title: Consolidate duplicate PRs #776 and #777: both implement the same #643 p2panda outputHash fix
body:
## Finding (PR diff review, 2026-10-24)

Two open PRs implement the **same fix for the same issue (#643)** and should be consolidated into one before either merges:

- PR #776 — `fix(id): correct the p2panda-da80c05 outputHash and group p2panda Renovate bumps` (head `6319600c4`, branch `id/build-fix`, opened 2026-10-24T18:00:03Z)
- PR #777 — `fix(id): update p2panda outputHashes for da80c05 rev (fixes #643)` (heads `7b898eabe` + `c72f17e77`, branch `sweep/643-p2panda-output-hash`, opened 2026-10-24T18:01:09Z, one minute later)

## Evidence

Both PRs change exactly the same three files with the same substantive change:

- `pkgs/id/default.nix` — `p2panda-core-0.7.1` outputHash `sha256-t1FDJkQ6B43clPF0lD36I+Uxav0YbqJ2e/UwWUoI6fk=` → `sha256-yq+ySfo14ucU1BWOUdJM0n7/FL3+Ria3Z+MxMHFa4Ls=` (identical hunk in both diffs)
- `pkgs/id/flake.nix` — the same hash replacement at all three `outputHashes` sites (identical hunks)
- `renovate.json` — both add a `packageRules` entry grouping all `p2panda-*` cargo deps into a single `p2panda` group

The only differences:

- #776 adds an explanatory comment in `pkgs/id/flake.nix` (keyed by crate name-version, not rev — hashes must be updated by hand, #643) that #777 lacks.
- The Renovate rule syntax differs: #776 uses `matchPackageNames: ["/^p2panda-/"]`; #777 uses `matchPackagePatterns: ["^p2panda-"]` plus `groupSlug`. Only one of these should survive, and it should be validated against the Renovate schema in use.
- #776's body still says "Local verification in progress; I'll update the description with results" and has no verification record; #777 carries the three-CI-run evidence for the `got` hash and is the PR the sweeps already treat as the #643 executor (backlog triage of #746/#750/#757/#771 points at #777).

## Why it matters

Merging both is impossible without a conflict in all three files, and merging the wrong one first leaves the second dangling as a stale duplicate of a closed issue. The blocked id PR queue (#746, #750, #757, #771, #778) is waiting on exactly one of these landing.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] One PR is chosen as the survivor (evidence favours #777) and the other is closed as a duplicate with a link to the survivor.
- [ ] If #776 is closed, its unique `flake.nix` explanatory comment is carried into the survivor or explicitly dropped.
- [ ] The surviving Renovate rule's syntax is the one intended for the repo's Renovate setup.
- [ ] #643 closes via the surviving PR only; no second PR for this fix remains open afterwards.

Refs #643. Filed by the pr-diff-review job; this job files only — a sweep does the consolidation.

title: id: store_traits.rs is rustfmt-dirty on main — treefmt check fails every id PR and cascades 'dependency failed' over all other id checks
body:
## Problem

`pkgs/id/src/store_traits.rs` on current main is not rustfmt-formatted, so the id flake `treefmt-check` / `id-web-fmt-check` fail on any PR that triggers the id checks — and every other id check in the same run then reports only "1 dependency failed", masking the real test/lint results.

## Evidence (verified this run)

- PR #757 (unrelated one-file change to `src/web/routes.rs`; `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` shows only that file) failed `nix flake check` in run 40093514156: the treefmt builder changed exactly one file —
  `ERRO file has changed path=src/store_traits.rs prev_size=35361 … current_size=35429`, `Error: unexpected changes detected, --fail-on-change is enabled` — after which `clippy-lint`, `web-lint`, `cargo-check`, `test`, `test-unit`, `test-int`, `test-web`, `test-web-unit`, `test-web-typecheck`, `crash-gate` and `doc` all failed with "1 dependency failed" without running.
- Independent local check on unmodified `origin/main`: `rustfmt --edition 2024 --check pkgs/id/src/store_traits.rs` reports diffs, e.g. at lines 628 and 897 the long single-line
  `assert_eq!(store.get_latest_entry_tx(&who, &ChainLog).await.unwrap(), None);`
  must be wrapped. The file was last touched by commit 3458742f ("chore(id): bump p2panda to da80c05 and port the vendored fork").

## Why it matters

The id PR gate is currently red for a reason unrelated to any PR's own change, and the dependency cascade hides whether the PR's tests, clippy and cargo-check pass at all. That trains everyone to ignore or force-merge past the gate — the exact failure mode #702/#711 fixed for the `|| true` checks.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `rustfmt --edition 2024 --check pkgs/id/src/store_traits.rs` (or the repo treefmt) is clean on main — formatting-only change, no logic edits.
- [ ] A PR touching only an unrelated id file then gets a `nix flake check` run whose treefmt checks pass and whose test/clippy/cargo-check legs actually execute and report their own results.

title: id(web): PR #747's is_body_limit_error can never match — axum MultipartError Display is a constant, so over-limit uploads still return generic 400, not the promised 413
body:
## Finding

PR #747 (https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/747, commit a3fba20e, OPEN) claims in its body that "multipart length-limit errors in the field/bytes reads map to the same clear 413 instead of a generic 400." That mapping can never fire: `is_body_limit_error` is dead code.

`pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs` on the PR branch (lines 1300–1304):

```rust
fn is_body_limit_error(err: &axum::extract::multipart::MultipartError) -> bool {
    let msg = err.to_string().to_lowercase();
    msg.contains("length limit") || msg.contains("body limit") || msg.contains("exceeded")
}
```

called at both error sites in `upload_handler` (branch lines 1329 and 1371 — the `next_field()` and `field.bytes()` error arms).

## Evidence

- This repo pins axum 0.8.9 (`pkgs/id/Cargo.lock`). In axum 0.8.9, `MultipartError`'s `Display` impl is a constant string that does not include the underlying multer error:

  ```rust
  impl fmt::Display for MultipartError {
      fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
          write!(f, "Error parsing `multipart/form-data` request")
      }
  }
  ```

  (axum-0.8.9 `src/extract/multipart.rs`, verified against the crate source; the multer error is only reachable via `Error::source()` / the error's own classification methods.) The constant contains none of "length limit", "body limit", or "exceeded", so `is_body_limit_error` returns `false` for every possible `MultipartError`.
- Consequence on the branch as written: an upload whose body exceeds the new 11 MiB route limit (`UPLOAD_BODY_LIMIT`) surfaces at `next_field()` as 400 `Invalid multipart data: Error parsing multipart/form-data request`, or at `field.bytes()` as 400 `Failed to read file data` — exactly the generic errors #716/PR #747 set out to replace. (The separate explicit `data.len() > MAX_IMAGE_SIZE` check does work, but it only covers files that fit inside the 11 MiB body limit; the body-limit path itself is the broken one.)
- axum already exposes the correct classification on the same error type: `MultipartError::status()` returns `413 PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE` for `FieldSizeExceeded`/`StreamSizeExceeded` and for stream read failures wrapping `http_body_util::LengthLimitError`, and `body_text()` returns "Request payload is too large" for those cases (axum's own internal `is_body_limit_error` operates on the `multer::Error` source, not on `Display`).
- The PR's only new test, `test_upload_body_limit_fits_max_image_plus_multipart_overhead`, pins the constants' arithmetic; no test exercises an over-limit multipart request through `create_router`, so nothing catches this. The PR body also notes the test binary's execution was blocked locally (linker OOM) and CI is the executor; the PR's `nix flake check` run is currently failing for an unrelated pre-existing reason (treefmt reformats `src/store_traits.rs` on main as well), so this path has effectively never been executed anywhere.
- Deduped: issue searches for `is_body_limit_error`, `MultipartError`, and `body_text` return nothing; #716 is the parent problem this PR partially fixes. Single-repo: per PR #747's own body, the upload route and client constant exist only in this repo.

## Why it matters

The one user-visible improvement #716 asked for on the over-limit path — a clear 413 saying the image is too large — silently does not happen for the largest, most confusing failures (body over the route limit). The code reads as if it handles the case, its PR description says it does, and its test suite cannot prove otherwise, so the defect would merge green and stay invisible until a user hits it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `upload_handler`'s body-limit detection uses a mechanism that can actually classify a body-limit `MultipartError` (e.g. `err.status() == StatusCode::PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE`, `err.body_text()`, or walking `std::error::Error::source()` to the multer/`LengthLimitError`), not substring-matching `MultipartError`'s `Display`.
- [ ] A test drives a multipart upload larger than `UPLOAD_BODY_LIMIT` through `create_router` (or an equivalent handler-level path) and asserts a 413 response with the clear "Image too large" message — and the test fails on PR #747's code as written.
- [ ] A test (or the same one) confirms a file of exactly `MAX_IMAGE_SIZE` still uploads successfully, and a file over `MAX_IMAGE_SIZE` but under the body limit still gets the explicit 413 from the length check.
- [ ] Non-size multipart errors still return 400 as before.

title: id(web): Go to Line miscounts and cannot navigate outside a single raw code_block — textContent has no block separators and position mapping hard-codes +2
body:
## Problem

Go to Line (Ctrl+G / Cmd+G) only works for a document that is a single raw-mode `code_block`. In every other mode the plugin is installed in, it miscounts lines and cannot navigate:

- The plugin is added unconditionally for all modes in `pkgs/id/web/src/editor.ts` (`createGotoLinePlugin()` in the shared plugin list, after the raw/rich branch), so rich, markdown and plain documents all get it. Those modes use `richSchema` (paragraphs, headings, list items, code blocks as separate textblocks).
- `getLineCount` (`pkgs/id/web/src/goto-line.ts:19-27`) counts `\n` characters in `doc.textContent`. ProseMirror's `textContent` concatenates textblocks with **no separator**, so block boundaries are invisible: a document of three paragraphs has `textContent === "alphabetagamma"` and counts as **1 line**.
- `getLineStartPos` (`pkgs/id/web/src/goto-line.ts:30-61`) maps a text offset to a document position with a hard-coded `pos + 2`, with a comment claiming rich mode is handled "via resolve" — there is no resolve; the +2 is only correct for `doc > code_block > text` with a single block. Each additional textblock adds its own position overhead, so even a correct count would land at the wrong position.

## Evidence (verified on main d7f99733 with a temporary vitest probe driving the real plugin, removed after)

Rich schema, doc = three paragraphs `alpha` / `beta` / `gamma`:

- `doc.textContent` is `"alphabetagamma"` (no newlines).
- Opening the dialog shows placeholder `Line # (1–1)` and `max=1` for a three-line document.
- Entering `2` and pressing Enter does nothing: the #712 strict validation rejects it as out of range, the dialog stays open and the selection does not move. Go to Line is effectively dead in rich/markdown/plain mode.

Raw schema, doc = two `code_block`s (`a\nb` and `c\nd`, four lines total):

- `textContent` is `"a\nbc\nd"` — the last line of the first block and the first line of the second are merged — and the dialog reports 3 lines instead of 4.

Dedup: #712 (closed) fixed invalid/out-of-range input handling for the single-block case; #718 (closed) fixed the dialog singleton across editor recreation. Neither touches line counting/position mapping outside a single code block. No open issue covers this.

## Why it matters

Ctrl+G is installed and advertised in every editable mode, but outside a single raw code block it tells the user their document has one line (or merges block-boundary lines) and refuses every jump past it. Plain-text and markdown files — primary id use cases — are exactly the affected modes.

## Acceptance criteria

- Line counting and line-start positions are computed from the document structure (walking textblocks and their positions), not from `doc.textContent` offsets plus a constant.
- A defined line semantics for non-raw modes (e.g. one line per textblock, plus `\n`-split lines inside code blocks) is implemented and documented in the module comment.
- Regression tests: rich doc of several paragraphs (dialog range matches, Enter on line N moves the cursor to the start of the Nth paragraph); mixed doc (paragraph + multi-line code_block + paragraph); raw doc with two code_blocks counts all lines; existing single-code_block tests and the #712 invalid-input tests still pass.
- Or, if Go to Line is deliberately raw-only, the plugin is not installed (or cleanly no-ops with feedback) in rich/markdown/plain modes, and that restriction is tested — silently offering a broken dialog is the unacceptable part.

title: id(ssh): PR #720's dropped-input notice still cannot fire in explorer sessions — the shared counter is counted for them but never claimed
body:
## Finding

PR #720 fixes #602 for world shells: the russh `data()` handler and `SshIo` now share one `Arc<AtomicUsize>` dropped-input counter, so bytes refused after the shell opens reach `SshIo::send`, which claims the notice at the documented `INPUT_DROP_NOTICE_BYTES` (1024) threshold.

The same handler and the same input queue also serve the other session type in the same function, and that branch is not wired:

- In `shell_request` on PR #720's head (`c7756f8c`, `pkgs/id/src/world_ssh.rs:319-325`), the `login.explore` branch creates its own `mpsc::channel(INPUT_QUEUE)` (256 frames, `:42` on the head), stores the sender in `self.input`, and spawns `run_explorer(explorer, handle, channel, bytes)` — with no dropped-input counter.
- The non-explorer branch right below it (`:352`) is the only place that clones the shared counter: `dropped_input: Arc::clone(&self.dropped_input)` into `SshIo`.
- The handler (`data()`, `:371`, counting at `:389` via `record_dropped_input`) counts refused bytes on `TrySendError::Full` regardless of which session type owns `self.input` — it cannot distinguish explorer input from world-shell input.
- `run_explorer` (`:1148-1153` on the head) takes only `explorer, handle, channel, bytes`; nothing in its loop ever calls `claim_dropped_input_notice` / `dropped_input_notice`. The only claim site in the file is `SshIo::send` (`:639`).

So for an explorer (`explore:`) session, refused bytes are still counted into a counter nobody reads and logged with `tracing::warn!` only — the viewer is never told their input was dropped. That is the exact silent-drop shape #549 / #602 were filed for, surviving in the second branch of the same `shell_request` after #720 lands. The explorer drains its queue one line at a time and awaits a hub/directory call per submitted line, so a paste/flood arriving while a line executes can fill the 256-frame queue in the same way.

This does not block PR #720: it correctly satisfies #602's acceptance criteria as written (which scope to the world shell / `SshIo`). This issue tracks the residual branch #602 did not name.

## Evidence

- PR: #720 (`fix(id): share the SSH dropped-input counter with the session so the notice can fire`, fixes #602, 1 commit `c7756f8ce520db275e51a5088b40f655068de9b4`, OPEN at filing, 1 file `pkgs/id/src/world_ssh.rs`, +95/-28). Its diff touches the handler counter, `SshIo`, and the two notice tests — no `run_explorer` / explorer-branch hunk.
- Verified on the PR head via `gh api .../contents/pkgs/id/src/world_ssh.rs?ref=c7756f8c`: `grep -n dropped_input` returns the handler, `SshClient`/`SshIo` fields, `record_dropped_input`/`claim_dropped_input_notice`, and the `SshIo::send` claim — no occurrence in the explorer branch or in `run_explorer`.
- Verified on current main (`df383659`, base of #720, local clone == `gh api commits/main`): the pre-fix structure is the same two branches — explorer at `shell_request` spawns `run_explorer` with no counter, world shell copies the (then-`usize`) counter into `SshIo`.
- Cross-repo: `git grep dropped_input_notice` is clean in the opencode, openchamber and nix clones — `pkgs/id` SSH code lives only in this repo.
- Dedup: `gh search issues "dropped input"` returns only #602 (OPEN, world-shell scope); searches for `explorer dropped`, `explorer input`, `run_explorer dropped` and `INPUT_DROP` return nothing. No open or closed issue tracks the explorer branch.

## Why it matters

An explorer user whose keystrokes/paste are refused under load gets the same "my input vanished" experience #549 set out to eliminate, with only a server-side warn log as evidence. Because the counter is now shared and incremented for explorer sessions too, the post-#720 code gives the impression the notice is handled uniformly — a reader of `data()` sees one counter and one notice mechanism, not a per-branch exception.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The explorer branch in `shell_request` passes the shared dropped-input counter (the same `Arc<AtomicUsize>` the handler counts on) into `run_explorer`.
- [ ] `run_explorer` claims the notice with the same helper/threshold as `SshIo::send` (`claim_dropped_input_notice`, `INPUT_DROP_NOTICE_BYTES`) and writes it to the channel before the next explorer output once the threshold is reached; a failed notice write restores the claimed bytes, so drops are neither lost nor double-counted (same reset-only-on-delivery rule as #602).
- [ ] A test drives the shared counter the way the handler does (or fills a live explorer session's input queue) and observes the `[-- input dropped: N bytes ... --]` notice on the explorer channel; below-threshold drops stay quiet and counted.
- [ ] World-shell behaviour from #720 is unchanged: the existing `world_ssh::` suite (incl. `dropped_input_notice_counts_and_quiet_zero` and `dropped_input_notice_follows_the_shared_counter`) still passes.
- [ ] Alternatively, if explorer sessions are deliberately excluded, that decision is recorded in a code comment at the explorer branch / counter definition and on this issue before closing — not left as a silent gap.

title: id(web): detectLanguage lets a special-name stem override a known extension — justfile.rs highlights as Just, makefile.md as Makefile
body:
## Summary

`detectLanguage` in `pkgs/id/web/src/highlight.ts` checks the file's *stem* against the special-filename table before it ever looks at the extension, so any file whose stem happens to be a special name is highlighted with the wrong language even when its extension unambiguously names another one.

## Evidence (verified on main df383659, temporary vitest probe since removed)

`highlight.ts:133-143` computes `nameWithoutExt` (basename minus its final extension) and returns `FILENAME_TO_LANG[nameWithoutExt]` before the extension lookup at `highlight.ts:158-162`.

Probe results against the real function:

| filename | returned | correct |
|---|---|---|
| `justfile.rs` | `just` | `rust` |
| `makefile.md` | `makefile` | `markdown` |
| `dockerfile.py` | `dockerfile` | `python` |
| `gemfile.json` | `ruby` | `json` |
| `vagrantfile.toml` | `ruby` | `toml` |
| `cmakelists.rs` | `cmake` | `rust` |
| `rakefile.ts` | `ruby` | `typescript` |

Controls that must keep working:

| filename | returned | correct |
|---|---|---|
| `Dockerfile.dev` | `dockerfile` | `dockerfile` (extension unknown) |
| `CMakeLists.txt` | `cmake` | `cmake` (`.txt` has no language) |
| `src/Dockerfile` | `dockerfile` | `dockerfile` (no extension) |

## Why it matters

The editor picks the Shiki grammar solely from this function (filename-detected language, `highlight.ts` `createSyntaxHighlightPlugin`). A mis-detected file is highlighted with a completely unrelated grammar — e.g. documentation about a Makefile (`makefile.md`) or a Rust source file named after the tool it drives (`justfile.rs`). The special-name rule was only ever meant for files that *are* the special file (`Dockerfile`, `Makefile`, `CMakeLists.txt`, `Dockerfile.dev`); it should not override a known extension.

## Acceptance criteria

- When the basename's extension is present in `EXT_TO_LANG`, the extension wins over the stem special-name match (`justfile.rs` → `rust`, `makefile.md` → `markdown`, `gemfile.json` → `json`).
- Special filenames still win when there is no extension (`Dockerfile`, `Gemfile`, `src/Makefile`) or the extension is unknown (`Dockerfile.dev`, `CMakeLists.txt`).
- Dotfile handling (`.env`, `.gitignore`, `.env.local`, …) is unchanged.
- New regression tests in `highlight.test.ts` cover at least the stem-vs-known-extension cases and the unknown-extension controls above; the existing `detectLanguage` suite passes unchanged.

title: id(web): Find panel and Go to Line dialog never appear after the editor is recreated — module singletons outlive the editor, destroy helpers have no production caller
body:
## Problem

Find (Ctrl+F / Ctrl+H) and Go to Line (Ctrl+G) silently stop working after the editor is recreated — e.g. after disconnecting from one world/session and opening another file. The shortcuts return `true` but no panel/dialog ever appears in the new editor.

## Root cause (same pattern, both modules)

Both modules keep their DOM in a **module-level singleton** that is created once for the first editor and never invalidated:

- `pkgs/id/web/src/search-panel.ts`: `panelState` (lines 47–54) is module-global. `openPanel` only creates the panel `if (!panelState.panelEl)`, and `panelState.view` / the event handlers captured by `setupPanelEvents` are bound to the **first** view forever.
- `pkgs/id/web/src/goto-line.ts`: `dialogEl` / `dialogInput` (lines 14–16) are module-global. `openGotoLine` only creates the dialog `if (!dialogEl)`. (It does refresh `activeView`, but the dialog element itself stays attached to the old container.)

Both modules export a destroy function (`destroySearchPanel`, `destroyGotoLineDialog`) documented as "Call this when the editor is being destroyed" — but **nothing in production calls either one**. The only callers are the test files' `afterEach`, which is why the existing suites never see the leak. Production teardown (`pkgs/id/web/src/main.ts`, disconnect path, ~line 1287) only calls `this.collab.editor.view.destroy()`.

When the old container is removed from the document, the singleton element is detached with it. The next Ctrl+F / Ctrl+G "opens" the panel by setting `style.display = ""` on the detached node and focusing a detached input — invisible, and for search the handlers still dispatch to the destroyed first view.

## Reproduction (verified this run, on main a8992eb7)

A vitest case mirroring the production lifecycle — create editor 1, open the panel, `view.destroy()` + remove container (**without** calling the destroy helper, exactly as production does), create editor 2, trigger the shortcut — fails for both modules:

- search: second container has no `.search-panel` after Mod-f (`expected null not to be null`)
- goto-line: second container has no `.goto-line-dialog` after Mod-g (same)

Both pass if `destroySearchPanel()` / `destroyGotoLineDialog()` is called between editors, confirming the missing invalidation is the whole defect.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] After an editor is destroyed and a new one created (no manual destroy-helper call in between), Ctrl+F/Ctrl+H shows a working find/replace panel **in the new editor's container**, bound to the new view (typing searches the new document; Enter/replace act on it).
- [ ] Same for Ctrl+G: the Go to Line dialog appears in the new container and jumps in the new document.
- [ ] Regression tests for both modules that recreate the editor **without** calling the destroy helpers (mirroring production teardown) and assert the panel/dialog appears and works in the second editor.
- [ ] Existing search-panel and goto-line suites still pass; typecheck clean.

Suggested fix shapes (either is fine): make `openPanel`/`openGotoLine` self-healing — if the singleton element is detached or belongs to a different container/view, destroy and recreate it bound to the current view — and/or call the destroy helpers from the editor teardown path in `main.ts`. The self-healing form is more robust: it also covers any future recreation path that forgets the teardown call.

Single-repo: no search-panel/goto-line copies exist in developing-today/opencode, developing-today/openchamber, or dezren39/nix (grep-verified this run).

title: id(web): images at the advertised 10 MiB max pass the client check but are rejected by the server's 10 MiB whole-body limit
body:
## Summary

An image at (or just under) the client's advertised 10 MiB maximum passes the
web UI's size check but is rejected by the server, because the client's limit
applies to the **file** while the server's identical 10 MiB limit applies to
the **whole multipart request body**, whose encoding adds overhead the file
budget does not account for.

## Evidence (verified on main `26c54292`, 2026-10-23)

- Client: `pkgs/id/web/src/image-upload.ts:34` — `MAX_IMAGE_SIZE = 10 * 1024 * 1024`;
  paste/drop handlers skip a file only when `file.size > MAX_IMAGE_SIZE`
  (`image-upload.ts:170` and `:198`), so a file of exactly 10 MiB is uploaded.
  The constant is pinned by `image-upload.test.ts:43-49`.
- Server: `pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs:265` — the whole router is layered with
  `DefaultBodyLimit::max(10 * 1024 * 1024)`. `upload_handler`
  (`routes.rs:1272`) has no size check of its own, so the body limit is the
  only server-side bound and it counts every byte of the multipart envelope.
- Measured with Node's `FormData`/`Request` (the same encoding the browser
  produces) for a file named `photo.png`:
  - file size 10,485,760 → multipart body 10,485,930 bytes (**170 bytes of
    overhead**: boundary, `Content-Disposition` with the filename, part
    `Content-Type`, closing boundary). Over the server limit → rejected.
  - file size 10,485,660 (100 bytes *under* the advertised max) → body
    10,485,830 → still rejected.
  - file size 10,485,560 → body 10,485,730 → accepted.
  So the effective maximum is ≈200 bytes below the advertised one, and it
  shrinks further with longer filenames. The user sees only a generic
  `Upload failed (…)` error from `uploadImageFile` with no hint that a file
  the UI explicitly allowed is "too large".

## Why it matters

The two sides disagree about what the limit measures, so the boundary of the
documented feature is broken in exactly the range a user who checks the limit
will hit: a 10 MiB image (a common phone-photo size class) is promised by the
client and refused by the server. The failure mode is silent/confusing rather
than a clear "image too large" message.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A file of exactly `MAX_IMAGE_SIZE` bytes (10 MiB) with a typical
      filename uploads successfully end to end, **or** the client limit is
      lowered/documented so the largest client-accepted file always fits the
      server body limit (including multipart overhead for long filenames).
- [ ] The server rejects an over-limit file with a clear size-related error
      (not a generic multipart/body error leaking through `upload_handler`).
- [ ] A test pins the relationship between the two limits (e.g. a Rust test
      asserting the upload route's effective body limit exceeds the client
      `MAX_IMAGE_SIZE` plus a multipart-overhead allowance, or a client test
      for the adjusted constant) so the two cannot drift back into conflict.
- [ ] Existing `image-upload` web tests and the Rust web route tests still pass.

Suggested fix direction: raise the body limit for the `/api/upload` route
only (route-scoped `DefaultBodyLimit` above 10 MiB + overhead, e.g. 11 MiB)
and/or add an explicit file-size check in `upload_handler` returning
`413` with a clear message — rather than raising the global router limit,
which also guards `/api/save` and the other POST routes.

title: id(web): Tab/Shift-Tab on a selection indents/dedents the wrong lines — unselected lines changed, selection's first line skipped
body:
## Summary

`pkgs/id/web/src/indent.ts` — Tab (indent) and Shift-Tab (dedent) with a
multi-line selection indent/dedent the wrong lines: lines outside the
selection are changed, and the line the selection starts in can be skipped.

## Evidence (verified on main `d495a5cd` with a temporary vitest probe driving the real commands; probe removed after the run)

Document `line1\nline2\nline3` in a `code_block` (content positions:
line1 at 1, line2 at 7, line3 at 13):

| Selection | Expected | Actual |
|---|---|---|
| line2 only (7–12) | only `line2` indented | `"  line1\n  line2\n  line3"` — all three lines indented |
| mid-line2 → mid-line3 (9–15) | `line2` + `line3` indented | `"  line1\nline2\n  line3"` — unselected line1 indented, line2 (where the selection starts) NOT indented |
| `a` only (1–2) in `a\nb\nc\nd\ne` | only `a` indented | all five lines indented |
| dedent: line3 only (17–23) in `  line1\n  line2\n  line3` | only `line3` dedented | `"line1\nline2\nline3"` — all three lines dedented |

## Root cause

`indentCommand` (indent.ts:55-58):

```ts
if (lineStart >= from || lineStart === blockStart) {
  if (lineStart <= to + offset) {
```

- `lineStart === blockStart` unconditionally indents the block's first line,
  whatever the selection.
- `lineStart >= from` excludes the line containing `from` whenever the
  selection starts mid-line (its line start is `< from`).
- `lineStart <= to + offset` compares an original-document line start
  against the selection end shifted by the insertions already made, so
  every inserted indent widens the range and pulls in following lines.

`dedentCommand` (indent.ts:107) has the mirror flaw for selections:
`lineStarts.filter((ls) => ls <= to)` has no lower bound, so every line
from the block start up to the selection end is dedented.

The existing test `indents only lines overlapping the selection`
(indent.test.ts) does not catch this: it asserts only that line2 is
indented and line3 is untouched, and its comment even records the
blockStart side effect as expected.

## Why it matters

Tab/Shift-Tab on a selection is a basic editor operation in the id web UI.
Today it silently reformats lines the user never selected — and with a
collaborator-shared document, that churn is broadcast to peers.

## Acceptance criteria

- Indent and dedent with a selection change exactly the lines the
  selection overlaps: the line containing `from` through the line
  containing `to` (state the rule chosen for a selection ending exactly
  at a line start, and pin it in a test).
- The four probe cases above behave as in the Expected column.
- Regression tests cover: selection on a single non-first line,
  selection starting mid-line, selection ending before later lines
  (no offset drift), and the dedent mirror cases.
- The existing indent/dedent tests still pass, updated where they
  encoded the buggy blockStart behaviour; single-cursor Tab/Shift-Tab
  behaviour unchanged.

Single-repo: `git grep indentCommand` in the opencode, openchamber and
nix clones returns nothing — the plugin lives only in pkgs/id/web.

title: id(web): Go to Line accepts 0/negatives as line 1, truncates fractions, and silently closes on out-of-range lines
body:
## Problem

The Go to Line dialog in the `pkgs/id` web editor (`pkgs/id/web/src/goto-line.ts`) does not validate the entered line number on Enter. The `<input type="number" min="1">` attributes are never enforced, because the `keydown` handler reads the raw value and acts on it directly — there is no `<form>` / constraint-validation step.

Verified on main `d495a5cd` with a temporary vitest probe driving the real dialog (probe since removed; the three cases below reproduce with the existing `goto-line.test.ts` harness):

1. **Line `0` (and negatives) are treated as line 1 — and create an invalid selection.** `goto-line.ts:88` does `parseInt(dialogInput?.value ?? "", 10)`; the only check is `Number.isNaN`. `getLineStartPos` (`goto-line.ts:36`) returns `0` for any `targetLine <= 1`, so `0` and `-3` both dispatch `TextSelection.create(doc, 0)`. ProseMirror logs `TextSelection endpoint not pointing into a node with inline content (doc)` and the selection lands at doc position `0`, outside the `code_block`. Typing `0` should be rejected, not silently reinterpreted as the top of the file.
2. **Fractional input is silently truncated.** `2.9` moves the cursor to line 2 (doc position `8` in a `first\nsecond\nthird` doc) because `parseInt` drops the fraction. A line number is an integer; `2.9` is invalid input, not line 2.
3. **Out-of-range input closes the dialog with no feedback.** `999` in a 3-line document: `getLineStartPos` returns `null`, nothing moves, and `closeGotoLine()` runs unconditionally (`goto-line.ts:100`) — the dialog disappears and the user cannot tell whether the jump happened, failed, or the line does not exist. The dialog already knows the line count (it renders `Line # (1–N)` and sets `input.max`), but the handler never compares against it.

Existing tests (`pkgs/id/web/src/goto-line.test.ts`) cover only valid inputs (`1`, `2`), Escape, and dialog lifecycle — none of these invalid cases.

## Why it matters

Go to Line is a primary navigation affordance in the editor. Silently treating `0`/negatives as line 1, truncating fractions, and swallowing out-of-range jumps with no feedback makes navigation unpredictable, and the `0` case additionally constructs a selection ProseMirror itself warns is not inside inline content.

## Acceptance criteria

- Entering `0`, a negative number, a fractional number (e.g. `2.9`), a non-numeric value, or a line greater than the document's line count does **not** move the cursor and does **not** silently close-and-forget: the dialog stays open (or reopens/focuses the input) with the invalid value visible/selectable so the user can correct it. A brief inline hint is welcome but not required.
- Valid integers in `[1, lineCount]` keep working exactly as today (line 1 → start of the code block content, line N → start of line N).
- New tests in `goto-line.test.ts` cover at least: `0`, a negative, a fraction, and a value greater than the line count — each asserting the selection did not move and the dialog did not silently succeed.
- The valid-path tests already in `goto-line.test.ts` continue to pass.

## Suggested fix

In the Enter handler, parse strictly (reject anything that is not a base-10 integer string, e.g. via a `Number` + `Number.isInteger` check on the trimmed value rather than bare `parseInt`), compare against `getLineCount(activeView)`, and only dispatch + `closeGotoLine()` on success; on failure, keep the dialog open and select the input text.

Single-repo: `getLineStartPos` / the goto-line dialog exist only in `developing-today/code` (`pkgs/id/web`); no copy exists in opencode, openchamber, or dezren39/nix.

id(ci): seven pkgs/id flake checks can never fail — treefmt/rustfmt/statix/shfmt/shellcheck/taplo/prettier buildPhases end in '|| true'
body:
## Problem

Seven per-formatter flake checks in `pkgs/id/flake.nix` can never fail: their `buildPhase` ends the formatter command with `|| true`, so the derivation always succeeds and the `installPhase` always writes "passed". Verified on main `b382bfb8`:

| Check | Location | Command swallowed |
|---|---|---|
| `treefmt-check` | `pkgs/id/flake.nix:413` | `treefmt --ci 2>&1 \|\| true` |
| `rustfmt-check` | `pkgs/id/flake.nix:446` | `find . -name '*.rs' … -exec rustfmt --check … + \|\| true` |
| `statix-check` | `pkgs/id/flake.nix:459` | `statix check -- "$f" \|\| true` (per-file, inside the loop) |
| `shfmt-check` | `pkgs/id/flake.nix:474` | `shfmt -d … \|\| true` |
| `shellcheck-check` | `pkgs/id/flake.nix:488` | `shellcheck … \|\| true` |
| `taplo-check` | `pkgs/id/flake.nix:502` | `taplo check … \|\| true` |
| `prettier-check` | `pkgs/id/flake.nix:519` | `prettier --check … \|\| true` |

All seven are in the PR gate: every name appears in `.github/scripts/id-pr-checks.txt`, so `id-check.yml` builds them on every PR and reports them green regardless of what the formatter found.

Contrast inside the same file: `nix-fmt-check` (`flake.nix:~400`, `xargs nixfmt --check`, no `|| true`) and `biome-check` (`flake.nix:~430`, no `|| true`) fail properly when their tool reports a problem, as do the `mkCheck`-based checks (e.g. `cargo-fmt-check`). The seven above are the outliers.

Shell semantics confirm the mechanism: under the generic builder's `set -e`, `false || true` still exits 0 — the check derivation succeeds, and nothing downstream reads the formatter output (it is not saved to `$out`).

## Why it matters

- The PR gate advertises rustfmt/treefmt/statix/shfmt/shellcheck/taplo/prettier coverage for `pkgs/id` that does not exist. A formatting or lint regression in any of those tools merges green and is only caught later (if at all) by a human or by the aggregate `default`/`ci` path — whose `just ci` recipes are a different code path from these derivations.
- `statix-check` is the weakest: the `|| true` is per-file inside the loop, so even the loop's aggregate exit status carries no signal.
- The `just check-<name>` recipes (`check-rustfmt`, `check-treefmt`, `check-statix`, `check-shfmt`, `check-shellcheck`, `check-taplo`, `check-prettier` in `pkgs/id/justfile`) all delegate to `nix build .#checks.….<name>`, so the documented local way to run these checks is equally vacuous.

## Suggested fix

Do NOT just delete the seven `|| true`s blind — they were likely added because the tree currently violates one or more of these tools, and flipping them all at once would turn the PR gate red for unrelated work. Instead:

1. Measure first: run each of the seven tools in check mode on current main and record the violation count per check (attach the counts to this issue / the PR).
2. For each check, either (a) clean up the violations and remove its `|| true`, or (b) if the violations are intentional/out of scope, rename/relabel the check as informational (or drop it from `id-pr-checks.txt`) so the gate no longer claims it enforces.
3. Fix `statix-check` structurally while there: collect failures across files (`fail=0; … statix check -- "$f" || fail=1; …; exit $fail`) instead of a per-file `|| true`.
4. Keep `nix-fmt-check`/`biome-check` as the reference shape (no `|| true`).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] No `|| true` remains on a formatter command in the `checks` set of `pkgs/id/flake.nix` (`grep -n '|| true' pkgs/id/flake.nix` returns no hits inside check derivations), OR each remaining one belongs to a check that has been removed from `.github/scripts/id-pr-checks.txt` and clearly labelled informational.
- [ ] A deliberately mis-formatted file of each covered kind (`.rs`, `.sh`, `.toml`, `.md`/`.yaml`, a statix-flagged `.nix`) makes the corresponding flake check FAIL (negative test, verified per check that was made enforcing).
- [ ] `nix flake check` for `pkgs/id` (or at minimum the seven named checks via `nix build .#checks.x86_64-linux.<name>`) passes on the cleaned tree.
- [ ] The per-check violation census from step 1 is recorded, so any check left informational has an explicit, tracked reason.

Single-repo: the `|| true` check pattern was grep-verified absent from the root `flake.nix` of developing-today/code and from the flakes of developing-today/opencode, developing-today/openchamber and dezren39/nix.

title: id: match_kind is defined four times — CLI, REPL, protocol and a dead helpers copy can silently diverge
body:
## Problem

`match_kind` — the exact/prefix/contains ranking that decides how `find` results are ordered — is defined **four times** in `pkgs/id`, with byte-identical bodies (verified on main `3d7b96a5`):

| # | Location | Visibility | Production caller |
|---|----------|-----------|-------------------|
| 1 | `pkgs/id/src/lib.rs:387` | `pub fn` (crate root, `id::match_kind`) | `pkgs/id/src/commands/find.rs:931,938` (imports `crate::match_kind` at `find.rs:81`) |
| 2 | `pkgs/id/src/helpers.rs:298` | `pub fn` (`id::helpers::match_kind`) | **none found** — only its own unit tests (`helpers.rs:422+`) and doctest (`helpers.rs:287`) reference it |
| 3 | `pkgs/id/src/protocol.rs:525` | private `MetaProtocol::match_kind` | server-side find in the same file (`protocol.rs:685,692`) |
| 4 | `pkgs/id/src/commands/repl.rs:771` | private `Self::match_kind` | REPL find in the same file (`repl.rs:725,732`) |

Each copy also carries its own partially-overlapping test suite (`lib.rs:617+`, `helpers.rs:422+`, `protocol.rs:754+`, plus `find.rs:974+` exercising copy 1). The suites have already drifted in coverage: e.g. the empty-needle and case-sensitivity cases are pinned in different subsets at different sites.

## Why it matters

The same user query is ranked through three different code paths depending on entry point — CLI `find` (copy 1), the server/protocol find (copy 3), and the REPL find (copy 4). Today they agree only because the bodies happen to be identical. Any future fix or ranking change (e.g. word-boundary scoring, case handling, empty-query handling) applied to one copy silently diverges the three surfaces, and the duplicated test suites give false confidence that "the" behaviour is pinned. Copy 2 is additionally a dead public API: it looks like the canonical helper, is documented with a doctest, and is the one a new contributor would most likely edit — to no effect.

## Suggested fix

Pick ONE canonical definition (the crate-root `id::match_kind` in `lib.rs` is the one the CLI already uses; `MatchKind` itself is defined in `protocol.rs:93` and re-exported at `lib.rs:269`), then:

- Delete the `helpers.rs`, `protocol.rs` and `repl.rs` copies; make `protocol.rs` and `repl.rs` call the canonical function.
- Decide explicitly what happens to the public `id::helpers::match_kind` path (remove it, or keep it as a re-export of the canonical fn) and note the choice in the PR.
- Merge the four test suites into one at the canonical site, keeping the union of cases (empty needle/haystack, case sensitivity, unicode, ordering).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Exactly one `fn match_kind` definition remains in `pkgs/id/src/` (`grep -rn "fn match_kind" pkgs/id/src` returns one hit, plus call sites).
- [ ] CLI find, REPL find and protocol find all resolve to that definition.
- [ ] The merged test suite covers every case the four old suites covered (no case silently dropped).
- [ ] `cargo test --no-default-features` (or the id `test-unit` flake check) passes; no behaviour change for any existing test.

title: clef-proxy: invalid client JSON returns 500 instead of 400 — body parse shares the upstream try/catch, non-JSON upstream is masked, and there are no tests
body:
## Problem

`bin/clef-proxy.mjs` is the only bin proxy whose client-body parse shares one `try/catch` with the upstream call, so a client error is reported as a server error:

- `bin/clef-proxy.mjs:115-157` — `JSON.parse(bodyText)` sits inside the same `try` as the Cloudflare fetch, and the single `catch` at :154-156 always answers `500`.
- Verified live on main (4f905d75): `POST /v1/systemone` with body `not-json{` returns **500** `{"error":"Unexpected token 'o', \"not-json{\" is not valid JSON"}`. Every sibling proxy returns **400** for the same input (e.g. muse-proxy.mjs, codex-proxy.mjs, agy-proxy.mjs, antigravity-ls-proxy.mjs all parse in a dedicated try and answer 400).
- Same catch also swallows upstream-shape errors: if the Cloudflare gateway returns a non-JSON body (e.g. an HTML 502/429 page), `await cfRes.json()` at :142 throws and the client gets a bare 500 with a JSON-parse message, losing the upstream status. If the upstream body parses to `null`, `cfData.success` at :144 throws a TypeError down the same path.

`bin/clef-proxy.mjs` also has no test file at all — every other bin proxy has one (`muse-proxy.test.mjs`, `codex-proxy.test.mjs`, `agy-proxy` via its suite, `design-code-proxy.test.mjs`, `antigravity-ls-proxy.test.mjs`, `proxy-port.test.mjs`).

## Why it matters

Clients (and OpenCode's error handling) treat 400 and 500 differently: a malformed request reported as 500 looks like a proxy outage, invites retries of a request that can never succeed, and hides real upstream failures behind a parse-error message with the wrong status.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `POST /v1/systemone` with a non-JSON body returns 400 (matching the sibling proxies), with the parse error in the body.
- [ ] A non-JSON upstream response does not surface as a client-facing JSON-parse 500; it is reported as an upstream failure preserving the upstream status (or 502).
- [ ] A `null`/non-object upstream JSON body does not throw on `cfData.success`.
- [ ] New `bin/clef-proxy.test.mjs` (run: `node --test bin/clef-proxy.test.mjs`) covers at least: health, invalid JSON → 400, missing token → 401. The 400 test fails on the pre-fix code.

title: antigravity-ls-proxy: reasoning_effort 'default'/'name' resolves to a non-enum model — MODEL_MAP metadata keys pass the family lookup
body:
## Bug

`bin/antigravity-ls-proxy.mjs` — `resolveModelEnum`, step 3 (family-with-effort lookup, lines 138–140):

```js
let effort = (requestedEffort || family.default || 'medium').toLowerCase().trim();
if (!family[effort]) effort = family.default || Object.keys(family)[0];
const enumVal = family[effort];
```

The guard only checks that `family[effort]` is *truthy*. A family entry in `MODEL_MAP` is not just effort → enum: it also carries the metadata keys `default` (an effort name, e.g. `'medium'`) and `name` (a display name, e.g. `'Gemini 3.8 Flash'`). A client that sends either of those strings as `reasoning_effort` / `effort` (both are read from the request body at the chat-completions handler) therefore "resolves" successfully — to a value that is not a model enum at all. That bogus value is then sent to the language server as `model:` in `GetModelResponse` and as `plannerConfig.requestedModel.model` in cascade mode, where it can only fail (or be misinterpreted) server-side, instead of falling back to the family's default effort the way a genuinely unknown effort does.

## Evidence (verified this run)

The function and `MODEL_MAP` were extracted verbatim from current `main` and driven directly:

| request | result `modelEnum` |
|---|---|
| `gemini-3.8-flash`, effort `"default"` | `"medium"` ❌ (an effort name, not an enum) |
| `gemini-3.8-flash`, effort `"name"` | `"Gemini 3.8 Flash"` ❌ (the display name) |
| `gemini-3.1-pro`, effort `"default"` | `"high"` ❌ |
| `gemini-3.8-flash`, effort `"high"` | `"MODEL_PLACEHOLDER_M318"` ✅ |
| `gemini-3.1-pro`, effort `"medium"` (not offered) | `"MODEL_PLACEHOLDER_M37"` ✅ correct default fallback |
| `gemini-3.8-flash`, no effort | `"MODEL_PLACEHOLDER_M319"` ✅ |

So an unrecognized effort falls back correctly, but an effort that happens to collide with a `MODEL_MAP` metadata key slips through with a garbage "enum".

## Why it matters

- The proxy's own contract (step 5 of the same function) is "refuse rather than quietly run a different model than the one asked for" — this path does the opposite: it quietly runs with a non-model value.
- `reasoning_effort` is client-controlled in the OpenAI-shaped API; values like `"default"` are plausible from generic clients/configs. The failure surfaces downstream as an opaque language-server error naming a model the user never asked for, far from the real cause.

## Suggested fix

In step 3, accept an effort only when its mapped value is actually an enum (e.g. a string starting with `MODEL_`, matching every effort value in `MODEL_MAP`); otherwise fall back to `family.default` (and validate that fallback the same way). Equivalently, restrict the accepted effort names to the known effort keys (`low` / `medium` / `high` / `extra-low`) before indexing the family object.

## Acceptance criteria

- `resolveModelEnum('gemini-3.8-flash', 'default')` and `('gemini-3.8-flash', 'name')` return the family's default-effort enum (`MODEL_PLACEHOLDER_M319`), never `"medium"` / `"Gemini 3.8 Flash"`.
- Existing correct behaviour is unchanged: valid efforts resolve to their enums, an unoffered effort (e.g. `medium` on `gemini-3.1-pro`) still falls back to the family default, and unknown models still throw the 400 "Unknown model" error.
- A regression test covers the metadata-key efforts (`default`, `name`) — this proxy currently has no test file, so a black-box test in the style of `bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs` (spawn the proxy against a stub language server via `ANTIGRAVITY_LS_ADDRESS`/`ANTIGRAVITY_CSRF_TOKEN` and capture the `model` the proxy sends) or an equivalent unit test of the resolver is acceptable.

title: design-code-proxy: forwarded Content-Length truncates the re-serialized success body (PR #682)
body:
## Finding

`bin/design-code-proxy.mjs`'s `writeHead()` helper (added by PR #682, fixing #681) forwards the backend's `Content-Length` header verbatim, but the non-stream success path then sends a **different body** than the backend sent: it re-serializes the parsed JSON with the `model` field rewritten and pretty-printing (`JSON.stringify(json, null, 2)`). Whenever the backend sets `Content-Length` — the normal behaviour of a buffered JSON HTTP server — the forwarded length is the length of the backend's original (usually compact) body, so the client reads exactly that many bytes and gets **truncated, unparseable JSON**.

Evidence (PR + current main):

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/682 (1 commit `be7244972df90becc95b70b018ab23489c6f8163`, merge `c6ec7bd623df42909fdfa2225d249b593ad2e44c` = current main)
- `bin/design-code-proxy.mjs:224-231` on main `c6ec7bd6`:

  ```js
  const writeHead = () => {
    if (!clientRes.headersSent) {
      clientRes.writeHead(localRes.statusCode || 200, {
        ...localRes.headers,
        'Access-Control-Allow-Origin': '*'
      });
    }
  };
  ```

  `...localRes.headers` includes the backend's `content-length`.
- `bin/design-code-proxy.mjs:270-272`: `json.model = modelId; writeHead(); clientRes.end(JSON.stringify(json, null, 2));` — the body actually sent is longer than the backend's body in essentially every case (pretty-printing alone guarantees it; the model rewrite usually changes the length too).

## Reproduced on current main (`c6ec7bd6`)

Ran the real `bin/design-code-proxy.mjs` with stub backends (same stub pattern as `bin/design-code-proxy.test.mjs`), except the primary stub sets an explicit `Content-Length` on its compact JSON success body, as a standard HTTP server does:

- Request: non-stream `design-code-flash` chat completion, primary returns 200 with `Content-Length: 191` and a 191-byte compact JSON body.
- Proxy response: status 200, `content-length: 191` forwarded — but the re-serialized pretty body is longer, so the client receives exactly 191 bytes, ending mid-JSON.
- `JSON.parse` of the received body fails: `Expected ',' or '}' after property value in JSON at position 191`.
- Control: the PR's own test suite passes 5/5 on the same main — its stubs never set `Content-Length` (Node then answers chunked), which is why the suite cannot see this. The sibling in-repo proxies (muse/codex/agy) also happen to answer chunked (they set only `Content-Type`), so the default local chain may not trigger it today; any backend that sets `Content-Length` — e.g. the real Antigravity LS backend this proxy fronts, or any Go/Rust/framework server — truncates every successful non-stream response through this proxy.

The streaming path uses the same `writeHead()` spread, so the same mismatch applies in principle there too (each SSE chunk's `model` is rewritten, changing lengths); SSE backends normally answer chunked, so the verified harm is the non-stream path.

## Why it matters

This turns the proxy's success path into corrupted output for a whole class of standards-compliant backends: the client gets a 200 with a syntactically invalid JSON body instead of the completion. It sits in the exact helper PR #682 introduced, and the new test file's stubs mask it by never sending the one header that triggers it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A non-stream success response from a backend that sets `Content-Length` arrives at the client complete and parseable, with `model` rewritten to the design model id (no truncation).
- [ ] The proxy does not forward a stale `Content-Length` for any body it re-serializes (drop the header and let Node frame the response, or set it to the actual sent length); headers for bodies forwarded byte-for-byte (the non-JSON catch branch) stay correct.
- [ ] Regression test: a stub backend that sets an explicit `Content-Length` on its JSON success body, asserting the client receives the full model-rewritten body; the existing 5 tests in `bin/design-code-proxy.test.mjs` still pass.
- [ ] Streaming success behaviour unchanged.

title: design-code-proxy: quota error in a 200 JSON body hangs the request forever — writeHead precedes the in-body check, so fallback can never fire
body:
## Finding

`bin/design-code-proxy.mjs`'s local-dispatch fallback can never fire for a quota error reported **in the JSON body of an HTTP 200 response**, and the client request **hangs forever** instead.

In `tryTarget` (`bin/design-code-proxy.mjs:213-266` on main `4b85ef69`):

1. The response callback calls `clientRes.writeHead(localRes.statusCode || 200, ...)` at **line 219** — before the body has been read. From that moment `clientRes.headersSent` is `true`.
2. The non-stream body handler (line 254-258) parses the body and, for a quota error, calls `return onFail(new Error('Quota exceeded in JSON body'))`.
3. The primary target's `onFail` wrapper (line 279-280) begins with `if (clientRes.headersSent) return;` — so it silently returns without trying the fallback target and **without ever ending `clientRes`**. The fallback target's own `onFail` (line 284) is guarded the same way, so the hang happens whichever target returns the quota body.

The status-based path works fine because the `429`/`>=500` check (line 213) runs *before* `writeHead` — only the in-body check, which the code explicitly added to catch quota exhaustion, is defeated by the ordering.

## Evidence (reproduced on current main `4b85ef6906a25c1a59694c64986cb17828b6c2b6`)

Ran the real `bin/design-code-proxy.mjs` locally with stub HTTP backends on the Antigravity/Codex ports (`DESIGN_CODE_PROXY_PORT`/`ANTIGRAVITY_LS_PROXY_PORT`/`CODEX_PROXY_PORT` pointed at the stubs), model `design-code-flash`, non-stream:

- Stub primary returns **HTTP 200** with `{"error":{"code":429,"message":"quota stub","type":"insufficient_quota"}}`:
  - `curl --max-time 5` → **timed out after 5002 ms with 0 bytes received** (curl exit 28); the proxy logged only the primary attempt — no "Falling back" line, the fallback stub was never contacted, and the response was never ended. Without a client-side timeout this hangs indefinitely.
- Control — stub primary returns **HTTP 429 status** with an error body:
  - Proxy logged `returned 429`, tried the fallback target, and answered **502 `All design code backends failed: HTTP 429` in under a second** — the intended behaviour the in-body path was written to provide.

## Why it matters

The in-body quota shape is exactly what this branch exists for (backends that report quota exhaustion in a 200 JSON error body). Today, instead of failing over to the fallback model/backend, every such request wedges an open client connection forever — the worst failure mode for a dispatch proxy whose whole job is fallback — and leaks the socket on both sides until the client gives up.

## Suggested fix

For the non-stream path, buffer the body and run the quota check **before** `clientRes.writeHead(...)`; only write the head once the response is known not to be a quota failure (the stream path must keep writing its head up front). Equivalently, restructure so the head is written at the point the body is ended for non-stream responses.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A non-stream request whose primary backend returns HTTP 200 with `{"error":{"code":429,...}}` or `{"error":{"type":"insufficient_quota",...}}` tries the fallback target instead of hanging; if the fallback succeeds, its (model-rewritten) response is returned; if it also fails, the client gets the existing 502 `All design code backends failed` response promptly.
- [ ] The same holds when the *fallback* target returns the in-body quota error: prompt 502, no hang.
- [ ] Unchanged behaviour: HTTP-status 429/5xx fallback, connection-error fallback, successful non-stream responses (status, headers, `model` rewritten to the design model id), and streaming responses.
- [ ] Regression tests cover the in-body quota case (primary and fallback) with stub backends — `bin/design-code-proxy.mjs` currently has no test file; `bin/codex-proxy.test.mjs` / `bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs` show the stub-backend pattern to follow.

Cross-repo check: `design-code-proxy` exists only in this repo (git grep across developing-today/opencode, developing-today/openchamber, dezren39/nix: no copies) — no cross-repo set.

title: codex-proxy: a turn.failed event with exit 0 is reported as a successful 'stop' — #677 judged failure by exit code only, no terminal-event check
body:
## Finding

PR #677 fixed `bin/codex-proxy.mjs` judging failure **only by the child's exit code** (`code !== 0` in the `close` handler, `bin/codex-proxy.mjs:412` on main `4b85ef69`). But `codex exec --json` also reports failure **in-band**: it emits a `{"type":"turn.failed","error":{"message": …}}` event for a fatal error during a turn, and that event can arrive on a run that **exits 0**. The proxy's event parser (`processJsonLine`, `bin/codex-proxy.mjs:340-380`) handles only `item.completed` and `turn.completed` — `turn.failed` is silently ignored, so an exit-0 failed turn is still reported as a successful `stop`:

- no output before the failure → HTTP 200, empty content, `finish_reason: "stop"` (non-stream) / a bare `stop` chunk + `[DONE]` (stream)
- partial output before the failure → HTTP 200 carrying the truncated text as a clean `stop` (both modes)

That is exactly the masked-failure shape #676 fixed for the exit-code half — and exactly the shape `bin/muse-proxy.mjs` already guards against by judging failure from the run's authoritative terminal event first and the exit code second (`failed = terminalState ? terminalState !== 'completed' : code !== 0`, the #672/#673 pattern PR #677's body says it mirrors). The codex half of that pattern — the event-state half — is missing.

Exit 0 does not rule out a failed turn for codex: other codex providers explicitly check for turn-failure events on exit 0 (e.g. the codex-cli AI SDK provider's exit-code logic: "0 | Success | Check for turn failure events; return results if none", with a dedicated event-based error-detection pass for "failures that may not manifest as non-zero exit codes"), and headless-codex guidance is to fail on a `turn.failed` event rather than trust the exit code. `turn.failed` (`TurnFailedEvent { error }`, "on fatal error during a turn") is part of the documented `codex exec --json` event protocol.

Note on scope: top-level `{"type":"error", …}` events also exist in the protocol, but some are transient reconnect notices; this issue only requires the unambiguous `turn.failed` case. Whether to treat non-reconnect `error` events as failures is a judgement call for the implementer.

## Evidence (reproduced on current main `4b85ef6906a25c1a59694c64986cb17828b6c2b6`)

Ran the real `bin/codex-proxy.mjs` (pristine copy from `origin/main`) with a stub `codex` at `$HOME/.local/bin/codex` (the proxy's own binary resolution):

- Stub prints `{"type":"turn.failed","error":{"message":"stub codex: model overloaded"}}`, exits 0:
  - non-stream → **200**, `content: ""`, `finish_reason: "stop"`
  - stream → **200**, one `finish_reason: "stop"` chunk, then `data: [DONE]` — no error anywhere
- Stub prints an `item.completed` agent_message (`partial answer`), then `{"type":"turn.failed","error":{"message":"stub codex: run failed midway"}}`, exits 0:
  - non-stream → **200**, `content: "partial answer"`, `finish_reason: "stop"`
  - stream → **200**, the `partial answer` chunk, then a `finish_reason: "stop"` chunk + `[DONE]`
- Control ( `item.completed` + `turn.completed`, exit 0) → 200 with the full text and `stop` in both modes, unchanged.
- The existing suites pass on the same main: `node --test bin/codex-proxy.test.mjs bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs` → 10/10 — no existing test emits `turn.failed`.

Source PR: #677 (`fix(codex-proxy): report failed codex runs as errors, not successful stops`, fixes #676, commit `a0a1b077`, merge `4b85ef69`). Its failure predicate is the single line `if (code !== 0)` at `bin/codex-proxy.mjs:412`; nothing in the PR's new `bin/codex-proxy.test.mjs` covers an in-band failure event.

Dedup: searches for `turn.failed` across all issues (open + closed) return nothing; `codex-proxy failed` returns only #676 (closed, the exit-code half), #670 (muse-proxy streaming), #496 and the open #678 (agy-proxy's separate exit-code masking — a different proxy and a different mechanism; this finding is codex-only). The `bin/codex-proxy.mjs` bridge exists only in this repo.

## Why it matters

Clients of the proxy (opencode's codex provider) cannot distinguish a failed codex turn from a successful empty or short answer: a rate-limited, overloaded, or otherwise fatally failed turn presents as a clean `stop`, so callers accept truncated/empty output instead of surfacing an error or retrying — the same silent-corruption failure mode #670/#672/#676 were filed and fixed for.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `bin/codex-proxy.mjs` tracks a `turn.failed` event during the run; on `close`, a run that emitted `turn.failed` is reported as a failure even when the exit code is 0: non-stream returns HTTP 500 with `Codex execution failed: <the turn.failed error message>` (falling back to stderr/signal/exit-code detail when the event carries no message), and stream mode writes a `data:`-framed error event + `data: [DONE]` with no chunk claiming `finish_reason: "stop"` — mirroring the existing #677 error framing.
- [ ] Partial output followed by `turn.failed` + exit 0 is an error in both modes, not a 200 `stop` carrying the truncated text.
- [ ] Successful runs (exit 0, `turn.completed`, no `turn.failed`) are unchanged in both modes.
- [ ] New stub modes in `bin/codex-proxy.test.mjs` pin the no-output and partial-output `turn.failed` + exit-0 shapes in both modes; ablating only the `turn.failed` check fails exactly those new tests, and the full codex-proxy + muse-proxy + proxy-port suites pass.

title: agy-proxy: failed agy run reported as successful 'stop' — stream handler never checks the exit code, non-stream masks failure when partial output exists
body:
## Finding

`bin/agy-proxy.mjs` reports a failed `agy` run as a successful completion in most shapes:

- **Stream mode** — the `child.on('close', code => ...)` handler (`bin/agy-proxy.mjs:467`) checks `code` only for the resume-retry case (`code !== 0 && !hasOutput && allowRetry && targetConvId`, :471). Every other non-zero exit falls through to the unconditional success ending at :481-510: a chunk with `finish_reason: 'stop'` plus `data: [DONE]`. The `stderrBuffer` collected at :463-465 is never read anywhere in the stream path, so the failure cause is discarded entirely.
- **Non-stream mode** — the failure branch is gated on empty output (`if (code !== 0 && !responseText)`, :553), so a run that fails after producing a partial response returns HTTP 200 with `finish_reason: 'stop'` and the truncated text. (This is the sighting noted for separate judgement in #672; the stream half above was not covered there or anywhere else.)

This is the agy-proxy counterpart of the defects already fixed in the sibling `bin/muse-proxy.mjs` (#670, #672, #674) and `bin/codex-proxy.mjs` (#676): a failed run presented as a clean `stop`.

## Evidence (reproduced on main `4b85ef69`)

Ran `bin/agy-proxy.mjs` with a stub `agy` at `$HOME/.local/bin/agy` (the proxy's own binary resolution) whose behaviour keys on the requested `--output-format`:

- Stub prints `stub agy: auth expired` to stderr and exits 3, no stdout:
  - stream: HTTP **200**, one chunk with `finish_reason: "stop"`, then `data: [DONE]` — no error anywhere
  - non-stream: HTTP **502** `{"error":"agy process exited with non-zero code","code":3,"stderr":"stub agy: auth expired"}` (correct — the control case)
- Stub emits one `step_update` text delta (`partial answer`) / `{"response":"partial answer"}`, prints `stub agy: run failed midway` to stderr, exits 3:
  - stream: HTTP 200, content chunk `partial answer`, then a `finish_reason: "stop"` chunk + `[DONE]`
  - non-stream: HTTP **200**, `content: "partial answer"`, `finish_reason: "stop"`
- Stub success case (delta + `result` event / `{"response":"full answer"}`, exit 0) correctly returns 200 with the full text and `stop` in both modes.

Dedup: searches for "agy-proxy" / "agy" across open and closed issues return only #434/#435/#437/#483/#661/#672 — #672 notes the non-stream gate at :553 as "judge separately" and explicitly excludes it from its acceptance criteria; none covers the stream handler or failure detection in this proxy. Cross-repo: `bin/agy-proxy.mjs` exists only in this repo (no copy in developing-today/opencode, developing-today/openchamber, dezren39/nix).

## Why it matters

OpenCode consumes this bridge in streaming mode as a provider. A failed agy run (expired auth, CLI crash, model rejection) presented as a clean `stop` with empty or truncated text is worse than an error: downstream code and users treat it as the complete answer, and an auth expiry presents as "the model said nothing" instead of a diagnosable failure. The two modes also disagree with each other — and with the proxy's own correct empty-output non-stream case (502 with stderr).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A child that exits non-zero (or is killed by a signal — `code` is `null` then) is reported as a failure in both modes, regardless of how much content was already produced: non-stream returns an error status (the existing 502 shape, with stderr, is fine) instead of 200/`stop`; stream mode emits a `data:`-framed error event naming the failure (last stderr line when present) followed by `data: [DONE]`, and no chunk claims `finish_reason: "stop"`.
- [ ] The resume-retry behaviour is preserved: a failed resume (`code !== 0`, no output, a conversation was being resumed) still retries once as a fresh conversation before any failure is reported.
- [ ] Successful runs (exit 0) are unchanged in both modes.
- [ ] A regression test with a stub `agy` (fail-with-no-output and fail-after-partial-output cases, both modes — the `bin/codex-proxy.test.mjs` / `bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs` stub pattern; there is currently no `bin/agy-proxy.test.mjs`) passes; the existing proxy test suites still pass.

title: codex-proxy: a failed codex run is reported as a successful 'stop' — close handler ignores exit code and signal in both modes
body:
## Finding

`bin/codex-proxy.mjs` never checks whether the spawned `codex exec` child actually succeeded. Its `child.on('close', (code, signal) => ...)` handler (bin/codex-proxy.mjs:401) ignores both `code` and `signal`, does not track stderr (no `stderrTail` — the stderr handler at :395 only logs), and unconditionally reports success: non-stream mode returns HTTP 200 with `finish_reason: "stop"`, and stream mode emits a `finish_reason: "stop"` chunk + `data: [DONE]`.

So a run that fails — auth expired, model rejected, CLI crashed — is indistinguishable from a successful empty (or partial) reply for the identical request.

This is the codex-proxy counterpart of the two defects already fixed in the sibling `bin/muse-proxy.mjs`: #670 (streaming failure invisible to SSE clients) and #672 (failure masked whenever any content exists). The muse-proxy fix judged failure on close and framed stream errors as SSE; codex-proxy has no failure detection at all (noted as "a different gap, not filed" in the #670 run's backlog entry).

## Evidence (reproduced on main d8bfe7c6)

Ran `bin/codex-proxy.mjs` with a stub `codex` at `$HOME/.local/bin/codex` (the proxy's own binary resolution) that reads the prompt from stdin:

- Stub prints `stub codex: auth expired` to stderr and exits 3, no stdout:
  - non-stream: HTTP **200**, `content: ""`, `finish_reason: "stop"`, `completion_tokens: 0`
  - stream: HTTP 200, one chunk with `finish_reason: "stop"`, then `data: [DONE]` — no error anywhere
- Stub emits one `item.completed` agent_message (`partial answer`), prints `stub codex: run failed midway` to stderr, exits 3:
  - non-stream: HTTP **200**, `content: "partial answer"`, `finish_reason: "stop"`
  - stream: content chunk `partial answer`, then a `finish_reason: "stop"` chunk + `[DONE]`
- Stub success case (agent_message + `turn.completed`, exit 0) correctly returns 200 with the full text in both modes.

Dedup: searches for "codex-proxy" across open/closed issues return only #434/#435/#437/#480/#483/#496/#661/#670 — none covers exit-code/failure detection. Cross-repo: `bin/codex-proxy.mjs` exists only in this repo (no copy in developing-today/opencode, developing-today/openchamber, dezren39/nix).

## Why it matters

OpenCode consumes this bridge in streaming mode as a provider. A failed Codex run presented as a clean `stop` with empty or truncated text is worse than an error: downstream code and users treat it as the complete answer, and an auth expiry presents as "the model said nothing" instead of a diagnosable failure.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A child that exits non-zero (or is killed by a signal) is reported as a failure in both modes, regardless of how much content was already produced: non-stream returns HTTP 500 with an `error.message` naming the failure (last stderr line when present, otherwise a fallback naming the signal or exit code — never `code null`/`code -2` style artifacts); stream mode emits a `data:`-framed error event followed by `data: [DONE]` and no chunk claims `finish_reason: "stop"`.
- [ ] Successful runs (exit 0) are unchanged in both modes.
- [ ] A regression test with a stub `codex` (fail-with-no-output and fail-after-partial-output cases, both modes) passes; the existing proxy test suites still pass.

title: muse-proxy: signal-killed runs report 'muse exec exited with code null', and #673's empty-stderr terminal-state fallback is untested
body:
## Finding

PR #673 (fixing #672) reworked `bin/muse-proxy.mjs`'s failure handling so failure is judged by the authoritative terminal state, and — when stderr is empty — the error detail names that terminal state instead of the misleading `muse exec exited with code 0`. The fallback expression it left behind (current `main`, `bin/muse-proxy.mjs:404-409`) has two remaining gaps in the same spot:

```js
const failed = terminalState ? terminalState !== 'completed' : code !== 0;
if (failed) {
  const stderrLine = stderrTail.trim().split('\n').pop();
  const fallback = terminalState && terminalState !== 'completed'
    ? `muse run terminated with state '${terminalState}'`
    : `muse exec exited with code ${code}`;
```

### 1. Signal-killed runs report `muse exec exited with code null`

The close handler is `child.on('close', (code, signal) => …)` (line 367), but `signal` is never used. When the child dies by signal (OOM `SIGKILL`, `SIGTERM`, …), Node reports `code === null`, the run correctly counts as failed (`code !== 0`), but with empty stderr the detail becomes the literal string `muse exec exited with code null` — the same class of misleading detail #673 set out to eliminate for the terminal-state case.

Reproduced on current main (`4a91edc3`, merge of #673) with a stub `muse` that kills itself and prints nothing:

```sh
#!/bin/sh
kill -9 $$
```

- Non-stream: `500 {"error":{"message":"Muse execution failed: muse exec exited with code null"}}`
- Stream: SSE error event with the same `code null` message, then `data: [DONE]`

### 2. The empty-stderr terminal-state fallback added by #673 has no test coverage

Both failure stubs added by #671/#673 emit a stderr line (`stub muse: run failed midway`, `stub muse: crashed midway`), and the #672 test only asserts `/Muse execution failed: stub muse:/` — so the `stderrLine` is always what satisfies the assertion and the new fallback string is never exercised.

Verified by ablation in a scratch copy: reverting **only** the fallback-detail lines to the pre-#673 form (`stderrTail… || \`muse exec exited with code ${code}\``), while keeping #673's failure predicate, still passes the full suite 4/4 (`node --test bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs`). The behaviour itself works today — a stub emitting `run.terminal.failed` with **no** stderr returns `Muse execution failed: muse run terminated with state 'failed'` in both modes — but nothing pins it, so a future refactor can silently regress it back to `exited with code 0`.

## Evidence

- PR #673: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/673 (commit `df1dd2502d98b2a7bf435e7a2789f49965354dbe`, merged in `4a91edc359063734da7d0b8a8dedbd2d49591216`), diff hunk changing the failure predicate and detail fallback in `bin/muse-proxy.mjs`.
- Current main: `bin/muse-proxy.mjs:367` (close handler signature `(code, signal)`), `:404-409` (predicate + fallback quoted above).
- Tests: `bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs` — `FAILPARTIAL`/`CRASHPARTIAL` stubs (lines 32-43) both write to stderr; the #672 test's error assertions (lines 175, 188) match only the stderr text.
- Live repro of both the `code null` message and the working-but-untested terminal-state message, run against current main as described above.

## Why it matters

This proxy is the OpenAI-compatible surface other tools drive `muse exec` through; when a run dies, the error detail is often the *only* diagnostic a client (or a human reading its logs) gets. `exited with code null` sends debugging in the wrong direction (a signal kill — e.g. OOM — looks like a corrupt message), and the one fallback #673 deliberately improved can regress unnoticed because no test reaches it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A run terminated by a signal with empty stderr and no terminal event produces an error detail that names the signal (e.g. `muse exec terminated by signal SIGKILL`) instead of `exited with code null`, in both stream (SSE error frame + `[DONE]`) and non-stream (500) modes.
- [ ] A stub mode that emits a non-`completed` terminal event with **empty** stderr is added to `bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs`, asserting the detail names the terminal state (e.g. `terminated with state 'failed'`) in both modes.
- [ ] A stub mode whose child dies by signal (e.g. `kill -9 $$`) with empty stderr is added, asserting the signal-naming detail in both modes.
- [ ] `node --test bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs` passes, and ablating either fallback branch makes exactly the new assertions fail.

title: muse-proxy: a run that fails after producing partial output is reported as a successful 'stop' — failure is masked whenever any content exists
body:
## Problem

`bin/muse-proxy.mjs` decides whether a `muse exec` run failed with this predicate (line 439):

```js
const failed = (code !== 0 && fullContent.length === 0) || (terminalState && terminalState !== 'completed' && fullContent.length === 0);
```

Both clauses require `fullContent.length === 0`. So whenever the CLI emitted **any** assistant text before failing, the failure is masked: the proxy returns the partial text as a normal successful completion with `finish_reason: 'stop'`.

## Evidence (verified 2026-10-23 with a stub `muse` on PATH, same harness style as `bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs`)

Case A — terminal event says the run failed, exit code 0:
- stub emits `run.output.delta` `"partial answer"`, then `run.terminal.failed` with `terminal: "failed"`, exit 0.
- Non-stream response: **200**, `message.content: "partial answer"`, `finish_reason: "stop"`.
- Stream response: partial chunk, then a finish chunk with `finish_reason: "stop"` + `[DONE]`. No error anywhere.

Case B — child crashes mid-run, exit code 3:
- stub emits `run.output.delta` `"partial answer"`, writes stderr, exit 3 (no terminal event).
- Both modes: **200 / finish_reason "stop"** with the partial text, exactly as Case A.

The empty-content cases are handled correctly (#670: non-stream 500, stream SSE error frame + `[DONE]`); only the partial-content cases slip through.

## Why it matters

Clients (opencode and any OpenAI-compatible consumer) cannot distinguish a truncated, failed run from a complete answer: they present the partial text as the model's full reply and record the request as successful. A mid-run auth expiry, rate limit, or CLI crash after the first tokens is indistinguishable from success — the worst failure shape for a bridge whose whole job is faithful translation.

## Acceptance criteria

- A run whose terminal state is present and not `completed` is reported as an error regardless of how much content was produced: non-stream → 500 with the `Muse execution failed: …` error body; stream → the already-streamed deltas are followed by the #670 SSE error frame + `[DONE]`, and **no** `finish_reason: 'stop'` chunk is emitted.
- A run with no terminal event and a non-zero exit code is likewise an error even when partial content exists (same surfacing as above).
- A run with terminal state `completed` stays a success even if the exit code is non-zero (the terminal event is authoritative), and all existing behavior for completed runs (tail reconciliation #484, usage accounting) is unchanged.
- New tests in `bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs` cover both cases above in both stream and non-stream modes (stub markers in the style of the existing FAILME/DIVERGE cases), and the existing three tests still pass (`node --test bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs`).

## Suggested fix

Make the terminal state authoritative and drop the content-length gate, e.g.:

```js
const failed = terminalState ? terminalState !== 'completed' : code !== 0;
```

## Related sighting (judge separately)

`bin/agy-proxy.mjs:553` has a similar content-gated check (`code !== 0 && !responseText`). That CLI exposes no authoritative terminal event, so the semantics differ; noted here only so the fixer can decide whether it deserves its own issue — it is not part of this issue's acceptance criteria.

title: muse-proxy: streaming execution failure is sent as unframed JSON on a 200 SSE response — clients see an empty successful stream
body:
## Finding

`bin/muse-proxy.mjs` sends the streaming response headers (`200` + `Content-Type: text/event-stream`) before the `muse exec` child runs. When the child then fails — non-zero exit with no content, or a non-`completed` terminal state with no content — the close handler's failure branch cannot change the status, and it ends the response with a bare JSON error object:

```js
if (!res.headersSent) {
  res.writeHead(500, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' });
}
res.end(JSON.stringify({ error: { message: `Muse execution failed: ${detail}` } }));
```

In stream mode `res.headersSent` is always true at that point, so the client receives an SSE response whose body is one unframed JSON line: no `data:` prefix, no error chunk, no `data: [DONE]`. An OpenAI-compatible SSE client parsing `data:` lines sees an empty, apparently successful stream (HTTP 200, zero events) — the failure is silently swallowed. The non-streaming path is correct (500 + JSON error), so the two modes disagree about the same failure.

## Evidence
