```
error: recipe `test-web-typecheck` failed
```

All other checks in that run passed, including 1633 unit tests and all 374 web unit tests (13 files). This failure blocks every open id PR (#820, #810, #808, #801, …) with an unrelated red `nix flake check`.

## Root cause

The #745 tests added in #746 (44c0cd3a) define a helper in `pkgs/id/web/src/goto-line.test.ts`:

```ts
function createViewFromDoc(
  schema: typeof rawSchema,
  doc: ReturnType<typeof rawSchema.node>,
)
```

`typeof rawSchema` is the narrow `Schema<"text"|"code_block"|"doc", never>` (rawSchema is built from a literal node map). `richSchema` is a generic `Schema` (built via `addListNodes(...)`), so passing `richSchema` at lines 354 and 394 does not typecheck. Line 372 passes `rawSchema` and is fine.

## Fix

Generalise the helper to the base ProseMirror types: `schema: Schema` and `doc: Node` from `prosemirror-model` (the same unparameterised `Schema` type `editor.ts:getSchema` already returns).

## Acceptance

- `bun run typecheck` (tsc --noEmit) in pkgs/id/web passes with no errors in goto-line.test.ts
- goto-line web unit tests still pass
- `nix flake check` test-web / test-web-typecheck go green on the PR

title: id(world-line): PR #808 — join pump --command-mode kills the session on a parse Message (SSH shows it and continues), and /logs [seconds] is parsed then discarded by both consumers

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: status/needs-triage
labels.description: Not yet triaged; needs a first look

labels.name: source/sweep
labels.description: Filed or worked by an issue-sweep job

body:
## Problem

PR #808 introduces the shared line grammar (`pkgs/id/src/world_line.rs`, branch `id/phase-11`) whose stated contract is that one line "works identically as an SSH command, a piped script line, and a CLI one-off" — and the PR body claims the `id world join --command-mode` pump and SSH command mode both speak it (#546). Two places break that parity:

### 1. A typo in the join pump kills the session; on SSH it just shows a message

- `world_line.rs` defines `WorldLine::Message(String)` as "A command that did not parse; the message is shown to the user" (unknown commands, `usage: /input <hex>`, `usage: /logs [seconds]`, `usage: /document <name>`).
- SSH command mode honours that: `pkgs/id/src/world_ssh.rs:667-672` renders `{message}\r\nworld> ` and the session continues.
- The join pump does the opposite: `pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs:1054-1056` maps `WorldLine::Message(message)` to `anyhow::bail!("{message}")`, and the pump loop calls `pump_command_frame(line)?` (`commands/world.rs:1007`), so the error breaks the writer loop, closes the connection, and ends `id world join` with a failure exit.

One mistyped `/imput …` or `/logs soon` in `--command-mode` therefore disconnects the user from the world instead of showing the usage line and a fresh prompt. The pump's own test even enshrines the divergence: `assert!(pump_command_frame("/nope").is_err())`.

### 2. `/logs [seconds]` is parsed, validated — and silently discarded by both consumers

- `world_line.rs:29, 78-87` — `WorldLine::Logs { seconds: Option<u64> }`; a non-numeric argument is a usage error, so the grammar promises the argument means something.
- SSH: `world_ssh.rs:846` maps `WorldLine::Logs { .. }` to `WorldCommand::Logs`, discarding `seconds` (the handler then prints the "event tailing is not available in command mode" stub regardless of the argument).
- Pump: `commands/world.rs:1051` maps `WorldLine::Logs { .. }` to `{"type": "logs"}` with no seconds field.

So `/logs 5` and `/logs 5000` behave identically everywhere, with no hint to the user. Either the frame/handler needs to carry the value, or the grammar should stop accepting (and validating) an argument nothing uses.

## Why it matters

The whole point of #546 / F11.5 is one grammar with one behaviour per surface; a shared parser whose error and argument semantics differ per consumer re-creates the divergence the refactor exists to remove, and the pump case is user-hostile: a recoverable typo becomes a disconnect (and a nonzero exit for scripted/piped use of `--command-mode`).

## Evidence

- PR #808 (OPEN, branch `id/phase-11`); file:line on the PR branch as fetched this run (`gh api .../contents/...?ref=id/phase-11`). Not on `main` yet — fix-before-merge.
- Dedup: #546 is the feature tracker this PR implements; #559/#807-style searches plus "pump command" found no issue covering the Message/`/logs` behaviour. The PR body itself notes "/logs in command mode is a documented stub" for SSH — it does not note the pump's session-killing Message handling or that the pump sends a bare `logs` frame.

## Acceptance

- In `--command-mode`, a line that parses to `WorldLine::Message` is shown to the user and the pump keeps running (matching SSH command mode); only `/quit` / EOF / a real I/O error ends the session. The pump test asserts the message path does not error and a following valid line still produces its frame.
- `/logs [seconds]` either takes effect identically on both surfaces (value carried into the logs request / stub message states what is ignored), or `world_line` rejects the argument with a usage message that says it is unsupported — in both cases, SSH and the pump behave the same.
- A parity test runs the same line corpus through both consumers' mappings (the structural-guard style PR #808 already uses for the projection) so the two mappings cannot silently drift again.

title: id(world-manifest): PR #801 — plan() treats omitted grants/ceiling/schedules as authoritative, contradicting 'empty fields are left alone' (omitted ceiling widens to whole catalog)
body:
## Problem

PR #801's new `world.toml` manifest model (`pkgs/id/src/world_manifest.rs`, branch `id/phase-12`) documents partial-manifest semantics that its own `plan()` does not implement — and the mismatch is destructive in one direction and privilege-widening in the other.

The struct doc (`world_manifest.rs:23-24`) says:

> A declarative description of a world. Empty fields are left alone by `plan`, so a minimal manifest drifts nothing.

That is only true for module/seed, and only against an already-empty world. `plan()` (`world_manifest.rs:179ff`) treats every other empty field as authoritative:

- **Grants** (`world_manifest.rs:197-205`): `grants` is a plain `Vec<String>` with no way to express "unspecified". An omitted/empty `grants` against a world with grants produces `SetGrants { grants: [] }` — `id world apply` revokes every grant.
- **Ceiling** (`world_manifest.rs:208-212`): an omitted `ceiling` is `None`, which the model defines as "the whole catalog". Against a world with a narrowed ceiling, a minimal manifest produces `SetCeiling { ceiling: None }` — apply **widens the ceiling to the entire catalog**. This is the security-sensitive direction: a manifest that never mentions the ceiling silently removes it.
- **Schedules** (`world_manifest.rs:224-233`): an omitted/empty `schedules` map produces a `CancelSchedule` step for every pending schedule in the current state.
- **Profile**: an omitted profile is the all-`None` default and replaces the current profile whenever it differs.

The PR's own test demonstrates the contradiction: `an_empty_manifest_drifts_nothing` (`world_manifest.rs`, tests) asserts an empty manifest against a default state drifts nothing, then asserts the same empty manifest against a state with grants + a ceiling produces exactly 2 steps (`SetGrants` + `SetCeiling`). The test's name and the struct doc claim the opposite of its second half.

A related rendering bug in the same file: `diff()` (`world_manifest.rs:321`) renders a `SetCeiling` step as `~ ceiling [{names}]` with `ceiling.as_deref().unwrap_or(&[])` — so `None` (whole catalog, the widening case) and `Some([])` (no capability allowed, the most restrictive case) both render as `~ ceiling []`. The two opposite operations are indistinguishable in `id world diff` output.

## Why it matters

`id world apply` is an admin operation meant to be safe to run with a partial manifest ("a minimal manifest drifts nothing" is the documented contract a user will rely on). Today, running it with a manifest that only sets, say, a module hash against a live world would also revoke all grants, remove the capability ceiling, and (once schedule state is exposed over the wire) cancel all schedules — none of which the manifest mentions.

## Evidence

- PR #801 (OPEN, branch `id/phase-12`), commits `408e664c3a50`, `0616553c34cd`; file:line on the PR branch as fetched this run. Not on `main` yet — fix-before-merge.
- Dedup: #807 tracks wiring module/schedule *apply* steps over the wire; it does not cover plan-level empty-field semantics or the diff rendering. No other open/closed issue mentions manifest empty-field behaviour (searched "manifest empty grants").

## Acceptance

- The manifest can distinguish "field unspecified — leave alone" from "field explicitly empty — clear it" for at least grants, ceiling, and schedules (e.g. `Option<Vec<String>>` / `Option<BTreeMap<..>>`, or an equivalent explicit design), and `plan()` leaves unspecified fields alone.
- The struct doc, the `an_empty_manifest_drifts_nothing` test name, and `plan()`'s actual behaviour agree; a regression test shows a minimal manifest (e.g. only `module_hash`) against a fully populated state produces only the module step.
- In particular, a manifest that omits `ceiling` can never widen an existing ceiling.
- `diff()` renders `None` (whole catalog) and `Some([])` (none allowed) distinctly.

title: id(world-doctor): PR #801 — a Warn finding exits nonzero claiming '6 problem(s)', and the ceiling/profile checks are dead from the CLI (inputs hardcoded None)
body:
## Problem

PR #801's new `id world doctor` (F12.16, tracking issue #559) does not behave the way its own severity model and PR description promise, in two independent ways:

### 1. A `Warn` finding exits nonzero, and the error counts every check as a problem

- `pkgs/id/src/world_doctor.rs:24` — `Severity::Warn` is documented as "Something is off but does not stop a world from running."
- `pkgs/id/src/world_doctor.rs:53-57` — `DoctorReport::healthy()` is `all(|f| f.severity == Severity::Ok)`, so a single Warn makes the whole report "unhealthy".
- `pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs:426-430` (branch `id/phase-12`) — the CLI bails whenever `!report.healthy()`, with `bail!("world doctor found {} problem(s)", report.findings.len())`. `findings.len()` is the total number of checks (always 6), not the number of non-Ok findings.

So the one Warn path that exists today (toolchain: a configured Roc binary that exists but differs from / is not the pinned nightly, `world_doctor.rs` `check_toolchain`) makes `id world doctor` exit nonzero while claiming "found 6 problem(s)" — even when the other five checks are Ok and nothing blocks a world. The PR body says the command "exits nonzero on failure"; Warn is not Fail.

### 2. The ceiling and profile checks can never fire from the CLI

- `pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs:413-422` — the Doctor handler constructs `DoctorInputs { caps_ceiling: None, profile: None, .. }` unconditionally. There is no flag, env var, or config source that supplies either value.
- `check_ceiling` with `None` always returns Ok ("no capability ceiling (whole catalog)") and `check_profile` with `None` always returns Ok ("no world execution profile (server defaults)").

Both checks are unit-tested in isolation, but through the only user-facing entry point they are dead: a world whose actual ceiling contains `*` or an unknown name, or whose profile has a zero bound, still gets `ok ceiling` / `ok profile` from `id world doctor`. The PR body advertises doctor as checking "the capability ceiling, the execution profile" — from the CLI it checks neither.

## Evidence

- PR #801 (OPEN, branch `id/phase-12`), commits `408e664c3a50`, `0616553c34cd`.
- All file:line references above are on the PR branch as fetched this run (`gh api .../contents/...?ref=id/phase-12`); the code is not on `main` yet, so this is a fix-before-merge finding, not a regression on main.
- No existing issue covers this: #559 is the F12.16 feature tracker PR #801 closes; searches for "doctor warn" / "doctor ceiling profile" found no defect issue.

## Acceptance

- A report whose worst severity is Warn exits 0 (or the severity model / PR description is changed so Warn is explicitly a failure — pick one and make code, docs, and tests agree).
- The failure message counts only non-Ok findings (e.g. "found 1 problem(s)"), not `findings.len()`.
- A test drives the CLI-level report path (not just `check_*` in isolation) with a Warn-only report and asserts the exit behaviour.
- `id world doctor` has a real source for the ceiling and profile it claims to check (flags, env, a live-world query, or local config), OR the two checks are removed from the CLI report and the docs stop claiming them.
- A test shows a bad ceiling / zero-bound profile actually producing a Fail finding through the wired path.

title: id(web): file-list tag pill truncation panics on a multi-byte character straddling byte 256 — templates.rs slices &v[..256] off-boundary
body:
## Problem

The web file list's tag-pill rendering truncates long tag values with a raw byte slice that **panics** when the cut point falls inside a multi-byte UTF-8 character — taking down the file-list request for any file carrying such a tag.

`pkgs/id/src/web/templates.rs:261-265` (`render_file_list`):

```rust
let truncated = if v.len() > crate::tags::TAG_DISPLAY_MAX_BYTES {  // 256
    format!("{}…", &v[..crate::tags::TAG_DISPLAY_MAX_BYTES])
} else {
    v.clone()
};
```

`&v[..256]` panics with `byte index 256 is not a char boundary` whenever byte 256 is mid-character. Tag values are user-controlled (set from the CLI, the bulk-tag UI, or synced from peers) and reach this code via `get_file_list` → `FileInfo.tags` (`routes.rs`), so one crafted/accidental tag value makes `/files` (and the `/api/files` partial) fail for that file list.

## Repro (verified on main `1161bcff`)

Verbatim harness of the two lines above with `v = "a"×255 + "é" + "tail-tail-tail"` (length 269 > 256; `é` occupies bytes 255..257):

```
thread 'main' panicked at trunc.rs:5:38:
end byte index 256 is not a char boundary; it is inside 'é' (bytes 255..257 of string)
```

Any value longer than 256 bytes whose byte-256 offset splits a 2–4-byte character triggers it (e.g. an emoji or CJK character at that offset, or a long CJK/accented value).

## The safe helper already exists in the same crate

`pkgs/id/src/commands/tag.rs:90-100` defines `pub fn truncate_on_char_boundary(s: &str, max: usize) -> String`, which walks back to a char boundary before slicing — and its tests already cover exactly this shape (`tag.rs:407`: a value with `é` straddling the limit). The web template re-implemented the truncation inline and missed the boundary walk.

## Suggested fix

In `templates.rs`, replace the inline slice with the existing helper:

```rust
let truncated = crate::commands::tag::truncate_on_char_boundary(v, crate::tags::TAG_DISPLAY_MAX_BYTES);
```

(`truncate_on_char_boundary` returns the string unchanged when it fits, so the `if` can go.) Add a regression test rendering a file list whose tag value has a multi-byte character straddling byte 256, asserting the pill shows the boundary-truncated value + `…` and nothing panics.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Rendering a file list containing a >256-byte tag value with a multi-byte character straddling byte 256 does not panic and shows the value truncated on a char boundary with `…`.
- [ ] Values ≤256 bytes and pure-ASCII long values render exactly as before.
- [ ] The web template uses the crate's existing `truncate_on_char_boundary` (no second inline implementation).
- [ ] New regression test in the web templates tests; `cargo test --features web` web template tests pass.

title: id(web): Origin check ignores the port — a different localhost port passes as same-origin (CSRF/CSWSH gap in security.rs)
body:
## Problem

The id web UI's Origin check (`pkgs/id/src/web/security.rs`) compares only the **host** of the `Origin` header against the host of the `Host` header — the port is stripped from both sides before comparison, so an origin on a *different port* of the same host passes as "same-origin".

This defeats the layer the module docs say it provides (security.rs:12-15): defeating cross-site request forgery and cross-site WebSocket hijacking for browser requests. An origin is scheme + host + **port**: a page served from `http://localhost:9999` (any other local web app, dev server, or attacker page proxied/served on another local port) is a different origin from the id UI on `http://localhost:3000`, but the guard treats them as the same. WebSocket handshakes carry no CORS preflight, so the Origin check is the only browser-side defence for the `/ws/*` routes when no token is configured (the default loopback setup relies on exactly these host/origin layers).

## Evidence (verified on main `1161bcff`)

- `security.rs:73-83` — `host_only()` strips an optional `:port` (and lower-cases) from a Host/Origin authority: `host_only("localhost:9999") == host_only("localhost:3000") == "localhost"`.
- `security.rs:138-145` — the guard's same-origin test is exactly that comparison:
  ```rust
  let same = origin_authority(origin).is_some_and(|a| host_only(a) == host_only(&host_header));
  ```
  So a request with `Host: localhost:3000` and `Origin: http://localhost:9999` evaluates `same == true` and is **not** refused.
- The existing test `same_origin_is_allowed_cross_origin_is_not` (security.rs:278) only exercises a same-port origin (`http://localhost:3000` vs Host `localhost:3000`) and a different-host origin (`https://evil.example`); no test covers a different-port origin.
- No other layer compensates: `grep -rn Origin pkgs/id/src/web` shows this guard is the only Origin check in the web stack.

Repro (verified by running the guard): a test added to the security tests in a scratch worktree driving `guard` with `Host: localhost:3000` and `Origin: http://localhost:9999`, asserting the *current* behaviour, **passed** on main `1161bcff` — i.e. the different-port origin was answered `200 OK` where a true same-origin check would refuse with `403`. Full run: `cargo test --features web --lib web::security::` → 12 passed, 0 failed (11 pre-existing + the repro case).

## Why it matters

- The loopback default has no token, so layers 2+3 (host allow-list + origin check) are the whole browser-attack defence. Layer 3 currently does not distinguish local origins, which is precisely the neighbour it exists to distinguish: other content reachable in the user's browser on another local port.
- The collab/world WebSocket routes are state-changing and long-lived; a cross-site WebSocket from a different local origin inherits the user's ambient access to the UI.

## Suggested fix

Compare the full authority (host **and** port) for the Origin check, while keeping the host allow-list check host-only as it is today:

- Keep `host_only()` for the allow-list comparison (step 2).
- For step 3, compare a port-preserving normalised authority (lower-cased host, explicit port when present; IPv6 brackets handled like `host_only` does) of `origin_authority(origin)` against the `Host` header authority.
- Decide and document the no-port cases: an Origin with no explicit port vs a Host with an explicit port (e.g. behind a proxy / default-port serving) — treat missing port as the scheme default, or refuse; either is defensible, but it must be a deliberate, tested choice, not an accident of stripping.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Request with `Host: localhost:3000` and `Origin: http://localhost:9999` (and the IPv4/`[::1]` equivalents) is refused with 403.
- [ ] Same-authority origins (same host, same port, any case) still pass; different-host origins still 403; `Origin: null` still refused.
- [ ] New regression tests cover different-port origin refusal and same-port acceptance; existing security tests pass (`cargo test --features web web::security`).
- [ ] Module docs updated so the stated Origin guarantee matches the implemented comparison.

title: id(web): detect_mode's .pm.json check is case-sensitive — document.PM.JSON opens Raw instead of Rich (and downloads as doc.PM.JSON.pm.json)
body:
## Summary

`detect_mode` treats every extension case-insensitively **except** the compound
`.pm.json` extension: a file named `document.PM.JSON` (or `Document.Pm.Json`)
opens in Raw mode instead of the Rich (ProseMirror) editor, and creating it
seeds empty bytes instead of the empty PM document `{}`.

## Evidence

`pkgs/id/src/web/content_mode.rs:143-152` — the extension is lowercased before
matching, but the Rich guard compares the raw filename:

```rust
let extension = path.extension().and_then(|e| e.to_str()).map(str::to_lowercase);
match extension.as_deref() {
    Some("json") if filename.ends_with(".pm.json") => ContentMode::Rich,
```

`ends_with` is case-sensitive, so the guard fails for any non-lowercase
spelling even though the `json` arm matched. Every other arm is effectively
case-insensitive, and the module's own tests pin that contract for simple
extensions (`test_detect_markdown` asserts `CHANGELOG.markdown` → Markdown).

Verified this run with a standalone rustc reproduction of the exact guard
(Path::extension + to_lowercase + ends_with, std semantics):

```
document.pm.json: rich=true
document.PM.JSON: rich=false
document.Pm.Json: rich=false
notes.MD ext lowercased: Some("md")   // simple extensions ARE case-insensitive
```

Consequences on current main (15f4885f):

- `pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs:1227` (`new_file_handler`): creating
  `notes.PM.JSON` takes the Raw content branch (`b""`) instead of Rich
  (`b"{}"`).
- Opening the file routes through `detect_mode_with_content`
  (routes.rs:452, collab.rs:121) → Raw, so a ProseMirror document is shown
  as raw text and edited without the rich editor.

Second site with the same root cause: `pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs:1676`
(download-as-JSON name) — `req.name.ends_with(".pm.json")` is case-sensitive,
so downloading `doc.PM.JSON` as JSON names the download
`doc.PM.JSON.pm.json`.

Precedent in the same codebase: `src/world_ssh.rs:985` lowercases before
`ends_with(".md")` checks.

## Why it matters

Filenames with uppercase extensions are common from Windows/macOS exports
and bulk renames. The mode detector's contract is "extensions are
case-insensitive" everywhere else; the one compound extension silently
violates it, and the file then opens in the wrong editor with the wrong
seed content.

## Acceptance criteria

- `detect_mode` returns `ContentMode::Rich` for `.pm.json` in any case
  (`document.PM.JSON`, `Document.Pm.Json`, …), with regression tests next
  to `test_detect_prosemirror_json` in content_mode.rs.
- Simple-extension behavior unchanged; the existing content_mode tests pass.
- The download-as-JSON path (routes.rs:1676) treats an existing `.pm.json`
  suffix case-insensitively too, or the issue is updated noting why that
  site was deliberately left.

title: PR #759's world-surface width check mis-measures astral-plane, ZWJ and ⚠️ glyphs (JS width 1 vs Rust unicode-width 2) — must not close #724 as-is

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: meta/enriched

body:
## Finding

Open draft PR #759 ("fix(web): match world surface presenter validation with rust wire rules", head `75a4be64`) claims `Fixes #724`, but its terminal-width measurement in `pkgs/id/web/src/world-surface.ts` mis-measures every wide glyph outside the BMP, plus ZWJ emoji sequences and ⚠️ — so it still diverges from the Rust validator in both directions, and merging it as-is would auto-close #724 with its own acceptance criteria ("ZWJ grapheme clusters handled as one grapheme", "width measurement matches Rust's unicode-width semantics") unmet for those cases.

## Evidence

PR head (cross-checked via `gh api contents?ref=75a4be64`):

```ts
const isEastAsianWide =
  /[\u1100-\u115F\u2329\u232A\u2E80-\u303E\u3040-\u33FF\u3400-\u4DBF\u4E00-\u9FFF\uA960-\uA97F\uAC00-\uD7A3\uF900-\uFAFF\uFE10-\uFE19\uFE30-\uFE6F\uFF01-\uFF60\uFFE0-\uFFE6]/;
const terminalWidth = isEastAsianWide.test(cell.symbol) ? 2 : 1;
```

All ranges in the regex are BMP-only. Probed the exact regex + `Intl.Segmenter` grapheme split in Node (each symbol is exactly 1 grapheme, so the grapheme-count check passes and the width check decides):

| Symbol | PR #759 width | Rust `unicode-width` 0.2 width |
|---|---|---|
| 😀 U+1F600 | 1 | 2 |
| 𠮷 U+20BB7 (CJK Ext. B) | 1 | 2 |
| 👨‍👩‍👧 (ZWJ sequence) | 1 | 2 |
| ⚠️ U+26A0 U+FE0F | 1 | 2 |
| 界 U+754C | 2 | 2 |
| x | 1 | 1 |

Rust side ground-truthed two ways: `pkgs/id/src/world_presentation.rs:219,350` requires `UnicodeWidthStr::width(symbol) == columns` with `unicode-width = "0.2"` (`pkgs/id/Cargo.toml:90`), and a scratch cargo program against the real `unicode-width` 0.2 crate printed width 2 for all four failing symbols above.

Consequences, mirroring #724's original failure modes:

- A **valid** Rust-produced cell `{symbol: "😀", columns: 2}` (+ empty continuation) is rejected by the presenter (`renderWorldSurface` returns `false`, world screen falls back) — valid surfaces containing emoji or astral CJK glyphs can never render.
- An **invalid** cell `{symbol: "😀", columns: 1}` is accepted and squeezed into a 1-column grid span — the exact misalignment #724 was filed for.

The PR's new tests in `world-surface.test.ts` cover only BMP cases (界, x, ab, ""), so none of this is caught. Separately, the PR also drops `"configVersion": 1` from `pkgs/id/web/bun.lock` — unrelated lockfile churn that should not ride along.

## Dedupe

#724 is the parent finding and is still open; this issue is specifically about PR #759's implementation shortfall and its `Fixes #724` closure. Searches for emoji/unicode-width/astral issues return only #724. Cross-repo: `world-surface.ts` exists only in this repo.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `world-surface.test.ts` gains cases for an astral wide glyph (e.g. 😀 or 𠮷) and a ZWJ cluster: `columns: 2` accepted, `columns: 1` rejected — matching `unicode-width` 0.2.
- [ ] The width measurement in `world-surface.ts` returns 2 for those cases (e.g. astral CJK ranges U+20000–U+2FA1F, emoji presentation ranges, and ZWJ sequences whose base glyph is wide), without changing the already-correct BMP/ASCII/combining behaviour.
- [ ] Either PR #759 is updated to satisfy the above before merge, or its `Fixes #724` is removed so #724 stays open for the remaining cases.
- [ ] The unrelated `bun.lock` `configVersion` removal is dropped from PR #759 or justified there.

title: Consolidate stale Jules PRs #753 and #755: both duplicate work already on main (cursor recycling / ARIA labels) — close as superseded, salvage two one-line hunks
body:
## Finding (PR consolidation / stale PRs)

Open draft Jules PRs **#753** (⚡ Bolt: Optimize ProseMirror cursor rendering) and **#755** (🎨 Palette: Add ARIA labels to icon-only buttons in templates) are both built on ancient bases and almost entirely duplicate work that is **already on `main`** via other commits. Neither should be merged as-is; together they are one cleanup finding.

## Evidence

### PR #753 — cursor DOM recycling, already landed, and its keys are weaker than main's

- Merge-base is `fcb1c982` (2026-10-12, merge of PR #198). `gh pr view 753` reports `mergeable: CONFLICTING`, `mergeStateStatus: DIRTY`, draft.
- Main already contains commit `09e3cc2b` (2026-10-20, Jules) "⚡ Bolt: Optimize cursor decoration DOM recycling" — the same change: factory functions for `Decoration.widget`, stable keys replacing the `decorationGeneration` counter.
- Main's current keys in `pkgs/id/web/src/cursors.ts` are strictly richer than #753's: standalone `cursor-${clientID}-${opacity}-${color}-${connectionState}-${encodeURIComponent(name)}`, cluster key includes group position plus per-cursor `clientID@head-opacity-color-connectionState-name`, own-cursor key includes `color`, selection key includes `color`. PR #753's keys drop `color` and `name` (own: `cursor-own-${clientID}`; cluster: clientIDs + opacities + connectionState only; selection: clientID + opacity only). Taking #753's version would regress colour/rename updates on recycled cursor DOM — the same omission class already tracked for a sibling draft in #331.
- The PR's only novel hunk is in `pkgs/id/web/src/image-upload.ts`: adding `key: placeholder-${action.id}` to the placeholder widget (main's widget at `image-upload.ts:136` still has only `id: action.id`, no `key`).

### PR #755 — ARIA labels, already landed except one line

- Merge-base is `7639d483` (2026-08-30).
- Main already contains commit `ac089859` (2026-10-22) "feat(ux): Add aria-labels to empty icon buttons", which added exactly #755's theme-button labels (both copies, `pkgs/id/src/web/templates.rs` lines 96–98 and 462–464 on main) and the `Add tag` label (line 478).
- The PR's only novel hunk is `aria-label="Download"` on the download button (main line 441 still has `title="Download">dl` with no aria-label).

### Dedupe

- #310 tracks triage of an older (2026-10-18) set of 11 overlapping Jules Bolt/Palette drafts (#207–#253); it does not name #753 or #755, which were opened 2026-10-24, and does not record that these two are superseded by main.
- #331 tracks colour/name key omission on PR #327 only.

## Why it matters

Merging or "fixing up" either PR risks reintroducing older, weaker versions of `cursors.ts` / `templates.rs` over main's newer ones (in #753's case, silently breaking cursor colour/rename refresh). Leaving them open adds two more stale Jules drafts to the pile #310 already complains about, and each future Jules run can point at them as prior art for yet another duplicate.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] PR #753 closed as superseded, with a comment linking commit `09e3cc2b` and this issue (do not merge its `cursors.ts`).
- [ ] PR #755 closed as superseded, with a comment linking commit `ac089859` and this issue.
- [ ] The two novel one-line hunks — `aria-label="Download"` on `#download-btn` in `templates.rs`, and `key: placeholder-${action.id}` in `image-upload.ts` — are either carried onto current main in one small fresh PR, or explicitly dropped with the reason recorded here.

title: id(web): parse_iso_timestamp accepts out-of-range dates — month 13, day 0/32, Feb 30, hour 25 and pre-1970 years all return plausible-but-wrong timestamps
body:
## Problem

`parse_iso_timestamp` in `pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs:148-201` — the parser behind `classify_tag` (`routes.rs:125-141`) for `auto-<ISO date>` backup tag names — performs **no range validation** on any component. Out-of-range values are silently rolled over into a different, plausible timestamp instead of returning `None`, and a pre-1970 year is clamped to the epoch. The resulting `FileInfo.timestamp` (`routes.rs:714`, second pass of the file-list builder) therefore shows/sorts an auto-backup under a date its name does not contain.

## Evidence (verified this run)

The function was extracted verbatim from current main and run standalone (`rustc -O`, unmodified logic). The valid control matches the known epoch exactly:

| Input | Result | Correct behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `2026-03-12T06:42:30Z` | `Some(1773297750)` | ✅ matches reference epoch |
| `2026-13-01T00:00:00Z` | `Some(1798761600)` (= 2027-01-01) | month 13 rolls into next year |
| `2026-00-01T00:00:00Z` | `Some(1767225600)` (= 2026-01-01) | month 0 silently becomes January |
| `2026-03-00T00:00:00Z` | `Some(1772323200)` | **identical to `2026-03-01`** — day 0 == day 1 |
| `2026-03-32T00:00:00Z` | `Some(1775001600)` (= 2026-04-01) | day 32 rolls into April |
| `2026-02-30T00:00:00Z` | `Some(1772409600)` (= 2026-03-02) | Feb 30 rolls into March |
| `2026-03-12T25:00:00Z` | `Some(1773363600)` | hour 25 rolls into the next day |
| `2026-03-12T00:60:00Z` / `T00:00:60Z` | `Some(...)` | minute/second 60 roll over |
| `1969-01-01T00:00:00Z` | `Some(0)` | **identical to the epoch** — the `1970..year` loop never runs and the date collapses to 1970-01-01 |

Contributing code:

- `routes.rs:165-168` — components are collected with `filter_map(|p| p.parse().ok())`, so only count is checked, never range.
- `routes.rs:182` — the month loop is capped only by the `month_days` array length, so month 13 accumulates a full year.
- `routes.rs:190` — `day.saturating_sub(1)` makes day 0 indistinguishable from day 1.
- `routes.rs:192` — `hour * 3600 + min * 60 + sec` accepts any hour/minute/second.

Related robustness note (same function): the days calculation loops `for y in 1970..year` with no upper bound, so a tag named e.g. `auto-999999999-01-01T00:00:00Z` makes the file-list handler iterate ~10⁹ times for that one name. A year-range check fixes this too.

Existing tests (`routes.rs:2236-2259`) cover only a valid date, garbage strings, and the epoch — no out-of-range component is tested.

## Why it matters

Auto-backup names are generated (`auto-2026-03-12T06:42:30.015Z`), but tag names are user/peer-controlled data in a p2p store: a malformed or adversarial `auto-…` name is displayed and ordered as if it were a real backup from a different date (a "Feb 30" backup sorting as Mar 2, a 1969 backup claiming the epoch), and an absurd year can stall the file list. A parser that cannot represent a date should say so (`None`, which `classify_tag` already handles) rather than invent one.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `parse_iso_timestamp` returns `None` for: month outside 1–12, day 0 or greater than the days in that month for that year (incl. Feb 29 on a non-leap year, Feb 30 always), hour > 23, minute > 59, second > 59.
- [ ] Years before 1970 return `None` (the `u64` result cannot represent them) instead of `Some(0)`.
- [ ] The year loop is bounded (the range check above suffices) — no per-year iteration for absurd years.
- [ ] Valid inputs are unchanged: `2026-03-12T06:42:30.015Z` → `1773297750`, `1970-01-01T00:00:00Z` → `0`, Feb 29 on a leap year (e.g. 2024-02-29) parses correctly.
- [ ] New unit tests next to the existing ones at `routes.rs:2236+` cover each rejected class and the leap-day cases; existing `test_classify_tag_*` / `test_parse_iso_timestamp_*` tests still pass.

title: id(web): world-surface presenter accepts cells the Rust wire validator rejects — symbol width/grapheme and continuation-symbol checks missing

body:
## Summary
The web world-screen presenter (`renderWorldSurface`) accepts wire cells that the Rust validator for the same wire model rejects, and renders them with a grid span that does not match the glyph — or silently drops a glyph entirely. The two validators for one wire format have diverged.

## Evidence (verified this run on current main)

Rust canonical validator — `pkgs/id/src/world_presentation.rs`, `ScreenSurface::render_ansi` (lines ~334–365):
- a `columns == 0` continuation cell must have an **empty** symbol (`!cell.symbol.is_empty()` → reject)
- a `columns == 1|2` cell must contain **exactly one grapheme** (`cell.symbol.graphemes(true).count() != 1` → reject)
- the grapheme's `UnicodeWidthStr::width` must **equal `columns`**
- the continuation of a wide glyph must also have an empty symbol

TypeScript presenter — `pkgs/id/web/src/world-surface.ts`, `renderWorldSurface` (lines ~57–147):
- only checks `cell.symbol.length > 16` (UTF-16 units) and rejects control characters
- never checks grapheme count, never checks symbol width against `columns`, never checks a continuation cell's symbol is empty

Probe run with vitest against current main (temporary test, since removed):
- `{symbol:"界", columns:1}` → returns `true`, rendered as `gridColumn: 1 / span 1` — a width-2 glyph squeezed into one column (Rust: width 2 ≠ 1, reject)
- `{symbol:"x", columns:2}` + continuation `{symbol:"Z", columns:0}` → returns `true`, rendered text is just `x` — the `Z` glyph is **silently dropped** (Rust: narrow glyph in 2 columns and non-empty continuation both reject)
- `{symbol:"ab", columns:1}` → returns `true` (two graphemes in one cell; Rust rejects)
- `{symbol:"", columns:1}` → returns `true` (zero graphemes; Rust rejects)

Existing tests: `pkgs/id/web/src/world-surface.test.ts` covers bounds, control characters and mismatched wide-cell styles, but no symbol/width or continuation-symbol cases.

## Why it matters
The presenter is the browser's safety/validity boundary for guest-supplied screen data ("Render a validated cell grid… return false on invalid wire data"). Accepting cells the producer's own validator would never emit means a malformed or hostile surface can misalign the whole grid (wide glyph in a 1-column span, narrow glyph spanning 2) or lose glyphs with no error — and the divergence will keep growing as either side is edited, since nothing pins them to the same rules.

## Acceptance criteria
- `renderWorldSurface` returns `false` (leaving the existing view untouched, as today) for:
  - a `columns == 1|2` cell whose symbol is not exactly one grapheme
  - a cell whose symbol's terminal width does not equal `columns` (e.g. `界` with `columns:1`, `x` with `columns:2`, `""` with `columns:1`)
  - a `columns == 0` continuation cell with a non-empty symbol
- Width measurement matches Rust's `unicode-width` semantics for the tested cases (at minimum: ASCII = 1, CJK/wide = 2, combining/ZWJ grapheme clusters handled as one grapheme); the chosen approach (small table, Intl APIs, or a dependency) is documented in the file header
- New cases added to `world-surface.test.ts` mirroring the Rust-side invariants; existing 3 presenter tests still pass

## Finding

PR #709 (🎨 Palette: Add aria-label to file select checkboxes, head `6365719c`) commits a Jules planning scratch file, `test_plan.sh`, at the repository root. It is not part of the change, it is executable, and it is the sole cause of the PR's failing `treefmt check`.

## Evidence

- `gh pr diff 709` adds a new file `test_plan.sh` (mode 100755) whose entire content is four `echo` lines of the agent narrating its plan ("I am Palette. Looking for a micro-UX improvement." / "I noticed the file select checkboxes…" / "I will add aria-label=…"). The actual fix is in `pkgs/id/src/web/templates.rs`; nothing references `test_plan.sh`.
- The PR's `treefmt check` run (40051219501) fails, and its log names exactly this file: `ERRO file has changed path=test_plan.sh prev_size=344 … current_size=342` followed by `Error: unexpected changes detected, --fail-on-change is enabled`. The formatter rewrites the scratch file, so the check can never pass while the file is in the PR.
- The PR's other checks (Nix flake evaluation, run) pass, so this one stray file is the only blocker — and if the PR were merged as-is, the scratch file would land on `main` permanently.

## Why it matters

Leftover agent scratch files pollute the repo root and, here, actively break CI for the PR that carries them. The same Jules flow that produced #709 will produce more PRs; the scratch file needs to be dropped before merge and ideally kept out of future automated PRs.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `test_plan.sh` is removed from PR #709 (or, if the PR has already merged, deleted from `main` in a follow-up).
- [ ] PR #709's `treefmt check` passes with the file gone.
- [ ] A quick scan of other open Jules-authored PRs confirms none of them carry a similar root-level scratch/planning file.

body:
## Finding

PR #695 (merged, merge commit `3d7b96a5cd4d5476942ec5efa6a7df128159e244`, commit `2446d3e999c86c16754bbda901c535b552395154`) dropped three dead OpenCode env vars from `home/common/default.nix`, citing developing-today/opencode#105 and developing-today/opencode#115 — but the same `sessionVariables` block still sets two more names those same issues adjudicated as dead, and one of them carries an active behavioural intent that is silently not happening.

Found by the pr-diff-review job reviewing PR #695; verified against current main of both repos on 2026-10-23 (code `3d7b96a5`, opencode `fe5d6c8e943882a01d7914264b710c7e8ac11b5a`), cross-checked via local clones and `gh api` contents.

## Evidence

### 1. `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_DISABLE_FILEWATCHER` — the file watcher is NOT off, despite the config saying it is

- `home/common/default.nix:1252-1255` on current main:
  ```
  # File watcher off by default (Drew, 2026-10-20): the working trees
  # are giant, and watching costs more than the live-external-edit
  # awareness it buys. Diffs are git-computed on demand either way.
  OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_DISABLE_FILEWATCHER = "1";
  ```
- Nothing in opencode reads that name: `git grep OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_DISABLE_FILEWATCHER` on opencode main returns only docs rows (`packages/web/.../cli.mdx`), no code reader.
- The actual gate is `packages/cli/src/server-process.ts:146` in opencode:
  ```ts
  filewatcher: !truthy(process.env.OPENCODE_FILEWATCHER_DISABLE ?? process.env.OPENCODE_DISABLE_FILEWATCHER),
  ```
  i.e. the watcher defaults to ON and is disabled only via `OPENCODE_DISABLE_FILEWATCHER` / `OPENCODE_FILEWATCHER_DISABLE`. Neither correct name is set anywhere in this repo (`git grep` on main: no hits).
- This exact dead name was already adjudicated in opencode: #104 ("filewatcher-disable sets a dead env name — OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_DISABLE_FILEWATCHER is read nowhere", CLOSED, fixed there by renaming opencode's own setters to `OPENCODE_DISABLE_FILEWATCHER`), and #115's body calls it out again. PR #695 removed `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_ICON_DISCOVERY` ~7 lines above this line, in the same block, but left this one.

### 2. `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_LSP_TOOL` — dead line from the same #105 set PR #695 was cleaning up

- `home/common/default.nix:1240` on current main: `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_LSP_TOOL = "1";`
- opencode#105 named this variable explicitly as one of its four dead vars ("the LSP-tool gate (`OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_LSP_TOOL`…)"), with `git grep` excluding docs returning zero hits; re-verified this run on opencode main `fe5d6c8e`: zero hits outside `packages/web`. #105 is CLOSED and its English docs row for this variable is gone.
- PR #695's stated four-var list covered three of #105's vars plus #115's icon-discovery var; this one — the fourth #105 var — was not in the list and survives.

## Why it matters

- Item 1 is not cosmetic: the home config's stated intent (Drew, 2026-10-20 — watcher off because the working trees are giant and watching costs more than it buys) is silently not in effect on any machine built from this config. The server spawns with the file watcher on by default.
- Item 2 is the same silent-no-op class PR #695 was created to eliminate; leaving it re-creates the "set but unread" trap for the next reader of this block.
- Cross-repo scope checked: neither dead name is set in developing-today/openchamber or dezren39/nix (`git grep` on their mains: no hits) — this is a code-repo-only setter, so this single issue tracks the whole finding.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `home/common/default.nix` sets `OPENCODE_DISABLE_FILEWATCHER = "1";` (the name `server-process.ts` actually reads) in place of the dead `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_DISABLE_FILEWATCHER` line, keeping the "file watcher off by default" comment accurate.
- [ ] The `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_LSP_TOOL = "1";` line is removed (mirroring PR #695's drop decision for its #105 siblings), or a reader is implemented in opencode with a test — dropping is the expected route.
- [ ] `git grep -n "OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_DISABLE_FILEWATCHER\|OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_LSP_TOOL"` over this repo's tracked tree returns no setters (a historical comment noting the rename, if kept, is fine).

body:
## Finding

Open Renovate PR #626 ("Update Rust crate rand [SECURITY]", head `20277913b714e3a96dd3961373da4bbe891946db`) bumps `pkgs/web-gen` from rand 0.9 to **rand 0.10.0** (`pkgs/web-gen/Cargo.toml`: `rand = "0.9.0"` → `"0.10.0"`; lock resolves rand 0.10.3) with **no source changes**. rand 0.10 removes/renames the exact APIs web-gen uses, so merging the PR as-is breaks the web-gen build. This was verified empirically, not inferred (probe below).

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/626 (OPEN at filing time; checks already red: `renovate/artifacts` FAIL and `treefmt check` FAIL).
- web-gen's only rand usage, on current main (`origin/main` ebb99893):
  - `pkgs/web-gen/src/main.rs:10` — `use rand::Rng;`
  - `pkgs/web-gen/src/main.rs:135-138` — `let mut rng = rand::thread_rng(); rng.gen_range(0..101)`
- PR #626's own release notes for rand 0.10.0 state: "Rename `Rng` -> `RngExt`" (#1717) and "Use Edition 2024 and MSRV 1.85" (#1653).
- Differential probe (scratch crate containing web-gen's verbatim three lines, run this review):
  - Against rand **0.9.5** (current main's lock): compiles — deprecation warnings only (`thread_rng` deprecated, `gen_range` renamed to `random_range`).
  - Against rand **0.10.3** (the version PR #626's web-gen lock resolves to): **fails** — `error[E0425]: cannot find function 'thread_rng' in crate 'rand'`, plus the `rand::Rng` import is no longer the extension trait.
- MSRV clash: rand 0.10 requires Rust 1.85, but `pkgs/web-gen/rust-toolchain` pins `nightly-2023-07-20`, so the crate's own pinned toolchain cannot build rand 0.10 at all.
- The same PR also bumps rand in two doc/ locations with no source adaptation (`doc/.../spikes/beekem/Cargo.toml` 0.8.5 → 0.9.0, whose `src/concurrency.rs` / `src/costs.rs` call `gen_range` throughout; and a vendored p2panda-core snapshot 0.8.5 → 0.9.3). Those are lower stakes but should be audited in the same pass.

## Why it matters

The PR is labelled [SECURITY] (GHSA-cq8v-f236-94qc, low severity, requires a custom logger calling `rand::rng()` during reseed — web-gen does not do this), so it looks like a routine safe merge. Merged as-is it silently breaks `pkgs/web-gen` compilation; no CI job in this repo builds web-gen, so nothing would catch it at merge time.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] PR #626 is not merged in its current form for `pkgs/web-gen`: either web-gen's rand requirement stays on the patched 0.9.x line, or the bump lands together with source adaptation (`rand::rng()`, `random_range`, `RngExt`) and a toolchain that satisfies rand 0.10's MSRV 1.85.
- [ ] `cargo check` for `pkgs/web-gen` passes against the rand version its lockfile pins after the change.
- [ ] The beekem spike and vendored p2panda-core rand bumps in the same PR are audited (adapt, pin, or drop from the PR) rather than carried silently.
- [ ] PR #626's failing checks (`renovate/artifacts`, `treefmt check`) are green or explicitly explained before any merge.

title: muse-proxy (PR #479): streaming responses silently drop the terminal text tail that non-streaming returns

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: source/human
labels.description: Filed directly by a human

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: meta/enriched
labels.description: Intake review done: acceptance criteria, links, and normalized labels added

body:
## Finding

In PR #479 (`bin/muse-proxy.mjs`, commit 9e7dcbde15e35bd71b7e50dd5762285477255c65), a streaming chat-completions response can silently lose the tail of the assistant's reply.

The proxy tracks two sources of response text:

- `run.output.delta` events are appended to `fullContent` and, in stream mode, written to the client immediately as SSE chunks (bin/muse-proxy.mjs:317-336 in the PR head).
- The `run.terminal.*` event carries the authoritative final text in `payload.text`, stored as `terminalText` (bin/muse-proxy.mjs:341-342).

On child close, the non-streaming path reconciles them:

```js
// Prefer the terminal event's authoritative text if deltas missed any
if (terminalText !== null && terminalText.length >= fullContent.length) {
  fullContent = terminalText;
}
```
(bin/muse-proxy.mjs:376-377)

But the streaming branch (bin/muse-proxy.mjs:~390-410) only writes a final chunk with `delta: {}`, `finish_reason: 'stop'`, and usage, then `data: [DONE]`. It never emits the part of `terminalText` that was not already streamed. So whenever the terminal text is longer than the sum of the deltas — the exact case the comment says the reconciliation exists for ("if deltas missed any") — streaming clients receive a truncated reply that nevertheless claims `finish_reason: "stop"`, while non-streaming clients receive the full text for the identical run.

## Evidence (reproduced against the PR head)

Ran the PR's `bin/muse-proxy.mjs` (fetched via the contents API at the PR head sha, byte-count matches the `gh pr diff` hunk: 459 lines) with a stub `muse` binary emitting:

```json
{"payload_type":"run.output.delta","payload":{"text":"Hel"}}
{"payload_type":"run.usage","payload":{"models":[{"input_tokens":100,"output_tokens":3}]}}
{"payload_type":"run.terminal.completed","payload":{"terminal":"completed","text":"Hello world"}}
```

- Non-streaming `POST /v1/chat/completions` returned content `"Hello world"` (correct).
- Streaming (`"stream": true`) returned exactly one content chunk `"Hel"`, then a finish chunk with `finish_reason: "stop"` and `data: [DONE]` — `"lo world"` was never sent.

Deduped: issue searches for "muse-proxy streaming terminal" and "run.terminal" return no existing issue. The sibling `bin/codex-proxy.mjs` has no terminal-text concept (its CLI stream differs), so this is muse-proxy only; `git grep muse-proxy` on the other three repos' mains (opencode/openchamber/nix) is empty.

## Why it matters

OpenCode (the stated consumer, wired as provider `muse`) typically consumes these bridges in streaming mode. A response that ends mid-sentence while reporting a clean `stop` is worse than an error: downstream code and users treat the truncated text as the complete answer, and the discrepancy is invisible unless someone compares against a non-streaming call.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] In stream mode, before the finish chunk, emit any suffix of the terminal text that was not already streamed (when `terminalText` starts with the streamed `fullContent`), or otherwise guarantee streamed content equals the non-streamed content for the same run.
- [ ] If the terminal text diverges from the streamed deltas in a way that cannot be reconciled as a suffix, the behaviour is explicit (documented) rather than silently truncated.
- [ ] A regression test with a stub `muse` emitting deltas that are a strict prefix of the terminal text passes in both stream and non-stream modes, asserting identical final content.

title: CI: nix flake check intermittently dies with 'No space left on device' in id-test/id-ci

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

body:
## Problem

`nix flake check` on GitHub-hosted runners intermittently dies with `No space left on device` while the parallel `id-test` / `id-ci` derivations are building, which masks real test results and burns a ~30-minute run.

## Evidence (two independent runs)

- Run [39081860390](https://github.com/developing-today/code/actions/runs/39081860390) (main @ `5bddbd33`): `rustc-LLVM ERROR: No space left on device` at link time in both the `id-test` and `id-ci` derivations.
- Run [39096263946](https://github.com/developing-today/code/actions/runs/39096263946) (PR #255 head `e3f9380f`): `id-test` failed to write `/build/id/target/debug/deps/rmeta…/full.rmeta`: `No space left on device (os error 28)`, and the runner itself reported ENOSPC writing its own diagnostic log (`_diag/pages/…_1.log`). In the same run `id-test-web` did complete (1487 passed), so the disk fills late, while the biggest derivations are still compiling/linking.
- A third run (main @ `e1f99237`, run 39090664953) completed the full suite with no ENOSPC, so this is intermittent — it depends on how the parallel derivations' disk footprints line up, not on any one change.

## Why it matters

- It has already hidden at least one verification: the #188 fix's first full-suite run was lost to ENOSPC, and PR #255's run lost its `id-test`/`id-ci` legs the same way.
- A red run caused by disk looks identical to a red run caused by code until someone reads 30k lines of log.

## Suggested directions (any one may suffice)

- Add a disk-reclaim step before `nix flake check` (e.g. remove preinstalled toolchains/dotnet/Android SDK the job never uses — the standard free-disk-space recipe recovers ~20–30 GB on `ubuntu-latest`).
- Reduce peak footprint: share one `target` dir between the test derivations instead of each building its own debug tree, or lower derivation parallelism for the heavy Rust checks.
- Move the job to a larger-disk runner if one is available to the org.

## Acceptance criteria

- Several consecutive `nix flake check` runs on main complete with no `No space left on device` anywhere in the log (including the runner's own annotations).
- If a reclaim step is added, the log shows the free space before/after so a future recurrence is diagnosable at a glance.

title: treefmt PR check sweeps merge-base drift: main-side unformatted files turn unrelated PRs red
body: Found 2026-10-28 while triaging code#1759: its treefmt check failed on nixos/home/laptop-repo-keeper.sh and nixos/home/openclaw-backup.sh — files the PR never touches. The check diffs base...head from the PR merge commit, so any unformatted file that lands on main (or drifts into the sweep) makes unrelated PRs red until someone formats main. Two gaps: (1) nothing format-checks main itself on merge, so unformatted files can land (both files arrived via merged PRs whose own checks evidently did not sweep them); (2) the sweep makes the failure surface on the wrong PR. Fix PR for the two current files: fix/treefmt-keeper-scripts. Longer-term options: run the treefmt check on push to main, and/or scope the PR check to files the PR actually changed relative to its merge-base.

title: laptop-repo-keeper: BUSY check never sees a merge/rebase in progress — rev-parse --git-dir is relative, so the keeper sealed a live merge as a 'snapshot' commit

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: area/nixos

labels.name: work/self-assigned

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Bug: laptop-repo-keeper's BUSY check never sees a merge/rebase in progress — it sealed a live merge as a "snapshot" commit

`nixos/home/laptop-repo-keeper.sh:64-65` (current main, ba51bec3):

```bash
gd="$(g rev-parse --git-dir 2>/dev/null)"
if [ -e "$d/.git/index.lock" ] || [ -e "$gd/MERGE_HEAD" ] || [ -d "$gd/rebase-merge" ] || [ -d "$gd/rebase-apply" ]; then
```

`git -C <repo> rev-parse --git-dir` prints a **relative** path (`.git`), relative to the target repo — but the script tests `$gd/MERGE_HEAD` relative to the **keeper's own cwd**. The systemd user unit (`nixos/home/laptop-repo-keeper.nix`) sets no `WorkingDirectory`, so the keeper runs with cwd `$HOME`, where `$HOME/.git/MERGE_HEAD` essentially never exists. The merge/rebase half of the BUSY guard therefore never fires (the `index.lock` half works because it is correctly prefixed with `$d/`). Symmetrically, if the keeper were ever launched from inside a merging repo, it would skip *every* repo as BUSY.

### Verified reproduction (laptop probe, 2026-10-28)

Probe dir on the laptop: `~/tmp/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-keeper-mergehead/` — a scratch repo put mid-merge (conflict resolved and staged, `MERGE_HEAD` present, `git status` = `M  f.txt`, HEAD = the branch tip), then the keeper run against a fake HOME containing only that repo:

- Before: `MERGE_HEAD=yes`, HEAD subject `main`
- Keeper output: `- merging: committed 1 tracked entries on main` / `- merging: ok (main, worktrees: 1)` — **no BUSY line**
- After: `MERGE_HEAD` **gone**; HEAD is `repo-keeper: snapshot merging 2026-10-28 13:39 CDT` with **two parents** (48ee2fd… + 74a4eeb…) — the keeper's `git add -u && git commit` (keeper script, commit block) *completed and sealed the human's in-progress merge* under a snapshot message. On the next hourly run it would also push that merge commit.

An unresolved-conflict merge is less lucky rather than safer: the same path reports `COMMIT FAILED` instead of `BUSY — skipped`, and a mid-rebase repo is not detected either (`rebase-merge`/`rebase-apply` use the same broken `$gd`).

### Why it matters

The keeper runs hourly, unattended, against *every* primary clone on the laptop, and its documented contract is "a dirty primary … is reported, never forced" / BUSY repos are "skipped". Instead, the one state where an unattended `git add -u && git commit` is most destructive — a half-finished merge or rebase — is exactly the state its guard cannot see. It can finalize merges with a junk message, commit conflict resolutions the owner had not finished reviewing, and push the result.

### Fix direction

Resolve the git dir absolutely, e.g. `gd="$(g rev-parse --absolute-git-dir 2>/dev/null)"` (or test `$d/.git/…` like the index.lock check, handling the `.git`-file/worktree case via the absolute path). Add a regression check: a fixture repo mid-merge (and one mid-rebase) must produce the `BUSY … — skipped` line and leave `MERGE_HEAD` and HEAD untouched.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A repo with `.git/MERGE_HEAD` present is reported `BUSY (lock/merge/rebase in progress) — skipped`; its HEAD, index and `MERGE_HEAD` are byte-identical after the run.
- [ ] Same for a repo with `.git/rebase-merge` (or `rebase-apply`) present.
- [ ] A healthy dirty repo is still snapshotted and a clean repo still reports `ok` (the existing behaviour the probe's control cases rely on).
- [ ] The fix works regardless of the keeper's cwd (test with cwd = another merging repo: healthy repos must NOT be skipped).

Found by new-issue-creator-code-a, 2026-10-28 run. Probe preserved on the laptop at `~/tmp/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-keeper-mergehead/` (keeper2.out + the sealed merge commit in `home/git/merging`).

title: mcpx(adapter): a negative timeout passes Validate and makes every tool call fail instantly — parseDuration accepts -5s, Run's WithTimeout is born expired and reports 'did not finish within -5s'

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

An mcpx adapter spec (or one of its tools) with a **negative** `timeout` — e.g. `"timeout": "-5s"` — passes `Spec.Validate()` cleanly, then makes **every** call of that tool fail instantly with a misleading timeout error, even for a command that finishes in milliseconds.

## Evidence (main `5ac81cae`, `pkgs/mcpx/internal/adapter/adapter.go`, blob `fbd12f85`)

- `adapter.go:148-158` — `parseDuration` returns whatever `time.ParseDuration` accepts; negative durations parse without error.
- `adapter.go:105` and `adapter.go:137-139` — `Spec.Validate()` checks the server and per-tool timeouts only for a parse *error*, so `"-5s"` and `"-1ns"` validate fine. Validation is documented as catching "the kind [of failure] that would otherwise surface as a confusing command line" (`adapter.go:94-97`) — this is exactly that kind, and it slips through.
- `adapter.go:230-234` — `Run` selects the timeout: `timeout, _ := parseDuration(spec.Timeout, 0)`; the server fallback applies only when `timeout == 0`, so a negative tool timeout is used as-is. `context.WithTimeout(ctx, -5s)` returns a context that is **already expired**.
- `adapter.go:237,256-260` — `exec.CommandContext` with the born-expired context fails immediately, `cctx.Err() != nil`, and the caller is told `"<server>.<tool> did not finish within -5s"` — the command never really ran, and the message blames its speed.

## Verification (this run)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-adapter-negtimeout/` (Go 1.26.8, on the laptop per the no-sandbox-builds rule): `parseDuration` copied verbatim from the blob above, plus a mirror of `Run`'s timeout selection / `WithTimeout` / `CommandContext` flow running `echo hi`:

- Control: `timeout=5s` → `out="hi"`, no error.
- Case: `timeout=-5s` → Validate-equivalent check passes (`err=nil`); the run fails instantly with `did not finish within -5s` and empty output.
- Case: tool `timeout=-1ns` with server `timeout=5s` → still fails instantly; the non-zero negative value suppresses the server fallback.

## Why it matters

Adapter specs are user/declaration files. A single typo (`-5s`, or a templated value that goes negative) produces a spec that every static check accepts and that then fails 100% of calls with an error message pointing at the tool's execution time rather than at the config — the hardest kind of misconfiguration to diagnose from the caller's side.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Spec.Validate()` rejects a negative timeout at both the server level and the per-tool level, naming the offending value (and a negative value can no longer reach `Run`).
- [ ] The pinned behaviour for `timeout: "0s"` / `"0"` is stated in a comment or doc at `parseDuration`/`Run`: today `0` at tool level silently means "use the server timeout"; whatever is decided (keep, or reject), a test pins it.
- [ ] Regression tests in `internal/adapter`: negative server timeout refused, negative tool timeout refused, positive timeout still runs a trivial command to completion.
- [ ] Existing `internal/adapter` tests still pass (laptop or CI).

## Scope / triage notes

- Fix site is `pkgs/mcpx/internal/adapter` only. Sibling duration parsers exist elsewhere (e.g. `internal/settings` `KindDuration`, `internal/execsvc`); whether they share the rule is a triage question — do not silently widen this issue to them.
- Not self-solved by the filing lane: the `0`-timeout semantics above are a small contract decision for triage, and the fix should land through the queue with the adapter tests.

title: bin/provider-catalog-sync: --open-pr pushes the current branch — from main it bypasses the PR it exists to create

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

body:
## Finding

`bin/provider-catalog-sync.mjs` (added in PR #1333, the PR-based successor to `bin/sync-models.mjs` for issue #1297) documents its `--open-pr` mode as: commit, push, and open a PR via `gh` — the tool "only ever **adds**, only through a reviewable PR". The implementation does not create a branch and does not check which branch is checked out:

```js
const git = (...a) => execFileSync('git', a, { cwd: repoDir, stdio: 'inherit' });
git('add', '.opencode/opencode.jsonc');
git('commit', '-m', `chore(opencode): catalog sync ${date} — add validated provider models (#1297)`);
git('push');
execFileSync('gh', ['pr', 'create', '--title', `chore(opencode): catalog sync ${date} (#1297)`, '--body-file', bodyFile], { cwd: repoDir, stdio: 'inherit' });
```

(current main, verified 2026-10-28 at main `32ab6b7600`: the `--open-pr` block is unchanged from PR #1333, commit `ae35af44c4`.)

## Why it matters

- Run from a checkout sitting on `main` — the natural state of the laptop checkout this tool is written to run on ("run this on the laptop") — `git push` pushes the catalog commit **directly to origin/main**, bypassing the reviewable-PR guarantee that is the tool's stated reason to exist. `gh pr create` then fails (no branch / nothing to compare), but only *after* the unreviewed change is already on main.
- Run from a brand-new local branch with no upstream, bare `git push` fails ("no upstream branch"), leaving a dangling local commit and no PR — the mode only actually works on an already-tracking non-main branch, which nothing in the tool sets up or documents.

Either way the `--open-pr` path cannot deliver its contract as written.

## Evidence

- PR: #1333 "feat(opencode): provider catalog sync — enumerate, classify, catalog-only PRs (#1297)", commit `ae35af44c4`, file `bin/provider-catalog-sync.mjs` (the `main()` `--open-pr` block; header comment lines stating the PR-only policy).
- Verified still present on current main (`32ab6b7600`, 2026-10-28) via the GitHub contents API: `git('push')` with no branch creation, no current-branch check, and no `--set-upstream` anywhere in the file.
- Deduped: no open or closed issue mentions this; #1297 (the parent epic) is closed and does not cover it.

## Acceptance criteria

- `--open-pr` creates a dedicated branch (e.g. `chore/catalog-sync-<date>`) before committing, or refuses to run when the current branch is the default branch — it must be impossible for the mode to push to `main`.
- The push sets the upstream for the new branch so `gh pr create` succeeds on a first run.
- A test or dry-run path pins the branch behaviour (the existing `bin/provider-catalog-sync.test.mjs` suite is the natural home).
- Header/usage text updated if the invocation contract changes.

Found by the pr-diff-review job reviewing PR #1333's diff.

title: id(local_events): a node with 33+ other authors in its store can never write again — record() builds an after frontier over the 32-hash cap

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

A local node can never record another event once its store holds events from 33 or more other authors. Every `LocalEvents` write — publish, set_tag, clear_tag, document remove — builds the new event's `after` frontier from the head of **every** other author in the store, and the chain layer refuses an `after` with more than 32 hashes. The failure is permanent and total for the node's own writes, and it arrives exactly when a node is well-connected: after syncing with 33+ peers.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `8c8d1bbb`)

- `pkgs/id/src/local_events.rs:343-352` — `other_heads()` returns the head of every author in `frontier()` except the node's own: no cap, no truncation, no selection.
- `pkgs/id/src/local_events.rs:355-378` — `record()` (the single path behind `publish` :171, `set_tag` :198, `clear_tag` :213 and the remove path) passes `other_heads()` straight into `ChainExt { after, .. }` and calls `chain::sign`.
- `pkgs/id/src/chain.rs:33` — `pub const MAX_AFTER: usize = 32;`
- `pkgs/id/src/chain.rs:187-189` — `ChainExt::validate` (run by `sign` before anything is encoded) refuses `after.len() > MAX_AFTER`: "after holds {0} hashes, the most allowed is {max}".
- `pkgs/id/src/event_store/mod.rs:425-438` — `chains()` returns one row per author in the store, so the frontier grows by one per distinct author ever synced; nothing prunes authors.
- Production callers of the blocked path: the web save flow (`pkgs/id/src/web/mod.rs:196` opens `LocalEvents` into `AppState`) and the doc CLI (`pkgs/id/src/commands/doc.rs:36`).

### Reproduction (probe in the real crate, run on the laptop)

Probe test (`tests/probe_lanea.rs` in a laptop worktree at origin/main; `local_events.rs`/`chain.rs` sha256-identical to sandbox main `8c8d1bbb`; probe + full log preserved in the goal bookkeeping, `probe-2026-10-28-laneA-after32/`):

- Control: fresh `LocalEvents`, no other authors → `set_tag` succeeds.
- Seed the same store with one seq-0 `tag.set` from each of 33 distinct other authors via `EventStore::ingest` (what sync leaves behind), reopen as `LocalEvents`:

```text
CTRL 0 other authors: set_tag ok = true
OBSERVED frontier heads = 34
OBSERVED set_tag FAILED: after holds 33 hashes, the most allowed is 32
test result: FAILED. 0 passed; 1 failed (the failure is the bug demonstration: the probe asserts the desired behaviour)
```

## Why it matters

This is the same shape as #1720 (a local operation that becomes permanently impossible once state crosses a cap) but broader: it does not block one tag name, it blocks **all** local writes — publishing documents, setting or clearing tags, removals — for any node whose store has accumulated 33+ authors. That is the normal end state of a node that syncs with a community, i.e. the nodes the system is built for. Reads still work, so the node looks healthy while silently being unable to write ever again; the error names the cap but offers no recovery path.

## Suggested direction (for triage to pin)

The frontier selection is a real design decision, which is why this is filed for triage rather than self-solved — semantics depend on `after`:

- A `tag.clear` only removes claims in its causal past, and causal past is computed from `after` + backlink (`local_events.rs:435-441`, `tag_claims.rs` `causal_past`), so dropping heads at random can silently un-see claims a clear was meant to remove.
- Options for triage to weigh: (a) raise/derive the cap in step with the header decoder's array bound; (b) select a bounded frontier with a documented rule (e.g. the heads the new event actually depends on for its kind — a document publish vs a clear have different needs); (c) compact/forget authors whose heads are already ancestors of others before counting.
- Whatever is chosen, `record()` must not fail solely because the store holds many authors.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] With 33 (and e.g. 100) other authors present in the store, `publish`, `set_tag` and `clear_tag` succeed (regression test at the probe's shape: seed ≥33 foreign authors, then a local write succeeds).
- [ ] A clear recorded with a bounded frontier still removes exactly the claims it names that were live when it was written — the causal-past semantics of clears are preserved (existing tag fold tests pass).
- [ ] Events the node produces still pass `ChainExt::validate` / decode on receipt by other nodes (no wire-format break unless deliberately versioned).
- [ ] The frontier rule is documented at `other_heads`/`record` (what is included, what is dropped, and what that means for clears).
- [ ] Existing id crate tests still pass (laptop or CI).

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues and code search for `MAX_AFTER`, `other_heads`, "after holds", and frontier terms before filing: no filing covers this interaction. #1720 is the sibling cap interaction inside `clear_tag` (claims per clear), not the `after` frontier. #1075 is a broad validation audit epic, not this bug.

title: mcpx(logging): Redact leaks credential fragments — a JWT's signature segment survives, and SESSION=/COOKIE=/PRIVATE= pairs inside MCPX_SCRIPT_ENV and URL userinfo passwords pass through verbatim

labels.name: task/triage

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
# mcpx(logging): Redact leaks credential fragments — a JWT's signature segment survives, and SESSION=/COOKIE=/PRIVATE= pairs inside MCPX_SCRIPT_ENV and URL userinfo passwords pass through verbatim

## Summary

`logging.Redact` (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/logging/trace.go:205-222`) is the only guard between the process's `MCPX_*` environment and the recorded ambient trace context: `gather` (:165-172) records every `MCPX_*` variable as `env.<name> = Redact(k, v)`. `Redact` elides whole values when the *name* matches `sensitiveName` (:176), and otherwise rewrites only the spans `sensitiveValue` (:189-201) matches. Three shapes fall through that second net, all verified against the real function this run:

1. **A JWT loses its first two segments but keeps its signature.** The JWT alternative is `\bey[A-Za-z0-9_-]{10,}\.[A-Za-z0-9_-]{10,}\.` — it ends at the *second* dot, so the match (and its `<elided>` replacement) covers `header.payload.` only. The third segment — the signature, the part that actually authenticates — is outside the match and is recorded verbatim: `Redact("MCPX_ANYTHING", "eyJ….eyJ….SflKxwRJSMeKKF2QT4fwpMeJf36POk6yJVadQssw5c")` returns `"<elided>SflKxwRJSMeKKF2QT4fwpMeJf36POk6yJVadQssw5c"`.
2. **Credential words the name pattern knows are missing from the value pattern.** `sensitiveName` refuses names containing `session[_-]?id`, `cookie`, `signature`, `private`, `auth` — but the KEY=VALUE alternative in `sensitiveValue` recognises only `token|secret|api[_-]?key|password|passwd|credential`. Pairs inside a container variable therefore leak when the container's own name is innocuous: `Redact("MCPX_SCRIPT_ENV", "DEBUG=1 SESSION=abc123def456ghi789")`, `… "COOKIE=sessionid-987654321-abcdef"` and `… "PRIVATE=hunter2hunter2hunter2"` all return their input **unchanged**. This is exactly the container shape the value check was added for (the comment at :182-188: "MCPX_SCRIPT_ENV carries KEY=VALUE pairs… an innocuous name holds a secret as its value") — the keyword lists of the two patterns were simply never reconciled.
3. **A password in a URL authority is invisible to both patterns.** `Redact("MCPX_ENDPOINT", "https://svc-user:hunter2pass@db.internal:8443/x")` returns the URL unchanged: no keyword precedes the `:`, and no known token prefix appears. Endpoint/DSN-style env values are precisely where userinfo passwords live.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 211aa58f)

Line trace, `pkgs/mcpx/internal/logging/trace.go` (sha256 `5de4a050…`, identical on the sandbox clone at 211aa58f and the laptop probe worktree):

- `sensitiveName` (:176): `(token|secret|key|password|passwd|pwd|credential|auth|session[_-]?id|cookie|signature|private)` — applies to the variable *name* only.
- `sensitiveValue` (:189-201): bearer, the KEY=VALUE alternative with the narrower keyword list above, `gh[pousr]_`, `sk-`, `xox[baprs]-`, `AKIA…`, and the JWT alternative ending in `\.` after the second segment.
- `Redact` (:205-222): name match → whole elision; otherwise only matched spans are replaced, keeping the text before the first `:`/`=`/space — unmatched tail text is never touched.

Probe executed on the laptop against the real package (worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-listfind-raw`, probe tests + log in the goal's `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-redact/`; `go test ./internal/logging/ -run TestProbeRedact -v`):

- CTRL: `MCPX_SCRIPT_ENV` `API_TOKEN=…` pair — elided (`leaked=false`); a `ghp_…` token under an innocuous name — elided.
- BUG (case 3): JWT — `leaked=true`; output is `<elided>` + the full signature segment.
- BUG (cases 4-6): `SESSION=`, `COOKIE=`, `PRIVATE=` pairs inside `MCPX_SCRIPT_ENV` — `leaked=true`, values returned verbatim.
- BUG (case 7): URL userinfo password in `MCPX_ENDPOINT` — `leaked=true`, returned verbatim.

The existing `redact_test.go` suite pins the name/value elisions and the partial-match context rule, but has no JWT case, no session/cookie/private pair case, and no URL case.

## Why it matters

The ambient env block exists to be recorded — it lands in trace/log records that are kept, shared for debugging, and read by tooling (and agents) that should never see a credential. A redactor that demonstrably catches `API_TOKEN=` pairs invites trust; the three shapes above break that trust in the directions real environments actually take (a JWT in an env var, a session/cookie pair bundled into `MCPX_SCRIPT_ENV`, a DSN with a password). The JWT case is the sharpest: the output *looks* redacted (`<elided>` prefix) while carrying the one segment that must never be recorded.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A JWT anywhere in a recorded value is elided in full — no segment, including the signature, survives; a regression test pins a three-segment JWT under an innocuous name.
- [ ] The KEY=VALUE value pattern recognises every credential word the name pattern recognises (at minimum `session`, `cookie`, `signature`, `private`, `auth`, `pwd`), so pairs inside container variables such as `MCPX_SCRIPT_ENV` are elided the same way `API_TOKEN=`/`PASSWORD=` pairs already are; regression tests pin SESSION=/COOKIE=/PRIVATE= pairs.
- [ ] A password in a URL authority (`scheme://user:password@host`) is elided while the rest of the URL stays readable; a regression test pins it, and a credential-free URL (the existing `MCPX_ENDPOINT` keep-case) is still kept verbatim.
- [ ] The existing keep-cases still pass: harmless values and harmless pairs (`DEBUG=1`, state dir, endpoint, level) are recorded unchanged, and partial matches keep their surrounding context with a visible `<elided>` marker.
- [ ] `go test ./internal/logging/` passes (laptop/CI).

## Notes

- Filed by the new-issue-creator (lane B) after a laptop-executed probe against the real package; not self-solved — how far to take generic high-entropy value detection (vs. the enumerated shapes above) is a contract pin for queue-lane triage, since over-elision is a pinned failure mode of this function too (`TestRedactKeepsValuesWorthSeeing`).
- Distinct from #1662 (mcpauth credential *expansion* rewriting literal `$` in values) — that is a different package and a correctness bug; this is the logging redactor's coverage.
