body:
## Problem

Laptop SSH has been unreachable from the sandbox since ~2026-10-28 11:16Z and remains down as of 13:1xZ. Every attempt via `~/tools/laptop-ssh.sh` fails with:

```
Connection closed by UNKNOWN port 65535 (rc 255)
```

That byte pattern matches the sshd MaxStartups early-drop signature root-caused on 2026-10-25 (see `~/TOOLS.d/laptop.md`), but it is equally consistent with the laptop being asleep/offline — it cannot be distinguished from the sandbox side, and that ambiguity is part of the problem.

## Impact

Fleet worktrees, edits, builds and tests live on the laptop by hard rule (worker instruction §3; sandbox builds banned 2026-10-27), so this single outage blocks all implementation work in the code queue. Queue tasks parked solely on this outage so far:

- 1777 / PR #1642 (#1637): CI-green, needs a one-file conflict resolution on the laptop
- 1616 (#1483): gate met, implementation not started
- 1824 (#1549): verified brief, implementation not started
- 1852 (#1603): gate met (PR #1608 merged), implementation not started

## Known pending permanent fix

From the 2026-10-25 root-cause: the laptop's NixOS config still needs `services.openssh.settings.MaxStartups = "100:30:300"` + a switch timed when no interactive laptop SSH is in use. The connection-multiplexing interim fix in `laptop-ssh.sh` does not help when no master connection can be established at all.

## Acceptance

- Laptop SSH reachable again from the sandbox via `~/tools/laptop-ssh.sh` (a plain `echo` round-trip succeeds).
- The parked tasks above can be claimed and worked.
- The MaxStartups permanent fix is either applied or explicitly scheduled, so a burst of fleet connections cannot reproduce the drop pattern.

body:
Part of the OpenCode-half redesign (design: `files/opencode-half-redesign-2026-10-28.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace; tracking: #1425). Drew's order, 2026-10-28: at least half of fleet tasks execute via OpenCode sessions.

## Scope

Claim-time execution-lane assignment for the repo queues:

- A per-queue **assignment ledger** stored with the queue (a small table beside `agent.tasks` in muse-dev): queue, task_id, assigned_lane (`opencode` | `direct`), executed_lane (filled at terminal state), fallback_reason, session_id, exclusion_reason, timestamps.
- A new verb in `~/tools/repo-queue.py`: `lane <TASK_ID> --worker <WORKER>` — atomically reads the ledger counts for the task's queue (in-flight + executed per lane), assigns **opencode iff opencode_count ≤ direct_count** (ties to opencode), writes the assignment row, and prints the lane. Safe under concurrent claims from two lanes.
- The terminal verbs (`complete` / `fail`, and `park` resume bookkeeping) record the executed lane back into the ledger row; a `repo-queue.py` helper or the existing result payload carries the execution block (see the measurement issue for the tally consumer).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Two lanes claiming alternately from the same queue receive a deterministic, replayable assignment sequence with ≥50% opencode at every prefix.
- [ ] A task assigned opencode that terminates as direct (fallback) moves its count to the direct side, and the next assignment for that queue is opencode until parity is restored.
- [ ] Ledger rows exist for 100% of tasks claimed after the verb ships; a claim with no ledger row is detectable by the fleet monitor.
- [ ] No change to claim atomicity, leases, or existing verbs' behavior for queues the verb is not invoked on.

title: mcpx: Phase 2 of #1634 — re-issue a broken modern request once (tools/call gated on annotations)

body:
Phase 2 of design #1634 (mcpx client session & stream recovery). Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-client-session-stream-recovery.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Independent of Phase 1 (different era, different trigger) — either may land first.

## Scope

Re-issue a modern (2026-07-28) request once when its response stream breaks — the 2026 spec's client MUST — without ever silently double-executing a tool call.

- Give the stream-lost error a stable, checkable identity. Today `lost()` (`internal/mcpclient/http.go` ~L378-389) synthesises code `-32000` (`codeStreamLost`), which the receive loop's "connection closed" failure shares; matching on message text is not acceptable. A marker in the error's `data` or an equivalent in-package sentinel — triage settles the shape.
- Re-issue at the request layer (`Client.roundTrip`, `internal/mcpclient/client.go` ~L953), so each MRTR `input_required` round is its own request: same method and params, once only, with a NEW request id. No re-issue when the caller's context is done. A second stream-lost surfaces the error.
- `tools/call` gate (decision recorded on #1634, from PM-06's own hazard note): every other method (lists, reads, ping/`server/discover`, completions, prompt gets — reads by protocol nature) is re-issued automatically. `tools/call` is re-issued automatically only when the tool's annotations declare `readOnlyHint` or `idempotentHint`; otherwise the stream-lost error surfaces unchanged and the host decides. Annotations are retained at list time for call time — `Tool.Annotations` (`client.go` ~L159-170) carries them raw, and the client's per-tool `toolHeaders` retention (modern.go) is the precedent.
- Legacy era is excluded: legacy's broken-stream mechanism is resumability (`resume()`, http.go ~L338); when resumption is exhausted the error surfaces, as today.
- Retire conformance gap `streamable-http-client-reissue-broken-request` (`internal/conformance/coverage_transport.go`).

## Evidence (main ed8e5910, 2026-10-28)

- Gap at `internal/conformance/coverage_transport.go:114` (origin dezren39/nix#203): "a broken 2026-07-28 response stream is reported lost to the caller (http.go); nothing re-issues the request with a new id".
- A modern SSE stream ending unanswered calls `t.lost(reqID)` (`internal/mcpclient/http.go` ~L190-205) and the call fails with the synthesised `-32000`.
- PM-06 (`docs/compare/register/process-model.md:133-146`): 2026-07-28 changelog — "clients MUST re-issue it as a new request with a new request ID"; and the register's own risk note — "re-issuing a non-idempotent tool executes it twice; nothing makes the server deduplicate" — which is why the `tools/call` gate exists and why a blanket re-issue was rejected on #1634.

## Acceptance

- Fake modern upstream that kills the response stream: a list call succeeds after exactly one re-issue, and the two attempts carried distinct request ids.
- A `tools/call` against a tool annotated `readOnlyHint` (and one annotated `idempotentHint`) is re-issued once and its result returned.
- A `tools/call` against an unannotated or destructive-annotated tool surfaces the stream-lost error, and the upstream observed exactly one execution.
- A stream that breaks on the re-issue as well → the error surfaces; no third attempt.
- Caller-cancelled context → no re-issue.
- Legacy broken-stream behaviour unchanged (resume path untouched).
- Gap `streamable-http-client-reissue-broken-request` retired; `go test ./...` for pkgs/mcpx passes in CI.

## Out of scope

Legacy session-404 recovery (Phase 1), register truth-up (Phase 3), a configurable re-issue count (open question on #1634 — one is the recorded default), re-issuing server-initiated requests from a dead stream.

body:
Phase 1 of design #1634 (mcpx client session & stream recovery). Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-client-session-stream-recovery.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace.

## Scope

Recover transparently when a legacy HTTP upstream forgets the session (restarts) mid-life: forget the dead session, re-initialize once, retry the request once.

- Trigger, narrowly: a request (never a notification, never `initialize` itself) fails with `HTTPStatusError` 404, the client era is legacy, and the failed request actually carried a session id. Any other 404 behaves exactly as today.
- `internal/mcpclient/http.go`: add a small transport seam the client can interface-assert (the `interface{ setNegotiated(string) }` pattern in `client.go`): atomically report-and-clear the held session id (working name `forgetSession() bool`). The fresh `initialize` must go out with no session id, and no later request may echo the dead one. Stdio transports do not implement the seam; recovery is HTTP-only.
- `internal/mcpclient/client.go`: recovery in the request path (`roundTrip`/`call` layer) reusing the existing `initializeLegacy`/`finishLegacy` unchanged. Re-initialize is singleflight across concurrent calls — a client-level mutex plus a session generation, so N concurrent 404s from one upstream restart produce exactly one `initialize`; calls whose generation was already replaced just retry on the new session.
- Retry the original request exactly once through `roundTrip` (fresh pending entry, new request id). A second 404, or a failed re-initialize, surfaces the error as today. No retry loop.
- After a successful re-initialize, fire the existing catalogue-invalidation signal (`invalidate` path → `Notifications.OnListChanged`) for `tools`, `resources` and `prompts` — a restarted upstream's catalogue is not the cached one. `finishLegacy` already refreshes ServerInfo/Capabilities and restarts the GET listen stream for ≥2025-03-26.
- Modern era is excluded: 2026 has no sessions (TR-30); a modern 404 stays an ordinary error.
- Retire conformance gap `streamable-http-client-reinit-on-404` (`internal/conformance/coverage_transport.go`).

## Evidence (main ed8e5910, 2026-10-28)

- Gap at `internal/conformance/coverage_transport.go:115` (origin dezren39/nix#203): "a 404 for the session is returned as an error; no new initialize".
- `HTTPTransport.Send` (`internal/mcpclient/http.go` ~L166-180) returns any non-2xx as `HTTPStatusError`; the session id is captured at ~L157-160 and echoed by `setHeaders`.
- Register TR-29 (`docs/compare/register/transports.md:550-565`): legacy spec 2025-03-26..2025-11-25 — a client receiving 404 for a session-carrying request MUST start a new session; mcpx @05c78b2 missing; "a restarted remote server leaves its mcpx instance failing every call" (the pool cannot reap an HTTP client that never dies).
- Decision recorded on #1634: recovery lives in the client, not the transport (protocol-free layer) and not the pool (reaping loses the in-flight call).

## Acceptance

- Fake legacy HTTP upstream test: session dropped upstream → the call succeeds after exactly one re-initialize, and the retried request carries the new session id.
- N concurrent calls 404ing from the same restart → exactly one `initialize` observed upstream.
- 404 with no session held (stateless legacy server) → error as today, no `initialize` sent.
- A second 404 after re-initialize → error surfaces; no further re-initialize for that call.
- Modern-era 404 → no recovery attempt.
- Gap `streamable-http-client-reinit-on-404` retired; `go test ./...` for pkgs/mcpx passes in CI.

## Out of scope

Modern broken-stream re-issue (Phase 2), register truth-up (Phase 3), persisting the new session into #1414's store (open question on #1634), notification-triggered lazy re-initialize (open question on #1634).

body:
## Finding

Open PR #1246 — `fix(id): complete integration VM suite` (commit `6c48403f`) — is stranded while its fix is still needed. It has had no update, labels, or agent note since it was opened, and the only failing check on it was a main-branch failure that has since been fixed on main.

## Evidence

- PR #1246, opened 2026-10-27T04:19Z, `updated_at` still 2026-10-27T04:25:36Z at this filing (2026-10-28T09:24Z — ~29 hours untouched), no labels, not draft.
- Its change: `pkgs/id/nix/tests/integration-test.nix` — `globalTimeout` 1200 → 3600 for the full `cli_integration` VM suite, plus `--nocapture --format=terse`. Body: the full suite "still hit the 20-minute global timeout in nightly run 40218257778"; verification of record is "the PR's CI and a manually dispatched full nightly run".
- Still needed: current main `ed8e5910` still has `globalTimeout = 1200; # 20 minutes` at `pkgs/id/nix/tests/integration-test.nix:30` — the suite CI already demonstrated cannot finish in 20 minutes.
- PR state cross-checked via `gh api` this run: `mergeable: true`, `mergeable_state: unstable`. Its check rollup is green except `nix flake check (clippy-lint)` (and the aggregate that includes it) — that clippy failure was the `panic!` in the MisplacedNode test **on main itself**, filed as #1245 and fixed by merged PR #1299, so a rebase/re-run should clear it; the PR's own diff touches no Rust.
- Tracking gap: #896 (the nightly-failure issue this follows up) is closed and #905 is merged; no open issue, label, or queue task tracks #1246's landing. Searches for "1246" / "integration timeout" returned nothing covering it.

## Why it matters

Until this lands, the nightly integration suite keeps terminating at 20 minutes — a long-running world test stays indistinguishable from a deadlock (the PR's own diagnosis), and the fleet's NixOS VM signal stays red/uninformative for the id package.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] PR #1246 is rebased onto current main (or superseded by an equivalent PR) and its checks re-run; the clippy-lint failure from main's #1245 bug is gone.
- [ ] The verification of record the PR body names — a manually dispatched full nightly/integration run at the 60-minute timeout — is dispatched and its result recorded on the PR.
- [ ] The PR is merged (main's `globalTimeout` becomes 3600 with `--nocapture --format=terse`), or closed with a comment naming the superseding change.

Filed by the pr-diff-review job as a PR-consolidation/stale-PR finding on PR #1246; PR #1246 itself is labelled `queue/queued` as the work subject of this finding.

body:
## Finding

PR #1310 split the aggregate `crash-gate` PR check into four parallel checks partitioned **by test-name filter**, and retired the aggregate from the PR gate (it now runs only in the nightly full flake check). The partition is complete today, but it is maintained by enumeration with **no guard**: any future `#[ignore]`d test added to the crash suite will silently run in **none** of the four PR checks, and nothing will fail.

## Evidence

- PR #1310 (commit `859726d5`, merged 2026-10-27) — body claim: "Together they run every test the aggregate runs except the corpus writers (excluded everywhere, as before)."
- Current main `ed8e5910`, `pkgs/id/justfile`:
  - aggregate (nightly only): `crash-gate: cargo test --release --features web --test crash -- --skip write_corpus --include-ignored`
  - `crash-gate-sampled: cargo test … --test crash -- --skip write_corpus` — **no `--include-ignored`**, so it runs zero ignored tests.
  - `crash-gate-sweep` / `crash-gate-control` / `crash-gate-ingest`: each `--include-ignored <one name substring>` (`full_sweep_has_no_failures`, `full_lying_sync_control_produces_failures`, `ingest_survives_every_crash_point`).
- The crash suite's ignored tests on current main are exactly the five the three named splits cover, plus the two corpus writers excluded everywhere by design:
  - `pkgs/id/tests/crash/main.rs:176,191` — `full_sweep_has_no_failures`, `full_lying_sync_control_produces_failures`
  - `pkgs/id/tests/crash/identity.rs:647,668` — same two names
  - `pkgs/id/tests/crash/store.rs:662` — `ingest_survives_every_crash_point`
  - writers: `main.rs:205 write_corpus`, `identity.rs:687 write_corpus_identity`
- `.github/scripts/check-id-pr-checks.sh` (updated by #1310) validates that flake check *names* match the PR check list — it never enumerates test names, so a new ignored crash test passes every guard while losing all PR coverage. The failure mode is silent: the new test would run only in the nightly aggregate, exactly the feedback delay #551 was closing.

## Why it matters

The crash gate is the redb/identity-store crash-safety gate. A heavy test added the documented way (`#[ignore = "… just crash-gate runs it"]`, per `pkgs/id/tests/README.md:42`) after this split gets no PR signal at all, and the justfile comment "together … they cover every test crash-gate runs" becomes false without anyone noticing.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A CI-visible guard exists that fails when an ignored test in the crash suite is not covered by any PR-gate split (e.g. a script/check that lists the crash binary's ignored tests and asserts each name is matched by a split filter or is a deliberately excluded corpus writer).
- [ ] The guard passes on current main (five covered gates + two named writer exclusions).
- [ ] Adding a dummy `#[ignore]`d test to the crash suite makes the guard fail, demonstrating the tripwire.
- [ ] The justfile / check-list comments point at the guard so the next split editor finds it.

Filed by the pr-diff-review job from PR #1310's diff; verified against current main twice (local `git show origin/main` + `gh` searches, 2026-10-28). Deduped: searches for "crash-gate ignored", "crash-gate-sampled", "silently excluded PR gate" returned no covering issue (#551 is closed; #1569 is unrelated flake-source corruption).

title: aggregator: roadmap Horizon dates are never validated — month 13 invents a Q5 lane and an 'undefined 2026' month, month 00 a Q0 lane, and ymdLabel throws on them

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: app/aggregator
labels.description: Package/app: aggregator (pm-stack in this repo)

body:
## Summary

The aggregator's roadmap date parsing accepts impossible calendar dates. `laneFor`'s date regex (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/derive.ts:65`, `DATE = /^(\d{4})-(\d{2})-\d{2}/`) and `rowDate`'s identical regex (`derive.ts:459`, `YMD`) check only the *shape* of a Horizon cell — two digits for the month — never that the month/day exist. A Grist "Program roadmap" Horizon typo such as `2026-13-15` or `2026-00-15` therefore does not fall into the "other / unscheduled" lane the code reserves for unrecognized horizons (`laneFor`, `derive.ts:71-82`); it is treated as a real date and produces nonsense lanes and labels, and one label helper throws on it:

- `laneFor("2026-13-15")` → `{ key: "2026-Q5", label: "Q5 2026", order: 8109 }` — a fifth quarter, sorting exactly where Q1 2027 sorts.
- `laneFor("2026-00-15")` → `{ key: "2026-Q0", label: "Q0 2026", order: 8104 }`.
- `monthTimeline` on a `2026-13-15` row → lane `{ key: "2026-13", label: "undefined 2026" }` — the literal text **"undefined 2026"** is what the month-grain roadmap page renders (`render.ts:1514` calls `timelineTable(monthTimeline(rows), …)`; `monthLabel`, `derive.ts:504-507`, indexes `MONTH_NAMES[m - 1]` unchecked).
- `ymdLabel("2026-13-15")` **throws** `TypeError: undefined is not an object (evaluating 'MONTH_NAMES[d.getUTCMonth()].slice')` (`derive.ts:499-502`) — an invalid `Date` yields `NaN` month/day indexes. Any present or future caller that labels a row-derived date (rather than a generated lane day) crashes on this input.
- `ymdLabel("2026-02-30")` silently relabels the impossible date as **"Mon Mar 2"** (JS Date roll-over), and `roadmapDayGrain` counts a `2026-02-30` / `2026-13-15` row as "dated, outside this window" (`outside = 1, coarse = 0`) instead of as an unparseable/coarse row, so the roadmap's own accounting misstates it.

## Verified (this run, on main be7cf629)

Probe ON THE LAPTOP (Bun 1.4.2, driving the real `derive.ts` — sha256 `312ac0fb…` identical in both clones; probe + log in the goal's `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-horizondate/`, run twice with identical results):

```
CTRL laneFor 2026-10-24: {"key":"2026-Q4","label":"Q4 2026","order":8108}
CTRL laneFor Q1 2027:    {"key":"2027-Q1","label":"Q1 2027","order":8109}
CTRL monthLabel 2026-10: October 2026
CTRL ymdLabel 2026-10-24: Sat Oct 24
BUG laneFor 2026-13-15:  {"key":"2026-Q5","label":"Q5 2026","order":8109}
BUG laneFor 2026-00-15:  {"key":"2026-Q0","label":"Q0 2026","order":8104}
BUG monthLabel 2026-13:  undefined 2026
BUG monthLabel 2026-00:  undefined 2026
BUG rowDate 2026-13-15:  2026-13-15        (accepted as a date)
BUG rowDate 2026-02-30:  2026-02-30        (accepted as a date)
BUG ymdLabel 2026-02-30: Mon Mar 2         (silently a different date)
BUG ymdLabel 2026-13-15: TypeError … MONTH_NAMES[d.getUTCMonth()].slice (throws)
BUG monthTimeline lanes for 2026-13-15: [{"key":"2026-13","label":"undefined 2026","order":24325}]
BUG dayGrain 2026-02-30: outside=1 coarse=0 laned=0
```

Existing tests cover only valid horizons (`test/render.test.ts:127-129`: `Q1 2027`, `2026-10-24`, `Ongoing`).

Reachability: Horizon is a free-text Grist cell, edited by humans and fleet jobs; the roadmap views are rendered from whatever it contains. One mistyped month (`2026-13-…` for a December/January slip, or a `00` from a spreadsheet export) is enough to put a phantom Q5/Q0 lane and an "undefined 2026" heading on the live roadmap, mis-sort the row into a neighbouring quarter, and count it as a real dated row outside the day-grain window.

## Why it matters

The roadmap is the Program view's backbone: quarter/month/day grains all derive from these same helpers, so one bad cell corrupts every grain differently (phantom quarter, undefined month heading, miscounted day window) instead of degrading once, visibly, into the existing "other/coarse" bucket. The helpers' own contract already anticipates unrecognized horizons — `laneFor` sorts "anything else" after every quarter — the date branch simply never validates that its digits form a date, so the fallback never fires for the most likely typo class.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A Horizon whose digits do not form a real calendar date (month `00`/`13`, day `00`, Feb 30, Apr 31, …) is treated as unrecognized: `laneFor` returns the "other" lane for it and `rowDate` returns `null`, so the row lands in the coarse/other bucket in every grain.
- [ ] No roadmap surface can render the literal `undefined` as a lane/month label, and `ymdLabel`/`monthLabel` cannot throw or silently relabel an impossible date (defensive behaviour for direct callers is pinned by a test).
- [ ] Regression tests cover at least: `2026-13-15`, `2026-00-15`, `2026-02-30` through `laneFor`, `rowDate`, `monthTimeline`, and `roadmapDayGrain` (counted coarse, not "outside"), plus the existing valid controls (`2026-10-24` → Q4 2026, a real Feb 29 on a leap year).
- [ ] Existing aggregator test suites still pass.

title: aggregator: OpenCode Go reset dates are paired by section position, not by workspace — one missing or extra 'monthly reset' line shifts both workspaces' resets

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: app/aggregator
labels.description: Package/app: aggregator (pm-stack in this repo)

body:
## Problem

The OpenCode Go quota extractor pairs each workspace with its monthly reset by **global position in the section**, not by the paragraph the reset appears in. One missing or one extra `monthly reset …` line silently shifts both workspaces' reset dates — each pool renders the other's reset, or a stale historical one, with no error anywhere.

`pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-extract.ts`, `goWorkspace` (:152-176):

```ts
// Resets appear in the same paragraph order as the workspaces.
const resets = [...s.matchAll(/monthly reset (\w{3}) (\d{1,2}), (\d{2}:\d{2}) UTC/gi)];
const r = name === "Personal" ? resets[0] : resets[1];
```

Both Go pools share the one `### OpenCode Go` section (`POOL_SPECS`, :276/:284 — the same `sectionOf` text is passed to both extractors). The workspace percentages are matched per-workspace by name, but the resets are collected section-wide and indexed `[0]`/`[1]`. The pairing holds only while every workspace paragraph carries exactly one reset line and nothing else in the section mentions one — and the quota view this parses is a human document that, per this file's own header, "preserves dated observations", so extra dated reset mentions in the section are expected over time.

## Evidence (verified on main be7cf629)

Probe on the laptop driving the **real** `extractQuotaPools` from `quota-extract.ts` (sha256 `29729137…`, identical in both clones; probe + log in the fleet bookkeeping `probe-2026-10-28-laneA-goreset/`, run twice with identical output), `now = 2026-10-28T12:00:00Z`:

- **CTRL** — Personal paragraph with `monthly reset Nov 3, 00:00 UTC`, Lab paragraph with `monthly reset Nov 9, 00:00 UTC` → Personal resetsAt `2026-11-03`, Lab resetsAt `2026-11-09`. Correct.
- **BUG** — Personal paragraph with **no** reset line, Lab paragraph with `monthly reset Nov 9, 00:00 UTC` → Personal resetsAt **`2026-11-09`** (Lab's reset), Lab resetsAt **`null`**. Personal inherits the other workspace's reset; Lab loses its own.
- **BUG2** — a stray historical line `monthly reset Oct 5, 00:00 UTC` earlier in the section, then the CTRL paragraphs → Personal resetsAt **`2026-10-05`** (the stale mention, rendered in the past), Lab resetsAt **`2026-11-03`** (Personal's reset). Both wrong, shifted by one.

`monthDayTime` (:37-45) compounds BUG2: its roll-forward only fires when the date is more than 30 days in the past, so the stale Oct 5 reset is served as a reset date three weeks in the past instead of being recognised as not-this-cycle.

## Why it matters

The quota page is the fleet's spend-steering surface: the Go workspaces carry a rotation order ("burn before Lab per rotation order", :168-170) driven by these windows and their reset dates. A shifted pairing tells the operator Personal resets six days later than it does and that Lab never resets — or, in the BUG2 shape, that Personal's reset already passed. Nothing fails loudly: the extractor is fail-soft by design, so the wrong dates render as authoritative.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each Go workspace's monthly reset is taken from its own paragraph (or an equivalently anchored match — e.g. the reset nearest/following that workspace's own percentage line), never by section-wide index.
- [ ] A workspace paragraph without a reset line yields `resetsAt: null` for that workspace and does not consume another workspace's reset.
- [ ] An extra `monthly reset` mention elsewhere in the section (historical note, prose) does not shift either workspace's reset.
- [ ] Regression tests cover all three shapes: the paired control, the missing-reset paragraph, and the stray-mention section (the probe fixtures in the fleet bookkeeping are directly reusable).
- [ ] Existing aggregator test suites still pass.

title: aggregator: proposal expiry is clocked from the delegation's updatedAt, not the proposal's draft time — a 72h-old proposal stays approvable, a 1h-old one reads expired

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: app/aggregator
labels.description: Package/app: aggregator (pm-stack in this repo)

body:
## Summary

Aggregator proposal expiry (#1293) is clocked from the delegation's `updatedAt`, not from the proposal's own draft time `proposal.at` — the two timestamps the sanitizer validates independently and nothing ties together. A proposal can therefore stay actionable long past the 48 h TTL, and a fresh proposal can read as expired:

- `PROPOSAL_TTL_MS` is documented as the age of the proposal: "A first-pass proposal older than this renders expired (#1293) and the publisher's self-check retires it on the next run" (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/tier-items.ts:46-47`).
- The proposal carries its own draft timestamp: `DelegationProposal.at` (`src/model.ts:532`), validated as ISO by the sanitizer and kept verbatim (`tier-items.ts:168-169`). The delegation state carries a separate `updatedAt` (`tier-items.ts:153-154`), also validated, with no rule that the two agree when `status === "proposal-ready"`.
- But `proposalExpired` (`tier-items.ts:306-310`) computes `Date.parse(d.updatedAt)` — the delegation clock, never `d.proposal.at`.
- Both consumers inherit the wrong clock: the render box (`src/render.ts:1035-1037`) prints "Proposal expired — drafted {proposal.at}" when the function fires, and prints the same drafted date in the live box (`render.ts:1047`) when it does not; the POST boundary (`tier-items.ts:381-382`, in `checkActionAgainstItem`) refuses/accepts approve-proposal and reject-proposal by the same function.

So whenever a publisher re-publishes a carried-forward proposal with a refreshed delegation `updatedAt` (the hourly section is re-published every run), the displayed draft age and the enforced TTL diverge in both directions.

## Verified (this run, on main 9752a47b)

Probe ON THE LAPTOP (Bun, driving the real `tier-items.ts`, sha256 `cdb1fd21…` identical in the sandbox clone and the laptop clone; items built through the real `sanitizeTierItemExtensions`; probe + log in the goal's `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-proposalttl/`):

- CTRL fresh (updatedAt and proposal.at both 1 h old) → `proposalExpired = false` (correct).
- CTRL old (both 72 h old) → `proposalExpired = true` (correct).
- BUG-A: proposal.at 72 h old, updatedAt 1 h old → sanitizer keeps the delegation as `proposal-ready`; `proposalExpired = false`; `checkActionAgainstItem(approve-proposal)` returns `null` — **approval ACCEPTED for a proposal drafted 72 h ago, past the 48 h TTL**. The card would render the live proposal box saying "Drafted 2026-10-25…".
- BUG-B: proposal.at 1 h old, updatedAt 72 h old → `proposalExpired = true`; approve-proposal is refused with "this proposal has expired" — **a 1-hour-old proposal is unactionable**.

Existing tests (`test/needs-user.test.ts`, "proposal identity + expiry (#1293)") only exercise the case where the two timestamps are equal, so the divergence is unpinned.

## Why it matters

The 48 h TTL is the mechanism that stops a stale first-pass proposal from being approved after the world has moved on (#1293: an expired proposal "is no longer actionable", and approval is the one dashboard action that applies a drafted change on the next orchestration pass). Clocking it from a state timestamp that any re-publish can refresh defeats it silently — the UI even displays the true draft date next to the wrong verdict, so the user sees "Drafted 3 days ago" on a box that still offers approval. The reverse direction refuses approval of a fresh proposal and tells the user a fresh first pass will be drafted, confusing the same flow.

Distinct from #1486 (yes/no survey answer validation, a different check in the same file) and from the freshness-family issues #1541/#1564/#1568 (feed/quota `generatedAt`/`measuredAt` gates in other modules; this is the delegation proposal TTL in `tier-items.ts`).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `proposalExpired` measures the proposal's age from `proposal.at` (the draft time the UI displays), or — if triage pins `updatedAt` as the intended clock instead — the TTL comment, the render text, and the proposal identity documentation are updated to say so explicitly, and the redundant-clock divergence is removed or explained.
- [ ] Regression tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/needs-user.test.ts` cover both divergent cases: old proposal.at + fresh updatedAt (expired; approve refused) and fresh proposal.at + old updatedAt (not expired; approve passes the expiry gate), alongside the existing equal-timestamp controls.
- [ ] `checkActionAgainstItem` approve/reject behaviour matches the pinned clock in both cases.
- [ ] Existing aggregator test suites still pass.

title: id(find): remote find fails outright past ~1k matches — server returns all matches unbounded, both clients cap the response at 64 KiB

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

Remote find has a hard ceiling of roughly a thousand matches, after which it fails outright instead of returning results:

- The server's `find` handler (pkgs/id/src/protocol.rs:661-695) collects **every** match — no limit — and the protocol handler writes the whole `MetaResponse::Find` unbounded (protocol.rs:719-724).
- Both hand-rolled remote-find clients read that response with `recv.read_to_end(64 * 1024)`:
  - CLI: pkgs/id/src/commands/find.rs:907 (`cmd_find_matches`, behind `id find` / `search` / `show` / `peek` with `--node`)
  - REPL: pkgs/id/src/commands/repl.rs:706 (`ReplContext::find` in connected/remote mode)
- `read_to_end(max)` errors when the stream exceeds the cap (the same API the unified client documents as "maximum accepted size of a single response" — meta_client.rs:28-29, where the cap is 64 **MiB**). So once the encoded response passes 64 KiB, the whole query errors — no partial results, no truncation notice.

For scale, the sibling whole-namespace call gets far more headroom: `List` responses are read with a 1 MiB cap (commands/list.rs:81,147), and the unified `MetaClient` path used by the tag commands uses `MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES` = 64 MiB (meta_client.rs:28,54). Find is the outlier at 64 KiB despite returning an unbounded, per-match-variable-size list.

Local find/search has no such cap (it iterates the store directly, find.rs local branch), so the same query works locally and fails against a remote node — the failure looks like a connectivity/protocol error, not a size limit.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Postcard sizing probe crate on the laptop (~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-findcap there; probe + log in the goal's hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-findcap/), encoding wire-shape replicas of `FindMatch`/`MetaResponse::Find` (protocol.rs:131-143 — hash as its 32 raw bytes on postcard's non-human-readable path, name string, enum discriminant, bool):

- one match with the repo test's own name (`found.txt`): 45 bytes encoded
- first match count whose encoded response exceeds 64 KiB, by name length:
  - 9-byte names → **1,490 matches**
  - 20-byte names → **1,192 matches**
  - 40-byte names → **874 matches**

(If the real `Hash` encoding carries a length prefix, the thresholds are a few percent lower; the conclusion is unchanged.) Broad queries reach this easily: `match_kind` matches on substring (`Contains`), so a one-letter query — or an empty one, whose match-all behaviour is pinned in lib.rs tests — matches most of a namespace; a remote with ~1k files is unremarkable.

## Why it matters

`find`/`search` are the discovery verbs for remote nodes. A node whose namespace grows past ~1k matching files silently becomes unsearchable from the CLI and the REPL: every broad remote query fails with a raw read error, while local search and `list` (1 MiB) keep working, sending debugging in the wrong direction.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Remote find/search (CLI `cmd_find_matches` and REPL `ReplContext::find`) succeeds against a node returning a `Find` response larger than 64 KiB — the read cap is raised to a named bound consistent with the other meta-protocol clients (1 MiB like `List`, or `MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES` via the unified client), or the response is paged/capped server-side with the client told the result is truncated.
- [ ] If a cap remains anywhere on this path, exceeding it produces an error that says the find response was too large / results were truncated — not a bare transport read error.
- [ ] A test pins the chosen behaviour: a synthetic `Find` response above 64 KiB (or above the new bound) is handled as specified at both call sites, or both call sites share one request helper so they cannot drift again.
- [ ] Local find/search behaviour and result ordering unchanged; small remote responses unchanged.

Related: #1614 covers the remote find *download-path* use of match names (different defect, same command family). The unified `MetaClient` (meta_client.rs) already solves the response-size problem for the tag commands — routing find through it, or sharing its bound, is one natural shape.

title: id(web): AutoSaveManager's generic-error path drops a coalesced follow-up — an edit made during a failed save is never autosaved

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`AutoSaveManager` (pkgs/id/web/src/auto-save.ts, added by PR #1545 for #1440) coalesces a save requested while one is in flight into exactly one follow-up — but only two of its three result paths honour that follow-up:

- **ok** (`onSaveResult`, auto-save.ts:161-169): runs the follow-up via `triggerSave()`.
- **rate-limited** (auto-save.ts:180-191): schedules a retry that "also serves as the follow-up for any edits that arrived during the failed save".
- **generic error** (auto-save.ts:192-206): sets state `error`, reverts to `unsaved` after 2s — and never acts on `followUpRequested`, and never clears it. No debounce, retry, or follow-up is pending at that point (the during-flight edit's debounce already fired and was consumed by the in-flight `triggerSave` at auto-save.ts:124-128), so **autosave silently stops for that edit**: the document sits at `save •` until the user happens to edit again or saves manually.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Probe driving the real `auto-save.ts` on the laptop (~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-autosave there; file sha256 ba898143929b3192ebc4f4b236a5c8d6fe09569aee83df715fc9e6fa6fab01a9, byte-identical to main b2adaf47; probe + log in the goal's hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-autosave/), run twice with identical results. Per case: edit → debounce fires → save #1 in flight; second edit during the flight; its debounce also fires during the flight (follow-up coalesced); then save #1 settles:

- `CTRL-OK`: calls after settle = **2** (follow-up ran), state saved/idle
- `CTRL-429` (`retryAfterMs: 100`): calls after settle = **2** (retry ran), state saved/idle
- `BUG-ERROR` (`{ok: false}`): calls after settle = **1**, and still **1** after a further 3s wait; state = `unsaved` — the during-flight edit is stranded, no save is scheduled

Relevant code: coalescing at auto-save.ts:124-135 (`followUpRequested = true; return`), ok-branch follow-up at :162-168, retry-branch follow-up at :180-191, error branch at :192-206 (no follow-up, flag left set). A throwing `saveFn` lands in the same branch (auto-save.ts:151-155).

Note the stranded case is specifically when the follow-up was *already consumed* before the failure: an edit whose debounce is still pending when the error lands does get saved when that debounce fires. The test suite from #1440 (auto-save.test.ts) covers the ok and 429 follow-up shapes but has no generic-error case.

## Why it matters

Autosave's contract after #1440 is "a save completion only marks the document saved when it covers the latest edit, and requested saves are never lost". The generic-error path breaks the second half silently: a transient failure (network blip, 500) during a save eats the next edit's autosave, and the only signal is the button reverting to `save •` — indistinguishable from "waiting for the debounce". The user can close the tab believing the 2s autosave had long since fired.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Pin the generic-error follow-up semantics in a test first: an edit that arrives during a save whose debounce fires before that save fails generically must not be stranded — it gets exactly one subsequent save attempt (a follow-up, or a re-armed debounce), OR the manager documents and tests a deliberate no-auto-retry pin in which the follow-up request is visibly dropped (flag cleared, state/behaviour intentional).
- [ ] If a follow-up is implemented: it is bounded (one attempt; a second generic failure stops again — no retry loop on a persistent outage), and `followUpRequested` is cleared on every `onSaveResult` path.
- [ ] New test in auto-save.test.ts mirroring the existing ok/429 serialization tests for the generic-error shape (deferred saveFn, edit + debounce during flight, resolve `{ok: false}`, assert the follow-up/strand behaviour pinned above).
- [ ] Existing auto-save tests (serialization, stale-completion, 429 coalescing, saveNow) still pass.

Related: #1440 (closed by PR #1545 — this is the one result path its serialization work did not cover). Not a duplicate of #1368 (collab reconnect cap — different module/mechanism).

title: id(find/search): a remote node's match name becomes the download path verbatim — ../ and absolute names overwrite arbitrary files

labels.name: kind/security
labels.description: Security issue or security hardening

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

`id find` (and `id search`) use the `name` of a find match **verbatim as the download path**. When the search targets a remote node, that name comes straight from the node's `MetaResponse::Find` — postcard-decoded with no validation — and the same node also supplies the blob content that gets written there. A malicious or compromised node can therefore make a client's `id find <NODE> <query>` overwrite arbitrary files the user can write: a match named `/home/user/.bashrc` (single-match mode uses the name as the whole output path), or `../victim.txt` (both single-match and `--all --dir` modes), is written with attacker-chosen content, truncating whatever was there.

Same defect family as CLOSED #1595 (a file name reaching a filesystem path with no working containment check), in the download path instead of the compile staging path.

## The chain (all on main `63ba1705`)

1. **Names arrive unchecked.** `cmd_find_matches` deserializes `MetaResponse::Find { matches }` from the remote node and returns them as-is (`pkgs/id/src/commands/find.rs:901-913`). `FindMatch.name` is a plain `String` (`pkgs/id/src/protocol.rs:131-143`). A hostile server need not run this codebase at all — the response is just postcard.
2. **Names become paths, four sites:**
   - `cmd_find` single/first-match: `let output = if to_stdout { "-" } else { &m.name }` (`find.rs:268` and `:280`) — the name IS the path, so absolute names land anywhere.
   - `cmd_find --all --dir`: `let output_path = format!("{}/{}", dir_path, m.name)` (`find.rs:237`) — `..` segments escape the requested directory.
   - `cmd_search --all --dir`: the same construction (`find.rs:369`).
   All four pass the path to `cmd_get_one_remote` / `cmd_get_one`, which fetch the blob (from the same remote node in the remote case) and export it.
3. **The write performs no containment.** `export_blob` (`pkgs/id/src/lib.rs:546-563`) passes the path through `to_absolute` (`lib.rs:357-363` — prepends the cwd if relative, no normalization of `..`, absolute paths pass through unchanged) into iroh-blobs `Store::export` (ExportMode::Copy), which creates-or-truncates the target (`File::create` / reflink-or-copy, iroh-blobs 0.103 `src/store/fs.rs:1272,1277`). Existing files are overwritten silently.
4. **Honest nodes can hold such names too.** Nothing stops a served store from containing a traversal name: blob rename validation (`fileops.rs:141-151` `validate_target`) checks only that the target is non-empty and different — `../../x` is an acceptable rename target today. So the exposure is not limited to hand-crafted protocol responses.

Contrast: `cmd_peek` fetches the same matches into a `NamedTempFile` instead (`find.rs:620-631`) — the safe shape already exists in this file.

## Verification (this run)

Verbatim-logic probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-findpath`; `find.rs` sha256 `5c6cb299…`, `lib.rs` `af81794b…` — identical in the sandbox and laptop clones; probe + log in goal bookkeeping `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-findpath/`, confirmed by two independent runs). The probe copies the `find.rs:237` and `find.rs:268` path constructions and `lib.rs`'s `to_absolute` character-for-character, and writes with `export`'s create-or-truncate semantics:

- `--dir` mode, name `../victim.txt`: writes `downloads/../victim.txt` — a pre-existing file **outside** the download dir is overwritten with the blob bytes.
- Single-match mode, name = an absolute path: the pre-existing file at that path is overwritten.
- Single-match mode, name `../victim2.txt` from a subdirectory cwd: the file one level up is overwritten.
- Control, name `plain.txt`: written inside the download dir as intended.

## Why it matters

`id find <NODE> query` is the documented way to pull a file from a peer ("Find and output first match", `find.rs` doc examples) — the victim does nothing unusual, names no output file, and may not even know the match's name is hostile, because find matches by query against the server's store. The overwrite target and content are both attacker-controlled, bounded only by the victim's filesystem permissions (dotfiles, SSH keys, project files are all in reach). The local-store variant also matters: any flow that lands a traversal name in a store (rename accepts one today) turns a later local `find` into the same escape.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A find/search match name can never cause a write outside the location the user asked for: in single/first-match mode the effective path is confined to the current directory tree the user invoked from (or the match is refused with a named error), and in `--all --dir` mode every write stays inside the given directory after path normalization — covering `..`, nested `a/../../b`, and absolute names at all four sites (`find.rs:237`, `:268`, `:280`, `:369`).
- [ ] Existing files outside the permitted location are never truncated by a find/search download; the probe cases above are pinned as tests (unit tests at the path-construction/sanitizing helper are enough — no network needed).
- [ ] The ruling for names that are not a single safe segment is stated in the PR: refuse, take the final component, or sanitize — including what happens to legitimate names containing `/` if any supported flow creates them (rename currently accepts them; if the ruling breaks those, that consequence is called out and rename-side validation is addressed or filed separately).
- [ ] Ordinary names (plain basenames, spaces, Unicode) download exactly as today in all modes, local and remote.

title: id(fileops): archive tags collide within one second — a second replace of the same name silently overwrites the first replace's archive

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`FileOps::rename` and `FileOps::copy` archive a file they replace under the name `<name>.archive.<unix-ts>`, where the timestamp has **one-second resolution** and the archive write is an unconditional tag `set`. Two replaces of the same destination within the same second produce the **same archive name**, so the second archive silently overwrites the first — the first replaced version loses its only archive reference (and, once its tag is gone, its protection from blob garbage collection). The web save path has the identical pattern in `archive_original_tag`.

## Evidence (verified on main 63ba1705)

- `pkgs/id/src/fileops.rs:153-162` — `archive_existing`: `let archive = format!("{name}.archive.{ts}"); store.tags().set(&archive, existing.hash)` — no existence check, no uniquifier; `set` replaces an existing tag (the same replace semantics `put`/`rename` rely on for the destination name itself).
- `pkgs/id/src/fileops.rs:238` (rename) and `:319` (copy) — `let ts = now_unix();` taken once per call; `pkgs/id/src/tags.rs:1735-1740` — `now_unix()` is `duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH).as_secs()`, i.e. second resolution.
- `pkgs/id/src/fileops.rs:248` — the rename-original archive uses the same `{from}.archive.{ts}` shape.
- `pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs:2170-2176` — sibling: `archive_original_tag` builds `format!("{name}.archive.{timestamp}")` with `as_secs()` and `store.tags().set(...)` — the web document-save path, where successive saves in one second are routine.
- `pkgs/id/src/fileops.rs:388-410` — `delete` enumerates archives by exactly this `<name>.archive.<digits>` pattern, so an overwritten archive is not merely mislabelled: from the store's point of view it never existed.

Verification: verbatim-logic probe crate run ON THE LAPTOP (probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-archive` there; `fileops.rs` sha256 d1e49762 and `routes.rs` sha256 2667e857 identical in the sandbox clone at main 63ba1705 and the laptop clone; probe models `tags().set` with its documented replace semantics):

```
BUG arch1=Some("b.md.archive.1730000000") arch2=Some("b.md.archive.1730000000")
BUG archive_tag_value=Some("HASH_A") (V1 archive survives? false)
BUG archive_count=1 tags={"b.md.archive.1730000000": "HASH_A", "b.md": "HASH_C"}
CTRL archive_count=2 v1_kept=true a_kept=true
```

Two replaces of `b.md` in the same second (V1 → A → C) leave **one** archive, pointing at A; V1's archive is gone. The same two replaces one second apart (control) leave two archives and both versions survive.

## Why it matters

The archive is the safety net the module doc promises: "rename and copy archive a file they replace" (`fileops.rs:14-18`). Scripted/bulk renames, REPL loops, test suites, and rapid web saves routinely replace the same name twice in one second — exactly the bursts where an operator most needs the earlier version back. The loss is silent: both operations report success, each returns an `archived_replaced` name, and the two names are identical strings, so even the `archive.replace` metadata tag cannot reveal that one archive replaced the other. Related but distinct from #1549 (web image-upload naming collision) and #1605 (mcpx exec artifact overwrite): this is the blob-tag archive namespace in `FileOps` plus its `routes.rs` sibling.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Archiving a replaced file never overwrites an existing archive: if `<name>.archive.<ts>` is taken, a distinct archive name is chosen (e.g. a suffix/counter) while staying inside the `<name>.archive.<...>` enumeration shape `delete` and `classify_tag` understand — or the enumeration/classification is updated in the same change.
- [ ] The same fix (or a shared helper) covers `archive_original_tag` in `web/routes.rs`, so the save path cannot collide either.
- [ ] Unit/integration tests: two replaces of the same destination with the same timestamp produce two distinct archives holding the two distinct hashes; the returned `archived_replaced`/`archived_original` names are the names actually written.
- [ ] Existing rename/copy/delete archive tests still pass; single-replace behaviour and archive naming for the common case are unchanged.

title: id(claim/doc/group): plain-text output renders names/values raw — a newline in a tag name or value forges extra rows and duplicate author=/event= fields

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The plain-text (non-`--json`) output of `id claim`, `id doc` and `id group` renders field values **raw** into a one-line `key=value key=value …` format, while the values it prints are only validated for byte length and NFC — spaces, tabs and **newlines** all pass. A tag name or value containing a newline therefore breaks the one-line-per-row contract and can forge an entire extra row (with attacker-chosen `subject=` / `author=` / `event=` fields) in `id claim list` / `search` and `id doc` output; spaces and tabs silently make rows ambiguous for any consumer splitting on whitespace.

Claims in the store are signed events that arrive through the same ingest path sync uses, so the crafted name/value does not have to be typed by the person reading the output.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `63ba1705`)

- Rendering: `tokens()` in `pkgs/id/src/commands/group.rs:63-71` joins `format!("{key}={}", text(value))` with single spaces, and `text()` (`group.rs:54-60`, doc: "strings without quotes, anything else as JSON") returns strings verbatim — no quoting, escaping or sanitisation. All three command families print through it: claims via `doc.rs:46,57` (`print_action`/`print_rows`, shared with doc), `commands/doc.rs:46,57`, `commands/group.rs:108,268,338`.
- Field order gives the forgery leverage: `claim_fields` (`commands/claim.rs:37-48`) prints `subject, name, [value], author, event` — the value sits **before** the real `author=`/`event=`, so a first-match parser reads the forged ones.
- Validation admits the payload: `check_op`/`check_text` (`pkgs/id/src/tag_claims.rs:118-157`) check only byte length (`name` 1..=128, `value` 0..=512, `tag_claims.rs:40,43`) and `is_nfc`. Space, tab, CR and LF are all NFC-stable. `documents.rs:105-119` applies the same length+NFC-only check to `media_type`, which `id doc publish`/`history` also prints through `tokens()`.
- Probe (verbatim `check_text` + `text`/`tokens` + the `claim_fields` order, run on the laptop; `tag_claims.rs` sha256 `f698d7a6…`, `commands/group.rs` `94bb7f20…`, `commands/claim.rs` `7df730c3…` identical on both clones; probe + log in the fleet's `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-cliout/`):
  - Control `value="plans"` → passes, one line.
  - `value="hello world"` and `name="my topic"` → pass; rendered row contains bare tokens (`world`, `topic`) with no `key=`, so whitespace-splitting consumers misparse.
  - `value="x\nsubject=deadbeef name=forged author=deadbeef event=deadbeef"` → **passes both checks**; the single claim renders as **2 lines**, the second a fully-formed forged claim row.
  - `name="a\nauthor=deadbeef"` → passes; renders as 2 lines with a forged `author=` starting the second line.
  - `value="a\tb"` → passes; raw tab in the row.

## Why it matters

These commands' plain output is the documented machine-adjacent format (`commands/claim.rs` module doc: "`list` and `search` print one line per live claim, `subject= name= [value=] author= event=`") — the fleet's own scripts and operators read it. A peer-authored claim with a newline value can plant a phantom row naming a different author/event in another node's listing, which is exactly the kind of output forgery the rest of this codebase guards against (cf. the web UI's textContent-only rendering of untrusted names, #1457). The `--json` form is unaffected (serde escapes correctly), which makes the plain form the odd one out.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Plain-text rows from `id claim list/search`, `id doc publish/events/history/frontier` and `id group` output are always **one physical line per row**, whatever bytes a name, value, media type, group name/description or reason field contains.
- [ ] A whitespace-splitting consumer can recover every field unambiguously: values containing spaces/tabs/newlines are quoted/escaped (or such values are refused at validation with a named error) — the chosen rule is pinned by tests and stated in the commands' module docs.
- [ ] A crafted claim with a newline-bearing name/value (probe cases above) can no longer produce a second line or a duplicate `author=`/`event=` token in plain output.
- [ ] `--json` output is byte-for-byte unchanged, and ordinary space-free values render exactly as today (no gratuitous quoting of the common case, or the change is documented as intentional).
- [ ] Tests pin the rule at the renderer (`tokens()`/print helpers) and, if refusal is chosen, at `check_text`/`DocumentRef::check` as well.

Triage note: quoting/escaping vs refusing control characters is a small contract pin for the queue lane — refusal alone would change what tags peers may set (sync-ingested events already in stores could hold such values), so the renderer-side fix is likely the load-bearing half either way.

title: id(tuple): decode accepts negative ints that wrap to zero/positive and NaN floats — the negative branch has no range check, unlike the positive branch

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/id/src/tuple.rs` `decode` / `decode_one` (380, 393) accepts integer and float encodings that the encoder can never produce and that the positive-int branch explicitly refuses — so a crafted or corrupted tuple key decodes to a *different* value than its tag claims, silently.

Verified this run by replicating the decoder's exact arithmetic (no code compiled on the sandbox):

### 1. Negative ints have no range check — they wrap to zero or positive

Positive branch (tuple.rs:446-461) checks the payload:

```rust
ensure!(i64::try_from(v).is_ok(), "positive integer exceeds i64::MAX");
```

Negative branch (tuple.rs:464-478) has no equivalent check on `abs` before `0u64.wrapping_sub(abs) as i64`:

- tag `0x13` (1-byte negative), payload `0xFF` → ones-complement `abs = 0` → decodes to `Int(0)` — zero via a negative tag (canonical zero is the single `0x14` tag).
- tag `0x0C` (8-byte negative), payload `0x00 × 8` → `abs = u64::MAX` → `0 - abs` wraps → decodes to `Int(1)` — a *positive* value from a negative tag, at the negative end of the sort order.
- tag `0x0C`, payload `0x7F 0x00…` → `abs = 9295429630892703743` (> 2^63) → decodes to `Int(9151314442816847873)`, again positive.

The encoder (`push_int`, tuple.rs:~335-350) can only emit `abs` in `1..=2^63` for values `i64::MIN..=-1`.

### 2. Floats decode to NaN, which the encoder refuses

Encoder `float()` (tuple.rs:260-264) rejects NaN ("NaN cannot be encoded in tuple keys"; `TupleValue::Float` is documented "NaN excluded"). The `FLOAT64` decode branch (tuple.rs:482-499) reverses the sort transform and returns `f64::from_be_bytes(b)` with no `is_nan` check — e.g. payload `21 FF F8 00 00 00 00 00 00` decodes to `Float(NaN)`.

### 3. Non-minimal int encodings are accepted

Both int branches accept leading-zero payloads the encoder's `byte_len` minimal encoding never emits — e.g. tag `0x16` (2-byte positive) payload `00 01` decodes to `Int(1)`, whose canonical encoding is `0x15 01`. Two distinct keys therefore decode to the same value.

## Why it matters

Tuple keys are the sort-preserving keys for the tag store: `tags.rs` `decode_alpha_key` / `decode_omega_key` (tags.rs:585, 609) run `decode` over keys read back from the namespace documents and trust the decoded subject/key/value. A key that decodes to a value outside its tag's range breaks the encoding's core invariant — byte order preserves semantic order (module doc, tuple.rs:1-25) — and does so silently: the positive branch proves the authors intended out-of-range payloads to be an error, the negative branch just misses it. This is the same asymmetry class as the store's other canonical-decoding rules (e.g. `chain.rs` refuses non-canonical encodings outright).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Decoding a negative-int payload with `abs == 0` or `abs > 2^63` returns an error (mirroring the positive branch's range check), with unit tests for `abs == 0`, `abs == 2^63` (valid, `i64::MIN`), `abs == 2^63 + 1`, and `abs == u64::MAX`.
- [ ] Decoding a float payload that reverses to NaN returns an error, with a unit test using a crafted NaN payload.
- [ ] Non-minimal int encodings (a payload whose first byte makes a shorter encoding possible) are either refused with tests, or explicitly documented as accepted — one behaviour, pinned.
- [ ] All existing tuple round-trip and sort-order tests still pass; no encoder change (encodings on disk/in documents are unchanged).

title: id(tags): parse_search_query only separates terms on ASCII space — tab/newline/NBSP fuse terms into one unmatchable term

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`parse_search_query` (pkgs/id/src/tags.rs:1466) separates search terms only on the ASCII space byte. A tab, newline, CRLF or non-breaking space between terms fuses them into a single bogus term, so a multi-term tag search silently returns the wrong (usually empty) result instead of the AND of its terms.

The separator checks are byte comparisons against `b' '`:

- tags.rs:1478 — the skip-separators loop: `bytes[i] == b' '`
- tags.rs:1492 — the term-end check: `bytes[i] == b' ' && !in_quotes`

Every other splitter in this codebase treats general whitespace as the separator (`split_whitespace` in directory_view.rs / repl, `char::is_whitespace` in directory_view::split_first). This parser is the outlier.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Verbatim probe crate on the laptop (functions copied unchanged from tags.rs at main 63ba1705; tags.rs sha256 c08d87fd identical on sandbox and laptop clones; probe + log in the fleet's hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-searchws/):

Controls — all correct:
- `name:foo bar:baz` → `[KeyValue("name","foo"), KeyValue("bar","baz")]`
- `"hello world" name:foo` → `[Literal("hello world"), KeyValue("name","foo")]`
- `"a<TAB>b" name:foo` → `[Literal("a\tb"), KeyValue("name","foo")]` — a tab *inside quotes* correctly stays part of the literal

Bug cases — terms fuse:
- `name:foo<TAB>bar:baz` → `[KeyValue("name", "foo\tbar:baz")]` — one term whose value can never equal a stored tag value
- `hello<TAB>world` → `[BareWord("hello\tworld")]`
- `name:foo<LF>bar:baz` and `name:foo<CRLF>bar:baz` → same fusion with `\n` / `\r\n` in the value
- `hello<NBSP>world` → `[BareWord("hello\u{a0}world")]`
- `name:<TAB>priority` → `[KeyValue("name", "\tpriority")]` instead of the space form's `[KeyOnly("name"), BareWord("priority")]` (the space behaviour is pinned by the existing test at tags.rs:~2479, `test_parse_search_multiple_terms`)

Consequence at the call site: `search_by_query` (tags.rs:1304) runs `find_by_key_value` / contains-matching with the fused value/word, which matches no stored tag, and the AND intersection then yields an empty result set — the search reports "no matches" for tags that exist.

Reachability: the HTTP search endpoint `GET /api/tags/search?q=` (web/tags_ws.rs:434-448) and the meta protocol `SearchTags` request (protocol.rs:629) pass the raw query string straight to `search_by_query`. A query pasted from a terminal, spreadsheet or document routinely carries tabs or newlines between terms. (The CLI/REPL paths join argv tokens with single spaces at commands/tag.rs:199 and repl/runner.rs:398, so they do not produce these separators themselves.)

## Why it matters

Tag search is the structured query surface for the whole namespace. A pasted query failing silently — empty results, no error, no hint that the separator was the problem — reads as "these tags don't exist" and sends the user debugging their data instead of their query string.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Term separation in `parse_search_query` recognises general whitespace (at minimum tab, LF, CR and NBSP — i.e. `char::is_whitespace` semantics), not only ASCII space, both when skipping separators and when ending a term.
- [ ] Whitespace inside a quoted section remains part of that term (the `"a<TAB>b"` control above still parses as one Literal).
- [ ] New unit tests next to the existing parser tests pin: tab-, newline- and CRLF-separated key:value terms, a tab-separated bare-word pair, and `name:<TAB>priority` matching the space form.
- [ ] All pre-existing `parse_search_query` tests pass unchanged.

body:
Phase 2 of design #1601 (mcpx client cache hints). **Gated on Phase 1** (the pool deadline/scope plumbing). Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-client-cache-hints.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace.

## Scope

Make `cacheScope` real at the disk boundary and define stale behaviour on refresh failure.

- Plumb the pool's catalogue scope/deadline through `SetSchemas` so the daemon registry can seed and save them.
- `internal/daemon/registry.go`: `SaveCache` skips pools whose catalogue scope is `private` — a private catalogue is never written to the on-disk schema cache. Cache-file entries record deadline + scope; bump `cacheVersion` (older files are already ignored on mismatch).
- `loadCache`: a public entry whose deadline has passed is seeded *expired* — the first `Schemas()` re-reads instead of serving a days-old catalogue as warm.
- Pool: when an expired modern entry's refresh fails, `Schemas()` serves the stale entry and records the error; the entry stays expired so the next call retries. A failed *first* fetch is unchanged (error, timestamp unset — per `RefreshSchemas`' existing discipline).
- Retire conformance gap `caching-private-no-cross-auth` (`internal/conformance/coverage_stateful.go`).

## Evidence (main 33a4e674, 2026-10-28)

- `Registry.loadCache`/`SaveCache` (`internal/daemon/registry.go` ~L249-285) persist and re-seed every catalogue; no TTL is applied to `FetchedAt`, no scope is recorded.
- Spec (register PG-10): `private` = reuse only within the same authorization context; MUST NOT be shared across contexts. A restarted daemon cannot prove its callers are the same context — hence never persist (decision recorded on #1601).

## Acceptance

- Test: a private-scoped catalogue is absent from the saved cache file; a public one is present with deadline + scope.
- Test: a public entry past its deadline at load is re-read on first `Schemas()`, not served as fresh.
- Test: expired entry + failing upstream → stale catalogue served, error recorded, next call retries the refresh.
- Test: failed first fetch still errors and leaves the cache unset.
- `caching-private-no-cross-auth` retired; pkgs/mcpx tests pass in CI.

## Out of scope

Register truth-up and the list_changed verification test (Phase 3); background revalidation (declined on #1601 — synchronous refresh is the recorded decision).

Phase 1 of design #1601 (mcpx client cache hints). Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-client-cache-hints.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace.

## Scope

Surface upstream `ttlMs`/`cacheScope` in the client and make the pool's catalogue cache expire for modern upstreams.

- `internal/mcpclient`: add `ttlMs`/`cacheScope` to `toolsListResult`, `resourcesListResult`, `resourceTemplatesListResult`, `promptsListResult`. title: id(world-doctor): journal check passes version 0 and a blank-line headerless journal, and fails a blank-line valid journal — first-entry test uses the raw line index, version range has no lower bound

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

`id world doctor`'s journal check (`validate_journal_file`, `pkgs/id/src/world_doctor.rs:361-395`) disagrees with the code that actually opens a journal in three ways, so doctor both clears journals the world refuses to open and condemns journals the world opens fine:

1. **Version 0 passes.** The check ensures only `version <= MAX_JOURNAL_VERSION` (`world_doctor.rs:382-385`). The real header check in `WorldCore::restore` requires `JOURNAL_VERSION..=MAX_JOURNAL_VERSION` (1..=2) (`pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs:152`). A journal headed `{"entry":"created","world_id":"w","version":0}` is reported by doctor as `1 entries, format version 0` / Ok, but restore refuses it: `unsupported world journal version 0`.
2. **A leading blank line makes a valid journal fail.** Doctor matches on the raw split-line `index` (`world_doctor.rs:368,377-381`), but skips empty lines with `continue` without adjusting that index, so a journal beginning with one blank line reports `entry 2 is Created, but it is not the first entry`. The real reader (`read_journal_entries`, `pkgs/id/src/world_store.rs:452-465`) skips empty lines before parsing, and restore sees `Created` as the first entry and opens it.
3. **The same blank line makes a headerless journal pass.** With a leading blank line, a first real entry that is not `Created` is at `index == 1`, so the `_ if index == 0` bail (`world_doctor.rs:387-389`) never fires, `version` stays `None`, and the function returns `Ok((1, JOURNAL_VERSION))` via the `unwrap_or` at `:394`. Restore refuses the same bytes: `world journal does not start with a header`.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Probe crate on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-doctor` there; `world_doctor.rs` sha256 `72559955a81526838c8266a65fbdea1c6b6fcc39d1d1e11625ebfc748aa61848` identical on the laptop clone and the sandbox clone; probe copies the `validate_journal_file` logic verbatim against a minimal `JournalEntry` shim and the restore header checks verbatim from `world/core.rs` + `world_store.rs`):

```
CTRL v1:                doctor=Ok((1, 1))  restore=Ok(())
V0 version0:            doctor=Ok((1, 0))  restore=Err("unsupported world journal version 0")
V3 future:              doctor=Err("journal format version 3 is newer than this binary supports (2)")  restore=Err("unsupported world journal version 3")
BLANK+Created v1:       doctor=Err("entry 2 is `Created`, but it is not the first entry")  restore=Ok(())
BLANK+headerless:       doctor=Ok((1, 1))  restore=Err("world journal does not start with a header")
CTRL headerless no blank: doctor=Err("the first entry is not `Created`")  restore=Err(...)
```

Controls behave: a normal v1 journal passes both, and a v3 (future) journal is refused by both — the validator is alive; its first-entry test uses the wrong counter and its version range is missing the lower bound.

## Why it matters

Doctor is the tool a user is told to run when a world will not open ("restore the journal from a backup, or recreate the world" is its own fix text). A check that says Ok for a journal restore will refuse — and Fail for one restore accepts — sends that user to recreate or restore over a working world, or to trust a broken one. Doctor's whole contract is that its verdict matches the opener's.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validate_journal_file` refuses a `Created` header with version 0 (lower bound `JOURNAL_VERSION`), matching `WorldCore::restore`'s `1..=MAX_JOURNAL_VERSION` range; versions 1 and 2 still pass, 3 still fails.
- First-entry checks are made against the first *parsed* entry, not the raw line index: a journal with leading/interior blank lines and a `Created` first entry validates; a journal whose first parsed entry is not `Created` is refused regardless of blank lines.
- Malformed-entry error messages may keep the raw line number (that is the useful diagnostic there).
- New unit tests in `world_doctor.rs` pin all three cases (version 0, blank-line + Created, blank-line + headerless) alongside the existing journal test; existing doctor tests still pass.
