body:
## Problem

`sanitize_file_name` in `pkgs/id/src/world_compile.rs:505-511` is the guard that is supposed to keep a compile request's file names inside the per-compile job directory at the staging write (`world_compile.rs:222`, `job.path().join(sanitize_file_name(name)?)` followed by `tokio::fs::write`). Its check can never fire:

```rust
fn sanitize_file_name(name: &str) -> Result<String> {
    ensure!(
        name.split('.').all(|part| part != "." && part != ".."),
        "file name {name:?} must stay inside the job directory"
    );
    Ok(name.to_owned())
}
```

`split('.')` yields maximal runs of non-dot characters, so no part can ever equal `"."` or `".."` (both contain a dot). Every input passes, including `".."`, `"../evil.roc"`, and `"/etc/passwd"`. The function returns every name unchanged and has no test.

Containment today rests entirely on a different layer: `validate_spec` (`world_compile.rs:157-168`) refuses any name outside `[A-Za-z0-9._-]` or starting with `.`, which incidentally excludes `/`. That is the only thing standing between a peer-supplied compile file name and a write outside the job tempdir — the dedicated guard at the write site enforces nothing, and its error message claims a guarantee it does not provide. Any future loosening of the `validate_spec` charset (e.g. allowing subdirectory module names like `modules/Foo.roc`, a natural Roc layout) silently turns this into a path-escape write of attacker-chosen content, with no failing test and no error at the write site.

## Evidence

Verified on main `65165193` with a probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-sanitize` there) evaluating the verbatim check expression from `world_compile.rs:505-511` (file sha256 `e9bb8327eb5647e3c40e7611cebb335660f1a127392085cb00622378df83f11f`; `ensure!` expanded by hand, plus a lexical `Path::components` normalization to test whether `job.join(name)` escapes). Log: `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-sanitize/out.log` in the goal workspace.

```text
"main.roc": sanitize_passes=true escapes_job=false
"Helper.roc": sanitize_passes=true escapes_job=false
"..": sanitize_passes=true escapes_job=true
"../evil.roc": sanitize_passes=true escapes_job=true
"../../evil.roc": sanitize_passes=true escapes_job=true
"a/../../evil.roc": sanitize_passes=true escapes_job=true
"sub/../..//evil.roc": sanitize_passes=true escapes_job=true
"/etc/passwd": sanitize_passes=true escapes_job=true
"a..b.roc": sanitize_passes=true escapes_job=false
split('.') of "...." = ["", "", "", "", ""]
```

Controls: legitimate flat names (`main.roc`, `Helper.roc`, `a..b.roc`) pass and stay inside the job dir. The existing test at `world_compile.rs:599` (`validate_spec` refuses `"../evil.roc"`) passes only because of the charset allowlist — it never exercises `sanitize_file_name`.

## Why it matters

- Defense in depth that isn't: the one function whose job is containment at the write site is dead code as a check, so a reviewer reading the staging loop reasonably believes traversal is handled there.
- The failure mode on any future charset loosening is silent: peer-supplied file content written outside the job tempdir (compile requests arrive from world-session clients; `world_session/mod.rs:1205-1212` passes wire files straight into `CompileSpec`), instead of a loud refusal.
- Sibling of #1593 (duplicate names, fixed): that fix hardened `validate_spec`; this is the remaining unverified guard in the same staging path.

## Acceptance criteria

- `sanitize_file_name` actually enforces its contract: it refuses any name whose `Path::components` are not exactly one `Component::Normal` (refusing `ParentDir`, `RootDir`, prefixes, separators, and empty names), or an equivalently sound component-based check.
- Unit tests in `world_compile.rs`'s test module call `sanitize_file_name` directly: `".."`, `"../evil.roc"`, `"a/../../evil.roc"`, `"/etc/passwd"` are refused; `"main.roc"`, `"Helper.roc"`, `"a..b.roc"` pass unchanged.
- No behavior change for any name `validate_spec` currently accepts (flat `[A-Za-z0-9._-]` names not starting with `.`).
- Existing `world_compile` tests still pass.

title: id(world-compile): duplicate file names in a compile request are never refused — the later file silently overwrites the earlier, and source_blake3 provenance describes sources that were never compiled

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

A world compile request (`ClientFrame::Compile` → `CompileSpec`) may carry two files with the same name. Nothing refuses that, and every stage of `pkgs/id/src/world_compile.rs` then treats the request differently:

1. **`validate_spec` (world_compile.rs:146-185)** checks the file count, that `files[0]` is `main.roc`, per-name safety, and per-file/total sizes — but never that names are unique.
2. **`digest_sources` (:423-442)** hashes *all* files in the spec, so `source_blake3` in the installed module's `ModuleProvenance::SourceBuild` (:213, :335-343) describes a source set that includes a file which is never compiled.
3. **The staging loop (:218-221)** writes each file to `job.path().join(name)` in order, so a later same-name file silently overwrites the earlier one. The compiler only ever sees the last file of each name, and the `main.roc` read back for the platform-path rewrite (:224-228) is the *last* `main.roc`, not the `files[0]` the validator checked.
4. **`check_imports` (:118-144)** scans all of `spec.files`, including shadowed files that never reach the compiler — a dead file importing an ungranted platform module refuses a compile whose actual sources are clean.

The session layer passes the wire files straight through (`world_session/mod.rs:1205-1212` maps `Vec<CompileFile>` into `CompileSpec` with no dedup), so any admin client that assembles a file list programmatically (or a buggy/duplicate-emitting client) can trigger this. Compilation is admin-only, which bounds the blast radius, but the outcome is either a confusing refusal, a silently different module than the admin sent, or — worst — an installed module whose recorded source provenance does not match the sources it was built from.

## Evidence

Verified on main `54f862c9` with a probe crate on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-dupcompile` there) driving verbatim copies of `check_imports`, `validate_spec`, `digest_sources`, and `sanitize_file_name` from `world_compile.rs` (sha256 `8a61af784d1698d96ef1d58ea5341432ebb82dc72fe2cb4053acca460cc3b580`), with the staging loop reproduced exactly (std::fs::write standing in for tokio::fs::write, same path and order). Log: `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-dupcompile/out.log` in the goal workspace.

```text
CTRL validate=Ok staged=[("Helper.roc", "HELPER"), ("main.roc", "MAIN")] digest_match=true
DUP1 validate=Ok staged=[("Helper.roc", "HELPER-SECOND"), ("main.roc", "MAIN")]
DUP1 digest(spec)=d30c2696ed39ad9f digest(staged)=4c07d9907fddb96e match=false
DUP2 validate=Ok files[0]="MAIN-FIRST" disk_main="MAIN-SECOND" staged=[("Helper.roc", "HELPER"), ("main.roc", "MAIN-SECOND")]
DUP3 check_imports=Err Helper.roc imports Chat, which this world does not allow (grant it with `id world caps --grant Chat`; …)
DUP3 staged=[("Helper.roc", "clean\n"), ("main.roc", "MAIN")] (the importing file is not among them)
```

- CTRL: unique names validate, stage loss-free, and `digest(spec) == digest(staged)`.
- DUP1: `[main.roc, Helper.roc="HELPER-FIRST", Helper.roc="HELPER-SECOND"]` validates; the first `Helper.roc` is silently lost at staging; the digest recorded as provenance (`digest(spec)`) differs from the digest of the sources actually compiled (`digest(staged)`).
- DUP2: `[main.roc="MAIN-FIRST", Helper.roc, main.roc="MAIN-SECOND"]` validates on the strength of `files[0]`, but the `main.roc` read back from the job dir — the one whose platform path is rewritten and which `roc build main.roc` compiles — is `MAIN-SECOND`.
- DUP3: `[main.roc, Helper.roc="import Chat\n", Helper.roc="clean\n"]` is refused by `check_imports` for an import in a file that is shadowed and never compiled.

## Why it matters

`ModuleProvenance` is the record of what a running world module was built from; `id world verify`/doctor-style audits and incident response lean on `source_blake3` meaning "these exact sources". A duplicate name quietly breaks that invariant while also discarding one of the admin's files without any error. Every sibling validator in this area refuses out-of-contract input by name (unsafe names, oversize files, ungranted imports); duplicate names are the one contract hole left.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `validate_spec` refuses a spec with duplicate file names, with an error that names the duplicated file (so `compile()`, which validates before imports/digest/staging at :202-203, refuses before any stage can diverge).
- [ ] Regression tests in `world_compile.rs` cover at minimum: a duplicated non-main file, a duplicated `main.roc`, and that a unique-name spec (control) still validates.
- [ ] Existing behaviour is unchanged for unique-name specs: the current `world_compile` test module keeps passing, including the source-digest order-independence test.
- [ ] No change to the digest format, the staging layout, or the provenance schema — refusal at validation is the whole fix surface.

title: id(repl): a non-ASCII character inside $(...) panics the whole REPL — the closing-paren scan mixes char and byte indices

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Bug

In the `id` REPL, any `$(...)` command substitution whose command text contains a non-ASCII (multibyte UTF-8) character **panics the whole REPL process** with a char-boundary slice error, instead of running the substitution or returning a handled error.

```text
> get $(echo café)
thread 'main' panicked at src/repl/input.rs:286:26:
end byte index 15 is not a char boundary; it is inside 'é' (bytes 14..16 of string)
```

The REPL loop cannot recover: `runner.rs:127` matches on the `Result` of `preprocess_repl_line` and handles `Err` gracefully, but a panic unwinds straight past it and kills the session (and any unsaved REPL state with it).

## Root cause

`pkgs/id/src/repl/input.rs:270-276` — the closing-paren scan mixes units:

```rust
for (i, c) in result[start + 2..].chars().enumerate() {
    match c {
        '(' => depth += 1,
        ')' => {
            depth -= 1;
            if depth == 0 {
                end = start + 2 + i;   // i is a CHAR index, end is used as a BYTE index
                break;
            }
        }
        _ => {}
    }
}
```

`find("$(")` returns a byte index and every slice after this (`&result[start + 2..end]` at :286, `&result[end + 1..]` at :296/:299) is byte-indexed, but `i` counts chars. For pure ASCII the two coincide, which is why all existing tests pass. One multibyte character before the closing paren makes `end` land inside that character (panic at :286), or — when the miscount happens to land on a boundary — silently truncates the command / corrupts the remainder slice (the `éé` case below panics at the second slice site, :299).

The backtick path right below (:303+) does not have this bug: it derives all offsets from `find`, which is byte-based.

## Verified (probe, this filing)

Probe crate on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-laneA-replsubst`) driving the verbatim `repl/input.rs` from main `996111fd` (sha256 `d6b25b5961312fafe2fafd8982e2e49e4309201caa4cdc4578e2595e42c6def6`, identical on both machines), each case under `catch_unwind`:

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| `get $(echo test)` (control) | `Ready("get test")` ✅ |
| `get $(echo $(echo nested))` (control) | `Ready("get nested")` ✅ |
| `get $(echo café)` | **PANIC** at `input.rs:286` — `end byte index 15 is not a char boundary; it is inside 'é' (bytes 14..16)` |
| `get $(echo ☕)` | **PANIC** at `input.rs:286` — inside '☕' (bytes 11..14) |
| `get $(echo éé)` | **PANIC** at `input.rs:299` — `start byte index 14 is not a char boundary` (second slice site) |
| `put $(echo café) name` | **PANIC** at `input.rs:286` (the put content-marker path is equally affected) |

So the trigger is not exotic: filenames, names, and content in most non-English languages — or an emoji — inside a substitution crash the REPL. E.g. `get $(echo résumé.txt)`, `put $(cat ☕.md) name`.

## Why it matters

- The REPL is the interactive front door of `id`; a panic on ordinary international text is a hard crash from a single typed line, with no error message the user can act on.
- The failure mode is the worst kind for a preprocessor: it runs on *every* REPL line before dispatch, so the blast radius is the whole session, not one command.
- The char/byte mix-up is exactly the class of bug that ASCII-only test suites never catch; the existing `repl::input` tests are all-ASCII.

## Suggested fix

Iterate byte offsets: `for (byte_i, c) in result[start + 2..].char_indices()` and set `end = start + 2 + byte_i`. All downstream slices then stay byte-consistent. No behavior change for ASCII input (existing tests pin it).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `preprocess_repl_line` never panics for any input: multibyte characters inside `$(...)` (before, between, and after nested parens) produce the correct substituted `Ready` line or a handled `Err`, never an unwind.
- [ ] New tests in `repl::input` cover at least: a 2-byte character (`get $(echo café)` → `get café`), a 3-byte character/emoji, two multibyte characters (exercises the remainder slice), and the `put $(...) name` content-marker path with multibyte content.
- [ ] All pre-existing `repl::input` tests pass unchanged (ASCII behavior, nesting, unterminated-substitution errors).
- [ ] No other preprocessor stage regresses: here-string, backtick, heredoc, and pipe cases in the existing suite stay green.

title: id(web): a partial issued before a navigation still writes into the new page — #1462's supersession slots never interact, so a stale search/tags refresh overwrites the navigated-to list

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem The #1462 supersession fix (PR #1550, `pkgs/id/web/src/navigation.ts`) gives `navigateTo` one token slot and `fetchPartial` one slot **per target selector** — but the two slots never interact. A `fetchPartial` issued on page A stays "current" in its own slot while a `navigateTo` swaps `#main` to page B, and when the stale partial finally resolves it queries the target selector **in the new page's DOM** and overwrites it. Page B's list is replaced by page A's stale results, with the URL and page agreeing — nothing looks wrong. This is the cross-slot remainder of #1462: that fix (and its tests in `navigation.test.ts`) covers navigate-vs-navigate and partial-vs-partial, but no navigate-vs-partial case. ## Evidence (verified this run, main 74514cc7) Probe on the laptop driving the **real** `navigation.ts` (sha256 `65cf1040…` identical both sides; deferred fetch + stub DOM, same spirit as the `navigation.test.ts` harness) — probe + log: goal `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-laneA-navcross/probe.ts` + `out.log`: - **CASE cross (bug):** `fetchPartial("/api/files?search=ab", "#file-list-content")` in flight → `navigateTo("/page-b")` resolves and swaps `#main` (list = "PAGE-B LIST (as navigated)", `onMainSwapped` fired, URL pushed) → then the stale partial resolves → **list becomes `
  • stale results for 'ab' (page A query)
    • ` and `onPartialSwapped` fires against the new page**. - **CONTROL same-slot:** two partials for the same target — newer kept, stale dropped (the #1462 fix works as intended). - **CONTROL reverse order:** a partial that resolves *before* the navigation lands writes the old page, which the navigation then replaces — correct. Code: `navigation.ts:36-38` (two independent token stores), `fetchPartial` checks only its per-target token (`:51-53`) and re-queries `document.querySelector(targetSelector)` at write time (`:64`); `navigateTo` bumps only `navigationToken` (`:84`). Reachability in the real app: - `#file-list-content` exists on every file-list view (`pkgs/id/src/web/templates.rs:176`), so navigating between list views (or home ↔ files) leaves a same-named target in the new page. - Partials are fired by sources that do not stop at navigation: the search debounce (300 ms, `main.ts:716`/`:735`), pagination buttons (`main.ts:1660`), and the **global tags WebSocket** — explicitly "stays connected across pages" (`main.ts`, connectTagsWs) — whose handler fires `fetchPartial(url, "#file-list-content")` at `main.ts:860` whenever a `fileListContent` element exists *at message time*, i.e. possibly the new page's, with the old page's in-flight request still outstanding. - `onPartialSwapped` (`main.ts:688+`) re-runs page side effects (e.g. re-applying the show-auto filter) against the wrong page's DOM. ## Why it matters #1462's whole point was that arrival-order application makes the UI silently show content the user did not ask for last, with URL and content agreeing. The cross-slot path reintroduces exactly that failure across the most common interaction pair (type a search / get a tags push, then click somewhere) whenever the destination page contains the same partial target — which for `#file-list-content` is the normal case. ## Acceptance criteria - [ ] A `fetchPartial` issued before a `navigateTo` swap never writes to the DOM after that swap lands, and never fires `onPartialSwapped` after it — regardless of target selector. - [ ] Symmetrically, a partial issued while a navigation is in flight must not write into the page that navigation installs (or is dropped if the navigation supersedes it — triage pins the exact rule; the invariant is: no write from a request issued against a previous page generation). - [ ] Same-slot behaviour from #1462 is unchanged: newer navigation supersedes older navigations; newer same-target partial supersedes older ones; different-target partials on the *same* page generation stay independent. - [ ] `navigation.test.ts` gains the cross cases: partial-then-navigate (stale resolves last), navigate-then-partial, and the reverse-order control (partial resolving before the swap still applies to the old page). - [ ] No behaviour change for the failed-current-navigation full-page fallback. Fix direction for triage: a page-generation counter bumped by every navigation swap (and possibly at navigation issue), captured by `fetchPartial` at issue time and checked at write time alongside its per-target token — or navigation invalidating all partial slots. The mechanism is triage's pick; the generation invariant above is the requirement.

title: id(groups): Policy::is_valid accepts History::Recent(0) — a zero-epoch window every other layer refuses, so the fold admits a history policy with no welcome mode

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Summary

`groups::Policy::is_valid` accepts `History::Recent(0)` — a history window of zero epochs — even though every other layer of the same system says that value is meaningless:

- `pkgs/id/src/groups/policy.rs:64-66` documents `Recent(u32)`: "The last N epochs (P4.5). … **N is at least 1**."
- `pkgs/id/src/encryption/history.rs:119-131`: `HistoryMode::recent(0)` returns `Err(HistoryModeError::EmptyWindow)` — "A window of zero epochs would welcome nothing" / "a recent window must hold at least one epoch" — and its `FromStr` likewise rejects the text form `recent:0`.
- `pkgs/id/src/encryption/history.rs:135-141`: `HistoryMode::from_policy(History::Recent(0))` therefore maps to `None` — the exact same bucket as `FromJoin` and `Causal`, which are documented as having no welcome mode at all.

But `is_valid` (`policy.rs:154-158`) checks only two things — `roles.change == Role::Admin` and `member_cap >= 1` — and never looks at `history`.

## Why it matters

`is_valid` is the fold's only policy gate, and the fold is the trust boundary for peer-supplied group events:

- create: `pkgs/id/src/groups/fold.rs:744-746` — `if !create.policy.is_valid() { return Err(Refusal::BadPolicy) }`
- policy change: `pkgs/id/src/groups/fold.rs:858-860` — same check

So a create or policy-change event carrying `history = Recent(0)` is **applied and stored** (templates do not save it either: `Template::Custom` admits everything at `policy.rs:186`, `Template::Channel` at `:180-184` checks only cap/scheme/join). The group then displays as `history = "recent:0"` (`pkgs/id/src/commands/group.rs:139`), a state no local constructor can produce — `HistoryMode`'s parser and constructor both refuse it — while the encryption layer silently treats the policy as modeless: a joiner gets no welcome bundle, indistinguishable from the deliberately modeless `FromJoin`/`Causal` policies, instead of the "last N epochs" the policy record claims.

This is the same validator-outlier shape as the closed empty-`module_hash` case (#1517): one layer states a `>= 1` rule, every sibling enforces it, and the one validator on the admission path does not.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `db6f7d00`)

Probe crate **on the laptop** (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-policy` there) driving the verbatim `policy.rs` (sha256 `8e9b9fba8be4c78de74fa70ae9e28e16b1687398c03a4cad132a2d88bf9f172b`, identical on sandbox main and the laptop clone), plus the verbatim `HistoryMode::recent`/`from_policy` logic from `encryption/history.rs:124-141`:

```
recent0:      is_valid=true  custom_admits=true  channel_admits=true  from_policy=None
recent1:      is_valid=true  custom_admits=true  channel_admits=true  from_policy=Some(Recent(1))
full-default: is_valid=true  custom_admits=true  channel_admits=true  from_policy=Some(Full)
fromjoin:     is_valid=true  custom_admits=true  channel_admits=true  from_policy=None
cap0:         is_valid=false   (control — the validator does refuse a zero cap)
recent0-cap0: is_valid=false   (refused for the cap, not the window)
mode_recent(0)=Err("EmptyWindow")  mode_recent(1)=Ok(Recent(1))
```

Controls confirm the validator is alive (cap `0` and a non-Admin role rule are refused, `policy.rs` tests at `:220-237`) — `Recent(0)` is simply not one of the things it checks.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Policy::is_valid` (or an equivalent single gate used by both fold paths) refuses `History::Recent(0)`, so a create and a policy-change carrying it both fold to `Refusal::BadPolicy`.
- [ ] A unit test in `groups/policy.rs` (or `groups/tests.rs`) pins it: `Recent(0)` invalid, `Recent(1)` still valid, existing cap/role cases unchanged.
- [ ] No other `History` variant changes validity: `Full`, `FromJoin`, and `Causal` remain admissible policy values (they are deliberate, documented modes even though they have no welcome bundle).
- [ ] Existing group/encryption tests keep passing (`cargo test` for the groups + encryption modules, on the laptop or CI — no sandbox builds).

Deliberately out of scope: changing `HistoryMode::from_policy`'s mapping, adding a CLI flag for history, or validating `Scheme` in `is_valid` (an unknown scheme is already refused downstream by `encryption::scheme::negotiate` as `UnsupportedScheme` — that path is deliberate).

title: meta-exporter: window_duration_secs is never validated — a missing/junk duration exports a 'window-NaNs' window as a successful reading

labels.name: effort/s

labels.name: app/pm-stack
labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

body:
## Bug

`pm-stack/meta-exporter/meta-quota-export.mjs` — `parseSubscriptionQuota` never validates `window_duration_secs`, even though the module's contract is fail-closed: "Parse a subscription-quota payload into export windows. Throws on any shape drift — fail-closed, never partial zeros." (`meta-quota-export.mjs:67-68`)

The parser carefully validates `window_weighted_used/limit`, `weekly_weighted_used/limit`, and both `*_resets_at` fields for finiteness and non-negativity (`:76-87`), and rejects zero limits (`:88-90`) — but `durationSecs` is read at `:79` and used unchecked at `:91` to name the short window:

```js
const shortName = durationSecs === 18_000 ? "5h" : durationSecs === 3_600 ? "1h" : `window-${durationSecs}s`;
```

## Verified this run (node, against the real module on main db6f7d00)

With an otherwise-valid payload (the captured fixture shape from `meta-quota-export.test.mjs`):

| `window_duration_secs` | Result |
| --- | --- |
| missing | **OK** — windows `["window-NaNs", "weekly"]` |
| `"abc"` | **OK** — windows `["window-NaNs", "weekly"]` |
| `-5` | **OK** — windows `["window--5s", "weekly"]` |
| `0` | **OK** — windows `["window-0s", "weekly"]` |

So a single drifted field in the console API response produces a *success* document (`status: "ok"`) carrying a garbage-named window with a real used-percent — exactly the "partial/fake reading" outcome the fail-closed design exists to prevent.

## Why it matters

The aggregator's file-export mapper passes window names through verbatim and only knows durations for the names `"5h"` and `"weekly"` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-gather-map.ts`: `FILE_EXPORT_WINDOW_SECONDS = { "5h": 18_000, weekly: 604_800 }`, and the window loop at `:144-155` pushes any named window with `windowSeconds: FILE_EXPORT_WINDOW_SECONDS[w.name] ?? null`). A `window-NaNs` window therefore lands in quota-current as a live "ok" window with a nonsense name and no duration, instead of the export failing closed with an `unparseable` failure document that consumers can alert on. Pool/quota consumers keying on the `5h` window silently lose the real short window while the service still reports healthy.

Parent feature: #1301 (Meta adapter Phase 1 — this exporter).

## Acceptance criteria

- `parseSubscriptionQuota` validates `window_duration_secs` like the other numeric fields: it must be a finite number `> 0`; a missing, non-numeric, zero, or negative value throws `ExportError("unparseable", 6, …)` naming the field.
- Well-formed payloads are unchanged: `18000` → `5h`, `3600` → `1h`, any other positive duration → `window-<n>s` (the forward-compatible naming for a genuinely new window length stays).
- Tests in `meta-quota-export.test.mjs` add the missing / `"abc"` / `0` / negative `window_duration_secs` cases to the existing "shape drift fails closed" test family, asserting they throw.
- No change to the success/failure document shapes or exit codes.

title: aggregator: a garbage or future-dated generatedAt is 'live' forever — the orchestration diagnosis and fleet-feed gate never check that the timestamp parses

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.description: Package/app: aggregator (pm-stack in this repo)

body:
## Summary

The aggregator's freshness gates accept a `generatedAt` that is not a date at all — and a date arbitrarily far in the future — and report the data as **live/fresh indefinitely**:

- `orchestrationSectionProblem` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/feed.ts:120-135, the check itself at :124) checks only `typeof s.generatedAt === "string"`. It never checks that the string parses as a date.
- `diagnoseOrchestrationSection` (feed.ts:165-176, age at :170) computes `ageMs = Math.max(0, now - Date.parse(s.generatedAt))`. For an unparseable string `Date.parse` is `NaN`, `Math.max(0, NaN)` is `NaN`, and `NaN > ORCHESTRATION_STALE_MS` is `false` — so the section diagnoses as **`live`**, with `ageMs: NaN`. For a future stamp the age clamps to `0`, so the section stays `live` until 90 minutes *after* its future date.
- `isFleetFeed` (feed.ts:193-204) has the same shape: `generatedAt` is string-only. A feed stamped `"not-a-date"` passes the gate and is served by `loadFeed`.
- `feedAgeText` (feed.ts:225-227) renders the garbage case literally as **`NaNd old`** in the provenance strings (`sources/live.ts:715,757,892,…`), and the future case as `fresh`.
- `buildHealth` (health.ts:229,249-250) derives `feedAgeMs` the same clamped way, so a garbage/future feed is never `stale` and never sets `degraded`.

## Verified (this run, on main db6f7d00)

Probe ON THE LAPTOP (Bun, driving the real `feed.ts`, sha256 identical both sides; probe + log in the goal's hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-feeddate/):

- Control, section stamped 10 min ago → `state=live` (correct); 2 h ago → `state=stale` (correct).
- Section stamped `"not-a-date"` → `state=live`, `ageMs=NaN`, `feedAgeText="NaNd old"`.
- Section stamped `+30 days` in the future → `state=live`, `ageMs=0`, `feedAgeText="fresh"` — and it stays live until 90 min after that future date.
- `isFleetFeed` accepts both the garbage and the +30d feed (`true`); the valid control also `true`.

## Why it matters

The diagnosis is the aggregator's honesty backbone (#1139/#1140): it decides whether Today / Needs-you render the orchestration section as current or show the "section is stale — its last published state" banners (render.ts:2215,2428), what provenance claims (`live (fleet feed · …)`), and whether /health reports the stack degraded. A publisher bug or clock skew that emits a malformed or future `generatedAt` therefore defeats every one of those surfaces at once — stale tiers, goals, and measurements present as live readings indefinitely, with no banner and no health signal. That is precisely the failure class the diagnosis was built to surface ("a publisher whose section is being rejected has a bug to fix"), except this input is never rejected.

Distinct from #1541 (quota-current's `measuredAt` freshness in a different module, different gate, different fix surface).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A section whose `generatedAt` does not parse as a date diagnoses as `invalid` (failing check named `generatedAt`), not `live`; `orchestrationSectionProblem` is still the single source of truth for the gate.
- [ ] A section/feed stamped implausibly in the future (beyond a small pinned clock-skew tolerance) is not reported `live`/`fresh` — it diagnoses stale or invalid per a documented rule, and the tolerance is pinned in a test.
- [ ] `isFleetFeed` rejects a feed whose `generatedAt` does not parse; `loadFeed` therefore returns null for it instead of serving it as current.
- [ ] `feedAgeText` / `ageMsText` can never render `NaNd old` for an input that reaches them (defence in depth at the validator is enough if the render paths are unreachable with NaN — say which in the fix).
- [ ] Regression tests in pm-stack/aggregator/test/orchestration.test.ts (and health tests if buildHealth's feed age changes): garbage date, future date, and the existing fresh/stale controls.
- [ ] Existing orchestration/health test suites still pass.

body:
Phase 1 of design #1554 (filed by the design architect, 2026-10-27). Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-tasks-one-store.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace.

**Decision in force (from #1554, do not re-litigate in triage):** one `tasks.Store` instance serves both the MCP surface and the daemon's `/v1` surface. The shared instance is the daemon's existing durable store (SQLite at `<state>/tasks.db`, in-memory fallback) — not the MCP server's in-memory one. Standalone `mcpserver` embeddings without a daemon keep a private in-memory store. MCP ownership/visibility semantics do not change; `/v1` keeps its unscoped operator view. Origin: dezren39/nix#209 rows TASK-27 (one store across MCP and `/v1`) and TASK-20 (durable creation).

## Scope

- Today: `internal/mcpserver/tasks.go` `tasks()` lazily creates `tasks.New()` (in-memory; field `taskStore` at `internal/mcpserver/server.go:273-274`, no seam), while `internal/daemon/ops.go:436-453` `taskStore()` creates the daemon's own store (`tasks.Open(<state>/tasks.db)`, fallback `tasks.New()`), used by `/v1` handlers and by `internal/daemon/routes_proto.go`, `routes_exec.go`, `input_required.go`.
- Add a store seam to `mcpserver.Server` (setter or exported field, following the existing wiring style — `srv.Notify`, `srv.Passthrough`, `srv.Timing` are set the same way in `App.MCPServer()`). When a store is injected, `tasks()` uses it and never creates its own; when none is injected, today's lazy in-memory behaviour is unchanged.
- Wire it in `internal/cli/serve.go` `App.MCPServer()` (~line 474): the daemon's store, constructed once, is shared by the daemon's `/v1` handlers and the MCP server. The daemon's lazy `taskStore()` construction may stay, as long as exactly one instance exists per daemon.
- One `PollInterval` source: today the MCP store takes `Timing.resolved().TaskPoll` and the daemon store takes the `protoTasks.pollInterval` setting. The shared store is configured once, from settings, at construction — and the PR states which setting won and what the other surface's cadence becomes.
- Retire the conformance gap `ext-tasks-durable-before-response` (`internal/conformance/coverage_stateful.go:112`) — its stated reason ("the task store is an in-memory map; a task does not survive the daemon") stops being true for the daemon's MCP surface.

## Acceptance

- Defining tests:
  - a task started through the MCP surface is visible via the daemon store (`Get`/`List`/result) under the same id, and a daemon-side task is reachable through the same shared instance — one store, both surfaces;
  - MCP cross-connection invisibility is preserved after the merge: connection B cannot get/list/cancel connection A's owned task, and `/v1`-started tasks (no MCP owner) are not listed by any MCP connection (legacy list requires an owner match);
  - restart durability: a terminal MCP-started task is still readable after the store is closed and reopened from the same `tasks.db`; a task that was `working` at close reloads as `Failed` with the existing "daemon restarted before task completion" message;
  - standalone construction (no injected store) behaves exactly as today (existing mcpserver task tests pass unmodified in behaviour).
- No protocol/wire changes on either surface; no changes to `internal/tasks` semantics (the store type is shared as-is).
- Verification via CI per fleet policy: `cd pkgs/mcpx && go test ./...` on the PR.

Out of scope: client-side task execution (Phase 2 of #1554); register/docs truth-up and nix#209 closure (Phase 3, gated on Phases 1–2); operational limits, cooperative cancel, audit logging (open questions on #1554).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `mcpserver.Server` accepts an injected `*tasks.Store`; the daemon injects its single store at `App.MCPServer()`; exactly one store instance exists per daemon.
- [ ] Cross-surface, visibility-preservation, and restart-durability tests above pass in CI.
- [ ] `PollInterval` for the shared store comes from one named settings source, stated in the PR.
- [ ] Gap `ext-tasks-durable-before-response` removed from `internal/conformance/coverage_stateful.go`.
- [ ] Standalone embeddings (`adapter.go`, `openapi.go`) unchanged in behaviour; full mcpx suite green via CI.

title: id(web): image upload stores by filename with no collision handling — a second paste named 'image.png' silently un-names the first

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`POST /api/upload` stores every image under its multipart filename as a blob tag, with no collision handling — so a second upload that arrives under the same name silently re-points that name to the new blob, and the first image disappears from every name-based surface. Uploaded names collide in ordinary use, because they are not unique:

- Paste/drop `File` names are caller/browser-assigned, not unique per image (a clipboard bitmap is `image.png`). The web upload path sends the `File` as-is (`uploadImageFile`, `web/src/image-upload.ts:76`: `formData.append("file", file)` — no filename argument), so the multipart filename the server reads is exactly `file.name`.
- The server's own fallback for a nameless upload is `paste-{unix_seconds}.{ext}` (`src/web/routes.rs:1491-1499`) — one-second granularity, so two nameless uploads in the same second also collide.
- The client's dedicated pasted-image name, `generatePasteFilename` (`web/src/image-upload.ts:57-60`, `` `paste-${Date.now()}.${ext}` ``), is never sent to the server at all — it is only the alt-text fallback at `image-upload.ts:217`. It has the same shape of problem anyway: millisecond-only entropy.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `a120b9a9`)

Laptop Bun 1.4.2 probe (real `image-upload.ts`, sha256 `d0ab2a43` identical both sides; probe + log in the goal's `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-laneA-uploadname/`):

- `P1 fixed-clock: call1=paste-1730000000000.png call2=paste-1730000000000.png identical=true`
- `P1 tight-loop: 200 calls -> 1 distinct name(s)`
- `P2 paste#1: bytes=3 -> server sees filename="image.png"` and `P2 paste#2: bytes=4 -> server sees filename="image.png"` — two *different* images present the same filename on the wire, which is the name `upload_handler` keys on.

Server chain, by code read (`src/web/routes.rs`):

- `:1491-1499` — `filename` = `field.file_name()` when non-empty (reconciled with the content type at `:621`), else `paste-{secs}.{ext}`.
- `:1553` — `state.store.tags().set(tag, hash)` with `Tag::from(filename)`: a bare overwrite of any existing tag of that name. No existence check, no uniquifying, no archiving.
- `:1562/:1575/:1588` — the `created` (`set_if_absent`), `modified` and `content-type` metadata tags are also keyed by that same filename, so the second upload's metadata merges into the first image's name record.
- `images_list_handler` (`:1613+`) lists images *by tag*, and `get_file_name` (`:1015+`) resolves a hash's name *by tag* — once the tag is re-pointed, the first image is gone from the image browser/list and from name lookup, even though its blob and any `/blob/{hash}` embeds keep working (which is why this stays silent).

Contrast with the house pattern: `FileOps::rename`/`copy` archive whatever they replace (`src/fileops.rs:15-16`, `archive_existing` at `:153` — `<name>.archive.<unix-ts>`). Upload is the outlier: it is the one name-writing path that destroys the previous occupant without a trace. A document *save* overwriting its own name is intended semantics; an image *upload* is the creation of a new object, so the replace semantics do not transfer.

## Why it matters

Pasting two screenshots into documents is a core editor flow. Today the second paste quietly un-names the first image: it vanishes from the image browser, name-based lookups return the newer image, and the shared metadata record mixes both uploads. Nothing errors anywhere, so the loss is only noticed when someone goes looking for the earlier image by name.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Two uploads that arrive under the same filename both remain listed by `images_list_handler` and resolvable by name afterwards — e.g. the later upload is uniquified (suffix/counter/hash-derived) or the replaced name is archived first, per the `fileops` pattern; triage picks and pins one behaviour.
- [ ] The nameless-upload fallback name cannot repeat for two uploads in the same second (and, if the client paste name is ever sent, `generatePasteFilename` gets the same guarantee).
- [ ] Regression coverage in the existing upload router tests (`upload_router_tests`, `src/web/routes.rs:2333+`): two same-name uploads with different bytes → both images still listed/resolvable, first upload's name record not silently merged with the second's.
- [ ] No change to document save semantics (a save still updates its own name's tag) and no change to the `/blob/{hash}` URL shape.

## Notes

- Not a duplicate of #1379 (upload completing after the document shrinks — insert-position, client side) or #908 (upload filename/type reconciliation — the `reconcile_upload_filename` step above is untouched by this).
- Deliberately not self-solved by the filing lane: the fix is a naming-semantics decision on the upload path (uniquify vs archive-first) that interacts with the image browser and metadata tags — queue-lane triage should pin it.

labels.name: task/triage

body:
# aggregator: a future-dated gatherer read is 'fresh' forever until its date passes — quota-current freshness has no upper bound, so one skewed measuredAt pins a pool's windows for weeks

## Summary

`entryState` in pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-current.ts:56-61 decides whether
a gatherer entry may replace a pool's windows:

```ts
const t = Date.parse(entry.measuredAt);
return Number.isFinite(t) && nowMs - t <= QUOTA_CURRENT_FRESH_MS ? "ok" : "stale";
```

The check bounds only the past. A `measuredAt` in the future gives a negative
age, which is always `<= QUOTA_CURRENT_FRESH_MS` (20 min) — so a read stamped
an hour, a day, or a month ahead is classified `"ok"`, replaces the pool's
windows in `overlayQuotaCurrent`, recomputes the pool state and the routing
choices (`computeChoices`), and keeps doing so on every render until 20
minutes after its future date arrives. The newest-entry sort in the overlay
(`Date.parse(b.measuredAt) - Date.parse(a.measuredAt)`, quota-current.ts:139-141)
also makes a future-dated entry win over every genuinely fresh entry for the
same service.

## Evidence (verified on main 3b559045, Bun 1.4.2, real quota-current.ts sha256 c528e1e3 on the laptop)

Probe drove the real `overlayQuotaCurrent` with a fixed `now`
(2026-10-27T07:00:00Z), one pool (weekly window at 68%), and one ok entry
carrying a 42% window:

| measuredAt | result |
|---|---|
| 5m ago (control) | state healthy, windows replaced (42), freshness ok |
| 19m ago (control) | healthy, windows replaced, freshness ok |
| 21m ago (control) | state **stale**, windows kept (68) |
| **1h in the future** | healthy, windows **replaced (42)**, freshness **ok** |
| **30d in the future** | healthy, windows **replaced (42)**, freshness **ok** |

`parseQuotaCurrent` (quota-current.ts:41-52) validates only that
`measuredAt` is a string, so nothing upstream of `entryState` catches this
either. The existing tests (test/quota-current.test.ts) construct entries
only with past offsets (`iso(msAgo)`), so the future case is uncovered.

## Why it matters

The module's own contract (header, quota-current.ts:7-19) is the dashboard's
data-honesty rule for the quota plane: a read past the freshness bound
"surfaces as the pool's state (error/stale, with the reason) — never as
zeros, and the pool's older windows are never silently presented as
current". A future stamp defeats that rule in the other direction: one
clock-skewed or mis-stamped gatherer write (the gatherer runs on a 15-minute
tick on another host) silently presents its numbers as the freshest truth
for as long as the skew lasts — a month in the verified case — and the
choices computed from those windows steer real session routing.

## Acceptance criteria

- An entry whose `measuredAt` is more than a small clock-skew tolerance in
  the future (tolerance pinned in triage; it should be minutes, not the
  unbounded current behaviour) is NOT classified fresh-ok: it surfaces as
  stale (or error) with the pool's older windows not replaced.
- The fresh-ok precedence sort cannot let a future-dated entry outrank a
  genuinely fresh entry for the same service.
- Regression tests in test/quota-current.test.ts for measuredAt at
  +1h and a far-future date, alongside the existing past-offset controls.
- No change to the freshness bound or semantics for past-dated reads.

## Notes

- Deliberately not self-solved by the creator lane: the skew tolerance is a
  small policy choice for triage (the gatherer and aggregator run on
  different hosts, so zero tolerance could flap on real skew).
- Sibling validator, different defect: #1540 (snapshot store records) —
  same app, unrelated module and mechanism.

title: id(sync): PR #1433 collect_batch lets refused arrivals grow a batch without bound — no total cap, grace restarts on every arrival

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Finding

PR #1433's new `collect_batch` (pkgs/id/src/log_sync.rs) caps a batch only by its **header** count, but stores **every** arrival in the batch `Vec` and restarts the batch grace on **every** arrival — including `Arrival::Refused`. A peer that keeps sending refused arrivals inside the grace window can therefore keep one batch open indefinitely: the `Vec` grows without bound, no write transaction ever commits, and the refused tally is never recorded.

Filed by pr-diff-review-b (lane B) from reviewing PR #1433. Refs #241 (the PR's parent issue).

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/1433 — OPEN, head `0c80543f842ecee1eab5da56ba910f1aed472877`
- PR head `pkgs/id/src/log_sync.rs:454` — `fn collect_batch(first: Arrival, arrivals: &mut mpsc::Receiver<Arrival>) -> Vec<Arrival>`
- PR head `pkgs/id/src/log_sync.rs:461-468` — `headers` increments only for `Arrival::Header(_)`; `batch.push(arrival)` runs for **every** arrival; the only break is `if headers >= INGEST_BATCH { break; }` (INGEST_BATCH = 256 headers)
- PR head `pkgs/id/src/log_sync.rs:470-476` — on every received arrival the grace is reset (`grace_end = None`), so the 5 ms `BATCH_GRACE` (`:73`) is an idle timeout that a steady refused stream never lets expire
- What a `Refused` arrival is (current main `3b559045`, `pkgs/id/src/log_sync.rs` ~:349-356): an `Operation` message that carries a body — "Events carry no body here, and a body is not stored, so a body is refused." It is entirely peer-controlled and costs the peer one frame per arrival.
- Behaviour on current main that the PR replaces: `ingest_arrivals` counts a refusal immediately (`tally.refused += 1`), never stores it in a `Vec`, and collects a batch with non-blocking `try_recv` only — a refused-heavy stream cannot accumulate or stall a batch.

So on the PR head: body-carrying operations spaced <5 ms apart keep `collect_batch` looping forever (headers stays 0, the cap never fires, disconnect is the only exit), the batch `Vec` grows by one element per frame for as long as the peer keeps sending, and the ingest worker (`spawn_blocking`, one per session) makes no progress — no commit, no tally — for the whole time.

The four new batch tests in the PR exercise only `Header` arrivals, so this mix is unpinned.

## Why it matters

LogSync ingest is a network-facing path: the peer pacing the arrivals is not necessarily a well-behaved client. One misbehaving or buggy peer can pin a blocking worker thread and grow host memory linearly with frames sent, for the duration of a session, instead of being counted-and-refused as on main today. It is also a silent stall: nothing is committed and no error surfaces while it happens.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `collect_batch` is bounded in **total** arrivals and/or wall time regardless of the header/refused mix (e.g. refusals count toward a cap, or are tallied and dropped during collection as on main, or a maximum batch duration is enforced) — the chosen bound is named in the doc comment, replacing the current "refusals do not count towards the cap, as before" wording if it no longer describes the whole story
- [ ] New regression test: a stream of `Arrival::Refused` paced inside the grace (and/or more refusals than `INGEST_BATCH`) terminates the batch at the bound, and the headers collected alongside are still handed to the store
- [ ] The PR's existing four batch tests (paced coalescing, grace restart, lone arrival, full-batch cap) still pass

Phase 2 of design #1531 (filed by the design architect, 2026-10-27). Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-stdio-exec-identity.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace.

**Dependency: gated on Phase 1 (the `internal/config` identity core) being merged.** Without it, this phase's cross-directory tests cannot pass — do not start implementation before Phase 1 lands; triage may still verify scope.

**Decision in force (from #1531):** a hashed script (`#!`) is identified by content + resolved directory, so a byte-identical script re-pointed into a **different** directory is a different program and its pool restarts; a re-point **within** one directory keeps its child. This phase proves that decision end-to-end on both paths that consume identity, and closes the originating records.

## Scope

- Reload path — `pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/reload_identity_test.go`: add the cross-directory case beside `TestReloadFollowsAForRePointedCommandByWhatItRuns` (line 162): a link re-pointed at a byte-identical script in a different directory replaces the pool (new pool, new child pid, old child gone). Rewrite that test's comment: the caveat it carries ("a program that finds its own files relative to its real location… is kept when the link points at an identical copy in another directory") is the behaviour #1531 removes; the same-directory keep case in the test must still pass as written in behaviour.

Out of scope: any change to `internal/config` identity semantics (Phase 1 — if this phase's tests expose a core defect, file it against Phase 1's issue rather than patching semantics here); interpreter-as-command servers; sibling-loading native binaries (open questions on #1531).

body:
Phase 1 of design #1531 (filed by the design architect, 2026-10-27). Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-stdio-exec-identity.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace.

**Decision in force (from #1531, do not re-litigate in triage):** for a hashed executable whose content begins with `#!`, the exec identity is its content **plus the resolved directory of the real file**; non-script hashed files stay content-only; files above `limits.execHashMax` stay stat/inode. This implements the first option named in `pkgs/mcpx/TODO.md` item 4 and the `planning/roadmaps/mcpx.md` row "Decide what a stdio server's identity is" (`proposed`).

## Scope

- `ExecStamp.Identity()` in `pkgs/mcpx/internal/config/execid.go` (currently lines 114–130) is the single identity implementation — callers are `Resolved.ExecState()` (execid.go:56), pool construction (`internal/pool/pool.go:199`) and the exec watch (`internal/pool/execwatch.go:84`). Keep it single: no second implementation in `internal/pool` or elsewhere.
- While the hashed branch streams the file (it is already read whole), note whether its first two bytes are `#!`. For a script, fold `filepath.Dir(s.Path)` — `s.Path` is already the `EvalSymlinks`-resolved real path (execid.go:94–99) — into the hash under a distinct framing (marker + separators, so no (content, directory) pair can alias another pair's hash input; exact framing is this issue's to settle). The identity string keeps the `sha256:<16 hex>` form.
- Non-script hash input must stay byte-for-byte today's, so existing binary identities do not move on rollout. The stat branch, the `missing:` form, and non-stdio servers are untouched.
- The `execid.go` header comment: replace the caveat paragraph ("a program that finds its own files relative to its real location is not [identified]… A restart (mcpx restart) is what moves it") with the new rule, including the one-time identity change for script servers on rollout (recorded handoff identities mismatch → script pools restart once at upgrade/first check, the existing binary-changed path).

## Acceptance

- Defining tests in `pkgs/mcpx/internal/config/execid_test.go`:
  - identical script bytes in two **different** directories → different identities;
  - identical script bytes at two names in **one** directory → same identity;
  - identical **non-script** bytes in two different directories → same identity (today's rule preserved);
  - a script and a non-script with identical bytes → different identities;
  - framing non-alias: pairs whose content/directory splits differ do not trivially collide;
  - large-file stat identity unchanged (existing `TestExecIdentityOfALargeFileIsItsInode` keeps passing).
- `TestExecIdentityFollowsTheExecutableNotTheCommandName` (execid_test.go:25) pins a `#!/bin/sh` script's identity to its bare content hash — the design knowingly changes this one expectation to the framed script hash; update it and say so in the PR. The same-directory identical-copy tests (`TestExecIdentityOfASmallFileIsItsContentNotItsPath`) must pass **unmodified in behaviour** — if one fails, the implementation is folding in more than the directory (e.g. the full path), which the design rejects.
- No changes needed in `internal/pool`, `internal/daemon`, handoff, or lifecycle code in this phase; `Identity()` staying platform-independent (the unix/other split is only `fileInode`) is confirmed, or any build-tag surprise is reported on this issue.
- Verification via CI per fleet policy: `cd pkgs/mcpx && go test ./internal/config/...`.

Out of scope: daemon-level reload/watch tests and the TODO/roadmap closure (Phase 2, gated on this phase); interpreter-as-command servers; sibling-loading native binaries (both are open questions on #1531).


## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ExecStamp.Identity()` folds the resolved directory into the hash for `#!` scripts only, under a framed (marker + separators) input that cannot alias another (content, directory) pair; non-script hashed input stays byte-for-byte today's.
- [ ] Defining tests in `pkgs/mcpx/internal/config/execid_test.go` pass: cross-directory identical script → different identity; same-directory identical script → same identity; cross-directory identical non-script → same identity; script vs non-script with identical bytes → different identities; large-file stat identity unchanged.
- [ ] `TestExecIdentityFollowsTheExecutableNotTheCommandName` is updated to the framed script hash and the PR says so explicitly; the same-directory identical-copy tests pass unmodified in behaviour.
- [ ] The `execid.go` header caveat is replaced with the new rule, including the one-time identity change / single restart for script servers on rollout.
- [ ] No changes in `internal/pool`, `internal/daemon`, handoff, or lifecycle code; CI green on the PR (fleet CI-first policy).

title: id(directory): a torn final line in directory.jsonl bricks the directory — Directory::replay refuses the crash-torn tail that ArtifactLog (loaded in the same open) drops and truncates

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

A crash-torn final line in the directory journal bricks the directory permanently: `Directory::open` / `Directory::replay` refuse the unterminated partial entry that a crash mid-append leaves behind, instead of dropping and truncating it the way the sibling JSONL stores in this codebase do.

## Evidence (verified this run on main 279c9739, code reading)

- `pkgs/id/src/directory.rs:527-543` — `Directory::append` writes one JSON line + `\n` with a single `write_all` followed by `sync_data`. A crash/power loss during that write leaves a final line that is a truncated JSON fragment with no terminating newline.
- `pkgs/id/src/directory.rs:505-525` — `Directory::replay` iterates `text.lines()` (which yields the unterminated final fragment as a line) and propagates any parse failure with `?` at `:516-517` (`directory journal line N is malformed`). There is no torn-tail special case: no check for a missing final newline, no truncation/repair.
- `pkgs/id/src/directory.rs:471-473` — `Directory::open` (the production load path) is `Self::replay(path)?` first, so one torn append makes every subsequent open fail the same way; the directory never recovers without manual file surgery.
- Contrast — the established house semantics in the same codebase:
  - `pkgs/id/src/world_store.rs:85-130` (`FileJournal::open`): an unterminated last line is a torn append — dropped, file truncated to `good_len`, with a comment explaining that a newline-terminated unparseable line is corruption and must still fail.
  - `pkgs/id/src/artifact.rs:575-600` (`ArtifactLog::open` — the very log `Directory::open` loads immediately after the journal): drops and truncates a final line cut short by a crash.
  - `pkgs/id/src/envelope_outbox.rs:143-165` and `pkgs/id/src/directory_log.rs:196-235`: same drop-the-torn-tail treatment.
- Existing test `replay_rebuilds_the_directory_and_refuses_a_broken_journal` (`directory.rs:2601`) covers an *apply-refused* complete entry, not a torn tail; no test covers an unterminated final fragment.
- Dedup: #1499 (open) is the same defect class in `Petnames::open` only (`pkgs/id/src/petname.rs`); it names FileJournal and Outbox as the good examples and does not cover the directory journal. No open or recently-closed issue mentions the directory journal / `Directory::replay` torn tail.

## Why it matters

The directory journal is the durable record of accounts, friendships and group membership for the directory service. Its own append path can produce exactly the torn tail its load path refuses — so a single ill-timed crash converts a recoverable restart into a permanently unopenable directory, while the artifact log sitting next to it (loaded in the same `open`) already survives the same crash.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Directory::replay`/`open` on a journal whose final line is an unterminated truncated fragment loads all complete entries, drops the fragment, and truncates the file to the last complete line (mirroring `FileJournal::open` / `ArtifactLog::open` semantics, including a warning log).
- [ ] A newline-terminated line that does not parse, anywhere including the last line, still fails with the existing `directory journal line N is malformed` error — corruption is never silently dropped.
- [ ] A complete entry that `apply` refuses still fails replay (existing test at `directory.rs:2601` keeps passing).
- [ ] New tests cover: torn final fragment (loads + file truncated), complete-but-corrupt final line (errors), torn fragment after valid entries (earlier entries intact).

title: id(world-manifest): plan/diff misreport seed and ceiling — a seed-only change reports 'no drift' and is never applied, while a ceiling reorder reports drift that grants (set-compared) ignore

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`plan()` / `diff()` in `pkgs/id/src/world_manifest.rs` misreport drift in both directions:

1. **False negative — seed-only changes vanish.** `WorldState` carries the live seed (`world_manifest.rs:63-64`, "The seed the active program was installed with"), and the manifest's `seed` is a declared field — but `plan()` only ever uses the seed as a ride-along on `InstallModule` (`:207-218`). If the module is unchanged and only the seed differs, the plan is empty and `diff()` prints **"no drift"**. The new seed is never applied and the admin is told nothing is wrong.
2. **False positive — ceiling reorder is "drift", grants reorder is not.** Grants are compared as `BTreeSet`s (`:231-240`), so reordering the same grants produces no step. The ceiling is compared as an ordered slice (`:242-249`: `current.ceiling.as_deref() != Some(ceiling.as_slice())`), so writing the same ceiling in a different order produces a `SetCeiling` step and a drift line — a semantically empty change that `id world apply` will "apply" and count.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 279c9739)

Probe (crate on the laptop compiling the **verbatim** `world_manifest.rs` sha256 `234f1dfc…` + `world_caps.rs` sha256 `679a2c25…`, identical sandbox↔laptop; log `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-manifest/out.log`):

- Manifest `module_hash = "abc123"`, `seed = 99` vs live state `{ module_hash: "abc123", seed: 7 }` → `steps=[]`, `diff="no drift"`
- Manifest `ceiling = ["time.now", "chat.say"]` vs live ceiling `["chat.say", "time.now"]` (same set) → `steps=[SetCeiling { ceiling: Some(["time.now", "chat.say"]) }]`
- Control, grants mirror of the same reorder → `steps=[]`
- Control, genuinely new schedule → `ScheduleAt` step as expected

## Why it matters

`id world diff` is the admin's drift oracle and `apply` reconciles from the same `plan()`. A false "no drift" silently strands a seed change (the seed drives the program's deterministic initializer, so the world keeps running with the wrong one while the manifest claims otherwise), and order-noise drift trains admins to ignore `diff` output — the exact failure mode a declarative manifest exists to prevent.

Distinct from #818 (the CLI wiring fabricates the *current* state the plan runs against — this defect is in pure `plan()` itself, reproduced against a correct, hand-built state) and from closed #817 (omitted-field semantics).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A seed-only difference produces an explicit reconciliation outcome — either a step that reinstalls with the new seed, or `diff`/`plan` surface the seed as unreconcilable-without-reinstall drift — pinned by a test; "no drift" for a differing seed is not an accepted outcome
- [ ] Ceiling comparison is set-based like grants: reordering the same ceiling names yields an empty plan, and a genuinely different ceiling still yields `SetCeiling`
- [ ] Tests cover: seed-only diff, ceiling reorder (no step), ceiling set change (step), grants behaviour unchanged
- [ ] `cargo test` for the `world_manifest` module passes; `apply_is_idempotent` and the #817 regression tests still pass

title: id(world-manifest): an empty module_hash passes validation — parse accepts "" and plan/apply install it, contradicting validate's own '1 to 64 hex digits' rule

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

`WorldManifest::validate` accepts an **empty** `module_hash`, even though its own error message says the hash "must be 1 to 64 hex digits". A manifest with `module_hash = ""` parses cleanly, `plan()` then emits an `InstallModule` step carrying the empty hash, and the pure `apply()` installs it into the state — the bad value is only ever caught (if at all) downstream at the server, far from the typo that caused it.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 279c9739)

`pkgs/id/src/world_manifest.rs:186-192`:

```rust
if let Some(hash) = &self.module_hash {
    let valid = hash.len() <= MAX_NAME_BYTES && hash.bytes().all(|b| b.is_ascii_hexdigit());
    ensure!(valid, "module hash must be 1 to {MAX_NAME_BYTES} hex digits");
}
```

`"".len() <= 64` is true and `all()` on an empty iterator is true, so the lower bound in the message is never enforced. Every sibling validator in `pkgs/id/src/world_caps.rs` does enforce it — e.g. `:248` `!spec.is_empty() && spec.len() <= MAX_NAME_BYTES`, `:274`, `:278` — the manifest hash check is the outlier.

Probe (crate on the laptop compiling the **verbatim** `world_manifest.rs` sha256 `234f1dfc…` + `world_caps.rs` sha256 `679a2c25…`, identical sandbox↔laptop; log `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-manifest/out.log`):

- `parse("module_hash = \"\"")` → **OK**, `module_hash=Some("")`
- control `parse("module_hash = \"not-hex!\"")` → Err("module hash must be 1 to 64 hex digits")
- control `parse("module_hash = \"abc123\"")` → OK
- `plan()` for the empty-hash manifest against a default state → `[InstallModule { hash: Some(""), source: None, seed: 0 }]`, and `apply()` sets `state.module_hash = Some("")`

## Why it matters

`world.toml` is the declarative admin interface for a world (`id world apply` / `diff`). Validation at `parse()` is the one place every bad manifest is supposed to die with a precise, field-naming error. An empty hash slipping through turns a one-character typo into a confusing downstream install failure (or a state whose module hash is the empty string), and the error text actively misleads: it claims a 1-digit minimum that the code does not check.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `parse("module_hash = \"\"")` fails with the existing "module hash must be 1 to {MAX_NAME_BYTES} hex digits" error
- [ ] Non-empty hex hashes (1..=64 digits) still parse; non-hex and >64-digit hashes still fail
- [ ] A regression test joins `validation_rejects_unknown_names_and_bad_hashes` in `world_manifest.rs` covering the empty hash
- [ ] `cargo test` for the `world_manifest` module passes; no other validation behaviour changes

## Gap (backup audit, 2026-10-27): atlas has no reliable routine backup

Two halves, both verified firsthand today:

**1. The canonical local atlas.db is never backed up routinely.**
- Canonical DB: `~/hatch-personal/workspace/turso-atlas/data/atlas.db` (1.49 GB, modified 2026-10-27 02:07). It and its dated snapshots are **gitignored** (hatch-personal .gitignore lines 33 and 48: `workspace/turso-atlas/data/*.db.gz`, `workspace/turso-atlas/data/**/*.db`), so the every-minute hatch-personal autocommit does NOT cover them.

**2. The nightly Turso atlas dump is failing.**
- cold-store-nightly-backup, 2026-10-27 03:12 CDT run: D1 backup OK, Supabase filing OK, 3 of 4 Turso databases filed to Drive — but **atlas failed**: `curl: (28) Operation timed out after 300001 milliseconds with 524901755 bytes received` / `turso export: ERROR: atlas: dump download failed`. Related exposure: the laptop's `~/atlas/v3/` embedding databases (incl. the Qwen3 pass, ~113h of compute) also have no backup; they are rebuildable from corpus.db only at full recompute cost, and corpus.db itself lives only on the laptop.

### Acceptance

title: aggregator: concurrent writes to the JSON stores share one temp path — most fail with ENOENT (returned as '400 invalid'), and persisted records don't match the calls that succeeded

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: app/aggregator
labels.description: Package/app: aggregator (pm-stack in this repo)

body:
## Summary

The aggregator's JSON stores persist through a temp file named only by process id — `` `${file}.tmp-${process.pid}` `` — and none of them serializes writes. Two writes that overlap in the same process share the one temp path: the first `rename` wins, the rest fail with `ENOENT`, and which records actually reach disk stops matching which callers were told succeeded.

Three sites share the pattern:

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/comments.ts:121` — `CommentsStore.persist()` (used by `add`, `markTriaged`, `markGithubResult`)
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/actions.ts:441` — `ActionsStore.persist()` (used by `add`, `markResult`)
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/sources/live.ts:594` — the session-registry merge write (same shared temp name; its `try/catch` swallows the failure as "best-effort", so registry updates are silently lost instead)

## Verified evidence (this run, main 931f1771)

Probe: the verbatim `pm-stack/aggregator/src` tree (comments.ts sha256 `5120ae7d…`, actions.ts `ca10a65f…`, model.ts `f801cde7…`, identical on both machines) under Bun 1.4.2 on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-laneA-persist` there; probe + log in the goal's `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-laneA-1435/`), firing concurrent `add()` calls at one store, then reloading through a fresh store instance (what survives a restart):

```
COMMENTS n=2  fulfilled=1  rejected=1   firstErr=ENOENT rename '…comments-2.json.tmp-2579588'  fileCount=1  reloaded=1
COMMENTS n=5  fulfilled=1  rejected=4   firstErr=ENOENT rename …                              fileCount=1  reloaded=1
COMMENTS n=20 fulfilled=1  rejected=19  firstErr=ENOENT rename …                              fileCount=1  reloaded=1
COMMENTS n=20 fulfilled=2  rejected=18  firstErr=ENOENT rename …                              fileCount=19 reloaded=19
ACTIONS  n=20 fulfilled=2  rejected=18  firstErr=ENOENT rename …                              fileCount=1  reloaded=1
ACTIONS  n=20 fulfilled=3  rejected=17  firstErr=ENOENT rename …                              fileCount=19 reloaded=19
```

Two distinct failures, both from the shared temp path + unserialized persists:

1. **Most concurrent writes error out.** The HTTP layer maps the failure to a misleading client error — `POST /api/comments` returns `400 {"error":"invalid comment: ENOENT: no such file or directory, rename …"}` (server.ts:324-332) and `POST /api/actions` likewise `400 "invalid action: ENOENT…"` — for a comment/action that was perfectly valid.
2. **Success and durability disagree in both directions.** Because each `persist()` stringifies the live in-memory array whenever its writes happen to land, a run where only 2 of 20 adds fulfilled still left 19 records on disk: callers told "400, not saved" had their comment/action silently persisted, so a client that retries creates a duplicate (comments have no dedupe token at all; actions are protected only when the client reuses its `clientToken`). The mirror image also occurs — in-memory state and the file diverge until some later, unrelated write happens to persist the whole array again.

## Why it matters

These stores are the dashboard's write path, and concurrency is the normal case, not an edge: a human clicking card actions in two tabs, the orchestrator posting `/api/comments/triage` and `/api/actions/result` while Drew posts a comment, and the live source's registry merges on its own schedule all hit the same processes. Today that yields spurious 400s on valid input, duplicate comments on retry, and silently dropped registry/result transitions — in the system whose whole job is to be the fleet's reliable triage surface.

## Acceptance criteria

- Concurrent `add` / `markTriaged` / `markGithubResult` / `markResult` calls on one store all fulfill, and a fresh reload returns exactly the records the fulfilled calls wrote — no ENOENT, no extras, no losses.
- Temp files are unique per write (or persists are serialized per store through a write queue/mutex) at all three sites: comments.ts, actions.ts, sources/live.ts.
- A persistence I/O failure is no longer reported to HTTP clients as `400 invalid comment/action` (a 5xx, or an explicit persistence-error body, is fine).
- A regression test fires ≥10 concurrent adds at a store and asserts fulfilled count == reloaded count (the probe above is a ready-made shape).
- Sequential behaviour is unchanged: same file format, same atomic rename publish, same dedupe-by-clientToken semantics for actions.

body:
# id(world-line): `/logs5` is silently executed as `/logs 5` — the logs verb has no word boundary, and bare `/document` / `/input` report "unknown command" instead of their usage

The shared one-line grammar (`pkgs/id/src/world_line.rs`, used identically by the SSH `cmd:` mode, the `id world join` stdin pump, and the CLI one-offs) parses its verbs inconsistently:

## Verified evidence (main 931f1771)

Probe: the verbatim `world_line.rs` (sha256 `5ed770895b0f644d425b86c612f1365ad4c58fefacedd62b9f34b612f0eb1bdb`, identical on sandbox and laptop) compiled standalone with `rustc` ON THE LAPTOP (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-worldline/`) and driven over boundary inputs:

| input | result | expected by the grammar's own conventions |
|---|---|---|
| `/logs 5` | `Logs { seconds: Some(5) }` | ✔ |
| `/logs5` | `Logs { seconds: Some(5) }` | unknown command / usage — no other verb accepts a glued argument |
| `/logs55` | `Logs { seconds: Some(55) }` | same |
| `/logs\t5` | `Logs { seconds: Some(5) }` | the other verbs require a literal space (`starts_with("/records ")`) |
| `/logsx` | `Message("usage: /logs [seconds]")` | (usage is fine here, but it proves the branch is entered by prefix alone) |
| `/document` | `Message("unknown command; type /help")` | `usage: /document <name>` — which is exactly what `/document ` (trailing space) returns |
| `/input` | `Message("unknown command; type /help")` | `usage: /input <hex>` — exactly what `/input ` returns |
| `/recordsx`, `/statsx`, `/helpme`, `/documentx y` | `Message("unknown command; type /help")` | ✔ controls: the other verbs do enforce their boundary |

## Root cause

- `world_line.rs:94` — the logs arm is `line.strip_prefix("/logs")` with no boundary check, then `rest.trim().parse::<u64>()`. Every sibling verb guards first: `/records` and `/documents` require `line == verb || line.starts_with(verb + " ")` (:57, :67), and `/stats`/`/caps`/`/help`/`/quit` are exact matches (:48-53).
- `/document` (:76) and `/input` (:106) only match `strip_prefix("/document ")` / `strip_prefix("/input ")` (trailing space included), so the bare verb falls through to the catch-all "unknown command" at :112 instead of the usage message those same arms produce for `"/document "` / `"/input "`.

## Why it matters

This grammar is the user-facing command surface on three transports at once (module doc, `world_line.rs:1-7`; consumers at `world_ssh.rs:1209` and `commands/world.rs:1544`). A typo like `/logs5` — or a script emitting `/logs60` — silently tails the world's event log for 5 (or 60) seconds instead of being refused, and a user who types `/document` or `/input` alone is told the command does not exist, sending them to `/help` for a verb that does exist. The parser's own tests (`world_line.rs:134-176`) pin the spaced forms and the unknown-command behaviour for `/nonsense`, but no test pins a glued or bare form of a real verb, so the inconsistency is invisible to the suite.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `/logs<digits>` with no separator (e.g. `/logs5`, `/logs55`) no longer parses as `Logs { seconds }` — it yields the same class of `Message` as other malformed/unknown commands; `/logs`, `/logs 5` keep working exactly as today.
- [ ] Bare `/document` and `/input` (no argument, no trailing space) produce their usage messages (`usage: /document <name>`, `usage: /input <hex>`), matching what the trailing-space forms already produce.
- [ ] New unit tests in `world_line.rs` pin the glued form, the tab-glued form (decide and pin: accept or refuse, consistently with the other verbs' space rule), and the bare-verb usage forms.
- [ ] Existing `world_line` tests and the SSH/pump mapping tests (`world_ssh.rs`, `commands/world.rs`) still pass; no consumer changes needed.

Related: #546 (the grammar itself, closed), #819 (closed — a different world-line defect: consumers discarding the parsed `/logs` seconds and the pump dying on a `Message`; this issue is parser-boundary behaviour only).
