body:
## Summary

In pkgs/id's web markdown codec (`pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs`), the save direction maps every PM `hard_break` to a comrak `LineBreak` node unconditionally (save arm at markdown.rs:1385), with no placement policy. A `LineBreak` renders in CommonMark as `\` + newline — which only means "hard break" inside a paragraph. In a **heading** (a single-line block) the emitted newline ends the heading: the text after the break is demoted to a paragraph, and the backslash comes back as literal heading text that gets escaped (doubled) on the next save. At the **end** of a paragraph or heading, and as the **only content** of a paragraph, the break is silently dropped on save.

`hard_break` is a schema-legal inline node in the rich editor (basic schema; `editor.test.ts:137` asserts `richSchema.nodes.hard_break` exists, and heading content is `inline*`), reachable by pasting line-broken content into a heading and by any client/collab peer sending schema-valid PM JSON — the same PM-originated standard as #1017 (hard_break in a table cell) and the other codec filings. Mid-paragraph breaks and a break at a paragraph start round-trip correctly; only the edge placements corrupt.

## Verified evidence (this run, main a1321fd5)

Verbatim-codec probe crate on the laptop (markdown.rs sha256 `f0b6b9cd…`, identical both sides; comrak 0.56.0; probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-laneA-1315` there; logs `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-laneA-1315/out2.log` + `out3.log` in the goal workspace). PM document → saved file → reopened PM → second save:

| PM document | Saved file | After reopen / 2nd save |
|---|---|---|
| heading `[a, hard_break, b]` | `# a\` ⏎ `b` | heading text is `a\` (literal backslash), `b` is a separate paragraph; 2nd save writes `# a\\` — the backslash doubles (then stabilizes) |
| heading `[hard_break, b]` | `## \` ⏎ `b` | heading text is `\`, `b` demoted to paragraph; 2nd save `## \\` |
| heading `[a, hard_break]` | `## a` | break silently dropped |
| paragraph `[text, hard_break]` (trailing) | `before` | break silently dropped |
| paragraph `[hard_break]` as only content, followed by `x` | `x` only | **the whole paragraph is deleted on save** |
| paragraph `[hard_break, text]` (control) | `\` ⏎ `after` | round-trips exactly |

## Why it matters

Every open→save→open cycle on a document with a break inside a heading visibly mangles it: the heading splits in two, a stray backslash appears in the heading text (and doubles once), and the demoted text loses its heading formatting. Trailing breaks and a break-only spacer paragraph vanish without any signal. The codec already has placement discipline elsewhere (the `MisplacedNode` guard at markdown.rs:47-56 rejects block/inline misplacement instead of emitting invalid markdown, #1043) — `LineBreak` placement is the unguarded remainder of that policy.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A placement policy for `hard_break` is picked and pinned in the codec: breaks inside a heading and at block edges are either preserved across open→save→open or normalized at save (e.g. to a space in a heading, dropped deliberately at block end) so the first saved file is already a byte fixpoint and no backslash ever appears as literal heading text.
- [ ] The heading cases above never split the heading or demote its trailing text to a paragraph.
- [ ] The break-only paragraph case is explicitly decided (round-trips as an empty paragraph, or is dropped at save by the documented policy) — not silently deleted as an emergent renderer effect.
- [ ] Regression tests in `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs` cover: break mid-heading, at heading start, at heading end, at paragraph end, break-only paragraph, and the paragraph-start control; mid-paragraph break behavior (#1017 cell case included) is unchanged.
- [ ] Existing `web::markdown` tests pass in CI.

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-a (Lane A), verified this run. Related: #1420 (edge *whitespace in text runs* lost on reopen — different node and direction: this is the `hard_break` node lost/corrupted on save), #1418 (marked-span edge spaces), #1017 (hard_break inside a table cell, which works).

title: aggregator: Needs-you 'Newest first' sorts tier cards by lastSeenAt while 'Oldest first' sorts by since — the two orders are not reverses, and a 30-day-old card can lead 'Newest first'

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

body:
## Summary

The Needs-you card order preference (#1456, closed) applies its sorts at render in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/render.ts`, but the two age orders use **different timestamp axes**:

- `newest` sorts by `seenMs` — the card's `lastSeenAt` (render.ts:2303)
- `oldest` sorts by `sinceMs` — the card's `since` (render.ts:2304)

For session cards both fields are the same value (`lastActivityAt`, render.ts:2284-2289), so the orders are exact reverses there. For tier-item cards they diverge: `sinceMs = Date.parse(item.since)` and `seenMs = Date.parse(item.lastSeenAt)` (render.ts:2295-2296). `since` is when the item entered the queue; `lastSeenAt` is refreshed whenever the publisher last saw the underlying item — so under "Newest first", a card that has been waiting 30 days but was seen 5 minutes ago outranks a card that entered the queue 1 hour ago. The two options present as opposite ends of one axis ("Newest first" / "Oldest first", render.ts:2151-2152) but are not reverses of each other.

## Verified evidence (this run, main 49e67083)

Probe on the laptop (verbatim `pm-stack/aggregator/src` tree; render.ts sha256 `005acc70…` and derive.ts sha256 `312ac0fb…` identical on sandbox main and the laptop copy; Bun 1.4.2; probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-laneA-needsorder` there, log `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-laneA-needsorder/out.log` in the goal workspace). Two tier cards rendered through the real `buildAttention` + `renderAttention` with `needsOrder` set:

- NEWCARD: `since` = 1h ago, `lastSeenAt` = 2h ago
- OLDCARD: `since` = 30d ago, `lastSeenAt` = 5m ago

Result:

```
newest: [ "OLDCARD", "NEWCARD" ]   ← the 30-day-old card leads "Newest first"
oldest: [ "OLDCARD", "NEWCARD" ]   ← identical order — not a reversal
control newest: [ "NEWCARD", "OLDCARD" ]
control oldest: [ "OLDCARD", "NEWCARD" ]
```

The control pair (where `since` and `lastSeenAt` agree in ordering) reverses correctly, which isolates the defect to the axis mismatch, not the sort machinery. The `deadline` order also ties/falls back on `seenMs` (render.ts:2305: `a.rank - b.rank || b.seenMs - a.seenMs`), so it inherits the same question.

The existing test suite only pins `newest` with cards that differ solely in `lastSeenAt` and share one `since` (`test/dashboard-overhaul.test.ts:274-286`, BASE `since` at :29) — `oldest` has no render test at all.

## Why it matters

The Needs-you list is Drew's triage surface; the saved order is a standing preference he set (#1456). "Newest first" that actually sorts by last-seen buries genuinely new arrivals under long-waiting cards that the orchestrator merely re-saw in its latest run — the opposite of what the control promises — and "oldest"/"newest" giving the same list makes the preference look broken.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `newest` and `oldest` sort tier-item cards on a single, documented axis (the natural reading: the card's queue age, `since` — matching what `oldest` already does), so the two orders are exact reverses for the same card set.
- [ ] Session cards keep behaving as today (their `since`/`lastSeenAt` are the same instant).
- [ ] The `deadline` tiebreak is decided consistently with the chosen axis and the choice is noted in a code comment.
- [ ] Regression tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/dashboard-overhaul.test.ts` cover tier cards whose `since` and `lastSeenAt` orderings disagree, for both `newest` and `oldest` (the divergent case above), plus the agreeing control.
- [ ] Full aggregator test suite passes in CI.

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-a (Lane A), verified this run. Related: #1456 (the feature this fixes), #1474 (sibling card-state derivation bug, different function).

body:
Phase 2 of design #1481 (JSON Schema validation of tool input and output). Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-json-schema-validation.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Origin gap: dezren39/nix#254.

**Dependency gate:** do not start until Phase 1 (the `internal/schemaval` core) is merged — this phase consumes its compile/validate API. If claimed earlier, park naming the dependency.

## Scope

Enforce at the one choke point every call surface funnels through — `internal/mcpclient`:

- **List time:** in `Client.ListTools` (`internal/mcpclient/client.go:1051`), compile each tool's `InputSchema` and `OutputSchema` with `schemaval`, as a sibling pass to `checkToolHeaders` (`internal/mcpclient/modern.go:495`). A tool whose schema does not compile (unsupported dialect, unresolvable/external `$ref`, invalid or oversized schema) is **excluded from the list with a `Warning`** carrying the cause — the x-mcp-header precedent; the pool already surfaces warnings as `server.warning` lifecycle events. Compiled validators are cached per client, per tool, keyed by schema hash so a re-list recompiles only changed schemas.
- **Inputs, enforced:** `Client.CallTool` (client.go:1164) validates the marshalled arguments against the tool's compiled input validator **before** the transport is touched. Failure returns an Invalid Params (-32602) error naming the tool and the path-qualified reason. Surfaces that translate generic call errors into an `isError` tool result (the gateway invoke path in `internal/mcpserver`) must pass this error through as the protocol error it is — a caller bug is not a tool failure. Scripts, `mcpx_call`, `/v1/call` and pass-through inherit the check via `Pool.Call` → `CallTool`; no per-surface duplication.
- **Outputs, warn-only:** when a `CallTool` result carries `structuredContent` and the tool declared an `outputSchema`, validate it. Failure produces a `Warning` (+ the lifecycle event that follows from it) and the result is delivered **unchanged**. Do not enforce outputs in this phase — the flip decision is an open question on #1481, answered with this phase's warning data.
- Tools with no `inputSchema`/`outputSchema` behave exactly as today.

Out of scope: elicitation answer validation (Phase 3); format assertion; any per-server validation-mode config; codegen changes; closing the conformance rows for elicitation (Phase 3) — this phase updates the matrix/gap registry for the tool input/output + dialect rows it closes.

## Acceptance

- Defining test: a call whose arguments violate the tool's `inputSchema` (wrong type; missing required; forbidden additional property — at least the first two) fails with -32602 naming the path, and the fake upstream's call count stays **0**.
- Defining test: valid arguments reach the upstream byte-identical to today's behaviour (existing call tests unmodified and green).
- Defining test: a tool whose schema declares an unsupported dialect (or carries an unresolvable `$ref`) is absent from `ListTools`, absent from a gateway tools/list, and a `Warning` with the cause was emitted.
- Defining test: a result whose `structuredContent` violates `outputSchema` is returned to the caller unchanged, with a `Warning` recorded; a conforming one records none.
- Benchmark sanity: argument validation on a representative nested schema (triage picks it from a real catalog tool) stays within a triage-set per-call budget; record the measured number on this issue.
- Conformance matrix rows for `json-schema-support-2020-12`, `json-schema-validate-per-dialect-and-error-on-unsupported`, `json-schema-document-dialects`, `json-schema-reject-unresolved-ref` and the matching gap-registry entries are updated to reflect enforcement (server + client sides as each applies).
- Full suite passes: `cd pkgs/mcpx && go test ./...` (via CI on the PR per fleet policy).

Filed as `task/triage`: triage confirms scope against current main once Phase 1 has landed (gate above) and enqueues the implementation packet; do not implement in the triage task.

body:
Phase 1 of design #1481 (JSON Schema validation of tool input and output). Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-json-schema-validation.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Origin gap: dezren39/nix#254 — its acceptance requires the validator decision recorded before implementation; that decision is recorded on #1481 (adopt `github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6` behind `internal/schemaval`; `internal/mcpspec` stays the test-only protocol-frame validator).

## Scope

Build the validator core only — **no call-path changes, nothing enforces yet**:

- New package `internal/schemaval` (name indicative; settle at triage) wrapping `github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6`; it is the **only** package importing the dependency. Add the dependency to `pkgs/mcpx/go.mod` (cause recorded on #1481: full 2020-12 support is a MUST row in mcpx's own conformance matrix; the library passes the JSON-Schema-Test-Suite and covers drafts 4/6/7/2019-09/2020-12).
- Dialect policy: a schema with no `$schema` compiles as 2020-12; a declared `$schema` must name 2020-12, 2019-09, draft-07, draft-06 or draft-04 — anything else returns a distinct, typed `UnsupportedDialect` error.
- **No network, ever:** the compiler's loader resolves only inline/already-registered resources. An external `$ref` is a typed `UnresolvedRef` compile error; an internal unresolvable `$ref` is likewise a compile error. Fetching is not an option the API exposes.
- Compilation is bounded: a maximum schema size (settle the number at triage against real catalog schemas) — an oversized or pathological schema fails compilation as invalid rather than consuming the daemon.
- Validation API: compile once from `json.RawMessage`, validate decoded instances; instances must be decoded the way the library requires (`jsonschema.UnmarshalJSON`) so >2^53 integers keep numeric fidelity. Validation errors flatten to a concise path-carrying form, e.g. `$.count: expected integer, got string`.
- Formats are annotations, not assertions, in v1 (`format: email` alone never fails validation).
- Dialect document: add the supported-dialect list + the policies above to `pkgs/mcpx/docs/`, and note in `internal/conformance/coverage_messages.go` that the validator mechanism exists (row closures land with Phases 2–3, not here).
- Package comment in `schemaval` must state the division of labour plainly: `mcpspec` = protocol frames, tests only; `schemaval` = tool/elicitation schemas, in the binary.

Out of scope: any change to `ListTools`, `CallTool`, `Client.answer`, codegen, or the daemon; enforcement of any kind; format assertion.

## Acceptance

- Defining tests pass: (a) 2020-12 keyword corpus incl. `prefixItems`, `unevaluatedProperties`, boolean schemas, `$defs` internal refs; (b) declared draft-07 schema compiles and validates per draft-07; (c) unsupported `$schema` dialect → `UnsupportedDialect` error, distinct from a generic compile error; (d) unresolvable `$ref` → compile error; (e) schema with a remote `$ref` → compile error and **zero** HTTP requests observed by a counting test server; (f) integer `9007199254740993` (2^53+1) validates as `integer` and fails a `maximum: 9007199254740992` check correctly; (g) a value violating a nested required/type rule returns the path-qualified error form.
- `go.mod` gains exactly one new direct dependency; `internal/mcpspec` is untouched and `TestNotImportedByBinary` still passes.
- Dialect document exists in `pkgs/mcpx/docs/` stating supported dialects, the no-network rule, and formats-as-annotations.

body:
# aggregator: a REJECTED restore still cancels its target in card-state — the card resurfaces even though the consumer refused the restore

## Summary

`pm-stack/aggregator/src/card-state.ts` derives each dashboard card's effective state at render time. Its documented contract (module header, lines 13–21) is that consumer **rejections are non-effective**: "A consumer REJECTION lifts the suppression again (the item resurfaces, with the rejection badge explaining why)." Every verb family honours that rule — snooze (:73), dismiss (:77), done (:79), answer (:86), ack (:92) all check `state !== "rejected"` — **except restore**. `cancelledActionIds` (:52–58) cancels the action named in a restore's `supersedes` for any restore whose state is merely not `"superseded"`, so a restore the consumer **rejected** still cancels its target at render time.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 7eca828d)

Probe: the verbatim aggregator `src/` tree (card-state.ts sha256 `76f9f438…`, identical on both sides) driven under Bun on the laptop, using the same `mkAction` fixture shape as `test/dashboard-overhaul.test.ts`:

```
control applied-dismiss + new restore:      suppressed=null       cancelled=da-dismiss  eff=da-restore
control applied-dismiss alone:              suppressed=dismissed  cancelled=            eff=da-dismiss
applied-dismiss + REJECTED restore:         suppressed=null       cancelled=da-dismiss  eff=da-restore   <-- BUG
future snooze + REJECTED restore:           suppressed=null       cancelled=da-snooze   eff=da-restore   <-- BUG
applied ack + REJECTED restore of ack:      acked=false           cancelled=da-ack                      <-- BUG
```

So with an applied dismiss in place and a restore that the consumer rejected (with a note, per `actions.ts:43-44`), the dashboard renders the card as restored — it leaves the hidden strip and returns to its main list — even though the restore never took effect. The same happens for a live snooze (card resurfaces before its `until`) and for an applied acknowledge (card loses its "seen, not resolved" quiet state).

Root cause: `card-state.ts:54` —

```ts
if (a.verb === "restore" && a.state !== "superseded" && a.supersedes) out.add(a.supersedes);
```

`state === "rejected"` must also exclude a restore from cancelling, exactly as the other verbs are excluded. (A *pending* restore must keep cancelling — that is the verified control above and the committed test at `dashboard-overhaul.test.ts:123`.)

## Why it matters

The dashboard is Drew's triage surface: a card that resurfaces reads as "this needs you again". A rejected restore (consumer could not apply it, e.g. the underlying object changed) silently resurrecting dismissed/snoozed items re-adds noise the user explicitly removed, and the rendered state disagrees with the store's applied truth — the exact class of divergence #1442/#1443 built this derivation layer to eliminate. No error is shown; the rejection badge logic never gets a chance to explain anything because the target action is filtered out of `effectiveActions` entirely.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `cardState([appliedDismiss, rejectedRestore(supersedes=dismiss)])` returns `suppressed.kind === "dismissed"`; the dismiss remains in `effectiveActions`.
- [ ] Same for snooze (future `until` → still `snoozed`) and acknowledge (applied ack + rejected restore → `acked === true`).
- [ ] Pending (`new`) and applied restores still cancel their target (existing test at `dashboard-overhaul.test.ts:123` keeps passing).
- [ ] New regression tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/dashboard-overhaul.test.ts` cover the rejected-restore cases, mirroring the existing rejected-dismiss test at :120.
- [ ] Full aggregator test suite passes in CI.

## Scope notes

- Fix is expected to be confined to `cancelledActionIds` in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/card-state.ts` (plus tests); if triage finds the store's own supersede transition has the same gap, note it on this issue rather than expanding scope silently.
- Distinct from #1452 (actions/comments store evaluation) and #1405 (Cost Explorer test coverage) — different module, different defect.

title: id(web): file-list pagination display still multiplies the raw page unchecked — debug panic / wrapped inverted range for page=usize::MAX (the #931 remainder in templates.rs)

body:
## Bug

`id(web)`: the file-list pagination **display** arithmetic in `render_file_list_content` still multiplies the raw page number unchecked — the remainder of #931 that its fix did not cover.

`pkgs/id/src/web/templates.rs:350` (main `1ff34134`):

```rust
let start = (page.page - 1) * page.per_page + 1;
let end = (start + page.files.len()).saturating_sub(1);
```

This runs whenever `total_pages > 1` (templates.rs:339-340). The values reaching it are not bounded above:

- `paginate()` in `pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs:934-946` (the #931 fix) clamps `per_page` to `1..=200` and computes its own offset with `saturating_sub`/`saturating_mul` — but it deliberately **echoes `page` back unclamped** (`page.unwrap_or(1).max(1)`), and its regression test `test_paginate_overflow_page` (routes.rs:3104) asserts `page == usize::MAX` is returned for `?page=18446744073709551615`.
- `get_file_list_page` passes that echoed `page` straight into `FileListPage`, which both `/files` and `/api/files` render through `render_file_list_content`.

So a well-formed query such as `/api/files?page=18446744073709551615&per_page=50` on any instance with more files than one page (e.g. 300 files) reaches line 350 with `page = usize::MAX`, `per_page = 50`, `files = []`.

## Verified this run

Standalone rustc probe on the laptop replicating templates.rs:339-351 verbatim, fed exactly the values `paginate()` returns for that query (probe: `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-templates-pagination/probe_tpl.rs`, log `out.log` in the goal bookkeeping):

- **Control** (page 2, per_page 50, total 300, 50 files shown): `51-100 of 300 (page 2 / 6)` — correct in both build modes.
- **Debug semantics** (overflow checks on — the dev/test profiles; `pkgs/id/Cargo.toml` sets no overflow-checks override): **panic `attempt to multiply with overflow`** at the `start` computation, exit 101. Through the real handler that is a panicked request task for `/files` and `/api/files`.
- **Release semantics** (overflow checks off): the range **wraps** to `18446744073709551517-18446744073709551516 of 300` — an inverted, bogus range (start > end, both astronomically larger than the total) rendered as if it were the requested page's range. With `per_page=200` (the clamp maximum): `18446744073709551217-18446744073709551216 of 300`.

## Why it matters

#931 closed the wrong-page/panic hole in the offset computation, but the same untrusted `page` value still flows into a second unchecked multiplication in the renderer — so the exact class of bug #931 was filed for (debug panic / release wrong output from a crafted or buggy client query) is still reachable on the web UI's main listing endpoint. Wrong-range output is worse than an error: the UI presents it as the requested page's position.

Related: #931 (closed — fixed `paginate()` in routes.rs only; this filing is its renderer remainder, not a duplicate: different file, different arithmetic, still live on current main).

## Acceptance criteria

- The pagination display arithmetic in `render_file_list_content` cannot overflow or wrap for any `FileListPage` values: use saturating/checked arithmetic for `start` (and audit `total_pages` at templates.rs:339 and `end` at :351 in the same pass).
- For an out-of-range page, the rendered range is sane (e.g. an empty/clamped range that never shows start > end and never exceeds the total), while normal pages render exactly as today (`51-100 of 300` for page 2 at per_page 50).
- Regression tests cover at least: `page=usize::MAX, per_page=50, total=300, files=[]`; `page=usize::MAX, per_page=200`; and the existing normal paging display cases still pass.
- Targeted test path: the existing templates/routes test modules (`cargo test --features web --lib web::templates` / `web::routes`), run on CI or the laptop — not a sandbox build.

## Suggested fix

In `render_file_list_content` (templates.rs:350-351), compute `start` as `page.page.saturating_sub(1).saturating_mul(page.per_page).saturating_add(1)` and clamp the displayed range to the total (an out-of-range page has `files.is_empty()`, so displaying `0-0 of {total}` or suppressing the range is defensible — pick one and pin it in the test). Alternatively clamp `page` to `total_pages` in `get_file_list_page` — but note `paginate()`'s echo-the-requested-page behaviour is pinned by its existing test, so the renderer-side fix is the smaller change.

Single-repo: `render_file_list_content` is `pkgs/id`-local; no copy exists in the other three fleet repos.

body:
## Summary

`richSchema` in the id web editor declares **no `tight` attr for `bullet_list`** and **no `tight` attr for `ordered_list`**, even though the Rust markdown codec carries `tight` on both. `Node.fromJSON` silently drops undeclared attrs on editor load, and the codec's save side defaults a missing `tight` to `false` (loose). Net effect: **every tight bullet or ordered list opened in the web editor is rewritten as a loose list on the next save** — blank lines are inserted between every item. This is the same schema-mirror defect class as #1036 (`task_list`, fixed) and #1436 (`code_block`, fixed today in PR #1447); those two fixes mirrored their node types and left the plain list types behind.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `1ff34134`)

TS side — `pkgs/id/web/src/editor.ts:46`:

- The schema is built as `addListNodes(basicSchema.spec.nodes, "paragraph block*", "block")` and then `.update(...)` is applied only to `code_block` (:47) and `image` (:73); the appended nodes (`task_list`, `table`, `html_inline`, …) include the `task_list` mirror from #1036. `bullet_list` / `ordered_list` / `list_item` are never updated.
- In `prosemirror-schema-list@1.5.1` (the version in `pkgs/id/web/package.json`), `bulletList` declares **no attrs at all** and `orderedList` declares only `{order: {default: 1}}`.

Probe — verbatim `richSchema` definition extracted from `editor.ts` (sha256 `81a60bfd…`), run under Bun **on the laptop** (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-laneA-lists`, log `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-laneA-lists/out.log` in the goal workspace):

```
bullet tight=true  IN : {"tight":true}            OUT: null            SPEC attrs: []
bullet tight=false IN : {"tight":false}           OUT: null            SPEC attrs: []
ordered order=3 tight=true  IN : {"order":3,"tight":true}  OUT: {"order":3}  SPEC attrs: ["order"]
ordered order=3 tight=false IN : {"order":3,"tight":false} OUT: {"order":3}  SPEC attrs: ["order"]
task_list tight=false (control, #1036)  IN : {"tight":false,"order":null} OUT: {"tight":false,"order":null}  SPEC attrs: ["tight","order"]
code_block params/htmlBlock (control, #1436) IN : {"params":"html","htmlBlock":true} OUT: {"params":"html","htmlBlock":true}  SPEC attrs: ["params","htmlBlock"]
```

`tight` is dropped in **both** directions for plain lists; `order` survives; the two previously fixed node types survive as controls.

Rust side — `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs`:

- Parse emits it: bullet `"attrs": {"tight": tight}` (:267-268), ordered `"attrs": {"order": list.start, "tight": tight}` (:257-261).
- Save requires it: `bullet_list` arm `let tight = json["attrs"]["tight"].as_bool().unwrap_or(false);` (:1193) and `ordered_list` arm the same (:1205) — a missing attr becomes a loose `NodeList`, which comrak renders with blank lines between items.

So `- a\n- b` (tight) → editor load (attr dropped) → save → `- a\n\n- b` (loose). Loose lists survive only by accident, because the save-side default happens to be `false`.

## Why it matters

Tight lists are the overwhelmingly common case. Any document containing one is silently reformatted — every item separated by a blank line — by a single open + save in the web editor, producing noisy whole-document diffs and changing list rendering semantics. It is silent data corruption of the same class the fleet has been fixing node type by node type (#1036, #1436); this is the remaining unmirrored node pair.

## Fix direction

Mirror the codec attrs into `richSchema` following the #1036/#1436 pattern: `.update("bullet_list", { attrs: { tight: { default: <see below> } }, … })` and `.update("ordered_list", { attrs: { order: { default: 1 }, tight: { default: <see below> } }, … })`, preserving the inherited `content`/`group`/`parseDOM`/`toDOM` fields exactly as the `code_block` update does. Choose the `tight` default deliberately (the codec's legacy-doc inference in the `task_list` arm at :1225 is the house precedent for absent-attr docs); a `false` default matches the codec's current save-side behaviour for editor-created lists.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `richSchema.nodeFromJSON` → `toJSON` round-trips `bullet_list` `attrs.tight` (`true` and `false`) and `ordered_list` `attrs {order, tight}` unchanged; `order` behaviour is not regressed.
- [ ] A tight bullet list and a tight ordered list survive a full open → editor load → save cycle byte-identically (codec round-trip test or editor + codec integration evidence).
- [ ] Regression tests in `pkgs/id/web/src/editor.test.ts` in the style of the #1436 `code_block` block (spec declares the attrs; `{params…}`-style fromJSON→toJSON cases for both list types).
- [ ] Existing `editor.test.ts` and `web::markdown` suites pass in CI; lists created fresh in the editor still save correctly (tight by default for single-paragraph items).

## Dedup

Checked open + closed issues for `tight` / `bullet_list` / `ordered_list` schema mirroring this run: #1036 (closed) covered `task_list` only; #1436 (closed, PR #1447) covered `code_block` only. #1380 (ordered-list `)` delimiter), #1397 (adjacent-list end comments), and #1370 (mixed task/plain lists) are different mechanisms in the Rust codec, not the editor schema.

# id(web): SPA navigation and partial swaps apply responses in arrival order — a slow earlier request overwrites the page/list the user asked for last ## Evidence (verified this run, main 95cd41f0) `pkgs/id/web/src/main.ts`: - `navigateTo(url)` (main.ts:656-689) awaits `fetch(url)` and then unconditionally assigns `main.innerHTML = html` (main.ts:676), pushes the URL into history (main.ts:678) and runs `onMainSwapped()`. There is no sequence token, no `AbortController`, and no check that a newer navigation has started since this fetch was issued. - `fetchPartial(url, targetSelector)` (main.ts:632-650) — used for file search, pagination, the tags-WebSocket refresh, and peers auto-refresh — has the same shape: it awaits the fetch and unconditionally assigns `target.innerHTML = html` (main.ts:644). - Callers issue these concurrently in normal use: rapid clicks on two `[data-nav]` links (click delegation at the bottom of main.ts calls `navigateTo` per click), a click racing a `popstate`, the debounced file search (300 ms) racing the tags-WS refresh (500 ms-debounced, same `#file-list-content` target), or pagination racing search. ### Probe (verbatim functions, laptop) `fetchPartial` and `navigateTo` extracted verbatim from main.ts:632-689 (file sha256 `43e3541e…` at main 95cd41f0) and driven under Bun on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-laneA-races/nav-probe.ts`; log `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-laneA-races/nav-out.log`) with a test-controlled deferred `fetch`: ``` Scenario A — navigateTo("/files") issued first but slow; navigateTo("/edit/b.md") second, fast: after B resolves: main = "

page B (second click)

" history = ["/edit/b.md"] after A resolves: main = "

files page (first click)

" history = ["/edit/b.md","/files"] onMainSwapped calls = 2 VERDICT A: final page is the FIRST click's page, not the last action's: true Scenario B — fetchPartial("/api/files?search=ab") issued first but slow; fetchPartial("/api/files?search=abc") second, fast; same target: file list final content: "
  • results for ab (stale)
    • " VERDICT B: stale first-issued response overwrote the newer one: true ``` In scenario A the user ends up viewing — and with a history entry for — the page they clicked *first*, even though their last action chose a different page; `onMainSwapped` also runs twice, so editor open/close, nav-history bookkeeping (`app.navHistory` gains the intermediate path) and the back-link/subtitle state are computed for a page that is immediately replaced. In scenario B the file list shows results for a query the search box no longer contains. ## Why it matters The whole id web UI is this SPA shell: every file open, file-list search, pagination step, tags refresh and peers refresh flows through these two functions. On a slow or loaded server (or a LAN peer with uneven latency) any two overlapping requests can put the UI into a state that contradicts the user's last action — wrong document on screen with a matching-but-wrong URL, or a file list silently filtered by a stale query. Because content and URL stay consistent with each other (both come from the stale response), the user has no visual cue that their click was effectively undone. Related but distinct: #1440 is the AutoSaveManager's concurrent-save race inside one document; this is the navigation/partial-swap layer. The AutoSaveManager fix does not touch these two functions. ## Acceptance criteria - Only the most recently issued `navigateTo` may swap `#main`, push history, or run `onMainSwapped`; a superseded navigation's response is dropped (or its fetch aborted) — verified by a deferred-fetch test in the style of the probe where the first-issued navigation resolves last and the final page/history reflect the second navigation only. - Only the most recently issued `fetchPartial` **per target selector** may write that target; a superseded partial response is dropped — verified by an out-of-order test against `#file-list-content` where the stale response resolves last and the newer content remains. - Error behaviour is preserved for the *current* request: a failed current navigation still falls back to `window.location.href = url`, and a failed current partial still just logs. - A superseded navigation must not close/reopen the editor or run `onMainSwapped` side effects for a page that never lands.

body:
# id(web): world page rejoin leaves a ghost WebSocket — the old socket's async close spawns a duplicate connection that double-joins and duplicates every frame

## Evidence (verified this run, main 95cd41f0)

`pkgs/id/web/src/world.ts`:

- The Join button handler (world.ts:514-523) tries to retire the old socket before reconnecting:
  ```ts
  joinButton.addEventListener("click", () => {
    if (socket) {
      intentionalClose = true;
      socket.onclose = null;          // <-- does not detach anything
      socket.close();
      socket = null;
    }
    intentionalClose = false;         // <-- reset synchronously, in the same task
    connect();
  });
  ```
- But `connect()` (world.ts:270-296) registered its handlers with `addEventListener` (open at :280, close at :287) — there is no `onclose` property handler to null out. Assigning `socket.onclose = null` removes nothing.
- A browser dispatches the `close` event asynchronously, after the click handler's task finishes. By then `intentionalClose` is already back to `false`, so the old socket's close handler (world.ts:287-295) treats the deliberate rejoin close as an unexpected drop: it sets status `Disconnected; retrying…` and schedules a reconnect.
- ~500 ms later that timer calls `connect()` again, creating a **third** socket and overwriting the module-level `socket` variable. The second socket (created by the rejoin click itself) is never closed — it stays live as a ghost.
- The handlers also reference the shared mutable `socket` variable instead of the socket they were attached to: the `open` handler at world.ts:282 sends the join frame via `socket?.send(...)`, so when the ghost socket opens, its join frame is sent on whichever socket is current.

### Probe (verbatim source, laptop)

Verbatim `world.ts` + its three dependency modules from main 95cd41f0 (world.ts sha256 `0a7217c4…`, matching the sandbox clone), driven under Bun on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-laneA-races/world-probe.ts`; log `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-laneA-races/world-out.log`) with a fake WebSocket modelling browser semantics (close event async; `onclose = null` does not remove `addEventListener` handlers) and a sessionStorage capability so the page auto-connects:

```
after init: sockets = 1
after rejoin click: sockets = 2
after ws1 close event: status = "Disconnected; retrying…" sockets = 2
after 700ms: sockets = 3
live sockets after opens: 2   join frames sent: 0+2   (ws2's open sent its join on ws3)
chat lines appended for ONE broadcast event: 2
```

So after one rejoin the browser holds two live world sockets, both joined (the server sees two participants/sessions for one browser), and one logical broadcast chat event is appended to the log **twice**. Every further rejoin multiplies this.

## Why it matters

Rejoin is the normal recovery path on the world page — it is the button a user clicks after pasting a fresh capability or when a session looks stuck. Instead of replacing the connection it accumulates them: duplicate participants in the roster, duplicated chat/input frames in the log, duplicate `records` pagination chains, and extra load on the server's per-connection state. The status line also flashes a spurious "Disconnected; retrying…" after every deliberate rejoin.

Distinct from #1368 (collab.ts reconnect-cap reset in the editor's collab socket): this is the world page's separate socket lifecycle in world.ts, and the defect is the rejoin teardown, not the backoff counter.

## Acceptance criteria

- Clicking Join/rejoin leaves exactly **one** live WebSocket: the retired socket's close event cannot schedule a reconnect, overwrite the current-socket reference, or change the status line.
- The close/open handlers act on the socket they were attached to (captured per-connection), not on the shared mutable `socket` variable; a stale socket's `open` cannot send a join frame on a newer socket.
- A regression test (fake WebSocket with async close dispatch, in the style of the probe) shows: init → open → rejoin click → old close event → backoff window elapses ⇒ exactly 2 sockets created total, exactly 1 live, exactly 1 join frame sent, and one broadcast frame appended once.
- Genuine unexpected drops still auto-reconnect with the existing backoff (the fix must not remove the reconnect path, only the ghost).

body: ## Summary `updateHeaderSubtitle` in `pkgs/id/web/src/main.ts` builds the header subtitle with `innerHTML` and interpolates the last-opened document's **raw filename** unescaped. A document whose name contains HTML markup turns into live DOM — including event-handler attributes — when the user navigates back to a main page. Document names are untrusted input in this codebase (the Rust templates escape them, `home.ts` renders them with `textContent`), and id is a peer-to-peer tool: a file received from a peer can carry a crafted name (any name without `/` is a legal filename on Linux, e.g. `.md`). ## Evidence (verified this run on main `95cd41f0`) Data flow: - Server: `pkgs/id/src/web/templates.rs:421-422,486` — `render_editor` URL-encodes the raw name into `data-filename="{name_urlencoded}"` (escaping is deliberately left to the encoding). - Client: `pkgs/id/web/src/main.ts:1196-1202` — `openEditor` does `decodeURIComponent(dataset.filename)`, recovering the **raw** name, and stores it as `this.lastFilename`. - Sink: `pkgs/id/web/src/main.ts:544-555` — `onMainSwapped` calls `updateHeaderSubtitle(app.lastFilename, app.lastFilePath, …)` (:743), which runs: ```ts subtitle.innerHTML = `// ${lastFilename}`; ``` No escaping of either interpolation. (The Rust shell spells the same name with `html_escape`, templates.rs:213/:420; `home.ts` renders document/tag names via `textContent` with the comment "tag values are untrusted user metadata".) Probe: the verbatim function (main.ts:544-555, sha256 `c32b3659…` identical both sides) driven under Bun + happy-dom 21 on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-subtitle`, log `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-subtitle/out.log`): | input filename | result | |---|---| | `notes.md` (control) | one `notes.md`, no extra elements | | `.md` | a real `` element inside the subtitle with `onerror="alert(1)"` — in a browser the failed `src=x` load fires it | | `x.md` renders as literal text inside a single anchor pointing at the file. - [ ] The `href` value is likewise set as a property/attribute (not string-interpolated into markup), so quotes in a path cannot break out of the attribute. - [ ] A regression test in `pkgs/id/web` (vitest/happy-dom) pins both cases above plus the benign control (`notes.md` → one anchor, correct text and href). - [ ] Audit note in the fix PR: the remaining `innerHTML` sinks in `main.ts` (`fetchPartial`/`navigateTo` swap server-rendered HTML — out of scope here, but confirm they only ever receive server-template HTML, never raw user strings). Found by new-issue-creator lane B, verified this run; distinct from closed #908 (/blob content-type XSS — different sink, already fixed).

title: id(web): AutoSaveManager runs concurrent saves and a stale completion marks newer edits saved

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

`AutoSaveManager` in `pkgs/id/web/src/main.ts` does not serialize saves. The debounce and rate-limit-retry paths call `triggerSave()` with no in-flight guard — the `state === "saving"` check exists only in `saveNow()` — so an edit made while a save is in flight starts a **second concurrent `/api/save` POST** once its debounce fires. A stale save completion also overwrites the state of newer edits: when the older save resolves after the user has typed more, `onSaveResult` sets the state to `saved` and the button reads "saved ✓" while the newer edit is still unsaved (its debounce still pending).

## Evidence (verified on main `95cd41f0`, 2026-10-27)

Verbatim extract of the manager from `main.ts` (`SaveResult` type :15, `AUTOSAVE_DEBOUNCE_MS` :22, `SaveState` :24, class :26–200; sha-verbatim lines driven under Bun on the laptop with a controllable `saveFn` whose promises resolve only when the probe says so; log in the goal's `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-autosave/out.log`):

```
after edit1 state: unsaved
after debounce: calls = 1 state: saving (save #1 in flight, unresolved)
after edit2 (during flight) state: unsaved
after edit2 debounce: calls = 2 maxInFlight = 2 state: saving
after resolving save#2: state: saved
after resolving stale save#1: state: saved calls: 2
scenario B: state after older save resolves with newer edit pending: saved (debounce still pending, calls: 1)
```

Code facts:

- `triggerSave()` (main.ts, class body) sets `state = "saving"` and awaits `saveFn()` unconditionally — no re-entry guard, no generation/dirty counter.
- `saveNow()` is the only guarded entry point (`if (this.state === "saving" || this.state === "rate-limited") return;`); the debounce timer in `onContentChange()` and the retry timer in `onSaveResult()` both call `triggerSave()` directly.
- `onSaveResult()` applies its transition unconditionally: a completion cannot tell whether the document changed after its save started.
- `saveFile()` (main.ts:1296) captures `state.doc` at call time and, on success, writes the returned hash into `editorContainer.dataset.hash`. Two overlapping saves therefore carry two different snapshots, and whichever response completes last wins the `dataset.hash` update — completion order, not capture order.

## Why it matters

- The save indicator can say "saved ✓" for content that has not been saved yet (scenario B). A user who trusts it and closes or navigates away in that window loses the pending edit — the debounce only saves it if the page stays open.
- Overlapping saves waste the server's save budget (the endpoint rate-limits, 429 + `retryAfterMs` handling exists for a reason) and can interleave the `dataset.hash` bookkeeping with the wrong save's result.
- Slow saves make this easy to hit: the debounce is 2s, so any save slower than ~2s (large document, slow network, server archiving on save) plus continued typing overlaps.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] At most one `saveFn()` invocation is ever in flight: an edit during a save schedules exactly one follow-up save after the current one settles (coalescing, not dropping, and not a second concurrent call).
- [ ] A save completion never moves the indicator to `saved` when an edit arrived after that save started (track a dirty generation/epoch, or equivalent); the indicator keeps showing the pending edit as unsaved until a save that covers it completes.
- [ ] The rate-limit retry path obeys the same serialization (a retry does not overlap a newer save, and a newer save does not silently cancel a pending retry without rescheduling).
- [ ] `saveNow()` behaviour is unchanged for the idle/unsaved cases (immediate save, no-op while saving).
- [ ] Regression tests drive the manager with a controllable `saveFn` (deferred promises) covering: edit-during-flight ⇒ exactly one follow-up save, max one in flight; stale completion ⇒ state stays `unsaved`; retry-after-429 ⇒ single serialized retry. (The class is currently private inside `main.ts`; exporting it for tests, as was done for `identity-refresh.ts` / `world-seed.ts` pure helpers, is an acceptable way to make it testable.)

## Notes

- Distinct from #1230 (e2e test-harness autosave save-count race in Firefox CI) — this is the production manager in `main.ts`, not the test setup.
- Verification was done with the verbatim class extract on the laptop, per the fleet's no-builds-on-the-sandbox rule; no production code was changed.

title: id(web): PR #1024's htmlBlock provenance attr is dropped by the editor schema — HTML blocks still re-fence on editor save (#982 regression path)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

PR #1024 (merged) fixed #982 in the Rust markdown codec by adding a provenance attr: the parse direction marks code blocks converted from raw HTML as `code_block` with `attrs: {"params": "html", "htmlBlock": true}` (`pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs:415`), and the save direction emits a real HTML block only when that attr is present (`pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs:1170`). The attr was never mirrored into the web editor's ProseMirror schema, so it does not survive the real editor save path — #982 still reproduces through the editor even though the codec's Rust tests pass.

## Evidence

- `grep htmlBlock pkgs/id/web/src/` on current main returns nothing. The codec-carried attrs that work in the editor all have schema mirrors with comments saying the codec reads/writes them: image `linkHref`/`linkTitle` (#880, `pkgs/id/web/src/editor.ts` image update), table `alignments` (#881), and — in the same batch as #1024 — `task_list` `tight`/`order` added by PRs #1041/#1042. #1024 changed only `markdown.rs`.
- `richSchema` (`pkgs/id/web/src/editor.ts:45`) inherits `code_block` from `prosemirror-schema-basic`, whose `code_block` spec declares **no attrs at all** (verified in `pkgs/id/web/node_modules/prosemirror-schema-basic/dist/index.js`: the `code_block` spec has content/marks/group/code/defining/parseDOM/toDOM and no `attrs`). The `code_block` with an attr at `editor.ts:262` belongs to the separate raw-mode schema.
- The editor parses the server-supplied document with `Node.fromJSON(editorSchema, initialDoc)` (`pkgs/id/web/src/editor.ts:375`). ProseMirror's `computeAttrs` builds a node's attrs by iterating only the attrs declared on its type (verified in `prosemirror-model/dist/index.js`), so undeclared attrs — `htmlBlock`, and likewise the codec's `params` — are silently dropped on load.
- Save posts that stripped document back: `main.ts` save handler sends `doc: state.doc` from `getEditorState()`, which is `state.doc.toJSON()` (`pkgs/id/web/src/editor.ts:662`; call sites `pkgs/id/web/src/main.ts:1330` and `:1421` for save/download). The server then runs `prosemirror_to_markdown` on a `code_block` with no `htmlBlock` attr and emits the ```html fence — exactly the #982 corruption.
- Same divergence class as open #1347 (footnote node types missing from richSchema), except here the node type exists, so nothing throws: the attr loss is silent.

## Why it matters

HTML comments, `<details>` and `<div>` blocks in any markdown document opened and saved in the web editor are still rewritten as visible ```html code fences. The fix for #982 only holds for server-side codec round-trips that never pass through the editor schema.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `richSchema`'s `code_block` declares the attrs the markdown codec carries (`htmlBlock`, and `params` if triage confirms it is dropped the same way — the basic-schema spec declares neither), following the #880/#881 mirror pattern in `pkgs/id/web/src/editor.ts`.
- [ ] A web-side test (e.g. in `editor.test.ts` or a codec-adjacent vitest) proves a `code_block` PM JSON with `htmlBlock: true` (and `params`) survives `Node.fromJSON(richSchema, …)` → `toJSON()` unchanged.
- [ ] An end-to-end style test or documented manual verification: a markdown doc containing an HTML block opens in the editor and saves back without gaining a ```html fence.
- [ ] No regression to authored ```html fences: a fence with no provenance attr still saves as a fence (existing Rust tests cover the codec side).

Found by the pr-diff-review job reviewing PR #1024 (batch 1023–1074, 2026-10-27).

title: id(web): world presenter rejects whole screen when a cell has a skin-tone emoji or tag flag — TS grapheme width sums modifiers instead of measuring the cluster

body:
## Problem

The browser world presenter refuses to render an entire screen when any cell contains an emoji with a skin-tone modifier (or a subdivision-flag tag sequence) — glyphs the Rust side of the same surface explicitly validates and emits as ordinary 2-column cells. One such glyph anywhere on the screen makes `renderWorldSurface` return `false` for the whole surface, so the world view silently stays on its previous/legacy content.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `37418e56`)

Rust side — `pkgs/id/src/world_presentation.rs:219` and `:350` validate a cell by `UnicodeWidthStr::width(symbol) == columns` using unicode-width 0.2.2 (pinned in `pkgs/id/Cargo.lock`). A probe crate compiled and run **on the laptop** (`unicode-width = "=0.2.2"`, `unicode-segmentation`) measures:

- `"👋🏽"` (U+1F44B U+1F3FD) — graphemes=1, width=2
- `"🧑🏽"` (U+1F9D1 U+1F3FD) — graphemes=1, width=2
- `"🏋🏽"` (U+1F3CB U+1F3FD) — graphemes=1, width=2
- England flag `U+1F3F4 U+E0067 U+E0062 U+E0065 U+E006E U+E0067 U+E007F` — graphemes=1, width=2

So the server legitimately produces `columns: 2` cells carrying these symbols, with a `columns: 0` continuation cell.

TS side — `pkgs/id/web/src/world-surface.ts:149-156` (`graphemeWidth`) has no modifier/tag-sequence case: outside the ZWJ (`:150-152`) and U+FE0F (`:153`) shortcuts it sums per-code-point widths. The skin-tone modifiers U+1F3FB–U+1F3FF fall inside the wide range `[0x1f3f8, 0x1f43e]` at `:95`, so a modified emoji measures 2 + 2 = 4; tag characters U+E0067… each measure 1, so the flag measures 8. At `:234-235` the presenter checks `graphemeWidth(cell.symbol) !== cell.columns` and returns `false`.

Probe against the verbatim `world-surface.ts` from main (sha256 `e92f95f99844db8553c8a60f2368305a8b4d654d4b03dfc4132c5b26ff62bd91`, run with Bun on the laptop, minimal DOM stub):

- controls render: `x`/1 → true, `😀`/2 → true, `👋`/2 → true, ZWJ family/2 → true, keycap `1️⃣`/2 → true
- `👋🏽`/2 → **false**, `🧑🏽`/2 → **false**, `🏋🏽`/2 → **false**, England tag flag/2 → **false**

## Why it matters

Skin-tone emoji are everyday user content in a world/chat surface. The Rust producer and the TS presenter disagree about the same contract (the TS file's own header at `:163-166` claims its width measurement "matches Rust's unicode-width 0.2 semantics"), and the failure mode is total: one cell rejects the whole frame, with no fallback rendering of the remaining cells. This is the same presenter/Rust width-parity class as closed #761, which special-cased ZWJ and U+FE0F sequences but missed emoji modifiers and tag sequences.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A 2-column cell carrying an emoji + skin-tone modifier grapheme (e.g. `👋🏽`, `🧑🏽`, `🏋🏽`) plus its continuation cell renders (`renderWorldSurface` returns `true` and produces the span), matching the Rust validator.
- [ ] A 2-column cell carrying a subdivision-flag tag sequence (e.g. the England flag above) renders the same way.
- [ ] Existing width behaviour is unchanged: plain wide glyphs, ZWJ sequences, U+FE0F sequences, keycaps, flags (regional-indicator pairs), combining marks, and the refusal cases in `world-surface.test.ts` (mismatched widths, multi-grapheme cells, control characters) all keep their current verdicts.
- [ ] New regression tests in `pkgs/id/web/src/world-surface.test.ts` cover skin-tone-modified emoji and a tag-sequence flag at columns=2 (accepted) — and, where the Rust width would differ, at columns=1 (refused).
- [ ] The fix is in the TS presenter's grapheme-width measurement; the Rust validator and the wire format do not change.

body:
## Summary

The #1019 fix for spaced link/image destinations only triggers on a literal space. Destinations containing a **tab** (authored or editor-originated) or a **newline** (editor-originated) take the unprotected path and are destroyed on save:

- **Tab**: `[x](</a\tb>)` parses to a link with href `/a\tb`, but saves as `[x](/a% 9b)` — comrak emits a `%`, a space, and a partial hex digit, which is not valid percent-encoding at all. **On reopen the link is gone**: the saved text parses as plain text. Images (`![a](</x\tb.png>)` → `![a](/x% 9b.png)`) and reference definitions (`[r]: </a\tb>`) fail identically.
- **Newline (PM-originated)**: a link mark whose href contains `\n` (e.g. set via the editor) saves as `[x](/a% Ab)` and likewise reopens as plain text; an image whose src contains `\n` saves as `![a](/x% Ab.png)` with the same result.

## Evidence

Verified on main `37418e56` with a verbatim-codec probe crate (comrak 0.56.0, compiled and run on the laptop; logs `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-1027-laneA-out.log` (probe8) and the probe9 run, cases `probe-2026-10-27-1027-laneA-probe8.rs` / `probe9.rs`):

```
=== angle-dest-tab pm_same=false
IN : "[x](</a\tb>)\n"          PM: link mark href "/a\tb"
OUT: "[x](/a% 9b)\n"          PM2: plain text "[x](/a% 9b)"  <- link destroyed, non-fixpoint
=== image-angle-dest-tab / ref-def-angle-tab / pm-link-href-tab / pm-image-src-tab: identical pattern
=== pm-image-src-newline pm_same=false
PM : image src "/x\nb.png"
OUT: "![a](/x% Ab.png)\n"     PM2: plain text                <- image destroyed
(PM link href "/a\nb" behaves the same: OUT "[x](/a% Ab)\n", PM2 plain text.)
```

A direct comrak parse→render control produces the same `% 9` output for the tab case, so the mangling itself is the renderer's — the codec defect is that its #1019 protection does not cover these destinations, exactly as it did not cover spaces before #1019.

Scope correction vs. the original filing: an *authored* angle-bracket destination containing a raw newline (`[x](</a\nb>)`) is **not** parsed as a link by comrak in the first place (it is plain text on both parse and save), so there is no authored-newline corruption — the newline case is editor-originated hrefs/srcs only. The tab case affects authored files directly.

## Root cause

`pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs:1091` — `substitute_spaced_destinations` (the #1019 placeholder mechanism, :1081-:1112) skips any destination that does not contain a space:

```rust
if !url.contains(' ') {
    continue;
}
```

Tab- and newline-bearing destinations therefore reach comrak's renderer unprotected. The placeholder-restore step writes the raw destination back in angle form `<{raw}>` (:1070-:1072), which represents tabs byte-identically (the probe's first parse proves `[x](</a\tb>)` parses to exactly that href). One caution: a destination containing a newline **and** literal document text matching the placeholder pattern interacts with #1348 (placeholder collision); the widened trigger should keep the placeholder tokens collision-safe.

## Why it matters

Angle-bracket destinations exist precisely for destinations the bare form cannot represent. A filename containing a tab is unusual but legal on Linux, and such a document is silently corrupted by simply opening it in the id web editor and saving — the link/image does not just get rewritten, it stops being a link/image at all. Same silent-corruption class as #1019, one whitespace character over.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `[x](</a\tb>)`, `![a](</x\tb.png>)`, and the reference-definition form round-trip open → save → open with the href/src byte-identical and the link/image intact (saved in angle form, no `% 9`).
- [ ] Editor-originated destinations with a tab or newline (link mark href, image src) round-trip with the link/image intact on reopen.
- [ ] Regression tests in `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs` cover tab destinations (link, image, reference definition) and newline destinations (PM-originated link/image); existing `web::markdown` tests (including the #1019 spaced-destination tests) still pass.
- [ ] The fix does not regress #1348's placeholder-collision concern (placeholder tokens remain unguessable / collision-checked).

Relates to: #1019 (space case, fixed), #1348 (placeholder collision).

body:
## Problem

In pkgs/id's web markdown codec, whitespace at the edges of a text run — state the rich editor readily holds — is written to the saved file but cannot survive the codec's own reparse. CommonMark strips up to three leading spaces on a paragraph line and ignores trailing spaces, so on the next open the spaces are gone. The worst case is structural: **a paragraph whose only content is spaces is deleted outright on reopen**, collapsing the document's block structure.

Verified on main `37418e56` with a verbatim-codec probe crate (comrak 0.56.0, compiled and run on the laptop; PM-first cases in `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-0927-laneA-out2.log` + `out3.log`):

| PM document | Saved file | After reopen |
|---|---|---|
| paragraph `  leading spaces` | `  leading spaces` | `leading spaces` — 2 spaces lost |
| paragraph `foo   ` (trailing) | `foo   ` | `foo` — trailing spaces lost |
| paragraphs [`   `, `x`] | `   ` + blank + `x` | only `x` — **the whitespace-only paragraph is gone** |
| `foo` + hard_break + `  bar` | `foo\` + newline + `  bar` | `foo` + hard_break + `bar` — spaces after the break lost |
| table header ` A `, cell ` x ` | `\|  A  \|` / `\|  x  \|` | `A` / `x` — cell padding lost |

All five are non-fixpoint across a full open→save→open cycle (the second save differs from the first: e.g. `  leading spaces` → `leading spaces`; the space-only case loses a whole block). Note the saved bytes look correct — the loss happens on reopen, because the codec emits plain spaces for state markdown cannot represent (compare the mark-wrapper path, which protects edge spaces with ` ` entities — no equivalent protection exists for unmarked run edges).

## Why it matters

Users typing in the rich editor create this state without doing anything exotic: indenting a paragraph's first line with spaces (a common writing habit), trailing spaces, or an empty spacer paragraph made of spaces. The editor shows one document, the file on disk appears to match it, and the next open silently shows a different one — in the spacer-paragraph case with a block deleted. Even where the resolution is "markdown cannot represent this, normalize it away", that normalization should happen at save (visibly, as a fixpoint) rather than as a silent reopen-time loss, and the whitespace-only paragraph deserves an explicit decision (map to an empty paragraph representation? drop at save?) instead of the current emergent deletion.

## Acceptance criteria

- A policy is picked and pinned for edge whitespace in unmarked text runs (paragraph start/end, after hard_break, table cells): either preserved across open→save→open, or normalized at save so the first saved file is already a byte fixpoint and the editor-visible result is the documented one.
- The whitespace-only paragraph case is explicitly decided: it must not silently vanish on reopen — either it round-trips (e.g. as an empty paragraph) or the save direction drops/normalizes it so file and reopen agree from the first save.
- The five probe cases above are covered by regression tests in `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs`; existing `web::markdown` tests pass, and the ` ` protection for marked spans (cf. #1418) is unaffected.

Related: #1418 (the marked-span counterpart — edge spaces inside delimiters), #1045 (unknown-mark policy — same pick-and-pin-a-policy shape), #1307 (.txt byte-faithfulness, different mode).

body:
## Problem

In pkgs/id's web markdown codec, a delimiter-mark span (em, strong, strikethrough) whose text **starts or ends with a space** loses its mark on the next open whenever a **word character touches the span on that same side**. The save emits the ` ` entity form inside the delimiters (e.g. `a* b*`), and that form cannot reparse as emphasis: the delimiter run is followed by `&` (punctuation, the entity start) and preceded by a word character, so it fails CommonMark's flanking rules for opening emphasis. On reopen the mark is gone and the delimiters remain as literal text — `a* b*` — and a second save escapes them (`a\* b\*`). The codec's own output is not readable by its own parser for these shapes.

Verified on main `37418e56` with a verbatim-codec probe crate (comrak 0.56.0, compiled and run on the laptop; `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-0927-laneA-out4.log`). PM documents below are editor shapes (a user selects a space-leading word mid-sentence and italicizes it):

| PM paragraph | Saved | After reopen |
|---|---|---|
| `a` + em(` b`) | `a* b*` | plain text `a* b*` — mark destroyed, literal `*`s remain |
| `a` + strong(` b`) | `a** b**` | plain text `a** b**` |
| `a` + strikethrough(` b`) | `a~~ b~~` | plain text (same failure) |
| `a ` + em(`b `) + `c` | `a *b *c` | plain text `a *b *c` |
| `a` + strong+em(` b`) | (same ` ` form) | mark destroyed |
| heading `a` + em(` b`) | `# a* b*` | mark destroyed (same) |

Controls in the same probe round-trip PM-identical and byte-fixpoint, which pins the trigger to the outside neighbor on the space-carrying side: span at paragraph start/end, neighbor is a space or punctuation, or the span is padded on both edges with spaced neighbours (`a * b * c` survives). An authored-markdown control confirms the mechanism at the parser level: the literal markdown `a* b*` parses to plain text, while `a * b*` (space before the delimiter) parses to em(` b`).

## Root cause

Save direction, `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs`: `create_marked_text` (:1737) builds the mark wrappers (em/strong/strikethrough arms :1762-1764) around the run's full text, keeping a leading/trailing space inside the wrapper; comrak's `format_commonmark` then renders that edge space as an ` ` entity inside the delimiters. Nothing in the codec checks whether the emitted delimited form can reparse — with a word character immediately outside the delimiter, it cannot (flanking rules above), so the first save writes a file the editor itself will misread on the next open.

## Why it matters

The shape is ordinary editor output: select ` b` (with its leading space) inside a sentence and press Ctrl+I, or apply bold to the last word of a sentence including the space before it. The loss is silent, destroys the formatting, and injects literal `*`/`~~` characters into the visible text; because the result is not a fixpoint, later saves compound it with backslash escapes. Siblings #1407/#1412 also leak ` ` entities but have different root causes (marks around an image node; marks spanning `html_inline` nodes) — this one is a single flat span with no other nodes involved.

## Acceptance criteria

- The full matrix round-trips PM-identical and byte-fixpoint: em, strong, strikethrough (and em+strong combined) × leading-edge space and trailing-edge space × word-character neighbour on that side, in paragraphs and headings.
- The fix preserves the rendered document (e.g. hoisting the edge space out of the mark wrapper — the space becomes unmarked, which renders identically — or another representation that reparses to the same PM doc); it must not regress the currently-working cases (span padded on both edges, space/punctuation/boundary neighbours) or the #953/#968/#981 mark tests.
- Regression tests in `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs` cover the matrix in both directions; existing `web::markdown` tests pass.

Related: #1407, #1412 (different ` ` mechanisms), #968 (nested-mark fragmentation, closed), #981 (softbreak-crossing spans, closed).

body:
## Problem

In pkgs/id's web markdown codec, any inline markup inside an image's alt text is silently stripped on the first open→save: emphasis, strong, code spans, and nested links in the description are flattened to their plain text. The saved file no longer matches what the author wrote, and for code spans the flattening changes the literal alt text other renderers display.

Verified on main `37418e56` with a verbatim-codec probe crate (comrak 0.56.0; `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-0854-laneA/out.log` + `out3.log`):

| Input | Saved |
|---|---|
| `![*alt* text](/x.png)` | `![alt text](/x.png)` |
| `![**bold alt**](/x.png)` | `![bold alt](/x.png)` |
| `` ![a `code` b](/x.png) `` | `![a code b](/x.png)` |
| `![a [link](/y) b](/x.png)` | `![a link b](/x.png)` |

Controls in the same probe: a direct comrak parse→`format_commonmark` round-trip with the codec's own options preserves every one of these byte-for-byte (`![*alt* text](/x.png)`, `` ![a `code` b](/x.png) ``), so this is a codec loss, not a comrak renderer behaviour. Alt text containing an escaped bracket (`![a\]b](/x.png)`) and entities round-trip fine — only markup structure is lost.

## Root cause

Parse direction, `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs:354-360` (the `NodeValue::Image` arm of `convert_node`): the alt is extracted with `get_text_content(node)` (:710), which concatenates only the text literals of the alt subtree. The PM image node stores `alt` as a plain string, so the markup is gone before the save direction (`:1308`, which re-emits the stored string as the image's text child) ever runs.

## Why it matters

Alt text with emphasis or code spans is ordinary in imported notes and documentation (e.g. `` ![the `resize` handler](/img.png) ``). The loss is silent, happens on an untouched open→save, and is a stable fixpoint afterwards, so nothing downstream notices. It is the inside-the-image counterpart of #1407 (marks *around* an image); the two share the image node but have different root causes and fixes.

## Acceptance criteria

- `![*alt* text](/x.png)`, `![**bold alt**](/x.png)`, and `` ![a `code` b](/x.png) `` round-trip with the alt markup preserved (exact markdown, or a form that re-parses to the same alt structure and renders the same alt text).
- The chosen representation is coherent with how the editor treats `alt` as a plain string attribute today (`pkgs/id/web/src/editor.ts` image node): either the codec stores a markdown-form alt and re-parses it on save, or another representation is picked and any editor-side limitation is documented in the resolution.
- Nested-link alt (`![a [link](/y) b](/x.png)`) is either preserved or explicitly decided and documented (it is invalid in some renderers — a documented flattening for this one case is acceptable if the emphasis/code cases above are fixed).
- Regression tests in `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs` cover emphasis, strong, and code-span alt text in both directions; existing `web::markdown` tests pass.

Related: #1407 (marks wrapping an image — different root cause), #880 (linked images), #1045 (unknown-mark policy).

body: # id(web): marks spanning inline HTML are broken on save — links fragment around the tags, emphasis leaks entities ## Summary In the pkgs/id web markdown codec (`pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs`), a mark (link, emphasis, …) that spans an `html_inline` atom does not survive a save. The parse direction is correct — the marked text runs carry the mark and the `html_inline` nodes sit between them — but the save direction reassembles the span wrongly: the HTML tags migrate outside the mark, a link is fragmented into one link per text run, and emphasis forms leak literal ` ` entities into the saved file. The corrupted output is a stable fixpoint, so nothing downstream ever notices or repairs it. This is the `html_inline` counterpart of #1407 (marks wrapping an *image*). The `html_inline` node type was introduced by the #943 fix (PR #1009); unlike the image arm, its save arm has no mark handling at all, so any fix scoped to images will not touch this. ## Evidence (verified this run on main `37418e56`) Verbatim-codec probe crate (markdown.rs copied byte-identical from main, comrak 0.56.0; log: goal `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-creator-a6/out2.log` + `out3.log`): | Input | Saved (first save) | |---|---| | `[a x](/y)` | `[a ](/y)[x](/y)` | | `[a x c](/y)` | `[a ](/y)[x](/y)[ c](/y)` | | `[a 2 c](/y)` | `[a ](/y)[2](/y)[ c](/y)` | | `*a x c*` | `*a **x** c*` | Parse shape for `[a x c](/y)` is correct (probe `out3.log`): PM paragraph = `text "a " [link]`, `html_inline ""`, `text "x" [link]`, `html_inline ""`, `text " c" [link]`. The information loss/fragmentation happens entirely on save. Controls that round-trip cleanly in the same probe: - `a x c` (inline HTML, no marks) — clean. - `# a x`, `a b` — clean. - `[x](/y)` and `**x**` (mark around a single atom run) — survive, because comrak re-nests the single marked text run equivalently. ## Root cause (from the code) - Parse: `NodeValue::HtmlInline` arm (`markdown.rs:421-433`) emits an `html_inline` atom with only an `html` attr; atoms carry no marks, so the surrounding mark context exists only as marks on the neighbouring text runs. - Save: the `"html_inline"` arm of `json_to_ast` (`markdown.rs:1360-1361`) emits a bare `NodeValue::HtmlInline` node. Mark wrapping is done by `create_marked_text` (`markdown.rs:1737`) per text run, and neither it nor `append_inline_child` (`markdown.rs:1712`) can carry a mark across the atom — contrast the image arm (`markdown.rs:1308+`), which at least special-cases the link mark (#880). The result: each text run gets its own mark wrapper, the tags land outside, boundary spaces inside emphasis wrappers are escaped by comrak as ` `. ## Why it matters Inline HTML inside links/emphasis is ordinary imported-markdown content (linked terms with ``/`` notation, ``/`` inside link text, formatted references). The first open→save silently rewrites it into fragmented links and entity-polluted emphasis; the rendered meaning changes (link scope and tag nesting invert) and the ` ` form is a stable fixpoint, so the corruption is permanent and invisible to later round-trip checks. ## Acceptance criteria - `[a x c](/y)` and `[a 2 c](/y)` round-trip with the link intact as a single link span containing the inline HTML (exact markdown or a form re-parsing to the same PM structure). - `*a x c*` (and strong/strikethrough equivalents) save as a single mark span containing the tags, with no ` ` or other HTML entities introduced. - Cases that already work stay working: unmarked inline HTML (`a x c`), single-run forms (`[x](/y)`), and the #943 sub/sup/u cases. - Regression tests in `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs` cover mark-spanning-html_inline in both directions; existing `web::markdown` tests pass. ## Related - #1407 — same failure class for image atoms (different arm, different fix surface). - #943 (closed) — introduced the `html_inline` node; its cases carry no marks. - #968 (closed) — text-run mark re-nesting; this issue is the atom-boundary remainder.

body:
## Summary

In pkgs/id's web markdown codec, a mark that wraps an image (emphasis, strong, strikethrough) is silently lost. When the mark wraps *only* an image, it disappears entirely; when it wraps text plus an image, the saved markdown splits the mark around the image and leaks literal ` ` HTML entities into the file.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `37418e56`)

Probe: verbatim copy of `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs` in a standalone crate (comrak 0.56.0), `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-creator-a4/out4.log`:

| Input | Saved output |
|---|---|
| `*![alt](/x.png)*` | `![alt](/x.png)` — emphasis gone |
| `**![alt](/x.png)**` | `![alt](/x.png)` — strong gone |
| `~~![alt](/x.png)~~` | `![alt](/x.png)` — strikethrough gone |
| `*[![alt](/x.png)](https://e.com)*` | `[![alt](/x.png)](https://e.com)` — link survives, emphasis gone |
| `*text ![alt](/x.png) tail*` | `*text *![alt](/x.png)* tail*` — one emphasis span becomes two, with literal ` ` entities in the saved file, and the image is no longer inside either span's text (re-parse gives the same split PM, so it is stable corruption, not a fixpoint error) |
| `**text ![alt](/x.png) tail**` | `**text **![alt](/x.png)** tail**` — same for strong |
| `- *![alt](/x.png)* item` | `- ![alt](/x.png) item` — same loss inside list items |

Control: `*text only*` round-trips exactly. The parsed ProseMirror for `*![alt](/x.png)*` is a bare `image` node with **no marks at all** (`{"type":"image","attrs":{"alt":"alt","src":"/x.png"}}`).

## Root cause

- Parse direction: the `NodeValue::Image` arm in `convert_node` (`pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs:354-393`) receives the surrounding marks in `active_marks` but only carries the `link` mark forward, copying it into the image node's `linkHref`/`linkTitle` attrs (the #880 precedent). `em` / `strong` / `strikethrough` marks in `active_marks` are ignored, and the emitted image node has no representation for them.
- Save direction: the `"image"` arm of `json_to_ast` (`pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs:1308-1360`) and the post-processing wrap (`:1503-1519`) only know how to re-wrap an image in a `Link` node from `linkHref`; there is no equivalent for emphasis/strong/strikethrough, and the marked text runs on either side of the image are emitted as separate mark-wrapper nodes, whose boundary spaces comrak escapes as ` `.

## Why it matters

Italic/bold captions and callouts that include an inline image are ordinary markdown (common in notes imported from other tools, which id syncs as plain files). Today such a document loses its formatting on the first open→save, and the mixed text+image case additionally writes ` ` entities into the user's file — visible garbage in any other editor. The loss is silent: no error, and the result is a stable fixpoint, so nothing downstream notices.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `*![alt](/x.png)*`, `**![alt](/x.png)**`, `~~![alt](/x.png)~~` and the linked-image form `*[![alt](/x.png)](href)*` round-trip with the mark preserved (exact markdown or an equivalent form that re-parses to the same marked structure, with no mark loss).
- [ ] `*text ![alt](/x.png) tail*` (and the strong/strikethrough equivalents) save as a single emphasis span containing the image, with **no ` ` or other HTML entities** introduced into the saved markdown.
- [ ] The representation chosen is coherent with the existing #880 `linkHref`/`linkTitle` pattern for wrapping an image, and the editor either renders it or the limitation is explicitly documented in the issue's resolution.
- [ ] Regression tests in `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs` cover image-only and mixed text+image mark spans in both directions; existing `web::markdown` tests still pass.

Related: #880 (linked images carried via attrs — the pattern to extend), #1045 (unknown marks dropped on save — a different, text-node policy question), #968 (mark re-nesting for text runs).

title: Upstream quirk: libsql /dump does not escape single quotes in sqlite_schema INSERTs for virtual tables (FTS5) — cold-store reaper works around it

labels.name: source/human

labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work
