labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Summary

In the id web markdown codec (`pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs`), saving a document with adjacent bullet lists that use different markers (`-`, `+`, `*` with no blank line between them — three separate one-item lists) writes literal `<!-- end list -->` HTML comments into the user's file. Worse, the result is **not a fixpoint and grows on every save**: on the next save each comment block additionally becomes a ```` ```html ```` code fence, and the save after that duplicates them again. A document with two list boundaries gains two more code blocks per save, forever.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 76672b97)

Standalone probe crate carrying a verbatim copy of `src/web/markdown.rs` (comrak 0.56.0, the locked version). Probe logs: goal `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-26-1815/` (`batch2.log` case `mixed_markers`, `inspect.log`).

Input:

```markdown
- a
+ b
* c
```

Parse (inspect.log): three separate `bullet_list` PM nodes — correct; the PM model has no marker attribute, so the three lists are indistinguishable from one list except for being separate nodes.

Save 1:

```markdown
- a

<!-- end list -->

- b

<!-- end list -->

- c
```

Save 2 (the comments from save 1 now reparse through the HTML-block path, cf. #982, and come back as code fences, while fresh comments are emitted again):

```markdown
- a

<!-- end list -->

```html
<!-- end list -->
```

- b

<!-- end list -->

```html
<!-- end list -->
```

- c
```

Save 3 doubles the accumulated ```` ```html ```` blocks again (two per list boundary; full sequence in `inspect.log`). Every open→save cycle permanently adds blocks to the file.

## Root cause (code evidence)

- Save direction `json_to_ast` (list arms, `markdown.rs:997-1045`) builds a separate comrak `List` node per PM `bullet_list`; comrak's CommonMark renderer separates two adjacent lists of the same type by emitting an `<!-- end list -->` HTML comment — the codec passes that through verbatim into the saved file.
- On reparse, a standalone comment is an HTML block; the codec's HTML-block handling (the behaviour tracked in #982) turns it into a ```` ```html ```` fenced block, while the renderer emits fresh `<!-- end list -->` comments for the still-adjacent lists — hence unbounded growth instead of a fixpoint.

## Why it matters

Mixed-marker adjacent lists appear in real notes (and in files produced by other editors). A user who opens such a file in the id web editor and saves repeatedly watches their document accumulate comment lines and then duplicated code fences — visible corruption that compounds, in the same non-fixpoint family as #944/#981 but with growth per save.

## Acceptance criteria

- `- a` / `+ b` / `* c` (and the two-list case) saves to a form that is a fixpoint from the first save: repeated open→save cycles are byte-stable.
- No `<!-- end list -->` comments or ```` ```html ```` artefacts are introduced into the saved file.
- The saved form still renders as the same list items with the same text (merging the adjacent bullet lists into one list on save is acceptable — the PM model cannot represent the marker distinction anyway; separating them by a construct that round-trips is equally acceptable).
- Regression tests in `web::markdown` assert byte-stability over at least three consecutive saves; existing markdown tests pass.

Suggested direction (triage decides): coalesce adjacent `bullet_list` nodes (same for ordered lists with a continuous `start`, if reproducible) in `json_to_ast` or in the parse direction, rather than letting comrak's renderer invent separators the codec cannot reparse. Interaction with #982 (HTML blocks → ```` ```html ````) should be noted: fixing #982 alone does not stop the comment emission, and fixing the emission alone leaves the comment-reparse path armed for user-authored comments between lists.

Dedup: searched open + closed issues for `end list`, `mixed marker`, `adjacent list` — no matches. #982 covers user-authored HTML blocks becoming code fences, a different trigger; this issue is about the codec's own renderer emitting comments it cannot round-trip.

body:
## Summary

In the id web markdown codec (`pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs`), a footnote definition with more than one paragraph loses the paragraph boundary on save: the paragraphs are fused into a single run of text with **no separator at all** — `first` + `second para` saves as `firstsecond para`. Words are glued together and the definition's block structure is destroyed.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 76672b97)

Standalone probe crate carrying a verbatim copy of `src/web/markdown.rs` (comrak 0.56.0, the locked version), round-tripping `markdown_to_prosemirror` → `prosemirror_to_markdown` twice. Probe logs: goal `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-26-1815/` (`batch2.log`, `inspect.log`).

Input:

```markdown
text[^a]

[^a]: first

    second para
```

ProseMirror after parse (inspect.log): the `footnote_definition` node's content is two bare text nodes — `[{"text":"first"},{"text":"second para"}]` — the paragraph wrappers are already gone.

First save:

```markdown
text[^a]

[^a]:
    firstsecond para
```

The output is a stable spelling from then on, but the document's words are fused and the second paragraph no longer exists as a paragraph.

## Root cause (code evidence)

- Parse direction, `markdown.rs:505-520` (`NodeValue::FootnoteDefinition` arm): iterates the definition's block children and extends one flat inline-content vec with `collect_inline_children(child, &[])` for each — block boundaries between children are discarded by construction.
- Save direction, `markdown.rs:1203-1220`: re-wraps **all** of that inline content in a single `Paragraph` before handing the AST to comrak, so nothing can reintroduce the boundary; adjacent text nodes render concatenated with no separator.

This is the footnote counterpart of #1003 (multi-paragraph table cells fusing), at a different code site with a different representation problem: the PM schema for `footnote_definition` currently cannot represent more than one block at all. A definition containing a list or code block flattens the same way.

## Why it matters

Multi-paragraph footnotes are ordinary markdown (the standard way to write a long footnote). Opening such a document in the id web editor and saving — even without touching the footnote — permanently fuses its paragraphs and glues words together. Silent data corruption on save, in the same family as #981/#1003/#1017.

## Acceptance criteria

- A footnote definition with two paragraphs round-trips with the paragraph boundary preserved (two paragraphs, or a representation that renders identically and is a fixpoint from the first save).
- No word fusion: saved text never concatenates two block children's text without a separator.
- A definition containing another block type (list, code block) either round-trips or degrades with an explicit separator, never silent fusion.
- Regression tests in `web::markdown` cover the two-paragraph definition (fixpoint asserted over two saves); existing markdown tests pass.

Suggested direction (triage decides): either carry block children on the PM `footnote_definition` node (schema change, editor side must tolerate it), or — if the flat inline representation stays — join block children with an explicit paragraph break on parse and split on save.

Dedup: searched open + closed issues for `footnote` — #945 (closed) covers basic footnote round-tripping and single-paragraph definitions; no issue covers multi-block definitions. #1003 is the table-cell site, distinct code path.

title: cold-store-reaper: project-budget enforcement in put-backup never counts backup bytes — cumulative backups can cross the 3 TiB budget unrefused (PR #988)

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.name: app/cold-store-reaper
labels.description: Package/app: cold-store-reaper (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Finding

PR #988 added project-budget enforcement to `put_backup()`, but the accounting it enforces against never counts backup bytes — so the cumulative backup stream can cross the 3 TiB project budget without ever being refused, and `status`'s `within_budget` verdict has the same blind spot.

## Evidence (verified on current main `76672b97df023607d8469d462f21420604fe92d5`, via `gh pr diff 988` and the local clone)

`pkgs/cold-store-reaper/cold_store.py`:

- `_upload_accounting()` (lines ~459–482) defines `cold_bytes` as verified **bundles only**:
  ```sql
  SELECT coalesce(sum(bytes),0) n FROM bundles WHERE state='verified'
  ```
- `_check_upload_limits()` (lines ~485–507) refuses when `cold_bytes + nbytes > project_budget_bytes`.
- `put_backup()` (lines ~933–960) calls `_check_upload_limits(conn, size, …)` before uploading, then records the backup **only** in the transfer ledger (`ledger_add(conn, "upload", size, "backup-upload", name)`). Backups are unbundled Drive files (`db-backups/<db>/`); they never enter the `bundles` table.

Consequences:

1. For a `put_backup` call, the budget side of the check compares *bundle* bytes + this one backup against the budget. Yesterday's backups contribute 0. A backup stream of any cumulative size passes as long as each individual file fits under `budget − bundle_bytes` and the rolling-24h hard stop (the only cumulative accounting backups do get, and it forgets after 24h).
2. This is now the main growth path: `backup-d1` and `backup-supabase` go through `put_backup`, and PR #993 added a nightly Turso export through the same path. Retention (`prune-backups`) bounds count by age class, but nothing bounds total backup bytes against the budget the PR claims to enforce.
3. `status_data()` reuses the same accounting, so its `cold_bytes` / `within_budget` readout also excludes every DB backup sitting in Drive.

PR #988's tests cover a single `put_backup` against a tiny budget (cold = 0 bundles + one file) and the bundle-path refusals, but no sequence of backups accumulating past the budget.

Deduped 2026-10-26: `gh issue list --search 'put-backup project budget'` returns only #938 (closed by PR #988 — this is a remainder of that enforcement, not a re-file of the original "never enforced" report) and #939 (retention, unrelated mechanism).

## Why it matters

#938 was filed because the limits were "reported but never enforced". After PR #988 the daily hard stop is genuinely enforced for all paths, but the project budget is still effectively unenforced for the backup class — the class that grows every night — while the README ("Upload guardrails (enforced, not just reported)") and `status` both present it as enforced. A silent Drive blow-out past 3 TiB is the failure the budget exists to prevent.

## Acceptance criteria

- Triage decides the correct cumulative accounting for backups (e.g. a backups total tracked in the manifest/meta, Drive folder totals, or ledger sums over the retention window — whatever can be kept truthful), and `put_backup`'s budget check uses it so that a sequence of backups whose cumulative total crosses `project_budget_bytes` is refused.
- Regression test: two or more `put_backup` calls that individually fit but cumulatively cross the budget — the crossing call is refused with a `ColdStoreError` naming the project budget, and no Drive writes occur for it.
- `status`'s budget readout reflects the same accounting the enforcement uses (one implementation, per PR #988's own design principle), or explicitly scopes its claim to bundles.
- Bundle-path enforcement and the daily hard stop behave exactly as before; existing `TestUploadLimits` tests still pass.

Source: PR #988 — https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/988 (commits `a6ac921`, `78f2707`, `0789776`); backup-stream growth via PR #993 — https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/993. Relates to closed #938. Filed by the pr-diff-review job, 2026-10-26.

body:
## Bug

In the id web markdown codec (`pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs`), an **ordered** task list loses its ordering on save: it comes back as a bullet task list, and a non-1 start number is lost with it.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `14dd66b6`)

Standalone probe crate compiling the verbatim codec from current main (logs: goal `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-26-1215/out2.log` + `out3.log`):

- Input:
  ```
  1. [ ] todo
  2. [x] done
  ```
  Parsed PM: a single `task_list` node (no `order` attr anywhere). Saved output:
  ```
  - [ ] todo
  - [x] done
  ```
- Input:
  ```
  5. [ ] five
  6. [x] six
  ```
  Saved output: `- [ ] five` / `- [x] six` — both the numbering and the start value 5 are gone.

Root cause, both directions:

- Parse: the `NodeValue::List` arm (markdown.rs:~205-220) checks only whether the first child is a `TaskItem`; when it is, it emits `{"type":"task_list"}` and discards `list.list_type` (Ordered vs Bullet) and `list.start`. The non-task branch right below does preserve both (`ordered_list` with `attrs.order`).
- Save: the `task_list` arm of `json_to_ast` (markdown.rs:~946) hardcodes `list_type: ListType::Bullet, bullet_char: b'-'` — there is no PM shape that could carry the ordering even if parse kept it.

For comparison, a plain ordered list round-trips correctly (`3. three` / `4. four` keep `order: 3` — same probe), and a plain bullet task list round-trips correctly. Only the ordered+task combination loses data.

## Why it matters

Ordered checklists are a natural way to write sequenced steps ("step 1… step 2…") with completion state. Opening such a file in id and saving any edit silently renumbers it into an unordered checklist — the sequence information the author encoded is destroyed without any visible warning in the editor.

## Acceptance criteria

- `1. [ ] todo\n2. [x] done` round-trips as an ordered task list; `5. [ ] five\n6. [x] six` additionally preserves the start number 5 (same `order` convention as `ordered_list`).
- The PM representation chosen (e.g. an `order` attr on `task_list`, or ordered list semantics for task items) must be one the web editor schema can actually render/edit — check `pkgs/id/web` before settling; if the editor cannot represent it today, the issue's fix note must say what was chosen and why.
- Mixed content keeps working: `- [ ] todo\n- plain` (task + plain items in one list, existing test `test_task_list_mixed_content`) does not regress.
- New unit tests in `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs` cover ordered task lists with start 1 and start >1, both directions.
- Existing codec tests pass.

## Related

- Plain task lists and plain ordered lists are both fine (probe-verified this run) — this is only the intersection.

body:
## Bug

In the id web markdown codec (`pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs`), a link with empty text is silently deleted on save — the href is lost entirely.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `14dd66b6`)

Standalone probe crate compiling the verbatim codec from current main (log: goal `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-26-1215/out.log` + `out3.log`):

- Input: `[](https://e.com)\n`
  - Parsed PM: `{"type":"paragraph"}` — no content at all
  - Saved output: `""` — the link and its URL are gone
- Input: `before [](https://e.com) after\n`
  - Parsed PM: two plain text nodes `before ` / ` after` (no link mark anywhere)
  - Saved output: `before  after\n` (note the double space where the link was)

Root cause, parse side: `NodeValue::Link` arm (markdown.rs:299) converts a link purely into a mark carried by its child text nodes (`collect_inline_children` with the link mark pushed). A link with no children produces no text node, so the mark — and the href/title — has nothing to attach to and vanishes. There is no other PM representation for a standalone link in this codec (contrast: images, which are nodes, survive empty alt — `[![](img.png)](https://e.com)` round-trips fine).

## Why it matters

Opening a markdown file containing an empty-text link (a placeholder link, a link inserted by another tool, or one whose text a user cleared in another editor) in id and saving any edit silently destroys the URL. It is unrecoverable from the saved file and invisible in the editor — the paragraph looks unchanged.

## Acceptance criteria

- `[](https://e.com)` and `before [](https://e.com) after` survive a parse→save round-trip with the href (and title, when present) preserved, OR the codec takes an explicit, documented alternative (e.g. emitting the href as visible autolink text) — silently dropping it is the one unacceptable outcome; the chosen representation must be a round-trip fixpoint.
- The editor-side implication is considered: if the chosen PM shape is one the web editor schema cannot represent, say so in the fix and choose the save-side preservation that keeps the file's data.
- New unit tests in `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs` cover: empty link alone, empty link mid-paragraph, empty link with a title.
- Existing codec tests pass; linked-image and normal link cases do not regress.

## Related

- Distinct from #953 (code+link drops the link mark on a non-empty text node — different mechanism: the `create_marked_text` code early-return) and #981 (softbreak fragmentation of non-empty links).

## Summary In the id web editor's markdown ↔ ProseMirror codec (`pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs`), any **HTML block** in a markdown file — an HTML comment, a `
` collapsible, a `
` — is rewritten on save as a fenced ```` ```html ```` code block. The rendered document changes completely: invisible comments become visible code blocks, and collapsible sections break into two code fences with their body stranded between them. ## Evidence (verified this run on main 24261355) Standalone probe crate compiling the verbatim codec from `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs` (logs: goal workspace `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-26-1015/out.log` + `out2.log`): Input: ``` text ``` After one save: ```` ```html ``` text ```` Input: ```
More body
``` After one save: the `
…` chunk and the closing `
` each become separate ```` ```html ```` fences with `body` as a plain paragraph between them — the collapsible is destroyed. ## Root cause - Parse side: the `NodeValue::HtmlBlock` arm (markdown.rs:329-352) converts non-`` HTML blocks to a `code_block` with `attrs.params = "html"` (comment in code: "safe fallback"). - Emit side: the `code_block` arm in `json_to_ast` (markdown.rs:872) has no special case for that marker — it always builds a fenced `NodeValue::CodeBlock`, so the fallback becomes permanent in the saved file. ## Design note (why this is triage, not a small fix) The PM shape for a converted HTML block (`code_block`, params `html`) is indistinguishable from a user-authored ```` ```html ```` block, which parses via `NodeValue::CodeBlock` with info `html` into the same shape. Emitting raw HTML for every params=`html` code block would corrupt genuinely authored html code blocks (they would turn into live HTML). A fix needs a way to tell the two apart — e.g. a distinct marker attr or node type for converted HTML blocks, with a migration story for documents already saved in the ambiguous shape — or another faithful-preservation design. Related but distinct: #943 covers *inline* HTML being backslash-escaped; this issue is block-level HTML only. ## Why it matters HTML comments and `
` blocks are common in notes, READMEs, and docs the web editor opens. A no-edit save currently vandalizes them into visible code fences. Until a faithful round-trip exists, opening such a file in the editor is destructive. ## Acceptance criteria - [ ] A design is chosen that distinguishes converted HTML blocks from authored ```` ```html ```` code blocks (or otherwise preserves both faithfully), and is recorded on this issue. - [ ] ``, `
…
`, and a bare `
` block each round-trip open → save byte-identical, and a second round-trip is a fixpoint. - [ ] A user-authored ```` ```html ```` fenced block still round-trips as a fenced code block. - [ ] New unit tests in `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs` cover HTML-block round-trips (comment, details, div, authored html fence). - [ ] Existing codec tests still pass; the sized/linked `` HTML-block handling (markdown.rs:332-340, #893) does not regress.

labels.name: task/triage

body:
## Summary

In the id web editor's markdown ↔ ProseMirror codec (`pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs`), any **nested mark combination** corrupts on save: when the active mark set changes mid-run (emphasis inside strong, strong inside emphasis, strikethrough or inline code nested inside strong/em, emphasis inside a link), the emitted markdown gains ` ` HTML entities in place of spaces and multiplied emphasis delimiters. Several cases are **not a fixpoint** — every subsequent save makes the output worse.

Single-mark and sibling cases are fine (plain `**strong**`, `*em*`, `~~strike~~`, `` `code` ``, and `***both***` all round-trip cleanly), which is why the existing tests miss this: the corruption only appears when adjacent text nodes carry *different overlapping* mark sets.

## Evidence (verified this run on main aa0d6d10)

Standalone probe crate compiling the verbatim codec from `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs` (current main), markdown → ProseMirror → markdown, twice:

| Input | After 1st save | After 2nd save |
|---|---|---|
| `**bold _em_ end**` | `**bold *****em***** end**` | `**bold *******em******* end**` (keeps growing) |
| `*em **strong** end*` | `*em ****strong**** end*` | stable in corrupted form |
| `**bold ~~strike~~ end**` | `**bold **~~**strike**~~** end**` | `**bold ****~~strike~~**** end**` (changes again) |
| `**bold \`code\` end**` | `**bold **\`code\`** end**` | — |
| `*em \`code\` end*` | `*em *\`code\`* end*` | — |
| `**_em_ rest**` | `***em***** rest**` | — |
| `[link *em* text](https://e.com)` | `[link ](https://e.com)*[em](https://e.com)*[ text](https://e.com)` | `[*em*]` migrates inside the link on the next save (not a fixpoint) |
| `**a *b \`c\` d* e**` | `**a *****b ***\`c\`*** d***** e**` | — |

The parsed ProseMirror is correct in every case (e.g. `**bold _em_ end**` parses to text nodes `bold ` [strong], `em` [strong, em], ` end` [strong]) — the corruption is introduced on the **emit** side.

Probe logs: goal workspace `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-26-0815/out.log` and `out2.log`.

## Suspected area

`prosemirror_to_markdown`'s inline emission: `create_marked_text` (markdown.rs:1117) and `build_mark_chain` (markdown.rs:1167). When consecutive text nodes have overlapping-but-different mark sets, the chain appears to close/reopen marks in an order that leaves boundary text nodes whose leading/trailing spaces comrak then renders as ` `, and re-parsing the result produces yet more mark boundaries — hence the per-save growth.

Related but distinct: #944 (strong+link mark-order oscillation — no nesting required), #953 (code+link drops the link via the code early-return at markdown.rs:1122). This issue reproduces with no link and no code mark at all (pure em+strong), so it is not a duplicate of either; a fix should be checked against both.

## Why it matters

Nested emphasis is ordinary writing (`**bold with *italic* inside**`). Today, opening such a file in the web editor and saving it — even without edits — rewrites it into entity-escaped, delimiter-doubled text, and repeated saves compound the damage. This is silent data corruption of user documents.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] New unit tests in `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs` cover nested-mark round-trips, including the fixpoint (double round-trip) property.
- [ ] Existing codec tests still pass, and the #944 / #953 cases do not regress.

title: id phase-9: a joiner's resize (up to 500x200) can permanently poison a world via the guest layout() call exceeding presentation_bytes

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/m
labels.description: Medium: expected under 1 day of work

labels.name: meta/enriched
labels.description: Intake review done: acceptance criteria, links, and normalized labels added

body:
## Finding

A session with only `join` scope can send `resize` up to 500×200, but the screen DTO is capped at 120×50 and the guest `layout(width, height)` result must fit `presentation_bytes` (default 8192). A reflowing app that fills a 120×50 grid exceeds 8192 bytes, so one participant resizing their window makes the world's program unhealthy for everyone until an admin reinstalls. This is the same trap-poisoning class as #547, but the trigger is an unprivileged joiner's window resize, which is meant to be per-connection and unjournaled.

## Evidence

- `pkgs/id/src/world_presentation.rs:15-17`: `MAX_SCREEN_WIDTH = 120`, `MAX_SCREEN_HEIGHT = 50`.
- `pkgs/id/src/world_session.rs:2309-2321`: `ClientFrame::Resize` accepts `width 1..=500 and height 1..=200` for any session holding join scope, and calls `send_view` with that viewport.
- `pkgs/id/src/world.rs:78`: `presentation_bytes: 8192` default.
- `pkgs/id/src/world.rs:3109-3125`: `ViewAt` sets `self.program_healthy = false` when the `layout` output exceeds `presentation_bytes`, and on any `layout` error — a world-wide state, not a per-session one.
- A 120×50 grid is 6000 cells plus JSON framing, which easily exceeds 8192 bytes; resize is documented as session-local (`viewport_is_session_local_and_never_advances_the_world_sequence`).

## Why it matters

An unprivileged participant can take a shared world offline with a single resize, and it stays unhealthy for every participant until someone reinstalls the module. This is a denial-of-service the current bounds do not prevent.

## Suggested fix (do not fix inline here — see note)

- Clamp `width`/`height` to `MAX_SCREEN_WIDTH`/`MAX_SCREEN_HEIGHT` before calling `view_at`/`send_view`.
- In `ViewAt`, treat an oversized `layout` result as a per-session error (fall back to `view()` plus cropping) instead of setting `program_healthy = false`.

## Proving test

A mock `WorldProgram` whose `layout` returns >8192 bytes when `width > 100`. Session A resizes to 500×200; assert session B still receives a `view` frame and that `input` is still accepted.

## Not fixed inline

Left as an issue (not fixed in PR #804) because the fix lands in `world.rs` / `world_session.rs`, which Session B's in-flight module split (PR #808, F11.10) is moving; an inline edit here would collide with that work.

## Related

#547 (F11.17: a trapping view must not poison the world) — this is a narrower, join-scope trigger.

## Acceptance criteria

- A join-scoped session's `resize` can no longer make a world permanently unhealthy: an oversized `layout()` result for one connection's viewport degrades to a per-connection fallback (crop/clamp to that connection's presentation budget) instead of setting world-wide `program_healthy = false`.
- Resize acceptance bounds and the screen DTO caps (120×50) / `presentation_bytes` budget are reconciled so the guest is never asked for a layout that cannot fit.
- A regression test reproduces the poison path (joiner resize to a large viewport on a reflowing app) and shows the world stays healthy for other participants.
- Existing world/presentation tests stay green.

title: sync-models: naive parseJsonc line-stripper breaks on block comments and string contents — multi-line /* */ or a ' // ' string fails the sync, a ', ]' string is silently corrupted

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: queue/queued
labels.description: Has a queued queue task

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: meta/enriched
labels.description: Intake review done: acceptance criteria, links, and normalized labels added

body:
## Problem

`bin/sync-models.mjs` reads the OpenCode config with a naive line-based JSONC stripper, `parseJsonc` (lines 224–231), even though the same file already contains a correct comment-aware parser, `parseJsoncTree` (line 238). `parseJsonc`:

- drops only lines that *start* with `//` or `/*`,
- strips everything after the first whitespace + `//` on each remaining line, whether or not it is inside a string,
- removes trailing commas with a whole-text regex (`/,\s*([}\]])/g`) that also matches inside strings.

Three verified failure modes follow (probe below, run against the verbatim function extracted from current main `b382bfb8`):

1. **A multi-line block comment makes the sync fail outright.** Only the line starting with `/*` is dropped; the continuation lines remain and `JSON.parse` throws. `main()` catches this at the config read (lines 391–398) and exits 1 — the sync-models service fails on every run for a config OpenCode itself accepts (block comments are legal JSONC).
2. **A string containing ` // ` makes the sync fail outright.** The line stripper cuts the string at the comment-like sequence: `{"note": "docs // see guide"}` is truncated mid-string and `JSON.parse` throws "Unterminated string".
3. **A string containing `, ]` or `, }` is silently corrupted.** `{"note": "a, ] b"}` parses successfully as `{"note": "a] b"}` — the comma is deleted from the value with no error. The object `parseJsonc` returns is the read model the sync decides its adds/updates/removals from (line 393), so a corrupted string can drive wrong edit decisions; the post-edit guard at lines 642–643 calls the same function, so it cannot catch this either.

Controls that work today and must keep working: a URL value (`"https://api.example.com/v1"` — the `//` is not preceded by whitespace), ordinary `//` line comments, and real trailing commas.

`bin/sync-models.mjs` also has no test file, unlike every sibling in `bin/` (`agy-proxy`, `antigravity-ls-proxy`, `clef-proxy`, `codex-proxy`, `design-code-proxy`, `muse-proxy` and `proxy-port` all have `*.test.mjs`).

## Evidence

`bin/sync-models.mjs` on current main (`b382bfb8`):

```js
function parseJsonc(text) {
  const cleanLines = text.split('\n').filter(l => {
    const s = l.trim();
    return !s.startsWith('//') && !s.startsWith('/*');
  }).map(l => l.replace(/\s+\/\/.*$/, ''));
  const cleaned = cleanLines.join('\n').replace(/,\s*([}\]])/g, '$1');
  return JSON.parse(cleaned);
}
```

Probe (function extracted verbatim with `sed -n '224,231p'`, run under Node):

```
blockComment          => THROWS Expected property name or '}' in JSON at position 2
stringWithCommentLike => THROWS Unterminated string in JSON at position 14
silentCorrupt         => OK {"note":"a] b","a":1}        (input was "a, ] b")
urlControl            => OK {"baseURL":"https://api.example.com/v1","a":1}
trailingCommaControl  => OK {"a":1}
```

Inputs: block comment = `{\n/* multi\nline comment */\n"a": 1\n}`; string cases as shown in the problem section.

Dedup: `gh issue list --search "sync-models"` returns only #591 (closed, Nix store config-path resolution) — no issue covers the parser. Cross-repo: `sync-models` exists only in this repo (no copy in the other three clones; OpenChamber's `parseJsonc` is the `jsonc-parser` library import in its VS Code package, unrelated code).

## Why it matters

sync-models runs as a service against Drew's real `~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc`, a hand-edited JSONC file. One block comment or one string with ` // ` in it stops model syncing entirely with a parse error that points at the config, not the parser; the `, ]` case is worse — it changes a config value silently and lets the sync act on the changed value.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The config read no longer uses the line-based stripper: parse the config with the file's own comment-aware machinery (`parseJsoncTree`, deriving the value from the recorded tree) or an equivalent string-aware JSONC parse, and use the same parse for the post-edit guard at lines 642–643.
- [ ] A config with a multi-line `/* … */` block comment parses to the same object as the same config without the comment.
- [ ] A string containing ` // `, `, ]` or `, }` round-trips byte-for-byte through the config parse.
- [ ] Existing good cases keep working: `//` line comments (whole-line and trailing), real trailing commas, URL values.
- [ ] New `bin/sync-models.test.mjs` (the script's first test file) pins the cases above; the parsing helpers need an export-for-test seam or equivalent, following the sibling proxies' test pattern.
- [ ] `node --check bin/sync-models.mjs` passes and a `--dry-run` against a fixture config exercising those cases completes without a parse error.

body:
## Finding

PR #685 fixed `design-code-proxy` forwarding the backend's `Content-Length` for bodies it re-serializes or rewrites — but only the non-stream half of that fix has a regression test. The streaming half is untested: no test in the suite can fail if the streaming path starts forwarding the stale length again.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/685 (merged, merge commit `0a405c64a908d14c68280959f49342a22ce11d0c`, fixes #684)
- The fix has two halves in `bin/design-code-proxy.mjs` on current main `4f905d75`:
  - Non-stream: `writeHead(sentBody)` advertises the re-serialized body's real length (`bin/design-code-proxy.mjs:239-240`, call sites `:287` and `:290`).
  - Streaming: `writeHead()` is called with no body at `:249`, which deletes the backend's `content-length` at `:241-243` so Node chunks the model-rewritten SSE stream.
- The new regression test (`bin/design-code-proxy.test.mjs`, "backend Content-Length does not truncate the re-serialized success body (#684)") only posts a non-stream request. Its stub mode `ok-length` is explicitly gated to non-stream requests: `stub.mode === 'ok-length' && !bodyText.includes('"stream":true')` (`bin/design-code-proxy.test.mjs:51`).
- The only streaming test, "streaming success is unchanged" (`bin/design-code-proxy.test.mjs:196-204`), uses the stub's streaming branch at `:58-66`, which answers `res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/event-stream' })` — it never sets a `Content-Length`, so the pre-fix and post-fix proxies behave identically for it.
- PR #685's own ablation confirms the gap: with only `bin/design-code-proxy.mjs` reverted, "exactly the new test fails; the other 5 design tests still pass" — i.e. reverting the streaming half of `writeHead` fails nothing.

Verified this run (pr-diff-review): design suite passes 6/6 on current main, and the diff/stub/test lines above were cross-checked via `gh pr diff 685`, `gh api pulls/685/files`, and the local clone at `origin/main`.

## Why it matters

The streaming path rewrites every SSE chunk's `model` field (`bin/design-code-proxy.mjs:255-267`), so a forwarded backend `Content-Length` is wrong for streamed responses in exactly the same way #684 documented for buffered ones: the client would stop reading at the backend's byte count, truncating the stream (and corrupting keep-alive framing for whatever follows). Today the code is correct; what is missing is the pin that keeps it correct. The sibling non-stream case shows this bug class has already shipped once in this file.

Single-repo: `design-code-proxy` exists only in this repo (per PR #685's git-grep check across the other three repos, re-confirmed by this job's sibling-proxy grep — no other proxy in `bin/` spreads backend response headers).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The stub backend gains a streaming mode that sets an explicit `Content-Length` on its SSE response (computed over the chunks it sends, whose `model` the proxy will rewrite to a different-length value).
- [ ] A regression test posts `{ stream: true }` against that stub and asserts the client receives the complete stream (all chunks plus `data: [DONE]`) and that any advertised `Content-Length` equals the byte count actually received.
- [ ] Ablation: with the streaming `delete headers['content-length']` behaviour reverted (stale length forwarded), the new test fails; with the fix in place, the full design-code-proxy suite passes.

body:
**Status: idea only, not a strong suggestion.** Recording it so it can be weighed later.

## What exists today (checked 2026-10-22)

Two different script environments can call MCP tools, and they handle imports in opposite ways:

| Environment | Imports | Observed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `mcpx run` / `mcpx exec` (Deno 2.9.7) | Anything, fetched at run time | `jsr:@std/async`, `jsr:@std/collections`, `npm:zod`, `npm:es-toolkit` and `https://esm.sh/p-limit@6` all import. Nothing pins versions or restricts which packages load. |
| OpenCode's Code Mode `execute` tool | None | `import()` fails with "Syntax 'ImportExpression' is not supported". No `setTimeout`, no `Deno`; only `fetch`. This interpreter is in the `opencode2` binary, not in mcpx. |

Related: mcpx scripts run with the `all` permission profile by default (`--allow-all` under deno, per `docs/runtimes.md`). A test script could read `/etc/hosts`, read `$HOME` from the environment, and see `Deno.Command`.

## Ideas to consider

1. **Import maps / pinned imports for mcpx scripts.** Let config (`script.importMap` or similar) name pinned versions such as `jsr:@std/async@1` and `npm:p-limit@6`, so scripts get reproducible versions and an operator can see and limit what loads. I have not checked whether the launcher already passes an import map or `deno.json` through.
2. **Whether to allow arbitrary remote imports by default at all,** or only those in the map, given that agents write many of these scripts.
3. **A small standard library for Code Mode (`execute`).** That runtime can't import, so common helpers get rewritten inline in every script, for example:
   - binding default arguments to a tool namespace, such as a fixed `aws_profile`
   - `chunk`, `uniqBy`, `keyBy`, `pick` / `omit`
   - `mapLimit` / bounded concurrency, `retry` with backoff, `withTimeout`

   mcpx might supply these as a projected helpers namespace, or the change might belong in OpenCode's Code Mode instead. Undecided.
4. **The default permission profile** (`all` vs `readnet`): `readnet` still allows imports and network access but blocks writes and subprocesses.

## Not proposing

- Baking libraries in as globals. That hides versions and doesn't help `execute`.
- Detecting imports and installing packages from mcpx itself. Deno already downloads and caches on first import.


## Acceptance criteria

This is an idea to weigh, not yet a commitment to build — "done" for this issue is a recorded decision plus, if the decision is to adopt, the smallest implementation that satisfies it:

- A decision is recorded on this issue for each of the four questions in the body: (1) pinned imports / import maps for mcpx scripts, (2) whether arbitrary remote imports stay allowed by default, (3) a small standard helper library for Code Mode `execute` (and whether it belongs in mcpx or in OpenCode), and (4) the default permission profile (`all` vs `readnet`).
- For any question decided "adopt": a linked implementation issue (or PR) exists with its own acceptance criteria — per the house rule, a design/idea issue is not finished work on its own.
- For any question decided "decline" or "defer": the reasoning is recorded on this issue so the idea does not get re-filed from scratch.
- If an import map is adopted: an mcpx script run with the map configured resolves the pinned versions (e.g. `jsr:@std/async@1`) and a script importing an unmapped remote package behaves as the decision specifies (allowed or refused), demonstrated by a test or a documented manual run.

title: Local proxy discovery: port files, sockets, or a registry instead of fixed ports?

labels.name: source/human
labels.description: Filed directly by a human

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: user/escalated
labels.description: Requires a Drew decision or access

labels.name: queue/blocked
labels.description: Queue or user escalation state

labels.name: effort/m
labels.description: Medium: expected under 1 day of work

labels.name: meta/enriched
labels.description: Intake review done: acceptance criteria, links, and normalized labels added

labels.name: kind/question
labels.description: Question or design decision to resolve

body:
## Question (Drew, 2026-10-20)

The four local proxies in `bin/` (clef 18742, agy 18743, codex 18744, antigravity-ls 18745) bind fixed localhost ports that other config must agree with. PR #431 + its follow-up single-sourced the numbers, so the copies can no longer drift — but a fixed port is still a fixed port: it can be taken by something else, and it must be known in advance by every consumer. Is there a better discovery mechanism? Options Drew named: pick ports randomly/nearby but stay findable; or first-launcher-takes-a-well-known-port and serves a registry of all running helpers. What do established apps actually do?

## The binding constraint

The main consumer, `.opencode/opencode.jsonc`, is **static config**: at load time it can substitute `{env:VAR}` and nothing else (developing-today/opencode `packages/core/src/config/variable.ts`). It cannot read files, query a registry, or follow a redirect. Any design that moves the port at runtime therefore needs one of:

- a launcher/shim that resolves the endpoint and exports the env vars before opencode starts, or
- a fork change (e.g. a `{file:...}` substitution, or `{env:VAR:-default}` fallback syntax — related: #434, the unset-variable case).

Every option below is judged against that constraint.

## Options

### (a) Port-file discovery — service binds, writes its endpoint to a well-known file

The service writes `$XDG_STATE_HOME/<name>/endpoint.json` (`{host, port, pid, url}`) on listen and unlinks it on exit. Clients that can read files always find the one running instance, whatever port it landed on.

Precedents: Chrome DevTools writes `DevToolsActivePort` (port + path) into the user-data dir for exactly this; Jupyter writes runtime connection files (`jpserver-*.json` with URL) under the runtime dir; VS Code's server/CLI handoff works the same way.

**Status: the publish half is implemented** in the follow-up PR to #431 (all four proxies now write/remove their endpoint file). The consume half exists only for future tooling until opencode or a launcher reads it.

### (b) Port fallback / increment — try the well-known port, else scan nearby

Dev servers do this (Vite, webpack-dev-server) — but their "client" is a human reading a printed URL. Here it is actively harmful: a proxy that lands on 18746 silently disagrees with the session's `{env:...}` value and the static config, recreating the exact silent-dead-provider failure #431 fixed, now nondeterministically. **Verdict: do not adopt** (except in combination with (a) + a file-reading client).

### (c) Registry on a well-known port (Drew's sketch)

First launcher binds a registry port and serves a stable interface listing every running helper and how to reach it.

Precedents: this is the classic **portmapper** pattern — Erlang's `epmd` (fixed port 4369) maps node names to the ephemeral ports nodes actually bound; ONC RPC's rpcbind is the same idea. It works there because the runtime speaks the protocol natively. Docker/Consul look similar but actually rendezvous on a Unix socket / agent API, not a TCP registry port.

Problems here: the recursion doesn't bottom out (the registry itself needs a fixed port or socket — if it uses a socket, option (d) alone was simpler); the loser of the bind race must reliably become a registry client; the registry is a new always-on component and a single point of failure; and opencode still can't query it. **Verdict: real pattern, wrong fit** — the registry's job is already done by systemd (it knows every unit and its state; `systemctl --user show` is the registry interface) for the service-managed case.

### (d) Unix domain sockets instead of TCP

No ports at all; each service listens on a deterministic path in `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`/state dir. **This repo already does it**: mcpx's daemon listens on `daemon-<confhash>.sock` in its state dir, overridable via `MCPX_DAEMON_ENDPOINT`, with `mcpx resolve` as the resolver. Also Docker (`docker.sock`), tmux, ssh-agent (`$SSH_AUTH_SOCK` env publication), D-Bus session bus.

Blocker: an opencode provider `baseURL` is an HTTP URL; the AI SDK cannot dial a Unix socket from a URL (undici needs a custom dispatcher). Closing this needs a fork change or a TCP→socket forwarder — which reintroduces a port. **Verdict: right answer for socket-capable consumers (mcpx proves it in-repo); blocked for opencode providers today.**

### (e) systemd socket activation

systemd owns the well-known listener and hands the fd to the service. Already in use in this repo: OpenChamber's `systemd.user.sockets.openchamber` holds `127.0.0.1:3000` across restarts so connections queue instead of being refused. Extending it to the four proxies removes the crash-loop failure when a previous instance still holds the port and makes restarts seamless, at the cost of a small `LISTEN_FDS` shim in each `.mjs` (`server.listen({ fd: 3 })`). It keeps fixed ports, so it solves reliability, not discovery. **Verdict: pragmatic, worth doing independently.**

## In-repo evidence that fixed ports already fail one layer up

The Antigravity language server — the upstream `antigravity-ls-proxy` wraps — binds a **random port every start**. `bin/antigravity-ls-proxy.mjs` and `bin/sync-models.mjs` discover it by scraping the process command line and logs for `--http_server_port N` / "listening on random port at N" and probing candidates. Log-scraping is the fragile worst form of discovery; it's what you're forced into when the service publishes nothing. (a) is the same idea with the service cooperating.

## Recommendation

1. Keep the single-sourced fixed ports as the default contract (done: #431 + follow-up PR fixing #435).
2. Port-file publication (a) is implemented publish-side in that PR; file-capable tooling should prefer it over assuming the port.
3. **Decision for Drew**: the only route to true dynamic ports (bind port 0 + port file, no fixed contract at all) is a fork change — teach opencode's config a `{file:...}` substitution (or `{env:VAR:-default}` fallback, cf. #434) so `baseURL` can resolve from `endpoint.json`. With that, the proxies could bind ephemeral ports and the fixed-port era ends. Without it, (e) is the pragmatic ceiling.
4. Do not adopt (b); (c) is superseded by systemd + (a).

## Related

- #431 — codex-proxy single-source
- #435 — single-source the remaining three proxies (fixed by the follow-up PR)
- #434 — `{env:...}` has no fallback when the variable is unset

## Acceptance criteria

- A decision is recorded on this issue (chosen option, or explicitly keep the fixed ports) with the reasoning against the static-config constraint in `.opencode/opencode.jsonc`.
- If a new discovery mechanism is adopted, follow-up implementation issues are filed and linked; if not, the port-file publish behaviour already shipped is documented as the standing answer.
- The decision addresses how a consumer that can only substitute `{env:VAR}` at load time finds a helper whose port moved, or states why that case cannot arise.

body:
## Problem

World resource profiles are stored as a new `JournalEntry::ExecutionProfile` variant. New binaries can read older journals, but an older binary cannot deserialize a journal after this entry has been written. The entry is currently appended under the journal's existing header version, so an old binary may fail while reading the entry rather than rejecting the file up front.

## Follow-up

Define the world-journal upgrade/rollback contract for new entry variants. Options include a versioned journal migration that atomically upgrades the header when the first new entry is written, an explicit no-downgrade policy with a reliable early refusal, or an operator-managed migration/backup workflow. Preserve read support for existing journals and ensure a failed migration cannot leave a partially rewritten journal.

This is not a blocker for forward-only upgrades, but operators must not roll back to an older binary after writing profile entries until a migration path exists.

## Acceptance criteria

- A written rollback/upgrade contract for new `JournalEntry` variants exists (versioned migration, explicit no-downgrade with early refusal, or operator-managed migration/backup) and is recorded in the journal code or docs it governs.
- An older binary refuses an incompatible journal early and clearly (at header/version check), not mid-read on an entry it cannot deserialize.
- Existing journals remain readable by new binaries (forward compatibility preserved).
- A failed migration cannot leave a partially rewritten journal (atomicity demonstrated by a test or a documented atomic-rename procedure).

body:
# id(web): classify_tag treats any '.archive.' filename as an archive — notes.archive.txt renders with an 'archive: ?' badge, sorts out of the primary list, and links by hash instead of by name

## Evidence (main `da42bfe7`)

- `pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs:165-169` (`classify_tag`): the archive branch returns `FileKind::Archive` for **any** name containing `.archive.`, whether or not the suffix after it parses as a unix timestamp:

  ```rust
  if let Some(pos) = name.rfind(".archive.") {
      let ts_str = &name[pos + ".archive.".len()..];
      let ts = ts_str.parse::<u64>().ok();
      return (FileKind::Archive, ts);   // Archive even when ts is None
  }
  ```

- The sibling `auto-` branch directly above it was fixed for exactly this flaw in #809/#810: it only returns `FileKind::Auto` when the remainder actually parses as an ISO date, and `test_classify_tag_auto_prefix_non_date_is_primary` (routes.rs:3119) pins that ordinary files like `auto-notes.txt` stay Primary. The archive branch never got the same treatment — `test_classify_tag_archive_no_timestamp` (routes.rs:3142) instead enshrines the loose behavior ("Even without a valid timestamp, .archive. pattern is recognized").
- No producer creates a non-numeric archive suffix: archives are minted as `{name}.archive.{unix-ts}` (`pkgs/id/src/fileops.rs:99-115`, `free_archive_name`), and fileops itself documents "Archive tags are named `<name>.archive.<unix-ts>`; match the numeric …" (fileops.rs:413-415). A non-numeric suffix is therefore never a real archive.

## Verified behavior (probe, laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-archiveclass/`)

`classify_tag` + `parse_iso_timestamp` copied verbatim from main, run over sample names:

```
notes.md.archive.1711000000         -> (Archive, Some(1711000000))   // genuine archive
notes.archive.txt                   -> (Archive, None)               // ordinary file
meeting.archive.notes               -> (Archive, None)               // ordinary file
backup.archive.draft                -> (Archive, None)               // ordinary file
x.archive.                          -> (Archive, None)               // empty suffix
photo.archive.2024-01-01            -> (Archive, None)               // date suffix, not a unix ts
auto-notes.txt                      -> (Primary, None)               // #809 control
my-document.md                      -> (Primary, None)
```

## Why it matters

An ordinary user file whose name merely contains `.archive.` (a file *about* archives is the obvious case) is misrendered in the file list, in the same ways #809 fixed for `auto-`:

- `pkgs/id/src/web/templates.rs:239-245`: it gets an `archive: ?` badge (parent `?` when no primary shares its hash; a fabricated parent link when one coincidentally does).
- `templates.rs:308-310`: its row links to `/hash/{hash}` instead of `/edit/{name}`.
- `routes.rs:897-916`: it sorts after every primary file (timestamp `unwrap_or(0)`), and `routes.rs:844-847` excludes it from `hash_to_primary`, so genuine auto/archive files sharing its hash lose their parent resolution and `get_file_name` (routes.rs:1027) won't prefer it.

## Acceptance criteria

- `classify_tag` returns `FileKind::Archive` only when the suffix after the last `.archive.` parses as a `u64` unix timestamp; otherwise the name falls through to `FileKind::Primary`.
- `test_classify_tag_archive_no_timestamp` is replaced with regression tests mirroring `test_classify_tag_auto_prefix_non_date_is_primary`: e.g. `notes.archive.txt`, `meeting.archive.notes`, `x.archive.` classify as Primary with no timestamp, while `notes.md.archive.1711000000` still classifies as Archive with its timestamp.
- Existing genuine-archive behavior is unchanged: rename/save archive naming (`free_archive_name`), sorting, badges, and parent resolution for numeric-suffix archives.

Dedup: #809/#810 cover the `auto-` prefix only; no open or recently closed issue covers the `.archive.` branch of `classify_tag`.

body:
# meta-exporter: parseSubscriptionQuota's num() reinterprets empty, hex and scientific strings as real measurements — a drifted '' used value exports as a measured 0% window

## Evidence (verified this run, main `da42bfe7`)

`pm-stack/meta-exporter/meta-quota-export.mjs`, `parseSubscriptionQuota` (line 69):

```js
const num = (v) => (typeof v === "string" || typeof v === "number" ? Number(v) : NaN);
```

The console API legitimately sends decimal strings (the captured-payload test at `meta-quota-export.test.mjs:19-21` uses `"100000000000"` / `"1023570000"`), so accepting strings is intentional. But bare `Number()` accepts far more than decimal spellings, and the parser's own contract (header, lines 66-68) is "Throws on any shape drift — fail-closed, never partial zeros":

Probe (laptop, importing the real module — file md5 `2f76d55332752bd1c43a86505f289007` on both clones; valid control payload, one field mutated per case; probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-metaempty/`):

| input | result |
|---|---|
| control (numeric fields) | `status`-ok windows: 5h usedPct 10, weekly usedPct 20 |
| `window_weighted_used = ""` | **OK — 5h usedPct exported as 0** (a fabricated measured-zero window) |
| `weekly_weighted_used = "   "` (whitespace) | **OK — weekly usedPct exported as 0** |
| `window_weighted_used = "0x10"` | **OK — usedPct 16** (hex reinterpreted) |
| `window_weighted_used = "1e2"` | **OK — usedPct 100** (scientific reinterpreted) |
| `window_resets_at = ""` with used = 10 | **OK — resetAt `1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z`**: `""` is neither `null` nor `undefined`, so it bypasses `resetField`'s absent-reset guard (lines 92-100), then `Number("") === 0` passes the finite/≥0 check |
| `as_of = ""` | **OK — consoleAsOf `1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z`** instead of `null` |
| controls: `window_weighted_used = "abc"` / `null` | correctly throws `unparseable` (exit 6) |

The existing malformed-reset test (`meta-quota-export.test.mjs:157-163`) pins `"soon"`, `-5`, `true`, `{}` as fail-closed — `""` slips past exactly the guard that test exists to enforce. Only the limit/duration fields are incidentally saved, by their separate zero checks (`window_limit = ""` → "zero limit"; duration `""` → ≤ 0): the *used* fields have no such backstop, so they are where the fake reading lands.

## Why it matters

This exporter's whole design is that "a failed tick can never be mistaken for a reading" (file header). An empty-string used value — the classic shape-drift / missing-value spelling from an upstream API — is currently exported in a `status: "ok"` document as a measured 0% window, and the quota gatherer ingests it as fact: real usage disappears from the burn/reset display precisely when the console API starts drifting. Hex/scientific spellings are silently reinterpreted into different numbers instead of failing closed.

## Acceptance criteria

- `parseSubscriptionQuota` accepts only plain decimal spellings (the API's actual format, per the captured payload) for its numeric fields: empty, whitespace-only, hex (`0x…`), scientific (`1e…`), and otherwise non-decimal strings throw `ExportError("unparseable", 6, …)`, for the used/limit/duration fields and inside `resetField` / `as_of` alike.
- `window_resets_at = ""` on a window with recorded usage fails closed like the absent-reset case; `as_of = ""` yields `consoleAsOf: null` or `unparseable`, never the 1970 epoch.
- New tests in `meta-quota-export.test.mjs` cover: `""` and `"   "` used values rejected; `"0x10"` / `"1e2"` used values rejected; `""` reset with usage rejected; the captured-payload (decimal-string) test and all existing tests still pass (`node --test pm-stack/meta-exporter/`).

## Dedup

- #2460 (open) is the timestamp *range/plausibility* gap (ms-scale and out-of-Date-range values) — a decimal-string or numeric input problem; it does not cover the used fields or the `Number("") === 0` coercion, and its fix would not stop a fake 0% window. The `""` → 1970 rows above are the same root cause (`num()`) surfacing in the timestamp fields; fixing `num()` here also removes those two spellings from #2460's surface.
- #2510 (open) is `parseBillingBanner` accepting *fractional numbers* — different function, different mechanism (no string coercion).
- #2743 is the same `Number()` pattern in supabase-export (different app/file). #1566 (closed) added the `window_duration_secs` validation only.

## Summary

`detectLanguage()` in `pkgs/id/web/src/highlight.ts` does plain-object lookups on three unguarded maps with keys taken from an arbitrary, user-chosen filename, so a filename whose extension or stem is an all-lowercase `Object.prototype` member name returns a prototype member instead of `undefined`:

- `highlight.ts:149-151` — `EXT_TO_LANG[ext]`, where `ext` is the lowercased extension of any document filename
- `highlight.ts:161-168` — `FILENAME_TO_LANG[nameWithoutExt]` and `FILENAME_TO_LANG[basenameLower]` with the lowercased stem / basename

Because the lookups are truthiness checks (`if (ext && EXT_TO_LANG[ext]) return EXT_TO_LANG[ext];`), inherited members count as hits. The declared return type is `string | undefined`, but at runtime the function returns a function or an object for these names.

## Evidence (verified this run, real module)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-highlightproto/probe.ts`, bun, importing the real `highlight.ts` from the laptop clone; file md5 `a88efa332c0483144cb896388e248cc9` matches sandbox `main` at `24ddc153`):

```
{"input":"notes.constructor","resultType":"function","result":"function Object() { [native code] }"}
{"input":"notes.__proto__","resultType":"object","result":"[object Object]"}
{"input":"constructor","resultType":"function","result":"function Object() { [native code] }"}
{"input":"__proto__","resultType":"object","result":"[object Object]"}
{"input":"notes.toString","resultType":"undefined"}   // lowercasing breaks the camelCase key — only all-lowercase prototype names leak
{"input":"app.ts","resultType":"string","result":"typescript"}        // control: correct
{"input":"Dockerfile","resultType":"string","result":"dockerfile"}    // control: correct
{"input":"notes.unknownext","resultType":"undefined"}                  // control: correct
```

Neither map has an own `constructor`/`__proto__` entry (`Object.hasOwn(...) === false` for both, verified in the same probe).

## Why it matters

- The "language" for a file named e.g. `notes.constructor` or `data.__proto__` is a function/object, not a Shiki language id. It flows into `createSyntaxHighlightPlugin` as `detectedLang` and into the parser / `languageExtractor` (`highlight.ts:325, 341, 379-386`), where `loadedLangs.has(lang)`, `getLoadedLanguages().includes(lang)` and the `LANG_IMPORTS` lookup all operate on a non-string: the file's code blocks silently never highlight, and any future consumer that treats the result as a string (concatenation, `import()` specifier, logging) gets `function Object() { [native code] }` / `[object Object]` instead of a language name.
- Same pattern in the same file: `ensureLanguage` (`highlight.ts:285`) does `LANG_IMPORTS[lang]` where `lang` can be the authored code-block `language` attribute (markdown fence info string — arbitrary text). `LANG_IMPORTS["constructor"]` is the `Object` constructor (callable — it gets *called* as an import function) and `LANG_IMPORTS["__proto__"]` is a non-function object that then throws when called; both are only saved by the surrounding try/catch marking the language loaded.
- Filenames are user/document metadata in a peer-to-peer file-sharing app — they are exactly the kind of untrusted string these lookup tables must not trust. This is the same plain-object-prototype class the fleet has fixed in the aggregator / pm-dispatch lookups; the id web maps were missed.

## Acceptance criteria

- `detectLanguage("notes.constructor")`, `detectLanguage("notes.__proto__")`, `detectLanguage("constructor")` and `detectLanguage("__proto__")` all return `undefined`.
- All three lookup sites in `detectLanguage` and the `LANG_IMPORTS` lookup in `ensureLanguage` only honour own properties of the maps (e.g. `Object.hasOwn` guard, `Object.create(null)` maps, or an equivalent own-key check) — a `language` attribute of `constructor`/`__proto__` is treated as an unknown language, never called as an import function.
- Existing behaviour is unchanged for real extensions / special filenames (the current `highlight.test.ts` suite passes, including the "every detected language has a grammar" guard from #749).
- New unit tests in `highlight.test.ts` cover the prototype-name cases above for both the extension and the bare-filename paths.

body:
## Problem

`id` web — Go to Line (Ctrl+G) still silently reinterprets non-decimal input as a line number, the #832 residual pattern in the #712 strict validation.

`pkgs/id/web/src/goto-line.ts:114` (main `12b7ec8a`):

```ts
const raw = (dialogInput?.value ?? "").trim();
const line = Number(raw);
...
activeView && raw !== "" && Number.isInteger(line) && line >= 1 && line <= lineCount
```

`Number()` accepts forms that are not decimal line numbers, and `Number.isInteger` does not exclude them. The #712 fix rejected `0`, negatives, fractions (`2.9`) and out-of-range values, but left every other `Number()` spelling:

| Input | `Number()` | Result today |
|---|---|---|
| `0x10` | 16 | jumps to line 16, dialog closes |
| `1e2` | 100 | jumps to line 100, dialog closes |
| `0b11` | 3 | jumps to line 3, dialog closes |
| `2.0` | 2 | jumps to line 2, dialog closes |

The user typed none of those line numbers in decimal; the jump is plausible-looking and silent — the same failure class #707/#832 fixed in `parseWorldSeed` by requiring a run of decimal digits (`/^\d+$/`) before `Number()`.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-gotoline/`): a copy of the real `pkgs/id/web/src` tree (goto-line.ts md5 `aae213d1b5004353f65638dd795260b6`, identical to main) with a vitest/happy-dom harness modelled on `goto-line.test.ts`, driving the real dialog over a 120-line code block (line *k* starts at doc pos `1 + (k-1)*3`):

- `0x10` → selection pos 46 (= line 16), dialog closed
- `1e2` → selection pos 298 (= line 100), dialog closed
- `0b11` → selection pos 7 (= line 3), dialog closed
- `2.0` → selection pos 4 (= line 2), dialog closed
- control `10` → pos 28 (= line 10), correct
- control `2.9` → no move, dialog stays open (the #712 behaviour, correct)

All 6 probe tests passed, confirming the reinterpretation in current code. Dedup: #712 (closed) covered 0/negatives/fractions/out-of-range only; #832 (closed) fixed the same `Number()` residual in `parseWorldSeed`, not here. No open issue covers goto-line input spelling.

## Why it matters

Go to Line is a navigation trust surface: a mistyped or pasted value (`2.0` from a spreadsheet, `0x10`, `1e2`) lands the cursor on a wrong line with no feedback, instead of keeping the dialog open with the text selected so the user can correct it — the exact contract #712 established.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Only an optional-whitespace-wrapped run of decimal digits is accepted as a line number (the `parseWorldSeed` rule in `world-seed.ts`); `0x10`, `1e2`, `0b11`, `2.0`, `+2` and any other non-digit spelling keep the dialog open with the input selected and do not move the cursor.
- [ ] Plain decimal input (including leading zeros, e.g. `007`) still jumps to the named line; the existing #712 rejections (`0`, negatives, fractions, out-of-range, empty) still hold.
- [ ] New cases are added to `goto-line.test.ts`'s invalid-input table using spellings that reinterpret to an *in-range* line on the 3-line fixture (e.g. `0x2`, `0b10`, `2.0`), so the tests would fail on the old code — out-of-range spellings alone cannot distinguish acceptance from rejection.

title: muse-proxy: direct mode — exchange the Muse CLI account token for the minted plan key and forward chat completions verbatim
body:
## What

Add a direct path to `bin/muse-proxy.mjs` so a chat completion no longer has to shell out to `muse exec --json` / a warm `muse serve` MSP host per request (which pays ~26k tokens of CLI harness scaffolding per call and flattens messages, losing native tool calling).

Requested directly by Drew on 2026-10-30 in the Muse side chat ("make the proxy do that", referring to the Muse CLI token-exchange mechanism).

## Verified mechanism (live on amd-6, 2026-10-30)

- The Muse CLI OAuth login token is an account token (`dca:…`, `~/.config/muse/auth.json` → `providers.meta.access_token`, device_code). It is NOT an inference credential: direct `/v1` calls with it return 401.
- Exchange: `POST https://api.meta.ai/muse-code/key` with `Authorization: Bearer <dca token>`, `x-api-version: 1.0.0`, body `{"onboard": false}` → 200. Response contains `api_key` (the `LLM|…` Muse Code plan key), `is_subs_active: true`, `require_payment: false`, `subs_tier_name`, `subs_usage`, etc.
- With the minted key: `GET /v1/models` → 200 (muse-spark-1.3, muse-wonder-1.0, -contributor variants). Chat completions reach the plan quota gate (429 Subscription quota exhausted when the 5h window is full — auth accepted).

## Scope

- Credential: read `$MUSE_AUTH_PATH || ~/.config/muse/auth.json`; use `providers.meta.access_token` for the exchange; if only `providers.meta.api_key` is present, use it directly. Never log secret values.
- Exchange + in-memory cache (10 min TTL); on upstream 401 invalidate + re-exchange once + retry once. `is_subs_active === false` / `require_payment === true` = hard error, no silent fallback to CLI paths.
- Forward `POST /v1/chat/completions` verbatim (messages/tools/tool_choice/response_format preserved; no formatPrompt flattening) to `{API_BASE}/v1/chat/completions` with the minted key; base model id via existing resolveModelAndEffort, reasoning_effort passed when explicitly requested; stream = untouched SSE passthrough; non-stream = upstream status+JSON verbatim. ANY upstream HTTP response (402/429/400) passes through as-is — never fall back after Meta has answered, never retry a quota wall.
- Fall back to existing warm/exec paths ONLY when direct is unavailable before any upstream response (no credential, exchange transport failure, upstream fetch throws).
- Kill switch `MUSE_PROXY_DIRECT=0`; API base override `MUSE_PROXY_META_API_BASE` (default https://api.meta.ai) for tests. /health gains a `direct` section (enabled, credential found, minted cached, tier/active — no secrets). /v1/models keeps the existing synthetic catalog.
- Tests in `bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs` against a local stub Meta API: exchange shape + minted-key auth, exchange caching, streaming tool_calls passthrough, 429 passthrough with NO exec fallback, and MUSE_PROXY_DIRECT=0 / no-auth.json leaving exec behavior unchanged. All pre-existing tests still pass (`node --test bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs` on the laptop).

## Related

- Warm-path work: #480. Proxy reconciliation: #484.

Capability only: this does NOT re-enable the OpenCode `muse` provider (disabled by Drew 2026-10-25) or any proxy service.

title: feat(dispatch): cross-repo grants + reusable Actions (starter/queuer) + workflow call-site migration

labels.name: source/dispatch
labels.description: Filed by pm-dispatch

body:
Drew's directive (2026-10-30): keep the pm-dispatch permission system, but establish grants so any allowlisted repo may target any other allowlisted repo; paper over the dispatch plumbing with centrally-updated reusable GitHub Actions referenced @main; migrate the fleet's workflow call sites onto them.

## Part 1 — Cross-repo grants (pm-stack/dispatch)
- OIDC rule changes from same-repo-only to a grant mesh: caller ∈ allowlist AND target ∈ allowlist (allowlist = the four fleet repos). Bearer unchanged.
- Grants model explicit in code + tests: cross-repo allowed, non-allowlisted caller rejected, non-allowlisted target rejected, same-repo still allowed, bearer unaffected.
- Small API extension: POST /v1/tasks accepts optional `issue_number` — attach to an existing issue in the target repo (task-id comment + queue/queued + source/dispatch labels) instead of creating a new one. Preserves tracker no-spam semantics for Part 3.
- Deploy to the laptop via install.sh; health version must move to the new main HEAD.

## Part 2 — Reusable actions (@main, this repo)
- `.github/actions/pm-dispatch-start` ("the starter"): OIDC fetch (aud pm-dispatch), POST /v1/sessions, outputs task_id/session_id/issue_number/issue_url.
- `.github/actions/pm-dispatch-queue` ("the queuer"): same plumbing over POST /v1/tasks, incl. issue / issue_number inputs.
- examples/dispatch-workflow.yml + dispatch README updated to the actions and the grants mesh.

## Part 3 — Call-site migration (all four repos)
Every Jules session-creation call in workflows → the starter; every direct issue creation → the queuer. Incidents that did both (tracker issue + Jules session) collapse to the starter alone — one issue per incident. Tracker-maintenance workflows keep no-spam: look up the open tracker, attach via the queuer's issue_number. Affected (enumerated 2026-10-30): code flake-inputs-update.yml, main-broken.yml, jules.yml, jules-daily-codebase-ideation.yml, jules-daily-flake-sync.yml; opencode jules-daily-upstream-sync.yml, main-broken.yml; openchamber opencode-update.yml, jules-daily-upstream-sync.yml, main-broken.yml; nix main-broken-watcher.yml (hybrid: dispatch's GitHub App is not installed on dezren39/nix, so its issue creation cannot move — the queue enqueue does).
Live proof: a workflow_dispatch-only pm-dispatch-smoke.yml in openchamber runs the queuer targeting developing-today/opencode (cross-repo), verified end-to-end, then cleaned up.

body:
## Problem

The NixOS pm-stack module (`nixos/services/pm-stack`) deploys the aggregator, projector, pm-git-sync, and quota-gatherer as home-manager user services, but three pieces of the pm stack still live outside it:

1. **pm-dispatch** — runs from a hand unit installed by `pm-stack/dispatch/install.sh` (deployed copy at `~/pm-stack/dispatch`).
2. **pm-tunnel** — the Cloudflare Tunnel connector is a hand-written user unit.
3. **The Kaneo docker stack** — `pm-stack/compose.yml` (Kaneo + PostgreSQL) is only started by running `pm-stack/deploy.sh` by hand; nothing starts it at boot, so it silently stays down (kaneo.security.cab 502s) until someone notices.

## Change

Extend `nixos/services/pm-stack/default.nix` so one `nixos-rebuild switch` deploys the whole pm stack:

- Add a `pm-dispatch` user service running from the primary checkout (`~/git/code/pm-stack/dispatch`), with its existing env files (`~/pm-stack/dispatch/.env` + `~/secrets/dispatch.env`) kept external to the module, exactly as the aggregator's state env files are.
- Add a `pm-tunnel` user service running cloudflared with the token from `~/pm-stack/tunnel.env`.
- Add a `pm-kaneo` oneshot user service that runs the stack's own `deploy.sh` flow from the `~/pm-stack` deployment dir (env render + compose pull/up), plus a self-heal timer so a docker-ordering failure at boot retries instead of leaving the stack down. `ExecStop` brings the compose stack down without touching the data volume.
- Teach `pm-git-sync` to redeploy `pm-dispatch` when the `pm-stack/dispatch` subtree changes.

Verification bar: the amd toplevel builds and the generated unit files carry the intended ExecStart/EnvironmentFile lines. Activation itself happens on Drew's next switch.

## Acceptance criteria

- `nixos/services/pm-stack/default.nix` gains a `pm-dispatch` user service running from the primary checkout (`~/git/code/pm-stack/dispatch`), with env files (`~/pm-stack/dispatch/.env` + `~/secrets/dispatch.env`) kept external to the module.
- A `pm-tunnel` user service runs cloudflared with its token from `~/pm-stack/tunnel.env`.
- A `pm-kaneo` oneshot user service runs the stack's own `deploy.sh` flow from `~/pm-stack` (env render + compose pull/up), with a self-heal timer retrying boot-time docker-ordering failures; `ExecStop` brings the compose stack down without touching the data volume.
- `pm-git-sync` redeploys `pm-dispatch` when the `pm-stack/dispatch` subtree changes.
- Verification: the amd toplevel builds and the generated unit files carry the intended ExecStart/EnvironmentFile lines. (Activation happens on Drew's next switch — not part of this issue's verification.)

title: mcpx cache: three Codex findings on merged PR #2555 — path traversal in cache remove, Put self-eviction, eviction/lease TOCTOU

body:
Filed by repo-queue worker lane C while completing queue task 3148. PR #2555 (implements #1908 Approach C, internal/cache) was merged at 2026-10-30T04:31:26Z (merge commit 674c4c6abf62b7071ef2cd9abe984bc2d152ff8a) with three Codex review findings (posted 2026-10-30T04:23:57Z by chatgpt-codex-connector[bot]) still undispositioned. All three are verified against the merged code on main (head 962a2757):

## 1. P2 — `mcpx cache remove` path traversal → recursive delete outside the cache root
`pkgs/mcpx/internal/cli/cache.go` passes the raw CLI args into `c.Remove(rest[1], rest[2], ...)`; `Cache.Path` is `filepath.Join(c.Root, kind, key)` with no validation (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/cache/cache.go`, Path/Remove), and `Remove` ends in `os.RemoveAll(p)`. Dot components / separators in kind or key escape the cache root (e.g. kind/key containing `../..`), so a mistyped or scripted `mcpx cache remove` can recursively delete unrelated directories, and can bypass lease pins on descendant entries.
**Fix:** reject dot components and path separators in kind/key (validate in `Remove` and ideally in `Path`/`Dir` for all callers), and verify the resolved target is exactly one entry inside the intended kind directory before deleting. Add a regression test with `../` inputs.

## 2. P2 — `Put` can evict the entry it just stored and still report success
`Put` renames the new entry into place, then calls `_ = c.Evict(kind, lim)`; `Evict` calls `SelectVictims(entries, lim, "")` — the keep argument is empty, so the just-stored entry is not protected. When the payload alone exceeds `lim.MaxBytes` (repro: 2-byte payload, MaxBytes 1), eviction removes the new entry and `Put` returns its now-nonexistent path with a nil error.
**Fix:** pass the new entry path as keep to the post-Put eviction, or explicitly reject oversized entries with an error instead of reporting success. Add the repro as a unit test.

## 3. P2 — eviction/lease TOCTOU: an entry leased after Scan can still be deleted
`Evict` and `Prune` decide victims from a `Scan` snapshot (`Leased: false`) and later `os.RemoveAll` them without re-checking the lease at deletion time. A runner that acquires a lease in the scan→remove window loses its pinned entry — `mcpx cache prune` can delete a workdir/program a running exec has successfully pinned, breaking the pinning guarantee #1908 is built on.
**Fix:** give lease acquisition and deletion a shared exclusion protocol (e.g. re-check `Leased()` immediately before each removal as a minimum, or a per-entry lock), and add a deterministic scan→lease→evict test.

## Acceptance
- All three findings fixed with regression tests; `go test ./...` for pkgs/mcpx passes in CI.
- The three Codex threads on PR #2555 are replied to (linking the fix) — worker note: replies/filing are being posted from queue task 3148 in the same pass this issue is filed.
- Parent: #1908 stays open/closed per its own state; this issue covers only these three defects in the merged mechanism.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Cache.Path`/`Remove` (and sibling entry points) reject kind/key values containing path separators or dot components; a regression test with `../` inputs proves nothing outside the cache root can be deleted
- [ ] `Put` never reports success for an entry that is no longer present: the just-stored entry is kept through post-Put eviction, or an oversized entry is rejected with an explicit error (the 2-byte payload / MaxBytes 1 repro becomes a unit test)
- [ ] Eviction/prune re-checks lease state at deletion time (or shares an exclusion protocol with lease acquisition), so an entry leased after the victim Scan is not deleted
- [ ] Existing internal/cache tests pass
