body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#818 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

## Problem

Server definitions are fully static: `internal/config/config.go` (`Server` struct) holds `Command`/`Args`/`Env`/`Cwd` with no placeholders — `grep '${'` across `internal/config` and `internal/pool` finds no templating at all.

That blocks argv-rooted servers from opting into per-scope roots. Example: codedb's index root is baked into its argv (the fleet points it at one big tree, `/home/user/git`, and relies on its per-call `project` argument for everything else). A future per-repo codedb entry — or any server that takes its root as an argument or env var — cannot express "the scope-resolved root" in config today.

## Proposed smallest design

Support two placeholders, substituted **at instance-spawn time only**:

- `${mcpx.root}` — the scope-resolved directory (repo common-dir's worktree / worktree top-level / caller cwd, per the server's scope)
- `${mcpx.cwd}` — the caller's cwd from `CallContext`

Substitution sites: `Args`, `Env`, and `Cwd`.

Constraints from the design note (2026-10-25):

- Substitute at spawn, never in the stored config — config stays static and hashable.
- The substituted values must feed the era-hash inputs: `eras.go` already hashes the spawn definition, and since substitution happens upstream of instance creation, the effective `Cwd`/`Args`/`Env` it sees are the substituted ones. Verify this holds rather than assuming it.
- Unknown or malformed placeholders are a config error at load/spawn, not silently passed through to the child.

## Relationship to the spawn-cwd issue

Companion to #817 (step 1 of the same design note). That issue covers the implicit default (child cwd when config `cwd` is empty); this one covers explicit opt-in via arguments/env. Either can land first, but both should land before fleet configs flip servers to `repo`/`worktree` scopes — and this one depends on the same resolved-root plumbing, so implementing them together is cheapest.

Step 3 of the note (initialize `rootUri`/`workspaceFolders`) is #819, and builds on the same resolution.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `${mcpx.root}` and `${mcpx.cwd}` in a server's `Args`, `Env`, or `Cwd` are replaced with the scope-resolved root / caller cwd when an instance spawns.
- [ ] The stored/merged config on disk and in `mcpx` config output remains unsubstituted.
- [ ] The era/instance identity reflects the substituted spawn definition (two instances differing only by substituted root do not collide).
- [ ] An unknown `${mcpx.*}` placeholder fails loudly with the server name and field.
- [ ] Servers whose config contains no placeholders behave exactly as before.
- [ ] Tests cover substitution in each of Args/Env/Cwd and the unknown-placeholder error.

https://github.com/wileai/codex-connectors-mcp exposes the apps connected in Codex (GitHub, Figma, ...) over MCP. Codex owns the OAuth, so credentials never pass through it or mcpx.

Set up: install the Codex CLI (not installed here today), `codex login`, connect apps, then add it to mcpx's config (`mcpx.config.nix` in this repo) as a stdio upstream: `npx -y @wileai/codex-connectors-mcp@latest` with `CODEX_CONNECTORS_ALLOW` naming the apps, and probably `CODEX_CONNECTORS_MODE=compact`, since mcpx's own catalogue does the discovery.

Gets authenticated services today; does not replace #253.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Codex CLI installed, `codex login` completed, and at least one app connected in Codex
- [ ] `codex-connectors-mcp` is configured as a stdio upstream in this repo's mcpx config with `CODEX_CONNECTORS_ALLOW` naming the connected apps (and `CODEX_CONNECTORS_MODE=compact` unless a reason against is recorded)
- [ ] A call through mcpx to one connected app succeeds end-to-end, demonstrating OAuth stayed entirely on the Codex side
- [ ] This is recorded as complementary to #253 (not a replacement), per the body

Relocated from dezren39/nix#340 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

mcpx's daemon decides this, for every call it forwards upstream, whichever client made it: a gateway-side setting, per server and globally.

- `ask` (default): confirm any call to a tool not marked read-only, through the caller's elicitation or mcpx's question queue, showing the exact tool and arguments. A caller that can answer neither gets a clear refusal.
- `allow`: no confirmation; the caller's own approval is trusted.
- `deny`: refuse tools not marked read-only, and every tool marked destructive.

Today `elicit.confirmDestructive` covers part of `ask` for tools annotated destructive (and, since #308, unannotated ones). This generalises it. Annotations are hints from the upstream, not proof (#257, annotation trust). Interacts with the autonomy dial and its ceiling (decision 0002).

Reference: https://github.com/wileai/codex-connectors-mcp#writes

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A gateway-side write policy setting exists per server and globally, with `ask` as the default
- [ ] `ask`: any call to a tool not marked read-only requires confirmation showing the exact tool and arguments (via the caller's elicitation or mcpx's question queue); a caller that can answer neither gets a clear refusal
- [ ] `allow`: no confirmation; `deny`: tools not marked read-only are refused, and every destructive-marked tool is refused
- [ ] The generalization subsumes today's `elicit.confirmDestructive` behavior without regressing it, and the interaction with the autonomy dial and its ceiling (decision 0002) is implemented and documented
- [ ] Tests cover all three modes, the unannotated-tool case (#308's extension), and the cannot-answer refusal path

Relocated from dezren39/nix#130 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #99

## Summary

A flaky test found only on the lead's third full-suite run is the motivating case: a flake that one run in three exposes is invisible to a CI that runs once, and invisible to agents who (per #127) will no longer run the full suite at all. This issue decides how flakes are **found** (race detector, shuffled order, repeat runs), **where** that costs time (changed tests per PR, everything nightly), and what happens when one is found (fix vs quarantine; never a silent retry). It also records that macOS vs Linux differences (#35) are a flake source CI cannot see today.

## Original notes

> - testing
>   - importantly, as we add more testing agents should not run every single test basically ever. below documents a rough idea of a ci job design/policy, the main priority is being short as possible.
>   - agents should make at least 1 simple, new test for every bug observed from any source, when cheap to do so-- aggresively test many permutations. 

(Why these: repeat runs and `-race` cost time the second line forbids spending on every PR, so most of it moves to scheduled jobs; "aggresively test many permutations" includes permutations of *order* and *schedule*, which is what `-shuffle` and `-race` supply. The seed bullet under the third line is owned by #93 and quoted in #128; the only part used here is that the shuffle seed derives from the run seed.)

## Current state

- CI runs `go test ./... -count=1` once, ubuntu-latest only, no `-race`, no `-shuffle` (`.github/workflows/mcpx.yml:65`, unchanged at 05c78b2). No test calls `t.Parallel()`, so the main nondeterminism is order, timing, subprocesses and goroutines inside the daemon.
- Today the only repeat runs are by hand, in the integrator's pre-merge routine: PR #69/#70 "Suite 2× clean", #171 "Suite 3× clean before my change and 2× after", #182 "Suite 3× clean" (plus a daemon count across the three). #127 rule 7 keeps that exception until the jobs below replace it.
- Flakes and races found so far, all by repetition or by `-race` run by hand:
  - PR #46: "A flaky client test: the older fake answered the client's own replies ... One run in three panicked. Found by running the suite repeatedly, not once."
  - PR #56 / #61: a data race in `internal/tasks` + `internal/mcpserver`, "~1 run in 5 under `-race`", "Invisible because the suite does not run `-race`."
  - `internal/testsupport/build.go:47-53`: building the binary per test under `go test ./...` load "produc[ed] a different spurious failure on each run".
  - #35: two tests passed on macOS and failed on Linux (the tests were wrong). Development happens on macOS; CI is Linux. Once agents stop running the full suite locally (#127), **nothing runs the full suite on macOS any more.**
- `go help testflag`: `-shuffle off,on,N` randomizes test order within a package and reports the seed; `-count n` runs each test n times; results are reported per run. The race detector costs roughly 2-20x CPU and 5-10x memory (https://go.dev/doc/articles/race_detector); since Go 1.20 it needs no cgo on macOS, and on Linux needs a C linker (present on ubuntu-latest) (https://go.dev/doc/go1.20).
- The repo is public, so GitHub-hosted macOS runners cost no minutes (they are slower to start and fewer run concurrently).

## Proposed policy

1. **No retries that hide flakes.** No `gotestsum --rerun-fails`, no "re-run failed jobs until green" as a merge path. A test that failed once and passed on retry is a found flake: it gets an issue.
2. **Changed tests are repeated before merge.** Tests added or modified in a PR (selected by the #127 script) run in a PR job with `-race -shuffle=<derived> -count=N` -- N=10 for unit, N=3 for e2e as a start. Runs in parallel with the main matrix so it does not lengthen the longest job (#95's budget).
3. **The whole suite is stressed on a schedule.** Nightly (or per N commits to `main`): `go test -race -shuffle=<derived> -count=3 ./...` on ubuntu **and macOS**. Failures open or update an issue automatically; the job never blocks a PR.
4. **`-shuffle` seed derives from the run seed** (#93), e.g. the first 63 bits of its hash, so a failing order is reproduced from the one seed CI printed. `-shuffle=on` (clock-seeded) is not used in CI.
5. **Fix now, or quarantine with an expiry.** A quarantined test calls a helper, e.g. `testsupport.Quarantine(t, "#123", "2026-11-15")`, that skips it until the date and then **fails** -- so a quarantine cannot become permanent. The nightly job runs quarantined tests anyway and reports them without blocking. A guard lists quarantine calls and fails on a missing issue link or an expired date (#129).
6. **Reproduce locally by name only:** `go test -count=20 -race -shuffle=<seed> ./internal/<pkg> -run '^TestX$'`. Never "run the whole suite a few times" locally as a way to reproduce (#127: cost; #52's leak is fixed by #182, so the cost is time only).

## Approaches

### A -- retry on failure (least recommended)
Let CI retry failed tests (or jobs) once or twice and merge on green. It is what many projects do because it makes the dashboard quiet. It is exactly wrong here: the #46 flake panicked one run in three, so a single retry passes it ~89% of the time and the bug ships; retries also double the time of every red run, against the "short as possible" priority, and teach everyone that red means "try again". Rejected.

### B -- fix-now always, no quarantine
Any flake blocks all merges until fixed. Honest and simple. In practice a flake in, say, the TUI blocks an unrelated protocol fix, and the path of least resistance becomes deleting or `t.Skip`-ing the test with no record -- a worse quarantine than a tracked one. Fine as the default *intent*; too rigid as the only rule.

### C -- detect by repetition off the critical path, fix-now by default, quarantine only with issue and expiry (recommended)
Policy 1-6 above: `-race`/`-shuffle`/`-count` on changed tests per PR (cheap, parallel), the whole suite stressed nightly on two OSes, no hiding retries, quarantine as a dated, linked, guarded exception. Recommended because it finds the classes that have actually bitten mcpx (order/timing flakes, data races, OS differences) at a cost outside the PR's longest job, and it makes the escape hatch visible and self-expiring instead of forbidding it and getting silent skips.

### Sub-choice: other operating systems

| Option | Catches #35-type bugs | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ubuntu only (today) | only Linux-side | none |
| macOS in the nightly stress job only | yes, within a day | nightly minutes only |
| macOS for e2e on every PR | yes, before merge | slower runner start; lengthens the longest job if e2e shards are not rebalanced (#95) |

Recommended: macOS nightly now, promote to a PR shard if a macOS-only bug escapes. Other OSes and distros (alpine, fedora, windows) belong to the environment matrix in #97; this issue only asks that at least one non-ubuntu OS runs the suite on a schedule.

## Open questions

- N for `-count` per tier (10 unit / 3 e2e is a guess; measure against #95's budget).
- Does `-race` on the e2e package help? The race detector instruments the test binary, not the `mcpx` binary it builds. A race-enabled *mcpx* needs `go build -race ./cmd/mcpx` in `testsupport` behind an env switch -- probably worth it for the nightly job.
- Is the nightly job allowed to open issues automatically, or only post to a tracker comment?
- Quarantine helper name and where the "expired" check runs (test itself vs a guard vs CI).

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** M · **Impact** high
**Depends on / related**: #93 (run seed -> shuffle seed), #95 (PR job, nightly job, budget), #97 (OS/environment matrix), #35, #52 (closed, fixed in #182), #46, #56, #61; siblings #127 (rule 7: the integrator's repeat runs, which this issue moves into CI), #128, #129, #131.

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

## Acceptance criteria

- A flake policy is decided and recorded (on this issue and in the contributor page, #1976): how flakes are found (race detector, shuffled order, repeat runs) and where that time is spent (changed tests per PR, full coverage nightly).
- The found-a-flake process is defined: fix vs quarantine, quarantine always with an expiry, and never a silent retry.
- The macOS-vs-Linux flake source is recorded with a route to visibility (second OS in CI) or an explicit deferral with its reason.
- The work described in the Summary/Scope above is delivered via a branch + PR (no direct push to main); verification runs in GitHub Actions CI, not on the sandbox.
- Evidence (policy text and any CI changes) is recorded on this issue before it is closed.

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#299 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #173

## Summary

mcpx runs scripts in JavaScript runtimes and notes its own problem with that:
"Only Deno has a permission model to speak of; bun and node run with the"
caller's full authority (`internal/runner/runner.go:43`). So the sandbox is a
flag set on one of three runtimes, and absent on the other two.

A WebAssembly module is the opposite default. It can reach *nothing* — no files,
no network, no clock, no environment — until a host hands it an import. And
**wazero** is a WASM runtime written in pure Go with no cgo, which means mcpx
could gain capability-based sandboxing without the toolchain cost that sinks
most such proposals in this codebase.

Two uses follow, and they are worth separating: a `.wasm` module as a **tool
source** (a server in a sandbox), and WASM as a **script runtime** (an untrusted
script that is safe by construction rather than by flag).

This is distinct from #84, which is about compiling *mcpx itself* to WASM.

## Original notes

> you can imagine what i might want build out your dreams

Arising from the same capability argument as the Roc platform proposal: the
interesting property is not the language, it is that the host decides what the
guest can reach, and the type system or the module boundary enforces it.

## Current state

**Three JS runtimes, one of which can be restrained.**
`runner.Detect` resolves `deno`, `bun`, `node` (`internal/runner/runner.go:73`),
and the package comment records the asymmetry at `:43`. #293 covers configurable
permission flag sets, which makes the Deno case better and does nothing for the
other two.

**Tool sources are processes or declarations.** An upstream MCP server is a
spawned process or an HTTP endpoint (`internal/mcpclient/stdio.go:67`,
`http.go`); an adapter is an `exec` of a binary
(`internal/adapter/adapter.go:237`); an OpenAPI document is HTTP calls. Every
one of them runs with the daemon's authority or the binary's own. #83 is
designing the tool-source interface that would let a fourth kind exist.

**WASM appears twice on the tracker, neither as this.** #84 is "embedding mcpx
-- a public Go API, the C ABI, WASM, and mcpx as its own upstream", i.e. mcpx
compiled *to* WASM. #156 mentions WASM for a runnable example on the docs home
page. Nothing proposes WASM as something mcpx *runs*.

**Why wazero specifically.** It is a pure-Go WASM runtime with no cgo and no
external dependency, which is the property that makes this proposal cheap where
the iroh and Roc-platform proposals are expensive. `nix build` keeps
cross-compiling for free and the release matrix (#158) does not grow.

## Approaches

### Approach A — least recommended: a WASI-preview-1 script runtime, and nothing else

Add `wasm` to the runtime list; `mcpx exec foo.wasm` runs it with WASI p1 and a
preopened directory.

Cheap and nearly pointless as stated. WASI p1 gives file and stdio access and no
networking, so the module cannot call a tool, which is the entire reason to run a
script under mcpx. Without a host import for `call`, a WASM script is a
calculator. Worth doing only as the substrate for B or C, never as the feature.

### Approach B — middle: a `.wasm` module as a tool source

A module exports `list_tools` and `call_tool`; mcpx instantiates it with wazero
and registers it as a namespace through #83's tool-source interface.

This is the smallest shape with a real payoff. A tool source that is a single
file, cannot read your home directory, cannot phone home, and runs
deterministically — compared with today's alternative, which is spawning
somebody's `npx` package with your full user authority. For the "I found an MCP
server on the internet" case, that difference is the whole ballgame.

Its limit is that WASM's ecosystem story for *writing* such a module is still
rough, so in practice the author is in Rust, Go, Zig or C, and the convenience
gap against writing a Node MCP server is large. It is a security feature people
will adopt only when they are already nervous.

### Approach C — recommended: the component model as the tool boundary, with B as the first slice

WASI preview 2 and the **component model** give typed, language-agnostic
interfaces defined in WIT, and `wasmtime`'s Go bindings or wazero's evolving
support can host them. Define the mcpx tool-source contract *as a WIT world*:
the guest exports tool listing and invocation; the host imports are exactly the
capabilities mcpx chooses to grant — `call` another tool, `log`, `emit`,
`artifact`, and nothing else unless declared.

What that buys over B:

- **The capability set becomes a declaration, per module.** A module's manifest
  states it needs `call` and `artifact`; the daemon grants that and no more, and
  the grant is reviewable in config. This is the same shape as the daemon
  permission model and should share its vocabulary.
- **Any source language.** Rust, Go, C, Zig, and increasingly Python and
  JavaScript, all compile to components. A tool source stops being tied to
  whoever writes Node.
- **The same world serves scripts.** An untrusted *script* is a component with
  the same imports, so the script-runtime and tool-source cases collapse into one
  mechanism rather than two.
- It composes with #83's tool-source interface instead of being a fifth special
  case, and with the daemon permission model (#298) as the thing that decides which
  modules get which imports.

The honest costs: the component model tooling is young and moving; wazero's
component support is less mature than wasmtime's, and wasmtime's Go bindings
reintroduce cgo, which would forfeit the main advantage — so **"pure Go" and
"component model" may not both be available yet**, and that tension is the first
thing to resolve. Start with B on wazero and core WASM, with the interface shaped
so the component world can replace the ABI underneath.

## Open questions

- Can wazero host components today at an acceptable maturity, or does C require
  wasmtime and therefore cgo? This decides whether C is reachable at all, and is
  the one piece of research that gates the rest.
- Performance: is per-call instantiation acceptable, or does a module need
  pooling like a server does? Instantiation is cheap but not free, and the pool
  already exists for processes (`internal/pool`).
- Does a WASM tool source go in the pool? Same question #83 asks about adapters,
  which have no long-lived process either. The answers should match.
- Distribution: a `.wasm` is content-addressable and would sit naturally in
  #187's cache. Is a module referenced by path, by URL, by hash, or by an OCI
  registry reference (the emerging convention)?
- Does an untrusted *script* in WASM actually help, given the script is usually
  the user's own? The threat model is sharper for third-party tool sources than
  for scripts, which argues for B's framing over A's.
- Debuggability: a panicking WASM module gives a worse diagnostic than a
  panicking process. What does `mcpx doctor` say about a module that will not
  instantiate?

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease:** M for B on wazero with core WASM; L–XL for C, with a hard research
gate on component-model hosting in pure Go. **Impact:** medium now, high later —
it is the only proposal on the tracker that makes "run somebody else's tool
source" safe by construction, and the cheapest of the three capability-sandbox
ideas (this, Roc's platform, a process sandbox) because it costs no new
toolchain.

**Depends on / related:** #83 (the tool-source interface this plugs into — do
not add a fifth `Extra` path), #173 (parent tracker: extensibility), #84 (mcpx
*as* WASM — the mirror image, and shares the C ABI question), #293 and
`internal/runner/runner.go:43` (the Deno-only permission model this is an answer
to), #175/#105/#106 (runtimes and languages, if WASM becomes a script runtime),
#187 (content-addressed cache — a natural home for modules), #158 (distribution),
#80/#82 (plugins — a WASM module is a strong candidate for the plugin contract,
since a plugin is the thing you least want running unsandboxed), #298 (a
permission vocabulary this could reuse later — not a dependency).

## Acceptance criteria

- A written decision separates the two uses — `.wasm` as a tool source vs WASM as a script runtime — with a recommendation for each.
- If a use proceeds: a wazero-hosted module runs with no filesystem, network, clock, or environment access except imports the host explicitly grants, demonstrated by a test module that is denied a capability it did not receive.
- Pure-Go constraint holds: no cgo introduced into the build.
- Existing JS-runtime script behaviour and process/HTTP tool sources are unchanged.

Relocated from dezren39/nix#297 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #174

## Summary

Reaching a daemon today means reaching an *address*. `daemon.endpoint`
(`internal/settings/registry.go:356`) takes a URL, the server listens on a unix
socket and a TCP port (`internal/daemon/server.go:205,220`), and #85 covers
getting to that port over ssh with tunnels. All of it assumes you can name a
route to the machine.

The thing that is actually wanted is to reach a daemon by **identity** — "my
laptop's mcpx", from a phone, from a different network, with no port forwarded,
no public IP, no dynamic DNS and no ssh key copied anywhere. iroh does exactly
this: QUIC between nodes named by an ed25519 public key, hole-punched directly
where possible and relayed where not, end-to-end encrypted either way.

The crux is not whether that is desirable. It is that **iroh is Rust and mcpx is
Go**, and this issue exists mostly to force that question into the open before
anyone starts, because the honest answer may be that a Go-native transport wins
on merit.

## Original notes

> add another for iroh support
>
> you can imagine what i might want build out your dreams

## Current state

**Two listeners, both address-shaped.** `Server.Start` binds a unix socket at
`s.paths.Socket` and a TCP listener on a host/port
(`internal/daemon/server.go:205,220`). `daemon.endpoint` lets a client point at
a remote daemon, with a documented fallback to a local one when the remote is
unreachable (`internal/settings/registry.go:356-364`).

**Remote reach is already a theme, already scoped to ssh.** #85 is "remote
access over ssh -- TUI, RPC, reverse tunnels, and why not a built-in ssh
server", under the #174 surfaces tracker. ssh solves authentication and
encryption and solves routing *only if* you can already reach the host. The
laptop-behind-NAT case is precisely where it does not help, and that is the case
worth solving.

**Content addressing is also already a theme.** #187 asks for "one
content-addressed cache for prepared dependencies, import graphs and flake
resolution". Artifacts shipped in #57. Both are BLAKE3-shaped problems that
`iroh-blobs` already solves as a library, with verified streaming and resumable
transfer.

**No Go implementation of iroh exists.** iroh is a Rust project (n0-computer).
`iroh-ffi` provides C bindings. There is no maintained Go port and writing one
is not a weekend.

## Approaches

### Approach A — least recommended: cgo against `iroh-ffi`

Link the Rust library into the Go binary through its C FFI.

This gets real iroh with its real guarantees and poisons the build. mcpx is
currently a pure-Go binary that `nix build` cross-compiles without ceremony;
cgo plus a Rust toolchain means per-platform native artefacts, a much larger
`package.nix`, cross-compilation that stops being free, and a release matrix
(#158) that multiplies. It also drags Rust's async runtime into a Go process,
which is a category of debugging nobody in this repository has signed up for.
The capability is not worth that unless everything else has failed.

### Approach B — middle: iroh as a sidecar, tunnelling to the existing socket

Run an iroh node as a separate process. It accepts an incoming connection by
`NodeId`, and proxies the stream to the daemon's existing unix socket. mcpx
learns one new thing: how to supervise and address a sidecar.

Honest and incremental. The daemon needs no new transport at all — it already
speaks HTTP over a unix socket, and the sidecar is a tunnel endpoint. It keeps
Go pure, it is testable, and it can be an optional component people install
rather than something in every binary.

Its costs are distribution and truth-in-advertising: a second binary from a
second toolchain in the release pipeline, and "mcpx supports iroh" meaning "mcpx
supports a thing you install next to mcpx".

### Approach C — recommended: write down the requirement, then pick the transport on Go-native merit

The property wanted is a short list, and iroh is one implementation of it:

1. a daemon reachable by stable cryptographic identity, not by address
2. NAT traversal without port forwarding, with a relay fallback
3. end-to-end encryption and mutual authentication from that identity

Who may then do what is a separate question, tracked separately (#298/#253),
and explicitly **not** a dependency of this issue.

Stated that way, the Go ecosystem has candidates that do not cost a Rust
toolchain, and they should be evaluated *against* iroh rather than assumed
inferior:

- **`tsnet`** (Tailscale) embeds a full Tailscale node **in a Go program**. It
  gives 1–3 outright, with mature hole-punching, a working relay network
  (DERP), identity tied to an existing account, and ACLs that are a real answer
  to 4. It is pure Go and already in this project's orbit — #115 proposes a
  Tailscale *server*, which means the dependency may be arriving anyway. The
  cost is a dependency on Tailscale's coordination service unless self-hosting
  Headscale, which is a genuine centralisation objection iroh does not have.
- **`go-libp2p`** gives 1–3 with no central coordinator, pure Go, at the price
  of being a large dependency with sharp operational edges around relays and
  peer discovery.
- **iroh**, via B, if the decentralisation and the blob story outweigh the
  sidecar.

**Where iroh wins on something the others do not have:** `iroh-blobs` is
BLAKE3-verified, resumable, content-addressed transfer, and #187 is already
asking for a content-addressed cache. If prepared dependencies, import graphs
and artefacts became iroh blobs, then "fetch this script's dependency closure
from whichever of my machines has it" is the same mechanism as "reach my
daemon", and that is a genuinely better story than tsnet or libp2p offer. If
that convergence is the goal, iroh's case is much stronger and B becomes worth
its cost.

So: do not start with a transport. Start with a short research issue that
answers "which of tsnet, libp2p and iroh-as-sidecar meets 1–4 for a pure-Go
binary, and does #187 want iroh-blobs badly enough to pay for a sidecar?" Then
implement the winner behind an interface the daemon can hold more than one of,
because the authorisation work in 4 is required regardless of who wins and is
probably the larger half of the job.

## Open questions

- Does the daemon hold more than one transport at once, or is it one at a time
  by configuration? Holding several is friendlier and multiplies the surface
  each has to be correct on.
- Does the TUI (#85's reverse-tunnel motivation) work acceptably over a relayed
  connection, or does the latency make it unpleasant precisely when hole
  punching fails?
- Is the real requirement "reach my daemon" or "reach my daemon *from a phone*"?
  If a browser is in the picture at all, none of iroh, tsnet or libp2p is
  directly reachable from a web page, and the answer is a hosted relay, which is
  a different project.
- Does `daemon.endpoint` grow a scheme (`iroh://<nodeid>`, `ts://<host>`), or
  does identity-based reach get its own setting? A scheme keeps one setting and
  one mental model.
- If a sidecar is acceptable here, is it acceptable for the Roc platform host
  too? Two issues wanting a Rust artefact is a different decision from one.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease:** S for the research comparison; M for a sidecar tunnel (B); L–XL for
cgo (A). **Impact:** high — "reach your own daemon from anywhere without
configuring a network" is the difference between mcpx as a local tool and mcpx
as personal infrastructure.

**Depends on / related:** #85 (remote access over ssh — the incumbent answer,
and this issue is the case ssh cannot reach), #174 (parent tracker: surfaces),
#187 (content-addressed cache — the strongest argument for iroh specifically,
via `iroh-blobs`), #115 (proposes a Tailscale server; if that lands, `tsnet` is
already a dependency and Approach C's calculus changes), #158 (release
artefacts, which a sidecar multiplies), #84 (embedding and the C ABI — the same
cgo question from the other direction), #113 (the operation surface where a
"who may call this" policy would be administered). Authorisation is tracked
separately in #253/#298/#300 and is **not** a dependency of this issue.

## Acceptance criteria

- A written comparison of iroh-from-Go options (bindings, sidecar, protocol reimplementation) against a Go-native identity transport, with a recommendation — the Go-binding question is answered, not deferred.
- If a transport is built: a client reaches a daemon by node identity from a different network with no port forwarding, no public IP, and no ssh key copying, authenticated by the identity key.
- Address-based endpoints (unix socket, TCP, ssh per #85) keep working unchanged.
- Failure modes (relay-only path, identity mismatch) produce clear errors, never a silent fallback to an unauthenticated route.

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#127 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #99

## Summary

Decide **which tests an agent working on mcpx runs, and when**, so that no agent runs the whole suite as a habit. The rule: an agent runs the smallest set that covers its change -- the edited packages' unit tests, a named handful of e2e tests, and the guard tests for any registry it touched -- and leaves the full suite to CI (#95). This issue decides the tiers, how an agent finds the tests that touch a change, what is never run locally, and how a CI failure is reproduced. The page that tells agents all this is #131.

## Original notes

> - testing
>   - importantly, as we add more testing agents should not run every single test basically ever. below documents a rough idea of a ci job design/policy, the main priority is being short as possible.

(The second line is also the joint strategy's framing in #91 and the CI tree's preamble in #95. This issue owns its *agent-side* half: what an agent runs locally. The CI half -- keeping the full run short -- is #95.)

## Current state (re-checked at 05c78b2)

Per-package cost, CI run 36693030957 at 05c78b2 (ubuntu-latest, `go test ./... -count=1`, step total 148 s, the rest is compilation). The d0b7e01 run 36673523537 had e2e at 100.7 s of a 135 s step; e2e grows with every test.

| Package | Time | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `internal/e2e` | **108.9 s** | 209 tests, serial (no `t.Parallel()` anywhere), each drives the real binary |
| `internal/tui` | 8.6 s | |
| `internal/pool` | 1.6 s | |
| `internal/events`, `internal/mcpserver` | ~1.0-1.3 s each | |
| every other package | < 0.6 s | 25 packages |
| `nix build .#mcpx` | 70 s | re-runs 18 unit packages in `checkPhase` (`package.nix:73-82`) |

Facts that shape the policy:

- **e2e sees every change, through the binary, not through imports.** `go list -test -deps ./internal/e2e` lists only `internal/api` and `internal/testsupport`. The binary under test is built by a `go build ./cmd/mcpx` *subprocess* (`internal/testsupport/build.go:54-74`). So Go's own dependency graph cannot say which e2e tests a change affects -- by that graph almost no change affects e2e, and in reality every change does.
- **Stale green risk (not reproduced; nobody has checked it yet).** `go help test`: results are cached for runs using only cacheable flags (`-run` is one), and a cached result is reused while the *test binary*, the env vars it reads and the files *it* opens are unchanged. The files the `go build` subprocess reads are not tracked. So after editing, say, `internal/runner`, `go test ./internal/e2e -run '^TestX$'` would plausibly print `ok ... (cached)` without building the new binary. CI is safe (`-count=1`, `mcpx.yml:65`). Any local e2e run must use `-count=1`. The same applies to a local `go test ./...`: its e2e line may have been cached.
- **`-run` is an unanchored regexp** (`go help testflag`): `-run TestEveryExec` also matches any longer name. Use `-run '^(TestA|TestB)$'`; subtests `-run '^TestA$/^case$'`.
- **Local e2e runs no longer leak daemons (#52, fixed in #182).** `newEnv`'s cleanup now runs `stop --all`, which reads the `daemon-<key>.json` info files instead of recomputing the socket path, and logs a failure instead of discarding it (`internal/e2e/e2e_test.go:71-85`). `newEnv` also sets `MCPX_AUTOSTART_IDLE_EXIT=60s` (`:68`, `:92`), so a daemon that escapes an interrupted run dies within a minute instead of 4h. `TestEnvCleanupStopsTheDaemonItStarted` (`:2630`) guards it and was falsified by reverting the fix. What remains: `testsupport` still leaves its `mcpx-bin-*` and `mcpx-fake-*` temp dirs behind on every test-binary run (`build.go:27,57`, `os.MkdirTemp` with no removal).
- Existing file split in e2e helps a little: `exec_test.go`, `settings_test.go`, `v1ops_test.go`, `proto_test.go`, `consumer_test.go`, `runtime_test.go`, `logs_test.go`, `multiconfig_test.go`, `unread_test.go` (#171) -- but `e2e_test.go` holds 129 of the 209 tests.
- No test recipe exists anywhere: the repo-root `justfile` has no mcpx recipes, `pkgs/mcpx` has no justfile; `scripts/` has only `bench.sh` and `stress.sh` (manual, real servers).
- History: #65 was merged with its own check red and unread. Whatever the local policy, reading the PR's CI result before merging is part of it.
- **In practice, integrators do run the full suite locally, repeatedly.** PR bodies: #69 and #70 "Suite 2× clean", #171 "Suite 3× clean before my change and 2× after", #182 "Suite 3× clean" plus a daemon count across the runs. The merge protocol the integrating agents follow asks for this. It is the only repeat-run flake detection mcpx has until #130's CI jobs exist. The policy below therefore has to say who runs the full suite (the integrator, before merging), not only who does not.

## Proposed policy (the tiers)

| Tier | When | Command | Typical cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| T0 format/vet | always, touched packages | `gofmt -l <files>`; `go vet ./internal/<pkg>/` | < 2 s |
| T1 unit | always, each package with an edited `.go` file | `go test -count=1 ./internal/<pkg>/` | < 2 s each (tui 8.6 s) |
| T1b dependents | only when an *exported* identifier changed | the same, for packages that import it (`go list -f '{{.ImportPath}} {{join .Imports " "}}' ./...` reverse lookup) | seconds |
| T2 targeted e2e | when behaviour visible through the binary changed | `go test -count=1 ./internal/e2e -run '^(TestA\|TestB)$'` | ~0.5 s/test average + one binary build; budget ~15 tests / ~30 s |
| T3 guards | when a registry was touched (flag, `/v1` op, setting, default constant) | the guard for that registry (list in #129), e.g. `-run '^TestEveryExecFlagChangesSomething$'` | seconds |
| T4 build | only when `package.nix`, `go.mod`/`go.sum` or `vendorHash` changed | `nix build .#mcpx` | 70 s |
| Full suite | **never locally for a routine change**; CI on push (#95). The integrator merging a PR is the exception (rule 7) | -- | ~110 s of serial e2e plus compilation, and growing |

Rules around the tiers:

1. **Never run** `go test ./...` or an unfiltered `go test ./internal/e2e` locally, unless the user asks for it by name or you are the integrator merging (rule 7). The reason is cost: ~110 s of serial e2e plus compilation, paid again on every run, and the number grows with every e2e test. There used to be a second reason: each run left daemons alive for up to 4 h (#52). #182 removed that one. The cost reason remains.
2. **Always `-count=1`** for e2e (stale green above). For unit packages the cache is correct and welcome.
3. **Push, then read CI.** The full run is CI's job; an agent must read the result of the PR's check before declaring done or merging (#65).
4. **Harness changes** (`internal/testsupport/**`, `newEnv`, the fake servers) affect every e2e test: run a small sample locally (`^(TestNoOrphanProcessesAfterStop|TestEnvCleanupStopsTheDaemonItStarted|TestEveryDeclaredRouteAnswersOverTheSocket)$`) and let CI run the rest.
5. **Reproducing a CI failure:** re-run only the failing test(s), by exact name, with the same run seed and shuffle order the CI shard printed (seed design and env var name: #93; shard layout: #95). If it does not reproduce once, it is treated as a possible flake and handled by #130 (`-count=N`, `-race`), not by re-running the whole suite.
6. ~~**Stopgap until #52 lands (unverified):** `newEnv` passes `os.Environ()` through, and the setting's derived env name is `MCPX_AUTOSTART_IDLE_EXIT` (`internal/settings/schema.go:225-230`), so exporting e.g. `MCPX_AUTOSTART_IDLE_EXIT=2m` before a T2 run should bound any leak to two minutes. Check that no e2e test asserts the default first.~~ **Done in #182:** `newEnv` sets `MCPX_AUTOSTART_IDLE_EXIT=60s` itself (`internal/e2e/e2e_test.go:68,92`), so there is nothing to export.
7. **The integrator's pre-merge run is the exception, and it is deliberate.** Whoever merges a PR runs the full suite locally more than once (current practice: 2-3 times, see Current state). Until #130 moves repeat runs and `-race` into CI, that is the only place mcpx looks for order- and timing-dependent flakes. Once #130's per-PR repeat job and nightly stress job exist, this step can drop to a single run or leave the local routine entirely.

## Approaches: how an agent finds the tests touching a change

### A -- judgment and grep (least recommended)
The agent reads its diff, greps `internal/e2e` for the feature's name, and picks tests. Costs nothing to set up. Risks: every agent picks differently; tests named for a behaviour rather than the flag or op (most of `e2e_test.go`) are missed; and an uncertain agent falls back to "run everything", which is the behaviour this issue exists to stop. Acceptable only as the documented fallback when C selects nothing.

### B -- a maintained map from package/feature to tests
Split `e2e_test.go` by feature and keep a map (`testdata/test-map.yaml` or comments) from `internal/<pkg>` and feature names to e2e files or regexes. Deterministic and readable. Costs: the map drifts as soon as a test is added under the wrong key, splitting `e2e_test.go` is a large mechanical diff, and the feature inventory is owned by #97 -- a second map here would compete with it. Worth doing only if #97's inventory becomes that map (then C can read it).

### C -- a selection script with a just recipe (recommended)
`scripts/affected-tests.sh` (or `go run ./internal/testsupport/affected`, to avoid bash portability questions) plus a recipe such as `just mcpx-test-affected [base]`:
1. `git diff --name-only <base>...HEAD -- pkgs/mcpx` (default base: `origin/main`).
2. Each edited `.go` file -> its package -> T1. If exported identifiers changed, add importers (T1b).
3. For e2e: pull the *names* the diff touches -- setting paths in `internal/settings/wire.go`, op names in `internal/api/ops*.go`, flag names in `internal/cli`, CLI command names, fake-server tool names -- and select e2e test functions whose bodies mention them; add the guard tests for any registry file touched (T3).
4. Print the commands and an estimate from per-test durations (from CI's `go test -json` artifact, #95). Dry-run by default; `--run` executes them with `-count=1`.
5. If nothing is selected, say "no e2e selected; CI runs the full suite" -- never fall back to all.

Recommended because it gives every agent the same answer for zero context cost, it is checkable (CI can later compare its selection with the tests that actually failed, i.e. measure the miss rate), and a miss costs one CI round-trip rather than a bug, since CI still runs everything. The same selector can later feed a PR fast lane in #95 if that tree wants one.

## Open questions

- Confirm the stale-cache hypothesis once, in a scratch worktree (safe to run now that #182 fixed #52): edit a non-imported package, run `go test ./internal/e2e -run '^TestX$'` twice without `-count=1`, look for `(cached)`.
- Where the recipe lives: repo-root `justfile` (the nix repo's) vs a new `pkgs/mcpx/justfile` vs only `scripts/`. A root recipe is discoverable; a package-local one keeps mcpx self-contained.
- The T2 budget: a count (~15 tests) or a time (~30 s)? Time is what matters; count is what an agent can see before running.
- The env var the run seed arrives in, and how a shard prints it (#93, #95).
- Should T0 include the linters #95 adopts (e.g. `golangci-lint run ./internal/<pkg>/...`)? Probably yes once they exist.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** S for the policy text; M with the selection script (C) · **Impact** high
**Depends on / related**: #52 (closed, fixed in #182; "never locally" now rests on cost alone), #93 (run seed, reproduction), #95 (full suite, shards, `go test -json` timings), #97 (feature inventory, if B's map is ever built), #65 (read the check before merging), #91; siblings #131 (states this policy), #129 (T3 list), #130 (non-reproducible failures; moves the integrator's repeat runs into CI).

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

## Acceptance criteria

- The test-tier rule is decided and recorded: an agent runs the smallest set covering its change (edited packages' unit tests, a named handful of e2e tests, guard tests for any registry it touched) and never the full suite locally as a habit; the full suite is CI's job.
- How an agent finds the tests that touch a change is defined (mechanism or documented procedure).
- How a CI failure is reproduced locally is defined.
- The decisions are handed to the contributor page (#1976) in a form it can carry verbatim.
- The work described in the Summary/Scope above is delivered via a branch + PR (no direct push to main); verification runs in GitHub Actions CI, not on the sandbox.
- Evidence (the recorded rule) is recorded on this issue before it is closed.

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#126 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #93

## Summary

The simple, explicitly requested issue: consider **deterministic execution** as a long-term design aspiration, two ways -- retrofit mcpx (inject clock, randomness, filesystem, process spawn and network behind interfaces) or a Rust rewrite, which the notes call "not a plan at all". Not a plan to build either; a short record of what each would take, what blocks it, and the cheap steps that pay off regardless.

## Original notes

>       - think a hack job of antithesis/tigerbeetle. this is the primary testing method is throw insane amount of variations. if something is found outside this system and a test that could have had missed it, make a different generator that uses the same seed and makes an infinite amount of things matching the offensive shape.
>         - we aren't shooting for deterministic execution to start, maybe we should but no. consider it a longterm design aspiration to retrofit or for rewrite in rust (not a plan at all, but could see it). separate simple issue for considering both those things.

## Current state

- Execution is nondeterministic by design today: Go goroutine scheduling; 78 `time.Now()` calls in non-test `internal/` code (05c78b2); ids from `crypto/rand` in `pool`, `tasks`, `elicit`, `artifacts`, `mcpserver`, `logging/trace`; 11 `exec.Command` sites; unix sockets (Deno/Bun) and TCP (Node) back to the daemon. The daemon's idle exit runs on wall-clock time. It is a setting, `autostart.idleExit` (default `4h`, `internal/defaults/defaults.json:138`; a setting since #56, not hardcoded), which #182 sets to 60 s for e2e.
- Some seams already exist: `pool.ReapIdle(now time.Time)` takes the clock as a parameter (`internal/pool/pool.go:697`); e2e isolates state/cache/config/registry/idle-exit by env (`internal/e2e/e2e_test.go:52-68`).
- The seeded-input design (#121, #124) reproduces inputs and test order, not interleavings. This issue is the other half.
- Go 1.25+ ships `testing/synctest`: inside a "bubble", `time` uses a fake clock that advances only when every goroutine in the bubble is durably blocked. Its own docs say to avoid the real network and external processes inside a bubble (`go doc testing/synctest`).

## What blocks determinism in mcpx

| Source | Retrofit difficulty | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wall clock / timers | Low-medium | inject a `Clock`; or run in-process components under `synctest` |
| `crypto/rand` ids | Low | inject an id source; seeded in tests |
| Filesystem | Medium | an `fs` seam for state/cache/artifacts; `t.TempDir` already isolates |
| Goroutine scheduling | High | Go has no deterministic scheduler; `synctest` makes time deterministic, not interleavings |
| Unix sockets / TCP / HTTP | High | real kernel I/O; in-process `net.Pipe` transports only for components that can run in one process |
| **Runtime subprocesses (deno, bun, node)** | **Not feasible** | separate processes with their own event loops, JITs and clocks; the core of `mcpx exec` |
| Real MCP servers (#97 real-software subset) | Not feasible | third-party processes |

## Approaches

### A -- Rust rewrite for determinism (least recommended; "not a plan at all", agreed)
What it would buy: Rust async simulation frameworks (e.g. madsim, turmoil for tokio) simulate time and network in one process, TigerBeetle/FoundationDB-style. What it would *not* buy: determinism for the deno/bun/node subprocess that runs every script, or for real MCP servers -- the part of mcpx most likely to misbehave. A full rewrite of a working Go codebase for a property it still would not achieve end to end is the wrong trade. Worth revisiting only if a rewrite happens for other reasons.

### B -- full retrofit: every nondeterminism source behind an interface, a simulated daemon
Clock, ids, fs, spawn and network all injected; a test harness runs the daemon, pool, events and a fake MCP server in one process on simulated transports, seeded from the run seed, VOPR-style. Achievable for the daemon's *internal* logic (pool admission/reaping, task lifecycle, elicitation broker, event store #6, state/cache #78), and it would find real concurrency bugs. Costs: interfaces threaded through most packages, a simulated transport layer, and it still stops at the runtime subprocess boundary. L-XL effort for partial coverage.

### C -- incremental seams where they pay today; Antithesis-style tooling as the end-to-end answer (recommended)
- Add seams only when a test needs them: a `Clock` for idle-exit (already configurable through `autostart.idleExit`, but a test of it still waits in real time), seeded id sources, `ReapIdle`-style `now` parameters.
- Use `testing/synctest` for in-process concurrent components (pool, tasks, elicit, events): deterministic time and "wait until everything is blocked" instead of `time.Sleep` polling -- which also removes the flake-prone sleeps found in #125.
- Derive every injected randomness source from the run seed (#121) so partial determinism composes with seeded inputs.
- For true end-to-end determinism including the runtime subprocesses, the realistic path is a deterministic hypervisor (Antithesis runs unmodified containers), not a rewrite. That needs a container image. One now exists: #182 added `pkgs/mcpx/Containerfile` (debian bookworm-slim runtime, bun, 413 MB; `docs/container.md`). It has no CI job and no tests yet (#134). This is a prerequisite that is now met, not a plan.
- Why C: each step is small, useful on its own (fewer flakes, faster tests), and moves toward B without committing to it.

## Open questions

- Is idle-exit the first `Clock` seam? #182 fixed #52 without one (cleanup plus a 60 s idle exit), so a bug no longer forces it. It is still the seam whose tests otherwise wait in real time.
- Which in-process components would `synctest` cover without refactoring (does anything inside them touch real sockets or processes)?
- The container image exists (#182). Is running it under a deterministic hypervisor worth one experiment once #134 gives it a CI job?

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** S (this issue: record + first seam list) · C incremental: S per seam · B: L-XL · A: XL, not planned · **Impact** low now, med long-term (flake reduction is the near-term win)
**Depends on / related:** #121, #124, #125; #52 (closed, fixed in #182), #78 (state/cache), #6 (event store), #97 and #134 (the container image and its CI job, real-software subset), #99 (flake policy).

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

## Acceptance criteria

- A short record exists (on this issue or in the docs tree and linked here) comparing the two routes to deterministic execution — retrofit (clock, randomness, filesystem, process spawn, network behind interfaces) vs a Rust rewrite — with what each would take and what blocks it.
- The cheap steps that pay off regardless of route are listed, and each is either filed as its own issue or explicitly dropped with a reason.
- No implementation is started under this issue (it is explicitly not a plan to build either route).
- Evidence (the record's location) is recorded on this issue before it is closed.

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#294 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

mcpx is mostly a gateway, but one planned surface turns a sentence into a script against the configured servers.

Today `mcpx prompt "<what you want>"` matches a saved recipe or generates a script to review, governed by `prompt.autonomy` (decision 0002: `off < advise < ask < propose < apply < run`).

Wanted, as one declared feature across CLI, `/v1`, MCP and the plugin:
- **Script only:** a sentence in, the script bytes out (typed against the generated client, type-checked), without running anything. This is the default at `propose`.
- **Run:** the same, executed, with the result returned (at `run`, subject to the daemon's `autonomy.max` ceiling).
- Where the model comes from must be stated: a caller-supplied model/provider, not MCP sampling (deprecated in 2026-07-28).
- Generated scripts saved as recipes on request, so a repeated sentence becomes a recipe match instead of a regeneration.

Related: #112 (hooks), #113 (administration by intent), decision 0002.

## Acceptance criteria

- `mcpx prompt "<sentence>"` can return the generated script bytes without executing anything (script-only mode), typed against the generated client and type-checked before it is returned.
- Run mode executes the same generated script and returns its result, gated by the caller's autonomy level and the daemon's `autonomy.max` ceiling.
- The model/provider used for generation is caller-supplied and stated in the response; MCP sampling is not used.
- A generated script can be saved as a recipe on request, and a later identical sentence matches the saved recipe instead of regenerating.
- The feature behaves the same across the CLI, `/v1`, MCP, and plugin surfaces, with tests covering script-only vs run gating.

## Repro

On pristine `origin/main` 408bc2b, with a real `~/.config/mcpx/config.json` present and `TMPDIR` pointing under $HOME (my case: TMPDIR on a btrfs volume at ~/tmp because /tmp is a 512M tmpfs):
