title: mcpx: the nix derivation's generated man page, completions and version are unverified, and one of them is not reproducible

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#178 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #177

## Summary

`pkgs/mcpx/package.nix` `postInstall` produces three artefacts from the binary it just built — a man page, three shell completion scripts, and a version string injected by `ldflags`. **Nothing asserts any of them, one of them is not reproducible, and the version exists in three places that no test keeps in agreement.** These are release prerequisites: #158 designs tags, release artefacts and install channels on top of a derivation whose generated half is currently unchecked, and a release that ships a man page dated by whichever day the builder ran is a release that cannot be rebuilt bit-for-bit.

This issue owns the three defects in `postInstall` and the version fan-out. It does **not** own the platform matrix (#136), the CI workflow shape and caching design (#135), the container image (#134), or the release pipeline (#158). (It previously named #161 and #168; both were closed as duplicates — the survivors are #134 and #135.)

## What was verified

All checks at `8001f23`, which is one commit ahead of the `d0b7e01` the earlier issues were written against; nothing in this area changed between them. **Every row was re-checked at `05c78b2` in the 2026-09-30 issues pass and every one still holds**: `internal/cli/manual.go:335` still stamps `time.Now()`; `package.nix:19` and `:61` and `cmd/mcpx/main.go:18` still carry three separate `0.1.0` literals; `internal/testsupport/build.go:63` still builds without ldflags; and `rg` over every `*_test.go` still finds no reference to `ManPage`, `CmdMan` or `CmdCompletion`. #171 and #182 changed nothing here.

| Claim | How verified | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The man page stamps a build date | `internal/cli/manual.go:335` — `date := time.Now().UTC().Format("2006-01-02")`, written into `.TH MCPX 1 %q ...` at `:337` | **VERIFIED** |
| `postInstall` runs the generator at build time | `package.nix` `postInstall`: `$out/bin/mcpx man > $out/share/man/man1/mcpx.1` | **VERIFIED** |
| Nothing asserts the man page or the completions | `rg -n 'ManPage\|CmdMan\|CmdCompletion\|--version\|a\.Version' --glob '*_test.go'` in `pkgs/mcpx` → **zero matches** | **VERIFIED** |
| The version is hard-coded in three places | `package.nix:19` `version = "0.1.0"`; `package.nix:61` `"-X main.version=0.1.0"`; `cmd/mcpx/main.go:18` `var version = "0.1.0"` (its own comment at `:17` says it "is overridden at build time with -ldflags"). `rg '0\.1\.0'` finds two further echoes that are not build inputs: `plugin/opencode/skills/mcpx-daemon/SKILL.md:35` (documentation example) and `plugin/opencode/mcpx/daemon.test.ts:132` (test fixture) | **VERIFIED — exactly three build-relevant sites, plus two documentation/test echoes** |
| The test binary is built without those ldflags | `internal/testsupport/build.go:63` — `exec.Command("go", "build", "-o", mcpxBin, "./cmd/mcpx")`, no `-ldflags` | **VERIFIED** |
| No `CGO_ENABLED` is set | `rg -n 'CGO\|env =' package.nix` → no matches; `buildGoModule` therefore inherits the nixpkgs default | **VERIFIED** (the static-linking consequences are #136's; **and the premise there was wrong — `CGO_ENABLED=0` yields a fully static linux binary, verified in #182, so #136 is a policy decision. This issue only records that `package.nix` sets no `CGO_ENABLED`.**) |

## Current state (with file refs)

### 1. The man page is not reproducible

```go
// internal/cli/manual.go:333-337
func ManPage(version string) string {
	var b strings.Builder
	date := time.Now().UTC().Format("2006-01-02")

	fmt.Fprintf(&b, ".TH MCPX 1 %q %q \"mcpx manual\"\n", date, "mcpx "+version)
```

`package.nix` runs `mcpx man` inside `postInstall`, so `$out/share/man/man1/mcpx.1` embeds the UTC date of the build. Everything else in the derivation is deterministic: Go builds reproducibly, `ldflags = [ "-s" "-w" ... ]` strips, and the vendor tree is a fixed-output derivation. `time.Now()` is the only wall-clock input.

Consequences, in increasing order of how much they will matter later:

- `nix build .#mcpx --rebuild` diffs across a UTC midnight boundary. Nothing runs that today, so nobody has seen it.
- A content-addressed or signed release artefact (#158) is not byte-stable, so "the tarball I built matches the tarball CI published" cannot be asserted.
- `man mcpx` shows the build date where a reader expects the documentation date, which is the wrong fact: a binary substituted from a cache shows the cache's build day.

The convention for exactly this is `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH`, which nixpkgs already exports in every build (it is set to `1` in the stdenv unless overridden) and which every reproducible-build toolchain honours.

### 2. Neither generated artefact is asserted

```nix
# package.nix postInstall
$out/bin/mcpx man > $out/share/man/man1/mcpx.1

installShellCompletion --cmd mcpx \
  --bash <($out/bin/mcpx completion bash) \
  --zsh <($out/bin/mcpx completion zsh) \
  --fish <($out/bin/mcpx completion fish)
```

`mcpx man` and `mcpx completion <shell>` are **executed** at build time and their output is **never inspected**, by the build or by any test. The build fails only if the process exits non-zero. A `ManPage` that returned the empty string, or a `completion zsh` that emitted a syntactically invalid `#compdef` block, would produce a green `nix build` and a broken installed package. `rg` over every `_test.go` in the tree returns no reference to `ManPage`, `CmdMan` or `CmdCompletion`.

This is worse than it looks because both generators read `Commands()`, which is itself incomplete — seven dispatched commands are missing from it (#159 item 1; re-measured in the sibling review issue). So the man page and the completions are known to be wrong, and there is no mechanism by which anyone would find out.

### 3. The version has three sources and no arbiter

| Site | Value | Who reads it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `package.nix:19` | `version = "0.1.0"` | the derivation name, `nix` metadata, any release artefact named from it |
| `package.nix:61` | `"-X main.version=0.1.0"` | the installed binary's `--version`, `/v1/health`, the OpenAPI `info.version`, the man page's `.TH` title |
| `cmd/mcpx/main.go:18` | `var version = "0.1.0"` | any binary built without ldflags — including **every end-to-end test**, via `internal/testsupport/build.go:63` |

They agree today only because nobody has changed one. The first bump breaks the property silently in two directions: the derivation name and the binary's self-report can diverge, and the e2e suite keeps exercising a binary that reports the pre-bump version while the packaged one reports the new one. `internal/api/openapi.go` and `internal/cli/openapi.go` both take `version` as a parameter, so a wrong value propagates into the published specification too.

## Approaches

### 1. Reproducible man page — no real choice

Honour `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH`: parse it when set, fall back to `time.Now()` when it is not, so an interactive `mcpx man` still shows today. Five lines in `internal/cli/manual.go`. The only sub-decision is what to show when the variable is absent from a *release* build, and the answer is that a release build always has it.

### 2. Asserting the generated artefacts

- **A — least recommended: assert in `postInstall`.** Add `grep -q` checks to the nix expression (`grep -q '^\.TH MCPX' mcpx.1`, non-empty completions). It works, and it puts test logic in the one place that only runs under `nix build`, is invisible to `go test`, cannot be run locally without a full derivation rebuild, and is written in bash inside a Nix string. Every future assertion accretes there.
- **B — middle: a Go golden test.** `internal/cli/manual_test.go` compares `ManPage("test")` against a checked-in golden file. Catches regressions in content, and catches *nothing* about the completions actually being valid shell, because a golden file of a zsh script only proves it did not change.
- **C — recommended: a Go presence test plus a shell-parser smoke test, and keep `nix build` dumb.** In Go: every entry in `Commands()` appears in `ManPage`, every entry appears in each of the three completion scripts, and the `.TH` line carries the version it was given. In CI (this belongs to #135's job graph, not to `postInstall`): pipe each completion script through `bash -n`, `zsh -n` and `fish --no-execute`, which is the only check that distinguishes "non-empty" from "valid". Once #159's `Commands()` gap is closed, the same presence test is what stops it reopening. Recommended because it moves the assertion to where it can be run in a second by anyone, and because the shell-parse check is the one that finds the failure mode that actually ships.

### 3. Single-sourcing the version

- **A — least recommended: a `//go:generate` step or a `version.txt` read by both.** A file both Nix and Go read is genuinely single-sourced, but it adds a build input that has to be kept in the `cleanSourceWith` filter, and it does not solve the test-binary problem: `go build` without ldflags still falls back.
- **B — middle: drop the fallback and make an un-stamped binary say so.** `var version = "dev"` in `cmd/mcpx/main.go` (which is already the convention used at `internal/pool/pool.go:39`, `var Version = "dev"`). Then a binary built without ldflags reports `dev` and can never be confused with a release. Cheap, honest, and leaves `package.nix`'s two copies still hand-synchronised.
- **C — recommended: B, plus derive the ldflag from the `version` attribute, plus a test.** `ldflags = [ "-s" "-w" "-X main.version=${version}" ]` removes one of the two Nix copies outright (`finalAttrs.version` or a `let`-bound name). `var version = "dev"` removes the third. That leaves exactly one literal, which #158 then replaces with the git tag. Add one e2e assertion that `mcpx --version` matches the derivation's version when run from `result/bin/mcpx` — which is the "handful of assertions against `result/bin/mcpx`" that **#134** identifies as the cheapest win in its area (formerly #161, closed as a duplicate), so the two should land together.

## Open questions

- Should `postInstall` keep generating the man page from the binary at all, or should the release pipeline (#158) generate and commit it so that the tarball, the nix package and the distro packages all ship the same bytes? Generating from the binary is the right call for correctness and the wrong call for a distro packager who does not want to execute a freshly built cross-compiled binary. This is a real fork and #158 should decide it, not this issue.
- Does `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` belong in `ManPage`'s signature (explicit, testable) or read from the environment inside it (fewer call sites to change)? Prefer the parameter, but it touches `CmdMan`.
- Is `lib.platforms.unix` plus an unasserted man page enough for a distro package's lintian/rpmlint pass, or does that need a `.TH` date in a specific format? Unknown; matters only once #158 picks a distro channel.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease: S** (the man-page date and the version fan-out are a handful of lines each; the presence test is the bulk, and it is one file) · **Impact: med** (nothing is broken for a user today; everything here is a prerequisite that gets more expensive the longer #158 waits on it)

Related: **#158** — this is largely a prerequisite for it: a release pipeline needs a reproducible derivation, one version source and generated artefacts it can trust. **#134** owns the container image and the "run assertions against `result/bin/mcpx`" step that item 3C plugs into (formerly #161, closed as a duplicate). #182 added a `Containerfile`; nothing in CI builds or tests it yet, so that step is still owed. **#159** item 5 records the man-page date as a documentation problem; this issue adds the nix-reproducibility consequence and the fix shape. **#159** item 16 and **#158** both record the three version sites; this issue adds the test-binary divergence via `internal/testsupport/build.go:63`. **#136** owns the platform matrix and the static-binary question, which is why `CGO_ENABLED` is only recorded here and not decided. **#135** owns the CI job graph the shell-parse check belongs in, and the rest of the caching design (its `cache-dependency-path` line landed in #182). **#144**/**#145** own generating a reference from `Commands()`, which shares the presence test. **#49** — the same "built but never exercised" gap for every other flake package.

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

title: mcpx: the socket-path fallback is deterministic but environment-dependent; resolve through the info file

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#88 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #174

## Summary

The socket-path fallback in `internal/daemon/paths.go` **is** deterministic — it is a pure function — but
it is a pure function of the *calling process's environment*, not of the daemon. Two processes that disagree
about `TMPDIR` or `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` compute two different paths for the same daemon, and the one that
computes the wrong one reports no daemon running. This was the mechanism behind #52: #182 confirmed it and
fixed the *test harness* by switching e2e cleanup to `mcpx stop --all`, which resolves through the info files
(see "What #182 changed" below). The CLI itself still recomputes. The redirect can be made safely followable,
but not by the obvious means: a symlink cannot work here, and this issue records why, with the test.

**Owns #181 collision 8:** the precedence of `MCPX_SOCKET` versus the info file and the computed path. #78
dropped that item and links here. The recommendation is step 6 of Approach C.

## Original notes

> - the following is a fixed thing but can that redirect path thing be deterministic so it can be safely followed? or no because reasons? does mac have a mac file length?
>   - > A leaked daemon is one the e2e suite started and never stopped. Each test builds a temp config, runs a command, and the command auto-starts a daemon to serve it. The daemon is deliberately detached so it outlives the command, with --idle-exit 4h. Cleanup calls mcpx stop, but when that can't reach the daemon — a different config fingerprint, a socket relocated because the temp path was too long, an interrupted run — the daemon stays up for four hours with a fakemcp child. Fifteen suite runs left 70.

## Current state (what mcpx does today, with file refs)

`socketPath(state, key)` in `internal/daemon/paths.go:103-133` (line numbers at 05c78b2):

1. `MCPX_SOCKET` if set (`paths.go:104-106`; wins over everything, for every key — see step 6 of C).
2. `<state>/daemon-<key>.sock` if it is ≤ **100 bytes** (`maxSocketPath`, `paths.go:96`, chosen as the
   portable floor: macOS `sun_path` is 104 bytes including the NUL, Linux 108).
3. Otherwise `sum = sha256(state + "\x00" + key)[:16]` and:
   - `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/mcpx/d-<sum>.sock` if `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` is set and the result fits, else
   - `$TMPDIR/mcpx-<uid>/d-<sum>.sock` (`privateRuntimeDir`, `paths.go:141-164`) if it fits, else
   - `os.TempDir()/mcpx-<sum>.sock`.

Separately, the daemon writes `<state>/daemon-<key>.json` with its **actual** socket path
(`Paths.WriteInfo`, `paths.go:280-290`; called from `internal/daemon/server.go:226-234`), removes it on
clean shutdown (`server.go:387`), and `ListDaemons()` reads every such file in the state dir
(`paths.go:225-246`).

The daemon's own resolver already follows the rule this issue recommends: `/v1/resolve` computes the keyed
path and then prefers `info.Socket` from the record when one exists (`internal/daemon/routes_resolve.go:110-121`).
Only the client side recomputes.

### The answer to "is it deterministic"

**Yes, as a function. No, across processes.** Nothing in it is random, time-dependent or ordering-dependent;
given identical inputs it always returns the same path. But two of the three fallback branches read
environment variables of *the process doing the computing*, and `os.TempDir()` on darwin returns `$TMPDIR`
when set and `/tmp` otherwise. So the result is a function of `(state, key, XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, TMPDIR)`, and
only the first two identify the daemon.

That is not hypothetical. On this machine, in this session:

```
$ echo $TMPDIR
/Users/drewry.pope/.local/share/opencode/tmp      # 44 chars, set by the tool that spawned the shell
```

A plain login shell on the same machine gets `/var/folders/<xx>/<24 chars>/T/`. Same daemon, same state
dir, same key — two different fallback socket paths, and `mcpx stop` from one shell cannot see the daemon
started from the other.

### How this reached #52

`mcpx stop` (no `--all`) uses `a.Client()`, whose dialler is `paths.Socket` — the **recomputed** path
(`internal/cli/client.go:115-127`, the dial at `:121`). `mcpx stop --all` and `mcpx daemons` instead iterate
`Paths.ListDaemons()` and use `info.Socket` — the path the daemon actually bound
(`internal/cli/commands.go:1271-1300` for `stopAll`, `:1316-1330` for `daemons`). Before #182 the e2e cleanup
called `e.try("stop")`, the recomputing one.

And the fallback threshold sits exactly in the middle of the suite's test-name distribution, because
`t.TempDir()` embeds the test name:

| path | bytes | branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/var/folders/j_/…/T/TestStop1234567890/001/state/daemon-abcdef123456.sock` | 93 | in state dir |
| `…/TestExecArtifacts1234567890/001/state/daemon-abcdef123456.sock` | 102 | **fallback** |
| `…/TestDaemonReloadsEditedConfig1234567890/001/state/daemon-abcdef123456.sock` | 114 | **fallback** |

Roughly nine characters of test name decide which branch a test takes. That matches #52's observation that
the leak is partial — "one test measured before/after went 46 → 45" — rather than total: the short-named
tests clean up, the long-named ones take the fallback and only clean up if every process in the chain
agreed on `TMPDIR`.

`docs/plugin-discovery.md:61-64` already states the rule the Go CLI does not follow: *"It must prefer the
info file's socket… A resolver that trusted the key would hand out a path with nothing behind it."* The
plugin's ladder is env-independent; `mcpx stop` is not.

### What #182 changed (evidence for Approach C)

#182 closed #52 by making the harness resolve through the info files, and its code comment states this
issue's diagnosis verbatim (`internal/e2e/e2e_test.go:72-83`, at 05c78b2):

> `stop --all` rather than `stop`: plain `stop` dials the socket path recomputed from the environment, and a
> long state path moves the real socket to a private runtime directory keyed to the *caller's* TMPDIR, so the
> computed path misses and the daemon survives. `--all` reads the daemon-<key>.json info files instead, which
> record the path the daemon actually bound.

It also set `MCPX_AUTOSTART_IDLE_EXIT=60s` in every test env (`e2e_test.go:68`, `testIdleExit` at `:92`) as a
backstop for interrupted runs. So the leak is fixed where the suite is concerned. What is **not** fixed:

- Every ordinary CLI command still dials the recomputed path (`client.go:121`), so `mcpx stop`, `mcpx status`
  and `mcpx call` from a process with a different `TMPDIR` still report "not running" for a live daemon whose
  state path is over 100 bytes.
- `stop --all` is scoped to a state directory, not a config. It was the right tool for a test env with its own
  `MCPX_STATE_DIR`; it is not a substitute for `mcpx stop` resolving *this* config's daemon.
- Follows from the code, not reproduced: on that miss, `EnsureDaemon` (`client.go:264-322`) pings only the
  computed path and then **starts a second daemon for the same key**. The second daemon's `WriteInfo` renames
  over `daemon-<key>.json` (`paths.go:285-289`), so the first daemon loses its record, and when the first one
  later shuts down, `os.Remove(s.paths.Info)` (`server.go:387`) deletes the *second* daemon's record. After
  that, `stop --all` and the plugin's rung 2 cannot see either daemon by record.

### "Does mac have a mac file length?"

Yes, and they are not the constraint. Verified with `getconf` on macOS 26.5.1 (arm64):

| limit | macOS | relevant? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `NAME_MAX` (one path component) | 255 bytes | no |
| `PATH_MAX` (whole path, for `open` etc.) | 1024 bytes | no |
| `sun_path` in `struct sockaddr_un` | **104 bytes incl. NUL** | **this is the one** |

A unix socket path is roughly a tenth of what an ordinary file path may be, and `bind()` fails with
`EINVAL`/`ENAMETOOLONG` rather than anything that names the cause. The existing comments at `paths.go:93-102`
call this out correctly.

### Verified: a symlink cannot fix this

Tested directly on macOS 26.5.1 (arm64), in `/tmp`, with Python's `socket` module — no repo files touched:

| test | result |
| --- | --- |
| `connect()` to a symlink pointing at a bound socket, symlink path short | **works** |
| `bind()` to a path 162 bytes long | fails, `AF_UNIX path too long` |
| `connect()` to a **symlink whose own path** is 162 bytes, target short | fails, `AF_UNIX path too long` |
| `bind()` through a dangling symlink at a short path | succeeds |

So symlinks resolve fine for `connect()` on macOS as they do on Linux — but the kernel checks the length of
the path *you hand it*, before resolution. A symlink placed at `<state>/daemon-<key>.sock` is unusable in
exactly the case that produces the fallback, because that path is over 100 bytes by definition. The obvious
fix does not work, and this is worth recording so nobody spends an afternoon rediscovering it.

(The relative-path escape — `chdir` to the directory and bind/connect the basename — does work, but
`chdir` is process-global and there is no `connectat()` on darwin. Not viable in a library.)

## Approaches

### Approach A — keep recomputing, document the environment dependence, least recommended

Change nothing in `paths.go`; add a paragraph to `docs/` saying that `TMPDIR` and `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` must
match between the process that starts a daemon and the process that talks to it, and have the e2e harness
pin `TMPDIR` to something short and fixed.

It would fix the suite. It does not fix the class: the failure is silent (`mcpx stop` prints "daemon: not
running" and exits 0 — the leaked daemon looks like a clean tree), it depends on every future caller
inheriting the right environment, and it leaves the CLI and the plugin computing the socket by two
different methods with the plugin's documented as the correct one. A documented landmine is still a
landmine, and this one already cost ~70 stray processes and a fair amount of debugging in #52. (#182 fixed
the suite a third way — `stop --all` through the info files — which is C applied to one command.)

### Approach B — hash into a fixed, environment-independent short location

Drop `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` and `TMPDIR` from the fallback entirely: always use a single well-known short
directory — `~/.mcpx/s/d-<sum>.sock`, or `/tmp/mcpx-<uid>/` unconditionally — so the computation depends
only on `(state, key)`. `$HOME` is far more stable than `$TMPDIR`, and a `~/.mcpx/s` prefix is ~20 bytes,
leaving plenty of room under 104.

This does make the function environment-independent, which is the stated goal, and it is a genuinely small
change — one branch deleted, one constant added. It keeps the property that a client can find a daemon with
zero I/O, which matters for CLI startup time (#79 is about exactly that).

Costs and risks. `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` exists for good reasons on Linux — it is tmpfs, it is cleaned on logout,
and moving off it puts sockets somewhere that survives a session and needs its own cleanup. `~` is not
always writable (containers, CI, some sandboxes) so a fallback-to-the-fallback returns anyway. It changes
where existing daemons' sockets live, so a version skew leaves old daemons unreachable by new clients —
survivable, since daemons are disposable, but it must be a deliberate one-time break rather than a
surprise. And it still does not make the *info file* and the *computed path* agree in every case, because
`MCPX_SOCKET` overrides both (step 6 of C).

### Approach C — recommended: the state directory is the anchor; resolve through the info file, always

Recommended. The invariant to establish is: **the daemon key identifies the daemon, the state directory
holds the record, and the socket path is a detail only the daemon itself chooses.** The record is
`<state>/daemon-<key>.json`, an ordinary file with a 1024-byte path limit and no environment dependence
beyond `MCPX_STATE_DIR`, which every caller already has to agree on anyway — it is the thing that defines
which daemon is being discussed.

Concretely:

1. **`Paths.Socket` stops being the connect path.** Introduce a resolve step — `Paths.Resolve()` — that
   reads the info file and returns `info.Socket` when it is present and live, and falls back to the
   computed path when it is not (a daemon whose info file was deleted is still a daemon; the plugin ladder
   makes the same allowance, `docs/plugin-discovery.md:98-102`). `NewClient` uses the resolved path.
   This is one function and a handful of call sites, and it makes `mcpx stop` behave like
   `mcpx stop --all` already does. The logic exists already inside the daemon's `resolveDir`
   (`routes_resolve.go:110-121`); extract it rather than writing a second copy. `EnsureDaemon` must resolve
   before deciding to spawn, or it keeps starting the second daemon described above.
2. **The computed path becomes a hint, not a contract.** Keep `socketPath` exactly as it is — it is still
   needed by the daemon at bind time, and it is still the right first guess for a client with no info
   file — but stop treating its output as authoritative anywhere a record exists.
3. **Write the info file before binding is announced; remove it on clean shutdown only if it is still
   yours.** `WriteInfo` is already atomic (`paths.go:285-289`) and shutdown already unlinks it
   (`server.go:387`, since #4), so a stale record is already evidence of a crash. What is missing is the
   ownership check: unlink only when the record's `pid` is this process, so a daemon that lost its record
   to a second one does not delete the survivor's.
4. **Fold in B's insight without B's breakage**: when the fallback *is* taken, log it once at daemon start
   (`socket relocated to <path>: state path is N bytes, limit 100`). #52 lists "the error from
   `e.try("stop")` is discarded" as a cause; a relocation that nobody can see is the same failure one level
   down.
5. **Do not add a symlink.** Record the measurement above in the code comment so the idea is closed.
6. **`MCPX_SOCKET` names one daemon, for the process it was given to (collision 8, decided here).** Today
   it is read inside `socketPath` (`paths.go:104-106`) and therefore overrides the path for *every* key
   the process computes, including answers about other directories. It is also what mcpx itself hands a
   child: `mcpx exec` and the exec service set it (`internal/cli/commands.go:682`,
   `internal/execsvc/execsvc.go:577`) and the generated client reads it (`internal/codegen/emit.go:268`).
   Recommended precedence for a client connecting to *its own* daemon: `daemon.endpoint` > `MCPX_SOCKET` >
   the info file for its key > the computed path. For anything answered *about another key* — `/v1/resolve`
   for another directory, `ListDaemons`, `stop --all` — `MCPX_SOCKET` is ignored: record first, computed
   path (without the override) second. Concretely, read it at the connect/bind call sites, not inside
   `socketPath`. Whether it becomes a declared setting is #172's call (it is one of the undeclared
   `MCPX_*` variables).

   #78 reported that a daemon started with `MCPX_SOCKET` "answers `/v1/resolve` with that socket for every
   directory". At 05c78b2 it is narrower: a directory whose daemon has a record gets the record's socket
   (`routes_resolve.go:112-119`); the override leaks only into the no-record branches — an unconfigured
   directory (`:97-104`) and a configured one with no running daemon (`:110-111`) — where `Running` then
   reports the asking daemon's own socket as live (`:121`). Step 6 closes both.

Why this is the right one: it is the only option that makes the answer *correct* rather than *agreed-upon*.
B makes two processes compute the same wrong-if-anything-moves answer; C makes both read the answer from
the process that knows it. It also aligns the Go CLI with the plugin's documented ladder instead of having
two discovery algorithms with different guarantees, and it composes with the `ssh -L` recipe in the sibling
issue, where a human needs to know the remote socket path and the info file is the only place that is
reliably written down.

The cost is one file read per client invocation on the fast path. Measurable against #79's startup budget
but small: a `stat` + read of a ~200-byte file in a directory that is about to be touched anyway. It can be
skipped entirely when the computed path is a live socket, which is the common case.

## Open questions

- Should `Paths.Resolve()` verify that `info.Socket` is owned by this uid before dialling, as the plugin
  ladder does (`docs/plugin-discovery.md:104-106`)? The Go CLI does not currently check.
- ~~Does the daemon's own `ListDaemons()`-based sweep belong in `TestMain` for the e2e suite as a backstop
  (#52 item 4), independent of this fix?~~ Answered by #182 another way: every test env runs `stop --all` in
  `t.Cleanup` and sets a 60s autostart idle exit, which clears an interrupted run within a minute
  (`e2e_test.go:68-92`). No `TestMain` sweep was added and none is needed for the suite.
- #52's item 5 (#52 is closed; this idea was not part of the fix) — "a daemon whose state directory has been deleted underneath it could notice and exit" —
  becomes more attractive with C, since the info file's absence is then meaningful rather than incidental.
  Does the daemon poll for its own record, or is that too clever?
- ~~Should `MCPX_SOCKET` (#78) be narrowed so it applies to `bind` but not to `/v1/resolve`'s answers for
  other directories?~~ Moved here from #78 (collision 8); the recommendation is C step 6. Open: whether a
  client whose `MCPX_SOCKET` does not answer should fall back to the record or fail. Failing is consistent
  with `daemon.endpoint`'s "never answer from the wrong daemon" rule; falling back is kinder to a stale
  shell. Related: a script run by `mcpx exec` inherits `MCPX_SOCKET`, so an `mcpx` it shells out to reaches
  the parent's daemon even from another project's directory. Under step 6 that stays true (the variable
  wins for the process's own connection); say explicitly whether that is intended (one run, one daemon) or
  whether a nested `mcpx` in a different config should resolve its own.
- Is the 100-byte constant worth raising to 104 on darwin / 108 on Linux with build tags? Probably not —
  the 8 bytes buy nothing and the uniform number is easier to reason about — but it is the kind of thing
  that gets asked.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease**: S for the resolve step and the relocation log; M once `Paths.Socket`'s call sites are audited.
**Impact**: med (was high; lowered in the 2026-09-30 issues pass because #182 removed the test-suite leak
that made it urgent). Still: it silently produces false negatives from `mcpx stop`, `mcpx status` and every
client command whenever the state path exceeds 100 bytes, it can start a second daemon for one key and orphan
the first one's record, and it gets worse as more surfaces (ssh, web, remote daemons) need to name a socket.
High for anyone with a long state path or a `TMPDIR` that differs between processes (opencode sets its own).
**Depends on / related**: #52 (closed, fixed in #182 — for the test suite only; see "What #182 changed"),
#78 (two digests under one name in the same info file; its `MCPX_SOCKET` item moved here, collision 8),
#183 (in flight: corrects the `ForConfig` comment in `paths.go`, same file — related, not a duplicate),
#87 (owns the daemon lifetime rule, collision 9), #79 (any added I/O on the client fast path is in its
budget), #76 (a `mcpx resolve` CLI command would surface this), #172 (`MCPX_SOCKET` is undeclared), #85 (a
forwarding recipe needs a knowable remote socket path), #86.

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

title: mcpx: a web frontend served by the daemon, without a second build system

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#86 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #174

## Summary

A browser view of a running daemon. The daemon is already a web server — HTTP over a unix socket and
loopback TCP, `/v1/*`, SSE at `/v1/events`, an OpenAPI document at `/v1/openapi.json`, MCP at `/mcp` — so
"web server" is done and "web frontend" is the whole of the work. The decision is not *whether* to serve
a UI but *how much build system* to accept for it, because mcpx is one `buildGoModule` derivation today and
a bundled SPA makes it two.

## Original notes

> - web frontend

> - web server

## Current state (what mcpx does today, with file refs)

- **The listener exists.** The daemon serves HTTP on a unix socket and, with `daemon.port`, on TCP;
  `daemon.address` (default `127.0.0.1`) chooses the interface
  (`internal/settings/registry.go:343-375`). Nothing serves static content — every route is registered
  explicitly in `internal/daemon/ops.go`, `routes_proto.go`, `routes_settings.go`, `routes_consumer.go`,
  `routes_resolve.go`, `routes_exec.go`; there is no `http.FileServer` and no `/` handler.
- **The data a UI needs is all there.** 60 operations across `internal/api/ops*.go`, one table that
  already generates routes, MCP tools and the OpenAPI document. Every view the TUI has —
  browse/log/stats/servers/sessions/storage (`internal/tui/tui.go:41-51`) — is a `/v1` call, and the
  read surface is captured as an eight-method interface (`internal/tui/data.go:19-28`).
- **Live updates exist.** `GET /v1/events` is SSE (`internal/api/ops.go:156`), honours `Last-Event-ID` so a
  reconnecting `EventSource` resumes by itself, and says `event: gap` in-band when it cannot
  (`internal/daemon/server.go:797-842`).
- **An open stream does not keep the daemon alive today.** The idle clock is stamped when a request starts
  (`server.go:344-353`), so an open tab holding `/v1/events` is not activity after it connects; see #87.
- **`go:embed` is already in use** (`internal/defaults/defaults.go:24`), so embedding assets costs no new
  mechanism.
- **The nix package is deliberately minimal**: `subPackages = [ "cmd/mcpx" ]`, one `vendorHash`, and a
  comment block that enumerates and justifies each of five direct Go dependencies
  (`pkgs/mcpx/package.nix:36-53`).

### `.lootbox/ui` — assess before reusing

36 tracked files under `.lootbox/ui`: React 18, Vite 6, Tailwind 3, a shadcn/radix component set
(`components/ui/*`), `@tanstack/react-query`, zustand, monaco, and exactly **one page**,
`src/pages/Dashboard.tsx` (193 lines) behind a 34-line `App.tsx`. A prebuilt bundle is committed
(`assets/index-B2p0eWoj.css`, `assets/index-BkA-9JbN.js`); `dist/` is empty; `node_modules/` is 279 MB and
untracked. #49 already records that this copy is **not built by the flake** — the lootbox that actually
runs is built from upstream (`flake.nix:388`) — so it has no build check and nothing depends on it.

Verdict for this issue: it is *lootbox's* dashboard, not mcpx's, and its one page is not a starting point
for an mcpx UI. The reusable part is the shadcn component set, which is a copy of an upstream generator's
output and can be regenerated at any time. It should not be adopted as mcpx's frontend, and #49's other
option — delete it — is not blocked by anything here.

## Approaches

### Approach A — vendor a React SPA into the repo and bundle it at build time, least recommended

`ui/` with Vite + React + Tailwind, `npm run build` into `internal/web/dist`, `go:embed` the result, serve
it at `/`.

Why not: it turns one derivation into two with two fixed-output hashes. `buildGoModule` grows a
`buildNpmPackage` stage and an `npmDepsHash` that Renovate will break on a cadence — #49 is *already* about
the vendorHash/npmDepsHash repair step never having run on a real bot PR, and this doubles the surface it
must handle. It also means the committed tree contains generated bundles (as `.lootbox/ui` does) or that
`nix build .#mcpx` requires network-free npm vendoring for a UI most users will never open. A 280 MB
`node_modules` in a repo whose Go side is proud of five dependencies is a values mismatch, not just a size
one. And the maintenance is not the initial build: it is React majors, Tailwind majors and Vite majors
arriving on a project whose owner is writing Go.

### Approach B — publish the contract and let the UI be someone else's repo

Do no frontend work. Make `/v1/openapi.json` good enough that `openapi-typescript` or `oapi-codegen`
produces a usable client, document the SSE stream in the same document, and point at it from the README.
Anyone who wants a dashboard generates a client and builds one outside this repo.

This is genuinely defensible and is most of the value at nearly no cost. The OpenAPI document is generated
from the same ops table as the routes (`internal/api/openapi.go`), so it cannot drift, which is exactly the
property a generated client needs. `docs/proposals.md:440` already gestures at this — "a dashboard, a test
harness, another language's client generator — use the same…".

Where it falls short: a contract is not a UI. Nobody gets a browser view by default, "open the dashboard"
stays a multi-step setup, and the honest outcome of "someone will build it" is that nobody does. It is also
not mutually exclusive with shipping something — the work below assumes the OpenAPI document is good, and
any gaps found while building a UI against it are bugs in the contract worth fixing anyway.

Worth checking cheaply as part of this: does `/v1/openapi.json` currently pass `openapi-typescript` and
`spectral lint` clean? If it does not, that is a small, high-leverage fix regardless of which approach wins.

### Approach C — recommended: a zero-build frontend embedded in the binary, plus a directory escape hatch

Recommended. Ship a small, dependency-free frontend — plain HTML, CSS and ES modules, no bundler, no npm,
no transpile — `go:embed`ed into the binary and served by the existing listener. Modern browsers run ES
modules and `import` directly; a five-file frontend that calls `fetch('/v1/...')` and subscribes to
`EventSource('/v1/events')` needs no build step at all. `nix build .#mcpx` stays one derivation with one
hash, and `mcpx daemon --ui` is a dashboard on a machine that has nothing installed but a browser.

Shape:

| decision | choice | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| where | the daemon's existing listener, at `/ui/` | a second listener is a second lifetime, a second address and a second thing to leak; the daemon's idle-exit and reload already work |
| enabling | one setting, `daemon.ui` (bool, scope daemon, default off) | matches how every other capability is exposed (`internal/settings/`); off by default so a daemon on `daemon.address=0.0.0.0` does not silently gain a UI |
| overriding | `daemon.uiDir` (string, default empty) serves a directory instead of the embedded assets | the escape hatch that makes A unnecessary: anyone who wants a React SPA builds it wherever they like and points the daemon at `dist/`. Also the dev loop — edit, reload, no rebuild |
| data | `/v1` + `/v1/events` only, no UI-specific endpoints | the parity rule (`docs/parity.md`) is CLI = `/v1` = MCP = plugin; a `/ui/api` prefix would be a fifth surface that drifts |
| scope v1 | the TUI's six views, read-only, plus answering elicitations | elicitation is the one thing a browser is *better* at than the terminal — a form with a schema beats a prompt — and `/v1/elicit/{id}/{action}` already exists |
| idle | apply #87's lifetime rule (#181 collision 9): activity on any surface renews the daemon's idle deadline, and nothing else does | today an open `/v1/events` stream counts only when it connects, so `daemon.idleExit` can kill the daemon under an open tab. Whether a delivering stream counts as activity is decided once, in #87, for this surface and ssh (#85) together -- not here |

Why this beats A: the cost that kills A is the toolchain, not the UI, and a no-build frontend has no
toolchain. Why it beats B: B's contract work is a *prerequisite* of C, not an alternative — building the
embedded UI against `/v1` is the thing that proves the OpenAPI document is usable, and C ends with B's
deliverable plus a working dashboard.

The real risk of C is scope creep: without a framework, view number seven is where hand-written DOM code
starts hurting. Mitigate by fixing the scope at "the TUI's views, plus elicitation forms" and treating
anything beyond that as a reason to reach for `daemon.uiDir` and an external project. If the UI outgrows
no-build, `daemon.uiDir` means moving it out is a configuration change rather than a rewrite.

One more reason to prefer the embedded route: it makes the remote story work end to end. With the ssh
endpoint scheme in the sibling issue, `ssh -L 7777:...` plus `http://127.0.0.1:7777/ui/` is a remote
dashboard with nothing installed locally — which is most of what the "ssh tui" want is actually asking for.

## Open questions

- `/ui/` or `/`? Serving at `/` risks a future `/v1`-adjacent path colliding and makes a 404 ambiguous
  between "no such route" and "no such asset". `/ui/` with a redirect from `/` is probably right.
- Does the UI need write operations in v1, or is read-only + elicitation the correct first cut? Write
  operations (`restart`, `shutdown`, `servers_remove`) are marked `Admin`/`Destructive` in the ops table
  (`internal/api/ops.go:451-466`, `internal/api/ops_settings.go:111`), and a browser is exactly where a
  misclick happens.
- Is `.lootbox/ui` deleted, kept as a reference, or given a CI build? #49 owns the decision; this issue's
  input is that it is not a useful base for mcpx.
- Does `/v1/openapi.json` currently generate clean with `openapi-typescript`? Cheap to check, informs both
  B and C.
- Browser support floor: ES modules and `EventSource` are universal, but import maps and `<template>`-based
  rendering vary. Writing the floor down avoids a debate later.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease**: S to serve a directory and add the settings; **M** for the embedded read-only frontend covering
the TUI's six views; **L** if a bundled SPA (A) is chosen. **Impact**: med — high for demos, remote
machines and anyone who will not open a terminal; low for the existing CLI-first user.
**Depends on / related**: #49 (`.lootbox/ui` has no build check and may be deleted; any new build stage
needs CI), #76 (CLI parity — a UI makes `/v1`-only operations visible to more people), #77 (protocol
follow-ups: inline answers and task status are what a live dashboard would want), #87 (owns the lifetime
rule this issue applies, collision 9; also touch-on-read for the elicitations the UI answers), #85 (a
forwarded port plus `/ui/` is the remote dashboard), #88 (the forwarded port needs a knowable socket path),
#52 (closed, fixed in #182).

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

title: mcpx: remote access over ssh -- TUI, RPC, reverse tunnels, and why not a built-in ssh server

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#85 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #174

## Summary

Reach a daemon, and the TUI, from another machine. Three separate wants get conflated under "ssh": a
**terminal UI over ssh**, **RPC over ssh** (the `/v1` API and MCP tunnelled through an ssh connection), and
**inbound access to a daemon behind NAT** (a reverse tunnel, or a built-in reverse shell). They have very
different costs, and two of the three are already mostly solved by transports mcpx has.

## Original notes

> - ssh rpc, ssh server, ssh tui

> - reverse-shell/shell/ssh/tui

## Current state (what mcpx does today, with file refs)

| capability | today | file |
| --- | --- | --- |
| full-screen TUI, six views | `mcpx tui` (browse/log/stats/servers/sessions/storage) | `internal/tui/tui.go:41-51` |
| the TUI reads through an interface, not the client | `tui.Source` — eight methods, a fake drives it in tests | `internal/tui/data.go:19-28` |
| talk to a daemon elsewhere | `daemon.endpoint`, scope client, accepts a URL or `unix:///path` | `internal/settings/registry.go:350-363`, `internal/cli/client.go:130-160` |
| listen wider than loopback | `daemon.address` (default `127.0.0.1`), `daemon.port` | `internal/settings/registry.go:343-375` |
| MCP over a spawned process | `mcpx serve --transport stdio`; every other transport is explicitly refused and redirected to the daemon's `/mcp` | `internal/cli/serve.go:358-383` |
| MCP over HTTP | the daemon serves it at `/mcp` | `internal/daemon/routes_proto.go` |
| events | `GET /v1/events` (SSE) | `internal/api/ops.go` |
| ssh is already an acknowledged transport | "A unix socket can be ssh-forwarded" | `docs/exec.md:189` |

Two facts that shape every option below:

1. **`ssh host mcpx <anything>` already works.** `ssh host mcpx tui` is an SSH TUI. `ssh host mcpx serve
   --transport stdio` is MCP-over-SSH and is a valid `command` for any MCP client's stdio transport, today,
   with no mcpx change. What does *not* work is talking to a remote daemon from a local `mcpx` when the
   remote is only reachable over ssh: `daemon.endpoint` understands `http(s)://` and `unix://` and nothing
   else.
2. **mcpx has five direct Go dependencies and the package file treats that as a design property**
   (`pkgs/mcpx/package.nix:36-53` enumerates and justifies each one). `charmbracelet/wish` v1.4.7 adds
   ~15 modules to the graph including `go-git/go-git/v5`, `ProtonMail/go-crypto` and `cloudflare/circl`
   (verified from `https://proxy.golang.org/.../wish/@v/v1.4.7.mod`). Unused packages are dropped by the
   linker, but `go.sum` and the nix `vendorHash` are not, and mcpx currently has no `golang.org/x/crypto`
   at all. wish v1.4.7 requires bubbletea v1.3.4; mcpx is on v1.3.10, so the bubbletea major line does match.

## Approaches

### Approach A — a built-in SSH server (`mcpx ssh` / `daemon.ssh.*`), least recommended

Import `charmbracelet/wish` and serve the existing bubbletea program over SSH with
`wish/bubbletea.Middleware`. Because `tui.Source` is already an interface and the model already takes its
size from the terminal, the TUI part genuinely is nearly free — an afternoon.

Everything around it is not. An SSH server needs a host key (generate where? rotate how? what does a client
do when it changes?), an authorised-keys policy, a per-connection identity that the `/v1` API has no concept
of, PTY allocation, window-change handling, and a listener whose lifetime is tied to a daemon that may
idle-exit under the connection. It is a second implementation of something every target machine already
runs, with worse defaults, and it makes mcpx a network daemon that accepts credentials — a category it is
not in today. `daemon.address` is currently documented as "the network it is reachable from is the access
control"; a built-in sshd is a promise that mcpx cannot keep at that level of care. The dependency cost
above is real but is the smaller objection.

If it is built anyway, it should be a *separate binary or a build tag*, not linked into the default `mcpx`,
and it should refuse to start without an explicit `authorizedKeys` path rather than defaulting to anything.

### Approach B — teach `daemon.endpoint` an `ssh://` scheme, tunnelled through the system `ssh`

No server, no keys, no crypto dependency: mcpx becomes an SSH *client*, and only by exec'ing the `ssh` the
user already has configured. `daemon.endpoint = ssh://user@host` makes `NewClientAt` install an
`http.Transport.DialContext` that spawns `ssh -q user@host mcpx <stdio-proxy-subcommand>` and returns the
process's stdin/stdout pipes as a `net.Conn`. The subcommand is a ~40-line pipe between stdio and the local
daemon socket. Everything downstream — `/v1`, SSE, `/mcp`, the generated client — is unchanged, because it
is all HTTP over a byte stream and the byte stream is the only thing that moved.

What this buys, in one setting:

- `mcpx tui --daemon-endpoint ssh://build-box` is a remote TUI, rendered locally, with local colours and
  local terminal handling. Better than a wish-served TUI, not worse: no PTY negotiation, no resize
  forwarding, works over a flaky link because only the HTTP stream is on the wire.
- `mcpx call`, `mcpx exec`, `mcpx status`, `mcpx ls` all point at the remote daemon for free — they already
  honour `daemon.endpoint` (`internal/settings/registry.go:361-362` lists the commands).
- Auth, host-key verification, `~/.ssh/config`, jump hosts, agent forwarding, `ProxyCommand`, Match blocks:
  all inherited, none implemented.

Costs and open edges. The remote needs `mcpx` on `PATH` (`ssh://host?bin=/opt/mcpx/bin/mcpx` covers the
rest). One ssh process per connection unless `ControlMaster` is set up — worth documenting, possibly worth
passing `-o ControlMaster=auto -o ControlPersist=60s` by default. Lifetime follows #87's rule (#181
collision 9, owned there): requests over the tunnel renew the remote daemon's idle deadline, a persisting
ssh master with no requests on it does not, and `ControlPersist` bounds only the ssh process. `mcpx` must not be started remotely with
autostart semantics that surprise (`daemon.endpoint` today deliberately refuses to autostart a remote
daemon; the ssh case is ambiguous and should follow the same rule: fail rather than start). Artifact
`sharedFs` must be false over ssh, which `docs/exec.md:189-193` already anticipates — remoteness is declared
by the caller, so this is a caller-side default, not an inference.

The pure-documentation variant of the same idea costs nothing and should ship regardless: OpenSSH has
forwarded unix sockets since 6.7, so `ssh -N -L 7777:/path/to/daemon-<key>.sock host` plus
`daemon.endpoint=http://127.0.0.1:7777` works today with no code. Put it in `docs/` as the zero-change
recipe. It is clunky enough (you must know the remote socket path — see the socket-path issue) that it is
not a substitute for the scheme.

### Approach C — recommended: B, plus name the three cases and close the reverse-access one with a tunnel, not a shell

Recommended. Ship the `ssh://` endpoint scheme from B, and alongside it settle the other two questions
explicitly rather than leaving "ssh" as one word:

**1. "ssh tui" — solved by B.** Document `ssh host mcpx tui` as the zero-config answer and
`--daemon-endpoint ssh://host` as the better one. Do not build a server for it. Reassess only if someone
wants a TUI on a machine that has no `mcpx` and cannot get one — a real but narrow case that a static
binary answers more cheaply than an SSH server does.

**2. "ssh rpc" — B is the whole of it.** Note that MCP-over-ssh needs no work at all: any MCP host can be
configured with `command: ssh, args: [host, mcpx, serve, --transport, stdio]`. This deserves a section in
`docs/protocol.md` because it is free and nobody will guess it. A `mcpx client --ssh host` generator that
emits that snippet for a given host is the useful sliver.

**3. "reverse shell" — use a tunnel, do not write one.** The underlying need is a daemon behind NAT that
something outside must reach. `ssh -R` already does this, and so does tailscale/wireguard, and both are
better at it than anything mcpx would grow: they reconnect, they authenticate, they are audited. mcpx's job
is to be *easy to put behind one*, which means (a) `daemon.address` already exists, (b) the daemon should be
able to bind an additional listener given as an address so a tunnel has a stable target, and (c) a
documented `ssh -R` recipe. An actual reverse shell — the daemon dialling out to a rendezvous and accepting
commands — is a backdoor with a friendly name, and the first thing an enterprise security review will
reject; it should not be built.

**4. "shell" — a separate, orthogonal feature worth one line.** The notes list `shell` beside the remote
items but it is a *local* gap: there is no `mcpx shell` REPL, only `mcpx tui` (full-screen, mouse-driven)
and `mcpx prompt` (one-shot, `internal/cli/consumer.go:399`). A line-oriented REPL that keeps one daemon
connection and accepts `call`, `ls`, `exec` lines would be cheaper than either and is what people reach for
over a slow link where a full-screen redraw hurts. It composes with B: `mcpx shell --daemon-endpoint
ssh://host`. Tracked here so it is not lost, but it is the smallest item in the issue.

## Open questions

- Does `mcpx <stdio-proxy>` want to be a public subcommand (discoverable, documented) or hidden (an
  implementation detail of the ssh scheme)? Hidden risks people reimplementing it; public risks it being
  treated as a supported protocol.
- Should `ssh://` reuse `daemon.endpoint`, or is a separate `daemon.transport` setting cleaner once there
  are three schemes? Current opinion: one setting, the scheme carries it, because every command that already
  lists `daemon.endpoint` then gets ssh for free.
- Over ssh, does SSE (`/v1/events`) behave? It is a long-lived HTTP response over a pipe; it should, but it
  is the one thing in B worth prototyping before committing.
- If a wish-based server is ever built, does it go behind a build tag, a separate `cmd/`, or a separate
  flake package? (#49 is relevant: every package needs a CI build.)
- `ControlMaster` by default: convenience, or a surprising process left behind? (The daemon side is
  settled by #87: an idle master does not hold the daemon. What remains is whether mcpx should leave an ssh
  process on the *local* machine for `ControlPersist` seconds.)

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease**: S for the documentation and the `ssh host mcpx serve` recipe; **M** for the `ssh://` endpoint
scheme and stdio proxy; **L** for a wish-based SSH server (A), mostly in policy rather than code.
**Impact**: med — high for anyone with a remote or containerised daemon, nil for a single-laptop user.
**Depends on / related**: #88 (an `ssh -L` recipe needs a knowable remote socket path; #88 also owns
`MCPX_SOCKET` precedence, collision 8, which matters once a second machine is asking), #87 (owns the
lifetime rule this issue applies, collision 9), #76 (CLI parity for `/v1`-only ops — a remote TUI makes the
gaps more visible), #49 (any new package or build tag needs CI), #86 (`ssh -L` plus `/ui/` is the remote
dashboard), #52 (closed, fixed in #182). A Containerfile now exists (#182, `pkgs/mcpx/Containerfile`), so
the "containerised daemon" in the Impact line is a shipped shape, not a hypothetical.

title: mcpx docs: overview, quick start, install page and 'now what'
body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#157 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #92

## Summary

The three pages behind the home page's two big links, plus the install page they point at:

1. **Overview** -- why you would install mcpx (the notes' three reasons, expanded) and one architecture
   picture.
2. **Install** -- every channel the notes list, with an honest status column, and the "install as" choices
   (just run the binary, per-user or per-host, local host, system service, persistent daemon).
3. **Quick start** -- the agent loop from `AGENTS.md` (`ls`, `search`, `types`, `run`/`exec`) in under one
   screen, every command real.
4. **Now what** -- a short page of links into level 2 (#94).

Each page must pass the note-line-8 test: a reader "skimming while doing 3 different things" gets the point
from headings, the diagram and the command blocks alone. Prose is the second layer.

## Original notes

> - documentation
>   - make a book using whatever is the most common and simple modern choice
>     - 3 main things, not book sections jsut like levels of detail-
>       - the 30 seconds look at home page click the overview page, click the quick start page, ctrl+w should be simple enough that even this person skimming while doing 3 different things will accidentally learn
>         - why you would install it
>           - code mode
>             - makes shareable, reusable scripts
>           - reclaim context, use less tokens
>             - smarter, cheaper
>           - tame mcp
>             - one mcp config
>             - share endpoint with your tailnet
>             - corral your scripts, apis, and binaries
>         - how to install it
>           - picture architecturally what it looks like
>           - aware of install
>             - bash/nix/agent-prompt
>               - (pwsh/rpm/flatpack/pkg/docker/justThePlugin)
>             - install as
>               - just exec the binary
>               - per-user|per-host
>               - optional:
>                 - local host
>                 - system service
>                 - persistent daemon
>             - quick start
>             - now what

## Current state (what mcpx does today, with file refs)

- **No overview, install or quick-start page exists.** The nearest material: the top of `docs/story.md`
  (a narrative, story.md:1-296), `AGENTS.md` (the loop, 109 lines), `package.nix` `meta.longDescription`,
  docs/dependencies.md (what mcpx needs), docs/configuration.md (settings).
- **Commands.** `internal/cli/manual.go` `Commands()` (`:33`) is the list behind `mcpx help`, `mcpx man`
  and the command table (32 entries). The dispatch table in `cmd/mcpx/main.go:119-162` has seven more that
  `mcpx help` does not list: `serve`, `openapi`, `adapter`, `registry`, `api`, `man`, `completion` (plus the
  aliases `list`, `namespaces`, `logs`). Any page may use
  either set, but a command missing from `mcpx help` needs a note or a fix (the generated reference owns
  this: #144).
- **Only nix installs today.** `flake.nix:385` builds `pkgs/mcpx/package.nix`; `flake.nix:494` exposes it as
  an app. Systems are `nix-systems/default` minus `x86_64-darwin` (`flake.nix:207-211`): aarch64-darwin,
  x86_64-linux, aarch64-linux. The wrapper puts `git`, `deno`, `bun` and `node` on `PATH`
  (`package.nix` postInstall), so a nix install is complete. No release or install script exists (#158).
  A `pkgs/mcpx/Containerfile` exists since #182 and builds a working image locally (bun as its only
  runtime, `git`; `docs/container.md`), but nothing builds or publishes it.
- **Runtime prerequisite outside nix.** `mcpx run`/`exec` need deno, bun or node; `mcpx doctor` fails the
  `runtime` check without one and warns if deno is absent ("the only runtime where --typecheck works",
  `internal/cli/doctor.go:47-60`). Node runs scripts with `--experimental-strip-types`
  (`internal/runner/runner.go:100`), so it needs Node 22.6 or later. `git` is optional (the `repo` and
  `worktree` scopes degrade to `cwd`, docs/dependencies.md).
- **Windows is not supported.** `syscall.SysProcAttr{Setpgid: true}` and `syscall.Kill` are used without
  build tags (`internal/runner/runner.go:413,428`, `internal/mcpclient/stdio.go:69,202`;
  `Setsid` in `internal/cli/client.go:312`), which do not compile for `GOOS=windows`; `package.nix` declares
  `platforms = lib.platforms.unix`. WSL is the Windows answer today.
- **Daemon lifecycle settings** (`internal/settings/registry.go`, `internal/settings/wire.go`):

  | Setting | Default | Meaning |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `daemon.autostart` | `true` | any command that needs the daemon starts one |
  | `autostart.idleExit` | `4h` (`internal/defaults/defaults.json:138`) | an auto-started daemon exits after this long idle |
  | `daemon.idleExit` | `0s` (never) | for a daemon started deliberately (`mcpx daemon`) |
  | `daemon.inline` | `false` | last resort: run servers inside the CLI process, nothing pooled |
  | `daemon.address` | `127.0.0.1` | interface for the TCP listener |
  | `daemon.port` | `0` (OS-assigned) | TCP port |
  | `daemon.endpoint` | empty (local socket) | a client setting: talk to a daemon elsewhere; mcpx will not autostart it |

- **Config search path** (`internal/config/config.go:542-579`): `MCPX_CONFIG` if set; else, walking up
  from the working directory, `.config/mcpx/config.json`, `.mcpx.json`, `.mcpx/config.json`, `.mcp.json`;
  then `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/mcpx/config.json`, `~/.config/mcpx/config.json`, `~/.mcpx.json`; then
  **`/etc/mcpx/config.json`**. So "per-host" configuration already exists as a file location, undocumented
  at level 1.
- **System service is `status: proposed`** (story.md "Service installation", :2498): wanted
  `mcpx service install` emitting a launchd plist or systemd unit; "Until then the daemon starts on demand
  from any command, which is the supported path." (That entry also still asks for
  `mcpx completions bash|zsh|fish`, which shipped as `mcpx completion`; reported for #150.)

## Overview page

### The why (expanded from note lines 9-17)

One section per reason, each: a display line, two or three sentences, one small proof (a command and its
real output, or a number from the story), one link to level 2.

| Reason | Proof to show | Link |
| --- | --- | --- |
| code mode: shareable, reusable scripts | `.mcpx/scripts/shot-flow.ts` and `mcpx run shot-flow <url> <outDir>` (story.md:196-271) | script page, #147 |
| reclaim context: smarter, cheaper | `mcpx ls`: "Seven namespaces, 43 tools, 171 tokens"; whole task ~4,600 tokens (story.md:142, :274) | #153 for the evidence behind "smarter" |
| tame MCP: one config | the `mcpServers` object is read as-is (`mcpx init`'s starter comment) | config page, #146 |
| tame MCP: share with your tailnet | `mcpx daemon --address <tailnet-ip> --port 8899` + `MCPX_DAEMON_ENDPOINT=http://<host>:8899` | remote/transport page, #146 |
| tame MCP: corral scripts, APIs, binaries | named scripts; `mcpx api tools --spec <url>`; `paths.adapters` + `mcpx adapter check` (API and adapter tools are served over MCP only, not in the script client yet: #102) | #147 |

The tailnet row must say plainly that the API is unauthenticated and that the network is the access
control (story.md:2120-2122).

### The architecture picture (note line 19)

One diagram, readable in five seconds, that also answers "what is running on my machine":

```
agent / harness
  ├─ CLI            mcpx ls | search | types | run | exec        (unix socket)
  ├─ plugin         plugin/opencode (no binary needed, #53)      (unix socket or URL)
  ├─ MCP            /mcp on the daemon, or `mcpx serve --transport stdio`
  └─ HTTP           /v1/*  (OpenAPI at /v1/openapi.json)
        │
        ▼
    mcpx daemon  ── one per config; autostarts; idle-exits
        ├─ pooled MCP server processes (stdio) and remote servers (Streamable HTTP)
        ├─ OpenAPI specs and CLI adapters as tools (MCP surfaces only today, #102)
        └─ script runner: deno | bun | node subprocess
              └─ calls back into the daemon: Deno and Bun over the unix socket, Node over loopback TCP
                 (.github/workflows/mcpx.yml:52-54; internal/codegen/emit.go:263-291)
```

The ASCII above is the content, not the proposed rendering. Rendering approaches:

- **Approach A -- client-side Mermaid** (least recommended). Most generators support it with a plugin
  (mdBook: `mdbook-mermaid`; MkDocs Material: native via superfences; Hugo: a render hook). Cheap to write.
  But it renders in the browser with a large JS bundle, shifts layout on load, shows raw text with JS off,
  and Mermaid's automatic layout makes nested boxes like the one above hard to control.
- **Approach B -- a hand-drawn SVG** (middle). Best-looking and fully controlled, loads instantly. But it
  drifts: nobody updates an SVG when a surface is added, and the agent twin (#120) gets an image with no
  text.
- **Approach C -- D2 rendered to SVG at build time** (recommended). D2 is a single Go binary in nixpkgs,
  gives better control of nested containers than Mermaid, and renders to static SVG during the docs build,
  so the page has no diagram JS and the `.d2` source ships in the agent twin as readable text. Works with any
  generator that can run a pre-build step (#117); mdBook has an `mdbook-d2` preprocessor. If
  #117 picks a generator with first-class Mermaid, build-time Mermaid (`mmdc`, which needs headless
  Chromium) is the fallback.

## Install page

### Channels (note lines 20-22), in the notes' order

Primary row first (`bash/nix/agent-prompt`), then the secondary row. Status must be honest on the page and
update from the release pipeline, not by hand.

| Channel | Command on the page | Status today | Designed in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| bash (install.sh) | per-user `curl -fsSL <short> \| sh`; system-wide `curl -fsSL <short> \| sh -s -- --system` | not started: no releases to download | #158, #155 (command forms) |
| nix | `nix profile install github:dezren39/nix#mcpx`; try without installing: `nix run github:dezren39/nix#mcpx -- ls` | **exists** (flake output) | this issue; #158 for a smaller flake |
| agent-prompt | the rotating prompt + `llms.txt` URL | not started | #155, #120 |
| pwsh (install.ps1) | `irm <short>/install.ps1 \| iex` | **blocked**: mcpx does not build for Windows | #158 |
| rpm (and deb) | `dnf install ./mcpx-<v>.rpm` | not started | #158 |
| flatpak | -- | not recommended (see #158) | #158 |
| pkg | open question: macOS `.pkg`, FreeBSD `pkg`, or Homebrew | not started | #158 |
| docker | `docker run ... ghcr.io/<owner>/mcpx` | **partly**: `pkgs/mcpx/Containerfile` builds locally (`docker build -f Containerfile -t mcpx .`, #182); no published image | #158 (publish), #134 (image design) |
| justThePlugin | copy `plugin/opencode/` into `~/.config/opencode/plugin/` (plugin README "Install") | **exists** as a manual copy. Needs no mcpx binary on that machine: it finds a daemon over the unix socket (info files) or `endpoint`, and spawns `mcpx --json status` only as the last-resort rung 4 (`bin: ""` forbids even that; #44, fixed in #53; `plugin/opencode/README.md:75-138`). It does need a daemon running somewhere. | #158, #148 |

**System-wide command.** The notes' home-page form `sudo $(curl <short> | sh)` is not used on any page: it
runs the installer unprivileged, then executes the installer's *stdout* as a root command line (#155,
"System-wide install command"). The install page shows `curl -fsSL <short> | sh -s -- --system` (the script
escalates only the copy into `/usr/local/bin`), with `curl -fsSL <short> | sudo sh` as the plain fallback for
environments where the script cannot call `sudo` itself. Same forms as #155; one source for both pages.

Nix caveats to state: the flake is the author's whole nix-darwin monorepo, so `nix profile install` fetches
and evaluates a large flake for one package (cost unmeasured; open question); x86_64-darwin is excluded.

Prerequisites box, above the table: a JavaScript runtime (deno recommended, bun, or node 22.6+) unless you
installed with nix (the container image ships bun); `git` recommended; macOS or Linux (Windows via WSL). Then "verify: `mcpx doctor`".

### Install as (note lines 23-29)

| Mode | What to do | Today |
| --- | --- | --- |
| just exec the binary | nothing: any command starts a daemon on demand (`daemon.autostart` true) and it exits after `autostart.idleExit` (4h) idle | shipped |
| per-user | binary in `~/.local/bin`; config `~/.config/mcpx/config.json` | binary location awaits #158; config shipped |
| per-host | binary in `/usr/local/bin` (`install.sh --system`); config `/etc/mcpx/config.json` (last on the search path) | binary location awaits #158; config shipped but undocumented |
| optional: local host | `mcpx daemon --address <ip> --port <n>` on one machine, `daemon.endpoint` / `MCPX_DAEMON_ENDPOINT` on clients (a client with an endpoint set never autostarts a local daemon) | shipped |
| optional: system service | launchd / systemd unit running `mcpx daemon`, with `daemon.autostart` false on clients so a stray second daemon cannot start | **proposed** (story.md :2498); designed in #158 |
| optional: persistent daemon | `mcpx daemon` (foreground) or `mcpx daemon --detached`; `daemon.idleExit` defaults to `0` (never) for a deliberately started daemon | shipped |
| fallback | `daemon.inline` true: no daemon, servers live inside each command; slower, nothing pooled | shipped, last resort |

"local host" is read as "run the daemon on a host other clients reach (a LAN or tailnet address)". If the
note meant "bind to localhost only", that is already the default (`daemon.address` `127.0.0.1`). Open
question below.

## Quick start (under one screen)

The loop from `AGENTS.md`, preceded by the minimum setup. Every line is a real command
(`internal/cli/manual.go`); the server example is the one `mcpx servers --help` itself uses.

```sh
mcpx doctor                                   # runtime, config, daemon: what is missing and how to fix it
mcpx servers add fs -- npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem /tmp
mcpx ls                                       # namespaces, tool counts, state
mcpx search directory                         # find a tool by name or description
mcpx types fs                                 # TypeScript signatures for one namespace
mcpx exec 'emit(await fs.list_directory({ path: "/tmp" }))'
```

Then one step that makes it an agent tool, not a CLI demo: "give your agent `AGENTS.md`" (or install the
opencode plugin, #148).

Notes for whoever writes it:

- Tool names come from the server; confirm `list_directory` with `mcpx types fs` when writing, and have
  CI run the block (Docs checks run in CI; see the testing trackers under #91 (CI pipeline #95, integration/environments #97)).
- The server example needs `npx` (Node). Someone with only deno or bun needs another first server; pick
  one that needs nothing extra, or show `mcpx registry search <words>` + `mcpx registry add <name> --write`.
- `mcpx init` writes a starter `.mcpx.json` whose servers are placeholders (`some-mcp-server`), so
  `mcpx ls` after `mcpx init` shows an error row. Do not use `init` as step one of the quick start unless
  the starter changes.
- #79 proposes `script.typecheck` on by default for `run`; if that lands, the first `run` of a new script
  takes ~400 ms longer and a type error stops it before side effects. The quick start should show the
  default that ships, and say "deno" where typecheck needs it.
- Output shown must be captured from a real run, not typed.

## Now what (note line 48)

One short page, four to six links into level 2 (#94), each a question: "Where does config go?" (#146),
"How do I call mcpx from my harness / over MCP / over HTTP?" (#147), "How does the opencode plugin
work?" (#148), "Something is wrong" (`mcpx doctor`, `mcpx status`, #149 FAQ), "Everything, in
depth" (the compendium, #98).

## Open questions

- "local host" (note line 27): a daemon other machines reach, or loopback-only? The table assumes the
  former.
- Does `nix profile install github:dezren39/nix#mcpx` evaluate in acceptable time from a cold machine, or
  does mcpx need its own small flake (or a flake at `pkgs/mcpx`) for users? Belongs with #158.
- Should the install page list `justThePlugin` beside binary channels, or under "harness integrations"?
  It is not an install of mcpx; it needs a daemon somewhere.
- Which first server for the quick start works with every runtime?
- Should the hidden commands (`serve`, `api`, `adapter`, `registry`, ...) be added to `Commands()` before
  the overview references them? (#144)

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease**: M (content from existing sources; the diagram pipeline is S once #117 is decided; honest
status needs #158 to exist first for most rows). **Impact**: high (the second and third pages of the
30-second path).
**Depends on / related**: #155 (links here; command forms), #158 (every "not started" row),
#117 (diagram tooling), #120 (agent twin), #144 (commands missing from `mcpx help`),
#146 #147 #148 #149 (now-what targets), #150 (story.md stale entries), #44 (closed, fixed in #53: plugin
without the binary), #134 (container image), #48 (other harnesses), #49 (CI), #79 (typecheck default), #102 (adapter/API tools not
in scripts), #94.
