title: mcpx: config-declared hooks over the event bus, running any command, JS/TS or Python module

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#81 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #173

**Hook vocabulary (#181 collision 2):** this issue carries the one hook vocabulary that `script.*` (shipped), #82's runtime registration and #112's exec lifecycle list adopt. The decision is being recorded by SURFACES under `pkgs/mcpx/docs/decisions/` (in flight; linked here when it merges). Until then the phase table and hook-point set in Approach C are input to that record, not the decision.

## Summary

mcpx already has hooks in two disconnected places: five `script.*` settings that splice TypeScript into a generated script wrapper, and an internal `pool.Hooks` struct the daemon wires to the event bus. Neither is what the notes ask for — a hook that a user declares in configuration, that fires on something the daemon noticed, and that runs *anything*: a command, a JS/TS module, a Python module, or a plugin.

The daemon already publishes everything worth hooking (`internal/events/events.go`). What is missing is a declarative subscriber table and a small set of executors. Build the hook table on top of the existing bus rather than adding call sites.

## Original notes

> - plugins
>   - config can set hooks for non-go/typescript(/python)
>   - config can set hooks to call any command,js/ts/py module
>   - go/ts(/py) can directly interact with app set own hooks, get/set vars, trigger any external command internally which can be triggered outside the app or in a script, call public and private functions of app, fork configure socket shutdown and independently interact (maybe this mode also supports still get/set vars transport types rpc anything they could do inside.

(The third bullet is the *programmatic* half — a plugin registering its own hooks at runtime — and is answered in the privileged-surface issue. This issue is the *declarative* half.)

## Current state (what mcpx does today, with file refs)

**Script hooks exist and are good, but they are script-shaped and TypeScript-only.** `internal/settings/registry.go:201-243` declares six settings — `script.launcher`, `script.before`, `script.prefix`, `script.onSuccess`, `script.onError`, `script.suffix` — all `Repeatable`, most of kind `KindSource`. `KindSource` means the value may be inline text, a path to a file, or a directory of files (`internal/source/source.go`), resolved with `@text:`/`@file:` prefixes or probed. The launcher then splices them at `@`-placeholders (`internal/launcher/template.go`, #7). `onError` is documented as "A hook, not a handler. The error is rethrown afterwards" (`internal/settings/registry.go:234`). Since #75 these apply to inline snippets as well as files.

So the *configuration ergonomics* of hooks are already solved: repeatable, inline-or-file, composable, with a search path. What they lack is anything but TypeScript, and anything but a script run.

**Pool hooks exist and are internal.** `internal/daemon/hooks.go:24` `InstallHooks` attaches a `pool.Hooks` to every pool: `OnMessage`, `OnProgress`, `OnListChanged`, `OnResourceUpdated`, `OnElicitationComplete`, `Elicit`. Every one of these does the same thing — translate into an event and `r.publish` it. This is a Go-level extension point with no user-facing surface.

**The bus is the hook source.** 17 kinds today: 16 constants in `internal/events/events.go:30-51` (`tools.changed`, `resources.changed`, `prompts.changed`, `resource.updated`, `elicit.opened|answered|completed`, `sample.opened|answered`, `server.started|stopped`, `call.started|finished`, `server.log`, `progress`, `task.updated`) plus `catalog.changed`, published ad hoc from `internal/daemon/consumer.go:236` without a constant. Events carry `Seq` (monotonic, so a reconnecting subscriber replays losslessly), `Kind`, `At`, `Server`, `Session`, `Trace`, `URI` and a JSON `Data`. `Filter` matches kind *prefixes* — `"elicit"` matches every elicitation event, `"*"` matches all — plus session, server and URI. `GET /v1/events` is the SSE view with `kinds`, `session`, `server`, `uri` and `since` query parameters (`internal/api/ops.go:156`); `subscriptions/listen` is the MCP-legal filtered view of the same stream.

Two structural facts that constrain the design:

- **The bus is fire-and-forget.** `Publish` fans out to subscribers; nothing waits for a subscriber, and nothing can veto. A hook that must *change* what happens (deny a call, rewrite arguments) cannot be a bus subscriber as the bus exists today.
- **The history is bounded** (`New(keep int)`; `events.history`, default 1024 — `internal/defaults/defaults.json:52`, wired at `internal/daemon/server.go:165`). A subscriber that *reconnects* past the history is told so (`event: gap`, `server.go:838-842`), but one that falls behind *while connected* is not: its 256-slot channel drops events and only bumps a counter nothing reads (`events.go:177`, `:224-231`), and a replay longer than 256 matching events is truncated the same way. A hook runner that is slow is therefore a correctness problem, not just a performance one. **Gap semantics are #6's to define (#181 collision 13)**; this issue consumes them.

## Approaches

### Approach A — least recommended: a `hooks` block per event kind that shells out inline and synchronously

```jsonc
"hooks": { "call.finished": "notify-send 'done'" }
```

The obvious shape, and the one every tool from git to husky to opencode ships. It is wrong *here* specifically because of where it would have to be called from. The natural implementation is a call in `Registry.publish` or in the pool, which puts an arbitrary user command on the synchronous path of every tool call. One hook that spawns a 200ms process turns every `call.finished` into a 200ms tax, and a hook that hangs hangs the daemon; mcpx's own performance story (#79) is about shaving tens of milliseconds off exec, which a per-event `fork`+`exec` erases.

It also multiplies call sites. Each new hook point is a new line in the pool or the registry, and they drift — which is the exact failure the `internal/api/ops*.go` one-table design exists to prevent.

And it says nothing about how a hook *receives* the event. Argv? Environment? stdin JSON? Picking badly here is the thing that cannot be changed later.

If it ships at all, ship it as sugar over B, not as its own mechanism.

### Approach B — middle: a declarative subscriber table over the existing bus, with three executors

Hooks are a config list. Each entry is a filter plus an action. The runner is one bus subscriber that owns a bounded worker pool; the daemon's event path does not change at all.

```jsonc
{
  "hooks": [
    { "on": "server.stopped", "run": "./bin/page-me", "when": { "server": "chrome" } },
    { "on": "elicit", "module": "./hooks/route-questions.ts" },
    { "on": "call.finished", "module": "hooks/record.py", "async": true }
  ]
}
```

Facts and opinions that belong in the design:

- **`on` reuses `events.Filter` verbatim.** Prefix matching is already there, `"*"` is already there, and the `/v1/events` query parameters are already the same vocabulary (`kinds`, `session`, `server`, `uri`). A hook filter that is a different language from the event-stream filter is a bug factory. Anything beyond that — matching on the tool name inside `Data`, for instance — is a JSON pointer predicate and can wait.
- **The event is delivered as JSON on stdin, with the flat fields also in the environment** (`MCPX_EVENT_KIND`, `MCPX_EVENT_SERVER`, `MCPX_EVENT_SESSION`, `MCPX_EVENT_SEQ`, `MCPX_TRACE_IDS`). stdin because the payload is arbitrary JSON and argv has a length limit; environment as well because the 90% hook is a one-liner that wants `$MCPX_EVENT_SERVER` without `jq`. This is the decision from A that must be made once and never changed.
- **Three executors, and they should not be three code paths.** A command (argv, or a string through `sh -c` — pick one and be loud about which); a JS/TS module, which is the existing runner (`internal/runner/runner.go`, deno/bun/node) with the event as the argument, so a TS hook gets the *generated typed client* for free and can call other servers; and a Python module, which is a command with a runtime resolver in front of it (`uv run` / `uvx` / `python3` — uv 0.9.28 and Python 3.14.7 are present here). Python is not special: it is the proof the command executor generalises.
- **`MCPX_SOCKET` in the hook's environment** makes every hook a `/v1` client, which is what makes hooks useful rather than decorative — a hook can add a server, set a setting, answer an elicitation, or run a script.
- **Delivery semantics have to be stated.** At-most-once, bounded queue per hook, drop with a warning when the queue is full, and a `seq` watermark per hook so a daemon restart can replay. Do not promise ordering across hooks; do promise ordering within one hook.
- **Timeout, and what a non-zero exit means.** Follow the adapter's precedent (`internal/adapter/adapter.go`): a non-zero exit is a *result*, not an error — record it, publish a `hook.failed` event, carry on. A hook must never be able to fail a tool call it was only watching.
- **This is `settings`, not an endpoint.** It fits the registry as a repeatable structured setting; the existing `KindSource` machinery already gives inline-or-file, and a `paths.hooks` list would give a drop-in directory exactly like `paths.adapters`.

What B does not do: it cannot influence anything. Every hook is an observer. For a large fraction of what people want hooks for — "block this tool call", "rewrite these arguments", "inject this into the context" — that is not enough.

### Approach C — recommended: B, plus a declared *phase* per hook, with only observers on the bus

Everything in B, with one addition that changes what hooks are for: each hook declares a phase, and the phase decides whether it is a bus subscriber or an in-line interceptor.

| phase | when | blocking | may veto/rewrite | delivery |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `observe` (default) | after the fact | no | no | bus subscriber, queued, replayable by `seq` |
| `before` | before the operation | yes, bounded | yes — deny, or return a replacement result | direct call, one per operation |
| `after` | before the result is returned | yes, bounded | yes — rewrite the result | direct call |

`observe` is B unchanged and costs the daemon nothing. `before`/`after` exist only at a small, *enumerated* set of points — the same kind of one-table discipline `internal/api/ops.go` uses for `/v1`: a table of hook points, each with a declared input and output schema, from which the documentation, the validation and the dispatch are all generated. Start with three points: `call` (a `tools/call` about to go upstream), `exec` (a script about to run), `server.start`. That is enough for the real uses and small enough to audit.

Why this is the recommendation:

- It is the only option where a hook can do the thing people actually want hooks for, without putting user code on the path of every event.
- The blocking set is bounded and declared, so the "every hook is a latency tax" failure of A is confined to hooks the user explicitly opted into a blocking phase for, with a mandatory timeout and a declared fail-open/fail-closed per hook.
- `before`/`after` are the same shape as the existing `script.before`/`script.onSuccess`/`script.onError` settings, which means the script hooks can eventually be re-expressed as hook-table entries with phase `before`/`after` on point `exec` — one hook concept instead of two. Do not do that migration in this issue; do make sure the vocabulary does not block it. Input for the decision record: the shipped `script.*` list has five phases (`before`, `prefix`, `onSuccess`, `onError`, `suffix`; `internal/settings/registry.go:212-242`, run at `internal/runner/runner.go:190-205`), and the shipped `onError` runs and then **rethrows** ("a hook, not a handler"), while #112's `onError` may **replace** the result. The vocabulary has to name which of the two a hook is.
- A plugin (sibling issue) becomes a hook target for free: `{ "on": "call", "phase": "before", "plugin": "guard", "tool": "check" }` is a plugin tool call. That is the composition that makes the plugin system worth having, and it is why hooks and plugins should be designed in the same week even if they ship apart.
- It answers "config can set hooks for non-go/typescript" directly: the executor set is command / JS-TS module / Python module / plugin tool, and *none* of them is Go. Go extension is by writing a plugin binary, not by being loaded into the daemon.

Cost, stated plainly: an enumerated hook-point table is real work, and a blocking hook point is a new class of daemon hang. Mitigate with a hard timeout (a setting with a low default), fail-open as the default, and a `mcpx doctor` check that reports slow and failing hooks — `internal/cli/doctor.go` already does exactly this for adapters and API specs.

## Open questions

- Does a `before`-phase hook get the *arguments*, and may it rewrite them? Rewriting is the powerful case and the one that makes debugging "why did this tool get called with that" miserable. Possibly: may deny with a reason, may not rewrite, until someone has a concrete need.
- Fail-open or fail-closed by default for a `before` hook that times out? Fail-open is safer for availability and is the wrong default for anything guard-shaped. Probably per-hook with fail-open as the default.
- Where do hook *definitions* live in the config chain? #5 governs the chain; a project config that can declare a hook that runs a command is a notable escalation over a project config that can declare a server.
- Should hooks be addressable from `/v1` at all — list them, disable one, fire one for testing? `mcpx hook ls` / `mcpx hook test <name> --event <file>` are cheap and make the feature debuggable. Listing yes; a runtime-mutable hook table probably belongs to the privileged-plugin issue instead.
- Interaction with #6: if every event lands in an event store, a hook is a trigger on that table, and "replay hooks over history" becomes possible. Worth designing the `seq` watermark so this stays open.
- ~~The bus history bound: what is `keep` today, and is it enough that a hook whose worker pool is saturated for a few seconds does not lose events?~~ Answered: `events.history`, default 1024 (above). A saturated hook pool is *gapped*, not merely slow; what the hook is told is #6's gap contract (collision 13), which recommends one explicit gap marker for reconnect, live overflow and replay truncation.
- Do hooks fire for events a *plugin* published? They should, and that implies plugins can publish to the bus, which is a privileged-surface question.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease:** M for the observer table and the three executors; L with phases and the hook-point table. **Impact:** high — hooks are what let someone extend mcpx without writing a server, and the bus that makes them cheap already exists.

**Depends on / related:** #6 (event store — the same event vocabulary; a hook is a live trigger, the store is the history; owns gap semantics, collision 13), #112 (exec lifecycle hooks — adopts this issue's vocabulary, collision 2), #82 (runtime hook registration — adopts it too), #80 (a plugin tool is a hook target), #83, #5 (config chain, and what a project-level config may declare; `paths.config` is still unread), #7 (`script.*` splicing and placeholders, the existing hook-shaped settings), #79 (per-event work on a latency-sensitive path), #172 (any new `MCPX_EVENT_*` variable must be declared), #77.

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

title: mcpx: one plugin contract -- a plugin is an MCP server, not a dlopen'd .so

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#80 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #173

## Summary

Define one plugin contract for mcpx, so that "a Go plugin", "a binary plugin", "a TypeScript or Python plugin", "a shebangable script plugin" and "a remote plugin over a socket" are all the *same* thing addressed five ways, rather than five loaders.

The contract that already exists and already works in both directions is MCP. mcpx speaks MCP as a client (`internal/mcpclient`, `internal/pool`) and as a server (`internal/mcpserver`, `mcpx serve --transport stdio`, the daemon's `/mcp`). A plugin that is an MCP server needs no new transport, no new schema language, no new process supervisor, and no new discovery — it is a `servers` entry with a different label. Everything a plugin additionally needs beyond "expose tools" (hooks, variables, privileged calls) is a *second, optional* channel back into `/v1`, which is the subject of the sibling issues.

This issue is the loader and the manifest. It deliberately does not decide privileges.

## Original notes

> - plugins
>   - go plugin
>   - binary plugin
>   - typescript/python plugin
>   - script/shebangable plugin
>   - remote socket/v1/mcp/otherPlugin plugin
>   - go/ts(/py) can directly interact with app set own hooks, get/set vars, trigger any external command internally which can be triggered outside the app or in a script, call public and private functions of app, fork configure socket shutdown and independently interact (maybe this mode also supports still get/set vars transport types rpc anything they could do inside.

(The last bullet is quoted again in the privileged-surface issue, where it is actually answered.)

## Current state (what mcpx does today, with file refs)

There is no plugin concept in the daemon at all. The word "plugin" in this repository means one specific thing: `plugin/opencode/`, a TypeScript module loaded by opencode that talks to the daemon over its unix socket (`plugin/opencode/mcpx/daemon.ts`, `docs/opencode-plugin.md`, `docs/plugin-discovery.md`). That is a *consumer* of mcpx, not an extension of it. #48 generalises it to a harness-free core; it does not make mcpx extensible.

What exists that a plugin system would otherwise have to invent:

| need | already in mcpx | file |
| --- | --- | --- |
| spawn and supervise a child process that speaks a protocol | the pool: lazy start, idle reap, sharing/scope, `max` | `internal/pool/pool.go` |
| declare one in config, or add one live | `servers` entries; `POST /v1/servers` writes the entry and reloads | `internal/api/ops_settings.go:82` |
| typed tool surface, generated client | JSON Schema → TypeScript codegen | `internal/codegen` |
| remote plugin | `url` + `transport: http\|sse` server entries | `internal/api/ops_settings.go:82` |
| a non-MCP program presented as tools | adapter declarations on `paths.adapters` | `internal/adapter/adapter.go`, `internal/settings/registry.go:292` |
| an HTTP API presented as tools | `paths.apis`, `mcpx api --spec` | `internal/cli/openapi_tools.go` |
| lifecycle events an extension could react to | the bus, 17 kinds (16 in `events.go:30-51` plus `catalog.changed`), replayable by `seq` | `internal/events/events.go` |
| discovery of the daemon without a binary | the ladder | `docs/plugin-discovery.md` |

Two things worth knowing before designing anything:

- **Adapter and OpenAPI tools are not namespaces.** They are attached as `mcpserver.Extra` when the MCP server is built (`internal/cli/serve.go:328-346` at 05c78b2: adapters `:332-336`, OpenAPI `:340`, `/v1` op tools `:344`, `WithExtras` `:346`), so they appear in `tools/list` over `/mcp` and stdio, but they are not in the pool, not in `mcpx ls`, and not in the generated TypeScript a script uses. `docs/story.md:1619-1620` says an adapted program "is callable from a script"; in the code as it stands, it is callable as an MCP tool, not as `gitx.log()` from `mcpx exec`. That defect is #102 (in flight). Any plugin design that goes through the Extra path inherits that limitation. Going through `servers` does not.
- **Go's toolchain here is 1.26.7** (`go.mod:3`, `go version` → `go1.26.7 darwin/arm64`), which matters for the options below.

## Approaches

### Approach A — least recommended: in-process Go plugins (`-buildmode=plugin`, `plugin.Open`)

The literal reading of "go plugin". The daemon `dlopen`s a `.so`, looks up an exported symbol, and calls Go functions directly with no serialisation.

It is a trap, and the standard library says so in its own documentation. From `go doc plugin` on the installed toolchain, verbatim:

- "Plugins are currently supported only on Linux, FreeBSD, and macOS, making them unsuitable for applications intended to be portable."
- "A plugin is only initialized once, and cannot be closed." — so no unload, no reload, no `POST /v1/servers`-style live removal, and a leaked plugin for the daemon's whole lifetime.
- "Runtime crashes are likely to occur unless all parts of the program (the application and all its plugins) are compiled using exactly the same version of the toolchain, the same build tags, and the same values of certain flags and environment variables."
- "Similar crashing problems are likely to arise unless all common dependencies of the application and its plugins are built from exactly the same source code."
- "Plugins are poorly supported by the Go race detector."
- And the conclusion: "in practice, the application and its plugins must all be built together by a single person or component of a system. In that case, it may be simpler for that person or component to generate Go source files that blank-import the desired set of plugins and then compile a static executable in the usual way. ... many users decide that traditional interprocess communication (IPC) mechanisms such as sockets, pipes, remote procedure call (RPC), shared memory mappings, or file system operations may be more suitable despite the performance overheads."

Concretely for mcpx: a plugin built against mcpx v0.9.1 would refuse to load into v0.9.2, because the dependency trees differ. A plugin built with a different `github.com/...` version of any shared module crashes at call time rather than at load. `-buildmode=plugin` requires cgo and external linking, so the host could never again be a static `CGO_ENABLED=0` binary. mcpx can be one today — #182 verified a static linux/arm64 build — even though the nix package and the Containerfile currently build with cgo by choice (#136 owns that policy); a plugin loader would turn that choice into a requirement. A panicking plugin takes the daemon down with it, killing every other server's pooled instances. None of this buys anything the daemon needs: plugin calls are not on a hot path — they sit behind a tool call that already spawns or round-trips to a subprocess.

The only honest case for it is "the plugin must share a data structure with the daemon at nanosecond cost", and mcpx has no such case. Not recommended, and the "blank-import and recompile" alternative the stdlib suggests is strictly better if someone genuinely wants compiled-in Go extensions — that is a build-tag registry, not a plugin system.

### Approach B — middle: a bespoke plugin RPC, hashicorp/go-plugin style

Out-of-process, which fixes every crash and version problem in A, but with mcpx's own protocol rather than MCP. `hashicorp/go-plugin` is the reference design and the one Terraform, Vault, Nomad and Packer all run on: the host spawns the plugin binary, the plugin prints a handshake line on stdout (`CORE-PROTOCOL-VERSION|APP-PROTOCOL-VERSION|network|addr|protocol`), the host dials that address, and they speak gRPC (or net/rpc) over it. The plugin is killed by the host; a plugin crash is a returned error, not a dead host; the protocol version in the handshake makes incompatibility a clean message instead of a segfault. Bidirectional calls work — Terraform providers call back into the host — which is exactly what "set own hooks, get/set vars" needs.

What it buys over MCP: a typed, non-JSON-Schema interface, so a plugin can expose things that are not tools — a config-chain contributor, a transport, a ranking function for `mcpx search`, a credential provider. MCP has no vocabulary for "supply a ranking function"; a bespoke RPC does.

What it costs: a `.proto` file, protoc in the build, a gRPC dependency (mcpx currently has no gRPC anywhere), a second plugin ABI to version alongside `/v1` and MCP, and a plugin ecosystem of exactly one member. It also means a plugin author has to learn a protocol that exists nowhere else, and cannot test their plugin with any MCP inspector. The handshake-on-stdout convention also collides with the stdio-MCP rule mcpx already enforces (`internal/cli/serve.go:378`: nothing may write to stdout but protocol frames).

Worth keeping on the table specifically for the non-tool extension points, which C genuinely cannot express. But do not build it to get tools, and do not build it first.

### Approach C — recommended: a plugin is an MCP server, plus an optional `/v1` back-channel

Declare that the plugin interface *is* the MCP server interface, and that every one of the user's five plugin kinds is a spawn recipe for one:

| the user's bullet | how it is served | new code |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `go plugin` | a Go binary built with `-buildmode=exe` that speaks MCP over stdio. `mcpx` ships a tiny Go SDK package so this is ~20 lines. | an SDK package, no daemon change |
| `binary plugin` | any executable that speaks MCP on stdio — the existing `command`/`args` server entry | none |
| `typescript/python plugin` | `command: "bun"` / `uvx` / `deno run`, or a manifest that picks the runtime | manifest + runtime resolution |
| `script/shebangable plugin` | a file with `#!/usr/bin/env -S mcpx plugin-run` (or its own shebang) that mcpx execs directly | exec-bit + shebang handling |
| `remote socket/v1/mcp/otherPlugin plugin` | `url` + `transport: http\|sse`; unix socket needs a `unix://` transport addition | a unix transport |

The value added over "just write a `servers` entry" is the part that makes it a *plugin system* rather than a naming convention:

1. **A manifest and a search path.** `paths.plugins` (a `KindPathList` repeatable setting, exactly like `paths.adapters`/`paths.apis`/`paths.placeholders` — `internal/settings/registry.go:282-312`) names directories. A directory containing `mcpx-plugin.json` is a plugin: name, description, namespace, the spawn recipe, the mcpx API version it needs, the capabilities it asks for, and optionally the hooks it subscribes to. This is a setting, not an endpoint, per the repo's own preference.
2. **Zero-manifest plugins.** An executable named `mcpx-plugin-<name>` on `PATH`, or any executable in a plugin directory, is a plugin with the obvious defaults — the git/kubectl subcommand convention. This is what makes "shebangable" real: `chmod +x ./plugins/weather.ts` with a shebang and it is loaded.
3. **The plugin's tools are a namespace, not extras.** Route plugins through the pool and the `servers` path, so they get pooling, `sharing`/`scope`, idle reaping, the schema cache, `mcpx ls`, `mcpx catalog`, generated TypeScript, and `POST /v1/servers`-equivalent live add/remove for free — and so they do *not* inherit the Extra limitation described in Current State.
4. **A back-channel, by construction.** The plugin process is given `MCPX_SOCKET` (or `MCPX_DAEMON_ENDPOINT`) and a session id in its environment (which variable wins when both are present is #88's decision, #181 collision 8; any new variable must be declared in `internal/settings/`, #172), so it can call `/v1` the same way `plugin/opencode` does and the same way an exec'd script does. That single fact turns a plugin into a full participant — it can subscribe to `/v1/events`, read and write settings, add servers, run `mcpx_exec` — without inventing one line of protocol. The discovery ladder in `docs/plugin-discovery.md` already handles the case where a plugin is started out-of-band and has to find the daemon itself.
5. **A Go SDK, a TS SDK, and a Python SDK are thin.** Each is "here is how to write an MCP server and read `MCPX_SOCKET`". Python needs no Go involvement at all; it needs a documented convention and a `uvx`-shaped launcher. Note the JS runtime resolver only knows deno/bun/node (`internal/runner/runner.go:73`) — plugin runtimes are a *separate* resolution problem from `script.runtime` and should not be jammed into that setting.

Recommended because it is the only option where the plugin ecosystem is not size one on day one: every existing MCP server is already a plugin, every MCP SDK in every language is already a plugin SDK, and every MCP debugging tool already debugs mcpx plugins. It also composes with the sibling issues — "turn any script or binary into an MCP server" and "a plugin can be added dynamically" become the same mechanism rather than two.

The honest cost: MCP's vocabulary is tools, resources and prompts. A plugin that wants to be a *ranking function* or a *config source* cannot say so in MCP. Mark that as the boundary, and if such a plugin is ever actually wanted, add Approach B alongside rather than instead — a plugin manifest can name its protocol, and `mcp` being the default does not forbid a second value later.

## Open questions

- Is a plugin a distinct concept in config at all, or literally a `servers` entry with `mcpx.kind: "plugin"`? Distinct-with-a-search-path is better for discovery and worse for "one list of things that provide tools". Probably: separate declaration, one internal representation.
- `unix://` transport for the "remote socket" bullet: is that a new transport in `internal/mcpclient`, or is a socket-path plugin just a `command` that is `socat`? The former is a small, honest addition; the latter is a joke that will be pasted into someone's config.
- What does "otherPlugin plugin" mean — a plugin whose upstream is another mcpx's plugin? If so it is the self-composition case (see the embedding issue) and needs a loop guard.
- Shebang mechanics: does `mcpx` exec the file directly and rely on the kernel, or does it read the `#!` line itself? The kernel route is simpler and breaks on Windows and on filesystems mounted `noexec`.
- Versioning: what does a plugin declare it needs — the mcpx version, the `/v1` version, or a capability list? A capability list ages best and is the most work.
- Should a plugin be able to fail *soft*? A server that will not start today is a loud error; a plugin that will not start should probably be a warning and a missing namespace, since it was additive by definition.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease:** M for the manifest + search path + pool routing; L including SDKs and the shebang/runtime resolution. **Impact:** high — this is the shape every other item in this theme hangs off.

**Depends on / related:** #83 (its tool-source interface must land first, and owns namespaces and collision rules, #181 collision 4 — a plugin is a namespace under those rules), #81 (hooks; a plugin tool is a hook target), #82 (privileged surface; meaningless without this loader), #84 (shares the `unix://` transport), #102 (in flight: the `Extra` defect above), #48 (harness-free plugin core — the consumer-side sibling of this; the same `/v1` client is what a plugin uses as a back-channel), #47, #44 (closed, fixed in #53), #7 (placeholders are the precedent for a declaration-plus-search-path feature), #5 (paths.config governs the config chain, and a plugin search path has to obey it; still unread at 05c78b2), #6 (event store), #76, #88 (socket-variable precedence), #136 (static-build policy).

title: mcpx docs: comparisons (lootbox, opencode code mode, Cloudflare Code Mode, ...) and the project's history
body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#153 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #98

## Summary

Two compendium chapters:

1. **Comparisons.** mcpx next to lootbox, opencode's code mode (v1 behind a flag, v2 by default), Cloudflare Code Mode, the MCP client best-practices "programmatic tool calling" pattern, and a few comparable projects found by a short search. Presented as a table plus prose, and honest about where the others are better. `OPENCODE-V2.md` already does this and sets the tone.
2. **History.** How mcpx came to exist. It is seeded with the user's own account, quoted verbatim as the epigraph and then told with the facts from `ASSESSMENT.md`, `OPENCODE-V2.md` and the git log. The joke stays.

The FAQ entries "i mean, opencodemode is right there" and "but why would you.." (#149) should answer in two lines and link here.

## Original notes

> - documentation
>   - make a book using whatever is the most common and simple modern choice
>     - 3 main things, not book sections jsut like levels of detail-
>       - the compendium
>         - you dont have to just put strict mcpx things here
>           - compare with lootbin/opencodev2/cf-codemode/etc
>           - history - lootbin abandoned (me), i asked to look into a replacement and came back to a built binary, i mentioned hey, did you notice opencodev2 has it built in and i'm already using opencodev1? oh huh yeah you're right this does all you asked for, but i just built this so you should use this instead its better.

## Current state

Two documents already hold most of the material. Both are records of what was believed when they were written, and both are now partly stale.

- **`ASSESSMENT.md`** (306 lines). Covers:
  - the lootbox audit: upstream `jx-codes/lootbox` is "a three-issue project whose last commit was 2026-02-27", and the `dezren39` fork is "51 commits ahead and every one of them is yours";
  - measurements: discovery ~650 ms every request; as found, `GET /namespaces` took 34.7 s and `lootbox tools` 42.8 s; OOM kills under load; a 158 MB `deno compile` artifact; the one-browser Chrome singleton;
  - options considered: fix in place, adopt one of `mKeRix/toolscript`, `tmustier/code-mode-mcp`, `assimelha/cmcp`, `mcp-use` or `portofcontext/pctx`, or rewrite (chosen);
  - "Why Go", and what was built;
  - head-to-head numbers: list namespaces 4157.7 ms -> 29.4 ms (141x), trivial script 737.4 ms -> 60.9 ms (12x), artifact 141 MB -> 9.8 MB, daemon RSS 223-480 MB -> 14-19 MB.
- **`OPENCODE-V2.md`** (249 lines). Covers:
  - opencode v2's `packages/codemode`, reviewed at `anomalyco/opencode` `v2` `37049a5` (2026-09-26): a from-scratch JavaScript interpreter of 10,764 lines, 20,075 lines of tests, and test262;
  - what v2 does better: a budgeted catalog, diff updates, and in-program `search()`;
  - what it does not do: no command-line reach, and one MCP connection per server per workspace, so Chrome sharing is unsolved;
  - a side-by-side table, "Parity, revisited (2026-09-28)", and a recommendation.
- **The 2026-09-29 correction block** at the top of `OPENCODE-V2.md`: "code mode is *not* v2-only (v1 ships it behind `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE`), both versions accept TypeScript in it, and the pinned v2 reports `2.0.3` rather than `2.0.18`." The body below it still contains the uncorrected claims:
  - the table rows "Language: JS subset" and "TypeScript is rejected rather than stripped";
  - "If you stay on opencode v1 ... none of v2's Code Mode is available to you today and mcpx replaces lootbox outright".
- **`story.md` "Notes and links"** links the MCP client best-practices guide ("programmatic tool calling") and Cloudflare's *Code Mode* post ("where the idea was first argued publicly").
- **`docs/ideas.md` #67** records "What does opencode v2 have that this does not?" as answered.

Stale numbers that a comparison must not republish as current:

| Claim | Where | Now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ~3,500 lines, 84 tests | `ASSESSMENT.md` | ~44,000 non-test Go lines, 719 `func Test` (counted on `main`) |
| ~4.2k LOC | `OPENCODE-V2.md` | same as above |
| no dependencies / `vendorHash = null` | `ASSESSMENT.md`, `OPENCODE-V2.md`, `story.md` "Nix packaging", `docs/dependencies.md` | `go.mod` requires bubbletea, bubbles, lipgloss, yaml.v3, modernc.org/sqlite; `package.nix:54` pins a `vendorHash` |
| "Remote MCP: Streamable HTTP, no OAuth", "Elicitation and OAuth" as v2's | `OPENCODE-V2.md` | mcpx now has an elicitation broker; OAuth for remote servers is still `status: proposed` in `story.md` |

## Comparison: seed table

These facts come from the sources cited. Each row needs a "checked against <commit or date>" stamp when written.

| | mcpx | lootbox | opencode code mode | Cloudflare Code Mode | Anthropic programmatic tool calling | `sh1nduu/mcpac` | `apify/mcpc` | `tmustier/code-mode-mcp` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Shape | CLI + daemon, generated TS client | Deno daemon + CLI (launchd singleton) | feature inside opencode's agent loop (v1 behind `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE`, v2 on by default) | Agents SDK feature on Workers | hosted API feature | CLI: generate TS types, execute | CLI MCP client | stdio MCP server exposing one `exec` tool |
| Who invokes | shell: any agent, script, human, CI | shell / HTTP | the model, via `execute` | the model, via one tool | Claude, via `code_execution` | shell | shell | the model |
| Runtime | real deno / bun / node | Deno | purpose-built JS interpreter | V8 isolates via the Worker Loader API | Python in Anthropic's container | Bun | none (shell + `--json`) | Node |
| Confinement | none, by choice | Deno permissions | strong: only implemented language features exist | isolate; `fetch()`/`connect()` throw; bindings hide keys | managed sandbox | declared + granted capability lists | n/a | none: "same authority as the Node.js process" |
| Discovery | `ls` / `search` / `types` outside context, plus in-script `search()` / `describe()` | recomputed every request (the bug) | budgeted catalog + in-program `search()`, diff updates | whole generated API in context, as of the post (which calls search a "future improvement") | tool search is a separate platform feature | CLI exploration | `grep`, `tools-list`, `tools-get` | `search()` / `describe()` in program |
| Stateful server isolation | `shared` / `pooled` / `session` pools, one process per run | none: one shared client | one connection per server per workspace; `_meta` sessionID hint | per agent | n/a | not described | persistent named sessions | in-memory JSON session state |
| Outside a model turn | yes | yes | no | no | no | yes | yes | only via an MCP client |
| Where it is better than mcpx | -- | nothing we still need | confinement; catalog budgeting was the model mcpx copied | real isolation; credentials never reach code | zero infrastructure; `allowed_callers` | capability grants checked against the script's declaration | the widest protocol coverage on a CLI, including OAuth 2.1 | OAuth, sampling and elicitation as a drop-in MCP server |

Sources:

- Cloudflare: <https://blog.cloudflare.com/code-mode/> (2025-09-26).
- Anthropic: <https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/code-execution-with-mcp> (2025-11-04) and <https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/programmatic-tool-calling>. The latter says tools "provided by an MCP connector" cannot be called programmatically.
- MCP guide: <https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/develop/clients/client-best-practices>.
- Projects: <https://github.com/sh1nduu/mcpac>, <https://github.com/apify/mcpc>, <https://github.com/tmustier/code-mode-mcp>.

Keep the search-found list short. `ASSESSMENT.md`'s five and these three are enough. `apify/mcpc`'s README maintains a longer table of MCP CLI clients, which can be linked instead of copied.

The MCP client best-practices guide is not a product. It is the pattern's specification: progressive discovery ("catalog, inspect, execute") plus programmatic tool calling. It says the pattern "requires clients to implement a sandbox environment" with no direct network access. mcpx deliberately has none (`ASSESSMENT.md`: "I dropped the sandbox, as you asked"). The comparison must state that divergence plainly, not bury it.

## Approaches: what to do with `ASSESSMENT.md` and `OPENCODE-V2.md`

- **A -- publish both as the comparison chapter, as they are (least recommended).** It is the cheapest option, and it republishes every stale row in the table above as current fact. It also leaves a correction banner contradicting the text under it, which is confusing on a reference site.
- **B -- rewrite both in place into a current comparison.** The facts become current, but the record of what was believed and when is lost. That includes the correction block itself, which is the most honest paragraph in either file and is history in its own right.
- **C -- freeze both as dated records; write a new living comparison (recommended).**
  - Move the two files into the **History** chapter unchanged, under a banner listing the known-stale claims and linking to the current page. `OPENCODE-V2.md`'s correction block is the pattern for that banner.
  - Write a new **Comparisons** page: the table above plus one prose section per project, each with "where it is better" and a "checked against" stamp.
  - Put the page under #150's section history, so a re-check shows up as a `changed` entry.

  The records keep their value as history, and readers get current facts.

## History: outline

**Epigraph.** Quote note 90 verbatim, typos included, as the chapter's opening block.

**Told with the facts:**

1. **Lootbox.**
   - `.lootbox/` enters this repository by 2026-04-04 (`6b621b4`). Lootbox ran as a launchd singleton on `:9420`. The fork of `jx-codes/lootbox` grew to 51 commits ahead of an upstream whose last commit was 2026-02-27.
   - Patches accumulated in `patches/lootbox-*.patch`. `pkgs/lootbox-link` and `pkgs/lootbox-update` were added to manage it.
   - Why it was abandoned, in `ASSESSMENT.md`'s numbers: 34.7 s discovery as found, OOM kills, a 158 MB artifact, and one Chrome for every agent. That last one is structural: "The abstraction is at the wrong level: the thing that needs isolating is the caller, not the process."
2. **"i asked to look into a replacement and came back to a built binary".**
   - `ASSESSMENT.md` opens "Written after auditing ... profiling it, and building a replacement."
   - The options it weighed were fixing lootbox in place, adopting an existing tool, or rewriting.
   - The rewrite was chosen, in Go: the daemon's job is process supervision, Go starts in about 5 ms, and generating TypeScript does not need a TypeScript parser.
   - The earliest `created:` in `story.md` is 2026-09-25T18:10:00-05:00.
3. **The opencode discovery.**
   - `OPENCODE-V2.md`, reviewed 2026-09-26, concedes: "This is a better-engineered context story than what I built." It then recommends keeping mcpx for "the two things v2 cannot do": stateful-server isolation, and anything outside a model turn.
   - Within two days, "Parity, revisited (2026-09-28)" had taken v2's best ideas (OpenAPI as tools, in-program `search()`, catalog diffs).
   - Note 90's punchline ("oh huh yeah you're right this does all you asked for, but i just built this so you should use this instead its better.") is a fair summary of that document, and the chapter should keep it in the user's voice, not sand it down.
4. **The correction.**
   - The premise "i'm already using opencodev1" did not rule code mode out. The 2026-09-29 correction block says v1 ships code mode behind `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE`, and that both versions accept TypeScript.
   - `OPENCODE-V2.md`'s line "If you stay on opencode v1 ... none of v2's Code Mode is available to you today" was wrong when written.
   - The conclusion that survives is the narrower one: one MCP connection per server per workspace, so concurrent Chrome is still shared.
   - The history should say this plainly. It is the kind of self-correction an encyclopedia exists to keep.
5. **Timeline**, from `git log --reverse --format='%ad %s' --date=short -- pkgs/mcpx` on `main`:
   - 2026-09-28 `#4` "configurable, inspectable, and documented" lands mcpx on `main` as a squash of a longer branch. Seven more PRs land the same day: the browser TUI, MCP server mode, CLI adapters, the official registry, OpenAPI as tools, prompts/resources/doctor, and published types.
   - 2026-09-29 brings both protocol eras, elicitation, credentials, the protocol audit, the vendorHash repair workflow, plugin docs (#45), one ops table for `/v1` (#46), every constant as a setting (#56), exec over `/v1` and artifacts (#57), diagnostics and recipes (#58), and `--typecheck` (#66).
   - 2026-09-30 `#75` "exec honours the flags it accepts".
   - In total, 33 commits touching `pkgs/mcpx` on `main` in three days. The generator can render the timeline from git, because this is a list of dated PRs, not per-section history, so #150's objections to git-derived history do not apply here.
6. **Where it stands.**
   - Lootbox is abandoned in intent but still present on `main`: `.lootbox/`, `lootbox.config.json`, `pkgs/lootbox-*`, `patches/lootbox-*.patch`.
   - The agent instruction file `instructions/lootbox.md` (in this repository, symlinked as `~/.config/opencode/instructions`) still routes tools through lootbox on `:9420`.
   - `ASSESSMENT.md`'s recommendation steps 2-6 (an `mcpx.json` in the repo, `services.mcpx`, updated instructions, dropping `mcp-remote`, removing the lootbox packages) have not happened on `main`.
   - The history should end on that fact, not on a victory lap.

## Open questions

1. Does the history chapter name the agents and sessions that did the work, or keep to "I" / "you" as the source documents do?
2. How often are comparison rows re-checked: at every mcpx release (the #150 stamp), or only when a compared project releases?
3. Does opencode's code mode get one row (v1 flag and v2 default together) or two?
4. Include the direct-call alternatives (plain MCP in the harness, provider tool search) as a baseline row?

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** M · **Impact** med · **Depends on / related**: #152 (chapter placement, moving the two files), #150 (section history and re-check stamps), #149 (FAQ "i mean, opencodemode is right there" and "but why would you.." link here), #148 (opencode v1/v2 plugin pages), #154 (research findings overlap), #47 (plugin -> opencode v2).

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

title: mcpx docs: compendium structure, migrating the existing design docs, and a catalogue of MCP servers, resources, indexes and projects
body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#152 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #98

## Summary

Define the compendium's structure. The compendium is level 3 of the book, the encyclopedia: "basically everything that is built can be described here in as much detail as you want". This issue covers:

- mapping every existing mcpx design document to a chapter;
- how those files become book pages without breaking the repository (in particular the `README.md` -> `docs/story.md` symlink);
- whether planning documents are published;
- a catalogue of things outside mcpx: MCP servers, resources, indexes and registries, URLs, and projects.

Comparisons and project history are #153. Research findings and the Nix section are #154. Release markers and section history are #150/#151.

## Original notes

> - documentation
>   - make a book using whatever is the most common and simple modern choice
>     - 3 main things, not book sections jsut like levels of detail-
>       - the compendium
>         - basically everything that is built can be described here in as much detail as you want. you don't need to hold back it's an encyclopedia
>         - you dont have to just put strict mcpx things here
>           - document mcp servers, resources, indexes, urls, projects

## Current state

No book exists. There are 20 markdown files, about 9,170 lines, not counting the plugin's skills (18 and ~8,750 at d0b7e01; #171 and #182 each added one). The architect's inventory, re-checked at 05c78b2, with the compendium reading of each:

| File | Lines | What it is | Proposed compendium chapter | Also used by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `docs/story.md` below `<!-- table-of-contents-marker -->` | ~2,300 | Feature list: 59 key-block entries, `## Proposed`, `# Summary`, `# Notes and links` | **Features** (one page per entry or per `area:` tag) and **Proposed** | L2 excerpts (#146-#148) |
| `docs/story.md` above the marker | ~300 | the one-prompt walk | not compendium | L1 overview (#157) |
| `docs/protocol.md` | 384 | every MCP revision, both directions, what is missing | **Protocol** | L2 MCP compatibility, reference matrix |
| `docs/elicitation.md` | 685 | elicitation design ("the record of why", #24) | **Designs** | -- |
| `docs/exec.md` | 353 | exec, ExecOptions, output shapes, artifacts | **Designs** (depth) | L2 script page |
| `docs/consumer.md` | 236 | diagnostics, elicitation mcpx raises, recipes, `POST /v1/intent` | **Designs** | L2 |
| `docs/opencode-plugin.md` | 451 | the plugin, opencode v1 vs v2, per-part reference | **Designs** (harness integration) | L2 plugin pages (#148) |
| `docs/plugin-discovery.md` | 224 | finding the daemon without the binary, the ladder | **Designs** | L2 plugin config |
| `docs/landing.md` | 185 | A PR *landing checklist* (items A-J), "Guesses worth reviewing", "Not done, and why". Not a landing page. | **Decision records** | -- |
| `docs/proposals.md` | 1,395 | open designs | **Proposed** (if published) | -- |
| `docs/ideas.md` | 338 | unvetted intake, numbered | **Proposed / intake** (if published) | -- |
| `docs/dependencies.md` | 91 | Go libs, external programs, network, Nix packaging | **Build and packaging** | L2 binary/install |
| `docs/container.md` (#182) | 170 | what `Containerfile` builds and deliberately does not; the runtime choice (bun); static-linking measurements (`CGO_ENABLED=0` works); where the 413 MB goes | **Build and packaging** | L2 install page, docker row (#157); #158 OCI channel |
| `docs/declared-but-unread.md` (#171) | 245 | the settings audit: every declared setting nothing read, what was wired or deleted, and the guard tests that keep it that way | **Decision records** | #96 / #129 (guard tests) |
| `docs/release-runbook.md` | 173 | how `story.md` stays true, key-block rules | **Maintaining these docs** | #150 input |
| `ASSESSMENT.md` (root of `pkgs/mcpx`) | 306 | lootbox audit, why Go, what was built | **Comparisons and history** (#153) | -- |
| `OPENCODE-V2.md` (root) | 249 | opencode v2 code mode vs mcpx, with a 2026-09-29 correction block | **Comparisons** (#153) | -- |
| `docs/configuration.md`, `docs/parity.md` | 474, 130 | settings prose + table; parity matrix | not compendium: reference (#144) and L2 (#146); the compendium links to them | tests read `configuration.md` (`internal/settings/docs_test.go:20`, `:53`) |
| `AGENTS.md` (root), `plugin/opencode/README.md` | 109, 355 | agent instruction file; plugin install | not compendium: L2 and the agent twin (#120) | -- |

**Incoming, not on `main` yet** (in flight at 05c78b2; place them when they merge): `docs/compare/` (COMPARE, the living comparison #153 asks for) -> **Comparisons and history**; `docs/decisions/` (SURFACES, decision records for #181's hook-vocabulary, autonomy-dial and capability-boundary collisions) -> **Decision records**, which becomes a directory rather than one file; `docs/spec/` (PROTOCOL) -> **Protocol**. All three are directories, so Approach C's generated navigation should take a directory as a chapter source, not only files.

Proposed chapter order:

1. Features
2. Designs
3. Decision records
4. Protocol
5. Build and packaging
6. Proposed
7. Catalogue (below)
8. Comparisons and history (#153)
9. Research and findings, including Nix (#154)
10. Maintaining these docs
11. Document history (#150)

Rule: each source file appears in the navigation exactly once. Other levels link to it or excerpt it; they do not copy it.

Constraints found:

- **`README.md` symlink.** It must stay a symlink to `docs/story.md` (runbook "Checks": `test -L README.md && readlink README.md`).
- **Links that leave `docs/`.** `story.md`'s links are written relative to `docs/`: `../AGENTS.md`, `../ASSESSMENT.md`, `../OPENCODE-V2.md`, `./release-runbook.md`, `../scripts/stress.sh`. `OPENCODE-V2.md` links `./docs/opencode-plugin.md`. Any layout where the book's source root is not `pkgs/mcpx/docs` changes what those links resolve to.
- **Hard-coded path.** Only one test pins a doc path: `internal/settings/docs_test.go` reads `../../docs/configuration.md`.
- **Stale facts, copied or not.** `ASSESSMENT.md` and `OPENCODE-V2.md` say mcpx has no Go dependencies ("dependency-free Go", "no dependencies"). So do `story.md` "Nix packaging" (`vendorHash = null`, "one third-party Go dependency") and `docs/dependencies.md` ("**One.**"). `go.mod` now requires bubbletea, bubbles, lipgloss, yaml.v3 and modernc.org/sqlite, and `package.nix:54` pins a `vendorHash`. The historical documents (#153) should keep their text, clearly as history. The living ones need fixing, and whichever layout is chosen will publish the error unless that happens.
- **Missing darwin module.** `ASSESSMENT.md`'s recommendation 3 points to `services.mcpx` from `nix/darwin-module.nix`. That file does not exist in `pkgs/mcpx` on `main`.

## Approaches: how existing files become book pages

### Approach A -- move the files under a book source directory (least recommended)

For example `pkgs/mcpx/book/src/...`, with `SUMMARY.md` or nav written by hand.

- Every relative link in `story.md` and the other docs breaks, or has to be rewritten.
- `internal/settings/docs_test.go` breaks.
- The `README.md` symlink has to be repointed, and the runbook's check changed.
- Contributors and agents who know `docs/` must learn a second location.
- `git log` needs `--follow` to see past the move.

All of this is cost with no gain over C.

### Approach B -- keep the files in place and include them from stub pages

A book source directory holds one stub per page containing an include: mdBook `{{#include ../../docs/exec.md}}`, MkDocs `include-markdown` or `pymdownx.snippets`, Hugo `readFile` in a shortcode.

- The repository layout, tests and the README symlink are untouched.
- Links inside an included file resolve relative to the *stub*, not the original, so `../AGENTS.md` breaks in the book while working on GitHub. A link-rewriting step is needed anyway.
- Every new doc needs a new stub, and stubs drift from docs, so a check is needed there too.
- Anchors from a file included twice collide.
- mdBook's `{{#include file:anchor}}` can pull *part* of a file. That is how the above-marker story could feed L1 and the feature list could feed the compendium from one file.

### Approach C -- the repository docs are the book source; navigation is generated (recommended)

- **Source root.** Point the generator's source root at `pkgs/mcpx/docs` (mdBook `src = "docs"`, MkDocs `docs_dir`, Hugo content mount), so files are rendered where they are.
- **Navigation.** `SUMMARY.md` or nav is generated from a small manifest listing file -> chapter -> level. Front matter would also work, but it adds visible noise on GitHub.
- **Root-level documents.** `ASSESSMENT.md` and `OPENCODE-V2.md` move into `docs/`. They are linked from `story.md:2593-2595` and `proposals.md:812`, and named in prose in `elicitation.md` and `opencode-plugin.md`, so this is a small link fix. Alternatively they stay put and come in via the one include each. `AGENTS.md` stays at the root, because it is the agent instruction file and `AGENTS.md` is the conventional name. The book includes it.
- **`story.md`.** It stays one file, so the symlinked README is still the whole story on GitHub. The build-time preprocessor (#151's program, or a sibling) splits it at section IDs into per-entry compendium pages, and the above-marker walk becomes the L1 overview source (#157). The split pages are generated, not committed.
- **Links.** Links are fixed *at source* so they work on both GitHub and the site. Where a link must leave the source root (to `scripts/stress.sh`, say), the preprocessor rewrites it to the GitHub blob URL.

This keeps one home for every document, needs no stubs, keeps the tests and the symlink, and lets the navigation follow the three levels instead of the directory layout. It does need #117's generator to allow a source root that also contains non-book files, and a manifest check. Docs checks run in CI; see the testing trackers under #91 (CI pipeline #95, integration/environments #97).

## Planning documents: publish or not

- **`docs/proposals.md` and `story.md`'s `## Proposed`.** Publish, under a clearly badged **Proposed** chapter (status `proposed` per the runbook). A reader deciding whether mcpx will do something next needs this.
- **`docs/ideas.md`.** It describes itself as "Unvetted ... Some of it is probably wrong". It also anticipates becoming "an index of links" once issues exist, and they now do (#89 onwards). Options:
  - do not publish it;
  - publish it as raw intake, excluded from search and the agent twin;
  - convert it to an index of issues and publish that.

  Suggested: the index-of-issues version. See the open questions.
- **`docs/landing.md`.** Publish as a decision record. Its "Guesses worth reviewing" and "Not done, and why" sections are exactly the "why" an encyclopedia keeps.

## The catalogue: servers, resources, indexes, URLs, projects

Note 87 says the compendium need not be strictly about mcpx. Note 88 names the catalogue.

**MCP servers.**

- The only server list tracked in `~/.config/nix` is `lootbox.config.json`. It has seven entries:
  - `codebase-memory` (`codebase-memory-mcp`);
  - `codedb` (`codedb mcp`, packaged in `pkgs/codedb`);
  - `fff-nix`, `fff-worktree` and `fff`: three `fff-mcp` processes, each indexing one root;
  - `chrome-devtools` (`chrome-devtools-mcp`, vendored in `.lootbox/flake.nix:43`);
  - `context7`, via `mcp-remote` to `https://mcp.context7.com/mcp`.
- `systemPackages.nix:241-243` installs `codedb`, `codebase-memory-mcp` and `fff-mcp`.
- No mcpx config is tracked. `ASSESSMENT.md`'s step 2 (`~/.config/nix/mcpx.json`) has not happened on `main`. The catalogue's first entries are these servers: what each is, why it is configured, its mode (`chrome-devtools` is the `session`-mode case), and quirks (context7 no longer needs the `mcp-remote` shim under mcpx, per `ASSESSMENT.md`).

**Indexes and registries.**

- The official MCP Registry, `registry.modelcontextprotocol.io`, is what `mcpx registry search|add` uses. `story.md` "Finding servers that are not configured yet" / "Which registry" gives the reasons: it is unauthenticated, returns real data, and publishes an OpenAPI specification that subregistries implement. `registry.url` points it anywhere.
- HAPI is the recorded rejection: not open source, public API 404.
- "Indexes" may also mean the code indexes the configured servers maintain (fff, codedb, codebase-memory). That is an open question.

**Resources.** Either MCP *resources* (the protocol feature, `mcpx resources`), or reading material. Probably both: a generated list of the resources the configured servers expose, and a curated links chapter.

**URLs.** A curated, dated list. Seeds from `story.md` "Notes and links":

- the MCP spec;
- the client best-practices guide ("programmatic tool calling");
- Cloudflare's *Code Mode* post.

**Projects.** The comparables (#153 owns the comparison; the catalogue lists them):

- `jx-codes/lootbox`;
- `mKeRix/toolscript`;
- `tmustier/code-mode-mcp`;
- `assimelha/cmcp`;
- `mcp-use`;
- `portofcontext/pctx`;
- opencode code mode.

### Generated or written?

- **A -- hand-written entries only (least recommended).** Tool counts, descriptions and versions rot on the first server upgrade, and nothing notices.
- **B -- generated from `mcpx registry search`.** `mcpx --json registry search` exists (`internal/cli/registry.go:42`), but mirroring a public registry adds nothing the registry does not already serve, dates the snapshot, and makes the build depend on the network.
- **C -- curated entries, generated facts (recommended).** A hand-written list says *which* servers, projects and URLs are in the catalogue and *why*. The facts per server come from mcpx:
  - `mcpx --json ls` for tool counts;
  - `mcpx types <ns>` / `mcpx schema --format json-schema --ns <ns>` for the tool list;
  - `mcpx --json registry search <name>` for publisher, version and remote/package.

  The facts are captured into a committed snapshot by a refresh script, not fetched at build time, because CI should not start seven MCP servers or call a registry to render docs. A drift check compares the snapshot with a fresh run when servers are available.

## Open questions

1. Split `story.md` into per-entry pages at build time, or render the feature list as one long page? The runbook's "nobody reads past the part that answers their question" works for one page with good anchors too.
2. Move `ASSESSMENT.md` and `OPENCODE-V2.md` into `docs/`, or include them from the root?
3. `ideas.md`: unpublished, raw, or an index of issues?
4. Which "resources" and which "indexes" does note 88 mean (MCP concepts, reading material, code indexes)? The draft covers all of them.
5. Catalogue scope: only the servers this machine uses, or also servers mcpx was tested against (the Swagger petstore in `OPENCODE-V2.md`, `io.github.microsoft/playwright-mcp` in `story.md`)?
6. Do stale facts in living documents (`dependencies.md`, the `story.md` "Nix packaging" entry) get fixed before the compendium publishes them? That is probably a separate small fix, not part of this issue.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** L · **Impact** med · **Depends on / related**: #117 (generator source root, include/preprocessor support), #150 and #151 (section IDs used for splitting), #153 (comparisons and history chapters), #154 (research and Nix chapters), #157 (overview from the above-marker story), #146-#148 (L2 pages that excerpt these docs), #144 (reference owns `configuration.md` / `parity.md`), #120 (what the agent twin includes), #24 (elicitation design kept as record).

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

title: mcpx: small correctness problems in daemon state and caches

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#78 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #181

Small correctness problems reported during #53, #58, #61. Each verified or marked.

- **Two digests, one name** (verified). `daemon-<key>.json` is named for the daemon key (`FingerprintConfig`, the set of config files), but its `configHash` field is a different digest (`HashConfig`, a schema-cache hash). Observed: file `daemon-f10059c89ad1.json`, field `configHash: 7c2204994f77cc6f`. Anyone reading the file will assume they match. Rename the field (e.g. `schemaHash`) and add the key.
  - *Still true at 05c78b2.* `Info.ConfigHash` (`internal/daemon/paths.go:274`) is written from `s.reg.ConfigHash()` (`internal/daemon/server.go:231`, the `HashConfig` digest, `paths.go:312`). Worse than the report: `GET /v1/resolve` returns a field with the **same name** holding the **key** (`Resolution.ConfigHash`, `internal/daemon/routes_resolve.go:30-37`), so one JSON name means two things on two surfaces. Both the resolver (`routes_resolve.go:25-29`) and the plugin (`plugin/opencode/mcpx/daemon.ts:771-775`, which reads the key from the file *name* and ignores the field) already code around it, so renaming the info-file field breaks no in-repo reader. `docs/plugin-discovery.md:66-76` records the collision and defers the rename to this issue.
- ~~**A daemon started with `MCPX_SOCKET` answers `/v1/resolve` with that socket for every directory** (reported by the plugin work, not re-verified). `socketPath` honours the env before the key, so the answer is right for the daemon itself and wrong for every other directory it is asked about.~~
  - *Moved to #88* (#181 collision 8): the precedence of `MCPX_SOCKET` versus the info file is socket resolution, which #88 owns. Verified there at 05c78b2 and narrower than stated: a directory whose daemon has a record gets the record's socket (`routes_resolve.go:112-119`); the override leaks only into the no-record branches.
- **The schema cache is not invalidated when an entry gains a field** (reported, one instance fixed). Adding `Annotations` parsed cleanly against an old cache and left it empty, so the destructive-call policy never fired. #58 bumped `cacheVersion`; the trap remains for the next additive field. Derive the version from the cached type's shape, or fail closed on a missing field.
  - *Still true at 05c78b2.* `cacheVersion = 4` is bumped by hand (`internal/daemon/registry.go:102-106`) and compared on load (`:217`). #187 (one content-addressed cache mechanism, #181 collision 12) owns the layout, keys and eviction of the *new* caches; this item is the existing schema cache's versioning and stays here unless #187 decides to absorb existing caches (its open question).
- **`mcpx status` does not autostart a daemon** (reported). Possibly intended -- status should not change what it reports -- but tests had to run `ls` first to get a socket. Decide and document.
  - *Still true at 05c78b2, still undocumented.* `CmdStatus` pings and prints `daemon: not running` (`{"running": false}` with `--json`) without calling `EnsureDaemon` (`internal/cli/commands.go:1107-1119`). Note it dials the recomputed socket, so "not running" can also be #88's false negative. Recommendation: keep it non-starting (a status query that starts what it reports on is a Heisenberg bug) and say so in `mcpx status --help` and `docs/`.

(Reported earlier and **no longer reproducible**: `mcpx --json status` exiting non-zero with no daemon. It exits 0.)

No real choice on any item: each has one fix, stated with it. The exec-workdir rework in #69/#70/#73 did not touch any of them (workdirs are evicted by count in `pruneWorkDirs`, `internal/runner/runner.go:808`; their future is #187's).

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** S (three independent small fixes) · **Impact** low-med -- none is user-visible on its own; each misleads the next person debugging which daemon answered, or lets a cache silently hide a field.

Related: #88 (socket resolution; owns the `MCPX_SOCKET` item, collision 8), #187 (cache mechanism, collision 12), #183 (in flight: the `ForConfig` comment in the same `paths.go` describes keying that #56 removed -- the same "which digest is which" confusion as item 1), #103 #104 #107 (the new caches #187 governs).

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.
