## Finding

`pkgs/mcpx/docs/opencode-plugin-v2.md` line 137 — the implementation map for the #1858 v2 plugin port — prescribes the wrong re-export path for the v2 `daemon.ts`:

> | `daemon.ts` | re-export of `../../mcpx/daemon.ts` | core reuse |

The row describes `plugin/opencode/v2/daemon.ts`. From that directory, `../../mcpx/daemon.ts` resolves to `pkgs/mcpx/plugin/mcpx/daemon.ts`, which does not exist. The daemon module actually lives at `pkgs/mcpx/plugin/opencode/mcpx/daemon.ts`, so from `plugin/opencode/v2/` the correct relative path is `../mcpx/daemon.ts`. A v2 file copied from this row fails to resolve its import.

## Evidence

- Source PR: #2457 (merged b1160f43d) added the doc as #1858 groundwork. CodeRabbit comment 4418944915 raised exactly this on the PR, with the one-line fix; it received no reply and the doc merged unchanged.
- Verified live on main 8f24c7db5a2a3412bb19262eb12f2cf86c5d6a3b: line 137 still reads `../../mcpx/daemon.ts`; `git ls-tree` shows `pkgs/mcpx/plugin/` contains only `opencode/`, and the daemon module is at `pkgs/mcpx/plugin/opencode/mcpx/daemon.ts` (with `daemon.test.ts` beside it).

## Why it matters

This doc is the map the #1858 rewrite (and its SET-REMAINDER #2841) is implemented from. A wrong path in the map becomes a broken import in the first v2 file that follows it, discovered later and further from the source.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Line 137 (and any other row in the map with a relative path) resolves to a file that exists in the tree at the commit it lands on.
- [ ] The v2 implementation, when it lands, can copy the row verbatim and have the import resolve.

## Finding

`pkgs/mcpx/docs/examples.md` presents four scripts as runnable as-is — "Four scripts you can run as they are… Run them from `pkgs/mcpx`" — but from a normal checkout none of the commands can produce the shown output, because the `demo` server the scripts call (`tools.demo.echo`, etc.) is never configured for the reader.

The only place the fixture is set up is the test harness: `pkgs/mcpx/examples/examples_test.go` (~lines 133–137) builds `internal/testsupport/fakemcp` and writes a temporary configuration mapping `mcpServers.demo` to the compiled fixture binary (`configTemplate … "demo": { "command": "FAKE" }`). Running an example directly does neither, so a reader following the page gets a missing-server failure instead of the printed output the page promises.

## Evidence

- Source PR: #2454 (merged 1caefdb81) added the examples page. Codex P2 comment 4418832039 raised exactly this on the PR; it received no reply and the page merged unchanged.
- Verified live on main 8f24c7db5a2a3412bb19262eb12f2cf86c5d6a3b: `docs/examples.md` contains no fixture/build/configuration instructions (its only "fixture" mentions are lines 4 and 146–147, describing the test), while `examples/examples_test.go:133-137` performs the setup privately.
- Renaming the namespace to an existing server is not a fix: the examples depend on the fixture's specific tools and deterministic responses.

## Why it matters

The page's whole premise — checked-in expected output, "an example that stops being true fails the build" — is about trustworthiness for a first-time reader. As written, the first thing a new user tries does not work, and nothing on the page tells them why or what to run first.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `docs/examples.md` (or a page it links before the first command) documents how to build the `fakemcp` fixture and configure the `demo` namespace so the four commands produce the shown output from a clean checkout.
- [ ] The documented steps are the same setup `examples/examples_test.go` performs (same fixture binary, same `mcpServers.demo` shape), so the page and the test cannot drift apart silently — or the page generates its instructions from that setup.
- [ ] Following the page from a clean checkout reproduces `demo.echo: hello from a script` for the first example.

body:
## Finding

`pkgs/mcpx/docs/faq.md` (the "is it safe?" answer, lines 47–48 on main) misdescribes mcpx's script permission profiles:

> `script.permissions` defaults to `all`, and the narrower profiles (`net`, `read`, `read-net`, `strict`) apply only on Deno: bun and node run with the user's own authority whatever you ask for.

That is not what the code does, in two ways:

1. **Node does enforce at least one narrower profile.** `pkgs/mcpx/internal/defaults/defaults.json` defines `readnet` / `read-net` with node flags `--permission --allow-fs-read=*` (verified on main). A reader who trusts the FAQ believes a restriction that exists is ineffective.
2. **A profile with no flags for a runtime is refused, not silently run with full authority.** In `pkgs/mcpx/internal/runner/runtimes.go`, the permission resolution returns a `refusal` when a named profile defines no flags for the selected runtime kind (~line 276), with the message at ~line 311: "permission profile %q defines no flags for %s, so %s cannot enforce it". So e.g. asking bun for `read-net` fails loudly rather than running unenforced.

## Evidence

- Source PR: #2454 (merged 1caefdb81) added the FAQ. Codex P2 comment 4418832041 raised exactly this on the PR; it received no reply and the text merged unchanged.
- Verified live on main 8f24c7db5a2a3412bb19262eb12f2cf86c5d6a3b: `faq.md:47-48` carries the sentence verbatim; `defaults.json` carries the node `readnet`/`read-net` flags; `runtimes.go` carries the refusal path.
- Tests in `pkgs/mcpx/internal/e2e/permissions_test.go` cover refusal of unsupported profiles and Node's write restriction (per the PR review).

## Why it matters

This is the safety answer of the FAQ — the page a user reads to decide how much authority a script gets. Telling them supported restrictions are ineffective (and that unsupported ones silently run at full authority, when they actually refuse) inverts the real risk picture in both directions.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The FAQ's "is it safe?" answer describes the actual behavior: which profiles are enforced on which runtimes (including node's `read-net`/`readnet` flags), and that a profile with no flags for the chosen runtime is refused with an error rather than run unenforced.
- [ ] The corrected text is checked against `internal/defaults/defaults.json` and `internal/runner/runtimes.go` at the commit it lands on.
- [ ] No other page repeats the "apply only on Deno / full authority whatever you ask" claim (grep the docs for it).

body:
# github-backup(inventory): a null `repositoryOwner` is silently read as "this owner has no repos" — reconcile then drops the owner's mirrors from plan.json and MANIFEST.json and exits 0

## Evidence (verified this run, 2026-10-31)

`infra/github-backup/bin/ghb_common.py`, `inventory_owner()`:

```python
data = json.loads(r.stdout)
conn = (data.get("data", {}).get("repositoryOwner") or {}).get("repositories")
if conn is None:
    return repos
```

Any successful (`gh` exit 0) GraphQL response whose `repositoryOwner` is `null` — the owner was renamed, the token lost visibility of the org (e.g. SAML enforcement, the exact failure mode config.json already records as a GAP for `vertexinc`), or the org is otherwise not visible — returns an empty repo list for that owner, indistinguishable from an owner that genuinely has zero repositories. The `errors` channel in `inventory()` is never populated for this case.

Laptop probe (real `ghb_common.py` from main `7d2f1f77`, sha256 `2eb427df…` matching the sandbox clone; `run()` stubbed to return canned GraphQL payloads; probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneA-ghb-inventory/` on the laptop):

```
control-visible:   repos=['some-owner/repo1'] errors={}
null-owner:        repos=[] errors={}                      <- the defect
gh-failure:        repos=[] errors={'some-owner': 'gh api graphql failed for some-owner: boom'}
null-repositories: repos=[] errors={}                      <- same defect, repositories field null
```

The control cases behave: a visible owner inventories normally, and a `gh` CLI failure raises and is recorded per-owner. Only the null-owner/null-repositories shapes are swallowed.

## Why it matters

`reconcile.py` is the system's correctness floor (its own docstring: inventory errors per owner are reported, and "Exit code is non-zero only on owner-level inventory failure, so the timer unit surfaces it"). With this defect, one invisible owner causes the weekly reconcile to:

1. overwrite `plan.json` with none of that owner's repos (they surface only as "no longer planned (mirrors kept on disk)", which reads as an intentional removal);
2. regenerate `MANIFEST.json` from the shrunken plan — `manifest.py` iterates the plan only — so the disaster-recovery source of truth silently stops recording mirrors that still exist on disk;
3. exit `0` (`return 1 if errors else 0`, and `errors` is empty), so the systemd unit reports success.

A backup system whose inventory layer cannot distinguish "owner has nothing" from "owner could not be seen" will eventually un-plan a live part of the estate and call it success.

Distinct from: #3219 (the drainer's ack path), #3215 (the umbrella system issue, which tracks the system as a whole, not this defect).

## Acceptance criteria

- `inventory_owner()` treats a null/missing `repositoryOwner` (and a null/missing `repositories` connection) in an otherwise successful GraphQL response as an owner-level error: it raises (or otherwise records an error for that owner in `inventory()`), naming the owner and the shape received.
- A legitimately empty owner (connection present, zero nodes, no next page) still inventories as zero repos with no error.
- Reconcile surfaces that failure the way its docstring promises: the owner appears in the report's inventory-errors section and the run exits non-zero, without overwriting `plan.json` in a way that drops the failed owner's previously planned repos (or, if plan.json is still written, the report makes the drop's cause unmistakable).
- Regression tests cover: null `repositoryOwner`, null `repositories`, a GraphQL response carrying a top-level `errors` field, and the empty-but-visible owner control.

## Finding (from PR review, unaddressed)

On PR #2549, Codex raised a P2 that was never fixed and never replied to:

> **Apply target time windows before expanding route candidates** — For the checked-in `background` route, object targets carry `window` gates referencing `experimental.model_route_windows`, but this normalization discards those gates and the resolver never evaluates them. Consequently, time-windowed route targets are expanded outside their windows.
> — chatgpt-codex-connector[bot], 2026-10-30T03:48:34Z

Evidence:
- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/2549
- Comment: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/2549#discussion_r4420257675 (bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs:318)
- No-response evidence: the comment thread has no reply, and no open issue covers it (searched open issues for route-proxy / window on 2026-10-31).

## Still live on current main (verified 2026-10-31)

`bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs` on current main contains no window handling at all (searching the file for `window` returns zero hits), and `normalizeTarget` still reduces an object target to its model ref and variant map:

```js
const normalizeTarget = (t) => {
  if (typeof t === "string") return { ...parseTargetRef(t), variantMap: null };
  if (t && typeof t.model === "string")
    return { ...parseTargetRef(t.model), variantMap: t.variants || null };
  return null;
};
```

Any `window` gate on a configured target is discarded at normalization, so time-windowed targets are eligible at all hours.

**Caveat for triage:** if the window-gates feature was deliberately retired in the proxy redesign, then the live defect is not the proxy but the stale checked-in config that still carries `window` gates — triage decides which side is wrong (restore window evaluation in the proxy, or remove the dead gates from the config) and closes accordingly.

## Acceptance criteria

- Triage records which is true: windows are a live feature (proxy must evaluate them) or a retired one (config must stop carrying them).
- If live: targets are only expanded inside their configured windows; a test pins an out-of-window exclusion.
- If retired: the checked-in config no longer carries `window` gates, and the removal is noted where the feature was documented.
- Or: resolve by a documented decision on this issue.

body:
## Bug: github-backup drainer acks webhook events even when the fetch failed or the mirror is missing — the freshness signal is silently dropped

**Where:** `infra/github-backup/bin/drain_queue.py` (landed in #3214; system tracked by #3215)

### Evidence

In `main()` (drain_queue.py:56-64), the per-repo fetch result is discarded:

```python
if repo in planned:
    fetch_mirrors.fetch_repo(root, repo, state)   # return value ignored
    fetched.append(repo)                          # reported as fetched either way
```

`fetch_repo` (`bin/fetch_mirrors.py:23-42`) returns `"ok"`, `"fail"` (git fetch non-zero), or `"missing"` (no valid mirror at the path). The drainer:

1. Appends **every** event id to `ack` up front (drain_queue.py:45) and POSTs the full ack list to the Worker at the end (drain_queue.py:67) — including events whose fetch just failed or whose mirror is missing. The Worker deletes them from KV (`worker/src/index.js` `/queue/ack`), so the event can never be redelivered.
2. Sets the 15-minute per-repo coalesce stamp `drain_last::<repo>` (drain_queue.py:52) before the fetch, so even a hypothetical redelivery inside the window would be skipped.
3. Writes nothing to `fetch.log` for the failure (only *unplanned* repos get a fetch.log line, drain_queue.py:61-64). The daily `fetch_mirrors.py` main loop logs failures; the drain path bypasses that logging entirely.
4. Prints the repo in the run summary's `fetched` list regardless of outcome, so the systemd journal shows a successful drain.

### Reproduced (laptop probe, main @ 96d13492)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-drainack/probe.py` drives the real `drain_queue.main()` with a stub Worker returning one push event for a planned repo and `fetch_repo` stubbed to return `"fail"`:

```
{"events": 1, "fetched": ["owner/repo"]}
ack calls: [('/queue/ack', {'ids': ['ev1']})]
fetch.log exists: False
state keys: ['drain_last::owner/repo']
VERDICT: event acked despite fetch failure: True
```

The `"missing"` return takes the same code path (return value ignored), so a planned repo whose clone previously failed also loses its events until the weekly reconcile notices the missing mirror.

### Why it matters

The webhook layer exists to keep mirrors fresh between weekly reconciles (Worker header: "Events are a freshness signal only; the weekly reconcile sweep is the correctness floor"). A transient fetch failure (network blip, GitHub 5xx, auth hiccup) currently converts into up-to-a-week of silent staleness for that repo: the event is deleted, the failure is in no log, and the run summary claims success. The correctness floor still catches the *data* eventually, but the failure is invisible — the opposite of this system's own observability pattern elsewhere (fetch_mirrors exits non-zero on 3-day chronic failures precisely so systemd surfaces them).

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Drain only acks an event for a planned repo when its fetch returned `"ok"`; on `"fail"`/`"missing"` the event stays queued for the next drain (or is acked only after an explicit retry policy), and the coalesce stamp is not advanced on failure.
- [ ] Fetch failures/missing mirrors on the drain path are appended to `fetch.log` in the same format the daily pass uses, and the run summary distinguishes fetched vs failed repos.
- [ ] A test (stub Worker + stub fetch, as in the probe) covers: success → acked; failure → not acked + logged; unplanned repo → acked + noted for reconcile (current intended behavior preserved).

body:
## Summary

The `log_sync` batch-collection tests race the production idle grace against wall-clock pacing from a second thread, and intermittently fail the `pkgs/id` check phase — which gates every NixOS system build (`id-web` → `unit-id-primary.service` → system toplevel). The assertions are correct; the timing margin is not.

Found while verifying the fix for #3160: with the five failures from that issue fixed, a `nix build .#id-web` check phase failed on exactly these two tests (1974 passed; 2 failed), and a local full-suite run failed one of them.

## The failing tests

- `log_sync::tests::test_batch_collection_coalesces_paced_arrivals` — batch length 2, expected 3 ("paced arrivals share one batch", src/log_sync.rs:1030)
- `log_sync::tests::test_batch_collection_refused_stream_ends_at_the_total_cap` — batch length 1, expected 256 ("a refused stream ends the batch at the total-arrival cap", src/log_sync.rs:1119)

A third sibling, `test_batch_collection_grace_restarts_on_each_arrival`, shares the design and the exposure.

## Mechanism

`collect_batch` (src/log_sync.rs:554) waits out an idle `BATCH_GRACE` of **5 ms** (src/log_sync.rs:86) for the next arrival, polling every 250 µs. The tests pace arrivals every **2 ms** from a spawned thread. Any scheduler delay over 5 ms on either thread — routine on a loaded 16-core build machine (observed at load 12–24 with parallel builds running) — splits the batch or ends it early. Measured behaviour tracks load exactly:

- Solo re-runs at load ~12: 26/26 passes across the three pacing tests.
- Solo re-runs at load 20+: `refused_stream` failed 4 of 6.
- Full-suite runs under load: at least one of the two fails most of the time.

## Prior attempt

ce8305622 ("fix(id): deterministic log_sync pacing & world_doctor mock", for #187) replaced the test-side first-arrival spin with `blocking_recv`. That removed one race but not this one: the pacer/grace wall-clock race is still live.

## Impact

The id check phase sits on the critical path of every system build, so this is a load-dependent coin flip on every deploy, unrelated to whatever change is being shipped.

## Suggested direction

Not prescribed, but one clean shape: give `collect_batch` an internal grace parameter (production call passes `BATCH_GRACE`; tests pass a generous grace), so the coalescing / grace-restart / cap behaviour is asserted without a 2 ms vs 5 ms wall-clock margin. The production 5 ms tuning stays exactly as is. These tests should not be excluded or ignored — what they assert is the ingest batching contract.

## Acceptance criteria

- The three pacing-sensitive `log_sync` batch-collection tests pass deterministically under load (repeated full-suite runs at load 20+), not only in solo re-runs.
- The fix removes the wall-clock race (deterministic synchronisation or an injected/controllable grace) rather than widening the 5 ms grace or the 2 ms pacing as a band-aid, unless the issue discussion records why a margin change is the right fix.
- The `pkgs/id` check phase passes with these tests included — no check-phase exclusions.

title: laptop-autocommit never pulls and swallows push failures: laptop primaries wedge silently (2076 behind)
body:
## laptop-autocommit never pulls and swallows push failures — laptop primaries wedge silently

Found during the 2026-10-31 hatch-autocommit wedge repair (dezren39/hatch-personal#10), where the sandbox script wedged via rebase-pull. The laptop's Nix-built `laptop-autocommit` (`nixos/home/laptop-autocommit.sh`, from #1723) has a worse variant of the same disease:

- Its whole sync logic was: `git add -u` -> commit -> `push` only if ahead, with failure swallowed (`|| true`).
- **It never pulls at all.** Once a laptop repo diverged from origin, every push was rejected non-fast-forward, invisibly, forever, while the unit showed success every minute.

### Evidence

- Laptop `hatch-personal` primary at discovery: **6 ahead / 2076 behind** origin/main (the originating repair brief had the numbers transposed; verified live). It had stopped receiving origin content — including merged PRs — while the sandbox side kept publishing.
- The one-time repair merged origin in (merge commit f00e1e23a in hatch-personal; pool-change-ledger append-vs-append resolved as chronological union) and pushed to 0/0. The other two swept repos (`~/hatch`, `~/.openclaw`) share the same exposure.
- The sandbox twin wedged the same week via `pull --rebase` + abort + exit 0 (hatch-personal#10).

### Fix

Drew's directive (2026-10-31): primaries merge-pull main and push back, stopping only on real conflicts. The fix PR rewrites the sync section to fetch -> merge-pull `--no-rebase --autostash` when behind -> push; real conflicts capture conflicted paths by name, abort, restore the autostash, and exit 1; rejected pushes exit 1. Scratch-tested both paths. Tracked-only scope and the daily untracked review are unchanged.

Deploy note: the script is baked into the Nix store via `writeShellScriptBin (readFile ...)`, so the fix takes effect on the next home-manager/NixOS switch after merge; until then the running binary is the old logic (primaries are 0/0 post-repair, so exposure is future divergence only).

body:
## Summary

Five `pkgs/id` lib tests fail on current main. Because the NixOS system toplevel depends on the id service (`id-web` package → `unit-id-primary.service` → `system-units` → `etc` → toplevel), these failures gate `nix build` of the whole system and are currently blocking a deploy. Verified against the failed build log on the laptop (`/nix/var/log/nix/drvs/d7/9c2azdf6l2km1gb0n3yzb9qqwh9s87-id-0.1.0.drv.bz2`): **1958 passed; 5 failed; 6 ignored**.

Drew has ruled: fix the tests properly — no check-phase exclusions.

## The 5 failures, by root cause

### 1. The no-SQLite guard vs the dev-only rusqlite dependency

`store_traits::tests::test_the_lock_has_no_sqlite_with_logsync_wired` (src/store_traits.rs)

```
Cargo.lock names rusqlite: SQLite is back in the build (see vendor/README.md)
```

The guard (added 2026-10-12, fedb1644e, with the vendored p2panda-sync) asserts the raw `Cargo.lock` text names none of sqlx/sqlite/rusqlite/libsqlite3-sys: p2panda-sync's store dependency defaults to SQLite via sqlx, the vendored copy turns that default off, and the shipped store is redb. On 2026-10-30, b3421ef18 (#2276, bridge sync PoC) added `rusqlite` 0.32 (bundled) as a **dev-dependency** — SQLite for the PoC's DO-shaped hosted store, used by dev targets only, never shipped. A raw lockfile scan cannot tell a dev-only edge from a shipped one, so the guard now false-fires.

Fix: make the guard inspect the resolved dependency graph instead of the raw lock text — a SQLite-family package is acceptable only when every package that depends on it is either another SQLite-family package or this package itself, and this package's manifest must declare SQLite names only under dev-dependencies. The guard keeps its teeth (it still fails if rusqlite enters the shipped graph through any other dependent, or if the manifest moves it out of dev-dependencies) and keeps the p2panda-sync presence + vendored p2panda-store `default-features = false` assertions. The PoC stays.

### 2. Fuel budgets left stale by the pf.Screen migration

`sandbox::tests::checked_in_examples_stay_within_fuel_budgets` (src/sandbox.rs)

```
roc-counter view: used 260269 fuel, budget 100000
roc-counter layout: used 323425 fuel, budget 100000
```

`commands::world::tests::measure_reports_fuel_per_call_kind_for_a_checked_in_module` (src/commands/world.rs)

```
assertion failed: report["worst_call_percent_of_limit"].as_f64().unwrap() < 1.0
```

720eb5770 (#565) migrated roc-counter to render through `pf.Screen` (boxed 20x3 screen) instead of a bare text view. Rendering a structured screen genuinely costs more wasmtime fuel than returning a string; the checked-in budgets were never re-baselined (old View/Layout baselines were 1,327/1,337). The sandbox test's own failure message prescribes the fix: "re-baseline deliberately: update the table and say why in the commit."

Fix: regenerate the roc-counter baselines/budgets with the shipped `print_fuel_baseline` generator (rule: baseline +25%, rounded up to the next 100,000 → View 400,000 on baseline 260,269; Layout 500,000 on baseline 323,425). The measure test does not read the table — it has its own bound (worst call < 1% of the 10,000,000 fuel limit, i.e. < 100,000 fuel, the same stale assumption). Update it consistently with the re-baselined envelope: the worst roc-counter call is now Layout at 323,425 (3.23%), and the largest per-call budget the table allows this module is 500,000 (5%), so the assertion becomes worst_call_percent_of_limit < 5.0 with a comment tying it to the budget table.

### 3. world_ws tests vs the Screen capability model

`web::world_ws::tests::browser_websocket_can_compile_install_and_run_roc_sources` (src/web/world_ws.rs)

```
compile failed: main.roc imports Screen, which this world does not allow
(grant it with `id world caps --grant Screen`; a capability ceiling may also exclude it)
```

examples/roc-counter/main.roc now imports `pf.Screen`, but the test world is a fresh `WorldCore` whose capability ledger has granted nothing, so the compile gate (`world_compile::check_imports` against the ledger's effective list) correctly refuses. Fix: grant the Screen capability to the test world (`world.update_caps`) before compiling — the same admin path the product exposes — not by weakening the ceiling check.

`web::world_ws::tests::browser_websocket_can_upload_and_run_a_roc_module` (src/web/world_ws.rs)

```
left:  "{\"kind\":\"screen\",\"version\":1,\"width\":20,\"height\":3,\"rows\":[\"+-counter----------+\",\"| count=0          |\",\"+------------------+\"]}"
right: "count=0"
```

The module's view now returns a screen frame instead of bare text. Fix: update the snapshot/event expectations to the screen frame and assert the count row content (`count=0`, then `count=1` after the `inc` input).

## Verification

- `cargo test` (release, lib): the 5 named tests, then the full lib suite.
- `nix build .#id-web` from the repo root flake (the package the system consumes) — check phase must pass end to end.

## Acceptance criteria

- All five named lib tests pass on current main (`store_traits` no-SQLite guard, and the remaining four grouped in the issue body), with the pkgs/id suite back to 0 failures.
- The no-SQLite guard still fails when a SQLite-family package enters the shipped (non-dev) dependency graph — the graph-based guard keeps its teeth, per the issue's fix direction.
- `nix build` of the id package / NixOS system toplevel passes the check phase with no check-phase exclusions (Drew's ruling in the issue).

## Finding
PR #2149's collector persists the charges surfaced-keys state at collection time — before the feed is published and before the laptop transfer (`scripts/push-fleet-feed.sh` collects first, transfers later). If publication or transfer fails, those unmatched charges are permanently suppressed: the keys say they were shown, the next collection omits them from `chargesAttention`, and they never reach the attention strip. Codex flagged this P2 on the PR (comment 4409381655); it merged unchanged and is still on main.

## Evidence
- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/2149 (merged, 7d064e5f, #1057)
- Current main: `pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/collect-fleet-feed.ts:451` — surfaced state `writeFile` inside the collection block; the feed itself is only written at :646, and delivery happens outside the collector entirely.

## Why it matters
Exactly-once surfacing is only correct if "surfaced" means "delivered". As written, one failed transfer silently deletes operator notifications about unrecognized charges — the failure mode the strip exists to prevent.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Surfaced keys are persisted only after the feed carrying them is successfully published/delivered, or pending keys survive a failed publication (e.g. written with the feed and confirmed on the next successful run).
- [ ] A simulated failed delivery leaves the charges surfacing on the next collection.

Amounts are the matcher's dedupe key; a systematically under-recorded amount both misstates spending and doubles the charge in the feed.

body:
## Finding
PR #2149's Gmail charge producer turns two kinds of NOT-a-charge mail into charge candidates:
1. **Declined/failed purchase alerts** — a subject like "Your $20.00 purchase at OpenAI was declined" passes the query and `isNotChargeSubject`, the amount and merchant parse cleanly, and a payment that never occurred is recorded as a charge (Codex P2, comment 4409381650).
2. **Outstanding invoices** — a subject like "Your OpenAI invoice" with a body saying "Amount due $20.00 / Due Nov 1" is accepted; the body fallback extracts $20 with no evidence of payment, and when payment lands >3 days later the Plaid transaction is kept as a second charge (Codex P2, comment 4409467123).

Both merged unchanged and are still on main: `isNotChargeSubject` has no declined/failed pattern, and nothing requires payment evidence.

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/2149 (merged, 7d064e5f, #1057)

## Why it matters
The producer's stated discipline is "never guessed at" — but declined and merely-due amounts are guesses that a charge occurred, and they flow into matched rows and the once-only attention strip as real spending.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Subjects/bodies indicating a declined or failed purchase produce no candidate (counted as skipped).
- [ ] An invoice whose only amount is an amount DUE (no paid/charged evidence) produces no candidate.
- [ ] Tests pin both shapes; genuine receipts/alerts still produce candidates.

The AI providers the hub tracks (Anthropic, OpenAI, …) live in `extractQuotaPools()` instead, so their charges can never match: an `ANTHROPIC` transaction always surfaces as an "unrecognized SaaS/AI charge" attention flag even though the hub already tracks that provider. Codex flagged this P2 on the PR (comment 4409381644); it merged unchanged and is still on main.

## Evidence
- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/2149 (merged, 7d064e5f, #1057)
- Current main: `pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/collect-fleet-feed.ts:435-437` — `matchCharges(candidates, (saas ?? []).map((s) => ({ name: s.name })))`.

## Why it matters
The attention strip's purpose is surfacing UNKNOWN charges. Flooding it with the fleet's best-known providers trains operators to ignore it — and every surfaced key is persisted, so the misclassification is sticky.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The matching catalog includes the hub's AI quota providers and their aliases (from the quota-pools extraction) alongside the SaaS services.
- [ ] A test shows an Anthropic/OpenAI candidate matching its provider instead of landing in unmatchedSaas.

PR #2148's auto-format workflow nightly sweep builds its file list with a `while` loop whose body is `[[ -n "$f" && -f "$f" ]] && printf …`. The nightly sweep is the backstop that keeps formatting drift from accumulating; a deleted file late in the alphabet silently disables it for that night with a red run nobody will connect to a deletion.

title: mcpx(cache): Scan counts a file entry's lease file as an entry — Prune can delete the live lease and strip the pin from an in-use entry

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/mcpx/internal/cache`'s `Scan` treats a file entry's lease file as a cache entry in its own right. A lease for a directory entry lives *inside* the entry (invisible to a scan of the parent), but a lease for a single-file entry lives *beside* it, named `<entry>.lease-<random>` (`leaseLocation`, cache.go:222-231). `Scan` (cache.go:265-310) only skips names starting with the bare lease prefix `.lease-` (cache.go:276) or `.tmp-` — a beside-file lease name starts with the *entry's* name, so it passes the skip, passes a nil `match`, and is returned as an `Entry` with `Leased: false`.

Consequences, all in the mechanism whose core promise is "eviction never removes a leased entry … the lease is what makes that safe" (cache.go:14-17):

- `List` / `mcpx cache` and every eviction accounting count phantom entries: a leased file entry reports as two entries, and its size/count budget is charged for the lease file too.
- Worse, `Prune`/`Evict` can select the lease file itself as a victim (it is not `keep`, and `Leased()` on the lease file's own path finds no `<leasefile>.lease-*`, so the #2566-finding-3 recheck in `removeAll`, cache.go:349-361, also passes) and delete it — silently stripping the pin from a live, in-use entry, which the next eviction pass can then delete mid-run.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `69b23978`)

Verbatim-copy probe on the laptop (cache.go sha256 `2782f988…` identical in both clones; probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-cachelease/` on the laptop):

- `Scan(dir, "kind", 0, nil)` over a directory holding one leased file entry returned **2 entries**: `key="entry.bin" size=7 leased=true` and `key="entry.bin.lease-3358895815" size=0 leased=false`.
- With the lease file aged oldest and the entry newest, `Prune(dir, Limits{MaxEntries: 1}, "", nil)` removed exactly one entry: **`entry.bin.lease-566081972` — the live lease file itself** — leaving the in-use entry unpinned.

The nil-`match` form is not hypothetical: `Cache.List` (cache.go:254) and the runner's `pruneWorkDirs` (internal/runner/runner.go:839-846) both scan with no pattern, and the package documents entries as "either a directory or a single file" (cache.go:8-9) with `Acquire` explicitly supporting file entries (cache.go:195-198). The runner's patterned pruners escape only because their suffix patterns (`.ts`, `.mcpx-entry.ts`) happen not to match a lease suffix.

## Why it matters

The lease is the cache mechanism's only protection against concurrent eviction (#1908, #2566). A scan that cannot tell a lease from an entry both corrupts eviction accounting and can destroy the pin itself, re-opening the exact failure #2566 finding 3 closed (an in-use entry deleted from under a running exec) through the lease file rather than the entry.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Scan` never returns a lease file as an entry: beside-file leases (`<name>.lease-*`) are skipped (or otherwise recognised) regardless of the `match` pattern, including the nil-pattern form.
- [ ] `Prune`/`Evict`/`removeAll` can never delete a lease file; a victim list containing one is impossible, not just rechecked.
- [ ] Regression tests in `internal/cache`: a leased file entry scans as exactly one entry with `Leased: true`, and a prune sized to force a victim leaves the lease file and the entry in place.
- [ ] Existing `internal/cache` and runner tests still pass (laptop or CI).

## Dedup

Distinct from closed #2566 (path traversal in `Remove`, `Put` self-eviction, scan→remove lease TOCTOU recheck): this is lease files being *enumerated as entries* by `Scan`, which neither the traversal validation nor the `removeAll` recheck addresses. Searched open + closed issues for cache/Scan/lease/Prune terms; no existing issue covers it. Parent mechanism: #1908.

body:
## Problem

The plain-text output of `id world list` prints each world name **raw** in a tab-separated, one-row-per-world format. The names come from the host's `worlds` reply over the wire and are accepted by the client with no validation, so a name containing a newline forges an extra row and a tab forges extra columns — the same row-forgery class fixed for peers in #1613 (`plain_field`, `commands/text.rs`) and filed for blob names (#1742) and meta-tags (#1735), but never filed for the world-directory renderer, which uses neither `plain_field` nor the `tokens()` renderer.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `33b6cb36`)

- Rendering: `pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs:677-688` — the non-JSON branch prints `println!("{name}{default_marker}\t{}", if open { "open" } else { "closed" })` with `name` interpolated verbatim.
- Wire receipt accepts anything: `pkgs/id/src/world_net.rs:690-697` — `WorldClient::list_worlds` collects `w["name"].as_str()` from the host's JSON reply with no validation or re-check against `validate_world_name`.
- A conforming current hub does validate at create time (`pkgs/id/src/world_hub.rs:48-63`, `a-z0-9-_` only), so the payload requires a non-conforming, older, compromised, or hand-provisioned host/storage — but the ruling recorded in `commands/text.rs:1-17` (#1613) is that the contract lives at the printer: *a printer never lets a value break row structure*, precisely because a store/host may already hold a value ingest validation could not have cleaned. The `--json` branch (world.rs:668-676, via `directory_json`) is safe.
- Probe (verbatim replication of the format string, python; output in the goal's `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-worldlist/probe.txt`): worlds `lobby`, `evil\nfake\topen`, `a\tb` render as **4 physical lines for 3 worlds** — the second line is a fully-formed forged row `fake\topen` — with tab-field counts `[2, 1, 3, 3]` instead of 2 per row.

## Why it matters

`id world list` plain output is the operator/script surface for the world directory (the JSON shape is the documented machine feed, #812; the plain rows are what terminals and shell pipelines consume). A hostile or merely buggy host can plant a phantom "open" world row in every listing a client prints, or shift the open/closed column — the exact output-forgery pattern #1611/#1613/#1742/#1735 eliminate renderer by renderer. This is the remaining unguarded TSV renderer in `commands/`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A world name (and the default-world marker comparison) in the plain branch of `id world list` renders through `plain_field` (`commands/text.rs`) or an equivalent quoting rule: a name containing `\n`, `\r`, `\t`, or other control characters produces exactly one physical line with exactly 2 tab fields.
- [ ] Names with no structure-breaking character (including ordinary valid world names) render byte-identically to today; the `--json` output is unchanged.
- [ ] Regression tests at the renderer level, mirroring the `commands/text.rs` / peers tests: a name with an embedded newline + forged `<name>\topen` payload produces one line; a tabbed name stays one field.
- [ ] Existing id crate tests still pass (laptop or CI).

## Dedup

Searched open + recently closed issues for world-list / TSV / forgery / `plain_field` / `validate_world_name` terms. #1613 is peers/gossip, #1742 is `list`/`find` blob names, #1735 is meta-tags, #2839 is a `plain_field` trigger-set gap for peers, #2960/#2890 are journal-restore display-name/scope validation in the world engine. None covers the `commands/world.rs` world-directory plain renderer or the `world_net.rs` receipt path.

title: proxy-relay: RELAY_TARGET_PORTS is parsed with bare Number()+filter — invalid entries are silently dropped and hex/scientific spellings are coerced to ports nobody configured

labels.name: status/duplicate
labels.description: Already tracked elsewhere

labels.name: source/creator

body:
# proxy-relay: RELAY_TARGET_PORTS is parsed with bare Number()+filter — invalid entries are silently dropped and hex/scientific spellings are coerced to ports nobody configured

## Evidence (verified this run, main d4279a45)

`bin/proxy-relay.mjs:47-50` parses its target-port list outside the house strict parser:

```js
const TARGET_PORTS = (process.env.RELAY_TARGET_PORTS || '')
  .split(',')
  .map((s) => Number(s.trim()))
  .filter((n) => Number.isInteger(n) && n >= 1 && n <= 65535);
```

Replicating that exact expression (node, this run) shows the failure modes:

| Input | Result |
|---|---|
| `18745,19745` | `[18745, 19745]` (correct) |
| `18745,abc` | `[18745]` — bad entry silently dropped |
| `18745,19745typo` | `[18745]` — typo'd fallback target silently dropped |
| `0x4a39` | `[19001]` — hex spelling coerced to a port nobody configured |
| `1e4` | `[10000]` — scientific spelling coerced |
| `18745.0` | `[18745]` — decimal spelling coerced |
| `99999,18745` | `[18745]` — out-of-range entry silently dropped |

This is exactly the class of bug `bin/proxy-port.mjs` was built to eliminate (#483, #494): its header states a bare parse "silently becomes" a different port, and every other fleet proxy routes its listen port through `parseProxyPort`/`parseAddressPortValue` so a bad value fails at startup naming the variable and its value. The relay's own listen/proxy ports do use the helper (`proxy-relay.mjs:39,55`); only the target list escapes it. The adoption guard in `bin/proxy-port.test.mjs` ("all eight parse sites in the six proxies use the shared helper") enumerates six files and `*_PROXY_PORT` names only, so it cannot see this site — and there is no `bin/proxy-relay.test.mjs`.

## Why it matters

The relay is a raw TCP forwarder whose whole job is trying target ports in order (`preferred` starts at `TARGET_PORTS[0]`, proxy-relay.mjs:57). A typo in the configured list does not fail startup: the relay starts healthy with a silently shortened target list, and the missing fallback target is only discovered when the primary target is down — i.e. at the moment the fallback was needed. A coerced spelling (`0x…`, `1e4`) makes it dial a port that was never configured at all.

## Dedup

Open+closed search 2026-10-31 for `RELAY_TARGET_PORTS` / "proxy-relay target ports" returned no issue. Neighbours are distinct: #483/#494 built the strict helper for listen/address ports; #2823 (open) covers `antigravity-direct`'s bare-`Number()` listen port/timeout, a different file and variable.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every entry of `RELAY_TARGET_PORTS` is validated strictly (decimal integer 1–65535, e.g. via a list parser in `bin/proxy-port.mjs` built on `parseProxyPortValue`); any invalid entry aborts startup with an error naming `RELAY_TARGET_PORTS` and the offending entry — no silent drops, no hex/scientific/decimal coercion.
- [ ] Valid lists (including entries with surrounding spaces, as today) parse unchanged; the "required" error for an absent/empty list stays.
- [ ] New tests (`bin/proxy-relay.test.mjs` or an extension of `bin/proxy-port.test.mjs`) cover: valid list, typo'd entry, hex entry, out-of-range entry, and the all-invalid case; the adoption guard is extended so a future bare-`Number()` port parse in `bin/` is caught.
- [ ] `node --test bin/proxy-port.test.mjs` (and the new tests) pass.

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-b (Lane B), 2026-10-31 run.

title: mcpx(nearmiss): Near is not symmetric — the prefix rule checks only the first argument's length, so Near("abcd","ab") is true while Near("ab","abcd") is false

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Summary

`nearmiss.Near` — the shared "is one name close to another" definition built by #1904 so diagnostics, search and the launcher all agree — is not symmetric: its prefix rule checks only the **first** argument's length, so swapping the arguments changes the answer.

`pkgs/mcpx/internal/nearmiss/nearmiss.go:90-99`:

```go
func Near(a, b string) bool {
	na, nb := Normalize(a), Normalize(b)
	if na == nb {
		return true
	}
	if len(na) > 2 && (strings.HasPrefix(nb, na) || strings.HasPrefix(na, nb)) {
		return true
	}
	return damerau(na, nb) <= 1
}
```

The guard is `len(na) > 2`; `len(nb)` is never checked. When the shorter name is 2 characters or fewer and the distance is more than one edit, the pair is a near miss in one order and not the other.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `5ff5d3cb`)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneA-nearmiss/` ran the package's own test harness against a verbatim copy of `nearmiss.go` (md5 `a3e96e3597912c10a64646c64921a883`, identical on sandbox and laptop):

```text
Near("ab","abcd")=false    Near("abcd","ab")=true
Near("en","entry")=false   Near("entry","en")=true
Near("ab","abcde")=false   Near("abcde","ab")=true
Near("cat","catalog")=true Near("catalog","cat")=true   (control: both names > 2)
```

The package's own test states the intended rule in the other direction only (`nearmiss_test.go:48-49`):

```go
{"cat", "catalog", true}, // prefix rule, both longer than two
{"ab", "abcd", false},    // prefix rule needs length > 2
```

"Both longer than two" is the documented shape — the test just never exercises the swapped pair, so the second case passes while its mirror image returns `true`.

## Why it matters

- `Near` is the one definition three surfaces share (#1904). A relation that depends on argument order reintroduces exactly the drift that issue removed: the same typo is "close" for a caller that passes `(candidate, known)` and not for one that passes `(known, candidate)`.
- The one live caller is the launcher typo guard, `looksLikePlaceholder(name, known)` in `pkgs/mcpx/internal/launcher/template.go:535-538`, which calls `Near(name, p)` — unknown word first. So today a 2-letter prefix of a known placeholder (`@en` for `@entry`, `@he` for `@header`, `@im` for `@import`) is **not** flagged as an unknown-placeholder typo, while the 3-letter `@ent` is — and any future caller that passes the arguments the other way will flag the 2-letter form. The guard's reach should not depend on which side of the call a name sits.
- `Distance` (the other shared relation in the same file) is symmetric, so `Near` disagreeing with itself under argument swap is inconsistent within the package's own contract ("whether one name is close to another", `nearmiss.go:86-89`).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Near(a, b) == Near(b, a)` for the probe matrix above: `Near("ab","abcd")` and `Near("abcd","ab")` give the same answer (per the test's stated rule, `false`: the prefix rule requires the shorter/prefix name to be longer than two characters), and likewise for `("en","entry")` and `("ab","abcde")` in both orders.
- [ ] The fix keys the prefix rule on the prefix (shorter) name's length — or on both names' lengths — not on the first argument alone; equal-after-normalisation and distance-≤1 behaviour are unchanged.
- [ ] Regression tests cover both argument orders for the boundary pairs (the existing `{"ab","abcd",false}` case gains its mirror `{"abcd","ab",false}`, plus a >2 control such as `{"cat","catalog",true}` / `{"catalog","cat",true}`), and the existing nearmiss and launcher test suites pass.
- [ ] Launcher behaviour is unchanged for names longer than two characters: `@ent` is still flagged as a likely `@entry` typo and ordinary words (emails, decorators) are still not flagged.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `nearmiss`, `Near`, `looksLikePlaceholder` and "prefix rule": #1904 (closed) built the shared matcher and is the origin, not a filing of this defect; no open or closed issue covers the asymmetry. Distinct from #2349/#2274/#2009 (REPL find parsing in pkgs/id).

# mcpx: user-facing docs and API/settings text still promise hardlink delivery — no code hardlinks anything since #3046

## Evidence (main `c6e099c9`, verified this run)

PR #3046 (commit `99597566`, fixing #1660) changed `artifacts.Store.PutFile` and `Store.Export` to **copy, never link**, because a blob sharing an inode with a file outside the store could be rewritten in place under its original hash. There is now **no `os.Link` / `Linkname` call anywhere in `pkgs/mcpx` Go code** (grep-verified this run). The code comments inside the two fixed functions say so explicitly:

- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/artifacts/artifacts.go:269-272` (PutFile body): "Copy, never link (#1660)…"
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/artifacts/artifacts.go:554-557` (Export doc): "Always a copy, never a link (#1660)…"

But the surrounding and user-facing text still describes the old hardlink behavior:

- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/artifacts/artifacts.go:223` — PutFile's own doc comment (directly above the fixed function) still says: "A hardlink where the filesystem allows one, a copy where it does not."
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/api/ops_exec.go:43` — the published API description for `artifact_put` says a caller may "send X-Mcpx-Path and have the file hardlinked, which is why handing back a large local file costs an inode rather than a copy."
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/settings/exec.go:84` — the `artifacts.dir` setting's long help says "the files are hardlinked into it rather than copied, so handing back a gigabyte costs an inode."
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/execsvc/execsvc.go:85` — `SharedFs` field doc: "Artifacts are placed there -- hardlinked, not copied"; `:1041` — deliver comment: "hardlinking them into its directory costs an inode and no I/O" (the path it describes calls `Store.Export`, which copies).
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/routes_exec.go:378` — `handleArtifactPut` doc: "the named file is hardlinked instead."
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/cli/exec.go:152` — `localStore` doc: the CLI "can hardlink a blob into an output directory rather than fetching its own copy."
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/cli/commands.go:1093` and `pkgs/mcpx/internal/codegen/emit.go:1507,1534` — generated-client / CLI comments saying the daemon/store hardlinks the named file.
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/artifacts/name.go:121` — `uniquePath` comment: "Removed again so Link can have the name" — there is no Link call left; the reservation is now for the copy in `copyInto`.
- Book docs: `pkgs/mcpx/docs/exec.md:219` ("the store **hardlinks** it"), `:229` ("hardlinked there"), `:284` ("hardlinking them into its directory costs an inode and no I/O"); `pkgs/mcpx/docs/remote.md:127` ("a `{path}` artifact is only hardlinked when…").

## Why it matters

- The settings help and API description are user-facing: they promise O(1)-inode delivery for large local files. Since #3046, handing back a gigabyte costs a full copy (time + disk) — a caller sizing timeouts/disk on the documented promise is misled.
- The stale text also inverts the safety story of #1660: a reader of `PutFile`'s doc comment or `docs/exec.md` would believe blobs still share inodes with outside files — exactly the mutation-under-hash hazard #1660 closed — and could design on top of that assumption (e.g. editing an exported file expecting the store to see it, or vice versa).
- `PutFile`'s doc comment contradicts the comment inside its own body, so the package disagrees with itself on the same screen.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every "hardlink" claim in `pkgs/mcpx` Go source (code comments, API operation descriptions, settings help) and in `pkgs/mcpx/docs/exec.md` / `docs/remote.md` describes the actual post-#3046 behavior: a copy into the store / into the delivery directory, never a shared inode.
- [ ] Wording preserves the reason where it is load-bearing (#1660: a blob must not share an inode with a file outside the store), so a future reader does not "optimize" the copy back into a link.
- [ ] A guard exists so the drift cannot silently return: e.g. a test or lint step that fails if `hardlink` reappears in these surfaces without an accompanying `os.Link` in the artifacts path (or an equivalent doc-current test in the style of `TestStoryDocumentIsCurrent`).
- [ ] `go test ./internal/artifacts ./internal/api ./internal/settings -count=1` passes (run on a dev machine / CI, per `pkgs/mcpx/internal/AGENTS.md` — package-scoped, not `./...`).

Dedup: searched open + closed issues for "hardlink" this run — only #1660 (closed, the behavior fix itself) and #1908 (unrelated cache design) match; no issue tracks the leftover text.

body:
# id(find/search/show/peek): a zero count is accepted everywhere — `--first 0`/`--last 0` report 'no matches found' for queries that do match, and `peek --lines 0` renders a preview with no content lines

## Problem

Every count-taking flag in the find/search/show/peek family accepts `0`, and `0` silently produces an empty or content-free result that blames the query instead of the limit:

- **CLI** (`pkgs/id/src/cli.rs`): `first`/`last` are plain `Option<usize>` with `num_args = 0..=1` (e.g. :727/:730) and peek's `lines` is a plain `usize` (:783) — no range validation anywhere, so `id find --first 0 config` and `id peek --lines 0 readme` parse cleanly.
- **REPL** (`pkgs/id/src/repl/runner.rs`): `parse_find_args` (--first branch :672-686, --last :687-701) and `parse_peek_args` (the duplicated --first/--last :1190-1213, --lines :1217-1224) accept a parsed `0` exactly like any other number.
- **The limit itself** (`pkgs/id/src/commands/find.rs:137-145`, `SearchOptions::apply`; REPL copy `apply_search_options` at runner.rs:987+): `first = Some(0)` is `take(0)` and `last = Some(0)` is `skip(len - 0)` — both yield an empty match list.
- **The handlers then misreport it**: CLI `find.rs:253` bails `no matches found for: <query>` and the REPL handlers print the same line (runner.rs:750, :811, :863, :911) — a user whose query *does* match is told it doesn't, with no hint the zero limit emptied the list.
- **Peek renders nothing**: `print_peek_lines` (runner.rs:1278+) with `lines = 0` takes the `total_lines <= n * 2` false branch for any non-empty file, prints the banner plus `... (N more lines)` and `... (N lines above)` and zero content lines — a "preview" containing no preview.

## Verified this run (2026-10-31, main `1f8ab4f6`)

Probe compiled and run on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-zero/` there; the `--first`/`--last` parse branches, the `SearchOptions::apply` limiting, and the `print_peek_lines` head/tail logic copied verbatim from `runner.rs`/`find.rs`; sandbox copies md5 `ee82b58f` runner.rs, `b64b2ede` find.rs):

- Control `["report", "--first", "2"]` → `first=Some(2)`, apply over `[1,2,3]` = `[1, 2]` ✓
- `["report", "--first", "0"]` → `first=Some(0)`, apply over `[1,2,3]` = `[]` → handler prints `no matches found for: report`
- `["report", "--last", "0"]` → `last=Some(0)`, apply over `[1,2,3]` = `[]`
- peek lines core with `n=0`, 10-line content → banner + `... (10 more lines)` + `... (10 lines above)`, content lines shown = **0 of 10**

## Why it matters

This is the silent-reinterpretation class this REPL keeps producing (#2009 non-numeric values becoming queries, #3029 --first+--last discarding --last), one step earlier: the value parses *successfully*, so nothing looks wrong, yet the answer is empty for a reason the output actively misstates. `0` is the most likely fat-finger/variable-substitution value (`--first $N` with `N` unset-ish or computed as 0 in a script), and scripts driving the CLI get a hard `no matches found` error (bail at find.rs:253) for files that exist.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A zero count is refused with a message naming the flag at every entry point — CLI `find`/`search`/`show`/`peek` (clap range validation or an explicit check) and REPL `find`/`search`/`show`/`peek` — OR triage pins a documented meaning for 0 and every handler implements it identically; the bare-flag documented defaults (first/last = 1, lines = 5) are unchanged.
- [ ] No path from a zero limit reaches the `no matches found` wording: with the refusal, `find --first 0 <matching query>` errors on the limit, not the query.
- [ ] Regression tests cover: REPL `parse_find_args`/`parse_peek_args` with `--first 0` and `--last 0`; `SearchOptions::apply` (or its replacement) never silently empties on a zero that slipped through; peek rendering with the zero case handled per the pinned contract.
- [ ] Both parser copies (find/search/show and peek) and both surfaces (CLI and REPL) behave identically — the fix is not applied to only one copy.

## Dedup / related

Distinct from #2009 (non-numeric --first/--last/--lines values becoming queries — a *rejected* parse; here the parse succeeds), #3029 (--first and --last together discarding --last), #2274 (unknown/mistyped flags swallowed), #1999 (selection-prompt numbers). Searched open + closed for zero-count/first-0/lines-0 coverage on 2026-10-31: none.

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-b (Lane B).

title: aggregator(dns): summarizeDns ages renewals against the UTC day, not Chicago's — a domain renewing today vanishes from nextRenewal and renewingSoon from 19:00 Chicago onward

labels.name: task/triage

body:
## Summary

`pm-stack/aggregator/src/dns.ts` `summarizeDns` (line 99) computes "today" as the **UTC** calendar day:

- `dns.ts:102` — `const today = now.toISOString().slice(0, 10);`
- `dns.ts:101` — the 45-day cutoff is likewise sliced from a UTC ISO string.

Every other calendar helper in the aggregator uses the **America/Chicago** calendar, via `chicagoYmd()` (`src/derive.ts:497`), because renewal/freshness dates are Chicago dates. `derive.ts:907-916` documents the exact failure mode #1629 fixed for freshness ageing: *"a stamp is a Chicago date, so ageing it against the UTC day called a read dated today '1d ago' — and stale — from 19:00 Chicago onward, when UTC had rolled over and Chicago had not."* `summarizeDns` was missed by that fix.

## Verified behaviour (this run, main `a9df3018`)

Runtime import of the unmodified `src/dns.ts` (Node type-stripping), with a two-entry register — `today.example` renewing `2026-10-31`, `later.example` renewing `2026-11-05` — at `now = 2026-11-01T01:00:00Z`, i.e. **20:00 CDT on 2026-10-31** (Chicago date still Oct 31; `chicagoYmd(now)` returns `2026-10-31`):

- `summarizeDns(...).nextRenewal` → `later.example` (2026-11-05) — **wrong**: the domain renewing that Chicago day is skipped because `2026-10-31 < "2026-11-01"` (the UTC date).
- `renewingSoon` → only `later.example`; `today.example` is dropped from the "Renewing in 45 days" spend card on the very day it renews.
- Control at `2026-10-31T17:00:00Z` (midday Chicago): `nextRenewal` → `today.example`, correct.

So for five hours every Chicago evening (19:00–24:00 CDT; six in CST), the DNS page and the domains summary card (`src/render.ts:2821-2832`, `src/sources/live.ts:854`) name the wrong "next renewal" and understate the renewing-soon spend.

## Why it matters

The summary exists so an upcoming renewal spend is visible before it lands. On the evening a domain actually renews, the page points at a later domain instead — precisely the moment the information matters — and the behaviour flips back at Chicago midnight, so it looks intermittent.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `summarizeDns` derives "today" from the Chicago calendar (e.g. `chicagoYmd(now)` from `src/derive.ts`), consistent with #1629; the renewing-soon window is computed on the same calendar basis.
- [ ] A regression test (in `test/slice3.test.ts` or a dns test) pins the evening case: at `2026-11-01T01:00:00Z` an entry renewing `2026-10-31` is `nextRenewal` and appears in `renewingSoon`.
- [ ] Existing `summarizeDns` tests (e.g. `test/slice3.test.ts:53-55`) still pass; behaviour at Chicago midday is unchanged.

## Scope notes

- Fix is local to `summarizeDns` (and its tests). Do not change the register parser (`parseDnsRegister`) or the renewal date format.
- Distinct from #1629 (freshness ageing in `derive.ts`, fixed) — this is the same UTC-day pattern in `dns.ts`, which that fix did not touch.

title: id(find/search/show/peek): --first and --last together silently discard --last — SearchOptions::apply is if/else-if, and none of the four commands declares the conflict Peek's own head/tail pair declares

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

`--first` and `--last` are mutually exclusive in effect — `SearchOptions::apply` can only honour one — but nothing says so, so setting both silently discards `--last`:

- `SearchOptions::apply` (pkgs/id/src/commands/find.rs:128) limits with `if let Some(n) = self.first { take(n) } else if let Some(n) = self.last { tail(n) }` (find.rs:137-139). When both are `Some`, the `last` branch is unreachable: the caller's `--last` value is dropped with no error and no warning.
- All four CLI commands that carry the pair define both flags with **no `conflicts_with`**: `Show` (cli.rs:727/730), `Peek` (cli.rs:808/811), `Find` (cli.rs:894/897), `Search` (cli.rs:961/964). So `id find --first 2 --last 3 config` parses cleanly, returns the first 2 matches, and never mentions that `--last 3` was ignored.
- The same file shows the house rule for mutually exclusive flags: Peek's own `--head-only` / `--tail-only` in the same command DO declare `conflicts_with` each other (cli.rs:786/789), as do `--words`/`--chars`. `first`/`last` are the exception.
- The REPL path has the same hole: `FindArgs::to_search_options` (repl/runner.rs:602) passes both fields straight into `SearchOptions::new`, and its parser sets both when both flags appear.

## Evidence (this run, main ab55f3c2)

- Laptop probe with `apply` + `should_exclude` copied verbatim from find.rs (stub `TaggedMatch` only; find.rs md5 `b64b2edef7c416f9357bc2c1d8c2de4f` on both clones; probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-firstlast/` on the laptop): 3 tests passed —
  - `first=Some(2), last=Some(3)` over 5 matches returns `[a, b]`: first wins, last silently ignored;
  - `last=Some(3)` alone returns `[c, d, e]`; `first=Some(2)` alone returns `[a, b]` — each flag works on its own, only the combination is silently misread.
- Callers: main.rs constructs `SearchOptions::new(first, last, …)` for Find, Search, Show and Peek with whatever clap accepted, so the CLI combination reaches `apply` unchallenged on all four commands.

## Why it matters

A user who writes `--first 2 --last 3` (or a script that assembles both flags from different layers) gets a result set shaped by only one of their two instructions, presented as if both were honoured. For `find`, the returned matches are the ones whose content is written to disk / stdout, so the silent choice changes which file the user ends up with — the worst kind of CLI surprise: no error, plausible-looking output, wrong semantics. The fix the codebase already uses for exactly this shape (`conflicts_with`, as on Peek's head/tail pair) costs one attribute per command.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Triage confirms on current main: `SearchOptions::apply` (find.rs:137-139) is if/else-if over first/last, and none of Show/Peek/Find/Search in cli.rs declares a first↔last conflict.
- [ ] Passing both `--first` and `--last` to any of `find`, `search`, `show`, `peek` is a loud parse error (clap `conflicts_with`, matching the head-only/tail-only precedent at cli.rs:786/789), not a silent precedence.
- [ ] The REPL find/search parser rejects (or loudly reports) the both-flags combination the same way, instead of passing both into `SearchOptions`.
- [ ] Single-flag behaviour is byte-identical: `--first N` alone and `--last N` alone return exactly what they return today; a regression test pins both-alone and both-together for at least one command.
- [ ] Alternatively, if triage decides both-set should mean something (e.g. last-within-first), that semantics is implemented in `apply`, documented in the flag help, and pinned by a test — silence is the only unacceptable outcome.

Distinct from: #2009 (REPL: a non-numeric --first/--last value becomes a query — different failure, REPL token parsing), #2274 (REPL: unknown/mistyped flags swallowed — REPL parser again; this issue is the CLI clap definitions plus the shared `apply` precedence, and the REPL's both-set case), #2178 (`--all --dir` overwrite in find downloads).

title: pm-dispatch(server): the 256 KiB body cap is measured in UTF-16 code units, not bytes — a 300 KB CJK body passes readJsonBody's 'too large' check

labels.name: task/triage

labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

body:
## Problem

pm-dispatch's request body cap is named and documented as a byte cap, but it is measured in UTF-16 code units — so a body well over the cap in bytes passes the check whenever the prompt text is non-ASCII.

## Evidence

- `pm-stack/dispatch/src/server.ts:36` (main `fbfd1454`): `const MAX_BODY_BYTES = 256 * 1024;`
- `server.ts:47-48`, `readJsonBody`: `const text = await req.text(); if (text.length > MAX_BODY_BYTES) throw new ValidationError("body: too large");` — `String.length` counts UTF-16 code units, not bytes.
- Verified this run with the runtime's own semantics: a string of 100,000 CJK characters has `length` 100,000 (≤ 262,144, so it passes) but encodes to 300,000 UTF-8 bytes — ~17% over the stated cap. Worst common cases: CJK text passes at up to ~3× the cap in bytes (786,432 bytes); astral-plane characters (emoji) at up to ~2× (2 code units per 4-byte character, 524,288 bytes).

## Why it matters

- The cap is the intake boundary's only size guard before `JSON.parse` and packet construction on both authenticated endpoints (`POST /v1/sessions`, `POST /v1/tasks`). Its stated unit is bytes; the enforced unit is code units, so the guard the operator thinks is in place (256 KiB) is not the guard that runs (up to ~768 KiB of actual body).
- Dispatch prompts are exactly the traffic that goes non-ASCII: callers paste prompts with CJK text, emoji and smart punctuation, so the miscount is on the common path, not an exotic one.
- Nothing else in the service re-checks size: the packet, issue body and queue task all carry the prompt onward at whatever size passed.

## Acceptance criteria

- `readJsonBody` rejects on the body's UTF-8 byte length (e.g. `new TextEncoder().encode(text).length` or `Buffer.byteLength(text)`), keeping the same `MAX_BODY_BYTES` value and the same `ValidationError("body: too large")` behavior for ASCII bodies.
- A test in `pm-stack/dispatch/test/` pins both sides of the boundary with multibyte text: a body just under the cap in bytes passes; a body under the cap in code units but over it in bytes is rejected.
- Existing dispatch tests still pass (`bun test` in `pm-stack/dispatch`).

Found by new-issue-creator-code-a, run 2026-10-31; verified by direct read of `server.ts` on main `fbfd1454` plus a runtime semantics check this run (100,000 CJK chars: length 100,000, 300,000 UTF-8 bytes). Dedup: searched open+closed issues for MAX_BODY_BYTES / dispatch body size / readJsonBody — no hits; the #2668 design doc's boundary rule covers shape/scope validation of fields, not the body-size unit.

body:
# fix(pm-dispatch): POST /v1/tasks issue_number attach never verifies the issue exists, is open, or is an issue

## Finding

PR #2676 (commit dbab526d0d) added the `issue_number` attach flow to `POST /v1/tasks`: instead of creating an issue, the task attaches to an existing one. The attach target is never verified. `parseIssueNumber` (`pm-stack/dispatch/src/validate.ts`) checks only that the value is a positive integer, and `handleTasks` (`pm-stack/dispatch/src/server.ts:280-284` on current main bfbd1454f1) constructs the issue reference purely from the request:

```ts
issue = {
  number: body.issueNumber,
  url: `https://github.com/${body.repo}/issues/${body.issueNumber}`,
};
```

There is no GitHub lookup anywhere on this path — `GitHubClient` (`pm-stack/dispatch/src/github.ts`) has no get-issue method at all (only `createIssue`, `addLabels`, `comment`, `ensureLabel`).

## Why it matters

- **Nonexistent number:** the task still enqueues (anchored to the canonical dedupe key for the phantom issue, `server.ts:292-295`), the response returns HTTP 201 with `issue_number` and an `issue_url` that 404s, and the only signal is two `warnings` entries after the comment/label calls fail. A caller typo silently mis-tracks the work.
- **Pull request number:** the GitHub issues API treats PRs as issues, so the agent-note comment and the `queue/queued` + `source/dispatch` labels succeed — on a PR, which then looks like queued fleet work.
- **Closed issue:** comment and labels also succeed, so a closed (possibly completed) issue is re-labelled `queue/queued` and noted as newly queued work.

Verified still present on current main `bfbd1454f10ab1c6e7f9e8bb173feee4b58d4223` (server.ts:280-284, same construction; no lookup added since #2676 merged 2026-10-30).

## Distinct from #2677

#2677 covers the attach flow returning a pre-existing dedupe-collided task as if new. This issue is the missing existence/state verification of the attach target itself; neither fix substitutes for the other.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Before enqueueing, the attach path verifies via the GitHub App (or the `gh` fallback) that `issue_number` in `repo` exists, is an issue (not a pull request), and is open; a failed check returns a 4xx naming the problem and enqueues nothing.
- [ ] For repos where the GitHub App is not installed (attach currently warn-skipped), the response makes the unverified state explicit rather than returning the same `issue_url` shape as a verified attach.
- [ ] Tests (stubbed GitHub client) cover: nonexistent number, PR number, closed issue, and the happy path of an open issue.

body:
## Bug

The projector's webhook dedupe treats a delivery whose apply **failed** as
applied, so a GitHub redelivery of that delivery is answered `200
{"status":"duplicate"}` and the event is never applied. One transient
failure (a DB hiccup, a store error mid-apply) permanently and silently
drops the event from the read model; the only recovery is the periodic
reconcile poll happening to cover that repo/stream.

### Evidence (main `689e47c0`)

- `pm-stack/projector/src/server.ts` — the webhook handler checks
  `store.deliveryApplied(db, deliveryId)` **before** applying, and on an
  `applyEvent` throw it records the delivery and returns 500:

  ```ts
  const already = await store.deliveryApplied(db, deliveryId);
  if (already) return jsonResponse(200, { status: "duplicate" });
  ...
  } catch (e) {
    await store.recordDelivery(db, { deliveryId, event, outcome: "error", detail: ... });
    return jsonResponse(500, { error: "apply_failed" });
  }
  ```

  The `invalid_json` path records `outcome: "error"` the same way.

- `pm-stack/projector/src/store.ts:337` — `deliveryApplied` ignores the
  recorded outcome entirely:

  ```sql
  SELECT 1 AS x FROM pmp_deliveries WHERE delivery_id = ?
  ```

  Any row — `applied`, `ignored`, or `error` — makes every later
  delivery of that GUID a "duplicate".

- `pm-stack/projector/schema.sql:98` — `pmp_deliveries.delivery_id` is
  the PRIMARY KEY ("a redelivered webhook is applied at most once"), so
  a fix that retries on redelivery must also make the second
  `recordDelivery` an upsert/replace rather than a bare INSERT, or the
  retry succeeds and its bookkeeping insert throws.

### Reproduction (verified this run)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneA-projredeliver/`,
real `handleRequest` + `migrate` + HMAC-signed fixture
`fixtures/02-issue-opened.json`, projector sources copied from main
`689e47c0`):

1. `pmp_items` briefly renamed away → signed delivery
   `probe-delivery-1` returns `500 {"error":"apply_failed"}` and
   `pmp_deliveries` gains `{delivery_id: "probe-delivery-1",
   outcome: "error", detail: "SQLITE_ERROR: no such table:
   pmp_items"}`.
2. Table restored, the **same** delivery redelivered →
   `200 {"status":"duplicate"}` and `pmp_items` count stays **0** —
   the issue-opened event is lost.
3. Control: the same body under a fresh delivery id →
   `200 {"status":"applied","refs":["developing-today/code#754"]}`,
   item count 1.

### Why it matters

The projector is the PM stack's read model for issues/PRs/comments.
Webhook intake is supposed to be at-least-once-safe: GitHub redelivers
(automatically on 5xx in some paths, and manually from the App UI after
an incident) precisely so transient failures heal. Here the failure is
recorded in the very table that gates redelivery, converting a
transient error into permanent, silent data loss — the deliveries audit
even shows the delivery as present, so nothing looks missing until
someone notices a stale item. Distinct from #2982 (a missing
`X-GitHub-Delivery` header collapsing distinct deliveries onto the
empty-string key): this is about deliveries that *have* an id and
*failed*.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A delivery recorded with `outcome = 'error'` does **not** count
      as applied: redelivering it re-runs `applyEvent` and, on success,
      returns `applied`/`ignored` and the writes land.
- [ ] Recording the retried delivery's outcome does not violate the
      `pmp_deliveries` primary key (upsert/replace semantics), and the
      audit row reflects the final outcome.
- [ ] A delivery recorded `applied` or `ignored` still short-circuits
      as `duplicate` (existing e2e idempotency test keeps passing).
- [ ] Regression test beside the projector tests: fail an apply
      (transient store error), redeliver the same delivery id, assert
      it applies; and a redelivery after an `error` does not throw on
      the deliveries insert.
- [ ] Triage pins the `invalid_json` case: a malformed-body delivery
      can never succeed on redelivery — either it stays deduped
      deliberately (documented) or it is excluded from the deliveries
      table; either way the choice is explicit, not accidental.

body:
## Finding

The /health dashboard-comments card added by PR #2098 tells operators that "a pending count that never drains means the triage/poster loop is not running". A pending count alone cannot prove that: comments can arrive faster than a running loop clears them, in which case a healthy loop leaves the count unchanged and an operator following the card's guidance misdiagnoses a stopped loop and goes looking for a dead process that is actually fine (or restarts a working loop). CodeRabbit flagged exactly this on the PR (Minor, Functional Correctness, at `render.ts:4500` in the PR diff); the PR merged with the wording unchanged and it is still on main verbatim.

## Evidence

- Source PR: #2098 (merged, head `84d2872b938c75c93ea031eec0d5cbf00de92660`) — https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/2098 — "feat(aggregator): pending dashboard-comment counts on /health (#1145)"
- CodeRabbit review comment on PR #2098 at `pm-stack/aggregator/src/render.ts:4500`: "Stop claiming a non-draining count proves a stopped loop. The new text … says a pending count that never drains means the triage or poster loop is not running. A count alone cannot show that. Comments can arrive faster than the external loop clears them. Then a running loop leaves the count unchanged, and operators get a wrong diagnosis." Codex reported no findings on the PR; the CodeRabbit thread was never answered and no follow-up commit changed the text.
- Verified still present on current main `6a19fec557c172b57e5f704d7b7f9163a76e43bb`, `pm-stack/aggregator/src/render.ts:4785`: `… (#1145 — a pending count that never drains means the triage/poster loop is not running)`.
- The counts themselves are fine — `pendingCommentCounts()` in `comments.ts` and the `buildHealth` plumbing were verified in the same review; only the diagnostic claim in the rendered text is wrong.
- Deduped 2026-10-31: `gh issue list --state all` searches for "triage poster loop not running", "health comments wording", and "pendingMessages render" find no issue covering this wording (#1145 is closed and was about exercising the loop end-to-end, not the card text).

## Why it matters

This card is the operator surface for an unworked comment queue. Its one diagnostic sentence points responders at the wrong conclusion in the high-arrival-rate case — the case where the queue matters most — and can send them restarting or debugging a healthy triage/poster loop while the real problem (arrival rate) goes unnamed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The rendered card no longer claims a non-draining pending count proves the loop has stopped; it names both causes (work arriving faster than it is cleared, or the loop stopped) and directs the operator to check the loop's last run before acting — CodeRabbit's suggested wording on PR #2098 is an acceptable starting point.
- [ ] The counts, labels, and layout of the card are otherwise unchanged, and the existing `health.test.ts` render assertions (updated for the new sentence) pass.
