body:
## Finding

PR #2099 taught the aggregator's two audit stores to quarantine a corrupt file instead of silently overwriting it (#1452), but the **read-error path still silently treats any failure as "no store yet"** — and the next persist then overwrites the existing store. In both stores, `doLoad`'s first `catch` swallows every `readFile` error, not just ENOENT, despite the code comment directly above it stating that "a missing file is the only silent empty start".

Concretely: if the store file exists and holds valid audit history but the read fails for a non-missing reason (EACCES after a permissions change, a transient I/O error, the path momentarily being something unreadable), the store starts empty with no log line at all, and the next `add()` persist — `mkdir` + write temp file + `rename` over the store path — replaces the unread history with a fresh file containing only the new record. That is exactly the silent audit-history loss #1452/#2099 set out to eliminate, reached through the read path instead of the parse path.

## Evidence

- Source PR: #2099 (merged, head `37ceccbe9f5b43a9fb0acdeaa803931e92b55eef`) — https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/2099 — "fix(aggregator): quarantine corrupt actions/comments stores (#1452)"
- Verified still present on current main `6a19fec557c172b57e5f704d7b7f9163a76e43bb`:
  - `pm-stack/aggregator/src/actions.ts:434-447` — `doLoad`: comment at :435-441 says a missing file is the only silent empty start; the `catch` at :444-447 around `readFile` (:443) treats **all** errors that way and returns with `this.actions = []`, no logging, no quarantine attempt.
  - `pm-stack/aggregator/src/comments.ts:114-127` — identical structure: comment :115-121, `readFile` :123, catch-all :124-127 setting `this.comments = []`.
  - Persist overwrites unconditionally in both stores: `actions.ts` `persist()` (mkdir + `writeFile(tmp)` + `rename(tmp, this.file)`) and the mirrored `persist()` in `comments.ts` — so the first write after a failed read destroys the on-disk history the read never saw.
- The parse/shape path in the same functions (actions.ts :448+, comments.ts :128+) does the right thing — quarantine to `<file>.corrupt-<timestamp>` plus a loud `console.error` — which makes the read path's silence an inconsistency in the same function, not a design choice.
- Deduped 2026-10-31: `gh issue list --state all` searches for "1452 quarantine", "corrupt store quarantine", "doLoad readFile", "store file unreadable overwrite" return only #1452 itself (closed, the eval this PR implemented) — no issue covers the read-error path.

## Why it matters

These two files are the dashboard's append-only audit history (actions and comments). #1452's whole point was that silently starting empty destroys that history. A permissions slip or transient read failure is at least as plausible as a truncated write, and today it produces the worst outcome in the matrix: no quarantine copy, no log line, and a routine persist that erases the original bytes.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] In both `ActionsStore.doLoad` and `CommentsStore.doLoad`, only ENOENT (file genuinely absent) takes the silent empty start; any other read error is loud: a `console.error` naming the file and the error, in the same style as the quarantine warning.
- [ ] After a non-ENOENT read failure, a subsequent persist must not silently overwrite the unread store — e.g. attempt the same `.corrupt-<timestamp>` quarantine rename before starting empty, and if that fails, surface it explicitly (as the parse path already does) rather than proceeding silently.
- [ ] Regression tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/store-corrupt.test.ts` (or a sibling) pin the non-ENOENT case for both stores (e.g. store path made unreadable / a directory-in-place probe where the platform allows, or an injected read error), alongside the existing missing/corrupt/wrong-shape/valid cases, which keep passing unchanged.
- [ ] Behaviour for the genuinely-missing-file case is byte-for-byte what it is today (silent empty start, first write creates the file).

body:
# projector: POST /links validates only subject/ref — a non-string note/createdBy throws out of the handler, relation is String()-coerced into garbage, and an empty subject is stored

## Evidence (verified this run, main `9b689eb5`)

`pm-stack/projector/src/server.ts`, the `POST /links` branch (bearer-gated): only `subject` and `ref` are type-checked —

```ts
const { subject, ref, relation = "relates", note, createdBy } = body ?? {};
if (typeof subject !== "string" || typeof ref !== "string" || !/^[\w.-]+\/[\w.-]+#\d+$/.test(ref)) {
  return jsonResponse(400, { error: "subject (string) and ref (owner/repo#N) required" });
}
await store.upsertLink(db, { subject, ref, relation: String(relation), note, createdBy });
```

`note` and `createdBy` go to the libsql bind unvalidated, `relation` is coerced with `String()`, and there is no `try/catch` around `upsertLink` (nor around `handleRequest` in `serve()`, server.ts fetch handler), so a driver throw escapes as Bun's bare 500 instead of this API's JSON error shape.

Probe (laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-projector/`, real `handleRequest` + migrated libsql DB, sources md5-matched to main `9b689eb5`, valid bearer token):

| body | observed |
|---|---|
| control: `{subject:"s:1", ref:"developing-today/code#1", relation:"tracks", note:"hi"}` | 201, stored verbatim |
| `relation: ["a","b"]` | 201; response echoes the raw array; **stored relation is `"a,b"`** |
| `relation: {x:1}` | 201; **stored relation is `"[object Object]"`** |
| `note: {x:1}` | **throws out of `handleRequest`**: `Error: SQLite3 can only bind numbers, strings, bigints, buffers, and null` — in production an uncaught 500, no JSON error |
| `createdBy: ["a"]` | same uncaught throw |
| `note: 42` | 201; stored note reads back as `"42.0"` (numeric bind into the TEXT column) |
| `subject: ""` | 201; a link with an empty subject is stored |
| `subject: 123` (control) | 400, as the existing check intends |

The garbage relations are durable: `pmp_links` is keyed `(subject, ref, relation)`, so `"a,b"` / `"[object Object]"` rows pollute the registry and answer later `GET /links` / subject-join queries (`getCommentsForSubject` joins on links), and the caller's 201 tells it the link was recorded as sent.

## Why it matters

This is the projector's only authenticated write API. A client bug or a hand-crafted request either (a) crashes the request with an uncaught driver error instead of the endpoint's own 400 JSON shape — the failure mode #1547/#2693 already removed from this server's read paths — or (b) silently stores a coerced relation/subject the caller never sent, corrupting the link registry the read model joins on. The handler already has the right validation shape for two fields; the remaining fields were never given it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `POST /links` validates the whole body before any store call: `relation`, `note`, and `createdBy`, when present, must be strings (absent/null keep today's defaults); a non-empty `subject` is required. Any violation returns the endpoint's JSON `400` shape — nothing is stored, nothing throws.
- [ ] No `String()` coercion of `relation`: a valid string relation is stored and echoed verbatim; the 201 response echoes what was actually stored.
- [ ] A store/driver failure on this path cannot escape `handleRequest` as an uncaught throw (same JSON-error discipline as the read paths).
- [ ] Tests (extending the projector suite, e.g. `test/limit.test.ts` style or a links test): the probe matrix above — array/object relation, object note, array createdBy, numeric note, empty subject — each returns 400 with no row stored; the valid control returns 201 and round-trips verbatim.
- [ ] No change to the bearer gate, the `ref` format check, link keying, or the GET/DELETE link endpoints.

title: id(world): journal restore issues participant 0 — an Issued entry for the reserved host identity restores, and its token chats and projects as the host

body:
## Problem

`WorldCore::restore` (`pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs:138`) accepts a `JournalEntry::Issued` for **participant id 0** — the reserved host/system identity that mint can never issue — and the restored capability then authorizes as participant 0.

Participant 0 is reserved throughout the world code:

- `WorldCore::new` starts `next_participant_id: 1` (core.rs:89) and `mint` assigns ids only from that counter (core.rs:873), so no live path ever issues id 0.
- Host-authored chat is committed as participant 0: "Commit a host-authored chat line as participant 0" (`system_chat`, core.rs:574-576).
- Journal `System` events are only accepted when they claim `participant_id == 0` (core.rs:303), and `ProgramInstalled` documents "`participant_id` is zero for this host-authored event" (`pkgs/id/src/world/mod.rs:341-342`).

The restore `Issued` arm (core.rs:172-232) checks for a duplicate id, a known parent, `uses >= 1`, and a delegate not outliving its parent — but never that `participant.id != 0`. A journal carrying an `Issued` entry for id 0 therefore rebuilds a capability record for the host identity itself, with a digest the journal author chose.

## Verified this run (laptop probe, main 17122875)

A probe test added to `src/world/tests.rs` on the laptop (worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-restore-id0`, since removed after the run) built a journal of `Created` + one `Issued` entry with `participant.id = 0`, display name `host`, GUEST scopes, and the digest of a self-chosen token `0.<secret>`:

- `WorldCore::restore` **succeeded** (the probe's first expectation).
- `core.chat(&cap, "forged host line")` with the forged token **succeeded**, and the committed event carries `participant_id == 0` — indistinguishable in the event log and in viewer projections from a genuine host/system line.
- `core.snapshot(&cap)` lists participant 0 among the world's participants.

Probe result: `world::tests::tests::probe_restore_issues_participant_zero ... ok` (1 passed, 1581 filtered out, `cargo test --lib`, default features).

## Why it matters

- **Host impersonation.** Anyone who can present a journal (world import, fork, backup restore, a compromised or malicious world export) gains a working capability for the host identity: chat and inputs committed as participant 0 read as host-authored to every client and to the world program.
- **It composes with #2894.** That issue covers restore never validating `Committed`/`Checkpoint` event authors. The natural fix there — "the author must be an issued participant or 0" — is defeated if a journal can also *issue* id 0 to itself: the forged record makes host-authored events "valid" and gives the forger the matching live token.
- **It persists.** `checkpoint_entries` (core.rs:448-460) re-emits an `Issued` entry for every capability record, so once restored, the id-0 record is carried into every compacted journal.
- Restore's own contract says a journal with "unknown participants" is refused, never partially applied (core.rs:130-136). Participant 0 is the one id that is never a participant.

Related but distinct: #2890 (Issued scopes), #2894 (Committed/Checkpoint authors), #2958 (participant count), #2960 (Issued display names), umbrella #2898.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `WorldCore::restore` refuses a journal whose `Issued` entry names participant id 0, with an error that names the reserved id; the refusal happens before any later entry is applied (no partial restore).
- [ ] A regression test in `pkgs/id/src/world/tests.rs` (in the style of `restore_refuses_a_delegate_outliving_its_parent`) covers the id-0 `Issued` case, including when the id-0 entry follows legitimate entries.
- [ ] Legitimate journals are unaffected: existing restore/checkpoint round-trip tests pass unchanged, and id 0 remains usable exactly where it is today — host-authored `System`/`ProgramInstalled` events and `system_chat` (participant 0 as an *author*, never as an *issued capability*).
- [ ] The fix does not mint or reserve any new participant id, and does not change the journal wire format.

body:
# projector: parseLimit still reinterprets non-decimal spellings — `limit=1e2`, `0x10`, `5.0`, `+5`, ` 5` are honoured as numbers instead of falling back to the default

## Evidence (verified this run, main `9b689eb5`)

`pm-stack/projector/src/server.ts:50-56` — the fix for #1547:

```ts
export function parseLimit(raw: string | null, defaultLimit: number, maxLimit: number): number {
  if (raw === null) return defaultLimit;
  const n = Number(raw);
  if (!Number.isInteger(n) || n < 1) return defaultLimit;
  return Math.min(n, maxLimit);
}
```

Its own doc comment (:42-49) says "Only a positive integer is honoured" and that negative/fractional/non-numeric values fall back to the endpoint default. But the check is on the `Number()`-coerced value, not the spelling, so any spelling `Number()` coerces to an integer passes:

Probe (laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-projector/`, real `parseLimit` imported from the md5-matched `server.ts` of main `9b689eb5`, defaults 200/1000):

| raw | result | expected per the #1547 contract |
|---|---|---|
| `"1e3"` | 1000 | default 200 (scientific spelling) |
| `"1e2"` | 100 (same mechanism) | default 200 |
| `"0x10"` | 16 | default 200 (hex spelling) |
| `"5.0"` | 5 | default 200 (fractional spelling — `2.7` falls back, `5.0` does not) |
| `"+5"` | 5 | default 200 |
| `" 5"` | 5 | default 200 |
| `"5"` | 5 | 5 (control, honoured) |
| `"2.7"`, `"abc"` | 200 | 200 (controls, fall back) |

Used by both read endpoints: `/items` (server.ts:139) and `/comments` (server.ts:148). The existing test matrix (`pm-stack/projector/test/limit.test.ts`) covers `-1`, `0`, `2.7`, `abc`, `""`, `NaN`, `Infinity` — none of the coercible spellings above.

## Why it matters

This is the exact reinterpretation class the repo keeps removing site by site (#2789/#2791/#2743 for measurement parsers, #832 for world seeds, the digits-only rule in `bin/proxy-port.mjs`): a client that sends `limit=0x10` or `limit=1e2` gets a silently different page size than the API contract states, and `5.0` vs `2.7` behaving differently is an inconsistency inside the fix's own test matrix. The bound itself still holds (results are clamped), so this is correctness/contract drift, not an unbounded-read hole — priority/low.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `parseLimit` honours only a plain decimal positive-integer spelling (digits only, e.g. `/^[0-9]+$/` after the absent-parameter check); `1e2`, `1e3`, `0x10`, `5.0`, `+5`, leading/trailing-whitespace, and empty spellings fall back to the endpoint default.
- [ ] Well-formed values behave exactly as today: honoured exactly, over-max clamped to the per-endpoint maximum, absent parameter keeps the default.
- [ ] `test/limit.test.ts` gains the coercible-spelling matrix above for both endpoints' defaults/maxima; existing #1547 tests pass unchanged.
- [ ] No change to the endpoints, defaults (items 200/1000, comments 500/1000), or the store layer.

title: id(web/collab): document step history grows without bound — no cap or compaction, and every joiner is sent a clone of the entire history

body:
## Problem

A collab document's step history grows without any bound for as long as the document lives, and every new joiner is sent a clone of the entire history. Any connected client — including an anonymous one, since collab auth is optional and failure proceeds as anonymous — can grow server memory and join-time catch-up cost without limit by sending Steps frames.

## Evidence (main `ed59bc6d`, `pkgs/id/src/web/collab.rs`)

- `:217` / `:250` — `Document.steps: RwLock<Vec<(Step, serde_json::Value)>>`, created empty; the module has no cap constant for it (contrast the encryption adapter, which bounds its held set by both count and bytes: `MAX_HELD_MESSAGES` / `MAX_HELD_BYTES`, `pkgs/id/src/encryption/scheme.rs:66,72`, enforced in #186 precisely so an unreadable-message flood cannot grow memory forever).
- `:1020-1028` — the only mutation site appends every step of every accepted Steps frame: `doc_steps.push(...)` per step. `grep` over the file shows no `truncate`, `drain`, `remove`, cap check, or compaction of `steps` anywhere; steps are never folded into the base document (`Document.doc` is the initial content, `:211`; the Init frame even hardcodes `version: 0` as "base", `:765` — see also #2799).
- `:1029-1033` — the version is just a counter (`fetch_add(steps.len())`); nothing ever resets it or the history when a save persists the document (`notify_new_version`, `:352-375`, only broadcasts and updates the stored hash).
- `:791-806` — on every join, the handler clones the whole history into a catch-up Update (`steps.iter().map(|(step, _)| step.data.clone())`), so join cost and allocation are O(total steps ever submitted) per joiner, forever.
- `:342-350` / cleanup in `handle_collab_socket` — a document is only removed after the last client has been gone for `DOCUMENT_CLEANUP` (1 hour, `:185`); a single client that stays connected (or reconnects within the hour) keeps the document — and its entire history — alive indefinitely.
- The Steps path itself has no per-message bound either: `CollabMessage::decode` (`:536-545`) accepts a steps vector of any length the WebSocket frame carries, and the handler checks only the version before appending all of them.

Verification this run: code-read verification on current main — full-text search of `collab.rs` for every `steps` mutation/read site (append at :1023 is the only push; reads are the catch-up clone and tests), plus the absence of any cap constant or compaction call in the module.

## Why it matters

This is an unbounded-memory / unbounded-work surface reachable by any peer that can open the collab socket (auth failure still proceeds as anonymous, `:716-753`). Long-lived shared documents — exactly the ones with the most history — become the most expensive to join and the largest memory residents, and a hostile or buggy client can accelerate that arbitrarily. The codebase's own precedent (#186) is that sets which grow on peer input get an explicit count+bytes bound with a refusal that neither poisons nor evicts; the collab history has neither a bound nor a compaction story.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Triage pins the remedy shape: e.g. periodic compaction of applied steps into the base document (advancing the Init base version — interacts with #2799, coordinate there), and/or a hard cap on retained steps / total step bytes with an explicit desync/reconnect error (the Lagged path at `:896-906` is the existing pattern) when the cap is hit.
- [ ] After the fix, retained history per document is bounded by a named constant (count and/or bytes), whatever traffic a client sends.
- [ ] Join-time catch-up no longer clones an ever-growing history: its size is bounded by the same constant, or by the compacted base + a bounded tail.
- [ ] A test submits steps past the bound (or past a compaction threshold) and asserts the bound/compaction behaviour and that a fresh joiner still reconstructs the same document.
- [ ] Normal editing below the bound is unchanged: Steps are Acked, broadcast, and replayed as before.

## Dedup / related

- #2799 (open) covers the Init frame always carrying version 0 — related (compaction would touch it) but distinct: this issue is the unbounded retention itself, which exists whatever the Init version says.
- #186 (closed) bounded the encryption held set — the precedent, not the same code.
- #2824 / #2830 (open) are collab-adjacent (TS frame shape, WS URL encoding) and do not touch server-side retention.
- Search of open + closed issues for "collab steps unbounded / step history growth / compaction" found no existing issue covering this.

body:
## Bug

The proxy-port drift guard — `.github/scripts/check-proxy-port-fallbacks.sh`, run as the
`basic: proxy port fallbacks` job in `.github/workflows/nix-ci.yml:50` on every PR — **fails on
current main**, and its proxy list no longer matches the fleet it guards: it still demands the
two proxies Drew retired on 2026-10-30, and it does not cover three live proxies whose port
copies can now drift silently. This is the inverse of #866 (guard missing proxies then in the
other direction), in the same script.

## Evidence (all on main `106b0571`, verified this run)

### 1. The guard exits 1 on main — it demands let definitions that were deliberately removed

```
$ bash .github/scripts/check-proxy-port-fallbacks.sh
::error::agyProxyPort definition not found in home/common/default.nix.
::error::antigravityLsProxyPort definition not found in home/common/default.nix.
EXIT:1
```

- The script's table (`.github/scripts/check-proxy-port-fallbacks.sh:36-44`) still lists
  `AGY_PROXY_PORT|agyProxyPort|bin/agy-proxy.mjs|yes` and
  `ANTIGRAVITY_LS_PROXY_PORT|antigravityLsProxyPort|bin/antigravity-ls-proxy.mjs|yes`.
- Commit `bce524fc` ("feat(antigravity-direct): nix service for the CLI-wire Gemini door;
  retire agy/ls proxy units") removed both lets and both units on purpose.
  `home/common/default.nix:660-670` documents the retirement: the two `bin/` scripts
  "remain in the repo as history, uninvoked", the matching opencode providers sit in
  `disabled_providers` (confirmed: `.opencode/opencode.jsonc:19,26` and the
  `antigravity-agy` provider at :2379 still carries `{env:AGY_PROXY_PORT:-18743}`),
  and undoing it means restoring the lets from git history. Nobody updated the guard.
- The failure is currently invisible in CI only because Actions runs are stuck queued
  (#1599). The moment runners recover, the `basic` job goes red on every PR and on main,
  for a reason unrelated to any PR's change — the #866 failure shape again.

### 2. Three live proxies are not guarded at all

Each has the same single-source let + copies pattern the guard exists to protect
(`home/common/default.nix:10-25` let block), agrees today, and can drift tomorrow with
no CI signal:

| proxy | let (default.nix) | bin/ fallback | opencode.jsonc baseURL |
|---|---|---|---|
| claude-code-proxy | `claudeCodeProxyPort = 18749` (:23) | `parseProxyPort('CLAUDE_CODE_PROXY_PORT', 18749)` (`bin/claude-code-proxy.mjs:42`) | `{env:CLAUDE_CODE_PROXY_PORT:-18749}` (:176) |
| opencode-route-proxy | `opencodeRouteProxyPort = 18750` (:22) | `parseProxyPort("OPENCODE_ROUTE_PROXY_PORT", 18750)` (`bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs:49`) | none in this repo (script-only row, like Clef) |
| antigravity-direct | `antigravityDirectProxyPort = 18751` (:24) | `Number(process.env.ANTIGRAVITY_DIRECT_PORT || 18751)` (`bin/antigravity-direct.mjs:60`) | `{env:ANTIGRAVITY_DIRECT_PORT:-18751}` (:2638) |

- Session-variable copies also exist for all three (`home/common/default.nix:779,848,1557,1565`).
- antigravity-direct additionally cannot be added as a row as-is: its fallback form
  (`Number(process.env.<VAR> || <number>)`, unquoted) matches neither of the two forms the
  guard accepts (`parseProxyPort('<VAR>', <port>)` or `process.env.<VAR> || '<port>'`).
  The guard needs a third accepted form, or the proxy should move to `parseProxyPort`
  (related: #2823 covers the runtime parsing hazards of that bare `Number()`; this issue
  is only about guard coverage).

## Why it matters

The guard is the only thing standing between the fleet and the #434/#435 failure mode —
a non-shell launch silently dialing the wrong or an empty port. Right now it is both
broken (red on main, masked by #1599) and blind (the newest proxy, claude-code, which
serves the default model, plus the router and the single Antigravity door, are exactly
the rows it doesn't check). A port edit in any one copy of those three passes CI today.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `bash .github/scripts/check-proxy-port-fallbacks.sh` exits 0 on main.
- [ ] The guard's table matches the live fleet: the retired agy/antigravity-ls rows are
      removed (or explicitly marked retired with the check adjusted), with a comment
      pointing at the retirement note in `home/common/default.nix`.
- [ ] claude-code-proxy (18749, with jsonc check), opencode-route-proxy (18750,
      script-only), and antigravity-direct (18751, with jsonc check) are covered; the
      antigravity-direct fallback form is either recognized by the guard or the proxy
      is migrated to `parseProxyPort` so the standard row applies.
- [ ] Deliberately breaking one copy (e.g. the jsonc fallback for claude-code) makes
      the guard fail naming that proxy — verified before merge.
- [ ] No port numbers change; no proxy behavior changes beyond (optionally) the
      antigravity-direct port-parse form.

Related: #866 (same script, opposite drift), #434/#435 (the failure mode the guard
exists for), #894 (claude-code-proxy wiring — the port copies exist; this issue is the
guard's coverage of them), #2823 (antigravity-direct bare `Number()` parsing),
#1599 (queued runners currently masking the red gate).

body:
## Bug

The id web UI's **Ctrl+S / Cmd+S save shortcut silently does nothing when CapsLock is on, and on non-Latin keyboard layouts** — instead of saving the document, the browser's own Save Page dialog opens, because the handler never calls `preventDefault`.

## Evidence

`pkgs/id/web/src/main.ts:1437-1446` (main `106b0571`) — the only Ctrl+S handler in the web UI:

```ts
// Ctrl+S to save, Enter to submit tags
document.addEventListener("keydown", (event: KeyboardEvent) => {
  if ((event.ctrlKey || event.metaKey) && event.key === "s") {
    event.preventDefault();
    if (app.collab?.editor && app.autoSave) {
      app.autoSave.saveNow();
    }
    return;
  }
  ...
```

`KeyboardEvent.key` is the *character produced*, not the physical key:

- CapsLock on (any OS): Ctrl+S produces `key === "S"` (with `shiftKey === false` — CapsLock is not Shift), so the `=== "s"` comparison never matches.
- macOS Cmd+S with CapsLock: same, `key === "S"`.
- Non-Latin layouts (e.g. Russian): the physical S key produces `key === "ы"` under Ctrl, so the shortcut is dead for every save on that layout.

The shortcut is user-facing and advertised: `pkgs/id/src/web/templates.rs:752` lists `<kbd>Ctrl+S</kbd> Save document (in editor)` in the shortcuts table, and the save button's title is `Save (Ctrl+S)` (templates.rs:458). The button itself (`triggerSave`) works — only the keyboard path is broken.

### Probe (laptop, verbatim predicate)

`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-ctrls/probe.mjs` — the exact predicate from `main.ts:1439` (file md5 `c04d43e9f5dbd1dbaf8ad7def9430234`, identical in the sandbox and laptop clones) run against the `key` values browsers deliver:

```
ok   control  Ctrl+S Win/Linux US, no caps: key="s" -> save fires: true
BUG  CapsLock Ctrl+S (any OS):              key="S" -> save fires: false
BUG  CapsLock Cmd+S macOS:                  key="S" -> save fires: false
BUG  Russian layout Ctrl+S (key=ы):         key="ы" -> save fires: false
ok   Ctrl+Shift+S (strikethrough, must NOT save): key="S" -> save fires: false
ok   plain s typing (must NOT save):        key="s" -> save fires: false

Physical Ctrl/Cmd+S presses that do NOT save: 3 of 3 (CapsLock x2 + non-Latin layout)
```

Distinct from #2834, which covers the separate Alt+T *theme* handler in `theme.ts`; this is the *save* handler in `main.ts`, and its failure mode is worse: the un-intercepted Ctrl+S opens the browser's Save Page dialog over an unsaved document.

## Why it matters

Ctrl+S is the primary explicit-save gesture for the editor (autosave exists, but the docs and footer teach Ctrl+S as "save document"). For CapsLock users it fails 100% of the time, and for users on non-Latin layouts it never works at all — and the failure is actively misleading: the browser Save Page dialog suggests the page itself is what gets saved, while the document's pending changes are not sent (`app.autoSave.saveNow()` is never reached and `preventDefault` is never called).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Ctrl+S / Cmd+S saves (calls `saveNow()` and `preventDefault`) with CapsLock on and on non-Latin layouts — the match is on the physical key (e.g. `event.code === "KeyS"`) or an equivalently layout/case-independent normalization, not on the produced character alone.
- [ ] Ctrl+Shift+S / Cmd+Shift+S does **not** trigger save: the editor's `Mod-Shift-s` strikethrough binding (editor.ts keymap) keeps that combination, so the save predicate must still exclude real Shift (`shiftKey`) presses.
- [ ] Plain `s` typing and Ctrl+other-key combinations do not trigger a save.
- [ ] New unit tests cover the save predicate for at least: `key:"s"` control, CapsLock `key:"S"` with `shiftKey:false`, a non-Latin `key:"ы"` with `code:"KeyS"`, and the Ctrl+Shift+S exclusion. (The handler currently lives inline in `main.ts`, which runs `init()` on import — extracting a small tested predicate, as `world-keyboard.ts` already does for the world view, is an acceptable shape.)
- [ ] Existing web unit tests still pass.

body:
## Summary

`id(petname)`: `Petnames::open` (`pkgs/id/src/petname.rs`) accepts a **parseable** torn final line — a complete petname record JSON whose trailing newline was lost to a crash mid-append — and the next `commit()` append glues the new record onto that same line. The resulting file can never be opened again: the glued line is unparseable, so `Petnames::open` fails fatally with "petname journal line N is malformed", and because `open_world` propagates that error (`world_store.rs:389`), **the whole world bricks** until someone hand-edits `petnames.jsonl`.

This is exactly the failure #1620 fixed for the envelope outbox ("a parseable torn tail is accepted, then merged into the next record") and #2947 filed for the group log. The sibling rule those fixes established — *an unterminated final line is torn, parseable or not, and is dropped and truncated at open* — was never applied to `Petnames`. #1499 (still open) covers `Petnames` only for the **unparseable** fragment case; its acceptance criteria drop only a final line that is "unterminated **and** unparseable", so a parseable torn tail survives that fix and still glues.

## Evidence (main `106b0571`)

- `Petnames::commit` (petname.rs:184-193) writes one JSON line + `\n` in a single `write_all` followed by `sync_data`, so a crash/power loss during that write can leave the full JSON with only its `\n` missing.
- `Petnames::open` (petname.rs:53-79) replays with `text.lines()` (line 63), which yields the final unterminated line like any other; a parseable record is applied via `store.apply(record)` with no completeness check and no truncation/repair — there is no torn-tail handling in the function at all.
- The next `set`/`remove` → `commit()` then appends its line directly after the unterminated one, merging two JSON records onto one line, and reports success.
- On the next open, that merged line fails `serde_json::from_str` and the open returns "petname journal line {N} is malformed". `open_world` (`world_store.rs:389`) propagates the failure, so every world open fails the same way.
- Contrast the established sibling rule: `Outbox::open` (envelope_outbox.rs:141-161) drops an unterminated final line "Parseable or not … Keeping a parseable torn line would let the next append merge two records onto one line and brick the queue (#1620)"; `Directory::replay` (directory.rs, #1521) and `ArtifactLog::open` (artifact.rs) drop and truncate the same way.

## Verified (laptop probe, real `petname.rs`)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-petparse/` on the laptop, compiling the **real** `petname.rs` (sha256 `ff6cba651a19ad5814a2540df12433d1444b44ff5fb258a8478cb891be88723e`, identical to the sandbox checkout at main `106b0571`) against a stub `directory::Refusal`; `cargo run` exit 0:

```
control journal bytes: "{\"op\":\"set\",\"owner\":\"00ff\",\"account\":\"aa11aa11\",\"name\":\"Ali\"}\n"
CONTROL clean journal: open OK, Ali=Some("Ali")
PARSEABLE TORN TAIL: open OK, Carol=Some("Carol") (accepted despite no newline)
AFTER NEXT APPEND bytes: "{\"op\":\"set\",\"owner\":\"00ff\",\"account\":\"aa11aa11\",\"name\":\"Ali\"}\n{\"op\":\"set\",\"owner\":\"00ff\",\"account\":\"cc33cc33\",\"name\":\"Carol\"}{\"op\":\"set\",\"owner\":\"00ff\",\"account\":\"dd44dd44\",\"name\":\"Dave\"}\n"
REOPEN AFTER APPEND: open FAILED: petname journal line 2 is malformed: trailing characters at line 1 column 64
```

- Control: a healthy newline-terminated journal opens and replays.
- Case: after appending a complete record with only its trailing `\n` stripped (the crash cut), reopen **accepts** Carol; the next `set` (Dave) succeeds but glues onto Carol's line; the final reopen is **bricked**.

## Why it matters

`petnames.jsonl` is a small private store, but `open_world` loads it on the world-open path, so one unlucky crash during a petname rename converts a recoverable one-byte tear into a permanently unopenable world on the next ordinary write — silently (the append reports success). Three sibling stores in the same crate already encode the correct rule with regression tests; `Petnames` is the remaining store that doesn't, and the open #1499 fix as scoped does not close this parseable half.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Petnames::open` treats an unterminated final line as torn **whether or not it parses**: the line is dropped and the file is truncated to the last complete line — mirroring `Outbox::open` (#1620) — ideally coordinated with the #1499 fix so both torn cases land in one replay rewrite (`split_inclusive('\n')`).
- [ ] Regression test in `petname.rs` mirroring the outbox's `a_parseable_torn_last_line_is_also_dropped`: write a valid record, strip only its trailing newline, reopen (record dropped, file truncated), set a new petname, reopen again and replay successfully.
- [ ] Existing behavior unchanged: a newline-terminated line that does not parse stays fatal with the line-numbered error; blank lines still skipped; healthy journals set/remove/reopen exactly as before.
- [ ] Related, do not duplicate: #1499 (Petnames unparseable torn tail — open; this is its parseable sibling case), #2947 (group log parseable torn tail — open, same pattern), #1620 (outbox parseable torn tail — closed), #1521 (directory torn tail — closed).

body:
## Summary

`handleLaunchFailure` (pm-stack/dispatch/src/launch_failure.ts, added for #2901) always tells the tracking issue the queue task "was cancelled" — even when the cancellation itself failed. The task is then still queued/claimed (exactly the orphaned-task state #2901 was filed to eliminate), while the only human-visible record says it was cancelled, so nobody goes looking for it.

## Evidence (main 70b2cec2)

- `pm-stack/dispatch/src/launch_failure.ts:30-48`: `cancelTask` is awaited inside a `try` whose `catch` discards the error and records nothing; the GitHub comment at :41 is then unconditionally `` `Dispatch launch FAILED and queue task #${taskId} was cancelled.` `` — the wording does not depend on whether the cancellation succeeded.
- The module header (:10-12) promises both steps are best-effort and independent — that part works — but the note's content asserts the first step's outcome instead of reporting it.
- Existing test `pm-stack/dispatch/test/launch_failure.test.ts` ("still notes the issue when the cancellation itself fails", stub `failCancel=true`) asserts only that the comment contains the launch error string; it never asserts what the comment says about the cancellation, so the false claim is unpinned.

## Verified this run (laptop probe)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-launchfail/`, verbatim copy of the file from main 70b2cec2, run with bun): a queue stub whose `cancelTask` throws `queue unreachable`, a GitHub stub capturing the comment, launch error `opencode refused the session`:

```text
returned msg: opencode refused the session
comment body: "Dispatch launch FAILED and queue task #4242 was cancelled.\n\nError: opencode refused the session"
comment claims cancelled: true
```

The cancellation never happened; the note says it did.

## Why it matters

#2901's failure mode was a launch failure leaving a task queued forever with no usable signal. This sub-case recreates it with a worse signal: an authoritative-looking note stating the cleanup already happened. Queue reconciliation then has to contradict the issue record to find the orphan.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] When `cancelTask` succeeds, the issue note keeps saying the task was cancelled.
- [ ] When `cancelTask` fails, the note says the cancellation FAILED (and that the task may still be queued/claimed and needs cleanup), including the cancellation error if available.
- [ ] The returned message / 502 path for wait:true does not claim cancellation on failure either, if it mentions it.
- [ ] Regression test: extend the `failCancel=true` case in launch_failure.test.ts to assert the comment's cancellation wording (and keep the success-case wording pinned).
- [ ] Header comment updated so the best-effort contract states the note reports each step's actual outcome.

Found by new-issue-creator-code-a (Lane A), 2026-10-30 run. Related: #2901 (the fix this helper came from), #2660 (different post-claim cancellation path).

body:
## Finding

`POST /v1/sessions` in pm-dispatch accepts a caller-supplied `directory` with no validation, and launches the OpenCode session there. For GitHub Actions OIDC callers — whose whole security model is repo scoping — this silently escapes the repo: any workflow in an allowlisted repo can start a session in **any directory on the laptop**, not just its own repo's clone.

## Evidence

- PR #2650 (commit `19f12cb2e2`, MERGED) introduced the service and the field.
- The OIDC boundary, `pm-stack/dispatch/src/auth.ts`: "The token's `repository` claim must be in the allowlist AND equal the request body's repo — a workflow can only dispatch for its own repo", enforced by `assertCallerRepo`.
- But on current main (`c4fb599617166d4c705eabeb34442ca179ecb9a6`):
  - `src/validate.ts:126` — `directory: optString(b, "directory")`: any non-empty string passes; no allowlist, no equality check against the repo's directory.
  - `src/server.ts:175` — `const directory = body.directory ?? REPO_DIRS[body.repo]!;` used verbatim.
  - `src/opencode.ts:59` — the session is created with `location: { directory: opts.directory }`, so the session's agent tools operate with that directory as their working root.
- `REPO_DIRS` (`src/config.ts`) maps each repo to exactly one laptop primary clone — the scoping the `directory` field bypasses. The packet built for the task even records `scope.include` as just the repo, while the session itself runs elsewhere.

## Why it matters

The static bearer token is the operator's own credential and is trusted accordingly; the OIDC path exists specifically so a repo's workflows can dispatch *for that repo only*. An unrestricted `directory` makes the repo claim decorative for the one thing that matters — where the agent session actually works. A compromised or over-eager workflow in any allowlisted repo could run a session in another repo's clone (cross-repo writes the packet scope explicitly excludes) or in a non-repo directory on the laptop.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] For OIDC callers, `directory` must be absent or equal to `REPO_DIRS[repo]`; anything else is rejected (400/403) before any issue/task/session is created.
- [ ] For bearer callers, the behaviour is a deliberate, documented choice: either the same restriction, or the README's `directory` entry is updated to state that bearer callers may override the directory and OIDC callers may not.
- [ ] Tests cover: OIDC caller + foreign directory → rejected; OIDC caller + omitted/own directory → accepted; the bearer case per the documented decision.

Found by the pr-diff-review job reviewing PR #2650 (batch 2630–2658, 2026-10-30). Deduped: `gh issue list --search 'dispatch directory'` and `'pm-dispatch directory validate'` (open + all) returned nothing covering this (only unrelated dispatch-workflow PRs).

body:
## Finding

In pm-dispatch (`pm-stack/dispatch`), a failed session launch on the `wait:false` path is **not** cleaned up: the queue task is left queued and the tracking issue is never noted. Only the `wait:true` path cancels the task and notes the issue — the exact behaviour PR #2650's description promises for failed launches generally ("a failed launch cancels the task and notes the issue").

## Evidence

- PR #2650 (commit `19f12cb2e2`, MERGED) introduced the service. Its body states: "`wait:false` answers `202` after the enqueue and finishes the launch asynchronously; a failed launch cancels the task and notes the issue."
- Verified on current main (`c4fb599617166d4c705eabeb34442ca179ecb9a6`), `pm-stack/dispatch/src/server.ts:222-240`: the async catch only does `patchTask(task.id, { last_error: "dispatch launch failed: …" })`. No `cancelTask`, no issue comment.
- Contrast the same file's `wait:true` path (~line 246+), whose comment states the invariant the async path violates: "Never leave a queued/claimed task behind for a session that did not launch: cancel it and note the failure on the issue."

## Why it matters

- The task stays `queued`, so a queue worker can claim and execute the packet — while in the partial-failure case (launch got as far as `createSession` + `sendPrompt` and failed afterwards, e.g. at the claim PATCH) a live OpenCode session is *also* working the same prompt. That is the double-booking the immediate-claim design exists to prevent.
- The caller received `202 {status: "launching"}` and the tracking issue says nothing further; the failure exists only as `last_error` on a still-queued task row, indistinguishable from a normally-queued dispatch at a glance.
- Follow-up PRs #2652/#2655/#2658 fixed three other launch-path defects found by deploy smoke tests (envelope, worker FK, lane ledger); none touched this branch.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The `wait:false` async failure path mirrors the `wait:true` one: `cancelTask(task.id, …)` is called and, when a tracking issue exists, a comment records that the launch failed and the task was cancelled.
- [ ] A regression test (stubbed queue/opencode clients, as in the existing `test/` suite) covers a `wait:false` launch failure and asserts the cancellation + issue note.
- [ ] The README's description of `wait:false` failure behaviour matches the implementation.

Found by the pr-diff-review job reviewing PR #2650 (batch 2630–2658, 2026-10-30). Deduped: `gh issue list --search 'pm-dispatch wait launch cancel'` and `'wait:false dispatch'` (open + all) returned nothing covering this.

body:
## Finding

PR #2630 re-added a **workflow-level** concurrency group to `.github/workflows/jules.yml` — the exact construct the file's own header comment says must not exist (#304).

## Evidence

- PR #2630 (commit `814c5146ad`, MERGED) added, as part of a blanket "cancel-in-progress everywhere" pass:

  ```yaml
  concurrency:
    group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
    cancel-in-progress: true
  ```

- Verified on current main (`c4fb599617166d4c705eabeb34442ca179ecb9a6`), `.github/workflows/jules.yml:35-43` — the comment directly above the added block still reads:

  > No workflow-level concurrency group (#304): for workflow_run events github.ref is the default branch, so one shared group let any noise completion cancel a pending ci-failure-fix run (queue: single). Each job carries its own group below, keyed by its target, so a run whose jobs all skip can never displace a run that would act.

- The contradiction is live, not historical: all three current triggers (`schedule`, `issues`, `workflow_dispatch`) resolve `github.ref` to the default branch, so every jules run shares the one workflow-level group `jules-refs/heads/main` with `cancel-in-progress: true`. A new run therefore cancels an in-progress run at the workflow level, defeating the per-job groups below it (`weekly-cleanup`, `issue-labeled`, `manual` — each `cancel-in-progress: false`, `queue: max`), which exist precisely so unrelated events queue instead of displacing each other.

## Why it matters

An `issues`-labeled noise event or a manual dispatch can silently cancel a scheduled/manual dispatch run that is mid-flight — the #304 failure mode, reintroduced by a blanket policy pass that did not read the in-file rule it was overwriting. The other workflows touched by #2630 only had their existing values flipped; jules.yml is the one that gained a brand-new workflow-level block against a documented prohibition.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The workflow-level `concurrency:` block is removed from `.github/workflows/jules.yml` (restoring the #304 state), OR it is re-keyed per event/target with `cancel-in-progress: false` and the #304 header comment is updated to match the new, deliberate design.
- [ ] The per-job concurrency groups (`weekly-cleanup`, `issue-labeled`, `manual`) are unchanged.
- [ ] A grep over `.github/workflows/` confirms no other workflow carries a workflow-level group that contradicts an in-file comment stating it must not have one.

Found by the pr-diff-review job reviewing PR #2630 (batch 2630–2658, 2026-10-30). Deduped: `gh issue list --search 'jules concurrency workflow-level'` (open + all) returned nothing covering this.

body:
# mcpx(daemon): `/v1/complete` never applies the 100-value spec cap — local fallback honors an unclamped `completion.maxValues` (0 = unlimited), upstream replies pass through verbatim

## Summary

The MCP specification caps a completion reply at 100 values (`CompleteResult.values`, `@maxItems 100` in the 2026 schema; prose in every earlier revision). The MCP-server surface enforces it; the daemon's HTTP `/v1/complete` surface does not — on either of its two reply paths. The same setting therefore produces a conforming reply over MCP and a non-conforming one over `/v1`.

## Evidence (main `c6564aa2`)

**Local (cache) fallback — the setting is applied raw:**

- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/ops.go:390-391` — `handleComplete` passes `cs.Int("completion.maxValues")` straight into `localCompletion`.
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/ops.go:427` — `localCompletion` truncates only `if max > 0 && len(values) > max`, to `max` itself. Nothing clamps `max` to 100, and `max <= 0` means *no truncation at all*.
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/settings/value.go:312` — `Set.Int` is a bare `strconv.Atoi`; there is no range validation for this setting anywhere.
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/settings/wire.go:185-191` — the setting's own help text says: "The MCP specification caps a completion reply at one hundred. Lower is legal; higher is not, and a server that sends more is sending something a conforming client will reject." It is user-settable (flag `--completion-max-values`, env `MCPX_COMPLETION_MAX_VALUES`, config) with default 100.

So with `completion.maxValues=250` and ≥101 cached prompt names / resource template URIs matching, `/v1/complete` returns up to 250 values. With `completion.maxValues=0` it returns every match, unbounded.

**Upstream passthrough — no cap at all:**

- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/ops.go:381-388` — when the upstream server answers, its `completion` payload is forwarded verbatim (`payload = res.Completion`); values/total/hasMore are never inspected, let alone truncated. An upstream that returns 250 values is relayed as 250 values.

**The MCP surface does it right (the contrast that proves the daemon path is the outlier):**

- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/mcpserver/server.go:2657-2669` — the same hot setting is read per request and then clamped: `if max > specMaxCompletions { max = specMaxCompletions }`, with `specMaxCompletions = 100` (`server.go:2695-2697`), and a non-positive setting keeps the 100 default instead of disabling the cap.

**Corroboration in-repo:** `pkgs/mcpx/docs/compare/register/completion.md` row CMP-06 already records that "`/v1/complete` passes an upstream's `completion` through without applying the cap" and that a value above 100 "fails 2026 schema validation" — but no issue tracks fixing the daemon surface (searched open + closed for CMP-06 / completion cap / localCompletion: only the #2386 design family, whose Phase 3 #2389 is a register truth-up for the rate-limit/security rows, out of scope for this cap).

## Verification this run

Code-read verification (the truncation arithmetic is deterministic in the source above), cross-checked against the MCP-server clamp and the CMP-06 register row. A laptop probe of `localCompletion` with `max=250` / 150 candidates could not be run this run: `~/tools/laptop-ssh.sh` failed on every attempt ("Connection closed by UNKNOWN port 65535") and sandbox builds are prohibited by fleet rule, so no probe result is claimed. The fix's regression test (below) is the executable proof.

## Why it matters

- A conforming (especially 2026-schema-validating) client can reject the whole completion reply, so completion silently breaks exactly for users who raised the setting or use a sloppy upstream — the two cases the cap exists for.
- The two surfaces disagree about the same setting, which is the class of divergence the hot-setting plumbing (`Server.MaxCompletions`, wp11 test) was built to eliminate on the MCP side.
- `max=0` disabling truncation entirely is a footgun with no documented meaning; on the MCP side 0 means "use the default".

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `/v1/complete` local fallback never returns more than 100 values, whatever `completion.maxValues` is set to; a setting of 0 or negative behaves like the MCP surface (default 100 applies), a setting between 1 and 100 still lowers the cap, and `total`/`hasMore` keep reporting the full ranked match count.
- [ ] `/v1/complete` upstream passthrough truncates an over-cap upstream reply to the effective cap and recomputes `total`/`hasMore` consistently (or documents and tests a deliberate alternative).
- [ ] Regression tests in `internal/daemon` cover: setting >100 with >100 matches, setting 0, setting below 100 (unchanged behavior), and an upstream reply with >100 values. Existing completion tests (`completion_rank_test.go`, handler tests) still pass.
- [ ] The fix routes both daemon paths through one shared cap computation with the MCP surface (or a shared constant), so the surfaces cannot drift again.

Related: #2386 (completion design epic), #2388 (ranked local completion — its cap-after-ranking behavior is preserved; this issue is only about the cap's ceiling), CMP-06 in `docs/compare/register/completion.md`.

title: id(world-manifest): unknown or misspelled world.toml keys are silently ignored — a typo'd grants/ceiling revocation parses clean, plans zero steps, and diff reports 'no drift'

body:
## Problem

`id world apply` / `id world diff` parse `world.toml` with `world_manifest::parse` (`pkgs/id/src/world_manifest.rs:151`), but `WorldManifest` is `#[serde(default, rename_all = "snake_case")]` (`world_manifest.rs:27-28`) with **no `deny_unknown_fields`** — and neither is the nested `WorldExecutionProfile` (`pkgs/id/src/world_limits.rs:39`, also `#[serde(default)]` only). Any misspelled or unknown key is silently dropped, so the manifest the admin wrote is not the manifest that is applied:

- A revocation written with a typo — `grant = []` instead of `grants = []`, `ceilin = []`, `schedule = {}` — parses cleanly, plans **zero steps**, and `diff` reports **"no drift"**. The admin believes every grant/ceiling entry was revoked; the world keeps them all.
- A typo inside `[profile]` (`wasm_fuell = 1`) likewise vanishes: the profile stays the all-default (inherit-everything) profile and no `SetProfile` step is ever planned.
- A typo'd `seeds = 99` next to a matching `module_hash` plans no reinstall, silently keeping the old seed.

`validate()` (world_manifest.rs) carefully refuses bad values for fields it *knows* (unknown capability names, bad hashes, zero fire times) — but a misspelled field name never reaches it.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `de59b343`)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-manifestunknown/`): real `world_manifest.rs` (md5 `7b3e4e0a…`) and real `world_caps.rs` (md5 `ac9d6bd5…`) copied from main, `WorldExecutionProfile` stubbed field-for-field from `world_limits.rs`; `cargo run` rc=0:

- CONTROL: `grants = []` / `ceiling = []` / `schedules = {}` against a populated `WorldState` (grants `[chat.say, time.now]`, ceiling same, one schedule) → **3 steps** `[set_grants, set_ceiling, cancel_schedule]`.
- CONTROL: `grants = ["time.nwo"]` → parse **error** (known-field validation works).
- CASE A: `grant = []` / `ceilin = []` / `schedule = {}` → parse Ok, all three fields `None`, **steps=0, diff="no drift"**.
- CASE B: `bogus_key = 12345` → parse Ok, steps=0.
- CASE C: `[profile] wasm_fuell = 1` → parse Ok, `wasm_fuel=None`, profile is default, steps=0.
- CASE D: `module_hash = "abc123"` + `seeds = 99` (state hash `abc123`, seed 7) → `seed=None`, steps=0.

Call path: `src/commands/world.rs:465,483` (`apply`/`diff`) → `parse_manifest_file` (`world.rs:861-864`) → `world_manifest::parse`.

## Why it matters

The manifest is the declarative, authoritative description of a world's grants, capability ceiling, execution profile and schedules — the security-relevant knobs of the world system. A one-character typo in the field that *narrows* access currently fails in the dangerous direction: silently, with a success-looking "no drift" / no-op apply. Strictness here is cheap and matches the house pattern: sibling wire/config structs in the same codebase already use `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` (e.g. `chain.rs` `Wire`, `documents.rs` `DocumentRef`, `seitan/accept.rs` `Wire`, `server_config/parse.rs`).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `world_manifest::parse` rejects a manifest with an unknown top-level key, naming the offending key in the error (e.g. via `deny_unknown_fields` on `WorldManifest`).
- [ ] An unknown key inside `[profile]` is likewise rejected (`WorldExecutionProfile` gains the same strictness, or the manifest parser validates profile keys explicitly) — without breaking the profile's JSON round-trip through `commands/world.rs` (`serde_json::from_value` at world.rs:889 and the host report path), which must be checked for extra keys the host legitimately sends.
- [ ] Tests: typo'd `grants`/`ceiling`/`schedules`/`seed` keys fail parse; a correctly spelled manifest (including the existing round-trip test manifest) still parses and round-trips unchanged.
- [ ] `id world diff` on a typo'd manifest surfaces the parse error instead of printing "no drift".

## Dedup notes

Related but distinct: #2166 (module_hash `blake3:<hex>` doc form that validate rejects — a documented form failing, not unknown keys being dropped). No open or closed issue covers unknown/misspelled manifest keys.

title: kill-collector drill: restore trap fires on precondition refusals — a refused drill still starts the collector (PR #1823)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: app/pm-stack
labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

body:
## Finding

The kill-collector chaos drill installs its restore trap **before** its precondition checks, so a drill that *refuses to start* still "restores" — starting the collector timer and immediately running the collector service. That contradicts the drill's own interlock contract and can mask exactly the real incidents the preconditions exist to protect.

## Evidence

- Source PR: #1823 (merged, merge commit `1720d64b308905f70b445029b993488dc142fd40`) — https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/1823
- Verified still present on current main `074485713b11745c5164a131aac6e80305abd228`, `pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/kill-collector-drill.sh`:
  - Line 9 (header contract): "Interlocks (any failure = refuse to start, **nothing is touched**)"
  - Lines 108–114: `restore()` runs `systemctl start "$COLLECTOR_TIMER"` **and** `systemctl start "$COLLECTOR_SERVICE"` (an immediate collection run).
  - Line 115: `trap restore EXIT INT TERM` — installed here.
  - Lines 118–122: the preconditions run *after* the trap is installed, and each failure path calls `die`, which `exit 1`s — firing the EXIT trap and therefore `restore()`:
    - line 118: collector timer not active — the script itself says "a stopped collector outside a drill is itself a finding", yet the trap silently restarts it and starts a collection, erasing that finding;
    - line 121: aggregator health unreadable — the drill "refuses to drill blind" but still starts the collector service blind;
    - line 122: feed already stale — explicitly "a real incident, not a drill", yet the trap starts an immediate collection run that can freshen the feed and interfere with / mask that incident.

## Why it matters

The drill runs on a weekly timer against the live PM stack. Its safety story is that interlock failures are pure refusals. As written, the three most safety-relevant refusals all mutate the system they refused to touch — worst case during a real stale-feed incident, where an unrequested collection run changes the evidence and the state an incident responder would see.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `restore()` only runs once the drill has actually stopped the collector (e.g. trap installed after the kill step, or restore gated on a `KILLED`/`STOPPED` flag set only after both `systemctl stop` calls succeed).
- [ ] Every precondition/interlock refusal (timer inactive, health unreadable, feed already stale, incident flag, lock held) exits without any `systemctl start` of the timer or service — verifiable by a stubbed-`systemctl`/`sudo` test harness or shell test that records invocations per refusal path.
- [ ] A drill that does kill the collector still restores exactly as today (trap on EXIT/INT/TERM plus the explicit restore + confirmation), and the result JSON / reporting behaviour is unchanged.
- [ ] Header comment updated if the resulting contract differs from "any failure = refuse to start, nothing is touched".

body:
# aggregator(cost-explorer): a setup named `__proto__` is silently never saved — the setups store assigns into a plain object, so the name becomes the store's prototype instead of an entry

## Evidence (main `f318fd59`)

The cost explorer's saved-setups store in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/render.ts` keeps setups in a plain object parsed from localStorage:

- `loadSetups()` (:4321) returns `JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("xpl-setups-v1") || "{}")` — a plain object carrying `Object.prototype`.
- Save handler (:4338): `all[name] = captureSetup();` then `storeSetups(all)` (:4324, `JSON.stringify`).
- Import handler (:4359): `Object.keys(parsed).forEach(function (k) { all[k] = parsed[k]; });` then `storeSetups(all)`.

Assignment `obj["__proto__"] = value` does not create an own property — it sets the object's prototype. So a setup whose name is exactly `__proto__` never becomes an entry:

### Verified (laptop probe, verbatim save/import logic; `render.ts` md5 `2f629fd585f6f281cb3be63ce55ce337` on sandbox main, assignment lines identical in the laptop clone)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-xplproto/` (`probe.mjs`, `probe2.mjs`)

Save path:
- save `Normal` → stored keys `["Normal"]`
- save `constructor` → stored keys `["Normal","constructor"]` (control: assignment *does* shadow for other prototype spellings)
- save `__proto__` → stored keys still `["Normal","constructor"]`; the stored JSON has no `__proto__` entry — **the setup is silently lost**, and the setup list (`refreshSetupList`, `Object.keys(loadSetups())`) never shows it.

Import path (file text built as a raw string, the way FileReader delivers it):
- `JSON.parse` itself preserves the entry: parsed own keys are `["__proto__","Real"]`.
- After the import loop, `Object.keys(all)` is `["Real"]` only; `all.tab === "polluted-tab"` and `Object.getPrototypeOf(all)` **is** the imported `__proto__` value — the assignment mutated the store object's prototype instead of storing the entry.
- The persisted JSON after import is `{"Real":{...}}` — the `__proto__` setup is silently dropped on import too.

## Why it matters

- Silent data loss in both directions of the setups feature: a user who names a setup `__proto__` (or imports a setups file containing one) loses it with no error, and the UI gives no signal — the name just never appears in the list.
- The import path additionally mutates the in-memory store's prototype for the rest of that handler's lifetime.
- This is the *write-side* counterpart of the own-key lookup design #2792, which explicitly puts write-side `__proto__` handling out of its scope ("write-side `__proto__` pollution is a different bug class"); the one filed write-side instance is #2828 (`bin/record.mjs` loose parser). This store is a separate instance in a separate surface (browser localStorage + file import).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Saving a setup named `__proto__` persists it: it appears in the setup list, survives reload (localStorage round-trip), and exports like any other setup — or the name is rejected with a visible signal; silent loss is the bug.
- [ ] Importing a setups file with a `__proto__` entry stores it as an entry (or visibly skips it); the store object's prototype is never mutated by save or import.
- [ ] Controls unchanged: `Normal`, `constructor`, `toString` setup names save/import/export exactly as before.
- [ ] A regression check covers the probe matrix (`__proto__`, `constructor`, ordinary name) across save → store → reload → export and across import.

body:
## Summary

Seven of the nine `bin/*-proxy.mjs` chat proxies **crash the whole process** on a
`POST /v1/chat/completions` whose body is valid JSON but not an object — the
literal `null`. Each handler `JSON.parse`s the body inside a try/catch (so
malformed JSON correctly gets a 400), but then dereferences the parsed value
without checking it is an object, so `null` throws a `TypeError` outside any
guard and Node exits. One malformed request from any client therefore kills a
long-lived fleet proxy until its supervisor restarts it.

The other two proxies already do this right and are the in-repo pattern to copy:

- `bin/clef-proxy.mjs:211` — `if (!body || typeof body !== 'object')` → 400
  "Invalid JSON body: expected an object", process stays up.
- `bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs:709` — `if (!isPlainObject(body))` → 400
  "request body must be a JSON object", process stays up.

## Evidence (main `c90fcbc7`, verified this run)

First unguarded dereference after `JSON.parse` in each affected handler:

| proxy | first deref |
|---|---|
| `bin/design-code-proxy.mjs` | `dispatchWithFallback` reads `body.model` at :247 (called from :236) |
| `bin/codex-proxy.mjs` | `Boolean(body.stream)` at :1088 |
| `bin/claude-code-proxy.mjs` | `Array.isArray(body.messages)` at :723 |
| `bin/agy-proxy.mjs` | `Boolean(body.stream)` at :847 |
| `bin/antigravity-ls-proxy.mjs` | `Boolean(body.stream)` at :770 |
| `bin/commandcode-proxy.mjs` | `Boolean(body.stream)` at :903 |
| `bin/muse-proxy.mjs` | `Boolean(body.stream)` at :1601 |

Probe (laptop, real modules, files md5-identical to main; probe dir
`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-nullbody/`): each proxy was spawned on a
scratch port, given a malformed-JSON control (`{bad json` → HTTP 400, process
alive in all nine), then `POST /v1/chat/completions` with body `null`:

- All seven above: fetch failed with `UND_ERR_SOCKET`, **process exited with
  code 1** (uncaught `TypeError` stack naming the deref line above).
- Controls: clef-proxy (`POST /v1/systemone`) and opencode-route-proxy both
  answered **HTTP 400 and stayed alive**.

Secondary (code-read, not probed): non-object scalars/arrays take inconsistent
paths instead of a uniform 400 — e.g. an array body reaches design-code's
dispatch with `body.model === undefined`, and `resolveModelConfig`
(`bin/design-code-proxy.mjs`, `requestedModel || 'design-code-pro'`) silently
substitutes the default model for a body that was never a chat request.

## Why it matters

These proxies are long-lived fleet infrastructure (supervised, shared by many
sessions). A single stray `null` body — a buggy client, a health-check tool, a
hand-rolled curl — takes the proxy down for every routed session, and the
failure mode (process exit, socket reset) points at the proxy rather than at
the bad request, so it is hard to attribute after the fact. The two guarded
siblings prove the intended contract: a non-object body is a client error
(400), never a process exit.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every `bin/*-proxy.mjs` JSON POST handler (chat completions at minimum;
      audit the other JSON POST routes in the same files) rejects a parsed
      body that is not a plain object with that proxy's existing 400 error
      shape, before any property dereference.
- [ ] `null`, array, string, and number bodies all get the 400; the process
      stays alive and answers a subsequent valid request.
- [ ] Each affected proxy's `bin/*.test.mjs` gains a regression test in the
      existing harness style: non-object body → 400 and the proxy still
      serves afterwards (the clef / opencode-route behaviour is the oracle).
- [ ] No behaviour change for object bodies, malformed JSON (still 400 from
      the parse catch), or the guarded clef / opencode-route proxies.

title: cold-store-reaper: resumable upload loops forever on a 308 whose Range stops advancing — no progress check or retry cap, and a Range-less 308 counts unacknowledged bytes as sent

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.description: Package/app: cold-store-reaper (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

`ColdStore._resumable_upload` (`pkgs/cold-store-reaper/cold_store.py:812-843`, main `c90fcbc7`) loops on HTTP 308 with no progress check, no retry cap, and no stall detection:

```python
while sent < total or total == 0:
    ...
    if status == 308:
        range_hdr = headers.get("Range") or headers.get("range") or ""
        try:
            sent = int(range_hdr.rsplit("-", 1)[1]) + 1
        except (IndexError, ValueError):
            sent += len(chunk)
        f.seek(sent)
        continue
```

Two verified failure modes in the same loop:

1. **A 308 whose `Range` stops advancing loops forever.** `sent` is recomputed from the server's acknowledged range on every iteration, so if Drive keeps answering `308 Range: bytes=0-0` (session wedged, bytes landing nowhere), `sent` is pinned at 1 and the client re-PUTs the same chunk indefinitely — no maximum attempts, no requirement that `sent` increase, no backoff. The upload never fails, never finishes, and the nightly job hangs while hammering the Drive API.
2. **A 308 with no `Range` header is treated as if the whole chunk landed.** The fallback `sent += len(chunk)` assumes bytes the server never acknowledged (per the Drive resumable protocol, a 308 without `Range` means zero bytes received so far). For a single-chunk file the client then exits the loop and reports `upload finished without a file id` — a misleading error that hides the actual incomplete upload; for a multi-chunk file it skips unacknowledged bytes and only the post-upload md5 check in `upload()` catches the resulting corruption, after the whole file has been sent.

The existing fake-Drive test (`tests/test_cold_store.py:186-212`) always returns a `Range` that advances by exactly the bytes received, so neither case is exercised.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `c90fcbc7`)

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-coldstore308/`, real module imported from the laptop clone; `cold_store.py` md5 `882a83a1d80b409192d5ae1db3ccb975` matches the sandbox clone). Transport monkeypatched; no credentials involved:

```
probe.py  (PUT always -> 308, Range: bytes=0-0; sentinel cap at 30 PUTs)
RESULT: PROBE-CAP: 30 PUTs reached, loop still going
PUTs issued: 31 (file is 1000 bytes, chunk cap 8MiB -> a healthy upload needs 1-2 PUTs)

probe2.py (PUT always -> 308, no Range header)
RESULT: ColdStoreError: upload finished without a file id
PUTs issued: 1 (server acknowledged 0 bytes, yet the client treated the chunk as sent and left the loop)
```

Dedup: title + keyword search over open and closed issues (`cold-store resumable`, `308`, `upload loop`) finds nothing covering this loop — #2733 is the S3 list-page parser in the same package, #938 (closed) was upload-limit enforcement in `upload()`/`put_backup`.

## Why it matters

cold-store-reaper is the fleet's backup path to Drive; its uploads run unattended (nightly). A wedged resumable session currently turns into an infinite, silent PUT loop instead of a failure the job can report and retry tomorrow — the bundle stays in `uploading` state and the run never completes. The missing-`Range` fallback additionally misreports an incomplete upload as a finished one.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `_resumable_upload` terminates with a `ColdStoreError` when a 308 response does not advance the acknowledged offset (no-progress detection), and/or after a bounded number of 308 retries — a stuck session fails the upload instead of looping forever.
- [ ] A 308 with a missing or unparseable `Range` header no longer assumes the whole chunk was received; the client re-sends from the last server-acknowledged offset (or queries the session status, per the Drive resumable protocol) — triage pins the exact approach.
- [ ] Tests extend the fake-Drive coverage with (a) a 308 whose `Range` never advances and (b) a 308 with no `Range` header; the existing resumable-upload tests still pass.
- [ ] Healthy-path behavior is unchanged: advancing 308s resume from the acknowledged byte, and a completed upload still returns the file id.

body:
# cloudflare-export: num() reinterprets empty, hex and scientific strings as real measurements — a drifted '' request count exports as a measured 0

## Evidence (verified this run, main `da42bfe7`)

`pm-stack/cloudflare-export/cloudflare-quota-export.mjs`, `num()` (lines 85–92):

```js
const num = (v, field) => {
  const n = typeof v === "string" || typeof v === "number" ? Number(v) : NaN;
  if (!Number.isFinite(n) || n < 0) {
    throw new ExportError("unparseable", 6, `graphql: field ${field} not a finite non-negative number`);
  }
  return n;
};
```

The helper is the exporter's fail-closed gate for every GraphQL measurement it publishes — its error text promises that anything not "a finite non-negative number" aborts the tick as `unparseable` (exit 6) instead of reaching a `status: "ok"` document. But bare `Number()` accepts far more than the API's decimal spellings, so the gate passes values it exists to reject. Every measurement flows through it: R2 request counts (`classifyR2`, line 136), KV request counts (`foldKv`, line 161), the generic `firstSum` totals (line 173), and R2 storage `payloadSize` (line 216).

Probe (laptop, importing the real module — file md5 `0fbd8dae4f5eba83adb88ec6092d1039` identical on both clones; probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-cfnum/`; one `sum.requests` value mutated per case through `classifyR2` with actionType `PutObject`):

| input | result |
|---|---|
| `""` | **OK — classA = 0** (a drifted empty value exports as a measured zero) |
| `"   "` (whitespace) | **OK — classA = 0** |
| `"0x10"` | **OK — classA = 16** (hex reinterpreted) |
| `"1e2"` | **OK — classA = 100** (scientific reinterpreted) |
| `"1.5"` | **OK — classA = 1.5** (fractional request count) |
| `" 12 "` | **OK — classA = 12** (whitespace-trimmed by coercion) |
| controls: `"12abc"` / `"-3"` / `"Infinity"` | correctly throw `unparseable` (exit 6) |

`foldKv` shows the same hole (`requests: ""` → `reads = 0`, no throw).

## Why it matters

This exporter follows the PM stack's fail-closed design: a drifted upstream shape must produce a failed tick, never a plausible reading (compare `classifyR2`/`foldKv`'s own missing-groups guards in the same file, which throw precisely so a missing field is not published as zero). An empty-string count — the classic shape-drift / missing-value spelling from an upstream API — currently sails through `num()` because `Number("") === 0`, and is published in a `status: "ok"` document as a measured 0 requests / 0 payload bytes. The aggregator ingests that as fact, so real Cloudflare usage silently reads as zero exactly when the GraphQL API starts drifting. Hex and scientific spellings are silently reinterpreted into different numbers instead of failing closed, and a fractional "count" is published as-is.

## Acceptance criteria

- `num()` accepts only plain decimal spellings for string inputs (the GraphQL API's actual format): empty, whitespace-only or whitespace-padded, hex (`0x…`), scientific (`1e…`), and fractional strings throw `ExportError("unparseable", 6, …)` naming the field, at every call site (R2, KV, `firstSum`, R2 storage payload).
- Numeric (non-string) inputs keep working exactly as today, including the existing finite / non-negative checks; legitimate decimal-string counts (e.g. `"1200"`) still parse.
- New tests in `cloudflare-quota-export.test.mjs` cover: `""` and `"   "` request counts rejected; `"0x10"` / `"1e2"` / `"1.5"` rejected; a decimal-string control still accepted; all existing tests still pass (`node --test pm-stack/cloudflare-export/`).

## Dedup

- #2789 (open) is the same `Number()` pattern in meta-exporter's `parseSubscriptionQuota` — different app, file, and parser; its fix does not touch this exporter.
- #2743 (open) is the same pattern in supabase-export's `parseDbSize`/`parseRequestCount` — different app/file again.
- #2574 / #2608 (open) are this same file but different mechanisms (R2 bucket enumeration failing open; GraphQL `errors` shape handling) — neither covers `num()`'s string coercion.

body:
## Problem

`bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs` parses its per-request deadline with a bare `Number()`:

- `bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs:51` — `const TIMEOUT_MS = Number(process.env.OPENCODE_ROUTE_PROXY_TIMEOUT_MS || 1_200_000);`
- `bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs:535-538` — the value goes straight into `setTimeout(() => deadlineCtl.abort(...), TIMEOUT_MS)`, the deadline that bounds every routed chat-completion request.

The proxy starts up happily with a bad value — nothing validates it — and then the deadline fires almost immediately on **every** request. The client gets a 502 that looks like a leaf/transport failure, the leaf is never contacted, and the route-attempt ledger records the attempt as a timeout — so the failure is misattributed to the backend pool, not to local configuration.

This is the one fleet proxy whose timeout env var did not get the strict treatment its siblings got: the listen ports all go through `parseProxyPort` in `bin/proxy-port.mjs` (#483, which exists precisely because "a bare parseInt is not a validator"), commandcode-proxy's identical timeout bug is filed as #1809, and agy-proxy's is inside #2096. The route proxy's was missed.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `24ddc153`)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-routetimeout/`): the real `opencode-route-proxy.mjs` + `proxy-port.mjs` copied verbatim (md5 `19286417…` / `9b6fc7c1…`, matching main), spawned against a fake leaf that delays 300 ms before answering, with the fixture config/ledger shape from `bin/opencode-route-proxy.test.mjs`:

| `OPENCODE_ROUTE_PROXY_TIMEOUT_MS` | Proxy starts | POST `/v1/chat/completions` | Leaf hits | Ledger |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `15000` (control) | yes | **200** in 342 ms, leaf content returned | 1 | outcome `success` |
| `abc` | yes | **502** in 23 ms — `leaf transport error: opencode-route-proxy deadline` | 0 | outcome `timeout`, tag `Transport` |
| `3000000000` (> 2³¹−1) | yes | **502** in 23 ms, same error (plus Node `TimeoutOverflowWarning`: the value is clamped to 1 ms) | 0 | outcome `timeout`, tag `Transport` |
| `-5` | yes | **502** in 24 ms, same error | 0 | outcome `timeout`, tag `Transport` |

Mechanism: `Number("abc")` is `NaN`, and `setTimeout(NaN)` / `setTimeout(-5)` fire in ~0–1 ms; a value above 2³¹−1 is clamped by Node to 1 ms. Non-decimal spellings are silently reinterpreted instead of rejected (`Number("0x493e0")` = 300000, `Number("1e6")` = 1000000).

## Why it matters

- A single typo in the one env var that tunes this proxy takes the whole routing door down while it reports itself healthy (`/health` is local and still answers 200) and blames the leaves in the ledger — the worst shape of config failure for a fleet that debugs from the ledger.
- The route proxy is the routing-only door (#2518); its deadline is the only bound on a hung leaf attempt chain, so the value being silently wrong removes or falsifies that bound.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `OPENCODE_ROUTE_PROXY_TIMEOUT_MS` is strictly validated at startup (decimal integer milliseconds within a stated sane range — e.g. via a `proxy-port.mjs`-style helper shared with the fix for #1809 if that lands first): an invalid value exits at startup with an error naming the variable and its value, like `parseProxyPort` does for ports.
- [ ] Valid values behave exactly as today (default 1,200,000 ms when unset/empty).
- [ ] Tests in `bin/opencode-route-proxy.test.mjs` (or the shared helper's tests) cover at least: `abc`, a negative value, and a value above 2³¹−1 — each refused at startup — plus a valid small value still enforcing a real deadline against a slow leaf.
- [ ] No behaviour change for any other env var or route.

*Filed by new-issue-creator-code-a, 2026-10-30. Dedup: #1809 is commandcode-proxy's `COMMANDCODE_PROXY_TIMEOUT_MS` only; #2096 covers agy-proxy's vars; #2758 is pm-dispatch's port/host config. No existing issue mentions `OPENCODE_ROUTE_PROXY_TIMEOUT_MS`.*
