body:
## Summary

PR #2782 (merged today, commit `edab2d29`) points all three CLI proxy home-manager units at **one shared workroot**, `%h/.local/state/cli-proxies` (`home/common/default.nix:757,786,823`). The three proxies' on-disk layouts were designed for private workroots, and two of them collide exactly: `commandcode-proxy` and `claude-code-proxy` derive per-conversation workdirs with the **same function over the same key space** — `WORKROOT/sessions/<sha256(key)[:16]>` — so the same conversation key now maps to the **same directory** in both proxies. `muse-proxy` compounds it: it runs its sessions with the workroot itself as cwd/workspace root, which is now the parent directory of the other two proxies' session trees.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `35c4c9c6`)

- One env value for three units: `home/common/default.nix` sets `COMMANDCODE_PROXY_WORKDIR` (:757), `CLAUDE_CODE_PROXY_WORKDIR` (:786), and `MUSE_PROXY_WORKDIR` (:823) all to `%h/.local/state/cli-proxies`. Before #2782 each proxy defaulted to its own `bin/work` under its own proxy dir.
- Identical workdir derivation:
  - `bin/commandcode-proxy.mjs:516-520`: `sessionWorkdirFor(key)` = `path.join(WORKROOT, 'sessions', sha256(key).slice(0,16))`.
  - `bin/claude-code-proxy.mjs:230-234`: the same body, verbatim.
- Identical key space, by design: `bin/claude-code-proxy.mjs:194-198` says its `getSessionKey` "mirrors commandcode-proxy's getSessionKey" — same sources in the same order: explicit `x-session-id`/`session_id`/… headers and body fields, then `user:<user>`, then `turn0:<sha256(first user message)[:16]>` (commandcode's at :472, claude-code's at :198-224). Keys are client/conversation attributes, not proxy attributes: an OpenCode session that switches provider, or two requests whose first user message is identical, produce the same key in both proxies.
- Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-sharedworkroot/`, functions extracted verbatim from the real files — `commandcode-proxy.mjs` md5 `b3bce253…`, `claude-code-proxy.mjs` md5 `7280c4bb…`, both byte-identical to this main — with `WORKROOT` set to one shared dir): for an explicit session id, for `user:drew`, and for a `turn0:` key, both functions returned the **identical path** (`<shared>/sessions/<same hash>`) in all three cases, and both created the same directories.
- The muse side: `bin/muse-proxy.mjs:50-51` takes `WORKDIR` as its root, runs sessions with `cwd: WORKDIR` (:455, :1673) and `workspaceRoots: [WORKDIR]` (:572), persists `warm-sessions.json` at its root (:319-320) and writes `prompt-<uuid>.txt` files there (:1651). With the shared root, a muse session's workspace **is** the directory containing commandcode's and claude-code's `sessions/` trees and commandcode's resident-ACP project dir (`bin/commandcode-proxy.mjs:553`: `WORKROOT/acp-project`).

## Why it matters

The per-conversation workdir exists so an agency agent's file work is confined to its own conversation (both proxies steer the CLI: do ALL file work inside this dir). Sharing the derivation and the root breaks that confinement across providers:

- A conversation continued on the other provider (same session id — the normal provider-switch path) lands in the previous provider's workdir: it inherits the other agent's half-finished files as its own starting state, and its writes mutate the first conversation's dir.
- Two unrelated conversations with the same first user message (the `turn0:` fallback — e.g. the same task prompt sent to two providers to compare) silently share one workdir even within the intended one-conversation-per-dir model.
- A muse session runs at the shared root, so its file tools can read, modify, or delete the other proxies' live per-conversation directories and `acp-project` state — state the other proxies treat as private.

Each proxy's own state files are safe (commandcode/claude-code keep `sessions.json` in their proxy dirs, not the workroot); this is specifically the workdir tree that #2782 merged.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The three units no longer share one flat workroot: each proxy gets its own subtree (e.g. `%h/.local/state/cli-proxies/{commandcode,claude-code,muse}` in `home/common/default.nix`, or a per-proxy subdirectory derived inside each proxy), so `sessionWorkdirFor` outputs can never coincide across proxies.
- [ ] muse-proxy's session cwd/workspace root is its own subtree, not the parent of the other proxies' `sessions/`/`acp-project` trees.
- [ ] A regression test (following the `bin/*.test.mjs` pattern) pins that the three proxies' workdir derivations, given the same key and the deployed env values, produce disjoint directories — or, if the fix is env-only, a check/test on the rendered unit env values asserting three distinct workroots.
- [ ] Existing per-proxy behaviour is unchanged apart from the root path: same key derivation, same `sessions/<hash>` layout inside each proxy's own root, warm-session files still found after the move (migration of existing state at the shared root is considered, per #2782's "runtime state preserved/moved at deploy time" note).

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for cli-proxies / shared workdir / WORKDIR collision terms this run: no filing. PR #2782 is the change that introduced the sharing (its stated goal — moving runtime state out of the primary checkout — is not in dispute; the collision is in the choice of one identical value for all three). Adjacent: #2780/#2770 are muse-proxy translator bugs in the same file family, different mechanism; #2753 is the muse-direct feature.

body:
## Summary

The repo carries two copies of `update-nixpkgs-inputs.{py,sh}`: the fleet copy at `scripts/` and the pkgs/id copy at `pkgs/id/scripts/`, which is the one the pkgs/id just recipes actually run (`pkgs/id/justfile` `update-nixpkgs`, `update-nixpkgs-all`, `update-nixpkgs-master`, `update-nixpkgs-unstable`). Closed #598 fixed a silent-failure bug in this tool — failed updates exited 0, and the wrapper would re-run the whole update on a genuine failure — but commit `4daf81e4` ("update-nixpkgs-inputs: exit non-zero when an input update fails (#598)") touched **only the `scripts/` copies**. The pkgs/id copies never received either half of the fix, so the exact bug #598 closed is still live on the pkgs/id door.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `35c4c9c6`)

- `pkgs/id/scripts/update-nixpkgs-inputs.py` (318 lines) ends `main()` after the summaries with no failure tally: there is no `failed_total` / `sys.exit(1)` anywhere in the file. The fixed root copy has it at `scripts/update-nixpkgs-inputs.py:316-323`.
- `pkgs/id/scripts/update-nixpkgs-inputs.sh:9` is still the pre-#598 one-liner `"$SCRIPT" "$@" || python3 "$SCRIPT" "$@"` — fallback on **any** non-zero exit. The fixed root wrapper (`scripts/update-nixpkgs-inputs.sh:9-16`) falls back only on cannot-execute exits 126/127 and propagates the status, with a header comment explaining that a genuine failure must never be re-run.
- `git show --stat 4daf81e4`: 2 files changed, both under `scripts/`; the pkgs/id copies are untouched by the fix (their last change is the earlier `cbd67753` fmt commit).
- The pkgs/id copy is live, not dead code: `pkgs/id/justfile:676,681,686,691` run `./scripts/update-nixpkgs-inputs.sh` (i.e. the pkgs/id copy, from the pkgs/id directory), and `pkgs/id/flake.lock` carries its own `nixpkgs` input that the script discovers (script's `repo_dir` is the parent of its `scripts/` dir).
- Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-idnixpkgsdrift/`, real scripts copied from the laptop checkout, md5-matched to this main: pkgs/id `.py` `b2b23b41…`, pkgs/id `.sh` `05b3ccd4…`, root `.py` `f35ee1ac…`, root `.sh` `c69843b2…`; minimal `flake.lock` with one NixOS/nixpkgs input + a stub `nix` that always exits 1):
  - pkgs/id `.py`: prints `Total: 1 / Failed: 1` and **exits 0**.
  - Root `.py` (control): same summary, **exits 1**.
  - pkgs/id `.sh` wrapper with the `.py` failing genuinely (no `flake.lock`): the script body executes **twice** (2 tracebacks in the output) before the wrapper exits 1.
  - Root `.sh` wrapper (control): executes **once** (1 traceback).

## Why it matters

#598's own rationale applies verbatim to the pkgs/id door: a run that failed to update any input reports success, so `just update-nixpkgs*` recipes, `&&` chains, and any caller trusting the exit code proceed as if pkgs/id's nixpkgs pin was updated when `nix flake update` actually failed — a stale pin under a success banner. The wrapper half compounds it: the first genuine non-zero exit the pkgs/id `.py` ever produces (a crash today; the failure exit itself once the tally is ported without the wrapper half) re-runs the entire update end-to-end, doubling the `nix flake update` work and masking the first run's results — exactly what #598's wrapper change was written to prevent. The two-copy drift is the root cause: a fix landed in one copy and silently not the other, and nothing in the repo warns when they diverge again.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `pkgs/id/scripts/update-nixpkgs-inputs.py` exits 1 after printing its summaries when any input's update failed (the `scripts/` copy's tally semantics), and still exits 0 on success / already-up-to-date.
- [ ] `pkgs/id/scripts/update-nixpkgs-inputs.sh` falls back to `python3` only on cannot-execute exits (126/127) and propagates the script's exit status — no re-run after a genuine failure.
- [ ] The two copies cannot silently drift again: either they are deduplicated to a single source (with the pkgs/id just recipes pointing at it), or an automated check/test compares them (or pins the shared contract for both copies, extending the harness #603 asks for to the pkgs/id pair as well).
- [ ] No behaviour change for the root `scripts/` copies, and the pkgs/id just recipes discover the same inputs from `pkgs/id/flake.lock` as before.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `update-nixpkgs-inputs`, exit-code, and pkgs/id scripts terms this run. #598 (CLOSED) is the original bug and fix — scoped, in its commit and PR, to the root `scripts/` copies only; this issue is the unfixed second copy. #603 (OPEN) asks for automated tests pinning the **root** copies' exit-code contract; it does not cover the pkgs/id copies' behaviour, and criterion 3 above complements it. #2769 (OPEN) is the owner-match regex in `discover_inputs` — a different defect, present in both copies; its fix should likewise land in both copies, but it is not this issue.

title: aggregator(quota-gather-map): plain-object lookups return prototype members as window metadata — a window named 'constructor'/'__proto__' gets a fabricated windowSeconds, and a Turso window with such a name fabricates a snapshot record with no unit/limit

body:
# aggregator(quota-gather-map): plain-object lookups return prototype members as window metadata — a window named `constructor`/`__proto__`/`toString` gets a fabricated `windowSeconds`, and a Turso window with such a name fabricates a snapshot record with no unit/limit

## Evidence (main `dccfec44`)

Two lookup tables in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-gather-map.ts` are plain object literals indexed by a window **name that comes from an external document**, with no own-key check:

1. `quota-gather-map.ts:99` + `:146` — `FILE_EXPORT_WINDOW_SECONDS: Record<string, number> = { "5h": 18000, weekly: 604800 }`, read as `windowSeconds: FILE_EXPORT_WINDOW_SECONDS[w.name] ?? null` inside `entryFromFileExport`. The window names come from the producer's file-export JSON (`latest.json` windows). `??` only catches `null`/`undefined`, and prototype members are neither.
2. `quota-gather-map.ts:263-267` + `:283` — `TURSO_NATIVE_RECORDS: Record<string, {unit, limit}>`, read as `const native = entry.serviceId === "turso" ? TURSO_NATIVE_RECORDS[w.name] : undefined` inside `recordsFromEntries`. Any truthy hit takes the native-record branch. Window names here come from quota-current entries (themselves built from producer documents).

Same pattern previously filed/fixed as #2734 (aggregator weights) and #2757 (pm-dispatch priority) — different file, different tables, different published artifacts.

## Verified repro (laptop probe, real module, md5-matched to main)

Probe: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-gatherproto/` (`bun run probe.ts`, module md5 `e6634146c5e436a18ae130fdfc7f48c0` = sandbox main copy).

`entryFromFileExport` with windows `5h` (control), `constructor`, `__proto__`, `toString`:

```
FE window "5h"          windowSeconds typeof= number   value= 18000
FE window "constructor" windowSeconds typeof= function value= function Object() { [native code] }
FE window "__proto__"   windowSeconds typeof= object   value= [object Object]
FE window "toString"    windowSeconds typeof= function value= function toString() { [native code] }
FE JSON published: [{"name":"5h","windowSeconds":18000},{"name":"constructor"},{"name":"__proto__","windowSeconds":{}},{"name":"toString"}]
```

So in the published quota-current document a `constructor`/`toString` window silently **loses** its `windowSeconds` field (functions are dropped by `JSON.stringify`; the contract at `model.ts:1245` says `number | null`), and a `__proto__` window publishes `windowSeconds: {}` — a wrong-typed value where consumers expect a number or null.

`recordsFromEntries` with a Turso entry carrying windows `storage` (control), `constructor` (value 42), `__proto__` (value 7):

```
REC storage     unit= gb        limit= 5         value= 2
REC constructor unit= undefined limit= undefined value= 42
REC __proto__   unit= undefined limit= undefined value= 7
REC JSON: [..., {"metricId":"constructor","value":42,"source":"api",...}, {"metricId":"__proto__","value":7,...}]
```

The prototype hit is treated as a native-unit window: a snapshot record is fabricated whose `unit` and `limit` are `undefined` (dropped in JSON), violating the `SnapshotRecord` contract (`model.ts:1291-1304`, `unit` is a required union member). An unknown window name should fall through to the normal pct path (or be skipped), never invent a native record.

## Why it matters

Both inputs are producer documents the aggregator does not control (the file-export convention is explicitly "a producer on the laptop writes latest.json"; quota windows are provider-shaped). One oddly-named window — a provider adding a window literally named e.g. `toString`, or a corrupt/hand-edited export — silently corrupts the published quota-current document and the append-only snapshot history: wrong-typed/missing `windowSeconds`, and unit-less snapshot records that downstream rollups cannot interpret. The module's stated philosophy is fail-closed at this boundary; these two lookups fail open via the prototype chain.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `entryFromFileExport`: a window whose name is not an **own** key of `FILE_EXPORT_WINDOW_SECONDS` gets `windowSeconds: null` — including `constructor`, `__proto__`, `toString`, `hasOwnProperty` — and the known keys `5h`/`weekly` still map to 18000/604800.
- [ ] `recordsFromEntries`: a Turso window whose name is not an own key of `TURSO_NATIVE_RECORDS` does **not** take the native-record branch (it follows the normal pct/label path or is skipped, as an unknown name does today); `databases`/`storage`/`sync` behavior unchanged.
- [ ] Tests alongside the existing quota-gather-map tests pin both sites with `constructor` and `__proto__` window names, asserting the published/serialized shapes (no function/object `windowSeconds`, no unit-less record).
- [ ] No other behavior change for ordinary window names.

Dedup: #2571 covers `entryFromFileExport`/`entryFromResult` percent **range** checks (different mechanism); #2553/#2568/#2582 are range checks in sibling mappers; #2734/#2757 are the same prototype-lookup pattern in different files/tables. No open or closed issue covers these two tables.

title: id(search): search_store_terms resolves every subject's event kind even when no kind term is present (PR #1806)

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Finding

`search_store_terms` (added by PR #1806) resolves the event kind of **every** subject in the store's live claims up front — one `event_by_id` store read per distinct subject — even when the term set contains no `Term::SubjectKind` at all. A pure name/author search (or even an empty term set) pays a full per-subject store scan it never uses, and worse, an `event_by_id` error on *any* subject aborts the whole search via `?`, including searches that never needed a kind.

## Evidence

- PR: #1806 (`id(search): author index, author/kind terms, multi-term AND — fix #800`), merged as 5a843a17283c380108dff9670553e1e8e3159806.
- Verified on current main dccfec446f1cb4671e75d5ff94d99dce709c6965, `pkgs/id/src/search.rs` (`search_store_terms`, ~:199-213):
  - The `kinds` map loop runs unconditionally over `claims.iter().map(|claim| claim.subject)` and calls `store.event_by_id(&subject)?` for each distinct subject, before `search_terms` is invoked.
  - `search_terms` only ever calls its `subject_kind` closure for `Term::SubjectKind` terms (its doc even notes a caller with no kind terms may pass a lookup that always returns `None`, as `search()` does) — so the eager work is discarded whenever no kind term is present.
  - The function's own error doc concedes the coupling: "Returns the errors of `EventStore::tag_claims` **and `EventStore::event_by_id`**" — for every call, not just kind searches.
- No production caller exists yet (only `pkgs/id/tests/search.rs`), so this is a latent API defect: the first CLI/web wiring of author or multi-term name search inherits the cost and the failure mode.

## Why it matters

Search-by-author and multi-term AND are the §9.4 surfaces this PR built for later wiring. As written, wiring them up makes every search O(subjects) in extra store reads and lets an unrelated subject's unreadable event fail a search that would otherwise succeed — a regression relative to `search_store`, which never touches `event_by_id`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] When `terms` contains no `Term::SubjectKind`, `search_store_terms` performs no `event_by_id` calls and cannot fail from one.
- [ ] Kind resolution is lazy/memoized per subject actually queried by a kind term (or equivalently gated on a kind term being present).
- [ ] Existing tests in `pkgs/id/tests/search.rs` still pass, plus a test pinning that a name/author-only search succeeds even when a subject's event cannot be read (or is absent in a way that errors), if the store test harness can express it.

title: id(serve): group-warning watcher ignores --groups-log — serve always reads the default groups.jsonl (PR #1805)

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

`id serve`'s group-warning watcher (P4.9, added by PR #1805) always reads the default `groups.jsonl`, ignoring the global `--groups-log` option. An operator who runs serve against a shared or relocated group log — the documented use case for `--groups-log` ("a log shared by several nodes is best given as an absolute path") — gets no group size/churn warnings at all, silently: the watcher either finds no file at the default path (evaluation returns empty) or watches a different, local log than the one `id group` / `delegate` / `revoke` are writing to.

## Evidence

- PR: #1805 (`id(serve): wire P4.9 group warning Evaluator into serve (#799)`), merged as 3675a4703d9cbb2df858dfe5725f101cbc5dad88.
- Verified on current main dccfec446f1cb4671e75d5ff94d99dce709c6965:
  - `pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:1295` — `let groups_log = PathBuf::from(GROUPS_FILE_NAME);` hardcoded; both the startup pass (:1296) and the 60s spawned task (:1304) use only this path.
  - `pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs` / `ServeOptions` carry no groups-log field, and `pkgs/id/src/main.rs` (Serve dispatch, ~:149-230) never passes `cli.groups_log` to `cmd_serve` — while the Group/Delegate/Revoke dispatch (~:274-277) passes `cli.groups_log` through.
  - `pkgs/id/src/cli.rs:174-178` — `--groups-log` is a global arg: "The group log that `group`, `delegate` and `revoke` read and append to. Defaults to `groups.jsonl` in the data directory. A relative path is relative to the data directory, so a log shared by several nodes is best given as an absolute path."
  - `pkgs/id/src/commands/group.rs:31-33` — the group commands resolve the option with the same default (`log_path()` falls back to `FILE_NAME`), so only serve diverges.
  - Failure mode is silent: `evaluate_group_warnings` returns an empty vec when the path does not exist, by design ("warnings never block serve").

Distinct from #1847 (open), which covers the same watcher's churn detection missing re-add cycles that complete between 60s evaluations; this issue is about which log file is watched at all.

## Why it matters

The warnings exist to surface group-size thresholds and device re-add bursts ("each re-add is a compromise recovery, so check the devices"). A shared-log deployment — the exact setup `--groups-log` documents — silently loses that signal while `id group` keeps working against the shared log, so nothing looks broken.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `id serve` honors `--groups-log` when given (absolute, or relative-to-data-dir like the group commands), falling back to `groups.jsonl` when absent.
- [ ] A test covers serve's warning evaluation against a non-default log path (the existing watcher tests in serve.rs pass explicit paths to `evaluate_group_warnings`; add coverage that the path serve actually uses comes from the option).
- [ ] Default behavior unchanged when `--groups-log` is not passed.

body:
# id(find/search): `--format` accepts any string and silently renders the tag format — a typo gets plausible-looking wrong output

## Evidence (main `fe47fa09`)

- `pkgs/id/src/cli.rs:891` (`Find`) and `pkgs/id/src/cli.rs:958` (`Search`): `--format` is a bare `String` with `default_value = "tag"` and **no `value_parser`**. The same file validates sibling options — `value_parser = [...]` lists at cli.rs:1412, 1946, 1966, 2004, 2007 and `ValueEnum` types at cli.rs:1345, 1355 — so the omission is local to these two args.
- `pkgs/id/src/main.rs:319-347` passes `&format` straight into `cmd_find` / `cmd_search` with no check.
- The printers treat every unrecognized value as `tag`:
  - `pkgs/id/src/helpers.rs` `print_match_cli` (lines 155-175): `"group"` / `"union"` arms, `_` arm renders the tag format.
  - `print_matches_cli` (lines 192-243): same `_` fallthrough.
  - `print_match_repl` (lines 246-268): same `_` fallthrough, fed by the REPL parser at `pkgs/id/src/repl/runner.rs:666`, which assigns the `--format` value verbatim.

## Verified behavior (probe, laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-findformat/`)

The printers' match logic, copied verbatim with the match type stubbed, run over one match:

```
--- format="tag"    -> abc123<TAB>config.json<TAB>(config)
--- format="group"  -> [config] / indented hash+name
--- format="union"  -> abc123<TAB>config.json
--- format="gorup"  -> abc123<TAB>config.json<TAB>(config)   (== tag)
--- format="yaml"   -> abc123<TAB>config.json<TAB>(config)   (== tag)
--- format="GROUP"  -> abc123<TAB>config.json<TAB>(config)   (== tag)
--- format=""       -> abc123<TAB>config.json<TAB>(config)   (== tag)
```

So `id find --format gorup config` and `id search --format yaml config` exit 0 and print tag-formatted output. Nothing tells the user the format was not understood.

## Why it matters

`--format` exists for scripts and for grouped/deduplicated reading. A mistyped or case-mismatched value silently produces a different shape than the caller asked for — the worst failure mode for a formatting flag, because the output still looks plausible and a script parsing `group` headers or `union` dedup semantics consumes tag rows instead. Every other enumerated CLI option in this file rejects bad values at parse time via clap; these two are the outliers.

Secondary, same surface: the module doc at `pkgs/id/src/commands/find.rs:24-28` says "**union**: Default format", while the CLI default is `tag` (cli.rs:890/957 `default_value = "tag"`, help text "tag (default)"). The doc should be corrected with the fix.

## Acceptance criteria

- `id find --format <anything other than tag|group|union>` and the same for `id search` fail at argument parsing with a clap error naming the accepted values (e.g. via `value_parser` or a `ValueEnum`, matching the file's existing patterns).
- The REPL `find`/`search` `--format` value is validated the same way, or the shared printers' fallthrough is otherwise made unreachable with an unknown value.
- The `commands/find.rs` module doc no longer calls `union` the default.
- A CLI parse test (alongside `test_cli_parse_find_with_format`, cli.rs:2609) pins that an invalid `--format` is rejected for both `find` and `search`.

Dedup: #2274 covers the REPL parsers swallowing unknown/mistyped *flags*; this is the distinct point that an accepted flag's *value* is never validated on either surface. No open or recently closed issue covers `--format` value validation.

title: pm-dispatch(validate): resolvePriority's plain-object lookup returns prototype members as priorities — 'constructor' becomes the Object constructor function and '__proto__' an object, instead of the documented 400

labels.name: task/triage

labels.name: app/pm-stack
labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

labels.name: source/design-architect

body:
## Problem

`pm-dispatch`: `resolvePriority` resolves a named priority through a plain-object lookup with no own-key check, so two prototype spellings are accepted as priorities instead of failing with the documented 400 — and the value that reaches the queue is not a number at all.

`pm-stack/dispatch/src/validate.ts:28-48` (main `58635f8d`):

```ts
export const PRIORITY_NAMES: Record<string, number> = {
  critical: 10, high: 20, normal: 40, low: 70,
};
...
if (typeof input === "string") {
  const v = PRIORITY_NAMES[input.trim().toLowerCase()];
  if (v === undefined) { throw new ValidationError(`priority: unknown name ...`); }
  return v;
}
```

`PRIORITY_NAMES["constructor"]` is the `Object` constructor function and `PRIORITY_NAMES["__proto__"]` is `Object.prototype` — neither is `undefined`, so neither throws.

## Verified (this run, real module)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-priorityproto/`, `validate.ts` copied verbatim from main, md5 `c1f61d5acf5c85da71de798f4c7056b8`, run under bun 1.4.2):

| input | result |
|---|---|
| `"high"` / `"normal"` (controls) | `20` / `40` (number) ✓ |
| `"bogus"` (control) | `ValidationError` 400 ✓ |
| `"constructor"` | returns **the `Object` constructor function** (`typeof === "function"`) |
| `"__proto__"` | returns **`Object.prototype`** (`typeof === "object"`) |
| `"toString"` / `"hasOwnProperty"` | 400 — they only escape because `toLowerCase()` changes their spelling; `constructor`/`__proto__` are already lowercase |

Downstream, through the real `parseSessionRequest`:

- `priority: "constructor"` yields a session/task request whose `priority` field is a function. `JSON.stringify({ p_priority: <that> })` produces `{}` — the field is silently dropped, so `QueueClient.enqueue` (`src/queue.ts`) sends the enqueue RPC with **no `p_priority` at all** instead of the request being rejected.
- `priority: "__proto__"` serializes as `p_priority: {}`, an object where the RPC expects the design-scale integer.
- `buildPacket` (`src/packet.ts`) interpolates the value into `priority_reason` ("resolved to `function Object() { [native code] }`…") and the `/v1/tasks` comment path interpolates it as `[object Object]`.

So a documented-error case (unknown priority name → 400, `validate.ts:36-38`) instead becomes a dropped/mistyped queue priority and garbage provenance text — the request is never told its priority was invalid.

## Why it matters

- The priority is the queue's claim-ordering input (design scale 10–90, `validate.ts:11-16`). Silently dropping it or sending `{}` means a caller who typo'd — or probed — a name gets a task at whatever the RPC does with a missing/object priority, with no error anywhere.
- This is the same own-key-lookup failure class as the aggregator weights lookup (#2734), in the dispatcher's own request boundary — the one place whose whole job is validating requests before they become queue tasks / launched sessions (cf. #2668's boundary-validation design).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `resolvePriority("constructor")` and `resolvePriority("__proto__")` (any case/whitespace variant that lowercases/trims to a prototype key) throw `ValidationError` (400, "unknown name"), like every other unknown name.
- [ ] The fix uses an own-key check (e.g. `Object.hasOwn` / a `Map` / a null-prototype table) rather than a denylist of the two spellings, so no other inherited member can leak through.
- [ ] Regression tests in `pm-stack/dispatch/test/validate.test.ts`: the two spellings above 400; the four real names and the numeric scale/snap behaviour are unchanged.
- [ ] No non-number can reach `Packet.priority` / `p_priority` from a named priority: a test through `parseSessionRequest`/`parseTaskRequest` with `priority: "constructor"` 400s instead of producing a request object.

## Dedup

Searched open + recently closed issues for `resolvePriority`, prototype/constructor priority, and dispatch priority validation. #2679 covers the composite actions sending a numeric priority as a JSON string (different mechanism, action side); #2734 is the same failure class in the aggregator's `weights.ts` (different module, already filed separately per app). No filing covers the dispatch lookup.

body:
# mcpx(resources): upstream resources/read results are never validated — null/missing contents becomes an empty successful read, an unparseable result is fabricated as a text entry, and malformed entries pass through

## Evidence (verified this run, main 9e8c3d02)

`prompts/get` got a fail-closed structural validator in #2193 (`internal/mcpclient/promptcheck.go`, `ValidatePromptResult`, called from `Client.GetPrompt`). `resources/read` never got one:

- `internal/mcpclient/client.go:1520` — `Client.ReadResource` returns the upstream `raw` bytes untouched (only the not-found error codes are translated).
- `internal/cli/serve.go:916` — `(*App).resourceContents` is the only transform on the `/mcp` serve path (also used by `internal/cli/serve_ask.go:282`), and it fails **open** in every direction (probe below).
- `internal/mcpserver/server.go:141` — `readResult` renders whatever it is given: blob wins over text, and an entry with neither renders as `text: ""`.

Probe (verbatim copies of `resourceContents` + `readResult`, laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-resread/`, `exposedURI` stubbed to identity — namespacing does not affect any case):

| Upstream result | What the client receives |
|---|---|
| `{"contents":null}` or `{}` | `{"contents":[]}` — a successful, empty read of a resource that may exist |
| `["not","a","result"]` or `{"contents":"nope"}` or an entry with `"uri":42` | the whole raw payload fabricated as one entry: `{"mimeType":"application/json","text":"<raw bytes>"}` |
| entry with neither `text` nor `blob` | `{"mimeType":"text/plain","text":""}` — fabricated empty text |
| entry with both `text:"WORDS"` and `blob:"aGk="` | `{"blob":"aGk="}` — the text is silently dropped |
| entry with `"blob":"!!not-base64!!"` | passed through verbatim as a blob no client can decode |

`ValidatePromptResult` rejects every analogous shape for prompts (no messages, a block with no type, a known type missing its fields, non-base64 image/audio data or embedded blob). Resources have no equivalent check anywhere in the chain: not in `mcpclient.ReadResource`, not in the daemon registry passthrough (`internal/daemon/registry.go:1111`), not in `resourceContents`.

## Why it matters

mcpx's contract to its clients is that an upstream's malformed or hostile response does not reach them "as if mcpx had produced it" — that is the stated reason #2193 exists. On the resources path the opposite happens, and two of the failure modes are silent data corruption rather than noise: a missing/null `contents` reads as "the resource is empty", and an unparseable result is re-labelled `application/json` text, so a client cannot distinguish a real resource body from mcpx's fabrication.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A structural validator for `resources/read` results (mirroring `ValidatePromptResult`): result is an object, `contents` is present and a list, every entry is an object with a string `uri`, exactly one of `text` / `blob` present and a string, and `blob` is valid base64.
- [ ] A result that fails validation is an error on the read (a clear reason, classified like the prompts path), never an empty/fabricated successful read — on both the direct `mcpclient` path and the `/mcp` serve path (`resourceContents` callers in `serve.go` and `serve_ask.go`).
- [ ] Tests covering the probe matrix above (null/missing/wrong-type contents, non-object result, neither-field entry, both-fields entry, non-base64 blob, wrong-type entry field) plus the valid text and blob cases continuing to pass through unchanged, including URI namespacing.
- [ ] If any current lenient behaviour is load-bearing for a real upstream, it is named and pinned by a test instead of falling out of the unmarshal fallback.

body:
# aggregator: Phase 1 of #2747 — guard the two path-segment decodes (/discuss, /item) on the shared contract

Phase 1 of design #2747 (one decode for path segments — a malformed percent-encoding is a 400, never a 500). Design doc: `files/designs/code-path-segment-decode.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace.

## Problem

The aggregator has the family's only unfiled sites — two of them (audit at origin/main `72545cb9`):

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/server.ts:730` — `GET /discuss/<ref>`: `const objectRef = decodeURIComponent(discussMatch[1]);`
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/server.ts:842` — `GET /item/<id>`: `const id = decodeURIComponent(itemMatch[1]);`

Both route patterns match any non-empty suffix, the decode is unguarded, and `fetchHandler` (`server.ts:900-909`) has no try/catch — a malformed percent sequence (`%`, `%zz`, a truncated escape, a truncated UTF-8 sequence like `%E0%A4%A`) throws a raw `URIError` out of the handler: under `Bun.serve` the request fails as an unhandled 500 with no error body. The same defect is filed for the three sibling apps (#2633 lab-ops-hub, #2693 projector, #2720 cf-container-hello); the aggregator instance was missed by all three filings.

## Scope (per design #2747)

- Add one guard helper in the aggregator's own code (a `decodePathSegment(raw) -> string | null`-shaped function in the module that best fits the app's layout) returning `null` on `URIError` — it wraps the decode only, nothing downstream.
- Both routes call it immediately after matching: `null` → a **JSON 400** naming the bad encoding (the aggregator's established bad-input shape — JSON 400s on its POST routes at `server.ts:412,423,432,456,484`, JSON 404 for an unknown project id). Only the decoded value proceeds downstream.
- Decode-once semantics for well-formed input are unchanged: `%2F` still decodes inside values, `100%25` still yields the literal `100%`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `GET /discuss/<malformed>` and `GET /item/<malformed>` (each of `%`, `%zz`, a truncated escape, `%E0%A4%A`) return a JSON 400 naming the bad encoding; no exception escapes the handler.
- [ ] Well-formed controls behave exactly as before: a plain ref/id, a `%20` segment, the routes' legitimate encoded forms, and `100%25` (a valid encoding of a literal `%` — must not 400).
- [ ] A well-formed ref/id naming nothing keeps its current behaviour.
- [ ] Handler-level tests pin the shared probe matrix from #2747 (the four malformed forms + the controls) for both routes.
- [ ] No other aggregator route changes behaviour; genuine downstream failures keep their current outcomes.

---
*agent-note:v1 — filed by the repo design architect (dedicated code job, pass 20) as Phase 1 of #2747. Sibling phases: Phase 2 adopts #2633 + #2720, Phase 3 adopts #2693 + the closing audit. Do not split this phase per-route — the helper and the matrix are the shared deliverable.*

body:
## Problem

The reviews stream in `pm-stack/projector/src/reconcile.ts` says it is guarded per-PR, but it isn't:

- The comment at `reconcile.ts:106-107` says: "Reviews hang off PRs; pull PRs and their reviews. **Guarded so a failure on one PR does not abort the whole stream.**"
- The loop at `:111-143` has no `try/catch` at all. `listResource` (`github.ts:170-180`) throws `github_api_<status>` on any non-OK response, so the first PR whose reviews endpoint fails (500, 404, rate limit) throws out of `reconcileStream` entirely.

Consequences, all verified below:

1. Every later PR in the repo is never fetched — its reviews never reconcile for as long as the one bad PR keeps failing (e.g. a PR whose reviews endpoint persistently errors).
2. `reconcileRepos` (`:160-168`) catches the throw at stream level and records `{ written: 0, error }` — even though earlier PRs' reviews **were** upserted to the store before the throw, so the run report understates what was written.
3. The sync cursor is only set on success (`:163`), so the next poll re-reads and re-upserts every earlier PR again — wasted work on every tick while the bad PR persists.

The other streams don't have this shape: issues/prs/comments are single collection reads, so a failure there is genuinely all-or-nothing. Reviews is the only per-item loop, and the only one whose comment promises a guard that doesn't exist.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `72545cb9`)

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-reviews/probe.ts`; real `reconcile.ts`/`github.ts`/`store.ts` copied from the laptop clone — md5s `5021e023…` / `a2516ee2…` / `448fc963…` match the sandbox clone at the same HEAD — in-memory libSQL, stub `fetch`):

Setup: 3 PRs; PR #1 reviews → one review (id 101); PR #2 reviews → HTTP 500; PR #3 reviews → one review (id 103).

```
reviews stream result: {"repo":"developing-today/code","stream":"reviews","written":0,"error":"github_api_500"}
PR3 reviews endpoint fetched: false
stored reviews: developing-today/code#1:101
total written reported: 0
```

So PR #1's review landed in the store, PR #3 was never even requested, and the stream reported `written: 0`.

Dedup: title+keyword search this run — #2455 (comment resurrection / monotonic guard), #2456 (webhook redelivery), and #2694 (bare comment-ID collisions in the same store) are distinct mechanisms; no open or closed issue covers the reviews loop's missing per-PR guard.

## Why it matters

Reconciliation is the projector's self-healing path beyond webhook delivery — it exists so missed reviews still land. One persistently failing PR silently freezes review projection for every later PR in the repo, indefinitely, while the run report claims nothing was written even for the PRs that succeeded. The code comment actively misleads the next reader into believing the failure is contained.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A failure fetching one PR's reviews is contained to that PR: later PRs in the same stream are still fetched and upserted in the same run, and the stream result reports the per-PR failure (repo, PR number, error) alongside the reviews actually written.
- [ ] The stream's `written` count reflects the upserts that actually happened, including in a run where a later PR fails.
- [ ] The cursor/reporting semantics for a partially-failed reviews stream are pinned by triage (advance-with-error-recorded vs hold) and match the code; the "guarded" comment and the code agree.
- [ ] Regression coverage: a stubbed-fetch run with PRs [ok, 500, ok] stores both ok PRs' reviews and reports exactly one per-PR error; the existing projector test suite still passes.

title: t3code-seed-providers: seed script crashes on parseable-but-wrong-shaped settings.json — one bad shape disables all seeding and the OpenCode-1.x safety disable

labels.name: task/triage

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Summary

t3code-seed-providers' seed script (`pkgs/t3code-seed-providers/seed.sh`, embedded Python) only guards against *unparseable* settings.json — a parseable-but-wrong-shaped document crashes it with a raw traceback, and because the script is `set -euo pipefail` and runs as the `t3code-seed-providers` oneshot user unit (`home/common/default.nix:528`, `Before=t3code.service`), one bad shape silently disables **all** seeding on every boot — including the OpenCode-1.x safety disable, which is the one part that exists to protect the shared 2.x session DB.

Hand-editing settings.json is explicitly supported upstream (the file's own header says so), so wrong shapes are a realistic input, not a theoretical one.

## Evidence (main `fa52fcb3`, `pkgs/t3code-seed-providers/seed.sh`)

- The only shape guard is the `try` around `json.loads` at :46-48: unparseable → `sys.exit(0)` ("don't clobber something we can't parse"). Nothing validates what the parsed value *is*.
- `doc.setdefault("providerInstances", {})` (:143) assumes `doc` is a dict.
- The add loop assumes `providerInstances` is a dict (`instances[k] = desired[k]`).
- The refresh-on-seed loop (:155-162) calls `instances[k].setdefault("config", {})` and `config.get(...)` with no isinstance checks — unlike the safety loop right below it (:173), which does guard `isinstance(inst, dict)`. A crash in refresh also means the safety loop never runs.
- The unit always sets all four binary env vars (`home/common/default.nix:544-549`: OPENCODE_V2_BIN, ANTIGRAVITY_ACP_BIN, MUSE_BIN, PI_BIN), so the refresh loop is always armed for the fleet-owned ids.

Verified this run with the real script (md5-matched copy of main's `seed.sh`; probe on the laptop at `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-t3seed/`, env mirroring the unit):

- control `{}` → rc 0, all instances added (OK)
- unparseable `{not json` → rc 0, file untouched (the designed path)
- `[]` → rc 1, `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'setdefault'`
- `null` → rc 1, `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'setdefault'`
- `{"providerInstances": []}` → rc 1, `TypeError: list indices must be integers`
- `{"providerInstances": null}` → rc 1, `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not a container`
- `{"providerInstances": {"muse": "oops"}}` → rc 1, `AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'setdefault'` (refresh loop)
- `{"providerInstances": {"opencode-v2": {"driver": "opencode", "config": null}}}` → rc 1, `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'get'`
- `config: "oops"` → rc 1, same site

In every crash case nothing is written and no seeding happens at all — the adds computed before the crash are discarded with the process.

## Why it matters

The seed runs before t3code starts, every boot. A single malformed entry — from a hand edit, a t3 version writing a new shape, or a partially migrated file — turns the unit into a permanent failure whose only trace is a Python traceback in the journal, and the fleet loses three things at once: new-instance seeding, binaryPath refresh (the fix for stranded store paths), and the 1.x safety disable that keeps a V1 binary away from the shared 2.x session DB. The script's own contract for input it cannot handle is "exit quietly and don't clobber" — wrong *shapes* should get the same treatment as unparseable bytes, or be repaired per-instance, not abort the whole run.

## Acceptance criteria

- A settings.json whose top level is not a JSON object, or whose `providerInstances` is not an object, no longer crashes the script: it exits without modifying the file and logs a legible reason (stderr), matching the unparseable path's don't-clobber contract.
- A fleet-owned instance whose stored value (or its `config`) is not an object does not abort the run: the remaining instances still seed/refresh, and the OpenCode-1.x safety disable still executes; the malformed entry is left untouched and named in the log line.
- Regression tests (or a scripted fixture run) cover: `[]`, `null`, `providerInstances: []` / `null`, a fleet instance as a string, `config: null` / `"oops"`, plus the `{}` control and the unparseable control.
- Well-formed files behave exactly as today (adds, refresh, disable, single stderr summary line).

## Dedup

- Searched open + closed issues for t3code seed / settings.json shape handling this run: no match. The seed script and its refresh/safety behaviour have no prior filing.

title: aggregator(weights): effortWeight's plain-object lookup returns prototype members as weights — 'effort/constructor' counts as sized and string-poisons every weighted summary

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

labels.name: app/aggregator
labels.description: Package/app: aggregator (pm-stack in this repo)

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Problem

`effortWeight` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/weights.ts:33-44) resolves an `effort/*` label through a plain-object lookup with no own-key check:

```ts
export const EFFORT_WEIGHTS: Readonly<Record<string, number>> = { xs: 1, s: 4, m: 12, l: 40 };  // :19

const size = label.slice("effort/".length);
const w = EFFORT_WEIGHTS[size];        // :37
if (w !== undefined) return w;         // :38
```

`EFFORT_WEIGHTS` is an object literal, so the lookup walks the prototype chain. Label text is lowercased before the lookup (:36), which happens to shield the camelCase members (`toString`, `hasOwnProperty`, `valueOf`), but the all-lowercase inherited keys still hit: **`effort/constructor`** resolves to the `Object` constructor function and **`effort/__proto__`** resolves to `Object.prototype` — both `!== undefined`, so both are returned as the item's "weight" instead of `null` (unsized).

That breaks the module's own contract (weights.ts:9-13): an item with no recognised effort label is UNSIZED and must be counted separately, "never silently zero-weighted". An item carrying one of these labels is instead counted as sized with a non-numeric weight.

## Verified this run (laptop probe, real module, main ec02aa14)

Probe: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-weights/probe.ts` (Bun, imports the real `weights.ts`, copied byte-for-byte from main ec02aa14; md5 9705f795f0a638f2b90a4f98aa432268):

- `effortWeight(["effort/constructor"])` → `function Object() { [native code] }` (typeof `function`), not `null`.
- `effortWeight(["effort/__proto__"])` → `Object.prototype` (typeof `object`), not `null`.
- Controls behave: `effortWeight(["effort/xs"])` → `1`; `effort/toString` / `effort/hasOwnProperty` → `null` (lowercasing shields them, as above).
- `summarizeWeights([{state:"closed", labels:["effort/constructor"]}, {state:"closed", labels:["effort/xs"]}])` → `totalWeight` and `closedWeight` become the **string** `"0function Object() { [native code] }1"` (number `+=` function coerces to concatenation), `weightedPct` is `null` while `unsizedCount` stays `0` — the summary claims everything is sized and nothing is weighted.
- `weightedLine(...)` then renders the function source into the dashboard text: `— (nothing sized) (0function Object() { [native code] }1/0function Object() { [native code] }1 weight closed) · 2/2 items closed`.

## Why it matters

`summarizeWeights` feeds the project page, the /projects per-Area rows and the /program cards (callers: render.ts:4873, :4877, :5090, :5092; project-config.ts:763; `effortWeight` also directly at render.ts:5095). Pool item labels come from the org Project / GitHub issues — label names are data, not code, and the taxonomy explicitly encourages coining labels freely, so an `effort/*` label outside the four known sizes is a when, not an if (a typo'd or experimental label is all it takes; it does not need to be one of the two prototype names — those are just the ones that collide today). Any unrecognised `effort/*` label should fall through to unsized; two of them instead corrupt every weighted summary on the page into string-typed weights and a nonsense progress line, with no error anywhere. The fix shape (own-key check, `Object.hasOwn`, a `Map`, or a null-prototype record) is triage's pin; silently treating a prototype member as a weight is the one outcome that is wrong either way.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `effortWeight` returns `null` for every `effort/*` suffix that is not one of the four defined sizes — including `effort/constructor` and `effort/__proto__` — so such items count as unsized.
- [ ] `summarizeWeights` over items carrying those labels produces numeric `totalWeight`/`closedWeight`/`openWeight` and the correct `unsizedCount`; `weightedLine` output contains no function/object source text.
- [ ] Regression tests in pm-stack/aggregator/test/weights.test.ts cover at least: `effort/constructor`, `effort/__proto__`, and one ordinary unknown size (e.g. `effort/xl`) — all unsized.

title: cold-store-reaper: S3 list-page parser trusts the body — non-XML/wrong-root pages and bad Size values crash raw or read as an empty bucket

labels.name: task/triage

labels.description: Package/app: cold-store-reaper (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Summary

cold-store-reaper's S3 ListObjectsV2 parser (`_parse_s3_list_page`) trusts the response body completely: it never validates that the XML root is a list result, never converts XML parse failures to the module's `ColdStoreError`, parses `Size` with a bare `int(...)`, and accepts negative sizes. A malformed or shape-drifted R2/proxy response therefore either crashes the CLI with a raw traceback, or — worse — is silently read as an empty/negative-sized listing that downstream backup and eviction code trusts.

## Evidence (main `ba5229e9`, `pkgs/cold-store-reaper/cold_store.py`)

- `_parse_s3_list_page` (:138) runs `ET.fromstring(body)` at :146 with no guard. `main()` catches only `ColdStoreError` (end of `main`, ~:2240), so a non-XML body escapes as a raw `xml.etree.ElementTree.ParseError` traceback.
- `Size` is parsed at :176 as `int(fields.get("Size") or 0)` with no guard: `"abc"` / `"1.5"` raise a raw `ValueError`; `"-5"` is accepted and stored as a negative object size.
- The root element is never checked: any well-formed XML that is not a `ListBucketResult` (e.g. an HTML/XML error or maintenance page returned with HTTP 200 — `_s3_check` at :1557 only rejects status >= 300) yields `([], False, None)`, i.e. "the bucket is empty", from `s3_list_objects` (:1563, parse call :1574).
- The parsed sizes are load-bearing downstream: `backup_supabase` passes `newest["size"]` as the byte-count verification for a downloaded backup (:1789), and `evict_apply` writes `entry["size"]` into the transfer ledger (:1915); `evict_scan` (:1817) plans deletions off this same listing.

Verified this run with the real module (md5-matched copy of main's `cold_store.py`; probe on the laptop at `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-s3parse/probe.py`, stdlib-only):

- control: valid `ListBucketResult` page → `[{'key': 'a.bin', 'size': 3, 'last_modified': 2026-10-01T00:00Z}]`, truncated False (OK)
- body `{"error": "nope"}` (non-XML) → RAW `ParseError: not well-formed (invalid token)`
- `<Size>abc</Size>` / `<Size>1.5</Size>` → RAW `ValueError: invalid literal for int()`
- `<Size>-5</Size>` → accepted, object size `-5`
- well-formed `<html><body>proxy error</body></html>` → silently `[]`, truncated False (read as an empty bucket)

## Why it matters

This listing is the input to `backup-supabase` and to eviction, which deletes objects. The module's own contract elsewhere is fail-closed with named `ColdStoreError`s (transport retries, the #2110 aware-or-None datetime rule, the curl size verification). The list parser is the one place a drifted body can either mask the real failure behind an unrelated traceback or, in the wrong-root case, present a non-empty bucket as empty to code that plans from it.

## Acceptance criteria

- `_parse_s3_list_page` raises `ColdStoreError` (naming the problem) for a body that is not well-formed XML and for a well-formed document whose root is not a list result.
- A `Contents` entry whose `Size` is missing keeps the current default; a `Size` that is non-numeric or negative raises `ColdStoreError` instead of a raw `ValueError` or a negative object size.
- Regression tests cover: non-XML body, wrong-root XML body, `Size` = `abc`, `1.5`, `-5`, plus the valid-page control (including the existing pagination and LastModified behaviour).
- Existing cold-store-reaper tests pass unchanged.

## Dedup

- #2618 covers the D1 response shapes in this same file and its queue packet explicitly scoped S3 response handling (`s3_error_message` / `_parse_s3_list_page`) OUT — this filing is that acknowledged remainder, a different subsystem (R2/S3 listing vs D1 API) with different failure modes.
- #1632 covers the `s3_list_objects` pagination loop (missing/repeated continuation token); #2110 (closed) covered offset-less `LastModified` parsing in this same function — neither touches root validation, XML parse failures, or `Size` parsing.
- Searched open + closed issues for S3 parse / malformed XML this run: no match.

title: id(ci): just-recipes.json drifts from the justfile with no guard — crash-gate-sampled's doc is already stale on main, and a recipe added without `just lockfiles` silently gets no nix app

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/id/flake.nix` generates every `nix run .#<recipe>` app from the checked-in
`pkgs/id/just-recipes.json` (`justRecipes = builtins.fromJSON (builtins.readFile ./just-recipes.json)`,
flake.nix:255; apps generated at flake.nix:727-728 from `publicRecipes`, flake.nix:276-278).
`pkgs/id/AGENTS.md` makes the sync a rule: when adding or modifying justfile commands, add the
corresponding nix app — which in practice means re-running `just lockfiles`
(justfile:185-203, `just-recipes` recipe) so the JSON matches the justfile.

Nothing checks that sync, and the file has already drifted on main.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `a0625480bc9e692243b384e0edcb5cc96bc4fa27`)

Regenerated the dump on the laptop (`just 1.58.0`, `just --dump --dump-format json` in
`pkgs/id/`, laptop clone at the same HEAD) and compared parsed JSON against the checked-in file:

```text
recipes only in fresh:   []
recipes only in checked: []
recipes differing:       ['bench', 'crash-gate-sampled']
```

- **`crash-gate-sampled` doc — real content drift.** Current justfile doc (justfile:238-248,
  ending “…losing all PR coverage.”) vs checked-in JSON doc (“excluded everywhere (they rewrite
  the checked-in corpus files).”). Commit `5b0a3031` (#1635) appended the guard paragraph to the
  justfile comment and touched only the justfile; `859726d5` (#551) was the last commit to touch
  both files. Because `mkRecipeApp` takes the app description from `recipe.doc`
  (flake.nix:264-269), `nix run .#crash-gate-sampled`'s description is the pre-#1635 text.
- **`bench` body + top-level `source` — generation noise a guard must handle.** The `bench`
  body serialises one argument list one nesting level differently under just 1.58.0, and the
  checked-in file's `source` is an absolute path from the machine that generated it
  (`/home/hatch/git/worktrees/queue-1283-551/pkgs/id/justfile`). A naive byte-diff guard would
  false-positive on both, forever.
- **No guard exists.** No flake check (flake.nix `checks`, :308ff), workflow, or script
  references `just-recipes` outside flake.nix's generation and the justfile's `lockfiles`
  recipe (grep this run).

## Why it matters

Today the drift is one stale description. The same silent path turns a future justfile change
into a missing or wrong nix app: a recipe added without `just lockfiles` gets no
`nix run .#<recipe>` at all, and a recipe whose parameters change keeps the old app signature —
exactly the Nix/justfile desync `pkgs/id/AGENTS.md` warns against, with no signal anywhere.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `pkgs/id/just-recipes.json` is regenerated so `crash-gate-sampled`'s doc matches the
      current justfile (and any other semantic drift at the time is resolved).
- [ ] An automated check (flake check or CI job, in the style of the existing id checks)
      fails when the justfile and `just-recipes.json` disagree on the semantic recipe fields
      (presence, doc, parameters, dependencies, private flag).
- [ ] The check normalises the known generation noise — the absolute `source` path and
      just-version serialisation differences such as the `bench` body nesting — so it is
      green on a correctly regenerated file regardless of which machine/just produced it.
- [ ] The check is demonstrated failing on the pre-fix tree (stale `crash-gate-sampled` doc)
      and passing after regeneration.

Related, distinct: #1797 (justfile formatting in CI / build hygiene) — this issue is only the
generated-file drift guard.

body:
# cf-container-hello: GET /name/<malformed percent-encoding> throws a raw URIError out of the Worker — 500 instead of 400

## Evidence

- `pkgs/cf-container-hello/src/index.ts:104` (main `a0625480`):

  ```ts
  const name = pathname.startsWith("/name/") ? decodeURIComponent(pathname.slice("/name/".length)) : undefined;
  ```

  The decode is unguarded and the default export's `fetch` handler has no try/catch anywhere, so a malformed percent sequence in the name segment throws straight out of the handler. In a deployed Worker that surfaces as a 500 / Worker exception, not a JSON error response like every other error this file returns (`json(...)` 401/503 paths).

- The route is reachable by any authenticated caller: the auth gate (lines 88–96) runs before the decode, and a valid Bearer token passes it, after which the bad segment throws.

## Reproduction (verified this run)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-cfhello/` importing the real `index.ts` (md5 `989af606a59525b334c2181765af025a`, identical on sandbox main and the laptop clone) with `@cloudflare/containers` stubbed (`getContainer` records the name and returns a marker response), `API_TOKEN` set, valid Bearer header:

| Request | Result |
|---|---|
| `GET /name/alice` | 200 `container:alice` (control) |
| `GET /name/%E0%A4%A` | **THREW `URIError: URI error`** |
| `GET /name/%zz` | **THREW `URIError: URI error`** |
| `GET /name/100%` | **THREW `URIError: URI error`** |
| `GET /worker-marker` | 200 (control) |
| `GET /name/%zz` without auth | 401 JSON (control — auth gate fires first) |

## Why it matters

This Worker is a diagnostic front door for container probes (`/probe`, `/lite` isolate image vs application faults). A malformed name — a typo'd URL, a scanner, a client that double-encodes — produces an unhandled exception and a non-JSON 500 instead of the file's otherwise consistent JSON error shape, which muddies exactly the Worker-vs-container distinction this app exists to make (an exception looks like an application fault). The same unguarded-decode defect has already been filed for two sibling apps (#2633 lab-ops-hub, #2693 projector); this is the cf-container-hello instance, in a different package with a different handler.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `GET /name/<malformed percent-encoding>` (e.g. `%E0%A4%A`, `%zz`, trailing `%`) returns a 400 JSON error response; no exception escapes the fetch handler.
- [ ] Valid names behave exactly as before, including legitimately percent-encoded names (e.g. `/name/a%20b` still resolves the container for `a b`).
- [ ] `/worker-marker`, the 401 path, and the 503 unconfigured-token path are unchanged.
- [ ] A test/regression check covers at least one malformed-percent name and one valid encoded name.

title: id(invite): the two invite parsers disagree on key/node spellings — the web handler percent-decodes them, Invite::from_query does not

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

pkgs/id has two parsers for the one invite format, and they accept different spellings of the security-relevant fields (`key` = the account key, `node` = the server node ID):

### 1. The string form — `Invite::from_query` (`pkgs/id/src/invite.rs:85-105`)

The hand-rolled parser percent-decodes **only `name`** (`decode(value)` at :94). `key` and `node` pass to `Invite::new` → `hex_key` (:108-115) **raw**, so any percent-encoded or `+`-carrying spelling of the key/node is refused as "must be 64 hex characters".

### 2. The HTTPS confirm page — `invite_handler` (`pkgs/id/src/web/explore.rs:356-360`)

The handler takes axum `Query<BTreeMap<String, String>>`, i.e. serde_urlencoded, which percent-decodes **every** field (and turns `+` into a space) before `Invite::new` ever sees them. So the page accepts — and confirms to the user — spellings the string parser refuses:

- `key=%61a11…` (percent-encoded hex) → page parses it as the account; `Invite::from_query` on the same query errors.
- `key=+aa11…` (leading `+`) → serde_urlencoded yields `" aa11…"`, and `hex_key`'s `trim()` then accepts it; the string parser refuses the `+`.

The page is the trust surface for this link: it displays the account key and name, emits the canonical `id:invite?…` string and its QR (`invite_page`, explore.rs:373-395). A link that the page happily confirms cannot be consumed in its raw form by the crate's own string parser, and intermediary tools that re-encode or normalize the query (shorteners, messengers, log pipelines) silently change whether a given spelling is valid at all. `key`/`node` are the identifiers the whole invite decision rests on — the same "one identifier, two spellings" class as #2517 (`hex_to_array`/`hex_bytes` accepting `+`-encoded pairs in directory_auth).

## Evidence (verified this run, main `74dde9c2`)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-invitedecode/` (compiled and run on the laptop; `src/invite.rs` copied **verbatim** from main, web side mirrors explore.rs:356-360 exactly: `serde_urlencoded::from_str::<BTreeMap<String,String>>` then `Invite::new(field("key"), field("node"), field("name"))`):

```text
control plain
  cli: Ok key=aa11aa11.. name="Ann"
  web: Ok key=aa11aa11.. name="Ann"
key fully %-encoded (%61)
  cli: Err the account key: must be 64 hex characters
  web: Ok key=aa11aa11.. name="Ann"
key first char %-encoded (%41 for A, upper)
  cli: Err the account key: must be 64 hex characters
  web: Ok key=aa11aa11.. name="Ann"
key with leading +
  cli: Err the account key: must be 64 hex characters
  web: Ok key=aa11aa11.. name="Ann"
node %-encoded first char
  cli: Err the node ID: must be 64 hex characters
  web: Ok key=aa11aa11.. name="Ann"
name percent-encoded (both should accept)
  cli: Ok key=aa11aa11.. name="Ann Lee"
  web: Ok key=aa11aa11.. name="Ann Lee"
```

(Duplicate fields were also probed: both parsers take the last occurrence — that behavior is already tracked by #2006 and is **not** part of this issue.)

## Why it matters

- One format, two acceptance sets: whether an invite link "works" depends on which door it enters through, for the two fields that identify *who* you are adding and *which server* vouches for them.
- The confirm page can bless a non-canonical spelling that the string-form parser (the crate's public API for the format, `Invite::parse`/`from_query`) rejects — the user sees a valid confirmation for a link they then cannot use as copied.
- Non-canonical spellings of an account key undermine string-level comparison anywhere links are logged, deduped, or blocklisted: `%61a11…` and `aa11…` are the same account but different strings until one specific parser decodes them.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] One decoding rule for `key`/`node` shared by both entry points: either `Invite::from_query` percent-decodes `key`/`node` exactly as it does `name` (and the web handler relies on that single parser instead of pre-decoding via `Query<BTreeMap<…>>`), or the web handler stops pre-decoding so both refuse non-hex spellings — triage pins which direction; the invariant is that the two paths never disagree on the same query string.
- [ ] `hex_key`'s acceptance is identical through both doors for: plain hex, percent-encoded hex, `+`-prefixed hex, and mixed-case hex (probe matrix above becomes the regression test cases).
- [ ] The web handler's existing tests (`explore.rs` invite page test, ~:1016) and `invite.rs` round-trip tests still pass; new tests cover the cross-parser agreement cases.
- [ ] No change to the canonical emitted form: `Invite::url()` / `https_path()` output is byte-identical to today for the same invite.

## Dedup

- #2006 (open) covers **duplicate** fields in both hand-rolled link parsers — distinct defect (this probe confirms duplicates behave the same in both parsers here; the asymmetry is decoding, not multiplicity).
- #1770 (open) covers control characters in the invite **name** via `Invite::new` — distinct field and defect.
- #2517 (open) is the same two-spellings class but in `directory_auth` hex parsing for signed requests — different code, different surface.

Found by new-issue-creator-code-a, 2026-10-30 run.

title: pm-dispatch(actions/workflows): prompt written to GITHUB_OUTPUT under a fixed heredoc delimiter — a prompt containing that line truncates and breaks the dispatch

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/low

labels.name: effort/s

labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

body:
## Summary

Three fleet dispatch sites write a multi-line **prompt** to `$GITHUB_OUTPUT` using a **fixed, hard-coded heredoc delimiter**. If the prompt text itself contains a line exactly equal to that delimiter — a realistic content for prompts *about these very actions* (a maintenance/ci-fix prompt quoting the action's own output block), for `prompt-url` text fetched from the web, or for the failure-entry / issue-body text embedded by `flake-inputs-update.yml` — the runner ends the `prompt` value at that line. The dispatched session loses the rest of its prompt, and the remaining prompt lines are then parsed as output-file lines: prose lines are invalid format (the runner throws and the step fails), and `key=value`-shaped lines are silently consumed as outputs. GitHub's own docs for multi-line output values recommend a delimiter "not present in the value" — in practice a randomly generated one per run; a constant string published in this repo cannot satisfy that for arbitrary prompt text.

## Evidence (main 59fed0e8)

- `.github/actions/pm-dispatch-task/action.yml` (resolve step, ~lines 221–229): writes `prompt<<PM_DISPATCH_TASK_PROMPT_EOF`, the resolved prompt, then the delimiter — the prompt comes from `prompt-file` (caller workspace), `prompt-url` (`curl -fsS` of an arbitrary https URL), the inline `prompt` input, or the bundled library, so its content is arbitrary text by design.
- `.github/workflows/flake-inputs-update.yml:336-338`: same pattern with `PM_DISPATCH_PROMPT_EOF`; the prompt file it cats embeds `$RUNNER_TEMP/entry.md` / `issue-body.md` (failure-entry / tracking-issue body text) verbatim.
- `.github/workflows/main-broken.yml:153-158`: same pattern with `MAIN_BROKEN_BODY_EOF` / `MAIN_BROKEN_PROMPT_EOF` for `body` and `prompt` (content built from workflow/job names and recurrence text — lower risk, same defect).

Verified this run with a laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-ghout/probe.py`) that reproduces the pm-dispatch-task write block byte-for-byte in structure and parses it with the runner's documented output-file rules (`name=value`; `name<<delimiter` until a line exactly equal to the delimiter):

```
CASE A benign: prompt intact: True | title: Scheduled Bolt - x/y | errors: []
CASE B delimiter-in-prompt: prompt intact: False
  parsed prompt: 'You are maintaining the pm-dispatch-task action. Its resolve step writes:\nprompt<<PM_DISPATCH_TASK_PROMPT_EOF\n...the prompt...'
  errors: ["invalid format line (runner throws): 'Then it dispatches the session with that prompt.'",
           "invalid format line (runner throws): 'IMPORTANT FINAL INSTRUCTION: also update the changelog.'",
           "invalid format line (runner throws): 'PM_DISPATCH_TASK_PROMPT_EOF'"]
CASE C delimiter+kv: prompt: 'Do the task.' | errors: ["invalid format line ... 'the rest of the real prompt, never delivered'", ...]
```

So a delimiter line in the prompt (Case B) truncates the prompt mid-text and turns the remainder into runner errors — the dispatch step fails, or, where following lines happen to parse, the session is launched with a silently shortened prompt and no warning anywhere.

## Why it matters

pm-dispatch is the fleet's session launcher: a truncated prompt means a dispatched agent works from partial instructions (the tail of these prompts is where the delivery/merge instructions live), and a failed resolve step means a scheduled/ci-fix dispatch silently never happens. The trigger content is not exotic — the prompt library's natural growth includes prompts that document or fix these actions themselves, and `prompt-url` is explicitly a fetch-arbitrary-text feature.

## Acceptance criteria

- No fixed delimiter: each site generates its output delimiter at runtime (e.g. `EOF_$(openssl rand -hex 8)` / `uuidgen`) so prompt content cannot practically collide with it, at all three sites above (pm-dispatch-task, flake-inputs-update, main-broken).
- A prompt containing the *old* fixed delimiter strings (and lines resembling them) round-trips intact through the resolve step's outputs — covered by a test or a documented simulation like the probe.
- Behaviour is otherwise unchanged: output names, ordering, and downstream consumers (`steps.resolve.outputs.prompt`, dispatch steps) untouched.

## Dedup

`gh` searches (open + closed) for "GITHUB_OUTPUT delimiter", "heredoc output", "EOF marker", and "pm-dispatch-task": no issue covers output-delimiter collision. #2679/#2681 are the pm-dispatch actions' priority/input defects — different mechanism. #2668 is the dispatch launch-pipeline design — this is a concrete defect inside it, not covered by its staging.

labels.name: source/design-architect

body:
## Problem

The projector's joined-subject read endpoint throws on a malformed percent-encoding instead of answering with a clean error (main b3f6d2b2):

**`pm-stack/projector/src/server.ts:175-176`**
```ts
if (path.startsWith("/subjects/") && method === "GET") {
  const subject = decodeURIComponent(path.slice("/subjects/".length));
```

`decodeURIComponent` is unguarded, and this handler has no try/catch (unlike `/health` and the webhook path in the same file). A subject containing an incomplete UTF-8 percent sequence (`%E0%A4%A`) or a non-hex escape (`%zz`) raises a raw `URIError` that escapes `handleRequest` entirely — under `Bun.serve` the request fails as an unhandled 500 with no JSON error body, instead of the endpoint's own `404 {"error":"subject_not_found"}` or a 400 naming the bad encoding.

Subjects are external keys (`kaneo:<projectSlug>/<taskId>`, `grist:<docId>/<tableId>/<rowId>`, `gh:<ref>` — schema.sql), i.e. caller-supplied strings interpolated into a URL path by the aggregator and other clients, so a malformed or hand-built link reaches this code as-is.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-projector/probe.ts`, real `handleRequest` + `migrate` against an in-memory libSQL DB, main b3f6d2b2):

```text
GET /subjects/%E0%A4%A     -> THREW URIError: URI error
GET /subjects/%zz          -> THREW URIError: URI error
GET /subjects/valid%20name -> status 404 body {"error":"subject_not_found"}
GET /subjects/plain        -> status 404 body {"error":"subject_not_found"}
```

Well-formed encodings decode and 404 cleanly; only the malformed forms escape the handler as a thrown exception.

## Why it matters

This is the projector's one joined read (links + item state + unified activity in one call — aggregator requirement #1 + #2). Any client that builds the path from an untrusted or hand-edited subject gets an opaque server error with no JSON body to handle, and the throw lands in the server log as an unhandled exception rather than a client error. Every other structured input on this server is validated at the boundary (webhook HMAC + bounded body, link `ref` regex); this decode is the loose one.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `GET /subjects/<malformed percent-encoding>` (e.g. `%E0%A4%A`, `%zz`, a trailing `%`) returns a JSON 400 (or the endpoint's 404) — `handleRequest` never throws for any path input.
- [ ] Well-formed subjects are unchanged: an existing subject still returns 200 with its view, an unknown one still returns `404 {"error":"subject_not_found"}`.

body:
# id(event_store): Mirror::release / present_proof expire due waiting events in the pool but never delete their rows — pool and rows diverge in the committed transaction

## Evidence (main c9f01089)

`pkgs/id/src/event_store/waiting_rows.rs` states the invariant the mirror exists to keep (module docs, lines 15–19):

> "The pool and the rows change together through `Mirror`. Each call on a `Mirror` makes one change to the pool and the matching change to the rows, inside one write transaction. If the transaction commits, the two agree…"

Two `Mirror` methods break it:

- `Mirror::release` (waiting_rows.rs:272–277) calls `self.pool.arrived(*id, now)` and then deletes only the released id's row and its dep index (`delete` + `drop_dep`).
- `Mirror::present_proof` (waiting_rows.rs:284–292) does the same.

But `WaitingPool::arrived` (pkgs/id/src/waiting.rs:342–343) begins with `self.expire_due(now_ms)`: every held event that has reached the age cap at `now` is removed from **every pool index** and pushed onto the pool's internal `expired` buffer. Those events are:

- not in `arrived`'s return value (it returns only released events),
- not deleted from the `waiting` / `waiting_by_dep` rows by `release`/`present_proof` — row deletion for expired events happens **only** in `Mirror::expire` (waiting_rows.rs:195–201), which these methods never call.

So a transaction whose only waiting-pool work is a release (the common `drain` path in `event_store/ingest.rs`, e.g. ingest.rs:641, 660) can commit with the pool and the rows disagreeing:

- in memory the due event is gone (`waiting_len`, `is_waiting`, rival checks in `held_rivals` all see it as absent),
- on disk its row — including its `waiting_by_dep` entries — is still present.

## Verified with a probe (verbatim `waiting.rs`, main c9f01089)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-waitmirror/` (crate copies `pkgs/id/src/waiting.rs` unchanged; `WaitingPool<u32, &str>`, default limits):

1. `insert(author, 1, [9], "X-due", 0)` and `insert(author, 2, [10], "Y-waiter", WEEK_MS - 1_000)` (Y fresh, X due at the cap).
2. Simulate exactly `Mirror::release(dep=10)`'s pool side at `now = 604_800_000` (the 7-day cap): `pool.arrived(10, WEEK_MS)` returns `["Y-waiter"]` only; afterwards `pool.len() == 0` and `pool.contains(&1) == false` — X left the pool without being returned anywhere.
3. Only a **later** `pool.expire(WEEK_MS)` surfaces X: `[(author, "X-due")]`.

In the store that later surfacing is what deletes X's row, so the cleanup — and the expiry count returned by `expire_waiting` (ingest.rs:396–401) — is attributed to a later, unrelated call. If no later ingest/expire call happens before shutdown, the row survives on disk; on the next open, `reload` (event_store/mod.rs:980–1013) silently drops it as due, so the expiry is never reported at all. Either way the expiry is not lost, but it is unreported/misattributed and the documented pool↔rows agreement does not hold for the committing transaction.

Distinct from the pool in isolation: `waiting.rs`'s caps/expiry/self-dep semantics were checked and found consistent in an earlier pass — this is specifically the Mirror layer's failure to flush the pool's expired buffer (rows + reporting) inside `release`/`present_proof`.

## Why it matters

- The mirror's pool↔rows agreement is the stated crash-consistency story for the waiting table; a silent exception in the hottest path (every release) makes the invariant un-auditable — the next divergence will be assumed impossible.
- Expiry is the waiting pool's only drop path and is supposed to be logged/counted by the caller (waiting.rs module docs, step 3: "Call `expire` regularly and log what it returns"). Expiries swallowed into the buffer during a release are logged late, under a different call, or never (restart case).
- The stale row keeps its `waiting_by_dep` entries, so `drop_dep` for a later-arriving dependency iterates and rewrites a row for an event the pool no longer holds.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Mirror::release` and `Mirror::present_proof` leave pool and rows in agreement when the transaction commits: due events expired inside `pool.arrived` have their rows deleted in the same transaction (or the methods flush/report the pool's expired buffer the way `Mirror::expire` does).
- [ ] An expiry that happens during a release is reported through the same channel/count as an expiry from `expire_waiting` — not silently attributed to a later unrelated call, and not lost across a restart.
- [ ] A regression test at the store level: hold two events, release a dependency at a time when the other event is due, then assert pool state, row state (e.g. via reopen/`waiting_len` after reload), and the expiry count agree immediately after the releasing call.
- [ ] Existing waiting/event-store tests still pass.
