body:
## Problem

The two daily pm-dispatch workflows declare `workflow_dispatch` inputs that never reach the dispatched session (main 65d87dff, call sites migrated in PR #2678). A manual dispatcher who sets them gets a run identical to a scheduled one — and in two cases the static prompt actively contradicts the input:

**`.github/workflows/jules-daily-codebase-ideation.yml`**
- `focus_app` (string, default `"all"`): "Optional specific package or subsystem to focus on (e.g. pkgs/id, pkgs/mcpx, or all)" — never interpolated into the title or prompt; the session is told to review everything regardless.
- `allow_direct_prs` (boolean, default `true`): "Allow opening small PRs for quick bugfixes…" — never read; the prompt unconditionally says the session is "actively encouraged to open small, focused Pull Requests", so `allow_direct_prs: false` does not stop PR creation.

**`.github/workflows/jules-daily-flake-sync.yml`**
- `auto_merge` (boolean, default `true`): "Automatically merge the PR if nix evaluation passes" — never read; the prompt's merge guidance ("Merge into `main` only when you are reasonably certain…") applies unchanged either way, so `auto_merge: false` does not prevent a merge the session judges certain.

The neighbouring `update_forks_only` input in the flake-sync file shows the honest pattern: it is explicitly described as "Legacy flag, ignored: …". These three inputs carry no such disclosure — their descriptions promise behaviour the workflow does not implement.

## Evidence (verified this run)

- `grep -n "inputs\." .github/workflows/jules-daily-codebase-ideation.yml .github/workflows/jules-daily-flake-sync.yml` at main 65d87dff returns **no matches**: neither file references any declared input anywhere (the only step is the `pm-dispatch-start` call with a fully static title/prompt in each).
- Reading both files end to end confirms the prompts are constant strings with no `${{ inputs.* }}` interpolation.
- Contrast in-file: `update_forks_only` (flake-sync) is labelled "Legacy flag, ignored" — the pattern the other three inputs do not follow.

## Why it matters

These are the manual override knobs for two autonomous daily sessions that can open and merge PRs. A human dispatching with `focus_app: pkgs/mcpx`, `allow_direct_prs: false`, or `auto_merge: false` reasonably believes they have scoped or de-fanged the run; the session never learns of it. The `auto_merge: false` case is the sharpest: the one control meant to keep a human in the merge loop is decorative.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every declared `workflow_dispatch` input on both workflows either observably changes the dispatched session (interpolated into the prompt/title, e.g. a focus directive, a no-PRs directive when `allow_direct_prs` is false, a do-not-merge directive when `auto_merge` is false) or is removed / explicitly described as ignored, following the `update_forks_only` pattern.
- [ ] With `allow_direct_prs: false`, the ideation prompt instructs the session not to open PRs; with `auto_merge: false`, the flake-sync prompt instructs it to leave any PR unmerged.
- [ ] Scheduled runs (no inputs) keep today's behaviour and prompt content.
- [ ] A grep-level check or workflow test pins that no declared input is unreferenced in either file.

Distinct from closed #359 (concurrency groups ignoring inputs dropped pending runs — a different mechanism in the pre-migration Jules form).

title: pm-dispatch(actions): documented numeric priority (10-90) always 400s — actions send it as a string, server only accepts names as strings

labels.name: effort/xs

labels.name: app/pm-stack
labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

body:
## Problem

The reusable pm-dispatch composite actions document a numeric priority form they can never deliver (main 65d87dff, actions added in PR #2678):

- `.github/actions/pm-dispatch-queue/action.yml` — input `priority`: "Optional priority: 10-90 or critical|high|normal|low."
- `.github/actions/pm-dispatch-start/action.yml` — same documented input.

Both actions build the request payload with jq `--arg` (queue action.yml payload step; start action.yml payload step):

```bash
payload="$(jq -n --arg priority "$INPUT_PRIORITY" ... \
  '{...} + (if $priority != "" then {priority: $priority} else {} end)')"
```

`--arg` always produces a JSON **string**, so a caller passing the documented numeric form sends `{"priority": "50"}`. The server's `resolvePriority` (`pm-stack/dispatch/src/validate.ts:28-48`) only accepts a string that is a scale *name* (`critical|high|normal|low`); a numeric string falls into the name lookup, misses, and throws `ValidationError` → HTTP 400 `priority: unknown name "50"`. The numeric path (integer 10-90, snapped to the scale) is only reachable from raw API callers who send a real JSON number — never through the Actions, which are the sanctioned cross-repo entry point under the grants mesh.

So any workflow in any allowlisted repo that follows the action documentation and passes `priority: "10"` … `"90"` gets a hard 400 from both `/v1/tasks` and `/v1/sessions`, while the name form works.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe importing the real `validate.ts` (md5 `c1f61d5acf5c85da71de798f4c7056b8`, identical in the sandbox clone at main 65d87dff and the laptop primary; probe at `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-priority/` on the laptop), feeding each parser the exact payload shape the actions construct:

```
A priority-input "50" (documented numeric form, via action) parseTaskRequest: THROW ValidationError status=400 msg=priority: unknown name "50" (use critical|high|normal|low or a number 10-90)
A priority-input "50" (documented numeric form, via action) parseSessionRequest: THROW ValidationError status=400 msg=priority: unknown name "50" (...)
B priority-input "10" (documented critical numeric, via action) parseTaskRequest: THROW ValidationError status=400 ...
B priority-input "10" (documented critical numeric, via action) parseSessionRequest: THROW ValidationError status=400 ...
C priority-input "high" (documented name form, via action) parseTaskRequest: OK priority=20
C priority-input "high" (documented name form, via action) parseSessionRequest: OK priority=20
D direct API numeric 50 (no action) parseTaskRequest: OK priority=50
D direct API numeric 50 (no action) parseSessionRequest: OK priority=50
E omitted priority (via action) parseTaskRequest: OK priority=40
E omitted priority (via action) parseSessionRequest: OK priority=40
```

No in-repo workflow passes `priority` to the actions yet (grep over `.github/workflows/`), so this bites the next caller — most likely another allowlisted repo following the published action docs — rather than a current in-repo call site.

## Why it matters

The actions are the documented, OIDC-authenticated way for any allowlisted repo to enqueue or launch dispatch work, and their input contract advertises the queue's full 10-90 scale. A caller using it gets an opaque 400 ("unknown name") for a value the docs told them was valid, with the failing layer (action jq typing vs server validation) not obvious from either side alone.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Passing any documented priority form through either composite action — numeric string `"10"`-`"90"` and the names — produces a request the server accepts, resolving to the same scale value a raw API caller gets for the numeric form.
- [ ] The fix layer is pinned by triage: actions emit a JSON number for numeric input (e.g. a numeric branch in the jq construction), or the server accepts numeric strings in `resolvePriority` — one canonical behaviour, tested at that layer. (If the server route is chosen, note it also changes raw-API behaviour for `"50"` string callers; if the action route, both actions must change identically.)
- [ ] Tests pin the through-the-action payload for a numeric priority (payload-shape test or a validate test fed the action-constructed JSON), plus the existing name/omitted cases.
- [ ] The action input descriptions and the server contract agree after the fix; existing dispatch tests still pass.

Related: #2668 (dispatch launch-pipeline boundary-validation design) — this is a concrete instance of a request the boundary mis-classifies, filed separately because the defect is in the action/server contract, not the launch pipeline ordering.

body:
# pm-dispatch(tasks): a second dispatch to an already-tasked issue silently vanishes — enqueue returns the old task, dispatch reports it as the new queued task

## Bug

`POST /v1/tasks` with `issue_number` (the attach flow added in #2676, commit dbab526d) derives the queue dedupe key canonically from (kind, repo, issue) — `pm-stack/dispatch/src/packet.ts:21` `canonicalDedupeKey`, used at `pm-stack/dispatch/src/server.ts:315-317`. The key carries nothing about the request's prompt/title. The enqueue RPC dedupes on `dedupe_key` against **all** tasks including terminal ones and returns the pre-existing row (documented at `pm-stack/dispatch/src/queue.ts:8-11`; proven live for the queue generally in #2323).

`handleTasks` never inspects the returned row. It uses `task.id` unconditionally (`server.ts:339`), posts a comment on the issue claiming `Queue task: #<old id> … Status: queued` (`server.ts:360`), and returns HTTP 201 with that id. So a second, different dispatch to an issue that already has a task under the canonical key:

- creates **no** new task — the new prompt is silently discarded;
- reports success (201) naming the **old** task, even when that task is `done` or `cancelled` (its prompt was different work);
- posts a fresh "Status: queued" agent note on the issue for a task that may have finished long ago.

The safety assumption recorded at `queue.ts:10-11` — "the canonical-key flows anchor to fresh issues, which cannot collide" — held for `/v1/sessions` and for `issue: true` (fresh issue per dispatch), but it is false for the `issue_number` attach flow, whose whole purpose is targeting an existing issue: exactly the case that can already have a canonical-key task (e.g. the fleet's own triage/fix task for that issue, or an earlier dispatch).

The same silent-drop is reachable without `issue_number`: a caller-supplied `dedupe_key` is accepted verbatim (`validate.ts` `optString`, no shape check; `server.ts:316`) and any repeat of a previously used key behaves identically.

## Evidence (this run, main 9d91d383)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-dispatchdedupe/`, real `packet.ts`/`validate.ts` copied verbatim from main, run with bun): two different prompts for the same issue produce byte-identical dedupe keys with different packet bodies —

```
kind=triage
  key A: repo-health:v1:triage:developing-today/code:issue:1234
  key B: repo-health:v1:triage:developing-today/code:issue:1234
  keys identical: true
  bodies identical: false
kind=small_fix
  key A: repo-health:v1:fix:developing-today/code:issue:1234
  key B: repo-health:v1:fix:developing-today/code:issue:1234
  keys identical: true
  bodies identical: false
```

Combined with the RPC's return-the-existing-row semantics (#2323, proven live 2026-10-29), the second packet never reaches the queue.

## Why it matters

Dispatch is the intake other repos' Actions workflows use to request fleet work. A caller that dispatches follow-up work to an existing issue — the documented attach use case — gets a success response and an on-issue confirmation for work that will never run, with no warning in the response (`warnings` is not populated on this path). This is the same silent-loss shape as #2323, but at the dispatch layer: even if #2323's RPC fix lands (dedupe only against non-terminal rows), the **live-row** case remains — a second dispatch while the first task is still queued/claimed still returns the live row and drops the new prompt while reporting success.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] When the enqueue returns a pre-existing row, dispatch detects it (e.g. compares the returned row's dedupe key + status/created_at, or an RPC-side created flag) and does **not** report it as a newly queued task.
- [ ] For the `issue_number` attach flow, a dispatch whose prompt differs from the existing task's work gets a distinct task (e.g. a dispatch-scoped suffix on the key for attach flows) or an explicit error/warning in the response — never a silent 201.
- [ ] The issue comment on the attach path states the truth: if it names an existing task, it says the task already existed and gives its actual status instead of `Status: queued`.
- [ ] The stale safety comment at `queue.ts:8-11` is corrected to cover the attach flow.
- [ ] A test (packet/server level, stubbed queue) covers: second attach dispatch to an issue with a terminal canonical-key task, and one with a live canonical-key task.

Related: #2323 (RPC dedupe semantics — root layer), #1298 (cancelled-row revival). This issue is the pm-dispatch layer's handling of the returned row, which neither of those covers.

title: mcpx(daemon): POST/DELETE /v1/servers handlers never hold reloadMu — concurrent adds lose servers while reporting success

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

The daemon's live server add/remove handlers — `handleServersAdd` (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/routes_settings.go:588`) and `handleServersRemove` (`routes_settings.go:623`) — are the only reload-path handlers that do **not** hold `s.reloadMu`, the mutex whose documented job is exactly this: “reloadMu serialises reloads, so two requests arriving together do not each rebuild the pool map from the same starting point” (`internal/daemon/server.go:137-139`).

Every other caller follows the rule:

- `handleSettingsSet` locks at `routes_settings.go:224`
- `handleAdaptersAdd` / `handleAdaptersRemove` lock at `routes_settings.go:845` / `:935` — and the adapters comment even asserts “The servers handlers hold reloadMu the same way” (`routes_settings.go:844`), which is not true
- `handleReload` and the SIGHUP path lock in `server.go`
- Adapters also got a regression test for exactly this property: `TestConcurrentAdapterAddsAllLand` (`internal/daemon/adapter_routes_test.go:88-116`). Servers have no equivalent test.

That leaves two races in the servers handlers:

1. **Lost file update.** `config.AddServer` / `config.RemoveServer` go through `config.Edit` (`internal/config/write.go:91`), an unsynchronised read-modify-write: read the file, mutate the decoded map, `os.WriteFile` the whole document back. Two concurrent `POST /v1/servers` calls (e.g. two CLI invocations, or a CLI racing a script) can both read the same starting document, each add a different server, and write back — the second write silently discards the first server. Both calls return 200.
2. **Racing reloads.** Each handler then calls `s.reloadConfig()` (`routes_settings.go:613`, `:654`) unlocked, so the two reloads can interleave their pool rebuilds from different starting points — the precise failure `server.go:137-139` says the mutex exists to prevent.

## Evidence (verified this run, main cc529762)

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-serverrace/` on the laptop) using the real `internal/config/write.go` from this main (md5 `3d8605b0c3d4340fbee7a9d1d96cf702`, byte-identical to the sandbox clone at cc529762; only its package-level `StripJSONC`/`DirMode`/`FileMode` dependencies are shimmed, and the probe inputs are plain JSON): two goroutines released simultaneously call `config.AddServer` for two different names against one config file seeded with 3,000 servers, 40 trials:

```
trial 0: both AddServer returned nil; alpha=false beta=true (one add silently lost)
RESULT lost_updates=40/40 trials (both calls reported success)
```

Both calls return nil in the lost trials — the add reports success for a server that is not in the file (and, because the handler's reload reads the file that survived, not in the running daemon either).

Code inspection this run confirms the missing lock is not compensated elsewhere: `grep reloadMu` over `internal/daemon` shows locks in the settings-set, adapters add/remove, watch, SIGHUP and reload handlers — and none in `handleServersAdd`/`handleServersRemove`; `config.Edit` itself takes no lock.

## Why it matters

Live server add is a headline mcpx workflow (`mcpx servers add`, used by scripts and parallel sessions against one shared daemon). A concurrent add that silently vanishes — while reporting success — is the worst failure shape: the caller proceeds believing the server exists, and the missing server is only discovered later, downstream, with no error pointing here. The adapters path was hardened against exactly this in PR #2565 after review; the older servers path was left with the same hole and a comment claiming it was covered.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `handleServersAdd` and `handleServersRemove` hold `s.reloadMu` across the file lookup/write and the reload, like the adapters handlers (and the stale comment at `routes_settings.go:844` becomes true, or is corrected).
- [ ] A daemon regression test mirroring `TestConcurrentAdapterAddsAllLand`: N concurrent `POST /v1/servers` adds all return 200 and all N servers are present in the written file afterwards.
- [ ] A concurrent add/remove mix cannot resurrect a removed server or drop an unrelated one (covered by the same lock, asserted in the test or a sibling).
- [ ] Existing daemon + config tests still pass in CI.

labels.name: app/pm-stack

body:
## Problem

pm-dispatch's `POST /v1/sessions` accepts a caller-supplied `directory` for the OpenCode session that is never validated — not for emptiness, and not against the repo the session is supposedly for (`pm-stack/dispatch/`, main 732ca26d):

- `optString` (`src/validate.ts:93-98`) returns string values verbatim: no trim, no non-empty check (contrast `reqString` at `:85-91`, which trims and requires non-empty). So `directory: ""` and `directory: "   "` pass validation.
- `handleSessions` resolves the directory as `body.directory ?? REPO_DIRS[body.repo]!` (`src/server.ts:180`) — `??` only catches `null`/`undefined`, so `""` defeats the per-repo default and is passed verbatim to `OpenCodeClient.createSession` as `location.directory` (`src/opencode.ts:53-61`).
- Any other absolute path is equally accepted: `directory: "/etc"` was accepted by `parseSessionRequest` in verification (below). Nothing ties the directory to the request's repo — no check against `REPO_DIRS[repo]`, no subtree/allowlist check.
- Authorization does not close this: `assertCallerRepo` (`src/auth.ts:190-201`) binds an OIDC caller to its own repo via the body's `repo` field only. A GitHub Actions workflow in repo X can therefore set `repo: X` (passing the check) with `directory: /home/user/git/<another repo>` — or any other directory on the laptop — and pm-dispatch will launch an OpenCode session there, with the caller's prompt, on the laptop's standing server. The static-bearer caller is Drew-shaped and trusted; the OIDC route is the one whose blast radius the repo binding was designed to limit, and the directory field escapes it.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe (bun, importing the real `validate.ts` from the laptop primary at main 732ca26d, md5-identical to the sandbox clone; probe at `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-dispatch/` on the laptop):

```
C empty title/directory accepted: {"title":"","directory":""}
C whitespace title + /etc directory accepted: {"title":"   ","directory":"/etc"}
```

(The same `optString` gap makes `title: ""` defeat the `titleFromPrompt` fallback in `handleSessions`/`launchSession`, which also use `??`.)

## Why it matters

The directory is where the launched agent session reads and writes. Letting the least-trusted caller class (any workflow in an allowlisted repo) point a session at an arbitrary laptop directory — including other repos' primaries or the home directory — silently widens the OIDC route from "launch work on your own repo" to "run an agent anywhere on the laptop". The empty-string case is the same gate failing at the other end: a malformed request produces a session with an unintended working directory instead of a 400.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Tests pin: `""`, `"   "`, `"/etc"`, and another repo's directory are rejected for a session request; the repo default and a subdirectory of it are accepted.
- [ ] Existing dispatch tests still pass.

# lab-ops-hub: `POST /api/machines` with a duplicate name returns 500 (raw SQLite UNIQUE error) — an already-registered machine is a 409, not a server fault

## Evidence (main `0144b0bd`, `pkgs/lab-ops-hub/src/index.ts`)

- The machines POST handler (`index.ts:269`) binds `b.name` raw into `INSERT INTO machines …` (`index.ts:271-285`) with no existence check and no local error handling.
- `schema.sql:7` declares `name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE` — a second POST for a machine that is already registered violates the constraint on every call.
- The only catch is the Worker's single outer handler (`index.ts:436-438`), which converts **every** throw into `500 {error: String(e)}`. So re-registering an existing machine returns **500 with the raw text `SQLiteError: UNIQUE constraint failed: machines.name`** — the same response shape as a genuine server fault.

## Verification (this run)

Bun probe replaying the handler's exact INSERT statement against the real `schema.sql` (`hidden_files/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-labops/probe.ts` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace, `bun:sqlite` in-memory):

- First insert of name `amd-6` → ok.
- Second insert of the same name with the handler's exact statement → throws `SQLiteError: UNIQUE constraint failed: machines.name`.

There is no code path in the handler that turns that throw into anything but the outer catch's 500.

## Why it matters

Re-adding a machine is the most predictable client mistake against this inventory API (a setup script re-run, a dashboard double-submit, a name typo'd then corrected). Today it reports "the server broke," leaks raw SQLite error text as the API contract, and gives the caller no way to distinguish "already exists — go look at it" from a real outage. The route family already has the right instincts elsewhere: `/api/crawl` returns 400 for a missing URL and the summarize route returns 404 for a missing note; the machines route just never got a conflict path. (Distinct from #2480, which covers missing fields and non-JSON bodies on these POST routes — a duplicate name is a well-formed request that conflicts with existing state.)

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `POST /api/machines` with a name that already exists returns **409** with an error naming the conflict (e.g. `machine "amd-6" already exists`); no raw SQLite text in the response.
- [ ] A first-time registration is unchanged: 201 + id, and the `machines:all` KV cache is still invalidated.
- [ ] Genuine D1 failures on the route still surface as 500.
- [ ] Regression coverage for the duplicate-name case (a unit test of the factored check/response per the #524 `src/lib.ts` pattern, or a handler-level test).

## Dedup

`gh` searches (open + closed) for lab-ops-hub + duplicate/409/UNIQUE return only #2478 (the upload `r2_key` UNIQUE collision — a server-generated key, fixed by changing the key, not a client-conflict response) and #2480 (missing-field/non-JSON 400s). Nothing covers a client-visible conflict response for the UNIQUE machine name.

— filed by new-issue-creator-code-b (Lane B), 2026-10-30 run

body:
## Summary

cold-store-reaper's D1 response handling assumes the Cloudflare D1 API body is always a JSON object with object-shaped `errors[0]` / `result[0]` entries. Any other shape — a JSON array, string, or number body, or an `errors`/`result` list holding a string or `null` — raises a bare `AttributeError` instead of the module's own `ColdStoreError` carrying the API's message. The error-extraction helper crashes in exactly the situation it exists for, so a shape-drifted D1 (or intermediary/proxy) error body masks the real failure with `'list' object has no attribute 'get'`.

## Evidence (main `541578ae`, `pkgs/cold-store-reaper/cold_store.py`)

- `d1_error_message` (:193-208) does `payload.get("errors")` and `errors[0].get("message")` with no shape checks. Its own docstring promises "best-effort extraction … so a sync failure is diagnosable from the CLI output alone".
- `_d1_select` (:1236-1243) repeats the assumption on the success path: `payload.get("success", True)`, `errors[0].get('message', …)`, `(payload.get("result") or [{}])[0].get("results")`.
- The manifest sync loop (:1340-1346) has the same `errors[0].get(...)` pattern, and both error paths call `d1_error_message(resp)` (:1233, :1333), so a malformed error body replaces the intended `ColdStoreError("D1 query/sync failed (HTTP …): <api message>")` with an `AttributeError` that callers catching `ColdStoreError` will not catch.

Verified this run with the real module imported (probe `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-d1shape/probe.py`, stdlib-only, transport stubbed for `_d1_select`):

`d1_error_message`:
- `{"errors":[{"message":"real d1 error"}]}` → `'real d1 error'` (control OK)
- `[{"message":"x"}]`, `"some error"`, `42` → `AttributeError: … has no attribute 'get'`
- `{"errors":[null]}`, `{"errors":["boom"]}` → `AttributeError` on the element

`_d1_select` (HTTP 200):
- normal body → rows returned (control OK)
- list payload, string payload, `{"success":false,"errors":["nope"]}`, `{"success":false,"errors":[null]}`, `{"success":true,"result":["x"]}` → all raise `AttributeError` instead of returning rows or raising `ColdStoreError`

## Why it matters

D1 is the manifest sync target for the backup system. When D1 (or a proxy in front of it) returns an unexpected body — maintenance pages are HTML (handled: non-JSON falls back to raw text), but JSON array/string bodies and shape-drifted `errors` entries are plausible from intermediaries and API changes — the operator gets a Python traceback about `.get` instead of the HTTP status and the API's own error text, and the failure escapes the `ColdStoreError` handling the CLI is built around. The diagnostic path should be the most defensive code in the file, not the least.

## Acceptance criteria

- `d1_error_message` never raises for any body: non-object JSON, non-dict `errors` entries, and non-list `errors` all fall back to the truncated raw-text behaviour it already has for non-JSON bodies.
- `_d1_select` and the sync loop raise `ColdStoreError` (naming the unexpected shape) for a 200 body that is not the expected object shape, and for `errors[0]` entries that are not objects; a rejected query still surfaces the API message when one is present.
- Regression tests cover: array body, string body, numeric body, `errors: [null]`, `errors: ["…"]`, `result: ["…"]`, plus the normal success and normal error controls.
- Existing cold-store-reaper tests pass unchanged.

## Dedup

Open cold-store issues cover the prune ledger (#2550), Drive pagination (#2426), S3 listing datetimes (#2110), and the S3 pagination loop (#1632) — none touches the D1 response-shape handling. Searched `d1_error_message` / D1 error across open and closed issues this run: no match.

body:
# mcpx(settings): non-positive durations pass validation, then panic the daemon at `time.NewTicker` — reapInterval/saveInterval/ssePing accept `-5s` and `0s`

## Summary

`KindDuration` settings are validated only for parseability, never for sign. Interval settings that are spent directly as `time.NewTicker` periods therefore accept `-5s` and `0s` at every layer (file / env / flag / preset / runtime override), and the daemon later panics with `non-positive interval for NewTicker` — at startup for the reap/save tickers, and on the first SSE events request for the ping ticker. This is the duration sibling of #1697 (byte sizes accept negatives/overflow and panic a `make` cap); that issue's fix does not reach this one, because the values here parse cleanly and overflow nothing.

## Evidence (verified this run, main fbedd805)

Line trace, `pkgs/mcpx`:

- `internal/settings/value.go:499-502` — `Validate`'s `KindDuration` case only checks `time.ParseDuration(raw)` succeeds. `-5s` and `0s` both parse, so both are *valid* settings. `SetRuntime`/`Apply` gate on `Normalize` → `Validate`, so the bad value is admitted at every layer.
- `internal/settings/value.go:317-320` — `Set.Duration()` re-parses with the error discarded and returns the value verbatim.
- Declarations with no floor/positivity constraint: `daemon.reapInterval` (`internal/settings/registry.go:474`, default `30s`), `daemon.saveInterval` (`registry.go:480`, default `5m`), `http.ssePing` (`internal/settings/wire.go:61`).
- Unguarded consumers: `internal/daemon/server.go:539-542` — `Serve()` does `time.NewTicker(s.set.Duration("daemon.reapInterval"))` and the same for `saveInterval`, unconditionally, before the serve loop; `internal/daemon/server.go:1447` — the SSE handler does `time.NewTicker(s.set.Duration("http.ssePing"))`.
- The guarded contrast exists in the same package: `internal/daemon/routes_exec.go:110-114` — `collectArtifacts` substitutes the default when `every <= 0` before calling `NewTicker`. The reap/save/ping sites have no equivalent guard, which is why this stayed hidden.

Laptop probe (real `internal/settings` package; worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-durticker` on the laptop at 541578ae — `internal/settings/value.go` sha256 `c669f256…` and `internal/daemon/server.go` sha256 `a5efbdc6…` are byte-identical to sandbox main fbedd805):

```
SetRuntime(daemon.reapInterval, "-5s") ACCEPTED; Duration()=-5s
time.NewTicker(-5s) PANICS: non-positive interval for NewTicker
SetRuntime(daemon.reapInterval, "0s") ACCEPTED; Duration()=0s
time.NewTicker(0s) PANICS: non-positive interval for NewTicker
SetRuntime(daemon.saveInterval, "-1s") ACCEPTED; Duration()=-1s  -> NewTicker PANICS
SetRuntime(http.ssePing, "-1s") ACCEPTED; Duration()=-1s         -> NewTicker PANICS
SetRuntime(http.ssePing, "0s") ACCEPTED; Duration()=0s           -> NewTicker PANICS
Validate(<real registry decl>, "-5s") err=<nil>; Validate(..., "0s") err=<nil>  (all three decls)
```

## Why it matters

The settings system is the one choke point whose job is keeping an invalid value out of a running process (the #1697 reasoning). An interval of `-1s`/`0s` is an easy typo or generated-config artefact, and here it does not degrade anything — it crashes the daemon outright at startup (reap/save) or takes down an SSE request handler goroutine (ping). Other duration settings may legitimately mean something at zero (e.g. `daemon.idleExit` defaults to `0s` = disabled), so this cannot be fixed by a blanket "all durations must be > 0" rule; the interval/poll class needs its own pin.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Interval-class duration settings — at minimum `daemon.reapInterval`, `daemon.saveInterval`, `http.ssePing`, and any other setting a consumer spends as a `NewTicker`/`Tick` period (triage to enumerate: e.g. `proto.askPoll`, `protoTasks.pollInterval`, `transport.sseKeepAlive`, `autostart.pollInterval`) — refuse zero and negative values at `Validate`/`Normalize` time, with an error naming the value, at every layer (file/env/flag/preset/runtime).
- [ ] Duration settings where zero is a documented "disabled/never" meaning (e.g. `daemon.idleExit`) keep accepting `0s`; triage pins which class each duration setting belongs to rather than applying one global rule.
- [ ] No `NewTicker` call site reachable from a settings duration can panic on a validated value (either validation refuses it, or the site guards like `collectArtifacts` does).
- [ ] Regression tests cover `-5s` and `0s` for at least the three named settings plus one legitimate-zero setting staying accepted; existing `internal/settings` and `internal/daemon` tests keep passing.

## Notes for triage

- Where the positivity pin lives (a per-setting floor/class on the declaration vs a consumer-side guard) is the decision this filing leaves to triage — hence `task/triage`, not a self-solve.
- Distinct from: #1697 (KindBytes negatives/overflow, `make` cap panic — different kind, different consumer); #1758 (closed; adapter's own `parseDuration`, not the settings system); #2309 (plugin `goDurationMs` overflow → Infinity, a JS-side conversion).
- Found by new-issue-creator lane A, 2026-10-30.

body:
# cloudflare-export: GraphQL `errors` is assumed to be an array of `{message: string}` — other shapes throw TypeErrors misclassified as fetch-failed, and a single-object `errors` is silently ignored

## Evidence (verified this run, main 819889bb)

`pm-stack/cloudflare-export/cloudflare-quota-export.mjs`, in `run()`:

- Line 407: `const gqlErrors = gql.body?.errors ?? [];`
- Line 408-409: `if (gqlErrors.length) { const msg = gqlErrors.map((e) => e.message.split("\n")[0]).join(" ; "); ... }` — this assumes `errors` is an array whose every entry is an object with a string `message`. Nothing validates that shape, in a file whose other parsers (`parseGraphqlUsage`, `classifyR2`, `foldKv`, `firstSum`) are deliberately fail-closed on shape drift.
- Line 451 (`main()`): any non-`ExportError` escaping `run()` is re-wrapped as `new ExportError("fetch-failed", 7, "unexpected: ...")`.

Probe (laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-cfgqlerr/probe.mjs`, Bun, the real `run()` imported from the laptop clone — md5 `0fbd8dae4f5eba83adb88ec6092d1039`, byte-identical to sandbox main — with `fetch` stubbed; billing probes 200, buckets well-formed):

- Control, valid payload with no `errors`: `status: ok`, 11 metrics.
- Control, `errors: [{message: "auth: permission denied"}]`: correctly throws `ExportError token-scope` exit 3.
- `errors: "upstream exploded"` (a string): **TypeError** — `gqlErrors.map is not a function` escapes `run()`; `main()` reclassifies it as **fetch-failed / exit 7** with detail `unexpected: ...`, instead of the file's own `unparseable / exit 6` for an unrecognised shape, and the GraphQL error text is lost.
- `errors: [null]`: **TypeError** — `null is not an object (evaluating 'e.message')`, same fetch-failed/7 misclassification.
- `errors: [{message: 12345}]`: **TypeError** — `e.message.split is not a function`, same misclassification.
- `errors: {message: "auth: permission denied"}` (single object, no array) **with** a valid `data` payload alongside (GraphQL permits partial data + errors): the error is **silently ignored** — `gqlErrors.length` is `undefined`, so the branch never runs — and `run()` publishes a `status: ok` document with 11 metrics despite an auth/permission error entry. Without `data`, the same shape falls through to the generic "no account node in data" unparseable, and the token-scope classification (exit 3) the array form gets never fires.

## Why it matters

This exporter's whole contract is its failure taxonomy (header comment, lines 36-40): `token-scope` (exit 3) tells the operator the token needs scopes, `unparseable` (6) says an endpoint answered an unknown shape, `fetch-failed` (7) says the network/other failed. A shape-drifted `errors` field currently lands in the wrong bucket — an on-call reader chasing a "fetch failure" finds a healthy network and no error text — and the single-object form can either hide an auth error behind a green `status: ok` document or strip it of its scope classification. The aggregator/gatherer side trusts these statuses to decide whether a Cloudflare reading is real.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The GraphQL `errors` value is normalised/validated before use: a non-array `errors`, or entries that are not objects with a string `message`, produce `ExportError("unparseable", 6, ...)` naming the shape — never a bare TypeError escaping `run()`.
- [ ] A single-object `errors` (or any truthy non-array form triage decides to accept) is not silently ignored: its message goes through the same auth/permission/scope classification as the array form, or it is rejected as unparseable — triage pins which; an auth/permission error must never coexist with a published `status: ok` document.
- [ ] `main()`'s classification of a GraphQL shape problem is `unparseable`/6, not `fetch-failed`/7.
- [ ] Regression tests in `cloudflare-quota-export.test.mjs` cover: `errors` as a string, `[null]`, `[{message: <number>}]`, and a single-object `errors`, alongside the existing array controls (valid payload still exports `status: ok`; `[{message: "auth: ..."}]` still yields token-scope/3).
- [ ] Well-formed responses are unaffected: the existing cloudflare-export test suite passes unchanged.

Dedup: #2574 covers the R2 bucket enumeration in the same `run()` (fails-open `r2Buckets: []` + pagination) — a different field and failure mode; this issue is only the GraphQL `errors` handling at lines 407-416. #2460 is the meta-exporter's timestamp misclassification, a different file.

body:
## Problem

The range-sync decoder accepts non-canonical (overlong) varints in every varint position, so one message has many wire spellings — the exact duplicate-spelling property this codebase's tuple decoder already refuses for integers and floats.

Evidence (pkgs/id/src/event_store/range.rs, main 3a425552):

- `put_varint` (lines ~400–408) always emits the minimal encoding: it stops as soon as the remaining value fits in one byte.
- `Reader::varint` (lines ~497–508) accepts any encoding of up to 5 bytes whose final byte is under 0x80 — including overlong forms with leading zero groups (e.g. `0x81 0x00` for 1, or a 5-byte encoding of 5). It never checks that a multi-byte encoding was necessary.
- The varint positions are: the frame entry count (`decode_frame` / `frame_entry_count`), the Fingerprint count, and the IDs count (`Reader::entry`).
- Contrast in the same crate: tuple decoding rejects a second spelling on purpose — "The encoder emits the minimal byte count, so a leading zero payload byte … is an encoding no encoder produces. Reject it rather than accept a second spelling of the same key" (src/tuple.rs, positive-int branch; the negative-int and float branches do the same, and the float branch rejects the -0.0 stored form for the same reason — see #2421).

## Verified this run (laptop probe, real crate, main 3a425552)

Probe: ~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-rangeenc/ (`id` path dependency, default-features off):

- Canonical frame `[more=0, count=0x01, entry(len 0, mode 0 Skip)]` → decode_frame Ok, 1 entry.
- Same frame with the count overlong-encoded as `0x81 0x00` → decode_frame Ok, 1 entry. Identical message, second spelling.
- A Fingerprint entry whose count 5 is overlong-encoded as the 5-byte `0x85 0x80 0x80 0x80 0x00` → decode_frame Ok, 1 entry.

## Why it matters

`/id-range-sync/1` flights are the reconciliation wire format between peers that may run different builds. A decoder that accepts spellings no encoder produces makes byte-equality useless for comparing flights (dedup, transcript logs, test vectors, any future flight hashing/signing), and hides peer encoder bugs behind silent acceptance — the same reasoning the tuple decoder already applies. It also leaves the 5-byte cap doing double duty: a 5-byte varint can carry 35 bits, so non-canonical forms smuggle values the field widths never intended (the Fingerprint count narrows to u32 afterwards; the IDs count and frame count are used as usize loop/allocation drivers first).

## Acceptance criteria

- `Reader::varint` rejects a non-minimal encoding (a multi-byte varint whose value fits in fewer bytes), in all three positions: frame entry count, Fingerprint count, IDs count.
- Tests: minimal encodings at each width boundary (0x7F, 0x80, 0x3FFF, 0x4000) still decode; overlong forms of the same values are refused in each position.
- Existing range.rs tests stay green.

body:
## Problem

The range-sync encoder never checks an entry's upper-bound length against the key length, so it happily emits frames that the crate's own decoder refuses — and past 255 bytes the one-byte length prefix wraps and garbles the entry stream.

Evidence (pkgs/id/src/event_store/range.rs, main 3a425552):

- Wire format (module doc, lines 19–24): an entry's upper bound is "one length byte, 0 for +infinity, then the prefix", and a bound is a prefix of a sync key — at most `KEY_LEN` = 72 bytes (line 35).
- `encode_entry` (line 415) writes the length as `out.push(b.len() as u8)` with no validation. `frames()` (lines ~446–465) checks only that the encoded entry fits the frame budget — never the bound length.
- The decoder enforces the limit the encoder ignores: `Reader::entry` rejects `len > KEY_LEN` with "a bound of {len} bytes is longer than a key".
- `check_bounds` (lines ~571–590) — the documented pre-flight check that `Party::respond` requires callers to have run on a message — checks only that bounds increase and that nothing follows +infinity. It does not check bound length either, so it approves every case below.

## Verified this run (laptop probe, real crate, main 3a425552)

Probe: ~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-rangeenc/ (`id` path dependency, default-features off; one `Entry { upper: Some(vec![0xAA; N]), mode: Skip }` per case):

- N=72: frames() OK, decode_frame round-trips equal. check_bounds Ok.
- N=100: frames() OK, decode_frame ERR "a bound of 100 bytes is longer than a key". check_bounds Ok.
- N=255: frames() OK, decode_frame ERR (same). check_bounds Ok.
- N=256: frames() OK, decode_frame ERR "unknown mode byte 170" — the length byte wrapped to 0 (+infinity) and the decoder started reading the bound's own bytes as the mode byte; the frame's remaining bytes are garbage. With different bound bytes the wrapped prefix can parse as a *different, valid-looking entry* instead of erroring. check_bounds Ok.
- N=300: frames() OK, decode_frame ERR "unknown mode byte 170" (300 wraps to 44, then the stream desynchronises). check_bounds Ok.

Internal producers are safe today only by construction: separators are at most KEY_LEN bytes and inbound entries pass through decode_frame. But `Entry`, `frames`, `check_bounds` and `Party::respond` are the public library surface of `/id-range-sync/1`, and respond() clones the upper bounds of the caller's message into its answer — any caller that builds or forwards a message without going through decode_frame (exactly the callers check_bounds exists for) can produce an undecodable or silently re-interpreted flight and kill the session with errors that point at the wrong layer ("unknown mode byte").

## Why it matters

A sender-side length bug should fail at the sender, with its own name on it. Today it surfaces on the peer (or the same process one step later) as a framing/mode error, and at ≥256 bytes the length-prefix wrap means the byte stream no longer means what the sender wrote. Fail-closed at encode time is the same pattern this module already uses for frame budgets ("an entry of {} bytes does not fit a {}-byte frame").

## Acceptance criteria

- `frames()` (or `encode_entry`) refuses an entry whose upper bound is longer than KEY_LEN, with an error naming the bound length and the 72-byte key limit.
- `check_bounds` also refuses an over-length bound, so the documented pre-flight check catches what respond() would otherwise clone into its answer.
- Tests cover bound lengths 72 (accepted, round-trips), 73/100/255 (refused at encode), and 256/300 (refused at encode — no wrap), plus check_bounds refusing an over-length bound.
- Existing range.rs tests stay green.

title: aggregator(attention): stuck-retrying is unreachable for live sessions — classifyAttention checks lastTurnError before repeatedErrorCount, and the only producer always sets both

body:
## Problem

The attention classifier's `stuck-retrying` state is unreachable for every live session entry: the only producer of `repeatedErrorCount` always sets `lastTurnError` on the same entries, and `classifyAttention` checks `lastTurnError` first.

- `classifyAttention` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/derive.ts:197-215) is first-match-wins: `awaitingQuestion` → `lastTurnError` ("errored", :203-205) → only then `repeatedErrorCount >= RETRY_LOOP_THRESHOLD (3)` ("stuck-retrying", :206-209).
- The sole live producer, the OpenCode mapper `mapOne` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/sources/opencode.ts), sets `entry.lastTurnError` whenever the last turn has any error (:246 `if (lastTurnError) entry.lastTurnError = lastTurnError`) and sets `entry.repeatedErrorCount` only as an addition to that same run of errors (:232-240, consecutive identical errors at the head of the run). Every entry that could ever satisfy the retry-loop test therefore already matched the `errored` branch one check earlier.
- Even the shipped fixture entry designed to demo this state (`ses_f_phase13`, src/sources/fixtures.ts:525-539: `repeatedErrorCount: 4` **and** `lastTurnError: "claude_session_limit (retry)"`) classifies as plain `errored`.
- The existing unit test (test/render.test.ts:233-237) passes only because it constructs the one shape no producer emits — `repeatedErrorCount: 4` with no `lastTurnError`.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `3a425552`)

Laptop Bun probe driving the **real** modules (aggregator `src/` copied verbatim; probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-retryloop/`): a fake v2 OpenCode server returns one session whose newest turn is 4 consecutive assistant messages carrying the identical tool error `boom`; the probe runs the real `mapServerSessions` and feeds its output to the real `classifyAttention`:

```
mapper entry: {"sessionId":"ses-retry","lastTurnError":"boom","repeatedErrorCount":4}
classifyAttention state: errored | evidence: Last turn error: boom
RETRY_LOOP_THRESHOLD: 3
control (no lastTurnError) state: stuck-retrying
```

The mapper emits `repeatedErrorCount: 4` (≥ threshold 3) with `lastTurnError` set — exactly as the code predicts — and the classifier returns `errored`. The control entry with the test's shape (count only) does return `stuck-retrying`, confirming the branch works only for shapes no live producer creates.

## Why it matters

`stuck-retrying` is a distinct published state with its own label ("stuck retrying", derive.ts:245), sort rank (ORDER, derive.ts:182), and orchestrator playbook ("Orchestrator breaks the retry loop and reroutes the work", derive.ts:294, applied via `tierEntry`'s `ORCHESTRATOR_NOTES[e.state]`). A session spinning on the same error — the exact failure the state exists to surface — is instead shown as a generic one-off error, sorted and narrated as such, so the retry-loop intervention never triggers and the taxonomy silently overstates its own coverage: the state lights up in tests and never in the live feed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An entry with `lastTurnError` set **and** `repeatedErrorCount >= RETRY_LOOP_THRESHOLD` classifies as `stuck-retrying` (treatment pinned at triage: reorder the checks in `classifyAttention`, or split the states in the mapper — either way the pinned precedence vs `awaitingQuestion` and vs the credential-error tiering in `tierEntry` is stated explicitly).
- [ ] A regression test classifies the mapper-shaped entry (both fields set, count ≥ 3) as `stuck-retrying`, plus a count of exactly `RETRY_LOOP_THRESHOLD - 1` still classifying as `errored`, and a single error with no count staying `errored`.
- [ ] The fixture entry `ses_f_phase13` renders as `stuck-retrying` in the fixture attention view (or the fixture is adjusted to the shape triage pins).
- [ ] Existing derive/render tests stay green.

## Dedup

- Searched open + closed issues for `stuck-retrying`, `classifyAttention`, `RETRY_LOOP` this run: no issue covers the classifier/producer shadowing. #852 (OPEN) is the original attention-taxonomy design that created the state — it does not track the state being unreachable.
- #2543 (OPEN) is `mapServerSessions` wire-*container* validation in the same mapper file (non-array data / null entries throw) — different failure: here both modules behave exactly as written on well-formed data; the defect is the precedence between them.
- #2286 (OPEN) is the mapper's `iso()` RangeError on out-of-range timestamps — unrelated mechanism.

body:
Follow-up to #1872 / PR #2541 (merged 2026-10-30, merge commit 1aef00ebaddd36e89508240a70bcd00dd4c6cfa7). The PR merged with 4 Codex review findings undispositioned (review 2026-10-30T03:27:58Z by chatgpt-codex-connector[bot]) and a red `basic: test` run. Filing per the Codex-findings gate so none of them evaporate.

## Codex findings to fix (all in the merged hooks implementation)

1. **P1 — `pkgs/mcpx/internal/hooks/runner.go:187` Bound descendant processes and output-pipe waits.** `CommandContext` kills only the direct child; descendants can hold stdout/stderr pipes open and keep `cmd.Run()` waiting for EOF indefinitely — so the hard timeout does not actually bound a hook that spawns children, contradicting #1872'\''s acceptance "a hanging hook cannot hang the daemon" for that case. Fix direction: process-group kill and/or bounded pipe draining.
2. **P2 — `runner.go:86` Account for event losses before per-hook fanout.** The shared bus subscription can overflow before events reach per-hook queues; `Subscription.Dropped` is never read, so `Stats.Dropped` under-reports and the gap contract (#6) is not honoured for bus-level drops.
3. **P2 — `runner.go:185` Cap retained hook output.** Both output streams accumulate unbounded in daemon memory, including successful runs whose output is discarded (a `yes` hook can allocate heavily inside the 2s default timeout). Cap and truncate.
4. **P2 — `pkgs/mcpx/internal/cli/hook.go:93` Check interpreter availability before marking a module ready.** A declared Python module with neither `python3` nor `uv` on PATH still reports ready in `mcpx hook ls` / doctor, then fails on every matching event. Readiness must check the interpreter, not just the file.

## CI-only `internal/hooks` failure

PR #2541'\''s `basic: test` (run 40997046260, head eb4cabc6) failed `internal/hooks` in 0.159s (the `internal/defaults`/`internal/settings` failures in the same run are the pre-existing doc-drift reds tracked in #2552). Reproduction attempt 2026-10-30 (queue task 3097, Lane D): `go test ./internal/hooks/ -count=1` on the laptop at the exact merged commit eb4cabc6 passes 11/11 tests. The workflow log prints only package-level output (per-test JSON is filtered out), so the failing test is not identifiable from CI logs. Investigate: likely environment- or timing-sensitive (candidates: TestTimeoutCutsHangingHookAndPublishProceeds under runner load, or an executor-availability assumption). Consider surfacing per-test failures in the mcpx workflow log so this class is diagnosable.

## Acceptance
- All 4 findings fixed with tests (descendant-spawning hanging hook is cut at timeout; bus drops counted; output capped; hook ls/doctor report unready when the interpreter is missing).
- `go test ./internal/hooks/...` green in CI on the fixing PR.
- Findings dispositioned on PR #2541 threads pointing here.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Timeout handling kills the hook's whole process group (or equivalently bounds pipe draining): a hook whose descendants hold stdout/stderr open cannot keep `cmd.Run()` waiting past the timeout
- [ ] Bus-level subscription drops are accounted: `Subscription.Dropped` is read and reflected in `Stats.Dropped`
- [ ] Retained hook output is capped per run with truncation, for both streams, including successful runs
- [ ] `mcpx hook ls` / doctor readiness for a declared Python module checks interpreter availability (`python3` or `uv` on PATH), not just the file
- [ ] The CI-only `internal/hooks` failure from PR #2541's run 40997046260 is identified (named test + mechanism) or per-test failure output is surfaced in the mcpx workflow so it becomes identifiable
- [ ] Existing hooks tests pass; new regression tests pin the descendant-timeout and output-cap behaviour

title: mcpx(cache): Put's own eviction can delete the entry it just stored — it returns success for a path that no longer exists

body:
## Problem

`cache.Put` can delete the entry it just stored, then return success for a path that no longer exists.

In `pkgs/mcpx/internal/cache/cache.go` (main `674c4c6a`):

- `Put` (line 117) renames the filled temp directory into place, then runs `_ = c.Evict(kind, lim)` (line 141) before returning `(dest, false, nil)`.
- `Evict` (line 272) calls `SelectVictims(entries, lim, "")` (line 277) — the keep argument is empty, so the just-stored entry is an ordinary eviction candidate. `SelectVictims` (line 305) only ever exempts `keep` and leased entries.
- By contrast `Prune` (lines 284-289), the runner-facing form of the same mechanism, passes its `keep` entry through to `SelectVictims` — the mechanism already has the exemption concept; `Put`/`Evict` do not use it for the entry being stored.

So whenever the bounds cannot be satisfied by evicting older unleased entries — one entry larger than `MaxBytes` alone, or every older entry leased while the total is over `MaxBytes` — the newest victim is the entry `Put` just wrote. The caller receives a path, `hit=false`, and a nil error, and only discovers the loss later as a cache miss / missing directory at use time.

## Evidence (verified this run, real module on the laptop)

Probe: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneA-cacheput/` — `internal/cache/cache.go` copied verbatim (md5 `9f9ce95f29c82804fb56487e47a29cd7`, matches main `674c4c6a`), driven by a small program:

- Control, `Put` with `Limits{}` for a 100-byte entry: `hit=false err=<nil> exists=true`.
- Scenario A, same entry with `Limits{MaxBytes: 10}`: `Put` returns `hit=false err=<nil>`, but `stat` on the returned path reports *no such file or directory*, and a following `Get` for the key misses — the entry is gone.
- Scenario B, a 100-byte older entry held under `cache.Acquire`, then `Put` of a second 100-byte entry with `Limits{MaxBytes: 150}` (total 200): `newExists=false oldExists=true` — the leased entry correctly survives and the just-stored entry is the one evicted, again with a nil error from `Put`.

No existing test covers `Put` under a binding limit: `cache_test.go`'s `writeEntry` helper always passes `cache.Limits{}`, and the eviction tests call `Evict` directly.

Context: `Put` is the store path of the one content-addressed cache mechanism from #1908 (merged in PR #2555). Today it is exercised directly only by tests, but it is the documented API the remaining kinds (prepared dependencies, import graphs, flake resolutions — #1915/#1921) are being migrated onto; each new caller inherits a silent store-then-delete on exactly the oversized/pressured stores that most need a loud outcome.

## Why it matters

A store API that reports success for data it has already deleted turns a configuration/size problem into a Heisenbug downstream: intermittent missing prepared deps and workdirs, retried work with no error anywhere in the log (the `Evict` result is discarded with `_ =`). It also makes the byte bound unenforceable as a diagnostic — an entry that can never fit should fail at `Put`, not vanish.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Put` never returns `(path, false, nil)` for a path that does not exist when the call returns: either the just-stored entry is exempt from the eviction pass its own store triggers (keep semantics, as `Prune` already has), or `Put` returns an explicit error when the entry cannot be retained under `lim`.
- [ ] The chosen semantics are pinned by tests in `internal/cache`: (a) a single entry larger than `MaxBytes`; (b) a store made while all older entries are leased and the total is over `MaxBytes`.
- [ ] Existing cache tests still pass (`TestEvictByBytesKeepsNewest`, `TestLeasedEntrySurvivesEviction`, `TestPruneCountWithPatternAndKeep`, round-trip/hit behaviour unchanged for unbounded stores).
- [ ] Triage pins which of the two semantics (exempt-just-stored vs error) callers of the #1908 migration should rely on, and the package doc comment for `Put` states it.

body:
# aggregator(token-adapter): the file-export adapter's fail-closed window check throws on a null window element — and accepts a non-string window name — instead of returning the retained unparseable outcome

## Summary

`pm-stack/aggregator/src/token-adapter.ts` is the browser-token adapter framework core (#1153). Its contract is fail-closed: any dashboard/export payload whose shape drifts produces an `AdapterOutcome` with a failure status and the RETAINED previous value — never a fabricated zero, and (for `collectAdapter`) never a throw from a parse step, because parse errors are caught and classified `unparseable` (token-adapter.ts:164-221).

`collectFileExportAdapter` (token-adapter.ts:229) implements the same discipline for file-export documents, with an explicit fail-closed window validation at :270-283:

```ts
for (const w of doc.windows) {
  if (!w.name || typeof w.usedPct !== "number" || !Number.isFinite(w.usedPct)) {
    return retainedOutcome("unparseable", ...);
  }
}
```

Two holes in that check:

1. **A `null` (or `undefined`) window element throws.** `w.name` dereferences the element before any object check, so a success document with `windows: [null]` throws `TypeError: null is not an object (evaluating 'w.name')` straight out of `collectFileExportAdapter`. Unlike `collectAdapter`, this function has no try/catch around its validation/mapping, so the throw escapes the framework entirely: no retained previous value, no `unparseable` classification, and any future caller that trusts the AdapterOutcome contract crashes (or must add its own catch, defeating the framework's purpose).
2. **A non-string window name passes.** `!w.name` is a truthiness check only, so `{ name: 42, usedPct: 1 }` validates and is handed to `entryFromFileExport` (:285), which stamps a numeric-named window into the published quota-current entry as a successful `ok` reading — exactly the "partial/fabricated value published instead of retained" outcome the module header says must never happen.

The existing test suite pins the neighboring case — a window missing `usedPct` is `unparseable` with the previous entry retained (test/token-adapter.test.ts, "a drifted success document (window without usedPct) is unparseable, previous retained") — but no test covers a null element or a non-string name.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 38917318)

Probe: laptop Bun 1.4.2, the real `src/token-adapter.ts` (verbatim copy of the aggregator `src/` tree, md5 334689a9912d2bb86a08ea26b0df8ac4, matching main 38917318) at `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneB-tokenadapter/probe.ts`, calling `collectFileExportAdapter` with a healthy `meta` file-export doc shape (mirroring the test fixture) and varying only `windows`:

- Control `[{ name: "5h", usedPct: 12.5 }]` → outcome status `ok`.
- Drift `[{ name: "5h" }]` (no usedPct) → outcome status `unparseable`, detail "file-export drift: window 5h lacks a finite usedPct" (the test-pinned behavior).
- `[null]` → **THREW** `TypeError: null is not an object (evaluating 'w.name')` — no outcome at all.
- `[undefined]` → **THREW** `TypeError: undefined is not an object (evaluating 'w.name')`.
- `["5h"]` (string element) → outcome `unparseable` (benign control: property reads on a string do not throw).
- `[{ name: 42, usedPct: 1 }]` → outcome status **`ok`** — a numeric window name is published as a successful reading.

File:line (main 38917318):

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/token-adapter.ts:270-283` — the window validation loop: no element object check, name checked by truthiness only.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/token-adapter.ts:285` — `entryFromFileExport(doc, ...)` runs on whatever passed the loop.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/token-adapter.ts:11-19` (module header) and `:255-269` — the stated contract: shape drift is `unparseable`, the previous value is retained, never a partial/fabricated publish.

## Why it matters

This framework is the template every per-provider quota adapter builds on (#1159/#1161/#1163/#1165/#1301 family), and its whole value is that callers can trust the outcome contract: failures arrive as classified outcomes with the last good value retained. A producer whose export gains one null window (a serializer edge, a hand-edited latest.json, a half-written document read mid-replace) currently breaks that contract at the framework's own validation step — the one place written specifically to convert drift into `unparseable`. The numeric-name hole is the same check under-validating in the other direction: malformed data stamped `ok` and published as measured quota data.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Triage pins the validation shape (expected: a window element that is not an object, or whose `name` is not a non-empty string, is drift → `retainedOutcome("unparseable", ...)` with the previous value retained, matching the existing missing-usedPct behavior — or triage pins a different shape; throwing out of `collectFileExportAdapter` for a parseable-but-malformed document is the one ruled-out option).
- [ ] Regression tests in test/token-adapter.test.ts: `windows: [null]`, `windows: [undefined]`, and `windows: [{ name: 42, usedPct: 1 }]` each return status `unparseable` with the previous entry retained and do not throw.
- [ ] No behavior change for well-formed documents or the already-pinned drift cases: the existing token-adapter.test.ts expectations pass unchanged.

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-b (lane B), run 2026-10-29 22:50 CDT. Dedup: gh searches for collectFileExportAdapter / "token-adapter windows" / file-export drift returned no covering issue; #1153 is the parent framework feature (in-review), not this bug; #2332/#2416 are quota-gather-map/quota-current window handling in different files; the meta-exporter window issues (#1566 closed, #2460) are the producer-side .mjs parser, not this aggregator-side adapter.

title: cold-store-reaper: prune_backups apply is not crash-consistent — a mid-run trash failure rolls back every ledger row, but the Drive trashes stay, and the trashed files are invisible to any retry

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

labels.name: app/cold-store-reaper
labels.description: Package/app: cold-store-reaper (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Summary

`ColdStore.prune_backups(apply=True)` performs the Google Drive trash calls **inside** the local SQLite transaction (`with conn:`), interleaved with the `transfer_ledger` inserts. Drive is not transactional: when any one trash PATCH fails part-way through a prune run, the files already trashed stay trashed, but the SQLite context manager rolls back — so **every** ledger row for the run, including the rows for backups that really were trashed, is discarded. Worse, the loss is unrecoverable: `list_backups` only lists untrashed files, so the already-trashed backups are invisible to every later prune plan and their ledger rows can never be written by a retry.

## Evidence

`pkgs/cold-store-reaper/cold_store.py` (main `28a70c2b`; file sha256 `d3fe48c5…`):

- `:1124-1143` — the apply block: `conn = self.db(); with conn:` wraps the whole multi-file loop; each iteration does `http_request("PATCH", …/files/{id}, {"trashed": True})` (Drive, external, immediate) and then `self.ledger_add(conn, "trash", f["size"], "backup-prune", f["name"])` (SQLite, uncommitted until the block exits). Any non-200 raises `ColdStoreError` (`:1137-1140`), the `with conn:` block rolls back, and all ledger inserts of the run vanish while the Drive trashes persist.
- `ledger_add` itself is a plain insert on the caller's connection (`:450-458`) — it commits only when the outer block commits.
- `list_backups` asks Drive for untrashed files only (the test harness documents the same contract: trashed files are invisible to the listing), so a retry's plan contains only the not-yet-trashed remainder.

### Reproduced this run (laptop probe, package's own FakeDrive harness)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneA-pruneledger/probe.py` on the laptop, against `pkgs/cold-store-reaper/tests/test_cold_store.py`'s `TestPruneBackups` seed series (5 prune candidates), with `cold_store.http_request` wrapped to return HTTP 500 on the **2nd** trash PATCH:

```text
PATCH attempts: 2
raised: ColdStoreError: trash failed for backup d1-20260331T010000Z-export.sql (HTTP 500)
fake Drive trashed_calls: 1
files actually trashed in Drive: 1
ledger backup-prune rows after failure: 0
trashed file visible to re-run plan: [False]
re-run prune count: 4
```

So one backup is really trashed, zero ledger rows survive, and the re-run plan (4 remaining candidates) never sees the trashed file again — its ledger row is permanently unwritable.

## Why it matters

- The `transfer_ledger` is the audit/accounting record for retention: #1028's backup-bytes accounting decrements counted backup bytes from `backup-prune` trash rows (`test_backup_prune_ledger_row_decrements_backup_bytes`). A missing row means the store permanently over-counts the pruned backup's bytes — budget/retention decisions are made from numbers that say a deleted backup still exists.
- The operator sees only `trash failed for backup … (HTTP 500)` for the *second* file; nothing reports that the *first* file was trashed without a ledger record. The divergence is silent.
- Partial failure is the normal case for a multi-file network operation (token expiry, quota, one bad file id), not an exotic one: any prune run with ≥2 candidates that fails after the first success hits this.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A prune run that fails part-way leaves the ledger consistent with Drive: every backup actually trashed has exactly one `backup-prune` ledger row, and no ledger row exists for a backup that was not trashed. (Shape is the fixer's choice — e.g. commit per file after its successful trash, or record-then-trash with reconciliation — as long as the invariant holds under the probe below.)
- [ ] A retry after a partial failure completes the remaining prunes and does not double-ledger or re-trash the already-trashed files.
- [ ] Regression test in `pkgs/cold-store-reaper/tests/test_cold_store.py`: using the FakeDrive harness, fail the 2nd trash PATCH of a multi-candidate apply (the existing tests cover only the dry-run plan and the all-success apply: `test_prune_dry_run_plan`, `test_prune_apply_trashes_and_ledgers`); assert (a) the error still surfaces, (b) the first file's ledger row is present, (c) a re-run plan/apply finishes the rest with exactly one ledger row per trashed backup in total.
- [ ] Existing cold-store-reaper tests still pass.

body:
Follow-up to #1884 (split remainder, named there per its acceptance criteria). The touch-on-read TTL convention is adopted in `pkgs/mcpx/docs/decisions/0005-ttl-touch-on-read.md` and implemented for the elicit family in PR #2544. This issue covers **artifacts**, in the opt-in form #1884 specified.

Verified 2026-10-29 at `origin/main` 7d1b081c (queue worker task 3120): `internal/artifacts/artifacts.go` put sets `Expires: now.Add(ttl)` once (~line 317) — absolute expiry, no renewal.

Per #1884's stated current opinion, artifacts stay absolute by default; renewal is opt-in.

## Acceptance

- A declared registry setting `artifacts.idleTtl` (off/zero = today's absolute behaviour). When set, an item read of an artifact renews it under decision 0005 (`lastTouched`, `min(created + maxAge, lastTouched + idleTtl)`), with a paired declared maxAge ceiling; collection reads do not touch.
- Artifact representations touched by the change carry `expiresAt` (RFC 3339), `lastTouched`, `ttlRemainingMs`.
- Default behaviour is unchanged when the setting is unset.
- No `/renew` endpoint or per-resource renew operation.
- Targeted tests cover opt-in renewal, the maxAge ceiling, collection-reads-do-not-touch, and unchanged default expiry; `go test ./...` in pkgs/mcpx passes via CI.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A declared registry setting `artifacts.idleTtl` exists; unset/zero keeps today's absolute-expiry behaviour exactly.
- [ ] When set, an item read renews an artifact under decision 0005 (`min(created + maxAge, lastTouched + idleTtl)`) with a paired declared maxAge ceiling; collection reads do not touch.
- [ ] Artifact representations touched by the change carry `expiresAt` (RFC 3339), `lastTouched`, `ttlRemainingMs`; no `/renew` endpoint is added.
- [ ] Targeted tests cover opt-in renewal, the maxAge ceiling, collection-reads-do-not-touch, and unchanged default expiry; mcpx tests pass via CI.

title: id(directory/auth): hex_to_array and hex_bytes accept '+'-encoded pairs — the same key/signature has two spellings, and a signed request's replay-guard id can be re-encoded

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Bug

Two of pkgs/id's hex decoders accept a non-hex encoding of the same bytes: any byte pair whose high nibble is `0` can be written with a leading `+` instead of `0` (`0a` → `+a`) and decodes identically. Both decoders guard only on length and ASCII, then parse each pair with `u8::from_str_radix(pair, 16)` — which accepts a leading `+` sign — and never check that the characters are actually hex digits.

- `pkgs/id/src/directory.rs:1873-1881` — `hex_to_array`: `text.len() != N * 2 || !text.is_ascii()` is the only gate before `u8::from_str_radix(&text[index * 2..index * 2 + 2], 16)` at :1879.
- `pkgs/id/src/directory_auth.rs:356-365` — `hex_bytes`: same shape, `from_str_radix` at :363.

The sibling decoders in the same codebase all pre-check `is_ascii_hexdigit` and are NOT affected: `invites/invitation.rs:114-124` (`parse_hex32`), `seitan/derive.rs:66-75` (`InviteId::from_hex`), `invite.rs:130-156` (`decode`), and `world/util.rs:56` (`hex_decode_32`, uses `to_digit(16)`).

## Evidence (verified this run)

Verbatim copies of both functions, compiled and run on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneA-hexplus/`, source = main `7d1b081c`):

```
canonical decodes: true
plus-form decodes: true
PLUS_EQUALS_CANONICAL=true          ("0a0b0c0d…" and "+a+b+c+d…" → identical [u8; 32])
plus-form string != canonical string: true
SIG_PLUS_EQUALS_CANONICAL=true      (hex_bytes::<64>: "0a"×64 and "+a"×64 → identical signature bytes)
control 'zz' rejected: true
control 'a+' (plus second) rejected: true
control '-a' rejected: true
```

Only a `+` in the FIRST position of a pair slips through — exactly the pairs for bytes `0x00`–`0x0f`.

## Impact

1. **Signed-request replay malleability (`directory_auth.rs`).** `verify_signed` (:315-353) normalizes the key via `normalize_key` (directory.rs:1788), which lowercases but preserves `+`, then feeds the resulting STRING to the replay guard: `replays.accept(&key, …)` at :352, and `ReplayGuard::accept` keys its seen-map on `format!("{key}:{nonce}")` (:251). A captured signed request whose key/signature contain any `0?` byte pairs can be re-encoded with `+` in those pairs: the bytes (and therefore the Ed25519 verification) are unchanged, but the replay-guard id is a different string, so the same `(key, nonce, at)` request is accepted a second time inside the signed window.
2. **Non-canonical keys pass the canonicality check (`artifact.rs`).** `Artifact::check` enforces `normalize_key(&self.author)? == self.author` (:275-278, "author is not a canonical key"), but a lowercase `+`-form author satisfies it, because `normalize_key` returns the `+` form unchanged. The same applies to `ensure_account_id` (directory.rs:1843-1849, "account ID must be 64 hex characters") and to server-config IDs via `parse_id` (server_config/parse.rs:382-389, error text "not 64 hex digits").
3. **Two textual identities for one key.** Directory records, directory-log records (directory_log.rs:94,98) and artifacts (artifact.rs:300,304) decode author/signature through `hex_to_array`, so the same key/signature has multiple accepted spellings anywhere these strings are compared, stored, or used as map keys.

Same defect family as #1804 (tag `hex_decode` prefix leniency), but these are different functions on the auth/directory path and the `+` form is not a prefix issue.

## Acceptance criteria

- `hex_to_array` (directory.rs) and `hex_bytes` (directory_auth.rs) reject any input whose characters are not all ASCII hex digits (either case), matching the strictness of `parse_hex32` / `InviteId::from_hex`.
- Regression tests: `+a`-style pairs rejected at both decoders for keys and signatures; canonical upper/lowercase hex still accepted; a `verify_signed` test shows the `+` re-encoding of a captured request is refused (malformed, not merely replay-detected).
- `normalize_key` output is guaranteed canonical hex (the artifact canonicality check then actually enforces it).
- No behaviour change for well-formed hex inputs anywhere (directory, directory_log, artifact, server_config callers).

Found by new-issue-creator-code-a, run 2026-10-29 (laptop probe cited above).

title: lab-ops-hub: crawl archive R2 key is Date.now() alone — same-millisecond crawls silently overwrite each other's archived full text, both D1 rows point at the second crawl

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/lab-ops-hub
labels.description: Package/app: lab-ops-hub (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Bug: lab-ops-hub crawl archive R2 key is `Date.now()` alone — same-millisecond crawls silently overwrite each other's archived full text, and both D1 rows point at the second crawl's object

`POST /api/crawl` in `pkgs/lab-ops-hub/src/index.ts:399` archives each crawl's full extracted result to R2 under a key derived from the wall-clock millisecond only — no URL, filename, random, or row-id component:

```ts
const key = `crawls/${Date.now()}.json`;
await env.FILES.put(key, JSON.stringify({ url: b.url, source, ...result }, null, 2), { ... });
const r = await env.DB.prepare(
  "INSERT INTO crawls (url, source, title, excerpt, links, status_code, r2_key) VALUES (?1,?2,?3,?4,?5,?6,?7)",
).bind(b.url, source, result.title ?? null, ..., key).run();
```

Unlike the sibling file-upload key (#2478), this collision does **not** surface: `pkgs/lab-ops-hub/schema.sql` declares `crawls.r2_key TEXT` with **no UNIQUE constraint** (the `files` table's `r2_key` is UNIQUE; the `crawls` table's is not). Two crawls that complete in the same millisecond therefore:

- derive byte-identical keys (`crawls/<ms>.json`);
- the second `FILES.put` silently **overwrites the first crawl's archived JSON** (full text, links, status) in R2;
- both D1 `INSERT`s succeed, leaving two crawl rows whose `r2_key` is the same object — the first row's metadata (url/title/excerpt) now describes an archive that actually contains the *second* crawl's content. The first crawl's full text is unrecoverable.

Millisecond collisions are realistic for this endpoint: scripted/retried crawls, a caller re-submitting after a container timeout (the handler itself falls back and retries via the Worker path), and test loops all land back-to-back crawls within one millisecond — and `Date.now()` resolution makes the window wider than it looks on coarse clocks.

### Verified this run (main `7d1b081c`)

Sandbox Python probe (probe dir `/tmp/probe-laneA-crawlkey/`, script `probe.py`) that extracts the verbatim key expression from `src/index.ts`, builds the `crawls` table from the real `schema.sql`, and replays the handler's put → insert order for two different URLs at one fixed millisecond:

- Key line found verbatim in `index.ts`: `const key = \`crawls/${Date.now()}.json\`;`
- `crawls` table definition contains no `UNIQUE`.
- Two crawls (`https://a.example/` → `TEXT-A`, `https://b.example/` → `TEXT-B`) at ms `1761782400000`: both inserts succeed (ids 1 and 2), distinct keys = **1**, R2 objects = **1**, and the archive served for row 1's `r2_key` is `TEXT-B`, not `TEXT-A`.

### Why it matters

The crawls table + R2 archive are the hub's record of what was crawled: the D1 row keeps only a 500-char excerpt inline, so the R2 object is the *only* full-text copy. A collision silently swaps the archive behind an existing row — the row looks healthy in `/api/crawls`, but its archive belongs to a different URL, and the original crawl's text is lost with no error anywhere.

### Acceptance criteria

- Two crawls completing in the same millisecond both succeed with **distinct** R2 keys and two D1 rows whose archives each contain their own crawl's content (e.g. a random/UUID or row-id component in the key, as #2478 prescribes for uploads).
- A regression test exercises back-to-back same-millisecond crawls (the key derivation should live somewhere testable, per the #524 pattern of moving logic out of the Worker entry into `src/lib.ts`).
- Existing behaviour otherwise unchanged: key prefix `crawls/`, `.json` suffix, the archived JSON shape, and the response body.

### Dedup

Distinct from #2478 (file-upload key `uploads/<ms>-<filename>`): that key at least carries the filename, and its collision is caught (as a 500) by the `files.r2_key` UNIQUE constraint. The crawl key carries nothing but the millisecond and its table has no UNIQUE guard, so the failure mode is silent archive loss, not an error. `gh` searches (open + closed) for lab-ops-hub crawl / `r2_key` / `Date.now` terms return the crawl-validator and timeout issues (#441, #460, #500, #511–#519, #532, #569, #571) and #2478 — none covers the crawl archive key derivation.

— filed by new-issue-creator-code-a (Lane A), 2026-10-29 run
