labels.description: bin/clef-proxy.mjs

body:
## Problem

clef-proxy interpolates the client-supplied `model` into the upstream Cloudflare URL with no validation, so a request body can rewrite the upstream request — and can run models this proxy is documented not to serve.

- The proxy's own header comment (bin/clef-proxy.mjs:106-107) says it is "a single-purpose SystemOne endpoint, not a chat router: its model universe is the Clef family".
- `resolveModel` (bin/clef-proxy.mjs:95-104) returns any string starting with `@cf/` **verbatim** (:97), maps the two exact aliases `clef`/`clef-flash` (:98-99), and for any other string containing `clef` returns `` `@cf/cloudflare/${model}` `` with the rest of the string untouched (:100). No character is refused: `/`, `..`, `?`, `#` and spaces all pass.
- The result is interpolated raw into the upstream URL at bin/clef-proxy.mjs:226-227: `` `https://gateway.ai.cloudflare.com/v1/${accountId}/${gatewayId}/workers-ai/run/${model}` ``, and fetched with the proxy's stored/fallback Cloudflare token (bin/clef-proxy.mjs:234-242; token from the caller's header or the proxy's env/config at :88-93).

## Evidence (verified this run on main `5a34fa70`)

Probe with `resolveModel` and the cfUrl construction copied verbatim (probe + log in the goal's `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-29-laneB-clefmodel/`; Node's URL resolution is what `fetch` applies — no network call was made):

- Controls behave: `clef` → `.../workers-ai/run/@cf/cloudflare/clef`; `clef-flash`, `@cf/cloudflare/clef`, `@cf/cloudflare/clef-omni` → the expected run URLs.
- A non-Clef model passes verbatim: `@cf/meta/llama-3.1-8b-instruct` → `.../workers-ai/run/@cf/meta/llama-3.1-8b-instruct` — any Workers AI model on the account can be run through this Clef-only proxy, billed to the proxy's token when the caller supplies none.
- Dot segments climb out of the run path: `@cf/cloudflare/../../ai/models/search` → `.../workers-ai/run/ai/models/search`; `clef/../../../../client/v4/accounts/OTHER/ai/models/search` → `.../workers-ai/client/v4/accounts/OTHER/ai/models/search` — the request no longer has the `/run/<model>` shape at all.
- Query injection: `@cf/cloudflare/clef?per_page=1#frag` → `.../run/@cf/cloudflare/clef?per_page=1#frag`.

## Why it matters

The proxy listens on loopback and spends a stored Cloudflare token for callers that present none. Anyone (or any local process / web page able to POST to the loopback port) who can reach `/v1/systemone` chooses not just the model but, via dot segments and `?`, the effective upstream path and query the proxy's credential is spent on — the exact steering the Clef-only design comment rules out. At minimum it silently breaks the documented model universe; the fix shape (allowlist against the live Clef list the file already fetches at :124-160, vs. a strict model-name grammar) is triage's pin.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `resolveModel` (or its replacement) refuses — with a 400 to the client, before any upstream fetch — any `model` that is not a plain model name: no `/` beyond the `@cf/<owner>/<name>` shape, no `..` segments, no `?`/`#`/whitespace/control characters.
- [ ] Only Clef-family models are served, per the :106-107 design comment (the `@cf/` verbatim branch no longer admits e.g. `@cf/meta/llama-3.1-8b-instruct`), OR the design comment is updated in the same change if triage rules the wider universe intentional.
- [ ] The documented spellings keep working unchanged: missing model, `clef`, `clef-flash`, `@cf/cloudflare/clef`, and newer Clef entries from the live catalog (e.g. `@cf/cloudflare/clef-omni`).
- [ ] A regression test in `bin/clef-proxy.test.mjs` (new file; cf. #692 on testability) pins the probe cases above: non-Clef `@cf/` model refused, both dot-segment payloads refused, `?` payload refused, controls unchanged.
- [ ] Existing proxy tests still pass (laptop or CI).

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `clef-proxy`, `resolveModel`, "model URL/path traversal": #2100 is the same file's missing upstream **timeout** (distinct defect), #692 is the missing regression tests / hardcoded-URL testability of the #691 fix (adjacent — it is why a test file does not exist yet — but it does not cover model validation), #690 (closed) was body-parse status codes. No filing covers model-to-URL interpolation. Sibling check: `grep` for `${model}` URL interpolation across `bin/*.mjs` hits only clef-proxy.mjs:227, so this is a single-file issue, not a cross-proxy set.

body:
# aggregator(registry): a non-array `taskRefs` passes `isSessionRecord` and crashes `mergeRecords`' spread — a string one silently splits into single-character refs

## Bug

The session registry's hygiene check validates only three fields, but the merge spreads a fourth, unchecked field as an array:

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/registry.ts:138-142` — `isSessionRecord` checks only that `id`, `source`, and `label` are strings. `taskRefs` may be any JSON value: a number, a boolean, `null`, a plain object, or a string.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/registry.ts:130` — when an incoming record shares a `(source, id)` key with a stored one, `mergeRecords` runs `taskRefs: [...new Set([...prev.taskRefs, ...r.taskRefs])]`. Spreading a non-iterable throws `TypeError: Spread syntax requires ...iterable[Symbol.iterator] to be a function` (or `...iterable not be null or undefined` for `null`). Spreading a **string** does not throw — it silently turns `"abc"` into the refs `["a","b","c"]`, corrupting the session's task linkage.
- The unchecked value reaches the merge from three directions, all filtered only by `isSessionRecord` / an id-only check: the durable store file (`src/sources/live.ts:611`, `loadRegistryStore`), the fleet feed's registry section (`src/sources/live.ts:980`), and Claude launch records (`registry.ts:100` — `parseLaunchRecords` checks only that `id` is a string; `registry.ts:88` — `recordFromLaunch` copies `l.taskRefs ?? []` verbatim, so `42` passes through and only `null`/`undefined` are replaced).

`registry()` (`src/sources/live.ts:976-1000`) calls `mergeIntoRegistry` → `mergeRecords` (`src/sources/live.ts:619`) with no guard whenever any incoming record exists. `/sessions` and `/api/registry.json` await `source.registry()` uncaught (`src/server.ts:543`, `src/server.ts:552`), so the request fails; the facet-priming callers catch and silently substitute `[]` (`src/server.ts:147`, `:160`, `:744`), so the registry reads as empty there. Because the poisoned record sits in the durable store, every later live read that merges anything re-throws — the wedge is permanent until the store file is hand-repaired.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 5a34fa70)

Sandbox Bun probe (`/tmp/probe-laneA-taskrefs/probe.ts`) importing the real `registry.ts`:

```
isSessionRecord(taskRefs=42) = true
isSessionRecord(taskRefs=null) = true
prev taskRefs=42 THROWS: TypeError: Spread syntax requires ...iterable[Symbol.iterator] to be a function
incoming taskRefs=null THROWS: TypeError: Spread syntax requires ...iterable not be null or undefined
prev taskRefs='abc' merged taskRefs = ["a","b","c"]
well-formed merge: OK
```

## Why it matters

One malformed record — a hand-edited or torn store file, a collector/feed entry whose `taskRefs` is a number or a bare string instead of an array, a launch-record line with `"taskRefs": 42` — permanently breaks the registry surface once any record with the same `(source, id)` is merged, and there is no signal about which record or field is responsible. The string form is worse in a way: it never crashes, it just invents single-character task refs that link the session to nothing real. This is the same validator/consumer mismatch family as #2376 (`lastSeenAt` crashing the merge sort, same file) and #2347 (comments/actions `createdAt`), but a different field, a different crash expression (spread at `registry.ts:130`, not `localeCompare` in the sort), and a silent-corruption mode neither of those has; #2376's acceptance criteria pin only `lastSeenAt` and would not fix this.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A record with a missing or non-array `taskRefs` can no longer crash `mergeRecords`, and a string `taskRefs` can no longer be split into character refs: either `isSessionRecord` rejects/coerces it at both load sites (store + feed), or the merge treats a non-array value as `[]` — the triage pin records which layer owns the rule, applied consistently to `recordFromLaunch`/`parseLaunchRecords` as well.
- [ ] A poisoned record already in the durable store does not wedge the registry: `/sessions` and `/api/registry.json` keep serving the remaining records.
- [ ] Regression tests (aggregator suite) cover: `mergeRecords` merging a duplicate-key record whose stored or incoming `taskRefs` is a number, `null`, and a string; a store/feed load containing such a record; existing merge tests keep passing.
- [ ] No behaviour change for well-formed records: the deduped union of refs and the merge special cases from #1560's contract are preserved.

## Related

- #2376 — same file, same validator: non-string `lastSeenAt` crashes the merge **sort**; different field and crash site, and its fix does not cover the spread.
- #2347 — same load-filter/consumer mismatch in the comments + actions stores (`createdAt`), different stores and validator.
- #1560 — `mergeRecords` field-wipe on sparse records; different defect in the same function (spread semantics over present fields, not unchecked types).

body:
# mcpx(exec): per-request exec `timeout` can disable the timeout entirely (0/negative) or raise it without any ceiling — the operator's `exec.timeout` is replaced, not bounded

## Summary

A `/v1/exec` caller controls the script timeout completely. `execsvc.Service.Run` replaces the operator-resolved `Limits.Timeout` (the `exec.timeout` setting, default **120s**) with any `time.ParseDuration`-valid per-request value, with no positivity check and no ceiling:

- `timeout: "0s"`, `"0"`, or any negative value (`"-1s"`, `"-100h"`) → the runner applies **no deadline at all** — the script runs unbounded.
- `timeout: "876000h"` (~100 years) → the bound is raised ~2.6 million× above the operator's 120s, again unbounded in practice.

## Evidence (main `5a34fa70`)

- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/routes_exec.go:218` — `handleExec` JSON-decodes the request, `Options` included, verbatim; nothing validates `options.timeout`.
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/execsvc/execsvc.go:349-356`:
  ```go
  timeout := s.Limits.Timeout
  if opts.Timeout != "" {
      d, err := time.ParseDuration(opts.Timeout)
      if err != nil { return nil, fmt.Errorf(...) }
      timeout = d
  }
  ```
  The only check is parseability. The resolved value is handed to the runner at `execsvc.go:377` (`Timeout: timeout`).
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/routes_exec.go:173` — `Limits.Timeout` is the operator's setting: `lim.Timeout = set.Duration("exec.timeout")`; `pkgs/mcpx/internal/settings/exec.go:16` declares `exec.timeout`, default `"120s"`.
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/runner/runner.go:62-63` — `Timeout` on the runner: *"Timeout bounds execution; 0 means no limit."* `runner.go:273`: `if opts.Timeout > 0 { runCtx, cancel = context.WithTimeout(...) }` — a zero or negative timeout therefore installs **no deadline**.
- The first-party CLI never sends a disabling value over the wire — `pkgs/mcpx/internal/cli/exec.go:562-564` guards `if rf.timeout > 0 { opts.Timeout = rf.timeout.String() }` — but the daemon side has no equivalent guard, so any non-CLI caller (plugin, MCP client, raw HTTP) can send one. (Locally, `--timeout 0 = no limit` at `internal/cli/commands.go:598` is a documented operator choice for the user's own process; the daemon path is a service acting on behalf of callers, where the operator's `exec.timeout` is the protection being silently removed.)

## Probe (this run, laptop, verbatim resolution + runner gate)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneA-exectimeout/` (main `5a34fa70`), operator limit 120s:

```
opt=""        -> effective timeout=2m0s    runner applies deadline: true
opt="30s"     -> effective timeout=30s     runner applies deadline: true
opt="0s"      -> effective timeout=0s      runner applies deadline: false
opt="0"       -> effective timeout=0s      runner applies deadline: false
opt="-1s"     -> effective timeout=-1s     runner applies deadline: false
opt="-100h"   -> effective timeout=-100h   runner applies deadline: false
opt="876000h" -> effective timeout=876000h runner applies deadline: true  (~100 years)
```

## Why it matters

`exec.timeout` exists so a daemon operator can bound how long any one script may run. Today that bound is advisory: a single request field removes it entirely (0/negative) or inflates it past any useful horizon, so a hung, looping, or hostile script holds a daemon worker, its runtime process, and any pooled upstream connections indefinitely. This is the same shape as the per-request TTL ceilings filed for tasks/artifacts (#2351, #2327) but for the execution bound itself — and it cuts against the house rule already recorded for the sibling setting in #1864: a caller may lower a daemon-set bound, not raise it past the operator's ceiling (the `ClampedBy` principle in `internal/settings/clamp.go`).

Not a duplicate: #1758 (closed) is the *adapter* timeout, where a negative value made calls fail instantly — the opposite failure in a different subsystem. #1864 is `pool.callTimeout` call-scoping for upstream tool calls, not the exec script timeout in `execsvc`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `POST /v1/exec` with `options.timeout` of `"0"`, `"0s"`, or any negative duration no longer produces an unbounded run: it is either refused with a named error or treated as "no override" (the operator's `exec.timeout` applies) — one rule, pinned at triage, applied in `execsvc.Run` so every entry point (HTTP, task mode) gets it.
- [ ] A positive per-request timeout larger than the operator's resolved `exec.timeout` is clamped to that ceiling (caller may lower, not raise), or refused — per the same pinned rule.
- [ ] A smaller positive timeout (e.g. `"30s"` against a 120s limit) still takes effect exactly as today.
- [ ] Regression tests cover the boundary inputs: `"0"`, `"-1s"`, a value above the limit, a value below it, and the absent-option default.
- [ ] The local CLI's documented `--timeout 0 = no limit` behaviour for direct local runs (`internal/cli/commands.go:598`, runner path) is unchanged.

title: fix(mcpx): supervised transport (PR #1495) — pumpStdout writes to the attached daemon while holding the supervisor mutex, so a stalled daemon wedges exit and detach

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Finding

PR #1495 (commit `18ba1ee35b`, "mcpx: supervised stdio transport behind a flag (#1385, Phase 1 of #1384)") added `pkgs/mcpx/internal/mcpclient/supervised.go`. In `pumpStdout` the supervisor performs a blocking socket write to the attached daemon **while holding the supervisor's global state mutex** — verified unchanged on current main (`origin/main` at `5a34fa7070`, 2026-10-29):

- `supervised.go:290` `pumpStdout()` — at `:297` it takes `s.mu.Lock()`, and at `:299` it calls `s.attached.Write(data)` inside that lock before unlocking.
- The child-exit goroutine at `:210-211` does `s.child.Wait()` and then needs the same `s.mu.Lock()` to record `exited`/`exitErr` and close `waitDone`.
- `detach()` (`:344`-area lock), `handleAttach()` (attach/drain path), and `finishWhenDone()` also need the same mutex.

Failure chain: if the attached daemon stops reading (paused, wedged, or slow enough that the unix-socket send buffer fills — the pump writes 32 KiB chunks), the `Write` blocks indefinitely **with the mutex held**. From that moment:

1. a child exit can never be recorded (the `Wait` goroutine blocks on the mutex), so `waitDone` never closes and `finishWhenDone` never runs — the supervisor wedges instead of surfacing the exit;
2. no detach or replacement attach can proceed (both need the mutex), so the stalled attach cannot be cleared;
3. child output stops being consumed, so the child can in turn block on a full stdout pipe — a full supervisor/child stall, behind the (default-off, Phase 1) supervised flag.

The existing tests from #1495 (`TestSupervisedPumpDetachReattach`, `TestSupervisedSingleAttachRefused`, `TestSupervisedBufferOverflow`, `TestSupervisedChildExitSurfaced`) cover a reading daemon and unattached buffering, but nothing covers an attached daemon that stops reading.

## Why it matters

The supervised transport exists precisely so a daemon going away never harms the child, and so a child exit always surfaces. A stalled-but-connected daemon is the one case the current locking defeats both guarantees for, and it fails silently (no error, no exit report, supervisor process lingers).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `pumpStdout` never performs a blocking write to the attached connection while holding the supervisor state mutex (e.g. a dedicated per-connection write mutex/queue owns attach writes and preserves the reply → buffered → live byte ordering that `handleAttach`'s under-lock flush was protecting).
- [ ] With an attached daemon that never reads: the child can still exit and the exit is recorded/reported (or the attach is dropped after a bounded write timeout), and a later attach/detach proceeds.
- [ ] A regression test pins the stalled-reader case (daemon attaches, stops reading, child emits more than a socket buffer of output and/or exits; the supervisor does not wedge).
- [ ] Existing supervised tests keep passing; unattached tail-buffer behaviour and `droppedBytes` accounting are unchanged.

body:
Phase 1 of design #2386 (mcpx completion, finished). Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-completion-rate-limit-ranking.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. The decision is recorded on #2386; this phase implements its first slice.

## Scope

One fixed-window, in-memory rate limiter for `completion/complete`, consulted in the daemon's `handleComplete` (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/ops.go:333`) after shape validation and **before** any pool lookup/acquisition — a refused request must never acquire a pool lease or wake an upstream.

- Keys: per (caller, server) and per server. Caller = the identity `handleComplete` already resolves (`callContext(r, req.Context, req.Session)`, `internal/daemon/server.go:836`); server = the configured name in `req.Server`, never anything self-reported.
- Hot settings in the existing `completion.*` namespace (beside `completion.maxValues`, `internal/settings/wire.go:185`): `completion.perMinute` default 120 (per caller per server), `completion.serverPerMinute` default 600 (per server, all callers — the backstop that does not depend on caller honesty, since caller identity is pre-principals). `0` disables that window.
- Count-on-admission: refusals do not consume quota (design #2333's recorded rule for the sibling limiter).
- Refusal: `/v1/complete` answers HTTP 429 with an error naming the limit; the MCP surface inherits it through `mcpBackend.Complete` → `Server.complete` as a named `-32603`. No new error code.
- The limiter is a small daemon-internal type, NOT completion-shaped in its interface (key + limit in, verdict out), so design #1554's `tasks-rate-limit` question can reuse it later. No new dependency (no limiter exists in-tree; fixed windows per #2333's precedent).

## Acceptance

- [ ] A completion flood from one caller against one server is refused with 429 (named limit) once `completion.perMinute` is exceeded in a window, while a second caller against the same server is still served until the per-server window trips
- [ ] Handler test proves a refused request never reaches the pool (no lease, no upstream call)
- [ ] Both settings are hot (change takes effect without restart) and `0` disables
- [ ] The MCP surface shows the refusal as a named `-32603` mentioning the completion rate limit
- [ ] Limiter unit tests cover window rollover, count-on-admission (refusals don't consume), and per-key independence
- [ ] Tests run via CI per fleet policy (no builds on the sandbox)

Out of scope: ranking (Phase 2), register changes (Phase 3), any change to upstream pass-through or to `completion.maxValues` semantics.

title: id(serve): is_process_alive treats EPERM as dead — a live foreign-owned serve's lock is deleted by get_serve_info

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

`is_process_alive` (`pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:200-206`) treats any `kill(pid, 0)` result other than `0` as "dead":

```rust
unsafe { libc::kill(pid as i32, 0) == 0 }
```

`kill(pid, 0)` also fails with `EPERM` when the process **exists** but is owned by another user — existence is exactly what the probe is asking about. On a multi-uid machine (serve started by one uid, a CLI/REPL process run by another — e.g. a user service vs an interactive shell, or a root-started serve inspected by the daily user) the function therefore answers "dead" for a live serve.

The only consumer, `get_serve_info` (`serve.rs:171-185`), acts on that answer destructively:

```rust
if !is_process_alive(info.pid) {
    // Stale lock file - remove it
    let _ = afs::remove_file(SERVE_LOCK).await;
    return None;
}
```

So a live serve's `.iroh-serve.lock` is **deleted** by a process running as a different uid, and discovery reports "no serve running" — every command that consults the lock first falls back instead of connecting to the serve that is actually up.

The codebase already knows the correct rule in the sibling component: mcpx's `ProcessAlive` (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/paths.go:299-313`) documents and implements "EPERM means the process is there but owned by somebody else, which is still alive". The converse bug in mcpx's pool checker is tracked separately as #2336.

This is distinct from #2142 (same function): that issue covers sentinel pids (0 / `u32::MAX`) being passed to `kill` and answering "alive" for no process. This issue covers the errno of a legitimate pid never being inspected, answering "dead" for a real process. Either fix alone leaves the other defect in place.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `5a34fa70`)

- `serve.rs:200-206`: the return value is compared to `0` only; `errno` is never read.
- `serve.rs:1873-1880`: the existing test `test_is_process_alive_pid_1` deliberately asserts nothing ("Just check that the function doesn't panic") — pid 1 is the canonical foreign-owned live pid, and the test cannot assert `true` because the function gets it wrong for non-root callers.
- Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneB-serveeperm/`, verbatim function logic via a direct `kill` extern, run as the laptop's non-root daily user):
  ```
  own pid 1582009 -> true
  pid 1 (alive, root-owned) -> false
  dead pid 1582067 -> false
  ```
- OS-level cross-check on the same host: `kill(1, 0)` returns errno 1 (`EPERM`) for the non-root user, while a dead pid returns errno 3 (`ESRCH`) — the information needed to distinguish the cases is present and is being discarded.

## Why it matters

Serve discovery is the front door for most CLI commands in a served directory. Deleting a live serve's lock is worse than misreporting it: the lock does not come back until the serve restarts, so one cross-uid invocation permanently (for that serve's lifetime) breaks discovery for everyone, with no error naming the cause.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `is_process_alive` distinguishes `EPERM` (alive) from `ESRCH` (dead): a live foreign-owned pid returns `true`.
- [ ] `get_serve_info` no longer removes the lock of a live foreign-owned serve; it returns that serve's info.
- [ ] Ordinary behaviour is unchanged: own live pid → `true`, dead pid → `false` (lock removed as stale).
- [ ] Regression test: `test_is_process_alive_pid_1` (or a successor) asserts pid 1 is alive on Unix when it exists, instead of asserting nothing — or an equivalent EPERM-path test is added.
- [ ] The fix composes with #2142's sentinel-pid guard (whichever lands first, the second rebases onto it rather than re-deciding the other case).

body:
# aggregator(registry): a non-string `lastSeenAt` passes `isSessionRecord` and crashes `mergeRecords`' sort — /sessions and /api/registry.json go down once the registry is big enough

## Bug

The session registry's hygiene check validates only three fields, but the merge that every live registry read runs sorts on a fourth, unchecked field with a string-only method:

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/registry.ts:138-142` — `isSessionRecord` checks only `id`, `source`, and `label` are strings. `lastSeenAt` (and `startedAt`) may be any JSON value: a number, a boolean, an object.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/registry.ts:134` — `mergeRecords` returns `[...byKey.values()].sort((a, b) => (b.lastSeenAt ?? "").localeCompare(a.lastSeenAt ?? ""))`. `localeCompare` exists only on strings, so a record whose `lastSeenAt` is e.g. `12345` throws `TypeError: (b.lastSeenAt ?? "").localeCompare is not a function` whenever the sort compares it in that position.
- The unchecked value reaches the merge from three directions, all filtered only by `isSessionRecord`: the durable store file (`sources/live.ts:611`, `loadRegistryStore`), the fleet feed's registry section (`sources/live.ts:980`), and Claude launch records (`registry.ts:82`, `recordFromLaunch` copies `l.lastSeenAt` verbatim; `parseLaunchRecords` checks only that `id` is a string).

`registry()` (`sources/live.ts:976-1000`) calls `mergeIntoRegistry` → `mergeRecords` (`sources/live.ts:619`) with no guard around it whenever any incoming record exists. The callers split: `/sessions` and `/api/registry.json` await `source.registry()` uncaught (`server.ts:543`, `server.ts:552`), so the request fails; the facet-priming callers catch and silently substitute `[]` (`server.ts:147`, `:160`, `:744`), so the registry reads as empty there.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 5a34fa70)

Sandbox Bun probe (`/tmp/probe-laneB-regsort/probe.ts`, `probe2.ts`) importing the real `registry.ts`:

```
isSessionRecord(good)= true
isSessionRecord(badNum)= true      (lastSeenAt: 12345)
isSessionRecord(badBool)= true     (lastSeenAt: true)
good+missing OK                    (lastSeenAt absent is fine: ?? "" )
big THROWS TypeError (b.lastSeenAt ?? "").localeCompare is not a function
rev THROWS TypeError (same, reversed input order)
```

The latency is part of the bug: with only two records Bun's sort happened to compare in the direction that coerces the number as the `localeCompare` *argument*, so a small registry can accept — and `mergeIntoRegistry` can persist (`sources/live.ts:627-631`) — a poisoned record without error. The same record throws reliably once the registry holds several records (8-record probe, both input orders). The durable store therefore accumulates the trigger silently and the failure switches on later, on an unrelated read, once enough sessions exist.

## Why it matters

One malformed record — a hand-edited or torn store file, a collector/feed entry with a numeric epoch instead of an ISO string, a launch-record line with a numeric `lastSeenAt` — permanently breaks the registry surface: every live `/sessions` and `/api/registry.json` request fails while that record is present, and there is no signal about which record or field is responsible. The neighbouring stores learned this exact lesson in #2347 (comments/actions: load filter checked only `id`, `all()` sorted via `createdAt.localeCompare`); the registry's filter is the same shape with a different field. This is distinct from #1560 (same file: sparse incoming records wipe fields via undefined spread — a data-loss semantics bug, no type check or crash involved) and its acceptance criteria do not cover this.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A record with a missing or non-string `lastSeenAt` can no longer crash `mergeRecords`: either `isSessionRecord` rejects/coerces it at both load sites (store + feed), or the sort (and the `>=` newest-comparison at registry.ts:131) treats a non-string value as absent — the triage pin records which layer owns the rule, applied consistently to `recordFromLaunch`'s unchecked copy as well.
- [ ] A poisoned record already in the durable store does not wedge the registry: `/sessions` and `/api/registry.json` keep serving the remaining records.
- [ ] Regression tests (aggregator suite, e.g. `test/slice3.test.ts`) cover: `mergeRecords` over several records including one with numeric and one with boolean `lastSeenAt`, and a store/feed load containing such a record; existing merge tests keep passing.
- [ ] No behaviour change for well-formed records: newest-`lastSeenAt` ordering and the merge special cases from #1560's contract are preserved.

## Related

- #2347 — same load-filter/sort-field mismatch in the comments + actions stores (`createdAt`), different stores and validator.
- #1560 — `mergeRecords` field-wipe on sparse records; different defect in the same function (spread semantics, not unchecked types).
- #1509 — registry store write atomicity; unrelated.

body:
## Summary

`pkgs/id/src/world_compile.rs` — the Roc compiler child's stdout and stderr are captured with unbounded `read_to_end` into `Vec`s living in the **server** process, even though only a 64 KiB tail of stderr is ever used and the stdout capture is discarded outright. A compiler run that spews diagnostics grows server memory without bound until the 120 s deadline kills the child; the child's own rlimits do not cap the parent's capture buffers.

## Evidence (main `5a34fa70`)

- `world_compile.rs:31` — `const MAX_CAPTURE_BYTES: usize = 64 * 1024;` is the stated capture intent.
- `world_compile.rs:283-295` — both reader threads do `let mut out = Vec::new(); stdout.read_to_end(&mut out)` (same for stderr): no cap, no truncation as it reads.
- `world_compile.rs:308-319,346,358` — the only uses of the captures are `tail(&captured_err, MAX_CAPTURE_BYTES)`; stdout is bound as `_captured_out` at `:313` and never used at all.
- `world_compile.rs:531-551` — `apply_rlimits` caps the **child** (CPU 120 s, AS 8 GiB, FSIZE 256 MiB), but the capture `Vec`s live in the parent (the long-lived `id serve` / world-session process, caller `world_session/mod.rs:275` with `COMPILE_TIMEOUT = 120s`, `world_compile.rs:29`), so those limits do not bound the memory at risk.
- Inputs are bounded (`MAX_COMPILE_TOTAL_BYTES` 256 KiB, `:27`), but diagnostic volume is not proportional to input size — error cascades / repeated warnings from a small source can produce arbitrarily large stderr within the deadline window.

## Verified this run

Verbatim-pattern probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneA-compilecap/`, the reader-thread code copied from `:283-295` plus the real `tail()`): a child writing 200 MiB to stderr and exiting 1 produced

```
status=exit status: 1 captured_err_bytes=209715200 captured_out_bytes=0 tail_used_bytes=65536
```

i.e. 209,715,200 bytes buffered in the parent to use 65,536.

## Why it matters

World compilation is a server-side operation reachable by whoever may submit a world source build. One spewing compile can OOM the serving process (taking down every other world/session it hosts), and concurrent compiles multiply the exposure. The 64 KiB constant shows the intended bound — it is just applied after the unbounded capture instead of during it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both reader threads cap captured bytes as they read (e.g. keep at most `MAX_CAPTURE_BYTES` tail, or a small multiple of it, draining/discarding the rest so the child never blocks on a full pipe).
- [ ] Stdout is either not captured at all (or capped the same way) while it remains unused.
- [ ] A regression test or probe with a child emitting ≫64 KiB to stderr shows peak captured size stays bounded and the failure message still contains the diagnostic tail.
- [ ] Compile success/failure behaviour and the returned diagnostics string are unchanged for ordinary (≤64 KiB) compiler output.

## Dedup notes

Searched open + closed issues for world_compile / compiler capture / stderr: no existing issue covers the capture path. Distinct from the bounded network `read_to_end(N)` call sites elsewhere in pkgs/id, which pass explicit caps.

title: mcpx(mcpclient): SSE retry interval is server-controlled with no ceiling — huge values stall resume/listen for years, larger ones wrap the Duration to microseconds or negative

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Bug

mcpx's Streamable HTTP client honours the SSE `retry:` field from an upstream MCP server with **no ceiling and a wrapping multiplication** — so one server-supplied line can stall reconnection effectively forever, or collapse the intended wait to microseconds and put the standalone GET stream into a hot reconnect loop.

`pkgs/mcpx/internal/mcpclient/http.go` (main `5a34fa70`):

```go
// :317-320 — the only check is ms >= 0
case field == "retry":
    if ms, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && ms >= 0 {
        st.retry = time.Duration(ms) * time.Millisecond
    }
```

Both consumers then wait on that value whenever it is positive, falling back to the operator default (`upstream.sseReconnectDelay` = 1s, `internal/defaults/defaults.json:254`) only when it is `<= 0`:

- `resume()` (:343-346) — `wait := st.retry; if wait <= 0 { wait = defaults.UpstreamSSEReconnectDelay }`, then `time.After(wait)`. Attempts are bounded (`sseReconnectAttempts`: 5), but the **wait itself is not**: a retry of e.g. 10 years means the resume never fires within any useful lifetime; the request's response is simply never recovered and the caller waits for its own deadline.
- The standalone GET-stream loop `listen()` (:471-474) — same wait selection, but the loop is **unbounded** (`for ctx.Err() == nil`, ctx cancelled only on transport close). A huge retry silences the stream (notifications / server requests lost) for years; a wrapped-to-microseconds retry makes it reconnect in a tight loop against the upstream.

### Overflow

`time.Duration(ms) * time.Millisecond` is int64-nanosecond arithmetic. Any `ms` above ~9.22e12 wraps:

- `retry: 10000000000000` (1e13) → `st.retry` is **negative** (-8446744073709551616 ns) → the `<= 0` fallback silently substitutes 1s — neither what the server asked nor a deliberate policy.
- `retry: 18446744073710` → wraps to a **small positive** 448384 ns (~448µs) → no fallback, near-instant reconnects.
- `retry: 8640000000000000` → wraps to a different positive value (6923773503929843712 ns ≈ 219 years instead of the ~273,972 years the digits denote) → used verbatim.

### Verified this run

Verbatim-logic probe (the parse expression and wait selection copied from http.go:317-320 / 343-346) compiled and run on the laptop, main `5a34fa70` — probe at `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneA-ssretry/`:

```
retry:3000                   -> st.retry=3s            -> effective wait=3s
retry:315360000000           -> st.retry=87600h0m0s    -> effective wait=87600h0m0s   (10 years, no ceiling)
retry:8640000000000000       -> st.retry=1923270h25m…  -> effective wait=same          (wrapped to ~219y)
retry:10000000000000         -> st.retry=-2346317h47m… -> effective wait=1s            (wrapped negative)
retry:18446744073710         -> st.retry=448.384µs     -> effective wait=448.384µs     (wrapped to ~zero)
retry:9223372036854775807    -> st.retry=-1ms          -> effective wait=1s
```

(The 448µs result cross-checks arithmetically: 18446744073710 × 1e6 ns − 2^64 = 448384 ns.)

## Why it matters

The `retry` value is **server-controlled input** — exactly the class of value mcpx must not trust unbounded, from a legacy or buggy upstream (the SSE resumability work in #1924 made the client honour this field; honouring it without a bound traded one robustness hole for another). Consequences today: a stuck resume that looks like a hung call, a silently dead standalone stream (lost notifications/server requests — the failure `listen()` exists to prevent), or a reconnect hot-loop hammering the upstream. Sibling per-request durations in mcpx already got ceiling/overflow issues for the same shape (#2231 waitMs, #2351 task TTL) — this is the client-side copy.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The parsed SSE retry interval is bounded before use: values above a named ceiling (operator default or a constant, triage's pin — e.g. relative to `defaults.HTTPSSERetry`/a max resume delay) are clamped or treated as absent, and the `time.Duration(ms) * time.Millisecond` conversion can no longer wrap (reject/clamp `ms` before multiplying).
- [ ] With `retry: 315360000000`, `retry: 8640000000000000`, `retry: 10000000000000`, and `retry: 18446744073710`, the effective wait in both `resume()` and the standalone `listen()` loop is the pinned bounded value — never years, never microseconds, never an accidental wrapped duration.
- [ ] Normal values are unchanged: `retry: 3000` waits 3s, absent/non-numeric/negative `retry` keeps the current default behaviour.
- [ ] Regression tests in `internal/mcpclient` cover the parse/wait selection for in-range, over-ceiling, and would-overflow inputs; existing mcpclient tests pass.

Related: #1924 (the resumability work that introduced honouring `retry`), #2231 / #2351 (same unbounded-duration shape in mcpx's daemon paths — distinct sites).

title: opencode-config-normalize: agents-only config silently loses every agent — the agents block is dropped even when the merge splice never lands

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/opencode-config-normalize/normalize.sh` silently deletes every agent definition from a config that has an `agents` key but no `agent` key — which is exactly the shape OpenChamber's v1→v2 migration produces (the script's own header: OpenChamber migrates `agent` -> `agents`). The script reports "repaired" and exits 0 while the user's agents vanish, so the v1 CLI loses all its agent definitions — the opposite of the script's purpose.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `5a34fa70`)

- `normalize.sh:52-68` (embedded Python): when `'agents' in doc`, it computes `merged = {**agents, **agent}` and, if `merged != agent`, tries to splice the merged map into the existing `"agent"` block with the regex `"agent"(\s*):\s*\{.*?\n  \}` (lines 61-65). When there is **no** `"agent"` key, that regex cannot match (`"agents"` does not match `"agent"` + closing quote), so nothing is inserted and `n = 0`.
- The drop on line 67 then runs **unconditionally**: `re.subn(r'\n\s*"agents"\s*:\s*\{.*?\n  \},?', '', out, count=1, ...)` removes the `agents` block regardless of whether the merge splice succeeded, and sets `changed`, so the mutilated text is written after only a parse check (lines 73-79) that cannot detect the loss.
- Probe (this run, `/tmp/probe-laneB-normalize/`, script run with `OPENCODE_CONFIG` pointed at a copy): input with only `agents` (`build` + `plan` entries) and `plugins` came out as just `{ "$schema": ..., "plugin": ["opencode-plugin-x"] }` — both agents gone, no `agent` key created, stderr `opencode-config-normalize: repaired ...`, exit 0.
- Controls in the same probe: a config with a standard pretty-printed `agent` block plus `agents` merges correctly, and a single-line `"agent": {}` also merges correctly — the loss is specific to the agents-only shape (and to any shape where the splice regex misses while the drop regex hits).

## Why it matters

This script runs unattended (it is designed for a path-unit trigger on the live `~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc`) precisely after OpenChamber launches — i.e. precisely when the config is most likely to be in the agents-only v2 shape. Each such launch can irreversibly strip every custom agent (models, prompts, permissions) from the shared config with no error, no backup, and a "repaired" log line. A repair tool must never be a data-loss path.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An agents-only config gains an `agent` block containing every `agents` entry (same merge precedence: existing `agent` wins per key) and loses the `agents` block — no entry is dropped.
- [ ] The `agents` block is removed only after its contents are verifiably present in the resulting `agent` block; if the splice/insert cannot be performed, the file is left byte-identical (no write, non-zero or silent no-op per the script's existing conventions — pin one).
- [ ] Regression fixtures: agents-only (2-space pretty), agent+agents merge (existing behaviour preserved), plugins-only rename, and an unparseable file left untouched; each asserts the full parsed document, not just substrings.
- [ ] Idempotence preserved: running the script on its own output is a no-op.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `opencode-config-normalize`, "normalize opencode config agents", and the script path: no issue covers this script's agents handling. #704 (closed) is a different tool (`sync-models`) with a different JSONC parser; #730 is v2 schema validation of `.opencode` project config, not this normalizer.

body:
# id(web): PR #1696's upload-name uniquifier is check-then-act — concurrent same-name uploads still silently un-name the first

## Finding

PR #1696 (merged) fixed #1549 for the sequential case: `upload_handler` resolves a collision-free stored name with `uniquify_upload_name` (`pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs:1473` on current main `5a34fa70`) and only afterwards sets the blob tag under that name (`routes.rs:1616`). The check and the claim are two separate awaited store operations with nothing serialising them — no lock in the handler or in `AppState`, and iroh-blobs `tags().set` is an unconditional write, not a create-if-absent.

Two uploads of the same filename with different bytes that are in flight at the same time can therefore interleave as: both call `upload_name_owner` (`routes.rs:1455`) and see the intended name free → both are handed the intended name → both `tags().set` it, the second overwriting the first. The first image loses its name exactly as in #1549 (its response even reported that name as its stored name and URL), and the filename-keyed metadata below the tag write is then set-if-absent under the same contested name, so the surviving name's metadata can describe the losing upload. The PR's tests exercise strictly sequential uploads, so the interleaving is untested.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/1696 (merged, commit `4d423fbd`) — "fix(id): uniquify colliding upload stored names" for #1549 (closed).
- Current main `5a34fa707001f297fd963ea7b8a33d0eb8b7951c`, `pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs`: `upload_name_owner` at :1455 (a plain `tags().get`), `uniquify_upload_name` at :1473-1500 (get-only loop, returns a name it has not claimed), the handler calls it at :1602 and performs the claiming `state.store.tags().set(tag, hash)` at :1616 — a separate awaited call with no lock, retry, or post-set verification between them.
- `AppState` (`pkgs/id/src/web/mod.rs:139-154`) holds the blob `store` shared by all requests and contains no upload/name mutex; axum serves `upload_handler` concurrently per connection.
- The uniquifier's own doc comment promises "a later upload never silently un-names an earlier, different image" (`routes.rs:1470-1472`) — under concurrency that guarantee does not hold.
- Deduped against open + closed issues: #1549 (closed) is the sequential origin and its fix is this PR; #1612 (closed) is the analogous archive-tag collision in fileops, a different store path. No issue covers the concurrent-upload interleaving.

## Why it matters

Pasting images is the upload path's normal use, and two pastes/uploads racing (two tabs, two collaborators on a shared node, a retry overlapping the original) is ordinary, not adversarial. When it happens, the failure is the precise silent data loss #1549 was filed to eliminate — one image quietly un-named while its uploader was told the name was theirs — just narrowed to the concurrent window the fix left open.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Name resolution and tag claiming are atomic in effect: two concurrent uploads of the same filename with different bytes both end up listed and resolvable under distinct stored names (e.g. the resolve+set sequence is serialised, or the claim is retried/re-resolved when the tag changed underneath), and each response reports the name that actually names its blob.
- [ ] A regression test drives two same-name different-bytes uploads concurrently (interleaved at the resolve/set boundary) and pins that neither un-names the other; the existing sequential #1549 tests stay green, including the idempotent identical-bytes re-upload.
- [ ] Filename-keyed metadata for a raced name cannot mix the two uploads (the surviving name's created/content-type records describe the blob the name resolves to).

body:
# id(web): PR #1688's table code-span pipe preprocessor also rewrites fenced code blocks — a table example inside a fence gains spurious backslashes

## Finding

PR #1688 (open, head `3895a266`) fixes #1424 by preprocessing the markdown source before comrak parses it: `escape_table_code_span_pipes` (called from `markdown_to_prosemirror`, `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs:129` on the PR head) scans line by line, treats any line followed by a table delimiter row as a header row and every following line until a blank line as a table body row, and escapes unescaped pipes inside code spans on those lines (`escape_table_code_span_pipes`, `markdown.rs:324-354` on the PR head).

The scanner has **no fenced-code-block state**. A fenced block that contains a markdown table example — exactly how docs and notes show table syntax — is therefore rewritten as if it were a live table: the header-looking line inside the fence gets its code-span pipes escaped. Comrak then renders the fence's contents verbatim, backslash included, so the code block displays `` `a\|b` `` where the author wrote `` `a|b` ``. That is silent corruption of literal code content on the parse direction, introduced by a change whose own guard test pins that lines *outside tables* stay untouched — a fence is the strongest form of "outside a table", and no test in the PR covers it.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/1688 (OPEN, head `3895a266633a5904a84e3ce42fa0c00510e1384b`) — "fix(id): keep pipes inside code spans from splitting table cells" for #1424.
- Call site (PR head): `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs:129` — `let protected = escape_table_code_span_pipes(&protected);` runs on the whole document inside `markdown_to_prosemirror`.
- Scanner (PR head): `markdown.rs:324-354` — the loop tracks only `in_table` (set by `is_table_delimiter_row`, `markdown.rs:226`) and `header_row` (next line is a delimiter row); there is no fence (` ``` `/`~~~`) tracking anywhere in the function, and its doc comment claims only "Lines outside tables are returned untouched".
- Contrast with the sibling preprocessor in the same file: `protect_newline_destinations` is documented on current main (`5a34fa70`, `markdown.rs:131-138`) as "Fenced code blocks are skipped — a destination-shaped string inside a fence is literal text, not a link." The new preprocessor does not follow that house pattern.
- Logic probe (faithful Python port of the PR's three functions, probe dir `hidden_files/probe-pr1688-fence/`): input fence
  ```` ```markdown ```` block containing `| `a|b` | H2 |` + delimiter row comes out with the header line rewritten to `| `a\|b` | H2 |` inside the fence, while a real (unfenced) table gets the same escaping as intended. The fence case is therefore a mis-fire of the table detection, not comrak behaviour.
- The PR's tests (5 new) cover body/header/only-content/one-column/outside-table cases; none puts a table or a delimiter row inside a fenced block. Deduped against open + closed issues: only #1424 (open, the origin) matches; it is about live tables and never mentions fences.

## Why it matters

Documents in this system routinely contain markdown-about-markdown: docs, specs, and notes that show table syntax inside fences. After this PR lands as written, merely opening such a document in the web editor rewrites its code samples (a spurious `\` appears in every code span containing a pipe on a header-looking line, and on body-looking lines after a delimiter-looking line inside the same fence), and a subsequent save persists the corruption. The fix in the PR is otherwise sound — this is a contained gap in the new scanner, cheapest to close before merge while the PR is still open.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `escape_table_code_span_pipes` (or its call path) skips fenced code blocks (``` and ~~~ fences): a table example inside a fence round-trips byte-identically through `markdown_to_prosemirror` / save.
- [ ] A regression test pins the fence case (table with a code-span pipe inside a fenced block renders as a code block with the literal pipe, no backslash) alongside the PR's existing #1424 tests.
- [ ] All five #1424 behaviours from PR #1688 are unchanged: live header/body code-span pipes still parse as one cell with the code mark intact, and lines outside tables remain untouched.

body:
# mcpx(plugin): shell.env hook throws RangeError on an out-of-range session created timestamp — the poisoned value is cached, so every full-level shell command for that session repeats the failure

## Summary

In the OpenCode mcpx plugin, the `shell.env` hook converts the session's
creation time with an unguarded `toISOString()`:

```ts
// pkgs/mcpx/plugin/opencode/mcpx-session.ts:718-721
if (s.created) {
  put(e, "MCPX_SESSION_CREATED", new Date(s.created).toISOString())
  put(e, "MCPX_SESSION_AGE_MS", String(Date.now() - s.created))
}
```

`s.created` is `s.time?.created` taken verbatim from the OpenCode server's
session response in `describe()` (`mcpx-session.ts:402`) — untrusted,
unvalidated server data (epoch milliseconds). A `Date` only accepts
±8,640,000,000,000,000 ms; any larger value (a corrupt / skewed /
differently-scaled server timestamp, e.g. `1e16`, a nanosecond-scale
value ~`1.7e18`, or `Infinity`) makes `toISOString()` throw
`RangeError: Invalid Date`.

## Why this is worse than a missing variable

- The throw is **outside** `describe()`'s fail-soft `try/catch`
  (`mcpx-session.ts:391-411`). The file states the invariant that wrapper
  exists for, at `mcpx-session.ts:380-383`: the walk "is bounded and every
  failure is swallowed: this runs in the path of every shell command, and
  a plugin that can break the shell is worse than a plugin that sometimes
  omits a variable." The conversion in the hook violates exactly that
  invariant — the hook's promise rejects instead of omitting
  `MCPX_SESSION_CREATED`.
- Everything after the block in that call never runs, including the
  `MCPX_TRACE_IDS` injection at `mcpx-session.ts:726`.
- `describe()` **caches** its result (`sessions.set(id, out)`,
  `mcpx-session.ts:412`), so the poisoned `created` value is reused: at
  `env: "full"` level, *every* shell command for that session repeats
  the throw for the life of the editor session, not just the first one.
- Secondary: even an in-range-but-absurd value (e.g. exactly
  `8640000000000000`) renders a year-275760 date and a hugely negative
  `MCPX_SESSION_AGE_MS` instead of being treated as absent.

Distinct from #2286: that is the aggregator's own `iso()` helper
(`pm-stack/aggregator/src/sources/opencode.ts:86-87`) dropping a server's
sessions on the dashboard. This is a different file, a different consumer,
and a different failure mode (the shell-command path itself, repeatedly).
Same lesson, second unguarded copy.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 5a34fa70)

Sandbox Bun probe (`/tmp/probe-laneA-mcpxcreated/probe.ts`) running the
verbatim guard + `put` + conversion lines from `mcpx-session.ts:718-721`:

```
control-normal  1727740800000      OK  MCPX_SESSION_CREATED=2024-10-01T00:00:00.000Z, trace marker set
max-valid       8640000000000000   OK  "+275760-09-13T00:00:00.000Z", AGE_MS=-8638206713466224
max+1           8640000000000001   THROWS RangeError: Invalid Date — env-so-far {}, trace marker never set
1e16                               THROWS RangeError: Invalid Date — env-so-far {}
Infinity                           THROWS RangeError: Invalid Date — env-so-far {}
ns-scale        1.7e18             THROWS RangeError: Invalid Date — env-so-far {}
negative        -1000              OK  1969-12-31T23:59:59.000Z
```

Code reading, same run:

- `mcpx-session.ts:402` — `out.created = s.time?.created`, no range or
  finiteness check.
- `mcpx-session.ts:385-413` — `describe()` wraps only the fetch walk in
  `try/catch`; it caches and returns the raw value.
- `mcpx-session.ts:708-726` — the `shell.env` hook calls `describe()`,
  then performs the conversion inline with no `try/catch` of its own.

Dedup: open + closed searches for `mcpx-session SESSION_CREATED`,
`toISOString plugin`, and `shell.env` return no covering issue
(#2286 aggregator, #2309 goDurationMs, #2231 waitMs are distinct sites).

## Acceptance criteria

- Triage pins the guard site (validate in `describe()` when caching, or
  guard the conversion in the hook) and the rule for absurd-but-in-range
  values (e.g. future / pre-epoch `created` → omit both variables, or
  keep — but recorded on this issue).
- With `created = 8640000000000001`, `1e16`, or `Infinity`, the
  `shell.env` hook resolves normally: `MCPX_SESSION_CREATED` /
  `MCPX_SESSION_AGE_MS` are omitted (or otherwise made safe), and the
  later `MCPX_TRACE_IDS` injection still runs.
- Normal values are unchanged: a real epoch-ms `created` still yields
  the ISO string and a non-negative age.
- A regression test covers the out-of-range cases alongside the normal
  case (plugin test suite, e.g. beside the existing `daemon.test.ts` /
  session tests), and existing plugin tests pass.

title: mcpx(tasks): per-request task TTL has no ceiling — past ~9.22e12 ms the duration overflows and the task deletes/cancels itself at birth; huge values keep results ~forever

body:
## Summary

A caller-supplied task TTL reaches `tasks.Store.Start` with only a `ttl <= 0 → operator default` rule and **no ceiling**, at every entry point:

- `internal/daemon/server.go:893` — `/v1` call tasks: `s.startCallTask(req.Task.TTL, ...)`
- `internal/daemon/routes_exec.go:238-245` — exec tasks: `req.Options.Task.TTL` (`internal/execsvc/execsvc.go:92-93`, "milliseconds the result is kept, as MCP spells it")
- `internal/daemon/routes_proto.go:422-425` — proto ask tasks: `req.TTL`

`internal/tasks/tasks.go:355-357` substitutes the default (`tasks.ttl`, 10m; `proto.askTTL`, 15m) only when `ttl <= 0`. Any positive value is accepted verbatim, and `tasks.go:389` converts it unsafely:

```go
time.AfterFunc(time.Duration(ttl)*time.Millisecond, func() { ... delete ...; cancel() })
```

Two failure modes follow:

1. **Overflow → instant self-destruct.** `time.Duration` is int64 nanoseconds, so any `ttl > ~9.22e12` ms (~292 years in ms — a plain JSON number like `10000000000000`) makes `time.Duration(ttl) * time.Millisecond` wrap negative. `time.AfterFunc` with a negative duration fires immediately: the task is deleted from the store and its context is cancelled at birth, before the work can run. The caller gets a 202 handle for a task that can never be collected.
2. **Huge-but-valid → retention the operator never chose.** `ttl = 1e12` ms (~31.7 years) is stored verbatim, so task results — tool-call and exec results, the payloads the retention exists to bound — are kept effectively forever, silently overriding the operator's `tasks.ttl` (10m default). This is the same shape as the artifact-PUT ceiling gap in #2327, in the task store instead of the artifact store.

## Evidence (main `5a34fa70`, laptop probe with the real `tasks.Store`)

Probe test in laptop worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneB-taskttl/pkgs/mcpx/internal/tasks/probe_taskttl_test.go` (`go test -run TestProbeTaskTTLOverflow -v`):

- Control `ttl=60000`: work (150ms) completes, task present with status `completed` after 400ms.
- `ttl=10000000000000` (1e13): after 400ms the task is **gone** (`Get` → not present) — deleted before its 150ms of work finished. Probe asserts this as the reproduced bug and fails as designed.
- `ttl=1000000000000` (1e12): accepted and stored verbatim (`stored TTL=1000000000000 ms`).

## Why it matters

The task handle is the contract for long-running tool/exec calls: the caller polls or collects the result later. An overflowing TTL silently breaks that contract in the worst way — accepted with a 202, then instantly uncollectable, with the work cancelled — and a merely huge TTL defeats the retention bound that keeps results (potentially sensitive tool/exec output) from living in the daemon's store and SQLite DB forever. Both are one JSON field from any local caller, and neither produces an error anywhere.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A per-request task TTL is validated at the daemon boundary (or in `tasks.Store.Start`): values above a defined ceiling are rejected with a 400-class error or clamped to the ceiling — triage pins which, and the ceiling's relationship to the operator's `tasks.ttl` / `proto.askTTL`.
- [ ] No accepted TTL can overflow the `time.Duration(ttl) * time.Millisecond` conversion (regression test at the boundary value, e.g. `ttl = 1e13`, asserting the task survives its work and completes).
- [ ] The rule applies uniformly to all three entry points (`server.go` call tasks, `routes_exec.go` exec tasks, `routes_proto.go` ask tasks) — a single guard in `Start` is the obvious way to guarantee that.
- [ ] Existing task tests pass; the persisted `expiresAtMs = createdMs + ttlMs` load path (`tasks.go:210`) stays consistent with the pinned rule.

Related: #2327 (the artifact-store sibling: per-request TTL with no ceiling overriding the operator default), #1653 (distinct — legitimate TTLs are clocked from creation, so a task is cancelled mid-run when its TTL lapses; this issue is about unbounded/overflowing TTL values, not the clock start).

body:
## Summary

`projectPace` in the pm-stack aggregator throws `RangeError: Invalid Date` on snapshot records that pass the store's own validator, and the throw propagates uncaught through the quota card render, the service detail page, and `/api/quota/service.json`. One poisoned pct record in the append-only snapshot store breaks those views for its service on every render until the record is removed by hand.

## Evidence (verified on main 5a34fa70)

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/derive.ts:939-940` — the projection is computed with no range guard:

  ```ts
  const projectedExhaustionAt =
    lastVal >= 100 ? last.ts : new Date(Date.parse(last.ts) + ((100 - lastVal) / slope) * 86_400_000).toISOString();
  ```

  The only guards above it are `days < 0.5 → null` and `slope <= 0.05 → null` (derive.ts:935-937). Nothing bounds `lastVal` from below, so a small positive slope plus a very negative last value pushes the projected instant past the maximum representable Date (±8.64e15 ms), producing an Invalid Date whose `.toISOString()` throws.

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/snapshots.ts:36-52` (`isSnapshotRecord`) — a numeric `value` is accepted iff `Number.isFinite(r.value)`. There is no pct range check, so a record with `unit: "pct"` and `value: -1_000_000_000` is a valid store record: `SnapshotStore.readAll()` returns it and `append()` happily persists it.

- Call sites do not catch: `render.ts` `paceLineHtml` (called per service card) calls `projectPace` directly; the service detail path maps `projectPace` over every metric (render.ts, `paces` construction); `src/server.ts` `/api/quota/service.json` maps it the same way. A throw in any of them aborts the whole render/response, not just the pace line.

## Reproduction (probe run this run, bun, against unmodified main)

Records (both pass `isSnapshotRecord`):

```ts
{ ts: "2026-10-20T00:00:00Z", value: -1_000_000_000, unit: "pct", metricId: "weekly", ... }
{ ts: "2026-10-22T00:00:00Z", value:   -999_999_999, unit: "pct", metricId: "weekly", ... }
```

`projectPace(recs, "weekly")` → **throws `RangeError: Invalid Date`** (slope = 0.5 pts/day over 2 days; projected offset ≈ 2×10⁹ days ≈ 1.7×10¹⁷ ms, past the Date maximum).

Control: ordinary records (30 → 40 over the same window) return a sane projection (`2026-11-03T00:00:00.000Z`).

A milder variant does not throw but is still wrong: values −5000 → −4999.88 (slope 0.06) project exhaustion in the year **2259** — a negative-percent metric should support no exhaustion projection at all.

## Why it matters

The snapshot store is append-only and written by several jobs (fleet-feed collector, stewardship-cycle, the Jules keeper, a Python mirror). A single bad pct observation — a misparse, a sign flip, a units mixup upstream — permanently poisons the quota views for that service: the store has no delete path, `readAll` keeps returning the record, and every affected page/API call throws instead of degrading to "no pace line", which is the function's own documented contract ("Null when history cannot support a projection — never invented", derive.ts:923-925).

Related but distinct: #1540 covers the validator accepting records it cannot read back (non-finite estimate pairs, non-ISO timestamps). This issue is downstream of the validator: even records the validator legitimately accepts can crash the projection, so the fix belongs in `projectPace` as well as (optionally) the validator.

## Acceptance criteria

- `projectPace` never throws for any records `isSnapshotRecord` accepts: out-of-range projections return `null` (or a clamped/`null` `projectedExhaustionAt`) instead of an Invalid Date exception.
- A last value below 0 (or otherwise outside the plausible pct domain) yields no exhaustion projection.
- Regression tests in the aggregator test suite cover: the extreme-negative pair above, the mildly-negative pair, and the existing sane cases (single point, flat slope) still behaving as before.
- Quota card render, service detail render, and `/api/quota/service.json` succeed for a service whose stored history contains such a record.

body:
## Finding (pool-intelligence, 2026-10-29)

The catalog leaf `commandcode/gpt-5.6-terra` fails **100%** of fleet
route attempts across two independently measured windows:

| window (route_attempt, laptop OpenCode store) | attempts | success | top error tags |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-10-26T12:01Z → 2026-10-27T12:01Z | 39 | 0 (0%) | — |
| 2026-10-28T13:12Z → 2026-10-29T13:12Z | 94 | 0 (0%) | UnknownProvider 56, Transport 38 |

Total: **0/133**. The dominant `UnknownProvider` tag points at a
provider/model-id mapping problem for this leaf (the model is
GPT-5.6 Terra served via CommandCode), not a transient outage —
and the sibling leaf `commandcode/deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash`
also managed only 4/25 (16%) in the latest window, so the
CommandCode door's model mapping deserves one look, not just this
leaf.

## Why it matters

The leaf is not seated in any pool, but until 2026-10-29 it was the
OpenCode server's first-available fallback default (canonical
config header note, origin/main 5a34fa70: default now pinned to
`opencode-route/workhorse`, verified against /api/model/default).
Any future fallback, probe, or direct-leaf session that resolves
to this leaf burns its whole attempt budget on a guaranteed
failure and fails over late.

## Acceptance criteria

labels.name: task/triage

body:
# mcpx(daemon): artifact PUT `ttl` has no ceiling — a per-request TTL overrides the operator's `artifacts.ttl` (24h) up to ~292 years, so GC never collects the artifact

## Evidence

`pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/routes_exec.go:371-379` (main `5a34fa70`), `handleArtifactPut` (`POST /v1/artifacts`, routes_exec.go:38):

```go
if ttl := q.Get("ttl"); ttl != "" {
    d, perr := time.ParseDuration(ttl)
    if perr != nil {
        writeErr(w, http.StatusBadRequest, fmt.Errorf("ttl %q: %w", ttl, perr))
        return
    }
    put.TTL = d
}
```

Any duration `time.ParseDuration` accepts is taken verbatim. There is no ceiling, and no comparison against the operator's configured retention.

The store then applies it verbatim — `pkgs/mcpx/internal/artifacts/artifacts.go:303-312` (`register`):

```go
ttl := p.TTL
if ttl <= 0 {
    ttl = s.opts.TTL
}
...
Expires: now.Add(ttl),
```

and GC is the only expiry path — `artifacts.go:515` (`GC`): `SELECT id FROM artifacts WHERE expires <= ?`. An expiry centuries out is, for GC, never.

The operator's retention setting this overrides: `artifacts.ttl`, default `24h` (`pkgs/mcpx/docs/configuration.md:257`; the store default is wired from the settings registry at `routes_exec.go:93` / `internal/cli/exec.go:163`).

### Probe (laptop, real `artifacts.Store`, main-identical files)

Probe worktree on the laptop: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneB-artifactttl/` (relevant files md5-identical to sandbox main `5a34fa70`: artifacts.go `0022b738…`, routes_exec.go `de9f0870…`). A test in `internal/artifacts` opened a store with the operator default `TTL: 24h` and called the real `Store.Put` with per-put TTLs:

| per-put TTL | result |
|---|---|
| `0` (control) | expires +24h (operator default) |
| `-1h` (control) | expires +24h (store's `ttl <= 0` fallback) |
| `876000h` (100 years) | **accepted — created 2026-10-29, expires 2126-10-05** |
| `2500000h` (~285 years) | **accepted — expires 2312-01-10** |

Parse-step controls: `time.ParseDuration("876000h")` and `("2500000h")` succeed; only a string overflowing int64 nanoseconds (~292.47 years, e.g. a 20-digit hour count) errors, and the handler correctly 400s on that parse error. So the effective ceiling today is Go's int64-nanosecond limit, not any retention policy.

## Why it matters

`artifacts.ttl` is the operator's retention promise: how long a registered file is kept before it is collected (configuration.md:257). The per-request `?ttl=` parameter silently repeals it for that artifact, with no bound and no log line. Any script or client that can reach the daemon — artifact registration is the normal `artifact()` script path, per the handler's own comment — can pin blobs effectively forever: a typo'd unit (`ttl=876000h` for `876000s`-ish intent), a careless "keep it a long time" value, or simple accumulation of large-TTL artifacts defeats GC and grows the blob store until the store quota (a hard ceiling checked at put time, not a retention mechanism) starts refusing new artifacts for everyone. The failure surfaces months later as disk/quota pressure, with nothing pointing back at the TTL that caused it.

This is the same shape as #2231 (per-request `waitMs` overriding operator wait settings with no cap), on a different surface: there the cost was a pinned handler, here it is pinned storage.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Triage pins the ceiling rule and records it on this issue: e.g. clamp per-request TTL to at most the operator's `artifacts.ttl`, reject above it with 400, or a named absolute maximum — including what a legitimate long-retention caller should do instead.
- [ ] `handleArtifactPut` enforces the pinned rule; a `ttl` beyond it no longer produces an `Expires` beyond the allowed horizon.
- [ ] Zero/negative `ttl` behaviour is unchanged (store default applies), and ordinary TTLs at or under the ceiling work exactly as before.
- [ ] A regression test covers an over-ceiling `ttl` (e.g. `876000h`) at the handler or store boundary, plus the happy-path and default controls.
- [ ] The effective rule is documented where `artifacts.ttl` is documented (`docs/configuration.md` / exec docs), so the per-request override's bound is discoverable.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for "artifact TTL", "artifacts ttl", and "ttl" generally (2026-10-29): #1884 is a TTL-renewal convention proposal (touch-on-read), #1653 is MCP task TTL clocked from creation — neither covers the artifact PUT ceiling. #2231 is the `waitMs` long-poll cap, a different endpoint and store; cross-linked as the same pattern, not a duplicate.

title: repo-queue: enqueue dedupe matches terminal rows — a completed dedupe key can never be re-enqueued, silently orphaning follow-ups

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: area/infra
labels.description: Infrastructure, deployment, and operations

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: source/fleet-monitor
labels.description: Filed or driven by the fleet monitor / operator reconciliation

body:
## Bug (proven live 2026-10-29, operator queue repair)

The enqueue RPC behind `~/tools/repo-queue.py` (`agent.enqueue_repo_task`) dedupes on `dedupe_key` against **all rows regardless of status** and returns the existing row. For a `done` (completed) task that means the key is permanently poisoned: any later packet for the same issue — a re-triage, a planned follow-up round — silently returns the completed row, creates nothing, and mutates nothing. The caller cannot tell; enqueue "succeeds."

This is the completion-side sibling of #1298 (cancelled rows), fixed 2026-10-27 by migration `0014_revive_on_enqueue.sql` for `cancelled` rows only. `done` rows were not covered, and the assumption recorded in several task completion notes — "the dedupe key frees on completion" — is **false** as the RPC behaves today. (Related queue-lifecycle gap: #1337, the missing claim/park verb.)

## Evidence (fresh reads before/after, 2026-10-29)

Seven Duty-1-style re-triage packets were built for open issues whose `queue/queued` labels promised work, and each enqueue was attempted:

| Issue | Returned existing task | Its status | New task created |
|---|---|---|---|
| #553 | 1261 | done | none |
| #785 | 2209 | done | none |
| #788 | 2214 | done | none |
| #806 | 2245 | done | none |
| #961 | 2298 | done | none |
| #1342 | 1327 | done | none |
| #1058 | 2328 | done | none |

The done rows' `updated_at` values were byte-identical before/after each attempt; a final count shows **0 live tasks across all seven dedupe keys** while all seven issues sit open with `queue/queued` labels.

## Consequences already observed

- **#553** (priority/high): triage 1261 done → fix 1305 done (slice 1 merged, PR #1437). Task 1305's planned "combined slices 2+3 follow-up" enqueue silently no-opped; the remaining acceptance criteria (Prometheus endpoint + tracing spans) are unowned.
- **#785**: triage 2209 done; the iroh-over-SSH fallback — an explicit acceptance criterion — has no code, and its planned follow-up packet was never enqueued (same silent no-op, recorded in 2209's own completion note).
- **#1058**: the real fix task 2992 was cancelled as a "duplicate of task 2329" on the strength of this behavior plus a phantom reference — task 2328's recorded `follow_up_task_ids [2329]` is erroneous (2329 is an unrelated nix triage for dezren39/nix#300). The fix for #1058 never ran.

## Per-issue state of the seven blocked issues

- **#553** OPEN, priority/high — slice 1 merged (PR #1437); slices 2+3 follow-up never enqueued.
- **#785** OPEN — SSH-over-iroh tunnel exists; iroh-over-SSH fallback criterion unimplemented.
- **#788** OPEN (XL) — disposition was re-queue gated on #534 + #538; both gates re-verified still OPEN 2026-10-29.
- **#806** OPEN — re-queue gated on F12.6/#534 + F11.12; #534 re-verified still OPEN.
- **#961** OPEN, status:blocked — requeue after #959 lands; #959 re-verified still OPEN.
- **#1342** OPEN — all three acceptance criteria appear covered (tasks 1327 triage, 1670 slice 1, 1671 slice 2 under #1409's key); needs only a close-out triage once enqueue works.
- **#1058** OPEN — fix never ran (see phantom-reference finding above); the re-triage must also correct the phantom `follow_up_task_ids` reference on the record.

## Fix options

1. **Root fix (recommended):** the enqueue RPC dedupes only against **non-terminal** rows (queued / claimed / parked / blocked). A key matching only a completed (or cancelled — already revived in place per #1298's migration 0014) row produces a fresh queued task. This is the semantics workers and the fleet monitor already assume everywhere.
2. **Pattern-side alternative:** extend the dedupe design patterns with a round suffix (e.g. `repo-health:v1:triage:developing-today/code:issue:553:r2`). No schema change, but every producer (lanes, creators, monitor, dispatcher) must learn the convention, round bookkeeping becomes a new failure surface, and already-poisoned base keys stay poisoned.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] After the fix, enqueueing a packet whose `dedupe_key` matches only a `done` task creates a **new** queued task.
- [ ] Enqueueing a packet whose key matches a **live** task (queued/claimed/parked/blocked) still returns the live task — no duplicates.
- [ ] The seven blocked issues above (#553, #785, #788, #806, #961, #1342, #1058) can be re-triaged; their re-triage packets will be rebuilt by the fleet monitor's Duty 1 once enqueue works.
- [ ] A regression test or documented probe (migration-style synthetic test, like the one for #1298/0014) covers both directions: terminal-key re-enqueue creates, live-key enqueue dedupes.
- [ ] The chosen semantics are written down where producers will see them (queue tooling docs / protocol), retiring the false "key frees on completion" assumption explicitly if option 1 lands differently than expected.

title: mcpx(plugin): goDurationMs returns Infinity for overflow durations Go rejects — one typo'd MCPX_PLUGIN_DISCOVERY_RETRY disables daemon rediscovery for the whole session
