body:
# mcpx(plugin): goDurationMs returns Infinity for overflow durations Go rejects — one typo'd MCPX_PLUGIN_DISCOVERY_RETRY disables daemon rediscovery for the whole session

## Summary

`goDurationMs` (`pkgs/mcpx/plugin/opencode/mcpx/daemon.ts:93-110`) is the plugin's
re-implementation of Go's `time.ParseDuration` spelling, used for exactly one setting:
`discoveryRetryMs: goDurationMs(env.MCPX_PLUGIN_DISCOVERY_RETRY) ?? TUNING.missCooldownMs`
(`pkgs/mcpx/plugin/opencode/mcpx-session.ts:196`). The settings registry declares
`plugin.discoveryRetry` as `KindDuration` (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/settings/plugin.go:49`,
default `1m0s`), and the Go side validates duration values with `time.ParseDuration`
(`pkgs/mcpx/internal/settings/value.go:500`), which **errors on overflow** (any duration
past ~2^63 ns ≈ 2562047h47m16s).

The plugin's parser has no overflow check: it multiplies `Number(m[1]) * unit` and only
rejects the input when the matched length differs from the input length. A long digit
string parses to `Infinity` and is returned as a valid duration.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 5a34fa70, sandbox Bun probe importing the real daemon.ts)

```
"60s"   => 60000        "1m30s" => 90000        "500ms" => 500
"3000000h" => 10800000000000          (finite, but Go: ParseDuration overflow error)
"1000…0h"  (370 digits) => Infinity
"999…9s"   (401 digits) => Infinity
"0" => undefined   (Go: ParseDuration("0") == 0, valid — plugin treats it as absent)
```

## Why it matters

`mcpx-session.ts:249` gates rediscovery on `Date.now() - missedAt < settings.discoveryRetryMs`.
With `discoveryRetryMs = Infinity` (or any absurd-but-finite value Go would have rejected,
e.g. `3000000h`), that comparison is true forever after the first discovery miss: a daemon
started later in the session is **never** discovered until the editor restarts — the exact
failure the cooldown exists to recover from, inverted, with no diagnostic anywhere. The
function's own doc comment states the design rule it violates: anything not understood is
treated as absent "because a cooldown of NaN would retry forever" — Infinity is the mirror
failure (never retry) and slips through precisely because the guard only thinks about NaN.

Secondary divergence in the same function: `"0"` is a valid Go duration (== 0, retry
immediately) but the plugin returns `undefined` for it (matched length 0), so an operator
who sets `MCPX_PLUGIN_DISCOVERY_RETRY=0` silently gets the 60s default instead.

## Acceptance criteria

- `goDurationMs` returns `undefined` for any input whose total would exceed what Go's
  `time.ParseDuration` accepts (overflow → absent, matching the function's stated rule);
  the result is always finite when defined.
- Parity tests in `daemon.test.ts` (the existing `goDurationMs` describe block) cover:
  overflow digit strings (`"9".repeat(400) + "s"`, `"3000000h"`), `"0"` (whatever behavior
  triage pins — Go parity says `0`), plus the already-covered happy paths unchanged.
- No behavior change for ordinary durations (`60s`, `1m30s`, `500ms`, `1.5h`, negatives
  staying absent is fine — that divergence is deliberate and documented in the header).

title: aggregator(opencode): iso() throws RangeError on out-of-range server timestamps — one bad session drops every session from that server

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

labels.name: app/aggregator
labels.description: Package/app: aggregator (pm-stack in this repo)

body:
## Summary

`iso()` in the aggregator's OpenCode session mapper converts a server-supplied millisecond timestamp with no range/finite gate, so one session whose `time.updated` (or `time.created`) is beyond the valid `Date` range makes `mapServerSessions` throw — and every caller fails soft at the whole-server level, so that one bad session silently drops **all** sessions from that OpenCode server from the attention feed and the durable registry.

## Evidence (main `5a34fa70`)

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/sources/opencode.ts:86-87`:
  ```ts
  const iso = (ms: number | undefined): string | null =>
    typeof ms === "number" && ms > 0 ? new Date(ms).toISOString() : null;
  ```
  `typeof` + `> 0` admit `1e16`, `Number.MAX_VALUE`, and `Infinity`-adjacent magnitudes. JS `Date` is only valid to ±8.64e15 ms; `new Date(1e16).toISOString()` throws `RangeError: Invalid Date`. (JSON cannot carry `Infinity`, but it happily carries `1e16`.)
- The throw sites are unguarded: entry construction in `mapOne` (`opencode.ts:174` `createdAt: iso(s.time?.created)`, `:179` `lastActivityAt: iso(s.time?.updated)`) and the long-running-call stamp at `:255`. `mapOne`/`mapServerSessions` have no per-session try/catch — one throw aborts the whole map.
- The bad session is reliably *included* before it throws: the attention filter at `opencode.ts:146` is `now - s.time.updated <= ATTENTION_WINDOW_MS`, and for a huge future `updated` that difference is negative, so the session passes the filter and sorts first (`:148`).
- Callers fail soft only at server granularity, which is what turns one bad row into a total loss:
  - `pm-stack/aggregator/src/sources/live.ts:878` (`attention()`) and `:983` (`registry()`): a throw from `laptopMapped()` is caught and the laptop part is dropped entirely (`laptopSeen = false`).
  - `pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/collect-fleet-feed.ts:456`: the sandbox `mapServerSessions` call sits in a try that leaves `attention = []` for the whole sandbox server on throw.

## Reproduction (this run)

Sandbox Bun probe driving the **real** `mapServerSessions` against a stub v2 server (probe in `/tmp/probe-laneB-ociso/probe.ts`):

- Control — one normal session: `entries: 1`, `lastActivityAt` stamped correctly.
- Experiment — the same good session plus one session with `time.updated = 1e16`: `mapServerSessions` **threw `RangeError: Invalid Date`**; zero entries returned, the good session included.

## Why it matters

The timestamps come from a remote OpenCode server's JSON — data this process does not control (a skewed clock, a corrupt store, a different server version). Today a single out-of-range stamp blacks out an entire server's sessions from attention + registry with no error naming the cause: the aggregator just reports the laptop/sandbox source as unreachable/fixtures. Per-session data faults should degrade per-session.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `iso()` (or its callers) returns `null` for any value that is not a finite, in-`Date`-range timestamp — no throw for `1e16`, `Number.MAX_VALUE`, or negative/huge magnitudes.
- [ ] One session with an out-of-range `time.created`/`time.updated`/message `time.created` does not prevent the remaining sessions from the same server being mapped (regression test with a mixed good/bad session list against the real mapper, in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/opencode.test.ts`).
- [ ] Triage pins whether far-future-but-valid stamps (e.g. +1 year) also count as "fresh" in the `:146` attention filter, or whether that stays as-is — record the decision on this issue.
- [ ] Existing aggregator tests pass.

## Dedup

Checked open + closed issues for `mapServerSessions`, "opencode iso", "toISOString throws": no existing issue covers this mapper. #2196 is quota-extract's `monthDayTime` throw (different file/mechanism); #1540/#2253/#2264 are store/quota/snapshot date gates, distinct modules.

title: id(repl): preprocessor rescans its own substitutions — $(...) and backticks inside single-quoted (literal) here-string content are executed instead of stored

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

The REPL preprocessor (`pkgs/id/src/repl/input.rs::preprocess_repl_line`) processes a line in stages — heredoc detection, here-string, `$(...)`, backticks, pipe — and each stage rescans the **whole** line, including content that an earlier stage inserted. Content supplied through a here-string is documented as literal when single-quoted (module docs: `put - name <<< 'literal content'`), but any `$(...)` or backtick span inside that content is then found by the later stages and **executed as a shell command**, with its output replacing the text. The same rescan applies to `$(...)` output, which the backtick stage then reprocesses.

## Evidence (main `5a34fa70`, verified this run)

Processing order in `preprocess_repl_line` (`pkgs/id/src/repl/input.rs`): here-string loop first, then the `$(...)` loop (`result.find("$(")` over the whole mutated line), then the backtick loop (`result.find('`')` over the whole mutated line). Neither loop excludes the `__STDIN_CONTENT__:` region inserted by the here-string stage.

Laptop probe (verbatim copies of `preprocess_repl_line`/`shell_capture`, only error plumbing adapted; probe at `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneA-replinput/` on the laptop):

```text
B1: put - name <<< 'price $(echo SUBSTITUTED) end'
    -> Ready("put __STDIN_CONTENT__:price SUBSTITUTED end name")   <- $(...) inside 'literal' content was EXECUTED
B2: put - name <<< 'a `echo TICK` b'
    -> Ready("put __STDIN_CONTENT__:a TICK b name")                <- backticks inside 'literal' content were EXECUTED
```

So `put - name <<< 'the price is $(cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519) today'` would store the command's output instead of the literal text — silently. The content a user explicitly quoted as literal is neither stored literally nor flagged.

For contrast, the other two content sources are **not** rescanned, which shows the intended boundary:

- Heredoc bodies are inserted by `repl/runner.rs` *after* preprocessing, so `$(...)` in a heredoc body stays literal.
- Pipe output is inserted by the last stage, so nothing rescans it.

## Why it matters

- **Correctness:** notes, snippets, and documentation text commonly contain `$(...)` or backticks (shell examples!). Storing them through a here-string silently rewrites them.
- **Safety:** literal-quoted content triggering shell execution is the kind of surprise that turns a paste into a command. The REPL already has an explicit shell escape (`!command` in `runner.rs`) and intentional substitution in command position; execution hidden inside quoted data is neither.
- The inconsistency across the three content sources (heredoc literal, pipe literal, here-string executed) makes the behavior impossible to predict from the docs.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Content inserted by the here-string stage is never rescanned by the `$(...)`/backtick stages: single-quoted here-string content is stored byte-for-byte (the documented "literal" behavior). Behavior for double-quoted and unquoted here-strings is pinned and documented either way.
- [ ] `$(...)` output is not rescanned by the backtick stage (or the rescan is pinned, documented, and tested).
- [ ] Substitution in command position keeps working: existing tests for `get $(echo test)`, backticks, nesting, and the `put $(...) name` content form still pass.
- [ ] New regression tests: `$(...)` and backticks inside single-quoted here-string content are stored literally; heredoc-body and pipe-output literalness is pinned by tests too.

## Dedup / related

- #1585 (open) covers the scans being quote-blind in the **original typed line** (a quoted `)` errors the line; a quoted `<<` triggers heredoc mode). This issue is the complementary defect: content **inserted by the preprocessor itself** is rescanned. A fix for either should be checked against the other, but neither issue's acceptance criteria cover the other's cases.
- #2280 covers the trailing `-` placeholder substitution in the same file — different defect.
- Searched open + recently closed issues for `here-string`, `preprocess`, `STDIN_CONTENT`, `command substitution` before filing; no existing issue covers rescanning of substituted content.

body:
## Summary

In the id REPL, the `-` content placeholder is only substituted when it appears mid-line (`" - "`). The end-of-line case was meant to be handled by a second replace, `.replace(" -$", ...)`, but Rust's `str::replace` is a **literal** string replace — `-$` is not a regex end anchor — so that pattern can only match the two literal characters ` -$`, which never occur. The end-of-line substitution is dead code at all three sites, and content addressed to a trailing `-` is silently lost or misrouted.

## Evidence (main `5a34fa70`, verified this run)

Dead-pattern sites:

- `pkgs/id/src/repl/input.rs` — here-string branch: `.replace(" - ", ...)` then `.replace(" -$", ...)`
- `pkgs/id/src/repl/input.rs` — pipe branch: `.replace(" - ", ...)`, `.replace(" -\n", ...)`, `.replace(" -$", ...)` (all literal)
- `pkgs/id/src/repl/runner.rs:140-141` — heredoc completion: same `" - "` / `" -$"` pair

Laptop probe (verbatim copies of `preprocess_repl_line`/`shell_capture` from `input.rs` and the heredoc-completion replace chain from `runner.rs`, only error plumbing adapted; probe at `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneA-replinput/` on the laptop):

```text
CTRL herestring mid:      Ready("put __STDIN_CONTENT__:payload name")
CTRL pipe mid:            Ready("put __STDIN_CONTENT__:hi name")
CTRL heredoc mid:         "put __STDIN_CONTENT__:BODY name"
A1 herestring dash-last:  Ready("put name -")                          <- 'payload' silently dropped
A2 pipe dash-last:        Ready("put name - __STDIN_CONTENT__:hi")     <- marker appended AFTER the '-'
A3 heredoc dash-last:     "put name -"                                 <- heredoc body silently discarded
PROOF replace:            "put name -".replace(" -$", " X") == "put name -"  (unchanged)
```

Downstream consequences, from `repl/runner.rs`:

- **Here-string** (`A1`): the line executes as `put name -` — the here-string content never reaches the store; the `-` is treated as an ordinary argument.
- **Pipe** (`A2`): the marker lands after the `-`, so `handle_stdin_content` (runner.rs:446) computes `before == "put name -"`, which is not `"put"`, and prints `unknown command with content: put name -` — the piped content is dropped with a misleading message.
- **Heredoc** (`A3`): after the user types the whole heredoc body, completion leaves the line as `put name -`; the body is discarded and the command runs as a plain file put.

## Why it matters

The REPL documents `-` as the content placeholder for `put` (module docs in `input.rs`), and users reasonably put it last (`put name - <<< '...'`, `... |> put name -`, `put name - <<EOF`). In each form the failure is silent data loss: the command appears to run, but the content the user supplied is not what gets stored — or nothing is stored and the error message points at the wrong cause. The dead `" -$"` pattern also misleads future readers into believing the end-of-line case is handled.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A trailing `-` placeholder is substituted in all three paths (here-string, pipe, heredoc completion), or the trailing form is rejected with a clear error naming the placeholder position — one consistent behavior, pinned in the issue/PR.
- [ ] No literal `" -$"` (or `" -\n"`) replace patterns remain; the substitution logic is shared or identically tested at all sites it is needed.
- [ ] Regression tests in `pkgs/id/src/repl/input.rs` / `runner.rs` covering: here-string with `-` last, pipe with `-` last, heredoc completion with `-` last, plus the existing mid-line controls.
- [ ] Existing REPL preprocessing tests still pass.

## Dedup / related

- #2274 covers the find/search/show/peek argument parsers swallowing unknown flags — different code path (argument parsing, not content-placeholder substitution).
- #1585 covers quote-blind heredoc/`$(...)` scans of the original line — different mechanism.
- Searched open + recently closed issues for `here-string`, `heredoc`, `STDIN_CONTENT`, `preprocess` before filing; no existing issue covers the trailing-placeholder substitution.

body:
# aggregator(snapshot-records): shape-only dates win freshestDate — a 2026-13-01 'Last checked' silently drops a pool's whole snapshot history, 2026-02-30 is stored as a phantom March date

## Summary

`pm-stack/aggregator/src/snapshot-records.ts` carries its own copy of the shape-only date logic already filed for saas-extract (#2206) — but this copy feeds the usage **snapshot store**, not the cards, and a fix to saas-extract will not touch it. `DATE_RE` (snapshot-records.ts:30, `/\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}/g`) has no calendar check; `freshestDate` (:42-45) string-sorts and takes the max; `lastCheckedDate` (:54-70) and `recordsFromPools` (:165, `lastCheckedDate(section) ?? freshestDate(section)`) stamp every snapshot record for a quota pool with that winner via `dayTs` (:35-37).

## Evidence (verified this run, main 5a34fa70)

Sandbox Bun probe driving the real `recordsFromPools` / `freshestDate` / `lastCheckedDate` plus the real `SnapshotStore` / `isSnapshotRecord` (probe: `/tmp/probe-laneA-snapdate/probe.ts`, `probe2.ts`):

- Control `**Last checked:** 2026-10-26` → record ts `2026-10-26T12:00:00Z`, valid, `SnapshotStore.append` returns 1.
- Same bullet plus a typo `2026-13-01` → `lastCheckedDate` returns `2026-13-01`; record ts `2026-13-01T12:00:00Z`; `isSnapshotRecord` is **false** (Date.parse is NaN) and `SnapshotStore.append` returns **0 of 1 with no error or log** — the pool's whole history point silently vanishes.
- `**Last checked:** 2026-01-15; typo 2026-02-30` → the impossible date wins string-max; record ts `2026-02-30T12:00:00Z` **passes** `isSnapshotRecord` because `Date.parse` rolls it over to 2026-03-02 — a phantom March observation is stored (in the `usage-2026-02.jsonl` file, since `snapshotFileFor` slices the string month), and pace/sort logic downstream ages it from a date that never existed. `2026-04-31` behaves the same (rolls to May 1).
- Leap control `2024-02-29` works correctly and must keep working.

File:line (main 5a34fa70):

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/snapshot-records.ts:30` — `DATE_RE` shape only.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/snapshot-records.ts:42-45` — `freshestDate` string-sort max.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/snapshot-records.ts:54-70` — `lastCheckedDate` built on `freshestDate`.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/snapshot-records.ts:159-165` — `recordsFromPools` stamps all pool records from that date.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/snapshots.ts:29,117` — store validation `Date.parse` NaN-rejects month-13 records (silent drop in `append`'s filter) but rollover-accepts Feb-30/Apr-31 records.

## Why it matters

Snapshot records are the hub's long-term usage history (§4 design): they feed pace projections and trend charts, and writers are explicitly safe-to-rerun because records keep their observation date. One typo'd date in the hand-edited quota-view section either (a) erases a pool's history point for that run with no signal anywhere — append just reports a smaller count — or (b) permanently writes a phantom-dated point into the append-only store, where dedupe keys on the phantom ts so a later corrected read appends a *second* point instead of replacing it. The store's own validation cannot catch case (b): the string is ISO-shaped and `Date.parse` rolls it over.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Triage pins the non-calendar-date rule for this module (expected: impossible dates are ignored by `freshestDate`/`lastCheckedDate` in snapshot-records.ts — a real date in the same text still wins — mirroring whatever rule #2206's triage pins for saas-extract, so the two copies cannot drift; sharing one implementation is also acceptable if triage prefers it).
- [ ] Regression tests in the aggregator test suite (snapshot-writers test home): a Last checked bullet with `2026-10-26` + `2026-13-01` yields records at `2026-10-26`; `2026-02-30` / `2026-04-31` never become a record ts; `2024-02-29` still counts.
- [ ] No behavior change for real dates: `recordsFromPools` output identical on the existing fixture (including the Last-checked-beats-2027-renewal case).

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-a (lane A), run 2026-10-29 06:05 CDT. Dedup: #2206 is the same shape-only pattern in saas-extract.ts (different file, different consumer — the cards vs the snapshot store; filed separately by the same convention as #2194/#2199); #1540 is SnapshotStore validation of non-finite pairs / non-ISO timestamps (store-side, distinct); #2253/#2242 are quota-current/health stamp paths, distinct.

body:
## Summary

In the aggregator's quota-current overlay, the stale-path "newest entry" pick is not
finite-gated, so a garbage or far-future `measuredAt` wins it — the pool's displayed
freshness (stamp + source) then comes from the bad write instead of the newest real read.

## Evidence (main 24901e7b, `pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-current.ts`)

- `parseQuotaCurrent` (:57) accepts any string `measuredAt` — no parseability check.
- `entryState` (:65-72) is correctly finite-gated (the #1541 fix): an unparseable or
  >60s-future stamp classifies `stale`, never `ok`.
- But when no fresh-ok entry exists, `overlayQuotaCurrent` picks the entry to represent
  the pool with a raw sort (:169):
  `[...entries].sort((a, b) => Date.parse(b.measuredAt) - Date.parse(a.measuredAt))[0]`
  and passes it to `applyEntry`, which stamps `pool.freshness = { measuredAt: entry.measuredAt, source: entry.source, state }` (:99-106).

Verified this run with a Bun probe calling the real `overlayQuotaCurrent` /
`parseQuotaCurrent` (fixtures mirrored from `test/quota-current.test.ts`), now =
2026-10-27T07:00:00Z, service `meta:high-usage`:

- `parseQuotaCurrent` ACCEPTS an entry with `measuredAt: "not-a-date"`.
- Garbage entry listed first + a real 2h-old read second → pool freshness =
  `{"measuredAt":"not-a-date","source":"garbage-src","state":"stale"}` — the NaN
  comparator (`Date.parse` diff) is treated as 0, so the winner is file-order dependent
  and the garbage stamp shadows the real read. Reversed order picks the real read.
- A +30d future entry vs a real 1h-old read → freshness =
  `{"measuredAt":"2026-11-26T07:00:00.000Z","source":"future-src","state":"stale"}` —
  the skewed write outranks the newest real stale read for as long as the skew lasts.
- Control (two real stale reads) correctly picks the newer one.

## Why it matters

The module's own stated intent (#1541, comment at :37-44) is that one skewed write
cannot pin a pool or outrank genuine reads. That holds for the fresh path, but the
stale path still lets a skewed/garbage write become the pool's displayed freshness:
the dashboard shows an unparseable or weeks-future stamp and the wrong source, and
 downstream age rendering (`Date.parse` on the stamp) produces NaN ages. The winner
also depends on provider order in the file when a stamp is unparseable.

## Acceptance criteria

- The stale-path newest pick ignores entries whose `measuredAt` does not parse to a
  finite time (or `parseQuotaCurrent` rejects them), so the newest *parseable* stale
  read represents the pool.
- A future-dated entry beyond `QUOTA_CURRENT_FUTURE_SKEW_MS` does not outrank a
  parseable past read in the stale-path pick.
- Regression tests in `test/quota-current.test.ts`: garbage-first vs garbage-second
  orderings give the same result; future-vs-stale picks the real stale read.
- Existing quota-current tests still pass.

Related: #1541 (closed — fresh-path skew gate; this is the stale-path residual),
#2242 (same stamp-validation pattern in health.ts, different module).

body:
# aggregator(health): dns/aa section stamps are never validated — garbage dns `generatedAt` renders ageMs NaN, future aa `generatedAt` renders age 0

## Evidence (verified this run, main `24901e7b`)

The `/health` view is the stack's honesty surface: `feedSections` in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/health.ts:184-207` reports each feed section's `generatedAt` and `ageMs`. Three sections carry their own stamps — `orchestration`, `dns`, `aa` (the rest inherit the feed's top-level stamp). Only the orchestration stamp is ever validated:

- Top-level feed stamp: `isFleetFeed` (`feed.ts:213-222`) requires `Number.isFinite(Date.parse(generatedAt))`, and `buildHealth` itself flags a top-level stamp >60s in the future as "never fresh" (`health.ts:234-235`, `:254-262`, `GENERATED_AT_FUTURE_SKEW_MS`).
- Orchestration stamp: `orchestrationSectionProblem` (`feed.ts:131`) requires a finite parse, and `diagnoseOrchestrationSection` (`feed.ts:180-186`) rejects >60s future stamps as invalid.
- dns stamp: `DnsSection.generatedAt` (`model.ts:644-646`) has **no validator on the read path** — `isFleetFeed` never inspects the dns section.
- aa stamp: `isAaSection` (`aa.ts:1070-1084`) checks only `typeof generatedAt === "string"` — no parse, no finiteness, no future bound. `isFleetFeed` doesn't inspect the aa section either.

`feedSections`' helper (`health.ts:186-189`) computes the age blindly:

```ts
const ts = generatedAt ?? feed.generatedAt;
return { present, generatedAt: ts, ageMs: Math.max(0, now - Date.parse(ts)), ... };
```

`Date.parse` of a garbage stamp is `NaN`, and `Math.max(0, NaN)` is `NaN`. A future stamp gives a negative age, clamped to `0` — maximally fresh — and stays `0` until the stamped date passes.

### Probe (Bun, real `buildHealth`, fixtures mode)

Feed with a valid top-level stamp, `dns.generatedAt = "not-a-date"`, `aa.generatedAt = now + 30 days`:

```
orchestration: present=false generatedAt="2026-10-29T10:47:56.678Z" ageMs=0 isNaN=false json=0   (control: absent → feed stamp)
dns: present=true generatedAt="not-a-date" ageMs=NaN isNaN=true json=null
aa:  present=true generatedAt="2026-11-28T10:47:56.678Z" ageMs=0 isNaN=false json=0
```

So the health JSON says the dns section is present with `ageMs: null` and no invalid/stale signal, and the aa section looks just-collected (`ageMs: 0`) for the next 30 days.

## Why it matters

The health page exists so a stale or broken section is *diagnosable* instead of silently "absent" or silently fresh (#1139/#1140, and #1564 established the finite + 60s-future-skew convention for the orchestration section and the top-level stamp). The dns and aa sections escaped that pass: a collector bug or clock skew that corrupts either stamp is invisible on the one surface meant to catch it — garbage reads as "present, age unknown", and a future stamp reads as "freshest possible" for as long as the skew lasts.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `feedSections` (or the section gates feeding it) applies the house convention to the dns and aa stamps: an unparseable stamp does not produce `ageMs: NaN` — the section is reported with a legible invalid/absent-style signal instead of `present` + `ageMs: null`.
- [ ] A section stamp more than `GENERATED_AT_FUTURE_SKEW_MS` (60s) in the future is not reported as `ageMs: 0` fresh; it gets the same treatment the top-level stamp gets ("never fresh" / invalid).
- [ ] Valid stamps render exactly as today; a regression test (health tests) covers garbage and future dns/aa stamps alongside the existing top-level/orchestration cases.

## Notes

- Dedup: searched open + closed for health/feedSections/section-stamp terms — no match. #1564 (closed) covered the orchestration diagnosis + top-level feed gate only; #2199/#2206 are the dns/saas *content* date parsers, not the health view's section stamps.
- Not self-solved by the filing lane: whether the fix lives in `feedSections`, in `isFleetFeed`/`isAaSection`, or in a dns section gate is triage's pin.

Filed by `new-issue-creator-code-a` (agent-note follows).

body:
# mcpx(daemon): long-poll `waitMs` is uncapped and overflows — a client can pin a handler past the operator's wait settings, and a ~317-year wait returns instantly

## Summary

Both mcpx daemon long-poll handlers take the client's `waitMs` query parameter verbatim, with no upper bound, and convert it with `time.Duration(ms) * time.Millisecond`, which overflows for large values:

- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/ops.go:476-480` — `handleTaskResult` (`GET /v1/tasks/{id}/result`): the operator's `tasks.resultWait` setting (default `2m`, `pkgs/mcpx/internal/defaults/defaults.json:83`; documented in `docs/configuration.md` as "how long collecting a task result blocks before giving up") is replaced by any positive `waitMs` the client sends.
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/routes_proto.go:514-518` — `handleAskPoll` (`GET /v1/ask/{id}`): the same pattern replaces the `proto.askPoll` default (500ms).

The daemon's HTTP server sets only `ReadHeaderTimeout` (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/server.go` `startHTTP`), so nothing else bounds how long these handlers hold a goroutine and a connection.

## Verified behavior (laptop probe, this run)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneA-waitms/` (laptop worktree at main `17819113`; both handler lines verified byte-identical at current main `24901e7b`). The probe drives the real `handleTaskResult` / `handleAskPoll` with a never-finishing task:

| Request | Result |
|---|---|
| task result `waitMs=300` | 408 after 300.2ms (control: small waits are honoured) |
| task result `waitMs=3600000` (1h = 30× the operator's 2m default) | still blocked after 2s; returned 200 only when the task was released — accepted, no cap |
| task result `waitMs=10000000000000` (1e13 ms ≈ 317 years) | 408 in **13µs** — `time.Duration(ms) * time.Millisecond` overflows int64 (threshold ≈ 9.22e12 ms) and wraps negative, so `context.WithTimeout` is already expired |
| ask poll `waitMs=300` | 200 after 300.6ms (control) |
| ask poll `waitMs=10000000000000` | 200 in **19.6µs** — same overflow, instant return, no error |

Legitimate in-tree clients only ever pass small waits (1ms polls in `internal/mcpserver/ask.go`, the 250ms `TaskEager` window, `daemonAsker.Poll` in `internal/cli/serve_ask.go:205`), so a cap at (or near) the configured defaults breaks nothing in-tree.

## Why it matters

- **Operator settings are silently overridden.** `tasks.resultWait` exists so the operator decides how long result collection may block; any local API client can currently multiply it without limit, pinning a handler goroutine + connection per request for hours.
- **The overflow is a silent wrong answer, not an error.** A wait past ~292 years (`ms > ~9.22e12`) wraps to a negative or arbitrary duration: the "wait" returns instantly (task result: a spurious 408 "has not finished yet"), indistinguishable from a genuine timeout. Nothing is logged and no 400 is returned.
- The same two-line pattern in both handlers means one ruling fixes both.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both handlers clamp or reject an out-of-range `waitMs` under one pinned rule (triage pins: clamp to the configured default/ceiling vs 400). The operator's `tasks.resultWait` / a named ask-poll ceiling is the maximum a client can obtain.
- [ ] No `waitMs` value can produce a negative or wrapped `time.Duration`: values above the overflow threshold (~9.22e12 ms) follow the same pinned rule as other out-of-range values, never an instant spurious timeout.
- [ ] Regression tests at the handler level: small `waitMs` honoured (as today); `waitMs` above the ceiling behaves per the pinned rule; `waitMs=10000000000000` does not return an instant 408/200.
- [ ] In-tree client behavior unchanged: 1ms–500ms polls and the `tasks.resultWait` default path work exactly as before.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `waitMs`, "task result wait", "long poll wait cap": no hit covers these handlers. Related but distinct: #1679 is the `/v1/events` `since` resume cursor (different endpoint, different parameter); #1864 covers call-scoped timeouts for MCP tool calls, not these HTTP long-polls.

body:
# mcpx(daemon): /v1/interactions score filters silently misbehave — a non-numeric minScore returns the unfiltered list, NaN/Inf return an empty one

## Evidence (verified this run, main `319e6c21`)

`pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/routes_feedback.go:95-115` (`handleInteractionsList`, GET /v1/interactions):

```go
if minStr := q.Get("minScore"); minStr != "" {
    if val, err := strconv.ParseFloat(minStr, 64); err == nil {
        filter.MinScore = &val
    }
}
if maxStr := q.Get("maxScore"); maxStr != "" {
    if val, err := strconv.ParseFloat(maxStr, 64); err == nil {
        filter.MaxScore = &val
    }
}
```

A parse failure leaves the filter unset and the handler returns 200 with the
**unfiltered** list — the caller asked for a score band and silently got
everything. A parse *success* is not safe either: Go's `ParseFloat` accepts
`NaN`, `Inf`, `+Inf`, `-Inf`, and the filter is passed straight into
`pkgs/mcpx/internal/logstore/feedback.go:303-310` (`score >= ?` / `score <= ?`
against SQLite, modernc driver). SQLite treats a NaN bound as NULL, so every
comparison is NULL and **no row matches**; `+Inf` as a minimum likewise
matches nothing.

Verified with a probe on the laptop (test file
`pkgs/mcpx/internal/logstore/probe_laneB_test.go` in worktree
`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneB-feedback-wt/`, whose feedback.go /
routes_feedback.go are md5-identical to this main; real
`logstore.FeedbackStore`, 3 seeded interactions scored 0.2 / 0.5 / 0.9,
handler parse block replicated verbatim; `go test` PASS):

- no filter → 3 rows; `minScore=0.4` (control) → 2 rows
- `minScore=abc` → filter never set → **3 rows (unfiltered)**
- `minScore=1e999` → ParseFloat range error → filter never set → **3 rows (unfiltered)**
- `minScore=NaN` → filter set to NaN → **0 rows**
- `minScore=Inf` → **0 rows**
- `maxScore=xyz` → filter never set → **3 rows (unfiltered)**
- `maxScore=NaN` → **0 rows**

`limit`/`offset` in the same handler (lines 107-115) have the same
silent-drop shape, but the store neutralizes them (`feedback.go` List:
`limit <= 0` falls back to the default page size, `offset` only applied when
`> 0`), so they are cosmetic; the score filters are the correctness bug
because both failure directions reach the caller as a plausible 200 result.

No test covers this: no test in `internal/logstore/feedback_test.go` or the
daemon tests references `MinScore`/`minScore`.

## Why it matters

/v1/interactions is the feedback-review surface: a reviewer (or a script)
asking "show me interactions scored below X" to find bad responses gets
either everything (typo'd / out-of-range bound) or nothing (NaN/Inf), with a
200 and no hint the band was not applied. Both directions look like real
answers — the unfiltered direction reads as "all interactions pass", the
empty direction as "no interactions in band".

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A non-numeric, NaN, or infinite `minScore`/`maxScore` on GET /v1/interactions is rejected with 400 naming the parameter (the handler already 400s on other bad input, e.g. `handleInteractionGet`'s missing id), OR is otherwise surfaced — never silently dropped.
- [ ] Valid finite bounds behave exactly as today (`minScore=0.4` over scores 0.2/0.5/0.9 returns the 0.5 and 0.9 rows).
- [ ] Handler/store tests cover: `abc`, `NaN`, `Inf`, `1e999` for both bounds, plus the finite control case.
- [ ] Triage pins whether the same 400 rule should extend to this handler's `limit`/`offset` (store-neutralized today) — recorded on the issue; not required for the score fix itself.

body:
## Problem

The peek printers exist twice in `pkgs/id`, and the two copies have drifted on the header's hash slice:

- `pkgs/id/src/commands/find.rs` — `print_peek_lines` (:719), `print_peek_chars` (:784) and `print_peek_words` (:845) each format the header with a bare `&hash[..12]`, with no length guard.
- `pkgs/id/src/repl/runner.rs` — the REPL copies of the same three printers (:1289, :1353, :1412) each compute `let hash_short = if hash.len() >= 12 { &hash[..12] } else { hash };` first.

So the `find.rs` helpers **panic on any hash string shorter than 12 bytes**, while the identical REPL helpers print it whole. The helpers are private and today the only production caller (`find.rs:647`) passes `m.hash.to_string()` — a full 64-char blob hash — so this is **not currently reachable from the CLI**. It is a latent panic sitting in a duplicated implementation that has already diverged once: the next caller that passes a short/abbreviated hash (the tests already pass hand-written hash strings, all exactly 12 chars, e.g. `find.rs:1307` `"abcdef123456"` — one character shorter would panic) hits it, and the drift guarantees future fixes keep landing in only one copy (cf. #1787, the `n * 2` overflow, which had to be filed against both copies).

## Verified this run (2026-10-29, main 319e6c21)

Probe compiled and run on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneA-find-peek/main.rs` there): the find-copy header expression vs the repl-copy guarded expression, same inputs —

- find copy, hash `"abcdef123456"` (12 chars): prints `hash: abcdef123456` ✓
- find copy, 64-char hash: prints first 12 chars ✓
- repl copy, hash `"abc123"` (6 chars): prints `hash: abc123` ✓
- find copy, hash `"abc123"` (6 chars): **panic — `end byte index 12 is out of bounds for string of length 6`, exit 101** ✗

Also verified by reading both files at 319e6c21: the three `&hash[..12]` sites in `find.rs` are the only unguarded ones; the three `runner.rs` sites all have the guard (diff of the two peek implementations shows the guard is the only functional divergence).

## Why it matters

A private display helper that panics on a plausible input is a landmine for the next caller, and the root cause — two hand-maintained copies of the same three printers — has already produced one cross-copy bug (#1787). Fixing the guard removes the panic; deduplicating the printers (or explicitly deciding not to) removes the class.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] No bare `&hash[..12]` remains in `pkgs/id/src/commands/find.rs`: all three peek printers handle a hash shorter than 12 chars the way the `repl/runner.rs` copies do (print it whole), OR the duplicated printers are deduplicated into one shared implementation used by both call sites.
- [ ] A regression test drives each of the three `find.rs` peek printers (lines/chars/words, non-quiet header) with a hash shorter than 12 chars (e.g. `"abc123"`): it prints the whole hash and does not panic.
- [ ] Existing peek tests in both `find.rs` and `repl/runner.rs` still pass, and the 12-char and 64-char header output is unchanged.

Related: #1787 (the `n * 2` overflow in the same duplicated printers — different defect, same drift).

body:
# aggregator(saas-extract): shape-only dates win freshestDate — a 2026-13-01 'Last checked' masks a real read (measuredAt goes stale/null), 2026-02-30 becomes a renewal date

## Summary

`pm-stack/aggregator/src/saas-extract.ts` accepts any `\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}` string as a date, with no calendar check. `datesIn` (saas-extract.ts:19-20, `DATE_RE` at :16) collects matches and string-sorts them, and `freshestDate` (:24) takes the string-max — so an impossible date always beats every real date in its text. That value becomes a service's `measuredAt` (saas-extract.ts:628, and the Cloudflare zone merge at :651-652), is shown as the freshest entry in `readsOf` (:63), and `extractSubscriptions` passes a shape-matched `renews 2026-02-30` through verbatim as `renewsAt` (:821-825). quota-view.md is a hand-edited local-record snapshot, so a single typo'd date in a "Last checked" bullet silently corrupts the card's freshness state.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 319e6c21)

Probe: real `extractSaasServices` / `extractSubscriptions` (Bun, sandbox) on a Turso section whose Last checked bullet carries a real read plus a typo, plus a Wispr section:

- Input Last checked: `2026-10-28 real read; typo line 2026-13-01`
- `turso.measuredAt` = `"2026-13-01"` — the impossible date wins string-max over the real 2026-10-28.
- `freshness("2026-13-01", 30, 2026-10-29)` (derive.ts:876-895) = `{ stale: true, ageDays: null }` (Date.parse is NaN), while the real read gives `{ stale: false, ageDays: 1 }` — the card renders stale/never-measured despite a read yesterday.
- `turso.reads` order: `["2026-13-01", "2026-10-27", "2026-02-30"]` — impossible dates are presented as the freshest reads.
- `freshness("2026-02-30", …)` ages from a phantom date instead: `Date.parse("2026-02-30T00:00:00Z")` rolls over to 2026-03-02 in Bun/V8, giving `ageDays: 241` at 2026-10-29 — the two impossible shapes take two different wrong paths (NaN vs rollover).
- `extractSubscriptions` returns Wispr Flow `renewsAt: "2026-02-30"` — a renewal date that does not exist, shown in the subscriptions strip.

File:line (main 319e6c21):

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/saas-extract.ts:16` — `DATE_RE = /\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}/g`, shape only.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/saas-extract.ts:19-27` — `datesIn` string-sort; `freshestDate` takes the last.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/saas-extract.ts:63-72` — `readsOf` sorts dated reads by the same strings.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/saas-extract.ts:628` — `measuredAt = freshestDate(Last checked bullet) ?? freshestDate(section)`.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/saas-extract.ts:651-652` — Cloudflare zone date replaces `measuredAt` on string `>`.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/saas-extract.ts:821-825` — Wispr `renews (\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2})` captured verbatim into `renewsAt`.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/derive.ts:880-887` — `freshness()` Date.parse: NaN → stale/null; Feb-30 → rolled-over phantom date.

## Why it matters

The SaaS cards' one trust signal is "when was this last actually read". An impossible date in a hand-edited snapshot currently either (a) masks a fresh real read and pins the card stale with no age, or (b) ages the card from a date that never existed — and a non-existent renewal date is displayed as fact in the subscriptions strip. There is no log line in any of these paths; the fail-soft shell discipline elsewhere in this file (a service whose patterns stop matching renders as a shell) has no equivalent guard for dates that match the shape but not the calendar.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Triage pins the non-calendar-date rule for this extractor (expected: impossible dates are ignored by `datesIn`/`freshestDate` — a real date in the same text still wins — and a non-calendar `renews` date yields `renewsAt: null`; or they are surfaced as a conflict line — triage decides, silence is the one ruled-out option).
- [ ] Regression tests in the aggregator test suite (saas-extract's test home): a Last checked bullet with `2026-10-28` + `2026-13-01` yields `measuredAt "2026-10-28"`; `2026-02-30` / `2026-04-31` never appear as a read's `at` or a `renewsAt`; `2024-02-29` (leap year) still counts.
- [ ] No behavior change for real dates: `measuredAt`, reads order, zone merge, and subscriptions output identical on existing fixtures.

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-b (lane B), run 2026-10-29 04:20 CDT. Dedup: #2194 is the same shape-only pattern in charges-collect and #2199 in dns.ts (different parsers, inputs, and consumers — filed separately by the same convention); #1568 is future-dated *valid* dates in derive.freshness (an upper-bound question, not calendar validity); #1684 is summarizeDns UTC-day aging.

body: # id(web/markdown): HTML `` width/height that aren't bare integers are silently dropped on markdown import — `200px`, `50%`, `200.0` sizing vanishes with no trace ## Evidence (verified this run, main `c58507a3`) `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs:1208-1217` (`parse_img_tag`, the #893 HTML-image import path): ```rust if let Some(w) = attr("width") && let Ok(n) = w.parse::() { attrs["width"] = json!(n); } if let Some(h) = attr("height") && let Ok(n) = h.parse::() { attrs["height"] = json!(n); } ``` A dimension that fails the bare-`u64` parse is not rejected, not preserved, and not reported — the attribute simply never enters the ProseMirror node. On the next save, `prosemirror_to_markdown` (markdown.rs:1953-1968) emits dimensions only from `attrs.width`/`attrs.height`, so the sizing is gone from the document permanently. Verbatim-probe (laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneA-imgwidth/`, `parse_tag_attrs` + `parse_img_tag` copied from main `c58507a3`): | input | resulting attrs | |---|---| | `width="200" height="100"` (control) | `width:200, height:100` — kept | | `width="200px" height="100px"` | both **dropped** | | `width="50%"` | **dropped** | | `width="200.0"` | **dropped** | | `width=" 200"` (leading space) | **dropped** | | `width="0"` | kept as `0` | | `width="+200"` | kept as `200` (Rust `u64` parse accepts a leading `+`) | `200px` is the form most of the world's HTML and Markdown-with-inline-HTML actually uses (CSS-style dimensions in exported notes, README badges, pasted web content); percentages are the standard responsive form. Both reach this parser through the raw-HTML image path (#893) and lose their sizing silently on the first load/save round-trip. ## Why it matters - Silent data loss on import: the document the user saved is not the document they wrote, and nothing anywhere says a dimension was discarded. - The accept set is accidental, not designed: `+200` and `0` pass while `200px`, `200.0` and `" 200"` fail — that is `u64::from_str`'s grammar, not an image-sizing policy. - Sibling asymmetry: the editor's own parseDOM side of this same problem is #2010 (TypeScript, bare `Number()`); this is the Rust markdown-import side, a separate code path with the opposite failure shape (drop instead of reinterpret). ## Acceptance criteria - [ ] Triage pins the dimension grammar for the markdown import path: which of `200px` (strip a `px` suffix), `50%` (percent — represent or refuse), `200.0`, and whitespace-padded values are accepted, and what happens to the rest. - [ ] A dimension the pinned grammar refuses is not silently dropped: it is either preserved in the node or the import surfaces it (the pinned behavior is recorded on this issue). - [ ] Regression tests in `web/markdown.rs` cover the pinned grammar end-to-end (import → node attrs → markdown emission) for at least: bare integer (control), `px`-suffixed, fractional, and padded values. - [ ] No behavior change for images whose dimensions already parse as bare integers. Dedup: #2010 is the TypeScript editor `parseDOM` path (bare `Number()` — NaN/fraction/hex pass through); #872 (closed) was substring attribute shadowing in this same function; #893 (closed) added the sized-image import form itself. None covers the Rust import-side dimension grammar.

body:
## Summary

`pkgs/id` world manifest: the only documented format for `module_hash` is rejected by the manifest's own validation. The field's rustdoc says the hash is written `blake3:<hex>`, but `WorldManifest::validate` accepts only 1–64 hex digits — a `blake3:`-prefixed value is 71 characters for a real 32-byte hash and contains non-hex characters (`:`, and the letters in `blake3` beyond `a`–`f`), so any `world.toml` written by following the documentation fails to parse, and `id world diff` / `id world apply` refuse it.

## Evidence (main `c58507a3`, verified this run)

- `pkgs/id/src/world_manifest.rs:29` — field doc: "A content hash of an already-installed module (`blake3:<hex>`)."
- `pkgs/id/src/world_manifest.rs:182-189` — validation: `!hash.is_empty() && hash.len() <= MAX_NAME_BYTES && hash.bytes().all(|b| b.is_ascii_hexdigit())`, with the error "module hash must be 1 to 64 hex digits". `MAX_NAME_BYTES = 64` (`pkgs/id/src/world_caps.rs:60`).
- The live producer is plain hex with no prefix: `pkgs/id/src/world_session/mod.rs:657-659` `module_hash()` is `iroh_blobs::Hash::new(wasm).to_string()` (64 hex chars), and the world-fixture doc also describes `module_hash` as `"<hex>"` (`pkgs/id/docs/2026-10-17T09-00-00Z_feature_world_fixtures/…md:20`). The `blake3:` form appears nowhere else in `src/` or the docs.
- Verbatim-predicate probe (the exact `valid` expression from `validate`, compiled and run on the laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-manifesthash/`):
  - plain 64-hex (the live form): `valid=true`
  - documented `blake3:<64 hex>` (71 chars): `valid=false`
  - `blake3:abc123` (short): `valid=false`

So the documented form fails on both independent grounds: length (71 > 64) and charset.

## Why it matters

`world.toml` is the declarative interface for reconciling a live world (`id world apply` / `id world diff`, `pkgs/id/src/cli.rs:1730-1759`). An operator who copies the documented hash form into a manifest gets a parse failure before any step is planned, with an error that contradicts the documentation they followed. One of the two sides is wrong, and until they agree, the documented interface is unusable as written.

## Acceptance criteria

- Triage pins the canonical form (the evidence points to plain hex: the live producer, the fixture doc, and the existing tests in `world_manifest.rs` all use bare hex; accepting/stripping a `blake3:` prefix is the alternative).
- The rustdoc on `WorldManifest::module_hash` and `validate`'s rule/error message agree on exactly one accepted form.
- A test in `world_manifest.rs` covers the pinned form: the documented example parses (or, if the doc is corrected, a regression test shows the previously documented `blake3:` form's behaviour is the intended one and the doc no longer names it).
- No change to plan/apply semantics for manifests that already parse.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed for `world_manifest`, `manifest module_hash`, `world.toml`, `blake3 prefix`: #1517 (closed) was the empty-string case of the same validator and is fixed on main; #817/#1519 are plan/diff semantics. None covers the documented-prefix mismatch.

The Make / Do / Tend role map is decided and recorded on #2131. This issue implements it in the fleet's working surfaces:

title: id(outbox): a blank line in outbox.jsonl bricks the world open — Outbox::open calls it corrupt while every sibling journal loader in the same open path skips blank lines

body:
## Problem

`Outbox::open` (`pkgs/id/src/envelope_outbox.rs:141-156`) treats a blank line in `outbox.jsonl` as fatal corruption, while every sibling journal loader in the same world-open path skips blank lines. One stray blank line — from a hand edit, a partial copy, or a tool that appends an extra newline — bricks the whole world open, because the failure is propagated, not degraded.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `8124cc0b`)

- `envelope_outbox.rs:141-156`: the replay loop iterates `text.split_inclusive('\n')`; any line that fails `serde_json::from_str::<Record>(line.trim_end())` and ends with `'\n'` returns `Err("envelope outbox line {} is corrupt")`. A blank line (`"\n"`) or whitespace-only line trims to `""`, which never parses, and it *is* newline-terminated — so it always takes the fatal branch. There is no empty-line skip.
- `world_store.rs:393-397`: world open does `Outbox::open(&outbox_path).await.context("outbox open task")??` — the error aborts opening the world entirely.
- Siblings in the *same* open sequence skip blank lines: `petname.rs:64-66` (`if line.trim().is_empty() { continue; }`), `directory_log.rs:202-209` (blank lines filtered/skipped in `load`), and the world journal restore (see `world_doctor.rs:549` — "world_store skips blank lines").
- Laptop probe (verbatim replay loop with a representative `Record` enum, `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-outboxblank/`, main `8124cc0b`):
  - clean two records: `OK applied=2`
  - blank line between records: `ERR envelope outbox line 2 is corrupt: EOF while parsing a value at line 1 column 0`
  - extra blank line at end: `ERR … line 3 is corrupt …`
  - whitespace-only line: `ERR … line 2 is corrupt …`
  - blank first line: `ERR … line 1 is corrupt …`
  - torn last line (unparseable, no newline): `OK applied=1` — the case the loader was designed to tolerate works; blank lines are the gap.

## Why it matters

The outbox holds undelivered envelopes; refusing to open the world over a blank line turns a cosmetic journal defect into total unavailability of that world, inconsistent with the petname/directory/journal loaders opened in the same function. #2128 fixed this exact class for the artifact journal; the envelope outbox is the remaining loader in the open path with the fatal-blank-line behaviour. (Not #1620: that is the parseable torn tail in this same file.)

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Outbox::open` skips blank and whitespace-only lines anywhere in `outbox.jsonl` (start, middle, end), matching `petname.rs` / `directory_log.rs`.
- [ ] A genuinely corrupt complete (non-blank) line still fails the open with the line number named.
- [ ] The torn-tail behaviour is unchanged: an unparseable unterminated final line is dropped and the file truncated as today.
- [ ] Regression tests in `envelope_outbox.rs`: blank line between records, trailing blank line, whitespace-only line — all open with every record applied.
- [ ] The `kept`/truncation accounting still excludes any dropped torn tail correctly when blank lines precede it.

body:
# id(artifact): a blank line in artifacts.jsonl bricks Directory::open — and its torn-tail truncation is silent

## Summary

`ArtifactLog::open` (`pkgs/id/src/artifact.rs:573-593`, main `0f5b4cbb`) parses
every line of the artifact journal strictly. A single blank line — in the
middle, as a trailing extra newline (`...\n\n`), or as the file's only
content — fails the whole open with `artifact line N is corrupt`, even though
every artifact in the file is intact. `ArtifactLog` is loaded by
`Directory::open` (`pkgs/id/src/directory.rs:473`), so the failure takes the
whole directory down with it.

The sibling journal loaded in the very same `Directory::open` treats blank
lines differently: `Directory::replay` explicitly skips them
(`directory.rs:535-537`: `if line.trim().is_empty() { continue; }`).

Second divergence in the same function: when `open` drops a crash-torn final
line it truncates the file with no log line at all (`artifact.rs:578-584`).
Both sibling loaders warn with the byte offset when they do exactly this —
`Directory::replay` at `directory.rs:525-528` ("dropping torn final entry at
byte {kept_len}") and `FileJournal::open` at `world_store.rs:116-119`. A torn
artifact tail therefore loses a signed artifact (e.g. a friend-removal record
replayed at `directory.rs:475-490`) with no trace anywhere.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-artifactlog/` — the `open` loop
copied verbatim from `artifact.rs` (main `0f5b4cbb`), artifacts as minimal
JSON objects, run 2026-10-29:

| case | `ArtifactLog::open` | directory-style parse |
|---|---|---|
| two valid lines (control) | Ok, 2 stored | Ok, 2 |
| valid, blank, valid | **Err "artifact line 2 is corrupt: EOF while parsing a value"** | Ok, 2 |
| valid, valid, blank (`\n\n` ending) | **Err "artifact line 3 is corrupt"** | Ok, 2 |
| file is only `"\n"` | **Err "artifact line 1 is corrupt"** | Ok, 0 |
| valid + torn tail (no trailing `\n`) | Ok, 1 — file truncated, **no warning emitted by the code path** | — |

Blank lines reach this file in ordinary ways: a hand edit, an editor that
adds a final newline, a restore/sync that appends one. Nothing in the append
path (`artifact.rs:601-608`, one line + `\n` per write) ever *needs* a blank
line to be fatal.

## Why it matters

- Availability: one stray newline makes `Directory::open` fail, which is on
  the world-open path (`world_store.rs` `open_world` loads the directory) —
  the directory is down until someone hand-repairs the file, despite zero
  corrupt artifacts.
- Observability: the silent truncation is the only one of the three JSONL
  loaders in this crate that drops data without a warning, so a lost
  artifact leaves nothing to investigate.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ArtifactLog::open` skips blank/whitespace-only lines the way
      `Directory::replay` does; a file with blank lines in any position
      (including a `\n\n` ending and a blank-only file) opens with all its
      artifacts intact.
- [ ] The torn-tail truncation in `ArtifactLog::open` emits a warning naming
      the file and the byte offset, matching the `Directory::replay` /
      `FileJournal::open` wording.
- [ ] A genuinely corrupt non-blank line still fails the open with the
      existing `artifact line N is corrupt` context.
- [ ] Regression tests cover: blank middle, blank final, blank-only, torn
      tail (opens, truncates, warns), and corrupt-line refusal.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for "ArtifactLog", "artifact blank line" and
"torn": #1521 (closed) fixed the same class for `Directory::replay` and notes
ArtifactLog is "loaded in the same open", but covered only the torn tail of
the directory journal, not the artifact log's blank-line refusal or its
silent truncation. #1499/#1522/#1523/#1544/#1620 are the petname, group,
world-fork, records and outbox loaders respectively — none touches
`artifact.rs`.

body:
## Summary

`check_imports` in `pkgs/id/src/world_compile.rs` — the only gate that keeps a compile request from importing platform modules the world was not granted — matches imports with the literal prefix `"import "` (exactly one ASCII space). Roc's parser accepts other whitespace between `import` and the module path, so an ungranted import written with two spaces or a tab passes the gate and compiles.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `bd880194`; `world_compile.rs` sha256 `11b5c8afaecdb8ddcd23e796cc588908b9cc39506485c87d8961617cecc0d583`)

The gate, `world_compile.rs:118-144`:

- `:121` — `line.trim_start().strip_prefix("import ")`: a tab after `import` makes the prefix miss, so the line is skipped entirely.
- `:124-127` — with two spaces, `rest` starts with a space and `split(whitespace | '[' | '{' | '(').next()` yields the empty string, so the path examined is `""` and no segment is ever checked.

`compile()` stages the **whole** platform (`copy_platform`, `world_compile.rs:~227`), so every platform module is resolvable by the compiler; this line scan is the sole grant enforcement before the compiler runs.

Verbatim-logic probe (laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-importws/probe_import.rs`, modules `[Key, Screen]`, granted `[]`):

- `import pf.Screen` → refused: "main.roc imports Screen, which this world does not allow" (control)
- `import  pf.Screen` (two spaces) → **Ok**
- `import<TAB>pf.Screen` → **Ok**
- leading-tab + single space, and `import pf.Screen exposing [x]` → refused (those paths work)
- sibling file `Helper.roc` with `import  pf.Key` → **Ok** (the sibling-smuggle test at `world_compile.rs:1281` only covers the single-space form)

Roc acceptance probe (laptop `roc fmt`, same probe dir): both the double-space and tab forms parse and are **normalized by the formatter to `import pf.Screen`** (exit 0). Checked and NOT a bypass: `import pf . Screen` passes the gate but Roc rejects it (`incomplete_import` parse error), so spaced dots are out of scope.

## Why it matters

Platform modules are the world's capabilities (Screen, Key, …). The grant list is the effective intersection of world grants with server/world ceilings (see `compile()` docs, `world_compile.rs:188-204`). A world author who was granted nothing — or whose ceiling excludes a module — can use it anyway by changing one space to two, silently defeating the ceiling the operator configured. The existing tests (`an_ungranted_platform_import_is_refused_by_name`, `a_sibling_file_cannot_smuggle_an_ungranted_import`) pin only the canonical single-space spelling.

## Acceptance criteria

- `check_imports` recognizes an import regardless of the whitespace Roc accepts between `import` and the path (at minimum: multiple spaces, a tab), in `main.roc` and in sibling files.
- Regression tests: the double-space and tab spellings of an ungranted platform import are refused by name, mirroring the existing single-space tests; the granted and `*` cases still pass for those spellings.
- No false refusals: comment lines (`# import pf.Screen`), non-platform imports, and `exposing [...]` forms keep their current behavior.
- Token-based parsing (first token `import`, second token the path) or an equivalent whitespace-flexible scan is fine; matching Roc's exact grammar is not required beyond the whitespace class.

title: id(artifact): ArtifactPullProtocol waits forever — no deadline on the request frame and an unbounded conn.closed() wait after answering

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

`ArtifactPullProtocol::accept` — the `/id-artifact-pull/1` handler (`PULL_ALPN`) served by `id serve` — waits forever at two points, with no deadline at either:

- `pkgs/id/src/artifact.rs:746-758` — after `conn.accept_bi().await?`, it awaits `read_frame(&mut recv)` (line 748) with no timeout: a peer that connects and sends nothing (or a partial frame) holds the handler indefinitely before any work happens. `crate::frames::read_frame` caps frame *size* (1 MiB) but waits indefinitely for the bytes to arrive.
- Line 757 — after answering, it awaits `conn.closed()` with no timeout: a peer that reads its page and simply never closes the connection holds the handler task indefinitely.

## Why this is the outlier

The sibling protocol that does the exact same post-session close wait bounds it, and says why in a comment:

- `pkgs/id/src/event_sync.rs:136` — `let _ = tokio::time::timeout(CLOSE_WAIT, conn.closed()).await;` with `CLOSE_WAIT` = 5 s (event_sync.rs:48) and the comment at lines 130-135: "The wait is bounded: … a dialer that never closes must not hold it (or this handler) forever."
- `event_sync.rs:40` also bounds the session itself (`SESSION_DEADLINE` = 60 s), and `log_sync.rs:59` does the same for sync sessions.

ArtifactPull is, after #2084 (envelope/artifact-push) and the meta protocol, one of the last `id serve` acceptors with unbounded peer-controlled waits. Its shape is distinct from both: it serves exactly one stream per connection, so the stall is per-connection (a leaked handler task per stalled peer) rather than head-of-line blocking of later streams — which is why this is filed separately and at lower priority.

## Why it matters

Every stalled pull connection leaks its handler task for as long as the peer cares to hold it — unbounded, peer-controlled, and free to repeat. On a long-running `id serve` this is a slow resource leak rather than a hard outage, but it is exactly the failure mode the event-sync close wait was explicitly bounded against, and the fix pattern (reuse `CLOSE_WAIT`-style bounding) already exists in the crate.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 39e8410b)

- Read `artifact.rs:746-758` directly: unbounded `read_frame` await and unbounded `conn.closed().await`; no `tokio::time::timeout` in the function.
- Contrast read at event_sync.rs:40,48,130-136 (bounded session + bounded close wait, with the rationale comment).
- Grepped all `conn.closed().await` sites in pkgs/id/src: artifact.rs:757 is the only production one without a timeout wrapper (event_sync.rs:136 is wrapped; the others are tests).
- Dedup: `gh issue list --state all` searches for "ArtifactPull closed", "conn.closed", "artifact pull deadline" returned no existing issue. Related distinct: #2084 (envelope + artifact-push `answer_frames`).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The pre-frame wait in `ArtifactPullProtocol::accept` is bounded by a deadline (triage pins the value — event_sync's 60 s session deadline is the in-repo precedent); a peer that sends no complete frame by then is dropped.
- [ ] The post-answer `conn.closed()` wait is bounded (event_sync's `CLOSE_WAIT` = 5 s precedent, or a shared constant), after which the handler returns and lets the router close the connection.
- [ ] Regression test: a peer that connects and sends nothing (or reads its page and never closes) does not hold the handler past the bound; normal pull clients (which close after reading) are unaffected.
- [ ] Existing artifact protocol tests still pass.

title: mcpx(daemon): a second set of routes reads request bodies with no size ceiling — chat completions, exec, intent, upgrade and five more bypass the configured http.*BodyLimit caps

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The mcpx daemon enforces its configured HTTP request-body ceilings (`http.bodyLimit` / `http.callBodyLimit` / `http.controlBodyLimit`, defaults in `pkgs/mcpx/internal/defaults/defaults.go:162,186-195`) on only some routes. A second set of handlers decodes or reads `r.Body` with no ceiling at all, and there is no global cap: the two `http.Server`s (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/server.go:307,360`) set only `ReadHeaderTimeout`, with no `MaxBytesHandler`. The defaults module's own comment states the intent — the ceiling was unified precisely because it used to differ per route — but the unification never reached these handlers.

Verified on main `264ba11549ddff607a38c72ff043e0cd0e7ef247`:

**Unbounded body reads (no `MaxBytesReader`, no limit):**
- `routes_proxy.go:44` — `handleChatCompletions`: `io.ReadAll(r.Body)` buffers the whole chat-completions request in memory
- `upgrade.go:106` — `handleUpgrade`: `io.ReadAll(r.Body)`
- `routes_consumer.go:45` — `handleDiagnose`: `json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode`
- `routes_consumer.go:203` — `handleRecipeSave`: same
- `routes_consumer.go:278` — `handleRecipeRun`: same
- `routes_consumer.go:369` — `handleIntent`: same
- `routes_embeddings.go:40` — `handleEmbeddings`: same
- `routes_exec.go:218` — `handleExec`: same
- `routes_feedback.go:32` — `handleFeedbackSubmit`: same
- `server.go:616` — `POST /v1/prompt` handler: same

**Bounded siblings (the house pattern these miss):**
- `server.go:870` (`http.callBodyLimit`), `server.go:963`, `server.go:1083` (`http.bodyLimit`), `server.go:1100` (`http.controlBodyLimit`)
- `routes_secrets.go:49,114` (`http.bodyLimit`), `routes_settings.go:200` (`http.controlBodyLimit`), `routes_settings.go:588`, `ops.go:336`
- `routes_proto.go:400` (`defaults.HTTPCallBodyLimit`), `routes_proto.go:627`, `routes_proto.go:879`

## Why it matters

The daemon listens on loopback TCP + a unix socket. Any local process — or any local client with a bug, e.g. a runaway script POSTing an ever-growing prompt/exec/chat body — can make the daemon buffer an unbounded request body and OOM the process that every other tool call depends on. `handleChatCompletions` is the worst case: it `io.ReadAll`s the entire body before parsing. The configured ceilings exist and are already honoured on the call/proto/secrets routes; the gap is pure inconsistency, and it is exactly the class #1893 asks to be guarded (a declared surface — "every body is capped" — with no guard walking it). Related but distinct: #1697 (settings byte-size values themselves accept negatives/overflow).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every daemon HTTP handler that reads a request body enforces a configured ceiling (`http.MaxBytesReader` or equivalent) with the limit for its route class (call / control / body), closing the enumerated list above; triage pins which class each route takes where ambiguous (chat completions and exec are call-shaped; upgrade/diagnose/recipes/intent/embeddings/feedback/prompt need an explicit ruling).
- [ ] An over-limit body gets a clean client error (400/413) and the daemon's memory stays bounded — no partial decode, no panic.
- [ ] Tests: an over-limit request to representative previously-unbounded routes (at least chat completions, exec, intent, upgrade) is refused; under-limit requests to those routes behave exactly as before.
- [ ] A guard (test or lint-style check, in the spirit of #1893 / #1971) fails when a daemon handler reads `r.Body` without a ceiling, so the next route cannot reintroduce the gap.
- [ ] Existing daemon test suites pass unchanged.

body:
Phase 3 of design #2077 (origin umbrella #1935, register rows ELI-12 server half + ELI-04/ELI-09 truth-up). Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-elicitation-era-edges.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Decision is recorded on #2077 — this phase implements it as scoped; do not re-file under #1935, this phase is what closes it.

**Gated on Phases 1–2 of #2077** (the truth-up needs their as-built state; the production trigger is settled against Phase 2's as-built flow).

## Scope

Server-side `-32042` (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/mcpserver`, the `viaAsk` path in `ask.go`): today a url question for a client that cannot take it stays with the broker and `-32042` is never returned — conformance gap `elicitation-server-must-return-32042` (`internal/conformance/coverage_clientfeatures.go`), against the 2025-11-25 error-handling MUST.

- Produce `-32042` for a host's call only when ALL hold: host negotiated 2025-11-25; host declared `elicitation.url`; a URL question raised by that call is pending; the question cannot be delivered to the host inline (no live channel for `elicitation/create` — the stateless/no-session case the error exists for). Triage settles the precise undeliverable trigger against Phase 2's as-built flow; the gating rules here are the design's and are not triage's to relax.
- The error's `data.elicitations` lists exactly the pending URL questions blocking the call, each url-mode with an `elicitationId` (the `paramsFor` `mcpx-<id>` synthesis where the upstream sent none).
- Never for form questions, never when inline delivery is possible, never at 2026 (MUST NOT emit). An upstream `-32042` that reaches the server side unhandled by Phase 2 is relayed only to a host that declared `elicitation.url`; otherwise it surfaces as a generic call error.
- Truth-up: compare-register rows ELI-04, ELI-09, ELI-12 in `pkgs/mcpx/docs/compare/register/elicitation.md` updated to as-built — ELI-09 recorded **landed** with its evidence (`Client.capabilities` declares `elicitation.url` when a handler is installed, `internal/mcpclient/modern.go` ~L71-84; pool installs it, `internal/pool/pool.go:508`) — plus gap `elicitation-server-must-return-32042` retired or explicitly recorded partial.
- Completion evidence comment on #1935 against each of its acceptance bullets, closing #1935 iff all are met; the ELI-21 bullet is answered by the design doc's documented-question record (the acceptance's own "or the broker-only path is documented as the deliberate design" ending), not by silence.

## Acceptance

- A 2025-11-25, url-declared host whose call is blocked by an undeliverable URL question receives `-32042` listing exactly those elicitations with ids; in every other configuration (form question, inline-deliverable, 2026 host, undeclared host) no `-32042` is emitted, proven by tests per configuration.
- Register rows ELI-04/ELI-09/ELI-12 match the as-built code; the conformance gap is retired or recorded partial with the reason.
- #1935 carries completion evidence per acceptance bullet and is closed iff all are met.

- -32042 is produced for a host's call only when all gating conditions hold: host negotiated 2025-11-25, host declared elicitation.url, a URL question from that call is pending, and the question cannot be delivered inline.

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/mcpx/internal/wasmtools` (the #1970 WASM tool-source spike, merged today in #2002) caps guest **output** at 1 MiB (`maxMsg = 1 << 20`, `wasmtools.go:58`, enforced in `readOutput`, `wasmtools.go:126-129`) but places **no bound at all on the granted `log` capability**:

- The host `log` handler appends every call to `s.logs` unconditionally — no per-line length limit, no line-count limit, no total-bytes limit (`wasmtools.go:105-112`).
- `Logs()` returns a copy of the full history and never drains it (`wasmtools.go:121-123`). There is no other accessor, so retention grows monotonically for the whole lifetime of a `Source`.
- A guest can invoke the `log` import any number of times *inside a single* `ListTools`/`CallTool` invocation, and each line's length is bounded only by the guest's own memory. The guest is exactly the untrusted party this package's capability model exists to contain (deny-by-default imports, no WASI — see the package doc, `wasmtools.go:1-13`).

So the one channel the host forgot to cap is the one a hostile or buggy guest can use to grow host memory without limit, while the result channel right next to it is carefully capped.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `26221fcc`)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-wasmlogs/`, verbatim copy of `pkgs/mcpx/internal/wasmtools` + `internal/mcpclient` from main `26221fcc`, Go test using the shipped `testdata/echo.wasm` — the well-behaved guest, which logs exactly one line per call):

```
=== RUN   TestProbeLogsUnbounded
    probe_wasmlogs_test.go:29: after 20000 CallTool calls: len(Logs())=20000
    probe_wasmlogs_test.go:32: second Logs() call: len=%d (drain? false)  // len=20000
--- PASS: TestProbeLogsUnbounded (1.09s)
```

20,000 ordinary calls → 20,000 retained lines, and a second `Logs()` call proves nothing is ever drained or trimmed. A looping guest reaches arbitrary retention within one call; the probe only needed the polite guest to prove no bound exists.

## Why it matters

The spike's stated purpose is hosting untrusted tool sources behind a capability boundary. An unbounded host-side accumulator reachable through a granted capability is a memory-DoS hole in that boundary, and it will be inherited by whatever production registration path (#1885) adopts this package if it is not fixed while the API is still cheap to change. It is also asymmetric with the package's own `maxMsg` discipline, so the fix is in keeping with the author's intent.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Log retention is bounded: a documented cap on line count and/or total bytes (and a sane per-line truncation or rejection), in the same spirit as `maxMsg` for output.
- [ ] The behavior when the cap is hit is explicit and observable (e.g. further lines dropped with a marker/counter, or an error) — not silent truncation that loses the fact logging overflowed.
- [ ] A test with a guest that logs excessively (looping guest or repeated calls past the cap) asserts retention stays at/below the cap; existing tests (`TestListAndCallWithGrantedLog`, grant-denial tests) still pass.
- [ ] The package doc / `Logs()` doc states the retention contract (bounded, and whether `Logs()` drains or is a snapshot).

Found by new-issue-creator-code-b (Lane B) this run; not self-solved — the cap value and drop-vs-error contract are triage's pin.

body:
# id(petname): skeleton look-alike map misses capital `I` (vs `l`) and `8` (vs `B`) — "PayPaI" and "8ob" pass the anti-spoof guard that refuses "PayPa1" and "B0b"

## Summary

`Petnames::set` refuses a petname that is confusable with another contact's
petname or alleged name, comparing `skeleton()` forms (`pkgs/id/src/petname.rs:120`
and `:128`). The skeleton's look-alike table (`petname.rs:240-256`) maps
`0→o`, `1→l`, `|→l`, `3→e`, `5→s`, `$→s`, `@→a`, plus `rn→m` and `vv→w` — but
two classic look-alikes are missing:

- **Capital `I` for `l`.** `fold()` lowercases first, so `I` becomes `i`,
  not `l`. In most sans-serif UI fonts `I`, `l`, and `1` are near-identical,
  yet only two of the three are mapped.
- **`8` for `B`.** The digit look-alikes `0`, `1`, `3`, `5` are all mapped;
  `8` is not.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `0fda29d1`)

Verbatim-copy probe of `fold`/`skeleton` (`petname.rs:233-256`), compiled and
run on the laptop in `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-skeleton/`:

```text
skeleton("PayPa1")="paypal"  skeleton("PayPal")="paypal"  equal=true   (refused today)
skeleton("PayPaI")="paypai"  skeleton("PayPal")="paypal"  equal=false  (accepted today)
skeleton("AIice") ="aiice"   skeleton("Alice") ="alice"   equal=false  (accepted today)
skeleton("8ob")   ="8ob"     skeleton("Bob")   ="bob"     equal=false  (accepted today)
skeleton("B0b")   ="bob"     skeleton("Bob")   ="bob"     equal=true   (refused today)
controls: "M0m"/"Mom", "vvill"/"will", "Rnoon"/"moon" all equal, as designed

set(other, "PayPa1") vs alleged "PayPal": refused_by_guard=true
set(other, "PayPaI") vs alleged "PayPal": refused_by_guard=false
set(other, "8ob")    vs alleged "Bob":    refused_by_guard=false
```

So an owner can be talked into (or a crafted flow can set) a petname for one
contact that reads as another contact's name — exactly the spoof the module
exists to prevent ("Account names are alleged, so the store refuses a petname
that could be taken for someone else's name", `petname.rs:1-6`).

Display does not rescue it: `labels()` (`petname.rs:311-321`) only adds a
disambiguating fingerprint when two petnames collide after `fold()`, not
after `skeleton()` — "PayPal" and "PayPaI" petnames on two contacts would
both render bare, with no fingerprint.

Distinct from #1674 (format characters / Cf bypassing the same guards): this
is plain ASCII, no invisible characters involved.

## Why it matters

The petname store is a trust surface: its one job is that a name the owner
sees cannot be mistaken for a different contact. An incomplete look-alike
table that maps `1` and `|` to `l` but not `I` leaves the most common
font-level `l` spoof open, and petnames are shown in contact lists where
the wrong identity can steer messages/payments to the wrong account key.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `skeleton("PayPaI") == skeleton("PayPal")` and
      `skeleton("AIice") == skeleton("Alice")`: capital `I` maps to the
      same class as `l`/`1`/`|`.
- [ ] `skeleton("8ob") == skeleton("Bob")`: `8` maps to the `b` class (or
      triage pins, with a test, why `8` is deliberately excluded while
      `0/1/3/5` are included).
- [ ] `Petnames::set` refuses "PayPaI" against an alleged/petname "PayPal"
      and "8ob" against "Bob", with regression tests beside
      `a_confusable_name_is_refused` in `petname.rs`.
- [ ] Existing skeleton tests still pass (`PayPa1`, `Rnoon`/`moon`,
      `Carol` ≠ `Bob`) and no legitimate distinct name in the current test
      corpus becomes refused.
- [ ] Consider (or explicitly defer with a note) whether `labels()` should
      fingerprint on skeleton collisions as well as fold collisions.

🤖 Filed by new-issue-creator-code-a (Lane A), 2026-10-28 run.

title: id(peers): peers --gossip silently drops invalid bootstrap node IDs — serve warns on the same input, peers collects for the full timeout and reports no peers

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/low

labels.name: app/id
