body:
## Problem

In the directory explorer's typed-line parser, the five no-argument commands silently ignore everything after the command word, while every argument-taking command in the same parser enforces its exact argument count with a usage error. A mistyped or pasted line therefore does something the user did not ask for instead of being refused:

- `signout anything` ends the session (and drops admin rights for the login) anyway.
- `session anything` opens a session anyway.
- `view anything` shows the full directory — there is no filtered view, so a user who typed an argument believes a filter applied when none did.
- `help anything`, `quit anything`, `exit anything`, `? anything` likewise act as if the extra text were not there.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `e91098f1`)

- `pkgs/id/src/directory_view.rs:612-627` — `parse_line`: `"help" | "?"` returns `Line::Help`, `"quit" | "exit"` returns `Line::Quit`, and `"view"` / `"session"` / `"signout"` build their actions with `Vec::new()` pairs — none of them look at `rest`/`words` at all.
- Same function, contrast: `addkey`/`removekey`/`addemail`/`verify` go through `words_n` (exact count or `usage: …` error), `friend_target` matches an exact token shape, and `group member` validates its level — wrong counts are refused everywhere else.
- `pkgs/id/src/directory_view.rs` test `a_malformed_line_is_refused_with_its_usage` pins refusal for wrong counts on argument-taking commands (`group member 3 account:x wizard`, `publish tag abc`, …) but has no trailing-argument case for a no-argument command.
- Both transports build actions through this parser / `action_from_fields` ("Both SSH and the HTML explorer build their actions through `action_from_fields`, so the two agree on every name and format", `directory_view.rs:606-610`), so the typed-line behaviour is the SSH explorer's command contract.

### Reproduction (probe in the real crate, run on the laptop)

Probe test (`id::directory_view::parse_line`, `--no-default-features`) in a laptop worktree of `origin/main` `e91098f1`; probe + full log in the goal bookkeeping (`probe-2026-10-28-laneA-dirview/`):

```text
PROBE "view junk" -> Ok(Action(View)) (expected usage error)
PROBE "session junk" -> Ok(Action(OpenSession)) (expected usage error)
PROBE "signout junk" -> Ok(Action(SignOut)) (expected usage error)
PROBE "help junk" -> Ok(Help) (expected usage error)
PROBE "quit junk" -> Ok(Quit) (expected usage error)
PROBE "exit junk" -> Ok(Quit) (expected usage error)
PROBE "? junk" -> Ok(Help) (expected usage error)
test result: ok. 1 passed
```

Controls in the same probe: bare `view` parses as `View`; `addkey` with zero or two arguments and `group member 3 account:x wizard` are all refused — the exact-count commands behave as documented.

## Why it matters

The explorer is an admin-capable surface (sign-up, verify, group administration, friend envelopes). A parser that silently discards trailing text turns typos into actions: the harmful direction is `signout`/`session`, where a line the user expected to be rejected changes their session state, and `view`, where ignored text can masquerade as a filter that never ran. The parser's own malformed-line test shows the house rule is "wrong shape → usage error"; the no-argument commands are the one hole in it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `parse_line` refuses a non-empty remainder for `view`, `session`, `signout`, `help`, `?`, `quit` and `exit`, with a usage message naming the command (e.g. `usage: signout` takes no arguments — exact wording is the fixer's choice, pinned by tests).
- [ ] Bare forms keep working exactly as today (`view`, `session`, `signout`, `help`, `?`, `quit`, `exit`, blank line).
- [ ] Regression tests cover trailing arguments on each no-argument command, added alongside `a_malformed_line_is_refused_with_its_usage` (or an equivalent test in the same module).
- [ ] Argument-taking commands are unchanged (existing `parse_line` tests keep passing).
- [ ] Existing directory_view tests pass (`cargo test` for the id crate on laptop or CI).

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `directory_view`, `parse_line`, "explorer", "trailing" and `signout` before filing: no filing covers the explorer parser's argument handling. #1770/#1778/#1674 are about control/format characters in names, a different layer; #1611/#1613 are about raw rendering of names in plain-text output, not parsing.

title: id(directory_mail): CommandSink has no timeout — a mail program that never exits hangs the directory request forever

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Bug

`pkgs/id/src/directory_mail.rs` — `CommandSink::send` runs the configured mail program and waits for it with **no timeout**:

- `directory_mail.rs:107` — `let status = child.wait().context("wait for mail program")?;` — a bare `wait()` with no deadline, and the child is never killed on any path.
- The sibling sink in the same file is bounded: `SmtpSink` sets `RELAY_TIMEOUT = Duration::from_secs(10)` (`directory_mail.rs:115`) on connect/read/write. `OutboxSink` is a single file write. Only `CommandSink` can block forever.

The wait is on a live request path. `WorldService::directory()` (`pkgs/id/src/world_session/mod.rs:108`) awaits the send for every mail-carrying directory action (`addemail`, `signin`):

```rust
tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || sink.send(&mail)).await
```

So a mail program that hangs (waiting on a lock, a network mount, a full pipe, a prompt) hangs that directory request — the SSH explorer / web request that asked for a confirmation or sign-in code — **forever**. Each retry spawns another blocked `spawn_blocking` thread and another hung child process; nothing is ever reaped or reported.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe (worktree of `origin/main` e561ab58f at `~/git/fleet/wt-laneB-mdprobe`, `directory_mail.rs` sha256 `dc6f7935…`, identical to sandbox main e91098f1), `pkgs/id/tests/mail_probe.rs`: `CommandSink` pointed at `/bin/sh -c 'sleep 30'` —

```text
send STILL BLOCKED after 3.000162752s (program sleeps 30s; no timeout in CommandSink)
```

i.e. `send()` returns only when the program exits, however long that takes; a program that never exits blocks it indefinitely.

## Why it matters

The command sink is one of the three documented mail transports an admin can configure for a world (`id serve`, `commands/serve.rs:468`). A single wedged helper program silently wedges every email-code flow for that world — no error, no log line, no recovery short of restarting the server — while the SMTP transport next door fails cleanly in 10 s.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `CommandSink::send` bounds the wait: after a deadline (a named constant; reusing the file's existing 10 s scale or a justified program-specific value is the triage pin), it kills the child, reaps it, and returns an error that says the program timed out.
- [ ] A test with a program that sleeps past the deadline returns the timeout error in bounded time (test uses a short injected deadline, not a real multi-second sleep).
- [ ] A slow-but-finite program inside the deadline still succeeds; a program exiting non-zero still errors as before (`a_failing_command_is_an_error` keeps passing).
- [ ] Existing `directory_mail` tests pass (laptop or CI).

Found by new-issue-creator-code-b. Dedup: `gh issue list --search 'directory_mail OR CommandSink OR "mail program"'` and `'mail timeout hang'` (open + closed) returned nothing on 2026-10-28.

title: id(peek): --lines is unbounded and every peek printer computes n * 2 — debug builds panic at -n 2^63, release builds wrap to 0 and print the content twice with a false omitted count

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

`id peek --lines/-n` takes an unbounded `usize` (`pkgs/id/src/cli.rs:784`, `#[arg(short = 'n', long, default_value = "5")] lines: usize` — no range), and every peek printer computes `n * 2` with plain multiplication:

- `pkgs/id/src/commands/find.rs:727,756` (lines), `:791,818` (chars), `:852,881` (words) — `if total <= n * 2` and `total.saturating_sub(n * 2)` for the "… omitted" count. The `saturating_sub` does not help: its argument already overflowed.
- `pkgs/id/src/repl/runner.rs:1302,1331,1364,1391,1423,1452` — the REPL copies of the same three printers have the identical expressions.

## Verified this run (2026-10-28, HEAD e561ab58)

Probe compiled and run on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-peek-overflow/main.rs` there; the exact expression shape `total <= n * 2` / `total.saturating_sub(n * 2)` with `total = 3`, `n` parsed from argv):

- Debug/test arithmetic (`-C overflow-checks=on`, the Rust default for the dev and test profiles in `pkgs/id/Cargo.toml`): `n = 9223372036854775808` (2^63) → **panic: `attempt to multiply with overflow`**, exit 101. So `id peek -n 9223372036854775808 <file>` crashes a debug/test-profile build outright.
- Release arithmetic (`-O -C overflow-checks=off`; the release profile sets no `overflow-checks`): `n = 2^63` → `n * 2` wraps to `0` → the small-enough check is `false`, the head+tail branch runs, `take(n)` prints the whole content, the banner claims `... (3 lines omitted)` for a 3-line file, and the tail prints the whole content a second time. Wrong output, silently.

## Why it matters

One user-supplied flag value either panics the CLI (debug/test builds) or makes peek print duplicated content with a fabricated omission count (release). This is the same unchecked-user-arithmetic class as #1472 (file-list pagination), which was fixed with saturating arithmetic — the peek printers were missed, in both copies (CLI and REPL).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] No `n * 2` (or equivalent unchecked doubling of the user-supplied count) remains in the peek printers in `pkgs/id/src/commands/find.rs` or `pkgs/id/src/repl/runner.rs`; the doubling is saturating (or the `--lines` value is range-clamped at parse time, with the printers still safe for any `PeekOptions` constructed in code/tests).
- [ ] A regression test drives a peek printer (each of lines/chars/words mode, at least in one of the two copies and ideally both) with `lines = usize::MAX / 2 + 1` and a short content string: it prints the content exactly once, with no omitted-count line, and does not panic.
- [ ] Existing peek tests in both files still pass.

title: id(invite): Invite::new has no control-character check at all — a crafted invite name carries newline/tab/CR into the /invite page and the prefilled petname

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem `Invite::new` is the only name validator in `pkgs/id` with **no control-character refusal at all**: an invite name may contain newline, tab and carriage return verbatim. Every sibling validator refuses them — `petname::normalize_name` and the directory's `clean_name` both reject `char::is_control` — but the invite name, which is attacker-chosen inside a link anyone can craft, goes straight to the `/invite` page. ## Evidence (verified this run on main `9874fe59`) - `pkgs/id/src/invite.rs:31-45` — `Invite::new` validates the name with exactly two checks: non-empty after trim, and `chars().count() <= MAX_NAME_CHARS` (64). No control, format or whitespace check. `Invite::parse` / `from_query` (the link a recipient actually opens) funnel through the same `new`, and percent-decoding (`invite.rs:133-158`) happily restores `%0A`, `%09`, `%0D` into the name. - Sibling house rule: `pkgs/id/src/petname.rs:217-230` — `normalize_name` ensures `!name.chars().any(char::is_control)` ("a petname cannot contain control characters"); `pkgs/id/src/directory.rs` `clean_name` does the same for account names. - Where the unchecked name lands: `pkgs/id/src/web/explore.rs:373-390` — `invite_page` renders it as the page headline (`

Add {name}

`), the submit button text (`Add {name}`), and **prefills it as the petname input's value**. `html_escape` neutralises markup, not control characters: a newline/tab/CR in the name renders into the page and the form field as-is, and a name the petname layer itself would refuse then fails the recipient's submit with an unexplained validation error. (Category-Cf/bidi characters in invite names are the display side of the same gap; the petname half of that class is already tracked in #1674 — this issue is the missing Cc check at the invite boundary, which #1674 does not cover.) ### Probe (verbatim mirror, run on the laptop) Mirror of `Invite::new`'s name checks vs `petname::normalize_name`'s (`invite.rs` sha256 `79c069aa…`, `petname.rs` sha256 `ff6cba65…`, main `9874fe59`). Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-replay-invite/` (laptop), copy + log in the goal bookkeeping `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-replay-invite/`: ```text P2 control plain 'Ann Lee': invite_ok=true petname_ok=true P2 newline 'Ann\nLee': invite_ok=true petname_ok=false P2 tab 'Ann\tLee': invite_ok=true petname_ok=false P2 CR 'Ann\rLee': invite_ok=true petname_ok=false P2 bidi U+202E in name: invite_ok=true petname_ok=true (Cf display class, cf. #1674) P2 zero-width U+200B in name: invite_ok=true petname_ok=true (Cf display class, cf. #1674) P2 65 chars (over cap): invite_ok=false petname_ok=false ``` ## Why it matters An invite link is a trust hand-off: the recipient's one confirmation screen says "Add {name}" for a key they cannot humanly verify. The name in that screen is the part a person actually reads, and it is entirely link-author-controlled. Today it can carry raw line breaks and tabs into the page and the prefilled petname field, and it is held to a weaker standard than every other name in the system — including the petname it is about to become, which refuses the same characters one step later. ## Acceptance criteria - [ ] `Invite::new` refuses a name containing control characters (at minimum Cc: `\n`, `\r`, `\t`), matching the `normalize_name` / `clean_name` rule, with the refusal reachable through `Invite::parse` and `from_query` as well. - [ ] Tests in `invite.rs`: newline, tab and CR names are refused; the existing round-trip, plus-as-space and 65-char refusal tests still pass (laptop or CI). - [ ] Triage pins whether category-Cf characters are also refused here or left to #1674's petname-side fix; either way the decision is recorded on this issue.

title: id(list/peers): hand-rolled clients still cap unbounded List/ListPeers responses at 1 MiB — a ~15–25k-item store cannot be listed at all, and #1617's shared read_capped_response was never applied to them

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`id list` fails outright against any node whose store is large enough that the `List` response passes 1 MiB — the same defect class #1617 fixed for remote find, left behind on every other hand-rolled unbounded-response read.

- The server's `List` handler collects **every** item, unbounded: `pkgs/id/src/protocol.rs:554-565` builds the full `Vec<(Hash, String)>` and the protocol writer sends it whole.
- Four hand-rolled clients read that response with a literal `recv.read_to_end(1024 * 1024)`:
  - `src/commands/list.rs:81` — `id list` via the local serve instance
  - `src/commands/list.rs:147` — `id list <remote-node>`
  - `src/commands/repl.rs:430` — REPL `list` in connected modes
  - `src/commands/repl.rs:839` — REPL `list_on_node` (`@NODE_ID`)
- `read_to_end(max)` errors when the stream exceeds the cap, and these sites propagate it with bare `?`, so the failure surfaces as a raw "stream too long" transport error — not a size message.
- #1617's fix (merged today in #1719, main `fb3d6372`) added the shared helper for exactly this: `src/meta_client.rs:63-75` — `read_capped_response` reads through `MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES` (64 MiB) and `capped_response_error` names the limit on overflow. Its doc comment says hand-rolled paths use it "instead of a per-call-site literal bound, so every response read shares the one named cap and cannot drift back to a smaller size" — but only the two find sites were migrated. List (and peers, below) still carry the literal bound the helper exists to eliminate.
- The same literal 1 MiB bound sits on the unbounded `ListPeers` response (handler `src/protocol.rs:643-649`; each `PeerAnnouncement` is ~51 wire bytes): `src/commands/peers.rs:215`, `src/commands/peers.rs:255`, `src/commands/repl.rs:1032`, `src/commands/repl.rs:1083`, and the serve-side stale-peer probe `src/commands/serve.rs:1329` (there an over-cap response reads as a dead peer and the still-live peer is removed as stale).

Fixed-size responses (`Get`/`Delete` at 64 KiB in `get.rs`/`repl.rs`) are **not** in scope — those responses are one hash / one bool and cannot grow with the store.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `fb3d6372`)

Postcard sizing probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-listcap/`, wire-shape replicas of `MetaResponse::List` / `ListPeers` exactly as in the #1617 find probe; log in the goal's `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-listcap/probe.log`):

- List item wire size: ~41 bytes (9-byte name), ~52 bytes (20-byte name), ~72 bytes (40-byte name)
- First item count whose encoded `List` response exceeds 1 MiB: **24,967** items (9-byte names), **19,785** (20-byte), **14,365** (40-byte)
- A 25,000-item list with 20-byte names encodes to 1,325,004 bytes — over the cap
- ListPeers crosses 1 MiB at ~20,165 announcements (~51 bytes each)

So a node with roughly 15–25k stored blobs — unremarkable for a long-lived store — cannot be listed at all from the CLI or the REPL, locally-served or remote, while the direct-store path (no serve running) iterates the store and works, and remote `find` on the same node now works to 64 MiB. The inconsistency sends debugging toward connectivity, exactly as #1617 did.

## Why it matters

`list` is the inventory verb: if a node's store outgrows ~20k entries, its contents become unlistable through every networked path, with a misleading transport error. The shared-cap helper and its regression-test pattern already exist from #1617/#1719; leaving four (plus five peers) call sites on the literal bound is the drift that fix's own doc comment warns against.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All four `List` response reads (`commands/list.rs` ×2, `commands/repl.rs` ×2) go through `meta_client::read_capped_response` (or the unified `MetaClient`), so a `List` response up to `MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES` succeeds at every site.
- [ ] The five `ListPeers` reads (`commands/peers.rs` ×2, `commands/repl.rs` ×2, `commands/serve.rs` probe) use the same shared helper; in the serve probe, an over-cap response is not silently indistinguishable from a dead peer (at minimum it follows the same named-error path before the stale decision, or the distinction is logged).
- [ ] Exceeding the shared cap on any of these paths produces the named "response too large: exceeds the 67108864-byte limit" error from `capped_response_error`, not a bare "stream too long".
- [ ] A regression test in the shape of `meta_client.rs`'s `find_response_larger_than_64_kib_reads_through` pins a `List` response above 1 MiB reading through intact.
- [ ] No remaining literal `read_to_end(1024 * 1024)` response reads in `pkgs/id/src/commands/` or `commands/serve.rs` (fixed-size `Get`/`Delete` 64 KiB reads are explicitly out of scope and may stay).
- [ ] Local direct-store list behaviour, ordering, and output format unchanged; existing id crate tests still pass (laptop or CI).

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for list/response-cap/read_to_end terms: only #1617 (closed, fixed by #1719) — it was scoped to find's 64 KiB bound and cited List's 1 MiB as the sibling with "far more headroom"; no filing covers the List/ListPeers sites hitting their own bound, and #1719 migrated only the find sites.

title: laptop-untracked-review: bare git commit sweeps pre-staged work into its commits — the junk-ignore commit also lands the newly tracked files and any unrelated staged edit

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/agent-backup
labels.description: Package/app: agent-backup (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`laptop-untracked-review.sh` commits with bare `git commit` — no pathspec — at both of its commit sites, so each commit lands **everything in the index**, not just the files the review itself staged. The daily unattended job therefore sweeps any pre-staged work in the personal primaries (an agent's or Drew's half-finished staged edit) into a commit whose message claims it only ignored junk paths or tracked N new files. Worse, the two commits interact: files the review stages for the *second* commit are already in the index when the *first* commit fires, so they land in the wrong commit and the second commit then has nothing to do.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `7b87168c`)

- `nixos/home/laptop-untracked-review.sh:77` — `git add -- .gitignore && git commit -q -m "untracked-review: ignore junk paths $DAY"`: the `add` is path-scoped, the `commit` is not.
- `nixos/home/laptop-untracked-review.sh:80` — `git commit -q -m "untracked-review: track $tracked_new file(s) $DAY"`: same unscoped commit; and by the time it runs, line 66 has already staged each newly tracked file during the scan loop, so those files are in the index for the line-77 commit whenever any junk file was also found.
- Probe (laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-untracked/`; drove the real script, sha256 `6c580a69…` identical to main, in a fixture HOME whose `hatch-personal` repo had a pre-staged unrelated edit to `tracked.txt`, an untracked junk `notes.tmp`, and an untracked normal `newnote.md`):
  - Report printed: `now tracking: newnote.md`, `junk ignored: notes.tmp`, `.gitignore updated` — and **no** "committed 1 newly tracked file(s)" line.
  - `git log --stat` shows exactly ONE review commit, `untracked-review: ignore junk paths 2026-10-28`, containing **3 files**: `.gitignore`, `newnote.md`, **and `tracked.txt` (the pre-staged unrelated edit)**.
  - The line-80 commit then ran against an empty index: git printed `nothing to commit, working tree clean` into the job's stdout, the `&& say` never fired, and the report silently omits that its tracking commit never happened.
  - Control shape: with no junk file present, line 77 never runs and line 80 still sweeps any pre-staged changes into the "track N file(s)" commit — the pathspec bug is at both sites independently.

## Why it matters

This job runs daily and unattended against `~/.openclaw` and `~/hatch-personal` — the two repos where agents and Drew most often have work in flight. Primaries are supposed to sit clean on main, but "clean" is a discipline, not a guarantee (the repo-keeper exists precisely because primaries drift), and a staged-but-uncommitted edit is exactly the state a human/agent leaves mid-task. The review converts that state into a pushed-history commit with a false message, mixing unrelated work into a junk-ignore commit where nobody will look for it, and its own report then misdescribes what was committed. House rule for this fleet is surgical staging: stage explicit paths, commit only those paths.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both commits are path-scoped (e.g. `git commit -m ... -- .gitignore` and `git commit -m ... -- <the files this run added>`), so a pre-staged unrelated change survives a review run still staged and uncommitted.
- [ ] The tracking commit contains exactly the files the review added this run, and the report's "committed N newly tracked file(s)" line fires only when that commit actually happened; a nothing-to-commit outcome is not silently swallowed.
- [ ] A regression test (fixture repo in the style of the probe: pre-staged edit + junk file + normal untracked file) pins all three outcomes: junk commit = `.gitignore` only, track commit = the new file only, pre-staged edit still staged afterwards.
- [ ] Report lines, secret-shaped and too-big handling, and the public-repo report-only mode are unchanged.

Triage note: the likely fix is pathspec commits plus collecting the tracked file list for the second commit's pathspec; whether the job should also refuse/skip a repo with pre-staged changes (the keeper's BUSY-style guard) is the triage pin — pathspec alone already stops the sweep.

title: openclaw-backup: a missing agent state DB is backed up as success — state/openclaw.sqlite is silently optional, no required-member check

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/agent-backup
labels.description: Package/app: agent-backup (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`openclaw-backup.sh` treats the one file the backup exists for — the agent state DB, `state/openclaw.sqlite` — as optional. If that file is absent at run time (state dir moved, DB renamed by an OpenClaw update, partial restore), the run still exits 0, prints the full success line, uploads the archive to both remotes, and advances the journal cursor. Every later restore from that date silently lacks the agent state, and nothing ever signals the loss: the manifest is generated from whatever staging produced, so archive verification is self-referential for this member.

This is the exact failure class the sibling script fixed with its expected set: `pm-dashboard-backup.sh` declares required members once (`EXPECTED_SET`, pm-dashboard-backup.sh:149-176, from #1025) and its verify step fails the run when a required member is missing. `openclaw-backup.sh` re-implemented the same pattern (DATE validation, lock, prune, journal cursor) but never got the expected-set half.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `7b87168c`)

- `nixos/home/openclaw-backup.sh:136-140` — the sqlite snapshot is guarded by `if [ -f "$OC/state/openclaw.sqlite" ]`; the absent case falls through with no log line at all. A present-but-failing `.backup` does fail the run — only absence is silent.
- `nixos/home/openclaw-backup.sh:160-176` — the manifest is built by walking the staged tree; `:259` prints `OK openclaw $DATE backed up to local + R2 + Drive` unconditionally once the legs succeed. No required-member check exists anywhere in the script (grep: no `expected` in openclaw-backup.sh, vs the EXPECTED_SET block in pm-dashboard-backup.sh).
- `nixos/home/openclaw-backup.test.sh` — the suite's `setup_home` always creates `state/openclaw.sqlite` (line ~188); no scenario covers its absence.
- Probe (laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-ocsqlite/`; drove the real script, sha256 `ade2b21e…` identical to main, with the test suite's stub pattern for bws/journalctl/sqlite3/rclone):
  - Control (sqlite present): exit 0, archive contains `./state/openclaw.sqlite`, full OK line, marker advanced.
  - Missing DB (`.openclaw` otherwise intact: `session.log`, `state/`, `tmp/`): **exit 0**, `local OK … (484 bytes …)` and the full `OK openclaw 2026-10-28 backed up to local + R2 + Drive` line, both offsite copies uploaded, journal marker advanced — and the archive listing contains `./state/` but **no `state/openclaw.sqlite`**.

## Why it matters

The backup's value is concentrated in that one file: it is the transaction-consistent snapshot the header (lines 14-18) calls out as the reason for the sqlite `.backup` step. A layout change upstream would degrade every daily backup to a state-less shell — logs and config survive, agent state does not — while the job reports success on all three legs indefinitely. The dashboard sibling already established the house rule: a required member missing at staging or verify fails the run, naming the member.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A run whose `$HOME/.openclaw/state/openclaw.sqlite` is absent fails non-zero, naming the missing member, before any upload (no local archive promoted, no offsite copy, journal marker un-advanced) — or, if triage decides absence must be tolerated (e.g. a pre-first-run host), the run prints an explicit WARN naming the file and the manifest records the member as missing; silence is the one outcome not allowed.
- [ ] The manifest/verify path records the state DB as a required member in the #1025 sense: recorded present in the archive is checked at verify, not just at staging.
- [ ] `openclaw-backup.test.sh` gains a missing-sqlite scenario in the existing stub harness pinning the chosen behaviour; all existing scenarios still pass.
- [ ] Behaviour with the DB present is unchanged: same archive layout, same OK line, marker advances only after all three legs succeed.

Triage note: fail-the-run mirrors pm-dashboard-backup's required-member rule and is the likely pin; the tolerated-with-WARN alternative is listed only because a brand-new host might legitimately have no state DB yet — triage decides which hosts that covers.

title: id(list/find): blob-name TSV output renders names raw — a newline in a remote node's blob name forges extra rows in id list and id find, and a tab forges columns

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The blob-name plain-text renderers in `pkgs/id` print stored names raw in a tab-separated, one-row-per-item format. A blob name containing a newline forges extra rows, and a tab forges extra columns — the same row-forgery class fixed for claim/doc/group in #1611 (merged in #1703) and filed separately for peers (#1613) and meta-tags (#1735), but never filed for the blob list/find renderers.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `0e245370`)

- Name storage accepts the characters: `src/fileops.rs:170-178` — `FileOps::put` rejects only a name that is empty after trim; a name containing `\n` or `\t` is stored as the blob's tag verbatim.
- Server pass-through: `src/protocol.rs:556-562` — the `MetaRequest::List` handler copies each tag name with `String::from_utf8_lossy` into `MetaResponse::List` items with no escaping or validation.
- `id list` renders raw in all three modes:
  - `src/commands/list.rs:91` (via local serve): `println!("{hash}\t{name}")`
  - `src/commands/list.rs:110` (direct store): `println!("{}\t{}", item.hash, name)`
  - `src/commands/list.rs:157` (remote node): `println!("{hash}\t{name}")` — this is the attacker-controlled case: listing a remote node's store prints that node's names.
- REPL list renders raw the same way: `src/commands/repl.rs:439` (serve) and `src/commands/repl.rs:452` (local).
- `id find` renders raw: `src/helpers.rs:158-166` (`print_match_cli`), `src/helpers.rs:190-220` (`print_matches_cli`, including the `[query]` group header), and `src/helpers.rs:246-257` (`print_match_repl`) interpolate `m.name` (and the query) with `\t` separators and no quoting. Find matches against a remote node carry that node's names.

So a node that stores a blob under the name `x\n<64-hex>\tfake.txt` makes every client that runs `id list <that-node>` or a remote `id find` print a forged row that is indistinguishable from a real `<hash>\t<name>` row — a script parsing the output (the documented format, `src/commands/list.rs:8-15`) reads a hash/name pair the listing node never had.

## Why it matters

`id list` / `id find` output is the machine-readable surface other tools and scripts parse. Row forgery by a remote (or merely careless) naming node corrupts inventories, can point a downstream `id get` at a name/hash pairing that does not exist on the listing node, and breaks the one-row-per-item invariant the rest of the fleet's plain-text output now guarantees after #1611/#1703.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A blob name containing `\n`, `\r`, `\t`, or other control characters renders in `id list` (CLI serve/store/remote modes and the REPL list) as exactly one physical line with the name unambiguously delimited (e.g. the JSON-string quoting rule #1611/#1703 adopted for `commands/group.rs` `text()`), and a tab in a name cannot create a second column.
- [ ] The same quoting applies to names (and the query header) in `print_match_cli`, `print_matches_cli`, and `print_match_repl` used by `id find` and the REPL.
- [ ] Names without whitespace/control characters render byte-identically to today, and any `--json` output is unchanged.
- [ ] Regression tests at the renderer level: a name with an embedded newline + forged `<hash>\t<name>` payload produces one line whose only unquoted hash column is the real one; a tabbed name stays one column.
- [ ] Existing id crate tests still pass (laptop or CI).

## Dedup

Searched open + recently closed issues for list/find/helpers TSV, newline and forgery terms. #1611/#1703 covered only the shared `tokens()` renderer in claim/doc/group; #1613 is peers/gossip; #1735 is `commands/tag.rs` meta-tag rows. The blob-name renderers in `commands/list.rs`, `commands/repl.rs`, and `helpers.rs` are not covered by any of them.

title: id(directory_auth): pending email codes are never evicted — the codes map keeps every expired code whose address never comes back

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`DirectoryAuth`'s pending email-code map grows forever: an entry is only ever removed when that same address comes back to `check_code` (or re-issues after the resend minute). A code that is issued and never checked — the normal case for a mistyped address, an abandoned sign-in, or a bot probing many addresses — stays in the map for the life of the process, long past its 15-minute expiry.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `8c8d1bbb`, line trace)

- `pkgs/id/src/directory_auth.rs:112` — `codes: HashMap<String, PendingCode>`, keyed by address.
- `pkgs/id/src/directory_auth.rs:157-179` — `issue_code` inserts/overwrites one entry per address; it never sweeps expired entries for other addresses.
- `pkgs/id/src/directory_auth.rs:186-200` — `check_code` is the only place an entry is removed (on success, on expiry, or on exhausted attempts) — and only for the address being checked.
- `pkgs/id/src/directory_auth.rs:27` — `CODE_TTL_MS = 15 * 60 * 1000`: entries are dead after 15 minutes but are retained indefinitely.
- The neighbouring maps in the same file DO sweep, so the omission is an asymmetry, not a design rule: sessions are swept in `open_session` (`directory_auth.rs:118`, `retain(|_, record| record.expires_at > now)`), and the signed-request replay guard sweeps in `accept` (`directory_auth.rs:250`, retain on `SIGNED_WINDOW_MS`).
- Callers: `pkgs/id/src/directory_view.rs:1219` (confirm) and `:1244` (sign-in) call `issue_code` for an address supplied in the request, so distinct addresses accumulate entries at request rate; nothing else touches the map (grep over `src/` for `issue_code`/`check_code`/`.codes` — only `directory_auth.rs` and those two call sites).

## Why it matters

This is a long-lived server process (a hosted world). The map grows by one entry per distinct address that ever requests a code and does not complete the flow, with no bound and no eviction — the same unbounded-growth class as #1713 (SaveRateLimiter) and #1730 (WaitingPool arrived set), but in the auth surface, where an unauthenticated caller controls the key (the email address). It also contradicts the module's own framing (`directory_auth.rs:5-7`): pending codes are supposed to live only until "its time is up".

## Suggested direction (for triage to pin)

Mirror the session sweep: retain only unexpired entries when `issue_code` runs (it already receives `now`), and/or sweep at the top of `check_code`. Keep behaviour otherwise identical: the resend-minute rule, the 5-attempt cap, and the digest-only storage all stay.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] After a code's 15-minute expiry, its entry is evicted without that address ever calling `check_code` (unit test: issue for address A, advance the clock past expiry, issue/check for address B, assert A's entry is gone — e.g. via the map's observable size or a re-issue behaving as a fresh entry).
- [ ] Unexpired codes still verify, the 60-second resend refusal still applies, and the 5-attempt exhaustion still removes the entry.
- [ ] Issue/check behaviour for live codes is unchanged; existing `directory_auth` tests still pass (laptop or CI).

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues and code search for `DirectoryAuth`, `issue_code`, and pending-code/expiry terms before filing: no filing covers this map. #1713/#1726/#1730 are the same unbounded-growth class in other components (web save limiter, outbox, waiting pool), not this one.

title: mcpx(searchpath): a ~name search-path entry is silently resolved under the caller's own home — ~alice/scripts becomes $HOME/alice/scripts

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`searchpath.Resolve` expands **any** entry starting with `~` into the caller's own home directory. A `~name` entry — which in every shell and in the usual `~user` convention names *that user's* home — is silently rewritten to a subdirectory of the caller's home, and a directory literally named `~scratch` relative to the working directory can never be named at all.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `211aa58f`)

- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/searchpath/searchpath.go:117-125` (`absolute`): `strings.HasPrefix(path, "~")` matches every leading `~`, then `filepath.Join(home, strings.TrimPrefix(path, "~"))` splices the remainder under the *caller's* home. There is no distinction between `~`, `~/…` and `~name[/…]`.
- Probe executed this run on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-lanea-searchpath/`, `searchpath.go` copied verbatim, sha256 `92c048ed…`; log in the goal's `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-searchpath/probe.log`), with `HOME=/home/testhome`:
  - `~alice/scripts` → `/home/testhome/alice/scripts`
  - `~nosuchuser/scripts` → `/home/testhome/nosuchuser/scripts`
  - `~scratch` → `/home/testhome/scratch`
  - Controls correct: `~/scripts` → `/home/testhome/scripts`, `~` → `/home/testhome`
- The resolved list is what actually gets searched: `internal/cli/scripts.go:58` (`scriptPath`, from the `paths.scripts` setting / `MCPX_PATHS_SCRIPTS`), `internal/cli/scripts.go:164` (`PlaceholderFiles`, `paths.placeholders`), and `internal/daemon/consumer.go:145` (`recipeDirs`) all pass configured entries through `Resolve`.
- `searchpath_test.go` has no `~` test at all, so neither the correct control cases nor the `~name` misresolution are pinned.
- `Describe()` (`searchpath.go:259`) renders the already-rewritten absolute path, so the "why is it not finding my script" diagnostic confidently shows a directory the user never wrote.

## Why it matters

Configured search paths are user-typed configuration. A user who writes `~alice/scripts` (a shared/team account's scripts) is silently searched in a lookalike directory under their own home instead — scripts are not found, and if `$HOME/alice/scripts` happens to exist, the *wrong* scripts are found and run with no hint why. Silent misresolution in a path that decides which code executes is worse than an error.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `~` and `~/…` keep expanding to the caller's home (existing correct behaviour, now pinned by tests).
- [ ] A `~name[/…]` entry is **not** resolved under the caller's home: triage pins the rule — expand to that user's home where the platform supports it, or leave the entry unexpanded/refuse it with a clear diagnostic — and the chosen rule is documented at `absolute`.
- [ ] Regression tests in `internal/searchpath` cover `~alice/scripts`, a `~name` for a nonexistent user, `~`, and `~/scripts`.
- [ ] `Describe()` output for a `~name` entry matches the locations `Find`/`List` actually search.
- [ ] Existing `internal/searchpath`, `internal/cli` and `internal/daemon` tests keep passing.

title: id(server_config): two user keys can name the same public key — parse accepts it, the second user silently vanishes, and its alias overwrites the first

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
# id(server_config): two user keys can name the same public key — parse accepts it, the second user silently vanishes, and its alias overwrites the first

## Summary

`ServerConfig::parse` (`pkgs/id/src/server_config/parse.rs`) guards the config's local keys carefully — `claim()` (:290-301) refuses a key declared twice (`DuplicateKey`), members are deduped, the creator may not be listed as a member, unknown/wrong-kind references are refused by name. But uniqueness is checked only on the key *string*, never on the identity it resolves to. Two `[[users]]` entries with different keys and the **same** Ed25519 public key (`id`) parse without any error, and the two declared users then silently collapse into one:

- `user_id("ann") == user_id("bo")` — every reference to either key resolves to the same account.
- The primary-alias table is keyed by the resolved object (`aliases: BTreeMap<Object, String>`, `server_config/mod.rs`), and `record_alias` (`parse.rs:303-322`) inserts by `Object::User(id)` — so the second user's alias **overwrites** the first's. `primary_alias` for the (single) user returns only the second alias; the first user's alias is lost with no diagnostic.
- Provisioning then silently creates only one account: `Provisioned::apply` (`server_config/provision.rs:146-160`) skips any user whose id the directory already has (`account(&id).is_some()` → `continue`), so a config declaring two users reports `users_created = 1` and starts a server on a state that does not match the file the operator wrote — no error, no warning naming the duplicate.

A config that lists its creator under two keys also trips over this in a confusing direction: a group whose creator is `ann` and whose member is `bo` (same key bytes) is refused as `CreatorListed` naming `bo` as if `bo` were the creator — accurate only after the silent merge, and baffling from the file alone.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 211aa58f)

Line trace, `parse.rs` (sha256 14673ade…):

- Users pass: `parse_id` (:331-339) validates each `id` on its own; `claim` checks only `names.contains_key(key)` — the local key string.
- `record_alias` inserts into `aliases` keyed by `Object::User(id)`; a second user with the same id replaces the first's alias entry.
- Groups/members/create-rule all resolve through `user_of`, which returns the shared `Key`, so no later pass can tell the two declared users apart.

Probe executed on the laptop in the real crate (detached worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-serverconfig-dupid`, removed after; probe + log in the goal's `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-serverconfig-dupid/`):

- CTRL: two users with distinct ids and aliases `Ann`/`Bo` — parse Ok, `user_id`s differ, both aliases kept.
- BUG: two users, same id, aliases `Ann`/`Bo` — parse **Ok**; `user_id(ann)==user_id(bo)`; `primary_alias` returns only `"Bo"`; `Provisioned::apply` reports `users_created=1` for 2 declared users and the directory holds 1 account. (Probe output in `probe.log`.)

The existing tests pin duplicate *keys* (`test_a_user_key_declared_twice_is_refused_naming_it`, `test_two_groups_with_one_key_are_refused_naming_it`) but no test declares the same *id* under two keys.

## Why it matters

The server config is the operator's declarative statement of who exists on a home server (P2.9). A copy-paste error — the most likely way a duplicate id happens — currently produces a server that silently runs with one fewer named user and the wrong primary alias shown for them, instead of the startup refusal every other shape of bad config gets ("Every refusal names the key it is about" is the module's stated contract). Alias display is identity surface: showing `Bo`'s alias for the merged account misattributes a name.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ServerConfig::parse` refuses two `[[users]]` entries that name the same public key, with an error that names both keys (a `ConfigError` variant in the existing style, e.g. `DuplicateId`).
- [ ] A regression test declares the same id under two keys and asserts the refusal; the existing duplicate-key tests still pass.
- [ ] Distinct ids under distinct keys are unaffected, including two users sharing an alias *text* (alias uniqueness is a separate, documented non-rule for claims — this issue is only about duplicate identities).
- [ ] `cargo test` for `server_config` (parse + provision suites) passes on laptop/CI.

## Notes

- Filed by the new-issue-creator (lane B) after a laptop-executed probe; not self-solved — whether the refusal lives in `parse_id`/`claim` or as a dedicated pass, and whether group IDs need the symmetric check (they are derived from creator+key, so two group keys cannot collide while user ids can), is a small contract pin for queue-lane triage.
- Distinct from the alias-claims design in `aliases.rs` ("Nothing is unique. Two objects may claim the same alias") — that is about *claims on different objects*; here two declared *objects* are one identity.

labels.name: task/triage

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body: ## Summary `logstore.Correlations` (pkgs/mcpx/internal/logstore/stats.go:539-570) counts **record pairs**, not sessions — but the dashboard renders its count as a session count. One busy session inflates a pair's "sessions" by the product of the two tools' call counts. The same method also breaks outright when called with an ordinary `Query` filter, because it splices the shared unqualified `where()` conditions into a self-join. ## Evidence (verified this run) Line trace, stats.go: - :548-556 — the query self-joins `records a JOIN records b ON a.session = b.session` with `a.tool < b.tool` and selects `count(*) AS cnt`. For a session where tool A was called *m* times and tool B *n* times, the join produces *m × n* rows for that session, and `count(*)` sums those products across sessions. - The consumer, internal/dashboard/dashboard.html:260-267, titles the table "Correlated Tool Pairs (Co-Occurring in Sessions)" with a "Co-Occurrences" column, and :415 renders each row as `` `${cr.count} sessions` `` — the count is presented to the reader as a number of sessions. - The only production caller is internal/daemon/routes_dashboard.go:52 (`st.Correlations(logstore.Query{}, 20)`), feeding `/v1/metrics/tools`. - :549-551 — when `q.where()` is non-empty, its conditions are appended verbatim (`AND ` + the trimmed where). Those conditions name unqualified columns (`server = ?`, `level IN (...)`, `ts_unix_ms >= ?`, …), which are ambiguous between `a` and `b` in a self-join. Sibling stats methods (Calls, Servers, Sessions, Slowest, Timeline) all accept filtered queries against a single table, so `Correlations` silently having a different, broken contract is a trap for the next caller (e.g. wiring it into the daemon ops path the way Sessions/Slowest are used in internal/daemon/ops.go:241-251). Laptop probe (real `internal/logstore` package, detached worktree at origin/main a2f85d95; stats.go sha256 cd723454, identical to the sandbox clone; probe + log in the goal's hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-corr/): Fixture: session s1 calls alpha ×3 and beta ×2; session s2 calls alpha ×1, beta ×1, gamma ×1. - BUG-A: `Correlations(Query{}, 20)` returns alpha/beta **count=7** (3×2 + 1×1). The dashboard would render "7 sessions"; alpha and beta actually co-occur in **2** sessions. - Controls: alpha/gamma = 1 and beta/gamma = 1 (one call each in one session — the shapes where the product happens to equal the session count). - BUG-B: `Correlations(Query{Server: "fff"}, 20)` returns `SQL logic error: ambiguous column name: server (1)` instead of filtered rows. - Baseline: with the probe removed, the full existing internal/logstore suite passes on the same tree. No existing test calls Correlations (grep: only feedback_test.go mentions "correlation" for a different check, and routes_dashboard_test.go only asserts the JSON field is non-nil with an empty store). ## Why it matters The dashboard's correlations table is the "which tools are used together" signal for the fleet. As written it ranks pairs by how *often the tools were called* in shared sessions, squared-ish — a chatty session dominates — while labelling the number "sessions", so the reader cannot tell 7 sessions from 1 session with 7 pair-products. Any future filtered use (per-server, per-window) fails with a raw SQL error instead of results. ## Acceptance criteria - [ ] The count for a tool pair equals the number of distinct sessions in which both tools were called (e.g. `COUNT(DISTINCT a.session)` or an equivalent per-session dedup), so the probe fixture above yields alpha/beta = 2, alpha/gamma = 1, beta/gamma = 1 — **or** the dashboard copy is changed to honestly name what is counted, with the semantics pinned by a test. (Session count is the recommended reading: it matches the existing dashboard copy.) - [ ] `Correlations` with a filtered `Query` (at minimum Server, Since/Until, Level) returns filtered results instead of an ambiguous-column SQL error — the where conditions are qualified/deduplicated for the self-join, and bound arguments stay in step with the placeholders. - [ ] Regression tests in internal/logstore cover: repeated calls of both tools in one session, the pair across multiple sessions, and a filtered query. - [ ] Existing internal/logstore and internal/daemon dashboard tests keep passing. ## Notes for triage - Tool identity here is the bare tool name (`a.tool`), matching how the rest of stats.go groups; whether a pair should also be keyed by server is a separate question — not required by this issue. - Found by new-issue-creator lane A, 2026-10-28. Distinct from #1664 (logstore read-only SQL guard in sql.go — different function/defect, same package).

title: mcpx(elicit): concurrent answers race Respond's check-then-insert — losers get a raw UNIQUE-constraint error, and an Await expiry that loses the race fails the asker

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

`elicit.Broker.Respond` decides "not yet answered" with a read, then records the answer in a separate transaction — so two answers that race (the broker's normal case: the asker and the answerer are *different processes* sharing one store file) both pass the check, and every loser but one gets a raw SQLite error instead of the outcome the code promises:

```
constraint failed: UNIQUE constraint failed: elicitation_answers.id (1555)
```

The documented contract (elicit.go, on `Respond`): "Answering twice is not an error worth failing a command over; the first answer stands and the caller is told so" — implemented as `"<id> was already answered"` for the sequential case and pinned by `TestAnsweringTwiceIsRefusedAndTheFirstStands`. Under concurrency the caller is told no such thing: it gets a driver error text, which the daemon's answer endpoint (`POST /v1/elicit/{id}/{action}`, daemon/server.go) forwards verbatim in its 409 body, and which the CLI prints as the command's failure.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `ea7272ce`)

Line trace of `pkgs/mcpx/internal/elicit/elicit.go` (sha256 `6a6298d4`):

- `Respond` (:298) reads the request with `Get` and refuses when `r.State != Pending` (:312-315, the `"%s was already %s"` error).
- Only afterwards does it open a transaction (:325) and `INSERT INTO elicitation_answers` (:334) — whose `id` is the table's primary key. Nothing makes the check-and-insert atomic across processes (no `UPDATE ... WHERE state='pending'` claim, no constraint-error translation).
- The store is explicitly multi-process: `Open` is per-process over a shared file, the package doc says the asker and answerer can be "different processes, on different days", and `Await` polls the table precisely because answers arrive from other processes (:278-295).

Probe executed this run in the real `internal/elicit` package ON THE LAPTOP (detached worktree from `origin/main` ea7272ce, removed after; full existing suite green on the same tree): two `Broker` handles on one store file (the daemon + CLI shape), one question, 8 goroutines barrier-released into `Respond(Accept, {"n":i})`, 10 trials.

- Every trial: exactly 1 winner; the stored answer is the winner's (integrity holds — the first answer does stand).
- Almost every loser: `constraint failed: UNIQUE constraint failed: elicitation_answers.id (1555)`.
- Occasionally a loser whose `Get` happened to run after the winner committed gets the documented `elc-… was already answered` — so the same race produces two different loser outcomes depending on timing.

Knock-on (line-traced, same defect): `Await`'s expiry path (:282-291) calls `Respond(Cancel, By:"expiry")` and returns its error verbatim. If that expiry loses the race — to a real answer, or to another process's `Pending()`-driven `expireOverdue` (:454) expiring the same question — the *asker* gets the raw constraint error out of `Await` instead of the answer that actually landed or the expiry-cancel it was manufacturing. `expireOverdue` itself ignores the error (`_ =`), so the two expiry paths treat the same race differently.

## Why it matters

Double-answering is not exotic here: a destructive-call confirmation or disambiguation can be answered from the CLI, the daemon API, and a plugin surface while an expiry is firing — the answer paths in daemon/server.go:1389, daemon/routes_proto.go:664, daemon/hooks.go:62, and cli/elicit.go:136-150 all call the same `Respond`. Today the race's losers — including a human who clicked a fraction late — see an SQLite internals error that reads like store corruption, and an asker in the expiry window can have its whole call fail with that error even though its question *was* answered.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The pending→answered transition is atomic across processes (e.g. the state change is claimed inside one transaction / conditional update), OR a primary-key/constraint failure from the answer insert is translated into the same `"<id> was already <state>"` outcome the sequential path returns.
- [ ] Concurrent answers from two broker handles on one file: exactly one winner, every loser gets the documented already-answered error (no raw `constraint failed` text escapes `Respond`).
- [ ] `Await`'s expiry path tolerates losing the race: if the question was answered (or expired) by someone else first, `Await` returns that answer instead of an error.
- [ ] A regression test races two brokers (or two handles) on one store file; the existing sequential test and the rest of the `internal/elicit` suite still pass.
- [ ] The daemon's 409 body for a lost race names the winning state, not a SQLite error code.

## Dedup / distinctness

Searched open + recently closed issues for `elicit`, `elicitation`, `Respond`, `UNIQUE constraint`: no filing covers this race. Adjacent, different defects: #1675-#1678 (broker hygiene — store permissions, retention, event redaction, review-first answering; none touches the answer transition), #1679 (internal/events resume), #1484 (form-answer schema validation in the client). The sequential double-answer behaviour is already pinned by `TestAnsweringTwiceIsRefusedAndTheFirstStands` — this is strictly its concurrent, cross-process counterpart.

title: aggregator: an empty github-result report marks a dashboard comment failed — a pending comment is written off unposted, and a posted comment flips back to failed

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

body:
## Summary

A GitHub-result report that carries **neither** a URL **nor** an error is recorded as a failure — and it can retroactively un-post a comment that already succeeded.

`CommentsStore.markGithubResult` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/comments.ts:202-214, sha256 3b0099d5):

```ts
if (result.url) {
  c.githubState = "posted";
  c.githubUrl = result.url;
} else {
  c.githubState = "failed";
}
await this.persist();
```

The `else` treats "no URL" as "failed", with no check that an error was actually reported, and no guard on the comment's current state. The HTTP boundary does not close the hole: `POST /api/comments/github-result` (src/server.ts:350-358) validates only that `id` is a string, then forwards `url`/`error` as `undefined` when absent — so a body of `{"id": "..."}` reaches the store as an empty result.

## Verified behaviour (probe run on the laptop, main d39e6111)

Probe test against the real `CommentsStore` (bun test, detached worktree, temp-dir store file):

- **CTRL** — a `{url}` report moves a pending comment to `posted`; an `{error}` report on a fresh comment moves it to `failed`. ✅
- **BUG-A** — `markGithubResult(id, {})` on a **pending** comment returns it with `githubState: "failed"` and persists that. Per the consumption contract in the comments.ts header, a kind-`github` comment "sits at githubState `pending` until a fleet poster posts it … then reports the result: `{ id, url }` or `{ id, error }`" — a report with neither field reports no outcome, yet the comment is written off as failed and will never be posted.
- **BUG-B** — after a successful `{url}` report (`posted`, `githubUrl` set), a later empty report flips the same comment back to `failed` (the stale `githubUrl` remains set, so state and URL now contradict each other; `githubCommentUrl` still renders the URL of a "failed" comment).

Existing tests (test/slice3.test.ts:149-154, :367-368) cover pending→posted and the happy-path endpoint, but no empty, conflicting, or repeat report.

## Why it matters

Dashboard comments of kind `github` are Drew's route for getting a comment onto an issue/PR via a fleet poster. A stray, truncated, or retried result report can silently mark an unposted comment as failed — the message never reaches GitHub and the dashboard says it was tried — or flip a genuinely posted comment to "failed", sending a poster to re-post a duplicate. The store is the system of record for this hand-off; it should refuse a result that reports nothing and never move a terminal state backwards.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A result report with neither `url` nor `error` is rejected (store returns an error / endpoint answers 400) and the comment's state is unchanged — pending stays pending.
- [ ] A comment already `posted` cannot be moved to `failed` by a later report (and a `failed` comment's path back, if any, is an explicit decision in the fix, pinned by a test); repeat identical reports are idempotent.
- [ ] A report carrying **both** `url` and `error` is rejected or resolved by a documented rule, pinned by a test — not silently decided by branch order.
- [ ] Regression tests cover: empty report on pending, empty report on posted, url+error report; the existing slice3 comment tests keep passing.

## Scope notes

- Two candidate homes for the validation: the store (defends every caller) and/or the server.ts endpoint (400 for the HTTP caller). The store-level refusal is the load-bearing one; triage pins whether the endpoint also validates.
- Out of scope: the load path's parse-failure handling in the same file, comment author validation, and the triage endpoint.

title: aggregator: summarizeDns ages renewals by the UTC day, not Chicago — a domain renewing today vanishes from Next renewal and the 45-day spend card every evening from 19:00 CDT

body:
## Summary

`summarizeDns` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/dns.ts:99-102) derives "today" and the 45-day spend-horizon cutoff from `Date#toISOString()` — the **UTC** calendar day:

```ts
const cutoff = new Date(now.getTime() + soonDays * 86_400_000).toISOString().slice(0, 10);
const today = now.toISOString().slice(0, 10);
```

The dashboard's house convention is America/Chicago: derive.ts:457-475 already provides `chicagoYmd(now)` ("2026-10-25" in America/Chicago for an instant) and `addDaysYmd(ymd, n)` for exactly this kind of date-only comparison — the helpers the #1629 fix introduced for `freshness()`. dns.ts uses neither.

## Verified behaviour (probe run on the laptop, main d39e6111)

Probe test in the real aggregator tree (bun test, detached worktree; dns.ts sha256 10933bba identical in both clones), with a register holding domains renewing 2026-10-27 and 2026-10-28:

- **CTRL** — `now = 2026-10-27T15:00:00Z` (10:00 CDT; UTC and Chicago agree on the date): `nextRenewal` = the 2026-10-27 domain, `renewingSoon` = both domains. ✅
- **BUG** — `now = 2026-10-28T01:30:00Z` (2026-10-27 **20:30 CDT** — still Oct 27 for the viewer): `nextRenewal` returns the **2026-10-28** domain and `renewingSoon` drops the 2026-10-27 domain entirely. The domain renewing *today* (Chicago) vanishes from both the "Next renewal" card and the "Renewing in 45 days" spend card (render.ts:2533-2545) every evening from 19:00 CDT until midnight — and symmetrically, tomorrow's renewal is presented as today's for those five hours.

The existing dns tests (test/slice3.test.ts, 19 pass on the same tree) exercise `summarizeDns` only at `2026-12-28T00:00:00Z` — midnight UTC, where UTC and Chicago dates differ too (Dec 27 18:00 CST) but the fixture's renewal dates are far enough away that the one-day shift changes nothing.

## Why it matters

The /dns page is the fleet's renewal-spend surface: "Next renewal" and "Renewing in 45 days · $total" are how upcoming domain spend is spotted. For five hours every evening the page skips the domain that renews that day and understates the 45-day total by that domain's price — a wrong answer on a money page, in the timezone the rest of the aggregator already standardised on.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `summarizeDns` computes `today` via the Chicago calendar (reuse `chicagoYmd` from derive.ts) and the cutoff via `addDaysYmd(today, soonDays)` or an equivalent Chicago-anchored computation — no `toISOString().slice(0, 10)` day derivation left in dns.ts.
- [ ] Regression test: at `2026-10-28T01:30:00Z` (Oct 27 evening CDT) a domain renewing 2026-10-27 is `nextRenewal` and appears in `renewingSoon`; a domain renewing 2026-10-28 also appears in `renewingSoon`.
- [ ] The existing slice3 dns tests keep passing, including the midnight-UTC summary case.
- [ ] A DST-boundary case is pinned (e.g. an instant during the CDT→CST transition week) so the cutoff arithmetic cannot drift by an hour into the wrong day.

## Scope notes

- Distinct from #1629 (derive.ts `freshness()` aging date-only stamps by the UTC day — fixed with the same helpers, different function and symptom) and from #1628 (Horizon dates never validated). This is the one remaining `toISOString().slice(0, 10)` day derivation in the aggregator's date-only comparisons — triage should grep to confirm no sibling remains.
- Fix direction is deliberately narrow: dns.ts only. Whether `parseDnsRegister` should also validate that a renewal date is a real calendar date is #1628-family territory and is **not** part of this issue.

title: mcpx(launcher): the placeholder typo guard misses user-defined names and never scans fill/definition bodies — misspellings reach the generated launcher verbatim

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

`pkgs/mcpx/internal/launcher` promises that a misspelled placeholder is caught at expansion time: `checkUnknown`'s doc (`internal/launcher/template.go:294-298`) says a typo "silently leaves the text in place, producing a syntax error from the runtime that points at a line the user did not write", and catching it "means the message names the misspelling and lists what was available". The guard only delivers that promise for near-misses of **built-in** names written **directly in the template text**. Two gaps leave the exact failure it exists to prevent:

1. **The near-miss test only knows built-ins.** `looksLikePlaceholder` (`template.go:344-360`) compares a name only against the `All` built-in list. A typo of a **user-defined** placeholder — the `@name`s declared in placeholder files (`internal/launcher/define.go`, loaded and bound by `internal/runner/runner.go:609-614`) — is not near any built-in, so it is never flagged, even in the template text. `Expand("@bannner", Fill{Entry: "E", "banner": "BANNER;"})` returns `"@bannner"` with **no error**.
2. **Fill and definition bodies are never scanned.** `Expand` calls `checkUnknown(t, fill)` (`template.go:92`), and `checkUnknown` iterates only `t.Text` (`template.go:305-330`). Bodies are where user definitions live — `define_test.go`'s own examples are bodies like `try { @inner } catch ...` — and `expand` (`template.go:136-140`) leaves an unknown reference in a body **verbatim** in the output. A definition body containing `@entyr` expands with no error and the literal `@entyr` lands in the generated launcher script.

## Verified (main `d39e6111`, laptop probe in the real package)

Probe test in `internal/launcher` (external test package), run on the laptop at the same main commit (`template.go` sha256 `ea09f4ca` identical in both clones); full existing `internal/launcher` suite passes alongside it:

- CTRL: template text `@entyr` with `Entry` filled → **refused**, error names `@entyr` (the pinned behaviour, also covered by the existing test at `template_test.go:94`).
- BUG-A: template text `@bannner` with a user-defined `banner` in the fill → output `"@bannner"`, **no error**.
- BUG-B: template `@wrap` whose fill body is `try { @entyr } catch {}` → output `try { @entyr } catch {}`, **no error** — the typo reaches the generated launcher, where it becomes a runtime failure in a generated file the user did not write.

A faithful premise mirror of `readRef`/`checkUnknown`/`looksLikePlaceholder`/`expand` reproduces the same three verdicts.

## Why it matters

User-defined placeholders are a documented, first-class feature (declarations via `// @mcpx:placeholder name(params)`, filename fallback, `Bind`), and the runner binds them into every custom-launcher expansion. The typo guard is the only thing standing between a misspelled `@name` and a broken generated launcher whose error points into a temp file. Today it protects the ten built-in names in one of the two places references can appear, and none of the user-defined names anywhere.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A near-miss of a user-defined placeholder name (from `Options.Defs` / the fill keys) in the template text is refused with the same "unknown placeholder …; available are …" error shape as a built-in near-miss, listing the user-defined names as available.
- [ ] References inside fill/definition bodies are checked too: a near-miss of any known name (built-in, user-defined, or a definition's declared parameters, e.g. `@innner` for `@inner`) in a body is refused at `Expand` time instead of being left verbatim in the output.
- [ ] Deliberately-unfilled names stay left alone (the existing behaviour pinned by `TestDeepNestingIsBoundedRatherThanUnbounded`'s premise and the email/decorator false-positive caution in `looksLikePlaceholder`'s doc): the widened check must keep the near-miss bar, not become an exact-match ban on unknown `@words` in bodies (generated header/entry fills contain ordinary JS with `@`-words).
- [ ] Tests cover: user-defined-name typo in template text, built-in typo inside a definition body, parameter-name typo inside its own definition body, and a body containing a non-near-miss `@word` still expanding cleanly.
- [ ] Existing `internal/launcher` tests pass.

title: mcpx(events): the /v1/events resume contract silently breaks at since=0 and on a malformed since — a trimmed history reports no gap, and a bad cursor is coerced to 0 or MaxUint64

body:
## Summary

The `/v1/events` resume contract — "a subscriber that missed events is told so, rather than silently given a stream with a hole in it" — breaks in two shapes on the same code path, so a resumable stream can be silently incomplete or silently mispositioned:

- **BUG-A (bus): an explicit `since=0` resume never reports a gap, even after the retained history has been trimmed.** The gap check in `SubscribeFrom` is gated on `since > 0`, so the one resume position that asks for *everything from the start* is the one position that can lose events 1..N with no `gap` signal.
- **BUG-B (daemon): a malformed `since` / `Last-Event-ID` is silently coerced to one of two opposite positions.** `handleEvents` discards the `strconv.ParseUint` error, so a syntax error behaves exactly like `since=0` (full retained replay) and an out-of-range value behaves like `since=MaxUint64` (no replay, no gap, live-only) — neither is rejected and neither is signalled.

## Evidence (verified on main `d39e6111`)

### BUG-A

`pkgs/mcpx/internal/events/events.go` (sha256 `370a935a…`):

- The package's promise, `New` (:~155): the history "is bounded… a subscriber gone longer than the history covers is told so rather than silently given a gap."
- `SubscribeFrom`'s own doc (:206-208): "**gap is true when since predates the retained history**, so the subscriber knows it missed something and can resynchronise instead of trusting a stream with a hole in it."
- The implementation (:218) is narrower than both docs:

```go
if since > 0 && len(h) > 0 && h[0].Seq > since+1 {
    gap = true
}
```

- The daemon deliberately distinguishes position zero from absent (`internal/daemon/server.go:1264-1265`): "Present-but-zero replays everything retained; absent is live only", and emits the in-band `event: gap` frame (:1277-1280) only when `SubscribeFrom` returns `gap=true`.
- So: daemon has published more than `eventHistory` (default 1024) events, a client connects with `?since=0` (or an SSE reconnect sends `Last-Event-ID: 0`), events 1..(first retained − 1) are gone, the replay starts mid-history, and no gap frame is emitted. The existing tests pin the neighbouring cases but not this one: `TestAGapBeyondHistoryIsReportedRatherThanHidden` uses `since=1`; `TestAReplayLargerThanTheSubscriberBufferMissesNothing` uses `since=0` with everything still retained (`h[0].Seq == 1`, where the uniform formula `h[0].Seq > since+1` also yields no gap).

Premise exercised this run (faithful mirror of the gap condition + `retained()`/trimming, `probe-2026-10-28-laneA-eventsgap/premise.py` in the fleet's hidden files): keep=3, seq 1..10 → retained [8,9,10]; CTRL since=1 → gap=true; CTRL since=0 with nothing trimmed → gap=false, all replayed; **BUG since=0 after trim → replay [8,9,10], gap=false — events 1..7 silently missing.**

### BUG-B

`pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/server.go:1262-1265`:

```go
raw := firstNonEmptyStr(r.Header.Get("Last-Event-ID"), q.Get("since"))
since, _ := strconv.ParseUint(raw, 10, 64)
// Present-but-zero replays everything retained; absent is live only.
sub, gap := s.Events.SubscribeFrom(f, since, raw != "")
```

The error is discarded. Per the installed Go stdlib source (`strconv/atoi.go`, `ParseUint`: a syntax error returns `0`, a range error returns `maxVal`):

| `since` value | effective position | result |
|---|---|---|
| `banana`, `-1` | 0 (syntax error, discarded) | full retained replay — as if the client asked from the start |
| `99999999999999999999999999` | MaxUint64 (range error, discarded) | no replay, no gap — live-only forever, client believes it is caught up at a position that can never exist |

Neither outcome is a 400, a gap frame, or a log line. `Last-Event-ID` is normally server-generated, but `since` is a documented query parameter of this endpoint (handler comment, server.go:~1243), so hand-written clients — the ones most likely to send a malformed value — get one of two silently opposite streams.

## Disclosure

A Go probe covering BUG-A (`probe_lanea_test.go`, same hidden-files folder) was prepared but **not executed**: the laptop was unreachable this run (SSH tunnel closes immediately — the ongoing outage, cf. #1667) and verification probes are never compiled on the sandbox. Triage should run the probe first and narrow this issue if either traced verdict differs. BUG-A is a line-trace + premise-mirror verification; BUG-B additionally rests on the Go stdlib source read this run.

## Why it matters

The gap signal is the only mechanism a `/v1/events` consumer has to know it must resynchronise instead of trusting the stream. BUG-A removes it for exactly the fresh-start resume (new client, reset cursor, `Last-Event-ID: 0`) once a busy daemon has rolled its 1024-event history — elicitation and server-lifecycle consumers then act on a partial history believing it complete. BUG-B makes a client bug (a bad cursor value) undetectable from either side: the daemon cannot log it and the client cannot distinguish the response from a legitimate one.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `SubscribeFrom(f, 0, true)` on a bus whose retained history starts at seq > 1 returns `gap=true`; with nothing trimmed it still returns `gap=false` (existing tests keep passing, plus a new regression test for the trimmed zero case).
- [ ] `GET /v1/events?since=0` after the daemon's history has rolled emits the in-band `event: gap` frame.
- [ ] A malformed `since` / `Last-Event-ID` (non-numeric, negative, or out of uint64 range) is rejected (e.g. 400) or otherwise explicitly signalled — never silently treated as 0 or MaxUint64; a test pins each malformed class.
- [ ] The `SubscribeFrom` doc comment and the implementation agree on when `gap` is set, for since = 0, since inside the retained window, and since beyond it.

*Filed by the fleet issue creator (lane A) with file:line evidence, premise log, and a prepared-but-unexecuted Go probe; see the agent note for the packet/state details.*
