Phase 3 of design #1675 (mcpx elicitation broker hygiene). Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-elicitation-broker-hygiene.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. **Gated on Phases 1–2** (the owner-only store and retention/events issues of #1675).

## Scope

Make `mcpx elicit` a review-first answering surface, then tell the truth in the registers.

- URL questions (`internal/cli/elicit.go` `renderQuestion` ~L201-232): print the URL's registrable domain on its own emphasised line apart from the full URL (the full URL still prints — do not regress the covered show-full-url behaviour). If the host contains `xn--` labels or non-ASCII that renders as punycode, print an explicit warning to check the domain is the one expected.
- Form questions: pre-fill the answer example (`exampleFor` ~L275-285, today `"..."` for every field) with each property's declared schema `default` where one exists; `describeSchema` (~L235-261) gains the default in the per-field detail. No default declared → `"..."` as today.
- Review step: `mcpx elicit answer` on an interactive terminal renders the parsed answer back against the question (field → value, with credential-shaped fields — the ones `elicit.Route` routes to humans — masked) and asks for confirmation before `Broker.Respond` relays it. An opt-out flag (name settled in triage, e.g. `--yes`) preserves one-shot behaviour for scripts; non-interactive use is byte-for-byte today's behaviour.
- Truth-up: retire the six elicit-ui conformance gaps (`elicitation-app-review-modify-responses`, `elicitation-client-form-review-modify-responses`, `elicitation-client-url-show-domain-and-consent`, `elicitation-client-handle-urls-carefully`, `elicitation-client-highlight-domain`, `elicitation-client-warn-punycode`) in `internal/conformance/coverage_clientfeatures.go`, and update the remaining `#255`-tagged gap texts that Phases 1–2 made stale (`elicitation-server-follow-best-practices` mentions world-readable storage).
- Post the completion evidence on dezren39/nix#255 — commenting, not closing: its answer-validation acceptance is only partly this design's (client slice is #1484; the server-relay slice `elicitation-server-validate-received-data` stays open and must be named as remaining in the evidence comment).

## Evidence (main d39e6111, 2026-10-28)

- Origin dezren39/nix#255 acceptance: "The answering surface shows which server is asking and allows review per the elicitation UI rows." (Server display already exists in `renderQuestion` — `from <server>.<tool>` — and is covered elsewhere; the open rows are review, defaults, and URL care.)
- Gap text for all six UI gaps: "mcpx elicit prints the raw request: no review step, no domain emphasis or punycode warning, no defaults pre-filled".
- Defaults precedent: the client-side path already applies schema defaults (`mcpclient.TestElicitationDeclarations` / `TestModernElicitationAppliesSchemaDefaults`, covered rows in the conformance register) — the CLI surface is the one place defaults are ignored.

## Acceptance

- URL question render: domain on its own line; a punycode host produces the warning; a plain host does not.
- Form question render: fields with schema defaults show those defaults in the detail and in the answer example; fields without keep `"..."`.
- Interactive `answer`: the parsed answer is rendered (credential-shaped values masked) and nothing is relayed until confirmed; declining the review relays nothing. With the opt-out flag, and non-interactively, behaviour matches today.
- Six elicit-ui gaps retired with tests/render fixtures as evidence; stale `#255` gap texts updated.
- Evidence comment posted on dezren39/nix#255 naming what landed and what remains (server-relay validation slice).
- CI green for `pkgs/mcpx` (tests run in GitHub Actions).

body:
## Summary

`pkgs/id` petnames exist so a contact can never be mistaken for someone else: the module doc (`src/petname.rs:1-7`) says the store "refuses a petname that could be taken for someone else's name", and `normalize_name` promises a petname "cannot contain control characters". Both promises are defeated by Unicode **format characters (general category Cf)**:

- `normalize_name` (`src/petname.rs:217-230`) refuses a name when `name.chars().any(char::is_control)`. Rust's `char::is_control` is category **Cc only**. Category-Cf characters — U+202E RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE, U+200B ZERO WIDTH SPACE, U+2060 WORD JOINER, U+FEFF, U+00AD SOFT HYPHEN — pass.
- `set()`'s confusability checks (`src/petname.rs:107-135`) compare `fold()` (lowercase) and `skeleton()` (look-alike map + `rn`→`m`, `vv`→`w`) verbatim. Neither strips Cf characters, so an invisible suffix changes both strings while changing nothing on screen.

## Verified shapes (main `d39e6111`, `src/petname.rs` sha256 `ff6cba65`)

Premise exercised this run with a faithful mirror of `normalize_name`/`fold`/`skeleton`/`set` (probe folder: `probe-2026-10-28-laneB-petnamecf/premise.py` + `premise.log`):

- CTRL: `Pay<TAB>Pal` → refused by normalize (Cc). `PayPa1` vs alleged `PayPal` → refused as confusable. Both guards work for the shapes they cover.
- **BUG-A (spoof):** petname `PayPal` + U+200B for a *different* contact, while another contact's alleged name is `PayPal` → **ACCEPTED** (`fold` unequal, `skeleton` unequal). The two names render identically in the directory view (`src/directory_view.rs` builds its labels from `petname::labels`), so the viewer sees two contacts apparently named exactly "PayPal" — precisely the impersonation shape the module exists to prevent.
- **BUG-B (bidi):** a petname containing U+202E is **ACCEPTED** by `normalize_name`, despite its documented "cannot contain control characters" rule. A right-to-left override in a displayed label (`Label::text`, `src/petname.rs:285-295`) can reorder the visible text around it.
- **BUG-C:** `PayPal` + U+2060 WORD JOINER → also ACCEPTED against alleged `PayPal`.

Existing tests (`src/petname.rs` `mod tests`) pin the Cc tab case and the `PayPa1` skeleton case, but no Cf character appears anywhere in the file's tests.

## Disclosure

The prepared Rust probe (`probe_laneb_test.rs`, same probe folder: asserts Cf names are refused by `normalize_name` and that the BUG-A spoof is refused by `set()`) was **NOT executed this run** — the laptop is unreachable (ongoing fleet-wide SSH outage) and verification probes are never compiled on the sandbox. Triage: run the probe first; it should currently fail on the BUG asserts. The line trace and the premise mirror above are the evidence this filing rests on.

## Why it matters

Petnames are a trust surface: they are how a viewer tells contacts apart when account names are self-asserted ("Account names are alleged"). An invisible-character spoof defeats the one check standing between an alleged name and a look-alike petname, and a bidi override in a label can misrender who is who. The fix is small and local to `petname.rs`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `normalize_name` refuses (or strips, with the choice pinned and documented) Unicode format characters (category Cf) — at minimum U+200B, U+202E/U+202A–U+202E, U+2060, U+FEFF, U+00AD — so the "no control characters" promise matches what callers and readers believe it says.
- [ ] The confusability comparison in `set()` cannot be bypassed by invisible characters: `PayPal`+ZWSP against alleged `PayPal` is refused (by the normalize refusal, an explicit Cf-strip in `fold`/`skeleton`, or both — triage pins which layer owns it).
- [ ] Tests cover at least: ZWSP suffix spoof vs an alleged name, RLO inside a name, and a Cf character against an existing petname (not only against alleged names).
- [ ] Existing petname tests still pass; legitimate names with ordinary punctuation/spaces are unaffected.

Related but distinct: #1499 (torn final line in `petnames.jsonl`) is the same file's crash-recovery defect — different function, different fix.

title: mcpx(recipes): a JSON default is truncated at the first bracket inside its strings — splitDefault counts brackets with no string state

body:
## Summary

`internal/recipes`' `@param` default splitter counts brackets without any string state, so a JSON default whose string values contain a bracket character is truncated at that character. The truncated fragment becomes the placeholder's `Default`: `Render` splices it verbatim into the script (invalid literal, script does not parse), the description is polluted with the remainder, and `FormSchema` silently drops the default — losing exactly the headless fallback the schema exists to carry.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `1b22a6e3`)

`pkgs/mcpx/internal/recipes/recipes.go` (sha256 `30dbbf05…`):

- `splitDefault` (:194-226): the quoted branch (first char `"`, `'`, `` ` ``) honours backslash escapes, but the bracket branch only counts `open`/`close` bytes — a `}` or `]` **inside a quoted string within the literal** decrements the depth and ends the value early, and the matching quote is never tracked.
- `Parse` (:115-124) stores that fragment as `Placeholder.Default` and takes the rest as the description, so the description also gains the garbage tail (`b"} the config`).
- `Render` (:316-317) uses `*p.Default` verbatim as the literal — the truncated, invalid fragment is what runs.
- `FormSchema`/`decodeLiteral` (:395-448): `json.Unmarshal` of the fragment fails and, for a `:json` placeholder, the default is omitted from the schema entirely — the broker contract documented on `FormSchema` ("a headless caller times out and the defaults are what remains") silently loses this default.
- `recipes_test.go` covers a plain numeric default (`= 30`) only; there is no object/array default test at all.

### Premise exercised this run

A faithful Python mirror of `splitDefault` (`hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-recipesdefault/premise.py` + `premise.log` in the goal workspace; premise held):

- CTRL: `{"a": 1} the config` → value `{"a": 1}` (valid JSON), description `the config`. CTRL: `"a}b" the label` (quoted first char) → whole string kept.
- **BUG-A**: `{"note": "a}b"} the config` → value `{"note": "a}` (**invalid JSON**), tail `b"} the config`.
- **BUG-B**: `["a]b", "c"] the list` → value `["a]`, tail `b", "c"] the list`.
- **BUG-C**: `[{"k": "v]"}] the list` → value `[{"k": "v]`, tail `"}] the list`.

So the reachable declaration shape is an ordinary one: `// @param cfg:json = {"note": "a}b"} …` or any list/object default mentioning a bracket inside a string (a glob, a format string, a closing-brace example).

### Disclosure

The prepared Go probe (`hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-recipesdefault/probe_lanea_test.go`, package `recipes_test`) was **not executed**: the laptop was unreachable for the whole run (`~/tools/laptop-ssh.sh` → "Connection closed by UNKNOWN port 65535", the ongoing fleet outage, cf. #1667) and verification probes are never compiled on the sandbox. **Triage step 1: run the probe in the real package on the laptop/CI and confirm or correct the verdict before fixing.**

## Why it matters

Defaults are not decoration in this system: they are what a recipe runs with when nobody answers the elicitation, and what the form schema advertises. A default that is silently cut in half produces a rendered script with a syntax error at run time — after the recipe was accepted, listed, and matched as healthy — and the failure surfaces in generated code far from the one declaration line that caused it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Triage runs the prepared probe first and confirms/corrects the verdict.
- [ ] `splitDefault` tracks quoted strings (with escapes) inside bracketed literals: a bracket character inside a string does not change the depth, for both `{…}` and `[…]` defaults, including nesting of the other bracket type.
- [ ] After the fix, the BUG-A/B/C declarations parse to the full literal as `Default`, the true description as `Description`, `Render` with no values emits the full literal, and `FormSchema` carries the decoded default.
- [ ] An unterminated literal (no closing bracket outside a string) keeps today's fall-back behaviour (whole rest as the value) or the new behaviour is stated and pinned by a test.
- [ ] New tests in `internal/recipes` cover object and array defaults containing brackets inside strings; existing tests pass.
- [ ] The ruling for apostrophes inside strings (e.g. `{"note": "don't }"`) is pinned by a test — only the active quote character may close a string.

Cross-link: sibling defect in the same file, #1670 (`refs`/`substitute` treat `@name` inside comments and strings as placeholders) — same lexical-state root, separate fix.

body:
## Summary

`internal/recipes`' placeholder scanner says it ignores comments and strings — but it implements neither. An `@name` mentioned in a `//` comment, a `/* */` comment, or inside a string literal becomes a **required** placeholder: the daemon elicits for it / returns 422 ("still needs …") when it is unfilled, and if it *is* filled, `Render` splices the JSON-encoded value **inside the string literal**, producing a script that does not parse.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `1b22a6e3`)

`pkgs/mcpx/internal/recipes/recipes.go` (sha256 `30dbbf05…`):

- `refs()` doc, :236-237: *"refs finds every `@name` in the body, ignoring declarations, comments and anything inside a string."*
- `refs()` implementation, :238-276: the only line ever skipped is a declaration line (`declLine.MatchString`, :242). There is **no comment state and no string state** — every line is scanned byte-by-byte, and any `@` not preceded by a word byte starts a name.
- `Parse` turns every undeclared ref into `Placeholder{Name, TypeString, Required: true}` (:158-166 of the listing in this run's trace: the "used but never declared" loop).
- `substitute()` (:335-356) repeats the same stateless scan, so a filled value is replaced in strings and comments too. For a string placeholder the literal is the JSON encoding **including the quotes** (`literal()`), which is correct in code position and corrupting inside an existing string.
- Consumers: daemon `routes_consumer.go:312,325` gates the run on `rec.Missing(values)` (elicitation, then 422 "… still needs …"), :331 `Render`s and runs the result; CLI `scripts.go:331` parses the same way. `recipes_test.go` pins a code-position ref and the email shape (`someone@example.com`, saved only by the preceding-word-byte rule) — there is no comment-mention or string-mention test.

### Premise exercised this run

A faithful Python mirror of `refs()` + `substitute()` + `Render()`'s placeholder logic (`hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-recipesrefs/premise.py` + `premise.log` in the goal workspace; all expectations held):

- CTRL-A: `await demo.echo({ message: @who });` → placeholder `who`, renders with `"hi"`, valid.
- CTRL-B: `const to = "someone@example.com";` → no placeholder (existing pinned behaviour).
- **BUG-A**: `// thanks @alice for the review` → placeholder `alice` (required); rendering with no values errors `recipe x needs alice` — a thank-you in a comment blocks the run behind an elicitation/422 for a value that is never used in code.
- **BUG-B**: `const note = "ask @admin first";` → placeholder `admin`; rendering with `admin="root"` yields `const note = "ask "root" first";` — **`node --check` rejects the rendered script**, while the original source passes `node --check`.
- **BUG-C**: `/* ping @oncall on failure */` → placeholder `oncall`, same as BUG-A.

### Disclosure

The prepared Go probe (`hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-recipesrefs/probe_lanea_test.go`, package `recipes_test`, three tests: comment mention, string mention, code-position control) was **not executed**: the laptop was unreachable for the whole run (`~/tools/laptop-ssh.sh` → "Connection closed by UNKNOWN port 65535", the ongoing fleet outage, cf. #1667) and verification probes are never compiled on the sandbox. **Triage step 1: run the probe in the real package on the laptop/CI and confirm or correct these verdicts before fixing.**

## Why it matters

Recipes are saved scripts run with the user's credentials. The ordinary ways a person writes a script — crediting someone in a comment, writing `"ask @admin first"` in a message string, a handle in a template — silently become holes that (a) block the deterministic, no-model recipe path behind a pointless question or a 422, and (b) when answered, corrupt the very string they were mentioned in, so the rendered script fails to parse at run time with an error pointing at generated code. The function's own doc comment already states the intended behaviour; the implementation just never grew the state machine.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Triage runs the prepared probe first and confirms/corrects the verdicts above.
- [ ] `@name` inside `//` comments, `/* */` comments, and string literals (single, double, and template literals) does **not** create a placeholder, is not listed by `Missing`, is not in the elicitation `FormSchema`, and is left byte-identical by `Render`.
- [ ] A code-position `@name` (including the email non-case, `someone@example.com`) behaves exactly as today; existing `recipes` tests pass unchanged.
- [ ] The ruling for template literals is stated explicitly (interpolations `${…}` are code; the literal text around them is string) and pinned by a test.
- [ ] The ruling for regex literals is stated (either handled, or explicitly documented as out of scope in the `refs` doc comment) — cf. the same lexical-state problem in #1659's scripting validator and #1644's secrets scanner; whether the three scanners share a helper is triage's call.
- [ ] New tests in `internal/recipes` cover: comment mention, block-comment mention, string mention (render leaves the line untouched), and a mixed script whose only real hole is in code position.
- [ ] Either `refs`' doc comment and code agree, or the doc comment is corrected to describe the behaviour triage pins.

Cross-link: sibling defect in the same file's declaration parsing filed separately (splitDefault bracket counting) — the two share the "scanner without lexical state" root but need separate fixes.

body:
## Problem

`openapi.Build` never applies the OpenAPI parameter-identity rule (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/openapi/openapi.go`, main c04a9430, sha256 79b465b9). Per the spec, a parameter is unique by *(name, location)*, and a parameter declared at path-item level can be **overridden** at operation level — the operation declaration replaces the shared one, it does not add a second parameter. The code concatenates both lists and treats every entry as distinct, with two observable consequences.

### Shape A — an overridden required parameter is duplicated in `required`: the advertised schema is invalid JSON Schema

- `Build` (:312): `params := append(append([]Parameter{}, item.Parameters...), op.Parameters...)` — no (name, `in`) dedup anywhere.
- `buildSchema` keys `properties` by name only (:491), so the property entry coincidentally ends up the operation's (matching override semantics), but it appends the name to `required` once **per occurrence** (:492-494).
- Example: path item `/pets/{id}` declares `{name: id, in: path, required: true}` and the GET operation redeclares it (the standard override, e.g. to refine its description). The generated tool's `inputSchema` is `{"type":"object","properties":{"id":…},"required":["id","id"]}`.
- JSON Schema requires the elements of `required` to be unique. The schema mcpx advertises for the tool (via `mcpx api tools` and the MCP server surface, `internal/cli/openapi_tools.go`) is therefore invalid for any spec using this spec-sanctioned pattern, and strict MCP clients/validators may refuse the tool outright.

### Shape B — same name in two locations: two distinct parameters conflated by the name-keyed schema

- A query parameter `key` and a header parameter `key` are *distinct* parameters per the spec (uniqueness is name+location), and both may legitimately apply to one operation (one at path level, one at operation level, or both at operation level).
- The flattened schema can only show one of them: `properties` is keyed by name (:491), so the later entry's type/description/location note silently replaces the earlier one's — one parameter is invisible to the caller.
- `Call` (:565-586) nevertheless iterates *both* entries in `Tool.Params` and routes each by its own `in`, sending the single `args["key"]` value in **both** locations. The wire behaviour and the advertised schema describe different operations.

## Evidence

1. Line trace on main c04a9430 (file sha256 `79b465b9636fa1e51025824ff395e27bf28d0849fcb0c4bd7a2490a097b7cde5`): concatenation at :312 with no dedup; `props[p.Name] = entry` :491; `required = append(required, p.Name)` :492-494 with no uniqueness check; `Call` routing loop :565-586 (`path` :572, `header` :576-577, default→query :585) iterates every entry in `spec.Params`. `openapi_test.go` has no path-item-vs-operation parameter case.
2. Premise exercised this run with a faithful mirror of the three code paths (goal `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-openapi-paramoverride/premise.py` + `premise.log`): shape A → `required == ["id","id"]`; shape B → schema advertises only the header entry while the mirrored Call sends the value in both query and header.

**Disclosure:** the prepared Go probe (`hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-openapi-paramoverride/probe_laneb_test.go`, package `openapi_test`; asserts a duplicate-free `required` for the override spec and pins shape B's schema/wire conflation against an httptest server) was **not executed** — the laptop was unreachable this run (SSH tunnel closes immediately) and probes are never compiled on the sandbox. Triage should run the probe first and correct this issue if any verdict differs.

## Why it matters

Path-level parameters with operation-level overrides are a normal, spec-endorsed way to write OpenAPI documents (shared path/header parameters refined per operation). For those documents mcpx currently publishes an invalid tool schema, and for same-name cross-location parameters it publishes a schema that does not describe what the call actually sends.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Triage runs the prepared probe and confirms/corrects both verdicts.
- [ ] Parameter resolution follows the spec: an operation-level parameter with the same (name, `in`) as a path-level one replaces it exactly once in `Tool.Params` and in the schema.
- [ ] Generated `inputSchema` never contains a duplicated `required` entry, for any spec; a regression test pins the override pattern.
- [ ] Shape B gets a stated ruling (e.g. schema disambiguation, a Build-time error naming the collision, or documented conflation with matching Call behaviour) pinned by a test — the schema and the wire must not silently disagree.
- [ ] Existing `internal/openapi` tests pass; specs without path-level parameters are unchanged.

Distinct from #1668 (same package, different defect: map-iteration nondeterminism in name disambiguation and the media pick; this issue is deterministic and concerns parameter identity).

body:
# mcpx(mcpheaders): the server's numeric header comparison only forgives the float form in the header — a body written `42.0` (or `4.2e1`) is rejected as 'not an integer' before the comparison runs

## Problem

For a 2026-07-28 `x-mcp-header` integer parameter, `mcpheaders.Check` (the server half, called from `mcpserver`'s `checkParamHeaders`) is supposed to compare the `Mcp-Param-*` header and the body value **numerically**: its own fallback comment says "Integers compare numerically: 42.0 in a header is 42", and the conformance catalogue quotes the spec's SHOULD the same way (`streamable-http-numeric-compare`: "servers **SHOULD** compare the header value and the body value numerically rather than as strings", `internal/conformance/requirements.json`).

That forgiveness is one-sided. The numeric fallback is only reached for a body value that `plain()` has already rendered, and `plain()` renders a JSON number exclusively through `strconv.ParseInt` — so any mathematically-integral body literal that is not plain decimal digits (`42.0`, `42.00`, `4.2e1`, `-0.0`) fails with `<path>: <literal> is not an integer` **before any comparison happens**, and `checkParamHeaders` turns that error into a header-mismatch rejection (HTTP 400 / JSON-RPC `-32020`). A client that serialises an integer argument as `42.0` — a form JSON Schema's `integer` type accepts, and a form several JSON encoders emit for a whole-valued number — is rejected even when its header says exactly `42`, and even when header and body are byte-identical (`42.0` / `42.0`).

mcpx's own Go client never trips this (its arguments are re-marshalled, and Go renders a whole float64 as `42`), which is presumably why it survived: the failing sender is any *other* MCP client talking to an mcpx server, or a raw-JSON argument forwarded into `Values` (which shares `plain()`).

## Evidence (verified this run, main `c5e06ee8`)

- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/mcpheaders/mcpheaders.go` (sha256 `d3332412…`):
  - `Check` (:195) decodes the arguments with `UseNumber`, so the body number keeps its raw literal text.
  - For each param, `Check` first calls `plain(root, p)` (:214) and returns its error immediately (:215-217).
  - `plain` (:282-310): a `json.Number` goes through `strconv.ParseInt(x.String(), 10, 64)` (:293) — an optional sign plus digits only — and errors `"<path>: <literal> is not an integer"` for `42.0` / `4.2e1` / `42.00`; it also refuses |value| > 2^53−1.
  - The numeric fallback (:232-240, `ParseFloat` on both sides) sits *after* `plain()` succeeds and the string comparison fails — unreachable for a float-form body.
- Pinned asymmetry: `internal/mcpserver/transport_test.go` (sha256 `9ad0a027…`) test `param-header-integer-compared-numerically` accepts body `{"n": 42}` with header `42.0` and rejects header `43` — the mirror-image cases (float-form body) are not tested anywhere; there is no `*_test.go` in `internal/mcpheaders` at all.
- Caller: `internal/mcpserver/transport.go` `checkParamHeaders` (:352+, sha256 `5b2ca2fe…`) maps any `Check` error to `headerMismatch` — so this is a request rejection, not a warning. Its own doc comment states the intent the code misses: "a value mcpx would send is a value mcpx accepts".
- Premise exercised this run (faithful mirror of `plain()` + `Check` control flow; `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-mcpheaders/premise.py` + `premise.log`):
  - CTRL body `42`, header `42.0` → ACCEPT (numeric fallback)
  - CTRL body `42`, header `42` → ACCEPT; header `43` → REJECT (true mismatch)
  - BUG-A body `42.0`, header `42` → REJECT, `n: 42.0 is not an integer`, before any comparison
  - BUG-B body `42.0`, header `42.0` → REJECT (identical values!)
  - BUG-C body `4.2e1`, header `42` → REJECT, same error
  - BUG-D body `42.00`, header `42` → REJECT; BUG-E body `-0.0`, header `0` → REJECT

**Disclosure:** the prepared Go probe (`hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-mcpheaders/probe_lanea_test.go`, a `Check` test in the real package) was **not executed** this run — the laptop was unreachable (the SSH tunnel closes immediately, the outage several fleet runs have now hit) and probes are never compiled on the sandbox. Triage: run the probe first; if any traced verdict differs, narrow this issue to what the probe shows.

## Why it matters

The header check exists so a gateway routing on the header and a server acting on the body cannot disagree about a request. Rejecting a request whose header and body *do* agree — numerically and, in BUG-B, byte-for-byte — turns an interoperability SHOULD into a hard failure for exactly the foreign clients the 2026-07-28 header scheme is meant to interoperate with, with an error message ("not an integer") that misdescribes a valid integer and points the sender at the wrong fix. The same `plain()` gate sits in client-side `Values`, so a raw-JSON `42.0` argument also cannot be *sent* by mcpx even though mcpx's server would have to accept its numeric equal.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Check` accepts every numerically-equal header/body pair for an integer-annotated parameter, whichever side carries the float/exponent form: at minimum body `42.0`/`42.00`/`4.2e1` with header `42`, body `42` with header `42.0` (already pinned), and body `42.0` with header `42.0`.
- [ ] Genuinely unequal pairs still reject (header `43` vs body `42` or `42.0`), and a non-integral body or header (`1.5`) still rejects — with an error that says the value is not an integer / does not match, not one produced before the comparison by the rendering step.
- [ ] Precision is not silently lost in the fix: two distinct integers above 2^53 must not compare equal via a float64 conversion (compare as integers / big values, or keep a named refusal for out-of-safe-range values — and state whether that refusal applies to the server `Check` path as well as client `Values`, since today `plain()`'s JS safe-range cap also rejects a perfectly matching `9007199254740993`/`9007199254740993` pair server-side).
- [ ] Tests pin the symmetric cases at the `mcpheaders.Check` level (the package currently has no test file of its own) and extend the `transport_test.go` numeric-compare case to a float-form body.
- [ ] `Values` (client side) renders the same canonical integer for a `42.0`-formed argument as for `42`, or the asymmetry between the two halves is explicitly documented in the package doc.

Triage note: where the canonicalisation lives (inside `plain()` vs a numeric-compare that runs before rendering) and the >2^53 server-side ruling are small contract pins for the queue lane; the defect — a comparison that never runs for one side's float form — is not in doubt.

title: mcpx(logstore): the 'read-only' log sql guard admits mutating PRAGMAs — journal_mode=DELETE persistently un-WALs index.db, user_version/application_id rewrite its header

labels.name: kind/security

labels.name: task/triage

body:
## Summary

`mcpx log sql` is documented as running **read-only** SQL (`internal/cli/manual.go:502`: "`log sql` runs read-only SQL"), and `CheckReadOnly` in `internal/logstore/sql.go` is the guard that is supposed to keep that promise. The guard allow-lists the `pragma` verb — and then never checks for an assignment. A value-carrying PRAGMA sails through, `RunSQL` executes it, and several of those PRAGMAs **mutate persistent database state**:

- `PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE` — switches `index.db` out of WAL mode **persistently**, undoing the mode `logstore.Open` deliberately sets (`internal/logstore/store.go:129-134`: "WAL, because the daemon may be writing while the CLI reads…") for every later process that opens the index.
- `PRAGMA user_version=42` / `PRAGMA application_id=7` — write header fields of the database file.
- `PRAGMA writable_schema=ON`, `PRAGMA synchronous=…`, `PRAGMA foreign_keys=…` — change per-connection state on a handle drawn from the shared `database/sql` pool, so the setting can leak into later statements in the same process.

The header comment on the guard even asserts the opposite of what the code does (`internal/logstore/sql.go:13-14`): "PRAGMA is allowed because that is how you ask SQLite about itself, and **the mutating pragmas need a value that this refuses anyway**." Nothing in `CheckReadOnly` (sql.go:20-51) refuses a value: it strips comments, checks for a second statement, allow-lists the first word, and — for `with` only — scans for write verbs. There is no `=` check, no pragma-name allow-list, nothing.

## Evidence (verified this run, main c69b7426)

Trace of `CheckReadOnly` (`internal/logstore/sql.go:20-51`, sha256 `458efae6…`) for `PRAGMA user_version=42`:

1. `stripSQLComments` — unchanged.
2. One-statement check — no `;`, passes.
3. Verb extraction splits on space/tab/newline/`(`/`;` → first field `PRAGMA` → lowercased `pragma` ∈ `readOnlyVerbs` (sql.go:15-17).
4. The write-verb scan runs only when the verb is `with`. Nothing else inspects the statement. **Returns nil.**

`RunSQL` (sql.go:101-105) then hands the string to `s.db.Query(query)` verbatim; SQLite executes a PRAGMA assignment as part of answering a query.

Premise exercised this run with Python's sqlite3 (same SQLite semantics; log in the creator's run records, `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-pragma/premise.py` / `premise.log` in the goal workspace):

```
initial journal_mode: wal
'PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE' executed via query path -> [('delete',)]
'PRAGMA user_version=42' executed via query path -> []
'PRAGMA application_id=7' executed via query path -> []
after reopen journal_mode: delete
after reopen user_version: 42
after reopen application_id: 7
```

All three assignments executed through the query path and **persisted across a reopen**; the read pragma `table_info` works normally for contrast.

Existing coverage: `TestReadOnlyGuardRejectsAnythingThatWrites` (`internal/logstore/logstore_test.go:610-634`) covers write verbs, multi-statements, comment-hidden verbs and a CTE-hidden DELETE, plus `PRAGMA table_info(records)` as an allowed read — but no value-carrying PRAGMA in either list.

**Disclosure:** the prepared Go probe (`probe_laneb_test.go` in the same probe folder — it asserts the three assignments pass `CheckReadOnly` today and that journal_mode/user_version mutations persist across `logstore.Open` after `RunSQL`) was **not executed**: the laptop was unreachable this run and verification probes are never compiled on the sandbox. Triage should run the probe first and correct this evidence if any traced verdict differs. The Python premise above *was* executed and is the load-bearing verification for SQLite's side of the behaviour; the Go-side half is the line trace of a 32-line guard function.

## Why it matters

- The one persistent mutation, `journal_mode`, attacks the store's own concurrency design: Open() pays for WAL + busy_timeout specifically so the daemon can ingest while the CLI reads. One `log sql` invocation silently reverts the file to rollback-journal mode for every future opener, and nothing anywhere reports the change — later lock contention would look like a flake, not like this.
- The guard's own comment tells the next reader the case is handled, so the gap is self-concealing: exactly the kind of "read-only" surface an agent (the manual addresses agents as much as people) will trust with generated queries.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `CheckReadOnly` rejects value-carrying PRAGMAs (any `PRAGMA name = value` / `PRAGMA name(value)` assignment form), or PRAGMA is restricted to a named allow-list of read pragmas.
- [ ] Read pragmas keep working, pinned by tests: `PRAGMA table_info(records)`, `index_list`, `journal_mode` (no value), `user_version` (no value).
- [ ] New guard tests pin the rejected shapes: at minimum `journal_mode=DELETE`, `journal_mode=WAL`, `user_version=42`, `application_id=7`, `writable_schema=ON`, including case/whitespace variants (e.g. `pragma  user_version = 42`).
- [ ] The header comment at sql.go:13-14 is corrected to describe what the guard actually enforces.
- [ ] Triage first runs the prepared Go probe (see Disclosure) and confirms the journal_mode/user_version mutations reproduce through `RunSQL` itself; if the modernc driver's query path does not step a no-row PRAGMA assignment, narrow this issue to the shapes that do execute and say which.

title: mcpx(tui): rendering measures strings in bytes, not terminal cells — truncation can emit invalid UTF-8 and wide-rune rows misalign every table

body:
## Problem

mcpx's terminal UI measures, pads and truncates strings in **bytes**, not terminal cells. Any non-ASCII text in a namespace name, tool name, log message or error — a server named with CJK characters, a path with an accented character, an em-dash in a log line — is rendered wrong in two distinct ways:

1. **Truncation can emit invalid UTF-8.** `truncate` slices the string by bytes, so the cut can land inside a multi-byte rune, leaving a lone lead byte in front of the ellipsis. The terminal receives bytes that are not valid UTF-8.
2. **Table columns misalign and the width budget is wrong.** Column widths are `len(cell)` (bytes) and `pad` pads to a byte length, so a wide-rune cell reserves too many columns and receives too little padding: rows in the same table end at different terminal-cell positions, and `shrink` spends the terminal's column budget in bytes.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `c69b7426`)

The measurement family is all in `pkgs/mcpx/internal/tui/data.go`:

- `data.go:159,163-164` — `Table.Render` computes column widths as `len(c)` / `len(cell)` (bytes).
- `data.go:168` — `shrink(widths, width-2*(len(widths)-1))` treats those byte widths against `width`, which is the viewport's **column** count (`m.body.Width`, `tui.go:657` / `tui.go:648`).
- `data.go:185` — every cell goes through `pad(truncate(cell, widths[i]), widths[i])`.
- `data.go:222-226` — `pad` compares and pads by `len(s)` bytes.
- `data.go:229-237` — `truncate` returns `s[:n-1] + "…"` — a byte slice.
- Callers beyond tables: `tui.go:648` truncates every log line to `m.body.Width`, `tui.go:650` pads the selected line to `m.body.Width`, and `tui.go:747` truncates error text to 60.

Premise exercised this run (script + log in the goal's `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-tuiwidth/`): applying the exact byte operations from `truncate`/`pad` to UTF-8 byte strings — bit-for-bit what Go does, since Go `len`/slicing are byte-based — gives:

- `truncate("héllo", 3)` → bytes `68 C3 E2 80 A6` — **invalid UTF-8** (lone `0xC3` lead byte before the ellipsis).
- `truncate("サーバーabc", 5)` → bytes `E3 82 B5 E3 E2 80 A6` — **invalid UTF-8** (cut inside the second rune).
- `truncate("café — done", 6)` → valid (control: the cut happened to land on a rune boundary).
- `pad("サーバー", 12)` adds **no** padding (the string is already 12 bytes) although it occupies only 8 terminal cells, so in a table whose ASCII row is padded to 12 the wide row ends 4 cells early.
- `len("サーバー")` = 12 bytes vs 8 cells; `len("héllo")` = 6 bytes vs 5 cells.

`grep` confirms no rune/cell handling anywhere in the package: no `utf8.` use in `internal/tui`, and `tui_test.go` exercises truncation only for ASCII log lines. The module already carries `github.com/mattn/go-runewidth` (indirect, via lipgloss/bubbletea) and `github.com/charmbracelet/x/ansi`, so a cell-width helper is available in-tree.

**Disclosure:** the prepared Go probe (`probe_lanea_test.go` in the same probe folder; tests `truncate` validity and `Table.Render` alignment for a mixed wide/ASCII table) was **NOT executed** — the laptop was unreachable for the whole filing run (SSH tunnel closes immediately, an outage several fleet runs have now hit) and verification probes are never compiled on the sandbox. Triage should run the probe first and correct this evidence if any verdict differs. The premise exercise above plus the line-by-line trace are the verification this run stands on.

## Why it matters

The TUI is the operator's live view of the daemon (namespaces, tools, logs, stats). Non-ASCII names and messages are ordinary — file paths, server names and log text are not ASCII-guaranteed. Today such rows render with replacement glyphs where truncation split a rune, and tables quietly lose their alignment, which is exactly the "findable row" property `Table.Render`'s own doc says the truncation order exists to protect.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Triage runs the prepared probe in `internal/tui` and confirms/corrects the two verdicts (invalid UTF-8 from `truncate`; cell misalignment in `Table.Render`).
- [ ] `truncate` never emits invalid UTF-8 for any input/width, and its result fits the requested number of terminal cells (ellipsis included).
- [ ] `pad` and `Table.Render` column widths are computed in terminal cells, so rows mixing ASCII, accented and wide (CJK) text align, and `shrink`'s budget is spent in cells.
- [ ] Regression tests cover at least: truncation cutting inside a multi-byte rune, a table mixing a wide-rune cell with ASCII cells, and the log-line path (`tui.go:648`).
- [ ] Existing `internal/tui` tests still pass; ASCII rendering is byte-for-byte unchanged.

body:
## Summary

`mcpauth` expands **every** credential field with `os.Expand`, so a *literal* credential containing a `$` segment is silently rewritten: `$2`, `$$`, `$5` are eaten as special shell variables, and `$NAME` splices the daemon's own environment into the credential. Literal credentials are an expected shape in these fields — `redactRef` exists precisely because a config may hold a literal secret — yet any literal password/token/value containing `$` followed by a letter, digit or shell-special character is corrupted, and the phantom variable name it invents lands in `Missing`, which the pool turns into a hard refusal naming a variable nobody referenced.

## Evidence (verified on main 7eb930a4, this run)

- pkgs/mcpx/internal/mcpauth/mcpauth.go:122-135 — `expand` runs `os.Expand(v, …)` unconditionally and appends the referenced name to `out.Missing` whenever the looked-up value is empty. It is applied to bearer `Token` (:166), basic `Username`/`Password` (:172), header `Value` (:182), query `ParamValue` (:193) and every non-passthrough `Env` value (:148).
- Go's `os.Expand` semantics, read this run in the installed stdlib (`~/tools/go/src/os/env.go:16-109`): `getShellName` treats a digit or one of `* # $ @ ! ? -` as a complete special-variable name, and otherwise consumes the longest `[A-Za-z0-9_]` run. So in a literal:
  - `hunter$2` → `hunter`, with phantom variable `2` reported missing;
  - `pa$$word` → `paword`, with phantom variable `$` reported missing;
  - `cost is $5` (an env value) → `cost is `, phantom `5`;
  - `s3cret$HOME` → `s3cret` + the daemon's actual `$HOME` value spliced in — **no** Missing entry, no error: the server silently receives a different password than the one configured and returns a 401 nobody can interpret, the exact failure this package's header says it exists to prevent.
- The phantom Missing is not advisory: internal/pool/pool.go `resolveAuth` (:766-777) refuses the server outright when `len(r.Missing) > 0`, with `auth: 2 not set in the daemon's environment` — naming a "variable" that appears nowhere in the user's config.
- Literals are expected in these fields: `redactRef` (mcpauth.go:226-237) redacts any value that is not a `$`-reference as "(literal, redacted)", i.e. `Describe` is built for literal secrets sitting in `Token`/`Password`/`Value`. The documented expansion contract names only the braced form: Token's doc (:34-35) says "Expanded, so ${GITHUB_TOKEN} works". No doc found this run states that a bare `$` in a literal is also a reference, and there is no escape mechanism.
- Existing tests cover only the `${VAR}` forms (mcpauth_test.go:14, :26, :79, :83; resolvewith_test.go:19, :38) — no literal containing `$` is tested.

**Disclosure:** the prepared probe test (in the goal's hidden_files, `probe-2026-10-28-laneB-authexpand/probe_laneb_test.go`) was NOT executed this run — the laptop probe host was unreachable for the whole run (the tailnet SSH tunnel closes immediately; the same outage the previous three creator runs hit) and probes are never compiled on the sandbox. The verdicts above follow deterministically from `os.Expand`'s source in the installed Go tree (cited above) traced through `expand`; triage should run the probe first and correct this evidence if any traced verdict differs.

## Why it matters

Passwords and opaque tokens containing `$` are ordinary. Today such a credential either (a) refuses the server before any request with an error naming a phantom variable (`2`, `$`, `5`), sending the user hunting for a config entry that does not exist, or (b) worse, when the invented name happens to be set in the daemon's environment (`$HOME`, `$USER`, `$PATH`…), silently sends a *different* credential than configured — splicing daemon environment values into a secret and producing an undebuggable 401. Both outcomes violate the package's stated purpose: report credential problems "before a request rather than as a 401" (mcpauth.go:99-101).

## Acceptance criteria

- A literal credential containing `$` reaches the transport byte-for-byte as configured: regression tests for at least the `$<digit>`, `$$`, and `$NAME-that-is-set` shapes across basic password, bearer token and an env value (run the prepared probe first and correct the issue's evidence if any traced verdict differs).
- The documented `${VAR}` reference form — and any bare-`$VAR` form triage decides to keep supporting — still expands, and a genuinely referenced unset variable is still reported in `Missing` (existing mcpauth tests pass unchanged, or are amended only where triage pins a deliberate contract change).
- The expansion contract is written down where a config author will find it (the `Auth` field docs and/or the package doc): which shapes are references, how a literal `$` is written, and what `Missing` means.
- No phantom names in `Missing`: every name it reports is a reference the config author actually wrote in a recognised reference shape.
- Full existing internal/mcpauth suite (and the pool auth tests, internal/pool/auth_test.go) pass on laptop or CI.

body:
## Summary

`mcpx completion` generates flag completion keyed only on canonical command names, so every command alias — the spellings users are steered toward — silently loses flag completion in bash and zsh, and fish never offers the aliases as subcommands at all.

## Evidence (verified on main 7eb930a4, this run)

Aliases are real, dispatchable spellings, not decoration:

- Hand-written: `ls` has aliases `list`, `namespaces` (pkgs/mcpx/internal/cli/manual.go:194); `log` has alias `logs` (manual.go:497).
- Generated operation groups derive more aliases from the operations' own names (internal/cli/opcmd.go:49-83 — `verbAliases` are described there as "the spellings a shell user reaches for before the one the operations' own names use").
- Dispatch registers a handler under every alias name (internal/cli/dispatch.go:95), and help resolves aliases to the canonical command (internal/cli/root.go:704).

But the three generators in pkgs/mcpx/internal/cli/completion.go never emit an alias:

- **bash** (completion.go:66-91): the word-1 candidate list is built from names **including** aliases (:58-65), so bash happily completes `mcpx lis<TAB>` to `list` — then the `case "$cmd"` arms are emitted per canonical `c.Name` only (:85). Under `mcpx list --<TAB>` no arm matches, `COMPREPLY` is never set, and `complete -o default` falls back to filename completion for what should be flags.
- **zsh** (completion.go:95-134): the `case "${words[2]}"` arms that carry `_arguments` are likewise canonical-only (:116). Under an alias, no arm matches and no flag is ever offered.
- **fish** (completion.go:136-157): the subcommand candidates are `-a <c.Name>` only (:141-142) — `list`, `logs`, `namespaces` are not even offered — and the flag rules are keyed `-n '__fish_seen_subcommand_from <c.Name>'` (:146), which does not fire when the token on the command line is the alias.

Existing tests do not cover this: internal/cli/completion_test.go (52 lines) pins only the zsh quoting regression from #272. Dedup: issue search (open + closed) for completion/alias finds #272 (zsh parse failure, closed) and no alias filing.

**Disclosure:** the prepared probe test (in the goal's hidden_files, `probe-2026-10-28-laneB-complalias/probe_laneb_test.go`) was NOT executed this run — the laptop probe host was unreachable for the whole run (the tailnet SSH tunnel closes immediately; the same outage the previous three creator runs hit) and probes are never compiled on the sandbox. The defect is established by a line-by-line trace of the three generators against the alias registration sites above; triage should run the probe first and correct this evidence if any traced claim differs.

## Why it matters

completion.go's own header states the point of generating the scripts: "a new flag is completable the moment it is declared" instead of rotting silently. Aliases are exactly where that promise breaks: they are the spellings opcmd.go says shell users reach for *first*, they are what help prints as "also: …", and under them the generated completion silently degrades (bash: filenames instead of flags; zsh: nothing; fish: the command itself is not offered). Users reasonably conclude the command has no flags, or that completion is broken generally. The three shells also disagree with each other about whether an alias exists at all.

## Acceptance criteria

- bash and zsh: typing any alias of a command offers that command's flags (e.g. `mcpx list --<TAB>` and `mcpx logs --<TAB>` behave like the canonical spellings), by combined case patterns, separate arms, or resolving the alias before the case — the mechanism is triage's choice.
- fish: aliases are offered as subcommand completions and the flag rules fire under them.
- Regression tests in internal/cli/completion_test.go assert alias coverage for all three shells, including at least one generated op-group alias (not only the hand-written `ls`/`log` aliases), so a future alias cannot silently strand again.
- Existing completion tests pass unchanged; canonical-name completion output is unchanged apart from the added alias coverage.
- Run the prepared probe first in triage; if any traced verdict differs, correct the evidence on this issue.

title: mcpx(artifacts): a content-addressed blob can change after registration — PutFile and Export hardlink it to files outside the store, and adopt() then cements the mutated bytes under the original hash

body:
## Problem

mcpx's artifact store is content-addressed — "The body lives under its sha256" (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/artifacts/artifacts.go:16-19`) — but two of its three ingestion/delivery paths make the blob share an inode with a file outside the store, so the bytes under a hash can change after registration:

- `PutFile` (artifacts.go:226) hardlinks the caller's file into the blob path: `os.Link(path, dest)` (artifacts.go:255). The same-filesystem case is pinned by `TestPutFileHardlinksRatherThanCopies` (artifacts_test.go:139-156, asserts `sameInode`).
- `Export` (artifacts.go:551) hardlinks the blob out to the caller's directory first: `os.Link(src, dest)` (artifacts.go:560). This is the delivery path used by execsvc (internal/execsvc/execsvc.go:746).

An in-place rewrite through either outside name — the normal shape for a screenshot tool overwriting the same path, or a caller annotating/cropping a delivered file in place — rewrites the blob. From then on:

1. `Bytes`/`OpenBody` serve bytes whose sha256 no longer equals the registered `Meta.SHA256` (and whose length may no longer equal `Meta.Size`): the hash a caller compares to skip a transfer (package doc, artifacts.go:16-19) now vouches for different content.
2. Worse, `adopt` (artifacts.go:288-295) trusts an existing blob path as "Identical content by definition": a later `Put` of the *genuine* original content finds the mutated blob in place, keeps it, and registers the original hash against the mutated bytes — permanently.
3. The daemon ingests script-produced files through this path (internal/daemon/routes_exec.go:380, `store.PutFile`), so a script/tool pair that reuses an output path can corrupt an earlier run's artifact after that run already reported its hash.

## Evidence

Verified on main 7eb930a4 by (1) deterministic trace of the code above, and (2) the hardlink premise, exercised this run:

```
$ printf 'ORIGINAL' > src.png && ln src.png blob && printf 'REPLACED!' > src.png
$ cat blob        -> REPLACED!
$ stat -c '%i' src.png blob   -> identical inode
```

(log: goal hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-artifactlink/premise.log)

Disclosure: the Go probe that drives the real `Store` (`hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-artifactlink/probe_lanea_test.go` in the goal workspace: PutFile → in-place overwrite → `Bytes` returns the replacement under the original hash; re-`Put` of the original content still serves the replacement; Export → in-place edit → stored body changes) was **not executed** — the laptop (the only sanctioned probe host) was unreachable for the whole creator run (SSH tunnel closes immediately, same outage the queue lanes hit earlier today), and probes are never compiled on the sandbox. Triage: run the probe first and correct this evidence if any verdict differs.

## Why it matters

The store's whole contract is that a hash names immutable bytes: dedup, transfer-skipping, and quota accounting (`Used`, distinct hash) all assume it. A silent mutation breaks that contract with no error anywhere, and `adopt` makes the corruption sticky for the genuine content too. The hardlink itself is a deliberate, tested optimisation — the defect is that nothing protects the blob from writes through the outside name (no copy-on-ingest for mutable sources, no read-only blob mode, no hash re-verification on serve/adopt).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Triage runs the prepared probe and confirms/corrects the three verdicts (PutFile mutation, adopt stickiness, Export mutation).
- [ ] After the fix, bytes served for a registration always hash to `Meta.SHA256` and match `Meta.Size`, even when the PutFile source or an exported copy is rewritten in place afterwards.
- [ ] Regression tests cover: PutFile source overwritten in place; Export target edited in place; re-Put of original content after a mutation attempt.
- [ ] The chosen remedy (e.g. copy instead of link on ingest, link + read-only blob, copy-on-export, or verify-on-adopt) is pinned in the package doc, including what happens to the existing `TestPutFileHardlinksRatherThanCopies` expectation if the link optimisation is dropped or narrowed.

body:
## Summary

mcpx's script validator promises, in its own doc comment, that "it never marks a valid script as invalid" — but its delimiter/string scanner has no regex-literal state, so perfectly valid TypeScript whose regex literals contain a quote, a delimiter, or a comment-like sequence is reported **fatally invalid**:

- `const re = /"/;` → the `"` inside the regex opens a string that runs to the newline: "unclosed string literal".
- `const re = /\(/;` → the escaped `(` is pushed as an opening delimiter: "unclosed delimiter '('".
- `const re = /}/;` → the `}` is an "unmatched closing delimiter".
- `const re = /'/;` → same false string opening as the double-quote case.
- `const re = /\/*/;` → the escaped slash followed by a bare `*` reads as a `/*` comment opener: "unclosed multi-line comment", and the rest of the script is swallowed as comment.
- `const re = /[)]/;` → the `)` inside a character class "mismatches" the class's `[`.

`Validate` is not advisory: the daemon's diagnose route returns its verdict (and triggers repair on fatal), the intent route returns a generated script **unrun** when its diagnostics are fatal, and `scripting.Repair`/`Synthesize` reject any model-produced candidate that fails `Validate`. A user (or a model) who writes an ordinary regex — splitting on `/\s*,\s*/` is fine, but matching a quote, a paren, or a comment marker is not — gets a valid script refused, repaired-against, or bounced, with an error that blames a string/delimiter the script does not contain.

## Evidence (verified on main `adb8ceaa`, this run)

Two independent halves, both checked this run:

1. **Every snippet below is valid JavaScript**: each was passed through `node --check` this run (all six BUG sources and the division control parse cleanly), and a regex literal after `=` is an expression position, so the regex reading is the only reading.
2. **The validator's verdict on each follows deterministically from `checkSyntaxAndDelimiters`** (`validator.go:103-242`), traced character by character this run: the scanner's only states are line comment, block comment and the three string kinds; a `/` is examined solely as a comment opener, quotes open strings wherever they appear outside a string/comment, delimiters are pushed/popped wherever they appear outside a string/comment, and backslash escapes are honoured only inside strings. There is no path through the function that treats a regex literal as opaque. Results:
   - CTRL plain code, division (`10 / 2 / 5`), delimiters/quotes inside strings and inside a `//` comment → `Valid=true` (strings/comments are opaque, division slashes are inert).
   - BUG-A `const re = /"/;` → `Valid=false`, fatal "unclosed string literal" (the `"` inside the regex opens a string that runs to the newline).
   - BUG-B `const re = /\(/;` → `Valid=false`, fatal "unclosed delimiter '('" (the escaped paren is pushed; the only later parens are `test(`'s own balanced pair).
   - BUG-C `const re = /}/;` → `Valid=false`, fatal "unmatched closing delimiter".
   - BUG-D `const re = /\/*/` → `Valid=false`, fatal "unclosed multi-line comment" (the escaped slash + `*` quantifier reads as `/*`; no `*/` follows anywhere in the script, so the rest is swallowed as comment).
   - BUG-E `const re = /'/;` → `Valid=false`, fatal "unclosed string literal".
   - BUG-F `const re = /[)]/;` → `Valid=false`, fatal "mismatched delimiter" (the `)` inside the character class is closed against the class's `[`).

A ready-to-run probe test for the real `internal/scripting` package covering exactly these cases accompanies this filing in the fleet's records (`hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-scriptingregex/probe_laneb_test.go`). Disclosure: it was **not** executed this run — the laptop (the fleet's designated probe host) was unreachable for the whole run (tailnet proxy closes the SSH CONNECT; the node is listed but port 22 does not answer) and probes are never compiled on the sandbox. Triage should run the probe first; if any traced verdict differs, this issue's evidence section is the thing to correct. The trace itself caught one drafting error this run (an earlier `/\/\*/` variant does **not** trigger the comment path — there is no adjacent `/*` in it), which is why BUG-D uses the quantifier shape above.

## Where it breaks

- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/scripting/validator.go:65-71` — `Validate` runs `checkSyntaxAndDelimiters` first and marks the script invalid on any fatal diagnostic from it.
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/scripting/validator.go:103-242` — `checkSyntaxAndDelimiters` tracks line/block comments and `'`, `"` and `` ` `` strings, but has **no regex state**: a `/` is only ever examined as a comment opener (`:170-183`), quote characters start strings wherever they appear (`:186-189`), and delimiters are pushed/popped wherever they appear (`:192-214`), including inside a regex literal and inside its character classes, with backslash escapes only honoured inside strings.
- Consumers that act on the fatal verdict: `pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/routes_consumer.go:55` (diagnose route; `recordDiagnosis(..., val.HasFatal())` and repair-on-fatal), `routes_consumer.go:444` (intent route: a generated script with fatal diagnostics is returned unrun, HTTP 422), `pkgs/mcpx/internal/scripting/repair.go:85` (a repair candidate is rejected if `Validate` fails it), `pkgs/mcpx/internal/scripting/synthesize.go:49` (same gate for synthesized scripts).

Distinct from #1644 (mcpx `internal/secrets` References scan — a different scanner, in a different package, gating secret preflight): this is the `internal/scripting` delimiter scanner gating diagnosis, repair, synthesis and the intent route. The two scanners share the missing-regex-state root cause, so a shared lexical helper is worth considering in triage, but the defects, consumers and fixes are separate.

## Why it matters

Regex literals are ordinary script code — validating input, parsing tool output, matching log lines. Every such script that happens to match on a quote, bracket or comment marker is falsely condemned by the one component whose documented job is to never do that, and the downstream machinery (repair loops, unrun 422s) spends model calls and user patience "fixing" code that was never broken.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Valid scripts whose regex literals contain quotes, delimiters, character classes with brackets, or comment-like sequences (`/*`, `//` shapes) validate as valid — regression tests for at least the quote, escaped-paren, close-brace, comment-like and character-class shapes above.
- [ ] Division is not misread as a regex start (e.g. `a / b / c`, `x /= 2` keep validating, and a genuinely unclosed delimiter/string after a division is still caught) — the regex-vs-division ruling (previous-significant-token heuristic, as in the secrets scanner's design space, or a pinned alternative) is documented in the code.
- [ ] Genuinely broken scripts still fail: the existing unclosed-paren, mismatched-delimiter and unclosed-string tests pass unchanged, and a truly unclosed regex literal does not silently validate.
- [ ] Full existing `internal/scripting` suite passes; the "never marks a valid script as invalid" guarantee in `Validate`'s doc is either met by the scanner or the doc is corrected to name the pinned blind spots.

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-b, 2026-10-28 run. Deliberately not self-solved: regex-vs-division disambiguation is context-sensitive (the same design pin #1644 faces in the secrets scanner), and whether the two scanners should share one lexical helper is a triage-level call — the fix is not a trivial one-liner.

title: mcpx(tasks): TTL is clocked from creation, not completion — a task still working at its TTL is deleted and cancelled mid-run, and a finished task's retention shrinks by its runtime

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

mcpx's task store (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/tasks`) starts a task's TTL clock at **creation**, but the TTL is documented — in mcpx's own configuration reference — as retention for a **finished** task: `tasks.ttl` "governs: how long a finished task's result is kept" (`pkgs/mcpx/docs/configuration.md:618`, default `10m0s`). The store instead expires a task `ttl` after it was started, whatever state it is in:

- `tasks.go:389-395` — `Start` arms `time.AfterFunc(ttl)` unconditionally; when it fires it deletes the task from the in-memory map and the DB **and calls `cancel()`**, killing the work's context mid-run.
- `tasks.go:210,254-255` — the persistent reload path computes the same creation-based deadline (`expiresAtMs := createdMs + ttlMs`) and re-arms deletion for the remainder, so a restart does not rescue the semantics.

Verified on main `adb8ceaa` with a probe test in the real `internal/tasks` package ON THE LAPTOP (detached worktree, removed after; tasks.go sha256 `3d274167…` identical in both clones; probe + log in the fleet bookkeeping `probe-2026-10-28-laneA-taskttl/`, run twice with identical output; the full existing `internal/tasks` suite passes). Control: a 50 ms task under a 5 s TTL completes and stays collectable.

## Bug A — a task still Working at its TTL is deleted and cancelled mid-run

Probe: TTL 300 ms, work that needs 900 ms:

- at +500 ms (work still running) `Get(id)` → missing;
- the work's context was cancelled at +301 ms;
- after the work finishes anyway, `Result(id)` → `ErrNoTask` ("no task …; it may have expired") — the produced result is uncollectable, and a polling client cannot distinguish "the work was killed by its own retention clock" from "you invented that handle".

This is the exact workload the package exists for — its doc: a task is "the right shape for a genuinely slow call — a build, a crawl, a browser session — where holding a request open for minutes invites every intermediary to time it out". With the default 10-minute TTL, any task-shaped call that legitimately runs longer than 10 minutes is cancelled by the store itself, and a client that requested a small `ttl` (e.g. the 1000 ms values used in the server's own tests) gets its still-running call killed almost immediately.

## Bug B — a finished task's retention shrinks by however long it ran

Probe: TTL 1000 ms, work that runs 800 ms and completes. At finish+300 ms the task is already gone. A task that runs 9m59s of a 10-minute TTL keeps its finished result for ~1 second; the client's window to collect `tasks/result` races the deletion regardless of how promptly it polls after completion. The retention a caller actually gets is `ttl − runtime`, not the documented `ttl`.

## Call-site nuance for triage

One caller passes a deadline-flavoured TTL: `internal/daemon/input_required.go:100` starts the parked `/v1/call` task with `proto.askTTL` (15 m, "how long the daemon keeps the call and its result", `docs/protocol.md:559`). If that call site relies on expiry to end an unanswered call, the fix must give it an explicit runtime deadline rather than quietly keeping today's overloaded meaning; the other call sites (`internal/mcpserver/tasks.go:74`, `internal/daemon/routes_exec.go:245`, `internal/daemon/routes_proto.go:434`, `internal/daemon/ops.go:525`) pass plain retention values from request `task.ttl` / `tasks.ttl`.

## Acceptance criteria

- A task still in `working` / `input_required` at its TTL is **not** deleted and its context is **not** cancelled by the retention clock; it runs to a terminal state.
- A terminal task is retained for a full TTL measured from when it reached the terminal state (finish time), in memory and across a store reopen (the reload path computes remaining retention from the finish/`lastUpdatedAt` of a terminal task, not from `created_at`).
- Regression tests in `internal/tasks` cover both probe shapes: (a) work outliving its TTL completes and its result is collectable; (b) a task that runs most of its TTL still keeps its result for the full TTL after finishing.
- The `input_required` ask-deadline behaviour is either preserved through an explicit mechanism or explicitly re-ruled, with the call site and `docs/protocol.md` updated to match.
- `Task.TTL`'s doc comment (tasks.go:39, currently "milliseconds after creation that the result is kept") and any other doc that describes the clock is updated to state the ruled semantics.
- All existing `internal/tasks` tests keep passing, including `TestTaskPersistenceAcrossReopen` and the cancellation tests.

body:
Implementation piece 1 of #1511 (repo-universe issue tracker) — the universe inventory.

## Scope
- Generator (script in this repo, e.g. `tools/fleet/repo-universe/` or the fleet's existing tooling home — pick at build time and document it) that builds the universe list from two sources:
  1. GitHub enumeration: `gh api --paginate orgs/developing-today/repos` (55 repos at 2026-10-28) and `gh api --paginate users/dezren39/repos`, plus any repo named in the census that belongs to neither (recorded with its owner).
  2. The 2026-10-27 census (`all-repos-census.md`, repo-health goal workspace): every clone remote on laptop + sandbox, including the nested clones inside `/home/user/repo-archive` (crosspoint-reader ecosystem, Nicolai-Electronics/tanmatsu-*, m5stack/M5GFX, Xinyuan-LilyGO/T-Display-K230, …).
- Each entry: `owner/name`, URL, class — `owned` (developing-today org or dezren39, not a fork), `fork` (GitHub fork flag or census-indicated), `upstream-dependency` (not owned; we depend on or track it — the four fleet repos' key upstreams and the hardware ecosystems named in #1511), `archive-nested` (exists only as a nested clone inside repo-archive) — plus `watch: issues|inventory-only` per the scope limits in the #1511 design.
- Output is a versioned, human-editable artifact (YAML or Markdown table) committed to this repo; hand edits (class/watch overrides) survive regeneration via an overrides section the generator merges, never overwrites blindly.

## Acceptance
- Artifact covers every developing-today + dezren39 GitHub repo and every census-named upstream, each classified.
- Re-running the generator on unchanged inputs produces a zero diff (idempotent).
- The four fleet repos and the side repos named in #1511 (dezren39/hatch, dezren39/hatch-personal, developing-today/hardware-doc, developing-today/opencode-auto-continue) are present and class `owned`.

Parent: #1511 (design posted there by queue task 1549).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A generator in this repo builds the universe list from both sources in the body (GitHub enumeration of developing-today + dezren39, and the 2026-10-27 census including repo-archive nested clones).
- [ ] Every entry carries owner/name, URL, class (`owned` / `fork` / `upstream-dependency` / `archive-nested`) and a `watch: issues|inventory-only` value.
- [ ] The committed artifact covers every developing-today + dezren39 GitHub repo and every census-named upstream, each classified (the body's Acceptance bullets, restated here as the criteria section).
- [ ] Re-running the generator on unchanged inputs produces a zero diff, and hand edits survive regeneration via the overrides merge.
- [ ] The four fleet repos and dezren39/hatch, dezren39/hatch-personal, developing-today/hardware-doc, developing-today/opencode-auto-continue are present and class `owned`.

title: mcpx(codegen): two servers can resolve to the same namespace — the generated client declares it twice and no script can run

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

mcpx namespaces are derived per server with no cross-server uniqueness check. Two distinct servers whose names sanitize to the same identifier — `my-server` and `my_server` are the ordinary case — both emit `export const my_server = { … }` into the generated client module. That module is a duplicate declaration: it does not parse in any runtime and does not type-check, so **every** script, `mcpx types` load and exec against that daemon breaks, for every namespace — not just the two colliding ones. Nothing warns at config load, resolve, or startup; the failure surfaces as a syntax error in a generated file the user never wrote.

## Evidence (verified on main `b97d8f32`, this run)

Probe test in the real `internal/config` package on the laptop (detached worktree, removed after; probe + log in the goal's `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-nscollide/`; run twice, identical; full existing `internal/config` + `internal/codegen` suites pass):

- `SanitizeNamespace("my-server")` → `my_server`; `SanitizeNamespace("my_server")` → `my_server` — collide=true
- `SanitizeNamespace("log")` → `log_`; `SanitizeNamespace("log_")` → `log_` — collide=true (the reserved-word suffixing in `codegen.SafeNamespace` walks straight into a name another server already owns)
- `SanitizeNamespace("a.b")` → `a_b`; `SanitizeNamespace("a_b")` → `a_b` — collide=true
- Control: `alpha`/`beta` stay distinct.

Feeding the two colliding namespaces through `codegen.Module` exactly as the daemon does (one `codegen.Namespace` per server, `internal/daemon/registry.go:731` appends with no dedup):

- The module contains `export const my_server = {` **twice**.
- `bun build` on the generated module: `error: "my_server" has already been declared`.
- `deno check` on it: `TS2451: Cannot redeclare block-scoped variable 'my_server'`.
- `codegen.GlobalDeclarations` emits the same name twice as an ambient global (`const %s: typeof __mcpx.%s`), so the globals file is broken the same way.

## Where the chain breaks

- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/config/config.go:530` — `nsSanitize` maps every non-`[a-zA-Z0-9_]` character to `_`, a many-to-one mapping (`-`, `.`, space, … all become `_`).
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/config/config.go:534-545` — `SanitizeNamespace` returns `codegen.SafeNamespace(out)`; `pkgs/mcpx/internal/codegen/ident.go:73-78` — `SafeNamespace` only avoids *reserved* names, never names already taken by another server.
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/config/config.go:631-634` — an explicit `mcpx.namespace` is checked only against `ReservedNamespace`; two servers may both declare the same explicit namespace, and an explicit namespace may equal another server's sanitized one.
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/config/config.go:644` — `Namespace: pick(ex.Namespace, SanitizeNamespace(name))` resolves each server in isolation; no pass ever sees two namespaces together until `codegen.Module` (`internal/codegen/emit.go:143`) prints both.

Tool-name collisions *inside* one namespace are already handled deliberately (`funcCollisions` in emit.go renders one throwing member naming both tools). Namespace collisions *across* servers have no equivalent.

## Why it matters

The generated client is the single entry point for all script execution (runner writes it beside every script; the preflight type-check runs against it). A config with two naturally-named servers — `chrome-devtools` next to a hand-added `chrome_devtools`, a dotted vendor name next to its underscored twin — silently poisons the whole catalogue, and the error ("has already been declared" in a generated temp file) points nowhere near the config that caused it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A config in which two servers resolve to the same namespace is caught before any client is generated: either a clear load/resolve error naming both servers and the shared namespace, or a deterministic, documented disambiguation — triage pins which (an error matches how alias chains and reserved explicit namespaces are already refused in `Resolve`).
- [ ] The check covers all three sources: sanitized-vs-sanitized (`my-server`/`my_server`), reserved-suffix-vs-plain (`log`/`log_`), and explicit `mcpx.namespace` vs either of the above.
- [ ] Regression tests for the three shapes; existing `internal/config` and `internal/codegen` tests pass unchanged.
- [ ] No change to the namespace a non-colliding server gets today (existing catalogues, scripts and `call("server", …)` names are unaffected).

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-b, 2026-10-28 run. Deliberately not self-solved: error-vs-disambiguate is a small contract pin for queue-lane triage (disambiguation would rename a namespace existing scripts may already import).

title: mcpx(adapter): buildArgs silently mistranslates three parameter shapes — a stdin param's enum is never checked, a positional boolean is dropped entirely, and an unknown argument is ignored

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage

labels.name: effort/s
