body:
## Summary

`ToolSpec.buildArgs` (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/adapter/adapter.go`) — the one function that turns a caller's named arguments into the wrapped program's command line — silently mistranslates three parameter shapes. Nothing upstream catches them: the `mcpserver` extra-tool path (`internal/cli/serve.go` `adapterTools`) unmarshals the caller's JSON into a map and hands it straight to `Spec.Call`, and `ToolSpec.Schema()` does not close the object (`additionalProperties` is absent, unlike mcpx's own meta-tools in `internal/mcpserver/server.go`, which set `"additionalProperties":false`). So what `buildArgs` drops or skips is dropped or skipped for the real invocation.

Verified on main `ed8e5910` with a probe test in the real `internal/adapter` package on the laptop (adapter.go sha256 `6d7976b8…` identical in both clones; probe + log in the fleet bookkeeping `probe-2026-10-28-laneA-adapter/`, run twice with identical output; the full existing adapter suite passes). Controls behave correctly: an enum on an ordinary positional parameter refuses `sideways` and accepts `fast`; a boolean **with** a flag emits `--loud`; a correctly-spelled `--tag` value reaches the command line.

## Bug A — an enum on the stdin parameter is never checked

`buildArgs` diverts the stdin parameter before the enum loop:

- `adapter.go:292-295` — `if p.Name == t.Stdin { stdin = toString(raw); continue }`
- `adapter.go:300-307` — the `p.Enum` check every other parameter goes through

Probe: a `cat` tool whose `body` parameter is the stdin parameter with `Enum: ["fast","slow"]`, called with `body="sideways"` → `err=<nil>`, stdout `sideways` — the out-of-enum value is piped to the program verbatim. `Param.Enum`'s doc says only "Enum restricts the value"; the generated schema advertises the same enum for a stdin parameter, so a caller is told a restriction exists that is never enforced. `TestEnumIsEnforced` (`adapter_test.go`) covers only a positional parameter.

## Bug B — a positional boolean is dropped entirely, true and false alike

The boolean branch only ever appends a flag:

- `adapter.go:310-315` — `if p.Type == "boolean" { if … values[0] == "true" && p.Flag != "" { out = append(out, p.Flag) }; continue }`

`Param.Flag`'s doc: "Empty makes it positional, in declaration order." Probe: an `echo` tool with positional parameters `text` (required) and `loud` (`Type: "boolean"`, no flag):

- `loud=true` → command `echo said: hello`, stdout `said: hello` — the `true` never appears
- `loud=false` → byte-identical command and output

A program that takes a positional boolean (plenty of CLIs take `true`/`false` positionally) can never receive either value through an adapter that declares one; both calls silently run as if the parameter had not been supplied. A non-single value (e.g. an array) for a flagged boolean is dropped the same way.

## Bug C — an argument naming no declared parameter is silently ignored

`buildArgs` iterates only the declared parameters (`adapter.go:281`), so a key in the caller's map that matches nothing is never examined and there is no error path for it. Combined with the open schema (above), a typo is indistinguishable from success:

Probe: an `echo` tool with an optional `--tag` flag parameter, called with `{"text":"hello", "tga":"important"}` → `err=<nil>`, command `echo said: hello` — the value vanishes and the program runs without the flag the caller asked for. The correctly-spelled control (`tag=important`) produces `echo said: hello --tag important`.

For an adapter — whose whole purpose is that "what is reachable is exactly what somebody wrote down" (package doc) — silently running a *different* command line than the caller specified is worse than an error: the caller believes an option (potentially a safety-relevant one like a dry-run or a target selector) was applied when it was not.

## Why it matters

Adapters expose arbitrary local CLI programs as MCP tools to model-driven callers, who cannot see the actual command line being run — `Result.Command` is the only trace, and nobody compares it per call. Each shape makes the executed command differ from the declared/called one with no signal: an unvalidated value reaches a program that was promised enum-restricted input, a declared parameter can never take effect, and a misspelled argument silently degrades the invocation instead of failing it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An out-of-enum value for the stdin parameter is refused with the same "must be one of …" error as any other parameter (and an in-enum value still reaches stdin unchanged); the stdin diversion happens after enum validation.
- [ ] A positional boolean (`Type: "boolean"`, no flag) is either passed positionally as `true`/`false` in declaration order, or refused at `Validate()` time with a message saying booleans need a flag — whichever triage pins, the silent drop is gone and the chosen behaviour is tested and matches the `Param` docs.
- [ ] A call carrying an argument that names no declared parameter fails with an error naming the unknown argument (and, ideally, the declared ones), OR the generated schema sets `additionalProperties: false` **and** the server path is shown to enforce it — silent ignoring is not an acceptable end state; triage pins which layer owns it.
- [ ] New `internal/adapter` tests cover all three shapes (stdin enum, positional boolean, unknown argument).
- [ ] All existing `adapter_test.go` cases keep passing, including the flag-boolean, stdin, repeated-flag and enum controls.
- [ ] Any shape deliberately left unhandled is named in the package/`Param` docs as a known restriction rather than left silent.

Found by the new-issue-creator (lane A) run of 2026-10-28; not self-solved because each shape has a small contract pin for triage (validate-vs-passthrough for positional booleans, which layer owns unknown-argument rejection), and the three should be ruled together in the one function they share.

title: mcpx(diagnose): CallError blames a field the server never named — fieldInMessage substring-matches prop names inside unrelated words ('valid' in 'invalid' beats the named 'id')

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`diagnose.CallError` maps a server's `-32602` back to an argument by finding a declared property name inside the server's message — but `fieldInMessage` (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/diagnose/diagnose.go:594-603`, called from `CallError` at :545) uses a bare `strings.Contains` with a longest-name-wins rule and no word boundaries. Any prop name that happens to be a substring of an unrelated word in the message is treated as named by the server, and a *longer* accidental substring beats the field the server actually named.

## Evidence (verified on main `ed8e5910`)

Probe test in the real `internal/diagnose` package (laptop worktree, file sha256 `9d9c9207` identical in both clones; probe + log in the creator's run records, run twice with identical results). All calls: `CallError` with code `-32602`, `Args: {}`, no required arguments missing (so the `fieldInMessage` branch is the one that fires):

- **CTRL** — props `{id, query}`, message `invalid params: "query" must be a string` → field=`query` ✅ (the field actually named)
- **CTRL** — props `{state, count}`, message `invalid params: schema mismatch` → field=`""`, generic diagnostic ✅
- **BUG-A** — props `{id, query}`, message `invalid params: validation failed` (names no field) → field=`id`, diagnostic reads *"the server rejected id (it wants string)"* — `id` was found inside in**valid** / val**id**ation
- **BUG-B** — props `{name, limit}`, message `invalid params: unnamed argument rejected` → field=`name` — found inside un**name**d
- **BUG-C (worst)** — props `{id, valid}`, message `invalid params: "id" must be a string` (names only `id`) → field=`valid`, *"the server rejected valid (it wants boolean)"* — `valid` is a substring of in**valid** and wins over the genuinely named `id` purely by being longer

The existing package tests pass unchanged; no existing test exercises a prop name that is a substring of a common error word.

## Why it matters

This diagnostic is the daemon's explanation layer for failed calls (`internal/daemon/callerr.go` calls `diagnose.CallError`): it is quoted to the user as fact — which argument the server rejected, what type it wants, and (via `Changed: cat.change(path, field)`) which schema change supposedly explains it. A misattributed field sends the user to fix the wrong argument, attaches the wrong field's change history, and in BUG-C's shape actively overrides the one piece of information the server did provide. Short prop names (`id`, `name`, `type`, `text`, `valid`, `limit`…) are extremely common, and "invalid"/"validation" are the most common words in exactly the messages this branch handles.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `fieldInMessage` (or its replacement) only attributes a field when the message names it as a token/word — substrings inside larger words (`valid`⊂`invalid`, `id`⊂`validation`, `name`⊂`unnamed`) never match
- [ ] When the message names a field exactly, that field is returned even if a longer prop name appears as a substring of another word (BUG-C shape is a regression test)
- [ ] When no field is named, `CallError` falls through to the generic diagnostic (field empty), as the CTRL generic case does today
- [ ] Regression tests cover BUG-A/B/C shapes; existing `internal/diagnose` tests pass unchanged
- [ ] Quoted names (`"query"`) and common server phrasings (`argument 'x'`, `x is required`) still match

## Scope notes

Fix surface is the one function plus tests in `pkgs/mcpx/internal/diagnose`. Whether matching should also handle quoted/backticked spellings preferentially is for triage to pin; the word-boundary requirement is the defect. Not self-solved by the creator: the matching contract (which token shapes count as "named") is a small pin for queue-lane triage, and the creator run's remaining time could not also do the laptop worktree + PR + CI cycle responsibly.

title: mcpx(secrets): References scan misreads regex literals, parameter/destructured bindings and phantom declarations — Preflight refuses scripts that reach nothing and clears scripts that do

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

`secrets.References` — the static scan that decides which servers a script reaches, feeding `Registry.Preflight` and the `refuseScript` gate — misreads three ordinary script shapes, in both directions:

- **A (false positive): a regex literal is scanned as code.** The scanner (`internal/secrets/refs.go:47` `code`) skips strings, comments and template text, but has no regex-literal state, so `/tools.fs.read/` or `/demo.echo/` in a pattern is counted as a namespace reach.
- **B (false positive): most binding forms are invisible to `declaredNames`.** Declarations are collected by three regexes over the raw source (`refs.go:209-216`) that only recognise `const|let|var|function|class|import <ident>`. Function parameters, arrow-function parameters, destructured bindings (`const {demo} = …`, `const {x: demo} = …`) and `catch (demo)` bindings are all *declared names the script binds itself* — exactly what the package doc says must not count — yet each is reported as a namespace reach.
- **C (false negative): a phantom declaration inside a comment or string suppresses a real reach.** Because `declaredNames` regexes the raw source without the lexical skipping the main scan does, the text `// const demo = make();` or `"let demo"` marks `demo` declared, and a genuine `demo.echo()` later in the script is then *not* reported.

## Evidence (verified on main `ed8e5910`)

Probe test in the real `internal/secrets` package on the laptop (detached worktree, removed after; `refs.go` sha256 `50e049f1` identical in both clones; probe + full log in the fleet's run records, run twice with identical output):

```
CTRL tools call                References=[fs]     (real reach, correct)
CTRL string not code           References=[]       ("tools.fs.read()" in a string, correct)
CTRL const local               References=[]       (const demo = {...}; demo.echo(), correct)
BUG-A4 regex unescaped tools   References=[fs]     (src is only: const re = /tools.fs.read/;)
BUG-A5 regex unescaped bare    References=[demo]   (src is only: const re = /demo.echo/;)
BUG-B1 function param          References=[demo]   (function run(demo) { return demo.echo(); })
BUG-B2 arrow param             References=[demo]   (const f = (demo) => demo.echo();)
BUG-B3 destructured const      References=[demo]   (const {demo} = opts; demo.echo();)
BUG-B4 destructured alias      References=[demo]   (const {x: demo} = opts; demo.echo();)
BUG-B5 catch binding           References=[demo]   (try { go(); } catch (demo) { demo.echo(); })
BUG-C1 phantom decl in comment References=[]       (// const demo = make();  then real demo.echo();)
BUG-C2 phantom decl in string  References=[]       (const s = "let demo";  then real demo.echo();)
```

Honest scope on A: the escaped-dot spelling `/tools\.fs\.read/` is *accidentally* safe — the backslash, not any lexical handling, breaks the scanner's `.` check — and a `[.]` char-class spelling is likewise not counted. The bug is the common unescaped spelling, which is valid JS and matches the same text with `.` as any-char.

Existing coverage (`internal/secrets/refs_test.go`) pins strings, comments, templates, member chains and the `const`/`import` declaration forms, but has no regex-literal case, no parameter/destructuring/catch case, and no phantom-declaration case.

## Why it matters

`References` is the only input to `Registry.Preflight` (`internal/daemon/secrets.go:272-296`), which is the only input to `refuseScript` (`secrets.go:306`), the gate a script passes before it starts:

- False positives (A, B) make Preflight report a server the script never reaches. If that server is missing secrets, the script is **refused before it runs** and a spurious secret request is created on the board (`board.Require`, `secrets.go:295`) — for a parameter that happens to share a namespace's name, or a regex that mentions one.
- The false negative (C) makes Preflight report `Ready: true` for a script that does reach a server lacking secrets, so the preflight's whole purpose — knowing before the run — is defeated for that script. (The at-call check still catches it mid-run, per the package doc; that is the degraded path preflight exists to avoid.)

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `References` returns no namespace for a reach that appears only inside a regex literal (at minimum the unescaped-dot spellings in the probe), in any position where a regex literal can appear (assignment, return, argument, test condition).
- [ ] Names bound as function/arrow parameters, destructured bindings (plain and renamed), and `catch` bindings are treated as declared, like `const`/`let`/`var`/`import` names are today.
- [ ] Declaration-shaped text inside comments, strings and template text does **not** mark a name declared: after `// const demo = …` or `"let demo"`, a real bare `demo.<tool>` reach is still reported.
- [ ] All existing `refs_test.go` cases keep passing (strings/comments/templates skipped, `${…}` interpolations scanned, `tools.<ns>` and `tools["<ns>"]` forms, member-of-something-else exclusion).
- [ ] New tests in `internal/secrets` cover the A/B/C shapes above.
- [ ] Handling stays a static scan (nothing evaluated), per the package's stated design; if any shape is deliberately left unhandled, it is named in the package doc as a known blind spot instead of silently diverging.

title: mcpx(catalog): VectorIndex silently drops non-384-dim vectors on reload — the remote-embedder cache vanishes on restart and mismatched dims score 0

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

mcpx's `catalog.VectorIndex` accepts embedding vectors of **any** dimension at write time — `Put` returns `nil`, `Import` counts them as imported, and the daemon's semantic search stores whatever the configured embedder produces — but the SQLite reload path silently discards every stored vector whose dimension is not exactly `VectorDim` (384). With a remote embedder configured (the default model, `text-embedding-3-small`, returns 1536 dimensions), every tool vector the daemon caches is thrown away on the next start, with no error and no log. In-process, the same dimension gap silently zeroes semantic scores: `CosineSimilarity` returns exactly 0 for mismatched lengths, so a query embedded by one backend against tool vectors cached under another scores every tool 0 and semantic search degrades to keyword-only without any signal.

## Evidence (verified on main `ed8e5910`)

- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/catalog/vector.go:159-182` — `loadFromDB` loads a row only when `len(blob) == VectorDim*4` (:172); any other dimension is skipped silently (no log, no error surfaced — `NewVectorIndex` ignores the outcome entirely).
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/catalog/vector.go:204-222` — `Put` stores a vector of any length in memory and on disk and never validates `len(vec)`; its `error` return is never used for this.
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/catalog/embeddings.go:346-376` — `Import` accepts and counts vectors of any length and persists them as blobs that `loadFromDB` will drop on the next open; `Export` (embeddings.go:324-343) stamps `Dim: VectorDim` regardless of the dimensions actually stored.
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/catalog/embeddings.go:67-127` — `RemoteEmbedder.Embed` L2-normalizes but never checks the returned dimension: the default model `text-embedding-3-small` returns 1536 floats, not 384. `CascadeEmbedder.Embed` (embeddings.go:268-302) tries remote first in `auto` mode.
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/catalog/vector.go:20-29` — `CosineSimilarity` returns 0 when `len(v) != len(other)`. The daemon's hybrid search (`internal/daemon/registry.go:534`) combines that 0 into the score with no mismatch signal; a tool with no keyword score is then dropped by the `combined > 15.0 || kwScore > 0` gate at registry.go:542.
- The write path that populates the cache with embedder-dimension vectors is live: `internal/daemon/registry.go:524-531` embeds each uncached tool with the configured embedder and calls `vIdx.Put(t.Function, tVec)` (:531, ignoring Put's error).

### Probe (laptop, real `internal/catalog` package)

Probe test in a detached laptop worktree at the same HEAD (`vector.go` sha256 `5e901780`, `embeddings.go` sha256 `19044242` — byte-identical to this clone), run twice with identical results (probe + log: `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-vecdim/`):

- CTRL: `Put` a 384-dim vector → close → reopen → present.
- BUG-A: `Put` a 1536-dim vector returns `err=nil` and is readable in-process; after close → reopen it is **missing** — silently dropped by `loadFromDB`.
- BUG-B: `Import` of a payload carrying one 1536-dim vector reports `count=1, err=nil`; after reopen it is **missing**.
- BUG-C: `CosineSimilarity(1536-dim, 384-dim)` = 0 exactly, while identical 384-dim vectors score > 0 — the silent in-process half of the same gap.

## Why it matters

The vector index is the semantic-search cache for `mcpx search`: with a remote (or WASM/Ollama) embedder configured, the daemon pays to embed every tool once, persists the results, and then silently loses all of them on restart — and any mid-flight backend switch (config change, remote outage falling back to local in the cascade) zeroes the semantic half of the hybrid score for already-cached tools. Nothing logs, errors, or tests the mismatch: existing tests (embeddings_test.go, vector_test.go) only ever exercise 384-dim local vectors.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A vector whose dimension is not the index's dimension cannot silently enter the persistent index: `Put`/`Import` either reject it with an error that names the expected and actual dimensions, or the index records and reloads vectors together with their dimension — one behaviour, pinned by tests.
- [ ] `loadFromDB` no longer drops rows silently: unloadable rows are surfaced (error or logged count).
- [ ] A restart round-trip test with a non-384 embedder vector exists and passes (either the vector survives, or the write failed loudly at write time).
- [ ] The daemon search path does not score a dimension-mismatched pair as a plain 0 without a signal (fallback to re-embed, or an explicit debug/log trace).
- [ ] Existing catalog tests pass unchanged for the 384-dim local path.

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-b. Whether to pin the index to one dimension per DB (reject at write) vs store per-vector dimensions is the triage call — the defect is the *silence*, which either ruling removes.

title: Design: mcpx client session & stream recovery — re-initialize on a legacy session 404, re-issue a broken modern request once

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: epic
labels.description: Meta-issue grouping multiple items (org Project Type=Epic)

labels.name: effort/l
labels.description: Large: multi-day or open-ended; expect staged check-ins

labels.name: meta/enriched
labels.description: Intake review done: acceptance criteria, links, and normalized labels added

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: A design proposal (design-architect): multi-step, phased, decision-bearing

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Summary

mcpx's client has no recovery from the two ways a live upstream connection goes stale. When a legacy HTTP upstream restarts and forgets the session, every later call 404s forever — the client never re-initializes, and the pool cannot reap an HTTP client that never dies, so only a daemon restart heals it. When a modern (2026-07-28) upstream's response stream breaks, the in-flight request is reported lost and never re-issued, though the 2026 spec makes re-issue a client MUST. This design puts both recoveries in `Client` (the layer that owns the handshake, the pending table and the era): forget + re-initialize + retry once on a session-carrying legacy 404, and re-issue once with a new id on a broken modern stream — with `tools/call` re-issued only on annotation evidence, so a destructive tool is never silently executed twice.

Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-client-session-stream-recovery.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace (full audit, alternatives, risks, open questions).

No Drew direction decision needed: the roadmap row is at `proposed`, both behaviours are spec MUSTs (TR-29; 2026 changelog / PM-06), and the judgment calls (client-layer recovery; the annotation gate) are recorded in the design doc.

## Current state (verified on main ed8e5910, 2026-10-28)

- The two gaps are open in the conformance register, `pkgs/mcpx/internal/conformance/coverage_transport.go:114-115`: `streamable-http-client-reissue-broken-request` and `streamable-http-client-reinit-on-404`, both client-side, origin dezren39/nix#203.
- 404 path: `HTTPTransport.Send` (`internal/mcpclient/http.go` ~L166-180) returns any non-2xx as `HTTPStatusError` (except a JSON-RPC error body naming the request, pushed as the reply). Nothing in `Client` treats a session-carrying 404 as expiry. Register TR-29 (`docs/compare/register/transports.md:550-565`): a restarted remote server "leaves its mcpx instance failing every call"; legacy spec (2025-03-26..2025-11-25): a client receiving 404 for a session-carrying request MUST start a new session with a fresh `initialize`.
- Broken-stream path: a modern SSE response stream that ends unanswered calls `t.lost(reqID)` (http.go ~L190-205), synthesising a `-32000` error (`lost`/`codeStreamLost` ~L378-389); the caller just fails. Legacy streams instead resume via GET + `Last-Event-ID` (`resume()`, http.go ~L338) — legacy has resumability, 2026 deliberately does not (PM-06, `docs/compare/register/process-model.md:133-146`).
- Reusable machinery: `Client.roundTrip` (`internal/mcpclient/client.go` ~L953) is the single request choke point; `initializeLegacy`/`finishLegacy` (~L343-388) already validate the version, refresh ServerInfo/Capabilities and restart the GET listen stream; the catalogue-invalidation signal (`invalidate` → `Notifications.OnListChanged`, ~L683-749) already reaches the pool; `Tool.Annotations` (~L159-170) carries readOnlyHint/idempotentHint/destructiveHint.
- Distinct from #1414: that design resumes a still-live session after *our* daemon restarts. This one handles the opposite event — the *upstream* restarted and the session is dead; the move is discard + new session, not resume.

## Proposal (decisions recorded in the design doc)

- **Recovery lives in the client.** Not the transport (protocol-free; `initialize` is a client exchange) and not the pool (reaping loses the in-flight call, and nothing marks an HTTP client dead for the pool to reap).
- **Legacy 404 (Phase 1):** trigger only when a request (not a notification, not `initialize`) 404s, era is legacy, and the request carried a session id. The transport gains a report-and-clear session seam (the `setNegotiated` interface-assertion pattern); re-initialize is singleflight across concurrent calls (session generation — one `initialize` per upstream restart); the request retries once with a new id; a second 404 surfaces. After re-initialize, all three catalogue kinds are invalidated through the existing signal.
- **Modern broken stream (Phase 2):** the stream-lost error gets a stable identity (not message matching); the request layer re-issues once with a new id. `tools/call` is gated: automatic re-issue only when the tool's list-time annotations declare `readOnlyHint` or `idempotentHint` (PM-06's double-execution hazard is the register's own warning); otherwise the stream-lost error surfaces and the host decides. Legacy is excluded — resumability is its mechanism.
- **Truth-up (Phase 3):** both conformance gaps retired with test evidence; TR-29 and PM-06 register rows rewritten as-built; the roadmap's "Legacy client robustness" row updated to name the umbrella's remainder; evidence comment on dezren39/nix#203 (comment, not close — the umbrella is its owners').

## Phases (each independently landable; filed as sub-issues)

1. **Legacy session-404 re-initialize + retry once** — transport seam, singleflight client recovery, one retry, catalogue invalidation; gap `streamable-http-client-reinit-on-404` retired.
2. **Modern broken-stream re-issue, annotation-gated** — stable stream-lost identity, once-only re-issue with a new id, annotations retained at list time, `tools/call` gate; gap `streamable-http-client-reissue-broken-request` retired. Independent of Phase 1.
3. **Register truth-up + nix#203 evidence** — TR-29 / PM-06 rows as-built, roadmap row updated, evidence comment on dezren39/nix#203. Gated on Phases 1–2.

## Acceptance (design level)

- A legacy upstream that restarts mid-life costs at most the calls in flight: they recover through exactly one re-initialize and one retry; later calls unaffected; no daemon restart involved.
- A broken modern stream loses no read-shaped request (re-issued once, new id); a tool call is re-executed only on annotation evidence, else its caller gets the stream-lost error.
- Both conformance gaps retired with tests; TR-29 and PM-06 tell the truth; dezren39/nix#203 carries the completion evidence.

<!-- agent-note:v1 agent=design-architect-code state=filed at=2026-10-28T09:32:00Z -->

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Legacy recovery is specified and landed via the phase issues (#1637, #1638, #1639): on a session-carrying legacy 404 the client forgets the session, re-initializes, and retries the request exactly once.
- [ ] Modern recovery: on a broken 2026-07-28 response stream the in-flight request is re-issued exactly once with a new id; `tools/call` is re-issued only on annotation evidence, so a destructive tool is never silently executed twice.
- [ ] The two conformance-register gaps named in the design (legacy session 404, broken modern stream) are closed in the register when the phases land.
- [ ] No daemon restart is required to heal either stale-connection case.

title: cold-store-reaper: s3_list_objects loops forever on a truncated page with a missing, empty, or repeated continuation token

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: app/cold-store-reaper
labels.description: Package/app: cold-store-reaper (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Summary

`ColdStore.s3_list_objects` (`pkgs/cold-store-reaper/cold_store.py:1555-1569`) paginates ListObjectsV2 with no progress guard: it loops `while True`, extending the result list, and returns only when a page says `IsTruncated` is false. If a page claims truncation but carries no usable continuation token — or repeats the token just used — the loop re-requests the same page forever, appending duplicate objects and growing memory without bound. There is no error, no page cap, and no token-progress check.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `ed8e5910`)

- `s3_list_objects` (cold_store.py:1559-1569): `token = None`; each iteration builds `query = {"list-type": "2"}` and adds `continuation-token` only `if token:` (:1561-1563 — an empty-string token is dropped too), calls `_s3_request`, extends `out`, and returns only `if not truncated`.
- `_parse_s3_list_page` (cold_store.py:138-172) returns `token = None` when the `NextContinuationToken` element is absent (:149, :154-155) and `child.text` verbatim otherwise — it never cross-checks the token against truncation.
- Probe on the laptop driving the real module (cold_store.py sha256 `d3fe48c5` identical in both clones; `_s3_request` stubbed to serve canned ListObjectsV2 pages; probe + log in the fleet's `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-s3list/`):
  - CONTROL — page 1 truncated with token `tok2`, page 2 not truncated: terminates, 2 calls, 3 objects.
  - BUG-A — every page `IsTruncated=true`, no `NextContinuationToken` element: still looping past the probe's 12-call cap (the first page is re-requested with no token each time).
  - BUG-B — every page truncated and repeats the same token `tokX`: still looping past the cap (each iteration re-requests the identical page and appends its objects again).
  - BUG-C — truncated with an empty token element: still looping past the cap (`if token:` drops it, same as BUG-A).
  - Probe run twice, identical results.
- Existing tests cover only well-behaved pagination: the FakeS3 server in tests/test_cold_store.py always emits a fresh `NextContinuationToken` when truncated (:760-785), and `test_list_pagination` (:1318-1332) asserts the 2/2/1 happy path. No test serves a truncated page with a missing, empty, or repeated token.
- Callers inherit the hang: `backup_supabase` (cold_store.py:1775) and the eviction scan (:1832) both start from `s3_list_objects`, so one malformed listing page wedges the nightly backup / evict-scan with no diagnostic — the same class of silent first-request death this package has been hardening against (cf. the transport-retry and curl-fallback work in #1625).

Real S3/R2 normally sends a token with `IsTruncated=true`, but this client already treats the endpoint as untrusted at every other layer (byte-count verification, transport retries, torn-body handling); a non-conforming, proxied, or partially corrupted listing response should be a loud `ColdStoreError`, not an infinite loop with unbounded memory growth in a long-lived nightly job.

## Why it matters

`backup-supabase` and `evict-scan` are unattended nightly paths. A single bad listing page turns them into a silent infinite loop: the job never completes, never errors, and accumulates duplicate object entries in memory until it is killed — indistinguishable from a slow run until someone notices the backup is stale.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `s3_list_objects` raises `ColdStoreError` (naming the bucket) when a truncated page arrives with a missing or empty `NextContinuationToken`.
- [ ] `s3_list_objects` raises `ColdStoreError` when the returned continuation token does not advance (equals the token used for the current request), instead of re-requesting the same page.
- [ ] Well-behaved multi-page listings behave exactly as today (existing `test_list_pagination` and the S3 transport-retry tests pass unchanged).
- [ ] New tests cover the missing-token, empty-token, and repeated-token pages and assert the call count stays bounded (the listing aborts on the offending page, it does not keep fetching).

title: mcpx(config): tool-pattern compiler silently mistranslates three entry shapes — unclosed /regex matches nothing, // matches everything, glob [^…] class inverts

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

`CompileToolPatterns` (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/config/toolpattern.go`) exists for one stated reason: "failing on the first entry that is not a valid pattern: a deny entry that silently matches nothing is the failure this exists to prevent." Three entry shapes still slip past it and silently mean something other than what the operator wrote — in the `tools`/`excludeTools` lists that decide which MCP tools are visible and callable (`Resolve`, `config.go:595-599`):

1. **An unclosed regexp is silently an exact name.** `/delete` (leading slash, no closing slash) compiles with no error and matches only a tool literally named `/delete` — never `delete_x`. In `excludeTools` that is precisely the prevented failure: a deny entry that matches nothing, so the tool the operator meant to block stays visible. The dispatch at `toolpattern.go:44` requires BOTH slashes before treating an entry as a regexp; a leading-slash entry that fails that test falls through to the glob/exact arms.
2. **An empty regexp is a silent match-all.** `//` compiles the empty RE2 pattern, which matches every tool name. In `excludeTools` it hides a server's entire tool set; in `tools` it allows everything — the dual of the match-nothing failure, equally silent.
3. **A glob class starting with `^` is inverted.** The glob translator (`globRegexp`, `toolpattern.go:84-120`) copies a character class's body into the regexp class escaping only `\`, `[`, `]`. Under the documented glob grammar the negation form is `[!a-z]`, so `^` is an ordinary member — but a class whose first member is `^` (e.g. `[^d]elete_*`, the set {`^`, `d`}) becomes the regexp `[^d]`, a NEGATED class: it matches `xelete_x` and `zelete_x`, and does NOT match `delete_x`. The meaning flips.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `1f0722cc`)

Probe test in the real `internal/config` package, run in a detached laptop worktree (`toolpattern.go` sha256 `6229ae25…` identical on sandbox main and the laptop clone; probe + log in the fleet's probe records for this run, executed twice with identical output):

- A: `CompileToolPatterns(["/delete"])` → `err=<nil>`, `Match("delete_x")=false`, `Match("/delete")=true`
- B: `CompileToolPatterns(["//"])` → `err=<nil>`, `Match("anything")=true`, `Match("delete_all")=true`
- C: `CompileToolPatterns(["[^d]elete_*"])` → `err=<nil>`, `Match("delete_x")=false`, `Match("xelete_x")=true`, `Match("zelete_x")=true`
- Control: the documented negation `[!d]elete_*` behaves correctly (`delete_x` false, `xelete_x` true), as do `/delete/` and `delete_*`.

Existing tests (`toolpattern_test.go:48-55`) pin refusal for `/(/`, `delete_[`, and `""` — a leading-slash entry is refused only when it happens to also end with `/` and fail RE2 compilation; the unclosed and empty shapes are untested.

## Why it matters

These lists are the operator's guardrail over which upstream tools an agent can see and call. Shape A is the exact silent-deny-failure the type was built to prevent, reachable by the most natural typo (a missing closing slash). Shape B turns a two-character entry into a wildcard over a whole server. Shape C inverts a class for anyone who writes `^` expecting glob semantics (or porting a class from another tool). All three fail silently at config load — the moment the design says must fail loudly.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An entry that begins with `/` but is not a complete `/…/` pair is a compile error naming the entry (or is otherwise refused, never silently exact) — triage pins whether a lone `/` is included.
- [ ] The empty regexp `//` is refused (or explicitly documented and tested as match-all, if triage decides it is a feature).
- [ ] A glob class whose body would begin the regexp class with `^` is escaped so the glob meaning (literal `^` member) is preserved; `[!…]` negation is unchanged.
- [ ] Regression tests cover all three shapes plus the existing controls (`/(/`, `delete_[`, `""`, `/delete/`, `[!d]…`, plain globs).
- [ ] Existing `internal/config` tests still pass.

## Dedup / distinctness

Searched open + closed issues for `ToolPatterns`, `tool pattern`, `excludeTools`: no filing covers the pattern compiler's entry shapes. Adjacent: #1414/#1415/#1416 are mcpx session-resume work; #1605 is mcpx exec artifact delivery — different packages and mechanisms.

title: aggregator: freshness() ages date-only stamps by the UTC day, not Chicago — a read dated today reports '1d ago' (and stale) from 19:00 Chicago onward

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: app/aggregator
labels.description: Package/app: aggregator (pm-stack in this repo)

body:
## Summary

`freshness()` in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/derive.ts:852-868` ages **date-only** stamps by the **UTC** calendar day, while the same file's calendar helpers define "today" in **America/Chicago** (`chicagoYmd`, `derive.ts:462-470`, under the header "Calendar helpers (America/Chicago — Drew's timezone)"). The date-only branch (`derive.ts:858-862`) computes:

```ts
const startOfToday = Date.UTC(now.getUTCFullYear(), now.getUTCMonth(), now.getUTCDate());
const ageDays = Math.max(0, Math.round((startOfToday - t) / 86_400_000));
return { stale: ageDays > cadenceDays, ageDays };
```

Its own comment states the intended semantics: "a read dated yesterday is 1 day old **all day today**". But with the UTC day boundary, "today" flips at 19:00 Chicago (CDT) / 18:00 (CST) — so for the last 5–6 hours of every Chicago day, a read dated **today** (Chicago) already reports `ageDays: 1`, and a service whose cadence is tight flips to **stale on the very day it was read**. The rendered surfaces inherit it: `freshnessStamp` (`render.ts:1651-1659`, prints "· 1d ago" / the stale badge) and the SaaS service cards/detail (`render.ts:1704`, `render.ts:1889`).

## Verified (this run, on main be7cf629)

Probe ON THE LAPTOP (Bun 1.4.2, driving the real `derive.ts` — sha256 `312ac0fb…` identical in both clones; probe + log in the goal's `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-horizondate/probe3.ts` + `out3.log`, output identical across runs):

```
now = 2026-10-28T01:30:00Z  (= 2026-10-27 20:30 Chicago)
chicagoYmd(now) = 2026-10-27                       (the file's own "today")
freshness('2026-10-27', 7, now) = { stale: false, ageDays: 1 }
    <- a read dated TODAY (Chicago) is already "1 day old"
freshness('2026-10-27', 0, now) = { stale: true,  ageDays: 1 }
    <- at cadence 0 it is STALE on the day it was read
now = 2026-10-28T06:30:00Z  (= 2026-10-28 01:30 Chicago)
chicagoYmd(now) = 2026-10-28
freshness('2026-10-27', 7, now) = { stale: false, ageDays: 1 }   (correct: yesterday)
```

So the same `measuredAt` is aged 0 for the first ~19 hours of its Chicago day and 1 for the remaining ~5 — the age (and any stale verdict at the boundary) depends on the time of day in a way neither the comment nor the file's Chicago convention intends. The datetime branch below it (`derive.ts:864-867`) ages by elapsed whole days and is unaffected; only date-only stamps (the hub's dated reads — quota-view / SaaS `measuredAt` dates) take the UTC-calendar branch.

## Why it matters

Every hub card's freshness stamp and stale badge derives from this function. Date-only reads are the common case for the manually-read SaaS/quota services, and their cadences are in days: being aged a day early for a quarter of every day makes cards flicker to "1d ago"/stale each evening and back — noise on exactly the honesty surface (#1139/#1140 family) whose job is to state data age truthfully, and a false stale can mask (or train Drew to ignore) a genuinely stale source. It is also an internal inconsistency: two functions in one file disagree about what day it is.

Distinct from #1568/#1541/#1564 (future/garbage timestamps pinning freshness *forever* in `freshness` callers / quota-current / feed gates — those are missing upper-bound/parse checks; this one is a wrong day-boundary for perfectly valid, past, date-only stamps) and from #1587 (julesSummary HHMM key rollover).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] For a date-only `measuredAt`, `ageDays` is the number of whole **America/Chicago** calendar days between the stamp's date and today-in-Chicago: a stamp dated today (Chicago) reports `ageDays: 0` at every hour of that day, and yesterday's stamp reports `1` all day.
- [ ] A date-only read cannot flip to `stale` before its Chicago calendar age actually exceeds `cadenceDays` (boundary case pinned by a test at e.g. 20:30 Chicago on the stamp's own date, cadence 0).
- [ ] Regression tests cover the evening-Chicago case (UTC date = Chicago date + 1) and the early-morning control, for both the age value and the stale verdict; the datetime branch's behaviour is unchanged.
- [ ] Existing aggregator test suites still pass.

title: id(outbox): a parseable torn tail is accepted, then merged into the next record — Outbox::open only drops unterminated final lines that fail to parse

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

`Outbox::open` (`pkgs/id/src/envelope_outbox.rs:130`) only drops a torn final line when it **fails to parse**. A crash that cuts an append after the record's closing `}` but before its `\n` leaves a *parseable* unterminated final line — and `open` accepts it as a committed record. The next `commit()` then appends the following record directly onto that same line, producing one line containing two JSON objects; on the next open that line is complete (newline-terminated) and corrupt, so `open` errors out and the envelope outbox is bricked until a human edits the file by hand.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `1658679c`)

- `src/envelope_outbox.rs:141-157`: the replay loop iterates `text.split_inclusive('\n')`; on parse success it applies the record and does `kept += line.len()` (line 146) **regardless of whether the line ends with `\n`**. The torn-tail drop is only the `Err(_) if !complete => break` arm (line 148). If the unterminated fragment parses, `kept == text.len()`, so no truncation happens and the file keeps its missing trailing newline.
- `src/envelope_outbox.rs:278-289` (`commit`): appends `serde_json::to_string(&record) + '\n'` with `OpenOptions::append` — no leading newline is written, so the next record is concatenated onto the unterminated line.
- Sibling stores treat *any* unterminated final line as torn, parseable or not, because an append that never got its newline was never durably committed:
  - `src/artifact.rs:565-583` (`ArtifactLog::open`): "A final line cut short by a crash was never synced, so it is dropped and the file is truncated to the last complete line" — implemented as `rfind('\n')` truncation *before* parsing.
  - `src/directory.rs:512-526` (the #1521 fix): drops the torn final fragment "parseable or not", warns, and truncates.
- The existing test `a_torn_last_line_is_dropped_and_not_mixed_into_the_next_record` (`src/envelope_outbox.rs:523`) covers only an *unparseable* fragment (`{"op":"queued","target"`). The parseable-fragment case — its exact title scenario, "not mixed into the next record" — is untested and currently fails by construction: fragment `{"op":"queued",...}` + appended record = `{"op":...}{"op":...}\n`, which no longer parses as a single record (demonstrated with a JSON parse of the concatenated line this run).
- Accepting the fragment also breaks the durability contract: `commit` does `write_all` then `sync_data` (line 285-288); a crash between the data write and the sync can leave exactly this parseable-but-unterminated tail for a record that was never acknowledged.

## Why it matters

The outbox is the durable delivery queue for envelopes/artifacts. One unlucky crash turns it into a file that loads once (silently accepting an unacknowledged record), then permanently fails to load after the next enqueue/withdraw/record — with a "line N is corrupt" error that gives no hint the real cause was a torn tail two restarts earlier.

Related but distinct: #1499 (petnames) and #1522 (groups) cite the Outbox as the *correct* sibling for refusing torn tails; neither covers this parseable-unterminated acceptance in the Outbox itself. #1521 (directory, closed) established the "drop parseable or not" policy this issue asks the Outbox to match.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Outbox::open` drops an unterminated final line **whether or not it parses**, truncates the file to the last complete (newline-terminated) line, matching `ArtifactLog::open` / directory replay semantics.
- [ ] After such a recovery, a subsequent `commit()` appends cleanly: reopening the outbox succeeds and contains exactly the pre-crash complete records plus the new one.
- [ ] A corrupt *complete* (newline-terminated) line still fails the load (existing test `a_corrupt_complete_line_stops_the_load` keeps passing).
- [ ] New regression test: final line is a complete JSON record missing only its trailing `\n`; open drops it (the record's envelope is not present), the file is truncated, a following enqueue round-trips through a reopen.
- [ ] Existing outbox tests pass, including `a_torn_last_line_is_dropped_and_not_mixed_into_the_next_record`.

body:
## Summary

`.github/scripts/id-bench-compare.sh` (added in #1589, slice 3 of #1513) compares benchmark medians by name only. It parses each line's `unit=` into a per-side table (parse function, script lines 48–62: `unit[name] = kv[2]`) but never compares the two sides' units: the percent change is computed from the raw numbers (line ~90) and the report row prints the **baseline's** unit for both medians (line ~98). A benchmark whose unit changed between the baseline capture and the current run is therefore compared as if the numbers shared a unit — in both directions:

- unit grows (e.g. `us_per_event` → `ms_per_event`, numbers drop ~1000×): a real regression reads as a huge improvement and is reported `ok`;
- unit shrinks (`ms` → `us`, numbers grow ~1000×): a phantom `+99900%`-class regression alarm.

The units are per-benchmark literals in the harness (`pkgs/id/benches/world_bench.rs:249-270`: `us_per_append`, `us_per_compact`, `us_per_event`, `us_per_delivery`), so a harness change that rescales one benchmark (plausible as a workload grows) lands exactly in the window this reporting exists for: the PR that changes the unit is compared against a `baseline.txt` that still carries the old unit, until someone re-baselines.

## Verified (this run, script at main 2617b73a, sha256 f16a21f1…)

Driving the real script with the harness's own line format:

```text
baseline: bench alpha unit=us_per_event median=100.000 …
current:  bench alpha unit=ms_per_event median=0.200 …
report:   | alpha | us_per_event | 100.000 | 0.200 | -99.8% | ok |
```

0.200 ms is 200 µs — a **+100% regression** — reported as **−99.8%, ok**, with the current value mislabelled as `us_per_event`.

Two adjacent comparability holes in the same computation, same probe run:

- A baseline median of `0.000` (the harness prints `median={:.3}`, so a sub-microsecond benchmark rounds to exactly this) yields change `+inf%` and a "regressed more than 20%" flag with an infinite percentage, instead of an incomparable/undefined note.
- A non-numeric `BENCH_REGRESSION_THRESHOLD_PCT` (the workflow exposes it as an env knob) silently disables all flagging: with `=abc`, a +10% row and the threshold line both pass and the report concludes "No benchmark regressed more than abc%" — the awk string comparison never fires. No validation error is printed.

## Why it matters

This report is the only regression signal for the F11.8 benchmarks (#539/#1512/#1513). It is deliberately non-blocking, so its entire value is that the numbers it prints can be trusted at a glance. A unit change currently makes it print a confident, wrong verdict — masking a real regression in one direction and crying wolf in the other — and the baseline-unit-only column hides the very fact a reader would need to notice.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] When a benchmark's current unit differs from its baseline unit, the row is reported as incomparable (both units shown, no percent change, no ok/regression verdict), and the summary calls out the unit change explicitly.
- [ ] A zero baseline median never produces `+inf%`/`-inf%`/`nan%`; it is reported as incomparable (or handled by a documented rule) instead.
- [ ] A non-numeric `BENCH_REGRESSION_THRESHOLD_PCT` is rejected with a clear message (usage-style exit or an explicit report warning), never silently treated as "flag nothing".
- [ ] Same-unit comparisons, `not run`, and `no baseline` rows behave exactly as today; the script still always exits 0 for missing files / no regressions (non-blocking design preserved).
- [ ] A test or fixture run covers the unit-mismatch and zero-baseline cases (the script currently has no tests at all).

body:
## Finding

The stale-branch cleanup workflow deletes candidates in a bare loop under `set -euo pipefail`, with no per-branch failure handling. One failed `git push origin --delete` aborts the whole run: later candidates are never attempted, the finish line never prints, and the same undeletable branch (ruleset protection, a concurrent delete, a transient push error) can starve every later candidate on every subsequent daily live run.

This is one cross-repo set — the workflow is byte-identical in the three repos below; file/fix it as a set, not per-repo duplicates.

## Evidence

- Source PRs (this repo): PR #1464 created the workflow; PR #1493 (`ci: run branch cleanup daily`, head `494e6dd5`) changed the schedule to daily, and its body states `BRANCH_CLEANUP_LIVE` has been set to true and verified — so scheduled runs perform live deletions daily.
- Current main `b2adaf47` (developing-today/code), `.github/workflows/branch-cleanup.yml`: `set -euo pipefail` at line 46; deletion loop at lines 150–159 with a bare `git push origin --delete "$branch"` at line 155 and no guard, failure collection, or `|| true`.
- Same loop, verified on current main today: developing-today/opencode (`9ba2221f`, workflow lines 46 and 155) and developing-today/openchamber (`93027f59`, lines 46 and 155).
- Mechanism: under `set -e`, a failing command in the loop body (not in a condition) terminates the script immediately — later loop iterations never run. This exact mechanism was reproduced and confirmed for the identical nix workflow when it was filed as dezren39/nix#1004.
- Reference fix: dezren39/nix already fixed its copy (nix#1004, now closed): the loop there uses `elif git push origin --delete "$branch"; then … else` to collect failures, keep going, and fail visibly at the end. Port that shape.

## Why it matters

The cleanup is live and daily in this repo. A single branch that cannot be deleted silently blocks cleanup of every candidate after it, indefinitely, and the run failure reads as a generic workflow failure rather than naming the branch that failed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A failed `git push origin --delete` for one candidate does not stop the run: remaining candidates are still attempted (code, opencode, and openchamber copies).
- [ ] Each failed deletion is reported by name in the log and step summary, with deleted/failed counts in the final summary.
- [ ] Partial failure is visible in the run outcome, not a clean full success.
- [ ] Dry-run behaviour, candidate criteria, open-PR head/base protections (PR #1586), the checkout pin (PR #1580), and the 50-candidate cap are unchanged.

Found by pr-diff-review lane B reviewing PRs #1464/#1493's workflow lineage (this run: PR #1493 in the >1468 batch).

title: mcpx(cli): exec artifact delivery silently overwrites same-named artifacts — applyFrame and fetchArtifacts rename onto the bare sanitized name, unlike Store.Export's never-overwrite rule

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The mcpx CLI's two exec artifact-delivery paths write incoming artifacts to `--artifacts-dir` under their sanitized name with **no collision handling** — a second artifact whose name sanitizes to the same file silently overwrites the first, and both artifacts' `Path` fields end up pointing at the one surviving file. This contradicts the artifact store's own documented rule: `Store.Export` resolves collisions by suffixing and never overwrites, because "a script that emits two files called `shot.png` has produced two files, and silently keeping one of them is data loss" (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/artifacts/artifacts.go:548-555`, guarded by `TestExportNeverOverwrites`).

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe driving the real code)

Probe test in `internal/cli` (package `cli`) on a laptop worktree at origin/main `63ba1705`; `internal/cli/exec.go` sha256 `292a18a0…` and `internal/artifacts/name.go` sha256 `8651feab…`, identical to the sandbox clone. Log: goal hidden_files `probe-2026-10-28-laneA-mcpxart/out.log`.

1. **Sanitize collisions are easy to hit** (real `artifacts.SanitizeName`): `"my shot.png"` and `"my-shot.png"` both → `my-shot.png`; `"a/b.png"` and `"b.png"` both → `b.png`; identical names trivially collide.
2. **Streaming path loses the first body**: real `App.applyFrame` fed two artifacts (`id1`, `id2`) both named `shot.png` with bodies `FIRST-BODY` / `SECOND-BODY` → the artifacts dir contains exactly one file, `shot.png` = `"SECOND-BODY"`, and `res.Artifacts[0].Path == res.Artifacts[1].Path`. Root cause: `FrameArtifactEnd` renames the temp file straight onto `filepath.Join(eo.ArtifactsDir, artifacts.SanitizeName(name))` (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/cli/exec.go:313-321`); `os.Rename` replaces the destination.
3. **Fetched path loses it too**: real `writeNew(dest, "FIRST-BODY")` then `writeNew(dest, "SECOND-BODY")` → dest holds only `SECOND-BODY`. `fetchArtifacts` computes the same bare dest (`exec.go:396`) and `writeNew` finishes with `os.Rename` onto it (`exec.go:407-420`) — the temp name protects against partial files, not against clobbering a finished one. This also means re-running the same script overwrites the previous run's artifact of the same name in the dir.
4. **Control**: the same probe's `Store.Export` of two `shot.png` artifacts returns `shot.png` and `shot-1.png` — the behaviour the store documents and tests.

## Why it matters

`mcpx run`/`exec --artifacts-dir` is how scripts hand files back to the caller. Two screenshots, two exports with a path-y or space-y name, or simply a repeat run, silently destroy the first file while the result JSON still lists both artifacts as delivered (with the same `Path`) — data loss that reports success, in the one subsystem that already wrote down why that must never happen.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both CLI delivery paths (`applyFrame`'s `FrameArtifactEnd` rename and `fetchArtifacts`/`writeNew`) place same-named artifacts at distinct paths, using the store's suffix convention (`shot.png`, `shot-1.png`, …) or an equivalent never-overwrite rule shared with `uniquePath`.
- [ ] Each artifact's `Path` in the result names the file that actually holds its body; a test in `internal/cli` mirrors `TestExportNeverOverwrites` for both delivery paths (two same-named artifacts → two files, both bodies intact, suffix before the extension).
- [ ] Re-running a script into a non-empty `--artifacts-dir` does not overwrite the previous run's same-named artifact (or, if that is judged intended, the overwrite is explicit in the flag help and the result — not silent).
- [ ] Existing artifact and CLI tests still pass; `TestExportNeverOverwrites` semantics unchanged.

body:
## Summary

mcpx's server half honours the 2026-07-28 caching contract; its client half never did. The client drops `ttlMs`/`cacheScope` on the floor, the pool's catalogue cache has a timestamp and no expiry, and the on-disk schema cache persists `private` catalogues and re-serves them after a restart as if they were public and eternally fresh. This design gives the pool cache a freshness deadline and a scope, era-scoped the way the spec is.

Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-client-cache-hints.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace (full audit, alternatives, risks, open questions).

## Current state (verified on main 33a4e674, 2026-10-28)

- Server side landed: `internal/mcpserver/server.go` stamps `ttlMs` + `cacheScope` on complete cacheable results for modern peers (scope table ~L690-706; envelope ~L730-740; values from `protoMessages.listMaxAge` / `readMaxAge` settings).
- Client side missing: list result types in `internal/mcpclient/client.go` (`toolsListResult` ~L183, `resourcesListResult` ~L204, `resourceTemplatesListResult` ~L209, `promptsListResult` ~L1117) carry no hint fields; `ListTools`/`ListResources`/`ListPrompts` return bare slices.
- Pool: `Pool.Schemas` (`internal/pool/pool.go` ~L815) serves the cache forever once `schemaAt` is set; only `Invalidate()` (list_changed, via `internal/daemon/hooks.go`) or manual refresh re-reads.
- Disk: `Registry.loadCache`/`SaveCache` (`internal/daemon/registry.go` ~L249-285) persist and re-seed every catalogue with no TTL applied to `FetchedAt` and no scope check.
- The conformance register says it nine times (`internal/conformance/coverage_stateful.go:113-121`, client gaps under dezren39/nix#200): "the client ignores ttlMs and cacheScope; the pool keeps upstream lists until list_changed or restart" — plus `caching-notification-invalidates` (#257) unverified.

## Proposal (decisions recorded in the design doc)

- **Freshness is era-scoped.** Modern upstream: hints rule — absent/zero/negative `ttlMs` = immediately stale; positive = hard deadline. Legacy upstream: unchanged (cache until list_changed / refresh / restart) — the TTL rules exist only in 2026-07-28, and legacy's invalidation channel is its notifications.
- **Aggregated hints.** A list's TTL is the minimum across its pages; its scope is `private` if any page says so. The pool cache expires at the earliest of its three lists' deadlines.
- **Private never persists.** `SaveCache` skips private catalogues; public disk entries carry deadline + scope (cacheVersion bump) and seed expired if their deadline passed.
- **Stale on error only.** A failed refetch of an expired entry serves the stale entry and records the error; a failed first fetch behaves exactly as today.

## Phases (each independently landable; filed as sub-issues)

1. **Client hints + pool TTL (modern era)** — hint fields/aggregation in `internal/mcpclient` (incl. templates `nextCursor` → `*string` + paging), hint-returning list variants with existing signatures kept as wrappers; pool deadline + `Schemas()` expiry; five `caching-*` gaps retired.
2. **Scope, disk persistence, stale-on-error** — scope plumbing, private-never-persisted, expired-on-load seeding, stale-on-refetch-failure; `caching-private-no-cross-auth` retired. Gated on Phase 1.
3. **Truth-up + notification verification + origin note** — the missing list_changed-invalidates-cache test; `docs/compare/register/pagination-caching.md` PG-08..PG-13 rewritten as-built; remaining gaps retired with reasons; roadmap row updated; evidence comment on dezren39/nix#200 (comment, not close — that umbrella tracks other rows). Gated on Phases 1–2.

Open questions stay in the design doc (resources/read client caching, discover/era TTL, a legacy default TTL knob, per-kind deadlines, background revalidation) — they are questions, not issues.

## Related

- Origin: dezren39/nix#200 (its summary names this remainder: "`ttlMs` on upstream lists is ignored")
- Roadmap: `planning/roadmaps/mcpx.md` → Next → "Legacy client robustness" (nix#203, nix#200, nix#201)
- Register: `pkgs/mcpx/docs/compare/register/pagination-caching.md` PG-08..PG-13
- Neighbouring designs (distinct): #1384, #1414, #1481, #1531, #1554

<!-- agent-note:v1 agent=design-architect-code state=filed at=2026-10-28T05:34:00Z -->

## Acceptance criteria

- The design decisions in the linked design doc are implemented by the three phase issues (#1602, #1603, #1604): the mcpclient list types carry `ttlMs`/`cacheScope`, aggregated hints (minimum TTL across pages, `private` if any page is private) drive pool cache expiry, and legacy-era upstreams keep the unchanged cache-until-list_changed behaviour.
- `Registry.SaveCache` never persists a `private` catalogue; public disk entries carry deadline + scope (cacheVersion bumped) and seed expired once their deadline has passed.
- The conformance register's client-caching gaps (coverage_stateful.go, under dezren39/nix#200) are updated to match the landed behaviour, and the stale-on-refetch-error behaviour is covered by a test.

body:
# aggregator: julesSummary presents a previous day's keeper totals as the last run's — the "freshest note" is picked by lexicographic HHMM key, which rolls over at midnight

## What

`julesSummary` in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/sources/jules.ts:81-99` picks the keeper run note whose totals it reports by taking the lexicographically largest `jules_note_<HHMM>` key in the keeper state:

```ts
if (/^jules_note_\d+$/.test(k) && typeof v === "string" && k > bestKey) { bestKey = k; bestText = v; }
```

The key carries a time-of-day only — no date. The keeper state file is long-lived (its `items` map persists across runs and days), so notes from more than one day coexist, and "largest HHMM" is not "freshest":

- After any run past midnight, yesterday's late-evening note (e.g. `jules_note_2359`) outranks every note from today until a run lands after 23:59 — the summary shows yesterday's totals **all day**.
- An unpadded key the regex happily accepts (`jules_note_905`) outranks a padded later one (`jules_note_1458`: `"905" > "1458"` lexicographically).

Meanwhile `summary.at` is taken from `state.last_run` (jules.ts:84-87) — the *actual* last run — so the two halves of the summary disagree. The consumer pairs them in one sentence: `src/sources/live.ts:1015-1019` renders "last keeper run ${j.at} · last run totals: ${j.total} sessions — …", attributing the stale totals to the fresh run. The collector bakes this summary into the fleet feed (`scripts/collect-fleet-feed.ts:438-444,559`).

## Evidence (verified this run)

Probe on the laptop (Bun 1.4.2) driving the verbatim `jules.ts` (sha256 `15b46caf8b7a052a2b37fcbd6de0bca489a9e5ab9286e77a41f59ba6ccabf5f9`, identical on main `7bd79a62` both sides; probe + log in the goal's hidden_files `probe-2026-10-27-laneA-julesnote/`):

- CONTROL — single note `jules_note_1458` (84 sessions / 77 completed / 6 failed), `last_run` 2026-10-27T14:58Z → totals 84/77/6. Correct.
- CASE 1 (midnight rollover) — notes `jules_note_2359` (84/77/6, yesterday) + `jules_note_0010` (12/3/1, today), `last_run` 2026-10-28T00:10Z → summary returns **84/77/6** with `at` = 2026-10-28T00:10Z. The dashboard sentence claims today's 00:10 run listed 84 sessions; it listed 12.
- CASE 2 (stale all day) — notes `jules_note_2359` (84/77/6) + `jules_note_0930` (20/9/2), `last_run` 2026-10-28T09:30Z → returns **84/77/6**.
- CASE 3 (unpadded key) — notes `jules_note_905` (50/40/5) + `jules_note_1458` (84/77/6), `last_run` 2026-10-27T14:58Z → returns **50/40/5**.

Existing tests (`test/slice2.test.ts`, "parses keeper totals") cover only the single-note same-day state.

## Why it matters

The Jules coverage line is how Drew (and the fleet's own health views) judge whether the Jules keeper is keeping up. After midnight it silently reports the previous day's session totals as the current run's — a wrong-but-plausible number, the worst kind of dashboard defect, and it persists for most of every day once the state file holds a late-evening note.

## Acceptance criteria

- `julesSummary` reports the totals of the note written by the run `last_run` names (e.g. match the note key against `last_run`'s HHMM), or the note selection is otherwise date-aware; when no note can be tied to the last run, the totals are omitted rather than guessed from another run.
- The key comparison, if any remains, is numeric on a zero-padded HHMM (an unpadded `jules_note_905` must not outrank `jules_note_1458`).
- New tests cover: notes spanning midnight (2359 yesterday + 0010 today), a stale late-evening note alongside a morning note, and an unpadded key.
- The existing single-note test keeps passing; `mapJulesItems` is unchanged.

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-a (lane A), 2026-10-27 run.

title: id(repl): the preprocessor's heredoc and $(...) scans are quote-blind — a quoted ')' errors the line and a quoted '<<' drops the REPL into heredoc mode with a garbage delimiter

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The REPL's input preprocessor scans for its shell-like operators with quote-blind substring searches, so quoted text that merely *contains* an operator character is misparsed — valid shell-shaped lines either error out or silently drop the REPL into heredoc mode with a garbage delimiter.

All in `pkgs/id/src/repl/input.rs` (`preprocess_repl_line`):

1. **Heredoc detection** (`:215`) is `line.find("<<")` over the whole raw line, before any other processing. A `<<` inside quotes or inside a `$(...)` substitution starts heredoc mode, and everything after the `<<` becomes the "delimiter".
2. **The `$(...)` closing-paren scan** (`:267-282`) counts `(`/`)` over every character, including parens inside single- or double-quoted strings within the substitution. A quoted paren closes the substitution early (or holds it open forever).

## Evidence

Verified on main `7bd79a62` with a probe crate on the laptop driving the verbatim `input.rs` (sha256 `a9138d2856f2bc7896d7e22455e6488068a86bdb28db2de96ad2a99f1a977f96`, identical both sides; anyhow 1 + rustyline 18 per `pkgs/id/Cargo.toml`). Controls behave correctly; every quoted case misparses:

| Input | Shell-correct result | Actual |
|---|---|---|
| `get $(echo hi)` (control) | `get hi` | `Ready "get hi"` ✅ |
| `put - name <<EOF` (control) | heredoc, delimiter `EOF` | `NeedMore delimiter="EOF"` ✅ |
| `get $(echo $(echo nested))` (control) | `get nested` | `Ready "get nested"` ✅ |
| `get $(echo ')')` | `get )` | **error**: the scan closes at the quoted `)`, so `shell_capture` runs `echo '` → `sh: unexpected EOF while looking for matching ''` |
| `get $(echo '(')` | `get (` | **error**: `unterminated $(...) in command` (the quoted `(` raises the depth forever) |
| `get $(echo ")")` | `get )` | **error**: same early-close failure via double quotes |
| `get $(printf 'a<<b')` | `get a<<b` | **heredoc mode**: `NeedMore delimiter="b')"` , original line truncated to `get $(printf 'a` |
| `get "a<<b"` | `get "a<<b"` | **heredoc mode**: `NeedMore delimiter="b\""` |

The heredoc cases are the worst: `repl/runner.rs:130-148` answers `NeedMore` by consuming further lines until one exactly equals the garbage delimiter (`b')`), then substitutes the collected text into the *truncated* original line. The user either Ctrl+C's and loses the command, or types the magic line and executes a mangled command. The substitution cases reject lines a shell accepts, with errors that blame the user's quoting (`unterminated…`, the shell's own EOF complaint) rather than the scan.

This is the same preprocessor whose closing-paren scan was just fixed for byte-vs-char indices in #1583; that fix made the scan offset-correct but it remains quote-blind.

## Why it matters

`preprocess_repl_line` is the front door for every interactive `id` session. Filenames and content with parens or `<<` in quoted arguments are ordinary (e.g. `get $(echo 'report (final)')`, tags or names containing `<<`), and the failure modes are silent-ish: a REPL that suddenly starts swallowing lines into a heredoc with an invisible delimiter looks hung.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The heredoc check and the `$(...)` paren scan skip over single- and double-quoted spans (with the quoting rules documented in the module doc comment), so the five quoted cases above preprocess to their shell-correct results.
- [ ] Regression tests in `repl/input.rs` cover at minimum: quoted `)` and `(` inside `$(...)` (both quote kinds), `<<` inside a quoted argument, and `<<` inside a quoted string within `$(...)`.
- [ ] Existing behaviour is unchanged for the control cases: genuine heredocs, here-strings, nested `$(...)`, backticks, and the `|>` pipe — the current test module keeps passing, including the #1583 multibyte tests.
- [ ] Backtick and here-string scans are audited for the same class of misparse; any case left quote-blind is named in the PR with a reason.
