The web world presenter (`pkgs/id/web/src/world-surface.ts`) still diverges from the Rust validator for four grapheme classes. CLOSED #1431 fixed emoji-modifier and tag sequences (PR #1542), but two classes that were folded into #1431 as evidence (comment 6446198995) were not touched by that fix, and two further classes in the same function were found this run. In every case a screen the Rust side validates and the SSH presenter renders (`world_presentation.rs:219` parse, `:350` `render_ansi`, both measuring with `UnicodeWidthStr::width` under unicode-width 0.2.2, pinned in `pkgs/id/Cargo.lock`) is either refused whole by the web presenter — `renderWorldSurface` returns `false`, so `world.ts:175-176` falls back to dumping the raw frame text — or, worse, accepted at the wrong column count, producing a misaligned grid.

## Verified on main 601af5a2 (2026-10-27, lane-B creator run)

Method: TS probe on the laptop driving the verbatim `world-surface.ts` (sha256 `3ee9823c` identical both sides; Bun 1.4.2, minimal DOM stub, `renderWorldSurface` called directly) against a Rust probe crate on the laptop using the pinned `unicode-width =0.2.2` + `unicode-segmentation` (the exact crates `world_presentation.rs` uses). Controls behaved: `x` Rust 1 / TS renders at 1; U+1F600 Rust 2 / renders at 2, refused at 1; the #1542 controls U+1F44D U+1F3FD and the England tag flag render at 2.

### 1. ⬛ U+2B1B and ⭕ U+2B55 — wide in Rust, missing from `WIDE_RANGES`

- Rust: both are 1 grapheme, width **2**.
- TS: refused at `columns=2`, wrongly **accepted at `columns=1`** (`WIDE_RANGES`, world-surface.ts:60-127, has no U+2Bxx entry; `codePointWidth` falls through to 1).
- This class was reported on #1431 (evidence comment 6446198995) and survived its fix.

### 2. Narrow base + skin-tone modifier — ☝🏻 U+261D U+1F3FB

- Rust: 1 grapheme, width **2** (unicode-width measures an emoji-modifier sequence at 2 even when the base alone is narrow).
- TS: refused at `columns=2`, accepted at `columns=1`. PR #1542's modifier rule (world-surface.ts:162-167) strips the modifier and measures the base alone, so a narrow base measures 1 — correct for the bases #1431 tested, wrong for narrow bases.
- Also reported on #1431 and survived its fix.

### 3. Composed Hangul jamo clusters — U+1100 U+1161 (LV) and U+1100 U+1161 U+11A8 (LVT)

- Rust: each is 1 grapheme, width **2** (a jamo syllable measures as the precomposed syllable U+AC00 does — and the precomposed form renders correctly in TS).
- TS: refused at **both** `columns=2` and `columns=1` — `codePointWidth` sums choseong 2 + jungseong 1 + jongseong 1. Any decomposed-Hangul screen (NFD text, jamo input methods) falls back whole.
- New this run; the #1431-era sweep tested jamo only as single code points, which match.

### 4. One grapheme longer than 16 UTF-16 units, and a lone spacing mark

- `e` + 17× U+0301 (combining acute): Rust 1 grapheme, width **1**. TS refuses at `columns=1` — pinned to the `cell.symbol.length > 16` check (world-surface.ts, cell validation in `renderWorldSurface`): the same grapheme at UTF-16 length 15 and 16 renders, at 17 and 18 it is refused. The Rust validator imposes no symbol-length limit — only exactly-one-grapheme and width 1–2 — so the cap is a TS-only rule that rejects Rust-valid cells.
- Lone U+0903 (Devanagari spacing combining mark, category Mc): Rust width **1**; TS width 0 via the `/^\p{M}$/u` rule (world-surface.ts:133,142), so the cell is refused at both column counts. (Inside a cluster after a base consonant both sides agree at the base's width; only the standalone mark diverges.)

## Why it matters

The presenter is the web half of a two-presenter contract: the same validated `ScreenSurface` must render on SSH and web. Every divergence either drops the whole screen to a raw-text dump (classes 1–4, at the correct column count) or silently misaligns it (classes 1–2, at the wrong count — a guest that disagrees with the Rust validator, or a future Rust change, would pass the web check it should fail). ⬛/⭕ are ordinary emoji a world program can plausibly draw as tiles; decomposed Hangul and accented Latin are ordinary text.

## Acceptance criteria

- `renderWorldSurface` agrees with `UnicodeWidthStr::width` (unicode-width 0.2.2) for: U+2B1B, U+2B55 (2, and refused at 1); U+261D U+1F3FB (2, refused at 1); composed jamo LV and LVT clusters (2); a lone U+0903 cell (1).
- The symbol-length rule is reconciled with the Rust side: either the TS cap is removed/raised so a 1-grapheme, width-1 symbol of 17+ UTF-16 units renders, or an explicit matching cap is added to `world_presentation.rs` with a comment naming the shared bound — the two validators must not disagree silently.
- A parity test in `world-surface.test.ts` covers each class above at its correct column count (renders) and at the wrong one (refused), in the style of the existing #761/#1431 tests.
- Existing presenter tests still pass; the #1542 modifier/tag controls (U+1F44D U+1F3FD, England flag) still render at 2.

## Notes

- Follow-up remainder of CLOSED #1431 / PR #1542 (classes 1–2 were its evidence comment 6446198995); classes 3–4 are new findings in the same function from this run's sweep. Distinct from OPEN #1322 (Playwright e2e coverage of the presenter — that is test-infrastructure, not a width defect).
- Probe artifacts: `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-surface2/` in the goal workspace (probe.ts, boundary.ts, main.rs, out.log, rust-out.log); laptop copies under `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-surface2/`.

title: id(encryption): welcome Reassembly has no size bound — one chunk may exceed the frame payload cap, and a forged chunk stream buffers without limit

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/id/src/encryption/welcome.rs` — the welcome chunking from P4.12 — bounds the **split** side carefully and the **receive** side not at all. `split()` never emits a chunk with more than `CHUNK_PAYLOAD_BYTES` (1 MiB frame − 256 header bytes) of payload, but `Reassembly::push` (welcome.rs:175-206) checks only the chunk's self-digest, the sequence, and total/digest consistency. It never checks:

1. **Per-chunk size** — a single chunk may carry far more than `CHUNK_PAYLOAD_BYTES`.
2. **Total reassembled size / chunk count** — `total` is a sender-claimed `u32`; the payload `Vec` grows with every accepted chunk and is only digest-checked when the *last* chunk arrives, which a sender can postpone forever (`total = u32::MAX`).

The chunk `check` is an unkeyed `Hash::digest` of the chunk bytes — any sender computes a valid one for arbitrary bytes, so these are not theoretical inputs: a forged stream is self-consistent by construction.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Probe crate on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-welcome` there; log in the goal's `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-welcome/out.log`) driving the verbatim `welcome.rs` from main `dd9eb979` (original sha256 `fabcbe9a…`; probe copy differs only in the import block — `Envelope`/`Hash`/CBOR stubbed, `MAX_FRAME_BYTES` = 1 MiB as in `frames.rs:20`):

- CONTROL: a genuine `split()` welcome reassembles; an altered chunk is refused with `AlteredChunk` — the existing checks work.
- CASE 1: one forged chunk of **1,113,856 bytes** (payload cap is 1,048,320) with `total = 2` → `push` returns `Ok(None)` — accepted.
- CASE 2: a forged stream with `total = u32::MAX`, 512 sequential chunks × 64 KiB, each with a correct self-check → **512/512 accepted, 32 MiB buffered, no error**. The probe stopped at 512; nothing in `push` ever stops it — the buffer grows until the sender runs out or memory does.

## Why it matters

The reassembly sits on the join path: the bytes it buffers are supplied by whoever sends the welcome, before the envelope is decoded or authenticated (the module doc is explicit that decoding happens only after the whole checks out). Every other refusal in this module is "as it arrives" — altered, out-of-sequence, foreign, zero-total — but size, the one resource a sender fully controls, is unbounded in both dimensions. When this is wired into the world join flow (the frame transport caps a single *frame*, not the number of frames), one peer can grow a joiner's memory without limit with a stream of individually well-formed chunks. The split side's contract ("chunks that each fit a frame") is currently a courtesy, not an invariant the receiver enforces.

## Acceptance criteria

- `Reassembly::push` refuses a chunk whose payload exceeds `CHUNK_PAYLOAD_BYTES` (new `WelcomeError` variant, e.g. `ChunkTooLarge`), before buffering it.
- The reassembly refuses — at the first chunk, not the last — a `total`/implied reassembled size above a named maximum welcome size (a constant with a rationale tied to the real welcome bound: ~40 bytes/epoch, epochs a group can actually accumulate), with a distinct error.
- Tests: oversized single chunk refused; a stream whose declared total exceeds the maximum refused on chunk 0; a genuine above-frame-cap welcome (existing `welcome-recent` round-trip test, 21 epochs) still reassembles; existing altered/out-of-sequence/other-welcome tests keep passing.
- The module doc states the receive-side bounds alongside the split-side ones.

Out of scope: signing chunks or changing the wire format — the digests already detect alteration; this is purely the missing size bound.

body:
## Problem

CI run 40617526037 (PR #1563, head 56f010e9) failed 7 `pkgs/id` flake checks (rustfmt-check, cargo-check, test-shard-1/2/3, crash-gate-sampled, crash-gate-ingest) with symptoms of a **corrupted source copy inside the build**, not the committed code:

- rustfmt job 122589807600 log shows Rust parse errors in the build copy of `pkgs/id/src/directory.rs`: `error[E0765]: unterminated double quote string` at :2925 and `prefix 'com' is unknown` at :2896 (`normalize_email("ok@example.com")`).
- The git content at the PR head (verified via the GitHub contents API at 56f010e9, 2026-10-28T02:44Z) has those exact lines intact and valid; the PR diff is that single file and its committed form parses.
- All failures are confined to the one run; other workflows on the same head (nix ci) passed.

So the source snapshot the nix builds received differed from the git tree — torn/corrupted in a way that split string literals. Every check that compiled that file failed the same way, which reads exactly like several independent code failures until the logs are compared.

## Impact

- Blocks PR #1563 (task 1622 / issue #1521) until the run completes and failed jobs can be re-run.
- Wastes reviewer/worker cycles root-causing phantom parse errors; similar in spirit to the Magic Nix Cache HTTP 418 flake seen on PR for #1418 (task 1485, 2026-10-28).

## Acceptance

- Identify where the build's source copy can diverge from the git tree (flake source filtering / cache / checkout path) for run 40617526037, or catch the divergence mechanically (e.g. a source-tree hash check early in the id workflow that fails fast with a clear "source snapshot mismatch" message instead of 7 downstream parse/test failures).
- A re-run of the failed jobs on the same head passes without any code change, OR the divergence mechanism is found and fixed.

Filed by repo-queue-worker lane A (task 1622 resume, 2026-10-28).

## Acceptance criteria
- The divergence point for run 40617526037 is identified — where the flake build's source copy can differ from the git tree (flake source filtering / cache / checkout path) — OR a mechanical guard exists (e.g. a source-tree hash check early in the id workflow) that fails fast with a clear "source snapshot mismatch" message instead of 7 downstream parse/test failures.
- A re-run of the failed jobs on the same head passes without any code change, OR the divergence mechanism is found and fixed.
- Root-cause findings are recorded on this issue either way, so the next phantom-parse failure is recognizable on sight.

title: aggregator: a future-dated read is 'today' forever until its date passes — derive freshness() has no upper bound, so one skewed measuredAt pins a hub card fresh for weeks

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: app/aggregator
labels.description: Package/app: aggregator (pm-stack in this repo)

body:
## Summary

`freshness()` in the aggregator's derive module has no upper bound: a **future-dated** `measuredAt` is reported as age 0 — "today", not stale — and stays that way until `cadenceDays` **after** its future date arrives. A read stamped +30 days in the future with a 7-day cadence is presented as fresh for 37 days; a read stamped +365 days is fresh for a year. Both branches (date-only and datetime) clamp the negative age to 0, so the stale check `ageDays > cadenceDays` can never fire for a future stamp.

This is the freshness stamp on the hub's SaaS-service and PAYG cards — exactly the surface whose job is to say a dated read is old (§1.1). Garbage and missing stamps are handled correctly (`stale: true, ageDays: null`); only the future direction is missing.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `db6f7d00`)

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/derive.ts:855-868` — `freshness(measuredAt, cadenceDays, now)`:
  - date-only branch (:862): `ageDays = Math.max(0, Math.round((startOfToday - t) / 86_400_000))`
  - datetime branch (:867): `ageDays = Math.max(0, Math.floor((now.getTime() - t) / 86_400_000))`
  - both then return `stale: ageDays > cadenceDays` — for any future `t`, age is clamped to 0 and `stale` is false.
- Laptop probe (Bun 1.4.2, real `derive.ts`, sha256 `312ac0fb` identical on sandbox and laptop; probe + log in the fleet's probe records for this run), fixed `now = 2026-10-27T12:00:00Z`, cadence 7:
  - controls correct: `2026-10-26` → `{stale:false, ageDays:1}`; `2026-10-19` → `{stale:true, ageDays:8}`; garbage → `{stale:true, ageDays:null}`; `null` → `{stale:true, ageDays:null}`
  - `2026-10-28` (+1d), `2026-11-26` (+30d, both date-only and datetime forms), and `2027-10-27T12:00:00Z` (+365d) all → `{stale:false, ageDays:0}`
  - the +30d stamp evaluated forward: still `{stale:false, ageDays:0}` at +29d and +30d, `ageDays:7` (still not stale) at +37d, and only stale at +38d.
- Render surface: `freshnessStamp` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/render.ts:1651-1659`) renders `ageDays === 0` as "· today" and adds the stale badge only when `f.stale`; callers are the PAYG card (`render.ts:1704` via `serviceCardHtml`'s freshness, and the PAYG line stamps), `serviceCardHtml` (:1704), and the service detail page (`render.ts:1889`).
- A future stamp is reachable, not hypothetical: the SaaS extractors set `measuredAt` from the freshest date in a section when no `**Last checked:**` bullet is present (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/saas-extract.ts:628`, `:651-652` — `freshestDate(section)`), and sections legitimately carry future operational dates (renewals, cycle ends — the exact hazard `snapshot-records.ts`'s `lastCheckedDate` comment warns about). One future renewal date in a section without a Last-checked bullet becomes that service's `measuredAt`, and this bug then certifies it "today" for weeks. A typo'd year in the human-maintained quota view does the same.
- Existing tests pin only the past/null directions: `pm-stack/aggregator/test/usage.test.ts:266-270` (1-day-old not stale, 25-day-old stale, null stale). No future-dated case exists.

## Why it matters

The freshness stamp is the dashboard's honesty mechanism for dated reads: it is what stops an old console read from being presented as current. A future stamp defeats it in the worst direction — the card claims the read happened today, carries no stale badge, and keeps claiming that until well after the stamped date — so a mis-dated or renewal-contaminated read silently pins a service's card as current while the real data ages underneath.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `measuredAt` in the future (beyond a small, named clock-skew tolerance that triage pins — e.g. 1 day for date-only stamps) is never reported as `ageDays: 0` / "today" with `stale: false`: it is stale, or carries an explicit future/invalid age state the render surfaces honestly.
- [ ] The rule applies to both branches (date-only and datetime) in `freshness()`.
- [ ] Controls unchanged: yesterday is 1 day old and not stale at cadence 7, a read older than its cadence is stale, garbage/null stay `{stale: true, ageDays: null}`.
- [ ] Tests in `usage.test.ts` (or the render freshness tests) pin: +1d, +30d, and +365d future stamps in both stamp forms; the boundary at the chosen skew tolerance.
- [ ] `freshnessStamp` does not render a future stamp as "· today" without a stale/future indication.

## Dedup / distinctness

Searched open + closed issues for `freshness`, `future-dated`, and `ageDays`: no filing covers `derive.ts freshness()`. Adjacent but different modules, gates, and fix surfaces:

- #1541 — `quota-current.ts entryState`: a future `measuredAt` on a **gatherer entry** replaces a pool's windows. Different input (gatherer JSON, 20-minute bound), different function, different consequence (window replacement vs the hub cards' stale badge/age).
- #1564 — `feed.ts` / `health.ts`: a garbage or future `generatedAt` on the **fleet feed / orchestration section** never goes stale. Different stamps (feed/section, not per-service dated reads), and that filing's garbage case is the opposite of this one (here garbage is already handled).

The fix for either of those does not touch `derive.ts freshness()` or its render callers.

title: id(waiting): the waiting pool has no total cap — the per-author cap is Sybil-defeated, so one peer can make a node hold (and persist) unbounded waiting events

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/m
labels.description: Medium: expected under 1 day of work

body:
## Bug / robustness gap

`pkgs/id/src/waiting.rs` — the waiting pool has **no total cap**. The only bounds are per-author and per-event age, so the module doc's claim is not true as written:

> "Two caps bound what a peer can make a node hold: at most `WaitingLimits::per_author` waiting events per author, and a drop once an event has waited `WaitingLimits::max_age_ms`." (`waiting.rs:5-7`)

Evidence on main db6f7d00:

- `WaitingLimits` carries exactly two fields, `per_author` (default 256) and `max_age_ms` (default 7 days) — `waiting.rs:44-61`, defaults `:33-38`.
- The single hold path, `WaitingPool::hold`, checks only the per-author count and nothing else (`waiting.rs:296-322`):
  ```rust
  if self.waiting_count(author) >= self.limits.per_author() {
      return Err(WaitRefusal::AuthorFull);
  }
  ```
  `insert`, `park`, and `restore` all funnel through it; no path ever consults `self.waiting.len()` against a bound.
- Author keys are self-certifying: an event's author is the Ed25519 public key embedded in its signed header, and `chain::decode` (`src/chain.rs:321+`) verifies the signature against that embedded key. Minting a new author identity is free — generate a keypair, sign events whose `after`/backlink dependencies never arrive, and each new author gets a fresh 256-event allowance.
- Held events are not memory-only: the event store mirrors every held event into redb waiting rows on disk (`src/event_store/waiting_rows.rs:1-12`, "the events held on disk"), and restores them on open. So the unbounded total is a disk bound failure as well as a memory one, and it survives restarts until each event individually ages out (up to 7 days at the default).

## Why it matters

A single hostile or buggy peer syncing events with unsatisfiable dependencies can grow a node's waiting pool — and its on-disk waiting table — without limit: 256 events × N minted authors × up to 7 days each. The per-author cap gives the appearance of a bound (and the doc asserts one) while bounding nothing an attacker controls. Every other ingest-side resource in this codebase is capped (wants entries/bytes, schedule count/horizon, tick intervals — `src/world_caps.rs`); the waiting pool is the outlier.

## Acceptance criteria

- `WaitingLimits` gains a total cap across all authors (a named constant default, e.g. `DEFAULT_TOTAL`), enforced in `hold` so `insert`/`park`/`restore` all respect it; refusal reuses or extends `WaitRefusal` so callers can distinguish total-full from author-full (or documents why one variant serves both).
- The cap interacts sanely with restore-on-open: a store whose on-disk rows exceed a newly lowered total does not brick on open (excess handling is defined — e.g. oldest-first expiry — and tested).
- `waiting.rs` module doc updated so the stated bound is the real bound.
- Tests: a pool under a small total refuses the (total+1)-th held event spread across distinct authors while per-author counts are all below their cap; existing per-author and age-cap tests keep passing.
- No change to release order, expiry semantics, or the sync contract (a refused event is, as today, dropped and not acknowledged, so sync re-sends it if its dependency ever exists).

title: id(web): unreferenced footnote definitions are silently deleted on save — a definitions-only document saves as an empty file

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/m
labels.description: Medium: expected under 1 day of work

body:
## Bug

In the id web editor's markdown ↔ ProseMirror codec (`pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs`), a **footnote definition that no `[^label]` reference in the document points at is silently deleted on save**:

```markdown
Hello world.

[^a]: orphan definition
```

loads and saves as just:

```markdown
Hello world.
```

The extreme case is total: a document consisting only of footnote definitions (a shared notes page collecting definitions, or a draft whose references are added later)

```markdown
[^a]: just a definition
```

loads as the empty-document placeholder paragraph and saves as an **empty file** (`""`).

Definitions that *are* referenced survive — the codec has dedicated `footnote_reference` / `footnote_definition` nodes for them (#945, #1031) and they round-trip. The loss is specifically: any definition whose label no reference in the current document uses. With two definitions where only one is referenced, the referenced one round-trips and the unreferenced one vanishes in the same save.

## Verified repro (this run, main db6f7d00)

Standalone probe crate compiling the verbatim `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs` (md5 `8478c0d4fdcb251801a8efc83379f213`, identical on sandbox main and the laptop copy) against comrak 0.56 + serde_json, built and run **on the laptop** (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-creator-a2` there; logs in the goal's `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-creator-a2/probe_out3.log`):

- `orphan-footnote-def-with-text`: `"Hello world.\n\n[^a]: orphan definition\n"` → PM is a single paragraph `Hello world.` (the definition appears nowhere) → save returns `"Hello world.\n"`.
- `only-footnote-def`: `"[^a]: just a definition\n"` → PM is `{"content":[{"type":"paragraph"}]}` (the empty-doc placeholder) → save returns `""`.
- `two-defs-one-referenced`: `"text[^a]\n\n[^a]: used\n\n[^b]: unused\n"` → PM carries only definition `a` → save drops `[^b]: unused`.
- `footnote-def-only-multiline`: a two-paragraph unreferenced definition likewise saves as `""`.
- **Layer isolation:** a raw comrak `parse_document` of `"[^a]: just a definition\n"` (footnotes extension on, exactly as `commonmark_options()`, markdown.rs:81-91) yields **zero** AST children, and `"Hello.\n\n[^a]: orphan\n"` yields only the `Paragraph` — comrak never emits a `FootnoteDefinition` node for an unreferenced definition, so the codec's parse direction (the `NodeValue::FootnoteDefinition` arm, markdown.rs:559-575) never sees it. The codec inherits the loss from its parser, exactly as #1004 does for link reference definitions.

## Relation to #1004 (not a duplicate)

#1004 tracks the same *phenomenon* for **link reference definitions** (`[label]: url`), which have no PM representation at all. Footnote definitions are a different construct with a different fix surface: the PM schema and editor already represent them (#945/#1031, and #1347 tracks their editor-schema wiring), referenced definitions already round-trip, and a source pre-scan fix for #1004 would not automatically know about `[^label]:` definition syntax. This issue tracks the footnote half so neither fix silently leaves the other construct losing data.

## Why it matters

Keeping footnote definitions at the foot of a note before (or without) referencing them is a normal authoring pattern, and footnote-heavy documents are exactly the ones this codec added dedicated support for. Opening such a file in the id web editor and saving — even with no edit — destroys every unreferenced definition with no warning. Same silent-loss-on-save family as #996 (empty links) and #1004 (unused reference definitions), in a distinct mechanism.

## Suggested direction (triage to decide)

Mirroring #1004's options: (a) preserve unreferenced definitions verbatim — the parse direction would need a source pre-scan for `[^label]:` definitions, diff them against the labels comrak actually emitted, and carry the leftovers (e.g. as a trailing raw block the editor displays but does not eat); (b) if neither preservation nor a PM representation is acceptable for the unreferenced case, document the limitation in the codec's module docs (top of markdown.rs) so the loss is a known, stated behaviour instead of a silent one. Doing nothing silently is the only unacceptable outcome. If a shared pre-scan lands for #1004, extending it to footnote definitions in the same change would close this issue by reference.

## Acceptance criteria

- A document with an unreferenced footnote definition no longer loses it silently on a load/save round trip — either the definition survives (verbatim or in an equivalent form), or the limitation is explicitly documented in the codec module docs and this issue is closed citing that documentation.
- Referenced footnote definitions (single- and multi-paragraph, with block children) keep round-tripping exactly as today (#945/#1031 behaviour unchanged).
- A definitions-only document does not save as an empty file under the chosen fix (or is covered by the documented limitation).

title: aggregator: registry merge wipes a session's model/title/directory when a later sparse record omits them — the durable store forgets what it knew

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator

labels.description: Package/app: aggregator (pm-stack in this repo)

body:
## Summary

`mergeRecords` in the aggregator's session registry wipes fields the stored record already knows whenever a later incoming record for the same session omits them. A sparse re-read of a session erases its `model`, `title`, and `directory`, nulls its `parentId`, and degrades its display `label` from the session title to the raw session id — and because the merged set is persisted to the durable registry store, the loss is permanent, not just in-memory.

## Evidence (verified on main `a120b9a9`, 2026-10-27)

Root cause — `pm-stack/aggregator/src/registry.ts:115-133`: the merge is `{ ...prev, ...r, ... }` with special cases only for `startedAt`, `tokensTotal` (max), `taskRefs` (union), and `lastSeenAt` (newest). The function's own doc comment (`registry.ts:110-114`) states the contract: "every other field takes the incoming value **when present**". But records built by `recordFromSessionEntry` (`registry.ts:31-52`) always carry the keys `model`/`title`/`directory`/`tokensTotal` — with `undefined` values when the source entry omits them — and a spread copies `undefined`-valued keys, so "absent" incoming fields overwrite present stored ones. `label` is always present on an incoming record, but `recordFromSessionEntry` falls back to the raw session id when the entry has no title (`registry.ts:40`), so a title-less re-read also replaces a good label with `ses_…`.

Sparse incoming records are a real shape, not a hypothetical: `sources/opencode.ts:171-178` (`mapOne`) builds entries with `title: s.title`, `directory: s.location?.directory`, `model: s.model?.id` — all legitimately absent for some sessions — and `sources/live.ts:965` feeds those entries through `recordFromSessionEntry` into `mergeIntoRegistry` (`sources/live.ts:614-631`), which persists the merged set with `JSON.stringify` to the registry file, dropping the wiped keys from the durable store.

Reproduction — Bun 1.4.2 probe driving the real `registry.ts` (sha256 `52c524d5…`, identical on both machines; probe + log in the fleet's run records):

- Stored record (from a full entry): `model="model-a"`, `title="Fix the thing …"`, `directory="/home/user/project"`, `parentId="ses_parent"`, `label="Fix the thing …"`, `tokensTotal=500`, `lastSeenAt=11:00Z`.
- Incoming: same session, newer `lastSeenAt=12:00Z`, no title/model/directory/parent (the `mapOne` sparse shape).
- Merged result: `model=undefined`, `title=undefined`, `directory=undefined`, `parentId=null`, `label="ses_1"` — while the special-cased fields behaved exactly as documented (`tokensTotal` stayed 500, `lastSeenAt` advanced, `startedAt` kept). The persisted JSON has no `model` key at all.
- Control: an incoming record that *does* carry `model="model-b"` correctly replaces the stored model (and tokens rise to 700) — present-value-wins works; only absent-value handling is broken.

Existing test coverage (`test/slice3.test.ts`, "merge keeps the record, maxes cumulative tokens, unions task refs") only merges records derived from the same full entry shape, so the sparse-incoming case is untested.

## Why it matters

The registry is the durable identity store behind the /sessions page (#906 §3): its whole purpose is that "a session stays in the registry after it expires out of the attention feed". Every live read merges feed + laptop records into that store, so any session that is ever re-read through a sparser source permanently loses its model, title, directory, and parent linkage, and its display name regresses to a raw session id — the exact durability the store exists to provide is silently undone by the merge itself.

## Acceptance criteria

- Merging an incoming record whose `model`/`title`/`directory` are `undefined` preserves the stored values; an incoming `parentId` of `null` does not erase a stored non-null parent unless that is an explicitly decided and documented semantic.
- A title-less incoming record does not degrade a stored `label` that came from a title.
- Fields the incoming record actually carries still win (present-value-wins), and the existing special cases (`tokensTotal` max, `lastSeenAt` newest, `startedAt` earliest, `taskRefs` union) keep working.
- A regression test in the aggregator suite merges a sparse incoming record (built via `recordFromSessionEntry` from an entry omitting title/model/directory) over a full stored record and asserts the stored fields survive; the existing slice3 merge test still passes.
- The fix's treatment of each `SessionRecord` field is consistent with the doc comment's "when present" contract (update the comment if any field is deliberately exempted).

body:
Phase 2 of design #1554 (filed by the design architect, 2026-10-27). Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-tasks-one-store.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace.

**Decision in force (from #1554, do not re-litigate in triage):** `mcpclient` executes a call as an upstream task when — and only when — the tool's declared `execution.taskSupport` is `"required"`. `"optional"` stays a plain call; `"forbidden"` is untouched. An upstream task that parks in `input_required` returns a distinct named error in this phase; relaying questions downstream is an open question on #1554, not part of this phase. Origin: dezren39/nix#209 row TOOL-21 (client half) and CAP-26 (client direction — the extension is never declared upstream).

## Scope

- Today: `internal/mcpclient/client.go:171-174` carries `Tool.Execution` raw for forwarding but nothing reads `taskSupport`; `CallTool` (`client.go:1164`) is a plain `tools/call`; the pool's call site is `internal/pool/pool.go:1051`; the client declares no tasks extension to upstreams. `Client.Era` already distinguishes legacy from modern (2026-07-28) upstreams.
- In `CallTool`'s path (or the narrowest seam above it that the pool and other callers share): when the named tool's listed `execution.taskSupport` is `"required"`, run the call as an upstream task instead of a plain call:
  - **Legacy upstream:** send `params.task` with the call; on the `{task}` result, poll `tasks/get` at the task's poll interval until terminal; fetch the outcome via `tasks/result` (the underlying request's result, `related-task` meta included).
  - **Modern upstream:** the client's initialize declares `extensions["io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks"]`; on a flat `Task` result (`resultType: "task"`), poll `tasks/get` — the `DetailedTask` inlines the terminal result or error; there is no `tasks/result` in the extension.
  - Honour the task's TTL as the outer bound; on context cancellation or deadline, send `tasks/cancel` (best effort) and return the context error. A failed task returns its fault in the client's existing error shapes, so callers (pool, code mode) see a call failure, not a new protocol type.
  - An upstream task that enters `input_required` ends the call with a distinct, named error stating the upstream task asked a question this phase does not relay.
  - A non-conforming task response (missing `{task}`, wrong shape, unknown status) is a call error — never a hang and never an unbounded poll.
- Tools whose `taskSupport` is absent, `"optional"`, or `"forbidden"` follow today's plain-call path byte-for-byte.

## Acceptance

- Defining tests against fake upstreams (the client's existing fake-server test rig):
  - legacy upstream, `required` tool: the call is sent with `params.task`, the result returned to the caller is the `tasks/result` payload, and exactly the expected get/result request sequence occurs;
  - modern upstream, `required` tool: initialize declared the tasks extension, the flat task is polled via `tasks/get`, and the inlined terminal result is returned;
  - `optional` tool on either era: plain call, no task methods issued;
  - cancellation: cancelling the call context issues `tasks/cancel` upstream and returns promptly;
  - failed upstream task: the fault surfaces as the call's error;
  - `input_required` upstream task: the distinct named error is returned;
  - malformed task response: call error, no hang (test completes under its deadline).
- No changes to the server side (`internal/mcpserver`) or to pooled-call behaviour for non-`required` tools; the pool call site needs no signature change, or any change is justified on this issue.
- Verification via CI per fleet policy: `cd pkgs/mcpx && go test ./...` on the PR.

Out of scope: Phase 1's store unification (independent — this phase does not depend on it); downstream relay of upstream `inputRequests` (open question on #1554); register truth-up and nix#209 closure (Phase 3, gated on Phases 1–2).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `CallTool` on a `taskSupport: "required"` tool completes through the upstream's task machinery in both eras, returning the task's result as the call result.
- [ ] Modern initialize declares `extensions["io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks"]`; legacy path uses `params.task` + `tasks/result`.
- [ ] Cancel, failure, `input_required`, and malformed-response behaviours match the scope above and are covered by the defining tests in CI.
- [ ] Non-`required` tools are byte-for-byte today's plain call; full mcpx suite green via CI.

title: id(discovery): peer announcements carry a timestamp nothing checks — a replayed or out-of-order announcement overwrites newer peer state and can keep a departed peer 'live' forever

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

Peer announcements carry a creation timestamp (`PeerAnnouncement.timestamp_secs`, `pkgs/id/src/discovery.rs:364`), but nothing on the receive path ever reads it:

- The gossip receive loop in `id serve` passes every deserializable announcement straight to the peer table (`pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:1278`, `recv_discovery.update(announcement)`), with no freshness or ordering check.
- `PeerDiscovery::update` (`pkgs/id/src/discovery.rs:430-437`) unconditionally inserts the announcement and stamps `last_seen = Instant::now()` — the *arrival* time, never the announcement's own timestamp.

Two consequences, both verified below:

1. **Out-of-order / replayed announcements regress live state.** An older announcement received after a newer one silently overwrites the stored name/blob_count with the stale values.
2. **A departed peer can be kept "live" forever by replay.** Freshness (`peers()`, `stale_peers()`) is measured only from the local arrival clock, so re-broadcasting one captured announcement at any cadence under `STALE_THRESHOLD` (120 s) refreshes the peer indefinitely. The cleanup task only probes peers that *are* stale (`serve.rs:1312-1352`), so a replay-refreshed peer is never probed and never removed. Announcements are unsigned plain postcard (`PeerAnnouncement` has no signature field) broadcast on a public topic with a public secret (`DEFAULT_TOPIC` / `DEFAULT_TOPIC_SECRET`), so a capture is available to anyone who has ever been on the topic — and ordinary gossip duplication/reordering triggers consequence 1 without any attacker at all.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `a120b9a9`)

Probe crate ON THE LAPTOP (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-discovery`) compiling the verbatim `pkgs/id/src/discovery.rs` (sha256 `52b897d2cfa2c620f54ac7945e1bad66435472e73327c43cd87ef2bc56ee3d99`, identical both sides; iroh-base pinned `=1.3.0` per `pkgs/id/Cargo.lock`). Log: `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-discovery/out.log`.

```
case1 after ts=2000: name=Some("new-name") blob_count=42 timestamp_secs=2000 count=1
case1 after replayed ts=1000: name=Some("old-name") blob_count=7 timestamp_secs=1000 count=1
case2 after ts=1000 then ts=2000: name=Some("new-name") blob_count=42 timestamp_secs=2000 count=1
case3 ancient ts=1 accepted: name=Some("ghost") blob_count=99 timestamp_secs=1 count=1
case3: peers()=1 stale_peers()=0
```

- Case 1: the replayed older announcement (ts=1000) overwrites the newer stored state (ts=2000, 42 blobs → 7, name regresses).
- Case 2 (control): normal in-order delivery works, so the gap is specifically the missing ordering/freshness check.
- Case 3: an announcement stamped `timestamp_secs = 1` (1970) is accepted as a currently-live peer: `peers()` returns it and `stale_peers()` does not — its claimed age is never compared to anything.

Existing tests cover insert/replace/stale-by-local-clock only; no test delivers announcements out of order or with an old timestamp.

## Why it matters

The peer table is what `id peers`, the REPL peer views, and the web `/peers` route show an operator, and blob_count is the only content signal in it. Today that table can be rolled back by ordinary gossip reordering, and — because the announcement is unauthenticated and replayable — pinned to a phantom peer indefinitely by anyone holding one old broadcast. The stale-probe cleanup that exists precisely to evict dead peers is structurally unable to see the replayed case.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An announcement whose `timestamp_secs` is not newer than the stored announcement's for that node does not overwrite the stored announcement (equal timestamps: keep the first, or a documented deterministic rule).
- [ ] An announcement stamped older than a pinned bound relative to local wall-clock time (e.g. `STALE_THRESHOLD`) does not make a peer live / does not refresh its freshness; the peer can still become live again from a genuinely new announcement.
- [ ] Regression tests in `discovery.rs`: out-of-order delivery keeps the newer announcement; an ancient-timestamp announcement is not returned by `peers()` as fresh (or is refused at `update`); in-order controls still pass.
- [ ] The receive path in `serve.rs` needs no new trust assumptions: the fix lives in `PeerDiscovery` (and/or a checked entry point it exposes), so every caller gets the ordering/freshness guarantee.
- [ ] Out of scope: signing announcements (a larger design question) — this issue is only about refusing to let an *old* announcement move state backwards or manufacture freshness.

title: projector: read-API limit is never validated — ?limit=-1 returns the whole table and ?limit=2.7 500s the request

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/pm-stack
labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

body:
## Summary

The projector's read API passes the `limit` query parameter to SQL `LIMIT ?` with no validation or clamp anywhere in the chain. `?limit=-1` (any negative) returns the **entire** table — SQLite treats a negative LIMIT as "no limit" — `?limit=1000000000` does the same in practice, `?limit=2.7` makes the driver throw a datatype-mismatch error (unhandled in the handler, so the request 500s), and `?limit=abc` sends `NaN` to the driver. The defaults (200 / 500) only apply when the parameter is absent.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `a120b9a9`)

- `pm-stack/projector/src/server.ts:119` — `/items`: `limit: Number(url.searchParams.get("limit") ?? 200)`. `Number("-1")` is `-1`, `Number("abc")` is `NaN`, `Number("2.7")` is `2.7`; nothing checks the result.
- `pm-stack/projector/src/server.ts:128` — `/comments`: same pattern with default 500, feeding both `getCommentsForSubject` and `getComments`.
- `pm-stack/projector/src/store.ts:188-191` — `listItems`: `const limit = opts.limit ?? 200` — `??` only catches `null`/`undefined`, so `-1`, `NaN` and `2.7` all pass through into `LIMIT ?`. Same shape at `store.ts:267` (`getComments`) and `store.ts:283` (`getCommentsForSubject`).
- SQLite semantics verified directly (python `sqlite3`, same SQLite core the libsql driver binds): `LIMIT ?` bound to `-1` or `-5` returned all 10 test rows; bound to `2.7` raised `datatype mismatch`; bound to `0` returned 0 rows.
- The `/items` and `/comments` handlers (`server.ts:110-141`) have no `try/catch` (unlike `/health` and the webhook path), so the fractional-limit driver error escapes `handleRequest` as an unhandled 500 instead of a 400 naming the bad parameter.
- No test covers a hostile `limit`: `pm-stack/projector/test/` has no `limit` cases (grep).

These are read endpoints (no bearer token — `server.ts` only gates writes/reconcile), served on the projector's port and consumed by the aggregator's live source, so any local caller can force a full-table dump of `pmp_items` / `pmp_comments` with one parameter.

## Why it matters

The `limit` parameter exists to bound response size; as written it bounds nothing. A negative or huge limit turns a paged read into an unbounded one (memory + payload blowup as the tables grow), and a fractional limit is a one-request 500. Every other numeric/structured input on this server is validated at the boundary (webhook HMAC + bounded body, link `ref` regex at `server.ts:159`) — `limit` is the loose one.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `limit` is parsed once, at the HTTP boundary (or in the store functions), as a positive integer and clamped to a named per-endpoint maximum; absent → the existing defaults (200 items / 500 comments).
- [ ] `?limit=-1`, `?limit=0`, `?limit=2.7`, `?limit=abc` and `?limit=999999999` can never produce an unbounded result or a 500: they get the default/clamp, or a 400 naming `limit`.
- [ ] Tests at the store or handler level pin: negative → bounded, fractional/non-numeric → bounded or 400, over-max → max, ordinary `?limit=3` still returns exactly 3.
- [ ] No behaviour change for well-formed callers (the aggregator's live reads use `refs=`, not `limit`).

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `projector limit` and related terms: no filing covers the projector read-API limit. Adjacent but in another repo/component: openchamber #604 (loose `Number` parsing in pool-health route — same defect family, different codebase), code #1485/#604-style aggregator sort issues (unrelated).

title: id(world): min_tick_ms (1000) is never enforced — a program can subscribe to time.tick:1 and drive ~1,000 journaled program updates per second

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Summary

`WorldLimits.min_tick_ms` defaults to 1000 and the architecture doc promises `time.tick:<ms>` is `>= 1000 ms`, but nothing ever reads the field. A world program can subscribe to `time.tick:1` (or `:10`, `:999`) and the host will run its `update`, publish its records, and journal a system event at that interval for as long as anyone is present — up to ~1,000 journaled program runs per second per interval, with up to 4 distinct intervals subscribed.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `a120b9a9`, and independently on the laptop clone)

- `pkgs/id/src/world/mod.rs:78,96` — `pub min_tick_ms: u64` ("Slowest tick a program may subscribe to, in milliseconds"), default `1000`. A repo-wide grep for `min_tick` returns only these two lines: the field is never read, and `WorldCore::new` (`pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs:59-75`) validates every other limit nonzero but not this one.
- `pkgs/id/docs/2026-10-07T00-20-00Z_architecture_roc_worlds/2026-10-07T00-20-00Z_architecture_roc_worlds.md:729` — the catalog contract: "`time.tick:<ms>` (>= 1000 ms, delivered only while someone is connected, so idle worlds stay idle)".
- `pkgs/id/src/world_caps.rs:165-172` — `Subscription::parse` accepts any `time.tick:<ms>` with `ms > 0` as `Subscription::Tick(ms)`; only `0` / non-numeric fall through to `Unknown`. Its tests (`world_caps.rs:725-737`) pin `1000` as a valid spec and `0` as unknown, but nothing at `1..999`.
- `pkgs/id/src/world/actor.rs:468-478` — `arm()` inserts the raw `ms` as the deadline offset (`now + Duration::from_millis(*ms)`), no clamp against `min_tick_ms`.
- `pkgs/id/src/world/actor.rs:230-246,481-500` — the run loop sleeps until the earliest tick deadline, `fire_ticks` re-arms at the same raw interval and `deliver()`s each tick; `deliver` (`actor.rs:341-376`) runs `program.update`, publishes records, and persists a `JournalEntry::System` (incrementing `since_checkpoint`) per tick.

So the intended floor exists in three places (field, default, doc) and is enforced in none.

## Why it matters

Ticks are not free: each one is a full program execution plus a journal append. A buggy or hostile program subscribed at 1 ms turns one connected viewer into a busy loop that grows the journal ~1,000 entries/sec (checkpoint churn included), burning host CPU and disk — exactly the idle/DoS bound `min_tick_ms` and the doc's `>= 1000 ms` were meant to provide. The dead field also misleads admins: setting `min_tick_ms` changes nothing.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A subscription below the floor cannot drive delivery below the floor: either `time.tick:<ms>` with `ms < min_tick_ms` parses/refuses as a refused subscription (consistent with `time.tick:0` → `Unknown`), or arming clamps the interval to `min_tick_ms` — one behaviour, chosen and documented.
- [ ] `WorldCore::new` validates `min_tick_ms` like the other limits (or the field is removed and the floor is a named constant where it is enforced — no dead config remains).
- [ ] Tests pin the boundary: `999` does not produce sub-second delivery, `1000` still works, and the existing `0`/non-numeric `Unknown` behaviour is unchanged.
- [ ] The architecture doc and the code agree on the floor afterwards.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `time.tick`, `tick interval`, `min_tick`: no filing covers the tick floor (only hit was the unrelated quota epic #1149). Adjacent but distinct: #1506 (joined-phase metrics capability check), #1537 (sync collect_batch cap).

body:
## Problem

A crash-torn or empty `records.namespace` file permanently bricks a world's startup: `RecordsStore::open` treats an unparseable namespace file as fatal, even though the records doc is explicitly a cache, and even though the same function already recovers gracefully when the doc itself is gone.

## Evidence (verified on main 194e32ca)

- `pkgs/id/src/world_records.rs:71-78` — `RecordsStore::open`: when the namespace file exists and reads OK, `text.trim().parse::<NamespaceId>()` failure is propagated with `?` ("parse records namespace in …"). There is no recovery case for empty/garbage content.
- `pkgs/id/src/world_records.rs:79-84` — the very next case *is* handled: a well-formed namespace whose doc no longer exists logs a warning ("records doc … is gone; creating a new one") and falls through to create a fresh doc. A torn file gets strictly worse treatment than a deleted doc.
- `pkgs/id/src/world_records.rs:86-92` — the file is written with a single non-atomic `tokio::fs::write(path, doc.id().to_string())` (truncate-then-write, no temp file, no rename, no fsync), so a crash, power loss, or kill mid-write leaves exactly the empty/partial file that `open` then refuses forever.
- `pkgs/id/src/world_records.rs:3-9` (module doc) — the records doc "is a cache of authoritative state, never a second source of truth" (records are recomputable from the journal), so discarding a torn namespace and creating a new doc loses nothing authoritative.
- `pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:575-577` — the only production caller passes `<world_dir>/records.namespace` and propagates the error with `await?`, so the affected world fails to start on every subsequent restart until a human manually deletes the file.
- Contrast with the house pattern elsewhere in pkgs/id: `FileJournal`/`ArtifactLog`/`Outbox` drop and truncate crash-torn tails and keep going (see #1499, #1521, #1522, #1523); the tag store writes via a temp file (`src/tags.rs:1587`).

Verification: laptop probe test against the real `RecordsStore::open` with a `Docs::memory` node (probe worktree on the laptop, test `probe_corrupt_namespace_file_bricks_open`): an empty `records.namespace` and a partial/garbage one both make `open` return `Err` ("parse records namespace in …"), while no file at all opens fine.

## Why it matters

The failure mode is worst-case timed: the torn write can only happen when the process dies unexpectedly — exactly the situation where an operator restarts `id serve` and expects worlds to come back. Instead one world never starts again, the error message points at parsing rather than at the safe remedy (delete the cache's namespace file), and nothing in the product ever heals it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `RecordsStore::open` with an empty or unparseable `records.namespace` succeeds: it logs a visible warning naming the file and the recovery, creates a new records doc, and rewrites the namespace file (the doc-gone path at :79-84 is the model).
- [ ] The namespace file is written atomically (write to a temp file in the same directory + rename, as the tag store does), so a crash mid-write cannot leave a torn file at the real path.
- [ ] A well-formed namespace pointing at an existing doc still reopens that doc (no behaviour change on the happy path); a well-formed namespace for a gone doc keeps the current warn-and-recreate behaviour.
- [ ] New tests: open with (a) empty namespace file, (b) garbage/partial namespace file, (c) valid namespace + live doc (round-trip), (d) valid namespace + gone doc.
- [ ] `id serve` world startup no longer fails solely because of a torn `records.namespace`.

body:
# aggregator: SnapshotStore accepts records it can never read back — non-finite estimate pairs and non-ISO timestamps pass validation, append reports success, and dedupe never sees them

## Summary

`isSnapshotRecord` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/snapshots.ts:26-42) is the shared
structural validator for the usage snapshot store: the store's own
`readAll`/`append`, the feed ingest in `sources/live.ts` (which appends
`feed.snapshots` into the local store), and the writer scripts
(`collect-fleet-feed.ts`, `gather-quota.ts`, `append-usage-snapshots.ts`) all
gate on it. Two classes of record pass that validator but can never be read
back by the store, so `SnapshotStore.append` reports them as written, they
never appear in history, and — because dedupe is computed from `readAll` —
re-appending the same record appends it again every time.

## Evidence (verified on main 3b559045, Bun 1.4.2, verbatim snapshots.ts sha256 49b14289 on the laptop)

Probe: `probe-2026-10-27-laneB-snapshots` (real `snapshots.ts`, only the
type-only `model.ts` import stubbed).

1. **Estimate pairs skip the finiteness check scalars get.** Scalar
   `value: NaN` → `isSnapshotRecord` false (line 34: `Number.isFinite`), but
   `value: { low: NaN, high: 10 }` → **true**, and `{ low: Infinity, high: 10 }`
   → **true** (lines 35-38 check only `typeof === "number"`). An inverted
   pair `{ low: 50, high: 10 }` also passes.
   - `append([NaN-pair])` returns **1**; the stored line has
     `"value":{"low":null,"high":10}` (JSON.stringify turns NaN into null),
     which `readAll` then rejects — `readAll()` returns **0** records.
   - `append([same NaN-pair])` again returns **1** (not 0): dedupe is built
     from `readAll` (snapshots.ts:99), which never sees the stored line, so
     every re-run of a writer appends another dead line and reports it as a
     new observation. The monthly file grows with records no reader will
     ever return.
2. **Any `Date.parse`-able `ts` passes, but file routing assumes an ISO
   prefix.** `snapshotFileFor` (snapshots.ts:20-22) routes by
   `ts.slice(0, 7)`, and `readAll` only reads files matching
   `usage-(\d{4}-\d{2})\.jsonl` (line 17). A record with
   `ts: "October 20, 2026"` passes `isSnapshotRecord` (line 29 only requires
   `Date.parse` to succeed), `append` returns **1** and writes it to
   `usage-October.jsonl` — a file `readAll` filters out, so `readAll()`
   returns **0**. Same silent-loss + no-dedupe shape as (1).
3. **Control:** a normal ISO record with a finite pair appends once, the
   second append returns 0 (dedupe works), and `readAll` returns 1.

## Why it matters

The snapshot store is the append-only usage history the hub's history views
are built from, and its contract (module header, snapshots.ts:1-10) is that
writers and the backfill are "safe to re-run" because dedupe makes appends
idempotent. Records in either class above break that contract silently:
append counts them as stored history, no surface ever shows them, and every
writer re-run adds another copy. The pair case is reachable from any writer
whose estimate arithmetic can produce NaN/Infinity (e.g. a division by a
zero denominator upstream) — the validator is exactly the boundary that is
supposed to keep such values out, and it already does so for scalar values.

## Acceptance criteria

- `isSnapshotRecord` rejects estimate pairs whose `low` or `high` is not a
  finite number (mirroring the scalar branch), and rejects a pair with
  `low > high`.
- `isSnapshotRecord` rejects a `ts` whose first 7 characters are not a
  `YYYY-MM` month the store can route (or, equivalently, `snapshotFileFor`
  output is guaranteed to match the `readAll` file pattern for every
  accepted record).
- Regression tests: appending a NaN/Infinity-pair record and a non-ISO-ts
  record each append 0 and write nothing; the existing finite-pair control
  still appends once and dedupes on re-append.
- No change to the on-disk format or to the dedupe key for valid records.

## Notes

- Deliberately not self-solved by the creator lane: the `low > high` ruling
  and the exact ts shape to require (full ISO vs `YYYY-MM` prefix) are small
  contract decisions for triage, and this validator is shared by four
  writer/reader paths.
- Related, different defect: #1509 (concurrent JSON-store writes in the
  aggregator) — same app, unrelated module and mechanism.

body:
# Fleet reliability: lane-shift instruction never pinned the queue worker id — an improvised id fails every claim (FK) and loses the whole shift

## What happened

On 2026-10-27 the opencode **lane B** shift (`repo-queue-worker-shift-opencode-b`) processed zero tasks: its claim called `repo-queue.py claim` with `--worker repo-queue-worker-shift-opencode-b` (its cron job id), which is not registered in `agent.workers`, so `claim_repo_task` failed with a foreign-key violation on every attempt and the shift ended having claimed nothing.

## Root cause

- `agent.workers` has exactly one registered worker per repo: `repo-worker-code`, `repo-worker-opencode`, `repo-worker-openchamber`, `repo-worker-nix` (verified 2026-10-28T00:1xZ; all opencode tasks in `agent.tasks` carry `worker_id = repo-worker-opencode`).
- The code-pilot runbook (`repo-queue-worker-instruction.md`) pins `--worker repo-worker-code` explicitly in every verb example.
- The multi-queue **lane-shift instruction** (`hidden_files/lane-shift-instruction.md`, used by the opencode/openchamber/nix lanes since the 2026-10-27 restructure) named the queue, repo, lane, and lock as parameters but **never named the worker id** — its claim step read just `claim --queue <QUEUE>`. Lane A shifts happened to use the registered id; lane B improvised one from its job name and lost the shift.

## Fix already applied (operator, 2026-10-27)

`lane-shift-instruction.md` §1 step 1 now pins the worker id per repo (same id for both lanes) and requires `--worker <WORKER>` on every helper verb, with the failure mode named so no lane improvises an id again.

## Acceptance criteria for closing

- [ ] One full cycle of lane B shifts (opencode + openchamber) completes with successful claims under the pinned ids.
- [ ] Consider hardening the helper: `repo-queue.py` could reject an unregistered `--worker` locally (or map queue → default worker) so a wrong id fails fast with a clear message instead of a raw FK error from the RPC. If that lands, link the PR here.
- [ ] Related hygiene noticed in the same pass: opencode task 1431 (#595) sat queued at attempts 2/2 (cap) — cap raised to 4 by the operator so the next claim cannot dead-end it.

## Links

- Epic: #1233 (fleet reliability)
- Runbook fixed: `~/workspace/goals/keep-the-four-repos-healthy/hidden_files/lane-shift-instruction.md`

body:
Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-stdio-exec-identity.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Register: central potential-projects list, same workspace (`files/potential-projects.md`).

**Identity decision (recorded here by the design architect, before implementation):** for a hashed executable whose content begins with `#!`, the exec identity is its content **plus the resolved directory of the real file** — a script's identity is *what it runs, where it runs from*. For a non-script hashed file the identity stays content-only, and above `limits.execHashMax` (1MB) it stays the stat/inode identity. No `user/review`: the roadmap row sits at `proposed` and `pkgs/mcpx/TODO.md` item 4 asks for exactly this decision ("Decide whether the identity should include the program's directory for scripts, or whether a re-pointed link should always restart"); the chosen rule is the TODO's first option, it is a small, reversible semantic change inside the existing identity mechanism, and no new surface, dependency, or behaviour beyond restart timing is introduced.

## Summary

A stdio server's identity today is the bytes of its executable (`ExecIdentity`, `pkgs/mcpx/internal/config/execid.go`). That is wrong for a program that finds its own files relative to its real location — the caveat is written into `execid.go` itself and into `pkgs/mcpx/TODO.md` item 4:

- A node script beside its `node_modules`, re-pointed at a byte-identical copy in another directory, keeps its child under the automatic check (`internal/pool/execwatch.go`) and on reload — the child keeps running with the **old directory's dependencies**. Only a manual `mcpx restart <server>` moves it.
- The pinning test is `TestReloadFollowsAForRePointedCommandByWhatItRuns` (`internal/daemon/reload_identity_test.go:162`), whose comment carries the same caveat.
- Above `limits.execHashMax` the identity is the inode instead, so an oversized copy *is* restarted — the current rule is not even self-consistent: whether a moved copy restarts depends on its size.

Roadmap: `planning/roadmaps/mcpx.md` → Next → "Decide what a stdio server's identity is" (status `proposed`, linked only to the TODO — no prior issue covers it; searched 2026-10-27 for ExecIdentity / stdio identity issues, none found).

**Proposal — directory-augmented identity for scripts, everything else unchanged:**

- `ExecStamp.Identity()` (`internal/config/execid.go:114`) is the single place identity is computed (used by `Resolved.ExecState`, pool construction `internal/pool/pool.go:199`, and the periodic watcher `internal/pool/execwatch.go:84`). When it hashes a small file, it also notes whether the content begins with `#!`. For a script, the resolved directory — `filepath.Dir` of the stamp's already-symlink-resolved `Path` — is folded into the hash under a distinct framing. The identity string format (`sha256:<16 hex>`) does not change.
- Directory, not full path: a rename or re-point **within** the same directory keeps the child (the location a script resolves siblings against has not moved); a re-point **across** directories changes the identity, so reload and the exec watch restart the pool through the existing `replaceChildren` path with the existing `server.restart` / "executable changed" lifecycle event. No watcher, pool, or daemon wiring changes are needed — the stamp already moves on a re-point, and identity comparison already decides.
- Non-script hashed files keep pure content identity (the deliberate anti-churn rule for binaries: `npx`/`uvx`/nix-profile re-points at identical bytes keep their child). Large files keep stat identity. Missing commands and non-stdio servers are untouched.

Grounding: `ExecStamp.Path` is already the `EvalSymlinks`-resolved real path (`execid.go:94-110`), so the directory folded in is the location the kernel/interpreter actually runs the script from. Both existing identical-copy tests (`TestExecIdentityOfASmallFileIsItsContentNotItsPath`, `TestReloadFollowsAForRePointedCommandByWhatItRuns`, `TestExecWatchFollowsARepointedLinkByWhatItRuns`) place their copies **in one directory**, so they keep passing under the directory rule — the rule change is visible exactly and only where the current tests are silent: copies in *different* directories. One exact-hash assertion does change: `TestExecIdentityFollowsTheExecutableNotTheCommandName` pins a `#!/bin/sh` script's identity to its bare content hash; Phase 1 updates that expectation to the framed script hash.

Alternatives (argued in the design doc): directory for *all* hashed files (pays binary restart churn to fix a script problem); always restart on any re-point (discards the content-identity anti-churn design the exec watch exists around); full path for scripts (a rename within a directory is not a location change for sibling resolution); per-script location-sensitivity detection (not statically knowable); status quo + manual restart (the TODO already calls the current choice wrong).

Risks: a one-time identity change for every script server when this lands — recorded handoff identities mismatch, pools are not adopted, each script pool restarts once at upgrade/first check (the safe direction; it is exactly the existing binary-changed path). Location-*independent* scripts moved across directories (e.g. a wrapper that only `exec`s an absolute path) now restart once needlessly — one drained child restart, correctness favoured over that churn. Residual gaps stay gaps, named as open questions in the design doc: native binaries that load sibling data (`$ORIGIN`-style), and interpreter-as-command servers (`node script.js`, where the script is an argument, not the command — its file is not part of `ExecIdentity` at all).

## Phased breakdown

- **Phase 1 — identity core in `internal/config`.** Script detection + directory folding in `ExecStamp.Identity()`, the `execid.go` header caveat rewritten as the new rule, unit tests: cross-directory identical script differs, same-directory identical script keeps, cross-directory identical non-script keeps, large-file stat identity unchanged. Filed as a sub-issue of this issue.
- **Phase 2 — daemon-level proof + closure.** Reload and exec-watch tests for a cross-directory re-point (pool replaced, child pid changes, one `server.restart` event) and a same-directory re-point (kept), on both the reload path and the live watch path; `pkgs/mcpx/TODO.md` item 4 and the roadmap row closed out. Filed as a sub-issue of this issue, gated on Phase 1.

### Open questions (NOT filed; stay as questions)

- Native binaries with sibling-data loading (`$ORIGIN` rpaths, `../share` relative to `bin/`): extend the directory rule to all hashed files if fleet evidence shows a real stale-location case?
- Interpreter-as-command (`node`/`python` + script path as an argument): should the first script-like argument join the watched identity? A different mechanism (arguments are config, in `PoolID`, but the file behind the path is unwatched) — separate design question.
- Should the restart lifecycle event distinguish "bytes changed" from "location changed" for operator visibility, or is `path` on the existing event enough?

When both phases land, this design's acceptance includes removing TODO item 4 and updating the `planning/roadmaps/mcpx.md` row — and noting the resolution on this issue.


## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Phase 1 (#1532, identity core in `internal/config`) and Phase 2 (#1533, daemon proof + closure) are both filed as sub-issues of this design — done at filing time — and both land.
- [ ] The recorded identity decision is implemented as written: `#!` script identity = content + resolved directory; non-script hashed files stay content-only; files above `limits.execHashMax` stay stat/inode.
- [ ] `pkgs/mcpx/TODO.md` item 4 is removed and the `planning/roadmaps/mcpx.md` row "Decide what a stdio server's identity is" is updated to link this issue.
- [ ] A completion note is posted on this issue summarising the resolution; the three open questions (native sibling-data binaries, interpreter-as-command, restart-event reason) remain recorded here as questions, not silently dropped.

body:
# projector: `GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY` documented "base64 of PEM" form fails — decodePem never unwraps it

## Summary

`pm-stack/projector/src/github.ts` documents `GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY` as "PEM (or base64 of PEM)" (line 6), but the base64-of-PEM form does not work: `appJwt` throws `Invalid keyData` at key import. Only raw PEM text and base64-of-DER actually work today, and the tests only cover base64-of-DER — so the documented input form most operators would produce (base64-encoding the `.pem` file GitHub gives them, e.g. for a one-line env var) is silently broken.

## Evidence

`decodePem` (github.ts:16-23):

```ts
function decodePem(pem: string): string {
  const trimmed = pem.replace(/-----[^-]+-----/g, "").replace(/\s/g, "");
  if (/^[A-Za-z0-9+/]+=*$/.test(trimmed) && !trimmed.includes("PRIVATE")) {
    // already base64 of the DER key
    return trimmed;
  }
  return trimmed;
}
```

Trace for base64-of-PEM input:

1. Input is base64 of the whole PEM text — it contains no `-----` markers, so the strip is a no-op; the string is pure base64, so the regex branch returns it unchanged.
2. `appJwt` (github.ts:66-67) then does a single `Buffer.from(b64, "base64")` — which yields the **PEM text bytes**, not DER.
3. `importRsaKey` feeds those ASCII bytes to WebCrypto as PKCS#8 (and then as PKCS#1-wrapped) → both fail with "Invalid keyData".

Verified behavior (reproduced on the laptop against the current code):

- plain PEM text → works (header/footer stripped, body is the DER base64)
- base64 of DER → works
- base64 of PEM → **FAIL `Invalid keyData`**

Test gap: `pm-stack/projector/test/github.test.ts:5-9` builds its "key formats" fixtures by exporting **DER** and base64-encoding that (`privateKey.export({ type, format: "der" })`). No fixture ever passes PEM text or base64-of-PEM, so the documented contract is untested in exactly the form that's broken.

## Why it matters

The projector's GitHub App auth is how it self-heals beyond webhook delivery. An operator who follows the header comment and stores the key base64-encoded (the standard way to put a PEM in an env var or secret store) gets a projector that cannot authenticate at all, with an error that points at the key data rather than the encoding — the worst kind of config failure to diagnose.

## Acceptance criteria

- `appJwt` succeeds with all three input forms of the same key: raw PEM text, base64 of DER, and base64 of PEM (both PKCS#1 "RSA PRIVATE KEY" and PKCS#8 PEM variants).
- Fix direction: make `decodePem` actually decode — if the input is base64 whose decoded text starts with `-----BEGIN`, treat the decoded text as PEM and extract its body (one recursive/iterative unwrap is enough); keep the existing DER and raw-PEM behavior unchanged.
- Tests in `test/github.test.ts` cover PEM-text and base64-of-PEM fixtures (generate the key, export `format: "pem"`, pass it raw and base64-encoded) alongside the existing DER controls.
- No change to the env var names or the documented contract — the code is brought up to the doc, not the other way around.

## Notes

- Found by new-issue-creator-code-b (run 2026-10-27 15:20 CDT), which verified the reproduction but timed out before filing; filed by the coordinator from its verified report and re-checked against source at github.ts:6,16-23,66-67 and test/github.test.ts:5-20.
- Dedup: `gh issue search` (open + closed) for `decodePem`, `base64 PEM`, `GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY` in this repo returned no existing issue.

## Bug: decided items persist in NEEDS DREW — code#1384 survived three orchestration passes after Drew's recorded decision

**Severity:** the dashboard's NEEDS DREW tier is Drew's action list. A decided item occupying it trains him to ignore the tier. This is the failure mode code#1454's triage gate exists to prevent, in reverse: the gate stops raw items arriving; nothing retires decided ones.

### Evidence (all verified 2026-10-27)

- **Decision:** Drew decided code#1384 on 2026-10-27 (adopt the per-instance mcpx supervisor design). Decision comment on the issue: https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/1384#issuecomment-6449925704 (~18:05Z). The `user/review` label was removed the same pass; the issue's labels since then carry no review marker.
- **Orchestrator-addressed retire note** posted on the issue after the first stale pass: comment 6451311158, naming the decision comment and asking the pass to retire the card.
- **Three consecutive passes kept the card:** runs at 18:12Z (run f3020dff), 19:12Z (run 2961b133), 20:12Z (orch-2026-10-27T20:12:19Z). Published reason, still verbatim at 20:12Z: "Only Drew can make the mcpx supervisor direction call: the #1385 triage verdict (comment 6447077814, 16:11Z) settled the 8 supervi…" — the cited verdict (16:11Z) **predates** Drew's decision (18:05Z). The classification is anchored to an older artifact and the NEEDS-DREW REVIEW's fresh-context re-check is not seeing the item's own newer comments.
- **Contrast:** the same 20:12Z pass DID retire openchamber#87 from recorded context (Drew's decision comment cited). The review mechanism can work — for #1384 it is looking at the wrong evidence (the #1385 verdict) or not re-reading #1384's comment stream.

### Acceptance

1. code#1384 leaves NEEDS DREW on the next pass (it is decided; follow-on work #1463/#1483/#1484 proceeds in the fleet tiers).
2. The NEEDS-DREW REVIEW, for every carried item, reads the item's OWN issue comments for a Drew decision newer than the item's classification `since` — and treats a decision comment (plus any review-label removal) as retirement evidence, before re-publishing.
3. When a carried item's reason cites evidence older than a newer comment on the item itself, the pass must reconcile the two explicitly in the run log (which evidence won, and why).
4. Add #1384's three stale passes to the case file so the fix is regression-checked against this exact pattern (decision recorded on the decided issue; classification anchored to a different issue's older verdict).

body:
## Problem

`read_journal_entries` — the raw journal reader behind `id world fork` — refuses a crash-torn final entry in a world journal that `FileJournal::open` on the very same file forgives: a world that opens, serves and verifies fine after a crash cannot be forked until someone hand-repairs its journal.

## Evidence (verified this run on main 279c9739, code reading)

- `pkgs/id/src/world_store.rs:452-466` — `read_journal_entries` splits the file bytes on `\n` and parses every non-empty chunk with `serde_json::from_slice(...)?` (`{path} is corrupt`). The final chunk after a crash-torn append is an unterminated truncated fragment; it is parsed like any other entry and fails the whole read. There is no torn-tail special case.
- `pkgs/id/src/world_store.rs:85-130` — `FileJournal::open`, the normal open path for the same journal, treats exactly this case as recoverable: an unterminated last line is a torn append (the crash came before the entry was acknowledged), so it is dropped, the file is truncated to `good_len`, and a warning is logged. Only a newline-terminated unparseable line is corruption there.
- `pkgs/id/src/world_store.rs:479` — `fork_world` starts with `read_journal_entries(&src_dir.join("journal.jsonl"))?`. Forking a *cold* world (not currently open — e.g. after the crash that tore the tail, before anything reopens it) therefore fails with `journal.jsonl is corrupt`, even though simply opening that world would have repaired the tail and proceeded.
- `pkgs/id/src/world_store.rs:190` — the second caller is `FileJournal::append`'s version-bump path (#227), which re-reads the journal through the same helper; it is normally shielded because `open` truncates first, which shows the helper's strictness is an accident of reuse, not a ruling: the fork path has no such shield.
- No test covers `read_journal_entries` / `fork_world` against a journal with an unterminated final fragment.
- Dedup: #1499 (open) covers `Petnames::open`; #1521 / #1522 (filed 2026-10-27) cover the directory journal and the group log. No open or recently-closed issue mentions `read_journal_entries`, `fork_world` and a torn journal tail.

## Why it matters

Forking (F12.2) is the template/backup path for worlds. The scenario where an admin most wants a fork — recovering or cloning a world after a crash — is exactly the scenario where the journal may carry a torn tail, and it is the one path that refuses it while the world's own open path quietly repairs it. The error message (`is corrupt`) also misdiagnoses a torn append as corruption, sending the admin toward discarding a journal that was never corrupt.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `read_journal_entries` (or the fork path) treats a final unterminated fragment the way `FileJournal::open` does: the fragment is excluded from the returned entries (and the exclusion is visible — a warning log or a fork note), so `fork_world` succeeds on a crash-torn source journal and the fork replays to the parent's last complete entry.
- [ ] A newline-terminated unparseable line, anywhere including the last line, still fails with the corrupt-journal error — corruption is never silently dropped.
- [ ] New tests cover: fork of a journal with a torn final fragment (succeeds, fork state = last complete entry), fork of a journal with a complete-but-corrupt final line (fails).
- [ ] `FileJournal::append`'s version-bump caller (#227) behaviour is unchanged for journals it has opened.
