body:
## Problem

A crash-torn final line in `groups.jsonl` bricks every group command: `GroupLog::open` refuses the unterminated partial event that a crash mid-append leaves behind, instead of dropping and truncating it the way the sibling JSONL stores in this codebase do.

## Evidence (verified this run on main 279c9739, code reading)

- `pkgs/id/src/groups/log.rs:137-150` — `GroupLog::append` writes one JSON line + `\n` with a single `write_all` followed by `sync_data`. A crash/power loss during that write leaves a final line that is a truncated JSON fragment with no terminating newline.
- `pkgs/id/src/groups/log.rs:48-71` — `GroupLog::open` collects `text.lines()` through `serde_json::from_str(...)?` for every non-empty line. `lines()` yields the unterminated final fragment as a line, so one torn append fails the whole open with `line N is not an event`. There is no torn-tail special case: no missing-final-newline check, no truncation/repair.
- `pkgs/id/src/commands/group.rs:200,361,395` — every group command (`cmd_group` and helpers) starts with `GroupLog::open(&log_path(path))?`, so one torn append makes all group operations fail the same way until someone hand-edits `groups.jsonl`.
- Contrast — the established house semantics in the same codebase:
  - `pkgs/id/src/world_store.rs:85-130` (`FileJournal::open`): an unterminated last line is a torn append — dropped, file truncated to the last complete line; a newline-terminated unparseable line is corruption and still fails.
  - `pkgs/id/src/envelope_outbox.rs:143-165` (`Outbox::open`): unterminated failing final line is dropped and the file truncated via `set_len(kept)`; a complete corrupt line still errors.
  - `pkgs/id/src/artifact.rs:575-600` and `pkgs/id/src/directory_log.rs:196-235`: same drop-the-torn-tail treatment.
- Existing test `test_a_line_that_is_not_an_event_is_an_error` (`groups/log.rs:386-392`) writes `"not json\n"` — a *complete*, newline-terminated line — and correctly asserts an error. No test covers an unterminated final fragment, which is the distinct torn case the sibling stores forgive.
- Dedup: #1499 (open) is the same defect class in `Petnames::open` only (`pkgs/id/src/petname.rs`); the directory journal instance is filed separately as #1521. No open or recently-closed issue mentions `GroupLog` / `groups.jsonl` torn tails.

## Why it matters

Groups are a user-facing feature whose entire local history lives in this one append-only log. Its own append path can produce exactly the torn tail its load path refuses — so a single ill-timed crash converts a recoverable restart into a permanently unopenable group log, while the envelope outbox written by the same binary already survives the same crash.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `GroupLog::open` on a log whose final line is an unterminated truncated fragment loads all complete events, drops the fragment, and truncates the file to the last complete line (mirroring `FileJournal::open` / `Outbox::open` semantics, including a warning log).
- [ ] A newline-terminated line that does not parse, anywhere including the last line, still fails — the existing `test_a_line_that_is_not_an_event_is_an_error` test keeps passing unchanged.
- [ ] New tests cover: torn final fragment (loads + file truncated), torn fragment after valid events (earlier events intact and `projection()` still folds).
- [ ] No change to the event format, the fold, or append behaviour.

title: id(world): joined-phase metrics frame is never capability-checked — the capability it carries is discarded, unlike query-phase metrics and joined-phase info

labels.name: kind/security

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The `metrics` session frame is capability-authorized in the query phase but never checked at all in the joined phase. The frame always carries a capability (`ClientFrame::Metrics { capability: String }`, `pkgs/id/src/world_session/types.rs:87-89`; the shell contract lists `metrics` in the opening, query, and joined phases), and the two phases treat it inconsistently:

- **Query phase** (`pkgs/id/src/world_session/mod.rs:1324-1352`): the handler takes the frame's `capability`, builds a `JoinCapability`, and gates on `service.world().snapshot(token)` — exactly like `info`. A bogus capability gets `join denied`. The scripted-session test pins this: `metrics_frame_reports_each_host_metric_after_a_scripted_session` (`pkgs/id/src/world_session/tests.rs:193`, bogus capability refused at :214, valid capability served at :230).
- **Joined phase** (`pkgs/id/src/world_session/mod.rs:2124-2134`): the comment says "Like `info`, the joined phase may read the world's metrics with the session's own capability", but the handler matches `ClientFrame::Metrics { .. }` — discarding the capability — and calls `world.metrics().await`. `WorldHandle::metrics` (`pkgs/id/src/world/handle.rs:116-128`) takes **no token parameter**, so no validation is possible on this path. Neither the frame's capability nor the session's join token is ever presented.

Contrast the joined-phase `info` handler directly above it (`mod.rs:2108-2123`), which passes `token.clone()` to `world.snapshot(...)` and refuses with `join denied` when the capability no longer joins.

## Why it matters

- A participant whose capability has been **revoked** keeps read access to the world's host metrics for as long as their frames win the race against the session loop's revocation branch (`mod.rs:1836-1843` breaks the loop when the revocation broadcast is received; a metrics frame already selected is served first). The codebase's stated enforcement model is per-delivery re-validation — "Projecting the event re-validates the capability on every delivery, which is what disconnects a revoked participant" (`mod.rs:1796-1798`) — and the metrics path bypasses it entirely.
- The metrics are operational data about a world the participant may no longer have any grant for: live session count, command/journal/checkpoint rates and latencies, frame bytes (`MetricsSnapshot`, `pkgs/id/src/world/metrics.rs:83-108`).
- The query phase and its test establish the intended authorization ("holding a capability that snapshots the world is enough to read its metrics", `mod.rs:1326-1327`); the joined phase silently not enforcing it is a defect in F11.7 slice 1 (#553, PR #1437), not a design difference — the joined handler's own comment claims the `info` pattern it does not implement.

Scope note for triage: the joined-phase `caps` handler (`mod.rs:2136-2149`) has the same token-less shape via `WorldHandle::caps_report` (`handle.rs:372`). It predates F11.7 and has no authorizing query-phase twin, so it is not filed here — triage should rule whether the fix pattern extends to it in the same pass or a follow-up.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Joined-phase `metrics` validates the session's capability the way joined-phase `info` does (gate on `snapshot(token)`, or a token-taking metrics path on `WorldHandle`); a metrics frame from a session whose capability no longer joins is refused (`join denied` / session ended), never served.
- [ ] A scripted-session test mirrors the query-phase test: join, revoke the participant, send a joined-phase `metrics` frame, assert no metrics reply is served. The existing query-phase metrics test and the metrics unit tests still pass.
- [ ] The joined-phase handler's comment matches the implemented behaviour.
- [ ] Triage records a ruling for joined-phase `caps` (same fix pass or a follow-up issue).

Found by new-issue-creator (lane A) on main `931f1771`, from a line-by-line read of the F11.7 slice-1 wiring (PR #1437). Related: #553 (the F11.7 epic — this is a defect in its shipped slice 1, not a duplicate).

body:
# id: a torn final line in petnames.jsonl bricks the whole world — Petnames::open refuses a crash-torn tail that FileJournal and Outbox both drop and truncate

## Summary

`Petnames::open` (`pkgs/id/src/petname.rs:56-70`) replays `petnames.jsonl` with `text.lines()` and fails the entire open on **any** malformed line — including a torn final line left by a crash mid-append. `Petnames::commit` (`petname.rs:186-199`) appends one JSON line + `sync_data()` per change, so a crash or power loss during `write_all` leaves exactly that: a partial JSON record with no trailing newline at the tail of the file.

That failure is not contained to petnames. `open_world` (`pkgs/id/src/world_store.rs:389-392`) propagates it with `??`, so **the whole world fails to open** — on every restart, forever, until someone hand-edits the journal. There is no recovery path: appends can't happen because open never succeeds.

The two sibling JSONL stores loaded by the same `open_world` already handle this exact case, deliberately:

- **FileJournal** (`world_store.rs:52-117`): "A torn final line, left by a crash mid-append, is truncated away" — unterminated last line is dropped, the file is truncated to the last good byte, and mid-file corruption is still refused. Test: `torn_final_entry_is_dropped_but_mid_file_corruption_is_refused` (`world_store.rs:1044`).
- **Outbox** (`envelope_outbox.rs:141-161`): iterates `split_inclusive('\n')`; an unparseable line that does not end with `'\n'` ends the replay, and the file is truncated to the kept prefix. Test: `a_torn_last_line_is_dropped_and_not_mixed_into_the_next_record` (`envelope_outbox.rs:523`).

`Petnames` (and `Directory::replay`, `directory.rs:517-535` — same strict `lines()` + `?` shape, also propagated by `open_world` at `world_store.rs:385-387`) never got the same treatment.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 67e0def2)

Probe crate on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-petname`) compiling the **real** `petname.rs` (sha256 `ff6cba651a19ad5814a2540df12433d1444b44ff5fb258a8478cb891be88723e`, identical to the checkout) against a stub `directory::Refusal`:

- Control — clean journal (two records written through `Petnames::set` itself): open OK, both names replay.
- **Torn tail** — the same bytes plus a partial record `{"op":"set","owner":"00ff","account":"cc33","name":"Car` (no trailing newline): `open FAILED: petname journal line 3 is malformed: EOF while parsing a string at line 1 column 55`.
- Control — malformed line in the **middle** (newline-terminated, valid record after it): open FAILED, as it should — mid-file corruption must stay refused.

Log: goal bookkeeping `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-petname/out.log`.

## Why it matters

Petnames are a small, private, append-only store; losing the ability to open them should never take down an entire world. Today one unlucky crash during a rename makes the world permanently unopenable without manual file surgery — while the world's main journal and its outbox, loaded seconds earlier in the same function, already survive the identical failure by design.

## Fix direction

Bring `Petnames::open` in line with the house pattern (Outbox is the closest model — same one-record-per-line JSONL, same append commit):

- Replay with `split_inclusive('\n')`; a final line that is unterminated **and** unparseable is a torn append: drop it and truncate the file to the kept prefix (so the next append is not glued onto the partial record — the failure the Outbox test name calls out).
- Any other malformed line (terminated, or mid-file) stays a hard error, exactly as today.
- Consider the same treatment for `Directory::replay` in the same pass — it is the other strict replay on the `open_world` path; if it is deliberately out of scope, say so on the issue.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `petnames.jsonl` whose final line is a partial JSON record (no trailing newline) opens successfully with all complete records replayed; the torn bytes are truncated from the file.
- [ ] After such a recovery, a subsequent `set`/`remove` appends a clean record that replays correctly on the next open (no gluing onto the torn bytes).
- [ ] A malformed line anywhere else (newline-terminated, or followed by more records) still fails the open with the line-numbered error.
- [ ] The existing test `a_malformed_line_fails_the_open` is updated/narrowed to the mid-file case, and a new test mirrors `torn_final_entry_is_dropped_but_mid_file_corruption_is_refused` for petnames.
- [ ] `cargo test` for the petname module passes; behaviour of clean journals is unchanged.

body:
## Bug

In the id web editor's markdown ↔ ProseMirror codec (`pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs`), saving a document whose **blockquote contains a fenced code block with no info string, followed by more quoted content**, silently **splits the blockquote in two**: everything after the code block is ejected from the quote. Reopening the saved file yields two separate blockquotes instead of the original one — the document's structure changes on a plain open→save with no edits.

Input (one blockquote: paragraph, no-info fence, paragraph):

```markdown
> before
>
> ```
> code
> ```
>
> after
```

After one load/save round trip:

```markdown
> before
> 
>     code

> after
```

The `after` paragraph has lost its place in the original quote (the blank line ends the quote; `> after` starts a new one). Re-parsing the saved output confirms the structure changed: the ProseMirror doc goes from `blockquote[paragraph, code_block, paragraph]` to `blockquote[paragraph, code_block]` + `blockquote[paragraph]`.

## Verified repro (this run, main a1321fd5)

Standalone probe crate compiling the verbatim `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs` against comrak 0.56.0 + serde_json, built and run on the laptop (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-laneA-codec` there; logs in the goal's `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-laneA-codec/`):

- **Ejects:** no-info fence mid-quote followed by a paragraph, a list, a heading, two paragraphs, or a second fence — every following block leaves the quote; reopen doc differs from the opened doc in all five cases.
- **Controls that save cleanly:** the identical document with an info string (``` ```rust ```) round-trips byte-identical and structure-stable; a table or thematic break in the same mid-quote position is fine; a no-info fence as the **last** block of the quote is structure-stable (only reformatted, cf. #954).
- **Layer isolation:** comrak's own parse → `format_commonmark` render of the original input produces the same ejection, so — like #1002 — the codec inherits this from the comrak CommonMark renderer behaviour its save direction relies on (`prosemirror_to_markdown` serializes a hand-built AST with `format_commonmark`). The parse direction is correct throughout: the PM doc has exactly the original structure.

## Relation to #954 and #1002 (not a duplicate of either)

- #954 tracks the no-info fence being rewritten as an indented block on save and asserts those rewrites "are currently stable fixpoints (a second round-trip does not degrade them further)". That assertion fails here: with trailing quoted content the rewrite is **not** a fixpoint — the first save changes the document structure. #954's evidence table includes a no-info fence inside a blockquote only as a lone block (nothing after it).
- #1002 tracks two stray blank lines when a blockquote **starts** with a non-paragraph block; its stated control — a blockquote where the code block is *not* first (`> intro` + fence) "saves with exactly the one normal separator line" — holds only when the fence is the quote's last block. Neither issue covers trailing content being ejected.

The likely shared root is #954's mechanism (no-info block rendered indented inside the quote, and the renderer then drops the quote prefix for the following sibling). Fixing #954 properly (info-less fences stay fenced) would very likely fix this too — the ```rust control proves the fenced form renders cleanly mid-quote — but this failure mode needs its own tests either way, because it is structural corruption, not formatting drift.

## Why it matters

Quoted code snippets followed by quoted commentary are a normal notes/docs pattern. A no-edit open→save silently restructures the document: quote attribution breaks (the trailing text no longer reads as part of the quote), subsequent saves treat the two quotes independently, and any tooling keyed on blockquote structure (extractors, renderers) sees a different document than the user wrote.

## Acceptance criteria

- Round-trip tests in `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs`: a blockquote containing a no-info fenced code block followed by (a) a paragraph, (b) a list, (c) a heading, (d) a second code block — each reopens to the **same ProseMirror structure** as the opened document (one blockquote, all blocks inside it).
- The ```rust mid-quote control and the table/thematic-break mid-quote controls still round-trip as today.
- Coordinated with #954/#1002: if the fix lands as part of #954 (fences stay fenced), these trailing-content cases are added to its test set and this issue closes by reference; a standalone workaround in the save direction is equally acceptable.
- Existing `web::markdown` tests pass.

body:
# id(web): saveFile decodes the wrong dataset field — files with `%` in their name save under a different name, or can never save at all (URIError wedges AutoSaveManager in "saving")

## Summary

`saveFile()` in `pkgs/id/web/src/main.ts` is the one place that reads the editor's filename from `dataset.docId` — and then runs `decodeURIComponent` on it. But the server never URL-encodes `data-doc-id`: it is written with plain HTML escaping, while the sibling `data-filename` attribute is the one that carries the URL-encoded name. Every other consumer reads `dataset.filename`. So for any filename containing a `%`:

- a valid `%XX` sequence is silently decoded — the save is posted under a **different file's name**, and the server obligingly sets that other tag to the new blob;
- an invalid `%` sequence throws `URIError` **before** `saveFile`'s `try` block, and `AutoSaveManager.triggerSave` has no `try/catch` either — the manager is left in state `"saving"` forever and `saveNow()` early-returns on that state, so the file can never be saved (autosave or manual) until reload.

## Evidence

The chain, all on main `a1321fd5`:

- Server emits the attributes at `pkgs/id/src/web/templates.rs:486-487`: `data-doc-id="{doc_id_escaped}" data-filename="{name_urlencoded}"`, where `doc_id_escaped = html_escape(doc_id)` (`templates.rs:418`) and `name_urlencoded = urlencoding::encode(name)` (`templates.rs:421`). The editor caller passes the raw file name as `doc_id` (`pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs`, `file_by_name_handler`: `render_editor(&name, &name, &content, &hash)`), so `dataset.docId` in the browser is the raw name, **not** a percent-encoded string.
- `openEditor` does it correctly — `main.ts:1195-1196` reads `dataset.filename` and decodes it. The tag panel (`:1004`, `:1044`), download (`:1410-1411`), rename (`:1459-1460`) and copy (`:1530-1531`) paths all read `dataset.filename` too. Only `saveFile` differs: `main.ts:1305-1306`

  ```ts
  const filenameEncoded = editorContainer.dataset.docId;
  const filename = filenameEncoded ? decodeURIComponent(filenameEncoded) : null;
  ```

- The throw escapes both layers: in `saveFile` the decode at `:1306` runs before the `try` at `:1318`; `AutoSaveManager.triggerSave` (`main.ts:121-127`) is `const result = await this.saveFn();` with no `try/catch`; `saveNow` (`:89-100`, guard at `:96`) returns early when `state === "saving"`. The fallback path in `triggerSave()` (`:1592-1611`) attaches only `.then(...)` to `saveFile()`, so it also produces an unhandled rejection.
- The server trusts the posted name completely: `save_handler` (`routes.rs:1195+`) detects the content mode from `req.name`, publishes with a `filename` tag of `req.name`, archives under `req.name`, and sets the tag `req.name → new_hash`. A decoded-wrong name is not an error — it is a cross-file overwrite.

Verified this run on main `a1321fd5` with a Bun + happy-dom probe **on the laptop** (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-docid`; `main.ts` sha256 `43e3541e…` identical on sandbox and laptop; probe + log in the goal's `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-docid/`). The probe rebuilds the exact attribute string `templates.rs` emits, parses it with a real DOM, and runs the verbatim `main.ts:1305-1306` expression (with the `main.ts:1195-1196` expression as control):

```
name="notes.md"       dataset.docId="notes.md"       saveFile: OK ("notes.md") | openEditor(dataset.filename): OK
name="a b.md"         dataset.docId="a b.md"         saveFile: OK ("a b.md") | openEditor(dataset.filename): OK
name="a%20b.md"       dataset.docId="a%20b.md"       saveFile: WRONG NAME -> save posts name="a b.md" | openEditor(dataset.filename): OK
name="%41.md"         dataset.docId="%41.md"         saveFile: WRONG NAME -> save posts name="A.md" | openEditor(dataset.filename): OK
name="caf%C3%A9.md"   dataset.docId="caf%C3%A9.md"   saveFile: WRONG NAME -> save posts name="café.md" | openEditor(dataset.filename): OK
name="100%.md"        dataset.docId="100%.md"        saveFile: THROWS URIError: URI error | openEditor(dataset.filename): OK
name="50%off.md"      dataset.docId="50%off.md"      saveFile: THROWS URIError: URI error | openEditor(dataset.filename): OK
name="résumé.md"      dataset.docId="résumé.md"      saveFile: OK ("résumé.md") | openEditor(dataset.filename): OK
autosave triggerSave REJECTED (URIError) — state stuck at "saving"
saveNow: early return (state === 'saving') — no save attempted | final state = saving
```

## Why it matters

Two failure classes from one wrong field:

1. **Silent cross-file corruption.** Editing `a%20b.md` and saving writes the content to the tag `a b.md` — overwriting a different real file if one exists — while `a%20b.md` itself keeps its old content. The decoded name also drives `convert_doc_to_bytes` mode detection on the server, so a name like `notes%2Etxt`-style decodings can even change how the document is converted.
2. **Total save failure with a wedged UI.** For `100%.md`, `50%off.md` and any other bare-`%` name, every save attempt throws, the save button stays on "saving…" (disabled), and neither autosave nor Ctrl+S/button (both route through the stuck manager) can ever succeed. The user's edits are unsaveable without a reload — and a reload loses them.

Percent signs in filenames are unremarkable (exports, URL-ish names, `100%.md` coverage notes), and the editor opens these files perfectly — only saving is broken, which is the worst place to discover it.

## Acceptance criteria

- `saveFile` posts the document's actual filename for names containing `%`: `a%20b.md` saves as `a%20b.md` (not `a b.md`), `%41.md` as `%41.md`, `caf%C3%A9.md` as `caf%C3%A9.md`. (Reading `dataset.filename` like every other consumer, or dropping the decode for `dataset.docId`, both satisfy this — the fix should match the server's actual encoding contract for whichever field it reads.)
- Saving `100%.md` / `50%off.md` succeeds: no `URIError`, a normal `/api/save` POST with the raw name, and the AutoSaveManager returns to `saved`/`idle`.
- Defense in depth: a `saveFn` that throws or rejects cannot leave `AutoSaveManager` in `state === "saving"` — `triggerSave` settles into an error/unsaved state and a later `saveNow()` can retry.
- Regression tests (web unit tests, e.g. alongside the existing `main.ts`-adjacent suites or an extracted helper) cover at least: a `%XX` name, a bare-`%` name, and a throwing `saveFn` leaving the manager retryable. Existing plain-name saves (`notes.md`, `a b.md`, `résumé.md`) are unchanged.

## Related

- #1457 is the same dataset family but a different sink (the header subtitle's `innerHTML`); this issue is the save path only.
- #1440 is the AutoSaveManager concurrency defect (concurrent saves / stale completion); this issue is its exception path — a throwing save wedging the state machine. The two fixes touch nearby code and should be checked against each other when either lands.

# id(web): .txt save still loses images — an image's alt text (and the image itself) vanish, despite the #1306 loss-free extraction

## Summary

PR #1448 (fixing #1306) made `.txt` save "loss-free" for block structure — lists, quotes, code blocks and tables now survive. Inline **atoms** still vanish: an `image` node contributes nothing at all to the extracted plain text. A paragraph containing only an image saves as an empty line; an image between text runs leaves a double space where it was. The image's alt text — the plain-text representation of an image, and the only part of it that can survive in a `.txt` file — is dropped along with it.

## Evidence

- `extract_plain_text` / `collect_plain_text_lines` / `extract_inline_text` in `pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs:2033-2107` (the #1306 implementation): the inline extractor handles `text` verbatim and `hard_break` as a newline, and recurses into any other inline node's **`content`** (`routes.rs:2090-2107`). The editor's image node is an inline atom with no content — its payload is `attrs {src, alt, title, …}` (`pkgs/id/web/src/editor.ts:73-90`) — so the recursion returns `""`.
- The #1306 policy comment (`routes.rs:2009-2032`) claims every block contributes its text and inline nodes are "recursed into rather than dropped"; the six new tests (`routes.rs:2822-2902`) cover blocks only — no inline-atom case.
- Reachability is the same as #1306's: `.txt` files open in the full rich editor (toolbar shown for Plain mode, `content_mode.rs:48`), and images can be inserted via the image-upload plugin / paste / a collab peer, exactly as lists and tables could.

Verified this run on main `b27dbe8e` with the three functions extracted **verbatim** (`routes.rs:2033-2107`) into a standalone Rust probe compiled and run ON THE LAPTOP (cargo, offline; `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-txtimg` there; probe + log in `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-txtimg/`):

```
control text para      -> "hello"
image-only para        -> ""                    <-- alt "diagram of the pipeline" and the image both gone
text+image+text para   -> "before  after"       <-- alt "ALT-TEXT" gone, double space remains
image in list item     -> ""                    <-- recursive path loses it too
footnote_ref para      -> "claim"               <-- footnote_reference atom likewise contributes nothing (secondary)
```

## Why it matters

#1306's whole point was that `.txt` save must not silently delete what the editor allowed the author to put in the document. That guarantee now holds for blocks but not for images: the save succeeds, the file reopens without the image, and nothing warns. Alt text is also an accessibility artifact — it is frequently the most information-dense part of an image in a notes file.

## Acceptance criteria

- Saving a `.txt` document containing an image preserves the image's alt text in the extracted plain text (e.g. an image-only paragraph saves as its alt text, or another pinned representation the triage chooses — but the choice must be explicit, documented in the `extract_plain_text` policy comment, and tested, not silent emptiness).
- An image with no alt text degrades to a pinned, tested representation (empty, or its src) — decided in triage, not by accident.
- The recursive paths behave the same: images inside list items, blockquotes and table cells follow the same policy as top-level paragraphs.
- New unit tests next to the #1306 tests in `routes.rs` cover at least: image-only paragraph, image between text runs, image in a list item, image without alt.
- The secondary observation (footnote_reference atoms contribute nothing) is either covered by the same policy or explicitly documented as out of scope in the policy comment.

body:
## Problem

In rich/markdown/plain documents, a fenced code block's own language (its info string) is never used for syntax highlighting. Every code block in the document is highlighted with the grammar derived from the *document's filename* — or not highlighted at all when the filename has no known extension.

So a ` ```rust ` block and a ` ```python ` block inside `notes.md` are both highlighted as Markdown, and the same blocks inside `notes.txt` or `README` get no highlighting at all.

## Evidence (verified on main `7eca828d`, 2026-10-27)

The language is lost at three stacked points; any one of them alone breaks it:

1. **The Rust codec stores the info string as `params`, never `language`** — `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs:198-211` (CodeBlock arm): `node_json["attrs"] = json!({"params": code_block.info})`.
2. **richSchema cannot carry a `language` attr** — `pkgs/id/web/src/editor.ts:56-72`: the rich `code_block` spec declares only `params` and `htmlBlock` (added by #1436). Only `rawSchema`'s code_block declares `language` (`editor.ts:294-296`). A probe with the real schemas (below) shows `Node.fromJSON` silently drops a `language` attr on rich code blocks while keeping it on raw ones.
3. **The highlight plugin only reads `language`** — `pkgs/id/web/src/highlight.ts:371-382`: `languageExtractor` returns `node.attrs.language ?? detectedLang(filename)`. Nothing in `web/src` ever reads `code_block.attrs.params` for highlighting (grep: the only `params` references are the schema declaration and its comment). The parser then uses that language at `highlight.ts:339`.

### Probe (Bun, laptop, verbatim sources)

Probe crate `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-hlparams` on the laptop, using the repo's real `editor.ts`/`highlight.ts` (sha256 `81a60bfd…` / `17411ef6…`, identical to main on the sandbox), a doc JSON shaped exactly as the codec emits it, and the `languageExtractor` body copied verbatim from `highlight.ts:371-382`:

```
rich code_block attrs after fromJSON: {"params":"rust","htmlBlock":null}
rich code_block attrs after fromJSON: {"params":"python","htmlBlock":null}
rich fromJSON with language attr -> {"params":"rust","htmlBlock":null}   (language dropped)
raw fromJSON with language attr -> {"language":"rust"}                  (raw schema keeps it)
filename=notes.md detected=markdown extractor-> [ "markdown", "markdown" ]
filename=notes.txt detected=undefined extractor-> [ undefined, undefined ]
filename=README detected=undefined extractor-> [ undefined, undefined ]
EXPECTED per-block languages: rust, python
```

## Why it matters

Fenced blocks with language tags are the common case in markdown documents — exactly the rich-mode documents this editor exists for. Today their highlighting is systematically wrong (the document's own format grammar applied to foreign code) or absent, and the carefully built grammar registry (`LANG_IMPORTS`, #749) is unreachable for the per-block languages it contains. The header comment in `highlight.ts:10-11` even documents the intended design ("manual override support via code_block node's `language` attribute") — an attribute the rich schema and the codec never provide.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A fenced block's info string determines its highlighting in rich/markdown/plain mode: e.g. ` ```rust ` and ` ```python ` blocks in one `.md` document highlight with the Rust and Python grammars respectively; the same blocks in an extensionless document also highlight.
- [ ] Info strings are normalized to Shiki language ids the way filenames are (author spellings such as `rs`, `py`, `js`, `sh`, `yml`, `c++` resolve via the existing extension/alias knowledge rather than failing silently); an info string with trailing attributes/words (e.g. `rust ignore`) does not break resolution.
- [ ] Blocks with no info string fall back to the current filename-detected language; raw mode (single code_block with a real `language` attr) keeps working unchanged.
- [ ] An `htmlBlock` code block (#982/#1436) is not syntax-highlighted as a language named by its `params` provenance value.
- [ ] Tests: unit coverage at the extractor/schema level proving a codec-shaped doc (`attrs.params`) yields the per-block language (the probe above is a ready-made failing case), plus the fallback and alias cases.

Related: #749 (grammar registry for filename-detected languages — different root cause: file-level, not block-level), #1436 (mirrored `params`/`htmlBlock` into richSchema but no consumer reads `params` for highlighting), #1229 (e2e identification of a highlighted span in a plain-text editor).

body:
# id(web): collab reconnects re-send the original identity token — the AUTH_OK refresh never reaches the socket that needs it

## Summary

`initCollab` captures the identity token **by value** at call time and its WebSocket `onopen` handler sends that captured value on every (re)connect. The refreshed token the server returns in `AUTH_OK` is handed to the `onTokenRefresh` callback (which updates `localStorage` and `currentIdentity` in `main.ts`) but is never written back into the collab closure — so every reconnect of the same `initCollab` instance re-authenticates with the token from when the editor was opened, no matter how many refreshes arrived in between.

That defeats the stated purpose of the refresh channel: the server includes a fresh token in `AUTH_OK` *"so long-lived WS sessions stay authenticated"* (`pkgs/id/src/web/collab.rs:461`), and the client comment says *"Save the refreshed token so long-lived WS sessions stay fresh"* (`collab.ts:384`). The one consumer that actually needs the token long-term — the reconnect AUTH — is the one place that never sees it.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `95cd41f0`)

Code path:

- `pkgs/id/web/src/collab.ts:92` — `token?: string | null` is a plain parameter of `initCollab(...)`; nothing in the closure ever reassigns it.
- `pkgs/id/web/src/collab.ts:378-388` — `MSG.AUTH_OK` handler extracts `refreshedToken` (msg[3]) and calls `onTokenRefresh(refreshedToken)` only.
- `pkgs/id/web/src/collab.ts:450-454` — `socket.onopen` sends `packr.pack([MSG.AUTH, token])` using the captured parameter. This handler runs for the initial socket **and** for every reconnect socket created by `scheduleReconnect`.
- `pkgs/id/web/src/main.ts:304-315` (`handleTokenRefresh`, passed at `:1220`) — saves the fresh token to `localStorage` and mutates `currentIdentity.token`; neither store is read by `collab.ts`.
- Server side: `pkgs/id/src/web/collab.rs:716-725` — on AUTH the server calls `identity_store.verify_and_refresh(token)` and returns a fresh token in `AUTH_OK`. Tokens are signed `{client_id, created_at}` payloads (`pkgs/id/src/web/identity.rs:325-348`); refresh does **not** revoke the old token, but `decode_token` rejects any token older than `TOKEN_MAX_AGE_SECS = 30 days` (`identity.rs:65`, `:379-381`). An expired token means *"Auth failed: invalid/expired token"* and the connection proceeds as anonymous (no `AUTH_OK`).

Probe (verbatim `collab.ts`, sha256 `0fb75f7015e070e982d2279ba84ef17e28e6363094ac31d05d3f159d175d826d` identical on both sides; `./editor` and `./cursors` stubbed, fake `WebSocket`, run under Bun on the laptop in `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-collabtoken`; log `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-collabtoken/out.log` in the goal workspace):

```
conn1 sent: [[8,"OLD_TOKEN_A"]]            <- AUTH with the init-time token (correct)
onTokenRefresh received: NEW_TOKEN_B       <- AUTH_OK [9, id, name, "NEW_TOKEN_B"] delivered
ws instances after drop: 2                 <- abnormal close 1006 -> reconnect socket created
conn2 sent: [[8,"OLD_TOKEN_A"]]            <- reconnect AUTH re-sends the ORIGINAL token
RESULT reconnect AUTH token = OLD_TOKEN_A
BUG CONFIRMED: reconnect used stale token
```

## Why it matters

- A long-lived editor tab (the exact case the AUTH_OK refresh was built for) silently loses its identity on the first reconnect that happens after the **original** token crosses the 30-day expiry: the server proceeds as anonymous, so the client's cursor identity / display name persistence is lost even though `localStorage` holds a perfectly fresh token the socket never used.
- The failure is silent and time-delayed — no error surfaces in the UI; the connection "works", just unauthenticated. It will look like an intermittent identity/name bug, not an auth bug.
- Scope honesty: opening a *new* editor calls `initCollab` with the then-current `currentIdentity?.token` (`main.ts:1219`), so fresh page loads and document switches are unaffected. The defect is specific to reconnects within one `initCollab` lifetime — which is precisely the long-lived-session scenario.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] After an `AUTH_OK` carrying a refreshed token, a subsequent reconnect AUTH sends the refreshed token, not the init-time token (regression test at the `collab.ts` level: fake WebSocket, deliver `AUTH_OK` with a new token, force a drop, assert the second socket's first frame decodes to `[8, <new token>]`).
- [ ] The fix keeps a single mutable source of truth for the token inside `initCollab` (e.g. a `currentToken` closure variable updated by the `AUTH_OK` handler, or a token getter supplied by the caller); the `onTokenRefresh` callback behaviour (localStorage + `currentIdentity` update in `main.ts`) is unchanged.
- [ ] Behaviour when no token was supplied at init and none arrives via `AUTH_OK` is unchanged (anonymous connect, no AUTH frame).
- [ ] Existing web unit tests pass; no change to the wire protocol or to the server (`collab.rs` / `identity.rs` untouched).

title: id(web): TS shell-contract checker rejects valid u64 values above 2^53-1 that the Rust checker accepts (seed, sequence, offset)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/low

labels.name: app/id

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

The TypeScript port of the shell contract checker (`pkgs/id/web/src/shell-contract.ts`) caps **every** `u64` field at `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (2^53−1), while the Rust original (`pkgs/id/src/shell_contract.rs`) caps `u64` at `u64::MAX` and the contract document (`pkgs/id/contract/shell-contract.v1.json`) puts no max on most `u64` fields. The TS checker therefore reports false violations for contract-valid frames — e.g. an `install_begin` whose `seed` is 2^53 or larger, a value class the system itself produces (`rand::rng().random::<u64>()`, `src/world_session/mod.rs:1162`).

## Evidence (verified on main `95cd41f0`, 2026-10-27)

Verbatim `shell-contract.ts` (sha256 `02baac39…`, identical both sides) plus the real `shell-contract.v1.json`, driven under Bun on the laptop (log: goal `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-u64/out.log`):

```
client install_begin seed=42:              {"ok":true}
client install_begin seed=9007199254740991 (2^53−1): {"ok":true}
client install_begin seed=9007199254740992 (2^53):   {"ok":false,"error":"`install_begin.seed` must be in 0..=9007199254740991, got 9007199254740992"}
client install_begin seed=u64::MAX (from wire JSON): {"ok":false,"error":"`install_begin.seed` must be in 0..=9007199254740991, got 18446744073709552000"}
server view sequence=u64::MAX (from wire JSON):     {"ok":false,"error":"`view.sequence` must be in 0..=9007199254740991, got 18446744073709552000"}
server view sequence=7: {"ok":true}
```

Code facts:

- TS: `INTEGER_MAX` in `shell-contract.ts` maps `u64` to `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, and `checkValue` clamps every integer field to `min(field.max ?? typeMax, typeMax)`.
- Rust: `check_value` in `shell_contract.rs` maps `FieldType::U64` to `u64::MAX`; only an explicit contract `max` narrows it.
- Contract fields with `u64` and **no** explicit max include `install_begin.seed` (required), `install_chunk.offset`, `view.sequence`, `program_changed.sequence`, `records.sequence`, `module_info.current_sequence`, `participant_id`, and the optional `expires_at` / `expires_in_secs` fields.
- The one `u64` field with an explicit max (`install_begin.total_bytes`, ≤ 16777216) is unaffected — the cap only bites where the contract leaves the range open, which is exactly where the Rust checker allows the full range.

## Why it matters

The contract's stated purpose (module docs, both ports) is that "a new shell proves conformance by running a check instead of reading host code." A shell (or a transcript checker — the Rust side ships `check_transcript`, the TS side `Conformance`) built on the TS port will fail frames the Rust host accepts, and its error message asserts a range (`0..=9007199254740991`) that appears nowhere in the contract — a conformance proof that disagrees with the contract is worse than none, because the failure looks like the *frame's* fault.

Scope honesty: no production web code imports the TS checker today (only `world-contract.test.ts`); this is a correctness/parity defect in the conformance library before it gains consumers, not a live user-facing outage — hence priority/low.

Note on precision: a JS consumer parsing wire JSON already loses integer precision above 2^53 (the probe shows `u64::MAX` arriving as `18446744073709552000`). The fix is therefore *not* "validate the exact value" — it is "do not reject values the contract allows": for `u64`, a non-negative integer number at or above the safe range cannot be proven out of range in JS and must be accepted (explicit field `min`/`max` bounds that lie within the safe range can still be enforced exactly).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `checkClientFrame` accepts `install_begin` with `seed` = 2^53 and with the JSON-parsed form of `u64::MAX`; `checkServerFrame` likewise accepts a `view`/`records` frame whose `sequence` is at/above 2^53. (Parity with the Rust checker's verdicts on the same frames.)
- [ ] Bounds that are exactly enforceable in JS still are: negative and non-integer values are still rejected for all integer kinds; `u16`/`u32` caps unchanged; explicit contract `max` values within the safe range (e.g. `total_bytes` ≤ 16777216) still reject above-max values, including for `u64` fields.
- [ ] Error messages for `u64` fields no longer cite `9007199254740991` as a contract bound.
- [ ] Regression tests in `world-contract.test.ts` pin the parity cases above, and a comment at the cap explains the JS precision constraint (mirroring how the Rust side documents its bound).
- [ ] Rust checker and the contract JSON are unchanged.

body:
## Finding

The cold-store-reaper test suite takes 162 s for 80 tests, and the cost is not the tests — it is per-test setup: every test creates a fresh cold-store home, and creating the manifest schema costs ~1.3–1.7 s each time.

Verified this run (main `37418e56`, sandbox VM):

- `python3 -m unittest discover -s pkgs/cold-store-reaper/tests` → `Ran 80 tests in 162.238s` (OK, 1 skipped).
- Per-test timing: slowest single test 6.2 s, only 13 of 80 under 2 s, test bodies near-instant (e.g. `test_auth_url_shape` body: 0.01 s; its `setUp`: 1.51 s).
- Isolation: `ColdStore(home).init()` on a fresh home = 1.67 s; second `init()` on the same home = 0.01 s. cProfile of a fresh `init()`: 1.30 s total, of which 1.295 s is a single call — `sqlite3.Connection.executescript` inside `ColdStore.db()` (`cold_store.py:369`), running `schema.sql` to create the manifest.
- Every test class derives from `ColdStoreTestBase.setUp` (`tests/test_cold_store.py:232`), which builds a brand-new `TemporaryDirectory` home and calls `store.init()` — so the suite pays the fresh-schema cost ~80 times (plus stacked fake Drive/S3/D1 servers in subclasses). The turso-export and drill tests pay it again per test through their own fixtures.

The absolute executescript cost varies with filesystem fsync speed (this VM is slow; a fast CI disk will be quicker), but the structure — full schema creation per test instead of once per suite — dominates the runtime anywhere and grows linearly with the test count.

## Why it matters

A 2–3 minute suite is a suite people stop running locally — which compounds #1427 (no CI runs these tests at all): the package's only safety net is both unwired and slow. It also slows every future CI wiring: a path-filtered workflow (per #1427) that takes ~3 minutes for one small package will pressure people to skip it. Backup-integrity code deserves a suite that runs in seconds.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The suite's wall-clock drops by at least ~5x on this VM (162 s → under ~35 s) with all 80 tests still passing and none deleted or weakened.
- [ ] Fresh-schema creation happens once per suite/run (e.g. a template manifest built once and copied per test, or an equivalent shared fixture), while each test still gets an isolated manifest it can mutate freely.
- [ ] Tests that specifically exercise first-run schema creation/migrations (fresh-home `init`, pre-v4 manifest migration) keep a genuinely fresh home — they are the exception, not the default fixture.
- [ ] The measurement is repeated and recorded on the PR (before/after wall-clock for the full discover run).

body:
## Finding (from PR #1373, merged)

`pkgs/cold-store-reaper/scripts/export-turso.sh` (validation added by PR #1373, still on main at lines 74–80):

```bash
DUMP_MAX_TIME="${TURSO_DUMP_MAX_TIME_SECONDS:-1800}"
case "${DUMP_MAX_TIME}" in
'' | *[!0-9]*)
  echo "turso export: ERROR: TURSO_DUMP_MAX_TIME_SECONDS must be a positive integer (got '${DUMP_MAX_TIME}')" >&2
  exit 1
  ;;
*) ;;
esac
```

The `case` rejects empty and non-digit values, but **`0` is all digits and passes** — despite the error message and the PR body both describing the check as validating "a positive integer". All-digit zero forms (`00`, `000`) pass the same way.

## Why it matters

The value is passed straight to `curl --max-time "${DUMP_MAX_TIME}"` for the /dump download. For curl, `--max-time 0` means **no timeout at all** — the transfer runs unbounded. PR #1373 exists because a ~500 MB dump outgrew the old fixed 300 s cap; setting `TURSO_DUMP_MAX_TIME_SECONDS=0` (a plausible "disable/zero" knob value, or a templating accident) silently removes the cap entirely while the operator believes a validated positive cap is in force. A stalled dump then hangs the export step indefinitely instead of failing loudly at the cap.

## Suggested fix

After the digit check, reject zero explicitly (e.g. strip leading zeros and require a non-empty/non-zero remainder, or `[ "$DUMP_MAX_TIME" -gt 0 ]` with the digit check first so the arithmetic is safe). Add a regression test beside `test_dump_max_time_env_override_is_honored` covering `0` (and ideally `00`) expecting exit 1 with the positive-integer error.

## Provenance

Identified by pr-diff-review-b run `04a1ab0f` (2026-10-27 04:18 CDT) during review of PR #1373; that run was interrupted before filing and later runs advanced the watermark past the PR. The run's own log did not survive the 2026-10-27 overload window, so the finding was re-verified firsthand against the merged diff and current main before filing (2026-10-27).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `TURSO_DUMP_MAX_TIME_SECONDS=0` (and all-zero forms like `00`) is rejected with the positive-integer error and exit 1.
- [ ] Non-zero positive values and the unset default (1800) behave exactly as before.
- [ ] A regression test beside `test_dump_max_time_env_override_is_honored` covers `0` (and ideally `00`) expecting exit 1.
- [ ] No other validation behavior in `export-turso.sh` changes.

## Finding

`pkgs/cold-store-reaper` has a substantial test suite — and no CI runs any of it.

Verified this run (2026-10-27, main `37418e56`):

- Suites exist: `tests/test_cold_store.py` (2,361 lines), `tests/test_export_turso.py` (246), `tests/test_nightly_backup.py` (133), plus the worker proof `worker/test/run-local-proof.mjs` (`npm test`).
- `grep -rn "cold-store|cold_store" .github/workflows/` → no workflow references the package. `grep` over `*.nix` / `flake.nix` → no check or derivation runs the tests either.
- The only documented way to run them is a manual command in `pkgs/cold-store-reaper/README.md` ("Tests" section): `python3 -m unittest discover -s pkgs/cold-store-reaper/tests -v`.
- Every comparable package has CI: `id-check.yml`, `mcpx.yml` + `mcpx-conformance.yml`, `go-modules-build.yml`, `identity-build.yml`, `map-build.yml`, `lab-ops-hub.yml`. cold-store-reaper is the outlier.

## Why it matters

The last three cold-store changes all shipped test changes that no automation executed:

- PR #1373 (nightly step isolation) — `tests/test_nightly_backup.py`, shell-script tests
- PR #1383 (turso GB-class hardening) — `tests/test_cold_store.py`, `tests/test_export_turso.py`
- PR #1398 (repair filter for #1391) — new `scripts/repair_dump.py` + 164 lines of tests

A regression in this package is a backup-integrity regression: this code verifies sha256s, enforces the 700 GB/day and 3 TiB budget stops, and produces the only portable exports of the Turso databases. "Tests exist but only run when a human remembers" is how a red suite lands on main unnoticed. (This run: the suite is currently green — 80 tests, OK, 1 skipped — but takes 162 s wall-clock, which is itself a reason it needs a proper CI home rather than ad-hoc runs.)

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A GitHub Actions workflow runs the cold-store-reaper Python suites (`python3 -m unittest discover -s pkgs/cold-store-reaper/tests`) on PRs and pushes to main that touch `pkgs/cold-store-reaper/**` (path-filtered, consistent with the repo's other per-package workflows).
- [ ] The workflow provisions the suite's documented requirements: Python 3.12, the `zstd` CLI, `curl`, and the `sqlite3` CLI (the export-turso tests shell out to it via the `SQLITE3_BIN` seam).
- [ ] The worker local proof (`worker/`: `npm test`, which cross-checks `src/decoder.js` against the real Python `pack`) runs in the same workflow or a sibling job.
- [ ] The workflow is green on main at merge time, and the README "Tests" section is updated to say CI runs the suites (keeping the manual command for local use).

body:
## Finding

PR #1387's new benchmark harness (`pkgs/id/benches/world_bench.rs`, head commit `b6f5b720e9fc7d117f44b46181818d114dbad3aa`) ships a `guest_replay` benchmark that never replays anything through the guest. It builds a journal of N `Committed` **chat** events, calls `WorldCore::restore`, and then pushes `restored.replay` through its `CountingProgram` — but on current main, `restore` does not put committed chat events into `replay` at all, so the guest pass iterates an empty vec and `guest.seen` stays 0. The reported `guest_replay` number is restore-only time, mislabeled as guest replay.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/1387 (OPEN, slice 1 of #539)
- `pkgs/id/benches/world_bench.rs:121` — `bench_guest_replay` builds the journal from `chat_event(...)` entries (`WorldEventKind::Chat`).
- `pkgs/id/benches/world_bench.rs:166` — `for event in &restored.replay { guest.update(event)?; }` — the loop that is supposed to be the measured guest workload.
- Current main `pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs:347` (verified at `37418e56`): in `WorldCore::restore`, the `JournalEntry::Committed` match arm is `WorldEventKind::System { .. } | WorldEventKind::Chat(_) => {}` — chat events are applied to core state via `commit_prepared` but are **not** pushed to `replay`. Only `Input` committed events (`core.rs:344`) and journal `System` entries (`core.rs:317`) land in `replay`.
- The bench's own inline comment half-notices this ("count the guest pass over the full journal's events as the replay workload when restore() consumed them into core state directly") but the code does not do that — it still iterates `restored.replay`.

## Why it matters

Slice 2 of #539 commits baselines recorded from this harness, and slice 3's CI job diffs medians against them. A `guest_replay` baseline that contains zero guest work will (a) understate the real replay cost the benchmark exists to track, and (b) make any future fix to the bench look like a massive regression when the guest pass starts doing real work. The failure is silent: the bench prints a plausible-looking line either way.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `guest_replay` actually pushes the N committed events through the guest (e.g. iterate the journal's committed events / core history, or build the journal from event kinds that `restore` returns in `replay`), OR the benchmark is renamed/re-scoped to state honestly that it measures restore only.
- [ ] The bench asserts the guest saw the expected count (e.g. `guest.seen == events`, or `restored.replay.len()` is checked non-empty) so a future restore-semantics change cannot silently re-empty the workload.
- [ ] `cargo bench --bench world_bench -- --quick --only guest_replay` (or the just/nix runner equivalent) completes with the assertion in place.

Refs #539. Found by pr-diff-review-b reviewing PR #1387's diff against current main.

body:
# id(web): Tab/Shift-Tab with a selection spanning multiple blocks corrupts a paragraph and skips later code blocks

## Summary

`indentCommand` / `dedentCommand` in `pkgs/id/web/src/indent.ts` assume the
selection lives inside a single `code_block`. When a selection starts in a
code block and extends across other blocks (select-all is the easy trigger),
the commands treat the whole span as one block's text:

- code blocks after the first are never indented/dedented, and
- the line-start math (computed over `doc.textBetween(blockStart, blockEnd)`,
  whose block separators do not exist as document positions) lands inside a
  neighbouring paragraph and inserts spaces into it — corrupting non-code
  content with a formatting keystroke.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 452d69e6)

Targeted vitest probes against the real commands + `richSchema` (probe files
preserved in the fleet's run records; run with `bunx vitest run` in
`pkgs/id/web`):

1. Doc = code_block(`x\ny`) + paragraph(`mid`) + code_block(`p\nq`), select
   all, Tab →
   - code_block 1 becomes `  x\n  y` (correct),
   - paragraph becomes `mid  ` — **two spaces appended to the paragraph text**,
   - code_block 2 stays `p\nq` — **never indented**.
2. Doc = code_block(`one`) + paragraph(`keep me`) + code_block(`two`), select
   all, Tab → only the first block is indented; `two` is untouched.
3. Controls behave: a selection entirely inside one code block works
   (existing `indent.test.ts` suite), and a selection entirely inside a
   paragraph returns `false` (the `inCode` gate at indent.ts:42-46 only
   inspects `$from`'s parent).

## Root cause

- `indent.ts:63-65` (indent) and `indent.ts:100-102` (dedent): `blockStart`
  comes from `$from.start($from.depth)` and `blockEnd` from
  `$to.end($to.depth)` — two different nodes when the selection spans blocks —
  and `textBetween(blockStart, blockEnd)` is then scanned for `\n` as if it
  were a single code block's text. Positions derived from that joined string
  do not correspond to document positions once block boundaries (and
  textBetween's separators) intervene.
- The `inCode` check (indent.ts:42-49, 93-97) only examines the selection's
  head parent, so a spanning selection is accepted and processed with the
  single-block math. This is the multi-block sibling of #714 (which fixed
  wrong-line selection *within* one block; its tests still only build
  single-code-block documents).

## Why it matters

Tab is a formatting key users hit with large selections reflexively
(select-all + Tab to reindent a file is a standard gesture). Today that
gesture silently edits prose paragraphs and leaves later code blocks
unindented — a data-corruption papercut in the editor's most basic
indentation path.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Tab with a selection spanning multiple blocks indents the selected
      lines of *every* code_block the selection overlaps, and modifies no
      non-code content (paragraph text byte-identical).
- [ ] Shift-Tab under the same conditions dedents every overlapped
      code_block's selected lines, with the same no-prose-edits guarantee.
- [ ] Single-block behaviour is unchanged: the existing `indent.test.ts`
      suite (including the #714 cases) passes unmodified.
- [ ] New tests cover multi-block selections (code+paragraph, and
      code+paragraph+code) for both commands, including select-all.

title: id(web): ImageNodeView.update() reassigns img.src on every update for relative sources — images reload/flicker on unrelated edits

body:
## Summary

`ImageNodeView.update()` reassigns `img.src` on **every** update for any image
whose `src` attr is relative (which is the normal shape for id's own images,
e.g. `/api/files/…`) — even when nothing about the image changed. In a browser,
assigning `img.src` restarts the image load, so images flicker / refetch /
re-decode whenever ProseMirror re-runs the node view during editing or collab
updates.

## Evidence (verified on main 95bfedb4, this run)

`pkgs/id/web/src/image-node-view.ts:240`:

```ts
if (this.img.src !== node.attrs.src) this.img.src = node.attrs.src || "";
```

The `img.src` **getter** returns the resolved absolute URL, while
`node.attrs.src` holds the authored (relative) value, so the comparison is
never equal for relative sources and the guard never guards.

Probe (targeted vitest, real `ImageNodeView` + `EditorView`/`richSchema`,
happy-dom; probe removed after the run, log in the creator's probe archive):

- node attrs src: `/api/files/cat.png`
- `img.src` getter: `http://localhost:3000/api/files/cat.png`
- `img.getAttribute("src")`: `/api/files/cat.png`
- Setter spy during `update()` with an **identical** fresh node (same src,
  alt): **1 src assignment** — the reload is triggered on a no-op update.

The neighbouring syncs in the same method are fine: alt/title are compared
against `node.attrs` directly (`:241-242`), only the src check compares
against the absolutizing DOM getter. The constructor (`:50`) assigns once and
is not affected.

## Why it matters

`update()` runs whenever ProseMirror reconciles the image node — local
typing near an image, remote collab steps, selection-driven re-renders.
Each pass silently restarts every relative-src image's load: visible flicker
in image-heavy docs, extra requests against the id server, and re-decode
jank, for zero benefit. It also makes the DOM churn under any future test
that asserts update() is a no-op for unchanged nodes.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `update()` with unchanged attrs performs no `img.src` assignment
      (compare against `getAttribute("src")` or a tracked last-applied src).
- [ ] Changing the src attr still updates the image exactly once; clearing
      it still clears the image.
- [ ] Regression test in `image-node-view.test.ts` (created by the #1389 fix
      or here, whichever lands first): setter-spy or attribute-based
      assertion that an unchanged update does not touch `img.src`, and a
      changed src does.
- [ ] Web unit tests + typecheck pass.

## Notes

Small, self-contained fix in `image-node-view.ts`. Sibling in the same file,
distinct defect: #1389 (west resize handles inverted).

# id(web): image upload completing after the document shrinks is silently lost — stale insert position throws, success is logged as "Upload failed"

## Evidence (verified this run, main 6f4532ab; `image-upload.ts` unchanged on current main 0c37bb15)

`pkgs/id/web/src/image-upload.ts`, `handleImageUpload` (line 209):

- The completion handler looks up the placeholder decoration and falls back to the **captured** insert position when the placeholder is gone: `const pos = found && found.length > 0 ? found[0].from : insertPos;` (line 228).
- It then inserts unconditionally at that position: `removeTr.insert(pos, imageNode);` (line 235).
- If the user edited the document while the upload was in flight and the text around the placeholder was deleted, the placeholder decoration is mapped away **and** the captured `insertPos` can be beyond the end of the now-smaller document. `insert` throws, the throw lands in the shared `.catch`, and it is logged as `[image-upload] Upload failed for <name>: RangeError: Position N out of range` (line 239) — even though the upload itself **succeeded** on the server. The image is never inserted and the user gets no feedback; the blob is orphaned server-side.

Reproduced this run with a targeted vitest probe (real `EditorView` + real plugin, deferred mocked `fetch`; probe removed after verification, log in the fleet's probe archive `probe-2026-10-27-creator-b2/out.log`):

- Doc `paragraph("abcdefghijabcdefghij")`, cursor at position 21, paste one PNG → placeholder added at 21.
- Before resolving the upload, the whole doc is replaced with `paragraph("x")` (doc size 24 → 5; the placeholder is gone).
- Resolve the upload successfully → final doc is still just `"x"` (no image), and the console warning is `[image-upload] Upload failed for a.png: RangeError: Position 21 out of range` at `image-upload.ts:235`.

Control in the same probe: with no shrink, the same upload inserts the image node normally.

## Why it matters

Paste an image, keep typing / undo / delete while a slow (10 MB, LAN) upload finishes, and the image silently vanishes — with a console log that actively misdirects debugging by claiming the upload failed. Collab edits from another client can shrink/move the document the same way, so this does not require fast local editing. This is a third, distinct failure mode in the same completion path as #1321 (oversized swallow) and #1323 (multi-image ordering).

## Suggested fix

Clamp/validate the fallback position against the current document before inserting (e.g. fall back to a valid position such as the current selection or the end of the document) so a successful upload still lands somewhere sensible; and do not route insertion errors through the upload-failure log message — distinguish "upload failed" from "insertion failed" so the log tells the truth. If the chosen policy is instead to drop the image when its anchor is gone, that must be an explicit, user-visible outcome, not a silent one.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Regression test: upload resolves after the document has shrunk past the captured insert position (placeholder deleted with the surrounding text) — the image is inserted at a valid in-range position (per the chosen policy), no `RangeError`, and the success path is not logged as an upload failure.
- [ ] The normal path is unchanged: placeholder still present → image inserts at the placeholder's mapped position.
- [ ] A genuinely failed upload (non-OK / network error) still removes only its placeholder and logs an upload failure.
- [ ] Existing web unit tests pass (`cd pkgs/id/web && bunx vitest run src/image-upload.test.ts`, plus the full web suite).

body:
## Work (Drew, 2026-10-27)

A standing steward job (`pool-quota-steward`, hourly) owns the
pools' health and the fleet's rate of use across models:

- Read every pool's quota each run: OpenChamber `/api/quota/*` for
  the listed providers, the provider snapshot tool for Meta, plan
  windows and reset times for all — a quota picture ≤60 min old is
  the license for any decision (the POOL MAP measurement gate).
- Compare burn rate against window remaining per pool and recommend
  the fleet's center of gravity: which pool should be absorbing the
  next hours of work, which is hoarding unused window that will
  expire unspent (burn-by-expiry), which is close enough to its wall
  that only finishing work belongs there.
- Make bounded ad-hoc decisions to correct the balance: routing
  changes land ONLY as PRs to the canonical repo config
  (developing-today/code `.opencode/opencode.jsonc`) or, for
  OpenChamber's category bindings, as recorded proposals until
  #1272's mapping lands. NEVER PAYG, never a credential change,
  never a pool Drew hasn't approved, Astra stays gated.
- **Change-event ledger** (append-only, goal workspace): every
  decision — including "no change, because" at a threshold crossing —
  is an event: timestamp, quota snapshot before, the change (PR link
  or proposal), rationale, expected effect, and the pool's window.
  On later runs the steward measures the change's actual impact
  (burn shift, session outcomes on that pool) and appends the
  outcome to the same event. A config change with no ledger event,
  or an event with no measured follow-up, is a defect the
  meta-reviewer should catch.
- Session token impact: using the babysitter log + queue outcomes,
  track whether a change moved cost per merged PR / per closed issue
  on the affected pool, and say so in the run report.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Job live; ledger exists with its first events, each carrying a
      before-snapshot and an expected effect.
- [ ] First impact follow-up measured and appended within 24h of
      the first change.
- [ ] Zero config changes outside the PR path (spot-check deployed
      configs against repo state).

Child of the pool & routing intelligence epic. Filed by Muse
(operator) 2026-10-27.

body:
## Bug

Pasting or dropping **multiple images at once** into the id web editor inserts them in **upload-completion order, not clipboard order**. Uploads race: whichever `/api/upload` request finishes first does not determine position — in the verified probe below, the image whose upload finished *first* ended up *second* in the document. The resulting order is effectively nondeterministic and depends on file sizes and network timing.

## Evidence

`pkgs/id/web/src/image-upload.ts`:

- `handlePaste` (~L185-202) and `handleDrop` (~L204-228) start every file's upload from the **same** insert position (`view.state.selection.from` / one `posAtCoords` result) via independent `handleImageUpload(view, file, insertPos)` calls — no sequencing or ordering token.
- `handleImageUpload` (~L232-245) adds a placeholder widget at that shared position; on completion it inserts the image node at its placeholder's mapped position (`found[0].from`). All placeholders sit at the same document position, so completion order — not paste order — decides the final sequence.

Verified this run on main `1bf2afb2` with a targeted vitest probe (real `EditorView` + plugin, mocked `fetch`; probe since removed):

- Pasted `[first.png, second.png]`; resolved **second.png's** upload first, then first.png's.
- Resulting document image order: **`[second.png, first.png]`** — reversed relative to the clipboard.

With equal timing the order varies run to run; larger files (slower uploads) systematically drift later/earlier than the user pasted them.

## Why it matters

Multi-image paste is the normal way users add screenshots and photo sets to a document. Silently scrambling their order corrupts the document's meaning (before/after shots, step-by-step screenshots, comic/panel sequences) and the user may not notice until the document is shared — in a collaborative editor, possibly after collaborators have seen the scrambled version.

## Acceptance criteria

- Images pasted or dropped together appear in the document in clipboard/file-list order, regardless of individual upload completion order (e.g. sequence the insertions, or give each placeholder a stable ordered slot that later completions insert after).
- A failed upload in the middle of a batch does not reorder or drop the remaining images; its placeholder is removed and the survivors keep their relative order.

body:
# pm-stack(grist): no supported API path to extend a Choice column's options

Filed from direct experience, 2026-10-26 (Drew: "make an issue documenting what you wished it would do").

## What happened
Adding the `id` area to the Program roadmap required extending the Area column's Choice list in the Grist doc. The REST API refused: `/apply` with `UpdateColumn` returns "'UpdateColumn' actions are not controlled" — the doc's access rules reject schema changes even for the SOPS-managed admin API key that can freely read/write all data. The only working route was: stop the Grist container, edit the doc's SQLite directly (`_grist_Tables_column.widgetOptions`), restart, verify. It worked and a backup was taken first, but no routine change should need database surgery.

## What I wished it did
- A supported, authenticated way for a doc owner/admin to modify column options (at minimum Choice lists) via the API — either by making access rules able to *grant* schema actions to a role instead of rejecting them as uncontrolled, or a dedicated admin endpoint/CLI for column metadata.
- Access rules that distinguish data edits from schema edits, so "this key may manage schema" is an expressible policy.

## To investigate first
Whether the block is our doc's access-rules configuration (fixable in config) or a Grist OSS limitation (then this becomes an upstream feature request + a documented local workaround: the stop/edit/restart runbook, kept with the pm-stack docs). Either way the end state is: scripted choice-list edits with no direct SQLite writes.

Context: doc `czYHYKgG9SHcm9CPwiKEq1` (Program roadmap), Grist OSS v1.7.21 pinned in `pm-stack/grist/compose.yml`.

## Acceptance criteria

- One of the issue's two end states is reached and recorded here: either (a) an upstream Grist path (newer version or API action) supports extending a Choice column's options via the REST API and is adopted/pinned, or (b) a documented local workaround exists — the stop/edit/restart runbook kept with the pm-stack docs — so choice-list edits are scripted end to end.
- Either way: no direct SQLite writes to the Grist document database are part of the procedure.
- The runbook/adoption note names the Grist version it was verified against (currently OSS v1.7.21).

labels.name: kind/feature

body:
## Problem (found by pilot #1188, 2026-10-26)

There are two scheduling systems in the house and they don't know
about each other:

- **The fleet's:** Supabase `agent.tasks` queues + cron-driven lane
  shifts / babysitter, with the lifecycle protocol (claims, parks,
  terminal states, monitor reconciliation).
- **OpenChamber's own:** per-project scheduled tasks
  (`/api/projects/:projectId/scheduled-tasks`, with `/run` and loop
  files) that fire sessions on their own schedule.

If both can start work on the same repo, the fleet gets a new class of
double-assignment the protocol can't see (an OpenChamber-scheduled
session and a queue worker fixing the same issue), and two places
claim to be the schedule of record.

## Work

- Inventory what OpenChamber scheduled tasks exist today on the
  laptop (which projects, what they run, whose work they do).
- Decide the integration shape, one of: (a) OpenChamber scheduled
  tasks become a *producer* that enqueues repo-task packets (the
  Phase 3 pattern) and never starts work directly; (b) the fleet
  treats OpenChamber scheduled tasks as an external holder in the
  monitor's tracker (labelled, watched, never double-claimed);
  (c) scheduled tasks are retired in favor of the queue. Recommend
  with reasons; Drew decides ties.
- Encode the decision in the lifecycle protocol doc so the monitor's
  duties cover whichever surface remains.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An inventory of live OpenChamber scheduled tasks exists.
- [ ] A decision is recorded (issue comment + protocol doc update)
      naming the single scheduling system of record.
- [ ] The monitor's tracker shows OpenChamber-scheduled work in
      whichever form the decision requires — no invisible holders.

Child of epic #1234. Filed by Muse (operator) 2026-10-26.

Part of epic #1184 (PM stack coherence — ideal-system design series, 2026-10-26).

## Why
History today is fragmented: GitHub timelines, Kaneo activity, session records, orchestration runs, and dashboard comments each tell part of a story, and reconstructing 'what happened to this item' means opening four systems. The ideal aggregator keeps one activity river — a unified, filterable audit timeline per item and globally — fed by every layer, including the dashboard's own actions.

## Design questions to answer
- Event model: the common event shape (actor, action, object, timestamp, source link) and which sources emit v1 (GitHub, Kaneo, sessions, orchestrator, dashboard writes, watchdog).

- Retention and storage: where events live (with the durability design), growth expectations, and what's pruned or archived when.
- Integrity: which events are append-only, who can annotate vs edit, and how gaps (a source was down) are shown rather than papered over.

## Acceptance
- Design note landed in repo `doc/` + implementation issues filed and linked as sub-issues of #1184; open questions needing Drew named explicitly in the design note.

The babysitter's core judgment is "progressing vs stalled." This pilot

title: Fleet observability: certify shift completion from queue state, not run self-report (uncertified runs)

labels.name: kind/debt
labels.description: Technical debt worth paying down deliberately

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: area/infra
labels.description: Infrastructure, deployment, and operations

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

Fleet shift runs keep ending "uncertified": a tool call or tool result inside the run never returns a success/failure status, so the run's own final report cannot confirm completion — even when every task it touched reached a verified terminal state. On 2026-10-26 this happened at least four times:

- 13:24 code worker shift: ended uncertified; outcomes (PRs #995, #999 merged) verified afterwards from GitHub.
- Lane B 16:44 shift: 8 tasks handled, 2 PRs merged (verified), run outcome marked failed over one unconfirmed tool result.
- Lane B 17:24 shift: 6 tasks worked, completion uncertain per its own report; verified afterwards from queue health (39 done, 0 failed) and PR states.
- Lane A 18:24 shift: reported its summary as "already delivered" — it had never reached the chat; the parent had to re-deliver from live state.

Today the recovery pattern is manual: the parent re-verifies merges, closures, and queue counts from GitHub/Supabase after the fact and reports what actually happened. That works, but it costs a verification pass on every affected shift and leaves a window where nobody knows whether work landed.

## Proposal

Certify shift completion from durable state, not from the run's self-report:

- A shift's completion record is the queue itself: per-task terminal states (complete/park/block with timestamps), the signal refresh, and the lane-lock release. A lightweight post-shift checker (the fleet monitor already reconciles queue ↔ GitHub hourly) compares the shift's claimed task set against terminal states and produces the certified summary line.
- When a run ends uncertified, the delivery automatically falls back to the state-derived summary ("uncertified run — outcomes verified from queue/GitHub state: …") instead of a bare failure, so the report Drew reads is always grounded.
- Track the uncertified-run rate per job as a fleet health metric; if it exceeds a threshold (say 2 in 24h for one job), the monitor flags it as an infrastructure problem in its summary rather than per-run noise.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A shift that ends with an unconfirmed tool result still produces a delivery whose every claim is derived from queue/GitHub state (no parent improvisation needed).
- [ ] The fleet monitor's summary includes, per shift job, runs completed vs uncertified for the last 24h.
- [ ] No shift outcome is reported as simply "failed" when its tasks verifiably reached terminal states.

Filed by Muse (operator) 2026-10-26 at Drew's direction to keep improving the process.

title: Queue workers: give the non-code queues lane-style long-budget shifts (claim evaporation is a run-budget problem)

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: New feature or capability request

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: area/infra
labels.description: Infrastructure, deployment, and operations

labels.name: effort/m
labels.description: Medium: expected under 1 day of work

body:
## Problem

The three non-code queues (repo-health-opencode-pilot, repo-health-openchamber-pilot, repo-health-nix-pilot) are worked by short-budget arrangements — a 2-hourly agent-queue-worker cron and per-queue hook workers — while the code queue runs two staggered lane shifts (40-min cadence, ~90-min budget, bundle of up to 10, per-lane locks, atomic claims). The short-budget workers keep dying mid-task: they claim, label, do real work, and their run ends without a terminal verb (complete/park/block). The lease expires, labels and queue state diverge, and the fleet monitor spends a duty repairing the divergence instead of the fleet making progress.

## Evidence (2026-10-26 alone)

- Task 1149 (opencode #530): evaporated 4 times, went dead-in-queue at 4/4; after an operator cap raise it was claimed again and the run was cut at its resolve cutoff mid-typecheck — branch unpushed, task left claimed. Its work has been verified-complete at checkpoint level (`targeted_tests_passed`) for most of a day without landing.
- Task 1157 (openchamber #495): evaporated 4 times, dead-in-queue at 4/4 (cap raised 2026-10-26 evening).
- Task 1160 (openchamber #500): reached its 2/2 cap the same way.
- Task 1187 (nix #907) and task 1177 (opencode #541): further evaporations the monitor repaired the same day.
- The fleet monitor repaired 10+ claim/label divergences on 2026-10-26 across the non-code queues; the code queue, on lane shifts, had one in-shift evaporation (task 1216) which the same shift self-recovered.

Migration 0012 (2026-10-26) fixed the attempt accounting (park/resume no longer consumes attempts), but evaporation itself is a run-budget problem: a worker whose run can be cut at any resolve/timeout boundary will keep stranding claims no matter how the attempts are counted.

## Proposal

Give each non-code queue the lane treatment the code queue proved out on 2026-10-26:

- One cron-driven shift worker per queue (or one worker rotating queues per shift), 40–60 min cadence, ~90-min run budget, bundle of up to 5 tasks strictly one at a time.
- Per-queue lock file; a lane gates out only on its own live lock.
- Same worker instruction as the code lanes (claim → checkpoint on claim → outcome-early ordering → park instead of waiting on CI → verified terminal state before claiming the next), including the §10 anti-evaporation discipline.
- Retire or repurpose the short-budget hook workers for those queues once the shifts are live (keep them as fallback, as the code hook was kept).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Shift worker(s) exist for the opencode, openchamber, and nix queues with the lane properties above (cadence, budget, bundle, own-lock gating).
- [ ] A full day of operation with zero claim evaporations on the non-code queues (monitor Duty 1 addendum finds no divergences to repair), or every evaporation traced to a named infrastructure cutoff with the task recovered by the next shift without operator help.
- [ ] Tasks 1149 and 1157 reach terminal states through the new workers without further operator cap raises.
- [ ] The fleet monitor's per-run evaporation-repair count for non-code queues trends to zero over the following week (measured at the queue-pilot interim check).

Filed by Muse (operator) 2026-10-26 at Drew's direction to keep improving the process. Related: migration 0012 (attempt accounting), the 2026-10-28 queue-pilot interim check.
