title: ci(flake-inputs-update): failure-issue lookup caps at the 100 newest open issues — this repo already has 143 open, so the one tracking issue will be missed, duplicated, and never closed

labels.name: kind/ci
labels.description: CI/CD pipelines, workflows, and build automation

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: area/ci
labels.description: CI/CD pipelines, workflows, and build automation (area)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: meta/enriched
labels.description: Intake review done: acceptance criteria, links, and normalized labels added

body:
## Finding

The `flake-inputs-update` workflow added in PR #907 (merged; the file is at current main HEAD `3645dda22adc`) tracks all of its failures in ONE issue, found by exact title. The lookup that finds it is capped at 100 open issues — and this repo already has more open issues than that, so the single-tracking-issue design breaks in production:

- `.github/workflows/flake-inputs-update.yml:61` ("Find an open failure issue" step):
  `gh issue list --state open --limit 100 --json number,title` followed by a `jq` exact-title match for `chore(deps): automated openchamber+opencode input update failing`.
- `gh issue list` returns newest-created first and stops at the limit. Verified 2026-10-25 by two methods: the search API reports 143 open issues in developing-today/code, and `gh issue list --state open --limit 200` returns 143. The cap is already exceeded before the workflow has ever opened its failure issue.
- This repo files new issues continuously, so a failure issue that is found when fresh will fall out of the newest-100 window quickly (edits do not change creation order).

## What goes wrong when the lookup misses

All of these are in the same workflow file and key off the step's `number` output:

1. The "Record the failure" step sees an empty `EXISTING_NUMBER` and runs `gh issue create` — a duplicate tracking issue, contradicting the workflow's stated "one issue per workflow, never a new one" contract (header comment and PR #907 body).
2. The attempt count and "First failure" timestamp are parsed from the old issue's body only when it is found, so the duplicate restarts at `Attempts: 1` with a fresh first-failure time and an empty failure history.
3. On the next success, both close paths (the "Publish and merge the update" step and the "Close the failure issue (pins already current)" step) close only the found number, and the update PR only carries `Fixes #<n>` for the found number — the original failure issue is never commented on or closed and stays open forever.

## Why it matters

The workflow merges flake-input updates on its own schedule; its failure issue is the only signal when updates start failing. Duplicated/reset tracking issues and a never-closed original make failures easy to miss and the failure history unreliable — exactly what the one-issue design in PR #907 was meant to prevent.

## Evidence

- PR: #907 "ci: scheduled flake-inputs-update workflow (openchamber + opencode)", head `9e95477519`, merged as `3645dda22adc` (current main HEAD at review time).
- File: `.github/workflows/flake-inputs-update.yml` line 61 (lookup), plus the create/edit and close logic in the failure-recording, publish, and pins-current steps of the same file.
- Live counts, 2026-10-25: `gh api "search/issues?q=repo:developing-today/code+type:issue+state:open"` → `total_count` 143; `gh issue list --state open --limit 200` → 143 issues.

## Acceptance criteria

- The failure-issue lookup no longer depends on the issue being among the newest N open issues: e.g. look it up with a title search (`gh issue list --search` / the search API), a dedicated label, or a fully paginated list.
- With >100 open issues and an existing failure issue older than the 100 newest, a failing run edits that same issue (attempt count increments, first-failure time and history preserved) instead of creating a new one.
- A subsequent successful run closes that same pre-existing issue on both success paths (update PR merged, and pins-already-current).
- Verification covers the >100-open-issues case explicitly (stubbed `gh` output or a documented live check), not only the fresh-repo case.

Found by the pr-diff-review job reviewing PR #907.

body:
## Design issue — aggregator "needs you" attention view

Parent context: the project-management stack design record
(`doc/2026-10-24T11-05-38Z_design_project-management-stack/`) and the
aggregator UI phase (session K, branch `pm/aggregator-ui`). Reference
design (concept only — FSL-1.1-MIT licensed, do NOT vendor its code):
https://github.com/amirfish1/claude-command-center (its whole board is
sorted by "which session needs you").

### What Drew asked for (2026-10-25)

An easier "needs you" dashboard. A nice GUI should be available, but
the priority is making it easy for **Muse** to analyze the fleet at a
glance: what is in motion, what is stopped, and what needs
intervention — so nothing stalls silently and no session sits waiting
on a question nobody saw.

### Session state taxonomy (Drew's list, 2026-10-25)

Every live agent session classified into exactly one state:

1. **in motion** — running, messages/tool calls progressing.
2. **stopped for a question** — idle because it asked something and is
   waiting on an answer (quote what it needs).
3. **errored** — last turn ended in an error (provider error, tool
   failure, crash).
4. **needs poke** — idle without a completion signal and without a
   question (finished a step, never continued).
5. **stalled on CLI** — a shell/CLI call has been running far beyond
   its normal envelope (hung subprocess, silent long build).
6. **stuck retrying** — repeated identical errors / retry loop /
   quota-wall spin with no file or commit progress.

### Required behavior

- The view is **machine-first**: a queryable state feed (projector /
  API) Muse can poll in one call, covering every OpenCode session
  across the fleet's servers, with per-session: state, session id,
  directory/branch, model + provider, last-activity timestamp,
  message count and its delta, current PR if any.
- Classification must combine server signals (session status,
  message growth, active tool calls) with the watch-cron heuristics
  already proven in the id-train watches (10-minute checks, interrupt
  for turns hung on subagents, model switch on quota walls — never to
  antigravity-ls from session environments, where it is unreachable).
- Attention ordering: stopped-for-question and errored first, then
  needs-poke / stuck-retrying / stalled-on-CLI, then in-motion.
  Every non-in-motion entry carries the evidence for its state (the
  question text, the repeated error, the long-running call) so Muse
  can act without opening the session.
- GUI renders the same feed as a board sorted by attention (CCC's
  model), one row per session, state-colored, with the evidence
  inline.

### Relationship to existing pieces

- The id wave-2/wave-3 watch crons already approximate this in text
  reports for 5 sessions; this view generalizes them and gives the
  watches a shared state source instead of per-cron scraping.
- Pairs with the quota/throughput view design issue: state feed +
  quota feed together are what let Muse route work (start, poke,
  switch model, or leave alone) without asking Drew.

Design first: this issue wants a written design (state model,
classification rules per state, feed schema) in the stack design
record before implementation.


## Acceptance criteria

- A written design lands in the project-management stack design record: the six-state session taxonomy (in motion / stopped for a question / errored / needs poke / stalled on CLI / stuck retrying), the classification rule for each state, and the feed schema.
- The machine-first feed answers in one call for every live OpenCode session across the fleet's servers: state, session id, directory/branch, model + provider, last-activity timestamp, message count and delta, and current PR if any.
- Every non-in-motion entry carries its evidence inline (the pending question text, the repeated error, or the long-running call), ordered stopped-for-question and errored first.
- The GUI board renders the same feed, one row per session, sorted by that attention order — no separate GUI-only data path.
- A linked implementation issue (or a tracked item with a named next action) is filed when the design lands, so the design does not sit as finished work.

## Design issue — aggregator quota + throughput view

Parent context: the project-management stack design record
(`doc/2026-10-24T11-05-38Z_design_project-management-stack/`) and the
aggregator UI phase (session K, branch `pm/aggregator-ui`). Reference
design (concept only — FSL-1.1-MIT licensed, do NOT vendor its code):
https://github.com/amirfish1/claude-command-center (throughput page +
share card).

### What Drew asked for (2026-10-25)

A view into **all pooled quotas and their resets** plus **throughput**,
so that Muse can quickly answer "what's the quota status" for every
provider and effectively choose the best model/pool for the next piece
of work. A nice GUI should exist, but the priority is machine
analyzability: this view is primarily a data surface for Muse, with
the GUI as a presentation of the same data.

### Required content

Per provider/pool:
- Plan name and pool identity (e.g. OpenCode Go Personal vs Lab are
  separate pools; Antigravity has TWO independent pools — Gemini models
  and the Claude models it supports; Meta Model API is a token quota
  under the Muse Code High Usage subscription).
- Current usage for each window the provider exposes (5-hour, weekly,
  monthly as applicable), % used, and **reset timestamps**.
- State flag: healthy / near limit / walled, with the wall/reset time
  when walled.

Throughput:
- Sessions currently burning, attributed per provider + model.
- Rough token rate per provider (tokens/min over recent windows) and
  cumulative tokens per session — enough to answer "which providers
  are you using at roughly what rate".
- Historical burn per pool between resets, so headroom can be
  projected, not just observed.

Model-choice support:
- Given the fleet burn order (Anthropic pools first, then other plan
  providers, OpenAI last), surface which pool has headroom for a new
  session and which pools are about to reset with unused headroom
  (burn-it-before-reset rule) or are close enough to their limit that
  no second session should start on them.

### Data sources (routes established 2026-10-25)

- Codex/ChatGPT: GET chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/usage (OAuth).
- OpenCode Go: opencode.ai/zen/go/v1/usage per org.
- CommandCode: api.commandcode.ai/alpha/usage/summary.
- Cline: api.cline.bot/api/v1/users/me/plan/usage-limits.
- DeepSeek: API /user/balance.
- Cloudflare: GraphQL workersInvocationsAdaptive.
- Turso: `turso plan show`.
- Meta Model API: dev.meta.ai Usage page (team quota; key must be the
  team-attached `meta.api-key-funded` — the orphaned key 402s).
- Claude (Anthropic): console only, claude.ai/settings/usage.
- Antigravity: agy `/usage` panel (both pools).
- Open Design: open-design.ai/cloud/dashboard.
- GitHub: REST /users/{user}/settings/billing/usage/summary
  (needs `user` scope; comped minutes net to $0 and do not consume
  the plan).

### Acceptance shape

- One joined, queryable model (projector output / API) that Muse can
  read in one call and answer a full quota question from.
- GUI page rendering the same data (pools, windows, resets,
  throughput) — the CCC-style share card is a nice-to-have on top.
- No estimator for pools already shown in the OpenChamber quota
  picker; log picker values instead (standing rule, 2026-10-24).

Design first: this issue wants a written design (data model, refresh
cadence per source, wall detection) in the stack design record before
implementation.


## Acceptance criteria

- A written design lands in the project-management stack design record: the joined quota/throughput data model, a refresh cadence per data source, and the wall-detection rule per pool.
- The machine-first model answers a full quota question in one call: per pool — plan/pool identity, usage and % used for each exposed window, reset timestamps, and a healthy / near-limit / walled flag with the wall/reset time when walled.
- Throughput is attributed per provider + model: sessions currently burning, rough token rate per provider, cumulative tokens per session, and historical burn per pool between resets.
- Model-choice support is explicit in the output: which pool has headroom for a new session (fleet burn order respected, OpenAI last), which pools are about to reset with unused headroom, and which are too close to their limit for a second session.
- The GUI page renders the same data (pools, windows, resets, throughput); no estimator is built for pools already shown in the OpenChamber quota picker — picker values are logged instead.
- A linked implementation issue (or a tracked item with a named next action) is filed when the design lands, so the design does not sit as finished work.

1. **Renovate's own artifact update failed.** `gh pr checks 827` shows `renovate/artifacts — fail — Artifact file update failure`, and `treefmt check` FAILS (run 40155013405). The other checks pass, so the PR looks superficially healthy while its lockfile generation is incomplete.
2. **All three changed files are under `doc/`:** the beekem spike's `Cargo.toml`/`Cargo.lock` (`doc/2026-10-11T03-44-33Z_design_groups_events_delegation/spikes/beekem/`, rand 0.8.5 → 0.9.0) and a downloaded upstream snapshot (`doc/2026-10-11T11-08-42Z_design_remaining_work/research-round2/toolchain/dl/p2panda-p2panda-core/Cargo.toml`, rand 0.8.5 → 0.8.6). Editing the `dl/` snapshot makes it no longer a faithful copy of the upstream source it documents. One PR also groups two different updates (0.9.0 for the spike, 0.8.6 for the snapshot).

Note: the beekem 0.9 bump itself is not a compile break — `gen_range` (call sites in `spikes/beekem/src/concurrency.rs` and `costs.rs`) is deprecated since rand 0.9.0, not removed. The problem is the failed artifact generation, the red check, and the scope, not the spike code.

title: id(world-manifest): PR #801 — 'id world apply' prints 'applied N step(s)' for steps it explicitly did not apply, and diff/plan run against a fabricated seed=0 / empty-schedules state

body:
## Problem

PR #801's `id world apply` / `id world diff` (branch `id/phase-12`, `pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs`) reports success and drift computed from state it does not actually have:

### 1. "applied N step(s)" counts steps that were explicitly not applied

- `commands/world.rs:461-476` — the Apply handler runs `apply_steps(...)` and then unconditionally prints `applied {} step(s)` with `steps.len()` — the full plan length.
- `commands/world.rs:721-722, 765-772` — `apply_steps` handles `InstallModule`, `ScheduleAt`, and `CancelSchedule` by printing `note: {} is reported but not applied here` to stderr and doing nothing.

So a manifest whose plan is, say, one module install + two schedule steps finishes with "applied 3 step(s)" and exit 0 while changing nothing on the world except (at most) the grants/ceiling/profile steps also in the plan. A script or admin trusting stdout/exit code believes the world was reconciled when the headline steps were skipped.

### 2. `diff`/`plan` run against a fabricated partial state

- `commands/world.rs:688-717` — `current_world_state()` hardcodes `seed: 0` and `schedules: BTreeMap::new()` (its own comment: "Schedules and the install seed are not exposed over the wire yet, so they read as empty here").
- Consequences for every live `diff`/`apply`:
  - Any manifest declaring schedules always shows `ScheduleAt` drift, even if the world already has exactly those schedules — apply is never idempotent for schedules through the CLI path, and `diff` cries wolf on every run.
  - A manifest that changes the module without naming a `seed` plans the install with `seed: desired.seed.unwrap_or(current.seed)` = `0`, not the live world's seed — once module install is wired (#807), applying such a manifest would silently re-seed the program.

## Relation to existing tracking

#807 ("F12.1 apply wiring — module install + schedules reconciliation") tracks building the missing apply path, and its acceptance already asks for idempotent module+schedules apply. This issue is the narrower, independently fixable truthfulness problem that exists *today, before* that wiring lands — and the seed/state-fetch half will still matter after it lands. Fix whichever lands first and cross-reference the other; do not close this as a duplicate of #807 unless #807's change also makes the reporting and the fetched state truthful.

## Evidence

- PR #801 (OPEN, branch `id/phase-12`), commits `408e664c3a50`, `0616553c34cd`; file:line on the PR branch as fetched this run (`gh api .../contents/pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs?ref=id/phase-12`). Not on `main` yet — fix-before-merge.

## Acceptance

- `id world apply` reports applied and not-applied steps separately (count and kinds), and does not print an unqualified "applied N step(s)" / exit as full success when any planned step was skipped — or it refuses to run a plan containing unwired steps before changing anything.
- `id world diff` / `apply` either fetch the real seed and schedule state, or explicitly mark those sections "unknown — not compared" instead of planning against `seed: 0` / empty schedules.
- A test (unit or integration) covers a plan containing an `InstallModule` / `ScheduleAt` step and asserts the reported outcome distinguishes it from an applied step.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `id world apply` reports applied and not-applied steps separately (count and kinds), and does not print an unqualified "applied N step(s)" / exit as full success when any planned step was skipped — or it refuses to run a plan containing unwired steps before changing anything
- [ ] `id world diff` / `apply` either fetch the real seed and schedule state, or explicitly mark those sections "unknown — not compared" instead of planning against `seed: 0` / empty schedules
- [ ] A test (unit or integration) covers a plan containing an `InstallModule` / `ScheduleAt` step and asserts the reported outcome distinguishes it from an applied step

## Finding

P7.2 (Cloudflare Workers pkarr option: HTTP PUT/GET and DNS-over-HTTPS) is design-only. Implementation is deferred pending owner approval, and deployment requires owner account/network access. The deferral is recorded only in plan/brief prose; there is no standalone GitHub issue tracking the remaining implementation and deployment work.

## Evidence

- `doc/2026-10-11T11-08-42Z_design_remaining_work/plan-phases.md` §12 Phase 7, step P7.2: "Cloudflare Workers pkarr option: HTTP PUT and GET and DNS over HTTPS only (round 2). Design complete; implementation deferred". Tests column: "design note ... no implementation tests".
- `doc/2026-10-12T21-22-53Z_phase_7_connectivity/2026-10-12T21-22-53Z_phase_7_connectivity.md` P7.2 row: "design complete; implementation deferred ... no deployment/account access".

- `doc/2026-10-14T_platform_completion/acceptance-brief.md` line 74 (checked): "P7.2: write the Cloudflare Workers pkarr design ... Design is complete; deployment and implementation remain out of scope for P7.2."

## Why it matters

P7.2 is the designed path for pkarr (HTTP PUT/GET + DoH) behind a Cloudflare Worker. Until it is implemented and deployed it is paper only; the work can silently drop out of view because no issue carries it forward.

## What's needed

- Owner approval to implement, plus owner-provided Cloudflare account/zone for any real deployment.
- A follow-up decision on whether implementation is still wanted given later connectivity work (Phase 7 was "nothing here is needed for a first working system").

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An owner decision is recorded on this issue: implement P7.2, or descope it (the Phase 7 record notes nothing in Phase 7 is needed for a first working system).

- [ ] Deployment is verified against an owner-provided Cloudflare account/zone — OR deployment is explicitly deferred into a linked follow-up issue, so this one can close on implementation alone.

body:
## Finding (PR diff review, 2026-10-24)

Open PR #768 — `warm: keep-alive pools for design-code-proxy + clef-proxy (#480)` (head `d452f7527`) — changes credential-caching and connection behaviour in two proxies but adds **no tests** for the new behaviour. Its changed-file list is only `bin/clef-proxy.mjs` and `bin/design-code-proxy.mjs`; the body cites the pre-existing suites passing (11/11), which by construction cannot cover code that did not exist when they were written.

## Evidence

1. **clef-proxy credential cache (new, untested).** The diff adds `configFileCache` to `bin/clef-proxy.mjs`: `readConfigFileSync` now stats each Cloudflare config file and serves the cached contents unless `mtimeMs` changes, so a rotated token is picked up without a restart. Verified: neither `bin/clef-proxy.test.mjs` nor `bin/design-code-proxy.test.mjs` on main mentions the cache, `mtime`, `readConfigFile`, or `getCredentials` at all. The failure mode this introduces is silent and credential-shaped: if the mtime check ever misfires (rotation tooling that preserves mtime, e.g. `cp -p` / atomic replace with a pinned timestamp), the proxy keeps presenting the **old** Cloudflare token indefinitely with no error.
2. **design-code-proxy keep-alive + error teardown (new, untested).** The diff adds module-level `http.Agent`/`https.Agent` keep-alive pools (`maxSockets: 32`) to every backend/upstream dispatch, plus new `error` handlers on backend and upstream responses that fall back when headers are unsent and `destroy()` the client response otherwise. No test pins: socket reuse across sequential requests, fallback on a mid-stream backend error before headers, or teardown (not hang) after headers are sent. The PR body's socket-reuse evidence is a manual sandbox smoke (4 requests, 1 source port), not a regression test.

## Why it matters

Both changes sit on hot, failure-sensitive paths (Cloudflare credential presentation; streamed chat completions through pooled sockets). Without tests, a future refactor can silently revert the rotation pickup or reintroduce the half-open-socket stall the PR exists to fix — the same class of proxy bug this repo has already had to re-fix (see #684's design-code-proxy Content-Length regression, which was caught by a stub test).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A clef-proxy test pins the cache contract: a second request does not re-read an unchanged config file; a config file whose contents **and** mtime change is re-read (rotated token served on the next request); a missing file still yields the fallback.
- [ ] A design-code-proxy test (stub backend) pins: sequential requests reuse the keep-alive pool, and a backend response error before headers triggers the fallback path while one after headers tears the client response down instead of hanging.
- [ ] The new tests fail against the pre-#768 behaviour where applicable (ablation), and pass on the PR head; existing proxy suites stay green.

Part of the #480 warm-proxy set. Filed by the pr-diff-review job; this job files only.

body:
## Finding (PR diff review, 2026-10-24)

Merged PR #764 (pm-stack Phase 2, merge commit `15f4885f` on main) hard-codes one host's tailnet IP address into both new compose files, which breaks the stack's own documented move-hosts procedure.

## Evidence (verified on current main `3184df61`)

- `pm-stack/pad/compose.yml:22` — port binding `"100.99.113.103:7777:7777"`
- `pm-stack/grist/compose.yml:26` — port binding `"100.99.113.103:8484:8484"`
- `pm-stack/README.md:23-24` repeats `100.99.113.103` as the tailnet bind for both services.

That address is the current laptop host's (amd-6's) Tailscale IP. It is not a value any other host can be assumed to have.

This contradicts the stack's own contracts, added in the same PR:

- `pm-stack/pad/deploy.sh:16` and `pm-stack/grist/deploy.sh:16` — "Host specifics (the ONLY host-specific values)" are listed as `PM_STACK_SECRETS` and `SOPS_AGE_KEY_FILE`. The tailnet bind address is a third host-specific value, and it lives in neither.
- `pm-stack/README.md:278-281` — "**Move hosts:** copy this directory + `../secrets`, ensure the new host's age key is a SOPS recipient, run `./deploy.sh`, install the unit, done." On any host whose tailnet IP is not `100.99.113.103`, `docker compose up` fails to bind that address (or, worse, the address belongs to a different tailnet node), so the documented procedure fails at the compose step with no hint that a tracked file needs editing.
- Same pattern, lower stakes: `pm-stack/grist/compose.yml:30` hard-codes `GRIST_DEFAULT_EMAIL: drewrypope@gmail.com` as a tracked literal rather than a rendered env value.

## Why it matters

The pm-stack is explicitly designed to be host-portable (token-based tunnel, SOPS-rendered `.env`, "only one connector should run at a time"). A hard-coded host IP in version-controlled compose files is the kind of thing that only surfaces during a host migration — the worst time to discover it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The tailnet bind address for Pad and Grist comes from the rendered `.env` / an env variable (e.g. `PM_STACK_TAILNET_IP`) produced by `deploy.sh`, with the loopback-only binding as the safe default when it is unset.
- [ ] `pm-stack/README.md`'s Move hosts section and services table no longer assume the current host's address, and the deploy.sh "ONLY host-specific values" headers are true again.
- [ ] `GRIST_DEFAULT_EMAIL` is likewise rendered from configuration, or the hard-coding is explicitly documented as intentional.
- [ ] Verified: rendering/deploying with a different (or unset) tailnet IP produces compose bindings matching that value, and the current host's deployment is unchanged in behaviour.

Filed by the pr-diff-review job from PR #764's diff, verified against current main; this job files only.

## Finding (PR diff review, 2026-10-24)

Open draft PR #765 — `⚡ Bolt: ProseMirror widget recycling and search counting optimization` (Jules, head `b9cf7303c`, opened 2026-10-24T15:06:36Z) — duplicates work already on main, conflicts with the sanctioned salvage PR #778, and its body claims a change its diff does not contain. It should be closed as superseded, not merged.

## Evidence

1. **The claimed search-counting change is not in the diff.** The body says it "replaced an O(N) document traversal for counting search matches with an O(1) read from a precomputed set", but the PR touches only two files (`pkgs/id/web/src/cursors.ts` +49/-60, `pkgs/id/web/src/image-upload.ts` +1/-0) and the full 183-line diff contains no search code at all. (The search-counting theme is also the subject of many earlier closed Bolt PRs — #142, #232, #235, #252, #447, #521 — and of open triage issue #310.)
2. **The cursor work is already on main.** Current main (`3184df61`) already has lazy `() => HTMLElement` widget factories and stable state-derived keys in `pkgs/id/web/src/cursors.ts` — e.g. line 655 `key: cursor-own-${ownCursor.clientID}-${ownCursor.color}` is byte-identical to #765's proposed own-cursor key (landed via `09e3cc2b`, the same landing that made Jules PR #753 superseded in #760).
3. **Where #765 differs from main it is weaker.** Main's standalone cursor key (cursors.ts:747) is `cursor-${clientID}-${opacity}-${color}-${connectionState}-${encodeURIComponent(cursor.name)}`; #765's version drops the cursor **name**, the exact weaker-keys flaw #760 cited for not merging #753 (recycled DOM can go stale when only the name changes — cf. #331).
4. **Direct overlap with PR #778.** #765 adds `key: image-upload-${action.id}` to the placeholder `Decoration.widget` call in `pkgs/id/web/src/image-upload.ts`; #778 (the #760 salvage PR, open) adds `key: placeholder-${action.id}` to the same call. Both cannot merge cleanly, and #778 is the tracked salvage vehicle.

## Why it matters

Merging #765 would regress main's cursor keys (dropping `name`), conflict with #778, and deliver none of the search improvement its body advertises. Leaving it open invites exactly the duplicate-Jules pile-up #310 and #760 are trying to clear.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] PR #765 is closed as superseded, with a comment linking this issue, main's cursor landing (`09e3cc2b` / cursors.ts on main), and PR #778 for the image-upload key.
- [ ] No part of #765 is merged unless a specific hunk is shown to be absent from main and stronger than main's version — in which case it is salvaged via #778 or a successor, not by merging #765.
- [ ] The discrepancy between the PR body (search-counting claim) and its diff is noted on the PR so future Bolt runs are not credited with it.

Related: #310, #760, #778, #331. Filed by the pr-diff-review job; this job files only — a sweep does the closing.

body:
## Summary

`pkgs/id/web` detects 13 Shiki languages that can never be highlighted: `detectLanguage()` returns them, the test suite pins that it returns them, but the static grammar registry `LANG_IMPORTS` has no entry for them, so no grammar is ever loaded and the file renders as plain text (line numbers only).

## Evidence (verified on main `85f0bb5b`)

- `pkgs/id/web/src/highlight.ts:26` `EXT_TO_LANG`, `:106` `FILENAME_TO_LANG`, plus the dotfile branch return **54** distinct language IDs (set computed mechanically from the source).
- `pkgs/id/web/src/highlight.ts:185` `LANG_IMPORTS` registers only **41** of them.
- Missing from the registry: `bat`, `dotenv`, `erlang`, `gitignore`, `hcl`, `just`, `less`, `ocaml`, `properties`, `protobuf`, `sass`, `viml`, `zig`.
  - Concrete user-visible cases: `.bat`/`.cmd` scripts, `.sass`, `.less`, `.proto`, `.zig`, `.erl`, `.ml`, `.vim`, `.tf`, `justfile`, `.env`, `.editorconfig`, `.gitignore`/`.dockerignore`.
- The failure is silent and permanent: `ensureLanguage()` (`highlight.ts:258`) finds no import function, adds the language to `loadedLangs` "to avoid retries" (`:261-265`), after which the parser's fast path checks `cachedHighlighter.getLoadedLanguages()` (which never contains the language) and returns `[]` forever.
- `pkgs/id/web/src/highlight.test.ts` pins the detection half only (e.g. `.sass` → `sass`, `.proto` → `protobuf`, `.zig` → `zig`, `.gitignore` → `gitignore`, `.env` → `dotenv`, `.editorconfig` → `properties`); no test connects detection to the registry, which is how the two halves diverged.

## Grammar availability (installed `shiki` ^4.5.0, `node_modules/@shikijs/langs/dist/`)

12 of the 13 have a grammar module ready to import in the installed package: `bat.mjs`, `dotenv.mjs`, `erlang.mjs`, `hcl.mjs`, `just.mjs`, `less.mjs`, `ocaml.mjs`, `properties.mjs`, `protobuf.mjs`, `sass.mjs`, `viml.mjs`, `zig.mjs`.

`gitignore` is the exception: `@shikijs/langs` in shiki 4.5.0 ships no gitignore grammar (only `git-commit` / `git-rebase`), so `.gitignore` / `.dockerignore` need a separate decision (stop claiming the language in `detectLanguage`, or supply a small custom grammar).

## Why it matters

The editor advertises syntax highlighting for these file types — detection is deliberate and test-pinned — but users editing Terraform, Protobuf, Zig, Erlang, OCaml, Vimscript, Sass/Less, batch files, Justfiles, `.env` or `.editorconfig` files get unhighlighted plain text with no indication anything is wrong, and the "mark as loaded to avoid retries" path makes the gap invisible to any future retry/loading fix.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every language `detectLanguage()` can return either has a `LANG_IMPORTS` entry whose grammar exists in the installed `@shikijs/langs`, or is explicitly removed/documented as intentionally unhighlighted (the `gitignore` decision).
- [ ] A regression test fails if the detected-language set and the registered-grammar set diverge again (the two sets are compared mechanically, not by a hand-maintained list).
- [ ] Files for the 12 available grammars actually highlight end-to-end through `createSyntaxHighlightPlugin` (decorations produced after the async load), not just detect.

title: id(web): world keyboard encoder drops or silently degrades modified special keys — Alt+Backspace sends plain Backspace, Alt+Arrow is dropped to the browser

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: meta/enriched

body:
## Summary

`terminalBytesForKey` in `pkgs/id/web/src/world-keyboard.ts` handles modified special keys inconsistently: some are silently dropped, and the rest are silently degraded to the *unmodified* key — so a world application receives a plain Backspace / Enter / Delete that the user never pressed, while other modified keys vanish entirely.

## Evidence (verified on main `5db60876`)

The special-key branch (`world-keyboard.ts:36-40`):

```ts
if (event.key in specialKeys) {
  if ((event.ctrlKey || event.altKey || event.shiftKey) && event.key.startsWith("Arrow")) return null;
  if (event.shiftKey && event.key === "Tab") return null;
  return new TextEncoder().encode(specialKeys[event.key]);
}
```

Only modified arrows and Shift-Tab are rejected; every other modifier combination falls through to the plain sequence. A temporary vitest probe driving the real function (removed after the run) produced:

| Input | Result | Plain-key result |
|---|---|---|
| Alt+Backspace | `\x7f` | `\x7f` (identical) |
| Ctrl+Backspace | `\x7f` | `\x7f` (identical) |
| Alt+Enter | `\r` | `\r` (identical) |
| Alt+Tab | `\t` | `\t` (identical) |
| Alt+Escape | `\x1b` | `\x1b` (identical) |
| Ctrl+Delete | `\x1b[3~` | `\x1b[3~` (identical) |
| Alt+Delete | `\x1b[3~` | `\x1b[3~` (identical) |
| Ctrl+Home | `\x1b[H` | `\x1b[H` (identical) |
| Shift+End | `\x1b[F` | `\x1b[F` (identical) |
| Alt+PageUp | `\x1b[5~` | `\x1b[5~` (identical) |
| Alt+ArrowUp | `null` (dropped) | `\x1b[A` |
| Alt+ArrowLeft | `null` (dropped) | `\x1b[D` |
| Shift+Tab | `null` (dropped) | `\t` |

Contrast with printable keys in the same function: Alt+`x` correctly returns `\x1bx` — the Alt modifier *is* preserved (as an ESC prefix) for printable input, just not for special keys.

## Why it matters

- **Wrong input delivered:** Alt+Backspace is word-delete in most editing contexts; the world app instead receives a single-character Backspace. Ctrl+Delete, Alt+Enter, Shift+End etc. all lose their modifier the same way. The caller in `pkgs/id/web/src/world.ts` (keydown handler, ~line 240) calls `preventDefault()` whenever bytes are returned, so the browser's own handling is suppressed and the degraded byte sequence is the *only* thing that happens.
- **Dropped input leaks to the browser:** when the function returns `null`, the caller does not `preventDefault()`. Alt+ArrowLeft / Alt+ArrowRight are browser history navigation in several browsers, so a user trying to send a modified arrow to the world can instead navigate away from the world page mid-session.
- **The decoder's design says nothing should be dropped or misreported:** the receiving side, `Key.parse` in `pkgs/id/examples/roc-world/Key.roc`, has no modified-key variants, but it deliberately surfaces unrecognised escape sequences as `Unknown(bytes)` ("nothing is dropped") — e.g. its own test pins `Key.parse("\u(1b)[1;5C") == [Unknown("\u(1b)[1;5C")]` for Ctrl+Right. The web encoder is the side that breaks that contract, in two opposite ways at once.

## Suggested directions (one consistent policy)

Pick one and apply it to *all* special keys, not just arrows/Tab:

1. **Encode the modifier** using the standard xterm modifier parameter (`;2`=Shift, `;3`=Alt, `;5`=Ctrl, …) for CSI sequences (`\x1b[3;5~` Ctrl+Delete, `\x1b[1;3A` Alt+Up, `\x1b[Z` for Shift-Tab) and the ESC-prefix convention the function already uses for Alt+printable where a CSI form doesn't exist (ESC+`\x7f` for Alt+Backspace). `Key.parse` will surface these as `Unknown` today — preserved, not misreported — and a later `Key` extension can name them.
2. **Or return `null` consistently** for every modified special key the Roc `Key` module cannot represent, so no modified press is ever silently rewritten as the plain key — and document that modified specials are unsupported (accepting that the browser keeps e.g. Alt+Left).

Option 1 matches the decoder's nothing-dropped contract; option 2 is the smaller change. Either is better than the current split.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] One documented policy covers every (special key × modifier) combination in `terminalBytesForKey`; no modified special returns the plain key's bytes, and the arrow/Shift-Tab special cases are no longer exceptions to a different rule.
- [ ] Regression tests in `world-keyboard.test.ts` pin the policy for at least: Alt+Backspace, Ctrl+Delete, Alt+Enter, Shift+Home/End, Alt+PageUp, Alt+Arrow, Shift+Tab — and the existing plain and Alt+printable expectations still pass.
- [ ] If option 1 is chosen, the emitted sequences are the standard xterm forms, and the `Key.roc` behaviour for them (currently `Unknown`) is noted in the PR.
- [ ] Unmodified special keys, control letters, and AltGr (Ctrl+Alt printable) behaviour are unchanged.

body:
## Finding

No PR check evaluates any NixOS host configuration, so a host definition that fails at evaluation merges green and is only discovered at `just switch` time on the machine itself. This already happened:

- PR #699 (commit `7beeff8b`) added `nixos/hosts/amd-krdp.nix` with `systemd.user.services.app-org.kde.krdpserver` unquoted. Unquoted, the dotted name parses as nested attrsets, and the value violates the systemd leaf-value type.
- PR #699's checks were all green — verified via its commit's check-runs: `run` success, `Nix flake evaluation` success, `treefmt check` success.
- PR #701's body records the first switch attempt on amd failing during evaluation:

  ```
  error: A definition for option `home-manager.users.user.systemd.user.services.app-org.kde.krdpserver' is not of type `boolean or signed integer or string or absolute path or list of (...)'
  ```

  PR #701 (commit `bfe44fe6`) fixed it by quoting the name — a second PR and a failed switch for a one-character-class bug that any host evaluation in CI would have caught pre-merge. PR #699's own body even claimed a targeted eval had verified the service, so the manual eval is demonstrably not a reliable net here.

## Evidence (current main `f7dfea35`)

- `.github/workflows/nix-ci.yml:60-70` — the `flake-check` job named "Nix flake evaluation" (the PR gate that passed on #699/#701) runs exactly three evals, none of them a host:

  ```
  nix eval .#devShells.x86_64-linux.default.drvPath
  nix eval .#packages.x86_64-linux.mcpx.drvPath
  nix eval .#apps.x86_64-linux.format-check.program
  ```

  (Verified two ways: local clone `git show origin/main:.github/workflows/nix-ci.yml` and `gh api repos/developing-today/code/contents/.github/workflows/nix-ci.yml` — lines 68-70 agree.)
- A grep of `.github/workflows/` for `nixosConfigurations` finds exactly one hit: `jules-daily-flake-sync.yml:71`, which evaluates `.#nixosConfigurations.nixos.config.system.build.toplevel.drvPath` (the Intel host, not amd) inside a scheduled Jules prompt — not a PR gate.
- Prior instance of the same discovery pattern: #158 (closed) — "amd host fails at evaluation" — was also found manually, not by CI.

Single-repo: the NixOS hosts (`nixos/hosts/`, `amd`, `nixos`) live only in this repo; dezren39/nix has no `nixos/` host tree and no equivalent workflow.

## Why it matters

The hosts are Drew's actual machines. An evaluation error that reaches main surfaces at the worst possible moment — mid-switch on the laptop — instead of on the PR that introduced it. Host modules are edited regularly (KRdp is one example), and the type system only protects them if something actually forces the evaluation.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A PR check evaluates at least `.#nixosConfigurations.amd.config.system.build.toplevel.drvPath` (and ideally the `nixos` host's too) — evaluating the drvPath only, no build — or an equivalently deep forced evaluation of the hosts' home-manager/systemd options.
- [ ] The check demonstrably fails on PR #699's original tree (i.e. with PR #701's quoting reverted) and passes on current main.
- [ ] The check is bounded so it does not blow up PR CI time (drvPath-only eval, a timeout, and/or path filtering to host-affecting changes are all acceptable ways to achieve this — the failure-on-#699 demonstration is the requirement, not the mechanism).

body:
## Finding

PR #693 (merged, commit `ed0a71ecc29befe03d4960926fb8ffcaf349d05e`, merge `b286aaaafb09375f685f4cd6fb43dbc85e1aa8b8`) added `turn.failed` handling to `bin/codex-proxy.mjs`, but only one of the three error shapes its own parser accepts is tested — and the shape with no usable message produces a self-contradictory error detail on current main.

The parser at `bin/codex-proxy.mjs:374-378` accepts three shapes:

```js
if (event.type === 'turn.failed') {
  const msg = typeof event.error === 'string'
    ? event.error
    : (event.error && typeof event.error.message === 'string' ? event.error.message : '');
  turnFailedMessage = msg;
}
```

1. `error: {message: "..."}` — tested (stub modes `INBANDFAIL` / `INBANDPARTIAL` in `bin/codex-proxy.test.mjs`).
2. `error: "..."` (a bare string) — **no test**. The stub never emits this shape.
3. `error` missing, `null`, or `{}` with no string `message` — **no test**, and this shape is broken in its detail (below).

## Evidence — reproduced on current main (`b286aaa`, = `gh api commits/main`)

Using a stub `codex` at `$HOME/.local/bin/codex` (the same resolution the test suite uses) emitting `turn.failed` + exit 0 with no stderr:

- String shape: `{"type":"turn.failed","error":"stub string error"}` → `500 {"error":{"message":"Codex execution failed: stub string error"}}` — works, but is unpinned.
- No-error shape: `{"type":"turn.failed"}` → `500 {"error":{"message":"Codex execution failed: codex exec exited with code 0"}}`
- Empty-object shape: `{"type":"turn.failed","error":{}}` → same: `Codex execution failed: codex exec exited with code 0`

The last two fall through at `bin/codex-proxy.mjs:434`:

```js
const detail = (turnFailedMessage || stderrLine || fallback).trim();
```

where `fallback` (lines 429-433) was written for the exit-code path and, for an in-band failure on an exit-0 run, reads `` `codex exec exited with code ${code}` `` with `code === 0`. The client is told the run failed *because it exited with code 0* — the same class of misleading fallback #676 fixed for the signal case (`code null`, pinned by the test asserting the detail does not match `/code (null|-2)\b/`), reintroduced for the new in-band path. Whether real `codex exec --json` ever emits a message-less `turn.failed` is beside the point: the parser explicitly handles that shape (it maps it to `''` rather than ignoring the event), so the detail it produces should be coherent.

Single-repo: `bin/codex-proxy.mjs` / `turnFailedMessage` exist only in this repo (git-grep clean in the developing-today/opencode, developing-today/openchamber and dezren39/nix clones).

## Why it matters

- The string and message-less shapes can regress silently (e.g. a parser refactor dropping the `typeof event.error === 'string'` branch) with the whole suite green, because no stub emits them.
- When the message-less shape does occur, the only diagnostic a client/operator gets actively misstates the cause, sending debugging toward the exit path that actually succeeded.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Add stub modes + tests (both stream and non-stream, via the existing `assertFailure` helper) for `turn.failed` with `error` as a bare string, pinning the string as the error detail.
- [ ] Add stub modes + tests for `turn.failed` with no usable error message (`error` absent and/or `{}`), no stderr, exit 0.
- [ ] For the message-less in-band case, the error detail no longer claims the run "exited with code 0" (e.g. a generic `codex turn failed` detail when the failure came from `turn.failed` and the exit code is 0); the detail for genuine non-zero exits is unchanged.
- [ ] Ablation: reverting only the parser's string branch, or only the new fallback, makes exactly the corresponding new tests fail.
- [ ] Full suite: `node --test bin/*.test.mjs` passes.

body:
## Finding

PR #691 fixed both halves of #690 in `bin/clef-proxy.mjs`, but only the client-body half got a regression test. The upstream half — a non-JSON or `null`/scalar gateway response is reported as an upstream failure preserving the upstream status instead of throwing into a 500 — has no test that can fail if it regresses, and as written it cannot be tested at all: the gateway URL is hardcoded, so no stub upstream can be injected.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/691 (merged 2026-10-23T21:39:55Z, merge commit `8e05af24341b321779851bc824177b14cfd57b9f`, commit `02183adb78c00e20fab4bebb2e7100a6f4e58bcc`, fixes #690, now CLOSED)
- Upstream guard on current main `8e05af24` (`bin/clef-proxy.mjs:157-165`, blob `b61de077` cross-checked via `gh api`): `cfData` starts `null`, `await cfRes.json()` is in its own `try {} catch {}`, and the success check is `cfRes.ok && cfData?.success && cfData.result?.answers`; the failure branch answers `cfRes.status >= 400 ? cfRes.status : 502`.
- The new test file's own header says the upstream is out of scope (`bin/clef-proxy.test.mjs:4-6`): "The proxy forwards valid requests to the Cloudflare AI gateway, which these tests never reach: they cover the paths that answer locally". Its four subtests are health 200, invalid JSON 400, non-object JSON 400, missing token 401 — none reaches the fetch. Verified this run (pr-diff-review): `node --test bin/clef-proxy.test.mjs` passes 5/5 on current main, and reverting only the upstream guard (unguarded `cfRes.json()` / `cfData.success`) would fail none of them.
- The gateway base is not overridable (`bin/clef-proxy.mjs:141`): `const cfUrl = \`https://gateway.ai.cloudflare.com/v1/${accountId}/${gatewayId}/workers-ai/run/${model}\``. Account, gateway and token all come from env/config (`getCredentials`, :56-73), but the host does not, so a test cannot point the proxy at a local stub gateway without a code change first.
- #690's acceptance criteria required tests only for the local paths (health / invalid JSON 400 / missing token 401), so the issue closed with the upstream behaviour — two of its own acceptance bullets — unpinned. Same pattern as #688 (the untested streaming half of PR #685's design-code-proxy fix).

## Why it matters

The upstream guard is the half that fires exactly when Cloudflare is misbehaving — an HTML 502/429 page or a malformed gateway body is when clients most need the real upstream status instead of a misleading JSON-parse 500. Today the code is correct; what is missing is the pin that keeps it correct, and the hardcoded gateway host means a future contributor cannot add that pin without first refactoring the URL construction.

Single-repo: `clef-proxy` and the `gateway.ai.cloudflare.com` URL exist only in this repo (git grep across the local clones of developing-today/opencode, developing-today/openchamber and dezren39/nix finds neither).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The gateway base URL is overridable for tests (e.g. an env var such as `CLEF_PROXY_GATEWAY_BASE_URL` / `CLOUDFLARE_GATEWAY_BASE_URL` defaulting to `https://gateway.ai.cloudflare.com/v1`), or an equivalent fetch/stub injection exists; production behaviour with the override unset is byte-identical.
- [ ] New tests in `bin/clef-proxy.test.mjs` run the proxy against a stub gateway and cover at least: a non-JSON upstream body with an error status (client gets that status / 502 upstream failure, not a JSON-parse 500), and a `null` (or scalar) upstream JSON body (no throw on `cfData.success`, reported as an upstream failure).
- [ ] Ablation: with the upstream guard reverted (unguarded `await cfRes.json()` and `cfData.success`), the new tests fail; with the guard in place, the full clef-proxy suite passes (`node --test bin/clef-proxy.test.mjs`).

title: agy-proxy: stream resume-retry judges 'no output' before flushing the final line — an unterminated partial delta is silently retried as a fresh conversation (PR #679)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: meta/enriched

body:
## Finding

PR #679 (fixes #678, head `f935ce0e`) judges a failed resume's "no output" condition inconsistently between the two modes of `bin/agy-proxy.mjs`, because the stream close handler checks `hasOutput` **before** flushing the final unterminated line, while the non-stream handler parses the whole stdout buffer before its retry gate:

- Stream (`bin/agy-proxy.mjs` on PR head): `child.on('close', (code, signal) => …)` runs the resume-retry check first — `if (code !== 0 && !hasOutput && allowRetry && targetConvId)` at :471 — and only afterwards flushes the tail line (`if (lineBuffer.trim()) { processJsonLine(lineBuffer.trim()); }` at :479-481) and the new exit-code failure check (:489). A `step_update` text delta that arrives as the child's final stdout bytes **without a trailing newline** is still sitting in `lineBuffer` at the retry decision, so `hasOutput` is `false` even though the run produced output.
- Non-stream (same file, PR head): `stdoutBuffer` is fully parsed into `responseText` before the `if (code !== 0)` block (:580), and the retry inside it is gated on `!responseText` — so the same run shape is correctly treated as "produced output": no retry, HTTP 502.

Consequence in stream mode: a resumed conversation whose run emits a partial delta in an unterminated final line and then exits non-zero is silently retried as a **fresh conversation**, and the client receives the fresh run's answer with `finish_reason: "stop"` and the resumed conversation's id — the failure is never reported, the partial output is discarded, and a second `agy` run executes even though the retry's own precondition ("failed without output", #678's acceptance criteria) does not hold. Whether the failure is reported or silently swapped for a fresh-conversation answer depends only on whether `agy` newline-terminated its last JSON line. The sibling proxies flush first: `bin/muse-proxy.mjs` and `bin/codex-proxy.mjs` both process a non-empty `lineBuffer` as the first step of their `close` handlers before judging the run.

Note the success path already relies on the flush at :479-481 to deliver an unterminated final line, so unterminated tails are a shape this file explicitly handles — just not at the retry decision.

## Evidence (reproduced on PR #679 head `f935ce0e1a5e4a2caf1880ee4f1badeec1638865`)

Ran the PR-head `bin/agy-proxy.mjs` with a stub `agy` at `$HOME/.local/bin/agy` (the proxy's own binary resolution; the `bin/agy-proxy.test.mjs` pattern from the PR), requests carrying `x-conversation-id: conv-123`:

- Stub, on `--conversation`: emits `{"event":"step_update","step_update":{"text_delta":"partial answer"}}` with **no trailing newline** (non-stream shape: `{"response":"partial answer"}` likewise unterminated), prints `stub agy: run failed midway` to stderr, exits 3; a fresh (no-conversation) run succeeds with `Hello world`:
  - stream → **200**, fresh run's `Hello world` chunk + `finish_reason: "stop"` + `[DONE]`; proxy log shows exactly 1 `retrying as fresh conversation` line — no error event, partial output never sent
  - non-stream → **502** `{"error":"agy process exited with non-zero code","code":3,"stderr":"stub agy: run failed midway"}` (correct — the control)
- Control, same stub but the partial line **is** newline-terminated:
  - stream → `partial answer` chunk, then `data:`-framed `agy execution failed: stub agy: run failed midway` error event + `[DONE]`, no `stop` chunk (the PR's intended new behaviour)
  - non-stream → **502**, same as above

So the two modes disagree on identical run shapes, and stream mode disagrees with itself based on a trailing newline. PR #679's new tests cover the resume-retry case only with no output at all (`RETRYME`) and the partial-output case only without a conversation (`FAILPARTIAL`, newline-terminated) — the resume + unterminated-partial shape is untested. This is filed against the PR as a follow-up; fixing it inside PR #679 before merge also satisfies this issue.

Dedup: issue searches for `agy-proxy` return only #678 (OPEN, the exit-code masking this PR fixes — its acceptance requires the retry be preserved for a failed resume with **no output**, which is exactly the precondition misjudged here) and unrelated port/discovery issues; searches for `lineBuffer` / `unterminated` / `resume retry` return only #678. Cross-repo: `bin/agy-proxy.mjs` exists only in this repo (no copy in developing-today/opencode, developing-today/openchamber, dezren39/nix — verified by `git grep` on each clone's `origin/main`).

## Why it matters

The retry exists to recover from a stale conversation id, not to replace a run that already answered in part. Triggering it on a run that produced output hides a real failure (expired auth, CLI crash) behind an unrelated fresh conversation's answer, presented under the resumed conversation's id as a clean `stop` — the same silent-substitution failure mode #678 was filed for, reachable only in stream mode (the mode OpenCode actually consumes) and only when the final line is unterminated.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The stream close handler flushes any non-empty `lineBuffer` (via `processJsonLine`) **before** the resume-retry decision, so `hasOutput` reflects all output the child produced — mirroring the non-stream ordering in the same file and the flush-first ordering in `bin/muse-proxy.mjs` / `bin/codex-proxy.mjs`.
- [ ] A failed resume (non-zero exit or signal) whose only output is an unterminated final `step_update` delta is reported as a failure in stream mode — `data:`-framed error event naming the failure + `data: [DONE]`, no chunk claiming `finish_reason: "stop"`, no fresh-conversation retry — matching the non-stream 502 for the same shape.
- [ ] A failed resume with genuinely no output still retries once as a fresh conversation in both modes (the existing `RETRYME` behaviour), and successful runs with an unterminated final line still deliver that line before the `stop` chunk.
- [ ] A new stub case in `bin/agy-proxy.test.mjs` pins the resume + unterminated-partial + non-zero-exit shape in stream mode (and the non-stream control); ablating the flush-reorder fails exactly that case, and the `agy-proxy` + `muse-proxy` + `codex-proxy` + `proxy-port` suites pass.

title: lab-ops-hub: container validator returns the raw U-label host for IDN targets — Worker returns the punycode A-label form it judged

body:
## Problem

The container validator (`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py`, `validate_crawl_url`) judges a non-ASCII host in its IDNA-encoded form — it even builds the A-labels at app.py:286-292 (`"xn--" + label.encode("punycode")`) for the RFC 1035 length check — but it never substitutes those A-labels into the URL it returns. The returned URL keeps the raw U-label host. The Worker validator (`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/src/lib.ts`) returns the WHATWG-canonical punycode host (`u.hostname`), so for **every** internationalized host the two validators certify different URLs for the same input.

## Evidence (verified 2026-10-23, both validators run on current main f1a8abf0)

| Input | Container returns | Worker returns |
|---|---|---|
| `http://café.com/` | `http://café.com/` | `http://xn--caf-dma.com/` |
| `http://münchen.de/path` | `http://münchen.de/path` | `http://xn--mnchen-3ya.de/path` |
| `http://bücher.example/` | `http://bücher.example/` | `http://xn--bcher-kva.example/` |
| `http://😀.com/` | `http://😀.com/` | `http://xn--e28h.com/` |

Repro: call `validate_crawl_url("http://café.com/")` in `container/app.py` and `validateCrawlUrl("http://café.com/")` in `src/lib.ts` and compare the returned URLs.

## Why it matters

The returned URL is the artifact the rest of the system stores, logs, dedupes on, and fetches. Two validators that are supposed to be interchangeable implementations of one policy disagree on the canonical form of every IDN target: the same crawl submitted through the container and through the Worker produces different stored URLs (breaking dedupe/comparison), and the container's form depends on the fetcher re-encoding the host at fetch time instead of the validator returning the wire form it actually judged. This is the same class of returned-URL divergence as #652 (UTS-46 ignored codepoints in the returned host), but it covers all non-ASCII labels, not just the ignored-codepoint subset — #652's fix alone would not close it.

## Acceptance criteria

- For any accepted non-ASCII host, the container validator returns the URL with the host in A-label (punycode) form, matching the Worker byte-for-byte (including the DNS root dot handling from #647 and UTS-46 mapping/ignored-codepoint deletion from #526/#652).
- ASCII hosts, IPv4/IPv6 literals, ports, userinfo, and path/query/fragment handling are unchanged.
- New tests in `pkgs/lab-ops-hub/test/test_container_validate.py` pin the returned A-label form for at least: a Latin-1 IDN (`café.com`), a multi-label IDN (`bücher.example`), and an astral-plane label (`😀.com` → `xn--e28h.com`); a Python↔TS differential over IDN spellings shows no remaining returned-host differences.

body:
## Finding

PR #599 (merged as `e9851e85`, fixes #598) gives `scripts/update-nixpkgs-inputs.py` a non-zero exit when any input update fails, and restricts the `scripts/update-nixpkgs-inputs.sh` wrapper's `python3` fallback to cannot-execute exits (126/127) so a genuine failure is never re-run end-to-end. The behavior is correct on current `main` — but nothing in the repo pins it: the PR's verification was a one-off manual stub-`nix` run in a scratch directory, and no automated test covers either script.

## Evidence

- `scripts/update-nixpkgs-inputs.py` on `main` (`e9851e85`): the exit tally at the end of `main()` sums `status == "failed"` results and calls `sys.exit(1)`.
- `scripts/update-nixpkgs-inputs.sh` on `main`: fallback only on 126/127, propagates the final status.
- `scripts/tests/` exists and covers the neighbouring scripts (`test_research_workflow.py`, `test_research_workflow_items.py`, `test_sync_research_workflow.py`) — there is no test file for `update-nixpkgs-inputs` in either form.
- PR #599's body documents the verification as manual: a stub `nix` plus a minimal `flake.lock` in a scratch dir, run once pre/post fix. None of that harness was committed.

## Why it matters

#598 was a silent-failure bug: failed updates exited 0, so `&&` chains, CI and cron proceeded as if inputs were updated. The fix's whole value is an exit-code contract across two files (the tally in the `.py`, the 126/127-only fallback in the `.sh`). A future refactor of either — e.g. "simplifying" the wrapper back to `|| python3 ...`, or restructuring the summary code — reintroduces the silent failure or the double full re-run with no test to catch it.

## Acceptance criteria

- A test under `scripts/tests/` (following the existing tests' style) runs the real `.py` against a stub `nix` and a minimal `flake.lock` with one NixOS/nixpkgs input and asserts: failing update → exit 1 with the `Failed:` summary still printed; succeeding update → exit 0.
- The same harness runs the `.sh` wrapper and asserts: a genuine update failure exits 1 with exactly one `nix` invocation (no double run); a cannot-execute first attempt (126/127) falls back to `python3` and propagates its result.
- The tests run in the repo's existing scripts-test path (same command that runs the other `scripts/tests` files).

title: lab-ops-hub: PR #584's A-label check still accepts decoded labels that are not valid UTS-46 labels — mapped/compatibility characters, IDNA-disallowed symbols, leading combining marks

body:
## Summary

PR #584 (fixes #580, commit `24566d9f`, merged as `22a4b98f`) added `_judge_a_label` to the container crawl validator (`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py:325`, called from `validate_crawl_url` at :213) so an `xn--` (A-label) host is judged by its punycode-decoded label. It checks: the label decodes, is non-empty/non-ASCII, re-encodes to exactly the same punycode (:351), carries no character in the validator's enumerated forbidden set, contains no unassigned (Cn) or format (Cf) codepoint, and passes `decoded.encode("idna")` (:383).

That still does not hold the decoded label to the UTS-46 validity the Worker's WHATWG parser applies, so whole classes of A-label spellings are certified by the container as ordinary public DNS names while the Worker's `validateCrawlUrl` (`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/src/lib.ts`) refuses them outright (`new URL` throws):

1. **Decoded labels that are not the canonical (mapped) form of anything.** UTS-46 processing maps uppercase, fullwidth and compatibility characters before punycode; a decoded label still containing one was never the encoding of a valid U-label. Examples: a decoded label containing `À` (maps to `à`), `²` (NFKC → `2`), U+FF0F `／` (NFKC → `/`, a host delimiter), U+3002 `。` (a label separator), or U+2000 (NFKC → space). The container's own raw-form path refuses or transforms every one of these (the mapped-delimiter re-check and the forbidden-character check in `validate_crawl_url`); the A-label path bypasses them because mapping was applied to the ASCII spelling, before decoding.
2. **IDNA-disallowed characters the stdlib IDNA-2003 codec passes.** Symbols and punctuation that IDNA2008/UTS-46 mark DISALLOWED (e.g. U+00A8 `¨`, U+00B4 `´`, U+037E, currency/math symbols) encode happily with `decoded.encode("idna")`, so the :383 check does not catch them.
3. **Labels beginning with a combining mark.** UTS-46/IDNA requires a label not to start with a non-spacing mark; `"\u0301abcé".encode("idna")` succeeds, so an A-label decoding to such a label passes.

## Evidence (verified 2026-10-22 on current main `22a4b98f`, the merge commit of PR #584 itself)

Headline cases — Python `validate_crawl_url` imported from `container/app.py` at main, TS `validateCrawlUrl` imported from `src/lib.ts` under Bun (the same differential method as #583):

| URL (A-label host) | Decoded label | Container | Worker |
|---|---|---|---|
| `http://xn--abc-dma09x.com/` | `\u0301abcé` (starts with combining acute) | **accepts** | refuses — `url is not a valid URL` |
| `http://xn--mnchende-65a9941j.com/` | `münchen。de` (contains U+3002) | **accepts** | refuses |
| `http://xn--ab-cja0631x.com/` | `a／bé` (contains U+FF0F) | **accepts** | refuses |
| `http://xn--mnchen-3ya5364d.com/` | `mün\u2000chen` (contains U+2000) | **accepts** | refuses |
| `http://xn--example-yoa.com/` | `exÀample` (uppercase in decoded label) | **accepts** | refuses |
| `http://xn--example-rla.com/` | `ex²ample` (compatibility digit) | **accepts** | refuses |
| `http://xn--mnchen-3ya.de/`, `http://xn--bcher-kva.de/`, `http://xn--fsq.com/` | `münchen`, `bücher`, `例` (controls, PR #584's own accepted set) | accepts | accepts |

Differential battery: 13,040 A-label hosts — every codepoint U+0080–U+32FF inserted into `ex<cp>ample` and punycode-encoded, plus labels beginning with U+0300–U+036F — run through both real validators: **2,449 divergences, all container-accepts / Worker-refuses** (by category of the inserted codepoint: Lu 866, So 512, Lo 355, No 155, Lm 140, Mn 139 incl. 112 leading-mark labels, Ll 94, Zs 14, plus smaller Po/Nl/Lt/Sk/Sm/Nd/Sc/Ps/Pe/Pd pockets). One smaller reverse pocket exists: **41 container-refuses / Worker-accepts**, all codepoints this Python's `unicodedata` 15.0.0 still classes Cn that Bun's newer Unicode has assigned — a Unicode-version skew in PR #584's new Cn check, noted here so the fix does not bake the skew in deeper.

Root cause: the canonical check at :351 compares raw punycode only (`decoded.encode("punycode") != body`) — punycode round-trips *any* string, valid U-label or not — and the validity check at :383 is the stdlib IDNA-2003 codec, which applies neither UTS-46 mapping/canonical-form verification nor the IDNA2008 disallowed/leading-mark rules. PR #584's battery (25 A-label hosts) only exercised the Arabic-Indic, malformed-punycode and ordinary-IDN classes it set out to fix, so the residual classes were untested.

Relation to existing issues: #583 tracks the same *kind* of gap for **raw-form** hosts (unassigned + bidi classes; its battery and acceptance corpus are raw spellings, and a raw-form fix that never decodes A-labels leaves this issue's spellings untouched). PR #584 already treated the A-label form of #583's bidi/unassigned classes as this validator's separate A-label work; this issue is the remaining A-label residue after that fix. Coordinate with #583 — one shared UTS-46 validity helper applied to the decoded label would close both. #531 is the opposite direction (raw-form over-refusal) and is unaffected.

## Why it matters

Same shape as #502/#507/#516/#574/#580: the two validators that are supposed to hold the same crawl-target policy (#441 defence in depth — the container is the component that actually fetches, re-validating independently) disagree on thousands of spellings. The container certifies a non-name as a public DNS name; the failure then surfaces deep inside the fetcher/resolver as a crawl failure instead of the validator's up-front refusal, and behaviour depends on which crawler runs.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validate_crawl_url` refuses an A-label whose decoded label is not a valid UTS-46 label: decoded form differs from its UTS-46 mapped/NFC form, contains an IDNA-disallowed codepoint, or begins with a combining mark — with the same accept/refuse verdict as the Worker's `validateCrawlUrl` on a differential battery over A-label hosts (the 13,040-host probe above, or an equivalent committed corpus).
- PR #584's pinned behaviour is unchanged: the Arabic-Indic A-label spellings and malformed A-labels stay refused; its accepted controls (`xn--mnchen-3ya`, `xn--bcher-kva`, `xn--fsq`, the Devanagari-digit A-label) stay accepted.
- New tests in `pkgs/lab-ops-hub/test/test_container_validate.py` pin the headline cases above (leading combining mark, U+3002/U+FF0F/U+2000 in decoded label, uppercase decoded label — refused; ordinary IDN A-labels — accepted).
- The 41-case reverse pocket is either closed (Cn judged against a Unicode version at least as new as the Worker's runtime) or explicitly documented as a known version-skew over-refusal.
- No regression in the existing Python or TS suites.

Single-repo: `validate_crawl_url` / `_judge_a_label` exist only in `developing-today/code` (the lab-ops-hub validator has no copy in opencode / openchamber / nix). Not an mcpx set.

body:
## Finding

PR #582 adds `.agents/skills/feature-plan/scripts/plan_check.py`, the mechanical gate the rewritten feature-plan skill runs before the fresh-context validator (SKILL.md step 11; `references/validation.md` §1: "Fix everything it prints before launching the validator"). Its `parse()` stores steps in a dict keyed by step number with no duplicate guard:

```python
# .agents/skills/feature-plan/scripts/plan_check.py:37 (PR #582 head d6d5c7a17e39d606ad7f1f73c7ac63afdbe8ca68)
steps[step] = {"wave": wave, "parallel": bool(found[2]), "text": ""}
```

A second step with the same number silently overwrites the first, so the overwritten step is never checked at all — and two same-numbered steps in one wave defeat the same-wave file-collision check, because both steps collapse into one dict entry.

## Evidence

Reproduced against PR #582's head (`d6d5c7a1`) with a plan containing two complete steps, both numbered `1`, both in Wave 1, both writing ``scripts/shared.py``:

```text
$ python3 -I .agents/skills/feature-plan/scripts/plan_check.py plan.md
ok: 1 steps in 1 waves        (exit 0)
```

Expected: a duplicate-step-number diagnostic (exit 1), and/or `wave 1: scripts/shared.py written by steps 1, 1`. Instead the checker reports one step and `ok`. A cross-wave variant (step `1` in Wave 1 and again in Wave 2) likewise produces no duplicate diagnostic — the Wave 1 step simply disappears from every check (fields, requires, files).

Step numbers are load-bearing in this format, which is why the silent overwrite matters:

- `references/plan-outline.md` §4 (PR #582): "Numbering. One sequence across the whole plan… Once issues exist, numbers never change."
- `references/issues.md` §1 (PR #582): implement-issue markers carry the step number (`"step":"3"`), and `blockedBy` links are built from `Requires:` step numbers — a duplicated number makes two steps indistinguishable downstream.
- `references/validation.md` §1 lists the file-collision and missing-field checks as what `plan_check.py` guarantees before the validator runs; both are void for an overwritten step.

## Why it matters

`plan_check.py` is the only mechanical check in the S7 flow; everything after it (validator, zero-context readers, issue creation) trusts its `ok`. A plan author who renumbers or copy-pastes a step — the exact accident a mechanical checker exists to catch — gets a green `ok` while one step escapes every field, wave and file-collision check, and two colliding writers can be scheduled into the same wave.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `plan_check.py` exits 1 and prints a clear diagnostic (e.g. `step 1: duplicate step number`) when a plan reuses a step number, in the same wave or across waves.
- [ ] The same-wave/same-file repro above no longer prints `ok`.
- [ ] A regression test or fixture covers duplicate step numbers (same-wave and cross-wave).
- [ ] Existing behaviour is unchanged for well-formed plans (the PR body's sample outputs still reproduce).

Found by the pr-diff-review sweep reviewing PR #582 (open, head `d6d5c7a17e39d606ad7f1f73c7ac63afdbe8ca68`). plan_check.py does not exist on `main` yet — this is a defect in the PR's new code, filed so it is not lost if the PR merges as-is.

body:
## Summary

The two lab-ops-hub crawlers disagree on redirect policy, so the same public URL can succeed via one crawler and fail via the other — and the Worker fallback (which exists to stand in when the container is unavailable) does not reproduce the container's behaviour.

## Evidence (verified 2026-10-22, on main `7a9ac873`)

**Redirect-count limit**
- Worker fallback: `fetchFollowingValidatedRedirects` defaults to `maxRedirects = 5` (`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/src/lib.ts:204`, error at lib.ts:216-218).
- Container: `_ValidatingRedirectHandler` (`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py:389-396`) subclasses urllib's `HTTPRedirectHandler` and inherits its defaults: `max_redirections = 10`, `max_repeats = 4`.

**Redirect status codes**
- Worker fallback follows *any* 3xx response that carries a `Location` header (lib.ts: `res.status >= 300 && res.status < 400`).
- urllib's handler only treats 301, 302, 303, 307 and 308 as redirects; any other 3xx raises `HTTPError`, which the container's `do_POST` surfaces as a 502.

**Reproduction (both sides run this run)**
- A 7-hop chain of 302s between public URLs, ending in 200:
  - Worker fallback (real `fetchFollowingValidatedRedirects` under `bun test` with a scripted fetcher): `Error: too many redirects (more than 5)`.
  - Container redirect handler (urllib opener against a local server): `200`.
- A single 300 Multiple Choices response with a `Location` pointing at a public 200 page:
  - Worker fallback: follows it, returns `200`.
  - Container: `HTTPError 300` → `/crawl` returns 502.

## Why it matters

`/api/crawl` tries the container first and silently falls back to the Worker on any container error (src/index.ts `crawlWithContainer` / catch → `crawlFallback`), recording only `source` in the result. Redirect-heavy public pages (shorteners, AMP/print chains, locale negotiation) therefore crawl or fail depending on which backend happened to serve the request, and a 6–10-hop page that the container handles fine hard-fails whenever the container is cold or down — exactly when the fallback is supposed to be equivalent. This is the same class of Worker/container divergence fixed for URL validation (#460, #474, #481, #500, #529, #567) and extraction (#569); redirect policy is the remaining unaligned piece.

## Acceptance criteria

- One redirect policy stated in one place both implementations follow: a single hop limit and a single set of followed status codes (suggested: align the Worker to the container's urllib semantics — 10 hops, codes 301/302/303/307/308 — or pick 5 deliberately and enforce it in the container handler too; either way the two must match, including a repeat/loop rule equivalent to urllib's `max_repeats`).
- The container handler sets its limits explicitly rather than relying on urllib defaults, so a Python/urllib default change cannot silently re-open the divergence.
- Tests on both sides pin the shared policy: a chain one hop over the limit fails identically, a chain at the limit succeeds identically, and a non-followed 3xx (e.g. 300/304 with `Location`) is handled identically (TS tests in `pkgs/lab-ops-hub/test/lib.test.ts`, Python tests alongside `test/test_container_validate.py` or a new container redirect test file).
- Per-hop SSRF re-validation of every redirect target is unchanged on both sides (#460).

body:
## Finding

Two open PRs are about to entrench opposite worker-branch namespaces. PR #566 unifies worker branch names on `research/<slug>/s<stage>-<unit>` *because that is the prefix the router's orphan-branch sweep searches*, and explicitly defers the remaining skills to PR #537 ("design-orchestrate, feature-plan and implementation-orchestrate are being rewritten in a separate PR and will follow the same name"). PR #537 — that separate PR — instead prescribes `wf/…` branches throughout its design-orchestrate rewrite, including its own orphan sweep over the `wf/` prefix. If both merge as-is, S6 worker branches are invisible to the router and the disagreement PR #566 set out to end survives for exactly the stages it deferred.

## Evidence

- PR #566 (open, commit `0f8a8d44`): changes concept-research, issue-handoff, notes-reconcile and `planning/workflow/vocabulary.md` to `research/<slug>/s2-c001`-style names; body: "which is what the router's orphan-branch sweep searches. … Not covered: design-orchestrate, feature-plan and implementation-orchestrate are being rewritten in a separate PR and will follow the same name."
- The router on current main: `.agents/skills/research-workflow/references/merge-and-restart.md:80` sweeps `refs/remotes/origin/research/<slug>/`; `references/worker-brief.md` gives worker branches as `research/<slug>/<stage>-<unit>`.
- PR #537 (open, commit `e4f29f74`), design-orchestrate rewrite:
  - `SKILL.md` step 1: bookkeeping branch `wf/<package-slug>/$CID-s6-books`
  - `references/dispatch.md` ("Names, branches and worktrees"): **Branch** `wf/<package-slug>/<item or step>-<stage>`, e.g. `wf/docs-pipeline/C001.3-s6`, `wf/docs-pipeline/C001-step-1.2.1-s8`
  - `references/dispatch.md` orphan sweep: `git for-each-ref … "refs/remotes/origin/wf/<package-slug>/"` — self-consistent within S6, but disjoint from the router's `research/<slug>/` sweep
  - `references/closeout.md`: `On wf/<package-slug>/$CID-s6-books…`; `references/merge.md` gate example: `wf/docs-pipeline/C001.3-s6`
- Post-#566 `vocabulary.md` will define a facet branch as `research/<slug>/s6-c002.3`, while PR #537's dispatch reference defines the same thing as `wf/docs-pipeline/C001.3-s6`.
- Both PRs' checks were green at review time (run / treefmt / workflow-contract 3.12+3.14 / Nix flake evaluation all SUCCESS on both), so nothing currently blocks the inconsistent pair from merging.

## Why it matters

The orphan sweep is a safety mechanism: it finds worker branches with commits and no PR so work is never lost (PR #537's own dispatch reference: "Never delete an orphan branch", restart-on-same-branch recovery). Branches created under a prefix nobody else sweeps silently defeat it at the router level, and two live namespaces recreate the exact three-way disagreement PR #566 documents as its motivation — with vocabulary.md then contradicting the S6 skill agents actually load.

## Acceptance criteria

- Before either PR merges (or as an immediate follow-up if they already have): design-orchestrate's `SKILL.md` and `references/` (dispatch, merge, closeout, decisions) use the unified `research/<slug>/s6-<unit>` worker-branch naming, and its orphan sweep scans `refs/remotes/origin/research/<package-slug>/`.
  - Or: an explicit, documented decision that orchestrator bookkeeping branches are a separate namespace **and** the router's sweep covers both prefixes — recorded in `planning/workflow/vocabulary.md` so the two PRs no longer contradict each other.
- The feature-plan (S7) and implementation-orchestrate (S8) rewrites in PR #537 land with the same naming, as PR #566's body promises.
- `grep` finds no remaining `wf/<` branch prescription in `.agents/skills/` or `planning/workflow/` outside historical records.
- `python3 -I scripts/research_workflow.py check --repo-root .` still reports ok.

title: wave-2 workflow: PR #488 notes-reconcile prescribes a deferred receipt disposition the tool rejects (resolve-note choices and check both allow only four)
