body:
## Finding

PR #488's deepened `notes-reconcile` skill prescribes a fifth note disposition, `deferred`, that the workflow tool does not accept anywhere — so a worker following the skill cannot complete step 5 for a deferred note.

- PR #488 (head 67c183fb), `.agents/skills/notes-reconcile/SKILL.md`: the frontmatter description (line 3) and step 4 (line 40) list five dispositions — `incorporated`, `acknowledged`, `declined`, `deferred`, `superseded` — and step 4 directs notes about files the receiver does not own to `acknowledged` or `deferred`.
- Its `references/receipts.md` ("The five dispositions", :5) defines `deferred` at :15 (with a mandatory `Revisit when: <event>` trigger in the reason) and repeats the unowned-file guidance at :19.
- The tool on current main (d20fe865), unchanged in this respect by PR #490: `scripts/research_workflow.py:1040` restricts `resolve-note --disposition` to `["incorporated", "acknowledged", "declined", "superseded"]`, and the receipt validation in `check` accepts only the same four (`scripts/research_workflow.py:826`).
- PR #489's `references/tool-fallbacks.md` covers the other not-yet-implemented commands these skills rely on (`lease`, `status --live`, `item`, `ids`, `render`, …) but has **no** fallback for a `deferred` disposition.

## Evidence (verified at PR #490 head 2b0cbbcb, which carries the current tool)

```text
$ python3 -I scripts/research_workflow.py resolve-note --package <pkg> --note x.md \
    --disposition deferred --target main.md --reason "test"
research_workflow.py resolve-note: error: argument --disposition: invalid choice: 'deferred'
(choose from 'incorporated', 'acknowledged', 'declined', 'superseded')   → exit 2
```

Hand-writing the receipt instead does not help: `check` fails it with `invalid receiver disposition/target/reason` (the :826 set). Yet PR #488 step 5's Done criterion is `check --package <pkg> --require-resolved` exits 0 — unreachable for any package with a note the skill says to defer.

## Why it matters

`deferred` is not an edge case in the skill's own design: it is the prescribed disposition for a valid note that must wait, and specifically for notes asking for changes in files the receiver does not own (another concept, `design.md`, `AGENTS.md`) — a routine S3 situation. A worker hitting it must either mislabel the receipt `acknowledged`/`declined` (losing the revisit trigger the receipts format requires, and misrecording the note's outcome in an immutable receipt) or stall. The pre-PR488 skill text mentioned "deferred" only in prose; PR #488 promotes it to a first-class, step-level disposition without the tool side landing.

## Acceptance criteria

- The skill and the tool name the same disposition set. Either:
  - the tool gains `deferred` end to end (`resolve-note` choices, the `check` validation set, `planning/workflow/records.md` if it enumerates dispositions, and tests), including the `Revisit when:` reason convention; or
  - the skill and `receipts.md` revert to the four tool-supported dispositions and express "valid but not now" through one of them (stating which, and where the revisit trigger is recorded instead).
- Every disposition named in the `notes-reconcile` skill can be written with `resolve-note` and then passes `check --require-resolved` (a test or fixture exercising each named disposition).
- If the tool route is chosen and cannot land with the skill, PR #489's `tool-fallbacks.md` gains an interim fallback entry for `deferred` so an S3 worker is never without a sanctioned path.

title: Warm-session proxies: hold CLI/language-server sessions open instead of spawning per request

labels.name: kind/performance
labels.description: Performance problem or optimization

labels.name: source/human
labels.description: Filed directly by a human

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/l
labels.description: Large: multi-day or open-ended; expect staged check-ins

labels.name: meta/enriched
labels.description: Intake review done: acceptance criteria, links, and normalized labels added

body:
Related: #479 adds `bin/muse-proxy.mjs`, the newest spawn-per-request proxy — this issue is its (and codex-proxy's) v2 design question.

## Problem: every proxy request pays a full cold start

The CLI-backed proxies in `bin/` (codex-proxy, and now muse-proxy) spawn a fresh CLI process per chat-completions request and flatten the entire message history into a single prompt. Measured on muse-proxy (2026-10-21):

- ~5–8 seconds of latency floor per request before model time — process spawn + runtime boot + agent/session setup dominates; generation is the tail.
- ~27k input tokens of CLI session context (system prompt, skills) are built and billed on **every** call, trivial prompts included.
- No context or prompt-cache continuity: request N+1 in a conversation re-sends and re-pays everything request N established.

Verified while filing: `bin/codex-proxy.mjs` contains no session handling at all — no `session`, `resume`, or `conversation` logic anywhere in the file; each request is an independent `codex exec`. muse-proxy is the same shape by design (it mirrors codex-proxy).

## Existing proof of concept in this repo

`bin/antigravity-ls-proxy.mjs` does **not** spawn per request: it attaches to a long-running language-server process (managed LS ports) and multiplexes requests over that warm process. That shape works in production here today. The CLI proxies are the odd ones out.

## Avenues

### (a) Muse — hold a warm `muse serve` host

The Muse CLI ships `muse serve` ("Serve an MSP session host over stdio") and `muse schema` (exports the MSP wire schema, JSON Schema or TypeScript). A v2 muse-proxy could:

- Spawn `muse serve` once and keep it warm for the proxy's lifetime.
- Open real sessions on the host per conversation, so session state, context, and any server-side caching persist across requests in that conversation.
- Translate OpenAI chat-completions ⇄ MSP using the exported schema rather than scraping `exec --json` output.

Unknowns to resolve in the spike: MSP session lifecycle (create/resume/close), concurrency model (one in-flight turn per session?), and whether prompt caching actually engages across turns on the plan allowance.

### (b) Codex — key resumable exec sessions by conversation ID

The Muse's exec sessions are resumable. codex-proxy could:

- Accept/derive a conversation key (client-supplied session/conversation id, falling back to a hash of the system prompt + first message) and map it to a CLI session id.
- Resume that session for follow-up requests, sending only the new turn instead of the flattened full transcript, so prompt cache and context carry over.

Unknowns: exact resume semantics of the installed CLI version, whether resumed sessions preserve cached prefixes measurably (check usage output across two turns), and session id storage/cleanup.

## Trade-offs to design around

- **Statefulness**: the proxy becomes a session owner. Restarts drop warm sessions; clients must tolerate a cold fallback (re-flatten and start fresh) as a normal path, not an error.
- **Serialization**: a warm session likely handles one in-flight turn at a time → per-conversation request queues, plus a small pool of warm sessions for concurrent conversations, with sane caps.
- **Hygiene**: a session's cwd and accumulated context bleed across requests if keying is sloppy. Conversation keys must be strict (never share a warm session across different clients/projects by accident), and idle sessions need a TTL + eviction.
- **Observability**: keep reporting real per-run usage (the CLIs already emit it) and add warm/cold markers so the win is measurable, not assumed.

## Spike acceptance criteria

- [x] Warm per-request latency measured against the ~8s cold baseline on the same prompt set (report both, same machine, same models).
- [x] Cache/context continuity demonstrated across two requests in one conversation: the second request answers a follow-up that requires the first turn's context **without** the client re-sending history, and/or usage numbers show the reused/cached input share.
- [x] Two concurrent conversations stay isolated (no cross-talk of context) and a third waits or cold-starts per the pool policy.
- [x] Killing the warm host/session mid-conversation degrades to a successful cold request, not a client-visible error.
- [x] No regression in the OpenAI-compatible surface (`/v1/models`, streaming + non-streaming chat completions) for either proxy the spike touches.

title: PR #327's ProseMirror widget keys omit cursor colour and name, so recycled cursor DOM goes stale

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

body:
## Finding

Open draft PR #327 (⚡ Bolt: Optimize ProseMirror decoration recycling, head `59decd10f6`) removes the `decorationGeneration` counter in `pkgs/id/web/src/cursors.ts` and gives the collaborative-cursor widgets stable, state-derived keys — but two of the new keys omit properties that are rendered into the widget DOM, so ProseMirror will keep showing the old DOM after those properties change.

ProseMirror compares a widget decoration's `key` instead of its DOM node to decide whether it needs to be redrawn (ProseMirror reference: widget spec `key` — "When comparing decorations of this type (in order to decide whether it needs to be redrawn), ProseMirror will by default compare the widget DOM node by identity. If you pass a key, that key will be compared instead"). A property that changes without changing the key therefore never reaches the screen.

## Evidence (PR #327 head, cross-checked via `gh api contents?ref=59decd10f6`)

- Standalone remote cursor, `cursors.ts:738` on the PR head:
  `key: cursor-${cursor.clientID}-o${cursor.opacity}-c${connectionState}`
  — includes opacity and connection state, but **not `cursor.color` and not `cursor.name`**. The widget it keys is built by `createStandaloneCursor` / `createCursorLine` (same file): caret `borderColor = cursor.color`, label `backgroundColor = cursor.color`, label text colour derived from `cursor.color`, and label `textContent = cursor.name`.
- Cluster/merged cursor lines, `cursors.ts:715` on the PR head:
  `key: cursor-cluster-${group.position}-${clusterKey}-c${group.mostRecentColor}`
  — the merged bar appended to the leftmost line renders one segment per cursor with that cursor's `color` (background), `name` (text), `opacity` and connection-state-driven strobe state (`createMergedBar`), and non-leftmost group lines render their first cursor's opacity/strobe state (`createCursorLine`); none of those per-cursor values are in the key (`clusterKey` encodes only `clientID@head` per cursor, and `mostRecentColor` is only the owning group's first cursor's colour).
- Contrast inside the same diff: the own-cursor key (`cursors.ts:651`) correctly includes its only rendered variable property, `ownCursor.color`. Contrast across the sibling drafts tracked by #310: PR #217's standalone key includes `-color-${cursor.color}`, its cluster key includes connection state plus an opacity hash, and its selection key includes colour — #327 drops colour from the standalone and selection keys.
- Colour/name are not session constants in this code: the plugin's `apply()` "update" case replaces `color` on every cursor update and takes `name` from the update when present (`name = cursorUpdate.name ?? existing?.name`), and `createCursorDecorations` falls back to `getColorForClient(clientID)` only when an update carries no colour — so a peer's colour source/value and display name can both change mid-session. While a peer is active their opacity stays at 1.0 (see `getOpacityForAge` in `cursor-utils.ts`: 1.0 for the first 30s after each update, and every update refreshes `lastUpdate`), so no other key component forces a redraw either.

## Why it matters

If #327 (or a variant with the same keys) merges as-is, a collaborator who changes colour or display name — or whose first updates arrive colourless and later carry an explicit colour — keeps rendering with the stale caret colour and stale name label for everyone else, indefinitely while they stay active. That is a correctness regression introduced specifically by removing the generation counter, in the one file the PR touches. The PR's own added learning note (`.jules/bolt.md`) states the rule it breaks: properties that dynamically dictate the widget's appearance (it names opacity, connectionState and colour) must be included in the key.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Whichever ProseMirror-recycling PR survives the #310 triage, every widget key in `cursors.ts` covers all properties rendered into that widget's DOM: standalone cursor keys include colour and name; cluster keys include the per-cursor segment values (colour, name, opacity) and connection state, not just the group's most-recent colour.
- [ ] The selection decoration's colour handling is checked the same way (PR #327's `selection-…-o${opacity}` key omits `cursor.color`, which is half of its rendered `background-color: ${cursor.color}${selectionOpacity}` style).
- [ ] A test or equivalent check pins the key construction: changing only a cursor's colour (or only its name) produces a different standalone key. There is currently no `cursors.test.ts` (only `cursor-utils.test.ts`), so the key derivation may need extracting to a pure helper to be testable.

Found by the pr-diff-review job reviewing PR #327 (open) in developing-today/code. Cross-repo check: `createCursorDecorations` / `collab-cursor` exist only in developing-today/code (GitHub code search), so this is a single-repo issue. Related triage: #310.

body:
## Problem

`dezren39/nix` vendors a copy of `pkgs/mcpx` because it has no cheap way to take mcpx from this repo. That copy has drifted: 29 files differ today, and each side holds fixes the other lacks (see dezren39/nix, the issue that removes the copy). This repo is the primary source for mcpx, so the vendored copy should go. First there has to be a way to consume mcpx from here.

## What exists

- The root flake already exposes `packages.<system>.mcpx` and `apps.<system>.mcpx` (`lib/default.nix`, `make-root-apps`), built with a plain `callPackage ../pkgs/mcpx/package.nix { }`.
- `overlays.mcpx` and `overlays.default` also provide `pkgs.mcpx` (`make-mcpx-overlay`).
- `pkgs/id` has its own flake, which is a precedent for a package that downstream users take without the rest of the repo.

## What is missing

Adding this repo as a flake input pulls the whole input graph (clan, disko and the NixOS inputs) into the darwin flake's lock file. I have not measured how large that gets, only that the root flake has far more inputs than mcpx needs.

Other points a consumer hits:

- `package.nix` takes `bun-bin ? bun`. The darwin flake passes its own `pkgs/bun-bin`.
- The package is built with `buildGo127Module`, so the consumer's nixpkgs needs it.
- The darwin build fails its own check phase on takeover tests that only work on Linux. That is the existing issue #237, and it blocks this one on aarch64-darwin.

## Options

1. A small `pkgs/mcpx/flake.nix` whose only input is nixpkgs, consumed as `github:developing-today/code?dir=pkgs/mcpx`.
2. Consume the root flake and use `follows` to keep the lock small.
3. Consume `overlays.mcpx` from the root flake.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] One option is chosen and the reason is written down here.
- [ ] `dezren39/nix` can build mcpx from a pinned rev of this repo on aarch64-darwin with no vendored source.
- [ ] The consumer can override `bun-bin` or the package pins the one it needs.
- [ ] CI here builds the package on a darwin runner, or the issue says why it does not.

title: CI caching: cache Go build cache by go.sum hash and reuse artifacts between legs

labels.name: kind/ci
labels.description: CI/CD pipelines, workflows, and build automation

labels.name: source/human
labels.description: Filed directly by a human

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: area/ci
labels.description: CI/CD pipelines, workflows, and build automation (area)

labels.name: effort/m
labels.description: Medium: expected under 1 day of work

labels.name: meta/enriched
labels.description: Intake review done: acceptance criteria, links, and normalized labels added

labels.name: design/ci-program
labels.description: Design: ci-program - all issues of this effort carry it

body:
Caching in the mcpx workflows is thinner than it should be:

- setup-go caches module downloads, but nothing caches the Go build cache (~/.cache/go-build), so the test leg recompiles packages from cold on most runs.
- The nix build leg (while it exists) starts from an empty store every run — no cachix and no magic-nix-cache anywhere in the repo.
- Artifacts produced by one leg are never reused by another; each workflow re-does setup (checkout + four toolchain installs) from scratch.

Proposal: add actions/cache for the Go build cache and module cache keyed on go.sum hashes (with restore-keys fallbacks), and share build artifacts between legs via actions/upload-artifact + download-artifact where a second leg currently recomputes them. Cache keys must be content hashes (go.sum / bun.lock), never branch names. If the nix-in-GHA replacement lands first, scope this to whatever legs remain.

Acceptance: cache hit rate visible in run logs; mcpx workflow wall time down measurably on repeat runs with unchanged go.sum.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The mcpx workflows cache the Go build cache and module cache with keys derived from content hashes (go.sum / bun.lock) and restore-keys fallbacks — never branch names.
- [ ] Run logs show cache hits on repeat runs with unchanged go.sum, and mcpx workflow wall time is measurably lower on those runs than on cold runs.
- [ ] Where a second leg currently recomputes a first leg's output, the artifact is shared via upload/download-artifact instead.
- [ ] If the nix-in-GHA replacement has landed by the time this is worked, the caching is scoped to the legs that remain.

body:
This repo has three Jules workflows: jules.yml, jules-daily-codebase-ideation.yml (cron 06:00 UTC) and jules-daily-flake-sync.yml (cron 05:00 UTC). Each carries its own triggers, pins and setup, and fixes (like the jules-action @v1 pin) have to be applied file by file and repo by repo.

Consolidate into a single jules.yml: one on: block with both cron schedules, jobs gated on github.event.schedule, plus the existing workflow_dispatch and event-driven jobs. Honest expectation: per-run cost today is ~6 seconds, so the minute savings are small — the win is one file to pin, audit and fix, and one place where Jules quota (free tier: 15 tasks/day, 3 concurrent) is managed.

Acceptance: one Jules workflow file remains; both daily jobs still run at their current times; dispatch inputs preserved.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Exactly one Jules workflow file remains (`jules.yml`); `jules-daily-codebase-ideation.yml` and `jules-daily-flake-sync.yml` are removed.
- [ ] Both daily jobs still run at their current times (05:00 and 06:00 UTC), gated on `github.event.schedule`.
- [ ] Existing `workflow_dispatch` inputs and event-driven jobs are preserved.
- [ ] The jules-action pin and Jules quota management live in exactly one place.

# pm-stack(aggregator): dnsSectionFromRegisterJson accepts impossible renewal dates (regex-only) and negative prices — the Markdown parser and isDnsSection in the same file refuse both

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe at main 5c53272ff)

`pm-stack/aggregator/src/dns.ts`:

- `:135` — the register.json parser gates `next_renewal` with only a format regex:
  `if (typeof renewal !== "string" || !/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/.test(renewal)) return null;`
  No `isIsoDate` re-check of the calendar components.
- `:57` (approx, `parseDnsRegister`) — the Markdown parser in the same file does it correctly, with the reason spelled out in its comment: an impossible calendar date (2026-02-30, 2026-13-01) "must be refused like a malformed row, or it string-sorts into the register, counts toward the annual total, and poisons nextRenewal / renewingSoon (#2199). isIsoDate re-checks the components, so leap dates (2024-02-29) still parse."
- `:161+` (`isDnsSection`, the shared gate) checks entry `renewal` only as `typeof string`, so a section built from an impossible date passes the gate too.
- `:136` — `renewal_price_usd` is gated finite-only, while `isDnsSection` (#4226) requires a present price and the total to be non-negative; the JSON parser can therefore build a section its own shared gate refuses.

Laptop bun probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-03-laneA-dns/probe.ts`, importing `dnsSectionFromRegisterJson` / `isDnsSection` / `summarizeDns` from main):

- `next_renewal: "2026-02-30"` → section ACCEPTED, `isDnsSection=true`, `summarizeDns(...).nextRenewal = "2026-02-30"`
- `"2026-04-31"` → ACCEPTED, `isDnsSection=true`, nextRenewal `2026-04-31`
- `"2026-13-01"` → ACCEPTED, `isDnsSection=true`, nextRenewal `2026-13-01`
- Controls `"2024-02-29"` (leap) and `"2026-03-15"` → ACCEPTED (correct)
- Two rows priced `20` and `-5` → section ACCEPTED with `totalAnnualListUsd=15`, prices `[20, -5]`, but `isDnsSection=false`

Production path: `pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/collect-fleet-feed.ts:697+` treats register.json as authoritative — when `dnsSectionFromRegisterJson` returns a section the collector marks the dns section "ok" and serves it; the Markdown fallback (which refuses these rows) runs only when the JSON parse returns null.

## Why it matters

register.json is the authoritative source for the DNS register (#902 slice 2). One impossible renewal date in it silently becomes the register's "next renewal", is rendered verbatim on /dns, and distorts `renewingSoon` (string comparisons in `summarizeDns`, dns.ts:242-248), exactly the poisoning #2199 fixed for the Markdown path. A negative list price produces a section that the shared `isDnsSection` gate refuses downstream, so the collector and the live source disagree about the same data.

## Acceptance criteria

- `dnsSectionFromRegisterJson` returns null for a row whose `next_renewal` is not a real calendar date (2026-02-30, 2026-04-31, 2026-13-01), mirroring `parseDnsRegister`'s `isIsoDate` rule; leap dates (2024-02-29) still parse.
- `dnsSectionFromRegisterJson` returns null for a negative `renewal_price_usd` (zero allowed), mirroring the #4226 non-negative rule in `isDnsSection`.
- New tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/slice3.test.ts` (or a dns test file) cover the refused shapes plus valid controls; every section the JSON parser returns satisfies `isDnsSection`.
- Aggregator bun test suite and typecheck pass.

# pm-stack(aggregator): sanitizeSaasServices accepts inverted/negative PAYG estimates and negative metric values — records derived from them are refused by isSnapshotRecord

## Evidence

The feed-boundary gate for SaaS services in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/feed.ts` checks only finiteness, never range or ordering:

- `isUsageMetric` (feed.ts:606, :611-615): `used`, `limit`, and `percent` need only `isFiniteNumber` — negative values pass.
- `isPaygEstimate` (feed.ts:622, :625-626): `low` and `high` need only `isFiniteNumber` — an inverted pair (`low > high`) and negative endpoints pass.
- `isSaasService` (feed.ts:632, :652, :659): `billedUsd` and `cadenceDays` likewise need only `isFiniteNumber` — negatives pass.

Sibling gates in the same codebase refuse exactly these shapes: `isSnapshotRecord` (`src/snapshots.ts:344`) requires a non-negative `limit` (`isNonNegative`), refuses negative `pct` values, and its estimate-pair branch (:358) requires `p.low <= p.high`. The producer-side extractors were fixed for the same class in #4942 / #2508, but this downstream sanitizer — the boundary that is supposed to drop malformed rows at feed read (#2451) — was not.

Verified with a laptop bun probe at main `d99399c1fde06102c6a8b8f53931e6ef99c59085` (probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-03-laneA-saas/probe.ts` on the laptop, importing `sanitizeSaasServices` / `recordsFromSaasServices` / `isSnapshotRecord` from the primary tree):

- Valid control service: kept (dropped=0). Garbage control (`high: "x"`): dropped.
- `paygEstimate {low:100, high:50}`: **kept**; `countedEstimate` (model.ts:1188, 1.2 × high) = 60 — a counted figure below the estimate's own low.
- `paygEstimate {low:-10, high:-50}`: **kept**; `countedEstimate` = -60, rendered verbatim by render.ts:2307/:2536 as a negative PAYG estimate.
- Metric `used=-500`, `limit=-100`, `percent=-20`, plus service `billedUsd=-99` and `cadenceDays=-30`: **all kept**.
- Round-trip loss: `recordsFromSaasServices` (snapshot-records.ts:105-115) turns the kept inverted estimate into a snapshot record `{low:100, high:50}`, and `isSnapshotRecord` returns **false** for it — so a service the feed accepts produces snapshot history that is silently dropped on readback.

## Why it matters

`sanitizeSaasServices` is the trust boundary for feed-supplied SaaS data: anything it keeps is rendered as measured usage/PAYG money (render.ts metric rows and PAYG cards, derive.ts:895-901 attention flags via `countedEstimate`) and converted into snapshot records. Inverted/negative estimates and negative usage/limits therefore display nonsense money, suppress or distort the payg-unbilled attention flag (counted is compared against the $5 bubble threshold), and create snapshot records the snapshot store itself refuses — silent history loss instead of a quarantined row at the boundary.

## Acceptance criteria

- `isPaygEstimate` rejects inverted pairs (`low > high`) and negative endpoints, mirroring the `isSnapshotRecord` pair rule in snapshots.ts.
- `isUsageMetric` rejects negative `used`, `limit`, and `percent` values (null/undefined allowances unchanged).
- `isSaasService` rejects negative `billedUsd` (when present and non-null) and negative `cadenceDays`.
- A service failing any of these is dropped by `sanitizeSaasServices` (counted in `dropped`), while valid services — including zero values and a `low === high` estimate — still pass.
- New tests cover each refused shape plus the valid controls; the aggregator bun test suite and typecheck pass.

body:
# id(publications): Registry::load restores records publish() would refuse — duplicates, empty worlds, non-canonical shadow paths

## Summary

`Registry::publish` (pkgs/id/src/publications.rs:195) enforces the registry's invariants: non-empty world name (:200), canonical mount path via `canonicalize_mount_path` (:204), one publication per placement (:207), and the #2147 shadow-acknowledgement gate (:216). `Registry::load` (:297) enforces none of them — it is a bare `serde_json::from_str`, so a persisted `publications.json` that is syntactically valid but semantically invalid is restored verbatim at boot.

That breaks the module's own stated contract: the module doc (publications.rs:40-49) and the boot call site (pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs, the #2147 slice-1 comment) both say a registry that cannot be honoured must fail loudly rather than silently restore the wrong set. Today only *unparseable* JSON fails; parseable-but-invalid records sail through.

## Verified behaviour (laptop probe, main 464467b7d)

Probe crate `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-03-laneB-pubload` (path-dep on pkgs/id, `Registry` public API only):

- Control — `publish()` refuses all three: empty world name, non-canonical path `//world`, duplicate placement `/arena`.
- A hand-written `publications.json` containing exactly those violations (duplicate `/arena` mounts for worlds a+b, an empty-world mount, an unacknowledged `//world` mount, an unacknowledged `/api/` trailing-slash mount) loads with `Ok` and restores all 5 records.
- `boot_warnings(KNOWN_EXPLORER_ROUTES)` on the loaded registry returns 2 warnings, and the one for the `//world` mount names the **wrong route**: `shadows()` (publications.rs:151) compares the raw stored string, so `//world` fails to match the `/world` route it denotes and instead matches route `/` via the `"//"` prefix — the warning claims the mount shadows `/`. The #2147 duty is to warn loudly *naming the shadowed route*; a non-canonical spelling makes the warning name a route the mount does not denote (and any future route-matching at apply time faces the same raw-string mismatch).
- `unpublish` canonicalises its argument (publications.rs:239), so a stored `/api/` record can never be removed by naming `/api` — the lookup compares canonical `/api` against stored `/api/` and reports "nothing published at path /api" (probe: `unpublish(/api)` against the loaded registry errors).

## Why it matters

- Slice 1 is the persisted half of #2147; later slices apply this set to live listeners. Duplicate placements will collide at bind time, an empty world name will fail (or worse, mis-target) at apply time, and an unacknowledged shadow mount that spells its path non-canonically overrides an Explorer route with no warning anywhere — exactly the failure #2147's binding rule exists to prevent.
- The file is operator-editable JSON by design (it lives in the store directory / `ID_PUBLICATIONS_FILE`); "only publish() writes it" is not a safe assumption for a persistence format, and the module doc already promises fail-loud behaviour for a file that cannot be read as a valid registry.

## Acceptance criteria

- `Registry::load` validates the parsed set against the same invariants `publish()` enforces: every world name non-empty, every path-mount path already canonical (or canonicalised on load with the change surfaced), no duplicate placements, and duplicate/invalid records produce an error naming the file — matching the existing malformed-JSON behaviour.
- Boot warnings fire for every unacknowledged persisted mount that shadows an Explorer route and name the route actually shadowed, for any spelling of the mount path.
- A stored record can always be removed by `unpublish` naming its placement in canonical form.
- Tests: load-rejection (or load-canonicalisation) cases for duplicate placement, empty world, and non-canonical path alongside the existing `save_load_round_trips_and_missing_file_is_empty` test; a boot-warning case for a non-canonical shadow spelling.
- Related: #2147 (slice 1 introduced the registry, PR #5114); #2898 (the reconstruction-is-admission design theme this is a concrete instance of).

# aggregator: isItemHistoryCutoff accepts impossible/non-ISO cutoffAt (and any string as coverage.fetchedAt)

## Evidence

`pm-stack/aggregator/src/item-history.ts:144` — the structural gate for stored item-history cutoff lines:

```ts
if (typeof c.cutoffAt !== "string" || Number.isNaN(Date.parse(c.cutoffAt))) return false;
```

`Date.parse` is lenient: impossible calendar dates roll over (`2026-02-30` → Mar 2) and non-ISO strings parse in a timezone-dependent way. The sibling gates in this codebase use the real-calendar rule instead — `isIsoDate` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/validate.ts:116`, via `parseIsoDate`), e.g. `snapshots.ts:328` ("Real calendar dates only (#2264/#2483): Date.parse rolls…") and the gates fixed in #5091/#5140/#5154.

`coverage.fetchedAt` is weaker still — `item-history.ts:147` checks only `typeof coverage.fetchedAt === "string"`, with no parse at all.

Verified with a laptop bun probe at main `298f35f75b4a62e71666810f9a972138a088fb55` (probe `/tmp/probe-ih.ts` on the laptop, importing `isItemHistoryCutoff` / `blockerFirstObserved` from the primary tree):

- `isItemHistoryCutoff` returns `true` for `cutoffAt` = `2026-02-30T00:00:00Z`, `2026-04-31T00:00:00Z`, `"March 2, 2026"`, and `"03/02/2026"`; control `"not-a-date"` → `false`, valid ISO → `true`.
- `coverage.fetchedAt` = `"not-a-date"` and `"2026-02-30T00:00:00Z"` both pass the gate.
- Downstream effect: `blockerFirstObserved` over cutoffs `2026-02-30` → `2026-03-10` reports `firstObservedAt: "2026-02-30T00:00:00Z"` verbatim with `lowerBoundAgeDays: 8` — the age is computed from the rolled-over Mar 2 instant, for a date that does not exist.

## Why it matters

`ItemHistoryStore.readAll()` (`item-history.ts:198-215`) trusts this gate for every line of `item-history.jsonl`, then sorts by `cutoffAt.localeCompare` (a non-ISO stamp like `"March 2, 2026"` sorts lexicographically, not chronologically) and feeds `weeklyTransitions`, `weeklyCompletions`, and `blockerFirstObserved`, whose ages are `Date.parse` differences (line 321). One corrupt or hand-edited cutoff line with an impossible/non-ISO stamp is therefore silently accepted and shifts blocker-age and weekly-flow numbers instead of being quarantined like other invalid stored records in this codebase.

## Acceptance criteria

- `isItemHistoryCutoff` rejects a `cutoffAt` that is not a real ISO calendar date/time (gate with `isIsoDate` from `validate.ts`, consistent with the sibling gates), including `2026-02-30`, `2026-04-31`, `"March 2, 2026"`, and `"03/02/2026"`.
- `coverage.fetchedAt` is validated to the same standard (not typeof-only).
- Valid ISO cutoffs captured by `captureItemHistory` still pass the gate (existing round-trip test at `test/item-history.test.ts:88` stays green).
- New tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/item-history.test.ts` cover the refused stamps above for both fields plus the valid control.
- Aggregator test suite and typecheck pass.

title: pm-stack(aggregator): validateStreamEvent accepts impossible calendar dates — Date.parse rolls 2026-02-30 over to March 2 instead of refusing it

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/pm-stack
labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

body:
## Problem

The aggregator's ingest contract (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/validate.ts:1-9`) says every ingested document is validated at its boundary for "shape, element types, value ranges, and **real calendar dates**", and `validate.ts` provides `parseIsoDate`/`isIsoDate` for exactly this: "impossible calendar dates FAIL instead of rolling over: 2026-02-30 and 2026-13-01 are null, not March dates."

The stream-event boundary never got that check. `validateStreamEvent` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/events.ts:54`) validates the event timestamp with Date.parse only:

```ts
if (typeof v.at !== "string" || !Number.isFinite(Date.parse(v.at))) {
  return { ok: false, error: "event.at must be an ISO timestamp string" };
}
```

`Date.parse` rolls day-overflow dates over instead of rejecting them, so an event stamped `2026-02-30T10:00:00Z` is accepted and stored verbatim, while every consumer (`pruneEvents` retention at `events.ts:96-105`, `filterEvents` newest-first ordering) parses it as 2026-03-02 — a different day than the record claims. The same validator gates both ingestion paths: `EventsStore.append` (`events.ts:243`) and the on-load filter `isStreamEvent` (`events.ts:88-89, 187-191`), so an impossible-date record also survives reload instead of being quarantined as malformed.

Sibling boundaries were hardened for this exact failure mode: the DNS register (#2199, PR #4835, plus #4858 for the JSON path) and the charges rows (#3458) all refuse impossible dates via `isIsoDate`. The event stream — the fleet's own audit trail, persisted to the events file with 30-day / 5000-record retention — was left on the lenient check.

## Verified this run (laptop probe, origin/main 1e3763faf)

Probe `/tmp/probe-events.ts` on the laptop (log `/tmp/probe-scan21.log`), importing `validateStreamEvent` and `pruneEvents` from current main:

```
2026-02-30            ok= true  stored_at=2026-02-30            parsed=2026-03-02T00:00:00.000Z
2026-02-30T10:00:00Z  ok= true  stored_at=2026-02-30T10:00:00Z  parsed=2026-03-02T10:00:00.000Z
2026-04-31T10:00:00Z  ok= true  stored_at=2026-04-31T10:00:00Z  parsed=2026-05-01T10:00:00.000Z
2026-13-01T00:00:00Z  ok= false event.at must be an ISO timestamp string
2024-02-29T10:00:00Z  ok= true  (valid leap date, control)
2026-01-15T10:00:00Z  ok= true  (control)
2026-01-01T25:00:00Z  ok= false (hour overflow already refused by Date.parse)
PRUNE_KEPT: 1  (the 2026-02-30 event is retained, treated as March 2)
```

So month-13 and hour-25 are refused only because `Date.parse` happens to return NaN for them; day-overflow within a real month — the case `parseIsoDate` was written for — sails through.

## Why it matters

Stream events are the fleet's shared audit/activity record: a producer (or a hand-edited / corrupt events file) that stamps an impossible date silently shifts the event to a different real day for retention, ordering, and filtering, and the stored string disagrees with every parsed view of it. The boundary's own contract and the shared primitive both say this input must be refused at ingest; every comparable aggregator boundary already does.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validateStreamEvent` refuses an `at` that is shape-valid ISO but not a real calendar date/time (e.g. `2026-02-30`, `2026-02-30T10:00:00Z`, `2026-04-31T10:00:00Z`), using the shared `parseIsoDate`/`isIsoDate` primitive from `validate.ts` rather than a new local parser.
- Real timestamps still validate, including leap dates (`2024-02-29T10:00:00Z`), offsets, and fractional seconds — the shapes the existing tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/events.test.ts` and `orchestration.test.ts` exercise.
- On load, an impossible-date record in the events file is treated as malformed by the existing `isStreamEvent` path (quarantine/drop behavior unchanged otherwise).
- New tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/events.test.ts` cover the impossible-date refusals and the leap-date control; existing events/orchestration tests stay green.
- Related site to check while in the area (separate change is fine): `isSavedView` in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/views.ts:100-102` uses the same Date.parse-only pattern for `createdAt`/`updatedAt`.

body:
# id(didit): interval verdicts split continuous activity at midnight — a gap crossing midnight escapes the max-gap check

## Summary

`interval_verdicts` (`pkgs/id/src/didit/eval.rs:174`) judges each active span in isolation. Spans come from `spans_for_date` (`eval.rs:333`), which returns one span **per local day** for `ActiveWindow::Always` (midnight→midnight) and splits a non-wrapping `SleepWindow`'s active complement at midnight too (yesterday's `(to_minute, midnight)` piece and today's `(midnight, from_minute)` piece are one continuous active stretch). Adjacent spans are sorted and deduped (`eval.rs:201-202`) but never **merged**, so a record gap that crosses midnight is judged as two edge gaps — "time from the last record to the span's end" (`eval.rs:255`) and "time from the next span's start to the first record" (`eval.rs:238`) — each of which can be ≤ `max_seconds` while the actual consecutive-record gap is up to ~2× `max_seconds`. The same consecutive gap inside one day is `Violated` via the pair check (`eval.rs:240-248`).

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe at 7d3dbd00b91e5cb8eeab89e5b24c90534f7179b0)

Probe test added in a throwaway laptop worktree (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-03-laneB-interval`, `pkgs/id/src/didit/tests.rs`), expectation `ActiveWindow::Always` (evaluates in UTC, `eval.rs:283-291`), `Window::Interval { min_seconds: 0, max_seconds: 3600 }`. Hourly records throughout, with exactly one hour skipped:

- Cross-seam: hourly 2026-06-15 00:00Z–23:00Z, then 01:00Z and 02:00Z on Jun 16 (00:00Z skipped; consecutive gap 23:00→01:00 = **7200s > 3600s max**), `now` = Jun 16 02:30Z → **no Violated verdict**:
  - `start=1781481600 state=Satisfied count=24 detail=every gap is inside the window`
  - `start=1781568000 state=Due count=2 detail=1800s since the last record`
- Control, the same 7200s gap inside one UTC day: hourly Jun 15 with 12:00Z skipped (11:00→13:00), `now` = 13:30Z → **Violated**: `start=1781481600 state=Violated count=23 detail=a 7200s gap is outside 0..=3600s`

## Why it matters

The body contract (`pkgs/id/src/didit/body.rs:325-326`) is "consecutive matching records no further apart than `max_seconds` … inside the active spans". For an always-active (or sleep-window) expectation the activity is continuous across midnight, so an overnight gap of up to nearly twice the tolerated max silently passes — exactly the overnight window these trackers exist to watch (e.g. "outside every 1–4 hours"). The evaluator already special-cases wrapping spans by scanning the previous day (`eval.rs:196-197`); the adjacent-span seam is the remaining hole.

## Acceptance criteria

- Adjacent (end == next start) or overlapping spans are merged before judging in `interval_verdicts`, or gaps are otherwise judged across span seams where the active window is continuous.
- A regression test in `pkgs/id/src/didit/tests.rs` reproducing the probe above: Always interval expectation (`max_seconds: 3600`), hourly records with only the 00:00Z hour skipped, yields a `Violated` verdict naming the 7200s gap; the same-day control keeps its current verdict. A non-wrapping SleepWindow case across its midnight seam should behave the same way.

# fleet-paperwork: ledger timestamp truncation defeats --pace — writes can go out ~0s apart and the pacing test flakes

## Summary

`infra/fleet-paperwork/fleet_paperwork.py`'s anti-rate-limit pacing silently under-waits by up to ~1 second because the ledger timestamp is truncated to whole seconds. With a small `--pace` the spacing can collapse to nearly zero — in the tool whose whole job is to file GitHub writes slowly enough to avoid the secondary rate limit (it is the fleet's rate-limit fallback path).

## Evidence (verified on laptop at main d6bf024a4)

- `fleet_paperwork.py:253` — `ledger_append` stamps the ledger with `datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(timespec="seconds")`, discarding the sub-second part.
- `fleet_paperwork.py:228` — `last_write_epoch` parses that truncated stamp back, so the last write appears up to ~1s older than it really is.
- `fleet_paperwork.py:241` — `pace(pace_secs)` sleeps `pace_secs - (now - last)`; with the truncated `last`, the sleep shrinks by the discarded fraction. Call sites at :320/:345/:412; `--pace` default is 3.0s (:442/:451/:473), so up to a third of the intended spacing can vanish; for `pace(1.0)` almost all of it can.
- Header contract (:26): "before each write the script waits out the remainder of --pace seconds since [the last ledger write]" — the truncation breaks that contract.

### Deterministic probe (laptop, /tmp/probe-pace.py)

Append executed at wall-clock fraction 0.880s, then read back and paced immediately:

```
real write at frac=0.880; stored age at readback = 0.881s (real age ~0.00s)
pace(1.0) waited 0.120s although the previous write was <0.05s ago (intent: ~1.0s spacing)
```

### Flaky test (observed this run)

`tests/test_fleet_paperwork.py:61` `test_pace_waits_remainder` asserts `pace(1.0)` takes >= 0.4s. First run of the suite this session FAILED with `AssertionError: 0.369... not greater than or equal to 0.4`; reruns passed. The test fails whenever the append lands late in a wall-clock second — i.e. it is flaky by construction, for the same root cause.

## Why it matters

fleet-paperwork is the developing.today GitHub App fallback used when the user token hits GitHub's secondary rate limit; its `--pace` spacing is the safety property that keeps App-token writes from re-triggering the limit. A pace that can silently collapse to ~0s undermines that, and the intermittent test failure trains operators to ignore the suite.

## Acceptance criteria

- `ledger_append` records sub-second precision (e.g. `timespec="milliseconds"`), and `last_write_epoch`/`pace` honour it: a probe that appends at wall-clock fraction ~0.9 and immediately calls `pace(1.0)` waits >= ~0.9s.
- `test_pace_waits_remainder` is deterministic — it no longer depends on where in a wall-clock second the append lands (fixing the stamp precision plus, if needed, asserting against the stored stamp rather than a fixed 0.4s floor).
- Full suite green on repeated runs: `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests` in `infra/fleet-paperwork/`, several consecutive runs.
- Backwards compatible: ledgers written with second-precision stamps still parse (they do — `fromisoformat` handles both).

title: Fix #4887: id(hosted_binding): a pending delayed rebind does not reserv

labels.name: source/dispatch

body:
Implement GitHub issue #4887 in developing-today/code: id(hosted_binding): a pending delayed rebind does not reserve its target key

## Summary

The delayed-rebind protocol added in #4885 (slice 2 of #3809, `pkgs/id/src/hosted_binding.rs` at `9d1464c05`) never reserves the **target** key of a pending delayed rebind, and `effect_due_rebind` never re-checks it. During the 30-day wait, another account can bind that exact key by an ordinary ceremony; when the wait elapses, the delayed rebind still effects and `apply_rebind` silently overwrites the other binding's `binding_by_iroh` entry. Two `active` binding records then claim the same `iroh_id`, and the by-key index points at only one of them — breaking the §1.2 rule the ceremony itself enforces ("one `sub` per `iroh_id` at a time", `submit_proof` conflict check).

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe at origin/main `9d1464c05`)

Probe test appended in a throwaway laptop worktree (`probe-2026-11-03-laneB-scan20`, removed after the run; log `/tmp/probe-scan20.log` on the laptop):

1. Account A binds key21, then `request_delayed_rebind` to key22 → request `Pending`, binding `rebind_pending`.
2. A third account completes an ordinary `complete_browser_ceremony` with **key22** → succeeds. Nothing consulted the pending request: `request_delayed_rebind` checks only `binding_by_iroh` at request time (hosted_binding.rs:1269), the pending target key is inserted into no index, and `submit_proof`'s conflict check (hosted_binding.rs:~997) checks only `binding_by_iroh`.
3. Time advances past `effective_at`; `effect_due_rebind` with a valid new-key countersignature → succeeds. Unlike both other paths, it has **no** `NewKeyBoundElsewhere` recheck: `rebind_with_old_key_authorization` checks `binding_by_iroh.contains_key(&new_iroh_id)` at effect time (hosted_binding.rs:1414) and `request_delayed_rebind` checks it at request time (:1269); `effect_due_rebind` (hosted_binding.rs:1462) checks neither that nor pending requests.
4. `apply_rebind` (hosted_binding.rs:1538-1540) unconditionally does `binding_by_iroh.remove(old)` + `binding_by_iroh.insert(new, this binding)`, overwriting the third account's index entry.

Probe outcome (asserted in the probe, all true on current main): both A's and the third account's records are `Active` with `iroh_id` = key22; `binding_by_iroh[key22]` names A's binding only; the third account's record is silently unindexed for its own key.

The symmetric hole also exists at request time: two different accounts can both open pending delayed rebinds to the same target key, and whichever effects second overwrites the first's index entry the same way.

## Why it matters

The delayed path is the account-recovery path for a lost root key — exactly the path whose target-key ownership must be unambiguous. The 30-day wait is the security property (§4.2), but it also creates a 30-day window in which the target key is claimable by anyone: a squatter who binds the target key during the wait is not stopped at effect time, is not notified, and loses their by-key index entry without any error, while their binding record still says `active`. Any consumer resolving a binding by `iroh_id` (device authorization, grant references — §1) then reaches the wrong account's binding.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A pending delayed rebind reserves its target key: an ordinary ceremony (`submit_proof`) naming a key that is the target of a pending rebind fails with a conflict (e.g. `IrohIdBoundElsewhere` or a dedicated pending-rebind conflict), and a second `request_delayed_rebind` from another account naming the same target key fails with `NewKeyBoundElsewhere` (or equivalent).
- [ ] `effect_due_rebind` re-checks at effect time, before any mutation: if the target key is now bound to a different binding (or is the target of another pending request that was created earlier), it fails with `NewKeyBoundElsewhere` and leaves the binding, the request, and both indexes unchanged (the `RebindError` no-mutation contract).
- [ ] `apply_rebind` cannot silently overwrite a `binding_by_iroh` entry owned by a different binding: it refuses (or its callers guarantee the check) when the existing entry names another binding.
- [ ] Regression tests cover: ceremony-bind of a pending target key during the wait; two pending rebinds to one target key; effect after the target key was bound elsewhere (state unchanged on refusal); the existing 21 hosted_binding tests still pass (`cargo test -p id --lib hosted_binding`, laptop or CI).

Distinct from: #4868 / #4871 (the §3 ceremony's consumed-challenge and pairing-code findings in the same file — different functions and defects), #3809 (the delayed-rebind implementation epic this landed under; this is a defect in that new code, found by reading it against the §1.2 conflict rules).



Context: a Jules session began this issue on 2026-11-03 and was stopped mid-flight when the owner retired the Jules service (decommission, developing-today/code#5098). Before starting, check for any pull request or branch that attempt may have produced (search PRs referencing #4887) and treat the issue text above as the source of truth.

House rules from the repo owner: (1) Deliver the finished work as a pull request in this run; put "Fixes #4887" in the PR description so the issue closes on merge. (2) Cover the whole set in the one PR: every instance of the same problem, and any directly related dependency updates batched in — never one PR per item or per dependency. (3) Run the relevant tests and checks before opening the PR. (4) Merging is permitted only when you are reasonably certain the PR is correct and complete (checks green, tests run, low-risk); you never have to merge — when in doubt, leave the PR open and state your confidence and what a human should check. (5) If you hit a genuine blocker (missing credentials, a decision only the owner can make), stop and say exactly what is needed in your final summary.

body:
# pm-stack(aggregator): freshness() ages impossible and non-ISO measuredAt stamps as fresh — Date.parse rolls 2026-02-30 to Mar 2 and accepts 'March 2, 2026'

## Evidence

`freshness(measuredAt, cadenceDays, now)` in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/derive.ts:941` (callers: hub/service card rendering in `src/render.ts:2234`, `:2300`, `:2513`, `:2526`) parses the stamp with raw `Date.parse` in both branches:

- Date-only branch (`derive.ts:951`): `Date.parse(\`${measuredAt}T00:00:00Z\`)` — an impossible calendar date rolls to the next real day instead of failing.
- Datetime branch (`derive.ts:962`): `Date.parse(measuredAt)` — any string V8/Bun can parse, ISO or not, is accepted.

Every sibling aggregator gate that consumes an external stamp uses the real-calendar ISO check `isIsoDate` / `parseIsoDate` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/validate.ts:66` / `:116`), which re-checks the components so impossible dates return null. `freshness()` never applies it.

Verified this run with a laptop bun probe importing `freshness` from origin/main `dda1def97`, `now = 2026-03-01T12:00:00Z`, `cadenceDays = 7` (`/tmp/probe-fresh.ts` on the laptop):

| measuredAt | result | expected |
|---|---|---|
| `2026-02-30` (impossible) | `{ stale: false, ageDays: 0 }` — rolled to Mar 2, reported as read today | invalid stamp → `{ stale: true, ageDays: null }` |
| `March 2, 2026` (non-ISO) | `{ stale: false, ageDays: 0 }` | invalid stamp → `{ stale: true, ageDays: null }` |
| `2026-04-31` (impossible) | `{ stale: true, ageDays: null }` — only via the future-tolerance bound, by accident of the chosen `now` | invalid |
| `2026-02-27` (control) | `{ stale: false, ageDays: 2 }` | correct |
| `not-a-date` (control) | `{ stale: true, ageDays: null }` | correct |
| `2026-03-01` (control) | `{ stale: false, ageDays: 0 }` | correct |

## Why it matters

`freshness()` decides whether hub and service cards render as stale. An extractor or upstream doc that emits an impossible or non-ISO `measuredAt` is currently reported as a read taken today (ageDays 0, not stale) — the exact failure the aggregator's ingest contract (#2576 family) exists to prevent: malformed stamps must read as unknown age, never as maximally fresh. The future-tolerance bound (#1568) catches only impossible dates that roll more than a day past `now`; one that rolls to today or tomorrow passes as fresh.

## Acceptance criteria

- `freshness()` returns `{ stale: true, ageDays: null }` for a present-but-invalid stamp: impossible dates (`2026-02-30`, `2026-04-31`) in both the date-only and datetime branches, and non-ISO strings (`March 2, 2026`, `03/02/2026`).
- Valid stamps are unchanged: date-only stamps still age by Chicago calendar day (the #1629 behavior), datetime stamps by elapsed whole days, and the #1568 future-tolerance bound still applies to real future dates.
- New tests cover impossible date-only, impossible datetime, non-ISO, and the existing valid controls; `bun test` in `pm-stack/aggregator` passes.

Dedup: distinct from #1568 (closed; future bound only), #2206 (closed; saas-extract freshestDate), #4987 (closed; parseQuotaCurrent measuredAt). No open issue covers `freshness()` in derive.ts.

body:
# pm-stack(aggregator): entryFromTurso computes windowSeconds with raw Date.parse — impossible/non-ISO billing-period stamps roll instead of yielding null

## Evidence

`entryFromTurso` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-gather-map.ts`, at origin/main `785247aad`):

- `:627-630` — the Turso subscription doc's `current_billing_period_start` / `current_billing_period_end` (and their aliases) are read as raw unknown values.
- `:631-635` — `windowSeconds` is computed directly from them:

```ts
const startMs = typeof periodStart === "string" ? Date.parse(periodStart) : Number.NaN;
const endMs = typeof periodEnd === "string" ? Date.parse(periodEnd) : Number.NaN;
const windowSeconds =
  Number.isFinite(startMs) && Number.isFinite(endMs) && endMs > startMs ? Math.round((endMs - startMs) / 1000) : null;
```

`Date.parse` is the only gate. It rolls impossible calendar dates to a different instant and accepts non-ISO strings (in a timezone-dependent way), so a malformed billing period silently produces a plausible-looking but wrong window length on every Turso window the entry publishes (`:643`).

Verified this run with a laptop bun probe importing `entryFromTurso` at `785247aad` (usage doc `{organization:{usage:{databases:3}}}`, Starter subscription):

| period start | period end | windowSeconds | expected |
|---|---|---|---|
| `2026-02-01T00:00:00Z` | `2026-03-03T00:00:00Z` (control) | 2592000 (30 d) | 30 d ✅ |
| `2026-02-30T00:00:00Z` (impossible) | `2026-03-30T00:00:00Z` | 2419200 (28 d) | null — Feb 30 does not exist; Date.parse rolled it to Mar 2 |
| `2026-02-01T00:00:00Z` | `2026-02-30T00:00:00Z` (impossible) | 2505600 (29 d) | null — rolled to Mar 2 |
| `February 1, 2026` | `March 3, 2026` (non-ISO) | 2592000 (30 d) | null — non-ISO stamps are accepted, and parsed in local time (the same probe's `resetsAt` came out `2026-03-03T06:00:00.000Z`, i.e. UTC-6) |
| `not-a-date` | `also-not-a-date` (control) | null | null ✅ |

## Why it matters

`windowSeconds` is the billing-window length attached to every Turso quota window; downstream pacing/burn math treats it as measured fact. A period stamp that is impossible (Feb 30) or non-ISO currently yields a window that is days off (28 d or 29 d instead of no window) with no signal anything was wrong — the exact failure class the aggregator has been closing site by site with its real-calendar ISO gate (`isIsoDate`, `pm-stack/aggregator/src/validate.ts:116`).

Related but distinct: #4968 covers `normalizeResetAt` (the `resetsAt` derived from the same `periodEnd`, `quota-gather-map.ts:44-57`). Fixing #4968 does not touch this computation — `windowSeconds` parses `periodStart`/`periodEnd` itself and never goes through `normalizeResetAt` — so this stays live after #4968 lands.

## Acceptance criteria

- `entryFromTurso` yields `windowSeconds: null` when either billing-period stamp is present but not a real ISO calendar date/time: impossible dates (`2026-02-30`, `2026-04-31`) and non-ISO strings (`February 1, 2026`, `03/01/2026`) included.
- Valid ISO start/end stamps (including offsets) still produce the exact window length; the valid control above stays 2592000.
- Absent/non-string period stamps keep yielding `windowSeconds: null` (unchanged).
- Tests cover the impossible-start, impossible-end, and non-ISO cases plus the valid control, through `entryFromTurso`; `bun test` in `pm-stack/aggregator` passes.
- Out of scope: `normalizeResetAt` itself (#4968), and any change to which subscription fields are read.

body:
## What happened

Laptop cascade deploy round 3 (2026-11-03): `home.activationPackage` built from code@8c065075 (the PR #5077 head) builds green, but activation aborts in the `reloadSystemd` step. Home Manager's sd-switch cannot build its switch plan because it cannot parse the generated `mcpx.service`:

```
Error: Error switching systemd units
Caused by:
    0: Failed to build switch plan
    1: Failed to load unit file /nix/store/wpmp9dh1019r5bxg85mzbn1fisx1ga3j-home-manager-generation/home-files/.config/systemd/user/mcpx.service
    2: .../mcpx.service: expected '=' but got '_' at line 20, column 11
```

## Root cause

`pkgs/mcpx/modules/home-manager.nix` passes the daemon environment through at the service level:

```nix
systemd.user.services.mcpx = {
  inherit (cfg) environment;
  ...
};
```

Home-manager's systemd service type serializes unknown top-level attributes as unit sections, so the generated unit contains a literal section (line 20 is the `[environment]` header):

```
[environment]
ANTIGRAVITY_BIN=/nix/store/...
CLAUDE_BIN=/nix/store/...
CODEX_BIN=/nix/store/...
OPENCODE_BINARY=/nix/store/...
OPENCODE_V2_BIN=/nix/store/...
PATH=/nix/store/...
```

The module comment says `Service.Environment` was avoided because home-manager injects its own `Service.Environment` (session variables) and "the two definitions do not merge". That premise needs re-testing: with list-form `Environment=` entries the definitions should merge, and the current shape is broken outright either way.

## Why it matters beyond the switch abort

systemd's own parser tolerates unknown sections (it logs and ignores them), so on any path where sd-switch does not block, the unit would load with the configured environment silently dropped: the daemon would run without the `ANTIGRAVITY_BIN` / `CLAUDE_BIN` / `CODEX_BIN` / `OPENCODE_BINARY` / `OPENCODE_V2_BIN` / `PATH` values from `services.mcpx.environment`.

## Deploy state

Activation aborted after linkGeneration/installPackages (files linked, the new generation registered) but before any unit switch and before `home.activation.mcpxDeploy` ran; no service was restarted by the failed attempt. Full rollback completed and verified: the pre-deploy generation was re-activated, and the mcpx daemon, openchamber, and the unit-less opencode incumbent on :13420 all serve as before, with `~/.config/mcpx/config.json` and `~/.local/bin/oc-password-sync.sh` restored. Round 3 is blocked on this issue. Rounds 1-2 never reached activation, so this is the first time this module's unit has been switched on a real machine.

## Fix direction / acceptance

- Render `cfg.environment` into `[Service] Environment=` (list form) in `pkgs/mcpx/modules/home-manager.nix`, merging with the session-variable Environment lines home-manager injects; re-test the merge premise quoted in the module comment. (The NixOS sibling module is unaffected: `systemd.services` there has a real service-level `environment` option.)
- Acceptance: activating the cascade configuration completes the `reloadSystemd` step, and the running daemon's environment (`/proc/<pid>/environ`) contains the configured keys. The cascade deploy round 3 then proceeds.

## Acceptance criteria
- The mcpx home-manager module renders services.mcpx.environment as proper environment assignments in the unit (not a literal [environment] block), shown in the rendered unit output
- Existing module behaviour is otherwise unchanged (render diff limited to the environment rendering)

body:
# pm-stack(aggregator): isSessionRecord accepts impossible and non-ISO lastSeenAt/startedAt — a non-ISO stamp wins merge recency forever, and impossible dates roll in registryActivityMs

## Evidence

`isSessionRecord` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/registry.ts:166`) gates the two
timestamps only on type: `(r.lastSeenAt === undefined || typeof r.lastSeenAt === "string")`
and the same for `startedAt`. That type check is the #2376 fix — it stops the
`mergeRecords` sort crash on non-string values — but it never checks that a
string timestamp is a real ISO calendar date. Every sibling store validator in
the aggregator gates timestamps with `isIsoDate`
(`pm-stack/aggregator/src/validate.ts:116`): snapshots (`isSnapshotRecord`),
quota rows (`isSubscriptionRow`, `isChargeRow`, `isBurnSegment`), saved views,
events, saas overlays. The registry record is the one boundary left on
string-only.

Verified on the laptop at origin/main `6a69ab52d` (bun probe importing the
real modules):

- `isSessionRecord` returns `true` for `lastSeenAt`/`startedAt` of
  `2026-02-30T10:00:00Z`, `2026-04-31T10:00:00Z`, `March 2, 2026`, and
  `not-a-date`.
- `registryActivityMs` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/registry-view.ts:62`,
  `Date.parse`) then reports the impossible stamps as different instants than
  the strings claim: `2026-02-30` → 2026-03-02, `2026-04-31` → 2026-05-01,
  `March 2, 2026` → 2026-03-02T06:00:00Z.
- `mergeRecords` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/registry.ts:136`, lastSeenAt pick
  at :158) compares the stamps as strings. Probe: merging a record stamped
  `2026-06-01T00:00:00Z` with one stamped `March 2, 2026` keeps
  `March 2, 2026` as lastSeenAt **in both merge orders** — lexicographic
  `M` > `2`, so a non-ISO stamp permanently wins recency and no later ISO
  record can ever displace it. The merged record is also what the final sort
  (`(b.lastSeenAt ?? "").localeCompare(...)`) orders by, so the poisoned
  stamp pins the session to the top of the registry ordering.

Consumers reached through the two load paths that filter on this validator
(`sources/live.ts:795` registry store load, `:1380` feed registry merge):
the sessions registry, `registryActivityMs`-based recency windows, and every
render that shows lastSeenAt/startedAt verbatim.

Control: `2026-03-02T10:00:00Z` validates and parses to itself.

## Why it matters

The registry is the fleet's session record of truth for the dashboard. One
malformed writer (or one hand-edited/corrupted store row) with a non-ISO
`lastSeenAt` becomes permanently "most recent" — it survives every later
merge, distorts recency windows and ordering, and displays a stamp that does
not mean what it says. Impossible dates silently shift a session's activity
by days. The fix is the house pattern already applied at every sibling
boundary.

## Acceptance criteria

- `isSessionRecord` refuses a record whose `lastSeenAt` or `startedAt` is
  present and not a real ISO calendar date (`isIsoDate`), e.g. `2026-02-30`,
  `2026-04-31`, `March 2, 2026`, `not-a-date`; absent timestamps stay allowed.
- Valid ISO timestamps (incl. offsets/fractional seconds) still validate.
- Tests cover the refused and control cases for both fields; `bun test` in
  `pm-stack/aggregator` passes.
- Out of scope: changing mergeRecords' comparison or the SessionRecord shape
  (both are correct once inputs are real ISO).

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-a (lane A). Dedup: searches for
`isSessionRecord`, `registry lastSeenAt` (2026-11-03) — #3414/#2376 cover
non-string types only, #3525 covers status/agentLabel/tokensTotal, #4890
covers taskRefs; none covers timestamp validity.

title: home profile: bin/opencode collision — consumer wrapper vs cascade opencode package blocks the generation build
body:
Found while implementing the #5027 fix (PR #5037): with the `bin/mcpx` collision resolved, the laptop's home-manager generation build stops at a second profile collision that was masked behind the first.

**The two providers of `bin/opencode`** in evaluated `home.packages` (`nixosConfigurations.amd`, user):

- `/nix/store/g6hvhvzhpl05pcf2nfysvkc2nwmps0m6-opencode` — this repo's consumer wrapper: `(pkgs.writeShellScriptBin "opencode" …)` in `home/common/default.nix` (the `home.packages` list, ~line 1530). It injects Cloudflare (`~/.config/cloudflare/*`) and Jules credentials into the environment, kicks a daily background `sync-models`, and execs `inputs.opencode.packages.<system>.opencode` — the root `opencode` input, pin `d66c71f5` (2.0.30+d66c71f).
- `/nix/store/b6mr9fv22rzajmpbnrib633945gmc1df-opencode-2.0.30+2d912e0` — the cascade's opencode package, added to `home.packages` by `services.opencode`'s home-manager module (openchamber `f46050fc` → opencode fork `2d912e02`).

Both ship a real, distinct `bin/opencode` file:

```
pkgs.buildEnv error: two given paths contain a conflicting subpath:
  `/nix/store/g6hvhvzhpl05pcf2nfysvkc2nwmps0m6-opencode/bin/opencode' and
  `/nix/store/b6mr9fv22rzajmpbnrib633945gmc1df-opencode-2.0.30+2d912e0/bin/opencode'
```

**Pre-existing:** both packages are present in unmodified main's evaluated `home.packages` at today's pins. In deploy round 2 (pin `8912c837e`) buildEnv reported the `bin/mcpx` conflict first, masking this one. It blocks the laptop cascade deploy (round 3) independently of #5027.

**Shape of the decision** — the same pattern as mcpx (Drew: "just enable openchamber and take that one"), except the wrapper carries behavior the cascade package doesn't:

- `lib.hiPrio` the wrapper, so it wins `bin/opencode` in the profile (smallest change; both builds stay installed; the cascade package's other files still link).
- Gate the fork module's profile contribution instead — an `addPackageToProfile`-style option in the opencode fork, like the one PR #5037 adds for mcpx in this repo — and keep the wrapper as the profile's only opencode.
- Drop the wrapper and take the cascade package as-is, moving its env injection + model sync elsewhere (session environment / a unit). Note the wrapper also execs a *different fork rev* (`d66c71f5`) than the service runs (`2d912e02`), so this option also unifies which build the CLI is.

Not decided here — filed so the deploy blocker is tracked with its evidence.

# id(web/world): upload and compile socket handlers cast JSON.parse straight to WorldFrame — non-object frames crash or hang the flow, and a non-integer chunk_bytes corrupts the chunk stream

## Evidence

Verified at origin/main 125789ddb in the laptop tree. In `pkgs/id/web/src/world.ts`:

- `:618` (module-upload socket) — `frame = JSON.parse(String(message.data)) as typeof frame;` and `:739` (Roc-compile socket) — the same cast to `WorldFrame`. The `try` covers only the parse; the very next reads (`frame.type` at `:624` / `:745`) are unguarded.
- `:631-636` — the only `chunk_bytes` validation is `!chunkBytes || chunkBytes < 1 || chunkBytes > 6 * 1024`: no integer/type check, so a fractional or string `chunk_bytes` passes and drives the chunk loop at `:641` (`offset += chunkBytes`, `file.slice(offset, offset + chunkBytes)`, `install_chunk` frames carrying that offset).
- Contrast in the same file: the main world `receive()` at `:188-200` parses to `unknown`, requires `isRecord(parsed)` and `typeof parsed.type === "string"`, and calls `rejectFrame()` otherwise. The upload/compile handlers skip the file's own established guard.
- The server side expects integer offsets: `pkgs/id/src/world_session/types.rs:287` and `:357` type `install_chunk`'s `offset` as `usize`.

Reproduction (laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-03-laneB-worldframe/probe.mjs`, replicating the handler logic at :616-645 verbatim with stubbed socket/file; run with bun at 125789ddb):

```
null                                  => UNCAUGHT THROW: TypeError - null is not an object (evaluating 'frame.type') | no status, socket never closed
123 / "hi" / [1,2]                    => no branch matched, socket left open, no status shown (flow hangs; install button stays disabled until a close that never comes)
{"type":"upload_ready","chunk_bytes":100.5} => install_chunk offsets sent: 0, 100.5, 201, ... (fractional offsets the server's usize field rejects)
{"type":"upload_ready","chunk_bytes":"512"} => offsets sent: 0, then the string "0512"; second chunk slices 1488 bytes (overlapping/oversized) — a corrupted chunk stream
{"type":"upload_ready","chunk_bytes":512}   => control: offsets 0, 512, 1024 — correct
{"type":"error"}                            => control: status shown, socket closed — correct
```

## Why it matters

These two handlers are the admin paths for installing a world program (wasm upload and Roc compile). Any malformed or unexpected frame from the host connection — a proxy/error page frame, a future server frame shape, a hand-rolled client test — either throws uncaught (no error surfaced, no cleanup), hangs the flow silently with the button disabled, or, for a non-integer `chunk_bytes`, sends a chunk stream the server cannot accept, failing the install opaquely partway through. The main socket in the same file already demonstrates the intended validation pattern, so the gap is an inconsistency, not a design choice.

## Acceptance criteria

- Both handlers validate the parsed frame before use (record + string `type`, mirroring `receive()`/`isRecord` in the same file); an invalid frame sets the existing "invalid upload/compile response" error status and closes the socket — no uncaught throw, no silent hang.
- `chunk_bytes` is accepted only as a finite integer within the existing 1..=6144 range (`Number.isInteger`); anything else takes the existing "invalid module chunk size" path.
- Web tests cover: `null`, a JSON number/string/array frame, fractional `chunk_bytes`, and string `chunk_bytes` for the upload handler (and the non-object cases for the compile handler); the existing world web tests still pass.

title: home profile: bin/mcpx collision between fork opencode package and standalone mcpx blocks cascade deploy

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

body:
## Symptom

Laptop cascade deploy round 2 (2026-11-03), worktree at 8912c837e building the Home Manager activation package: the build fails at `home-manager-path` — a buildEnv collision on `bin/mcpx` between the two packages in the profile:

- `/nix/store/b6mr9fv22rzajmpbnrib633945gmc1df-opencode-2.0.30+2d912e0/bin/mcpx` (fork opencode package)
- `/nix/store/n35r5vj80rpnhszsb8zr5bqmfpy2hisp-mcpx-0.1.0/bin/mcpx` (standalone mcpx)

## Context

- The openchamber FOD gate that blocked round 1 is cleared; everything else in the activation realised (31 built / 123 fetched in the round-2 build). This collision is the sole remaining blocker for the cascade deploy.
- Nothing was switched: Home Manager generation 189 is still current, the pre-deploy state is intact.
- The deploy retries from the build step once a fix merges (worktree at 8912c837e + post-fix main).

## Grounding (source + evaluated, 2026-11-03)

Evaluated for `nixosConfigurations.amd.config.home-manager.users.user`:

- `services.mcpx.package` → `mcpx-0.1.0 /nix/store/n35r5vj80rpnhszsb8zr5bqmfpy2hisp-mcpx-0.1.0`
- `services.opencode.package` → `opencode-2.0.30+2d912e0 /nix/store/b6mr9fv22rzajmpbnrib633945gmc1df-opencode-2.0.30+2d912e0`
- `home.packages` contains both names — exactly the two colliding store paths.

How each package enters the profile:

**(a) Standalone mcpx** — not listed directly in `home/common`. The let binding in `home/common/default.nix:56`:

```nix
mcpx = pkgs.callPackage ../../pkgs/mcpx/package.nix { };
```

is pinned as the service package in `home/common/default.nix` (`services.mcpx`, ~line 916-921):

```nix
# This repo's own mcpx build — the package the hand-rolled unit
# ran (pkgs/mcpx) — rather than the fork's re-export default.
package = mcpx;
```

and code's own mcpx home-manager module (`pkgs/mcpx/modules/home-manager.nix:32`) puts it in the profile under `lib.mkIf cfg.enable`:

```nix
home.packages = [ cfg.package ];
```

So `services.mcpx.package` resolves to this repo's standalone `pkgs/mcpx` build (mcpx-0.1.0), deliberately overriding the fork module wrapper's `mkDefault` (the fork's `packages.<system>.mcpx`).

**(b) Fork opencode package** — arrives only via the service cascade modules. `home/common/default.nix` imports `inputs.openchamber.homeManagerModules.openchamber` (re-declared in `home/user/default.nix`'s merge element); openchamber's module (pin f46050fc) imports `opencode.homeManagerModules.opencode` from its nested opencode pin 2d912e02. The fork's home-manager module (`nix/modules/home-manager.nix:40` in developing-today/opencode) does:

```nix
{ home.packages = [ cfg.package ]; }
```

with `services.opencode.package` defaulted (`mkDefault`, fork `flake.nix` opencodeModule wrapper) to the fork's own `packages.<system>.opencode`. That opencode derivation bundles its own `bin/mcpx` (the fork's mcpx build is, in the fork flake's words, "the one opencode bundles") — hence the second `bin/mcpx` in the profile env.

## Decision needed

Which `bin/mcpx` should the home profile expose? Candidates:

- **(A)** Standalone mcpx owns `bin/mcpx`: exclude the fork opencode package's bundled copy from the profile env (e.g. strip/wrap the opencode package as it enters `home.packages`, or a dedicated profile-facing variant), keeping the standalone in the profile and the service pins as they are.
- **(B)** Drop the standalone from `home.packages`: the fork's bundled mcpx owns PATH. The daemon is unaffected — `services.mcpx` still pins its own package via `services.mcpx.package` — but shells/agents resolving bare `mcpx` would get the fork's bundled build instead of `pkgs/mcpx`'s.
- **(C)** Priority-mask one of them (`lib.hiPrio` / `meta.priority`): keeps both packages in the profile, hides the duplication behind buildEnv priority. Least structural change; the losing binary is silently shadowed.

This is an open decision — the deploy is blocked on the choice, not on implementation difficulty.

# id(world_fixture): tic-tac-toe determinism fixture was recorded under a module hash the checked-in wasm no longer matches — replay test red on main

## Evidence

Verified on the laptop at origin/main 27f12c6e6 (also failing at eef89b983), file-captured logs `/tmp/scan20-full.log` and `/tmp/scan20b.log`:

```
cargo test -p id --lib -- checked_in_session_snapshot_hashes
test world_fixture::tests::replay_tests::checked_in_session_snapshot_hashes_are_stable ... FAILED
panicked at src/world_fixture.rs:1175:56:
called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: the module hashes to
a3fbe44805adfbec2fe7000dc9440af23171da997ca088d13f150debe4a3c583,
but the fixture was recorded under
8aaca464562944fa0832a9d42e97c838cad45a58fc8a12c293f3a222d884b9f9
```

- `pkgs/id/src/world_fixture.rs:328-339` — `check_module` compares the fixture header's recorded `module_hash` against `module_hash(wasm)` and refuses a mismatch; the test at `:1175` unwraps it.
- The module under test is the checked-in `pkgs/id/apps/tic-tac-toe/program/tic-tac-toe.wasm` (world_fixture.rs:1082); the fixture is `pkgs/id/tests/fixtures/tic-tac-toe-determinism.jsonl`, whose header records the older hash.
- So one side drifted: either the wasm was rebuilt/changed without re-recording the fixture, or the fixture was re-recorded against a wasm that was never committed. The test never reaches the snapshot comparisons, so the determinism guarantee this fixture exists to pin is currently unenforced on main.

## Why it matters

This fixture is the replay/determinism tripwire for world programs: if the recorded snapshots ever genuinely diverge, this test is how the fleet finds out. While it fails at the module-hash gate, that protection is off and the red suite masks other failures.

## Acceptance criteria

- Determine which side is stale: rebuild the tic-tac-toe wasm from its committed source and compare hashes; if the committed wasm is the intended module, re-record the fixture against it (regenerating the snapshot expectations through the fixture's own recording path); if the wasm drifted unintentionally, restore/rebuild the correct wasm instead.
- `cargo test -p id --lib world_fixture` passes on main, including the snapshot-hash comparisons (not just the module gate).
- The resolution states, in the closing comment, which side was stale and what changed it.
