labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The binding-layer parser for a packaged app's `[interfaces.web]` section, `web_interface_from_app_toml` (`pkgs/id/src/web/app_interface.rs:117`), validates only `mode`. It accepts any `route` / `socket` string and hands it to `create_router_for_app` (`pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs:306`), which feeds both straight into axum route registration:

- `route` → `.route(&world_route, get(world_page_handler))` at `src/web/routes.rs:322`
- `socket` → `world_routes_at(socket)` at `src/web/routes.rs:382`, which does `.route(socket, ...)` at `src/web/world_ws.rs:60`

Axum **panics** on a path that does not start with `/` and on a path that collides with an already-registered route. So a packaged app whose `app.toml` carries a malformed or colliding binding crashes router construction (server startup / host binding) with an axum panic instead of a named `WebInterfaceError`.

This is the public flow the crate itself exercises in `public_entry_point_honours_a_configured_binding` (`src/web/routes.rs`): parse `[interfaces.web]` with `web_interface_from_app_toml`, then build the router with `create_router_for_app`. The host-discovery work (#2324) will feed real third-party app folders through exactly this path.

## Verified (probe on laptop, origin/main cb190a312)

A probe test in a scratch worktree parsed each `[interfaces.web]` below with `web_interface_from_app_toml` (all parsed `Ok`) and built the router with `create_router_for_app` under `catch_unwind`:

| route | socket | parse | router |
|---|---|---|---|
| `arena` | `/ws/arena` | Ok | **panic** at routes.rs:322 (path must start with `/`) |
| `/` | `/ws/arena` | Ok | **panic** at routes.rs:322 (collides with the index route) |
| `/files` | `/ws/arena` | Ok | **panic** at routes.rs:322 (collides with the files page route) |
| `/arena` | `ws/arena` | Ok | **panic** at world_ws.rs:60 (path must start with `/`) |
| `/arena` | `/ws/tags` | Ok | **panic** at routes.rs:382 merge (collides with the live-tags channel) |
| `/arena` | `/ws/arena` | Ok | no panic (control) |

## Why this is not #4060

#4060 covers `parse_app_manifest` / `discover_apps` in `src/app_manifest.rs` (segment sanity for `route`, any validation at all for `socket`, cross-app duplicate routes at discovery). This issue is the **other** parser — the binding layer in `src/web/app_interface.rs`, which #4060 does not name — and a different failure mode: even values that pass `app_manifest`'s only web check (`route.starts_with('/')`, app_manifest.rs:174) **and** all of #4060's proposed segment-sanity criteria (`/`, `/files`: leading slash, no `..`, no whitespace, no `?`/`#`) still panic the router, because the host's own route table is never consulted.

## Why it matters

A packaged app is data, not code the host author wrote. One bad `app.toml` in an apps folder turns a recoverable configuration error into a process panic at startup, with an axum/matchit message that names neither the app nor the field. Every other malformed-manifest path in this codebase returns a named error (`WebInterfaceError::UnknownMode` is the existing precedent in the same function).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `web_interface_from_app_toml` rejects a `route` or `socket` that does not start with `/`, returning a `WebInterfaceError` variant that names the field and the value.
- [ ] A `route` or `socket` that collides with a route the host router always registers (at minimum `/`, `/files`, `/settings`, `/peers`, `/ws/tags`, `/ws/collab/{doc_id}`, the `/api/world/*` surface, and the other side of the same binding) cannot panic router construction: it is rejected at parse/bind time with a named error, or router construction validates and reports it.
- [ ] Unit tests cover the five verified cases above (no-slash route, `/`, `/files`, no-slash socket, `/ws/tags` socket) plus the `/arena` + `/ws/arena` control still building a working router.
- [ ] The world app's own binding (`/world`, `/ws/world`) and the checked-in `pkgs/id/apps/tic-tac-toe/app.toml` binding are unchanged.

title: id(chat-presence): HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL (25s) is defined and documented but never used — serve broadcasts presence on the 30s announcement cadence

labels.name: task/small-fix

labels.name: app/id

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/id` documents a 25-second presence heartbeat cadence that nothing in the repo actually runs.

- `pkgs/id/src/chat_presence.rs:68` defines `pub const HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL: Duration = Duration::from_secs(25);` with the doc: "How often a node broadcasts its presence heartbeat. Two to three heartbeats land inside one TTL window, so a single dropped gossip message never flickers a live node stale." (`PRESENCE_TTL_SECS` is 75, chat_presence.rs:64.)
- A repo-wide search for `HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL` returns exactly one hit — the definition itself (verified this run two ways: a full-tree grep on the laptop checkout at origin/main c128305c4, and `gh search code`, which returns only `pkgs/id/src/chat_presence.rs`). The constant is never used.
- The only presence broadcast in the codebase is in `pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs` (the `PresenceHeartbeat::new` + `encode_frame` broadcast at ~:1925/:1934), and it sits inside the peer-announcement task, whose timer is `tokio::time::interval(ANNOUNCE_INTERVAL)` (serve.rs:1878). `ANNOUNCE_INTERVAL` is 30 seconds (`pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/discovery.rs:317`).

So the effective heartbeat cadence is the 30s announcement cadence, not the documented 25s. The resilience the doc relies on is thinner than stated: with a 75s TTL, a 25s cadence tolerates two consecutive dropped broadcasts before a live node flickers stale (stamps at 0/25/50/75s); at 30s only one drop is tolerated (stamps at 0/30/60s, then nothing until 90s, past the 75s expiry).

## Why it matters

The constant is public (`pub mod chat_presence`, lib.rs:167) and reads as the contract for presence timing; the #2809 design band (TTL 75s inside 60–90s) was paired with this interval. Either the serving code should honour it, or the constant and its doc should stop promising a cadence the system does not have — a silent mismatch here is exactly the kind that later debugging trusts and loses time to.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Presence heartbeats in `id serve` are broadcast on the documented cadence: either a dedicated timer driven by `HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL` in the gossip loop, or `HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL` is removed/redefined so the named cadence and the actual cadence are the same value from one source.
- [ ] A test or assertion pins the wiring (e.g. the broadcast loop's interval equals `HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL`), so the constant cannot silently become dead again.
- [ ] The doc comment on the interval and the TTL resilience claim match the shipped behaviour.

`delete_top_level_entry` in `pkgs/opencode-config-normalize/normalize.sh` finds the start of a preceding block comment with a plain backward `rfind('/*')`. title: id(world_manifest): apply() re-checks only grants/ceiling/schedule-id — ScheduleAt fire time and the 64 cap, SetProfile bounds, and InstallModule hash fold unvalidated

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/id/src/world_manifest.rs` — `WorldManifest::validate()` (lines 216–256) refuses:

- a schedule with `at_ms == 0` ("must fire in the future", line 236),
- more than `MAX_PENDING_SCHEDULES` (64) schedules (lines 229–233),
- a `module_hash` that is not 1..=64 hex digits (lines 244–255),
- a profile whose bounds fail `WorldExecutionProfile::validate()` (line 227: `wasm_fuel == Some(0)`, memory below the floors, etc.).

`apply()` (lines 373–424) is documented as the defensive re-check ("A step that names an unknown capability (a manifest should be validated first; this is a defensive re-check)"), and it does re-check two step kinds — `SetGrants`/`SetCeiling` re-run `validate_grant_names`/`validate_ceiling_names` (lines 386, 394) and `ScheduleAt` re-runs `validate_schedule_id` (line 405). But the other step kinds get no re-check at all:

- `ScheduleAt` accepts `at_ms == 0` and folds any number of schedules into state, past the 64 cap.
- `SetProfile` accepts a profile that `profile.validate()` refuses (e.g. `wasm_fuel: Some(0)`).
- `InstallModule` accepts a non-hex, over-long, or empty `hash` and stores it as the live module hash.

So a step list that did not come from a validated manifest (programmatic construction, a future caller, a deserialized plan) can fold a state that `parse`/`validate` would never let a manifest describe — and `apply`'s own changed-count then reports it as a successful reconciliation. The re-check is inconsistent: either it is load-bearing (then it should cover every invariant `validate()` enforces) or it is decoration on exactly the fields that happen to have a helper handy.

## Evidence (verified this run, origin/main a8aa52dc4)

Laptop probe (worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-scan7`, `pkgs/id/tests/probe_manifest_apply.rs` against the real `id` crate, `cargo test`, probe removed after the run):

- `apply([ScheduleAt { id: "wake", at_ms: 0 }])` → Ok(1), schedule stored with fire time 0.
- `apply([SetProfile { wasm_fuel: Some(0), .. }])` → Ok(1), profile stored.
- `apply([InstallModule { hash: Some("zz!" × 40), source: None, seed: 1 }])` → Ok(1), 120-char non-hex hash stored as `module_hash`.
- `apply(65 distinct ScheduleAt steps)` → Ok, 65 schedules in state (cap is 64).
- Control: `apply([SetGrants { grants: ["no.such.cap"] }])` → Err — the re-check exists for grants, confirming the gap is the missing coverage on the sibling steps, not a design of "apply never validates".

Dedup: searches (all states) for `world_manifest apply`, `ApplyStep`, and open `manifest` issues found #2876 (closed; unknown TOML keys), #2882 (closed; `check_schedule_replacing` cap), #3015/#1519 (cited in the code; parse-time profile validation and seed/ceiling plan semantics). No open or closed issue covers `apply()`'s partial re-check.

## Why it matters

`apply` is the pure fold the manifest tests and the server-side reconciliation model are checked against; a fold that accepts states the manifest layer forbids makes the model lie about what a live world can look like, and any future caller that builds steps without going through `parse` inherits the hole silently. The inconsistency is the bug: two of five step kinds re-validate, three do not.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `apply` refuses a `ScheduleAt` step with `at_ms == 0`, naming the schedule id, in the style of `validate()` line 236.
- [ ] `apply` refuses a step list that would leave the state with more than `MAX_PENDING_SCHEDULES` schedules.
- [ ] `apply` refuses a `SetProfile` step whose profile fails `WorldExecutionProfile::validate()`.
- [ ] `apply` refuses an `InstallModule` step whose `hash` is not 1..=64 hex digits (the `validate()` rule at lines 244–255).
- [ ] Regression tests sit alongside the existing `world_manifest` tests covering each refusal above, plus the already-working grant/ceiling/id refusals; valid step lists fold exactly as before (existing tests green, changed-count semantics unchanged for valid input).
- [ ] No change to `plan()` output or to `WorldManifest::validate()` itself.

title: id(tag_claims): check_op accepts a tag.clear naming the same claim twice — every sibling hash-set field in a chain extension refuses duplicates

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Bug

`pkgs/id/src/tag_claims.rs` — `check_op` for `tag.clear` is the only hash-set field in a chain extension whose duplicates are not refused. Every sibling set-field validated through `ChainExt::validate` rejects a repeated hash; a clear naming the same claim twice (or 256 times) passes both the builder and the decoder check, so any node accepts and folds it on receipt.

## Evidence (verified this run, origin/main a8aa52dc4)

- `tag_claims.rs:132-141` — the `Clear` branch of `check_op` checks only `claims.len() > MAX_CLEAR_CLAIMS` (256). No duplicate check.
- Sibling rules in the same validation tree:
  - `chain.rs:219-223` — a hash repeated in `after` is `ChainError::DuplicateAfter`.
  - `notes.rs:124-130` — a revision naming a parent twice is a `NoteError::Field` ("a revision names a parent twice").
  - `session_checkpoint.rs:235-242` — a session naming a participant twice is a `CheckpointError::Field`.
- Laptop probe (worktree `probe-2026-11-02-laneB-scan6`, test against the real `id` crate, since removed):
  - `check_op(CLEAR_KIND, Clear{claims:[claim, claim]})` = `Ok(())` — duplicates accepted.
  - `check_op(CLEAR_KIND, Clear{claims: vec![claim; 257]})` = `Err("257 claims, the most is 256")` — the cap counts copies, so a clear naming ONE distinct claim 257 times is refused while one naming 256 distinct claims passes.
  - `check_op(CLEAR_KIND, 256 distinct claims)` = `Ok(())`.
- The folds (`live_claims` / `compacted_claims`, tag_claims.rs) treat the claims as a set, so duplicates change no outcome — the gap is purely at the admission check every other set-field enforces. Local producers never emit duplicates (`LocalEvents::clear_tag` builds its lists from distinct live claims and chunks them, #1720), so only a foreign or buggy peer's signed event exercises it — exactly the input `check_op` exists to police on decode (`ChainExt::validate` is applied by both `chain::sign` and `chain::decode`).

## Why it matters

- The header is the wire contract: a non-canonical clear (the same claim spelled many times) is admitted, stored, and synced to other peers instead of being refused at the choke point, mirroring the canonical-form discipline the tuple decoder and the other extension checks enforce.
- The 256-claim cap's meaning is currently "256 entries", not "256 claims": padding a clear with copies of one claim trips the cap, and a legitimate-looking count cannot be trusted when auditing a clear's size.

## Acceptance criteria

- `check_op(CLEAR_KIND, …)` refuses a `Clear` whose `claims` repeat a hash, with a `TagError::Field` in the style of the sibling messages (e.g. "a clear names a claim twice").
- Regression tests alongside `test_a_clear_naming_too_many_claims_is_refused`: duplicate claims refused (adjacent and non-adjacent); 256 distinct claims still pass; 257 copies of one claim refused as duplicates (either error accepted, but the duplicate case with ≤256 entries must fail specifically on duplication).
- No fold behavior change: `live_claims`/`compacted_claims` results for duplicate-free clears are unchanged, and existing tag_claims/chain tests stay green.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed for "tag.clear duplicate claims" and "check_op clear": only #1720 (closed — clear_tag chunking over the cap, a different defect, fixed). No issue covers duplicate claim IDs inside one `tag.clear`.

body:
## Finding

In `.github/workflows/auto-format.yml`, the workflow-only early exit introduced by PR #3198 never records success, so the `AUTO_FORMAT_LAST_SUCCESS_SHA` fast path never engages after a workflow-only head.

PR #3198 (merged 5018339fd, for #3118) partitioned changed files into `format_files` / `skipped_workflow_files` and added this branch:

```bash
if ((${#format_files[@]} == 0)); then
  echo "Only workflow files changed; nothing for the auto-format bot to push."
  exit 0
fi
```

The 2026-11-02 scheduled redesign added `record_success` (which stores the current HEAD in the repo variable `AUTO_FORMAT_LAST_SUCCESS_SHA`) to every other terminal success path in the same run block — verified on current main (two independent reads of the file via the contents API, full text + grep):

- no changed files → `record_success` then exit (lines 93–94)
- treefmt made no changes → `record_success` then exit (lines 122–123)
- after a successful push → `record_success` (line 142)
- **workflow-only branch → plain `exit 0` (line 115), no `record_success`**

## Why it matters

The workflow header states the design intent: "a run whose HEAD still equals it [LAST_SUCCESS_SHA] exits immediately". After any merge whose changed-file range is workflow-only, that never happens: every 15-minute scheduled run re-checks out the repo, installs Nix, re-diffs the same range, and re-logs the same skipped workflow files, until an unrelated non-workflow change happens to land and a later branch records success. The variable is documented as an optimization rather than a correctness input, so nothing breaks — it is pure recurring CI burn (up to 96 scheduled runs/day) plus noisy duplicate "Skipping workflow file(s)" logs that make the skip look unhandled.

## Acceptance criteria

- The workflow-only branch calls `record_success` before exiting (or an equivalent advance of `AUTO_FORMAT_LAST_SUCCESS_SHA`), matching the other no-op success branches.
- A subsequent scheduled run with an unchanged HEAD takes the "main is unchanged since the last successful format pass" fast path.
- Workflow files are still never formatted/staged by the bot (the #3118 behavior PR #3198 added is unchanged), and the skipped files are still logged on the run that first sees them.
- The existing `scripts/tests/test_auto_format_workflow.py` coverage for the workflow-only exit still passes, ideally extended to assert the success recording.

Found by the pr-diff-review job reviewing PR #3198 (batch #3190–#3217, developing-today/code). Deduped: #3118 (closed) is the original push-rejection bug this branch fixed; no open or closed issue mentions `record_success` or the workflow-only stall.

body:
## Problem

`compute_state` in `pkgs/id/src/attestation.rs` treats a player's duplicate claim as a fork (→ `Disputed`) when the whole `ResultClaim` struct differs — including `frontiers` — while the cross-player agreement check at line 275 compares only `outcome` and `final_state_hash`. The two comparisons disagree about what a claim *asserts*.

## Evidence (verified this run, origin/main d05c22e7a)

- `pkgs/id/src/attestation.rs:267`: `Some(first) if first != claim => return MatchState::Disputed` — `first != claim` is full-struct equality on `ResultClaim`, whose `frontiers: Vec<Hash>` field (line 119) is documented as "both chain frontiers the claimant had seen at match end" — observation evidence, not part of the asserted outcome.
- `pkgs/id/src/attestation.rs:275`: the inter-player check is `a.outcome == b.outcome && a.final_state_hash == b.final_state_hash` — frontiers are (correctly) ignored there.
- The function's own doc (line ~230) states the rule: two claims that concur on outcome and final-state hash are `Agreed`; a player claiming twice *with different claims* is a fork. A re-issued claim with the same outcome and final-state hash but a longer frontier list (the natural case: the player re-claims after seeing the opponent's genesis/claim events, so what they "had seen" has grown) is not a different position, yet it computes `Disputed`.
- Probe (laptop worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-scan2`, test `pkgs/id/tests/probe_lanea_attestation.rs`, run on the laptop): player X claims twice with identical `agreement`, `outcome` and `final_state_hash`, second claim's `frontiers` extended by one hash; player O concurs exactly. Result: `STATE=Disputed` — the probe's assertion of the documented `Agreed` rule failed. Frontier *order* alone (same set, different order) triggers the same false dispute, since `Vec` equality is order-sensitive.

## Why it matters

A duplicate/re-issued claim is the normal recovery path in an offline-first PoC (re-broadcast, second device, claim sent after more of the match had synced). Today that turns an attested match into a permanent dispute even though both players concur on the only two fields the protocol says decide agreement — and no later claim can repair it, because the early `return Disputed` fires regardless of what else is in the set. It also makes `compute_state` order-sensitive in a second way: the same claim set in a different arrival order can pick a different "first" claim.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Two claims from the same player that agree on `agreement`, `outcome` and `final_state_hash` do not create a fork, whatever their `frontiers` (content or order).
- [ ] A same-player pair that differs in `outcome` or `final_state_hash` still computes `Disputed` (existing negative case preserved).
- [ ] The probe case above (duplicate claim, extended frontiers, concurring opponent) computes `Agreed`, as a regression test in `pkgs/id/tests/attestation_poc.rs` or the module tests.
- [ ] The doc comment on `compute_state` states explicitly which fields define a claim's position for fork detection.

Related: #2863 (distinct-player check, open), #2868 (outcome domain, closed) — different defects in the same function; this one is the frontiers/fork-comparison asymmetry.

body:
## Finding (from PR review, never addressed)

Replication frame writes are unbounded: `write_envelope` awaits `write_frame` with no timeout, so a peer that stops reading can stall the stream indefinitely — holding the world lease and the hub session permit for the entire stall, and blocking the update loop for that feed. The request read at the top of `serve_stream` is timeout-bounded (30s); the writes are not.

Raised on PR #4589:
- CodeRabbit (Major, Stability & Availability, "Quick win"), 2026-11-02T21:37:25Z: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/4589#discussion_r4448051681 — `pkgs/id/src/world_replication_net.rs:307`: bound the write in the replication frame flow with a timeout so a stalled peer cannot hold the world lease and session permit indefinitely

## No-response evidence

- PR #4589 had a single commit; the comment predates the merge (merged 2026-11-02T22:21:20Z as-is).
- All 12 review threads on PR #4589 are unresolved (GraphQL `reviewThreads`, checked 2026-11-03); no reply to this comment.

## Still live on current main (verified 2026-11-03 via `gh api` raw reads)

`pkgs/id/src/world_replication_net.rs` on main (:296-308): `write_envelope` still ends with a bare `write_frame(send, &bytes).await.context("write replication frame")?` — no timeout wrapper, while the request path in the same file (:101-104) uses `tokio::time::timeout(30s, ...)`.

## Acceptance criteria

- Frame writes in the replication feed are bounded by a timeout; on expiry the stream errors (distinguishably from an ordinary write error) and the lease/permit is released.
- A regression test covers a non-reading peer being cut off by the timeout.
- Or: a documented decision on this issue.

body:
## Finding (from PR review, never addressed)

Every replication subscription materializes a complete copy of the world journal, and keeps it for the whole session:

1. `replication_snapshot` does a full `std::fs::read` of the journal file, and it runs inside the world actor's serial command handler — so each new feed blocks that world's writes while the whole journal is read, and each subscriber gets its own full copy (CodeRabbit, Major).
2. In the network layer, the owned initial `snapshot` local in `serve_stream` stays in scope across the indefinite update loop after `send_snapshot` finishes with it, so every long-lived follower retains a full historical journal copy for its entire session, even after compaction replaces that history (Codex, P2).

Raised on PR #4589:
- CodeRabbit (Major, Stability & Availability), 2026-11-02T21:37:25Z: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/4589#discussion_r4448051699 — `pkgs/id/src/world_store.rs:208`: replace the full-journal read in the actor's feed handling with an incremental or bounded read
- Codex (P2), 2026-11-02T21:31:55Z: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/4589#discussion_r4447988632 — "Release the initial snapshot before following updates" (`pkgs/id/src/world_replication_net.rs:125`): explicitly drop the snapshot after the initial transfer or scope its ownership to that transfer

## No-response evidence

- PR #4589 had a single commit; both comments predate the merge (merged 2026-11-02T22:21:20Z as-is).
- All 12 review threads on PR #4589 are unresolved (GraphQL `reviewThreads`, checked 2026-11-03); no replies to either comment.

## Still live on current main (verified 2026-11-03 via `gh api` raw reads)

- `pkgs/id/src/world_store.rs` on main (:206-207): `replication_snapshot` still begins `let bytes = std::fs::read(&self.path)`.
- `pkgs/id/src/world/actor.rs` on main (:1577-1591): the `ReplicationFeed` handler still calls that snapshot synchronously in the actor's command handling.
- `pkgs/id/src/world_replication_net.rs` on main (:114-127): `serve_stream` binds `snapshot` and passes `&snapshot` to `send_snapshot`; the owned buffer remains in scope for the whole update loop that follows.

## Acceptance criteria

- Feed setup no longer performs an unbounded full-journal read inside the actor's serial handler (incremental/bounded read, or the read moved off the actor), and the network layer drops the initial snapshot buffer once the initial transfer completes.
- A test or measurement shows per-subscriber memory no longer scales with full journal size for the session's lifetime.
- Or: a documented decision on this issue.

body:
## Finding (from PR review, never addressed)

After a journal storage failure, new replication feeds can still receive a signed snapshot containing a mutation that was never durably committed. If `FileJournal::append` writes a complete entry but `sync_data` then fails, `persist` marks the actor storage-failed and publishes no update — but the `ReplicationFeed` handler reads the journal without checking that state, and `replication_snapshot`'s newline check accepts the fully written but unconfirmed bytes. A newly connected replica therefore receives a terminal-committed snapshot containing the failed mutation while existing replicas stay at the previous durable cursor; a writer crash can also lose that mutation.

Raised on PR #4589:
- Codex (P2), 2026-11-02T21:31:55Z: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/4589#discussion_r4447988624 — "Reject replication snapshots after a storage failure" (`pkgs/id/src/world/actor.rs:1587`)
- CodeRabbit (Major, Data Integrity), 2026-11-02T21:37:25Z: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/4589#discussion_r4448051727 — same handler: check `storage_failed` before calling `replication_snapshot`
- Related, same failure family — CodeRabbit (Minor), 2026-11-02T21:37:25Z: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/4589#discussion_r4448051710 — when `journal.append` bumps the header and then fails, subscribers are never told the header version went stale; the `Err` branch should publish `ReplicationUpdate::ResetFailed` when `replication_header_version()` changed (`pkgs/id/src/world/actor.rs:421`)

## No-response evidence

- PR #4589 had a single commit; all three comments predate the merge (merged 2026-11-02T22:21:20Z as-is).
- All 12 review threads on PR #4589 are unresolved (GraphQL `reviewThreads`, checked 2026-11-03); no replies to any of these comments.

## Still live on current main (verified 2026-11-03 via `gh api` raw reads)

- `pkgs/id/src/world/actor.rs` on main, `WorldCommand::ReplicationFeed` handler (:1577-1591): subscribes and calls `journal.replication_snapshot()` with no `storage_failed` check.
- Same file, `persist` (:421-425): the append `Err` branch sets `storage_failed = true` and returns without publishing `ResetFailed` (or any update) even when the header version changed.
- `pkgs/id/src/world_store.rs` on main (:206-218): `replication_snapshot` reads the raw file and accepts any newline-terminated bytes as the snapshot.

## Acceptance criteria

- The replication feed refuses (or bounds snapshots to a known-durable boundary) once storage has failed.
- The append-failure path notifies subscribers (e.g. `ResetFailed`) when the journal header version changed.
- A regression test simulates an append whose `sync_data` fails after a complete write and shows new feeds do not receive the unconfirmed entry.
- Or: a documented decision on this issue.

title: bug(queue): claimed task 6700 rejected by lane/checkpoint/heartbeat/park RPCs; claim-response titles diverge from tasks table

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

body:
## Problem

On 2026-11-03 ~02:02–02:25Z, lane code-i (repo-queue-worker-shift-i) claimed task 6700 via `repo-queue.py claim --queue repo-health-code-pilot --worker repo-worker-code --lane code-i`. The claim returned success (status claimed, lease_until 2026-11-03T02:47:51Z), and a direct read of `agent.tasks` (id=eq.6700) confirms: status=claimed, worker_id=repo-worker-code, lane_id=code-i, attempts=1.

However every subsequent worker RPC for task 6700 rejects the claim:

- `repo-queue.py lane 6700` → HTTP 400 `assign_repo_task_lane: task 6700 does not exist`
- `repo-queue.py checkpoint 6700` → HTTP 400 `checkpoint_task: task 6700 is not claimed by repo-worker-code`
- `repo-queue.py heartbeat 6700` → HTTP 400 `heartbeat_task: task 6700 is not claimed by repo-worker-code`
- `repo-queue.py park 6700` → HTTP 400 `park_task: task 6700 is not claimed by repo-worker-code`

Repeated across ~20 minutes; not a transient single-call failure. The worker could not checkpoint, park, or work the task; its lease will expire and requeue it.

## Second observation: claim-returned titles vs tasks-table titles

For all three tasks claimed by this shift, the title in the claim RPC response did not match the title in a direct `agent.tasks` read minutes later:

- task 6562: claim returned `fix(id/world): track retained admin-history bytes incrementally (#4633)`; table title is `Reconcile merged PR #4655 into packets for sibling id P9 test issues #4643/#4644/#4645/#4646`
- task 6695: claim returned `Update all four repo-health lane instructions to pass remaining budget`; table title is `Promote the verified D2 finding in #3107 into an implementation packet for id P9a`
- task 6700: claim returned `Curate #2888: promote into a packet for id P9 lanes removing per-OS predicate duplication`; table title is `Curate #2955: stale review — no queue review artifact has ever covered merged PR #2955`

For task 6562 and task 6695 the checkpoint/park RPCs worked normally, so the divergence there is limited to the returned-vs-stored title (or titles are being rewritten after claim — also worth ruling out). For task 6700 the claim is unusable through the RPC surface at all.

## Impact

- A claimed task that no worker verb can touch is indistinguishable from a claim evaporation until its lease expires (the pattern §10 anti-evaporation discipline exists to prevent).
- If claim responses can describe a different task than the row actually claimed, a worker may do GitHub work (notes, labels, parks) against the wrong issue.

## Acceptance

- Reproduce or explain the task 6700 RPC rejections against a table row that reads claimed by the same worker.
- Explain the claim-response vs tasks-table title divergence for task 6562, task 6695, and task 6700 (response construction, post-claim title rewrite, or read-path difference).
- Add a check (helper self-test or fleet-monitor probe) that a fresh claim can immediately lane + checkpoint; alert when it cannot.

Filed by repo-queue-worker-shift-i (lane code-i) from its 2026-11-02 19:48 CST shift; related design surface: issue #3424.

title: id(world): mint can produce a display name restore refuses — sanitize trims before the 48-char cap, so truncation landing on whitespace leaves a name that is a fixed point of neither sanitizer

labels.name: task/triage

labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

Mint can produce a participant display name that journal restore then refuses as one "mint could not have produced" — so a world that accepted the participant can no longer be restored at all.

`sanitize_display_name` (`pkgs/id/src/world/util.rs:69-77`) orders its steps: filter control/format characters → `trim()` → `take(48)`. The trim runs **before** the 48-character cap, so when truncation lands exactly on a whitespace character, the stored name ends in whitespace:

- Input: 47 × `a` + `" "` + 10 × `b` (58 chars)
- Minted/stored name: 47 × `a` + `" "` — exactly 48 chars, ending in a space

That stored name is a fixed point of **neither** sanitizer:

- `sanitize_display_name(stored)` trims the trailing space → the 47-`a` string ≠ stored
- `legacy_sanitize_display_name(stored)` (`util.rs:86-94`: filter → `take(48)` → `trim()`) also trims it → ≠ stored

Restore's #2960 check (`pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs:388-398`) accepts an `Issued` display name only when it is non-empty and equal to one of those two sanitizations, and refuses the **whole restore** otherwise ("participant {} has a display name mint could not have produced"). Mint itself is at `core.rs:1220` (`let display_name = sanitize_display_name(display_name);`) and accepts this shape: the result is non-empty, so the participant is issued, the `Issued` entry is journaled — and every later restore of that journal fails.

The same shape works with any trim-removed whitespace at position 48 (two spaces at 47–48, or a U+00A0 no-break space at 48 — all probed below). This is the residual edge of two closed fixes colliding: #3709 moved the trim before `take(48)` (fixing leading padding spending the budget), and #2960 made restore demand a fixed point of one of the two sanitizers; neither order is trimmed **after** truncation.

## Evidence (verified this run, origin/main `4ee46c0ea`; `world/util.rs` md5 `ffd968e6fd638d1ac2229c7e5f668725`)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-sanitizefixedpoint/` — `sanitize_display_name`, `legacy_sanitize_display_name`, and `is_format_char` extracted verbatim from origin/main (`util.rs.orig` / `unicode.rs.orig` saved alongside), plus a `restore_accepts` helper mirroring the `core.rs:388-398` condition exactly:

| case | minted | restore accepts minted? |
|---|---|---|
| `Bob` (control) | `Bob` | yes |
| 48 × `x` (control) | 48 × `x` | yes |
| family emoji (legacy control) | sanitized name | yes |
| 47 × `a` + ` ` + 10 × `b` | 47 × `a` + ` ` (48 chars, ends in space) | **no** — fixed point of neither sanitizer |
| 46 × `a` + `  ` + 10 × `b` | 46 × `a` + `  ` (48 chars, ends in spaces) | **no** |
| 47 × `a` + U+00A0 + 10 × `b` | 47 × `a` + U+00A0 (48 chars) | **no** |

## Why it matters

- A display name is user-chosen text arriving at a join/delegate mint; a >48-char name whose 48th character is a space is ordinary (e.g. a long full name or a phrase). The participant joins successfully — nothing fails at mint time — and the poisoned name is written into the journal.
- The failure surfaces later and out of proportion: restore refuses the whole journal, so the world cannot be reopened/restored from that journal at all, and the error text actively misleads diagnosis by claiming the name is one mint could not have produced.
- Any fix must consider journals already written by the current mint: changing only the sanitizer leaves already-journaled trailing-whitespace names refused by restore, so the restore side (or a migration of the check) needs a deliberate decision in the fix packet.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `sanitize_display_name`'s output is always a fixed point of itself: re-sanitizing any minted name returns it unchanged (in particular, no minted name ends in whitespace; truncation is followed by a final trim or equivalent).
- [ ] A participant minted with the probed shapes (space / double space / U+00A0 at the 48-char boundary) restores successfully from its journal — including a journal entry carrying the exact name the **current** mint produces, if the fix keeps restore strict.
- [ ] The #3709 cases still hold: leading padding does not spend the 48-char budget (48 spaces + `Bob` → `Bob`; 1 space + a 48-char name keeps all 48 chars), and the #2960 refusal still rejects names no mint path could produce (empty, control-bearing, over-length).
- [ ] Regression tests cover the boundary shapes above at the sanitizer level and, if practical, at the mint → journal → restore level.

Related: #2960 (closed — the restore fixed-point check), #3709 (closed — trim/take ordering for leading padding), #2112 (closed — Cf stripping in this sanitizer). Distinct from all three: this is the trailing-whitespace-at-truncation shape their combination leaves behind, verified against current main.

Found by new-issue-creator-code-a (lane A) this run.

body:
## Summary

`bin/check-opencode-metered-providers.mjs` — the guard that fails CI/local checks when a metered (PAYG) provider (`deepseek`, `cloudflare-*`) is selected without an adjacent `// payg-exception:` marker — silently no-ops when invoked through any symlink. Its entry-point check at line 359 (origin/main `03b5817dc`) is:

```js
if (process.argv[1] && resolve(process.argv[1]) === fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)) {
  await main();
}
```

`path.resolve()` only normalizes the invoked path; it does not resolve symlinks, while `fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)` is the module's real path. Invoked via a symlinked file or through a symlinked directory (e.g. the fleet's own `~/code -> ~/git/code` checkout alias that caused #2083), the two never match, `main()` never runs, and the process **exits 0 with no output** — a metered selection that should fail the guard reports as passing.

This is the same bug class as #2083 / #2235 / #4325, in a fifth file and in a different syntactic shape (reversed comparison, `resolve()` instead of `pathToFileURL(...).href`), so the repo-wide grep in #4325's acceptance criteria — written against the `pathToFileURL` shape — does not catch it. A grep for `fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)` entry-point comparisons in `bin/` at origin/main shows this is the only remaining instance in that shape (the other hits are `dirname(...)` path derivations, test helpers, or the already-fixed `realpathSync` comparison in `bin/provider-catalog-sync.mjs:936`).

## Evidence (laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-meteredentry/`, file extracted verbatim from origin/main `03b5817dc`, md5 `72912190ea823ae65c7ef6898f9b64fb` both sides)

Config under test: `{ "model": "deepseek/deepseek-chat" }` (a metered selection with no payg-exception marker).

- Direct: `node real/check.mjs config.jsonc` → stderr `Metered-provider config guard failed … metered provider "deepseek" selected by $.model …`, exit 1 — the guard ran and failed the config.
- Via a file symlink: `node link.mjs config.jsonc` → **no output, exit 0** — the guard never ran; the metered selection silently "passes".
- Via a symlinked directory: `node linkdir/check.mjs config.jsonc` → **no output, exit 0** — same silent no-op.
- Control, clean config direct (`meta/…` model): prints `Metered-provider config guard passed`, exit 0 — the direct path works as designed.

## Why it matters

This guard is the automated backstop for the house rule that PAYG providers are a reserve, never a routine route. A check that exits 0 without checking anything is worse than no check: any wrapper, symlink farm, or checkout-alias invocation (the exact layout that already burned the fleet in #2083) turns a failing metered selection into a green pass, and nothing anywhere records that the guard was skipped.

Distinct from #4325 (open): that issue names four files (`bin/codedb-bridge.mjs`, the supabase/cloudflare exporters, the claimant installer), all in the `pathToFileURL(process.argv[1]).href` shape. This file is not named there and its reversed `resolve(...) === fileURLToPath(...)` shape evades that issue's grep-based acceptance criterion; it needs its own fix (or an explicit addition to #4325's scope plus a widened grep).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `bin/check-opencode-metered-providers.mjs` runs `main()` when invoked via a symlinked file path and via a symlinked directory path (use the `fs.realpathSync`-on-both-sides comparison proven in `bin/proxy-supervise.mjs` and applied in #4123, or an equivalent).
- [ ] Importing the module as a library (its test suite does this) still does **not** run `main()`.
- [ ] A regression test spawns the guard via a symlink against a metered config and asserts exit 1 with the failure message (and via a symlink against a clean config, exit 0 with the pass message).
- [ ] The repo-wide entry-point grep is widened to catch both shapes (`pathToFileURL(argv[1])` and `resolve(argv[1]) === fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)`), and #4325's acceptance grep is updated or cross-linked so this shape cannot survive that sweep either.

Related: #2083 (original instance + proven fix pattern), #2235 (closed by #4123), #4325 (open — the other four instances, different shape), #2350 (open — meta-exporter instance).

body:
# id(abuse): `budget_usage` never rolls its window counters — it reports a full window's usage forever after the window has passed

## Evidence (origin/main @ 6f54447c0)

`pkgs/id/src/abuse.rs`:

- `AbuseEvaluator::budget_usage` (:885) is `&self` and computes each row directly from the stored counters:
  `counter.estimate_bytes(now_ms)` / `estimate_messages(now_ms)`.
- `WindowCounter::estimate_bytes` (:447) / `estimate_messages` (:452) are just
  `cur + prev_weighted(prev, now_ms)`. `prev_weighted` (:440) assumes `cur_start_ms`
  is the *current* fixed window's start.
- The only places that advance `cur_start_ms` are `roll` (:421), called from the
  *mutating* paths `budget_refusal` (:742) and `record_budget` (:770). Nothing on the
  read path rolls, and `budget_usage` cannot roll through `&self`.

So once a scope has been charged, `budget_usage(now)` keeps counting the whole
current-window charge no matter how far `now` has moved past the window:

- at one window + half, the charge should count only as the previous window,
  weighted by the fraction still inside the rolling span (50%);
- at two windows or later, it should count as 0 — the same aged-out state
  `prune_budget_state` / `WindowCounter::aged_out` (:488) already recognise, and the
  same recovery admission already exhibits.

### Reproduced this run (laptop probe, verbatim module)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-abuseusage/` on the laptop — `abuse.rs`
copied verbatim from origin/main (md5 481cd01f583f95f6155b7ecf0043826a, matched
against `git show origin/main:pkgs/id/src/abuse.rs`). Per-peer limit
`BudgetLimit::bytes(1_000, 100)`, one 100-byte charge at t=0:

```
usage t=0      = 100 (expect 100)
usage t=500    = 100 (expect 100, still in first window)
usage t=1500   = 100 (expect 50: prev window weighted 500/1000)
usage t=2000   = 100 (expect 0: fully aged out)
usage t=100000 = 100 (expect 0)
admit t=2000 after full charge = true (expect Ok — admission DOES recover)
usage t=2000 after new charge  = 100 (expect 100)
```

Admission is correct; only the observability surface is stale. That split is the
proof this is a read-path bug, not a window-math bug: `can_admit` sees the rolled
counter, `budget_usage` sees the un-rolled one.

## Why it matters

`budget_usage` is the documented operator-visibility surface for the #2247 budgets
("the operator-visibility surface for budgets, alongside `counters`"). An operator
(or a dashboard/alert built on it) watching a peer that charged its full window an
hour ago still sees it at 100% usage — indistinguishable from a peer actively
saturating its budget right now — until some unrelated charge or refusal happens
to roll that scope's counters. Stale-at-full usage invites false abuse responses
and hides real recovery.

Related: #2247 (the budget design this implements). Not a duplicate: no open or
closed issue covers `budget_usage` (title/keyword search this run).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `budget_usage(now_ms)` returns the rolled sliding-window estimate: a charge
      counts at its previous-window weight once `now_ms` is past its fixed window,
      and as 0 once it has fully aged out (>= 2 windows), for both bytes and messages.
- [ ] `budget_usage` results agree with admission at the same `now_ms`: if
      `check_budget` would admit a full-window charge at `now`, the prior usage it
      reports for that scope/window is 0.
- [ ] A regression test charges a scope, advances time past 1.5 and past 2 windows
      with no intervening charges, and asserts the reported usage (the existing
      `budget_recovers_after_the_window_rolls` test covers admission only).
- [ ] Existing abuse/budget tests still pass; in-window usage reporting (t within
      the first window) is unchanged.

title: id(currency_poc): preflight passes requests build_legs cannot build — fee_amount>0 with no fee_account, and transfer_ids count never checked (extra IDs silently dropped)

body:
## Problem

`ConversionExecutor::preflight` (`pkgs/id/src/currency_poc/executor.rs:141`, origin/main `0400795a8`) is the §4 gate whose contract is that a request it passes can be built and submitted — the #4124/#4132 fixes added its same-account and duplicate-transfer-ID checks for exactly that reason. Two build requirements are still checked only inside `build_legs`, and one is checked nowhere, so `preflight` returns `Ok` for requests that can never execute, and silently discards caller-supplied transfer IDs:

1. **Fee with no fee account.** `preflight` only rejects `fee_account == Some(user_source)` (`:148`) and only checks the fee account's ledger `if let Some(fee_account)` (`:196-198`). With `fee_amount > 0` and `fee_account: None` it returns `Ok`; `prepare` then fails in `build_legs` at `:115` ("fee_amount > 0 requires a fee_account").
2. **Too few transfer IDs.** The duplicate check (`:160-166`) never counts. With one ID supplied for a three-leg conversion (T1 + fee + T3), `preflight` returns `Ok`; `build_legs` fails at `:97` ("transfer_ids must cover every leg (T1, fee, T3)").
3. **Extra transfer IDs are silently dropped.** `build_legs` consumes only the IDs the legs need (`:92-97`). With `fee_amount == 0` and four IDs supplied, `preflight` returns `Ok`, two legs are built, and the fourth pre-generated ID appears in no leg and in no persisted intent record — a caller that pre-generated and recorded that ID (the write-ahead discipline the module docs describe) is never told it went unused.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe `probe-2026-11-02-laneB-preflight` (verbatim `currency_poc` modules from origin/main `0400795a8`, executor.rs md5 `500df828`; setup mirrors `currency_poc/tests.rs` funded ledger), `cargo test`: 4/4 pass, including the defect assertions —

- CONTROL: valid request → `preflight` Ok, `execute` posts, 3 legs.
- PROBE2: `fee_amount=25, fee_account=None` → `preflight` **Ok**; `prepare` Err "fee_amount > 0 requires a fee_account".
- PROBE3: `transfer_ids=[601]` (3 legs needed) → `preflight` **Ok**; `build_legs` Err "transfer_ids must cover every leg (T1, fee, T3)".
- PROBE4: `fee_amount=0, transfer_ids=[601,602,603,604]` → `preflight` Ok; 2 legs built; supplied ID 604 used by **no** leg.

## Why it matters

`preflight` is a public, separately callable gate (the scenario tests call it as the §4 rejection surface). A gate that passes unbuildable requests pushes the failure into `prepare`, after the caller has been told the conversion is sound — the same false-pass shape #4124 and #4132 were filed and fixed for. The silently dropped extra ID is the worst case: nothing fails at all, so a pre-generated transfer ID can be reused or audited against a conversion that never carried it.

## Acceptance criteria

- `preflight` rejects `fee_amount > 0` with `fee_account: None`, with a message naming the missing fee account.
- `preflight` rejects a `transfer_ids` count different from the leg count the request implies (2 without a fee, 3 with one): too few **and** too many.
- `prepare`/`execute` behaviour for valid requests is unchanged (existing scenario tests pass), and no request that `preflight` passes can fail in `build_legs` for these three reasons.
- Regression tests in `pkgs/id/src/currency_poc/tests.rs` cover all three cases at the `preflight` surface (the #4124/#4132 test pattern: fails preflight, no intent persisted).

Dedup: #4124 (same-account legs in preflight) and #4132 (duplicate transfer IDs in preflight) are closed/fixed and cover different checks; #4133 covers malformed leg vectors in persisted records (recovery side); #4578 covers `FileIntentStore` listing vs `get`. No open or closed issue covers the fee-account-presence or transfer-ID-count checks.

body:
## Problem

In staged mode (#4641), the charge-candidates producer takes its period from the fetcher's `charge-inputs-manifest.json` — and never validates it:

- `pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/produce-charge-candidates.ts` `main()` (:371-378): `start = manifest.start; end = manifest.end;` straight from `JSON.parse`, with no presence, format, calendar, or ordering check. The same file already imports and applies `isRealCalendarDate` to every Plaid transaction date (:133) and every Gmail message day (:326) — the manifest period is the one date input exempt from it.
- A manifest whose `start`/`end` are missing (e.g. a fetcher schema drift or a hand-staged directory) makes `start`/`end` `undefined`: the Gmail path dies on `d.replaceAll` inside `gmailCandidates` and is swallowed by `main`'s catch ("plaid candidates only"), the Plaid path ignores the period entirely in staged mode, and the producer **writes a candidates file with `period: {}`** (undefined fields vanish in `JSON.stringify`), logs `undefined..undefined`, and **exits 0**.
- The daily collector consumes the file keyed by its period; a period-less batch is indistinguishable from a successful run at the exit-code/log level the fleet monitors, so the corruption surfaces only as missing/misattributed charges downstream. A malformed date string (e.g. `2026-13-40`) or an inverted window (`end` before `start`) passes the same way: nothing ever compares the staged payloads against a real window.

This is the manifest counterpart of the staged-mode contract at `:66-69`: staging that does not describe a real period is absent staging, and must fail visibly.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe at origin/main 17610f555)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-chargestaged/` — producer extracted verbatim from origin/main (script md5 70bff805), complete staging (both Gmail triage responses, one Plaid transaction, one Gmail receipt), manifest replaced with `{"note":"no period fields"}`:

- Output: `producer: wrote out-probe2.json — 1 candidates for undefined..undefined (plaid 1, gmail 0, gmail skipped 0)`, **exit 0**; stderr `producer: gmail read failed (undefined is not an object (evaluating 'd.replaceAll')); plaid candidates only`.
- The written file's period is literally `"period": {}`.
- Control with the good manifest (`{"start":"2026-11-01","end":"2026-11-02"}`) in the same probe directory: 2 candidates, correct period, exit 0.

Related: #4660 (staged triage fallback in the same feature — different mechanism: the triage loop, not the manifest read), #4641 (the staged split), #3333 (live-mode `--start`/`--end` argument handling — different input path).

## Acceptance criteria

- In staged mode, a manifest with a missing, malformed, non-calendar, or inverted (`end` < `start`) period fails the run visibly: non-zero exit and no candidates file presented as a successful batch.
- Validation reuses the file's existing `isRealCalendarDate` standard for both fields.
- With a valid manifest, staged output is unchanged (control case above).
- Live mode (env unset) is unchanged.
- A regression test or scripted fixture covers the missing-fields manifest case.

body:
## Finding

PR #3110 (merged) threaded `--groups-log` into `id serve`'s group-warning watcher (#2778). To add its path-resolution helper it inserted the new `serve_groups_log_path` function between `cmd_serve`'s doc comment / `#[allow(unused_variables)]` attribute and `cmd_serve` itself. In Rust an outer attribute binds to the next item, so the allow — whose own comment says it exists because "web/port only used with web feature" — now decorates `serve_groups_log_path` (which uses its only parameter and needs no allow), and `cmd_serve` has lost it.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/3110 — merged, head `9f5f2832789bfaff8feac9957f04115324de01bf`. Its serve.rs hunk inserts the doc comment + `fn serve_groups_log_path` directly after the context line `#[allow(unused_variables)] // web/port only used with web feature` and before `pub async fn cmd_serve`.
- Current main (`17610f5553`): `pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:832` — `#[allow(unused_variables)] // web/port only used with web feature` immediately precedes the `serve_groups_log_path` doc comment and function at `:833-839`; `cmd_serve` follows at `:841` with no attribute.
- `cmd_serve` destructures `web` and `port` out of `ServeOptions` (serve.rs, just below `:841`); those bindings are the ones the allow was written for — without the `web` feature they are unused.
- Verified still present on current main by reading serve.rs:825-849 directly. Dedupe: searched open + closed issues 2026-11-02 for `unused_variables`, `serve_groups_log_path`, and `allow attribute serve` — no match.

## Why it matters

Feature-reduced builds of the id crate (`--no-default-features` / web disabled) get the `unused_variables` warnings on `web`/`port` that the attribute existed to suppress — warning noise that can mask real warnings and fails any `-D warnings` invocation — and the stray allow on the helper misleads the next reader about which function needs it.

## Acceptance criteria

- `#[allow(unused_variables)]` (with its web/port comment) sits on `cmd_serve` again, and `serve_groups_log_path` carries no allow attribute.
- Building the id crate with the web feature disabled produces no `unused_variables` warnings for `web`/`port` in `cmd_serve` (checked in CI).
- No behavior change: `serve_groups_log_path` resolution and the #3110 regression tests are untouched and still pass.

body:
## Finding

PR #3143 (merged) added pre-existing enqueue-row detection for pm-dispatch (#2677): a returned task row is classified as pre-existing when its `created_at` predates the request, or when its status is terminal. The timestamp half of that test compares two different clocks: `requestStartedAt` is `new Date()` on the dispatch host (taken at the top of `handleTasks`), while the row's `created_at` is assigned by the Supabase Postgres server when the enqueue RPC inserts the row. CodeRabbit raised exactly this as a Minor on PR #3143 (inline comment 4432530400); it was never replied to and the merged code still classifies by the cross-clock comparison. The sibling CodeRabbit Major / Codex P2 on the same PR (caller-supplied dedupe keys) WAS fixed in-PR (commit 97e60a7eb) — this one was not.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/3143 — merged, final head `3ad9e717e21220f06982e057dbab7694e7fc2072`; final Codex state on that head is clean, but the CodeRabbit Minor thread (comment 4432530400, `pm-stack/dispatch/src/server.ts`) is unreplied and unaddressed in the final diff.
- Current main (`17610f5553`): `pm-stack/dispatch/src/server.ts:312-317` — `isPreExistingTaskRow` returns `parsed < requestStartedAt.getTime()` for a non-terminal row; `:390` — `const requestStartedAt = new Date()` at the start of `handleTasks` (dispatch-host clock); `:350/:365` — both the first enqueue result and the dispatch-scoped retry are classified by this function.
- The row's `created_at` comes from the queue database (the enqueue RPC returns the created row, `pm-stack/dispatch/src/queue.ts`), i.e. the Postgres server's clock — not the dispatch host's.
- Failure mode, DB clock behind dispatch clock by more than the enqueue latency: a genuinely fresh row reads as pre-existing. In the attach flow that queues a SECOND task under a random `:dispatch:` dedupe key (duplicate work — the exact outcome dedupe exists to prevent); in other flows the response reports "no new task was queued" for a task that was just queued.
- Failure mode, DB clock ahead: a live pre-existing row created instants before the request (e.g. a concurrent duplicate dispatch, or the same-millisecond case CodeRabbit named) reads as fresh — reported as newly queued, attach retry skipped: the original #2677 silent-vanish symptom in miniature.
- The terminal-status half of the test is clock-independent, so the exposed cases are precisely live (queued/claimed) pre-existing rows and fresh rows — the concurrent-duplicate window where this detection matters most.
- Dedupe: searched open + closed issues 2026-11-02 for `isPreExistingTaskRow`, `pre-existing enqueue clock`, and `2677` — only the parent issue #2677 (closed by #3143) matches; no issue covers the classification mechanism itself.

## Why it matters

#2677's fix replaced a silent wrong answer with a clock-dependent one. Dispatch and Supabase are different hosts; NTP skew of a second or more between a laptop and a cloud database is unremarkable, and the misclassification both duplicates queued work and misreports what was queued — in a component whose entire job is truthful queue reporting.

## Acceptance criteria

- Pre-existing classification no longer depends on comparing timestamps from two hosts (e.g. an authoritative inserted-vs-existing signal from the enqueue path, or a pre-enqueue dedupe-key lookup whose row id is compared with the returned row's id).
- Tests cover both skew directions: a fresh row whose `created_at` precedes `requestStartedAt` is reported as newly queued (no spurious `:dispatch:` retry), and a live pre-existing row whose `created_at` follows `requestStartedAt` is still detected (attach retry / truthful `pre_existing` response preserved).
- Existing `dispatch_preexisting.test.ts` cases still pass (terminal rows, caller-supplied keys, retry-also-pre-existing).
- Full dispatch suite passes in CI.

body:
## Problem

The charge-candidates producer's new staged mode (#4641, commit 7757c2ef1) is supposed to run on the laptop, where the Plaid/Gmail connector CLIs do not live, reading only staged inputs. But the Gmail triage loop falls back to the live CLI for any query whose staged response is missing:

- `pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/produce-charge-candidates.ts:286-298` — `stagedResponses[i] ?? (await run(GMAIL_CLI, ["gmail", "+triage", ...]))`. `gmail-triage.json` is documented as "the two +triage responses, in query order", but nothing checks that both are present.
- On the laptop the default `GMAIL_CLI` (`/opt/hatch/bin/hatch_gws_cli`) does not exist, so the fallback throws ENOENT, `gmailCandidates` rejects as a whole, and `main`'s catch (`:402`, "gmail read failed …; plaid candidates only") swallows it: the run **exits 0 and writes a candidates file with the entire Gmail source missing** — including messages the staging *did* deliver.
- This contradicts the staged contract the same change documents at `:66-69` (`stagedText`): "a stale or absent staging must fail visibly, never silently produce an empty batch." A short staging is exactly stale/absent staging, and the batch it produces is silently *partial* instead: the daily collector consumes it as the period's complete candidate set, so that period's Gmail charges simply never match.

The Plaid path does not have this flaw: a missing `plaid-transactions.json` throws out of `plaidCandidates`, which `main` does not catch, so the run fails visibly. The Gmail triage path is the inconsistent one. (Missing `gmail-bodies.json` is different and correct by design: bodies are requested via `gmail-body-requests.json` for a later run.)

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe at origin/main 17610f555)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-chargestaged/` on the laptop — the producer extracted verbatim from origin/main (script md5 70bff805), staged inputs for period 2026-11-01..2026-11-02 with one Plaid transaction (Coffee Shop $12.34) and one Gmail receipt ("Your Bakery order receipt $9.99").

- CONTROL — `gmail-triage.json` = both responses staged: exit 0, **2 candidates** (gmail Bakery $9.99 + plaid Coffee Shop $12.34), `gmail skipped 0`.
- PROBE — `gmail-triage.json` = only the first of the two responses staged: stderr `producer: gmail read failed (ENOENT: no such file or directory, posix_spawn '/opt/hatch/bin/hatch_gws_cli'); plaid candidates only`, **exit 0**, output file contains **only the Plaid candidate**. The staged Gmail message was discarded along with the unstaged query.

Related: #4641 (the staged-mode split this defect ships in), #2448 (a different whole-batch Gmail discard, fixed — same failure shape, different cause).

## Acceptance criteria

- In staged mode (`CHARGE_INPUTS_DIR` set), the producer never invokes the Plaid/Gmail CLIs, for any input.
- A `gmail-triage.json` that is missing, unparseable, or holds fewer responses than the producer issues queries fails the run visibly (non-zero exit, no candidates file written or the file clearly marked failed) instead of producing a plaid-only batch with exit 0.
- With complete staging, output is unchanged from today (control case above: both sources' candidates present).
- Live mode (env unset) is unchanged.
- A regression test or scripted fixture covers the short-staging case.

body:
## Summary

In `pkgs/id/src/references.rs` (the #2259 friendly-name PoC), the Tier-1 petname match in `LocalIndex::best_match` hardcodes `ClaimState::Uncontested`, and the `claimants()` helper that computes contested state counts only titles and alias claims — never petnames. `LocalIndex::set_petname` also places no uniqueness constraint on the name: the petname map is keyed by target, so one viewer can give two different actors the same petname.

Result: when two actor targets share one viewer petname, `resolve` returns both as Tier-1 `MatchKind::Petname` candidates whose provenance both claim `ClaimState::Uncontested`, and `Resolution::is_contested()` returns `false`. That contradicts the module's own stated rule (module docs): "A surface claimed by two or more targets is **contested**: every candidate is shown with its provenance and nothing is picked silently." The exact-claim and exact-title tiers do compute the state through `claim_state()`/`claimants()`; only the petname tier bypasses it.

The auto-pick itself is safe — the top-tier tie makes `Resolution::single()` return `None`, so `insert_unambiguous` still refuses. What is wrong is the provenance every consumer reads: `Candidate::contested()` and `Resolution::is_contested()` both report "no contest here", so a UI or caller that warns on contested surfaces (the reason `ClaimState` exists) stays silent for exactly the viewer's own names, the tier ranked most trustworthy.

Relevant code (main `b3eb4ef8a`, `pkgs/id/src/references.rs`):

- `set_petname` (:348-350): inserts into `petnames: BTreeMap<Hash, String>` keyed by target — duplicate names across targets are accepted.
- `claimants` (:382-396): counts objects of the sigil whose **title or alias claims** fold-equal the surface; petnames are not counted.
- `best_match` Tier 1 (:446-456): on a petname match returns `candidate(MatchKind::Petname, petname.clone(), object.author, ClaimState::Uncontested)` — the state is a literal, never computed.
- Contrast Tier 2 (:458-470): `ExactClaim`/`ExactTitle` pass `claim_state(&claim.text)` / `claim_state(&object.title)`.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-petname-contested/` — verbatim `references.rs` from origin/main `b3eb4ef8a` (pristine md5 `1a64cc11233f79484159fc53cf53ea23`; the probe copy differs by exactly one line, the `p2panda_core::Hash` import swapped for a deterministic stub with the same API, md5 `9be8f7cc3866c7109f2a3769a753601a`). The module's own 14 tests all pass in the probe. Three added probe tests (`tests/petname_contested.rs`):

```
shared_petname_candidates_are_both_marked_uncontested ... ok
  — two live actors, viewer petname "ann" set on BOTH: resolve(Actor, "ann")
    returns 2 candidates, both MatchKind::Petname, both
    provenance.claim_state == Uncontested; is_contested() == false;
    single() is None (the tie alone blocks the auto-pick).
control_shared_title_candidates_are_marked_contested ... ok
  — control: two actors titled "Minutes" both get ClaimState::Contested
    and is_contested() == true, so the claimants path works for titles.
control_single_petname_is_uncontested_and_pickable ... ok
  — control: one actor with petname "ann" resolves Uncontested and
    single() returns it (existing intended behavior, references.rs:648ff).
```

## Why it matters

`ClaimState` is the signal the design gives an author that a surface needs a second look before a reference is committed (`Provenance` docs: "enough for the author to tell duplicates apart and to judge a claim"). A shared petname is precisely a duplicate surface — and petnames are viewer-private, so no one else can see the collision coming. The codebase already treats set-time refusal as insufficient elsewhere: `petname.rs`'s `labels()` adds fingerprints for legacy stored names that `set` would now refuse (#2069), because stored state outlives the guard. `LocalIndex` has no set-time guard at all, so the resolve-time state is the only line of defence, and it currently always says "uncontested" for the petname tier.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] When two or more actor targets share the viewer's petname (folded comparison, as all tiers fold), their Tier-1 candidates carry `ClaimState::Contested` and `Resolution::is_contested()` returns `true`.
- [ ] A petname held by exactly one target still resolves `ClaimState::Uncontested` and remains auto-pickable via `single()` / `insert_unambiguous` (existing test `petname_outranks_an_exact_claim_for_actors` still passes).
- [ ] The rule is implemented in one place (e.g. `claimants` also counts petname holders for the actor sigil, and the petname tier uses `claim_state()` like Tier 2) rather than a second ad-hoc counter; module docs state the outcome.
- [ ] New tests cover: shared petname → both candidates contested; shared petname where one holder is a topic (sigils do not cross — topics have no petname tier, so no contest); the module's existing tests still pass.

Distinct from: #4455 (same module: `resolve` ignores the `cleared` flag — this issue is about live targets and the petname tier's claim state, and remains after a cleared-filter fix), #2259 (the PoC tracker this module implements), #2069 / `petname.rs` (the replicated petname store's own conflict refusal — `LocalIndex::set_petname` is a separate in-memory API with no such refusal).

title: Split charge-candidates producer: staged inputs staged on the sandbox, producer runs on the laptop

labels.name: meta/follow-up
labels.description: Follow-up spun out of earlier work

body:
## Problem

`pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/produce-charge-candidates.ts` (#1057, #2205) runs from a sandbox checkout of this repo solely because it shells out to the sandbox-only connector CLIs (`/opt/hatch/bin/plaid`, `/opt/hatch/bin/hatch_gws_cli`). Drew's 2026-11-02 rule removes ALL repo copies from the sandbox (work runs on the laptop via SSH), and the producer's standing trigger has already lapsed silently once (runs stopped 2026-11-02 09:18Z).

## Split (approved by Drew 2026-11-02)

- **Sandbox = thin fetcher, no repo.** A standalone script runs the exact CLI calls the producer makes today (one Plaid `transactions-get`, two Gmail `+triage` searches, plus `+read` for message bodies the producer requests) and stages the raw responses as JSON in the hatch-personal-synced hidden-files area: `plaid-transactions.json`, `gmail-triage.json`, `gmail-bodies.json`, `charge-inputs-manifest.json` (period + fetch times + per-source status).
- **Producer = laptop.** The producer gains a staged-input mode (`CHARGE_INPUTS_DIR`): it reads the staged raw responses instead of shelling out; the manifest's period governs. Gmail bodies it needs but staging lacks are written to `gmail-body-requests.json` and picked up on a later run once the fetcher stages them (each body fetched exactly once). Live CLI mode stays the default when the env is unset.
- Producer output (`charges-candidates.json`) is written directly at the laptop path the fleet-feed collector already reads. The cross-machine output ride and the sandbox clone both go away.

## Acceptance

- Parity: for a fixed historical window, staged-mode output candidates are identical to live-mode output candidates (verified before merge).
- Aggregator tests/typecheck green in the worktree.
- After cutover, one full cycle observed: fresh staged inputs -> fresh `charges-candidates.json` on the laptop -> collector consumes it.
- Old sandbox runner (`~/tools/produce-charge-candidates-scheduled.sh`) retired; no sandbox repo copy recreated.

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/opencode-config-normalize/normalize.sh` — when both v1 `plugin` and v2 `plugins` are present, the merge re-serialises the combined array with `json.dumps` and replaces the whole `plugins` value span:

- normalize.sh:304-308 — `span = find_value_span(out, 'plugins')` … `out = out[:vs] + json.dumps(legacy + native) + out[ve:]`
- normalize.sh:309 — the v1 `plugin` entry is then deleted whole via `delete_top_level_entry`.

That destroys every comment inside either array, collapsing multi-line formatting, even though the script's own header promises the opposite:

- normalize.sh:33-36 — "preserving everything else including comments"
- normalize.sh:282-284 — for the bare-rename path: "array contents are byte-preserved, comments included"
- normalize.sh:290-291 — "a repair tool must never be a data-loss path (#2364)"

The pre-write verification cannot catch the loss: it compares `json.loads(jsonc_to_json(out))` against the expected document (normalize.sh verification block), and `jsonc_to_json` strips comments first, so a comment-free result verifies as correct.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop, main 51535c2b4)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-plugincomments/` (`run.sh`, runs the real `normalize.sh` via `OPENCODE_CONFIG` on temp files)

Input:
```jsonc
{
  // leading comment
  "plugin": ["legacy-a" /* legacy note */],
  "plugins": [
    // native note inside plugins
    "native-b" // trailing native
  ],
  "other": 1
}
```
Output (exit 0, "repaired"):
```jsonc
{
  // leading comment
  "plugins": ["legacy-a", "native-b"],
  "other": 1
}
```
All three comments inside the two arrays are gone; only the comment outside the spliced spans survives. A second probe shows the same re-serialisation also escapes non-ASCII entry text (`café-plugin` → `caf\u00e9-plugin`, `snowman-☃` → `snowman-\u2603`) — semantically equal, but further proof the value is re-serialised rather than spliced.

Existing test coverage: `normalize_test.sh` case 13 (`plugins-merge`, :301-311) covers the both-present merge with a comment-free fixture only, so the loss is untested.

Distinct from #4612: that issue is the `agent`→`agents` fold's layout-bound regex splices (exit-1 / silent-no-op convergence failures). This is the `plugin` path, which already uses the locators #4612 points to — the loss here is in what the located span is replaced with, not in how it is located. The two fixes are independent (though a textual element-splice helper could serve both).

## Why it matters

This script runs on a path-unit trigger against the live opencode config. Comments in a hand-maintained config are documentation — why a plugin is pinned, disabled, or ordered. A normalise pass that silently deletes them on the one occasion both spellings coexist (exactly when a human has been hand-editing) is data loss from a repair tool, the failure class #2364 exists to prevent.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The both-present `plugin`/`plugins` merge preserves comments inside both arrays (and, where practical, their formatting): splice the legacy array's element texts into the native array textually instead of replacing the span with `json.dumps(...)`, or refuse (exit 1, file byte-identical) when either array contains a comment that cannot be preserved.
- [ ] The probe case above round-trips with `/* legacy note */`, `// native note inside plugins`, and `// trailing native` all present in the output, with entries in legacy-first order.
- [ ] `normalize_test.sh` gains a both-present fixture with comments inside both arrays; existing cases (including case 13 plugins-merge) still pass.
- [ ] A splice that cannot be done safely still exits 1 with the file byte-identical (#2364 discipline).

Related: #4612 (agent fold, same script), #2364 (never a data-loss path), #3179/#4312 (comment-aware handling in this script).

body:
# id(world): `admin_history_bytes` re-serializes the entire retained admin history on every accepted event — track retained bytes incrementally

**Scope:** PR #3998 head `47937fe3e73707eaefbaddc6d196a45f26ddc366` (`fix(id): export host events through authorized journal history`). The admin-history machinery does not exist on `main` yet — it is introduced by that PR — so this is a follow-up on the PR's new code, cross-linked both ways. Independent origin: Codex P2 review comment `r4437438581` on PR #3998; re-verified line-by-line against the PR head this run, and left unfiled by the 2026-11-02 pr-comment-review run only because that run hit its per-repo filing cap.

## Evidence (all line numbers on PR head `47937fe3`)

- `pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs:7-12` — the helper itself:

  ```rust
  fn admin_history_bytes<'a>(events: impl IntoIterator<Item = &'a WorldEvent>) -> usize {
      events
          .into_iter()
          .map(|event| serde_json::to_vec(event).map_or(usize::MAX, |bytes| bytes.len()))
          .fold(0usize, usize::saturating_add)
  }
  ```

  Every call allocates and JSON-serializes **every** event it is given, just to sum the byte lengths.

- `pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs:1317-1336` — `record_admin_history` pushes the new event, then evaluates the helper in the trim-loop condition:

  ```rust
  while self.admin_history.len() > self.limits.retained_events.min(MAX_ADMIN_HISTORY_EVENTS)
      || admin_history_bytes(&self.admin_history) > MAX_ADMIN_HISTORY_BYTES
  ```

  In steady state (length within cap) the byte total is computed on **every** call, and each `pop_front` re-evaluates the condition — so trimming *k* events costs *k+1* full re-serializations of the remaining deque.

- Call frequency: `record_admin_history` runs on the accept path — `pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs:1312` (inside event acceptance), also `core.rs:457`, `core.rs:650`, and `pkgs/id/src/world/actor.rs:445`. Every accepted input, chat message, or host event pays the full scan even when no admin export is ever requested.

- Bounds: `pkgs/id/src/world/mod.rs:57` `MAX_ADMIN_HISTORY_EVENTS = 4096`; `mod.rs:59` `MAX_ADMIN_HISTORY_BYTES = 64 MiB`. With the default 1,024-event retention and valid 16 KiB inputs, one accepted event can re-encode ~16 MiB of JSON; at the 4,096-event cap, up to the full 64 MiB byte budget is re-encoded per event.

- Secondary edge in the same helper: a single event whose serialization fails counts as `usize::MAX`, so the total saturates and the trim loop would drain the entire retained history one pop (and one full re-scan) at a time.

- `WorldCore` is deliberately serialized: `core.rs:28` — "Keep it behind one actor/mutex so event sequencing is serialized." The re-serialization is synchronous work inside that single world actor, so it delays subsequent inputs, ticks, and view requests for everyone in the world.

- One legitimate one-shot use exists: `restore_admin_history` (`core.rs:1349`) validates a checkpoint's history once at restore time. That call can stay, or reuse the same cached sizes.

## Why it matters

This is an O(retained-history) tax on the hottest path in the world actor, paid per accepted event, forever, in exchange for a byte total that changes by exactly one event's size per call. Busy worlds (the ones that accumulate a large retained history) get slower per event the more history they retain — precisely backwards. The fix is mechanical and local: cache each event's encoded size when it enters the deque and maintain a running total as events enter and leave.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `record_admin_history` is O(1) in the retained-history size per accepted event (amortized): encoded sizes are cached per retained event and a running byte total is maintained incrementally on push/pop; no per-event full re-serialization on the accept path.
- [ ] Trim behavior is unchanged: the same events are retained/evicted under both the event-count cap (`retained_events.min(MAX_ADMIN_HISTORY_EVENTS)`) and the byte cap (`MAX_ADMIN_HISTORY_BYTES`), and `admin_history_complete` flips exactly as before.
- [ ] `restore_admin_history`'s byte-bound validation still rejects an over-budget checkpoint history (it may reuse the cached sizes or keep the one-shot scan — restore is not the hot path).
- [ ] The serialization-error edge is handled deliberately (an event that cannot be serialized cannot silently poison the running total or drain the whole history); the chosen behavior is pinned by a test.
- [ ] A regression test or benchmark demonstrates the improvement (e.g. a test with a large retained history asserting the trim outcome, plus a comment/measurement showing per-event cost no longer scales with history size), and the existing `world` test suite passes.

Cross-links: PR #3998 (introduces the code), Codex review comment `r4437438581`.

title: openclaw ACP adapter: cancellation marker survives a finished prompt and mislabels the next prompt as cancelled (#3997)

labels.name: task/triage
