labels.description: Filed by the pr-comment-review job

body:
## Finding (from PR review)

A cancellation that races with a prompt's completion leaves a stale cancellation marker that mislabels the next normally completed prompt. Codex (P2, PR #3997):

> When a cancellation notification races with the prompt's final idle event, the prompt can finish before this handler runs. The handler still records the session as cancelled, but an ensuing idle event cannot remove that marker because cleanup in `handleServeEvent` requires a pending prompt. The next normally completed prompt then incorrectly returns `stopReason: "cancelled"`. The marker also survives a cancelled prompt ending through `session.error`. Only mark active prompts as cancelled and clear their cancellation state on every terminal path.

## Evidence

- Source PR: #3997 — https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/3997 (merged 2026-11-02 as-is)
- Review comment: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/3997#discussion_r4437436119 — chatgpt-codex-connector[bot], 2026-11-01T21:31:19Z, `bin/opencode-acp-adapter.mjs:422`
- No-response evidence: the review thread is unresolved (GraphQL `reviewThreads`, checked 2026-11-02), the comment has no replies, and PR #3997 contains a single commit (8e67215808, 2026-11-01T21:26:51Z) that predates the comment — no fix followed it before merge.
- Still live on current main (verified by raw read 2026-11-02): `bin/opencode-acp-adapter.mjs:422` — `session/cancel` calls `cancelledSessions.add(sessionId)` unconditionally; the marker is deleted only at `:308-312`, inside the `session.idle` branch gated on `pendingPrompts.has(sessionId)`, and the `session.error` path (`finishPrompt`) never clears it.

## Acceptance criteria

- Cancellation is recorded only for prompts actually in flight, and cancellation state is cleared on every terminal path (`session.idle`, `session.error`, prompt finish).
- A regression test covers: cancel arriving after a prompt finished, followed by a normal prompt that must return `stopReason: "end_turn"`.
- Or the finding is resolved by a documented decision on this issue.

body:
## Finding (from PR review)

In the configured OpenClaw gateway, the ACP adapter (`bin/opencode-acp-adapter.mjs`) only authenticates if `OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD` happens to be inherited, but `home/openclaw/default.nix` neither supplies that variable nor installs a wrapper to load it. Codex (P1, PR #3997):

> The standing server requires the password stored in `~/.local/state/opencode/service-prod.json`: `bin/openchamber-start.sh` loads it explicitly, as does the dispatch client. Unlike the previous private-server ACP command, this adapter therefore sends unauthenticated session and event requests in the declared gateway environment, preventing session creation even after the API contract is corrected. Read the standing server's credential at runtime or explicitly wire it into the adapter's launch environment.

## Evidence

- Source PR: #3997 — https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/3997 (merged 2026-11-02 as-is)
- Review comment: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/3997#discussion_r4437436108 — chatgpt-codex-connector[bot], 2026-11-01T21:31:18Z, `bin/opencode-acp-adapter.mjs:67`
- No-response evidence: the review thread is unresolved (GraphQL `reviewThreads`, checked 2026-11-02), the comment has no replies, and PR #3997 contains a single commit (8e67215808, 2026-11-01T21:26:51Z) that predates the comment — no fix followed it before merge.
- Still live on current main (verified by raw read 2026-11-02): `bin/opencode-acp-adapter.mjs:65` reads the password only from `process.env.OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD`; `home/openclaw/default.nix` (lines 59 and 442) launches the adapter with a bare command and no `OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD` wiring and no reference to `service-prod.json`.

## Acceptance criteria

- The adapter, as launched by the OpenClaw gateway config in `home/openclaw/default.nix`, authenticates to the standing server — either by loading the credential from `~/.local/state/opencode/service-prod.json` at runtime (as `bin/openchamber-start.sh` and the dispatch client do) or by explicit environment wiring in the launch definition.
- Verified against the gateway launch path, not only a hand-exported shell environment.
- Or the finding is resolved by a documented decision on this issue.

body:
## Finding (from PR review)

The OpenClaw ACP-to-HTTP adapter (`bin/opencode-acp-adapter.mjs`) implements the older v1 session contract against a target that is the OpenCode 2.x standing server pinned in `flake.nix`. Codex (P1, PR #3997):

> The existing client for that same standing server, `pm-stack/dispatch/src/opencode.ts`, creates sessions with `POST /api/session`, supplies `location.directory` in the body, unwraps the `{data: …}` response, and submits prompts through `/api/session/:id/prompt`. Here, session creation instead uses `/session?directory=…` and expects a bare `id`; subsequent prompts likewise use the incompatible `prompt_async` route. Consequently, switching OpenClaw to this adapter does not provide a working session flow against its intended server. Implement and test against the pinned server's contract rather than the v1-shaped stub.

## Evidence

- Source PR: #3997 — https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/3997 (merged 2026-11-02 as-is)
- Review comment: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/3997#discussion_r4437436106 — chatgpt-codex-connector[bot], 2026-11-01T21:31:18Z, `bin/opencode-acp-adapter.mjs:388`
- No-response evidence: the review thread is unresolved (GraphQL `reviewThreads`, checked 2026-11-02), the comment has no replies, and PR #3997 contains a single commit (8e67215808, 2026-11-01T21:26:51Z) that predates the comment — no fix followed it before merge.
- Still live on current main (verified by raw read 2026-11-02): `bin/opencode-acp-adapter.mjs:387` creates sessions via `serveJson(withDirectory('/session', cwd), { method: 'POST', body: {} })` and expects a bare `session.id`; `:408` submits prompts via `/session/${sessionId}/prompt_async`. No `/api/session` v2 contract is used.

## Acceptance criteria

- The adapter creates sessions and submits prompts using the pinned standing server's v2 contract (`POST /api/session` with `location.directory` in the body, `{data: …}` unwrapping, `/api/session/:id/prompt`), matching `pm-stack/dispatch/src/opencode.ts`.
- A test exercises session creation + prompt submission against the v2-shaped contract (not only a v1-shaped stub).
- Or the finding is resolved by a documented decision on this issue.

title: opencode-config-normalize: agent->agents fold uses layout-bound regex splices — inline/other-indent/comment-lookalike configs exit 1 or silently never converge

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/opencode-config-normalize
labels.description: Package/app: opencode-config-normalize (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/opencode-config-normalize/normalize.sh` folds the v1 `agent` map into `agents` with raw regex splices, while the `plugin` -> `plugins` path in the same script was moved to string/comment-aware locators (`find_value_span` / `delete_top_level_entry`, normalize.sh:304-309, per the #4312 review). The agent path still uses:

- normalize.sh:341-347 — replace the `agents` block: `re.subn(r'"agents"(\s*):\s*\{.*?\n  \}', ...)`
- normalize.sh:349 / :356 — delete the `agent` block: `re.subn(r'\n\s*"agent"\s*:\s*\{.*?\n  \},?', ...)`

Both patterns hard-code one exact layout (block closes with a newline + exactly two spaces + `}`) and match the first textual occurrence, live key or not. Verified on current main `9f730f1c2` (normalize.sh md5 `c484608106940bd49bae9e26e2013d6e`), laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-normagent/`:

- Control (canonical 2-space layout, `agent` adds a new key): merges correctly, exit 0.
- `agents` written inline (`"agents": {}` or `"agents": { "a": { ... } }`) with a standard `agent` block: **exit 1, file unchanged** — the fold can never land.
- Whole document in 4-space indent: **exit 1, file unchanged**.
- A `//` comment above the real keys containing an `"agents": { ... }` example shape: **exit 1** — the regex hits the comment first; only the whole-document verification keeps the file safe.
- Fully-duplicated `agent` entries (`merged == agents` branch, normalize.sh:356) with the `agent` block on one line: **exit 0, file unchanged** — the duplicate v1 block is silently left in place forever, so the script reports success while the config never converges.

The whole-document verification (#2364) prevents corruption, so this is a convergence/robustness failure, not data loss: legitimate hand-edited configs either fail the normalize unit on every trigger (exit 1) or are silently never normalised (exit 0 no-op), and the v1/v2 flap the script exists to end persists for exactly the hand-edited files most likely to carry both spellings.

## Why it matters

This script runs on a path-unit trigger against the live opencode config. A permanent exit 1 trains everyone to ignore a failing unit; a silent exit 0 leaves `agent` and `agents` coexisting, where the fork's merge semantics (native wins per key) can shadow hand edits made to the v1 block. The plugin family in the same file already demonstrates the correct locator approach.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The agent fold and the agent-block deletion use the string/comment-aware top-level locators (`find_top_level_key` / `find_value_span` / `delete_top_level_entry`, or equivalents) instead of layout-bound regexes — no hard-coded `\n  }` closing shape, no first-textual-match selection.
- [ ] Probe cases B/C/D (inline `agents`, single-line `agents`, 4-space document) all normalise to the expected merged document with exit 0.
- [ ] The comment-lookalike case (probe F) normalises the live keys and leaves the comment byte-identical.
- [ ] The duplicated-entries case (probe E) actually removes the v1 `agent` block, whatever its layout, or exits 1 — never a silent exit-0 no-op while `agent` remains.
- [ ] `pkgs/opencode-config-normalize/normalize_test.sh` gains fixtures for these layouts and passes; existing 13 cases still pass; a splice that truly cannot be done still exits 1 with the file byte-identical (#2364).

Related: #2364 (fail-closed discipline), #3179 / #3180 (same script), #4594 (the v2 flip that kept these splices).

title: agent-backup: PREV selection picks a future-dated snapshot — dedup compares against the wrong snapshot and `latest` repoints backwards

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/low

labels.description: Package/app: agent-backup (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Bug: agent-backup compares against a future-dated snapshot and repoints `latest` backwards

`pkgs/agent-backup/backup.sh` (at origin/main `12da9503c`) chooses the "previous" snapshot by name order, not by position relative to the new snapshot, and unconditionally repoints `latest` at the new stamp:

- `backup.sh:87-88` — `PREV="$(find "$ROOT" -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 -type d -not -name "$STAMP" -printf '%f\n' | sort | tail -n1)"` picks the lexicographically greatest directory that is not the new one. The header contract (`backup.sh:9-11`) is "the most recent **previous** snapshot" — a directory with a stamp **later** than the new run's (clock stepped backwards after an NTP correction or a VM restore, a backup root restored/copied from another machine, or any future-dated snapshot planted by a test) is not previous, but it wins this selection.
- `backup.sh:96` — `ln -sfn "$STAMP" "$ROOT/latest"` runs whenever the new snapshot survives the comparison, even when a newer snapshot already exists, so `latest` regresses behind the newest snapshot, contradicting the header: "A `latest` symlink points at the **newest** snapshot."

### Reproduction (verified this run, laptop probe `probe-2026-11-02-laneB-backupfuture/`, `backup.sh` md5 `32956cfd09b8f2b61b21d1b679af9088` = origin/main)

Seed a backup root with two snapshots and `latest -> 2027-01-01T00-00-00`, stub `date` to `2026-06-01T00-00-00` (the pattern `test-backup.sh` already uses), and make the current content (`CURRENT`) identical to the true previous snapshot `2026-01-01T00-00-00` but different from the future snapshot `2027-01-01T00-00-00` (`FUTURE`):

```
$ bash backup.sh
agent-backup: snapshot 2026-06-01T00-00-00 (1 files)   # kept — dedup compared against 2027, not 2026-01-01
$ ls backups
2026-01-01T00-00-00  2026-06-01T00-00-00  2027-01-01T00-00-00  latest
$ readlink backups/latest
2026-06-01T00-00-00                                     # regressed behind 2027-01-01T00-00-00
```

Control, same setup without the future-dated directory: `agent-backup: no change since 2026-01-01T00-00-00`, no new directory, `latest` unchanged. So both defects are caused by the future-dated entry alone:

1. **Duplicate snapshot kept.** Content unchanged since the actual previous snapshot is stored again, because the no-change comparison ran against the future snapshot — the history grows when nothing actually differs (header contract, `backup.sh:9-11`).
2. **`latest` points at stale content.** Any consumer resolving `latest` (restores, audits) silently gets an older snapshot than the newest one on disk.

The mirror-image case also misbehaves: current content identical to the future snapshot but changed versus the true previous one is dropped as "no change since <future>", erasing the transition from the history ordering.

### Why it matters

This script is the safety net for irreplaceable agent credentials/config. Its two promises are exactly the ones broken here: dedup against the previous snapshot, and `latest` = newest. Both fail silently (exit 0, normal-looking output) in the clock-skew/restore situations a backup tool is most likely to meet.

### Acceptance criteria

- The dedup comparison runs against the newest snapshot with a stamp **strictly before** the new stamp (same-second suffixed names from #3340 order within their second), never against a later-stamped directory.
- `latest` is only repointed when the new snapshot is the newest on disk; a run that creates an older-stamped snapshot leaves `latest` at the newer snapshot.
- Regression coverage in `pkgs/agent-backup/test-backup.sh` (or a sibling test) for the future-dated-directory case, using the existing fake-`date` pattern: duplicate not kept when content matches the true previous snapshot, and `latest` does not regress.
- Existing same-second behaviour (#3340) unchanged.

Distinct from #3340 (same-second collision, fixed in b974eb6ed): this is about a snapshot directory stamped later than the running clock, which the #3340 fix does not address.

title: provider-catalog-sync: OPENCODE_CONFIG_PATH now names the runtime overlay — catalog-sync diffs (and would --apply into) the wrong file, and the env var beats an explicit --config

body:
## Bug

Since the #4544 config split, `bin/provider-catalog-sync.mjs` resolves its target config from the wrong variable — and an explicit `--config` flag cannot override it:

```js
// bin/provider-catalog-sync.mjs:828-829 (main)
const configPath =
  process.env.OPENCODE_CONFIG_PATH || opt('--config', path.join(root, '.opencode', 'opencode.jsonc'));
```

`OPENCODE_CONFIG_PATH` is sync-models' variable. Before the split it happened to name the same file catalog-sync wanted. #4544 changed its meaning: `home/common/default.nix:1610` now exports it in `home.sessionVariables` — i.e. into every user session — pointing at the **runtime overlay**:

```nix
OPENCODE_CONFIG_PATH = "$HOME/.local/state/opencode/opencode-runtime.jsonc";
```

(the sync-models service is pinned to the same value at `home/common/default.nix:883`.)

## Verified this run (laptop probe, verbatim file from main `e22084504`, md5 `33b72d9142987ac2e75b9ffde51f82ba`)

Fixtures: `tracked.jsonc` = `{provider:{acme:{models:{m1}}, openai:{models:{}}}}`, `overlay.jsonc` = `{provider:{openai:{models:{g1}}}}`, empty `--source-dir`, local `--models-dev`.

- **Bug case** — `OPENCODE_CONFIG_PATH=<overlay>` (the new session default) plus an explicit `--config <tracked>`:
  report `"config": ".../overlay.jsonc"`, `"runtime_overlay": ".../overlay.jsonc"` (the file merged over itself), and `providers` contains **only `openai`** — `acme`, present in the file named by `--config`, never appears.
- **Control** — env unset, same flags: `"config": ".../tracked.jsonc"`, providers `{acme, openai}` (the merged effective config, exactly the #4544 intent).

Probe dir (laptop): `~/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-catsync/`.

## Why it matters

In any normal post-split user session, catalog-sync silently diffs the runtime overlay instead of the tracked configured default:

- Every non-sync-owned provider in the tracked default becomes invisible — its validated additions and vanishings never surface, so the catalog silently stops being maintained (the tool's whole job, #1297).
- `--apply` would write additions into the overlay — a state file outside the repo — instead of the tracked default via a reviewable PR; the #4544 sync-owned skip is also computed against the wrong provider set.
- `--open-pr` derives the repo dir as `dirname(dirname(configPath))` = `~/.local/state`, so the PR flow runs git in a non-repo directory.
- The precedence inversion (environment beats an explicit flag) means there is no way for a caller who knows the right file to say so.

## Acceptance criteria

- `provider-catalog-sync` resolves its config as: explicit `--config` first; otherwise the tracked configured default (`<repo>/.opencode/opencode.jsonc`). It must not take its target from `OPENCODE_CONFIG_PATH` (that variable now names the runtime overlay, sync-models' file). If an env override is kept, give it a catalog-sync-specific name (e.g. `OPENCODE_CATALOG_SYNC_CONFIG`) and document it in the header comment.
- With `OPENCODE_CONFIG_PATH=<overlay>` set in the environment and `--runtime-config` defaulting to the same overlay, a run against the tracked default reports the same provider set as the env-unset control (probe fixtures above).
- A regression test in `bin/provider-catalog-sync.test.mjs` covers the resolution precedence (env-set + explicit `--config` → the flag wins / the env var is ignored), alongside the existing #4544 merge tests.
- The header comment block is updated so the documented config resolution matches the code.

Related: #4544 (the split; this is a defect in its rollout), #2827 (open, different catalog-sync defect — enumerateProxy shape), #4387 (sync-models, different file).

title: id(currency_poc): FileIntentStore listing ignores canonical file names — duplicate copies reconcile twice, and a misnamed record is invisible to prepare()'s identity guard

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

`FileIntentStore` (pkgs/id/src/currency_poc/intent.rs) has two inconsistent notions of where an intent record lives:

- `get(conversion_id)` reads only the canonical path `path_for(id)` = `{id:032x}.json` (intent.rs:175-177, 199-209).
- `unresolved()` ignores file names entirely: it scans every `*.json` entry in the directory and returns whatever parses as an `IntentRecord` (intent.rs:211-256).

Nothing ties a listed record to its canonical file name, and nothing deduplicates by `conversion_id`. Two verified consequences:

1. **Duplicate listing / duplicate reconciliation.** Every copy of a record file in the same directory (an operator backup copy, a copy under another name) is listed again. Recovery then reconciles the same conversion once per copy and emits duplicate `(conversion_id, outcome)` pairs.
2. **A misnamed-only record is invisible to the identity guard.** A record that exists only under a non-canonical name (older naming scheme, operator rename) is seen by `unresolved()` but `get(id)` returns `None` for it. `ConversionExecutor::prepare`'s identity guard — "a conversion ID is the identity of ONE conversion: never replace its persisted intent" (executor.rs:238-258) — is built on `get()`, so it happily persists a second, conflicting intent for the same conversion. The store then holds two records for one conversion with different legs, and `unresolved()` returns both.

This is the identity counterpart of #4125 (closed): that fix made the listing skip *unparseable* entries; parseable-but-misnamed or duplicated entries still pass through unchecked. It is also adjacent to #4133 (closed), which made `reconcile` distrust the leg vector; the record-identity layer has the same trust problem one level up.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 874ca86a9)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-intentname/` — verbatim copies of `currency_poc/{intent,ledger,recovery}.rs` from origin/main (md5 intent d276f6cc, ledger 093c818d, recovery 8d40cf83, all matching the sandbox clone at 874ca86a9); `cargo test` 2/2 pass:

- PROBE1: `put` record for conversion 7, then copy its file to `backup.json` and `999.json` in the same directory → `unresolved()` returns **3** records for conversion 7; `reconcile(.., Abandon)` returns **3** outcomes `[(7, Abandoned), (7, Abandoned), (7, Abandoned)]`.
- PROBE2: write a Recorded record for conversion 9 only as `intent-9.json` → `get(9)` returns `None` while `unresolved()` returns `[9]`; after `put` of a conflicting record for conversion 9 (different leg ID), `unresolved()` returns **2** records for conversion 9.

## Why it matters

The intent store is the write-ahead recovery surface for conversions: its whole contract is one durable record per conversion that the scanner can trust. Duplicate listings make recovery reports (and any consumer counting outcomes) double-count a conversion, and repeated `put`s from duplicate entries rewrite the canonical file once per copy. The misnamed case is worse: it silently defeats prepare()'s never-replace guard, the exact mechanism that prevents a retry from erasing/conflicting with the recovery record of an earlier, possibly-posted submission — two divergent leg sets for one conversion ID is precisely the state the recovery scanner cannot reconcile safely.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `FileIntentStore::unresolved()` returns at most one record per `conversion_id`.
- [ ] A parseable record whose file name is not the canonical `{conversion_id:032x}.json` for the `conversion_id` it carries is handled explicitly: either it is reported through `unreadable_entries()` (the #4125 skip-and-report channel, with a reason naming the mismatch) and not listed, or the store's identity contract is changed so `get()` and `unresolved()` agree — with the chosen semantics documented on the `IntentStore` trait.
- [ ] Regression tests: (a) duplicate copies of one record file in the directory list/reconcile once; (b) a misnamed-only record cannot coexist with a conflicting `put` for the same conversion — after the fix, prepare()'s guard sees every record the scanner sees.
- [ ] Existing currency_poc tests stay green, including the #4125 unreadable-entry tests.

Drew's order (2026-11-02): "no, remove it if it's not used" — following the ruling that there should be no dezren39/nix builds anywhere.

### Verified basis

- flake.nix's own comment at the input: "a pin source: other inputs follow its nixpkgs-hoisted. Its laptop home-manager modules (laptop-backups, codex-remote-control) moved into this flake on 2026-10-28 (nixos/home/; #1723) — nothing here consumes its homeModules output anymore. Its package set targets darwin and nothing here builds from it."
- The name `dezren39-nix` appears only in flake.nix / flake.lock repo-wide.
- Lock analysis (202 nodes): every `follows` path rooted at `dezren39-nix` (42 edges) sits on nodes reachable **only** through the dezren39-nix subgraph — they are dezren39/nix's own internal hoisting declarations for its own input tree (its duplicate copies of home-manager, openchamber, flake-parts, treefmt-nix, sops-nix, systems, plus determinate / mac-app-util / nixpkgs-terraform / homebrew-* / etc.). No node in this flake's own graph carries an edge into that subgraph; the only direct reference is `root.dezren39-nix` itself.
- Removing the input therefore prunes exactly 49 nodes (dezren39-nix + its 48-node private subgraph) and leaves every remaining node's locked rev untouched.

### Scope

- Remove the input block + comment from flake.nix; regenerate flake.lock.

body:
## Summary

The REPL preprocessor's heredoc scan mistakes a `<<` inside an unquoted `$(...)` or backtick substitution body for a REPL heredoc operator. The line is dropped into heredoc mode (`ReplInput::NeedMore`) with a garbage delimiter carved out of the substitution body, the substitution never executes, and the original line is truncated at the `<<`.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `6e12642d4`)

`pkgs/id/src/repl/input.rs`, `preprocess_repl_line` (stage 1, before the here-string / `$(...)` / backtick / pipe stages):

- The heredoc check is `find_unquoted(line, "<<")` — quote-aware only. It has no notion of `$(...)` or backtick spans, so a `<<` inside a substitution body is treated as a top-level operator.
- The module's own quoting contract states the substitution body is shell code; the later `$(...)` stage scans paren depth quote-aware and would execute the body via `shell_capture` — but it never runs, because stage 1 returns `NeedMore` first.

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-heredocsub/` (verbatim `find_unquoted` / `find_unquoted_from` / `is_protected` / `has_trailing_placeholder` + the heredoc branch of `preprocess_repl_line`, from `input.rs` @ `6e12642d4`, file md5 `2a80a51fa5d4b64e0a413abc15753bc2`):

```text
"get $(echo a<<b)"            => NeedMore delimiter="b)"        original_line="get $(echo a"
"get `echo a<<b`"             => NeedMore delimiter="b`"        original_line="get `echo a"
"get $(echo $(echo a<<b))"    => NeedMore delimiter="b))"       original_line="get $(echo $(echo a"
"put $(echo a<<b) name"       => NeedMore delimiter="b) name"   original_line="put $(echo a"
"get $(printf 'a<<b')"        => NoHeredoc   (quoted control — #1585 fix holds)
"put - name <<EOF"            => NeedMore delimiter="EOF"       (real heredoc control)
"put - name <<< 'x'"          => NoHeredoc   (here-string control)
```

Ground truth for the body alone: `sh -c 'echo a<<b'` exits 0 and prints `a` — the substitution is valid shell that the REPL's own `shell_capture` would have run.

## Why it matters

- The user is silently dropped into heredoc continuation mode and must type a line exactly equal to `b)` / `b\`` to escape; the command they typed is lost (the collected heredoc content is substituted into a truncated `original_line`).
- This is the same substitution-span blindness as #4427 (the pipe scan mistaking a `|>` inside `$(...)`/backticks for an outer pipe), but at an earlier stage and with a worse failure mode: #4427's scan only mis-rejects; this one hijacks the line into heredoc mode before any substitution executes.

## Distinct from

- #1585 (closed): quoted `<<` / `)` — fixed by making the scans quote-aware; the quoted control above still passes. This issue is about *substitution spans*, not quote spans.
- #3395 (open): a real top-level heredoc whose delimiter is the raw rest of the line. Here there is no top-level heredoc at all.
- #4427 (open): `source_pipe_position` mistaking a `|>` inside `$(...)`/backticks. Same root-cause class, different scan, different stage, different symptom — fixing #4427's validation scan does not fix stage-1 heredoc detection.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `preprocess_repl_line` does not enter heredoc mode for a `<<` that lies inside a `$(...)` (including nested) or backtick span; such lines reach the substitution stages and execute as shell.
- [ ] A genuine top-level `<<DELIM` still returns `NeedMore` with the correct delimiter and `original_line`, including when a substitution appears earlier on the line with no `<<` inside it.
- [ ] Tests cover: unquoted `<<` in `$(...)`, nested `$(...)`, and backticks; the quoted control (`$(printf 'a<<b')`) and the here-string (`<<<`) controls keep passing.
- [ ] Existing `repl::input` tests pass unchanged.

title: fix(scripts): gate nixpkgs-unstable input updates on the Hydra channel (cached) revision

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: status/needs-triage
labels.description: Not yet triaged; needs a first look

labels.name: source/human
labels.description: Filed directly by a human

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: effort/m
labels.description: Medium: expected under 1 day of work

labels.name: meta/enriched
labels.description: Intake review done: acceptance criteria, links, and normalized labels added

body:
## Problem

`scripts/update-nixpkgs-inputs.py` updates the nixpkgs inputs to branch HEAD (`nix flake update --refresh`). For the `nixos-unstable` ref set that is the wrong target: branch HEAD runs days ahead of what Hydra has built and what cache.nixos.org actually serves. An update can therefore pin a revision whose binaries do not exist in the cache yet, turning the next system build into a massive source build.

This is not hypothetical: the 2026-10-30 update pinned nixpkgs-unstable at `31ecbaca` before Hydra had built it, and the amd toplevel became a multi-day source build (55k derivations, thin cache coverage). See #2715 and PR #4519 for the full fallout, including the temporary overrides that had to be bisected and pinned on top of that update.

## Fix: gate the unstable ref set on the Hydra channel revision

For every input whose `original.ref` is `nixos-unstable` (currently `nixpkgs-unstable` and `nixpkgs-25`), the update target is no longer branch HEAD. It is the newest revision Hydra has fully built for the channel:

1. `GET https://hydra.nixos.org/job/nixos/unstable/tested/latest-finished` (JSON, follow redirects; jobset `nixos:unstable`, renamed from `nixos:trunk-combined`) → take `jobsetevals[0]`.
2. `GET https://hydra.nixos.org/eval/<id>` (JSON) → target revision is `jobsetevalinputs.nixpkgs.revision`.
3. Pin each gated input to that revision in `flake.lock`: rewrite its `locked` entry (rev + narHash + lastModified taken from a real nix fetch of that exact revision, e.g. `nix flake metadata github:NixOS/nixpkgs/<rev>`) while leaving its `original` entry untouched, so `original.ref` stays `nixos-unstable` and input discovery (this script and `nix/nixpkgs-inputs.nix`) keeps matching.
4. If an input is already at the Hydra revision, the run is a clean no-op for it and says so.

Verified live 2026-11-02: latest-finished build 351844113 (finished, status 0), eval 1830926, revision `0bb2eedc20e4739f29e8045034f2828ad7054f8f` — which is exactly the revision the 2026-11-02 scheduled update run converged on by hand.

Dead ends, do not use: `channels.nixos.org/<channel>/git-rev` returns 404; `NixOS/nixpkgs-channels` has been untouched since 2021.

## Fail closed

If the Hydra lookups fail, time out, or return an unexpected shape (missing fields, a revision that is not a full 40-char commit hash), the script exits non-zero with a clear message and leaves `flake.lock` untouched. No update is better than an uncached update.

## Scope

- Only the `nixos-unstable` ref set is gated. The master / no-ref set keeps its current branch-HEAD behavior (the fleet procedure does not run it, and nixpkgs-master is being removed per #3327 — its semantics are not changed here).
- This changes the updater script only; it does not move any pins on main by itself.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] For every input whose `original.ref` is `nixos-unstable`, `scripts/update-nixpkgs-inputs.py` pins the Hydra channel revision (latest-finished `nixos:unstable` tested eval's nixpkgs revision) instead of branch HEAD, rewriting only the `locked` entry (rev/narHash/lastModified from a real fetch) and leaving `original` untouched.
- [ ] An input already at the Hydra revision is a clean no-op and the run says so.
- [ ] On any Hydra lookup failure, timeout, or unexpected response shape, the script exits non-zero with a clear message and leaves flake.lock unchanged (fail closed).
- [ ] Non-unstable inputs keep the existing branch-HEAD update behavior.

title: aggregator(feed): sanitizeQuotaView never checks pool-level freshness, and session tokens / freshness dates are value-blind — malformed freshness and negative counts survive the #3921 pass

labels.name: app/pm-stack

body:
## Problem

The #3921 sanitization added in PR #4508 (merged today, main `c84bbcfa1`) validates quota credential rows and active sessions by shape in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/feed.ts` — but three value/pool-level gaps remain in the same `sanitizeQuotaView` pass, all verified this run:

1. **Pool-level `freshness` is never sanitized at all.** `isQuotaPool` (feed.ts:473-480) does not look at `pool.freshness`, and `sanitizeQuotaView` (feed.ts:596-625) rewrites only `windows`, `credentials`, and `activeSessions`. `isQuotaFreshness` exists (feed.ts:486-495) but is applied only inside credential rows. So a pool carrying `freshness: "error"` (a bare string) or `freshness: { measuredAt: "2026-02-30T00:00:00Z", source: "quota-current", state: "banana" }` survives sanitization untouched and renders in `renderQuota` (render.ts:2278-2280) as an empty/bogus "gatherer · · measured — ·" line or a literal `banana` state; the health error count in render.ts:3306 (`pool.freshness?.state === "error"`) also misses every malformed form. The model's `QuotaPool.freshness` is `PoolFreshness` (model.ts:257) — the same shape credential rows are now dropped for failing.
2. **Active-session `tokens` is finite-only.** `isQuotaActiveSession` (feed.ts:505-512) uses `isFiniteNumber(v.tokens)`, so a cumulative token count of `-12345` passes and renders as `burning: s-neg (gpt-5) -12,345 tok` (render.ts:2262-2267). Every sibling numeric guard in the same section is non-negative for exactly this reason: window `used`/`limit` (#3427, `isNonNegative`), burn-segment `tokens` (#3428, `isNonNegative`).
3. **Credential-row freshness `measuredAt` is never date-checked.** `isQuotaFreshness` accepts any string, so a credential row with `freshness.measuredAt: "banana"` is kept with `droppedCredentials: 0`, while window `resetsAt` and burn `from`/`to` in the same file must pass `isIsoDate` (real calendar dates — "2026-02-30" fails). The sanitized view is projected publicly via `/api/quota.json`, so the bogus stamp reaches consumers as if measured.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-quotapool/probe.test.ts` on the laptop, importing the real `feed.ts`/`render.ts` at main `c84bbcfa1` (feed.ts md5 `0d344ffcc96d83587ae2aa511da23c1e`, render.ts md5 `93546815e6efb4e2530a05de67c991aa`, identical on sandbox and laptop clones). `bun test`: 6/6 pass, documenting the current (buggy) behavior:

- P1: session `tokens: -12345` → kept, `droppedActiveSessions: 0`, HTML contains `-12,345 tok`.
- P2: pool `freshness: "error"` → kept verbatim, `droppedPools: 0`, HTML contains the empty `gatherer ·  · measured —` line.
- P3: pool freshness `{measuredAt: "2026-02-30T00:00:00Z", state: "banana"}` → kept verbatim, HTML renders `banana`.
- P4: credential row `freshness.measuredAt: "banana"` → kept, `droppedCredentials: 0`.
- P5: pool `burnTokensPerMin: -500` → kept and renders `-500 tok/min` (same unsanitized pool-scalar pattern; render.ts:2281 interpolates it unchecked).
- C1 control: a well-formed pool (valid freshness, session `tokens: 42`) passes sanitization unchanged with zero drops — the guards above are the only gap.

## Why it matters

`sanitizeQuotaView` is the feed boundary whose contract (validate.ts header, #2576) is that no consumer, store append, or render sees unvalidated values. #3921 closed the crash class for credential/session *shapes*; the pool's own freshness stamp — the field that tells Drew whether a pool's numbers are current or walled — still passes through in any shape, and negative cumulative counts render as measured fact on the quota page and in the public `/api/quota.json` projection.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] `sanitizeQuotaView` validates pool-level `freshness` with the same `isQuotaFreshness` guard used for credential rows: a present-but-malformed pool freshness is dropped from the pool (pool itself survives, like the non-array `activeSessions` treatment) and the loss is surfaced in the dropped counts (extend the counts shape or document the chosen bucket).
- [x] `isQuotaFreshness` requires `measuredAt` to be a real ISO calendar date (`isIsoDate`), for both pool and credential-row freshness.
- [x] `isQuotaActiveSession` requires `tokens` to be non-negative (`isNonNegative`), consistent with window `used` and burn `tokens`; negative-token sessions drop individually and count in `droppedActiveSessions`.
- [x] Pool `burnTokensPerMin`, when present, is validated as a non-negative finite number or dropped from the sanitized pool.
- [x] New regression tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/feed.test.ts` covering P1–P5 above; the well-formed control (C1) and all existing #2429/#3427/#3428/#3921 quota tests still pass.

## Related

- #3921 — parent finding (credential-row/session shape sanitization, implemented by PR #4508); this issue is the pool-level/value residual its criteria did not cover.
- #3427 / #3428 — the value-rule precedents for quota windows and burn segments in the same file.

title: Split opencode.jsonc into tracked configured default + runtime overlay (stop config drift)
body:
## Problem

`.opencode/opencode.jsonc` in this repo is simultaneously (a) the tracked, deliberate OpenCode configuration and (b) the file several automated processes rewrite in place in the live `~/git/code` tree. That dual role is what fed the #4464 divergence: any in-tree rewrite dirties the primary, pm-git-sync cannot pull a dirty tree, the primary falls behind, and (pre-#4525) the repo-keeper snapshot-committed the dirt onto the stale base. #4525 fixed the keeper; this issue removes the drift source.

## Writers found (evidence, 2026-11-02)

Automatic/runtime writers of the tracked file today:

1. **`bin/sync-models.mjs`** — the big one. Runs daily (`sync-models.timer`) and opportunistically from the `opencode` CLI wrapper (24h stamp). Rewrites the file in place, editing **only** `provider.*.models` for five providers, from models.dev / agy discovery / the Codex cache:
   - `antigravity-direct` — add/update/**remove** entries, incl. `variants` + `limit`
   - `openai-codex` — add entries, fix `limit`
   - `google`, `openai`, `cloudflare-gateway` — add-only from models.dev
   Current footprint: 238 model entries (62 openai, 65 openai-codex, 54 google, 30 cloudflare-gateway, 27 antigravity-direct). The provider blocks for `google` and `openai` contain *only* `models`; the other three keep deliberate shells (`npm`/`name`/`options`) alongside.
2. **OpenChamber launch rewrite + `opencode-config-normalize`** — OpenChamber migrates the v1 `plugin`/`agent` keys to v2 `plugins`/`agents` spellings in the file on launch; the path-unit normalize service rewrites them back (idempotent; net drift zero once it runs, but the file flaps on every launch). These keys are deliberate config and stay in the tracked file; the split does not change this pair's behavior.
3. **The fork server's `Config.update`** — writes exactly one key, `shell`, into the global config file when a client calls the config.update RPC (fork `packages/core/src/config.ts`). Rare, but it is a runtime write into the tracked file.

Deliberate writers (must keep landing in the tracked file, via PRs): human/agent config edits (routes, pools, provider shells, `disabled_providers`).

Direct readers that must see the same effective config: the fork server (native config layering), `bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs` (own JSONC parse), OpenChamber (via the server), and the pm-stack aggregator collector (AA coverage reads provider catalogs from this file).

## Design

Split by ownership, using the fork's native config layering — verified empirically against the deployed build (2.0.30+6fb3bac): config documents from multiple sources are **deep-merged per provider/model**, and the `OPENCODE_CONFIG` env source ranks above the global file and is watched for hot reload.

- **Configured default (tracked)**: `.opencode/opencode.jsonc` keeps everything deliberate — provider shells, routes, pools, settings — minus the five sync-owned `models` maps above. `google`/`openai` blocks disappear entirely (they were models-only). Changes land only via PR.
- **Runtime changes (untracked)**: new file `~/.local/state/opencode/opencode-runtime.jsonc` (XDG state, alongside the other relocated runtime state) holding only `{ provider: { <the five>: { models: {…} } } }`. The server layers it over the default via `OPENCODE_CONFIG`; effective config is unchanged.
- **sync-models** targets the runtime file (it already honors `OPENCODE_CONFIG_PATH`): service environment in `home/common/default.nix` + resolution default in the script so bare/wrapper invocations land there too once the file exists. `provider-catalog-sync` reads the merged effective config for diffing and skips the five sync-owned providers on `--apply` (sync-models owns them).
- **route proxy** deep-merges the runtime file over its config at load (env `OPENCODE_ROUTE_PROXY_RUNTIME_CONFIG`, default the state path), cache keyed on both files. The aggregator collector merges it the same way when present (AA coverage parity).
- **fork change** (developing-today/opencode): `Config.update` writes its patch into the explicit (`OPENCODE_CONFIG`) file when one is configured, else the global file as today — so the server's one runtime write also lands in the runtime file.
- Session durability: `OPENCODE_CONFIG` (+ `OPENCODE_CONFIG_PATH` for sync-models) set in HM session variables so the server, CLI invocations, and children inherit the layering across relaunches/logins.

Migration: the five providers' current `models` maps move verbatim from the tracked file into the runtime file; a parse-compare proves the merged result deep-equals today's effective catalog before adoption.

## Verification bar

1. After adoption, exercising the system (server up, route calls, a sync-models run) leaves `git status` in ~/git/code clean — runtime writes land only in the runtime file.
2. A deliberate config edit lands in the tracked file only, as a clean reviewable diff.
3. Effective-config parity for server + proxy + OpenChamber against the pre-split config (same providers/models/routes; route decisions flowing; no reader errors).

## Coordination

#4464's reconciliation/soak runs on the same tree: worktree/PR work proceeds independently; the live adoption (tracked-file slimming landing in the primary, server relaunch) is sequenced so it does not invalidate an in-progress soak.

title: projector(reconcile): the prs stream reads the issues endpoint, so reconcile can never learn draft/merged/merged_at — first-sight PRs are stored draft=0/merged=0 forever

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: app/pm-stack
labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

body:
## Summary

The projector's reconcile poller can never learn a PR's `draft` / `merged` / `merged_at` — and for a PR it discovers first, it stores the wrong values permanently.

Both item streams in `pm-stack/projector/src/reconcile.ts` read the **issues** endpoint:

- `reconcile.ts:47-49` — the `issues` and `prs` streams share one path: `` `repos/${repo}/issues?${q}&filter=all` ``; the `prs` stream only filters the same list to objects with a `pull_request` link (`:55-57`).

Objects from that endpoint are issue-shaped for PRs: a `pull_request` link (whose nested object carries `merged_at`) but **no top-level `draft` / `merged` / `merged_at`** — the same shape the repo's own test documents for webhook issue objects (`pm-stack/projector/test/projector.test.ts`, the #4158 describe block: "it has a pull_request link but NO merged / merged_at / draft").

Since the #4158 fix (merged today as #4516), `fromIssueOrPr` (`projector.ts:52-58`) emits `null` for those three fields on issue-shaped payloads, and `upsertItem` (`store.ts`) preserves stored values for `null`. That is correct for webhooks. For reconcile it means:

1. **First sight materializes false defaults.** A brand-new row INSERTs with `COALESCE(?,0)` (`store.ts`, upsertItem insert step), so a draft PR reconcile discovers is stored `draft=0` (ready for review) and a merged PR is stored `merged=0, merged_at=null` (closed-unmerged).
2. **Reconcile can never heal it.** Every later poll re-reads the same issue-shaped objects, emits `null` again, and the store preserves the wrong stored values. Only a later `pull_request` webhook with a newer `updated_at` can correct the row — exactly the delivery reconcile exists to not depend on ("poll GitHub … so the projection self-heals beyond webhook delivery", `reconcile.ts:1-4`).
3. **The truth is already in the same run, and is discarded.** The `reviews` stream fetches `repos/${repo}/pulls?per_page=100&state=all` (`reconcile.ts:128`) — pulls-shaped objects that DO carry `draft` / `merged` / `merged_at` — and uses them only to enumerate PR numbers for review fetching. No item row is upserted from them.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-reconcileprs/` on the laptop — verbatim copies of `pm-stack/projector/src/{reconcile,projector,store,github}.ts` + `schema.sql` at main `4c42670d0` (md5-matched against the primary clone), driven through the real `reconcileRepos` with a fake GitHub fetch:

- `/issues?…` returns two issue-shaped PR objects: #7 an open **draft** PR, #8 a **merged** PR (`pull_request.merged_at` nested in the link object only).
- `/pulls?…` (reviews stream) returns the pulls-shaped truth: #7 `draft:true`, #8 `merged:true, merged_at:"2026-10-03T00:00:00Z"`.

Stored rows after reconcile run 1 **and** run 2 (identical):

```
PROBE run1 #7 draft/merged/merged_at: 0 0 null
PROBE run1 #8 draft/merged/merged_at: 0 0 null
PROBE run2 #7 draft/merged/merged_at: 0 0 null
PROBE run2 #8 draft/merged/merged_at: 0 0 null
```

Control: the repo's own `reconcile.test.ts` + `projector.test.ts` pass in the same probe directory (0 fail).

## Why it matters

`pmp_items.draft/merged/merged_at` is what the aggregator/dashboard reads as fact about PR state. Any PR whose `pull_request` webhook was missed, predates the projector, or lands while webhooks are down is projected by reconcile with merge fields that are silently wrong — a merged PR reads as closed-unmerged and a draft reads as ready — and no amount of re-polling fixes it. This is the reconcile-side counterpart of #4158: that issue fixed issue-shaped payloads *resetting* known values; this one is reconcile *never being able to learn* them, because its item source is an endpoint that does not carry them.

Distinct from: #4158 (webhook reset, fixed), #4302/#4303 (the application contract and its writer-inventory audit — this is a concrete writer defect that inventory should disposition), #4210 (item deletion path).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Reconcile sources PR-shaped data for the `prs` stream (e.g. upsert items from the `/pulls` list response it already fetches, or fetch pulls-shaped objects for the prs stream), so a reconcile-discovered PR is stored with its real `draft` / `merged` / `merged_at`.
- [ ] A PR first projected by reconcile as a draft reads `draft=1`; a merged PR reads `merged=1` with its `merged_at`; a second reconcile pass over unchanged data changes nothing.
- [ ] A row previously materialized with the false defaults is healed by a later reconcile pass (the pulls-shaped upsert carries a non-null carrier signal, so the #4158 preservation logic does not pin the wrong values).
- [ ] Regression tests in `pm-stack/projector/test/reconcile.test.ts` (fake-GitHub style, like the existing streams tests) cover draft-first-sight, merged-first-sight, and heal-after-webhook-gap; the existing projector suite stays green.
- [ ] Issues stream behavior is unchanged (plain issues still project from `/issues`).

title: id(replication): ReplicationTracker::accept never checks the payload's own journal header — a snapshot with no header, a foreign world's header, a version-99 header or a duplicate header is verified and advances the cursor, though WorldCore::restore refuses every one

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: task/fix
labels.description: has a fix task queued

body:
## Summary

`ReplicationTracker::accept` in `pkgs/id/src/world/replication.rs` (F12.13 replication contract, issue #806) verifies that every payload line **decodes** as some `JournalEntry` — but it never checks the payload's own journal header against the frame or the world. A correctly signed frame from the pinned source is accepted, and the tracker's verified cursor advances, for payloads `WorldCore::restore` refuses wholesale:

- **Snapshot with no header at all** — payload is a single `CapsGranted` entry. Restore: "world journal does not start with a header" (`world/core.rs:221`).
- **Snapshot whose `Created` entry names a different world** — the envelope's `world_id` matches the tracker, the payload's header does not. Restore: "journal belongs to world …" (`world/core.rs:210-215`).
- **Snapshot whose `Created` entry claims version 99** while the envelope's `header_version` is 1 — the envelope field passes the `<= MAX_JOURNAL_VERSION` check (`replication.rs:626`), the entry's own version is never read. Restore accepts only `1..=3` (`world/core.rs:217`).
- **Snapshot with a duplicate header** — two `Created` entries in one payload. Restore: "duplicate world journal header" (`world/core.rs:232`).
- **Tail carrying a `Created` entry** — appending it to an already-headed journal is the same duplicate-header refusal at restore.

The only payload-shape check in the chain path is decodability: `chain_payload` (`replication.rs:367`, decode at `:384`) maps each line through `serde_json::from_slice::<JournalEntry>` and otherwise treats its bytes as chain arithmetic. Its own comment states the intended guarantee — "refuse it here so a verified cursor never covers data the restore path cannot read" — and PR #4447 added the decode check for exactly that reason. The header rules are the part of restore's contract that check does not cover: restore's first-entry and no-second-header rules (`core.rs:210-232`) have no counterpart in `accept`'s Snapshot branch (`replication.rs:651-666`) or Tail branch (`:667-686`), and the payload header's `world_id`/`version` are never compared with `envelope.world_id` / `envelope.header_version`.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-replpayload/` on the laptop — `replication.rs` copied **verbatim** from current main `5c49f4807` (md5 `f807510cedc0884c513f5a49ea81bfe6`, matched against the sandbox clone), with only a minimal `JournalEntry` stub (the three variants the module's own tests use, same serde tagging) around it. `cargo test`: **7/7 probe tests pass, plus the module's own 10 tests** (`probe-output.txt`).

- `probe1_snapshot_without_any_header_entry_is_accepted` — signed Snapshot, payload `[CapsGranted]` only, `header_version=1`: `accept` returns `Ok`, tracker cursor advances to ordinal 1.
- `probe2_snapshot_header_entry_version_99_is_accepted` — signed Snapshot, payload `[Created{world, version: 99}, CapsGranted]`, envelope `header_version=1`: `Ok`, cursor ordinal 2.
- `probe3_snapshot_header_entry_for_other_world_is_accepted` — signed Snapshot, payload `[Created{"someone-elses-world", 1}, CapsGranted]`, envelope world matches tracker: `Ok`, cursor ordinal 2.
- `probe4_snapshot_with_duplicate_header_entry_is_accepted` — payload `[Created, Created, CapsGranted]`: `Ok`, cursor ordinal 3.
- `probe5_tail_carrying_a_header_entry_is_accepted` — after a good snapshot (cursor ordinal 2), a signed Tail whose payload is `[Created{world, 1}]`: `Ok`, cursor ordinal 3.
- Controls pass: the well-formed snapshot (`[Created{world, 1}, CapsGranted]`) is accepted, and a hand-crafted signed frame with an undecodable entry line is refused (`MalformedPayload` from the chain step) — so the gap is exactly the header semantics, not the decode or signature machinery.

The signing key is the pinned source, so this is not a forgery scenario: it is a writer bug or a confused peer producing frames the contract says the receiver verifies — and the receiver's verified state then describes a journal no binary can restore.

## Why it matters

The tracker is the trust boundary for replication (issue #806): later phases build the writer feed, the durable receiver, and spectator serving on the guarantee that accepted frames form a restorable journal. Today that guarantee holds only for line decodability. A snapshot that rebases the chain onto a headerless / foreign-world / version-99 / double-headed journal poisons the replica at the exact moment it is supposed to replace state wholesale, and the failure only surfaces later — at restore — far from the frame that caused it, with the verified cursor already advanced past it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ReplicationTracker::accept` refuses a Snapshot whose payload does not begin with exactly one `JournalEntry::Created` header whose `world_id` equals the envelope's `world_id` and whose `version` equals the envelope's `header_version` (which is itself in `1..=MAX_JOURNAL_VERSION` per issue #4471), with a named `ReplicationError` variant; tracker state unchanged on refusal.
- [ ] A Snapshot or Tail payload containing a `Created` entry anywhere other than a Snapshot's first entry is refused (duplicate-header rule, mirroring `core.rs:232`); a Tail payload never carries a header.
- [ ] Regression tests in `replication.rs` for all five probe cases above (no header, foreign-world header, entry version ≠ envelope header version, duplicate header in a snapshot, header in a tail), each asserting refusal and unchanged cursor/header version; the existing snapshot/tail round-trip and rebase tests still pass.
- [ ] `cargo test -p id --lib world::replication` passes.

Distinct from: issue #4471 (the **envelope** `header_version` field's missing lower bound — this issue is the **payload's own header entry**, which is never checked at all; the two fixes are complementary and both belong in `accept`), issue #4454/#4455 (references.rs), and the PR #4447 fixes already on main (trailing frame bytes, undecodable entries).

title: id(replication): ReplicationTracker accepts journal header_version 0 — accept checks only the upper bound, so a signed Snapshot rebases a v1-v3 chain onto a version WorldCore::restore refuses (1..=3)

body:
## Summary

`ReplicationTracker::accept` in `pkgs/id/src/world/replication.rs` (F12.13 replication contract, landed today in PR #4447 for issue #806) refuses a journal header version only when it is **newer** than this binary supports — it has no lower bound. A correctly signed frame with `header_version = 0` is accepted:

- `replication.rs:626`: `if envelope.header_version > MAX_JOURNAL_VERSION { return Err(UnsupportedJournalVersion(...)) }` — `0` passes.
- A `Snapshot` frame with `header_version = 0` then rebases the tracker: the Snapshot branch computes the chain base for version 0, chains the payload, and sets `self.header_version = envelope.header_version` (0).
- A `Tail` frame with `header_version = 0` is likewise accepted by a tracker constructed with header version 0 (`ReplicationTracker::new` performs no range check either).

But journal header version 0 does not exist and can never be restored:

- `pkgs/id/src/world/mod.rs:928`: `pub const JOURNAL_VERSION: u32 = 1;` — journals are created at version 1; `mod.rs:946`: `MAX_JOURNAL_VERSION = 3`.
- `pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs:217`: `WorldCore::restore` accepts only `(JOURNAL_VERSION..=MAX_JOURNAL_VERSION).contains(&version)`, i.e. `1..=3`, and refuses any other header version before applying entries.

So the replication receiver's verified state can advance onto a chain (and a stored header version) that the restore path — phase 3's durable receiver — must refuse wholesale. That is the same class of divergence the follow-up fix on PR #4447 closed for undecodable entries ("a verified cursor never covers data the restore path cannot read"), one check earlier: the envelope's own header version is never held to the restore range.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-replhdr/` on the laptop — `replication.rs` copied **verbatim** from current main `4843f2e21` (md5 `f807510cedc0884c513f5a49ea81bfe6`, matched against the sandbox clone), with only a minimal `JournalEntry` stub (the three variants the module's own tests use, same serde tagging) and the real `MAX_JOURNAL_VERSION = 3` around it. `cargo test --offline`:

- `probe_header_version_zero_snapshot_is_accepted` — a signed `Snapshot` envelope with `header_version = 0`, sent to a tracker on a legitimate v1 chain, returns `Ok`, and the tracker's `header_version()` becomes `0`.
- `probe_header_version_zero_tail_is_accepted` — a signed `Tail` envelope with `header_version = 0` returns `Ok` from a tracker constructed at version 0.
- Controls pass: `header_version = 4` (`MAX + 1`) is refused with `UnsupportedJournalVersion(4)`, and a legitimate v2 snapshot is accepted and rebases to 2 — so the gap is exactly the missing lower bound, not the version machinery in general.
- The module's own in-file tests also pass in the probe (no other behavior disturbed).

The signing key in the probe is the pinned source, so this is not a forgery scenario: it is a writer bug / downgrade / confused peer producing a frame the contract says the receiver verifies — and the receiver's verified cursor then describes a journal no binary can restore.

## Why it matters

The tracker is the trust boundary for replication (design `pkgs/id/doc/2026-11-01_design_id806.md`): phases 2–5 build the writer feed, durable receiver, and spectator serving on the guarantee that accepted frames form a restorable journal. Accepting header version 0 breaks that guarantee at the first field the receiver checks, and a Snapshot makes it worse by silently **downgrading** an established v1–v3 chain to 0. Every later phase that trusts `tracker.header_version()` or the verified cursor inherits the poisoned state.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ReplicationTracker::accept` refuses any envelope whose `header_version` is outside `JOURNAL_VERSION..=MAX_JOURNAL_VERSION` (i.e. `0`, and any future below-minimum value) with `ReplicationError::UnsupportedJournalVersion`, for all three kinds (Snapshot, Tail, Terminal — a Terminal with header version 0 against a v0 tracker is the same hole).
- [ ] `ReplicationTracker::new` cannot be constructed on an out-of-range header version, or its construction is documented/checked so a v0 tracker can never accept frames (choose the shape that matches the crate's conventions; the accept-side check above is the mandatory part).
- [ ] A Snapshot can no longer move a tracker to a header version below `JOURNAL_VERSION`.
- [ ] Regression tests in `replication.rs`: signed Snapshot and Tail frames with `header_version = 0` are refused and leave tracker state (cursor + header version) unchanged; the existing v2-snapshot rebase test and the `MAX + 1` refusal test still pass.
- [ ] `cargo test -p id --lib world::replication` passes.

Distinct from: issue #4454 / issue #4455 (references.rs, PR #2756 — different module), and the two PR #4447 Codex fixes already on main (trailing frame bytes, undecodable entries — both payload-side; this is the envelope header-version bound).

title: id(references): from_markdown silently drops the character after an unescaped ']' in the label

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage

labels.name: source/creator

body:
## Problem

In `pkgs/id/src/references.rs`, `Reference::from_markdown` (:106-135) silently drops a character when it parses a label containing an unescaped `]` that is not the closing delimiter. The label loop's delimiter arm is guarded:

```rust
']' if chars.next() == Some('(') => { /* delimiter: break */ }
chr => surface.push(chr),
```

When the guard fails — the `]` is followed by anything other than `(` — the match falls through to the `chr` arm and pushes the `]`, but the character the guard already consumed with `chars.next()` is gone. It is neither pushed nor re-examined (so a dropped `(` can also destroy a real delimiter). The parse still returns `Some` with a corrupted surface instead of the intact surface or `None`.

`to_markdown` escapes every `]`, so text produced by this crate round-trips (verified: control below). The corrupted input is the degradation as written by anyone else — a hand-written note, another client, or a future renderer that does not escape — and `from_markdown`'s own doc presents it as the inverse of the degradation ("the ID and surface — the meaning and the label — round-trip exactly, whatever the surface contains"). A parser for a stored-reference format must not silently rewrite the label it was given: the surface is what a citation displays, and a one-character deletion is exactly the kind of quiet corruption the escaping exists to prevent.

Related but distinct: this module currently does not compile on main (#4454; one of its two errors is also in `from_markdown`, at the `strip_suffix` line a few lines below this guard). Whoever rewrites that line will be working in this exact loop — this issue exists so the guard semantics are fixed in the same pass, not preserved by accident.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-refcleared/` (same probe as the companion cleared-resolution issue filed this run; `references.rs` from main `466cf98fb`, md5 `b939a8c3b71faa4fef2958834888ce1c`, with only the stub Hash/AuthorKey surface and two disclosed compile shims for the #4454 errors — the label-loop guard is byte-identical to production):

- P3: parsing the hand-written text `[a]b](id://<64-hex>)` returns `Some` with surface `"a]"` — the `b` after the unescaped `]` was consumed by the failed guard and dropped.
- CONTROL3: a `Reference` with surface `"a]b"` written by `to_markdown` (which escapes the `]` as `\]`) parses back to exactly `"a]b"` — the crate's own output is unaffected; only unescaped input corrupts, silently.

Dedup: title/keyword searches for `from_markdown reference`, `LocalIndex`, `references cleared resolve` across open and closed issues find only the #2259 PoC epic and #4454 (the compile errors) — neither covers the guard's character drop.

## Why it matters

A stored reference's surface is a historical label: the module doc stresses it is "kept verbatim" and "never silently rewritten". A parser that deletes a character and reports success breaks that promise at the exact boundary where foreign text enters — and because it returns `Some`, no caller can detect the corruption. The fix is small (peek instead of consume, or refuse an unescaped `]`), but it has to be chosen deliberately while #4454's rewrite touches the same lines.

## Acceptance criteria

- `from_markdown` on a label containing an unescaped `]` either returns the surface intact or returns `None` — it never returns `Some` with a character missing. The chosen behaviour is documented at `from_markdown`.
- The delimiter detection does not consume a character it does not use (e.g. it peeks, as the iterator is already `Peekable`).
- New unit tests cover: an unescaped `]` mid-label, an unescaped `]` as the label's last character before the delimiter, and the existing escaped round-trip cases; the existing `references` tests pass once the module compiles again (#4454).

title: id(references): resolve and insert_unambiguous ignore the tombstone — cleared targets still resolve, receive new commits, and contest live targets

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: status/duplicate
labels.description: Already tracked elsewhere

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

In `pkgs/id/src/references.rs` (the friendly-name reference-resolution PoC, #2259), resolution never reads `IndexedObject.cleared`. The tombstone flag is written by `LocalIndex::clear` (:353-360) and read in exactly one place — `render` (:553) — while `resolve` (:383), `claimants` (:365), `best_match` (:408) and `insert_unambiguous` (:497) all treat a cleared target as fully live. Two consequences, both verified below:

- **A fresh reference can be committed to a tombstone.** When the only matching target is already cleared, `resolve` returns it as an ordinary candidate and `insert_unambiguous` returns `Ok` — the author's "unambiguous" commit succeeds, and the reference renders `Cleared` the first time it is shown. The `Cleared` render state exists for a target cleared *after* a reference was stored (module doc, four rendering states); nothing in the module's contract contemplates committing a new reference to a target the store already tombstoned.
- **A tombstone contests like a live rival.** `claimants` counts cleared objects, so when one live and one cleared object share a title/alias surface, the live target's exact match is marked `Contested` and `insert_unambiguous` refuses with `Ambiguous(2)` — byte-for-byte the same outcome as two live rivals (the by-design contested case). A dead claim blocks the live target's auto-commit indefinitely, because the tombstone never leaves the index.

Note: this module currently does not compile on main — that is tracked separately as #4454 (two errors, neither in the resolution path). This issue is about the resolution logic, which is independent of those errors; sequencing it after #4454 is fine.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Full-file read plus a laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-refcleared/` (`cargo run --release`, rustc 1.98, edition 2024) with `references.rs` copied from main `466cf98fb` (md5 `b939a8c3b71faa4fef2958834888ce1c`). The resolution code (`resolve`/`claimants`/`best_match`/`insert_unambiguous`/`render`/`clear`) is byte-identical to production; the probe carries only the surface the module uses — a stub `p2panda_core::Hash` (digest/to_hex/FromStr), `AuthorKey = [u8;32]` — plus two disclosed compile shims for the #4454 errors (a probe-local `Default for StoreId` impl, and owning the stripped hex `String` in `from_markdown`), neither of which touches the resolution path.

- CONTROL (one live object, title "Roadmap"): `candidates=1 contested=false`, `insert_unambiguous = Ok`, renders `Resolved`.
- P1 (the same object, cleared before resolution): `candidates=1 contested=false`, `insert_unambiguous = Ok` (reference committed), and rendering that just-committed reference gives `state=Cleared`.
- P2 (one live + one cleared object, both titled "Atlas"): `candidates=2 contested=true single=None`, `insert_unambiguous = Err(Ambiguous(2))`.
- CONTROL2 (two live objects titled "Atlas"): `candidates=2 contested=true` — P2 is indistinguishable from the by-design live-rival case.

Grep on current main confirms the mechanism: `cleared` occurs at :274 (field), :357 (set by `clear`), :553 (read by `render`) and in tests — nowhere in the resolution path.

Dedup: title/keyword searches for `references cleared resolve`, `LocalIndex`, `insert_unambiguous`, `friendly-name references` across open and closed issues find only the #2259 PoC epic and unrelated items — none covers cleared-target resolution. #4454 covers only the module's two compile errors.

## Why it matters

The module's core promise is "nothing is picked silently" — contested and ambiguous phrases are shown, never auto-committed. That promise is about *live* alternatives. Today a tombstone both (a) silently receives new commits as if it were the unambiguous live answer, producing citations that are dead on arrival, and (b) silently vetoes auto-commit for a genuinely unambiguous live target forever. As the PoC's index is fed from real store state (the v2 fan-out the spec plans), cleared documents/notes are common, so both failure modes would be routine, not exotic.

## Acceptance criteria

- `resolve` does not return cleared targets as candidates (or, if returning them is decided to be intentional, they are marked distinctly from live candidates and the module doc says so — silence is not an accepted outcome).
- `insert_unambiguous` never commits a reference whose only match is a cleared target: it returns `NoMatch` (or a dedicated error) in that case.
- `claimants` does not count cleared objects: a live target whose only surface rival is tombstoned resolves uncontested and `insert_unambiguous` succeeds for it.
- `render`'s `Cleared` state is unchanged (a target cleared *after* its reference was stored still degrades to its label).
- New unit tests cover: cleared-only match, live+cleared same-surface, and the existing live+live contested control; the existing `references` tests pass once the module compiles again (#4454).

body:
Follow-up filed from the Phase 3b closing inventory (issue #3456, design #3455).

## Problem

`sanitize_name` (`pkgs/id/src/web/identity.rs:559-569`) strips control characters plus only the bidi override/isolate subset (`is_bidi_override_or_isolate`: U+061C, U+200E/U+200F, U+202A-U+202E, U+2066-U+2069):

```rust
.filter(|ch| !ch.is_control() && !is_bidi_override_or_isolate(*ch))
```

The rest of the shared Cf set passes through to collab display names and cursor frames: U+200B (zero-width space), U+FEFF (zero-width no-break space), U+00AD (soft hyphen), U+2060-U+2064, U+FFF9-U+FFFB, etc. The existing test even pins ZWJ/ZWNJ pass-through (`a\u{200d}b\u{200c}c` unchanged). A zero-width look-alike name renders identically to a plain one — the look-alike half of the #3455 contract.

## Why not fixed in the audit branch

Extending the filter to the full shared set (`crate::is_format_char`, Unicode 16 Cf in `id-core/src/unicode.rs`) changes existing-name behavior: ZWJ/ZWNJ-joined names (family emoji sequences) that collab currently keeps would be stripped, and collab display names are user-visible persistent state. That needs a product decision (strip-all vs strip-with-joiner-exception like `sanitize_chat`), not an audit drive-by.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Decide: full shared Cf strip, or strip with the ZWJ/ZWNJ exception (`sanitize_chat` precedent in `pkgs/id/src/world/util.rs:95-103`).
- [ ] Wire the decision to the shared `crate::is_format_char` set — no local subset.
- [ ] Regression tests: U+200B/U+FEFF/U+00AD stripped; joiner decision pinned; bidi behavior unchanged.

body:
## Summary

`LocalIndex::resolve` in `pkgs/id/src/references.rs` (landed by PR #2756 for #2259) never looks at `IndexedObject.cleared`. A tombstoned target is offered as an ordinary candidate, is auto-picked by `Resolution::single()`, and can be committed by `insert_unambiguous` — a fresh reference that `render` immediately reports as `RenderState::Cleared`. A cleared object also still counts in `claimants`, so a tombstone sharing a title with a live object makes the **live** object read as contested and blocks its unambiguous insert. The `Candidate` type carries no cleared marker, so nothing downstream can tell a dead candidate from a live one.

Relevant code (main 466cf98fb, `references.rs`):

- `resolve` (:383-407) iterates all objects of the sigil and calls `best_match` — no `cleared` filter.
- `best_match` (:410-475) never reads `object.cleared` either; the petname tier (:430-444) likewise.
- `claimants` (:368-380) counts cleared objects as claimants for contested determination.
- `render` (:543-578) is the only place `cleared` is honored — after the reference already exists.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-references/` — verbatim `references.rs` (md5 `b939a8c3b71faa4fef2958834888ce1c`) plus the two minimal compile fixes described in #4454 (the module does not compile as landed; the fixes touch only the `StoreId` Default impl and an owned `String` in `from_markdown`, neither of which affects resolution). The module's 12 own tests pass in the probe; two added probe tests (`tests/cleared.rs`, log `patched-output.txt`) demonstrate:

```
cleared_target_still_resolves_and_auto_inserts ... ok
  — index holding ONLY a cleared "Roadmap": resolve("roadmap") returns 1 candidate
    for the tombstone, single() returns it, insert_unambiguous succeeds, and the
    fresh reference immediately renders as RenderState::Cleared.
cleared_duplicate_makes_live_target_contested ... ok
  — one live "Minutes" + one cleared "Minutes": resolve returns 2 candidates,
    is_contested() is true, insert_unambiguous("minutes") fails Ambiguous(2)
    even though only one live target exists.
```

## Why it matters

The design record (`doc/2026-10-30T13-25-00Z_design_friendly_name_references.md` §4) defines the cleared state for **rendering stored references** — a citation degrades to its label. It never sanctions minting new references to tombstones, and the contested rule it adopts ("two or more claims for the same surface") is about live claims an author must choose between. As written, deletion of a document silently (a) keeps it insertable by anyone resolving its name, and (b) poisons the name for the live document that replaced it — the exact ambiguity the contested rule exists to surface only when a real choice exists.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `resolve` does not return candidates for cleared objects (all tiers, including petname matches), **or** candidates for cleared objects are explicitly marked as cleared in `Candidate` and excluded from `single()` / `insert_unambiguous` — one stated rule, documented in the module docs.
- [ ] `claimants` does not count cleared objects: a live target whose only same-surface namesake is cleared resolves uncontested and `insert_unambiguous` succeeds.
- [ ] Existing behavior for stored references is unchanged: `render` still reports `RenderState::Cleared` for a reference whose target was cleared after insertion (existing test `a_cleared_target_degrades_to_its_label` still passes).
- [ ] New tests cover: cleared-only phrase resolves to no auto-insertable candidate; live+cleared duplicate inserts unambiguously; the module's existing 12 tests still pass (after the #4454 compile fix).

Distinct from: #4454 (the same module's compile errors — this issue is the resolution semantics, visible only once the module compiles), #2259 (the PoC tracker this module implements), #4298 (notes.rs cyclic revise parents — different module).
