body:
## Summary

`pkgs/id/src/references.rs`, landed today by PR #2756 (merge 4b6d1f930, 2026-11-02T16:04Z, for #2259), does not compile. The module is declared unconditionally (`pub mod references;`, `pkgs/id/src/lib.rs:213`), so the `id` lib build on current main (verified at 466cf98fb) fails with two errors, both in `references.rs`:

1. **E0277 — `LocalIndex` derives `Default` over a field whose type has none.** `references.rs:301-303`: `#[derive(Clone, Debug, Default)] pub struct LocalIndex { store: StoreId, ... }`, but `StoreId` (`references.rs:61-63`) derives only `Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord`, and there is no `impl Default for StoreId` anywhere in `pkgs/id/src`, `pkgs/id/crates`, or `pkgs/id/tests` (grep-verified this run).
2. **E0597 — `Reference::from_markdown` breaks out of its parse loop with a borrow of a loop-local `String`.** `references.rs:122-124`: the arm binds `let rest: String = chars.collect();` and then `break rest.strip_prefix("id://")?.strip_suffix(')')?;` — the break value is a `&str` borrowed from `rest`, which is dropped at the end of the match arm while the borrowed value is stored in `hex` outside the loop.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-references/` on the laptop — `references.rs` copied **verbatim** from main (md5 `b939a8c3b71faa4fef2958834888ce1c`, matched against the sandbox clone, the laptop copy, and the GitHub API copy of the file at main), with only a minimal `p2panda_core::Hash` shim and a `waiting::AuthorKey = [u8; 32]` stub around it. `cargo test --offline` on the verbatim file (log: `verbatim-output.txt` in the probe dir):

```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `StoreId: Default` is not satisfied   (src/references.rs:303)
error[E0597]: `rest` does not live long enough                      (src/references.rs:124)
error: could not compile `probe` (lib) due to 2 previous errors     (cargo-exit:101)
```

Both error patterns were additionally reproduced as minimal standalone files on **both** rustc 1.98 and the repo-pinned rustc 1.99 (edition 2024), so neither is a shim or toolchain artifact. With exactly two minimal fixes applied to the probe copy only — a `Default` impl for `StoreId` in the probe's `lib.rs`, and `.to_owned()` on the `from_markdown` break value — the module compiles and **all 12 of its own unit tests pass** (`patched-output.txt`), confirming these are the only two errors and that the tests were written against a compiling version that never landed.

Caveat: a full `cargo check -p id --lib` on the real crate was started in a laptop fleet worktree but stayed blocked behind another lane's build-directory lock for the duration of this run; the verbatim-file probe plus the isolated reproductions are the verification. PR #2756's checks at merge were CodeRabbit only (skipping) — no CI compile ran on it.

## Why it matters

Every `id` build, test run, and Nix build on main is broken until this is fixed, and the failure is invisible to the feature-gated build-rot issues already tracked (#4340 web-feature tests, #4159 `--no-default-features`, #3962 ssh feature — all different feature sets; this one is the **default** lib build). Any lane now building pkgs/id on current main will hit these two errors first and may misattribute them to its own change.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `cargo check -p id --lib` (default features) compiles on main: `StoreId` gains a `Default` impl (or `LocalIndex` drops the derive and constructs its store explicitly), and `from_markdown` no longer borrows across the loop break (e.g. the hex slice is owned, or `rest` is bound outside the loop).
- [ ] `cargo test -p id --lib references` passes — the module's 12 existing unit tests, including the markdown round-trip tests that exercise `from_markdown`.
- [ ] No other module's behavior changes; the fix is confined to `references.rs` (plus, if the `Default` impl is placed there, that same file).

Distinct from: #4340 (web-feature test rot in `web/routes.rs`), #4159 (`--no-default-features` gating in chat.rs/invite.rs), #3962 (ssh-feature compile), #3923 (id-core test compile — different crate).

body:
## Summary

`pm-stack/grist/update-choice-options.py` makes every Grist API call through `api()` (line 60–69), which calls `urllib.request.urlopen(req)` with **no `timeout` argument** — so all three calls the tool makes (GET columns, PATCH columns, GET read-back verification) block forever if the server accepts the connection but never responds. The sibling script in the same directory, `reload-doc.sh` (line 57–60), bounds every one of its curl calls with `--max-time 30`; the Python tool is the outlier.

## Evidence

- `pm-stack/grist/update-choice-options.py:67` — `with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as resp:` — no timeout is passed anywhere in the file (only urlopen call site; `grep -n "urlopen\|timeout"` shows no timeout).
- `pm-stack/grist/reload-doc.sh:57-60` — the house pattern in the same directory: `curl --fail --silent --show-error --max-time 30` for every API call.
- Verified this run on the laptop with the verbatim script @100098293 (md5 `7b363aa70281e4b7abffee872b466791`, matching the sandbox checkout): imported the module's own `api()` and called it against a black-hole TCP server that accepts the connection and never sends a byte — `api()` was **still blocked after 5.0 s** with no error and no diagnostic (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-gristtimeout/probe.py`, output `api() STILL BLOCKED after 5.0s against a silent server`). Python's `urlopen` default is an infinite socket timeout, so it would block indefinitely.
- The stall scenario is realistic for this stack: a Grist server mid-restart or mid document-reload (the exact condition `reload-doc.sh` exists to manage, #1288) accepts connections before it can answer them.

## Why it matters

The tool is run by an operator (and is the documented way to extend Choice columns, per CHOICE-OPTIONS.md) precisely when the Grist doc is being changed or reloaded — the moments a stall is most likely. Today that produces a silent, unbounded hang with no output after "adding […]" is printed, indistinguishable from a slow success; the operator cannot tell whether the PATCH landed. A bounded timeout turns it into a clear exit-1 failure, matching the tool's documented exit-code contract and the sibling script's 30 s bound.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `api()` passes an explicit timeout to `urlopen` (30 s, matching `reload-doc.sh`'s `--max-time 30`, or a `--timeout` flag defaulting to it).
- [ ] A stalled server produces a non-zero exit with a message naming the timeout, instead of hanging (cover GET, PATCH, and the read-back GET — they all share `api()`).
- [ ] Existing behaviour is unchanged against a healthy server: `test_update_choice_options.py` still passes, and a stub-server test (accept-and-never-respond) proves the call fails within the bound rather than blocking.

## Dedup note

Checked open and closed issues for `grist` / `update-choice-options` / timeout on 2026-11-02: #1288 (live-apply of external doc changes) and the other grist issues do not cover this tool's HTTP calls. The unbounded-fetch findings in sibling tools (#4191 codedb-bridge, #2175 meta-exporter) are different programs; this one is the grist tool's own call sites.

body:
## Problem

`resolve_web_bindings` (`pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:422-462`) returns the
listener list exactly as supplied, with no duplicate check, on both
non-legacy paths:

- `--web-listen` flags (serve.rs:439-442): the flag values are mapped
  straight into `WebBinding`s.
- `[web_bindings]` entries from `defaults.conf` (serve.rs:444-461): each
  line is parsed and collected, duplicates included.

Startup then binds the listeners one by one (serve.rs:~1302, bind loop
under the #2145 comment "any bind failure aborts startup"). Binding an
address that is already bound by the same process fails, so a repeated
entry — an easy copy-paste error in `defaults.conf`, or a repeated
`--web-listen` flag — aborts `id serve --web` startup with:

```text
web: failed to bind listener 127.0.0.1:3000: Address already in use (os error 98)
```

That message points at a *foreign* process holding the port; nothing
tells the operator the address appears twice in their own listener set.

## Evidence (verified this run, 2026-11-02)

- serve.rs:422-462 — read directly at main `d1de7ee86`: neither the flag
  branch nor the config branch deduplicates or rejects duplicates; the
  only validations are the `--bind`/`--port` conflict and per-line parse
  errors.
- serve.rs:~1302 — the startup bind loop binds each resolved binding in
  order and aborts on the first failure, so the second copy of a
  duplicated address always fails there.
- OS semantics re-verified this run on the laptop: two listeners on the
  same `127.0.0.1:<port>` (even with `SO_REUSEADDR`, which Rust's
  `TcpListener` sets on Unix) — the second bind fails with
  `EADDRINUSE` / "Address already in use".
- Existing tests (serve.rs:2382-2495) cover legacy fallback, flags-win,
  config-only, IPv6 scope IDs, the flag conflict, and malformed config
  lines — no duplicate-entry case.
- Contrast: the bootstrap list in the same binary *is* deduplicated
  preserving order (`crates/id-core/src/discovery.rs`, `resolve_config`:
  "Append CLI-provided bootstrap nodes, then deduplicate (preserving
  order)"), so the listener list is the inconsistent outlier.
- Dedup check this run: open + recently closed issue search for
  `web_bindings` / `resolve_web_bindings` / duplicate listener returned
  no covering issue. The bindings model itself is #2145.

Note on scope: port `0` entries are *not* duplicates after binding (the
OS assigns distinct ports), and overlapping-but-not-identical addresses
(e.g. `0.0.0.0:3000` vs `127.0.0.1:3000`) also conflict at bind time —
the acceptance criteria below leave both decisions to the fix, as long
as the identical-entry case is diagnosed clearly.

## Why it matters

`[web_bindings]` is a build-time embedded config edited by hand, and
`--web-listen` is repeatable by design — a duplicated line is a likely
operator error, and today it costs a full startup abort with an error
that sends the operator hunting for a nonexistent other process.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A listener set containing the same socket address twice (from
      `--web-listen`, from `[web_bindings]`, or split across both is
      impossible by precedence — flags win entirely) is either
      deduplicated preserving order, or refused at resolve time with an
      error that names the duplicated address and its source. Either
      behaviour is acceptable; silently passing duplicates to the bind
      loop is not.
- [ ] The chosen behaviour is covered by unit tests next to the existing
      `test_resolve_web_bindings_*` tests, for both the flag path and
      the config path.
- [ ] Existing `test_resolve_web_bindings_*` tests still pass; distinct
      listeners (including IPv6 scope-ID forms and port-0 entries) are
      unaffected.

body:
## Finding

PR #3096 (merged, head `1b0327c346`) removed the pipe stage's `" -\n"` replacement on the grounds that the dead literal replaces never matched. That is true of `" -$"`, but `" -\n"` was functional: it substituted a mid-line `-` placeholder that is followed by a newline (a form a substitution can produce). Without it, a newline-separated mid-line placeholder is no longer substituted — the content is appended at the end instead and the literal `-` stays in the command, which the stdin-content handler then rejects, so nothing is stored. Codex raised this as a P2 on the PR (comment 4432995820); it was never replied to, and the PR's final Codex review state on the merged head is `has_unresolved_findings: true`.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/3096 — merged 2026-11-01, merge commit `d00c6d10aafb479cc92d6ae85b8b78f04c3cba54`, final head `1b0327c3467ddb1b366d6c7b6f7e1aa8a82755eb`.
- Current main (`d1de7ee86`): `pkgs/id/src/repl/input.rs:639` — the pipe stage substitutes only `right.replace(" - ", ...)`; when no marker is produced, the fallback at `input.rs:641-645` appends `__STDIN_CONTENT__:<output>` at the very end of the right side.
- Codex example: `echo hi |> $(printf 'put -\n name')` previously produced `Ready("put __STDIN_CONTENT__:hi\n name")`, which `handle_stdin_content` accepts and stores under `name`. On current main it produces `Ready("put -\n name __STDIN_CONTENT__:hi")`, whose prefix that handler rejects as an unknown command, so nothing is stored.
- Verified still present on current main by reading the pipe stage at `pkgs/id/src/repl/input.rs:627-649` — no `" -\n"` (or equivalent newline-boundary) case exists.
- Dedupe: searched open + closed issues for `3096 placeholder`, `pipe placeholder newline` (2026-11-02) — only the parent fix #2280 (closed) matches; it does not cover this regression.

## Why it matters

A supported placeholder form silently changed meaning in a merged PR: content that used to be stored under the intended name now makes the whole command fail downstream with an unrelated "unknown command" error. Either the form should keep working, or it should be rejected at preprocessing with the clear placeholder diagnostic — the current fall-through does neither.

## Acceptance criteria

- `echo hi |> $(printf 'put -\n name')` once again yields a `Ready` line that `handle_stdin_content` accepts and stores under `name` (placeholder substituted in place), OR the form is rejected during preprocessing with the trailing/misplaced-placeholder diagnostic — with the chosen behavior pinned by a test.
- A regression test covers a mid-line placeholder followed by a newline in the pipe stage.
- Existing #3096 tests still pass (trailing placeholders still rejected before execution; mid-line space-separated placeholders unchanged).
- `cargo test --lib repl::` passes in CI.

title: id(currency): RateAuthorisation::validate checks only issuer and rate_den — inverted amount bounds, empty/inverted validity window, >100% fee_bps, zero rate and same-ledger bodies all fold Live, and a malformed higher version shadows a good one

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

In `pkgs/id/src/currency.rs`, `RateAuthorisation::validate` is the only validity gate the fold trusts — and it checks exactly two things (issuer match, `rate_den != 0`). Every other validity condition the type's own field docs state is never checked anywhere, `sign_authorisation` never calls `validate` at all, and the fold crowns the highest "valid" version — so a malformed authorisation signs, folds `Live`, and a malformed higher version permanently shadows a good lower one (the fold doc: no older version revives once a higher exists).

- `pkgs/id/src/currency.rs:152-163` — `validate()` checks only `issuer_id == author` and `rate_den == 0`. Its rustdoc (:146-151) names only those two errors, matching the one field with explicit validity language: `rate_den` is "non-zero in a valid authorisation" (:104-106).
- The unchecked documented conditions: `min_amount` is the "Smallest convertible amount" and `max_amount` the "Largest" (:108-112) — `min > max` is a contradiction no conversion can satisfy; `not_before` is "No conversions before this time" and `expires_at` the "Mandatory expiry: no conversions at or after" (:118-121) — `expires_at <= not_before` is an empty/inverted window; `fee_bps` is a "fee in basis points" (:124-126) — above 10,000 bps the fee exceeds 100% of the conversion; the module doc (:10-14) defines the object as one direction `source_ledger` → `dest_ledger` — identical ledgers are a degenerate self-conversion; `rate_num == 0` makes `apply_rate` return `Some(0)` for every amount (:169-175).
- `pkgs/id/src/currency.rs:279-311` — `fold_authorisation` filters candidates by `body.validate(author).is_ok()` (:291, under the doc at :262-277: "Among the expected issuer's valid versions the highest is the candidate") and crowns the highest version `Live`. An unchecked-malformed v2 therefore displaces a good v1, and since revocation/supersession never revives a lower version, the authorisation is bricked by its own malformed successor.
- `pkgs/id/src/currency.rs:313-336` — `sign_authorisation` serializes and signs any body without calling `validate`: even the two existing checks are sign-time unenforced, so an issuer can publish a zero-denominator authorisation the fold will silently drop (`fold` → `None`) while believing it live.

This is Phase 1 library code (#3800, closed), but the Phase 2/3 gateway (#3801/#3802, on #2290) will consume `fold_authorisation`'s `Live` state as its trust input — the gate should mean what the docs say before a gateway builds on it.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-currencyvalidate/` with `currency.rs` copied verbatim from `pkgs/id/src/currency.rs` (production code, md5 `291c105842289c856635a2b69ffd1d72`, identical in the sandbox clone at main `a0ff47b41` and the laptop checkout; only the `#[cfg(test)]` module was stripped and `crate::chain` stubbed to the surface `currency.rs` uses — `validate`/`fold_authorisation`/`apply_rate` are pure and unmodified), `cargo run --release`, using the #2290 worked example from the module's own tests as the baseline body:

- BASELINE (min 1 ≤ max 10,000, window 0 → 4102444800, no fee): `validate=Ok(())`, fold = `Live`.
- P1 `min_amount=10_001, max_amount=10_000`: `validate=Ok(())`, fold = `Live`.
- P2 `not_before=1000, expires_at=1000` (empty window): `validate=Ok(())`, fold = `Live`.
- P3 `not_before=2000, expires_at=1000` (inverted window): `validate=Ok(())`, fold = `Live`.
- P4 `fee_bps=Some(20_000)` (a 200% fee): `validate=Ok(())`, fold = `Live`.
- P5 `rate_num=0`: `validate=Ok(())`, `apply_rate(100)=Some(0)`, fold = `Live`.
- P6 `source_ledger == dest_ledger == "ABC"`: `validate=Ok(())`, fold = `Live`.
- CONTROL `rate_den=0`: `validate=Err(ZeroRateDenominator)`, fold = `None` — the one documented check beyond issuer works.
- P7 shadowing: good v1 + inverted-bounds v2 → fold = `Live` version 2 (min 10001, max 10000); the good v1 is unreachable.

Dedup: title/keyword searches for `RateAuthorisation`, currency-validate, fee_bps and min_amount across open and closed issues find only the #2290 design (open), the closed Phase 1 implementation #3800, and the gateway phases #3801/#3802 — none covers validation completeness.

## Why it matters

`Live` is the fold's promise that an authorisation is usable. Today it also covers authorisations that can never convert (inverted bounds, empty window), that charge more than the converted amount in fees, or that convert a ledger into itself — and because version selection trusts `validate`, one malformed successor silently retires every good earlier version. The issuer-side sign path compounds it: nothing stops publishing a body the fold will drop or crown wrongly. Fixing the gate now is cheap; after the #3801/#3802 gateway treats `Live` as authoritative, each unchecked case becomes a gateway bug instead of a library inconsistency.

## Acceptance criteria

- `RateAuthorisation::validate` rejects, with named `ValidateError` variants: `min_amount > max_amount`; `expires_at <= not_before`; `fee_bps > 10_000`. For `rate_num == 0` and `source_ledger == dest_ledger`, the fix either rejects them in `validate` too or documents explicitly at the field why they are intentionally valid — silence is not an accepted outcome.
- `sign_authorisation` refuses a body that `validate` rejects (sign/validate symmetry), or the asymmetry is documented as intentional at `sign_authorisation` with the reason.
- New unit tests cover each rejected case at both `validate` and the fold (a malformed higher version no longer crowns over a good lower version — it is skipped by the fold's validity filter, like the zero-denominator control), and the existing `currency` tests pass unchanged.
- The `validate` rustdoc lists every condition it checks, so the Phase 2 gateway (#3801/#3802) can rely on the doc as the contract.

title: id(world_caps): CapLedger usage accounting grows one entry per distinct unknown cap name forever — a guest program mints unbounded host memory and CapsReport size

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

In `pkgs/id`, the world capability ledger's usage accounting inserts a new map entry for **every distinct capability name it is asked about, including names that are not capabilities at all**, and nothing ever bounds or evicts those entries. A world guest program — the untrusted code the capability system exists to confine — can therefore grow host memory for the whole life of the world actor, one ≤64-byte key at a time, and every `CapsReport` then clones the whole map.

- `pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/world_caps.rs:544-552` — `CapLedger::decide_for` does `self.usage.entry(cap.to_owned()).or_default()` **before** the `is_known(cap)` check, so an unknown name is permanently recorded with `denied = 1` instead of being refused without state. The catalog (`CATALOG`, :72-90) has 17 names, so legitimate per-name accounting could never exceed 17 entries.
- The names are program-controlled and renewable without limit: `parse_wants` bounds **one** document (`MAX_WANTS_ENTRIES` = 64 requests, `MAX_NAME_BYTES` = 64 bytes per name), but a program issues requests across unlimited calls. The host feeds them straight to the ledger: `pkgs/id/src/world/actor.rs:631` (`execute` → `decide_for(&request.cap, …)`) and `pkgs/id/src/world/actor.rs:526` (`apply_subscriptions` → `decide(sub.cap())`).
- Subscriptions are worse: for an unrecognized spec, `Subscription::cap()` returns the **whole spec string** (`world_caps.rs:176-182`), so every distinct junk spec — not just distinct cap names — mints its own ledger entry.
- The cost is paid repeatedly: `pkgs/id/src/world/actor.rs:998` clones `ledger.usage()` into every `CapsReport`. The module docs (:44-46) say a usage count "bounds nothing" — true of the counts, but the map **key set** is unbounded host state, unlike the sibling bounds this module does enforce (`MAX_PENDING_SCHEDULES`, `MAX_TICK_INTERVALS`, chat-presence's bounded tables in #4004/#3991).

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-capusage/` with `world_caps.rs` copied verbatim from `pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/world_caps.rs` (md5 `cddc6508d0796d07a808bc472c9bafac`, identical in the sandbox clone at main `4e95fc59c` and the laptop checkout), `cargo run --release`:

- PROBE1: 10,000 × `decide("bogus-{i}")` with distinct unknown names → `usage().len() == 10_000` (sample entry `bogus-9999` has `denied = 1`). Growth is exactly 1 entry per distinct junk name, unbounded.
- PROBE2 (control): 10,000 × `decide("time.now")` with one known name → `usage().len() == 1`. Known-name accounting is already bounded by the catalog; only unknown names leak.
- PROBE3: 1,000 × `decide(Subscription::parse("bogus-sub-{i}").cap())` → `usage().len() == 1_000`. The subscription path mints entries per distinct spec.
- PROBE4: 4 successive `parse_wants` documents × 64 distinct unknown request caps each (every document individually inside the `MAX_WANTS_ENTRIES` bound) → `usage().len() == 256`. Per-document bounds do not accumulate into any ledger bound.

## Why it matters

The ledger lives in the host for the lifetime of a world, and world programs are guest code run under fuel/memory caps precisely because they are not trusted with host resources — yet this map sits outside every cap (`SandboxLimits` bounds the guest, not the host's ledger). A buggy or malicious program that randomizes cap names (or subscription specs) inflates host RAM and makes each caps report bigger, forever, with no error anywhere. Denied-unknown is also the highest-frequency junk case, so the leak is on the default path, not an edge case.

## Acceptance criteria

- Asking about an unknown capability no longer grows `CapLedger::usage` without bound: distinct unknown names/specs aggregate into a fixed number of entries (e.g. one shared unknown bucket) or the map is otherwise capped at a named bound; the refusal (`Decision::Deny(CapError::unknown())`) is unchanged.
- Per-name allowed/denied counts for the 17 catalog capabilities are unchanged, and `CapsReport.usage` stays ≤ catalog size plus the fixed unknown accounting.
- A unit test drives ≥10,000 distinct unknown cap names (and distinct unknown subscription specs) through `decide`/`decide_for` and asserts the bounded usage length; existing `world_caps` and world actor tests pass.
- The chosen bound/aggregation is named in the module docs next to the other `MAX_*` bounds in `world_caps.rs`.

title: id(id-core): ScreenSurface::fit returns a dimension-invalid screen for a zero viewport — fit(0, h) / fit(w, 0) yield width/height 0 that from_cells and render_ansi reject

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

body:
## Problem

`ScreenSurface::fit` (`pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/world_presentation.rs:85-113`) can return a screen that the same module's own validation rejects: fitting to a zero width or zero height produces a `width == 0` / `height == 0` surface with zero cells.

- `fit` clamps only above: `width.min(usize::from(self.width))` (line 86) — a requested `0` passes straight through.
- The constructor `from_cells` (lines 56-66) requires width `1..=MAX_SCREEN_WIDTH` (120) and height `1..=MAX_SCREEN_HEIGHT` (50), and `is_valid` (lines ~505-515) returns `false` for `width == 0 || height == 0`, so `render_ansi()` on the fitted screen returns `None`.
- `fit`'s own doc says it crops "so the returned grid remains valid" — true for the wide-glyph case it handles, false for a zero dimension.
- The only existing fit test (`viewport_crops_rows_and_does_not_split_wide_graphemes`) covers `fit(1, 1)`; no test pins a zero dimension.

## Evidence (verified this run, 2026-11-02)

Verbatim copy of `fit` plus the dimension arm of `is_valid` compiled and run on the laptop (probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-fit/`, `main.rs` md5 `5018a9e61183ce295dad328fba3ca40f`, source @ `086474ee3`):

```
fit(0,2)   -> width=0 height=2 cells=0 dims_valid=false
fit(4,0)   -> width=4 height=0 cells=0 dims_valid=false
fit(0,0)   -> width=0 height=0 cells=0 dims_valid=false
fit(1,1)   -> width=1 height=1 cells=1 dims_valid=true
fit(4,2)   -> width=4 height=2 cells=8 dims_valid=true
fit(500,200) -> width=4 height=2 cells=8 dims_valid=true
```

Reachability today: the two in-repo callers happen to be guarded upstream — `world_session` validates `Resize` frames to width 1..=500 / height 1..=200 before clamping (`src/world_session/mod.rs`, "viewport dimensions must be…"), and the actor fallback (`src/world/actor.rs:1245`) passes those same session dimensions. But `fit` is a public `id-core` API whose contract is the valid grid; nothing in its signature or docs states a non-zero precondition, and a presenter that fits to a terminal reporting 0 columns/rows (a real state for detached/resizing terminals) gets a silently unrenderable screen instead of a defined result. `WorldHandle::view_at` (`src/world/handle.rs:690`) also takes raw `u16` width/height with no zero check of its own.

## Why it matters

A crop helper that can emit a value its own type considers invalid pushes an invisible failure downstream: `render_ansi() -> None` reads as "no frame", not "bad viewport", so the symptom is a blank client with nothing pointing at the cause. Every other constructor/parser in this module (`from_cells`, `parse_surface`, `ScreenPatch::apply`) enforces the 1..=MAX dimension invariant at the boundary; `fit` is the one producer that doesn't.

## Acceptance criteria

- `fit(0, h)`, `fit(w, 0)` and `fit(0, 0)` no longer return a dimension-invalid surface: either clamp each dimension to at least 1 (consistent with the module's other producers), or change the API so the zero case is explicit — with the chosen behaviour documented on `fit`.
- New tests pin the zero-width, zero-height and zero-both cases, plus a fit to the source's own dimensions remaining the identity.
- Existing `world_presentation` tests still pass, including the wide-glyph crop test.
- If the fix clamps, a comment/doc line states that a zero viewport is treated as 1, so future presenters don't re-derive it.

Distinct from #2910 (ScreenPatch::apply cell validation) and #942 (actor oversized-layout fallback size check): neither covers `fit`'s dimension invariant.

title: sync-models: removeJsoncPath silently deletes a trailing comment on the removed member's closing line

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

labels.name: app/sync-models
labels.description: bin/sync-models.mjs model catalog sync

body:
## Problem

`bin/sync-models.mjs` edits `opencode.jsonc` as text specifically so comments survive: "comment-preserving JSONC edits. The file is edited as text, one member at a time, so every byte outside the edited span (comments included) is kept" (bin/sync-models.mjs:283-284). The removal path breaks that contract for one comment position: a `//` comment trailing the removed member on its value's closing line is silently deleted with the member.

`removeJsoncPath` (bin/sync-models.mjs:406-424) deletes the span from the member's line start through the end of the line its value ends on: it advances `end` past the value, spaces, and at most one comma (:419-421), then cuts to the next newline (:421-422). Anything between that comma and the newline — typically a trailing comment explaining the entry — is inside the deleted span. The function's own doc comment (:404-405) only promises "Comments on other lines are kept", which is exactly the gap: the sibling inserter `setJsoncMember` goes out of its way to insert "after the last value, so any comma or comment that followed it stays put", so the editor's intent is to preserve trailing comments; removal is the asymmetric path.

Removals are not rare: the one production caller is the policy reconciliation in `run()` — every model a provider policy disallows is removed through `removeJsoncPath` (the `antigravity-direct` policy in `bin/sync-models.policy.json` keeps five families, so any other discovered/existing model entry is removed on the next sync). A hand-written note on such a model's closing line (why it was pinned, when its quota resets, why it must not come back) disappears with no warning, no diff summary mention, and the output still parses — the loss is silent.

## Evidence (verified this run, main aebaa7f85)

Verbatim-extraction probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-removecomment/`, source md5 5834afc1a18fd9f1a22c4e44d3fadb0f, identical on sandbox and laptop clones) — the same extraction method as `bin/sync-models.test.mjs`. Input models object:

```
"kept-model": { "name": "Kept" },
"old-model": {
  "name": "Old"
}, // retired 2026-10-30: argon quota gone
// standalone note about the next model
"other-model": { "name": "Other" }
```

`removeJsoncPath(config, ['provider','antigravity-direct','models','old-model'])` produced output where:

- `trailing comment survives: false` — `// retired 2026-10-30: argon quota gone` is gone;
- `standalone comment survives: true`, `kept-model`/`other-model` intact, `old-model` removed, output still parses (`parseJsoncTree` accepts it);
- control (removing `kept-model`, which has no trailing comment) is clean and leaves the `old-model` trailing comment untouched — the loss is specific to the removed member's own closing line.

## Why it matters

The whole reason sync-models edits JSONC as text instead of round-tripping JSON is that `opencode.jsonc` is a hand-maintained file whose comments carry operational knowledge. A sync that silently eats a comment on exactly the entries it deletes — the entries someone most likely annotated with *why* they are special — erodes trust in running the sync at all, and the information is unrecoverable once the file is written (the `.backup` keeps one generation only).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Removing a member whose value's closing line carries a trailing `//` comment (after the comma, or after the value when it is the last member) preserves that comment in the output (e.g. re-homed onto its own line or the following line) — or, if preservation is judged impossible, the removal refuses with a named error in the same style as the existing shares-a-line refusal instead of deleting silently.
- [ ] A comment between the value and the comma (`"x": {…} /* note */,`) is likewise not silently dropped.
- [ ] Standalone comments on their own lines, comments inside the removed member's own span, and all existing behavior are unchanged; the post-edit `parseJsoncTree`/`parseJsonc` re-parse in `run()` still passes.
- [ ] Tests in `bin/sync-models.test.mjs` style (verbatim extraction) cover: trailing comment after comma, trailing comment on a last member with no comma, comment before the comma, and the no-comment control.

## Dedup / related

Checked open + closed issues for `removeJsoncPath` and sync-models comment handling (2026-11-02): #704 (closed) fixed the `parseJsonc` reader; #3430 covers `provider-catalog-sync`'s `stripJsonc` (a different script); #2832 covers wrong-shaped-config TypeErrors in `run()`/the tree editor; #1799 covers limit/variant reconciliation. None covers comment loss in `removeJsoncPath`.

title: cloudflare-export: neurons/day alert threshold accepts 0, zeroing the alert its contract says must never be zeroed

body:
## Problem

`aiNeuronsDayAlertThreshold` in `pm-stack/cloudflare-export/cloudflare-quota-export.mjs` accepts `0` as a valid `CLOUDFLARE_AI_NEURONS_DAY_ALERT_THRESHOLD`, zeroing the Workers AI neurons/day alert threshold — the exact outcome the function's own contract says must never happen. With the threshold at 0, the alert added by #2287 fires on any day with even a single neuron of Workers AI usage, so the loud dashboard alert (aggregator `cloudflareAlertsNote`) cries wolf daily instead of only surfacing a burn day.

## Evidence (main @ a5d04734b, verified this run)

- `cloudflare-quota-export.mjs:78-87` — the doc comment states: "Unset, empty, non-numeric, or negative values fall back to the default — a typo must never silently disable (or zero) the alert." The implementation is `Number.isFinite(n) && n >= 0 ? n : AI_NEURONS_DAY_ALERT_THRESHOLD_DEFAULT`, so `0` passes the gate.
- Laptop probe (verbatim file, md5 8284db5c770dcbc5904212ced72b3118, node import of the module): `"0"` → 0, `"-0"` → -0, `"0.0"` → 0, `" 0 "` → 0, while `"-5"`, `"abc"`, `""`, `"Infinity"` all correctly fall back to 50000.
- Consequence, same probe: `aiNeuronsDayAlerts` with a single group of 1 neuron for one day returns a firing `workers-ai-neurons-day` alert at threshold 0 (`totalNeurons: 1, threshold: 0`), and no alert at the 50000 default.
- Existing tests (`cloudflare-quota-export.test.mjs:387-393`) cover unset/empty/`abc`/`-5` but never a zero spelling — the gap is untested.
- Secondary, same loose parse: `"0x10"` → 16 and `"0.5"` → 0.5 are silently accepted as thresholds.

## Why it matters

The #2287 alert exists because a 4.11M-neuron (~$45) burn stayed invisible for days; its value is that it is rare and loud. A single typo (`0` instead of a real value, or a templating slip that renders `0`) turns it into a daily false alarm on the Cloudflare card, training exactly the ignore-the-alert habit the feature was built to break — and it does so silently, since 0 is indistinguishable from an intentional setting in the export document.

## Acceptance criteria

- `aiNeuronsDayAlertThreshold` falls back to `AI_NEURONS_DAY_ALERT_THRESHOLD_DEFAULT` (50000) for every zero spelling (`"0"`, `"-0"`, `"0.0"`, `" 0 "`) — i.e. the accepted range is strictly positive, matching the documented contract.
- Regression tests in `cloudflare-quota-export.test.mjs` pin the zero spellings alongside the existing unset/empty/non-numeric/negative cases.
- An intentional sub-1 or hex-spelled value is either rejected to the default or explicitly documented as accepted; the behaviour is pinned by a test either way.
- Existing cloudflare-export tests pass unchanged otherwise; a day at exactly the (positive) threshold still does not fire, and a day above it still does.

Distinct from #2287 (the feature itself, closed/implemented — this is a residual validation gap in its threshold parser) and from #2288 (opencode config guard, unrelated).

title: id(peers): --gossip collection bypasses the announcement freshness/ordering guards — replayed, ancient and far-future announcements are reported as discovered peers

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Problem

`id peers --gossip` collects peer announcements through a path that never applies the freshness or ordering guards the rest of the system relies on — so a replayed, ancient, far-future, or out-of-order announcement is reported as a discovered peer, and can displace a fresher result for the same node.

## Evidence (main `15af52b2d`)

- `pkgs/id/src/commands/peers.rs:373` `discover_via_gossip` collects into a raw map at `peers.rs:442`:
  ```rust
  let mut peers: HashMap<EndpointId, PeerAnnouncement> = HashMap::new();
  ```
  and inserts every postcard-decodable announcement unconditionally at `peers.rs:449`:
  ```rust
  peers.insert(announcement.node_id, announcement);
  ```
  `timestamp_secs` is never read in the function. This is one of only two `PeerAnnouncement` ingest sites in `pkgs/id/src` (grep-verified this run); the other, `commands/serve.rs:1633`, goes through the guarded table.
- The guarded path it bypasses: `PeerDiscovery::update` (`pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/discovery.rs:456-472`) refuses announcements stamped more than `STALE_THRESHOLD` (120 s) in the past **or** the future, and drops an announcement older than the stored one for the same node. Its doc comment states why the guard lives in the table: "so every caller gets them (the `serve.rs` receive loop needs no trust logic of its own)" — this caller does not use the table at all.
- The merge in `cmd_peers` compounds it: gossip results are inserted into `all_peers` at `peers.rs:165-176` **after** the RPC results (`peers.rs:150`), so a stale gossip announcement also overwrites a fresher RPC/`ListPeers` entry for the same node in the printed output.

## Verification (this run, laptop probe)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-peersgossip/` (laptop; single-file `rustc`, replicating the exact unconditional-insert collection loop — `discover_via_gossip` itself needs a live gossip topic, so the merge it performs is what was exercised):

- announcement stamped `1` (1970, the #1552 "ghost" case) → **collected, 1 peer** (guard would refuse)
- newer announcement (`now`, `new-name`, blob 42) followed in-window by an older replay (`now-60`, `old-name`, blob 7) → **final entry is the older one** (guard would refuse the regression)
- announcement stamped `u64::MAX` → **collected** (guard would refuse)
- control: fresh in-order pair → newest kept, as expected

Distinct from #1552 (closed: it fixed `PeerDiscovery::update`, the serve path — this CLI collection path was not covered) and from #2944 (open: the serve peer table's authentication/bounds — this is the one-shot CLI collector, which has no table and needs only the freshness/ordering checks, not authentication).

## Why it matters

`id peers` is the diagnostic an operator runs to answer "who is out there". A departed peer replayed (or simply slow-gossiped) inside the collection window is printed as discovered with its stale name/blob count/timestamp, and a fresher RPC answer for the same node is silently replaced by the older gossip copy — the exact failure #1552 closed for `serve`, still live in the CLI.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `discover_via_gossip` (or a shared helper it uses) refuses announcements stamped more than `STALE_THRESHOLD` from the local wall clock, in either direction — the same bound `PeerDiscovery::update` applies.
- [ ] Within the collection window, an announcement older than the already-collected one for the same node does not replace it (equal timestamps may keep last-arrival-wins, matching the table's tie rule).
- [ ] A stale gossip announcement cannot overwrite a fresher RPC result when `cmd_peers` merges the two sources (or the merge is shown to be safe because both sources are now freshness-checked).
- [ ] Unit tests cover: 1970-stamped announcement excluded, `u64::MAX`-stamped announcement excluded, older-after-newer does not regress, fresh in-order announcements still collected.
- [ ] Existing peers/discovery tests pass.

title: id(id-core): WorldExecutionProfile::validate rustdoc is two half-merged blocks with lost words, and resolve() has no doc comment

body:
## Problem

The rustdoc on `WorldExecutionProfile::validate` in id-core is two half-merged doc blocks with lost words, and `resolve` — the method the text partly describes — has no doc comment at all. This is the validator the #3015 fix made load-bearing ("a manifest can never accept bounds that apply would later refuse"), so its documentation is the contract other callers read.

## Evidence (main @ 9f472b401, read this run)

`pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/world_limits.rs:135-156` (doc comment on `validate`, fn at line 157):

1. The first half describes **resolve**, not validate: "Validate values and resolve them beneath the server's hard limits. A request may lower a bound or inherit it, but can never raise the server ceiling. The Wasm module-size cap is always taken from `hard`." — `validate(&self)` takes no `hard` and resolves nothing.
2. A sentence loses its subject: "every bound that is set must be positive and at or above its floor.  inherits the server ceiling and is always valid." (the "`None`" that inherits is missing; note the double space).
3. A caller reference is an empty bracket: "This is the single source of truth for the bound checks: [] runs it against the live profile at apply time, and the world manifest validator runs it at parse time…" — the apply-time caller's name/link was lost.
4. There are two `# Errors` sections in the one comment.
5. `pub fn resolve` (line ~184) has no doc comment, despite being the public entry point that clamps a profile beneath the server ceilings.

## Why it matters

#3015 deliberately made this `validate` the single source of truth shared by manifest parse time and apply time. A reader tracing either caller lands on a comment that describes the wrong method, drops the apply-time caller's name, and leaves `resolve` undocumented — the next editor cannot tell from the docs which guarantees belong to which method, which is how the parse/apply divergence #3015 fixed creeps back.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `validate`'s doc describes only validation: which bounds are checked, their floors, and that `None` inherits and is always valid — with the lost words restored.
- [ ] The "single source of truth" sentence names both callers (apply time and the world manifest validator) with resolvable references.
- [ ] Exactly one `# Errors` section per method.
- [ ] `resolve` carries its own doc comment (lower-or-inherit semantics, clamping, module-size cap from `hard`, its errors).
- [ ] Docs only: no signature or behavior change; `cargo doc` for id-core builds without new warnings for this file.

title: id(note_links): check_note_link_op refusal messages state the opposite of the failed condition — empty surface 'is not empty', non-NFC surface 'is NFC'

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

Two of the three field-error messages in `check_note_link_op` state the opposite of the condition that produced them. A peer (or operator) whose `note.link` event is refused is told the surface satisfies the very rule it broke.

## Evidence (main @ 9f472b401, read this run)

`pkgs/id/src/note_links.rs:97-115`:

- Line 100: when `surface.is_empty()` is true, the error is `"a link's authored surface is not empty"` — the surface **is** empty; the message asserts it is not.
- Line 111: when `!is_nfc(surface)` is true, the error is `"a link's authored surface is NFC"` — the surface **is not** NFC; the message asserts it is.
- The third message in the same function (line 104-107, over-long surface: "is {} bytes, it may be at most {MAX_SURFACE_BYTES}") is factual, which makes the other two read as copy slips, not a style.

House style in the sibling validator states the fact: `pkgs/id/src/tag_claims.rs` `check_text` returns `"the {field} is not NFC"` for the same condition, and `pkgs/id/src/idset.rs` `check_scope` returns `"the scope is not NFC"`.

These errors are not local-only: `check_note_link_op` is called on the chain receipt path (`pkgs/id/src/chain.rs:307`), so the inverted text is what a refused event's sender/operator sees in logs and error propagation.

## Why it matters

Refusal reasons are the debugging surface for a signed-event protocol: a sender told their surface "is not empty" when it is empty (or "is NFC" when it is not) will fix the wrong thing or conclude the receiver is broken. The values are also pinned by no test — `test_check_rejects_a_bad_surface_and_a_wrong_kind` (note_links.rs tests) matches only `Err(NoteLinkError::Field(_))`, so the inversion survived review.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The empty-surface error states the surface is empty (e.g. "a link's authored surface is empty" / "must not be empty" phrased as a fact about the input).
- [ ] The non-NFC error states the surface is not NFC, matching the `tag_claims`/`idset` phrasing.
- [ ] A test pins the message text (or at least the distinguishing wording) for both cases, not just the `Field(_)` variant.
- [ ] No behavior change: the same inputs are accepted/refused as before.

title: id(chat-presence): receipt never scopes heartbeats to sender membership — update_scoped has no production caller, serve stores channels unscoped

labels.name: source/design-architect

labels.name: status/triaged

body:
## Summary

Chat presence documents a receipt-side membership-scoping guarantee that no production code path implements: `PresenceTable::update_scoped` — the only entry point that filters a heartbeat's channels to channels the *sender* is a member of — has **no caller outside its own module**. The one production receipt path, the gossip receive task in `id serve`, stores verified heartbeats through the explicitly unscoped `PresenceTable::update`, so any channels a heartbeat names are kept as claimed.

## Evidence (verified this run, main @ 97e3e8e0a)

- `pkgs/id/src/chat_presence.rs:24-31` — module doc, "Membership scoping": *"On receipt, [`PresenceTable::update_scoped`] filters a heartbeat's channels to those the sender is a member of (the caller's membership predicate), so a node cannot advertise presence in — or probe — a channel it does not belong to."*
- `pkgs/id/src/chat_presence.rs:222-228` — `update()` is documented as *"with no membership scoping (the transport layer's view; scoping is the receiver's job — see `update_scoped`)"*.
- `pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:1615-1628` — the only production receipt path: `decode_frame` → `heartbeat.verify()` → `recv_presence.update(heartbeat)`. Signature verification stops *forgery of another node's* heartbeat, but a node signs its own key freely, so verification does not stop a node claiming channels it does not belong to — that is exactly what scoping was for.
- Caller search (run twice, independently: sandbox clone @ 97e3e8e0a and laptop clone): `grep -rn "update_scoped" pkgs/id/src/` returns only references inside `chat_presence.rs` itself (the definition, its doc comments, and its tests). No production caller exists.
- The sender side shows the wiring is half-built: `serve.rs:1591-1599` broadcasts this node's heartbeat with **no channels**, with the comment *"Channel membership lives in the chat layer above serve, so this heartbeat names no channels; receivers scope and read it through PresenceTable."* The chat layer that would name channels — and the receiver-side membership predicate that would scope them — do not exist yet.

## Why it matters

The module doc states the scoping as a present-tense property of the system, and it is the only thing standing between "presence is scoped to authorized channel members" and "any node that learns or guesses a channel's group hash can advertise presence in it and keep a live entry in every peer's table." Today the exposure is latent — the built-in sender names no channels, and no production reader renders rosters yet (`roster_at` / `roster_for_viewer_at` / `live_nodes_at` also have no production callers). But the moment the chat layer starts naming channels on send and reading rosters, it will inherit an unscoped table while believing the documented guarantee holds. This is the same failure shape as #4227 (a protective evaluator that exists, is tested, and is never wired in).

## Acceptance criteria

- The production receipt path in `id serve` scopes incoming heartbeats to the sender's membership — i.e. it calls `update_scoped` with a membership predicate backed by the group fold (or an equivalent mechanism) — **or** the module documentation is corrected to state plainly that receipt scoping is not wired, and `update()` is not described as leaving scoping "to the receiver" when no receiver does it.
- A test demonstrates the end-to-end property at the serve/receipt level (not only `update_at` unit tests): a correctly self-signed heartbeat naming a channel the sender does not belong to does not leave that channel in the receiver's table.
- Existing `chat_presence` tests still pass; the signature-verification behaviour in `serve` is unchanged.
- Distinct from #3991 (typing list dedup/bounding) and #4004 (table node-count bound) — this issue is only about the missing membership scoping on receipt.

title: id(tag_claims): compacted_claims returns a claim twice when the applied list repeats an ID — the production fold diverges from live_claims on duplicate input

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.name: app/id

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: task/fix
labels.description: has a fix task queued

body:
## Summary

`compacted_claims` — the fold production actually uses — returns a claim **twice** when its input contains two `Applied` entries with the same event ID, while the reference fold `live_claims` returns it once. The module header promises the two folds always agree: "Both give the same result (P5.3, #184)" (`pkgs/id/src/tag_claims.rs:21`).

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop fuzz probe)

- `live_claims` (`tag_claims.rs:182`) collects sets into a `BTreeMap` keyed by claim ID (`:192`), so a duplicated ID collapses to one claim (last entry wins).
- `compacted_claims` (`tag_claims.rs:232`) builds its result by iterating `applied` directly (`:281` ff.) and filtering only on the `removed` set — it never dedupes by ID. Its internal `by_id` map (`:233`) dedupes, but the output list does not.
- Probe (laptop, verbatim `tag_claims.rs` @ `3d6deeae7`, only the `Hash`/`AuthorKey` imports stubbed; probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-tagfold/`):
  - Randomized DAG fuzz, duplicate-free inputs: **50,000 cases, 0 divergences** — the folds agree on well-formed input.
  - Same fuzz with duplicate `Applied` entries injected: divergences on iteration 4 already — `compacted_claims` emits the duplicated claim twice, `live_claims` once.
  - Equivocation case (same ID, values `Some("A")` then `Some("B")`): `live_claims` → 1 claim (`"B"`); `compacted_claims` → **2 claims with the same ID**, one per spelling.

## Why it matters

`EventStore::tag_claims` (`pkgs/id/src/event_store/claims.rs:76`) returns `compacted_claims` output verbatim, and it feeds `TagIndex` and alias display. A duplicated claim in that output is not cosmetic: `aliases_of` (`pkgs/id/src/aliases.rs`) counts claims, so one real claim appearing twice reads as two claims and the view shows the alias as **Contested** instead of **Only** — and the tag index carries a phantom second claim. Today the store's caller happens to build `applied` from a table keyed by event, so duplicates should not occur; but the fold's documented contract is unconditional, nothing in either function states a no-duplicates precondition, and the reference fold already tolerates duplicates. The production fold should not be the fragile one. (Related: #1421 asks for a mutation/planted-bug check for this fold; this is a concrete divergence such a check would catch.)

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `compacted_claims` returns at most one claim per claim ID for any input, matching `live_claims` on duplicate and equivocating inputs (state the chosen winner — the reference fold's last-wins — in the doc comment).
- [ ] The module docs state the input precondition or the dedup behaviour explicitly, so "both give the same result" is true as written.
- [ ] Regression tests in `tag_claims.rs`: verbatim duplicate `Applied` set entry, and same-ID entries with different values, asserting both folds agree.
- [ ] Existing tag-claims and event-store claim tests still pass (`cargo test` for the id lib on laptop/CI).

title: id(note_links): project_links validates target/pin before the head check — a superseded link with a bad pin or unknown target fails the whole projection

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

`project_links` (pkgs/id/src/note_links.rs, added by PR #4131 for issue #3816) validates a link's target and pin **before** checking whether the link's asserting revision is still a head of its source note. A link asserted by a superseded revision contributes nothing to the projection — the function drops it with `continue` — but only *after* the target/pin checks have had the chance to fail the **entire** projection. One stale link with a bad pin or a not-yet-known target therefore takes down every link and backlink in the store, even though the link itself would have been silently dropped.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Code order in `project_links` (pkgs/id/src/note_links.rs, main @ a205ae3bd):

1. source note lookup → `UnknownSource` error
2. revision-of-source check → `RevisionNotOfSource` error
3. target note lookup → `UnknownTarget` error
4. pin check → `PinNotOfTarget` error
5. **only then**: `if !source_note.heads.contains(revision) { continue; }`

Laptop probe (worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-notelinks`, note_links.rs byte-identical to main, md5 594803d785fafc1ad0c82deffaf306dc; source note created then revised so revision 10 is superseded by head 11):

- superseded link pinning a revision of a *different* note → `Err(PinNotOfTarget)` — projection fails
- superseded link naming an unknown target → `Err(UnknownTarget)` — projection fails
- control: the same bad pin asserted by the *head* revision → `Err(PinNotOfTarget)` (correct)
- control: a well-formed superseded link → `Ok`, 0 edges (dropped as intended)

## Why it matters

The projection is derived from applied events, including events that arrive via sync before the notes they reference (the prune path in pkgs/id/src/event_store/mod.rs already special-cases link references so a rebuild after prune does not fail with `UnknownTarget`). A single stale or early link should not be able to blank the whole link/backlink view for a store. Head-asserted links must keep failing loudly — their errors are real — but links that are not part of the projection at all should be dropped before their target/pin validity is judged.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `project_links` drops a link whose asserting revision is not a head of its source note **without** erroring on that link's target existence or pin validity (the source/revision-of-source checks needed to establish headship still apply).
- [ ] A link asserted by a head revision with an unknown target or a pin that is not a revision of the target still fails the projection with `UnknownTarget` / `PinNotOfTarget` (existing behaviour, covered by existing tests).
- [ ] New tests in pkgs/id/src/note_links.rs cover: superseded link + bad pin → Ok with the link dropped; superseded link + unknown target → Ok with the link dropped.
- [ ] Existing note_links tests pass (`cargo test` for the id package on the laptop or CI).

body:
## Problem

`cargo test -p id --lib --features web` does not compile on current main: the test modules in `pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs` have rotted against current `id-core` / iroh APIs. The `web` feature is not in the crate's default features (`default = ["sandbox", "world"]`), so the default test build never compiles this code and the rot is invisible.

## Evidence (2026-11-02, main 3d5023d07, laptop)

`cargo test -p id --lib --features web collab_route_tests` fails with 8 errors, all in pre-existing test code in `pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs`:

- `routes.rs:2532` — E0308: `TagStore::init_in(&docs, ...)` test helper: expected `TagStoreError`, found a different error type (id-core API drift).
- `routes.rs:3421` and `routes.rs:3433` — E0599: `get_file_tags(&store)` called with `iroh_blobs::api::Store` where the method now needs `&iroh_docs::api::Doc` (iroh API drift).
- Plus E0255/E0277 errors of the same character (detailed explanations E0255, E0277, E0308, E0599; 8 errors total).

Found while working #2830 (queue task 5436): a new route-level test module could not be executed in-crate at all; its axum behavior had to be verified with a standalone probe against the locked axum 0.8.9 instead.

## Acceptance

- `cargo test -p id --lib --features web` compiles.
- The routes.rs test modules (`upload_router_tests`, handler tests around the file-tag endpoints) run and pass, or stale tests are removed with a note.
- Ideally CI gains a `--features web` check build for pkgs/id so this cannot rot silently again.

## Acceptance criteria
- `cargo test -p id --lib --features web` compiles on current main: the test modules in `pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs` are updated to the current `id-core` / iroh APIs (or stale tests removed with a note explaining why).
- The web-feature test suite (routes / file-tag handler tests) runs and passes locally.
- Ideally, CI gains a `--features web` check build for pkgs/id so the feature cannot rot silently again; if CI wiring is out of scope, that gap is recorded on the issue before closing.

title: bin(proxies): response-side per-chunk decode corrupts multibyte UTF-8 split across chunks — stdout line buffers and design-code response accumulators stringify each chunk separately (response-side twin of #3186)

body:
## Bug: bin proxies decode subprocess/response streams per chunk — multibyte UTF-8 split across chunks is corrupted to U+FFFD on the response side (the response-side twin of #3186)

#3186 fixed the **request-body** side: eight proxies collected request bodies with per-chunk stringification, and the fix introduced the shared `bin/request-body.mjs` collector (Buffer-concat, decode once). The **response side** was never given the same treatment. Across `bin/`, subprocess stdout line buffers and upstream response accumulators still do `buffer += chunk.toString('utf-8')` per chunk, with no `StringDecoder` anywhere in `bin/` (grep-verified). A multibyte UTF-8 sequence straddling a chunk boundary decodes to U+FFFD on both sides. Because the damage lands inside JSON string values, the line still parses — assistant/response text containing emoji, CJK, or accented characters is silently garbled before it reaches the client, with no error anywhere. (Flagged as an unverified lead by lane A earlier today; verified this run.)

### Sites (main f576a6c2)

JSON-line stdout buffers (parsed events / content deltas flow through these):

- `bin/agy-proxy.mjs:574` — `this.lineBuffer += chunk.toString();` in `_onStdout`
- `bin/claude-code-proxy.mjs:369` — `this.lineBuffer += chunk.toString('utf-8');` in `_onStdout`
- `bin/codex-proxy.mjs:947` — `lineBuffer += chunk.toString('utf-8');`
- `bin/commandcode-proxy.mjs:592` and `bin/commandcode-proxy.mjs:1145` — two stdout handlers
- `bin/muse-proxy.mjs:464` and `bin/muse-proxy.mjs:1774` — two stdout handlers

Upstream response accumulation (design-code-proxy):

- `bin/design-code-proxy.mjs:412` — SSE streaming `buffer += chunk.toString('utf-8');` (lines are JSON-parsed, model-rewritten, and re-serialized to the client)
- `bin/design-code-proxy.mjs:437` — non-streaming `fullBody += chunk.toString('utf-8');` before `JSON.parse(fullBody)`

Same pattern, lower impact (ASCII-shaped output today, still in scope for the audit): `bin/agy-proxy.mjs:271` (`stdout += d` feeding `parseAgyModelsOutput`) and `bin/muse-proxy.mjs:243` (`out += c.toString('utf-8')` feeding a `--flag` scan). The per-chunk stderr tails in the same files share the flaw for diagnostic text.

The correct house patterns already exist in the same directory: `bin/request-body.mjs` (Buffer-concat / decode-once for request bodies) and `node:string_decoder`'s `StringDecoder` for streaming line buffers.

### Evidence (verified this run, main f576a6c2)

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-stdoututf8/`, laptop clone at the same HEAD f576a6c2; `bin/claude-code-proxy.mjs` md5 5bc03524c6d6874a5c14156d939de4e2 and `bin/agy-proxy.mjs` md5 d63469ac6958f95bdee8403d78a6f259, identical to sandbox main): the verbatim `_onStdout` method bodies extracted by line range from both files were fed a JSON line `{"type":"assistant","text":"before-☃é😀-after"}` as two chunks split 1 byte into the ☃ (3-byte) sequence:

- claude-code-proxy `_onStdout`: parsed message text = `"before-���é😀-after"` — ☃ destroyed (3× U+FFFD)
- agy-proxy `_onStdout`: parsed message text = `"before-���é😀-after"` — same corruption
- StringDecoder control (same chunks): `"before-☃é😀-after"` — intact

Chunk boundaries on a pipe/socket are not exotic: a busy CLI emitting large JSON lines will routinely split output at 64 KiB (or smaller) boundaries, and any non-ASCII character near one is garbled.

### Why it matters

These proxies are the fleet's front door to the model CLIs. Response text is the product: garbled characters in streamed assistant output, code comments, and non-English text are silent data corruption in exactly the place #3186 already established is unacceptable on the request side. It is also a latent trap for any future structured field that must round-trip exactly (ids, hashes, signatures) if one ever lands in a split string value.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every stdout line buffer and response accumulator listed above decodes via a streaming `StringDecoder` (or Buffer-concat/decode-once where the consumer is whole-body), including the end-of-stream flush (`decoder.end()` tail is processed through the same line path).
- [ ] A regression test in the house style (cf. `bin/antigravity-ls-proxy.test.mjs` "preserves UTF-8 split across HTTP request-body chunks (#3186)") feeds a multibyte character split across two chunks through at least the claude-code-proxy and agy-proxy stdout paths and one design-code-proxy response path, and asserts the parsed/forwarded text is byte-identical.
- [ ] No per-chunk `chunk.toString()` accumulation remains on stdout/response paths in `bin/*.mjs` (grep-auditable), except demonstrably ASCII-only uses that are commented as such.
- [ ] Existing per-proxy test suites pass on the laptop or CI.

Related: #3186 (request-body twin, closed), #4335 (opencode-route-proxy request body, open — same class, different file/side).

title: id(web): classify_tag timestamp parsers accept non-canonical spellings — non-padded, '+'-signed and over-wide components classify as Auto/Archive with the canonical instant

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

`classify_tag` (pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs:153) decides whether a file is an auto-backup or an archive from the *shape* of its name — the rule built by #809/#2793 is that only a producer-shaped name classifies. Both of its timestamp parsers still accept non-canonical spellings that no producer mints, and map them onto the canonical instant, so an ordinary user file with a near-miss name is pulled out of the primary list and rendered/sorted as an auto-backup or archive.

- `parse_iso_timestamp` (routes.rs:184) parses each component with `p.parse::<u64>()` (routes.rs:210-215) and checks only the numeric *range*. Rust's `u64` parser accepts a leading `+` and any digit width, and nothing checks the fixed widths of the documented format (`2026-03-12T06:42:30.015Z`, routes.rs:156-159).
- The archive branch (routes.rs:168-175) does `ts_str.parse::<u64>()` — its own comment (#2793) says the producer "always formats a u64" (Display form: no sign, no padding), yet a `+`-signed suffix parses.

This is the residual of the closed fixes in this same function family: #756 (range checks), #1879 (non-numeric components, fixed today in PR #4062), #2793 (archive suffix must parse). None of them checked spelling/canonical form.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe @ aa4fbe89)

Verbatim `classify_tag` + `parse_iso_timestamp` + `is_leap_year` extracted from routes.rs (file md5 e8b5543a20890f367ade0261931e3836), compiled and run on the laptop in `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-isowidth/`:

- Control: `auto-2026-03-12T06:42:30.015Z` -> Auto, ts=1773297750 ✓
- `auto-2026-3-12T6:42:30Z` (non-padded month/day/hour) -> **Auto, ts=1773297750** (same instant)
- `auto-2026-03-12T06:4:2Z` (non-padded minute/second) -> **Auto, ts=1773295442**
- `auto-+2026-03-12T06:42:30Z` (`+`-signed year) -> **Auto, ts=1773297750**
- `auto-02026-03-12T06:42:30Z` (5-digit year) -> **Auto, ts=1773297750**
- `auto-2026-003-12T06:42:30Z` (3-digit month) -> **Auto, ts=1773297750**
- Control: `notes.archive.123` -> Archive, ts=123 ✓; `notes.archive.txt` -> Primary ✓
- `notes.archive.+123` (`+`-signed suffix) -> **Archive, ts=123**
- Direct: `parse_iso_timestamp("2026-3-2T6:4:2Z")` -> Some(1772431442)

## Why it matters

Classification drives the file list: Auto/Archive files get badges, sort out of the primary list, and (per #2793) link by hash instead of by name. A user file that merely *resembles* a backup name in a non-canonical spelling is therefore hidden/mislabelled exactly as in #809/#2793 — those fixes' stated rule ("only an auto-backup when the remainder actually parses as an ISO date", in the documented fixed-width format) is not yet enforced for spelling.

## Acceptance criteria

- `parse_iso_timestamp` requires the canonical component widths (4-digit year; 2-digit month/day/hour/minute/second) and rejects `+`-signed components; regression tests sit beside `test_parse_iso_timestamp_rejects_malformed_components` in routes.rs.
- The archive branch of `classify_tag` rejects a `+`-signed suffix (a plain unsigned decimal in producer Display form only), with a regression test beside the #2793 cases.
- Canonical names still classify exactly as today: `auto-2026-03-12T06:42:30.015Z` -> Auto/1773297750, `notes.archive.123` -> Archive/123, and the existing routes.rs test suite passes (laptop or CI).

body:
## Summary

Four entry points still use the pre-#2083 raw-path entry-point check — the exact bug class fixed today for `bin/record.mjs` and `bin/provider-catalog-sync.mjs` in #4123 (closing #2235):

```js
if (process.argv[1] && import.meta.url === pathToFileURL(process.argv[1]).href) {
  await main();
}
```

`process.argv[1]` is the path exactly as invoked; `import.meta.url` is the module's resolved URL. Invoked through any symlink — a symlinked file, or a path through a symlinked directory such as the `~/code -> ~/git/code` checkout alias that caused #2083 — the two never match, `main()` never runs, and the process **exits 0 with no output and no files written**: a silent no-op.

Remaining instances on main `c08b27f2`:

- `bin/codedb-bridge.mjs:317` — the MCP stdio bridge added in #4120, after #2235 was filed; #2235's "no remaining raw-path instances in `bin/`" acceptance criterion is unmet in `bin/` itself because of this file.
- `pm-stack/supabase-export/supabase-quota-export.mjs:399`
- `pm-stack/cloudflare-export/cloudflare-quota-export.mjs:491`
- `pm-stack/opencode-claimant/install.mjs:97-98` (same check, stored in an `isMain` const)

Not in scope: `pm-stack/meta-exporter/meta-quota-export.mjs:535` has the same check but is already tracked by #2350 — fix it there, not here. This issue is the four instances no open issue names.

## Evidence (main `c08b27f2`, laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-entryguard/`, all four files md5-matched between the sandbox clone and the laptop clone)

codedb-bridge (ping request on stdin):

- Direct: `node bin/codedb-bridge.mjs` → `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"result":{}}`, exit 0 — main ran.
- Via a file symlink and via a symlinked directory: **no response at all**, exit 0 — main never ran; an MCP client sees a bridge that starts "successfully" and never answers.

supabase-quota-export (no token available, `BWS_BIN=/bin/false`, scratch `--out-dir`):

- Direct: exit 3, stderr `supabase-quota-export: no-token: …`, and the failure document is written (`latest.json` + `history.jsonl`).
- Via a file symlink and via a symlinked directory: exit 0, no output, **out-dir empty**.

cloudflare-quota-export (no token in env, scratch `--out-dir`):

- Direct: exit 2, stderr `cloudflare-quota-export: no-token: …`, failure document written.
- Via a file symlink and via a symlinked directory: exit 0, no output, **out-dir empty**.

opencode-claimant install (`--store <scratch> --dry-run`):

- Direct: prints the summary JSON (`action: "inserted"`, task id, …), exit 0.
- Via a file symlink and via a symlinked directory: exit 0, **no output** — the claimant task is silently never installed/refreshed.

## Why it matters

All four tools are designed to be quiet on success, and the two exporters' whole failure-visibility design is the failure document: a tick that cannot read its source still writes a `no-token` document so consumers can tell "source down" from a reading. The symlink no-op defeats exactly that — no document, a green exit 0, and the only signal is `latest.json` quietly going stale. The codedb bridge is worse: it is spawned by MCP clients as a subprocess, so a symlinked invocation path (wrapper, symlink farm, checkout alias — the fleet's own `~/code -> ~/git/code` layout) yields a server that accepts the spawn and never speaks. This pattern has already burned the fleet three times (#2083, #2235, #2350); each fix repaired the named files and left the siblings behind.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All four files above run their `main()` when invoked via a symlinked file path and via a symlinked directory path (use the `fs.realpathSync`-on-both-sides comparison proven in `bin/proxy-supervise.mjs` and applied in #4123 to `bin/record.mjs` / `bin/provider-catalog-sync.mjs`, or an equivalent).
- [ ] Importing any of the four modules as a library (their test suites do this) still does **not** run `main()`.
- [ ] A regression test covers the symlinked invocation for at least the codedb bridge (its test suite already spawns the bridge as a subprocess) and at least one exporter, so the check cannot silently regress again.
- [ ] A repo-wide grep for entry-point comparisons (`process.argv[1]` vs `import.meta.url`) shows no remaining raw-path instances except `pm-stack/meta-exporter/meta-quota-export.mjs`, which is tracked separately by #2350.

Related: #2083 (closed — original instance + proven fix pattern), #2235 (closed by #4123 — the `bin/` pair fixed today), #2350 (open — the meta-exporter instance, explicitly out of scope here), #4120 (added the codedb bridge with the old check).

title: aggregator(card-state): a restore cancelled by a later restore still cancels its target — undo-of-undo is a no-op when the first restore was applied

labels.name: app/pm-stack
labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

body:
## Bug

`cardState`'s restore derivation is not transitive: a restore that is itself cancelled by a later restore still cancels its own target. Undoing an undo is a no-op — but only when the first restore was already `applied`; when it is still `new`, the store supersedes it and the undo-of-undo works. The same user intent therefore has opposite outcomes depending on consumer timing.

## Evidence (main `b7cc5356`)

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/card-state.ts:55-62` — `cancelledActionIds` collects the `supersedes` target of every restore whose state is not `superseded` and not `rejected`. It never checks whether that restore's own id is cancelled by another restore.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/card-state.ts:66-69` — `effectiveActions` removes the cancelled restore itself from the effective set, so the second restore demonstrably registered — yet the first restore's cancellation of its target survives in the set computed from the full list.
- Contrast the two paths that do work: a `rejected` restore does not cancel (#1474, pinned by tests in `test/actions.test.ts`), and a still-`new` restore loses its cancellation when a later action supersedes it, because `ActionsStore.add` marks it `superseded` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/actions.ts:612-614`, new-state only) and `cancelledActionIds` excludes `superseded`. An `applied` restore cannot be superseded by the store, so the derivation is the only place its cancellation can be lifted — and it isn't.
- `validateNewAction` (`actions.ts:405-407`) accepts a restore naming any action id in `supersedes`, including another restore, so this state is reachable through the public boundary.

Verified this run with a laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-restorechain/probe.ts` on the laptop, importing the byte-identical `card-state.ts` at md5 `c8c1372e`, run with bun):

- A: dismiss(applied) + restore(new, supersedes=dismiss) → cancelled=[dismiss], suppressed=null — restore works.
- B: dismiss(applied) + restore1(applied, supersedes=dismiss) + restore2(new, supersedes=restore1) → cancelled=[dismiss, restore1], effective=[restore2], **suppressed=null** — restore2 removed restore1 from the effective set but the dismiss stays cancelled; the card never comes back.
- C: dismiss(applied) + restore(rejected, supersedes=dismiss) → cancelled=[], suppressed=dismissed — the #1474 behavior.
- D: dismiss(applied) alone → suppressed=dismissed.

## Why it matters

`cardState` is the documented single derivation truth for renderers and consumers ("renderers and tests share one truth", card-state.ts header). A card dismissed, restored by an applied restore, and then un-restored stays restored forever: the suppression the user explicitly reinstated silently never applies, and no later action short of a fresh dismiss/snooze/done re-suppresses it. The same flaw applies to every verb a restore can cancel (ack, answer, snooze, done), not just dismiss.

## Acceptance criteria

- `cancelledActionIds` (or its replacement) computes cancellations to a fixpoint: a restore whose own id is cancelled by an effective restore does not cancel its target — mirroring the existing `superseded`/`rejected` exclusions.
- Regression tests in the aggregator suite cover: applied dismiss + applied restore + new restore-of-restore → card is suppressed again (`dismissed`); the chain also works at depth 3 (restore-of-restore-of-restore re-restores); #1474's rejected-restore tests and the existing restore tests still pass.
- No change to store persistence or the action record shape; derivation-only fix in `card-state.ts`.

title: id(notes): cyclic note.revise parents (incl. self-parent) pass the gate and the notes() drop-filter, then fail every note query with a false UnknownParent
