labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

A `note.revise` whose parents form a cycle — including the degenerate case of a revision naming **itself** as its only parent — passes every gate pkgs/id has, survives the defensive drop-filter in `LocalEvents::notes()`, and then makes `fold_notes` fail the **whole store's** note view with `UnknownParent` — an error that falsely claims the named parent "is not a note event", when the parent is present in the set (in the self-parent case it is the revision itself). One signed cyclic revision from any peer therefore takes down `notes()`, `note_history()` and `revise_note()` for every note in the store, and the diagnosis points investigators at a missing event that is not missing.

## Evidence (verified this run, main @ beed98f2)

- Gate: `check_note_op` (`pkgs/id/src/notes.rs:97-141`, called from `pkgs/id/src/chain.rs:279` on receipt and from `pkgs/id/src/local_events.rs:397/450` locally) checks parent count (1..=32) and duplicates only. A parent list containing the revision's own future event ID, or two revisions naming each other, is structurally acceptable to it.
- Drop-filter: `LocalEvents::notes()` (`pkgs/id/src/local_events.rs:498-525`) already defends against unknown/foreign parents by dropping revises whose parents are not revisions of the same note — but its `owners.get(parent) == Some(note)` test passes for self-parents and cycles, because every cyclic parent *is* a revision of the same note.
- Fold: `fold_notes` (`pkgs/id/src/notes.rs:274-335`) folds a revision only once all its parents have folded. When nothing can progress it takes `rest[0]` and returns `NoteFoldError::UnknownParent` (notes.rs:316-332) for the first unfolded parent — for a cycle that parent is in the set, so the error text ("names parent {parent}, which is not a note event", notes.rs:203-209) is false. `notes()` propagates the error (`Ok(fold_notes(&applied)?)`), so one cyclic event fails every note query, not just its own note.

### Reproduction (laptop probe, verbatim module)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-notecycle/` on the laptop compiles `pkgs/id/src/notes.rs` **verbatim** (md5 3055ade17c6a57dd46ec351a6792721f, identical in both clones @ beed98f2; only `p2panda_core::Hash`, `documents::DocumentRef` and `waiting::AuthorKey` are minimal stubs) plus a verbatim copy of the `local_events.rs` drop-filter loop:

```text
gate check_note_op(self-parent-shaped op): Ok(())
self-parent: drop_filter kept 2 of 2 events
self-parent: fold_notes -> Err("revision 0b0b… names parent 0b0b…, which is not a note event")
2-cycle: drop_filter kept 3 of 3 events
2-cycle: fold_notes -> Err("revision 0b0b… names parent 0c0c…, which is not a note event")
control unknown-parent: fold_notes -> Err("revision 0b0b… names parent 4d4d…, which is not a note event")  (correct: 0x4d is genuinely absent)
control healthy: fold_notes ok = true
```

Cases: create(0x0a) + revise(0x0b, parents=[0x0b]) — self-parent; create(0x0a) + revise(0x0b, parents=[0x0c]) + revise(0x0c, parents=[0x0b]) — 2-cycle. Both pass the gate and the drop-filter, both fail the fold with the false `UnknownParent`.

## Why it matters

- Availability: note events are replicated signed events; a buggy or malicious peer can inject one cyclic revision and every note query on the receiving store fails until the event is dealt with out-of-band. The existing drop-filter (added precisely so one bad peer revision cannot fail every note query — see the comment at local_events.rs:498-503) does not cover this shape.
- Diagnosis: the error names a present event as missing, sending an operator to hunt sync/replication for an event that already arrived.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A self-parent revision and a cyclic parent set (2-cycle minimum) are refused or excluded with an accurate diagnosis — e.g. a distinct `NoteFoldError` variant (or a drop-filter extension in `notes()`) that names the cycle/self-reference as the problem, never `UnknownParent` for a parent that is in the set.
- [ ] One cyclic revision in a store no longer fails `notes()` / `note_history()` for the store's healthy notes (whichever layer the fix lands in, the consumer-visible behaviour matches the existing unknown/foreign-parent defence).
- [ ] Genuinely unknown parents still report `UnknownParent` with the absent parent named (existing tests at notes.rs:~526-545 keep passing).
- [ ] Regression tests cover: self-parent, 2-cycle, and a longer cycle (3+), at the layer(s) changed; healthy chains, concurrent heads and explicit merges fold exactly as before.
- [ ] `check_note_op`'s documented contract is updated if the gate gains a rule it can actually evaluate (it has no event ID, so self-parent may be fold/filter-layer only — say so in the docs rather than leaving the gap implicit).

Dedup: searched open + closed for fold_notes / note parent cycle variants on 2026-11-02 — only #3814 (the closed build issue for the notes module itself). No covering issue.

body:
## Problem

One `answer` action may carry the same survey question twice in a single `payload.answers` array — with contradictory values — and every layer accepts it:

- `validateNewAction` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/actions.ts:275-303) converts each answers entry independently (array of at most 50) and never tracks which `questionId`s it has already seen.
- `checkActionAgainstItem` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/tier-items.ts:348-362) checks each entry's membership/value against the published question, again per entry, with no duplicate detection.

The item side enforces the opposite invariant: `sanitizeQuestions` / `sanitizeOptions` (tier-items.ts) drop later entries whose id repeats (`seen` sets). The answer side has no mirror of that rule.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe against real code @ cc819feb, md5-matched)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-answeroption/` (verbatim imports of src/tier-items.ts; item fixture mirrors test/needs-user.test.ts — single question `audience`, options internal/public):

- control — `answers: [{questionId: "audience", value: "internal"}]` → `null` (accepted, correctly)
- control — an answer naming an unknown question or an unpublished option value is rejected by the same function (existing tests, test/needs-user.test.ts:316-330)
- **bug — `answers: [{questionId: "audience", value: "internal"}, {questionId: "audience", value: "public"}]` → `null` (accepted, both entries stored)**

## Why it matters

The stored action is self-contradictory, and its two readers resolve the contradiction differently and silently:

- `cardState` (src/card-state.ts:89-99) merges answers into a `Map` per question, latest entry wins — the rendered card shows only `public`, with no trace that the same submit also said `internal`.
- The consumer receives the raw payload (actions.ts header: the orchestration pass "delivers payload text/option/answers like its own classifications") — which of the two values it applies is an accident of its own iteration, not a contract.

A double-submit race, a stale form, or a buggy client can therefore record two opposite answers to a *required* question in one auditable action, and the dashboard's merged view will disagree with what a consumer reading the payload in order applies first.

## Acceptance criteria

- A single `answer` action whose `answers` array names the same `questionId` more than once is rejected at the boundary — either in `validateNewAction` or in `checkActionAgainstItem` — with a legible error naming the duplicated question. (Rejecting, not silently deduping, matches the boundary's fail-legible style; if dedupe is chosen instead, the surviving value must be the one both the card merge and the consumer see, and that choice must be tested.)
- Regression tests in pm-stack/aggregator/test/needs-user.test.ts: duplicate questionId with the *same* value and with *contradictory* values; distinct questions in one submit still pass; partial submits (#1451) are unaffected.
- Aggregator test suite passes (`bun test` in pm-stack/aggregator).

Distinct from: #1476 (the dashboard *UI* presenting one question through multiple answer widgets — this is the POST boundary accepting duplicates from any client), and from the optionId-shielding gap filed this run as #4286.

title: aggregator(tier-items): a valid answers array shields optionId from membership checking — checkActionAgainstItem's else-if chain never validates optionId when answers is present

body:
## Problem

`checkActionAgainstItem` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/tier-items.ts:342-376) validates an `answer` action's payload with an `if / else if / else if` chain over `answers` → `optionId` → `text`. As soon as a payload carries a non-empty `answers` array, the `optionId` branch is never reached — so an `optionId` that is **not one of the item's published options** is accepted unchecked, even though the same value submitted on its own is rejected.

`validateNewAction` (src/actions.ts:272-273, 368-378) accepts the combination: it only requires that *at least one* of `text` / `optionId` / `answers` be present, and stores all of them verbatim. The stored action is then delivered to the consumer as-is (actions.ts header: the pass "delivers payload text/option/answers"), and `cardState` (src/card-state.ts:100) records the unchecked value as the card's `answeredOptionId`, which render.ts:1361 compares against the published options.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe against real code @ cc819feb, md5-matched)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-answeroption/` (verbatim imports of src/tier-items.ts + src/card-state.ts; item fixture mirrors test/needs-user.test.ts: options csv/json, single question `audience` with options internal/public):

- control — `optionId: "yaml"` alone → `"option \"yaml\" is not one of this item's published options"` (rejected, as the existing test at test/needs-user.test.ts:310 expects)
- control — `optionId: "csv"` alone → `null`; valid `answers` alone → `null`
- **bug — `answers: [{questionId: "audience", value: "internal"}]` + `optionId: "yaml"` → `null` (accepted)**
- **bug — same valid answers + `optionId: "bogus-zzz"` (never published) → `null` (accepted)**
- downstream — `cardState` on that accepted action: `answeredOptionId => "bogus-zzz"`

## Why it matters

`checkActionAgainstItem` is the POST boundary whose documented contract (tier-items.ts:335-338) is "option and survey membership" checking — the consumer trusts that an accepted answer's option was actually published on the item. The else-if short-circuit lets any client (or a buggy/stale form) attach an arbitrary, never-offered option id to a legitimate survey submit, and that id propagates to the consumer and into the card's answered state, where it matches no published option.

## Acceptance criteria

- An `answer` action carrying `optionId` is membership-checked against the item's published options **regardless** of whether `answers` (or `text`) is also present — or combined content payloads are rejected outright at `validateNewAction` with a legible error. Either resolution is acceptable; silent acceptance is not.
- Regression tests in pm-stack/aggregator/test/needs-user.test.ts: valid answers + unpublished optionId is rejected (or the combination is rejected); valid answers + a *published* optionId behaves per the chosen contract; the existing single-field cases are unchanged.
- Aggregator test suite passes (`bun test` in pm-stack/aggregator).

Distinct from: #1486 (yes/no answer values unvalidated), #3393/#3396 (impossible calendar dates), #1476 (duplicate answer *widgets* in the UI).

title: aggregator(registry): isSessionRecord admits a record with taskRefs absent — merge keeps it undefined and the registry query/render path throws

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: app/aggregator

body:
## Problem

`isSessionRecord` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/registry.ts:155-175`) treats `taskRefs` as absence-friendly: a record with **no `taskRefs` at all** passes the gate. But `SessionRecord.taskRefs` is a required field (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/model.ts:1112`), both real producers always set it (`recordFromSessionEntry` registry.ts:31-55, `recordFromLaunch` registry.ts:73-90), and several consumers dereference it unconditionally — unlike `mergeRecords`, which is the only consumer that guards with `?? []`:

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/registry-view.ts:114` — `matchesText` spreads `...r.taskRefs` (runs for any `/sessions` or `/api/registry.json` request with `?q=`)
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/registry-view.ts:147` — the `?task=` filter calls `r.taskRefs.some(...)`
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/render.ts:2057` — `sessionRecordLine` reads `r.taskRefs.length` (every record line on `/sessions` and item pages)
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/server.ts:1520` — the item page's linked-sessions filter calls `r.taskRefs.some(...)`

The absence is never normalized away:

- `mergeRecords` (registry.ts:135-152) sets a **new-key** record into the map exactly as admitted — `taskRefs` stays `undefined` — and the merged set is then persisted back to the durable registry store by `mergeIntoRegistry` (`sources/live.ts`), so the poisoned shape is self-perpetuating.
- When no live source is reachable, `registry()` (`sources/live.ts`) returns the store records **directly, with no merge at all**, so a store record missing `taskRefs` reaches the renderers untouched.

This is the residual the #2408 fix left: it made a *present-but-non-array* `taskRefs` fail the gate, while the *absent* case — which the model's type says cannot happen — still passes and crashes the query/render path instead of dropping at the gate.

## Verified (laptop probe, verbatim sources at main `d6bcc30b`)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-regtaskrefs/` on the laptop — `registry.ts` (md5 `667312dd`), `registry-view.ts` (md5 `708c6072`), `model.ts` (md5 `6189406b`), all md5-matched to main `d6bcc30b`, run with bun.

The probe record is well-formed in **every other field** (string `status`, `agentId`, `agentLabel`, timestamps — the shapes #3525 covers are all present and valid); only `taskRefs` is absent:

- `isSessionRecord(minimal)` → `true`; control with `taskRefs: []` → `true`
- `mergeRecords([], [minimal])[0].taskRefs` → `undefined` (absence preserved on the new-key path)
- `queryRegistry([control], ?q=probe)` → OK, matched 1
- `queryRegistry([minimal], ?q=probe)` → **THROW** `TypeError: Spread syntax requires ...iterable not be null or undefined`
- `queryRegistry([control], ?task=code)` → OK, matched 0
- `queryRegistry([minimal], ?task=code)` → **THROW** `TypeError: undefined is not an object (evaluating 'r.taskRefs.some')`
- `queryRegistry([minimal], no filters)` → OK (the crash needs a filter, a record line, or the item-page session filter — the plain page render still hits `sessionRecordLine`'s `r.taskRefs.length`)

## Why it matters

The registry store is durable and grows forever; one record from a poisoned/hand-edited store file or a malformed feed `registry` entry (the two untrusted admission paths, `live.ts` store filter and feed filter) permanently breaks `/sessions` search/filter, the item page, and every record line — the same failure family #2376/#2408/#3525 address in this gate, one field-shape over. The gate is the designated hygiene boundary (validator owns the rule, reject-don't-coerce); the consumers are written against the model's required-field contract and should be able to trust it.

## Acceptance criteria

- `isSessionRecord` rejects a record whose `taskRefs` is absent (present values keep the #2408 rule: array of strings only) — or, equivalently, every admission path normalizes an absent `taskRefs` to `[]` before merge/persist, with the chosen contract stated in the gate's comment. Reject-at-gate is the house precedent (#2376/#2408).
- The #2376/#2408 hygiene tests' minimal fixture (`{id, source, label}`) is updated to the new contract, coordinated with #3525's planned fixture update for the same gate (land them together or sequence explicitly to avoid conflicting fixture edits).
- Regression tests: a taskRefs-less record in the store file and in the feed `registry` section drops individually; `queryRegistry` with `?q=` and `?task=`, `sessionRecordLine`, and the item-page session filter all render without throwing; well-formed records from both producers pass unchanged.
- No consumer-side `?? []` scattering as the sole fix: the contract must hold at the gate so future consumers can dereference `taskRefs` per the model.

## Distinct from

- #2408 (closed): present-but-non-array / non-string-element `taskRefs` in this same gate — absence was explicitly left allowed.
- #3525 (open): absent/non-string `status`, `agentId`/`agentLabel`, and non-finite `tokensTotal` in this same gate — this issue's probe record has all of those well-formed; only `taskRefs` absence is exercised.
- #2485 (open): malformed `taskRefs` *elements* (array present, bad refs) crashing `refUrl` at render.
- #2539 (open): `isFleetFeed` never checking the `registry` container shape — a different gate, upstream of this one.

title: aggregator(alerts): mergeQuiet accepts any string as the quiet-hours timezone — an invalid tz is stored verbatim and inQuietHours then silently never suppresses

labels.name: task/triage

labels.name: app/pm-stack

body:
## Problem

`pm-stack/aggregator/src/alerts.ts` `mergeQuiet` (alerts.ts:88-99) accepts any non-empty string as the quiet-hours timezone:

```ts
if (typeof q.tz === "string" && q.tz.trim()) out.tz = q.tz.trim();
```

There is no validity check. The value is persisted via `validateNewSubscription` → `upsertSubscription`, and the only consumer, `inQuietHours` (alerts.ts:108-132), builds an `Intl.DateTimeFormat` with that zone inside a try/catch whose catch returns `false` — "unknown tz — do not suppress". So a subscription stored with `tz: "Not/AZone"` or `tz: "banana"` has quiet hours that **silently never apply, forever**: dashboard-class notifications are never suppressed, at any hour, with no error anywhere. That is the opposite failure direction from a typo'd time, and it contradicts this parser's own established contract — every other malformed field in `mergeQuiet` falls back to the default instead of being stored verbatim.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe importing the real `alerts.ts` at main `fa28f499` (md5 `933468e2…`, identical in both clones; probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-quiettz/`, log `probe.log`):

- Control: `inQuietHours(mergeQuiet({}), 2026-01-15T06:00Z = 00:00 CST)` → `true`; at `18:00Z = 12:00 CST` → `false` — default prefs behave correctly.
- `mergeQuiet({ tz: "Not/AZone" })` → stored verbatim: `{ start: "23:00", end: "07:00", tz: "Not/AZone", enabled: true }`
- Same prefs at 00:00 CST (deep inside the 23:00–07:00 window) → `inQuietHours` returns `false` — quiet hours never apply.
- `mergeQuiet({ tz: "banana" })` → `tz: "banana"` stored; at midnight CST → `false`.

## Why it matters

Quiet prefs are user-supplied subscription input. A client bug or hand-edited payload that emits a bad zone name is silently stored and then silently disables suppression for that subscription — the user believes they have quiet hours and gets woken at 03:00 anyway, and nothing in the ledger or logs says why. The fix follows the parser's own precedent: validate and fall back to the default, don't store garbage.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `mergeQuiet` accepts a `tz` only if it is a real IANA zone name (e.g. constructing `Intl.DateTimeFormat` with it does not throw); anything else (`"Not/AZone"`, `"banana"`) falls back to the default `America/Chicago`, like other malformed fields do today.
- [ ] Regression tests pin: invalid zones fall back to the default; a valid non-default zone (`UTC`, `Europe/London`) is accepted and honoured by `inQuietHours`; existing quiet-window tests still pass.
- [ ] No other `mergeQuiet` / `inQuietHours` behaviour changes (the `inQuietHours` catch may stay as defence in depth for rows already stored with a bad zone).

Distinct from: #3686 (open — same function, but only the start/end *time* ranges; its acceptance criteria say nothing about `tz`), #3676 (the alert throat itself).

title: aggregator(snapshots): isSnapshotRollup still admits negative pct values and inverted min/max — the #3365 hardening missed the value domain

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.description: Package/app: aggregator (pm-stack in this repo)

labels.name: app/pm-stack
labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

labels.name: task/fix
labels.description: has a fix task queued

body:
## Bug

`isSnapshotRollup` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/snapshots.ts:93`) still does not apply the value-domain rules `isSnapshotRecord` applies to the same data — the residual left after #3365 (timestamps / `limit` / `resetsAt` / pair shape / `month`) and #3443 (`count`) hardened the rest of this gate:

1. **Negative `pct` values pass.** The record gate refuses a scalar `pct` value below 0 (`snapshots.ts:329-332`: "Negative percent-of-limit is never legitimate (#2346): refuse new negative numeric pct records at the boundary"). The rollup gate's `val()` helper (`snapshots.ts:108-114`) accepts any finite number for `valueMin`/`valueMax`/`valueLast`, whatever the unit. `expandRollup` (`snapshots.ts:254-264`) then emits those values as records straight into the `readAll` reading path (`snapshots.ts:568`) — records that `isSnapshotRecord` itself would refuse — and compaction seeding (`snapshots.ts:725`) carries them forward into every later compaction.
2. **Inverted min/max passes.** No writer can produce `valueMin > valueMax`: `aggAddRecord` (`snapshots.ts:167-175`) only ever lowers the min and raises the max, ordered by `rollupOrderKey`/`cmpValue`. The gate never compares them, so a hand-edited or corrupt rollup line with `valueMin=90, valueMax=10` is certified, expanded, and re-seeded — `aggFromRollup` trusts the seeded min/max, so the inversion persists indefinitely (rollup files are kept forever).

## Evidence (verified this run, main 5ae6ee7a)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-rolluppct/` (`probe.ts` + `probe.txt`), driving the real `snapshots.ts` (md5 `1eb8d550`, identical on sandbox main 5ae6ee7a and the laptop copy; `validate.ts`/`model.ts` also md5-matched):

- Control (valid pct rollup): `isSnapshotRollup=true`; all 3 expanded records pass `isSnapshotRecord`.
- `valueLast=-5` (unit `pct`): `isSnapshotRollup=true`; expanded records pass `[true, true, false]` — the `last` record, the one latest-value readers consume, is a record the record gate refuses.
- `valueMin=-20, valueLast=-5` (unit `pct`): `isSnapshotRollup=true`; expanded records pass `[false, true, false]`.
- Record-side controls: a raw record with `value=-5, unit="pct"` → `isSnapshotRecord=false`; `value=50` → `true`.
- `valueMin=90, valueMax=10` (unit `pct`): `isSnapshotRollup=true` (expanded records individually pass the record gate — the violation is the rollup's own min/max invariant, which only this gate can enforce).
- Non-pct control: unit `usd` with `valueMin=-20, valueLast=-5` passes both gates — negative non-pct values are legitimate record-side and must stay legitimate rollup-side.

## Why it matters

The snapshot store is the usage hub's history and rollups are its permanent form (raw files age out at 13 months; rollups are kept indefinitely and re-seed every compaction). #3365 established the principle that the rollup door must not re-admit shapes the record door was hardened to refuse; the pct value domain is the one value rule that hardening missed, so a single corrupt rollup line permanently falsifies a pool's pct history (latest value, min) where a corrupt raw line would simply be dropped. The inverted min/max is the same class: a structural invariant every writer maintains and only this gate can check at the boundary.

## Acceptance criteria

- `isSnapshotRollup` refuses a rollup with `unit="pct"` whose scalar `valueMin`, `valueMax`, or `valueLast` is negative, mirroring `isSnapshotRecord`'s #2346 rule. (Pair values are the `usd-est` estimate shape and are unaffected, as record-side.)
- `isSnapshotRollup` refuses a rollup whose `valueMin` orders after `valueMax` under the existing `rollupOrderKey`/`cmpValue` ordering (scalar and pair forms).
- Negative values for non-pct units (e.g. `usd`) still pass, and a valid pct rollup still passes and expands to records that all pass `isSnapshotRecord`.
- Regression tests beside the existing snapshot gate tests pin each refused shape plus the valid and non-pct controls.
- No change to the rollup file format, `expandRollup` semantics for valid rollups, or compaction output for valid rollups.

Distinct from #3365 (same gate's timestamp/`limit`/`resetsAt`/pair-shape/`month` rules — its acceptance does not cover the pct value domain or min/max ordering) and #3443 (same gate's `count` rule). Distinct from #2568/#3460 (writer-side `used_percent` range in snapshot-records).

body:
## Finding

The feed's PAYG gate — `isPaygLine` in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/feed.ts:584-610` — checks only the *shape* of a line: dollar fields need only be finite (`nullableFinite`, feed.ts:586), the estimate pair needs only finite `low`/`high` (feed.ts:587-596), and `measuredAt` needs only be a string or null (feed.ts:605). It accepts values no producer can emit:

- negative `accruedUsd` / `collectedUsd` / `unbilledUsd`
- a negative estimate pair (`low: -10, high: -5`)
- an inverted estimate pair (`low: 25, high: 20`)
- a non-date `measuredAt` (`"banana"`, `"2026-02-30"`)

These lines survive `loadFeed`'s drop-and-count sanitization (`sanitizePayg`, feed.ts:618-627) and reach every consumer verbatim:

- `paygCardHtml` (render.ts:2139-2151) renders `$<accrued> accrued · $<unbilled> unbilled` and sums `unbilledUsd` into the card total whose `total > 5` badge class decides the health styling — a negative line silently offsets real unbilled spend.
- `countedEstimate` (model.ts:1172-1174, `1.2 × high`) returns **-6** for the negative pair ("counted $-6.00 as used") and **24** for the inverted pair — a counted figure below the pair's own `low`.
- `buildAttentionFlags` (derive.ts:872-882) keys the payg-unbilled flag's severity on the raw `unbilledUsd`.
- `recordsFromPaygLines` (snapshot-records.ts:127-159), the snapshot writer for this same `PaygLine` shape, emits a record with `value: -5` for a negative `accruedUsd`, and `tsFor` (snapshot-records.ts:38-40) turns `measuredAt: "banana"` into the record timestamp **`"bananaT12:00:00Z"`**.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-payggate/` — verbatim copy of the aggregator `src/` at main `9a3c52de` (feed.ts sha256 prefix `0b4b9b77`, matched on both hosts), run with `bun probe.ts`:

```text
control valid: true
negative_accrued isPaygLine: true sanitizePayg kept: 1
negative_collected isPaygLine: true sanitizePayg kept: 1
negative_unbilled isPaygLine: true sanitizePayg kept: 1
negative_estimate_both isPaygLine: true sanitizePayg kept: 1
inverted_estimate isPaygLine: true sanitizePayg kept: 1
garbage_measuredAt isPaygLine: true sanitizePayg kept: 1
countedEstimate(neg high -5): -6
countedEstimate(inverted 25/20): 24
snapshot records for negative accrued: [{"ts":"2026-10-25T12:00:00Z","serviceId":"meta:high-usage","metricId":"payg-accrued","value":-5,...}]
snapshot records for banana measuredAt: [{"ts":"bananaT12:00:00Z",...}]
```

## Why it matters

The feed file is hand-editable and collector-produced; every sibling gate in this file was hardened to values, not just shape, after exactly this class of falsification: `isBurnSegment` refuses negative tokens and inverted ranges (#3428), the charge gates' negative/non-date gap is tracked in #3458, and subscription `renewsAt` in #3513. The PAYG gate is the remaining shape-only one: one drifted or hand-edited line falsifies the /quota PAYG total, publishes a negative "counted as used" figure, and — through the snapshot writer — can append a negative measured record and a non-date timestamp to the usage history.

Distinct from: #3458 (charge rows / unmatched charges only), #3513 (subscription renewsAt), #2450 (closed; shape-only PAYG gate introduction), #2568/#2571 (quota-gather / provider-usage percents).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `isPaygLine` refuses negative `accruedUsd`, `collectedUsd`, and `unbilledUsd` (the shared `isNonNegative` primitive in validate.ts:33, null still allowed where it is today).
- [ ] `isPaygLine` refuses an estimate whose `low` or `high` is negative, or whose `low > high`.
- [ ] `isPaygLine` refuses a `measuredAt` that is neither null nor a real ISO date/timestamp (the shared `isIsoDate` primitive), so `tsFor` can never mint a `bananaT12:00:00Z` record.
- [ ] Malformed lines drop individually through `sanitizePayg` with the drop count surfaced, exactly as today — the whole feed is never rejected for one bad PAYG line.
- [ ] Regression tests in `test/feed.test.ts` beside the existing #2450 PAYG block: each shape above fails `isPaygLine`, drops in `sanitizePayg`, and a valid control line (including all-null figures) still passes.

title: opencode-route-proxy: window times are never range-checked — parseHHMM accepts 24:60 and 99:99, so a typo'd window silently becomes always-on, always-off, or end-less

labels.name: task/triage

body:
## Summary

`bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs`'s window-time parser accepts out-of-range times and silently reinterprets them: `parseHHMM` (bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs:398-401) only checks the shape `^([0-9]{1,2}):([0-9]{2})$` and returns `hour * 60 + minute` with no range check, so `24:60` parses to 1500 and `99:99` to 6039. Nothing else validates the windows either — `normalizeWindowGate` (:372-377) only extracts the gate name/invert flag, and the window definitions come straight from config (`model_route_windows`, :175).

## Verified behavior (this run)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-routewindow/`) extracted `parseHHMM` + `windowActive` verbatim from the real file @ 6cdfaee0 (md5 c7ad071278474a5b4bfe0a181714cc0e) and ran them:

- `parseHHMM('09:30') = 570` (control, correct); `parseHHMM('24:60') = 1500`; `parseHHMM('99:99') = 6039` — all accepted.
- Window `99:99`–`99:98` (a wrapping window) is **active at Mon 12:00 UTC**: the wrap branch (`mins < end`, :443-447) is true for every real wall minute (max 1439 < 6038), so a nonsense window is effectively always-on — and with `invert: true` on the gate, always-off.
- Window `25:00`–`26:00` is **never active** (no wall minute reaches 1500 in the non-wrapping branch) — a typo'd window silently kills the route target, or, inverted, makes it permanently eligible.
- Window `09:00`–`24:60` behaves as if it had no end (active at 23:30), silently extending a curfew-style gate past its intent.

## Why it matters

Window gates decide which model routes are eligible at which times (quota windows, overnight routes). A single typo in a window definition does not fail at startup or log anything — it silently flips a gate to always-on, always-off, or end-less, which misroutes traffic in exactly the hours the window exists to control. The fleet already treats this shape as a bug in the sibling surface: aggregator `mergeQuiet` accepting `99:99`/`24:60` is filed as #3686. This is the same class in the route proxy, which has never had the range check.

## Acceptance criteria

- `parseHHMM` (or window loading, one place) rejects hour > 23 and minute > 59 — a window with an out-of-range start or end is not silently reinterpreted.
- The failure mode is visible: an invalid window definition is refused/logged by name at config load (consistent with how this proxy surfaces other config errors), rather than the gate quietly evaluating as always-on/always-off.
- Regression tests in `bin/opencode-route-proxy.test.mjs`: `24:00`, `24:60`, `99:99`, `25:00` as start and as end are rejected/refused; valid boundary windows `00:00`, `23:59`, and the #3874 wrapping-window cases still evaluate as before.
- Existing route-proxy tests pass (`node --test bin/opencode-route-proxy.test.mjs`).

## Dedup / related

- #3686 (open) is the aggregator's quiet-window parser, a different file and surface; this issue is the route proxy's own parser.
- #3874 (closed) fixed the wrapping window's day attribution in this same `windowActive`; it did not add range validation.
- #3225 (closed) added window gates to this proxy; no range check was part of it.

title: id(worker-poc): a /step that fails after guest.update but before the journal insert keeps the advanced guest — the failed event is silently journaled inside the next step's snapshot

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage

labels.name: source/creator

body:
## Problem

In the `id` worker-poc Durable Object host, a `/step` request whose guest work fails **after** `guest.update(...)` has succeeded but **before** the journal `INSERT` commits leaves the advanced guest in place — so the failed request's event is silently journaled as part of the *next* step's snapshot, and the journal's own event list can no longer reproduce its snapshots.

`pkgs/id/worker-poc/src/worker.ts` (WorldObject.handle, `/step` branch):

- The update → view → records → snapshot → hash → insert sequence runs as one unit (the file header states the invariant: "a /step runs its update -> hash -> journal-insert as one serialized unit, so journal order always matches guest evolution order").
- Only the `INSERT` is guarded: its catch calls `this.dropGuest()` with the comment "The guest advanced but nothing was journaled: discard it, so the next request restores from the journal and the unjournaled event cannot contaminate later snapshots."
- `guest.view()`, `guest.records()`, `guest.snapshot()` and `sha256Hex(snapshot)` all run **between** the update and that guarded insert with no such protection. If any of them throws, the exception propagates, nothing is journaled, `this.step` is unchanged — but `this.guest` keeps the advanced model.
- The same window includes a trapping `guest.update(...)` itself: `PlazaGuest.update` (guest.ts) only commits its model pointer on success, but a trap mid-update can already have mutated guest linear memory, and the native host treats any failed update as poisoning (sandbox.rs `update`: `if result.is_err() { self.poisoned = true; }`). The TS host keeps using the guest.

The native host's distinction underlines the gap: a trapped **view** does not poison the native instance (F11.17, sandbox.rs `view`) precisely because rendering never changes the model and no journaling is tied to it there. In the worker host the view sits *inside* the journaling unit, so the safe native behaviour becomes state corruption here.

## Verified this run (2026-11-02, sandbox main @a1294111-lineage, files byte-identical on the laptop clone)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-workerstep/`, Node v24): verbatim copies of `worker-poc/src/worker.ts` (md5 `dcb1af9f9e01cff861385ba010382cc4`; only the CompiledWasm import line adapted to compile the same bytes from disk, as wrangler supplies the module in production), `guest.ts` (`410a375ac6cbb0ba3ff26d36eeff29b6`), `manifest.ts` (`19b5e7b0bb0bd93fc21652057460fef5`) and the prebuilt `examples/roc-counter/counter.wasm` (`451971d91b22c0dcb0a5ac5147842257`), with an in-memory SQL shim for the DO journal. `PlazaGuest.prototype.view` was made to throw exactly once (the F11.17 trapped-view case) during the first `/step {participant:1, event:"inc"}`:

```
step1: fetch rejected: simulated trapped view (F11.17 case) | journal rows: 0
step2: status 200 body.step 1 body.records {"count":2}
journal rows: 1 | row.step 1 | row.event "inc" | row.records {"count":2} | row snapshot (count) 2
after cold start: step 1 records {"count":2}
```

So: the caller of step 1 got a failure and the journal recorded **zero** events for it, yet its `inc` is inside step 1's journaled snapshot (`count: 2` from a single journaled `"inc"` event, where replaying the journal's events gives `count: 1`), and a cold start restores the phantom state from that snapshot. The journal — the DO's stated source of truth — is internally inconsistent from that point on.

Distinct from #4076 (/cold-start reporting `this.step`) and #4074 (participant coercion in `PlazaGuest.update`): different failure window, different lines, different consequence.

## Why it matters

The worker host's whole design contract (#2271) is journal equality with the native host: the SQLite journal is the source of truth and cold-start restore must reproduce guest evolution from it. One transient guest fault (a trapping view/records/snapshot, a hash failure, a trapping update) permanently desyncs the journal's event list from its snapshots, with no error recorded anywhere — every later cold start faithfully restores state that includes an event the journal says never happened and whose caller was told the step failed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Any failure inside the `/step` unit after (or during) `guest.update(...)` and before the journal insert commits — update trap, view/records/snapshot throw, snapshot missing, hash failure — discards the guest (`dropGuest()` or equivalent), exactly as the insert-failure path already does, so the next request restores from the journal.
- [ ] A regression test (smoke or unit, alongside `worker-poc/smoke/`) drives a `/step` whose post-update stage fails once, then a second `/step`, and asserts: the second response is step 1, its records/snapshot reflect only the second event, the journal holds exactly one row naming the second event, and a cold start reproduces that same state.
- [ ] The existing counter smoke / compare checks still pass (`worker-poc` smoke scripts or CI equivalent).

body:
# mcpx(artifacts): the never-overwrite delivery rule is a check-then-rename race — uniquePath's O_EXCL reservation is deleted before the write, and copyInto/writeNew finish with an overwriting os.Rename

## Summary

Every artifact delivery path in mcpx documents the same rule — a delivered file **never overwrites** an existing one; a same-named second delivery is suffixed instead (`shot-1.png`). That rule is what #1605 restored for the exec paths and what `Store.Export` has always claimed. The implementation is a check-then-act pair with the claim released in the middle:

1. `uniquePath` (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/artifacts/name.go:90-137`) finds a free name by creating the candidate with `O_CREATE|O_EXCL` (:118) — then **removes the placeholder again** (:124, "Removed again so Link can have the name") and returns the bare path. From that moment the name is unclaimed: the directory looks exactly as it did before the call.
2. The caller then writes through a temp file and finishes with `os.Rename(tmp, dest)` — `copyInto` (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/artifacts/artifacts.go:394-408`, used by `Store.Export` at :780-797), `writeNew` (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/cli/exec.go:426-439`, used by `fetchArtifacts`), and the streaming delivery path's direct `os.Rename(w.Name(), dest)` (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/cli/exec.go:330`). POSIX rename **replaces** an existing destination silently.

So any file that appears at the chosen path between the two steps — most realistically the first of two concurrent same-named deliveries finishing — is silently overwritten by the second, which is precisely the #1605 data-loss outcome ("silently destroyed the first artifact's body and left both Path fields pointing at the one surviving file"), through the narrower window the current code's own comment believes is closed (:120-123: "without the reservation two concurrent exports pick the same name and one is lost" — but the reservation is deleted before the payload is written, so two deliveries that resolve their names before either writes do pick the same name, as the probe below shows).

## Evidence

- `name.go:118-125`: the O_EXCL create is followed immediately by `_ = os.Remove(p)` and `return p, nil` — no file, no claim.
- `artifacts.go:407`: `copyInto` ends in `os.Rename(tmp.Name(), dest)` with no existence check; `Export` (:784-794) composes `uniquePath` + `copyInto` and documents "collisions are resolved by suffixing, never by overwriting".
- `cli/exec.go:326-330` and `:412-439`: both exec delivery paths compose the exported `UniquePath` with a renaming write the same way (comments cite the #1605 never-overwrite rule).
- Verified this run on main `9456d017` with the verbatim module on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-artifactrace/`; name.go md5 `bf6d33f0`, artifacts.go md5 `6a819621`), an in-package probe test driving the real `uniquePath` + `copyInto`:
  - two `uniquePath(dir, "shot.png")` calls before any write return the **same** path;
  - a foreign file written to that path in the window is **silently replaced** by `copyInto` (final content is the new delivery's bytes, no error).

## Why it matters

The never-overwrite rule is a data-loss guarantee, not a nicety: concurrent `mcpx exec` runs of the same script (the exact scenario in uniquePath's comment) delivering same-named artifacts into one directory can still destroy the first artifact and report two `Path`s for one surviving file. The guarantee currently holds only when deliveries are strictly sequential and nothing else writes the directory.

## Acceptance criteria

- A destination that exists (or appears) at write time is never silently replaced on any delivery path: `Store.Export`, the exec streaming path, and `fetchArtifacts` all land the new delivery under a suffixed name (or fail loudly), with the returned `Path` matching the file actually written.
- The claim is held across the write (e.g. keep the O_EXCL placeholder and rename-over-it only when it is still the placeholder this call created, link/renameat2-style no-replace semantics, or an equivalent atomic claim), not released before it.
- Regression tests cover the interleaving: resolve destination → foreign file appears → deliver → foreign bytes intact and the delivery lands under a different name; plus a concurrent same-name delivery test (two goroutines, both files survive with distinct paths).
- The stale "Removed again so Link can have the name" comment is updated to match the post-#1660 copy-based design.

## Dedup notes

#1605 (closed) fixed the exec paths renaming onto the *bare sanitized name without consulting uniquePath at all*; they now call `UniquePath` — this issue is the residual race inside the `uniquePath` + rename composition itself, which #1605's fix relies on. #1660 (closed) replaced hardlink delivery with copies (and left the stale Link comment above); it did not change the claim or rename semantics. #3064 was docs-only fallout of #1660.

title: id(world_net): the abuse evaluator's per-peer connection cap (max_connections_per_peer=4) is never wired in — WorldProtocol::accept registers no connection, so one peer can open unlimited connections

body:
## Summary

The shared abuse evaluator's per-peer concurrent connection cap is implemented and unit-tested but never wired into any transport. `AbusePolicy::max_connections_per_peer` (default **4**) and `AbuseEvaluator::open_connection` / `close_connection` exist only for `abuse.rs`'s own tests: no production code path calls them. The P0-A integration (PR #3960, for #3882) wired frame/byte charging into `WorldProtocol`, but `WorldProtocol::accept` never registers a connection with the evaluator — so a single remote endpoint can open an unbounded number of QUIC connections to the world protocol, each allowed its own 16 sessions, and nothing ever refuses the 5th, 50th, or 500th connection.

## Evidence (verified this run, 2026-11-02, main @762f32af)

- `pkgs/id/src/abuse.rs:237` — `AbusePolicy.max_connections_per_peer`; `:255` — default value 4; `:625` — a test pins the default.
- `pkgs/id/src/abuse.rs:433-460` — `open_connection` enforces the cap (returns a `RateLimited` refusal at the cap) and `close_connection` releases it; unit tests at ~:661-687 exercise cap/refusal/release.
- Caller search across the whole crate (run independently on the sandbox clone @762f32af and on the laptop clone @12ea94d17, same result): `grep -rn "open_connection|close_connection" pkgs/id/src --include="*.rs"` returns **no callers outside `abuse.rs`** (definition + its own tests only). File md5s: `abuse.rs` 52884455f31e10e13e0da898053fc872, `world_net.rs` 4692a53fb89c3600be435f0e8adad7e1.
- `pkgs/id/src/world_net.rs:129-158` — `WorldProtocol::accept` prunes abuse state, then loops on `conn.accept_bi()` with only a per-connection session semaphore (`MAX_SESSIONS_PER_CONNECTION = 16`, :54, :136). It clones the shared evaluator into each session for frame/byte charging but never calls `open_connection`/`close_connection`, and iroh invokes `accept` once per incoming connection with no per-remote accounting anywhere else in the handler.
- Contrast: the SSH transport does bound connections globally (`pkgs/id/src/world_ssh.rs:71` `MAX_CONNECTIONS: usize = 64`), so the world QUIC transport is the unbounded one — and its bound was supposed to be per-peer, via the evaluator.

## Why it matters

The evaluator's module doc states the design premise (#2244 P0-A): an endpoint's allowance is a property of the endpoint, "never multiplied by opening more connections to it", and the evaluator owns "the concurrent connection cap per peer". Frame/byte buckets are indeed shared per endpoint, but connections themselves are the resource a flooding peer spends on the host: each accepted connection carries an accept task, a `JoinSet`, QUIC connection state, and up to 16 session tasks with reader tasks — all before any frame is charged (a peer that opens connections and sends nothing is never charged at all). The cap that was designed, implemented, and tested for exactly this is dead code in production, so the pre-auth connection-flood surface the #2032/#2033 design set out to close is still open on the world protocol.

Distinct from #3927 (oversize requests get a temporary refusal from `check_bytes`/`check_frame` — a refusal-contract issue inside the evaluator) and from #4004/#3991 (chat-presence state bounds). This is about the evaluator's connection-count contract having no consumer.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `WorldProtocol::accept` (and any other transport the integration charges frames on) registers each incoming connection with the shared evaluator (`open_connection` keyed by the remote endpoint) and releases it (`close_connection`) when the connection ends, on all exit paths.
- [ ] A connection refused by the cap is rejected/closed without spawning session tasks, and the refusal is logged/counted so operators can see cap hits.
- [ ] Regression test: one endpoint opening `max_connections_per_peer + 1` concurrent connections to a `WorldProtocol` sees the extra connection refused, while a second endpoint is unaffected; after one connection closes, a new one is admitted.
- [ ] If the intended scope is deliberately narrower (e.g. the cap is meant only for a future transport), the policy field and evaluator doc say so explicitly instead of presenting a cap no transport enforces.

Related: #2244 (parent), #3881 (core, closed — introduced the cap), #3882 / PR #3960 (integration, closed/merged — wired frame/byte charging but not the connection cap), #2033 (design).

body:
# aggregator(dns): isDnsSection accepts negative money after the #2412 finite fix — a poisoned feed renders $-50.00/yr, negative entry prices, and a negative renewing-soon total, and records a negative snapshot value

## Summary

The #2412 fix (merged today in PR #4174, commit fd1321d4) hardened `isDnsSection` so `totalAnnualListUsd` and each entry's `priceUsd` must be **finite** numbers and `status` must be in the enum. It did not bound them below: a **negative** finite value passes the gate on both fields. No producer can emit a negative price — `parsePriceUsd` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/dns.ts:24-27`) only matches `^\$([\d,]+(?:\.\d+)?)$` (no sign), and the section total is a sum of those — so a negative value is exactly the poisoned-feed case the gate exists to reject, and it currently certifies it as valid.

## Evidence

- Gate: `pm-stack/aggregator/src/dns.ts:74-107` (`isDnsSection`) — `totalAnnualListUsd` checked only `typeof === "number" && Number.isFinite(...)` (:83-84); entry `priceUsd` checked only null/undefined or finite number (:94-96). No `>= 0` anywhere.
- Render paths that trust the gate: `pm-stack/aggregator/src/render.ts:3488` prints `$${section.totalAnnualListUsd.toFixed(2)}/yr`; :3466 prints each entry's `$${e.priceUsd.toFixed(2)}`; :3486-3488 sums `priceUsd` over `summarizeDns(...).renewingSoon` into the "renewing soon" spend total.
- Snapshot path: `pm-stack/aggregator/src/snapshot-records.ts:250` (`recordsFromDns`) appends `dns.totalAnnualListUsd` verbatim as the `total-annual-usd` snapshot record value, so a negative total also enters the usage history series.
- Verified this run on main `6be48a69` with the verbatim sources on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-dnsneg/`; dns.ts md5 `efb3954e`, derive.ts md5 `dcdefb5e`, model.ts md5 `6189406b` — identical on sandbox and laptop), under Bun:

```
producer section (dnsSectionFromRegister): totalAnnualListUsd = 30, prices 10 / 20
control good isDnsSection:            true
control string total rejected:         false   (gate rejects)
control NaN price rejected:            false   (gate rejects)
BUG negative total -50 isDnsSection:   true    -> renders as $-50.00/yr
BUG negative priceUsd -999 isDnsSection: true  -> entry renders $-999.00
BUG negative-price section isDnsSection: true
renewingSoon: soon.example             render.ts soonTotal = $-999.00
```

## Why it matters

`isDnsSection` is the shared structural gate for the collector and the live source; everything downstream (the /dns page, the usage view, snapshot records) dereferences these fields without re-checking, which is precisely why #2412 moved the finite/status rules into the gate. A corrupted or hand-edited feed section with negative money currently sails through and publishes nonsense spend figures — and a negative snapshot record, which later compaction/reporting treats as measured history. This is the same range-check family as #2582 (out-of-range `pctOfLimit` dropped at both readers) and #2568, applied to the field #2412 just hardened.

## Acceptance criteria

- `isDnsSection` rejects a section whose `totalAnnualListUsd` is negative, and rejects any entry whose present `priceUsd` is negative; zero remains valid, and null/absent `priceUsd` remains valid.
- A producer-built section from `dnsSectionFromRegister` over a normal register still passes the gate unchanged.
- Regression tests (e.g. alongside the #2412 cases in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/slice3.test.ts`) cover negative total, negative entry price, and the zero/null controls.
- No change to the renewal-date or generatedAt validation — those are tracked separately (#2199, #3441).

## Dedup notes

#2412 (closed today) covered missing/string/null/NaN/Infinity totals and prices plus the status enum — not sign. #3441 covers the impossible `generatedAt`; #2199 covers impossible renewal dates in `parseDnsRegister`. Neither covers negative money at this gate.

title: design-code-proxy: DESIGN_CODE_PROXY_BACKEND_TIMEOUT_MS has no upper bound — a value over 2^31-1 is silently truncated to ~24.8 days, defeating the #2097 silent-backend timeout (house parseProxyMillis bypassed)

labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

body:
## Summary

`bin/design-code-proxy.mjs` parses `DESIGN_CODE_PROXY_BACKEND_TIMEOUT_MS` with a hand-rolled `Number()` guard that checks only `Number.isFinite(raw) && raw > 0` — no upper bound and no integer-spelling check. Values above 2^31−1 are silently truncated by Node's timer layer to 2147483647 ms (~24.8 days), so a too-large value defeats the #2097 backend-inactivity timeout instead of extending it modestly; non-decimal spellings (`0x10` → 16 ms, `1e5`) are also admitted. The house helper for exactly this — `parseProxyMillis` in the sibling `bin/proxy-port.mjs`, which this file already imports `parseProxyPort` from — refuses anything outside integer 1..2147483647 at startup, naming the variable.

## Evidence (verified this run, 2026-11-02)

- `bin/design-code-proxy.mjs:27-30` (md5 `c1460c96f7a72fa35231051f93c33de0`):

  ```js
  const BACKEND_TIMEOUT_MS = (() => {
    const raw = Number(process.env.DESIGN_CODE_PROXY_BACKEND_TIMEOUT_MS);
    return Number.isFinite(raw) && raw > 0 ? Math.floor(raw) : 60_000;
  })();
  ```

- The value feeds `clientReq.setTimeout(BACKEND_TIMEOUT_MS, …)` (`bin/design-code-proxy.mjs:249`) and `localReq.setTimeout(BACKEND_TIMEOUT_MS, …)` (`bin/design-code-proxy.mjs:463`) — the #2097 silent-backend protection.
- `bin/proxy-port.mjs:50-70` (md5 `b833b6038a74d5a34b78306c70702f0f`): `MAX_TIMEOUT_MS = 2147483647` and `parseProxyMillis`/`parseProxyMillisValue` refuse non-integer or out-of-range values with a startup error naming the env var. `design-code-proxy.mjs:4` already imports from this module (ports only).

Laptop probe (Node v24.21.0): an HTTP request to a silent local server with `req.setTimeout(2147483648, cb)`:

```text
(node) TimeoutOverflowWarning: 2147483648 does not fit into a 32-bit signed integer.
Timer duration was truncated to 2147483647.
no timeout callback within 3000ms
```

So `DESIGN_CODE_PROXY_BACKEND_TIMEOUT_MS=2147483648` (or any larger finite value, e.g. a typo'd extra zero) does not produce an error and does not produce the requested timeout — it produces a ~24.8-day inactivity timeout, i.e. a silent backend holds the client request and a pooled keep-alive socket effectively forever, which is exactly the hang #2097 added this timeout to prevent. Conversely `0x10` is admitted as a 16 ms timeout, which would kill every slow-but-alive backend call.

## Why it matters

The timeout is a hang-protection mechanism; a configuration path that silently converts it to ~25 days (or to 16 ms) removes the protection while the process starts healthy and logs nothing. Sibling proxies' env numbers are being moved onto the strict helper family (#2835 design; per-file instances filed for other proxies), and this one was missed because it has a partial guard — finite-and-positive looks validated at a glance.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `DESIGN_CODE_PROXY_BACKEND_TIMEOUT_MS` is parsed through `parseProxyMillis` (or an equivalent strict check): decimal integer, 1..2147483647, startup error naming the variable and value otherwise.
- [ ] Unset/empty keeps the 60_000 ms default.
- [ ] Tests in `bin/design-code-proxy.test.mjs` cover: `2147483648` refuses to start (or is refused by the parse), `0x10` / `1e5` refused, a valid value (e.g. `5000`) honoured.
- [ ] Existing design-code-proxy tests still pass.

title: codedb-bridge: parseDaemonUrl silently drops query, fragment and userinfo — CODEDB_DAEMON_URL validation rejects paths but strips the rest instead of failing fast

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: app/codedb-bridge
labels.description: bin/codedb-bridge.mjs — stdio MCP bridge to the shared codedb daemon

body:
## Problem

`parseDaemonUrl` in `bin/codedb-bridge.mjs:37-51` is meant to accept only a bare `http://` origin — it rejects a non-URL, a non-`http:` protocol, and any path other than `/`:

```js
if (url.protocol !== 'http:' || (url.pathname !== '/' && url.pathname !== '')) {
  throw new Error(`CODEDB_DAEMON_URL="${value}" must be an http:// origin with no path ...`);
}
return url.origin;
```

But it never inspects `url.search`, `url.hash`, or `url.username`/`url.password`, and `url.origin` silently strips all three. So configuration the operator wrote is silently discarded instead of either honoured or rejected:

- `CODEDB_DAEMON_URL=http://127.0.0.1:7719/?token=abc` → accepted, query dropped
- `CODEDB_DAEMON_URL=http://user:pass@127.0.0.1:7719/` → accepted, credentials dropped
- `CODEDB_DAEMON_URL=http://127.0.0.1:7719/#frag` → accepted, fragment dropped
- `CODEDB_DAEMON_URL=http://127.0.0.1:7719/?next=/explore/tree` → accepted, query dropped

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneA-codedb/` (verbatim copy of `bin/codedb-bridge.mjs` from main `199a7d27`, md5 `ca05ede20d2ae1a4760297bbe9320c58`, node v24.21.0), calling `parseDaemonUrl` directly: all four inputs above returned `"http://127.0.0.1:7719"` with no error.

Controls in the existing suite (`bin/codedb-bridge.test.mjs:16-24`) confirm the intended strictness for the cases that are checked: `https://…` throws, `http://127.0.0.1:7719/explore` throws, a non-URL throws. Query/fragment/userinfo are simply untested and unchecked.

## Why it matters

This is the bridge's only configuration knob, and its errors are supposed to fail fast at startup with a message naming the bad value (that is the whole design of `parseDaemonUrl`, and `main` exits 1 on its throw, `:245-250`). A typo'd or pasted URL carrying a query or credentials instead starts the bridge against a different effective configuration than the operator wrote, with no trace — a silent third path of the kind issue #3352 bans, at the config layer. Dropping embedded credentials silently is the worst case: the operator believes the daemon is being reached with auth; it is not, and nothing says so.

## Acceptance criteria

- `parseDaemonUrl` rejects (with the existing error style naming the value) any URL with a non-empty query string, fragment, username, or password — or, if one of those is deliberately supported, it is honoured and documented in the header instead of stripped.
- Tests in `bin/codedb-bridge.test.mjs` cover query, fragment, and userinfo inputs alongside the existing protocol/path cases; the default and trailing-slash cases still pass.

title: aggregator(opencode): an in-range future time.updated earns freshness forever — a future-dated session pins the attention feed and can crowd out every recent session

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: app/aggregator
labels.description: Package/app: aggregator (pm-stack in this repo)

body:
## Problem

`mapServerSessions` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/sources/opencode.ts) treats an in-range **future** `time.updated` stamp as fresh forever: the freshness inclusion is one-sided, so a session dated days or years ahead stays in the attention feed, sorts to the top, and can crowd genuinely recent sessions out of the detailed cap.

## Evidence (main `687ac07a`)

- `validMs` (opencode.ts:100-101) accepts any finite stamp `0 < ms <= 8.64e15` — including stamps far in the future. It gates both `iso()` and the freshness inclusion, per its own comment.
- Inclusion (opencode.ts:151-156): `now - (s.time?.updated as number) <= ATTENTION_WINDOW_MS` (12h). For a future stamp this difference is negative, so the test passes for *any* future date, however far. The included set is then sorted newest-first (`.sort((a, b) => (b.time?.updated ?? 0) - (a.time?.updated ?? 0))`) and capped with `.slice(0, opts.maxDetailed ?? 60)` — future sessions take the first slots.
- The existing test coverage (test/opencode.test.ts, `ses_bad_updated`) covers only the out-of-Date-range stamp `1e16`, which `validMs` rejects. An in-range future stamp is not covered.

Verified this run on the laptop with the verbatim file (md5 `042391fd` for opencode.ts, `6189406b` for model.ts, matching the sandbox clone at `687ac07a`), stub v2 server, `NOW = 2026-11-01T22:50:00Z`:

- Control set {future = NOW+365d, recent = NOW−5m, stale = NOW−20h}: mapped entries are `[ses_future, ses_recent]` — the future session is included and first, with `lastActivityAt: 2027-11-01T22:50:00.000Z`; the stale session is correctly excluded.
- Crowd-out set {1 recent session + 61 future sessions}: mapped count is 60 and the genuinely recent session is **not** included — the future sessions fill the whole detailed cap.

Probe: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneB-futureupdated/` (probe.ts + verbatim src copies).

## Why it matters

The attention feed is the dashboard's "what needs eyes now" surface (consumers: the live source in sources/live.ts and scripts/collect-fleet-feed.ts). One clock-skewed or buggy server stamp pins a dead session at the top of the feed until real time catches up to the stamp plus 12h — for a year-ahead stamp, a year. Enough future stamps (a single server with a wrong clock produces them wholesale) evict every genuinely recent session from the 60-session detailed window, so real work disappears from the feed while phantom-fresh sessions remain. The aggregator already has the opposite convention elsewhere: feed/orchestration generatedAt stamps implausibly in the future are invalid (`GENERATED_AT_FUTURE_SKEW_MS = 60_000`, feed.ts) and quota-current rejects future measuredAt beyond a skew bound (quota-current.ts) — the session mapper is the one-sided outlier.

Distinct from: #2286 (closed — out-of-range stamps throwing / earning freshness; in-range future stamps were not covered), #1800 (id web token future-dated expiry, different subsystem), #3947 (board done-item recency, different consumer).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A session whose `time.updated` is more than a small future-skew tolerance (suggest the aggregator's existing 60s convention) ahead of `now` does **not** earn freshness inclusion in `mapServerSessions` — it is treated like a stale/absent stamp for inclusion (active-set and pending-permission inclusion are unaffected).
- [ ] Such a session does not consume a detailed-cap slot ahead of genuinely recent sessions; with 61 future-stamped sessions and 1 recent session, the recent session is mapped.
- [ ] `lastActivityAt` handling for a future stamp is decided and tested (null it, clamp it, or document why the raw future value is safe for derive/registry consumers).
- [ ] New tests in test/opencode.test.ts style cover: in-range future updated (excluded from freshness), future updated at/inside the skew tolerance (included), and the crowd-out case; the existing #2286 out-of-range cases still pass.

body:
## Problem

`parse_app_manifest` (`pkgs/id/src/app_manifest.rs`, main @ 56e66c9a) validates every list field in the manifest except one:

- `interfaces.cli.commands` rejects blank entries (app_manifest.rs:124-131, "must not contain empty command names");
- `capabilities.request` rejects blank entries (:133-140) and duplicates (:141-152, with the pinned rationale that a repeat is an authoring mistake the gate should name rather than silently absorb);
- `[resources].files` (`Resources`, app_manifest.rs:76-79) is never inspected at all — `parse_app_manifest` (:97-193) has no resources block.

Verified this run with a probe crate on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneA-resources/`) compiling a byte-identical copy of `app_manifest.rs` from main 56e66c9a (md5 `d786541ff7045e599df9516605b129db`):

```
baseline-web:             ACCEPTED
design-example-files:     ACCEPTED files=["assets/**", "web/templates/**"]
control-blank-cli-command: REJECTED interfaces.cli.commands must not contain empty command names
control-blank-capability:  REJECTED capabilities.request must not contain empty entries
control-dup-capability:    REJECTED capabilities.request must not contain duplicates
blank-entry:               ACCEPTED files=["assets/a.txt", ""]
whitespace-entry:          ACCEPTED files=["  "]
duplicate-entry:           ACCEPTED files=["assets/a.txt", "assets/a.txt"]
padded-duplicate-entry:    ACCEPTED files=["a.txt", " a.txt "]
empty-list:                ACCEPTED files=[]
```

## Why it matters

Per the app-packaging design (`doc/2026-10-29T12-50-36Z_design_id_app_packaging` §2/§5), `[resources].files` is the set the pack step will package and content-hash as a unit. A blank entry names nothing (or, resolved against the folder, the folder itself); a duplicate entry double-counts one file in that set; a padded entry (`" a.txt "`) names a file that does not exist under that spelling. All three are exactly the authoring mistakes the same function already refuses for `commands` and `capabilities.request` — the strict gate reads as deliberate where it is actually missing a field. The failure surfaces later, at pack time or as a silently wrong bundle, with no diagnostic naming the entry.

Scope boundaries (already tracked, not this issue): path confinement of `files` entries (absolute / `..`) is #4059; duplicate/padding handling for `cli.commands` and `capabilities.request` is #4085. This issue is only the missing blank/duplicate gate for `[resources].files` itself.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `parse_app_manifest` rejects a `[resources].files` entry that is empty or whitespace-only, with an error naming the field — mirroring the `cli.commands` / `capabilities.request` blank rules.
- [ ] `parse_app_manifest` rejects duplicate `files` entries under the same normalisation rule the #4085 fix chooses for the other list fields (a padded duplicate such as `" a.txt "` must not parse as a distinct entry).
- [ ] Unit tests in `app_manifest.rs` cover: blank entry rejected, whitespace-only entry rejected, exact duplicate rejected, padded duplicate rejected (or stored trimmed, per the #4085 rule), and the design example `files = ["assets/**", "web/templates/**"]` still accepted.
- [ ] The checked-in `pkgs/id/apps/tic-tac-toe/app.toml` (no `[resources]` section) and the existing manifest tests still pass unchanged.

title: github-backup(clone_all): family members never wait for an in-flight anchor — the wait condition requires the anchor to still be pending, so members full-clone without --reference

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: app/github-backup
labels.description: infra/github-backup estate mirror system

body:
## Bug: github-backup clone_all family members never wait for an in-flight anchor — they full-clone without `--reference`

`infra/github-backup/bin/clone_all.py` documents its contract in the module docstring:

> Repos with a `reference` wait for their anchor; if the anchor failed they fall back to a full clone.

The scheduling loop does not implement that. The wait branch (clone_all.py, main loop) is:

```python
ref = p.get("reference")
if (
    ref
    and state.get(ref) is None
    and any(q["repo"] == ref for q in pending)
):
    continue
```

A member is only deferred while its anchor is **still in `pending`**. But plan order (build_plan / reconcile `_dependency_order`: depth, then name) always places the anchor **before** its members, and the loop submits items in that order — so by the time a member is considered, its anchor has already been removed from `pending` and is merely **in flight** (`state.get(ref) is None`, but the `any(...)` clause is false). The member is submitted immediately with `ref_ok = state.get(ref) == "ok"` = `False`, and `clone_one` therefore clones **without** `--reference`: a full, self-contained clone.

The wait branch is effectively dead in the common case: a member uses `--reference` only if its anchor happens to complete before the member's turn comes up. For the families this design exists for — the config's `tier_rules.families` note: forks sharing an upstream are "cloned with git alternates against the family anchor", e.g. the nixpkgs family with several multi-GB copies — the anchor is the slowest clone in the family, so members virtually always full-clone, duplicating the shared history per member and defeating the alternates pool's disk saving. (Data is not lost — a full clone is self-contained — but the tree's disk footprint and clone time blow up exactly where the family mechanism was meant to prevent it, and MANIFEST/FAMILIES bookkeeping then describes a pool the members are not actually part of.)

### Evidence (laptop probe, this run)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneB-cloneanchor/` on the laptop — verbatim `clone_all.py` + `ghb_common.py` (md5 `8199073eb58d494495aed5f86631f9bd`, matching main `56e66c9a`), a fake `git` on PATH that logs clone argv and makes the anchor clone take 3s (others 0.2s), and a plan of `o/anchor` (reference null), `o/member` (reference `o/anchor`), and two fillers (PAR=4):

- Clone argv log: `clone --mirror https://github.com/o/member.git <dest>` — **no `--reference`**, started concurrently with the anchor.
- `clone-status.jsonl`: `o/member` finished `ok` at 0s with `"reference_used": null`; `o/anchor` finished at 3s. The member completed a full clone before its anchor existed.

Expected per the docstring: the member is deferred while the anchor is in flight, then cloned with `--reference <anchor path>` once the anchor is `ok` (full clone only when the anchor's state is `fail`).

### Fix sketch

Defer a member whenever its reference is unresolved — `state.get(ref) is None` — regardless of whether the anchor sits in `pending` or in `inflight`; only proceed without the reference when the anchor's state is `fail` (or the reference names a repo not in the plan and not already a valid mirror on disk). The existing no-progress fallback (submit with `False` when nothing is in flight) already guards against a reference cycle deadlocking the loop; keep it reachable for that case.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] With a plan where an anchor clone is still in flight, a member with `reference` set is not submitted until the anchor resolves.
- [ ] When the anchor resolves `ok`, the member clones with `--reference <anchor mirror path>` and its status record shows `reference_used` set.
- [ ] When the anchor resolves `fail`, the member falls back to a full clone (no `--reference`) in the same run.
- [ ] A reference cycle or a reference to a repo outside the plan cannot deadlock the driver (the existing no-inflight fallback still fires).
- [ ] A probe/test in the style of the evidence above (fake `git`, slow anchor) demonstrates the ordering; existing behaviour for reference-less repos is unchanged.

title: id(repl): peek never learned the >file redirect — --first/--last/--lines >out.txt hard-error as 'requires an integer' and a trailing >out.txt becomes a search query

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

The REPL `peek` parser never learned the `>file` redirection that `find`/`search`/`show` support, and the #4072 fix (merged in c8a21912, closing #2009) widened the gap: it taught `parse_find_args` to exclude a `>` token from the optional numeric operand of `--first`/`--last`, but the same change converted `parse_peek_args` to hard integer errors without the exclusion — and `parse_peek_args` has no `>` branch at all.

Evidence on main `fddd4ad6`:

- `parse_find_args` handles `>file` at `pkgs/id/src/repl/runner.rs:684-686` (`strip_prefix('>')` → `output_file` + `to_file`) and excludes `>` operands at `:715` / `:731`.
- `parse_peek_args` (`runner.rs:1244`) has no `>` branch; its `--first` (`:1273`), `--last` (`:1284`), and `--lines`/`-n` (`:1300`) branches accept any next token not starting with `-` as the numeric operand.
- The peek handler already honors `output_file` — `handle_peek_command` writes the preview to a file when `args.output_file` is set (`runner.rs:991`) — but today only `-o`/`--output` can set it for peek.

## Verified behavior (laptop probe, verbatim parsers from main fddd4ad6, runner.rs md5 7de48728480a2975a55ebbfad09bd428; probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneA-peekredirect/`)

| Input | Result |
|---|---|
| `find q --first >out.txt` | Ok — `first=Some(1)`, `output_file=Some("out.txt")`, `to_file=true` |
| `find q --last >out.txt` | Ok — `last=Some(1)`, `output_file=Some("out.txt")` |
| `peek q --first 2` (control) | Ok — `first=Some(2)` |
| `peek q -o preview.txt` (control) | Ok — `output_file=Some("preview.txt")` |
| `peek q --first >out.txt` | **Err `--first requires an integer (got ">out.txt")`** |
| `peek q --last >out.txt` | **Err `--last requires an integer (got ">out.txt")`** |
| `peek q --lines >out.txt` | **Err `--lines requires an integer (got ">out.txt")`** |
| `peek q >out.txt` | **Ok but wrong — `queries=["q", ">out.txt"]`, `output_file=None`: the redirect token becomes a search query** |
| `peek q --first abc` (control) | Err `--first requires an integer (got "abc")` — the #4072 rejection itself works |

## Why it matters

`find` and `peek` are sibling REPL commands sharing `FindArgs`, limits, and output plumbing; a user who learns `find q --first >out.txt` reasonably expects `peek q --first >out.txt` to preview the first match into the file. Instead peek hard-errors with a message that blames the user's "integer", or — worse, with the redirect in final position — silently searches for a blob literally named `>out.txt` and reports no matches. The error message is actively misleading: `>out.txt` is not a malformed integer, it is a token peek's parser doesn't know.

Distinct from #2274 (unknown/mistyped `-`-flags silently swallowed, value-flags missing values, and the bare `>` empty-target case in `parse_find_args`): this issue is peek's missing `>` handling and the asymmetric operand exclusion left by the #4072 fix. If triage judges the `>out.txt`-as-query half belongs to #2274, the `--first`/`--last`/`--lines` hard-error half still stands alone as a #4072 residual.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `peek q --first >out.txt` and `peek q --last >out.txt` parse like find: limit defaults to 1 and the redirect is honored (no integer error).
- [ ] `peek q >out.txt` sets `output_file=Some("out.txt")` (and the handler writes the preview there) instead of adding `>out.txt` to the query list.
- [ ] `peek q --lines >out.txt` no longer fails with an integer error (triage pins: redirect honored with default lines, consistent with `--first`/`--last`).
- [ ] Non-numeric operands still error (`peek q --first abc` keeps the #4072 message); bare `>` handling matches whatever #2274 pins for find.
- [ ] Regression tests in `runner.rs` cover all three `>` positions for peek plus the find-parity cases; existing parser tests pass.
