body:
# projector(items): an `issues`/`issue_comment` event for a merged PR resets `merged` to 0 and clears `merged_at`

## Summary

The projector's item projection is built from two different GitHub payload
shapes, and the issue-shaped one silently erases PR merge state:

- `pull_request` events carry the full PR object (`merged`, `merged_at`,
  `draft`).
- `issues` events — and `payload.issue` in `issue_comment` events — carry the
  *issue* view of a PR, which has **no** `merged`, `merged_at`, or `draft`
  fields at all.

`fromIssueOrPr` (pm-stack/projector/src/projector.ts:41-71) defaults the
missing fields instead of treating them as unknown:

- projector.ts:60 — `merged: obj.merged ? 1 : 0`
- projector.ts:67 — `merged_at: iso(obj.merged_at)` (→ `null`)
- projector.ts:59 — `draft: obj.draft ? 1 : 0` (same pattern)

`applyIssue` (projector.ts:146-151) and `applyComment`
(projector.ts:153-165) upsert that row unconditionally, and the store's
monotonic guard (pm-stack/projector/src/store.ts:133) only requires
`excluded.source_updated_at >= pmp_items.source_updated_at`. Any later —
or even same-timestamp — issue-shaped event for a merged PR therefore
overwrites the merged row with `merged = 0, merged_at = NULL`.

## Reproduction (verified this run)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneB-prmerged/` — verbatim
`src/projector.ts` + `src/store.ts` from main `ac777161` (md5
projector.ts `d692044cac211608f474e157083cfe36`, store.ts
`448fc963eedcaffaf4191ee6891120c3`), real libSQL store, real `applyEvent`:

1. `pull_request` event, action `closed`, PR object with
   `merged: true, merged_at: "2026-11-01T10:00:00Z", updated_at: "…T10:00:00Z"`
   → stored row: `merged=1, merged_at="2026-11-01T10:00:00Z"`.
2. `issues` event, action `labeled`, with the issue-shaped view of the same
   PR (`pull_request` key present, no `merged`/`merged_at`/`draft` keys,
   `updated_at: "…T11:00:00Z"`)
   → stored row: `merged=0, merged_at=null`.

The probe's assertions (`merged` stays 1, `merged_at` stays set) fail on
current main exactly as shown above.

## Why it matters

- The trigger is routine: labelling, assigning, or commenting on a merged
  PR fires `issues` / `issue_comment` events. The fleet itself labels PRs
  after merge constantly, so merged PRs in the projection routinely lose
  their merged flag and merge timestamp.
- Everything downstream that distinguishes "closed because merged" from
  "closed unmerged" (the read model, `pmp_v_links_items`, the aggregator's
  subject views) then misreports those PRs as closed-unmerged.
- Reconciliation does not heal it reliably: the reconcile issues/prs
  streams derive rows from the list API (which does carry merge fields
  only in the PR shape), while the next webhook event re-breaks the row —
  the projection flaps depending on which writer ran last.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A repro test (fake or real store) applies a merged `pull_request`
      event followed by an `issues` (e.g. `labeled`) event and an
      `issue_comment` event for the same PR, and the stored row keeps
      `merged = 1` and its original `merged_at` after both.
- [ ] Fields a payload shape does not carry (`merged`, `merged_at`,
      `draft` in issue-shaped payloads) never overwrite a stored value
      with a default; a genuinely unmerged/draft state arriving in a
      PR-shaped payload still updates the row.
- [ ] Existing projector tests pass (`bun test` in pm-stack/projector),
      including the e2e fixture sequence.

## Dedup notes

Distinct from #2456/#2982 (delivery dedup), #2455 (comment resurrection),
#2694 (comment id keying) and #3087 (review created_at) — this is the
item row's merge fields being defaulted away by a partial payload shape.
Searches for projector merged/upsertItem/"issues event" returned no
covering issue.

title: bug(id): put path:name spec is hijacked by stdin auto-detection whenever stdin is not a terminal (breaks toplevel build)

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

body:
Seventh breakage in the #3720 fold chain — the second fold-switch attempt (2026-11-01 21:5x CST) failed its in-sandbox checkPhase on exactly one test:

```
test put_get_tests::test_put_with_custom_name ... FAILED
Command failed: ["put", "/build/.tmpVLBYe6/test.local.txt:test.custom-name"]
stderr: Error: name must be a safe relative path: /build/.tmpVLBYe6/test.local.txt:test.custom-name
```

Reproduced deterministically on a host: `cargo test -p id --test cli_integration -- test_put_with_custom_name < /dev/null` fails in 0.27s with the same error; with a terminal stdin it passes (which is how it stayed hidden — interactive runs mask it).

Root cause (`src/commands/put.rs`, `cmd_put_multi`): the stdin auto-detection

```rust
if items.len() == 1 && !stdin().is_terminal() && !from_stdin {
    let path = PathBuf::from(&items[0]);
    if !path.exists() { return cmd_put_local_stdin(name /* the whole spec */).await; }
}
```

checks the LITERAL spec string as a path. A `path:name` spec never exists as a literal path (the colon), so every non-interactive `id put file:name` is misrouted into stdin-content mode, and `FileOps::put` then rejects the whole spec as an unsafe name (leading `/`). With a name that passed validation it would silently store stdin under a garbage name instead.

Fix: the existence check must use the path part of the spec (`parse_put_spec`). Plain names and missing files keep the current stdin behavior; an existing file behind a `path:name` spec goes to the normal file-put loop. Blocks the #3720 fold switch (the toplevel's id checkPhase runs non-interactively by construction).

title: aggregator(views): ViewsStore load keeps malformed rows — a missing/non-string name makes save()/rename() throw TypeError, and a non-object filters silently becomes a match-everything default view

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: app/aggregator
labels.description: Package/app: aggregator (pm-stack in this repo)

body:
## Problem

`pm-stack/aggregator` saved views (#1276): `ViewsStore.doLoad` promises in the module header that "an unparseable or wrongly-shaped file is quarantined … never silently overwritten" (views.ts:11-14), but the row-level check only requires each row to be an object with a string `id` (views.ts:198-200). Malformed-but-parseable rows are neither quarantined nor dropped, and they break the store in two verified ways:

1. A row whose `name` is missing or not a string makes every later `save()` (views.ts:257, `v.name.toLowerCase()`) and `rename()` for that owner throw a `TypeError` — the owner can never save or rename a view again while that row is in the file, and nothing tells them why.
2. A row whose `filters` is not an object (e.g. the string `"repo:x/y"`) is served as-is: `defaultFor()` returns it, and `itemMatchesView` reads `filters.repo` etc. as `undefined`, so every filter dimension is skipped and the "filtered" default view silently matches **every** item. `viewQuery` likewise encodes none of its filters.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `c8a21912`)

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/views.ts:198-200` — `doLoad` filter: `(v) => typeof v === "object" && v !== null && typeof v.id === "string"`; no check of `name`, `owner`, `filters`, `isDefault`, or `createdAt`.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/views.ts:255-258` — `save()` duplicate-name scan calls `v.name.toLowerCase()` on every same-owner row.
- Laptop probe (verbatim `views.ts` from main `c8a21912`, md5 `dfe51cfc329ba111f8603f112f5787eb`; stub `model.ts` type only; probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneA-views/` on the laptop, bun):
  - File with one good-shaped row except `name` omitted → no quarantine file created; `all()`/`forOwner()`/`defaultFor()` return the row; `save({owner:"gh:1", …})` → `TypeError: undefined is not an object (evaluating 'v.name.toLowerCase')`.
  - Same with `name: 42` → `save()` → `TypeError: v.name.toLowerCase is not a function`.
  - File with `filters: "repo:x/y"` on an `isDefault: true` row → `defaultFor("gh:1")` returns it with `filters` still the string; `applyView([{repo:"a/b",…},{repo:"x/y",…}], filters)` returns **both** items — the repo filter is silently not applied.
  - Control: a fully well-formed row loads, saves, and defaults normally.

## Why it matters

The store's stated discipline (comments-store #906 pattern) is that a wrongly-shaped file is quarantined loudly rather than half-trusted. Today one hand-edited, partially migrated, or foreign-written row in `PM_AGG_VIEWS_FILE` (a) wedges that owner's view mutations with an unhandled TypeError on the mediated action path, and (b) can silently widen a person's default landing view from a narrow filter to the whole board — the exact failure a saved view exists to prevent, with no log line naming the bad row. Distinct from #4140 (CoverageSnapshotStore) and #2347 (comments/actions store): this is the new views store from #1276/#4013, whose only corrupt-file test covers unparseable JSON, not parseable-but-malformed rows.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ViewsStore` load validates each row's full shape (`id`/`name`/`owner` strings, `filters` passing `validateViewFilters` or an equivalent row check, boolean `isDefault`, string timestamps): a file with a malformed row is either quarantined per the header contract or the malformed rows are dropped with a loud log naming the row — behaviour pinned by a test; well-formed rows in the same file are not silently lost without that quarantine/log trail.
- [ ] With a malformed row present in the on-disk file, `save()` and `rename()` for the affected owner no longer throw `TypeError`.
- [ ] A malformed `filters` value can never reach `defaultFor()`/`applyView` as a match-everything view.
- [ ] Existing views tests pass, including the corrupt-file quarantine test.

title: projector(github): GITHUB_APP_ID is never validated — appJwt signs a JWT with any iss ("abc", "0", "-1", " 123 "), unlike the GITHUB_APP_INSTALL_ID validation added in #4106

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

labels.name: app/pm-stack
labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

body:
## Bug

`pm-stack/projector/src/github.ts`: `appJwt` uses `env.GITHUB_APP_ID` verbatim as the JWT `iss` claim with no shape validation at all, while the sibling credential added in the same fix (#4106, commit caacf3ae) — `parseConfiguredInstallId` (github.ts:104-115) — rejects any `GITHUB_APP_INSTALL_ID` that is not a positive decimal integer, with a clear error naming the variable and the expected form.

`appJwt` (github.ts:78-91):

```ts
const appId = env.GITHUB_APP_ID;
const rawKey = env.GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY;
if (!appId || !rawKey) throw new Error("github_app_credentials_missing");
...
const claims = { iat: now - 60, exp: now + 540, iss: appId };
```

A mistyped app id (a slug, a copy-pasted install id with spaces, `0`, a decimal) therefore does not fail fast at credential resolution. It produces a locally well-formed, correctly signed JWT that GitHub rejects downstream, and the failure surfaces far from the cause:

- `discoverInstallationId` (github.ts:125-144) swallows any non-OK response (`if (!res.ok) return undefined;`), so a bad `iss` looks exactly like "app not installed on this repo";
- `apiTokenFor` then falls through to the configured install id / `GITHUB_TOKEN`, or throws the misleading `no_github_credentials_for_<repo>` — none of which names the actual problem.

## Evidence (verified this run, main @ bc0afe2f)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneB-projcov/` (verbatim `github.ts`, md5 65529a67e3c34d041f1e91a27c1d68c6, throwaway generated RSA key, claims decoded from the issued JWT):

```
APP_ID "123456"                   -> JWT ISSUED, iss="123456"   (control)
APP_ID "abc"                      -> JWT ISSUED, iss="abc"
APP_ID "0"                        -> JWT ISSUED, iss="0"
APP_ID "-1"                       -> JWT ISSUED, iss="-1"
APP_ID "12.5"                     -> JWT ISSUED, iss="12.5"
APP_ID " 123 "                    -> JWT ISSUED, iss=" 123 "
APP_ID "999999999999999999999999" -> JWT ISSUED, iss="999999999999999999999999"
INSTALL_ID "abc"  -> THREW Invalid GITHUB_APP_INSTALL_ID "abc"; expected a positive decimal integer
INSTALL_ID "0"    -> THREW Invalid GITHUB_APP_INSTALL_ID "0"; expected a positive decimal integer
INSTALL_ID "12.5" -> THREW Invalid GITHUB_APP_INSTALL_ID "12.5"; expected a positive decimal integer
```

## Why it matters

#4106 established the house rule for this module: numeric GitHub identifiers from the environment are validated at parse time with an error that names the variable, because the downstream GitHub errors are opaque. The app id is the one identifier in the same credential set that was left out — and it is the first one used (every app-auth path goes through `appJwt`, including installation discovery, so a bad app id corrupts the diagnosis of every later step).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `appJwt` (or a shared parse helper alongside `parseConfiguredInstallId`) rejects a `GITHUB_APP_ID` that is not a positive decimal integer (safe-integer range), throwing an error that names `GITHUB_APP_ID` and the expected form — mirroring the `GITHUB_APP_INSTALL_ID` message.
- [ ] Valid decimal app ids (e.g. `"123"`, `"123456"`) keep issuing JWTs with the identical `iss` claim as today.
- [ ] A missing/empty `GITHUB_APP_ID` keeps the existing `github_app_credentials_missing` behaviour.
- [ ] Unit tests in `pm-stack/projector/test/github.test.ts` cover the rejected spellings (`"abc"`, `"0"`, `"-1"`, `"12.5"`, `" 123 "`, an out-of-safe-range digit string) beside the existing install-id cases.
- [ ] Existing projector tests still pass.

Dedup: searched open + closed issues for `GITHUB_APP_ID`, `appJwt`, and the #4106 follow-up space — #1529 (private-key base64 form) is the only adjacent hit and is a different input. No issue covers app-id validation.

title: id(currency_poc): reconcile counts legs per entry, not per distinct transfer — an empty or duplicate leg list is marked Posted with nothing (or half) in the ledger

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/id` currency_poc: the recovery scanner decides "all legs posted" by counting per-leg lookup matches — `matched == record.legs.len()` — without ever checking that the legs are distinct or that there are any legs at all. A record with an empty leg list, or with the same transfer listed twice, is marked `Posted` / `AlreadyPosted` even though the ledger does not hold the conversion's legs.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `11cb8966`)

- `pkgs/id/src/currency_poc/recovery.rs:56-71` — the scanner increments `present`/`matched` once per entry in `record.legs` and treats `matched == record.legs.len()` as proof of posting. For `legs == []` that is `0 == 0`: unconditionally true. For `legs == [t, t]` a single posted transfer `t` counts twice.
- `pkgs/id/src/currency_poc/intent.rs` — neither `IntentStore::put` nor the `IntentRecord` type validates the leg list (non-empty, distinct IDs, IDs matching `transfer_ids()`/conversion), so a malformed record — hand-edited or foreign file-store JSON that still parses (cf. #4125), a buggy producer, a future store implementation — reaches the scanner as-is.
- Laptop probe (verbatim currency_poc modules from main `11cb8966`, md5-matched; probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneA-dupids/` on the laptop):
  - Record with `legs: []`, state `Recorded`, `amount_in: 100`: `reconcile(Resubmit)` → `[(4242, AlreadyPosted)]`, stored state advanced to `Posted`, zero transfers in the ledger for the conversion.
  - Record with `legs: [t, t]` (the same transfer twice), state `Submitted`, with `t` posted exactly once: `reconcile(Resubmit)` → `AlreadyPosted`, state `Posted`, while only 1 distinct transfer exists.

## Why it matters

`Posted` is the scanner's terminal verdict: the record leaves the unresolved set and no one looks at it again. Declaring a conversion posted when its legs are absent or short is the failure the scanner exists to prevent — a conversion silently treated as settled when the money never (fully) moved. The executor's own records always have 2–3 distinct legs today, which is exactly why the guard belongs in the scanner/record validation rather than relying on every present and future producer being well-formed; the file store already admits, by design, whatever JSON parses into an `IntentRecord`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `reconcile` never returns `AlreadyPosted` for a record with an empty leg list; such a record is reported (e.g. `Inconsistent`) and left unresolved, or rejected with an error — with a test pinning the chosen behaviour.
- [ ] A record whose legs contain a duplicate transfer ID is not counted as fully posted on the strength of one distinct transfer; distinct-ID counting (or an equivalent leg-set validation) is used, with a test.
- [ ] Existing recovery tests pass, including `recovery_does_not_trust_transfer_id_existence_alone` and both crash-recovery scenarios.

Related: #2289 (parent PoC), #4125 (foreign/corrupt files in the same store directory — the plausible route by which a malformed-but-parseable record arrives).

title: id(currency_poc): preflight never checks duplicate transfer_ids — a reused ID passes prepare, fails in submit, and strands a Submitted intent

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/id` currency_poc: neither `preflight` nor `prepare`/`build_legs` checks that a `ConversionRequest`'s `transfer_ids` are distinct. A request that reuses one transfer ID for two legs passes preflight, gets its write-ahead intent persisted, and only fails inside `submit` — stranding the record in `Submitted`, the same failure shape as #4124 but with a different, unchecked cause.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `11cb8966`)

- `pkgs/id/src/currency_poc/executor.rs:138-195` — `preflight` checks the quote, account existence/ledger, and balances; it never inspects `request.transfer_ids`.
- `pkgs/id/src/currency_poc/executor.rs:99-136` — `build_legs` pulls IDs from `transfer_ids` in order with no uniqueness check, so `vec![601, 601, 603]` builds legs `[601 (T1), 601 (fee), 603 (T3)]`.
- `pkgs/id/src/currency_poc/ledger.rs:171-181` — the ledger (correctly) rejects a second, different transfer reusing an ID inside one chain with `ExistsWithDifferentFields`; the executor's own test `duplicate_transfer_id_in_one_chain_is_rejected` (tests.rs) pins that ledger behaviour, but nothing stops the executor from constructing such a batch.
- Laptop probe (verbatim currency_poc modules from main `11cb8966`, md5-matched to the sandbox checkout; probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneA-dupids/` on the laptop):
  - request with `transfer_ids = [601, 601, 603]`: `prepare` → Ok, record persisted with leg IDs `[601, 601, 603]`; `submit` → Err, record left `Submitted`, zero transfers posted for the conversion.
  - control, distinct IDs `[601, 602, 603]`: `execute` → Ok, state `Posted`.

## Why it matters

Transfer IDs are the idempotency key the whole write-ahead/recovery design rests on (#2289). A caller bug (an ID generator collision, a hand-built request reusing an ID) is knowable entirely at preflight time, before any state exists. Instead it is discovered only after the intent is persisted and submission attempted, leaving an unresolved `Submitted` record that the recovery scanner will keep resubmitting and rejecting — the exact stranded-record cost #4124 documents for same-account legs. Preflight's contract is "failing here means no intent is written and nothing is submitted" (executor.rs module/`preflight` docs); duplicate IDs break that contract.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `preflight` (or `prepare` before persisting) rejects a request whose `transfer_ids` contain a duplicate, with an error naming the duplicated ID; no intent record is written for such a request.
- [ ] A test at the executor level (not only the ledger level) covers duplicate IDs across T1/fee and T1/T3, asserting `prepare` errors and the store stays empty.
- [ ] Existing currency_poc tests pass, including `duplicate_transfer_id_in_one_chain_is_rejected` and the identical-retry test (`conversion_id_reuse_cannot_replace_persisted_intent`).

Related: #2289 (parent PoC), #4124 (same stranding shape, different unchecked preflight cause — same-account legs).

title: id(currency_poc): TigerBeetle pin check is a substring test — a drifted 0.17.99 binary passes verify_pinned_version for pinned 0.17.9

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

`verify_pinned_version` (pkgs/id/src/currency_poc/harness.rs:46-60) checks the TigerBeetle pin with a substring test:

```rust
let text = String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stdout);
if !output.status.success() || !text.contains(TIGERBEETLE_PINNED_VERSION) {
```

`TIGERBEETLE_PINNED_VERSION` is `"0.17.9"` (harness.rs:28), and `"0.17.99"`, `"0.17.90"`, `"0.17.9-anything"` — and any other output that merely *contains* the digits, e.g. in a commit hash or a build suffix — all satisfy `contains`. The module's stated purpose is the opposite (harness.rs:9-13): the pin "is verified against `tigerbeetle version` output before a cluster starts, so a developer-machine-only or drifted binary fails loudly instead of silently testing against the wrong release." A drifted 0.17.99 binary passes the gate today and the PoC scenarios run against the wrong release while the harness claims the pin was verified.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe, main caacf3ae)

Probe crate with a verbatim copy of harness.rs (md5 9dc31fc00143dfb6655f2a7946940005, matching main caacf3ae), calling the real `verify_pinned_version` against stub shell scripts as the "binary":

- script printing `tigerbeetle 0.17.9` → `Ok(())` (intended).
- script printing `tigerbeetle 0.17.99` → **`Ok(())`** (the bug: a different, drifted release passes the pin).
- script printing `tigerbeetle 0.16.0` → `Err(...)` (control: unrelated versions are rejected, so the check works — it is the boundary that is wrong).

## Why it matters

The harness is step 0 of the #2289 PoC: its whole value is that scenario results against a "real cluster" are results against the pinned 0.17.9 release. A substring check silently voids that guarantee for any version whose spelling extends the pin (0.17.90+ is a plausible future patch line), producing test evidence attributed to a release that never ran.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `verify_pinned_version` accepts only an exact version match: the version token parsed from the binary's output must equal `TIGERBEETLE_PINNED_VERSION` (word/token boundary, not substring).
- [ ] Tests (the function is testable without a real binary via a stub executable, as in the probe): `0.17.9` accepted; `0.17.99`, `0.17.90`, and `0.16.0` rejected; output that contains `0.17.9` only inside a longer token (hash/suffix) rejected.
- [ ] The real binary's actual `version` output format is accounted for (parse the version field rather than scanning the whole stdout), and the existing ignored cluster smoke test still works with a genuine 0.17.9 binary.
- [ ] All existing currency_poc tests pass unchanged.

Related: #2289 (the PoC this harness belongs to).

title: id(currency_poc): one corrupt or foreign .json file in the FileIntentStore directory aborts recovery for every pending conversion

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`FileIntentStore::unresolved()` (pkgs/id/src/currency_poc/intent.rs:165-181) aborts on the **first** file it cannot read or parse:

```rust
let bytes = fs::read(&path)?;
let record: IntentRecord = serde_json::from_slice(&bytes)
    .map_err(|error| io::Error::new(io::ErrorKind::InvalidData, error))?;
```

and `recovery::reconcile` propagates that error before reconciling anything (recovery.rs:54, `store.unresolved().context("listing unresolved intents")?`). One stray file in the intent directory — a truncated or hand-edited record, a file written by an older/newer record schema, any unrelated `*.json` file someone dropped in the directory, or a subdirectory named `*.json` (`fs::read` fails on it) — therefore blocks recovery of **every** pending conversion, indefinitely, with a single opaque listing error. The scanner's own design already rejects this failure mode for resubmissions ("One rejected resubmission must not abort recovery of every later record", recovery.rs) but not for the listing step that gates the whole scan.

Note the store's writes are atomic (tmp + rename + fsync, intent.rs put), so this is not about torn writes from this implementation — it is about the directory being a long-lived recovery surface that must survive schema evolution, operator handling, and foreign files.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe, main caacf3ae)

Probe crate with verbatim copies of the currency_poc modules (md5 intent.rs 4b413d6505f423428eabe27ba5e0b753, recovery.rs f4885f69754643cb92e946aaf33ff758, matching main caacf3ae):

- Control directory (one valid `Recorded` intent, conversion 777): `reconcile(Resubmit)` returns `[(777, Resubmitted)]`, 3 legs posted.
- Same valid record plus one file `deadbeef.json` containing `{not json`: `unresolved()` returns `Err("data did not match any variant of untagged enum AdjacentValue @ line 1 column 12..")`, `reconcile` returns the same error, **0 legs posted**, and the valid record is still `Recorded` — total recovery blockage from one bad file.

## Why it matters

The recovery scanner is the component that runs precisely when something has already gone wrong (a crash mid-conversion, #2289). A design where one damaged record silently freezes reconciliation of all the healthy ones turns a single-record incident into a full stop, and the operator gets no list of what was skipped — the valid records are not even reported.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `reconcile` processes every readable unresolved record even when other files in the store directory are unreadable or unparseable; the bad entries are surfaced (returned in the outcome list under a distinct outcome, logged, or collected into the error report) rather than silently dropped or fatal.
- [ ] A subdirectory named `*.json` and a non-JSON-content `*.json` file are both covered by tests.
- [ ] The valid-record control scenario (resubmission posts its legs) still passes with a corrupt sibling file present, and the corrupt entry remains identifiable for an operator afterwards (not deleted by the scanner).
- [ ] All existing currency_poc tests pass unchanged; the `IntentStore::unresolved` trait contract documents whatever error/skip semantics are chosen so the in-memory store and future stores agree.

Related: #2289 (the PoC this store belongs to).

title: id(currency_poc): conversion preflight never checks same-account legs — user==LP, fee==user, LP-dest==user-dest pass prepare, fail in submit, and strand a Submitted intent

labels.name: task/triage

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`ConversionExecutor::preflight` (pkgs/id/src/currency_poc/executor.rs:138-194) never checks that the accounts taking part in a conversion are **distinct where a leg requires two different accounts**. Every leg is a transfer, and the ledger rejects any transfer whose debit and credit accounts are the same (`TransferError::AccountsMustBeDifferent`, ledger.rs:172-174), but preflight only checks existence and ledger for each role (executor.rs:149-168) and the two balance checks. So a request with

- `user_source == lp_source` (T1 debits and credits the same account), or
- `fee_account == user_source` (the fee leg debits and credits the same account), or
- `lp_dest == user_dest` (T3 debits and credits the same account)

passes preflight, `prepare()` persists the write-ahead intent, and `submit()` fails mid-submission — leaving the record in state `Submitted`, unresolved forever: the recovery scanner can only resubmit the same doomed legs (`ResubmissionRejected`) or abandon a conversion that should never have been recorded. This breaks preflight's own contract (executor.rs:132-136): "Failing here means no intent is written and nothing is submitted." These configurations are statically knowable before any write.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe, main caacf3ae)

Probe crate with verbatim copies of the currency_poc modules (md5 executor.rs d12b3b971441cb271cec2abc9ada0798, matching main caacf3ae), funded-ledger fixture and request copied from tests.rs:

- `lp_source = user_source`: `prepare()` returns `Ok(Recorded)` and the intent is persisted; `submit()` errors `AccountsMustBeDifferent`; the stored record stays `Submitted` (unresolved).
- `fee_account = Some(user_source)`: same outcome — `prepare()` Ok, `submit()` errors, record stuck `Submitted`.
- Control: the unmodified request `execute()`s to `Posted` — the fixture is sane.

## Why it matters

The write-ahead intent is the crash-recovery contract of the PoC (#2289): anything in `Recorded`/`Submitted` is owed a reconciliation. Letting a deterministically-invalid conversion into that store pollutes it with records no recovery policy can ever post, and in a production-shaped successor the same gap means a misconfigured conversion (e.g. an LP configuration that aliases the user account) is only discovered after the intent is durable and submission has been attempted.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `preflight` (or `build_legs`) rejects any request where a single leg's debit and credit account coincide: `user_source == lp_source`, `fee_amount > 0 && fee_account == Some(user_source)`, and `lp_dest == user_dest` — with an error naming the conflicting roles.
- [ ] A rejected request writes **no** intent record and submits nothing (store lookup for the conversion ID returns none after `prepare()` errors).
- [ ] New tests cover all three coincidences plus a control showing a normal request (with and without a fee leg) still prepares and posts.
- [ ] All existing currency_poc tests pass unchanged.

Related: #2289 (the PoC this executor belongs to). Distinct from #4071 (RateAuthorisation body validation in pkgs/id/src/currency.rs, a different module).

title: id(currency_poc): InMemoryLedger posts an unterminated linked chain — a batch ending with linked=true commits instead of being rejected

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: task/fix
labels.description: has a fix task queued

body:
## Problem

`InMemoryLedger::create_transfers` (pkgs/id/src/currency_poc/ledger.rs:249-258) posts a linked chain that is never terminated. The trait documentation (ledger.rs, `LedgerBackend::create_transfers`) defines a chain as a contiguous run **ending at a transfer with `linked == false`**, but the chain-splitting loop

```rust
let mut chain_end = chain_start;
while batch[chain_end].linked && chain_end + 1 < batch.len() {
    chain_end += 1;
}
let chain = &batch[chain_start..=chain_end];
```

stops at the end of the batch even when the last leg still has `linked == true`, and the resulting "chain" is validated and committed like a properly terminated one. A real TigerBeetle submission leaves such a chain open (the linked flag promises a following leg), so scenario tests that pass against the in-memory reference backend can rely on behavior a production binding over the official client would reject — exactly the divergence this backend exists to prevent (mod.rs: "a production binding would implement the same trait"; tests.rs header: the same scenarios are to run against a real cluster).

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe, main caacf3ae)

Probe crate with verbatim copies of the currency_poc modules (md5 ledger.rs 3c2ccc964b2bcc0e29232fae8966c41d, matching main caacf3ae), funded-ledger fixture copied from tests.rs:

- Single transfer id 700, amount 100, `linked: true`, no terminator: `results=[Ok(())]`, `lookup_transfer(700)` returns the transfer, user spendable rises to 10100 — the unterminated chain **posted**.
- Two legs (ids 710/711, amounts 100/200), **both** `linked: true`, no terminator: `results=[Ok(()), Ok(())]`, both transfers stored.
- Control: the same transfer with `linked: false` posts (expected) — the probe fixture is sane.

## Why it matters

The in-memory backend is the reference semantics for the future TigerBeetle client binding and the only ledger the #2289 scenario tests run against today. Silently accepting an open linked chain lets malformed batches (e.g. a caller that builds legs and forgets to clear `linked` on the last leg, or a truncated batch) pass every PoC test while failing — or behaving differently — against a real cluster. The executor itself always terminates its batch (executor.rs sets `linked: false` on T3), so this is a backend-fidelity gap, not an executor bug.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `create_transfers` rejects a batch whose final chain is unterminated (last leg `linked == true`): no leg of that chain posts, no balance moves, and the per-leg results report an error for every leg of the open chain (a dedicated `TransferError` variant if the existing codes cannot express it).
- [ ] Properly terminated chains and single unlinked transfers behave exactly as before; all existing currency_poc tests pass unchanged.
- [ ] New tests: single unterminated transfer rejected; multi-leg unterminated chain rejected atomically; a terminated chain following an unterminated one in the same batch is handled per the documented per-chain result contract.
- [ ] The `LedgerBackend::create_transfers` doc comment states the unterminated-chain behavior so a future client binding implements the same rule.

Related: #2289 (the PoC this backend belongs to). Distinct from #4071 / #4069 (pkgs/id/src/currency.rs authorisation validation/fold, a different module).

body:
Implements the determination recorded on #2225 (task 5226, 2026-11-02): codedb stops running one stdio process per MCP session (~1.1 GB RSS warm / ~2.1 GB cold-peak per instance on the largest project, measured) and becomes one shared daemon per project root plus a thin MCP bridge.

## Spec (from the #2225 determination)

1. **Verify the daemon surface first**: `codedb serve` is an HTTP daemon on :7719 with routes mirroring the query surface (`/tree`, `/outline`, `/search`, `/searchq`, `/word`, `/hot`, `/health`) and no MCP route. Confirm exact request/response shapes against codedb's MCP tool surface, and daemon behaviour on a stale index.
2. **Daemon unit**: user systemd unit running `codedb serve` for the `~/git/code` root first (add further primary roots only as needed; the daemon is per-root).
3. **Bridge**: a small stateless stdio MCP shim, fleet-owned in this repo, exposing codedb's MCP tools and forwarding to `http://127.0.0.1:7719` for the session's project root. No index state in the shim.
4. **Config PR**: in `.mcpx.json`, move codedb from `disabledMcpServers` back to `mcpServers` with `command` = the bridge, retaining `CODEDB_NO_TELEMETRY=1`. This lifts the PR #2220 park in the new shape and closes #2225.

## Acceptance

- One `codedb serve` daemon serves multiple concurrent MCP sessions through the bridge; no per-session codedb process holds an index (verify with `ps` + RSS during ≥3 concurrent sessions).
- codedb MCP tools (search/find/outline/tree/word/hot) return the same results via the bridge as via direct stdio for a fixed query set on `~/git/code`.
- `.mcpx.json` on main has codedb in `mcpServers` (bridge) and out of `disabledMcpServers`; #2225 closed by the config PR.

Refs: #2225 determination comment, PR #2220 (the park).

## Acceptance criteria

- The daemon surface is verified first: `codedb serve` routes and request/response shapes are confirmed against codedb's MCP tool surface, including behaviour on a stale index.
- One shared `codedb serve` daemon runs per project root (user systemd unit), replacing one stdio process per MCP session.
- A thin MCP bridge connects sessions to the shared daemon; existing MCP tool behaviour is unchanged for callers.
- The #2220 park condition that this work lifts is recorded as resolved on the issue, with the measured per-instance RSS cost gone (one daemon per root instead of ~1.1 GB warm per session instance).

## Finding — consolidation set (one finding, two PRs)

Two open PRs rewrite the same two functions in the same file and overlap in at least one hunk. Landing them independently guarantees a conflict in exactly the code both are trying to fix; they should be shepherded as one set (land one, rebase the other onto it in the same pass — or combine into a single PR).

## The set

- PR #3092 — "fix(id): reject malformed REPL flags" (branch `queue/4318-2274-repl-flags`, for #2274). Changes `parse_find_args` / `parse_peek_args` in `pkgs/id/src/repl/runner.rs` to return `Result`, rejects unknown flags, missing values, invalid `--format`, and bare `>`; validates peek `--lines` non-numeric values. Currently **mergeable: CONFLICTING / mergeStateStatus: DIRTY** against current main.
- PR #4072 — "fix(id/repl): reject nonnumeric result limits" (branch `queue/5075-2009-repl-numeric-flags`, for #2009, opened 2026-11-01T23:29Z from a newer main). Same two functions, same file: rejects non-numeric `--first` / `--last` in both parsers and non-numeric `--lines` / `-n` in peek — the `--lines` validation duplicates PR #3092's peek change, and both PRs edit the same parser test module.

## Evidence

- PR #3092 diff: `parse_find_args` / `parse_peek_args` signature change to `Result<...>` (commit `06fc15565`), peek `--lines` branch replaced with `required_value` + `parse::<usize>()` error.
- PR #4072 diff: based on main `957cf6625` (which already carries a *different* partial parser evolution — `format_error` deferred validation and `validate_result_limits` from PR #3738), changes the `--first` / `--last` / `--lines` branches of the same functions.
- Current main (`d9636237`) still does not reject unknown flags: `parse_find_args` at `pkgs/id/src/repl/runner.rs:655` keeps the silent fall-through (only non-`-` tokens become queries), `--dir` / `--exclude` missing values are still silent no-ops, and `>` still accepts an empty path — so #2274 is not fixed on main and PR #3092 is not superseded; it is stale-based and conflicting.
- Dedupe: no existing issue names this pair (searched "3092 4072" and "consolidate repl parsers"); #2274 and #2009 are sibling issues from the same probe family but neither tracks the PR overlap.

## Why it matters

Whichever PR merges second will conflict in `runner.rs`'s parser branches and tests, and a careless conflict resolution can silently drop one issue's validation (e.g. PR #4072's `--first`/`--last` rejection or PR #3092's unknown-flag rejection) while both issues auto-close. Handling them as one shepherd set keeps both acceptance sets intact.

## Acceptance criteria

- One shepherd pass dispositions both PRs: either (a) one combined PR carrying both #2274 and #2009 behavior, with the other PR closed as superseded by it, or (b) a documented merge order with the second PR rebased onto the merged first and its full test set re-run.
- After the set lands, on main: unknown/mistyped flags error, value-flags missing values error, invalid `--format` errors, bare `>` errors, and non-numeric `--first` / `--last` / `--lines` values error — in both `parse_find_args` and `parse_peek_args`.
- #2274 and #2009 each close only when their own behavior is verified on main, not merely when one PR of the set merges.

Found by the pr-diff-review job reviewing PR #3092 (PR #4072 is the overlapping counterpart).

title: Design: one signed set, one meaning — BoardGraph's gates hold at insert, projection and replication (pkgs/id)

body:
## Summary

`pkgs/id/src/boards.rs` makes one promise in four places, and the fleet has now filed a counterexample at every one of them. The module header (boards.rs:3-9) says `BoardGraph` "checks signatures, canonical references, board scope, and the authority rules needed to accept an object". The `has_role` design note states the determinism rule the module is built around: peers holding the same signed set must reach the same verdict, in any arrival order. `compose_view`'s own comment states the projection rule: "a superseded record … has no effect in the projection, whatever it once said." And the federation docs promise a lagging replica is "never silently presented as current". Five filings in three days span all three gates of the graph:

- **#3963** — insert: `validate_links`' `Post` arm checks thread, parent post and every attachment via `require_scoped`, and never reads `embed_ref`. A dangling or cross-board embed inserts `Ok`; the same hashes as attachments are refused.
- **#4109** — insert: the `BoardListing` arm enforces the chain for `supersedes = Some` but for `supersedes = None` checks only `version == 1`, never whether a listing for that (board, host) exists. A second "first" listing is accepted and `latest_listings` resolves the tie by content hash — listed-vs-withdrawn becomes hash luck (probe at main `d9636237`).
- **#4003** — projection: `compose_view` inserts every RoleAttestation's `supersedes` edge into `attestation_superseded`, including attestations the generic frontier just nullified. An owner who reverses a revocation by superseding it gets a view where the reversal silently did nothing.
- **#3964** — projection: two different revision-1 `Rules` texts for one board both insert (`validate_shape` checks only `revision > 0`; the links arm checks only moderator authority), and no graph-level rule says what "rules at revision N" means. The origin leaves reject-vs-resolve open.
- **#4081** — replication: `board_ref()` returns `None` for `BoardFork` and `board_object_set` expands only Board/Theme dependencies, so a fork record is in no board's set. Fork provenance never replicates, and `replica_status_against` still reports `Complete` (probe: expected=2/present=2 on a 4-object graph). No test constructs a `BoardFork` at all.

Pass 34 of the design architect assessed #3963/#3964 as a pair and named the trigger ("a third instance makes it a cluster"); #4003, #4081 and #4109 have since filed. This design is the cluster's origination — a sibling of #2898/#4000 (same crate, same validate-at-the-gate family, different surface: BoardGraph has no reconstruction path; objects are inserted, projected and replicated, never restored), not a phase of either.

Full design doc: `files/designs/code-id-boardgraph-one-signed-set.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Audit baseline: origin/main `d9636237` (all sites read verbatim at HEAD this pass).

## The contract

> **One signed set, one meaning.** Every reference an object carries is validated at insert (existence + board scope, the kind rule stated). Where a kind carries a signed chain, the chain's head is unique at insert. Where a kind has no chain, competing versions are signed history and the projection resolves them by a stated deterministic rule — never by arrival order. A record contributes its edges to a projection only while it is itself active. And a board's replication set is exactly the objects scoped to it plus the closure those objects need to be accepted on a fresh graph — so `Complete` means the whole set, including its provenance records.

## Recorded decisions

1. **`embed_ref` is a reference like the others (Phase 1, #3963).** The `Post` arm validates it with `require_scoped` (existence + same-board), per #3963's acceptance. Kind rule stated, not implicit: in v1 the only game-post object kind in the graph is `Post`, so the target must be a `Post`; when a dedicated game-post kind lands, the kind check updates in the same change that adds the kind, and the module doc says so. Lazy validation at projection loses — the graph is the substrate later layers are told they can trust.
2. **A second "first" listing is refused (Phase 1, #4109).** Per #4109's acceptance, including its convergence argument. Listings are where rejection is right: single-author chain (only the board creator signs), and the supersedes link *is* the ordering — a chain-less second head is a malformed chain, not a race between peers.
3. **Duplicate `Rules` revisions are history; projections resolve them deterministically (Phase 2, #3964 — option (b), recorded).** Option (a), insert rejection, loses for the module's own stated reason: `Rules` has no supersedes chain and its authorised signers are plural (owner + any moderator, `require_moderator`). Two moderators can sign revision N concurrently in good faith; first-arriver-wins rejection makes acceptance depend on arrival order — the property the `has_role` note rejects for this module — and a graph holding both would stall replication instead of converging. Instead: duplicates are legal signed history; one resolution rule for every projection — for a given revision the greater content hash wins (the tie-break `latest_listings` already documents for signed forks); "current rules" is the highest revision, resolved the same way — exposed as one graph helper with the rule in the module doc, so the board-view layer consumes it instead of re-deriving a pick. Hash-pinned `Thread.rules_ref` is unaffected.
4. **Only active records contribute edges — attestations included (Phase 2, #4003).** `attestation_superseded` is computed only from RoleAttestations not themselves in the generic `superseded` set — the fixed-point frontier `compose_view` already computes for Supersede records, whose comment already states this rule. Per #4003's acceptance and its three preserved-behaviour controls. Attestation-to-attestation supersession is unchanged; this governs generic-supersede nullification only.
5. **The fork record travels with the fork board (Phase 3, #4081).** A `BoardFork` belongs to its **fork board's** set — not the source's, not both. A source replica does not need to learn it was forked to serve the source, and adding the record to the source's set would flip every source replica to `Incomplete` because of an object about a different board. The closure follows acceptance: the fork's set additionally pulls the source root and every `source_frontier` object (the record's `validate_links` arm requires both roots and the frontier's source scope), with frontier objects' own dependencies through the existing closure expansion. `replica_status_against` needs no special case once the record is in the set. Source membership is revisited only if a consumer that queries a source for its forks is ever filed.
6. **No wire-format or writer change.** No struct, kind string or hash changes in any phase.

Alternatives that lose (in the doc): five independent fixes with the two open rulings left to triage; rejecting duplicate Rules (decision 3); fork record in both sets or source-only (decision 5); folding into #2898/#4000 (no reconstruction surface — see Summary); resolving the listings tie by hash instead of refusing the second first (leaves listed/withdrawn to hash luck where the single-author chain lets insert refuse outright).

## Phased breakdown

- **Phase 1 — insert gates (adopted: #3963 + #4109).** `embed_ref` via `require_scoped` with the v1 kind rule stated; second-first listing rejected naming the existing listing. Per both origins' acceptance, including regression tests and #4109's replication-convergence control. Lands first.
- **Phase 2 — projection determinism (adopted: #4003 + #3964).** Attestation edges only from active attestations (decision 4) with #4003's regression + preserved-behaviour controls; the Rules resolution rule documented + one graph helper + insertion-order-independence test (decision 3). Independent of Phase 1 in code.
- **Phase 3 — replication completeness (adopted: #4081).** Fork record in the fork board's set + acceptance closure; first-ever `BoardFork` tests; end-to-end replication including record and frontier; a fork replica missing the record no longer reports `Complete`. Independent of Phases 1–2 in code.
- **Phase 4 — closing audit (new issue, gated on Phases 1–3).** A kind-by-gate inventory for `boards.rs` — every `BoardObject` variant dispositioned against shape / every reference validated at insert / chain-or-resolution posture / projection effect under the active-records rule / replication membership + closure — recorded as a table in the module header doc; any confirmed same-shape gap fixed under the audit only if small, else filed as a named follow-up.

Open questions stay in the design doc (source-side fork discovery if a consumer is ever filed; whether `compose_view` surfaces current rules via the Phase 2 helper now or the board-view layer adopts it on first use; replication stall diagnostics naming a two-first-listings equivocation — Phase 1 triage notes it, not a phase; the embed kind rule when a dedicated game-post kind lands).

Related: #2898 / #4000 (sibling designs — see Summary), #3806 (federation origin for Phases 1/3), #2813 (board views, Phase 2), #3231 (envelope gate in `artifact.rs` — no field overlap), #3455 (unrelated, same crate).

🤖 Design architect pass 35 (2026-11-01), audit at origin/main `d9636237`.

## Acceptance criteria

- The design names, for each of BoardGraph's three gates (insert, projection, replication), the single enforcement point where the gate's promise is checked, and which of the filed counterexamples (#3963 and its sibling filings) each enforcement point closes.
- Every counterexample filing referenced by the design is either closed by the design's proposed change or explicitly carried as a named exception with a reason.
- The design's implementation is filed as linked follow-up issue(s) (phase issues, in the pattern of #4114) before the design is considered done; the design issue itself closes on the design landing, not on the code.

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/id/web`'s test suite is red on main: all 3 failures in `src/world-contract.test.ts` come from the shell contract's server `view` frame gaining a **required** `view_revision` field that the TypeScript test fixtures never adopted.

- `pkgs/id/contract/shell-contract.v1.json` (revision 4) — server frame `view` declares `"view_revision": "u64"` (required; `base_view_revision` is the optional one). The field arrived in d488f321 ("revisioned JSON ScreenPatch view frames — #805 Phase 1"), which updated the Rust host (`pkgs/id/src/world_session/mod.rs:2154-2204` sends it on every view frame) and the Rust contract tests (`pkgs/id/src/shell_contract/tests.rs:146` sends `view_revision: 0`) — but not the web tests.
- `pkgs/id/web/src/world-contract.test.ts` — the `view` frames at :33 and :70 and the recorded-flow frames behind :330 carry no `view_revision`, so the TS checker (correctly, per the contract) rejects them:
  - `shell contract validator > accepts the frames a joined shell sends` — `checkServerFrame({type: "view", sequence: 1, data: …})` returns not-ok.
  - `shell contract validator > accepts u64 values at and above 2^53, like the Rust checker (#1441)` — the `view` frame with `sequence: 2**53…` returns not-ok (the u64 case is collateral of the same missing field, not a u64 regression).
  - `web shell conformance > sends only contract frames, in the right phases, across every flow` — violation `socket 0 frame 4 (server): `view` needs field `view_revision``.
- Related surface to check while fixing: `pkgs/id/web/src/world.ts:31-32` types `view_revision?: number` as **optional** on the client side, while the contract makes it required on every host `view` frame — triage should decide whether the client type should match the contract or the optionality is deliberate (older hosts).

## Verified this run (2026-11-01)

- Laptop, pristine primary clone at main 7a0da2fc (no local changes): `bun x vitest run src/world-contract.test.ts src/search-panel.test.ts` → the same 3 world-contract failures plus the search-panel failure already tracked as #3243. Full web suite on the same clone: 4 failed / 569 passed / 9 skipped, and those 4 are exactly these + #3243.
- The sandbox clone at ceba688a carries the same contract JSON (revision 4, `view_revision` required) and the same test file, so the failure is not a laptop-local artifact.

## Why it matters

A permanently red suite trains everyone to ignore it — the next real conformance regression in the TS shell-contract checker (the browser-side twin of `src/shell_contract.rs`) will land unnoticed, the same failure mode as the aggregator's red-main baseline (#4023). The drift pattern is also the recurring one for this contract: a revision lands on the Rust side and the TS port's fixtures lag one revision behind.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `bun run test` in `pkgs/id/web` passes for `src/world-contract.test.ts` (the 3 tests above) on main, with the fixtures sending contract-valid `view` frames (including `view_revision`).
- [ ] The fix does not weaken the contract: `view_revision` stays required in `shell-contract.v1.json` unless triage determines the field itself was mis-declared — in which case the JSON, the Rust tests, and the host are changed together instead.
- [ ] Triage records a decision on `world.ts:31` (`view_revision?: number` optional vs the contract's required).
- [ ] No other test in the web suite regresses (the #3243 search-panel failure is pre-existing and out of scope).

title: id(fileops): put stores names verbatim while rename/copy targets are trimmed — padded names create untargetable twin files

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Summary

`pkgs/id` file names are normalized inconsistently inside `FileOps` itself: `put` stores a name **verbatim**, while `rename`/`copy` targets are **trimmed** — so `put` can create files that rename/copy can never target, and two files whose names differ only by surrounding whitespace can coexist.

## Evidence (main `7a0da2fc`, `pkgs/id/src/fileops.rs`, md5 `365ad4ab9ec7d1e589d854ed0df627fa`)

- `FileOps::put` (fileops.rs:243-255) calls `Self::validate_name(name)` and then uses `name` **untrimmed** as the tag name. `validate_name` (fileops.rs:200-217) uses `trim()` only for its emptiness test — a padded name passes and is stored as-is.
- `FileOps::rename`/`copy` go through `validate_target` (fileops.rs:219-227), which does `let to = to.trim();` before validating, and stores the trimmed name. Both web handlers trim a second time (`web/routes.rs` rename handler ~:1757 and copy handler ~:1804: `req.new_name.trim().to_owned()`).
- `FileOps::delete` (fileops.rs:432-435) likewise only checks blank-after-trim and uses the name verbatim, so it agrees with `put`, not with rename/copy.

Verified this run on the laptop with verbatim copies of `validate_name`/`validate_target` (probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneB-fileopstrim/`):

```
validate_name(" report.txt ") = Ok(())            -> put() stores " report.txt " verbatim
validate_target("other.txt", " report.txt ") = Ok("report.txt")  -> rename/copy store "report.txt"
validate_name("report.txt") = Ok(()) and validate_name(" report.txt") = Ok(())
                                                  -> both can exist as distinct files
control: "../x" refused on both paths
```

## Why it matters

`fileops.rs`'s own module doc says the operations "used to be implemented separately… and they drifted apart" and that this module is the single implementation every entry point calls. The drift now exists *inside* the single implementation, at the validation layer added for #1621: the name a file is created under and the names rename/copy will produce follow different rules. A padded name created via `id put` (CLI `commands/put.rs:169` calls `ops().put(name, …)` untrimmed) renders almost identically to its trimmed twin in listings, cannot be produced or matched by a rename/copy target, and sorts/compares differently everywhere names are keys.

## Acceptance criteria

- One stated name-normalization rule for `FileOps`, applied identically by `put`, `rename`, `copy` (and documented for `delete`): either every entry point trims before validating/storing, or padded names are refused everywhere with `InvalidName`.
- Tests in `fileops.rs` pinning the rule: the same padded input yields the same stored name (or the same refusal) through `put` and through `validate_target`; `"x"` and `" x"` cannot silently become two files under the chosen rule.
- Existing fileops tests and the #1621 traversal refusals (`/…`, `…\`, drive prefixes, `.`/`..` components) still pass.

title: id(web/editor): task_list parseDOM reads el.start unvalidated — the #2005 ordered_list fix does not cover ordered task lists; fractional/negative starts save as bullet lists, hex/scientific starts are reinterpreted

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

In the `id` web editor, the `task_list` node's `parseDOM` rule for `<ol>` reads the list start from the DOM's own `el.start` reflection instead of the validated `parseOrderedListStart` helper that #2005 / PR #4078 added for the sibling `ordered_list` rule in the same file — so ordered **task** lists still admit every start value that fix was created to reject:

- `pkgs/id/web/src/editor.ts:210-218` — both branches of the task_list `<ol>` rule return `{ order: el.start }`. `el.start` is whatever the DOM implementation makes of the raw attribute; nothing checks it is a plain non-negative decimal integer.
- `pkgs/id/web/src/editor.ts:46-57,118` — `parseOrderedListStart` (plain `\d+`, safe-integer, fallback 1) is applied only to `ordered_list`. The `task_list` attrs (`editor.ts:203`) declare `order: { default: null }` with no validation.
- `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs:4378` — on save, the codec reads task_list `attrs.order` via `as_u64()`: a negative or fractional order reads as `None`, and the list is rebuilt as a **bullet** task list (markdown.rs:4379-4390). A pasted ordered task list silently loses its ordering on save.
- `pkgs/id/web/src/editor.ts:220-227` — the task_list `toDOM` emits `start="<order>"` for any order ≠ 1, so a stored `-3` or `2.5` round-trips into the rendered HTML verbatim until the save drops the ordering entirely.

## Verified this run (2026-11-01, main `ceba688a`; laptop clone at `7a0da2fc`, `editor.ts` md5 `82283862fb30369b0bc9864a49c2568d` identical on both)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneA-tasklist-start/`, happy-dom — the DOM implementation of the repo's own test suite, `pkgs/id/web/vitest.config.ts` — reading `el.start` exactly as editor.ts:214/216 does, against `parseOrderedListStart`, the helper copied verbatim):

| start attr | task_list `el.start` → saves as | ordered_list `parseOrderedListStart` |
|---|---|---|
| (absent) | 1 → ordered from 1 | 1 |
| `5` / `0` / `42` | 5 / 0 / 42 → preserved | 5 / 0 / 42 |
| `2.5` | 2.5 → **bullet** (as_u64 None) | 1 |
| `-3` | -3 → **bullet** (as_u64 None) | 1 |
| `""` | 0 → ordered from 0 | 1 |
| `0x10` | 16 → **saved as 16** (reinterpreted) | 1 |
| `1e3` | 1000 → **saved as 1000** (reinterpreted) | 1 |
| `9007199254740993` | 9007199254740992 → saved rounded | 1 |

In a spec-compliant browser `el.start` is the IDL signed-long reflection, whose details differ (it truncates `2.5` to 2, parses `0x10` as 0, clamps huge values to 2147483647) — but it still bypasses the fallback-to-1 rule, still truncates instead of rejecting, and still admits negatives that the u64 codec cannot represent. Neither reflection is the validated read #2005 established.

## Why it matters

This is the residual half of #2005 in the same schema: the plain ordered list was hardened, the ordered task list — which shares the `<ol start>` surface and the same u64 save codec — was not. Pasted web content is the realistic source (task lists copied from rendered HTML carry whatever `start` the source page had), and the failure shapes are the two #2005/#2010 classics: silent reinterpretation (`0x10` → 16) and silent loss on save (negative/fractional → bullet list). Distinct from #2010 (image width/height `Number()` in the same file) — different node, different expression, different downstream failure.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The task_list `<ol>` parseDOM rule derives `order` from `parseOrderedListStart(el.getAttribute("start"))` (or an equivalent validated read): only a plain non-negative decimal integer within safe range is preserved (0 included); malformed, fractional, negative, hex/scientific, empty, or unsafe values fall back to 1, exactly as `ordered_list` — in both branches (class-matched and checkbox-detected).
- [ ] Tests mirroring the #2005 `ordered_list start parsing` block cover the task_list rule's getAttrs for the same value set (`5`, `0`, `42` preserved; `abc`, `2.5`, `0x10`, `1e3`, empty, `-3`, `9007199254740993` → 1; absent → 1).
- [ ] The editor test suite passes (`bun run test` in `pkgs/id/web` or CI equivalent).

body:
# proxy-supervise: loadConfig validates ports per proxy but never across proxies — two same-host proxies can claim the same canonical or alternate port

## Evidence (main `ceba688a`)

PR #4049 (for #1952) taught `loadConfig` in `bin/proxy-supervise.mjs` to validate the whole config before reconcile: proxy names are deduplicated (`bin/proxy-supervise.mjs:172-178`, `seenNames`), each `canonicalPort` must be an integer in 1..=65535 (`:182`), and each proxy's own `canonicalPort + altPortOffset` must not exceed 65535 (`:187-188`). The checks are all **per proxy** — nothing compares the port sets of different proxies against each other.

Every proxy ends up using **two** ports at runtime — its canonical port and its alternate (`canonicalPort + altPortOffset`, default offset 1000) — on the same host (default `127.0.0.1`, `bin/proxy-supervise.mjs:233-241` defaults in the `cfg` mapping). Reconcile health-checks exactly those two ports (`:482`, `const ports = [proxy.canonicalPort, altPort]`) and spawns instances on them (`waitHealthy(proxy, proxy.canonicalPort, …)` at `:527` and `:633`; `checkHealth` at `:282` keys only on host+port+healthPath, and a non-JSON 200 or a `{status:"ok"}` body from *any* server counts as healthy).

### Verified (laptop probe, this run)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneB-superviseports/` on the laptop — `node probe.mjs` importing `loadConfig` from a byte-identical copy of `bin/proxy-supervise.mjs` (sha256 `14441e61c8f60841a197f1199ca46c7e9865fb52e45866188d7c4ff36a504e5f`, matching main `ceba688a`):

- control, distinct ports (9000 / 9100, both alt +1000) → **ACCEPTED** (correct)
- two proxies, same host, `canonicalPort` 9000 and 9000 → **ACCEPTED** ← collision
- proxy A canonical 9000 (alt 10000), proxy B canonical 10000 → **ACCEPTED** ← A's alternate port is B's canonical port
- proxy A canonical 9000 offset 500 (alt 9500), proxy B canonical 9200 offset 300 (alt 9500) → **ACCEPTED** ← alternate/alternate collision
- same canonical 9000 on different hosts (`127.0.0.1` vs `127.0.0.2`) → **ACCEPTED** (legitimate — must stay accepted)

## Why it matters

- With two same-host proxies claiming one port, the second instance cannot bind it. Worse, the supervisor's health check is satisfied by *the other proxy's* server answering on that port (same default `healthPath` `/health`): reconcile can judge its own dead child healthy, record it as the serving instance, and publish an endpoint file pointing at a port owned by a different proxy. The failure surfaces as cross-wired traffic or a phantom "healthy" service, not as a config error.
- This is exactly the class #1952/#4049 set out to eliminate — "never pass unsafe … ports through to runtime calculations" — and the validator already does the cross-entry check for names; ports are the remaining cross-entry field it misses.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `loadConfig` rejects a config where two proxies **on the same host** claim the same port in any combination: canonical/canonical, canonical/alternate, alternate/alternate — with an error naming the config file, both proxies, and the colliding port (the existing `fail()` shape).
- [ ] Same port on **different** hosts stays accepted (the probe's `127.0.0.1` vs `127.0.0.2` case), as do fully distinct port sets.
- [ ] Unit tests in `bin/proxy-supervise.test.mjs` cover the three collision shapes and the different-host control, alongside the existing #1952 validation tests.
- [ ] No behavior change for configs that validate today and have no same-host collision.

body:
## Summary

The field-value gate added for #4063 (PR #4082, `parse_app_manifest` in `pkgs/id/src/app_manifest.rs`) rejects duplicate `capabilities.request` entries — with the stated rationale that a repeat is an authoring mistake the gate should name rather than silently absorb — but the same gate is inconsistent for the manifest's other list fields, and its own duplicate check is evadable by whitespace padding:

1. **Duplicate `interfaces.cli.commands` are accepted.** `commands = ["play", "play"]` parses fine (app_manifest.rs:119-131 validates only non-empty + non-blank). The duplicate rule was applied to `capabilities.request` (lines 146-155) but not to the CLI command list in the same function.
2. **The capability duplicate check compares raw strings while the blank check trims.** `request = ["store.read", " store.read "]` is accepted as two distinct requests (lines 133-155: blank check uses `capability.trim()`, the `HashSet` insert uses the raw `capability`), and the padded entry is stored verbatim in the parsed manifest — so the manifest's "strict record of what an app asks for" carries a capability name (`" store.read "`) that no exact-match capability check will ever match, silently granting nothing while looking granted. The same padding evasion works for commands: `["play", " play "]` is accepted.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneA-manifest/` — a crate that compiles the real `app_manifest.rs` from main `78b2bd26` (md5 `d786541ff7045e599df9516605b129db`, byte-identical to the repo file) and calls `parse_app_manifest`:

```
dup-cli-commands:    ACCEPTED cmds=["play", "play"]
ws-evaded-cli-dup:   ACCEPTED cmds=["play", " play "]
ws-evaded-cap-dup:   ACCEPTED caps=["store.read", " store.read "]
untrimmed-cap-entry: ACCEPTED caps=[" store.read "]   (stored verbatim, padding kept)
baseline-cli / baseline-web: ACCEPTED (unchanged)
```

## Why it matters

#4082's gate is the strict authoring contract for app manifests; an app author who duplicates a command or pads a capability gets no error, and the padded capability silently never matches at enforcement time — the worst failure shape for a permission request (looks declared, never granted, no diagnostic anywhere). The inconsistency is also in the exact code the #4063 fix just touched, so the contract reads as deliberate where it is actually partial.

## Acceptance criteria

- `parse_app_manifest` rejects duplicate `interfaces.cli.commands` entries, with an error naming the field, mirroring the `capabilities.request` duplicate rule.
- Duplicate/blank comparisons for list entries use one consistent normalisation: either entries are trimmed before storage and comparison (and the stored manifest carries the trimmed values), or padded entries are rejected outright — a padded duplicate of an existing entry must not parse as a distinct entry.
- Unit tests in `app_manifest.rs` cover: duplicate commands rejected; `["store.read", " store.read "]` rejected (or stored as one trimmed entry only if trimming is the chosen rule — the test pins whichever rule is chosen); the checked-in tic-tac-toe manifest and the existing #4082 tests still pass.
- Not in scope: route/socket validation (#4060), `[resources].files` confinement (#4059), symlinked app folders (#4067).

title: id(worker-poc): POST /cold-start on a fresh Durable Object instance reports journaledStep 0 regardless of the journal — this.step is only populated by ensureGuest, which the route never calls

body:
## Summary

In the Worker isolate host (`pkgs/id/worker-poc/src/worker.ts`), `POST /cold-start` answers `{cold: true, journaledStep: this.step}` — but `this.step` is purely in-memory state that starts at `0` and is only populated inside `ensureGuest()` when the guest is (re)built from the journal. The `/cold-start` branch never reads the journal itself.

So on a genuinely fresh Durable Object instance — an evicted/redeployed isolate whose SQLite journal already holds steps, which is exactly the situation `/cold-start` exists to exercise — a `/cold-start` as the first request reports `journaledStep: 0` no matter how long the journal is. The route also drops nothing (the guest is already null), so the response is doubly misleading: it claims a cold start happened and names the wrong journal position.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneA-coldstart/` (`probe.mjs`): a `WorldObject` constructed over a fake `SqlStorage` whose journal already contains steps 1–2 receives `POST /cold-start` as its first-ever request:

```
POST /cold-start (fresh instance, journal at step 2) -> {"cold":true,"journaledStep":0}
actual journal max step: 2
```

The probe drives the real `worker.ts` (md5 `dcb1af9f`, matching main `070f0d99`); the only probe-copy change is stubbing the compiled-Wasm import line, which the `/cold-start` path never reaches (it calls neither `ensureGuest` nor the guest).

Code path: `worker.ts` constructor creates the table but never reads it; `step = 0` field initializer; `handle()` answers `/cold-start` from `this.step` directly; `this.step` is assigned only in `ensureGuest()` (from the journal's latest row) and after a journaled `/step`.

Why the existing harness misses it: `compare/do-cold-start.mjs` asserts `cold.journaledStep == 2`, but only on a warm instance whose guest was already built by prior `/step` calls. Its genuinely-fresh-instance leg (after the `wrangler dev` restart) calls `GET /state` first — which runs `ensureGuest()` and populates `step` — and never re-checks `/cold-start` on the fresh instance.

## Why it matters

`journaledStep` is the operator-facing proof that the journal survived a cold start; reporting 0 against a non-empty journal reads as "the journal is empty / state was lost" — the exact failure the cold-start route exists to rule out — and would send an operator debugging in the wrong direction. Responses from a stateful route should be derived from the source of truth (the journal), not from a cache that may never have been filled.

## Acceptance criteria

- `POST /cold-start` on a fresh instance reports the journal's actual latest step (e.g. by reading `SELECT step … ORDER BY step DESC LIMIT 1`, or by routing through the same lazy load `/state` uses) — 2 in the probe scenario, 0 only when the journal is genuinely empty.
- `compare/do-cold-start.mjs` gains a fresh-instance `/cold-start` check (after the wrangler restart, before any `/state` call) asserting the restored `journaledStep`.
- Warm-instance behaviour unchanged: the existing harness assertions (`journaledStep == 2` after two steps, restore equality after cold start and after restart) still pass.

Dedup: open+closed search for worker-poc /cold-start / journaledStep found only #2271 (closed; the PoC itself) — this response field is not covered anywhere.

title: id(worker-poc): PlazaGuest.update collapses NaN and -Infinity to participant 0 (host-event routing) and passes negative/fractional participants the native u64 host can never produce

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/low

labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

`PlazaGuest.update()` in the Worker isolate host (`pkgs/id/worker-poc/src/guest.ts`) converts the caller's `participant: number` with a top-end clamp only:

```ts
const clamped = Math.min(participant, 2147483647);
this.model = this.ex.plaza_update(this.model, clamped | 0, ptr, len);
```

The native host it must evolve state identically to takes `participant: u64` (`pkgs/id/src/sandbox.rs:444`) and clamps only the top end (`i32::try_from(participant).unwrap_or(i32::MAX)`, sandbox.rs:452). Negative, fractional, and non-finite participants **cannot exist** on the native side — but on the isolate side they silently become values the native host would never deliver:

| participant | guest receives | effect (roc-chat) |
|---|---|---|
| `NaN` | `0` (`NaN \| 0`) | routed as a **host event** — input not appended |
| `-Infinity` | `0` | routed as a **host event** — input not appended |
| `-1`, `-2147483648` | the negative value itself | appended, as a participant class native can never produce |
| `1.5` | `1` (truncation by `\| 0`) | silently delivered as participant 1 |

Collapsing into participant 0 is exactly the failure the i32::MAX clamp fix (#2271, Codex P2 on PR #3726) was written to prevent for `4294967296` — `smoke/participant-clamp.mjs` pins "clamped participant must not collapse into participant 0" — but the same collapse is still reachable via `NaN` and `-Infinity`, and the negative/fractional classes diverge from native state evolution in the other direction.

The Worker's `/step` route validates its input (`worker.ts`: non-negative integer required), but `PlazaGuest` is the host API itself — `loadHostedGuest` / `loadHostedModule` expose it, the compare harness (`compare/isolate-runner.mjs`) and smoke scripts drive it directly, and any future caller inherits the silent coercion.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneA-guestclamp/` (`probe.mjs`, driving the real `guest.ts`/`manifest.ts` — md5 `410a375a`/`19b5e7b0` matching main `070f0d99` — with the checked-in `examples/roc-chat/roc-chat.wasm`, md5 `829ff79c`), one `update(p, "x")` per fresh guest:

```
participant=0          -> view="chat seen=0 last= input="     (host-event routing)
participant=1          -> view="chat seen=0 last= input=x"
participant=-1         -> view="chat seen=0 last= input=x"    (native-impossible value delivered)
participant=-2147483648-> view="chat seen=0 last= input=x"    (native-impossible value delivered)
participant=NaN        -> view="chat seen=0 last= input="     (collapses to participant 0)
participant=-Infinity  -> view="chat seen=0 last= input="     (collapses to participant 0)
participant=Infinity   -> view="chat seen=0 last= input=x"    (clamps to i32::MAX, correct)
participant=1.5        -> view="chat seen=0 last= input=x"    (silently truncated to 1)
participant=4294967296 -> view="chat seen=0 last= input=x"    (clamps to i32::MAX, correct)
```

## Why it matters

The worker-poc's whole contract is journal/state equality with the native host (#2271). A participant value that is a host event on one host and an appended message on the other — or a participant class that exists on only one host — makes the two hosts evolve different state from the same call sequence, with no error anywhere. The values are not exotic: `NaN` is what JSON-adjacent JS produces from a missing/garbled numeric field, and `-Infinity`/`NaN` both arise from ordinary arithmetic on unvalidated inputs.

## Acceptance criteria

- `PlazaGuest.update` rejects (throws, naming the value class) any participant that is not a non-negative integer: negative, fractional, `NaN`, and both infinities other than the top-end clamp behaviour already pinned — or, if a coercion is deliberately chosen for some class, it is documented in guest.ts and pinned by a test; `NaN` and `-Infinity` must never reach the guest as participant 0.
- Participants in `[0, i32::MAX]` pass through unchanged and values above `i32::MAX` keep the existing clamp (regression: `smoke/participant-clamp.mjs` still passes).
- A smoke/regression script (extending `smoke/participant-clamp.mjs` or a sibling) covers `-1`, `1.5`, `NaN`, `-Infinity` against roc-chat and asserts the chosen behaviour.
- The native/isolate comparison harness (`compare/`) still produces identical lines for its scripted sequences.

Dedup: open+closed search for PlazaGuest/participant/worker-poc validation found only #2271 (closed; the clamp fix itself) — this is its residual input class, not a duplicate. The Worker's `/step` route validation in `worker.ts` is a different layer and does not cover direct `PlazaGuest` callers.
