body:
## Finding

PR #3058 (merged `facf6481b5`, for #1674) added `is_format_char` in `pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/petname.rs` — a hand-listed range set whose doc comment claims "Ranges are the Cf set of Unicode 16". The set is incomplete: **U+061C ARABIC LETTER MARK is category Cf (since Unicode 7) and is not in the list.**

Verified live on current main (`c3fda1c4e6327f7d4e9824608e77fd6461ab0075`): `is_format_char` at `petname.rs:244-266` covers `0600–0605`, `06DD`, `070F`, `0890–0891`, `08E2`, … — no `061C` entry anywhere in the function.

## Why it matters

U+061C is an invisible bidi control — exactly the spoof/reorder class #1674 and #3058 set out to close (the PR's own pinned cases use U+200B and U+202E). Because the set is shared, the gap reaches every consumer:

- `normalize_name` (`petname.rs:293`) accepts a petname carrying U+061C;
- the fold/skeleton comparison path strips only listed Cf, so a stored or alleged name carrying U+061C does not compare by what it renders as;
- invite names reuse the same function (`pkgs/id/src/invite.rs:43`, via PR #3759), so an invite name carrying U+061C also passes.

Dedupe (2026-11-01): searches for `061C` and for petname Cf completeness return only unrelated width/cursor issues (#2962, #1833) and the broader Cf-contract design #3455 — no issue covers this missing code point in `is_format_char`. #1674 is closed by #3058.

## Acceptance criteria

- `is_format_char('\u{061C}')` returns true; a petname and an invite name carrying U+061C are refused, and the fold/skeleton strip removes it.
- A regression test pins U+061C explicitly (named-codepoint style, matching the existing tests in the PR).
- The doc comment's completeness claim is made true — ideally a test or generation note that checks the hand-listed set against the full Unicode Cf set so the next omission is caught mechanically rather than by review.
- Existing petname/invite tests keep passing.

Found by pr-diff-review lane B reviewing PR #3058's diff against the Unicode Cf set.

body:
## Summary
`pkgs/id/src/currency.rs` `fold_authorisation` (landed today via PR #3888, closing #3800) selects the live version with `max_by_key(|(_, body)| body.version)` (currency.rs:313-320). When two distinct signed bodies from the expected issuer carry the **same highest version** (a forked/duplicated issuer chain, or a re-issued v2 with a different rate), `Iterator::max_by_key` returns the **last** maximal element in slice order — so the folded `Live` authorisation depends on the order the caller happens to present the objects, not on the objects alone. The module header promises "State is a fold over the objects alone" (currency.rs:20-23), and the revoke side of the same fold was made explicitly deterministic ("ties break to the smallest `revoked_version_from`, deterministically", currency.rs:296-300) — the version selection has no such tie-break.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe)
Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneB-currency/` on the laptop — verbatim `validate` + version-selection core of `fold_authorisation`, against `currency.rs` at main `c3fda1c4` (sha256 `8f68982526219dff920586495a076d2c1a33f87fe3b6716a74e561ea821b9493`, reference copy in the probe dir).

Two issuer-signed v2 bodies for authorisation 7, `rate_num` 8000 vs 9000:

```
order [8000,9000] -> rate_num 9000
order [9000,8000] -> rate_num 8000
test duplicate_version_fold_depends_on_input_order ... ok
```

Same object set, two presentation orders, two different live rates.

## Why it matters
The fold is the library source of truth every later phase consumes: Phase 2 (#3801) folds "highest version" at submission time and Phase 3 (#3802) binds quotes to it. Two nodes (or one node after a re-sync that changes object order) can fold the same signed object set to different live rates and both be "correct" per this code — a consensus-style divergence in a money-adjacent type, created by the issuer merely signing two bodies at one version (which the chain permits on forked chains; nothing in `validate` or the fold rejects duplicate versions).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Duplicate highest versions fold deterministically regardless of input order: either a canonical tie-break (e.g. by body hash / canonical bytes) documented in the fold's doc comment, or duplicate versions at the maximum are rejected / fold to no live authorisation with the rule stated.
- [ ] Regression test: the same duplicate-version object set in both orders folds to the identical state.
- [ ] Existing currency tests (golden rates, hijack, revoke tie-break) still pass.
- [ ] The chosen rule is recorded on #2290 (parent design) if it changes the design record's fold semantics.

Distinct from: #3801 (gateway live-state checks — it consumes this fold), #3802 (quote binding), #4060/#4063 (app_manifest validation, different module).

labels.name: source/design-architect

body:
## Problem

`discover_apps` (`pkgs/id/src/app_manifest.rs:152-200`, main @ df3f836e) follows symlinks when scanning the apps root, so an "app folder" that is actually a symlink to a directory **outside** the apps root is registered as a local app:

- candidate folders are filtered with `path.is_dir()` (app_manifest.rs:182), which follows symlinks;
- the manifest is loaded via `folder.join("app.toml")` + `is_file()` (:186-190), also following symlinks;
- the folder name used for the id-match check is the **symlink's** name (:187-190), so an external folder registers whenever its manifest `id` matches the symlink's name.

Verified this run with a probe crate on the laptop compiling a sha256-identical copy of `app_manifest.rs` from main df3f836e (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-appmanifest-20261101` on the laptop; result confirmed in two independent runs): apps root containing two real folders plus `linked-app` → symlink to a directory outside the root holding a valid `app.toml` with `id = "linked-app"` → `discover_apps` returns `apps=["app-one", "app-two", "linked-app"], errors=0`.

## Why it matters

The app-folder model (design `doc/2026-10-29T12-50-36Z_design_id_app_packaging` §2/§3) treats the folder as the unit of trust: everything is relative to it, its name must equal the app id, and discovery "registers the app". A symlink hop silently breaks that unit — the registered app's `program.source`, `[resources].files`, and templates all resolve in a directory the operator never placed under the apps root, and a later folder-copy/backup of the root captures a dangling or different app than the one registered. The fleet hit this exact shape in pm-dispatch and fixed it as #3999 (symlink confinement, merged today); discovery has no equivalent stance — it does not even record that a folder was a symlink.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Discovery takes an explicit stance on symlinked app folders: either skip them with a named per-app error in `AppDiscovery.errors`, or resolve and register them only when the resolved target stays inside the apps root — the chosen rule is documented in the module docs.
- [ ] A unit test builds an apps root with a symlinked folder pointing outside it and asserts the chosen behavior (not silently registered as a plain local app).
- [ ] Real (non-symlink) app folders, including the checked-in tic-tac-toe app, discover exactly as today.
- [ ] Symlinks *inside* a real app folder (e.g. a linked `program/` entry) are either covered by the same rule or explicitly called out as out of scope in the module docs.

body:
## Problem

`parse_app_manifest` (`pkgs/id/src/app_manifest.rs`, main @ df3f836e) is strict about manifest *shape* (`#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` on every struct, kebab-case `app.id`, folder/id match) but barely checks field *values* — and the checks it does have are applied inconsistently:

- `program.kind` must be non-empty (app_manifest.rs:117-120) and `program.module_hash` must be non-empty after trim (:130-135) — but `app.name` and `app.version` have **no** checks at all: `name = ""` and `version = ""` are accepted.
- The "at least one interface" rule (:110-113) checks `interfaces.cli.is_some()`, so `[interfaces.cli]` with `commands = []` satisfies it — an app declaring **no commands and no web surface** passes the rule whose entire purpose is to require an interface.
- `capabilities.request` entries are unchecked: blank strings and duplicates are accepted (`request = ["", "", "../../etc"]`).
- `program.module_hash = "not-a-hash"` is accepted. The sibling world-apply manifest validates exactly this field: `world_manifest.rs:229-235` requires 1..=64 plain hex digits. The app-packaging design (§2) presents the app manifest's `module_hash` as the same concept ("a prebuilt module", mutually exclusive with `source`, "same rule as the world-apply manifest").

Verified this run with a probe crate on the laptop compiling a sha256-identical copy of `app_manifest.rs` from main df3f836e (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-appmanifest-20261101` on the laptop) — all of these were **ACCEPTED**: empty name+version; cli-only manifest with `commands = []`; `module_hash = "not-a-hash"`; `capabilities.request = ["", "", "../../etc"]`.

## Why it matters

Discovery (#2324) registers whatever passes this parser, and serve logs it as a discovered app. Blank names/versions, zero-command CLI interfaces, and non-hash "hashes" are exactly the authoring mistakes a strict v1 schema (the module's own doc comment: "The strict, version-one description of one unpacked app folder") exists to catch at the gate — instead they pass silently and will surface as broken display, unroutable apps, or unresolvable module references in the consumers (#2325, the pack step) that trust the gate.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `parse_app_manifest` rejects empty/blank `app.name` and `app.version`.
- [ ] An `[interfaces.cli]` section with an empty `commands` list does not satisfy the at-least-one-interface rule (and blank command names are rejected).
- [ ] `capabilities.request` entries must be non-blank; duplicates are rejected or deduplicated with the rule documented in a test.
- [ ] `program.module_hash` is validated to the same shape the world-apply manifest uses (hex digits, bounded length — see `world_manifest.rs:229-235`), or the divergence is explicitly documented in the module docs with a reason.
- [ ] Unit tests cover each rejection above; the checked-in tic-tac-toe manifest and all existing tests still pass.

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Problem

When the apps root does not exist, app discovery fails **silently**:

- `discover_apps` (`pkgs/id/src/app_manifest.rs:155-167`, main @ df3f836e) special-cases `ErrorKind::NotFound` from `fs::read_dir(root)` and returns a default `AppDiscovery` — zero apps, **zero errors**. Every other `read_dir` error is recorded in `errors`; a missing root is the one failure mode that leaves no trace.
- `cmd_serve` (`pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:782-792`) resolves the root from `ID_APPS_DIR` or the literal relative path `apps`, then logs one `info!` per discovered app and one `warn!` per discovery error. For a missing root it logs **neither** — and it never logs the root path it scanned.

So running `serve` from a working directory without an `apps/` folder (or with `ID_APPS_DIR` mispointed, or from a packaged install whose apps live elsewhere) is indistinguishable in the logs from a host that legitimately has zero apps installed: the #2324 discovery feature appears to do nothing, with no signal pointing at the cause.

Verified this run with a probe crate on the laptop compiling a sha256-identical copy of `app_manifest.rs` from main df3f836e (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-appmanifest-20261101` on the laptop): `discover_apps("/nonexistent-apps-root-probe-xyz")` returns `apps=0, errors=0`.

## Why it matters

Discovery's design contract (#2324, design §3) is "degrade, don't die — **with a named error**": a malformed app disables only itself *with a named error*. A missing root is the same class of operator error at one level up, and it is currently the only silent one. As apps move from PoC to real installs (the flake already copies `apps/` into the test package's share dir, `pkgs/id/flake.nix`), "no apps found" will be the first symptom of every packaging/path mistake.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A nonexistent apps root produces a visible signal at serve startup: either `discover_apps` records a named error entry for the missing root (which serve already logs as a warning), or serve logs a warning naming the resolved root path when it does not exist — triage picks the layer, but the signal must name the path.
- [ ] A unit test covers the missing-root case and asserts the new signal (error entry or equivalent) is produced.
- [ ] Existing behavior is preserved otherwise: a present-but-empty root and a root with valid/invalid apps behave as today, and the checked-in tic-tac-toe app still discovers.
- [ ] Serve startup logs (or the discovery result) make it possible to tell "root missing", "root present, 0 apps", and "root present, N apps" apart.

body:
## Problem

The `[interfaces.web]` validation in `parse_app_manifest` (`pkgs/id/src/app_manifest.rs`, main @ df3f836e) checks `mode` against `adapter|direct` and requires `route` to start with `/` (app_manifest.rs:136-148) — and nothing else:

- `route` may contain `..` segments, spaces, or a query/fragment: it is never checked for path-segment sanity.
- `socket` (`WebInterface`, app_manifest.rs:57-64) is never validated at all — any string, including an absolute URL, is accepted, although the design (`doc/2026-10-29T12-50-36Z_design_id_app_packaging` §2) shows it as a local live-channel route (`socket = "/ws/world"`).
- `discover_apps` (app_manifest.rs:152-200) performs no cross-app check: two different apps declaring the **same** `route` are both returned in `apps` with zero errors.

Verified this run with a probe crate on the laptop compiling a sha256-identical copy of `app_manifest.rs` from main df3f836e (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-appmanifest-20261101` on the laptop):

- manifest with `route = "/../escape path"` and `socket = "https://evil.example/ws"` → **ACCEPTED**
- two app folders (`app-one`, `app-two`) both with `route = "/same"` → `discover_apps` returns `apps=2, errors=0`, both carrying route `/same`

## Why it matters

Issue #2325 (open) will parameterise the host's `/world` page route and `/ws/world` live channel from exactly these fields. A route is a routing key: if discovery can register two apps on one route — or an app on a route with traversal segments — the collision surfaces later as one app shadowing another in the router, with no named error at the gate that exists to catch it. Discovery already guarantees per-app error isolation; uniqueness and route shape are the cross-app half of that contract and are missing.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `parse_app_manifest` rejects a web `route` containing `..` segments, whitespace, `?`, or `#`, and rejects a `socket` that is present but does not start with `/` (same segment sanity as route).
- [ ] `discover_apps` reports a named error for the second (and later) app whose web `route` duplicates an already-discovered app's route, and does not register the duplicate — the first app (folder sort order, as today) is unaffected.
- [ ] Unit tests cover: traversal route rejected, absolute-URL socket rejected, duplicate-route discovery yields 1 app + 1 error naming the route.
- [ ] The checked-in `pkgs/id/apps/tic-tac-toe/app.toml` (`route = "/tic-tac-toe"`, no socket) still validates and discovers unchanged.

body:
## Problem

`parse_app_manifest` (`pkgs/id/src/app_manifest.rs`, main @ df3f836e) enforces folder confinement for exactly one path field and leaves `[resources].files` unchecked:

- `program.source` is validated component-by-component (app_manifest.rs:124-133): every component must be `Component::Normal`, so absolute paths, `..`, and `.` are rejected.
- `Resources::files` (app_manifest.rs:70-77) is a bare `Vec<String>`; `parse_app_manifest` (app_manifest.rs:97-149) never inspects its entries at all.

Verified this run with a probe crate on the laptop compiling a sha256-identical copy of `app_manifest.rs` from main df3f836e (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-appmanifest-20261101` on the laptop): a manifest with

```toml
[resources]
files = ["../../etc/passwd", "/etc/passwd", "assets/**"]
```

is **ACCEPTED** by `parse_app_manifest`.

That contradicts the app-packaging design (`doc/2026-10-29T12-50-36Z_design_id_app_packaging/2026-10-29T12-50-36Z_design_id_app_packaging.md` §2): "Everything is relative to the app folder. No absolute paths, no references outside the folder" — and `[resources].files` are the entries the pack step (§5) will package and content-hash as a set, so a traversal entry accepted at discovery is the entry a later pack/serve step will read.

## Why it matters

Discovery is the validation gate for app folders (#2324, closed). Every other consumer — the pack step, the `[interfaces.web]` adapter binding (#2325), any resource serving — will reasonably trust that a discovered manifest's declared files live inside the app folder. Today that trust holds for `program.source` only.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `parse_app_manifest` rejects any `[resources].files` entry that is absolute or escapes the app folder via `..` components, with an error naming the offending entry.
- [ ] In-folder entries from the design example keep working, including glob patterns such as `assets/**` and `web/templates/**` (glob metacharacters live inside otherwise-normal components).
- [ ] Unit tests in `app_manifest.rs` cover: absolute entry rejected, `../` entry rejected, nested `a/../../b` entry rejected, `assets/**` accepted.
- [ ] The checked-in `pkgs/id/apps/tic-tac-toe/app.toml` (and the module's existing tests) still validate/discover unchanged.

body:
# id(doc): `note.revise` rows in `id doc events`/`history` omit the revision's size and media_type

## Problem

The CLI's per-event listing formatter gives every content-bearing entry its
content hash, size, and media type — except a note revision. A `note.revise`
row shows its note, content hash, and parents, but never the revision's size
or media type, even though the revision carries exactly the same
`DocumentRef` the other rows render. A consumer of `id doc events --json` /
`id doc history --json` (or the plain-text rows) cannot learn a revision's
size or media type from the listing; it has to fetch the blob instead.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 2a93f3f6)

`pkgs/id/src/commands/doc.rs`, `entry_fields` (the only field source for
`DocCommand::Events` at :155 and `DocCommand::History` at :162; `print_rows`
at :51-59 renders exactly these fields in both text and JSON modes):

- `Entry::Document` (:78-82): `content`, `size`, `media_type`
- `Entry::NoteCreate` (:100-104): `content`, `size`, `media_type`
- `Entry::NoteRevise` (:106-115): `note`, `content`, `parents` — no `size`,
  no `media_type`

The asymmetry came in with the note listing support in PR #3908 (#3814):
the create arm copied the document arm's three content fields, the revise
arm did not. `Entry::NoteRevise` holds `content: DocumentRef`
(`pkgs/id/src/local_events.rs`, `entry_of`), so both fields are already in
hand at the formatter — nothing needs to be fetched or recomputed.

## Why it matters

The listing is the discovery surface for note history: it is how a user or a
script decides which revision to fetch. Size and media type are the two
fields that decision needs (is this revision the big attachment or the small
markdown edit?), and they are present for the note's first revision (the
create row) and for every document row — just missing for every later
revision, which is most rows of any real note history.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Entry::NoteRevise` rows from `entry_fields` include `size` and
      `media_type` from the revision's `DocumentRef`, matching the
      `Document`/`NoteCreate` arms.
- [ ] A test covers a note revision's listing fields (unit test on
      `entry_fields` or a CLI-level history/events test) showing `size` and
      `media_type` present for a revise row.
- [ ] No other entry kind's fields change.

Dedup: open + closed searches for `entry_fields`, "note revise media_type
size history", and "notes doc listing fields" returned only #3814 (the
closed implementation tracker) and unrelated hits — nothing covers the
revise row's missing fields. Notes landed on main today (PR #3908, merged
16:08 CST), after Lane A's last sweep of pkgs/id, so this is uncovered new
code, not a re-check of a swept area.

title: id(boards): compose_view applies supersedes edges from superseded attestations — a nullified revocation still revokes

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Summary

`BoardGraph::compose_view` (pkgs/id/src/boards.rs, merged today in PR #3971 for issue #2813) computes the "current moderator frontier" from RoleAttestation `supersedes` edges collected from **every** attestation in the graph — including attestations that have themselves been superseded and therefore, by the module's own rule, have no effect. A revocation that was later nullified by a generic `Supersede` record still revokes the grant it named, so a moderator the owner reinstated (by superseding the revocation) silently keeps no authority in the composed view.

## Evidence (main @ 9e1be520)

- The generic-supersede frontier is resolved to a fixed point at boards.rs:899-925, and the module's stated rule (compose_view comments, boards.rs:884-891) is: "a superseded record (a moderation action, a tombstone, any content object) has no effect in the projection, whatever it once said." The test `superseded_supersede_record_has_no_effect` (boards.rs:2058) pins the same principle for Supersede records, and `generic_supersede_of_a_grant_also_revokes_authority` (boards.rs:1997) pins that superseding a *grant* ends its authority.
- But the attestation frontier at boards.rs:932-941 inserts `value.supersedes` into `attestation_superseded` for **all** RoleAttestations of the board, with no check that the attestation carrying the edge is itself still active (not in the `superseded` set computed just above). The filter at boards.rs:943-944 excludes a superseded attestation as a grant *source*, yet its outgoing `supersedes` edge is still applied.

### Reproduction (verified this run)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneB-attsuper/` over verbatim pkgs/id/src/boards.rs (sha256 b041c747c05745465d8043a8ab8b089ff512a68a8e78ff3e0964c6272918d19a, matching main @ 9e1be520; artifact.rs sha256 c3332474b111453df5b68688aed35f977f8125a6cec6a3a69daedfbc913ae1c7):

1. Owner grants Moderator to M (attestation A1, `granted=true`); M hides a post → view hides it (control passes: hidden=1).
2. Owner revokes with A2 (`granted=false`, `supersedes=A1`) → post visible again (control passes).
3. Owner signs an unrelated attestation A3 (grants a *different* member) and a generic Supersede record S (`previous=A2`, `replacement=A3`; same kind, same author — valid per validate_links boards.rs Supersede arm). S nullifies the revocation A2.
4. Expected per the module's rule: A2 has no effect, so A1 is again the current grant and M's Hide applies (post hidden). **Observed: the post stays visible** — A2's stale `supersedes` edge still excludes A1 from `current_moderators`, so `has_authority(M)` is false and the Hide is treated as unauthorized.

Note the asymmetry this creates: superseding a grant revokes (tested, boards.rs:1997), but superseding a revocation does not reinstate (untested, broken) — the two directions of the same record-nullification rule were only half-applied when the frontier was built.

## Why it matters

Moderator authority in the composed view decides whose Hide/Restore records change what every viewer sees. An owner who reverses a revocation via the generic supersede mechanism (the same mechanism the module tests for grants, tombstones, and moderation actions) gets a view where the reversal silently did nothing: the formerly-revoked moderator's actions are ignored, with no error anywhere. Authority frontiers that disagree with the signed record set undermine the order-independence/determinism the module is designed around.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `compose_view` only applies a RoleAttestation's `supersedes` edge when that attestation is itself active (not superseded), mirroring the generic frontier rule — or an equivalent formulation with the same observable behavior.
- [ ] Regression test: grant → revocation (attestation `supersedes`) → generic Supersede nullifying the revocation (replacement is a same-kind attestation that does not itself decide the subject's role) → the subject's moderation actions take effect again in the composed view.
- [ ] Existing behavior preserved: grant → revocation keeps the subject without authority; generic supersede of a grant still revokes (boards.rs:1997 test); superseded-supersede test (boards.rs:2058) still passes.
- [ ] All existing boards tests pass.

## Scope / notes

- Fix is local to `compose_view`'s moderator-frontier computation in pkgs/id/src/boards.rs; insert-time validation is unchanged.
- Related, distinct filings on the same file: issue #3963 (Post embed_ref unvalidated), issue #3964 (Rules revision uniqueness). This issue is only about the attestation frontier in the view projection.

title: id(chat-presence): heartbeat typing list is never deduplicated or bounded — one channel yields a 3.3 MB signed frame, defeating MAX_HEARTBEAT_CHANNELS

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Summary

`pkgs/id` chat presence bounds a heartbeat's `channels` list but not its `typing` list: `typing` is documented as a subset of `channels` ("The channels the node is currently typing in. A subset of `channels`", chat_presence.rs:107-109), yet neither the constructor, the table's receive path, nor the codec deduplicates or caps it. A heartbeat can carry an unbounded number of duplicate typing entries, so one signed heartbeat produces an arbitrarily large gossip frame and an arbitrarily large stored table entry — defeating `MAX_HEARTBEAT_CHANNELS`, whose stated purpose is to "bound the frame size and the work a single received heartbeat can make the table do" (chat_presence.rs:76-78).

## Evidence (verified this run, main 70a595a7)

- `PresenceHeartbeat::new` (chat_presence.rs:138-161) deduplicates `channels` and truncates it to `MAX_HEARTBEAT_CHANNELS` (64), but for `typing` it only filters to entries present in `channels` — duplicates survive and there is no length cap.
- `PresenceTable::update_at` (chat_presence.rs:296-301), the receive path, applies the same filter-only treatment to a decoded heartbeat's `typing`; heartbeats decoded from the wire never pass through `new`, so the constructor's invariants would not save this path anyway.
- The production receiver in `serve` (commands/serve.rs:1575-1591) verifies the signature and then calls `recv_presence.update(heartbeat)`. Signature verification does not help here: the sender signs its own bloated heartbeat with its own key, so `verify()` passes.
- Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneA-presencetyping/` (verbatim `chat_presence.rs`, md5 68590664a175bd4a17937c28a2f0fb6b, matching sandbox main 70a595a7; minimal stubs for `groups::GroupView` / `waiting::AuthorKey`):
  - `PresenceHeartbeat::new(node, vec![chan], vec![chan; 100_000], ts)` → `channels.len() = 1`, `typing.len() = 100_000`, `encode_frame(...).len() = 3_300_087` bytes (~3.3 MB frame naming one channel).
  - Control: `new` with 500 distinct channels → `channels.len() = 64` (the cap works for channels).
  - A wire-shaped heartbeat with `typing = vec![chan; 50_000]` round-trips through `encode_frame`/`decode_frame` at full length and is accepted by `update_at`.

## Why it matters

Presence is an unauthenticated-reach, always-on gossip surface: any peer on the topic can get its own heartbeats accepted. The one size bound the protocol declares (64 channels) can be bypassed by three orders of magnitude through the sibling field, inflating every receiver's stored entry (retained until the TTL prune) and every re-gossiped frame. It is also a shape bug independent of size: duplicate typing entries mean the stored heartbeat's `typing` is not the set the docs promise, so any future consumer that iterates or counts it inherits the duplicates.

## Acceptance criteria

- `PresenceHeartbeat::new` deduplicates `typing` (after filtering to `channels`), so `typing.len() <= channels.len()` for every constructed heartbeat.
- `PresenceTable::update_at` applies the same dedup/bound to decoded heartbeats, so a wire heartbeat with duplicate or excess typing entries is stored in bounded form (or refused), regardless of the constructor.
- Regression tests: a heartbeat built or decoded with duplicate typing entries (e.g. 100_000 copies of one channel) is stored/encoded with at most one entry per channel; existing chat_presence tests keep passing.
- The bound is stated next to `MAX_HEARTBEAT_CHANNELS` so the frame-size guarantee covers the whole heartbeat, not just `channels`.

Distinct from: #2809 (the presence protocol itself, closed — this is a residual bound gap in its merged implementation), #3927 (abuse evaluator oversize, different module), #3950 (chat v1 core remainder — membership/store/rate, not presence frame bounds).

body:
## Bug

`BoardGraph` validates every object reference a `Post` carries — thread, parent post, and each attachment get existence + same-board scope checks via `require_scoped` — **except `embed_ref`**. A post whose `embed_ref` names a hash that is not in the graph at all, or a post that lives in a different board, is accepted into the graph. The module header promises the graph "checks signatures, canonical references, board scope, and the authority rules needed to accept an object" (`pkgs/id/src/boards.rs:3-9`); `embed_ref` is the one reference class that escapes that promise.

## Evidence (verified this run, main @ e860d3a9)

- `pkgs/id/src/boards.rs:62-68` — `GamePostRef { object: ArtifactHash }`, "Hash of the immutable signed game-post object."
- `pkgs/id/src/boards.rs:145` — `Post.embed_ref: Option<GamePostRef>`.
- `pkgs/id/src/boards.rs:505-524` — the `BoardObject::Post` arm of `validate_links` checks `require_board`, `require_scoped(thread)`, the parent post (incl. same-thread), and every attachment — `embed_ref` is never read.
- Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneB-boards/` (verbatim `boards.rs`, sha256 `bcc08b3e…` matching the repo file @ e860d3a9; faithful minimal `SignedArtifact` harness; all 8 built-in boards tests pass):
  - post with `embed_ref` = hash of a nonexistent object → **insert Ok** (accepted)
  - post with `embed_ref` = a real post in a *different* board → **insert Ok** (accepted)
  - controls: the same missing hash as an attachment → insert Err; the same foreign post as an attachment → insert Err

## Why it matters

The board graph is the validation substrate every later layer (replication #3806, board views #2813) will trust: an object in the graph is supposed to have had its references checked. A dangling embed reference means projections must re-validate (or render broken embeds), and a cross-board embed reference breaks the board-scope invariant the rest of the module enforces everywhere else — including for the attachments on the very same post.

## Acceptance criteria

- A `Post` whose `embed_ref` names an object not present in the graph is rejected at `BoardGraph::insert` with a clear error.
- A `Post` whose `embed_ref` names an object scoped to a different board is rejected at insert.
- The expected kind of the referenced object is decided and documented (a dedicated game-post object kind does not exist yet in v1; at minimum existence + same-board scope via `require_scoped`, with the kind rule stated in the code/docs for when the game-post type lands).
- Regression tests in the `boards.rs` test module cover the missing-object and cross-board `embed_ref` cases, mirroring the existing attachment controls.
- All existing boards tests still pass.

title: id(world): restore's EntityImported epoch check uses plain + 1 — prior=u64::MAX wraps to an accepted epoch 0 in release and panics in debug/test

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Finding

`WorldCore::restore`'s standalone `EntityImported` journal arm validates the owner-epoch advance with a plain `+ 1` on a `u64`:

```rust
// pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs:367-370 (restore, JournalEntry::EntityImported arm)
ensure!(
    new_owner_epoch == prior_owner_epoch + 1,
    "journal import for handoff {handoff_id:?} does not advance the owner epoch"
);
```

`prior_owner_epoch` / `new_owner_epoch` are `u64` (`pkgs/id/src/world/mod.rs:513`, `:814`), and `pkgs/id/Cargo.toml` sets no `overflow-checks` override in any profile, so the check behaves differently by build:

- **Release** (overflow checks off): `prior_owner_epoch = u64::MAX`, `new_owner_epoch = 0` satisfies `0 == MAX + 1` (wrapping) — restore **accepts** an import whose owner epoch wraps to 0, i.e. the epoch goes *backwards* to the start. Owner epochs are the fencing currency for the region-seam handoff (#3870 phases 2–5 build on this foundation): an epoch that can wrap to 0 defeats the monotonicity the fence relies on.
- **Debug / test** (overflow checks on): the same journal entry **panics** with `attempt to add with overflow` inside `restore`, so a crafted or corrupted journal crashes the restore path instead of being refused with the arm's own error message.

## Evidence (main 92682232, verified this run)

- `pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs:368` — the plain `+ 1` above (file md5 `6b67846b2091c327ba9af2cdf93b687a`, identical on the sandbox clone and the laptop clone).
- Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneA-epochwrap/` — the verbatim predicate extracted from core.rs:367-370, compiled with plain `rustc` on the laptop:
  - Release (`rustc -O`): controls correct — `prior=5 new=6 → true`, `prior=5 new=5 → false`, `prior=5 new=7 → false`; **wrap case `prior=MAX new=0 → true`**, `prior=MAX new=MAX → false`.
  - Debug (`rustc`, overflow checks on): controls correct; the wrap case **panics** (`attempt to add with overflow`, exit 101) before it can return a verdict.
- Sibling checks in the same restore already avoid plain arithmetic where it matters: the checkpoint consecutiveness check is the subject of #3736, and `since_checkpoint` accounting uses `saturating_add` (core.rs, EntityExported/EntityImported arms).

## Why it matters

This arm is the *validating* path for journal-carried imports — the checkpoint-carried variant is separately unvalidated (#3942). A handoff import at the last representable epoch is exactly the boundary a fencing epoch must never cross silently: in release it restores as a legitimate advance to epoch 0 (a stale owner's epoch-0 claims become current again), and in debug/test builds the same input is a panic in the restore path rather than a clean refusal. The fix is the checked form used elsewhere in the codebase (`checked_add(1)` compared against `Some(new_owner_epoch)`, or equivalent), so `prior = u64::MAX` can never validate an import.

## Acceptance criteria

- `WorldCore::restore` refuses a standalone `EntityImported` journal entry with `prior_owner_epoch = u64::MAX` (any `new_owner_epoch`) with the existing "does not advance the owner epoch" error — in both debug/test and release builds, with no panic and no wrapping acceptance.
- Ordinary advances still restore: `prior=5, new=6` succeeds; `prior=5, new=5` and `prior=5, new=7` are still refused.
- A regression test in `pkgs/id/src/world/tests.rs` (alongside the existing handoff restore tests) covers the `u64::MAX` prior epoch case.
- The same plain-`+1` pattern is checked for the other epoch/sequence comparisons added by the #3900 handoff foundation, and any sibling site found is either fixed in the same change or filed separately with a link here.

Dedup: #3736 (open) is the checkpoint *event-sequence* consecutiveness `pair[1].sequence == pair[0].sequence + 1` at core.rs:476 — a different field, arm, and consequence. #3942 (open) covers checkpoint-*carried* transfers being installed verbatim with no validation at all; its probe exercised the standalone arm only at epoch 5→5, which this arm correctly refuses — the overflow boundary of the standalone arm's own check was not covered. #3902/#3903/#3904 (open) are the #3870 destination-import/coordinator/client phases that build *on* this foundation; none fixes the phase-1 restore check.

body:
## Summary

The same epic, over the same Project pool, reports two different done-counts depending on which page you read:

- **Epic rollup** (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/epics.ts:35`, rendered on /projects, /program and the epic's /item page): a child counts as done when it is `closed`/`merged` in GitHub **or marked Done in Project Status** — `child.state === "closed" || child.state === "merged" || status === "Done"`. This is the documented contract on the `EpicRollup.done` field (epics.ts:6): "Children closed/merged in GitHub or marked Done in Project Status."
- **Roadmap drill-down** (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/render.ts:1757`, `roadmapDrilldown`, landed in #1168): progress counts only GitHub state — `drill.children.filter((c) => c.state === "closed" || c.state === "merged")`. A child whose Project Status is "Done" but whose issue is still open is **not** counted.

## Evidence (verified this run, main @ 92682232)

Probe on the laptop (`probe-2026-11-01-laneB-epicdrill/probe.ts`) importing the real `buildEpicRollups`, `buildRoadmapDrill`, `reconcileRoadmap` and `renderRoadmap`, using the exact fixture shape of `test/epics.test.ts` (epic with 4 children: one merged, one status "Done" + state open, one In Progress, one Todo):

- `buildEpicRollups(pool)` → `{ total: 4, done: 2, blocked: 1 }` (matches the pinned expectation in `test/epics.test.ts`)
- `renderRoadmap(...)` drill-down for the same epic → `Progress: 1/4 child issues done`

So /projects says "2/4 done" for an epic while /roadmap's expansion of the same epic says "Progress: 1/4". Neither test suite exercises the other surface's rule: `test/roadmap-drill.test.ts` never includes a status-Done/open child, and `test/epics.test.ts` never renders the drill-down.

## Why it matters

The dashboard's pages are supposed to be one coherent read of the pool (#1184). A reader comparing /roadmap against /projects or an epic's item page sees contradictory progress for the same work, and the drill-down silently under-reports completion for the common workflow where the Project board is marked Done before (or instead of) the issue being closed.

## Acceptance criteria

- One shared done-rule for epic children across the rollup and the roadmap drill-down (ideally the drill-down reuses `buildEpicRollups` or a shared helper instead of re-deriving the count in `roadmapDrilldown`).
- A child with Project Status "Done" and GitHub state "open" counts the same way on /roadmap, /projects, /program, and the epic /item page.
- A regression test puts a status-Done/open child in front of both surfaces and asserts the same done/total.
- Existing `epics.test.ts` and `roadmap-drill.test.ts` expectations still pass (or are updated with the reason recorded in the PR).

body:
## Summary

In the aggregator's **month** roadmap view (`/roadmap?h=month`), lanes are sorted by `Lane.order`, but month lanes and quarter lanes compute `order` on incompatible scales, so quarter lanes always render before month lanes regardless of the actual dates. A `Q1 2030` lane renders ahead of October 2026; a `Q1 2027` lane renders ahead of the October–December 2026 month lanes it follows (and ahead of its own January 2027 month lane, which lands several lanes later).

## Evidence

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/derive.ts:612-638` — `monthTimeline` builds month lanes with `order: y * 12 + m` (e.g. October 2026 → 24322) and falls back to `laneFor` for non-dated rows; lanes are sorted once at the end with `sort((a, b) => a.order - b.order)`.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/derive.ts:86-101` (+ `quarterLane`) — `laneFor` gives quarter lanes `order: year * 4 + quarter` (e.g. Q1 2030 → 8121, Q1 2027 → 8109), ongoing `1e6`, other `1e6 + 1`, unscheduled `1e6 + 2`. Every quarter order (~8.1k) is below every month order (~24.3k), so the final sort groups all quarters first, then all months.
- Rendered by `pm-stack/aggregator/src/render.ts:1767`: `timelineTable(monthTimeline(rows), …)` for grain `month`. Mixed grains are the normal case: the roadmap fixture itself mixes ISO-date horizons with `Qn YYYY` horizons, and the existing test only asserts both lane kinds are present (`pm-stack/aggregator/test/slice2.test.ts`, "month timeline places dated rows by month and keeps quarter grain"), never their relative order.
- The quarter view does not have this bug: `timeline()` folds dated rows into quarter lanes via `laneFor`, so all its lanes share one scale.

Verified this run (main @ `0b3719ee`) with a laptop Node probe over the verbatim functions copied from `derive.ts` (file sha256 `3f57f42b…`, identical on sandbox and laptop clones; probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneA-monthlane/`). Rows: `2026-10-24`, `Q1 2027`, `2027-01-15`, `Q4 2026`, `Q1 2030`, `Ongoing`. Resulting lane order:

```
2026-Q4 (order 8108)
2027-Q1 (order 8109)
2030-Q1 (order 8121)   <- a 2030 quarter ahead of Oct 2026
2026-10 (order 24322)
2027-01 (order 24325)
ongoing (order 1000000)
```

Chronologically, October 2026 and Q4 2026 cover the same quarter, January 2027 sits inside Q1 2027, and Q1 2030 belongs after every 2026/2027 lane.

## Why it matters

The month view is the planning view: a reader scanning top-to-bottom reads it as a timeline. As soon as the roadmap mixes dated rows with quarter rows for a later year — the normal state of a roadmap that plans into next year — future quarters jump the queue and the view silently stops being chronological, with no flag that anything is off.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] In `monthTimeline`, lanes sort chronologically across grains: a quarter lane orders by the months it spans (e.g. Q1 2027 alongside/around Jan–Mar 2027, Q1 2030 after all 2026/2027 lanes), and no quarter lane for a later year renders before a month lane for an earlier date.
- [ ] Ongoing / other / unscheduled lanes keep sorting after all dated lanes, in their current relative order.
- [ ] The quarter view (`timeline()`) ordering is unchanged.
- [ ] Regression test in the aggregator test suite (e.g. `slice2.test.ts` or `render.test.ts`): a mixed set such as `2026-10-24`, `Q4 2026`, `2027-01-15`, `Q1 2027`, `Q1 2030` asserts the full lane-key sequence, not just lane presence.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `monthTimeline`, lane order/sort, and quarter/month timeline on 2026-11-01: no covering issue. #1628 (closed) fixed date *validation* in these functions (impossible months, `undefined` labels, `ymdLabel` throws) — different defect; #2601 (open) is the `ymdLabel` trailing-text residual. Neither touches lane ordering.

body:
## Summary

`doneItemIsRecent` in the aggregator's board policy has no upper bound on `updatedAt`, so a future-dated done card never ages out of the 7-day done window until its (future) date plus 7 days have passed. One skewed Kaneo `updatedAt` can pin a finished card on the WIP board for months — the exact failure the aggregator's own "a future stamp is never fresh" rule was created to prevent on every other surface.

## Evidence (on main `1b1e3abd`)

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/board-policy.ts:20` — `DONE_BOARD_WINDOW_MS` is 7 days; the module header (lines 5–6) states the contract: "Done items stay on the board for DONE_BOARD_WINDOW_MS (7 days) after their last update, then drop off entirely".
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/board-policy.ts:40-45` — the only check is one-sided:

  ```ts
  export function doneItemIsRecent(item: BoardItem, now: number): boolean {
    if (!item.updatedAt) return true;
    const t = Date.parse(item.updatedAt);
    if (Number.isNaN(t)) return true;
    return now - t <= DONE_BOARD_WINDOW_MS;
  }
  ```

  For any future `t`, `now - t` is negative, so the comparison is always true — no matter how far in the future the stamp is.
- The policy is applied in both board paths, so no source bypasses it and no source is protected from it either: `pm-stack/aggregator/src/sources/live.ts:204` (`applyBoardDonePolicy(out)` in the Kaneo reader) and `pm-stack/aggregator/src/render.ts:1582` (`renderBoardBody`).
- The `updatedAt` value is the Kaneo API's verbatim stamp (after #1197 / #3938, `pm-stack/aggregator/src/sources/live.ts` passes `t.updatedAt` through with no validation), so a clock-skewed or buggy upstream write reaches this check unchecked.
- The house rule this violates already exists in the same codebase: `pm-stack/aggregator/src/feed.ts:189` defines `GENERATED_AT_FUTURE_SKEW_MS = 60_000` ("Future-skew tolerance for generatedAt stamps (#1564; the aggregator-wide 60s convention ruled for #1541)"), and the closed precedents #1541, #1564 and #1568 all fixed the same one-sided-age shape on other surfaces (quota freshness, orchestration/feed generatedAt, derive freshness). The board policy was never given the upper bound.

## Verified this run

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneB-boardfuture/` (Bun 1.4.2) importing the verbatim `board-policy.ts` from main (sha256 `aa40a1f72cd590f753301bf03ee799542b18db3f452486947789bd3693f79710`, identical in the sandbox clone at `1b1e3abd` and the laptop clone), with `now = 2026-11-01T12:00:00Z`:

- Control passes: a done card updated 1 day ago is kept, one updated 30 days ago is dropped, an undated done card is kept (age unproven — the documented behaviour).
- A done card with `updatedAt` **+30 days** in the future: `doneItemIsRecent` returns `true` and `applyBoardDonePolicy` keeps it.
- A done card with `updatedAt` **+365 days** in the future: still `true` at `now`, and still `true` at `now + 180 days` — it would only drop off more than a year from now.

Probe result: 3/3 tests pass (the two "BUG" tests assert the current, buggy behaviour so the finding is reproducible, not inferred).

## Why it matters

The board is a WIP view, not a completion log (#1146). A single future-dated done card defeats the 7-day age-out indefinitely, inflates the "Done recently (N)" strip, and — because the undated/invalid cases are deliberately kept — there is no other layer that will ever remove it. The stamp is presented to the user as recent finished work for as long as the skew lasts.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A done item whose `updatedAt` is more than the aggregator's future-skew tolerance (60s, `GENERATED_AT_FUTURE_SKEW_MS`) in the future is not treated as recent solely because `now - t` is negative: it is either dropped by `applyBoardDonePolicy` or handled under an explicitly documented future-stamp rule in `board-policy.ts` (the fix chooses one and says why; silently keeping it forever is not an option).
- [ ] Undated and unparseable `updatedAt` keep their current documented behaviour (kept — age unproven), and non-done items are unaffected.
- [ ] Regression tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/board-done-policy.test.ts`: future-dated done at +30d and at a far-future date, a within-skew (≤60s) future stamp if the chosen rule keeps it, plus the existing recent/ancient/undated controls.
- [ ] Both application points (`sources/live.ts` board assembly and `render.ts` `renderBoardBody`) exhibit the fixed behaviour (they share `applyBoardDonePolicy`, so one fix should cover both — the tests should say so).

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `doneItemIsRecent`, board-policy / DONE_BOARD_WINDOW, and future-dated done/board terms on 2026-11-01: no covering issue. #1146 (closed) is the feature that introduced the policy; #1541 / #1564 / #1568 (closed) fixed the same one-sided-age shape on other aggregator surfaces and are precedents, not duplicates — none touches `board-policy.ts`.

body:
## Summary

`WorldCore::restore` (`pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs`) treats the journal as untrusted input and validates handoff state strictly when it arrives as standalone entries — but a `JournalEntry::Checkpoint`'s `transfers` list is installed verbatim with none of those checks. A journal whose checkpoint carries duplicate handoff sides, a non-advancing import epoch, or a transfer event that claims a sequence/participant is restored successfully, while the identical facts as standalone entries are refused. The checkpoint path is exactly the path compaction produces, so this is the durable-state trust boundary for the region-seam handoff state added in #3870 phase 1 (PR #3922).

## Evidence (current main c1675d64)

Standalone arms validate (core.rs restore):

- `EntityExported` arm (core.rs:322-330): refuses when `source_event.sequence != 0 || source_event.participant_id != 0` ("journal export event claims a sequence"), and refuses a second export with the same `handoff_id` ("journal exports handoff … twice").
- `EntityImported` arm (core.rs:363-375): same event check, plus `new_owner_epoch == prior_owner_epoch + 1` ("does not advance the owner epoch"), plus the duplicate-import refusal.

Checkpoint arm (core.rs:502-504):

```rust
// A checkpoint comes first in its journal, so its
// transfer list is the whole active-handoff state.
core.handoff_transfers = transfers.unwrap_or_default();
```

No duplicate check, no epoch check, no transfer-event check, no bound. (The same arm does validate the checkpoint's `execution_profile`, `caps_ceiling`, and schedule agreement — transfers are the unvalidated remainder.)

Verified this run with a laptop probe calling the real `WorldCore::restore` (transient integration test in the laptop clone `~/git/code` at c1675d64, `pkgs/id/tests/probe_ckpt_transfers.rs`, since removed; log at `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneA-ckpttransfers/run.log`; sandbox and laptop `core.rs`/`mod.rs` md5-identical):

- CONTROL standalone duplicate export → Err "journal exports handoff "h1" twice"
- CONTROL standalone import epoch 5 → 5 → Err "does not advance the owner epoch"
- CONTROL standalone export event sequence 7 / participant 9 → Err "journal export event claims a sequence"
- CONTROL standalone valid import 5 → 6 → Ok
- CASE checkpoint, one valid export transfer → Ok
- CASE checkpoint, duplicate export transfers (same `handoff_id`) → **Ok** (expected Err)
- CASE checkpoint, import transfer epoch 5 → 5 → **Ok** (expected Err)
- CASE checkpoint, export transfer event sequence 7 / participant 9 → **Ok** (expected Err)

## Why it matters

Restore is the journal's trust boundary everywhere else in this function: forged `Issued` entries for participant 0 (#2972), duplicate issues, out-of-bounds delegation expiry, unknown caps, and schedule disagreement are all refused at restore, precisely so a corrupt or crafted journal cannot resurrect state the live writers would never produce. Checkpoint-carried handoff state is the exception. Duplicate export records break the dedupe invariant the coordinator phases of #3870 rely on (an exact retry returns the existing receipt; two export sides for one `handoff_id` make that ambiguous), a non-advancing import epoch defeats the epoch fencing the design (#2818 §3) uses to stop a stale source region from re-owning an entity, and a transfer event claiming a sequence/participant violates the host-event invariant replay assumes. Because compaction rewrites the journal behind a checkpoint, any bad transfer state that ever reaches a checkpoint is laundered into the canonical durable form.

## Acceptance criteria

- `WorldCore::restore` applies the same validation to checkpoint-carried transfers as to standalone `EntityExported`/`EntityImported` entries: no duplicate (handoff_id, direction) pair, import records advance the owner epoch (`new_owner_epoch == prior_owner_epoch + 1`), export records carry no `new_owner_epoch`, and each transfer's `event` has `sequence == 0` and `participant_id == 0`.
- Restore refuses (with a clear error naming the handoff) a checkpoint exhibiting any of: duplicate export side, duplicate import side, non-advancing import epoch, or a transfer event claiming a sequence/participant — matching the standalone-arm error style.
- New world tests cover each refused checkpoint case plus a control: a checkpoint with valid export and import transfers restores, and the checkpoint/compaction round-trip test from PR #3922 still passes.
- Existing world/journal tests still pass; no change to the journal wire format or to what `checkpoint_entries` writes for live (valid) state.

## Dedup notes

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-a. Searched open + closed issues for checkpoint/handoff/restore validation: #3900/#3870 (the phase-1 implementation and its umbrella — this is a validation gap in that landed code, not one of the phase 2-5 implementation issues #3901-#3904), #3911 (WaitingPool::restore duplicate guards — different type), #3373 (journal restore under revoked parent — different invariant). None covers checkpoint-carried transfer validation.

**Failing on main** (verified 2026-11-01, lane D worker): `store_traits::tests::test_the_lock_has_no_sqlite_with_logsync_wired` in pkgs/id panics at `src/store_traits.rs:701`:

```
sqlx-sqlite depends on libsqlite3-sys: SQLite is back in the shipped build (see vendor/README.md)
```

**Evidence it is pre-existing, not a recent regression from the nearest merge:**
- The test reads only `pkgs/id/Cargo.lock` + `pkgs/id/Cargo.toml` (via `CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR`) and asserts no package outside the allow-list has a SQLite-family edge. The committed `Cargo.lock` at 33aefa7f (parent of the PR #3922 merge) already contains the `sqlx-sqlite` 0.9.0 package whose dependencies include `libsqlite3-sys` — the exact edge the test rejects (the `sqlx` facade's optional backend packages are recorded in the lock even when inactive).
- The test FAILS identically at 33aefa7f and at post-merge main (876b4028d) in clean worktrees on the laptop; PR #3922 changed zero Cargo files.
- Repro: `cargo test -p id --lib test_the_lock_has_no_sqlite_with_logsync_wired` in pkgs/id at either commit → 0 passed, 1 failed, panic at store_traits.rs:701.

**What a fix looks like:** either the test's allow-list learns the sqlx facade shape (a package whose sqlite edge is optional/inactive in the default-feature graph — the test's second half already asks `cargo tree` for the shipped graph, so the lock-edge half may need the same treatment for `sqlx` → `sqlx-sqlite`), or the lock is regenerated so the inactive backend packages are absent. The test's own doc comment says the lock records optional edges even when inactive, which is exactly the sqlx-sqlite case.

Related: #3160 (closed) previously tracked lib-test failures on main including a rusqlite guard.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `cargo test -p id --lib test_the_lock_has_no_sqlite_with_logsync_wired` passes on current main.
- [ ] The fix addresses the lockfile-vs-allow-list mismatch directly (allow-list learns the sqlx facade's inactive backend packages, or the lock no longer records them) without weakening the test's actual guarantee: no SQLite edge in the shipped build's active dependency graph.
- [ ] The test still fails if a real SQLite dependency is introduced into the shipped graph (negative check).

title: id(repl): peek accepts --head-only with --tail-only and --chars with --words — one of each pair is silently discarded, unlike the CLI which rejects both pairs

body:
## Problem

The REPL `peek` parser accepts flag pairs that are mutually exclusive in effect, and one of each pair is then silently discarded — the exact failure the CLI version of the same command already rejects with clap `conflicts_with`:

- `parse_peek_args` (pkgs/id/src/repl/runner.rs:1235) sets `peek_opts.head_only` (runner.rs:1299) and `peek_opts.tail_only` (runner.rs:1301) independently, and likewise `chars` (runner.rs:1302-1303) and `words`. Its only validations are `FindArgs::validate_result_limits` (first/last, zero limits — #3029/#3059) and the `--lines 0` check (runner.rs:1314-1318). Nothing rejects `--head-only --tail-only` or `--chars --words` together.
- The printers are if/else-if chains, so one flag wins silently: `print_peek` (runner.rs:1347-1353) dispatches `chars` before `words`; `print_peek_lines` checks `head_only` (runner.rs:1385) before `tail_only`, and the chars/words printers repeat the same head-before-tail order. With both set, `--tail-only` / `--words` have no effect and no warning.
- The CLI `Peek` command declares the house rule for this same struct: `head_only` `conflicts_with = "tail_only"`, `chars` `conflicts_with = "words"`, `words` `conflicts_with = "chars"` (pkgs/id/src/cli.rs:810-819), so `id peek --head-only --tail-only …` is a loud parse error while `peek --head-only --tail-only …` at the REPL prompt silently shows the head.

## Evidence (this run, main 5b2eca7a)

- Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneA-replpeek/` (laptop clone at the same HEAD; runner.rs md5 `c73b99fe9e4644d66ca3a6763edbbb00` on both clones) with `parse_peek_args`, `FindArgs::validate_result_limits`, and `print_peek` copied verbatim (only `anyhow::bail!` mechanically rewritten to a `return Err`, and the leaf printers stubbed to name the mode; the lines stub preserves the head-before-tail branch order of runner.rs:1385ff):
  - `parse_peek_args(&["q", "--head-only", "--tail-only"])` returns Ok with `head_only=true tail_only=true`; dispatch renders HEAD-ONLY — the tail request vanishes.
  - `parse_peek_args(&["q", "--chars", "--words"])` returns Ok with `chars=true words=true`; the verbatim `print_peek` dispatch renders CHARS mode — the words request vanishes.
  - Control: `--tail-only` alone dispatches TAIL-ONLY, so each flag works on its own; only the combinations are silently misread.
- Existing REPL tests pin each flag alone (`test_parse_peek_args_head_only` / `_tail_only` / `_chars` / `_words`, runner.rs:1834-1863) but no test passes a conflicting pair.

## Why it matters

A REPL user who types `peek --head-only --tail-only report` (or a pasted command line that assembles both flags) gets a head-only preview presented as if both instructions were honoured — plausible-looking output with the wrong semantics, and a behavioural split from the CLI, where the same combination is an error. The codebase's own precedents (#3029 first/last, #3059 zero limits) put this rejection in the parser, right next to the existing `--lines 0` bail in the same function.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Triage confirms on current main: `parse_peek_args` (runner.rs:1235) accepts both `--head-only --tail-only` and `--chars --words`, and the printers' if/else-if order (runner.rs:1347, 1385) silently discards `--tail-only` / `--words`.
- [ ] Passing `--head-only` with `--tail-only`, or `--chars` with `--words`, to REPL `peek` is a loud parse error from `parse_peek_args` (matching the CLI `conflicts_with` pairs at cli.rs:810-819 and the `--lines 0` bail style in the same function), before any search or fetch work starts.
- [ ] Single-flag behaviour is unchanged: each of `--head-only`, `--tail-only`, `--chars`, `--words` alone renders exactly what it renders today.
- [ ] Regression tests pin both conflicting pairs as errors and at least one single-flag case per pair as still accepted (extending the existing `test_parse_peek_args_*` tests in runner.rs).

Distinct from: #3029 (first/last conflict — CLI clap plus the REPL find/search parser's `validate_result_limits`, which `parse_peek_args` already calls; this issue is the two peek-only pairs that neither that fix nor the CLI covers on the REPL path), #3714 (value-flags consuming the next flag as their value), #2274 (unknown/mistyped flags swallowed by the REPL find/peek parsers).

title: repo-archive stored twice in R2 (~24 GB): raw bundle/tar pass + daily restic of a static directory

labels.name: status/needs-triage

body:
## Finding (R2 review, 2026-11-01)

The laptop's `~/repo-archive` directory is stored **twice** in the R2 bucket `supabase-backups`, ~24 GB total for ~13.5 GiB of content:

1. `repo-archive/` — a one-off manual upload pass from 2026-10-27: `repo-archive-2026-10-27.bundle` (3.94 GB) + `repo-archive-worktree-2026-10-27.tar` (10.63 GB) + .sha256 files. The pass **did complete** (both payloads and checksums are present; this was unverified until this review).
2. `restic-repo-archive/` — the daily restic job (`repo-archive-backup`, ~05:15, script `~/tools/repo-archive-backup.sh` on amd): 9.46 GB stored, 7 snapshots, retention keep-last 7 / keep-daily 7 / keep-weekly 4 with prune — healthy and declared.

Two further observations:

- The directory is **static**: all 7 restic snapshots are byte-identical at 13.509 GiB. A daily snapshot cadence buys nothing over weekly/on-change for a frozen archive (dedup keeps the cost near zero, but the schedule and watchdog surface are real).
- The raw bundle/tar are the only *restic-independent* copies in R2; the restic snapshots are the only *versioned* copies. Nothing was deleted in the review — which form is canonical is a decision, not a cleanup.

Related: #1849 (laptop backup coverage; its "timer has never fired" premise is stale — the timer is flake-declared and fires daily now), #1854 (backup completion contract).

## Ask

Designate one canonical R2 form for repo-archive:

- If restic is canonical: retire the raw `repo-archive/` prefix (14.57 GB) once a restore from restic is proven, or keep the raw bundle only (drop the 10.63 GB worktree tar, which restic covers better).
- If the raw form is canonical: drop the daily restic cadence to weekly, or exclude R2 from that job (it already writes local + Drive copies).

Either way the ~24 GB should become ~9–14 GB with no loss of restorability.

## Acceptance criteria
- One canonical R2 form for `~/repo-archive` is designated and the decision is recorded on this issue (restic snapshots, or the raw bundle/tar pass).
- A restore from the designated canonical form is proven (restic restore check or bundle/tar checksum verification) *before* anything is retired.
- The non-canonical copy is retired accordingly (raw `repo-archive/` prefix removed, or the restic cadence dropped to weekly / R2 excluded), bringing the R2 total from ~24 GB to roughly 9–14 GB.
- Restorability is unchanged after the cleanup: the surviving form verifies clean (checksums / `restic check`).

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

body:
# mcpx(source): naturalLess silently drops digit runs that overflow int64 — directory concatenation order is wrong or arbitrary for large-numbered fragments

## Evidence (verified this run, main @ fec6a9df)

`pkgs/mcpx/internal/source/source.go:210-235` (`naturalLess`), used by `sortNatural` (:206) to order the files `Resolve` (:167) concatenates for a directory read:

```go
an, aerr := strconv.ParseInt(a[as:ai], 10, 64)   // :222
bn, berr := strconv.ParseInt(b[bs:bi], 10, 64)   // :223
if aerr == nil && berr == nil && an != bn {
    return an < bn
}
continue
```

When either digit run overflows `int64` (>19 digits, or 19 digits above 9223372036854775807), the numeric comparison is silently skipped and comparison resumes *after* the digit runs — so the number that was supposed to control the order is ignored entirely and the suffix (or nothing) decides.

Laptop probe (verbatim copy of `naturalLess`/`isDigit`/`sortNatural` from source.go, md5 `ea6a8c5521476daf62b8a0e089104007`; probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneA-naturalless/` on the laptop):

- `x = "f99999999999999999999999z"` (23-digit run) vs `y = "f100000000000000000000000a"` (24-digit run): numerically x < y, but `less(x,y)=false`, `less(y,x)=true` — **actively inverted** (the suffix `z` vs `a` decides). End-to-end: `sortNatural([y, x])` returns `[y, x]`.
- `p = "f99999999999999999999999"` vs `q = "f100000000000000000000000"`: numerically p < q, but `less` is false in both directions — the pair compares **equal**, so their concatenation order is arbitrary (sort.Slice is not stable).
- `r = "f9999999999999999999"` (19 nines, overflows) vs `s = "f8999999999999999999"` (parses): numerically r > s, but `less(s,r)=false` — again equal both ways. One overflowing side is enough.
- Control: `less("2-b.ts","10-c.ts")=true`, `less("10-c.ts","2-b.ts")=false` — ordinary numbers order correctly, which is why the existing test (`TestADirectoryIsConcatenatedInNaturalOrder`, 1/2/10 only) passes.

## Why it matters

`sortNatural` exists for exactly one job, per its own comment (:200-205): directory concatenation serves "a set of fragments numbered to control their order". A fragment set numbered with large counters — timestamps, epoch-nanosecond names, long zero-padded sequences past 19 digits — silently concatenates in the wrong or an arbitrary order, producing a merged source text whose content differs from what the numbering says, with no error anywhere. The failure is silent and the comparison is not even a consistent order for the equal-treated pairs.

## Acceptance criteria

- Digit runs of arbitrary length compare numerically (e.g. compare by trimmed length, then lexically, instead of `ParseInt`), including runs longer than 19 digits and mixed overflow/non-overflow pairs.
- `naturalLess` remains a strict weak ordering for these inputs: exactly one of `less(a,b)` / `less(b,a)` holds when the numeric values differ.
- New tests in `pkgs/mcpx/internal/source` cover: both-overflow runs with differing suffixes, both-overflow runs with no suffix, a one-side-overflow pair, and an end-to-end directory concatenation in that order — alongside the existing 1/2/10 test.
- Existing source package tests still pass.

body:
## Summary

`validateProjectConfigs` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/project-config.ts:659) is the registry's only guardrail — "strict in tests, never throws at render" — but two of its checks are looser than the code that consumes the values, so a registry entry can pass validation clean and still break or misrender a /program page:

1. **Refs the validator accepts, `parseRef`/`refUrl` throw on.** The validator's `REF_PATTERN` (project-config.ts:641) is `/^[^/\s]+\/[^#\s]+#\d+$/`. The canonical parser (model.ts:452-456) is `/^([\w.-]+\/[\w.-]+)#(\d+)$/` — exactly one slash, `[\w.-]` segments. Refs such as `a/b/c#12`, `a$/b#12`, and `a+b/c#3` pass validation with zero errors, but `parseRef` throws `not a repo-qualified ref` and so does `refUrl`. Config tracked refs are rendered through `refUrl` (render.ts:5459, project detail page) and resolved through the shared ref set (`allProjectRefs`, project-config.ts:843), so one such entry turns a green registry test into a render-time throw.
2. **`openIssuesAsOf` is shape-only.** The check at project-config.ts:696 is `/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/`, so `2026-02-30`, `2026-13-01`, `2026-00-00`, and `2026-04-31` all pass. The value is rendered verbatim as the snapshot's date (render.ts:5462: "Open issues (GitHub search, \<openIssuesAsOf\>)"), so an impossible date ships as the stated provenance of the count. The same package already has the real-calendar helper for exactly this — `isCalendarDate` (derive.ts:75), used by `rowDate`/`ymdLabel` — the validator just doesn't use it.

## Evidence (verified this run, main e764f4e7)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneB-projcfg/probe.ts`, importing the real `validateProjectConfigs`, `parseRef`, and `refUrl` from the laptop checkout (project-config.ts sha256 acd7cbe0…, model.ts sha256 f987be93…, both matching sandbox main e764f4e7):

```
asOf 2026-02-30: errors=[]
asOf 2026-13-01: errors=[]
asOf 2026-00-00: errors=[]
asOf 2026-04-31: errors=[]
asOf control 2026-02-28: []
ref a/b/c#12: validationErrors=[] parseRef=THROW: not a repo-qualified ref: a/b/c#12 refUrl=THROW
ref a$/b#12: validationErrors=[] parseRef=THROW: not a repo-qualified ref: a$/b#12 refUrl=THROW
ref a+b/c#3: validationErrors=[] parseRef=THROW: not a repo-qualified ref: a+b/c#3 refUrl=THROW
ref developing-today/code#1: validationErrors=[] parseRef=ok refUrl=https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/1
```

## Why it matters

The registry is edited by hand as the documented way to add a project ("Adding a project is a config change here"). The validator plus its test (`validateProjectConfigs(PROJECT_CONFIGS)` must equal `[]`, test/program.test.ts:171) are the whole safety net for those edits. A check that disagrees with the consumer gives false confidence in both directions the fleet has already been bitten by: #2485 is the same failure shape one layer down (bad refs pass a gate, `refUrl` throws at render), filed for feed data; this is the static-registry instance of it.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validateProjectConfigs` rejects any ref that `parseRef` (model.ts) would reject — ideally by sharing one pattern/parser instead of a second hand-rolled regex — including extra path segments and characters outside `[\w.-]` in either segment.
- `openIssuesAsOf` validation requires a real calendar date (month 01-12, day valid for the month/year, leap years correct), reusing `isCalendarDate` from derive.ts or an equivalent check; `2026-02-30`, `2026-13-01`, `2026-00-00`, `2026-04-31` produce errors, `2026-02-28` and `2024-02-29` do not.
- Regression tests in test/program.test.ts alongside the existing "validation catches duplicates and malformed entries" cases; the shipped `PROJECT_CONFIGS` still validate to `[]`.
- No render-path changes needed: this is the validator agreeing with its consumers.

Related: #2485 (feed taskRefs, same throw-at-render shape, different gate and data path).

body:
## Problem

`aggregateBillingUsage` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/sources/github-billing.ts) validates each billing item's date and numeric fields (#2493), but two element-level gaps remain at the same boundary — the items array itself and the one field derived by parsing a free-text SKU:

1. **A `null` (or otherwise non-object) item crashes the whole month's collection.** `fetchUsageItems` (scripts/collect-github-billing.ts) returns `usageItems` cast unchecked (`items as BillingUsageItem[]`), and the aggregator loop dereferences the item immediately: `typeof item.date` at github-billing.ts:91. A `null` element throws `TypeError: null is not an object (evaluating 'item.date')`. `main()` calls `aggregateBillingUsage(items)` before anything is written (collect-github-billing.ts:74), so one bad element discards every well-formed item in the month — the exact whole-collection loss #2493's fix comment says must not happen.

2. **The Codespaces core multiplier parsed from the SKU is never range-checked.** `codespacesCoreMultiplier` (github-billing.ts:72-76) returns `Number(m[1])` for any `(\d+)\s*-core` capture, and :109 multiplies the quantity by it verbatim:
   - `Codespaces 0-core` → multiplier 0 → 5 real Codespaces hours aggregate to 0, and because zero aggregates emit no record, the day's codespaces-hours silently vanish (gross/net for the same row are still counted).
   - `Codespaces 999999999999999999999999999999-core` → multiplier 1e30 → a 2-hour row aggregates to `2e+30` codespaces-hours and `recordsFromBillingUsage` emits a snapshot record with `value: 2e+30` — finite, so it passes the collector's `isSnapshotRecord` filter (collect-github-billing.ts:84) and is stored as measured usage.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `d4e19229`)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneB-ghbilling-items/` running the verbatim `src/sources/github-billing.ts` (sha256 ce946a38…) and `src/validate.ts` (sha256 1f72539a…), with `dayTs` stubbed to its real one-line implementation; full output in `probe.log`:

- Control: `Codespaces 4-core` × 2 h + Actions 30 min → `codespacesHours: 8, actionsMinutes: 30` — correct.
- `[null, ...control items]` → `aggregateBillingUsage` throws `TypeError: null is not an object (evaluating 'item.date')`; nothing aggregates.
- `Codespaces 0-core`, quantity 5 → `codespacesHours: 0` (gross/net 1/1 still counted).
- `Codespaces 999…-core` (30 digits), quantity 2 → aggregate `codespacesHours: 2e+30`; derived record `{metricId: "codespaces-hours", value: 2e+30, unit: "hours"}`.
- A string element (`"x"`) is skipped harmlessly — the crash is specific to `null`/non-object elements whose property access throws.

## Why it matters

This collector is the GitHub billing source of truth for the usage hub: its records are stamped at the usage day and deduped, so a poisoned `2e+30` record is durable, and a crashed month is a silent gap (the collector runs daily; the failure looks like a gh/API error, not bad data). #2493 established the contract for this exact function — validate at the boundary so one bad item can neither be stored as usage nor discard the whole collection — and these are the two inputs that fix did not cover: the element itself, and the SKU-derived multiplier.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `aggregateBillingUsage` never throws on a non-object element (`null`, number, array): such elements are skipped (and ideally counted/logged by the collector), and the remaining items aggregate normally.
- [ ] `codespacesCoreMultiplier` returns a plausible positive core count only (real Codespaces SKUs are small integers — e.g. 1–64): a 0, absurd, or non-finite multiplier falls back to face value (×1, matching the existing no-parseable-count rule) rather than zeroing or exploding the row.
- [ ] Regression tests pin: `[null, validItem]` aggregates the valid item; a `0-core` SKU does not erase the row's hours; a huge-digit `-core` SKU cannot produce a codespaces-hours value beyond the plausible bound; the control case (4-core × 2 h = 8) is unchanged.

## Dedup

- #2493 (CLOSED) validated item dates and quantity/amount fields in this same function — it did not check element objectness or the SKU multiplier (its acceptance list covers date/quantity/gross/discount/net only).
- #3419 (OPEN) is the collector script's `--year/--month/--user` CLI arguments — different input, different failure.
- #2553 / #2571 / #2508 (OPEN) are other mappers' range checks (turso, gather-map, saas-extract) — no overlap with github-billing.ts.
- Searches for `codespacesCoreMultiplier` / "core multiplier" / "github-billing" over open+closed issues returned no match for either defect.

body:
## Problem

In `pkgs/id`, `WorldCore::restore` validates a journal checkpoint's events with a plain `+ 1` — the one sequence-consecutiveness check in the file that does not use the checked/saturating arithmetic every sibling check uses — so a checkpoint whose penultimate event carries sequence `u64::MAX` behaves differently in each build profile, and neither behaviour is the intended rejection:

- **Debug / test builds** (overflow checks on — `pkgs/id/Cargo.toml`'s `[profile.dev]`/`[profile.test]` set no `overflow-checks` override, so the default applies): the check **panics** with "attempt to add with overflow" instead of returning restore's `journal checkpoint events are out of order` error.
- **Release builds** (overflow checks off): `u64::MAX + 1` wraps to `0`, so a checkpoint whose events run `[…, u64::MAX, 0]` **passes** the consecutiveness gate as if MAX → 0 were a valid step (the trailing check `events.last().sequence == sequence` then anchors the checkpoint at sequence 0).

## Evidence (verified this run, main `51dee687`)

- `pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs:380-384` (the `JournalEntry::Checkpoint` arm of `restore`, `core.rs:138`; reached from journal load at `world_store.rs:380`):

  ```rust
  ensure!(
      events.last().is_none_or(|last| last.sequence == sequence)
          && events
              .windows(2)
              .all(|pair| pair[1].sequence == pair[0].sequence + 1),
      "journal checkpoint events are out of order"
  );
  ```

- `WorldEvent.sequence` is `u64` (`pkgs/id/src/world/mod.rs:319`).
- Every sibling sequence check in the same file uses saturating or checked arithmetic: `core.rs:335` and `core.rs:1038` use `saturating_add(1)` for the same "next sequence" comparison; `core.rs:220`, `:885`, `:1027`, `:1148` use `checked_add(1)`. Line 383's plain `+ 1` is the lone exception.
- Laptop probe (verbatim predicate, source md5 `607e68c2` in both copies; `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneA-ckptseq/` on the laptop):
  - `rustc -C overflow-checks=on`: `[1,2,3] → true`, `[1,3] → false`, `[MAX-1,MAX] → true`, and the `[MAX,0]` case **panics** — `attempt to add with overflow`, exit 101.
  - `rustc -O -C overflow-checks=off`: `[MAX,0] → true` (wrap accepted as consecutive), `[MAX,5] → false`.

## Why it matters

`restore` is the integrity gate for a world's journal on load: its `ensure!` checks are what stand between a damaged or crafted journal file and the world state rebuilt from it. A gate that panics in one profile and silently accepts a wrapped sequence in another is neither — the panic turns a corrupt-checkpoint error into a crash of the loading process, and the wrap-accept lets a checkpoint claim a sequence chain no writer can produce (writers advance via the saturating/checked paths). The fix is also the file's own established convention, so this is a consistency defect, not a design question.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The checkpoint consecutiveness check uses checked arithmetic (e.g. `pair[0].sequence.checked_add(1) == Some(pair[1].sequence)`, or the file's `saturating_add(1)` convention — either makes MAX → anything non-consecutive): a checkpoint with a penultimate `u64::MAX` sequence is rejected with the existing "journal checkpoint events are out of order" error in **both** debug and release profiles, with no panic.
- [ ] A regression test restores a checkpoint whose events are `[…, u64::MAX, 0]` (checkpoint `sequence` 0) and asserts the out-of-order error; ordinary consecutive checkpoints (including `[MAX-1, MAX]` as the final pair) still restore.
- [ ] No other restore validation changes behaviour; existing `world` / `world_store` restore tests pass.

Distinct from #2396 (CLI `--seconds`/`--timeout-secs` added to an `Instant` — different site, different input path).
