body:
## Problem

`pkgs/pkarr-worker/deploy.mjs` performs **no argument validation**: it reads only the two spellings it knows and silently ignores everything else on the command line. A misspelled `--dry-run`, the conventional `--deploy-version=<id>` equals form, or any stray flag is dropped without a word — and the script proceeds to make a **real production deploy**. For a deploy tool, an ignored argument is not a cosmetic papercut: the operator believes they asked for a preview (or a rollback to a named version) and instead ships HEAD at 100%.

This is the sibling of #3252 (a *known* flag ignored on one path): here the flag is never recognized at all, on *every* path.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `f4f800e7`)

- Arg parsing is two lookups and nothing else (`deploy.mjs:39-45`):

  ```js
  const args = process.argv.slice(2);
  const dryRun = args.includes("--dry-run");
  const deployVersionAt = args.indexOf("--deploy-version");
  const deployVersion = deployVersionAt >= 0 ? args[deployVersionAt + 1] : null;
  if (deployVersionAt >= 0 && !deployVersion) {
    throw new Error("--deploy-version needs a version id");
  }
  ```

  No loop over `args`, no rejection of unrecognized entries. `--deploy-version=<id>` does not match the exact-string `indexOf`, so `deployVersion` stays `null` and the script falls through to the deploy-HEAD flow. A typo'd `--dry-rnu` leaves `dryRun === false`.

- Laptop probe (sha-matched copy of `deploy.mjs`, sha256 `805d407348729bf00a6010a5502b66455d66c559d79d4659a786faf067d80ff9` — same hash as current main; stub `cf`/`bws`/`git` on PATH logging argv, `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` stubbed, stub `cf workers get` failing so the bootstrap path runs; probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-deployargs/` on the laptop):

  - Control `node deploy.mjs --dry-run` → cf log: `cf -q deploy --worker pkarr --tag git-aaaaaaaaaaaa --message … --dry-run`; exit 0; "dry run: config builds, nothing uploaded".
  - `node deploy.mjs --dry-rnu` (one transposed letter) → cf log: `cf -q deploy --worker pkarr --tag git-aaaaaaaaaaaa --message …` — **no `--dry-run`**: a real `cf deploy` call. The run then continued to `workers versions list` and stopped only because the stub returned no version; against the real account it would have proceeded to create the 100% deployment.
  - `node deploy.mjs --deploy-version=v-rollback-123` → the named rollback version is never mentioned again; cf log shows the same real bootstrap deploy of HEAD (`git-aaaaaaaaaaaa`). The operator asked to roll back and instead deployed current HEAD.
  - `node deploy.mjs --prod` (unknown flag) → silently ignored; same real deploy of HEAD.

## Why it matters

`deploy.mjs` is the one sanctioned path for shipping and rolling back the pkarr Worker (#1828 standard). Its safety rests entirely on the operator typing exactly `--dry-run` or exactly `--deploy-version <id>` — one typo or the ubiquitous `--flag=value` habit converts a preview or a rollback into a live deploy of whatever HEAD happens to be, with no warning that anything was ignored. Tools that perform irreversible outward actions must fail closed on input they do not understand.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Any argument that is not `--dry-run`, `--deploy-version <id>`, or `--deploy-version=<id>` (if the equals form is supported) aborts before any `bws`/`cf` call, with an error naming the offending argument and the usage.
- [ ] `--deploy-version=<id>` either works identically to the space form or is refused as above — it must never fall through to deploying HEAD.
- [ ] A misspelled safety flag (e.g. `--dry-rnu`) can no longer produce a real deploy: covered by the unknown-argument refusal, with a regression test/probe case.
- [ ] The known-good invocations in the header comment (`deploy.mjs [--dry-run]`, `deploy.mjs --deploy-version <id>`) behave exactly as today (including #3252's dry-run semantics once that lands).
- [ ] Verification is reproducible with stub `cf`/`bws` on PATH: unknown/equals-form arguments make zero `cf` calls.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for pkarr-worker deploy argument handling. #3252 covers `--dry-run` being ignored *on the `--deploy-version` path* (both flags recognized, one branch drops the check); #3261 is `RETENTION_SECONDS` parsing in `src/index.ts`; #1828/#1829 are the deployment standard and the original implementation. No issue covers unrecognized/misspelled arguments or the `--deploy-version=<id>` form being silently ignored.

title: pkarr-worker(retention): RETENTION_SECONDS is parsed with a bare Number() and no guard — '0'/'7d'/'  ' schedule the deletion alarm at/before now (or NaN), so stored packets vanish right after a 204, and '1e9' never expires

body:
## Summary

`pkgs/pkarr-worker`: `RETENTION_SECONDS` is parsed with a bare `Number(...)` and no validity guard in `PkarrStore.putPacket` (`src/index.ts:67-68`), and the resulting timestamp is handed straight to `setAlarm`, whose handler unconditionally deletes the stored record. Any value that is not a plain positive decimal silently breaks retention for every record in that object:

- `"0"`, `"-1"`, or a whitespace-only `"  "` (truthy, so the `|| "604800"` fallback does not fire; `Number("  ")` is 0) → the deletion alarm is scheduled at or before now, so the record a PUT just stored (and returned 204 for) is deleted again almost immediately; later GETs 404.
- `"7d"` or any non-numeric spelling → `retentionMs` is `NaN` and the alarm time is `NaN` — the expiry behaviour is whatever the runtime does with an invalid alarm time, instead of the documented 7 days.
- `"1e9"` → silently reinterpreted as 1,000,000,000 seconds (~31,700 years): records effectively never expire, contradicting the header contract that "records expire after RETENTION_SECONDS without refresh".

The same file already shows the house pattern for exactly this: `DNS_TTL` is parsed in `handleDoh` (`src/index.ts:224-226`) with `Number.isFinite(ttl) && ttl > 0 ? ttl : 30` — a guarded parse with a sane fallback. The retention parse has no equivalent guard.

## Evidence (main `f4f800e7`)

- `src/index.ts:67-68` — `const retentionMs = Number(this.env.RETENTION_SECONDS || "604800") * 1000; await this.ctx.storage.setAlarm(Date.now() + retentionMs);` No `isFinite`, no positivity check, no fallback beyond the empty-string `||`.
- `src/index.ts:86-88` — `alarm()` runs `DELETE FROM record WHERE id = 1` unconditionally, so a past-due alarm removes the current record, including one stored seconds earlier.
- `src/index.ts:224-226` — the guarded `DNS_TTL` contrast in the same file.
- `wrangler.jsonc:18` sets `"RETENTION_SECONDS": "604800"` — the value is operator-edited config (a var, not code), so a units slip (`"7d"`, `"604800 "` variants, `"0"` while testing) reaches the parse unvalidated.
- Distinct from #3252 (deploy.mjs `--dry-run` on the deploy-version path — deploy tooling, not the Worker's runtime config) and #1828/#1829 (the deployment standard this Worker pilots).

## Verified (laptop probe, exact expressions from `index.ts:67`)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneA-pkarr-retention/` on the laptop — `src/index.ts` sha256 `a751bb4d…` identical in the laptop clone and the sandbox checkout at main `f4f800e7`; the probe evaluates the verbatim `:67` expression:

```
undefined  -> retentionMs = 604800000     | alarm in past / invalid: false
"604800"   -> retentionMs = 604800000     | alarm in past / invalid: false
"0"        -> retentionMs = 0             | alarm in past / invalid: true
"-1"       -> retentionMs = -1000         | alarm in past / invalid: true
"7d"       -> retentionMs = NaN           | alarmAt = NaN
"  "       -> retentionMs = 0             | alarm in past / invalid: true
"1e9"      -> retentionMs = 1000000000000 | ~31,700-year retention
"3600.5"   -> retentionMs = 3600500       | fractional seconds accepted silently
```

(The Durable Object alarm itself was not executed — no node_modules on the laptop for the workers vitest pool; the claim verified here is the parse layer plus the unconditional-delete alarm handler in the source. A past-due `setAlarm` firing promptly is documented Durable Object behaviour.)

## Why it matters

Retention is the only expiry mechanism for stored pkarr packets: the store has one row per key and `getPacket` performs no age check, so the alarm is the whole contract. A config slip therefore fails in the worst two directions at once — live records vanishing right after a successful publish (clients see 204, then 404), or records never expiring at all — with no error anywhere: `putPacket` returns `"stored"` in every case above except a possible runtime throw on the NaN alarm.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `RETENTION_SECONDS` is parsed with the same discipline as `DNS_TTL`: a non-finite, non-positive, or non-plain-decimal value falls back to the 604800s default (or is rejected loudly at startup), never reaching `setAlarm` as 0/negative/NaN.
- [ ] With `RETENTION_SECONDS` set to `"0"`, `"7d"`, and `"  "` (one test each), a PUT still stores the packet and a subsequent GET returns it, with the alarm scheduled ~7 days out.
- [ ] Scientific/fractional spellings (`"1e9"`, `"3600.5"`) are either rejected-to-default or explicitly documented as accepted — not silently reinterpreted.
- [ ] Regression tests in the workers vitest suite cover the bad-value cases alongside the existing `"604800"` behaviour, which is unchanged.

body:
## Summary

`github-backup(fetch)`: the chronic-failure alarm in `infra/github-backup/bin/fetch_mirrors.py` does not implement its own contract. The module docstring promises: "A repo failing on 3 distinct days **in a row** makes the run exit non-zero." The implementation instead counts every distinct failure day **since the last success**, with no consecutiveness check and no expiry: `fail_days` is only ever appended to (one entry per calendar day) and is only cleared by a successful fetch. A repo that fails once in January, once in February and once in March — never on consecutive days — is declared a chronic failure, and from then on **every** daily run exits 1 until that repo next succeeds, even on days when nothing failed.

## Evidence (main `f4f800e7`)

- `fetch_mirrors.py:1-9` — module docstring: "Failures are appended to fetch.log. A repo failing on 3 distinct days in a row makes the run exit non-zero (so systemd shows the failure)."
- `fetch_mirrors.py:29-38` — on failure, `today` is appended to `st["fail_days"]` if not already present; the list is never pruned, windowed, or checked for consecutiveness. It is reset to `[]` only on success (`:31`).
- `fetch_mirrors.py:72-75` — the chronic test is purely `len(fail_days) >= 3` over the persisted `state.json`, and `main()` returns 1 if any repo qualifies. Because the list persists in `state.json`, once the count reaches 3 the exit-1 result latches across all later runs until a success clears it.
- Distinct from #3250 (a fetch timeout raises out of `main()` and is never recorded at all — the opposite failure-recording defect), #3240 (non-atomic state writes), #3219 (drainer ack on returned failures). This issue is only about what a *recorded* failure day counts toward.

## Verified (laptop probe, real `fetch_mirrors.py`)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneA-fetchchronic/` on the laptop — the real `fetch_mirrors.py` from the laptop clone (sha256 `f0115270…`, identical to the sandbox checkout at main `f4f800e7`), a real bare mirror for the `valid_mirror` sanity check, then the fetch stubbed to fail (rc=1) with the calendar stubbed to three non-consecutive days:

```
valid_mirror(real bare) = True
2026-01-05 -> fail fail_days = ['2026-01-05']
2026-02-10 -> fail fail_days = ['2026-01-05', '2026-02-10']
2026-03-20 -> fail fail_days = ['2026-01-05', '2026-02-10', '2026-03-20']
chronic_condition(main's exit-1 test) = True
```

Three failures spaced weeks/months apart — never 3 days in a row — trip the chronic condition.

## Why it matters

The exit code is the systemd-visible alarm for the daily mirror fetch. An alarm that fires for intermittent, self-recovering flakiness (a laptop asleep one day in January, a network blip one day in February, a GitHub incident one day in March) and then stays latched trains the operator to ignore it — the exact failure mode a "3 days in a row" streak rule exists to prevent. Conversely the persisted count means the alarm's state depends on ancient history in `state.json`, not on the repo's current health.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Chronic means a streak: a repo counts as chronic only when its failures fall on 3 consecutive calendar days (per the docstring), or the docstring and implementation are changed together to a clearly stated window rule (e.g. 3 failures within N days) — code and contract must agree.
- [ ] Failure days that fall outside the streak/window no longer count: failures on 2026-01-05, 2026-02-10 and 2026-03-20 do not produce a chronic exit 1.
- [ ] A success still resets the streak, and 3 truly consecutive failure days still exit 1.
- [ ] Regression tests/probe cover: three non-consecutive failure days (no chronic), three consecutive failure days (chronic), failure–failure–success–failure–failure (no chronic), and the no-failure control unchanged.

title: github-backup(fetch): a git fetch that hits the 3600s timeout raises TimeoutExpired out of fetch_mirrors.main() — every later repo is skipped, no failure is recorded, and state.json/MANIFEST.json are never written

body:
## Summary

`github-backup(fetch)`: `fetch_repo` in `infra/github-backup/bin/fetch_mirrors.py` runs `git fetch` with `timeout=3600` and no `TimeoutExpired` handling — one hanging fetch raises out of `main()` and kills the whole run: every later repo is never attempted, no failure is recorded for the timed-out repo, `state.json` is never written (so the coalesce/fail stamps of repos already fetched in the same run are lost too), `fetch.log` gets no line, and `MANIFEST.json` is not rebuilt. The module's own contract — "Failures are appended to fetch.log. A repo failing on 3 distinct days in a row makes the run exit non-zero" — never applies to the slowest, most failure-prone failure mode: a timeout can recur daily forever and never count toward the chronic-failure exit, because it is never recorded as a failure at all.

## Evidence (main `8e4ef90e`)

- `fetch_mirrors.py:25-26` — `subprocess.run(["git", "-C", path, "fetch", "--all", "--prune"], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=3600, env=env)` with no `try`/`except` anywhere in the file. `subprocess.run` raises `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` on expiry.
- `fetch_mirrors.py:36-63` — `main()` loops over repos calling `fetch_repo` unguarded; `state.json` is written only after the loop (`:52-53`), the chronic check and summary print come after that, and `manifest_mod.build(root)` is called at `:54`. An exception anywhere in the loop skips all of it.
- Contrast the sibling driver: `clone_all.py:55-60` catches `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` explicitly and returns a recorded failure for that repo, so one repo's timeout never wedges the others.
- The same unguarded call reaches the 5-minute drainer: `drain_queue.py:59` calls `fetch_mirrors.fetch_repo(root, repo, state)` with no handling, so a fetch timeout there also raises out of `drain_queue.main()` before its state write (`:64-65`) and before the remaining queued repos are fetched. (Distinct from #3219, which is about the ack sent after a *returned* failure; on this path no ack is sent and the crash is the defect.)
- Distinct from #3240 (non-atomic state writes / bare `json.load`), #3233 (clone_all partial destination), #3238 (valid_mirror bareness), #3229 (inventory null owner), #3215 (umbrella).

## Verified (laptop probe, real `fetch_mirrors.py`)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-fetchtimeout/` on the laptop — the real `fetch_mirrors.py` / `ghb_common.py` / `manifest.py` copied verbatim (sha256 `f0115270…`, `2eb427df…`, `a489798e…`, identical in the sandbox checkout at main `8e4ef90e` and the laptop clone), three real bare mirrors, the subprocess layer raising `TimeoutExpired` for the first repo exactly as `git fetch` hitting the 3600s timeout does, real git for the rest:

```
CASE hang-first: main([prog, hang/aaa, good/bbb, good/ccc])
  RAISED TimeoutExpired (unhandled): Command '['git', '-C', '.../hang/aaa.git', 'fetch', '--all', '--prune']' timed out after 3600 seconds
  fetch attempts: [only hang/aaa — good/bbb and good/ccc never attempted]
  state.json exists: False
  fetch.log exists: False
  MANIFEST.json exists: False
CONTROL no-hang: main([prog, good/bbb, good/ccc])
  {"results": {"ok": 2, "fail": 0, "skip": 0, "missing": 0}, "chronic_failures": []}
  returned rc = 0
  state.json exists: True (both repos stamped last_fetch, fail_days [])
```

## Why it matters

The daily fetch is the freshness mechanism for the whole mirror estate. Mirrors of large/active repos are exactly the ones that can hit a 3600s fetch (slow network, laptop sleep mid-fetch, a wedged remote). Today one such repo silently stops the entire daily pass — every repo after it in plan order goes stale — and leaves no per-repo record, so the chronic-failure alarm that exists precisely to surface a repeatedly failing repo can never fire for it. The only trace is an unhandled traceback in the systemd journal.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `git fetch` that exceeds the timeout is recorded as that repo's failure (same shape as a non-zero exit: `last_error` noted, today appended to `fail_days`, a `fetch.log` line written) and the run continues with the remaining repos.
- [ ] `state.json` is written and `MANIFEST.json` is rebuilt even when one or more fetches time out; the summary/chronic-failure exit behaviour applies to timeouts exactly as to other failures (3 distinct fail days → exit 1).
- [ ] `drain_queue.py`'s fetch path inherits the same behaviour: one repo's timeout does not abort fetching the remaining queued repos or lose the drainer's state write.
- [ ] Regression tests/probe cover: timeout on the first repo (later repos still fetched, state + log + manifest produced), timeout counted in `fail_days`, and the no-timeout control unchanged.

title: github-backup(clone_all): a clone killed mid-flight leaves a partial destination every rerun rejects — the 'resumable' driver never resumes that repo

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

labels.name: app/github-backup
labels.description: infra/github-backup estate mirror system

body:
## Problem

`infra/github-backup/bin/clone_all.py` is documented as the *resumable* parallel mirror-clone driver (module docstring, lines 2–8; README.md:59): re-running it skips verified mirrors and retries the rest. That resume works only when a failed clone leaves **no** destination behind. A clone that is killed mid-flight — the driver's own `TIMEOUT = 5400` expiry (clone_all.py:17, 55–60), an interrupt, a laptop sleep/reboot during the multi-GB initial estate clone — leaves a partial `<owner>/<repo>.git` directory on disk. From then on, every rerun fails that repo permanently:

- `clone_one` (clone_all.py:41–47) checks `valid_mirror(dest)`; a partial directory is not a bare repository, so it falls through to `git clone --mirror … dest` (lines 48–57).
- git refuses a non-empty existing destination: `fatal: destination path '…' already exists and is not an empty directory.`
- Nothing in the driver ever removes, quarantines, or retries around the partial directory, so the repo can never be mirrored until a human finds and deletes the leftover by hand. `reconcile.py` invokes `clone_all.py` whenever mirrors are missing (reconcile.py:64–70), so the weekly correctness floor inherits the wedge: that repo reports a clone failure on every sweep and stays unmirrored while the rest of the plan proceeds.

The timeout path makes this a designed-in outcome, not an exotic accident: `clone_one` explicitly catches `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` and returns a plain `fail` record (lines 58–60) — after `subprocess.run` has killed git mid-transfer, which is exactly the case where git cannot clean up its own destination (a git that exits on its own error removes the destination it created; a killed one cannot).

## Evidence (verified this run, main 357ec7fb)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-clonepartial/` (on the laptop), driving the **real** `clone_all.py` (sha256 `59a0abd6…` for clone_all.py and `2eb427df…` for ghb_common.py, identical in the sandbox clone, the laptop clone, and the probe copy), with `backup_root` pointed at a scratch tree and a one-repo plan (`octocat/Hello-World`):

1. Pre-seeded the destination with a partial-clone leftover (`Hello-World.git/objects/pack/tmp_pack_XXXX`, not a valid mirror) — the state a killed clone leaves:
   - Run 1: `octocat/Hello-World fail` — error `fatal: destination path '…/Hello-World.git' already exists and is not an empty directory.` — exit 1.
   - Run 2 (the "resume"): identical failure, identical error, exit 1. The driver never self-heals.
2. Control — leftover removed, same plan, same script: `octocat/Hello-World ok`, exit 0, destination is a valid bare mirror (`git rev-parse --is-bare-repository` → `true`). So the clone itself is fine; only the partial-leftover state wedges it.

## Why it matters

The initial estate clone and the reconcile clone pass are how new or recovered mirrors come into existence. The repos most likely to hit the 90-minute timeout or an interrupted laptop session are the giant ones (multi-GB nixpkgs-class mirrors in `config.json`'s force-include list) — exactly the ones a backup system most needs to land. Today one interrupted attempt silently converts into a permanent per-repo failure that only manual filesystem surgery fixes, and the status log just records the same opaque git fatal each week.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Before cloning, a destination that exists but is **not** a valid mirror is handled explicitly: removed (it was created by this driver and is not a verified mirror) or moved aside to a clearly named quarantine path, and the clone is then attempted — a rerun after a timeout/interrupt/kill converges to a mirrored state with no manual cleanup.
- [ ] A destination that **is** a valid mirror is never deleted or re-cloned (current `already-present` behaviour preserved); any cleanup is limited to the exact per-repo destination path the driver itself manages.
- [ ] The timeout path is covered: after a `TimeoutExpired`, the next run can succeed for that repo.
- [ ] Regression tests drive `clone_one`/`main` with (a) a pre-existing partial destination, (b) a valid-mirror destination (untouched), and (c) an absent destination (normal clone), and fail on the current code for (a).
- [ ] `clone-status.jsonl` distinguishes a cleared-partial retry from an ordinary failure, so the recovery is visible in the log.

Dedup (this run): title/keyword searches for `clone_all`, "resumable mirror clone", and the git fatal text return no covering issue. Related but distinct: #3219 (drain ack path), #3229 (inventory null owner), #3215 (umbrella estate issue).

title: cold-store-reaper: put_backup files DB dumps with no read-back verification — a corrupted Drive copy is ledgered as a good backup, unlike bundle upload which md5-verifies

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.description: Package/app: cold-store-reaper (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/cold-store-reaper/cold_store.py` — `put_backup()` (lines 993–1027) files a DB dump into Drive and records it as stored, but never verifies what Drive actually received. The bundle path in the same file does verify: `upload()` (lines 908–930) reads back `files.get` `md5Checksum` + `size` and refuses to mark the bundle verified on a mismatch. `put_backup()` has no equivalent step:

1. `file_id = self._resumable_upload(src, name, folder_id)` (line 1019)
2. a `transfer_ledger` row `upload / backup-upload` is written immediately (lines 1020–1024)
3. the result dict is returned as success

That ledger row is load-bearing: `_upload_accounting()` (lines 497–541) computes the project-budget backup bytes from `backup-upload` rows, and `backup_supabase()` / `backup_d1()` / `scripts/export-turso.sh` all file through `put_backup()`. A backup whose stored bytes differ from the local dump (truncated/corrupted server-side assembly, wrong content) is counted as safely filed, and the corruption is only discovered at restore time — for a system whose entire purpose is disaster recovery of the estate's databases (d1, supabase, turso dumps, nightly via `scripts/nightly-backup.sh`).

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-backupverify/probe.py` against the real `cold_store.py` (sha256 `fba42e08027514abae2de1602e755854ebfd6a3b578a5eece34b6c0becd39b95`, identical on the sandbox and laptop clones, main `357ec7fb`):

- `_resumable_upload` stubbed to return a file id while Drive holds different bytes, and `cold_store.http_request` rigged to raise if any verification request is attempted.
- Result: `put_backup("d1", dump.sql)` **returned success** (`{'db': 'd1', 'name': 'd1-20261031T212413Z-dump.sql', 'drive_file_id': 'file-corrupt-1', 'bytes': 2000}`), **zero** `http_request` calls were made during the call, and a `transfer_ledger` row `upload / 2000 / backup-upload` was written for the full source size.

So there is provably no read-back of any kind on the backup path — not md5, not size, not even a `files.get`.

## Why it matters

- The bundle path's verification exists precisely because an unverified upload cannot be trusted; DB backups are at least as critical as bundle objects (they are the recovery source for the estate's databases, and the restore drill in `scripts/restore-drill.sh` exercises d1 backups).
- Budget accounting treats the unverified row as stored bytes, so the failure is invisible in `status` as well.
- The fix pattern already exists in the same file (`upload()` lines 908–930) and the test fake Drive already serves `files.get` with `md5Checksum`/`size` for the bundle tests.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] After `_resumable_upload`, `put_backup()` reads back the uploaded file's `md5Checksum` and `size` (Drive `files.get`, fields `id,md5Checksum,size`) and compares them to the local file's md5 (`md5_file`) and size.
- [ ] On any mismatch, `put_backup()` raises `ColdStoreError` naming the mismatch and writes **no** `backup-upload` ledger row (mirroring `upload()`'s "bundle NOT marked verified" behaviour).
- [ ] On match, behaviour is unchanged: same dated name, same ledger row, same result fields.
- [ ] A regression test in `pkgs/cold-store-reaper/tests/test_cold_store.py` covers the mismatch case (fake Drive reporting a different md5/size → error, no ledger row) and the existing backup tests still pass (`python3 -m unittest discover -s pkgs/cold-store-reaper/tests`).

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-b, 2026-10-31. Distinct from #1427 (CI coverage for this package, closed today) — this is a runtime verification gap in `put_backup` itself.

title: aggregator(charges): amountFromBody's verb evidence treats future and negated charges as paid — 'will be charged $X', 'to be paid $X' and 'not charged $X' all return $X, bypassing #3120's due veto (PR #3193 residual)

body:
## Problem

`amountFromBody` in `pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/produce-charge-candidates.ts:169-186` treats **future** and **negated** charge wording as paid evidence. The verb-evidence tier added today in PR #3193 (commit `d6dfa4c1`, the Codex-P2 follow-up to #3120) is:

```ts
/\b(?:charged|paid)[:\s]*\$([\d,]+\.\d{2})/i   // line 175
```

It matches the verb wherever it appears, with no check on what precedes it, and it runs **before** #3120's due-language veto (lines 178-182). So a body that says the money has *not* moved — or has not moved *yet* — yields an amount, and `gmailCandidates` (line 235: `amount ??= amountFromBody(text)`) turns it into a charge candidate for the message's date.

## Evidence (verified this run, 2026-10-31)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneA-chargeverb/` (on the laptop): the real `produce-charge-candidates.ts` from `origin/main`, sha256 `999f2dd904924bc718aa278f209441656e85da05db75aa33c6a95e6d8b0eefe3` — identical on the sandbox and laptop clones — imported under `bun test`. Control passes; all five target cases return an amount today and should return `undefined`:

| Body | Today | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| `Receipt\nYou were charged $20.00 for OpenAI\nBalance due $0.00` (control, PR #3193's own test) | `"20.00"` | `"20.00"` |
| `Your subscription renews Nov 5\nYou will be charged $20.00 on Nov 5` | `"20.00"` | `undefined` |
| `Reminder: your card will be charged $42.50 tomorrow` | `"42.50"` | `undefined` |
| `Invoice\nAmount to be paid $20.00 by Nov 15\nAmount due $20.00` | `"20.00"` | `undefined` |
| `The attempt failed. You were not charged $20.00` | `"20.00"` | `undefined` |
| `Good news: your card was never charged $20.00 for this order` | `"20.00"` | `undefined` |

Result: 1 pass / 5 fail (`probe.txt` in the probe dir).

## Why it matters

This is exactly the class #3120 closed today — money that is merely due, scheduled, or explicitly not charged becoming a charge candidate — re-entering through the fix's own new tier:

- A renewal/reminder mail ("will be charged … tomorrow") becomes a candidate dated the *reminder's* day, then the real charge arrives later and the pipeline carries both (or dedupes against the wrong date).
- An invoice body's "to be paid $X" defeats the due veto that is the whole point of lines 178-182: the veto only runs when the paid tiers found nothing.
- A failure/declined body that reassures "you were not charged $X" produces the candidate #3120's subject gate was built to stop, whenever the subject itself doesn't carry a gated word (the Gmail body read at line 235 is reached for receipt/invoice subjects whose subject carried no amount).

## Acceptance criteria

- `amountFromBody` returns `undefined` for future forms: `will be charged $X`, `will be charged $X tomorrow/on <date>`, and `to be paid $X`.
- `amountFromBody` returns `undefined` for negated forms: `not charged $X`, `never charged $X`, `was not charged $X`, `will not be charged $X`.
- Genuine past-tense evidence still wins exactly as PR #3193 requires: `You were charged $20.00` (including with a trailing `Balance due $0.00` line), `Paid $20.00`, `Amount paid $21.60`, `Total charged $21.60` all return their amounts.
- The #3120 due-only cases still return `undefined` (`Amount due $20.00`, `Balance due: $42.50`).
- New tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/produce-charge-candidates.test.ts` pin the future and negated cases above; the existing #3120/#3121 tests still pass.

Related: #3120 (closed by PR #3193 — this is a residual in that fix, not a reopen: the subject gate and due veto themselves work as designed), #3121 (the sibling body-fallback issue), #3161 (the charges evidence contract design).

body:
## Context
Atlas production search is switching to hybrid FTS + Snowflake 768 (decision 2026-10-31; golden v3: pool 100/branch, RRF k=60, MRR 0.3829 vs current production hybrid 0.3282). Query serving is currently one-query-at-a-time. Drew asked (2026-10-31) whether batching is worth anything in a busy system; filing this as a low-priority exploration so the question gets a measured answer instead of an opinion.

## Question
At what query load, if any, does batching pay for this search — and where?

## Scope of exploration
- **Embedding stage:** micro-batching incoming queries (collect for a few ms, embed together with Snowflake on GPU) — expected large per-query cost reduction vs one-at-a-time embedding.
- **Scoring stage:** batched cosine against the corpus is a single matrix multiply (queries x 101,471 chunks) vs repeated single-query scans.
- **FTS stage:** assess whether BM25 lookups batch or amortize at all (connection reuse, prepared statements).
- **Costs/risks:** added per-query latency while a batch fills; complexity; result quality must be identical (batching is a throughput change, never a ranking change — verify fused top-10 outputs match the unbatched path on golden v3 questions).
- **Scale check:** current corpus 101,471 chunks, brute-force scan is fine; note the load level at which an ANN index would matter more than batching.

## Acceptance
- A short findings note (on this issue) with: measured per-query latency/throughput at 1 / 8 / 32 concurrent queries, batched vs unbatched, on the laptop.
- A recommendation: adopt micro-batching (with a stated window), defer until a stated load threshold, or drop.
- No production change under this issue — implementation, if recommended, gets its own issue.

Priority: low. Nothing is blocked on this; current query volume is modest.

body:
## Problem

`SshTarget::from_str` (`pkgs/id/src/world_ssh.rs:1013-1017`, main `bb16cb89`) parses the port with a bare `digits.parse::<u16>()`. That accepts port **0** — and the signed spelling `+22` — even though no SSH server can be reached on port 0 and the parser's own contract is `[user@]host[:port]`.

```rust
let port = |digits: &str| {
    digits
        .parse::<u16>()
        .map_err(|_| anyhow::anyhow!("`{digits}` is not a port"))
};
```

So `id world join --via ssh example.org:0` (via `commands/world.rs:763`, `target.parse::<SshTarget>()`) parses successfully, and the failure only surfaces later inside russh's connect as a low-level OS/socket error that never names the real problem: the port itself. The parser already refuses the neighbouring bad spellings — its test at `world_ssh.rs:2387-2410` rejects `host:`, `host:99999`, `::1`, `[::1`, `@host`, `[::1]x` — port 0 is the one out-of-range value that slips through, because `u16` range is not the port range.

This also diverges from the house rule for ports: `bin/proxy-port.mjs` (#483) requires an integer **1-65535** for every bin proxy's listen port, for exactly this reason — a bare numeric parse is not a validator.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneA-sshtarget/`, rustc, replicating the verbatim port closure; `world_ssh.rs` sha256 `5c6900cdb2412280…` identical on the sandbox clone at `bb16cb89` and the laptop clone):

```text
"0"     -> Ok(0)
"+22"   -> Ok(22)
"022"   -> Ok(22)
"22"    -> Ok(22)
"65535" -> Ok(65535)
"65536" -> Err(PosOverflow)
"-1"    -> Err(InvalidDigit)
"22x"   -> Err(InvalidDigit)
""      -> Err(Empty)
```

Dedup: open + closed search for `SshTarget` / SSH target port found no existing issue covering this parser (#536 is a broad transport-design issue, not this defect).

## Why it matters

A typo'd or scripted `:0` target starts down the SSH path and fails with a misleading connect error, sending the user to debug host keys/network instead of the target string. Every other malformed target is refused at parse time with the target named; port 0 should be too.

## Acceptance criteria

- `SshTarget::from_str` refuses port 0 (e.g. `example.org:0`, `[::1]:0`) with an error naming the target/port, consistent with the existing bad-spelling tests.
- The signed spelling `+22` is refused, or explicitly accepted-and-documented — no silent third behaviour.
- Valid targets keep parsing exactly as today: `example.org` → 22, `ada@example.org:2222`, `[::1]:2022`, `me@[::1]` → 22.
- Tests in the `ssh_targets_parse_user_host_and_port` test (or a sibling) pin the port-0 refusal.

**Low priority — documentation only, no action scheduled.** Measured 2026-10-31 as part of a fleet-wide repo hygiene census. Full source data: `repo-history-census-2026-10-31.md` and `repo-inventory-2026-10-31.md` (sandbox workspace, `~/workspace/`).

## Repo snapshot

- **Commits:** 5,532 on `main` — first commit 2023-04-17, last 2026-10-31
- **Visibility:** public
- **Fresh clone of `main`:** ~78.4 MB pack (GitHub repo size 79 MB) — tip is 5,510 files / 67 MB
- **Local clone:** 217 MB `.git`
- **Open PRs:** 53 (re-measured 2026-10-31)

## Junk in history (main-branch history, measured by blob census)

**337 MB uncompressed / ~26 MB packed, almost all in 65 objects** — stripping them would shrink a fresh clone from 78.4 MB to ~52.4 MB (saves 26.0 MB, 33%). Nearly all of it is already dead history (335 of 337 MB is not at the tip):

- **Roc build outputs, recommitted across versions:** `pkgs/roc/**/build` — 133 MB + 91 MB across versions; `platform/libhost.a` — 66 MB total (11.7 MB × 5 versions); `dynhost`, `*.rh`
- **Compiled binaries, committed then deleted:** `pkgs/launcher/launcher` (17.4 + 15.6 MB), `pkgs/database/database` (12.0 MB), `pkgs/import/import` (8.7 MB), `pkgs/chat/chat` (7.9 MB), `pkgs/tea/tea` (7.6 MB)
- **One-offs:** `infra/dns/terraform.log` — 20.9 MB (the single largest blob in the repo's history is a log file); `sources/map/data/data.kz` — 6.5 MB
- All-refs census (including side branches): 837 MB of the 900 MB total blob bytes are not at the tip.

**At the tip today there is exactly one file over 2 MB:** `doc/NanoPi…` at 12.5 MB.

## Verdict: NO history rewrite

26 MB packed does not justify orphaning 53 open PRs, invalidating ~150 fleet worktrees, and changing every commit SHA cited across the fleet's issues and docs. As a public repo, a rewrite also wouldn't erase the old history — forks, existing clones, and GitHub's PR refs (`refs/pull/*`) keep the objects alive until GitHub's own GC.

## Already done

- Nothing needed at the tip: it is already clean except for the one `doc/NanoPi` file below. The junk is history-only.

## Open questions (human calls, no deadline)

1. **Roc platform artifacts — intentional or accidental?** `pkgs/roc/**/platform/libhost.a`, `*.rh`, `dynhost`, and the `build` outputs may be intentional platform *distribution* artifacts (Roc platforms ship prebuilt hosts) rather than accidental commits. If accidental: untrack + gitignore the classes at the tip. If intentional: document that here and close the question permanently.
2. **`doc/NanoPi` (12.5 MB at tip)** — keep as a doc asset, or move to release/artifact storage?

## Standing forward-hygiene rules

- No build outputs, compiled binaries, or log files committed at the tip; build artifacts belong in releases or artifact storage (subject to the Roc question above).
- Gitignore scratch classes (scratch/output dirs, API/monitor dumps, probe dirs, `*.err`/`*.out`).
- Runtime state files belong outside repos (`~/.local/state/`) per the pm-aggregator precedent; repos hold summaries.
- Re-run the hygiene census quarterly, or sooner if this repo's main pack crosses ~250 MB or junk classes appear at the tip. Fleet tracking issue: "Standard task: per-repo hygiene census + cleanup documentation" (this repo).

## Acceptance criteria

- The measured census for this repo (blob census, junk classes, fresh-clone size, verdict) is on record in this issue.
- No history rewrite is performed: the recorded verdict stands unless a future census shows a materially larger saving.
- Forward hygiene: no build outputs, binaries, or log files are committed at the tip going forward.

body:
# chat: session program registry never pruned — unbounded growth, per-message fan-out to dead programs, and a data race on the shared slice

## Problem

`pkgs/chat` is a long-running SSH chat server (wish + bubbletea). Its broadcast registry only ever grows, and it is shared across goroutines without synchronization:

- `pkgs/chat/main.go:32` — `app.progs []*tea.Program` is the broadcast registry.
- `pkgs/chat/main.go:92` — `ProgramHandler` appends the new session's program: `a.progs = append(a.progs, p)`. This is one of only three references to `progs` in the package (declaration, append, iterate) — nothing ever removes an entry, so every SSH session that has ever connected stays in the registry for the life of the server.
- `pkgs/chat/main.go:36-40` — `app.send` ranges over the whole slice and spawns one goroutine per entry for **every** chat message: fan-out cost per message grows linearly with the total number of sessions ever served, not the number currently connected.
- No mutex guards the slice: wish invokes `ProgramHandler` on per-session goroutines (append) while any connected client's `Update` calls `app.send` (range) on its own goroutine — a concurrent append during iteration is a data race on the slice header/backing array.
- Dead programs are not cleaned up by bubbletea: in the pinned bubbletea v0.25.0 (`pkgs/chat/go.mod`), `Program.Send` is `select { case <-p.ctx.Done(): case p.msgs <- msg: }`, so sends to finished programs return immediately — the cost is the unbounded slice, the per-message goroutine fan-out over dead entries, and the race, not a block.

## Why it matters

The server is meant to run indefinitely (`Start` blocks until SIGINT/SIGTERM). A busy or long-lived instance accumulates one registry entry per session forever, every message gets slower to broadcast, and the unsynchronized append/iterate can corrupt the slice or panic under concurrent connect + chat — exactly the load pattern a chat server exists for. There are no tests in `pkgs/chat` to catch any of this.

## Acceptance criteria

- A session's program is removed from the broadcast registry when the session/program ends, so registry size tracks live sessions, not cumulative sessions.
- Registry access is race-free: a test that connects/disconnects sessions while messages are sent passes under `go test -race`.
- Broadcast still reaches every live session's program exactly once per message.
- Existing behaviour otherwise unchanged (same host/port, same TUI).

## Evidence

Verified this run on main `c9877f8a`: `grep -n "progs" pkgs/chat/main.go` returns exactly lines 32, 37, 92 (no removal path exists anywhere in the package); bubbletea v0.25.0 `Program.Send` source read from the module cache (`tea.go:599-604`).

title: id(artifact): check() accepts duplicate after hashes — the same hash can fill all 32 frontier slots, unlike chain.rs which refuses DuplicateAfter

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Problem

`SignedArtifact::check()` (the verification gate behind `verify()` and `ArtifactLog::insert`) validates the `after` causal frontier only for count and shape — never for duplicates:

- `pkgs/id/src/artifact.rs:280-287` — `after.len() <= MAX_AFTER` (32) and every entry `is_hash(...)`. Nothing rejects the same hash appearing twice.
- The sibling type for the identical concept refuses it explicitly: `ChainExt::validate()` in `pkgs/id/src/chain.rs:187-193` caps `after`, then builds a `HashSet` and returns `ChainError::DuplicateAfter` ("after names the same hash twice", chain.rs:53-55) when a hash repeats. `ChainExt.after` is documented as "the author's causal frontier … At most [`MAX_AFTER`] hashes, none repeated" (chain.rs:104-107).

So a signed artifact whose `after` is `[h, h]`, or even the same hash repeated 32 times — filling the entire frontier with ONE distinct artifact — verifies and is stored by `ArtifactLog`, while an event header carrying the same frontier is refused at decode.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 236cb985)

Laptop probe `probe-2026-10-31-laneA-dupafter` (in `~/git/fleet/` on the laptop) driving the real `id` crate (`SignedArtifact::sign_after` → `verify()` → `ArtifactLog::insert`), `artifact.rs` sha256 `bdc11bbe0cafa72c4017df93523699cad99303520b65c71365e1ca7d3e1bc86b` matched on both clones:

```
control distinct [h1,h2]: verify=Ok(()) insert=Ok(New)
duplicate [h1,h1]: verify=Ok(()) insert=Ok(New)
duplicate x32 (whole frontier, 1 distinct): verify=Ok(()) insert=Ok(New)
duplicate x33 (over cap): verify=Err(an artifact names at most 32 artifacts before it) insert=Err(same)
control distinct x32: verify=Ok(()) insert=Ok(New)
```

Controls show the existing checks work: 32 distinct hashes pass, and 33 entries are refused for count — but the count is spent by duplicates, so the "32 artifacts" the frontier claims to name can be as few as 1.

## Why it matters

- `after` is signed ordering evidence: the module doc (artifact.rs:11-13) says a receiver can order concurrent statements by it and "enforcing that order is up to the consumer". A frontier that repeats one hash is ambiguous evidence — a consumer counting distinct dependencies, or checking whether a specific set was seen, reads a padded list as more causal history than exists.
- The cap's intent is per distinct artifact: `MAX_AFTER` bounds how many artifacts one statement may name. Duplicates spend the budget without naming more, so the same statement can simultaneously satisfy `len == 32` (maximally "informed") and name a single predecessor.
- Cross-type drift: two signed frontier types in one crate enforce different rules for the same field name and concept, so a statement can be valid as an artifact and invalid as an event for the same reason. The chain side already decided the rule — repeated hashes are an error, not a normalization case.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `SignedArtifact::check()` (or `ArtifactLog` insert) refuses an artifact whose `after` names the same hash twice, with an error naming the duplication.
- [ ] Regression tests: `[h, h]` refused; the same hash ×32 refused; 32 distinct hashes still accepted; over-cap still refused.
- [ ] `sign_after` (the local signing path) refuses or dedupes a repeated `after` hash so a local author cannot mint an artifact remote peers will refuse — signing and verification apply the same rule, as `ChainExt`'s builder/decoder pair does (chain.rs:174-176).
- [ ] Existing artifact tests (paging, sync, directory application) still pass.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for artifact `after` duplicates / `DuplicateAfter` before filing: no existing issue covers the artifact side. Distinct from #3146 (friend_remove `requests` validation), #3187 (home_declared `world_id`), #3192 (document/tag NFC) — different field and rule; this one is the envelope-level `after` check in `check()`, not a `parsed()` kind arm.

title: id(artifact): parsed() accepts non-NFC text in document and tag — media_type, tag name and value bypass the NFC rule documents.rs and tag_claims.rs both enforce

body:
## Problem

`SignedArtifact::parsed()` (`pkgs/id/src/artifact.rs`) accepts non-NFC text in the two known kinds that carry free text, while every sibling text path in the same crate refuses non-NFC:

- `DOCUMENT` arm (artifact.rs:356-371): checks only `media_type` empty / >128 bytes and content size. A decomposed media type such as `text/cafe\u{301}` (e + combining acute U+0301) is accepted and stored.
- `TAG` arm (artifact.rs:372-385): checks only subject hash, name 1–64 bytes, value ≤256 bytes. A decomposed tag name (`aute\u{301}ur`) or value (`cafe\u{301}`) is accepted and stored.

The sibling rules that these kinds bypass:

- `documents.rs` `DocumentRef::check()` (documents.rs:105-121) refuses a media type that is not NFC — its doc comment states the rule and it is pinned by `test_the_media_type_is_one_to_128_bytes_in_nfc`. Same 128-byte cap as the artifact arm, minus the NFC half.
- `tag_claims.rs` `check_text()` (tag_claims.rs:146-160), used by `check_op` for `tag.set`, requires NFC for name and value.
- `chain.rs` (chain.rs:198, chain.rs:367) requires NFC for event kinds and text strings.

## Why it matters

An artifact is a signed, stored, propagated statement: `parsed()` is the trust-boundary check before a known kind is applied (directory.rs publishes/applies `Kind::Document` and `Kind::Tag`). Two spellings of the same media type / tag name — NFC and decomposed — are different byte strings, so lookups, equality, and tag-name matching split on a difference no user can see: a document published with a decomposed media type does not match the NFC spelling a reader asks for, and a decomposed tag name forms a separate tag from the composed one. The event/chain side of the same system canonicalizes on NFC; the artifact side silently does not, so the same logical statement is valid in one store and refused in the other.

## Evidence (verified this run)

- Code: artifact.rs:356-385 (above) vs documents.rs:113-117 and tag_claims.rs:152-154 — the NFC check exists in both sibling validators and is absent from both artifact arms.
- Laptop probe (probe-2026-10-31-laneA-nfc, on the laptop clone at the same HEAD 236cb985, artifact.rs sha256 bdc11bbe on both clones) driving the real `SignedArtifact::sign` + `parsed()`: control NFC document/tag ACCEPTED; non-NFC media_type, tag name, and tag value all ACCEPTED by `parsed()`.
- Dedup: open + recently closed search for NFC / non-NFC / normalization against artifact kinds found no existing issue covering the artifact `document`/`tag` arms (sibling of #3187 home_declared world_id and #3146 friend_remove requests — same function, different kinds/fields/rules; the parsed-shape contract design is #3068).

## Acceptance criteria

- `parsed()` refuses a `document` whose `media_type` is not NFC, with a `Refusal::Forbidden` naming the rule, pinned by a parsed()-level test using a decomposed spelling.
- `parsed()` refuses a `tag` whose `name` or `value` is not NFC, likewise pinned.
- Ordinary NFC documents and tags (existing artifact tests) parse exactly as today.
- The check is shared with, or explicitly mirrors, the existing NFC rules in `documents.rs` / `tag_claims.rs` so the three validators cannot drift again (e.g. one helper, or a test that walks all three).

body:
## Bug: bin proxies corrupt multibyte UTF-8 split across request-body chunks

Eight proxies in `bin/` accumulate the request body with `bodyText += chunk`, where `chunk` is a `Buffer` and no handler calls `req.setEncoding`. Each chunk is therefore stringified on its own: a multibyte UTF-8 sequence straddling a chunk boundary decodes to U+FFFD replacement characters on both sides, and the corrupted text is parsed and forwarded upstream as if the client had sent it. JSON still parses (the damage lands inside string values), so prompts containing emoji/CJK/accented text are silently garbled — no error anywhere.

### Evidence (verified this run, main fe62dc72)

Handlers with the pattern (no `setEncoding` in any of these files):

- `bin/clef-proxy.mjs:194-196`
- `bin/agy-proxy.mjs:844-846`
- `bin/antigravity-ls-proxy.mjs:751-753`
- `bin/claude-code-proxy.mjs:721-723`
- `bin/codex-proxy.mjs:1069-1071`
- `bin/commandcode-proxy.mjs:897-899`
- `bin/design-code-proxy.mjs:180-182`
- `bin/muse-proxy.mjs:1484-1486` and `bin/muse-proxy.mjs:1582-1584` (two handlers)

The correct house pattern already exists in the same directory: `bin/antigravity-direct.mjs:700-701` collects Buffer chunks and decodes once with `Buffer.concat(chunks).toString('utf8')`; `bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs` uses a streaming `TextDecoder`.

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-chunksplit/`, real `bin/clef-proxy.mjs` from the laptop clone, sha256 `7eac5569…` identical to sandbox main, stub upstream via `CLEF_PROXY_GATEWAY_BASE`): POST `/v1/systemone` with `{"questions":{"q":"before-😀-after"}}`:

- Control (single write): stub upstream receives `q = "before-😀-after"` — intact.
- Split (first write ends 2 bytes into the emoji's 4-byte sequence, rest 150 ms later): stub upstream receives `q = "before-���-after"` — 3× U+FFFD, emoji destroyed.

Chunk boundaries are not exotic: Node's HTTP parser emits data per socket read (64 KiB high-water mark), so any non-ASCII character landing on a read boundary of a large body — or simply split by client/network segmentation, as in the probe — is corrupted.

### Why it matters

These proxies front the fleet's model traffic (Muse, Codex, Muse, CommandCode, design, agy, antigravity-ls, clef). A user prompt, file content, or tool result with non-ASCII text near a chunk boundary reaches the model with replacement characters substituted in, silently — the request succeeds, the answer is just computed over garbled input. The larger and more international the payload, the more likely a hit.

### Acceptance criteria

- Every handler listed above decodes the body exactly once over the complete byte stream (`Buffer.concat` + single `toString('utf8')`, a streaming `TextDecoder` with `{stream: true}`, or `req.setEncoding('utf8')`), matching the `antigravity-direct.mjs` pattern; the byte-based size caps keep working (count bytes, not decoded characters, if the accumulation changes form).
- A regression test per affected proxy (or one shared test driving the pattern): a body with a multibyte character split across two writes arrives/parses byte-identical; the existing per-proxy test files (`bin/*.test.mjs`) still pass.
- No behavior change for ASCII bodies, oversize bodies (413 path), or malformed JSON (400 path).

### Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `bodyText`, chunk-boundary / U+FFFD / replacement-character / split-UTF-8 proxy terms on 2026-10-31: no existing issue covers this. Related but distinct: #1844 (proxy-relay `RELAY_TARGET_PORTS` parsing), #483/#494 (strict port parsing in `bin/proxy-port.mjs`), #690 closed (clef-proxy JSON parse error shape).

— filed by new-issue-creator-code-b (Lane B), 2026-10-31 run

body:
## Problem

In reactive mode (`serve.mode = "reactive"`), every tool named in `catalog.pinnedTools` appears **twice** in the `tools/list` surface.

`reactiveSurface` (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/mcpserver/reactive.go:59-77`) builds the surface in three sections:

1. the meta tools (`request_tools`, `batch_call`),
2. **pinned tools** — appended from `s.PinnedTools` (lines 60-64),
3. **retained working-set tools** — appended from `ReactiveWorkingSet.List()` (lines 67-73).

But the working set already contains every pinned tool: `catalog.NewWorkingSet`'s constructor inserts each pinned entry itself (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/catalog/retention.go:65-68`, `ws.Add("", p, OriginPinned)`), and the serve path builds the set from the very same list (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/cli/serve.go:631-634`: `srv.PinnedTools = settings.List("catalog.pinnedTools")`, then `NewWorkingSet(maxTools, stickyWindow, srv.PinnedTools)`). The lazy constructions in `reactive.go:129` and `server.go:2832` do the same. So section 3 re-appends each pinned tool that section 2 just added. Nothing downstream dedupes: `tools/list` (`server.go:964-978`) pages the surface verbatim.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-reactivepin/` (full copy of `pkgs/mcpx` at main `fd7ef4526`; `reactive.go` / `retention.go` / `serve.go` sha256 identical in the sandbox and laptop clones) with one same-package test: a server with extras `alpha` + `beta`, `Reactive=true`, `PinnedTools=["alpha"]`, `ReactiveWorkingSet = catalog.NewWorkingSet(24, time.Hour, PinnedTools)`:

```
=== RUN   TestProbeReactivePinnedDuplicate
    probe_reactive_test.go:34: surface names=[request_tools batch_call alpha alpha] counts=map[alpha:2 batch_call:1 request_tools:1]
--- FAIL: TestProbeReactivePinnedDuplicate (pinned tool alpha appears 2 times)
```

The unactivated, unpinned `beta` correctly appears zero times. With no pinned tools configured (the default) the surface is correct, which is why this needs a non-empty `catalog.pinnedTools` to reproduce.

## Why it matters

`tools/list` is the contract a client reads its callable surface from. Duplicate entries with the same name inflate the page count, and strict MCP clients that index tools by name (or validate uniqueness) can reject or mis-render the whole list — in exactly the mode whose purpose is a small, curated surface. The duplication also makes the pinned section's ordering guarantee meaningless: the second copy lands in recency order at the end of the working-set section.

## Acceptance criteria

- With `catalog.pinnedTools` non-empty, each pinned tool appears exactly once in the reactive `tools/list` surface, in a deterministic position.
- A regression test in `internal/mcpserver` builds the surface the way `serve.go` does (working set constructed from the same `PinnedTools`) and asserts no duplicate tool names, for at least: one pinned tool, a pinned tool that is also activated via `request_tools`, and no pinned tools.
- Activated (sticky/injected) tools still appear once; pinned tools are still never evicted from the working set (`internal/catalog` retention tests keep passing).
- `go test ./internal/mcpserver ./internal/catalog -count=1` passes (on the laptop or CI, per fleet rules).

Dedup note: searched open + closed issues for reactive / pinned / duplicate tools/list on 2026-10-31 — no existing issue covers this; #1877 mentions reactive embedding only in passing.

title: opencode-config-normalize: the repair write discards the config's permissions (0600 -> 0644) and silently severs a symlinked config — tmp+replace with no mode copy and no symlink handling (normalize.sh:126-128)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

body:
## Problem

When `pkgs/opencode-config-normalize/normalize.sh` does repair `opencode.jsonc`, its write path discards the file's existing permissions and breaks symlinks: a `0600` config comes back `0644` (umask default), and a symlinked config is replaced by a brand-new regular file at the link path while the link target keeps the unrepaired v2 keys forever.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `fc88d0a9`, script sha256 `c59dd79b…`)

- `normalize.sh:126-128`: the repaired text is written to a fresh sibling temp file and moved over the config —
  ```python
  tmp = path.with_suffix(path.suffix + '.normalize-tmp')
  tmp.write_text(out)
  tmp.replace(path)
  ```
  Nothing copies the original file's mode onto `tmp`, and `Path.replace` on a symlinked `path` replaces the symlink itself, not its target. Nothing in the script checks `path.is_symlink()` or `stat` mode.
- Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneA-normalize/`, verbatim copy of the script, sha-matched to main):
  - Case B: a `chmod 600` config needing repair → repaired correctly, but `stat` afterwards shows `644`.
  - Case C: config as a symlink to `target.jsonc` needing repair → after the run the link path is a regular file (`-rw-r--r--`, no longer a symlink) holding the repaired content, while `target.jsonc` still contains the unrepaired `"plugins"` key.

## Why it matters

An opencode config can carry provider credentials, so silently widening `0600` → `0644` exposes them to other local users — the same defect filed for the t3code seed write in #3170, in a second script. The symlink half is a correctness break in exactly the setups this fleet uses (dotfiles/home-manager style linked configs): the normalizer reports "repaired", the file the user actually manages through the link target is never repaired, and the link is silently severed so future target updates stop reaching the live config.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] After a repair, the config's permission bits equal those it had before (a `0600` fixture stays `0600`); a test fixture asserts the mode, not just the content.
- [ ] A symlinked config is repaired through the link (target content updated, symlink intact), or the script refuses with a non-zero exit and leaves both link and target byte-identical — never a silent link sever. The chosen behaviour is covered by a fixture in `normalize_test.sh`.
- [ ] All existing `normalize_test.sh` cases still pass, including byte-identical-on-failure and idempotence.

## Related

- #3170 — same mode/symlink defect class in the t3code-seed-providers seed write (different script, different config file); fixing both with one shared pattern would be ideal, but each stands alone.
- #3179 — the same script's JSONC comment gap (probe/parse side; this issue is the write side).

## Dedup

Searched open + closed for `opencode-config-normalize` / `normalize.sh`: only #2364 (closed, agents-drop). No existing issue covers this script's write path, mode, or symlink behaviour.

title: opencode-config-normalize: an inline // or /* */ comment anywhere in opencode.jsonc silently disables every repair — the probe stripper only removes full-line comments, the parse fails, and the script exits 0

labels.name: kind/bug

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/opencode-config-normalize/normalize.sh` silently performs **no repair at all** on an `opencode.jsonc` that contains an inline `//` comment or a `/* */` block comment — the two comment forms JSONC allows anywhere, and the forms a hand-edited user config most often contains. The config keeps its v2 `plugins`/`agents` keys, which opencode 1.x ignores (the script's own header documents this), so the user's plugins/agents stay broken while the path-unit trigger reports nothing.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `fc88d0a9`, script sha256 `c59dd79b…`)

- `normalize.sh:36-41`: the membership probe strips only full-line comments — `re.sub(r'^\s*//.*$', '', raw, flags=re.M)` — then `json.loads(probe)`; on any exception it does `sys.exit(0)` ("unparseable: leave it alone"). An inline comment after a value, or a `/* */` block, is not stripped, so the parse fails and the script exits 0 having changed nothing. The same weak probe is reused for the pre-write verification at lines 108-109.
- Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneA-normalize/`, verbatim copy of the script, sha-matched to main):
  - Case A: config with `"plugins": ["opencode-plugin-x"] // migrated by OpenChamber` → exit 0, file byte-identical, `plugins` still present.
  - Case A2: config with a `/* user config */` header comment and `"plugins": [...]` → exit 0, file byte-identical, `plugins` still present.
  - Control case B (no comments) repairs correctly, proving the fixtures are otherwise in the script's recognised shape.

## Why it matters

The script exists because OpenChamber rewrites the config to v2 spellings and v1 opencode silently ignores them. A user who annotates their config — the normal thing to do in a JSONC file — falls entirely outside the repair, with no log line, no non-zero exit, and no way to tell the normalizer gave up versus found nothing to do. The failure is silent in exactly the population (hand-editors) most likely to also hand-merge OpenChamber's rewrites.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A config whose only JSONC features are inline `//` comments is repaired the same as the comment-free equivalent (full parsed-document equality, as in `normalize_test.sh`).
- [ ] A config with a `/* */` block comment is repaired likewise, or — if block comments are deliberately out of scope — the script says so in its header and the limitation is covered by an explicit test fixture asserting the untouched-exit-0 behaviour.
- [ ] Comment stripping is string-aware: a `//` or `/*` sequence inside a string value (e.g. a URL or prompt) is never treated as a comment, and a `,}` / `,]` sequence inside a string is never treated as a trailing comma (the current regex probe at line 37 has the same string-blindness — cf. closed #704 for the same failure in the sync-models stripper).
- [ ] New fixtures in `normalize_test.sh` cover inline-comment, block-comment, and comment-like-text-inside-a-string configs, asserting full parsed documents and idempotence.
- [ ] All existing `normalize_test.sh` cases still pass, including the byte-identical-on-failure contract.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed for `opencode-config-normalize` / `normalize.sh`: #2364 (closed) is the agents-drop data-loss bug, fixed with the verification block this issue builds on; #704 (closed) is the same string-blind stripper class in a different tool (sync-models). No existing issue covers this script's comment handling.

title: pm-dispatch(validate): titleFromPrompt truncates by UTF-16 code units — an astral character at the cap leaves a lone surrogate in the title

labels.name: task/triage

body:
## Problem

`titleFromPrompt` in pm-stack/dispatch caps a fallback title by **UTF-16 code units**, not characters: `first.slice(0, max - 1) + "…"`. When an astral character (an emoji, most CJK extension characters, musical symbols) straddles the cut, the slice keeps its high surrogate and drops the low surrogate, producing a title that ends in a **lone surrogate** before the ellipsis. That string is not well-formed Unicode: `JSON.stringify` emits it as the invalid escape `"\ud83d…"`, and strict JSON/UTF-8 consumers downstream (the queue packet, the GitHub issue created from the title) receive a title no conforming parser has to accept.

## Evidence (verified this run on current main)

- `pm-stack/dispatch/src/validate.ts:218-226` — `titleFromPrompt(prompt, max = 120)`: picks the first non-empty line, then `first.length > max ? first.slice(0, max - 1) + "…" : first`. `length` and `slice` are code-unit based; nothing aligns the cut to a character boundary.
- Call sites: `pm-stack/dispatch/src/server.ts:107` (`title: req.title ?? titleFromPrompt(req.prompt)`) and `server.ts:182` — the fallback title becomes the session/task title, and from there the created issue's title and the queue packet's title.
- Existing tests cover the cap with ASCII text only; no astral-character boundary case exists in `pm-stack/dispatch/test/validate.test.ts`.

### Probe (real code, run on the laptop)

Imported the repo's own `validate.ts` (sha256 `8f3b727b5a49dfdf48ae0421db290c2bacc2969863f87bd5eb9470fb534a8d55`, identical in the sandbox clone at main and the laptop clone) with bun 1.4.2; probe at `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-modeltrim/probe.ts` (laptop). Input: a first line of 118 `x` characters + 😀 (U+1F600, two code units) + 10 `y` characters (131 code units, over the 120 cap, emoji straddling the cut):

```text
title len(cu)= 120
last codes: [ "78", "d83d", "2026" ]   (x, LONE HIGH SURROGATE, …)
title has lone surrogate: true
title JSON: xxxxxxxxxxxx\ud83d…"
```

## Why it matters

Prompts are free text from callers; an emoji near column 120 of the first line is unremarkable. The dispatch service then mints an issue and a queue record whose title contains an unpaired surrogate — a value that cannot be encoded as UTF-8 and is invalid in strict JSON — so the failure, when it comes, appears in a downstream consumer (packet store, GitHub API client, a Rust/Python reader) rather than at the truncation that caused it. Every other length cap in this codebase's neighbourhood that cuts user text is expected to cut on a character boundary; this one silently doesn't.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `titleFromPrompt` truncates on a character (code-point) boundary: the returned title never contains a lone surrogate, for any input and any `max`.
- [ ] Tests in `pm-stack/dispatch/test/validate.test.ts`: a line with an astral character straddling the cap produces a well-formed title (no lone surrogates, ends with `…`, length within the cap's intent); ASCII behaviour is byte-identical to today.
- [ ] Triage pins whether the cap is then measured in code points or grapheme clusters; either is acceptable if the no-lone-surrogate property and the test land.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `titleFromPrompt`, lone-surrogate and dispatch title truncation: no existing filing covers it. Distinct from the `parseModel` string-form finding filed the same run (different function, different failure) and from #2679/#2757 (`resolvePriority`).

body:
## Problem

`parseModel` in pm-stack/dispatch validates the two model-hint forms to different standards. The **object form trims** `providerID` and `id` (and requires each non-empty after trimming); the **string form trims only the whole string**, then returns the two slash-separated segments verbatim. A model hint with spaces around the slash — the natural way a human writes one in a workflow input — is accepted by `POST /v1/sessions` and `POST /v1/tasks`, and the untrimmed segments are sent verbatim to the opencode server as the session's model, where no such provider or model exists. The request validates, the issue/task is created, and the failure only surfaces at session launch as an unknown-provider/model error far from the actual cause.

## Evidence (verified this run on current main)

- `pm-stack/dispatch/src/validate.ts:73-80` — string form: `const t = input.trim()`, split on first `/`, `return { providerID: t.slice(0, slash), id: t.slice(slash + 1) }` — neither segment is trimmed or checked for interior whitespace.
- `pm-stack/dispatch/src/validate.ts:82-87` — object form: requires `providerID.trim()` and `id.trim()` non-empty and returns both **trimmed**. Same input, different result depending on form.
- Downstream: `pm-stack/dispatch/src/opencode.ts:61` sends the parsed ref verbatim (`body.model = { id: opts.model.id, providerID: opts.model.providerID }`); `parseModel` is reached from `parseSessionRequest` (`validate.ts:139`) and `parseTaskRequest` (`validate.ts:214`), so the spaced form passes request validation entirely.
- Existing tests (`pm-stack/dispatch/test/validate.test.ts:84-112`) cover the clean string form, first-slash splitting, both object spellings, and malformed forms — no spaced-segment string case exists.

### Probe (real code, run on the laptop)

Imported the repo's own `validate.ts` (sha256 `8f3b727b5a49dfdf48ae0421db290c2bacc2969863f87bd5eb9470fb534a8d55`, identical in the sandbox clone at main and the laptop clone) with bun 1.4.2; probe at `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-modeltrim/probe.ts` (laptop):

```text
string spaced both:     {"providerID":"anthropic ","id":" claude-sonnet"}
string spaced id:       {"providerID":"anthropic","id":" claude-sonnet"}
string spaced provider: {"providerID":"anthropic ","id":"claude-sonnet"}
object spaced:          {"providerID":"anthropic","id":"claude-sonnet"}
string clean:           {"providerID":"anthropic","id":"claude-sonnet"}
```

The object form of the same spaced input returns the trimmed pair; only the string form leaks the spaces into the launched model.

## Why it matters

Model hints arrive as strings from composite/workflow callers — exactly the callers most likely to write `provider / model` with spaces, and the same caller class the priority parser was already hardened for (numeric strings, #2679). Today that input is not a clean 400 and not a working launch: it is an accepted dispatch whose session fails later against a provider named `"anthropic "` (trailing space), with the error pointing at opencode's model lookup rather than at the hint the caller actually sent.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The string form of `parseModel` returns segments held to the same standard as the object form: each segment trimmed (or a segment carrying surrounding whitespace refused with a `ValidationError` — triage pins one behaviour; trimming matches the object form and the whole-string trim the string form already does).
- [ ] Tests in `pm-stack/dispatch/test/validate.test.ts`: string forms with spaces around the slash (provider side, model side, both) produce the same `ModelRef` as the clean string and the object form; all existing model-parsing tests still pass.
- [ ] First-slash splitting is unchanged: `meta/claude/sonnet` still yields provider `meta`, id `claude/sonnet`.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `parseModel`, model-hint trimming and dispatch model parsing: no existing filing covers the string form's untrimmed segments. Distinct from #2679/#2757 (same file, `resolvePriority` only) and from #3113 (aggregator credential refs, different package).

title: t3code-seed-providers: the seed write does not preserve settings.json's file mode — a 0600 settings file becomes umask-default (0660/0644), and a symlinked settings.json is silently replaced by a regular file

body:
## Problem

`t3code-seed-providers`' write path does not preserve the existing `settings.json` file mode — and silently destroys a symlink.

Evidence on main (`47214f1c`), `pkgs/t3code-seed-providers/seed.sh` (the embedded Python, final write block):

```python
tmp = path.with_suffix(".seed-tmp")
tmp.write_text(json.dumps(doc, indent=2) + "\n")
tmp.replace(path)
```

- `tmp` is a brand-new file, so it gets the process umask's default mode; `replace()` then swaps it in for the original. Nothing reads or reapplies the original file's mode (no `stat` / `chmod` anywhere in the script).
- The same `replace()` replaces a symlink itself rather than writing through it: if `settings.json` is a symlink, the link is silently replaced by a regular file and the link target is never seeded.

This file is a credential-bearing one by the script's own header: it notes upstream settings hand-edited by users, mentioning "Bitbucket tokens hand-edited into settings.json". A user who keeps that file at `0600` loses that protection on the first seed run that changes anything, with no warning.

## Verified this run

Probe (sandbox, actual `seed.sh` from main `47214f1c`, temp `T3CODE_HOME`, `settings.json` = `{"providerInstances": {}}`, all `*_BIN`/`GROK_*` env empty; record in the fleet backlog probe dir `probe-2026-10-31-laneA-seed-mode/probe.txt`):

- Mode case: `settings.json` chmod `0600` before the run. Run exits 0 ("added antigravity, claudeAgent, codex, grok") and afterwards the file's mode is `0660` — the sandbox umask (0002) default. Under the more common umask 022 the same path yields `0644`, i.e. world-readable.
- Symlink case: `settings.json` a symlink to a sibling file. Run exits 0; afterwards `settings.json` is no longer a symlink (a regular file holds the seeded content) and the link target's content is unchanged — the seeded settings silently went somewhere the user's setup does not read through the link.
- Control nuance: on a run that changes nothing the script exits before the write block, so the mode/symlink survive — the damage happens exactly on the runs that write.

## Why it matters

The seed runs automatically before t3 starts, so the first store-path refresh or 1.x safety-disable silently widens a token-bearing file from owner-only to group/world-readable on the user's own machine, and breaks a symlinked settings layout without any message. Both are properties of the one shared write path, so one fix covers both.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] When the seed writes, the resulting `settings.json` has the same permission mode the file had before the run (a newly created file keeps the current default). A test in `test_seed.py` sets `0600`, runs a seed that changes something, and asserts the mode is still `0600`.
- [ ] If `settings.json` is a symlink, the write goes through to its target (the link survives and the target receives the seeded content), or the script refuses with a clear stderr message and changes nothing — it must not silently replace the link with a regular file. A test pins whichever behavior is chosen.
- [ ] Existing behavior is unchanged otherwise: malformed settings still left untouched with a warning (#2738), no-change runs still write nothing, and the current `test_seed.py` cases still pass.

Distinct from: #2738 (closed — malformed settings shapes crash/disable seeding; different failure in the read/validate path, not the write path).
