body:
🤖 Design-architect pass 27 (2026-10-31) — design issue. Full design doc: `files/designs/code-charges-pipeline-contract.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Audit at origin/main `8bae502f`, all code references verified on current main this pass.

## Summary

The charges pipeline built for #1057 has a pure core whose header states its philosophy — `charges-match.ts`: *"this module only decides what a charge IS, never what was already shown"* — but the pipeline never stated the three rules that philosophy needs: **what counts as a charge (admission), when two observations are the same charge (identity), and when an unmatched charge counts as shown (delivery).** Nine open filings are those three unstated rules, one per pipeline stage:

- **Admission** (`scripts/produce-charge-candidates.ts`): `isNotChargeSubject` (~L148–157) has no declined/failed pattern and nothing requires payment evidence, so declined alerts and amount-due-only invoices become candidates (#3120); the body amount fallback (~L208) matches `total` inside **Subtotal** and first-match wins, recording $20.00 for a $21.60 charge (#3121) — the wrong amount then defeats dedupe.
- **Identity** (`charges-match.ts`, `charges-collect.ts`): `matchCharges` dedupes on (amount, normalized merchant, ±3 days) without requiring **different sources** despite the header/#1057 scoping dedupe to across-sources, and empty-normalized merchants merge across merchants (#2130); `sameCharge` (charges-collect.ts:74) merges hand-fed rows on squashed **substring containment** (`Meta` vanishes against `METAMUCIL`, `AI` against `RAILWAY`, #3049) and never compares payment methods, so conflicting card masks merge away (#3123).
- **Classification**: `isSaasLooking`/`matchService` match substrings with no token boundary — `METAMUCIL` and `METAL ROOFING` classify as Meta (#3048) — and the collector's catalog is built only from `extractSaasServices()` (collect-fleet-feed.ts:435–437), so Anthropic/OpenAI charges can never match and always flood the attention strip (#3119).
- **Delivery**: surfaced keys are persisted at collection time (~L451), before the feed is written (~L646) and before the out-of-collector laptop transfer, so one failed delivery permanently suppresses flags (#3122); the live source consumes charges only inside the `saas` gate (live.ts:869), so a quota-view failure hides all auto-matched charges (#3124).

Pass 26 of this series assessed #3048/#3049 as a candidate to revisit "if a third instance files" — six more filed today. The condition is met.

**The rules (recorded here; full text, alternatives and risks in the design doc):**

> **A charge is evidence.** (1) **Admission requires payment evidence** — declined/failed and merely-due amounts produce no candidate; the amount is the amount *paid* (explicit paid/charged labels outrank a bare total; a bare total must be a standalone label, never a substring of "Subtotal"). (2) **Identity is one rule everywhere** — same charge only when provenance differs (cross-source dedupe; hand-fed vs auto merge), amounts equal, dates within the existing 3-day window, merchant identity holds at **token boundaries** (exact normalized equality for dedupe; token-boundary containment for the hand-fed merge, preserving the documented `METAPAY` / "Meta PAYG spill" pair), an empty normalized merchant never matches, and **conflicting known payment methods veto** the merge. (3) **Surfaced means delivered, and consumption is independent** — surfaced keys persist only for charges in a successfully published feed, and the live source consumes the charges sections on their own validity, never gated on an unrelated section. Classification corollary: names/aliases/markers match at token boundaries only, and the catalog is SaaS services **plus** quota pools and aliases from their existing extractors.

**Boundaries:** input-validity neighbours are NOT adopted — #2194 (impossible dates), #2445/#2439 (feed charges shape), #2448 (batch-discarding producer throw) are governed by #2576's fail-closed ingest contract and #3068's shape contract; this design governs identity, evidence and lifecycle of candidates that pass them. #3005 owns count/size measurement grammar; the producer's paid-amount labels are admission evidence, owned here. Producer scheduling (#2205) is operational and untouched.

## Phased breakdown (phases adopt the origins — no parallels)

- **Phase 1 — Identity.** #2130 + #3049 + #3123: one shared identity rule across `matchCharges` and `sameCharge`, one probe matrix (same-source repeats, empty-normalized pairs, Meta/METAMUCIL, AI/RAILWAY, the METAPAY control, conflicting/agreeing/absent methods).
- **Phase 2 — Admission & classification.** #3120 + #3121 + #3048 + #3119. Independent of Phase 1.
- **Phase 3 — Delivery.** #3122 + #3124, plus the closing truth-up on landing: the three rules written into the `charges-match.ts` / `charges-collect.ts` / producer headers and evidence posted on #1057. No separate audit issue — the surface inventory is closed (verified by repo-wide grep this pass: producer + collector scripts, charges-match, charges-collect, feed/live consumption only).

Open questions stay in the design doc (`unmatchedKey` gaining the method; #3122's confirm-after-publish vs pending-keys mechanism — either satisfies the rule, Phase 3 picks against the as-built publish flow).

## Acceptance

- [ ] Phase 1 origins (#2130, #3049, #3123) closed under the recorded identity rule, probe matrix as tests
- [ ] Phase 2 origins (#3120, #3121, #3048, #3119) closed under the admission + classification rules
- [ ] Phase 3 origins (#3122, #3124) closed; rules written into the module headers; evidence posted on #1057
- [ ] Register row for this design in `files/potential-projects.md` kept truthful as phases land

## Acceptance criteria

- The design doc (`files/designs/code-charges-pipeline-contract.md` in the goal workspace) states the three contract rules — admission, identity, delivery — for the charges pipeline.
- Each of the nine open filings named in the issue is linked to the contract section that governs it.
- Implementation of the contract is tracked by linked implementation issues (this design issue does not itself change pipeline code).

title: mcpx(config): an explicit mcpx.namespace is never checked as an identifier — 'my-ns', '9lives', 'a b' resolve verbatim and the generated client does not parse

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

An explicit `mcpx.namespace` in a server's config is only checked against the reserved-word list — never for being a valid identifier at all. A namespace like `my-ns`, `9lives`, `a b` or `foo.bar` passes `Resolve` unchanged and is printed verbatim into the generated client, which then does not parse in any runtime: **every** script, `mcpx types` load and exec against that daemon breaks, for every namespace — not just the misconfigured one. This is the same failure class #1649 fixed for *derived* namespaces (collision), through the door #1649 left open: the explicit override bypasses `SanitizeNamespace`, the one place that guarantees identifier shape.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe on current main)

Probe in the real `internal/config` + `internal/codegen` packages (laptop worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-nsident/`, detached at origin/main cd8c1137e; probe test + generated module kept there):

- `Config.Resolve` with `Mcpx.Namespace` set to each of `my-ns`, `9lives`, `a b`, `x;evil//`, `café`, `foo.bar`: **all ACCEPTED**, resolved namespace returned verbatim. Control `good_ns1` also accepted, as it should be.
- Feeding the resolved namespace through `codegen.Module` exactly as the daemon does emits, e.g.:
  - `export const my-ns = {`
  - `export const 9lives = {`
  - `export const a b = {`
  - `export const foo.bar = {`
- `bun build` on the generated module for `my-ns`: `error: Expected ";" but found "-"` at the `export const my-ns` line — the module does not parse.

## Where the chain breaks

- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/config/config.go:783` — `Namespace: pick(ex.Namespace, SanitizeNamespace(name))`: the explicit value wins and is never sanitized or shape-checked.
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/config/config.go:770-773` — the only explicit-namespace check is `codegen.ReservedNamespace(ex.Namespace)`.
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/codegen/ident.go:68-70` — `ReservedNamespace` is a denylist (reserved words ∪ runtime globals ∪ prelude names); `my-ns`, `9lives`, `a b`, `foo.bar` are none of those, so they pass.
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/config/config.go:651-665` — `SanitizeNamespace` (the derived path) guarantees a valid identifier by construction (`[^a-zA-Z0-9_]` → `_`, leading digit prefixed, reserved words suffixed); the explicit path gets none of that.
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/codegen/emit.go:144` — `Module` prints `export const %s = {` with the namespace verbatim; `emit.go:30` does the same for `declare namespace %s {` in `mcpx types` output. The Python target (#1917) has the same shape problem with its own identifier rules.

## Why it matters

The generated client is the single entry point for all script execution. One typo'd or hand-written explicit namespace (`my-ns` is the natural spelling a user would pick, mirroring their server name `my-server`) silently poisons the whole catalogue, and the error ("Expected ; but found -" in a generated temp file) points nowhere near the config that caused it. #1649's fix established the house rule — catch namespace problems at resolve time with an error naming the server — this is the remaining input that skips that rule.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Resolve` (or the same single choke point #1649 used) refuses an explicit `mcpx.namespace` that is not a valid identifier for the generated targets — leading letter/`_`/`$`, then letters/digits/`_`/`$` — with an error naming the server and the offending namespace, parallel to the existing reserved-word refusal at config.go:770.
- [ ] The check is shape-only: every explicit namespace that is a valid, non-reserved identifier today (e.g. `aa`, `good_ns1`) resolves exactly as before; derived namespaces are untouched.
- [ ] Regression tests cover the invalid shapes (hyphen, leading digit, space, dot, non-ASCII) and the valid control; existing `internal/config` and `internal/codegen` tests pass unchanged.
- [ ] Triage pins whether the Python target's stricter rules (no `$`) need the check tightened further, or whether that is a separate follow-up.

title: repo(opencode-config): 34 backup files (3.2 MB) are tracked on main — 24 dated opencode.jsonc snapshots, bin/ proxy .bak copies and a 0-byte .new — a recurrence of #367 that the 2026-10-29 residue cleanup never reached

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.description: Infrastructure / host-portability work

body:
## What

34 editor/tooling backup files — 3,233,450 bytes — are tracked on main at `9d8e191c` (verified this run, 2026-10-31, via `git ls-files`). This is a recurrence of #367 (closed 2026-10-20): that cleanup covered the `.bak` files of its day, and a fresh generation has been committed since.

### The set

- `.opencode/` — 25 files: 24 dated snapshots of the live config (`opencode.jsonc.bak-2026-10-24-*`, `opencode.jsonc.bak-2026-10-25-*`, `opencode.jsonc.bak-20261024*`, `opencode.jsonc.bak-20261025*`, each ~4,100–5,100 lines) plus `opencode.jsonc.backup` (189,518 B, the largest single file).
- `bin/` — 6 files: `codex-proxy.mjs.pre-warm-20261024`, `codex-proxy.mjs.resume-build.bak`, `commandcode-proxy-start.sh.bak-20261025003957-netfix`, `muse-proxy.mjs.bak-20261024-flag-tolerance`, `muse-proxy.mjs.bak-20261024121323-laptop-deploy`, and `proxy-supervise.mjs.new` (0 bytes — an empty placeholder).
- Root — `opencode.json.bak` (the live file is `opencode.jsonc`; the `.json` config no longer exists).
- `doc/2026-10-11T03-44-33Z_design_groups_events_delegation/spikes/s11-relay/certs/live/` — `leaf.key.bak-20261011T122827Z` and `leaf.pem.bak-20261011T122827Z`, duplicates of the spike's own tracked `leaf.key`/`leaf.pem` fixtures sitting next to them.

### How they landed

- `11fc50d2` "chore(config): snapshot local working state on amd" (2026-10-25) added most of them in one commit: 122,147 insertions across 35 files, including all 24 `.opencode` dated backups and the `bin/` copies.
- `8e06e88f` (2026-10-28, the sanctioned parked-dirt commit) carried `opencode.jsonc.backup` in with the live config edits.

### Why the obvious fix is the wrong fix here

The root `.gitignore` tail (2026-10-29 note) records Drew's explicit call: config backups (`.opencode/*.bak-*`) are **NOT** to be gitignored — they are audit references, and hiding them behind `.gitignore` loses work; they are cleaned by moving them to dated residue dirs (e.g. `~/primary-residue-2026-10-29`). So this issue is **not** "add ignore rules". It is: the residue move prescribed on 2026-10-29 has never been applied to the copies already committed to main, so every clone still carries 3.2 MB of superseded config snapshots, and the snapshot-commit path that swept them in is still the way the next generation will arrive.

Verified this run: `git check-ignore` matches none of the 34 paths (exit 1), and `git grep` finds no reference to any of these filenames anywhere else in the tree — nothing builds, runs, or documents from them; the live files (`opencode.jsonc`, the `bin/*.mjs` proxies) are all present separately.

## Why it matters

- Every clone and every CI checkout carries ~3.2 MB of stale config copies that differ from the live config in ways nobody tracks — a reader (human or agent) who opens the wrong copy gets provider/model settings that are days stale and look authoritative.
- 24 near-identical 5,000-line config snapshots make repo-wide searches for config keys return two dozen dead hits, burying the live one.
- The spike-cert `.bak` pair normalizes keeping backup copies of key material in the tree next to the fixtures themselves.
- Sibling, not duplicate: #3097 covers the same class inside `pkgs/id` (clippy/cargo scratch at the package root); this issue covers the `.opencode/` + `bin/` + root set and the snapshot-commit mechanism behind it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The 34 listed backup files are preserved outside the repo first (dated residue dir on the laptop, per the 2026-10-29 policy), then removed from tracking on main; the live files (`opencode.jsonc`, `bin/*.mjs`, the spike's `leaf.key`/`leaf.pem`) are untouched.
- [ ] No `.gitignore` rule is added for `*.bak` / `*.bak-*` / `*.backup` / `*.new` — the 2026-10-29 decision stands; the fix is the residue move, not hiding.
- [ ] A lightweight guard exists that names this class at commit/snapshot time (e.g. the snapshot/keeper path refuses or flags tracked paths matching `.bak`, `.bak-*`, `.backup`, `.pre-warm*`, `*.mjs.new`), so the next snapshot commit cannot silently re-add a generation — or the issue documents why the existing keeper already does and this set predates it.
- [ ] After removal, a repo-wide search for a key that only exists in the live config returns exactly one config file, and `git ls-files | grep -E '\.backup$|\.bak|pre-warm|resume-build|\.mjs\.new$'` is empty.

title: id(artifact): friend_remove `requests` is the one known-kind body parsed() never validates — any count, any shape, any length passes, and every string lands permanently in the directory's removed_requests void guard

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Problem

`SignedArtifact::parsed()` validates every field of the other known artifact kinds — but a `friend_remove` body's `requests` list is checked for nothing at all: not its length, not the shape of its entries, not their size.

Evidence on main (`b3b9ad33`, `pkgs/id/src/artifact.rs:318-335`): the `FRIEND_REMOVE` arm of `parsed()` decodes `FriendRemove`, calls `check_key` on `a` and `b`, refuses `a == b`, and requires the author to be one of them. It never inspects `body.requests`. Compare the sibling arms in the same function: `HOME_DECLARED` caps servers at `MAX_HOME_SERVERS` and validates each endpoint/world, `DOCUMENT` caps content at `MAX_DOCUMENT_BYTES`, `TAG` requires a hash-shaped subject and caps name (64 B) and value (256 B). `FriendRemove` is defined at `artifact.rs:139-148` with `requests: Vec<String>` and `#[serde(default)]` — no bound anywhere.

Every legitimate producer builds this list in exactly one place, `Directory::friendship_requests` (`pkgs/id/src/directory.rs:1710-1721`): the request that formed the friendship (`friend_requests`, at most one) plus `pending_id(a, b)` and `pending_id(b, a)` (at most one each), sorted and deduped — **at most 3 IDs**. And every real request ID is an envelope ID: `Envelope::signed` (`directory.rs:366-376`) sets `id = hex_encode(&nonce)` over a 16-byte nonce, i.e. exactly 32 lowercase hex characters.

## Verified this run

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-friendremove/` (verbatim test against the laptop checkout, whose `artifact.rs`/`directory.rs` sha256-match sandbox main; output in `probe.txt` there): a `friend_remove` artifact signed by account `a`, naming 100 request IDs — 99 of the form `not-an-envelope-id-<n>` and one 500-character string — passes both gates:

- `artifact.parsed()` returns `Ok(Some(Kind::FriendRemove(..)))` with all 100 entries verbatim;
- `ArtifactLog::insert(..)` accepts it as `Stored::New`.

## Why it matters

The list is not inert. `Directory::receive_artifact` (`directory.rs:1392-1403`) applies a `FriendRemoved` entry whenever `requests` is non-empty, even for a pair that was never friends, and `Directory::apply` (`directory.rs:1698-1705`) extends the permanent `removed_requests` set with **every** string in the list. That set is the void guard consulted for every future `FriendRequested` entry (`directory.rs:1665-1671`) and it is replayed from the journal on every open, so junk entries persist and are re-processed forever. One signed artifact (bounded only by the 1 MiB frame) can therefore plant thousands of arbitrary strings — up to ~1 MiB of them — into every receiving server's directory state, none of which can ever name a real request. It also breaks the invariant the rest of the module maintains: a stored known-kind artifact is one whose body passed the same shape rules its producers obey.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `SignedArtifact::parsed()` (or an equivalent single validation point on the receive/store path) refuses a `friend_remove` body whose `requests` has more entries than a legitimate removal can carry (at most 3 today: formed-by + one pending per direction; if a named constant is introduced, producers and the check share it).
- [ ] Each entry in `requests` must be a well-formed envelope/request ID (32 lowercase hex characters, matching `Envelope::signed`'s `hex_encode` of a 16-byte nonce); anything else is refused with a `Refusal::Forbidden` naming the rule, consistent with the sibling arms.
- [ ] A test signs a `friend_remove` with (a) 4 well-formed IDs, (b) one non-hex / wrong-length ID, and (c) one over-long ID string, and asserts all three are refused by `parsed()` and by `ArtifactLog::insert` / `Directory::receive_artifact`; a legitimate removal produced by `Directory::remove_friend` (via `friendship_requests`) still parses, stores, and applies.
- [ ] No change to the wire format, to `FriendRemove`'s fields, or to the semantics of `removed_requests` for legitimate removals.

Distinct from: #2637 / #2404 / #1899 (directory_mail validation gaps — different module, different fields); the tag/document/home-declared caps above (those kinds are already validated; this is the one arm that is not).

title: id(cli): space-form `--new` swallows the subcommand as the instance name — the documented `id --new serve` creates .iroh/serve/ and starts the REPL instead of serving under a random name

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`id --new` is declared with an optional value (`num_args = 0..=1`), and clap greedily consumes the next token as that value — including when the next token is the subcommand. The documented random-name example therefore does the opposite of what it says:

- `pkgs/id/src/cli.rs:170-171` — `#[arg(long, global = true, num_args = 0..=1, default_missing_value = "", value_name = "NAME", conflicts_with = "data_dir")] pub new: Option<String>`
- `pkgs/id/src/cli.rs:162-168` — the doc examples: `id --new my-dev serve --port 0`, `id --new serve` ("Random name (auto-generated)"), `id --new my-dev list`.
- `pkgs/id/src/cli.rs:189-191` — `command: Option<Command>`; "If `None`, the REPL is started." `main.rs:147` dispatches `None => run_repl(None)`.
- `pkgs/id/src/main.rs:88-112` — a non-empty `--new` name creates `.iroh/<name>/` and bails if it already exists.

So `id --new serve` creates an instance literally named `serve` under `.iroh/serve/` and starts the interactive REPL — it does not start a server, and it does not use a random name. A second run of the same documented command then fails outright: "instance directory already exists: .iroh/serve (use --data-dir to reuse an existing directory)". The same swallowing hits every bare subcommand: `id --new list`, `id --new id`, `id --new repl`, … all become instance names with no subcommand.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneA-clap-new/`): a minimal clap 4.6.7 derive struct replicating the exact `Cli` shape (global `--data-dir` with `conflicts_with = "new"`, global `--new` with `num_args = 0..=1` + `default_missing_value = ""`, and an optional subcommand enum), run against the pinned clap version in `pkgs/id/Cargo.lock` (clap 4.6.7):

```text
--new serve        => new=Some("serve")   command=None        BUG (documented as random-name serve)
--new my-dev serve => new=Some("my-dev")  command=Some(Serve) control, works
--new list         => new=Some("list")    command=None        BUG (any bare subcommand is swallowed)
--new              => new=Some("")        command=None        random name, as intended
--new=serve        => new=Some("serve")   command=None        explicit name via =, expected
serve --new        => new=Some("")        command=Some(Serve) trailing form works
```

Coverage gap that let this ship: every `--new` integration test uses the `=` form (`pkgs/id/tests/cli_integration.rs:3696ff` — `--new=`, `--new=test-instance`, `--new=dup`, `--new=../escape`); no test exercises a space-form `--new` followed by a subcommand.

## Why it matters

`--new` is the documented way to spin up a throwaway instance, and its own help text gives the broken command as the example. A user following the docs gets an interactive REPL in a directory named after their subcommand instead of a running server, and the leftover `.iroh/serve/` directory then makes the same command fail on retry. The failure is silent about the real cause — nothing says the subcommand was eaten as a name.

## Acceptance criteria

- `id --new serve` behaves as documented: a randomly-named instance directory is created and the `serve` subcommand runs. More generally, a bare token that names a subcommand is never consumed as the `--new` value (e.g. `--new list`, `--new id` likewise).
- The forms that work today keep working: `--new` alone (random name), `--new=<name> <cmd>`, `--new <name> <cmd>` (named instance), and a trailing `--new` after the subcommand.
- Help text / doc examples and the actual parsing agree for every form shown at `cli.rs:152-168`.
- New integration tests in `pkgs/id/tests/cli_integration.rs` cover the space forms — at minimum `--new serve`-style subcommand non-consumption (using a fast subcommand such as `id`) and `--new <name> <cmd>` — alongside the existing `=`-form tests.

title: mcpx(stats): CallStats/Calls row order is nondeterministic on equal totals — the Server+Tool concatenation tie-break is not a total order ("a"+"bc" == "ab"+"c")

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The call-statistics tables in mcpx have no deterministic order when two
server+tool rows tie on total time and their names concatenate to the same
string. Both implementations collect rows by ranging a Go map, then sort
with the same tie-break:

```go
return out[i].Server+out[i].Tool < out[j].Server+out[j].Tool
```

- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/eventstore/stats.go:92-97` (`Store.CallStats`)
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/logstore/stats.go:107-112` (`Store.Calls`) — the
  eventstore file header says the aggregation "mirrors logstore.Calls
  exactly — same grouping, same nearest-rank percentiles, same ordering".

Concatenation is not an ordering on pairs: `("a","bc")` and `("ab","c")`
both produce `"abc"`, so the comparator reports them equal in both
directions. `sort.Slice` is not stable, and the pre-sort order comes from
Go map iteration, which is randomized — so the row order of the two rows
varies from call to call whenever their `TotalMs` values are equal
(equal totals are common: every row whose calls carry no duration sits
at 0, and identical durations tie exactly).

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-statstie/` (on the
laptop, per fleet rules): a verbatim copy of the aggregation tail —
map collection plus the exact comparator above — over the two
concat-colliding keys `("a","bc")` and `("ab","c")` with equal totals,
400 iterations in one process:

```text
 351 x a/bc then ab/c
  49 x ab/c then a/bc
RESULT: NONDETERMINISTIC ORDER for equal-total concat-colliding pairs
```

Code reading confirms both production sites share the comparator and
both build `out` by ranging `counts` (eventstore stats.go:83-91,
logstore stats.go:96-106).

## Why it matters

- The two stores are contractually the same table (#1850): the package
  test `TestCallStatsAgreeWithLogstore`
  (internal/eventstore/eventstore_test.go:162) compares the two outputs
  **row by row, in order**. Its fixture uses distinct totals (45 vs 75),
  so the tie path is never exercised; a fixture with an equal-total
  concat-colliding pair would make that test flaky in both directions.
- Any consumer rendering or diffing the stats table (dashboard, CLI)
  sees rows swap positions between calls with no data change.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The tie-break in both `CallStats` (eventstore) and `Calls`
  (logstore) compares server, then tool, as separate fields (no string
  concatenation), so the ordering is a total order on distinct
  (server, tool) pairs.
- [ ] `TestCallStatsAgreeWithLogstore` (or a sibling test) gains a
  fixture with at least one equal-total, concatenation-colliding pair
  such as `("a","bc")` / `("ab","c")`, and passes deterministically
  (`go test ./internal/eventstore ./internal/logstore -count=5
  -shuffle=on` on laptop or CI).
- [ ] A repeated-call determinism check: calling `CallStats`/`Calls`
  many times over the same fixture returns the identical row order
  every time.
- [ ] No other ordering changes: TotalMs-descending primary order and
  the percentile math stay exactly as they are.

Related: #1850 (the one-table-for-every-statistic work that made the
two implementations mirror each other). Distinct from #3103 (diagnose
fieldInMessage map-order tie — different package, different mechanism:
that one picks a blameworthy field; this one is a sort comparator that
is not a total order).

title: id(world): the plain `id world join` pump bypasses the shared line grammar for /input — unvalidated hex is sent to the server and dropped, a bare /input is posted as chat, and the two-space form is accepted here but rejected by the grammar

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: status/needs-triage
labels.description: Not yet triaged; needs a first look

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: queue/queued
labels.description: Has a queued queue task

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/id/src/world_line.rs` declares itself the single parser for the world's line grammar — its module docs (lines 1–7) say the SSH command mode, the `id world join` stdin pump, and the `id world` CLI subcommands "all speak the same verbs", with `parse_line` mapping one line to one action "so a sentence works identically" on every surface. The command-mode pump honours that (`pump_command`, `pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs:1694` calls `parse_line`). The plain (non-command-mode) pump does not: at `pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs:1630–1633` it hand-rolls `/input` handling —

```rust
match line.strip_prefix("/input ") {
    Some(hex) => serde_json::json!({"type": "input", "data_hex": hex.trim()}),
    None => serde_json::json!({"type": "chat", "text": line}),
}
```

— with no hex validation, no lowercase normalisation, and no usage message. The same typed line therefore behaves differently depending on whether the user passed `--command-mode`:

| Line typed | Shared grammar (`parse_line`, command mode / SSH) | Plain pump |
|---|---|---|
| `/input ZZ` | local `usage: /input <hex>`, nothing sent | frame sent; server replies error frame `input data must be hexadecimal` (`world_session/mod.rs:2212–2219`), input dropped |
| `/input 0` (odd length) | local `usage: /input <hex>`, nothing sent | frame sent; same server error, input dropped |
| `/input` (bare) | local `usage: /input <hex>`, nothing sent | sent as **chat text** — the literal word `/input` is posted into the world |
| `/input  00af` (two spaces) | local `usage: /input <hex>`, nothing sent | **accepted** (`hex.trim()`), input delivered — the inverse divergence |
| `/input 00AF` | normalised to `00af` before sending | sent as typed (`00AF`); the server happens to accept it |

Verified this run with a verbatim-copy probe (parse_line copied byte-for-byte from main `b878339e`, diff-checked; the plain-pump arm and the server's `decode_hex` gate replicated): laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneA-pump-input/probe.txt`.

## Why it matters

- The plain pump is the scripted surface (`id world join` reading stdin lines from a pipe). A typo'd hex string silently becomes a dropped input plus a server error frame on stdout — the pump's own contract is that stdout stays a clean stream of frames and user-facing notes go to stderr (`commands/world.rs` pump docs) — instead of an immediate local usage message.
- A bare `/input` (easy to type when a script emits a verb with an empty argument) is posted into the world as chat text.
- The two surfaces disagree in both directions (the plain pump also *accepts* the two-space form the grammar rejects), so a script tested against one surface breaks on the other.

## Distinct from existing issues

- #1946 is about `parse_line` *internally*: `/document` and `/input` there reject two spaces while siblings trim. This issue is the plain pump not calling `parse_line` at all for `/input`. Fixing #1946 does not fix this, and vice versa.
- #1507 / #819 covered word boundaries and the command-mode pump's handling of parse messages; neither touches the plain pump's `/input` arm.

## Acceptance criteria

- The plain pump validates `/input` through the shared grammar's rules (even length, ASCII hex only) before sending: invalid hex and a bare `/input` produce the local `usage: /input <hex>` message on stderr and send nothing.
- `/input` is never delivered to the world as chat text.
- Valid hex is normalised the same way on both pump paths (lowercased), so the frame bytes do not depend on `--command-mode`.
- The two-space behaviour matches the grammar's (whatever #1946 decides there, both surfaces agree).
- Tests cover the plain-pump mapping for: valid hex, uppercase hex, non-hex, odd-length hex, bare `/input`, and a non-`/input` chat line.

title: mcpx(elicit): the deadline is never checked on the answer path — Respond accepts answers to overdue questions and Get still presents them as pending

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

mcpx elicitation deadlines are enforced only on the wait/list paths, not on the answer path. A question whose deadline (`expiresAt` = min(lastTouched+ttl, created+maxAge), decision 0006 touch-on-read) has passed stays `state='pending'` in the store until something lazily expires it — and in that window it can still be **answered successfully**, and is still **presented as a live pending question**. Expiry is lazy by design ("expire on read, no sweeper"), but the two reads/writes that matter most don't expire:

- `Broker.Respond` (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/elicit/elicit.go:465ff`) checks only `r.State != Pending` and claims the row with `UPDATE … WHERE state='pending'`. It never compares `ExpiresAt` to now. Its callers don't either: the daemon's `POST /v1/elicit/{id}/{action}` handler (`internal/daemon/server.go`, `handleElicitAnswer`) and the CLI's `elicit answer|decline|cancel` (`internal/cli/elicit.go`) pass straight through.
- `Broker.Get` (`elicit.go:580ff`) — the item read behind `GET /v1/elicit/{id}` and `mcpx elicit show` — never calls `expireOverdue`. Its `touch` refuses to *revive* an overdue question (`elicit.go:619`), but `Get` still returns it with `state: pending` and `ttlRemainingMs: 0`, so an answerer polling the item (the documented answerer flow) sees a live question and answers it — and `Respond` accepts.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 37df0a65)

Complete enumeration of the deadline enforcement in the broker (grep over `internal/elicit/elicit.go`, non-test):

- `ExpiresAt` is compared against now in exactly two places: `Await`'s poll loop (`:457`, expires only while a waiter is actively waiting) and `touch` (`:619`, no-revive only).
- `expireOverdue` (`:701`) is called from exactly two places: `Open` (`:210`) and `Pending` (`:674`). Not from `Get`, not from `Respond`.
- `Respond`'s claim is `UPDATE elicitations SET state=? WHERE id=? AND state='pending'` — no `expires_ms` condition.

Scenario: a question is opened with a 1-minute TTL; the asker's `Await` is bounded by its own ctx (e.g. `internal/daemon/consumer.go` sampling bounds the wait by ctx precisely because reads renew TTL) and gives up. No `Pending`/`Open` call happens. An hour later `mcpx elicit answer <id> '<json>'` (or the equivalent POST) succeeds: the row becomes `answered`, an answer row is stored, `Lookup` returns it — an answer to a question that died an hour earlier, potentially carrying form/sampling content (incl. credential-shaped fields, cf. #1678's review-before-relay) to a flow that has moved on. Symmetrically, `mcpx elicit show <id>` / `GET /v1/elicit/{id}` report the dead question as `pending`.

Distinct from: #1691 (concurrent-answer race — the claim itself, fixed), #1677/#1675 (retention/hygiene of terminal rows), #1884 (TTL renewal convention). None of them checks the deadline on `Respond`/`Get`.

## Why it matters

The deadline is the safety property of the broker: it's what makes an abandoned or much-glimpsed question "still die by maxAge" (the `deadline` doc comment). A write path that ignores it means expiry is advisory — any answerer (human at the CLI, an event-driven hook, another process holding the id) can resurrect-and-answer a dead question indefinitely, as long as nobody happens to list pending questions or open a new one first.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Broker.Respond` refuses (or first settles as expired, per the #1691 loser semantics) an answer for a pending question whose `ExpiresAt` is in the past; the refusal/settlement is covered by a failing-first test with an overdue-but-unexpired row.
- [ ] `Broker.Get` on an overdue pending question settles/reports it as expired (mirroring `Pending`'s expire-on-read), so `GET /v1/elicit/{id}` and `mcpx elicit show` never present a dead question as pending.
- [ ] A live question within its deadline still answers and touches exactly as before (existing elicit tests green, package-scoped: `go test ./internal/elicit -count=1`).
- [ ] The expiry race stays #1691-clean: an answer that lands concurrently with expiry resolves to the documented already-answered/expired outcome, not a raw store error.

body:
## Summary

Both hand-maintained command lists for the `id` CLI omit entire top-level command families that exist in the clap definition, and nothing guards either list against drifting again.

Verified on main `de4663ec056ac5852522422e7de62370ee4c1d68`:

- `pkgs/id/src/cli.rs:200` `pub enum Command` declares **20** top-level commands: `serve, repl, put, put-hash, get, get-hash, cat, show, peek, find, search, list, group, doc, claim, tag, migrate-tags, id, peers, world` (`Group` at cli.rs:1056, `Doc` at 1081, `Claim` at 1101, `World(Box<WorldCommand>)` at 1043).
- The module-doc command list at `pkgs/id/src/cli.rs:10-27` names only **15** — it omits `group`, `doc`, `claim`, `world`, and `migrate-tags`.
- The user-facing "CLI Commands" table at `pkgs/id/README.md:102-121` names only **16** — it omits `group`, `doc`, `claim`, and `world`.
- The omitted `world` family alone is `pub enum WorldCommand` at `pkgs/id/src/cli.rs:1398` with 27 subcommand variants (create/join/invite/install/records/mirror/download/ssh-tunnel/compile/caps/logs/stats/replay/verify/…), i.e. the largest command family in the CLI is invisible in both command lists. `group`, `doc`, and `claim` are the Phase-5 claims/groups surface (see `pkgs/id/src/commands/group.rs`, `doc.rs`, `claim.rs`).

## Why it matters

A new user (or an agent) reading the README or the `cli` module docs cannot discover that `id group`, `id doc`, `id claim`, or `id world …` exist at all; the only complete list is `id --help` output or the enum itself. The repo already treats this drift class as worth a guard elsewhere — `just-recipes.json` got a drift guard in #2729 — but the two prose command lists have no guard, so they will drift again the next time a command is added (the lists already disagree with each other: README has `migrate-tags`, the cli.rs doc does not).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `pkgs/id/README.md` "CLI Commands" table lists all 20 top-level commands from `Command` in `pkgs/id/src/cli.rs`, with correct aliases (clap `alias`/`aliases` attributes) and one-line descriptions.
- [ ] The command list in the `pkgs/id/src/cli.rs` module doc (lines 10-27) lists the same 20 commands.
- [ ] A guard test (e.g. in `pkgs/id/src/cli.rs` tests or `pkgs/id/tests/cli_integration.rs`) enumerates the top-level subcommands via clap (`Cli::command().get_subcommands()`, including aliases' canonical names) and fails if any canonical command name is missing from the README table or the module-doc list — so adding a command without updating both lists turns CI red.
- [ ] Existing CLI parse tests stay green; no command behavior changes.

Found by new-issue-creator-code-a, 2026-10-31. Dedup: searched open + closed issues for id README / CLI command list / command table drift — no existing issue covers these lists (#1883/#1893/#1903 are mcpx docs surfaces; #2729 is the just-recipes guard, a different file).

body:
## Finding
PR #2149's `sameCharge` merge predicate drops a hand-fed charge row whenever an auto row has the same amount, a date within the dedupe window, and a squashed merchant containment — it never compares payment methods. Two genuinely different charges on different cards (e.g. an auto $20 METAPAY row on Visa •7535 vs a hand-fed $20 Meta PAYG incident on Visa •9545) collapse into one, deleting evidence — where the pre-existing `extractCharges()` deduplication explicitly includes the card in a charge's identity. Codex flagged this P2 on the PR (comment 4409381665); it merged unchanged and is still on main.

## Evidence
- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/2149 (merged, 7d064e5f, #1057)
- Current main: `pm-stack/aggregator/src/charges-collect.ts:74` — `sameCharge` compares amount, date window, and squashed label only; `method` is never read.

## Why it matters
Hand-fed rows exist precisely for incidents the auto read cannot see properly (PAYG spills on a specific card). Merging them away on a merchant+amount coincidence loses exactly that evidence.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] When both rows carry known, conflicting card masks, they are NOT treated as the same charge.
- [ ] Same-charge merging still works when masks agree or either row lacks a method; existing charges-collect tests pass.

title: fix(ci): auto-format push is rejected when the format diff touches workflow files (PR #2148)

labels.name: kind/ci
labels.description: CI/CD pipelines, workflows, and build automation

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding
PR #2148's auto-format workflow formats every changed file with treefmt (whose prettier set includes `.github/workflows/*.yml`), stages with `git add -A`, and pushes with the default `GITHUB_TOKEN`. GitHub refuses pushes that update workflow files from a token without workflow-write authorization, so whenever a merged change needs a formatting fix in a workflow file, the bot's push — and every retry — is rejected, and the unrelated formatting fixes in the same commit are lost with it. Codex flagged this P2 on the PR (comment 4409644280, with GitHub docs links); it merged unchanged and is still on main.

## Evidence
- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/2148
- Current main: `.github/workflows/auto-format.yml` — `permissions: contents: write` only, default checkout token, `git add -A` at :82, push/retry loop after.
- Related but distinct: #2014 investigates fleet-wide token strategy as a design question; this issue is the concrete failure in the workflow as shipped.

## Why it matters
The workflow's promise is that formatting drift is fixed within seconds of merge. The one class of files most likely to be hand-edited in this repo — its many workflow files — makes the whole auto-format commit unpushable.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A format diff touching `.github/workflows/*.yml` no longer blocks the rest of the commit: either the push uses a token authorized for workflow updates, or workflow files are excluded/handled separately with the remainder still landing.
- [ ] The loop-safety guards (bot-commit skip, GITHUB_TOKEN non-retrigger) still hold.

title: fix(aggregator): validateCredentialRef checks credential-value keys with 'in' (prototype chain), not own keys (PR #2115)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.name: effort/xs

labels.name: app/pm-stack
labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

body:
## Finding

`validateCredentialRef` in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/token-adapter.ts` (added by PR #2115, the browser-token adapter framework core for #1153) checks for credential-value keys with the `in` operator, which walks the prototype chain — so the framework's "references only, never values" contract can be both bypassed in spirit and tripped by inheritance:

- A ref object created with `Object.create({ token: "…" })` (or a class instance whose prototype carries one of the listed keys) is rejected even though it carries no own credential value.
- More importantly, the check's semantics are the opposite of the house own-property rule used everywhere else in this codebase family (e.g. the own-key rule in `quota-gather-map.ts`, #2781): validation of a security contract should inspect the object's OWN keys (`Object.hasOwn`), not inherited ones. As adapters start consuming refs built by other code (#1159/#1161/#1163/#1165/#1301), inherited-key false positives and inconsistent semantics are a live trap.

CodeRabbit flagged exactly this as a P2 on PR #2115 (token-adapter.ts, "Minor: Use own-key checks for credential fields in validateCredentialRef"); the PR merged unchanged, with no reply and no follow-up commit, and the code is still in this shape on current main.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/2115 (merged, commit 48e9aebc)
- Current main `4c34c57c10ed7ef9aa979e90277e9440459dd52f`: `pm-stack/aggregator/src/token-adapter.ts:49` defines `VALUE_BEARING_KEYS`; `:57-58` — `for (const key of VALUE_BEARING_KEYS) { if (key in record) { … } }`.
- The module's own header contract (same file): "Any other shape — above all, any object carrying a credential VALUE — is a contract violation and is rejected before an adapter runs."
- Existing tests (`pm-stack/aggregator/test/token-adapter.test.ts`) cover own-key value-bearing refs only; no test pins the inherited-key case in either direction.

## Why it matters

This is the credential-safety gate for every per-provider browser-token adapter that will be built on this framework. A validation primitive whose key semantics differ from the rest of the stack invites both false rejections (refs built on prototypes) and false confidence (reviewers reading `key in record` as an own-key check). It is a one-line fix now, before five adapters inherit the pattern.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `validateCredentialRef` rejects value-bearing keys based on the ref's OWN properties only (e.g. `Object.hasOwn` / `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call`).
- [ ] A test pins both directions: a ref with an own `token`/`cookie`/… key is rejected; a plain `{ kind: "bitwarden", name }` / `{ kind: "file", path, mode: 0o600 }` ref validates (including one whose prototype happens to carry a listed key name, if that is the chosen semantics — or the rejection of inherited keys is documented as deliberate in the module comment).
- [ ] No change to the accepted ref shapes, the `0600` file contract, or `credentialRefLabel` output.

body:
## Problem

The shared `key=value` plain-text renderer for `id group`, `id doc` and `id claim` — `text()` in `pkgs/id/src/commands/group.rs:64-72`, used by `tokens()` (group.rs:75) and reached from doc.rs `print_action`/`print_rows` (doc.rs:40,51) and claim.rs `print_set`/`claim_fields` (claim.rs:26,36) — passes Unicode format characters (category Cf) raw to the terminal in both of its paths:

```rust
Value::String(string) if string.chars().any(|c| c.is_whitespace() || c.is_control()) => {
    Value::String(string.clone()).to_string()
}
Value::String(string) => string.clone(),
```

1. **Unquoted path:** the quoting trigger is `is_whitespace() || is_control()`. `char::is_control()` is category Cc only and `is_whitespace()` is the White_Space property; every Cf character — U+202A–U+202E (bidi embedding/override, incl. RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE), U+2066–U+2069 (isolates), U+200E/U+200F (LRM/RLM), U+200B, U+FEFF, U+00AD — is neither, so a stored claim name/value carrying only an override is returned byte-identical.
2. **Quoted path:** even when quoting does trigger (e.g. the value also contains a space), the quoted form is a serde_json string literal, which escapes only control characters, `"` and `\` — the Cf character is emitted raw inside the quotes, where it still acts on terminal rendering.

A RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE in a claim value therefore visually reorders the rest of the row on a terminal: the stored name/value sit before the row's real trailing `author=` and `event=` fields (the exact field order the #1611 fix protected against *textual* forgery), so the spoof the renderer exists to prevent can still be done *visually*. Zero-width/format characters (U+200B, U+FEFF, U+00AD) likewise reach the terminal invisibly, so two rows that look identical can carry different bytes.

## How the values get there

Claim names/values are signed tag events that sync between nodes. Ingest validation (`check_text`, `pkgs/id/src/tag_claims.rs:145-153`) checks only byte length and NFC; Cf characters are NFC-stable, so a claim authored by another node with a U+202E in its name or value passes `check_op`, is stored, and is printed by `id claim list` / `id claim search` (and the same renderer serves `id doc` rows and `id group` output).

## Evidence (verified this run, main `201e0c35`)

- Source read: group.rs:64-72 (trigger + both paths), group.rs:75 (`tokens`), claim.rs:26/36 (stored name/value fields placed before `author=`/`event=`), doc.rs:40/51 (shared use), tag_claims.rs:145-153 (length + NFC only).
- Laptop Rust probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneA-group-text-cf/`, rustc, replicating the exact predicate): for U+202E, U+202A, U+2066, U+200B, U+200E, U+FEFF and U+00AD — `is_control=false is_whitespace=false quoted_trigger=false` in every case.
- Python `unicodedata` cross-check: all seven are category Cf and not White_Space.

## Distinct from existing issues

- #2839 covers the *other* renderer, `plain_field` in `pkgs/id/src/commands/text.rs` (TSV rows in `id peers` / REPL). Its fix extends `breaks_row` there; it does not touch `group::text`, whose trigger, quoting rule and consumers are different code.
- #1611 (closed) fixed this same renderer for whitespace/control (newline forgery); Cf was outside its trigger set, as it was for the petname fix in #1674 (closed).
- #1778 is ingest-side validation for directory account/group names — a different store, and this renderer's ruling (see text.rs module doc) is that rendering must be safe regardless of what ingest allowed, because a store may already hold the value.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A claim name or value containing U+202E (alone, and combined with a space so the quoted path is taken) renders with the Cf character escaped (e.g. `\u202e`) in `id claim list`/`search` plain output — it never reaches the terminal raw; same for the other Cf characters named above.
- [ ] Regression tests in the group.rs renderer tests (alongside `test_newline_in_value_stays_one_line` etc.) cover: Cf-only value (unquoted path) and Cf-plus-space value (quoted path).
- [ ] Values with no structure-breaking or format characters still render byte-identically to before (existing tests, incl. `test_space_free_values_render_byte_identically` and `test_json_output_is_unchanged`, stay green); `--json` output is unchanged.
- [ ] The fix is in the shared renderer (`text`/`tokens`), so `id group`, `id doc` and `id claim` all inherit it — no per-command copies.

title: mcpx(diagnose): fieldInMessage breaks equal-length ties by Go map order — the same rejection message blames a different field on different runs

body:
## Problem

`fieldInMessage` in `pkgs/mcpx/internal/diagnose` — the function that decides which declared argument a server's rejection message "wants" — iterates the shape's property map and keeps the longest matching name, but breaks **equal-length ties by Go map iteration order**. When a message names two same-length fields in the same class (both bare tokens, or both quoted), the blamed field changes from run to run, and with it the diagnostic's `Field`, its "it wants \<type\>" text, and its `Changed` attribution.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `facf6481`)

- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/diagnose/diagnose.go:582-607` — `fieldInMessage` ranges `for name := range shape.Props` (a map) and replaces the incumbent only when `len(name) > len(best)` within the same quoted class (lines 597-603: quoted-vs-bare mismatch handled first, then `len(name) <= len(best)` skips). Nothing orders equal-length candidates, and Go map range order is deliberately random per iteration.
- The doc comment (diagnose.go:571-580) specifies the ranking — quoted occurrence outranks bare token, "within a class the longest name wins" — and is silent on ties, so the tie outcome is unspecified *and* unstable.
- The result is load-bearing at the only call site, `diagnose.go:523-533`: the returned field becomes `Diagnostic.Field`, is interpolated into the message (`the server rejected %s (it wants %s)`), and drives `cat.change(tool.Path(), field)`.

First-hand probe on the laptop (the four functions copied verbatim from current main into a scratch module; `Shape` stubbed with the same map type), same input, 4000 calls in one process:

```
msg "user and name are incompatible; host and port conflict", props {user,name,host,port} (all 4 chars, all bare tokens):
  run 1: map[host:514 name:498 port:507 user:2481]
  run 2: map[host:498 name:514 port:473 user:2515]
msg "'user' and 'name' are both wrong", props {user,name} (both quoted):
  run 1: map[name:484 user:3516]
  run 2: map[name:472 user:3528]
```

Every tied candidate wins some iterations; nothing but map order varies. (The skew toward the first-inserted key is Go's small-map iteration bias — the point is that all outcomes occur.)

## Why it matters

mcpx diagnostics are the user-facing explanation of a failed call, and the fleet's own standard elsewhere in this codebase is deterministic tie-breaking: `nearmiss.Nearest` (internal/nearmiss/nearmiss.go:105-108) explicitly breaks ties lexicographically "so the answer never depends on the order candidates were enumerated in". `fieldInMessage` missed that treatment when #1646/#3041 rebuilt its matching: the same failed call can blame `user` in one run and `name` in the next, pointing the user (and any test or snapshot built on the diagnostic) at different arguments and different schema types for identical input. It also makes any future regression test over a tie case flaky by construction.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `fieldInMessage` is deterministic: for a fixed message and shape, repeated calls always return the same field, including when two or more same-length fields match in the same class (bare or quoted). The tie rule is stated in the doc comment (e.g. lexicographically smallest name, matching `nearmiss.Nearest`, or first occurrence in the message — either is acceptable if documented and tested).
- [ ] The existing ranking is preserved: a quoted occurrence still outranks a bare token, and a longer name still beats a shorter one within a class; the #1646 token-boundary and empty-name behaviours are unchanged.
- [ ] Regression tests in `internal/diagnose` cover a bare-token tie and a quoted tie, asserting one stable winner across repeated calls (e.g. loop the call and require a single outcome).
- [ ] `go test ./internal/diagnose -run 'TestFieldInMessage|TestDiagnose' -count=1` (or the package's equivalent targeted tests) passes on laptop or CI.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for fieldInMessage tie / nondeterministic / map: the only hit is #1646 (closed — the substring/token-boundary rebuild this function came from, including the #3041 quote-preference and empty-name fixes). Neither it nor any other issue covers equal-length tie determinism; the defect is present on current main.

title: mcpx(nearmiss): distance is measured in bytes, not characters — one accented-letter edit counts as two, so Near misses it and Threshold inflates for non-Latin names

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/mcpx/internal/nearmiss` measures name distance over **bytes**, but its own `Normalize` deliberately keeps non-ASCII letters — so for any name containing a multi-byte letter, one character edit counts as two (or more) edits, the prefix rule's length guard counts bytes instead of characters, and `Threshold` inflates with byte length. The three consumers of the shared definition (#1904) — diagnostics suggestions (`internal/diagnose/diagnose.go:432`, `Nearest`), launcher placeholders (`internal/launcher/template.go:538`, `Near`), and `Distance` — therefore disagree with the character-level semantics the package documents.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `facf6481`)

- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/nearmiss/nearmiss.go:22-39` — `Normalize` ranges over runes and keeps every `unicode.IsLetter` (lower-cased via `unicode.ToLower`): `Normalize("café")` = `"café"`. Non-ASCII letters are in scope by design; they are not dropped as boundaries.
- `nearmiss.go:49-52` — the `damerau` comment claims it operates on "already-normalised (lowercase **ASCII-folded**) strings", but nothing ASCII-folds: `Normalize` preserves é, ü, Cyrillic, etc. verbatim. `damerau` then uses `len(a)` (bytes, line 52) and byte indexing `a[i-1]` (lines 64-69).
- `nearmiss.go:99` — `Near`'s prefix rule guards on `len(na) > 2 && len(nb) > 2` in bytes: a 2-rune name like `"éé"` (4 bytes) passes the ">2 characters" guard its comment (lines 86-93, and test table "prefix rule needs length > 2") describes in characters.
- `nearmiss.go:118` — `Nearest` passes `Threshold(len(nn))` with the byte length, inflating the allowance: a 6-rune Cyrillic name gets threshold 5 (12 bytes) instead of 3.

First-hand Go probe on the laptop (the package copied verbatim from current main into a scratch module, `go test -run TestProbeByteVsRune -v`):

```
Distance(café,cafe)=2        Near(café,cafe)=false
Distance(entrée,entree)=2    Near(entrée,entree)=false
Distance(привет,привед)=2
Normalize(café)="café" len=5   (4 runes, 5 bytes)
```

A byte-faithful Python replication of `damerau()` agrees, and contrasts with the rune-wise result: café/cafe byte 2 vs rune 1; é/e 2 vs 1; über/uber 2 vs 1; naïve/naive 2 vs 1; an adjacent transposition involving a multi-byte rune likewise costs more than the documented one edit. ASCII names are unaffected (byte = rune), which is why the existing test table — all ASCII — is green.

## Why it matters

#1904 made this package the *one* definition of "close" so search, diagnostics and the launcher cannot diverge. They don't diverge from each other, but the shared definition silently changes meaning at the ASCII boundary: a one-character typo in an accented or non-Latin name is not a near miss (`Near` false, `Distance` 2), while `Nearest`'s threshold simultaneously *loosens* for the same names (byte-inflated), so suggestion quality degrades in both directions depending on which consumer asks. The misleading "ASCII-folded" comment invites future callers to rely on a guarantee `Normalize` never provides.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Distance`/`Near`/`Nearest` operate on runes (or `Normalize` genuinely folds to ASCII, with the choice documented and the `damerau` comment made true): a single-character substitution, insertion, deletion or adjacent transposition involving a multi-byte letter costs exactly one edit — `Distance("café","cafe") == 1`, `Near("café","cafe") == true`, `Distance("entrée","entree") == 1`, `Distance("привет","привед") == 1`.
- [ ] The prefix rule's ">2" guard and `Threshold` count characters, not bytes: `Near("éé","éééé")` follows the same 2-character rule as `Near("ab","abcd") == false` (#3075 table), and `Threshold` for a 6-rune Cyrillic name is the value its rune length gives.
- [ ] Regression tests in `internal/nearmiss` cover multi-byte names for `Distance`, `Near` (both argument orders) and `Nearest`, alongside the existing ASCII table — ASCII behaviour byte-for-byte unchanged.
- [ ] `go test ./internal/nearmiss -count=1` passes (laptop or CI per the mcpx testing rules).

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for nearmiss / Damerau / damerau: #1904 (closed, created the shared package) and #3075 (closed, `Near` prefix-rule symmetry) are the only hits; neither mentions bytes, runes or non-ASCII names. The byte-vs-rune defect remains on current main.

title: id(repo): ~509 KB of raw clippy/cargo scratch output is tracked at the pkgs/id root — clippy_out4.txt, clippy_out5.txt and cargo-build-output.txt are unreferenced, and nothing stops the next dump

body:
## Problem

Three raw tool-output scratch files are tracked at the root of `pkgs/id` — about 509 KB of clippy/cargo output that no build, test, doc, or script reads:

- `pkgs/id/clippy_out4.txt` — 274,569 bytes. First lines: `Checking id v0.1.0 (/app/pkgs/id)` followed by clippy `warning: empty line after doc comment` output for `src/commands/find.rs:212`.
- `pkgs/id/clippy_out5.txt` — 228,300 bytes. Same shape: `Checking id v0.1.0 (/app/pkgs/id)`, then clippy diagnostics.
- `pkgs/id/cargo-build-output.txt` — 6,264 bytes. A `cargo tree -i iroh` dump (`iroh v0.95.1`, `distributed-topic-tracker v0.2.5`, `id v0.1.0 (/home/user/code/pkgs/id)`).

## Evidence (verified this run, main `68d59a37`)

- `git ls-files` lists all three as tracked files on current main.
- `clippy_out4.txt` and `clippy_out5.txt` were both added by commit `1646db17` ("style(id): resolve clippy-lint check failures in CI", 2026-10-30) — the lint output was committed alongside the lint fixes it described. `cargo-build-output.txt` was last touched by `1a291185` ("amd 414").
- A repo-wide search for `clippy_out` / `cargo-build-output` across `*.nix`, `*.toml`, `*.md`, `justfile`, and `*.json` finds no reference: nothing consumes these files. (Contrast the legitimate tracked text files in the same package — `benches/baseline.txt`, `proptest-regressions/*.txt`, `tests/regressions/*.txt` — which are read by benches/tests and are NOT part of this issue.)
- `pkgs/id/.gitignore` covers only `.iroh*`, `test.*`, `.identity.db`, `.identity.redb` — no pattern stops the next `clippy_outN.txt` / build-output dump from being committed the same way.
- A scan of the other `pkgs/*` package roots finds no sibling scratch dumps (the other tracked `.txt` files are resources/fixtures: schema files, migration text, mcpx `.expected.txt` fixtures), so this is a one-package cleanup, not a cross-repo set.

## Why it matters

Half a megabyte of stale diagnostics sits in every clone and in every `pkgs/id` listing, and the contents are actively misleading: `clippy_out5.txt` reports lint *errors* (e.g. at `src/commands/find.rs:212`) that were fixed in the very commit that added the file, so anyone (or any agent) grepping the tree for open lint problems finds a phantom backlog that no longer exists. This is the same failure mode as #2464 (a stray agent-scratch file carried by a PR), except these reached main directly and have no guard against recurrence.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `pkgs/id/clippy_out4.txt`, `pkgs/id/clippy_out5.txt`, and `pkgs/id/cargo-build-output.txt` are deleted from the tree.
- [ ] A `.gitignore` guard (in `pkgs/id/.gitignore` or the repo root one) prevents committing the same scratch shapes again — at minimum `clippy_out*.txt` and `cargo-build-output.txt` at the `pkgs/id` root — without ignoring any legitimately tracked text file (`benches/baseline.txt`, `proptest-regressions/`, `tests/regressions/`, `src/defaults.conf` neighbours).
- [ ] After the change, `git check-ignore` / a fresh `git status` in a tree with a locally generated `clippy_out6.txt` shows it ignored, and the id crate's checks that read tracked text fixtures still pass (CI).
- [ ] No other file contents change.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `clippy_out`, `cargo-build-output`, and scratch-file terms. #2464 (open) covers a stray `get_plan.py` at the repo root carried by PR #1715 — a different file, path, and landing path; it does not name these files. No existing issue covers the `pkgs/id` scratch outputs or a gitignore guard for them.

body:
## Summary

`aggregator(aa)`: three plain-object lookups in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/aa.ts` return `Object.prototype` members for prototype-named inputs instead of the unknown-key fallback — the #2792 own-key rule (fixed for quota-gather-map in #3022, weights in #2734) was never applied to this file's maps. The inputs are data-controlled: effort/variant names and model names come from the opencode config, and CAI `creatorSlug` values come from the Supabase AA payload.

## Evidence (main `1f8ab4f6`, aa.ts md5 `969672a1a6e49152544ceca205a2fedc`, identical in both checkouts)

- `effortRank` (aa.ts:347-351): `return AA_EFFORT_ORDER[effort.toLowerCase()] ?? 50;` — for `"constructor"` the lookup returns the `Object` constructor **function** (not nullish, so `?? 50` never fires); for `"__proto__"` it returns `Object.prototype`. Declared return type is `number`. Its only caller sorts variant names with `effortRank(a) - effortRank(b)` (aa.ts:869), which becomes `NaN`, silently corrupting the variant sort order.
- `caiFromRaw` (aa.ts:998): `creator: slug ? (CAI_CREATORS[slug.toLowerCase()] ?? slug) : ""` — a `creatorSlug` of `"constructor"` yields the `Object` constructor as the creator; `"__proto__"` yields `Object.prototype`, instead of falling back to the slug itself.
- Catalog (aa.ts:886): `goCapUsd: … (AA_GO_CAPS[norm] ?? null)` where `norm = normalizeModelName(modelId)` (aa.ts:271-279; `"constructor"` normalizes to itself) — under an `opencode-go*` provider, a model named `constructor` gets `goCapUsd` = the `Object` constructor function instead of `null`. render.ts:3560 then prints `Published OpenCode Go cap: $function Object() { [native code] }/mo → ~NaN AA tasks…`.
- Note on scope: `AA_PLAN_FACTS[providerId]` (aa.ts:859) has the same shape but is observably benign today — the result is only read through `fact?.plan/.multiplier/.note`, all absent on prototype members, so it degrades exactly like an unknown provider. Fix it in the same pass for uniformity, but it is not the bug's impact. `TEST_RUN_FIELDS`' `in` check (aa.ts:81) is likewise benign: the map built from it is only queried with fixed literal names.

## Verified (laptop probe, real `aa.ts`)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneA-aaproto/` on the laptop, importing the real `aa.ts` from the laptop clone at `1f8ab4f6` (md5 above), bun run:

```
effortRank high: 3 number
effortRank constructor: function function Object() { [native code] } sortDiff: NaN
effortRank __proto__: object [object Object] sortDiff: NaN
effortRank toString: number 50 sortDiff: 49   (lowercasing saves camelCase names — only all-lowercase prototype keys leak)
planFacts constructor: function plan field: undefined
goCaps constructor: function [class Object]
goCaps unknown-model: null
```

End-to-end through `aaSectionFromSupabase` with CAI rows `creatorSlug: "constructor" | "__proto__" | "acme"`:

```
cai creator: function function Object() { [native code] }
cai creator: object [object Object]
cai creator: string acme
json cai: [null,{},"acme"]
```

So a prototype-named creator slug serializes to `null`/`{}` in the feed JSON instead of its own name, and a prototype-named effort label poisons the catalog variant sort with `NaN`.

## Why it matters

These maps are indexed by names that arrive in external data (Supabase AA payload, opencode.jsonc provider/model/variant keys). One such name silently produces a function/object where a number, string, or null is typed — breaking a sort, blanking a creator in the published feed, and printing native-function source into the dashboard's cap line. This is exactly the failure class the fleet has been closing file by file under design #2792; aa.ts is a remaining embodiment, in the same aggregator the #3022 fix just landed in.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `effortRank("constructor")` and `effortRank("__proto__")` return `50` (the unknown-label rank); known efforts return their ladder values unchanged.
- [ ] A CAI row with `creatorSlug: "constructor"` or `"__proto__"` gets `creator` equal to the slug itself (the unknown-slug fallback); known slugs still map to display names.
- [ ] A catalog entry for a model whose normalized name is `constructor` under an `opencode-go*` provider gets `goCapUsd: null`; real Go model names keep their caps.
- [ ] All plain-object lookups in aa.ts indexed by data-controlled keys (`AA_EFFORT_ORDER`, `CAI_CREATORS`, `AA_GO_CAPS`, `AA_PLAN_FACTS`) use an own-key guard (`Object.hasOwn`) or equivalent, per #2792.
- [ ] Regression tests in the aggregator test suite covering the probe matrix above (constructor/__proto__ + a known-key and an unknown-key control for each site).

Related: #2792 (design: own-key rule), #3022 (quota-gather-map embodiment, fixed), #2734 (weights embodiment, fixed), #2985 (aa `num()` hex reinterpretation — distinct, value parsing not key lookup).

body:
## Summary

`sameCharge` in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/charges-collect.ts` decides that a hand-fed charges row duplicates an auto-matched row when their squashed normalized labels merely *contain* one another — no token boundary and no minimum length (charges-collect.ts:74-80). `mergeChargeRows` (:89-92) then silently drops the hand-fed row. With equal amounts and dates within the 3-day dedupe window, unrelated charges eat hand-fed rows:

- a hand-fed `Meta` row is dropped because an auto row labelled `METAMUCIL` exists ("METAMUCIL" contains "META");
- a hand-fed `AI` row is dropped because an auto row labelled `RAILWAY` exists ("RAILWAY" contains "AI").

## Evidence (verified this run, main `0f84fe08`; laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-charges/probe2.ts` importing the shipped file — `charges-collect.ts` md5 `246eca2b01496bf280146a2e506785d7` identical in the sandbox and laptop clones)

- Case A: auto `[{2026-10-06, "METAMUCIL", $20}]` + hand-fed `[{2026-10-05, "Meta", $20}]` → merged output is **only the METAMUCIL row**; the Meta row is gone.
- Case B: auto `[{2026-10-05, "RAILWAY", $10}]` + hand-fed `[{2026-10-05, "AI", $10}]` → merged output is **only the RAILWAY row**.
- Control (documented intent, must keep working): auto `"METAPAY"` + hand-fed `"Meta PAYG spill"`, same amount/day → one row, the auto row (charges-collect.ts:68-73 names this pair as the reason for squash containment).

## Why it matters

The merge's stated rule is conservative — "a hand-fed row is only dropped when an auto row plausibly IS that charge" (charges-collect.ts:70-73) — but substring containment with no floor is not conservative: short hand-fed labels (`Meta`, `AI`, any 2–4 letter service shorthand) are substrings of unrelated merchant names, so real hand-fed charges vanish from the feed with no trace. The feed is financial evidence (#1057); a silently missing row is the same failure family as #2130's under-count, by the opposite door.

Distinct from #3048 (same run): that issue is classification in `charges-match.ts` (`matchService`/`isSaasLooking`). This one is the hand-fed/auto merge in `charges-collect.ts`. Also distinct from #2194, which reaches `sameCharge` only via impossible calendar dates (NaN window); here the dates are valid and the containment alone drops the row.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `sameCharge` no longer treats substring containment inside a longer token as a match: the Meta/METAMUCIL and AI/RAILWAY pairs above both keep their hand-fed rows.
- [ ] The documented intended pair still merges: hand-fed `Meta PAYG spill` against auto `METAPAY` (same amount, within window) drops the hand-fed row.
- [ ] New tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/charges-collect.test.ts` cover both false-merge pairs and the intended pair; all existing charges-collect and charges-match tests pass.

Related: #1057 (feature), #3048 (classification substring matching in charges-match), #2130 (dedupe collapse), #2194 (impossible dates in this file), #1047 (epic).

body:
## Summary

`matchService` and `isSaasLooking` in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/charges-match.ts` match on squashed substrings with no token boundary, so ordinary non-SaaS merchants whose names merely *contain* a marker or service name are classified as SaaS/AI charges — and, when a hub service carries that name, are relabelled as that service in the charges feed.

- `isSaasLooking` (charges-match.ts:158-160): `SAAS_MARKERS.some((marker) => flat.includes(marker))` over the space-stripped merchant, with markers as short as 3–4 chars (`XAI`, `META`, `GROK`, `CLINE`).
- `matchService` (charges-match.ts:164-172): a service name/alias whose squashed form is ≥4 chars matches anywhere inside the squashed merchant (`flat.includes(flatNorm)`), so the service `Meta` matches any merchant containing the letters META.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `0f84fe08`; laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-charges/probe.ts` importing the shipped file — `charges-match.ts` md5 `bec11791e5b91a32acf78529d4960087` identical in the sandbox and laptop clones)

- `normalizeMerchantName("METAMUCIL")` → `"METAMUCIL"`; `isSaasLooking` → **true**; `matchService(..., [{name:"Meta"}, ...])` → **Meta**. A full `matchCharges` run on a single Plaid `METAMUCIL $12.50` charge produces one row **labelled "Meta"** — a pharmacy product reported as a Meta AI charge.
- `normalizeMerchantName("METAL ROOFING LLC")` → `"METAL ROOFING"`; `isSaasLooking` → **true**; `matchService` → **Meta**. A roofing contractor is likewise classified as a Meta charge.
- Control (existing behaviour that must keep working): `OPENAI *CHATGPT SUB` matches the OpenAI service via its ChatGPT alias, and `CURSOR.COM` normalizes to `CURSOR` (covered by `test/charges-match.test.ts`).

## Why it matters

The charges strip is financial evidence (see #1057/#2130): a mislabelled row attributes one vendor's charge to a hub service, and a false SaaS-looking flag pushes household merchants (pharmacy, trades) into the unmatched-SaaS attention strip. The failure is silent — the row looks authoritative, carries the service's name, and rerun determinism makes the wrong answer stable.

Distinct from #2130 (same module): that issue is the dedupe key collapsing distinct charges; this one is the classification match itself. #2130's acceptance criteria do not touch matching boundaries.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Service names/aliases and SaaS markers match only at token boundaries (a whole normalized token, or a whole multi-token sequence), never as a substring inside a longer token: `METAMUCIL` and `METAL ROOFING` match neither the `Meta` service nor the `META` SaaS marker.
- [ ] Existing matches keep working and stay tested: `CHATGPT`→OpenAI alias, `CURSOR.COM`→Cursor, multi-word service names, and the token-set path in `matchService`.
- [ ] New tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/charges-match.test.ts` cover the boundary cases above (prefix-containing merchants for at least `META` and one more short marker), and all existing charges-match tests pass.

Related: #1057 (feature), #2130 (dedupe defect in the same module), #1047 (epic).
