body:
## Summary

In `pm-stack/aggregator`, the /health topology table's **Port** column is hard-coded per service in `src/topology.ts`, while the probe target for the same row follows the configured base URL. When a configured URL carries a non-default port, the page probes one port and displays another — a service can show "up" next to a port nothing was probed on.

## Evidence (main a9df3018)

- `src/topology.ts:99` — the aggregator row does take `port: cfg.port`, but the other probed rows hard-code theirs: Kaneo `port: 5173` (:118), ready-for-agent `port: 6056` (:152), Pad `port: 7777` (:168), Grist `port: 8484` (:183), projector `port: 7801` (in `projectorDef`, :72 and :89) — while their `loopbackUrl` values come from config (`cfg.kaneo.baseUrl`, `cfg.readyForAgent.baseUrl`, `cfg.pad.baseUrl`, `cfg.grist.baseUrl`, `cfg.projector.baseUrl`).
- `src/config.ts` — those base URLs are env-overridable: `KANEO_URL` (:113), `PM_AGG_RFA_URL` (:140), `PM_AGG_PAD_URL` (:136), `GRIST_URL` (:121), `PM_PROJECTOR_URL` (:128-131). The topology module's own header (:12-13) says probe targets come from config "so an env override moves the probe with the reader" — but the port column does not move with it.
- `src/render.ts` (renderHealth) renders `s.def.port` as the row's Port column on the same /health page whose state comes from probing `loopbackUrl` (`src/health.ts:286` iterates `buildServices(cfg)`).

Verified this run by importing the real `src/config.ts` + `src/topology.ts` (Node type-stripping) with explicit-port overrides:

```
loadConfig({PM_AGG_SOURCE:'live', PM_PROJECTOR_URL:'http://127.0.0.1:9999',
  PM_AGG_RFA_URL:'http://127.0.0.1:7778', KANEO_URL:'http://127.0.0.1:6000',
  GRIST_URL:'http://127.0.0.1:9000', PM_AGG_PAD_URL:'http://127.0.0.1:3131'})
buildServices(...) =>
  kaneo           port=5173  probe=http://127.0.0.1:6000
  ready-for-agent port=6056  probe=http://127.0.0.1:7778
  pad             port=7777  probe=http://127.0.0.1:3131
  grist           port=8484  probe=http://127.0.0.1:9000
  projector       port=7801  probe=http://127.0.0.1:9999
```

With default config every row agrees, so this only bites on a non-default deployment / local stack — exactly when an operator is most likely to trust the topology table while debugging.

## Why it matters

The topology registry's stated job (#1137, module header) is to be the one home for "what runs where, bound how" so the /health page never duplicates or invents identity facts. A port column that silently disagrees with the probe target on the same row breaks that contract: the state dot is earned at one address while the table names another.

## Acceptance criteria

- For every probed service whose configured base URL carries an explicit port, the topology row's `port` equals that port (derived from the URL), for Kaneo, Grist, Pad, ready-for-agent, and the projector (both branches of `projectorDef`).
- A configured base URL with no explicit port keeps the current documented default port for that service.
- Default-config output is unchanged: `buildServices(loadConfig({}))` returns the same ports as today, and the existing health tests still pass.
- A regression test covers at least one explicit-port override (e.g. `PM_PROJECTOR_URL=http://127.0.0.1:9999` in live source mode yields projector `port: 9999`).

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for topology / port / config / baseUrl combinations on 2026-10-31: no existing issue covers the topology port column diverging from configured probe URLs. Distinct from #2161/#2758/#2172 (boot-time env port *validation* for PM_AGG_PORT / DISPATCH_PORT / projector PORT — those are about `loadConfig`/server startup parsing, not the topology table's displayed identity facts) and from #2835 (the shared strict-parse design).

body:
# aggregator(validate): `parseIsoDate` mishandles years 0000–0099 — rejected without an offset, silently shifted to 1900–1999 with one

## Evidence (main `27940ab3`, verified this run)

`parseIsoDate` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/validate.ts:68-110`, added in #2577) extracts the components, range-checks them against the real calendar (`:51-57`, `:73-80`), then builds the instant with `Date.UTC(year, …)` at `:82`. `Date.UTC` maps years 0–99 to 1900–1999 (the JS legacy year mapping), and the two code paths cope with that differently:

- **No offset / `Z`:** the round-trip re-check at `:97-109` compares the UTC components and returns `null` — so perfectly valid ISO dates are rejected.
- **Explicit numeric offset:** the re-check is skipped (comment `:92-96`: "only the instant is checked there"), so the 1900-shifted instant is returned as if correct — off by exactly 1900 years. Worse, `0000-02-29` is a real date by the module's own leap rule (`:51-52`: `0 % 400 === 0`), but 1900 is not a leap year, so the offset form rolls over to a different month/day entirely.

Verified this run by importing the real `src/validate.ts` (Node 24 type-stripping, no modification):

| input | result | correct |
|---|---|---|
| `0099-01-01` | `null` | 0099-01-01 |
| `0099-01-01T00:00:00Z` | `null` | 0099-01-01T00:00:00Z |
| `0099-01-01T00:00:00+01:00` | `1998-12-31T23:00:00.000Z` | 0098-12-31T23:00:00Z |
| `0000-02-29` | `null` | 0000-02-29 (leap, year 0) |
| `0000-02-29T12:00:00+01:00` | `1900-03-01T11:00:00.000Z` | 0000-02-29T11:00:00Z |
| `0001-06-15T00:00:00-05:00` | `1901-06-15T05:00:00.000Z` | 0001-06-15T05:00:00Z |
| `2026-10-25T17:00:00+02:00` | `2026-10-25T15:00:00.000Z` | ✓ (control) |

The regex (`:48-49`) accepts any `\d{4}` year, so `0000`–`0099` are inside the grammar the function claims to parse; the test matrix (`test/validate.test.ts:136-182`) exercises only years 2024/2026, so nothing pins this range.

## Why it matters

`parseIsoDate` is the shared ingest-validation primitive from #2576/#2577 — "validated ONCE, at its boundary" — and its results gate real consumers: `isFleetFeed` requires `isIsoDate(f.generatedAt)` (`src/feed.ts:255`), and `isTimestampNotFuture` (`validate.ts:126-136`) judges freshness from the parsed instant. A document stamped with a year below 100 is therefore either dropped as invalid or — with an offset — accepted with an instant 1900 years in the future relative to its stated date, corrupting any age/freshness reasoning built on it. The same input being valid-or-not depending on whether it carries `Z` or `+01:00` is exactly the kind of boundary inconsistency the ingest contract exists to eliminate. Practical likelihood is low (real feeds stamp current dates), hence low priority — but the fix is small and the primitive is meant to be total and trustworthy.

Distinct from #2196 (quota-extract `monthDayTime` rollover — a different parser) and #3005/#2985 (measurement-number grammar, not dates). #2577 built these primitives; this is a bug in them, not a reopening of its scope.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `parseIsoDate` returns the correct instant for years 0000–0099 in all forms: date-only, `Z`, and numeric offsets (e.g. build the date with `setUTCFullYear` or an equivalent that bypasses the 0–99 → 1900s mapping).
- [ ] `0000-02-29` (leap by the module's own rule) parses to Feb 29 of year 0 in every form; a non-leap small year (e.g. `0099-02-29`) still returns `null`.
- [ ] Acceptance is offset-independent: the same calendar date/time with `Z` vs an equivalent numeric offset yields the same instant.
- [ ] Regression tests in `test/validate.test.ts`: the table above (or equivalent) is pinned, including the `0000-02-29` offset rollover case; existing valid/invalid matrices and the exact-instant test keep passing.

title: id(connectivity): await_home_relay and check_qad_order have no production caller — serve binds, writes its lock and prints ready with no home-relay wait, and the QAD relay-order refusal can never fire

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: task/fix
labels.description: has a fix task queued

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/id/src/connectivity.rs` defines two startup safeguards for wider-network endpoints, each with its own tests, and **neither has a production caller anywhere in the repo** (verified this run, below):

1. **The home-relay startup wait is never awaited.** `HOME_RELAY_DEADLINE` (connectivity.rs:92, "How long startup waits for the home relay before carrying on without one") and `await_home_relay` (connectivity.rs:96-105, "Waits until the endpoint has a connected home relay, for at most `limit`") exist so startup does not announce a server before it is reachable through its home relay. `cmd_serve` (commands/serve.rs:776-806) builds the endpoint with `public_builder`, binds it, and never calls `await_home_relay`; it goes on to write the serve lock file and print `node: <id>` status (serve.rs:~1158-1168) immediately after bind. A server can therefore present itself as ready — lock file written, node ID printed, callers detecting it via stdout — while its home relay is not yet connected (or never connects, e.g. a dead relay entry), and nothing ever reports that: the 10-second bounded wait that was built and tested for exactly this is dead code.

2. **The QAD relay-order check never runs.** `check_qad_order` (connectivity.rs:117-139) refuses a relay map with no QAD-capable relay among the first 5 entries iroh probes, because such a map "gives no public address a direct path needs". No production code calls it, and no production path constructs a custom `RelayMap` for it to check (`public_builder`, connectivity.rs:44-50, offers only the N0 preset or relays disabled), so the refusal the doc describes can never fire: the safeguard is a tested function guarding a door nothing walks through.

## Evidence (this run, main ab55f3c2)

- Whole-repo search for `await_home_relay`, `check_qad_order`, and `HOME_RELAY_DEADLINE` over all `*.rs`: every hit is inside `connectivity.rs` itself (definitions at :92/:99/:121 and the unit tests at :~290-360). Independent second grep over `pkgs/id/src` for production callers outside `connectivity.rs` returned no callers; `cmd_serve`'s endpoint construction (commands/serve.rs:776-806) contains no relay wait and no QAD check, and a search for `.online()` / `home_relay` outside connectivity.rs found no substitute wait.
- The functions are not dead in the compiler's eyes (they are `pub` in `pub mod connectivity`, lib.rs:164), so no dead-code warning ever surfaces the gap; only a call-graph check finds it.
- Contrast inside the same file: `connect` and `public_builder` ARE wired (commands/get.rs, list.rs, put.rs, find.rs, serve.rs all call them), so the module's policy is only half applied — dials get the deadline policy, startup gets neither of its two safeguards.

## Why it matters

- Startup readiness is a contract other tooling relies on (the serve lock file comment at serve.rs:~1158 says integration callers detect the server via its stdout/lock). Announcing readiness before relay reachability means early dials by node ID alone can fail or hang until their own 45s `DIAL_TIMEOUT`, with no log line naming the relay as the cause.
- The QAD check's doc states a real failure mode (a relay map whose first five probed entries lack QUIC address discovery yields no public address). Leaving the check unwired means the day a custom relay map IS introduced (config, tests, a deployment flag), it lands without the guard its author built for it — silently.
- This is the same unwired-policy shape as pull_policy.rs's module doc ("`id serve` does not read it yet", tracked in #798 for pull policy specifically); connectivity's two safeguards have no tracking issue at all.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Triage confirms on current main: `await_home_relay` and `check_qad_order` have no production callers (repo-wide call search), and `cmd_serve` binds + writes the lock file + prints status with no home-relay wait.
- [ ] A decision is recorded on this issue: wire them, or remove/deprecate them. Wiring looks like: `cmd_serve` awaits the home relay under `HOME_RELAY_DEADLINE` when relays are enabled (skipping the wait — with a status/log line — when `--no-relay` is set, per `await_home_relay`'s own doc), carrying on after the deadline as the doc promises, and logs the outcome; `check_qad_order` is applied to any relay map a production path actually constructs, or the function is explicitly scoped as a guard for a named future caller.
- [ ] If wired: a test or startup log line demonstrates the bounded wait (relay disabled → no wait; dead relay → startup proceeds after the deadline with a warning naming the relay wait).
- [ ] If removed instead: the constants, functions, and their tests are deleted together and the module doc no longer describes startup policy that does not run.
- [ ] No change to `connect` / `public_builder` behaviour or to the `DIAL_TIMEOUT` policy.

Distinct from: #798 (pull-policy / freshness config unwired in serve — different policy, different module), #795 (real-network QAD/holepunch tests owner-blocked — this issue is about the in-process check/wait never being called, not about network test access), #3023 (meta_client response deadlines).

body:
**Decision (Drew, 2026-10-31):** tasks assigned the **opencode execution lane** must be triggered by scheduled tasks on the laptop/OpenChamber side. No Muse cron boots, launches, or hands off to OpenCode. Muse lanes keep claiming and assigning; execution starts without Muse in the loop.

**Why:** execution already spends only provider-plan quotas, but the triggers and supervision are Muse cron jobs — in the Oct 30 check-in window the conductor burned 96M input and its still-running predecessors (openchamber-dispatcher + openchamber-babysitter) ~199M more, i.e. Muse tokens spent just to start and watch work that runs entirely elsewhere.

**Mechanism — OpenChamber scheduled tasks (corrected 2026-10-31, Drew):** OpenChamber **does** have native scheduled tasks, and they are the mechanism for this change: the schedule lives on the OpenChamber side, not in Muse cron and not in OS timers. OpenCode itself lacks the capability — the #2019 investigation (comment 6494101941) audited OpenCode core and the fleet fork and correctly found no scheduler there (upstream request anomalyco/opencode#41906 open), but it did not audit OpenChamber's own feature set; its systemd-timer + `opencode run` composition is a fallback only, for anything OpenChamber's scheduler genuinely cannot express.

**Work:**
1. **OpenChamber-scheduled claimant/executor.** An OpenChamber scheduled task on the laptop (any supporting service units defined in the developing-today/code flake — laptop services live there, never in dezren39/nix) that polls the four repo-health queues for tasks whose execution lane is `opencode`, and for each: claims/binds it in the lane ledger **at launch, with the session id recorded** (this closes the launch-binding gap behind the Oct 28 duplicate PRs), launches the session with the route the task packet specifies (Workhorse default; Specialist / Summit for complex work), enforces the 12-session concurrency cap, and records the terminal state (complete / park / block / fail) via the queue helper when the session ends.
2. **Parallel-run gate.** Run beside openchamber-conductor for a defined window (24h or the first 20 executions, whichever is later), comparing bindings and completions. The Muse launch path stands down only after the gate passes.
3. **Stand-down.** Disable the conductor's launch role and retire openchamber-dispatcher and openchamber-babysitter. Muse lanes keep claiming/assigning lanes and verifying results from queue + ledger records.
4. **Supervision.** Scheduling is not supervision (#2019): name how stalled sessions are caught laptop-side (an OpenChamber-scheduled session health check) with Tend's fleet-watchdog reading the ledger as the backstop, and record the choice on this issue.

**Acceptance:**
- A full day with the Muse launch path disabled and opencode-lane completions continuing at or above the pre-change rate.
- 100% of laptop-side launches have a ledger binding with session id at launch time; zero duplicate PRs attributable to unbound launches during the gate.
- Daily check-in reports the opencode lane's per-item cost before/after the change.
- The Muse token cost of the launch path (conductor + predecessors) goes to ~0 for opencode executions.

Routes, pools and the measurement gate are unchanged — this moves *who pulls the trigger*, not what the sessions run on.


## Acceptance criteria
- An OpenChamber scheduled task on the laptop polls the four repo-health queues for opencode-lane tasks, claims/binds each at launch with the session id recorded in the lane ledger, launches it on the packet's route, enforces the 12-session concurrency cap, and records the terminal state via the queue helper.
- The parallel-run gate (24h or the first 20 executions, whichever is later) passes beside openchamber-conductor: 100% of laptop-side launches bound with session id at launch time, zero duplicate PRs attributable to unbound launches.
- After the gate passes, the Muse launch path stands down: openchamber-conductor's launch role disabled, openchamber-dispatcher and openchamber-babysitter retired.
- A full day with the Muse launch path disabled shows opencode-lane completions continuing at or above the pre-change rate, and the Muse token cost of the launch path at ~0 for opencode executions.
- Laptop-side stall supervision is named and recorded on this issue (OpenChamber-scheduled session health check, fleet-watchdog ledger backstop).

title: id(meta_client): meta response reads have no deadline — a peer that accepts the stream but never answers (or trickles under the 64 MiB cap) hangs find/put/REPL forever, and put's 2-minute retry deadline never fires

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

Every client-side meta-protocol response read in `pkgs/id` is bounded in **bytes** but not in **time**. A peer that accepts the stream and then never answers — or trickles bytes under the cap — hangs the calling command forever:

- `src/meta_client.rs:77-84` — `request_over()` does `open_bi` → `write_all` → `finish` → `read_capped_response()` with no timeout anywhere.
- `src/meta_client.rs:70-75` — `read_capped_response()` is `recv.read_to_end(MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES)` (64 MiB). The cap bounds size, not duration: `read_to_end` returns only when the stream ends, so a silent peer waits forever and a peer sending 1 byte/minute stays under the cap indefinitely.
- `src/commands/find.rs:949` — remote find (`id find --node <peer>`, an arbitrary user-supplied node ID) hand-rolls the same unbounded read.
- `src/commands/repl.rs:735` — the connected REPL's find does the same, so one silent peer wedges the interactive session.
- `src/commands/put.rs:131-147` — put's retry loop *looks* bounded: a 2-minute `deadline` wraps `request_over`, but the deadline is only checked **between** attempts, after `request_over` returns. A single hung attempt never returns, so the 2-minute bound never fires.

## Contrast inside the same crate

The house pattern is deadlines everywhere else:

- `src/connectivity.rs:54-57,63-85` — dialing runs under `DIAL_TIMEOUT` (45 s) via the `within()` helper, whose error names the wait ("timed out after … while connecting to a peer").
- `src/envelope_net.rs:80` — envelope delivery is timeout-wrapped.
- `src/commands/peers.rs:339` — the remote peers query is timeout-wrapped.
- #2087 (closed) added exactly this kind of deadline to the artifact-pull protocol's frame read.

The meta client paths are the remaining unbounded ones.

## Verification (this run, main fa7e71b7)

Laptop probe (worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneA-metadeadline`, integration test `pkgs/id/tests/meta_deadline_probe.rs`, built and run on the laptop): a loopback server accepts the connection and stream, reads the request, and then never sends anything. The real `id::meta_client::request_over` was still pending when a 5-second observation window elapsed — it has no deadline of its own. (Result line from the probe run is quoted in the filing agent note.)

## Why it matters

`id find --node`, remote put, tag commands via `MetaClient::connect_node`, and the connected REPL all talk to peers the user does not control. One dead-but-connected peer (crashed handler, half-open relay path, malicious silence) turns a one-shot CLI command into a permanent hang with no error and no recourse but Ctrl-C — and in put's case it silently defeats a deadline the code already claims to enforce.

## Related

- #2086 (open) is the server-side sibling: `MetaProtocol`'s accept loop is sequential with no stream deadline. This issue is the client side; the two fixes are independent.
- #2087 (closed) fixed the same shape for artifact pull.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `request_over()` completes under a named deadline constant; on expiry the error names the wait, in the style of `connectivity::within`.
- [ ] The hand-rolled reads in `commands/find.rs` and `commands/repl.rs` get the same bound (or are routed through the bounded helper).
- [ ] Put's 2-minute retry deadline bounds the total wait **including** an in-flight attempt.
- [ ] A regression test with a silent loopback peer returns the deadline error within the bound; the existing meta_client loopback tests (large-response read-through, over-cap error) still pass.
- [ ] The deadline value is pinned in triage (suggestion: align with `DIAL_TIMEOUT`, 45 s, or the envelope-delivery limit).

body:
# id(world-manifest): `validate()` never checks the execution profile or the schedule count — manifests parse and plan clean, then fail partway through a live apply

## Evidence (main `6bbb065b`, verified this run)

`WorldManifest::validate()` (`pkgs/id/src/world_manifest.rs:164-196`) — the only gate `parse()` runs (`:151-155`) — checks grant names, ceiling names, schedule **ids** and positive fire times, module-hash shape, and hash/source exclusivity. It never looks at two fields it carries:

1. **The execution profile.** Every bound `WorldExecutionProfile::resolve()` refuses (`pkgs/id/src/world_limits.rs:71-92`) sails through `parse()`:
   - `wasm_fuel = 0`, `wasm_message_bytes = 0`, `native_cpu_seconds = 0`, `native_call_deadline_ms = 0`
   - `wasm_memory_bytes = 1024` (below the 64 KiB one-page minimum)
   - `native_memory_bytes = 1024` (below the 16 MiB minimum)

   `plan()` then emits a `SetProfile` step for each (any non-default profile that differs from current, `world_manifest.rs:285-289`). The live apply reaches `WorldService::set_execution_profile`, which resolves **first** and refuses (`pkgs/id/src/world_session/mod.rs:266`: `profile.resolve(self.runtime)?`). `world doctor`'s `check_profile` (`world_doctor.rs:326-366`) flags exactly these values — the doctor and the manifest validator disagree about what a valid profile is.

2. **The schedule count.** A present `schedules` map is reconciled *exactly* (`world_manifest.rs:293-308`: add missing, cancel undeclared), so the desired end state has exactly `len(schedules)` pending. `validate()` accepts **65** entries — one past `MAX_PENDING_SCHEDULES = 64` (`world_caps.rs:95`), the cap `WorldCore::check_schedule` enforces on every live set (`world/core.rs:613-617`, called from `world/actor.rs:759`). No live world can ever hold the state the manifest declares.

## Verified with a probe (laptop, this run)

Probe crate `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneA-manifestvalidate/` (laptop) built from **verbatim** `world_manifest.rs` (md5 `7b3e4e0a…`), the verbatim validators/constants of `world_caps.rs` (md5 `ac9d6bd5…`), and the verbatim `WorldExecutionProfile` + `resolve()` of `world_limits.rs` (md5 `94fccbd8…`) — both clones at `6bbb065b`:

- All six profile values above: `parse()` → **Ok**, `plan()` → exactly one `SetProfile` step, `resolve(RuntimeLimits::default())` → **Err**.
- A 65-entry `schedules` map: `parse()` → **Ok**, `plan()` against an empty state → **65 `ScheduleAt` steps**.

## Why it matters

`id world apply` is not atomic: `apply_steps` runs the steps in reachability order (`commands/world.rs` `ordered_steps`: cancels → **profile** → grants → ceiling → module → schedule additions) and stops at the first error. So a manifest that `parse()` blessed can:

- fail at the `SetProfile` step after schedule cancels have already landed, or
- fail on the 65th `ScheduleAt` step after the profile, grants, ceiling and module install have all been applied and journaled —

leaving the world half-reconciled to a manifest that can never be fully applied, with `diff` still promising the remaining steps will converge. Validation is the manifest's contract ("a manifest should be validated first; this is a defensive re-check", `world_manifest.rs:311-314` on `apply()`) — the two fields it skips are exactly the two whose live refusals arrive mid-apply.

Distinct from #2876 (unknown/misspelled keys silently ignored — serde-level) and #2166 (module_hash `blake3:<hex>` doc mismatch): this is about declared, known fields whose *values* `validate()` never checks. The schedule *horizon* (30 days, `check_schedule`) is deliberately **not** part of this issue: it is relative to the apply-time clock, so a pure `validate()` cannot judge it — only the count is time-free.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `WorldManifest::validate()` (or `parse()`) refuses a profile that `resolve()` would refuse: zero `wasm_fuel` / `wasm_message_bytes` / `native_cpu_seconds` / `native_call_deadline_ms`, `wasm_memory_bytes < 64 KiB`, `native_memory_bytes < 16 MiB` — naming the offending bound, consistent with `check_profile`'s problem list.
- [ ] `validate()` refuses a `schedules` map with more than `MAX_PENDING_SCHEDULES` (64) entries, naming the cap.
- [ ] Regression tests in `world_manifest.rs`'s test module (extending `validation_rejects_unknown_names_and_bad_hashes` or new tests): each bad profile bound fails `parse()`; a 65-entry schedule map fails `parse()`; a 64-entry map and a boundary-valid profile (exactly 64 KiB / 16 MiB) still parse.
- [ ] Existing manifest tests keep passing (`parses_and_round_trips` uses `wasm_fuel = 5_000_000` and one schedule — both stay valid).

title: id(search): search_terms re-calls the subject_kind lookup once per SubjectKind term per subject — its doc promises at most once per subject, so a two-kind-term search does twice the store reads

labels.name: task/triage

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/low

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Summary

`search_terms` documents that its `subject_kind` lookup "is called at most once per subject", but the lookup is re-run once per subject **per `SubjectKind` term** — a search with two kind terms calls it twice for every subject, three kind terms three times, and so on.

## Evidence (main 6bbb065b)

- `pkgs/id/src/search.rs:85-88` — the doc comment on `search_terms` says: "`subject_kind` resolves a subject to the kind of the event it names, for [`Term::SubjectKind`]; it is called at most once per subject, and a subject it cannot resolve (`None`) never matches a kind term."
- `pkgs/id/src/search.rs:108-145` — the implementation builds the matched-subject set in a `for term in terms` loop, and the `Term::SubjectKind(kind)` arm (lines 135-141) filters **all** subjects by calling `subject_kind(&Hash::from_bytes(*subject))` for each one. There is no memoization across terms, so the per-subject call count is exactly the number of `SubjectKind` terms in the query.
- Verified this run on the laptop with a probe carrying the `search_terms` loop verbatim (stub `TagIndex`/`Hash`/`Claim` types only; `search.rs` md5 `59987199ef6eb85becd589f51c434c86`, identical on both clones; probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-searchkind/`). Two subjects (one claim each) and a counting lookup:

  | terms | lookup calls | doc promise |
  |---|---|---|
  | one `SubjectKind` term | 2 | ≤ 2 ✓ |
  | two different `SubjectKind` terms | **4** | ≤ 2 ✗ |
  | the same `SubjectKind` term twice | **4** | ≤ 2 ✗ |

## Why it matters

The "at most once per subject" sentence is the contract a caller relies on when supplying an expensive lookup — the natural implementation reads the subject's event from the store (that is exactly what `search_store_terms` wires it to, `EventStore::event_by_id`). `search_store_terms` happens to pre-resolve and cache kinds before calling `search_terms`, so the store caller is shielded today; any direct caller of the public `search_terms` who follows the documented contract with an uncached lookup pays one store read per subject per kind term instead of one per subject. Multi-kind queries are also the case where the extra work is pure waste: a subject has exactly one kind, so two distinct kind terms can never both match — yet every subject is still looked up for both. The fix is small and local: resolve each subject's kind once (memoize in a map) before/within the term loop and reuse it for every kind term.

Related but distinct: #2779 covers `search_store_terms` resolving every subject's kind even when **no** kind term is present (wasted work on the caller side). This issue is the dual gap inside `search_terms` itself: with kind terms present, the lookup runs more than the documented once per subject.

## Acceptance criteria

- `search_terms` calls `subject_kind` at most once per distinct subject, regardless of how many `SubjectKind` terms the query contains (memoize the resolved kind per subject).
- Search results are unchanged for all existing cases: single kind term, multiple kind terms (AND semantics — distinct kinds still match nothing), kind-only term sets, and mixed name/author/kind term sets.
- A unit test with a counting lookup pins the contract: N subjects × K kind terms (K ≥ 2) results in at most N lookup calls, and the duplicate-same-kind-term case is covered.
- The doc comment and the implementation agree after the fix.

Dedup: issue search for `search_terms`/`subject_kind` returned only #2779 (the `search_store_terms` no-kind-term over-resolution — a different function and the opposite waste); no open or closed issue covers the per-term re-calling inside `search_terms`. NOT self-solved: filed-only this run (time discipline); the memoization is a small, clearly scoped fix for the queue.

title: pm-dispatch(sessions): a failure between createSession and the claim PATCH orphans a live OpenCode session — task cancelled, 'launch FAILED' noted, session id recorded nowhere

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

labels.name: app/pm-stack
labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

body:
## Problem

In pm-dispatch (`pm-stack/dispatch/src/server.ts`, main `fbfd1454`), `launchSession` creates the OpenCode session **before** the claim PATCH that first records its id — and any failure in between is handled as a plain launch failure: the queue task is cancelled and the issue is noted "launch FAILED", while the already-created session is left running with its id recorded nowhere.

## Evidence

- `launchSession` order (`server.ts`): `opencode.createSession(...)` at :105, `sendPrompt(session.id, ...)` at :111, `queue.ensureWorker()` at :117, then the claim `patchTask(task.id, { status: "claimed", progress: { session_id: session.id, ... } })` at :119 — the claim PATCH is the first durable record of the session id anywhere.
- Any throw from :111, :117 or :119 propagates out of `launchSession`. Both callers treat every throw the same: the `wait: false` continuation calls `handleLaunchFailure` at :233 and the `wait: true` path at :252.
- `handleLaunchFailure` (`src/launch_failure.ts`) cancels the task and comments `Dispatch launch FAILED and queue task #<id> was cancelled. Error: <msg>` on the issue. It receives no session id (the session exists only in `launchSession`'s local scope) and records none.
- `OpenCodeClient` (`src/opencode.ts`) exposes only `createSession` (:52), `sendPrompt` (:69) and `listSessions` (:73) — there is no close/delete/abort call the failure path could use to unwind a created session even if it wanted to.
- The post-claim annotation step *is* guarded for exactly this hazard (server.ts, comment above the annotation try/catch: a failure there "must not reject the launch — callers cancel the task on a rejected launch (#2901), which would orphan a live session"). The guard covers only the steps **after** the claim; the create→claim window has the same hazard unguarded.

## Why it matters

- Worst case: `sendPrompt` succeeds and the claim PATCH fails (a Supabase/PostgREST blip). A live OpenCode session is now **actively working the prompt** in the repo directory while the queue task is cancelled and the tracking issue states the launch FAILED. The fleet believes nothing is running; an unrecorded agent session is editing the repo.
- Lesser cases (sendPrompt or ensureWorker fails): the session exists, unprompted, with no record of its id on the task, the issue, or anywhere else — it can only be found by listing all sessions on the OpenCode server and guessing.
- This is also a counterexample to the invariant stated in the #2668 design (Rule 2): cancel+502 "remains the failure outcome only for failures at or before the commit point, where it is correct: **no live session is left untracked**". Session creation precedes the commit point (the claim PATCH), so pre-commit failures *can* leave a live session untracked. Distinct from #2660 (post-claim annotation failure — that step is already guarded on current main) and #2901 (wait:false cancellation parity — the shared handler both paths use is the one that drops the session).

## Acceptance criteria

- On any `launchSession` failure after `createSession` has succeeded, the session id is recorded somewhere durable and visible: at minimum in the cancellation reason / task `last_error` and in the issue failure note (i.e. `handleLaunchFailure` or its call sites learn the session id).
- Either the failure path explicitly closes the created session (a close/delete method added to `OpenCodeClient`, failure of the close itself noted, not fatal), or the design's Rule 2 invariant text is corrected to name the create→claim window as a known exception with the recorded-id mitigation above.
- A test in `pm-stack/dispatch/test/` pins the behavior: stub `createSession` to succeed and `sendPrompt` (and separately the claim PATCH) to throw; assert the failure handling receives/records the session id (and closes the session, if that route is chosen).
- Existing dispatch tests still pass (`bun test` in `pm-stack/dispatch`).

Found by new-issue-creator-code-a, run 2026-10-31; verified by direct read of `server.ts`, `launch_failure.ts`, `opencode.ts` on main `fbfd1454` this run. Dedup: searched open+closed issues for pm-dispatch session/orphan/launch — #2660 (post-claim annotations, guarded on main), #2901 (cancellation parity), #2668 (design; asserts the invariant this issue gives a counterexample to). None covers the create→claim window.

title: id(world-doctor): clock check accepts absurd future readings — its doc promises a zero-or-absurd check but only zero is tested, so a clock set to year 2100 (or u64::MAX) reports ok

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Summary

`id world doctor`'s clock check promises to catch an absurd clock reading but only checks that the reading is positive — a clock set years or millennia in the future reports `ok`.

## Evidence (main bd137984)

- `pkgs/id/src/world_doctor.rs:399-411` — the doc comment on `check_clock` says: "The clock reads a positive unix time. A zero (or absurd) reading means the system clock is before the epoch, which breaks every schedule and expiry." The implementation is only:

  ```rust
  match inputs.now_ms {
      Some(now) if now > 0 => ok("clock", format!("{now} ms since the epoch")),
      _ => fail(/* ... */),
  }
  ```

  No upper bound / absurdity check exists anywhere in the check.
- The CLI feeds it the real system clock: `pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs:445` sets `now_ms: Some(crate::time::unix_ms())`.
- Verified this run on the laptop with a verbatim copy of `check_clock` (world_doctor.rs md5 `d82936864cfb68121393220ece88f98f`, identical on both clones; probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-doctorclock/`):

  | input | result |
  |---|---|
  | `Some(0)` / `None` | Fail (correct) |
  | realistic 2026-10-31 ms | Ok |
  | year 2100 (4102444800000 ms) | **Ok** |
  | year 3000 (32503680000000 ms) | **Ok** |
  | `u64::MAX` | **Ok** |

## Why it matters

Doctor exists to mechanically diagnose a broken world setup, and a mis-set clock is one of its six named checks. A far-future clock (bad RTC, mis-set VM/container clock — the classic failure this check is for) silently breaks the things the fix text itself names: schedules are bounded relative to now (`MAX_SCHEDULE_HORIZON_MS`, 30 days, `world_caps.rs:99-101`) and expiries compare against now, so a clock years ahead makes expiries instantly due and schedules un-settable — while `id world doctor` reports the clock check `ok` and sends the operator looking elsewhere. The module's other checks are carefully aligned with the code they diagnose (e.g. the journal check matches restore semantics, the profile check matches `WorldExecutionProfile::resolve` exactly); the clock check is the one whose implementation does not deliver what its own contract states.

## Acceptance criteria

- Triage pins the absurdity rule: the upper bound (e.g. a fixed sanity ceiling or a bound relative to a plausible range) and the severity (Fail vs Warn) for a beyond-bound reading, including what the detail/fix text should say for the future case (the current Fail text only covers "before the unix epoch").
- `check_clock` implements the pinned rule; realistic current timestamps still report Ok, zero/None still Fail.
- Unit tests in `world_doctor.rs` cover: zero, a realistic now, the pinned boundary, and a far-future value (year 2100 / u64::MAX class).
- The doc comment and the implementation agree after the fix.

Dedup: no open or closed issue covers the doctor clock check (issue search for doctor/clock returned only #2093, the doctor *journal* disagreement — distinct check). NOT self-solved: the bound and severity are triage's pin.

title: aggregator(saas-extract): Cloudflare, Turso and GitHub count patterns still use bare \d+ — grouped counts truncate (1,234 → 234) or drop the whole metric

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: app/aggregator
labels.description: Package/app: aggregator (pm-stack in this repo)

labels.name: app/pm-stack
labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Summary

Three more `saas-extract.ts` extractors parse counts with bare `\d+`, so a comma-grouped figure is either silently truncated to its last digit group or drops the metric(s) entirely. This is the same defect class as #2997 (bitwarden), in extractors that issue does **not** name: Cloudflare counts, the Turso database count, and the GitHub comped-minutes pair. The wrong `used` values flow into durable snapshot records the same way #2997 describes (`recordsFromSaasServices`, `snapshot-records.ts:85`).

## Evidence (main `1c6d5174`)

`pm-stack/aggregator/src/saas-extract.ts`:

- **:308 (Cloudflare)** — `/(\d+) Workers, (\d+) R2 buckets[^;]*; (\d+) D1, (\d+) KV, (\d+) Queues/`. `\d+` cannot cross a comma. When the **first** count is grouped, the engine slides and records only the last group. When a **later** count is grouped, the pinned literal separators (`, `, `; `) leave nowhere to slide, so the whole match fails and all five count metrics vanish.
- **:324 (Turso)** — `/(\d+) DB/` records the last group of a grouped database count.
- **:395 (GitHub)** — `/(\d[\d,]*) Linux \+ (\d+) macOS minutes/`: the Linux group already accepts commas (and strips them at :426), but the macOS group is bare `\d+` pinned by the ` Linux + ` literal, so a grouped macOS figure makes the whole comped-minutes metric disappear instead of being recorded.

Verified this run on the laptop with the **real** `extractSaasServices` (`saas-extract.ts` md5 `2b540acdb7924e834941a63b0416cf44` on both clones; probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneA-saascounts/`):

```text
CF grouped-first  "1,234 Workers, 56 R2 buckets ~2 GB; 7 D1, 8 KV, 9 Queues"
  -> workers-count=234 (want 1234), r2=56, d1=7, kv=8, queues=9
CF grouped-later  "3 Workers, 2 R2 buckets ~2 GB; 2 D1, 1,234 KV, 2 Queues"
  -> {} — all five count metrics missing (want kv=1234, rest present)
CF control        "3 Workers, 2 R2 buckets ~2 GB; 2 D1, 2 KV, 2 Queues" -> 3/2/2/2/2
Turso grouped     "1,234 DB total" -> databases=234 (want 1234); control "12 DB" -> 12
GitHub grouped    "5,000 Linux + 1,234 macOS minutes" -> actions-comped-minutes missing
                  (want 6234); control "5,000 Linux + 234 macOS minutes" -> 5234
```

## Why it matters

- The truncated figures are indistinguishable from true reads (234 could be a real Workers count), and they persist as snapshot history — silent corruption, not a display glitch.
- The drop modes are worse in a different way: one grouped figure in the wrong position erases the whole Cloudflare footprint line or the comped-minutes metric, so the hub reports "not measured" for data that was recorded in the view.
- The house pattern already exists in the same file: `allowance()` captures `[\d,.]+`, `dns.ts` `parsePriceUsd` and `snapshot-records.ts:177` use `[\d,]+` + strip-commas, and the GitHub extractor's own Linux group does it — these three sites are the outliers. Existing fixtures only exercise ungrouped counts (`3 Workers, 2 R2 buckets…`, `1 DB`), so the suite cannot see the gap.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Cloudflare counts parse comma-grouped figures at face value in **every** position: `1,234 Workers, …` → 1234, and `…, 1,234 KV, …` → kv-count 1234 with the other four counts still present.
- [ ] Turso `databases` parses `1,234 DB` → 1234.
- [ ] GitHub comped minutes parse `5,000 Linux + 1,234 macOS minutes` → 6234.
- [ ] Regression tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/usage.test.ts` cover grouped figures for all three extractors alongside the existing ungrouped fixtures; ungrouped reads are unchanged and a bullet with no counts still yields no count metrics.

## Dedup

Searched open and closed issues 2026-10-31 for `cloudflare counts comma`, `turso comma`, `macOS minutes`, `saas-extract grouped counts`, and the counts-line text: the only hit is #2997, which is scoped to the bitwarden extractor (landed in PR #2987) and names only the Modal comma-dollar patterns as a sibling for triage ruling. The Cloudflare, Turso, and GitHub sites predate that commit and are not mentioned there. #2985/#2791 concern `num()` *reinterpretation* of non-decimal strings in different functions, not grouped-decimal truncation/dropping.

body:
## Summary

The Bitwarden extractor added today in PR #2987 (#1111) parses the dated `bws` counts with bare `\d+`, so a comma-grouped count is silently truncated to its last group — and the wrong figure then flows into the snapshot store as a permanent record. `1,121 secrets` is recorded as **121** (indistinguishable from a real 121 read) and `1,000 projects` is recorded as **0**.

## Evidence (main `74afc26e`)

`pm-stack/aggregator/src/saas-extract.ts:475-478` (`bitwardenMetrics`, added by commit `795bbdb4`, merged in #2987):

```ts
const secrets = /(\d+)\s*secrets?/i.exec(usage);
const projects = /(\d+)\s*projects?/i.exec(usage);
```

`\d+` cannot cross the comma, so the regex engine slides forward and matches only the final digit group before the noun: for `1,121 secrets` it matches `121 secrets`; for `1,000 projects` it matches `000 projects` → `Number("000")` = 0.

Verified this run on the laptop with the **real** `extractSaasServices` (laptop clone at the same main, `saas-extract.ts` md5 `2b540acdb7924e834941a63b0416cf44` on both clones; probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-bwcomma/`):

```text
Usage bullet: "1,121 secrets, 1,000 projects (bws count-only read 2026-10-26)"
measuredAt 2026-10-26
secrets-count used = 121     ← want 1121
projects-count used = 0      ← want 1000
control ("121 secrets, 1 project"): secrets-count = 121, projects-count = 1
```

Note the corrupted secrets figure is *identical to the control* — there is no signal in the output that anything was lost.

## Why it matters

- These metrics are not display-only: the extractor's commit message and `recordsFromSaasServices` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/snapshot-records.ts:85`, called from `scripts/collect-fleet-feed.ts:598` and `scripts/append-usage-snapshots.ts:67`) turn `used` into durable snapshot records keyed by (service, metric, ts, value). A misparsed count becomes wrong history, not a transient render glitch.
- Every sibling extractor in this codebase already handles grouped numbers: `parsePriceUsd` in `dns.ts` and the DeepSeek ¥ parse in `snapshot-records.ts:177` use `[\d,]+` and strip commas; the Cloudflare limits in the same file parse `10M`-style figures. The new extractor (merged hours ago) is the outlier, and its own test fixture only exercises ungrouped counts (`121 secrets, 1 project`), so the gap is invisible to the suite.
- The Modal extractor added in the same commit has the same `\d+`-only shape for its dollar figures (`saas-extract.ts:448-455`); there the failure is fail-soft (a `$1,250 credits used` read matches nothing and stays null). Triage should decide whether to harden it in the same pass or leave it as a noted sibling.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `bitwardenMetrics` parses comma-grouped counts at face value: `1,121 secrets` → 1121, `1,000 projects` → 1000 (accept the house `[\d,]+` + strip-commas form, or an equivalent grouped-number parse).
- [ ] Regression tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/usage.test.ts` cover grouped secrets and projects counts alongside the existing ungrouped case.
- [ ] Ungrouped reads are unchanged (`121 secrets, 1 project` → 121 / 1), and a bullet with no counts still yields no metrics.
- [ ] Triage rules on the Modal comma-dollar sibling (same-commit `\d+`-only patterns): fix in the same change, or record it as an explicit follow-up — not silently left.

## Dedup

Searched open and closed issues for `bitwarden`, `bws count`, and comma/thousands parsing in `saas-extract` on 2026-10-31: no existing issue covers this extractor (it landed today in #2987). The extractor's parent work is #1111 / #2990 (per-credential rows and remainders — different items). Sibling number-reinterpretation issues (#2985 `aa.ts` `num()`, #2791 cloudflare-export `num()`) concern different functions that *reinterpret* non-decimal strings; this one *truncates* a grouped decimal.

body:
# mcpx(recipes): a declared `@param` default is never validated against its type — Render splices it verbatim, bypassing literal() entirely

## Evidence (verified this run, main `c1b9052c`)

In `pkgs/mcpx/internal/recipes/recipes.go`:

- `Placeholder.Default` is documented (lines 54–56) as "the literal as written in the declaration, **already valid for the type**" — but nothing enforces that. `Parse` (lines 134–139) stores whatever `splitDefault` takes off the declaration line, with no check against the declared type.
- `Render` (lines 354–355) uses the default verbatim — `lits[p.Name] = *p.Default` — and never passes it through `literal()`, the one function that validates supplied values. So even the checks that do exist for caller-supplied values (and the gaps in them, #2993) do not apply to defaults at all.
- The inconsistency is visible inside the same file: `FormSchema` (lines 451–455) only exposes a default when `decodeLiteral` can JSON-decode it (or, for strings, after trimming quotes), so the form and the renderer disagree about what the default is.

Probe (laptop, real package copied from `origin/main` at `c1b9052c`, `recipes.go` md5 `053282eb929febab57c74a5646c4950f` on both clones; probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneA-recipedefault/`, `go test ./internal/recipes/ -run TestProbeDefaults`): each recipe rendered with **no values supplied** and returned `err=nil`:

| Declaration | Rendered splice | Problem |
|---|---|---|
| `@param n:number = banana` | `n: banana` | bare identifier — runtime `ReferenceError`, or whatever `banana` happens to be in scope |
| `@param s:string = hello` | `s: hello` | a supplied string value is JSON-quoted by `literal()`; the default is spliced unquoted as an identifier |
| `@param b:boolean = yes` | `b: yes` | not a boolean literal at all |
| `@param n:number = 1+1` | `n: 1+1` | an arbitrary expression from the declaration line is spliced verbatim |
| `@param n:number = 30` (control) | `n: 30` | correct |
| `@param s:string = "hi"` (control) | `s: "hi"` | correct |

## Why it matters

`Render`'s own safety comment (lines 340–342) says values are written as JSON precisely because "substituting raw text would make every recipe an injection site, and a recipe is run with the user's credentials." The default path is exactly that raw substitution, for the value most likely to be exercised headlessly: the broker's contract (`FormSchema` docs) is that a headless caller times out and **the defaults are what remains**. A mistyped or unquoted default therefore either silently changes the executed script's semantics (bare identifier / expression) or fails at runtime in the recipe, instead of being refused at the boundary where the declared type is known. It also composes with #2993: fixing `literal()` alone does not fix defaults, because defaults never reach it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A declared default is validated/rendered through the same type path as a supplied value (or an equivalent check at `Parse`/`Render`): a default whose form does not match the placeholder's declared type is refused with an error naming the placeholder and expected type — no verbatim splice.
- [ ] An unquoted string default renders as a JSON string (quoted), matching what a supplied string value renders as; a number/boolean default renders only when it is a valid literal of that type in JavaScript.
- [ ] `FormSchema` and `Render` agree on defaults: a default one of them rejects is rejected (or omitted) consistently by the other.
- [ ] Regression tests in `pkgs/mcpx/internal/recipes/recipes_test.go` cover the probe table (number=`banana`, string=`hello` unquoted, boolean=`yes`, number=`1+1`) plus the correctly-typed controls (`30`, `"hi"`).
- [ ] Existing recipe tests still pass (`go test ./internal/recipes/`).

## Dedup / scope notes

- Distinct from #2993 (open): that issue is caller-supplied values passing through `literal()` in `Render`. This one is the declaration-default path, which bypasses `literal()` entirely (`Render` lines 354–355) and is never validated in `Parse`.
- Distinct from #1671 (closed): `splitDefault` bracket truncation of JSON defaults — a parsing bug in how much of the line becomes the default, not whether the resulting default is valid for the type.
- Distinct from #1670 (open): where substitution happens (@name inside comments/strings).
- NOT self-solved: where validation belongs (Parse-time vs Render-time) and whether an unquoted string default should be quoted or refused is triage's pin; this filing goes the producer-queue route.

# mcpx(recipes): Render's literal() type-checks only string inputs — a mistyped JSON value is spliced verbatim, and Go-only number spellings render as invalid JS

## Evidence (verified this run, main `c1b9052c`)

`pkgs/mcpx/internal/recipes/recipes.go`, `literal()` (lines 401–441), is the one place a caller-supplied value becomes code in the rendered recipe script: `Render` (lines 343–377) splices its result at each `@name`. The type switch only validates **string** inputs:

- `TypeNumber` + string: `strconv.ParseFloat` check, error on failure (`%s is a number, got %q`).
- `TypeBoolean` + string: `strconv.ParseBool` check, error on failure.
- `TypeJSON` + string: only when the string is valid JSON.

Every other combination falls through to `json.Marshal(v)` and is spliced with **no type check at all**, and the two validated string paths return the caller's spelling verbatim after a *Go* parse — but the rendered script is JavaScript, whose number grammar is narrower than Go's.

Probe (laptop, real package copied from `origin/main` at `c1b9052c`, `recipes.go` md5 `053282eb929febab57c74a5646c4950f` on both clones; probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-recipeliteral/`, `go test -run TestProbeLiteralTypes`). Recipe: `@param n:number`, `@param s:string`, `@param b:boolean`, body `demo.run({ n: @n, s: @s, b: @b })`. All of these returned `err=nil`:

| Given value | Rendered splice | Problem |
|---|---|---|
| `n = true` (bool) | `n: true` | number placeholder silently becomes a boolean |
| `n = "Inf"` (string) | `n: Inf` | Go `ParseFloat` accepts `Inf`; JS has no `Inf` identifier — runtime `ReferenceError` |
| `n = "0x10p0"` (string) | `n: 0x10p0` | Go hex-float spelling; not valid JS numeric syntax — script does not parse |
| `n = math.Inf(1)` (float64) | `n: +Inf` | `FormatFloat` Go spelling; JS name is `Infinity` — `ReferenceError` |
| `s = 42` (number) | `s: 42` | string placeholder splices an unquoted number |
| `s = true` / `s = ["a"]` | `s: true` / `s: ["a"]` | string placeholder splices bool/array literals |
| `b = 1` (number) | `b: 1` | boolean placeholder splices a number |

Control (all correctly typed values) rendered exactly as expected: `n: 3, s: "x", b: true`.

## Why it matters

Recipes run with the user's credentials (the module's own docs make this point about substitution safety), and values arrive from elicitation answers and headless/API callers — i.e. JSON whose types are whatever the caller sent, not what the `@param` declaration promised. Today a mistyped value produces no error at the boundary where the type is known: it either silently changes the value's type in the executed script (bool for number, number for string, …) or produces a script that fails to parse / throws `ReferenceError` at runtime, with the failure pointing at the recipe instead of the bad input. The string-input branches show the intended contract — reject with `%s is a number, got %q` — the fall-through just doesn't extend it to non-string JSON values or to JS-invalid spellings.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `literal()` rejects (with the existing error style, naming the placeholder and the expected type) any value whose JSON type does not match the placeholder's declared type, for all types — including non-string inputs for `number`/`boolean`/`string` placeholders. (If triage prefers coercion for a specific case, pin it explicitly instead of the current accidental fall-through.)
- [ ] Number rendering never emits a spelling JavaScript cannot read: non-finite floats (`±Inf`, and `NaN` if triage rules it out for a *declared number input*) and Go-only string spellings accepted by `ParseFloat` (e.g. `Inf`, `0x10p0`) are rejected or rendered in JS form — pinned by tests.
- [ ] Regression tests in `pkgs/mcpx/internal/recipes/recipes_test.go` cover the probe table above (bool→number, number/bool/array→string, number→boolean, `"Inf"`, `"0x10p0"`, `math.Inf(1)`) plus the correctly-typed control.
- [ ] Existing recipe tests still pass (`go test ./internal/recipes/`).

## Dedup / scope notes

- Distinct from #1670 (open): that issue is about *where* substitution happens (@name inside comments/strings). This one is about *what* `literal()` splices for a legitimately-placed placeholder when the value's type is wrong.
- Distinct from #1671 (closed): `splitDefault` bracket truncation of JSON defaults.
- Not self-solved: the reject-vs-coerce ruling per type (and the `NaN` ruling) is triage's pin; this filing goes the producer-queue route.

body:
## Summary

`pkgs/mcpx/internal/source/source.go`'s `abs()` (line 118-126, main `90f69428`) still expands **any** leading `~` under the caller's own home — the exact bug #1702 pinned for search paths and fixed for `searchpath` in #2967 (landed `6bee50a8`). The `source` resolver was missed:

```go
func abs(path, dir string) string {
	if filepath.IsAbs(path) { return path }
	if strings.HasPrefix(path, "~") {
		if home, err := os.UserHomeDir(); err == nil {
			return filepath.Join(home, strings.TrimPrefix(path, "~"))
		}
	}
	...
	return filepath.Join(dir, path)
}
```

So `~alice/secret.ts`, `~nosuchuser/x.ts`, and `~scratch` are silently resolved to `$HOME/alice/secret.ts`, `$HOME/nosuchuser/x.ts`, and `$HOME/scratch` — inventing a home for users who may not exist — instead of being treated as literal relative entries under `Dir`, which is the rule #1702's triage pinned (only a bare `~` and `~/...` name the caller's home) and which the two sibling helpers now implement:

- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/searchpath/searchpath.go:127` — `path == "~" || strings.HasPrefix(path, "~/")` (fixed in #2967)
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/routes_dashboard.go:84` — `dir == "~" || strings.HasPrefix(dir, "~/")`

`source.abs()` is the path resolver for every string-shaped mcpx source setting (launchers, prefixes, error hooks — see the package doc): it is reached via `@file:`, `@dir:`, and the bare-value probe path in `Resolve()`.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-sourcetilde/` — the real `source.go` copied verbatim (md5 `ea6a8c5521476daf62b8a0e089104007`, matching both clones at main `90f69428`), with a test calling the real `abs()` / `Resolve()` with `HOME` set to a temp dir and `Dir` set to a different temp dir containing a literal `~alice/` directory:

```
abs("~alice/secret.ts")   = "$HOME/alice/secret.ts"        want "$DIR/~alice/secret.ts"
abs("~nosuchuser/x.ts")   = "$HOME/nosuchuser/x.ts"        want "$DIR/~nosuchuser/x.ts"
abs("~scratch")           = "$HOME/scratch"                want "$DIR/~scratch"
Resolve("@file:~alice/secret.ts") text="FROM_HOME_ALICE"   (read $HOME/alice/secret.ts)
                                  want "FROM_LITERAL_TILDE" (the file under $DIR/~alice/)
```

Controls behaved correctly and are not in the failure list: `abs("~/own.ts") = $HOME/own.ts` and `abs("~") = $HOME`.

## Why it matters

A source value beginning `~name` reads a *different file than the one named* — a lookalike file under the caller's own home — with no error. For launcher/prefix/hook sources that is silent wrong-code execution potential if such a lookalike exists, and a confusing "file not found / wrong content" failure otherwise. It also makes the three mcpx path helpers disagree: the same `~alice/...` string means one thing as a search-path entry and another as a source value.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `source.abs()` expands only a bare `~` and `~/...` to the caller's home; `~name` entries resolve literally against `Dir`, matching `searchpath.absolute()` and the dashboard helper.
- [ ] Regression test in `pkgs/mcpx/internal/source/source_test.go` covering `~`, `~/x`, `~alice/x`, `~nosuchuser/x`, and `~scratch` (mirroring `TestOnlyBareTildeAndTildeSlashExpandHome`), including an end-to-end `Resolve("@file:~alice/...")` case that reads the literal directory.
- [ ] No other mcpx path helper retains the bare-`HasPrefix(path, "~")` form (grep-verifiable).

## Dedup / relations

- #1702 (closed) covered `searchpath` only; its fix #2967 touched `searchpath.go` only. This is the missed sibling helper from the same rule, not a duplicate filing of #1702.
- #1727 (open, `mcpx(source)`) is about non-regular files in directory sources — different defect, same package.

body:
## Summary

In the PM projector's webhook intake, the delivery id is taken from the
`X-GitHub-Delivery` header with an empty-string fallback, and that empty
string is used as the delivery's identity everywhere. The first
header-less delivery is recorded under `delivery_id = ""`, and every
later — completely distinct — header-less delivery is answered
`200 {"status":"duplicate"}` and silently dropped: its event is never
applied. Push events collapse the same way (`recordPush` keys on the
same id with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`).

GitHub itself always sends the header, but the intake accepts any
correctly HMAC-signed POST (replay tooling, a future non-GitHub sender,
a proxy that strips the header), and for all of those the dedup
identity silently degrades to a single shared bucket: one event is
applied, the rest vanish with a success response.

## Evidence (main 6a19fec5, verified this run)

- `pm-stack/projector/src/server.ts:108` —
  `const deliveryId = req.headers.get("x-github-delivery") ?? "";`
- `pm-stack/projector/src/server.ts:117-120` — `deliveryApplied(db, "")`
  is true as soon as any header-less delivery has been recorded, so the
  handler returns `{status: "duplicate"}` before parsing/applying.
- `pm-stack/projector/src/store.ts` — `recordDelivery` stores the `""`
  row verbatim; `recordPush` (server passes the same `deliveryId`)
  uses `ON CONFLICT(delivery_id) DO NOTHING`, so header-less pushes
  after the first are lost too.

Probe (laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-projector/probe2.ts`,
real `handleRequest` + migrated file DB, valid HMAC, repo allow-listed):

```
event#101 NO delivery header            -> 200 {"status":"applied","refs":["developing-today/code#101"]}
event#102 NO delivery header (distinct) -> 200 {"status":"duplicate"}
event#103 with delivery header          -> 200 {"status":"applied", ...}
event#104 with delivery header          -> 200 {"status":"applied", ...}
event#103 redelivery same header        -> 200 {"status":"duplicate"}   (control, correct)
items in DB: developing-today/code#101, #103, #104     — #102 never arrived
delivery row: {"delivery_id":"","event":"issues","outcome":"applied"}
```

## Why it matters

Silent data loss with a success response is the worst failure shape
for a projection whose whole job is not missing GitHub activity: the
sender believes the event was deduplicated, the item/comment/push
simply never exists downstream, and nothing logs an anomaly. It is
the mirror image of #2456 (a *recorded failure* blocking retry): here
a *missing identity* makes unrelated deliveries collide.

## Acceptance criteria

- A webhook POST without a usable delivery id is never deduplicated
  against a different event: either it is rejected (e.g. 400
  `missing_delivery_id`) or it is applied with a locally generated
  unique delivery identity — triage picks one contract and pins it.
- The chosen behaviour is covered by a handler test: two distinct
  header-less deliveries produce the pinned outcome for both, and the
  `pmp_deliveries` rows show no shared `""` identity.
- Normal dedup is unchanged: a repeated real delivery GUID still
  returns `{"status":"duplicate"}` and applies once.
- Push events from header-less deliveries follow the same contract
  (no silent `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` loss under a shared id).

Related: #2456 (error-row blocks redelivery — same dedup table,
different mechanism).

title: id(web/collab): Steps version check and append are not atomic — two clients at the same base version both pass, both append, and the document silently diverges

body:
## Problem

In the collab WebSocket handler, the Steps version check and the step append are not atomic, so two clients connected to the same document can both pass the version check with the same base version and both have their steps appended — silently diverging the shared document instead of one of them getting the version-mismatch error the protocol relies on.

## Evidence (main `ed59bc6d`, `pkgs/id/src/web/collab.rs`)

- `:1002-1003` — the handler reads the current version: `let current_version = doc.version();` (`Document::version` is a plain `AtomicU64` load, `collab.rs:268-270`) and compares it to the version the client's Steps frame claims.
- `:1019-1028` — only afterwards does it take `doc.steps.write().await` and push the steps. The `.await` on the steps lock sits between the check and the append, so the task can yield there.
- `:1030-1033` — the version is bumped only after the push: `doc.version.fetch_add(steps.len() as u64, SeqCst)`. The version and the steps vector are two separate synchronization objects; nothing holds a lock across check → append → bump.
- Each socket is handled by its own task (`handle_collab_socket`), and the server performs no transform/rebase of incoming steps: steps are stored verbatim (`:1023-1026`) and broadcast verbatim (`:1036-1040`). The version equality check is the only guard against a client submitting steps computed against a stale document state — ProseMirror's collab protocol depends on exactly that rejection.

Interleaving that breaks it:

1. Clients A and B are both at version V (the normal state after a broadcast).
2. A sends Steps(version=V, steps=[a]); B concurrently sends Steps(version=V, steps=[b]), where `b` was computed against the document at V (not V+[a]).
3. A's handler checks V == V, then yields awaiting the steps lock (or B's handler runs first — either order works).
4. B's handler also checks V == V and passes.
5. Both append; the version advances by len(a)+len(b). B's steps are now recorded as if they followed A's, and every other client replays them in that order via the broadcast Update and the join-time catch-up (`:791-806`). No client ever sees a version mismatch, so no client rebases or reconnects; the replicas have applied non-commuting steps in an order one author never intended.

Verification this run: code-read verification of the handler on current main (the check/append/bump sequence and the per-socket task structure are as cited above; no lock or atomic spans them). The race needs no exotic timing — any two editors typing at the same moment on the same document can hit the await window, and the window widens under load (steps lock contention with the catch-up read at `:792`).

## Why it matters

Silent divergence is the worst collab failure mode: the server reports success (Ack with the new version, `:1046-1053`) to both authors, so the corruption is only discovered later as mangled text on save. The codebase already treats the neighbouring failure (broadcast lag) as a desync worth an explicit error + reconnect (`:896-906`); this path produces the same desync with no signal at all.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Steps acceptance is atomic per document: the version check, the steps append, and the version bump happen under one per-document lock (or an equivalent compare-and-swap discipline), so a second Steps frame with the same base version is rejected with the existing `Version mismatch` error once the first has been applied.
- [ ] A regression test drives two concurrent Steps submissions with the same base version against one document and asserts exactly one is Acked and the other gets the version-mismatch error, and that the stored steps/version reflect only the winner.
- [ ] Single-client behaviour is unchanged: sequential Steps at the correct version are Acked, broadcast, and replayed by the join-time catch-up exactly as before.
- [ ] The fix does not hold the steps lock across network sends (broadcast/Ack stay outside the critical section, or the ordering is argued in the PR).

## Dedup / related

- #2799 (open) is the Init-frame version (`Init` always carries version 0 while the document replays to a later version) — a different frame and a different defect; this issue is about two live Steps submissions racing.
- #2824 (open) is the TypeScript client's trust of MessagePack frame shape — client-side, distinct.
- #2830 (open) is the collab WS URL encoding — distinct.
- Search of open + closed issues for "collab steps version race / concurrent steps / version mismatch" found no existing issue covering this interleaving.

title: id(web): world presenter residual width divergences vs unicode-width 0.2.2 — 2529 code points in classes #1581 never scoped (trigrams, CJK radicals, format chars)

body:
## Problem

After the #1581 fix (PR #2945), the TS world presenter (`pkgs/id/web/src/world-surface.ts`) and the Rust validator (`pkgs/id/src/world_presentation.rs`, unicode-width 0.2.2) still disagree on the **alone width of 2529 single code points** — classes #1581 never scoped. Same failure mode as #1581: a Rust-valid screen can fall back to raw text in the browser (TS refuses a width the Rust side admitted), or TS accepts a width Rust refused.

## Evidence (gathered 2026-10-31, queue task 1842)

Exhaustive differential: the real `graphemeWidth` from `world-surface.ts` (driven under bun) vs `UnicodeWidthStr::width` on the pinned unicode-width 0.2.2 (standalone Rust probe), every code point U+0020..U+2FFFF, alone and +U+FE0E. The PR #2945 work zeroed all #1581/FE0E divergences (57 alone + 93 FE0E fixed, zero new); the residual **alone-width** mismatches, by class:

| Rust | TS | count | examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 1 | 2295 | U+17A4 (Khmer vowel), U+2630..U+2637 (trigrams) |
| 1 | 2 | 76 | U+2E9A, U+2EF4..U+2EFA (CJK radicals inside TS's broad `0x2E80..0x303E` / `0x3040..0x33FF` wide ranges) |
| 0 | 1 | 143 | U+00AD, U+0605, U+061C, U+070F, U+0890..U+0891, U+08E2 (format/invisible chars) |
| 0 | 2 | 13 | U+302A..U+302F (ideographic tone marks), U+3099, U+309A |
| 1 | 0 | 1 | U+2D7F |
| 3 | 1 | 1 | U+17D8 |

Reproduction is mechanical: rebuild the two probes (a ~30-line Rust binary pinned to `unicode-width = "=0.2.2"` dumping `cp / alone / +FE0E`, and a bun script importing `graphemeWidth`) and diff — counts above must reproduce exactly against PR #2945's head or later main.

## Reachability note (why this needs triage, not a blind table sync)

The Rust validator admits only graphemes of width 1..=2 per cell, so classes with Rust width 2 / TS 1 are reachable in principle (e.g. a screen cell `U+2630` at `columns: 2` is Rust-valid and TS-refused). Other classes may be unreachable: U+17D8 is Rust width 3 alone (never admittable as a lone cell), and some rust=0 classes may be excluded upstream by the presenter's control-char refusal. Each class needs a disposition before table surgery on 2529 code points is justified.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each residual class above is dispositioned reachable-as-a-cell or unreachable, with the reasoning recorded (single-grapheme admission, control-char refusal, segmenter behavior in clusters — clusters may differ from the alone table)
- [ ] Reachable classes are fixed in `world-surface.ts` with parity tests in `world-surface.test.ts`, re-verified by the exhaustive differential (target: zero alone and +FE0E mismatches outside proven-unreachable classes)
- [ ] #1581 / PR #2945 are not reopened — this issue covers only the residual classes

Filed by the queue worker (Lane B, task 1842) from evidence gathered fixing the Codex P2 on PR #2945; a queue triage task keyed to this issue carries the same evidence.

title: id(world): journal restore never sanitizes Issued display names — empty, control-bearing, and over-length names restore verbatim, though mint refuses or strips all three

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage

body:
## Problem

`WorldCore::restore` (`pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs`, the `JournalEntry::Issued` arm) inserts the journaled `Participant` verbatim — including its `display_name`. The struct's own contract is "Caller-provided display name, **sanitized and bounded at issue time**" (`src/world/mod.rs`, `Participant`), and the one live producer enforces it:

- `WorldCore::mint` (core.rs) runs every name through `sanitize_display_name` (`src/world/util.rs`: strip control characters, cap at 48 chars, trim) and refuses the result if it is empty: "participant display name must not be empty".

Restore does neither. A journal no live code path can produce (hand-edited, corrupted, or fork-copied — restore's contract is "a bad journal is refused, never partially applied") therefore restores participants whose names are:

1. **Empty** — a participant no join flow could ever create, shown as a blank entry in every snapshot's participant list and in the presence "left" lines restore itself synthesizes from the name (`presence_event(participant, &name, false)` at the end of restore).
2. **Control-bearing and unbounded** — names with newlines / BEL / other control characters, and names far past the 48-char bound, carried verbatim into snapshots (`WorldSnapshot.participants`), the players list a world program reads (`players_list` in `src/world/actor.rs`), and presence events. Every other name producer in the system sanitizes first; a restored name is the one that reaches those consumers raw.

This is the restore-side gap, distinct from #2112: that issue is about the sanitizer itself letting format characters (Cf) through on the *live* path. Here even the sanitizer's existing guarantees (no control characters, ≤48 chars, non-empty) are skipped entirely by the *restore* path.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `51033658`)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneA-restorecap/`, a detached worktree of `origin/main` at `51033658f73a`; integration test `pkgs/id/tests/probe_restorecap.rs` against the real `id` crate, token digests built exactly as `mint` builds them):

- CONTROL: live `issue_capability` with a control-only name (`"\u{1}\u{2}"`, which sanitizes to empty) returns `Err`.
- CASE B: restore of `Created + Issued(1, display_name="")` returns `Ok`; a snapshot taken with participant 1's legitimate token lists the participant with name `""`.
- CASE C: restore of `Created + Issued(1, display_name="a\u{7}\n" + 98 more chars)` returns `Ok`; the snapshot participant's name is **verbatim** (`verbatim=true`, 101 chars, `has_control=true`) — no stripping, no 48-char cap, no trim.

Code points (main `51033658`): restore's `Issued` arm at `src/world/core.rs:168-222` inserts `participant` unchecked at :212-221; `mint`'s sanitize + empty refusal at `core.rs:864-868`; `sanitize_display_name` at `src/world/util.rs:69-76`; the `Participant` doc contract at `src/world/mod.rs:307-313`.

## Why it matters

Display names are the human-facing identity of a participant: they render in participant lists, presence join/leave lines, and program-visible player lists. The system treats sanitization as an issue-time invariant — the type documents it, `mint` enforces it — so downstream consumers reasonably trust names to be single-line, bounded, and non-empty. Restore silently breaks that trust for exactly the journals that deserve the most suspicion, and once restored, the name is re-journaled verbatim by the next checkpoint (`checkpoint_entries` re-emits the stored `Participant`), so the unsanitized name becomes permanent.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Restore either refuses an `Issued` entry whose `display_name` is empty after sanitization, or sanitizes journaled names on restore exactly as `mint` does — triage pins which (refuse matches restore's "bad journal is refused" contract for the neighbouring fields; sanitize-and-keep matches fork/legacy tolerance). Whichever is chosen, a restored name must never be empty, control-bearing, or over the 48-char bound.
- [ ] Regression tests beside the existing restore tests: empty name case; control-char name case; >48-char name case; a normal minted journal (names already sanitized) still restores byte-identical names.
- [ ] Triage checks historical/compacted journals: `checkpoint_entries` re-emits stored participants, and all stored participants came through `mint`, so legitimately produced journals always carry already-sanitized names — confirm no legitimate shape is broken by the pinned rule.
- [ ] Out of scope: strengthening the sanitizer itself against format characters — that is #2112, on the live path.

Dedup checked this run: open+closed search for restore / display name / sanitize — #2112 (open; the sanitizer's own Cf gap on the live path — different mechanism), #1833 (collab cursor names, different surface), #2890/#2894/#2958 (restore `Issued` scopes / event authors / participant limit — same function, different fields). No filing covers display-name validation in restore.
