body:
Phase 3 of design #2953 ("define, don't assign" — the write-side prototype contract). Phases 1–2 are adopted origin issues: Phase 1 = #2941 (aggregator snapshots), Phase 2 = #2828 (bin/record) + #2851 (aggregator cost-explorer). This phase is the closing inventory audit + contract statement. **Gated on Phases 1–2 landing** — do not start the audit before both land.

Design doc: `files/designs/code-proto-write-side.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace.

## Scope

1. **Inventory.** Grep the repo's TS/JS/mjs (excluding vendored assets such as `pm-stack/aggregator/src/assets/datastar.js`, and tests) for the four non-conforming write forms with dynamic keys:
   - `obj[key] = v` where the key is not a literal;
   - `obj[key] ??= …` accumulators;
   - copy loops `dst[k] = src[k]` over `Object.entries` / `Object.keys`;
   - `Object.assign(dst, src)` with a non-literal `src`.
2. **Disposition every hit** as exactly one of:
   - (a) covered by Phases 1–2 of #2953;
   - (b) external-key (a caller, document, feed, file, peer, or user can spell the key) — fix it under this design before closing, or file it as a named follow-up issue linked here;
   - (c) internal-only (all keys code-constructed) — named in the closing evidence with the reason.
   Candidates already visible at design time — disposition them, do not pre-judge: antigravity-direct's schema walkers in `bin/antigravity-direct.mjs` (`merged[k]`, `sub[name]`, `props[name]` — keys from external tool schemas); `bin/provider-catalog-sync.mjs` (`report.providers[providerId]`, `(added[pid] ??= [])`); `pkgs/id/web/src/world.ts:181` `Object.assign(records, frame.records ?? {})` (a peer-supplied frame); `bin/sync-models.mjs`'s `prov.models[baseId]` family (parsed config keys). Also report any recursive/deep-merge helper the sweep finds (the design doc's open question — report, don't pre-decide its shape).
3. **Contract statement.** Write the define-semantics rule (one paragraph + the probe matrix) into the docs that already state contracts for the covered surfaces: the aggregator README (or its snapshots/cost-explorer docs, wherever its store contracts live) and the `bin/record.mjs` header comment if it does not already carry it. No new docs files.
4. **Close #2953** with the audit evidence (the disposition table) posted as a comment on #2953 and on this issue.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The disposition table covers every grep hit from step 1, with the grep commands recorded so the sweep is reproducible.
- [ ] Every (b) hit is either fixed under this issue (with the design's probe matrix as tests: `__proto__` string value, `__proto__` object value, `constructor`, `toString`, ordinary key — own property present, JSON round-trip preserves, container + `Object.prototype` prototypes unmoved) or filed as a named follow-up issue linked here.
- [ ] #2792's Phase 3 read-side audit is not duplicated: read-only lookup sites found by the sweep are listed in the closing evidence as "#2792 scope" and not fixed here.
- [ ] Contract statement landed in the docs named in step 3.
- [ ] Closing evidence posted on #2953 and this issue; #2953 closed or its remaining follow-ups named.

## Out of scope

- Re-litigating the decisions recorded on #2953 (preserve-don't-reject; accumulators fixed by container construction, not `hasOwn`).
- Read-side lookups (#2792's phases own them, including today's #2920/#2919).
- Any site whose keys are verified internal-only — disposition (c) is a complete outcome for those.

title: Design: define, don't assign — untrusted keys are stored with define semantics, never through the __proto__ setter

labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Summary

One rule for the write side of the prototype family: **a value keyed by an externally-spellable name is stored with define semantics, never assignment semantics.** Assignment (`obj[key] = v`, `obj[key] ??= …`, `dst[k] = src[k]` copy loops, `Object.assign(dst, src)`) goes through `[[Set]]`, and for exactly one spelling — `__proto__` — `[[Set]]` invokes the `Object.prototype` setter instead of creating an own property: a non-object value is silently ignored, an object value replaces the container's prototype. Three filed instances in three surfaces prove the class; this design adopts them as its phases and closes with an inventory audit.

This is the write-side counterpart of #2792 (read-side own-key lookups), whose design doc explicitly scoped this class out ("a different bug class with a different fix… a future design decides") and whose pass-23 assessment recorded the trigger: originate when a second write-side instance files after #2851. There are now three.

Design doc: `files/designs/code-proto-write-side.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace (problem, evidence, alternatives, risks, open questions).

## The instances (audited at origin/main `106b0571`)

- **#2941 — aggregator snapshots (Phase 1, the polluting instance).** `SnapshotStore.byService()` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/snapshots.ts:562-565`) groups with `(grouped[r.serviceId] ??= []).push(r)` and `compactInner()` (:703-711) accumulates its report the same way; `serviceId` is validated only as a non-empty string (:303) and arrives from external feed jobs. A `__proto__`/`constructor`/`toString` id makes `byService()` throw (its only caller swallows the throw into `{}` — all snapshot history blanks, persistently, since the record passes validation and is stored), and `compact()` with a `__proto__` id writes its counts onto `Object.prototype` itself (`({}).before === NaN` afterwards). The same file already groups with `Map` at `appendLocked` (~:620) and in `compactRecordsToRollups` — these two sites are outliers in their own file.
- **#2851 — aggregator cost-explorer (Phase 2).** Saved setups live in a plain object from localStorage (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/render.ts:4338` save `all[name] = …`, :4359 import `all[k] = parsed[k]`). A setup named `__proto__` is silently never saved; an imported one mutates the store object's prototype. Silent data loss both directions.
- **#2828 — bin/record (Phase 2).** `parseLoose` (`bin/record.mjs:110`) builds fields by assignment; a loose `__proto__` field counts toward the keyed-segment threshold but never reaches the appended JSONL line — breaking record's never-lose-a-field contract for exactly the key an agent records while reporting this bug class. The JSON path preserves it (parse + spread = define semantics); the two paths disagree.

## Decisions recorded

1. **Preserve, don't reject.** The key is data: a `__proto__` field / setup name / serviceId is stored, listed, exported and re-read like any other key. (#2851's acceptance permits visible rejection for setup names; this design records *preserve* so all surfaces behave identically and #2941's already-stored records become readable instead of stranded. Validation-side rejection is also not the fix — #2941's acceptance already states the grouping fix must not depend on it.)
2. **The prototype must not move** — asserted as a test property: after any covered write, the container's prototype is unchanged (or `null` by design) and `Object.prototype` gains no own properties.
3. **Accumulators are construction, not lookup.** Grouping/counting sites are fixed by changing the container (`Map`, converted at the boundary via `Object.fromEntries`/spread), not by `hasOwn` guards — that is the boundary with #2792. (`byService()`'s crash is a `??=` read, but its fix is container construction, so it lives here; #2792's Phase 3 audit should disposition it as covered by this design.)
4. **One probe matrix everywhere:** `__proto__` with a string value *and* an object value (the setter treats them differently), `constructor`, `toString`, an ordinary key — asserting own-property presence, JSON round-trip preservation, and decision 2.

## Phased breakdown

- **Phase 1 = #2941** (aggregator snapshots): `Map` grouping in `byService()` + `compactInner()`, converted at the boundary. Lands first — the only instance that corrupts global state and blanks a whole surface, and its store may already hold a poisoned line.
- **Phase 2 = #2828 + #2851** (silent loss at the edges): define-semantics construction in `record.mjs`'s loose parser and in the cost-explorer save/import paths. Independent of Phase 1.
- **Phase 3 = new issue (filed with this design)**: closing inventory audit — grep TS/JS/mjs (vendored assets and tests excluded) for the four non-conforming forms with dynamic keys, disposition each (covered / external-key → fixed here or filed as a named follow-up / internal-only → named in the closing evidence), state the contract in the app docs that already state contracts, and close this design with the evidence. Candidates already visible, to be dispositioned not pre-judged: antigravity-direct's schema walkers (`merged[k]`, `sub[name]`, `props[name]` — external tool-schema keys); provider-catalog-sync's `report.providers[providerId]` and `(added[pid] ??= [])`; pkgs/id/web `Object.assign(records, frame.records)` (`world.ts:181`, a peer-supplied frame); sync-models' `prov.models[baseId]` family. Gated on Phases 1–2.

Phases 1–2 adopt the origin issues (no parallels — they carry explicit acceptance with verified probes and queued triage packets). Related, deliberately NOT adopted: today's read-side filings #2920 / #2919 (id/web) belong to #2792's Phase 3 audit — their fix is a read guard.

## Open questions (stay in the design doc, not filed)

- Lint enforcement of define-semantics (false-positive rate known only after Phase 3's inventory — same deferred question as #2792's for reads).
- Recursive/deep-merge helpers, if Phase 3's audit finds one in-tree (none known).
- Cost-explorer storage-format change (per-name keys) — unnecessary once names are safe; revisit only if that format is revised for another reason.

---
*Filed by the repo design architect (pass 24, 2026-10-31) for developing-today/code. Implementation phases are the linked sub-issues; phases with open questions stayed in the design doc.*

## Acceptance criteria
- The design doc (`files/designs/code-proto-write-side.md`, goal workspace) is adopted or amended with the decision recorded on this issue.
- Each filed write-side instance (the three surfaces named in the design, incl. #2851) is linked as a phase of this epic, with its fix approach stated in define-semantics terms.
- The closing inventory audit is posted: every externally-keyed write site in the prototype family is listed and dispositioned (define semantics, guarded, or filed as a follow-up).
- Read-side counterpart #2792 is cross-linked and the boundary between the two classes stays explicit.

title: id(groups): a parseable torn final line in groups.jsonl is accepted, glued onto by the next append, and then bricks every group command

labels.name: task/small-fix

body:
## Summary

`id(groups)`: `GroupLog::open` (`pkgs/id/src/groups/log.rs`) accepts a **parseable** torn final line — a complete event JSON whose trailing newline was lost to a crash mid-append — and the next `record()` append glues the new event onto that same line. The resulting file can never be opened again: the glued line is newline-terminated and unparseable, so `GroupLog::open` fails fatally with "line N is not an event" and **every group command bricks** until someone hand-edits `groups.jsonl`.

This is exactly the failure #1620 fixed for the envelope outbox ("a parseable torn tail is accepted, then merged into the next record") and #1521 fixed for the directory journal. The sibling rule those fixes established — *an unterminated final line is torn, parseable or not, and is dropped and truncated at open* — was never applied to `GroupLog`. #1522 fixed `GroupLog` only for the **unparseable** fragment case.

## Evidence (main `b90f91a9`)

- `GroupLog::append` (log.rs:172-183) writes one JSON line + `\n` in a single `write_all` followed by `sync_data`, so a crash/power loss during that write can leave the full JSON with only its `\n` missing.
- `GroupLog::open` (log.rs:60-92): `complete` is computed (`line.ends_with('\n')`, :68) but is only consulted on the **error** arm (`Err(_) if !complete` → drop torn fragment). On the `Ok(event)` arm the event is pushed and `kept += line.len()` **regardless of `complete`** — so a parseable unterminated tail is kept, `kept == text.len()`, and no truncation/repair happens.
- `record()` → `append()` (log.rs:155-183) then appends the next event's line directly after the unterminated one, merging two JSON objects onto one line.
- On the next open, that merged line **is** newline-terminated, so it takes the fatal arm: `"{path}: line {N} is not an event"`. Every group command starts with `GroupLog::open` (commands/group.rs), so all of them fail the same way.
- Contrast the established sibling rule: `Outbox::open` (envelope_outbox.rs:141-150) drops an unterminated final line "Parseable or not … Keeping a parseable torn line would let the next append merge two records onto one line and brick the queue (#1620)"; `Directory::replay` (directory.rs:514-525, #1521) drops and truncates the same way.

## Verified (laptop probe, real `id` crate)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-grouplog/` (path-dep on the real `id` crate from a laptop worktree at origin/main `b90f91a9`; log.rs md5 `e70afe7a2262351c65dfd69a701ae0f4`, identical in both checkouts):

```
control healthy: events=2
case first outcome: Applied
case reopen-after-tear: ACCEPTED events=1
case second record: Ok(Applied)
case file lines after append: 1
case final reopen: BRICKED /home/user/tmp/.tmp2e4gPn/groups.jsonl: line 1 is not an event: trailing characters at line 1 column 427
```

- Control: a healthy newline-terminated log records two events and reopens with `events=2`.
- Case: after stripping only the trailing `\n` from a one-event log (the crash cut), reopen **accepts** the event; the next `record()` succeeds (`Applied`) but the file has **1 line** for 2 events (glued); the final reopen is **bricked**.

## Why it matters

`groups.jsonl` is the node's only group record; every group command opens it first. The one-byte tear (a complete JSON missing its newline) is precisely the crash outcome `append`'s single `write_all` + `sync_data` can leave, and the current open converts that recoverable state into permanent, fatal corruption on the next ordinary write — silently (the append reports success). Two sibling stores in the same crate already encode the correct rule with regression tests; `GroupLog` is the remaining store that doesn't.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `GroupLog::open` treats an unterminated final line as torn **whether or not it parses**: the line is dropped (with the same warn log as the fragment case) and the file is truncated to the last complete line — mirroring `Outbox::open` (#1620) and `Directory::replay` (#1521).
- [ ] Regression test in `groups/log.rs` mirroring the existing torn-fragment tests and the outbox's `a_parseable_torn_last_line_is_also_dropped`: write a valid event, strip only its trailing newline, reopen (event dropped, file truncated to empty/previous complete lines), record a new event, reopen again and fold successfully.
- [ ] Existing behavior unchanged: a newline-terminated line that does not parse stays fatal; blank lines still skipped; healthy logs record/reopen exactly as before.
- [ ] Related, do not duplicate: #1522 (GroupLog unparseable torn tail — closed, this is its parseable sibling case), #1620 (outbox parseable torn tail — closed), #1521 (directory torn tail — closed), #2128 (artifact journal blank lines — distinct).

title: id(discovery): peer announcements are unauthenticated and the peer table is unbounded — a fresh-timestamp announcement spoofs another peer's entry, and invented peers stall stale cleanup for N×10s

labels.name: kind/security
labels.description: Security issue or security hardening

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`id serve`'s gossip peer table trusts a `PeerAnnouncement`'s self-asserted `node_id` completely, and the table has no size bound:

- The receive loop (`pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:1531-1537`) deserializes an announcement from `msg.content` and passes it straight to `recv_discovery.update(announcement)`. It never compares `announcement.node_id` to anything about the message's origin — and the announcement carries no signature (the struct is plain postcard fields: `node_id`, `name`, `blob_count`, `timestamp_secs`).
- `PeerDiscovery::update` (`pkgs/id/src/discovery.rs:430-441`) inserts/replaces purely by that self-asserted `node_id` and stamps `last_seen = Instant::now()`.
- The discovery topic is public with a public secret (`DEFAULT_TOPIC` / `DEFAULT_TOPIC_SECRET`, `discovery.rs`), so anyone can broadcast announcements claiming any node ID.

Two consequences, both verified below:

1. **Fresh-timestamp identity spoofing.** An announcement claiming a victim's node ID, with a *fresh* (newest) timestamp and attacker-chosen `name`/`blob_count`, silently overwrites the victim's live entry. This is NOT covered by #1552: that issue's ordering/freshness fix refuses *old* announcements, and explicitly scopes signing out — a spoof with the newest timestamp passes every check #1552 adds. `id peers`, the REPL peer views, and the web `/peers` route then show the attacker's name/blob_count for the victim's node ID.
2. **Unbounded table + sequential probe amplification.** `update` has no cap and nothing evicts before staleness, so N invented node IDs are all retained and returned by `peers()`. Worse, the stale-cleanup task (`serve.rs:1571-1611`) probes stale entries **sequentially**, each with `PROBE_TIMEOUT` = 10 s (`serve.rs:1480,1582`): N attacker-chosen fake peers that go stale make one cleanup pass spend up to N×10 s dialing attacker-chosen node IDs before `remove_stale` runs — 1,000 fakes ≈ 2.8 hours of cleanup-loop time, during which genuinely stale peers are not evicted (the loop is the only eviction path).

## Evidence (verified this run, main `e19c953d`)

Probe crate on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-peerspoof/`) compiling the verbatim current `pkgs/id/src/discovery.rs` (md5 `050562c661c4c430c4c57c338bf71ea6`, identical on laptop and sandbox checkouts of main; iroh-base pinned `=1.3.0` as in the earlier discovery probes):

```
case1 spoof: count=1 name=Some("attacker-fake") blob_count=0 ts=1700000100
case2 unbounded: count=20000 peers=20000 all_peers=20000
case3 control: count=1 name=Some("honest")
```

- Case 1: after the victim's real announcement (name `victim-real`, blob_count 42, ts 1700000000), an announcement for the **same node_id** with a newer timestamp (ts 1700000100), name `attacker-fake`, blob_count 0 replaced it — `peers()` returns the attacker's values. Code inspection confirms there is no other gate: the receive path uses only `msg.content`, and `update` keys only by `announcement.node_id`.
- Case 2: 20,000 announcements with distinct invented node IDs were all inserted, counted, and returned — no cap, no eviction before the 120 s staleness threshold.
- Case 3 (control): a single honest announcement behaves exactly as before.

Probe-loop timing is code-read from `serve.rs:1563-1611` (sequential `for info in &stale` with a 10 s per-probe timeout wrapping a connect+ListPeers RPC; `remove_stale` runs only after the loop finishes).

## Why it matters

The peer table is the operator's view of the network (`id peers`, REPL, web `/peers`) and the cleanup loop is its only eviction mechanism. Today any participant on the public discovery topic can (a) impersonate another server's entry with values a freshness check cannot catch, and (b) flood the table with invented peers that turn the eviction loop into hours of dialing attacker-chosen endpoints. #1567 fixed the same Sybil/no-total-cap shape for the waiting pool; the peer table has neither a cap nor an identity binding.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Triage pins the identity fix shape: e.g. announcements signed by the node's key (verify `node_id` == signer before `update`), or another binding that makes a fresh-timestamp announcement for someone else's node ID refuse at the receive/update boundary. A timestamp/ordering check alone does not satisfy this (see #1552 scope note).
- [ ] `PeerDiscovery` gains a total size bound (cap with a documented eviction rule, e.g. oldest-`last_seen` first), so invented peers cannot grow the table without limit; the bound is exercised by a regression test inserting well past it.
- [ ] Stale cleanup cannot be stalled by table size: probing is bounded per pass (probe budget, concurrency cap, or eviction before probing), so one cleanup pass completes in bounded time regardless of how many stale entries exist.
- [ ] Regression tests: a spoofed announcement for an existing peer's node ID does not replace that peer's name/blob_count; honest in-order announcements (existing tests) still pass.
- [ ] Related, do not duplicate: #1552 (timestamp ordering/freshness — old-announcement replay), #2839 (peer name sanitization at display), #1567 (waiting-pool total cap precedent).

body:
# aggregator(snapshots): SnapshotStore groups by serviceId into plain objects — a `__proto__`/`constructor`/`toString` serviceId crashes byService (blanking all snapshot history) and pollutes Object.prototype during compact

## Evidence (verified this run, main `df6d9f58`)

`SnapshotStore` validates records with `isSnapshotRecord`, which checks only that `serviceId` is a non-empty string (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/snapshots.ts:303`). Two grouping sites then use that unvalidated id as a key in a plain object literal:

- `byService()` — `snapshots.ts:563-565`:
  ```ts
  const grouped: Record<string, SnapshotRecord[]> = {};
  for (const r of await this.readAll()) {
    (grouped[r.serviceId] ??= []).push(r);
  }
  ```
- `compactInner()` per-service report — `snapshots.ts:703-711`: the same `(perService[r.serviceId] ??= { before: 0, after: 0 })` accumulation in three loops.

For a prototype spelling, the `??=` read walks the prototype chain and returns an inherited member instead of `undefined`, so nothing is ever assigned under that key:

- `grouped["__proto__"]` → `Object.prototype` (no `.push`)
- `grouped["constructor"]` → the `Object` constructor function (no `.push`)
- `grouped["toString"]` → `Object.prototype.toString` (no `.push`)

### Probe (laptop, real module md5-identical to main)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-snapproto/` on the laptop — verbatim `snapshots.ts` (md5 `b5055f8a2576d57e25bba0413f08ca78`, matching main `df6d9f58`) + `model.ts`, run under bun 1.4.2, one process per case. Store file `usage-2026-10.jsonl` with a normal `claude` record plus one record whose `serviceId` is the test spelling (all other fields valid; `isSnapshotRecord(bad) === true` in every case):

| case | result |
|---|---|
| control (serviceIds `claude` + `whatever`) | `byService()` ok, keys `["claude","whatever"]` |
| `byService()` with `__proto__` | **THREW** `TypeError: (grouped[r.serviceId] ??= []).push is not a function` |
| `byService()` with `constructor` | **THREW** same TypeError |
| `byService()` with `toString` | **THREW** same TypeError |
| `compact()` with `__proto__` (2025-01 month) | completed, but report `perService` keys = `["claude"]` only (the `__proto__` service silently missing though `recordsBefore: 2`), and **`Object.prototype` gained own properties `before`/`after` (both `NaN`)** — `({}).before === NaN` afterwards |
| `compact()` with `constructor` | completed, `perService` keys = `["claude"]` only; counts were written onto the `Object` constructor function instead |
| `compact()` control (`claude` + `claude2`) | report keys `["claude","claude2"]`, no prototype change |

## Why it matters

- **One poisoned record blanks ALL snapshot history, persistently.** `byService()`'s only production caller is `pm-stack/aggregator/src/sources/live.ts:849`: `const history = await store.byService().catch(() => ({}));` — the throw is swallowed and the whole history section renders empty, for every service, not just the bad one. And because the record passes `isSnapshotRecord`, `store.append(feed.snapshots)` (live.ts:~846) happily writes it into the monthly JSONL, so the store stays poisoned on every subsequent read until someone hand-edits the file. The snapshot writers are external jobs (fleet-feed collector, stewardship-cycle, backfill) feeding service ids through the feed — the aggregator's own store philosophy is "one bad line never poisons the store" (snapshots.ts:~550), and this line does exactly that.
- **Compaction corrupts its own report and the process.** With `__proto__`, compact's counts are added onto `Object.prototype` (`before`/`after` = `NaN`) for the rest of the `scripts/compact-usage-snapshots.ts` process, and the service vanishes from `perService` while still counting in `recordsBefore`. With `constructor`, counts land on the `Object` function. (The rollup data itself is built with a `Map` at snapshots.ts:201-205 and is unaffected — only the report and the prototype are hit.)
- **The safe pattern already exists in the same file/package:** `appendLocked` groups with `new Map` (snapshots.ts:~620), `compactRecordsToRollups` groups with a `Map`, and `quota-current.ts:153` groups by serviceId with a `Map`. These two sites are the outliers. Related but distinct: #2792 (read-side own-key lookups; its scope note explicitly leaves write-side instances to be reported/fixed separately, cf. #2851), #2483 (isSnapshotRecord limit/resetsAt — different fields/effect).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `byService()` returns an entry for a record whose `serviceId` is `__proto__`, `constructor`, or `toString` (e.g. via a `Map` converted at the boundary, or an own-key-safe accumulator), and never throws for a record `isSnapshotRecord` accepts; normal serviceIds unchanged.
- [ ] `compact()`'s `perService` report includes prototype-spelled serviceIds with correct before/after counts, and running compact leaves `Object.prototype` untouched (`Object.getOwnPropertyNames(Object.prototype)` unchanged, `({}).before === undefined`).
- [ ] Regression tests in the aggregator suite (e.g. `pm-stack/aggregator/test/snapshot-retention.test.ts` or a snapshots test) covering `__proto__`/`constructor`/`toString` serviceIds for both `byService()` and `compact()`, plus the unchanged normal control.
- [ ] Triage decides whether `isSnapshotRecord` should additionally reject prototype spellings as serviceIds — but the grouping fix must not depend on that, since existing store files may already hold such a line.

Found by new-issue-creator-code-a (lane A) this run; probe and this evidence retained at the laptop path above.

body:
## Summary

`bin/clef-proxy.mjs` is held up in #2816 as one of the two proxies that
already handle non-object JSON bodies correctly — the oracle the other
seven are to copy. Its guard does not actually reject arrays:

```js
// bin/clef-proxy.mjs:211 (main 16bae8ea)
if (!body || typeof body !== 'object') { /* 400 */ }
```

`typeof [] === 'object'`, so a JSON array body passes the guard. The
handler then reads `body.model` / `body.state` / `body.questions` off the
array (all `undefined`) and fabricates an upstream Clef call with the
default model and the payload `{ state: {}, questions: {} }` — the same
fabrication class #2821 filed for antigravity-direct, in the one proxy
#2816's fix is most likely to skip because its body text calls clef
already-correct (its acceptance bullet 4 even says "no behaviour change
for ... the guarded clef / opencode-route proxies").

The sibling oracle gets this right: `opencode-route-proxy.mjs:659-660`
defines `isPlainObject` as
`typeof v === "object" && v !== null && !Array.isArray(v)`. Clef is the
only `bin/*-proxy.mjs` handler using the bare `typeof` guard (grep over
`bin/*.mjs`, this run).

## Evidence (verified this run, main `16bae8ea`)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-clefarray/`,
real `clef-proxy.mjs` + `proxy-port.mjs`, md5-identical to main —
clef-proxy `5e55c6637574d1c69c143bd4430bc030`), proxy spawned on a
scratch port with a dummy `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`, `POST /v1/systemone`:

| body | result |
|---|---|
| `[]` | **HTTP 401 from the upstream call** — i.e. NOT a 400: the proxy fabricated `{state:{}, questions:{}}`, called the Cloudflare gateway with the default model, and relayed its auth error |
| `[1,2]` | same 401 upstream relay |
| `{}` (valid control) | same 401 upstream relay — the array responses are indistinguishable from a valid empty-object request |
| `"hello"` | HTTP 400 "Invalid JSON body: expected an object" |
| `null` | HTTP 400 (the #2816 case — this part of the guard works) |
| `42` | HTTP 400 |

Process stayed alive throughout (this is a fabrication bug, not the
#2816 crash).

## Why it matters

- A client bug or stray probe that POSTs an array gets a real upstream
  Clef execution attempted with a defaulted model and empty
  state/questions, and the response it gets back (an upstream
  status/error) points at Cloudflare, not at its own malformed request.
- Process-of-record risk: #2816's evidence names clef as the pattern to
  copy. If its fix lands by copying clef's guard shape — or by skipping
  clef per its "no behaviour change" bullet — the array hole is
  cemented into whichever proxies adopt the bare `typeof` check, and
  #2816 closes with this still live. This issue exists so clef is in
  somebody's evidence set; if the #2816 PR fixes clef too, close this
  as completed by that PR and say so.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `POST /v1/systemone` (and `/systemone`, `/`) with a JSON array
      body returns the proxy's existing 400 "expected an object" error
      before any upstream call is attempted; `null`, string, and
      number bodies still 400; object bodies are unchanged.
- [ ] The guard matches the `opencode-route-proxy.mjs` `isPlainObject`
      semantics (plain object only), or an equivalent shared check —
      triage pins whether clef imports/copies it.
- [ ] A regression test in `bin/clef-proxy.test.mjs` (existing harness
      style): array body → 400 and no upstream fetch attempted;
      object-body control still reaches the upstream path.
- [ ] Cross-check #2816's PR when it lands: any proxy that adopted a
      bare `typeof body !== 'object'` guard gets the same array test.

Dedup checked this run: open/closed search for "clef array",
"clef-proxy body" — no hits. #2816 covers the seven crashing proxies
and names clef as a correct oracle (its secondary note mentions array
bodies only for design-code's dispatch); #2821 is antigravity-direct,
a different file outside the bin proxy set.

Not found

Contrast, same file, same run of the handler: - `/program/` passes 404 explicitly (server.ts:696-697). - The JSON twins pass 404: `/api/program-project.json` (server.ts:710), `/api/quota/service.json` (server.ts:767). - The fallthrough route returns `json({ error: "not found", path }, 404)` (server.ts:888). ## Verified this run (main `48f7c867cbf95e9ed51ece83ae0d68d58785ca54`) Laptop probe (fixture source, loopback only, `server.ts` sha256 `d68163b8…` identical on sandbox main and the laptop clone; probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-item404/`): | Request | Result | |---|---| | `GET /item/no-such-item-xyz` | **200** | | `GET /quota/service/no-such-svc` | **200** | | `GET /program/no-such-proj` (control) | 404 | | `GET /api/quota/service.json?id=nope` (control) | 404 | | `GET /nope-route` (control) | 404 | ## Why it matters - Machine consumers, link checkers, uptime/health probes, and browser history treat these misses as successful pages; a mistyped or stale item/service link is indistinguishable from a real page by status. - `fetchHandler` (server.ts:~905) records a render as OK when `res.status < 400`, so every hit on a missing `/item/…` page is recorded in the #1147 render registry as a successful page render — the health page's per-page "last rendered OK" signal is polluted by not-found traffic. - The inconsistency is in-file: a reader cannot tell whether 200 is deliberate for these two routes (nothing documents it) — the explicit 404s elsewhere say it is not. body:
# id(web): mimeToExtension returns Object.prototype members for prototype-named MIME types — 'constructor' yields the Object constructor instead of 'bin', corrupting paste filenames

## Evidence (verified this run, main 321dc21da15af25211cdaec0e9fc7d367d8ead98)

`pkgs/id/web/src/image-upload.ts:43-54` — the extension table is a plain object literal and the fallback relies on nullish coalescing:

```ts
export function mimeToExtension(mime: string): string {
  const map: Record<string, string> = { "image/png": "png", /* … */ };
  return map[mime] ?? "bin";
}
```

`?? "bin"` only fires for `null`/`undefined`. For a key that exists on `Object.prototype`, the lookup returns the inherited member — never nullish — so the fallback never runs and the function returns a **function or object** despite its declared `string` return type.

Probe (the function's verbatim lines 43-54 extracted from this HEAD; laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-mimext/`, `bun run probe.ts`):

| mime | result (runtime type) |
|---|---|
| `image/png` | `"png"` (string, correct) |
| `application/octet-stream` | `"bin"` (correct) |
| `""` | `"bin"` (correct) |
| `constructor` | `function Object() { [native code] }` (**function**) |
| `toString` | `function toString() { [native code] }` (**function**) |
| `hasOwnProperty` | `function hasOwnProperty() { [native code] }` (**function**) |
| `__proto__` | `[object Object]` (**object**) |

Downstream, `generatePasteFilename` (`image-upload.ts:76-79`) interpolates the result into a filename, so `mimeToExtension("constructor")` yields `` paste-<ts>.function Object() { [native code] } `` — a filename containing spaces, braces and parentheses — instead of `paste-<ts>.bin`. That name is used for pasted images whose `File.type` is empty/unrecognized (`handleImageUpload`, :237), a value ultimately supplied by the clipboard/drag source.

## Why it matters

Same plain-object-lookup class fixed for `detectLanguage` in #2787 and for `LANG_IMPORTS` in `highlight.ts:284-286` (own-key check, with an explanatory comment) — `image-upload.ts` was missed, and its `??` fallback makes the failure silent: no error, just a non-string "extension" flowing into a generated filename and upload metadata. The existing tests (`image-upload.test.ts:109-143`) pin the seven real types plus two unknown-string cases, but no prototype-name case.

## Acceptance criteria

- `mimeToExtension` returns `"bin"` for every `Object.prototype` member name (`constructor`, `toString`, `hasOwnProperty`, `valueOf`, `__proto__`, …) and for any other unlisted MIME string.
- The seven listed types still map exactly as before; existing `image-upload.test.ts` cases unchanged and green.
- New tests pin the prototype-name cases.
- Fix uses an own-key check (`Object.hasOwn`) or an equivalent prototype-free table (`Object.create(null)` / `Map`), consistent with the #2787 precedent in the same package; the declared `string` return type holds at runtime for all inputs.

Dedup: searched open + closed issues for `mimeToExtension` / `image-upload prototype` this run — no hits. #2787 covers `highlight.ts` only. Sibling filed the same run: #2919 (`terminalBytesForKey` in `world-keyboard.ts`, same class, different file/function/caller — independently fixable).

# id(web): terminalBytesForKey treats Object.prototype members as special keys — 'toString'/'constructor' send native-function source bytes as world terminal input instead of null

## Evidence (verified this run, main 321dc21da15af25211cdaec0e9fc7d367d8ead98)

`pkgs/id/web/src/world-keyboard.ts:20-35` — `specialKeys` is a plain object literal (`Record<string, string>`), and membership is tested with the `in` operator, which walks the prototype chain:

```ts
if (event.key in specialKeys) {
  ...
  return new TextEncoder().encode(specialKeys[event.key]);
}
```

The function's own contract (docstring, :23-25) is: "Returns null for browser/OS shortcuts and keys the Roc `Key` module does not recognize yet." Prototype-member names are not in the table, but `in` says they are, and the lookup returns the inherited `Object.prototype` member — a function or object — which `TextEncoder.encode` string-coerces.

Probe (verbatim copy of the file at this HEAD, md5-verified; laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-keyboard/`, `bun run probe.ts`):

| key | result |
|---|---|
| `Enter` | `"\r"` (correct) |
| `F5` | `null` (correct) |
| `toString` | `"function toString() { [native code] }"` |
| `constructor` | `"function Object() { [native code] }"` |
| `hasOwnProperty` | `"function hasOwnProperty() { [native code] }"` |
| `valueOf` | `"function valueOf() { [native code] }"` |
| `__proto__` | `"[object Object]"` |
| `isPrototypeOf` | `"function isPrototypeOf() { [native code] }"` |

## Why it matters

The only production caller is `pkgs/id/web/src/world.ts:258`, which forwards the returned bytes as terminal input to the running world (Roc) program. Any key event whose `key` is a prototype-member name — synthetic/programmatic events, IME or virtual-keyboard oddities, future callers feeding non-DOM key sources into this exported pure function — injects the JS engine's native-function source text into the world program as if the user typed it, instead of being dropped as unrecognized. This is the same plain-object-lookup class fixed for `detectLanguage` in #2787 and for `LANG_IMPORTS` in `highlight.ts:284-286` (own-key check with an explanatory comment); `world-keyboard.ts` was missed, and it uses the even broader `in` operator.

## Acceptance criteria

- `terminalBytesForKey` returns `null` for every `Object.prototype` member name (`toString`, `constructor`, `hasOwnProperty`, `valueOf`, `isPrototypeOf`, `__proto__`, …) with no modifiers, matching the documented unrecognized-key behavior.
- All twelve real special keys still encode exactly as before (existing `world-keyboard.test.ts` cases unchanged and green).
- New tests in `pkgs/id/web/src/world-keyboard.test.ts` pin the prototype-name cases.
- Fix uses an own-key check (`Object.hasOwn`) or an equivalent prototype-free table (`Object.create(null)` / `Map`), consistent with the #2787 precedent in the same package.

Dedup: searched open + closed issues for `world-keyboard`, `specialKeys`, `terminalBytesForKey` this run — no hits. #2787 covers `highlight.ts` only. Sibling filed the same run for `mimeToExtension` in `image-upload.ts` (same class, different file/function/caller — independently fixable).

body:
## Summary

`id(event_store)`: when a group-operation event is refused with
`Refusal::WaitingFull` (its author is at the waiting-pool cap), `settle`
has already written its membership action into the `actions` table —
and that row **commits** whenever the same ingest call also expired an
unrelated held event. The refused event is neither held nor stored, yet
its action row persists forever (nothing ever deletes `actions` rows),
contradicting the table's own contract (event_store/mod.rs, `ACTIONS`:
"Written when the event arrives, **held or stored**, so a release reads
it back without the caller").

## Evidence (main a51aab2c; ingest.rs md5 d935efc7, identical at e7039cdb)

- `settle`, Decision::Wait (ingest.rs:668-672) and Decision::Park
  (:674-678): `store_action(m.txn, &id, action)?` runs **before**
  `m.hold(...)`. `held()` maps `Hold::Full` to
  `Settled::Refused(Refusal::WaitingFull)` (ingest.rs:711).
- `ingest_in` (ingest.rs:549, 555): the call first expires due events,
  and `changed = expired > 0 || ...` — a refusal in a call that expired
  anything counts as "changed".
- `EventStore::attempt` (event_store/mod.rs:983-987): the transaction
  commits iff `changed`. So a WaitingFull refusal with no expiry aborts
  (action row discarded), but the same refusal in a call that expired
  an unrelated author's held event commits — action row included.
- No code path ever removes an `actions` row (grep: only insert/read).

## Verified (laptop probe, real `id` crate)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-actionsrefused/` (path-dep on
a laptop worktree at origin/main; scenario run twice, differing only in
the clock of the refused call):

- Setup: `WaitingLimits::new(1, 1_000)` (per-author cap 1, max age 1s).
  Author B's seq-1 event held at t=0 (due at t=1000); author A's seq-2
  event held at t=500 (A at cap). A's seq-3 group event (backlink to
  the held seq-2, so it must wait) is then ingested via
  `ingest_with_action` with a `GroupAction::Create`.
- Control (t=500, nothing due): outcome
  `Refused(WaitingFull)`; after dropping the store, the `actions`
  table in `events.redb` has **0 rows**.
- Expiring (t=1000, B's held event due): outcome
  `Refused(WaitingFull)` — the event is not waiting
  (`is_waiting(a3) == false`) and never stored — yet the `actions`
  table has **1 row, keyed by the refused event's ID**.

## Why it matters

1. **A refused group operation is pre-armed.** `attach_action`
   (ingest.rs:852-866) deliberately attaches an action only to an
   event that `is_stored`, and `stored_action`/`resolve::load` read
   the `actions` table for any stored event. If the refused event
   later arrives via sync (which carries no bodies,
   ingest_events/ingest.rs) and is stored, the stale row makes the
   resolution treat it as the group operation its earlier, refused
   arrival claimed — without that arrival ever being held or stored.
2. **`plain()` flips forever.** `plain()` (ingest.rs:875-879) is
   "no actions and no forks". One stray row permanently disables the
   plain fast path: every later accept takes the full `refresh()`
   re-resolution instead.
3. The outcome depends on unrelated expiry timing in the same call —
   the same refusal leaves opposite on-disk state depending on whether
   a stranger's held event happened to come due.

## Acceptance criteria

- A `WaitingFull` refusal (Wait or Park) leaves no `actions` row for
  the refused event, regardless of what else the call expired or
  changed; the transaction-commit condition cannot resurrect it.
  (Natural shapes: write the action only after the hold succeeds, or
  delete/skip it on the Full path — triage's pin.)
- Regression test at the store level mirroring the probe: capped
  author + group event that must wait + an unrelated held event due
  in the same call → `Refused(WaitingFull)` and an empty `actions`
  table (read back after reopen), with the no-expiry control unchanged.
- Existing behaviour preserved: a successfully held group event still
  keeps its action (`stored_action` on release), and a stored event's
  action still attaches via `attach_action` only when stored.

body:
# id(world-presentation): ScreenPatch::apply never validates the replacement cells — a patch carrying control characters, an orphaned wide-glyph continuation, or an impossible column count produces an invalid screen instead of falling back to a full frame

## Summary

`ScreenSurface` is a validated type everywhere it is built from untrusted data:

- `parse_surface` (`pkgs/id/src/world_presentation.rs:260`) rejects control characters, glyphs that occupy 0 or 3+ columns, wide glyphs split by style spans, and continuations that do not match their leading glyph.
- `ScreenSurface::from_cells` (`world_presentation.rs:54`) refuses any cell set whose `render_ansi()` is `None` — the constructor enforces the portable-screen invariant.

`ScreenPatch::apply` (`world_presentation.rs:188-218`) is the exception. It checks only the patch header (version/dimensions match `prev`) and run geometry (runs in order, non-overlapping, inside the grid), then splices the runs' replacement cells into a clone of `prev.cells` and returns `Some(ScreenSurface { .. })` built by struct literal — the replacement cells are never validated. A patch is a wire-shaped value: `ScreenPatch`, `CellRun`, and `ScreenCell` all derive `Deserialize` (with `deny_unknown_fields`, but no cell-content checks), so a deserialized patch can carry cells no guest view could ever produce:

- a cell whose symbol is a raw ESC string (`"\u{1b}[2J"`, columns 1) — the exact guest control sequence `parse_surface` exists to keep out of presenters;
- a run that replaces only the leading cell of a two-column glyph with a one-column cell, orphaning the continuation cell at the next index;
- a cell with `columns: 3` (no glyph occupies 3 columns) or `columns: 2` in the last column of a row (no room for its continuation).

In every case `apply` returns `Some(screen)` and the produced screen is invalid: its own `render_ansi()` returns `None`. That breaks `apply`'s documented contract (`world_presentation.rs:183-187`): `None` is the signal that "the patch does not belong to `prev` — the caller falls back to a full frame". A malformed-cells patch returns `Some`, so the caller applies it, gets an unrenderable screen, and never falls back. `diff` only ever emits valid cells (it clones them from validated screens), which is why the existing tests — all built on `diff` round-trips — never see this.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `c4fb5996`)

Probe on the laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-screenpatch/`: the real `world_presentation.rs` compiled as a module (md5 `8477cb3bf70ca698ce0b0720b0d32864`, identical to main), patches built by deserializing JSON into the real `ScreenPatch`:

```text
control diff-patch: apply==next:true render_ok:true
case1 esc-cell: apply=Some render_ansi_is_some:false
case2 orphan-continuation: apply=Some render_ansi_is_some:false cell1_columns:0
case3 columns-3: apply=Some render_ansi_is_some:false
case4 wide-at-last-column: apply=Some render_ansi_is_some:false
```

Case 2 detail: `prev` is the valid screen for rows `["界ab"]`; the patch replaces only index 0 with `("x", columns 1)`, leaving index 1 as the wide glyph's continuation (`columns: 0`, empty symbol) with no leading wide glyph.

## Why it matters

The module's whole purpose is that guests never supply terminal escapes or malformed glyphs to presenters (module doc, `world_presentation.rs:1-7`). `ScreenPatch` is the F12.11 delta type (#805) that clients will apply to reconstruct screens from patch data; the moment a patch arrives over a transport instead of being produced locally by `diff`, its cells are untrusted input, and `apply` is the reconstruction point — the one place that can refuse and trigger the documented full-frame fallback. Today it rebuilds an invalid screen and reports success, degrading the client to a blank/error view (the ANSI presenter returns `None`) with no recovery signal, and leaving non-ANSI presenters to consume cells that violate the invariants they were promised.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ScreenPatch::apply` returns `None` when the produced screen would be invalid — at minimum for: a replacement cell containing a control character or a symbol that is not exactly one grapheme; a `columns` value other than 0/1/2, or a width that disagrees with the symbol's actual width; a wide glyph whose continuation is missing/mismatched, a continuation with no leading wide glyph, or a wide glyph starting in a row's last column (the same rules `render_ansi`/`parse_surface` enforce).
- [ ] A patch that is valid except for its cells must behave exactly like a mismatched patch today: `None`, so the caller falls back to a full frame.
- [ ] Regression tests beside the existing patch tests: ESC-symbol cell refused, orphaned continuation refused, `columns: 3` refused, wide glyph at the last column refused; the existing `diff` round-trip and parity tests still pass unchanged.
- [ ] Triage pins the enforcement shape (validate the spliced result once, e.g. the `from_cells`/`render_ansi` check, vs per-cell validation during the splice) — either is acceptable if the cases above return `None`.

Related: #805 (F12.11 delta frames — this is a correctness gap in its first slice, not the remaining binary/resume work). Distinct from #2802/#2824 (world/collab WebSocket frame-shape trust on the session path; this is the presentation patch type).

# id(petname): skeleton confusable check is ASCII-only — Cyrillic/Greek homoglyph petnames pass the anti-mimicry guard and render with no fingerprint

## Summary

`Petnames::set` refuses a petname that is confusable with another contact's petname or alleged name, comparing `fold()` and `skeleton()` forms (`pkgs/id/src/petname.rs:113-135`). The design decision is "Mimicry: refuse, for both exact (folded) and confusable matches" (`pkgs/id/docs/2026-10-10T07-00-00Z_feature_petnames_invites/2026-10-10T07-00-00Z_feature_petnames_invites.md`, Decisions). But `skeleton()` (`petname.rs:240-257`) maps only ASCII look-alikes (`0→o`, `1→l`, `|→l`, `3→e`, `5/$→s`, `@→a`, `rn→m`, `vv→w`). `normalize_name` (`petname.rs:217-231`) admits any non-control characters, so a petname or alleged name written with Cyrillic or Greek homoglyphs — visually identical in the terminal and web UI — produces a different skeleton and is accepted:

- "PayP**а**l" with U+0430 (Cyrillic small a) vs "PayPal"
- "**А**lice" with U+0410 (folds to U+0430, still not Latin `a`)
- "B**о**b" with U+043E, "**е**ve" with U+0435, "**С**arol" with U+0421, "T**ο**m" with U+03BF (Greek omicron)

Display does not rescue it: `labels()` (`petname.rs:311-330`) adds the disambiguating fingerprint only when two petnames collide after `fold()` — fold also differs for these pairs, so both contacts render bare, visually identical, with no fingerprint.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `ffa86396`)

Verbatim-copy probe of `fold`/`skeleton` (`petname.rs:233-257`), compiled with rustc and run on the laptop in `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-petuni/`:

```text
control "PayPal" vs "PayPa1": skeleton_eq=true   (refused today, as designed)
control "PayPal" vs "paypa1": skeleton_eq=true   (refused today)
control "Mum" vs "rnurn":     skeleton_eq=true   (refused today)
homoglyph "PayPal" vs "PayPаl" (U+0430): fold_eq=false skeleton_eq=false  skeleton_b="paypаl"
homoglyph "Alice"  vs "Аlice"  (U+0410): fold_eq=false skeleton_eq=false
homoglyph "Bob"    vs "Bоb"    (U+043E): fold_eq=false skeleton_eq=false
homoglyph "Eve"    vs "еve"    (U+0435): fold_eq=false skeleton_eq=false
homoglyph "Carol"  vs "Сarol"  (U+0421): fold_eq=false skeleton_eq=false
homoglyph "Tom"    vs "Tοm"    (U+03BF): fold_eq=false skeleton_eq=false
```

`set()`'s only confusable checks are those two equalities (petname.rs:120, :128), so every homoglyph case above is accepted today, for both the existing-petname comparison and the alleged-name comparison.

Related but distinct: #2069 (skeleton misses ASCII `I`/`l` and `8`/`B` — two map entries), #1674 (Cf format characters bypassing the guards). This issue is the cross-script class: the fix shape is a Unicode confusable skeleton (e.g. UTS #39 confusables) and/or a mixed-script rule, not two more ASCII entries. Triage may fold this into #2069 if it prefers one skeleton-hardening item — the acceptance criteria below are written to survive either way.

## Why it matters

The petname store is a trust surface: a name the owner sees must not be taken for a different contact (module doc, `petname.rs:1-6`). Cross-script homoglyphs are the standard, best-known way to defeat exactly this kind of check, they need no invisible characters (#1674's class), and the resulting pair of contacts renders with no fingerprint to tell them apart — a wrong-identity steer for messages or payments to the wrong account key.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `skeleton()` (or its replacement) equates the common cross-script confusables: at minimum Cyrillic а/е/о/р/с/х/у and А/В/Е/К/М/Н/О/Р/С/Т/Х and Greek ο/ν/ρ/τ/χ look-alikes with their Latin counterparts, so `Petnames::set` refuses the six verified cases above (against both an existing petname and an alleged name).
- [ ] Alternatively/additionally, a documented mixed-script rule: a petname mixing Latin with Cyrillic/Greek letters is refused or skeleton-normalized — whichever shape triage pins, the six cases above must not be silently accepted.
- [ ] Legitimate non-Latin names are not broken wholesale: a petname written entirely in one non-Latin script (e.g. a genuinely Cyrillic name with no Latin look-alike target) still works, or its refusal is an explicit, documented decision.
- [ ] Regression tests beside the existing petname tests: homoglyph-vs-petname refused, homoglyph-vs-alleged refused, ASCII controls (`PayPa1`, `rnurn`) still refused, unrelated names still accepted.
- [ ] If triage folds this into #2069, close as duplicate pointing there and extend #2069's criteria with the cases above rather than dropping them.

title: id(world): journal restore never validates Issued scopes — unnamed bits and JOIN-less capabilities restore clean, and a CHAT-/INPUT-only token can act without ever joining

labels.name: task/triage

body:
## Problem

`WorldCore::restore` (`pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs`, the `JournalEntry::Issued` arm) rebuilds a participant's scopes with a direct tuple construction — `scopes: WorldScopes(scopes)` — and never validates the raw journaled `u8`. Every other path that creates a scope set validates it:

- `WorldScopes::from_bits` (`src/world/mod.rs`) exists for exactly this: "Scopes from raw bits; `None` if any bit names no scope. The admin authority bits round-trip here even though they are outside `ALL`" — i.e. it is the journal round-trip validator, and restore does not call it.
- `WorldCore::mint` refuses any capability whose scopes lack `JOIN`: "world capability must include join scope". `WorldScopes::attenuate` likewise returns `None` unless the requested set keeps `JOIN`, and every role preset in `from_role` includes `JOIN`.

Restore validates the neighbouring `Issued` fields — duplicate participant id, parent must already exist, `uses >= 1`, a delegate's expiry may not outlive its parent's (there is a dedicated test, `restore_refuses_a_delegate_outliving_its_parent`) — but the scopes byte gets none of that: no `from_bits` check, no JOIN requirement, nothing.

Consequences, both from a journal no live code path can produce (a hand-edited, corrupted, or fork-copied journal — restore's own contract is "a bad journal is refused, never partially applied"):

1. **Unnamed bits are silently carried.** `scopes = 0x87` (GUEST + bit `0x80`, which names no scope) restores `Ok`, even though `WorldScopes::from_bits(0x87)` is `None`. The bit is inert in today's `effective_scopes` (it intersects from `ALL`), but the journal now holds a scope set the type itself calls invalid, ready to acquire meaning if a future bit is assigned.
2. **A capability can act without ever joining.** `scopes = 0b00010` (CHAT only, no JOIN) restores `Ok`, and its token then passes `chat()` — which authorizes only `WorldScopes::CHAT` (`core.rs`, `authorize(token, WorldScopes::CHAT)`) — and posts chat into a world it cannot snapshot or join (`snapshot()` authorizes `JOIN` and fails). Same shape for INPUT-only (`0b00100`) through `prepare_input`/`input()`, which authorizes only `INPUT`. No live issuance path can mint such a capability: `mint` refuses it outright (verified control below).

## Evidence (verified this run, main `690e4722`)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-restorescope/`, a detached worktree of `origin/main` at `690e4722`; `core.rs`/`mod.rs` md5-identical to the sandbox clone) — an integration test against the real `id` crate (`tests/probe_restorescope.rs`), token digests built exactly as `mint` builds them (`"<id>.<hex secret>"`, SHA-256):

- CONTROL: `Issued` with GUEST scopes (`0b00111`) restores `Ok`; its token chats `Ok`.
- CONTROL: live `issue_capability` with CHAT-only scopes on a fresh `WorldCore` returns `Err` (the JOIN requirement in `mint`).
- CONTROL: restore refuses `Issued` with `uses = Some(0)` — restore does validate sibling fields.
- CASE A: `WorldScopes::from_bits(0x87)` is `None`, but restore with `scopes = 0x87` returns `Ok`.
- CASE B: restore with `scopes = 0` returns `Ok`.
- CASE C: restore with `scopes = 0b00010` (CHAT, no JOIN) returns `Ok`; `core.chat(token, …)` is `Ok`; `core.snapshot(token)` is `Err`.
- CASE D: restore with `scopes = 0b00100` (INPUT, no JOIN) returns `Ok`; `core.input(token, …)` is `Ok`.

Code points (main `690e4722`): restore's `Issued` arm validates digest shape, duplicate id, parent existence, `uses >= 1`, expiry-vs-parent, then inserts `WorldScopes(scopes)` unchecked at `src/world/core.rs:215`; `WorldScopes::from_bits` is at `src/world/mod.rs:189`; the JOIN requirement in `mint` is at `core.rs:862`; `chat()` authorizes only CHAT at `core.rs:965` and `prepare_input()` only INPUT at `core.rs:1004`, while `snapshot()` authorizes JOIN at `core.rs:1042` — so the JOIN invariant is the only thing keeping a non-join capability from acting, and restore is the one producer that skips it.

## Why it matters

Restore is the trust boundary for persisted world state: its whole design is to refuse internally inconsistent journals rather than partially apply them, and it already enforces the delegate-narrowing rule for expiry. Scopes are the authorization substance of the entry — the one field where an inconsistent value changes what a bearer token may do — yet they are the field restored without a check. A journal produced by a bug, a partial write outside the journal format's own protections, or a future writer that trusts restore to catch bad scopes yields capabilities that act in a world they never joined, in a shape no operator ever issued.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Restore refuses an `Issued` entry whose scopes fail `WorldScopes::from_bits` (any bit outside `ALL_BITS`), naming the participant in the error, in the style of the neighbouring restore errors.
- [ ] Restore refuses an `Issued` entry whose scopes lack `JOIN`, matching the invariant `mint` and `attenuate` enforce for live issuance.
- [ ] Regression tests beside the existing restore tests (cf. `restore_refuses_a_delegate_outliving_its_parent`): unnamed-bit scopes refused; JOIN-less scopes refused; a valid GUEST/builder/moderator journal still restores (the `from_bits` admin bits must keep round-tripping).
- [ ] Triage confirms there is no legitimate historical journal shape with JOIN-less or unnamed-bit scopes that must keep restoring; if one exists, name it explicitly instead of loosening the check silently.
- [ ] Triage also rules on the adjacent gap in the same arm: a delegated entry's scopes are not checked against its parent's implied scopes the way expiry is (partly mitigated at use time by `effective_scopes` chain intersection — confirm whether restore should still refuse).

body:
## Summary

`WorldCore::check_schedule_replacing` (`pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs:600-627`) trusts a caller-supplied `replacing: bool` to discount the pending-schedule count, instead of checking its own map:

```rust
let pending = self.schedules.len() - usize::from(replacing);   // core.rs:612
ensure!(pending < crate::world_caps::MAX_PENDING_SCHEDULES, ...); // 64, world_caps.rs:95
```

The flag is redundant — whether the id being set is actually pending is knowable from `self.schedules` — and a mismatched flag breaks the cap in both directions:

1. **Full map, absent id, `replacing=true`:** with 64 schedules pending, `pending` computes as 63, the check passes, and the caller inserts a **65th** pending schedule — one more than `MAX_PENDING_SCHEDULES` (64). That state is one journal replay refuses: restore rejects a journal whose pending `ScheduleSet` entries reach the cap (`world/core.rs:263-275`, `core.schedules.len() < MAX_PENDING_SCHEDULES` per insert), so a journal ever written in that state would make the world unopenable.
2. **Empty map, `replacing=true`:** `0 - 1` on `usize` panics in debug builds (arithmetic overflow) and wraps to `usize::MAX` in release, making the check refuse a schedule that should be admitted.

## Evidence (main `b4136991`, code-read verified this run)

- `pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs:612` — the subtraction above; the duplicate check at :607-610 is keyed on the same flag (`replacing || !contains_key`), so the flag controls both guards while the map, which knows the truth, is consulted for neither.
- `pkgs/id/src/world_caps.rs:95` — `MAX_PENDING_SCHEDULES: usize = 64`.
- `pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs:271-275` — journal restore enforces the same cap per `ScheduleSet`, i.e. the cap is a hard invariant of persisted state, not an advisory limit.
- Sole production caller, `pkgs/id/src/world/actor.rs:1376-1383` (`WorldCommand::AdminScheduleAt`), currently computes the flag correctly (`let replacing = self.core.schedules.contains_key(&id);`) — so today this is a latent trap, not a live breach: the invariant holds only by caller discipline, in exactly the function whose job is to enforce it.
- Coverage gap: `pkgs/id/src/world/tests.rs:3405-3444` (`a_replacement_is_validated_as_a_replacement_not_as_an_addition`) exercises `replacing=true` only with the id actually pending (`"taken"`, `"s0"`). No test passes a mismatched flag.

Verification note: verified by reading the code at the lines above and tracing the arithmetic for the boundary cases (64 pending + absent id + `true`; 0 pending + `true`). No compiled probe this run: the laptop SSH tunnel is down (see #2879), and the sandbox does not build. The boundary trace is deterministic from the quoted lines; triage can confirm with the two unit cases in the acceptance criteria in seconds.

## Why it matters

The pending-schedule cap bounds journal size and wakeup work per world, and restore treats it as a hard invariant. An enforcement helper that can be talked out of the cap — or into a panic — by a redundant boolean is a footgun for the next caller (the manifest-apply path already grew one new caller in #807; `SetSchedule` frames and program `schedule.at` are adjacent surfaces). Deriving the discount from the map removes the whole class.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `check_schedule_replacing` derives whether the id is being replaced from `self.schedules` itself (or otherwise cannot be desynchronised from the map); no caller-supplied flag can discount a schedule that is not pending.
- [ ] Unit test: 64 schedules pending + set of a *new* id through the replacement path is refused with the "pending schedules" error.
- [ ] Unit test: replacement path on an empty map (and on a map not containing the id) neither panics nor wraps.
- [ ] Existing tests still pass, including `a_replacement_is_validated_as_a_replacement_not_as_an_addition` (a true replacement at capacity still fits) and the #807 guarantee that a refused replacement leaves the existing schedule standing.
- [ ] The duplicate guard and the capacity discount agree: both keyed on the same map lookup.

body:
## CodeRabbit minor findings on PR #2840 — deferred follow-ups

PR #2840 (fix for #2573) was reviewed by CodeRabbit at head `831ac5dc` (2026-10-30T23:17Z), which raised 3 Minor findings. One was already fixed by the next head; two are valid-but-minor and are tracked here instead of blocking the merge (Codex reviewed the final head `8db2e07b` clean; the PR's own acceptance in #2573 covers the 4 Codex findings from #2541, all fixed).

### 1. Workflow log formatter retains every parsed event in memory — `.github/workflows/mcpx.yml:187`
The readable-output formatter appends every parsed `go test -json` event to `lines` before printing in two passes. Retained memory grows with the full stream. Suggested fix (from the review thread): re-read the file per pass with a generator instead of retaining events. Thread: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/2840#discussion_r4429279438

### 2. Hook failure text can be polluted by stdout — `pkgs/mcpx/internal/hooks/runner.go`
`execute()` points both `cmd.Stdout` and `cmd.Stderr` at one shared `cappedWriter`, and the failure text is `firstLine(out.String())`. A hook that fills the cap with stdout (no newline) before writing its stderr diagnostic records truncated stdout as the "error". Suggested fix: give stderr its own capped writer, build the failure text from stderr's first line, and fall back to stdout's first line when stderr is empty. Add a regression test (hook writes >cap stdout, then a one-line stderr diagnostic, exits non-zero; `Stats().LastError` names the diagnostic). Thread: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/2840#discussion_r4429279452

### Already fixed (no action)
The third finding (wildcard hook's `Dropped` counting `hook.*` events, thread https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/2840#discussion_r4429279447) was fixed in head `8db2e07b` by `Hook.SubFilter()` (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/hooks/hooks.go`), which expands a wildcard to the hookable kinds so `hook.*` events are excluded before the bus buffers them.

### Acceptance
- [ ] Formatter streams per pass (no full event retention) with identical log output
- [ ] stderr has its own capped writer; failure text prefers stderr, falls back to stdout; regression test above passes
- [ ] `go test ./internal/hooks/...` green in CI

## Acceptance criteria
- The mcpx workflow log formatter streams parsed `go test -json` events without retaining the full event list in memory (or the retention is bounded and documented).
- Each deferred CodeRabbit minor finding from PR #2840 listed in this issue is either fixed or explicitly dispositioned as wontfix with a reason.
- mcpx CI stays green on the change; no behavior change to the formatted output content.

# id(attestation): `compute_state` never validates the claim outcome's domain — claims naming a third party (or any string) as winner compute `Agreed`

## Evidence (main `07448571`, merged today in PR #2854 for #2248)

`pkgs/id/src/attestation.rs` documents the claim outcome's domain on `ResultClaim.outcome` (:106-108): "the winning player's id as hex, or `"draw"`". But the viewer checks concurrence only:

- `compute_state` (:223) accepts two claims when `a.outcome == b.outcome && a.final_state_hash == b.final_state_hash` (:253) — a pure string-equality check. Neither claim's outcome is ever compared against the agreement's two player ids (hex) or the `"draw"` sentinel.
- So any outcome string both players sign — the hex of a key that is **not in the match**, or arbitrary text — computes `Agreed`, even though no such result is possible for the tic-tac-toe example the PoC models (the winner is one of the two seats, or a draw).

Distinct from #2863 (duplicate seats): there the seats collapse to one key; here the seats are two genuine, distinct players and the genesis pair is complete — the gap is purely that the *asserted result* is outside the documented domain.

### Verified (laptop probe, verbatim `compute_state` + object types, real p2panda-core `Hash` at the pinned rev `da80c05b`)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-attdup/` on the laptop (same verbatim extraction as #2863; `attestation.rs` md5 `530fcdf45da5d8688dc0e4e319b641b2`), distinct players `[A, B]`, complete genesis pair, concurring claims throughout:

- both claims name third party C (hex of a key that is not a player) as winner → **`Agreed`** ← the bug
- both claims give outcome `"banana"` → **`Agreed`** ← the bug
- both claims give outcome `"draw"` → `Agreed` (control: the documented non-player outcome stays valid)
- both claims name A (a seat player) → `Agreed` (control, from the #2863 probe run)

The shipped tests (`tests/attestation_poc.rs`) only ever use seat-player hex outcomes and the wrong-winner dispute case (which names the *other seat*), so the out-of-domain case is uncovered.

## Why it matters

- The viewer's `Agreed` is the attestation: downstream consumers (the #2039 v1 design, audit/replay in #2038's line) will read it as "both players conceded this result". An out-of-domain outcome — above a nonsense string, a result naming someone who never played — should not be attestable at all; if it computes `Agreed`, every consumer must re-validate the outcome itself, which is exactly the invariant a viewer exists to own.
- It also masks claim-construction bugs: a claimant whose outcome encoding is wrong (raw bytes instead of hex, a display name, a seat index) produces claims that can still concur and attest, instead of failing visibly at the viewer.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Two concurring claims whose outcome is neither a seat player's id-as-hex nor `"draw"` do **not** compute `Agreed` (they compute `Proposed` or `Disputed` — triage pins which, and whether a claim with an out-of-domain outcome is ignored like a non-player claim or counts as a position).
- [ ] Documented outcomes unchanged: seat-player hex (either seat) and `"draw"`, with concurring final-state hash, still compute `Agreed`; differing in-domain outcomes still compute `Disputed`.
- [ ] A regression test covers the probe matrix: third-party hex, arbitrary string, and the `draw`/seat-hex controls.
- [ ] Triage pins the encoding contract being enforced (lowercase hex of the 32-byte player id, as produced by the example/tests) so the check and claim constructors cannot drift apart.

body:
## Finding

The no-origin rule added for the laptop repo keeper falls back to `main` when a no-origin repo is in detached HEAD, which reintroduces exactly the flag/move behaviour the change exists to remove: a clean detached no-origin repo gets checked out onto `main` (or flagged when `main` does not exist).

## Evidence

- Source PR: #1819 (merged, merge commit `528886ebad10a4a5a0d4004cf88e0a25a1ea5258`, commit `14ad4beb`) — https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/1819
- PR intent: for a repo with no origin, "whatever branch it is on IS its default — never flag it, never move it."
- Verified still present on current main `074485713b11745c5164a131aac6e80305abd228`, `nixos/home/laptop-repo-keeper.sh`:
  - Lines 79–81: the no-origin branch sets `db="$(g branch --show-current)"`, then `[ -z "$db" ] && db=main`. In detached HEAD, `git branch --show-current` prints nothing, so `db` becomes `main` — a branch the repo may not even have (the motivating local clan repos sit on `master`-style defaults).
  - Line 86: `br` is likewise empty in detached HEAD, so `br != db` below (branch-mismatch block, checkout at line 98, "primary was on $br (clean) — moved to $db" at line 99): a clean detached repo is **moved** to `main`; a dirty one is flagged "PRIMARY ON  with N dirty entries — left alone (needs a human)" with an empty branch name.

## Why it matters

Detached HEAD is a normal working state for a local-only repo (inspecting an old commit, bisecting, a tool's checkout). The keeper runs hourly and auto-moves clean primaries, so a local-only repo left detached is silently switched to `main` — the exact class of surprise the #1819 change was written to stop, just through the detached-HEAD door instead of the wrong-default door.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A no-origin repo in detached HEAD is skipped by the branch-alignment logic entirely (never flagged, never moved), the same as a no-origin repo on any branch — e.g. detect the empty current branch in the no-origin case and `continue`, or treat "no branch" as aligned by definition.
- [ ] The dirty-detached case produces no "PRIMARY ON  …" flag line with an empty branch name.
- [ ] No-origin repos on a real branch, and origin repos' existing default-branch behaviour, are unchanged.

body:
# id(attestation): `compute_state` never checks the two players are distinct — an agreement with `players = [A, A]` attests `Agreed` from one key's single genesis + single claim

## Evidence (main `07448571`, merged today in PR #2854 for #2248)

`pkgs/id/src/attestation.rs` (md5 `530fcdf45da5d8688dc0e4e319b641b2`) implements the mutual-concession viewer:

- `GenesisAgreement.players: [PlayerId; 2]` (:56-62) — "Both players, in seat order." Nothing in `sign_genesis`, `GenesisAgreement`, or `compute_state` requires the two seats to be **different** keys.
- `compute_state` (:223) checks the genesis pair with `agreement.players.iter().all(|player| genesis.iter().any(|(author, signed)| author == player && signed == agreement))` (:228-232). With `players = [A, A]`, **one** genesis event from A satisfies both seats, because `any` is re-evaluated per seat against the same entry.
- The claim phase (:239-250) enumerates the seats and, for each seat, scans the claims for that player. With `[A, A]`, A's **single** claim fills `per_player[0]` and `per_player[1]` both — the `(Some(a), Some(b))` arm (:251) then compares A's claim with itself, so outcome and final-state hash trivially "concur" and the state is `Agreed`.

The module's own contract says the opposite: "`Proposed` until both players have signed the same genesis and concurred" (module doc), "`two claims (one per player)` that concur … are `Agreed`" (`compute_state` doc, :216-221).

### Verified (laptop probe, verbatim `compute_state` + object types, real p2panda-core `Hash` at the pinned rev `da80c05b`)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-attdup/` on the laptop (`src/main.rs` md5 `83aab30df89c89f1549f314d795f6fde`; the extracted types/`compute_state` are byte-identical copies from `attestation.rs` — only the chain-signing helpers are omitted, because `compute_state` consumes pre-decoded author/object pairs exactly as the shipped tests call it, e.g. `one_claim_only_stays_proposed` in `tests/attestation_poc.rs:202`):

- `players=[A,A]`, genesis = `[ (A, agreement) ]` (one event), claims = `[ (A, claim) ]` (one event) → **`Agreed`** ← the bug: a single key attested a "mutual" result entirely alone
- `players=[A,A]`, genesis = `[ (A, agreement) ]`, claims = `[]` → `Proposed` (control: the claim is what completes it)
- `players=[A,B]`, both genesis, both claims concur → `Agreed` (control: normal path unchanged)
- `players=[A,B]`, both genesis, A's claim only → `Proposed` (control: the existing one-claim test's expectation)

The shipped tests (`tests/attestation_poc.rs`) cover the distinct-player happy path, the wrong-winner dispute, and the one-claim case — no duplicate-seat case.

## Why it matters

- The entire point of the attestation shape (#2037/#2248) is that a result is only `Agreed` when **two independent players** concede it. A self-match agreement collapses that to one signature set: anyone can mint an "agreed" match result naming themselves as both seats (and, with the outcome string naming themselves the winner, a one-sided "conceded" win) with no second party ever involved.
- It is a PoC today, but the module doc says production API may be built on these object shapes after the #2056 review round — this is exactly the class of invariant that review (and #2039, the v1 design) needs pinned **in the viewer**, because agreements arrive as signed objects from peers: a viewer that trusts `players` without checking distinctness will accept self-attestations from anyone, not just from local callers.
- A genesis-signing guard alone would not fix it: `compute_state` is the component that faces untrusted, already-signed objects, so the distinctness check belongs there (and, defensively, at signing time too).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `compute_state` never returns `Agreed` (or `Disputed`) for an agreement whose two player seats are the same key: a `[A, A]` agreement with any genesis/claim set from A computes `Proposed` (or the chosen explicit invalid-agreement result — triage pins which), because there is no second player.
- [ ] The distinct-player behavior is unchanged: `[A, B]` with both genesis + concurring claims → `Agreed`; differing claims → `Disputed`; one claim → `Proposed`.
- [ ] A regression test covers the probe matrix: `[A,A]` with one genesis + one claim, `[A,A]` with two distinct claims from A, and the distinct-player controls.
- [ ] Triage also pins whether `sign_genesis` should refuse to sign a duplicate-seat agreement (defense in depth) or whether the viewer check alone is the intended invariant — either way the viewer must not attest a self-match.

title: id(fileops): rename/copy onto an existing file merges the replaced file's metadata into the new file — two created values, both files' values for shared keys, and the archive keeps none

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.name: app/id
