labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`FileOps::rename` and `FileOps::copy` (`pkgs/id/src/fileops.rs`) archive a file they replace at the destination — the replaced content gets a blob tag `<to>.archive.<unix-ts>` — but the replaced file's **metadata tags are neither moved to that archive nor removed**. The transfer/copy then layers the source file's tags on top of whatever the destination already had:

- `rename` (`fileops.rs:262-335`): `archive_existing(&to, ts)` archives only the blob tag (`archive_existing`, `fileops.rs:182-194`, sets a blob tag and nothing else). Then `transfer_all_tags(ns, from, to)` (`tags.rs:983-1009`) copies each source tag onto `to` with `set_tag` and deletes the source's tags. Nothing ever reads, moves or deletes `to`'s pre-existing tags.
- `copy` (`fileops.rs:345-390`): same shape via `copy_all_tags` (`tags.rs:1018-1034`). Its trailing `stamp(&to, true)` resets `created`/`modified` singletons, but every other pre-existing destination tag survives the same way.

`set_tag` (`tags.rs:820-850`) is keyed by `(subject, key, value)`, so tags are multi-valued per key: the same key with a different value is a *separate* entry, not a replacement. Consequences for a destination that is replaced:

1. **Keys only the replaced file had stay on the new file.** E.g. the replaced file's `color=red` now describes the source's content.
2. **Keys both files had end up with both values.** E.g. `status` is both `wip` (source) and `done` (replaced file) after the rename.
3. **Singleton-intended keys duplicate (rename path).** `created`/`modified` are maintained as singletons everywhere else (`stamp` uses `set_singleton`/`set_if_absent`, `fileops.rs:215-247`), but rename never stamps, so after a rename onto an existing file the new name carries *two* `created` values — its own and the replaced file's.
4. **The archive is left with no metadata at all.** The archived version's tags are stranded on the destination name (points 1-3), so the archive tag `<to>.archive.<ts>` has zero metadata tags: the version it preserves cannot be found by the metadata that described it.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `07448571`)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA2-replacemeta/`, a worktree of origin/main with a probe-only test module appended to `fileops.rs` in the worktree; real `FileOps` over a MemStore blob store + a real `TagStore` over in-memory iroh-docs):

Setup for both tests: `put a.md` (content A), `put b.md` (content B); `a.md` gets `status=wip`, `created=111` (singleton); `b.md` gets `status=done`, `color=red`, `created=222` (singleton).

```text
BEFORE b.md:        ["color=red", "created=222", "file=b.md", "modified=1793402633", "name=b.md", "status=done"]

rename a.md -> b.md (archived_replaced = "b.md.archive.1793402633"):
AFTER-RENAME b.md:  ["archive.replace=b.md.archive.1793402633", "color=red",
                     "created=111", "created=222", "file=b.md", "modified=1793402633",
                     "name=b.md", "status=done", "status=wip"]
ARCHIVE b.md.archive.1793402633 tags: []

copy a.md -> b.md (fresh store, same seed; archived_replaced = "b.md.archive.1793402633"):
AFTER-COPY b.md:    ["archive.replace=b.md.archive.1793402633", "color=red",
                     "created=1793402633", "file=b.md", "modified=1793402633",
                     "name=b.md", "status=done", "status=wip"]
ARCHIVE b.md.archive.1793402633 tags: []
```

So after the rename, `b.md` (now holding content A) has **two** `created` values (`111` from A, `222` from the replaced B), **both** `status` values (`wip` and `done`), and B-only `color=red` — while the archive tag preserving B's content has **no metadata at all**. Copy shows the same merge; only `created` escapes duplication there because copy's trailing `stamp(..., reset_created=true)` happens to reset that one singleton. (In this probe both files' `modified` values fell in the same second, so that key did not visibly duplicate; it goes through the identical transfer path as `created` in rename, which never stamps.)

## Why it matters

Rename-onto-existing and copy-onto-existing are normal flows (the meta protocol renames with archiving, `protocol.rs:572`; the web UI exposes both). Metadata is how this system describes files — tag list/search, the web file list's user-visible tags, and `archive.*` bookkeeping all read it. After such a rename/copy, the destination's metadata is a blend of two different files' metadata, with duplicated `created` timestamps and contradictory values for the same key, while the archived version that metadata partly belongs to is undiscoverable by it. Nothing errors; the corruption is silent and persists in the synced tag store.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] After `rename` or `copy` replaces a file at the destination, no metadata tag that belonged only to the replaced file remains on the destination name (whether the ruling is move-to-archive-subject or delete-with-the-replace — triage pins it, consistently for both operations).
- [ ] After a rename onto an existing file, the destination has exactly one `created` and one `modified` value, belonging to the renamed file.
- [ ] A key both files had carries only the source file's value(s) on the destination after rename/copy.
- [ ] The archive subject (`<to>.archive.<ts>`), if the ruling is move-to-archive, carries the replaced file's metadata; if the ruling is delete, a test pins that the archive intentionally has none and the destination is clean either way.
- [ ] Regression tests in `fileops.rs` (real `FileOps` + `TagStore`): rename onto an existing file with disjoint and overlapping tag keys; copy onto an existing file likewise; rename/copy onto a *fresh* name behave exactly as today.
- [ ] Triage pins the ruling for the replaced file's `archive.*` system tags and for `put`-style overwrite (which intentionally keeps metadata) so this fix does not change `put` semantics.

Dedup checked this run: open+closed search for fileops rename/copy metadata — #2856 (delete misses previous-name archives) is the same module but a different operation and defect; #1612/#2462 cover archive *blob-tag* naming/races only; no issue covers replaced-file metadata handling in rename/copy.

body:
## Summary

`id` file hard delete does not remove archives that were created under a previous name. After a rename, deleting the file under its current name leaves the rename-created archive (and any earlier archives of the old name) behind as orphan blob tags — contradicting `FileOps::delete`'s documented contract.

## Evidence (main b706a837; file:line at 21f43a4f, same code)

- `pkgs/id/src/fileops.rs` module docs (lines 19–20): "`FileOps::delete` is a *hard* delete: the name, its metadata and its archive tags are removed."
- `FileOps::rename` with `archive=true` (the meta-protocol path, `pkgs/id/src/protocol.rs:572`) archives the original under the OLD name: `free_archive_name(store, from, ts)` → `<from>.archive.<ts>` (fileops.rs, `archived_original` block in `rename`), points the new name at the content, deletes the old name, and records that archive on the new name's own metadata as the `archive.rename` tag.
- `FileOps::delete` (fileops.rs:415) enumerates archive tags only by the CURRENT name's prefix: `let prefix = format!("{name}.archive.");` plus an all-digits suffix check. `<from>.archive.<ts>` never matches `<to>.archive.`, so it is not deleted and not counted in `DeleteOutcome.archives_removed`.
- Every delete surface goes through this one implementation (web `routes.rs:2013`, meta protocol `protocol.rs:564`, local `local.rs:159`), so no caller cleans the orphan up.
- The same applies to archives made before the rename: replace a file twice at name A (creating `A.archive.<t1>`, `A.archive.<t2>`), rename A→B, delete B — both archives survive. They still render in the file list as Archive-kind entries whose file no longer exists, and the only cleanup is an undocumented second delete of the already-gone old name.

## Probe (this run)

Laptop worktree probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-fileops/`, test appended to fileops.rs in the worktree only, never committed): put `doc` → `rename("doc", "doc2", true)` → `delete("doc2")` against an in-memory store + real `TagStore`, then list remaining blob tags.

Result: **bug reproduced** — `rename` created archive tag `doc.archive.1793401009`; `delete("doc2")` returned `existed=true, archives_removed=0`; the blob-tag list after the delete still contains `doc.archive.1793401009`. The probe test fails on exactly this assertion (`BUG REPRODUCED: rename-created archive doc.archive.1793401009 survives hard delete of doc2`).

## Why it matters

Hard delete is the operation a user reaches for to actually remove a file and its history. A version the user believes is gone stays in the store, still listed as an archive of a file that no longer exists, and still downloadable by name — a correctness and privacy footgun (delete-after-rename is a normal flow: the meta protocol always renames with `archive=true`).

## Acceptance criteria

- Deleting a file removes the archives recorded for it, including archives created under previous names (at minimum the `archive.rename` / `archive.replace` targets named in its own metadata, and/or archives discoverable by shared hash).
- `DeleteOutcome.archives_removed` counts every archive tag actually removed.
- A regression test covers put → rename (archive=true) → delete and asserts no `<old>.archive.<digits>` blob tag remains; a second test covers replace-at-A ×2 → rename A→B → delete B.
- Existing fileops behaviour is unchanged for files that were never renamed (same-second archive tests keep passing).

## Dedup

- #1612 (closed) was same-second archive-name collisions in `free_archive_name`; #2462 (open) is the check-then-act race in the same helper. Neither covers delete's archive enumeration missing previous names.

title: proxy-relay: bytes sent while the tunnel CONNECT is in flight are silently dropped — the peek removes the only data listener and the client is never paused, so request bodies truncate and upstreams hang

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: app/proxy-relay
labels.description: bin/proxy-relay.mjs sandbox-to-laptop relay

body:
## Summary

`bin/proxy-relay.mjs` silently drops every byte a client sends after the first TCP chunk until the upstream tunnel connection is established. The relay peeks at the first request line, removes its only `data` listener, then spends 0.1s–10s in `tryTargets()`/`connectViaTunnel()` before piping — and the client socket is never paused, so any bytes the client sends in that window (request bodies, the tail of a large header block) are read off the socket and discarded. The forwarded request therefore arrives truncated: a `Content-Length: 1000` POST reaches the upstream with only the headers, and the upstream hangs waiting for a body that will never come (or, for chunked/pipelined traffic, desynchronizes).

## Evidence (verified this run, main `497c820f`)

`bin/proxy-relay.mjs`:

- L152–187 (server handler): `client.on('data', onData)`; inside `onData`, once the first `\r\n` is seen, `client.removeListener('data', onData)` runs, then `tryTargets(order).then((upstream) => { upstream.write(buf); client.pipe(upstream); ... })`. Nothing calls `client.pause()` between the listener removal and the `.then`, and no buffering listener replaces `onData`.
- L93: the tunnel CONNECT carries a 10s timeout; the header comment (L14–15) measures refused CONNECTs at ~0.1–0.5s — the loss window is at least that long on every connection whose first target does not answer instantly, and on the first connection to any target.

Probe (laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-relaypeek/probe.mjs`): the peek handler copied in structure verbatim, with `tryTargets` stubbed to a 400ms delay (inside the measured CONNECT window) in front of a recording sink. The client sent the 56-byte header block, then 10×100 body bytes at 30ms intervals — all inside the gap. Two consecutive runs:

```
{"expected":1056,"sinkReceived":56,"lost":1000}
{"expected":1056,"sinkReceived":56,"lost":1000}
```

Only the peeked first chunk reached the sink; 100% of the bytes sent during the connect window were lost, deterministically.

Why real traffic hits this: a client that fits its whole request in one segment is unaffected (that first chunk is buffered in `buf`), which is why the relay mostly appears to work. Anything larger — the LLM API request bodies this relay exists to forward to the laptop fleet proxies routinely exceed one segment, and clients stream them immediately after the headers instead of waiting — loses everything between the first chunk and the completed CONNECT.

## Why it matters

Silent data corruption on a byte-forwarder whose whole contract is "pipe bytes untouched" (header comment, L11–12). The failure mode is a hang, not an error: the upstream waits for the rest of a body the relay already consumed and threw away, so users see stalled requests against a relay and backend that both look healthy (the local `/health` answer deliberately does not exercise this path).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Bytes a client sends at any point after connecting — including during the upstream CONNECT window — are forwarded to the upstream byte-for-byte and in order (e.g. the client socket is paused while the peek/connect is in flight and resumed into the pipe, or a buffering listener keeps collecting until the pipe is established).
- [ ] A regression test (this file currently has no `proxy-relay.test.mjs` sibling, unlike every other `bin/*.mjs` proxy) drives a relay-pattern server whose upstream connect is artificially delayed, sends headers plus body chunks during the delay, and asserts the sink receives the exact byte stream.
- [ ] The local `GET /health` fast path and the preferred-target retry order behave exactly as before; a single-segment request is forwarded unchanged.

## Dedup / relations

- Distinct from #1844 (RELAY_TARGET_PORTS parsing) and #2234 (accepted connections have no timeout — an idle-client hold; this is live-client data loss). Neither covers the peek/connect window.
- Found by: new-issue-creator-code-a, this run.

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

body:
# proxy-supervise(swap): a failed final start leaves NOTHING serving — the old instance is already stopped, contradicting the documented failure contract

**File:** `bin/proxy-supervise.mjs` (main `8808dfad`)
**Strategy affected:** `swap` (the sandbox proxies whose wiring hard-codes the canonical port)

## The contract

The header (line 56) promises:

> Exit code: 0 when every selected proxy reconciled (or was already correct); 1 when any roll failed (**the old instance is left running**).

The `ab` strategy honours this (`roll-failed-old-kept`). The `swap` strategy cannot: its sequence destroys the fallback before the risky step.

## The mechanism

Main swap path, `bin/proxy-supervise.mjs:541-555`:

1. The candidate is validated on the alternate port (healthy).
2. `:543-544` — the candidate **and the old instance are both stopped**.
3. The same build is spawned on the canonical port and health-checked.
4. If that final start is unhealthy → `swap-failed` (:550), the failed final instance is stopped, `lastError` is written — **and nothing is restarted**. The state file keeps the pre-roll `current` (old hash, now-dead pid).

The interrupted-swap completion path has the same shape (`:430-446`): the validated instance live on the alternate port is stopped first (`:438`); if the canonical start then fails → `swap-failed` (:442) with nothing left serving and no state update at all.

A build can pass validation on the alternate port and still fail the canonical start (canonical port momentarily occupied, a port-dependent startup fault, a transient resource failure during the swap window). When that happens the proxy is down on **both** ports until the artifact changes or a human intervenes — the exact outcome the supervisor exists to prevent (its whole design is "a rebuild must not kill a running proxy").

## Verified this run (laptop probe, real module)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-swapfail/` on the laptop — `proxy-supervise.mjs` copied verbatim (md5 `20dc2fcf9980046a94fd3215d2376963`, matches sandbox main), driven with the same fake-proxy harness pattern as `bin/proxy-supervise.test.mjs`. The v2 fake serves `/health` on any port **except** it exits immediately on the canonical port (a port-dependent startup fault, so the alt validation passes and the final start fails deterministically):

| step | result |
|---|---|
| reconcile #1 (v1, swap) | `started` on canonical; health 200 |
| reconcile #2 (v2) | **`swap-failed`** |
| old (v1) pid after #2 | **dead** |
| health on canonical after #2 | **no answer (connection refused)** |
| health on alternate after #2 | **no answer** |
| state file after #2 | still records the dead pid as `current` with the **old** hash; only `lastError` was added |
| reconcile #3 (unchanged) | `roll-failed-old-kept` — still nothing serving |
| control (v2 healthy on all ports) | `rolled`, settles on canonical, health 200 with the v2 marker |

## Why it matters

`swap` is the strategy for the proxies whose consumers hard-code the canonical port (the sandbox OpenCode config) — i.e. the ones with no endpoint-record fallback to save them. A single transient failure during the seconds-long swap window converts a graceful roll into an unbounded outage of a fleet proxy, silently (the run exits 1 with `swap-failed`, but no instance is serving and the state file claims a dead pid is current).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] When the final canonical start of a swap fails, the supervisor leaves a working instance serving: e.g. restart the previous build on the canonical port (its artifact files are unchanged on disk), or keep/restart the validated new build on the alternate port and flip the endpoint record to it — the chosen recovery is stated in the result/log line.
- [ ] The same recovery applies to the interrupted-swap completion path (`:430-446`), which today stops the only live instance before its risky start.
- [ ] After a failed swap, the state file never records a dead pid as `current` without an explicit marker of the failure state.
- [ ] Regression tests in `bin/proxy-supervise.test.mjs` (existing fake-proxy harness): a build that serves on the alternate port but fails on the canonical port ends the reconcile with *something* healthy serving and the old-or-recovered instance's pid recorded; the healthy-swap control still settles on canonical.
- [ ] The header contract at line 56 and the observed behaviour agree (either the recovery makes the contract true, or the contract is rewritten to state the real semantics and why).

title: id(peers): plain_field passes bidi/format controls raw — a gossip peer name with U+202E reaches the terminal unescaped and visually reorders the row's columns

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Problem

`plain_field` (`pkgs/id/src/commands/text.rs:42-44`) — the renderer whose whole job is making untrusted values row-safe in plain-text output (#1613) — treats a value as structure-breaking only when it contains a `char::is_control` character or U+2028/U+2029:

```rust
fn breaks_row(c: char) -> bool {
    c.is_control() || matches!(c, '\u{2028}' | '\u{2029}')
}
```

Unicode bidirectional and format controls are category Cf, not Cc, so `is_control()` is false for all of them: U+202A–U+202E (embedding/override, incl. RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE), U+2066–U+2069 (isolates), U+200E/U+200F (LRM/RLM), U+200B, U+FEFF. They reach the terminal raw in both paths:

1. **Unquoted path:** a peer name carrying only an override (no tab/newline) is returned byte-identical by `plain_field`.
2. **Quoted path:** even when quoting does trigger (e.g. the name also contains a tab), the escape loop in `plain_field` (text.rs:62-86) only escapes characters `breaks_row` matches — the override is emitted raw inside the quotes, where it still acts on the terminal rendering.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `a8ea41ae`)

Probe crate on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-bidi/`) running `breaks_row`/`plain_field` copied verbatim from `src/commands/text.rs`:

- `U+202A..U+202E, U+2066..U+2069, U+200E, U+200F, U+200B, U+FEFF`: `is_control=false`, `breaks_row=false` for every one.
- `plain_field("mallory\u{202e}9 0")` returns the input **byte-identical, unquoted**, with a raw U+202E in the output.
- A name with a tab + U+202E is quoted, but the output still contains the raw U+202E.

Callers put the result in fixed-column rows whose trailing fields are exactly what an override reorders visually:

- `format_peer_row` (`src/commands/peers.rs:206-219`): `<node_id>\t<name>\t<blob_count>\t<timestamp>` — the name arrives over **unsigned gossip**, is stored and served verbatim (peers.rs:116-121), so any peer can announce such a name. In a terminal, U+202E reverses the visual order of the text after it: the blob-count/timestamp columns can be made to read swapped or falsified, defeating the column structure #1613 exists to protect.
- Same renderer in the REPL peer list (`src/commands/repl.rs:116-123`).

Sibling surfaces with the same `is_control`-only assumption, to audit in the same pass (not necessarily the same fix): the `key=value` renderer `text()` in `src/commands/group.rs:66` (quotes only on whitespace/control; serde_json string rendering does not escape Cf either) and `sanitize_display_name`/`sanitize_chat` in `src/world/util.rs:69-84` (filter only `is_control`).

## Why it matters

The #1611/#1613 ruling is that a printer never lets an untrusted value be mistaken for structure. A bidi override does not add a row or shift a byte column — it corrupts what the row *appears* to say, which is the terminal-level equivalent: a malicious peer name can visually falsify the numeric columns next to it. This is the Trojan-Source class of characters (CVE-2021-42574) applied to live CLI output.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `plain_field` quotes and escapes (`\uXXXX`) the bidi/format controls — at minimum U+202A–U+202E, U+2066–U+2069, U+200E, U+200F — whether they appear alone or alongside an already-escaping character; a rendered field never contains a raw Cf override/isolate/mark.
- [ ] Ordinary names are unchanged byte-for-byte: spaces, CJK, emoji, accented letters (the existing test corpus in text.rs) still render unwrapped.
- [ ] Regression tests in `src/commands/text.rs` covering: override-only name is quoted+escaped; override+tab name has no raw override inside the quotes.
- [ ] The sibling surfaces (`group.rs` `text()`, `world/util.rs` sanitizers) are audited and either fixed in the same PR or explicitly filed as follow-ups from triage.
- [ ] Triage pins the exact character set (embeddings/overrides/isolates/marks, and whether zero-width chars U+200B–U+200D/U+FEFF are in scope) before the fix packet is routed.

Dedup checked this run: open+closed search for bidi/plain_field/Trojan/unicode-spoof — no hits; #1611/#1613/#1856 cover tab/newline/space escaping only.

body: ## Bug The id web UI's **Alt+T theme-cycling shortcut never fires on macOS**, and also fails everywhere when Shift (or CapsLock) is held — even though the editor footer advertises `Alt+T theme` as a working shortcut. ## Evidence `pkgs/id/web/src/theme.ts:65-72` (main `dc9b1179`) — the only Alt+T handler: ```ts document.addEventListener("keydown", (event: KeyboardEvent) => { if (event.altKey && event.key === "t") { event.preventDefault(); cycleTheme(); } }); ``` `KeyboardEvent.key` is the *character produced*, not the physical key: - macOS Option+T produces key `"†"` (U+2020), Option+Shift+T produces `"ˇ"` (U+02C7) — the `=== "t"` comparison never matches, so the shortcut is dead on macOS. - Alt+Shift+T (or CapsLock on) on any platform produces key `"T"` — also never matches. ### Probe (laptop, verbatim predicate, theme.ts md5-matched `5c0e856b…` against both clones) `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-altt/probe.mjs` — the exact predicate from `initTheme` run against the `key` values browsers deliver: ``` control Alt+T (Win/Linux US): key="t" -> shortcut fires: true macOS Option+T: key="†" -> shortcut fires: false macOS Option+Shift+T: key="ˇ" -> shortcut fires: false any Alt+Shift+T: key="T" -> shortcut fires: false control plain t (no Alt): key="t" -> shortcut fires: false Alt+T physical presses that do NOT fire: 3 of 4 ``` The shortcut is also user-facing: `pkgs/id/src/web/templates.rs` renders `Alt+T theme` in the editor footer, and clicking that footer link (`window.cycleTheme?.()`) works — only the keyboard path is broken. Note `pkgs/id/web/src/world-keyboard.ts` already exists as a tested helper that normalizes exactly these `KeyboardEvent` edge cases (`Unidentified`/`Dead`/`Process` keys, modifier handling) for the world view; the theme handler predates / bypasses that care. ## Why it matters A documented, footer-advertised shortcut silently does nothing for every macOS user (Option is the Mac Alt key) and for anyone whose press includes Shift/CapsLock. Theme switching is a small but visible feature — the sneak/arch/mech themes are a deliberate part of the id UI — and a dead shortcut reads as "the app is broken" rather than "wrong key". ## Acceptance criteria - [ ] Alt+T (Option+T on macOS) cycles the theme in current browsers on macOS, Windows, and Linux, including when Shift is held or CapsLock is on. - [ ] The match is on the physical key (e.g. `event.code === "KeyT"`) or an equivalently layout-independent normalization — not on the produced character alone. - [ ] Plain `t` typing and unrelated Alt combinations do not trigger a theme change; `preventDefault` still suppresses the character insertion where the shortcut fires. - [ ] New unit tests for the handler predicate cover at least: `key:"t"` control, `key:"†"` + `code:"KeyT"`, `key:"T"`, and a non-T control. (There is currently no `theme.test.ts`.) - [ ] Existing web unit tests still pass.

# id(web): collab WebSocket URL interpolates the raw filename unencoded — names with `/ ? #` never connect, and a `%20` name silently opens a different file

## Summary

`openEditor` in `pkgs/id/web/src/main.ts` builds the collab WebSocket URL by interpolating the raw document name into the path with no encoding:

```ts
// main.ts:955 (main cd21b77c)
const wsUrl = `${wsProtocol}//${window.location.host}/ws/collab/${docId}`;
```

`docId` is `dataset.docId`, which the server writes as the **raw, HTML-escaped only** name: `templates.rs:436` `doc_id_escaped = html_escape(doc_id)`, emitted at `templates.rs:505` as `data-doc-id="{doc_id_escaped}"`, and the editor route passes the raw name as that argument (`routes.rs:508`: `render_editor(&name, &name, &content, &hash)`). The sibling `data-filename` attribute is the URL-encoded one (`templates.rs:440`, `urlencoding::encode(name)`) — but the WS path never uses it encoded.

The server route is a single path segment: `routes.rs:307` `.route("/ws/collab/{doc_id}", …)`, and `ws_collab_handler` treats the percent-decoded segment as the filename (`collab.rs:661-662`: "doc_id is now a filename — resolve to hash"). Filenames with URL-significant characters are legal: `new_file_handler` (`routes.rs:1348ff`) rejects only empty names, and `/edit/{*name}` is a wildcard route, so these files open in the editor page fine — only the collab connection breaks.

## Verified behavior (laptop probe, this run)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-wsurl/`, Node, WHATWG URL — the browser's parser): the verbatim `main.ts:955` construction plus `collab.ts`'s `initCollab` query append (`?filename=…` via `URLSearchParams`), then single-segment route matching and percent-decoding of the segment, as axum does:

```
name="notes.md"   -> /ws/collab/notes.md            server doc_id="notes.md"   filename param ok   OK
name="a b.md"     -> /ws/collab/a%20b.md            server doc_id="a b.md"     filename param ok   OK (URL parser encodes the space)
name="résumé.md"   -> /ws/collab/r%C3%A9sum%C3%A9.md server doc_id="résumé.md" filename param ok   OK
name="a/b.md"     -> /ws/collab/a/b.md              NO ROUTE MATCH (two segments) — upgrade 404s, editor never initializes
name="a#b.md"     -> /ws/collab/a                   server doc_id="a" (fragment eats the rest; filename param lost) — wrong/empty doc
name="a?b.md"     -> /ws/collab/a                   server doc_id="a" (query eats the rest; filename param garbled) — wrong/empty doc
name="a%20b.md"   -> /ws/collab/a%20b.md            server doc_id="a b.md" — SILENTLY OPENS A DIFFERENT FILE
name="100%.md"    -> /ws/collab/100%.md             percent-decode of the segment fails (URI malformed) — no connection
```

Controls (`notes.md`, `a b.md`, `résumé.md`, `a&b.md`, `a+b.md`) all round-trip correctly, which is why plain names never notice.

## Why it matters

- **Cross-file corruption risk, load side:** editing `a%20b.md` connects the editor to `a b.md`'s collab session — the user sees and edits a different file's content under the first file's title. This is the load-path counterpart of #1494 (which is the *save* path reading `dataset.docId`); fixing #1494's `saveFile` field does not fix this URL.
- **Unopenable files:** any name containing `/`, `?`, or `#` renders an editor page whose WebSocket can never connect (404 or truncated doc_id), so the document never loads and the status sits at connecting/reconnecting — with no hint that the filename is the cause.
- Every other URL this client builds encodes the name (`/edit/${encodeURIComponent(name)}` at `main.ts:1142/1261/1327`, `/api/tags?subject=${encodeURIComponent(filename)}` at `main.ts:724`, home.ts links). The collab WS path is the outlier.

## Acceptance criteria

- `openEditor` connects for names containing `/`, `?`, `#`, `%`, and spaces: the server receives the exact filename as `doc_id` in every case (e.g. encode the segment with `encodeURIComponent`, and if `/` must stay supported, confirm axum's `{doc_id}` capture vs a wildcard/catch-all or encoded `%2F` decoding behavior — encoded `%2F` must round-trip to `a/b.md`, not 404).
- `a%20b.md` opens `a%20b.md`'s own session, never `a b.md`'s; `100%.md` connects normally.
- The `filename` query parameter appended in `initCollab` still arrives intact for all of the above (no `#`/`?` truncation upstream of it).
- Web unit tests cover the URL construction for at least: a slash name, a `#`/`?` name, a `%20` name, a bare-`%` name, plus the plain/space/unicode controls unchanged.
- No behavior change for existing plain names; reconnect logic in `collab.ts` is untouched except as needed for the URL.

## Related / dedup

- #1494 (open) is the save path: `saveFile` decodes `dataset.docId`. Same dataset family, different sink and different failure — this issue is the collab *connect/load* path (`main.ts:955`), which #1494's acceptance criteria do not cover.
- #2824 (open) is MessagePack frame-shape validation in `collab.ts` `handleMessage`; unrelated to URL construction.
- Searched open + closed issues this run for `ws/collab`, collab WebSocket URL/encoding, and `saveFile` — no existing issue covers the WS URL construction.

body:
# record(loose): a `__proto__` field in loose text is silently dropped — parseLoose assigns into a plain object, so the field never reaches the JSONL line (the JSON path preserves it)

**Repo:** developing-today/code · **Main:** `a047d531` · **File:** `bin/record.mjs` — `parseLoose` at lines 104–126 (field assignment at :115), `normaliseInput` at :132–145.

## Evidence (verified this run, real module)

`record`'s contract (file header, :12–19) is NEVER REJECT and "Agent-supplied fields are never rewritten, flattened, or validated — unknown keys pass through untouched." The loose-text path breaks that for exactly one key:

`parseLoose` collects segments into a plain object literal (`const fields = {}`, :105) and assigns `fields[key] = value` (:115). The key grammar (`/^\s*([A-Za-z_][\w .-]*?)\s*[:=]/`, :108) admits `__proto__`, and assigning to `fields.__proto__` invokes the `Object.prototype` setter instead of creating an own property: a string value is ignored outright, and an object value silently replaces the fields object's prototype. Either way the key counts toward the two-keyed-segment threshold (:122) but never becomes a field.

Laptop probe (real module, md5 `47b3304a4ee676b5b19b8129af5a3f49` matching main; probe retained at laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-recordproto/`):

- Control: `parseLoose('category=bad | finding: something broke')` → `{"category":"bad","finding":"something broke"}`.
- `parseLoose('__proto__=hello | category=bad')` → `{"category":"bad"}` — `__proto__` gone, `Object.keys` = `["category"]`.
- `parseLoose('__proto__={"polluted":1} | category=bad')` → `{"category":"bad"}`, and the fields object's prototype IS `{polluted:1}` (the value went to the prototype, not a field; `Object.prototype` itself is not polluted — `({}).polluted` stays `undefined`).
- End-to-end `record('__proto__=hello | category=bad', …)` returns `recorded` and appends `{"category":"bad","raw":"__proto__=hello | category=bad","ts":…,"pwd":…}` — no `__proto__` field (it survives only inside the verbatim `raw` string, and any later normalisation pass that re-runs `parseLoose` on that raw drops it again).
- Asymmetry control: the JSON path preserves the same key — `record('{"__proto__":"hello","category":"bad"}', …)` appends a line with an own `"__proto__":"hello"` field (`Object.hasOwn(entry,'__proto__') === true`), because JSON.parse + spread create it as a data property.
- `constructor=x` in loose text is preserved as an own field — `__proto__` is the only setter-special key the grammar admits.

## Why it matters

`record` is the fleet's append-only observation log (#1853): its one hard rule is that a supplied field must not be lost, because a lost field costs the observation permanently. A loose recording that legitimately names a `__proto__` field — exactly the kind of key an agent records when reporting a prototype-lookup bug (the fleet filed four of those this week: #2734/#2757/#2781/#2790) — is silently normalised into a line without that field, and the recording still reports success. The two input paths also disagree: the same observation sent as JSON keeps the field, sent as loose text loses it.

Related but distinct: #2792's design covers read-side own-key *lookups* and explicitly scopes write-side `__proto__` handling out ("a different bug class", Phase 3 reports instances). This is that write-side instance, with field loss (not lookup fabrication and not global pollution) as the concrete harm — triage may route it under #2792's Phase 3 audit instead of a standalone fix; either disposition is fine, but it should be on record.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A loose-text `__proto__` field reaches the appended JSONL line as an own field with its parsed value, exactly as the JSON path already does — for both string and object values.
- [ ] Building the loose fields object never changes any object's prototype (the fields object keeps `Object.prototype`, and no other object is affected).
- [ ] Tests in `bin/record.test.mjs` pin: loose `__proto__` with a string value, loose `__proto__` with an object value, and the JSON-path control — all three lines carry the field.
- [ ] All other loose/JSON behaviour is unchanged: the two-keyed-segment threshold, `raw` ride-along, stamp filling, quarantine path, and exit-0 / never-throw contract.

Dedup: searched open + closed issues for `record.mjs`, `parseLoose`, `ai_recordings`, `__proto__` + loose — no filing covers this. #2235 covers record's entry-point check only; #2792 is read-side lookups with write-side explicitly out of scope (see above). NOT self-solved: the fix shape (null-prototype fields object vs defineProperty assignment) interacts with the spread/stamp code and is triage's pin.

body:
## Problem

`bin/provider-catalog-sync.mjs` trusts the shape of a proxy's `/v1/models` response (and of `--source-dir` snapshot files) past "it parsed as JSON". `enumerateProxy` (lines 443–451) is:

```js
return (data.data ?? []).map((m) => m.id);
```

with no check that `data` is an object, that `data.data` is an array, or that the mapped ids are non-empty strings. The header contract (lines 22–25) promises the opposite failure shape: "A provider that fails to enumerate degrades to a per-provider note, never a failed run", and `additions_validated` is "the only class --apply will ever add" (line 8). Two verified consequences on current main (`1281cb37`):

1. **A parseable 200 body with no `data` field is silently treated as a live empty model list.** `data.data ?? []` turns a shape drift (e.g. `{}` or `{"unexpected": []}` from a proxy whose response format changed) into `live_count: 0` with NO error status/note, and `classify` then flags **every** model in the config as a vanishing with `vanishings_basis: "live"`. A reader of the report (or a catalog PR body built from it) sees "the provider serves nothing" instead of "the provider's response shape changed".
2. **An entry without a string `id` poisons `--apply` and crashes the whole run.** An entry like `{"name": "no-id"}` maps to `undefined`, which lands in `additions_validated` (serialized as `null` in the report). That class is exactly what `--apply` acts on: `applyAdditions` → `makeEntry` (line 408) → `prettifyModelName` (line 352, `modelId.split('/')`) throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'split')` — outside the per-provider try/catch in `runSync` (line 511), so one malformed entry from one proxy fails the entire sync instead of degrading that provider.

Other malformed shapes DO degrade correctly, which shows the gap is missing validation, not design: `data: "oops"` → `not-enumerable` ("(data.data ?? []).map is not a function"), `data: [null]` → `not-enumerable` ("Cannot read properties of null (reading 'id')"). Only the missing-`data` and missing-`id` shapes slip through silently / fatally.

## Evidence (this run, laptop probe with the real module)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-catalogsync/` on the laptop — real `bin/provider-catalog-sync.mjs` (md5 `521dfab189aa83e1202691ba48f195b6`, identical on sandbox main `1281cb37` and the laptop copy), driven through the exported `runSync` with `--source-dir`-style snapshot files; config fixture has provider `claude-code` (port 18749) with models `model-a`/`model-b` and `commandcode` (18748) as a healthy control.

- Snapshot `18749.json = {"unexpected": []}` → `{"status":null, "live_count":0, "additions_validated":[], "vanishings":["model-a","model-b"], "basis":"live", "note":null}` — silent false vanishings.
- Snapshot `18749.json = {"data":[{"name":"no-id"}]}` → `{"live_count":1, "additions_validated":[null], "vanishings":["model-a","model-b"], "basis":"live"}`; then `applyAdditions(...)` → `THREW TypeError Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'split')`.
- Snapshot `{"data":"oops"}` → `status:"not-enumerable"` with explanatory note (intended degradation — control).
- Snapshot `{"data":[null]}` → `status:"not-enumerable"` with explanatory note (intended degradation — control).
- Snapshot `{"data":[{"id":"model-a"},{"id":"model-b"}]}` → `live_count:2`, no additions/vanishings (valid control).

The same code path serves the live HTTP enumeration (`fetchJson` → `res.json()` → same `.map`), so a live proxy returning either shape hits the same outcomes; snapshots are just the reproducible offline door the tool itself documents.

## Why it matters

This tool's whole job is trustworthy drift classification for the provider catalog, and its safety story rests on two promises: enumeration failures degrade per-provider, and only validated additions are ever applied. A proxy whose `/v1/models` shape drifts (a real event in this fleet — the proxies are actively rewritten) currently either manufactures a full-catalog "vanishings" alarm with a `live` basis, or takes down the scheduled sync run entirely at `--apply` time with a stack that names neither the provider nor the offending entry.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `enumerateProxy` validates the response shape: body is an object, `data` is present and an array, and every entry yields a non-empty string `id`; any violation throws an enumeration error naming the port/shape problem, so `runSync` records that provider as `not-enumerable` with a note (the existing degradation path).
- [ ] A missing or non-array `data` field is never classified as a live empty list (no `vanishings_basis: "live"` vanishings from an unvalidated body).
- [ ] Entries without a valid string `id` never reach `additions_validated`, and `--apply` / `applyAdditions` cannot be crashed by an enumeration result.
- [ ] `bin/provider-catalog-sync.test.mjs` gains cases for: no-`data` body, non-array `data`, id-less entry, and null entry — each asserting the per-provider `not-enumerable` outcome (or the pinned equivalent), plus the valid-list control unchanged.
- [ ] Valid enumerations (live and snapshot) produce identical reports to today.

body:
# mcpx(progspec): concurrent resolves of one nix spec each run their own `nix build` — the memo only dedupes sequential calls

**Repo:** developing-today/code · **Main:** `1281cb37` · **File:** `pkgs/mcpx/internal/progspec/progspec.go` — memo check at lines 136-158, `resolveNixMemoized` at 168-177 (new in PR #2585, merged 2026-10-30)

## Summary

`progspec` memoises resolved nix specs so "a daemon that restarts a server repeatedly pays the build once" (package doc, lines 22-24). The memo is only consulted **before** resolving and only populated **after** a resolution finishes:

```go
memoMu.Lock()
if r, ok := memo[key]; ok { ... return r, nil }
memoMu.Unlock()
return resolveNixMemoized(ctx, spec, dir, key)   // resolves, then stores
```

There is no in-flight tracking, so N concurrent `Resolve`/`ResolveInDir` calls for the same spec — the normal shape when a daemon starts or restarts several servers at once, or several servers share one `nix:` command — each spawn their own `nix build --no-link --print-out-paths`. Nix's store locking serialises the actual build, but every invocation still pays full flake evaluation (the expensive part for a large flake such as nixpkgs), and each is independently allowed up to `DefaultTimeout` (3 minutes, line 43).

## Evidence (verified this run, real module)

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-progspec/`; the repo's real `progspec.go`, md5 `69fd5418546542c4de1f127906d59ed5` identical on sandbox main `1281cb37` and the laptop copy; stub `nix` on PATH in the style of the package's own tests, sleeping 0.3 s per invocation and counting calls):

| Scenario | `nix` invocations |
|---|---|
| 8 goroutines calling `Resolve(ctx, "nix:nixpkgs#faketool")` concurrently, same spec/dir | **8** (elapsed 312 ms — fully parallel, no dedupe) |
| 2 sequential resolves of the same spec (existing test `TestResolveNixSpecBuildsOnceAndSpawnsTheStorePath`) | 1 (memo works sequentially — not in dispute) |

Callers that resolve at spawn time, all reachable concurrently: `pkgs/mcpx/internal/mcpclient/stdio.go:103` (`ResolvePathInDir`), `pkgs/mcpx/internal/mcpclient/supervised.go:243` (`spawnChild`, per child restart) and `:609` (`ResolvePathFreshInDir`).

## Why it matters

The memo's stated purpose is paying the build once per daemon. Concurrent first-resolves — daemon startup with several `nix:` servers, a supervisor restarting children together, pooled servers sharing one spec — silently pay it once **per caller** instead, multiplying the slowest, most failure-prone step of launch (a network/flake evaluation with a 3-minute timeout) exactly when the daemon is busiest. It also multiplies the failure surface: one transient nix failure can surface as N slightly-different launch errors for what is logically one resolution.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Concurrent `Resolve`/`ResolveInDir` calls for the same memo key share one in-flight `nix build`: a regression test with the stub-`nix` harness (slow stub, N concurrent resolves) counts exactly 1 invocation and all callers receive the same `Resolved`.
- [ ] A failed in-flight resolution is **not** memoised (today's behaviour): every waiter receives that error, and a later call retries the build.
- [ ] The deleted-output eviction behaviour (`TestResolveNixSpecMemoEvictsDeletedOutput`) and the per-directory memo keying still hold; a resolution whose memo entry is evicted mid-flight does not resurrect a dead path.
- [ ] `ResolveFreshInDir`'s contract is preserved or explicitly re-pinned in its doc comment (it bypasses the memo *read* by design — triage decides whether fresh callers also share an in-flight resolution or stay fully independent).
- [ ] Existing `pkgs/mcpx/internal/progspec` tests still pass (`go test ./internal/progspec -count=1` in CI / on the laptop — not `go test ./...` locally, per `pkgs/mcpx/internal/AGENTS.md`).

Dedup notes: searched open + closed issues this run for progspec / singleflight / concurrent resolve / memo — no hit. Related but distinct: #1921 (the feature this shipped in, still open for its environment half), #1908 (a *durable, cross-process* content-addressed cache for flake resolutions — this issue is only the in-process concurrent case), #2754/#2726 (mcpx result-validation / settings panics, unrelated paths). NOT self-solved: the singleflight shape (and the `ResolveFreshInDir` question above) is triage's pin, and fleet verification for Go changes runs on the laptop/CI, not in a creator run.

body:
# id(web): collab `handleMessage` trusts MessagePack frame shape — a `null` frame throws out of `onmessage`, and a field-less INIT silently initializes an empty editor at an undefined version

**Repo:** developing-today/code · **Main:** `df9381ff` · **File:** `pkgs/id/web/src/collab.ts` — `handleMessage` at lines 198-206, INIT case at 210-265

## Summary

The collab WebSocket handler guards only the MessagePack **decode** step:

```ts
try {
  msg = unpackr.unpack(new Uint8Array(data)) as unknown[];
} catch (err) {
  console.error("[collab] Failed to decode MessagePack message:", err);
  return;
}
const msgType = msg[0] as number;   // :206 — outside the try, shape never checked
```

Two verified failure modes for frames that decode fine but are not the expected array shape:

1. **A `null` frame throws out of the handler.** MessagePack `0xc0` unpacks to `null`; `msg[0]` then throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading '0')` at `collab.ts:206`, escaping `onmessage` as an uncaught error. Any non-array unpack result that cannot be indexed the same way is one peer bug away from the same path; the decode-error path right above shows the intended behaviour (log + drop), the shape path just never got it.
2. **A field-less INIT is silently accepted as an empty document.** `case MSG.INIT` reads `version = msg[1]`, `doc = msg[2]`, `mode = msg[3] || "raw"` with no presence/type check (:212-214) and calls `initEditor(container, doc, version, mode, …)` (:221). `initEditor` (`editor.ts`) treats a missing/non-object doc as "create an empty document" — so a truncated or buggy INIT presents the user with a **blank editor for a document that is not blank**, running the ProseMirror collab plugin at version `undefined`, and fires `onEditorReady` (which enables the save button and wires AutoSaveManager in `main.ts`). Nothing logs an error, no resync is requested, and the status reads "connected". Code-read consequence: an edit + save from that phantom editor posts the near-empty doc to `/api/save` under the real file's hash — the server archives the previous version, but the working document has been replaced by the blank one the client fabricated.

## Evidence (verified this run, real module)

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-collabframe/`; `collab.ts` md5 `fff3e0f4bdf0165f40a56f683fa03434` identical on sandbox main `df9381ff` and the laptop; vitest + happy-dom, `FakeSocket` global + the real `initCollab`, frames packed with the repo's own `msgpackr`):

| Frame delivered | Result |
|---|---|
| `null` (msgpack `0xc0`) | **TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading '0')** thrown out of `onmessage` |
| `42`, `"hello"`, `{}`, `[999, 1]` (controls) | no throw — dropped / unknown-type warning, as expected |
| `[0]` — INIT, no version/doc/mode | **no throw, but `onEditorReady` fired, editor initialized, mode `raw`** — an empty editor built from an absent doc at an undefined version |
| `[0, 0, {doc…code_block "hi"}, "raw"]` (well-formed control) | no throw, editor initialized with the real doc — well-formed handling unchanged |
| `[4]` — CURSOR with no fields, after valid INIT | no throw (cursor plugin tolerates it — checked, not part of this filing) |
| `[2, "nope", [123]]` — UPDATE with string steps | no throw out of the handler; the existing step-apply catch closes with 4001 and reconnects (the resync behaviour INIT should arguably share — noted, not part of this filing) |

## Why it matters

Collab frames originate from the serving node / peer, not from this client — the same untrusted-shape boundary the codebase already defends for world frames (#2802) and shell frames (`shell-contract.ts`). The throw is the loud half; the silent half is worse: a user whose INIT arrives truncated (or who connects to a buggy/experimental server build) is shown an empty document, told they are connected, and given a working save path over the real document's hash. "My file went blank" with no error anywhere is the hardest class of report to attribute after the fact.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A frame whose unpacked value is not an array (including `null`) is dropped with a logged error and does **not** throw out of `handleMessage`/`onmessage`; a subsequent well-formed INIT on the same connection still initializes the editor.
- [ ] An INIT frame without a numeric version or without a document object is rejected — logged, and handled as an invalid/desynced state (error status and/or the resync-reconnect the UPDATE path already uses) — and never initializes an editor from an absent doc or an `undefined` version; `onEditorReady` does not fire for it.
- [ ] Regression tests in a new `pkgs/id/web/src/collab.test.ts` (FakeSocket harness in the style of `world-records.test.ts`) pin: the `null` frame, the field-less INIT, an INIT with a non-object doc, and the well-formed INIT control; existing web tests still pass (`bunx vitest run` in `pkgs/id/web`).
- [ ] Well-formed frames of every existing type (INIT/UPDATE/CURSOR/ACK/ERROR/CURSOR_REMOVE/NEW_VERSION/AUTH_OK) behave byte-for-byte as today.

Dedup notes: searched open + closed issues this run for collab frame shape / handleMessage / INIT — no hit. Distinct from #2802 (the world page's JSON `receive()` in `world.ts`; different protocol, handler and consequences), #1618 (server-side step validation), #1463/#1368 (collab reconnect/token behaviour), and closed #1783 (the Rust codec's tag-6 decode).

# antigravity-direct: ANTIGRAVITY_DIRECT_PORT / _TIMEOUT_MS are bare Number() — the new door bypasses the house strict port helper, so bad ports crash with a stack or bind the wrong port, and bad timeouts start healthy then 502 every request

**Repo:** developing-today/code · **Main:** `2a91ea6c` · **File:** `bin/antigravity-direct.mjs:60-62` (landed 2026-10-30 in `b0058ec7`)

## Summary

```js
const PORT = Number(process.env.ANTIGRAVITY_DIRECT_PORT || 18751);        // :60
const TIMEOUT_MS = Number(process.env.ANTIGRAVITY_DIRECT_TIMEOUT_MS || 300000); // :62
```

Every other `bin/*` proxy parses its listen port through the strict house helper `bin/proxy-port.mjs` (`parseProxyPort`, built for #483 precisely because "a bare parseInt is not a validator"): agy (:39), antigravity-ls (:10), claude-code (:42), clef (:8), codex (:12), commandcode (:58), design-code (:6), muse (:39), opencode-route (:49), proxy-relay (:39/:55). The door seated today is the sole exception — it validates neither value, and each bad spelling fails differently, none of them naming the variable at fault.

## Evidence (verified this run, real module)

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-antigrav-port/`; `bin/antigravity-direct.mjs` md5 `de11cfa24df8200d66fd788422667ef8`, identical on sandbox main `2a91ea6c` and the laptop). Stub `secret-tool` + local stub/hanging upstreams; no real keyring read, no real Google call.

PORT cases:

| `ANTIGRAVITY_DIRECT_PORT` | Result |
|---|---|
| `abc`, `18941abc` | Process exits 1 at startup: `RangeError [ERR_SOCKET_BAD_PORT]: options.port should be >= 0 and < 65536. Received type number (NaN)` at `antigravity-direct.mjs:660` — a Node stack that never names `ANTIGRAVITY_DIRECT_PORT` or the offending value |
| `18941.9` | Same exit-1 `ERR_SOCKET_BAD_PORT` (`Received type number (18941.9)`) |
| `99999` | Same exit-1 `ERR_SOCKET_BAD_PORT`, variable/value unnamed |
| `0` | Starts "healthy", binds a **random ephemeral port**, while `endpoint.json` records `{"port":0,"url":"http://127.0.0.1:0"}` and the log claims `listening on http://127.0.0.1:0` — every client reading the endpoint file dials port 0 and fails |
| `0x4a35` | Silently binds **18997** — a port nobody configured — and `endpoint.json` ratifies it (`"port":18997`); `/healthz` answers there |
| `18941` (control) | Starts, `endpoint.json` correct, serves normally |

TIMEOUT_MS cases (upstream stub that accepts and never responds):

| `ANTIGRAVITY_DIRECT_TIMEOUT_MS` | Result |
|---|---|
| `300` (control) | Request fails in ~0.32 s: HTTP 502 `upstream timeout after 300ms` — the intended behaviour |
| `abc` | Proxy starts and listens healthy, but **every** upstream request returns HTTP 502 in ~14 ms with Node's raw `The value of "timeout" is out of range. It must be a non-negative finite number. Received NaN` — naming neither the variable nor that this is a config error; the catalog pull fails the same way at startup and is logged only as "keeping fallback list" |
| `-5000` | Same healthy-start / 502-every-request shape (`Received -5000`) |
| `3000000000` | Starts with `TimeoutOverflowWarning: 3000000000 does not fit into a 32-bit signed integer`; a request against the hanging upstream is still unanswered after the client's 6 s cap — the configured 50-minute bound is neither honoured nor rejected |

## Why it matters

This door was seated in opencode today as the replacement for the agy / antigravity-ls seats, so its systemd unit will be started with these env vars by home-manager like every sibling proxy. The failure taxonomy is the worst available per value: a typo'd port either kills the unit with a stack that doesn't say which variable is wrong (triage starts from Node internals, not the config), or — worse — the unit stays up on a random or hex-decoded port while `endpoint.json` advertises a dial-nothing address, so the seat looks alive and every client fails. A typo'd timeout is worse still: the service passes a health check, then converts every real request into a 502 that blames the upstream transport. The fix already exists in-repo and is imported by all ten sibling entry points; this file just never got it.

## Dedup

#2821 covers this file's non-object JSON body; #2822 its `tool_choice` flattening — neither touches env parsing. #2786 is the same bare-`Number()` timeout pattern in `opencode-route-proxy` only; #2758 is pm-dispatch's port/hosts. #483 built `proxy-port.mjs` for the other proxies, before this file existed. No open issue covers `ANTIGRAVITY_DIRECT_PORT` / `ANTIGRAVITY_DIRECT_TIMEOUT_MS`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ANTIGRAVITY_DIRECT_PORT` is parsed through `parseProxyPort` from `bin/proxy-port.mjs` (the sibling import every other `bin/*` proxy uses), so a non-decimal, fractional, hex, zero, or out-of-range value exits at startup with the variable name and value in the message and no stack; the default stays 18751.
- [ ] `ANTIGRAVITY_DIRECT_TIMEOUT_MS` is validated at startup with the same strictness shape (decimal integer within a stated positive range that fits a Node timer, i.e. ≤ 2^31−1): an invalid value fails startup naming the variable and value, instead of starting healthy and 502-ing every request or overflowing silently.
- [ ] `endpoint.json` is only ever written with the actually-bound, validated port.
- [ ] Tests in the existing `bin/*.test.mjs` node-test style (extend `bin/antigravity-direct.test.mjs` from #2821 if it exists, else create it) cover: `abc`, `18941abc`, `18941.9`, `0`, `99999`, `0x4a35` ports rejected at startup; timeout `abc`, `-5000`, `3000000000` rejected at startup; valid port + `300` timeout control still serves and times a hanging upstream out at ~300 ms.
- [ ] Well-formed default startup (no env overrides) is byte-for-byte unchanged.

# antigravity-direct: a specific-function `tool_choice` is flattened to `functionCallingConfig: ANY` — the function the client required is never pinned, and any declared function may be called instead

**Repo:** developing-today/code · **Main:** `df9381ff` · **File:** `bin/antigravity-direct.mjs:355-357` (landed today in `b0058ec7`)

## Summary

OpenAI's Chat Completions API lets a caller force one specific function: `tool_choice: { "type": "function", "function": { "name": "get_weather" } }`. `buildV1Request` translates `tool_choice` to the Cloud Code / Gemini `functionCallingConfig` like this:

```js
if (body.tool_choice) {
  const mode = body.tool_choice === 'none' ? 'NONE' : body.tool_choice === 'auto' ? 'AUTO' : 'ANY';
  request.toolConfig = { functionCallingConfig: { mode } };
}
```

Every non-`none`/`auto` value — including the specific-function object — becomes bare `ANY`, and the `allowedFunctionNames` field that `functionCallingConfig` provides for exactly this case is never set. `ANY` means "must call **some** declared function", not "must call **this** function": a client that required `get_weather` can be answered with a call to any other declared function (in the probe: `send_email`).

The string forms are fine (`"none"` → `NONE`, `"auto"` → `AUTO`, `"required"` → `ANY` is the correct semantic). Only the object form loses information.

## Evidence (verified this run, real module)

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-antigrav-body/`; `bin/antigravity-direct.mjs` md5 `de11cfa24df8200d66fd788422667ef8` identical on sandbox main `df9381ff` and the laptop; stub `secret-tool` + stub upstream recording every payload — no real keyring read, no real Google call). Sent:

```json
{
  "model": "gemini-3.8-flash",
  "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": "weather?" }],
  "tools": [
    { "type": "function", "function": { "name": "get_weather", "parameters": { "type": "object", "properties": {} } } },
    { "type": "function", "function": { "name": "send_email",  "parameters": { "type": "object", "properties": {} } } }
  ],
  "tool_choice": { "type": "function", "function": { "name": "get_weather" } }
}
```

The recorded upstream `streamGenerateContent` payload carried both declarations but:

```json
"toolConfig": { "functionCallingConfig": { "mode": "ANY" } }
```

— no `allowedFunctionNames`, nothing naming `get_weather`. The response to the client was a normal HTTP 200, so the downgrade is silent.

## Why it matters

Callers use a specific-function `tool_choice` as a control-flow guarantee (structured extraction, a router that must invoke exactly one named tool, a safety gate that must not fire side-effecting tools). Through this door the guarantee silently degrades to "some function": the model may invoke a different — possibly side-effecting — declared function, and the client, which never opted into that, will execute it under the assumption its choice was honoured. The fleet's own pattern already preserves the choice end-to-end: `bin/muse-proxy.mjs:1161-1164` maps the object form through (`{type:'function', name}`), pinned by `bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs:598,648`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A specific-function `tool_choice` (`{type:"function", function:{name:"X"}}`) produces an upstream `functionCallingConfig` that restricts calling to `X` (e.g. `mode: "ANY"` with `allowedFunctionNames: ["X"]` — triage pins the exact upstream shape), where `X` is one of the declared functions.
- [ ] String forms are unchanged: `"none"` → `NONE`, `"auto"` → `AUTO`, `"required"` → `ANY` (no allowed list).
- [ ] A `tool_choice` naming a function that was not declared does not silently widen to unrestricted `ANY` — it is rejected with a 400 or handled by an explicit, documented fallback (triage pins which).
- [ ] Regression tests in a new `bin/antigravity-direct.test.mjs` (stub-upstream payload recording, in the style of `bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs:598`) cover the specific-function case and the three string forms; requests without `tool_choice` send no `toolConfig`, as today.

Dedup notes: searched open + closed issues this run for `tool_choice` / `functionCallingConfig` / `allowedFunctionNames` against antigravity — no hit. Distinct from #2821 (same file, request-body shape guard; this is a translation-fidelity bug on a well-formed object body).

body:
## Problem

The match-result attestation design (#2037, doc PR #2805) rests on move evidence being **player-signed**: a witness replays both players' signed move logs, and a rewritten move history is supposed to collapse via the event store's fork proofs. Codex review of PR #2805 (2026-10-30) found that the world/game path does not produce player-signed move chains today:

- `pkgs/id/src/world/mod.rs` — `WorldEvent` carries only a host sequence, a server-assigned participant ID, and a payload. No signature, no chain link; it is "committed by the world authority".
- `pkgs/id/src/world/actor.rs` — game inputs are persisted as `JournalEntry::Committed` without signing through `pkgs/id/src/chain.rs`.
- The tic-tac-toe example (the attestation PoC's target, #2248) uses this world path.

So the signed chains that exist in the event store (`chain.rs`: canonical encoding, `verify_strict`, per-author sequence/backlink chains; fork proofs in `event_store/ingest.rs`) are not what game moves currently are. Without this layer, witness adjudication and equivocation guarantees in the attestation design have nothing to stand on for world-path games.

## Scope

Design + build (or explicitly scope into the #2039 synthesis, with the decision recorded there):

- Capture each player's game input as a player-signed chained event (author key, per-author sequence/backlink per `chain.rs`), at the world input seam (actor `WorldCommand::Input` path) or as a signed log the world journal references.
- Integrate the signed capture with the event store so fork/equivocation on a move chain produces the existing fork-proof behavior.
- Keep the host journal working as today (this is an evidence layer, not a rewrite of world execution); the world authority's `WorldEvent` stream and the players' signed input chains must be cross-referenceable (sequence/frontier links both ways).

## Acceptance criteria

- A tic-tac-toe game played through the world path yields two player-signed input chains, verifiable with `chain.rs` verification, whose replay reproduces the journal's `WorldEvent` sequence.
- Tampering with a recorded move after the fact is detectable (signature/chain failure), and producing two versions of a move at one sequence yields a fork proof under existing ingest rules.
- The attestation objects in the #2037 design can cite these chains' frontiers as their evidence base without further capture work.

## Context

- Origin: #2037 investigation (wave 2, queue task 3921), Codex P2 finding on PR #2805, verified against `main` c90fcbc7 on 2026-10-30.
- Related: #2248 (attestation PoC — depends on or must explicitly scope around this), #2266 (signed turns for playable board posts — a different surface, share learnings), #2039 (synthesis — this is a named prerequisite input).
- Program rule: this is a permanent-feature prerequisite, so it gets its own review round — it is not folded silently into the PoC.

body:
## Summary

`scripts/sync_research_workflow.py` parses three JSON documents with `json.loads` and then uses the results as dicts with no shape validation: the target's upstream manifest (`.agents/research-workflow.upstream.json`), and the source/target repository profiles (`.agents/research-workflow.json`). A document that is **syntactically valid JSON but the wrong shape** — a top-level array, a `files` value that is a list or string, a numeric `workflow_docs`, a non-string `lifecycle_skills` element — raises `TypeError`/`AttributeError`, which `main()` does not catch (it catches only `ValueError, OSError, KeyError, subprocess.CalledProcessError` at :173). The tool therefore dies with a raw traceback naming Python internals instead of its own contract: a one-line diagnostic on stderr and exit 1.

One shape is actively misleading rather than crashing: a **string** `lifecycle_skills` is iterated character by character, so the tool reports `missing source directory: .agents/skills/r` — blaming a directory that was never configured.

## Evidence (main `c90fcbc7`, script md5 `319a3caa2fdbf117b4ba2a3867dfdf1d`, identical in the sandbox clone and the laptop primary)

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-syncshape/probe.py`, real module, fixture repos built exactly like `scripts/tests/test_sync_research_workflow.py`):

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| control: valid fixture, `--check` after a `--write` | returns cleanly |
| manifest with a JSON **syntax** error | `JSONDecodeError` (a `ValueError`) — caught by `main`, clean error + exit 1 ✅ |
| manifest = `[]` (top-level array) | `TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not str` — **not caught** |
| manifest = `{"files": ["x"]}` | `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'keys'` (:112) — **not caught** |
| manifest = `{"files": "abc"}` | `AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'keys'` — **not caught** |
| source profile = `[]` | `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'` (:46) — **not caught** |
| source profile `workflow_docs: 123` | `TypeError: argument should be a str or an os.PathLike… not 'int'` (:47) — **not caught** |
| source profile `lifecycle_skills: [123]` | `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for /: 'PosixPath' and 'int'` — **not caught** |
| source profile `lifecycle_skills: "research-workflow"` (string) | misleading `ValueError: missing source directory: .agents/skills/r` (iterates the string's characters) |

Relevant code: profiles loaded at `scripts/sync_research_workflow.py:44-47`; manifest loaded at :96-99 and used as `old["files"].get(...)` / `old["files"].keys()` at :109, :112, :122; the catch tuple at :173 omits `TypeError` and `AttributeError`.

## Why it matters

This script is the guard that keeps the mirrored research-workflow copy honest: it is supposed to refuse bad states with a readable reason ("local edits need reconciliation", "workflow mirror differs"). The manifest and profiles are exactly the files that get hand-edited, truncated by a bad merge, or regenerated by another tool — the moment the guard is most needed is the moment its input is malformed. Today that moment produces a traceback that points at `PosixPath` arithmetic instead of at the offending file and field, and the string-`lifecycle_skills` case sends the operator hunting for a directory named `r`. Sibling tool `scripts/research_workflow.py` already validates its profile shapes with `isinstance` checks (`profile()` at :77-102); the sync tool does not.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A parseable-but-wrong-shaped manifest or profile (top level not an object; `files` not an object of string digests; `workflow_docs` not a string; `lifecycle_skills` not a list of strings) fails with a one-line diagnostic naming the file and the offending field, on stderr, exit 1 — no traceback.
- [ ] A string `lifecycle_skills` is rejected as a shape error, never iterated as characters.
- [ ] Valid fixtures behave exactly as before: the four existing tests in `scripts/tests/test_sync_research_workflow.py` still pass.
- [ ] New tests cover at least: top-level-array manifest, non-object `files`, non-object profile, and string `lifecycle_skills`.
- [ ] Scope is validation at the load sites only — no change to the sync/check semantics, the manifest format, or the local-edit protection rules.

body:
## Summary

The dogfood plugin copy has drifted from the canonical mcpx plugin again — the exact failure #314 added a CI guard for — and because that guard sits inside the push-only `basic: test` job, the drift merged silently and now fails that job on main, skipping the entire mcpx Go test suite and plugin tests on every main push.

## Evidence (main `da42bfe7`, verified this run)

`diff -r pkgs/mcpx/plugin/opencode/mcpx .opencode/plugin/mcpx` exits 1:

1. `pkgs/mcpx/plugin/opencode/mcpx/instructions.test.ts` exists **only** in the pkgs copy (added in `43ab3040`, #1938, 2026-10-30 02:25 CDT) — never copied to `.opencode/plugin/mcpx/`.
2. `ops.gen.ts` differs: the pkgs copy gained the `adapters_add` / `adapters_remove` operations (table entries at pkgs lines 25–47, client methods `adaptersAdd`/`adaptersRemove` at lines 886–902) when it was regenerated in `2aec81c0` (#2565, 2026-10-30 04:36 CDT). The `.opencode` copy this repo's own opencode sessions load has neither — a session here cannot call the daemon's live adapter add/remove endpoints through the typed client.

`mcpx-session.ts` copies are identical (diff exits 0).

## The guard is running — too late, and it takes the test suite down with it

`.github/workflows/mcpx.yml`, job `test` ("basic: test"):

- The sync check is step 3 of that job, and the job is gated `if: github.event_name == 'push'`. Pull requests never run it (the PR-triggered jobs are `stress-pr` and `vendorhash-repair`, neither of which diffs the copies), so drift introduced by a PR is invisible until after merge.
- On push it now fails before anything else runs: e.g. run `41067448387` (push, 2026-10-30T13:56Z) — step 3 "Check the dogfood plugin copy is in sync" = failure; setup-go, `go mod tidy -diff`, the full `go test ./...` suite and the plugin bun tests all **skipped**. Every push run of this workflow today (11:44Z, 12:13Z, 12:15Z, 12:47Z, 12:59Z, 13:56Z) concluded failure — main currently gets no mcpx test coverage from this job at all.

This is #314 recurring: that fix synced the copies and added this guard precisely because "the generation guard inside pkgs/mcpx only compares the pkgs copy" — but placing the new guard in a push-only job left the pre-merge hole open.

## Why it matters

- The repo's own opencode sessions load a stale plugin client missing two daemon operations that shipped today.
- Main's mcpx CI is red for a non-code reason and, worse, the failure pre-empts the actual test suite — regressions in mcpx on main are currently undetectable by this workflow.
- Each future regeneration of `ops.gen.ts` (or plugin test addition) will re-drift the copy the same way until the check runs pre-merge.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `.opencode/plugin/mcpx/` is byte-identical to `pkgs/mcpx/plugin/opencode/mcpx/` again (`diff -r` exits 0), including `ops.gen.ts` (with `adapters_add`/`adapters_remove`) and `instructions.test.ts`; `mcpx-session.ts` copies remain identical.
- [ ] The sync check runs on pull requests that touch `pkgs/mcpx/**` or `.opencode/plugin/**` (e.g. its own lightweight job, or a step in a PR-triggered job), so drift fails the PR that introduces it instead of main after merge.
- [ ] A push run of `mcpx.yml` on main completes the `basic: test` job past the sync step — the Go test suite and plugin bun tests actually execute.
- [ ] Deliberately drifting one file in a test PR (or an equivalent local demonstration) makes the new PR check fail with the diff shown.

## Notes

- Cross-repo: mcpx also stands alone in dezren39/nix, which has no repo-root `.opencode` copy — the guard must stay in this repo's workflow, not move into `pkgs/mcpx` (per #314's reasoning). No nix-side change is owed.
- Related: #314 (original sync + guard), #2565 (adapters regeneration that drifted the ops table), #1938 (instructions test added to the pkgs copy only), #1978 (plugin bun tests step that is currently being skipped along with the rest of the job).

body:
# Own keys only — a plain object is not a map for untrusted keys

**Design doc:** `files/designs/code-own-key-lookups.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace (design-architect pass 21, 2026-10-30). Audited against origin/main `da42bfe7`.

## The problem in one paragraph

Five times in two days the fleet has found the same bug in five files: a plain object literal used as a lookup table for a key that comes from outside the process. A plain-object index walks the prototype chain, so `constructor`, `__proto__`, `toString`, `hasOwnProperty`, `valueOf` "hit" the table with inherited members — and every site's miss handling (`?? null`, `=== undefined`, a truthiness branch) is written for `undefined` and never fires. The one fixed instance, #2787 (id/web, closed today, commit 9ee4a5dd), states the rule this design generalises; the four open instances were each filed and probed individually and will keep recurring individually without it.

## The rule

> A plain object is never a map for an externally-controlled key. Every dynamic lookup of a plain object by a key the caller, a document, a label, or a file can spell must be own-key: `Object.hasOwn(table, key)` at the read site (the #2787 / `pkgs/id/web/src/shell-contract.ts:107` idiom). A `Map`, or `Object.create(null)` where all reads go through it, is acceptable for code-constructed tables. Objects from `JSON.parse` always carry `Object.prototype`, so for them the `Object.hasOwn` guard is the only conforming form.

Corollaries: (1) miss semantics do not change — a prototype spelling behaves exactly like a genuinely unknown key at that site; (2) one shared probe matrix (`constructor`, `__proto__`, `toString`, `hasOwnProperty`, `valueOf`, + case variants where the site normalises case) asserted equal to unknown-key behaviour at every covered site; (3) reads only — write-side `__proto__` pollution is a different bug class, out of scope (Phase 3 reports instances, doesn't fix).

## The four open instances

- **#2790** sync-models: family validation passes for `constructor`; the allowed set comes out empty and the sync's removal pass wipes every model of that provider. `__proto__` crashes on a regex built from `"[object Object]"`. The destructive instance.
- **#2781** aggregator `quota-gather-map.ts:99/:263` — a window named `constructor`/`__proto__` gets a fabricated `windowSeconds`; a Turso window with such a name fabricates a snapshot record with no unit/limit.
- **#2734** aggregator `weights.ts:37` — `effort/constructor` resolves to the `Object` constructor as an item's weight, breaking the module's unsized contract and string-poisoning weighted summaries.
- **#2757** pm-dispatch `validate.ts:28` — priority `"constructor"` returns the `Object` constructor function instead of the documented 400; `JSON.stringify` then silently drops it at enqueue.

Not #2576's scope: that design validates document *contents* (dates/percents/shapes); lookup semantics are a different mechanism with a different fix — settled in the design doc.

## Phases (origins adopted as phases — no parallel issues)

- **Phase 1 = #2790** — own-key family validation in sync-models; lands first, it is the only instance that destroys data.
- **Phase 2 = #2734 + #2781** — own-key guards in aggregator `weights.ts` + `quota-gather-map.ts`, shared probe matrix as tests.
- **Phase 3 = #2757 + closing audit** — own-key guard in `resolvePriority`, then the inventory sweep over the repo's TS/JS/mjs (vendored assets excluded): every plain-object table indexed by a dynamic key dispositioned as covered / external-key (filed under this design) / internal-only (named in closing evidence). Phase 3 closes this issue with the audit evidence.

Alternatives, risks, and open questions (lint enforcement, write-side pollution as a future design, Go maps unaffected) are in the design doc.

agent-note:v1 — filed by design-architect pass 21 (2026-10-30). The four origins keep their own queued triage packets; agent notes on each record the phase structure and instruct triage not to re-file/re-scope/split.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Phase 1 (#2790, sync-models): family validation is own-key — `constructor`/`__proto__`/`toString` spellings behave exactly like an unknown family, and no provider's models are wiped by a prototype spelling.
- [ ] Phase 2 (#2734 + #2781, aggregator): own-key guards in `weights.ts` and `quota-gather-map.ts`, with the shared probe matrix (constructor, __proto__, toString, hasOwnProperty, valueOf, plus case variants where a site normalises case) asserted equal to unknown-key behaviour.
- [ ] Phase 3 (#2757 + closing audit): own-key guard in pm-dispatch `resolvePriority`, plus the repo inventory sweep — every plain-object table indexed by a dynamic key dispositioned as covered / external-key (filed under this design) / internal-only, named in the closing evidence.
- [ ] This issue closes only with the Phase 3 audit evidence attached; miss semantics at every covered site are unchanged for genuinely unknown keys.

title: sync-models(policy): family validation is a prototype lookup — 'constructor'/'toString' pass and wipe a provider's models, group-less patterns crash unnamed
