body:
## Problem

`bin/sync-models.mjs`'s policy validation does not actually validate two things it is there to validate, and the failure modes are a silent provider wipe and an unnamed crash.

### 1. Family-name validation is a plain-object lookup — prototype names pass

`loadPolicy` (bin/sync-models.mjs:180-192, check at :185):

```js
if (!policy.families?.[family]) {
  throw new Error(`sync-models.policy.json: ${name} keeps unknown family "${family}"`);
}
```

`policy.families[family]` walks the prototype chain. A `keep` entry of `constructor`, `toString`, or `hasOwnProperty` finds an inherited member (truthy), so validation passes for a family that does not exist in the policy. `allowedModelIds` (:202-218) then builds `new RegExp(policy.families[family])` from that inherited value:

- `constructor` / `toString` / `hasOwnProperty`: the resulting regex (the function's source text) matches no real model id, so the allowed set is **empty**. The sync's removal pass (:503-515) treats an empty allowed set as authoritative: it removes **every** existing model of that provider ("not in its policy") and adds none. One typo'd `keep` entry that happens to be an `Object.prototype` member name silently wipes a provider's model list on the next sync, instead of failing at startup like a real typo does.
- `__proto__`: `policy.families['__proto__']` is `Object.prototype`; `new RegExp(Object.prototype)` stringifies to the character-class pattern `[object Object]`, which matches most model ids — and then `match[1]` is `undefined` (see below), crashing the sync.

A genuinely unknown family (`gemini-flah`) correctly throws the naming error above, so the validator's intent is clear — it just doesn't own-key check.

### 2. A family pattern with no participating capture group crashes unnamed

`allowedModelIds` (:208-210):

```js
const match = id.match(new RegExp(policy.families[family]));
if (!match) continue;
const version = match[1].replace(/-/g, '.').split('.').map(Number);
```

Nothing checks that the family's pattern captures a version in group 1. A pattern with no capture group (`^gemini-\d+-flash$`), or one whose group is optional and does not participate for a matching id (`^gemini-(\d+)?flash$` vs `gemini-flash`), yields `match[1] === undefined` and the sync dies with:

```
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'replace')
```

— naming neither the family, the provider, nor the model id.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-syncpolicy/probe.mjs`), using the same verbatim source-extraction method as `bin/sync-models.test.mjs` (#704) against the real `bin/sync-models.mjs` (md5 `89c914c87a4b4eb444795ee00e4118a9`, identical on sandbox main `da42bfe7` and the laptop clone):

```
CONTROL known family: [ 'gemini-3-flash' ]
CASE keep=constructor:    loadPolicy PASSED (no throw) | allowed=[]
CASE keep=__proto__:      loadPolicy PASSED (no throw) | allowedModelIds THREW: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'replace')
CASE keep=toString:       loadPolicy PASSED (no throw) | allowed=[]
CASE keep=hasOwnProperty: loadPolicy PASSED (no throw) | allowed=[]
CASE keep=gemini-flah (typo): loadPolicy threw: sync-models.policy.json: p keeps unknown family "gemini-flah"
CASE groupless regex THREW: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'replace')
CASE optional group THREW:  TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'replace')
```

The shipped `bin/sync-models.policy.json` is not affected today (all five families are own keys with a participating group 1) — this is about the next policy edit landing wrong.

## Why it matters

The policy file is hand-edited (families are added as new model lines appear). The validator exists precisely to catch a bad edit at startup with the provider and family named. Two classes of bad edit currently bypass it: one converts the sync into a provider-wiping run, the other into a stack trace with no pointer to the offending entry.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `loadPolicy` rejects a `keep` entry that is not an **own** key of `policy.families` (e.g. via `Object.hasOwn`), so `constructor`, `__proto__`, `toString`, `hasOwnProperty` produce the same named "keeps unknown family" error as any other typo.
- [ ] A family pattern that can match without a participating capture group 1 is rejected at load time (named family + provider), or `allowedModelIds` treats a match with no group 1 as a non-match / named error — never an unnamed `TypeError` from `match[1].replace`.
- [ ] Tests in `bin/sync-models.test.mjs` style cover: prototype-named keep entries, a group-less family pattern, and an optional-group pattern against a non-participating id; the shipped policy still loads and the known-family control still selects the newest version.
- [ ] No behavior change for the current shipped policy.

title: muse-proxy(direct): a failed upstream Responses body is reported as a successful chat completion — non-streaming translator never checks status, partial output masks the failure

body:
## Problem

muse-proxy's direct (minted-key Responses) path reports a failed upstream generation as a successful chat completion on the non-streaming door. The Responses API signals generation failure in the response body (`status: "failed"` with an `error` object, HTTP 200) — the streaming translator handles the equivalent event, the non-streaming translator never looks at `status` at all.

- `responsesToChatCompletion` (bin/muse-proxy.mjs:1225-1242, main `dccfec44`) converts any parsed body into a chat completion: `extractResponsesOutput` (:1178) reads only `output`, and `finishReasonFromResponses` (:1198-1206) checks only tool calls and `incomplete` + `max_output_tokens`. `status: "failed"` and `respBody.error` are never read.
- The non-streaming branch of `tryDirectChat` (:1386-1391) writes the result as HTTP 200 unconditionally once the body parses.
- The streaming translator in the same file *does* handle failure: `response.failed` → an SSE error frame (:1303-1305), and `error` events likewise (:1306-1308). The two doors disagree about the same upstream outcome.
- An `incomplete` body whose reason is not `max_output_tokens` (e.g. `content_filter`) also falls through to `finish_reason: "stop"`, presenting a truncated answer as complete.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `dccfec44`)

Laptop probe at `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-directfailed/` running the real `bin/muse-proxy.mjs` (md5 `86f6d34295ef7488760535e242f3f575`, identical to main) against a stub Meta API (key exchange + `/v1/responses`) and stub auth, warm path off:

- Control — upstream `{status: "completed", output: [text "Hello direct"]}` → HTTP 200, content `Hello direct`, `finish_reason: "stop"` ✓
- Upstream `{status: "failed", error: {code: "server_error", message: "upstream exploded"}, output: []}` → **HTTP 200, content `""`, `finish_reason: "stop"`, no error anywhere** — the upstream error message is dropped entirely.
- Upstream `{status: "failed", error: …, output: [text "half an answer"]}` → **HTTP 200, content `half an answer`, `finish_reason: "stop"`** — the failure is masked whenever partial output exists.
- Upstream `{status: "incomplete", incomplete_details: {reason: "content_filter"}, output: [text "partial"]}` → HTTP 200, content `partial`, `finish_reason: "stop"` — a filtered/truncated answer presented as complete.

## Why it matters

Direct mode is the default door for the muse-direct provider seats (#2753, live since 2026-10-30). A client on the non-streaming door cannot distinguish "the model answered with empty text" from "the generation failed": it receives a well-formed successful completion, retries nothing, and logs nothing — the upstream `error.message` that would explain the failure is discarded. This is the same failure-masking shape the fleet already fixed on the exec door (#672) and the streaming door (#670), arriving with the new direct door's non-streaming half. Failure with partial output is the worst case: truncated text is consumed downstream as a complete answer.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A non-streaming direct response whose body has `status: "failed"` surfaces an error to the chat client (an error body with the upstream `error.message`, with a non-200 status or the door's established error shape) instead of a 200 completion with `finish_reason: "stop"` — whether or not partial output is present.
- [ ] A body with `status: "incomplete"` and a reason other than `max_output_tokens` does not report `finish_reason: "stop"` (mapped distinctly or surfaced as an error — triage pins which).
- [ ] `status: "completed"` and `incomplete` + `max_output_tokens` → `length` behavior are unchanged.
- [ ] Regression tests in `bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs` (stub Meta API pattern) pin the failed-empty, failed-partial, and incomplete-non-token cases, plus the completed control.

## Dedup

- Searched open+closed for the direct translator / `responsesToChatCompletion` / `incomplete_details`: no filing covers it. #2753 (CLOSED) is the direct-mode feature itself.
- #672/#676/#678 (CLOSED) are the same masking pattern on the exec/other-proxy doors, not this translator. #2770 (OPEN) is the direct path's tool-name alias inverse — different mechanism, same file. #2159 (OPEN) is the exec door's missing turn deadline.

title: update-nixpkgs-inputs: owner match is an unanchored prefix regex — lookalike owners (NixOS2, nixos-fork) are updated as NixOS/nixpkgs, while NIXOS/NiXoS spellings are silently skipped

labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

body:
## Summary

`scripts/update-nixpkgs-inputs.py` decides which flake inputs are "NixOS/nixpkgs inputs" — the set it then runs `nix flake update` on — with an owner check that is neither the exact match nor the case-insensitive match its own docstring promises. It misses real NixOS spellings and, worse, claims inputs that belong to other owners.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `7363b499`)

- `scripts/update-nixpkgs-inputs.py:100`, in `discover_inputs` (defined :79):

  ```python
  if not re.match(r"[Nn]ix[Oo][Ss]", original.get("owner", "")):
      continue
  ```

  `re.match` anchors at the start only, and the character classes cover only two case spellings per letter. The docstring (:83-92) says the match is `original.owner ~= NixOS (case-insensitive)`. The neighbouring checks show the intended style: `type` is compared with `.lower() != "github"` (:97) and `repo` with exact `!= "nixpkgs"` (:103).
- Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-nixpkgsowner/`, the real script, md5 `f35ee1ac721a8519333a4de3dae37498` — byte-identical to main) against synthetic `flake.lock` data, one input per case, `repo="nixpkgs"`:

  | owner | discovered | documented expectation |
  |---|---|---|
  | `NixOS`, `nixos`, `Nixos` | yes | yes |
  | `NIXOS`, `NiXoS`, `nIxOs` | **no** | yes (case-insensitive) |
  | `NixOS2`, `nixos-fork`, `NixOSx`, `nixoss` | **yes** | no (not the NixOS owner) |
  | `evilNixOS`, `someuser` | no | no |
  | control: `NixOS` / repo `home-manager` | no | no |

- Today's `flake.lock` is not affected: all four nixpkgs inputs carry owner exactly `NixOS` (checked this run). The bug is latent — it fires the day a lock gains a differently-cased NixOS spelling or an owner whose name merely starts with a NixOS-like prefix (e.g. a fork org), both realistic additions to a flake this size.

## Why it matters

This script is the fleet's nixpkgs-update tool (wrapped by `scripts/update-nixpkgs-inputs.sh`; the scheduled nixpkgs updates are built on it). Its one job is to update exactly the NixOS/nixpkgs pins:

- A false positive means a "NixOS/nixpkgs inputs" run silently runs `nix flake update` on someone else's `nixpkgs` fork input and reports it in the NixOS summary — an unreviewed pin bump to a third-party fork under a trusted banner.
- A false negative means a real NixOS input is silently skipped: the run reports success while a pin stays stale.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The owner test is an exact, case-insensitive comparison (`owner.lower() == "nixos"` or an anchored full match): every case spelling of `NixOS` matches; `NixOS2`, `nixos-fork`, `NixOSx`, `nixoss` and any other prefix/superstring owner do not.
- [ ] A test (under `scripts/tests/`, alongside the existing script tests) pins both directions: the case table above, plus the existing controls (non-`nixpkgs` repo excluded, non-string/follows inputs skipped, ref filtering unchanged).
- [ ] No behaviour change for the current `flake.lock`: the same four inputs (`nixpkgs-25`, `nixpkgs-master`, `nixpkgs-stable`, `nixpkgs-unstable`) are discovered.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `update-nixpkgs-inputs`, `discover_inputs`, and owner/regex terms this run: no filing covers the owner match. Adjacent: open #603 asks for automated tests of this script's exit-code contract — it does not cover `discover_inputs` matching, and the test criterion above complements it.

title: pm-dispatch(config): DISPATCH_PORT / DISPATCH_HOSTS are never validated — port 0 silently binds a random port, a typo crashes with a Bun RangeError naming neither variable, hex/scientific spellings become other ports, and an all-separator DISPATCH_HOSTS exits 0 serving nothing

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

labels.name: app/pm-stack
labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Problem

`pm-dispatch`: `DISPATCH_PORT` and `DISPATCH_HOSTS` are never validated — the last pm-stack service with this gap (the aggregator's version is #2161, the projector's is #2172; dispatch was never filed).

`pm-stack/dispatch/src/config.ts:87-91` (main `58635f8d`):

```ts
port: Number(s(env.DISPATCH_PORT, "4879")),
hosts: s(env.DISPATCH_HOSTS, "127.0.0.1")
  .split(",")
  .map((h) => h.trim())
  .filter(Boolean),
```

and `src/server.ts:412-416` consumes both verbatim:

```ts
const servers = cfg.hosts.map((hostname) =>
  Bun.serve({ hostname, port: cfg.port, fetch: handler }),
);
```

## Verified (this run, real module)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-dispatchcfg/`, `config.ts` copied verbatim from main, md5 `0bfdc1a7a2e3cce4ab4ca900d6e586a9`, bun 1.4.2):

| env | `loadConfig` result | consequence at `Bun.serve` |
|---|---|---|
| (unset) | port `4879`, hosts `["127.0.0.1"]` ✓ | normal |
| `DISPATCH_PORT=abc` | port `NaN` | throws `The value of "options.port" is out of range… Received NaN` — names neither `DISPATCH_PORT` nor the offending value's source |
| `DISPATCH_PORT=4879.5` | port `4879.5` | same RangeError (`Received 4879.5`) |
| `DISPATCH_PORT=0` | port `0` | Bun binds a **random** port — the service is up somewhere nobody (including `install.sh`'s `/health` poll on `${DISPATCH_PORT:-4879}` and the aggregator's topology row, port 4879) is looking |
| `DISPATCH_PORT=0x1234` / `1e4` / `-1` / `99999` | `4660` / `10000` / `-1` / `99999` | hex and scientific spellings silently become *different ports*; negative/oversize throw the same opaque RangeError |
| `DISPATCH_HOSTS=","` or `" , ,"` | hosts `[]` | `server.ts` maps over an empty array: **zero servers are created, nothing is logged, and the process exits 0 serving nothing** — a systemd unit that "started" with no listener |

`install.sh:33,110` renders whatever `DISPATCH_PORT` it is given straight into the service env file with no check either, so the typo survives the deploy path and only surfaces as the opaque Bun error (or, for `0`/hex spellings, as a healthy-looking service on the wrong port whose `/health` version check polls the *intended* port and fails for an unrelated-looking reason).

## Why it matters

Dispatch is the fleet's authenticated intake for sessions and queue tasks (GitHub Actions workflows call it). A one-character env typo today produces one of: a crash loop with an error that doesn't name the variable, a service silently listening on a random/different port while health checks poll the configured one, or a clean exit-0 with no listener at all. All three burn operator time on a config error that a boot-time check could state in one line. #2161/#2172 set the house pattern for the sibling services; dispatch is the remaining hole.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `loadConfig` (or an explicit boot check in `server.ts`) rejects a `DISPATCH_PORT` that is not a decimal integer in 1–65535, with an error that names `DISPATCH_PORT` and the offending value; `0` is rejected too (a random port is never the intent for a service other components address by number).
- [ ] A `DISPATCH_HOSTS` that parses to zero hosts is rejected at boot with an error naming `DISPATCH_HOSTS`, instead of exiting 0 with no servers.
- [ ] Tests in `pm-stack/dispatch/test/config.test.ts`: `abc`, `4879.5`, `0`, `-1`, `99999`, `0x1234` rejected; unset/`4879` and a normal host list unchanged.
- [ ] (Optional, same shape as the fix) `install.sh` validates its rendered `PORT` before writing the env file.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed for `DISPATCH_PORT` / `DISPATCH_HOSTS` validation: no filing. #2161 covers the aggregator's `PM_AGG_PORT`/`PM_AGG_HOSTS` and #2172 the projector's `PORT` — same failure class, different services, each filed separately; this is the dispatch sibling, not a duplicate.

## Problem

`Question.carriesMultiSelect` (pkgs/mcpx/internal/mcpserver/conn.go:316-344, landed today in #2719 for #2078) decides whether an elicitation question must be withheld from a pre-2025-11-25 host by unmarshalling the whole `requestedSchema` into one strict typed struct — every property's `type` as a `string` and every property's `items` as a JSON object. If **any** property in the schema does not fit that struct, the unmarshal fails, the function returns `false` for the entire question, and `Sendable` (conn.go:538-547) offers the question — multi-select included — to the old host verbatim. That is exactly the shape #2078 promised to refuse whole: a strict old host rejects the request, or answers a multi-select in a form the upstream rejects.

One nonconforming sibling property disables detection for every other property; the detector's own property can also defeat it directly.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `72545cb9`)

- conn.go:320-327 — the typed struct: `Type string`, `Items map[string]json.RawMessage`; any mismatch (a union type, a boolean `items` schema) makes `json.Unmarshal` return an error, and the error path is `return false` — "no multi-select anywhere".
- Probe on the laptop (~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-multiselect/, a verbatim copy of pkgs/mcpx at this main — conn.go md5 `72e199e66f1838bbf2b36ca12c3a5a8f` both sides) with a test in package `mcpserver_test` calling the real `Question.Sendable` for a 2025-06-18 peer:
  - control, plain multi-select (`type:"array"`, `items.enum`) → `Sendable=false` (withheld, correct)
  - control, plain single-select → `Sendable=true` (correct)
  - multi-select **plus a sibling** `{"type":["string","null"]}` (nullable union type) → `Sendable=true` — LEAK
  - multi-select **plus a sibling** with `"items":true` (boolean schema) → `Sendable=true` — LEAK
  - the multi-select property itself with `"type":["array","null"]` → `Sendable=true` — LEAK
- The loose-map style used everywhere else in this file (e.g. `carriesSamplingTools`, conn.go:301-309, and `paramsFor`'s `map[string]any` walk) does not have this failure mode; only the new detector uses a whole-schema typed unmarshal.
- Today's regression tests (enum_downgrade_test.go) cover only schemas whose every property fits the struct, so the leak class is untested.

## Why it matters

The withholding is a correctness gate, not a nicety: #2719's own comment (conn.go:541-546) says a multi-select is "refused whole for an older host, never flattened or downgraded", because the old host cannot express the answer type. A detector that silently turns itself off whenever an unrelated property uses a union type or a boolean subschema — both ordinary JSON Schema spellings an upstream of a different revision can legitimately send — reintroduces the failure #2078 closed, with no error anywhere: the question is simply offered.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `carriesMultiSelect` detects a multi-select property regardless of sibling properties' shapes: detection is per-property and tolerant (e.g. walk `map[string]any` / per-property raw messages), so one property's unmarshal failure cannot mask another's `items.enum`/`items.anyOf`.
- [ ] A multi-select property whose own `type` is a union containing `"array"` (e.g. `["array","null"]`) is detected and withheld from a pre-2025-11-25 host.
- [ ] Regression tests (failing-first, per pkgs/mcpx/internal/AGENTS.md) cover at least: the two controls from enum_downgrade_test.go, a union-typed sibling, a boolean-`items` sibling, and a union-typed multi-select property.
- [ ] Plain single-select and non-elicitation behaviour are unchanged; `go test ./internal/mcpserver/ -count=1` passes on laptop or CI.

body:
## Problem

pm-dispatch's OIDC verification assumes the decoded JWT header and payload are JSON objects (`pm-stack/dispatch/src/auth.ts`, main 732ca26d), but `parseJwt` (`auth.ts:53-67`) accepts any JSON value: `JSON.parse` of the base64url-decoded first segment can be `null`, a number, a string, or an array, and the result is cast straight into `JwtParts.header`/`payload` typed as `Record<string, unknown>`.

`verifyOidcToken` then dereferences it before any check can run:

```ts
if (jwt.header.alg !== "RS256") throw new AuthError("oidc: unexpected alg (want RS256)");  // auth.ts:101
```

For a token whose header decodes to JSON `null`, that line throws a raw `TypeError`, not an `AuthError`. The server's error mapping (`src/server.ts` handler catch) turns `AuthError` into 401 but everything else into **500** — so a malformed credential, the most routine bad input an auth endpoint receives (truncated tokens, non-GitHub JWTs, scanner probes), is answered as a server fault instead of an authentication failure. (The payload segment has the same shape of hole at `auth.ts:129-131`, reachable after a signature passes.)

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe (bun, importing the real `auth.ts` from the laptop primary at main 732ca26d, md5-identical to the sandbox clone; probe at `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-dispatch/` on the laptop), token = `base64url("null") + "." + base64url({iss:…}) + "." + base64url("sig")`:

```
D parseJwt(null header): null
D verify throws: TypeError - null is not an object (evaluating 'jwt.header.alg') | status= undefined
```

An `AuthError` carries `status = 401`; this throw carries none. Control: a well-formed header with an unknown `kid` correctly throws `AuthError` ("signing key not found in JWKS").

## Why it matters

Auth endpoints should fail closed *and* fail classified: a 500 for a bad credential pollutes error monitoring with phantom server faults, can page like an outage, and hides real 500s in the noise. It also leaks an implementation detail (the service 500s on `null` headers but 401s on other bad tokens) to unauthenticated callers probing the endpoint.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `parseJwt` rejects any header/payload segment that does not decode to a plain JSON object (returns null → "malformed JWT" `AuthError`), covering `null`, arrays, and scalar JSON.
- [ ] Every malformed-token input to `verifyOidcToken`/`authenticate` surfaces as `AuthError` (HTTP 401), never a raw `TypeError`/500.
- [ ] Tests pin the null-header, array-payload, and scalar-segment cases alongside the existing auth tests.
- [ ] Existing dispatch tests still pass.

body:
## Problem

In pm-dispatch (`pm-stack/dispatch/src/server.ts`, main 732ca26d), the steps after a session is already launched and its queue task already claimed are not failure-isolated, so a GitHub API hiccup at the very end of a successful launch is reported — and acted on — as a launch failure:

- `launchSession` creates the OpenCode session and sends the prompt (`server.ts:117-123`), registers the worker and PATCHes the task to `status: claimed` with the session id in progress (`server.ts:130-143`).
- The lane-ledger call right after IS guarded: its failure is noted on the task with "launch unaffected" (`server.ts:148-158`).
- But the final GitHub calls are NOT guarded: `github.comment(...)` (`server.ts:161-165`) and `github.addLabels(...)` (`server.ts:166`) throw straight out of `launchSession`. (`GitHubClient.comment`/`addLabels` in `src/github.ts` do fall back from the app route to the `gh` CLI, but a failure of both routes throws `GitHubError`.)

Consequences by caller mode:

- **`wait: true` (default):** `handleSessions` treats any `launchSession` throw as a launch failure, calls `cancelTask` on the task (`server.ts:253`) and returns `502 {task_id, error}`. The OpenCode session, however, was already created and prompted — it keeps running the work, now untracked: its queue task is cancelled, and the caller was told the dispatch failed, inviting a duplicate retry dispatch.
- **`wait: false`:** the async continuation catches the same throw and PATCHes `last_error: "dispatch launch failed: …"` (`server.ts:225-234`) onto a task that is in fact `claimed` with a live, running session — the task record actively misstates the state of the work.

This also contradicts the README contract for `POST /v1/sessions`: "a task is never left `queued` for a session that launched, nor `claimed` without a session id" — the cancel path leaves a launched session with a cancelled task, which is the mirror-image violation.

## Evidence

- Code trace at main 732ca26d (file:line above): prompt is sent BEFORE the claim PATCH, the claim PATCH precedes the unguarded comment/label calls, and both caller paths treat a post-claim throw as launch failure. The guarded `assignLane` block (`server.ts:148-158`) shows the intended pattern for post-launch steps.
- No test covers `launchSession`'s failure ordering: `pm-stack/dispatch/test/` contains only `auth.test.ts`, `packet.test.ts`, `validate.test.ts` — `server.ts`/`queue.ts`/`github.ts` have no tests.

## Why it matters

pm-dispatch is the fleet's authenticated launch intake (merged 2026-10-30, PRs #2652/#2655/#2658). A transient GitHub failure at the last step converts a healthy, running session into a cancelled tracking task + a 502 that invites a duplicate dispatch of the same prompt — exactly the double-booking the service exists to prevent.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A failure in the post-claim issue comment or label calls does NOT cancel the task and does NOT change the success response: the launch still returns 201/`claimed` (wait:true) with the failure surfaced as a warning and/or recorded on the task (e.g. `last_error`/progress note), mirroring the existing `assignLane` guard.
- [ ] In the wait:false path, a post-claim note/label failure is not recorded as "dispatch launch failed" on a claimed task.
- [ ] Cancellation + 502 remains reserved for failures before/at the actual launch and claim (session create, prompt send, claim PATCH).
- [ ] A test (stubbed GitHub client failing on comment/addLabels after a successful claim) pins the behavior for both wait modes.
- [ ] Existing dispatch tests still pass.

title: id(web): TS shell-contract checker never validates the contract document — one bad field type passes silently for every other frame and throws uncaught on its own

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

The TypeScript port of the shell contract checker (`pkgs/id/web/src/shell-contract.ts`) never validates the contract document itself. The Rust original parses the document eagerly — `ShellContract::parse` runs every field of every frame through `Field::try_from` and refuses the whole document, naming `frame.field`, if any field type is unknown. The TS port has no parse/validate entry point at all: consumers `JSON.parse` the document and cast it to `ShellContract` (as `world-contract.test.ts` does), and the only validation is `parseField`, called lazily inside `checkFields` for the fields of the one frame being checked — where it **throws** an uncaught `Error` instead of returning a `Check` result or failing at load.

So a contract document with one bad field type (a typo like `u65` in a future revision) is silently accepted by the TS checker: frames of every other type check normally, and the first frame of the affected type crashes the checker (the throw propagates straight out of `checkClientFrame` / `checkServerFrame`, and out of `Conformance.client()` / `.server()`, which call them without a guard) instead of producing a violation or a load error.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `06be46dd`)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-shellcontract/`, Bun; verbatim `shell-contract.ts` sha256 `02baac39…`, identical to main, plus the real `contract/shell-contract.v1.json`; one field type mutated to `u65` in `client_frames.join.capability` and `server_frames.view.sequence`):

```
baseline join: {"ok":true,"type":"join"}
unrelated chat vs broken contract: {"ok":true,"type":"chat"}
join vs broken THREW: unknown field type `u65`
view vs broken THREW: unknown field type `u65`
```

Code facts:

- TS: `parseField` (`web/src/shell-contract.ts:69`) throws ``unknown field type``; its only caller is `checkFields` (`:165`), per-field, per-frame-check. No exported parse/validate function exists; `ShellContract` is a bare type, so a malformed spec for a frame type that is never checked never surfaces at all.
- TS: `Conformance.client` (`:257`) and `.server` call the checkers unguarded, so the throw escapes the session checker rather than landing in `violations`.
- Rust: `ShellContract::parse` (`src/shell_contract.rs:305`) → `frames()` (`:273`) → `Field::try_from` (`:164`) validates **every** field of **every** client and server frame at load and fails with `frame.field: unknown field type \`…\`` before any frame is checked. The embedded contract goes through the same parse (`ShellContract::embedded`).

Scope honesty: like #1441 (the u64-cap parity defect in the same file), no production web code imports the TS checker today — only `world-contract.test.ts`. This is a correctness/parity defect in the conformance library before it gains consumers, not a live outage — hence priority/low. It is distinct from #1441: that is about integer *ranges* at check time; this is about *when and how* a malformed contract document is rejected.

## Why it matters

The contract's purpose (module docs, both ports) is that a new shell proves conformance by running a check instead of reading host code. A checker that accepts a broken contract document and then crashes mid-session — on exactly the frame type whose spec is broken, with a raw exception instead of a recorded violation — makes a contract-authoring error look like a shell bug and can take down the whole conformance run. The Rust side's fail-fast-at-load behaviour is the contract author's safety net; the port should offer the same.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The TS port exposes a load-time validation step (e.g. `parseContract` / `validateContract`) that checks every field spec of every client and server frame — type names, and the shorthand `?` forms — and reports an unknown type naming the frame and field, mirroring `ShellContract::parse`'s error shape.
- [ ] `checkClientFrame`, `checkServerFrame`, and `Conformance` never throw for a malformed field spec: with an unvalidated contract they return/record a `{ ok: false }` violation naming the bad spec instead of propagating `parseField`'s exception (or the checkers validate up front — either way, no uncaught throw).
- [ ] Regression tests in `world-contract.test.ts`: a contract with one field type replaced by an unknown name (a) is rejected by the load-time validation naming that frame/field, (b) does not crash a `Conformance` session that checks an unrelated frame first and the affected frame second — the affected frame becomes a violation.
- [ ] The real `shell-contract.v1.json` still passes validation and all existing world-contract tests pass unchanged; the Rust checker and the contract JSON are unchanged.

# aggregator(aa): two AA_GO_CAPS entries are unreachable — "contributor" is a noise token the normalizer strips, so Muse Spark 1.3 and Gemini 4 Argon publish goCapUsd: null instead of $12

## Evidence (main a2ea43bf)

`pm-stack/aggregator/src/aa.ts`:

- `AA_GO_CAPS` (line 660) is keyed by `normalizeModelName` output — the table's own comment (lines 661-662) says so, and the only lookup is `AA_GO_CAPS[norm]` in `aaCatalogFromConfig` (line 886), where `norm = normalizeModelName(modelPart(id))`.
- `normalizeModelName` (lines 271-280) drops every token in `NOISE_TOKENS` (line 255), which includes `"contributor"`.
- Two cap entries carry that token in their keys:
  - line 678: `"muse spark 1 3 contributor": 12`
  - line 679: `"gemini 4 argon contributor": 12`

Those keys can never be produced by the normalizer, so the entries are dead. The fleet's Meta/Gemini model ids are exactly the `-contributor` ids (see the AA_PLAN_FACTS note at line 612: "pools use the -contributor ids wherever a Meta model is seated"), so the affected models are the ones the caps were written for.

## Verified this run (probe on the laptop, real `aa.ts` from main, md5-matched)

```
opencode-go/muse-spark-1.3-contributor  => norm: "muse spark 1 3"   cap lookup: null
opencode-go/gemini-4-argon-contributor  => norm: "gemini 4 argon"   cap lookup: null
opencode-go/deepseek-v4.1-flash         => norm: "deepseek v4 1 flash" cap lookup: 80
UNREACHABLE KEY: "muse spark 1 3 contributor" normalizes to "muse spark 1 3"
UNREACHABLE KEY: "gemini 4 argon contributor" normalizes to "gemini 4 argon"
catalog opencode-go/deepseek-v4.1-flash         goCapUsd: 80
catalog opencode-go/gemini-4-argon-contributor  goCapUsd: null
catalog opencode-go/muse-spark-1.3-contributor  goCapUsd: null
```

Probe: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-gocaps/` (real module via `aaCatalogFromConfig`, minimal opencode-go config).

## Why it matters

The Model Explorer catalog publishes `goCapUsd: null` for these two models, so the "Published OpenCode Go cap: $12/mo → ~N AA tasks at the measured cost" line (render.ts:3550) and the explorer's `goCapFor` lookup never fire for them — the two caps silently read as "not recorded", the exact outcome the catalog code says a missing fact must not be confused with ("a miss means 'not matched', never 'does not exist'"). Every other entry in the table works, so the failure is invisible without checking these two models specifically.

## Acceptance criteria

- `aaCatalogFromConfig` returns `goCapUsd: 12` for `opencode-go/muse-spark-1.3-contributor` and `opencode-go/gemini-4-argon-contributor` (and 80 for the deepseek-v4.1-flash control).
- Every key of `AA_GO_CAPS` is a fixed point of `normalizeModelName` (`normalizeModelName(key) === key`), pinned by a test so a future cap entry with a noise token fails loudly instead of going dead.
- Existing aa tests still pass (the non-Go luna null case and the deepseek 80 case in test/aa.test.ts unchanged in spirit).

title: id(directory_mail): plain_address accepts '@', 'a@', '@b' and 'a@@b.c' — SmtpSink's only address-shape gate never counts the @ or checks either side is non-empty

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

`plain_address` in `pkgs/id/src/directory_mail.rs:199-205` — the only shape check behind `SmtpSink` — is just:

```rust
fn plain_address(text: &str) -> bool {
    text.contains('@')
        && text
            .chars()
            .all(|c| c.is_ascii_graphic() && !matches!(c, '<' | '>' | ',' | ';' | '"' | '\\'))
}
```

It never checks that there is exactly one `@`, or that either side of it is non-empty. So strings with no local part, no domain, or several `@`s all pass as a "plain address".

## Evidence (verified this run, main `dd2c88ff`)

Laptop probe over a verbatim copy of `plain_address` (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-plainaddr/`, rustc, main `dd2c88ff`):

```text
"a@b.co" => true            "first.last+tag@example.test" => true
"@" => true                 "a@" => true
"@b" => true                "a@@b.c" => true
"a@b@c.d" => true           "a@b@c" => true
"no-at-sign" => false       "a b@c.d" => false
```

Call sites that trust it:

- `SmtpSink::new` (`directory_mail.rs:129-144`) documents "Fails if … `from` is not a plain address" and gates the operator-supplied sender (`--world-mail-from`, `commands/serve.rs:478-485`) on `is_ascii` + `plain_address` only. `SmtpSink::new(relay, "@")`, `"a@"`, `"@b"`, `"a@@b.c"` all return `Ok`.
- `SmtpSink::send` (`directory_mail.rs:150-166`) gates the recipient on the same function, then formats both addresses straight into the wire: `MAIL FROM:<{from}>`, `RCPT TO:<{to}>`, and the `From:`/`To:` headers. A bogus sender therefore surfaces only at send time as an opaque relay reply error from `expect()` — or, against a lenient relay, goes out as a null / double-`@` reverse-path, so confirmation mail (the directory's email codes, `directory_view.rs:1466` `code_mail`) fails or bounces nowhere instead of the configuration being refused at startup.

Contrast with the directory's own email shape: `normalize_email` (`directory.rs:1800-1828`) requires exactly one `@` in effect (`split_once` + a domain charset that excludes `@`), a non-empty local part (≤64, no leading/trailing/doubled dots), and a domain with at least one dot and valid labels. Recipients that arrive through account confirmation are held to that; the SMTP sink's own gate — the layer whose job is not to trust its caller — is held to almost nothing. The module's tests (`directory_mail.rs:405-412`) pin the no-`@` and non-ASCII cases but no empty-side or multi-`@` case.

Related, distinct: #2404 (OutboxSink header injection — missing control checks), #1899 (reply-reader deadline), #1788 (CommandSink timeout). None covers this shape gap.

## Why it matters

`SmtpSink` is the fail-closed layer for confirmation mail: its constructor and `send` checks exist so a bad address is refused before a connection is opened (a property its tests assert for the internationalised case). A shape check that accepts `@` alone defeats that for the one address no other layer validates — the configured sender — turning a startup-time config error into a per-message relay failure, or into mail sent with an unusable reverse-path.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `plain_address` (or its replacement) refuses an address with zero or more than one `@`, an empty local part, or an empty domain — at minimum `"@"`, `"a@"`, `"@b"`, `"a@@b.c"`, `"a@b@c.d"` all return false / are refused.
- [ ] `SmtpSink::new` refuses those senders at construction with the existing "not a plain address" error, and `SmtpSink::send` refuses those recipients before connecting (pinned by a no-connection test like the SMTPUTF8 one).
- [ ] Legitimate addresses keep passing: `a@b.co`, `first.last+tag@example.test`, and the existing test set at `directory_mail.rs:405-412`.
- [ ] Triage pins the intended strictness: whether the sink should reuse `crate::directory::normalize_email`'s shape (one `@`, dotted domain, label rules) or a deliberately weaker exactly-one-`@` + non-empty-sides rule — either way the choice is recorded and tested, and any divergence from `normalize_email` is documented in the module.
- [ ] Existing `directory_mail` tests pass.

body:
# lab-ops-hub: `GET /api/files/<malformed percent-encoding>` returns 500 (raw URIError) — the key decode is unguarded, so a bad key spelling is never a 400/404

## Evidence (main `0144b0bd`, `pkgs/lab-ops-hub/src/index.ts`)

- The file-download route matches any non-empty suffix: `const fileMatch = p.match(/^\/api\/files\/(.+)$/)` (`index.ts:362-363`), then immediately calls `env.FILES.get(decodeURIComponent(fileMatch[1]))` (`index.ts:364`) with no guard on the decode.
- `decodeURIComponent` throws `URIError` on any malformed percent sequence — a bare `%`, `%zz`, a truncated escape (`uploads%2`), or a truncated UTF-8 sequence (`%E0%A4%A`). A request path can carry all of these: `new URL()` keeps the raw percent spelling in `url.pathname`, and the `(.+)` route match accepts it.
- The throw lands in the Worker's single outer catch (`index.ts:436-438`), which returns **500 `{error: String(e)}`** — so a misspelled key returns a raw `URIError: URI malformed` server fault instead of a client error. The route's own not-found path (404, `index.ts:365`) is never reached.

## Verification (this run)

Bun probe of the exact decode the handler performs (`hidden_files/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-labops/probe.ts` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace):

- `decodeURIComponent("%")` → throws `URIError`
- `decodeURIComponent("%zz")` → throws `URIError`
- `decodeURIComponent("uploads%2")` → throws `URIError`
- `decodeURIComponent("%E0%A4%A")` → throws `URIError`
- Control: `decodeURIComponent("uploads%2F123-a.txt")` → `uploads/123-a.txt` (normal encoded keys decode fine)

There is no code path in the route that turns the throw into anything but the outer catch's 500.

## Why it matters

File keys arrive in URLs — copied from dashboard links, scripts, and chat messages, where truncation and re-encoding happen. A truncated or double-mangled key is a client error, and today it reports as "the server broke" with raw engine error text, misdirecting debugging toward the deployment exactly as the #2480 POST-route cases did (those covered JSON POST bodies; this is the GET download route, which they do not touch). It also makes the route's behaviour untestable against a stable contract: the same bad key gives 500 here and would give 404 if spelled with valid-but-wrong escapes.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `GET /api/files/<malformed percent-encoding>` (bare `%`, `%zz`, truncated escape or UTF-8 sequence) returns **400** (or 404) with a plain error naming the bad key encoding — never a 500, and no raw `URIError` text.
- [ ] Valid encoded keys are unchanged: `uploads%2F<name>` still downloads the object, and a well-formed key for a missing object still returns the existing 404.
- [ ] Genuine R2 failures on the route still surface as 500.
- [ ] Regression coverage for the malformed-spelling cases (a unit test of the factored decode/response per the #524 `src/lib.ts` pattern, or a handler-level test).

## Dedup

`gh` searches (open + closed) for lab-ops-hub + decodeURIComponent/percent/URIError return only the crawler-validator percent-host issues (#505/#529/#567 family — the crawl URL validator, a different code path). #2480 covers missing fields and non-JSON bodies on the JSON POST routes only. Nothing covers the file-download route's unguarded decode.

— filed by new-issue-creator-code-b (Lane B), 2026-10-30 run

title: id(range-sync): an empty flight ends reconciliation as all-skip — a zero-entry first flight completes a session that transfers nothing

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

In `pkgs/id` range sync (`/id-range-sync/1`), an **empty flight** — a single frame carrying zero entries — is accepted as a successful end of reconciliation. `all_skip` is vacuously true for an empty message, and nothing on the read path ever requires a flight to contain at least one entry:

- `src/event_store/range.rs:215-217` — `pub fn all_skip(msg: &[Entry]) -> bool { msg.iter().all(|e| e.mode == Mode::Skip) }` — `all` on an empty iterator is `true`.
- `src/event_store/range.rs:443` — `frames(&[], budget)` happily encodes an empty message as one frame, `[0, 0]` (flag `0`, count `0`).
- `src/event_store/range.rs:539` — `decode_frame(&[0, 0])` returns `Ok((false, vec![]))`; there is no minimum entry count.
- `src/event_store/range.rs:576` — `check_bounds(&[])` returns `Ok(())`.
- `src/event_store/sync.rs:493-505` — `read_flight` returns that empty `Vec` as a complete flight.
- `src/event_store/sync.rs:594` — `run_session`'s reconciliation loop does `if all_skip(&incoming) { break; }`, so the empty flight terminates reconciliation exactly like a genuine all-skip answer.
- `src/event_store/sync.rs:643` — `simulate` has the same vacuous-truth termination.

## Verified this run (laptop probe, verbatim code)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-emptyflight/` on the laptop — `range.rs` copied verbatim from main `a680bf89` (md5 `26980b5f7ca4499c0b1f446df73ba571` matches the source file), compiled and run there:

```
ALL_SKIP_EMPTY=true
FRAMES_EMPTY=[[0, 0]]
DECODED_MORE=false ENTRIES=0
CHECK_BOUNDS_EMPTY_OK=true
RECEIVER_TERMINATED=true LEARNED=0 RECEIVER_KEYS=3
HONEST_OPEN_ALL_SKIP=false HONEST_MODE_IS_FP=true
```

The receiver-side step mirrors `run_session`'s loop shape: fed the decoded empty flight, it terminates with `learned = 0` even though the receiver's `Party` holds 3 keys.

## Why it matters

Reconciliation ending is what moves a session into the data phase, and the data phase derives everything from `learned`: `need` (what to expect) and `offers` (what to send) at `sync.rs:609-622`, and the only cross-check is `count == need.len()` at `sync.rs:722` — which compares the peer's count against the same truncated `learned` set, so it passes at `0 == 0`. A peer (buggy, hand-rolled, or hostile) whose first flight is the two bytes `[0, 0]` therefore gets a session that completes the full protocol — data phase and the phase-4 `APPLIED_FRAME` handshake included — having transferred nothing, with an `Outcome` indistinguishable from a sync between two genuinely identical stores. No honest peer built from `respond` ever sends an empty flight (`respond` emits at least one entry per incoming entry, and the opening flight is the `full_range` fingerprint), so an empty flight is always a protocol violation that is currently rewarded with success. Silent no-op "successful" syncs are the worst failure shape for a replication protocol: stores diverge while every observable says they converged.

This is the same wire-validation family as #2595 / #2596 / #2607 (peer-supplied range-sync input accepted in shapes the protocol never produces), but a distinct hole: those concern bound lengths, varint spellings, and the zero-length bound sentinel; this one concerns the flight-level entry count and the termination predicate.

## Acceptance criteria

- A flight with zero entries is refused on the read path (in `read_flight` / `decode_frame` / `check_bounds` — triage pins the layer), with an error that names the empty flight; **or** `all_skip` is made false for an empty message and every caller is audited so an empty flight cannot terminate reconciliation any other way. Either way the behaviour is pinned by tests, not just by the predicate change.
- Regression tests: `decode_frame`/`read_flight`-level refusal of the `[0, 0]` frame as a complete flight; a session-level (loopback or simulate) test in which an empty first flight does **not** produce a successful zero-transfer `Outcome`.
- Honest flows are unchanged: identical stores still end via a genuine all-skip flight (which always carries at least one entry), and the existing range/sync test suites pass.
- `frames(&[])` either refuses an empty message or is documented/tested as never being called with one by the session code.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `all_skip`, "empty flight", and "empty message" in this repo: no hits. #2595 (bound length), #2596 (varint overlong), #2607 (zero-length bound as +infinity sentinel) are sibling wire-validation gaps in the same module, each a different check; none covers the zero-entry flight or the vacuous `all_skip`.

title: id(store): load_or_create_keypair's first read has no creation-race wait — a concurrent first start reading the winner's key file between create_new and write_all fails 'invalid key length: got 0'

body:
# id(store): `load_or_create_keypair`'s first read has no creation-race wait — a concurrent first start that reads the winner's key file between `create_new` and `write_all` fails with "invalid key length: expected 32, got 0"

## Evidence (main `c90d6acf`, `pkgs/id/src/store.rs`)

`load_or_create_keypair` (`store.rs:91`) handles the first-run creation race in exactly one interleaving and misses the other:

- **Handled:** the loser's first `afs::read` returns `NotFound`, its `write_private_file` then gets `AlreadyExists` from `create_new` (`store.rs:156`), and it falls back to `read_key_after_creation_race` (`store.rs:123-140`) — a 1-second retry loop that waits for the winner to finish writing the 32-byte key.
- **Missed:** the loser's first read lands *after* the winner's `create_new` has made the (still empty) file visible but *before* its `write_all` (`store.rs:157`) completes. That read succeeds with 0 bytes (or a partial key), so the function takes the ordinary "existing key" branch (`store.rs:92-99`) and immediately errors `invalid key length: expected 32, got 0` — no wait, no retry, and no second chance, even though the valid key lands milliseconds later.

The two operations in `write_private_file` are separate syscalls with no atomicity between them, so the window is real on every concurrent first start (two `id` processes / a CLI invocation racing `id serve` on a fresh directory). The existing test `test_concurrent_key_creation_preserves_one_identity` (`store.rs:553`) joins two calls but cannot hit the window reliably, because in-process the winner writes almost immediately after creating.

## Verification (this run, laptop probe)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-keyrace/` on the laptop — verbatim copies of `load_or_create_keypair`, `read_key_after_creation_race` and `write_private_file` from main `c90d6acf` (only the `SecretKey` type stubbed), with a slow winner that creates the key file, waits 600 ms, then writes the 32-byte key:

- **A — `load_or_create_keypair` called during the create→write window:** `ERR 'invalid key length: expected 32, got 0'` after **3 ms**.
- **B — control, `read_key_after_creation_race` on the identical window:** waits **601 ms** and returns the winner's key (`OK key7=true`).
- **C — sanity, load after the write completes:** `OK`.

So the wait logic exists in the same file and is proven correct — the ordinary load path just never uses it.

## Why it matters

First-run identity creation is the one moment two `id` processes are most likely to start together (scripted setup, a service and a CLI probe, test harnesses sharing a fresh home). In the missed interleaving one process dies with a misleading "invalid key length" error that reads like on-disk corruption, inviting the operator to delete a key file that is in fact the winner's valid, just-written identity. The sibling SSH host-key loader (`world_ssh.rs` `load_or_create_host_key`) has no race handling at all and may deserve the same treatment — triage should decide whether it is in scope here or a follow-up.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A load whose first read observes a 0-byte or partial key file waits/retries for a bounded period (consistent with `read_key_after_creation_race`'s 1 s) and returns the winner's key once the write completes, instead of erroring immediately.
- [ ] A key file that is *still* the wrong length after the wait errors with the same clear "invalid key length" message — a genuinely corrupt/truncated key must never be silently replaced or regenerated.
- [ ] A deterministic regression test covers the missed interleaving (a writer paused between create and write, or an equivalent seam), alongside the existing concurrent-creation test.
- [ ] Both concurrent first-start processes end up with the same identity (the winner's), as the existing test asserts.

title: agy-proxy: eviction sweep kills session workers with a turn in flight — no busy guard in the TTL or cap branches

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: app/agy-proxy
labels.description: bin/agy-proxy.mjs warm-session proxy

body:
## Finding

PR #1759 (merged 2026-10-29, commits c55b2bcd..81765bab) replaced agy-proxy's spawn-per-request path with resident warm workers plus an eviction sweep, `evictLiveWorkersIfNeeded` in `bin/agy-proxy.mjs`. The sweep never checks whether a worker is mid-turn, so it can kill a worker that is actively serving a request:

- TTL branch (current main 541578ae, `bin/agy-proxy.mjs:692-699`): a worker is killed when `now - w.lastUsedAt > SESSION_IDLE_TTL_MS`. `lastUsedAt` is set at spawn (:476) and on turn *completion* (:611) — never at turn start — so a worker whose current turn has been running longer than the TTL looks "idle". The two knobs are independent env vars with no cross-check (:453 `TURN_TIMEOUT_MS`, default 300000; :457 `SESSION_IDLE_TTL_MS`, default 30 min): a legitimate tuning such as `AGY_PROXY_SESSION_TTL_MS=60000` with default turn timeout makes every turn longer than a minute eligible for mid-flight eviction by the 60 s interval sweep (:707).
- Cap branch (:700-705): when live workers reach `MAX_LIVE_WORKERS` (default 32), the sweep kills least-recently-used workers until the count drops — again with no in-flight check, and `acquireWorker` calls the same sweep (:720) before registering a new session worker. A busy worker whose turn started earliest is exactly the LRU entry while 31 other sessions complete quick turns and refresh their `lastUsedAt`.

## Why it matters

`kill()` settles the in-flight turn via `_fail` (:541, :652): the client request fails with `agy worker killed` (502 non-stream, or an SSE error event after any partial deltas). The fresh-conversation retry only fires for a resumed worker with no output yet, so a stateless request, or a session turn that had already streamed deltas, surfaces the failure to the caller — caused not by the upstream but by the proxy's own housekeeping. Eviction is a resource control; it should never be able to take down the work it is protecting.

Related but distinct: #2096 covers the bare `Number()` parsing of these same knobs (NaN / 0 / negative shapes). This issue is the missing busy guard, which applies with perfectly valid knob values.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `evictLiveWorkersIfNeeded` skips any worker with a turn in flight (`turnWaiter != null`) in both the TTL and cap branches; such a worker becomes eligible again once its turn settles.
- [ ] The cap branch never drops the live set below the cap by killing busy workers: if all candidates are busy, it evicts nothing this pass.
- [ ] A regression test (stub `agy`, in the style of `bin/agy-proxy.test.mjs`) pins: a session worker mid-turn survives an eviction pass that would otherwise select it (TTL-expired and cap-pressure variants), and is evicted once idle after the turn completes.

title: id(range-sync): a zero-length upper bound encodes as +infinity — Some(vec![]) is the one bound length the sentinel swallows, and check_bounds approves it as finite

labels.name: task/triage

body:
## Problem

The range-sync wire format uses a bound's length byte as a sentinel: `0` means +infinity, anything else is the length of the key prefix that follows (module doc, `pkgs/id/src/event_store/range.rs` lines 19–24). That makes a zero-length bound unrepresentable — but nothing refuses one. An entry built with `upper: Some(vec![])` encodes byte-for-byte identically to `upper: None` (+infinity), so the encoder silently changes what the entry says, and `check_bounds` — the documented pre-flight check a caller runs before `Party::respond` — approves the entry as a finite bound that does not end the flight.

Evidence (pkgs/id/src/event_store/range.rs, main f9268e24; file sha256 identical on the laptop clone at 819889bb):

- `encode_entry` (~line 411): `Some(b) => { out.push(b.len() as u8); out.extend_from_slice(b); }` — with `b` empty it pushes the `0` sentinel and no bytes, exactly the `None` arm's output.
- `Reader::entry` (~line 510): `let len = self.byte()? as usize; … let upper = if len == 0 { None } else { Some(…) }` — the decoder can never produce `Some(vec![])`, so the value exists only on the constructing side, where it is silently rewritten.
- `check_bounds` (~line 571): treats `Some(bound)` as a finite bound — it does not set its `ended` (+infinity) flag, and an empty bound sorts below every other bound, so `[Some([]), Some([1]), None]` passes.
- Internal producers are safe today only by construction: `Party::separator` always returns at least one byte, and inbound entries come through `decode_frame`. `Entry`, `frames`, `check_bounds` and `Party::respond` are the public library surface of `/id-range-sync/1`, and `respond` clones the caller's upper bounds into its answer.

## Verified this run (laptop probe, real crate)

Probe: ~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-zerobound/ (`id` path dependency, default-features off; range.rs sha256 2e8a2255… matches sandbox main f9268e24):

- Case 1: `frames([Entry { upper: Some(vec![]), mode: Skip }])` succeeds (4 wire bytes); `decode_frame` returns the entry with `upper = None`; round-trip equality is **false**. `check_bounds` on the original entry: Ok.
- Case 2: the flight `[Some([]), Some([1]), None]` passes the sender-side `check_bounds`; after encode/decode its uppers are `[None, Some([1]), None]`, which the receiver-side `check_bounds` **rejects** ("an entry follows +infinity") — a flight the sender's own pre-flight check approved kills the session at the peer.
- Case 3: `frames([Some(vec![])])` is byte-identical to `frames([None])`.

Related but distinct: #2595 covers bounds **over** KEY_LEN (decoder rejection at 73–255, u8 wrap at ≥256). A fix that only refuses `len > KEY_LEN` does not catch the empty bound — the empty bound is the one length that collides with the format's own sentinel rather than exceeding its limit. This issue tracks that remaining case; the two fixes belong in the same functions (`encode_entry`/`frames` and `check_bounds`).

## Why it matters

A bound that silently widens to +infinity changes the meaning of a flight: as the last entry it reconciles the whole remaining key space instead of an empty range; anywhere else it makes the peer reject the flight. Either way the failure surfaces at the wrong layer (a bounds error on the receiver, or a mysteriously widened range), never at the constructor that wrote an unrepresentable value. The module's own pattern is fail-closed at encode time (frame budgets, bound length in the decoder); the empty bound is the one input that slips through because its length is *too small*, not too large.

## Acceptance criteria

- `frames()` (or `encode_entry`) refuses an entry whose upper bound is `Some` with length 0, with an error naming the problem (a bound is a key prefix of 1..=KEY_LEN bytes, or `None` for +infinity).
- `check_bounds` also refuses a zero-length bound, so the documented pre-flight check catches what `respond()` would otherwise clone into its answer and re-encode as +infinity.
- Tests cover: `Some(vec![])` refused at encode and by `check_bounds`; a 1-byte bound still round-trips; `None` still encodes as the sentinel.
- Existing range.rs tests stay green.

body:
## Summary

Residual of closed #1628: `ymdLabel` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/derive.ts:534-542) was made defensive — an impossible date is echoed verbatim instead of throwing, pinned by the test "ymdLabel and monthLabel neither throw nor relabel impossible dates" (test/render.test.ts:197-201). That contract still breaks for a **valid calendar date with trailing text**: the `YMD` regex (derive.ts:494) is not end-anchored, so `"2026-10-25xyz"` matches and passes `isCalendarDate`, but the label is then built from `new Date(`${ymd}T12:00:00Z`)` over the **whole raw string**, which is an Invalid Date — `MONTH_NAMES[NaN]` is `undefined` and `.slice` on it throws a `TypeError`.

## Evidence (verified this run, main efeea69c)

Laptop Bun probe importing the real `ymdLabel` from derive.ts (probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-titlerefs/probe2.ts`):

- `ymdLabel("2026-10-25")` → `"Sun Oct 25"` ✓
- `ymdLabel("2026-13-15")` → `"2026-13-15"` (echoed, the #1628 fix ✓)
- `ymdLabel("2026-02-30")` → `"2026-02-30"` (echoed ✓)
- `ymdLabel("2026-10-25xyz")` → **throws** `TypeError: undefined is not an object (evaluating 'MONTH_NAMES[d.getUTCMonth()].slice')`
- `ymdLabel("2026-10-25 (today)")` → **throws** the same
- `ymdLabel("2026-10-25T99")` → **throws** the same

Root cause in one line: the regex validates a *prefix* of the input, and the Date is constructed from the *unvalidated remainder included* — the function should build the date from the captured `m[1]-m[2]-m[3]` groups (as `rowDate` at derive.ts:556-560 already does when it returns `` `${m[1]}-${m[2]}-${m[3]}` ``), or echo the input when the match is not the whole string.

## Why it matters / reachability (stated honestly)

Today's in-repo callers pass only internally generated dates (roadmapDayGrain lanes), so this is not a live 500: it is a hole in a deliberate, test-pinned defensive contract — the exact contract #1628 added after this helper threw in production-adjacent roadmap rendering. The next caller that hands `ymdLabel` a feed- or section-derived string (the pattern that produced #1628) re-opens the throw. The fix is one line plus regression cases in the existing test.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ymdLabel` never throws for any string input: a valid date followed by trailing text either labels the captured date or echoes the input verbatim — triage pins which, consistent with the #1628 echo contract.
- [ ] The existing cases stay green: `"2026-13-15"` and `"2026-02-30"` echo verbatim, `"2026-10-24"` → `"Sat Oct 24"`.
- [ ] Regression tests add the suffix shapes: `"2026-10-25xyz"`, `"2026-10-25 (today)"`, `"2026-10-25T99"`.
- [ ] Construction uses the captured groups (or an anchored match), matching `rowDate`'s existing practice in the same file.

## Dedup

#1628 (CLOSED) fixed the month-13 / Feb-30 throw shapes and added the defensive contract + test; it did not cover the valid-date-plus-suffix shape, which throws through a different line (Invalid Date from the raw-string construction, not a rollover). Searched this run for `ymdLabel` open + closed — no other issue covers it. Not self-solved: echo-vs-label for suffixed input is triage's pin against the #1628 contract.

body:
## Summary

`titleRefs` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/sources/live.ts:436-462) fabricates a fleet ref that appears nowhere in a linedUp title: its shorthand `#N` pass (line 448, `/#(\d+)/g`) re-processes the `#N` that is already part of an explicit `owner/repo#N` ref extracted at line 442, and attributes that number to the nearest preceding repo alias (`code|opencode|openchamber|nix`, lines 444-460). When the explicit ref names a repo that is not one of the four aliases — or any alias word appears earlier in the title — the result is a phantom ref to an unrelated issue in a fleet repo.

## Evidence (verified this run, main efeea69c)

Laptop Bun probe importing the real `titleRefs` from the laptop clone (live.ts md5 9809c45fca6066bf77415aa0876c1b94, identical to sandbox main; probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-titlerefs/probe.ts`):

- `titleRefs("code #811 blocked on developing-today/kaneo#42")`
  → `["developing-today/kaneo#42", "developing-today/code#811", "developing-today/code#42"]`
  — `developing-today/code#42` is fabricated: the title's `#42` belongs to `developing-today/kaneo`, and no `code#42` is named anywhere.
- Controls behave: `"nix #889 queued; see dezren39/nix#501 for the pre-seed"` → only `dezren39/nix#889`, `dezren39/nix#501` (the alias inside the explicit ref happens to be the nearest preceding alias, so the duplicate is deduped); `"code #944 fix - PR #985 opened"` → exactly the two shorthand refs. The bug needs an explicit ref whose repo name is not itself an alias word, plus an alias word earlier in the title — a normal shape for orchestrator linedUp titles, which routinely lead with a shorthand ref and then name blockers in other repos.

## Why it matters

`titleRefs` feeds `inFlightBoardItems` (live.ts:497), whose refs become the synthetic board entry's rendered GitHub links (relation `tracks`) and participate in two decisions:

- Kaneo dedupe (live.ts:498): `refs.some((r) => existingRefs.has(r))` drops the whole entry — a phantom ref that happens to be linked from a Kaneo card suppresses a genuinely new in-flight item.
- The entry's repo is `parseRef(refs[0]).repo` (live.ts:508); phantom/mis-ordered refs degrade that attribution.

So the in-flight lane can link Drew to an unrelated issue (e.g. code#42) as if it were the blocking work, and can silently hide real work.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `titleRefs("code #811 blocked on developing-today/kaneo#42")` returns exactly `developing-today/code#811` and `developing-today/kaneo#42` — the `#N` of an explicit `owner/repo#N` (or GitHub URL) ref is never re-attributed to an alias.
- [ ] Shorthand behaviour is unchanged for the existing test shapes (`code #944 … PR #985`, `nix #889; nix #848`, alias-less numbers stay unlinked) — existing `board-in-flight.test.ts` cases stay green.
- [ ] New regression tests cover: explicit non-fleet ref + earlier alias word; explicit ref to a fifth repo with no alias word (no phantom); mixed shorthand + explicit refs in one title.
- [ ] Triage pins the mechanism (e.g. mask/consume the spans of explicit refs before the shorthand pass, or skip `#N` matches immediately preceded by `owner/repo`).

## Dedup

Searched open + closed for `titleRefs` / `inFlightBoardItems` this run: #1196 is the deliberate coarse per-ref dedupe in the same function (documented, distinct mechanism), #1206 is the canonical-projection design — neither covers phantom ref fabrication. Not self-solved: the fix shape (span-masking vs match filtering) and its interplay with the deliberate alias-attribution heuristics is triage's pin.

body:
## Problem

The reader side of the quota-current contract never range-checks `pctOfLimit`, so a finite-but-impossible percent in a fresh `state:"ok"` gatherer read is applied verbatim to the pool — and steers placement:

- `pctWindows` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-current.ts:88-97) gates only on `typeof w.pctOfLimit === "number" && Number.isFinite(w.pctOfLimit)` (:90) and then copies the value verbatim into `used` and `percent` against a hardcoded `limit: 100` (:95-96). There is no [0,100] check.
- `applyEntry` (quota-current.ts:118+) installs those windows on the pool and recomputes `pool.state = poolState(pool)`; `poolState` (src/derive.ts:164-168) returns `"walled"` when any window percent is >= 100, and `overlayQuotaCurrent` then recomputes `computeChoices` — so one glitched read at 150% marks a healthy pool **walled** and lands it in `doNotStart`, steering new work away from a pool that is actually fine. A read at -20% publishes a negative percent window that renders as negative usage.
- `overlayTursoUsage` (quota-current.ts:225) is weaker still: `...(w.pctOfLimit != null ? { percent: w.pctOfLimit } : {})` — no type or finite check at all, so any non-null value (150, -20, a string) becomes the Turso metric's `percent`.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `3a425552`)

Laptop Bun probe importing the real `quota-current.ts` (aggregator `src/` copied verbatim to the laptop probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-quotacurrent/`, run with `bun probe.ts` against a one-pool view):

- Fresh ok entry, window `pctOfLimit: 150` → pool state `"walled"`, window `{used: 150, percent: 150, limit: 100}`, and `choices.doNotStart: ["anthropic:claude-pro"]` — the healthy pool is excluded from placement by a single out-of-range read.
- Fresh ok entry, window `pctOfLimit: -20` → pool state `"healthy"` with window `percent: -20` published as-is.
- Control: the module's own tests show in-range reads overlay normally — the defect is only the missing range gate at this reader.

## Why it matters

quota-current.json is written every 15 minutes by a gatherer on another host and embedded into the fleet feed by the collector; this reader is the trust boundary for that file (the same rationale as #2416's shape gate). #2571 pins the writer-side mappers in quota-gather-map.ts, but the reader must not depend on every present and future writer being correct: a stale gatherer build, a hand-edited file, or a new provider adapter with a percent bug currently reaches pool state and placement choices unchecked. The failure is also silent — the pool simply reads walled (or negative), with freshness stamped ok.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `pctWindows` never emits a window whose percent is outside [0,100] from a gatherer read (treatment pinned at triage: drop the window — the function's existing pattern for unusable pct — or clamp; sibling in-range windows of the same entry still apply).
- [ ] `overlayTursoUsage` only forwards a `percent` that is a finite number in [0,100]; other values omit `percent` rather than passing through.
- [ ] Regression tests in test/quota-current.test.ts pin: 150 and 1e9 do not wall the pool nor enter `doNotStart`; -20 never publishes as a window percent; in-range reads (including exactly 0 and exactly 100) overlay unchanged.
- [ ] Existing quota-current / quota tests stay green.

## Dedup

- #2571 (OPEN) is the writer side: `entryFromResult`/`entryFromFileExport` in quota-gather-map.ts. Its packet names quota-current.ts:90-96 as a downstream flow-through, but its acceptance pins only the mappers — no reader-side gate is tracked anywhere.
- #2416 (OPEN) is this file's *shape* gate (null/non-object window entries crash the overlay) — different failure: a well-formed numeric 150 passes every shape check.
- #2568 (OPEN) is `recordsFromProviderUsage` in snapshot-records.ts; #2253 (OPEN) is the stale-path `measuredAt` pick in this file — both distinct.
- Searched open + recently closed issues for `quota-current pctOfLimit`, `parseQuotaCurrent`, `overlayQuotaCurrent` this run: no range-check issue for the reader side.

# cloudflare-export: R2 bucket enumeration fails open — a 500/malformed buckets response publishes `r2Buckets: []` in a status:ok document, and pagination past 100 buckets is silently dropped

## Evidence (verified this run, main `af19d7fd`)

`pm-stack/cloudflare-export/cloudflare-quota-export.mjs`, in `run()`:

- `:393` — the bucket enumeration is a single request: `` `/accounts/${acct}/r2/buckets?per_page=100` ``. No further page is ever requested and `result_info` is never read.
- `:394` — only 401/403 are treated as errors (`scopeError`). Every other non-200 status falls through.
- `:395` — `const r2Buckets = (buckets.body?.result?.buckets ?? []).map((b) => b.name).filter(Boolean);` — a missing/malformed `result.buckets` silently becomes `[]`.

Probe (this run; stubbed `fetch`, real exported `run()` imported from the repo module; probe dir `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-cfbuckets/`):

| Scenario | Result |
|---|---|
| Buckets endpoint returns HTTP 500 (`result: null`) while GraphQL storage data exists | `status: "ok"` document with `r2Buckets: []` (count 0) **and** `r2-storage` metric `used: 5` GB — the document contradicts itself |
| Buckets endpoint returns 200 with a malformed `result` (no `.buckets`) | `status: "ok"`, `r2Buckets: []` |
| Buckets endpoint returns 100 buckets with `result_info: { total_count: 150, total_pages: 2 }` | `status: "ok"`, `r2Buckets` lists exactly those 100 — the other 50 buckets are absent with no marker |
| Control: 200 with 2 buckets | `r2Buckets: ["alpha", "beta"]` — normal path works |

## Why it matters

This exporter is deliberately fail-closed everywhere else in the same file: `classifyR2`/`foldKv`/`firstSum` throw `unparseable` on a missing groups field ("a missing/null groups field is shape drift, not zero operations"), and the r2-storage metric carries an explicit `lowerBound: true` marker when its group count saturates the query limit. The bucket enumeration is the one place that breaks that contract:

1. A transient Cloudflare 500 or a response-shape drift publishes a successful export asserting the account has **no** R2 buckets, in the same document that reports gigabytes of R2 storage. A consumer (or a human reading `latest.json`) cannot distinguish "enumeration failed" from "account has no buckets".
2. Past 100 buckets the list is silently truncated — exactly the silent-undercount failure mode the file's storage path was written to flag with `lowerBound`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A non-200 buckets response (other than the existing 401/403 scope path) or a malformed `result.buckets` shape does not publish as an empty bucket list in a `status: "ok"` document: it either fails the run with the file's existing failure-document taxonomy, or the document explicitly marks the enumeration as failed/unknown — triage pins which.
- [ ] Bucket enumeration follows pagination (cursor or `result_info` page count) so accounts with more than 100 buckets are fully listed, or the document carries an explicit truncation marker analogous to r2-storage's `lowerBound`.
- [ ] `cloudflare-quota-export.test.mjs` covers: buckets-endpoint 500, malformed buckets body, and a multi-page bucket list; the existing tests stay green.

## Dedup

Searched this run: `cloudflare-export`, `r2Buckets`, "r2 buckets enumeration" — no open or recently closed issue covers the buckets enumeration path. #2287 is the separate Workers-AI alerting ask; #1048 (the collector's origin issue) specified the storage total, not this enumeration's failure/pagination behaviour.
