body:
## Problem

`pkgs/id/src/directory_mail.rs` defines three `MailSink`s for the same `Mail { to, subject, body }`, but only one of them validates the header fields:

- `SmtpSink::send` (directory_mail.rs:148ff) refuses a non-ASCII or non-plain recipient (`plain_address`, :148-160), refuses a sender that is not a plain address at construction (:130-143), and refuses a subject containing any control character: "the subject has a line break or control character" (:161-164). The module's own test at :453 sends a smuggled `a@b.co>\r\nRCPT TO:<x@y.z` recipient and expects refusal.
- `OutboxSink::send` (directory_mail.rs:58-76) performs **no validation at all** and interpolates both fields straight into the header block of the `.eml` file it writes:

```rust
write!(file, "To: {}\nSubject: {}\n\n{}", mail.to, mail.subject, mail.body)
```

A `subject` (or `to`) containing `\n` therefore forges arbitrary extra headers in the stored message — `Bcc:`, a second `Content-Type:`, or a whole second message after a blank line — in a file whose entire purpose is to be read/picked up as email. `Mail`'s fields are `pub` (directory_mail.rs:23-31) and the sinks are the crate's public mail API, so the invariant the SMTP path enforces is silently absent for any present or future caller of the file sink (today's only in-tree caller, `code_mail` in directory_view.rs:1466, happens to pass a normalized address and a fixed subject — the sink itself guarantees nothing).

## Evidence (verified this run, main `5a34fa70`)

Laptop probe test added to the verbatim `directory_mail.rs` tests in a laptop worktree (file md5 `58718d786ae90d6ea7cb65688cbc20e2`, identical on sandbox main and the laptop; worktree removed after the run):

```rust
let sink = OutboxSink::new(dir.clone());
let mail = Mail {
    to: "victim@example.com".into(),
    subject: "Your code\nBcc: attacker@evil.example".into(),
    body: "hello".into(),
};
sink.send(&mail).unwrap();
// read back the single .eml file written
assert!(found.contains("\nBcc: attacker@evil.example"));
```

Result: `test directory_mail::tests::probe_outbox_writes_injected_header ... ok` — the `.eml` on disk contains a real forged `Bcc:` header line. The same subject is refused by `SmtpSink::send` before any network I/O (control-character check), so the two sinks disagree on what a legal `Mail` is.

Existing tests cover the outbox happy path only (`text.starts_with("To: a@b.co\nSubject: Your code\n\n")`, :290); no test feeds a control character to `OutboxSink`.

## Why it matters

The outbox directory is a trust boundary: files dropped there are mail. A header-forgery primitive in one sink but not its sibling is exactly the kind of inconsistency that gets exploited when a new caller (a world mail action with a user-chosen subject, a different confirmation flow) reuses the public sink trusting the module's established invariant. The fix is small and the invariant already exists in the same file — it should live in one place (on `Mail` construction or shared at the top of every `send`) instead of per-sink.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `OutboxSink::send` refuses a `Mail` whose `to` is not a plain ASCII address or whose `subject` contains a control character, with the same error wording/classes as `SmtpSink` — or the validation moves to a single shared place (e.g. a checked `Mail` constructor / `Mail::validate`) that all three sinks use; either way, no sink writes unvalidated header fields.
- [ ] A regression test mirrors the SMTP smuggling test (:453) for the outbox sink: a subject of `"Your code\nBcc: x@y.z"` and a recipient containing `\r\n` are both refused and **no `.eml` file is created**.
- [ ] The legitimate path is unchanged: the existing outbox test (:290) and the directory confirmation flows (`code_mail`, directory_view.rs:1466 — normalized address, fixed subjects) pass unmodified.
- [ ] Out of scope: `CommandSink` timeout behaviour (#1788) and the SMTP reply-reader bounds (#1899) — already tracked separately.

body:
## Problem

The `basic: nix flake check (clippy-lint)` PR check fails on `pkgs/id` with two `clippy::expect_used` errors in code this repo has not changed:

```
error: used `expect()` on an `Option` value
   --> src/tags.rs:1484:22
    |
1484 |     let ch = input[i..].chars().next().expect("i is a char boundary");
     |                      ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
     = note: requested on the command line with `-D clippy::expect-used`

error: used `expect()` on an `Option` value
   --> src/tags.rs:1499:22
    |
1499 |     let ch = input[i..].chars().next().expect("i is a char boundary");
```

## Evidence it is pre-existing, not PR-local

- Observed on PR #1820 (`queue/2661-807-apply-wiring`), run [40894646360](https://github.com/developing-today/code/actions/runs/40894646360) job 123626426997 — the failure was first misread as nix-cache throttling (HTTP 418 on a *different*, earlier attempt); the rerun reached clippy and produced these two real errors.
- `pkgs/id/src/tags.rs` is **not** in PR #1820's file list (13 files changed, none in `src/tags.rs`).
- The same two `expect()` calls are present verbatim in `origin/main:pkgs/id/src/tags.rs` at the same lines, so the check should be red for any PR that touches `pkgs/id`.

## Impact

Every PR touching `pkgs/id` is unmergeable: `clippy-lint` is a required check. #1820 is parked on this, and other `app/id` work will queue behind it.

## Expected fix

Either replace the two `expect()` calls with a non-panicking form, e.g.

```rust
let Some(ch) = input[i..].chars().next() else { break };
```

(the enclosing loops already break when `i >= input.len()`), or, if the panic is genuinely intended as an invariant, `#[allow(clippy::expect_used)]` with a comment — but prefer the `let-else`, since `i` is always advanced by `len_utf8`.

Verify with the clippy-lint check (`nix build .#checks.<system>.id-clippy-lint` or `cargo clippy -p id --all-targets -- -D clippy::expect-used`), not just `cargo check`: the 366 warnings in the same log are non-fatal and must not be "fixed" here.

## Related

- #1820 (blocked on this)
- #807 (F12.1 apply wiring, the parent)

## Acceptance criteria

- `basic: nix flake check (clippy-lint)` passes on main with no `clippy::expect_used` errors at `pkgs/id/src/tags.rs:1484,1499` — fixed in place or via the keystone PR #2335 fmt/clippy change set, not both.
- No behaviour change to the char-boundary parsing those lines implement; existing pkgs/id tests pass in CI.

body:
## Summary

Two `id world` CLI commands turn an unchecked `u64` seconds argument into a deadline by adding it to an `Instant`, and a huge value panics the process with `overflow when adding duration to instant` instead of being refused or clamped:

1. **`id world logs --seconds <huge>`** — `pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs:563-564`:
   ```rust
   let deadline =
       tokio::time::Instant::now() + std::time::Duration::from_secs(seconds.max(1));
   ```
   `seconds` is a plain clap `u64` (`pkgs/id/src/cli.rs:1820-1828`, `--seconds`, default 5, no range). The deadline is computed after connect + join, so the command connects successfully and then crashes with a panic.
2. **`id world mirror --timeout-secs <huge>`** — `pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs:152` builds `Duration::from_secs(timeout_secs.max(1))` (`--timeout-secs`, plain `u64`, `pkgs/id/src/cli.rs:1490-1491`) and passes it to `crate::world_records::replicate`, which at `pkgs/id/src/world_records.rs:218` computes:
   ```rust
   let deadline = std::time::Instant::now() + timeout;
   ```
   The earlier `tokio::time::timeout(timeout, …)` at `world_records.rs:205` survives huge durations (tokio caps its internal deadline — verified), so the panic lands on the std `Instant` addition at :218, after the initial sync has already run.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `5a34fa70`)

Laptop probe crate `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-logsinstant/` (verbatim deadline expressions):

- `std::time::Instant::now() + Duration::from_secs(u64::MAX)` → panics `overflow when adding duration to instant`, exit 101.
- `tokio::time::Instant::now() + Duration::from_secs(u64::MAX)` → same panic, tokio 1.54.1 at `tokio/src/time/instant.rs:161` (id's `Cargo.lock` pins tokio 1.53.2, same documented panic-on-overflow semantics).
- Control: `Duration::from_secs(86400)` deadline computes normally, exit 0.
- `tokio::time::timeout(Duration::from_secs(u64::MAX), …)` does **not** panic (completes normally) — confirming Mirror's crash site is the std addition at `world_records.rs:218`, not the timeout at :205.

Other `Instant::now() + …` sites in the crate use constants or internal durations (`world_compile.rs:296` uses the `COMPILE_TIMEOUT` constant; `event_store/sync.rs:314`, `store.rs:124` fixed values) and are not user-reachable with arbitrary values — only these two CLI paths are.

## Why it matters

A typo'd or script-generated `--seconds 99999999999999999999`-class value crashes the CLI with a Rust panic (exit 101, backtrace hint) instead of a clean "value too large" error, in one case after a successful connect/join and in the other after the initial sync. It is the same unchecked-seconds shape the fleet has been filing in mcpx (#2231/#2351/#2368), here in the id CLI's own argument surface.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `id world logs --seconds 18446744073709551615` no longer panics: it is either refused at parse time with a message naming `--seconds`, or clamped to a documented maximum deadline.
- [ ] `id world mirror --timeout-secs 18446744073709551615` no longer panics at `world_records.rs:218` (same rule: refuse or clamp, naming `--timeout-secs`).
- [ ] The chosen rule is applied consistently at both sites (one shared helper or identical clap `value_parser` range), and the maximum is documented in the `--help` text or the error message.
- [ ] Regression tests: a unit test for the clamp/refusal at the boundary value, and existing `world logs` / `world mirror` argument-parsing tests still pass.
- [ ] Normal values are unchanged: `--seconds 5` (default) and `--timeout-secs 30` (default) behave exactly as before.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for "world logs", "logs seconds", "Instant overflow": no covering issue. #2125 (peers `--depth=-1`) is a different argument/mechanism; #2231/#2351/#2368 are mcpx (TypeScript) duration ceilings in other code paths.

body:
🤖 **Agent note** · design architect (repo-design-architect-code), pass 15, 2026-10-29
- **Design doc:** `files/designs/code-mcpx-completion-rate-limit-ranking.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace
- **Origin:** the two remaining conformance gaps under dezren39/nix#213 — `completion-security` and `completion-server-should` in `pkgs/mcpx/internal/conformance/coverage_utilities.go:102-103`. nix#213 itself is CLOSED in nix; its main bug (completion ignoring ref) has landed. No code-side origin issue exists for the remainder, so this design originates it. Audited against origin/main `5a34fa70`.

## Summary

`completion/complete` is mcpx's cheapest-looking and most expensive request: every call acquires a pool lease and may wake an upstream process, and completion is the request a client sends once per keystroke. Nothing bounds that rate, and the one answer mcpx composes itself — the cached-names fallback for upstreams that never declared `completions` — comes back in alphabetical order with prefix-only matching, where the spec asks for relevance ranking and fuzzy matching where appropriate.

**The design, in one paragraph:** both surfaces converge on one handler — MCP `completion/complete` (`internal/mcpserver/server.go:2573`) delegates to `mcpBackend.Complete` (`internal/cli/serve.go:992`), which forwards via `POST /v1/complete` "so the two surfaces give the same answer", landing in the daemon's `handleComplete` (`internal/daemon/ops.go:333`). So: **one fixed-window in-memory limiter at `handleComplete`, consulted after shape validation and before any pool acquisition** (a refused request must never wake an upstream — that churn is the cost being limited), keyed per (caller, configured server name) + per server, settings `completion.perMinute` (default 120) / `completion.serverPerMinute` (default 600), `0` disables, count-on-admission; refusal is HTTP 429 on /v1 naming the limit, reaching MCP clients as a named `-32603` (the #1834 expiry precedent). And **relevance ranking for the local fallback only** (`localCompletion`, `ops.go:402`): exact → prefix (shorter first) → substring tier; upstream answers pass through in upstream order untouched — the upstream owns relevance and its `total`/`hasMore` meaning.

## Evidence highlights

- No rate-limit machinery exists anywhere in `pkgs/mcpx/internal` (grep finds only the gap rows); `handleComplete` goes straight from validation to `p.Complete(...)` (`ops.go:367`) → pool lease (`internal/pool/request.go:60`).
- `localCompletion` matches with `hasPrefixFold` (case-insensitive prefix, `ops.go:590`) over pool-cached prompts sorted by name (`internal/pool/pool.go:915`) — the register's "sorted alphabetically" is exact; its "matched by substring" is stale (prefix-only is the opposite failure: mid-name typing finds nothing). Phase 3 corrects the wording.
- Input validation (the other clause of both spec rows) already exists at both layers — not part of the remaining gap.
- Settings precedent: `completion.maxValues` already lives in the `completion.*` namespace (`internal/settings/wire.go:185`).

## Phases

1. **Phase 1** — rate limit at the choke point: limiter + settings + `handleComplete` integration before pool acquisition + refusal shapes + tests. (Filed as a sub-issue.)
2. **Phase 2** — relevance-ranked local completion: tiered ranking + substring tier in `localCompletion`; upstream pass-through untouched. Independent of Phase 1. (Filed as a sub-issue.)
3. **Phase 3** — register truth-up: retire both gap rows (the security row goes to *partial* with the principals dependency recorded — per-caller access control waits on #1968/#1972 and this design does not pretend otherwise), correct the substring wording, update requirements/matrix notes. Gated on Phases 1–2. (Filed as a sub-issue.)

## Alternatives recorded in the doc

Two limiters (mcpserver + daemon) — double-counts MCP, misses the shared budget; limiter in the pool — sees a session key, not a caller; re-ranking upstream answers — destroys context-aware upstream ordering; token bucket / x/time/rate — new dependency, second limiter shape beside #2333's fixed windows; client debounce — a caller SHOULD, not the server-side MUST.

## Open questions (in the doc, not filed)

Per-caller access control over sensitive suggestions (waits on #1968/#1972); a shared dedicated rate-limit error code with #2333's limiter if one is ever coined; whether #1554's `tasks-rate-limit` gap reuses this limiter type (the type must not be completion-shaped); in-flight request coalescing only on fleet evidence.

This issue is the design record. Implementation lives in its sub-issues; please do not implement from this issue directly.


## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Phase 1 (#2387) landed: completion rate limit enforced at the /v1 choke point with completion.* settings, refusal before any pool acquisition
- [ ] Phase 2 (#2388) landed: local completion answers relevance-ranked (exact → prefix → substring); upstream answers pass through unranked
- [ ] Phase 3 (#2389) landed: conformance register truthful — both #213 gap rows retired/moved to partial with the #1968/#1972 reason recorded
- [ ] This issue's own truth-up comment summarises what landed per phase against this design

title: id(web/markdown): heading level is truncated to u8 before the 1-6 clamp — level 256 saves as H1, 261 as H5

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

In `json_to_ast`'s heading arm (`pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs:1782-1790`), the ProseMirror heading level is truncated to `u8` **before** it is clamped to the valid 1–6 range:

```rust
#[allow(clippy::cast_possible_truncation)] // level is clamped to 1-6
let level = json["attrs"]["level"].as_u64().unwrap_or(1) as u8;
NodeValue::Heading(comrak::nodes::NodeHeading {
    level: level.clamp(1, 6),
    …
```

The comment's reasoning is wrong for any level ≥ 256: the `as u8` cast wraps first, so the clamp then operates on the wrapped value, not the author's level. The clamp only does what the comment claims for levels 0–255.

This converter runs on the save path: `convert_doc_to_bytes` (`pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs:2050-2053`) feeds the client-supplied document JSON through `prosemirror_to_markdown` for every `.md` save. A document whose heading node carries `attrs.level` ≥ 256 — a crafted or buggy editor client, a collab peer's document, or an imported/forwarded PM JSON — is silently saved at a wrong heading level: a level-256 heading becomes H1, level 261 becomes H5, level 512 becomes H1. Nothing errors; the document's structure is quietly rewritten.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `5a34fa70`)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneB-headlvl/`, the two lines copied verbatim):

```
level 1    -> 1      level 7    -> 6 (clamp works)
level 3    -> 3      level 100  -> 6
level 6    -> 6      level 255  -> 6
                     level 256  -> 1 (expected 6)
                     level 257  -> 1 (expected 6)
                     level 261  -> 5 (expected 6)
                     level 512  -> 1 (expected 6)
                     level 1000 -> 6 (only by accident: 1000 mod 256 = 232, clamped)
absent     -> 1
```

## Why it matters

The clamp exists precisely so out-of-range levels degrade predictably to the nearest valid heading. The truncation defeats it for the largest inputs — the ones most in need of clamping — and does so silently on a save path, permanently rewriting the stored markdown at a wrong level. It is also a misleading-comment hazard: the `#[allow]` annotation tells future readers the cast is safe because of the clamp, which is only true below 256.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The level is clamped in the `u64` domain before any narrowing cast (e.g. `.clamp(1, 6) as u8`), so every level ≥ 6 saves as H6 and 0/absent still save as H1.
- [ ] Regression tests cover levels 0, 6, 7, 255, 256, 261, and a large value (e.g. 1000 / `u64::MAX`) through `prosemirror_to_markdown` or `json_to_ast`.
- [ ] The `cast_possible_truncation` allow comment is corrected to match the actual order of operations.
- [ ] No behaviour change for levels 1–6 or for documents without a heading level.

title: aggregator(readJsonBody): the 100 KB body cap runs after req.text() buffers the whole body — oversized and drip-fed POSTs are fully read before any rejection

labels.name: task/triage

labels.name: app/pm-stack

body:
## Problem

`readJsonBody` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/server.ts:183-187`) checks the body size only *after* buffering the entire body in memory:

```ts
async function readJsonBody(req: Request): Promise<unknown> {
  const text = await req.text();
  if (text.length > 100_000) throw new Error("body too large");
  return JSON.parse(text);
}
```

The 100,000-character cap is the aggregator's only stated body limit, but it runs after `req.text()` has already read the whole request into a string. There is no `Content-Length` pre-check, no streaming/byte-counting read, and `Bun.serve` is configured with no `maxRequestBodySize` (server.ts:809-815). A client can therefore make the server buffer a body orders of magnitude larger than the cap on every write route — the cap costs the memory it was meant to save before it fires.

All five POST write routes go through this helper:
- `POST /api/comments` (server.ts:327)
- `POST /api/comments/triage` (server.ts:344)
- `POST /api/comments/github-result` (server.ts:353)
- `POST /api/actions` (server.ts:371)
- `POST /api/actions/result` (server.ts:405)

## Evidence (verified this run, main `5a34fa70`)

- Code order is unambiguous: `await req.text()` (line 184) completes before the `text.length > 100_000` check (line 185). The length of an already-buffered string is the only measurement taken.
- Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-aggbody/probe.ts`, Bun 1.4.2) running a verbatim copy of `readJsonBody` behind `Bun.serve`, instrumented to record `text.length` after `req.text()` returns:
  - Single 5,000,000-char POST → `status=400 {"error":"body too large"}`, but `serverReadLength=5000000`: the server buffered 50× the cap before rejecting.
  - Drip-fed body (200,000 chars, 700 ms pause, then 200,000 more) → after the pause `serverReadLength=null` (no early rejection; server still buffering), final `status=400` with `serverReadLength=400000`. A slow client holds the buffered prefix — and the connection — with no deadline or early abort from the cap.
  - Small valid JSON body (7 chars) → `status=200`, parsed normally.
- A missing or lying `Content-Length` cannot save this either: `req.text()` reads chunked/streamed bodies the same way, as the drip test shows.

## Why it matters

The aggregator is a long-lived dashboard process on the laptop serving the comment/action write paths the fleet itself polls and posts to. Concurrent oversized POSTs multiply the buffered memory (each request buffers its full body before any rejection), and a drip-fed body is never cut off early. The intended 100 KB contract exists in the code but is not enforced at read time, so it provides no protection — only a late error message.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The body limit is enforced *while reading*: a body over 100,000 bytes/chars is rejected without the full body being buffered (e.g. `Content-Length` pre-check where present plus a streaming read that aborts as soon as the accumulated size crosses the cap, or an explicit `Bun.serve` `maxRequestBodySize` set at/below the intended limit in addition to the post-read check).
- [ ] Oversized bodies still get the existing 400 + `body too large`-class error shape on all five POST routes; a body delivered in chunks (no trustworthy `Content-Length`) is rejected as soon as it crosses the cap, not after the stream ends.
- [ ] Bodies at/under the cap, including valid JSON posted to `/api/comments` and `/api/actions`, behave exactly as today.
- [ ] Regression tests: oversized single-shot POST, oversized chunked/drip POST (assert rejection before the stream completes / bounded buffered size), and an at-cap body that succeeds.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `readJsonBody`, "body too large" + aggregator, and aggregator request-body terms (2026-10-29): no covering issue. #2082 is mcpx's daemon routes bypassing its configured body limits — a different codebase and mechanism; the favicon finding in openchamber (#817) is likewise a read-then-cap pattern in a different repo/component.

body:
# mcpx(pool/mcpclient): upstream `ttlMs` cache hint has no ceiling — huge values pin the catalogue for decades, larger ones wrap the Duration and make it instantly stale

## Summary

The pool catalogue cache honours a modern upstream's `ttlMs` hint (#1601/#1602) with no ceiling and no overflow guard at either boundary where the server-controlled value enters:

1. **Merge (client):** `pkgs/mcpx/internal/mcpclient/client.go:215-224` — `CacheHints.merge` folds each page's `ttlMs` (JSON `int64`, declared at client.go:230, :272, :279, :1355) into the aggregate verbatim: the smallest declared value wins, with no range check of any kind.
2. **Deadline (pool):** `pkgs/mcpx/internal/pool/pool.go:928-948` — `consider()` takes `eff = h.TTLMs` whenever `TTLMs > 0`, and the deadline is computed as `fetchedAt.Add(time.Duration(minTTL) * time.Millisecond)` (pool.go:948). The freshness gate at pool.go:829 (`time.Now().Before(p.schemaDeadline)`) then trusts that deadline directly, and the deadline also flows to the disk-seed path (pool.go:1025).

## Verified behaviour (this run, real pool + real era test server)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneB-cachettl/`, a copy of `pkgs/mcpx` whose `pool.go` / `client.go` / `cachettl_test.go` are md5-identical to main `5a34fa70`; probe tests added in `internal/pool/probe_cachettl_test.go` on top of the existing `cachettl_test.go` harness, `ERAMCP_TTL_MS` declared by the test server on every list result):

| Server `ttlMs` | Meaning | Observed |
|---|---|---|
| `1000000000000` (1e12 ms) | ~31.7 years | 3 `Schemas()` calls → **1** `tools/list` call: catalogue served from cache for ~31.7 years, no ceiling ever re-checks it |
| `18446744073710` ms | ~584 years | `time.Duration(ms) * time.Millisecond` wraps to ~448µs: after a 10 ms sleep the second `Schemas()` call refetched (**2** `tools/list` calls) — a server asking for centuries gets a sub-millisecond cache |
| `10000000000000` (1e13 ms) | ~317 years | Duration wraps **negative** (deadline in the distant past): every `Schemas()` call refetches (**2** calls for 2 calls) — the catalogue is permanently instantly-stale and the upstream is hammered with list calls on every read |

All existing `cachettl_test.go` cases still pass (0 / −5 / absent → immediately stale; 60000 → cached; 120 → expires). Those tests cover only small values — nothing at or above any plausible ceiling, and nothing in the overflow range (> ~9.22e12 ms, where `Duration(ms) * Millisecond` exceeds int64 nanoseconds).

## Why it matters

- `ttlMs` is **server-controlled**: any modern upstream mcpx connects to — including a buggy or hostile one — picks the value. A buggy server emitting a huge TTL silently freezes the tool/resource/prompt catalogue (new or removed tools never appear; only `list_changed` invalidation or a restart unsticks it). A server emitting a value in the wrap range turns the cache into a no-op, so every catalogue read becomes three upstream list calls — the opposite failure, and just as silent.
- Both directions fail **silently**: no log, no clamp, no error — the deadline is simply wrong by decades or by sign.
- This is the same unchecked-server-duration shape as #2368 (SSE `retry`), but a different field, file, and failure: that one stalls a reconnect wait; this one corrupts catalogue freshness in both directions. #2351/#2327 are per-request/operator TTLs on the daemon side, also distinct.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A declared `ttlMs` above a documented ceiling is clamped (or treated as the ceiling) before it reaches the pool deadline — the ceiling's value and site (merge vs pool) are the fix's design call, recorded on the PR.
- [ ] No `ttlMs` value a server can send (up to int64 max) can produce a wrapped/negative or past deadline via the `time.Duration(ms) * time.Millisecond` conversion.
- [ ] New tests in the `cachettl_test.go` style cover: a huge-but-representable TTL (e.g. 1e12 ms), a wrap-range TTL (e.g. 1e13 ms and/or 18446744073710), asserting bounded, sane freshness behaviour in both cases.
- [ ] Existing behaviour is preserved: 0 / negative / absent → immediately stale; ordinary positive TTLs honoured as today (existing `TestPoolCacheTTL*` tests pass unmodified).
- [ ] `go test ./internal/pool/ ./internal/mcpclient/` passes.

## Related

- #1601 / #1602 — the design + Phase 1 that introduced honouring `ttlMs`/`cacheScope`; neither mentions a ceiling or overflow (checked this run).
- #2368 — SSE retry interval, same unchecked-duration family, different field/site/consequence.
- #2351, #2327 — daemon-side TTL ceilings, distinct values and stores.

title: id(repl): interactive find --dir selection fetches every selected blob twice — once to the directory file, once dumped to stdout

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Summary

In the `id` REPL, interactively selecting matches from a `find`/`search` result with `--dir` fetches every selected blob **twice**: once to the file inside the requested directory, and once again to **stdout**. The user asked for files in a directory; they also get the blobs' full contents (binary included) dumped to their terminal, and in connected mode every blob crosses the network twice.

## Evidence (main `5a34fa70`)

`pkgs/id/src/repl/runner.rs`, `select_and_output_matches_filtered`, the `dir` branch (lines 1128–1142):

```rust
for n in &selections {
    let (_, m) = &filtered_matches[n - 1];
    let output_path = format!("{}/{}", dir_path, m.name)
    if let Err(e) = ctx.get(&m.name, Some(&output_path)).await {
        println!("error: {e}");
    }
    if let Err(e) = ctx.get(&m.name, Some("-")).await {   // <-- second, unconditional fetch
        println!("error: {e}");
    }
}
```

- `Some("-")` is the stdout destination: `ReplContext::get` documents `"-"` as stdout (`pkgs/id/src/commands/repl.rs:539`), and the sibling branches of the same function treat the modes as alternatives — `to_file` fetches only to the file, the default branch fetches only to `"-"`. Only the `dir` branch does both.
- The `--all` counterpart, `output_all_matches_filtered` (`runner.rs:1014`), shows the intended `--dir` shape: fetch to the file only, then print the match line — no content dump.
- In connected mode each `get` is a full round trip (`commands/repl.rs:550 ff.`): a `MetaRequest::Get`, a blob fetch over `BLOBS_ALPN`, and an export — so the second call doubles transfer as well as output.
- The double call is longstanding (present before the 723e4f08 reformat, per `git log -L`).

## Verification (this run)

Verbatim-logic probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneA-dirselect/`): the branch copied line-for-line from main `5a34fa70` with `ctx.get` replaced by a recording mock of the same call shape. Results:

- Selection `[1]` with `--dir downloads` → **2** get calls: `get("report.bin", Some("downloads/report.bin"))` then `get("report.bin", Some("-"))`.
- Selection `[1, 2]` → **4** get calls (2 files × 2).

## Why it matters

`find --dir` + interactive selection is a bulk-download flow. Dumping every selected blob to stdout corrupts the terminal for binary content, leaks file contents into scrollback/logs the user never asked to print, and doubles the network and store work for every selection. The `--all --dir` path proves the dump is not the designed behavior for directory downloads.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] In `select_and_output_matches_filtered`'s `dir` branch, each selected match is fetched exactly once, to its file in the requested directory; nothing is written to stdout except the usual status/match lines.
- [ ] Behavior of the other branches is unchanged: `to_file` fetches once to the output file, the default branch fetches once to stdout.
- [ ] A regression test (recording/fake `get` or an extracted output loop) pins one fetch per selected match in `--dir` mode, matching the probe cases above.
- [ ] Existing id crate tests still pass (laptop or CI).

## Dedup

- #1999 (open) covers the same function's selection *parser* (silently dropped tokens, duplicate numbers fetched twice — its acceptance is parser strictness/dedup). It does not cover this: a single, valid, non-duplicate selection in `--dir` mode still fetches twice, once to stdout. Fixing #1999 alone leaves this bug; fixing this alone leaves #1999.
- #2307 (open) covers the *paths* these same calls write to (match names verbatim, #1614 confinement) — orthogonal to the extra stdout fetch.
- Searched open + recently closed issues for "dir stdout twice double fetch select_and_output" — no match.

Found by new-issue-creator lane A (`new-issue-creator-code-a`), 2026-10-29 run.

body:
# aggregator(comments+actions): one store record that passes the load filter but lacks a string `createdAt` crashes every comments/actions read — and persist() re-writes the poisoned record forever

**Scope note:** this covers BOTH dashboard JSON stores, which share the identical load-filter/sort code shape — `CommentsStore` (comments.ts) and `ActionsStore` (actions.ts:434-463, same id-only filter at :438-440, same `createdAt.localeCompare` sort at :463, same persist re-write). Both probes below were run against both stores with identical results. One fix, one issue.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 5a34fa70)

`pm-stack/aggregator/src/comments.ts`:

- `CommentsStore.doLoad()` (comments.ts:114-124) filters the on-disk records with a single check — `typeof c.id === "string"` (comments.ts:118-120). Every other field a record needs is accepted unchecked.
- `all()` (comments.ts:149) then unconditionally calls `a.createdAt.localeCompare(b.createdAt)` on every loaded record. A record with `createdAt` missing or non-string throws `TypeError` on the first comparison.
- Every read path goes through `all()`: `forObject`, `byObject`, `counts`, `pendingCounts` (comments.ts:153-196), and the server's `/api/comments.json` handler (server.ts:436/440). `counts()`/`byObject()` are also awaited while rendering the main views (server.ts:270, 288-289), so the throw is not confined to the comments endpoints.
- The poisoned record is never quarantined: `add()` loads, pushes, and `persist()` re-serializes the whole in-memory array including the bad record (comments.ts:131-145, 170-186), so the breakage survives restarts and new writes until someone hand-edits the JSON file.

Probe (sandbox Bun, real `CommentsStore` imported from main, temp files):

- control (one well-formed record): `all()` OK, counts correct.
- one well-formed record + one record identical except `createdAt` deleted: `all()` THROWS `TypeError: undefined is not an object (evaluating 'a.createdAt.localeCompare')`.
- `createdAt: 123` (number): `all()` THROWS `TypeError: a.createdAt.localeCompare is not a function`.
- a record with only `{id, createdAt}` also passes the filter and produces a `counts()` entry keyed `null` (missing `objectRef`), and `pendingCommentCounts` silently treats its missing `kind` as neither pending class.

## Why it matters

The comments file is a hand-inspectable JSON store in the aggregator's data directory, and the load filter exists precisely to tolerate records the current build didn't write (older/newer writers, partial hand edits, a restore from backup — cf. the #1509 load-race history in the same file). Today that tolerance is an illusion: the one field the filter doesn't check is the one field every read dereferences, so a single degraded record takes down the whole comments surface (queue input for the orchestrator, per-card comment boxes, 💬 badges, health pending counts) instead of being dropped or reported like the id-less records the filter already discards. Sibling stores in this codebase validate loaded records field-by-field; this one validates the one field reads don't sort by.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Load-time validation checks the fields reads actually use (at minimum `id`, `objectRef`, `kind`, `createdAt` as an ISO string; author/body per the DashComment shape), and records failing it are excluded from the in-memory set (dropped or quarantined with a logged count — triage pins which), matching the existing id-filter precedent.
- [ ] `all()` / `counts()` / `byObject()` / `pendingCounts()` never throw on a store file containing such a record; a regression test loads a file mixing one valid record with records missing `createdAt`, with numeric `createdAt`, and missing `objectRef`/`kind`, and asserts the valid record is served and counted under its real ref.
- [ ] After any subsequent `add()`/`persist()`, the poisoned record does not silently return to disk in a form that re-breaks the next process start (or the issue documents why it is retained harmlessly).
- [ ] Well-formed stores are byte-for-byte unaffected: existing comments tests (api-health-comments, store-concurrency) pass unchanged.

Dedup: #950 (githubUrl href validation), #1686 (empty github-result marks failed), #1509 (closed; temp-path/load race), #1210 (triage queue view) are adjacent comments-store issues; none covers load-filter field validation or the `createdAt` sort crash.

labels.name: task/triage

labels.name: source/creator

body:
# mcpx(pool): keyPIDAlive treats an EPERM pid as dead — pid-scoped instances for a live foreign-owned caller are reaped, never replaced, and skipped on restart

## Summary

`keyPIDAlive` (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/pool/pool.go:1238-1248`) decides whether the
process named by a pid-scoped instance key still exists:

```go
proc, err := os.FindProcess(pid)
if err != nil {
    return false
}
return proc.Signal(syscall.Signal(0)) == nil
```

`Signal(0)` returns **EPERM** when the process exists but belongs to another
user. This helper treats any error as "dead", so a live caller owned by a
different user reads as exited. The daemon already has the correct version of
this exact check — `ProcessAlive` (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/paths.go:302-312`):

```go
if pid <= 0 {
    return false
}
...
err = proc.Signal(syscall.Signal(0))
return err == nil || errors.Is(err, syscall.EPERM)
```

The two helpers disagree on precisely the cross-user case, and the pool is the
one that acts destructively on the answer.

## Where the wrong answer lands (all on current main, 5a34fa70)

1. **Reaper** — `pool.go:1218`: `orphaned := in.holders == 0 && p.cfg.Scope.WatchesPID() && !keyPIDAlive(in.key)`
   → the instance is stopped immediately (not after the idle timeout) even
   though its caller is alive.
2. **No replacement** — `internal/pool/execwatch.go:253` (`replaceable`):
   a retired child for that caller gets no replacement.
3. **Restart skip** — `pool.go:1426-1429`: restart skips the key with the error
   text `owning process has exited` — a false statement in the EPERM case.

The caller pid itself is client-supplied and unvalidated for ownership:
`internal/daemon/server.go:857-861` takes `X-Mcpx-Pid` verbatim into
`cc.PID`, and `ScopePid.Key` (`internal/config/scope.go:103-107`) keys the
instance `pid:<n>` for any `n > 0`. Cross-user is a real configuration for a
shared/system daemon serving per-user MCP clients — and even in the
single-user case, a client naming a system pid (e.g. 1) gets an instance that
can never survive the reaper.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneB-pidalive/` (Go module with
`PIDOf`, `keyPIDAlive`, and `ProcessAlive` copied verbatim; source files at
main 5a34fa70, md5 pool.go `007347aeca38d00f12eeb6024a68263a`, scope.go
`5ba59164fb560a0b95e928eaccc9cb18`, paths.go `1d922b391432f7e8275828d8b20da1b3`),
run unprivileged (uid 1337; pid 1 is root-owned and alive):

```
pid 1 (root-owned, alive, EPERM for unpriv caller)   keyPIDAlive=false ProcessAlive=true
own pid (alive, same owner)                          keyPIDAlive=true  ProcessAlive=true
dead pid                                             keyPIDAlive=false ProcessAlive=false
Signal(0) pid=1 err=operation not permitted (EPERM=true)
```

Checked and **not** part of this filing: pid 0 / pid -1 keys. The Rust id
analogue (#2142) is real because `kill(0, 0)` probes the caller's own process
group; in Go the os layer rejects both (`process not initialized` /
`process already released`), so `keyPIDAlive("pid:0")` and `("pid:-1")` both
return false in the same probe. Adding `ProcessAlive`'s `pid <= 0` guard for
parity is harmless but is not the bug.

## Why it matters

Pid scope exists to tie an instance's lifetime to its caller's. With the EPERM
blind spot, exactly the deployments where caller and daemon differ in uid —
the ones that most need the daemon to be conservative about killing instances —
get silent instance churn, unreplaced children, and restart output that
misreports a live process as exited, which sends diagnosis in the wrong
direction.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `keyPIDAlive` treats EPERM from `Signal(0)` as alive, matching
      `daemon.ProcessAlive` semantics for the same pid (or the pool calls one
      shared helper — triage pins which).
- [ ] Regression test: a pid that exists but is not signalable by the test
      process (or a seam/fake that injects EPERM) is reported alive; a dead
      pid is still reported dead; same-owner live pid unchanged.
- [ ] Restart no longer reports `owning process has exited` for an
      EPERM-only pid.
- [ ] No change to `daemon.ProcessAlive` / `PruneStale` behaviour (#278,
      closed) or to pid-scope key production.

## Dedup

`gh` searches (open + closed) for `keyPIDAlive`, `ProcessAlive`, `EPERM pid`,
`pool orphan pid alive`, `pid-scoped instance`: no filing covers the pool
helper. #2142 is the Rust `id` serve lock (different codebase, and its pid-0
arm does not transfer to Go — see Evidence). #278 (closed) was daemon-record
pruning via `ProcessAlive`, which already handles EPERM correctly.

body:
Design — filed by repo-design-architect-code pass 14, 2026-10-29. Origin: #2192 (split of #1957, ex-nix#257). Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-upstream-question-rate-limits.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. No `user/review`: #2192's acceptance is explicit and the judgment calls below are the architect's recorded decisions.

## Problem

An upstream MCP server can ask mcpx's client questions — sampling (`sampling/createMessage`: a model call or a person's review) and elicitation (`elicitation/create`: a person's attention) — at any rate. A buggy upstream loops; a hostile one floods the broker with questions, each holding a TTL and a slot in every watching UI. The spec's security considerations say clients **SHOULD** implement rate limiting for both features; mcpx's conformance register records both as gaps (`internal/conformance/coverage_clientfeatures.go:118-119`): sampling has "no per-server or per-session limit", elicitation "no per-server limit" — the only bounds today are per-request (`proto.askRounds` = 8) and per-question TTL. #2192 names the work and its acceptance but leaves the mechanism open; this design records it and adopts #2192 as Phase 1 instead of filing a parallel.

## Recorded decisions

1. **One limiter, at `Client.answer`** (`internal/mcpclient/modern.go:288`) — the single dispatch both eras reach (legacy via `handleServerRequest`, client.go:607; 2026 via `resolveInput`, modern.go:377). Enforced at entry, for `sampling/createMessage` and `elicitation/create` only, before the handler: an over-limit question never reaches the handler, the broker, or a person.
2. **Keyed by the configured server, never the claimed one.** Per-server bucket keyed by the pool's `cfg.Name`, pool-owned and passed via a new `mcpclient.Options` field; `ServerInfo.Name` is self-reported and is never a key. Per-session bucket is a field on `Client` (one Client = one session). Non-pool clients degenerate to per-session only — recorded, acceptable.
3. **A question counts when admitted, once** — whether later answered, declined or expired (the bounded resource is spent on the asking). Refusals count against neither bucket. Each 2026 `inputRequests` entry counts separately; `askRounds` still bounds rounds underneath.
4. **Fixed per-minute windows, in memory, no new dependency** (no limiter exists in-tree and `x/time/rate` is not in go.mod). Windows reset with the daemon; nothing persists.
5. **Settings in the `proto.*` family** (following `proto.askRounds`/`proto.askTTL`): `proto.samplingPerMinute` default 60 (per server), `proto.samplingSessionPerMinute` default 20, `proto.elicitationPerMinute` default 30; ScopeDaemon ints; 0 disables that bound.
6. **Refusal is a named -32603 error, never a fabricated answer**: `rpcError` -32603 with a message naming the limit, plus the refusal emitted via `c.warn` — following design #1834's "expiry stays -32603 named" precedent (the spec assigns no rate-limit code). For elicitation the refusal is the JSON-RPC error, NOT `{action: "cancel"}` — nobody declined; #2192 requires clear failure, not a silent drop.

## Phases

- **Phase 1 (ADOPTED — #2192):** the limiter + the three settings + enforcement at `answer` per decisions 1–6, with #2192's named tests (burst refused, under-limit passes, per-server isolation) plus per-session isolation and the modern `input_required` path. #2192 already carries `queue/queued` with a triage packet in flight — triage records this phase structure instead of re-scoping or splitting it.
- **Phase 2 (filed, gated on Phase 1):** register truth-up — retire the two gap rows in `coverage_clientfeatures.go`, update the `requirements.json` client notes, verify the conformance-matrix rows, and post evidence on tracker #1957 closing its rate-limits cluster.

## Alternatives rejected (detail in the design doc)

Broker-side enforcement (misses non-broker handlers and the modern in-client path); pool-side enforcement (server-initiated requests are only visible inside `Client`); token bucket (flood bound, not burst shaping; no new dependency); delay/queue instead of refuse (stale questions, invisible stalls, teaches a looping upstream nothing).

## Explicitly out of scope

The server-side `tasks-rate-limit` gap (`coverage_stateful.go:120`, citing #209) — the other side of the protocol; it belongs to design #1554's operational-limits open question. Daemon-originated `/v1/ask` questions from local scripts — bounding those waits on the principals work (#1968/#1972).

<!-- agent-note:v1 — Design filed by repo-design-architect-code pass 14, 2026-10-29. Origin #2192 is adopted as Phase 1; Phase 2 is a sub-issue of this design. Decision is recorded here and in the design doc. -->

## Acceptance criteria

- A per-server rate limiter for upstream sampling/elicitation questions exists at the mcpx client choke point, keyed by the configured server, per the recorded decisions.
- The conformance register entries (internal/conformance/coverage_clientfeatures.go:118-119) are updated from gap to implemented with the limits named.
- #2192 (adopted as Phase 1 by this design) is updated with the implementation link, and its acceptance is checked off or carried into a follow-up issue.

body:
## Summary

`entryFromResult` in the quota gatherer (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-gather-map.ts:173-177`) converts a provider result's `fetchedAt` epoch-ms value with `new Date(result.fetchedAt).toISOString()` after checking only `typeof === "number"` and `Number.isFinite`. A finite value outside the JS Date range (max ±8.64e15 ms) makes `new Date(...)` an Invalid Date, and `.toISOString()` on it throws `RangeError: Invalid Date`. Because the gatherer maps every result for a provider in one `.map()` call, that one bad result discards the provider's whole tick.

The same file already knows this guard: `normalizeResetAt` (quota-gather-map.ts:44-49) checks `Number.isNaN(d.getTime()) ? null : d.toISOString()` for window `resetAt` values — `fetchedAt` is the one conversion in the file left unguarded.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `5a34fa70`)

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-gather-map.ts:173-177` — `measuredAt` is `typeof result.fetchedAt === "number" && Number.isFinite(result.fetchedAt) ? new Date(result.fetchedAt).toISOString() : tickIso`. The `tickIso` fallback exists for missing/non-finite values, but a finite out-of-range value takes the throwing branch instead of the fallback.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/gather-quota.ts:199` — `const entries = results.map((r) => entryFromResult(r, tickIso))` runs inside `runProvider`'s try/catch (~:196-215): a throw returns `{ state: "error", entries: [] }` for that provider, so every credential/window that provider returned correctly in the same tick is dropped with it.
- Probe (Bun, real `quota-gather-map.ts` imported from main, `/tmp/probe-laneB-fetchat/probe.ts`):
  - control `fetchedAt: 1793075143879` → OK, `measuredAt=2026-10-27T04:25:43.879Z`
  - `fetchedAt: 1e16` → **THREW RangeError Invalid Date**
  - `fetchedAt: 9e15` (just over the Date maximum) → **THREW RangeError**
  - `fetchedAt: -1e16` → **THREW RangeError**
  - batch map of [good result, `fetchedAt: 1e16` result] → **THREW — whole map lost**
  - in-file control: `normalizeResetAt(1e16)` → `null` (guarded, no throw)
- Secondary, same gate: `fetchedAt: 0` yields `measuredAt=1970-01-01…` instead of the tick fallback, so a zero stamp renders a fresh read as ~56 years old / instantly stale. (`normalizeResetAt` requires `v > 0`; `entryFromResult` has no such check.)

## Why it matters

`fetchedAt` is produced by the OpenChamber quota module, outside this repo — the mapper is exactly the boundary that is supposed to absorb a provider's bad stamp (its header, quota-gather-map.ts:1-15, promises a provider whose usage is not well-shaped "yields no windows (never zeros)", i.e. degrade per-entry, never fail the tick). Today one out-of-range stamp — e.g. a provider computing in microseconds or nanoseconds (1e16 is a plausible µs-scale value for 2026), or a corrupted upstream timestamp — turns a successful fetch into a provider-wide error entry every 15-minute tick until the provider is fixed, with the gatherer's error text (`RangeError: Invalid Date`) naming neither the provider field nor the value.

This is the same defect class as #2286 (`iso()` in the OpenCode session mapper), in a different module with a different data source and blast radius: there one bad session dropped a server's session feed; here one bad stamp drops a provider's quota tick.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `entryFromResult` never throws for any numeric `fetchedAt`: a finite value that does not produce a valid Date (out of range, or `<= 0`) falls back to `tickIso`, exactly as a missing/non-finite value already does.
- [ ] One result with a bad `fetchedAt` no longer discards the other results in the same provider batch — the bad entry is still produced (with the tick stamp), not dropped.
- [ ] Regression tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/quota-gather-map.test.ts` pin: `1e16`, `-1e16`, and `0` → `measuredAt === tickIso` with windows intact; the existing ms control (`1793075143879` → `2026-10-27T04:25:43.879Z`) is unchanged.
- [ ] No change to `normalizeResetAt`, the file-export path (`entryFromFileExport`, whose `measuredAt` parse is already NaN-gated), or the quota-current contract shape.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `quota-gather-map`, `entryFromResult`, `fetchedAt`, and `RangeError Invalid Date aggregator`: #2286 is the OpenCode session mapper (`sources/opencode.ts`), distinct file/source; #1624 is gatherer snapshot dedupe by credentialId, distinct; no filing covers the `entryFromResult` `fetchedAt` conversion. The 2026-10-29T10:58Z backlog check that cleared quota-gather-map covered `entryFromFileExport`'s NaN-gated `measuredAt` only.

body:
## Summary

`id`'s log-level resolution documents a default of `warn` but implements a default of `debug`, so every invocation with no `--debug`, no `--log-level`, and no log env vars runs with debug-level logging to stderr.

## Evidence (main at 5a34fa70)

- `pkgs/id/src/main.rs:15-24` — the `get_log_level` doc comment lists the priority order and states step "6. Default → `warn`".
- `pkgs/id/src/main.rs:47-49` — the actual step 6 in the same function is:

  ```rust
  // 6. Default to debug
  "debug".to_owned()
  ```

- `pkgs/id/src/main.rs:128-160` — the returned string is used verbatim as the base `EnvFilter` for `tracing_subscriber::fmt()` writing to stderr (only the listed noisy third-party modules are capped at `info`). So the implemented default is debug-level output from `id` itself and from every non-listed dependency, on every plain `id list` / `id repl` / `id serve` run.
- Nothing else overrides this: `pkgs/id/src/cli.rs:120-124` gives `--log-level` no default value, and `--debug` is documented as the opt-in equivalent of `--log-level debug` (`cli.rs:114-116`) — which is meaningless as an opt-in if debug is already the default.

Verified this run by reading the full path (CLI definition → `get_log_level` → filter construction) on current main; there is no test covering `get_log_level` (`main.rs` has no test module), so nothing pins either behaviour.

## Why it matters

- The documented and implemented defaults disagree inside one function; one of them is wrong and nobody can tell which from the code.
- If `warn` is intended: every default run pays debug-log volume on stderr (startup diagnostics from iroh/discovery at debug, interleaved with REPL/command output consumers may capture), and `--debug` is a no-op flag.
- If `debug` is intended: the doc header is a trap for anyone configuring logging from it, and the noise is a deliberate default that should be stated as such.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Triage pins the intended default (the doc's `warn`, or `debug` with the doc corrected and the `--debug` help updated to match).
- [ ] Code and the `get_log_level` doc comment agree on the full priority list, including the default.
- [ ] A test pins `get_log_level`'s resolution for the no-flag/no-env case (and ideally the flag > `RUST_LOG` > `LOG_LEVEL` > `DEBUG` ordering), so the default cannot silently flip again.

title: id(repl): find/search download paths use the match name verbatim — the #1614 confinement never reached the REPL copies (../ and absolute names overwrite arbitrary files)

labels.name: kind/security
labels.description: Security issue or security hardening

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

The `id` REPL's `find`/`search` file outputs build the local write path from the match's `name` **verbatim**. The confinement that closed #1614 — `download_output_path` in `commands/find.rs`, which reduces a match name to its final path component and refuses names with none — was applied only to the CLI handlers. The REPL has its own copies of the same path constructions, and they were never updated. A match named `/home/user/.bashrc` or `../victim.txt` is written, with blob content, wherever the name points — in connected mode both the name and the content come from the remote node being queried, exactly the #1614 threat model, through the interactive surface instead of the one-shot CLI.

Same defect family as #1614 (CLOSED) and #1595: a file name reaching a filesystem path with no working containment check. This issue covers the REPL copies only; the CLI sites are fixed.

## The chain (all on main `5a34fa70`)

1. **Names arrive unchecked.** In connected mode, `ReplContext::find` (`pkgs/id/src/commands/repl.rs`, `find` at ~:696) returns the remote node's `MetaResponse::Find` matches postcard-decoded as-is; `FindMatch.name` is a plain `String`. In local mode the names come from the local store, where blob rename still accepts traversal targets (#1621, open).
2. **Names become paths, five sites, all in `pkgs/id/src/repl/runner.rs`:**
   - `handle_find_command` single match (`:769`): `args.output_file.unwrap_or(&m.name)` — with `--file` and no explicit output name, the match name IS the path; absolute names land anywhere.
   - `handle_search_command` first match (`:834-835`): the same construction.
   - `output_all_matches_filtered` (`:1029`, used by find/search `--all --dir`): `format!("{}/{}", dir_path, m.name)` — `..` segments escape the requested directory.
   - `select_and_output_matches_filtered` with a directory (`:1131`): the same `"{dir}/{name}"` construction for interactively selected matches.
   - `select_and_output_matches_filtered` to-file (`:1142-1143`): `output_file.unwrap_or(&m.name)` — name verbatim again.
3. **The write performs no containment.** All five pass the path to `ReplContext::get` (`commands/repl.rs:550`), which calls `export_blob` (`pkgs/id/src/lib.rs:547`): `to_absolute` (`lib.rs:358`) prepends the cwd if relative, does not normalize `..`, and passes absolute paths through unchanged; iroh-blobs export then creates-or-truncates the target. Existing files are overwritten silently.
4. **The fixed helper is out of reach.** `download_output_path` (the #1614 fix) is a private function of `commands/find.rs`; the REPL never calls it. Contrast inside the REPL itself: `peek` fetches via a temp file (`runner.rs:1251`) — the safe shape already exists in this surface too.

## Verification (this run)

Verbatim-logic probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneA-replpath/`; the `runner.rs` constructions, `lib.rs`'s `to_absolute`, and the CLI's `download_output_path` copied character-for-character from main `5a34fa70`; writes use export's create-or-truncate semantics). Run 2026-10-29 ~12:16Z:

- **Default file output, name = an absolute path:** the pre-existing file at that path is overwritten with the blob bytes (`victim_now="ATTACKER-BYTES"`).
- **Default file output, name `../victim-rel.txt`:** the file one level above the cwd is overwritten (`"ATTACKER-BYTES"`).
- **`--all --dir downloads`, name `../victim-dir.txt`:** writes `downloads/../victim-dir.txt` — the file one level above the requested directory (`work/victim-dir.txt`) ends up containing `ATTACKER-BYTES`; the write escaped the directory the user named.
- **Control, name `plain.txt`:** written inside `downloads/` as intended.
- **Contrast — the CLI helper on the same names:** `download_output_path(Some("downloads"), "../victim-dir.txt") = Ok("downloads/victim-dir.txt")`, absolute name → final component only, and `..` / `/` are refused with a named error.

Candidate verified by code-reading in the 2026-10-29 07:05 CDT creator run; the probe was prepared by that run and executed by its follow-up run after the original ended early.

## Why it matters

The REPL is the interactive way to browse and pull files from a peer (`find`/`search` with `--file` or `--all --dir` are its documented download flows). The user names a query, not an output path; the match's name is invisible until after the write unless they list first. The overwrite target and content are both attacker-controlled in connected mode, bounded only by the user's filesystem permissions. The local variant matters too: any traversal name that lands in a store (#1621 — rename accepts one today) turns a later REPL `find --file` into the same escape.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A REPL find/search match name can never cause a write outside the location the user asked for, at all five sites (`runner.rs:769`, `:834-835`, `:1029`, `:1131`, `:1142-1143`): match-derived default paths are confined to the cwd tree (default mode) or the requested directory (`--dir` mode), covering `..`, nested `a/../../b`, absolute names, and names with no final component (refused with a named error, nothing written).
- [ ] The REPL and the CLI share ONE implementation of the final-component ruling (e.g. `download_output_path` moved somewhere both can call) — not a third copy of the rule that can drift again.
- [ ] The `--all --dir` collision behavior (two matches reducing to the same final component) is stated in the PR and matches the CLI behavior tracked in #2178, or is explicitly coordinated with it.
- [ ] The probe cases above are pinned as tests at the path-construction level (no network needed); ordinary names (plain basenames, spaces, Unicode) download exactly as today in all modes, local and remote.
- [ ] Output paths the user names explicitly (`--file <path>`, `> path`) remain the user's choice — only match-derived defaults are confined.

body:
## Problem

The fleet's standing rule is **plan quotas only, never PAYG** — but nothing enforces it at the config layer. In October 2026 that gap cost real money: OpenCode sessions burned **4,114,515 Workers AI neurons (~$44.95 estimated)** because a metered provider was selectable as a session model and sat in route fallbacks. The providers are disabled now; this issue makes the mistake structurally hard to repeat.

## Verified facts (Workers AI cost investigation, 2026-10-29)

- 99.2% of the burn was one model — `@cf/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4-pro-0813` — via the `cloudflare-gateway` provider in the laptop's OpenCode config, in a two-day burst Oct 24–25 (sessions under `~/work/id-train/`).
- Mechanism: every agent turn re-sent a ~200–500k-token context and Workers AI bills full input per call (336M cache-read tokens billed, not free).
- Workers AI is PAYG beyond 10k free neurons/day — there is no plan allowance to burn against, so it should never have been a workhorse/route target.
- Current state: `cloudflare-gateway`, `cloudflare-workers-ai`, and `cloudflare-ai-gateway` are all in `disabled_providers`; usage has been zero since Oct 25.

## Ask

Add a **config-level guard** on the canonical pool config (this repo's `.opencode/opencode.jsonc`, the config-canonical source) so a PAYG/metered provider cannot silently become a route target or default again:

- Maintain an explicit metered-provider designation (the `cloudflare-*` providers, plus any provider whose billing is per-call metered rather than a plan allowance).
- A schema/CI check that **fails** when a metered provider appears in route targets, fallbacks, or session defaults — unless the config carries an **explicit, visible exception marker** at that spot (so any future exception is a deliberate, reviewable act, not an accident).
- Document the exception mechanism in `ci-policy.md` or in the config itself.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The check fails on a fixture config naming `cloudflare-gateway` as a route fallback without an exception marker.
- [ ] The check passes on the current canonical config (Cloudflare providers disabled, no metered route targets).
- [ ] A fixture with a properly marked exception passes, and the marker format is documented in `ci-policy.md` or the config.
- [ ] The check runs in CI on changes to `.opencode/opencode.jsonc`.

Related: the companion collector alert issue (neurons/day threshold in `pm-stack/cloudflare-export/`) covers detection; this one covers prevention.

Workers AI is pay-as-you-go beyond the 10k free neurons/day allowance — it is not a plan pool. A same-day alert on the dataset the new collector already reads would have caught this on day one.

## Verified facts (Workers AI cost investigation, 2026-10-29)

- 4,114,515 neurons total for October; **99.2% on one model** — `@cf/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4-pro-0813` — reached via the `cloudflare-gateway` provider in the laptop's OpenCode config.

- Mechanism: every agent turn re-sent a ~200–500k-token context, and Workers AI bills the full input on every call — 336M cache-read tokens were processed and billed, not free.
- The three Cloudflare providers (`cloudflare-gateway`, `cloudflare-workers-ai`, `cloudflare-ai-gateway`) are now in `disabled_providers`; usage has been zero since Oct 25. This issue is about detection, not the (already stopped) burn.

## Ask

The Cloudflare collector (#1048, `pm-stack/cloudflare-export/`, PR #2228) already reads the `aiInference` dataset every 15 minutes, but it has **no threshold alert**. Add one:

- Compute Workers AI neurons/day from the same dataset the collector already ingests.
- When a day's total crosses a **configurable threshold (suggested default: >50k neurons/day** — 5× the free daily allowance, far below the 2.99M single-day burn), surface it loudly the same day through the collector's existing reporting path.
- Document the threshold, how to change it, and where the alert lands.

## Acceptance criteria

body:
Follow-up B from the Durable Object jurisdiction investigation on #2061
(doc: `doc/2026-10-29T11-43-02Z_investigation_do_jurisdiction_pinning/`, §2).

Parent epic: #2056. Context: #2044 (§6 shared worlds, §7 bridge), #2059 (hot-world sharding).

## The problem

A shared world is one Durable Object, and a Durable Object has **one** jurisdiction (`eu`, `us` or `fedramp`), fixed when the ID is created. Its writers do not share that jurisdiction: an `eu`-pinned user and a `us`-pinned user writing into the same world means one of them is writing outside their jurisdiction. The platform cannot fix this — it is a product decision.

## Questions to answer

1. **Partition or consent?** Either worlds are jurisdiction-partitioned (an `eu` world and a `us` world, no cross-participation, and the same world name resolves differently per jurisdiction — exactly as Durable Object names already do), or cross-jurisdiction participation is explicit, consented and disclosed. Both are defensible; the doc must pick one and say what it costs.
2. **What does a world's *participant list* reveal?** Even if content stays put, the DO holding the world learns which users participate. Is that metadata crossing a boundary?
3. **Blobs in a shared world.** Content-addressed blobs follow the user's R2 jurisdiction bucket, but a world's participants share world content. Which bucket holds world blobs, and what happens when a user from the other jurisdiction reads them?
4. **The bridge.** Native Iroh nodes are not jurisdiction-pinned at all. When a native node syncs with a hosted `eu` user, what residency claim survives?
5. **Federation and relay paths** (#2035, #2036): same question one layer down.

## Acceptance

body:
Follow-up A from the Durable Object jurisdiction investigation on #2061
(doc: `doc/2026-10-29T11-43-02Z_investigation_do_jurisdiction_pinning/`).

Parent epic: #2056. Context: #2044 (Cloudflare Workers fit), §3 and §7.

## What to design

Make the per-user hosted store **jurisdiction-aware from the first request**, without exposing a user-facing region choice yet.

1. **A `jurisdiction` field on the user record**, written at account creation (default `us`, policy constant), immutable in the app layer from the first Durable Object creation.
2. **One ID-derivation function** `userObjectId(sub, jurisdiction)` with **no default argument** — because `idFromName("google:"+sub)` and `jurisdiction("eu").idFromName("google:"+sub)` are different objects, a routing bug that drops the jurisdiction silently creates a second, empty user store (investigation §4.1).
3. **Restricted-namespace binding**: select `env.USERS.jurisdiction(<stored>)` at runtime rather than using the unrestricted binding, so a mismatched ID throws instead of working (the unrestricted namespace "will not run into an error").
4. **A `ctx.id.jurisdiction` assertion** on every identity-touching entry point, failing closed — including the two `undefined` cases (unrestricted namespace; alarm scheduled before 2026-03-15).
5. **R2 bucket per jurisdiction**, bound with the `jurisdiction` field repeated in `wrangler` config; content-addressed dedupe becomes jurisdiction-local.
6. **The shared D1 directory's residency story**: it has one jurisdiction for all users, so it must be data-minimal (hashed subject, public keys, public server records — never graph content) and documented as the single residency exception.
7. **The migration path** as a first-class state, not an ops script: `jurisdiction_pending` + export → create in target → import → verify → switch directory record → delete. Signatures survive unchanged.

## Out of scope

The user-facing region choice UI (design the field and routing now; ship the control when a customer needs it). Cross-jurisdiction shared worlds — that is follow-up B. Vendor-guarantee confirmation — follow-up C.

## Acceptance

- Design doc under `doc/` covering the seven points above, with the failure modes named.
- A concrete migration runbook sketch for a single account.
- Follow-on implementation issues for whatever is buildable.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Design doc under doc/ covers all seven numbered points in the body, with the silent-second-store failure mode (dropping jurisdiction in ID derivation) named and designed out
- [ ] The ctx.id.jurisdiction assertion covers both undefined cases and fails closed
- [ ] Migration path specified as a first-class state (jurisdiction_pending → export → create → import → verify → switch → delete)
- [ ] A single-account migration runbook sketch is included
- [ ] Follow-on implementation issues filed for the buildable parts

title: id(repl): find/search/show/peek parsers silently swallow unknown and mistyped flags — a typo'd flag vanishes and its value becomes a query

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The REPL's find/search/show/peek argument parsers silently swallow malformed flags. Both parsers return plain values (no `Result`), and any token they don't recognize is dropped without a word:

- `parse_find_args` — `pkgs/id/src/repl/runner.rs:627`; the fall-through at `:706` only collects tokens that do **not** start with `-`, so every unknown `-`-flag vanishes.
- `parse_peek_args` — `runner.rs:1162`; same fall-through at `:1234`.

## Verified behavior (laptop probe, verbatim parsers extracted from main `5a34fa70`, `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneB-replflags/`)

| Input | Result |
|---|---|
| `find report --bogus` | `queries=["report"]`, no error — flag silently gone |
| `find report --fist 2` (typo of `--first`) | `queries=["report", "2"]` — the typo'd flag is dropped **and its would-be value becomes a search query** |
| `find report --format yaml` | `format="yaml"` accepted verbatim; the match printers (`helpers.rs` `print_match_cli`/`print_matches_cli`, `print_match_repl`) fall through to the default format for any unknown value, so the user gets the default rendering with no hint their format was ignored |
| `find report --dir` / `--exclude` / `--format` (trailing, no value) | silently no-op (`runner.rs:659`, `:664`, `:701` guard on `i + 1 < rest.len()` and otherwise do nothing) |
| `find report >` | `output_file=Some("")`, `to_file=true` (`runner.rs:656` `strip_prefix('>')` accepts the empty path); the single-match path then calls `ctx.get(name, Some(""))` |
| `peek report --bogus`, `peek report -o`, `peek report --lines` | same silent drops in `parse_peek_args` |

Control: `find report --all` parses as expected (`all=true`).

## Why it matters

The REPL is the interactive surface of `id`. A mistyped flag doesn't just fail to apply — it can change the query set (`--fist 2` searches for `2`), redirect output to an empty path, or render a different format than asked, all silently. Users have no way to tell their command wasn't the command that ran. The CLI side (clap) rejects unknown flags loudly; the REPL should not be the silent exception.

Distinct from #2009 (non-numeric `--first`/`--last`/`--lines` values becoming queries — a value-consumption bug in the same functions): this issue is about tokens the parsers never recognize at all, value-flags missing their value, and the bare `>` redirect.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An unknown `-`-flag in find/search/show/peek REPL commands produces a visible error or usage message naming the flag (triage pins: hard error vs warning-and-continue), and never silently alters the query set.
- [ ] A value-flag (`--dir`, `--format`, `--exclude`, `-o`/`--output`, `--lines`/`-n`) with no following value is reported, not silently dropped.
- [ ] A bare `>` (empty redirect target) is reported instead of setting `output_file=Some("")`.
- [ ] `--format` with a value outside {tag, group, union} is reported (or the printers stop falling through silently — triage pins which layer owns this).
- [ ] Regression tests in `runner.rs` cover: unknown flag, typo'd flag with a following value, trailing value-flag, bare `>`, bad `--format` value; existing parser tests still pass.

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-b (Lane B), verified this run.

title: agy-proxy: bridge drops tool schemas — the workhorse-primary agy leg cannot execute tools and masks it as success (Codex P1 on #2200, now on main)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: effort/m
labels.description: Medium: expected under 1 day of work

labels.name: meta/enriched
labels.description: Intake review done: acceptance criteria, links, and normalized labels added

body:
## Defect

The agy bridge drops tool schemas: `bin/agy-proxy.mjs` formats only `body.messages`, never forwards the caller's offered tool schemas, and emits only content with `finish_reason: 'stop'` — so OpenCode can never receive structured tool calls through this leg, and because the responses look successful, no failover triggers. Tool-dependent workhorse jobs routed here silently cannot complete. Codex flagged this as a P1 on PR #2200 (the Gemini-burn PR, which added agy to the workhorse primary pool, sending roughly half of primary selections through this bridge). PR #2200 has since **merged (2026-10-29)**, so **this defect is on main today**.

## The Codex finding (verbatim, PR #2200)

> **Require tool-call support before adding agy to the primary pool**
>
> For workhorse tasks that need the caller's tools, this new leg routes roughly half of primary selections through a text-only bridge. `bin/agy-proxy.mjs` formats only `body.messages` (lines 865–867), never forwards the offered tool schemas, and emits only content with `finish_reason: 'stop'` (lines 1022–1028 and 1054–1060), so OpenCode cannot receive structured tool calls. These responses appear successful rather than triggering failover, leaving tool-dependent jobs unable to complete their work. Add tool-call translation to the bridge or keep this provider out of the primary pool until it supports it.

Finding: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/2200#discussion_r4410496158 (filed against `.opencode/opencode.jsonc` line 6626, PR #2200)

## Fix direction (as Codex prescribed)

Either add tool-call translation to `bin/agy-proxy.mjs` (forward tool schemas; translate model tool calls into OpenAI `tool_calls` with a truthful `finish_reason`), or keep this provider out of the workhorse primary pool until it supports it. Note #865 (closed) fixed the same defect class for the sibling `antigravity-ls-proxy`; this issue is the `agy-proxy` bridge specifically.

## Source

Codex review-value audit 2026-10-29 (`research_notes/codex-review-value-20261029/findings.md` §2, best catch #5): classified REAL-CATCH; PR #2200 merged 2026-10-29 with the finding unacted, so the defect is on main. Verification: defect confirmed present on main 2026-10-29.


## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The agy bridge forwards the caller's offered tool schemas and emits structured tool calls OpenCode can execute — or agy is removed from the workhorse primary pool until it does
- [ ] A tool-dependent workhorse job routed through the agy leg completes with real tool calls (evidence linked), and a text-only response can no longer masquerade as success for a tool-requiring request
- [ ] The masking is gone: when the bridge cannot honour tools, the response fails over instead of returning finish_reason 'stop' content

title: cold-store: hash/compress two-pass race seals objects whose manifest hash never matches their bytes — silently unrestorable backups (Codex P1 on #923, merged unacted)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: meta/enriched
labels.description: Intake review done: acceptance criteria, links, and normalized labels added

body:
## Defect

The cold-store reaper can seal an archive that can never be restored: hashing and compression read the source in two separate passes, so a file that changes between them is recorded in the manifest with the old hash but compressed with the new bytes. Upload verification passes and the object is marked `cold`, but every future `fetch` rejects the restored bytes with a SHA-256 mismatch. Codex flagged this as a P1 on PR #923; the PR merged without the finding being acted on. **Defect confirmed present on main 2026-10-29** (audit: REAL + never engaged + merged anyway).

## The Codex finding (verbatim, PR #923)

> **Hash and compress the same stable source snapshot**
>
> If a source file changes between `sha256_file(src)` and the separate read performed by zstd, the manifest records the old content hash while the bundle contains the new content. The subsequent upload verification still succeeds and marks that object `cold`, but `fetch` will always reject its restored bytes with a SHA-256 mismatch. This can silently create an unusable archive for actively written files. Hash and compress a stable snapshot, or verify that the compressed frame decodes to the recorded object hash before sealing.

Finding: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/923#discussion_r4372844010 (filed against `pkgs/cold-store-reaper/cold_store.py` line 392, PR #923)

## Fix direction (as Codex prescribed)

Hash and compress a single stable snapshot of the source, or verify that the compressed frame decodes to the recorded object hash before sealing the object as `cold`.

## Source

Codex review-value audit 2026-10-29 (`research_notes/codex-review-value-20261029/findings.md` §2, best catch #3): 636 Codex findings classified, this one REAL-CATCH, never engaged, PR merged anyway. Verification: defect confirmed present on main 2026-10-29.


## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Hash and compression consume one stable snapshot of the source (or the compressed frame is verified to decode to the recorded hash before sealing) — the two-pass race in the body can no longer seal a mismatched object
- [ ] A regression test mutates the source between the old pass points (or simulates it) and shows the object is either sealed consistently or refused, never sealed `cold` with a hash its bytes fail
- [ ] Objects already sealed mismatched, if any are identifiable, are reported on this issue rather than silently left
