body:
## Defect

The laptop repo-keeper's secret guard can be bypassed by directory nesting: the guard regex runs over collapsed `git status` output, so a credential file inside a wholly untracked directory (status shows only `?? config/`) is never matched — and the autocommit snapshot then commits and pushes it. Codex flagged this as a P1 on PR #1740 and reproduced it in a temp clone; the PR merged without the finding being acted on. **Defect confirmed present on main 2026-10-29** (audit: REAL + never engaged + merged anyway).

## The Codex finding (verbatim, PR #1740)

> **Check individual untracked paths in the secret guard**
>
> When a sensitive file is inside a wholly untracked directory, this status output can contain only the directory name, such as `?? config/`, so the regex never sees `config/credentials.json`. The subsequent snapshot commits the nested file despite the advertised secret-path guard. I reproduced this with a temporary `hatch` clone; the enabled autocommit script then pushed that snapshot. Inspect individual untracked paths, as the size check already does, rather than relying on collapsed status entries.

Finding: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/1740#discussion_r4403720975 (filed against `nixos/home/laptop-repo-keeper.sh` line 78, PR #1740)

## Fix direction (as Codex prescribed)

Inspect individual untracked paths in the secret guard — as the size check already does — rather than relying on collapsed status entries.

Related but distinct: #1751 (laptop-untracked-review bare `git commit` sweeping pre-staged work) is a different mechanism in a sibling script; this issue is only the keeper secret-guard bypass.

## Source

Codex review-value audit 2026-10-29 (`research_notes/codex-review-value-20261029/findings.md` §2, best catch #2): 636 Codex findings classified, this one REAL-CATCH, never engaged, PR merged anyway. Verification: defect confirmed present on main 2026-10-29.

title: security(pm-aggregator): reflected XSS — decoded /item/<subject> interpolated unescaped into the not-found HTML response (Codex P1 on #856, still on main)

labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Defect

Reflected XSS in the PM aggregator: for an unknown `/item/<subject>` URL, the decoded subject is interpolated unescaped into the HTML not-found response. Codex flagged this as a P1 on PR #856; the PR merged without the finding being acted on, and the defect is **confirmed present on main 2026-10-29** (audit spot-check: `pm-stack/aggregator/src/server.ts` on main still interpolates `${id}` raw at line 774, same pattern at 496/603).

## The Codex finding (verbatim, PR #856)

> **Escape the decoded subject in the not-found response**
>
> For an unknown `/item/<subject>` URL, the decoded path is interpolated directly into an HTML response. A link to `/item/%3Cimg%20src%3Dx%20onerror%3Dalert(document.domain)%3E` therefore returns an executable image element rather than displaying the subject as text, allowing reflected JavaScript execution in the aggregator's origin when someone follows the link. Escape `id` with the renderer's HTML-escaping helper before including it in this response.

Finding: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/856#discussion_r4370123338 (filed against `pm-stack/aggregator/src/server.ts`, PR #856)

## Fix direction (as Codex prescribed)

Escape `id` with the renderer's HTML-escaping helper before including it in this response — and audit the same raw-interpolation pattern at the other sites the audit named (server.ts lines ~496/603) so the fix covers the class, not just the one line.

## Source

Codex review-value audit 2026-10-29 (`research_notes/codex-review-value-20261029/findings.md` §2, best catch #4): 636 Codex findings classified, this one REAL-CATCH, never engaged, PR merged anyway. Verification: defect confirmed present on main 2026-10-29.

title: id(comms): per-peer frame/byte accounting + structured rate-limit refusal (P0 of #2032)

labels.name: task/triage

body:
From the #2032 investigation ([record](https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/2243/files)); this is the prerequisite for every budget in #2033.

## Problem

`pkgs/id` has no per-peer counters. The five existing limiters are keyed by file name, world capability, e-mail address or nonce — none by the remote endpoint public key — and there is no byte accounting anywhere. "Max MB per window, per IP or per ID" therefore cannot be evaluated at all today, and a rate refusal is a prose string with no retry value ("chat rate exceeded; try again later", `world/core.rs:955-975`).

## Work

- Per-`(local node, remote endpoint key)` counters for frames and bytes, incremented at the frame read/write boundary in `pkgs/id/src/frames.rs` before decode.
- Token bucket over those counters (defaults from the record: 60 frames/s burst 180, 512 KiB/s burst 4 MiB authorized; 10/s burst 30 before authorization; 4 connections per peer).
- One structured refusal type carrying `reason` (`rate_limited` | `budget_exhausted` | `blocked_by_operator` | `unauthorized`) and `retry_after_ms` (1 s floor, 60 s cap), replacing the prose refusals; HTTP routes map it to `429` + `Retry-After`.
- Counters observable (metrics or `id peers`), so an operator can tune what they can see.

## Done when

A peer exceeding the bucket is refused with a machine-readable retry value, the counters are visible, and no existing limit is duplicated — the world chat limiter becomes a consumer of the same bucket.

title: id: design: session header + segment checkpoint event kind

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
Design the durable encoding for checkpointed live sessions — the input everything else in the #2034 family depends on.

## Why

[#2034](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/2034) investigation (doc: `doc/2026-10-29T10-45-00Z_investigation_ephemeral_live_data_retention/`) concluded on a two-tier model: durable facts stay on the per-author signed hash chain (`ChainExt`), keystroke/cursor/input traffic moves to an ephemeral per-session stream authenticated by a session header + per-session MAC key, closed by intermittent **segment checkpoints**. Nothing in the tree defines what a session header or a checkpoint *is*.

## Scope

- Define `SessionHeader` and `SegmentCheckpoint` records and a new `ChainExt.kind` (`session.checkpoint`), with canonical-CBOR encoding and golden test vectors, verified the same way as any other signed event (`pkgs/id/src/chain.rs:282-342`).
- Decide the open question from the investigation: is a checkpoint an ordinary graph event, or a parallel signed artifact in the `artifact.rs` shape referenced from the graph? State the trade-off and pick one.
- Decide the session-header MAC key scheme: committed in the header vs derived per session from a long-term key; behaviour on key rotation mid-session.
- Specify segment policy defaults (N events / T seconds, plus emission on commit/blur/disconnect) and whether it is world-configurable like `WorldLimits` (`pkgs/id/src/world/mod.rs:59-99`).
- Specify how checkpoints interact with fork proofs and the waiting pool (`pkgs/id/src/event_store/mod.rs:12-22`, `waiting.rs`) so a later compaction cannot break `after` resolution.
- Peer countersignature (`peer_signature`) variant: which classes must require it (#2037/#2038 consume this).

## Acceptance

- A design doc under `doc/` linked from this issue with the record shapes, encoding, verifier walk, and the decisions above.
- Wire fields and a verifier algorithm concrete enough that the PoC issue can be built from it without further design.
- No permanent feature built here — this is design only.

Refs #2034, #2056.

title: bin: provider-catalog-sync and record still use the pre-#2083 raw-path entry-point check — invoked via any symlink they silently no-op with exit 0

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: app/provider-catalog-sync
labels.description: bin/provider-catalog-sync.mjs catalog sync

body:
## Summary

Two `bin/` entry points still use the pre-#2083 entry-point check that compares the **raw** invoked path against the module's resolved URL. When either script is invoked through a symlink — a symlinked file, or a symlinked directory such as the `~/code -> ~/git/code` checkout alias that caused #2083 — the check fails, `main()` never runs, and the process **exits 0 with no output and no error**: a silent no-op.

`bin/proxy-supervise.mjs` was fixed for exactly this in #2083 (its comment at `:644-656` spells the mechanism out, and it now compares `fs.realpathSync` on both sides). The same pattern survives verbatim in:

- `bin/provider-catalog-sync.mjs:750` — `path.resolve(process.argv[1]) === new URL(import.meta.url).pathname` (`path.resolve` makes the path absolute; it does not resolve symlinks, and `import.meta.url` is the resolved module URL).
- `bin/record.mjs:206-209` — `import.meta.url === pathToFileURL(path.resolve(process.argv[1])).href` (same flaw in URL form).

## Evidence (main `24901e7b`, sandbox probes this run)

provider-catalog-sync:

- Direct: `node bin/provider-catalog-sync.mjs --json` → exit 0, **14,177 bytes** of report on stdout.
- Via a symlink to the file: `node /tmp/isMain-probe/catalog-link.mjs --json` → exit 0, **0 bytes**.
- Via a symlinked directory (the #2083 scenario): `node ~/code-link/bin/provider-catalog-sync.mjs --json` → exit 0, **0 bytes**.

record (with `AI_RECORDINGS_FILE` pointed at a scratch target, loose-text input):

- Direct: the target's `.quarantine` sibling is created with the verbatim line (its never-reject contract for unkeyed text) — main ran.
- Via a symlink to the file: **neither** the target nor the quarantine file is created — main never ran, and the recording is silently lost.

Probe outputs saved in the goal's hidden_files `probe-2026-10-29-ismain/` (direct.out / link.out / dirlink.out / README.md).

## Why it matters

Both tools are built to be quiet: catalog-sync's no-additions path is a "silent run" by design, and record's contract is exit-0-always. That makes this failure mode invisible — a timer, wrapper, or Nix-store/symlink invocation path that reaches either script through a symlink gets a green exit and nothing happens: catalog additions never materialise, session recordings vanish. This is precisely how the supervisor timer no-oped unnoticed from 2026-10-27 until #2083; the fix landed for one file and the sibling instances of the identical check were left behind.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both `bin/provider-catalog-sync.mjs` and `bin/record.mjs` run their `main()` when invoked via a symlinked file path and via a symlinked directory path (use the `fs.realpathSync`-on-both-sides comparison already proven in `bin/proxy-supervise.mjs:648-656`, or an equivalent).
- [ ] Importing either module as a library (their test suites do this) still does **not** run `main()`.
- [ ] A regression test covers the symlinked invocation for at least one of the two (catalog-sync's subprocess-style test or a scripted probe), so the check cannot silently regress again.

body:
## Summary

`bin/proxy-relay.mjs` never times out an accepted client connection. The only socket timeout in the file guards the **outbound** tunnel CONNECT (10s, `proxy-relay.mjs:93`, cleared at `:116`); the accepted client socket gets none — not while the relay waits for the first request line, and not after the connection is piped upstream.

## Evidence (main `24901e7b`)

- `bin/proxy-relay.mjs:155-184` — the `net.createServer` handler buffers the first line in `onData` (`headEnd === -1 && buf.length < 8192` → keep waiting). No `client.setTimeout(...)` is ever called on the accepted socket; `grep setTimeout bin/proxy-relay.mjs` returns only lines 93 and 116, both on the upstream socket.
- Probe (this run, sandbox, relay on loopback :18999, target 18745): opened (1) a TCP connection that sent **nothing**, and (2) a connection that sent a partial request line `GET /hea` with no CRLF. After **12s** — longer than the upstream CONNECT timeout — both sockets were still open (`idleClosed=false partialClosed=false`, neither destroyed). The partial-line socket was still holding its buffered bytes in the peek stage. Nothing in the code ever reaps either state, so they live until the client or the OS gives up.
- After the peek stage the same gap continues: `client.pipe(upstream); upstream.pipe(client)` (`:178-179`) with no idle timeout on either side, and the upstream's CONNECT timeout is explicitly cleared (`sock.setTimeout(0)`, `:116`) once the tunnel is up.

## Why it matters

The relay is a long-lived loopback forwarder supervised for fleet proxies. Any local client that connects and stalls — a hung OpenCode/proxy client, a crashed process that left a half-open socket, a health prober that connects but never writes — pins a file descriptor and its buffered bytes in the relay forever. Enough of them accumulate into fd exhaustion on a process whose whole job is to stay up, and the failure mode is silent: nothing logs, nothing expires. Every other timeout-sensitive surface in this fleet has been pinned down one by one (upstream CONNECT here included); the accepted-socket side is the unguarded one.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An accepted client connection that does not deliver a complete first line within a bounded time is closed by the relay (triage pins the value; the upstream CONNECT timeout of 10s is the in-file precedent).
- [ ] The timeout behaviour after piping (idle forwarded connections) is decided explicitly — either an idle timeout is applied, or the code comments why forwarded connections are intentionally exempt.
- [ ] A test (alongside `bin/proxy-relay` coverage or a scripted probe) shows an idle connection and a partial-line connection are both reaped within the bound, while a normal `/health` answer and a forwarded request still work.
- [ ] No change to target selection, `/health` local answering, or endpoint publishing behaviour.

Found by new-issue-creator-code-b (lane B) this run; probe in the goal's hidden_files `probe-2026-10-29-relayidle/` (probe.mjs + relay.log), main `24901e7b`.

body:
## Problem

codedb (the MCP code-index/search server in the fleet's mcpx config, `.mcpx.json` → `command: /home/user/bin/codedb`) runs as **one process per client session**. Observed 2026-10-29: ~7 simultaneous `codedb mcp` children on the laptop, parented by the OpenClaw gateway supervisor and MCP-client node processes. There is no codedb systemd unit in either manager — process count scales with session count, and each instance presumably maintains its own index state.

Tonight its mcpx entry was **parked** (PR #2220: moved out of `mcpServers` into a top-level `disabledMcpServers` key, definition retained verbatim) pending this determination. Existing per-session children retire with their sessions; the park only stops new spawns once the PR lands and the primary checkout is pulled.

## Determination to make

Evaluate, with evidence:

- **(a) One shared codedb service** — a single long-lived codedb instance (daemon/service shape) that all MCP clients connect to, instead of per-session children. What does codedb support today (transport, shared state, concurrency), and what config changes does each client need?
- **(b) Replace codedb with the fleet's built-in embedding machinery** — OpenCode core already ships a local embedding stack (llama.cpp + Qwen3-Embedding tiers, `packages/core/src/messaging/embedding.ts` in developing-today/opencode), but today it indexes **messages and session transcripts** for messaging search, not source code. Atlas (hatch-personal `workspace/turso-atlas/`) indexes conversations + repo *docs*, not source code either. Is extending one of these to code search realistic, and what would it cost vs (a)?
- **(c) Another existing fleet component** — e.g. mcpx's own catalog embeddings are tool-catalog-scoped (semantic tool search), not code-scoped; state plainly if nothing existing fits.

## Acceptance

- A written determination in this issue (or a linked doc) naming the recommended path and the evidence for/against each candidate.
- The per-client / per-config changes the recommended path implies (mcpx config, OpenClaw, OpenCode, any service units).
- The PR #2220 park is then either lifted (codedb returns in its new shape) or made permanent with the replacement in place.

## Related

- developing-today/code#2218 — Make Qwen configurable on mcpx/OpenCode (tonight's local-model disable pass; the local-model feature audit behind this issue is summarized there).
- PR #2220 — the codedb park itself.
- Atlas code indexing (hatch-personal) — the corpus-side question if path (b) wins.

## Acceptance criteria

- A determination is recorded on this issue with evidence for each option: (a) one shared codedb service, (b) a replacement for codedb, or (c) per-session instances by design — including measured per-instance cost (memory/index state) from the observed ~7-instance state.
- The chosen option is either implemented (PR linked, mcpx config updated from the parked state in PR #2220) or filed as a linked follow-up issue with the determination as its spec.
- The interim park state is explicitly resolved: codedb either returns to `mcpServers` under the chosen model or stays parked with the reason recorded here.

# aggregator(dns): parseDnsRegister accepts impossible renewal dates — 2026-02-30 and 2026-13-01 enter the register, count toward the annual total, and string-sort into wrong positions

## Summary

`parseDnsRegister` in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/dns.ts` validates a register row's renewal cell with a shape-only regex — `/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/` (dns.ts:51) — so impossible calendar dates pass as real renewals. Every downstream consumer treats the string as a date: `parseDnsRegister` sorts entries by `renewal.localeCompare` (dns.ts:66), `dnsSectionFromRegister` sums every entry's price into `totalAnnualListUsd` (dns.ts:73), and `summarizeDns` picks `nextRenewal` and the 45-day `renewingSoon` spend horizon by string comparison against today (dns.ts:104-110). A typo'd renewal in the hand-produced #902 register therefore lands in the fleet feed as fact: a `2026-13-01` domain can never appear in `renewingSoon` (month 13 sorts after every real date) yet its price still counts toward the annual total, and a `2026-02-30` sorts ahead of real February/March renewals and becomes `nextRenewal` whenever "today" precedes it.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 318ca58a)

Probe: real `parseDnsRegister` / `dnsSectionFromRegister` / `summarizeDns` under Bun, register with three rows (renewals `2026-11-01` @ $10, `2026-02-30` @ $20, `2026-13-01` @ $30):

- Parsed renewals: `b.example=2026-02-30`, `a.example=2026-11-01`, `c.example=2026-13-01` — both impossible dates accepted, sorted by string (`2026-02-30` first, `2026-13-01` last).
- `totalAnnualListUsd: 60` — the $20 and $30 prices of the impossible rows are counted.
- With `now = 2026-01-15` the `2026-02-30` row would be `nextRenewal` and inside the 45-day horizon; the `2026-13-01` row is in no horizon, ever.

File:line (main 318ca58a):

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/dns.ts:51` — the shape-only renewal check: `if (!domain || !/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/.test(renewal)) continue;`
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/dns.ts:66` — renewal sort by `localeCompare`.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/dns.ts:71-75` — `dnsSectionFromRegister` totals all parsed entries' prices.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/dns.ts:99-112` — `summarizeDns` string-comparison `nextRenewal` / `renewingSoon`.

## Why it matters

The register is a Markdown file produced by the #902 pipeline and edited by hand; a single typo'd renewal (`2026-13-01`, `2026-02-30`) currently flows into the collector's feed section with no rejection and no log line, corrupting the two things the section exists for — what renews next (and within the 45-day spend horizon) and what the estate costs per year. The parser is documented as the fallback of record for the register ("if #902's job ever emits register.json, this parser is the fallback"), so its validation bar is the system's bar.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Triage pins the rule for a non-calendar renewal date (expected: the row is refused at parse, like a row with too few cells or a missing domain — the register keeps only real dates; or, if refused rows must stay visible, they are excluded from the sort/total/horizon and marked — triage decides, silence is the one ruled-out option).
- [ ] Regression tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/slice3.test.ts` (the dns parser's test home): rows with `2026-02-30`, `2026-13-01`, `2026-00-10`, `2026-04-31` do not enter the entries/total; `2024-02-29` (leap year) still parses; existing register fixtures unchanged.
- [ ] No behavior change for real dates: sort order, `totalAnnualListUsd`, `nextRenewal`, and `renewingSoon` identical on the existing fixtures.

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-b (lane B), run 2026-10-29 03:50 CDT. Dedup: #1684 (open) is summarizeDns's UTC-day aging — a different bug in the consumer, not parse validity; #2194 is the same shape-only pattern in charges-collect (different parser, input, and consumers); #902 is the register pipeline epic.

# aggregator(quota-extract): dateTimeCDT hardcodes UTC-5 year-round — winter (CST) reset reads render an hour early

## Summary

`dateTimeCDT` in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-extract.ts:43-46` converts a quota-view dated read (`2026-12-16` + `14:00 CDT`) into an ISO timestamp by stamping a fixed `-05:00` offset:

```ts
/** "2026-10-28" + "14:00" CDT (UTC-5) -> ISO. */
function dateTimeCDT(date: string, hhmm: string): string {
  return `${date}T${hhmm}:00-05:00`;
}
```

US Central Time is UTC-5 only during daylight saving (CDT, mid-March to early November). For the rest of the year it is CST, UTC-6. The quota view's dated reads are Central wall-clock times (the stewardship writer stamps them "CDT" by convention — every extractor pattern matches the literal `CDT`), so for any read dated in the CST months the extractor emits a `resetsAt` **one hour earlier than the wall time it claims to encode**. The same codebase already knows the right model: `pm-stack/aggregator/src/derive.ts:473-480` has "Calendar helpers (America/Chicago — Drew's timezone)" built on `Intl.DateTimeFormat` with `timeZone: "America/Chicago"`.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 318ca58a)

Probe: real `extractQuotaPools` under Bun, minimal Claude section, `now = 2026-12-10T12:00:00Z`:

- Input: `weekly 68% used, weekly reset Wed 2026-12-16 14:00 CDT`
- Emitted window: `resetsAt: "2026-12-16T14:00:00-05:00"` = **19:00Z**
- Ground truth: 2026-12-16 falls in CST — `Intl.DateTimeFormat` with `timeZone: "America/Chicago"` reports `CST` for that date, and 14:00 Central wall time = `2026-12-16T20:00:00.000Z`. The emitted reset is one hour early.

Call sites (all Central-time reads, all affected):

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-extract.ts:100` — `extractClaude`: weekly reset → the window's `resetsAt`.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-extract.ts:132` — `extractMeta`: weekly reset → `resetsAt` and `wallLiftsAt`; `extractMeta` also compares `now >= Date.parse(resetIso)` (line 134) to decide the window has reset, so a winter wall lifts / window clears an hour early in the model, not just in display.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-extract.ts:189` — `extractClinePass`: the measured-read base instant from which both relative resets (weekly/monthly) are computed — a winter ClinePass read shifts both derived resets by an hour.

## Why it matters

Reset and wall-lift times drive the hub's pool state (`poolState`, the "walled" rendering, burn/rotation decisions in stewardship). For roughly 4.5 months of the year every Claude, Meta, and ClinePass reset derived from a dated read is an hour off — pools shown as reset (or walls shown as lifted) an hour before they actually are. October reads are correct only by accident of the calendar; the first winter dated read (the quota view is already accumulating late-October reads) silently inherits the error, and no test pins a CST-month date.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Triage pins the conversion rule (expected: interpret the stamped wall time in `America/Chicago` — DST-aware, matching derive.ts's calendar helpers — rather than a fixed `-05:00`; or, if the fixed-offset convention is deliberately kept, rename/document it so the winter error is a stated choice, not an accident).
- [ ] Regression tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/quota.test.ts`: a December/January dated reset read yields the UTC-6 instant (e.g. `2026-12-16 14:00` → `2026-12-16T20:00:00.000Z`); an October read still yields UTC-5; a read on a DST transition date is covered or explicitly ruled out of scope on the issue.
- [ ] All three call sites covered (Claude reset, Meta reset/wallLiftsAt + the reset-passed comparison, ClinePass measured base).
- [ ] No behavior change for reads dated inside CDT.

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-b (lane B), run 2026-10-29 03:50 CDT. Dedup: searches for `dateTimeCDT`, "CDT offset", "daylight" (open+closed) found no covering issue; #1541 (closed) was quota-current future-skew, a different aggregator time bug.

# aggregator(quota-extract): a lowercase or non-month reset month silently discards a pool's whole read — and an out-of-range day rolls over into an invented reset date

## Summary

`monthDayTime` in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-extract.ts` converts a quota-view reset read like `resets Oct 30, 18:01 UTC` into an ISO timestamp. Its callers capture the month with **case-insensitive** regexes (`/resets (\w{3}) (\d{1,2}), (\d{2}:\d{2}) UTC/i`), but `monthDayTime` looks the capture up in the **case-sensitive** `MONTHS` table. A lowercase (`oct`) or all-caps (`OCT`) month — or any other 3-letter word the `\w{3}` capture accepts (`Foo`) — makes `MONTHS[mon]` `undefined`, so `Date.UTC(year, undefined, …)` is `NaN` and `d.toISOString()` throws `RangeError: Invalid time value`. `extractQuotaPools` catches the throw per pool and treats the extractor as if it had matched nothing: **the pool's entire read is discarded** — including the usage percentage the extractor had already matched — and the pool renders with its shell "No current read" note.

Separately, an out-of-range day silently rolls over instead of failing: `resets Oct 39, 18:01 UTC` produces a reset of **2026-11-08** — an invented date, the exact outcome the module header says the extractors must never produce ("renders with its identity and a 'no current read' note instead of vanishing or inventing numbers").

## Evidence (verified this run, main 318ca58a)

Probe: real `extractQuotaPools` under Bun, minimal ChatGPT section, `now = 2026-10-29T12:00:00Z`:

| reset line in the quota view | Codex pool result |
|---|---|
| `7-day 42% used; resets Oct 30, 18:01 UTC` | window: 42%, `resetsAt 2026-10-30T18:01:00.000Z` ✅ |
| `7-day 42% used; resets oct 30, 18:01 UTC` | **no windows, "No current read" shell** ❌ |
| `7-day 42% used; resets OCT 30, 18:01 UTC` | **no windows, "No current read" shell** ❌ |
| `7-day 42% used; resets Foo 30, 18:01 UTC` | **no windows, "No current read" shell** ❌ |
| `7-day 42% used; resets Oct 39, 18:01 UTC` | window: 42%, `resetsAt 2026-11-08T18:01:00.000Z` (rolled over) ❌ |

File:line (main 318ca58a):

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-extract.ts:17-30` — `MONTHS` table, title-case keys only.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-extract.ts:33-40` — `monthDayTime`: `MONTHS[mon]` unchecked; `Date.UTC(...)` with `undefined` month → `NaN`; `d.toISOString()` throws. No day-range check, so `Date.UTC` rolls day 39 into the next month.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-extract.ts:113` — `extractCodex` reset regex `/resets (\w{3}) (\d{1,2}), (\d{2}:\d{2}) UTC/i`.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-extract.ts:168` — `goWorkspace` reset regex (same shape, `/i`) — affects both OpenCode Go pools.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-extract.ts:203` — `extractCommandCode` "period ends" regex (same shape, `/i`).
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-extract.ts:351-358` — `extractQuotaPools` wraps each extractor in `try/catch` and maps a throw to `raw = null` (the shell pool), so the failure is silent and total for that pool.

## Why it matters

The quota view is a human-written document; month case in a dated read is exactly the kind of variation the fail-soft design is meant to absorb. Today one lowercase `oct` in the Codex or OpenCode Go section makes a healthy, current read vanish from the hub with no log line and no diagnosable difference from "the pattern stopped matching" — and a typo'd day invents a reset date the stewardship rotation decisions then trust. Four pools share the helper (Codex, OpenCode Go Personal, OpenCode Go Lab, Command Code), so one fix covers all of them.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Triage pins the rule for `monthDayTime` (expected: normalize the captured month case-insensitively against `MONTHS`; an unrecognized month token or an out-of-range day yields a `null` reset for that window — the matched percentage read is kept — rather than throwing or rolling over).
- [ ] Regression tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/quota.test.ts` (or the extractor's test home): `oct`/`OCT` resets produce the same `resetsAt` as `Oct`; a non-month token and day 39 produce the window with `resetsAt: null`; title-case behavior unchanged.
- [ ] All four `monthDayTime` call sites (Codex, both Go workspaces, Command Code) covered by the fix.
- [ ] No change to the per-pool try/catch in `extractQuotaPools` semantics for genuinely unmatched sections (shell note still renders).

body:
## Bug

`parseChargeCandidates` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/charges-collect.ts:42), the structural validation boundary for the charges candidates state file the daily collector consumes, checks a candidate's date with a shape-only regex:

```ts
if (typeof c.at !== "string" || !/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}/.test(c.at)) continue;
```

That accepts impossible calendar dates — `2026-13-45`, `2026-02-30`, `2026-00-00`, `2026-10-00` all pass as "an ISO date" (the function's own doc comment, charges-collect.ts:25-29). The existing test (test/charges-collect.test.ts:24) only covers the non-date string `"not-a-date"`, which the regex does reject.

The bad dates then corrupt both consumers in opposite directions, because both `daysBetween` implementations (charges-collect.ts:63-66, charges-match.ts:118-121) are `Math.abs(Date.parse(a) - Date.parse(b))`:

- **Month 13+ (`Date.parse` → `NaN`):** in `matchCharges` (charges-match.ts:196) `NaN <= DEDUPE_WINDOW_DAYS` is false, so the same real charge seen by Plaid and Gmail is never deduped — it publishes as **two rows**. In `mergeChargeRows`/`sameCharge` (charges-collect.ts:79) `NaN > DEDUPE_WINDOW_DAYS` is also false, so the window check passes vacuously — a hand-fed row is **dropped as a "duplicate"** of an auto row whose date is actually years away.
- **Feb 30 / day-00 (`Date.parse` rolls over):** `Date.parse("2026-02-30")` is 2026-03-02, so window arithmetic silently uses a date different from the one in the file and in the published row's `at`.

The producer writes this file with the same shape-only checks (scripts/produce-charge-candidates.ts:111 for Plaid, :207 for Gmail), so the collector's validator is the only place a real calendar check can be enforced for the file as persisted state (hand edits, an older/buggier producer, a partially migrated file).

## Evidence (verified this run, main 478797cd)

Verbatim copies of the shipped `charges-collect.ts` + `charges-match.ts` (sha256 identical to main) run under Bun 1.4.2 on the laptop — probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneA-chargedates/`:

```
parse "2026-10-28" -> ACCEPTED at=2026-10-28        (control)
parse "2026-13-45" -> ACCEPTED at=2026-13-45
parse "2026-02-30" -> ACCEPTED at=2026-02-30
parse "2026-00-00" -> ACCEPTED at=2026-00-00
parse "2026-10-00" -> ACCEPTED at=2026-10-00
parse "not-a-date" -> dropped                        (existing test case)
Date.parse 2026-13-45 = NaN   2026-02-30 = 2026-03-02T00:00:00.000Z
matchCharges rows (plaid 2026-10-28 + gmail 2026-13-45, same merchant/amount): 2   (control, both valid: 1)
mergeChargeRows (auto at=2026-13-45 vs hand-fed at=2020-01-01, same merchant/amount): hand-fed row DROPPED  (control: kept, 2 rows)
```

Collector wiring: scripts/collect-fleet-feed.ts:421-427 — `parseChargeCandidates(JSON.parse(...))` → `matchCharges(...)` → `mergeChargeRows(auto.rows, charges ?? [])`.

Note: the `at.slice(0, 10)` truncation of a full timestamp (`"2026-10-27T14:03:00Z"` → `"2026-10-27"`, test line 22) is intended behavior and is **not** part of this issue — only the calendar validity of the resulting 10 chars is.

## Why it matters

This file is the charges feed's source of record for a period. A single impossible date silently (a) double-publishes a charge in the hub, or (b) suppresses a legitimate hand-fed row — the exact hand-fed rows the merge exists to preserve — with no log line either way (`parseChargeCandidates` drops malformed entries silently by design, and these entries are not even seen as malformed). Validation that only checks shape is what the function's doc promises it does not do.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `parseChargeCandidates` rejects candidates whose `at` (after the existing 10-char slice) is not a real calendar date: month 01-12, day valid for that month/year (leap years included) — `2026-13-45`, `2026-02-30`, `2026-00-00`, `2026-10-00` are dropped; `2026-02-29` is dropped but `2024-02-29` is kept.
- [ ] Regression tests in test/charges-collect.test.ts cover the impossible-date cases above alongside the existing `"not-a-date"` case, and the intended full-timestamp slice case (test line 22) keeps passing.
- [ ] With only real dates able to enter, `matchCharges` dedupe and `mergeChargeRows` hand-fed preservation behave as in the controls above (a same-charge Plaid+Gmail pair yields 1 row; a years-apart hand-fed row is kept).
- [ ] Triage pins whether the same calendar check is also applied at the producer's two shape-only sites (scripts/produce-charge-candidates.ts:111, :207) in this fix or as a follow-up.

## Dedup

Checked open + closed issues and the repo backlog this run: #2130 covers the matcher's clustering rules (same-source repeats inside the window; empty-normalized merchants merging) — different defect, in `charges-match.ts` clustering, with all-valid dates. #1057 (closed) is the feature. #2161/#2172 are config env-var validation in other components. No existing issue covers calendar validity of charge candidate dates.

title: id(world_line): bare verbs with an argument report 'unknown command' — /help me, /quit now, /stats all, /caps list fall through, while argument-taking siblings answer with usage

body:
## Problem

In the shared world line grammar (`pkgs/id/src/world_line.rs`, `parse_line`), the four no-argument verbs — `/help`, `/quit`, `/stats`, `/caps` — are matched only as exact whole lines (world_line.rs:54-60). Any space-separated argument makes the line fall through every other branch to the catch-all at the end of the parser:

```rust
if line.starts_with('/') {
    return Some(WorldLine::Message("unknown command; type /help".to_owned()));
}
```

So a user who types a known command with an extra word is told the command does not exist:

- `/help me` → `unknown command; type /help` (the message even directs the user to the very command they just typed)
- `/quit now` → `unknown command; type /help` — and the session does **not** quit
- `/stats all` → `unknown command; type /help`
- `/caps list` → `unknown command; type /help`

The argument-taking siblings in the same parser behave differently and correctly: a malformed argument produces a usage message naming the verb (`/logs soon` → `usage: /logs [seconds]`; bare `/document` → `usage: /document <name>`). The bare verbs are the only commands in the grammar with no such path.

This grammar is shared by all three surfaces (SSH `cmd:` mode via `world_ssh.rs` `world_command`, the `id world join` stdin pump via `commands/world.rs` `pump_command`, and CLI one-offs), so the misleading message appears identically everywhere.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 324c6b10)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneB-worldline-verbs/` — verbatim `WorldLine` enum + `parse_line` copied from `world_line.rs` (enum :13-38, parser :44-109), compiled and run on the laptop:

```
"/help"          => Some(Help)
"/help me"       => Some(Message("unknown command; type /help"))
"/help extra words" => Some(Message("unknown command; type /help"))
"/quit"          => Some(Quit)
"/quit now"      => Some(Message("unknown command; type /help"))
"/stats"         => Some(Stats)
"/stats all"     => Some(Message("unknown command; type /help"))
"/caps"          => Some(Caps)
"/caps list"     => Some(Message("unknown command; type /help"))
"/logs soon"     => Some(Message("usage: /logs [seconds]"))   <- sibling behaviour
"/document"      => Some(Message("usage: /document <name>"))  <- sibling behaviour
"/nonsense arg"  => Some(Message("unknown command; type /help"))  <- correct for a genuinely unknown verb
```

## Why it matters

- The message is factually wrong: the command exists. `/help me` answering "unknown command; type /help" is a self-contradictory dead end for exactly the users who asked for help.
- `/quit now` silently not quitting is a (minor) control surprise: the user believes they may have left / or is told their exit command doesn't exist.
- Consistency: #1507 established the grammar's boundary discipline (glued forms are unknown; bare argument-verbs answer with usage). Space-separated arguments on bare verbs are the remaining unhandled cell of that table.

## Not this issue

- Glued forms (`/logs5`, `/logs<TAB>5`) staying "unknown command" is the pinned #1507 behaviour — do not change it.
- `/document` / `/input` rejecting two spaces after the verb is #1946 (open), a different branch of the same parser.
- Whether a bare verb with an argument should execute (ignore the argument) or refuse with usage is the triage pin this issue asks for — either is defensible; the current "unknown command" answer is not.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `/help <anything>`, `/quit <anything>`, `/stats <anything>`, `/caps <anything>` (space-separated) no longer return `unknown command; type /help`.
- [ ] The chosen behaviour (execute the verb ignoring the argument, or a usage message such as `usage: /stats` / "…takes no arguments") is the same for all four verbs and is pinned in a test.
- [ ] Exact bare forms still parse to `Help`/`Quit`/`Stats`/`Caps`; genuinely unknown verbs (`/nonsense arg`) still return the unknown-command message; glued forms keep the #1507 behaviour.
- [ ] Regression tests in `world_line.rs` cover at least one argument-bearing form per bare verb.

body:
## Summary

`get_file_list` in `pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs` resolves each file's `display_name` from its `name` / `file` / `path` identity tags with a stated preference — the comment at routes.rs:802 says "prefer name > file > path" — but the implementation is first-tag-wins over whatever order `TagStore::list_all` returns, so the preference is never actually applied.

## Evidence (main c58507a3)

- `pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs:802-811`: the loop inserts into `display_name_map` only when the subject is absent (`if !display_name_map.contains_key(&subj)`), i.e. the first of the three tags encountered wins, regardless of which key it is.
- `pkgs/id/src/tags.rs:1275-1284`: `list_all` streams α-doc entries in stored key order. α keys are encoded `(subject, key, value)` (tags.rs:505-509), so within one subject the identity keys arrive in byte order: `file` < `name` < `path`.
- `pkgs/id/src/tags.rs:1049-1073` (`auto_tag`, run for every stored file): every file subject normally carries all three tags — `name` = the subject itself, `file` = the basename, `path` = the original source path when known.

So for a nested file such as `docs/report.txt`, the common-case result is the `file` value (`report.txt`), not the preferred `name` value (`docs/report.txt`): two different files `a/report.txt` and `b/report.txt` render with the same display name in the file list / `/api/files` response. If a `path` tag ever arrives first (entries from another author sort differently in the α doc), the display name becomes the original absolute source path (e.g. `/home/<user>/docs/report.txt`) — leaking a local filesystem path into the UI/API for a shared file.

## Verification

Verbatim copy of the routes.rs:802-811 loop in a standalone probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneB-displayname/`, main c58507a3), fed the exact tag values `auto_tag` writes for subject `docs/report.txt`:

- α order (file, name, path) → `Some("report.txt")` — basename, not the stated preference
- name-first order → `Some("docs/report.txt")`
- path-first order → `Some("/home/u/docs/report.txt")`

The result depends entirely on tag arrival order; the documented priority is not implemented anywhere.

## Why it matters

`display_name` is what the file list and `/api/files` show (routes.rs:866-870, and the dedup key at routes.rs:883-895 also keys on it, so two same-basename files with equal tags can even be deduplicated against each other under the wrong name). Nested files become indistinguishable, and the path-first case discloses the uploader's absolute local path.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Display-name resolution implements the stated priority explicitly (name, then file, then path), independent of tag iteration order
- [ ] A regression test covers a subject carrying all three identity tags in α (file-first) order and asserts the `name` value wins
- [ ] The absolute source `path` value is never used as a display name when a `name` or `file` tag exists
- [ ] No behavior change for subjects carrying only one identity tag

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for "display name", "get_file_list", "display_name_map": #1793 (file origin/scope in listings) and #2112/#1833 (world/collab display-name sanitizing) are different surfaces; nothing tracks the file-list priority resolution.

body:
# id(find/search): PR #1622's final-component confinement makes distinct `--all --dir` matches silently overwrite each other

## Finding

PR #1622 confined find/search download writes to the match name's **final path component only** (`download_output_path`, `pkgs/id/src/commands/find.rs:163` on current main `c58507a3`). That closed the #1614 traversal, but it flattens the namespace: in `--all --dir` mode, two distinct matches whose names differ only in their directory part now map to the **same** output path, and the second download silently truncates/replaces the first.

Match names reaching this code are unvalidated remote strings that can carry directory components — that is the premise of #1614 itself. The `--all` loops dedupe by `hash:name` (`find.rs:268` cmd_find, and the matching cmd_search loop), so two matches with different hashes and different names (e.g. `a/report.txt` and `b/report.txt`) both pass the dedupe, both are printed as downloaded — and both are written to `out/report.txt`. The user asked for every match and ends up with only the last one, with no error or warning.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/1622 (merged, merge commit `19802757`, branch commit `b5e56e28`) — "fix(id): confine find/search download writes to the match name's final component (#1614)".
- `download_output_path` (current main `c58507a3630e1a5a4935b3279a61c7fb59e3c65b`, `pkgs/id/src/commands/find.rs:163-186`) derives the write path from `Path::file_name` only; call sites: `find.rs:271` (cmd_find `--all --dir`) and `find.rs:411` (cmd_search `--all --dir`).
- The PR's own pinning test shows the flattening: `download_output_path(Some("out"), "../victim.txt") == "out/victim.txt"` (current main `find.rs:1051-1063`). By the same rule `a/victim.txt` and `b/victim.txt` both map to `out/victim.txt` — no test in the PR or on main covers two distinct matches sharing a final component.
- Writes are create-or-truncate (the #1614 chain: `cmd_get_one` / `cmd_get_one_remote` → export), so the collision is a silent overwrite, not an error.
- Verified on current main `c58507a3` (2026-10-29): helper, both `--all` call sites, and the `hash:name` dedupe are unchanged since the merge. Deduped against open + closed issues: #1614 (closed) chose final-component confinement and never addressed same-final-component collisions; no other issue covers this.

## Why it matters

`--all` is the bulk-download mode: its contract is "every match lands on disk". A collision breaks that contract silently — the output listing shows both matches as downloaded while one file has already replaced the other. In remote mode the names are attacker-influenced, so a hostile node can also shadow a legitimate match with a later same-named one; in honest use, any store holding directory-carrying names loses files the same way.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Two distinct matches (different hash and/or name) that share a final path component, downloaded with `id find --all --dir` or `id search --all --dir`, no longer silently overwrite each other: either both land on disk under disambiguated names, or the colliding write is refused with a clear error naming the collision — triage pins which.
- [ ] A regression test pins the collision case (two distinct names, one final component, `--all --dir` semantics) for both find and search paths, or at the shared helper/call-site level if both route through it.
- [ ] #1614's confinement is unchanged: no write escapes the target directory, names with no final component are still refused, and ordinary single-segment names keep byte-identical output paths.

title: meta-exporter: CDP plumbing has no timeout — an endpoint that accepts but never answers hangs the exporter forever and writes no failure document

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/s

labels.name: app/pm-stack
labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

body:
## Summary

`pm-stack/meta-exporter/meta-quota-export.mjs` has **no timeout anywhere in its CDP plumbing**, so a browser debug endpoint that accepts the connection but never answers hangs the exporter forever instead of producing one of its designed failure documents:

- `httpJson` (meta-quota-export.mjs, CDP plumbing section) — `await fetch(url)` with no `AbortSignal`; used for `${cdpBase}/json/list` in both `run()` and `fetchPaygBalance()`.
- `connectWs` — the promise resolves only on `ws.onopen` and rejects only on `ws.onerror`; if the socket opens but the page never answers, `send()`'s per-call promise is stored in `pending` and **never settled** (no `onclose` handler rejects pending calls), so `evaluate()` (which awaits `client.send("Runtime.evaluate", …)`) hangs indefinitely.
- The in-page `fetch` calls in `fetchQuotaPayloads` likewise carry no timeout, though `Runtime.evaluate` with `awaitPromise: true` means a hung in-page fetch also never returns.

The module's own header documents the contract this breaks: every failure mode is supposed to write a failure document (`cdp-unavailable` exit 4, `fetch-failed` exit 7, …) so a failed tick "can never be mistaken for a reading", and consumers derive `laptop-unreachable` only from the *age* of `latest.json`. A hang produces **no document at all** — under the shipped systemd units the only backstop is `meta-quota-export.service`'s `TimeoutStartSec=120`, which SIGTERMs the process: still no failure document, no exit-code semantics, and the stale `latest.json` is then misread downstream as the laptop being unreachable rather than the browser/CDP being wedged.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `c58507a3`)

- Grep: no `timeout` / `AbortSignal` / `setTimeout` anywhere in `meta-quota-export.mjs`.
- `connectWs`: `pending` promises are resolved/rejected only in `ws.onmessage`; there is no `ws.onclose` handler at all, so a socket that closes mid-`Runtime.evaluate` also leaves `evaluate()` pending forever.
- Sandbox probe: started a TCP server on `127.0.0.1:19299` that accepts connections and never replies, then ran the shipped exporter against it:
  `node meta-quota-export.mjs --cdp-port 19299 --out-dir /tmp/probe-metaexp/out` under `timeout 8` → **exit 124** (killed by `timeout`; the exporter never returned), and the out-dir contained **zero files** — no `latest.json` failure document, no `history.jsonl` entry.
- Control behaviour by contrast: an unreachable port (connection refused) does produce the designed `cdp-unavailable` failure document via the `catch` in `run()` — it is specifically the *accepts-but-never-answers* case that has no path to any outcome.

## Why it matters

This exporter is the Meta pool's only quota feed (code#1301, epic #1149); the aggregator's pool decisions ingest its file export every 15 minutes. A wedged browser page or CDP endpoint currently turns into up to 120 s of systemd kill-wait per tick, zero diagnostics in the export stream (the failure taxonomy exists precisely to name this state), and a downstream signal that points operators at the laptop's reachability instead of the browser session.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every CDP HTTP fetch (`/json/list`) carries a bounded timeout (e.g. `AbortSignal.timeout(...)`) that surfaces as the existing `cdp-unavailable` failure document + exit 4.
- [ ] WebSocket `send()` calls carry a bounded deadline, and `ws.onclose`/`onerror` rejects all pending promises, so a hung or closed socket surfaces as `fetch-failed` (exit 7) instead of hanging.
- [ ] The in-page quota fetch is bounded (directly, or transitively via the `Runtime.evaluate` deadline above).
- [ ] A test (the file already has `meta-quota-export.test.mjs`) covers the accepts-but-never-answers endpoint: the run terminates with a failure document well inside the systemd 120 s budget.
- [ ] Healthy-path behaviour unchanged: success document shape, failure taxonomy, and exit codes all as documented in the module header.

## Dedup / distinctness

- #1566 (CLOSED) was `window_duration_secs` validation in the quota parser — unrelated to CDP transport timeouts.
- #1301 / #1167 / #1149 (OPEN) are the feature/epic for this exporter; none tracks a transport-deadline gap (searched `meta-exporter OR meta-quota-export`, all states).
- The proxy timeout issues (#2102, #2157, #2159, #2100) concern other services' upstream calls, not this exporter's CDP channel.

body:
## Summary

The pm-stack projector's two numeric environment inputs are parsed with bare `Number()` and never validated:

- `PORT` (`pm-stack/projector/src/index.ts:6`): `const port = Number(env.PORT ?? 7801)` is passed straight to `Bun.serve` in `pm-stack/projector/src/server.ts` (`serve(db, env, port)`). `PORT=0` silently binds a **random ephemeral port** while every consumer expects 7801; `PORT=abc` / `99999` / `-1` / `4870.5` crash at startup with a Bun `RangeError` that names neither `PORT` nor the projector.
- `GITHUB_APP_INSTALL_ID` (`pm-stack/projector/src/github.ts:121`): `installId = Number(env.GITHUB_APP_INSTALL_ID)`. `'abc'` becomes `NaN`, which is falsy, so the configured installation is **silently skipped as if unset** — reconcile then falls back to `GITHUB_TOKEN` or throws `no_github_credentials_for_<repo>`, an error that blames credentials when the real problem is a typo'd install ID. `'12.5'` is truthy and is interpolated verbatim into `https://api.github.com/app/installations/12.5/access_tokens`, producing a misleading `installation_token_failed_404`.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `c58507a3`)

- `pm-stack/projector/src/index.ts:6` — the only parse of `PORT`; no range/integer check anywhere in `src/` (grep).
- `pm-stack/projector/src/github.ts:121` — the only parse of `GITHUB_APP_INSTALL_ID`; the result is used at `:122` (`&& installId`) and `:125` (URL interpolation).
- Sandbox Bun probe of the exact pattern (`port = Number(raw)`, then `Bun.serve({port, hostname:"127.0.0.1"})`):
  - `"abc"` → `NaN` → `RangeError [ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE]: The value of "options.port" is out of range. It must be an integer. Received NaN`
  - `"99999"` → `RangeError ... must be >= 0 and <= 65535. Received 99999`
  - `"-1"` → same RangeError; `"4870.5"` → `RangeError ... must be an integer. Received 4870.5`
  - `"0"` → **bound port 36647** (random ephemeral) and reported as listening; `"7801"` → bound 7801 (control)
- Install-ID coercion probe: `Number("abc")` → `NaN`, `!!NaN === false` (so the `:122` gate treats a configured-but-garbage ID exactly like an unset one); `Number("12.5")` → `12.5`, truthy, used verbatim in the access-token URL.
- No test covers either input: `pm-stack/projector/test/` has no `PORT` / `GITHUB_APP_INSTALL_ID` validation cases (grep).
- The fleet already has the strict precedent: `bin/proxy-port.mjs` (`parseProxyPort`) rejects non-integer / out-of-range ports with an error naming the variable.

## Why it matters

The projector is the PM stack's GitHub→database intake; its consumers (the aggregator's live source, per `pm-stack/projector/README.md`) find it at the expected port. A one-character typo in `PORT` either makes the service silently live on a random port (unit healthy, data stale, nothing in the log points at the cause) or kills it with a runtime error that does not name the variable to fix. A typo in `GITHUB_APP_INSTALL_ID` silently downgrades or breaks reconcile auth with an error that sends the operator to check the wrong credential.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `PORT` that is not an integer in 1–65535 (including `0`, unless 0 is made an explicit documented opt-in) fails at startup with an error naming `PORT`, the offending value, and the valid range — before any bind.
- [ ] A `GITHUB_APP_INSTALL_ID` that is not a positive integer fails (or at minimum logs a loud warning naming the variable and value) instead of being silently treated as unset; a fractional value is never interpolated into the access-token URL.
- [ ] Defaults unchanged: unset `PORT` → 7801; unset `GITHUB_APP_INSTALL_ID` → existing discovery/token fallback path.
- [ ] Tests cover `'abc'`, `'0'`, `'-1'`, `'99999'`, `'4870.5'` for `PORT` and `'abc'` / `'12.5'` for the install ID, plus the unset defaults.

## Dedup / distinctness

- #1547 (OPEN) is the projector's read-API `?limit=` validation — a different input surface (query param → SQL) in the same service.
- #2161 (OPEN) is the aggregator's `PM_AGG_PORT`/`PM_AGG_HOSTS` in a different service (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/config.ts`); this issue is the projector's own entry-point/auth env parsing (`src/index.ts`, `src/github.ts`). If triage prefers, the fix patterns should be shared, but the code paths and failure modes are separate.
- #1529 (OPEN) is `GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY` PEM decoding in the same file — unrelated to the install-ID number parse.

body:
## Problem

`loadConfig` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/config.ts:64-69`) performs no validation on the aggregator's bind configuration:

- `port: Number(s(env.PM_AGG_PORT, "4870"))` — a bare `Number()` with no integer/range check.
- `hosts` is split/trimmed/filtered with no non-empty check.

`server.ts:807-817` then maps one `Bun.serve` per host and logs whatever port Bun reports.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `b2b885b9`)

Probe 1 — `loadConfig` itself (bun, importing the real `src/config.ts`):

- `{PM_AGG_PORT:"0"}` → `port 0`
- `{PM_AGG_PORT:"abc"}` → `port NaN`
- `{PM_AGG_PORT:"4870.5"}` → `port 4870.5`
- `{PM_AGG_HOSTS:","}` → `hosts []`
- `{PM_AGG_HOSTS:" , "}` → `hosts []`

Probe 2 — what Bun does with those ports (sandbox bun 1.4.4, `Bun.serve` on 127.0.0.1):

- `NaN`, `99999`, `-1`, `4870.5` → `RangeError [ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE]: The value of "options.port" is out of range…` — the process dies at startup with an error that names neither `PM_AGG_PORT` nor the accepted range, so an operator typo presents as a Bun internals crash.
- `0` → binds a **random ephemeral port** (probe got 36279) and `server.ts` happily logs `aggregator listening on http://127.0.0.1:36279`. Every consumer of the aggregator expects 4870, so the service is "up" in systemd terms and unreachable in practice — a silent misconfiguration, worse than a crash.
- `hosts []` → `servers` is an empty array, nothing is bound, nothing is logged, and the process exits 0 immediately — the unit looks like it ran fine while no dashboard exists.

## Why it matters

The aggregator is the PM stack's single dashboard URL. Its only two bind knobs can each turn a one-character env typo into either a misleading crash or a silently absent/wrong-port service, and none of the failure modes name the offending variable. Sibling services in this repo already learned this lesson the hard way (the proxy fleet's strict `parseProxyPort` in `bin/proxy-port.mjs` exists for exactly this class).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `loadConfig` rejects a `PM_AGG_PORT` that is not an integer in 1–65535 (0 included — an ephemeral aggregator port is never useful) with an error naming `PM_AGG_PORT`, the received value, and the accepted range; the process fails at startup, before binding.
- [ ] `loadConfig` rejects a `PM_AGG_HOSTS` that yields zero bind addresses with an error naming `PM_AGG_HOSTS`.
- [ ] Valid configurations are unchanged: unset → port 4870, hosts `["127.0.0.1"]`; explicit valid port/hosts pass through.
- [ ] Tests for `loadConfig` cover: `"abc"`, `"0"`, `"-1"`, `"99999"`, `"4870.5"` rejected; `","` / `" , "` hosts rejected; defaults accepted.

Triage should pin whether validation lives in `loadConfig` (throwing) or in `server.ts` before serving, and whether port 0 deserves a deliberate opt-in instead of a rejection.

title: muse-proxy: exec fallback path has no turn deadline — a hung muse exec child hangs the request forever

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: app/muse-proxy
labels.description: bin/muse-proxy.mjs OpenAI-compatible Muse bridge

body:
## Problem

`bin/muse-proxy.mjs`'s exec (cold) path has no turn deadline. When the warm MSP path is disabled (`MUSE_PROXY_WARM=0`) or a request falls back to exec, the handler spawns `muse exec` (`bin/muse-proxy.mjs:979`) and the HTTP response is completed only from the child's `close` handler (`:1083`). There is no timer on this path: the only kill is on client disconnect (`res.on('close')` → `child.kill('SIGTERM')`, `:992-996`). If the spawned `muse exec` child hangs — alive but never emitting a terminal event (upstream stall, a CLI waiting on input the proxy never sends, a wedged run) — and the client is a patient programmatic caller (an OpenCode session, a queue worker), the request hangs forever and the child accumulates.

Every sibling path is bounded, including in this same file:

- The warm path in this file: `WARM_TURN_TIMEOUT_MS = 300 * 1000` (`:300`), applied per turn (`:585-587`); MSP `rpc()` defaults to a 30s timeout (`:513-519`); even the `--help` capability probe kills its child after 10s (`:216-219`).
- `bin/claude-code-proxy.mjs`: `TURN_TIMEOUT_MS = 300 * 1000` (`:55`) on its spawned turns, with SIGKILL escalation (`:480`).
- `bin/codex-proxy.mjs`'s app-server path: 10s connect / 30s RPC timeouts (its exec path has the same defect as this one and is filed separately this run).

The exec path is the fallback taken exactly when the bounded warm path is unavailable or has failed — the moment a hang is most likely — and it is the one path with no bound.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `b2b885b9`)

Sandbox probe with a fake `muse` binary (`$HOME/.local/bin/muse` under a scratch HOME; the fake answers `--help` probes with a flags line and sleeps 60s for any other invocation), `MUSE_PROXY_WARM=0`:

- Proxy log: `CLI probe: exec advertises 6 flags...` then `Spawning: .../muse exec --json --prompt-file ... --model muse-spark-1.3 --reasoning-effort low --user-input-auto-resolve --approval-mode never` — the request reached the exec spawn at `:979`.
- `curl -X POST /v1/chat/completions` (non-streaming): **no response after 8s** (curl killed by `timeout 8`, exit 124, 0 response bytes) while the fake child (`sleep 60`) was still running. Nothing in the proxy would have ended the request before the child's own exit — and a truly hung child never exits.

Dedup: `gh` searches for `muse-proxy timeout` and `muse-proxy hang` (open + closed) return no covering issue. Adjacent but distinct: #2097/#2100/#2102 are the same no-timeout class in design-code-proxy, clef-proxy, and antigravity-ls-proxy (HTTP fetch / RPC paths in other files); the codex-proxy exec path is filed separately this run.

## Why it matters

This proxy is the only door from OpenCode sessions into the Meta pool (see the pool map in `~/hatch-personal/AGENTS.md`), so a wedged exec turn stalls the session routed through it with no error, no log line, and no recovery short of the client dying — at which point the accumulated child is killed only as a side effect of the disconnect. A bounded fallback would surface the same stall as a prompt, actionable error, consistent with how the warm path already behaves at 300s.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `muse exec` turn that exceeds a named deadline (consistent with the house convention — this file's own `WARM_TURN_TIMEOUT_MS` 300s, or a strictly parsed `MUSE_PROXY_*` env override) is terminated (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after a short grace) and the request settles with the existing error-response shape (including the SSE error framing for streaming requests, #670).
- [ ] The partially accumulated content / terminal-state reconciliation on `close` (#484/#672) still runs for a deadline-killed child, or the deadline path produces an equivalent explicit failure — never a silent successful `stop`.
- [ ] The existing client-disconnect kill (`:992-996`) keeps working and races safely with the deadline kill.
- [ ] Regression tests in `bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs` style: a fake child that never exits is killed at the deadline and the request errors; a fake child that completes normally is unaffected; the warm path is unchanged.
- [ ] Prompt-file cleanup (`fs.unlinkSync(promptFile)`) happens on the deadline path as it does on `close`.

title: id(serve): design — how does a program appear as a website? (program-only ports, mixed ports, path mounts)

body:
Design question from Drew (2026-10-29): how does a program appear as a website in id?

Today `id serve` can host a world (`--world`, `--world-module <wasm>`), but the program is only reachable through the World Explorer's `/world` page, behind an interactive guest join. There is no way to give a program its own web presence. Define the serving model for programs, covering at least these launch shapes:

1. **Program-only port:** launch flags bind a specific program to a port — that port serves the program and NOT the World Explorer.
2. **Mixed ports, one process:** the Explorer on one port and a program on another port, from the same `serve` invocation.
3. **Path mount:** a program served at a path on the same listener as the Explorer.

Questions the design must answer:
- What is a "program" for serving purposes — a world program (Roc/Wasm module) only, or any addressable program/document in the node? How is the program identified on the command line / in config (name, id, path)?
- Per-listener and per-mount authentication: does the `--web-token` model extend, and what is public-by-default?
- How does this relate to the existing world hosting (`--world-admin-token`, guest capabilities) — is a served program a world with a web front door, or a separate concept?
- What does the program receive per request/session (identity, capabilities), and what can it render?

Companions: the bindings model (multiple listeners by flag/config) and dynamic publish/unpublish are separate issues; this one is the model they implement.

body:
From the 2026-10-29 walkthrough of `id serve --web`, and Drew's direction on serving:

Today the web interface has exactly ONE listener: `ServeOptions` carries a single `bind: IpAddr` and `port: u16` (serve.rs), used for the World Explorer, with `--web-token` required when binding non-loopback (`web/security.rs`). The demo had to be reached through an SSH tunnel purely because the listener was loopback-only. There is no way to describe a SET of listeners — by flags or by config — and no foundation for serving anything except the Explorer.

Wanted:
- A bindings model for `id serve`: multiple listeners, each an (address, port) pair, declared by repeatable flags and/or the config file (the `defaults.conf` mechanism is the obvious home), with per-listener token policy following the existing non-loopback rule.
- The Explorer remains the default content of a listener; what else a listener can serve is the program-as-website design (companion issue).
- Binding failures (address in use, permission) fail loudly at startup with the listener identified — no silent unbound listeners (the walkthrough already hit one silent no-bind failure mode via the web cargo feature, noted on #190).

Acceptance: a node can be launched with two listeners on different interfaces/ports from config alone, both answering, and the startup log lists every bound listener.

From the 2026-10-29 screenshot walkthrough of `id serve --web`:

A hosted world cannot actually be *viewed* from the web UI without interactive choreography. The `/world` page renders a pre-join lobby shell ("Not connected"): viewing anything requires pasting a guest capability into the join form interactively, and the Records panel reads `{}` unless a world program (Roc/Wasm module) has been installed into the world and a guest session has joined and written records. There is no host-side view of a world this node is already serving.

Gaps to close:
- A node that hosts a world (`serve --world`, optionally `--world-module`) should be able to display that world's live view and records in its own web UI without minting and pasting a guest capability by hand — the host is already trusted locally.
- Installing a world program into a world should have a discoverable path (CLI at minimum, documented; web UI ideally), so "the world is empty" is a state a user can act on rather than a dead end.

Design questions to answer in triage:
- What is the intended viewing model for a hosted world — is the guest-join flow meant to be the only door, with the host view a convenience, or should a hosted world render server-side by default?
- What does the world program's output surface look like when rendered for the host (same program view as guests see, plus host-only panels)?

Related: #2057 (world-VM Wasm portability audit) touches the runtime, not this serving/viewing gap. Walkthrough notes: ~/workspace/id-walkthrough/NOTES.md (screenshot 07-world.png shows the pre-join shell).

title: id(serve): is_process_alive answers 'alive' for pid 0 and u32::MAX — a lock file with either pid is never stale and wedges serve discovery

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

`get_serve_info()` decides whether the serve lock (`.iroh-serve.lock`, `pkgs/id/src/lib.rs:311`) is stale by calling `is_process_alive(info.pid)`, where `pid` comes straight from the lock file's JSON (`ServeInfo.pid: u32`, `pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:130-141`). `is_process_alive` (`serve.rs:196-210`) casts that `u32` to `i32` and calls `libc::kill(pid as i32, 0)`, with a comment claiming the cast is safe because "valid PIDs on Unix are always positive and fit in i32". That holds for a pid written by `create_serve_lock` (`std::process::id()`), but not for the pid **read back from disk**: serde accepts any `u32`, and two values make the stale check answer "alive" for no process at all:

- `pid: 0` → `kill(0, 0)` checks the caller's own process **group** — it succeeds whenever the calling process exists, i.e. always.
- `pid: 4294967295` (`u32::MAX`) → casts to `-1` → `kill(-1, 0)` succeeds if *any* process the caller may signal exists, i.e. always.

A lock file carrying either value is therefore never treated as stale: `get_serve_info` returns the bogus `ServeInfo` and never deletes the lock (`serve.rs:171-185`). Every command that consults the lock first — `get`, `put`, `list`, `peers`, the REPL and the meta client (`commands/get.rs:101`, `put.rs:153`, `list.rs:72`, `peers.rs:204`, `repl.rs:235`, `meta_client.rs:103`) — then tries to reach a serve instance that does not exist instead of falling back to a local node / "no serve running".

Reachability is mundane, not adversarial: a hand-edited, corrupted-but-still-JSON-parseable, or partially migrated lock file (or any future writer that records a sentinel pid) permanently wedges serve discovery for that directory until a human deletes `.iroh-serve.lock` by hand.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `8124cc0b`)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-pidalive/`), running `is_process_alive` copied verbatim from `serve.rs:196-210`:

```
own pid 3726549 -> true
pid 0 -> true
pid u32::MAX (4294967295, casts to -1) -> true
pid 4294967294 (casts to -2) -> false
dead pid 3727865 -> false        (spawned, reaped, then checked)
pid 999999 (likely dead) -> false
```

So ordinary dead pids are correctly reported dead; only the sentinel/wrapped values lie. Dedup: `gh` searches for `is_process_alive`, `serve lock`, and `pid reuse` returned no issue covering this (only closed #443, about gitignoring serve artifacts).

## Why it matters

Serve discovery is the front door for most CLI commands in a served directory. A lock that can never go stale turns a recoverable state (dead serve) into a permanent, confusing failure (connection attempts to a dead/wrong endpoint), with the fix — deleting a dotfile — undiscoverable from any error message.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `is_process_alive` (or `get_serve_info`) refuses non-positive / out-of-range pids: `pid == 0` and any pid that does not fit a positive `i32` are treated as "not alive" (stale lock), never passed to `kill`.
- [ ] A lock file with `pid: 0` or `pid: 4294967295` is removed by `get_serve_info` and `None` is returned, exactly as for an ordinary dead pid.
- [ ] A live pid and an ordinary dead pid behave exactly as before.
- [ ] Regression tests cover pid 0, `u32::MAX`, a dead pid, and the caller's own pid.
- [ ] The misleading cast-safety comment is corrected to state where the pid is validated.

The usage & billing hub already compiles provider numbers continuously, but pool-quota-steward re-probes every pool hourly (3.45M input/run, 51.8M per 15h at check-in #5) to feed the dispatch measurement gate, plus ledger and impact follow-up work every run.

Change: (1) read the hub's compiled snapshot and the quota registry first; (2) probe ONLY pools whose picture is stale — and keep hourly probing only for pools the dispatcher is actively drawing from, so the ≤60-min measurement gate stays honest; (3) impact follow-ups move hourly → daily. Target ≤1.7M input/run with no loss of gate freshness for active pools.

title: aggregator(charges-match): dedupe collapses distinct charges — same-source repeats within 3 days merge into one row, and empty-normalized merchants merge across merchants

labels.name: app/pm-stack
labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Summary

`matchCharges` in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/charges-match.ts` (merged in PR #2113 for #1057) dedupes on `(amountUsd, normalizedMerchant, ±3 days)` only — it never requires the two candidates to come from *different* sources, and it never rejects an empty normalized merchant. Two distinct real charges therefore collapse into one row, under-counting the charges strip that #1057 exists to automate.

The module's own contract is narrower: the header says dedupe is *across sources* ("Deduped across sources", "Charges from two sources for the same purchase post within days", charges-match.ts:4-9, :54, :178-182), and #1057's acceptance is "a charge is never double-counted **across sources**".

## Evidence (verified this run, main `58621026`, laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneB-charges/probe.ts` importing the shipped file)

Control — cross-source pair dedupes correctly:

- Plaid `CURSOR.COM $20 2026-10-27` + Gmail `Cursor $20 2026-10-28` → **1 row** (expected).

Bug A — same-source distinct charges collapse:

- Two **Plaid** candidates, `CURSOR.COM $20` on 2026-10-27 and 2026-10-28 → **1 row** (real charges: 2). Code path: charges-match.ts:190-202 finds the existing cluster by amount/normalized/window regardless of source; the second Plaid candidate sets neither `existing.plaid` (already set) nor `existing.gmail`, and is silently dropped (`continue`).
- Two **Gmail** candidates, same merchant/amount/day → **1 row** (real charges: 2).

This is not exotic: usage-based AI/API charges, per-seat charges, and two purchases from the same vendor within three days at the same price are exactly the charges this strip reports.

Bug B — empty-normalized merchants collide across merchants:

- `normalizeMerchantName("1234567") === ""` and `normalizeMerchantName("9876543") === ""` (digit-only tokens are dropped, charges-match.ts:84-93). A Plaid charge from merchant `1234567` ($9.99) and a Gmail alert from the *different* merchant `9876543` ($9.99, same day) → **1 row** labelled `1234567`. Any two descriptors that normalize to `""` with equal amount within the window merge, whatever they are.

## Why it matters

The charges strip is financial evidence: under-counting hides real spend (the failure mode is silent — no error, just a missing row), and Bug B can attribute one vendor's charge to another. Rerun determinism (a stated design goal) makes the wrong answer stable, so it will not self-correct on the next collector run.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Dedupe only merges candidates from different sources (a cluster holds at most one Plaid and one Gmail candidate); two same-source candidates with the same merchant/amount inside the window produce two rows.
- [ ] Candidates whose normalized merchant is empty never merge with a different raw merchant; they are kept as their own rows (or explicitly handled and tested).
- [ ] The existing cross-source control case still produces one Plaid-of-record row, and all existing `charges-match.test.ts` tests pass.
- [ ] New tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/charges-match.test.ts` cover: same-source repeats inside the window, and two distinct empty-normalizing descriptors with equal amounts.

Related: #1057 (the feature this shipped under — distinct from its cross-source double-count acceptance), #1047 (epic).
