body:
Design (repo design architect, pass 12, 2026-10-29): **one policy evaluator in a new `internal/policy` package, evaluated inside `resolveAndGuard` after it gains the call's arguments**, in a fixed order — hidden-tool check (existing) → unknown-write ledger check → argument rules → write mode → `confirmDestructive` floor. The three origin issues below are three separately-filed slices of one design; they share one seam, one write classification, and one evaluator (#1986's own body: "Design the two together… the evaluator is one function so the two can never disagree"). This design adopts them as its phases instead of filing parallel implementation issues.

Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-write-policy.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace (problem, current-state audit against origin/main `73ba3a96`, proposal, alternatives, risks, open questions).

## Why now / grounding

- The only write gate today is `elicit.confirmDestructive` (default off, `internal/settings/consumer.go:65`; `internal/daemon/consumer.go:382`) — a boolean aimed at one annotation. It never shows the arguments, because `resolveAndGuard` (`internal/daemon/registry.go:868`) and `confirmDestructive` are both argument-blind even though all three call paths (`Call` registry.go:852, `CallReporting` input_required.go:75, `CallAsk` routes_proto.go:302) hold `args` in hand.
- The validator argument rules were blocked on (ex-nix#254) now exists: `internal/schemaval`, landed by #1482 and wired in by #1483 (`internal/mcpclient/schemacheck.go`). Tool-pattern keys are `config.ToolPatterns`; the classification precedent is `destructiveHint` (`internal/daemon/consumer.go:439-444`, spec defaults — inverted, it is the write classification).
- No unknown-outcome recording exists anywhere in `pkgs/mcpx/internal` (grep-verified): a write lost after dispatch leaves no trace and the next write proceeds.

## Decisions recorded in the design doc

1. Classification shared and annotation-derived (write iff `readOnlyHint` is not true); annotation dishonesty stays owned by #1957 — argument rules are the annotation-independent control.
2. Modes are settings (`policy.write`, daemon scope, `ask` default per #1979's acceptance; per-server `writePolicy` override); rules are per-server config (`argumentRules`, kept over a folded `policy` block — #1986 open question 1 resolved); the evaluator is the shared part.
3. `ask` renders the exact call (tool + canonical arguments) through the existing broker confirmation; `elicit.confirmDestructive` is subsumed as a floor (destructive asks even under `allow` — decision 0002's "no level skips a consent gate").
4. Rule refusals render natively per surface (daemon 400 `HiddenTool`-style naming argument path/value/constraint/rule origin; MCP pass-through `isError: true` result) — #1986 open question 3 resolved by the hidden-tool precedent. Rules only tighten (`allOf` across pool/server/layered files); bad schema or non-RE2 `pattern` is a load-time config error; dead rules warn at load and on catalog change.
5. Unknown-outcome ledger is a versioned state-dir file (server, tool, args SHA-256 — never the arguments — time, surface), written atomically, persisted across restarts, never auto-cleared; "ambiguous" is conservative (post-dispatch marker only once request bytes were written).
6. The policy is an operator consent gate, not the autonomy dial (decision `0002`, `pkgs/mcpx/docs/decisions/0002-autonomy-dial.md`: `confirmDestructive` classed "not the dial"); neither clamps the other, and Phase 1 documents the interaction.

## Phased breakdown (each independently landable)

- **Phase 1 — the gate: #1979** (sub-issue). Plumb `args` into `resolveAndGuard`; `internal/policy` + classification; `policy.write` + per-server `writePolicy`; exact-call ask; `deny`; `confirmDestructive` subsumption; dial documentation. Leaves ledger/rules steps as no-op hooks. Acceptance: #1979's own checklist.
- **Phase 2 — argument rules: #1986** (sub-issue, gated on Phase 1, `status/blocked`). `argumentRules` config + `schemaval` compilation, evaluation before the mode step, per-surface refusals, dead-rule warnings. Acceptance: #1986's own checklist including its four worked examples. Triage first confirms #1951's in-review reconciliation does not reopen the validator question.
- **Phase 3 — unknown-outcome ledger: #1977** (sub-issue, gated on Phase 1, `status/blocked`). Post-dispatch error marker, state-dir ledger, guard step, `mcpx writes` / `mcpx writes clear <server>` + `/v1` clear route, restart-persistence tests. Acceptance: #1977's own checklist. On landing, post evidence on tracker #1984 for its #1979/#1977 checkboxes.

## Not in this design (open questions in the doc)

Schema advertising of rules (`allOf` in `mcpx types` / `tools/list`); pinning/`set` (#1933's slice); redaction of secret-shaped values in ask renderings; per-principal policy (waits on #1968/#1972); ledger visibility in `mcpx status`.

Related: #1984 (tracker that lists #1979/#1977), #1481 (validation — dependency, not a slice), #1957 (annotation trust), #1634 (landed; its client recovery sits below this design's recording point).

title: id(peers): a negative --depth is an undocumented unlimited crawl — --depth=-1 maps to i32::MAX and stops only when the frontier runs out

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage

body:
## Problem

`id peers --depth` accepts negative values, and the crawl treats **any** negative depth as unlimited — a sentinel that is documented nowhere a user can find it:

- `pkgs/id/src/cli.rs:1191-1193` — the flag is a plain `i32` with `default_value = "1"` and no range validation. Its help text documents only `0 = no crawl, 1 = query direct peers (default), N = recursively query up to N levels deep`.
- `pkgs/id/src/commands/peers.rs:292` — `let max_depth = if depth < 0 { i32::MAX } else { depth };`
- The module doc (`peers.rs:26-38`) likewise documents only depth 0/1/N and lists the safeguards as `--max-peers`, `--timeout`, and visited tracking.

So `--depth=-1` (the `=` form; clap rejects the space form) silently selects an unbounded crawl. There is no overall deadline: the crawl loop (`peers.rs:295-347`) queries frontier peers **sequentially**, each allowed the full per-query timeout (`--timeout`, default 30s, `peers.rs:319`), so wall-clock grows with frontier size × timeout. The only stops are the frontier running out or the max-peers check — and per #1765 that cap is not hard on all paths (the crawl inserts a whole `ListPeers` response without re-checking it, `peers.rs:328-335`).

## Evidence (verified this run, main 42796be5)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneB-peersdepth/`): the clap derive replicated exactly from `cli.rs` (clap 4, `#[arg(long, default_value = "1")] depth: i32`) plus the `crawl_peers` loop structure copied from `peers.rs:291-347` with an in-memory chain graph (peer *i* announces peer *i+1*), per-peer timeout dropped (it only makes the negative case slower, never shorter):

```
CLI --depth=-1 parses to depth=-1
CLI --depth=-7 parses to depth=-7
CLI --depth -1 (space form) rejected: error: unexpected argument '-1' found
depth=  0 -> discovered 1 peers (chain of 51)
depth=  1 -> discovered 2 peers (chain of 51)
depth=  2 -> discovered 3 peers (chain of 51)
depth=  3 -> discovered 4 peers (chain of 51)
depth= -1 -> discovered 51 peers (chain of 51)
depth= -7 -> discovered 51 peers (chain of 51)
depth=-1 max_peers=10 -> discovered 10 peers (cap is the only stop)
```

## Why it matters

A typo, a script that computes a depth and underflows below zero, or a user guessing that `-1` means "one level less" turns a quick lookup into a crawl of the whole reachable network — up to the 1000-peer default cap at up to 30s per sequential query in the worst case (hours), issuing a connection + `ListPeers` RPC to every node it visits. Nothing in `--help`, the module doc, or any output line tells the user an unlimited mode was selected. Everywhere else this CLI parses numbers strictly and answers misuse with a usage error (e.g. `world_line` `/logs`, the REPL's strict parsers); this flag is the outlier.

Related but distinct: #1765 (max-peers is not a hard cap — different defect, the cap check placement; this issue is the depth sentinel). Fixing #1765 does not fix this, and vice versa.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Triage pins the contract: either (a) negative `--depth` is refused at parse time with a clear error (preferred — matches the CLI's strict-parser convention and the documented 0/1/N range), or (b) negative depth is kept as an intentional unlimited mode and is documented in the `--help` text and module doc, with a startup warning line naming the max-peers bound.
- [ ] A test pins the chosen contract: `--depth=-1` either fails to parse / errors before any crawl starts, or (under (b)) crawls past a positive bound in a stubbed-graph unit test of `crawl_peers`.
- [ ] Positive depths 0/1/N behave exactly as today (existing peers/cli tests pass).
- [ ] If (a): programmatic `PeersOptions` with a negative depth cannot reach the unlimited branch either (the guard lives at, or below, the `crawl_peers` entry — not only in clap).

title: id(tuple): decode recurses on NESTED with no depth limit — a crafted 100 KB tag key (50k nested tags) aborts the process with a stack overflow

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`tuple::decode` recurses on the `NESTED` tag with no depth limit, so a crafted
key of repeated `0x05` bytes aborts the whole process with a stack overflow —
an error no caller can catch or recover from.

## Evidence (main `42796be5`)

- `pkgs/id/src/tuple.rs:380` — `pub fn decode(bytes: &[u8]) -> Result<Vec<TupleValue>>`
  walks the input via `decode_one`.
- `pkgs/id/src/tuple.rs:393,428` — `decode_one`'s `NESTED` arm loops by calling
  itself recursively (`match decode_one(data, pos, true)?`). There is no depth
  counter, no input-length guard, and no cap anywhere in the file (the only
  `MAX`-style checks in the decoder are the per-field canonicality rules added
  for #1610).
- Contrast in the same crate: `pkgs/id/src/chain.rs` decodes peer-supplied CBOR
  with an explicit `.recursion_limit(64)` (`RECURSION_LIMIT`, chain.rs:39,350).
  The tuple decoder — which parses the same class of untrusted bytes — has no
  equivalent.
- Reachability: the decoder runs on iroh-docs entry keys, which are written by
  other replicas of a shared namespace: `pkgs/id/src/tags.rs:585,609`
  (`decode_alpha_key` / `decode_omega_key` call `decode(raw)` on the raw key)
  and `tags.rs:1401-1415` (`entry_to_tag_alpha` / `entry_to_tag_omega`, called
  from the tag query paths at tags.rs:1240,1281,1383,1395). One crafted key in
  a synced α/Ω doc crashes every node that lists/searches that namespace's tags.

## Reproduction (verified this run)

Probe crate on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-tuple-depth/`) that
compiles the crate's own `tuple.rs` at main `42796be5` verbatim
(md5 `8fd9b15126d0772d28bb984bd86f83f2`, identical in both clones) and calls
`tuple::decode` on `[0x05; N] ++ [0x00; N]`:

- N=1,000 and N=10,000 on a 2 MiB stack: decode OK.
- N=50,000 (a 100 KB input) on a 2 MiB stack: `thread has overflowed its
  stack / fatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting`, exit 134 (SIGABRT).
- N=100,000 on an 8 MiB stack: same abort, exit 134.

A stack overflow in Rust is a process abort, not a `Result::Err` — the
`?`-based error handling in every caller is irrelevant once it trips.

## Why it matters

Tag namespaces sync between peers; the α/Ω key space is not written only by
this node. A single malicious or corrupt entry key turns a routine tag
list/search on any replica into a full process crash (denial of service that
repeats on every query until the entry is removed by other means). The crate
already treats this exact risk as real for CBOR headers (recursion limit 64);
tuple keys deserve the same bound.

## Acceptance criteria

- `tuple::decode` rejects nesting deeper than a named, documented limit
  (consistent with the crate's CBOR `RECURSION_LIMIT` of 64, or a justified
  value) with a normal `Err`, at any input size and on a small (e.g. 2 MiB)
  stack — no abort.
- Regression tests: `[0x05; 100_000] ++ [0x00; 100_000]`, a just-over-limit
  nested value, and a legitimately nested value at/under the limit (round-trip
  through the encoder) — the first two error, the last decodes.
- `decode_alpha_key` / `decode_omega_key` surface the depth error as an
  ordinary tag error (no panic/abort) on a crafted doc entry key.
- The encoder side is considered too: if the encoder can still *produce*
  nesting deeper than the decoder accepts, that asymmetry is either fixed or
  explicitly documented.

Split from #1877 (triage task 2771, 2026-10-29); parent tracker #1885 (extensibility).

## What is needed

A decision-ready proposal for mcpx's public Go API surface — step 1 of #1877's sequence (public Go package → C ABI → WASM, each step only if the one before it has a caller).

Confirmed at triage (2026-10-29, current main): there is **no public Go API at all** — `pkgs/mcpx` top level is `cmd/`, `daemon/`, `internal/`, `plugin/`, `docs/`; every implementation package is under `internal/` and cannot be imported by another module. Today "embedding" means exec the binary or speak `/v1` over the socket.

## The proposal must name

1. The candidate public packages (smallest surface that serves a real first caller) and the first caller each serves.
2. The compatibility promise that attaches to them.
3. Honest weighing of the status-quo alternatives (exec the binary; `/v1` over the socket) — if they suffice for the named callers, say so and close the sequence.
4. Sequencing for the C ABI (`-buildmode=c-shared` / `c-archive`) and WASM (`wasip1` reactor via the same exported surface), per #1877.

## Out of scope

- Implementing the API, C ABI, or WASM build (a follow-up implementation packet follows the decision).
- The self-connection loop guard — split 1 from #1877, queue task 3108.

- Proposal posted (here or on #1877) covering points 1–4 with file:line evidence for claims about the current package layout.

title: id(web/tags_ws): /ws/tags WebSocket has no message-size cap — a client can force 64 MiB buffered-and-discarded messages on a socket that expects no inbound payload at all

labels.name: task/triage

labels.name: app/id

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

The `/ws/tags` WebSocket upgrade in `pkgs/id` sets no message-size cap, unlike the repo's other WebSocket:

- `pkgs/id/src/web/tags_ws.rs:205-208` — `ws_tags_handler` calls plain `ws.on_upgrade(...)` with no `max_message_size(...)`.
- `pkgs/id/src/web/world_ws.rs:279` — the world WebSocket pins `ws.max_message_size(MAX_FRAME_BYTES)` (1 MiB) before upgrade.
- `pkgs/id/src/frames.rs:14-20` — `MAX_FRAME_BYTES` is documented as the shared bound: "the WebSocket has `max_message_size(MAX_FRAME_BYTES)`".

With no pin, the framework default applies: tungstenite 0.29's `WebSocketConfig::default()` is `max_message_size: Some(64 << 20)` = 64 MiB (verified in the vendored crate source, `tungstenite-0.29.0/src/protocol/mod.rs:101` — the same default #1965 established for the collab socket).

## Why it matters

`/ws/tags` expects **no inbound messages at all** — its own module doc says so (`tags_ws.rs:14`, and the handler doc at :200-203: "No inbound messages are processed (ping/pong only for keepalive)"). But `handle_tags_socket` (`tags_ws.rs:215-228`) spawns a drain task that `receiver.next().await`s whole messages just to ignore everything except `Close`. So every connected client can force the server to buffer a full 64 MiB message per frame batch — 64× the repo's own 1 MiB bound — for data that is definitionally discarded. There is no per-connection or aggregate bound on top of that, so N idle clients × one in-flight 64 MiB message each is pure unbounded-by-design memory pressure on `id serve`, on a socket whose legitimate inbound traffic is zero bytes of payload.

This is distinct from #1965 (collab): that socket *processes* inbound steps and retains them; this one retains nothing and needs no inbound payload at all — the fix surface and the acceptance test are different (here the drain simply must never see an oversized message).

## Evidence (verified this run, main 42796be5)

- Read `tags_ws.rs:195-260` directly: no `max_message_size` anywhere in the file (`grep -n "MAX_FRAME_BYTES\|max_message" pkgs/id/src/web/tags_ws.rs` returns nothing); the file also has no test module.
- Contrast read at `world_ws.rs:279` (cap pinned) and `frames.rs:14-20` (1 MiB constant + the documented WebSocket convention).
- Framework default verified in a second, independent source: vendored `tungstenite-0.29.0/src/protocol/mod.rs:101` — `max_message_size: Some(64 << 20)`.
- Route registered at `pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs:303` (`/ws/tags`).
- Dedup: `gh issue list --state all` searches for `tags_ws`, "ws/tags websocket size" returned no existing issue for this socket; #1965 covers only the collab WebSocket (`/ws/collab`, `collab.rs:627-632`) — cross-linked, not duplicated.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The `/ws/tags` upgrade pins a message-size cap consistent with the repo convention (triage pins the exact value — `MAX_FRAME_BYTES` 1 MiB is the in-repo precedent at `world_ws.rs:279`; a smaller cap is defensible since no inbound payload is legitimate).
- [ ] A client that sends a message over the cap has its connection closed/refused by the framework instead of the server buffering the whole message in the drain task.
- [ ] Regression test: an oversized inbound message to `/ws/tags` does not get delivered to the drain loop (connection terminated), while ping/close handling and the outbound tag-event stream keep working.
- [ ] Existing `pkgs/id` web tests still pass; the outbound `/ws/tags` event stream is unchanged for well-behaved clients.

title: mcpx(daemon): chat-completions proxy has no upstream timeout and buffers the whole upstream response in memory — proxyToUpstream uses http.DefaultClient and an uncapped TeeReader buffer

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Problem

The mcpx daemon's chat-completions reverse proxy (`proxyToUpstream`, `pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/routes_proxy.go:215`) has no bound on either direction of its upstream call:

**1. No upstream timeout.** `routes_proxy.go:237` calls `http.DefaultClient.Do(upReq)`. `http.DefaultClient` has no `Timeout`, and the client sets no `ResponseHeaderTimeout` — the only cancellation is the inbound request's context, i.e. the downstream client disconnecting. The daemon's own HTTP servers set only `ReadHeaderTimeout` (`internal/daemon/server.go:309,361`) — no write/response deadline rescues a stuck handler. An upstream that accepts the connection and never answers (or trickles forever) holds the handler, its goroutine and the downstream connection indefinitely. This is reachable per-request: `handleChatCompletions` takes the upstream URL from the `X-Upstream-Url` request header when present (`routes_proxy.go`, step 4, ~:150), so any local client can aim the daemon at a slow-loris endpoint.

**2. The whole upstream response is buffered in memory, uncapped.** `routes_proxy.go:245-262`: the response body is streamed through an `io.TeeReader` into a `bytes.Buffer`, then `buf.String()` is stored as the feedback interaction record after `io.Copy` finishes. The copy itself streams, but the buffer defeats it — memory grows with the full response size, with no cap. A streamed request makes this worst-case: `chatCompletionReq.Stream` (`routes_proxy.go:38`) is marshalled straight into the proxied payload (`:227`) and `handleChatCompletions` proxies unconditionally (`:164`), so a long SSE stream accumulates in the buffer for its entire life.

Verified on main `42796be5bbe8824545df570f3b239d23d4ef93ac` by reading the code this run.

## The house pattern this misses

Every other outbound HTTP call in mcpx pins a timeout or a body bound:

- `internal/catalog/embeddings.go:52` — `&http.Client{Timeout: defaults.EmbeddingsRemoteTimeout}`
- `internal/mcpclient/sse.go:58` — `&http.Client{Timeout: timeout}`; error bodies read via `io.LimitReader(..., defaults.HTTPErrorBodyLimit)` (`sse.go:76,225`)
- `internal/cli/client.go:118-162` — all daemon clients built with explicit timeouts
- `internal/daemon/ops.go:285` — registry calls use `cs.Duration("registry.timeout")`

`routes_proxy.go:237` is the only `http.DefaultClient` use in `internal/daemon`.

## Why it matters

The daemon is the process every other tool call depends on. One hung upstream (a crashed provider gateway, a misconfigured `proxy.upstreamUrl`, a header-aimed slow endpoint) leaks a handler + connection pair forever per request, and one large or streamed response can grow daemon memory without limit — the daemon-side mirror of the inbound body-cap gap in #2082 (request bodies), on the response path #2082 does not cover. Distinct from #2097/#2100/#2102: those are the standalone proxy packages; this is mcpx's own daemon proxy route.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `proxyToUpstream` uses a client with a configured timeout (a `proxy.*` setting with a sane default, in the style of `registry.timeout` / `defaults.EmbeddingsRemoteTimeout`), covering at least time-to-headers and total response time; a timed-out upstream yields a clean 502 to the downstream client.
- [ ] The feedback-record copy of the upstream response is capped (e.g. `io.LimitReader` at a named constant, in the spirit of `defaults.HTTPErrorBodyLimit`); over-cap responses are still proxied in full to the client, only the recorded copy is truncated, and the truncation is visible in the record.
- [ ] Tests: a stub upstream that accepts and never responds makes the handler return within the configured timeout; a stub upstream returning an over-cap (or streamed) response is proxied completely while daemon-side buffering stays bounded.
- [ ] Existing daemon test suites pass unchanged.

title: id(world): sanitize_display_name / sanitize_chat filter Cc only — Cf format characters (U+202E, U+200B, bidi isolates) pass into participant names and broadcast chat, and a zero-width-only name passes the join empty check

body:
## Problem

The world runtime's two text sanitizers promise to strip control characters from participant display names and chat text, but they filter with `char::is_control` — Unicode category **Cc only**. Category-**Cf** format characters (U+200B ZERO WIDTH SPACE, U+202E RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE, U+2066/U+2069 bidi isolates, U+2060 WORD JOINER, U+FEFF, U+00AD SOFT HYPHEN) pass both sanitizers untouched, so a participant can join with an invisible or bidi-reordering display name, and chat lines broadcast to every other participant can carry the same characters. A display name consisting solely of zero-width spaces also passes the join path's non-empty check, so a participant can be present under a literally invisible name.

This is the same Cf class as #1674 (petname), #1778 (directory) and #1770 (invite), but a different module and fix surface: none of those covers `pkgs/id/src/world/util.rs` or the world join/chat paths in `world/core.rs`. #1833 covers web/collab cursor names, a different subsystem.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `42796be5`)

- `sanitize_display_name` (`pkgs/id/src/world/util.rs:69-76`): `.filter(|ch| !ch.is_control())`, then `take(48)`, then trim. Rust's `char::is_control` is general category Cc only.
- `sanitize_chat` (`pkgs/id/src/world/util.rs:78-85`): same filter (allowing `\n`/`\t`), then trim.
- Call sites: join — `world/core.rs:847` sanitizes the display name, `core.rs:848-851` refuses only if the sanitized name is empty; chat — `world/core.rs:955` (participant chat) and `core.rs:578` (host/system chat) sanitize before the event is committed and broadcast.
- Laptop probe (verbatim copies of both functions, main `42796be5`, `world/util.rs` sha256 `6c6cab01…`; probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-worldcf/`):
  - `"Ann\u{202E}nimdA"` → name and chat output unchanged (RLO survives).
  - `"\u{200B}\u{200B}"` (zero-width only) → output unchanged and **non-empty**, so the join empty-name refusal does not fire.
  - `"Ann\u{200B}"`, `"An\u{00AD}n"`, `"\u{2060}\u{FEFF}Bo"`, chat `"hi \u{2066}evil\u{2069}"` and `"pay \u{202E} 100"` → all unchanged.
  - Control: Cc `U+0007` is stripped from both (`"A\u{0007}nn"` → `"Ann"`), as documented.
  - `is_control()` returns `false` for U+200B, U+202E, U+2066, U+2060, U+FEFF and U+00AD.

## Why it matters

Display names and chat are the identity other participants see inside a shared world. A RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE in a name or chat line reorders the text around it for every viewer (the classic spoofing primitive), zero-width characters make two visually identical names distinct (or one name invisible), and bidi isolates can hide or fake quoted text. The sanitizers are the single choke point for both surfaces, so this is the layer where the Cf class has to be closed for worlds — the directory/petname fixes do not reach it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `sanitize_display_name` and `sanitize_chat` in `pkgs/id/src/world/util.rs` remove (or refuse, per a contract pinned in triage) the Cf characters U+200B, U+202E, U+2066–U+2069, U+2060, U+FEFF and U+00AD — consistent with whatever shared rule #1674/#1778 settle on, if one exists by then.
- [ ] A display name that is only Cf/whitespace sanitizes to empty, so the existing join refusal in `world/core.rs` fires for invisible names.
- [ ] Chat text containing Cf reaches other participants without those characters; legitimate text (including `\n`/`\t` in chat, non-Latin scripts, emoji/ZWJ sequences if the pinned rule allows them — ZWJ U+200D is also Cf and the rule must say explicitly what happens to it) is otherwise unchanged.
- [ ] Unit tests in `world/util.rs` (or `world/core.rs`) cover: RLO in a name, a zero-width-only name, bidi isolates in chat, and the Cc control case continuing to pass.
- [ ] Existing world tests pass.

body:
## Proxy service-model redesign: automatic flake services, supervisor retirement

Design decision (Drew, 2026-10-28 23:05 CDT): make the fleet proxies proper automatic flake-declared user services, retire the proxy-supervisor's process-ownership role, and restore consumers' `Wants` against the real units.

### Current state

- Seven proxies serve canonical ports: clef :18742, antigravity-agy :18743, codex :18744, antigravity-ls :18745, design-code :18746, commandcode :18748, claude-code :18749. (muse :18747 is supervised the same way and must not be stranded by a supervisor retirement.)
- They currently run as supervisor-owned transient `fps-*` units (`bin/proxy-supervise.mjs`, run by the `proxy-supervisor` user timer every ~2 min; endpoint state under `~/.local/state/<proxy>/endpoint.json`).
- The supervisor had a symlink-guard bug (#2083) making it a silent no-op from 2026-10-27 until manual cold-starts on 2026-10-28. PR #2085 (guard fix) is open.
- The flake also declares manual one-off units for the proxies in `home/common/default.nix` (no `Install.WantedBy`), currently stopped. `claude-code-proxy` and `muse-proxy` have no declarative unit at all — supervisor config only.
- Consumers on `main` still `Wants` the manual units: `openclaw-gateway` (`home/openclaw/default.nix`: commandcode/design-code/agy + mcpx) and `openchamber.service` (`home/common/default.nix`: clef/codex/antigravity-ls/design-code).

### Redesign

1. One automatic user service per proxy: flake-declared (home-manager `systemd.user.services`), canonical port, `ExecStart` running the same checkout entry points the supervisor runs today (`~/code/bin/*.mjs`, `commandcode-proxy-start.sh`, `muse-proxy-start.sh`), `Restart` per flake patterns, `Install.WantedBy = [ "default.target" ]`.
2. Retire the supervisor's ownership in the same change: remove/disable the `proxy-supervisor` timer + oneshot service and its config so it cannot respawn `fps-*` units. No second owner may remain; the cutover must end in exactly one ownership model.
3. Consumers' `Wants` stay/restored against the (now real, automatic) units with `Wants`+`After` semantics — soft pull-in, ordering when co-started, never blocks the consumer if a proxy is not live. mcpx `Wants` are legitimate and stay.
4. The manual one-off declarations are replaced by the automatic units (same unit names), so nothing startable remains that can fight the services for a canonical port.

### Supersedes / related

- PR #2092 (gateway wants removal) and PR #2094 (openchamber wants removal) are superseded by this redesign: the wants are no longer wrong once the units they name are real automatic services. Both PRs stay open, unmerged.
- #2083 / PR #2085: the guard fix becomes moot if the supervisor's process-management role retires here.
- #883: related — the declarative commandcode unit's store-path `ExecStart` was the stale-bin casualty; the redesign runs the checkout entry points like the supervisor does.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] After a switch: all proxy services active on canonical ports, `proxy-supervisor` timer gone/disabled, no `fps-*` units.
- [ ] `/v1/models` spot-checks on :18745, :18746, :18748 return live lists.
- [ ] `openclaw-gateway` and `openchamber.service` restart cleanly (Wants+After soft semantics).
- [ ] One end-to-end route smoke through the background OpenCode serve (:13420).
- [ ] `systemctl --user --failed` clean for proxy units.
- [ ] Cutover safety: never leave supervisor + services fighting over ports; if the cutover cannot complete, the supervisor-owned status quo stays fully intact.

title: antigravity-ls-proxy: callRpc has no timeout — a language server that heartbeats but never answers an RPC hangs /v1/models and every chat request forever

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator

labels.description: Package/app: antigravity-ls-proxy (bin/ in this repo)

body:
## Summary

`bin/antigravity-ls-proxy.mjs`'s `callRpc` — the single method every language-server RPC goes through — calls `fetch` with **no timeout signal**. A language server that is alive enough to pass the proxy's heartbeat but wedged on real RPCs (deadlocked, stuck on its own upstream) hangs every dependent request forever: `/v1/models`, and every `/v1/chat/completions` (which blocks on `GetAvailableModels` before it even starts a cascade). The heartbeat in the same file pins `AbortSignal.timeout(1500)` (:224), and `bin/sync-models.mjs`'s identical `GetAvailableModels` call pins 3000 ms — `callRpc` is the one unguarded path.

## Evidence (main `82b019a0`)

- `bin/antigravity-ls-proxy.mjs:372-383` — `callRpc(method, payload)` does `await fetch(url, { method: 'POST', headers, body })` with no `signal`, no `AbortSignal.timeout`, no deadline of any kind; callers: `GetAvailableModels` (:420, via `getLiveCatalog`), `StartCascade` (:793), `SendUserCascadeMessage` (:806), `GetCascadeTrajectorySteps` (:824), `GetModelResponse` (:913).
- Same file, :217-226 — `checkHeartbeat` uses `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(1500)`, so a wedged-but-listening server passes health checks while its RPCs hang: `ensureActive` succeeds, then the request waits indefinitely.
- The cascade poll loop (:822-843) has a nominal cap (120 attempts × 250 ms, then "Cascade execution timed out after 30 seconds") that a single hung `GetCascadeTrajectorySteps` callRpc defeats — the loop never advances to the next attempt.
- `getLiveCatalog` (:417-430) caches for 60 s, but a hung first pull never resolves and never caches, so every `/v1/models` and chat request piles onto the same indefinite wait.

## Probe (laptop, 2026-10-28, shipped file unmodified)

Probe dir: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-lsrpc/` (laptop) — stub language server that answers `Heartbeat` with 200 and never responds to any other RPC (the test file's own env attach path, `ANTIGRAVITY_LS_ADDRESS`/`ANTIGRAVITY_CSRF_TOKEN`), shipped proxy on an alternate port:

- Proxy starts and `/health` answers (heartbeat path works against the stub).
- `GET /v1/models`: **no response after 8001 ms** (client-side abort fired; stub logged the hanging `GetAvailableModels` RPC).
- `POST /v1/chat/completions`: **no response after 8002 ms** (blocked on the same hanging `GetAvailableModels` callRpc, before any cascade RPC).

## Why it matters

This proxy fronts a language server that is a separate, crash- and deadlock-prone process. The failure mode "process alive, RPCs wedged" is exactly the one the heartbeat cannot distinguish — and it converts a backend wedge into indefinitely hung client requests with no error, no log line, and no recovery short of restarting the proxy (which doesn't unwedge the server). Every sibling call site in the fleet already bounds this wait (heartbeat 1500 ms here; sync-models 3000 ms for the same RPC; clef-proxy 10 s, #2100; design-code-proxy dispatch, #2097).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `callRpc` carries a bounded timeout (triage pins the value; it must comfortably exceed normal `GetModelResponse`/cascade-step latency — a generous per-RPC bound, not a total-request deadline), and a timed-out RPC surfaces as an error the existing `catch` paths already handle (e.g. `getLiveCatalog`'s last-known-good fallback engages instead of hanging).
- [ ] A language server that heartbeats but never answers RPCs: `/v1/models` answers within a bounded time (live catalog or static floor), and a chat request fails with a clean error within a bounded time — never an indefinite hang.
- [ ] The cascade poll loop's 30-second cap becomes effective: a hung poll RPC counts against it instead of defeating it.
- [ ] Tests in `bin/antigravity-ls-proxy.test.mjs` style: stub LS in heartbeat-ok/RPC-hang mode → models and chat requests resolve (value or clean error) within a bounded time; slow-but-alive LS (answers after a delay under the bound) still succeeds.
- [ ] Existing behaviours unchanged: heartbeat timeout, live-catalog 60 s cache + last-known-good, model resolution (#686 tests), cascade and direct-RPC chat paths against a healthy stub.

## Dedup

`gh issue list --search "antigravity-ls-proxy timeout callRpc"` and `--search "antigravity"`: no issue covers a missing `callRpc` timeout. Related but distinct: #2097 (design-code-proxy backend dispatch), #2100 (clef-proxy data-path fetch), #494 (closed, LS address parsing).

body:
# clef-proxy: data-path upstream fetch has no timeout — a gateway that accepts and never responds holds the /v1/systemone request open (the models fetch in the same file pins 10s)

## Evidence

`bin/clef-proxy.mjs` (main `82b019a0`, sha256 `12e3415ff346ac25…`):

- `:234` — the data path, the proxy's only inference call, awaits the Cloudflare gateway with **no signal and no deadline of any kind**:

```js
const cfRes = await fetch(cfUrl, {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'Authorization': `Bearer ${token}`, 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify(payload)
});
```

  `cfUrl` is built at `:227` (`https://gateway.ai.cloudflare.com/v1/<account>/<gateway>/workers-ai/run/<model>`). The follow-up `await cfRes.json()` at `:248` is likewise unbounded, so a gateway that sends headers and then trickles or stalls the body hangs the same handler a second way.

- `:128-130` — the **same file** already knows the fix pattern: the live-model-catalog fetch pins `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10000)`. Only the catalog got a deadline; the request that actually serves user traffic did not.

- The handler is the `POST /v1/systemone` route: until the fetch settles it never writes a response, so the client connection, the request handler, and (for the hosted SystemOne caller) the turn all stay open. Nothing maps a stall to a 504 — if the runtime eventually errors the fetch, the shared catch at the end of the handler reports it as a generic 500.

### Probe (this run, sandbox Node, verbatim call shapes)

A local HTTP server that accepts and never responds, called two ways:

| call | result |
|---|---|
| `fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2000) })` (control) | rejected after ~2000 ms (`TimeoutError`) |
| `fetch(url, { method: 'POST', headers, body })` — exactly the `:234` shape, no signal | **still unsettled after 12 s**, probe exited with the request pending |

So the data path's only bound is whatever the fetch runtime's global defaults happen to be (undici's multi-minute headers/body defaults) — roughly 30× the 10 s deadline this same file chose for its catalog fetch, and not a contract anything pins or tests.

## Why it matters

Clef is a decision endpoint: a stalled gateway turns into a stalled caller with no error, no log line naming a timeout, and no response to retry against, for minutes at a time. The proxy process stays healthy (`/health` answers), so supervision sees nothing. This is the same failure class as #2097 (design-code-proxy dispatch, no timeout, fallback never fires) in a different proxy whose upstream is a hardcoded public gateway — there is no operator-side workaround short of editing the file.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The data-path fetch at `:234` carries an explicit deadline (e.g. `AbortSignal.timeout(<pinned value>)`), and the deadline also bounds reading the response body (`cfRes.json()`).
- [ ] A deadline expiry is reported as an upstream timeout (a 504-class response naming the timeout), not folded into the generic 500 catch.
- [ ] The pinned value is a named constant (parity with the models fetch's 10000, or a triage-pinned Clef-appropriate value), with the choice recorded on this issue.
- [ ] Tests in `bin/clef-proxy.test.mjs` cover: a never-responding upstream fails the request at the deadline with the timeout response, and a normally responding upstream is unchanged.
- [ ] The models-catalog fetch behaviour is unchanged.

Related: #2097 (same no-timeout class, design-code-proxy), #2096 / #1809 (this proxy family's env-parsing cases — different failure, same "starts healthy, fails silently" shape).

body:
## Summary

`bin/design-code-proxy.mjs` dispatch has **no timeout on its backend requests**: if a backend accepts the connection (or connects and then stalls) and never answers, the client request hangs forever and the proxy's own primary→fallback machinery never fires — fallback only triggers on a socket `error`, an HTTP 429/5xx response, or an in-body quota error, and a silent backend produces none of those. Each hung request also holds one socket from the shared keep-alive pool (`maxSockets: 32` per scheme) indefinitely, so a wedged backend can gradually exhaust the pool for the healthy backend too.

## Evidence (main `bd880194`, file sha256 `27e9fc8c…`)

- `bin/design-code-proxy.mjs` — `tryTarget` (in `dispatchWithFallback`) builds the backend call with `http.request({ hostname: '127.0.0.1', port: target.port, path: '/v1/chat/completions', agent: httpAgent, … })` and registers only `localReq.on('error', …)` → `onFail`. There is no `localReq.setTimeout(...)`, no `timeout` option, and no abort anywhere in the dispatch path. The only `AbortSignal.timeout` in the file is 2500 ms on the background `/v1/models` catalog probes (:95).
- The AMR upstream forward in the same file (`clientReq = https.request(...)`, same handler) likewise sets no timeout; its `error` handler falls back to local dispatch, which a hanging upstream also never triggers.
- The fallback contract is otherwise proven working: a primary that answers 500 falls back immediately (see probe control below).

## Probe (laptop, 2026-10-28, shipped file unmodified)

Probe dir: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-designtimeout/` (laptop) — two stub backends (primary switchable 500/hang, fallback healthy) + the shipped proxy on alternate ports (`ANTIGRAVITY_LS_PROXY_PORT`/`CODEX_PROXY_PORT`/`DESIGN_CODE_PROXY_PORT` env):

- Control, healthy primary (`gpt-6-luna` → codex stub): **200 in 94 ms**.
- Control, primary answers 500 (`design-code-pro` → antigravity stub 500, codex stub healthy): **200 in 31 ms via fallback** — the fallback machinery works when failure is signalled.
- Test, primary accepts and never responds (`design-code-pro`, primary in hang mode): **no response within 8000 ms** (client-side `AbortSignal` timeout fired); the healthy fallback was never tried. The proxy itself stayed alive (`GET /v1/models` → 200 immediately after), so this is a per-request permanent wedge, not a crash.

## Why it matters

`dispatchWithFallback` exists precisely so one bad backend doesn't take down design-code requests — the file already handles backend response errors, 429/5xx, and in-body quota errors (#681 fixed a sibling "hangs forever instead of falling back" bug in this same function). A backend that wedges silently (deadlocked language server, a proxy sibling stuck on its own upstream) is the remaining failure mode, and it is worse than a clean error: the client waits indefinitely and pooled sockets accumulate.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A backend that connects but does not respond within a bounded time (triage pins the value; it should be generous enough for slow streaming first-byte, e.g. a time-to-first-response / socket-inactivity timeout rather than a total-stream deadline) causes `onFail` → fallback, and if both targets time out, a clean 502 — never an indefinite hang.
- [ ] The AMR upstream forward (`https.request` path) gets the same treatment: a silent upstream falls back to local dispatch instead of hanging.
- [ ] Streaming responses that are actively flowing are not killed by the timeout (inactivity-based, or reset on data).
- [ ] Tests in `bin/design-code-proxy.test.mjs` style: hanging-primary → fallback serves; both-hang → 502 within a bounded time; slow-but-alive backend still succeeds.
- [ ] Existing behaviours unchanged: 429/5xx fallback, in-body quota fallback, model rewriting on stream and non-stream paths.

title: id(world-doctor): journal check disagrees with FileJournal::open both ways — passes blank-line journals open refuses as corrupt, fails the crash-torn tail open drops and repairs

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`id world doctor`'s journal check (`validate_journal_file`, pkgs/id/src/world_doctor.rs) disagrees with the journal's actual open path (`FileJournal::open`, pkgs/id/src/world_store.rs) in **both directions**, so its verdict — and its repair advice — cannot be trusted:

1. **Doctor fails a journal that open repairs.** Doctor parses every non-empty line and errors on any malformed one (world_doctor.rs:367-371). A crash-torn final entry (unterminated, partial JSON — the normal state after a crash mid-append) therefore fails the check, and `check_journal` advises: *"restore the journal from a backup, or recreate the world"* (world_doctor.rs:348). But `FileJournal::open` drops and truncates exactly that torn tail and opens the world fine (world_store.rs:107-125; test `torn_final_entry_is_dropped_but_mid_file_corruption_is_refused`, world_store.rs:1044). Following the doctor's advice destroys a world that would have opened cleanly.

2. **Doctor passes a journal that open refuses as corrupt.** Doctor skips empty lines (world_doctor.rs:367). `FileJournal::open` does not: a blank line (`"\n"`) fails `serde_json::from_slice`, and because the line is newline-terminated (`complete == true`) open bails with "world journal … is corrupt at byte …" (world_store.rs:84-106). A journal with a leading, middle, or trailing blank line is reported healthy by doctor and then refuses to open.

## Why this happened

#1598 aligned doctor to `read_journal_entries` (world_store.rs:452 — the fork/compaction reader, which skips blank lines) rather than to `FileJournal::open`, which is the path that actually opens and restores a world. The two readers in world_store.rs themselves diverge on blank lines and on the torn tail (#1523 covers the fork reader's torn-tail gap).

## Evidence (verified at main 39e8410b)

- pkgs/id/src/world_doctor.rs:361-396 `validate_journal_file`: `if line.is_empty() { continue; }` (:367); any other unparseable line → "entry {} is malformed" (:370-371). No torn-tail case.
- pkgs/id/src/world_doctor.rs:336-351 `check_journal`: failure fix text is "restore the journal from a backup, or recreate the world" (:348).
- pkgs/id/src/world_store.rs:82-125 `FileJournal::open`: blank line parses as an error with `complete == true` → corrupt bail (:84-106); unterminated unparseable final line with nothing after it → `torn = true`, dropped and truncated (:107-125).
- pkgs/id/src/world_store.rs:1044 test proves the torn-tail repair on the open path.
- pkgs/id/src/world_store.rs:452-466 `read_journal_entries` skips empty lines — the reader #1598 matched doctor against.

## Acceptance criteria

- Doctor's journal verdict matches `FileJournal::open`'s accept/refuse outcome for at least: a crash-torn final entry, a blank line (leading, middle, and trailing positions), mid-file corruption, and a fully-written entry from a newer binary.
- Triage pins the fix direction per case: for the torn tail, doctor must stop advising restore/recreate for a journal open repairs (report it as repaired/repairable instead). For blank lines, either open learns to skip them or doctor fails them — one behaviour, named in the issue resolution, with the other reader (`read_journal_entries`) brought into line if it diverges from the pinned rule.
- Regression tests in world_doctor's test module mirroring the world_store journal cases (torn tail, blank lines, mid-file corruption), so the two cannot drift apart again silently.

Related: #1598 (closed, prior doctor/restore alignment), #1523 (open, fork reader torn-tail gap — distinct path, this issue is the doctor check).

title: id(protocol): MetaProtocol accept is sequential with no stream deadline — one idle or trickling stream stalls every meta request on the connection

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`MetaProtocol::accept` — the `/id-meta/1` handler (`META_ALPN`) served by `id serve` — handles streams strictly one at a time, with no deadline on any stream:

- `pkgs/id/src/protocol.rs:705-727` — the accept loop awaits `recv.read_to_end(MAX_REQUEST_BYTES)` (line 708) and then `self.handle(&remote, req).await` **inline** before accepting the next stream. There is no `tokio::time::timeout` anywhere in the function, and no per-stream spawn.
- `read_to_end` caps the request *size* (1 MiB, `MAX_REQUEST_BYTES` at protocol.rs:238) but waits indefinitely for the peer to finish (or close) the stream. A peer that opens a stream and sends a partial request — or nothing — and never finishes it stalls the loop forever.
- The client side reuses ONE connection per server: `MetaClient::Remote` holds a single `Connection` (`pkgs/id/src/meta_client.rs`, `MetaClient::open`/`connect_node`), and every request goes through `request_over(&conn, …)` opening a new stream on that same connection. So one stalled stream on a connection black-holes every subsequent meta request (Put/Get/List/Find/Delete/Rename/…) on it, not just one call.

## Why this is the outlier

Sibling acceptors in the same crate do both things this one does not:

- `log_sync.rs` — `SyncProtocol::accept` spawns each stream into a `JoinSet` and wraps sessions in `timeout(SESSION_DEADLINE)` (60 s, log_sync.rs:59).
- `world_net.rs:73-95` — `WorldProtocol::accept` spawns per-stream sessions under a `Semaphore` (`MAX_SESSIONS_PER_CONNECTION`), refusing only the over-limit stream.
- `world_ssh.rs:123` — `SshTunnelProtocol` spawns per stream under a semaphore.
- `event_sync.rs:40,48` — sessions bounded by `SESSION_DEADLINE` (60 s) and even the post-session close wait is bounded (`CLOSE_WAIT` 5 s).

Related but distinct: #2084 covers the envelope + artifact-push acceptors (`answer_frames`). The meta protocol does not use `answer_frames` and is not in that issue's scope — it is the remaining sequential, deadline-free acceptor in `id serve`'s router (serve.rs:941).

## Why it matters

The meta protocol is the primary request path into a running `id serve` — local CLI/REPL clients and remote peers both use it. An idle or trickling stream is free for any connected peer to create and currently pins the connection's handler indefinitely; because clients multiplex all their requests over that one connection, the failure mode is a silent total stall of that client's meta operations, with no error and no recovery short of reconnecting.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 39e8410b)

- Read `protocol.rs:705-727` directly: sequential loop, inline `read_to_end` + `handle` awaits, no timeout, no spawn.
- Read `meta_client.rs`: `MetaClient::Remote` holds one `Connection`; `request_over` opens a stream per request on it.
- Contrast reads: log_sync.rs:59 + JoinSet accept; world_net.rs:73-95; world_ssh.rs:123-147; event_sync.rs:40-48,136.
- Enumerated every `ProtocolHandler` impl in pkgs/id/src: MetaProtocol is the only production acceptor that is both sequential and deadline-free besides the two in #2084 (ArtifactPull is filed separately — its waits are single-stream and its close-wait is unbounded, a different shape).
- Dedup: `gh issue list --state all` searches for "MetaProtocol", "meta protocol stall", "answer_frames" returned no existing issue for this (closest: #2084, envelope/artifact-push only; #697, closed, unrelated match_kind duplication).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A meta stream that does not deliver a complete request within a bounded deadline (triage pins the value — log_sync/event_sync's 60 s is the in-repo precedent) is abandoned/closed, and the acceptor moves on.
- [ ] One stalled or slow stream no longer blocks later streams on the same connection (per-stream spawn, or an equivalent structure; a per-connection concurrency bound like world_net's semaphore is welcome).
- [ ] Regression test: a peer that opens a stream and sends nothing (or a partial request) does not prevent a second stream's request from being answered; the stalled stream is closed at the deadline.
- [ ] Existing protocol/meta tests still pass; well-behaved one-request-per-stream clients (the current `request_over` paths) are unaffected.

title: id(envelope_net): envelope + artifact-push acceptors answer streams one at a time with no deadline — an idle or trickling peer stream stalls the whole connection forever

body:
## Problem

The two frame-answering Iroh acceptors in `pkgs/id` handle streams strictly one at a time, with no deadline on any stream:

- `pkgs/id/src/envelope_net.rs:137-160` — `answer_frames` loops `while let Ok((mut send, mut recv)) = conn.accept_bi().await` and awaits `read_frame(&mut recv)` (line 143) and then `receive(body)` **inline** before accepting the next stream. There is no timeout anywhere in the function.
- `answer_frames` is the shared accept path for both live protocols: `EnvelopeProtocol` (`/id-envelope/1`, `envelope_net.rs:125-135`) and `ArtifactPushProtocol` (`/id-artifact-push/1`, `pkgs/id/src/artifact.rs:779`). Both are registered in `id serve` (`pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:962,966`).
- `crate::frames::read_frame` caps the frame *size* (1 MiB, `frames.rs`) but waits indefinitely for the length prefix / body bytes to arrive.

So a peer that opens a bidirectional stream and sends nothing — or trickles a partial frame — stalls that connection's handler forever: no later stream on the connection is ever read, and the handler task (plus the receive-side work queued behind the stuck stream) never progresses. A slow `receive()` (directory apply) blocks the next stream the same way.

## Why this is the outlier

The send side of the same module is deadline-bound: `send_within` wraps the whole delivery, address lookup included, in `TIMEOUT` = 30 s (`envelope_net.rs:29`, `send_within`). The receive side has no counterpart.

The sibling sync protocol does both things `answer_frames` does not (`pkgs/id/src/log_sync.rs`):

- `SyncProtocol::accept` (lines ~200-217) spawns each accepted stream into a `JoinSet`, so one stream cannot starve the next.
- `answer()` wraps the session in `timeout(deadline, session)` with `SESSION_DEADLINE` = 60 s (`log_sync.rs:59`).

## Why it matters

`/id-envelope/1` and `/id-artifact-push/1` are served to Iroh peers — the peer is not the local user. An idle or trickling stream is free to create and currently pins a connection handler indefinitely while silently black-holing every subsequent envelope/artifact on that connection (the sender's own 30 s timeout fires, the outbox retries, and each retry can land behind the same stuck stream shape on a fresh connection the peer keeps stalling). It's a small availability/robustness hole with an established in-repo pattern for the fix.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 17249b05)

- Read `envelope_net.rs:137-160` directly: sequential loop, inline `read_frame` + `receive` awaits, no `tokio::time::timeout`.
- Grepped all `answer_frames` callers: only `EnvelopeProtocol::accept` and `ArtifactPushProtocol::accept` (artifact.rs:779); both registered in serve.rs:962,966.
- Contrast read at log_sync.rs:59 (`SESSION_DEADLINE`), ~200-217 (JoinSet spawn per stream), ~268/~313 (`timeout(deadline, session)`).
- Dedup: `gh issue list --state all` searches for `answer_frames`, "envelope idle timeout stream", and slow-loris/idle-connection terms returned no existing issue for this (closest hits were unrelated mcpx testing issues and the distinct collab-WS cap #1965).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A stream on `/id-envelope/1` or `/id-artifact-push/1` that does not deliver a complete frame within a bounded deadline (triage pins the value — sender-side 30 s or log_sync's 60 s are the in-repo precedents) is abandoned/closed, and the acceptor moves on.
- [ ] One stalled or slow stream no longer blocks later streams on the same connection (per-stream spawn, or an equivalent structure).
- [ ] Regression test: a peer that opens a stream and sends nothing (or a partial frame) does not prevent a second stream's envelope/artifact from being answered; the stalled stream is closed at the deadline.
- [ ] Existing `envelope_net` and `artifact` protocol tests still pass; well-behaved one-frame-per-stream senders (the current `deliver`/`push` clients) are unaffected.

title: mcpx(wasmtools): Load never checks the memory export — a guest with the four ABI functions but no memory is accepted, then ListTools/CallTool panic the host

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: status/needs-review
labels.description: Ready for review

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: queue/needs-review
labels.description: Queue task finished and is awaiting review

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/mcpx/internal/wasmtools` (the #1970 WASM tool-source spike, merged today in #2002) documents a guest ABI whose **first required export is `memory`** (package doc, `wasmtools.go:19-27`), but `Load` validates only the four ABI **functions**:

```go
for _, fn := range []string{inputPtrFn, outputPtrFn, listFn, callFn} {
    if mod.ExportedFunction(fn) == nil {
        rt.Close(ctx)
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("wasmtools: guest does not export %s", fn)
    }
}
```
(`wasmtools.go:116-122` — no `mod.Memory()` check.)

A guest that exports the four functions but no memory is therefore accepted, and the first use crashes the host with a nil-pointer panic instead of returning an error:

- `readOutput`: `s.mod.Memory().Read(...)` (`wasmtools.go:133-136`) — `Memory()` is nil for such a guest.
- `CallTool`: `s.mod.Memory()` then `mem.Write(...)` (`wasmtools.go:163-166`) — same nil dereference.
- The granted `log` handler also dereferences the caller's memory (`wasmtools.go:107-110`).

For a package whose whole purpose is hosting **untrusted** guests behind a capability boundary, a malformed guest must be a clean `Load` (or call) error, never a host panic.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `26221fcc`)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-wasmlogs/`, verbatim copy of the package from main `26221fcc`). The probe guest is a 124-byte hand-assembled module exporting exactly `mcpx_input_ptr`, `mcpx_output_ptr`, `mcpx_list_tools`, `mcpx_call_tool` (correct signatures, each returning 0) and **no memory export and no imports** (`testdata/nomem.wasm` in the probe dir):

```
=== RUN   TestProbeNoMemoryGuest
    probe_nomem_test.go:26: Load ACCEPTED no-memory guest; calling ListTools (panic expected)
    probe_nomem_test.go:29: PANIC from ListTools on no-memory guest: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
--- PASS: TestProbeNoMemoryGuest (0.00s)
```

The panic was caught by the probe's `recover()`; in production it propagates out of `ListTools`/`CallTool` into the caller. Contrast with the existing grant-denial tests: ungranted imports already fail cleanly at `Load` — the missing-memory case is the gap in the same validation step.

## Why it matters

Deny-by-default instantiation is the spike's headline property (three tests prove import denial). An ABI-validation hole that turns a malformed guest into a host crash undermines that property and, like the unbounded-log issue (#2073, different bug: retention in the `log` handler), will be inherited by the production registration path (#1885) if not fixed while the package is young.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Load` rejects a guest with no exported `memory`, with a descriptive error naming the missing export (mirroring the existing `guest does not export %s` errors), and closes the runtime on that path as the function-check path does.
- [ ] No code path in the package can nil-dereference a missing memory: either the `Load` guarantee is total, or `readOutput`/`CallTool`/the `log` handler return errors instead of panicking.
- [ ] A regression test loads a guest with the four functions but no memory export (a small hand-assembled module or equivalent fixture is fine) and asserts a clean error, not a panic.
- [ ] Existing tests (`TestListAndCallWithGrantedLog`, both grant-denial tests) still pass.

Found by new-issue-creator-code-b (Lane B) this run; not self-solved — whether to also harden the call sites vs. relying on the Load guarantee is triage's pin.

title: id(tags): tag search quote handling degenerates silently — "" matches every tag, name:"" widens to all values, an unterminated quote keeps its stray quote and matches nothing

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

In `pkgs/id` tag search, the query parser's quote handling degenerates silently on empty and unterminated quoted components — three distinct wrong-result shapes, none of which reports anything to the user:

- **An empty quoted literal matches everything.** `id tag search '""'` parses to `Literal("")` (`parse_single_term`, `src/tags.rs:1540-1542` via `strip_quotes`, :1563-1569). `search_by_query` (`src/tags.rs:1321-1337`) matches a `Literal`/`BareWord` term with `field.to_lowercase().contains(&text_lower)` on subject/key/value, and `"anything".contains("")` is true — so the empty literal returns **every tag**, the same output as no query at all. ANDed with real terms it is a silent no-op instead of a constraint.
- **A quoted empty component is silently dropped from `key:value`.** `name:""` parses to `KeyOnly("name")` and `"":high` to `ValueOnly("high")`: `parse_single_term` (`src/tags.rs:1523-1535`) branches on `key.is_empty()` / `value.is_empty()` *after* `strip_quotes`, so it cannot tell "no value was written" (`name:`) from "the value written was explicitly empty" (`name:""`). Empty-string tag values are real (a `tag set` with an empty value is distinct from a bare tag), so `name:""` should not widen to every value of `name`.
- **An unterminated quote is kept as a literal quote character.** `"abc def` parses to `BareWord("\"abc def")` — the term extractor (`src/tags.rs:1497-1513`) consumes to end-of-input while `in_quotes`, and `strip_quotes` only strips a *pair*, so the stray `"` stays in the search text and the search silently matches nothing. `key:"unclosed` similarly becomes `KeyValue("key", "\"unclosed")` — a value with a leading quote that no tag has.

## Evidence (verified this run, 2026-10-28, main `38f1f00f`)

Probe compiled and run on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-searchquotes/` there; `SearchTerm`, `parse_search_query`, `parse_single_term`, `split_on_unquoted_colon` and `strip_quotes` copied verbatim from `src/tags.rs:1434-1569`, sha256 of the source file `e2483c0b…`):

```text
"\"\""            => [Literal("")]                    control should be: no match / error, not all tags
"\"hello world\"" => [Literal("hello world")]         control ✓
"\"abc def"       => [BareWord("\"abc def")]          BUG: stray quote kept, silently matches nothing
"name:\"\""       => [KeyOnly("name")]                BUG: explicit empty value dropped → widened to all values
"\"\":high"       => [ValueOnly("high")]              BUG: explicit empty key dropped
"key:\"unclosed"  => [KeyValue("key", "\"unclosed")]  BUG: value carries the stray quote
"\"a\" \"\""      => [Literal("a"), Literal("")]      the empty term is a silent no-op in the AND
"name:foo"        => [KeyValue("name", "foo")]        control ✓
```

Existing parser tests (`src/tags.rs:2425-2580`) pin the empty *query*, bare colon, `key:` and quoted forms with content, but no test pins `""`, `name:""`, or an unterminated quote.

## Why it matters

Tag search is the discovery surface for the whole store (CLI `id tag search`, REPL `find`/`search` paths share this parser's terms via `search_by_query`). A typo'd closing quote — the common case when typing a quoted phrase by hand in the REPL — turns the search into a silent empty result, and an empty quoted phrase turns it into a silent full dump. Both are the silent-reinterpretation class this codebase keeps fixing one parser at a time (#1609 whitespace separators in this same function, #1999, #2009); the quote paths are the un-pinned remainder in this function.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `parse_search_query("\"\"")` does not produce a term that matches every tag: either the empty literal is refused/reported at the command layer, or it matches only empty fields — the chosen contract is pinned by a test.
- [ ] `name:""` and `"":high` keep their explicitly-empty component (distinct from `name:` / `:high`), or are refused the same way; a test pins whichever contract is chosen.
- [ ] An unterminated quote (`"abc def`, `key:"unclosed`) never leaves a stray `"` in a search term: the term is parsed as if the quote closed at end of input, or the query is refused with a message naming the unterminated quote; a test pins it.
- [ ] New parser tests in `src/tags.rs` cover at least `""`, `name:""`, `"abc def`, `key:"unclosed`; all existing parser tests (src/tags.rs:2425+) still pass, and the documented forms (`"key:":":value"`, quoted phrases with spaces) are unchanged.

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-a. Related: #1609 (same function, whitespace separators), #2009 / #1999 (same silent-reinterpretation class in the REPL parsers).

title: id(web/editor): image parseDOM bare Number() lets NaN/fraction/hex dimensions through — pasted image sizing silently lost or reinterpreted on save

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

In the `id` web editor, the image node's `parseDOM` converts the `width`/`height` attributes with a bare `Number()` and the attrs declare no validation, so non-integer dimensions are stored verbatim and then silently dropped (or reinterpreted) downstream:

- `pkgs/id/web/src/editor.ts:145-146` — `width: el.getAttribute("width") ? Number(el.getAttribute("width")) : null` (same for `height`). The image attrs at `editor.ts:125-126` are `{ default: null }` with no `validate`, unlike `ordered_list`'s `order` which at least declares `validate: "number"` (and still lets NaN through — #2005).
- `pkgs/id/web/src/editor.ts:157-158` — `toDOM` emits the attr only `if (node.attrs.width)`: `NaN` and `0` are falsy, so they vanish; a fraction (`2.5`) or negative (`-5`) is emitted as the invalid attribute `width="2.5"` / `width="-5"`.
- `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs:1953-1954` — on save, `json["attrs"]["width"].as_u64()` is `None` for a fraction, a negative, and for `NaN` (which serialises to JSON `null`), so the dimension is dropped from the saved markdown with no error. The Rust-side HTML parse (`markdown.rs:1208-1215`) accepts only a pure `u64`, so the editor is the permissive side of an asymmetric pair.
- `pkgs/id/web/src/image-node-view.ts:58-62` — the node view sets `img.style.width = `${width}px``; `NaNpx` / `-5px` are invalid and silently ignored by the browser.

## Verified this run (2026-10-28, main `38f1f00f`)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-imgdim/`, the shipped `getAttrs` conversion copied verbatim; `editor.ts` sha256 `4340aef4…` identical on laptop and sandbox main), with the `toDOM` truthiness check and the save-side `as_u64()` semantics modelled from the shipped code:

- Control `width="200"` → parseDOM `200`, toDOM `"200"`, saved `200` ✓
- `width="200px"` → `NaN` → toDOM omits the attribute, saved `null` — dimension silently lost
- `width="50%"` → `NaN` → same silent loss
- `width="2.5"` → `2.5` → toDOM emits `width="2.5"`, saved `null` — lost on save
- `width="-5"` → `-5` → toDOM emits `width="-5"`, saved `null` — lost on save
- `width="abc"` → `NaN` → silently lost
- `width="0x10"` → `16` and `width="1e3"` → `1000` — silently *reinterpreted* as values the author never wrote (an HTML dimension attribute is a leading-digits value, not a JS numeric literal)

Pasted web content is the realistic source: images in copied HTML routinely carry `width="200px"`, percentage widths, or fractional/negative junk from CMS markup, and every one of those pastes loses its sizing on the next save without any signal.

## Why it matters

This is the same silent-coercion class as #2005 (ordered-list `start`) in the adjacent node of the same file, but with a different failure shape: the list renumbers, the image *loses its dimensions* (or gains ones nobody typed, `0x10` → 16). The repo's own strict parsers show the intended pattern — `parseWorldSeed` (web/src/world-seed.ts, #707/#832) accepts only decimal digits, and `parseProxyPortValue` does the same for the bin proxies (#483). The image attrs are an unhardened spot the earlier passes missed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Image `width`/`height` from `parseDOM` are either a non-negative integer or `null`: a value that is not a plain run of decimal digits (e.g. `200px`, `50%`, `2.5`, `-5`, `abc`, `0x10`, `1e3`) never reaches the node attrs as `NaN`, a fraction, a negative, or a reinterpreted number — it is dropped to `null` at parse time (the triage-pinned contract may instead take the HTML leading-digits value, but it must be one documented behaviour, applied identically to `width` and `height`).
- [ ] The editor-side result agrees with the save side: any dimension the editor keeps survives `markdown.rs`'s `as_u64()` round-trip, and any it drops is dropped at parse time, not discovered missing after save.
- [ ] Regression tests (web/src/editor.test.ts or a sibling) cover at least: `"200"` (kept), `"200px"`, `"50%"`, `"2.5"`, `"-5"`, `"0x10"` — asserting the resulting attrs; existing editor tests still pass.
- [ ] The fix is scoped to the image node (the ordered-list site is #2005's, already filed).

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-b. Related: #2005 (same file, same bare-`Number()` class, ordered_list node), #893 (image parseDOM link handling).

title: id(repl): a non-numeric --first/--last/--lines value silently becomes a search query — 'find report --first two' searches for 'two' too, truncated to 1

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

In the `id` REPL, a non-numeric value after `--first` / `--last` (and after `--lines` in `peek`) is silently reinterpreted as a search query, and the limit silently falls back to 1 (or, for `--lines`, to the default 5). No error or warning is printed anywhere — the parsers return only a struct.

- `pkgs/id/src/repl/runner.rs:675-700` — `parse_find_args` (used by REPL `find`, `search`, and `show`): when the token after `--first`/`--last` does not start with `-` and fails `parse::<usize>()`, the branch sets `first`/`last = Some(1)` ("default to 1") but does **not** consume the token (`i += 1` happens only on parse success). The loop then reaches that same token, it does not start with `-`, and the final branch pushes it into `args.queries`.
- `pkgs/id/src/repl/runner.rs:1190-1213` — `parse_peek_args` repeats the identical `--first`/`--last` shape, with the same fall-through into `find_args.queries`.
- `pkgs/id/src/repl/runner.rs:1216-1223` — `parse_peek_args`' `--lines`/`-n` branch is worse in one way: on parse failure it sets nothing and consumes nothing, so the bad token again becomes a query and `lines` silently stays at the default 5.

## Verified this run (2026-10-28, main `d069a613`)

Probe compiled and run on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-replfirst/` there; the `--first`/`--last`/query branches and loop increment copied verbatim from `parse_find_args`):

- Control `["report", "--first", "5"]` → `queries=["report"] first=Some(5)` ✓
- Control `["report", "--first"]` → `queries=["report"] first=Some(1)` ✓ (documented bare-flag default)
- `["report", "--first", "two"]` → `queries=["report", "two"] first=Some(1)` — the typo became a second search term **and** the result set was narrowed to 1
- `["report", "--last", "abc"]` → `queries=["report", "abc"] last=Some(1)`
- `["--first", "two", "report"]` → `queries=["two", "report"] first=Some(1)`

So `find report --first two` does not fail, does not warn, and does not search what the user asked: it searches for `report` AND `two`, truncated to the first match (`apply_search_options`, runner.rs:987-1013, applies the limit after collecting matches for all queries).

## Why it matters

A one-character-class typo in an interactive session silently changes *which blobs are searched for* and *how many come back* — the same silent-reinterpretation class as #1999 (selection prompt dropping unparseable numbers), one parser earlier. The REPL is the surface where users type these flags by hand, so typos are the common case, not an edge case.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A non-numeric token following `--first`/`--last` in `parse_find_args` and `parse_peek_args`, or following `--lines`/`-n` in `parse_peek_args`, is never added to `queries` and never silently defaults the limit: the command reports the bad value (usage/error line naming the flag and the token) and runs no search, OR the triage-pinned contract is documented in the help text and implemented identically in both parsers.
- [ ] The bare-flag form (`--first` with no following token, or followed by another flag) keeps its documented default of 1.
- [ ] Regression tests in `runner.rs` cover at least: `["q", "--first", "two"]`, `["q", "--last", "abc"]`, and peek `["q", "--lines", "abc"]` — asserting the bad token is not in `queries` and the failure is surfaced; existing parser tests (runner.rs:1540+) still pass.
- [ ] Both parser copies behave identically (find/search/show and peek), so the fix is not applied to only one copy.

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-a. Related: #1999 (same REPL, same silent-parse class, different site).

body:
## Problem

`nix flake check`'s `clippy-lint` check fails on current `main` for the `id` crate, blocking the aggregate flake check on every PR (observed on PR #1838, a docs-only change to `pkgs/id/TODO.md`, run 40775308431, job 123141230630, 2026-10-28T23:31Z):

```
error: used `expect()` on an `Option` value
    --> src/tags.rs:1484:22
     |
1484 |             let ch = input[i..].chars().next().expect("i is a char boundary");
error: used `expect()` on an `Option` value
    --> src/tags.rs:1499:22
     |
1499 |             let ch = input[i..].chars().next().expect("i is a char boundary");
error: could not compile `id` (lib) due to 2 previous errors
```

The code is on `main` today (introduced by #1743, commit 35726e8e: `parse_search_query` in `pkgs/id/src/tags.rs`), and the crate denies `clippy::expect-used` on the command line (`-D clippy::expect-used`), so this is a hard error, not one of the ~150 tracked warnings in #803.

## Fix

Replace both `expect("i is a char boundary")` calls with a non-panicking boundary step (e.g. `let Some(ch) = ... else { break }`), preserving the parser's behavior — `i` is maintained as a char boundary by construction, so the `None` arm is unreachable in practice but must not panic.

## Acceptance

- `clippy-lint` flake check passes on main.
- `parse_search_query` behavior unchanged (existing tags/search tests pass).

## Acceptance criteria

- The `clippy-lint` flake check passes on `main` (both `expect()` sites in `parse_search_query`, `pkgs/id/src/tags.rs`, replaced with non-panicking char-boundary handling).
- `parse_search_query` behaviour is unchanged: the existing tags/search tests pass in CI.
- The work is delivered via a branch + PR (no direct push to main); verification runs in GitHub Actions CI, not on the sandbox.

labels.name: kind/bug
