labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Summary

The web editor's `ordered_list` DOM parser (`pkgs/id/web/src/editor.ts:100`) reads the list start with a bare `Number(el.getAttribute("start"))`. Non-numeric and fractional `start` values from pasted HTML therefore enter the ProseMirror node unchecked:

- `start="abc"` → `order = NaN`. The schema's only guard is `validate: "number"` (`editor.ts:115`), and ProseMirror's string validator checks only `typeof value` (`prosemirror-model` `validateType`: `typeof NaN === "number"`), so NaN passes.
- `editor.ts:105` `toDOM` then renders any `order !== 1` as `start: NaN` — an invalid HTML attribute.
- On save, the node JSON carries `order: null` (`JSON.stringify(NaN)`), and the Rust markdown codec reads it as `json["attrs"]["order"].as_u64().unwrap_or(1)` (`pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs:1844-1845`) — the list is **silently renumbered from 1**.
- `start="2.5"` → `order = 2.5` (same validate pass, `start="2.5"` rendered) → `as_u64` on a fractional JSON number is also `None` → silently renumbered from 1 on save.
- `start="0x10"` → reinterpreted as 16, `start="1e2"` as 100 — forms an HTML `start` attribute never means (the sibling task-list parser at `editor.ts:196` correctly uses the `el.start` IDL property, which follows HTML's integer parsing rules).

So a pasted ordered list whose `start` is not a plain integer either displays with a bogus start attribute or loses its numbering entirely on the next save, with no signal at any step. The control case works end to end: `start="5"` → order 5 → rendered 5 → saved 5.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-olstart/`, node, main `6a284efd`) evaluating the verbatim `editor.ts:100` expression, the vendored `prosemirror-model` `validateType` semantics, the `editor.ts:105` `toDOM` branch, JSON round-trip, and the `markdown.rs:1845` `as_u64().unwrap_or(1)` read:

```
start="5"    -> order=5   validate=ok toDOM start=5     json=5    rust_save_order=5
start="abc"  -> order=NaN validate=ok toDOM start=NaN   json=null rust_save_order=1
start="2.5"  -> order=2.5 validate=ok toDOM start=2.5   json=2.5  rust_save_order=1
start="-3"   -> order=-3  validate=ok toDOM start=-3    json=-3   rust_save_order=1
start="0x10" -> order=16  validate=ok toDOM start=16    json=16   rust_save_order=16
start="1e2"  -> order=100 validate=ok toDOM start=100   json=100  rust_save_order=100
(no attr)    -> order=1   validate=ok toDOM (no attr)   json=1    rust_save_order=1
```

Source lines: `editor.ts:100` (bare `Number()`), `editor.ts:111-116` (`order: { default: 1, validate: "number" }`), `editor.ts:105` (toDOM), `markdown.rs:1844-1845` (`as_u64().unwrap_or(1)`). The image attrs at `editor.ts:145-146` use the same bare `Number()` for `width`/`height` (`"100px"` → NaN, silently dropped by the falsy check in `toDOM`) — same fix shape, worth covering in the same change if triage agrees.

This is the parser-strictness class the web code has been fixing one site at a time: go-to-line strict validation (#712), world seed digits-only (#832), identity refresh finite check (#847). This `parseDOM` site is unguarded.

## Why it matters

Paste is how existing documents arrive in the editor. A list pasted from a web page or another editor with an unusual `start` keeps its numbering on screen (or shows `NaN`) and then silently renumbers from 1 when saved — the saved markdown no longer says what the user saw and confirmed. Silent reinterpretation (`0x10` → 16) is the same class of harm in the other direction.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The `ordered_list` `parseDOM` getAttrs produces only a valid list start: a finite integer the save codec can represent (non-negative safe integer), or falls back to 1 — never NaN, a fraction, or a hex/scientific reinterpretation. Using `el.start` (as the task-list parser at `editor.ts:196` does) plus a range/integer check is an acceptable shape; triage pins the exact fallback for negative starts, which markdown cannot represent.
- [ ] A pasted `<ol start="5">` still round-trips: order 5 in the node, `start="5"` rendered, 5 in the saved markdown.
- [ ] Tests in `editor.test.ts` (or the schema's test home) cover at least: `start="abc"`, `start="2.5"`, `start="0x10"`, and the `start="5"` control.
- [ ] If triage includes them, the image `width`/`height` attrs at `editor.ts:145-146` get the same treatment (`"100px"`/non-numeric → null, plain integer preserved).
- [ ] Existing web unit tests pass.

Found by new-issue-creator lane B, 2026-10-28 run. Dedup: `gh search issues` for "ordered list start", "parseDOM start", "ol start NaN editor" (open + closed) returned no matching issue. Related but distinct closed issues: #1469 (lists lose their `tight` flag — a different attr) and #997 (ordered *task* lists rewritten as bullet lists on save — the `contains-task-list` branch at `editor.ts:196`, not the plain `ordered_list` getAttrs at `editor.ts:100` covered here).

Relocated from dezren39/nix#143 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #95

## Summary

Build the first version of the skeleton from #135 and measure it: split the one serial job into `init`, `unit`, three static `e2e` shards, a minimal lint leg, the `nix` build (with the vendorHash repair moved over from `mcpx.yml`), and a final `ci-ok` job that prints a timing table. Fix the broken Go cache on the way. Record the baseline in this issue so #139 and #140 start from numbers, not estimates. This is deliberately the smallest thing that produces those numbers: no splitter, no budget gate, no autofix.

## Original notes

> - testing
>   - make a comprehensive github action ci.yaml workflow (or test.yaml) that is as fast as possible,

> - testing
>   - make a comprehensive github action ci.yaml workflow (or test.yaml) that is as fast as possible,
>     - splitting sets of tests into as small groups as practical, eg split out unit/integration tests into 2 jobs, whichever one takes longer: shard it into 4 logical groups (or however many) based on an appropriate category, then find the longest job at that point and repeat (you dont want to iterate on this forever, at some point start splitting logical units by like, e.g. maybe a-f/g-s/t-z, balance number of letters by time.

## Current state

One `ubuntu-latest` job in `.github/workflows/mcpx.yml`, 3m57s wall on run 36673523537: ~33 s setup (Go cache broken: `Restore cache failed: Dependencies file is not found ... go.mod`), `go test ./... -count=1` 134.8 s (~31 s compile, e2e 100.7 s serial), `nix build` 59.6 s run *after* the tests. Full table and log reference in #135.

Since #182 (05c78b2): the Go cache key is fixed (`cache-dependency-path: pkgs/mcpx/go.sum`, `mcpx.yml:50`) -- that was step 8's first half and option B below, landed on its own. The first run after it (36693030957, push to main) was still a miss by construction: 4m09s wall, setup 22 s, `go test` 148 s (~39 s download + compile before the first `ok`; e2e 108.9 s for 209 tests), `nix build` 70 s (`buildPhase` 28.7 s, `checkPhase` 18.5 s). The next push to main is the first that can hit; its number goes in the baseline table below.

## Scope

1. `.github/workflows/mcpx-test.yml` (`name: mcpx-test`) with the triggers, draft `if:`, and concurrency from #135 decisions 3 and 5. For this first iteration, keep `mcpx.yml`'s path list inside `init` as the relevance check (decision 4 C) -- do not make anything a required check yet (main is unprotected).
2. `init` (small): sparse depth-1 checkout; output `mcpx=true|false`; output the seed placeholder per #93 if #93 has decided, otherwise leave the slot; output a **static** matrix:
   - `e2e-1`: the first half of `e2e_test.go`'s tests (65 names at 05c78b2, alphabetical)
   - `e2e-2`: the second half (64)
   - `e2e-3`: every test in the other nine e2e files (80; `unread_test.go` arrived with #171)
   The regexes are generated by a few lines of shell from `grep -h '^func Test'`, so nothing is hand-maintained. By test count this is roughly even (~33 s each if tests are uniform); it is a stopgap until #139's splitter replaces the static list.
3. `unit`: `go test -count=1 $(go list ./... | grep -v /internal/e2e)`.
4. `e2e` (matrix): `go test -count=1 -json -run "$REGEX" ./internal/e2e`, human output via `gotestsum --format testname --jsonfile ...` or a `jq` filter; upload the JSON as an artifact. Each leg writes its exact `go test -run` line to `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY`. After `go test`, count surviving `mcpx daemon` processes and print the number (warn only) -- #52 is fixed in #182, and this is the check that notices if it regresses.
5. `lint` (minimal, only checks that are already clean): `gofmt -l` must be empty, `go vet ./...`. Everything else is #141.
6. `nix`: `mcpx.yml`'s vendorHash repair and `nix build` moved over unchanged, with job-level `permissions: contents: write`; all other jobs `contents: read` and `persist-credentials: false`. Delete `mcpx.yml` in the same PR (Renovate's grouped Go PR must keep working -- watch the next one, #49).
7. `ci-ok` (`needs:` all, `if: always()`): fail if any needed job failed/was cancelled; print the #140 measurement table (wall, matrix span, longest leg + name, queue max/sum, per-leg fixed cost) from the jobs API. No gating on time yet.
8. Every Go job: `actions/setup-go` with `cache-dependency-path: pkgs/mcpx/go.sum` (**done for the existing job in #182**, `mcpx.yml:50`; carry it into every new job), restore-only on PRs, save on main (today every PR run saves its own branch-scoped copy).
9. Pin `setup-deno`/`setup-bun`/`setup-node` versions to the flake's (today CI gets deno 2.9.7, bun 1.4.2, node 24.21.0 while the Nix wrapper uses `bun-bin` 1.3.14).

Out of scope here: the timing-driven splitter (#139), the budget number and runbook (#140), formatters beyond gofmt (#141), format automation (#142), shared binary artifacts, dev-shell toolchains, the docs-examples leg.

## Prediction to check

With a working Go cache, each e2e leg ≈ 30-40 s fixed + ~33 s tests ≈ 65-75 s. The `nix` leg ≈ 3 s set up + 2 s checkout + 8 s installer + 60 s build ≈ **75 s** -- so after this change the **Nix build is likely the longest job**, and the next win is in the Nix leg (store cache, and what to do about `checkPhase` re-running the unit packages CI already ran -- #135 decision 6 argues for keeping it, off the critical path; decision 7 has the store cache), not in more e2e shards. Expected wall ≈ 1.5-2 min, down from ~4.

## Baseline to record (comment on this issue)

From 5 main runs and 3 PR runs of the new workflow, plus the last 10 `mcpx.yml` runs for comparison (`gh run list --repo dezren39/nix --workflow mcpx.yml`, `gh api .../runs/<id>/jobs`):

| | old `mcpx.yml` | new, median | new, max |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| wall (`max(completed_at) - run_started_at`) | 3m57s-4m30s | | |
| longest leg (name) | 3m53s (build) | | |
| e2e legs: fixed cost / test time | -- | | |
| unit leg | -- | | |
| nix leg | 59.6 s step | | |
| queue delay max / sum | 2-3 s (one 37 s) | | |
| Go cache hit? compile time per leg | miss / ~31 s (after #182, run 36693030957: miss by construction / ~39 s incl. download) | | |

Also attach the merged per-test timings (top 20 slowest e2e tests) -- the input #139 needs to choose between "rebalance" and "fix the slowest tests first".

## Approaches

No real choice on *whether*; the design choices are made in #135. One scoping choice:
- **A -- do the full skeleton at once** (splitter, budget gate, all linters, autofix). One large PR, nothing measured before deciding. Not recommended.
- **B -- only fix the Go cache in `mcpx.yml`.** A one-line change. **Landed in #182** exactly this way; it splits nothing, which is why this issue stays open.
- **C -- this issue as scoped (recommended)**, on top of B. Smallest change that yields the numbers every other CI issue needs.

## Acceptance

- `mcpx-test` runs on push to main and on non-draft PRs (and on undraft); a new push to a PR cancels the previous run; main runs are never cancelled.
- `ci-ok` is green only if every leg is green or skipped; it prints the timing table.
- `setup-go` logs a cache hit on the second run.
- A Renovate/Dependabot Go bump still gets its vendorHash repaired (or the gap is written down on #49).
- The baseline table above is filled in on this issue.

## Open questions

1. ~~Land the one-line Go cache fix in `mcpx.yml` immediately, before this PR?~~ Done in #182.
2. Does `ubuntu-slim` work for `ci-ok` (needs `gh`/`jq`)? Try it here.
3. Keep `mcpx.yml`'s file name for the Nix job to avoid disturbing Renovate's config comments, or rename everything at once?

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** M · **Impact** high (roughly halves CI wall time and produces the data for everything else) · **Depends on / related**: #95, #135 (design), #139 (replaces the static shards), #140 (turns the table into a gate), #141 (grows the lint leg), #93 / #121 (seed slot), #49 (vendorHash repair moves), #138 (environment allowlist; the e2e shards inherit the runner's environment until it lands), #52 (closed, fixed in #182; the daemon count after e2e guards it), #97 (legs added later), #99.

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

## Acceptance criteria

- Split CI (init/unit/3 e2e shards/lint/nix build/ci-ok) runs in GitHub Actions and the baseline timing table is recorded on this issue, superseding the serial-job numbers in the body.
- The work described in the Summary/Scope above is delivered via a branch + PR (no direct push to main); verification runs in GitHub Actions CI, not on the sandbox.
- Evidence (CI links, timings, or probe output as applicable) is recorded on this issue before it is closed.

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#142 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #95

## Summary

The notes ask for a separate `format.yaml` that auto-commits formatting to `main` after the formatters succeed and the test workflow is green. This issue works through what that actually requires (trigger, token, loop guard, branch protection, the race with newer commits) and finds a logical conflict with the check-mode formatters in the test matrix (#141). Plain conclusion: **auto-committing to `main` is worse than formatting the PR head**; the recommendation is a blocking format check on PRs plus an autofix push to the PR branch, and a `main`-side workflow that opens a PR rather than committing directly. If the direct-to-main version is still wanted, the safe way to build it is written out below.

## Original notes

> - testing
>   - separately, format.yaml which auto-commits to main when format has changes and successfully completes all formatters, receives a green test workflow

## Current state

- No formatting automation. The only bot push today is the vendorHash repair in `mcpx.yml` (`:67-95` at 05c78b2), which commits to `renovate/*` / `dependabot/*` PR branches with `GITHUB_TOKEN`. Its comment states the repository's policy on rewriting branches (`mcpx.yml:68-70`): "A human changing dependencies should see the failure and fix it deliberately rather than have it rewritten under them." The step ran on a real Renovate PR for the first time in #184 (run 36693225089) but took the no-op path ("builds as-is; nothing to repair"), so the push-back itself has still never run.
- `main` has **no branch protection and no rulesets** (`.../branches/main/protection` -> 404; `.../rulesets` -> `[]`), so a direct push from Actions would succeed today, and would start failing the day protection is turned on.
- Token behaviour ([trigger docs](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-when-workflows-run/trigger-a-workflow)): events caused by `GITHUB_TOKEN` do **not** start new workflow runs -- so a push to `main` with it is never tested. The exception is `pull_request` `opened`/`synchronize`/`reopened`, which now create runs in an **approval-required** state. A GitHub App installation token or PAT does trigger runs normally.
- `workflow_run` ([events docs](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#workflow_run)): only fires for a workflow file on the default branch; types `completed`/`requested`/`in_progress`; exposes `workflow_run.conclusion`, `head_branch`, `head_sha`, `event`; chains at most three levels deep.

## The conflict to resolve first

#141 puts formatters in **check mode** in the test matrix. If an unformatted commit reaches main, the `fmt` leg fails, the test workflow is red, and a `format.yaml` gated on "a green test workflow" **never runs**. Conversely, whenever the test workflow *is* green, formatting is already clean and there is nothing to commit. As written, the two notes cancel out. Ways out:
1. Make the `fmt` leg non-blocking on `main` pushes (`continue-on-error: ${{ github.event_name == 'push' }}`) and have `format.yaml` check the individual job results through the API (`workflow_run.conclusion` is for the whole run). Works, but main can then be "green" while unformatted.
2. Make formatting blocking on PRs, so main is always formatted by construction, and use `format.yaml` only for drift that does not come through a PR: a formatter version bump in `flake.lock`, a direct push. That is the recommended framing below.

## Approaches

### A -- auto-commit to `main` after a green run (the notes' design), least recommended

How to build it safely if chosen:
- `on: workflow_run: { workflows: [mcpx-test], types: [completed] }`; `if: conclusion == 'success' && event == 'push' && head_branch == 'main'` (ignore `cancelled`, PR runs, and dispatches).
- Check out `workflow_run.head_sha`; run the same pinned formatters (#141: `nix fmt`); if `git diff --quiet`, exit.
- Race: if `main` has moved past `head_sha`, **skip** (the newer commit's own run will trigger `format.yaml` again) rather than rebase -- rebasing a bot commit onto untested code is the worst of both.
- Verify the diff is formatting-only before pushing: `go build ./...` and `go vet ./...`, `deno check`, `nix eval` of the package -- seconds, and it catches a formatter bug or a bad version bump.
- Bound what the bot may write (from #170): stage the explicit list from `git diff --name-only`, never `git add -A` (the repair step already stages one named file, `mcpx.yml:93`); **abort on an unexpectedly large diff** (a formatter version bump can legitimately reformat the whole tree -- a threshold such as 500 lines or 50 files, or any file outside a configured set, hands it to a human PR instead); re-run the check after committing and fail if it is still dirty, which catches two formatters fighting over one file.
- Add `workflow_dispatch` beside `workflow_run`: `workflow_run` only fires for the workflow file on the default branch, so without it the workflow cannot be exercised before it merges (from #170).
- Loop guard: commit as `github-actions[bot]` with a marker (`[mcpx-format]`) and skip when the triggering head commit carries it; with `GITHUB_TOKEN` no run is triggered anyway. With an App token, the push triggers a test run, which triggers `format.yaml`, which finds no diff and stops -- "no diff" is the real guard, the marker is belt and braces.
- Branch protection: when it is turned on, the pusher must be on the bypass list; that requires a GitHub App (PATs belong to a person and bypassing as a person is worse).

Why it is least recommended:
- With `GITHUB_TOKEN`, the formatted commit on main is **never tested**. For gofmt that is nearly safe (it only rewrites layout); for `deno fmt`, `shfmt`, `nixfmt` after a version bump it is "probably fine", which is the wrong standard for main.
- Every unformatted merge becomes two commits on main (the change, then "format"), permanently in history and in `git blame`.
- It needs `contents: write` on the default branch in an automated job, and it fights branch protection.
- It only ever fires if the conflict above is resolved by making main's format check non-blocking.

### B -- open a formatting PR from `main` drift

Same trigger as A; instead of pushing to main, `peter-evans/create-pull-request` (or `gh pr create`) opens or updates a single branch `bot/mcpx-format` with the diff. The PR runs the full test workflow (with an App token; with `GITHUB_TOKEN` it lands in the approval-required state), and a human or auto-merge merges it. Tested, reviewable, protection-compatible, one extra PR when drift happens. Good as the **main-side** fallback.

### C -- blocking check on PRs, autofix pushed to the PR head, B as the main fallback (recommended)

- The `fmt` leg in the test workflow is blocking on PRs (check mode, prints the diff and the one command to fix: `nix fmt`; the diff also goes into `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` as a `git apply`-able patch, from #170).
- An `autofix` job (same workflow, after `fmt` fails, same-repo branches only -- forks cannot be pushed to) runs `nix fmt` and pushes a commit to the PR branch, exactly like the existing vendorHash repair. Merge it into one "bot push-back" job with the vendorHash repair so a bot PR gets one push, not two. **Scope it the way the repair is scoped** (changed in the 2026-09-30 pass, from #170): always on bot branches (`renovate/*`, `dependabot/*` -- where a formatter bump lands, open question 3), and on a human's branch only when the author opts in (e.g. an `autofix` label). The repository has already written down that a human's branch is not rewritten under them (`mcpx.yml:68-70`); an unconditional autofix contradicts that and rewrites a branch mid-review, invalidating review comments and forcing a pull before the next push. If the user wants autofix on every PR anyway, that is a policy change to make explicitly, together with the repair step's comment.
- Token: a GitHub App token, so the push triggers a normal (not approval-gated) run of the full workflow; the superseded run is cancelled by the PR concurrency group (#135). Loop guard: no diff -> no push; and skip when the head commit author is the App.
- `format.yaml` exists only for drift on main that did not come through a PR (formatter bump, direct push): approach B.
- Result: every commit on main is formatted **and tested**; with squash merges the autofix commit leaves no trace on main.
- Off-the-shelf alternative to a custom job: autofix.ci (a GitHub App, free for OSS) does the PR-head push with its own loop/fork handling; it requires trusting a third-party app with write access. Worth considering; decide with the App-token question.

Recommended because it keeps the notes' intent (nobody hand-formats; formatting never blocks a human for long) without an untested commit on main, and without overriding the branch-rewriting policy the repository already has.

## Open questions

1. Is the user OK replacing "auto-commit to main" with "autofix the PR head + a formatting PR for drift"? If not, build A with the safeguards above.
2. GitHub App (new, owned by the user) vs autofix.ci vs a fine-grained PAT for the push-back? The same token would fix the vendorHash repair's approval-required runs (#49).
3. Should Renovate/Dependabot formatter bumps (a new nixfmt in `flake.lock`) reformat inside the bump PR via the same autofix job? That is the cleanest place for format drift to land.
4. Does the user merge by squash? (If merge commits are used, autofix commits appear in main's history.)
5. A pre-commit hook (and which framework), or is `nix fmt` / `just fmt` plus the blocking check enough? A hook makes the blocking check nearly unreachable and `format.yaml` almost dead code -- which is fine; it is a backstop (from #170).
6. Bot identity: reuse `mcpx-hash-bot` (`mcpx.yml:91-92`) or a separate `mcpx-format-bot` so `git log` says which bot did what? Cosmetic; decide once (from #170).
7. Should the same push-back machinery regenerate derived artefacts CI checks (man page, OpenAPI, settings table)? That is #96/#145's drift problem; build the mechanism once (from #170).

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** M (needs a token decision) · **Impact** low-med (convenience; quality comes from the blocking check) · **Depends on / related**: #95, #141 (the formatters and their pinning), #135 (concurrency cancels superseded runs; the vendorHash push-back job this merges with), #49 (bot push-back for every package, token choice), #99 (agents run `nix fmt` before pushing; CI is the backstop).

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

## Acceptance criteria

- format.yaml auto-formats only after a green run, distinguishes PR-head vs main behaviour as specified, and its CI run is green.
- The work described in the Summary/Scope above is delivered via a branch + PR (no direct push to main); verification runs in GitHub Actions CI, not on the sandbox.
- Evidence (CI links, timings, or probe output as applicable) is recorded on this issue before it is closed.

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#817 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

## Problem

mcpx scopes choose *which* process serves a caller, but nothing tells that process *where the caller is*.

Scope keys already resolve the caller's cwd to a git root: `internal/config/scope.go` (`CallContext`, `Scope.Key()`) yields `repo:<git-common-dir>` / `worktree:<top-level>` using the native git discovery in `internal/config/gitdiscover.go`. But instance spawn ignores that resolution: `internal/pool/pool.go` `dial()` builds `StdioOptions{Cwd: p.cfg.Cwd}` — the config's static string, verbatim — and `internal/mcpclient/stdio.go` sets `cmd.Dir = opts.Cwd`. A `repo`- or `worktree`-scoped server therefore still *runs* in the daemon's cwd.

Concrete casualty (observed live, 2026-10-25, fleet config of 16 servers): gopls is a workspace server whose workspace is its process cwd. Scoped per-checkout it would still run in the daemon's cwd, so it loads files ad hoc ("command-line-arguments" package) instead of as a module workspace session.

## Proposed smallest design

When a server's scope is `repo` or `worktree` **and** its config `cwd` is empty, spawn the instance with `Dir` = the resolved scope root (the common-dir's worktree / the checkout top-level) instead of the daemon's cwd.

This needs the scope resolution to hand the pool the root, not just the opaque key string: return the resolved root alongside the key from `Scope.Key()`, or recompute it via `locateGit` at spawn time. One branch in `pool.dial()`.

Explicit config `cwd` always wins — the scope root is only the default when `cwd` is unset.

## Why this order

This is step 1 of the per-project design note (2026-10-25). With it, `"mcpx": {"scope": "worktree"}` on gopls becomes a real per-project workspace server: one gopls per checkout, rooted in that checkout. Flipping scopes *before* this lands only multiplies processes for little gain, so config scope flips wait for this issue.

Related: #818 — the `${mcpx.root}` / `${mcpx.cwd}` substitution issue (companion, step 2) — and #819 — the initialize `rootUri`/`workspaceFolders` issue (step 3, builds on the root resolution here).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `worktree`-scoped server with no config `cwd` is spawned with its working directory set to the caller's checkout top-level; a `repo`-scoped one to the resolved worktree of the common dir.
- [ ] Two callers in different checkouts of the same repo get distinct `worktree`-scoped instances rooted in their own checkouts; `repo` scope keeps sharing one instance per common dir.
- [ ] An explicit config `cwd` overrides the scope root in all cases.
- [ ] `global`/`cwd:`/`session` and other scopes are unchanged.
- [ ] A `worktree`-scoped gopls answers a package-level query (e.g. `go_package_api` on a module path) with the module's real API instead of an empty result.
- [ ] Tests cover the spawn-cwd decision (scope root vs explicit cwd vs daemon cwd fallback).

Relocated from dezren39/nix#339 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

If a call to a non-read-only tool is cancelled, times out, or loses its upstream after dispatch, mcpx cannot know whether it took effect. Retrying can duplicate it.

codex-connectors-mcp marks that outcome **unknown** and refuses further writes until someone checks the app. Proposed for mcpx: record such calls (server, tool, arguments hash, time), refuse further non-read-only calls to that server until cleared (`mcpx writes clear <server>` or a `/v1` route), and say why in the error. Scope: per server, persisted across daemon restarts, unlike theirs.

Related: #77 (cancellation), the destructive-call confirmation (`elicit.confirmDestructive`), the write-policy issue.

Reference: https://github.com/wileai/codex-connectors-mcp#writes

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A non-read-only tool call whose outcome is unknown (cancelled, timed out, or upstream lost after dispatch) is recorded with server, tool, arguments hash, and time.
- [ ] Further non-read-only calls to that server are refused with an error that says why, until the record is cleared (`mcpx writes clear <server>` or a `/v1` route).
- [ ] The block persists across daemon restarts; read-only calls are unaffected.
- [ ] Tests cover: unknown-outcome write blocks the next write, clearing unblocks, restart preserves the block.

Parent: #99

## Summary

Write **one contributor page** that tells agents working *on* mcpx the test policy -- what to run (#127), a test per bug (#128), guards per class (#129), flakes (#130) -- and make sure agents editing mcpx code actually load it, **without** adding it to `pkgs/mcpx/AGENTS.md`, which is the user-facing guide to *using* mcpx. (The book itself belongs to the documentation tree; this is only the contributor page.)

## Original notes

> - testing
>   - importantly, as we add more testing agents should not run every single test basically ever. below documents a rough idea of a ci job design/policy, the main priority is being short as possible.
>   - agents should make at least 1 simple, new test for every bug observed from any source, when cheap to do so-- aggresively test many permutations. 

(The page states the policies decided in the sibling issues; the notes above are quoted there in full with their context.)

## Current state

- `pkgs/mcpx/AGENTS.md` (109 lines) is about using mcpx ("Every MCP server on this machine is reachable from the shell through `mcpx`" ... "The loop") and says nothing about tests. `docs/release-runbook.md:44` treats it as the instruction file "quoted in full" in the published material, so its length is a user-facing cost. There is no repo-root `AGENTS.md`.
- There is no `CONTRIBUTING.md`, no `docs/testing.md`, no PR template. The closest contributor material is scattered in PR bodies ("Verified it fails without the fix", "suite 3x clean", "`-race` clean").
- **How opencode picks up instruction files** (source of the version in the nix store, `packages/opencode/src/session/instruction.ts`):
  - at session start: the first `AGENTS.md` (else `CLAUDE.md`) found walking *up* from the working directory, plus the global file, plus `instructions` globs from `opencode.json` (lines 115-150);
  - **on every file read**: `Instruction.resolve` (lines 179-221, called from `tool/read.ts:300`) walks up from the file being read to the project root and attaches each directory's `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` not already loaded, once per message.
  - Consequence 1: a nested `pkgs/mcpx/internal/AGENTS.md` reaches exactly the agents that read mcpx source, and nobody else.
  - Consequence 2: an agent reading `pkgs/mcpx/internal/...` from the repo root *already* gets `pkgs/mcpx/AGENTS.md` attached (the walk passes through `pkgs/mcpx/`). Everything added to that file is paid by contributors as well as users.
- Other harnesses: Claude Code loads nested `CLAUDE.md` files on demand when it reads files in that subtree; Codex concatenates `AGENTS.md` from the repo root down to the working directory. So a nested file is the portable mechanism; the exact trigger differs (open question for non-opencode harnesses).
- Not verified: the mechanism by which `pkgs/mcpx/AGENTS.md` reaches *consuming* agents outside this repo. Nothing in `package.nix` installs it and the plugin's `instructions` option injects a fixed four-sentence string instead (`plugin/opencode/mcpx-session.ts:737-746` at 05c78b2, off by default). Either way it is published as the user guide, so the conclusion stands.

## Approaches

### A -- append a "Developing mcpx" section to `pkgs/mcpx/AGENTS.md` (least recommended)
One file, zero discovery questions, and opencode's read-time walk already attaches it for contributors. But every consumer of the user guide pays for contributor rules it cannot use (tiers, `-count=1`, quarantine), the release runbook's "quoted in full" material grows, and the file stops being about one audience. The user asked for this concern to be weighed; it loses.

### B -- a contributor file only (`pkgs/mcpx/CONTRIBUTING.md` or `pkgs/mcpx/docs/testing.md`)
The conventional home, readable by humans on GitHub, and the book can link it. But no harness loads `CONTRIBUTING.md` on its own; it reaches an agent only if someone adds it to an `instructions` list (per-user config, not the repo) or the agent happens to open it. Agents would keep running `go test ./...` because nothing told them otherwise.

### C -- the page in `docs/testing.md`, plus a short nested `pkgs/mcpx/internal/AGENTS.md` that points at it (recommended)
- `pkgs/mcpx/docs/testing.md`: the full policy -- tiers and commands with timings, the per-bug rule and checklist, when to add a guard and how, flake handling, how to reproduce a CI failure. Human-readable; the book (docs tree) links it; `CONTRIBUTING.md`, if wanted, is a three-line pointer to it.
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/AGENTS.md` (~15-25 lines): the rules an agent must not miss -- never `go test ./...` or unfiltered e2e locally for a routine change (#127; the reason is time, now that #182 fixed #52's leak), always `-count=1` for e2e, the `just`/script command from #127, one failing-first test per bug, guards when touching a registry, read CI before merging -- and "details: `docs/testing.md`". Placed under `internal/` so it is attached only when an agent reads Go source there, which is when it is about to change or test something. (`cmd/` is one file; a second copy there is unnecessary.)
- A `CLAUDE.md` symlink beside it is unnecessary for opencode (it prefers `AGENTS.md`) but cheap for Claude Code users; decide in open questions.
- `pkgs/mcpx/AGENTS.md` stays untouched.

Recommended because it costs users nothing, reaches contributor agents automatically through the read-time walk, keeps one source of truth (the nested file is a summary with a pointer, not a copy), and survives a harness change since it relies only on the nested-file convention.

A guard (per #129) can keep the summary honest: a unit test that every command quoted in `internal/AGENTS.md` names a test or recipe that exists.

## Tasks

- [ ] Write `pkgs/mcpx/docs/testing.md` once #127, #128, #129, #130 are decided (can start with #127 alone; it is the one agents need first).
- [ ] Write `pkgs/mcpx/internal/AGENTS.md` (short), link it from `docs/testing.md`.
- [ ] Hand the book's "Contributing / testing" link to the documentation tree.

## Open questions

- `docs/testing.md` vs `CONTRIBUTING.md` as the canonical file name (GitHub surfaces `CONTRIBUTING.md` in the PR UI only at repo root or `.github/`, and this repo is a whole nix config -- so a package-level `CONTRIBUTING.md` gets no special treatment).
- Should the nested file sit at `pkgs/mcpx/internal/AGENTS.md` or at `pkgs/mcpx/internal/e2e/AGENTS.md` (narrower, only loaded when touching e2e, but then misses unit-only changes)?
- A `CLAUDE.md` alongside for Claude Code, or rely on its `AGENTS.md` support?
- Should the repo root get its own short `AGENTS.md` for the nix repo as a whole? Out of scope here; note for the owner.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** S · **Impact** high (it is what makes the other policies reach agents)
**Depends on / related**: siblings #127, #128, #129, #130; #52 (closed, fixed in #182), #93 (seed/repro wording), #95 (CI facts the page quotes), #97; the documentation tree (#89, the book); #91.

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

## Acceptance criteria

- One contributor test-policy page exists in the documentation tree (not in `pkgs/mcpx/AGENTS.md`, which stays the user-facing guide to using mcpx), covering: what to run, a test per bug, guards per class, and the flake policy — referencing the sibling policy issues rather than duplicating them.
- A loading mechanism is in place so agents editing mcpx code actually load the page, and the mechanism is named on this issue.
- The work described in the Summary/Scope above is delivered via a branch + PR (no direct push to main); verification runs in GitHub Actions CI, not on the sandbox.
- Evidence (the page path and the loading mechanism) is recorded on this issue before it is closed.

Today anything that can reach the daemon's socket or loopback port is trusted; the `Origin`/`Host` check stops browsers, not callers.

**Optional, off unless set**: a setting (e.g. `transport.bearerToken`, from env so it need not live in a config file) that, when set, makes every `/v1` and `/mcp` request carry `Authorization: Bearer <token>` or get 401. Unset keeps today's behaviour. Reject tokens shorter than 32 characters, as codex-connectors-mcp does.

The CLI, plugin and scripts read the same setting so they keep working. A first, cheap step toward #253 (authorization) and #300 (the permissive interface that authorizes everyone); principals per surface are #298.

Reference: https://github.com/wileai/codex-connectors-mcp (`CODEX_CONNECTORS_HTTP_TOKEN`).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] With `transport.bearerToken` set (sourced from env), every `/v1` and `/mcp` request without a matching `Authorization: Bearer <token>` gets 401; with the token it succeeds.
- [ ] With the setting unset, behaviour is byte-for-byte today's (no auth check).
- [ ] Tokens shorter than 32 characters are rejected at startup/config load with a clear error.
- [ ] The CLI, plugin, and scripts read the same setting and keep working when it is set.

Parent: #99

## Summary

Two parts. **Policy:** every bug observed from any source gets at least one new test, in the same PR as the fix, that fails without the fix -- when that is cheap -- and the test covers the bug's *permutations*, not just the one input that tripped it. **Review:** audit the recently fixed mcpx bugs against that policy, and file the missing tests. The checklist that enforces it (PR template vs CI check) is decided here too.

## Original notes

> - testing
>   - agents should make at least 1 simple, new test for every bug observed from any source, when cheap to do so-- aggresively test many permutations. 
>     - you can absolutely rely on fuzzing anywhere you can fit it and you should whenever you can-- but you _must_ use a single seed per-run to generate all inputs. (this could eventually be discussed with careful consideration.) it should be appended into a test tracking structured file in the repo and it can be committed. ideally main branch commit's seed or pr merge seed should make it back into file eventually. to prevent churn, maybe ci appends the seed into a gha var (race/overwrite risk?), or attached as artifact to each workflow in init job before tests begin-- a collector job can scoop them up sometime later. once a day/week/on-release/every-100-commits. im thinking touch tests/seeds/<seed> or uv has a seed generate job. anyways ci it should end up in that dir, then as an artifact if gha and main branch, then passed into the test matrix. if uv test without arg- warn, generate and write it yourself pass it to all tests, if some other testing method there should not be a static seed, throw for empty or setup should make the seed. avoid changing how seed generates data. im not sure if a convenient uuid with time, v7?, is valid, but as long as its enough entropy whatever works. either put nothing in their or compact json, consider seeds/v1/id/<first 2 char>/<seed><--symlink: seeds/yyyy/mm/dd/<seed> avoiding conflicts is important.

The seed bullet is quoted here because it is the second half of this policy ("aggresively test many permutations" is how, "a single seed per-run" is the constraint). **Its design -- seed format, storage under `tests/seeds/`, GHA artifacts, the collector job, `uv` -- is owned by #93** and is not decided here. This issue only commits to: permutation generators in regression tests take their randomness from the run seed #93 defines, never from their own clock or a hardcoded constant.

## Current state

- No `Fuzz*`, property tests, `math/rand` or `testing/quick` anywhere; permutations today are hand-written table tests (e.g. `TestEveryExecFlagChangesSomething`, `internal/e2e/e2e_test.go:2877`, four rows).
- No PR template (`.github/` holds only `workflows/`). Agents open PRs with `gh pr create --body ...`, which does **not** apply a template, so a template checkbox alone would not reach them.
- The best existing example of the policy is PR #62: "The new test exercises the script path. Verified it fails without the fix and passes with it." -- and it names why the old test missed it ("only the first direction was tested"). Two later PRs are as good or better. #75 found that its own guard's first `--typecheck` assertion matched output present either way; the table's without-flag check caught it. #182 reverted its cleanup fix to watch the new leak test fail before trusting it.

### First-pass review of recent fixes (from PR bodies and changed-file lists, merged PRs through #182 at 05c78b2; to be confirmed)

| settings declared and never read (24 wired, 3 deleted; `script.env` dead twice); `logging` capability declared and undelivered; `subscribe`/`listChanged` gated per server, not per connection; `POST /v1/diagnose` `session` and `GET /v1/log?chain=` filters dropped | agent audit | PR #171 | yes: the `consumed_test.go` guard (`internal/settings/consumed_test.go:73,145,209`), nine effect tests in `internal/e2e/unread_test.go` (nine of the 24 settings it wired), plus `logs_test.go`, `proto_test.go`, `server_test.go`, `registry_test.go` changes | not stated for the tests. The `listChanged` over-correction was caught against the binary, not by a test | The `/v1/log?chain=` e2e test had hidden the bug by passing `--level debug`, so it was a test that could not fail. The new guard proves a setting is *read*, not that reading it matters: `registry.pageSize` passed it (#179) -> #129 (#181 collision 15) |

## The policy (proposed wording for the contributor page, #131)

1. **Sources that count:** user reports, CI failures (including ones that "went green on retry"), an agent noticing something while doing other work, review comments, flaky runs, `-race` reports, and bugs in tests themselves (#35).
2. **Where:** the test lands **in the same PR as the fix**. A fix without a test says why in the PR body (`No test: <reason>`).
3. **Red first:** the test must fail without the fix. Either commit the test before the fix (reviewable in history), or state "fails without the fix" in the PR body as #62 did. Better still, revert the fix and quote the failure, as #182 did. "Fails without the fix" means the *assertion* discriminates, not just that the test runs. #75's first `--typecheck` assertion matched text present with or without the flag and would have passed either way.
4. **"Cheap" means** roughly: a unit test, or an e2e test that adds < ~2 s. When it is not cheap (needs a real server, an OS CI does not have, minutes of setup), file an issue labelled `testing` with the reproduction instead of dropping it.
5. **Permutations, aggressively.** Test the bug's *shape*: a Go table test over the dimensions the bug lives in (runtime deno/bun/node x snippet/file x daemon/inline x socket/TCP is mcpx's usual cross-product; add "one configuration vs two" and "one run vs concurrent runs" after #69/#70/#73), or a generator seeded from the run seed (#93). Keep the cross-product in unit or in-process tests; in e2e, pick the rows only the binary can prove, because every e2e row is a subprocess and CI is budgeted (#95).
6. **Name it for the behaviour**, not the issue number (`TestInlineScriptReachesTheDaemon`, not `TestIssue62`), and put the issue number in a comment.
7. **If the bug is one of a class** (the same shape has shipped before, or a declaration and its use live apart), the fix also adds or extends a guard test -- #129.

## Approaches: how the policy is enforced

### A -- a PR template checkbox (least recommended alone)
`.github/pull_request_template.md` with "[ ] regression test added / fails without the fix". Cheap. But the template is repo-wide (this is a whole nix config repo, most PRs are not mcpx), GitHub supports per-template files only via `?template=` URLs, and `gh pr create --body` -- how agents open PRs -- skips templates entirely. A checkbox is also self-attested.

### B -- the checklist in the contributor page and the review step
The rule lives in the contributor page (#131), and whoever reviews (human or review agent) checks it. Reaches agents where they actually read instructions, costs nothing in CI. Still self-attested, and misses PRs nobody reviews.

### C -- B plus a cheap CI check (recommended)
B, plus a CI step (#95) on PRs touching `pkgs/mcpx/**`: if the PR is a fix (title starts with `fix`, body has `Fixes #`/`Closes #` on a `bug` issue, or a label says so) and changes no `*_test.go` / `*.test.ts`, the step fails unless the body contains `No test: <reason>`. It does not prove the test fails without the fix; that stays a review item (an optional later step could run the PR's new tests against the merge base and expect failure). Recommended because it catches the common miss for seconds of CI, leaves an escape hatch that is visible in history, and does not depend on templates agents never see.

## Tasks

- [ ] Confirm or correct each row of the review table; for each "no"/"unclear", file or write the missing test (small PRs, one per bug).
- [ ] Settle the policy wording and hand it to #131.
- [ ] Specify the C check for #95 (inputs, exact match rules, escape hatch).

## Open questions

- Is "fails without the fix" proven by commit order, by PR-body statement, or by a CI job that runs new tests against the merge base? The last is the only non-attested option and the most expensive.
- Does a bug found and fixed inside the same unmerged PR count? (Proposed: yes if it reached a pushed commit or CI.)
- Label for flaky-found bugs: reuse `testing` + `bug`, or add a `flaky` label? (Label set is fixed today.)

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** S (policy) / M (review + missing tests) / S (CI check) · **Impact** high
**Depends on / related**: #93 (run seed, generators, the quoted seed bullet), #95 (the CI check, plugin tests), #97 (integration inventory), #35, #52 (closed, fixed in #182), #65, #74 (closed, fixed in #75), #75, #78, #46, #56, #58, #61, #62, #66, #69, #70, #73, #171, #179 (the setting #171's guard passed), #182; siblings #127, #129, #130, #131.

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

## Acceptance criteria

- The failing-first policy is recorded: every bug gets at least one new test in the same PR as its fix, failing without the fix (when cheap), covering the bug's permutations — and the enforcement checklist (PR template vs CI check) is decided and in place.
- Recently fixed mcpx bugs are audited against the policy, with the audit result recorded on this issue.
- Missing tests the audit finds are filed (issues or PRs) and linked here.
- The work described in the Summary/Scope above is delivered via a branch + PR (no direct push to main); verification runs in GitHub Actions CI, not on the sandbox.
- Evidence (audit list and links) is recorded on this issue before it is closed.

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#298 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #253

## Summary

The daemon has no notion of *who* is calling. That is deliberate and documented
three times over — "the API is unauthenticated, so the network it is on is the
access control" (`internal/daemon/server.go:214`), "the socket's file
permissions are the access control" (`internal/daemon/origin.go:13`), "Every
endpoint is unauthenticated" (`internal/api/openapi.go:40`) — and for a daemon
on a unix socket it is the right model.

This issue is the **authorisation model**: one notion of a principal that each
surface can construct, and a permission declared on each operation. Built
permissively, in the same spirit as #253: every principal resolves to the owner,
every permission check answers yes, and the daemon behaves exactly as it does
today. What the work buys is that the *vocabulary exists* and is declared in one
place, so a future surface has something to populate and a future policy has
something to constrain.

**This blocks nothing.** No surface, transport or feature waits on it. An
unauthenticated local daemon is a complete answer and stays one. Ordered behind
#253 so the auth work proceeds in one line rather than two.

## Original notes

> security is just off the table right now, there's no blocker for adding
> security, there's no blocker for not having auth. just dont mix auth with
> other things in issues

Raised after an earlier draft of this issue framed itself as a precondition for
remote surfaces. It is not one, and the framing was wrong.

## Current state

**Unauthenticated by design, and consistently so.** Three separate places state
the model in the same terms, which indicates a decision rather than a drift. The
TCP listener's host is deliberately not defaulted
(`internal/daemon/server.go:216-220`): "that has to be somebody's decision
rather than a default." The daemon will bind a port and declines to guess you
meant to expose it.

**The peer uid is available and unread.** A unix socket connection carries peer
credentials (`SO_PEERCRED` / `LOCAL_PEERCRED`). mcpx never looks. "Which local
user is calling" is a principal obtainable today for free.

**The ops table is the asset.** Every operation is declared once in
`internal/api/ops*.go`, and that declaration drives the CLI command, the MCP
tool and the OpenAPI operation. #114 names this as the project's own precedent —
"one declaration should drive every surface". A permission attached there is
enforced everywhere by construction, including on surfaces that do not exist
yet.

**What is adjacent and is not this.** #253 is the authorization *interface*
(OAuth, resource server, 61 conformance rows). #300 is real credential
validation, behind #253. #240 and #205 are configured upstream auth never being
applied — mcpx as a client, the opposite direction. #204 is `Origin` validation,
a browser-threat defence, not authentication. #185 is a settings ceiling a
caller may lower but not raise — the same *shape* as a permission and worth
sharing machinery with.

## Approaches

### Approach A — least recommended: a principal only when a surface needs one

Leave it until ssh or a browser surface lands, then add identity to that
surface.

This is how a codebase ends with four authentication systems: each surface
invents a principal because none existed when it was written. The cost of
declaring the vocabulary now is small precisely *because* nothing depends on it
— there is no migration, no compatibility surface and no behaviour to preserve.
Doing it later means doing it four times, against live surfaces.

### Approach B — middle: principals now, permissions when needed

Construct a principal per surface, carry it through, and defer the permission
declarations.

Half the value for most of the work. A principal nothing consults is a field
that rots; without a permission to check it against, nothing exercises it and it
will be wrong by the time it matters.

### Approach C — recommended: both, permissively, and a decision that is always "yes" but always *recorded*

**1. Every surface constructs a principal.** One internal notion, built from
what each transport natively knows:

| surface | principal from |
| --- | --- |
| unix socket | peer credentials — the uid, available today, read nowhere |
| loopback TCP | nothing native; explicit configuration, or anonymous |
| ssh (#85) | the authenticated key |
| browser (#174) | a session, alongside #204's `Origin` check |
| plugin (#82) | a declared plugin identity rather than ambient trust |

**2. Every operation declares a permission.** A field on the ops-table entry,
checked at the one place all surfaces funnel through. Default policy: the
socket's owner gets everything, anonymous gets everything, and **the check
always returns yes**. Behaviour is identical to today.

**3. The decision is recorded even though it is always yes.** This is the piece
that makes the permissive stage worth shipping rather than merely harmless.
With principals constructed and permissions declared, mcpx can answer "what
would a policy have refused?" from real traffic, before any policy exists. That
is the same dry-run property #300 wants for credential checks, and the two
should share one mechanism.

What this deliberately does **not** do: define a policy file format, decide
which scopes may grant, or enforce anything. Those are a later issue, and they
are the parts with actual risk.

## Open questions

- Is the permission vocabulary per-operation, or a small set of tiers
  (`read`/`run`/`admin`) operations are tagged with? Tiers are comprehensible
  and coarse; per-operation becomes a 200-row table nobody reads. Leaning tiers.
- Does a *tool call* carry a permission, or only mcpx's own operations? Upstream
  tools are not in the ops table, and they are the interesting surface. Possibly
  #114's tool views are the natural grant unit.
- Does the principal belong in the request context, or in the existing session
  notion? There is already a session key (`_meta["ai.opencode/sessionID"]`,
  #211); a principal is not a session but they travel together.
- Should `mcpx doctor` report "authorisation: permissive" so nobody deploys
  believing otherwise? Same hazard #300 flags for the credential interface, and
  the same answer: yes, loudly.
- Shared machinery with #185's clamping — same ceiling shape, probably one
  implementation.
- Does the socket peer uid distinguish anything useful on a single-user laptop?
  Honestly, rarely. It matters for a shared host and for #255's elicitation
  storage concern, and it is nearly free, which is the whole argument.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease:** M for principals and the declaration field; S for the permissive check
and the decision log. The enforcement, policy format and config-chain
constraints are explicitly **out of scope** and belong to a later issue.
**Impact:** low and deferred — this is vocabulary, not capability. Worth doing
early only because it is cheap while nothing depends on it. **Blocks nothing.**

**Depends on / related:** **#253 (the auth interface — this is ordered behind
it)**, #300 (real credential validation — the sibling second stage, also behind
#253, also blocking nothing), #185 (clamped settings — same ceiling shape,
share machinery), #204 (Origin validation — adjacent, not a substitute), #240
and #205 (configured upstream auth never applied — mcpx as client, the other
direction), #255 (elicitation storage permissions — a case a principal would
make expressible), #82 (plugins as a principal), #114 (tool views as a possible
grant unit), #113 (the operation surface where a policy would be administered),
#174 (surfaces — each would supply a principal as it lands, none waits on this).

## Acceptance criteria

- A principal type exists that every surface (unix socket, TCP, HTTP) can construct, and a permission is declared per operation in one place.
- Built permissively: every principal resolves to the owner and every check answers yes — daemon behaviour is byte-for-byte unchanged for existing clients.
- The vocabulary is documented where the current unauthenticated model is stated (`server.go`, `origin.go`, `openapi.go`), superseding those comments.
- Tests pin the permissive behaviour so a future policy change is a deliberate diff, not an accident.

body:
## Problem

The collaborative-editing WebSocket (`/ws/collab/{doc_id}`) applies **no message-size cap and no per-message step-count cap**, even though the repo's own framing standard is 1 MiB:

- `pkgs/id/src/frames.rs:16-19` — `MAX_FRAME_BYTES` is 1 MiB, documented as: "Both transports enforce it: the Iroh frame reader refuses longer frames and the WebSocket has `max_message_size(MAX_FRAME_BYTES)`."
- `pkgs/id/src/web/world_ws.rs:279` — the world WebSocket does exactly that: `ws.max_message_size(MAX_FRAME_BYTES)`.
- `pkgs/id/src/web/collab.rs:626-632` — `ws_collab_handler` calls plain `ws.on_upgrade(...)` with no `max_message_size` / `max_frame_size`, so the upgrade inherits the framework default. Verified in the vendored tungstenite 0.29.0 source (the version axum 0.8.9 uses here): `WebSocketConfig::default()` is `max_message_size: Some(64 << 20)`, `max_frame_size: Some(16 << 20)` — **64× the repo's frame standard**.

Nothing downstream compensates:

- `CollabMessage::decode` (`collab.rs:513`, Steps attempt at :536-545) deserializes a `Vec<serde_json::Value>` of steps with no length or byte check.
- The Steps handler (`collab.rs:1016-1029`) pushes **every** step in the message into the document's permanent step history (`doc_steps.push(...)` at :1019), clones the whole vector for the broadcast `Update`, and advances the version by `steps.len()`.
- That history is retained for the life of the document and re-serialized in full as the catch-up `Update` to **every** later joiner (`collab.rs:784-810`), so one oversized message is paid for in server memory and in every subsequent join's bandwidth, not just once.

Any client that can open a collab socket (the first-message auth is optional — anonymous clients proceed, `collab.rs` auth-timeout path) can therefore send a single ~64 MiB message, or one message carrying hundreds of thousands of steps, and have all of it decoded, cloned several times, stored, broadcast, and replayed to future joiners. The sibling world socket and every length-prefixed transport in the crate refuse anything over 1 MiB unread.

Related but distinct: #1833 covers the collab *cursor name* path (no length/control filtering); this issue is the message/step-count size bound on the same socket. #1839 is the same bug class in codex-proxy's hand-rolled WS parser.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `6a284efd`)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-collabws/` — the Steps decode attempt copied verbatim from `collab.rs` (file sha256 `55e042705c0389140eb2b50aa617cd4cac388806b44e116ecba69af0a7d9f6e0` = main), plus the handler's history-push loop:

```
CONTROL ok: 33 bytes, version=0 steps=1 client=7
OVERSIZE_FRAME_ACCEPTED: 4194337 bytes (4x the 1 MiB frame cap) decoded to 1 step(s); no size check in decode
MANY_STEPS_ACCEPTED: 200000 steps in one 6937097-byte message; simulated handler history now holds 200000 steps, version would jump by 200000
```

Framework default verified in the laptop cargo registry: `tungstenite-0.29.0/src/protocol/mod.rs:101-102` — `max_message_size: Some(64 << 20)`, `max_frame_size: Some(16 << 20)`.

Dedup: `gh issue list --search` (all states) for "collab websocket message size", "max_message_size", and "collab steps history unbounded" returned only #1833 (cursor names — different) and closed audit #1075. No existing issue covers a collab message-size or step-count bound.

## Why it matters

A long-lived `id serve` process can be made to allocate and retain hundreds of MiB (decode + history clone + broadcast clone + per-joiner catch-up clones) from a single unauthenticated socket message, and the retained history inflates every later join for that document. The crate already decided this bound: 1 MiB, enforced on the Iroh reader, the SSH/byte-stream readers, and the world WebSocket. The collab socket is the one WebSocket that missed it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ws_collab_handler` sets `max_message_size` (and `max_frame_size` if triage judges it needed) to the repo standard `MAX_FRAME_BYTES`, matching `world_ws.rs:279`; an over-limit message closes/refuses the connection without being decoded into the step history.
- [ ] A per-message step-count bound (a named constant) is enforced on the Steps path — in `decode` or in the handler before any step is pushed — so a within-size but step-stuffed message cannot grow the history or jump the version by an unbounded count in one frame. (Triage pins the value; it should comfortably cover legitimate ProseMirror step batches.)
- [ ] Regression tests: an over-`MAX_FRAME_BYTES` collab message is refused; a Steps message past the step-count bound is refused with the document version and history unchanged; ordinary small Steps messages still apply, ack, and broadcast.
- [ ] The `frames.rs` doc claim ("the WebSocket has `max_message_size(MAX_FRAME_BYTES)`") is true for every WebSocket the crate serves after the fix — triage also checks `tags_ws.rs` (its inbound side only drains, so exposure is smaller, but the same one-line bound applies).

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#123 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #93

## Summary

Pick the engine that turns the run seed (#121) into test inputs. Candidates: Go native fuzzing (`go test -fuzz`), `testing/quick`, `pgregory.net/rapid`, and hand-rolled generators on `math/rand/v2`. The deciding constraint is the notes' hard rule -- **one seed per run for all generated inputs** -- plus per-test substreams and "avoid changing how seed generates data". Findings below are from docs and source; recommendation at the end, including how native fuzz corpora fit.

## Original notes

> - testing
>   - agents should make at least 1 simple, new test for every bug observed from any source, when cheap to do so-- aggresively test many permutations. 
>     - you can absolutely rely on fuzzing anywhere you can fit it and you should whenever you can-- but you _must_ use a single seed per-run to generate all inputs. (this could eventually be discussed with careful consideration.) it should be appended into a test tracking structured file in the repo and it can be committed. ideally main branch commit's seed or pr merge seed should make it back into file eventually. to prevent churn, maybe ci appends the seed into a gha var (race/overwrite risk?), or attached as artifact to each workflow in init job before tests begin-- a collector job can scoop them up sometime later. once a day/week/on-release/every-100-commits. im thinking touch tests/seeds/<seed> or uv has a seed generate job. anyways ci it should end up in that dir, then as an artifact if gha and main branch, then passed into the test matrix. if uv test without arg- warn, generate and write it yourself pass it to all tests, if some other testing method there should not be a static seed, throw for empty or setup should make the seed. avoid changing how seed generates data. im not sure if a convenient uuid with time, v7?, is valid, but as long as its enough entropy whatever works. either put nothing in their or compact json, consider seeds/v1/id/<first 2 char>/<seed><--symlink: seeds/yyyy/mm/dd/<seed> avoiding conflicts is important.

## Current state

No fuzz, property, or random tests exist (735 tests at 05c78b2, none use `testing.F`, `testing/quick`, rapid or `math/rand`). Go 1.26.7. Zero test-only dependencies today; `go.mod` deps are bubbletea/bubbles/lipgloss, yaml.v3, modernc.org/sqlite (chosen, per `package.nix`, to avoid a C toolchain -- the project leans toward few, pure-Go deps).

## Findings

| | Native fuzz (`testing.F`) | `testing/quick` | rapid v1.3.0 | Hand-rolled on `math/rand/v2` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Seedable from our run seed | **No.** The mutator's randomness is internal; there is no seed flag. | Yes: `Config.Rand *rand.Rand` (math/rand **v1**; wrap a ChaCha8 in a v1 `Source` adapter). | Partly: `-rapid.seed` / `RAPID_SEED` (uint64, `0` = random from `maphash`), **process-global** (`data.go:21 baseSeed()`); settable in-process via `flag.Set("rapid.seed", ...)` because it is read at check time. | Yes, fully. |
| Per-test substream keyed by test name | n/a | Yes (we build the `*rand.Rand` per test) | **No.** Every `rapid.Check` in the process starts from the same base seed and uses `base + iter` per case (`engine.go:420`). Only achievable by `flag.Set` before each `Check`, which breaks under `t.Parallel`. | Yes |
| Runs under plain `go test ./...` | Only the seed corpus (`f.Add` + `testdata/fuzz/FuzzX/`) runs, as regular tests. Actual fuzzing needs `-fuzz`, which must match **exactly one package and one target** per invocation (`go help testflag`). | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Structured inputs | Args limited to `[]byte`, `string`, bool, ints, floats; structure must be decoded from bytes | reflection over Go types; poor for "valid config document" shapes | Excellent (`Custom`, `OneOf`, `SliceOfN`, state machines via `T.Repeat`) | Whatever we write |
| Shrinking | Yes (`-fuzzminimizetime`) | **No** | **Yes**, automatic | No (cheap substitute: draw sizes small-first) |
| Coverage guidance | **Yes** | No | No | No |
| Output stability across upgrades | n/a | Frozen package ("not accepting new features", `go doc testing/quick`) | Tied to rapid's version: fail files record rapid's internal format version (`persist.go:21`) and are ignored when it differs (`engine.go:376`) -- rapid itself treats an upgrade as possibly changing what a bitstream generates | Ours, guarded by the golden test in #121 section 3 |
| Writes into the repo | failing inputs to `testdata/fuzz/FuzzX/` (wanted: they are the regression corpus) | no | fail files to `testdata/rapid/<Test>/` unless `-rapid.nofailfile` | no |
| Timing sensitivity | `-fuzztime` | fixed count | cases cut short by a deadline heuristic (`engine.go:413`), and `-short` divides checks by 5 -- same seed, variable number of cases (a prefix of the same sequence) | fixed count per budget |
| Dependency | stdlib | stdlib | 1 module, MPL-2.0, no transitive deps | stdlib |

Also: rapid's failure message prints its own `-rapid.seed=N`, not our run seed, so the reproduce line would need translating; and `rapid.MakeFuzz(prop)` turns a rapid property into a native fuzz target (bytes become rapid's bitstream).

## Approaches

### A -- `testing/quick` (least recommended)
Seedable and stdlib, but frozen, reflection-driven (hard to express "a valid layered config" or "a JSON Schema"), no shrinking, and on math/rand v1. Nothing it offers is not better in B or C.

### B -- rapid as the primary engine
The best off-the-shelf generator and shrinker in Go; property code is pleasant (`rapid.Check(t, func(t *rapid.T){ ... Draw(t, "x") })`), and `MakeFuzz` bridges to native fuzzing for free. Seeding works via `RAPID_SEED` derived from the run seed (#121 section 2), so the "one seed per run" rule is satisfiable. The costs: no per-test substream (all tests share `base + iter`; adding a case to one property does not shift another, but the scheme is rapid's, not ours), generation output is coupled to rapid's version (an upgrade is an implicit generator-version bump for every rapid-backed generator -- in tension with "avoid changing how seed generates data"), its deadline heuristic makes the case count timing-dependent, and it writes fail files into `testdata/rapid/` unless disabled. It would also be mcpx's **sixth direct Go dependency**. `package.nix:36-53` names and defends each of the five, and a test-only module still lands in `go.mod`'s direct block and changes `vendorHash` (`package.nix:54`). Adopting rapid therefore means amending that comment in the same PR (addendum below). A defensible choice if shrinking turns out to matter more than stream control.

### C -- hand-rolled generators on ChaCha8 behind a tiny `Source` interface, native fuzz for parsers (recommended)
- `internal/testsupport/gen`: generators are `func(src Source, size int) T` where `Source` is just `Uint64() uint64`. In property mode, `src` is ChaCha8 keyed by `stream(t, gen@version)` from #121.
- **The same generator also serves native fuzzing**: a `bytesSource` that reads `Uint64`s from the fuzzer's `[]byte` (zeros when exhausted) lets any generator become a `Fuzz*` target -- the pattern `rapid.MakeFuzz` uses, in ~20 lines. So coverage-guided fuzzing of structured shapes is available without a second generator.
- Native `Fuzz*` targets for byte-oriented parsers where coverage guidance pays: `config.StripJSONC` (`internal/config/config.go:718`), `codegen.TypeFor` over raw schema bytes (`internal/codegen/ts.go:70`), `launcher.Expand` templates (`internal/launcher/template.go:80`), `settings.ParseBytes` (`internal/settings/value.go:415`). Their **seed corpora** (`f.Add` + `testdata/fuzz/FuzzX/`) run in every `go test` as deterministic regression tests; the minimized failing input from a seeded failure is committed there too. Long `-fuzz` sessions are a scheduled/soak job (one target per invocation) owned by #95's budget, not part of the per-run seed rule -- they are explicitly *outside* "one seed per run", which the notes' "(this could eventually be discussed with careful consideration.)" leaves room for.
- Shrinking substitute: generators take a `size` that the runner grows from small to large across a test's budget, so the first failure is usually small; revisit rapid if that is not enough.
- Why C: it is the only option that satisfies all three hard requirements (one run seed, per-test substreams, versioned stable output) without fighting the library; it is stdlib-only; and it keeps a clean upgrade path to B (rapid can later be driven by `RAPID_SEED` from the same root).

## Open questions

- Is shrinking worth a dependency? Decide after the first ~5 generators exist (#125): if failures are routinely unreadable, adopt rapid for new generators (B) with its version pinned and treated as a generator-version input.
- Native fuzz corpora: commit only failure-derived inputs, or also a curated set of generator outputs (`gen -> testdata/fuzz/FuzzX/<hash>`)?
- Scheduled `-fuzz` soak: which targets, how long, on which runner (#95)? It cannot share the run seed (the mutator is unseeded); is that acceptable as a documented exception?
- Does `testing/synctest` (Go 1.25+) belong in the same helper package for time-dependent properties (#126)?

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** S (research is done here; the choice gates #124/#125) · **Impact** high (fixes the shape of every generator)
**Depends on / related:** #121 (seed, derivation, golden guard), #124 (generator registry), #125 (first generator), #126; #95 (soak `-fuzz` job and budget), #99 (policy on committing fuzz corpora).

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#252 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Baseline from the official suite (`@modelcontextprotocol/conformance@0.2.0-alpha.11`) against the daemon's `/mcp` endpoint at `408bc2b`:

| requirement set | passed | failed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `2026-07-28` | 115 | 54 |
| `2025-11-25` | 45 | 21 (2 of them #251) |

**Read the 54 correctly before acting on it.** About 50 are scenarios that never reach a protocol assertion, because they assume the suite's own fixture surface: tools named `slow_compute`, `confirm_delete`, `failing_job`, `test_missing_capability`, `json_schema_2020_12_tool`; prompts named `test_simple_prompt`, `test_prompt_with_arguments`; resources under `test://`; and a tool carrying `x-mcp-header` annotations. mcpx is a proxy — it publishes its own small tool set and namespaces upstream resources as `mcpx://<namespace>/<uri>` — so those report failures that say nothing about conformance. Every `input-required-result-*`, every `tasks-*`, `prompts-get-*`, `tools-call-{image,audio,embedded-resource,mixed-content,with-progress}`, `http-custom-header-server-validation` and `json-schema-2020-12` failure is in this bucket.

Chasing that number as if it were 54 defects would be weeks of work for four fixes.

## The four genuine gaps

**1. `-32021 MissingRequiredClientCapability` is never raised.**
`sep-2575-server-rejects-undeclared-capability`. When a tool needs a client capability the request's `_meta` did not declare, 2026-07-28 requires `-32021` (HTTP 400). mcpx runs the tool. The code exists as `codeMissingCapability` in `internal/mcpserver/server.go` but nothing in the `tools/call` path consults the declared capabilities before dispatching.

**2. The tasks extension does not gate on the extension capability.**
`sep-2663-tasks-methods-non-declaring`: `tasks/get`, `tasks/update` and `tasks/cancel` must answer `-32021` to a client that did not declare `io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks`; mcpx answers `-32602`. The extension overview is explicit: *"Never return a task to a client that did not declare support."*

**3. No server-directed task creation.**
`tasks-server-directed-creation-no-hint`, `sep-2663-result-type-task-on-create`. In 2026 the server decides per request whether to return a `CreateTaskResult` (`resultType: "task"`); the per-request opt-in of 2025-11-25 is gone. mcpx only ever creates a task when asked. Also `CreateTaskResult` must carry `ttlMs` (renamed from v1 `ttl`).

**4. `Mcp-Method` on a `tools/call` changes the result.**
`tasks-headers-tolerate-mcp-method-on-tools-call`: *"tool result content MUST be unaffected by the Mcp-Method header."* The body is the source of truth; headers are mirrors for intermediaries to route on. Something in the header path is feeding dispatch.

(1)-(3) are properly exercisable only against a server that publishes the fixture tools, which argues for #133's scriptable mock MCP server rather than guessing.

## Also worth recording

- **An official suite exists and is governance-critical.** SEP-2484 (*Final*) makes a merged conformance scenario a condition of a Standards Track SEP reaching `Final`; SEP-1730 ties official SDK tiering to a percentage from it (Tier 1 = 100%). Its `requirements/<revision>.yaml` sets are frozen on purpose.
- **The npm `latest` tag is a 0.1.x that predates 2026-07-28.** Install `@alpha` or you will score against the wrong revision.
- **SEP-1627, the earlier "conformance testing" proposal, is closed and superseded** by SEP-2484; its golden-trace design was explicitly not carried forward. Reading 1627 and stopping is how you conclude no suite exists.
- `pkgs/mcpx/scripts/conformance.sh` already runs both legs, including mcpx as the client under test via `internal/conformance/officialclient`. It needs `CONFORMANCE_DIR`; the install is the only step needing network, and nothing in `go test` touches it.
- A per-revision record of what a server owes, including the obligations the prose implies but never states, is now at `pkgs/mcpx/docs/spec/server-obligations.md` §7.

## Suggested next step

Wire `scripts/conformance.sh` into CI as a **non-blocking** job with a recorded baseline and an expected-failures file (the suite supports `--expected-failures`), so the number moves only deliberately. That is the cheap way to stop this regressing again — #251 is exactly the kind of drift it would have caught the same day.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The ~50 fixture-artefact failures are documented as artefacts (suite surface assumptions named), so the count is never again read as 54 defects.
- [ ] The four genuine gaps are each tracked by a live issue (the #253–#259 set or successors) — this issue links them and closes when they do.
- [ ] A conformance re-run on current main replaces the 408bc2b baseline numbers in the matrix doc.

## Summary

mcpx speaks stdio and Streamable HTTP. The 2024-11-05 HTTP+SSE transport (two endpoints, a persistent event stream) is neither served nor spoken, `transport: sse` in config is ignored, and there is no fallback from Streamable HTTP to it, which the backward-compatibility guidance in every later revision describes. The transport is deprecated and on a short removal clock (`2026-07-28/deprecated.mdx:31`), so this is worth doing only if a server someone uses still needs it; opencode v1 has the fallback.

## What to do

## Summary

Four daemon-state defects. `/v1/exec` never marks its runs ephemeral, so session-scoped instances (a browser) are not released at the end of the run and wait for idle reaping; the CLI path sets `MCPX_EPHEMERAL` (read from code, not driven). Found while writing the comparison register (`pkgs/mcpx/docs/compare/`) and checked against the code at `05c78b2`. Each row below links its register entry, which carries the value, effort, risk, the specification text and every source.

| [PM-15](https://github.com/dezren39/nix/blob/main/pkgs/mcpx/docs/compare/register/process-model.md#pm-15-v1protocol-reports-nativeelicit-from-the-default) | `/v1/protocol` reports `nativeElicit` from the default | ✗ — compiled default, not the setting | S |
| [PM-21](https://github.com/dezren39/nix/blob/main/pkgs/mcpx/docs/compare/register/process-model.md#pm-21-opencode-database-filename-depends-on-release-channel) | opencode database filename depends on release channel | ✗ — `mcpx stats opencode` reads `opencode.db` only | S |

## Evidence

`internal/execsvc/execsvc.go:573-593` vs `internal/cli/commands.go:694`; `internal/cli/serve_ask.go:234-254`; `internal/daemon/routes_proto.go:530` (the comment at `:495-497` says it cannot disagree); `v1:packages/core/src/database/database.ts:49`, `v2:packages/cli/src/database-path.ts:7`.

## What to do

One change each; the ephemeral release needs a test that fails today.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** S · **Impact** med · **Related**: #78 (daemon state and caches), #189

## Acceptance criteria

- `mcpx stats opencode` finds the opencode database filename for the installed release channel, not only `opencode.db`.
- Regression tests cover each of the four defects.
