## Summary

mcpx declares `sampling` to every upstream because the daemon always installs an elicitation handler, and `docs/protocol.md` says it is declared only when a handler exists. It declares `roots` to every upstream and always answers `[]`; the doc says "the configured roots" and the daemon passes `nil`. Toward hosts, the elicitation gate treats any declared `elicitation` as form-capable, so a host that declared only `url` would be sent a form. Sampling is relayed after checking only that `sampling` is present, not `sampling.tools` or `sampling.context`. mcpx never asks its host for roots, which would be the honest source for the roots it answers upstream.

Found while writing the comparison register (`pkgs/mcpx/docs/compare/`) and checked against the code at `05c78b2`. Each row below links its register entry, which carries the value, effort, risk, the specification text and every source.

## Register rows

| row | difference | mcpx @ 05c78b2 | effort |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [CAP-02](https://github.com/dezren39/nix/blob/main/pkgs/mcpx/docs/compare/register/capabilities.md#cap-02-client-roots) | client `roots`; deprecated to a bare `{}` in 2026 | partial — declared to every upstream; always answers an empty list | S |
| [CAP-04](https://github.com/dezren39/nix/blob/main/pkgs/mcpx/docs/compare/register/capabilities.md#cap-04-client-sampling) | client `sampling`; structured in 2025-11-25, deprecated in 2026 | partial — declared to every upstream; only a broker agent answers | S |
| [SMP-09](https://github.com/dezren39/nix/blob/main/pkgs/mcpx/docs/compare/register/sampling.md#smp-09-client-declares-sampling-only-when-something-can-answer) | Client declares `sampling` only when something can answer | ✗ — declared to every upstream; doc says otherwise | S |
| [CAP-08](https://github.com/dezren39/nix/blob/main/pkgs/mcpx/docs/compare/register/capabilities.md#cap-08-client-elicitationform) | client `elicitation.form`; `{}` means form only | partial — form gate ignores a url-only declaration | S |
| [SMP-11](https://github.com/dezren39/nix/blob/main/pkgs/mcpx/docs/compare/register/sampling.md#smp-11-relaying-sampling-to-a-host-checks-sub-capabilities-and-revision) | Relaying sampling to a host checks sub-capabilities and revision | ✗ — only `sampling` presence checked | S |
| [ROOT-04](https://github.com/dezren39/nix/blob/main/pkgs/mcpx/docs/compare/register/roots.md#root-04-server-asks-its-host-for-roots) | Server asks its host for roots | ✗ — never sends `roots/list` to a host | M |

## Evidence

- `internal/mcpclient/modern.go:46-58` (sampling when a handler exists), `internal/daemon/hooks.go:69` (always a handler), `internal/daemon/server.go:176` (`nil` roots).
- `internal/mcpserver/conn.go:191-211` (`CanElicit`, `CanSample`).

## What to do

Declare `sampling` only when a sampler is configured; answer roots from configuration or the host (or stop declaring `roots`); gate form mode on `form` present or neither key present; check `sampling.tools`/`context` before relaying.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** S · **Impact** low · **Related**: #177, #110 (where the model comes from, after Sampling's deprecation)

## Acceptance criteria

- mcpx declares `sampling` and `roots` to an upstream only when the corresponding handler actually exists — code matches `docs/protocol.md` (CAP-02/CAP-04).
- `roots/list` is answered from configured or host-provided roots, not unconditionally `[]`.
- Host-facing gates check sub-capabilities: `elicitation` form vs url, `sampling.tools` / `sampling.context` — not merely the parent capability's presence.
- mcpx obtains roots from its host where the host offers them, as the honest source for what it answers upstream.
- Tests cover declaration and gating per sub-capability.

title: mcpx: where a script's packages come from -- npm/deno/bun dependency configuration chain

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#103 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #175

**Cache: deferred to #187** (#181 collision 12). #187 owns the cache mechanism
(layout, keys, byte/age eviction, leases); this issue owns only what it puts in
it — the resolved dependency set as the key, and the prepared directory as the
entry. The cache design text below stays as input to #187.

## Summary

Where does a script's third-party code come from, and who decides? Today: the
runtime decides, entirely, and mcpx has no opinion, no setting and no way for a
caller to state one. This issue defines the dependency-source chain — host
default, CLI config, config directory, the working directory's
`package.json`/`node_modules`, an explicit package list over `/v1`, `/mcp`, the
CLI and the plugin, and a pre-baked set shipped with the binary — and picks a
precedence order for it.

## Original notes

> - how to config npm
>   - from host default
>   - from cli config
>   - from cli config dir
>   - from pwd dir nodepackages
>   - from /v1 /mcp (and cli/plugin)
>     - command to pass list of packages, package.json(c) (package.lock supported too)
>   - baked into binary

## Current state

Nothing in mcpx configures packages. `runner.Run` writes the client and the
launcher next to the script, sets `MCPX_RUNTIME`, `MCPX_ENTRY`, `MCPX_CLIENT`
and whatever `script.env` carries, and spawns the runtime with `cmd.Dir =
opts.Dir` (`internal/runner/runner.go`). Resolution is then whatever the runtime
does from that directory. `docs/proposals.md:301` states the position
explicitly — "Scripts run on a real runtime, so imports already work: `npm:`,
`jsr:`, `https:` on Deno, `node_modules` on bun and node. What is missing is a
declared place to put shared code" — and proposes `.config/mcpx/lib/` with a
generated import map. That proposal is still `status: proposed`.

Two consequences that matter:

1. **Working directory determines dependencies, and the working directory
   differs by surface.** `mcpx run ./x.ts` inherits the caller's cwd on purpose
   ("a relative path in a script should mean what it means on the command
   line"). `POST /v1/exec` takes `cwd` from `ExecOptions` — the *caller's*
   context, which on a remote daemon names a directory that does not exist
   there. So the same script resolves packages differently depending on how it
   was invoked, and nothing says so.
2. **A remote exec sends text, not a path** (`docs/exec.md`), so there is no
   project directory on the daemon side at all. A remote script cannot import
   anything but `npm:`/`jsr:`/`https:` specifiers today.

The one place mcpx does touch npm is unrelated: `internal/registry/registry.go:248-255`
(`Runtimes`) maps a registry package type to a launcher (`npm` → `npx -y`,
`pypi` → `uvx`, `oci` → `docker`, `nuget` → `dnx`) when adding an MCP *server*.

### How each runtime resolves packages (verified, deno 2.9.6 / bun 1.3.11 / node v24.20.0)

| | deno | bun | node |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| bare specifier `import {z} from "zod"` | needs `deno.json` `imports` or a `node_modules`/`package.json` | resolves `node_modules`, **auto-installs when none exists** (verified: fresh dir, no `node_modules`, `bun b.ts` fetched zod and ran) | `node_modules` upward walk only; fails otherwise |
| `npm:zod@3` specifier | native, no install step (verified) | **rejected** — "Cannot resolve invalid URL 'npm:zod'" | rejected |
| `jsr:` / `https:` | native | `jsr:` no, HTTP no | no |
| cache location | `DENO_DIR` (default `~/.cache/deno`) | `~/.bun/install/cache`, `BUN_INSTALL` | `node_modules` on disk; npm cache under `~/.npm` |
| materialise `node_modules` | `nodeModulesDir: "auto"\|"manual"\|"none"` in `deno.json` | always | always |
| declared deps | `deno.json` `imports`, `--import-map` | `package.json` + `bun.lock`, `bunfig.toml` | `package.json` + lockfile |
| auto-install control | n/a (specifier-level) | `--install=auto\|fallback\|force`, `-i` | none |
| registry/auth config | `.npmrc` is honoured for `npm:` | `bunfig.toml` `[install]`, `.npmrc` | `.npmrc` chain: project → `~/.npmrc` → global → builtin, plus `NPM_CONFIG_*` env |

The asymmetry to design around: **deno pins in the specifier, bun and node pin
in a file.** `npm:zod@3` is self-contained and travels with the script text —
which is exactly what a remote exec needs — while `package.json` needs a
directory. Any scheme that works on all three has to be able to produce both.

`docs/story.md:1672` already states the project's stance on this: "npm versions
are pinned. A configuration that silently upgrades is one that…". Bun's
auto-install resolves to *latest* unless the specifier carries a range, so
auto-install-by-default contradicts that line and should be opt-in.

## Approaches

### Approach A — least recommended: a `mcpx npm` command group that shells out

`mcpx npm install <pkg>`, `mcpx npm config set …`, writing into a
mcpx-owned `node_modules`. The user's note ("command to pass list of packages")
reads most directly as this.

Why not, and this is the brief's point 2 in practice: it is a new command
surface that duplicates a tool the user already has, in a project whose parity
rule is CLI = `/v1` = MCP = plugin — so one command becomes four surfaces, an
ops-table entry and an OpenAPI path, all to wrap `npm install`. It also has to
pick a package manager (npm? bun? pnpm is on this box too) and then owns every
lockfile-format question forever. And it says nothing about deno, where the
answer is not an install at all. A *setting* that names where dependencies come
from is strictly smaller and reaches all four surfaces automatically.

### Approach B — middle: one `deps.*` setting group over the existing search-path machinery

Add settings in the one registry:

| setting | kind | default | meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `deps.source` | enum `host\|config\|cwd\|explicit\|none` | `host` | which of the chain below is authoritative |
| `paths.deps` | path list | — | directories searched for `package.json`/`deno.json`/`bunfig.toml`, nearest first, with the `null` splice |
| `deps.packages` | list, repeatable | — | explicit specifiers, e.g. `zod@3`, `npm:zod@3` |
| `deps.manifest` | source (inline or path) | — | a `package.json`/`package.jsonc` or `deno.json` given directly |
| `deps.autoInstall` | enum `off\|fallback\|always` | `off` | maps to bun `--install=`, to a materialise step for node, ignored by deno |

`paths.deps` reuses `internal/searchpath` exactly as `paths.scripts`,
`paths.adapters` and `paths.placeholders` do — same `null` splice, same
nearest-wins, same `Describe()` for error messages — so "from cli config dir"
and "from pwd dir nodepackages" are two entries on one list rather than two
features. `KindSource` already accepts "inline source, a path to a file, or a
directory", which is what `deps.manifest` needs, and `settings.Scope` already
distinguishes client from daemon, which is what makes `cwd` mean the right thing
on each side.

This is most of the answer and it is small. What it leaves open: nothing is
*declared* per script, so two scripts in one project cannot want different
versions; and the daemon still has to be told what the caller's `cwd` contained
on a remote run.

### Approach C — recommended: Approach B, plus a resolved **dependency set** computed per run and carried on `ExecOptions`

The addition is one idea: mcpx resolves the chain once, into a concrete
*dependency set* — a list of pinned specifiers plus optionally a manifest and a
lockfile — and that resolved set is what travels, gets hashed, and keys the
cache. Everything else is where the set comes from.

The chain, most specific wins:

| rank | source | how it is expressed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | the script itself | a pinned `npm:`/`jsr:` specifier in the source, or a PEP-723-style inline block (PEP 723 is #105's; #104 reads a script's own specifiers statically) |
| 2 | explicit request | `--package zod@3` (repeatable), `--manifest ./package.json`, `ExecOptions.deps` on `/v1/exec` and `mcpx_exec` |
| 3 | project | nearest `package.json`/`deno.json`/`node_modules` on `paths.deps` from the working directory |
| 4 | mcpx config dir | `.config/mcpx/package.json` and `.config/mcpx/lib/` — `docs/proposals.md:301`'s proposal, which this subsumes |
| 5 | user/host | `~/.npmrc`, `DENO_DIR`, `~/.bun/install/cache` — whatever the host already has |
| 6 | baked in | a set shipped with the binary or the Nix derivation |

Why this one:

- **It is the only version that makes remote exec work.** A remote run sends
  text; a *resolved set* is also text. `ExecOptions.deps` is one more field on
  an object whose stated design is "one flat object that grows, rather than a
  new endpoint per capability" (`docs/exec.md`), and it lands on `/v1`, MCP, the
  CLI and the plugin at once because that is how `ExecOptions` already works. No
  new endpoint is needed, which is the answer to "from /v1 /mcp (and
  cli/plugin)".
- **It gives caching something to key on.** The runner already content-addresses
  the exec workdir by the hash of the generated client, precisely so two
  catalogues cannot overwrite each other's `node_modules`-adjacent state. A
  dependency set hashes the same way: same set, same prepared directory, warm
  runtime cache; different set, different directory, no interference. Without
  this, two projects sharing one exec workdir would fight over `node_modules`
  the same way they once fought over the client — a mistake this codebase has
  already made once and fixed. (The key is this issue's; where the prepared
  directory lives and how it is evicted and pinned is #187's.)
- **It normalises the deno/bun/node split at one point.** From a resolved set
  mcpx can emit whichever form the selected runtime wants: rewrite to `npm:`
  specifiers or a `deno.json` `imports` map for deno; write `package.json` +
  lockfile and run `bun install --frozen-lockfile` for bun; materialise
  `node_modules` for node. The caller states *what*, mcpx decides *how*, and the
  comparison table above stops being the user's problem.
- **Lockfiles get honoured rather than reinvented.** The user asks for
  `package.lock` support; the right reading is "if a lockfile is present next to
  the manifest, use it and do not resolve" — `bun install --frozen-lockfile`,
  `npm ci`, `deno.lock`. mcpx never writes one into somebody's project
  uninvited.

**"Baked into binary"** deserves its own note because it has three real
meanings and they are not equivalent:

1. *Vendored cache* — the Nix derivation prefetches a fixed dependency set into
   a store path and mcpx points `DENO_DIR`/`BUN_INSTALL`/`NODE_PATH` at it. Pure,
   offline, reproducible, and the natural fit for this repo: `package.nix`
   already wraps the binary with `PATH` additions for exactly this kind of
   reason. Recommended reading of the bullet.
2. *Embedded source* — `go:embed` a small standard library of `.ts` helpers into
   the binary and write it into the exec workdir. Cheap, no network ever, but
   only viable for first-party code.
3. *Self-contained executable* — `deno compile` a script and its graph into one
   binary. Real, and interesting for shipping a *recipe* as a command, but it is
   a distribution feature rather than a dependency-configuration one.

Only (1) and (2) belong in this issue; (3) is worth a line in the comparison
doc.

`.jsonc` is asked for explicitly: `deno.json` is JSONC already, `package.json`
is not and npm will not read comments. If mcpx accepts `package.jsonc` it must
strip comments and write plain JSON before any package manager sees it.

## Open questions

- Precedence: does an explicit `--package` *replace* the project manifest or
  merge with it? Merging invites two versions of one package; replacing
  surprises someone in a project directory. A conflict that is reported rather
  than silently resolved is likely right, matching #5's rule for config chains.
- Does mcpx ever run an installer itself, or only ever point the runtime at
  something already prepared? Running one means network, timeouts and a lock on
  a shared directory inside what is meant to be a fast exec path.
- Where does a prepared dependency directory live — under the content-addressed
  exec workdir (pruned by count by `pruneWorkDirs`, `internal/runner/runner.go:808`,
  keeping `exec.workDirs: 8`, `internal/defaults/defaults.json:98`) or in its own
  cache with its own retention? `node_modules` is far larger than a generated
  client and the existing pruning policy was not sized for it. **Owned by #187**
  (collision 12); kept here as input. #187's first open question — lean on the
  runtimes' own caches and store only the resolved manifest — is the one this
  issue should answer.
- For the daemon: does `ExecOptions.cwd` imply the daemon may read a manifest at
  that path when it happens to share the filesystem? That is the same
  shared-filesystem question artifacts answered with an explicit
  `capabilities: ["artifacts"]` / `sharedFs` declaration rather than inference —
  the same answer probably applies.
- Does `deps` need to reach `mcpx api --spec` adapters and launcher placeholder
  files, or is it strictly a script-execution concern?

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** L — five sources, three runtimes, and a cache key · **Impact** high;
without it a script cannot use a library, which is most of what scripts do.

**Depends on / related**: #187 (owns the cache mechanism, #181 collision 12),
#5 (`paths.config` chain and its two-pass rule, the model for precedence here),
#40 (closed, fixed in #57 — ExecOptions, which `deps` extends), #7 (launcher
placeholders, same settings machinery), #78 (daemon state/cache correctness —
a prepared dependency directory is new cached state), and siblings #100
(runtime selection), #101 (comparison doc), #104 (automatic imports; fills in
the set), #105 (Python parity; PEP 723) and #107 (flake environments; a
Nix-vendored set). `docs/proposals.md` "Modules and libraries" (`:295`) is
subsumed by this.

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

body:
# id(directory_mail): SmtpSink's reply reader has no total deadline and no line bound — a trickling or never-terminating relay reply hangs the directory request forever and buffers without limit

## Evidence (verified this run, main `d2cb60fe`)

`pkgs/id/src/directory_mail.rs`:

- `:115` `RELAY_TIMEOUT = 10s` is applied at `:164-165` as the socket **read/write timeouts** — per-read inactivity timeouts, not a deadline for a reply or for the exchange.
- `:233-252` `expect(reader, code)` loops on `read_line` (`:238`): every line whose first 3 chars parse to the expected code and whose 4th byte is `-` continues the loop. There is **no cap on the number of continuation lines, no cap on one line's length, and no overall deadline**. `read_line` buffers a whole line before `expect` can inspect any of it.
- The caller awaits the send: `pkgs/id/src/world_session/mod.rs:108` runs `sink.send(&mail)` in `spawn_blocking` and `.await`s it before the directory action returns, so a hung reply hangs the directory request (and permanently occupies a blocking-pool thread per attempt).

This is the sibling of #1788 (CommandSink has no timeout at all). #1788's framing called SmtpSink "10s-bounded" — it is only inactivity-bounded, as the probe shows.

## Probe (laptop, verbatim logic)

Probe crate `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-smtpexpect/` (laptop): `expect()` copied verbatim from `directory_mail.rs` at main `d2cb60fe` (file sha256 `dc6f7935…`, identical on laptop and sandbox), same 10s socket timeouts, fake relays on loopback:

- CONTROL: ordinary multiline reply (`250-fake` / `250 OK`) → `Ok(())` in ~0.3 ms.
- TRICKLE: relay sends a valid `250-…` continuation line every 2 s forever → **expect still blocked after 25 s**; the 10s timeout never fires because every read completes in-window.
- GIANT: relay sends `250-` then floods bytes with no CRLF → **expect still blocked after the relay sent up to 32 MiB**; `read_line` keeps buffering the unterminated line without limit.

## Why it matters

The relay is loopback and operator-chosen, but it is still a separate process that can be buggy, wedged, or compromised — and the failure mode is the worst kind: not an error, but a directory request (e.g. an email-code sign-in) that never returns, plus unbounded memory growth in the server for the giant-line case. A stalled local SMTP daemon or a misbehaving spam-filter milter in front of it turns into a silent sign-in outage.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A reply (and/or the whole `send`) has a total deadline: a relay that keeps every read in-window but never finishes a reply causes `send` to fail with a clear timeout error in bounded time.
- [ ] One reply line's buffered length is capped (a named constant); a line past the cap fails the send instead of buffering without limit.
- [ ] The number of continuation lines per reply is capped, or the deadline demonstrably bounds them.
- [ ] Regression tests with a fake relay: trickling continuation lines time out; an over-long line is refused; the existing plain/multiline/dot-stuffing tests still pass.
- [ ] The fix states the chosen bounds where `RELAY_TIMEOUT` is defined, so the "10s" a reader sees is the bound that actually applies.

## Acceptance criteria
- SmtpSink's reply reader has a total deadline and a maximum line length; a trickling or never-terminating relay reply fails the directory request with a bounded error instead of hanging it.
- A regression test drives a slow/never-terminating reply and asserts the request completes (with an error) inside the bound; existing directory_mail tests stay green in CI.

## Purpose

Level 2: "a more normal set of docs". A new user who stops here should have everything they need and never feel the
compendium was withheld. Every item in the notes gets its own page or its own anchored section.

## Original notes

> - documentation
>   - make a book using whatever is the most common and simple modern choice
>     - 3 main things, not book sections jsut like levels of detail-
>       - the 'ok i just installed this thing what even is it' layer
>         - basically a more normal set of docs
>         - new person might assume this is all there is and wont be upset
>         - a page or section in a page for

(The 30 items, lines 53-82, are quoted verbatim in #146's page map and again in the child that writes each.)

## Children

- [ ] #146 mcpx docs: level-2 page map, and the configuration, modes and transport pages
- [ ] #147 mcpx docs: interface pages -- abstract and client interfaces, CLI, MCP, binary, script, /v1 and the SDKs
- [ ] #148 mcpx docs: plugin pages -- plugins, compatibility, interface and config, opencode v1 and v2, vibeMcp
- [ ] #149 mcpx docs: the FAQ, in the notes' own voice

## Proposed order

1. #146's page map first (ten grouped pages, a fixed anchor per item), then its configuration/modes/transport pages.
2. #147 and #148 in parallel; both embed filtered slices of the generated reference (#96) rather than only linking.
3. #149 FAQ, and the examples gallery it proposes (scripts CI runs).

## Ease and impact

| # | Title | Kind | Ease | Impact |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| #146 | page map + config, modes, transport | design, docs | M | high |
| #147 | interface pages | docs | M | high |
| #148 | plugin pages | docs | S-M | med |
| #149 | FAQ | docs | S (gallery M) | med-high |

## Warnings

- "plugin" means two things: a harness plugin (the opencode one) and an extension of mcpx (#80). #148 always qualifies it.
- "vibeMcp" appears nowhere; its meaning is #148's first open question.
- "/v1 sdk" does not exist beyond the plugin's DaemonClient; #147 recommends documenting generation from
  `/v1/openapi.json`. Three OpenAPI documents exist and describe different things (#159).
- The server block key is `mcpServers`, not `servers`.
- Four corrections every child must carry (checked at `05c78b2`). (1) The shipped binary is not static, by choice; `CGO_ENABLED=0`
  builds a static one (#147, #136). (2) The opencode plugin never *needs* the binary; it spawns `mcpx --json status` only
  as discovery rung 4 (#148). (3) `MCPX_SESSION` is a live variable the generated client reads, distinct from the
  plugin's `MCPX_SESSION_ID`; nothing is renamed (#159 item 13, struck). (4) The undeclared `MCPX_*` count is #172's
  (44), not "about 49" (#146).

## Related

#96 (generated reference), #5, #44 (closed, fixed in #53), #47, #48, #76, #77, #80, #83 (anything as MCP -- a vibeMcp
candidate), #101 (docs/runtimes.md, from the runtimes theme -- a level-2 page), #102, #136 (static-binary policy, for
`binary#binary`), #159, #172 (the env-var page's source).

## Ease · Impact · Related

See the table above; related issues listed above.

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

- The level-2 pages named in this issue exist, are linked from the level-1 layer, and match the daemon's actual behaviour at current main.
- A reader who installed mcpx five minutes ago can answer 'what is this and what do I do next' from these pages alone.

body:
## Bug

`parse_iso_timestamp` in `pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs` (lines 196-197 at main `d2cb60fe`) collects date/time components with `filter_map(|p| p.parse().ok())`. Any component that fails to parse is **silently dropped** instead of failing the parse, so a malformed timestamp with an extra non-numeric segment still parses — as long as exactly three numeric components remain on each side of the `T`. The dropped segment simply disappears, and the surviving numbers are interpreted as a complete, valid timestamp.

```rust
let date_parts: Vec<u64> = parts[0].split('-').filter_map(|p| p.parse().ok()).collect();
let time_parts: Vec<u64> = parts[1].split(':').filter_map(|p| p.parse().ok()).collect();
```

This is the hole left by the #756 fix: that fix range-checked the components that survive, but never made the parse strict about components that don't.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Verbatim copy of `parse_iso_timestamp` + `is_leap_year` + the `classify_tag` auto branch, compiled and run on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-isoparse/`, source = main `d2cb60fe`):

```
control valid            -> Some(1773297750)
2026-03-12-junkT06:42:30Z            -> Some(1773297750)
2026-03-12T06:42:xx:30Z              -> Some(1773297750)
2026-03-12T06:xx:42:30Z              -> Some(1773297750)
junk-2026-03-12T06:42:30Z            -> Some(1773297750)
2026-13-01T00:00:00Z                 -> None
MALFORMED_EQUALS_CONTROL=true
```

Four different malformed strings all return **exactly** the control timestamp for `2026-03-12T06:42:30Z`. Note the in-tree tests themselves rely on the drop: `test_parse_iso_timestamp_valid` / `test_parse_iso_timestamp_epoch` pass `"auto-2026-03-12T…"` (with the `auto-` prefix still attached) directly to `parse_iso_timestamp` and expect `Some` — that only works because the `auto` segment is silently discarded.

## Impact

`parse_iso_timestamp`'s only caller is `classify_tag` (routes.rs:155-164), which decides whether a file named `auto-…` is a generated auto-backup (`FileKind::Auto`, sorted by timestamp out of the primary list, rendered with the auto badge) or an ordinary primary file. #809 established that an ordinary file that merely starts with `auto-` must stay Primary. The drop defeats that for a plausible ordinary filename:

```
classify auto-2026-03-12-draftT06:42:30       -> (Auto, Some(1773297750))
classify auto-2026-03-12T06:42:30.015Z        -> (Auto, Some(1773297750))
classify auto-notes.txt                       -> (Primary, None)
```

A user's own file named e.g. `auto-2026-03-12-draftT06:42:30` is rendered and sorted as a system auto-backup with a fabricated timestamp, indistinguishable from a real generated backup of that instant.

## Acceptance criteria

- `parse_iso_timestamp` rejects any input whose date or time side has a component that does not parse as a number, or has more/fewer than exactly three `-` / `:` separated components (no silent drops). The malformed cases above all return `None`; the #756 out-of-range cases stay `None`.
- Legitimate generated names keep working: `2026-03-12T06:42:30.015Z`, `2026-03-12T06:42:30Z`, leap day `2024-02-29T00:00:00Z` → `Some(1709164800)`, epoch → `Some(0)`.
- The in-tree tests that pass an `auto-`-prefixed string straight to `parse_iso_timestamp` are corrected to pass the bare timestamp (the prefix is `classify_tag`'s job), or the function's contract is explicitly changed and documented — the current accidental reliance on the drop is removed either way.
- Regression tests: extra date segment, garbage time segment (both positions), and garbage prefix segment all return `None`; `classify_tag("auto-2026-03-12-draftT06:42:30")` is `(Primary, None)` while a real generated auto-backup name still classifies `Auto`.

Relocated from dezren39/nix#974 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): legacy Porkbun DNS Terraform project — Drew's Porkbun configuration lives in developing-today/code (infra), so the validation project belongs beside it. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

## Validate the legacy DNS Terraform project (Porkbun bulk changes)

There is a Terraform project from a couple of years ago that manages DNS for Drew's Porkbun domains, built for mass/bulk changes. Its current state is unknown: it may or may not still match reality, and bulk-apply tooling that has drifted is dangerous.

### Work (read-only validation — NO apply without Drew's explicit go-ahead)

1. Locate the project (repo, state backend, where state lives) and identify which domains/zones it manages, including which Porkbun account they sit in.
2. `terraform validate` and a read-only `terraform plan` against current state; report whether it plans cleanly.
3. Diff the project's declared records against live Porkbun DNS for the managed zones; report drift (records changed outside Terraform, records in Terraform that no longer exist, zones/domains moved or lapsed).
4. Assess the state file itself: age, backend health, provider version pins, whether the Porkbun provider credentials it expects still exist (note the second Porkbun account's API access is a separate open item — see the account-connection campaign).
5. Also check: the project's YAML DNS config — confirm whether it is embedded in the fleet's semantic index; per Drew, configs of this class should qualify for embeddings. Report its embedding status and file the gap if it is missing.

### Done when

A written verdict exists: safe to keep using for bulk changes as-is / safe after listed repairs / retire it — with the drift report attached. No DNS changes are made by this issue.


## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The legacy Porkbun DNS Terraform project is located (repo, state backend, state location) and the domains/zones it manages are listed, including which Porkbun account they sit in.
- [ ] `terraform validate` and a read-only `terraform plan` are run and reported — NO apply or DNS change is made under this issue.
- [ ] A drift report compares the project's declared records against live Porkbun DNS for the managed zones (out-of-Terraform changes, stale records, moved/lapsed zones).
- [ ] The state file is assessed: age, backend health, provider version pins, and whether the Porkbun provider credentials it expects still exist.
- [ ] The project's YAML DNS config embedding status in the fleet semantic index is reported, and the gap is filed if it is missing.
- [ ] A written verdict is posted: safe as-is / safe after listed repairs / retire it.

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#1024 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): backup design epic for the same jobs as #976/#1026; follows their home. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

## Summary

`modules/laptop-backups.nix` is the laptop's backup system of record (its header, citing #976 and developing-today/code#1516): two daily jobs, `pm-dashboard-backup` (local tar.zst + R2 + Drive, each leg sha256-verified) and `repo-archive-backup` (restic). The machinery works — but a run's success signal does not mean a complete, verified archive exists, and the fleet has now found that six times in the nine days since the dashboard script landed (PR #977):

- #981 — journal cursor advanced on a failed offsite leg (closed)
- #982 — a run's own retention sweep pruned the archive it had just built (closed)
- #989 — unvalidated DATE argument wrote outside the backup root (closed)
- #1010 — a second EXIT trap silently discarded FAILED logging (closed)
- #1021 — `prune_remote` swallows a failed remote listing: retention silently stops, full success reported (open)
- #1023 — dataset copies unchecked and the manifest generated **from whatever staged**, so a dropped file is invisible to the script's own verify chain; incomplete archive exits 0 (open)

Three structural causes, all on current main `23551fd`:

1. **The manifest is descriptive, not normative** — `modules/pm-dashboard-backup.sh:172-193` builds it by walking the staging tree; verification (`:196-219`) checks the archive against that same list. Nothing states what a complete backup *contains*.
2. **Failure accounting is per-step and ad hoc** — some steps `|| fail`, some tolerate deliberately (journal placeholder, optional-file WARN), some swallow by accident (`|| true` at `:242`, unchecked `cp -a` at `:147,150,152,156`). Every new step re-decides whether its failure counts.
3. **Success leaves no durable record** — stdout/journal lines and the journal-window cursor are all a run leaves. #976 (2026-10-27) verified neither timer had ever fired and asked for a freshness check; there is still no artefact such a check could read, and no restore of either job has ever been recorded.

This design is the contract those six issues point at, in five rules:

1. **Expected-set manifest** — each job declares its expected members (required vs optional) in one place; the manifest records expected vs present vs missing per member; verification compares the archive against the *expected* set, so a missing required member fails the run before upload, and a missing optional member is recorded in the manifest, not just a WARN.
2. **One failure ledger per run** — every step's outcome lands in a single ledger; exit status and the success line derive from it at the end. A step is non-fatal only when named as tolerated; an undeclared swallow is a defect.
3. **A durable run record** — one JSON record per run at a fixed path outside every prune scope: job, date, result, failing steps, archive sha256, per-destination results. Written on complete *and* failed exits.
4. **A freshness watchdog** — a third unit beside the jobs reads the run records + both timers' last-trigger times and exits non-zero naming the job when the last *complete* run is older than a threshold option. It fixes nothing; it makes a stopped backup named, per #976's acceptance.
5. **The contract is the adoption unit for #976 coverage** — new datasets join by declaring expected members + destinations under this contract, never as another script with a private notion of success.

## Phased breakdown

1. **Phase 1 — the open instances land** → the existing **#1023** and **#1021** (linked as sub-issues below; #1021 already in progress, #1023 already enqueued). Their regression suites are the seed of the contract's test coverage. No new issue for this phase.
2. **Phase 2 — expected-set manifest for pm-dashboard-backup** → new sub-issue filed with this design (enqueued): declared required/optional member list; manifest gains expected-vs-present; verify fails on a missing required member; stubbed-harness regression cases for deleted-required (run fails, nothing uploaded) and missing-optional (run completes, manifest records it).
3. **Phase 3 — run record + freshness watchdog** → new sub-issue filed with this design (enqueued): rule-3 record on every exit path; `laptop-backups-watchdog` service+timer + threshold option in `modules/laptop-backups.nix`; watchdog test suite in the repo's established style wired as a flake check. The repo-archive side is covered via timer-firing only — its script and restic credentials live outside this repo (stated honestly in the design doc).

Alternatives considered and why they lose, the full risk analysis (expected-set drift, watchdog false alarms vs `Persistent = true` catch-up, run-record placement per #982's lesson), and the open questions (scheduled restore drills; whether the repo-archive script is vendored into the repo; eventual restic migration; off-machine alerting; the missing ROADMAP backup row) are in the design doc — they stay questions, not issues, until answered.

## Links

- Design doc: `files/designs/nix-laptop-backup-completion-contract.md` in the fleet goal workspace (`keep-the-four-repos-healthy`), registered in `files/potential-projects.md`
- Coverage parent: #976 (this design supplies its "freshness check exists" acceptance mechanism)
- Phase 1 vehicles: #1023, #1021 (sub-issues)
- Phases 2–3: sub-issues filed with this design
- Non-goals: no change to dataset membership, destinations, 30-day retention, or schedule; no opencode-db script changes (#659's territory); no credential-handling change; no external monitoring service

🤖 **Agent note** · state: filed
- **Agent:** repo-design-architect job
- **Session / ID:** repo-design-architect cron run 2026-10-28 08:33 CDT (split rotation: opencode / openchamber / nix; nix's first pass)
- **Found via:** design pass over ROADMAP.md, TODO.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, planning/, docs/ (incl. the 2026-10-19 reliability review), and the open issue list; #976, #1021, #1023 read in full; code evidence verified against the local clone on current main `23551fd`
- **Task:** Design issue — the contract above is the deliverable; phase 1 lands as #1023/#1021, phases 2–3 as their own sub-issues, all enqueued to repo-health-nix-pilot
- **Expectation:** effort/l across the three phases; this issue closes when all sub-issues land or are explicitly retired
<!-- agent-note:v1 agent=repo-design-architect state=filed at=2026-10-28T13:33:00Z -->

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Phase 1 lands: #1023 and #1021 close with their filed acceptance met.
- [ ] Phase 2 lands: a pm-dashboard-backup run with a required dataset member missing or uncopyable fails before any upload, and the manifest of a completed run records every expected member as present or explicitly missing.
- [ ] Phase 3 lands: every pm-dashboard-backup run — complete or failed — leaves a JSON run record, and the watchdog exits non-zero naming the job when the last complete run exceeds the threshold.
- [ ] No run of either laptop-backups job can print/report full success while a declared-required step failed undeclared.
- [ ] This issue closes only when all sub-issues have landed or been explicitly retired.

title: mcpx docs: interface pages -- abstract and client interfaces, CLI, MCP, binary, script, /v1 and the SDKs

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#147 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #94

## Summary

This issue covers the level-2 pages for every way into mcpx: the abstract interface (one ops table behind every surface), client interfaces, the CLI (overview, arguments, commands), MCP (overview, SDK, compatibility), the binary, scripts, `/v1`, and a `/v1` SDK. Anchors are in #146's page map: `interfaces#…`, `cli#…`, `mcp#…`, `binary#binary`, `scripts#script`, `http-api#…`.

Four facts found while reading the code change what these pages can promise:

1. `Commands()` is not every command. Seven dispatched commands are missing, including the only MCP stdio entry point.
2. mcpx publishes three different OpenAPI documents, and one of them describes a server that was removed.
3. "Global flags from the settings registry" is not how flags work. Registry flags are bound per command.
4. `docs/dependencies.md` says mcpx has one Go library, but `go.mod` lists five.

Details are in "Current state".

## Original notes

Source-notes lines 1, 2, 7, 49-52 (parents) and 60-71 (this issue). The lines in between are quoted in sibling issues.

> - documentation
>   - make a book using whatever is the most common and simple modern choice
>     - 3 main things, not book sections jsut like levels of detail-
>       - the 'ok i just installed this thing what even is it' layer
>         - basically a more normal set of docs
>         - new person might assume this is all there is and wont be upset
>         - a page or section in a page for
>           - abstract interfaces
>           - client interfaces
>           - cli
>           - cli arguments
>           - cli commands
>           - mcp
>           - mcp sdk
>           - mcp compatibility
>           - binary
>           - script
>           - /v1
>           - /v1 sdk

## Current state (what mcpx does today, with file refs)

Paths are relative to `pkgs/mcpx/` on `main` (`d0b7e01`); re-checked at `05c78b2` in the 2026-09-30 issues pass, and drifted line numbers re-cited.

### Finding 1: `Commands()` omits seven dispatched commands

`internal/cli/manual.go` says "Commands is every subcommand mcpx has", and describes each command once "so that help, the man page and the command table cannot disagree about what exists". `Commands()` has 32 entries: run exec scripts recipes prompt diagnose ls catalog types search call client status daemons refresh restart stop daemon config settings servers init schema elicit doctor prompts resources tui explore log stats help.

The dispatch map in `cmd/mcpx/main.go:119-161` also routes **`serve`, `api`, `registry`, `adapter`, `openapi`, `man`, `completion`**, and the alias `logs`. `mcpx help`, the man page and shell completions (`internal/cli/completion.go` reads `Commands()`) all leave them out. Current docs already rely on them:

- `docs/protocol.md` §5: `mcpx serve --transport stdio`
- `docs/configuration.md` "Servers": `mcpx registry add`
- `OPENCODE-V2.md`: `mcpx api --spec`

A "cli commands" page generated from `Commands()` would silently omit the only way an MCP host can spawn mcpx.

**Prerequisite, outside docs:** add the seven commands to `Commands()`, plus a test that the dispatch keys equal the `Commands()` names plus their aliases. Routed as #159 item 1 (still open at `05c78b2`). This issue does not implement it.

(The inventory in the docs worker notes says "35 commands" but lists these same 32 names.)

### Finding 2: three OpenAPI documents, and the docs must never confuse them

| document | produced by | describes | state |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /v1/openapi.json` | `api.OpenAPI` (`internal/api/openapi.go:8-17`), from the ops table | the **daemon API** (`/v1/*`) | correct; the source for `http-api#v1` |
| `mcpx schema --format openapi` | `CmdSchema` (`internal/cli/publish.go`) | **the tools** of your MCP servers, as operations for a client generator | correct; a different subject |
| `mcpx openapi` | `cli.OpenAPI` (`internal/cli/openapi.go:14-100`) | `/mcp`, `/health`, `/openapi.json`, `/v1/tools/*`, with server `http://127.0.0.1:8787` labelled "mcpx serve --transport http" | **stale**: `docs/protocol.md` §5 says that separate server was removed, `/health` became `/v1/health` and `/openapi.json` became `/v1/openapi.json` |

The comment at `internal/api/openapi.go:15-17` also still refers to "`mcpx serve --http` ... at /openapi.json".

**Recommendation:** point `mcpx openapi` at `api.OpenAPI`. Then the docs build can produce the `/v1` spec with no daemon running, and the CLI name means what a reader assumes. Until then, the pages name each document explicitly.

### Finding 3: flags come in two kinds

- **Hand-parsed global flags**, before the subcommand (`cmd/mcpx/main.go:61-104`): `--json`, `--tui`, `--profile <a,b>`, `--skip-default`, `--all-profiles`, `--config <file>`, `--version`/`-v`, `--help`/`-h`.
- **Registry flags, bound per command.** `parseFlags` calls `BindFlags(fs, cmd)`, which calls `sch.Bind(fs, cmd)` over `ForCommand(cmd)` (`internal/cli/root.go:52-67`, `internal/settings/bind.go:69-88`). A command only accepts the settings it reads. Plumbing flags are marked `[plumbing]` rather than hidden.

The generated "cli arguments" page therefore has two parts: the global list, and a per-command flag list. It is not one global table.

### Finding 4: the binary's dependencies

`docs/dependencies.md` says "Go libraries: **One.** `modernc.org/sqlite`". `go.mod:5-11` also requires `bubbletea`, `bubbles`, `lipgloss` and `yaml.v3`. story.md "The browser › The dependency" records the TUI libraries: 1.2 MB, taking the stripped binary from 11.2 to 12.4 MB. The binary page must use `go.mod`, not that sentence.

### Other facts the pages use

- **One ops table.** `internal/api/ops*.go` declares 60 operations (60 `Method:` entries across `ops.go`, `ops_consumer.go`, `ops_exec.go`, `ops_proto.go`, `ops_resolve.go`, `ops_settings.go`). From it come the `mcpx_<op>` MCP tools and `/v1/openapi.json`. Routes are *not* generated: they are registered by hand with `mux.HandleFunc` (e.g. `internal/daemon/ops.go:28-38`), and `internal/api/parity_test.go:21` reads them out of the daemon source with a regex and checks them against the table. `parity_test.go` enforces three of the four parity columns this way, and the plugin column is not enforced (`docs/parity.md`).
- **No MCP SDK.** mcpx is built on none: `go.mod` has no MCP module. The MCP client (`internal/mcpclient`), the server (`internal/mcpserver`) and the JSON-RPC framing are its own code. `docs/dependencies.md` says so.
- **Protocol revisions.** mcpx serves `2025-03-26`, `2025-06-18`, `2025-11-25` and `2026-07-28`. Upstream it speaks `2025-11-25` by default (`docs/protocol.md` §1). The matrix lives as data in `internal/mcpserver/revisions.go` and is served by `GET /v1/protocol`: "the document defers to the endpoint". There is no CLI command for it (#76).
- **The `/v1` SDK today** is the plugin's `DaemonClient` (`plugin/opencode/mcpx/daemon.ts:338`): generic `raw`/`get`/`text`/`post`/`postRaw`/`putRaw` plus 22 typed methods (`status`, `exec`, `call`, `logQuery`, `tasks`, `putSetting`, ...), and `connect()` for discovery. It is not published as a package.
- **Bare invocation.** A first argument that looks like a file (`.ts`, `.js`, `.mts`, `.mjs`, or an existing file) or like source code runs without `run`/`exec` (`cmd/mcpx/main.go:25-50`, `:164-179`). Bare `mcpx` opens the TUI, or prints help when there is no terminal.

## Content per item

### `interfaces#abstract-interfaces`

Explain the design in one diagram: one declaration (`Op` in `internal/api/ops.go`) produces the `mcpx_<op>` MCP tool and the OpenAPI entry, and a test holds the hand-registered `/v1` route to it (the diagram must not show the route as generated). The CLI and the plugin sit on top of `/v1`. Quote the parity claim word for word: "Everything the CLI can do can be done from a plugin, can be done over `/v1`, can be done from MCP." Then state honestly what enforces it (`parity_test.go`, three of four columns) and what does not (the plugin column, and the CLI gaps in #76). The parity table is generated (#144). This page is the map. The other interface pages are the territory.

### `interfaces#client-interfaces`

Every way code can drive mcpx, with one runnable snippet each:

| client interface | for | reference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| generated TypeScript client: `tools.<ns>.<fn>(args)`; globals `tools`, `log`, `emit`; namespaces as bare identifiers in `exec`; `import tools from "./mcpx-client.ts"`; in-script `search()` / `describe()` | scripts | `AGENTS.md` "Scripts"; `mcpx client [-o file] [--ns a,b]` prints it; `mcpx types` shows signatures |
| the CLI | people, shells, CI | `cli#cli` |
| `mcpx call <ns>.<tool> [json]` | one call, no JS runtime needed | `docs/dependencies.md` "External programs" |
| `DaemonClient` / `connect()` | harness plugins, and any Bun/TypeScript program | `plugin/opencode/README.md` "Talking to the daemon directly" |
| any MCP client, through `/mcp` or `mcpx serve --transport stdio` | MCP hosts | `mcp#mcp` |
| raw HTTP on `/v1` | curl, other languages | `http-api#v1` |

### `cli#cli`

- The loop: `ls`, then `search`, then `types`, then `run`/`exec` (`AGENTS.md` "The loop").
- `--json` for machines; never parse human output.
- Exit codes worth knowing: 75 (`EX_TEMPFAIL`) when a call is waiting on an elicitation (`manual.go`, `elicit` Detail); 2 for an unknown command or a settings conflict (`cmd/mcpx/main.go`).
- Bare invocation and runnable-first-argument behaviour.
- The man page (`mcpx man`, installed by `package.nix` to `share/man/man1/mcpx.1`) and shell completions (`mcpx completion bash|zsh|fish`). Both commands are dispatched but not in `Commands()` (Finding 1).

### `cli#cli-arguments`

Generated (#144), in two parts (Finding 3): the global flags, then each command's registry flags with their aliases (`--runtime` for `--script-runtime`, and so on). Short prose around the tables covers:

- the precedence chain, linking `configuration#common-config`;
- the fact that two different spellings of one setting on one command line is an error (`bind.go` `ApplyTo`);
- the fact that derived names are published as-is (`--daemon-lease-t-t-l`).

### `cli#cli-commands`

Generated from `Commands()`, grouped as `help` groups them (running, discovery, daemon, configuration, inspection). Each command gets its usage, detail and examples. **Blocked on Finding 1's prerequisite.** Without it, the page leaves out `serve`, `api`, `registry`, `adapter`, `openapi`, `man` and `completion`.

### `mcp#mcp`

- **mcpx as an MCP client** of every configured server: four revisions, two eras; the server-initiated requests it answers (sampling passthrough, the elicitation broker, roots; `docs/protocol.md` §4).
- **mcpx as an MCP server:** `/mcp` and stdio, the small tool surface and why (story.md "mcpx speaks MCP"), and `subscriptions/listen`.

Link `modes#server-modes` and `modes#transport-options` rather than repeating them.

### `mcp#mcp-sdk`

The item is ambiguous. The page answers the first two readings and routes the third:

1. **Which MCP SDK mcpx uses:** none, and why (dependencies stay small; the client, server and framing are about one package each). One paragraph.
2. **Using mcpx from an MCP SDK:** any official SDK client (TypeScript, Python, Go, etc.) connects to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/mcp`, or spawns `mcpx serve --transport stdio`. Include one tested snippet using the official TypeScript SDK client.
3. **An SDK mcpx provides for writing servers or extensions:** does not exist. Link the extensibility issues #80 and #83.

### `mcp#mcp-compatibility`

- The revision matrix, generated from `internal/mcpserver/revisions.go` rather than copied from `docs/protocol.md` §1, since the document itself says it defers to the code. #144 decides the mechanism.
- The "accept liberally, send conservatively" rule in two sentences.
- The known gaps from `docs/protocol.md` §6, linked to #77.
- A second table for host compatibility: which MCP hosts have actually been pointed at mcpx. None are recorded today (open question 3).

### `binary#binary`

- One Go binary. Every dependency is pure Go (the SQLite driver is `modernc.org/sqlite`), so `CGO_ENABLED=0` builds a fully static binary. #182 verified one: a 21 MB linux/arm64 ELF, "statically linked". The **shipped** artifacts are not static, by choice. The nix package uses the nixpkgs cgo default and is wrapped with a `PATH` suffix, and the Containerfile keeps `CGO_ENABLED=1`. Whether to ship static is a policy question owned by #136: pure-Go `os/user` reads `/etc/passwd` rather than NSS/LDAP, and the pure-Go resolver bypasses NSS modules -- on Linux only; on macOS `CGO_ENABLED=0` changes nothing, since Go 1.20 uses the system resolver and user database there without cgo. The page states what is shipped, not what is possible, and never says `os/user` or `net` prevent a static build.
- Size, from story.md figures, or measured at release (#158).
- External programs, from the `docs/dependencies.md` table: `git` for the `repo`/`worktree` scopes (`git rev-parse`, `internal/config/scope.go:152-159`; GIT's in-flight native resolution may remove this dependency, so re-check when it merges); `deno`/`bun`/`node` for `run`/`exec` only (`call`, `ls`, `types`, `catalog` and `search` work without one); the configured servers.
- The Nix wrapper appends `git`, `deno`, `bun-bin` and `nodejs` to `PATH` (`--suffix`, `package.nix:96-104`), so a runtime already on the user's `PATH` wins.
- A container image: `pkgs/mcpx/Containerfile` (added in #182; `docs/container.md`). It is Debian bookworm-slim, ships bun, and sets `MCPX_SCRIPT_RUNTIME=bun`. The page links `docs/container.md` rather than restating it, because GIT is still changing the container.
- The version is hard-coded at `0.1.0` (`package.nix:19`, `:61`; `cmd/mcpx/main.go:18`). Release and install channels belong to #158. This page only states what the binary needs.

### `scripts#script`

The page a script writer lives on:

- **The contract** (`AGENTS.md` "Script contract"; story.md "The script contract"): stdout is the result, stderr is diagnostics; a default export is the entry point; `--export <name>` spreads arguments; `emit()` streams; `log.info("…{x}", {x})`; `--json` gives one envelope.
- **Named scripts:** `.mcpx/scripts/<name>.ts`, searched upward, then `~/.config/mcpx/scripts/`, nearest wins; `mcpx scripts` lists them and marks shadowed ones.
- **Results:** unwrapped values, `.raw` for the envelope, `ToolError` on `isError`.
- **Runtimes:** deno, then bun, then node (`script.runtime`, `--runtime`). Node runs only erasable TypeScript: an `enum` fails. `--typecheck` / `script.typecheck` runs `deno check` and only applies on Deno. Link #79.
- **Authority:** scripts run with the user's full permissions; link `faq#is-it-safe` (#149).
- **Where a script runs:** `exec.where`, linking `modes#client-modes`.
- **Checking before running:** `mcpx diagnose`, and the automatic preflight (`diagnose.preflight`).
- **Recipes** (`// @param`), and pointers onward to the launcher and placeholders (#7), artifacts (`docs/exec.md`, #40) and `mcpx prompt`.

### `http-api#v1`

- Rendered from `/v1/openapi.json` (#144), ideally produced without a daemon (Finding 2's recommendation).
- Prose around it covers: how to reach the API (`curl --unix-socket <sock> http://mcpx/v1/health`, or the TCP port); the `X-Mcpx-Settings` header for call-scoped settings; `GET /v1/events` as SSE with `?since=N`; which operations are admin (`Op.Admin`); request body limits (`http.*`).
- Link #76 for operations that exist here and in MCP but have no CLI command.

### `http-api#v1-sdk`

There is no `/v1` SDK beyond the plugin's unpublished `DaemonClient`.

**Approaches:**

- **A (least recommended): hand-written SDKs per language, shipped by mcpx.** Each one is a second copy of the ops table that drifts. That is the exact failure `internal/api/ops.go`'s header comment exists to prevent. It also carries release and packaging cost per language before there is one outside user.
- **B (middle): publish `DaemonClient` as the TypeScript SDK.** It already exists, is tested (`daemon.test.ts`) and knows the discovery ladder, which no generated client will. But it is Bun-first (`fetch(url, {unix})`), only 22 of the 60 operations have typed methods, and its natural home is the harness-free core in #48, not a general SDK. Worth doing as part of #48, not as the answer to this item.
- **C (recommended): document generation from `/v1/openapi.json` with standard tools, and test it.** Name the tools: `openapi-typescript` + `openapi-fetch`, `openapi-generator`, `oapi-codegen` for Go, `openapi-python-client`. Show the one mcpx-specific step: most generated clients assume a TCP base URL, so use `daemon.port` or `MCPX_ENDPOINT`, or a transport that can dial a unix socket. A CI job generates one client and compiles it against the current spec, so the promise cannot rot (docs checks; see the testing trackers under #91 (CI pipeline #95, integration/environments #97)). It adds no new code to maintain, works for every language at once, and stays correct because the spec is generated. Mention `DaemonClient` (B) as the option for harness plugins.

Warning for the page: `mcpx schema --format openapi` describes **tools**, while `/v1/openapi.json` describes the **daemon**. A reader who feeds the wrong one to a generator gets a working client for the wrong thing. Say so in a callout.

## Open questions

1. **Finding 1 prerequisite:** add the seven commands to `Commands()` with a dispatch-parity test? Some of them (`openapi`, `adapter`) may be meant as plumbing. Then `Command` needs a `Plumbing`/hidden group, not an omission.
2. **Finding 2:** repoint `mcpx openapi` to the daemon spec, or remove it in favour of `mcpx schema` plus `/v1/openapi.json`?
3. **Host compatibility:** which MCP hosts should the compatibility page claim, and should each claim be backed by a CI smoke test?
4. **"mcp sdk":** does the notes' item mean any of the three readings above, or something else?
5. **Script arguments:** `AGENTS.md` says run arguments "arrive in `Deno.args`". The scripts page needs the rule for bun and node. Is `Deno.args` shimmed on those runtimes, or does a default export's `main(args)` cover it?

Docs checks run in CI; see the testing trackers under #91 (CI pipeline #95, integration/environments #97).

## Ease · Impact · Related

title: id(serve): group churn warning is blind to re-add cycles that complete between evaluations — the watcher compares net device sets every 60s, so a revoke+re-add inside one interval counts as zero

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`id(serve)`: the group churn warning (P4.9, #799) cannot see a device re-add that completes between two warning evaluations. Serve re-evaluates group warnings every 60 s, and the watcher derives re-adds by comparing the *net* authorized-device set at consecutive evaluations — so a revoke + re-add cycle that starts and finishes inside one interval leaves the evaluated set unchanged, counts as zero re-adds, and is lost forever, even though the group log the watcher re-reads on every pass contains both events.

A burst of re-adds is exactly the signal the warning exists for ("each re-add is a compromise recovery, so check the devices", `groups/warnings.rs`). Four cycles straddling evaluations warn; the same four cycles inside a single minute never warn — and a process cycling a device faster than once a minute can churn indefinitely without ever reaching the threshold of 4.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `3675a470`)

- `pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:1191,1228` — the spawned task re-evaluates on `GROUP_WARNING_INTERVAL = 60s`.
- `serve.rs:1266-1292` (`GroupWarningWatcher::evaluate`): a device counts as re-added only if it is in the current `group_active_devices` set, was **not** in the previous evaluation's set (`devices`), and **was** in `seen_devices`. Two evaluations that see the same set therefore record nothing, whatever happened in between. The intermediate states are available — `evaluate_group_warnings` (`serve.rs:1315`) re-opens and re-folds the whole group log on every pass — but the watcher only ever receives the final `Projection`.
- `pkgs/id/src/groups/warnings.rs:39,139-148` — the evaluator itself is sound: it warns at `CHURN_THRESHOLD = 4` re-adds in the 24 h window. It is starved of input, not wrong.
- The shipped test pins only the visible shape: `serve_group_warnings_fire_on_device_readd_churn` (`serve.rs:1598`) calls `evaluate_group_warnings` after **every** revoke and **every** re-add, so each cycle straddles an evaluation by construction. No test performs two log writes between evaluations.
- Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-churninterval/` (faithful transcription of the `serve.rs:1270-1292` counting block + the `warnings.rs` window/threshold rule; `serve.rs` sha256 `1fc3be8d…`, `warnings.rs` sha256 `f05bf215…` at main `3675a470`):
  - CONTROL (4 cycles straddling evaluations): `counted=4 churn_fires=true`.
  - **BUG (the identical 4 revoke+re-add cycles completed between two evaluations): `counted=0 churn_fires=false`** — the same group-log event history produces no warning.
  - A single intra-interval cycle also counts 0.

## Why it matters

The churn warning is a security signal: a device re-add is the N8 compromise-recovery path, and a burst is supposed to make an operator look. The current sampling makes the signal depend on the phase alignment between the burst and a 60 s poll, and the fastest churn — a loop or an attacker cycling a device many times a minute — is the shape most reliably missed. The warning shipped in #799 / PR #1805 today; this is its detection blind spot, not a new feature request.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A revoke + re-add cycle that completes between two warning evaluations is counted as a re-add (e.g. the watcher tracks progress through the group log / fold instead of comparing only net device sets, or evaluates on log change rather than only on the 60 s poll) — one mechanism, pinned by tests.
- [ ] Regression test at the watcher level: four revoke+re-add cycles written to the group log with **no** evaluation in between, then one evaluation, produce the churn warning (readds = 4); the existing straddling-cycles test keeps passing unchanged.
- [ ] Re-add timestamps: cycles recovered from the log are stamped no later than the evaluation that finds them and still age out of the 24 h window; the once-per-burst / re-arm behaviour of `groups/warnings.rs` is unchanged.
- [ ] Size warnings and the startup evaluation pass are unchanged; existing id crate tests still pass (laptop or CI).

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for group-warning/churn/evaluator terms. #799 (closed) is the feature request this implementation satisfied (merged as PR #1805 on current main); it does not cover the intra-interval blind spot. No other filing names the watcher's set-comparison derivation.

body:
# proxy-relay: RELAY_TARGET_PORTS silently drops invalid entries and reinterprets non-literals — a typo'd target list starts a healthy relay with the wrong targets

## Evidence (verified this run, main `3675a470`)

`bin/proxy-relay.mjs:44-52` parses the target list with a forgiving filter, unlike every other port in the same file:

```js
const TARGET_PORTS = (process.env.RELAY_TARGET_PORTS || '')
  .split(',')
  .map((s) => Number(s.trim()))
  .filter((n) => Number.isInteger(n) && n >= 1 && n <= 65535);
if (TARGET_PORTS.length === 0) { /* only the all-invalid case errors */ }
```

- The listen and tunnel ports in the **same file** go through the strict `parseProxyPort` from `bin/proxy-port.mjs` (:39, :58), whose header (#483) spells out why: a bare numeric coercion must fail at startup naming the variable and its value, never silently reinterpret or drop. The target list — the one that decides where traffic actually goes — is the only port input exempt from that rule.
- A non-empty remainder masks the mistake completely: the relay starts, `/health` answers `ok`, and `endpoint.json` is published, all with a target set smaller (or different) from the one the operator configured.

### Probe (laptop, verbatim parser)

Probe dir: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-relayports/` — `proxy-relay.mjs` copied byte-identical to main (sha256 `2ed8aa8dded4f041abb4157d662f5e918b7efdabeadfebe5c57236f07e6edf16`), the `TARGET_PORTS` expression extracted verbatim and run with `node probe.mjs`:

| input | result |
|---|---|
| `18745,19745` (control) | `[18745, 19745]` |
| `18745,19745junk` | `[18745]` — typo'd target silently gone |
| `18745,99999` | `[18745]` — out-of-range target silently gone |
| `18745,19745.9` | `[18745]` — fractional target silently gone |
| `1e4` | `[10000]` — scientific notation silently reinterpreted as a port |
| `0x4a39` | `[19001]` — hex silently reinterpreted as a port |
| `18745,,19745` | `[18745, 19745]` — empty segment silently gone |

No case throws, warns, or names the variable/value.

## Why it matters

This relay is the sandbox's only path to the laptop fleet proxies, and its whole configuration surface is these env vars. A single typo in one target (`19745junk`, a transposed digit making `99999`, a pasted hex/scientific value) does not fail the service — it degrades it silently: the relay reports healthy, the supervisor is satisfied, and connections to the missing target fail later, elsewhere, looking like a backend outage — the exact failure shape #483's strict parsing was built to eliminate for the other ports. Partial validity is the dangerous case; the all-invalid case already errors today.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every comma segment of `RELAY_TARGET_PORTS` is validated with the strict rule from `bin/proxy-port.mjs` (exactly an integer 1–65535, decimal digits only — e.g. via `parseProxyPortValue` per segment, or an equivalent strict helper): any invalid segment exits at startup naming `RELAY_TARGET_PORTS` and the offending value.
- [ ] Empty segments (`18745,,19745`, a trailing comma) get one pinned behaviour — refused at startup or explicitly documented as ignored — and a test pins whichever is chosen.
- [ ] The all-invalid / unset cases keep failing at startup as they do today.
- [ ] Tests in a new or existing `bin/proxy-relay.test.mjs` (or the parser's test file): the control list parses unchanged; each invalid class above (junk suffix, out of range, fractional, `1e4`, `0x…`) refuses; valid multi-target order is preserved (preferred-target order matters at :161).
- [ ] No behaviour change for valid lists: listen/proxy port handling and the `/health` + forwarding paths are untouched.

body:
## Phase 2 of #1834 — sampling message + result validation at the broker

Design: #1834 (mcpx sampling trust boundary). Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-sampling-trust-boundary.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Origin: dezren39/nix#256.

### Problem

Sampling messages and results are relayed without validation, in either direction. `sampleViaBroker` (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/hooks.go`) unmarshals only `maxTokens`/`systemPrompt` from a request — the `messages` array is never inspected, so tool-result messages holding non-`tool_result` content, or a `tool_result` whose id no earlier `tool_use` issued, pass through untouched (compare register SMP-06). On return the only checks are JSON-object / not-null, after which a missing `role`/`model` is *silently filled in* (`result["role"] = "assistant"`, `result["model"] = "unknown"`) and the result is never checked against its request: `stopReason: "toolUse"` or `tool_use` content against a tools-less request, and era-wrong content shapes (2025-11-25 made message content single-or-array; earlier eras single only — SMP-05), all relayed as-is. Gaps: `sampling-both-validate-message-content` (client + server rows) in `pkgs/mcpx/internal/conformance/coverage_clientfeatures.go`.

### Scope — one validator at the broker choke point

One validation helper used by `sampleViaBroker` (the point legacy wire requests and modern `input_required` answers both converge on); do not copy checks into mcpclient/mcpserver separately.

- **Request side, on open** (before a broker question is opened): `messages` decode as sampling messages for the upstream's era — content single block before 2025-11-25, single-or-array from 2025-11-25; tool-result messages hold *only* `tool_result` blocks; every `tool_result` id pairs with a `tool_use` in the preceding messages. Violations raise the typed `-32602` from Phase 1 back to the upstream immediately — a malformed request must not consume an answerer's attention.
- **Result side, on answer**: the result must carry `role` and `model` and era-legal content; `stopReason: "toolUse"` / `tool_use` content blocks are valid only when the request carried `tools` — against a tools-less request, `-32602`. Where the answer arrived through the broker, refuse it at the answer step with the question left open (the pattern the existing null-answer refusal in `internal/elicit/elicit.go` established); where discovered after acceptance, refuse upstream with `-32602`.
- **Remove the silent `role`/`model` fill-in.** It manufactures fields the answerer never supplied and hides exactly the malformation validation exists to catch. This behaviour change is deliberate and must be visible in the PR description.
- Model-hint mismatch is NOT a failure: model preferences are expressly ignorable, so a result naming a different model than the hint asked for passes.

Out of scope: declaring any new sampling sub-capability (that is #1753's ground), rate limits (nix#257), CLI rendering (Phase 3), a genuine pre-delivery staging hold (open question on #1834).

### Open seam for triage (recorded on the design)

Validation needs the upstream's negotiated era at the broker, which today receives params, not era. Settle where era comes from (the client connection that raised the question knows it). If it cannot be threaded without new plumbing, the recorded fallback is the permissive union (single-or-array accepted in all eras) with the era-strict half stated on this issue — do not silently shrink the scope.

Equally: this phase is independent of Phase 1 in code, but raises Phase 1's typed `-32602`; if Phase 1 has not landed, carry the error type with this phase (triage settles the seam — not a hard gate).

### Tests (defining)

- Well-formed exchange in each era relays byte-identical (control case, both eras).
- Tool-result message mixed with text content → `-32602`, no broker question opened.
- `tool_result` with an unpaired id → `-32602`, no question opened.
- Result missing `role` or `model` → refused (question left open on the broker path); no fill-in occurs.
- Result with `tool_use` content / `stopReason: "toolUse"` against a tools-less request → `-32602`; the same result against a tools-carrying request passes.
- Result naming a model different from the request's hint → passes.

<!-- agent-note:v1 agent=design-architect state=filed at=2026-10-28T21:34:31Z -->

## Acceptance criteria

- The validator lives in one place and is exercised from `sampleViaBroker` in both directions; no duplicated checks in mcpclient/mcpserver.
- Request violations are refused with `-32602` before a broker question opens; result violations never reach the upstream; the `role`/`model` fill-in is removed and the removal is called out in the PR.
- Gaps `sampling-both-validate-message-content` (both rows) are retired.
- The era-source question is settled on this issue (threaded era, or the recorded union fallback with reasons).

title: id(web/collab): a client's cursor name is broadcast verbatim — no length cap and no control-character filtering on the frame path, and identity sanitize_name does not remove control characters either

body:
## Problem

A collaborative-editing client's cursor name is broadcast to every other client in the document with **no sanitization at any layer** — no length cap and no control-character filtering — and the one name path that does sanitize (`IdentityStore`) only trims and truncates, so control characters pass there too.

Two ingest paths feed the same cursor labels:

1. **The cursor frame itself (any connected client, no identity needed).** `CollabMessage::Cursor` carries `name: Option<String>` (`pkgs/id/src/web/collab.rs:441-455`, decoded at `:557-575` with no constraint on the string). In the socket handler (`:1054-1111`), when the connection has no verified identity name cached, the client-supplied frame name is used verbatim: `let effective_name = cached_display_name.clone().or(name);` (`:1075`). It is stored in the document's cursor table (`:1088-1102`), broadcast to all clients (`:1104-1111`), and replayed to every later joiner in the existing-cursor snapshot (`:820-845`).
2. **The identity path.** `IdentityStore::register` / `update_name` run the name through `sanitize_name` (`pkgs/id/src/web/identity.rs:181`, `:257`), but that function (`:412-427`) only trims and truncates to 64 **bytes** — it does not remove control characters, so a registered name containing `\n`, `\t`, ESC or U+202E is stored, persisted, and pushed into cursors via `CollabState::update_client_name` (`collab.rs:378-415`) unchanged.

Contrast with the codebase's own rules for every other display name:

- `crate::world::sanitize_display_name` (`pkgs/id/src/world/util.rs:69-76`) filters out control characters and caps at 48 chars.
- `directory::clean_name` and `petname::normalize_name` refuse control characters outright.
- The world WebSocket sets a message-size bound (`web/world_ws.rs:279`, `ws.max_message_size(MAX_FRAME_BYTES)`); the collab upgrade sets none (`web/collab.rs:626-642`, route at `web/routes.rs:301`), so a cursor frame's name is bounded only by the framework default, not by any name rule.

## Verified this run (2026-10-28, HEAD 528886eb)

Probe tests added (uncommitted) in a laptop worktree of `origin/main` and run with `cargo test --features web probe_lane_b`:

- `CollabMessage::Cursor` with name `"Alice\nFORGED\u{1b}[31m"` + 100,000 `x` characters encodes and `decode()`s back **byte-for-byte verbatim** (probe prints `PROBE cursor name verbatim: len=100017 has_newline=true has_esc=true`; both probe tests pass, 2 passed / 0 failed).
- `sanitize_name(Some("Alice\nFORGED\t\u{1b}[31m\u{202e}Bob"))` returns the string with the newline, ESC and U+202E **all still present** (probe asserts each survives).

The handler/storage/broadcast steps between decode and the other clients' screens are the verbatim assignments cited above; the frontend renders the name with `textContent` (`pkgs/id/web/src/cursors.ts:362`, `:441`), so this is not an HTML-injection hole — it is a display-integrity and amplification hole: forged multi-line cursor labels, ANSI/bidi control bytes in every peer's tooltip and cursor bar, and a multi-hundred-KB "name" re-broadcast on every cursor move and replayed in full to every new joiner.

## Why it matters

Cursor presence is how collaborators tell who is who in a shared document. One client — including a guest with no identity at all — can impersonate/confuse with a name that spans lines, embeds terminal escapes, or reverses text direction, and can make every cursor update and every join snapshot carry an arbitrarily large name payload. Every other name-like input in this codebase is bounded and stripped of control characters at ingest; the collab cursor name is the unguarded exception, on both of its paths.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A cursor name arriving in a `Cursor` frame is sanitized before it is stored, broadcast, or replayed: control characters (per `char::is_control`, and the ruling states whether format characters/Cf are also handled) removed or the frame's name refused, and a length cap in the same class as the existing name rules (48 chars world display names / 64 identity names — triage pins one) enforced.
- [ ] `sanitize_name` in `web/identity.rs` removes control characters too, so the identity path and the frame path cannot diverge; names that are ordinary text (spaces, Unicode letters) are unchanged.
- [ ] The collab WebSocket upgrade gets an explicit message-size bound comparable to the world socket's, or triage records why the framework default is the ruling.
- [ ] Regression tests: a `Cursor` frame whose name carries `\n`/`\t`/ESC (and one far over the cap) is stored/broadcast in sanitized form (or refused) at the handler or codec level; `sanitize_name` tests cover control characters, not only trim/truncate.
- [ ] Existing id web tests still pass (laptop or CI).

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for "collab cursor name", "cursor name sanitize" and related terms on 2026-10-28: #1783 is the collab codec's CursorRemove decode tag, #1790 is cursor presence UX (tooltip modes/pin/lifecycle logging), #331/#765/#778/#780 are cursor DOM recycling — none covers sanitizing or bounding the cursor **name** on either ingest path. #1778 covers Cf characters in directory account/group names (a different surface); #1613 covers peer-announcement names in CLI TSV output (different transport and fix surface).
