body:
## Origin

Design follow-up to #802. Drew's ruling (2026-10-28) reopens P8.1 as a proof of concept (branch A), scoped by the direction below. This issue settles the exact mechanics Drew flagged as 'need to get worked out' before the PoC is built.

## Owner direction (condensed from Drew's 2026-10-28 ruling)

- **Order stays the backbone.** For ~99% of the system's mechanics — merges, code sharing — causal/order validity is all that matters. Provable time must NOT become the backbone of merges; server-side cooperation just uses order.
- **Provable time is still required** for apps that need it — above all multiplayer / no-trust or limited-trust situations with winners and losers.
- **Witness = time oracle.** A witness service records each second: the time plus a value signed with its own secret key — a stream of signed ticks. Every id server could run one, but primarily they would all use the same one: a central witness we operate. Third parties are the product here — almost everyone would use our central/secondary witness servers.
- **Before/after proofs from ticks:** an event carrying a recent witness tick proves it occurred at-or-after that tick; submitting a record to a witness that countersigns it proves it occurred at-or-before that countersigning. Witnesses act as the 'before or current' anchor.
- **Witnesses are graph participants.** Direction of travel is a mostly graph-based model, not just a DAG. A witness can act on a message — judge it valid, sign it, and emit that as its own message in the graph. Candidate checkpoint record: a hash over the concatenation of all graph tips a message contains (to be evaluated, not pre-decided).
- **Untrusted ordering:** in no-trust settings, ordering aids like the bubble-merge concept or a coordinator who determines arrival order; a coordinator can also supply time, or a party can obtain a witnessed 'occurred before T' record for itself.
- **Modes:** timekeeping/witness capability is built into the core app — a dedicated witness-only mode, or witness functions switched on alongside other functions via a flag; if running in server mode it could simply be on. Made available for all operations but only USED by apps that need it.
- **P2P option:** a peer group can run its own witness cluster and accept answers marked valid by a quorum/consensus of its nodes instead of depending on our central server. Their Sybil / Byzantine-generals exposure is their problem; a blockchain is explicitly another day (non-goal here).

## This issue must settle

- Tick format and chaining (per-second signed records; how a tick commits to history; clock-source expectations).
- The two proof constructions (not-before via embedded recent tick; not-after via witness countersignature) and their exact verification rules.
- Witness-as-participant: the witness message type, what 'valid' attests, and whether/how the tip-set hash checkpoint works.
- Modes and flags in the core app (witness-only mode; timekeeping flag; server-mode default).
- Quorum model for P2P witness clusters (threshold semantics; what a client accepts).
- Trust assumptions stated plainly for each deployment shape (central witness vs own cluster).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A design document in `doc/` answering every point above, updating (not replacing) `task-09-time-and-witnesses.md`, with remaining open questions listed explicitly for the owner.
- [ ] The PoC issue (linked from #802) is scoped from the accepted design.

---

## Problem

Set up an Oracle OCI account and automate running the **technical maximum of the Always Free tier** — free, geo-dispersed capacity alongside the home cluster. Drew believes the free tier is more than the headline 2 instances; verify the current terms before building anything.

Source: [idea register 2026-10-20](https://github.com/dezren39/hatch-personal/blob/main/workspace/goals/stand-up-lab-cluster-talm-talos-cozystack-postgres-rustfs/files/idea-register-2026-10-20.md) (goal `stand-up-lab-cluster-talm-talos-cozystack-postgres-rustfs`).

## What we believe (verify all of it)

- Always Free includes **2 × AMD E2.1.Micro** instances.

Relocated from dezren39/nix#505 on 2026-10-28 - it was filed in the wrong repo; developing-today/code is its home. Original content follows, verbatim.

---

## Problem

**Bandwidth is the scarce resource, not compute.** The basement fleet has very fast CPUs, ≥3 TB RAM and ~200 TB of disks at near-zero marginal cost — behind exactly **2 Gbps symmetric** of home fiber. Design the egress strategy before anything popular lands on this cluster.

Source: [idea register 2026-10-20](https://github.com/dezren39/hatch-personal/blob/main/workspace/goals/stand-up-lab-cluster-talm-talos-cozystack-postgres-rustfs/files/idea-register-2026-10-20.md) (goal `stand-up-lab-cluster-talm-talos-cozystack-postgres-rustfs`).

## What we know

- One fiber provider (Brightspeed) in his part of Osseo: 2 Gbps up/down. A second line = 4 Gbps total — still small at scale. Cable offers 100 Mbps, more expensive (possible redundancy pickup). TriCounty Communications fiber may reach his part of Osseo → then buy both fibers.
- Hotspot plans and Starlink investigated for emergency backup; Starlink would likely need a business plan for this use.
- Strategy direction (Drew): "tunnel most or much of that to Cloudflare or Turso or anywhere we connect with Tailscale" — shunt bulk traffic to SaaS with cheap or **free egress** (e.g. Cloudflare R2's zero-egress pricing, CF cache/tunnels), compress aggressively, and only cross the home link with what must.
- Budget guardrails: Turso $5 plan and Cloudflare $5 Workers plan in play; free tiers preferred; a $25–$30 Cloudflare plan is possible; **$75 is out**.

## Acceptance / first steps

- [ ] Classify the app's traffic: what can be cached at the edge (CDN), what can live on free-egress object storage (R2), what genuinely must be served from home.
- [ ] Design the tunnel topology: cloudflared from the cluster, Tailscale links, Turso edge replicas — with per-path egress costs written down.
- [ ] Compression plan per traffic class (static assets, API payloads, media) and the CPU cost of doing it on the Threadrippers (plenty available).
- [ ] Failure/redundancy matrix: fiber cut, cable fallback (100 Mbps — what degrades, in what order), Starlink/hotspot emergency tier.
- [ ] Output: a one-page egress budget model — expected GB/month per class vs the ~2 Gbps link and each SaaS allowance — kept current in the subscription/usage ledger.

## Open questions

- Is TriCounty fiber actually available at the address? (Needs an address check.)
- Which SaaS egress allowances are we already paying for but not using (ties into the cloud ideation ledger)?

## Acceptance criteria

- An egress design is recorded on this issue (or a linked design doc/PR) covering which traffic classes go via Cloudflare / Turso / Tailscale / direct, and why.
- The design states the bandwidth budget against the 2 Gbps symmetric constraint and what happens when it is exceeded.
- Follow-up implementation issues are filed and linked for any build work the design calls for.

The cluster must be bootstrapped with TALM (cozystack/talm) — turn on bare machines running Talos, connect them, and TALM harvests each node's actual hardware into named per-node configs that we keep in git. Drew got this working locally with a couple of containers, barely; the full bare-metal flow is unproven. Hard constraints: everything bootstrappable/declarative, **no HashiCorp anything**.

## What we know

- Target: 3–5 machines (chosen by the hardware-inventory issue) as the first Talos/Cozystack nodes.
- Host OS approach: Talos's small, **frozen read-only host image** on each machine's NVMe boot drive; the rest of the NVMe is for minor logs and wear-leveling headroom across consumer SSDs (best: 990 Pro).
- Per-node drives differ (SSD models/sizes vary; HDD counts vary) — the per-node config harvest is presumably the answer; document exactly how disks get matched/named per node.

- [ ] Document the frozen read-only host-image layout (OS partition vs logs/wear space) for our NVMe boot drives.
- [ ] Write the runbook: adding a node, replacing a disk, wiping/rebuilding a node from config only.

## Open questions

- How are non-identical system disks handled if a boot NVMe dies and is replaced with a different model/size?
- Where do the harvested per-node configs live — this repo, or a dedicated cluster-config repo?

body:
# laptop-autocommit: no merge/cherry-pick-in-progress guard — the every-minute sweep finalizes a live merge (or cherry-pick) as an "autocommit:" commit and pushes it

## Evidence

`nixos/home/laptop-autocommit.sh` (29 lines, sha256 `e58fea91…` on main `e91098f1`) is run **every minute** per repo by the timers in `nixos/home/laptop-autocommit.nix` (`OnCalendar = "*-*-* *:*:00"`, repos: `~/.openclaw`, `~/hatch`, `~/hatch-personal`).

Its only in-progress guard is the index lock:

- `:11` — `[ -e "$d/.git/index.lock" ] && exit 0` — the *only* busy check.
- `:14-15` — it then requires only that the current branch is the default branch. During a merge or cherry-pick on `main`, the branch **is** `main`.
- `:16-22` — `git add -u`, and if the index differs, a bare `git commit -q -m "autocommit: …"`.
- `:24-28` — the result is then **pushed to `origin <default-branch>`**.

There is no check for `MERGE_HEAD`, `CHERRY_PICK_HEAD`, `REVERT_HEAD`, `rebase-merge`/`rebase-apply`, or `.git/sequencer` anywhere in the script. The sibling keeper script learned exactly this lesson in #1771 and now guards on all of them (`nixos/home/laptop-repo-keeper.sh:65`, using the absolute git dir since a worktree's `.git` is a file). The autocommit script, added the same day (#1723), never got the guard.

### Probe (laptop, verbatim script from the laptop primary clone, sha-identical to main)

Probe dir: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-autocommit/` (throwaway repos with a local bare origin):

- **Control** — ordinary tracked change on `main`, no operation in progress: committed as `autocommit: …` and pushed. PASS (intended behaviour).
- **Merge in progress** — conflicting merge of `feature` into `main` started (`MERGE_HEAD` present), conflict resolved and staged by hand, **not yet committed** (no `index.lock` at that moment): one run of the script produced a **two-parent merge commit** with subject `autocommit: merge1 2026-10-28 15:26`, cleared `MERGE_HEAD`, and **pushed it to `origin main`** (`ls-remote` = the new merge HEAD). The user's unfinished merge — which they might still have wanted to test, amend, or abort with `git merge --abort` — was finalized and published within a minute of staging the resolution.
- **Cherry-pick in progress** — conflicting cherry-pick stopped (`CHERRY_PICK_HEAD` present), conflict resolved and staged: one run committed it as `autocommit: cp1 …` (the picked commit's own subject/message lost), cleared `CHERRY_PICK_HEAD`, and pushed it.

## Why it matters

The repos this sweeps are personal working repos where merges and cherry-picks on the default branch are routine. Any conflict resolution that takes more than a minute while staged — i.e. essentially all of them, since the timer fires every 60 s — is silently committed under a meaningless `autocommit:` message and pushed to origin, with no chance to abort, squash, write a real message, or run a check first. For a merge, `--abort` becomes impossible once pushed; recovering means a revert or a history rewrite of a published branch.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `laptop-autocommit.sh` exits 0 without staging, committing, or pushing when a merge, cherry-pick, revert, or rebase is in progress in the target repo (state detected via the **absolute** git dir, per the #1771 keeper fix — a worktree's `.git` is a file, and `.git` may also be a submodule pointer).
- [ ] The sequencer state (`.git/sequencer`, e.g. a multi-commit cherry-pick/revert sequence paused between picks) is also treated as busy, or the issue's triage comment explicitly pins why the per-operation HEAD files suffice.
- [ ] A test (shell test beside the script, in the style of `nixos/home/openclaw-backup.test.sh`) covers: merge-in-progress → no commit, `MERGE_HEAD` intact; cherry-pick-in-progress → no commit; ordinary tracked change → still committed and pushed (control).
- [ ] No behaviour change for the clean-tree, detached-HEAD, off-default-branch, and index-locked cases.

Related: #1771 (same guard, keeper), #1751 (sibling sweep script committing more than its mandate — different script, different mechanism).

title: id(web/identity): a future-dated token never expires — decode_token's age check is one-sided (saturating_sub), unlike the envelope and signed-request windows

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage

body:
## Bug

`pkgs/id/src/web/identity.rs` — the identity token's 30-day expiry check is one-sided, so a **future-dated token never expires until 30 days after its future date arrives**:

- `pkgs/id/src/web/identity.rs:65` — `TOKEN_MAX_AGE_SECS = 30 * 24 * 60 * 60`.
- `pkgs/id/src/web/identity.rs:381`, in `decode_token` (after the Ed25519 signature verifies):

```rust
if now.saturating_sub(payload.created_at) > TOKEN_MAX_AGE_SECS {
    return None;
}
```

`created_at` is a `u64` seconds timestamp set at issuance (`register`, :188; refresh, :235). When `created_at > now`, `saturating_sub` yields 0, the check passes, and it keeps passing for the entire future offset plus another 30 days. There is no future-date / skew refusal anywhere in `decode_token`, `verify_token` (:222), `verify_and_refresh` (:232) or `verify_token_client_id` (:245).

The crate's other time-window checks are two-sided, which makes this the odd one out:

- Directory envelopes refuse the future explicitly: `envelope.at <= now.saturating_add(ENVELOPE_SKEW_MS)` (5 min), "envelope is dated in the future" (`pkgs/id/src/directory.rs:303`, `:1234-1237`), before the same-shaped TTL check at `:1239`.
- Signed directory requests use `signed.at.abs_diff(now) <= SIGNED_WINDOW_MS` (`pkgs/id/src/directory_auth.rs:327`).

Tokens are minted only by the server, so the trigger is a server clock fault: the clock runs ahead at registration or refresh (NTP step, VM time sync, manual set), is later corrected, and every token minted in that window gains the full skew as extra lifetime — minutes in the common case, unbounded in the worst case. A token's stated 30-day maximum age is therefore not a bound.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-tokenfuture/probe.mjs`: the exact predicate from :381 with Rust `u64` saturating-sub semantics, `TOKEN_MAX_AGE_SECS` from :65:

```text
control old token (31d ago): expired=true
control fresh token: expired=false
future token (+10y): expired=false
future token (+10y) checked 5y later: expired=false
future token (+10y) expires only at created+30d: expired=true
BUG CONFIRMED: a future-dated token is never expired until 30d AFTER its future date
```

Line trace on main `e91098f1` confirms the predicate is the only age check on all three verify paths, and no caller re-checks `created_at`.

## Why it matters

The web identity token is the credential for the web UI and WebSocket auth (`verify_token_client_id`). Its 30-day cap is the only lifetime bound — identities themselves are kept indefinitely (see #1766). A clock incident at issuance silently stretches that cap by the size of the incident for every affected token, with no log or signal; the two sibling protocols in the same crate both treat a future date as a refusal, so this reads as an oversight, not a policy.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `decode_token` refuses a token dated implausibly in the future: `created_at` more than a pinned skew allowance (small — minutes, on the scale of the envelope's 5-minute `ENVELOPE_SKEW_MS`, or a justified value) ahead of `now` is rejected.
- [ ] Regression tests alongside `test_token_expiry` (identity.rs:~1054): a token dated past the skew allowance is refused; a token dated within it is accepted; the existing 30-day expiry test keeps passing.
- [ ] Existing identity tests pass (laptop or CI).

Found by new-issue-creator-code-b. Dedup: `gh issue list --search 'identity token future OR created_at OR TOKEN_MAX_AGE'` (open + closed) and the open-issue list on 2026-10-28 show no token-expiry filing; #1766 covers identity retention, not token lifetime.

body:
## Problem

On 2026-10-28 the `treefmt check` job in `nix-ci.yml` became the fleet's dominant false-red: of the last 28 completed `nix-ci` runs sampled 19:12Z (17 success / 8 failure / 3 cancelled), **all 8 failures are the `treefmt check` job** — including runs on `main` pushes (e.g. run 40744776742 @ 18:24Z, run 40748461479 @ 18:48Z) — while `Nix flake evaluation` passed throughout.

Worse, PR runs fail for files outside the PR's diff: PR #1731 (diff = `pkgs/id/web/src/navigation.ts` + test only, per `gh pr diff`) failed treefmt with 13 flagged files, all unrelated: `nixos/home/laptop-autocommit.nix`, `nixos/home/laptop-backups.nix`, `nixos/home/*.sh`, `.github/workflows/flake-inputs-update.yml` (job 122995015603 log). A later failed job (123028438014) flags `nixos/home/laptop-repo-keeper.sh`. The flagged set looks like files that landed on main unformatted (laptop-autocommit family) being swept into other branches' changed-file computations — the job diffs `$base_sha...$GITHUB_SHA` (nix-ci.yml:51), so the base/head semantics for `pull_request` merge commits vs moved main need checking.

## Impact

Every PR's nix-ci verdict is currently unreliable; queue workers park merge-ready PRs (tasks 1841/#1578 today, plus at least PRs in runs 40741007599, 40741900122, 40743077092, 40744747559, 40747684674) and burn shifts re-diagnosing the same red.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Root cause identified: why files outside a PR's three-dot diff are format-checked (or, if the files are simply unformatted on main, why main pushes pass the pre-merge gate)
- [ ] The currently-flagged files on main are formatted (or the check's changed-file set is corrected), and `nix-ci` on main is green again
- [ ] A PR whose diff touches none of the flagged files shows a green `treefmt check`

Found by queue task 1076's investigation of #774 (Lane B shift, 2026-10-28) — related but distinct: #774 is Magic Nix Cache 418s, which were NOT observed in today's sample.

body:
## Design: fast PR tier, full main tier, self-healing main

Design doc: `files/designs/ci-fast-pr-full-main.md` in the repo-health
goal workspace
(`~/workspace/goals/keep-the-four-repos-healthy/files/designs/ci-fast-pr-full-main.md`).
Directive: Drew, 2026-10-28. Capacity tracker: #1599.

### Summary

CI execution is already fast — the fleet's pain is GitHub runner
**queue wait** (2026-10-28 evidence in the doc and on #1599: 127+
runs queued at once; a 27-job `id` run waited 16–105m per job for
0.4–13.8m of execution; opencode `test` e2e jobs waited 65–76m for
0.1m of execution). The fix is structural, in three phases:

1. **Phase 1 — cancel-in-progress everywhere it is missing**
   (Drew-approved outright). Standard pattern: ref-keyed group +
   `cancel-in-progress: true`; main runs keyed by run_id, never
   cancelled. Audit gaps are enumerated in the doc §2.2
   (openchamber nix-eval/release/vscode-extension, opencode
   publish*, openchamber pr-review, code goreleaser). jules.yml is
   deliberately untouched (#304).
2. **Phase 2 — PR tier slimming.** PRs get basic validation only:
   changed-path lint/format, syntax/typecheck of affected packages,
   affected-package unit tests. Full matrices (flake check, e2e,
   cross-platform builds, conformance, benches) move to main. The
   dividing line is an explicit path-glob **change-class policy**
   (doc §3.3, classes 0–4) that is tuned over time using the
   main-breakage rate — not pipeline rewrites.
3. **Phase 3 — main tier + remediation chain.** One watched
   main-gate workflow per repo runs ALL checks on merge to main. On
   failure: breakage issue filed under the pattern (Breakage-ID
   dedupe, `main-broken` + `priority/critical` labels) → Jules
   first via the existing `jules` label trigger (budgeted: free
   tier 15/day, 3 concurrent) → on Jules failure/timeout, release
   to a **priority-90 Muse fix packet**, dedupe
   `repo-health:v1:fix:<repo>:main-breakage:<id>`. Ownership is
   singular and visible at all times (exactly one of the `jules`
   label or a live queue task holds the breakage; every transition
   is an agent-note:v1), so the orchestrator never double-assigns
   and dropped items are recovered by the monitor's existing
   claim-evaporation/dead-in-queue repairs.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Design reviewed; phase issues (filed alongside this one) are
      the implementation path.
- [ ] The change-class policy table (doc §3.3) is adopted as the
      tuning surface for PR-tier scope.
- [ ] Rollout order Phase 1 → 2 → 3 is followed; each phase lands
      via its own queue task and PRs.

### Notes

- Jules today: code's jules.yml has the `jules`-label trigger and a
  `ci-failure-fix` job that explicitly excludes main — Phase 3
  builds on both facts (doc §2.3).
- Releases must not cut from a red main; that gate is a Phase 3
  acceptance item, not part of this design issue.

body:
## Problem

The directory's name and description cleaners in `pkgs/id` promise "must not contain control characters", but the check is `char::is_control` — Unicode category **Cc only**. Category-**Cf** format characters (U+200B ZERO WIDTH SPACE, U+202E RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE, U+2066/U+2069 bidi isolates, U+2060 WORD JOINER, U+FEFF, U+00AD SOFT HYPHEN) pass both cleaners, so an account name, a group name, or a group description can carry invisible or text-reordering characters into every view that displays it. This is the same Cf class as #1674, but a different module, different functions, and a different fix: #1674 is scoped to `petname.rs` (`normalize_name`/`fold`/`skeleton`), and #1770 is scoped to `invite.rs`, which has no check at all. Neither covers the directory — the layer that creates the *alleged* names the petname layer then has to defend viewers against.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `35726e8e`, `src/directory.rs` sha256 `9ef8669c…`, identical on sandbox and laptop clones)

- `clean_name` (`pkgs/id/src/directory.rs:1846-1859`): trim, non-empty, ≤64 chars, then `!name.chars().any(char::is_control)` with error text "name must not contain control characters". Rust's `char::is_control` is general category Cc only.
- `clean_description` (`directory.rs:1861-1875`): same check (allowing `\n`), same gap.
- Call sites: account creation (`insert_account`, `directory.rs:1463`, reached from `sign_up`/`sign_up_keyed` apply paths), group creation (`directory.rs:1588`), group update — both the entry point (`update_group`, `directory.rs:862`) and the journal apply path (`directory.rs:1611`). Because the journal apply path re-cleans, a fix here covers replayed entries too.
- Display surfaces: `directory_view.rs:1609` feeds `account.name` as the `alleged` name into `petname::labels` (the viewer-facing contact labels); `directory_view.rs:1666,1679` render group and member names; `web/explore.rs:399` renders `group.description` through `html_escape`, which neutralises markup but not bidi/format characters.
- Probe (faithful Python mirror of `clean_name`/`clean_description` — Rust `is_control` ≡ category Cc — run on the laptop; probe + log at `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-dircf/`):
  - Control: `Alice<TAB>Admin` name → **REFUSED** (the Cc guard works); LF in a description → accepted, by design.
  - **BUG:** `Alice`+U+200B → ACCEPTED; `Alice`+U+202E+`Admin` → ACCEPTED; `Alice`+U+2066+`Admin`+U+2069 → ACCEPTED; `Owners`+U+2060 → ACCEPTED; U+FEFF+`Alice` → ACCEPTED; `Al`+U+00AD+`ice` → ACCEPTED; description `safe text`+U+202E+`evil` → ACCEPTED. All are category Cf.
  - Plain `Alice Smith` → accepted, unchanged.

## Why it matters

Directory names are self-asserted and shown to other people: account names become the "alleged" half of every contact label, and group names/descriptions are rendered in the directory and web views. An invisible-character account or group name renders identically to a legitimate one (the exact spoof shape the petname module exists to prevent, created here at the source), and a U+202E override in a name or description can reorder the visible text around it. The cleaners' own error messages claim a guarantee they do not deliver.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `clean_name` refuses (or strips, with the choice pinned and documented) Unicode format characters (category Cf) — at minimum U+200B, U+202A–U+202E, U+2060, U+2066–U+2069, U+FEFF, U+00AD — so the "must not contain control characters" promise holds; `clean_description` gets the same rule (keeping its `\n` allowance).
- [ ] Tests in `directory.rs` cover at least: ZWSP in an account/group name, RLO in a name, RLO in a description, and a plain name/description with ordinary spaces and punctuation still accepted.
- [ ] Existing directory tests still pass (laptop or CI).
- [ ] Triage records the layering against #1674 (petname-side) and #1770 (invite-side): whether one shared name-cleaning helper should own the Cf rule for all three, or each module keeps its own check.

## Dedup

Searched open + recently closed issues for Cf / format character / U+200B / `clean_name` terms: only #1674 (petname.rs-scoped), #1770 (invite.rs, no Cc check at all), and closed lab-ops-hub UTS-46 items (#652/#516, different package). No filing covers `directory.rs` `clean_name`/`clean_description`.

title: id(directory_auth): a signed request replays at exactly at+SIGNED_WINDOW_MS — the replay guard evicts the nonce 1 ms before the verifier's window closes

body:
## Problem

A captured signed directory request can be replayed successfully at exactly one instant: `signed.at + SIGNED_WINDOW_MS` (5 minutes after its timestamp). At that millisecond the replay guard has already forgotten the nonce, while the verifier still considers the request inside its time window — so the same signed request is accepted twice.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `9874fe59`)

- `pkgs/id/src/directory_auth.rs:28` — `pub const SIGNED_WINDOW_MS: u64 = 5 * 60 * 1000;`
- Verifier gate (`directory_auth.rs:327`, in `verify_signed`): `let window_ok = signed.at.abs_diff(now) <= SIGNED_WINDOW_MS;` — the boundary instant is **inclusive**: at `now == at + SIGNED_WINDOW_MS` the request is still in-window.
- Replay guard eviction (`directory_auth.rs:249-250`, in `ReplayGuard::accept`): `self.seen.retain(|_, seen_at| *seen_at + SIGNED_WINDOW_MS > now);` — the entry is **exclusive**: at `now == seen_at + SIGNED_WINDOW_MS` the nonce is already evicted. (`seen_at` is the original request's `signed.at`, stored at `directory_auth.rs:266`.)
- `accept` is called only after the signature verifies (`directory_auth.rs:352`), and a replay carries the original valid signature, so nothing else stops the second acceptance.

### Probe (verbatim mirror, run on the laptop)

Mirror of `ReplayGuard::accept` + the `verify_signed` window gate (comparisons and the retain predicate character-exact; `directory_auth.rs` sha256 `fab8803d…` on main `9874fe59`). Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-replay-invite/` (laptop), copy + log in the goal bookkeeping `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-replay-invite/`:

```text
P1 first use at at:             Ok(())
P1 replay at at+WINDOW-1:       Err("request was already used")
P1 replay at at+WINDOW (exact): Ok(())  <-- replay accepted
P1 replay at at+WINDOW+1:       Err("signed request is outside its time window")
```

The controls bracket the bug exactly: refused 1 ms before the boundary (nonce still remembered) and 1 ms after it (window closed), accepted **only** at the boundary millisecond.

## Why it matters

The replay guard is the only thing standing between a captured signed request (method + target + body hash are all in the signed message) and a second execution of it inside its validity window. The window is narrow — one millisecond per captured request — but it is deterministic: an attacker who captured a request knows its `at` exactly and can flood replays around `at + 300000` so one lands on the boundary millisecond on the server's clock. The two boundary conventions (`<=` in the verifier, `>` in the guard) were clearly meant to describe the same interval; they disagree at exactly one point.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] One convention, both places: a signed request is acceptable at a given `now` **iff** its nonce is still remembered at that `now` — e.g. the guard retains while `seen_at + SIGNED_WINDOW_MS >= now`, or the verifier uses `<` — with the choice pinned and commented so the two cannot drift apart again.
- [ ] Regression test in `directory_auth.rs` tests: first use at `at`, replay at `at + SIGNED_WINDOW_MS - 1`, at `at + SIGNED_WINDOW_MS`, and at `at + SIGNED_WINDOW_MS + 1` — only the first use succeeds.
- [ ] Existing `directory_auth` tests still pass (laptop or CI).

body:
## Design: mcpx sub-capability gating — gate on what was actually declared, not on the parent capability

**Design doc:** `files/designs/code-mcpx-subcapability-gating.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace (developing-today/code design architect, pass 9, 2026-10-28).
**Origin:** [dezren39/nix#210](https://github.com/dezren39/nix/issues/210) — capabilities declared to upstreams that nothing answers, and host gates that ignore sub-capabilities. This design scopes only its remainder (audit below); no Drew direction decision is needed — nix#210's acceptance is explicit and the spec dictates which end errors and which end degrades.

### Problem

Since 2025-11-25, capabilities have sub-capabilities: `sampling.tools` gates tool use inside sampling, `sampling.context` gates `includeContext`, `elicitation.form`/`elicitation.url` gate the two elicitation modes. mcpx still keeps only the parent-level promise, verified on main `f6760a69`:

1. **Client side enforces elicitation modes but not sampling shapes.** `Client.answer` (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/mcpclient/modern.go` ~L277-296) refuses an undeclared elicitation mode with `-32602` — but the adjacent `sampling/createMessage` case has no shape check. mcpx declares `sampling` as a bare `{}` (`capabilities()` ~L85-87: no `tools`, no `context`), yet a request carrying `tools`/`toolChoice` or `includeContext` reaches the handler untouched. Gap: `sampling-client-error-on-tools-without-capability`.
2. **Server side gates sampling on presence only.** `Peer.CanSample` (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/mcpserver/conn.go` ~L251-252) is `Declared("sampling")`. `Question.Sendable` therefore offers any sampling question to any host that declared the parent, and `Question.paramsFor` shapes elicitation params per era but passes sampling params verbatim. Gaps: `sampling-server-no-tools-without-capability`, `sampling-server-includecontext-only-with-context-capability`.
3. **The elicitation form gate has the same shape.** `Peer.CanElicit` (~L232-249) special-cases `url` but returns `true` for form against any elicitation declaration — including a 2025-11-25+ host that declared only `{"url": {}}`, which cannot render a form. Register row CAP-08: "`{}` means form only"; the gate ignores a url-only declaration.

### Already landed since nix#210 was written (register is stale on these — not this design's work)

- Roots answered from configured roots, and a server's `roots/list` is relayed to the client whose call raised it (`modern.go` roots answer; `internal/daemon/hooks.go` `rootsViaBroker`) — ROOT-04 exists.
- Sampling declared upstream only when a handler exists (`capabilities()`); the elicitation url gate and the client-side `-32602` mode enforcement exist and are this design's precedent.

### The design (decisions recorded in the doc)

One rule at every gate: **a question, or a field inside it, crosses a boundary only if the receiving side declared the specific sub-capability that field needs.**

- **Client side (Phase 2):** tools/`toolChoice` without declared `sampling.tools` → `-32602` naming the sub-capability (mirrors `elicitModeDeclared`; the schema gate says the client MUST error, and stripping would falsify a `toolChoice: "required"` request). `includeContext` without declared `sampling.context` → field dropped, request proceeds (context inclusion is expressly ignorable). mcpx does **not** start declaring `sampling.tools`/`context` upstream — the broker answers plain messages; declaring more would recreate the lie.
- **Server side (Phase 1):** tools-carrying sampling questions are not sendable to a host that declared no `sampling.tools` (they follow the existing unsendable/broker-fallback path); `paramsFor` strips `includeContext` for hosts that declared no `sampling.context`. `CanSample` stays the parent check; shape logic lives in `Sendable`/`paramsFor`, where the question's shape is known — the split elicitation already uses.
- **Elicitation form gate (Phase 3):** for 2025-11-25+ peers, form is sendable iff the declaration carries a `form` key or is empty (`{}` = form-only declaration); url-only is not form-capable. Older peers unchanged.

### Phases (sub-issues of this issue)

- **Phase 1** — server-side sampling relay gating (`internal/mcpserver`). Independent.
- **Phase 2** — client-side sampling enforcement (`internal/mcpclient`). Independent of Phase 1.
- **Phase 3** — elicitation form gate + compare-register truth-up (CAP-02/04/05/06/08, SMP-09/11) + nix#210 completion evidence. Gated on Phase 1 (same file, `conn.go`).

### Open questions (kept in the design doc, NOT filed)

- `includeContext` values across a relay (gap `sampling-server-avoid-includecontext-values`): `thisServer`/`allServers` are answerer-relative and soft-deprecated; downgrade vs pass vs strip needs a spec reading at triage — the gap stays open meanwhile.
- Whether mcpx should ever declare `sampling.tools` upstream (only on evidence of an upstream that requires it; sampling's 2026 deprecation argues no).
- Whether the always-declared `roots` capability should follow configuration (CAP-02's scope-derived roots is a feature question, not gating).

### Acceptance (design level)

- Phases 1–3 landed. No host receives sampling `tools`/`includeContext` beyond its declaration; no upstream tools-carrying sampling request reaches mcpx's handler against its bare declaration (it gets `-32602`); a url-only host is no longer offered form elicitations while `{}`/form hosts still are, in every era.
- The three scoped `#210` conformance gaps retired (`sampling-server-avoid-includecontext-values` explicitly remains, named above); compare register matches the code again.
- dezren39/nix#210 carries completion evidence against each acceptance bullet and is closed iff all are met.

<!-- agent-note:v1 agent=design-architect state=filed at=2026-10-28T17:38:00Z -->


## Acceptance criteria

- Phases 1–3 (sub-issues of this design) have landed: server-side sampling relay gating, client-side sampling enforcement, and the elicitation form gate with compare-register truth-up.
- No host receives sampling `tools`/`includeContext` beyond its declared sub-capabilities; an upstream tools-carrying sampling request against mcpx's bare declaration is refused with `-32602` naming the sub-capability.
- A host that declared only `elicitation.url` (2025-11-25+) is no longer offered form elicitations, while `{}` (form-only) and form-declaring hosts still are, in every era.
- The three scoped dezren39/nix#210 conformance gaps are retired (`sampling-server-avoid-includecontext-values` explicitly remains open, as named in the design); the compare register matches the code again.
- dezren39/nix#210 carries completion evidence against each of its acceptance bullets and is closed if and only if all are met.

body:
## Gap

The PM stack has no first-class event log. The audit/activity pieces exist but are scattered across separate stores in the aggregator state dir (~/.local/state/pm-aggregator/):

- the actions store (dashboard triage actions + their applied outcomes)
- the orchestrator's published actions[] in orchestration.json
- the session registry (agent/session identity + outcomes)
- the dashboard comments store (note / message / github kinds)
- per-item derived activity (derive.ts merges linked refs' comments — but comment resolution depends on the projector, which is not deployed; see code#1199)

There is no single chronological "what happened across the stack" stream a human (or the /today page) can read.

## What to build

- An append-only event record in the aggregator: {at, actor (drew / orchestrator / keeper / job id / session), kind (action-applied, tier-change, comment, session-outcome, status-write, wall, ...), ref (item/session/goal), summary}.
- Writers: the aggregator's own action-result route, the orchestration publish step, and the session registry merge — events are emitted where the facts already occur, not scraped afterward.
- A page + machine-first /api twin (e.g. /events and /api/events.json) with filters by kind/ref/actor, newest first, bounded retention (e.g. 30 days or N=5000, whichever first).
- /today links its "progressed since last run" entries to the underlying events.

## Acceptance

- Dashboard actions, orchestration tier changes, and session outcomes all appear in one stream with timestamps and refs.
- The /api twin carries the same records; filters work.
- Writing an event never blocks the underlying action (fire-and-forget append with the same durability as the existing stores).

Raised by Drew 2026-10-28 in the PM-stack non-Git data review; companion to the roadmap-files integration issue filed the same day.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Dashboard actions, orchestration tier changes, and session outcomes all appear in one chronological stream with timestamps and refs.
- [ ] The /events page and its /api/events.json twin carry the same records; filters by kind/ref/actor work.
- [ ] Writing an event never blocks the underlying action (fire-and-forget append with the same durability as the existing stores); retention is bounded (e.g. 30 days or N=5000, whichever first).

body:
# mcpx(source): a directory source reads non-regular files — a FIFO blocks resolution forever, a socket or symlink-to-directory aborts it

## Summary

`internal/source`'s directory resolution collects **every** non-directory entry a walk finds and reads it, although the package documents the opposite. One FIFO in a source directory hangs `Resolve` indefinitely; one unix socket or one symlink to a directory aborts the whole resolution with a low-level OS error. All of the directory's ordinary script fragments are lost either way.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Code, on current main (`source.go`, sha256 `e6834f6e3557c9d26239f86cd912af82428cc9c5d5e69ce01fe0212d07763b68`, identical in both clones):

- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/source/source.go:59` — the `Options.Extensions` doc: *"Empty takes every regular file."*
- `source.go:149-158` — the `readDir` walk callback: a directory entry is descended into / skipped per `Recursive`; the only other filter is `wanted(path, opt.Extensions)` (extension only). Every remaining entry — FIFO, socket, device, symlink-to-directory — is appended to `files`.
- `source.go:131-137, 161-…` — each collected path is opened with `os.ReadFile`. Opening a FIFO for reading blocks until a writer appears; opening a socket fails `ENXIO`; opening a symlink to a directory fails `EISDIR`. Any error aborts the whole `Resolve`.

Consumers: plumbing sources (launchers, prefixes, error hooks) resolve through `source.Resolve` at `internal/cli/commands.go:263` and `internal/cli/commands.go:2180`, so a directory a user points one of those settings at is the reachable input.

Probe — executed this run **on the laptop** in a detached worktree at `origin/main` `2217171d`, as a test in the real `internal/source` package (probe + full log preserved by the filer; existing package suite: 14 tests pass, only the three probe bug-cases fail):

- CTRL: a directory of two regular `.ts` files resolves and concatenates both — PASS.
- CTRL: a symlink to a regular file inside the directory resolves and is read — PASS (this behaviour must be preserved).
- BUG-A (FIFO): directory with `a.ts` + a FIFO → `Resolve` still blocked after 3 s (it blocks until a writer opens the FIFO — potentially forever in a CLI/daemon call).
- BUG-B (symlink to a directory): directory with `a.ts` + a symlink to a real subdirectory → `Resolve` fails: `reading …/linkdir: read …/linkdir: is a directory`. A real subdirectory is silently skipped when not recursive; the symlink form aborts everything.
- BUG-C (unix socket): directory with `a.ts` + a live unix socket file → `Resolve` fails: `reading …/sock: open …/sock: no such device or address`.

## Why it matters

Directory sources exist for exactly the messy real-world case: a folder of script fragments that grows over time. Sockets and FIFOs appear in such folders in practice (a dev server's socket, a logging pipe, an editor/tool leftover), and today any one of them either wedges an mcpx invocation with no diagnostic at all (the FIFO case — the worst failure mode: no error, no timeout) or discards every fragment in the directory over one entry the resolver was never supposed to read. This contradicts the package's own documented contract ("every regular file").

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `readDir` only reads regular files: walk entries that are not regular (FIFO, socket, device) are skipped, not read — a directory containing one still resolves its regular files.
- [ ] A symlink is judged by its target: a symlink to a regular file is still read (current behaviour, pinned by a test); a symlink to a directory is treated like a directory (skipped when not recursive, descended when recursive), never an `EISDIR` abort.
- [ ] No regression for the plain cases: natural-order concatenation, extension filtering, and the non-recursive subdirectory skip keep working; the existing `internal/source` suite stays green.
- [ ] New tests in `internal/source` cover at least: FIFO in a directory (resolution completes), unix socket in a directory, symlink-to-directory (both recursive settings), and symlink-to-regular-file.
- [ ] Triage pin to decide: whether skipping a non-regular entry should be silent (matching how non-recursive subdirectories are silently skipped) or logged — either is acceptable if it is deliberate and tested; hanging or aborting is not.

## Notes

- Not a duplicate of #1702 (searchpath `~name` expansion): different package and defect. `internal/source`'s own `abs` shares the `~name` shape — worth a grep during triage, but it is not this issue.
- Filed by the new-issue-creator (lane B); verification was a live probe in the real package, not a premise mirror.

## Problem

`commands::serve::tests::world_names_are_bounded_and_are_a_single_path_segment` fails on clean `main`.

## Evidence (2026-10-28, queue worker lane C, task 1853 verification)

- Laptop, branch worktree for #1611 (only `pkgs/id/src/commands/group.rs` changed): full `cargo test --no-default-features --lib` → **825 passed, 1 failed** — this test.
- Laptop, **clean `origin/main` (211aa58f)** detached worktree, same command filtered to this test: **fails identically** (0 passed, 1 failed). So the failure is pre-existing on main, not caused by the #1611 renderer change or PR #1703.
- The test exercises `validate_world_options` in `pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs` (~line 1447): names like `""`, `"../evil"`, `"Tic-Tac-Toe"`, `"a/b"`, `"sp ace"`, `"wörld"` must be refused; `"tt-2_x"`, 64×`a`, `"lobby"` must pass; 65×`a` refused. Found while verifying PR #1703 / issue #1611; that PR's own targeted tests (7 renderer tests) pass.

body:
## Finding

PR #1543 added `protect_newline_destinations` (`pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs:138`, current main `211aa58f`) to the parse side of the id markdown codec: before comrak parsing, it replaces each newline inside an angle-form link/image destination (`](<...>)`, `]: <...>`) with a collision-safe token, and `restore_attr_newlines` (`markdown.rs:217`) restores the token to a newline afterwards — but only in link `href` / image `src` attrs.

The destination/context classification is incomplete in two directions, both verified on current main (function unchanged since #1543 merged):

### 1. Literal code contexts other than plain fenced blocks are not skipped — the token leaks into text

The doc comment skips fenced code blocks because "a destination-shaped string inside a fence is literal text, not a link". The same applies to contexts the scanner does not track:

- **Inline code spans**: `` `[x](<a\nb>)` `` — the newline inside the span is replaced by `idweb-newline-0-token`. Comrak parses span content literally, so the converted PM text node contains the token string; `restore_attr_newlines` never rewrites text nodes, so the document now literally reads `` `[x](<aidweb-newline-0-tokenb>)` `` and a save writes the token into the file. The newline is destroyed.
- **Indented code blocks** (4-space indent): same corruption — fence tracking only recognises lines whose first non-space characters (up to 3 spaces) are a fence, and the `](<` scan itself is not line-anchored.
- **Longer fences**: fence state toggles on any line starting with ` ``` ` regardless of the opening fence's length, so inside a ` ```` ` block a ` ``` ` line flips the state early and protection fires inside the still-open literal block.

Probe (faithful port of the function's detection/substitution logic, run this review): all three inputs above come out `protected=True` with the token substituted into the literal text; the control fenced block and a genuine link behave as intended.

### 2. The blank-line guard misses whitespace-only blank lines — a non-destination becomes a link

The closing-`>` scan only breaks on a blank line spelled exactly `\n\n` (`markdown.rs`, `b'\n' if bytes[k+1] == b'\n'`). A blank line containing spaces/tabs (`\n \n`) does not break the scan, so `[x](<a\n \nb>)` — which is not a link in CommonMark, the paragraph break ends any destination — is protected across the break and comrak then parses it as a real link whose restored `href` contains `"\n \n"`. Literal text silently becomes a link node.

## Why it matters

`markdown_to_prosemirror` is the reopen path for every id document; the codec's core contract (the whole #1019/#1423 line of work) is a save/reopen fixpoint that never rewrites content the author didn't touch. Documents that quote markdown link syntax inside code — documentation about linking/markdown is the obvious case — are silently corrupted on open + save, and a paragraph-broken destination can invent a link. Both failure modes are silent: no error, the file on disk changes.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/1543 (merged; head commits `5baa46dc`…`c5e0491f`), fixing #1423.
- Current main `211aa58f97800e7eacf78dad09f8ae31c9ff22ce`: `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs:110` (`markdown_to_prosemirror`), `:138` (`protect_newline_destinations`), `:217` (`restore_attr_newlines` — rewrites only `href`/`src` string attrs).
- Probe script and outputs from this review are kept in the goal workspace (`hidden_files/probe-1543/probe.py`): inline code span, indented block, and 4-backtick fence cases all substitute the token into literal text; the `\n \n` case is protected across the paragraph break; controls (plain fence, `\n\n`, genuine link) behave as designed.
- Dedupe: open + closed issue search for `idweb-newline`, "code span destination", "newline token", `protect_newline_destinations` — only #1423 itself (closed, the space/tab/newline save-direction fix); nothing covers the parse-side literal-context or whitespace-blank-line gaps.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A destination-shaped string inside an inline code span or an indented code block is left byte-identical by `markdown_to_prosemirror` (no token in any text node after conversion).
- [ ] Fence tracking respects the opening fence's character and length: a shorter fence line inside a longer fence does not end the literal block.
- [ ] A whitespace-only blank line (spaces/tabs between the newlines) breaks the destination scan exactly like `\n\n`.
- [ ] Regression tests in `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs` pin all of the above plus the existing #1423 behaviours (genuine inline + reference destinations with newlines still round-trip).
- [ ] No converted document ever contains the protection token outside an `href`/`src` attr.

title: mcpx(settings): byte sizes accept negatives and int64 overflow — http.streamBufferInit=-1 passes validation, then panics the CLI with 'makeslice: cap out of range' at the first streaming read

labels.name: effort/s

body:
## Summary

Byte-size settings (`KindBytes`) accept negative and overflowing values: `settings.ParseBytes` returns them with no error, `Validate`/`Normalize` pass them through, and at least one consumer spends the value as a slice capacity with no guard — so a config file, env var, or runtime override that sets `http.streamBufferInit` to `-1` (or to a size so large it overflows int64) crashes the CLI with `makeslice: cap out of range` the first time it reads a streaming response.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Line trace, pkgs/mcpx/internal/settings/value.go:

- `ParseBytes` (:450-479) strips a suffix and does `strconv.ParseFloat` + `int64(f * float64(mult))` with no sign or range check. A negative literal parses cleanly; a huge one converts out-of-range float → int64 (on amd64/arm64: `math.MinInt64`).
- `Validate` (:481+, KindBytes case at :503) only checks that `ParseBytes` returned no error — so every value above is a *valid* setting. `Apply` and `SetRuntime` both gate on `Normalize` → `Validate`, so the bad value is admitted at every layer (file, env, flag, preset, runtime API).
- Unguarded consumer: internal/cli/client.go:965-966 and internal/cli/opcmd.go:556-557 both do `sc.Buffer(make([]byte, 0, c.set.Bytes("http.streamBufferInit")), int(c.set.Bytes("http.streamBufferMax")))` — a negative init value is a negative `make` cap, which panics.
- Other consumers happen to be guarded, which is why this stayed hidden: artifacts treats `MaxBytes > 0` / `Quota <= 0` as "no ceiling" (internal/artifacts/artifacts.go:191,354-355) and logging substitutes the default when `maxBytes <= 0` (internal/logging/file.go:86-88). Those guards silently reinterpret a negative a user actually set — worth a triage look, but the crash is the headline. `http.bodyLimit` / `http.callBodyLimit` feed `http.MaxBytesReader` in internal/daemon/routes_secrets.go:49,114 and server.go:870 with whatever `Bytes()` returns.
- The one existing ParseBytes test (internal/settings/registry_test.go, TestByteSizesAcceptBothDecimalAndBinarySuffixes) covers only well-formed positive sizes.

Laptop probe (real `internal/settings` package, detached worktree at origin/main 211aa58f; value.go sha256 c669f256, identical to the sandbox clone; probe + log in the goal's hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-bytes/):

```
ParseBytes(-1) = -1, err=<nil>
ParseBytes(-5MB) = -5000000, err=<nil>
ParseBytes(999999999999999999999999TB) = -9223372036854775808, err=<nil>
Validate accepted byte size "-1" / "-5MB" / "999999999999999999999999TB"   (KindBytes, http.streamBufferInit decl)
Normalize accepted the same three
make([]byte, 0, ParseBytes(-1)) panicked: runtime error: makeslice: cap out of range
```

Baseline: with the probe removed, the full existing internal/settings suite passes on the same tree.

## Why it matters

The settings system is the one choke point whose whole job is keeping an invalid value out of a running process ("a runtime change that skips the parser is the one way to get an invalid value into a running process" — value.go, SetRuntime). A size is the easiest typo to make (`-1` is a common "unlimited" idiom in other tools), and here it either crashes the client at first stream or — at the guarded consumers — silently turns a set limit into "no limit / default", the opposite of what was configured. Overflow needs no malice either: `999999999999999999999999TB` is what a fat-fingered or generated config produces, and it lands as the most negative int64 there is.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ParseBytes` (or `Validate` for KindBytes) refuses negative results and magnitudes that do not fit in an int64, with an error that names the offending value — `ParseBytes("-1")`, `ParseBytes("-5MB")` and the overflow case above all error.
- [ ] A `KindBytes` setting therefore cannot be applied at any layer (file/env/flag/preset/runtime) with such a value; the error surfaces at apply time, not at first use.
- [ ] Regression tests cover negative (bare and suffixed), overflow, and the existing well-formed cases (the current suffix table test keeps passing).
- [ ] Triage confirms no consumer still spends a `Bytes()` value unguarded in a way a *valid* value can crash (e.g. an init buffer larger than the max, at the two scanner sites) — or files that separately.
- [ ] Existing internal/settings, internal/cli and internal/daemon tests keep passing.

## Notes for triage

- Where the check lives (ParseBytes itself vs Validate-only) is the pin: ParseBytes is also called by `Set.Bytes()` at read time and by defaults' `mustBytes` for built-ins, so refusing inside ParseBytes protects every caller; refusing only in Validate leaves direct ParseBytes callers exposed.
- Whether "0" keeps meaning "no ceiling/default" at the guarded consumers is existing documented behaviour — not part of this issue.
- Found by new-issue-creator lane A, 2026-10-28. Distinct from #1641 (settings Clamp validating a dial against the ceiling's enum — different mechanism, same package) and #1695 (logstore Correlations).

body:
Phase 2 of design #1675 (mcpx elicitation broker hygiene). Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-elicitation-broker-hygiene.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. **Gated on Phase 1** (the owner-only store issue of #1675): same open sequence and store files.

## Scope

Bound the broker store's retention and stop broadcasting question/answer content on the event bus.

- Retention, enforced by the broker on `Open` (the codebase's expire-on-read discipline: no timer, no sweeper): delete terminal rows (answered/expired) from both `elicitations` and `elicitation_answers` when they exceed the bounds in `internal/defaults/defaults.json` — recorded defaults from the design: **30 days old or more than 1000 terminal rows, whichever bound hits first** (triage confirms names/values against the defaults file's conventions). **Pending rows are never pruned** — a pending question is live state with its own expiry (`expireOverdue`).
- Sampling rows obey the same bound (same table): this retires `sampling-messages-not-retained-between-requests`.
- Event payloads become summary-only at all publish sites: `events.ElicitOpened` and `events.ElicitAnswered` carry id, server, tool, mode, audience, state, expiry — never a question's `message`, `schema` or `url`, and never an answer's `content`. Sites: `internal/daemon/hooks.go` ~L164-171, `internal/daemon/consumer.go` ~L325/424/505, `internal/daemon/routes_proto.go` ~L669, `internal/daemon/server.go` ~L1395 (today: `Data: mustJSON(req)` / `mustJSON(ans)`, the full objects).
- Tree-wide audit of consumers of these two event kinds' `Data` before the shrink lands; anything in-tree that read content is rerouted to the broker read path. The design's audit found no in-tree consumer reading answer content from the bus (askers use `Broker.Await`). Also confirm during implementation whether the out-of-tree OpenCode plugin reads payload fields being removed; if it does, route it through the broker read path — do not restore the leak.
- Retire conformance gaps `sampling-messages-not-retained-between-requests` and `sampling-both-handle-sensitive-data` (client + server sides) in `internal/conformance/coverage_clientfeatures.go`.

## Evidence (main d39e6111, 2026-10-28)

- `internal/elicit/elicit.go` contains no `DELETE`; `expireOverdue` (~L437) only transitions state. Origin dezren39/nix#255 acceptance: "Stored elicitations are pruned (age or count bound, documented)."
- Gap texts (coverage_clientfeatures.go ~L108-110): "prompts and answers are stored unredacted in state/logs/elicit.db under a 0755 directory and published on the event bus"; "every CreateMessageRequest is kept in state/logs/elicit.db and never pruned".
- Decision recorded on #1675: payload shrink at the source, not per-subscriber filtering (the bus has no field-level filtering; every future subscriber would inherit the leak). The migration path for any external consumer is the broker read path, named here and in the nix#255 evidence comment at Phase 3.

## Acceptance

- Broker open with aged terminal rows deletes them (both tables); pending rows and fresh terminal rows are kept; the count bound trims oldest-first.
- Retention bounds are settings in `defaults.json` with the documented defaults, not hard-coded constants.
- Published `ElicitOpened`/`ElicitAnswered` event data contains none of a fixture question's message/schema/url or a fixture answer's content (canary strings asserted absent), while id/server/mode/audience/state fields are present.
- Consumer audit recorded on this issue: every in-tree `Data` consumer of the two kinds accounted for.
- Gaps `sampling-messages-not-retained-between-requests` and `sampling-both-handle-sensitive-data` (both sides) retired with the tests as evidence.
- CI green for `pkgs/mcpx` (tests run in GitHub Actions).

body:
## Summary

The elicitation broker is where mcpx puts the most sensitive data it handles — questions routed to a human precisely because an agent should not hold them (password/credential-shaped fields, per `elicit.Route`), sampling prompts "stored exactly as sent", and the answers — and it is the least protected store in the daemon. On current main the broker DB sits in a `0755` directory any local user can read, no row is ever deleted, and the full question and answer are broadcast as event-bus data to every subscriber. The one human surface over the store, `mcpx elicit`, prints raw URLs with no domain emphasis or punycode warning, pre-fills `"..."` instead of schema defaults, and answers with no review step. This design gives the broker an owner-only home with migration for existing installs, a documented retention bound, summary-only event payloads, and a review-first answering surface.

Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-elicitation-broker-hygiene.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace (full audit, alternatives, risks, open questions).

No Drew direction decision needed: origin dezren39/nix#255's acceptance is explicit (owner-only store verified on disk; pruning with a documented bound), the owner-only precedent is already in-tree (`internal/artifacts` and the state dir at `0o700`), and the judgment calls (dedicated `0700` subdir rather than tightening the shared logs dir; summary-only events; retention defaults of 30 days / 1000 terminal rows) are recorded in the design doc.

## Current state (verified on main d39e6111, 2026-10-28)

- Both broker open sites create the shared `<state>/logs` dir with `defaults.PublicDirMode` (`0755`, `internal/defaults/defaults.json:214`): `internal/daemon/hooks.go` `OpenBroker` (~L288-294) and `internal/cli/elicit.go` `broker()` (~L37-44). `elicit.Open` (`internal/elicit/elicit.go` ~L155) creates `elicit.db` (+ WAL/SHM) with default modes. Gaps `elicitation-state-storage-protected` and `elicitation-server-follow-best-practices` (`internal/conformance/coverage_clientfeatures.go`, origin dezren39/nix#255).
- `internal/elicit/elicit.go` contains no `DELETE`: `expireOverdue` (~L437) only transitions pending → expired. Every question, answer, and sampling request accumulates forever. Gap `sampling-messages-not-retained-between-requests`.
- Full payloads on the bus: `events.ElicitOpened` with `Data: mustJSON(req)` and `events.ElicitAnswered` with `Data: mustJSON(ans)` at `internal/daemon/hooks.go` ~L164-171, `internal/daemon/consumer.go` ~L325/424/505, `internal/daemon/routes_proto.go` ~L669, `internal/daemon/server.go` ~L1395. No in-tree consumer reads answer content from the bus — askers use `Broker.Await`. Gaps `sampling-both-handle-sensitive-data` (client + server).
- `renderQuestion` (`internal/cli/elicit.go` ~L201-232) already shows the asking server/tool; what is missing is exactly the #255 UI slice: URL domain emphasis + punycode warning, schema defaults pre-filled (today `exampleFor` ~L275-285 emits `"..."`), and a review step before an answer is relayed. Six gaps: `elicitation-app-review-modify-responses`, `elicitation-client-form-review-modify-responses`, `elicitation-client-url-show-domain-and-consent`, `elicitation-client-handle-urls-carefully`, `elicitation-client-highlight-domain`, `elicitation-client-warn-punycode`.
- Explicitly NOT this design: validating answers against `requestedSchema` — the client slice is #1484 (Phase 3 of design #1481, queued); the server-relay slice (`elicitation-server-validate-received-data`) stays open on nix#255 until #1484's as-built shape is known. Also distinct: the tasks store's own `0755` dir creation (`internal/tasks/tasks.go:149`) belongs to #1554's store, not this one.

## Proposal (phased; each phase independently landable)

1. **Phase 1 — owner-only store.** One path helper in `internal/elicit`; the store moves to a dedicated state subdir at `0700`, DB files `0600`; a legacy `logs/elicit.db` is migrated on open with pending questions preserved; modes are tightened on open for pre-existing installs and failure to tighten is an error. Both open sites use the helper.
2. **Phase 2 — bounded retention + redacted events** (gated on Phase 1). Terminal rows pruned on open by age + count bounds from `defaults.json` (30 days / 1000 rows, recorded defaults); pending rows never pruned. `ElicitOpened`/`ElicitAnswered` payloads become summary-only (id, server, tool, mode, audience, state, expiry — never message/schema/url/content) at all publish sites, with a tree-wide consumer audit.
3. **Phase 3 — review-first answering surface + truth-up** (gated on Phases 1–2). URL domain emphasis + punycode warning; schema defaults pre-filled in form rendering; interactive render-and-confirm for `mcpx elicit answer` with a script-preserving opt-out (non-interactive behaviour unchanged). Retire the six elicit-ui gaps; completion evidence on dezren39/nix#255 — commenting, not closing (its validation acceptance is only partly this design's).

## Open questions (stay questions; not filed)

- Should the logs directory itself go owner-only later (log index can carry tool-call arguments)? Its own design if evidence appears.
- Should sampling rows get a different retention bound than form answers? One bound until size evidence argues otherwise.
- Does the OpenCode plugin (out-of-tree) read bus payload fields Phase 2 removes? To confirm in Phase 2 triage; the fix is routing it through the broker read path, not restoring the leak.
- Full TUI edit-in-place for answers vs render-and-confirm? Evidence from actual use first.

## Acceptance (design level)

- Phases 1–3 filed as sub-issues of this issue and landed.
- Fresh and upgraded installs: `elicit.db` + its directory owner-only, verified on disk; a question pending across the upgrade is still answerable.
- Terminal history bounded by the documented age/count limits; pending never pruned.
- No bus event carries a question's message/schema/URL or an answer's content.
- `mcpx elicit` shows the asking server, the URL domain called out (punycode warning where applicable), defaults pre-filled, and an interactive review before relay.
- dezren39/nix#255 carries the completion evidence with its remaining validation slice named honestly.

title: mcpx(openapi): Build is nondeterministic — duplicate operationIds swap tool names between runs, and the body schema is whichever JSON media type the map yields first

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/normal

body:
## Problem

`openapi.Build` (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/openapi/openapi.go`, main c04a9430, sha256 79b465b9) is nondeterministic for two spec shapes it explicitly handles: the same specification, built twice by the same binary, can produce different tools. `Build` is re-run on every `mcpx api` invocation and every MCP-server start (`internal/cli/openapi_tools.go:59-77` `buildAPI`, used by `CmdAPI` and `apiTools`), so the flips happen between ordinary restarts/invocations, not just in theory.

### Site 1 — duplicate-operationId disambiguation depends on map iteration order

- `PathItem.operations()` (openapi.go:75-86) returns a `map[string]*Operation`; `Build` ranges it at :291. Go randomises map iteration order on each range.
- Paths themselves are sorted (:285-288) and the final tool list is sorted by name (:325), but neither fixes *which operation owns which name*: the collision loop (:302-310) keeps the bare name for the first operation visited and appends `_2` to the later one.
- The code's own comment (:302-305) says duplicate operationIds occur in practice and are "disambiguated rather than dropped" — but the disambiguation is a coin flip. Example: `GET /pets` and `POST /pets` both declaring `operationId: listPets` (with methods `all`) yield `api_listpets → GET, api_listpets_2 → POST` on one Build and `api_listpets → POST, api_listpets_2 → GET` on the next.
- Consequence: a caller (script, saved command, model) invoking `api_listpets` can silently reach the *other* endpoint after a restart — a read can become a create — or a name it used yesterday now belongs to a different operation. Tool names are the stable surface everything else keys on; here they are not stable.

### Site 2 — the request-body schema is whichever JSON media type the map yields first

- `buildSchema` (:498-511) ranges `op.RequestBody.Content` (a Go map) and `break`s on the first media type whose name contains `"json"`.
- A request body declaring two JSON media types with *different* schemas — e.g. `application/json` and `application/vnd.api+json` (JSON:API), both containing "json" — advertises one schema on one Build and the other on the next. The tool's published `inputSchema` (what a caller validates against and what a model reads) flips accordingly, while `Call` always sends the same body.

## Evidence

1. Line trace on main c04a9430 (file sha256 `79b465b9636fa1e51025824ff395e27bf28d0849fcb0c4bd7a2490a097b7cde5`): `operations()` :75-86 builds a map; `Build` ranges it :291; disambiguation :306-310 is visit-order dependent; `buildSchema` media loop :498-511 breaks on the first map-yielded `"json"` key. Existing tests (`openapi_test.go`) cover neither duplicate operationIds nor multi-JSON-media bodies.
2. Premise exercised this run with a faithful mirror of both loops (goal `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-openapi-nondet/premise.py` + `premise.log`): iteration GET,POST → `api_listpets=GET`; iteration POST,GET → `api_listpets=POST`; media iteration json-first → schema A, vnd.api+json-first → schema B. The only input that changes is iteration order, which Go supplies randomly per range.

**Disclosure:** the prepared Go probe (`hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-openapi-nondet/probe_laneb_test.go`, package `openapi_test`; builds the same spec 200× and fails if the bare name's owner or the body schema ever flips) was **not executed** — the laptop was unreachable this run (SSH tunnel closes immediately) and probes are never compiled on the sandbox. Triage should run the probe first and correct this issue if any verdict differs.

## Why it matters

Generated tool names and schemas are a contract: scripts, the catalogue/codegen surface and callers' saved invocations all assume the same spec yields the same tools. Nondeterminism here is silent (no error, both outputs look valid) and, for site 1, can route a call to the wrong HTTP method/path.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Triage runs the prepared probe and confirms/corrects both verdicts.
- [ ] `Build` is deterministic: building the same spec any number of times yields byte-identical tool names, method/path bindings and input schemas.
- [ ] Duplicate operationIds are disambiguated by a stable rule (e.g. method/path order), pinned by a test that builds a colliding spec repeatedly; the operation that keeps the bare name does not depend on iteration order.
- [ ] The request-body media pick follows a stated, stable preference (e.g. exact `application/json` first, then lexicographic media type), pinned by a test with two JSON media types carrying different schemas.
- [ ] Existing `internal/openapi` tests pass; no change to single-media-type or unique-operationId behaviour.

body:
## Problem

Two `log_sync` batch-collection timing tests flaked in the same full `nix flake check` run, failing the id-ci check (and, by dependency, the whole nightly):

Run: https://github.com/developing-today/code/actions/runs/40666995402 (id e2e nightly, dispatched at cc46ea3f, job "nix flake check (full)", 2026-10-28)

Failures in the id lib test suite (src/log_sync.rs):
- `log_sync::tests::test_batch_collection_coalesces_paced_arrivals` — suite result: 1784 passed, 1 failed, finished in 38.90s
- `log_sync::tests::test_batch_collection_grace_restarts_on_each_arrival` — panicked at src/log_sync.rs:968:9: `assertion left == right failed: arrivals each inside the grace of the previous one share one batch` (left: 1, right: 8); suite result: 1815 passed, 1 failed, finished in 552.91s

Both tests assert batching behaviour over wall-clock grace windows; under the full flake check's parallel load (dozens of checks building/testing concurrently, plus Magic Nix Cache throttling early in the same run: GitHub API `ResourceExhausted` / HTTP 418), the paced arrivals miss their grace windows. The same tests pass in the PR-level sharded test checks.

Impact: the nightly's `nixos-integration` check was blocked by the id-ci dependency failure, so the integration VM suite produced no signal in that run — this flake masks exactly the signal the nightly exists to provide (found while shepherding PR #1246 / issue #1636).

## Acceptance

- [ ] The two batch-collection tests are made load-insensitive (e.g. drive the collection clock/batching deterministically instead of relying on wall-clock pacing, or scale the grace window to the observed scheduler delay) — without weakening what they assert about batching semantics.
- [ ] A full `nix flake check` run under load passes the id lib suite with both tests green.

Filed by queue worker lane D from run-log evidence; not a duplicate of closed #241 (different LogSync test).

body:
Implementation piece 2 of #1511 (repo-universe issue tracker) — the scheduled checker. Depends on the inventory artifact (piece 1).

## Scope
- A scheduled, read-only checker (fleet cron, same home as the other read-only fleet checks) that, for every universe repo with `watch: issues`:
  - fetches issues via `gh api --paginate repos/<owner>/<name>/issues?state=all&since=<last-run watermark>` (issues endpoint; filter out pull requests),
  - diffs against a persisted state file (per repo: issue number → state, title, updated_at, html_url),
  - emits a delta report (new / changed / closed per repo) to the repo-health goal workspace and appends state.
- Watermark/state handling: first run baselines without reporting the full history as "new" (report counts only); a failed repo fetch is reported as an error line, never silently treated as zero issues.
- The checker performs NO writes to GitHub. Creating/updating tracking entries is piece 3's job; the delta report is its input.

## Acceptance
- Two consecutive runs with no upstream changes produce an empty delta and zero state churn beyond the run timestamp.
- A test issue opened in dezren39/hatch-personal appears in the next run's delta as `new`; closing it appears as `closed` on the following run.
- Runs unattended on its schedule and leaves a dated delta report per run.

Parent: #1511 (design posted there by queue task 1549).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A scheduled, read-only checker runs unattended for every universe repo with `watch: issues` and performs no writes to GitHub.
- [ ] Two consecutive runs with no upstream changes produce an empty delta and zero state churn beyond the run timestamp (the body's Acceptance bullets, restated here as the criteria section).
- [ ] A test issue opened in dezren39/hatch-personal appears in the next run's delta as `new`; closing it appears as `closed` on the following run.
- [ ] A failed repo fetch is reported as an error line in the delta report, never silently treated as zero issues.
- [ ] Each run leaves a dated delta report in the repo-health goal workspace and advances the persisted watermark/state.

title: mcpx(settings): Clamp validates a dial request against the ceiling's enum, not the dial's — prompt.autonomy accepts apply/off/advise/ask

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

`settings.Set.Clamp` validates a requested dial value against the **ceiling's** enum, not the dial's own enum. For the one dial whose enum is a strict subset of its ceiling — `prompt.autonomy` (`{propose, run}`, clamped by `autonomy.max`'s full ladder `{off, advise, ask, propose, apply, run}`) — a request for a value the dial can never hold passes through untouched, unlowered and unerrored, as long as it is anywhere on the ceiling's ladder and at or below the ceiling. The error for a truly unknown value also lists the ceiling's values, telling the caller that `apply`/`off`/`ask` *are* acceptable for `prompt.autonomy`.

## Evidence (verified on main `ed8e5910`)

`pkgs/mcpx/internal/settings/clamp.go:36-48` (`Set.Clamp`): the only rank check is

```go
want, ok := cdecl.Rank(requested)   // cdecl = the CEILING's declaration (autonomy.max)
if !ok {
    return Clamp{}, fmt.Errorf("%s: %q is not one of %v", path, requested, cdecl.Enum)
}
```

`decl.Rank(requested)` (the dial's own enum) is never consulted. The declarations (`internal/settings/consumer.go:118-119` and `:156-157`): `autonomy.max` has `Enum: AutonomyLevels` (`off, advise, ask, propose, apply, run`, `consumer.go:12`); `prompt.autonomy` has `Enum: []string{"propose", "run"}, ClampedBy: "autonomy.max"`. `checkClamp` (`clamp.go:82-115`) deliberately allows this shape — a dial's values must be an *ordered subset* of the ceiling's — so subset dials are a designed-for case, not a misconfiguration.

Probe on the laptop driving the real `internal/settings` package with the real registry (default `autonomy.max = run`; probe + log in the fleet's run records, run twice with identical output):

```
Clamp(prompt.autonomy, "propose") -> value="propose" lowered=false err=nil     (control, valid)
Clamp(prompt.autonomy, "run")     -> value="run"     lowered=false err=nil     (control, valid)
Clamp(prompt.autonomy, "apply")   -> value="apply"   lowered=false err=nil     (BUG: not a prompt.autonomy value)
Clamp(prompt.autonomy, "off")     -> value="off"     lowered=false err=nil     (BUG: same)
Clamp(prompt.autonomy, "advise")  -> value="advise"  lowered=false err=nil     (BUG: same)
Clamp(prompt.autonomy, "ask")     -> value="ask"     lowered=false err=nil     (BUG: same)
Clamp(prompt.autonomy, "plan")    -> err=prompt.autonomy: "plan" is not one of [off advise ask propose apply run]  (error lists the CEILING's enum)
Clamp(repair.autonomy, "apply")   -> value="apply" err=nil                     (control: repair's enum IS the full ladder)
Clamp(repair.autonomy, "plan")    -> err=... "plan" is not one of [off advise ask propose apply run]  (correct list here)
```

Existing coverage misses exactly this: `internal/settings/clamp_test.go` builds the same subset shape (`t.dial` = `{propose, run}` under the full ladder) but only ever clamps `run`, `propose`, and `plan` — a value outside *both* enums. No ceiling-enum-but-not-dial-enum request (`apply`/`off`/`advise`/`ask`) is tested.

## Reachability today (honest scope)

The two prompt routes are *not* currently exploitable end-to-end: `promptAutonomy` (`internal/daemon/routes_consumer.go:507-518`) pre-validates the request body to `propose`/`run` before calling `Clamp`, and the call-settings header path (`callSettings`, `routes_settings.go:79` / `Normalize`) and file/env layers validate against the dial's own enum. What is broken is `Clamp` itself — the function its own doc names as the choke point for this job ("A handler that takes the dial from a request body calls this", `clamp.go:23-26`). Any present or future handler that relies on `Clamp` alone (as its contract invites) gets out-of-enum values back labelled as the request's autonomy: e.g. `apply` satisfies `AutonomyAtLeast(level, "propose")` (`routes_consumer.go:337,:400`) yet is neither `run` nor a handled level, so a recipe/intent resolution would return its source unexecuted under a nonsense `autonomy: "apply"` label, with no error anywhere.

## What must NOT change

Lowering *to* a ceiling value below the dial's whole range is intentional and pinned by the existing test (`clamp_test.go`: ceiling `off` lowers a `propose` request to `off`, and `routes_consumer.go`'s `belowPropose` exists for exactly those levels). The defect is only the **unlowered pass-through** of a requested value that is not in the dial's enum (and the wrong enum in the error). A fix that rejects lowered-to-ceiling results would break that design.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Clamp("prompt.autonomy", x)` for `x` in `{apply, off, advise, ask}` (in the ceiling's enum, not the dial's) with ceiling `run` returns an error instead of passing `x` through as the value — or, if triage prefers a different ruling, that ruling is pinned by tests and documented on `Clamp`.
- [ ] The error for an invalid request names the **dial's** permitted values (`propose, run` for `prompt.autonomy`), not the ceiling's ladder.
- [ ] Valid requests are unchanged: `propose`/`run` pass at or below the ceiling; a request above the ceiling is lowered to the ceiling value (including a ceiling below the dial's range, e.g. ceiling `off` lowering `propose` → `off`, per the existing pinned behaviour).
- [ ] `repair.autonomy` / `hooks.autonomy` (dial enum == ceiling enum) behave exactly as before.
- [ ] New tests in `internal/settings` cover the ceiling-enum-but-not-dial-enum shapes against a subset dial (the `clamp_test.go` fixture shape already supports this).

title: id(world): id world verify (PR #1468) never surfaces the header verdict — exits 0 saying 'records verify' when both replays mismatch the fixture header

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient
