body:
## Finding

`id world verify` (added by PR #1468) computes the fixture-header verdict for both of its replays — and then never prints or acts on it. When the two replays agree with each other but **both mismatch the fixture's recorded header records**, the command prints `records verify (two replays agree at all N steps)` and exits **0**, with no hint that the replayed records differ from the records the fixture was recorded with. `id world replay` on the same fixture prints `records differ` and exits nonzero — the two commands give contradictory operator signals and `verify` hides the half that failed.

Filed by pr-diff-review-b (lane B) from reviewing PR #1468. Parent: #544 (closed by that PR).

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/1468 — MERGED, commit `b0ee0cd0`
- Verified on current main `3b559045`, `pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs`:
  - `verify_fixture` (starts :1095) matches only on `verification.divergence`, prints the first replay's records and view, and bails only when a divergence exists. It never reads `verification.first.verdict` or `verification.second.verdict`.
  - Contrast `replay_fixture` (:1036): prints `records match` / `records differ` / `records not compared (…)` from `replayed.verdict` and bails on `Verdict::Mismatch`.
- `pkgs/id/src/world_fixture.rs` (`replay_collecting`, added by the same PR): each replay's `Replayed.verdict` **is** computed against the header (`verdict(header, records.as_deref())`) and stored in the `Verification` — the CLI layer discards it.
- The agree-but-mismatch case is not hypothetical: it is the documented #242 shape. A guest whose live behaviour depended on host events (e.g. territory/presence) replays deterministically to records that differ from the header — both replays omit host events equally, so they agree with each other and both carry `Verdict::Mismatch`. The fixtures doc (updated by the PR) says verify "proves the recorded fixture replays deterministically, nothing more" — but the CLI output does not say even that; it reads as a full pass.

## Why it matters

`verify` is the determinism self-check an operator runs to trust a fixture. A fixture that no longer reproduces the recorded world — exactly the regression class #544 was built to catch early — currently produces a success line and a zero exit, indistinguishable from a fixture whose replays also match the header. Anyone scripting on the exit code, or skimming the verdict line, is told the fixture verified when only the weaker run-to-run property held.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `verify_fixture` prints the header verdict (Match / Mismatch / NotCompared, as `replay_fixture` renders it) alongside the two-replays-agree/diverge line
- [ ] For a complete fixture whose replays agree but mismatch the header, the output names that explicitly, and the exit-code behaviour for that case is a deliberate, documented choice (bail like `replay`, or a clearly worded pass-with-mismatch line in the CLI help and the fixtures doc) — not silence
- [ ] A test covers the agree-but-mismatch case at the CLI or `verify` layer (e.g. a tampered-header fixture, whose replays agree with each other and mismatch the header — the existing `world_fixture` tests already build tampered-header fixtures for `replay`)

body:
## Finding

PR #1453 added the `wasm-opt -Os` + `wasm-tools strip` shrink pipeline to all seven Roc example `build.sh` scripts, and its body states the pipeline ends with "`wasm-tools validate`" — but two of the seven scripts, `roc-chat` and `roc-grid`, have **no validate step at all** (they never had one, and the PR did not add one). Their post-strip modules are echoed as "Built" without ever being validated by the script that produces the checked-in artifact.

Filed by pr-diff-review-b (lane B) from reviewing PR #1453. Parent: #555 (closed by that PR).

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/1453 — MERGED, commit `9c5ba735`. PR body: "After the build: `wasm-opt -Os --all-features`, then `wasm-tools strip` …, then `wasm-tools validate`."
- Verified on current main `3b559045`:
  - `pkgs/id/examples/roc-chat/build.sh:40-42` — `$WASM_TOOLS strip roc-chat.wasm …`, `mv … roc-chat.wasm`, `echo "Built roc-chat.wasm …"` — no validate line anywhere in the file
  - `pkgs/id/examples/roc-grid/build.sh:40-42` — same shape, no validate line
  - `pkgs/id/examples/lounge/build.sh:42` — `$WASM_TOOLS validate lounge.wasm` (present); the same step is present in `roc-counter` (after strip, before its import check comment), `roc-screen`, `territory`, and `tic-tac-toe` — five of seven

## Why it matters

The checked-in `.wasm` files are artifacts other work trusts (e.g. the F11.9 bytes-per-frame baseline in #542 instantiates them). For five examples the producing script itself proves the optimized+stripped module is still valid before it can be committed; for `roc-chat` and `roc-grid` a `wasm-opt`/`strip` regression would be committed silently at build time and only surface later, in a different context, if a test happens to instantiate that example. The scripts also diverge from the contract #555's PR states, so the next reader cannot tell the omission is accidental.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `pkgs/id/examples/roc-chat/build.sh` and `pkgs/id/examples/roc-grid/build.sh` run `$WASM_TOOLS validate <module>` after the strip step and before the "Built" echo, matching the other five example scripts (or the deviation is explicitly documented in both scripts and in #555's follow-up notes)
- [ ] All seven example `build.sh` scripts have the same build → optimize → strip → validate sequence

body:
## Problem (observed live, 2026-10-27)

Every dashboard page is supposed to show its data's age — the freshness-chips row (`freshnessChips`, #1138) is the standard, and most pages render it. Cost Explorer doesn't.

Field evidence (live HTML grep, ~13:56 CDT): the chips row is present on /today, /quota, /sessions, /program, /dns, /roadmap, /health — and **absent on /aa** (and /pages). `/aa` is served `renderAa(await source.aa(), prov())` — no `provDetail()`, so no chips. What /aa shows instead is one prose line, "collected <date>", covering only the AA section. The page's second tab, Model Explorer, renders a fleet catalog built from a *different* read (the collector's catalog build over the fleet's `.opencode/opencode.jsonc`) whose age appears nowhere: when the catalog is missing the page says so (good), but when it is present its vintage is invisible.

This matters because the AA section has silently vanished before (#1349): an age chip that flips to stale is the at-a-glance tripwire, and /aa is the one page without it.

## Design

- `renderAa` takes the provenance detail like every other page and renders the standard chips row (aa facet at minimum).
- The two tabs carry their own ages: AA section age from the feed facet; catalog age from the catalog's own collected-at (carried in the section model by the collector if present, otherwise the chip states the feed age and labels it as such — never an unlabeled guess).

## Acceptance

- `/aa` renders the freshness-chips row, vocabulary identical to the other pages (live/stale/absent + age).
- AA tab and Model Explorer tab each display their own data age.
- A stale AA section (older than one collector cycle) reads stale in the chip.

Related: #1349 (AA section vanished silently once), #1260 (freshness SLOs consume the same facet states), #1204 (extractor health on /quota — same pattern, different page).

body:
## Problem (observed live, 2026-10-27)

Drew's two daily questions are "what needs me?" and "is everything healthy?". Today answers only the first.

Field evidence (aggregator live, ~13:56 CDT): `/today?full=1` contains the NEEDS DREW / NEEDS USER counts, but **zero health signal** — no degraded-service, feed-age, or stack-state content anywhere in the render (`src/render.ts`'s Today path has no reference to the health assembly at all). If Kaneo, the fleet-feed collector, or the orchestration pass dies, Today looks identical; the only place that shows it is `/health`. Meanwhile `/api/health` already assembles everything needed in one view: `services[]` with per-service state, `degraded`, feed `generatedAt`/`fileMtime`, section ages — computed, cached (60 s probes), and unused by the landing page.

## Design

A one-row **system strip** directly under Today's H1, in both the shell (first paint — it is the glanceable answer) and the full/fragment render:

- Services: `stack 8/8 up` — or the down/degraded service names in the warning colour, linking to `/health`.
- Feed age: `feed 4m` (warning state past 15m), linking to `/health`.
- Orchestration age: `orchestrator 39m`, linking to `/health`.
- Quota read errors: count when > 0 (today: 2 provider reads sit in error state in `/api/quota.json`), linking to `/quota`.

Each cell is one glanceable token; the strip adds no new data source — it renders the health assembly's existing outputs where Drew actually lands. Mobile: the strip wraps to at most two rows at 390 px.

## Implementation path

`todayContext()` in `src/server.ts` gains the health view (the same `healthContext()` `/health` and `/api/health` use — probe results are already 60 s-cached, so this adds no per-request fan-out); `renderTodayShell` / `renderTodayBody` in `src/render.ts` render the strip from it. Fail-soft like every other facet: if the health assembly errors, the strip renders its own unknown state rather than breaking Today.

## Acceptance

- All services up + fresh feed: the strip reads green in one line on `/today` (shell and full render).
- Any service down/degraded, feed > 15m old, or a quota pool in error state: the strip names it on `/today` without visiting `/health` or `/quota`.
- Strip present in first paint (shell), not only after the fragment lands.

Part of epic #1184 (PM stack coherence). Related: #1147 (built the health assembly this reuses), #1260 (freshness SLOs — the strip is the human surface for the same states).

body:
# aggregator: yes/no survey answers are never validated — any string (or even an array) is accepted as a yes/no answer

## Summary

The Needs-you survey's POST-boundary check (`checkActionAgainstItem`) promises that survey answers are checked against the published question's options — and it works for `single` and `multi` questions. For `yesno` questions it never fires: **any** value is accepted and stored as the answer to a yes/no question, including nonsense strings and even an array of both options. The card then renders that value as "✓ answered: banana".

## Evidence

Three pieces line up into the hole:

- The sanitizer only attaches `options` to `single`/`multi` questions — `sanitizeQuestions` in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/tier-items.ts:117-134`. A `yesno` question's options are dropped even when the publisher supplies them (verified: a yesno question published with `options: [{id:"yes"},{id:"no"}]` sanitizes to a question with **no** `options` field).
- The boundary check validates a yesno answer only when options exist — `checkActionAgainstItem`, `tier-items.ts:347`: `if ((q.type === "single" || q.type === "yesno") && q.options) { ... }`. Since yesno questions never carry options after sanitization, the guard is dead code for them.
- The renderer knows the real option set — `questionFieldHtml` in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/render.ts:963-968` synthesizes `[{id:"yes",label:"Yes"},{id:"no",label:"No"}]` when `q.options` is absent. The UI can only ever submit `yes`/`no`; the API accepts everything else anyway.

Verified this run on main `b27dbe8e` with the verbatim `tier-items.ts` (sha256 `cdb1fd21…`, identical on sandbox and laptop) under Bun on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-yesno`; log `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-laneB-yesno/out.log`):

```
control single bogus value        : REJECTED: answer for "audience" must be one of its options
control single valid value         : ACCEPTED (null)
control multi string (not array)   : REJECTED: answers for "tags" must be chosen from its options
control multi bogus entry          : REJECTED: answers for "tags" must be chosen from its options
yesno valid 'yes'                  : ACCEPTED (null)
yesno BOGUS 'banana'               : ACCEPTED (null)   <-- bug
yesno BOGUS array ['yes','no']     : ACCEPTED (null)   <-- bug
yesno-with-opts BOGUS 'banana'     : ACCEPTED (null)   <-- bug (sanitizer stripped the options)
text BOGUS array ['a','b']         : ACCEPTED (null)   <-- same shape: no per-type value-shape check for text either
```

Downstream, the bogus value is merged into the card state verbatim (`card-state.ts` `answered` map, latest answer wins) and printed as the answered value (`render.ts` question state line), and it is what the consumer of the answer action receives — a yes/no answer it cannot interpret.

## Why it matters

The boundary check is the contract the consumers rely on (#1291/#1293 design: "option and survey membership … checks"). Every other question type is enforced; yes/no is the most common triage question shape ("Go ahead?"), and its answers silently escape validation, so a malformed or hand-crafted POST can record an unanswerable "answer" that marks a required question as answered on the card.

## Acceptance criteria

- A `yesno` answer whose value is not exactly `"yes"` or `"no"` (or one of the question's published option ids, if the sanitizer is changed to keep publisher-supplied yesno options) is rejected by `checkActionAgainstItem` with a legible error, in the same style as the `single` case.
- A non-string value (e.g. an array) for a `yesno` or `single` question is rejected; an array value for a `text` question is rejected (per-type value shape: `single`/`yesno`/`text` → string, `multi` → string array).
- Valid answers still pass: `yes`/`no` for yesno, a published option for single, a string for text, an option-id array for multi; partial submits (#1451) are unaffected.
- Regression tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/needs-user.test.ts` cover the yesno bogus-value and array cases and the text array case, alongside the existing single/multi controls.

body:
Phase 3 of design #1481 (JSON Schema validation of tool input and output). Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-json-schema-validation.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Origin gap: dezren39/nix#254 (acceptance: "Elicitation schemas are validated with the same mechanism").

**Dependency gate:** do not start until Phase 1 (the `internal/schemaval` core) is merged. Independent of Phase 2 — either order after Phase 1 is fine. If claimed earlier, park naming the dependency.

## Scope

Validate elicitation form answers against the schema the server itself supplied, at the single answer choke point:

- In `Client.answer` (`internal/mcpclient/modern.go:253`, the `elicitation/create` case), **after** `applyDefaults` runs (defaults first — an omitted field is valid only once its default is in): when the mode is form (or undeclared, which the codebase already treats as form) and the handler's answer has `action: "accept"` with `content`, compile the request's `requestedSchema` with `schemaval` and validate `content` against it.
- On failure: return an Invalid Params (-32602) `rpcError` to the requesting server naming the failing path, emit a `Warning`, and **do not relay the answer**. The unvalidated answer never reaches the upstream.
- On a `requestedSchema` that itself does not compile: warn and relay the answer unvalidated (the server authored the schema; its defect must not wedge the user's answer) — record this choice in a code comment.
- Untouched: `decline`/`cancel` answers (no content to validate), URL mode, sampling (`sampling/createMessage` — gap #256, separate), and the broker/daemon layers (the modern input-required flow inherits this check because `resolveInput` routes through `answer()`).
- Update the conformance matrix / gap registry for the elicitation validation rows this closes (`elicitation-both-validate-against-schema`, `elicitation-client-validate-responses`, `elicitation-server-validate-received-data` — the mechanism rows shared with #255).

Out of scope: everything else under #255 (elicitation storage protection, redaction, CLI review UI); re-ask/retry UX for a rejected answer (open question territory — v1 surfaces the -32602 to the server, matching how the undeclared-mode check already behaves in the same function).

## Acceptance

- Defining test: a handler answers `accept` with a wrong-typed field against `requestedSchema` → the upstream receives -32602, not the answer; a `Warning` was emitted.
- Defining test: an answer omitting a field that `requestedSchema` gives a `default` validates and is relayed with the default applied (defaults-before-validation order proven).
- Defining test: a conforming answer is relayed byte-identical to today's behaviour; decline and cancel answers pass through with no validation attempted.
- Defining test: an uncompilable `requestedSchema` → answer relayed, warning emitted, no error to the server.
- The same wrong-typed answer arriving via a modern input-required round is likewise rejected (the `answer()` inheritance is covered by a test, not just asserted).
- Full suite passes: `cd pkgs/mcpx && go test ./...` (via CI on the PR per fleet policy).

---

Filed as `task/triage`: triage confirms scope against current main once Phase 1 has landed (gate above) and enqueues the implementation packet; do not implement in the triage task.

body:
Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-json-schema-validation.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Register: central potential-projects list, same workspace (`files/potential-projects.md`).

**Validator decision (recorded here per nix#254's acceptance, before implementation):** adopt `github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6` behind a thin `internal/schemaval` wrapper — a new dependency *with cause* (full JSON Schema 2020-12 is a MUST row in mcpx's own conformance matrix, and the library passes the JSON-Schema-Test-Suite and covers drafts 4/6/7/2019-09/2020-12). Do **not** extend `internal/mcpspec`: it is a deliberately test-only subset validator for the vendored protocol schemas (`TestNotImportedByBinary` keeps it out of the binary), and growing it into a general 2020-12 engine is writing a JSON Schema implementation as a side quest. No `user/review`: the direction is already set by the roadmap row at `proposed` and nix#254's acceptance criteria.

## Summary

mcpx forwards tool schemas it never enforces. The conformance matrix (`pkgs/mcpx/docs/spec/conformance-matrix.md`, 2025-11-25 lines 1380–1382; 2026-07-28 lines 2068–2075) carries the gap under nix#254, and `internal/conformance/coverage_messages.go` registers it:

- `json-schema-support-2020-12` (MUST) — "mcpx never validates arguments against a tool's inputSchema; schemas pass through"
- `json-schema-validate-per-dialect-and-error-on-unsupported` (MUST) — "no validator in the binary, so an unsupported $schema is forwarded, not refused" / "is accepted"
- `json-schema-document-dialects` (SHOULD) — "no document states which dialects mcpx supports"
- `json-schema-reject-unresolved-ref` (SHOULD) — "an unresolvable $ref is rendered permissively (codegen) rather than rejected"

Roadmap: `planning/roadmaps/mcpx.md` → Next → "JSON Schema validation of tool input and output" (status `proposed`, nix#254). Origin gap: dezren39/nix#254 (OPEN) — mcpx's canonical home is this repo, so the design and implementation live here and cite it; no fresh nix issue for the same change.

**Proposal — one validator, compiled once per tool at list time, enforced at the client choke point:**

- `internal/schemaval` (name indicative) wraps the library as the only import site. Dialect policy: no `$schema` → 2020-12 (MCP default); declared dialect must be one of 2020-12 / 2019-09 / draft-07 / draft-06 / draft-04, else a distinct `UnsupportedDialect` error. **No network, ever:** external `$ref` is an `UnresolvedRef` compile error, never a fetch (preserves the tested `json-schema-no-network-ref` MUST NOT). Formats are annotations, not assertions, in v1. Compilation is size-bounded. Errors carry instance paths (e.g. `$.count: expected integer, got string`).
- **List time:** `Client.ListTools` compiles each tool's `InputSchema`/`OutputSchema` beside the existing `checkToolHeaders` pass (`internal/mcpclient/modern.go:495`) and caches compiled validators per tool keyed by schema hash. A tool whose schema cannot compile is **excluded with a `Warning`** — the established x-mcp-header precedent ("a definition mcpx cannot honour is not forwarded"); the pool already wires `OnWarning` to `server.warning` lifecycle events.
- **Call time, inputs enforced:** `Client.CallTool` (`internal/mcpclient/client.go:1164`) validates arguments before send. Failure = -32602 Invalid Params (tool + path-qualified reason), surfaced by gateway paths as the protocol error it is, not an `isError` tool result; the upstream sees zero calls. The client is the choke point: `Pool.Call` (`internal/pool/pool.go:1028`), daemon `Registry.Call`, scripts, `mcpx_call` and pass-through all funnel through it.
- **Call time, outputs warn-only:** `structuredContent` validated against `outputSchema` when both present; failure = `Warning` + lifecycle event, result delivered unchanged. The caller did nothing wrong; flipping outputs to enforced is an open question answered with this warning data.
- **Elicitation answers enforced:** in `Client.answer` (`internal/mcpclient/modern.go:253`), after `applyDefaults` (which already parses `requestedSchema`), an `accept` answer's `content` is validated against `requestedSchema` (form mode); failure = -32602 to the requesting server, answer not relayed. The modern input-required flow inherits this via `answer()`. Only the mechanism slice of the elicitation rows — #255's storage/redaction/UI items are out of scope.

Grounding: `mcpclient.Tool` already carries both schemas raw (client.go:163-164); `internal/mcpspec/validate.go` header documents the subset validator's test-only scope and keyword list; codegen (`internal/codegen/ts.go`) stays a permissive type renderer — rejection belongs at list time, after which an excluded tool never reaches codegen through the catalog. Alternatives (extend mcpspec; xeipuuv/qri-io libraries — neither reaches 2020-12; validate in daemon/gateway instead of client; enforce outputs day one; do nothing) and risks (sloppy real-world schemas — mitigated structurally, no speculative per-server opt-out in v1; performance — compile cached, benchmark in Phase 2 acceptance; >2^53 number precision — library-required decoding + a Phase 1 test; dependency weight — one pure-Go module behind one package) are argued in the design doc.

## Phased breakdown

- **Phase 1 — validator core and dialect policy.** `internal/schemaval` + dependency + dialect document in `pkgs/mcpx/docs/`; no call-path changes, nothing enforces yet. Defining tests: 2020-12 keyword corpus, unsupported dialect refused, unresolvable `$ref` refused, remote `$ref` triggers zero requests against a counting test server, >2^53 integer validates as integer. Filed as a sub-issue of this issue.
- **Phase 2 — tool input enforcement + output warning at the client choke point.** List-time compile/exclude, `CallTool` argument validation (-32602, upstream call count 0 on failure), `structuredContent` warn-only validation, argument-validation benchmark. Requires Phase 1 merged. Filed as a sub-issue of this issue.
- **Phase 3 — elicitation form-answer validation.** `requestedSchema` check in `Client.answer` after defaults; wrong-typed answer → upstream receives -32602, not the answer. Requires Phase 1 merged; independent of Phase 2. Filed as a sub-issue of this issue.
- **Open questions, NOT filed.** Output enforcement flip (on Phase 2 warning data); format assertion for a named subset; per-server validation mode knob (only on fleet evidence); prompts/sampling reuse of `schemaval` (#256 is separate); codegen hard-fail for schemas from non-catalog sources.

---
agent-note:v1 — filed by the repo design architect (dedicated code job, pass 3, 2026-10-27). Design doc + register entry as linked above. Phases 1–3 are filed as sub-issues with `queue/queued` + `task/triage` packets enqueued to repo-health-code-pilot. Cross-repo note: dezren39/nix#254 is the origin gap record; this issue is the mcpx-canonical design that satisfies its acceptance — do not file a duplicate in nix.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The validator decision above (adopt santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6 behind `internal/schemaval`; mcpspec stays test-only) is the recorded decision nix#254's acceptance requires, or is superseded on this issue with reasons before implementation starts.
- [ ] Phases 1–3 land with their own acceptance criteria met, and the four #254 conformance gaps (support-2020-12, validate-per-dialect, document-dialects, reject-unresolved-ref) are updated in `pkgs/mcpx/docs/spec/conformance-matrix.md` / the gap registry as each phase lands.
- [ ] dezren39/nix#254 is closed or commented with a link to this issue once the phases land, so the origin record does not outlive the fix.

body:
## Policy (Drew, 2026-10-27)

Lint, format checks, and builds for this repo run in **GitHub Actions**. Contributors and fleet workers do **not** need to run them locally before pushing.

## Rules

- Push the branch and let CI run lint, format, and build/test workflows. Review the CI results on the PR.
- A local worktree or copy used **for review and edits only** is fine anywhere (including the Muse sandbox VM).
- **Running builds, test suites, linters, or formatters locally on the sandbox VM is not allowed** — the VM is a 2-core coordination box and local builds saturate it. When a check genuinely cannot run in CI, it runs on Drew's laptop (amd-6) instead, never on the sandbox.
- A red CI run is the signal to fix and re-push — not a reason to move the build back onto a local machine.

## Why

On 2026-10-27 the sandbox VM sat at load ~25 on 2 cores from fleet workers compiling in local worktrees (rustc in two fleet worktrees plus a probe crate), repeatedly dropping the owner's app connection. The work itself was fine; the location was the problem. CI runners exist for exactly this.

## Acceptance

- [ ] This policy is reflected in the repo's contributor/agent guidance (AGENTS.md or equivalent) in one short section.
- [ ] CI workflows cover lint + format + build for the main packages, so no change needs a local run to be verified.
- [ ] Fleet shift instructions reference CI as the verification path (they already route heavy work to the laptop; CI is preferred where it covers the check).

## Finding

PR #1390 (merged, merge commit `37418e56339c315cf0ddf3e61c9c55c1e9d0c0a2`) added roughly a thousand lines of new computation to the Cost Explorer's inline browser script in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/render.ts` — the recommendations engine, the Pareto frontier tables, the Pareto-gap inequality filters, and the task-assumptions projection — with no committed tests for any of that logic. The PR's test changes cover only the data layer (`aaCaiPoints`, `caiFamily`, catalog rate windows) plus HTML `toContain` assertions that the new sections' element ids exist. The PR body says the script was "runtime-smoke-tested against the fixture data" — a one-off manual check that is not in the repo and cannot regress.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/1390 (MERGED 2026-10-27)
- New untested logic on current main, all inside the `AA_EXPLORER_SCRIPT` template string in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/render.ts`:
  - `render.ts:2092` `pctRank` — percentile ranks shown in every Pareto table cell
  - `render.ts:2105` `paretoSet` — non-dominated set behind all four frontier tables
  - `render.ts:2170` `gapMetrics` — score gap / price premium / speed gap behind the inequality filters
  - `render.ts:2814` `computeRecs` — banding, near-top floors, relative price/speed ceilings, dominance removal, tradeoff ranking `(relative time)^w × (relative price)^(1−w)`, lab-diversity passes
  - `render.ts:3191` `project` (+ `pjBand` band/window selection) — projected $/task and time/task; the PR body hand-verifies one fixture case (~$0.106/task, ~5m 53s) that is not encoded as a test
- `pm-stack/aggregator/test/aa.test.ts` on current main contains zero references to `computeRecs`, `project`/`pjBand`, `gapMetrics`, or `pctRank` (grep-verified); the new render assertions are `expect(html).toContain('id="xpl-pf-score"')`-style presence checks.

## Why it matters

These functions produce numbers a reader acts on (shortlists, projected costs). Because they live in a template string, neither `tsc` nor the existing test suite exercises them at all — a sign flip in `pctRank`, a band-selection off-by-one in `pjBand`, or a dominance error in `computeRecs` ships silently. The one hand-verified projection example in the PR body is exactly the kind of case that should have become a fixture test.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The explorer script's pure computations (at minimum `project`/`pjBand`, `paretoSet`, `pctRank`, `gapMetrics`, and `computeRecs` banding/ranking) are covered by committed tests that run in the aggregator's normal `bun test` — e.g. by extracting them into an importable module the template string also uses, or by evaluating the script against the fixture data in a test harness.
- [ ] The PR body's hand-verified projection case (Luna fixture rate: 3 turns × (10k uncached @ $0.75 + 10k cache reads @ $0.075 + 6k output @ $4.50) ≈ $0.106/task; time ≈ 5m 53s) is encoded as a test expectation.
- [ ] Existing suite stays green (`bun test` in `pm-stack/aggregator`, `bunx tsc --noEmit` clean).

Found by pr-diff-review-b reviewing PR #1390's diff against current main. Remainder items for the same PR are already tracked in #1400; this test-coverage gap is not among them.

## Finding

PR #1387's benchmark harness (`pkgs/id/benches/world_bench.rs`, head commit `b6f5b720e9fc7d117f44b46181818d114dbad3aa`) silently succeeds when `--only <name>` names no known benchmark: it prints nothing and exits 0. The same applies to any misspelled or renamed benchmark name.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/1387 (OPEN, slice 1 of #539)
- `pkgs/id/benches/world_bench.rs:216-218` — `main` parses `--only` into an optional string; each benchmark is then gated by `run(name) = only.is_none() || only == Some(name)`. An unmatched name gates off all four benchmarks, `main` returns `Ok(())`, and the process exits 0 with no output and no error.

## Why it matters

The harness's stated contract (file header) is that slice 3's CI job will parse its `bench <name> unit=... median=...` lines and diff medians against the committed baseline. A typo'd or stale `--only` name in that CI job would produce an empty run that passes — the exact silent-green failure a benchmark gate must not have.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `--only <unknown>` exits non-zero with an error naming the valid benchmark names.
- [ ] Running with no `--only` and with each valid `--only <name>` behaves exactly as today (one `bench ...` line per selected benchmark).

Refs #539. Found by pr-diff-review-b reviewing PR #1387's diff.

**Covered sites** — the shared fixtures in `pkgs/id/src/test_forgeries.rs` (`IDENTITY_KEY` small-order key, `identity_forgery()`, `with_non_canonical_s()`) are used by per-site regressions at 5 of the 7 direct `verify_strict` call sites in `pkgs/id/src`: `artifact.rs:306`, `directory.rs:396`, `directory_auth.rs:349`, `directory_log.rs:100`, `web/identity.rs:373`.

Existing coverage is generic only: `pkgs/id/tests/invites.rs` `a_bad_event_signature_refuses_the_accept_with_no_send` (bit flip) and `changing_the_role_or_the_expiry_breaks_the_signature` (tamper). Neither pins the strict-only rejections (an identity-key forgery that plain `verify` would accept, or an S+L non-canonical signature).
2. `pkgs/id/src/seitan/accept.rs:142` — `accept::verify` for seitan proofs. `pkgs/id/src/seitan/tests.rs` covers wrong key, tampered message bytes, a forged key, and a zero signature, but not the small-order identity forgery or non-canonical S via the shared fixtures.

The indirect 8th site (event headers via p2panda-core `AnyHeader::decode`, used at `pkgs/id/src/chain.rs:323`) is upstream code; its mutation resistance is covered locally by `pkgs/id/tests/chain_properties.rs` (`test_a_single_changed_byte_is_always_refused`) — no action needed there unless the audit decides otherwise.

## Acceptance criteria

- A regression at the invites site proving `verify_signature` rejects (a) an invite event signed under the small-order identity key with the `identity_forgery()` signature, and (b) a valid signature mutated with `with_non_canonical_s()`.
- A regression at the seitan site proving `accept::verify` rejects both fixture classes the same way.
- Tests use the shared `crate::test_forgeries` fixtures (no new fixture copies) and pass in the normal Rust unit layer.

title: id(web): ordered lists with ) markers are rewritten to . on save — list delimiter style is dropped by the codec

body:
## Summary

An ordered list written with parenthesis markers (`1) one`) is silently rewritten to period markers (`1. one`) the first time the document is saved from the web editor. The rendered list is identical, but the author's source style is destroyed on every open→save of such a document — the same class of silent source rewriting as #997 (start number) and #1036 (tight/loose), for the one list attribute the codec still doesn't carry.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `17c2be5d`)

Round-trip through the verbatim codec (probe crate, `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-creator-a/out5.log`, case `paren-delim-ordered`; control in `probe8`):

- Codec: `1) one\n2) two\n` → PM `ordered_list` with attrs `{order: 1, tight: true}` (no delimiter) → save → `1. one\n2. two\n` (fixpoint thereafter — the `)` form is unrecoverable after one save).
- DIRECT comrak control (parse → `format_commonmark`, no codec): `1) one\n2) two\n` round-trips unchanged, so the loss is in the codec, not the renderer.

Root cause, `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs`:

- Parse direction, `NodeValue::List` arm (~:254-264): `ordered_list` attrs store only `order` (`list.start`) and `tight`. comrak's `NodeList` carries the marker style in `delimiter: ListDelimType` (`Period`/`Paren`, comrak nodes.rs:373) — it is never read. The ordered `task_list` arm (~:234-240) drops it the same way.
- Save direction, `ordered_list` arm (~:1200-1211) and ordered `task_list` arm (~:1238-1244): `NodeList { list_type: ListType::Ordered, ..Default::default() }` — `Default` is `ListDelimType::Period`, so every ordered list is emitted with `.`.
- `pkgs/id/web/src/editor.ts`: the `ordered_list`/`task_list` schema likewise has no delimiter attr, so the editor cannot round-trip it either (cf. the `order`/`tight` attrs added there for #997/#1036).

## Why it matters

- Silent, irreversible source churn for any document authored with `)` markers (a common style, and the default in some editors that users paste/import from).
- It is the last uncarried `NodeList` field: `start` (#997) and `tight` (#1036) were both fixed by carrying the attr both directions; `delimiter` was left behind.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `1) one\n2) two\n` round-trips byte-identically through markdown → PM → markdown (codec test), and is a fixpoint.
- [ ] `1. one` lists render exactly as before (no change for period-style lists).
- [ ] Ordered task lists keep their delimiter too (e.g. `1) [ ] x` if the parser accepts the form; otherwise the exclusion is noted in the test).
- [ ] Legacy PM docs without the new attr save exactly as today (delimiter defaults to period).
- [ ] `editor.ts` `ordered_list` (and `task_list`, if applicable) schema carries the attr with a period default, mirroring the #997/#1036 pattern.
- [ ] Existing `web::markdown` tests still pass.

Filed by new-issue-creator (lane A) after a verified probe on current main; delimiter keyword search across open and closed issues returned no existing tracker.

The fleet's publish step evaporates the same way its claims used to: work finishes in a worktree and the push/PR step never happens.

- **62 commits on no origin branch, across 37 trees** — almost all finished queue/sweep work (worst: `wt-1058`, 10 commits). Includes task 1149's completed #530 branch commit.
- **13 trees with uncommitted work (139 entries)** — worst: the home repo (`~`): 98 dirty files **and the fleet's own Supabase migration commits 0009–0012 unpushed**.
- **143 GitHub branches ahead of main with no open PR** (code 66, opencode 44, openchamber 19, nix 14) — a mix of Jules debris, bot branches, and real feature work (opencode `session-messaging` +44, `github-tools` +33).

- **Hazard:** task 1157's cursor-quota work sits dirty in TWO worktrees with divergent heads (`~/git/devtoday-openchamber-wt-1157`, `~/work/oc-wt-1157`).
- Primary clones are healthy (code/openchamber/nix clean+pushed; opencode 2 behind). One fleet submodule fetch timed out during the audit — one tree's status unverified.

## This effort

1. Push every already-committed local-only branch (no force-push; rejections recorded, not fought).
2. Open PRs for finished queue-task branches whose work is complete and whose issue is still open (body notes the reconciliation origin); skip branches whose issue is closed or whose PR already merged.
3. Classify — do not commit — every dirty tree: in-flight lane work vs abandoned vs the divergent 1157 pair (flagged for a decision, untouched).

body:
## Problem

A `.md` file that starts with YAML front matter is destroyed by one open → save cycle in the id web editor. The front matter is not preserved, hidden, or rejected — it is silently rewritten into unrelated document structure.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `0cbb91b1`)

Probe: verbatim copy of `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs` in a standalone crate (comrak 0.56.0), `markdown_to_prosemirror` → `prosemirror_to_markdown` round-trip. Logs: fleet bookkeeping `probe-2026-10-27-creator-a/out.log` + `out4.log`.

Input:

```markdown
---
title: Hello World
date: 2026-01-02
tags: [a, b]
---

# Heading

Body text.
```

Parsed PM doc: a `horizontal_rule`, then a level-2 **heading** whose text is `title: Hello World date: 2026-01-02 tags: [a, b]` (the YAML lines fused by soft breaks; the closing `---` became the setext underline), then the real heading and body.

Saved output:

```markdown
-----

## title: Hello World date: 2026-01-02 tags: \[a, b\]

# Heading

Body text.
```

The front matter is gone as metadata: any static-site/tooling consumer of the file loses title/date/tags, and the document gains a spurious rule and a nonsense heading. The mangled form is a fixpoint, so the loss is silent and permanent after the first save. A blank line inside the YAML block mangles differently again (first key becomes a paragraph, a later key becomes the heading) — no front-matter shape survives.

Root cause: `commonmark_options` (`pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs:81-91`) enables strikethrough/tasklist/table/footnotes but not comrak's front-matter support, and the codec has no node representation for front matter, so the `---` fences parse as a thematic break + setext heading.

## Why it matters

Front matter is the default header format for markdown notes and docs (Obsidian, Hugo, Jekyll, Astro, Docusaurus, GitHub Pages). id is a general markdown file editor; any user who opens such a file and saves — including an unrelated one-character edit, or autosave — silently corrupts the file's metadata and structure. Same loss class as #1306/#1307 (plain-mode fidelity), but for the much more common `.md` path.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `.md` doc beginning with YAML front matter round-trips byte-identically (or semantically identically with the front-matter block verbatim) through open → save, including multi-key blocks, blocks containing blank lines, and a doc whose body starts with a heading or with plain text.
- [ ] The front matter is not editable-as-body by accident: whatever representation is chosen (dedicated PM node, codec-level strip-and-restore, or equivalent), the editor does not present the YAML lines as a heading/paragraph the user can half-delete.
- [ ] A leading `---` that is NOT front matter (e.g. a thematic break after a paragraph, `Para one.\n\n---\n\nPara two.`) still round-trips as a horizontal rule — verified control case in the probe.
- [ ] Regression tests in `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs` cover the shapes above (round-trip + fixpoint), mirroring the existing codec test style.
- [ ] TOML (`+++`) front matter is either supported the same way or explicitly documented as out of scope in the fix PR.

body:
## Purpose

Drew (2026-10-27): a regular check on quotas and route pools — whether the latest models are incorporated, whether the best model per pool is chosen, and whether pool members are right-sized against each other and against the pool's speed/cost/performance requirements.

The fleet already has an hourly steward (balances burn across pools as composed) and daily pool-intelligence (AA market data + our measured speeds + add/retire flags). Neither owns *membership*: twice a day, this review audits whether each pool's composition is still correct and hands the steward changes that are ready to land.

## The three checks (every run, every pool)

Pools in scope: scout / workhorse / specialist / summit + *-plan variants in the canonical config (developing-today/code `.opencode/opencode.jsonc`), plus OpenChamber's routing categories.

1. **Latest-model check** — newly released models (from pool-intelligence's AA data + provider catalogs) missing from the pool where they'd belong, named with AA standing vs current members, plan/quota home, and the member displaced or joined.
2. **Best-per-pool check** — is each pool's current lead the right choice given AA values, the pool's quota window + reset time, AND our historical per-model/per-effort statistics from real sessions (babysitter log, session store, meta-reviewer scorecards)? A lead that wins on AA but loses on our sessions — or draws on a window about to reset while an equal model sits on a fresh window — is a misalignment, with numbers.
3. **Right-sizing check** — members matched to each other and to the pool's job: measured speeds differing ~3× inside one pool doing the same work, a summit-class model on mechanical work, a fast-cheap member carrying work its success rate says it shouldn't, or interchangeable members where one burns a scarcer window — each named with numbers.

## Outputs

- A review section appended per run to `hidden_files/pool-composition-log.md` (per-pool verdicts; aligned is a verdict too).
- Ledger-ready change proposals handed to the steward (pool, change, expected measurable effect, evidence). The review NEVER edits config itself — changes land through the steward's PR path.
- Add/retire flags filed as their own issues when they clear the quantified bar (same pattern as pool-intelligence).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The `pool-composition-review` job is live at a 12h cadence with its instruction file in the goal workspace.
- [ ] The first review covers every pool in the canonical config plus the OpenChamber routing categories, with per-pool verdicts in the composition log.
- [ ] The first run produces at least one steward-ready recommendation, or a verified-aligned result per pool with the numbers that show it.

body:
PRIORITY — Drew, 2026-10-27 02:18 CDT ("make it a priority"). Context: the sandbox opencode server is STOPPED for good (Drew's laptop-only ruling, 2026-10-27) — all opencode work now runs against the laptop. Two access patterns exist; which one should be the fleet's default for opencode work is an open, measurable question.

THE COMPARISON (benchmark, don't opinion-shop):
A) SSH onto the laptop and run opencode there — CLI/TUI/sessions execute on the laptop, driven over ~/tools/laptop-ssh.sh (multiplexed). Agent tooling shells in, runs commands, reads output.
B) Attach to the laptop's opencode server over the network — the fork's attach/remote modes and/or the HTTP API (and OpenChamber pointed at the laptop server via OPENCODE_HOST + OPENCODE_SKIP_START), with the server reached directly over Tailscale or via an SSH port-forward.

MEASURE, on identical scripted workloads (session create, prompt round-trips on a small model, a multi-step file task, quota CLI run, session list/read):
- Latency: time-to-first-token and per-call round-trip overhead (local-on-laptop vs Tailscale-direct vs SSH-forward), incl. connection setup cost per invocation.
- Throughput/reliability: long-running session behavior, dropped-connection recovery (SSH session death vs server attach reconnect), concurrent sessions.
- Locality: where config/credentials/plan store/db live in each pattern (both are laptop-side in A; in B the server holds them and the client is thin — spell out what still executes client-side, e.g. the quota CLI's credential resolution).
- Failure modes: laptop asleep/rebooting, Tailscale down (SSH also rides it — note the shared dependency), server not running vs sshd not running.
- Fit with our tooling: stewardship dispatch, OpenChamber (its Remote Instances are SSH-based — mechanism (a) from the 2026-10-22 linking research), the quota gatherer (already laptop-resident), mcpx.
Prior art to reuse, not redo: 2026-10-22 OpenChamber linking research (three mechanisms; SSH forwards of laptop :3000 + opencode :40671 proven from the sandbox); laptop serve ports observed then: 43853 / 40671 / 13420.

DELIVERABLE: a short benchmark report in the usage-billing-hub goal files (or a more fitting fleet location — name it in the report), a DECISION RECORD with the recommended default pattern per use case (interactive agent work / scripted API calls / OpenChamber use), and follow-on implementation issues for whatever wiring the winner needs. If the answer differs by use case, say so with the measurements — a split verdict is a fine outcome.
Acceptance: both patterns benchmarked on the same workloads with numbers; decision recorded; follow-ons filed.

## Acceptance criteria

- Both access patterns (SSH-on-laptop vs attaching to the laptop opencode server over the network) are benchmarked on the same workloads, with numbers recorded on this issue.
- A decision is recorded: the fleet default pattern, or a split verdict by use case where the measurements differ.
- Follow-on implementation issues are filed for whatever wiring the winning pattern needs (including OpenChamber use).

## Question

`openai-codex` and `chatgpt` — two provider ids that both front the same Codex proxy door (127.0.0.1:18744) — sit in `disabled_providers`. They entered that list in commit f5749275 ("chore(config): commit laptop fleet config working-tree state"), a bulk state commit, so the repo records no reasoning. Meanwhile the plan pools (luna-plan, sol-plan, terra-plan) address the bare `openai` provider + `openai.alternate` for OpenAI traffic, and the codex proxy itself is healthy and supervised.

## Why it matters

- If the disable is **deliberate** (e.g. the two ids duplicate one quota and route traffic should never split across them), it should be documented in the config header like the other disables (the 2026-10-24 provider-alignment note explains google/antigravity-agy but not these).
- If it is **debris** from the working-tree commit, the fleet's intended OpenAI door for plan traffic may actually be the codex proxy, and the bare `openai` provider leaves in every plan pool deserve a second look (what credential/quota do they draw on?).

## Ask

Decide and record: (a) un-disable one or both ids and adjust plan-pool doors accordingly, or (b) keep them disabled and add the reasoning to the config header note. Surfaced by the 2026-10-27 validation sweep that caught terra-plan (PR #1296) pointing at these disabled providers; terra-plan was retargeted to openai + openai.alternate in the meantime.

## Acceptance criteria

- The question is answered on this issue with evidence: either (a) the disable was deliberate, with the reasoning recorded in the opencode config header note, or (b) it was an accident of the bulk commit f5749275 and `openai-codex`/`chatgpt` are re-enabled (or the plan-pool doors adjusted) accordingly.
- Whichever outcome: the config in the repo and the recorded reasoning agree, and no plan-pool door points at a disabled provider (the terra-plan failure mode from PR #1296).

body:
# id(web): every .txt open→save drops the final newline (and rewrites CRLF to LF) — Plain mode is not byte-faithful unlike Raw

## Summary

Opening a plain-text (`.txt`) file in id and saving it — even with no
edits — rewrites the file: the final newline is always removed, and
CRLF line endings are converted to LF. Raw mode round-trips
byte-exactly; Plain mode does not.

## Evidence

- Load: `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs:1825` `plain_text_to_prosemirror`
  splits with `str::lines()`, which yields no element for a single
  trailing newline and strips the `\r` of CRLF endings.
- Save: `pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs:2009` `extract_plain_text` joins
  paragraphs with `"\n"` and appends nothing at the end — so the
  trailing newline the load discarded can never come back.
- Verified this run on origin/main 90f7ea00 with a probe crate running
  the real load function plus the verbatim save function (log:
  `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-26-2352/out3.log`):
  - `"alpha\nbeta\n"` → `"alpha\nbeta"` (final newline lost)
  - `"alpha\n"` → `"alpha"`; `"\n"` → `""`; `"alpha\n\n"` → `"alpha\n"`
  - `"alpha\r\nbeta\r\n"` → `"alpha\nbeta"` (CRLF rewritten to LF)
  - Controls that round-trip exactly: `"alpha\nbeta"` (no trailing
    newline) and `""`.
- Contrast: Raw mode (`raw_text_to_prosemirror` /
  `extract_raw_text`) keeps the whole file in one code block and
  round-trips byte-exactly, including the trailing newline.

## Why it matters

Every POSIX text file ends in a newline; a no-op open→save in id
produces a spurious diff (`\ No newline at end of file`), breaks
tools that require a terminating newline, and silently converts
CRLF files (common for notes shared with Windows editors) to LF.
Fidelity loss in the mode whose entire job is plain bytes.

## Acceptance criteria

- A documented, tested policy makes no-edit open→save of a `.txt`
  file byte-stable for the common shapes: trailing newline present
  or absent, and CRLF endings (either preserved, or — if LF
  normalization is the deliberate choice — called out in the mode's
  docs and pinned by a test, not accidental).
- Regression tests cover at least: `"a\nb\n"`, `"a\nb"`, `"a\n"`,
  `""`, and a CRLF sample, through the real load→save pair.
- Markdown and Raw save/load behavior unchanged.

## Notes

The information loss happens at load (`lines()` cannot distinguish
`"a"` from `"a\n"`), so a fix likely needs the load side to carry the
trailing-newline fact (e.g. a trailing empty paragraph, mirroring how
`"a\n\n"` already loads) or the save side to adopt an
always-terminate policy — triage should pick and pin one.

# fleet(queue): repo-queue.py — add list/inspect, surface dedupe hits, document priority direction

Three frictions hit while sequencing the Path-to-Phase-12 queue (2026-10-26), each verified live:

1. **No way to see the queue.** `repo-queue.py` has validate/enqueue/claim/.../health, but health is counts only. Answering "what is queued, in what order?" required direct SQL against `agent.tasks` via the Supabase Management API. Add `list --queue <q> [--status ...]` printing id, priority, status, dedupe key, title, age — ordered the way `claim_repo_task` will claim them.
2. **Enqueue dedupe is silent and cross-queue.** Enqueueing a packet whose dedupe key matches an existing task returns that task — including tasks in OTHER queues (a completed `repo-health-code-shadow` investigation ate the #551 triage packet) and terminal states (a done Oct 25 task ate the #229 packet). The caller can't tell "created" from "deduped against task N in queue Q with status S". Print that explicitly, and warn when the match is terminal or in a different queue.
3. **Priority semantics are undocumented and coarse.** `claim_repo_task` orders `priority ASC, created_at ASC` (lower = sooner) — the helper never says so, and the validator's scale [10,20,30,40,50,70,90] has too few rungs to encode a 14-step sequence (we used 10–22 by direct DB update). Document the direction in the helper + schema, and either widen the scale or document the intended sequencing mechanism (same-priority FIFO by enqueue order).

None of these blocked the work — the DB is fully accessible and was used — but every fleet operator re-derives them by hand today.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] repo-queue.py gains `list --queue <q> [--status ...]` printing task id (rendered `task <id>`), priority, status, dedupe key, title, and age, ordered the way claim_repo_task will claim them.
- [ ] Enqueue surfaces a dedupe hit explicitly: when the returned task already existed — in any queue or terminal state — the output says so and names that task's queue/status, instead of looking like a fresh enqueue (see also #1298).
- [ ] The priority direction (which end claims first) is documented in the helper's help/docs, and the #1274 prefix convention is followed in the new output.

# pm-stack(grist): apply external doc changes live — no full server restart

Companion to the Choice-options API gap. Tonight's dropdown fix required stopping and restarting the whole Grist server to make it re-read its own document database; during the window the PM aggregator served fallbacks.

## Wanted
A way to make a running Grist server pick up an externally-applied document change without a process restart, any of:
- an admin "reload/reopen document" endpoint,
- a file-watch on the doc store that safely reopens changed docs (with the doc idle / no active editors),
- or a documented, safe `grist` CLI subcommand for offline doc edits that a running server tolerates.

## Why it matters beyond tonight
The pm-stack direction is more generated content (roadmap seed sync, dashboard build-out #1239). Every generated-schema or bulk-metadata change currently costs a restart window. Live-apply turns those into routine, automatable operations. If upstream Grist can't do this, the fallback ask is a first-class maintenance mode in OUR stack: aggregator drains to fixtures, Grist restarts, health-verified return — scripted end to end instead of by hand.

## Acceptance criteria

- A running Grist server picks up an externally-applied document change (e.g. a Choice-options extension) without a full server restart — or, if upstream Grist (OSS v1.7.21, pinned in pm-stack/grist/compose.yml) cannot do this, the fallback ships instead: a scripted maintenance mode in our stack (aggregator drains to fixtures, Grist restarts, health-verified return) that runs end to end unattended.
- During the operation the PM aggregator never serves silent stale/fallback data without signalling it.
- The procedure is documented with the pm-stack docs and exercised once against the Program roadmap doc.

Part of epic #1184 (PM stack coherence — wave 2, 2026-10-26).

Opening an item today means assembling its story by hand: state on one page, blockers as prose, last activity in the projector/GitHub stream, sessions on another page. A per-item AI brief panel — "explain this item" — does that assembly: current state in plain language, why it is blocked (with the blocker named and linked), who or what acted last and when, and a suggested next action, each claim carrying an evidence link into the underlying data. The brief is derived from the canonical projection + item activity at request time, is labelled as derived wherever it renders, and is never silently authoritative: where the data disagrees with itself, the brief says so and shows both sides rather than picking one. It renders on the item page and inside Needs-you cards, and its JSON twin exposes the same brief so agents read the identical summary Drew does.

Acceptance:
- Every board/roadmap/Project item can render a brief containing state, blocker (or "not blocked"), last actor + time, and a suggested next action, each with an evidence link.
- Briefs are visibly labelled as derived, and a source disagreement on the item is stated in the brief instead of resolved silently.
- The brief is available via the item's machine-first JSON twin with identical content.
- A brief for an item with no activity/blocker renders honestly (states what is unknown) rather than inventing a narrative; covered by fixture tests for blocked, in-flight, and idle items.

## Acceptance criteria

- A per-item 'explain this item' brief panel exists assembling: current state in plain language, blocker (named and linked), last actor/activity, and a suggested next action.
- Nothing in the brief is asserted without a source in the underlying data — unknowns are stated as unknown, not narrated over.

Views are stored dashboard-side like comments are (the aggregator's own store), operate over the canonical work-item projection, and render through the existing pages rather than forking new ones — a saved view is a parameterisation of Board/Projects/Roadmap, not a new surface to keep coherent.

Part of epic #1149; supports #1151 (gatherer). Priority P1. Observed 2026-10-26: a full `openchamber quota --json` run over 7 configured providers took ~19s wall — fetching appears effectively sequential and unbounded per provider. At ~30 catalogue providers on a 15-minute gatherer tick, that profile risks tick overruns and head-of-line blocking by one slow dashboard API.
Work: parallelize provider fetching in the CLI/module list path with a bounded concurrency (e.g. 6) and a per-provider timeout (default 10s, configurable); a timed-out provider returns a timeout state row, never blocks the batch; the gatherer gets a total tick budget with per-adapter time reported in its heartbeat (feeds #1116/#1175).

## Acceptance criteria
- A refresh fetches all providers' quota data in parallel instead of serial awaits.
- The refresh is bounded by a timeout budget, so total wall time is capped regardless of provider count.
- A slow or hung provider degrades to its last-known snapshot with the staleness visible, instead of stalling the whole refresh.

body:
Found live 2026-10-26 (Drew: "there should always be a server listening... ensure everything is correctly handled"). Part of epic #1149's world; boot persistence itself is code#903 — this issue is the quota-plane side.

Facts: on the current sandbox boot the opencode-serve system unit did not exist (recycle wiped it; init.sh's install run_step had not restored it), so `openchamber quota` failed wholesale with "Transport: fetch failed" — every provider dark at once. Restored manually via the sanctioned path (bash ~/tools/install-opencode-service.sh): unit active, /api/provider 200, CLI then returned per-provider results (cline-pass/deepseek/opencode-go/openai.alternate/codex-legacy ok).
Work:
1. Boot verification: something in the boot path (init-ensure or the installer run_step) must VERIFY opencode-serve is active + API 200 each boot and restore it if not — not merely attempt install. Coordinate with code#903 rather than duplicating its scope.
2. CLI/module resilience: when the server is unreachable, the quota module should fall back to its direct credential-store read (readOpenCodeCredentials) for providers whose fetchers accept injected reads, and report per-provider errors — never one wholesale transport failure.
3. Claude credential expiry (found in the same pass): the claude provider errors "Claude session expired. Open Claude Code to sign in again." Define + document the re-login path for the sandbox's Claude Code credential and who/what performs it; expiry must surface as a user/owned item, not a silent stale card.
Acceptance: kill the server -> quota reads degrade per-provider with clear errors; reboot the sandbox -> server verified listening without manual steps; claude expiry produces a visible re-login task.

## Acceptance criteria

- With opencode-serve killed, `openchamber quota` degrades per-provider: providers with a direct credential-store read still report, and unreachable ones return clear per-provider errors — never one wholesale transport failure.
- After a sandbox reboot/recycle, the boot path verifies opencode-serve is active and its API answers 200, restoring it without manual steps when it is missing (coordinated with #903, not duplicating it).
- Claude credential expiry produces a visible re-login task/item (user/owned lane) with the documented re-login path, instead of a silently stale quota card.

title: OpenClaw: share one opencode serve via a small ACP-to-HTTP adapter

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/m
labels.description: Medium: expected under 1 day of work

labels.name: meta/enriched
labels.description: Intake review done: acceptance criteria, links, and normalized labels added

body:
## Problem

OpenClaw's only coding-harness protocol is ACP, and `opencode acp` starts a **private** OpenCode server per process by design (OpenCode v2 docs: "starts a private OpenCode server for its own use. It doesn't connect to the shared background service"). Meanwhile every other OpenCode client (TUI `opencode attach`, `opencode run --attach`, JS SDK `createOpencodeClient({ baseUrl })`, desktop, web, OpenChamber via `OPENCODE_HOST` + `OPENCODE_SKIP_START=true`) can drive **one** shared `opencode serve`. Result on the laptop today: OpenChamber's managed serve + a background `serve --service` + per-session ACP processes, each spawning its own llama.cpp embedding child — duplicate processes, split session state, and per-turn cold boots against the shared SQLite DB (a third-party integrator measured 0/24 success under 8-concurrent load cold-booting vs 6/6 through one shared server).

Research (2026-10-26): `~/workspace/research_notes/openclaw-opencode-single-server-research-20261027-0359/report.md` — no fork of OpenClaw or OpenCode is needed; no existing ClawHub plugin bridges ACP to the serve HTTP API.

## Design: a small ACP↔HTTP adapter

A single-purpose shim executable that speaks ACP (JSON-RPC over stdio) on one side and the OpenCode serve HTTP API on the other, registered in OpenClaw exactly where `opencode acp` sits today:

```nix
plugins.entries.acpx.config.agents.opencode = {
  command = "<adapter>";
  args = [ "--server" "http://127.0.0.1:4096" ];
};
```

Mapping:
- ACP `session/new` → `POST /session` (cwd → directory scoping)
- ACP `session/prompt` → `POST /session/:id/message` (or `prompt_async` + `GET /event` SSE for streaming updates back as ACP session/update notifications)
- serve permission events → ACP `session/request_permission` → reply via `POST /session/:id/permissions/:permissionID`
- ACP `session/cancel` → `POST /session/:id/abort`
- Auth: `OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD` basic auth, sourced from sops like the other OpenClaw secrets.

Companion changes:
- Run ONE `opencode serve` as a user service on a fixed port (4096, loopback; password via sops) started before front-ends.
- OpenChamber pointed at it (`OPENCODE_HOST`, `OPENCODE_SKIP_START=true`) so it stops spawning its own managed server.
- Retire the stale background `serve --service` instance once the shared server is canonical.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `/acp spawn opencode` in OpenClaw creates a session **on the shared server** (visible via `GET /session` and in OpenChamber/TUI attached to the same server).
- [ ] A prompt round-trip through OpenClaw streams output and completes; permission requests surface in OpenClaw and resolve via the permissions endpoint.
- [ ] Only one `opencode serve` process (and one embedding child) on the laptop during an OpenClaw coding session.
- [ ] Adapter lives in this repo, is covered by the OpenClaw Nix config, and the interim `opencode acp` override remains a one-line fallback.

## Notes

- Interim state (already live): ACP per-session processes; keep sessions non-persistent by default.
- Related adoptables from the same research pass, tracked separately: memory-lancedb in `plugins.slots.memory` (verify the official npm package name first — two candidates claim it), OmOC-style persona/tool-restriction shapes remapped to fleet quota pools (do NOT adopt its flagship-model category defaults).

## Acceptance criteria

- The adapter executable speaks ACP (JSON-RPC over stdio) on one side and the OpenCode serve HTTP API on the other, and registers in OpenClaw exactly where `opencode acp` sits today (agents.opencode command/args).

body:
Follow-up to #229, from queue task 1240's classification of the isolated Firefox dispatch run [40402931464](https://github.com/developing-today/code/actions/runs/40402931464) (PR #987 branch). Nine of the 13 persistent failures are timing/environment artefacts of the nix-VM e2e sandbox, in two clusters:

**A. Autosave exact save-count race** — `autosave.spec.ts:145/:191/:226` fail only on exact request-count assertions (expected 1/2, received 2/3; one retry 3). The tests race the app's 2s debounce autosave against a manual Ctrl+S/click save (test comment: "Hit Ctrl+S immediately (before 2s debounce)"); under VM-Firefox slowness the debounce also fires, the parallel saves hit the server's real 5s per-file save rate limiter (`DEFAULT_SAVE_COOLDOWN`, `pkgs/id/src/web/mod.rs`) — the save button visibly entered `retry…` in :145 attempt 1 — and the 429-retry adds further requests. All saves themselves succeed; no content assertion failed. Open sub-question a local repro can settle: does a manual save fail to cancel a pending debounce (product defect), or is this purely test timing?

**B. Websocket-spec server stall window** — `websocket.spec.ts:488/:519` fail with `apiRequestContext.get: socket hang up` on the post-save `GET /blob/<hash>`; `:644/:657/:676/:713` all time out in `setupCollabPair` (`page1.fill("#new-file-name")` never satisfiable). Timeline: tests 1–12 pass in 2–4s each; one degraded window 23:33:54–23:39:41Z (connection resets → brief recovery, Error Recovery tests pass → ~4 min home page unservable → spontaneous recovery, :761/:779 pass). All pure-websocket behaviour tests passed.

## Acceptance criteria
- Cluster A: either the count assertions are made timing-robust (await debounce quiescence / count only post-trigger saves), or the debounce-cancellation product defect is proven with a local repro and filed as a fix packet.
- Cluster B: server-side evidence for the stall is captured (VM resource pressure vs server stall) and a concrete hardening is proposed/recorded (resource bump, per-test server restart, or harness retry-on-stall).
- Findings posted on this issue. Merging PR #987 is out of scope (recommended separately on #229).

Evidence pack: goal `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-27-t1240/` (`failures.txt`, `progress.txt`), classification comment on #229 by queue task 1240.

body:
## Papercut / inconsistency

The save direction of the id web markdown codec treats unknown names inconsistently:

- Unknown **node** type → hard error: `ConversionError::UnknownType` (pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs:1186). The caller learns the document could not be converted faithfully.
- Unknown **mark** type → silently skipped: `create_marked_text` (markdown.rs:1442-1459) matches `em` / `strong` / `strikethrough` / `link` and falls through with `_ => continue, // Skip code (handled below) and unknown marks`. The text survives; the formatting vanishes with no error and no signal.

## Evidence (verified 2026-10-26 on main cf60812d)

Standalone probe crate carrying a verbatim copy of `src/web/markdown.rs` (comrak 0.56.0 locked) — log in goal hidden_files `probe-2026-10-26-2145/out3.log`:

- `SAVE unknown_node` (doc containing a `mention` node) → `ERR=UnknownType("mention")`
- `SAVE unknown_mark` (paragraph text `hi` carrying an `underline` mark) → `ok="hi\n"` — mark gone, no error

## Why it matters

ProseMirror documents reach this codec from the editor, collab peers, imports, and API writers — producers whose mark vocabularies can be larger than the codec's four-plus-code (underline and highlight are the obvious examples). Today a document using one saves "successfully" while quietly losing that formatting everywhere it appears. Either behavior can be defended — erroring like nodes, or skipping marks by design — but the split is currently accidental, undocumented at the API level, and untested: the `continue` arm's comment lumps deliberate `code` handling together with arbitrary unknown marks.

## Acceptance criteria

- A documented, tested policy for unknown marks: either `Err(ConversionError::…)` (consistent with unknown nodes), or an explicitly documented skip with a regression test pinning the behavior and a doc comment on `prosemirror_to_markdown` naming it.
- The `code` mark's special handling stays intact and covered by existing tests.
- Existing `web::markdown` tests still pass; documents using only known marks render byte-identically to before.

body:
## Bug In the id web editor's markdown ↔ ProseMirror codec (`pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs`), a table cell that contains **more than one paragraph** is fused into a single run of text on save — the paragraphs are concatenated with **no separator at all**, so words merge: ProseMirror document (editor/collab-originated; a user pressing Enter inside a cell produces exactly this shape): ```json {"type":"table_cell","content":[ {"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"first"}]}, {"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"second"}]} ]} ``` Saved markdown cell: `| firstsecond |` — "first" and "second" have become one word. Reparsing that output yields the single text node `firstsecond`; the paragraph boundary is unrecoverable. ## Root cause (verified in code) `json_to_ast`'s table-cell special case (markdown.rs, the `table_header`/`table_cell` branch after the main match, ~:1080-1098 on main 3b9d1592) unwraps each paragraph in the cell and appends its inline children directly to the cell node, in sequence, with nothing inserted between paragraphs. The markdown parse direction never produces multi-paragraph cells (GFM table cells are inline-only), so this only fires for editor-authored or collab-merged documents — which is precisely the population the unwrap special case exists to serve (its own comment: "ProseMirror wraps cell content in paragraphs, so we unwrap them here"). ## Verified repro (this run, main 3b9d1592) Standalone verbatim-codec probe (evidence log: goal `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-26-1415/out4.log`, case `cell-two-paras`): - Input PM: header `h`, one data cell with paragraphs `first` and `second` (JSON in the log). - `prosemirror_to_markdown` → `"| h |\n| --- |\n| firstsecond |\n"`. - Reparse → cell text is the single node `firstsecond`; `SAMEPM: false`. ## Why it matters Silent content corruption (word fusion) on save for anyone who puts a line break / second paragraph in a table cell in the editor — the same codec data-loss family as #996/#997, in the save direction's cell handling rather than the parse direction. ## Suggested fix In the cell unwrap loop, insert a separator between consecutive paragraphs — a single space is the least-surprise choice for a GFM cell (a literal newline cannot appear in a table row, and `
` would change rendering semantics); alternatively join with a space text node via `append_inline_child` so mark handling stays consistent. Whichever separator is chosen, pin it with a test so the behaviour is deliberate rather than accidental. ## Acceptance criteria - A table cell with two paragraphs saves with a separator between them (no word fusion) and reparses to text containing both words as separate words. - Single-paragraph cells (the common case, and everything the markdown parse direction produces) save byte-identically to today. - A cell with three paragraphs, and a header cell with two paragraphs, behave the same way. - Existing `web::markdown` table tests pass.

body:
## Improvement

In the id web markdown codec (`pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs`), bare URLs and email addresses in markdown are never recognized as links: the comrak **autolink extension is not enabled**, so they load into the editor as ordinary text and are never clickable link marks — unlike on GitHub and in essentially every other markdown renderer, where they autolink.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `14dd66b6`)

`commonmark_options()` (markdown.rs:67-76) enables exactly three extensions:

```rust
options.extension.strikethrough = true;
options.extension.tasklist = true;
options.extension.table = true;
// (no autolink)
```

Standalone probe crate compiling the verbatim codec from current main (log: goal `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-26-1215/out.log`):

- Input: `visit https://example.com/path?a=1 now\n`
  - Parsed PM: one plain text node `visit https://example.com/path?a=1 now` — no link mark
- Input: `mail me@example.com now\n`
  - Parsed PM: one plain text node — no link mark
- Control, same probe: the angle form `<https://example.com>` DOES parse to a link-marked text node and round-trips stably — the codec's link machinery handles autolink-shaped links fine; only the extension that recognizes the bare form is off.

## Why it matters

Documents written in other tools (or pasted from the web) routinely rely on bare URLs. In id they render as dead text: a reader cannot click them in the web editor, and any feature built on link marks (link editing UI, link extraction) cannot see them. The file on disk looks identical, so users only discover the gap when a link doesn't work.

## Acceptance criteria

- `visit https://example.com/path?a=1 now` parses with a link mark over exactly the URL (href = the URL), and `mail me@example.com now` parses with a link mark over the email (href per comrak's autolink convention).
- Round-trip is a fixpoint: saving the parsed doc and re-parsing yields the same PM (whichever spelling the save side emits — `<url>` or `[url](url)` — it must be stable on the second save, not oscillate).
- No false positives in code: bare URLs inside inline code spans and code blocks remain unlinked (probe/test both).
- URLs at punctuation boundaries behave sensibly (e.g. `(see https://e.com/x).` — trailing punctuation not swallowed into the href), covered by a test.
- New unit tests in `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs` cover www/URL/email autolinks + the code-span negative; existing codec tests pass.

## Notes

- This is the same class of gap as #945 (footnotes): a GFM/CommonMark extension the codec never turned on. The two are independent — this one needs no new PM node/mark types, since the link mark already exists.
- If there is a deliberate reason autolink was left off (e.g. editor typing behaviour), record it on this issue and close with the rationale instead.

body:
Slice 2 of decision record 0004 (`pkgs/mcpx/docs/decisions/0004-scope-resolved-roots.md`, PR #957). Design source: dezren39/nix#818 — this issue carries its acceptance criteria. Depends on slice 1 (#958, ResolvedScope plumbing).

## What to build (spec §4)
- At instance-spawn time only, substitute `${mcpx.root}` (the instance's resolved root) and `${mcpx.cwd}` (the creating CallContext's canonical cwd) in `Args`, every `Env` value, and `Cwd`.
- Placeholder names validated at config load: an unknown `${mcpx.<name>}` or a malformed `${mcpx.` sequence is a config error naming the server and the field. Only the `mcpx.` namespace is touched; every other `${…}` passes through verbatim.
- Referencing `${mcpx.root}` for an instance whose root is empty (e.g. a `global`-scoped server) fails the spawn loudly, naming server and field — never substitute an empty or daemon-cwd root.
- `pool.Identity` (era cache) must hash the effective per-instance (substituted) spawn definition, not the static Resolved config.

## Acceptance criteria (from nix#818, verbatim intent)
- [ ] `${mcpx.root}` and `${mcpx.cwd}` in a server's `Args`, `Env`, or `Cwd` are replaced with the scope-resolved root / caller cwd when an instance spawns.
- [ ] The stored/merged config on disk and in `mcpx` config output remains unsubstituted.
- [ ] The era/instance identity reflects the substituted spawn definition (two instances differing only by substituted root do not collide).
- [ ] An unknown `${mcpx.*}` placeholder fails loudly with the server name and field.
- [ ] Servers whose config contains no placeholders behave exactly as before.
- [ ] Tests cover substitution in each of Args/Env/Cwd and the unknown-placeholder error.

## What to build (spec §1, §2, §3, §6)
- `internal/config`: add `ResolvedScope{Key, Root, Degraded}` and `Scope.Resolve(ctx)`; `Scope.Key` becomes `Resolve(ctx).Key` — one resolution path. Root semantics per spec §1 (worktree → checkout top-level; repo → parent of the common dir only when its base is `.git`, else no root; cwd → canonical caller cwd; degraded repo/worktree → that cwd; global/session/psession/pid/call → no root).
- Plumbing: `Registry.keyFor` switches to `Resolve` and passes the ResolvedScope into `Pool.Acquire`; the pool stores the root on the Instance at creation and `startLane`/`dial()` read it from the instance (never re-resolved at redial — root is a pure function of the key).
- Spawn cwd (stdio only): config `cwd` when non-empty, else the resolved root when non-empty, else unset (daemon cwd, today's behavior).
- Observability: one spawn log line (server, key, root, cwd source: config/scope/daemon); `mcpx status` instance JSON gains `root`.

## Acceptance criteria (from nix#817, verbatim intent)
- [ ] A `worktree`-scoped server with no config `cwd` spawns with its working directory set to the caller's checkout top-level; a `repo`-scoped one to the resolved worktree of the common dir.
- [ ] Two callers in different checkouts of the same repo get distinct `worktree`-scoped instances rooted in their own checkouts; `repo` scope keeps sharing one instance per common dir.
- [ ] An explicit config `cwd` overrides the scope root in all cases.
- [ ] `global`/`cwd:`/`session` and other scopes are unchanged.
- [ ] Tests cover the spawn-cwd decision (scope root vs explicit cwd vs daemon fallback) as a pure function, plus degraded-root cases.

(The gopls live-proof criterion from nix#817 belongs to slice 4, which has the full stack.)
