body:
## Why

Follow-up to [#5468](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5468). The Atlas writer and the cleanup/remediation are already identified there, but the quota feed no longer provides a fresh storage or rows-read window, so the 5 GB storage state and the over-limit monthly rows-read state cannot be verified.

This is a quota-measurement fix only. It does not authorize deleting or rewriting Atlas data, changing a Turso plan, or spending money.

## Evidence at triage

- Laptop `quota-current.json` at `2026-11-05T13:00:15.401Z`: the Turso row is `state=ok`, `source=opencode-quota`, but contains only databases (44/100), rows-written (1,672,071/10,000,000), and sync (0/3 GB). Storage and rows-read are absent.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-gather-map.ts` defines `entryFromTurso()` to map `storage_bytes` and `rows_read`, but repository search found no runtime call site; the gatherer currently maps provider results with `entryFromResult()`.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-current.ts:432-468` overlays the latest fresh Turso entry by replacing the card's metrics with the windows present in that entry. A partial fresh entry can therefore hide previously dated storage/read metrics.
- The earlier 2026-11-05 00:27Z measurement recorded 7.358009 GB storage and 821,437,321 rows-read; the 02:15Z read still recorded ~165.6% rows-read but omitted storage and rows-read windows. Those over-limit measurements are not evidence of present recovery.
- Related: #5638 records the gatherer import outage and a successful recovery at 02:21Z; the current 13:00Z sample confirms the feed is ticking but still partial.

## Acceptance

- The live quota path provides authoritative Turso storage and rows-read measurements when the service response carries them, with source and measured-at timestamps preserved.
- Missing metrics are represented as missing/stale, never as zero or as proof the issue recovered; a partial fresh Turso row does not silently erase the last dated storage/read values.
- Add targeted fixtures/tests for complete, partial, and error Turso reads and the SaaS-card overlay behavior.
- Keep credentials runtime-resolved and out of source, logs, packets, and comments. No plan changes, purchases, or Atlas data mutations.

## Scope

Include the quota gatherer/provider wiring and its mapping/overlay tests under `pm-stack/aggregator/`.

Exclude changes to the Atlas producer or mirrored data, other providers, and plan/billing changes. Validate the Turso API/credential integration against the existing runtime resolution pattern before implementation.

title: Fix #6224: pm-stack(aggregator): a pool item with an invalid blockedBy/blocks edge

labels.name: source/dispatch
labels.description: Filed by pm-dispatch

body:
Implement GitHub issue #6224 in developing-today/code: pm-stack(aggregator): a pool item with an invalid blockedBy/blocks edge 500s the project page and throws the brief — isProjectPoolItem validates edges by shape only, brief + pool-graph + epic-graph call refUrl unguarded

## Summary

A Project-pool item whose `blockedBy` / `blocks` edge carries a ref `parseRef` rejects breaks three aggregator surfaces at render/derive time. The chain has two mismatched layers:

1. **The shared pool gate admits it.** `isProjectPoolItem` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/projects.ts:280-283) checks the edge fields only by shape: `parentRef`/`epicRef` are any string, `blockedBy`/`blocks` are any array of strings. There is no `isValidRef` check — exactly the disagreement model.ts:463-466 documents for the shared rule (#4952): a boundary validator must route through `isValidRef` instead of a local shape check whose values `parseRef` (and `refUrl`) then throw on. So `developing-today/code#99999999999999999999` (unsafe integer) and `812` (not repo-qualified) both pass the gate.
2. **The feed path trusts it.** `poolFromFeed` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/feed.ts:466-470) keeps any item passing that gate, so a feed-published pool section carrying such an edge reaches every consumer verbatim.
3. **Three consumers call `refUrl` unguarded on those edges:**
   - Per-item brief: `buildItemBrief` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/brief.ts:92-96) maps each `blockedBy` ref to `target?.issueUrl ?? refUrl(ref, "issue")` — an out-of-pool bad blocker throws, so the brief (and any page/API building briefs for the pool) fails.
   - Project page, pool graph section: `blockedSummary` (graph.ts) follows `blockedBy` edges and reports the bad ref in `longestChain`; `poolGraphHtml` (render.ts:6479) renders the chain with unguarded `refUrl(r)` — one bad edge 500s the whole project page.
   - Project page, per-epic graph: the ranked list (render.ts:6590) and the dependency list (render.ts:6645 `blocked by:`, :6648 `blocks:`) render `blockedBy`/`blocks` refs with unguarded `refUrl(b)` — a member item with a bad edge 500s that epic's project page.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop, aggregator sources at origin/main 04f78696ab)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-pool-edges/probe.ts` (bun, real aggregator sources, run synchronously):

```
isValidRef BAD_UNSAFE: false | BAD_PLAIN: false | GOOD: true
gate blockedBy=[BAD_UNSAFE]: true
gate blockedBy=[BAD_PLAIN]: true
gate blocks=[BAD_UNSAFE], parentRef=BAD_PLAIN: true
poolFromFeed keeps bad item: 1
brief BAD_UNSAFE blocker (out of pool): THREW: ref number is not a safe integer: developing-today/code#99999999999999999999
brief GOOD blocker control: OK len=49
blockedSummary chain with BAD: ["developing-today/code#1","developing-today/code#99999999999999999999"]
projectPage graph BAD_UNSAFE chain: THREW: ref number is not a safe integer: developing-today/code#99999999999999999999
projectPage graph GOOD chain control: OK len=34510
projectPage epic BAD_PLAIN blocker: THREW: not a repo-qualified ref: 812
projectPage epic GOOD blocker control: OK len=38578
```

BAD_UNSAFE is `developing-today/code#99999999999999999999`; BAD_PLAIN is `812`; controls use `developing-today/code#3` in the same positions and render/derive cleanly.

## Why it matters

The pool's edge fields are the native dependency graph the dashboard is built on (#2399 contract): the collector writes them from GitHub's native relations, but the feed is a published artifact other producers can write, and the gate is explicitly the shared contract both sides must not drift from (feed.ts:440-446). One malformed edge in one feed item — a hand-edited feed, a buggy producer, a non-GitHub dependency written as a bare number — permanently breaks the brief for that item and 500s the affected project pages until the feed is fixed by hand. Siblings already filed cover other producers of the same throw (projector registry links #6211 — which covers render.ts:6741 roadmap rows and /search, not these sites; lined-up titles #6210/#6195; objectives #6174; overview #6205), and #5202 covers a different field of this same gate (`updatedAt`). None covers the pool edge fields or the brief / pool-graph / epic-graph consumers. The session-record path (render.ts:1912) already shows the house pattern for untrusted refs: try/catch and omit only the bad link.

## Acceptance criteria

- A pool item whose `blockedBy`/`blocks` (and, for consistency, `parentRef`/`epicRef`) edge fails `isValidRef` never reaches a renderer: either `isProjectPoolItem` validates edge refs through `isValidRef` (bad item drops individually in `poolFromFeed`, per the gate's existing fail-soft contract), or the three consumer sites guard `refUrl` the way `sessionRecordLine` (render.ts:1912) does. The gate layer is preferred — it is the shared contract — but stored/in-memory pools that bypass the feed must not stay lethal, so a consumer-side guard in addition is welcome.
- The brief, the project page's pool-graph section, and the per-epic graph all survive a pool item carrying an unsafe-integer or non-repo-qualified edge: the item renders, the bad edge is omitted or shown unlinked, valid edges still render as links.
- Regression tests alongside the existing aggregator suites (graph / epic-graph / brief / projects gate tests) pinning: unsafe-integer `blockedBy`, non-repo-qualified `blockedBy`, and unsafe `blocks`, each with a valid-ref control.
- Existing behavior unchanged for valid refs (controls above).

Related: #6211 (projector registry links; render.ts:6741 + /search), #6210, #6195, #6174, #6205, #5202 (same gate, `updatedAt` field), #4952 (the shared ref-validity rule), #2399 (pool edge contract).


Rules from the repo owner: (1) Deliver the finished work as a pull request in this run; put "Fixes #6224" in the PR description so the issue closes on merge. (2) Cover the whole set in the one PR: if the issue names a set (files, subcommands, cases), fix every member, and batch any directly related dependency updates into the same PR — never one PR per item or per dependency. (3) Run the relevant tests and checks before opening the PR. (4) Merging is permitted but never required: merge only when checks pass and you are reasonably certain the PR is correct and low-risk — otherwise leave it open, and state your confidence and what a human should check. (5) If you hit a genuine blocker (missing credentials, a decision only the owner can make), stop and say exactly what is needed in your final summary instead of guessing.

---

  - The natural home, `.github/workflows/pm-stack-tests.yml`, wires the

    and exactly two Python suites by explicit name
    (`pm-stack/opencode-claimant/test_poll.py`,
    `pm-stack/grist/test_update_choice_options.py`) — external-comms is absent.
  - No flake check or justfile recipe mentions it either.

## Why it matters

This suite is the only regression pin for #6154, where the external-comms
pusher silently deleted spilled send records — the fallback copy of an
already-sent external message — while reporting a clean drain. The standing
rule for this subsystem is "external comms are never silent"; if the pusher
regresses, nothing in CI notices, and the failure mode is precisely the one
that hides itself. The sibling pm-stack Python suites were wired for exactly
this reason (#5951); this one was added later, with the #6154 fix, and missed
the same wiring step.

## Acceptance criteria

- A workflow (extending `pm-stack-tests.yml` in its existing style, or a
  dedicated workflow in the house style of e.g. `id-hosted-worker-tests.yml`)
  runs `test_push_quarantine.py` on changes to `pm-stack/external-comms/**`
  and on dispatch.
- The step asserts the suite file exists before running it (the
  anti-silent-skip guard used by the existing pm-stack Python step), so a
  green run cannot be a silently skipped suite.
- The suite passes in CI as it does locally (6 tests, offline, ~1s).

body:
You are "Bolt" ⚡ - a performance-obsessed agent who makes the codebase faster, one optimization at a time.

Your mission is to identify and implement ONE small performance improvement that makes the application measurably faster or more efficient.


## Boundaries

✅ **Always do:**
- Run commands like `pnpm lint` and `pnpm test` (or associated equivalents) before creating PR
- Add comments explaining the optimization
- Measure and document expected performance impact

⚠️ **Ask first:**
- Adding any new dependencies
- Making architectural changes

🚫 **Never do:**
- Modify package.json or tsconfig.json without instruction
- Make breaking changes
- Optimize prematurely without actual bottleneck
- Sacrifice code readability for micro-optimizations

BOLT'S PHILOSOPHY:
- Speed is a feature
- Every millisecond counts
- Measure first, optimize second
- Don't sacrifice readability for micro-optimizations

BOLT'S JOURNAL - CRITICAL LEARNINGS ONLY:
Before starting, read .jules/bolt.md (create if missing).

Your journal is NOT a log - only add entries for CRITICAL learnings that will help you avoid mistakes or make better decisions.

⚠️ ONLY add journal entries when you discover:
- A performance bottleneck specific to this codebase's architecture
- An optimization that surprisingly DIDN'T work (and why)
- A rejected change with a valuable lesson
- A codebase-specific performance pattern or anti-pattern
- A surprising edge case in how this app handles performance

❌ DO NOT journal routine work like:
- "Optimized component X today" (unless there's a learning)
- Generic React performance tips
- Successful optimizations without surprises

Format: `## YYYY-MM-DD - [Title]
**Learning:** [Insight]
**Action:** [How to apply next time]`

BOLT'S DAILY PROCESS:

1. 🔍 PROFILE - Hunt for performance opportunities:

  FRONTEND PERFORMANCE:
  - Unnecessary re-renders in React/Vue/Angular components
  - Missing memoization for expensive computations
  - Large bundle sizes (opportunities for code splitting)
  - Unoptimized images (missing lazy loading, wrong formats)
  - Missing virtualization for long lists
  - Synchronous operations blocking the main thread
  - Missing debouncing/throttling on frequent events
  - Unused CSS or JavaScript being loaded
  - Missing resource preloading for critical assets
  - Inefficient DOM manipulations

  BACKEND PERFORMANCE:
  - N+1 query problems in database calls
  - Missing database indexes on frequently queried fields
  - Expensive operations without caching
  - Synchronous operations that could be async
  - Missing pagination on large data sets
  - Inefficient algorithms (O(n²) that could be O(n))
  - Missing connection pooling
  - Repeated API calls that could be batched
  - Large payloads that could be compressed

  GENERAL OPTIMIZATIONS:
  - Missing caching for expensive operations
  - Redundant calculations in loops
  - Inefficient data structures for the use case
  - Missing early returns in conditional logic
  - Unnecessary deep cloning or copying
  - Missing lazy initialization
  - Inefficient string concatenation in loops
  - Missing request/response compression

2. ⚡ SELECT - Choose your daily boost:
  Pick the BEST opportunity that:
  - Has measurable performance impact (faster load, less memory, fewer requests)
  - Can be implemented cleanly in < 50 lines
  - Doesn't sacrifice code readability significantly
  - Has low risk of introducing bugs
  - Follows existing patterns

3. 🔧 OPTIMIZE - Implement with precision:
  - Write clean, understandable optimized code
  - Add comments explaining the optimization
  - Preserve existing functionality exactly
  - Consider edge cases
  - Ensure the optimization is safe
  - Add performance metrics in comments if possible

4. ✅ VERIFY - Measure the impact:
  - Run format and lint checks
  - Run the full test suite
  - Verify the optimization works as expected
  - Add benchmark comments if possible
  - Ensure no functionality is broken

5. 🎁 PRESENT - Share your speed boost:
  Create a PR with:
  - Title: "⚡ Bolt: [performance improvement]"
  - Description with:
    * 💡 What: The optimization implemented
    * 🎯 Why: The performance problem it solves
    * 📊 Impact: Expected performance improvement (e.g., "Reduces re-renders by ~50%")
    * 🔬 Measurement: How to verify the improvement
  - Reference any related performance issues

BOLT'S FAVORITE OPTIMIZATIONS:
⚡ Add React.memo() to prevent unnecessary re-renders
⚡ Add database index on frequently queried field
⚡ Cache expensive API call results
⚡ Add lazy loading to images below the fold
⚡ Debounce search input to reduce API calls
⚡ Replace O(n²) nested loop with O(n) hash map lookup
⚡ Add pagination to large data fetch
⚡ Memoize expensive calculation with useMemo/computed
⚡ Add early return to skip unnecessary processing
⚡ Batch multiple API calls into single request
⚡ Add virtualization to long list rendering
⚡ Move expensive operation outside of render loop
⚡ Add code splitting for large route components
⚡ Replace large library with smaller alternative

BOLT AVOIDS (not worth the complexity):
❌ Micro-optimizations with no measurable impact
❌ Premature optimization of cold paths
❌ Optimizations that make code unreadable
❌ Large architectural changes
❌ Optimizations that require extensive testing
❌ Changes to critical algorithms without thorough testing

Remember: You're Bolt, making things lightning fast. But speed without correctness is useless. Measure, optimize, verify. If you can't find a clear performance win today, wait for tomorrow's opportunity.

If no suitable performance optimization can be identified, stop and do not create a PR.---

body:
## Summary

A projector registry link whose issue number is an unsafe integer breaks two aggregator pages at render. The chain has three mismatched gates:

1. **The projector admits it.** `POST /links` validation (pm-stack/projector/src/server.ts:246) is a shape regex, `/^[\w.-]+\/[\w.-]+#\d+$/`. Its `\d+` admits numbers `parseRef` rejects — exactly the anti-pattern model.ts:463-466 documents for the shared rule (#4952). `developing-today/code#99999999999999999999` (20 digits) passes with a 201.
2. **The aggregator trusts it.** `projectorLinks` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/sources/live.ts:484-488) maps `row.ref` verbatim — no `isValidRef` filter — and `enrichWithRegistryLinks` (live.ts:496-507) merges those links into board items (live.ts:1164) and roadmap rows (live.ts:1198). Legacy/seeded rows in `pmp_links` bypass the POST gate entirely and take the same path.
3. **Two render sites call `refUrl` unguarded on those links.** `parseRef` (model.ts:454-460) throws `ref number is not a safe integer`, so:
   - `/search`: `renderSearch` (render.ts:510) calls `refUrl(ref)` for every result ref not in the items map — a registry ref is unresolved by construction, so any search matching that board item or roadmap row 500s.
   - Project pages: `renderProgramProject`'s roadmap rows (render.ts:6741) call `refUrl(l.ref)` for every link on the row, so one bad registry link on one roadmap row takes down that project's whole page.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop main 04f78696ab)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-search-ref/probe.ts` (bun, real aggregator sources from the laptop checkout):

```
projector POST /links gate regex admits BAD: true
isValidRef(BAD): false | isValidRef(GOOD): true
search(board BAD): THREW: ref number is not a safe integer: developing-today/code#99999999999999999999
search(board GOOD control): OK len=19929 hasGoodLink=true
search(roadmap BAD): THREW: ref number is not a safe integer: developing-today/code#99999999999999999999
project(roadmap BAD): THREW: ref number is not a safe integer: developing-today/code#99999999999999999999
project(roadmap GOOD control): OK len=29872 hasGoodLink=true
```

BAD is `developing-today/code#99999999999999999999` carried as a registry `Link` — the exact shape `enrichWithRegistryLinks` produces from a `pmp_links` row. GOOD is the same cases with `#123`.

## Why it matters

Registry links are the cross-repo linking mechanism the board and roadmap are built around ("the registry is where a `code` task's link to an `opencode` PR lives", live.ts:492-495), and they are writable through an authenticated API whose only ref check disagrees with the consumer. One stored link — a typo'd or pasted oversized number is enough — permanently 500s `/search` for matching queries and the affected project page until someone deletes the row from the database by hand. Siblings already filed cover other producers of the same throw (lined-up task titles, #6210 board strip at render.ts:1506 — the same registry links also reach that strip; objectives #6174; reconciled overview #6205); this is the registry-link producer plus the two render sites none of them cover. The session-record path (render.ts:1912) already shows the house pattern for untrusted refs: try/catch and omit only the bad link.

## Acceptance criteria

- A registry link whose ref fails `isValidRef` never reaches a renderer: filter (with a logged/provenance-visible drop) in `projectorLinks` or `enrichWithRegistryLinks`, and/or align the projector's `POST /links` gate with `parseRef` semantics (safe-integer number) so the row cannot be stored in the first place. Both layers preferred — stored legacy rows must not stay lethal.
- `/search` and project-page roadmap rendering survive a board item / roadmap row carrying such a link: the item renders, the bad link is omitted or shown unlinked, sibling good links still render as links.
- Regression tests alongside the existing aggregator suites (search-view / program rendering) pinning: unsafe-integer registry ref on a board item, on a roadmap row, and a non-GitHub-shaped stored ref if the filter is the chosen layer.
- Existing behavior unchanged for valid refs (controls above).

Related: #6210 (same links reach the board strip via titleRefs; registry links are a second producer), #6174, #6205, #3766 (project-config validator, same gate-disagreement shape, different gate), #2485 (session taskRefs, fixed with the try/catch pattern at render.ts:1912).

title: pm-stack(aggregator): overview front door throws on a lined-up task with a non-GitHub ref — reconciledInProgress reaches refUrl unguarded

body:
## Problem

The aggregator's overview — the front door at `/`, served via `/frag/overview` and `/api/overview.json` — throws (500 / dead fragment) whenever the orchestration section contains a goal with an **in-progress lined-up task whose ref is not a GitHub `owner/repo#N` ref**, or whose title mentions `owner/repo#<number>` with a number too large to be a safe integer.

Lined-up tasks legitimately carry non-GitHub refs in the real feed (goal ids, bare numbers — the same data reality behind #6174 and #6195), and the feed gate does not check the field: `isLinedUpElement` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/feed.ts:223-232`) validates `title`/`horizon`/`status`/`horizonWhy` only. `LinedUpTask.ref` is typed `RefKey` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/model.ts:640-642`) but nothing enforces that promise at the boundary.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ `36b346f399`)

`reconciledInProgress` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/render.ts:3552`, called by `deriveOverview` at `render.ts:3703`) walks `orchestration.goals[].linedUp`:

- `render.ts:3592-3593` — `if (task.ref) { signal(task.ref, "active-session", task.title); continue; }` — no validity check.
- `signal` → `ensure` (`render.ts:3574`) falls back to `url: project?.issueUrl ?? item?.url ?? url ?? refUrl(ref)` whenever the ref is absent from the pool and the items map (always true for a non-GitHub ref). `refUrl` → `parseRef` (`model.ts:454-460`) **throws** on anything that is not `owner/repo#<safe integer>`.
- Second vector, same function: the no-ref title path first routes through `refsInText` (`render.ts:3596`), which correctly filters with `isValidRef` (`model.ts:467-484`, the shared #4952 rule) — then the very next loop (`render.ts:3597-3599`) re-scrapes the title with a raw `matchAll(/([\w.-]+\/[\w.-]+)#(\d+)/g)` and signals every match **without** the safe-integer check, re-admitting exactly what `refsInText` refused.

Call sites have no guard around the throw: `server.ts:1329` (`/frag/overview`), `server.ts:1781` (`/api/overview.json`), and `renderOverview` (`render.ts:3771`, the `/?full=1` no-JS path).

Probe (bun, real `deriveOverview` imported from the tree, `~/git/fleet/probe-overview-ref/probe.ts`):

| case | result |
|---|---|
| no orchestration section | OK, `inProgress=[]` |
| lined-up in-progress, ref `developing-today/code#42` | OK, row url `https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/42` |
| lined-up in-progress, ref `goal_a243772844c3` | **THREW `not a repo-qualified ref: goal_a243772844c3`** |
| lined-up in-progress, ref `812` | **THREW `not a repo-qualified ref: 812`** |
| lined-up in-progress, no ref, title `Work on developing-today/code#99999999999999999999 next` | **THREW `ref number is not a safe integer: developing-today/code#99999999999999999999`** |
| lined-up in-progress, no ref, title `Work on developing-today/code#42 next` | OK |
| lined-up **queued** (not in-progress), ref `goal_a243772844c3` | OK (status gate at `render.ts:3591` skips it) |

## Why it matters

The overview is the aggregator's front door — the first page every viewer (and the dashboard's own refresh fragment) loads. One in-progress lined-up task with a goal-id or numeric ref takes the whole overview down for everyone until the orchestrator's next run happens to change the lined-up set; it does not degrade to a missing row. This is a different surface and failure mode from its siblings: #6174 (/today objectives, `render.ts:3368`), #6195 (board in-flight lane swallowed by a catch, `sources/live.ts:634`), #4316 (lined-up `blockedBy` gate → `todayFromSection`). Same root family: consumers reaching `parseRef`/`refUrl` without routing through the shared `isValidRef` rule (#4952).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `deriveOverview` never throws for a feed-valid orchestration section: a lined-up in-progress task with a non-GitHub ref (`goal_…`, bare number, any other string) produces no in-progress row for that ref (or a row with no GitHub URL), and the rest of the overview renders normally.
- [ ] The title-scrape path applies the same validity rule as `refsInText` (`isValidRef`, including the safe-integer check) — e.g. by dropping the duplicate raw `matchAll` loop or guarding its matches — so `owner/repo#<unsafe integer>` in a title cannot throw either.
- [ ] Valid refs behave exactly as today: a lined-up in-progress task referencing a real `owner/repo#N` (in pool/items or not) still yields an in-progress row with the correct GitHub URL, from both the `ref` field and a title mention.
- [ ] Pinning tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/overview.test.ts` (or a sibling suite) cover: goal-id ref, numeric ref, unsafe-integer title mention, and the valid-ref controls; the aggregator test suite passes.
- [ ] Related but out of scope: the feed-gate question (should `isLinedUpElement` validate `ref` when present?) is #6174's layer — do not change gate semantics here beyond what the overview fix needs. Cross-ref #5082 (same endpoints, different failure mode: ~12s empty replies) in the fix PR if it touches these handlers.

title: id(seitan): accept::parse ignores trailing bytes — appended data (even a second accept map) decodes as the bare accept

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/id/src/seitan/accept.rs:119` — `accept::parse` decodes the joiner's signed accept message with `rmp_serde::from_slice`, which returns after the first complete msgpack value and never checks that the input is exhausted. Any trailing bytes after the accept map are silently ignored, so one `Fields` value has many byte spellings: the bare message, the message plus a stray byte, the message plus a whole second value — even the message concatenated with a second complete accept map.

This matters in this module specifically:

- The module's stated rule (accept.rs header) is that the admin "verifies the signature over the bytes exactly as received, and only then reads the fields out of them" — but `admit` (`admit.rs`) runs `parse` first and bases its UnknownInvite / Revoked / Expired / Used / freshness decisions on fields read from what may be only a strict prefix of the received bytes.
- `parse` is public API (`pub mod accept`, re-exported through `seitan`), so any future caller that parses without the admit path's signature check inherits silent truncation.
- The rest of this codebase treats one-object-many-spellings as a defect class (tuple decode refuses non-minimal ints and the encoder-unproducible -0.0 form — #1610 / #2421; directory auth refused `+`-encoded hex pairs — #2517). This is the same class in the Seitan accept decoder, and it is also the only peer-facing `rmp_serde::from_slice` in pkgs/id.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe against the real `id` crate @ f55e16cfcc)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-seitan-trailing` on the laptop (path dependency on `pkgs/id`, `default-features = false, features = ["world"]`). It signs a genuine proof with `accept::sign`, parses the bare message as a baseline, then parses mutations of `proof.message`:

```text
baseline ok: uid=user123 seqno=7 ctime=1700000000000
trailing 0x00: Ok("user123")
trailing 0x2a: Ok("user123")
trailing str: Ok("user123")
duplicated map: Ok("user123")
```

All four trailing forms — one `0x00` byte, one msgpack integer (`0x2a`), one msgpack string (`"hello"`), and the complete accept map concatenated a second time — parse `Ok` with the first message's fields instead of returning `ProofError::Malformed`.

`accept.rs`'s own doc for `parse` says it returns `Malformed` "for any message that is not a version 2 accept with a valid invite ID" — a message followed by a second complete message is not a version 2 accept message; it is two messages.

Dedup: title/keyword search over open and closed issues for seitan / trailing / msgpack accept found #194 (Keybase accept capture), #1386 and #5226 (verify_strict call sites), #2517 (directory-auth hex spellings) — none covers trailing-data acceptance in `accept::parse`.

## Acceptance criteria

- `accept::parse` returns `ProofError::Malformed` when any byte remains after the first complete msgpack value: tests pin a trailing single byte, a trailing scalar value, a trailing string, and a second concatenated accept map.
- A genuine message produced by `accept::message` / `accept::sign` still parses, and the existing seitan test suite (Keybase vectors, admit freshness/expiry/single-use) stays green: `cargo test -p id seitan`.
- The fix consumes the decoder's actual consumed length (or an equivalent full-consumption decode); it does not re-encode-and-compare, which would also reject honest non-canonical msgpack width encodings the current decoder accepts and Keybase clients may emit.
- `admit`'s behaviour for honest proofs is unchanged (same check order, same `Reject` values).

## Why not fixed in this run

Filed-only: the fix is small, but choosing the full-consumption mechanism against `rmp_serde` 1.x's API (and not breaking non-canonical-but-honest encodings) deserves a deliberate pass through the queue rather than a rushed creator self-solve.

body:
**Decision needed from Drew (one line):** 20 of the repo's 53 workflows are `disabled_manually` in Actions — including most test venues — so wiring alone cannot restore test coverage: re-enable the test venues, fold their suites into the active workflows, or accept the dispatch-only coverage definition in this design? Phase 3 cannot land until this is ruled.

Design doc: `files/designs/code-test-suite-coverage-contract.md` in the `keep-the-four-repos-healthy` goal workspace. Filed by the design architect (pass 54, 2026-11-05). Audit HEAD: origin/main e3626d1e3.

## The defect

The repo keeps writing regression suites and then never running them. On 2026-11-05 alone, twenty-one issues were filed of the form "ci(X): <suite> is run by no workflow — verified nowhere" (03:30–06:32Z), joining #1439 (2026-10-27) and #5582. The root is not any one missing step: **the repo has no statement of which suite runs where, and no check that the statement stays true** — so the fleet rediscovers the gap one hand audit at a time, each wiring fix wires exactly the suite it was filed for and misses the sibling in the same app (#5951 → #6091 + #5993; #5937 → #6085; #6034's 6-of-13), and several closed fixes wired suites into venues that cannot run at all.

## Evidence

- **Unwired family (filed today):** #5935 (program-tending), #5942 (fleet-paperwork), #5946 (worktree-reaper — the destructive reap gates), #5952 (cargo-target-janitor deletion-safety; the hourly timer runs the deleter, never its tests), #5992 (t3code seed), #5993 (pm-git-sync 23 checks + tailnet-bindings), #6065 (opencode-config-normalize), #6082 (id-mail deploy guard), #6084 (three quota-exporter suites), #6085 (github-backup Worker), #6091 (claimant install), #6092 (mcpx v2 plugin, 61 tests), #6099 (pkgs/chat go tests — the touching workflow builds and vets but never tests). Seven more closed in-window by per-site wiring: #5937, #5945, #5951, #6034, #6081, #6090, #6094, #6095.
- **Venue reality (Actions API, audit time):** 53 workflows, **20 `disabled_manually`** — including `scripts-test.yml` (the venue #5935 names), `pm-stack-tests.yml` (#5954), `go-modules-build.yml` (the venue #6099 names), `research-workflow.yml`, `mcpx.yml`, `mcpx-test.yml`, `lab-ops-hub.yml`, `cf-container-hello.yml` (#1439's venue), `cold-store-reaper.yml`, `opencode-config-guard.yml`, `mod-tidy.yml`. Enablement is settings state, invisible in the tree. #5954 records #5951's acceptance as unverifiable until its workflow runs again (dispatch returns HTTP 422).
- **"Runs" unproven:** build+vet counted as coverage (#6099); self-skip exits 0 (#5993's tailnet suite); suites not runnable at all — live-network tests (#5935), clean-checkout lockfile break (#6093), import-time argv theft (#5943, closed).
- **Trigger reality:** every workflow on main is `workflow_dispatch`-only while headers and `.github/ci-policy.md` still describe PR/push tiers (#1779). Per Drew's 2026-11-05 ruling (#6126), this design does **not** propose restoring auto triggers; it defines coverage truthfully inside the dispatch-only regime.

## The contract (recorded decisions)

A suite counts as covered only when all five hold:

1. **Registered** — one registry naming exactly one venue + invocation per suite; a suite added without a registry entry is an incomplete change.
2. **Real venue** — the venue is enabled (`active` in Actions, or a flake check that actually runs) and dispatchable; a suite whose only venue is disabled is uncovered, full stop.
3. **Proven run** — the venue step names the suite's files explicitly and asserts they exist first; a suite-reported SKIP is a visible failure for coverage; build/vet/typecheck does not count as running a suite.
4. **Runnable and hermetic** — passes from a clean checkout with networking disabled (mock seams, no import-time side effects, lockfile/runner in agreement).
5. **Ratcheted** — a check compares on-disk suite inventory ↔ registry ↔ venue contents; rule 2's enablement half is audited from the Actions API by the recurring check Phase 3 establishes (it cannot be checked from inside the tree).

## Phases (each independently landable)

- **Phase 1 — the registry** (filed with this design): inventory every suite on main, one entry per suite (paths, venue, invocation, enablement at audit time); uncovered suites get an explicit row pointing at their Phase 2 issue; contract statement lands in `.github/ci-policy.md`.
- **Phase 2 — wire the filed suites (ADOPTED origins, no parallels):** #5935, #5942, #5946, #5952, #5992, #5993, #6065, #6082, #6084, #6085, #6091, #6092, #6099 into their registry-named venues; #6093 made runnable, then wired; #5582 dispositioned to a named check. Each origin keeps its own acceptance, amended by rules 2–3.
- **Phase 3 — venue reality:** #5954 adopted (pm-stack instance) + a filed enablement audit covering every other registry venue: API state, a recorded disposition per disabled test venue (re-enable / fold / retire with reason), and the recurring enablement re-audit's owner + cadence. **Gated on Drew's ruling above.**
- **Phase 4 — the ratchet** (filed with this design, gated on Phases 1–2): the inventory check of rule 5 in an enabled venue, plus trigger-text truth-ups (#6126 disposition) and #5919 dispositioned as venue hygiene.

Open questions stay in the design doc (dispatch cadence — Drew's runner strategy; the enablement audit's home; registry granularity for pkgs/id and pkgs/mcpx; doc/ and vendored-tree boundary).

## Acceptance

- [ ] All four phases closed or dispositioned with evidence.
- [ ] Every suite on main is in the registry with a real, enabled venue or a recorded waiver.
- [ ] The ratchet fails on a deliberately unwired test suite added in a scratch branch (probe evidence on Phase 4).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Drew's one-line ruling is recorded on this issue: re-enable the test venues, fold their suites into the active workflows, or accept the dispatch-only coverage definition.
- [ ] The coverage contract (design doc in the goal workspace) is updated to match the ruling and names, per app/suite, the venue that runs it.
- [ ] A mechanical check exists (CI step or scheduled audit) that enumerates the repo's test suites and fails/lists any suite no active venue runs — the statement stays true without hand audits.
- [ ] The unwired family filed 2026-11-05 (e.g. #5935, #5942, #5946, #5952, #5992, #5993, #6065, #6082, #6084, #6085, #6091, #6092, #6099) is dispositioned against the contract: wired, folded, or explicitly accepted as dispatch-only.
- [ ] Phase 3 of the design lands or is explicitly deferred with the reason recorded here.

labels.name: kind/performance

labels.name: task/triage

labels.name: task/small-fix

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/cold-store-reaper
labels.description: Package/app: cold-store-reaper (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/cold-store-reaper/worker/src/index.js:125-146` requests one frame from Google Drive with a `Range` header. When Drive responds with HTTP 200 instead of 206, `rehydrate` calls `resp.arrayBuffer()` for the entire bundle and only then slices out the requested frame. Peak memory therefore scales with the whole remote bundle rather than `frame_length`.

## Required behavior

Handle a range-ignoring 200 response without materializing the entire response in memory. Stream/discard bytes before `offset`, retain only the requested frame, and stop once the frame is complete; continue to validate exact length, decompression, and SHA-256 before returning bytes.

## Acceptance criteria

- A test stubs Drive to ignore `Range` and return a large streaming bundle; rehydration returns the correct requested frame without buffering the full response.
- Short responses and malformed/truncated frames still fail closed.
- A normal 206 range response retains current behavior and hash verification.

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/agent-backup/test-backup.sh` — the only regression suite for `pkgs/agent-backup/backup.sh` — is run by no workflow, flake check, or justfile recipe. `backup.sh` is not dead code: it is inlined verbatim into a live systemd user service, so its snapshot/dedup logic runs on the laptop continuously, while the suite that pins its two worst historical bugs executes only when a human remembers to run it.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ f2a72d9478, HEAD == origin/main)

- `home/common/default.nix:582-622` declares `systemd.user.services.agent-backup` plus a path watcher; at `:590-591` the service's script is `builtins.readFile ../../pkgs/agent-backup/backup.sh` — the exact file the suite tests is the file that runs live.
- Whole-tree grep for `test-backup` across `.github/workflows/`, `flake.nix`, `justfile`, Nix files, and docs returns zero references. No automated check ever runs the suite.
- Hand run on the laptop this run: `bash pkgs/agent-backup/test-backup.sh` → `agent-backup same-second collision regression: PASS` and `agent-backup future-dated PREV/latest regression: PASS`, exit 0. The suite is fully offline and isolated (it stubs `date`, points `HOME`/`AGENT_BACKUP_DIR` at a `mktemp -d` tree).
- What the 88-line suite pins, against the 119-line `backup.sh`:
  - A second run in the same second gets its own `-0000000001` directory and must not delete the first run's snapshot or leave `latest` dangling — the regression suite for closed #3340.
  - A future-dated snapshot must neither become the dedup baseline nor lose/regress the `latest` pointer — the regression suite for closed #4602 (cases seeded with 2026/2027/2028 stamps).
  - A duplicate-content run removes only its own newly reserved directory and leaves `latest` resolving to a real snapshot.

## Why it matters

Both pinned bugs were data-loss class: a same-second rerun could delete the previous snapshot, and a future-dated snapshot made dedup compare against the wrong baseline while `latest` pointed backwards. The backup service runs unattended via a path watcher; if either behaviour regresses, the failure mode is silently losing the very snapshots the service exists to keep — discovered only when a restore is needed. The suite exists, is fast, offline, and deterministic; it is simply never executed.

## Acceptance criteria

- An automated check (a workflow step, flake check, or equivalent) runs `bash pkgs/agent-backup/test-backup.sh` on changes under `pkgs/agent-backup/` (and ideally `home/common/default.nix`'s agent-backup unit).
- The check asserts the suite file exists first, so a green run cannot be a silently skipped suite.
- The check passes on current main (both PASS lines at filing).
- Breaking a pinned behaviour (e.g. letting a same-second second run reuse/delete the first snapshot directory, or letting a future-dated snapshot become the dedup baseline) makes the check fail.

title: id(currency_poc): InMemoryLedger posts new legs behind an Exists head leg in a linked chain — real TigerBeetle breaks the chain and posts nothing

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Summary

The two `LedgerBackend` implementations disagree on a linked chain whose first leg is an idempotent resubmission (`Exists`) and whose later legs are new:

- `InMemoryLedger` (`pkgs/id/src/currency_poc/ledger.rs`, `validate_and_stage` + `create_transfers`): an `Exists` leg is treated as non-failing — "An idempotent `Exists` leg does not fail the chain" — so the remaining new legs stage, commit, and move balances, reported `Ok(())`.
- Real TigerBeetle breaks a linked chain on **any** non-`Created` status. That is the repo's own documented semantics in `pkgs/id/src/currency_poc/tb_ledger.rs` (`create_transfers`, the PR #5072 linked-chain-retry comment): a resubmitted chain reports `Exists` for its first leg and `LinkedEventFailed` for every later leg. The binding compensates **only** for the whole-chain-already-posted pattern (it verifies every stored leg is identical before rewriting the later legs to `Exists`). A mixed chain — first leg `Exists`, later legs genuinely new — is **not** compensated: on the live backend those new legs report `LinkedEventFailed` and nothing new posts.

So the same `create_transfers` call posts money on the in-memory reference backend and posts nothing on TigerBeetle. The executor layer cannot paper over this: `executor::submit` and the recovery scanner both accept per-leg `Err(Exists)` as success, so code tested green against `InMemoryLedger` for a mixed-chain resubmission silently behaves differently against the live cluster.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe @ 231eb9ccb1)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-linked-exists` on the laptop — a crate against the real `id` crate (`pkgs/id`), `InMemoryLedger`, all accounts on ledger 100, issuer-funded:

- `chain1 [601,602]` (601: user→LP 100, `linked=true`; 602: LP→dest 100): `[Ok(()), Ok(())]` — balances user `{debits 100, credits 1000}`, LP `{100, 100}`, dest `{0, 100}`.
- Mixed chain `[601 identical, 603, 604]` (603: LP→user 50, `linked=true`; 604: user→dest 50): **`[Err(Exists), Ok(()), Ok(())]`** — `lookup_transfer(603) = Some((603, 50))`, `lookup_transfer(604) = Some((604, 50))`, balances move to user `{150, 1050}`, LP `{150, 100}`, dest `{0, 150}`. The new legs **posted** behind an `Exists` head leg.
- Control — whole-chain identical resubmit of chain1: `[Err(Exists), Err(Exists)]`, balances unchanged. The divergence is specifically the mixed shape, not idempotent resubmission in general.

TigerBeetle-side evidence is in-repo and already pinned by live tests: `tb_ledger.rs` documents the chain-break on any non-`Created` status, and `tests.rs` (`live_same_request_twice_posts_once`, ~line 1653) records that TigerBeetle reports `Exists` + `LinkedEventFailed` for a resubmitted chain — the pattern the binding must translate. No equivalent translation exists for `InMemoryLedger`, because it never produces it.

## Why it matters

`InMemoryLedger` is the reference oracle every currency_poc scenario test runs against in CI (the live-TB tests are `#[ignore]`d). A parity gap here means the test suite can certify executor/recovery behavior — e.g. a resubmission path that reuses an already-posted leg ID alongside new legs — that the real backend rejects atomically. That is exactly the class of divergence #6150 (failed-ID memory) and #6135 (ID validity) already filed for this backend; this is the linked-chain member of the same family, and it is not covered by either (nor by #4669's short-result-vector issue or #6108's tb_ledger status-mapper panics).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The two backends agree on the mixed chain `[Exists leg, new leg, ...]`: either `InMemoryLedger` fails the new legs with `LinkedEventFailed` and posts nothing (matching TigerBeetle + the tb_ledger compensation contract), or the trait contract in `ledger.rs` is amended to state the `Exists`-leg semantics explicitly and the tb_ledger binding is extended to implement them — with the decision recorded on this issue
- [ ] A pinning test in `pkgs/id/src/currency_poc/tests.rs` covers the mixed chain on `InMemoryLedger` (first leg byte-identical to a posted transfer, later legs new): result vector, `lookup_transfer` for the new legs, and balances all match the chosen semantics
- [ ] The whole-chain identical-resubmit control stays all-`Exists` and moves nothing on both backends
- [ ] `cargo test -p id currency_poc` passes

## Related

- #6150 — InMemoryLedger forgets failed transfer IDs (sibling parity gap)
- #6135 — InMemoryLedger accepts zero/int-max IDs TigerBeetle refuses (sibling parity gap)
- #6108 — tb_ledger status mappers panic on unmodelled statuses
- #4669 — submit()/recovery treat a short result vector as success

body:
# pm-stack(external-comms): pusher silently drops unparseable outbox lines — a spilled send record vanishes with the pusher reporting a clean drain

## Summary

`record-external-send push` (the external-comms ledger pusher, landed in #6130) discards any outbox line it cannot parse, with no trace anywhere: not kept in the outbox, not counted in `pusher-health.json`, not surfaced in `last_error`, and not in the pusher's stdout summary. When the outbox contains only an unparseable line, the pusher reports a fully successful drain (`pending: 0`, `last_error: null`, `last_drain_ok_at` set).

This is the module whose own header states Drew's ratified rule (2026-11-05): "EXTERNAL COMMS ARE NEVER SILENT" (`pm-stack/external-comms/record-external-send:4-7`), and whose docstring promises that on push "failures stay with `_attempts`/`_last_error` bookkeeping" (`:24-26`). An unparseable line is a failure that gets neither.

## Evidence

`pm-stack/external-comms/record-external-send:201-204` (main @ `7e7b418bf5`):

```python
try:
    rec = json.loads(ln)
except Exception:
    continue  # unparseable line: drop, it can never land
```

The line is not appended to `pending`, so the outbox rewrite at `:225-229` deletes it permanently, and no counter or health field records that anything was dropped.

How a line becomes unparseable in practice: `spill()` appends + fsyncs (`:143-151`), but a crash/power loss mid-append, a torn write, disk-full truncation, or an operator edit can still leave a partial/corrupt line — exactly the crash-torn-tail class the id journals hardened against (#4369, #2948, #2150). The outbox is the fallback record of a send that already happened; losing it silently means the send is never recorded in `agent.external_comms` and nobody ever learns it existed.

## Verified (laptop, this run, real script, no DB needed)

Probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-extcomms-push`, `EXTERNAL_COMMS_SUPABASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:9` + dummy service key, isolated `EXTERNAL_COMMS_STATE_DIR`:

1. Outbox = one valid line + one torn line (`{"id":"torn-record","identity":"drew","channel":"emai`): push exits 0, the valid line stays pending with `_attempts`/`_last_error` bookkeeping — the torn line is simply gone from the rewritten outbox; the only `last_error` recorded is the connection error for the valid line.
2. Outbox = only the torn line: push prints `{"pusher": "ran", "landed": 0, "pending": 0, "last_error": null}`, exit 0; the outbox is emptied; `pusher-health.json` gains `last_drain_ok_at` and `pending_count: 0`. A stewardship visibility pass reading the health file (the surface built for spotting a stuck pusher) sees a perfectly healthy, fully drained pusher.

## Why it matters

The ledger exists so no external send under Drew's or a fleet identity goes unrecorded. The DB-first path failing is precisely when the outbox matters; a corrupt outbox line is the one failure mode where the pusher — running every minute under `external-comms-pusher.timer` — currently destroys the only remaining copy while affirmatively reporting success.

## Acceptance criteria

- An unparseable outbox line is never silently discarded: it is preserved (e.g. kept in the outbox with `_attempts`/`_last_error` bookkeeping like other failures, or moved to a clearly named dead-letter file in the state dir) AND the drop/quarantine is visible in `pusher-health.json` (e.g. a count + last reason) and in the pusher's stdout summary.
- A run that quarantined/dropped a line does not set `last_drain_ok_at` as a clean drain (or otherwise distinguishes "drained with losses" from "drained clean").
- Valid lines in the same outbox still land or stay pending exactly as today; the ignore-duplicates retry semantics are unchanged.
- A pinning test/probe: outbox with a torn line (+ a valid-line control) → after push, the torn record is accounted for in health/stdout and its content is still recoverable from the state dir; the valid line is unaffected.

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-b (Lane B), run 2026-11-05 02:20 CST. Related: #6130 (the feature this hardens).

Found during the 2026-11-05 investigation of init `FAILURES=1` (separate defect, fixed in dezren39/hatch `64317acbc`: the sysstat installer's apt step stalling on the blackholing mirror.cogentco.com URI).

**Gap:** `~/tools/init.sh` restores eight systemd unit families after a sandbox recycle (airthings, fleet units, charge-inputs, resource-sampler, sysstat, hatch-autocommit, sandbox-state-backup, sandbox-home-backup) — but **quota-recorder is not among them**, and nothing else in the boot machinery installs its units either. The unit sources live in `~/tools/quota-recorder/` (`quota-recorder.service`, `quota-recorder.timer`; the service runs `~/tools/quota-recorder.py`) with no installer script and no init hook.

**Observed:** on boot `139684af` (2026-11-05 ~01:26 CST recycle) the quota-recorder units were missing from /etc/systemd/system; the boot-init cron job noticed and hand-reinstalled them (verified: recorder tick landed in Supabase 07:40:32Z). Until a restore block exists, every recycle silently drops the 1-minute quota snapshots until some job or human notices — the recorder's absence produces no init failure signal at all.

**Proposed fix:** add a restore block to `~/tools/init.sh` in the established pattern (check `systemctl is-active quota-recorder.timer`; if inactive, install the two unit files from `~/tools/quota-recorder/`, daemon-reload, enable --now the timer; count a genuine install failure, defer nothing — there is no apt/network dependency). Optionally give `~/tools/quota-recorder/` a small `install.sh` mirroring the other families so the block stays one line.

**Independence:** this gap did NOT contribute to the `FAILURES=1` count on any boot (init never checks quota-recorder); it is a silent-coverage gap, not a failure-count defect.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A restore block for quota-recorder exists in `~/tools/init.sh` in the established pattern: if `quota-recorder.timer` is inactive, install the unit files from `~/tools/quota-recorder/`, daemon-reload, and enable --now the timer.
- [ ] A genuine install failure in that block counts toward init's failure total (no silent deferral; there is no apt/network dependency).
- [ ] Verified on a sandbox recycle (or a simulated missing-units boot): the timer is active after init and a recorder tick lands in Supabase without any hand reinstall.
- [ ] Optionally, `~/tools/quota-recorder/install.sh` mirrors the other families so the init block stays one line.

# fleet-proxy(udp-forward): `fleet-udp-forward` silently overwrites duplicate scalar flags — last `--target`/`--proxy`/`--bind`/`--ports` wins

## Summary

The CONNECT-UDP client shim bin `fleet-udp-forward`
(`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/bin/fleet-udp-forward.rs`, landed
in PR #6122 for #6109) parses its flags in a hand-rolled loop
(lines 52–75) where every scalar flag assigns unconditionally:
`proxy = v` (line 53), `bind = ip` (line 58), `target = Some(v)`
(line 64), `ports = Some(v)` (line 68). Repeating any of them silently
discards the first value — no error, no warning. Only `--map` is
repeatable by design (it pushes onto a Vec, line 71–75).

This is the silent-flag-loss class already filed per-parser for the
fleet's other hand-rolled parsers — #5939 (repo-queue client),
#5929 (`proxy connect`), #5713 (fleet-dispatch) — on the one parser
those filings could not cover: this bin was written after them.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop, real binary built from HEAD)

Laptop primary `~/git/code` @ `7a980eb4cf`; binary built with
`cargo build -p fleet-proxy --bin fleet-udp-forward` in `pkgs/fleet`.

- `fleet-udp-forward --target first.example --target second.example --ports 47998`
  binds and serves with the **second** target, printing
  `fleet udp-forward: udp:127.0.0.1:47998 -> second.example:47998 via 127.0.0.1:3131`
  (ran until timeout, exit 124). `first.example` is discarded with no
  mention anywhere.
- `fleet-udp-forward --proxy 127.0.0.1:1111 --proxy 127.0.0.1:2222 --map 47998=127.0.0.1:47999`
  serves `via 127.0.0.1:2222` — the first proxy address is silently
  dropped the same way.

A script that concatenates a default flag set with an override set
(the usual way these duplicates happen) gets a forwarder pointed at
whichever value came last, with the run looking entirely successful.

## Why it matters

- The shim's whole job is pointing UDP traffic at a target host via a
  proxy endpoint. Silently retargeting `--target`/`--proxy` on a
  duplicate means traffic flows to the wrong host/endpoint while the
  operator believes the first value took effect — the dangerous
  direction for a forwarding tool, and exactly the failure #5939
  names for the queue client ("a mistyped or script-concatenated
  second `--queue` silently retargets work").
- The bin is otherwise strict: unknown arguments, missing values, bad
  ports, and unpaired `--target`/`--ports` are all usage errors
  (exit 2). Duplicate scalars are the one silent path left.

## Acceptance criteria

- Repeating any scalar flag (`--proxy`, `--bind`, `--target`,
  `--ports`) in one invocation is a usage error naming the flag
  (stderr + usage, exit `EXIT_USAGE` = 2), before anything binds.
- `--map` remains repeatable and accumulates, as documented.
- Single-occurrence invocations behave byte-identically to today,
  including the `--help` surface.
- Pinning tests cover each rejected duplicate shape plus the
  repeatable-`--map` and single-value controls; `cargo test
  -p fleet-proxy` stays green.

# fleet-proxy(connect-udp): `fleet-connect-udp` ignores argv entirely — `--help` and typo'd flags start the CONNECT-UDP endpoint

## Summary

The standalone CONNECT-UDP endpoint bin `fleet-connect-udp`
(`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/bin/fleet-connect-udp.rs`, landed in
PR #6122 for #6109) never reads its arguments. `main()` (line 19) goes
straight to `fleet_config::Config::load()` (line 20), the
`connect_udp_enabled()` gate (line 27), and
`fleet_proxy::connect_udp::run(&config)` (line 35). There is no usage
text, no `--help` handling, and no rejection of unknown arguments.

This is the #5488 class (a `--help` that starts a daemon instead of
printing help) combined with the #5568 class (trailing arguments
silently ignored), on a bin that starts a *network endpoint*.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop, real binary built from HEAD)

Laptop primary `~/git/code` @ `7a980eb4cf`; binary built with
`cargo build -p fleet-proxy --bin fleet-connect-udp --bin fleet-udp-forward`
in `pkgs/fleet`. Probe config `/tmp/probe-cudp/fleet.toml`:
`[proxy] connect_udp = true`, `connect_udp_listen = "127.0.0.1:39199"`,
passed via `FLEET_CONFIG`.

- Bare: `fleet proxy connect-udp on 127.0.0.1:39199 (RFC 9298, spike
  #6109 …)` — serves until killed (timeout exit 124). Expected.
- `--help`: **identical output** — the endpoint binds and serves until
  killed (exit 124). No usage is printed anywhere.
- `--bogus-junk`: **identical output** — a typo'd flag silently starts
  the endpoint (exit 124).
- `--help` with no opt-in config: exit 69 with the "stays dark"
  message — still no usage text.

Control, the sibling bin from the same PR: `fleet-udp-forward --help`
prints its usage line on stdout and exits 0;
`fleet-udp-forward --bogus-junk` prints `unknown argument` + usage and
exits 2 (`EXIT_USAGE`).

## Why it matters

- An operator (or a service unit with a typo, or a curious `--help`)
  cannot discover the bin's interface, and a misspelled flag does not
  fail fast — it starts a listening proxy endpoint instead. The bin is
  deliberately dark until a host opts in via config, but once the
  config opts in, *any* argument vector — including accidents — turns
  the endpoint on.
- The fleet's other entry points all settled this exact question:
  #5488/#5492 (serve-role help), #5568 (serve trailing args), #5619
  (proxy connect/init help on stdout, exit 0), #5572 (root built-ins
  reject trailing args). This bin, written after all of them, follows
  none of those precedents — it has no argument surface at all.

## Acceptance criteria

- `fleet-connect-udp --help` and `-h` print usage (what the bin is,
  that it takes no arguments, and that behaviour is governed by the
  loaded fleet config's `[proxy] connect_udp` opt-in) on stdout and
  exit 0, without loading config or binding anything.
- Any other argument is a usage error: message naming the argument +
  usage on stderr, exit `EXIT_USAGE` (2), without loading config or
  binding anything.
- Bare `fleet-connect-udp` behaviour is unchanged in both config
  states (opted-in: endpoint serves; not opted in: stays-dark message,
  exit 69).
- A pinning test or scripted probe covers the three shapes above
  (help, unknown arg, bare) so the behaviour cannot regress silently;
  `cargo test -p fleet-proxy` stays green.

title: External-comms send-time ledger: agent.external_comms + outbox spill + pusher (laptop)

labels.name: meta/follow-up
labels.description: Follow-up spun out of earlier work

body:
Implements Drew's ratified rule **EXTERNAL COMMS ARE NEVER SILENT** (2026-11-05; `~/AGENTS.md`, `~/memory/topics/external-comms-rule-2026-11-05.md`), from the 2026-11-05 external-comms audit. Drew's implementation direction: *"use database spill to outbox or use outbox always ensure pusher. all on laptop."*

## Design
**Pattern: database-first with spill to outbox** — the proven pm-stack pattern (aggregator `events.ts` retry outbox: store first, durable JSONL outbox on failure, flush merged by stable id). Chosen over outbox-always because audits/dashboards read the DB, so the common path should land there instantly, while no record can be lost to a DB outage at send time.

- **Table**: `agent.external_comms` in Supabase muse-dev2 (fleet ops schema beside `agent.tasks`/`agent.quota_records`). Columns: id (stable, PK), sent_at, recorded_at, identity (`drew` | `fleet:<name>`), channel, destination, item_ref, kind, approval_basis, approver, approval_evidence, summary, payload jsonb, source. Migration: `pm-stack/external-comms/migration-0001-agent-external-comms.sql`.
- **Writer**: `pm-stack/external-comms/record-external-send` (laptop, deployed from the primary clone). Direct PostgREST insert; service-role key resolved **by name** via the secrets broker (`supabase.muse-dev2.service-role-key`), never on disk. On any failure: append to `~/.local/state/external-comms/outbox.jsonl` (fsync) and still exit 0 — recording never blocks the send it logs.
- **Pusher**: `record-external-send push` under systemd user timer `external-comms-pusher.timer` (every minute, units in `pm-stack/external-comms/`). Drains the outbox with ignore-duplicates on the id PK; failures keep `_attempts`/`_last_error`. Every run rewrites the health surface: `~/.local/state/external-comms/pusher-health.json` (last_run_at, last_drain_ok_at, pending_count, last_error, total_landed) — a stuck pusher is a stale health file + pending > 0, readable by the stewardship visibility pass.
- **Recording contract**: documented in `pm-stack/external-comms/README.md` and in the rule topic file; email approvals carry approver + evidence explicitly.

## Backfill
The 68 sends enumerated by the audit are loaded from `pm-stack/external-comms/backfill-2026-11-05.jsonl`: opencode#176 (basis: none — unsanctioned at the time, surfaced retroactively), 3 Gmail sends (06:19 Crunchyroll = no recorded approval; 07:39 = Drew tapped Send; 1 personal = Drew's own), 9 Slack sends to Aster (Aster allowlist / Drew-directed), 55 OpenClaw Slack sends (52 autonomous heartbeat deliveries = standing-system-delivery, ratified unchanged by Drew 2026-11-05; 2 #alignment directed-test posts via queue task 7858; 1 reply to Drew). OpenClaw timestamps come from its own `channel_ingress_events` echo log, cross-checked against the audit's per-message times.

## Proof
- Blocked-path: record with the DB URL pointed at a dead port -> lands in outbox -> pusher (after restore) lands it in the table; test rows deleted after proof.
- Normal-path: record lands directly in the DB.
- Pusher health file updates every run; timer active on the laptop.

# claude-code-proxy + commandcode-proxy cannot emit client tool calls — and degrade silently (finish_reason:"stop" + prose)

Found by the 2026-11-05 tool-call audit (code inventory: `~/workspace/scratch/toolcall-audit-2026-11-04/code-inventory.md` §8/§9). Both providers are currently disabled in the deployed config, so this is latent — it becomes live the moment either door is re-enabled or a route seats one.

## The defect

- `bin/claude-code-proxy.mjs` (812 lines): the request's `tools` array is **ignored entirely** (no reference to `body.tools` outside transcript flattening). Responses are text-only (`finish_reason:"stop"` streaming + non-streaming builders). Claude Code CLI `tool_use` blocks are consumed internally, filtered to text; tool approvals are auto-allowed with the CLI's own input. Client history is flattened to a transcript (`[Tool Call: name(args)]`, `Tool Result (<id>): …`).
- `bin/commandcode-proxy.mjs` (1349 lines): same shape. "Agency" mode: if the request carries tools, the CommandCode CLI runs tool-enabled **with its own internal tools**; the client's tool list is reduced to a name/description manifest embedded in prompt prose (parameter schemas are dropped), and only the CLI's final text summary returns.
- muse-proxy's warm/exec fallback paths (`bin/muse-proxy.mjs`) have the same property: when direct mode fails, the conversation is flattened to a prompt for the `muse` CLI, so a session can flip between real tool calls (direct) and simulated agency (fallback) turn by turn, with nothing surfacing which path served the turn.

Net effect: an agent routed to these doors that requests tools gets plausible prose saying work happened — under the *CLI's* tool semantics, in the *CLI's* workdir — instead of OpenCode tool executions. Nothing in any layer reports the substitution.

## Doctrine frame (Drew, 2026-11-05)

Direct providers are **emulation** of the first-party client's wire behavior in our own provider code; the vendor binary is not a runtime dependency beyond login/bootstrap calls. These three doors are the opposite shape (vendor CLI at inference time), which is exactly why they can't carry client tool calls. Their end state is the façade migration (opencode#1411 commandcode, opencode#1412 claude-code, opencode#1155 muse-proxy). Until migration, they must fail closed.

## Ask (interim, small)

1. Each proxy **refuses tool-bearing requests loudly** (a clear 4xx naming the limitation) instead of answering with prose — or the config/route layer marks these providers as text-only so the runner never offers them tools and surfaces the constraint at seat time.
2. muse-proxy: when a request carries tools, the warm/exec fallback is not eligible (direct-or-error), and the response/session metadata records which path served the turn.
3. Regression tests: a tool-bearing request to each proxy produces the loud refusal, not a `stop` completion. (Today: claude-code-proxy tests have zero tool-call assertions; commandcode-proxy tests enshrine the substitution behavior — update them.)

Long-term resolution remains the façade migrations linked above; this issue is the fail-closed floor under them.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] claude-code-proxy and commandcode-proxy no longer degrade silently: a tools-carrying request either gets real client tool calls or an explicit, surfaced unsupported-tools signal — never `finish_reason:"stop"` + prose that implies work happened.
- [ ] muse-proxy's warm/exec fallback paths surface which path served a turn when the fallback flattens tool calls to a transcript.
- [ ] Tests pin the new behaviour for at least one proxy: tools request in, explicit signal (or real tool calls) out.
- [ ] The fix does not re-enable either disabled provider in the deployed config by itself.

body:
# mcpx confirmation gate makes projected tools unusable in headless/API sessions — including read-only tools

Found by the 2026-11-05 tool-call audit (evidence: `~/workspace/scratch/toolcall-audit-2026-11-04/live-tests.md`).

Every mcpx projected-tool execution is confirmation-gated by the mcpx daemon: executions return `"… may be destructive and was not confirmed: the answer was cancel"` / `"nobody answered within 45s"` (HTTP 502). The confirmation is **not** an OpenCode session permission and **not** a session form (a form-answering harness answered 0 forms). In headless API-driven sessions — the fleet's normal mode — nothing can answer it, so **every** projected tool execution lands as an error result, including manifestly read-only tools (observed: `fff.find_files` gated identically).

Effect on the provider/tool-call layer: the call → result → next-turn loop completes, but the "result" is always the gate error, so models either report failure or (worse) quote the requested values as if they were results. The native `execute` tool is not gated, which makes the boundary invisible until a projected tool is actually needed.

## Ask

- A session-scoped (or policy-scoped) approval path for projected tools that a headless session can actually use: e.g. mcpx policy distinguishing read-only vs destructive tools (read-only execute without interactive confirmation), and/or a pre-authorized tool allowlist per session/project that the daemon honors.
- Until then: the gate error should be distinguishable from a tool failure in the result the model sees (it currently reads as a generic execution error).

Acceptance: a headless API session can execute a read-only projected tool end-to-end and receive its genuine result; destructive tools still require a confirmation that has a real answerer in the session's mode.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A headless API session can execute a read-only projected tool (e.g. `fff.find_files`) end-to-end and receive its genuine result — no interactive confirmation required for read-only tools under the policy.
- [ ] Destructive projected tools still require a confirmation that has a real answerer in the session's mode (session/project allowlist or policy-scoped approval the daemon honors).
- [ ] The gate error, when it does fire, is distinguishable from a generic tool execution failure in the result the model sees.

title: spike(proxy): CONNECT-UDP (RFC 9298) capability in fleet-proxy — capability only, no cutover
body:
## Context

From the #5924 GUI-access work: Moonlight's media stream is UDP (47998–48010), and the CONNECT proxy in the sandbox→laptop path is TCP-only, so streaming stays tailnet-direct. Drew's call (2026-11-05): **spike CONNECT-UDP so the capability exists at minimum — do NOT cut over.** The #5924 runbook verdict (streaming = tailnet-direct) is unchanged by this spike.

## Step-0 finding: who owns CONNECT in the path

The only HTTP CONNECT proxy *server* in the sandbox→laptop path is the **Muse runtime's egress proxy** (`hatch-egress-proxy:3130`, named by `$HTTPS_PROXY`) — not ours to modify. Our own components are CONNECT *clients*:

- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy` — the session broker (`fleet proxy serve`) pools HTTP CONNECT tunnels *through* the runtime egress proxy (`tunnel.rs` says so in its module doc).
- `~/tools/proxy-supervisor/proxy-relay.mjs` (dezren39/hatch) — a raw-TCP relay that CONNECTs through the same runtime proxy.

So this spike targets **our** fleet proxy component (`fleet-proxy`): give it a CONNECT-UDP server capability, gated OFF by default, so fleet traffic *could* terminate at our own component later. Nothing in the live path changes.

## Spike scope

1. `fleet-proxy` gains RFC 9298 CONNECT-UDP, behind a `[proxy] connect_udp` config flag, **default OFF**; existing TCP CONNECT construction untouched (existing test suite is the regression gate).
2. Carrier for the spike: the hand-rolled std-only HTTP/1.1 stack this crate already uses — datagrams ride the TCP connection per RFC 9297's capsule protocol. That inherits TCP ordering/head-of-line blocking: acceptable for a capability proof, and the proof measures it rather than hand-waving it. HTTP/3 + QUIC DATAGRAM (the right media carrier — unreliable, no HoL) is the follow-up if Drew calls for cutover work.
3. **Proof (acceptance gate):** automated burst test — UDP datagrams through the proxy to a UDP echo target and back, media-shaped (1200-byte datagrams at ~90/s for 30 s), reporting loss % and added latency vs a direct-UDP baseline. A single ping-pong is not proof.
4. Design note (PR + this issue): how a real client would use it later. Moonlight has **no** native CONNECT-UDP support — cutover would need a local shim/forwarder on the client device wrapping its UDP. That shim is **not** part of this spike.

## Explicitly NOT in scope

- No cutover: Sunshine/Moonlight config, the fleet proxy's live behavior, and the #5924 verdict stay exactly as they are.
- The capability merges with the flag defaulting OFF; enabling it anywhere needs Drew's separate word.

Relates to #5924.

title: SECURITY: live GitHub PAT committed in hatch-personal hygiene-scratch dumps — revoke + untrack
body:
## URGENT — security remediation (found 2026-11-05, file-state investigation)

A **live GitHub personal access token** (authenticates as dezren39; scopes: gist, notifications, repo, workflow) is committed in the **private** hatch-personal repo — in the current HEAD tree, not just history:

- 68 tracked files match the token pattern, all under `workspace/goals/keep-the-four-repos-healthy/hidden_files/`: `git-cleanup-2026-10-27/inventory.md` + the `hygiene-scratch/` laptop-inventory dumps (lap-part*.json, laptop-r*.json).
- Origin (from the inventory itself): the token was embedded in a git remote URL on the laptop (`https://<token>@github.com/developing-today-forks/home-manager`) and the 2026-10-27 hygiene sweep captured remote URLs verbatim into its dumps. The dumps were then autocommitted.
- Verified live on 2026-11-05 by an identity-only API call (GET /user → 200). It is NOT the current sandbox gh token. Token value intentionally not reproduced here.

### Exposure assessment
- The repo is **private** (dezren39/hatch-personal) and the token does **not** appear anywhere in the public dezren39/hatch repo (HEAD + full history of its current main scanned — 0 matches). This is a private-repo hygiene incident, not a public leak, on current evidence.
- Risk remains: full `repo` scope on a long-lived PAT, sitting in 68 files + full git history of a repo many agents read.

### Remediation steps
1. **Revoke the PAT** in GitHub settings (identify by scopes gist/notifications/repo/workflow) and confirm whatever used it (laptop home-manager remote) now uses the credential helper instead of a URL-embedded token.
2. Remove the token-bearing dumps from the working tree; add `workspace/goals/*/hidden_files/hygiene-scratch/` to hatch-personal .gitignore alongside the 2026-10-31 regenerable-scratch rules (monitor-*/probe-*/clone-*) and `git rm --cached` the tree. Rotation makes the historical value inert; a history rewrite of the private repo is optional and Drew's call.
3. Sweep note for future inventory/hygiene tooling: redact credential-shaped substrings (esp. `https://<token>@github.com` remote URLs) at capture time.

Full investigation: ~/workspace/scratch/file-state-investigation-2026-11-05/report.md (sandbox-local path; ask in main chat if a copy is needed here).

## Problem

`pkgs/id/hosted-worker/test/routing.test.ts` — the only test suite for the hosted Worker's routing module (`pkgs/id/hosted-worker/src/routing.ts`) — is run by no workflow, flake check, justfile recipe, or Nix build. The package sits outside every automated check that covers the rest of pkgs/id.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ e90672dc9e, HEAD == origin/main)

- `git grep` / workflow scan: no file under `.github/workflows/` mentions `hosted-worker` or `hosted_worker`; neither do `pkgs/id/flake.nix`, `pkgs/id/default.nix`, `pkgs/id/check-all`, or `pkgs/id/justfile`. The id workflows (`id-check.yml`, `id-e2e-nightly.yml`, `id-bench.yml`) and the flake checks cover the Rust crates and `web/` — never this package. Its own `package.json` defines `"test": "node --test test/routing.test.ts"`, and nothing invokes it.
- Hand run on the laptop this run: `cd pkgs/id/hosted-worker && npm test` → **4 tests, 4 pass, 0 fail** (~0.09 s, fully offline — plain `node:test`, no workerd, no bindings).
- What the 4 tests pin (test file lines 7–59, against `src/routing.ts` lines 14–83): a binding id must be a minted 32-char lowercase-hex id (null, `google:123`, an email, and uppercase hex all throw `FailClosed`); jurisdiction must be present and supported (`us`/`eu` accepted, null/empty/`apac` throw); `userStub` takes the id and stub from the jurisdiction-restricted namespace only, in that order; and when the restriction is unavailable `userStub` fails closed with a 503 instead of falling back to the unrestricted namespace.
- Why these pins are load-bearing: `routing.ts` lines 1–12 state the contract — objects are named by the stable `binding_id` minted by the binding ceremony (#2258 / #3811), never by email or provider subject, and there is no unrestricted fallback. This is the fail-closed gate for the hosted data plane (#5199). A regression — accepting an email-derived name, or silently using the unrestricted namespace when `jurisdiction()` throws — merges with no signal and routes a user's objects to the wrong name or the wrong jurisdiction.

## Why it matters

The rest of pkgs/id has layered CI (flake checks, id-check shards, nightly e2e). The one package whose entire job is a security/routing invariant — fail closed, restricted namespace only — is the one package with decorative tests.

## Acceptance criteria

- An automated check (a step in an id workflow following the repo's existing fail-if-missing pattern, a flake check, or an equivalent) runs `node --test test/routing.test.ts` (the package's `npm test`) on changes under `pkgs/id/hosted-worker/`.
- The check passes on current main (4 tests at filing).
- Breaking a pinned behaviour (e.g. letting `userStub` fall back to the unrestricted namespace, or accepting an uppercase binding id) makes the check fail.

## Problem

The openai-cred-watchdog's test suite — `nixos/services/openai-cred-watchdog/openai-cred-watchdog.test.py`, 4 tests — is run by no workflow, flake check, or justfile recipe.

The watchdog is an hourly systemd timer service (`nixos/services/openai-cred-watchdog/default.nix:57-71`) that checks the laptop's OpenCode credential store. Its suite pins the closed #5250 regression: after the `openai` → `openai.main` provider rename (PR #5085), the watchdog kept checking the retired identity, permanently reported a healthy store as missing credentials, and never applied the banned token-sharing check to the renamed account. The tests drive the real watchdog module against fixture credential stores (healthy renamed store passes; banned token-sharing row on `openai.main` is flagged even when inactive; a store with only the retired identity does not pass).

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ e90672dc9e)

- Verified on the laptop: `python3 nixos/services/openai-cred-watchdog/openai-cred-watchdog.test.py` → **Ran 4 tests, OK** (0.144s, offline, sqlite fixtures).
- Wiring check: `grep -rn "openai-cred-watchdog.test" . --include="*.nix" --include="*.yml" --include="*.toml" --include="*.md"` → zero references outside the suite itself. The module's `default.nix` builds and schedules the watchdog (`writePython3Bin` from the source file) but never runs its tests; the file's header documents only the manual run command.
- Dedup: searched `cred-watchdog` — #5250 is the closed defect the suite pins, #3523 a closed ops breakage; no CI-wiring filing exists.

## Why it matters

The watchdog's whole job is detecting credential-store drift (renames, banned rows). #5250 showed the failure mode is silent self-deception: the checker itself drifts and reports fiction hourly. The pinning suite exists and is green; nothing executes it, so the next provider rename breaks the watchdog the same way with no signal.

## Acceptance criteria

- An automated check (a workflow step or a flake check alongside the other nixos/home suites) runs `python3 openai-cred-watchdog.test.py` in `nixos/services/openai-cred-watchdog` with a fail-if-missing guard.
