body:
## Problem

The pm-stack quota aggregator degrades any provider run whose entries carry no measured window: `finalizeRun` in `pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/gather-quota.ts` flips ok entries to `state: "error"` with the reason `no-data: provider reported ok but no window carried a percentage` (mapper rule in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-gather-map.ts`, `entryFromResult`). That rule is correct for its motivating case (Meta's post-roll ok-but-null shape silently replacing last-good percentages since 2026-11-03).

It is wrong for **key-validity-class providers** — providers whose credential class provably cannot expose a usage window and which declare that honestly. The first such provider landed 2026-11-05: openchamber's `mistral` provider (developing-today-forks/openchamber#1619, PR #1633, merged). Mistral usage/balance return 404 for a standard API key and the Admin usage API is Enterprise-only, so the provider reports key validity with usage `{ windows: {}, usageAvailability: 'console-only' }`. Every production tick now shows mistral as a permanent `error / no-data` — indistinguishable from a broken read, and it trains exactly the ok-but-null blindness the rule exists to prevent, in reverse.

## Ask

Exempt entries from the no-data degradation when the provider result **declares** the key-validity class. The declaration channel already exists: the mapper copies `result.usage` onto the entry verbatim, and the mistral provider sets `usage.usageAvailability: 'console-only'`. Rule change, either in the mapper or in `finalizeRun`:

- If every ok entry of a run carries `usage.usageAvailability === 'console-only'` (or an equivalent declared marker the aggregator chooses), keep `state: "ok"`, do not attach the no-data error, and let #1268 retention treat the entry as a healthy credential-watch row.
- Meta's case must stay an error: it declares no such marker (its windows exist; their percentages are null), so the existing rule keeps firing there unchanged.

Add a case to `pm-stack/aggregator/test/quota-gather-map.test.ts` (or the gather-quota equivalent): a console-only-declared provider stays ok; an undeclared ok-but-null provider still degrades.

## Evidence

Production `quota-current.json` (laptop, tick 2026-11-05T06:03:33Z, gatherer service on merged openchamber main 36e12d7b8):

```json
{
  "providerId": "mistral",
  "state": "error",
  "credentialWatch": true,
  "credentialLabel": "Mistral (drewrypope)",
  "usage": { "windows": {}, "usageAvailability": "console-only" },
  "error": "no-data: provider reported ok but no window carried a percentage"
}
```

The provider result behind it was `ok: true` (key verified live against `GET /v1/models`).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An entry whose provider result declares `usage.usageAvailability === 'console-only'` (all ok entries of the run) keeps `state: "ok"` through `finalizeRun` — no `no-data` error is attached.
- [ ] An undeclared ok-but-null provider (the Meta shape) still degrades to `error` with the existing no-data reason — the original rule is unchanged for that case.
- [ ] A regression case in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/quota-gather-map.test.ts` (or the gather-quota equivalent) covers both directions: console-only-declared stays ok; undeclared ok-but-null degrades.
- [ ] #1268 retention treats the console-only entry as a healthy credential-watch row.

## Problem

19 of the 20 `bin/*.test.mjs` suites — the regression tests for the live provider proxies in `bin/` — are run by no workflow, flake check, or package script. They execute only when a human remembers to run `node --test` by hand.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ aee78ac310, HEAD == origin/main)

- `bin/` holds 20 `*.test.mjs` suites: agy-proxy, antigravity-ls-proxy, check-opencode-metered-providers, claude-code-proxy, cli-proxy-workroots, codedb-bridge, codex-proxy, commandcode-proxy, design-code-proxy, muse-proxy, opencode-acp-adapter, provider-catalog-sync, proxy-port, proxy-relay, proxy-supervise, record, request-body, socket-activation, stream-decode, sync-models.
- The only wiring in the repo is `.github/workflows/opencode-config-guard.yml:23`, which runs exactly one of them: `node --test bin/check-opencode-metered-providers.test.mjs`. Grep across `.github/workflows/`, `nixos/`, `home/`, `infra/`, `scripts/`, and the flake finds no other reference to the remaining 19 files; the root `package.json` declares no scripts at all.
- Hand run on the laptop this run: `node --test bin/*.test.mjs` → **315 tests, 314 pass, 1 skipped, 0 fail** (~13.5 s). The suites are green and fast; they are simply never run.
- These are not toy scripts: `bin/muse-proxy`, `bin/codex-proxy`, `bin/claude-code-proxy`, `bin/commandcode-proxy`, `bin/design-code-proxy`, `bin/agy-proxy`, `bin/provider-catalog-sync`, and `bin/proxy-supervise` are the live session/provider path. Their suites pin behaviour that has regressed silently before and was caught only by hand runs — e.g. #3355 (agy-proxy suite failing on fleet hosts), #3769 (codex-proxy suite hang), #3114 (cached_tokens emission unpinned for two transports).

## Why it matters

Every proxy fix lands with tests that then bit-rot unwatched: a later change can break a pin (streaming terminal-text reconciliation #484, warm-session handling #480, UTF-8 chunk decoding #3186/#4336, per-key chain cleanup #2407) and nothing signals it until a user-facing proxy misbehaves. The one wired suite proves the pattern works; the other 19/20 of the coverage is illusory.

Note for the implementer: #3355 recorded the agy-proxy suite's `findAgyBinary` stub being shadowed by a system `agy` on fleet hosts — the suite passed on the laptop this run and a clean CI runner has no `agy`, but the wiring run should confirm all 20 suites pass on the runner, not just locally.

## Acceptance criteria

- A workflow (new, or extending an existing guard workflow) runs all `bin/*.test.mjs` suites — e.g. `node --test bin/*.test.mjs` — on changes to `bin/`, following the repo's existing workflow conventions (dispatch + the house concurrency pattern used by the other test workflows).
- The run is green on a clean runner for the current main tree (315 tests at time of filing).
- Deliberately breaking one pin in any previously unwired suite (e.g. muse-proxy or codex-proxy) makes the workflow fail.
- No suite is silently dropped from the enumeration when a new `bin/*.test.mjs` file is added (glob, not a fixed list).

title: fix(quota-plane): Meta percentage read — restore portal-API fetcher (subscription-quota) as the gatherer's source

body:
## Problem

The Meta (Muse Code High Usage) pool's percentage read rests on `POST https://api.meta.ai/muse-code/key` (`subs_usage`), which Meta's server currently does not populate — and has a proven history of not populating in non-exhausted states too (51 consecutive null probes 2026-10-28→11-02 while the console showed 9%→100%). Determination with full evidence: #3347 comment 6650593668. The key endpoint is a valid subscription-active/tier signal but **cannot be the system of record for percentages**.

The faithful source is the dev.meta.ai portal API (the #1301 exporter's source, retired by #5040 in favour of the key endpoint — that trade should be reversed for percentages).

## Fix: laptop-side portal fetcher for the gatherer

On the existing ~15-min gatherer tick, from the LAPTOP (same egress/device as the session, per the 2026-10-26 console investigation's Phase 1 design):

1. **Cookie capture:** read the `llama_dev_sess` cookie (plus `datr` for the same host) for `dev.meta.ai` from the live Helium profile via CDP (`Storage.getCookies` against the laptop Helium debug port). The session is in the desktop Helium's **default** profile, which currently runs without a debug port — the capture step needs Helium launched/attached with `--remote-debugging-port` (or an equivalent profile-copy launch) at capture time. Cookie value goes directly into the gatherer's secret handling — never into a file, log, or this repo. Expected lifetime ~1 year (captured cookie expiry 2027-10-27); treat 401/`Not authenticated` as failure class `session-expired` → row goes stale-with-reason per the #5719 retention behaviour, never zeros.
   - Note (2026-11-04): the Oct-era profile copy at `~/atlas/helium-chatgpt-profile-copy` no longer authenticates (401 on `/api/auth/me`) — do not reuse it; capture from the live profile.
2. **Reads (cookie-auth GETs, base `https://dev.meta.ai`, team `1073226932208501` = "My Team"):**
   - `GET /api/portal/teams/{team_id}/subscription-quota` → `{subscription_quota: {tier: "Muse Code High Usage", as_of, window_weighted_used, window_weighted_limit: "100000000000", window_duration_secs: 18000, window_resets_at, weekly_weighted_used, weekly_weighted_limit: "300000000000", weekly_resets_at}}` — used/limit are stringified integers in weighted units; % = used/limit; the 18000s window is the rolling window, plus the weekly window. Proven live payload 2026-10-27 (window 1.02%, weekly 8.83%; resets matched the key endpoint's boundaries exactly).
   - `GET /api/portal/teams/{team_id}/billing-banner` → `{kind, remaining_minor_units, currency}` — free credits remaining (minor units = cents; $148.57 at last read).
   - Map into the existing meta row shape (`meta:high-usage`): rolling + weekly windows with usedPercent + resetsAt, free credits as the balance figure. The portal's own note applies: "new usage can take up to an hour to appear" — carry `as_of` as measuredAt.
3. **Keep the key-endpoint fetcher as a cross-check**, not the source: its `is_subs_active` / `subs_tier_name` / `require_payment` remain the cheapest active/tier signal, and an inference-path 429 (quota exhausted, with reset) corroborates a 100% weekly. If portal and key-endpoint disagree about exhaustion, prefer the portal's percentages and record the disagreement in the row's reason.
4. **Testing:** fixture tests from the captured 2026-10-27 payload shape (stringified weighted units, % derivation, reset mapping) + the session-expired and portal-error classes; oracle = the recorded payload + a live console read at verification time.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Two consecutive gatherer ticks carry a fresh ok meta entry with real (non-null) rolling + weekly percentages sourced from the portal API.
- [ ] The laptop live route (`/api/quota/meta`) and the hub entry agree.
- [ ] A forced session-expired test (bad cookie) yields the `session-expired` stale-with-reason row, not zeros and not a silent null.
- [ ] #3347's remaining acceptance (recovered read recorded in the pool-change ledger by the next steward pass) can be satisfied.

Related: #3347 (root-cause determination), #1301 (original exporter, closed), #5040 (source switch being partially reversed), #5719 (retention behaviour), #5101 (board stale-fallback display).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The gatherer's Meta percentage read comes from the dev.meta.ai portal API (`subscription-quota`) fetched laptop-side on the existing gatherer tick; both the rolling (18000s) and weekly window percentages are computed from used/limit.
- [ ] The cookie is captured from the live Helium profile at capture time and passes only through the gatherer's secret handling — it appears in no file, log, or repo content.
- [ ] A 401 / `Not authenticated` response is failure class `session-expired`: the row goes stale-with-reason per #5719 retention, never zeros.
- [ ] The key endpoint remains only as a subscription-active/tier signal; it is no longer the system of record for percentages.

body:
Parent: [#6026](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/6026) (content versioning + retention). Research source: prior-art doc `~/workspace/scratch/atlas-ingestion-brief-2026-11-04/prior-art-research.md` (2026-11-04). Follow-up 14 (Cluster 2).

## Decision to record (research, in substance)

Turso Cloud PITR (restore/branch at any timestamp within a plan window — **24 h free; 10/30/90 days by paid tier**; restores create a *new* database and count against the plan's DB quota; https://docs.turso.tech/features/point-in-time-recovery) is **disaster recovery for the database**, not corpus retention:

- Whole-database granularity, ≤90-day windows — far shorter than corpus retention horizons, and no per-file version semantics.
- Atlas retention (version lineage, cold rollout to rustfs, deletion triggers) lives in Atlas's own tables + rustfs, permanently policy-driven.
- The two never substitute for each other: PITR answers "the shard DB broke"; retention answers "this file version aged out."

## Done looks like

A one-page decision record linked from #6026, so no future design reaches for PITR as a versioning mechanism.

body:
# ci(nixos/home): 6 of the 13 nixos/home script suites are wired into no check — the flake-check list in lib/default.nix covers only the 7 backup suites

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ ec2ac0e8eb)

`lib/default.nix:1106` defines `make-laptop-backups-checks`, which turns a
hard-coded `suites` list (`lib/default.nix:1110-1117`) into root flake checks
(`laptop-backups-<suite>`), each a `runCommandLocal` that copies `nixos/home`
somewhere writable and runs one `<suite>.test.sh`. The list names exactly 7
suites, all backup-related:

- `laptop-backups-watchdog`, `pm-dashboard-backup`, `pm-dashboard-backup-copy`,
  `pm-dashboard-backup-date`, `pm-dashboard-backup-manifest`,
  `pm-dashboard-backup-prune`, `pm-dashboard-backup-record`

The same directory holds 13 `*.test.sh` suites. The other 6 appear in no
workflow, no flake check, and no other runner (repo-wide grep for their names
finds only the test files themselves):

| suite | lines | what it pins |
|---|---|---|
| `nixos/home/laptop-autocommit-in-progress.test.sh` | 90 | #1807 regression: the every-minute autocommit (`nixos/home/laptop-autocommit.nix:52`, `OnCalendar = "*-*-* *:*:00"`) must not finalize a user's in-progress merge/cherry-pick |
| `nixos/home/laptop-autocommit-merge-abort.test.sh` | 75 | #3367 regression: pull-conflict abort must resolve MERGE_HEAD to an absolute path |
| `nixos/home/laptop-repo-keeper.test.sh` | 200 | keeper snapshot rules; an untracked secret inside a wholly untracked directory must block snapshots (#2268) |
| `nixos/home/laptop-untracked-review.test.sh` | 230 | #1751: the review's commits stay isolated to the literal paths the run produced; pre-staged unrelated edits survive |
| `nixos/home/openclaw-backup.test.sh` | 478 | #1036 suite for openclaw-backup.sh — the largest suite in the directory: required-member checks (#1748 class), upload-failure journal/cursor behavior |
| `nixos/home/pm-dashboard-backup-pmp-links.test.sh` | 282 | #1744 P0: `pmp_links` is the only non-rebuildable table in the projector DB, so the dashboard archive must carry its export; corrupt DB uploads nothing |

All six were run by hand this run on the laptop (in a scratch copy of
`nixos/home`, the same copy-then-run shape the flake check uses): **all six
pass** (exit 0; `all … tests passed` / `PASS:` lines). So this is purely a
wiring gap, not a red suite being hidden.

## Why it matters

These scripts run unattended on the laptop — one of them every minute — and
several guard destructive or data-loss-shaped behavior: autocommitting a
user's half-resolved merge, snapshotting a tree that contains an untracked
secret, or silently producing an incomplete backup. Their regression pins
(#1807, #3367, #1751, #2268, #1748) were each written after a real incident.
Today a regression in any of them is caught only when a human remembers to
run the suite by hand — exactly the failure the existing
`make-laptop-backups-checks` wiring was created to stop for the other seven
suites (see its comment at `lib/default.nix:1100-1105`).

## Acceptance criteria

- The six suites above are added to the `suites` list in
  `make-laptop-backups-checks` (`lib/default.nix`), or are otherwise run by
  an automated check that executes on the relevant changes.
- `nix flake check` (or the chosen check route) builds
  `checks.<system>.laptop-backups-laptop-autocommit-in-progress`,
  `…-laptop-autocommit-merge-abort`, `…-laptop-repo-keeper`,
  `…-laptop-untracked-review`, `…-openclaw-backup`, and
  `…-pm-dashboard-backup-pmp-links` and they pass.
- If any suite cannot run in the nix sandbox as-is (tool assumptions in the
  `runCommandLocal` environment), that is documented in the check or the
  suite header instead of the suite being silently dropped from the list.

Filed by the new-issue-creator (lane B) after verifying each suite passes by
hand at ec2ac0e8eb; deduped against open and recently closed issues (no
existing issue covers wiring these six suites).

body:
Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Wave-2 follow-up from the prior-art research (Lane B item 7); parent topic issue: [#5963](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5963). Research source: `workspace/scratch/worlds-capabilities-brief-2026-11-04/prior-art-research.md`.

## Scope

Roc has no effect-row inference and no content-addressed code. Two research languages prove properties id wants; this note decides which to emulate in tooling rather than envy:

- **Koka** — row-polymorphic effect types; effects compile to capability-passing. Proves the *used-effect set is inferable from types* — the theoretical basis for automatic capability derivation (https://koka-lang.github.io/koka/doc/book.html). Still research-grade per its own README.
- **Unison** — abilities in type signatures (`I ->{A} O`, compile-time ability-check failure) and **content-addressed definitions** (keyed by AST hash): free dedup/cache identity for libraries and compiled artifacts — directly applicable to the compile-cache design (https://www.unison-lang.org/docs/fundamentals/abilities/).
- **Cautionary:** OCaml 5 algebraic effects are *untyped* — unhandled effects are a runtime `Effect.Unhandled`, losing the compile-fail guarantee. Dead end for a security boundary if copied naively.
- **Zig** comptime context structs are the closest mainstream analogue to `context.platform.fn`: capabilities are struct fields; absence = compile error. No inference, all manual.

## Deliverable

Per property (effect-row inference, content addressing, ability-checked signatures): emulate in id tooling / approximate / skip, with the cost of emulation stated. Feeds #5963 (programming model) and the derivation-tool follow-up under #5955.

## Done looks like

Short spec note landed and linked from #5963.

title: id(didit): entity aliases and expectation hours spans have no count cap — the encoder produces bodies the decoder's 8192-element limit refuses

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

body:
## Summary

`pkgs/id/src/didit/body.rs` can **encode** did-it bodies that its own **decoder refuses**: two collections have no count cap in `check()`, so they can exceed the CBOR decoder's per-array element limit. A body this code writes is then unreadable by itself and by every peer — the module's stated contract ("a body that decodes is a body that would re-encode to itself", and encoders/decoders applying the same shape rules) only holds in one direction.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ `ec2ac0e8eb`)

- The decoder is configured with a declared-element limit: `top_level()` (`body.rs:873-895`) decodes with `DecodeOptions … .length_limit(LENGTH_LIMIT)` where `const LENGTH_LIMIT: u64 = 8192` (`body.rs:63`, "Declared element limit for one array, map, or string").
- The model checks cap the collections the authors remembered: `check_subjects` refuses more than `MAX_SUBJECTS = 512` (`body.rs:54, 839-858`) and `Record::check` refuses more than `MAX_DETAILS = 512` details (`body.rs:57, 253-258`). The sibling CBOR modules do the same: `idset.rs` caps `MAX_ENTRIES = 4096` against the same 8192 decoder limit, and `chain.rs` caps `MAX_AFTER = 32` against its 512 limit.
- But `Entity::check` (`body.rs:96-110`) validates each alias's text and rejects duplicates — with **no cap on the alias count** — and `ActiveWindow::check` / `HoursSpan::check` (`body.rs:399-430, 453-500`) validates each span's minutes/days with **no cap on the span count**. Nothing else bounds these counts before `check_size` (which only caps total bytes at `MAX_BODY_BYTES = 1 MiB`, `body.rs:816-821`).
- Probe (laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-didit-aliases`, real `id` crate @ `ec2ac0e8eb`, `cargo run --release`):
  - Entity with **8,193** distinct aliases (`a0`…`a8192`): `encode_entity_body` → **Ok, 48,143 bytes** (well under the 1 MiB cap); `decode_entity_body` on those exact bytes → **Err** `DiditError::Cbor("the did-it body is not CBOR: length exceeds reasonable size")` — the decoder's length limit refusing the array the encoder just wrote.
  - Control at the limit, **8,192** aliases: encodes (48,137 bytes) **and** decodes Ok — the failure is exactly the 8,192 element boundary, not size or content.
  - Expectation with **8,193** identical hours spans (420→1320, days `None`): `encode_expectation_body` → **Ok, 65,689 bytes**; `decode_expectation_body` → **Err**, same Cbor length error.
  - Normal control (entity with 1 alias): encodes and decodes Ok.

## Why it matters

`encode_entity_body` / `encode_expectation_body` are the write path for did-it events (#2031 tracker, body persistence in #4837). An entity with many aliases (importers and household merges are the realistic source — an entity accumulates aliases over its life) or an expectation with many active-hours spans can be constructed, pass `check()`, encode, and be signed/published — and then **no decoder in the fleet can read it back**, including the writer's own store on the next load. That is a self-inflicted unreadable event in an append-only log: it cannot be repaired by editing, only by superseding events that themselves reference data peers cannot decode. The caps exist for exactly this reason on subjects/details; aliases and hours spans were simply missed.

The fix direction (for triage to confirm): add explicit count caps for entity aliases and hours spans in `check()` — sized like the sibling caps (well under the 8192 decoder limit, e.g. in line with `MAX_SUBJECTS`/`MAX_DETAILS`) — with tests pinning that a body at the cap round-trips and one over the cap is refused at encode time with a named `DiditError::Invalid`, rather than producing an undecodable body.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Entity::check` (and therefore both `encode_entity_body` and `decode_entity_body`) refuses an entity whose alias count exceeds a named maximum, with the error naming the count and the limit — mirroring `check_subjects` / the details cap.
- [ ] `ActiveWindow::Hours` checking refuses an expectation whose hours-span count exceeds a named maximum, same error shape.
- [ ] Pinning tests: an entity/expectation exactly at each new cap encodes and round-trips through its decoder; one over the cap is refused by `encode_*_body` (this is the regression test for this issue — pre-fix the over-cap bodies encode successfully and fail decode).
- [ ] Existing didit tests stay green: `cargo test -p id --lib didit` on the laptop or in CI.
- [ ] A sweep of the other `didit` body collections confirms no remaining uncapped `Vec` field can exceed the decoder's 8192 element limit under the 1 MiB body cap (subjects, details, `about`, days are already bounded — see the issue body).

body:
Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Statements S5–S7 of the 2026-11-04 brief.

## Task (Drew, in substance)

Find — or build — a **demo library and a demo app** demonstrating the Roc library import model for worlds:

- The demo library **relies on platform capabilities**, so it is technically not pure.
- The demo app imports that library and uses it successfully on a platform that provides those capabilities.
- Existing starting points: `pkgs/id/examples/{roc-world,roc-chat,roc-counter,roc-grid,roc-screen}` (the roc-world example already carries the capability protocol helpers in `RocCap.roc`). Prefer extending an existing example's pattern over inventing a parallel one.

## Acceptance criteria — BOTH negative tests are required

1. **Negative test A (capability not on the platform):** a variant of the demo app (or the same app compiled against a reduced platform) that tries to use something that is **not on the platform** must **fail** — compile-time failure preferred; if the failure is at load/admission time instead, the test must pin exactly that behavior and say why.
2. **Negative test B (platform used wrong):** a variant that imports the platform and **tries to use it wrong** (wrong signature, wrong protocol order, malformed capability request) must **fail** as a test.
3. The positive path (app + platform-dependent library on a sufficient platform) passes and runs.
4. All three cases are wired into the repo's normal test flow so they cannot silently rot — this is also a down payment on the Phase 9–10 Roc-library verification debt in [#796](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/796) (cf. the closed [#813](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/813): `roc test` was never wired into CI for library code).

## Related

- Import model design (filed alongside this task under [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955))
- Capability catalog: `pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/world_caps.rs`
- Core/app platform design: [#2028](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/2028)

## Done looks like

Demo library + app in the tree, both negative tests running in CI/test flow and failing for the right reason (asserted error, not just any failure), positive path green.

## Finding

Two pm-stack Python test suites are run by no workflow, justfile recipe, or flake check — they only run when someone executes them by hand:

- `pm-stack/opencode-claimant/test_poll.py` — 36 tests (classes at :32 `TestIsActiveRoot`, :102 `TestSummarizeCap`, :121 `TestIsCandidate`, :173 `TestParseLeaseMs`, :197 `TestIsStuckBound`) pinning `poll.py`'s active-only cap counting, the #3026 gate that decides whether the claimant launches new sessions. The file's own docstring (:2-6) documents only a manual run command.
- `pm-stack/grist/test_update_choice_options.py` — 7 tests (first at :28) pinning `update-choice-options.py`'s Choice-column option merging (append-preserving-order, idempotence, empty widget options) — the script behind the Grist Choice-options workaround.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ d82a48a3dd)

- `grep -rn "test_poll|test_update_choice" .github/workflows/ justfile flake.nix pm-stack/*.md` → zero references.
- `.github/workflows/pm-stack-tests.yml` runs only: aggregator `bun test`, projector `bun test`, and two bash smoke scripts (`seed-smoke.test.sh`, `deploy-install-smoke.test.sh`). No Python step exists.
- `.github/workflows/pm-aggregator-tests.yml` is likewise bun-only (aggregator + projector).
- Both suites pass today, run by hand on the laptop: `python3 -m unittest pm-stack/opencode-claimant/test_poll.py` → Ran 36 tests, OK (0.001s, offline); `python3 -m unittest discover -s pm-stack/grist -p 'test_*.py'` → Ran 7 tests, OK (2.0s).

## Why it matters

The claimant's cap counting is a safety gate: if `is_active_root` / `summarize_cap` regress, the claimant can over-launch sessions against the cap (the failure class behind #5016) or stall launches entirely — and nothing would signal it, because the pinning suite never runs. The grist suite similarly guards a script that mutates live Grist Choice columns; a regression there corrupts dashboard data silently. This is the same gap class as the recently wired suites (#5935, #5937, #5942, #5945, #5946).

## Acceptance criteria

- A CI step (extending `pm-stack-tests.yml` or a sibling workflow, following the repo's CI tier policy in `.github/ci-policy.md`) runs both suites: `test_poll.py` (36 tests) and `test_update_choice_options.py` (7 tests), on changes to `pm-stack/opencode-claimant/**` and `pm-stack/grist/**` respectively (or on the workflow's existing dispatch/main-tier cadence).
- The step fails when either suite fails (no continue-on-error).
- Both suites pass in CI on main after the change.

# ci(repo-universe): test_generate.py + test_check_issues.py are run by no workflow — the #1650/#1651 regression suites are verified nowhere

## Summary

`scripts/fleet/repo-universe/test_generate.py` and `scripts/fleet/repo-universe/test_check_issues.py` (16 tests together) are enumerated by no workflow and no other automation: they run only when a human happens to invoke them by hand. These suites are the only automated guard on the repo-universe generator (#1650, which maintains `doc/fleet/repo-universe.yaml`) and the issue checker (#1651, whose delta reports feed the #1511 tracker).

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ 2b476fd0453c8b6de423154b8b645b33ed8e76f4)

- `grep -rn "repo-universe" .github/workflows/ scripts/tests/ justfile flake.nix` → zero references to the tests (or the tooling). The only scheduled runner in the repo is `scripts/fleet/repo-universe/systemd/repo-universe-issue-check.{service,timer}`, and its `ExecStart` runs `check_issues.py` itself (the production checker, daily) — never its tests.
- `scripts-test.yml` enumerates individual files under `scripts/tests/` only (`test_update_nixpkgs_inputs.py`, `test_worker_preflight.py`); the repo-universe tests live in `scripts/fleet/repo-universe/`, outside that directory, so they are not picked up.
- The suite passes today, run on the laptop: `python3 -m unittest discover -s scripts/fleet/repo-universe -p "test_*.py" -v` → `Ran 16 tests in 0.461s — OK`. The tests are fixture/offline (tempdir state, mocked fetches; `test_live_refuses_wrong_authenticated_account` exercises the refusal path, not the network), so wiring them is cheap.
- What the suites guard is load-bearing for the tracker: `test_generate.py` pins overrides survival across regeneration, byte-identical idempotence, classification, and owned-repo coverage for the eight fleet/side repos named in #1511/#1650; `test_check_issues.py` pins the delta semantics (new/changed/closed/reopened), pull-request filtering, and the rule that a failed fetch is explicit and preserves prior state. A regression in either shape currently surfaces only as a corrupt inventory or a wrong delta report in production.
- Precedent for this exact gap shape: #5937 (github-backup suite, since wired), #5942 (fleet-paperwork suite), and closed #1427 (cold-store-reaper). This filing is the repo-universe instance — a different tool and suite, in a different directory.

## Why it matters

The repo-universe inventory is the tracker's map of every repo the fleet owns or depends on, and the daily checker is what turns that map into delta reports. Their tests exist, pass in under a second, and are fully offline — but nothing runs them, so a generator regression (a lost hand-edit override, a non-idempotent regeneration, a misclassified repo) or a checker regression (a missed reopen, a state file clobbered by a failed fetch) would be discovered from bad production output, not from a failing check.

## Acceptance criteria

- Some workflow runs both `scripts/fleet/repo-universe/test_generate.py` and `scripts/fleet/repo-universe/test_check_issues.py` and fails when a test fails (a dispatch-triggered workflow is consistent with the house pattern since 5a94833ea3; the scripts-test workflow is a possible home).
- The full suite (16 tests) passes under the new wiring on the workflow's Python.
- A green run cannot be a silently skipped suite: the wiring names the test files/discovery directory explicitly.
- No behaviour change to `generate.py` or `check_issues.py`.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues this run for "repo-universe tests / CI / workflow", "test_generate.py", and "test_check_issues": #5615 (generator org enumeration, open — a behaviour change, not CI wiring), #1511 (the tracker epic, open), #1650/#1651 (the pieces that built the generator/checker, closed) — no CI-wiring filing for this suite. Sibling same-class filings cover different suites: #5935 (scripts/tests program-tending), #5937 (infra/github-backup), #5942 (infra/fleet-paperwork).

body:
# t3code-seed-providers: test_seed.py steals sys.argv[1] at import — the suite fails under every standard test runner (only a bare `python3 test_seed.py` passes)

## Summary

`pkgs/t3code-seed-providers/test_seed.py` reads an optional comparison-script path out of `sys.argv` at module import time (line 14). That is the test runner's argv, not the suite's: under `python3 -m unittest`, `unittest discover`, or pytest, `sys.argv[1]` is the runner's own first argument (a test name, a flag, a path), so the suite treats it as a script to execute, and its golden-comparison test fails. The suite — the regression guard for the #2738 and #3170 seed.sh fixes — only passes when invoked in exactly one way: a bare `python3 test_seed.py` with no arguments. No workflow runs it in any form, so the breakage is invisible.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ f8bac9f840a9a474ac590346141ab217345f60a5)

- `pkgs/t3code-seed-providers/test_seed.py:14`:
  ```python
  ORIGINAL = Path(sys.argv.pop(1)).resolve() if len(sys.argv) > 1 else None
  ```
  The docstring (line 2) states the intent: "Run with python3 test_seed.py; optionally pass the original seed.sh to compare." The pop also mutates the runner's argv.
- `test_well_formed_matches_original` (test_seed.py:~124-156) runs `run_seed(content, ORIGINAL)` whenever `ORIGINAL` is truthy — i.e. it `bash`-executes whatever path argv[1] resolved to.
- Direct invocation, as documented: `python3 test_seed.py` → `Ran 6 tests — OK` (argv has no second element, `ORIGINAL is None`, comparison skipped).
- Standard runner: `python3 -m unittest test_seed` → `FAILED (failures=3)`. All three subtests of `test_well_formed_matches_original` fail identically: `AssertionError: 127 != 0 : bash: /home/user/git/code/pkgs/t3code-seed-providers/test_seed: No such file or directory` — argv[1] was the string `test_seed` (the module-name argument), resolved against the cwd into a path that does not exist (the file is `test_seed.py`).
- Discovery form fails the same way: `python3 -m unittest discover -s . -p "test_*.py"` → `FAILED (failures=3)`.
- The other five tests pass under every invocation — the seed.sh behaviour itself is fine; only the harness's argv handling is broken.
- No automation would have caught this: `grep -rn "test_seed\|t3code-seed" .github/workflows/` → zero references; the suite runs nowhere.

## Why it matters

This suite is the only automated regression coverage for seed.sh's settings.json safety behaviour — malformed entries preserved, symlinked settings refused, file mode preserved (#2738, #3170). A suite that fails under the standard runners trains everyone to ignore it or to run it in the one fragile way that happens to work, and it cannot be wired into CI as-is: the first attempt to add it to a workflow (the natural fix for its invisibility) goes red for a reason unrelated to the code under test. The failure message also misleads — it points at a missing file, not at the argv theft — so a future maintainer's first CI run reads as an environment problem.

## Acceptance criteria

- `python3 -m unittest test_seed`, `python3 -m unittest discover -s pkgs/t3code-seed-providers`, and pytest (if used) all run the suite to `OK` (6 tests) with no comparison configured.
- The optional original-script comparison is configured in a way that cannot collide with a test runner's arguments (e.g. an environment variable such as `SEED_ORIGINAL`, or an argument parsed only under `__main__` before `unittest.main()` consumes argv), and the documented way to use it still works.
- With the comparison configured to a real original seed.sh, `test_well_formed_matches_original` still compares outputs (the golden check is not simply deleted).
- A missing/nonexistent comparison path, if it can still be expressed, produces a clear configuration error naming the path — not a bash 127 inside a subtest.
- Bonus, not required: wire the suite into a workflow (cf. #5942 / #5937 for the house pattern) so the fix stays verified.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for "t3code seed" and "test_seed" this run: #2738 and #3170 are the closed seed.sh behaviour bugs this suite guards (both fixed); no issue covers the test harness's argv handling or the suite's runner-dependence.

body:
# fleet(queue): the repo-queue client's parser silently overwrites duplicate flags, accepts `--dry-run=false` as true, and silently defaults a non-numeric `--limit`

## Summary

The `repo-queue` / `fleet queue` client's hand-rolled argument parser
(`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/client.rs`, `parse_args`, lines
471–512 at `1cf701651a`) silently discards or misreads user input in
three ways. This is the #5713 / #5929 silent-flag-loss class on the
queue leaf: #5713 is scoped to fleet-dispatch and #5929 to
`proxy connect`; neither covers the queue client's own parser, which
every fleet lane uses to enqueue, claim, and complete work.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop, real binary built from HEAD)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-queue-args` on the laptop: the freshly built
`repo-queue` binary (cargo build at `1cf701651a`) driven against a
recording loopback broker (`REPO_QUEUE_BROKER_URL` +
`REPO_QUEUE_TOKEN_FILE`, the client's documented direct transport).
Recorded broker requests are the ground truth for what the parser
decided:

- **Duplicate value flags last-win silently.**
  `list --queue alpha --queue beta` → exit 0, no warning; the broker
  received `{"queue": "beta", …}`. Same for `enqueue packet.json
  --queue alpha --queue beta --dry-run` → the `/enqueue` body carried
  `"queue": "beta"`. Root cause: `opts.insert(name, …)` overwrites
  (client.rs:487/490). A mistyped or script-concatenated second
  `--queue` silently retargets work to the other queue.
- **A boolean flag ignores an inline value — including `=false`.**
  `enqueue packet.json --queue alpha --dry-run=false` → exit 0; the
  broker received `"dry_run": true` and the client printed
  `{"_dry_run": true, …}`: nothing was enqueued, while the caller
  explicitly wrote `false` intending a real enqueue. Root cause:
  `parse_args` checks `bools.contains(name)` before looking at the
  inline `=value` (client.rs:485–488), so `--dry-run=<anything>`
  means true. This is the dangerous direction: the verb reports
  success for work it deliberately did not do.
- **A non-numeric `--limit` silently becomes the default.**
  `list --limit abc` → exit 0, "(no tasks)"; the broker received
  `"limit": 20`. Root cause: `get_i64` is `parse().ok()`
  (client.rs:521–523) and `cmd_list` does `.unwrap_or(20)`. A typo'd
  limit is indistinguishable from asking for the default.
  (Contrast inside the same file: `pos_i64` dies with a usage error
  on an unparsable positional — the flag path has no such guard.)

Control case: `list --queue alpha` recorded exactly
`{"queue": "alpha", "limit": 20, …}` — single, well-formed flags
parse exactly as intended.

## Why it matters

`repo-queue` is the fleet's work-order CLI: producers enqueue with it
and workers claim/checkpoint/complete through it, usually from
generated command lines where a duplicated or mistyped flag is a
realistic accident. Silent last-wins can enqueue or claim against the
wrong queue; `--dry-run=false` reporting success while enqueueing
nothing is a lost-work failure that no downstream check can see (the
queue simply never receives the task); a silently defaulted `--limit`
misreports queue depth to whoever is auditing it.

## Acceptance criteria

- Repeating any value flag or boolean flag in one invocation is a
  usage error (exit 2, naming the flag), for every verb — no silent
  overwrite.
- A boolean flag given an inline value (`--dry-run=false`,
  `--dry-run=anything`) is a usage error naming the flag; booleans
  keep working in their bare form.
- `--limit` (and any other numeric flag read via `get_i64`) with a
  non-numeric value is a usage error naming the flag and the value,
  matching the existing `pos_i64` behaviour for positionals.
- Single well-formed invocations are byte-identical to today
  (control case above stays green), and pinning tests cover the
  three rejected shapes plus the control.

## Notes

- Same bug class as #5713 (fleet-dispatch parser) and #5929
  (proxy-connect parser); the fix here is scoped to
  `fleet-queue/src/client.rs` — a shared parser is a separate call.
- Filed-only by the creator lane; not self-solved (the parser is
  shared by all 15 queue verbs, so the rejection semantics deserve
  the queue worker's normal review pass).

## Finding

The `infra/github-backup` regression suite — 10 test files under `infra/github-backup/tests/`, ~250 checks over the org backup estate (clone/mirror, reconcile retention, queue drain, worker deploy/rollback) — is run by **no workflow in the repo**:

- `grep -rn "github-backup" .github/workflows/*.yml` returns nothing (verified on laptop primary @ `9ddf6a8216`, 2026-11-05). There is no `github-backup` workflow at all; the systemd units under `infra/github-backup/systemd/` run the backup jobs, not the tests.
- The suite's own README entry (`infra/github-backup/README.md:68`) describes `tests/` only as "regression tests (plain python3, no deps)" — no documented CI runner exists.

Same gap shape as closed #1427 (cold-store-reaper tests executed only when a human remembered — fixed by adding a workflow) and #5582 / #5935, in the backup subsystem.

## Verified state of the suite

Run on the laptop @ `9ddf6a821658` (HEAD == origin/main), each file as a plain script — **all 10 pass**:

| file | result |
|---|---|
| test_clone_all_partial.py | pass |
| test_clone_all_references.py | 4/4 |
| test_deploy_dry_run.py | 11/11 |
| test_deploy_rollback_version.py | 16/16 |
| test_deploy_unknown_args.py | 53/53 |
| test_drain_queue.py | 82/82 |
| test_fetch_mirrors.py | OK |
| test_inventory_owner.py | 18/18 |
| test_reconcile_clone_pass.py | 9/9 |
| test_reconcile_retention.py | 9/9 |

These tests guard safety-critical behaviour that has already bitten once: the deploy `--dry-run --deploy-version` combination that performed a real 100% deployment (#3474), rollback verify-before-deploy (#3475), retention of a failed owner's mirrors in plan/MANIFEST, and the drain-queue contract. A regression in any of them currently surfaces only when someone happens to run the files by hand.

## Wiring caveat (verified)

A naive `python3 -m unittest discover -s infra/github-backup/tests` step does **not** work as-is: the three `test_deploy_*.py` modules execute their checks at import time and end in `sys.exit(...)` at module level (e.g. `test_deploy_dry_run.py:112`), so discovery reports `FAILED (errors=3)` with `SystemExit: 0` even though every check passed. The other seven files are a mix of unittest classes and the same script style. The wiring must either run each file as a script (`python3 tests/test_*.py`, the documented plain-python3 mode) or first move the script-style checks behind a `__main__` guard / into TestCase classes.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Some workflow runs all 10 files in `infra/github-backup/tests/` and fails when any file exits non-zero (a dedicated workflow or an added job/step in an existing scripts/infra workflow; dispatch-triggered is consistent with the house pattern since `5a94833ea3`).
- [ ] The wiring copes with the script-style modules (runs them as scripts, or the modules are restructured so `unittest discover` is clean) — a green run that silently skipped the three deploy suites does not count.
- [ ] Full suite passes under the new wiring on the workflow's Python.
- [ ] No behaviour change to `infra/github-backup/bin/*`, `worker/*`, or the systemd units.

## Evidence

- File/line and grep evidence above, read on laptop primary `~/git/code` @ `9ddf6a821658c8700fb78c06b024e2a1b024f754`.
- Suite runs on laptop, 2026-11-05: all 10 files exit 0 as scripts (results table above); `unittest discover` over the directory reports `FAILED (errors=3)` solely from the three import-time `sys.exit` deploy modules.
- Related: #1427 (closed precedent, same shape), #3474 / #3475 (incidents the deploy tests pin), #5222 (one specific untested drain-wrapper branch — distinct from this whole-suite wiring gap).

body:
# design: remote GUI evaluation — a more performant desktop for the human client, and a cheaper answer for agents

Context: RustDesk is the incumbent remote GUI. Measured 2026-11-04 (WS-C, #5775): a displayed session burns 26–45% of a core — it renders via llvmpipe software-GL and encodes in software on our Linux/AMD path — it is launched by hand (`~/tools/rustdesk-gl/launch.sh`) and has no supervisor (#5775 carries the idle auto-exit ruling). Drew asks: are there more performant GUIs for the client side (a human viewing/controlling a machine), or better ones for agent use?

Environment constraints that score everything below: NixOS laptop **with** a GPU; sandbox VM with **no GPU** (4 vCPU, oversubscribed — see #5701); tailnet-only access; self-hosted; declarative packaging matters (nixpkgs presence checked 2026-11-04 via by-name tree).

## Part A1 — human client side

| Candidate | CPU, software-render case | CPU, hardware case | Latency posture | Wayland / X11 | Nix packaging | Self-host / tailnet | Unattended |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **RustDesk** (incumbent) | **High — measured 26–45% of a core** displayed; VP9 (libvpx) default; Linux hw-encode via FFmpeg hwcodec exists but is the uneven path (solid NVENC/QSV, weak AMD — field reports + our measurement agree it fell back to software) | Good where NVENC/QSV engage; VAAPI hit-or-miss | Decent on LAN; remote quality depends on relay vs direct | Wayland experimental (portal capture); **login screen needs X11** | `rustdesk`, `rustdesk-server` in nixpkgs; server module exists | Self-host hbbs/hbbr; fleet splice designed in #5694 | **Yes — permanent password; strongest suit. Covers the sddm greeter, which nothing else here does** |
| **Sunshine + Moonlight** | x264 fallback = last resort, same-or-worse bill than VP9. Do not run it in software mode | **Best in field**: VAAPI/NVENC/QSV first-class on all three vendors; host CPU ~nil while encoding; 10–25 ms glass-to-glass on LAN-class links | Lowest of the set (built for game streaming) | X11 solid; Wayland via KMS capture (works, rough edges on some compositors); **cannot serve the login/greeter screen** | `sunshine` + `services.sunshine` module; `moonlight-qt` client | Fully self-hosted, direct UDP — tailnet-perfect | Service runs pre-login but has no greeter; pair with a greeter-capable fallback |
| **KasmVNC** | **Very low for desktop content** (damage-based RFB + WebP, not a video pipeline); poor at full-motion/video | No HW-encode story (not a video pipeline) | Fine for admin/desktop work | **X11 only** — it is its own Xvnc; cannot share a Wayland session | **Not in nixpkgs** (upstream .deb/Docker, GPL-2.0) — packaging cost | Self-hosted, browser client, tailnet-friendly | Yes — own virtual session, no console tie |
| **Selkies 2.0** (2026-09) | Vendor claim: 1080p60 software encode <100% CPU (x264/vpx) — **unmeasured, treat as a target not a fact** | VAAPI/NVENC incl. zero-copy paths | WebRTC-class, low | X11 + **headless-Wayland** backends in 2.0 | **Not in nixpkgs** | Self-hosted, browser client, single-port WebSocket/WebRTC | Yes for virtual sessions; upstream maintenance health was flagged ("in need of maintainers") pre-2.0 — watch item |
| **wayvnc + neatvnc** | Low (damage-aware capture, tight/zlib encodings, optional H.264) | H.264 with GPU assist where the compositor hands over dmabuf | Low on LAN | **Wayland, wlroots only** (sway/labwc/Hyprland — not GNOME/KDE) | `wayvnc` in nixpkgs | Self-hosted; also runs against headless sway (`WLR_BACKENDS=headless`) | Yes, incl. fully headless sessions |
| **TigerVNC** | Low for static X11 desktops (Tight encoding) | None | Moderate | X11 only | In nixpkgs | Self-hosted | Yes (own X session via Xvnc); better as the standard viewer than a new server bet |
| **X2Go** | Low (NX compression) | None | Good on thin links | X11 only, aging | Client only; **server not in nixpkgs** | Self-hosted | Yes, but upstream is in maintenance twilight — skip |
| **NoMachine** (proprietary) | Low–moderate, efficient NX | H.264 HW paths on some platforms | Low | X11, partial Wayland | **Not packaged** (vendor binaries) | Self-host server, but vendor licensing/account surface | Yes — capable; costs the self-host purity |
| **AnyDesk** (proprietary) | Low–moderate | Some | Low | X11/Wayland varies | In nixpkgs (unfree) | Cloud-mediated by default | Yes; proprietary + account surface |
| **Chrome Remote Desktop** (incumbent: `amd-crd` container) | Moderate (VP8/VP9 inside a container on a GPU-less box) | Client-side HW decode only | Variable — Google relay in the path | X11 virtual session | Container image, not a NixOS citizen | **No** — Google account + Google relays; breaks the tailnet-only/self-host posture | Yes (PIN). Verdict: keep as break-glass only, never expand |
| **Apache Guacamole** | Adds a gateway hop; the backend VNC/RDP still pays the full encode bill | n/a | +1 hop | Whatever the backend supports | `guacamole-server` in nixpkgs | Self-hosted browser access layer | n/a — **a gateway, not an encoder**; only enters if "browser access with no client install" becomes a hard requirement |

### Reading of the table

- The software-render case has **no winner**: on a GPU-less box every video pipeline pays roughly the same x264/VP9 bill, and llvmpipe rendering stacks on top. The only real answers for the sandbox are *don't stream* or *stream rarely, on demand*.
- The hardware case has a clear winner: **Sunshine**, because hardware encoding is its design center on all three GPU vendors, while RustDesk's Linux hardware path is the part that demonstrably fell back to software here.
- RustDesk's moat is real but narrow: **greeter/login-screen access and unattended permanence**. Sunshine structurally cannot do the greeter. This argues for a split, not a swap.

### Recommendation — human side

1. **Laptop (has GPU): adopt Sunshine + Moonlight as the primary interactive remote desktop**, declared via `services.sunshine`; Moonlight clients on Drew's devices. Acceptance spike before committing: confirm from Sunshine's log that a hardware encoder actually engaged on the laptop's GPU (the `software` encoder line is the silent-failure mode), and measure host CPU during a displayed 1080p session against RustDesk's 26–45%-of-a-core baseline.
2. **RustDesk is demoted, not deleted**: greeter/fallback duty + the #5694 fleet-splice role, with #5775's idle auto-exit applied. It stops being the default interactive path.
3. **Sandbox (no GPU): no standing GUI streaming at all.** The `amd-crd` container stays as break-glass. If a recurring sandbox-GUI need ever appears, spike KasmVNC or Selkies **on-demand** (both need packaging work — that cost is the gate) rather than running anything resident.
4. Guacamole, X2Go, NoMachine, AnyDesk: not adopted (gateway-not-encoder / unmaintained / proprietary-account surface, per the table).

## Part A2 — agent side: stop eating pixels

The hierarchy, cheapest truth first:

1. **Structured APIs / CLI** (fleet verbs, gh, files, Supabase) — zero pixels, exact answers. Most "GUI" agent tasks are actually this.
2. **CDP against the Helium browser** (already live: 127.0.0.1:19222 on the laptop) — DOM-level truth, deterministic input, screenshots on demand.
3. **AT-SPI accessibility trees** for native apps — semantic widgets/labels, no rendering, no encode.
4. **Screenshot on demand** from whatever session exists — a single-frame encode costs milliseconds; a 30–60 fps stream costs the 26–45% core measured above. Pixels are for *visual verification*, taken as stills.
5. **A persistent virtual desktop** — only when an app genuinely demands a real display/session.

Where a virtual desktop is needed, run it per-agent and headless: **Xvfb** (X11 apps) or **headless sway** (`WLR_BACKENDS=headless`, Wayland apps) — order ~10–30 MB RAM and ~zero idle CPU per session, versus a continuously encoded real desktop. Attach **wayvnc** to the headless sway session only when a human or agent truly needs a live view; otherwise the session is driven via CDP/AT-SPI/xdotool-class input and read via stills.

**Recommendation — agent side:** standardize on CDP → AT-SPI → stills, with Xvfb/headless-sway as the display of last resort. No agent consumes a standing video stream, ever; that single rule is worth more than any encoder choice in the table.

Links: #5694 (RustDesk fleet splice — this issue narrows its role, does not replace it), #5775 (idle auto-exit + standing-load rulings).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Candidates are scored against the stated constraints: GPU NixOS laptop (human client), GPU-less 4-vCPU sandbox (llvmpipe today), agent-driven use, and supervision/launch requirements.
- [ ] The RustDesk incumbent's measured cost (26–45% of a core, software GL + software encode) is the baseline every candidate is compared against.
- [ ] The evaluation gives a separate answer for the human client and for agent use — they may differ — each with expected CPU cost and evidence quality (measured vs claimed).
- [ ] It ends with a concrete next step: a named pilot (with what to measure) or an explicit stay-with-RustDesk recommendation.

body:
## Finding

The Python-compatible JSON/text writers that define atlas-search's output-parity contract exist as two verbatim copies with no mechanical drift guard:

- `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-search/src/pyjson.rs` (279 lines) and `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-search/src/pyjson.rs` (282 lines) — `diff` on main 83f78ed234 (2026-11-05) shows the ONLY difference is fleet-search's 3-line header comment ("Ported verbatim from pkgs/atlas-search's bin crate in fleet step 5 (#5433)").
- Same for `render.rs`: atlas-search 187 lines vs fleet-search 190 lines, diff is only the header comment.

The port is deliberate and documented (#5433): the fleet verb must render service envelopes byte-identically to atlas-search. But nothing enforces that after the port — `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-search/` has no `tests/` directory, and no test or CI step compares the two copies or renders the same envelope through both binaries. A future fix to a float-formatting or escaping edge case in one copy (the exact class of bug these hand-rolled writers exist to control — CPython `repr` semantics in the small-value range) will silently break the byte-parity contract the port was created to guarantee.

## Why it matters

Output parity is a stated contract ("the output-parity contract lives in these writers", pyjson.rs module doc). Unenforced verbatim copies drift; the failure mode is subtle stdout differences between the atlas-search binary and the fleet verb, found by users rather than CI.

## Suggested fix shape

Direction only, pick one: (a) extract the two modules into a small shared crate both binaries depend on; (b) add a cheap CI/repo check that diffs the two copies modulo the header comment; or (c) a cross-binary parity test rendering a fixed envelope corpus through both writers. (b) is the smallest step that makes drift loud.

## Evidence

Verified 2026-11-05 on main 83f78ed234: `diff` of both file pairs (4 diff lines each, header only), `ls pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-search/` (Cargo.toml + src only, no tests/).

Filed by the Scheduled Suggestions pass, tracking issue #5648 (task 9736).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A mechanical drift guard (CI check or test) fails when `pyjson.rs` or `render.rs` in atlas-search and fleet-search diverge by anything beyond the documented header comment.
- [ ] The guard runs in an existing CI workflow on changes to either copy.
- [ ] Both copies reference the #5433 byte-parity contract and the guard, so the next porter finds the rule where the code is.

## Finding

`.github/workflows/pm-aggregator-tests.yml` pins its actions inconsistently with the rest of the repo's workflows:

- Lines 42, 59, 76: `actions/checkout@v4` — every other workflow in `.github/workflows/` uses `actions/checkout@v7` (62 uses counted 2026-11-05).
- Lines 43, 60, 77: `oven-sh/setup-bun@v2` — a floating major tag. The sibling workflow `.github/workflows/pm-stack-tests.yml` (line ~16) and 7 other call sites pin the same action by SHA: `oven-sh/setup-bun@0c5077e51419868618aeaa5fe8019c62421857d6 # v2.2.0`. Third-party actions elsewhere (DeterminateSystems nix-installer / magic-nix-cache, denoland/setup-deno, oven-sh/setup-bun) are likewise SHA-pinned with a version comment.

## Why it matters

A floating `@v2` tag on a third-party action is a supply-chain surface the rest of the repo has deliberately closed by SHA-pinning, and `checkout@v4` is three majors behind the version the repo standardized on — the pm-stack aggregator workflow is the only outlier on both, so a repo-wide pin audit or bump silently misses it.

## Suggested fix shape

Align the three jobs in `pm-aggregator-tests.yml` with the repo norm: `actions/checkout@v7` and the SHA-pinned `oven-sh/setup-bun` reference used by `pm-stack-tests.yml`. No trigger or job changes.

## Evidence

Verified by direct reads on main 83f78ed234 (2026-11-05): `grep -rn "uses:" .github/workflows/` tallies and line reads of `pm-aggregator-tests.yml` and `pm-stack-tests.yml`.

Filed by the Scheduled Suggestions pass, tracking issue #5648 (task 9736).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `.github/workflows/pm-aggregator-tests.yml` uses `actions/checkout@v7` at all three sites, matching the repo-wide convention.
- [ ] `oven-sh/setup-bun` is pinned by SHA with a version comment (as in pm-stack-tests.yml: `0c5077e51419868618aeaa5fe8019c62421857d6 # v2.2.0`) at all three sites.
- [ ] The workflow still passes on a run after the change; no other workflow behaviour changes.

# fleet-search(client): home_dir() falls back to a literal "~" when HOME is unset (and to the CWD when HOME is empty) — a planted ./~/.config/atlas-search/client.json token is loaded and submitted, and a planted service.json marker flips seat routing to standalone

## Evidence

`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-search/src/client.rs:53-57` (laptop primary @ 102bfa62ba):

```rust
fn home_dir() -> PathBuf {
    std::env::var_os("HOME")
        .map(PathBuf::from)
        .unwrap_or_else(|| PathBuf::from("~"))
}
```

`PathBuf::from("~")` is a *relative* path — nothing expands a tilde — and an empty `HOME` maps to `PathBuf::from("")`, whose joins are plain CWD-relative. Every consumer of `home_dir()` therefore resolves under the process's current working directory when `HOME` is unset or empty:

- `client_token()` — `client.rs:84-87`: reads the bearer token from `~/.config/atlas-search/client.json` (unset) or `.config/atlas-search/client.json` (empty).
- `serving_host_marker()` — `client.rs:65-69`, used by `resolve_route` (`src/lib.rs:323`): existence of `~/.local/state/atlas-search/service.json` is the seat signal that routes searches **standalone** instead of via-service.
- `ensure_sandbox_forward()` — `client.rs:163`: probes `~/tools/laptop-ssh.sh` under the same bogus root.

Verified this run on the laptop with the installed `fleet` binary (behaviour matches the code above; scratch dirs under `/tmp/probe-search-home/`):

- **HOME unset, clean CWD:** `fleet search probequery --via-service` → `no service client token (set ATLAS_SEARCH_TOKEN or create ~/.config/atlas-search/client.json)` — the error names a literal-`~` relative path.
- **HOME unset, planted `./~/.config/atlas-search/client.json` containing `{"token": "PROBE-PLANTED-TOKEN"}`:** the token was **loaded and submitted** to the live service — `service at http://127.0.0.1:18760 rejected the job submit: HTTP 401 (unauthorized: invalid client token)`. A file planted in the working directory became the client's bearer credential.
- **HOME empty (`HOME=`), clean CWD:** the token error names `.config/atlas-search/client.json` (plain CWD-relative); with that file planted (`PROBE-PLANTED-TOKEN2`) it was likewise loaded and submitted (401 from the service).
- **HOME unset, planted `./~/.local/state/atlas-search/service.json`, no routing flag:** the search went **straight to standalone** (no via-service token attempt at all), while the identical run in a clean CWD (control) attempted via-service first. A planted empty file flips the Q3 seat routing.

## Why it matters

`fleet search` is run from arbitrary working directories (agent sessions, scripts, shells inside checked-out repos). When `HOME` is unset or empty — cron/systemd-style environments, `env -i`, scrubbed agent shells — whoever controls the CWD controls (a) which bearer token the client presents to the search service: a planted token is a credential-substitution / confused-deputy path, and a planted *valid* token file (e.g. dropped into a shared checkout) would be silently used; and (b) the seat routing, via a zero-byte marker file. The sibling fallbacks were already ruled wrong in this codebase — fleet-config's `"."` fallback (#5737, open) and fleet-queue's empty-string `home()` (#5673, open) — but fleet-search's literal-`"~"` variant is a third, distinct mechanism in a third crate, and it is the only one whose fallback file is a *credential that gets transmitted*.

## Acceptance criteria

- With `HOME` unset or empty, `fleet search` never resolves the client config, the service marker, or the sandbox-forward probe against the CWD (no literal-`~` directory, no bare `.config/...`): it fails closed with a clear error naming the missing `HOME`, or resolves through a non-CWD source of truth — one behaviour chosen, documented in the module doc, and pinned by tests.
- A test plants `./~/.config/atlas-search/client.json` and `./.config/atlas-search/client.json` in a scratch CWD with `HOME` unset and empty in turn, and shows the planted token is never read/submitted in either case.
- A test shows a planted `./~/.local/state/atlas-search/service.json` with `HOME` unset does not flip routing to standalone.
- With `HOME` set normally, token resolution, the marker check, and routing behave exactly as before (existing behaviour pinned by a control test).
- Sibling consistency is considered in the fix note: #5737 (fleet-config) and #5673 (fleet-queue) are the same ruling in other crates; this issue covers only `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-search`.

## Related

- #5737 — fleet-config `home_dir()` `"."` fallback (open, distinct crate/mechanism)
- #5673 — fleet-queue client `home()` empty-string fallback (open, distinct crate/mechanism)

body:
## fleet-proxy(shims): a planted `.services.json` stamp makes `sync_shims` delete symlinks OUTSIDE the shim dir

`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/shims.rs` regenerates the PATH shim dir on every connect/init. Its conservative-removal rule is stated in the module doc (shims.rs:9-12): *"it removes only symlinks it previously created (named in the old stamp), never foreign files"*.

The removal loop does not enforce that. `stamp_tools` (shims.rs:81-92) returns the `tools` strings from the on-disk stamp `.services.json` **unvalidated**, and the removal loop (shims.rs:133-139) does `dir.join(&old_tool)` + `remove_file` on anything that `is_symlink()`. `Path::join` semantics do the rest:

- a stamp entry `"../victim-link"` resolves **outside** the shim dir;
- a stamp entry that is an **absolute path** replaces the shim dir entirely.

The names fleet itself writes come from the fixed table in `tools_for_service` (`laptop-agent`, `repo-queue`), so a stamp carrying `../…` or `/…` names is by definition not one fleet wrote — a corrupt stamp, or one planted in the state dir (the same planted-file class as #5473 / #5640 / #5737, where a file a fleet tool trusts is placed ahead of it). As written, the trust is backwards: the stamp is treated as proof of ownership, and any symlink it names — anywhere on the filesystem the user can unlink — is deleted on the next `fleet proxy` / `fleet init` sync (callers: `fleet-proxy/src/client.rs:220-225`, invoked at client.rs:385/477/487/504).

### Verified (this run, laptop probe against the real crate)

Probe crate `~/git/fleet/probe-shims-traversal` (path-dep on `fleet-proxy` @ c2bf5fca29), calling `sync_shims(shims_dir, &BTreeMap::new(), exe)` with a pre-planted stamp:

1. Stamp `{"services":{},"tools":["../victim-link"],"exe":"/bin/true"}`, with `victim-link` a symlink in the **parent** of the shim dir → after sync: `victim symlink still exists: false` (target file itself untouched — only the link is unlinked).
2. Stamp with `tools:["<absolute path to a symlink outside the dir>"]` → same result: `abs-victim symlink still exists: false`.

Controls: a stamp naming a plain in-dir tool behaves as designed (existing tests `sync_adds_then_removes_as_the_map_changes`, `sync_never_replaces_a_foreign_file` pass on main).

### Why it matters

- It breaks the module's own headline safety invariant ("never foreign files") using only the contents of a file the module reads — no race, no permissions beyond what fleet already has.
- The deletion is silent (`let _ = remove_file`, no warning entry in `ShimSync.warnings`), so the user discovers it as a mysteriously missing link.
- Tool names are a closed set in practice; accepting anything else from the stamp is pure downside.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Stamp tool names are validated as plain file names before any removal: a single normal path component, no `/` (or `\`), not `.` / `..`, not absolute. Entries failing validation are never joined/removed (skipping with a `ShimSync.warnings` entry is fine).
- [ ] A regression test: a stamp listing `../<name>` and an absolute path pointing at symlinks outside the shim dir leaves both symlinks intact after `sync_shims`.
- [ ] Existing shim behaviour is unchanged: the fixed-table tools still sync/remove as before (`cargo test -p fleet-proxy` green, including the three existing shims tests).

Found by new-issue-creator-code-a, 2026-11-04 run. Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-shims-traversal` on the laptop.

title: fleet-proxy(broker): method/path CRLF injection — one frame smuggles a second request onto the pooled tunnel

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/fleet
labels.description: pkgs/fleet multicall binary + platform crates

body:
# fleet-proxy(broker): request `method`/`path` are interpolated into the HTTP request line with no validation — CRLF injection and request smuggling onto the pooled tunnel

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ a719a69907)

The broker turns a client frame into an HTTP request to a laptop service in two steps, and neither validates the two caller-controlled strings:

1. `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/serve.rs:415` `parse_request` — `method` and `path` are required only to be JSON strings; any content is accepted and passed on.
2. `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/serve.rs:312` `do_request` hands them straight to `HttpConn::request`, and `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/http.rs:132` builds the head by interpolation:

```rust
let mut head = format!(
    "{method} {path} HTTP/1.1\r\n\
     Host: {host_header}\r\n\
     X-Agent-Token: {token}\r\n\
     ...
```

There is no control-character, whitespace, or token check anywhere in the chain (both files read in full this run). The Python broker this succeeds got the validation for free from `http.client`, which rejects control characters in the URL and non-token methods; the Rust port dropped it.

Behavioral probe (laptop probe crate `~/git/fleet/probe-crlf`, path-dep on the real `fleet-proxy`, `HttpConn::request` against a recording loopback service):

- Control `GET /health` → the service received exactly one well-formed request head.
- Crafted path `/health\r\nX-Injected: yes\r\nContent-Length: 0\r\n\r\nGET /admin HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\nX-Agent-Token: forged\r\n\r\n` → the service received the injected `X-Injected: yes` header, a `Content-Length: 0` that terminates the first request early, and then a **complete second, smuggled request** (`GET /admin` with a forged `X-Agent-Token` header) ahead of the broker's own head — on the connection the pool will reuse for the next client.
- Crafted method `GET\r\nX-Method-Injected: 1` → the service received `GET\r\nX-Method-Injected: 1 /health HTTP/1.1…` — header injection through the method as well.

## Why it matters

The broker is the fleet's confused-deputy boundary: it reads the agent token from disk and attaches it to whatever a socket client asks for, over pooled keep-alive tunnels. One frame is supposed to be exactly one request. With CRLF in `method`/`path` a frame becomes *two* requests: the second one's response is read as the *next* broker client's response (cross-client response confusion on the pool), injected headers land ahead of the broker's own (a service reading the first `X-Agent-Token` sees the forged one), and a forged `Content-Length` desyncs the pooled stream — the exact failure family #5579 hardened the *response* reader against, left open on the *request* side. Same class as #2404 (newline in a header field forges arbitrary headers), which this repo treats as a bug worth fixing.

## Acceptance criteria

- The broker rejects a frame whose `method` is not a valid HTTP token, or whose `path` is empty or contains a control character, space, or DEL — with the usual `{status: 502, body: {error}}` response and **no bytes written to any tunnel** (no pool checkout consumed by the smuggled request).
- Defense in depth at the second layer: `HttpConn::request` itself returns `HttpError::Malformed` for an invalid method/path before writing anything, so no present or future caller can smuggle through it.
- Legitimate traffic is unchanged: ordinary methods (`GET`/`POST`/…) and paths (including query strings and percent-encoded bytes) pass byte-for-byte as today.
- New pinning tests cover: CRLF in path, CRLF in method, space in path, empty path, and a well-formed control — at whichever layer(s) the fix lands.
- `cargo test -p fleet-proxy --all-features` green on the laptop.

title: Atlas search: SPLADE investigation — third retrieval signal, eval harness, query-adaptive weighting

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

body:
# Atlas search: SPLADE investigation — third retrieval signal, eval harness, and query-adaptive signal weighting

Promoted from a paragraph in #5733 to its own issue at Drew's direction (2026-11-04: "file SPLADE so the idea isn't lost"). Context: hybrid design = dense cosine scan + FTS/BM25 fused (RRF), Jaccard at ingest/promotion (dedup) and rescore (#5733), scan-over-shards on TursoDB (#5669 restore). This issue owns the SPLADE question end to end.

## Drew's framing (2026-11-04) — the constraints that shape this

- **Ingest time is not a problem** if results improve. The expensive-at-ingest objection is retired.
- **The bar is query time "sameish"**: SPLADE's query-side cost is one small-model encoding of the query plus an inverted-index lookup (BM25-class speed). If total query latency stays in the current band, the investigation is worth it.
- Open questions this issue must answer with measurements, not opinion: run BM25 *and* SPLADE both? Does the full stack (dense + BM25 + SPLADE, Jaccard at both ends) actually score higher on *our* corpora?

## Does SPLADE fit SQLite natively? (Yes — structurally.)

SPLADE retrieval **is** inverted-index retrieval: the model emits a sparse, vocabulary-sized vector per text (~30k dims, ~100 nonzero, with *learned* term weights and *expanded* terms not literally present). Scoring = Σ over shared terms of w_query(t) · w_doc(t) — a postings lookup and a sum.

- **Implementation A (portable): a postings table** `(term_id, chunk_id, weight)` in the same shard DB as the chunks. Pure SQL join + aggregate; works in libSQL/TursoDB and even D1. This is the same shape FTS5 already maintains internally — SPLADE is, in effect, an FTS index whose term weights come from a model instead of term statistics.
- **Implementation B (native, later):** TursoDB's sparse-vector support (its experimental sparse-IVF index is aimed at exactly this type). Not required for v1; A is the boring, shard-friendly route.

## Test plan — the eval harness comes first

No signal earns a permanent place on intuition. Build the harness, then ablate:

1. **Held-out eval set** from real query shapes against our corpora: code questions, documentation questions, pasted errors, concept questions — with judged relevant chunks. (Reuse the parity/eval methodology from the 2026-11-04 spike.)
2. **Ablation matrix** over signal combinations: {dense} / {BM25} / {SPLADE} / {dense+BM25} (today's design) / {dense+SPLADE} / {dense+BM25+SPLADE} / each ± Jaccard rescore. Metrics: recall@10, MRR, per query class.
3. **Latency budget**: p50/p95 per-shard and fan-out totals for each combination; the SPLADE configs must stay in the current query-time band (Drew's "sameish" bar). The query encoder's latency counts — measure it where queries will actually be served.
4. **Decision rule**: a signal stays only if removing it measurably hurts the fused result. Correlated signals (BM25 and SPLADE are both lexical) may not both earn their keep — let the ablation say.

## Query-adaptive weighting (Drew, 2026-11-04)

Fixed fusion weights assume every query is alike. They're not:

- **Explicit hint wins**: a caller-supplied target (code vs documentation vs all) sets the weighting profile directly.
- **Rules second**: cheap shape detectors — identifiers / paths / extensions / stack-trace shape → code or error profile (lexical signals up); plain prose question → documentation profile (dense up).
- **Classifier last**: when no hint and no rule fires, classify the query — the Jev classifier already in the façade stack is the natural home (a query-class task beside its intent work); a small LM is acceptable given the cost lands on ambiguous queries only.
- **Hard rule: weights are floored, never zeroed.** A misclassified query degrades gracefully to slightly-wrong weights, never to a missing signal.
- Log (query class, weights used) per query so the eval can score per-class quality and tune the profiles from evidence.

Expected profiles (to be validated, not assumed): code → BM25/SPLADE high, dense medium; documentation → dense high, lexical medium; error paste → exact/Jaccard features high, dense low.

## Query encoding + the cache tie-in

- The query SPLADE encoding is a pure function of (text, model) — exactly like a dense query embedding. It therefore belongs in the **query-embed cache from #5668** beside the dense one: cache both encodings under the same key discipline, and repeat/phrased-alike queries skip both inferences.
- Encoder placement follows wherever queries are served (laptop today; possibly Workers later per the read-distribution direction on #5681). The model is small (BERT-base class); CPU inference is tens of ms — inside the "sameish" budget, and cache hits erase it.

## Success bar

Adopt SPLADE (and any weighting profile) only on measured improvement over the shipped dense+BM25 hybrid on our eval set — recall@10 / MRR up by a margin that justifies a permanent query-time inference dependency, at query latency within the current band. Otherwise the finding "SPLADE doesn't earn it here" is itself the deliverable, recorded with its numbers.

body:
## Problem

The ID-mail Worker continues per-recipient limiter checks after the caller-level rate limiter has already rejected a request. In nixos/services/id-mail/worker/src/index.js around lines 45–53, recipient checks still run when callerAllowed is false; each check calls env recipient Durable Object idFromName around lines 64–70. nixos/services/id-mail/worker/src/limiter.js:10–20 stores limiter counters without expiry.

A caller that has exceeded its own limit can therefore keep sending rejected requests with new recipient addresses and still cause recipient Durable Objects/counters to be created or written. The caller throttle rejects delivery but does not bound downstream Durable Object work or persistent state growth.

## Required behavior

Once caller-level admission fails, return the rejection without resolving or mutating recipient Durable Objects. Ensure recipient limiter state is bounded/expiring so accepted traffic cannot grow it indefinitely.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A denied-caller Worker test proves no recipient Durable Object is looked up, instantiated, or written after callerAllowed is false.
- [ ] Accepted requests still enforce recipient limits, including the configured per-request recipient cap.
- [ ] Limiter state has an explicit expiry/retention bound; test expiration or cleanup behavior.
- [ ] Tests run against the Worker handler/runtime contract, not only deploy.mjs argument parsing.
