title: ci: keep non-default daily ideation dispatches from launching duplicate production tasks

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: area/infra
labels.description: Infrastructure, deployment, and operations

body:
## Problem

The daily review workflow can start two separate agent tasks for the same daily prompt when a non-default-branch manual run overlaps the default-branch schedule. This happened on 2026-11-05: issue #5724 was created from a workflow run on queue/9572-5499-local-dispatch-action, then identical issue #5727 was created about two minutes later from main. They launched distinct queue tasks (#9775 and #9780), so the duplicate is operational work, not just duplicate GitHub issue text.

## Root cause

In .github/workflows/jules-daily-codebase-ideation.yml, the side-effecting "Run Codebase Innovation & Review Agent via pm-dispatch" step at lines 62–64 runs for every workflow_dispatch ref. That step calls .github/actions/pm-dispatch-start, whose action.yml:138–141 POSTs a new session to /v1/sessions; it has no idempotency key. The workflow concurrency group at lines 22–25 is scoped by github.ref, so a manual run on a queue/feature branch is not serialized with the scheduled run on main.

The queue-branch run was a verification dispatch for PR #5723. It successfully demonstrated that the job reached dispatch, but also launched a full production task. The scheduled run on main then launched the same daily task again.

## Requested change

Make branch verification side-effect-free while preserving intentional runs from the default branch. Prefer guarding the dispatch step so it runs only on the repository's default branch (or an equivalent explicit default-branch condition). Keep checkout and input validation available on non-default refs so workflow syntax/action setup can still be tested without calling pm-dispatch.

If manual dispatches from non-default branches are intended to produce work, use an explicit opt-in input and make the safe default skip dispatch; do not rely on branch-scoped concurrency as deduplication.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A workflow_dispatch from a non-default ref completes validation but does not POST to pm-dispatch or create an issue/session/task.
- [ ] Scheduled runs and explicit workflow_dispatch runs from the default branch still create exactly one task, preserving focus_app and allow_direct_prs behavior.
- [ ] Add a deterministic test or workflow-level assertion for the dispatch guard (including default-branch and feature-branch cases).
- [ ] Document the safe verification procedure in the workflow so future action tests do not launch duplicate production work.

## Evidence / related work

- Duplicate runs: #5724 and #5727; launch comments identify refs queue/9572-5499-local-dispatch-action and main, respectively.
- PR #5723 changed the action reference to a local path and used a branch dispatch to verify setup; that PR is merged and correctly fixes the staging failure, but exposed this dispatch-side-effect gap.
- Workflow: .github/workflows/jules-daily-codebase-ideation.yml; action: .github/actions/pm-dispatch-start/action.yml.

body:
Perform a comprehensive daily codebase review, innovation scan, and issue/PR maintenance pass across developing-today/code.

You are acting as an unrestricted principal architect and senior systems engineer. Do not hold back: generate bold ideas, surface hidden gaps, polish proposals, and solve immediate problems opportunistically.
Follow these directives and areas of focus:
### 1. COMPREHENSIVE REPOSITORY & ACTIVITY AUDIT - Inspect recent commits on `main` to understand the latest velocity and architectural direction. - Review open, recently closed, and merged issues and PRs (`gh issue list --state all --limit 50`, `gh pr list --state all --limit 30`). - Review each major package, tool, and subsystem in the repository:
  - **`pkgs/id`**: Distributed identity, cryptographic event log, p2panda synchronization, local event store, group encryption, discovery, and capability delegation.
  - **`pkgs/mcpx`**: Model Context Protocol daemon, multi-server multiplexing, protocol compliance, session leasing, JIT secret prompt vault, and Code Mode projection.
  - **`pkgs/jules` / `pkgs/jules-fleet` / `pkgs/jules-merge`**: Automated multi-agent coding workflows, issue triage, and parallel agent execution.
  - **NixOS System Infrastructure & Web Services**: Modules, cloud functions, background daemons, and system services.

### 2. UNRESTRICTED INNOVATION & NEW FEATURE GENERATION - You are NOT restricted by what currently exists. Brainstorm things that *should* exist, would be exceptionally useful, or incorporate frontier concepts:
  - Edge architectures using Cloudflare Workers, Durable Objects, KV, and Queues.
  - Distributed SQLite / libSQL / Turso primitives for offline-first, syncable state.
  - Advanced autonomous coding loops, speculative tool execution, and local verification loops.
  - Cross-platform bridges, native desktop integrations, and performance optimizations.
- **Bias Toward Capture**: It is far better to create an issue to triage later than to let a valuable opportunity or insight pass.
### 3. ACTIVE ISSUE & PR MAINTENANCE - **Scope Variety**: Create single large architectural vision issues for strategic direction, or narrow, highly focused issues for targeted improvements. - **Issue Decomposition**: If an existing issue is too broad, ambiguous, or monolithic (including issues created by others), break it apart into a series of clear, modular, linked sub-issues with explicit dependencies. - **Deduplication & Consolidation**: Identify overlapping or duplicate proposals/issues and consolidate them into unified, high-quality reference issues. - **Comments & Spec Refinement**: Leave comments or edit existing issues/PRs to provide missing technical specifications, edge-case analysis, data schemas, or suggested test cases. - **Zero-Context Hand-off Standard**: Every issue you author must be self-contained, citing exact file paths, interfaces, architectural rationale, and verifiable acceptance criteria so a new agent with zero prior context can execute it.

### 4. OPPORTUNISTIC IMPLEMENTATION (QUICK-WIN PRS) - If you identify straightforward bugs, unhandled edge cases, missing test coverage, or clean opportunities to refactor code to prevent future merge conflicts:
  - You are actively encouraged to open small, focused Pull Requests implementing the fix or feature directly.
  - Ensure all added code follows repository standards, includes tests, and passes formatting/linting hooks (`treefmt`, `conform`).
  - Never introduce breaking regressions to existing stable flows.
  - **One PR per coherent set**: batch every instance of the same problem — and all related dependency updates — into a single PR, or a few PRs split by coherent group. Never one PR per item or per dependency.
  - **Prefer tracked, higher-impact work**: before inventing a new micro-fix, check the open issues and implement the highest-impact one you can complete and verify, even when it spans several files.
  - **Merging is permitted, never required**: merge your PR only when checks pass and you are reasonably certain it is correct and low-risk. Otherwise leave it open and state your confidence and what a human should check in the description.

This looks like flake.lock input drift: the current lock no longer matches the four inputs the test asserts. Either the lock legitimately gained/lost an input (test expectation is stale) or an input was dropped/added unintentionally (lock is wrong).

## Found during

Queue task 9769 / issue #5712 (moving mid-file `unittest.main()` guards) — the failure is pre-existing on clean main and unrelated to that change; discover outcome before and after is identical (14 tests, same 2 failures).

## Acceptance

- Determine whether the flake.lock state or the test expectation is correct.
- Fix whichever is wrong so the test passes on main.

# worktree-reaper: run-log filename collides for same-second runs — the gate test suite fails 6/6 and a second run's audit log overwrites the first

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ af0847d00a)

The reaper names its per-run decision log with second resolution plus the process id:

- `infra/worktree-reaper/bin/worktree_reaper.py:542` — `ts = time.strftime("%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ", time.gmtime(int(now)))`
- `infra/worktree-reaper/bin/worktree_reaper.py:603` — `log_path = os.path.join(state_dir, "runs", f"run-{ts}-{os.getpid()}.jsonl")`, opened `"w"` at :605.

Two runs started in the same second by the same process therefore share one
log path: the second run truncates and rewrites the first run's log.

The gate suite drives the reaper in-process
(`infra/worktree-reaper/tests/test_worktree_reaper.py`, `ReaperRun.run`),
and discovers a run's decisions by diffing the `runs/` directory listing
before/after. When a run's log path already exists (same second, same pid),
the diff is empty and the run returns `{}` decisions, so assertions die with
`KeyError` on the tree path.

Reproduction (laptop, current main):

- `python3 -m unittest discover -s infra/worktree-reaper/tests` — FAILED in
  6 of 6 consecutive full-suite runs (1–2 errors each: `test_03_reap_matrix`
  KeyError at test line 234 on the patch-equivalent tree, `test_04_quiet_gate`
  KeyError at test line 253 on the fresh tree). Each test passes standalone.
- Micro-repro with the suite's own harness: two `runner.run()` calls in the
  same second produced exactly one log file
  (`run-20261105T002713Z-57087.jsonl`); the first run returned its tree's
  decision, the second returned `[]` decisions while overwriting the file.

## Why it matters

- The suite is the only gate-logic coverage for a tool that deletes
  worktrees and branches, and it is effectively red whenever runs land in
  the same second — so nobody can trust a green/red signal from it (it is
  also not wired into any workflow, so the failure is invisible until a
  human runs it by hand).
- In production the same naming means two invocations that share a pid in
  one second (pid reuse, wrapper re-exec) silently lose the first run's
  audit log — the only record of what the reaper deleted and why.

## Acceptance criteria

- Run-log filenames are unique per run even for same-second, same-process
  invocations (e.g. sub-second component, monotonic sequence, or exclusive
  create with a disambiguating suffix); a second run never truncates a
  previous run's log.
- `python3 -m unittest discover -s infra/worktree-reaper/tests` passes 10
  consecutive full-suite runs on the laptop.
- A regression test (or the existing gate tests run back-to-back) covers
  two runs in the same second both producing readable decision logs.

# Two Python suites carry `unittest.main()` mid-file — direct-script runs silently skip every test class defined after it

Verified on main `af0847d00a2231c71f6ebb59eba4cc7db197599e` (2026-11-04, `gh api` raw reads + executed copies of the committed files).

## Evidence

### 1. `pkgs/cold-store-reaper/tests/test_cold_store.py`

- Lines 3223–3224: `if __name__ == "__main__": unittest.main(verbosity=2)` — mid-file.
- Line 3227: `class TestResumableUploadStalls(ColdStoreTestBase)` is defined **after** that guard, with 3 tests (lines 3252, 3261, 3270). They are the regression tests for closed #2797: a resumable-upload 308 whose Range stops advancing must raise instead of looping forever, and a Range-less 308 must not count unacknowledged bytes as sent.
- The file's own header (lines 4–5) documents two run modes: `python3 -m unittest discover -s pkgs/cold-store-reaper/tests -v` **or** `python3 pkgs/cold-store-reaper/tests/test_cold_store.py`.
- Executed this run from a verbatim copy of the committed files (+ `cold_store.py`, `schema.sql`):
  - Direct: `python3 tests/test_cold_store.py` → **Ran 109 tests**; zero `TestResumableUploadStalls` tests appear.
  - Discover: `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v` → **Ran 112 tests**; all 3 stall tests run and pass.
  - (13 failures in both modes in the verification copy are an artifact of the partial copy — missing `scripts/drill_compare.py` / export-turso fixtures — identical in both modes and unrelated.)
- CI (`.github/workflows/cold-store-reaper.yml`) uses discover, so CI is **not** affected; the documented direct-script mode silently is.

### 2. `scripts/tests/test_update_nixpkgs_inputs.py`

- Lines 377–378: `if __name__ == "__main__": unittest.main()` — mid-file, followed by a fresh `import` block (line ~380) and the entire #4553 section.
- Defined after the guard: `TestHydraGateParsing` (line 473, 2 tests), `TestGatedPinEndToEnd` (line 611, 2 tests), `TestHttpsContext` (line 671, 1 test) — 5 tests pinning the #4553 Hydra cache-gate contract and the HTTPS-verification-stays-on contract for both copies of `update-nixpkgs-inputs`.
- Executed this run from a verbatim copy (with both script copies in place):
  - Direct: `python3 scripts/tests/test_update_nixpkgs_inputs.py` → **Ran 9 tests**.
  - Discover: `python3 -m unittest discover -s scripts/tests -p 'test_update_nixpkgs_inputs.py'` → **Ran 14 tests**; the 5 after-guard tests run and pass.
  - (1 identical error in both modes is the verification copy's missing repo-root `flake.lock` — unrelated.)
- CI (`.github/workflows/scripts-test.yml` line 31) uses discover, so CI is **not** affected; a direct run silently is.

## Why it matters

`unittest.main()` raises `SystemExit` when the module is executed as a script, so any class defined below the guard is never even defined in that process — the suite reports a smaller, green-looking run with no warning. In both files the stranded tests are safety contracts (#2797 upload-stall protection; #4553 pin gating). Anyone verifying a change with the documented/quick direct invocation — exactly what the cold-store header offers — gets illusory coverage. Sibling instance, filed separately because its mechanism differs (dead defs are outside any class, so they never run in *any* mode): #5710.

A repo-wide scan this run (all 41 Python test files) found exactly these two remaining mid-file-guard instances besides #5710's file.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] In both files, the `if __name__ == "__main__": unittest.main()` block is the last executable statement in the file (nothing defined after it).
- [ ] `python3 pkgs/cold-store-reaper/tests/test_cold_store.py` reports **112 tests** (was 109), including the 3 `TestResumableUploadStalls` tests.
- [ ] `python3 scripts/tests/test_update_nixpkgs_inputs.py` reports **14 tests** (was 9), including `TestHydraGateParsing`, `TestGatedPinEndToEnd`, and `TestHttpsContext`.
- [ ] Discover invocations report the same counts as before the change (112 / 14) and no test outcome changes; no production code is modified.

# cargo-target-janitor: the two `owner_changed` tests never run — they are defined after `unittest.main()`, outside the test class

## Evidence (verified this run @ af0847d00a)

`infra/cargo-target-janitor/tests/test_cargo_target_janitor.py`:

- Line 191-192: the file ends its class body and closes with
  ```python
  if __name__ == "__main__":
      unittest.main()
  ```
- Lines 194 and 208: `test_owner_changed_when_worktree_switched_branch` and
  `test_owner_changed_ignores_adhoc_targets` are defined **after** that call,
  indented inside the `if __name__` block — not as methods of `JanitorTests`.
  `unittest.main()` also exits the process, so the two `def`s are never even
  reached at runtime, and unittest discovery never sees them either way.

Reproduction (run against the file as committed):

```
$ python3 tests/test_cargo_target_janitor.py -v
...
Ran 11 tests in 0.053s
OK
```

An AST walk of the file finds **13** `test_*` functions; only the 11 class
methods run. The two dead tests are the only coverage for
`owner_changed()` (`infra/cargo-target-janitor/bin/cargo_target_janitor.py:69`),
the guard the `--apply` path re-checks immediately before `shutil.rmtree`
(same file, line 548): if the worktree owning a target switched branch/task
since the plan, deletion must stop (the #4175 Codex P2 fix).

The function itself is currently correct — calling it directly with the dead
tests' fixtures gives the expected results (switched → True, same → False,
unregistered → True, ad-hoc → False) — so this is illusory coverage, not a
live logic bug: any future regression in `owner_changed` would pass CI green
while the file appears to test it.

## Why it matters

This tool deletes directory trees (`shutil.rmtree`) under `~/git/fleet`.
`owner_changed` is one of the last-moment safety re-checks that keep it from
removing a target whose checkout was repurposed after planning. A safety
guard whose tests silently never execute is exactly the kind of coverage
that fails only when it is needed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `test_owner_changed_when_worktree_switched_branch` and
      `test_owner_changed_ignores_adhoc_targets` are methods of
      `JanitorTests` (moved above the `if __name__ == "__main__":` guard).
- [ ] `python3 tests/test_cargo_target_janitor.py` reports **13 tests** and
      passes (previously 11).
- [ ] No change to `bin/cargo_target_janitor.py` behavior is needed; if the
      rescued tests fail against the current implementation, that failure is
      reported on this issue rather than edited away in the tests.

# id(issuer-rotation): `fold_rotation_chain` dedups candidates by event id only — duplicate-id entries with a different author/body make the fold input-order dependent, contradicting its determinism contract

## Evidence (verified this run against main `af0847d00a2231c71f6ebb59eba4cc7db197599e`, via `gh api` raw reads; laptop unreachable this run)

`pkgs/id/src/issuer_rotation.rs:497` documents the fold's core contract:

> The fold is deterministic and independent of input order.

The candidate reduction at `pkgs/id/src/issuer_rotation.rs:560-561` does not uphold it:

```rust
candidates.sort_by_key(|(_, event_id, _)| *event_id);
candidates.dedup_by_key(|(_, event_id, _)| *event_id);
```

`sort_by_key` is stable and `dedup_by_key` keeps the *first* of each equal-key run, so when the input slice contains two entries with the **same event id but different rotation bodies**, whichever entry happens to be listed first survives dedup, and the surviving entry alone decides the generation transition (or the fork resolution) afterwards. The filters at lines 543–559 do not save this: they validate each entry on its own merits, and two *distinct, individually valid* bodies can share one event id in the fold's input. Concretely, this changes the folded result under a mere permutation of the same input multiset:

- Same event id, two valid `Routine` bodies by the current generation key naming **different successor keys** (each correctly countersigned by its own successor). Both pass every filter. Listed A-first, generation *g+1*'s key is A's successor; listed B-first, it is B's — instead of the `ChainStatus::Conflicted` the design (§3.2 rule 5) prescribes for two valid transitions claiming the same predecessor.
- Same event id, one valid `Routine` body and one valid `CompromiseRecovery` body (recovery key author). The survivor decides whether the step is a plain advance or a recovery advance with a `RecoveryStep` recorded — purely by input order.

In the production path the event id is the hash of the signed header, so two *decoded events* cannot collide this way today. But `fold_rotation_chain` is a public, documented-as-order-independent pure function over caller-supplied `(author, event_id, rotation)` tuples — its callers supply authors and rotations extracted from events (`fold_rotation_chain` docs, lines 490–496), and any future caller that merges rotation sets from two sources (store + sync feed, journal replay + live) can present the same id twice with divergent extracted fields. The sibling currency fold had exactly this bug class and it was treated as a real defect: #4069 (closed) — "fold_authorisation duplicate highest version folds by input order — no deterministic tie-break". This fold's contract is stronger (it promises order independence outright) and its reduction is weaker (id-only).

## Why it matters

- The fold is the authoritative answer to "which key speaks for generation *g*" for a currency issuer. An order-dependent fold means two replicas folding the same rotation set can disagree on the active issuer key — the exact failure the module exists to prevent (§3.2 rule 5 refuses arrival-order tie-breaks for the same reason).
- The gap is invisible to the current test suite: every fold test passes distinct event ids (`event(1)`, `event(2)`, …), so no test exercises a duplicate id with divergent fields.

## Acceptance criteria

- `fold_rotation_chain` returns the identical `GenerationChain` for every permutation of the same input multiset, including inputs containing duplicate event ids whose author or rotation body differ. (Deterministic rule for duplicates: e.g. dedup on the full `(event_id, author, rotation)` tuple with a total order over the tuple, or refuse/ignore all-but-one by a content-derived order — any rule that is a function of the multiset, not of the listing order.)
- A property test (per the repo testing doctrine: the oracle is permutation invariance of the fold) shuffles inputs — including duplicate-id/divergent-field entries — and asserts identical output; it fails on the current code and passes after the fix.
- Existing `issuer_rotation` tests still pass (`cargo test -p id --lib issuer_rotation` on the laptop or CI per house rules).
- Dedup behaviour for the ordinary duplicate case (identical tuples listed twice) is unchanged: the transition still counts once.

body:
# id(chain): `ChainExt::validate` never checks the issuer-rotation body — every other payload kind gets its `check_*`, rotation gets `(true, Some(_)) => {}`

## Evidence (verified this run against main `af0847d00a22`, via `gh api` raw reads)

`pkgs/id/src/chain.rs` — `ChainExt::validate()` applies a payload check for every
payload-carrying kind:

- tag → `check_op(&self.kind, op)`
- document → `document.check()`
- note → `check_note_op(&self.kind, op)`
- note link → `check_note_link_op(&self.kind, op)`
- session checkpoint → `check_session_checkpoint(&self.kind, checkpoint)`

The rotation arm (chain.rs:352–367) checks only presence/absence:

```rust
match (is_rotation_kind(&self.kind), &self.rotation) {
    (false, None) => {}
    (false, Some(_)) => { /* error: carries a rotation */ }
    (true, None) => { /* error: needs its rotation */ }
    (true, Some(_)) => {}   // ← no check of the body at all (chain.rs:366)
}
```

`pkgs/id/src/issuer_rotation.rs` — `IssuerRotation::validate()` exists
(issuer_rotation.rs:295) but is never called from `chain.rs` (code search:
`IssuerRotation` is referenced only in `chain.rs`, `issuer_rotation.rs`, and
the #2804 design doc). Its context-dependent half (recovery author vs the
currency's committed recovery key; routine author is the current generation
key) does need the fold's context — but a stateless subset is decidable from
the body alone, exactly like the sibling `check_*` functions:

- consecutive generations: `to_generation == from_generation + 1`
  (issuer_rotation.rs:300–303)
- predecessor rule: generation 0 names no `previous_rotation`; any later
  generation names one (issuer_rotation.rs:305–311)
- routine mode carries no `asserted_compromise_from`
  (issuer_rotation.rs:313–317)
- `verify_successor_proof()` — a pure function of the body
  (issuer_rotation.rs:268)

## Observed behaviour

`chain::sign` will sign, and `chain::decode` will accept, an
`issuer.rotation` event whose body:

- has `to_generation != from_generation + 1` — including the
  `from_generation == u64::MAX` saturating case that `IssuerRotation::unsigned`
  documents as "an object validation always rejects" (issuer_rotation.rs:198–200;
  no validation runs on the sign/decode path, so nothing rejects it there);
- is a generation-0 transition naming a `previous_rotation`, or a later
  transition naming none;
- is a routine rotation carrying `asserted_compromise_from`;
- carries a zeroed successor proof (`unsigned()` leaves `successor_proof`
  as `[0; 64]` until `prove_successor` runs).

That contradicts `validate()`'s own contract (chain.rs, doc on `validate`):
"Both the builder and the decoder apply them, so a signed event always
passes them on receipt" — rotation is the one payload kind for which no
body rule is applied by either the builder or the decoder. The malformed
event is a fully valid signed event: it is stored and synced as one, and
only a future fold consumer would ever refuse it. `chain.rs` tests never
exercise rotation at all (every `ChainExt` literal in its tests has
`rotation: None`).

## Why it matters

The header is the trust boundary: receivers call `decode` and nothing else
(chain.rs module docs). Every other signed body is refused at that boundary
when malformed; a malformed rotation body crosses it silently, so the
failure surfaces far from its cause — at fold time, in a different
component, against an event other nodes have already accepted and stored.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `check_rotation(kind, &IssuerRotation)` (or equivalent) runs the
      stateless subset above — consecutive generations, predecessor rule,
      routine/no-asserted-compromise, successor-proof verification — and
      `ChainExt::validate` calls it in the `(true, Some(rotation))` arm,
      mapping failures to `ChainError::Extension` like the sibling arms.
- [ ] The context-dependent rules (recovery author vs committed recovery
      key; routine author is the current generation key) stay in
      `IssuerRotation::validate` / the fold, with a comment naming why they
      are not part of the chain check.
- [ ] Tests in `chain.rs`: `sign`/`decode` refuse a rotation event with a
      non-consecutive generation, a generation-0 predecessor, a routine
      `asserted_compromise_from`, and a zeroed/invalid successor proof; a
      well-formed rotation (built via `unsigned` + `prove_successor`)
      signs and decodes.
- [ ] `cargo test -p id --lib chain` (and the issuer_rotation tests) pass
      on the laptop or CI per house rules.

body:
## Incident record — 2026-11-04 afternoon responsiveness loss (sandbox ↔ laptop path)

Drew's chat went unresponsive shortly after 15:00 CST ("connection error / reconnecting" at ~16:09, last activity ~15:0x). Two orchestration passes failed (14:12 no execution; 15:12 timeout after prelude). An independent workstream (Mistral-provider build, chat f3937a75) reported the fleet session proxy "closing EVERY CONNECT to the laptop (`laptop-agent: proxy closed during CONNECT` — three consecutive failures after earlier intermittent ones)". Drew powered the laptop OFF at ~17:01 CST and responsiveness returned — but the sandbox also recycled at 16:57 CST, which is the more mechanical explanation for the recovery (a fresh boot clears the wedged state, whatever it was).

### Timeline (UTC; CST = UTC−6)

- 14:38–20:57 — boots 0a18fb7e, da56f9ed (16:20), ad076b64 (18:27), d50de26a (20:57). Baseline load already high: resource sampler shows load 11–13 on 4 CPUs at 00:0x, and .rustdesk-wrapper ~45% CPU through the ad076b64 evening.
- ~20:43–21:16 — the repo-queue → fleet-queue migration completed (29 cron jobs) and the exceptions coordinator finished; heavy parallel agent work in flight (Atlas revision, Mistral build, ID sessions).
- 21:00–21:28 (boot d50de26a) — client trip log: **280 laptop-agent trips, ALL status 200**, 10–19/min, 15 slow (>5 s, worst 217 s — a long exec that completed). The laptop path itself was working. Load 2–8, mem avail 1.0–4.4 GB. Init re-running every 2–7 min in the background (see the init-loop issue — fixed separately).
- 21:22:46 — sandbox recycled again (boot 3ed35cc9, only 25 min after d50de26a).
- 21:25–21:29 — post-boot thundering herd: sampler shows load climbing; at **21:29:17 load 30.39 (1-min) / 12.61 (5-min), a `.gh-wrapped` process tree at 1645% CPU, and the Muse daemon restarted (pid 67 → 10918)**.
- **21:29:17 → 22:57 — the resource sampler produced NO further lines** (it had sampled every 2 min all day). Sandbox-side agent trips also essentially cease (2 trips in ~90 min vs ~280 in the prior 28 min). This ~88-minute window is Drew's dead period.
- 22:57:31 — sandbox recycled (boot 6989413c). Sampler, daemon, and trips resume immediately. Drew's connectivity returns ~17:01 CST (23:01 UTC) — in the new boot.
- After 23:01 — trips fail with ~25–32 s timeouts and `status: null` because the LAPTOP IS OFF (Drew powered it down) — expected, not a fault.

### What the evidence establishes

1. **The laptop and the laptop-agent path were not the failure** in the 21:00–21:28 window: 280/280 trips succeeded. The failure begins with a sandbox recycle (21:22) and a post-boot load explosion (21:29).
2. **The sandbox side wedged, not the transport**: a daemon restart + a sampler that stopped sampling for 88 minutes + agent traffic ceasing all point at the sandbox VM/daemon being frozen or CPU-starved, not at CONNECT refusals. (The Mistral agent's "proxy closed during CONNECT" errors are consistent with a sandbox-side proxy process starved/frozen mid-handshake — the broker log also holds a `ConnectionRefusedError` from `tunnel_socket` to the runtime proxy port and repeated client BrokenPipes — but the broker log has no timestamps, so those cannot be placed in the window. That is a logging gap to fix.)
3. **Recycle cadence is part of the story**: six boots on 2026-11-04 (02:25, 04:18, 06:03, 10:34, 12:33, 14:38, 16:20, 18:27, 20:57, 21:22, 22:57 — the sampler's boot list is even longer). Every recycle triggers catch-up cron firings + full init + the platform's apt replay; the 21:22 boot's herd is the one that tipped over.
4. **The fleet-queue migration is not implicated by any direct evidence**: migrated jobs invoke `fleet queue` on the sandbox, which reaches the queue-broker on the laptop through the same proxy pools as before; trip-log volume in the healthy window is agent execs (unchanged path), and no queue-connection errors appear in any timestamped log. The migration coincided with the incident window but the failure signature (daemon restart, sampler death) is sandbox CPU/life-cycle, not queue-client behavior. Remaining unknown: the Rust client's per-call connection behavior (pool reuse vs new CONNECT per call) — source is in the code repo (laptop, off at filing time); verify when it returns.
5. **Contributors, honestly weighted**: (a) post-boot thundering herd (catch-up crons + lanes + coordinators + platform apt replay) — strongest fit for the 21:29 spike; (b) the init re-run loop (fixed separately) added a ~65 s job every few minutes all day; (c) standing oversubscription — load 11–13 at idle-ish times on a 4-CPU box, .rustdesk-wrapper ~45% for hours; (d) a `.gh-wrapped` burst at 1645% at the spike moment (many agents shelling to gh simultaneously after the boot).

### What is NOT established (and the tests that settle it)

- **Concurrent-connection ceiling**: Drew's proposed clean ramp test (50 → 64 → 128 concurrent proxied connections sending real messages, find where errors start) has NOT been run — it needs the laptop ON (every proxied target terminates there). Run it when the laptop returns, against the queue-broker port and the daemon port, and record where "proxy closed during CONNECT" first appears, if anywhere.
- **Why the sampler stopped**: service death vs whole-VM freeze cannot be distinguished from surviving logs (the sampler's own log IS the missing data). sysstat collection (added 2026-11-04) would have answered this; ironically its install was blocked all day by the init-loop bug (now fixed), so the next incident should have sadc data.
- **Laptop-side state in the window** (broker/daemon logs, laptop load): pending — laptop is off by Drew's choice; gather when it returns: laptop trips.jsonl (daemon side), `fleet serve` broker journals, daemon journal for 21:00–22:10 UTC.
- **Why the platform recycled the sandbox at 21:22 and 22:57**: no platform-side reason is visible from inside the VM.

### Transport findings from the same pass (code-cited; full analysis in the investigation report)

- **"proxy closed during CONNECT" decoded**: the literal string (`laptop-agent.py:78`) fires on exactly one condition — EOF before the runtime proxy finishes answering a CONNECT. It is the **runtime proxy closing mid-handshake**, distinct from a refusal (non-200 → `CONNECT refused: …`) and from TCP-refused (an exception, surfaced via the broker as a 502). Three consecutive occurrences in the Mistral agent therefore mean the runtime proxy path itself was dropping handshakes during the window — consistent with the sandbox/runtime side being wedged, and NOT evidence of a laptop-daemon fault (the daemon is never reached when CONNECT itself fails).
- **Broker-mode failure chain**: in broker mode, that same EOF makes `tunnel_socket` raise `SystemExit`, which the Python broker's `except Exception` does not catch — the handler thread dies silently, the client sees "broker closed", auto-retries once, then falls back to a direct re-POST. A timed-out `/exec` can consequently be **submitted up to three times** (broker attempt + client retry + direct fallback). Duplicate-execution risk on long execs is a real, separate defect worth its own fix.
- **Broker ownership flaps between implementations**: the Python broker and `fleet proxy serve` share one socket; `broker.log` (untimestamped — a gap) shows them alternately owning it across boots, and at investigation time the **Python fallback was the live broker** — pool **12**, no overflow wait — while the fleet broker (pool **50**, 300 ms overflow wait) is what `init-ensure.sh` intends to launch with `LAPTOP_AGENT_POOL=50`. The two have materially different saturation behavior, so "which broker was live" is a variable in any future incident; making the broker log timestamped and the ownership deterministic belongs in the follow-ups.
- **The 660 s synchronous cap is ours**: `laptop-agent.py:108` (broker-socket timeout; the operative one) — a fleet-authored constant (daemon cap 600 + 60 headroom), not a platform default. The daemon caps a synchronous exec at **600 s total wall-clock per command** regardless of output (output is buffered, never streamed; there is no idle-timeout reset, and `/exec` has no stdin channel at all — interactive programs like vim cannot run over it; detached jobs are the multi-hour path).

### Actions taken in the same pass

- Init FAILURES=1 loop root-caused and fixed (separate issue): sysstat apt-lock deferral; the marker now gets written and init stops re-running per-prelude.
- Monitor + lane A + remaining `repo-queue` cron bodies migrated repo-first (hatch-personal a8f942c8d) per Drew's method.
- Trip-log v2 designed (separate issue): four timestamps per trip so the next incident attributes each leg.
- Quota-recorder laptop-broker redesign filed with recommendation (separate issue).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The incident timeline and root-cause analysis are complete on this issue.
- [ ] Every follow-up action is either filed as a linked issue or explicitly recorded as decided-against.
- [ ] The responsiveness-loss trigger (post-boot wedge) is named with the evidence that supports it.

title: init: FAILURES=1 forever — sysstat apt-lock collision kept the boot marker unwritten and init re-running every prelude (fixed 2026-11-04)
body:
## Summary

Every sandbox boot on 2026-11-04 recorded `result=FAILURES=1` from `~/tools/init.sh`, and the single failing step was the same in every run of every boot inspected (da56f9ed, ad076b64, d50de26a, 6989413c): the **sysstat collector restore**, failing instantly with:

```
E: Could not get lock /var/lib/apt/lists/lock. It is held by process 774 (apt-get)
E: Unable to lock directory /var/lib/apt/lists/
```

## Root cause chain

1. `scripts/sysstat/install-sysstat-units.sh` runs `apt-get update && apt-get install sysstat` whenever `sar` is missing — which is every boot, because apt packages do not survive sandbox recycles.
2. The lock holder is the sandbox platform's own post-boot **os-intent replay** (`apt-get update`, pid 774 in boot d50de26a; pid 753 in boot 6989413c, still running 12+ minutes after boot, fetching through the runtime proxy). It holds `/var/lib/apt/lists/lock` for many minutes after every recycle.
3. init counted the collision as a failure → `FAILURES=1` → **the boot marker is only written on a clean run**, so it was never written.
4. With no marker, `~/tools/init-ensure.sh` (run as the prelude of essentially every agent turn and cron job) took its cold path and re-spawned the **full init** every time. Observed: init END records every 2–7 minutes all day (boot d50de26a: 20:59, 21:02, 21:05, 21:09, 21:11, 21:14, 21:19, 21:21 UTC).
5. Each re-run costs ~65 s, dominated by the deferred-telemetry `du -sh /home/hatch/nix-persist` (60 s timeout, returns `unknown`, every time) — a persistent, pointless background load on a 4-CPU box, plus an apt attempt that could never succeed while the replay held the lock.

All other restore steps (nix, fleet units, charge fetcher, resource sampler, autocommit, backups, airthings) succeed in ~1 s; sysstat was the only failure. The recurring "init FAILURE" records Drew kept seeing were this one step, not a series of different problems.

## Fix (landed 2026-11-04, `~/tools/init.sh`)

- The sysstat block now captures the installer output. If it failed with `Could not get lock` / `Unable to lock directory`, the run logs `sysstat restore DEFERRED (apt lock held by another process)` and does **not** count a failure; a detached retry (up to 6 attempts, 5 min apart) converges the collector once the lock frees.
- Any other installer failure still counts as a real init failure, so `result=` stays truthful.
- Verified live in boot 6989413c (2026-11-04 23:11:45 UTC): the first full run under the new code logged `init: sysstat restore DEFERRED (apt lock held by another process — not counted as a failure; detached retry queued)` and ended **`result=SUCCESS`**; the boot marker was written for 6989413c and `init-ensure.sh` now warm-exits in 0.04 s instead of re-spawning a ~65–97 s init on every prelude. (Two transitional runs that started before the edit landed still showed the old FAILURES=1; the first run started entirely under the new code is the SUCCESS above.)

## Notes / follow-ups

- The platform replay holding the apt lock for 12+ minutes is itself worth watching: in boot da56f9ed its fetches were failing (`Connection failed [IP: 198.19.0.1 3128]` — the runtime proxy), so on a degraded-proxy boot the lock window can stretch much longer. Nothing fleet-side can shorten it; the defer makes us immune to it.
- The 60 s `du` telemetry timeout fires once per init run; with the loop fixed it is once per boot. If it still returns `unknown` every boot, consider dropping the measurement to a cheaper source (df on the mount) — separate small cleanup, not done here.
- Related incident record: the 2026-11-04 15:00–17:00 CST responsiveness loss (session proxy CONNECT failures, two failed orchestration passes, a Muse daemon restart at 21:29 UTC, and a sampler-silent window 21:29–22:57 UTC) is filed separately; this init loop was a contributor to baseline load, not the established cause.

body:
# atlas-search + fleet-search: results-paging cursor guard catches only an immediate repeat — a cycling cursor (A→B→A) spins the no-sleep paging loop until the 330s deadline

## Summary

The via-service results-paging loop in both client copies guards against a
non-advancing cursor only by comparing `next_cursor` with the cursor
**immediately before it** (#5424). A service (buggy or malicious) that cycles
cursors with period ≥ 2 — A → B → A → B … — passes that check on every page.
The paging loop contains no sleep and no page/iteration cap, so the client
hammers the service's results endpoint at full loopback speed until the
330-second client deadline expires, accumulating duplicate results the whole
time (for a large `--k`, the `results.len() >= k` break does not save it).
Only then does the loud standalone fallback engage.

## Evidence

- `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-search/src/service.rs`, `search_with_token`,
  paging loop (~lines 190–252): the only progress checks are
  `page.next_cursor.is_none()`, empty-page-with-cursor, and
  `cursor.as_deref() == Some(next_cursor.as_str())` (immediate repeat).
  No seen-cursor set, no page cap, no sleep between pages (the poll loop
  sleeps 100 ms; the paging loop does not).
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-search/src/client.rs`, `search_with_token`,
  paging loop (~lines 300–390): the fleet-step-5 port carries the identical
  loop and the identical guard ("The cursor guards from code#5424 ride
  along unchanged").
- Verified this run on the laptop with a stub service (fleet-search test
  harness, `StubMode::CyclingCursor` added in probe worktree
  `~/git/fleet/wt-probe-cycle`): the stub alternates `cursor-A`/`cursor-B`
  with one result per page and `k = 100_000`. After 10 s the client was
  still paging and the stub had received **2,307 results-endpoint hits**
  (~230 req/s). The existing repeating-cursor stub (period 1) is rejected
  promptly by contrast (`search_repeating_cursor_returns_err_promptly`).

## Why it matters

#5424's stated contract is that a non-advancing page stream "is a malformed
response and an error — never a loop". A period-2 cycle is exactly a
non-advancing page stream: the ranking never progresses, yet the client
burns up to 330 s and thousands of requests against the service before
falling back, and the spliced result list fills with duplicated pages.
The fleet-search port (#5433) doubles the exposed surface.

## Acceptance criteria

- Both copies (`atlas-search/src/service.rs`, `fleet-search/src/client.rs`)
  reject any `next_cursor` already seen during this paging session (e.g. a
  `HashSet` of used cursors), returning the same style of malformed-page
  error as the existing guards so the caller falls back to standalone loudly.
- A regression test in each crate with a cycling-cursor stub (period ≥ 2)
  returns `Err` promptly (comparable to the repeating-cursor test), and the
  existing happy-path / repeating-cursor / empty-page tests still pass.
- Behaviour for a well-behaved service is unchanged: distinct, advancing
  cursors page exactly as before.

body:
# fleet(help): `fleet help <domain> <extra>` silently ignores every argument after the domain name

## Summary

The root `help` built-in takes exactly one argument — a domain name — but never
checks for extras. `fleet help queue --bogus-junk` (or any trailing token)
prints the queue domain help and exits 0, silently discarding the extra
argument. Every sibling root built-in rejects this shape: `version`,
`capabilities`, and `--version`/`-V` all route through `reject_extra_args`
and exit 2 naming the unexpected argument (#5572: "Root built-ins take no
arguments: a trailing argument is a usage error naming it, not silently
discarded output"). The `help` arm is the one root built-in the #5572 sweep
missed, because its first argument is legitimate.

## Evidence

`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet/src/main.rs`, `run_root`:

- Lines 669–672: bare `fleet help` (one token) prints the full registry help.
- Lines 673–684: the `Some("help")` arm resolves `args.get(1)` as a domain and
  prints its help — `args.get(2..)` is never inspected.
- Contrast lines ~686–707: `--version`/`version`/`capabilities` each call
  `reject_extra_args(args)` first (which names `args[1]`, correct there
  because those built-ins take no argument at all).

Verified this run against the real binary on the laptop
(`pkgs/fleet/target/debug/fleet`, built 2026-11-04 12:09 CST from this tree;
the `run_root` help arm at HEAD `9af042edd0` is the code quoted above):

```
$ fleet help queue --bogus-junk
fleet queue — Repo work queue: enqueue, claim, and complete tasks through the queue broker.
... (full domain help) ...
EXIT:0

$ fleet help queue            # control: identical output
EXIT:0

$ fleet version --bogus-junk  # sibling control (#5572 behavior)
error: unexpected argument '--bogus-junk' for 'fleet version'
EXIT:2
```

## Why it matters

This is the same silent-discard bug class the fleet CLI has been closing leaf
by leaf (#5572, #5575, #5592, #5603, #5607): a user who mistypes
`fleet help queue claim` — plausibly asking for help on the `claim`
subcommand — gets the domain help with a success exit and no signal that the
second word was dropped, instead of either subcommand help or a usage error.
Scripts and muscle memory both read exit 0 as "that was a valid invocation."

## Acceptance criteria

- `fleet help <domain> <extra>` (one or more extras) exits 2 with a usage
  error naming the first unexpected argument, consistent with the
  `reject_extra_args` message shape (`unexpected argument '<extra>' for
  'fleet help'`).
- `fleet help`, `fleet help <domain>`, `fleet --help`, and the unknown-domain
  error (`fleet help nosuchdomain`) behave exactly as today.
- A pinning test covers the extra-argument rejection alongside the existing
  root built-in arity tests in `crates/fleet/src/main.rs`.

title: bitwarden-load-secrets: multiline values are split into bogus variables

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: area/infra
labels.description: Infrastructure, deployment, and operations

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

`bitwarden-load-secrets.sh` stores secret records in a newline-delimited `PAIRS` string (`lib/bitwarden-load-secrets.sh:185-196`). The BWS and Vault loaders emit raw `jq` values into tab/newline-delimited records (`:223-225`, `:271-273`), and each output mode later reads `PAIRS` one line at a time (`:304-310`, `:315-320`, `:323-329`). A newline inside a legitimate secret therefore becomes another record instead of remaining part of that secret.

Reproduced with a stub `bws` returning `TLS_CERT = "BEGIN CERT\\nPRIVATE KEY\\nEND CERT"`: `--format json` produced `TLS_CERT: "BEGIN CERT"`, plus bogus empty `PRIVATE_KEY` and `END_CERT` entries. The script documents direct CLI and sourced use (`:5-8`, `:110-113`); no in-repository callers or tests were found.

## Why it matters

Multiline values such as private keys and certificates are silently truncated, so consumers receive invalid credentials; continuation text is also exposed as unintended environment-variable names in source/export modes. This is a functional defect in the loader's documented use.

## Suggested fix

Keep key/value pairs in a representation that preserves newlines (rather than embedding raw values in a newline-delimited string), and add regression coverage for multiline values across the supported output formats. Shell output values are currently quoted; this finding is about record corruption, not a demonstrated shell-injection path.

body:
Follow-up from Phase 4 audit issue #5048 (epic #5047); intentionally not changed in the audit PR.\n\nObserved in `pkgs/id/src/hosted_binding.rs`:\n- Expired challenges that are never successfully consumed remain in `challenges`; expiry is state-free, so `submit_proof` does not remove them.\n- Expired, unexchanged pairing codes remain in `pairing_codes` until exchange or replacement for the same challenge. They continue to occupy their six-digit value in the collision check.\n- `consumed_challenges` retains every consumed challenge ID for the service lifetime. The per-account hourly issuance cap is not a lifetime/global bound.\n\nDefine and implement a retention policy that bounds these one-time ceremony maps without weakening single-use/replay behavior or allowing stale pairing-code collisions to make code minting unbounded. Add tests for the selected expiry/replay semantics and stale-code cleanup.

## Acceptance criteria
- Expired, unconsumed challenges are removed from `challenges` (on access or on a bounded sweep) instead of being retained for the service lifetime.
- Expired, unexchanged pairing codes stop occupying their six-digit value in the collision check once expired, so code minting stays bounded.
- `consumed_challenges` retention is bounded by a stated policy that still prevents replay of a consumed challenge within its validity window.
- Tests cover the selected expiry/replay semantics and stale pairing-code cleanup; single-use and replay protections are not weakened.

# cold-store-reaper: `evict` / `evict-scan` accept a negative `--min-age-days` — the age safety gate silently turns off

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe at main 1f2cad1074)

`pkgs/cold-store-reaper/cold_store.py`:

- `evict_scan()` (def at line 2074) converts the argument unchecked at line 2107:
  `min_age = timedelta(days=min_age_days)`, and the age verdict is
  `now - obj["last_modified"] < min_age` → `too-young`. With a negative
  `min_age_days` that comparison is false for **every** object, however new —
  the age condition (condition (c) in the docstring: an object is evictable
  only if it is at least `min_age_days` old) can never fail.
- The neighbouring guard *was* hardened for negatives: line 2105 clamps
  `keep_newest` with `max(keep_newest, 0)`. `min_age_days` got no equivalent.
- Both CLI verbs take the argument with plain `type=int` and no range check:
  `p_evict_scan` lines 2335–2336, `p_evict` lines 2342–2343.

Probe (laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-evict-negage/probe.py`, reusing the package's
own `EvictTestBase` fake-S3 harness; the `young` fixture object is 1 day old,
cold, in a verified bundle):

```
CONTROL  min_age=14   keep=0  young verdict: too-young
NEGATIVE min_age=-1   keep=0  young verdict: evictable
NEGATIVE min_age=-365 keep=0  young verdict: evictable
CLI rc: 0   (cold_store.main(["evict-scan","--min-age-days","-1","--keep-newest","0"]))
CLI summary: 7 object(s) scanned: bundle-unverified 1, evictable 4, hash-unknown 1, not-in-manifest 1
```

## Why it matters

`evict --apply` **deletes** R2 objects based on this scan (each evictable entry
is re-verified against the manifest at deletion time, but age is not part of
that re-verification). A typo'd or scripted `--min-age-days -1` therefore
deletes cold objects of *any* age — including one uploaded yesterday — with no
warning, where every other invalid value in this package's CLIs is rejected
loudly (cf. the `TURSO_DUMP_MAX_TIME_SECONDS` positive-integer validation in
`scripts/export-turso.sh`, filed/fixed as #1428 for the same
zero/negative-disables-a-guard class).

## Acceptance criteria

- `evict_scan()` rejects a negative `min_age_days` with a `ColdStoreError`
  (or the CLI rejects it before the scan), so both `evict-scan` and
  `evict --apply` fail loudly on `--min-age-days < 0`; `--min-age-days 0`
  keeps its current meaning (no age floor, operator's explicit choice).
- Negative `keep_newest` handling is made consistent (today it is silently
  clamped to 0 at line 2105 — either reject it the same way or document the
  clamp in the help text).
- A regression test pins the rejection (scan-level and/or CLI-level), in the
  style of the existing `TestEvictScan` / export-turso validation tests.

# id(web): .txt save drops the front_matter block — the #1369 node's payload lives in attrs.text, which extract_plain_text never reads

## Summary

Plain-text (`.txt`) save in the id web editor silently deletes a document's entire YAML front matter block:

- `front_matter` is a first-class block node since #1369 (closed): the markdown codec emits it as `{"type": "front_matter", "attrs": {"text": "---\n…\n---\n"}}` — its payload is the `text` **attribute**; the node has no `content` array and no top-level `text` field (`pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs:17`, `:2911`, `:4095-4097`, `:5101-5103`).
- `extract_plain_text` (`pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs:2657`) dispatches blocks in `collect_plain_text_lines` (`routes.rs:2671`). `front_matter` matches no named arm, so it lands in the catch-all `_` arm (`routes.rs:2693-2708`), which contributes a line only when the node has a `content` array or a top-level `text` field. A `front_matter` node has neither — so it contributes **nothing at all**, not even an empty line.
- This is the exact failure mode #1491 pinned for the `image` atom ("Inline atoms carry no `content`, so recursion alone loses them", `routes.rs:2651-2653`): a payload-in-`attrs` node that the recursive extraction cannot see. The image fix handled the inline case; the block-level twin was missed. The doc comment at `routes.rs:2651` names `footnote_reference` as the known remaining gap (filed as #5366); `front_matter` is not named anywhere — it is untracked.

The extraction's stated contract is "loss-free (#1306)" and "Any other block type: recursed into rather than dropped, so new node types degrade to their text instead of vanishing" (`routes.rs:2622-2624`). `front_matter` does not degrade to its text — it vanishes, fences and all.

## Verified this run (2026-11-04, laptop probe)

Probe worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-creator-b-frontmatter` on the laptop (branch `probe/creator-b-frontmatter` at main `e25ebcdec8`), one temporary test added to the existing `routes.rs` test module (which already tests `extract_plain_text` directly):

- Doc: `front_matter` node with `attrs.text = "---\ntitle: Hello\n---\n"` followed by a paragraph `Body`.
- `extract_plain_text(&doc)` returned `"Body"` — the front matter is absent, and no separator line marks where it was.

## Why it matters

- Front matter is where a markdown document's metadata lives (title, tags, publish state). A doc that carries a `front_matter` node — authored or opened via the markdown path, or received via collab — loses all of it on a plain-text save, silently, with no placeholder. That is the same data-loss class #1306/#1491 established as a bug for `.txt` save ("loss-free extraction").
- The #1369 fix created this node specifically so front matter survives save; the plain path is the one save mode that still destroys it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `collect_plain_text_lines` (or `extract_plain_text`) renders a `front_matter` block from its `attrs.text` verbatim (including the `---` fences, as authored), at its document position, following the one-block-per-line join policy.
- [ ] New tests in `pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs` pin: front matter followed by a paragraph, front matter as the only block, and the missing/empty `attrs.text` case (contributes nothing, does not panic).
- [ ] Existing `extract_plain_text` / routes tests still pass; markdown-mode (`prosemirror_to_markdown`) front matter handling is unchanged.
- [ ] The `extract_plain_text` doc comment's "known remaining gap" note is updated to reflect the state after this fix and #5366.

## Evidence

- `pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs:2585-2605` (`convert_doc_to_bytes`: `.txt` → `extract_plain_text`, "loss-free plain-text extraction (#1306)")
- `pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs:2622-2624` (policy: any other block type recursed into rather than dropped), `:2651-2655` (the #1491 attrs-payload warning; only `footnote_reference` named as remaining gap)
- `pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs:2671-2710` (`collect_plain_text_lines`: `front_matter` falls to the `_` arm, which requires `content` or top-level `text`)
- `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs:17` (front_matter: "YAML front matter block with `text` attribute"), `:2911` (emitted node shape), `:4095-4097` ("front_matter carries no PM child content (its payload is the `text` attr)"), `:10751` (test fixture shape `{"type": "front_matter", "attrs": {"text": "---\na: b\n---\n"}}`)
- Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-creator-b-frontmatter` on the laptop, 2026-11-04, main `e25ebcdec8` — `extract_plain_text` over `[front_matter("---\ntitle: Hello\n---\n"), paragraph("Body")]` returned `"Body"`.
- Related: #1306 (loss-free .txt extraction, closed), #1491 (image attrs payload, closed), #1369 (front_matter node created, closed), #5366 (footnote_reference atoms dropped — the inline sibling, open; distinct node, distinct fix site)

The 15-minute quota gatherer has produced no successful tick since
2026-11-04T18:30:15Z. Every tick from 18:45Z onward (18:45, 19:00,

(In 'auth.openCodeLocalCredentialSource({ dbPath })',
'auth.openCodeLocalCredentialSource' is undefined)

  same import error.

- Timeline: the last good tick ran at checkout HEAD `45be0757b`;
  the first failed tick (18:45Z) ran after HEAD advanced to include
  PR #5263 (merge `e25ebcdec8`, "queue/6561-1171-quota-lazy-refresh").
  The lazy-refresh change is the prime suspect for the renamed/removed

  OpenChamber `/api/quota/*` probes (per the standing rule, a stale

  leg, which has no live-probe route — cannot refresh until this is

body:
# id(outbox): journal replay accepts a `Queued` target the live path refuses — `Outbox::open` loads a malformed target that `enqueue` rejects

## Summary

`Outbox::enqueue` / `enqueue_artifact` validate the delivery target with
`check_target` before anything is queued, but journal replay in
`Outbox::open` does not: `apply` → `insert_queued` inserts a `Queued` /
`QueuedArtifact` record's target verbatim. A journal containing a target that
is neither an endpoint ticket nor a node ID — a record the live API can never
produce — loads cleanly, and the entry sits in the queue as due until the
first `flush` burns a delivery cycle on it and finishes it `Refused`.

This is the one live-path invariant replay does not re-check. After #4347,
replay strictly validates the state machine (attempt counts must advance by
one, no attempt/finish after finish, withdraw only before any attempt,
finish/detail pairing, gave-up only at the retry limit). Target validity is
checked on the write path (`enqueue`) but not on the read path (`apply`).

## Evidence

All in `pkgs/id/src/envelope_outbox.rs` (laptop primary `~/git/code`, main at
time of filing):

- `enqueue` (line 189) and `enqueue_artifact` (line 200) both call
  `check_target(target)?` before `enqueue_payload`.
- `check_target` (line 457): parses the target as an `EndpointTicket` or a
  bare `EndpointId`; anything else is an error — "fails if `target` is
  neither, so nothing is queued for it."
- `apply` (line 308) dispatches `Record::Queued { target, envelope }` and
  `Record::QueuedArtifact { target, artifact }` straight to
  `insert_queued(target, …)` (line 393), which only checks for a duplicate
  key. No `check_target` call anywhere on the replay path.
- `flush` (line 426) is where the bad target is finally caught: it maps a
  `check_target` error to `Outcome::Refused`, so the poisoned entry costs one
  flush cycle and a `Finished(Refused)` journal record instead of failing
  fast at open the way every other invalid record does (`Outbox::open`'s own
  contract: "Fails if … a journal record violates the outbox state machine").

Verified this run on the laptop (worktree `~/git/fleet/wt-outbox-probe`,
probe test added to the module's test suite):

- `enqueue("not a target", …)` → `Err` (live path refuses).
- A journal file containing one `{"op":"queued","target":"not a target",…}`
  record → `Outbox::open` returns `Ok` and `due(u64::MAX)` returns the entry
  as deliverable.

Same shape as the petname journal gap in #5225 (replay loads what the write
path refuses) and the replay half of #4347 for this same module.

## Why it matters

The journal is the durable record; replay is the trust boundary for anything
the file contains (older binary versions, hand edits, partial corruption that
still parses). Every other invariant `enqueue`/`record` enforce is
re-validated on replay — this one slipped through, so a bad target is
discovered late (at flush, as a spurious "refused" delivery outcome
indistinguishable from a recipient-side refusal) instead of at open with the
line number, like every other corrupt record.

## Acceptance criteria

- `Outbox::open` replay refuses a `Queued` / `QueuedArtifact` record whose
  target fails `check_target`, with the standard "envelope outbox line N is
  refused" context naming the line.
- Regression tests in the module's replay-error style
  (`assert_replay_error`): malformed target in a `Queued` record and in a
  `QueuedArtifact` record both fail open; a valid ticket target and a valid
  bare node-ID target both still replay fine.
- Live-path behavior unchanged: `enqueue` / `enqueue_artifact` errors,
  `flush`'s handling of entries already in memory, and all existing outbox
  tests keep passing (`cargo test -p id --lib envelope_outbox`).

body:
# atlas-search: service config silently ignores unknown/misspelled keys — a typo'd `limits` or `listen` key loads with defaults instead of erroring

## Summary

The atlas-search service config (`service.json`, parsed by `load_service_settings` in `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-search/src/server.rs`) deserializes into three structs that all use `#[serde(default)]` with **no `deny_unknown_fields`**:

- `ServiceConfigFile` (server.rs:183-190) — top level: `listen`, `vec_table`, `limits`, `clients`
- `RuntimeLimitsFile` (server.rs:131-141) — the `limits` block: `max_queued_jobs`, `job_ttl_ms`, …
- `RawClientConfig` (server.rs:174-180) — per-client rows: `name`, `token`, `ceiling_cap`

Any misspelled or unknown key is silently dropped and the documented default takes its place. This is the exact failure class fixed for fleet.toml in #5460 (closed: fleet-config gained `deny_unknown_fields` on every struct, fleet-config/src/lib.rs:50,82,93,118,129,141) and for world.toml in #2876 (closed) — the atlas service config, which carries **client tokens, per-client sensitivity ceilings, the listen address, and the runtime limits**, never got the same treatment.

It also undercuts the validation that does exist: #5630 (closed today) made `validate_limits` reject zero queue caps at startup — but that check only fires if the `limits` key is spelled exactly right.

## Verified this run (2026-11-04, laptop probe)

Probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-atlas-config-typo`; binary rebuilt from laptop main `b1328b51de`; each config mode 0600 with one valid client (`ceiling_cap: "personal"`):

- **Control** — `"limits": {"max_queued_jobs": 0}` → startup fails: `atlas-search: max_queued_jobs must be at least 1` (the #5630 validation works when the key is spelled right).
- **Typo, top level** — `"limts": {"max_queued_jobs": 0}` → **serves normally** on the configured listen address; the limits block is silently discarded and defaults apply.
- **Typo, inside limits** — `"limits": {"max_queued_job": 0}` (missing `s`) → **serves normally**; the cap is silently discarded.
- **Typo, listen** — `"listn": "127.0.0.1:18798"` with no `listen` key → the service ignores the intended address and tries to bind the **default** `127.0.0.1:18760` (`cannot bind 127.0.0.1:18760: Address already in use` — the production instance already holds it).

## Why it matters

- The operator-facing knobs in this file are safety knobs: queue/concurrency caps (#5630), job TTLs, the loopback listen address, and which sensitivity ceiling each client's token gets. A one-character typo silently reverts any of them to defaults with no error and no log line — the service looks healthy while running a different configuration than the one on disk.
- The file is hand-edited JSON (mode 0600, tokens inside) — exactly the surface where typos happen, and the crate's own sibling configs (fleet.toml, world.toml) already established the house rule: unknown keys are a loud parse error, never a silent default.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `load_service_settings` rejects a service config containing an unknown key at any level (top level, `limits`, client rows) with a parse error naming the offending key — e.g. `deny_unknown_fields` on `ServiceConfigFile`, `RuntimeLimitsFile`, and `RawClientConfig`, mirroring the #5460 fleet-config fix.
- [ ] Configs written by `atlas-search init` (which emits only `listen`/`vec_table`/`clients` with `name`/`token`/`ceiling_cap`) still load unchanged.
- [ ] A pinning test covers at least: typo'd top-level key rejected, typo'd limits key rejected, and a valid config with all fields spelled correctly accepted.
- [ ] No change to the defaults themselves or to `validate_limits` behavior for correctly-spelled configs.

## Evidence

- `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-search/src/server.rs` — `ServiceConfigFile` (`#[serde(default)]`, no deny), `RuntimeLimitsFile` (same), `RawClientConfig` (no deny); `load_service_settings` parses via `serde_json::from_str` and substitutes defaults per missing key.
- Contrast: `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs:50,82,93,118,129,141` — `deny_unknown_fields` on every config struct after #5460.
- Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-atlas-config-typo` (2026-11-04): control/typo-top/typo-inner/typo-listen configs + the serve outputs quoted above, binary built from `b1328b51de`.

# atlas-search(serve): `max_queued_jobs` / `max_queued_jobs_per_client` of 0 passes startup validation, then every job submission is 429 forever

## Summary

The atlas service's startup validation (`validate_limits`, `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-search/src/server.rs:318-332`) refuses two of the four capacity limits at 0 —

- `max_concurrent_branch_executions` → `"max_concurrent_branch_executions must be at least 1"`
- `max_concurrent_jobs_per_client` → `"max_concurrent_jobs_per_client must be at least 1"`

— and validates both TTLs (positive, `hard_ttl >= job_ttl`). It does **not** validate the other two capacity limits, `max_queued_jobs` and `max_queued_jobs_per_client`, both settable from the service config's `limits` block (`RuntimeLimitsFile`, server.rs:132-137, applied at :153-162).

The admission check makes 0 a brick, not a "no queueing" mode: `new_computation` (server.rs:1372-1373) rejects when `queued_for_client >= max_queued_jobs_per_client || queue.len() >= max_queued_jobs` — with either cap at 0 the comparison is `0 >= 0`, true on an empty queue, so **every** fresh job submission is rejected `429 rate_limited` forever. The 429 body even reports `"queue_depth":0` while claiming the service is "saturated", and clients honor `retry_after_seconds: 5` — the service looks healthy (starts, binds, answers health), yet can never accept a job.

## Verified this run (2026-11-04, laptop, real binary built from main `448019bbfc`)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-atlas-limits/` (temp 0600 service configs, one authenticated client, `POST /v1/search/jobs` with a valid bearer token):

- `limits: {"max_queued_jobs": 0}` → server starts and serves; POST jobs → **429** `{"code":"rate_limited", "queue_depth":0, "retry_after_seconds":5}`.
- `limits: {"max_queued_jobs_per_client": 0}` → server starts and serves; POST jobs → **429**, same body.
- Control `limits: {"max_concurrent_branch_executions": 0}` → process exits at startup, code 2: `atlas-search: max_concurrent_branch_executions must be at least 1`.
- Control `limits: {}` → POST jobs → **202** with a job id (accepted).

## Why it matters

- A single mis-typed config value (0 reads naturally as "no limit" / "disabled" to many operators) silently bricks the service in the most confusing possible way: startup succeeds, health is green, and every client gets a saturation 429 pointing at load that does not exist — the exact shape of an incident that burns hours before anyone re-reads the config.
- The validation function's own contract is inconsistent: sibling fields in the same struct, loaded by the same code path, get the guard; these two do not. `validate_limits` is called from both `load_service_settings` (server.rs:297) and `start_server` (server.rs:1925), so one fix covers config-file and programmatic settings alike.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `validate_limits` rejects `max_queued_jobs == 0` and `max_queued_jobs_per_client == 0` with messages in the existing style (`"<field> must be at least 1"`).
- [ ] A pinning test covers both new rejections plus the already-validated zero fields and a valid default `RuntimeLimits` (e.g. a `validate_limits` unit test in server.rs's test module).
- [ ] `atlas-search serve` with either zero queue cap in the service config now exits at startup with the validation error instead of serving 429s.

## Evidence

- `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-search/src/server.rs:318-332` (`validate_limits` — the two missing checks)
- `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-search/src/server.rs:132-162` (`RuntimeLimitsFile` → `into_limits`: both fields flow in from the config file)
- `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-search/src/server.rs:1372-1373` (admission check: `>=` makes 0 reject on an empty queue)
- Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-atlas-limits/run2.py` + per-config logs on the laptop, 2026-11-04, binary built from `448019bbfc`

# fleet(secrets): `secrets get --help` and `secrets list --help` answer help through the error channel — exit 2 on stderr instead of usage on stdout at exit 0

## Evidence (verified this run, real binary on the laptop @ 6499f5148)

`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet/src/secrets.rs` is the only fleet domain whose leaf verbs have no help handling:

- `cmd_get` (secrets.rs): any leading-`-` argument is treated as a usage error — `args[0].starts_with('-')` → one line `usage: fleet secrets get <name>` on **stderr**, exit 2.
- `cmd_list` (secrets.rs): any argument at all → `usage: fleet secrets list` on **stderr**, exit 2.

Probe of the shipped debug binary (temp `HOME`, no network reached in any form):

| invocation | exit | stdout | stderr |
|---|---|---|---|
| `fleet secrets get --help` | 2 | 0 bytes | `usage: fleet secrets get <name>` |
| `fleet secrets get -h` | 2 | 0 bytes | same |
| `fleet secrets get some-name --help` | 2 | 0 bytes | same |
| `fleet secrets list --help` | 2 | 0 bytes | `usage: fleet secrets list` |
| `fleet secrets list -h` | 2 | 0 bytes | same |
| `fleet secrets --help` (control) | 0 | 192 bytes, domain help | 0 |
| `fleet dispatch status --help` (control) | 0 | 182 bytes, verb usage | 0 |

## Why it matters

This is the exact defect class fixed three times in sibling domains this week: #5619 (proxy connect/init), #5575 (proxy serve), #5560 (dispatch status). The fleet-wide leaf convention is now: a `--help`/`-h` flag in a leaf verb prints that verb's usage on **stdout** and exits **0** (dispatch `verb_status`/`verb_launch`/`verb_enqueue`, search's `EXIT_OK` help sentinel, proxy's classify helpers in `main.rs`). The secrets domain — the newest domain, step 6 (#5554) — is the one remaining domain that answers a help request as if it were a caller error, so scripts and users probing `fleet secrets get --help` get a failure exit and an error-channel one-liner instead of the verb's usage.

Note the existing guard is otherwise correct and must stay: a secret name is never flag-shaped, so non-help stray arguments to `get`/`list` should remain usage errors (exit 2, stderr). Only the help forms change channel.

## Acceptance criteria

- `fleet secrets get --help`, `get -h`, and `get <name> --help` print the `get` verb's usage on stdout and exit 0, with no resolver/broker contact.
- `fleet secrets list --help` / `list -h` print the `list` verb's usage on stdout and exit 0, with no broker contact.
- Non-help misuse is unchanged: `secrets get` with zero or 2+ names, a non-help flag-shaped name, and `secrets list <stray>` still print usage on stderr and exit 2.
- A pinning test covers the help forms for both verbs (following the dispatch/main.rs classify-helper pattern so the check is testable without a Config or a broker).
- `cargo test -p fleet` passes on the laptop or in CI.

## Receipt-audit follow-up from #3232 / design #3231

The new receipt checks for duplicate after hashes (#3196) and NFC in document.media_type / tag.name / tag.value (#3192) are unconditional on local replay today. ArtifactLog::open re-runs verify() and parsed_for_replay(), but verify() always checks the duplicate-after rule and parsed_mode(replay=true) still checks those NFC fields.

Before those checks landed, the supported artifact producer path could persist these shapes: SignedArtifact::sign_after accepted duplicate after entries, and Directory.publish_document / publish_tag passed text through the then-lenient parser. Such logs were accepted at the time; reopening them now fails, contrary to #3231's replay-compatibility criterion. Tests cover the home_declared replay exception and duplicate friend_remove replay, but not these pre-upgrade after/NFC cases.

## Scope

- Decide and implement a trusted legacy boundary or narrowly scoped replay compatibility for these rules, while keeping fresh receipts strict.
- Add fixtures proving legacy logs reopen and new receipts with the same invalid shapes remain refused.
- Keep genuinely corrupt/authenticity failures strict.
- Coordinate with #4459's artifact-format cutoff for remote peer pulls; do not reuse local replay leniency as a blanket remote-receipt policy.

This follow-up is separate from the #3232 audit; the audit records the gap and links this issue without changing validation behavior.

## Acceptance criteria
- Pre-upgrade artifact logs containing duplicate `after` entries or non-NFC `document.media_type` / `tag.name` / `tag.value` values reopen successfully under a narrowly scoped, trusted legacy replay boundary.
- Fresh receipts with the same invalid shapes are still refused.
- Genuinely corrupt or inauthentic logs still fail verification.
- Fixtures/tests prove both directions (legacy reopen + fresh refusal), and local replay leniency is not reused as a blanket remote-receipt policy (coordination with #4459's cutoff noted on the PR).

body:
# fleet(proxy): `proxy connect --help` and `init --help` report help through the error channel — exit 2 on stderr instead of usage on stdout at exit 0

## Summary

Two `fleet` proxy leaves answer a help request as if it were a usage
error. Every other leaf in the binary prints its usage to stdout and
exits 0 when asked (`proxy serve --help` since #5575, `dispatch
status/launch/enqueue --help` since #5560, `search --help`, the root
and domain help). These two are the remaining outliers:

- `fleet proxy connect --help` / `-h` — exit **2**, usage text on
  **stderr** prefixed `fleet:`, nothing on stdout.
- `fleet init --help` / `-h` and `fleet proxy init --help` — exit
  **2**, stderr `fleet: fleet init takes no arguments (got "--help")`:
  the help flag is reported as an illegal argument.

Scripts and agents that probe a leaf with `--help` (the standard
"how do I call this" check, and the smoke-harness pattern) read a
failure where the binary was simply asked for its own usage.

## Evidence (verified this run, real binary built from laptop primary @4733d598f, temp HOME)

```
$ fleet proxy connect --help   → exit 2, stdout empty, stderr: fleet: usage: fleet proxy connect [--print-path] [--stdio [--host H] [--port N]] [--request METHOD PATH [--service-port N] [--token-file F] [--body JSON]]
$ fleet proxy connect -h       → exit 2 (same)
$ fleet init --help            → exit 2, stderr: fleet: fleet init takes no arguments (got "--help")
$ fleet init -h                → exit 2 (same)
$ fleet proxy init --help      → exit 2 (same)
controls:
$ fleet proxy serve --help     → exit 0, usage on stdout
$ fleet dispatch status --help → exit 0, usage on stdout
$ fleet search --help          → exit 0, usage on stdout
$ fleet --help                 → exit 0
```

## Root cause (file:line at 4733d598f)

- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/client.rs:335-343` —
  `ConnectArgs::parse` handles `--help`/`-h` by returning
  `Err(ClientError::Usage(<usage text>))`; `ClientError::Usage`
  maps to exit 2 (`client.rs` `exit_code()`), and the caller in
  `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet/src/main.rs:589-595` prints it with
  `eprintln!("fleet: {e}")`. The usage text exists — it is only
  reachable through the error channel.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/client.rs:435-446` —
  `run_init` rejects *any* non-empty argv with the usage error
  before checking for a help flag, so `--help`/`-h` hit the
  "takes no arguments" rejection. Both entry points land here:
  root `fleet init` (`main.rs:692` → `cmd_init` → `run_init_call`,
  main.rs:610) and `fleet proxy init` (`main.rs:605`).

No pinning test covers either leaf's help behavior (`client.rs`
has no test module).

## Why it matters

- Consistency is the multicall binary's contract (epic #5412): the
  #5488/#5560/#5575 fixes established "help flag at a leaf prints
  usage, exit 0, no side effects" leaf by leaf; these are the two
  leaves that series missed.
- `fleet init` is the autostart door run from shell/tool startup
  lines — the leaf an operator is *most* likely to probe with
  `--help` when wiring it up, and the one that currently answers
  with an error naming the help flag as illegal input.

## Acceptance criteria

- `fleet proxy connect --help` and `-h` print the connect usage to
  stdout and exit 0, with no broker connection or spawn attempted.
- `fleet init --help` / `-h` and `fleet proxy init --help` / `-h`
  print the init usage to stdout and exit 0, with no probe, spawn,
  or shim sync attempted.
- Non-help argument handling is unchanged: `fleet init <bogus>`
  still exits 2 naming the argument; `proxy connect` unknown
  arguments still exit 2.
- New pinning tests cover both leaves' help forms (and the init
  non-help rejection), in the style of the existing
  `proxy_serve_args_classify_help_and_reject_strays` /
  `status_help_and_rejection_need_no_service` tests.
- `cargo test -p fleet -p fleet-proxy` green on the laptop or CI;
  `cargo fmt` clean.

Design amendment request for #3455, discovered while implementing #5530.

## Evidence

The design's Phase 1 acceptance requires pkgs/id to compile with default features, --no-default-features --features world, and bare --no-default-features. On the fresh origin/main base used for #5530, the bare no-default test fails before reaching invite.rs:

error[E0432]: unresolved import crate::world
  --> pkgs/id/src/chat.rs:43
use crate::world::sanitize_chat;

chat.rs is unconditionally included, while the world module is feature-gated. This pre-existing issue is tracked by #4159. The #5530 branch changes invite validation to the unconditional crate::is_format_char helper, removing the invite-side world gate, but the package-level no-default build still stops at chat.rs.

## Amendment requested

Please record the no-default package build as blocked on #4159, or explicitly extend the design scope to resolve the chat feature boundary. The Cf contract, renderer behavior, and no-new-ingest-rejection decisions are unchanged. The #5530 implementation should not silently absorb the unrelated chat refactor.

This request does not replace #4159, which remains the implementation/fix tracker.
