body:
## Bug

`fleet search --version` (and `-V`) silently ignores **all** trailing arguments — including a real verb. The version shortcut in `fleet_search::run` matches only the first argument and returns success, discarding the rest.

This is the exact bug class fixed today for the queue domain in #5603 / PR #5605 (and earlier for the root built-ins in #5572). The search domain was missed because it does not use `fleet` main's shortcut: `run_domain` delegates the whole arg vector to `fleet_search::run` (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet/src/main.rs`, search branch), whose own shortcut never checks arity.

## Evidence

`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-search/src/lib.rs:528` `pub fn run(...)`; `:544`:

```rust
Some("--version") | Some("-V") => {
    println!("fleet search {}", env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"));
    EXIT_OK
}
```

No `args.get(1)` check — compare the queue-domain fix at `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet/src/main.rs` (commit 79124573c), which rejects a trailing argument with a usage error naming it.

Verified this run with a probe crate on the laptop against current main (79124573c), calling `fleet_search::run(&Config::default(), args)` directly (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-search-version` on the laptop):

```
fleet search 0.1.0
PROBE ["--version"] -> exit 0
fleet search 0.1.0
PROBE ["--version", "--bogus-junk"] -> exit 0
fleet search 0.1.0
PROBE ["-V", "extra"] -> exit 0
fleet search 0.1.0
PROBE ["--version", "get-chunk"] -> exit 0
```

The last case is the sharp one: `fleet search --version get-chunk …` prints the version and exits 0 instead of running (or rejecting) the chunk request — a typo'd or scripted invocation silently does nothing while reporting success. The same path serves the `atlas-search` argv0 route (see the `run` doc comment), so the flaw is reachable there too.

## Why it matters

Silent success on malformed input is the fleet CLI's recurring correctness trap (#5488, #5560, #5575, #5592, #5603): scripts and agents that compose flags cannot trust exit 0. The queue domain was hardened today; the search domain should match the house contract — a version flag takes no trailing arguments.

## Acceptance criteria

- `fleet search --version <anything>` and `-V <anything>` exit with the usage code (2), print a usage error naming the first unexpected argument, and print no version line.
- Bare `fleet search --version` / `-V` still print `fleet search <version>` and exit 0.
- A pinning test in `fleet-search` covers both flags with a trailing argument plus the bare controls (mirroring `queue_domain_version_rejects_trailing_arguments` from #5605).
- `cargo test -p fleet-search` passes.

# fleet(queue): `fleet queue --version` / `repo-queue --version` silently ignore trailing arguments

## Summary

The queue domain's `--version` shortcut in the `fleet` multicall binary checks only the first argument and returns success no matter what follows it:

- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet/src/main.rs:458-475` (`run_domain`, `#[cfg(feature = "queue")]` arm): when `args.first()` is `--version` or `-V`, it prints the version and returns `EXIT_OK` — `args[1..]` is never inspected.
- The root built-ins in the same file got exactly this fix in #5572: `run_root`'s `--version`/`-V`/`version`/`capabilities` arms all call `reject_extra_args` first (`main.rs:661-682`), and the queue client's own verbs got the same treatment in #5592. The domain-level shortcut that sits *in front of* the queue client is the one surface both fixes missed — it intercepts the invocation before `fleet_queue::client::run(args)` is ever reached.

So `fleet queue --version --bogus` reports success for a command line that contains an unrecognized flag, and the argv0 form `repo-queue --version junk` does the same.

## Verified this run (2026-11-04, laptop, binary rebuilt from main `18f0aa1a6`)

```
$ fleet queue --version            → "fleet 0.1.0", exit 0   (control, correct)
$ fleet queue --version junkextra  → "fleet 0.1.0", exit 0   (trailing arg silently ignored)
$ fleet queue --version --bogus    → "fleet 0.1.0", exit 0   (unrecognized flag silently ignored)
$ fleet queue -V junk              → "fleet 0.1.0", exit 0   (same for -V)
$ repo-queue --version junk        → "repo-queue 0.1.0", exit 0  (argv0 alias route, same arm)
$ fleet --version junk             → usage error, exit 2     (control: root arm, fixed by #5572)
```

## Why it matters

- A version probe in a script or CI step that accidentally appends an argument (or a caller who mistypes a flag) gets a clean success and a version string instead of the usage error every sibling surface now returns — the exact silent-misparse class #5572/#5592/#5568/#5575 have been eliminating across the fleet surfaces one leaf at a time.
- The shortcut is also the argv0 `repo-queue` binary's only version surface (the census fix noted in the arm's own comment), so the laxity ships in two binaries' shapes from one arm.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `fleet queue --version <anything-else>` and `fleet queue -V <anything-else>` (including via the `repo-queue` argv0 alias) exit 2 with a usage error naming the unexpected argument, before printing the version — mirroring `run_root`'s `reject_extra_args` behavior for the root built-ins.
- [ ] Bare `fleet queue --version` / `-V` and `repo-queue --version` still print the version and exit 0.
- [ ] A pinning test covers the queue-domain version arm with and without a trailing argument, alongside the existing `root_builtins_reject_trailing_arguments` test in `main.rs`.

## Evidence

- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet/src/main.rs:458-475` (unguarded queue-domain version arm), `:661-682` (root arms with the `reject_extra_args` guard), `:626-639` (`reject_extra_args` itself)
- Probe: `fleet` binary rebuilt on the laptop from main `18f0aa1a6` (2026-11-04), outputs above
- Related: #5572 (root built-ins, closed), #5592 (repo-queue client verbs, closed), #5412 (fleet multicall epic, open)

body:
# fleet(queue): repo-queue silently ignores extra positional arguments on every verb

## Evidence

`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/client.rs`:

- `parse_args` (line 471) collects positional arguments into `Args.pos`, and rejects unknown `--flags` with exit 2 — but no verb ever checks how many positionals it received.
- `cmd_validate` (line 669) and `cmd_enqueue` (line 687) use only `args.pos.first()` — a second packet path is silently dropped, so `repo-queue validate a.json b.json` validates (and `enqueue` enqueues) only `a.json` while the caller believes both were processed.
- `cmd_health` (line 1137), `cmd_list` (line 768), and `cmd_signal` (line 1174) never read `pos` at all — any stray positional is silently ignored.
- The task verbs (`lane`, `bind`, `heartbeat`, `checkpoint`, `park`, `block`, `cancel`, `fail`, `complete`) read only `pos_i64(0, "task_id")` — a second positional (a typo'd extra id, a stray word) is silently dropped, so `repo-queue complete <task> <something-else>` completes the task and reports success.

Verified this run with the shipped binary on the laptop (`~/.local/bin/repo-queue`, probe `~/git/fleet/probe-rq-posargs`):

- `repo-queue health junkpositional` → exit 0, full health table printed (positional ignored).
- `repo-queue list junkpositional --limit 1` → exit 0, task list printed (positional ignored).
- Control: `repo-queue health --bogus-flag` → exit 2, `unrecognized argument` — flags are validated, positionals are not.

## Why it matters

repo-queue is the fleet's own control-plane client: creator/monitor/worker automation and humans drive queue state through it. A silently ignored positional means a mistyped command does something other than what the caller asked — validating/enqueueing the wrong (first) packet, or completing/parking the intended task while an extra argument the caller meant as a guard vanishes — and exits 0, so scripts cannot detect the mistake. This is the same silent-arg-discard class fixed for the fleet multicall leaves in #5560/#5575, on the one client those fixes did not cover.

## Acceptance criteria

- Every repo-queue verb rejects an unexpected positional argument count with a usage error (exit 2) naming the verb and the offending argument, before any broker call: exactly 1 positional for `validate`/`enqueue` (packet path) and the task verbs (task_id); exactly 0 for `list`/`health`/`signal`.
- A unit test pins the arity check (extra positional rejected; correct counts accepted).
- Existing behavior is otherwise unchanged: unknown `--flags` still exit 2, valid invocations of every verb behave as before.
- `cargo test -p fleet-queue` passes.

body:
# fleet(secrets-broker): `url_decode` maps '+' to a space in the /secret/<name> path segment — a client-legal '+' name can never be fetched, and a space-spelled key is returned in its place

## Evidence

- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/secrets_broker.rs:291-311` — the broker's private `url_decode` applies form-encoding semantics inside a URL **path** segment: any `+` byte becomes a space (`out.push(if bytes[i] == b'+' { b' ' } else { bytes[i] })`). Under RFC 3986, `+` in a path segment is a literal plus; the `+`-means-space rule applies only to `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` query strings.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/secrets_broker.rs:267-271` — `GET /secret/<name>` extracts the name with `path.trim_start_matches("/secret/")`, runs it through `url_decode`, and looks the decoded string up in the secret cache.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-secrets/src/lib.rs:112-130` — the client's `validate_name` **permits** `+` in a secret name (it refuses only empty, `.`/`..`, `/ ? # %`, whitespace, and control characters; tightened in #5469 for percent/dot spellings, `+` deliberately left legal).
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-secrets/src/lib.rs:281-283` — `BrokerSource::resolve` interpolates the name raw: `format!("/secret/{name}")` — it never percent-encodes, so a `+` name goes on the wire as a literal `+`.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/http.rs:79-81` — the session broker writes the request line raw (`{method} {path} HTTP/1.1`), so the `+` reaches the secrets broker unencoded.

Chain: `fleet secrets get 'a+b'` (a legal name) → request `GET /secret/a+b` → broker decodes the name to `a b` → cache lookup for `a b`.

## Verified this run

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-secret-plus` (the verbatim `url_decode` extracted mechanically from `secrets_broker.rs:291-311` at main `908b22f09`):

```
decode(a+b)   = "a b"    <- wrong: the '+' name is looked up under the space spelling
decode(a%2Bb) = "a+b"    <- the percent-encoded spelling decodes correctly
decode(alpha) = "alpha"  <- control
decode(a%20b) = "a b"    <- %20 is the correct way to name a space
```

`secrets_broker.rs` has no test module at all — `url_decode` is entirely untested.

## Why it matters

- A vault secret whose key contains `+` is **unreachable** through the broker path: the lookup always misses (404 "no such secret"), with no hint that the name was rewritten in transit.
- Worse, if a *different* key spelled with a space exists in the vault cache, the broker silently returns **that secret's value** for the `+` name — automation receives the wrong credential with a 200 and a matching-looking response.
- The client contract (#5469) treats the name as one raw path segment; the broker must decode that segment with path semantics, not form semantics.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `url_decode` no longer maps `+` to a space in the `/secret/<name>` path segment: a request for a name containing `+` looks up the exact `+` spelling.
- [ ] Percent-decoding behavior is unchanged: `%2B` still decodes to `+`, `%20` still decodes to a space, malformed `%` sequences stay literal.
- [ ] New pinning tests for `url_decode` cover at least: `a+b` → `a+b`, `a%2Bb` → `a+b`, `a%20b` → `a b`, a plain name unchanged.
- [ ] `cargo test -p fleet-queue` passes.

body:
# fleet-proxy(http): response reader trusts peer-declared sizes (unbounded preallocation) and silently drops the body on a malformed Content-Length, desyncing the pooled connection

## Problem

`HttpConn::request` in `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/http.rs` — the pooled HTTP/1.1 client the broker's `serve` side uses for tunneled services (`serve.rs` pools these connections per target port) — reads responses with none of the bounds the rest of the crate applies, and misparses malformed length headers instead of failing:

1. **Unbounded preallocation from the declared length.** At `http.rs:147`, a `Content-Length` body is allocated in full before a single body byte arrives: `data.resize(len, 0)`. There is no cap anywhere in the reader. The chunked path has the same shape at `http.rs:190` (`out.resize(start + size, 0)` per chunk, parsed straight from the peer's hex chunk-size line, with no cumulative bound either). The status line and header lines are read with unbounded `read_line` (`http.rs:98`, `:118`). Contrast the same crate's own discipline: `fleet-proxy-proto` refuses frames over `MAX_FRAME_BYTES` before allocating, and `tunnel.rs` caps a CONNECT response at 65536 bytes.
2. **A malformed `Content-Length` silently becomes "no body".** At `http.rs:133`, `content_length = value.parse().ok()` — an unparsable value (e.g. `Content-Length: abc`) turns into `None`, so the response is treated as a bodiless keep-alive response: the real body bytes are left in the stream, the caller gets an empty body with a success status, and the connection stays `reusable` and returns to the pool, where the leftover bytes desync the next response parsed on it. Duplicate `Content-Length` headers with differing values get the same silent treatment (last one wins). Every other malformed element in this reader (status line, header line, chunk size) is a `Malformed` error that marks the connection non-reusable — the length header is the one exception.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe crate `~/git/fleet/probe-proxy-http` (path dep on the real `fleet-proxy` crate @ main 9cf2688e4), canned loopback servers:

- **Invalid CL:** response `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` + `Content-Length: abc` + body `hello` → `request` returns `Ok((200, ""))` — body silently dropped — and `reusable() == true`. A second request on the same connection returns `Ok((200, "hi"))` from a correctly-formed second response: the leftover `hello` bytes were consumed as the start of the next status line, which only parses by accident (`helloHTTP/1.1 200 OK` splits so token 1 is `200`). A body whose first token differs would corrupt the next caller's response instead.
- **Duplicate differing CLs:** `Content-Length: 5` then `Content-Length: 0`, body `hello` → same result: `Ok((200, ""))`, reusable, silent desync of the next response.
- **Preallocation:** response headers declaring `Content-Length: 536870912` (512 MiB) with **zero** body bytes sent and the socket closed → the request errors on EOF only after allocating the full declared body: probe process `VmHWM` measured **526,616 KiB**. A peer can declare up to `usize::MAX`; the allocation attempt itself is the failure (abort/OOM in the broker daemon), no payload ever needs to arrive.

The response peer is a service the broker tunnels to — not fully trusted input: a buggy or compromised local service, or anything that can answer on a tunneled port, can OOM the broker or poison pooled connections for unrelated later requests.

## Why it matters

The broker is long-lived infrastructure; its pooled connections are shared across requests and callers. Today a single malformed response can (a) crash the daemon by allocation, or (b) silently return an empty body to one caller and shift the byte stream under the next caller — a correctness failure that surfaces far from its cause and is nearly impossible to diagnose from the second caller's symptoms.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An unparsable `Content-Length`, or duplicate `Content-Length` headers whose values differ, is a `Malformed` error (like the other header defects) and marks the connection non-reusable.
- [ ] Response bodies have a documented maximum size (a named constant, sized for the JSON payloads this client carries, e.g. aligned with an existing crate ceiling): a declared `Content-Length` above it, a chunk size above it, and a chunked body whose cumulative size exceeds it all fail with an error *before* allocating the declared amount; the connection is marked non-reusable.
- [ ] Status/header/chunk-size lines have a bounded read (no unbounded `read_line` accumulation from a peer that never sends a newline).
- [ ] Regression tests (canned loopback responses, following the crate's existing integration-test pattern): invalid CL → `Malformed` + not reusable; conflicting duplicate CLs → `Malformed`; oversize declared CL → error with no outsized allocation; oversize chunk → error; a well-formed CL response and a well-formed chunked response still round-trip and stay reusable.

body:
# fleet: `proxy serve --help` (and any trailing argument) silently starts the session-proxy daemon

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ 6d7845ebb, real `fleet` binary)

`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet/src/main.rs`, `run_proxy`: the `serve` branch dispatches straight to the daemon without ever inspecting the trailing arguments:

```rust
Some("serve") => {
    #[cfg(feature = "proxy-serve")]
    {
        fleet_proxy::serve::run(config)
    }
    ...
}
```

`fleet_proxy::serve::run` (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/serve.rs:346`) takes only `&Config` — it has no argument list at all — so everything after `serve` is dropped on the floor before the socket is bound. The domain-help shortcut in `run_domain` (`wants_domain_help`) only special-cases the *serve domain's* role position (the #5488 fix); the proxy domain's `serve` subcommand sits one level deeper and is not covered. The argv0 alias lands in the same place: `laptop-agent-broker` implies `serve`, so `laptop-agent-broker --help` becomes args `["serve", "--help"]` and also starts the daemon.

Behavioral probe (real binary built on the laptop, fake HOME, `FLEET_BROKER_SOCKET` pointed at a temp path, 3s timeout):

```text
$ fleet proxy serve --help
fleet proxy serve on /tmp/probe-proxy-home/broker.sock   # killed by timeout, exit 124
$ fleet proxy serve --bogus-junk
fleet proxy serve on /tmp/probe-proxy-home/broker.sock   # killed by timeout, exit 124
$ laptop-agent-broker --help                             # argv0 symlink
fleet proxy serve on /tmp/probe-proxy-home/broker.sock   # killed by timeout, exit 124
$ fleet proxy --help                                     # control
fleet proxy — The session proxy: …                       # domain help, exit 0
$ fleet proxy connect --help                             # control
fleet: usage: fleet proxy connect …                      # usage error, exit 2, no daemon
```

## Why it matters

`--help` is the safe, reflexive first command for any operator or agent meeting a daemon binary; here it silently performs the most consequential action the binary has — binding the session-broker socket and serving — instead of printing help, and a typo'd flag is swallowed the same way. This is exactly the bug class already fixed twice in this binary (#5488 for `fleet serve <role> --help`, #5560 for `fleet dispatch status` swallowing its arguments); the proxy domain's `serve` leaf is the remaining surface with the same shape: a no-argument daemon entry point reached through an argument-discarding dispatch. The §3 dispatch contract in `main.rs` says domain help is "always available, even where the domain itself is not" — the serve leaf defeats it.

## Acceptance criteria

- `fleet proxy serve --help` / `-h` prints usage for the serve leaf (or the proxy domain help) and exits 0, without binding the socket.
- `fleet proxy serve <any other argument>` fails with a usage error (exit 2) before binding anything.
- The argv0 form `laptop-agent-broker --help` behaves the same.
- Bare `fleet proxy serve` still starts the broker exactly as today; `fleet proxy connect`, `fleet proxy init`, and `fleet proxy --help` behavior are unchanged.
- A test pins the serve-leaf argument handling at the dispatch level so the implied-arg alias route cannot regress it.

body:
## Problem

The fleet binary's root built-in commands silently discard trailing arguments: `fleet version <anything>`, `fleet capabilities <anything>`, and `fleet --version <anything>` all print their normal output and exit 0, whatever follows. The root dispatcher itself is strict everywhere else — an unknown subcommand is a usage error (exit 2) — so a typo'd invocation like `fleet version --bogus-flag` (or a wrapper passing a stale flag) succeeds silently instead of failing as a usage error.

Same fail-open class as #5560 (fleet-dispatch status, fixed) and #5568 (serve broker roles) — but a different code path: those live in the domain dispatchers; this one is `run_root` in the top-level binary, whose `version` / `capabilities` / `--version` arms never check `args.len()`.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary at e844ed152)

Code — `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet/src/main.rs`, `run_root`:

- `Some("--version") | Some("-V")` arm prints and returns `EXIT_OK` unconditionally (the `--help` arm right above it does guard with `args.len() == 1`; these do not).
- `Some("version")` → `print_version(...)` → `EXIT_OK`, no arity check.
- `Some("capabilities")` → `print_capabilities(...)` → `EXIT_OK`, no arity check.

Probe (fleet binary rebuilt on the laptop from e844ed152, `Source rev: e844ed152dd1`):

| invocation | result |
|---|---|
| `fleet version` | version block, exit 0 (control) |
| `fleet version --bogus` | identical version block, exit 0 |
| `fleet capabilities --bogus` | identical JSON, exit 0 |
| `fleet --version --bogus` | `fleet 0.1.0`, exit 0 |
| `fleet versio` (control) | `error: unrecognized subcommand 'versio'`, exit 2 |

## Why it matters

These are the exact surfaces scripts and agents parse (`fleet version` for the census/source rev, `fleet capabilities` for the capability JSON). A caller passing a misspelled or retired flag gets valid-looking output and a success exit, so version/capability gating in automation silently runs on the wrong assumptions — the fleet has been removing this shape wherever it appears (#5560, #5460, #3287 series) because silent success on a typo is how stale invocations survive migrations.

## Acceptance criteria

- `fleet version <extra>`, `fleet capabilities <extra>`, and `fleet --version <extra>` / `fleet -V <extra>` exit 2 with a usage error naming the unexpected argument.
- Bare `fleet version`, `fleet capabilities`, `fleet --version`, `fleet -V` are unchanged (same output, exit 0).
- The existing `--help`-arm arity behavior is unchanged.
- A pinning unit test covers the rejection; `cargo test -p fleet` passes on the laptop or in CI.

title: fleet-proxy: pool sized for the fleet's work — default 50 + bounded wait in pool_get
body:
## Order

Drew, 2026-11-04: "build something that supports all our work — that was always the goal — fix it." Both arms approved: the env raise now, and the code fix behind it.

## Evidence

The concurrency report on #5412 (comment 6634809392) isolated the defect in `crates/fleet-proxy/src/serve.rs`:

- The per-port tunnel pool is an idle cache capped by `LAPTOP_AGENT_POOL`, default **12**.
- `pool_get` never waits: no idle tunnel ⇒ open a brand-new tunnel immediately, which costs seconds under burst; only 12 are retained, so the next burst pays again.
- Benchmark (32 concurrent, production): queue-broker p50 **1001.7 ms** through the proxy vs 213.0 ms direct, ~1/6 the throughput; the cliff starts exactly at the cap (at 16 concurrent, p95 already 851 ms). The identical binary with the pool at 32 (scratch control) restored direct-class performance (p50 137.8 ms). Backends are exonerated; the cap + no-wait overflow is the cause.

## Scope

1. **Default idle cap 12 → 50.** Brokers are auto-spawned by `fleet proxy connect` (`ensure_broker`) from arbitrary consumers whose environments do not carry the knob — a production broker was observed respawned by a random consumer with no `LAPTOP_AGENT_POOL` in its environment, silently reverting an env-only raise. The right size must be the compiled default; the env var remains an override. (The immediate arm — `LAPTOP_AGENT_POOL=50` at the sandbox broker's owning launch surface, `init-ensure.sh` — lands with this issue and stays as an explicit override.)
2. **Bounded wait in `pool_get`.** When no idle tunnel exists and opening another would exceed the pool size in live tunnels, wait (condvar signalled by `pool_put`) up to a bounded budget (250–500 ms, justified from the benchmark's tunnel-return times) for a returned tunnel before opening a new one. Hard requirements: a request must never hard-fail because of the pool (timeout ⇒ open a new tunnel, as today); the existing failure path (discard dead pooled connection, retry once on a fresh tunnel, then 502) is preserved; the pool mutex is never held during network I/O; keepalive behavior unchanged (never resets idle-exit).
3. **Legibility.** Named constants, the overflow policy (idle → wait-bounded → grow) commented at `pool_get`, and the effective pool size rendered in the broker's startup line.
4. **Tests/smoke.** Unit coverage for the wait (a waiter is woken by `pool_put`; a waiter times out into a fresh tunnel; live-count accounting). The workspace smoke gains a 32-concurrent hermetic burst against a scratch broker on default config asserting no request hangs or fails, plus the startup-line pool rendering.

## Acceptance

- Workspace tests + full smoke suite green.
- Merged, and the production sandbox broker redeployed onto the merged build: health on all three ports, `repo-queue health`, framed secrets request, and a 32-concurrent burst spot-check at direct-class p50.
- A broker auto-spawned with no `LAPTOP_AGENT_POOL` in its environment verifiably runs the 50 default (startup line).

body:
## Bug: `fleet dispatch status` silently ignores all arguments — `--help` performs a live `GET /health` instead of printing help, and typos are swallowed

`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-dispatch/src/lib.rs` (new in step 4, #5432):

- `run()` routes the verb and **discards the rest of argv for `status`**:

```rust
Some("status") => verb_status(config),
```

- `verb_status(config)` takes no argument list at all — it unconditionally
  picks a transport and exchanges `GET /health`.
- Its sibling verbs behave differently: `verb_launch` / `verb_enqueue` both
  scan for `--help`/`-h` first and print their usage with **no network
  call**, and their arguments go through `parse_args`, which rejects
  unknown options with a usage error (exit 2).

So `fleet dispatch status --help` does a real network request (possibly a
CONNECT tunnel through the proxy egress on the sandbox seat) and prints the
service's health JSON; `fleet dispatch status --bogus-junk` (or any stray
positional/typo) is silently accepted and does the same. There is no way to
ask what `status` accepts, and a mistyped invocation looks like a
successful health check.

### Verified this run (laptop probe, real crate @ main 7cd293eff)

Probe crate `~/git/fleet/probe-dispatch-status` (path-dep on the real
`fleet-dispatch`) calling `fleet_dispatch::run` with
`[dispatch] url = http://127.0.0.1:48931` pointed at a fake pm-dispatch
server that logs requests and returns `{"ok":true,"build":"probe"}`:

- **Case 1 — `status --help`**: printed the health JSON + transport line,
  exit 0; server log shows `GET /health`. No help text.
- **Case 2 — `status --bogus-junk`**: identical output, exit 0; server log
  shows `GET /health`. The unknown argument was never rejected.
- **Case 3 — control, `status`**: same output, exit 0, `GET /health`
  (correct behavior).
- **Case 4 — control, `launch --help`**: printed `Usage: fleet dispatch
  launch …`, exit 0, **no** server hit.

Server log after all four cases: exactly three `GET /health` lines
(cases 1–3).

### Why it matters

- Same bug class as #5488 (`serve <role> --help` starting the daemon):
  a help flag that triggers real work instead of printing help erodes the
  CLI contract the fleet multicall is built around (§3: help is always
  available, never has side effects).
- Silently ignored arguments hide operator typos — e.g. an intended
  filter/limit flag on a status check appears to succeed, so scripts and
  humans trust output for a different invocation than the one they typed.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `fleet dispatch status --help` (and `-h`) prints a status usage
      text and performs **no** network request, mirroring
      `launch`/`enqueue`.
- [ ] `fleet dispatch status <anything-else>` fails with a usage error
      (exit 2) naming the unexpected argument, before any transport is
      opened.
- [ ] Bare `fleet dispatch status` is unchanged: `GET /health`, health
      JSON + `transport` line, exit 0.
- [ ] Unit tests pin all three behaviors (help returns without touching
      the network; unknown args are usage errors; the help/rejection
      paths need no live service).
- [ ] `cargo test -p fleet-dispatch` green.

title: fleet step 6: secrets domain — `fleet secrets` verb (broker-first, Bitwarden fallback)
body:
Part of the #5412 epic family (fleet multicall binary; steps #5429–#5433). Filed 2026-11-04 on Drews direct order: setup the `secrets` subcommand that uses the local broker and falls back to Bitwarden.

## Why

Step 1 (#5429) shipped the fleet-secrets resolver platform — broker framed source first, Bitwarden (`bws`) fallback behind an injectable runner (`default_chain`) — but no shipped verb consumes it: the binarys only reference is a type assertion in `main.rs`. The 2026-11-04 attribution proof verified the broker legs wire exchange end-to-end against the live laptop secrets-broker (token discrimination + wire-level negative control), and its coverage note flagged exactly this gap: wiring a real resolve verb.

## Scope

- `fleet secrets get <name>` — resolve by name through `default_chain`: (1) BrokerSource framed exchange through the session proxy to the laptops secrets-broker (8-byte BE length + JSON; token file `~/tools/secrets-broker-token`; socket default `~/.cache/laptop-agent/broker.sock`); (2) on broker error/unreachable/not-found, fall back to Bitwarden via the existing bws runner seam. Value to stdout only; diagnostics to stderr; clean nonzero exit when both legs fail; the value is never logged anywhere else.
- `fleet secrets list` — names only, from the brokers names endpoint. Broker-leg failure is loud (stderr + nonzero), no silent substitution of a differently-shaped bws listing.
- Registry/stub semantics: the domain registers under the existing secrets capability; builds/profiles without it get the exit-69 stub taxonomy; hyphenated-name narrowing unchanged; capability→profile mapping stays as step 1 established it (flag any gap in the PR, do not silently widen).
- Reuse `default_chain`/`Resolver` as-is; smallest platform fix only if the error types cannot distinguish broker-404 from broker-down for clean fallback semantics, called out in the PR.

## Gates

- Verb shipped in the merged tree; `fleet secrets --help` renders from the registry like the other domains.
- Smoke extended: hermetic (scratch broker + stub bws runner: broker-first resolution; broker leg killed → fallback resolves; unknown name → clean failure) AND live attribution on the sandbox (a low-stakes name matches the bws copy by SHA-256/length with the value in no log; forced-broker-down still resolves via bws, designed so connect auto-spawn cannot mask the down state).
- D7 variant size gates stay green.
- Evidence comment here with attribution results + profile/capability placement before close.

title: fleet-proxy(stdio): relay never exits after remote close while stdin stays open — up.join() waits on a stdin-blocked thread

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/fleet
labels.description: pkgs/fleet multicall binary + platform crates

body:
## Bug: `fleet proxy connect --stdio` never exits after the remote side closes, when stdin stays open

`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/stdio.rs`, `relay_stdio` (merged in step 3, PR #5515):

```rust
let up = std::thread::spawn(move || {
    let mut stdin = std::io::stdin().lock();
    pump(&mut stdin, &mut inbound);
    let _ = inbound.shutdown(std::net::Shutdown::Write);
});
// tunnel → stdout on this thread.
let mut stdout = std::io::stdout().lock();
pump(&mut tunnel, &mut stdout);
drop(tunnel);
let _ = up.join();   // <-- blocks until stdin reaches EOF
Ok(0)
```

When the tunnel side closes first (server closes / SSH session ends), the
download pump returns — but `up.join()` then waits for the upload thread,
which is blocked in `stdin.read()` and also holds the `try_clone()` of the
socket, so `drop(tunnel)` closes nothing. The process hangs until stdin
also reaches EOF. As an SSH `ProxyCommand` this wedges session teardown:
the remote is gone, the bytes are delivered, and the relay process never
exits.

### Verified this run (laptop probe, real crate @ main 5521f3f11)

Probe crate `~/git/fleet/probe-stdio-hang` (path-dep on the real
`fleet-proxy`, `default-features = false`) calling
`relay_stdio` in direct mode against a loopback server that sends
`hello-from-server\n` and closes:

- **Case A — stdin held open** (pipe write-end open, no data, no EOF):
  stdout received `hello-from-server`, then the process **hung**;
  `timeout 6` killed it (exit 124).
- **Case B — control, stdin at EOF** (`< /dev/null`): exit 0 promptly,
  same bytes delivered.

### Why it matters

`--stdio` exists to be SSH's ProxyCommand. A ProxyCommand that outlives
the connection leaks a process per dead session and can stall `ssh`
exit; the Python relay it replaces exits when either side is done.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] When the tunnel reaches EOF/errors, `relay_stdio` returns promptly
      even if stdin is still open with no data.
- [ ] The stdin-EOF-first half-close behavior is preserved: stdin EOF
      still `shutdown(Write)`s the tunnel and the download side drains
      until the remote closes.
- [ ] Probe case A above exits 0 within ~1s of the server closing;
      case B unchanged.
- [ ] `cargo test -p fleet-proxy` green.

title: fleet-queue(validate): dedupe keys accept leading-zero spellings (issue:05424) and number 0 in the fix/triage/pr/set families

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/fleet
labels.description: pkgs/fleet multicall binary + platform crates

body:
## Bug

`fleet-queue` packet validation (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/validate.rs`, `match_dedupe`, lines 147–215 at main `864ed8a4a`) accepts **non-canonical numeric spellings** in `dedupe_key`s for the plain-number families: the number check is `all_digits(s)` followed by `s.parse()`, with no requirement that the spelling be the canonical decimal rendering of the parsed value, and no minimum of 1.

So all of these validate (`valid: true`) against a payload naming issue/PR/origin **5424**:

- `repo-health:v1:fix:developing-today/code:issue:05424`
- `repo-health:v1:fix:developing-today/code:issue:0005424`
- `repo-health:v1:pr:developing-today/code:pr:05424` (pr_shepherd packet, `prs: [{number: 5424}]`)
- `repo-health:v1:set:05424:owed:developing-today/code` (pr_shepherd packet, `set.origin_issue: 5424`)
- `repo-health:v1:fix:developing-today/code:issue:0` against a payload with `issue.number: 0` — issue/PR numbers start at 1, so 0 names nothing.

This is the same canonicality class #5482 fixed for the `pr-set` and `maintenance` families (single/repeated pr-set numbers, impossible ISO weeks), left open for the plain-number families (`fix`, `triage`, `pr`, `set` origin — and `pr-set` parts spelled with leading zeros, e.g. `0100-5424`, pass the same `parse()` path).

## Why it matters

The `dedupe_key` is the queue's deduplication identity: the database treats the key string as the identity of a unit of work. `…issue:5424` and `…issue:05424` are **different strings**, so a packet spelled with leading zeros gets a fresh dedupe identity for the same issue — exactly the duplicate-work evasion the canonical-spelling rules in `DEDUPE_PATTERNS_DOC` (same file) exist to prevent. The validator is the gate that is supposed to keep non-canonical keys out; for these families it approves them and even confirms the parsed number matches the payload, so nothing downstream flags the second spelling.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Shipped validator (laptop `fleet` multicall binary at main `864ed8a4a`, invoked as `repo-queue validate`) on packets derived from the known-good `packet-5424-fix.json` (probe dir on laptop: `~/git/fleet/probe-dedupe-zero`):

- control packet (`issue:5424`): `valid: true`
- `issue:05424`, `issue:0005424`: `valid: true`
- pr-family `pr:05424` and set-family `set:05424:owed:…`: `valid: true`
- `issue:0` with payload `issue.number: 0`: `valid: true`
- control for the overflow path: a 26-digit issue number is correctly rejected (parse failure surfaces as a number mismatch), so the gap is specifically canonical spelling / zero, not numeric parsing in general.

Dedup: #5482 (closed) covered only pr-set shapes and maintenance weeks; searches for leading-zero/canonical dedupe coverage returned no open or closed issue for the plain-number families.

## Acceptance criteria

- `match_dedupe` rejects any numeric component whose spelling is not the canonical decimal rendering of its value (no leading zeros) in the `fix`, `triage`, `pr`, `pr-set`, and `set` families.
- Numeric components must be ≥ 1 (issue/PR/origin numbers start at 1); `issue:0` / `pr:0` / `set:0:owed:…` do not validate.
- Canonical keys (e.g. `issue:5424`, `pr-set:100-5424`, `set:5424:owed:…`) validate exactly as before.
- Unit tests in `validate.rs` pin the rejected spellings (leading zeros per family, zero) and the accepted canonical controls.
- `cargo test -p fleet-queue --all-features` green (laptop or CI; no builds on the sandbox).

title: ci: required check 'basic: proxy port fallbacks' fails on every PR since ff971acc4 (antigravity-direct baseURL removed, guard still expects it)

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

body:
## What is broken

The required merge check **`basic: proxy port fallbacks`** fails on every PR (and on `main`) — the job exits in ~10s before any test runs.

## Evidence

Run on this branch (PR #5493): <https://github.com/developing-today/code/actions/runs/41846554696/job/126631459383>

```
::error::.opencode/opencode.jsonc has no {env:ANTIGRAVITY_DIRECT_PORT:-18751} baseURL — the fallback must match the antigravityDirectProxyPort definition (18751); a bare {env:ANTIGRAVITY_DIRECT_PORT} resolves to an empty port outside a home-manager shell (#434).
```

Reproduced locally on `origin/main` (clean, no branch diff in `.opencode/`):

```
$ bash .github/scripts/check-proxy-port-fallbacks.sh
::error::.opencode/opencode.jsonc has no {env:ANTIGRAVITY_DIRECT_PORT:-18751} baseURL ...
exit=1
```

## Cause

- `.github/scripts/check-proxy-port-fallbacks.sh:57` still declares the antigravity-direct row as `has_config=yes`:
  ```
  "ANTIGRAVITY_DIRECT_PORT|antigravityDirectProxyPort|bin/antigravity-direct.mjs|yes"
  ```
- `ff971acc4` ("opencode config: repoint antigravity-direct to the native in-fork provider (opencode#1414)") removed the `ANTIGRAVITY_DIRECT_PORT` baseURL from `.opencode/opencode.jsonc` entirely (`grep -r ANTIGRAVITY_DIRECT_PORT .opencode` is now empty), while `antigravityDirectProxyPort = 18751` still exists in `home/common/default.nix:23`.

So the guard demands a baseURL that the config no longer has.

## Fix options

1. Set the row to `has_config "no"` (the `CODEX_PROXY_PORT` / `OPENCODE_ROUTE_PROXY_PORT` precedent in the same array) — the proxy script fallback check still applies.
2. Or restore `"baseURL": "http://127.0.0.1:{env:ANTIGRAVITY_DIRECT_PORT:-18751}/..."` in `.opencode/opencode.jsonc` if the native repoint still routes through the local proxy.

Option 1 matches the commit that removed the baseURL; please confirm which is intended.

## Impact

`basic: proxy port fallbacks` is the branch-protection required check, so this blocks every PR until fixed.

title: github-backup(queue): #3476 pagination fix is merged but the Worker was never redeployed — live /queue still returns 500 events with no cursor, drainer blind to ~5.9k queued events
body:
## Summary

The #3476 fix (PR #3484, merged 2026-11-04, merge commit 8d2666741) added cursor pagination to the backup Worker's `GET /queue` and taught the drainer to follow it. The drainer half is live (it runs from the laptop clone), but the Worker half was never deployed: the live Worker still runs the pre-fix build, so the drainer remains blind past the first 500 queued events.

## Live evidence (2026-11-04, ~08:19-08:24 CST, two independent read-only probes)

- Authed `GET <worker>/queue` returns a JSON object whose ONLY top-level key is `events` — no `cursor`, no `list_complete` — with exactly 500 events.
- All 500 visible events are from 2026-11-02 11:13-15:55 UTC: dezren39/openclaw-personal 284, developing-today/code 204, dezren39/hatch-personal 12. The head was identical across probes ~5 minutes apart.
- `bin/drain_queue.py` treats a metadata-less response as a complete one-page queue (its documented legacy fallback), so every drain run reports `"events": 500` and can only ever ack events from that first page.
- True backlog measured this morning (Cloudflare port run): ~6,444 events (dezren39/openclaw-personal ~2,868, developing-today/code ~2,458). Roughly 5.9k events are therefore invisible and unackable, aging toward the Worker's 7-day event TTL. Events are a freshness signal and the weekly reconcile remains the correctness floor, but the drain is head-of-line blocked until this ships.
- Source check: `infra/github-backup/worker/src/index.js` on current main DOES return `{events, cursor, list_complete}`. The fix exists in the tree; only the deploy is missing.

## Secondary: ack-path timeouts against the current Worker

Four drain runs today (07:19, 07:33, 07:49, 08:04 CST) crashed with `TimeoutError` inside `ack_events` (60s client timeout reading the `/queue/ack` response; the Worker deletes ids sequentially, one KV op per id). The 08:04 crash is why the successful 08:03 fetches of dezren39/hatch-personal and dezren39/openclaw-personal did not ack their queued events in that run. Worth re-verifying the ack path under a full 500-id batch after the redeploy.

## Not this issue (already recovered)

The DRAIN-CHRONIC fetch failures for dezren39/hatch-personal and dezren39/openclaw-personal (05:56-07:12 CST today, 15 consecutive, fetch.log) were caused by the laptop's invalid `gh` token (private-repo auth: first "could not read Username", finally a 403 at 07:12). They recovered when the token was restored: both repos fetched ok at 08:03, their `drain_fail::*` counters are cleared, and `git ls-remote` for both succeeds (08:19). Minor residue: `state.json` still carries the stale 07:12 403 string in `last_error` after successful fetches, which made this diagnosis harder than it needed to be.

## Fix direction

1. Redeploy the Worker from `infra/github-backup/worker` (deploy.sh / deploy.mjs) so the deployed build matches main.
2. Verify: `GET /queue` returns `cursor` + `list_complete`; a drain run summary shows `events` > 500 and the backlog count falls across consecutive runs.
3. Confirm the ack path survives a full 500-id batch without the drainer timing out.

BOLT'S JOURNAL - CRITICAL LEARNINGS ONLY:
Before starting, read .jules/bolt.md (create if missing).

Your journal is NOT a log - only add entries for CRITICAL learnings that will help you avoid mistakes or make better decisions.

⚠️ ONLY add journal entries when you discover:
- A performance bottleneck specific to this codebase's architecture
- An optimization that surprisingly DIDN'T work (and why)
- A rejected change with a valuable lesson
- A codebase-specific performance pattern or anti-pattern
- A surprising edge case in how this app handles performance

❌ DO NOT journal routine work like:
- "Optimized component X today" (unless there's a learning)
- Generic React performance tips
- Successful optimizations without surprises

Format: `## YYYY-MM-DD - [Title]
**Learning:** [Insight]
**Action:** [How to apply next time]`

BOLT'S DAILY PROCESS:

1. 🔍 PROFILE - Hunt for performance opportunities:

  FRONTEND PERFORMANCE:
  - Unnecessary re-renders in React/Vue/Angular components
  - Missing memoization for expensive computations
  - Large bundle sizes (opportunities for code splitting)
  - Unoptimized images (missing lazy loading, wrong formats)
  - Missing virtualization for long lists

  - Missing lazy initialization

  - Consider edge cases
  - Ensure the optimization is safe
  - Add performance metrics in comments if possible

4. ✅ VERIFY - Measure the impact:
  - Run format and lint checks
  - Run the full test suite
  - Verify the optimization works as expected
  - Add benchmark comments if possible
  - Ensure no functionality is broken

5. 🎁 PRESENT - Share your speed boost:

  - Title: "⚡ Bolt: [performance improvement]"

    * 📊 Impact: Expected performance improvement (e.g., "Reduces re-renders by ~50%")
    * 🔬 Measurement: How to verify the improvement
  - Reference any related performance issues

BOLT'S FAVORITE OPTIMIZATIONS:
⚡ Add React.memo() to prevent unnecessary re-renders
⚡ Add database index on frequently queried field
⚡ Cache expensive API call results
⚡ Add lazy loading to images below the fold
⚡ Debounce search input to reduce API calls
⚡ Replace O(n²) nested loop with O(n) hash map lookup
⚡ Add pagination to large data fetch
⚡ Memoize expensive calculation with useMemo/computed
⚡ Add early return to skip unnecessary processing

BOLT AVOIDS (not worth the complexity):

body:
# fleet: `serve <role> --help` (and `queue-broker --help` / `secrets-broker --help`) starts the daemon instead of printing help

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ eb3e71c31)

`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet/src/main.rs`, `run_domain`: the domain-help shortcut only inspects `args.first()`:

```rust
if matches!(args.first().map(|s| s.as_str()), Some("--help") | Some("-h") | Some("help")) {
    print_domain_help(surface, d);
    return EXIT_OK;
}
```

For the `serve` domain the first argument is the *role*, so a help flag in position 2 is never seen. The call falls through to the broker entry points — `fleet_queue::queue_broker::run()` and `fleet_queue::secrets_broker::run()` (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/queue_broker.rs:589`, `secrets_broker.rs:170`) — which take **no arguments at all** and ignore argv entirely, proceeding to bind and serve.

The argv0 aliases hit the same path: `main()` prepends the implied arg (`queue-broker` → `serve queue-broker`), so `queue-broker --help` becomes args `["queue-broker", "--help"]` and also starts the daemon.

Behavioral probe (real `fleet` binary built on the laptop, fake HOME with probe token files, `QUEUE_BROKER_BIND=127.0.0.1:0`, 3s timeout):

```text
$ fleet serve queue-broker --help
queue-broker: listening on 127.0.0.1:0        # stderr; killed by timeout, exit 124
$ queue-broker --help                          # argv0 symlink
queue-broker: listening on 127.0.0.1:0        # stderr; killed by timeout, exit 124
$ fleet serve --help                           # control
fleet serve — Run a fleet daemon role …        # domain help, exit 0
```

## Why it matters

`--help` is the safe, reflexive first command for any operator or agent meeting a new daemon binary. Here it silently performs the most consequential action the binary has — binding a port and serving the repo-queue / secrets brokers with whatever token files the host carries — instead of printing help. The §3 dispatch contract in the same file says domain help is "always available, even where the domain itself is not"; the role-shaped invocation defeats that contract. It is also an operational footgun for the fleet's own automation, which routinely probes `<tool> --help` to learn a surface.

## Acceptance criteria

- `fleet serve queue-broker --help`, `fleet serve secrets-broker --help` (and `-h` / `help` in the same position) print the serve domain help and exit 0, without binding anything.
- The argv0 forms `queue-broker --help` and `secrets-broker --help` behave the same.
- `fleet serve <role>` with no help flag still starts the role exactly as today; `fleet serve --help` and all other domains' help behavior are unchanged.
- A test pins the help-after-role routing (e.g. at the dispatch level) so the implied-arg alias route cannot regress it.

title: helium-cdp can wedge with CDP answering but every page load hanging; nothing detects or repairs it

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.description: Medium: expected under 1 day of work

body:
## What happened

The laptop's managed Helium instance (`helium-cdp.service`, a transient `systemd-run` unit, CDP on 127.0.0.1:19222) spent at least ~1.5 h in a state where **every page load hung**, while the browser process itself stayed up and answered CDP:

- `PUT /json/new` returned a target with a valid `webSocketDebuggerUrl`;
- `Page.navigate` never replied (30 s timeout);
- `Runtime.evaluate` on the new target never replied (20 s timeout);
- the same probes succeeded in ~1 s against a throwaway second Helium instance (port 19223, fresh profile), so this was the instance, not the machine or the caller.

Consequences: `meta-quota-export.service` failed every 15-minute tick from ~2026-11-04T12:49Z to 13:16Z with `no-console-page: created dev.meta.ai tab did not finish loading within 75s` (the fix for #5121 creates its own tab, so the failure moved from "no tab" to "tab never loads"). No measurement was exported for over 30 h (last `status: ok` at 2026-11-03T07:45Z).

`systemctl --user restart helium-cdp.service` restored it immediately: the first post-restart probe navigated and evaluated in ~1 s. The instance had no signed-in session to lose (its only page tab was a logged-out GitHub login redirect plus the extension background page).

## Why it matters

- Nothing supervises the browser's *renderer* health. The unit is `active (running)`, CDP answers, and `/json/list` lists targets — every cheap health signal is green while no page can load.
- The wedge is indistinguishable, from the exporter's point of view, from "the tab I created did not load in time", so its failure record says `no-console-page` even though a page was created and the browser was the broken part.

## Suggested fixes

1. A readiness probe the timer (or a supervisor) runs before the export: create a target, navigate to `about:blank`/`data:`, `Runtime.evaluate("1")` with a short timeout, close it. On failure, restart `helium-cdp.service` (bounded, e.g. max once per 15 min) and record the restart in the export document.
2. A distinct exporter status/exit for "target created but never became usable" (e.g. `page-not-ready`, exit 5 alongside `no-console-page`) so the record names the browser, not the tab, as the culprit.
3. Keep `session-expired` (HTTP 401) separate as it already is — during the same investigation the laptop's `dev.meta.ai` session turned out to be expired as well, which needs a human re-login and cannot be fixed by any agent.

## Evidence

- Task 9492 / issue #5121 blocked-escalated note: https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5121#issuecomment-6632791182
- `~/atlas/meta-quota-export/history.jsonl` around 2026-11-04T12:49Z–13:16Z (`no-console-page`, 75 s timeout).

## Acceptance criteria
- A wedged state (CDP answering while page loads hang) is detected by an explicit health check rather than going unnoticed
- On detection the driver recovers or fails fast with a diagnosable error naming the wedge
- A regression test or scripted repro covers the hang scenario

title: fleet-queue(validate): pr-set dedupe keys accept non-canonical spellings (single/repeated number) and maintenance keys accept impossible ISO weeks (W99)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/normal

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/validate.rs` — `match_dedupe` accepts dedupe-key spellings that the validator's own pattern contract forbids, so the same queue work can be enqueued under two different "deterministic" keys and the dedupe guarantee is bypassable at validation time (the DB backstop only catches identical keys, not alternate spellings of the same coverage).

The contract is in the same file, `DEDUPE_PATTERNS_DOC` (validate.rs:24-30, also printed verbatim in the validator's own error messages):

```
pr-set:      repo-health:v1:pr-set:<repo>:<n>-<n>[-...] (sorted)
maintenance: repo-health:v1:maintenance:<repo>:<kind>:<YYYY-Www>
```

## Verified this run (shipped `repo-queue validate`, packets derived from the known-good packet for issue #5424)

1. **Single-number pr-set validates.** Key `repo-health:v1:pr-set:developing-today/code:5424` (kind `pr_shepherd`, payload `prs: [{number: 5424}]`) → `{"valid": true}`. The doc pattern requires `<n>-<n>` — at least two numbers. Root cause: the pr-set arm (validate.rs:203-215) splits the tail on `-` and only checks every part is digits; a one-element split passes. Consequence: one PR can be enqueued as either `pr:…:pr:5424` or `pr-set:…:5424` — two valid keys, one unit of work, dedupe defeated.
2. **Repeated-number pr-set validates.** Key `…:pr-set:developing-today/code:5424-5424` with `prs` listing 5424 twice → `{"valid": true}`. A "set" with a repeated element is not a set; the sortedness check in `dedupe_errors` (validate.rs:337-355) treats equal neighbours as sorted, and the payload comparison compares the same duplicated list, so nothing rejects it.
3. **Impossible ISO week validates.** Key `repo-health:v1:maintenance:developing-today/code:weekly:2026-W99` (kind `triage`) → `{"valid": true}`. The week check (validate.rs:231-235) verifies only shape (`YYYY-W` + two digits); ISO weeks run 01–53, so `W99` (and `W00`) name no real week — a maintenance key for a week that does not exist can never collide with the correctly-spelled key for any real week, splitting maintenance dedupe by spelling.

Controls in the same run: a proper two-number pr-set key (`…:100-5424`) validates, and a non-numeric pr-set tail (`…:abc`) is rejected with the pattern doc — the matcher is live and the shapes above are genuine holes, not a disabled validator.

## Why it matters

Dedupe keys are the queue's determinism contract: producers rely on `validate` to guarantee one canonical key per unit of work before enqueue. Every non-canonical spelling that validates is a second key for the same work — duplicate tasks for one PR set, or a maintenance task that the correctly-keyed weekly packet cannot dedupe against.

## Acceptance criteria

- `match_dedupe`'s pr-set arm requires at least two numbers, all distinct (equivalently: strictly ascending at match time, with the existing `dedupe_errors` sortedness/payload checks unchanged).
- Maintenance keys require the ISO week number in `01..=53`.
- Unit tests in `validate.rs` pin all three rejected shapes above plus the valid controls (single `pr:` key, two-number pr-set, `2026-W44`-style maintenance key).
- `cargo test -p fleet-queue` green (laptop or CI); the shipped `repo-queue validate` rejects the three repro packets and still accepts the controls.

Found by new-issue-creator-code-b (Lane B) during the 2026-11-04 run; verified against the live validator binary and the source at main 49d11b5b7.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe against the real crate @ main 3b3df1be3)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-fleetconfig-env` on the laptop — a binary crate with a path dependency on `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config`, driving the public API with controlled env vars (`HOME=/tmp/fakehome123`):

- **A** — `XDG_CONFIG_HOME=""`: `Config::file_path()` returns `"fleet/fleet.toml"` — a **relative** path. (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs`: `file_path()` maps `var_os("XDG_CONFIG_HOME")` straight into `PathBuf::from` with no empty check; XDG base-directory spec says an empty value is invalid and must be treated as unset.)
- **B** — with a planted `./fleet/fleet.toml` in the working directory (`[domains] queue = false`), `Config::load()` loads **that file**: `domain_enabled("queue") == false`. So from any directory containing a stray `fleet/fleet.toml`, fleet silently takes its config — including domain disables, broker socket, and token-file path — from the CWD instead of the user's `~/.config/fleet/fleet.toml`.
- **C** — control, `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` unset: `file_path()` is `/tmp/fakehome123/.config/fleet/fleet.toml` and the planted file is ignored (`queue_enabled=true`).
- **E** — same flaw in `state_dir()`: `XDG_STATE_HOME=""` returns relative `"fleet"`, so the state/shims dirs also land in the CWD.
- **D** — `broker_socket()`: a relative `FLEET_BROKER_SOCKET` (e.g. `.cache/laptop-agent/broker.sock`, the default's own spelling) is returned **as-is, CWD-relative**, while the config-file value and the compiled default both go through `resolve_under_home` — despite the field doc "relative paths resolve under $HOME". The same operator spelling therefore names different sockets depending on which source supplied it. Control: env unset → `/tmp/fakehome123/.cache/laptop-agent/broker.sock`.

## Why it matters

fleet-config is the one place fleet configuration resolves, and its crate docs make a loud-error / no-silent-surprises contract (#5460 just enforced it for typos). Empty-string env vars are a routine artifact (systemd units, `env -i` wrappers, templated exports that expand to nothing), and here they quietly relocate the config file, the state dir, and — via a relative env socket — the broker endpoint to whatever directory the process happens to start in. The CWD-planted config case is the sharp edge: config content (domain disables = the incident lever, socket and token-file paths) becomes directory-dependent.

## Acceptance criteria

- Empty `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` / `XDG_STATE_HOME` are treated as unset (fall back to `~/.config` / `~/.local/state`); empty `FLEET_CONFIG` likewise falls through to the XDG path instead of naming an empty path.
- A relative `FLEET_BROKER_SOCKET` env value resolves under `$HOME`, exactly like the config-file and default values.
- Regression tests pin: empty-XDG file/state paths are the HOME-based absolutes, and the env socket spelling `.cache/laptop-agent/broker.sock` resolves to the same path as the default.
- `cargo test -p fleet-config` green (laptop or CI; no builds on the sandbox).

title: libvirtd.service fails to start on the 2026-11-02 generation: systemd credential decryption fails (243/CREDENTIALS)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

body:
## Summary

On the fleet switch to the 2026-11-02 generation (switch attempt 4, 2026-11-04, log `/home/user/switch-20261104-070428.log`), activation completed and the system profile advanced, but `switch-to-configuration` exited 4 because **libvirtd.service failed to start**. It is the only failed unit on the system.

## Evidence

- Generation advanced: `/run/current-system` and the system profile both moved from `b0zkpr8p41ckyagml89qaiw0szshv92c-nixos-system-amd-26.11.20261010.6510408` to `vvxbyg7w01s0cqq21q1sbw240lqq25gn-nixos-system-amd-26.11.20261102.f9887a8`.
- `systemctl --failed` shows exactly one unit: `libvirtd.service`.
- Failure mode (2026-11-04 07:24:43 CST, at activation):

```
(libvirtd)[950748]: libvirtd.service: Decryption failed (incorrect key?): No OpenSSL errors.
(libvirtd)[950748]: libvirtd.service: Failed to set up credentials: Bad message
(libvirtd)[950748]: libvirtd.service: Failed at step CREDENTIALS spawning .../libvirt-12.8.0/sbin/libvirtd: Bad message
systemd[1]: libvirtd.service: Main process exited, code=exited, status=243/CREDENTIALS
```

- The unit carries a `LoadCredentialEncrypted=` directive; systemd cannot decrypt the credential blob on this host/boot, so the daemon never starts. Socket units (`libvirtd.socket`, `libvirtd-ro.socket`, `libvirtd-admin.socket`) are present, so any VM/libvirt client connection attempt will hit this.

## Notes

- First observed at this activation; whether the same start would have failed under the previous generation is not established (libvirtd had not been started since the 05:47 reboot, and the journal is volatile).
- The switch itself was not rolled back: the rest of the new generation is live and verified. This issue tracks only the libvirtd credential defect.
- Likely area: how the encrypted credential is produced/sealed (host key / TPM binding vs. the credstore the unit reads) in the NixOS libvirt configuration.

title: fleet-secrets: validate_name accepts dot segments and percent-encoded spellings — '..', '%2e%2e', 'a%2fb' pass the single-path-segment check and leave /secret/<name>

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/fleet
labels.description: pkgs/fleet multicall binary + platform crates

body:
## Summary

`fleet-secrets`' `validate_name` (pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-secrets/src/lib.rs:104) is the
gate that guarantees a secret name is safe as a single URL path segment — it is
interpolated raw into the broker request path at lib.rs:213,
`path: format!("/secret/{name}")`. It rejects `/`, `?`, `#`, whitespace, and
control characters, and its own doc/error text states that purpose:

> Names become URL path segments (`GET /secret/<name>`); validate before any source sees them.

But the encoded and dot-segment spellings of exactly those characters pass:

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-secret-name`, real `fleet-secrets` crate via path-dep @ main ec28a3dd1)

```
"."       validate_ok=true   path="/secret/."
".."      validate_ok=true   path="/secret/.."
"%2e%2e"  validate_ok=true   path="/secret/%2e%2e"
"%2f"     validate_ok=true   path="/secret/%2f"
"a%2fb"   validate_ok=true   path="/secret/a%2fb"
"a%3fb"   validate_ok=true   path="/secret/a%3fb"
"a%23b"   validate_ok=true   path="/secret/a%23b"
"a/b"     validate_ok=false  (control case — the literal spelling is refused)
"normal.name" validate_ok=true (legitimate dotted names must keep working)
```

Reference normalization (Python `urllib`, same semantics as RFC 3986 §5.2 /
percent-decoding layers in HTTP stacks):

- `/secret/..` normalizes to `/` and `/secret/.` to `/secret/` — the request
  no longer names a secret under `/secret/` at all.
- `/secret/%2e%2e` percent-decodes to `/secret/..`; `/secret/a%2fb` decodes
  to `/secret/a/b` — the very shapes the validator exists to refuse, arriving
  at any decoding broker/router layer in decoded form.

## Why it matters

`fleet-secrets` is documented as *the one secrets-by-name path for fleet*
(design §1, epic #5412): "secrets are resolved by name through this crate
only." Its validation is the boundary every caller relies on. A name that
passes validation but does not stay a single literal segment under
`/secret/` breaks that contract — at best the broker resolves a different
route/name than the caller asked for; at worst a crafted name (`..`,
`%2e%2e`, `a%2f..`) walks the broker's routing in a secrets-bearing service.
This is the same class as #5427 (dot segments evading an exact-string path
check in `is_safe_web_path`), one crate over. The `bws` fallback matches
names literally, so the two sources also disagree about what these names
mean.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validate_name` refuses `.` and `..` as complete names, and any name
  containing `%` (the introducer of every encoded spelling of the refused
  characters) — or, equivalently, the path construction percent-encodes the
  name so the wire segment is always the literal name; either way the
  guarantee "the broker receives exactly one literal segment, the name
  itself" must hold and be tested.
- The `InvalidName` error text is updated to name the newly refused shapes.
- New tests in the existing `name_validation_rejects_path_material` style pin
  `.`, `..`, `%2e%2e`, `%2f`, `a%2fb`, `a%3fb`, `a%23b` as refused, and
  legitimate dotted names (`supabase.service-role-key`, `a.b-c_d`) still pass.
- `cargo test -p fleet-secrets` green.

title: fix(fleet): daily top-issue dispatch jobs race on shared state — same issue double-dispatched (2026-11-04: #5421)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: effort/m
labels.description: Medium: expected under 1 day of work

labels.name: meta/enriched
labels.description: Intake review done: acceptance criteria, links, and normalized labels added

body:
## Problem

The two daily top-issue dispatch jobs — `opencode-daily-top-issue` (rotating) and `opencode-daily-top-issue-code` (code-dedicated) — both fire at 07:12 and share `opencode-top-issue-state.json` as their dedupe record. The state file is read-then-written with no atomic claim step, so when both runs select concurrently they cannot see each other.

On 2026-11-04 both jobs walked the code backlog to #5421 and launched OpenCode sessions ~22 seconds apart (sessions ses_e5e594cc7dbffeQhm3TWhSNM38 / task 9531 / tracking #5458, and ses_e5e594c5081ffeAPNQmQjGx2sC / task 9533 / tracking #5461). The later session was stood down manually (deleted via the OpenCode server API) and #5461 closed; a queue lane (task 9434, from triage 9432) was also already working the same issue, so three channels converged on one small fix.

## Why it matters

Double-booking is exactly what the shared state file exists to prevent (the feeder's dedupe rule was written after the opencode#831 / queue-task-3137 double-booking). Duplicate sessions burn laptop build capacity, produce competing PRs for the same issue, and need manual cleanup.

## Fix directions (any one, or combined)

- Claim before dispatch: at selection time, atomically mark the issue (e.g. apply `queue/claimed` via gh and re-read to confirm this run won) before calling pm-dispatch; the loser walks to the next backlog entry.
- Stagger the two jobs so the code-dedicated job runs after the rotating job has written state (and have the rotating job skip code on days the sibling owns it, or vice versa).
- Have each job re-read the state file (and the issue's labels) immediately before the dispatch call, not only at run start.

## Acceptance

- A repeat of the 2026-11-04 morning (both jobs firing the same minute with the same top backlog entry) results in exactly one dispatch; the other job records a dedupe skip.
- The dedupe check covers queue-lane claims too: an issue with a live queue fix task is not dispatched.

## Acceptance criteria
- Two dispatch jobs racing on the same state cannot dispatch the same issue twice
- The claim on shared state is atomic or lock-guarded, with the losing job standing down visibly
- A test or scripted repro demonstrates the race is closed

title: Fix #5421: fix(pm-stack): apply-config.sh treats DRY_RUN=0/false as dry-run — ready

labels.name: source/dispatch
labels.description: Filed by pm-dispatch

body:
Implement GitHub issue #5421 in developing-today/code: fix(pm-stack): apply-config.sh treats DRY_RUN=0/false as dry-run — ready-for-agent config silently never applies

## Finding

`pm-stack/ready-for-agent/apply-config.sh` (added by PR #3311, for #1203) decides dry-run mode with Python truthiness on the raw environment string:

- `apply-config.sh:28` — `export DRY_RUN="${DRY_RUN:-}"`
- `apply-config.sh:38` — `dry_run = bool(os.environ.get("DRY_RUN"))`

`bool("0")` and `bool("false")` are `True` in Python, so `DRY_RUN=0 ./apply-config.sh` — or an ambient `DRY_RUN=false` in the caller's environment — runs as a **dry run**: every mutation becomes a `DRY-RUN would ...` print, the script exits 0, and the final line reads `ready-for-agent config applied (dry run)`. Nothing is registered, configured, or unpaused, and nothing fails.

This matters because the same PR wired `./apply-config.sh` into `pm-stack/ready-for-agent/install.sh` to run on **every** install run after the harness is verified serving. An operator or unit environment that carries a conventional false-y `DRY_RUN=0` therefore silently defeats the declarative config (#1203) forever: the harness settings (including the fleet's `mergePolicy: OFF` human-merge posture) never converge, with a success exit and no error anywhere.

Verified live on current main (991bb496a, 2026-11-04): lines 28 and 38 above are unchanged from the PR. The PR's own test, `pm-stack/ready-for-agent/test-apply-config.sh`, covers `DRY_RUN=1` (mutates nothing) and unset (applies) only — no false-y value is pinned.

## Evidence

- Source PR: #3311 `feat(pm-stack): declarative ready-for-agent config + aggregator dispatch source (#1203)`, merged 8ee2e1cd0b61e24e5b123645556a968deeb1ef6d; apply-config.sh introduced in commit dcea7fa21.
- `pm-stack/ready-for-agent/apply-config.sh:38` on main: `dry_run = bool(os.environ.get("DRY_RUN"))`.
- Contrast with the fleet's dry-run semantics findings in the dangerous direction (#3297, #3287): there an unrecognised flag meant a real mutation; here a recognised false-y value silently means *no* mutation, reported as success.

## Acceptance criteria

- Only an explicit truthy value (`1`, and if supported `true`) enables dry-run; `0`, `false`, `no`, empty, and unset all apply for real (case-insensitive where applicable).
- `test-apply-config.sh` gains a case proving a false-y `DRY_RUN` value (e.g. `DRY_RUN=0`) actually sends mutations to the stub harness.
- The script header documents the accepted dry-run values.
- Existing test cases (dry-run mutates nothing; first apply registers/configures/unpauses; second apply is a no-op) still pass.

title: fleet-config: misspelled fleet.toml section/key is silently ignored — a typo'd [domains] disable loads Ok and the domain stays enabled

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/fleet
labels.description: pkgs/fleet multicall binary + platform crates

body:
## Summary

`fleet-config` (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs`, landed in step 1, #5429) parses `fleet.toml` with serde's default unknown-field handling: **any misspelled section or key is silently ignored and the compiled-in default rules instead**. That is exactly the failure mode the crate's own docs say must never happen:

> "A missing file is not an error (defaults rule); a malformed file is a loud error, never a silent fallback, because a silently ignored disable would defeat the lever." (crate doc, `lib.rs:13-15`)

A typo is not a parse error under TOML/serde, so today it *is* a silent fallback.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-fleetconfig` against the real crate as a path dependency, main `be7dae6ca`)

`Config::load_from` on three misspelled files:

- `[domain]` (misspelled `[domains]`) with `queue = false` → `Ok`, `domain_enabled("queue") == true` — **the operator's domain disable is silently lost**; the domain the operator meant to kill via the §7 incident lever stays enabled.
- `[proxy]` with `idle_exit_sec = 60` and `broker_soket = "/tmp/x.sock"` → `Ok`, `idle_exit_secs() == 3600` (default), `broker_socket()` == the default under `$HOME` — both overrides silently lost.
- Unknown top-level key (`domainz = 1`) → `Ok`.

Control with correct spellings (`[domains] queue = false`, `[proxy] idle_exit_secs = 60`) resolves as intended (`domain_enabled("queue") == false`, `idle == 60`), so the loss is specifically the unknown-field handling, not the resolution logic.

Root cause: `Config`, `ProxyConfig`, and `SecretsConfig` (`lib.rs:36-60`) derive `Deserialize` with `#[serde(default)]` but no `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]`, so unknown sections/keys deserialize without error.

## Why it matters

The `[domains]` disable is the per-host incident lever for the fleet binary (design §7, epic #5412). An operator disabling a misbehaving domain during an incident, with one character wrong in the section name, gets a successful load, no warning, and a still-enabled domain — the worst possible outcome for a safety lever, and a direct contradiction of the crate's stated contract. The same silent loss applies to the broker socket and secrets token-file overrides, where a typo reroutes (or un-routes) broker traffic with no signal.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Config`, `ProxyConfig`, and `SecretsConfig` reject unknown fields (`#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` or equivalent), so a misspelled section or key in `fleet.toml` makes `Config::load_from` return `ConfigError::Parse` naming the offending field.
- [ ] `[domains]` remains an open map: arbitrary domain names as keys still load (the deny applies to struct fields, not domain names).
- [ ] Unit tests pin: misspelled section (`[domain]`), misspelled key (`idle_exit_sec`), and unknown top-level key all error; the existing tests (missing file → defaults, correct spellings resolve) still pass.
- [ ] `cargo test -p fleet-config` green.

title: id(group/doc/claim): key=value renderer leaves DEL, C1 controls and U+2028/U+2029 raw inside its quoted literal

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Bug: `id group`/`doc`/`claim` key=value renderer leaves DEL, C1 controls, and U+2028/U+2029 raw inside its "quoted" literal

The shared key=value renderer in `pkgs/id/src/commands/group.rs` (`text` / `quoted`, used via `tokens` by `id group`, `id doc`, and `id claim` via `commands/doc.rs` `print_action`/`print_rows`) quotes a value when it contains whitespace, a control character, or a format character — but its escape arm only escapes part of that trigger set:

- `pkgs/id/src/commands/group.rs:122` (at 54b9c3b06):
  ```rust
  c if crate::is_format_char(c) || (c.is_control() && (c as u32) < 0x20) => {
      push_unicode_escape(&mut rendered, c);
  }
  ```
  The `< 0x20` bound excludes the rest of category Cc: DEL `U+007F` and the C1 controls `U+0080`–`U+009F` (including NEL `U+0085`).
- `U+2028` / `U+2029` are also missed: they trigger quoting via `is_whitespace` in `text` (group.rs:80), but they are neither `is_control` nor Cf (`is_format_char`), so `quoted` pushes them raw.

That contradicts the renderer's own doc (group.rs: "the whitespace and control bytes escaped (`\n`, `\t`, `\u00XX`, and so on)" / "a plain row is therefore always exactly one physical line") and the shared plain-output contract in `pkgs/id/src/commands/text.rs:35-57` (design #3455 Phase 3b): structure characters are category Cc **plus** `U+2028`/`U+2029`, and row renderers — explicitly including this key=value renderer — "render each offending character as `\uXXXX`".

### Verified this run (laptop probe, verbatim functions)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-group-quote` on the laptop, copying `text`/`quoted`/`push_unicode_escape` verbatim from group.rs, `is_format_char` verbatim from `crates/id-core/src/unicode.rs`, and `plain_field` from `commands/text.rs` as the reference renderer, at main 54b9c3b06:

```
DEL 0x7F:  group="\"a<RAW 0x7F>b\""  raw_char_present=true  | plain_field="\"a\\u007fb\""
NEL 0x85:  group="\"a<RAW 0x85>b\""  raw_char_present=true  | plain_field="\"a\\^Eb\""
C1 0x9F:   group="\"a<RAW 0x9F>b\""  raw_char_present=true  | plain_field="\"a\\^_b\""
U+2028:    group="\"a<RAW 2028>b\""  raw_char_present=true  | plain_field="\"a\\u2028b\""
U+2029:    group="\"a<RAW 2029>b\""  raw_char_present=true  | plain_field="\"a\\u2029b\""
C0 0x1F:   group="\"a\\^_b\""     raw_char_present=false | plain_field="\"a\\^_b\"" (control case OK)
Cf 0x202E: group="\"a\\u202eb\""     raw_char_present=false | plain_field="\"a\\u202eb\"" (control case OK)
```

So C0 controls and Cf are correctly escaped (#3111), but DEL/C1 and the line/paragraph separators reach the terminal raw inside the quotes.

### Why it matters

A stored group/doc/claim name or value is untrusted text (the #1611/#3111 threat model). Raw DEL/C1 bytes can act on a terminal, and NEL / `U+2028` / `U+2029` are treated as line breaks by some consumers — `plain_field` includes them for exactly that reason (text.rs: "some consumers treat them as line breaks"). Inside the key=value row they can therefore split or falsify a row that the quoting was meant to keep to one physical line with its real `author=`/`event=` tail unambiguous.

### Acceptance criteria

- `quoted` in `pkgs/id/src/commands/group.rs` escapes **every** character that can trigger quoting in `text`: all `char::is_control` (including `U+007F` and `U+0080`–`U+009F`), all Cf, and `U+2028`/`U+2029`, as `\uXXXX` (with the existing short escapes for `\b \f \n \r \t` kept).
- The rendered literal still parses back as the same JSON string (`serde_json::from_str` round-trip), as the existing Cf tests pin.
- New tests in `commands/group.rs` pin DEL, a C1 control (e.g. NEL `U+0085`), `U+2028`, and `U+2029` — alone and embedded — asserting the `\uXXXX` spelling and that no raw offending character remains; existing group/text renderer tests stay green.
- No change to `--json` output or to values with no offending character (byte-identical rendering preserved).

Related: #1611, #3111 (Cf in this same renderer — fixed), #2839 / #3455 / #3456 (the plain-output contract and its is_control inventory; this is the residual Cc-beyond-0x1F + Zl/Zp gap in the quoted arm).
