## Summary

The `idset.writer` body codec (`pkgs/id/src/idset.rs`, writer-set spec slice 1, #3854) accepts duplicate entries that carry contradictory semantics: the same author key twice with opposite `include_history` flags, the same group twice with different `role_min` values, `public` twice with opposite flags, and duplicates inside `excludes`. Neither the encoder nor the decoder refuses them — `WriterSet::check()` validates only the scope (length/NFC) and the total entry count.

## Evidence (verified on `origin/main` @ fd961f654, this run)

- `pkgs/id/src/idset.rs:134-146` — `WriterSet::check()` checks scope and `entries.len() + excludes.len() <= MAX_ENTRIES` (4096) only; no uniqueness check over entries or excludes.
- `pkgs/id/src/idset.rs:256-289` — `encode_writer_body` and `decode_writer_body` both gate on `check()` (decode also re-checks canonical CBOR, tag, and version in `top_level`), so the one missing check leaves both paths open.
- `pkgs/id/src/idset.rs:499-511` — `entries_field` maps each entry through `entry_field` and collects; it never compares an entry against the ones before it.
- Sibling precedent in the same crate, all refused at the codec boundary: `chain.rs` `ChainExt::validate` refuses a repeated `after` hash (`ChainError::DuplicateAfter`); the group-event codec's identical gap was filed as #5217 (duplicate/self causal predecessors, duplicate create members with conflicting roles); the artifact codec's version was fixed as #3196.
- The open expansion slice, #4998 (writer-set expansion — `expand`/`expand_retro` over group grants, spec slice 2 of #3789), will consume exactly these lists: for a duplicated key, whether history is admitted depends on which copy an expander honours (first, last, or either); for a duplicated group, the effective `role_min` is undefined. Two conforming expanders can therefore disagree about who is a writer for the same signed set.

Verified with a laptop probe at `origin/main` fd961f654 (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-04-laneA-idset/pkgs/id/tests/probe_idset.rs`, `cargo test --test probe_idset` — 1 passed):

- Control: an ordinary single-entry set encodes and decodes round-trip unchanged.
- `entries = [key([9;32], include_history=true), key([9;32], include_history=false)]`: `encode_writer_body` = Ok, `decode_writer_body` = Ok with 2 entries.
- `entries = [group(H, role_min=Read), group(H, role_min=Admin)]` (same group id, conflicting roles): encode Ok, decode Ok with 2 entries.
- `entries = [public(include_history=true), public(include_history=false)]`: encode Ok, decode Ok with 2 entries.
- `excludes = [key([5;32], true), key([5;32], false)]`: encode Ok, decode Ok with 2 excludes.

## Why it matters

This codec is the signed wire format writer sets will sync by, and its expansion consumer (#4998) is not yet built — now is the cheapest moment to tighten it, before lax acceptance is baked into peers' stored sets and before the expander has to pick an arbitrary duplicate winner. Duplicates also burn the bounded entry budget: one author repeated 4096 times is a valid body that admits one writer. Every other causal/entry codec in pkgs/id refuses duplicates at the boundary; this one should match the house rule while it is still version 1 with no deployed peers.

Note: the same key appearing once in `entries` and once in `excludes` is NOT a duplicate — exclusions win by design (spec §D6) and that shape must keep decoding.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `WriterSet::check()` (or an equivalent single gate used by both `encode_writer_body` and `decode_writer_body`) refuses a repeated entry identity within `entries`, and separately within `excludes`: same author key for `key` entries (regardless of `include_history`), same group id for `group` entries (regardless of `role_min`/`include_history`), and more than one `public` entry in one list.
- [ ] The refusal is an `IdsetError::Shape` naming the duplication.
- [ ] Tests in `pkgs/id/src/idset.rs` cover all three duplicate shapes on the decode path (hand-built bodies, not just encode), plus the entries-vs-excludes same-key shape still decoding (spec §D6).
- [ ] Existing idset tests still pass (`cargo test -p id idset` on the laptop/CI).

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-a after verification this run; not a duplicate of #5217 (group-event codec), #3196 (artifact codec, fixed), #5225 (petname journal replay), or #4998 (the expansion slice that will consume these lists).

Step 6 of the Atlas binary+service epic (#5350). Design of record: `doc/2026-11-04T08-07-13Z_design_atlas_binary_service/` (§5 gates B/C + migration phases, §7 Q2/Q3).

**Scope**
- **Gate B run:** the golden 311 (golden-queries-v3) through the binary vs the Python production path, **both against the production corpus** (107,639 chunks; the reference is a same-day Python run on the same corpus, not the historical v3-corpus 189/0.3894). Run through the eval3.py harness shape adapted to call the binary, so per-question rank diffs are inspectable. Tolerances (design §5): hits@10 within ±2 questions, overall MRR within ±0.005, no category (exact-fact / paraphrase / dictated-garbled / cross-session) regressing > 0.01 MRR. Configuration identical both sides, with the Gate C (A/B-winning) vector backend as the default.
- **Cutover phases** (design §5, additive-first; each flip is Drew's per-surface call):
  1. CLI opt-in: binary installed as `atlas-search` from its own profile position; the Python wrapper renamed — not removed — to `atlas-search-py`.
  2. Service opt-in: unit enabled on amd; the §3 v1 client tokens issued (with Drew; Q2 decides caps above `personal`); `--via-service` live from laptop + sandbox CLIs; standalone remains default.
  3. Default flip per surface (laptop first, sandbox after a soak; Q3 recommends the sandbox default to via-service at this phase).
- Rollback at every phase is repointing the name/flag — there is no data migration anywhere in this program. The Python remains installed as fallback and **permanent eval reference** after cutover.

**Dependencies:** step 5; Gate A green (step 1); the A/B verdict (Gate C). Drew's answers to design Q2/Q3 gate phases 2–3 details, not the Gate B run.

**Verification gate (exit criteria)**
- Gate B results recorded on this issue with the paired per-category table; a tolerance miss stops the cutover (the binary does not flip defaults on a failed gate — the miss gets its own issue and this step stays open).
- After each flip: the deployed `atlas-search --version`-equivalent and one golden spot query verified on that surface, and the Python fallback demonstrated still working.
- Epic #5350 closes when phase 3 has run on both surfaces or Drew rules a surface stays on the Python.

**Out of scope:** decommissioning the Python (explicitly never — it is the eval reference), new clients beyond §3 v1, publish-pipeline changes.


## Acceptance criteria
- Gate B run completed: golden-311 through the binary vs a same-day Python reference run, both against the production corpus, via the eval3.py-shaped harness; per-category paired table recorded on this issue.
- Tolerances met (design §5): hits@10 within ±2 questions, overall MRR within ±0.005, no category regressing >0.01 MRR — a miss stops the cutover and spawns its own issue.
- Cutover phases (CLI opt-in → service opt-in → per-surface default flip, laptop first) each land only on Drew's per-surface call, with the deployed binary version + a golden spot query verified per surface and the Python fallback demonstrated working.
- Epic #5350 closes when phase 3 has run on both surfaces or Drew rules a surface stays on the Python.

Step 5 of the Atlas binary+service epic (#5350). Design of record: `doc/2026-11-04T08-07-13Z_design_atlas_binary_service/` (§4 packaging/deploy, §7 Q1).

**Scope**
- `pkgs/atlas-search/default.nix`: `rustPlatform.buildRustPackage` with `cargoLock.lockFile`, pkgs/id pattern. Two hard requirements carried from the fork's native-embeddings work (opencode#1554/#1559) — do not rediscover them:
  1. ONNX Runtime is **dynamically loaded from the nix closure** (the `ort` crate must not download a prebuilt runtime at build or run time).
  2. The closure must carry **`libstdc++.so.6` and `libz.so.1`** — verified by closure inspection + a smoke run, not assumed.
- Post-install smoke check in the derivation: start the binary, run one FTS-only and one embedded query against a fixture DB.
- Model provisioning: `atlas-search fetch-model` downloads the pinned HuggingFace revision of `snowflake-arctic-embed-m-v2.0` into `~/.local/state/atlas-search/model/<rev>/`, verifying sha256 hashes recorded as constants in the repo; atomic rename into place; rerun is a no-op when the pinned set verifies. (Design §7 Q1 recommends state-dir over a nix-store FOD; if Drew flips Q1 before this step starts, implement the FOD instead and note it here — the rest of the design is unaffected.)
- Deploy on amd: systemd **user service** declared in home-manager (`atlas-search.service`, `ExecStart` = `serve`, `Restart=on-failure`), landed **disabled**. `tailscale serve` exposure on the MagicDNS name in front of 127.0.0.1. Proposed port 18760 — **verify against the fleet port inventory** (`check-proxy-port-fallbacks.sh`, `home/common/default.nix`) and take the next free 187xx if taken; record the final port on this issue.
- State dir `~/.local/state/atlas-search/` holds `service.json` (0600), `model/`, logs. The deploy provisions structure, **not** real client tokens (token generation is step 6, with Drew).

**Dependencies:** step 3 (CLI), step 4 (serve).

**Verification gate (exit criteria)**
- `nix build` of the package green on the laptop (never the sandbox); the smoke check runs inside the build.
- A laptop switch is **not** required to close this step: the package + disabled unit land on main; activation is step 6. If a switch is ridden anyway, the unit must come up disabled and the Python must remain the resolved `atlas-search`.

**Out of scope:** enabling the service, issuing tokens, any default flip (all step 6).


## Acceptance criteria
- `pkgs/atlas-search` builds green via `rustPlatform.buildRustPackage` on the laptop (never the sandbox), with the in-derivation smoke check (FTS-only + embedded query against a fixture DB) passing.
- ONNX Runtime is dynamically loaded from the nix closure (no prebuilt download at build or run time); closure inspection verifies `libstdc++.so.6` and `libz.so.1` are present, plus a smoke run proves it.
- `atlas-search fetch-model` provisions the pinned HuggingFace revision of `snowflake-arctic-embed-m-v2.0` into `~/.local/state/atlas-search/model/<rev>/` with sha256 verification and atomic rename; a rerun is a no-op.
- The home-manager `atlas-search.service` user unit lands on main DISABLED; tailscale serve exposure is declared in front of 127.0.0.1 on the verified-free 187xx port (proposed 18760), and the final port is recorded on this issue.
- No real client tokens are provisioned (step 6); the Python remains the resolved `atlas-search` after this step.

body:
Step 4 of the Atlas binary+service epic (#5350). Design of record: `doc/2026-11-04T08-07-13Z_design_atlas_binary_service/` (§2 protocol, §3 clients/auth, §6 non-goals).

**Scope**
- `atlas-proto` crate: the job protocol's request/response types, shared by the server and the CLI's via-service client so they cannot drift.
- `serve` subcommand: HTTP+JSON on 127.0.0.1 — `POST /v1/search` (one-shot), `POST /v1/search/jobs` (202 + job_id + per-job capability token), `GET /v1/search/jobs/{id}` (status), `GET /v1/search/jobs/{id}/results?cursor=&limit=` (pages of the **immutable** fused ranking), `DELETE /v1/search/jobs/{id}`, `GET /v1/search/jobs/{id}/chunk/{chunk_id}` (ceiling-checked), `GET /health` (no auth, no data).
- Worker pool: FTS and vector branches of a job execute concurrently; fusion runs once over complete branch pools; fetch-to-fill escalation happens inside the vector branch only.
- Temp store: **in-memory**, sharded by job_id, TTL 10 min from completion / 60 min hard cap from submit, sweeper-enforced. Nothing persists across restart; in-flight jobs fail `expired` on restart and clients resubmit. (Rationale — reproducible + snippet-bearing + perishable — is design §2; do not re-litigate it into a database without an epic-level decision.)
- Auth + ceiling enforcement: bearer tokens from `~/.local/state/atlas-search/service.json` (0600), per-client `ceiling_cap`; effective ceiling = min(requested, cap), recorded on the job and reported in the envelope; the `init` verb generates the client table (Drew's CLI + the §3 v1 rows). A `get-chunk` outside the job ceiling returns the missing-chunk shape.
- Backpressure (design §2, config-tunable): ≤4 concurrent branch executions globally, ≤2 concurrent + 8 queued jobs per client, pool ≤400 at submit, index-fill escalation ≤3200, saturation → 429 + `Retry-After` + queue depth; queued-too-long jobs fail `expired` (120 s).

**Dependencies:** step 2 (core); step 1 via step 3's embedder wiring. Serves the Turso backend only in v1 (local backend stays CLI-side).

**Verification gate (exit criteria)**
- Protocol conformance tests: submit→page a full ranking and confirm page-concatenation == the one-shot result == the standalone CLI's result for the same query/config.
- Ceiling tests: a `personal`-capped token cannot obtain local-only content via search, paging, another job's token, or get-chunk — each attempted path demonstrated closed.
- Restart test: in-flight jobs fail `expired`, no result data survives on disk anywhere under the state dir.
- Saturation test: the 5th concurrent branch execution queues/429s per the configured behavior.

**Out of scope:** packaging/deploy (step 5), issuing real client tokens for other machines (step 6 cutover), Aster (not a v1 client — design §3/§6).


## Acceptance criteria
- `atlas-proto` crate defines the job protocol types shared by server and CLI via-service client; `serve` exposes the full §2 surface (one-shot search, job submit/status/results paging, chunk fetch, delete, unauthenticated `/health`) on 127.0.0.1.
- Protocol conformance: page-concatenation of a job's results == the one-shot result == the standalone CLI result for the same query/config.
- Ceiling enforcement proven by tests: a `personal`-capped token cannot obtain local-only content via search, paging, another job's token, or get-chunk.
- Temp store is in-memory only: restart fails in-flight jobs as `expired` and no result data survives on disk under the state dir; TTLs (10 min post-completion / 60 min hard cap) are sweeper-enforced.
- Backpressure behaves per design §2: the 5th concurrent branch execution queues/429s with `Retry-After` + queue depth.

**Scope**
- The `atlas-search` binary's one-shot mode at full Python surface parity: `search` and `get-chunk` subcommands, the Python's flags (`--model` / `--vec-table` / `--embedder`-equivalents where they still make sense, `--trunc`, `--max-sensitivity`, filters, `--pool`, `--vector-backend`, `--backend turso|local`, `--text`), JSON envelope output identical in shape to the Python's, and the human-readable `--text` rendering.
- Standalone operation is the default and must be complete: embed the query in-process (step 1), talk to Turso or a local publish file directly (step 2). No daemon required, ever.
- Token resolution for Turso identical to the Python's order: env, Bitwarden by name (`turso.atlas-ro-token` / `turso.atlas-read-only-token` / `atlas-ro`), `turso` CLI read-only mint with the 20 h cache.
- `--via-service` / `ATLAS_SEARCH_VIA=service`: route through a running service (step 4) using `atlas-proto`; contract is *prefer service, fall back to standalone loudly* (a note in the envelope's `notes`), never a silent hang or failure. Until step 4 lands, via-service against no service exercises exactly that fallback path.
- Degradation parity: with no model present, FTS-only search and `get-chunk` work; vector/hybrid fail loudly (design §4).

**Dependencies:** step 1 (embedder), step 2 (core).

**Verification gate (exit criteria)**
- A flag-for-flag comparison run: a fixed battery of representative queries (filtered, ceiling-raised, FTS-only, get-chunk with neighbors, local-backend against a publish copy) produces envelopes matching the Python's (same results, same order, same `rank_sources`; scores within float formatting).
- Cold one-shot latency measured and recorded on this issue vs the Python's ~35 s baseline (the embedder load is the expected win; report the real number either way).

**Out of scope:** serve mode (step 4), packaging/deploy (step 5), any default flip (step 6).

**Scope**

- Query embedding is consumed through a trait so fixture vectors stand in during this step (the real embedder is step 1).

**Dependencies:** none hard (fixture vectors stand in for step 1). The **default** `VectorBackend` is decided by the golden-311 A/B running on the Python (design Gate C): start with `Scan` (the incumbent); if the A/B verdict lands during this step, set the default to the winner — a one-line change, recorded on this issue.

**Verification gate (exit criteria)**

body:
## Design: laptop-agent — resident execution agent on the laptop (fleet infra)

Directed by Drew 2026-11-04. Full design: `files/laptop-agent-design-2026-11-04.md` in the repo-health goal workspace (Muse-side); substance summarized here.

### Problem

Sandbox load ~11 on 4 cores. The SSH CONNECT relay measures 0% CPU — the cost is **process-spawn volume** (a fresh bash→ssh→helper→remote-shell tree per fleet action, ×26 code lanes, dozens of calls per shift) and **session fragility** (long laptop test runs strand when a session/claim lease ends mid-run — Lane H, 2026-11-04, task 9108; files move by tar-pipe because heredocs through the SSH helper mangle quoting). A Rust rewrite of the CONNECT relay was evaluated and rejected: it is a byte pipe after a ~30 ms handshake.

### Verified fact the design rests on

The sandbox reaches the laptop via the VM's tailnet tunnel proxy (HTTP CONNECT). On 2026-11-04 it was proven live that the proxy CONNECTs to **arbitrary ports** on the laptop's tailnet IP (100.99.113.103), not just :22 — a throwaway HTTP server on the laptop served a full response to a raw CONNECT client on the sandbox. So a laptop daemon is reachable with **no SSH in the data path**.

### Proposal

- **Daemon** (laptop, host `amd`): single-file Python-stdlib HTTP service, systemd user unit, binds only 100.99.113.103:4799, token auth (`X-Agent-Token`, mode-600 token files both ends, never in argv/git). API:
  - `GET /health`
  - `POST /exec` — a **batch** of commands in one request, per-command exit/stdout/stderr/duration, bounded timeout + output caps
  - `POST /jobs` / `GET /jobs/<id>` (byte-offset polling) / `POST /jobs/<id>/kill` / `GET /jobs` — detached jobs that survive client/SSH death; output spooled to disk, reaped after 24 h
- **Client** (sandbox): `~/tools/laptop-agent.py` — performs the CONNECT handshake (credential from `HTTPS_PROXY`, inside the request only), subcommands `health|exec|run|poll|kill|jobs`.
- `laptop-ssh.sh` stays for interactive/sudo use; the daemon is additive. Fleet rules unchanged (no sandbox worktrees; builds on laptop/CI).

### Phases

1. **MVP** — daemon + client + user service; verified end-to-end vs the ssh baseline. (Built 2026-11-04 alongside this filing.)
2. **Migrate hot call sites** — creator/lane laptop probes and test runs move to `run`/`poll`; measure lane shift wall-time before/after.
3. **Durable form** — declare the service in the laptop's NixOS config (dezren39/nix) so a rebuild can't drop it.

### Risks

Daemon = RCE for token/proxy-credential holders; mitigations are the tailnet-only bind, token auth, and secrets kept out of argv and git. A wedged daemon blocks migrated call sites; ssh remains the fallback and the unit restarts on failure.

## Acceptance criteria
- MVP daemon + client are verified end-to-end against the SSH baseline (health, exec batch, detached jobs with byte-offset polling).
- The daemon binds only the laptop tailnet address, requires token auth, and the token never appears in argv, git, or logs.
- Phase 2 migration of hot call sites (creator/lane laptop probes and test runs) is done with lane shift wall-time measured before and after.
- Phase 3 durable form is declared in the laptop's NixOS config (dezren39/nix), or an exception is recorded on this issue.
- Each phase is tracked by a linked implementation issue or native sub-issue — a design with no implementation link is not finished work.

title: id(web): /api/upload trusts the declared multipart Content-Type — uploaded bytes are never checked against the image type they are stored and served as

body:
## Problem

`POST /api/upload` in pkgs/id's web server validates an uploaded image only by the **multipart field's declared `Content-Type`** — the bytes are never inspected. Any bytes at all are accepted, stored, and served as a genuine image of the declared type, as long as the client claims an allowed type.

## Evidence (at origin/main 8bb1e43bf)

- `pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs:1770-1780` (`upload_handler`): the only type check is `field.content_type()` (the client-supplied multipart header) against `ALLOWED_IMAGE_TYPES`. The handler then reads the bytes (`field.bytes()`), checks only size and non-emptiness, and stores them.
- No magic-byte/format sniffing exists anywhere in `pkgs/id/src` (no PNG/JPEG/GIF/WebP signature check).
- The surrounding code documents the opposite premise: `reconcile_upload_filename` (routes.rs:711-715) says a name is reconciled with "the type the upload was validated as" so it cannot "masquerade as a different type than the bytes were checked as" — but the bytes are never checked; only the claim is. The existing tests encode the gap: `blob_png_is_served_inline_with_protective_headers` uploads the literal bytes `b"png-bytes"` as `image/png` and expects success.
- Verified by a laptop cargo probe test in the routes test harness (scan worktree at 8bb1e43bf, probe test since removed): HTML/script bytes (`<html><script>alert(1)</script></html>`) uploaded with declared type `image/png` and filename `evil.png` returned **200 OK**, were stored, and were served back from `/blob/<hash>?filename=evil.png` with `Content-Type: image/png`; plain-text bytes declared `image/jpeg` were likewise accepted with 200.

## Why it matters

- The stored blob's filename extension, its stored content-type metadata tag, and the type it is served with all assert a format the content may not have. Every downstream consumer that trusts that metadata (the editor's image rendering, the file listing, any future thumbnail/transcode step) inherits the lie.
- The #908 serving mitigations (allowlisted inline types, `nosniff`, sandboxing CSP) limit the XSS blast radius of a mislabeled blob, but they were designed on the premise that an `image/*` blob is actually an image. A declared-`image/svg+xml` upload, for example, need not be XML at all.
- It is also a correctness bug independent of security: a corrupt or mislabeled "image" is accepted silently and only fails later, in the renderer, with no connection to the upload that caused it.

## Acceptance criteria

- `upload_handler` verifies the bytes against the declared type before storing: magic signatures for PNG (`89 50 4E 47…`), JPEG (`FF D8 FF`), GIF (`GIF87a`/`GIF89a`), WebP (`RIFF…WEBP`), BMP (`BM`), ICO (`00 00 01 00`), and for `image/svg+xml` a check that the content (after optional BOM/whitespace/XML prolog) is an `<svg` document.
- A mismatch returns `400` with a clear message naming the declared type and the detected mismatch; nothing is stored or tagged.
- Existing upload tests are updated to use real minimal valid headers for each type instead of placeholder bytes (`b"png-bytes"`), and new tests cover: HTML-as-PNG refused, text-as-JPEG refused, a valid-header upload of each allowed type accepted, SVG with prolog accepted, non-SVG-as-SVG refused.
- Client behavior is unchanged for genuine images (the web client's `ALLOWED_IMAGE_TYPES`/`MAX_IMAGE_SIZE` in `web/src/image-upload.ts` stay in sync with the server constants).

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-b after verification this run; not a duplicate of #908 (serving-side headers, closed), #1549/#2363 (name collisions, closed), or #716 (body limit, closed) — no open issue covers byte-level validation of uploads.

## Finding (from PR review)

Codex (chatgpt-codex-connector[bot]) raised this P2 finding on merged PR #5166 and it was never fixed or replied to:

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/5166 — "fleet: unified schedule registry — Muse cron + OpenCode + Jules (#4988)"
- Comment: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/5166#discussion_r4460792846 (2026-11-03T21:43:42Z, on `doc/fleet-schedule-registry.md:199`)
- Essence: "Record execution routes separately from work queues. The repo-health queue identifies the work scope, not the execution route or quota pool, so it cannot supply the route/pool field required by the Fields section. This information is available for at least the claimant: `pm-stack/opencode-claimant/install.mjs:21-26,75-84` sets its execution route to `opencode-route` / `workhorse`, but neither its registry row nor this explanation records that route. Omitting execution routes prevents the intended placement/shared-pool audit from identifying which routes recurring model jobs consume. Add the actual execution route/pool to the records, retain queue names as scope, and explicitly mark unavailable routes as `not recorded`."

## No-response evidence

- The inline thread contains only the Codex comment; no reply followed it (reviewThreads check 2026-11-04: thread unresolved, sole author chatgpt-codex-connector).
- PR #5166 merged at 2026-11-03T21:44:28Z, under a minute after the review was submitted — no fix commit could have followed the comment on the PR, and the conflation is present in the merged result on main.

## Still live on current main (verified 2026-11-04 by gh api raw read)

`doc/fleet-schedule-registry.md`:
- The Fields section requires, per schedule: "surface, name/id, repo/scope, cadence, route or pool, prompt/brief pointer, budget expectation, owner, kill criteria, date created, last review."
- Section 2a's preamble (line ~199) instead says: "Route/pool for queue-lane tasks is the repo-health queue named in the task name" — a queue name is work scope, not an execution route or quota pool.
- The claimant row (`f1b4a33b-14d5-4a69-9ad6-d221e42e3ac9`, "Opencode lane claimant/executor - #3026") has no route/pool recorded at all.
Meanwhile the route is recorded in source: `pm-stack/opencode-claimant/install.mjs:24-25` sets `PROVIDER_ID = "opencode-route"` and `MODEL_ID = "workhorse"`, and `buildTask` writes them into the task's execution block.

## Acceptance criteria

- The registry records the actual execution route/pool separately from the work queue (scope) for the schedules where it is known — at minimum the #3026 claimant (`opencode-route` / `workhorse`) — and explicitly marks routes that are genuinely unavailable as `not recorded` instead of substituting a queue name.
- The section 2a preamble no longer presents a repo-health queue name as a route/pool.
- Or: the finding is resolved on this issue by a documented decision, with the reasoning recorded.

Since this registry is explicitly an input to the placement audit, these entries misrepresent execution frequency and workload. Preserve the complete calendar expressions when collecting the timer specs."

## No-response evidence

`doc/fleet-schedule-registry.md`, section 2b (laptop systemd user timers):

body:
# opencode-route-proxy: known-100% seating gate — exclude legs whose binding quota window is known exhausted until reset (#4370 acceptance (c))

Implementation slice scoped by triage task 8950 (lane W, 2026-11-04) extending #3325 leg-shedding to the #4370 death classes. Findings and full evidence are on #3325 (task 8950 comment) and #4370.

## Problem (verified at main, blob 70f01618, bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs, 1095 lines)

- Seating has no known-100% gate. `demotedPairs` (lines ~330–345) learns only from the attempt ledger (≥3 quota failures in 4 h), and `applyDemotion` (lines ~662–670) reorders demoted pairs to the back — it never excludes them.
- A leg whose binding window is already known to be at 100% with a future reset (cline-pass monthly, #4370: 11 sessions killed 2026-11-01) is a normal first-choice candidate until it has failed three times.

## Scope

- Seating-time gate in `bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs`: a (provider, model) pair whose binding quota window is known exhausted (ledger quota detail carrying a future reset, or an equivalent known-100% record the proxy already stores) is EXCLUDED from candidates until that reset — the credential-less exclusion pattern (#3228).
- Fail-safe: if exclusion would empty the route, keep current demoted order rather than hard-failing; record the gate decision in existing diagnostics.
- Tests with the pinned-now clock (`OPENCODE_ROUTE_PROXY_NOW_MS`): known-100% pair excluded while a live pair exists; pair returns after reset; all-exhausted route still walks in demoted order.

Out of scope: external quota-service reads at request time, demotion threshold changes, transport timeouts (companion slice), in-stream shedding (task 8932).

## Acceptance criteria

# pm-stack(aggregator): isAaSection accepts impossible/non-ISO testRuns snapshotDate — summarizeAa reports a fabricated snapshot vintage on /aa

## Summary

The AA section gate checks a test run's `snapshotDate` only as string-or-null, never as a real calendar date. A gate-passing section whose test runs carry `2026-02-30` or `not-a-date` produces a snapshot-vintage range built from those strings, and the /aa provenance card presents it as the batch's real Test_Runs snapshot range.

## Evidence (verified this run, origin/main @ ef55926de)

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/aa.ts:1170-1171` — `isAaSection`'s testRuns element check is `(typeof snapshotDate === "string" || snapshotDate === null)`. The same gate validates `generatedAt` with `isIsoDate` (aa.ts:1158 and the absent-form check), so the date rule exists in this function and this one field skips it.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/aa.ts:1206-1213` — `summarizeAa` collects the string snapshotDates, sorts them lexicographically, and reports `{ min, max }` as `snapshotVintage`.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/render.ts` (renderAa provenance card) — renders `Test_Runs snapshots in this batch: ${summary.snapshotVintage.min} – ${summary.snapshotVintage.max}` verbatim.
- Laptop bun probe (scan worktree at ef55926de, `probe-aa.ts`, run this run): a complete minimal valid section passes the gate (control); the same section with testRuns snapshotDates `"not-a-date"` and `"2026-02-30"` also passes (`isAaSection` = true) and `summarizeAa(...).snapshotVintage` = `{"min":"2026-02-30","max":"not-a-date"}`.
- `isIsoDate` (src/validate.ts:116) accepts the date-only form real snapshot dates use (`"2026-09-28"`, see fixtures in src/sources/fixtures.ts) while rejecting both probe strings, so gating on it does not break legitimate producer output (aa.ts:112 builds the field from the import's `snapshot_date` column via `str()` — arbitrary upstream text).

## Why it matters

The vintage range is the /aa page's provenance claim about which AA snapshot batch the figures came from. An impossible or garbage date in one upstream row silently falsifies that claim for the whole batch — the aggregator-wide rule (#2199/#3513/#5172 family) is that a date field a consumer treats as a date is gated as a real ISO calendar date at the boundary, not merely typed as a string. This is distinct from #4169 (dereference depth: gate-passing sections throwing in renderAa) and from #2415, which added the string-or-null check itself: neither covers the value validity of this field, and this section does not throw — it renders wrong data.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `isAaSection` requires a testRuns `snapshotDate` to be `null` or `isIsoDate(...)` (date-only forms included), so a section carrying an impossible/non-ISO snapshot date reads as absent/degraded at the live-source gate (src/sources/live.ts) instead of serving a fabricated vintage.
- [ ] Gate tests in the style of test/aa-gate-2415.test.ts: `2026-02-30`, `2026-04-31`, and `not-a-date` snapshotDates fail the gate; `2026-09-28` and `null` pass; collector-built sections (aaSectionFromRaw output) still pass unchanged.
- [ ] Existing aggregator tests still pass.

# pm-stack(aggregator): #4942 fix never landed — PR #5256 closed unmerged, applyCloudflareExport still accepts negative used on main

## Summary

Issue #4942 (applyCloudflareExport accepts negative `used`) is CLOSED, but the bug is still live on `main`. Its fix was written and then lost: the implementing PR was closed without merging, and no equivalent change ever reached `main`.

## Evidence (verified this run, 2026-11-03, at origin/main 85c0e0b89)

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/saas-extract.ts` — in `applyCloudflareExport`, the metrics filter is still finite-only:
  `.filter((m) => m && typeof m.id === "string" && typeof m.used === "number" && Number.isFinite(m.used))`
  The sibling `applySupabaseExport` in the same file drops `used < 0` / `limit < 0` metrics.
- Laptop bun probe at origin/main 85c0e0b89 (probe test mirroring `test/cloudflare-export.test.ts`'s freshDoc): a fresh Cloudflare export doc with `workers-requests used: -500` overlays as-is — stored `used = -500`, derived `percent = -0`, note stamped `Live via cloudflare-graphql-analytics`, card `sourceClass = "api"`. Control metric `kv-reads used: 1420` overlays normally.
- The fix exists but is stranded: commit `59c03cad6` ("fix(pm-stack/aggregator): drop negative Cloudflare export metrics", `Closes #4942`) is present only on branch `queue/8048-4942-cf-negative-used`; `git merge-base --is-ancestor 59c03cad6 origin/main` fails — it is NOT in main.
- PR #5256 from that branch is CLOSED with `mergedAt: null` (never merged), yet issue #4942 was closed at 2026-11-03T22:57Z. `test/cloudflare-export.test.ts` on main has no negative-used regression test.

## Why it matters

A broken/negative Cloudflare export measurement is stamped onto the live card as measured API data with a negative percent, instead of keeping the metric's prose/null fallback — the exact harm #4942 described. The closure of #4942 also makes the fleet believe this is handled, so nobody re-checks it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Land the negative-metric guard in `applyCloudflareExport` (the stranded commit `59c03cad6` on `queue/8048-4942-cf-negative-used` can be cherry-picked, or the one-filter change re-implemented): metrics with `used < 0` are dropped from the overlay, matching `applySupabaseExport`.
- [ ] The regression test from that commit (negative `workers-requests` keeps its fallback while a valid metric in the same doc still overlays) is present in `test/cloudflare-export.test.ts` and passes.
- [ ] Re-run the probe above against the fixed tree: `workers-requests` keeps its prose/null used value and no `Live via` note; `kv-reads` still overlays.
- [ ] Cross-link #4942 and PR #5256 in the fixing PR so the lost-fix path is traceable.

body:
## Problem

`isSaasService` in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/feed.ts:697` (the element gate behind `sanitizeSaasServices`, applied at the `loadFeed` boundary) accepts any string as a SaaS service's `measuredAt`:

```ts
(typeof v.measuredAt === "string" || v.measuredAt === null) &&
```

That is weaker than every sibling `measuredAt` gate in the same file:

- `isQuotaFreshness` — `feed.ts:548`: `isIsoDate(v.measuredAt)`
- `isPaygLine` — `feed.ts:969`: `(v.measuredAt === null || isIsoDate(v.measuredAt))`

`isIsoDate` (`validate.ts:116`) requires a real ISO calendar date. The SaaS gate does not, so impossible and non-ISO stamps survive sanitization verbatim.

## Verified (laptop bun probe at origin/main 12fcad972, probe in `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-03-laneA4-scan`, removed after the run)

A minimal otherwise-valid service was passed through `sanitizeSaasServices`, then `recordsFromSaasServices` + `isSnapshotRecord`:

| measuredAt | kept by sanitizeSaasServices | derived record ts | isSnapshotRecord |
|---|---|---|---|
| `2026-02-30` | yes (dropped=0) | `2026-02-30T12:00:00Z` | **false** |
| `2026-04-31` | yes (dropped=0) | `2026-04-31T12:00:00Z` | **false** |
| `March 2, 2026` | yes (dropped=0) | `March 2, 2026` | **false** |
| `not-a-date` | yes (dropped=0) | `not-a-dateT12:00:00Z` | **false** |
| `2026-03-01` (control) | yes | `2026-03-01T12:00:00Z` | true |

## Why it matters

- `recordsFromSaasServices` (`snapshot-records.ts:85`, via `tsFor` at `:32`) derives one snapshot record per measured metric at the service's `measuredAt`. With a bad stamp every derived record fails `isSnapshotRecord`, so the service's snapshot history is silently dropped at append — the same failure shape as #5140, through a different gate.
- `conflicts.ts:133-134` feeds `svc.measuredAt` to `ageDaysFrom`, which uses raw `Date.parse`: `2026-02-30` rolls to Mar 2 and reports a concrete conflict age instead of `null` (unknown).
- `render.ts` `freshnessStamp` prints `measuredAt.slice(0, 10)` verbatim, so `2026-02-30` / `March 2, 2` render as the measured date on the service card (freshness itself is strict since #5102, so the stamp also reads stale with a nonsense date attached).

Distinct from: #5188 (same sanitizer — PAYG/metric range gates, now fixed; it left `measuredAt` type-only), #5018 (the saas-extract export-overlay documents, a different input path), and #5102 (`freshness()` consumer).

## Acceptance criteria

- `isSaasService` requires `measuredAt` to be `null` or `isIsoDate(...)`, matching `isPaygLine` in the same file; a service with an impossible or non-ISO `measuredAt` is dropped by `sanitizeSaasServices` and counted in `dropped`.
- Regression tests cover at least `2026-02-30`, `2026-04-31`, and a non-ISO string (`March 2, 2026`) being dropped, with a valid ISO date and a `null` stamp kept as controls.
- Aggregator test suite and typecheck stay green.

## aggregator(forecast): resampling estimator for epic ETA (design §1) — zero-median bursty buckets return no_measurable_pace

Found by Codex review round 4 on PR #5236 (finding comment 4463375210), dispositioned there as a follow-up because it is an estimator redesign, not a defect fix in that PR's scope.

**Problem.** `deriveEpicEta` in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/forecast.ts` derives P50/P80 from the median / lower-quartile weekly pace. When the four complete primary weeks are `[0, 0, 0, 4]` closures and work remains, the local evidence floor passes (4 completions, 4 weeks) but the median weekly bucket is zero, so the result is `no_measurable_pace` with no dates despite positive measured throughput. Batch-delivery scopes (sufficient evidence, bursty weeks) get no forecast.

**Contract.** The forecasting design (`doc/2026-11-01T21-07-00Z_design_pm-stack_forecasting/2026-11-01T21-07-00Z_design_pm-stack_forecasting.md` §1, line 36) specifies: "Estimator: resample complete weekly completion buckets (including observed zero weeks) to estimate a distribution for remaining units / weekly throughput. Publish P50 and a conservative P80 completion range… If no weekly pace is measured, emit 'no measurable pace'". The current median/lower-quartile implementation is a simplification that does not implement the resampling estimator.

**Acceptance criteria.**
- Deterministic (seeded) resampling over the complete weekly completion buckets, zero weeks included, estimating the distribution of weeks-to-complete for the remaining units; P50 and conservative P80 derived from that distribution.
- `[0, 0, 0, 4]` with remaining work returns a forecast with finite P50 <= P80 instead of `no_measurable_pace`.
- A truly zero total pace (all buckets zero) still returns `no_measurable_pace` with no dates.
- Pinned tests updated with rationale where behavior changes (notably "zero lower-quartile pace: P50 present, P80 explicitly unmeasurable" in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/forecast-3982.test.ts`); new tests cover the bursty case and determinism (same input → same output).
- Decide and record whether the estimator change bumps `FORECAST_MODEL_VERSION` (`forecast/v1`).
- Full aggregator suite green (`bun test` in `pm-stack/aggregator`).

body:
# mcpx(daemon): full-package test run is killed by SIGTERM — an in-process server's delayed self-signal terminates the test binary

## Observed (verified this run, laptop, origin/main 1ed5d038b)

`go test ./internal/daemon/` in `pkgs/mcpx` fails reproducibly with the test
binary itself dying of SIGTERM:

- Full suite `go test ./...`: `FAIL internal/daemon 38.699s` — output is just
  `signal: terminated`, no failing test named.
- Standalone `go test -count=1 ./internal/daemon/`: same result at 16.6s,
  31.5s, 36.0s and 68.3s across four runs (the variance is the tell: the
  signal lands on whatever test happens to be running).
- A clean isolated re-run (no other mcpx test suite active on the machine)
  still fails the same way at 36.0s.
- Individual tests pass alone, e.g. `go test -run TestAHiddenToolCannotBeCalled
  ./internal/daemon/` → PASS in 0.41s (in the `-v` full-package run that same
  test was the one running when the binary died).

The other red packages in the same full-suite run are already tracked
(internal/settings #5242/#2716, internal/conformance #2716,
internal/defaults #5211); this daemon failure is not covered by any open
issue (searched: "daemon terminated", "signal terminated", "mcpx daemon
test").

## Likely mechanism (leads, not proven)

`internal/daemon/server.go:1518` `handleShutdown` — and the restart handler
at `:1530` — schedule a delayed self-signal in a goroutine:

```go
go func() {
    time.Sleep(defaults.DaemonRestartSettle)
    p, _ := os.FindProcess(os.Getpid())
    _ = p.Signal(syscall.SIGTERM)
}()
```

In production the server *is* the daemon process, so this is its graceful
exit. In tests the server runs in-process inside the test binary: any test
that drives a shutdown/restart request (or leaves one of these goroutines
pending past its own end) SIGTERMs the entire test process
`DaemonRestartSettle` later, mid-way through an unrelated test. Tests in
this package also register `os.Getpid()` as a fake daemon PID
(`paths_test.go:333,406,428`; `takeover_test.go:224`), so stop/takeover
paths that signal PIDs read from info records are a second suspect route
to the same outcome.

## Why it matters

- The daemon package's tests cannot be trusted as a gate: the package is
  red on main for a reason unrelated to any assertion, and the failure
  report names no test, so real regressions hide inside it.
- The same in-process self-signal pattern is a hazard for any embedder
  that runs the daemon server inside a longer-lived process.

## Acceptance criteria

- `go test -count=1 ./internal/daemon/` passes repeatedly (say 5
  consecutive runs) on a machine with no other mcpx suite running, and
  also when run as part of `go test ./...`.
- The shutdown/restart self-signal is suppressed or redirected when the
  server runs in-process for tests (e.g. an injectable exit hook, like
  the existing `execSelf` seam at server.go:1527), without changing the
  production daemon's exit behaviour.
- A regression test proves that handling a shutdown request in-process
  does not deliver SIGTERM to the host process.

`nixos/home/dashboard-backup.nix` still declares, in `systemd.user.services.dashboard-backup.Service`:

```nix
Path = servicePath;
```

labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Summary

The `group.op` membership body codec in id-core (`pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/membership/body.rs`, the CBOR codec whose `decode_body` is the ingest gate for group operations at `pkgs/id/src/event_store/ingest.rs:436`) accepts a `create` action that lists the **same member twice** — including with conflicting access levels such as `Read` then `Manage`. `decode_kind`'s create arm (body.rs:225-244) checks only the member count (≤ `MAX_CREATE_MEMBERS`, 256) and decodes each pair independently; it never compares members against each other. `encode_body`'s create arm (body.rs:98-112) has the same gap, so the codec both produces and accepts a shape whose meaning depends on the reader.

This is a distinct codec from `pkgs/id/src/groups/event.rs`, whose duplicate-create-member gap was filed separately as #5217 — that issue covers the JSON `group.event` codec only, not this CBOR `group.op` codec.

## Evidence (verified on `origin/main` @ 1a8e6e7a2, this run)

- `pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/membership/body.rs:225-244` — the `create` arm of `decode_kind` enforces `pairs.len() > MAX_CREATE_MEMBERS` and decodes `[member, access]` pairs; no uniqueness check on the decoded `GroupMember`s. Encode side (body.rs:98-112) checks the same count only.
- The codec is otherwise strict about member identity: `decode_member` (body.rs:274-293) refuses a member whose outer kind and identity tag disagree (fixed as #3358), and `decode_body` demands canonical CBOR that re-encodes byte-identically (body.rs:138-160). Duplicate members are the remaining identity hole.
- Downstream, the two group models disagree about the shape: the event-store bridge (`pkgs/id/src/event_store/resolve.rs:295-330`) copies every `initial_members` entry into a `GroupCreate`, and the group fold refuses a repeated member outright — `pkgs/id/src/groups/fold.rs:81-82` `Refusal::BadMembers`, "The members list repeats an account, or names the author" (raised at fold.rs:1587). So a create the membership codec blesses bridges into a form the fold can only refuse, while the membership layer itself collapses the duplicate by map order — which access level the member ends up with is reader-dependent.

Verified with a laptop probe at `origin/main` 1a8e6e7a2 (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-03-laneA2-membership/pkgs/id/crates/id-core/tests/probe_membership_dup.rs`, `cargo test -p id-core --test probe_membership_dup` — 1 passed):

- Control: create with two distinct members encodes and decodes unchanged.
- Create with the same individual (`Key([7;32])`) listed as `Read` then `Manage`: `encode_body` = Ok (97 bytes), `decode_body` = Ok with `initial_members` of length 2 carrying both conflicting levels.
- Create with the same member twice at identical `Read` access: encode Ok, decode Ok.

## Why it matters

`decode_body` is the trust boundary for group operations arriving in event bodies: ingest refuses whatever it refuses (`Refusal::Malformed`, ingest.rs:436) and stores whatever it accepts. A signed create body that names one member at two access levels has no single meaning — the membership layer, the resolve bridge, and the group fold each resolve the contradiction differently (map-order collapse vs. bridging both entries vs. `BadMembers` refusal), so two honest nodes can disagree about a group's founding membership. The sibling `group.event` codec is being tightened for the same shape (#5217), and this codec already refuses subtler identity contradictions (#3358); the duplicate check belongs at the same boundary, in both encode and decode, while the format is still version 1.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `decode_body` refuses a `create` whose `initial_members` list names the same `GroupMember` twice (regardless of access level) with a `BodyError::Shape` naming the duplication.
- [ ] `encode_body` refuses the same shape with `BodyError::Unencodable`, so local callers cannot produce a body peers will refuse.
- [ ] Tests in `membership/body.rs` cover both refusals (conflicting-level and identical duplicates, decode of hand-built CBOR plus encode) and the distinct-members control still round-trips.
- [ ] Existing id-core membership tests still pass (`cargo test -p id-core membership` on the laptop/CI).

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop, clean worktree at origin/main 1391b59e2)

The v2 plugin gained a new environment knob today, and the settings registry — the package whose whole point is that every knob is declared there — never heard about it:

- `pkgs/mcpx/plugin/opencode/v2/options.ts:135` — `disabledTools: nameList(o.disabledTools) ?? nameList(env.MCPX_PLUGIN_DISABLED_TOOLS)` (documented at options.ts:55; exercised by `plugin/opencode/v2/tool-filter.test.ts:247`).
- The read landed in commit d4f1c2416 ("mcpx v2 plugin: wire disabledTools option as the tool-filter policy writer (#5122)"), merged via PR #5170.
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/settings/plugin.go:18` — `pluginSettings()` declares plugin.bin, plugin.binArgs, plugin.backend, plugin.discoveryRetry, plugin.toolTiming, plugin.env, plugin.instructions, … but no `plugin.disabledTools` entry, so the derived env name `MCPX_PLUGIN_DISABLED_TOOLS` is declared nowhere (grep for the name across `internal/settings/*.go` hits only tests' prose).

Repro (standalone, deterministic):

```
$ cd pkgs/mcpx && go test ./internal/settings/ -run TestThePluginReadsNoUndeclaredSetting -count=1
--- FAIL: TestThePluginReadsNoUndeclaredSetting (0.01s)
    consumed_test.go:283: the plugin honours variables nothing declares:
          MCPX_PLUGIN_DISABLED_TOOLS (plugin/opencode/v2/options.ts:135)

        Add them to pluginSettings() so `mcpx settings` can report them.
```

## Why it matters

- `mcpx settings` cannot report a live plugin knob: a user asking what `MCPX_PLUGIN_DISABLED_TOOLS` does gets nothing, which is exactly the failure `plugin.go`'s header says the registry exists to prevent ("a knob is a knob regardless of which process reads it").
- It is a fresh regression from today's #5122 landing, not part of the pre-existing settings redness: the older guard failures are tracked separately in #2716 / #2697 / #2552 (filed 2026-10-30, acceptances scoped to the scriptenv/compendium/env-doc failures), and no open or closed issue mentions `MCPX_PLUGIN_DISABLED_TOOLS` (searched 2026-11-03). Keeping this one separate keeps the #5122 follow-up owned instead of dissolving it into the older umbrella.

## Fix shape (per the guard's own instructions)

Add a `plugin.disabledTools` entry to `pluginSettings()` in `pkgs/mcpx/internal/settings/plugin.go` (ScopePlugin; the name derivation from the path produces exactly `MCPX_PLUGIN_DISABLED_TOOLS` — do not hand-write an Env override). Watch the follow-on guards that enumerate plugin settings: the path→env map in `internal/settings/registry_test.go` (~:352), the effect-probe-or-exemption guard for the new setting, and any settings/Plugin README snapshots that list plugin settings.

## Acceptance criteria

- `go test ./internal/settings/ -run TestThePluginReadsNoUndeclaredSetting -count=1` passes on clean main.
- The settings registry reports `plugin.disabledTools` / `MCPX_PLUGIN_DISABLED_TOOLS` with plugin scope (e.g. via `mcpx settings`).
- No other `internal/settings` test regresses relative to the pre-existing red baseline tracked in #2716 / #2697 / #2552.

title: id(chat-presence): PresenceHeartbeat::verify uses plain verify — the #1386 small-order identity forgery passes the presence authentication gate

labels.name: kind/security
labels.description: Security issue or security hardening

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Summary

`pkgs/id` chat presence is the one signature-verification site in the crate that still uses plain Ed25519 `verify` instead of `verify_strict` — so the shared small-order identity forgery from #1386, which every sibling verifier refuses, is accepted as an authenticated presence heartbeat.

## Evidence (origin/main a51be0e22)

- `pkgs/id/src/chat_presence.rs:157-165` — `PresenceHeartbeat::verify()` ends with `verifying_key.verify(&self.signing_bytes(), &signature).is_ok()` (line 164). This is the production gate for gossip presence: `pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:2021` (`receive_presence_heartbeat`) drops a heartbeat only when `verify()` returns false.
- Every sibling verifier in the same crate uses `verify_strict`: `invites/event.rs:126`, `seitan/accept.rs:142`, `artifact.rs:321`, `peer_announcement.rs:79`, `directory_log.rs:100`, `directory.rs:383`, `web/identity.rs:523`, `world_session/mod.rs:846`, `hosted_binding.rs` (multiple).
- `pkgs/id/src/test_forgeries.rs:19-27` documents why: the identity point is a small-order public key, and the forgery (R = identity, S = 0) passes plain `verify` for **any** message under it; only `verify_strict` refuses it because the key is small-order. The helper's own test (`test_forgeries.rs:51`) pins `verify = Ok`, `verify_strict = Err` for exactly this pair.
- Verified this run on the laptop at a51be0e22 (probe worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-03-laneB3-presence`, sources kept): a test constructing a `PresenceHeartbeat` with `node = IDENTITY_KEY`, `signature = identity_forgery()`, one channel and a current timestamp prints `PROBE presence verify() on identity forgery = true` and passes its bug assertion on unpatched main (`cargo test --lib probe_identity_forgery_against_presence_verify`, 1 passed) — i.e. a heartbeat nobody signed passes the authentication gate.
- The existing presence auth test (`chat_presence.rs:717` `heartbeats_authenticate_by_signature`) covers unsigned/tampered heartbeats only — no #1386 forgery fixtures, unlike the regression tests #1386/#4676 added at the invites and seitan sites.

## Why it matters

Presence is scoped by group membership after the signature gate, which bounds the blast radius today — but the module's own contract (`chat_presence.rs` module doc, "Authentication") states the signature **is** the authentication for a heartbeat's claimed node, because the gossip plane does not authenticate authors. A verifier that accepts a known, fixture-grade forgery for a small-order claimed node breaks that contract and diverges from the crate-wide #1386 posture: any future caller that trusts `verify()` without the membership filter (the exact failure mode #4502's guarded-door design warns about) inherits a forgeable gate. The fix shape is already established at five sibling sites.

## Dedup / related

- #1386 (closed) and #4676 (closed) covered the invites and seitan call sites only; neither names chat_presence.
- #4502 (open, gossip-admission design) covers canonicalisation/bounds/scoping of presence and peers; it does not disposition signature strictness.
- Presence signature issues #4363/#4541 (scoping) and #4404/#3991/#4004 (bounds) are different defects.

## Acceptance criteria

- `PresenceHeartbeat::verify()` refuses the small-order identity forgery: a heartbeat with `node = IDENTITY_KEY` and `signature = identity_forgery()` (from `crate::test_forgeries`) returns `false` from `verify()` and is dropped by `receive_presence_heartbeat`.
- A regression test at the presence site mirrors the invites/seitan #1386 tests (identity forgery refused; a genuine signature still verifies — non-canonical-S disposition matching the sibling sites).
- No behaviour change for honestly signed heartbeats: the existing `chat_presence` test suite passes (`cargo test --lib chat_presence` in `pkgs/id` on the laptop or CI).

body:
Surfaced by the code#5195 investigation (2026-11-03, evidence on that issues closing comment). #5195s test proved fully bounded (all waits are clamped tokio sleeps / timeout-wrapped charges), so it cannot explain the 2026-11-03 fleet-switch hang: a workspace cargo test binary sat single-threaded at 0 CPU for 52 minutes inside a nix check phase and had to be killed by hand (the laptop nix config sets max-silent-time = 0 / timeout = 0, so nothing reaps a hung build).

## Lead
The id lib test binary carries live-iroh tests whose connects/receives have no outer timeout. An unbounded network await is the only identified mechanism in the id test surface consistent with an indefinite 0-CPU wait. This is a lead, not an attribution — the hang could not be attributed from outside the nix sandbox.

## Ask
Audit the id test suites (lib + integration) for unbounded awaits — iroh connects/receives and any other network or channel waits without deadlines — and bound every one with a loud timeout, so a wedged test fails in seconds with its name attached instead of hanging a build forever. If the audit finds the surface already bounded elsewhere, record that; the remaining value is the inventory.

## Related
code#5195 (the flake fix; closed), code#5216 (host-side clap stack overflow, separate).

## Acceptance criteria
- Every iroh connect/receive await — and any other network or channel wait without a deadline — in the pkgs/id lib and integration test suites is wrapped in a bounded timeout that fails the test loudly with its name attached.
- A deliberately wedged await demonstrates the bound: the test fails within its timeout instead of hanging (evidence recorded on the implementing PR).
- The full pkgs/id test suite passes in the nix check phase / CI with no test deleted or ignored to achieve the bound.

# pm-stack(aggregator): entryFromResult launders impossible/non-ISO credentialExpiresAt into a shifted valid ISO date

## Summary

`entryFromResult` in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-gather-map.ts` (string branch, ~line 328-330) accepts any string that `Date.parse` can handle and re-stamps it with `toISOString()`:

```ts
} else if (typeof expiry === "string" && Number.isFinite(Date.parse(expiry))) {
  entry.credentialExpiresAt = new Date(expiry).toISOString();
}
```

`Date.parse` normalizes impossible calendar dates and accepts non-ISO formats, so a provider-reported expiry that does not exist (or is not ISO) is silently rewritten to a *different, valid* date before it is stored.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop bun probe at origin/main c7e442a21)

Calling `entryFromResult({...base, credentialExpiresAt: exp}, tick)`:

| input | stored `credentialExpiresAt` |
|---|---|
| `"2026-02-30T00:00:00.000Z"` | `"2026-03-02T00:00:00.000Z"` (rolled over) |
| `"2026-04-31"` | `"2026-05-01T00:00:00.000Z"` (rolled over) |
| `"March 2, 2026"` | `"2026-03-02T06:00:00.000Z"` (non-ISO accepted) |
| `"not-a-date"` | dropped (correct) |
| `"2027-01-15T00:00:00.000Z"` | unchanged (control, correct) |

## Why it matters

The consumer gate for this exact field is strict: `parseQuotaCurrent` (`quota-current.ts:79-80`) requires `isIsoDate(value.credentialExpiresAt)`. But because the producer normalizes first, the gate can never reject the bad value — the corruption is laundered into a valid ISO string upstream. The stored expiry is a date the provider never reported, so credential-expiry warnings/rotation prompts fire on the wrong day (here: +2 days for Feb 30, +1 day for Apr 31). This is the producer-side counterpart of the `normalizeResetAt` bug (#4968, same file) and the consumer-side gaps in #4955/#4987: every other date field in this pipeline is gated with `isIsoDate` (`validate.ts`), this one string branch is not.

## Acceptance criteria

- `entryFromResult` only sets `credentialExpiresAt` from a string when it passes the same `isIsoDate` check used by `parseQuotaCurrent` (quota-current.ts:80); impossible or non-ISO strings leave the field unset (numeric epoch-ms handling unchanged).
- Regression tests: `"2026-02-30T00:00:00.000Z"`, `"2026-04-31"`, and `"March 2, 2026"` produce no `credentialExpiresAt`; a valid ISO string and a numeric epoch both still populate it.
- Existing aggregator tests pass.

title: id(didit): a self-superseding expectation passes decode, and evaluate() silently drops it — a supersede cycle drops every member the same way

body:
## Summary

A did-it expectation that supersedes **itself** passes body validation, and a pair of expectations that supersede **each other** passes validation too — but `evaluate()` then silently evaluates none of them. The tracker produces no verdicts and no error for an expectation its author believes is live, and the empty result is indistinguishable from "nothing to evaluate".

## Evidence (verified on `origin/main` @ 540ed0173, this run)

- `pkgs/id/src/didit/body.rs:524-545` — `Expectation::check()` validates subjects, act text, window, active window and note. It never compares `supersedes` (field at body.rs:517) against the expectation's own `id`. Both `encode_expectation_body` and `decode_expectation_body` (body.rs:727/754) gate on this `check()`, so a self-superseding body is refused by neither path.
- `pkgs/id/src/didit/eval.rs:91-95` — `evaluate()` builds `superseded` as the set of every expectation's `supersedes` target, then skips any expectation whose own `id` is in that set:
  - Self-supersede: `e.supersedes == Some(e.id)` puts `e.id` in the set, so `e` is skipped. Zero verdicts, `Ok` result.
  - Two-cycle: A supersedes B and B supersedes A — both ids are in the set, so both are skipped. Zero verdicts, `Ok` result.
- The only supersede test, `supersede_is_order_independent` in `pkgs/id/src/didit/tests.rs`, covers the normal one-directional case. Nothing pins the self or cycle cases.

## Why it matters

Superseding is how a user corrects an expectation (design §8: superseding is a set operation, order-independent). A self-reference is a certain authoring/encoding bug, and a cycle is reachable whenever two devices each replace the other's expectation concurrently — exactly the multi-device setting this evaluator is built for ("the same inputs always produce the same verdicts, on every device"). Today both fail silently: no verdicts, no error, nothing in the output that says the expectation was dropped, so the act simply stops being tracked and nobody can tell why.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Expectation::check()` refuses a body whose `supersedes` is its own `id` with `DiditError::Invalid`, so both encode and decode reject it (with a test through `decode_expectation_body`).
- [ ] `evaluate()` handles a supersede cycle deterministically and visibly: cycle members are not silently dropped — either they are evaluated under a stated tie-break rule, or `evaluate` returns an `EvalError` naming the cycle. The chosen rule is documented in the `eval.rs` module docs (the module already documents superseding as a set operation).
- [ ] Tests cover: self-supersede refused at decode; a two-expectation cycle; a three-expectation cycle; and a normal chain (A←B←C) still evaluating only the head.
- [ ] Existing didit tests still pass (`cargo test -p id didit` or the pkgs/id equivalent on the laptop/CI).

labels.name: kind/bug

body:
## Observed failure

On the laptop, `github-backup-drain.timer` last triggered at **2026-11-01 22:07:10 CST**. At the 2026-11-03 verification it reported `NextElapseUSecMonotonic=infinity`, no realtime next elapse, `Trigger: n/a`, and the drain-service journal was empty. The timer unit was active but had no scheduled next run. The fetch and reconcile timers continued to fire.

## Current unit configuration

At repository `main` (`dcca6cd510866556a00dedb2c92b7d21cf817e2b`), `infra/github-backup/systemd/github-backup-drain.timer` is monotonic-only:

```ini
[Timer]
OnBootSec=3min
OnUnitActiveSec=5min
Persistent=true
```

It has no `OnCalendar=` trigger. The timer was reactivated at about 22:16 CST during the home-manager unit migration in #3720, so the timing is associated with that reload. However, the recorded last service trigger at 22:07 is recent enough that an `OnUnitActiveSec` anchor would ordinarily be expected. The available evidence does **not** establish the precise systemd state transition that produced `infinity`; confirm that mechanism during implementation rather than assuming the migration discarded an otherwise valid anchor. `Persistent=true` applies to calendar timers and does not itself provide a calendar trigger here.

## Scoped fix and verification

Give the drain timer a calendar-based five-minute trigger, independent of the service's last activation, for example:

```ini
[Timer]
OnCalendar=*:0/5
OnBootSec=3min
Persistent=true
```

Keeping `OnBootSec` is optional if the calendar schedule alone is sufficient for the first run. Reload/restart the user timer and verify a finite next elapse plus one successful drain tick. Add a runbook or test check that every github-backup timer has a finite next elapse after unit installation/reload.

## Relations

- Umbrella rollout tracker: #3215 (the initial webhook proof is recorded there; this issue tracks the standing timer failure).
- #3720 is the temporally associated home-manager unit migration; causation is not yet confirmed.

## Acceptance criteria

- `github-backup-drain.timer` has a calendar-based five-minute trigger that is independent of the service's last activation (not monotonic-only).
- After a unit reload / daemon-reload, the timer reports a concrete next elapse (never `NextElapseUSecMonotonic=infinity` with no realtime elapse) and the drain service actually runs on the cadence.
- The mechanism that produced the infinity state is confirmed during implementation, or the calendar trigger is verified to fire across a reload regardless of that mechanism.
- The fetch and reconcile timers' behaviour is unchanged.

body:
Implementation issue for item (1) of #2841 (SET-REMAINDER of #1858, the set tracker). Filed by queue worker lane code-p, triage task 8566, 2026-11-03.

## Decision recorded (worker review, 2026-11-03)

Item (1) as originally worded — register a filtered MCP server set **per session** via `mcp.transform` — is **not implementable on the pinned opencode v2 surface**. Verified across tasks 3997 and 6867 and re-verified at current main by task 8566:

- The pinned `mcp.transform` editor (`packages/plugin/src/promise/mcp.ts:6-16`) is synchronous and location-wide, with no session ID.
- Host reconciliation changes shared connections (`packages/core/src/mcp/index.ts:534-574`), so a transform cannot own a per-session server set safely, and a blind implementation risks deleting or duplicating a user's hand-configured servers.

**Decision:** item (1) is dispositioned as a **recorded deviation** — the same closest-supported-equivalent treatment #2841 already sanctions for items (3) and (4). The landed equivalent is per-session filtering of **model-visible** mcpx tool definitions via `session.hook("context")` (`packages/plugin/src/promise/session.ts:25-35`; core filtering at `packages/core/src/session/model-request.ts:249-275,300,406-407`). This is explicitly **not** access control and not session-scoped registration: connections stay shared, and gateway/shell calls can bypass it. That limitation is part of the acceptance record, not a hidden gap.

## Scope

- In `pkgs/mcpx/plugin/opencode/v2/`: implement a context-hook filter that, per session, hides model-visible tool definitions for mcpx servers/tools the session's policy marks disabled.
- Policy source: the plugin's existing per-session state only (ctx.storage remembered daemon choice / session-env) — the filter must close over asynchronously refreshed plugin state (the established pattern from `v2/permission.ts`), never query the daemon synchronously from the hook.
- Filter only mcpx-namespaced tool definitions. Never mutate the location-wide MCP registry; never remove or alter user-configured servers.

## Out of scope

- Session-scoped MCP registration/discovery in the opencode host itself (upstream surface change; revisit if the pinned API gains a session-scoped transform).
- Items (3) and (5) of #2841 — they follow in order after this and item (4) (PR #4997) land.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Context-hook filter implemented in the v2 tree with targeted tests (`bun test plugin/opencode/v2/` on the laptop or CI green on the PR)
- [ ] Tests prove: disabled mcpx tools are hidden for the session, enabled ones remain, non-mcpx tools are untouched, and the MCP registry is not mutated
- [ ] PR references #2841 and #1858, and the deviation (model-visible filtering only, not access control) is stated in the PR body
- [ ] Outcome noted on #2841 and #1858 when merged

body:
## Problem

`pm-stack/dispatch/src/config.ts:107` defaults `SUPABASE_URL` to `https://nltgxorqwxhgfzseiirt.supabase.co` (the legacy **muse-dev** project) when the env var is unset:

```ts
supabaseUrl: s(env.SUPABASE_URL, "https://nltgxorqwxhgfzseiirt.supabase.co").replace(/\/$/, ""),
```

That project has been **deleted**: the Management API returns 404 `{"message":"Resource has been removed"}` for it, and its public hostname is NXDOMAIN. Any environment missing `SUPABASE_URL` therefore fails at DNS with `getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND nltgxorqwxhgfzseiirt.supabase.co` — before any request is even made.

## How it bit (2026-11-03)

title: Fix #4887: id(hosted_binding): a pending delayed rebind does not reserv

labels.name: source/dispatch
labels.description: Filed by pm-dispatch

body:
Implement GitHub issue #4887 in developing-today/code: id(hosted_binding): a pending delayed rebind does not reserve its target key

## Summary

The delayed-rebind protocol added in #4885 (slice 2 of #3809, `pkgs/id/src/hosted_binding.rs` at `9d1464c05`) never reserves the **target** key of a pending delayed rebind, and `effect_due_rebind` never re-checks it. During the 30-day wait, another account can bind that exact key by an ordinary ceremony; when the wait elapses, the delayed rebind still effects and `apply_rebind` silently overwrites the other binding's `binding_by_iroh` entry. Two `active` binding records then claim the same `iroh_id`, and the by-key index points at only one of them — breaking the §1.2 rule the ceremony itself enforces ("one `sub` per `iroh_id` at a time", `submit_proof` conflict check).

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe at origin/main `9d1464c05`)

Probe test appended in a throwaway laptop worktree (`probe-2026-11-03-laneB-scan20`, removed after the run; log `/tmp/probe-scan20.log` on the laptop):

1. Account A binds key21, then `request_delayed_rebind` to key22 → request `Pending`, binding `rebind_pending`.
2. A third account completes an ordinary `complete_browser_ceremony` with **key22** → succeeds. Nothing consulted the pending request: `request_delayed_rebind` checks only `binding_by_iroh` at request time (hosted_binding.rs:1269), the pending target key is inserted into no index, and `submit_proof`'s conflict check (hosted_binding.rs:~997) checks only `binding_by_iroh`.
3. Time advances past `effective_at`; `effect_due_rebind` with a valid new-key countersignature → succeeds. Unlike both other paths, it has **no** `NewKeyBoundElsewhere` recheck: `rebind_with_old_key_authorization` checks `binding_by_iroh.contains_key(&new_iroh_id)` at effect time (hosted_binding.rs:1414) and `request_delayed_rebind` checks it at request time (:1269); `effect_due_rebind` (hosted_binding.rs:1462) checks neither that nor pending requests.
4. `apply_rebind` (hosted_binding.rs:1538-1540) unconditionally does `binding_by_iroh.remove(old)` + `binding_by_iroh.insert(new, this binding)`, overwriting the third account's index entry.

Probe outcome (asserted in the probe, all true on current main): both A's and the third account's records are `Active` with `iroh_id` = key22; `binding_by_iroh[key22]` names A's binding only; the third account's record is silently unindexed for its own key.

The symmetric hole also exists at request time: two different accounts can both open pending delayed rebinds to the same target key, and whichever effects second overwrites the first's index entry the same way.

## Why it matters

The delayed path is the account-recovery path for a lost root key — exactly the path whose target-key ownership must be unambiguous. The 30-day wait is the security property (§4.2), but it also creates a 30-day window in which the target key is claimable by anyone: a squatter who binds the target key during the wait is not stopped at effect time, is not notified, and loses their by-key index entry without any error, while their binding record still says `active`. Any consumer resolving a binding by `iroh_id` (device authorization, grant references — §1) then reaches the wrong account's binding.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A pending delayed rebind reserves its target key: an ordinary ceremony (`submit_proof`) naming a key that is the target of a pending rebind fails with a conflict (e.g. `IrohIdBoundElsewhere` or a dedicated pending-rebind conflict), and a second `request_delayed_rebind` from another account naming the same target key fails with `NewKeyBoundElsewhere` (or equivalent).
- [ ] `effect_due_rebind` re-checks at effect time, before any mutation: if the target key is now bound to a different binding (or is the target of another pending request that was created earlier), it fails with `NewKeyBoundElsewhere` and leaves the binding, the request, and both indexes unchanged (the `RebindError` no-mutation contract).
- [ ] `apply_rebind` cannot silently overwrite a `binding_by_iroh` entry owned by a different binding: it refuses (or its callers guarantee the check) when the existing entry names another binding.
- [ ] Regression tests cover: ceremony-bind of a pending target key during the wait; two pending rebinds to one target key; effect after the target key was bound elsewhere (state unchanged on refusal); the existing 21 hosted_binding tests still pass (`cargo test -p id --lib hosted_binding`, laptop or CI).

Distinct from: #4868 / #4871 (the §3 ceremony's consumed-challenge and pairing-code findings in the same file — different functions and defects), #3809 (the delayed-rebind implementation epic this landed under; this is a defect in that new code, found by reading it against the §1.2 conflict rules).



Context: a Jules session began this issue on 2026-11-03 and was stopped mid-flight when the owner retired the Jules service (decommission, developing-today/code#5098). Before starting, check for any pull request or branch that attempt may have produced (search PRs referencing #4887) and treat the issue text above as the source of truth.

House rules from the repo owner: (1) Deliver the finished work as a pull request in this run; put "Fixes #4887" in the PR description so the issue closes on merge. (2) Cover the whole set in the one PR: every instance of the same problem, and any directly related dependency updates batched in — never one PR per item or per dependency. (3) Run the relevant tests and checks before opening the PR. (4) Merging is permitted only when you are reasonably certain the PR is correct and complete (checks green, tests run, low-risk); you never have to merge — when in doubt, leave the PR open and state your confidence and what a human should check. (5) If you hit a genuine blocker (missing credentials, a decision only the owner can make), stop and say exactly what is needed in your final summary.

body:
# id(didit): count windows drop records in the after-midnight tail of a wrapping active span

## Evidence

`pkgs/id/src/didit/eval.rs` at origin/main `7de65a8fe`:

- `count_verdicts` (line 139) builds the active spans for a count period with
  `active_spans_between(tz, &expectation.active, start, end)`.
- `active_spans_between` (lines 401–420) generates spans only for the local
  dates the period itself touches (`first = local_date(start)` …
  `last = local_date(end - 1)`).
- `spans_for_date` (lines 353–367) treats a wrapping `HoursSpan`
  (`from_minute > to_minute`) as one span that starts on that date and crosses
  midnight into the next.

So on the **first date of a count period**, the tail of the wrapping span that
began the *previous* day (e.g. 20:00–06:00 covering 00:00–06:00 of the period's
first day) is never generated, and records in that tail satisfy the period
filter (`record.at >= start && record.at < end`) but fail `in_spans`
(line 139–149) — they are silently not counted.

The interval path in the same file handles exactly this case:
`interval_verdicts` (lines 188–199) scans both today and the previous local
day, with the comment "A span that wraps past midnight began on the previous
local day, so both days are scanned." The count path has no equivalent.

## Verified (laptop probe, this run)

Probe test appended to `pkgs/id/src/didit/tests.rs` in a throwaway worktree at
origin/main `7de65a8fe` (probe since removed):

- Expectation: `CountPerPeriod { count: 1, period: Day }`, active
  `Hours { spans: [20:00–06:00], tz: America/Chicago }`, subject dog A.
- Record: act at **2026-06-16 02:00 Chicago** (inside the span that began
  2026-06-15 20:00). `now` = 2026-06-16 12:00 Chicago.
- Result: the 2026-06-16 verdict is `count=0, state=Due` — the record was
  dropped. Expected: `count=1, state=Satisfied`.
- The interval evaluator's own golden test (`wrapping_active_span_is_handled`)
  counts records at 02:00/05:00 on the second day as part of the span begun
  the previous evening, confirming the intended semantics.

The same hole hits `Period::Week` (a span begun Sunday night covering Monday
00:00–06:00 of a new week) and any custom period whose first date is preceded
by a wrapping span.

## Why it matters

The evaluator is the pure, replayable core of the did-it tracker (#3788,
Phase 1 of #2031): every device must produce the same verdicts from the same
inputs. A whole class of legitimate records — anything done after midnight
inside an overnight active window, on the first day of a period — is silently
excluded, so satisfied expectations report `Due` (and, once the period closes,
`Violated`). Overnight spans are a headline case for this tracker (the design's
own worked example is a 20:00–06:00 "outside" span).

Related but distinct: #5049 (a count verdict's `Due`→`Violated` timing once
the last active span of a period has closed). This issue is about span
*generation* at the period's leading edge; #5049 is about state choice.

## Acceptance criteria

- `active_spans_between` (or `count_verdicts`) includes the previous local
  day's wrapping span when it overlaps the period start, so a record in the
  after-midnight tail of a span begun the day before the period counts.
- A regression test mirrors the probe above: Day count window, 20:00–06:00
  active span, record at 02:00 on the period's first day → `count=1`,
  `Satisfied`; and an equivalent Week-boundary case (span begun Sunday,
  record early Monday).
- Existing didit tests still pass (`cargo test --lib didit` in `pkgs/id`),
  including the DST-day and interval wrapping-span golden tests.
- No change to interval-window behavior or to the CBOR body format.
