# didit evaluator: a count window whose active spans have all closed still reports `Due` — the requirement can no longer be met, but the verdict never turns `Violated` until the period ends

## Evidence

`pkgs/id/src/didit/eval.rs`, `count_verdicts` (main `8e151e895`): the state for a
count window is chosen from the **period** bounds only:

```rust
let state = if count >= required {
    VerdictState::Satisfied
} else if end <= now {
    VerdictState::Violated
} else {
    VerdictState::Due
};
```

`end` is the period end (e.g. local midnight for `Period::Day`). But records only
count when they fall inside the expectation's active spans (`in_spans(record.at,
&spans)` in the same function). For an `ActiveWindow::Hours` expectation whose last
span of the period has already ended, no further record in this period can count —
yet the verdict stays `Due` until the period ends.

That contradicts `VerdictState::Due`'s own contract in the same file: "The window
is still open and the requirement **can still be met**." After the last active span
closes, it cannot.

### Probe (laptop, worktree at `8e151e895`, test appended to `didit/tests.rs`)

Expectation: `CountPerPeriod { count: 2, period: Day }`, active hours 07:00–22:00
America/Chicago (the test helper's default span), no records.

- `now` = 2026-06-15 23:00 Chicago (span closed at 22:00, period ends at midnight):
  current-period verdict state = **Due** (expected: Violated — the day's last chance
  to record has passed).
- Control, `now` = 2026-06-15 12:00 Chicago (mid-span): **Due** (correct).

## Why it matters

The did-it tracker (#2031) surfaces these verdicts to the household: an item that
can no longer be done today keeps showing as still-doable ("Due") for hours after
its last active window closes, and only flips at midnight — for a weekly period,
an unmeetable requirement can report `Due` for days after the week's last active
span. Every consumer of `evaluate` inherits the wrong state; the evaluator is pure,
so the fix belongs here, not in callers.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] In `count_verdicts`, when the count is unmet and no active span of the current
      period is still open or yet to come (i.e. `now` is at/after the end of the
      period's last active span), the verdict is `Violated`, not `Due`.
- [ ] `ActiveWindow::Always` behavior is unchanged (its span is the whole period).
- [ ] Regression test in `pkgs/id/src/didit/tests.rs`: hours-windowed count
      expectation evaluated after the last span of the day ends reports `Violated`
      for the current period; evaluated mid-span it still reports `Due`; a wrapping
      (past-midnight) span is handled (the span that began yesterday and is still
      open keeps the verdict `Due`).
- [ ] Existing didit tests pass (`cargo test -p id didit`).

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-b (Lane B), verified this run at origin/main
`8e151e895`.

# id(hosted_binding): closing lifecycle audit — transition table for every public method + module-header contract statement (Phase 4 of #5047)

Phase 4 of design #5047 ("A name is claimed once — the hosted binding lifecycle contract", design doc `files/designs/code-id-hosted-binding-lifecycle.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace). Gated on Phases 1–3 (#4868, #4871, #4887).

## Scope

Audit every public method of `HostedBindingService` (`pkgs/id/src/hosted_binding.rs`) against the lifecycle contract recorded on #5047 — a challenge, a pairing code, and a rebind target key are each claimed exactly once, by exactly one holder, for exactly their stated lifetime; every transition out of a live state (consumption, supersession, expiry, reservation, release) is named — and write the resulting transition table into the module header beside the §3.4 failure-semantics prose it completes. Close #4868/#4871/#4887 with evidence if their phases have not already closed them.

## Required dispositions

(a) **Expired pairing codes:** `pairing_codes` entries whose challenge expired are swept only when presented to `exchange_pairing_code`. State whether mint/lookup sweeps them, or record that the leak is bounded by the challenge TTL (5 min) and why that is acceptable.
(b) **`consumed_challenges` growth:** consumed IDs accumulate for the life of this in-memory service. State the bound, or the reason none is needed at this slice (e.g. tied to challenge issuance rate limits), in the header table's notes.
(c) **Reservation scan cost:** the target-key reservation (Phase 3, #4887) is a predicate over pending requests. If the pending set can grow beyond a trivial scan, disposition the named alternative — an index keyed by target key — with the reason it is or is not taken (the design doc records why a second index loses by default: it is a second place for state to disagree).
(d) **Old-key-side symmetry:** confirm the delayed path's old key needs no symmetric reservation statement (it is already reserved via the binding's `rebind_pending` status) — confirm in the table, do not re-derive.

title: fix(ci): auto-format stages only the listed files — treefmt companion changes (rustfmt mod children) fail the commit or are silently dropped (#3198)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

The auto-format workflow decides "treefmt changed something" with a whole-worktree check but stages only the files it passed to the formatter. treefmt's rustfmt invocation can change files that were never in that list — rustfmt formats a file's out-of-line `mod` children along with it — so a companion change is either stranded or breaks the run:

- `.github/workflows/auto-format.yml` on current main (`0467ae0f9887`): line 111 runs `nix run .#format -- "${format_files[@]}"`, line 112 checks `git diff --quiet` (whole worktree), line 119 stages with `git add -- "${format_files[@]}"` and line 120 commits unconditionally.
- If the listed files were already formatted but a companion changed, nothing is staged and `git commit` exits 1 ("no changes added to commit"); under `set -euo pipefail` the step fails, nothing is pushed, and `record_success` never runs — so every later 15-minute run re-diffs the same range and fails the same way until the range moves on.
- If some listed file did change, the commit succeeds and the companion change is silently discarded with the runner: the unformatted child stays on main.

PR #3198 introduced the restricted staging (it replaced `git add -A` to keep workflow files out of the bot's push, #3118). The later PAT rework (PR #4797, commit df09437d) removed the workflow-file exclusion — `format_files` is now all changed files and the header comment says nothing is excluded from the write pass — but kept the restricted `git add`, so the companion gap survived. CodeRabbit flagged exactly this on PR #3198 (Minor / potential_issue, https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/3198#discussion_r4433106457); it was never addressed or replied to, and the PR merged as-is (2026-11-02).

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/3198 — MERGED, head `1cc7de210e`; the hunk replaced `git add -A` with `git add -- "${format_files[@]}"` while `git diff --quiet` stayed whole-worktree.
- Current main `0467ae0f98876cef0dfffe9fc75d61c68aeacd67`: `.github/workflows/auto-format.yml:111-120` as quoted above; `treefmt.toml` configures rustfmt as plain `rustfmt --edition 2024` with no `skip_children` / `--skip-children`.
- Verified on the laptop (2026-11-03, rustfmt 1.9.0): a formatted `parent.rs` declaring `mod child;` plus an unformatted `child.rs` — running `rustfmt --edition 2024 parent.rs` (only the parent passed, treefmt's exact invocation shape) reformats `child.rs`. Replaying the workflow's git sequence on that tree: `git diff --quiet` reports dirty, `git add -- parent.rs` stages nothing, `git commit` exits 1 with "no changes added to commit".
- Dedupe: issue searches for the auto-format staging / companion-file problem (titles and bodies, all states, 2026-11-03) return no covering issue. #3118/#3198 are the closed workflow-push problem; open #4787 is about scheduled runs not firing and the record_success token scope — a different failure.

## Why it matters

The auto-format bot is the fleet's formatting safety net: it runs every 15 minutes and keeps main formatted without gating merges. This gap makes it fail loudly and repeatedly for an entire diff range whenever a merged PR leaves an unformatted module child next to a formatted parent (formatting never gates a merge, so drift on main is expected), and in the mixed case it silently throws away formatting it already computed. Either way the bot stops doing the one job it exists for, with no issue on file.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The write pass stages every tracked change treefmt actually made (or equivalently decides "nothing to commit" from the staged diff, not the worktree diff), so a companion-file change can neither fail the commit with "no changes added to commit" nor be silently discarded.
- [ ] Workflow files remain pushable under the current REPO_AUTOMATION_TOKEN PAT arrangement (the #3118 regression does not return in another form).
- [ ] A regression test in `scripts/tests/test_auto_format_workflow.py`, executing the workflow's real run block like the existing tests, covers the companion case: a listed file already formatted whose formatter run changes an unlisted tracked file — the run exits 0 and the companion change is in the pushed commit.
- [ ] The existing auto-format workflow tests still pass.

title: opencode-claimant: requeue/lease expiry never clears a bound session_id — a live session can sit on a claimable task (7787), and a relaunch can never re-bind

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: source/queue-worker
labels.description: Filed or worked by the queue/worker pilot

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: effort/m
labels.description: Medium: expected under 1 day of work

labels.name: app/pm-stack
labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

body:
## Summary

A task can be **requeued while a claimant-bound session is still live or while a
dead binding still exists**, and nothing clears `progress.session_id`:

1. **Launch race (live, task 7787).** The claim lease expired 2026-11-03T15:31:38.44Z.
   The 09:20 CT claimant fire — using a poll snapshot taken before expiry —
   created and bound session `ses_e5e5df699f1ffeTb5Z3gWDNsYI` for it at
   **15:31:40.62Z**, two seconds after expiry. The task row is now
   `status=queued`, `worker_id=null`, `lease_until=null`, while that session is
   **LIVE** in `GET /api/session/active` and executing the task.
2. **Stale bindings on requeued rows.** Of 36 `queued` tasks that still carry a
   bound `session_id`, 33 have a terminal session, 2 a marker-less stale one, and
   1 (7787) a live one. The claim was released; the binding was not.

## Impact

- **Double execution.** A `queued` task is claimable by any lane. For 7787 the
  next claim executes the same issue alongside the live session. The atomic bind
  in migration 0021 cannot prevent this: binding runs at *launch*, and by then
  the task is no longer claimed, so `bind` raises no conflict at all.
- **Orphan sessions that can never bind.** `bind_repo_task_lane_session` refuses
  to overwrite a *different* existing binding. So a relaunch of any of the 35
  dead-session queued rows would create a session whose bind is rejected —
  exactly the Oct-28 unbound-launch defect #3026 exists to close, reached by the
  opposite path.
- The claimant's step 4a re-verify does not catch facet 1 unless it re-reads the
  ledger in the same instant as the create; the lease can die between poll and
  `POST /api/session`.

## Reproduction / current state

Read-only snapshot from the 2026-11-03 09:30 CT claimant fire
(`~/.local/state/opencode-claimant/fires.jsonl`):

```
task 7787 | repo-health-code-pilot | status=queued | stage=launched
          | session_id=ses_e5e5df699f1ffeTb5Z3gWDNsYI
          | launched_by=opencode-claimant | worker_id=null | lease=null
          | stage_at=2026-11-03T15:31:40.617952Z | attempts=3
session ses_e5e5df699f1ffeTb5Z3gWDNsYI -> in GET /api/session/active (LIVE)
```

Ledger query for facet 2:

```
GET tasks?status=eq.queued&progress->>session_id=not.is.null   -> 36 rows
per-id session read: terminal 33 | markerless-stale 2 | LIVE 1
```

### State at fire close (~15:40Z)

The bound session noticed its own claim had lapsed and **re-claimed the task
itself** (`status=claimed`, `worker_id=repo-worker-code`, stage `verified`), so
no second executor appeared and no duplicate work occurred. But that repair was
ad-hoc, taken by a worker whose prompt said the task was "already claimed", and
it was only possible because a worker may claim. For **~6.5 minutes (15:31:38 →
~15:38)** the task was `queued` and claimable by any lane while a live session
was already executing it. Avoid the exposure window, not the repair.

## Suggested direction (not prescriptive)

- **Requeue/reap must disposition the binding**, not just the claim: clear
  `progress.session_id` + `launched_by` when the bound session is terminal and
  the task returns to `queued`, record the old id in history, and leave `bind`
  free to overwrite.
- **Claimant launch must re-assert the claim under the launch**, e.g. heartbeat
  or claim-guard the row in the same transaction/step as create+bind, and treat
  "lease lost between poll and create" as a skip (no session created).
- **A queued task with a live bound session should be unclaimable** (claim should
  refuse, or the row should carry a `bound_live` guard).
- Task 7787's live session needs a decision from the ledger backstop: adopt it
  (re-claim to the worker) or let it finish without any lane claiming the row.

## Scope note

Found during supervision of #3026 slice 1; the claimant correctly launched and
mutated **nothing** this fire (cap saturated, 14 active roots vs cap 12). Related:
#4757 (session-list truncation), #4758 (bound session with no prompt, stuck
claimed), #4912 (session contract design), #3026 (slice 1).

## Acceptance criteria
- When a task is requeued (lease expiry, park expiry, or lane release), any `progress.session_id` bound to a previous claim is cleared or superseded in the same transition, so a queued row never carries a live or stale binding.
- A relaunch of a previously bound task can bind its new session (the 0021 bind no longer refuses because of a dead predecessor binding).
- The launch race is closed: a session created from a pre-expiry poll snapshot cannot end up executing a task that has already been requeued — the claimant re-verifies the claim at bind time and aborts/rebinds on mismatch.
- The 36 queued rows carrying bound session_ids measured at filing are reconciled (bindings cleared or verified live-and-owned).

body:
Disposition 1 of design #3702 Phase 3 (audit task 5613, 2026-11-03). `mergeQuiet` now rejects out-of-range clock times (#3686), so no *new* bad row can be stored, but rows written before that fix are still read raw:

- `inQuietHours` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/alerts.ts:168`) converts `quiet.start`/`quiet.end` with `toMin()` without validating them, so a stored `99:99` becomes minute 6039 and `24:60` becomes 1500 — the window silently becomes a different one (often suppressing almost the whole day).
- The `/alerts` prefs form renders the stored string straight back (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/render.ts` `formQuietStart`/`formQuietEnd`).

Design decision 3 says stored rows are **not** silently rewritten, so the fix is a read-side sanitize (pass stored values through `mergeQuiet` before use, or clamp per field to the default) and/or a one-off data fix with the row ids recorded. Either way the audit wants the old rows' fate to be explicit rather than a silent reinterpretation.

Also covers the stored-invalid-`tz` half of disposition 3: an unknown stored zone makes `inQuietHours` fail open (`return false`, no suppression) — deliberate for delivery, but the read path should probably fall back to the default zone instead of disabling quiet hours.

Acceptance: a test that a stored `99:99`/`24:60`/bad-tz row produces the default window (or a documented fail-open), and a note on #3702 saying whether production rows were found and fixed.

Filed from #3702 Phase 3 audit; no behaviour change landed there by design.

title: id(world): bound every journal entry at write time by splitting the compacted checkpoint (fixes #4630)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
Follow-up from the design note in [#4962](https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/4962) (`doc/2026-11-03T14-55-00Z_design_id4630_oversized_replication_entries.md`), which chose **bounded checkpoint at write time** for [#4630](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/4630). Implementation issue — the fix for #4630 itself; #4630 closes when this merges.

## Problem

`WorldCore::checkpoint_entries` (`pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs:1063-1200`) emits the whole compacted world as **one** `JournalEntry::Checkpoint`. Nothing bounds its size:

- the program snapshot `String` (passed in from `world/actor.rs:275`) has no `WorldLimits` bound (`snapshot_bytes` bounds only the client-facing snapshot's event selection, `core.rs:2063`);
- retained `events` (≤ `retained_events`, default 1024, each ≤ `input_bytes` 16 KiB, hex-encoded entity inputs double that);
- `admin_history` (≤ min(`retained_events`, 4096)).

One such entry over `MAX_REPLICATION_PAYLOAD_BYTES` (256 KiB, `pkgs/id/src/world/replication.rs:79`) makes `split_entry_payload` return `PayloadTooLarge` and `send_snapshot` (`world_replication_net.rs:206-243`) fail before the first frame. No other entry kind can grow unboundedly (chat ≤ 2 KiB, input ≤ 16 KiB, participant/ceiling/schedule entries small, `open_presence` capped at 4096 IDs), so bounding the checkpoint bounds every entry.

## Required change

Split the checkpoint into bounded part entries at compaction time, mirroring the existing pre-`Checkpoint` entry pattern (`CapsCeiling`, `ScheduleSet`, `Isolation`, `ExecutionProfile`, transfer entries):

- new part entry kinds for the program snapshot, retained events, and admin history, each `{ sequence, part_index, part_count, ... }`, split by **encoded** size (`serde_json::to_vec` of the assembled part) at UTF-8 boundaries for the string;
- `MAX_CHECKPOINT_PART_BYTES = 192 * 1024` — deliberately below the 256 KiB payload bound, leaving headroom for the part's scalar fields and JSON framing;
- `Checkpoint` keeps scalars plus `open_presence` (≈86 KiB worst case at the 4096-ID cap, under the part bound);
- restore assembles parts for the same `sequence`, refusing missing / duplicate / out-of-order / mismatched `part_count` parts, and applies exactly today's state;
- bump `JOURNAL_VERSION` to 6 and map the new kinds in `journal_version_required_by`, per the existing header-bump contract (`world/mod.rs:980-1060`);
- keep `MAX_REPLICATION_PAYLOAD_BYTES` and the envelope at v1 — **no wire change, no envelope bump, no `ReplicationTracker::accept` change**.

Constraint: a checkpoint that would exceed the part bound must be split, never skipped or truncated — compaction may not silently keep the untrimmed journal for size reasons, except for the already-documented open-presence limit.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A compacted journal from a world whose program snapshot is > 256 KiB contains no entry over `MAX_CHECKPOINT_PART_BYTES`, and `restore` reconstructs the identical `WorldCore` state (snapshot bytes, retained events, admin history, presence, transfers, schedules, profile).
- [ ] **#4630 regression test:** the same oversized-Checkpoint journal image round-trips the feed path — `journal_entry_line` per entry → `split_entry_payload` (no `PayloadTooLarge`) → `ReplicationEnvelope::snapshot`/`tail` + `send_snapshot` framing → `ReplicationTracker::accept` — and the accepted cursor equals the sender's final cursor; the received journal `restore`s to the same state.
- [ ] Boundary tests: a part of exactly `MAX_CHECKPOINT_PART_BYTES` passes; one byte over is split, not errored; a multi-byte UTF-8 character is never cut mid-character.
- [ ] Journal-version tests: a v6 journal is refused by a version-5 reader at the header check; a journal needing only v1-v5 keeps its existing version.
- [ ] `cargo test -p id --lib world::replication` passes.
- [ ] The `world_store` replication feed tests pass (they build snapshot bytes through the same path).
- [ ] The existing journal-version / restore / compaction suites pass (`cargo test -p id --lib world`).
- [ ] The module doc of `pkgs/id/src/world/replication.rs` states the resulting per-entry guarantee from the design note (every writer-emitted entry ≤ 192 KiB, hence ≤ one v1 payload frame), replacing "such an entry can never be replicated in v1".

## Out of scope

- Sub-entry fragmentation / continuation frames (rejected in the note: v1→v2 wire bump plus permanent receiver buffering for a writer-controlled entry kind).
- Raising `MAX_REPLICATION_PAYLOAD_BYTES` (deferred; it changes a receiver-side constant, so it is a compatibility decision).
- Legacy journals already holding an oversized `Checkpoint` — handled by the companion residual issue.

body:
## Problem

`nixos-integration` runs the SSH world tests against an `id` binary that is
built **without** the `ssh` feature, so those tests cannot pass on current
`main` even when the harness itself is green.

- `pkgs/id/flake.nix:649-659` builds `id-web` with
  `buildFeatures = [ "web" "sandbox" "world" ]` — no `ssh`.
- `pkgs/id/flake.nix:637-641` passes `idPackage = self.packages.${system}.id-web`
  to `nix/tests/integration-test.nix`.
- `flake.nix:127` builds `integrationTestRunner` with
  `cargo test --all-features --test cli_integration --no-run`, so the test
  binary contains the SSH tests.

The spawned server therefore exits with:

```
Error: this build has no SSH support (feature `ssh`)
```

## Evidence

VM run of `checks.x86_64-linux.nixos-integration` on branch
`queue/7796-1372-legible-vm-timeout` (PR #4913, the legibility fix for #1372),
2026-11-03, reusing the branch's built test runner and `id` binary:

```
[id-integration] 126 tests in 4 named groups: fast_unit=49, serve=43, tag=29, harness_unit=5
[id-integration] group 'fast_unit' finished in 7.4s
[id-integration] waiting on group 'serve' (filters: serve_tests::); per-group deadline 2200s, 3393s of suite budget left
...
test result: FAILED. 40 passed; 3 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 83 filtered out; finished in 14.40s
```

Failures:

- `serve_tests::test_world_join_via_ssh_carries_the_frame_protocol`
- `serve_tests::test_world_ssh_tunnel_carries_join_via_ssh`
- `serve_tests::test_world_module_shared_over_iroh_and_web_presentations`
  (assertion `join denied`; its server stderr shows the same missing-ssh exit)

Two are explicitly SSH tests; the third's server dies before the forged-join
assertion. The shared root cause in the captured stderr is
`Error: this build has no SSH support (feature 'ssh')`.

## Why it matters

#1372's acceptance is "the suite passes, or it fails fast with a named
assertion". The legibility half now holds (the run fails in seconds naming the
group and tests), but the "passes" half cannot be met while the binary under
test lacks a feature the test binary was compiled with.

## Options

1. Build the integration test's `id` binary with the `ssh` feature (matching
   the runner's `--all-features`), so the SSH tests exercise real behaviour.
2. Gate the SSH tests on the spawned binary's capabilities and skip them
   otherwise — weaker, and it reduces coverage.

Preferred: option 1. A separate pre-existing blocker (#4850, `ChainExt`
literals missing the #3794 `checkpoint` field) also makes `id-web`'s
checkPhase fail to build on `main`; both have to be cleared before a stock
`nix build .#checks.x86_64-linux.nixos-integration` can be green.

Refs #1372, PR #4913, #4850.

body:
# pm-stack(aggregator): validateNewComment / validateNewAction accept ref keys parseRef rejects — GH_REF number group is unbounded

## Summary

Two POST boundary validators in the aggregator check GitHub refs with a local regex whose number group is an unbounded `\d+`:

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/comments.ts:43` — `GH_REF`, used by `validateNewComment` (:119) for a `kind: "github"` comment's `githubRef`, and by the store-load gate `commentRecordProblem` (:65).
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/actions.ts:253` — the same `GH_REF`, used by `validateNewAction` for `targetRef` (:396) and for the `request-status` target derived from `objectRef` (:469-470).

Both validators therefore accept refs like `developing-today/code#99999999999999999999` and store them typed as `RefKey`. But a `RefKey` is only meaningful if the canonical parser accepts it: `parseRef` (`src/model.ts:460-466`) throws `ref number is not a safe integer` for any number above `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` — the rule established for #2485/#4284 and applied at the registry gate (`isValidTaskRef`, registry.ts) — and `refUrl` inherits the throw.

The comment module's own consumer proves the breakage in-repo: `githubCommentUrl` (`src/comments.ts:482-485`) returns `refUrl(c.githubRef)` for a stored comment, so a comment that passed validation and the store-load gate throws when its URL is derived, instead of rendering a link. Action `targetRef`s carrying the same shape are handed to downstream status-request consumers as valid `RefKey`s they cannot parse.

This is the validator-side sibling of #4890 (open): that issue covers `refsInText` *manufacturing* unsafe keys from text; this one covers the two *boundary validators* (and the comments store-load gate) accepting unsafe keys a client posts directly. The fix in one does not touch the other.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop bun probe at origin/main a8dbda7fc)

Probe imported `validateNewComment`, `validateNewAction`, `githubCommentUrl`, and `parseRef` from the laptop primary's aggregator sources:

- `validateNewComment({kind:"github", githubRef:"developing-today/code#99999999999999999999", …})` → `ok: true`, ref stored verbatim
- `githubCommentUrl({githubRef: that ref})` → **throws** `ref number is not a safe integer: developing-today/code#99999999999999999999`
- `validateNewAction({targetRef: that ref, …})` → `ok: true`; a `request-status` action with `objectRef: "gh:developing-today/code#99999999999999999999"` → `ok: true`, `targetRef` derived to the same unsafe key
- Boundary: `#9007199254740991` (MAX_SAFE_INTEGER) — validate `true`, `parseRef` ok; `#9007199254740992` — validate `true`, `parseRef` throws
- Controls: `#123` — validate `true`, `parseRef` → `{repo, number: 123}`, `githubCommentUrl` → `https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/123`

## Why it matters

- The boundary is the one place the aggregator's ingest contract (validate once, at the boundary) can keep an unparseable `RefKey` out of the durable stores; once stored, the comments store-load gate (`commentRecordProblem`, same regex) re-admits it on every load, so the poisoned record is permanent until hand-edited.
- The failure surfaces far from the cause: a render/URL derivation throw (or a downstream consumer refusing the ref) for a comment/action that every validator said was fine.
- Two copies of the same flawed regex (comments.ts:43, actions.ts:253) guarantee the sites drift; the registry already solved this by routing through `parseRef` (`isValidTaskRef`) — the validators should share that one rule.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `validateNewComment` rejects a `githubRef` whose number is not a safe integer (same rule as `parseRef`), and `commentRecordProblem` applies the same rule at store load.
- [ ] `validateNewAction` rejects an unsafe-number `targetRef`, including the `request-status` target derived from `objectRef`.
- [ ] The check is one shared rule (e.g. a `parseRef`-based `isValidRef` helper in model.ts, as registry.ts already uses), not a third copy of a patched regex.
- [ ] Regression tests: oversized-number refs rejected at both validators and at the comments store-load gate; `#9007199254740991` and ordinary refs (e.g. `#123`) still accepted; existing comments/actions tests stay green.

Distinct from: #4890 (refsInText builder emitting unsafe keys from session text), #2485/#4284 (registry gate hardening, already landed).

body:
# pm-stack(aggregator): applyCloudflareExport accepts negative `used` values — the Supabase overlay refuses them

## Evidence

`pm-stack/aggregator/src/saas-extract.ts`, `applyCloudflareExport` (line ~831): the export-metric filter accepts any finite `used`:

```ts
.filter((m) => m && typeof m.id === "string" && typeof m.used === "number" && Number.isFinite(m.used))
```

The sibling overlay in the same file, `applySupabaseExport` (lines ~941-947), explicitly drops negative measurements:

```ts
!(typeof m.used === "number" && m.used < 0) &&
!(typeof m.limit === "number" && m.limit < 0),
```

and the Supabase billing gate in the same function also requires `billedUsd >= 0` (line ~982). The Cloudflare path has no equivalent guard, so a negative `used` from the file-export document is copied onto the card and its percent is derived from it (line ~843: `percent: ... Math.round((live.used / m.limit) * 1000) / 10`), and the card is stamped `sourceClass = "api"` — presented as live measured data.

## Verified this run (laptop bun probe at origin/main 115fe4f44)

Fresh, in-cycle Cloudflare export doc with `workers-requests: used = -500` (control `kv-reads: used = 1420`):

```
workers-requests used= -500 percent= -0
kv-reads used= 1420 percent= 0
sourceClass= api
```

The negative measurement is stored on the service card. With a larger magnitude (e.g. `used = -5,000,000` against the 10M limit) the derived percent is -50 — a negative usage percentage rendered as measured fact.

## Why it matters

The export document is produced by an external collector writing a file; a buggy or drifted collector value flows straight through this overlay onto the usage card as authoritative "live" data. The Supabase overlay in the same file already encodes the house rule — negative usage/limit measurements are not measurements and are dropped, keeping the tracker prose fallback. The Cloudflare overlay is the inconsistent half of the pair.

## Acceptance criteria

- `applyCloudflareExport` drops export metrics with `used < 0` (mirroring `applySupabaseExport`'s filter), so the affected metric keeps its prose/null state instead of a negative measured value.
- A regression test in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/cloudflare-export.test.ts`: a fresh doc carrying a negative `used` leaves that metric unchanged (and does not set a negative percent), while other valid metrics in the same doc still overlay.
- Existing cloudflare-export and saas test suites pass.

labels.name: meta/enriched

body:
## Problem

`.github/ci-policy.md` says the basic-validation (PR) tier is the only merge requirement, and that `basic: proxy port fallbacks` is the required status context branch protection and the merge queue enforce. But the workflow that defines it — `.github/workflows/nix-ci.yml` — has no `pull_request` trigger:

```yaml
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  schedule:
    - cron: "17 8 * * *"
  workflow_dispatch:
```

So on an ordinary PR the job never starts, and the PR shows only bot reviewers. Observed on PR #4935 (`bin/antigravity-direct.mjs` only): `statusCheckRollup` was `[CodeRabbit NEUTRAL]` with `mergeStateStatus: CLEAN` — no `basic:` context at all, neither pending nor absent-but-required.

## Why it matters

- The policy's stated merge gate cannot run on the thing it is meant to gate. A PR that breaks proxy-port fallbacks (the exact failure #434/#435 built this job for) merges with a clean state.
- The merge-queue note in the same doc says `nix ci` also runs on `merge_group` events "which is why" the queue can validate a combined head — that trigger is absent too, so the queue's validation is also unproven.
- A worker following "CI-first verification" cannot distinguish "check green" from "check never ran" from `gh pr view` output; both read as no failing check.

## Suggested fix

Add `pull_request:` (and `merge_group:`) to `nix-ci.yml`'s triggers for the `proxy-port-fallbacks` job, or split that job into its own workflow with a `pull_request` trigger if the rest of `nix ci` is deliberately main-only (host-eval and full flake checks are the expensive parts). The job is pure bash/grep with a 5-minute timeout, so it belongs on every PR.

## Evidence

- `.github/workflows/nix-ci.yml:1-9` — triggers.
- `.github/ci-policy.md` "Merge requirement" and "Merge queue (pilot, 2026-10-29)".
- PR #4935: `gh pr view 4935 --json statusCheckRollup` → CodeRabbit only; merged 2026-11-03T13:59:30Z with `mergeStateStatus: CLEAN`.

Found while landing #2823 (queue task 8037, `repo-health-code-pilot`, lane `02cafe76-eafd-4d0b-aaa6-2b7a737d68dc`).

## Acceptance criteria

- `.github/workflows/nix-ci.yml` (or a split workflow) runs the `proxy-port-fallbacks` job on `pull_request` events, so a PR's statusCheckRollup contains the `basic: proxy port fallbacks` context.
- The `merge_group` trigger is present (or the ci-policy doc is corrected where it claims it), so the merge queue's combined-head validation actually runs.
- Verified on a real PR after the change: the basic context appears (pending → success/failure) instead of being absent.

body:
# pm-stack(aggregator): refsInText emits ref keys parseRef rejects — builder-made session records fail isSessionRecord and drop whole

## Summary

`refsInText` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/model.ts:471-475) extracts GitHub issue/PR URLs with the `GH_URL` regex (model.ts:468), whose number group is an unbounded `\d+`. It returns the matches typed as `RefKey[]`, but a `RefKey` is only meaningful if `parseRef` (model.ts:460-466) accepts it — and `parseRef` throws when the number is not a safe integer.

So a session whose title, PR, or branch contains a GitHub URL with a very large issue number (≥ 2^53, e.g. `https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/99999999999999999999`) produces a task ref that is not a valid ref key. `taskRefsOf` (src/registry.ts:32-38) collects it into the record built by `recordFromSessionEntry` (registry.ts:41), and that record then fails the registry's own structural gate `isSessionRecord` (registry.ts:165, via `isValidTaskRef`, registry.ts:12-20) — so the whole session record is dropped by the drop-and-count sanitizers (`sanitizeRegistry` in src/feed.ts, the `parseLaunchRecords` hygiene filter in registry.ts) instead of keeping the session with its valid refs.

This is the builder-side residual of #2485: that issue hardened the gate so malformed `taskRefs` can no longer crash /sessions at render, but the producer still manufactures gate-failing refs, and the failure mode is now silent loss of the entire session record over one bad URL in its title.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe at origin/main 9d1464c05c84f5536bb32d937c13e584175413c3)

Probe (bun, run against the laptop primary's aggregator sources):

- `refsInText("see https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/99999999999999999999")` → `["developing-today/code#99999999999999999999"]`
- `parseRef("developing-today/code#99999999999999999999")` → throws `ref number is not a safe integer: developing-today/code#99999999999999999999`
- `recordFromSessionEntry({ sessionId: "s1", source: "opencode-sandbox", title: "work <that URL>", createdAt: "2026-11-03T00:00:00Z" })` → `taskRefs: ["developing-today/code#99999999999999999999"]`, and `isSessionRecord(record)` → `false`
- Control: same entry with `.../issues/123` → `taskRefs: ["developing-today/code#123"]`, `isSessionRecord(record)` → `true`

## Why it matters

- The registry is the durable record of fleet sessions; a session disappears from it entirely because of one cosmetic string (its title), not because anything about the session is malformed.
- The drop is at record granularity: the session's valid refs, tokens, and identity are lost with the bad one.
- `refsInText`'s declared return type (`RefKey[]`) promises keys `parseRef` can read; every current and future caller inherits the trap.

## Acceptance criteria

- `refsInText` never returns a key that `parseRef` rejects (skip matches whose issue/PR number is not a safe integer), OR `taskRefsOf` filters extracted refs through the same validity rule `isSessionRecord` applies — one shared rule, not two copies.
- A session entry whose title/PR/branch contains an oversized-number GitHub URL yields a record that passes `isSessionRecord`, keeping its valid refs.
- Regression tests cover: oversized number URL in title, in PR field, and in branch; a mix of one oversized and one normal URL keeps the normal ref; existing refsInText/registry tests still pass.
- Related: #2485 (gate hardening this builds on).

title: id(hosted_binding): a pending delayed rebind does not reserve its target key — another account can bind it during the 30-day wait, and effect_due_rebind silently overwrites that binding's by-key index entry

body:
## Summary

The delayed-rebind protocol added in #4885 (slice 2 of #3809, `pkgs/id/src/hosted_binding.rs` at `9d1464c05`) never reserves the **target** key of a pending delayed rebind, and `effect_due_rebind` never re-checks it. During the 30-day wait, another account can bind that exact key by an ordinary ceremony; when the wait elapses, the delayed rebind still effects and `apply_rebind` silently overwrites the other binding's `binding_by_iroh` entry. Two `active` binding records then claim the same `iroh_id`, and the by-key index points at only one of them — breaking the §1.2 rule the ceremony itself enforces ("one `sub` per `iroh_id` at a time", `submit_proof` conflict check).

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe at origin/main `9d1464c05`)

Probe test appended in a throwaway laptop worktree (`probe-2026-11-03-laneB-scan20`, removed after the run; log `/tmp/probe-scan20.log` on the laptop):

1. Account A binds key21, then `request_delayed_rebind` to key22 → request `Pending`, binding `rebind_pending`.
2. A third account completes an ordinary `complete_browser_ceremony` with **key22** → succeeds. Nothing consulted the pending request: `request_delayed_rebind` checks only `binding_by_iroh` at request time (hosted_binding.rs:1269), the pending target key is inserted into no index, and `submit_proof`'s conflict check (hosted_binding.rs:~997) checks only `binding_by_iroh`.
3. Time advances past `effective_at`; `effect_due_rebind` with a valid new-key countersignature → succeeds. Unlike both other paths, it has **no** `NewKeyBoundElsewhere` recheck: `rebind_with_old_key_authorization` checks `binding_by_iroh.contains_key(&new_iroh_id)` at effect time (hosted_binding.rs:1414) and `request_delayed_rebind` checks it at request time (:1269); `effect_due_rebind` (hosted_binding.rs:1462) checks neither that nor pending requests.
4. `apply_rebind` (hosted_binding.rs:1538-1540) unconditionally does `binding_by_iroh.remove(old)` + `binding_by_iroh.insert(new, this binding)`, overwriting the third account's index entry.

Probe outcome (asserted in the probe, all true on current main): both A's and the third account's records are `Active` with `iroh_id` = key22; `binding_by_iroh[key22]` names A's binding only; the third account's record is silently unindexed for its own key.

The symmetric hole also exists at request time: two different accounts can both open pending delayed rebinds to the same target key, and whichever effects second overwrites the first's index entry the same way.

## Why it matters

The delayed path is the account-recovery path for a lost root key — exactly the path whose target-key ownership must be unambiguous. The 30-day wait is the security property (§4.2), but it also creates a 30-day window in which the target key is claimable by anyone: a squatter who binds the target key during the wait is not stopped at effect time, is not notified, and loses their by-key index entry without any error, while their binding record still says `active`. Any consumer resolving a binding by `iroh_id` (device authorization, grant references — §1) then reaches the wrong account's binding.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A pending delayed rebind reserves its target key: an ordinary ceremony (`submit_proof`) naming a key that is the target of a pending rebind fails with a conflict (e.g. `IrohIdBoundElsewhere` or a dedicated pending-rebind conflict), and a second `request_delayed_rebind` from another account naming the same target key fails with `NewKeyBoundElsewhere` (or equivalent).
- [ ] `effect_due_rebind` re-checks at effect time, before any mutation: if the target key is now bound to a different binding (or is the target of another pending request that was created earlier), it fails with `NewKeyBoundElsewhere` and leaves the binding, the request, and both indexes unchanged (the `RebindError` no-mutation contract).
- [ ] `apply_rebind` cannot silently overwrite a `binding_by_iroh` entry owned by a different binding: it refuses (or its callers guarantee the check) when the existing entry names another binding.
- [ ] Regression tests cover: ceremony-bind of a pending target key during the wait; two pending rebinds to one target key; effect after the target key was bound elsewhere (state unchanged on refusal); the existing 21 hosted_binding tests still pass (`cargo test -p id --lib hosted_binding`, laptop or CI).

Distinct from: #4868 / #4871 (the §3 ceremony's consumed-challenge and pairing-code findings in the same file — different functions and defects), #3809 (the delayed-rebind implementation epic this landed under; this is a defect in that new code, found by reading it against the §1.2 conflict rules).

title: fix(pm-dispatch): JWKS URL has a bogus .json suffix — every GitHub OIDC validation 401s (JWKS fetch 404)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

body:
## Bug

Every pm-dispatch OIDC validation fails: `POST /v1/tasks` answers **401 `oidc: JWKS fetch failed (HTTP 404)`** for valid GitHub Actions OIDC tokens, fleet-wide. The whole dispatch mesh is down — cross-repo queueing, CI failure escalation, and the smoke test all hit it.

## Root cause (verified 2026-11-03)

`pm-stack/dispatch/src/auth.ts:73`:

```ts
const GITHUB_JWKS_URL = "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com/.well-known/jwks.json";
```

GitHub's JWKS endpoint has **no `.json` suffix**. Live checks just now:

- `GET https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com/.well-known/jwks.json` → **404**
- `GET https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com/.well-known/jwks` → **200** (this is the `jwks_uri` in GitHub's OIDC discovery document)

`fetchGithubJwks()` (auth.ts:79-80) throws `oidc: JWKS fetch failed (HTTP 404)` on the 404, so no GitHub OIDC token can ever validate.

## Evidence of impact

- openchamber `pm-dispatch smoke test` run 41631575281 (2026-11-03T11:59Z): vendored `pm-dispatch-queue` action mints a valid token (audience `pm-dispatch`), POST fails 401 with exactly this error — tracked as openchamber#1449.
- Same 401 in openchamber `opencode-update` run 41631990938's pm-dispatch escalation step (openchamber#805) and the main-broken watcher track (openchamber#1429).

## Fix

Drop the `.json` suffix at auth.ts:73 (or read `jwks_uri` from the discovery document). Add/adjust a test that pins the JWKS URL to GitHub's discovery `jwks_uri` so this cannot regress silently — the injectable `jwksSource` seam (auth.ts:89) meant unit tests never exercised the real URL.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `GITHUB_JWKS_URL` matches the discovery document's `jwks_uri`; a test pins it.
- [ ] After deploy, a cross-repo smoke dispatch succeeds: openchamber `pm-dispatch smoke test` run on main completes with conclusion success (closes openchamber#1449).

Origin issue for the set: this one. Downstream tracks (do not duplicate the fix there): openchamber#1449, openchamber#805, openchamber#1429.
Filed by repo-queue lane openchamber-b (queue task 7530 triage/fix investigation).

title: id(hosted_binding): create_pairing_code does not supersede earlier codes — multiple live pairing codes per challenge, none revocable

body:
## Problem

In `pkgs/id/src/hosted_binding.rs` (own-node ceremony variant, §3.3b), `create_pairing_code` (hosted_binding.rs:813) mints a fresh 6-digit pairing code for a challenge **without invalidating any previously minted codes for the same challenge**. Each code is stored independently in `pairing_codes` (insert at hosted_binding.rs:851-857; `PairingCode` records the `challenge_id`, hosted_binding.rs:390-397), and `exchange_pairing_code` (hosted_binding.rs:870) honours every live code — exchanging a code does not consume the challenge or any sibling code.

So one pending ceremony can have many simultaneously valid bearer codes (bounded only by `MAX_PAIRINGS_PER_HOUR` = 10 per account), each able to fetch the full challenge (sub, iroh_id, nonce) until the challenge's 5-minute expiry. The §3.3b flow describes *a* short-lived pairing code tied to the pending ceremony; nothing in the module documents multiple live codes per ceremony, and there is no way to revoke an earlier code (e.g. one displayed to the wrong screen, or mistyped into the wrong node) short of abandoning the whole challenge.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Re-verified by new-issue-creator lane A at origin/main 2194bd4c2 (laptop worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-03-laneA-hosted`, since removed; temporary integration test `pkgs/id/tests/probe_hosted_a.rs`, log `/tmp/probe-laneA-hosted.log` on the laptop):

- One challenge, two `create_pairing_code` calls: two distinct live codes (probe printed `096628` vs `017728`). Exchanging the first succeeded, exchanging the second also succeeded, and both returned the same challenge — the first code was not superseded or invalidated by minting the second, and neither exchange affected the other code.

Code reading at the same commit: `create_pairing_code` (hosted_binding.rs:813) never removes or marks existing `pairing_codes` entries whose `challenge_id` matches; the collision loop only avoids reusing a code string that is currently present. Originally found by lane B (creator-b) at 550b611eb; its filing was blocked by a GitHub secondary rate limit, so lane A re-verified and filed it.

## Why it matters

The pairing code is the bearer handoff between the authenticated browser session and the user's node. Keeping every previously minted code valid for the challenge's whole lifetime multiplies the exposure of a 6-digit (10^6) secret and defeats the natural user recovery action — "that code went to the wrong place, give me a new one" — because the old code keeps working. Binding still requires the root key's signature, so this is a hardening/contract gap rather than a direct takeover; it is cheap to fix now, in the slice that introduced the flow (#3808), before the Worker API slice (#3811) exposes it over HTTP.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Minting a pairing code for a challenge supersedes (invalidates) all previously minted, unexchanged codes for the same `challenge_id` — or the module docs are amended in the same change to state that multiple live codes per ceremony are intended, with the reasoning recorded.
- [ ] Regression test: code A minted, code B minted for the same challenge, exchanging A fails (`UnknownChallenge`), exchanging B succeeds and returns the challenge.
- [ ] Existing behaviour preserved: a single code still exchanges once and only once; per-account pairing rate limit unchanged; expired codes still return `ChallengeExpired` on exchange.
- [ ] Existing hosted_binding tests still pass (`cargo test -p id --lib hosted_binding`).

Found by new-issue-creator lane B (creator-b) during a scan of the newly landed #3808 module, re-verified and filed by lane A; not covered by #3808/#3809/#3811 as filed.

title: opencode-claimant: session create sends a top-level `directory`, which the v2 API ignores — launched workers land in /home/user, not the repo primary

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/queue-worker
labels.description: Filed or worked by the queue/worker pilot

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: app/pm-stack
labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Summary

`pm-stack/opencode-claimant/prompt.md` tells the claimant to create the worker session with a **top-level** `directory`:

```
POST /api/session with JSON body {"directory": <the repo's laptop primary>, "title": ..., "model": {...}, "agent": "build"}
```
(prompt.md:79-82)

The v2 OpenCode server does not accept a top-level `directory`. `session.create` decodes `location` (`Location.PublicRef` = `{directory}`) and strips unknown keys, so the field is silently dropped and the session is created at the server default location — `/home/user` — not the repo primary.

## Evidence

- `packages/protocol/src/groups/session.ts:221-234` — `session.create` payload is `{id, parentID, title, agent, model, location, metadata, permissions, subagentPolicy}`; there is no `directory` field.
- `pm-stack/dispatch/src/opencode.ts:52-58` — the working dispatch client sends `location: { directory: opts.directory }`.
- `pm-stack/opencode-claimant/prompt.md:79-82` — the claimant's instruction still says top-level `directory`.
- Observed sessions launched by the claimant with this shape:
  - task 7077 → `ses_e5e5ef40dccffesEpg4GoSqzeZ`, `location.directory=/home/user`
  - task 7316 → `ses_e5e5ef64873ffedhQFx8Dz4k6h`, `location.directory=/home/user`
  - task 3275 → `ses_e5e5fd27fa1ffeOpTSf2l3D84t`, `location.directory=/home/user`
  - all three resolve to project `a3b70b365cae…` (the `/home/user` project), not the code-repo project.

## Impact

Workers do still do the right work because the prompt text names the directory ("Work in /home/user/git/code"), but the session runs under the wrong project: the server's per-project context (AGENTS.md discovery, project attribution, session listing/aggregation by project) is the `/home/user` project. It also makes session→repo attribution in the aggregator unreliable, and it is why bound-session listings mix `dir=/home/user` and `dir=/home/user/git/code`.

## Fix

In `prompt.md` step 4b, replace the top-level `directory` with the v2 location object, keeping the model in the `model` object:

```json
{"title": "...", "location": {"directory": "<repo primary>"},
 "model": {"id": "workhorse", "providerID": "opencode-route"}, "agent": "build"}
```

A regression guard is worth having for the next launcher: assert that a created session's `location.directory` equals the requested repo primary before binding (the claimant can check the create response, which already returns `location`).

Found during the 2026-11-03 11:20Z fire of the opencode-claimant; this fire launched nothing because Supabase returned HTTP 544 (see the fire log), so the defect was documented rather than fixed inline.

title: id(hosted_binding): expired challenge is recorded as consumed — a second presentation returns ChallengeReplay, and create_pairing_code's documented ChallengeReplay branch is unreachable

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Problem

In `pkgs/id/src/hosted_binding.rs` (hosted account + ID binding ceremony, slice 1 of #3808), the handling of *dead* challenges (expired or consumed) contradicts the module's own §3.4 failure-semantics table in two places:

1. **An expired challenge is recorded as consumed on first presentation.** The module header (hosted_binding.rs:43-44) says "expired challenges die without state", and `CeremonyError::ChallengeExpired`'s own doc (hosted_binding.rs:415) says "State change: none; the challenge is dead." But the expiry branch of `submit_proof` (hosted_binding.rs:674-678) removes the challenge **and inserts its ID into `consumed_challenges`**. Observable consequence: presenting the same expired challenge a second time returns `ChallengeReplay` ("already presented") instead of `ChallengeExpired` — even though expiry was specified as creating no state. It also makes the consumed set retain IDs whose only sin was expiring.

2. **`create_pairing_code`'s `ChallengeReplay` branch is unreachable.** Its doc comment (hosted_binding.rs:807-812) promises `ChallengeReplay` for a dead (consumed) challenge. But the function first looks the challenge up in `self.challenges` and returns `UnknownChallenge` if absent (hosted_binding.rs:818-822), and only *then* checks `consumed_challenges` (hosted_binding.rs:823-825). Consumed challenges are always removed from `self.challenges` (`consume()`, hosted_binding.rs:769-772; the expiry branch above), so a consumed ID can never reach the replay check — the branch is dead code, and callers get `UnknownChallenge` for a challenge that was in fact consumed.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Re-verified by new-issue-creator lane A at origin/main 2194bd4c2 (laptop worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-03-laneA-hosted`, since removed; temporary integration test `pkgs/id/tests/probe_hosted_a.rs`, log `/tmp/probe-laneA-hosted.log` on the laptop):

- Expired challenge presented twice: first `Err(ChallengeExpired)`, second `Err(ChallengeReplay)` — expiry did create state (the consumed entry), contradicting the "state change: none" specification.
- Challenge consumed by a bad-signature submit (`Err(BadSignature)`), then `create_pairing_code` for it: `Err(UnknownChallenge)` — never the documented `ChallengeReplay`.
- Control: `create_pairing_code` for a live challenge succeeds.

Code reading at the same commit confirms the mechanism for both: expiry inserts into `consumed_challenges` (hosted_binding.rs:676); `create_pairing_code` checks the live map (hosted_binding.rs:820) before the consumed set (hosted_binding.rs:824), and `consume()` (hosted_binding.rs:769-772) always removes from the live map first. Originally found by lane B (creator-b) at 550b611eb; its filing was blocked by a GitHub secondary rate limit, so lane A re-verified and filed it.

## Why it matters

This module is the security ceremony that binds a Google identity to an Iroh root key. Its error taxonomy is the contract the §3.4 table specifies for clients and for the follow-up slices (rebind #3809, Worker API #3811): "expired" and "replayed" drive different client behaviour (plain retry vs. replay handling/logging). Today the two are conflated for expired challenges, one documented error can never be returned, and the consumed-ID set grows with expired IDs it was not specified to hold. The divergence is in brand-new code (landed today in #3808), so fixing the contract now is cheap; after slice 2/3 build on it, it is not.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Presenting an expired challenge repeatedly yields the §3.4-specified result for expired challenges on every presentation (per the table, expiry records no consumed state), OR the §3.4 docs/header/`ChallengeExpired` doc are amended in the same change to specify the recorded-as-consumed behaviour — code and docs agree either way, with the chosen semantics stated on the issue/PR.
- [ ] `create_pairing_code` for a consumed challenge returns the error its documentation promises (`ChallengeReplay`), i.e. the consumed check is reachable — regression test covers consumed, expired, unknown, and live challenges.
- [ ] Regression tests in `hosted_binding.rs`: expired challenge presented twice; pairing-code creation against a challenge consumed by a failed submit.
- [ ] Existing hosted_binding tests still pass (`cargo test -p id --lib hosted_binding`).

Found by new-issue-creator lane B (creator-b) during a scan of the newly landed #3808 module, re-verified and filed by lane A; not covered by #3808/#3809/#3811 as filed.

body:
Title: pm-stack(aggregator): dnsSectionFromRegisterJson accepts impossible renewal dates (2027-02-30, 2026-13-01) — the #2199 fix covered only the Markdown register path

## Problem

`parseDnsRegister` (the Markdown path) refuses impossible calendar renewal dates since the #2199 fix (PR #4835): `pm-stack/aggregator/src/dns.ts:56` requires `isIsoDate(renewal)` in addition to the `YYYY-MM-DD` shape, because an impossible date "string-sorts into the register, counts toward the annual total, and poisons nextRenewal / renewingSoon".

The JSON path — `dnsSectionFromRegisterJson`, whose register.json is *authoritative* for the fields it carries (`dns.ts:95-103`) — never got the same check:

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/dns.ts:135`: `if (typeof renewal !== "string" || !/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/.test(renewal)) return null;` — shape only, no `isIsoDate`.
- The shared section gate `isDnsSection` (`dns.ts:183`) likewise only requires `renewal` to be a string, so a section carrying an impossible renewal certifies as valid for the render paths.

That contradicts the function's own contract (`dns.ts:100-103`): "Returns null on ANY malformation … so the caller falls back to the Markdown parse instead of serving a half-invented register."

## Verified this run (laptop probe, origin/main 8e76c6fa5)

Probe script `/tmp/probe-dns.ts` on the laptop, importing `dnsSectionFromRegisterJson`, `isDnsSection`, and `summarizeDns` from current main, with a register.json containing `next_renewal` values `2027-02-30` ($20), `2026-13-01` ($30), `2024-02-29` ($5, valid leap date), and `2027-01-15` ($10):

```
SECTION_NULL: false
DOMAINS: leap.example,month13.example,real.example,feb30.example
TOTAL: 65
IS_DNS_SECTION: true
NEXT_RENEWAL: month13.example 2026-13-01
```

So the impossible rows are accepted, their $50 counts toward `totalAnnualListUsd`, the section passes `isDnsSection`, and `summarizeDns` (`dns.ts:232`, string comparison `e.renewal >= today`) reports the nonexistent `2026-13-01` as the next renewal — exactly the harm #2199 documented for the Markdown path.

## Why it matters

The JSON register is the authoritative source (#902 slice 2); a single bad `next_renewal` from the register job silently poisons the /dns totals, `nextRenewal`, and `renewingSoon` instead of falling back to the Markdown parse as the contract promises. The Markdown path was fixed for this exact failure mode in #4835; the authoritative path was left open.

## Acceptance criteria

- `dnsSectionFromRegisterJson` returns `null` when any row's `next_renewal` is shape-valid but not a real calendar date (e.g. `2027-02-30`, `2026-13-01`, `2026-00-10`, `2026-04-31`), falling back to the Markdown parse.
- Real dates still parse, including leap dates (`2024-02-29`).
- `isDnsSection` refuses an entry whose `renewal` is not a real calendar date.
- New tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/slice3.test.ts` mirror the #4835 Markdown cases for the JSON path (impossible dates refused, leap date kept); existing slice3 DNS tests stay green.

body:
## Two findings from the 2026-11-03 investigation of the auto-format redesign (#4731)

### 1. Scheduled runs have not fired since the redesign merged

- PR #4731 merged 2026-11-03T02:17:54Z, switching `auto-format.yml` to `schedule: "*/15 * * * *"` + `workflow_dispatch`.
- Since then: **zero** `schedule` runs (checked repeatedly through 2026-11-03T07:47Z, ~22 slots). The last schedule run is 2026-11-02T16:33:52Z, under the old design.
- The workflow's state is `active`, and other workflows' schedules in this repo fire normally (e.g. repo sweeper, 2026-11-03T03:56:36Z). `workflow_dispatch` runs work fine.
- Under the old design the nightly run also fired 7–10h late (cron `47 6 * * *` landing 13:05–16:33Z), so GitHub's scheduler appears to heavily delay this workflow specifically. Unknown whether the */15 schedule will fire late/bunched or never.
- Impact: formatting passes currently happen only when someone dispatches one. Drift accumulates in the meantime (formatting never gates merges, by design).

Options: (a) accept and drive passes from the laptop sync timer below (it can also dispatch), (b) investigate repo/org Actions settings for schedule throttling, (c) wait and see whether GitHub's scheduler starts firing late.

### 2. `record_success` can never succeed with the workflow's GITHUB_TOKEN

- The workflow's `record_success` PATCHes `AUTO_FORMAT_LAST_SUCCESS_SHA` with the GITHUB_TOKEN. It failed in the verification run (41565232921) and will always fail: **GitHub's workflow `permissions:` vocabulary has no key for repository variables.**
- Proven empirically 2026-11-03 on throwaway branches: adding `variables: write` or `vars: write` to `permissions:` makes GitHub reject the workflow file at parse time — `failed to parse workflow: Unexpected value 'variables'` (HTTP 422 on dispatch). Probe branches deleted after the test.
- The REST variables endpoints require a user-grade credential: a fine-grained PAT or GitHub App with the **Variables** repository permission, or a classic PAT with `repo` scope. The workflow token cannot be granted it.

### Mitigation installed (2026-11-03)

- Laptop user timer `auto-format-var-sync.timer` (every 15 min at :07/:22/:37/:52) runs `~/.local/bin/sync-auto-format-var.sh`: sets the variable to the newest successful run's verified point (its headSha, or the treefmt bot commit when the pass pushed one as the direct child of its head), using the owner's gh credentials. Monotonic — it never moves the variable backward, and it repairs values that are not commits.
- First run (2026-11-03T07:46:36Z) repaired the variable from `a56101c3…` — a SHA that is not a commit in this repo, set by hand during the PR #4752 work — to `8bd11c59` (the #4731 merge, the last pass-verified head).
- Source copies: `~/workspace/goals/keep-the-four-repos-healthy/hidden_files/auto-format-var-sync/` in hatch-personal.

### Correction to the #4731 verification record

Run 41565232921 did **not** push a bot commit: treefmt traversed the 4 candidate files and changed 0 (`formatted 0 files (0 changed)` / "treefmt made no changes"), then `record_success` hit the warning path described above. Earlier reports saying it "formatted 4 files and pushed" were wrong.

Related: #2014 (fleet-wide format auto-fix tracker). The workflow-only-exit gap in `record_success` was already fixed by #4752.

## Acceptance criteria

- A decision is recorded on this issue for finding 1: either the */15 schedule is observed firing (late/bunched counts, with run ids), or passes are driven by the laptop sync timer dispatching the workflow, or an Actions-settings cause is identified and fixed.
- `record_success`'s mechanism is settled: either the workflow no longer attempts the variables PATCH with GITHUB_TOKEN (the laptop sync timer is documented in the workflow/repo as the mechanism of record), or a credential with the Variables permission is provisioned and a verification run shows the variable advancing.
- The AUTO_FORMAT_LAST_SUCCESS_SHA variable only ever holds a verified commit SHA in this repo, advanced monotonically by the sync timer (or its successor).
- The correction to the #4731 verification record stands: no report claims a bot commit or formatted-file count that the run log does not show.

title: id(directory): confirm_email refuses re-confirming the account's own address as a Conflict, though its contract only refuses addresses another account holds

body:
## Problem

`Directory::confirm_email` (pkgs/id/src/directory.rs:667) refuses to re-confirm an email address that the **same account** already holds, returning `Refusal::Conflict` ("that address already belongs to an account") — even though its own documented contract says it fails only for "an address **another** account holds" (directory.rs:664-666).

The fold is the cause: `DirectoryEntry::AccountEmailConfirmed` in `change_mode` (directory.rs:1556-1566) guards with `self.account_for_email(email).is_none()`, and `account_for_email` (directory.rs:723) matches **any** account, including the confirming account itself. The final `emails.insert(...)` is a `BTreeSet` insert — idempotent — so nothing about the state requires the refusal.

The web flow has the same over-broad guard one layer up: `DirectoryAction::AddEmail` in pkgs/id/src/directory_view.rs:1241-1247 refuses to even issue a confirmation code when `account_for_email(&address).is_some()`, again including the requester's own address.

## Why the current behavior is the outlier

- The sibling `add_key` contract (directory.rs:613-615) deliberately says "a key held by **any** account already" — the email contract's "**another** account" is a different, deliberate wording, and the code does not implement it.
- Other re-applies in the same fold are idempotent-Ok: `AccountVerified` (directory.rs:1526) simply sets `verified = true` again; `GroupVisibility` re-setting the same value also applies cleanly. Email re-confirmation is the only one that turns a no-op repeat into a Conflict.
- Practical effect: a server-side confirmation retry (code re-sent / double submit / client retry after a lost response) for an address the account already confirmed fails as if someone else owned the address, with a message that falsely claims another account holds it.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe (scratch worktree at origin/main a41cba35d, unit probe added to directory.rs tests, removed after the run):

```text
directory.confirm_email(Actor::Server, &ann, "ann@example.com")  → Ok
directory.confirm_email(Actor::Server, &ann, "ann@example.com")  → Err("that address already belongs to an account")
PROBE reconfirm own email: Err(that address already belongs to an account)
test result: FAILED (assert is_ok) — 0 passed; 2 failed (lib + binaries)
```

Cross-checks from the existing test suite (directory.rs:2987-3007): confirming an address for a **different** account (Bo) correctly returns Conflict — that case must keep failing.

## Acceptance criteria

- `confirm_email` (and the `AccountEmailConfirmed` fold) succeeds when the address is already held by the **same** account (idempotent no-op success); it still returns `Refusal::Conflict` when a **different** account holds the address, and still refuses account actors and malformed addresses.
- `DirectoryAction::AddEmail` in directory_view.rs no longer refuses solely because the requester's own account already holds the address; another account holding it still returns Conflict before any code is issued.
- Regression tests: same-account re-confirm is Ok and leaves state unchanged; different-account confirm still Conflicts (existing test at directory.rs:3002-3006 stays green).
- `cargo test --lib directory` passes (laptop or CI).

## Dedup

Searched all states 2026-11-03 for `confirm_email`, `AccountEmailConfirmed`, "re-confirm email directory": no covering issue. Nearest hits are unrelated (#1732 closed — directory_auth pending-code eviction; #1521 closed — torn directory journal line).

title: patchelf 0.19.x corrupts Node SEA binaries (t3 0.1.2 segfaults; blocked the fleet switch)

body:
## Problem

patchelf 0.19.x corrupts Node SEA (single-executable) binaries. The `t3` package in `pkgs/latest-cli` (t3 0.1.2, a Node SEA build) is patched by `autoPatchelfHook`, which on the current nixpkgs pin drives patchelf 0.19.2. The rewritten binary segfaults at startup:

- The build's own `installCheck` (`t3 --version`) dies with SIGSEGV, exit 139.
- The same output binary segfaults when run directly on the host, outside any sandbox.
- Patching the pristine upstream binary by hand with patchelf 0.19.2 (only `--set-interpreter` + `--set-rpath`) reproduces the failure byte-for-byte (md5 `46ceed45f828c4d395fa167d553b1729`).
- Patching the same pristine binary with patchelf 0.15.2 produces a working binary. The older nixpkgs pin shipped 0.15.x, which is why earlier t3 builds in the store work.

This failure is what blocked the fleet `nixos-rebuild switch` on 2026-11-02 (retry attempt: `t3-0.1.2.drv` builder failure took down the toplevel closure). The first attempt also saw a builder segfault in `nodejs-24.22.1.drv` — possibly a relative of the same patchelf regression; worth a look if it recurs.

## Fix landed for t3

The t3 derivation now holds its main binary out of the hook's pass (moved aside in `preFixup`) and patches it in `preInstallCheck` with a pinned patchelf 0.15.2 built inline in `pkgs/latest-cli/default.nix`. The rest of the tree is still patched by the hook. Verified: package builds, installCheck passes, and the built server starts and serves HTTP 200.

## Wider hazard

Any other prebuilt SEA / pkg-style binary that enters the fleet through `pkgs/latest-cli` (or anywhere `autoPatchelfHook` runs on the current pin) will hit the same corruption, and most packages have no installCheck that would catch it — t3 was caught only because it checks `--version`. Worth auditing the other `latest-cli` entries for runtime smoke checks.


## Acceptance criteria

- An audit of the other `pkgs/latest-cli` entries (and any other fleet package where `autoPatchelfHook` runs on the current nixpkgs pin) identifies every prebuilt SEA / pkg-style binary that patchelf 0.19.x would rewrite, and the audit result is recorded on this issue.
- Each identified binary either gets a runtime smoke check (an installCheck or equivalent that actually executes the binary, like t3's `--version` check) or is held out of the hook's pass and patched with the pinned working patchelf, following the t3 pattern in `pkgs/latest-cli/default.nix`.
- A binary patched by the current pin is demonstrated to start successfully (no SIGSEGV) in CI or on the laptop before the fix is called done.
- The possibly-related `nodejs-24.22.1.drv` builder segfault from the first 2026-11-02 switch attempt is either reproduced and linked, or explicitly noted as not recurring.

body:
## Summary

Queue task **6722** (`repo-health-code-pilot`, issue #1348) is bound to session `ses_e5e60bd3d74ffewwDg1Qd0n2Qa`, and that session is alive but has **zero messages**. No rule in the claimant contract can unstick it:

- it is not a launch candidate (it carries `progress.session_id`, and `poll.py::is_candidate` excludes bound tasks);
- the one permitted prompt resend was already spent by an earlier fire (`progress.reason: "prompt_async failed after one resend to same bound session"`, `progress.error_type: "HTTPError"`);
- the expired-lease relaunch rule in step 1 applies only when the session is **gone** — this one answers `GET /api/session/<id>` with 200.

State observed 2026-11-03T04:43Z:

| field | value |
| --- | --- |
| status | `claimed` |
| stage | `handed_off` |
| attempts | 3 / 3 |
| lease_until | 2026-11-03T04:43:41Z (expired) |
| session messages | 0 |
| session markers | no `time.idle`, no `outcome`, `created == updated` (2026-11-03T04:35:14Z) |

## Impact

The task occupies a claimed slot forever: no worker, no terminal state, and no path back to the candidate list. Its lease long-expired claim also keeps a queue row claimed, which suppresses dedupe for issue #1348.

## Proposed fix

Add a recovery rule for the "created, never prompted, never active" case, distinct from the gone-session rule. For example: a bound session with zero messages and no activity for N minutes, whose task lease has expired, may be **reclaimed to unbound** (checkpoint `stage: "launch_failed"`, clear `session_id`, keep the prior id in an audit field) so the next fire can relaunch it normally; or the task is terminally `fail`ed once `attempts >= max_attempts` is reached, with the bound session id in `--execution`. Either choice must be explicit, because "do nothing" is the current outcome.

Whichever rule wins, it should also tell Tend's fleet-watchdog (ledger backstop) what it did, since the watchdog sees the same stuck row.

## Acceptance criteria

- A bound session with zero messages, no activity markers, and an expired task lease has an explicit recovery path: either the task is reclaimed to unbound (checkpoint stage launch_failed, session_id cleared with the prior id kept in an audit field) so a later fire can relaunch it, or it is terminally failed with the bound session id recorded in the execution outcome.
- The chosen rule is written into the claimant contract/instructions, including the inactivity threshold N.
- Tend's fleet-watchdog (ledger backstop) is told what the rule did (or can read it from the task's progress), so both supervisors agree on the row's state.
- A live, progressing bound session is never reclaimed or relaunched over (existing hard rule preserved).

title: id(fileops): archive tag namespace is not reserved — a user file named <name>.archive.<digits> is misclassified as an archive, hard-deleted by delete(<name>), and a put to an existing archive's name silently overwrites it

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.description: Triaged and routed (see agent note)

body:
## Summary

FileOps mints archive tags in a reserved-looking namespace — `<name>.archive.<unix-ts>` (`claim_archive_name`, `pkgs/id/src/fileops.rs:166`) — but nothing reserves that namespace against user-created files. `validate_name` (`fileops.rs:221-242`) rejects empty, rooted, drive-prefixed, and `.`/`..` names, but accepts archive-shaped names, and every consumer of the namespace then treats a user file with that shape as an archive:

1. **Misclassified in the web file list.** `classify_tag` (`pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs:153-184`) returns `(FileKind::Archive, Some(ts))` for any name ending in `.archive.<digits>` — a user file named `report.archive.1700000000` renders as an archive of `report`, sorted/grouped with archives, instead of as the primary file its owner created.
2. **Hard-deleted by deleting a different file.** `FileOps::delete` (`fileops.rs:496+`) collects the base name's archives by a prefix scan (`{name}.archive.` + all-digit suffix, `fileops.rs:523-545`) and via `archive.*` metadata references filtered by `is_archive_tag_name` (`fileops.rs:155-160`), then deletes those tags **and their metadata**. Deleting `report` therefore hard-deletes the independent user file `report.archive.1700000000` and its metadata with it.
3. **Archives can be silently overwritten.** `put` (`fileops.rs:307-318`) validates the name, then unconditionally `tags().set(name, hash)`. A put (directly, or as a rename/copy target — `validate_target` uses the same `validate_name`) to the exact name of an existing archive replaces the archived version's hash, destroying the one copy the archive mechanism exists to preserve, with no archive-of-the-archive and no error.

The non-numeric lookalike case is already defended and pinned by a test (`delete_only_removes_numeric_archive_suffixes`, `protocol.rs`: `a.archive.notes` survives `delete("a")` because the suffix is not digits). The numeric-suffix case — the only shape that actually collides — has no equivalent guard, because the guard lives in the *readers* (classification/delete) while the *writer* (`validate_name`) never got the reservation.

## Evidence (verified this run, origin/main `b882c9d5e`)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-archivename/` — verbatim extracts of `validate_name` and `is_archive_tag_name` from `fileops.rs` (blob md5 `721b667fe3bb56a6198e49328ea7b3b7`), `classify_tag`/`parse_iso_timestamp` from `web/routes.rs`, and `delete()`'s prefix-scan collection logic over an in-memory tag list. Results:

- `PROBE1 validate_name("report.archive.1700000000") == Ok (put accepts it): PASS` (controls: `"../x"` and `"  "` are rejected)
- `PROBE2 classify_tag("report.archive.1700000000") == (Archive, Some(1700000000)): PASS` (control: `"a.archive.notes"` classifies Primary)
- `PROBE3 delete("report") collects user file report.archive.1700000000 for deletion: PASS` (controls: `report.archive.notes` and `report2.archive.5` are spared)
- `PROBE4 is_archive_tag_name("report.archive.1700000000") == true: PASS`

## Why it matters

Archives are the only recovery copy when a file is replaced or renamed over (`archive_existing`, #1612/#2462 hardened their claiming precisely so a replaced version is never lost). A namespace collision breaks that guarantee in both directions: user data that merely *looks* like an archive is destroyed by an unrelated delete, and a genuine archive can be clobbered by an ordinary put — silently in both cases, since each operation reports success. Any surface that can create files (meta protocol Put/Rename/Copy, web routes, REPL — all funnel through `FileOps`) can trigger it, accidentally (a user naming an export `data.archive.2024`… the shape only needs trailing digits, e.g. `notes.archive.1`) or deliberately.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Creating a file whose name matches the archive shape (`<something>.archive.<all-digits>`) is refused with a clear error at the FileOps layer (`validate_name` / `validate_target`), so put, rename, and copy all inherit it; the error is distinguishable like the existing `InvalidName`/`EmptyName` variants.
- [ ] Regression test mirroring `delete_only_removes_numeric_archive_suffixes` from the writer side: put/rename/copy to an archive-shaped name fails, and a pre-existing archive tag's hash is unchanged after such an attempt.
- [ ] The chosen spelling rule matches the readers exactly (unsigned decimal digits only — no `+` sign, per #4329's note in `classify_tag`); non-numeric lookalikes such as `a.archive.notes` remain valid user files and still survive `delete("a")`.
- [ ] If reserving the namespace is judged too breaking, the alternative is implemented instead and this issue updated: archives move to a namespace users cannot mint (or delete/classify stop inferring archives from names alone and use the `archive.*` metadata references as the sole source) — with the same writer/reader agreement tests.

## Related

- #4574 (archive references orphaned by rename — different defect: metadata references travelling, not user files colliding with the archive namespace; this issue's `delete` archive-reference path is the `is_archive_tag_name` half of PROBE4)
- #1612 / #2462 (archive-name collision hardening for producer-minted names)
- #2793 / #4329 (classification-side spelling rules for archive suffixes)
