body:
## Problem

In `pkgs/id/src/currency_poc`, the terminal intent states are not enforced by the executor. A record the recovery scanner (or an operator) deliberately abandoned can be posted afterwards by nothing more than an identical retry — the abandon decision is silently undone and the money moves.

- `intent.rs:33-37` (origin/main) — `IntentState::Abandoned` is documented as "The scanner (or an operator) decided not to resubmit", and `is_unresolved()` (`:41-43`) treats it as resolved/terminal: the scanner will never look at the record again.
- `executor.rs:256-266` — `prepare()`'s never-replace guard compares a persisted record against the new request with the state deliberately normalised away (`comparable.state = record.state`, `:262-263`), so an identical request against an **Abandoned** (or already-**Posted**) record returns the existing record as-is, terminal state included.
- `executor.rs:284-307` — `submit()` never inspects `record.state` at all: it unconditionally overwrites it with `Submitted` (`:285`), submits the legs, and persists `Posted` (`:302`).
- `executor.rs:310-314` — `execute()` is `prepare()` + `submit()`, so the normal retry path composes the two gaps: retrying an abandoned conversion posts it.

`recovery.rs:129-136` is where `Abandon` lands: the record is persisted `Abandoned` precisely so the conversion does **not** happen (e.g. the rate authorisation is stale, an operator intervened). Nothing downstream of that decision checks it.

## Verified this run (laptop probe, verbatim origin/main sources)

Probe crate `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-abandoned/` on the laptop compiles the `currency_poc` modules extracted from `origin/main` (10e4ec1b7; blob-verified — `executor.rs` blob `0582e8ea`, md5 `500df828`; `intent.rs` md5 `d276f6cc`; `recovery.rs` md5 `8d40cf83`) against the in-repo `InMemoryLedger`/`InMemoryIntentStore`:

- **Probe A (retry resurrects):** `prepare()` a conversion (id 777) → `reconcile(RecoveryPolicy::Abandon)` returns `[(777, Abandoned)]`, stored state `Abandoned`, 0 legs in the ledger → an identical `execute()` retry returns `Ok` with state **`Posted`** and **3 legs** in the ledger.
- **Probe B (no guard in `submit` itself):** a record hand-set to `Abandoned` and persisted, passed directly to `submit()`, returns `Ok(())`, ends `Posted`, 3 legs posted.

`cargo test` on the probe: 2 passed (both probes assert the buggy outcome).

Note on provenance: the laptop primary's working tree is currently a dirty repo-keeper snapshot (local HEAD `04286381a`, off origin/main), so the probe was built from `git show origin/main:...` extractions, not the working tree; the cited line numbers are origin/main's.

## Why it matters

`Abandoned` is the recovery system's only "do not move this money" verdict. If any later identical retry — a client timeout retry, a caller re-running `execute()` after a crash it misread, an operator script — silently reverses that verdict and posts the conversion, the state machine's terminal states are decorative. The asymmetry is the tell: the scanner respects `Abandoned` forever (`is_unresolved` excludes it), while the executor ignores it completely, so the two halves of the same module disagree about what the state means. (Re-submitting an already-`Posted` record is harmless today only because every leg returns `Exists`; the missing guard is the same hole.)

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ConversionExecutor::submit` refuses a record in a terminal state (`Posted`, `Abandoned`) with an error naming the conversion and its state, instead of overwriting the state and submitting.
- [ ] `execute()` on a conversion whose persisted intent is `Abandoned` fails (does not post, state stays `Abandoned`); on an already-`Posted` intent it returns the posted record without resubmitting, or fails explicitly — either way the behaviour is deliberate and tested.
- [ ] Regression tests in `currency_poc/tests.rs`: abandon-then-retry (via `reconcile` + `execute`) posts nothing and leaves the record `Abandoned`; direct `submit()` on an `Abandoned` record errors; existing scenario tests still pass.

Related: #2289 (the PoC), #2063 (design), #4133 (leg-vector vacuous Posted, fixed). Distinct from #4669 (short result vector), #4664 (preflight gaps), #4578 (FileIntentStore listing).

title: id(world-replication): a journal whose Checkpoint line exceeds 256 KiB can never be replicated — split_entry_payload refuses the single entry and send_snapshot dies before the first frame

labels.name: task/small-fix

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

A world whose journal contains a single entry larger than `MAX_REPLICATION_PAYLOAD_BYTES` (256 KiB) can never be replicated over the new `/id-world-replication/1` feed (PR #4589, phase 2 of #806). `send_snapshot` splits the journal image with `split_entry_payload`, which refuses any *single entry* over the cap — and the one journal entry that routinely grows past it is the compaction `Checkpoint`: it carries the program's own state snapshot (uncapped) plus **all** retained events on one line. Once such a checkpoint exists, every replication stream for that world dies before the first frame, deterministically, on every reconnect; live subscribers are dropped the same way when the post-compaction `Reset` snapshot is sent.

## Evidence (origin/main `51535c2b4`)

- `pkgs/id/src/world/replication.rs:79` — `MAX_REPLICATION_PAYLOAD_BYTES = 256 * 1024`.
- `pkgs/id/src/world/replication.rs:164-192` (`split_entry_payload`): chunks are split only at entry (newline) boundaries; at `:179-181` a single entry with `entry_end - start > MAX` returns `ReplicationError::PayloadTooLarge`.
- `pkgs/id/src/world_replication_net.rs:197` (`send_snapshot`): `let chunks = split_entry_payload(&snapshot.bytes).context("split journal snapshot")?;` — the error ends the stream before any frame is written. The same function serves the `Reset` path, so a live stream dies at the reset after compaction too.
- `pkgs/id/src/world/mod.rs:874-908` — `JournalEntry::Checkpoint { .., snapshot: String, events: Vec<WorldEvent> }`: the program's state serialization and the retained events ride in this one entry.
- `pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs:731-743` (`checkpoint_entries`): the checkpoint's `events` is `self.events.iter().cloned().collect()` — **all** retained events (`WorldLimits::retained_events` defaults to 1024, `world/mod.rs:103`), with no byte budget applied to the entry (the `snapshot_bytes` budget at `world/mod.rs:80-83` bounds participant snapshot *frames*, not this journal entry).
- `pkgs/id/src/world/actor.rs:261-268` (`compact_journal`): `program.snapshot()` is journaled with no size check. Compaction is routine: `checkpoint_every` defaults to 1000 commits (`world/mod.rs:106`), and `compact_if_due` publishes the reset afterwards (`world/actor.rs:1618`, `:1630`).
- `pkgs/id/src/world_store.rs:242-245` — `FileJournal::compact` writes each entry as exactly one `serde_json` line, so the checkpoint is a single line in the journal file; `replication_snapshot` (`:206-218`) returns those exact bytes to `send_snapshot`.

So both growth routes land on the same line: a program whose serialized state exceeds ~256 KiB, or ~1024 retained events whose serializations sum past it. Neither is exotic for a long-lived world, and compaction is the normal state of such a world — precisely the worlds read replicas (#806) exist for.

## Reproduced this run (laptop probe)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-replcheckpoint/` on the laptop: `split_entry_payload` + the cap constant extracted verbatim from origin/main `51535c2b4` (snippet md5 `5dda768b`; source `replication.rs` md5 `99ceb4bf`), fed journal byte images in the exact on-disk shape (one `Created` line + one `Checkpoint` line):

- PROBE1 PASS: checkpoint line with a 300,000-byte program snapshot → `Err(PayloadTooLarge)` — the snapshot can never be sent.
- PROBE2 PASS (control): 100,000-byte snapshot → `Ok(1 chunk)`, chunks reassemble to the exact journal bytes.
- PROBE3 PASS (boundary): a single entry of exactly 262,144 bytes (incl. newline) → `Ok`; 262,145 bytes → `Err(PayloadTooLarge)`.

## Why it matters

The failure is silent from the replica's side (the stream just ends, with the error only in the server's debug log), total (no snapshot, no tail, no reset — the world is unreplicable, not degraded), and permanent (the checkpoint stays in the journal; retrying reproduces the identical refusal). It strikes exactly the worlds that have lived long enough to compact with substantial state — the ones whose writer most needs a surviving replica per #806's acceptance ("Replicas serve spectators while the writer is offline").

## Acceptance criteria

- A world whose compacted journal contains a `Checkpoint` entry larger than 256 KiB replicates end to end: a fresh subscriber receives the full snapshot and reaches the terminal cursor, and a live subscriber survives the post-compaction reset.
- The chosen mechanism (e.g. sub-entry payload splitting with the chain/cursor contract updated, a larger single-entry allowance within the 1 MiB transport frame bound, or a bounded checkpoint) is applied consistently to the snapshot, tail, and tracker-accept paths, and the replication module docs state the resulting per-entry guarantee.
- Regression test: a journal image whose checkpoint line exceeds `MAX_REPLICATION_PAYLOAD_BYTES` ( program-snapshot route and/or retained-events route) round-trips through the feed split/send path and is accepted by `ReplicationTracker` with a cursor that matches a recomputation from the journal bytes.
- Existing replication tests (`cargo test -p id --lib replication` and the world_store replication feed tests) still pass.

Related: #806 (the replication epic this feed implements), #4592/#4593 (replication admission contract — receiver side; this issue is the sender side).

body:
# id(world_line): the shared line grammar splits on whitespace for bare verbs but demands a literal space for argument verbs — a tab after /logs, /records, /documents, /document or /input is "unknown command" while /help<tab>me parses

## Summary

`pkgs/id/src/world_line.rs` is the single parser for the world's three surfaces (SSH `cmd:` mode, the `id world join` stdin pump, the `id world` CLI), so one sentence should parse identically everywhere. Its verb-boundary rule is internally inconsistent about tab separators:

- The bare verbs are matched on the first whitespace token (`split_whitespace().next()`, world_line.rs:52-58), so `/help\tme`, `/stats\tall`, `/quit\tnow`, `/caps\tlist` all parse.
- The argument verbs are matched with literal-space prefixes (`line == "/logs" || line.starts_with("/logs ")`, and the same shape for `/records`, `/documents`, `/document`, `/input` at :60-125), so `/logs\t5`, `/records\tfoo`, `/documents\tfoo`, `/document\treport.txt`, `/input\tab` all fall through to `Message("unknown command; type /help")`.

This contradicts both of the grammar's own stated rules:

- #1507 pinned `/logs\t5` → "unknown command" (test `glued_and_bare_verbs_do_not_parse_as_commands`), i.e. the boundary rule as decided there rejects the tab — but the bare verbs accept it for the same input shape.
- #1946's fix comment at world_line.rs:88-90 says "The separator is whitespace, not exactly one space" — but the implementation only accepts exactly the space character for argument verbs.

One of the two verb classes is wrong under either reading; today the answer depends on which verb a user happened to type.

## Evidence (this run, verbatim probe on the laptop)

Probe crate `probe-2026-11-02-laneB-worldline` (~/git/fleet/ on the laptop) compiled `parse_line` + `WorldLine` extracted verbatim from `pkgs/id/src/world_line.rs` at main 9c4ba5d6b (file md5 413096c48a245fe1354046394cc5a977, identical on sandbox and laptop clones):

```
"/help\tme"            => Some(Help)
"/stats\tall"          => Some(Stats)
"/quit\tnow"           => Some(Quit)
"/caps\tlist"          => Some(Caps)
"/logs\t5"             => Some(Message("unknown command; type /help"))
"/records\tfoo"        => Some(Message("unknown command; type /help"))
"/documents\tfoo"      => Some(Message("unknown command; type /help"))
"/document\treport.txt" => Some(Message("unknown command; type /help"))
"/input\tab"           => Some(Message("unknown command; type /help"))
"/logs 5"              => Some(Logs { seconds: Some(5) })   (space control)
"/document report.txt" => Some(Document("report.txt"))     (space control)
```

Pasted or script-generated lines are exactly where tabs appear (the stdin pump and SSH command mode both consume machine-fed lines), and the failure mode is the misleading "unknown command" for a verb that exists.

## Why it matters

The module's stated purpose is that the three surfaces cannot drift apart; an inconsistent boundary inside the one parser reintroduces the drift at the grammar level, and whichever rule is intended, one verb class currently violates it — including a pinned test (#1507) that contradicts the bare-verb behaviour for tab input.

## Acceptance criteria

- One verb-boundary rule for tab separators, applied uniformly to all verbs in `parse_line` (either whitespace boundaries everywhere, or literal-space-only everywhere with the bare verbs fixed to match).
- The chosen rule reconciles the #1507 pinned test and the #1946 separator comment: update whichever of the test/comment/code disagrees, so all three state the same rule.
- New tests cover tab-separated forms for at least one bare verb and one argument verb under the chosen rule.
- Space-separated behaviour is unchanged.

Distinct from #3134 (the join pump bypassing the grammar for /input) and #1507/#1946/#2189 (closed; boundary, multi-space, and bare-verb-argument cases respectively — none covers the tab split between verb classes).

body:
## Defect

The route proxy resolves the plan-backed GPT providers (`openai`, `openai.alternate`) to the wrong backend door.

code#3256 recorded that both provider blocks in the deployed config are empty shells. OpenCode tolerates that because its built-in `openai` provider wires the ACTIVE credential to its proper backend: `chatgpt-browser` (main) and `chatgpt-headless` (alternate) both talk to the ChatGPT/Codex backend, not to `api.openai.com`.

code PR #3830 closed the proxy symptom by adding built-in endpoint defaults in `bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs`, including `https://api.openai.com/v1` for `openai`. That is the PAYG platform door. Live proof on 2026-11-02 (see code#2518 evidence: https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/2518#issuecomment-6581998868) showed both GPT members answering 429 through the proxy, with the main leaf reporting "no credits remaining" from the platform door, while the fork's internal routing to the same plans works.

## Required fix

The proxy must resolve a leaf provider the way OpenCode itself resolves it: provider + its active credential determines the backend. No invented vendor defaults.

- Configured `baseURL` wins when present.
- Otherwise use built-in resolution keyed by the provider's ACTIVE credential type: `chatgpt-browser` / `chatgpt-headless` -> ChatGPT/Codex backend using the fork's exact request contract; a genuine platform/API-key credential -> platform door.
- Remove the `api.openai.com` default for plan-backed providers.
- Fail closed on unresolvable leaves. NEVER fall back to the PAYG API door.

## Acceptance

- Proxy tests cover the credential-keyed resolution and the fail-closed behavior.
- After merge + one restart of `opencode-route-proxy.service`, live proof on production :18750: `terra-plan` reaches the Codex backend (main member success, or a genuine Codex-backend plan/quota response); the alternate member's wall (weekly, until Nov 6) presents as the Codex backend's quota response, never "no credits remaining" from api.openai.com.
- OpenCode session counts in opencode.db unchanged across the proof; route_attempt rows recorded with `session_id` NULL.


## Acceptance criteria
- The route proxy resolves the `openai` and `openai.alternate` leaves by their active credential the way OpenCode does — to the ChatGPT/Codex backend (chatgpt-browser / chatgpt-headless) — and never defaults a plan-backed provider to `https://api.openai.com/v1`.
- A route attempt through the proxy for both GPT providers reaches the credential-backed backend: no platform-door 'no credits remaining' 429 of the kind recorded on issue #2518 while the same plans answer via the fork's internal routing.
- Proxy tests cover provider resolution by active credential, including the case where a leaf's config block is an empty shell (issue #3256).

body:
## Summary

`pkgs/id` chat presence caps a heartbeat at `MAX_HEARTBEAT_CHANNELS` (64) channels, but the receive path applies that cap to the **raw** channel list without deduplicating first — while the constructor deduplicates before capping. A wire heartbeat whose channel list repeats one channel 64 times and then names a second, genuinely distinct channel is stored with only the repeated channel: the distinct channel is silently dropped, and the node reads as not present in it, even though the heartbeat names just 2 distinct channels, far under the cap.

## Evidence (verified this run, main d1de7ee86; `chat_presence.rs` md5 68590664a175bd4a17937c28a2f0fb6b, unchanged at this HEAD)

- `PresenceHeartbeat::new` (pkgs/id/src/chat_presence.rs:110-118) deduplicates `channels` into `unique` first, and only then truncates to `MAX_HEARTBEAT_CHANNELS` — so a constructed heartbeat keeps up to 64 **distinct** channels.
- `PresenceTable::update_at` (chat_presence.rs:261, channels filter at :273-279), the receive path for heartbeats decoded from the wire (which never pass through `new`), does `.filter(is_member).take(MAX_HEARTBEAT_CHANNELS)` on the raw list — no dedup step — so duplicate entries consume cap slots.
- `MAX_HEARTBEAT_CHANNELS` (chat_presence.rs:74-77) is documented as "The most channels one heartbeat may name" — a bound on distinct channels, which the receive path does not deliver.
- Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-presencechannels/` (verbatim `chat_presence.rs`, md5 68590664a175bd4a17937c28a2f0fb6b, matching current main; same stub harness as the #3991 probe):
  - Control: `PresenceHeartbeat::new(node, [A×64, B], …)` → `channels.len() = 2`, B kept.
  - Wire shape: the same list round-tripped through `encode_frame`/`decode_frame` (65 raw entries) and accepted by `update_at` → `liveness_at(node, A) = Live`, `liveness_at(node, B) = Offline`. B was crowded out by the duplicates.
  - Second shape: `[A×63, B, C]` (3 distinct) via the wire path → B `Live`, C `Offline`; the constructor with the same list keeps all 3.

## Why it matters

Presence correctness depends on the stored channel set being the set the heartbeat actually claims. On the receive path — the only path untrusted wire data takes — that set is currently "the first 64 raw entries", so a buggy or crafted (but validly self-signed; the sender signs its own heartbeat, so `verify()` passes) heartbeat loses presence in channels it genuinely belongs to, with no error anywhere: the heartbeat is accepted, the node simply never shows as live in the displaced channels. It also makes the stored `channels` list a multiset rather than the set the type documents, so any future consumer that iterates or counts it inherits the duplicates. The constructor already implements the intended semantics; the receive path diverges from it.

## Acceptance criteria

- `PresenceTable::update_at` deduplicates a decoded heartbeat's `channels` (preserving first-seen order, as `new` does) before the `MAX_HEARTBEAT_CHANNELS` cap is applied, so the cap bounds distinct channels on the receive path just as in the constructor.
- Stored heartbeats never contain duplicate channel entries, regardless of the path they arrived by.
- Regression tests: a wire-shaped heartbeat with `[A×64, B]` is stored present in both A and B; a heartbeat with `[A×63, B, C]` is stored present in all three; existing chat_presence tests keep passing.

Distinct from: #3991 (the `typing` list is never deduplicated or bounded — a frame-size/DoS gap in the sibling field; this issue is the `channels` list on the receive path, where duplicates displace distinct channels rather than inflate the frame), #4004 (PresenceTable node-count bound), #4363 (receive path does not scope heartbeats to sender membership — `update_scoped` has no production caller).

- `openai-plan/gpt-6-luna` is attempted as provider `openai-plan` and fails instantly: "no endpoint configured for provider openai-plan" (route_attempt error_tag UnknownProvider). openai-plan is a provider_routes entry (providers [openai.alternate, openai], ordered) - the OpenCode server router expands it correctly (route_decision for luna-plan chooses it sticky; ~49k openai + ~2.8k openai.alternate Luna successes in the same 24h), but the proxy does not expand it.
- `opencode-go/gpt-6-luna` (base workspace leaf) fails "no credential for provider opencode-go" in the proxy context (it rides the Lab login when the server router resolves it).
- `opendesign/gpt-6-luna` fails "no credential for provider opendesign".

Effect: direct proxy calls waste 3+ attempts (and add quota-failure noise to the demotion ledger) before reaching a working leaf. Failover eventually lands, so this is latency/noise, not an outage - but the demotion accounting counts these as leaf failures.

Fix direction: when the proxy expands a plan route, expand nested provider_routes entries (openai-plan) into their member providers, and skip leaves the proxy cannot credential rather than attempting them - or reuse the server's expansion wholesale.

Evidence: route_attempt ids 115071-115082 (2026-11-02 ~12:46Z), route_id workhorse-primary, session_id NULL.

## Acceptance criteria
- When the standalone route proxy expands a plan route, nested `provider_routes` entries (e.g. `openai-plan`) are expanded into their member providers instead of being attempted as providers themselves.
- Leaves the proxy cannot credential in its own context are skipped without an attempt, and are not recorded as leaf failures in the demotion ledger.
- A direct proxy call to model `workhorse-primary` reaches a working leaf without burning attempts on `openai-plan`, `opencode-go`, or `opendesign` as configured in the evidence.
- The OpenCode server router's existing (correct) expansion behaviour is unchanged.

title: id(outbox): Outbox::open replay accepts state transitions the live API refuses — a finished entry can be re-attempted, overwritten, and an attempted entry withdrawn

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`Outbox::open` replays the `outbox.jsonl` journal through `Outbox::apply` (`pkgs/id/src/envelope_outbox.rs:329-371`), which applies each record's fields unconditionally. The live API refuses the same transitions:

- `Outbox::record` refuses to record any outcome for a finished entry ("envelope {id} already finished", `envelope_outbox.rs:285-287`).
- `Outbox::withdraw` refuses an attempted or finished entry ("was already attempted", `envelope_outbox.rs:267-274`).
- `Outbox::record` derives `attempts` itself, always `entry.attempts + 1` (`envelope_outbox.rs:287`).

Replay enforces none of this. A journal containing those records — from a damaged store, a hand repair, an older/newer writer, or a future bug in a second writer — is silently accepted and produces entry states the live code can never produce.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe @ fc34d3af)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-outboxreplay/` (worktree of origin/main fc34d3af5; `envelope_outbox.rs` md5 `db129e3cb9e410afcf31f4363f024dba`, identical in the probe and the laptop primary). Probe tests append crafted journal lines after a real `enqueue`, then reopen:

- PROBE1 — journal `finished(delivered, attempts 1)` → `attempted(attempts 7)` → `finished(gave_up, attempts 8)`: replayed entry is `finish=Some(GaveUp) attempts=8 last_error=Some("overwritten")`. A delivered delivery is retroactively rewritten as gave-up, and a finished entry gains later attempts.
- PROBE2 — journal `attempted(attempts 5)` → `attempted(attempts 2)`: replayed entry is `attempts=2`. The attempt count skips and then regresses, so the `attempts >= MAX_ATTEMPTS` give-up rule in `record` (`envelope_outbox.rs:303`) can be bypassed or re-armed by journal contents alone.
- PROBE3 — journal `attempted(attempts 1)` → `withdrawn`: replayed entry is gone, although live `withdraw` refuses exactly this.
- PROBE4/PROBE5 (controls) — the live path refuses both: `record` after finish errors, `withdraw` after an attempt errors. All 4 probe tests pass (`cargo test --no-default-features --lib outbox_probe`, 517 lib tests pass overall).

Contrast in the same codebase: `Directory::replay` runs journal entries through the same checked transition function as live writes (`directory.rs` `change_mode` conflict/refusal checks, with the test `replay_rebuilds_the_directory_and_refuses_a_broken_journal`). The outbox journal is the only one of the sibling loaders whose replay path performs no transition checking at all — its replay care stops at torn-line handling (#1620).

## Why it matters

The outbox is the durable record of what this server still owes other servers. Its state decides redelivery: a finished entry rewritten to `gave_up`, an attempts count regressed below `MAX_ATTEMPTS`, or an attempted entry withdrawn all change what gets delivered, silently, at the next restart — with no error anywhere. Every other journal in this open path treats replay as admission and refuses a broken journal loudly; the outbox should meet the same bar.

## Acceptance criteria

- `Outbox::open` refuses (with the line/record identified, in the style of the existing "envelope outbox line N is corrupt" error) a journal whose records violate the live state machine: an `attempted` or second `finished` record for a finished entry; a `finished` record whose outcome would overwrite an earlier finish; an `attempted`/`finished` record whose `attempts` is not exactly the entry's previous attempts + 1; a `withdrawn` record for an attempted or finished entry.
- Journals written by the current live code replay unchanged (all existing outbox tests pass, including the torn-tail and blank-line cases).
- New tests cover each refused transition above, plus the matching accepted sequences, mirroring the Directory replay tests.
- Design note: if some historical journal shape legitimately needs tolerance (as Directory's #1778 Cf case did), name it explicitly in a replay-only allowance rather than leaving replay unchecked.

title: id(shell-contract): parseShellContract never validates top-level fields — missing routing_fields/projection throw TypeError at check time, missing max_frame_bytes silently disables the frame cap

labels.name: task/triage

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/normal

body:
## Problem

`parseShellContract` in `pkgs/id/web/src/shell-contract.ts` (line 115) validates every client/server **field spec** at load — that was the #4238 / #2657 fix, so a malformed spec cannot make `checkValue` throw later. But it never validates the contract's **top-level fields**: it checks only that `client_frames`/`server_frames` are objects with object `fields`, then returns `value as unknown as ShellContract` (line ~141). The Rust checker it ports (`pkgs/id/src/shell_contract.rs`, `RawContract` at lines 238–249) requires all of these with no `#[serde(default)]`: `max_frame_bytes: usize`, `routing_fields: Vec<String>`, and `projection.redacted_keys: Vec<String>`. A contract document the Rust side refuses to load is accepted by the TS side, and the failure surfaces later — as a thrown `TypeError` instead of a recorded violation, or as a silently disabled check.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-shellcontract/`, verbatim `shell-contract.ts` @ main `8052d96f`, md5 `59dc2d096669f95b8ef29f714d1ea8d2`, real `contract/shell-contract.v1.json`, bun). Controls on the unmodified contract behave: a valid `join` passes, a 1,100,041-byte frame is rejected with "frame of 1100041 bytes exceeds 1048576", and a `world_state` frame with `seed: 7` is rejected as a projection leak.

With top-level fields removed or mistyped, `parseShellContract` accepts every variant:

- **`routing_fields` deleted** → `checkClientFrame` **throws** `TypeError: undefined is not an object (evaluating 'routing.includes')` (line 226) instead of returning a `Check`/recording a violation.
- **`projection` deleted** → `checkServerFrame` **throws** `TypeError` (evaluating `contract.projection.redacted_keys`, line 298). Same throw when only `projection.redacted_keys` is deleted.
- **`max_frame_bytes` deleted** → the frame-size cap is silently off: the same 1,100,041-byte frame no longer gets the size error and falls through to field checking ("`join` has no field `pad`").
- **`max_frame_bytes: -1`** → accepted; then *every* frame is rejected ("frame of 32 bytes exceeds -1"). Rust's `usize` refuses this document at load.
- **`routing_fields: "world"`** (a string, not an array) → accepted; `String.includes` then does substring matching, so a frame field named `orl` is treated as a routing field ("routing field `orl` must be a string").

## Why it matters

The shell contract is the conformance boundary between shell and host: the size cap, the routing-field exemption, and the redacted-key leak check (`seed` must never reach a session nonzero) are three of its load-bearing checks. All three depend on top-level fields the TS parser never validates, so a truncated, hand-edited, or version-skewed contract document either crashes the checker mid-session with an uncaught `TypeError` or quietly disables the cap/leak checks — precisely the failure mode #4238 fixed for field specs, one level up.

## Acceptance criteria

- `parseShellContract` rejects, with a named error at load time: missing/non-object `projection`, missing/non-string-array `projection.redacted_keys`, missing/non-string-array `routing_fields`, and missing/non-finite/negative `max_frame_bytes`.
- After the fix, no input to `parseShellContract` can make `checkClientFrame`/`checkServerFrame`/`Conformance` throw a `TypeError` from these fields; malformed contracts fail at parse, malformed frames return violations.
- Regression tests in `pkgs/id/web/src/world-contract.test.ts` cover each case above (missing routing fields, missing projection, missing redacted_keys, missing/negative frame cap, string routing fields), mirroring the existing field-spec tests added by #4238.
- The real `contract/shell-contract.v1.json` still parses and all existing shell-contract tests pass.

body:
## Phase 4 (audit) of design #4202 — closing field-by-field disposition for pkgs/id app_manifest

Parent design: #4202 ("the app folder is the unit of trust — one gate for what an app manifest may name"). Design doc: `files/designs/code-id-app-manifest-folder-contract.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Audit baseline: origin/main `cc5effd8`.

**Gated on Phases 1–3 of the design**: Phase 1 = #4059 + #4067 (folder confinement: `[resources].files` under `program.source`'s component rule; symlinked folders resolved and contained), Phase 2 = #4085 + #4168 (one entry rule for every list field — non-blank, unpadded, no duplicates), Phase 3 = #4060 + #4061 (route/socket shape + uniqueness across the discovered set; missing root as a named error). Do not start the inventory before all three land.

## Scope

A field-by-field disposition of `pkgs/id/src/app_manifest.rs` against the #4202 contract, recorded in the module doc: every `AppManifest` field (`app.id/name/version/description`, `program.kind/source/module_hash`, `interfaces.cli.commands`, `interfaces.web.mode/route/socket`, `capabilities.request`, `resources.files`) and every `discover_apps` behaviour (root read, entry filtering, per-app error isolation, the `program.source` existence check, sort order), each dispositioned as gated-by-a-named-rule / deliberately ungated with the reason.

Required dispositions (named in the design; each must be answered explicitly, not passed over):

1. **Symlinks inside a real app folder** — the posture for the `program.source` existence check and for pack-time `[resources].files` resolution (the pack step's confinement question): state the discovery-side rule and name the pack step as the owner of the pack-time half, or file it.
2. **Empty `files = []`** — decision 3 of #4202 keeps it legal (optional section, packages nothing); record the posture in the module doc so it is deliberate, or file the change if the inventory shows a consumer that reads it as a defect.
3. **Route edge spellings** — trailing slash, `//` segments, `route = "/"`: disposition each against the Phase 3 segment-sanity rule (holds / tightened here if small / filed).
4. **App-`id` uniqueness** — structural via the folder-name-equality check (one folder name, one directory entry): state it in the module doc, do not add a redundant check.
5. **`[program].kind` vocabulary** — a free string today with one checked-in value ("roc-world"): disposition only (no enumeration without a second kind).
6. **Uniqueness against the host's own routes** — #4202 decision 4 leaves this to #2325's binding (it owns the host route table): record that disposition and confirm #2325's scope names it, or file the gap.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The disposition table is in the `app_manifest.rs` module doc, covering every field and discovery behaviour above, each cell dispositioned (gated by rule / deliberately ungated with reason / filed follow-up).
- [ ] All six required dispositions are answered explicitly in the table.
- [ ] A summary with any findings is posted on design #4202.
- [ ] Any confirmed same-shape gap (a field a consumer trusts that no rule gates, a discovery behaviour that can fail silently) is either fixed under this issue — only if small and within one field — or filed as a named follow-up issue linked from #4202. Never left as a comment-only finding.
- [ ] No behaviour changes beyond the dispositions taken; existing app_manifest tests still pass (CI).

🤖 Filed by the design architect (pass 36, 2026-11-01) as Phase 4 (audit) of design #4202.

- `pkgs/id/src/chat.rs:43`: `use crate::world::sanitize_chat;` (used at :155 and :180) — `crate::world` is `#[cfg(feature = "world")]` (src/lib.rs:233-234), so the import is unresolved without the feature: `error[E0432]: unresolved import crate::world`.
- `pkgs/id/src/invite.rs:43`: `crate::petname::is_format_char` in `Invite::new` — the `petname` re-export is `#[cfg(feature = "world")]` (src/lib.rs:207-208): `error[E0433]: cannot find petname in crate`.

## Verification (2026-11-02, queue worker lane D, task 5043)

On clean main bc0afe2f5c642501a01823adb237ee6fc9298d32 (laptop worktree, no modifications):

```
cargo check --no-default-features --lib   (in pkgs/id)
error[E0432]: unresolved import `crate::world`
error[E0433]: cannot find `petname` in `crate`
```

The same two errors block `cargo test --no-default-features --lib <any test>` — this is what prevents the #1708 acceptance variant 1 (`world_names_are_bounded_and_are_a_single_path_segment` without default features) from even compiling, independent of the test gating fixed by PR #4028 (merged 21dd7cc3f). With `--features world` the focused test passes.

## Why it matters

The no-default-features build is a supported configuration (the #1708 test matrix names it). Right now it is silently broken at the lib level: any contributor running the reduced-feature build hits compile errors in modules unrelated to their change, and feature-gated test coverage (like the world-name test) cannot run in that configuration at all.

## Acceptance criteria

- `cargo check --no-default-features --lib` succeeds in pkgs/id on main.
- `cargo test --no-default-features --lib world_names_are_bounded_and_are_a_single_path_segment` compiles and passes (the test itself is feature-gated by PR #4028; it must not assert world-only behaviour when the feature is absent).
- The fix preserves behaviour with default/world features: chat sanitisation and invite name validation semantics unchanged (e.g. move `sanitize_chat` / `is_format_char` to an ungated home, or gate the dependent code — pick the smaller, semantics-preserving option and pin it in the PR).
- Existing test suites in the default configuration still pass.

## Dedup

Found during task 5043 (the #1708 fix) on 2026-11-02. Searched open + closed for no-default-features / sanitize_chat / petname coverage — none found. Distinct from #1708 (the serve.rs test gating, fixed by PR #4028).

body:
## Finding

Codex review on PR #4099 (round 2, 2026-11-02) flagged a quadratic lookup in the membership layer replay added for issue #165:

- `pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/membership/layer.rs`: when a concurrent create displaces the standing create, the layer re-decides held events in canonical order and finds each event's latest outcome by scanning the accumulated `latest` vector — O(N²/2) event-ID comparisons over a history of N events.
- This is on a production path: `event_store::resolve` feeds the entire history into the layer, and both `EventStore::roster` and `ingest::refresh` invoke that resolver, so the cost repeats on subsequent resolutions once conflicting creates are retained.

## Fix

Index replay outcomes instead of scanning: keep a hash-indexed outcome-position map (event ID -> position in `latest`), or append outcomes directly when they cannot repeat. Preserve the exact canonical-order semantics and the latest-outcome-per-event truth rule from PR #4099.

## Acceptance

- Replay outcome lookup is O(1) amortized per event (map-based), with the existing PR #4099 convergence tests (both arrival orders, derived friendship group ID) still passing.
- A test or benchmark note demonstrating the replay no longer scans `latest` per event.

Filed by queue worker lane A (task 2950) as the tracked follow-up for the Codex P2 disposition on PR #4099.

## Acceptance criteria

- The membership layer replay in `pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/membership/layer.rs` no longer finds each event's latest outcome by scanning the accumulated `latest` vector: outcomes are hash-indexed (event ID -> position) or appended under a proven no-repeat invariant.
- Replay verdicts are byte-identical to the scanning implementation for the same event histories (existing membership/layer tests pass unchanged; a conflicting-create history is covered).
- The fix lands on or after PR #4099's layer code (it is a follow-up to that PR's replay), not as a conflicting rewrite of it.

body:
Found during the task 4848 differential for #659 (PR #3781, 2026-11-01): three accepted IDN spellings where the container validator's returned host still differs from the Worker's WHATWG return, all on the stdlib-IDNA-codec path in `pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py` (`_return_label`: `candidate.encode("idna")` — IDNA2003 nameprep, Unicode 3.2 tables), not the punycode fallback fixed in PR #3781.

Reproduction (container return vs `new URL().href`):

| Spelling | Container | Worker (WHATWG/UTS-46) |
|---|---|---|
| `http://ß.com/` | `http://ss.com/` | `http://xn--zca.com/` |
| `http://ς.com/` | `http://xn--4xa.com/` (σ) | `http://xn--3xa.com/` (ς) |
| `http://ꭰ.com/` (U+AB30) | `http://xn--kz9a.com/` | `http://xn--58d.com/` |

Causes: nameprep maps ß→ss (UTS-46 nontransitional keeps ß) and final sigma ς→σ (UTS-46 keeps ς; only U+03F2 maps to σ), and the codec's Unicode 3.2 tables encode newer/changed codepoints differently from current UTS-46.

These change the domain the fetcher resolves versus the one the Worker certified — the same defect class as #659/#665, different mechanism.

Acceptance:
- A Python↔WHATWG differential over these spellings (and neighbours: ß in multi-label hosts, ς/σ/ϲ family, post-3.2 codepoints) shows no returned-host differences.
- All existing pinned returns stay green (`test_container_validate.py`, including the #659 A-label tests and the #652/#660/#667 families) — in particular ϲ.com must keep returning xn--4xa.com.
- Judging (accept/refuse) is unchanged; only the returned form moves.

## Acceptance criteria

- For the three filed spellings, the container validator returns the same host as the Worker (WHATWG/UTS-46): `ß.com` → `xn--zca.com`, `ς.com` → `xn--3xa.com`, `ꭰ.com` (U+AB30) → the current UTS-46 punycode, verified by a differential test against `new URL().href`.
- The fix replaces or corrects the stdlib IDNA2003 nameprep path in `pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py` (`_return_label`) rather than special-casing the three filed inputs.
- Existing lab-ops-hub container validator tests pass, and the PR #3781 punycode-fallback behavior is unchanged.
- A regression differential (container vs Worker) over the filed cases is added to the test suite.

title: id(design #3455): plain_field escape form corrupts supplementary-plane Cf — surrogate-pair escaping not specified

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

body:
## Finding (from PR review, unaddressed)

Codex P2 on PR #3861 — **Specify surrogate-pair escaping for supplementary Cf characters**

> For supplementary-plane Cf characters such as U+110BD and U+E0001, extending `plain_field` to use its existing escape branch would silently corrupt the represented value. That branch in `pkgs/id/src/commands/text.rs` uses `write!(rendered, "\\u{:04x}", u32::from(c))`, so U+110BD becomes `\u110bd`, which a JSON parser reads as U+110B followed by `d`, rather than the original character. The shared set includes these characters, but the proposed test criteria cover only BMP examples. Explicitly require surrogate-pair escaping and supplementary-plane JSON round-trip tests rather than prescribing the existing escaped form unchanged.

- Source PR: #3861 "design(id): #3455 shared Cf contract for plain output" — https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/3861 (merged 2026-11-01T17:10:07Z; the Codex review landed after the merge)
- Comment: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/3861#discussion_r4436581752 — chatgpt-codex-connector[bot], 2026-11-01T17:11:28Z, on `doc/2026-11-01_design_id3455.md:142`
- Parent design issue: #3455; Phase 1 implementation issue: #2839

## No-response evidence

- The review thread is unresolved (GraphQL `reviewThreads`: `isResolved=false`) and has no replies — the inline comment is the only comment in its thread.
- No fix followed: the PR merged before the comment was posted, and the design doc on current main is unchanged on this point (see below).

## Still live on current main (verified 2026-11-01, origin/main 9e1be52063)

- `doc/2026-11-01_design_id3455.md` §3 step 2 still prescribes: "In `plain_field`, treat Cf as a reason to use the existing quoted/escaped representation" — with no mention of surrogate pairs or supplementary-plane characters anywhere in the document (grep for surrogate/supplementary/U+110BD/U+E0001: no hits). Its §4 acceptance tests cover only BMP examples (bidi overrides/isolates including U+202E, zero-width/join controls).
- `pkgs/id/src/commands/text.rs:83` still has the escape branch the comment flags: `let _ = write!(rendered, "\\u{:04x}", u32::from(c));` — a `\u` escape followed by 5–6 hex digits for any character above U+FFFF, which a JSON parser reads as the first four hex digits' code point plus literal trailing characters.
- The shared Cf set the design adopts (`is_format_char`, `pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/petname.rs`) explicitly includes supplementary-plane Cf: U+110BD, U+110CD, U+13430–U+1343F, U+1BCA0–U+1BCA3, U+1D173–U+1D182, U+E0001, U+E0020–U+E007F. So a Phase 1 implementation (#2839) that follows the design literally will silently corrupt exactly those characters in quoted output — the value the design promises "remains represented" would not round-trip.

Dedupe (2026-11-01): searches for surrogate / supplementary / plain_field / 110BD / "Cf contract" across open and closed issues found no issue covering surrogate-pair escaping. #2839's acceptance criteria cover BMP Cf only (U+202A–U+202E, U+2066–U+2069, U+200E/U+200F, U+200B, U+FEFF); #3455 is the parent design this issue refines.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The #3455 design contract (doc and/or #2839's scope) explicitly requires supplementary-plane Cf characters to be escaped as JSON surrogate pairs (`\uXXXX\uXXXX`) — or another form that provably round-trips — rather than the existing `\u{:04x}` form unchanged.
- [ ] JSON round-trip tests cover at least one supplementary-plane Cf character (e.g. U+110BD or U+E0001): the escaped `plain_field` output parses back as JSON to the original character.
- [ ] Or: this is resolved by a documented decision on this issue explaining why supplementary-plane Cf cannot reach the escaped path.

Found by Codex review round 4 on PR #3918 (comment 4437512013), dispositioned there as a follow-up because the fix (complete HTML5 named-reference data + semicolon-omission rules) is larger than a review-fix round. Sibling of #569. ## Evidence (verified against the container Extractor, Python 3.13.13) Input: `Α &

→ A & B

` - Container: title `Α &`, text `→ A & B` - Worker fallback: every reference preserved literally ## Scope - Decode the complete HTML5 named character references (the data behind Python's html.entities.html5), including the legacy semicolon-less forms and the spec's semicolon-omission rules for text content (e.g. `A` -> `A`, `&` -> `&` in the cases html.unescape expands). - Keep the existing numeric-reference normalization (C1 remap, U+FFFD rules) intact. - Add shared parity fixtures (test/extractor-fixtures.json) pinning the cases above plus a spread of named references; expected values verified against the container suite before pinning. ` yields title `Α &` and text `→ A & B` from the Worker fallback, identical to the container Extractor. - A differential test corpus (named references with/without semicolons, numeric references with/without semicolons, ambiguous ampersands in text and in attribute-like contexts) matches `html.unescape` output case for case. - Existing extractor test suites pass; no change to the container Extractor.

Parent chain: #1184 → #1256 → this issue. GitHub currently caps #1184 at 100 direct sub-issues and rejects additional links (REST 422), so implementation slices are nested under #1256, already a native child of #1184; no existing parent links were changed.

Design context: #1256; `doc/2026-11-01T21-07-00Z_design_pm-stack_forecasting/2026-11-01T21-07-00Z_design_pm-stack_forecasting.md` (§1, §3). Depends on the reusable item-history source in #3981. Coordinate with #1281: reuse its history/throughput seam, but do not duplicate its charts.

## Goal
Add pure, deterministic derivations for project/epic ETA distributions and item stall-risk explanations. The current project/coverage inputs do not contain enough item-level history to calculate these values.

## Acceptance criteria
- ETA uses complete observed weekly item-history buckets, including zero-completion weeks, over trailing 4-week and 8-week windows; incomplete windows are excluded and the scope/sample are returned.
- One direct native child closure is the documented default unit; merged PRs do not double-count. Reopened issues are not counted as currently complete. Existing effort weights and open-ended/unsized work remain explicit and never create invented precision.
- With fewer than 3 completions or 4 complete weeks, the result is low-confidence/borrowed from a clearly named comparable scope or “not enough history”; with no defensible baseline, no ETA date is returned. Numeric forecasts include P50/P80 ranges, confidence, input coverage, and model version.
- Stall risk is a versioned, explainable 0–100 rule score with contributing reason codes/timestamps; first-observed blocker age is labelled a lower bound, and unavailable heartbeat/requeue signals stay unknown.
- Score ≥60 is surfaced as informational “at risk”; score alone does not create a Needs-you escalation. Tests cover missing history, zero pace, reopen, sparse samples, borrowed baseline, and each risk signal.

Prior related audit: #1516 (2026-10-27 coverage audit) — this is the current, narrower failure: db-dump step failing + no offsite verification.

(3) Backfill the missing 2026-10-29 → 2026-11-01 date dirs to R2 from the local archives once the dump step is fixed.

body:
## Summary

`WaitingPool::restore` (`pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/waiting.rs:312-326`) applies a narrower duplicate guard than `insert` and `park`: it checks only `by_key` (already held). `insert` (`waiting.rs:234`, guard at `:243-246`) and `park` (`waiting.rs:273`, guard at `:281-284`) refuse a key that is already held, **has arrived**, or **is sitting in the ready queue**. `restore` checks none of the latter two, so a key the pool already knows is finished or ready-to-hand-out can be held a second time — and later handed out a second time. That is exactly the double hand-out class closed #2001 fixed for `insert` (which is why the `ready_keys` index exists, `waiting.rs:170-176`); the fix never reached `restore`.

`restore` is not a test-only path: the event store uses it for **every** hold. `Mirror::hold` (`pkgs/id/src/event_store/waiting_rows.rs:241`) calls `pool.restore(...)`, `Mirror::park` (`waiting_rows.rs:320`) re-holds proof headers through it, and the reload-on-open loop (`pkgs/id/src/event_store/mod.rs:1015`) restores every waiting row through it.

## Verified this run (laptop probe, current main 33aefa7f)

Probe crate on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneA-restoreguard/`) `#[path]`-includes the real `waiting.rs` from the laptop clone at the same HEAD (md5 `9654300d490a030f3f5513c79692e717`, identical in both clones) and exercises `WaitingPool<u32, &str>`:

- **Case A — already-arrived key:** `arrived(10)` then `restore(author, 10, [99], ev)` → the event is **held** (`len=1`, `contains(10)=true`); a later `arrived(99)` **releases it**, handing an already-applied event to the caller a second time. Control: `insert` of the same arrived key is ignored (`len=0`).
- **Case B — ready-queue key (#2001 class):** `insert(author, 1, [], ev)` (goes to the ready queue) then `restore(author, 1, [99], ev2)` → the same key is **also held**; `arrived(99)` releases the held copy and `take_ready()` returns the ready copy — the same key is handed out **twice**. Control: `park` of a ready key is ignored (`len(held)=0`).

## Why it matters

The pool's contract is that a key is in exactly one state — held, ready, or arrived — and is handed out at most once. `restore` silently breaks that invariant for two of the three states:

- An already-arrived (applied) event re-held via `restore` occupies per-author/total cap slots until its dependency happens to arrive or the 7-day age cap drops it, and if the dependency does arrive it is released and applied **again**.
- A ready key re-held via `restore` can be handed out twice (once from the ready queue, once on release), the precise failure #2001 closed for `insert`.
- At the store layer, `Mirror::hold`'s Held/Skipped decision keys off `pool.contains(&id)` after `restore` (`waiting_rows.rs:242-262`), so the phantom hold also writes/keeps a waiting row for an event that is not waiting.

## Design constraint — one caller does this on purpose

`Mirror::present_proof` (`waiting_rows.rs:288-301`) marks a fork-proof header arrived via `pool.arrived(...)` and then deliberately re-holds it through `restore` (`Mirror::park`, `waiting_rows.rs:313-323`): a proof header never applies, so it is parked for good to keep its conflicts seen. A blind copy of `insert`'s arrived-guard into `restore` would silently break that park (the header would never be re-held). The fix therefore has to separate the intents — e.g. `restore` guards the ready queue unconditionally (no caller parks a ready key on purpose) and the arrived case gets an explicit held-for-good route for proofs — rather than one shared guard pasted over all three entry points. This is also why this issue is filed-only, not a trivial self-solve.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `WaitingPool::restore` can no longer hold a key that is in the ready queue, and a non-proof event whose key has already arrived is not re-held/re-released through the `Mirror::hold` path; the chosen guard shape is documented on `restore` like the other two entry points.
- [ ] The fork-proof park still works: `present_proof`/`park_proof` keep a proof header held for good after its arrival, with a test pinning that behaviour (existing proof-header tests stay green).
- [ ] Regression tests at the pool level, alongside `test_restore_keeps_the_cap_and_ignores_a_key_already_held` (`waiting.rs:728`): restore-after-arrived holds nothing and releases nothing when its deps later arrive; restore-of-a-ready-key holds nothing and the key is handed out exactly once.
- [ ] The reload-on-open and `Mirror::hold`/`park` paths behave as before for genuinely waiting/parked events (existing waiting + waiting_rows tests stay green).

## Dedup

Open/closed searches for "restore WaitingPool duplicate" and "waiting restore" (2026-11-01) return only #2001 (insert's ready-queue guard — closed, restore not covered), #1567 (total cap — closed), and #1730 (arrived-set growth — open, different defect). No issue covers `restore`'s guard.

body:
## Finding

The orchestration section's per-goal gate, `isGoalMeasurement` in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/feed.ts`, checks only that `linedUp`, `stalled`, and `gaps` are arrays and that `progressedSinceLastRun` is a string or an array. It never checks the array *elements*, and it never checks `goal`, `momentum`, `summary`, or `goalId` at all — even though `GoalMeasurement` (model.ts) requires all of them and `todayFromSection` (derive.ts) dereferences them. The gate's own header comment states its contract (#949): "`todayFromSection` dereferences `linedUp`, `stalled`, and `gaps` on every goal, so a goal missing any of them must fail validation here — this validator is the only gate on every path, and a rejected section falls back to the derived view by design." A goal that passes this gate with a `null` element defeats both halves of that contract: the section is not rejected, and the consumer crashes instead of falling back.

## Evidence (main f7c942b1, verified this run)

- `feed.ts:122-131` `isGoalMeasurement`: `Array.isArray` on `linedUp`/`stalled`/`gaps` only; no element checks; `goal`, `momentum`, `summary`, `goalId` unchecked. Used by `orchestrationSectionProblem` at `feed.ts:172`, the single source of truth behind `isOrchestrationSection` and `diagnoseOrchestrationSection`.
- The contract it under-checks: `model.ts:626-639` `GoalMeasurement` requires `goalId: string | null`, `goal: string`, `momentum: "moving" | "stalled" | "blocked" | "no-work-lined-up"`, `summary: string`, `linedUp: LinedUpTask[]` (element shape at `model.ts:615-623`: `title`, `status` enum, `horizon`, `horizonWhy`), `stalled: { title: string; since: string; blocker?: string }[]`, `gaps: string[]`.
- The consumer that trusts the gate: `derive.ts:687` `todayFromSection` — `g.linedUp.filter((t) => t.horizon === "today")` at :694, `g.stalled.filter((s) => s.blocker)` at :713, `project: g.goal` at :717, the momentum ternary at :718 (any non-"moving"/non-"blocked" value silently renders as `"stalled"`), `[g.summary, ...g.gaps].join(" ")` at :721. Production path: `sources/live.ts:1036` `normalizeOrchestrationSection` (the gate) → `server.ts:474` `todayContext()` → `deriveToday` → `todayFromSection`, with no catch in `todayContext`.

Laptop Bun probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneB-goalgate/`, importing the real `feed.ts`/`derive.ts` from the laptop clone at the same HEAD — md5 `fb3693f1…` / `dcdefb5e…`, identical to sandbox main f7c942b1):

- Control (fully valid goal): gate `true`, `todayFromSection` renders correctly.
- `linedUp: [null]`: gate `true` (problem `null`) → `todayFromSection` **throws** `TypeError: null is not an object (evaluating 't.horizon')`.
- `stalled: [null]`: gate `true` → **throws** `TypeError … (evaluating 's.blocker')`.
- Goal with only the four checked fields (no `goal`/`momentum`/`summary`/`goalId`): gate `true` → renders momentum entry with no project name and state `"stalled"`, objective with no title.
- `gaps: [{ finding: "x" }]`: gate `true` → rendered detail contains the literal text `[object Object]`.
- `momentum: "flying"`: gate `true` → silently rendered as state `"stalled"`.
- `linedUp: ["Task A"]` (bare string): gate `true` → the task silently vanishes and the fallback objective replaces it.

## Why it matters

The orchestration section is published by an automated job into a JSON file the aggregator reads fail-soft everywhere else; this gate is the one place a drifted or hand-edited section is supposed to be diagnosed as "invalid" (with the failing check named, #1140) and demoted to the derived view. As written, one malformed goal element turns that designed degradation into an uncaught TypeError on the today page's request path, and milder drift (missing name, nonsense momentum, non-string gaps) renders falsified state — a goal reported as "stalled" that never said so, a nameless objective, `[object Object]` in the detail line — with no diagnosis anywhere.

## Acceptance criteria

- `isGoalMeasurement` validates the full `GoalMeasurement` shape: `goal` a non-empty string, `momentum` one of the four enum values, `summary` a string, `goalId` a string or null; `linedUp` elements are records with a string `title` and a valid `horizon` (and `status`/`horizonWhy` per `LinedUpTask` when present per the type); `stalled` elements are records with string `title` and `since` (optional string `blocker`); `gaps` elements are strings; a `progressedSinceLastRun` array's elements are strings (the single-string form stays accepted, per the existing tolerance).
- A section whose goal fails the tightened gate is diagnosed through the existing machinery: `orchestrationSectionProblem` still reports `"goals (per-goal shape)"`, the section renders as invalid/falls back to the derived view, and `todayFromSection` can no longer be reached with an element it would throw on.
- Regression tests beside the existing feed gate tests cover at least: `linedUp: [null]`, `stalled: [null]`, a goal missing `goal`, a nonsense `momentum`, and a non-string `gaps` element — all rejected — plus the valid-goal control still passing.
- Existing feed/derive tests stay green.

Dedup: #949 is the original gate-design issue whose comment states the contract above — it predates the element-shape gap and does not name it. #3458 covers the charge gates (`isChargeRow`/`isUnmatchedCharge` amount/date semantics), #3766 the project-config registry validator, #3427/#3428 the quota window/burn gates — different validators, fields, and consumers. No open or closed issue covers `isGoalMeasurement`'s missing element and field checks.

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-b (Lane B) from a verified laptop probe; filed only, not self-solved — the element rules must match the publisher's real shapes, which is a triage decision, not a trivial fix.

body:
## Bug: /quota roster flickers — two fleet-feed producers write divergent quota sections to the same file

Found in the 2026-11-01 PM-stack page-by-page review.

`~/.local/state/pm-aggregator/fleet-feed.json` has TWO producers running the same collector (`scripts/collect-fleet-feed.ts`) on a ~5 min cadence:

1. The laptop's `fleet-feed-collector.timer` — reads the LAPTOP's deployed opencode config for the #1114 disabled_providers filter and runs current code.
2. A sandbox-side push (`scripts/push-fleet-feed.sh`, "systemd, sandbox" per its header) — runs the collector against the sandbox's code checkout and the sandbox's config, then overwrites the laptop file.

Their quota sections diverge, so /quota's roster changes depending on which producer wrote last. Measured live 2026-11-01:

- 16:58Z file: 11 pools, no `openai.alternate` (sandbox-shaped: unfiltered disabled-door pools present).
- 17:01Z file (laptop collector, post-#3837): 6 pools — `openai.alternate` present; meta:high-usage, anthropic:claude-pro, commandcode:go, antigravity:gemini, antigravity:claude-gpt, deepseek:api filtered per #1114 (the laptop config disables their doors: meta, claude-code, commandcode, deepseek, antigravity-ls+agy+google).
- 17:03Z file (sandbox push): back to 11 pools, alternate gone again.

The laptop collector's journal shows the #1114 filtering firing all day (612 "filtered —" lines on 2026-11-01, 0 unreadable-config fallbacks), while the sandbox producer evidently assembles with a different (emptier) disabled set and, until its checkout syncs, older code.

## Why it matters

- Pools appear and disappear from /quota every few minutes — this is the direct cause of "where's alternate openai and so on": whether a pool is visible depends on refresh timing.
- The #1114 filtered pools are "noted" only in the laptop collector's journal; the page/API carries no trace of them, so a reader cannot distinguish "pool filtered because its door is disabled" from "pool missing".

## Suggested direction (needs an owner decision)

- Give the quota section a single producer (the laptop — the pools describe laptop-served providers and the laptop's deployed config is the #1114 source of truth), and have the sandbox push preserve the existing quota section the way the AA section is already reused/carried; OR make both producers read the same config + code rev (fragile).
- Surface the #1114 filtered pools on /quota itself (a "filtered — door disabled" note listing them), not only in the collector journal.

## Acceptance criteria
- The fleet-feed quota section has a single effective producer: either the laptop collector alone writes it, or the sandbox push (`scripts/push-fleet-feed.sh`) preserves the existing quota section the way it already carries the AA section.
- Two consecutive producer cycles (~10 minutes apart) yield an identical /quota pool roster — no pool appears or disappears depending on which producer wrote last, and the roster matches the laptop's #1114 disabled_providers filtering.
- Pools filtered by the #1114 disabled-door rule are surfaced on /quota itself (e.g. a "filtered — door disabled" note naming them), not only in the collector journal, so "filtered" is distinguishable from "missing" on the page.

body:
Regression of #193 (closed): the `id` lib again does not build with `--no-default-features`.

**Evidence (2026-11-01, found during PR #3471 verification, queue task 5371):**
- `cargo check -p id --no-default-features` on the PR #3471 head fails with exactly one error: `E0433: cannot find petname in crate` at `pkgs/id/src/invite.rs:43` — `Invite::new` validates names with `crate::petname::is_format_char`, but the `petname` re-export is gated `#[cfg(feature = "world")]` (`pkgs/id/src/lib.rs`, `pub use id_core::petname;`).
- This is **pre-existing on main**, not introduced by PR #3471: at main `73423be04`, `pkgs/id/src/invite.rs` is byte-identical (no diff to the PR branch) and `petname` was already world-gated in the root `lib.rs` before the crate split. The same E0433 therefore occurs on clean main.
- Default features build fine (`cargo check -p id` passes); only the no-default / no-world combination is broken.

**Fix shape:** `Invite::new` is ungated core functionality, so either `is_format_char` moves to an ungated leaf (it has no world dependencies — it is a pure char predicate) or the name validation stops depending on a world-gated module. Moving the predicate to an ungated home is the smaller, safer change; gating `invite` would remove core invite creation from no-world builds.

**Acceptance:** `cargo check -p id --no-default-features` passes on main; a CI check exercises a no-default-features (or equivalent minimal-feature) build of the `id` lib so #193 does not regress a third time.

## Acceptance criteria
- `cargo check -p id --no-default-features` passes on main (the `E0433: cannot find petname in crate` at `pkgs/id/src/invite.rs:43` is gone).
- `cargo check -p id` with default features still passes, and name-validation behavior is unchanged (the predicate moves to an ungated home or the dependency is otherwise removed — `invite` is not feature-gated away).
- A CI check exercises a no-default-features (or equivalent minimal-feature) build of the `id` lib, so the #193 regression cannot recur a third time unnoticed.

body:
## What happened (found 2026-11-01, during the "fix all errors" service sweep)

Kaneo and its PostgreSQL had **two competing managers**, and for ~10 hours **two PostgreSQL postmasters ran against the single `pm-stack_postgres_data` data volume**:

- The **pm-stack module's compose path** (`pm-kaneo.service` + `pm-kaneo.timer` running `~/pm-stack/deploy.sh`) — live and healthy throughout; the compose postmaster holds Kaneo's connection pool.
- The **pm-apps module's oci-containers** (`docker-pm-kaneo.service`, `docker-pm-postgres.service`) from the code#1752 migration, whose activation never completed: the compose units were never disabled, and the compose self-heal timer resurrected the compose stack at **2026-11-01 00:35**, bringing the compose postmaster up alongside the oci postmaster (running since 2026-10-30) on the same PGDATA.

Verified live before intervening: both postmasters accepting connections on the same mounted volume; the oci postmaster had **zero** established client connections, the compose postmaster had Kaneo's 4 backends. Separately, `docker-pm-kaneo.service` failed at every activation (`Bind for 127.0.0.1:5173 failed: port is already allocated`) and restart-looped into `start-limit-hit` — that failure is what the 2026-11-01 09:30 generation-524 activation surfaced.

PostgreSQL does not support two postmasters on one data directory; that the compose stack kept serving cleanly for 10h is luck (buffer/checkpoint interleaving), not safety.

## Interim actions (applied 2026-11-01, verified)

- `docker-pm-postgres.service` stopped — the idle second postmaster is gone; the compose postmaster is now the only postmaster on the volume.
- `docker-pm-kaneo.service` stopped; both units `reset-failed`. Kaneo never went down (compose stack healthy, `GET 127.0.0.1:5173` → 200 before and after).
- `/etc/systemd/system` is read-only on this host, so the units **cannot be disabled outside a NixOS switch**: if the laptop reboots before the fix below lands via a switch, both units start again. Treat reboot-before-switch as re-opening this incident.

## Durable fix

PR #3847 removes the `pm-kaneo` + `pm-postgres` declarations from `nixos/services/pm-apps`, making compose the single declared manager (Grist/Pad/ready-for-agent stay oci; they were never contested). It lands with the next switch (which also carries the flake fold, code#3720).

## Decision left open for Drew/fleet

The alternative is completing the #1752 migration for Kaneo/PostgreSQL: disable the pm-stack compose service+timer in the flake and plan the cutover window. PR #3847 deliberately takes the compose branch because that is what has actually been running the PM stack — but the migration intent in #1752 was the opposite, so the call should be explicit. Either way, **exactly one manager** must survive the next switch.

Related: code#3720 (flake fold), code#1752 (pm-apps migration).


## Acceptance criteria
- Exactly one manager owns Kaneo and its PostgreSQL: the losing path's units (pm-apps oci-containers `docker-pm-kaneo` / `docker-pm-postgres`, or the pm-stack compose units if the oci path is chosen instead) are disabled/removed in the NixOS configuration, not merely stopped, so a reboot cannot resurrect the dual-postmaster state.
- After a switch (and ideally a reboot or service restart cycle), verification shows exactly one postmaster on the `pm-stack_postgres_data` volume and Kaneo healthy (`GET 127.0.0.1:5173` → 200).
- The `docker-pm-kaneo` start-limit loop is gone (unit removed or fixed), and the interim state recorded in the body is superseded by the final disposition on this issue.

body:
# aggregator(alerts): getSupabaseClient and getAlertsStore both memoize a transient null forever — the alerts ledger stays "unavailable" until restart

## Evidence

Two stacked "resolved once" latches in the alert-throat landing (#3676),
both in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/` (main `d3225b99`):

**Layer 1 — `supabase.ts:48-68`:**

```ts
let clientPromise: Promise<SupabaseClient | null> | null = null;

export function getSupabaseClient(): Promise<SupabaseClient | null> {
  if (!clientPromise) {
    clientPromise = (async () => {
      const token = await resolveBwsSecret("supabase.access-token-muse-cli");
      if (!token) return null;
      ...
    })().catch(() => null);
  }
  return clientPromise;
}
```

**Layer 2 — `alerts.ts:482-489`:**

```ts
let storePromise: Promise<AlertsStore | null> | null = null;

export function getAlertsStore(): Promise<AlertsStore | null> {
  if (!storePromise) {
    storePromise = getSupabaseClient().then((db) => (db ? new AlertsStore(db) : null));
  }
  return storePromise;
}
```

`resolveBwsSecret` (`src/secrets.ts`) fails soft to `null` on any
transient problem (bws unreachable, token file briefly unreadable, 30s
timeout) — by design, and it caches that `null` for only 5 minutes so
the failure heals. Neither consumer honors that design: the first
`null` is memoized in a module-level promise that is never cleared, at
BOTH layers independently. Fixing only the client layer would not heal
the store, whose settled `null` promise never re-asks the client; and
the store layer is the only path the alerts surface uses, so the whole
alert throat (intake ledger, dedupe, delivery state, ack) reports
itself unavailable for the process lifetime after one transient hiccup
at first use.

This is the same defect shape as #3729 (`push.ts`
`ensurePushConfigured`), filed separately because the fix sites and the
affected surface differ: there, push delivery; here, the ledger/store
every alerts route depends on.

## Verified (laptop probes, verbatim files)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneB-supalatch/` on the laptop.

1. `supa/` — the repo's real `supabase.ts` (sha256 `7a0969f7…`, identical
   on sandbox main `d3225b99` and the laptop clone) with its
   `./secrets.ts` import stubbed fail-once-then-succeed
   (`probe-supabase.log`):

```text
1st getSupabaseClient (bws transiently down): null resolveCalls=1
2nd getSupabaseClient (bws recovered):        null resolveCalls=1
RESULT: LATCH CONFIRMED — null client memoized forever, secret never re-read
```

2. `alerts/` — the repo's real `alerts.ts` (sha256 `fb07caf8…`) with
   only its `./supabase.ts` and `./push.ts` imports stubbed; the stub
   client is unavailable on the first ask and available thereafter
   (`probe-alerts.log`):

```text
1st getAlertsStore (client unavailable): null clientCalls=1
2nd getAlertsStore (client available):   null clientCalls=1
RESULT: LATCH CONFIRMED — storePromise memoizes the null store; the client is never re-asked
```

## Why it matters

The alerts surface is deliberately fail-soft ("callers fail soft — the
alerts surface reports itself unavailable instead of taking the
dashboard down", `supabase.ts` header). A transient secret-store failure
around the first alerts request after a restart turns that soft
degradation into a hard, silent, permanent one: sentinels keep posting,
but intake/dedupe/delivery bookkeeping has no store until someone
restarts the aggregator. Nothing distinguishes "no token configured"
from "failed once at startup" in the outcome.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `null` result is not memoized at either layer: after a
  transient failure, a later `getSupabaseClient()` / `getAlertsStore()`
  retries resolution and can return a live client/store without a
  process restart.
- [ ] A successful resolution is still memoized (no per-request bws
  spawns), and concurrent first callers still share one in-flight
  resolution.
- [ ] Regression tests cover fail-then-recover at both layers
  (client: first token `null`, then a token → `null` then a client;
  store: first client `null`, then a client → `null` then a store).
- [ ] Genuinely unconfigured (no token reachable at all) still fails
  soft: callers get `null`, no throw, the dashboard stays up.

Distinct from: #3729 (the `push.ts` VAPID configure latch — same shape,
different module and surface), #3685 (closed; delivery marking),
#3693 (subscriptions GET key leak).

body:
# id(repl): find/peek value-flags consume the next flag as their value — `--dir --all` saves to a directory literally named `--all`, `-o --quiet` writes a file named `--quiet`

## Problem

The REPL's hand-rolled argument parsers take the next token as a value-flag's value unconditionally, even when that token is itself a flag:

- `parse_find_args` (`pkgs/id/src/repl/runner.rs:631`): `--dir` (runner.rs, `--dir` branch) and `--exclude` assign `rest[i + 1]` with no check; `--format` does the same and then reports the flag as an invalid format value.
- `parse_peek_args` (`pkgs/id/src/repl/runner.rs:1210`): `-o`/`--output` and `--exclude` do the same.

So a flag the user typed is swallowed as a value, and the flag itself never takes effect:

- `find report --dir --all` → `dir = Some("--all")`, `all = false` — results are saved into a directory literally named `--all` (via the selection path's `create_dir_all`), in interactive-selection mode instead of output-all mode.
- `find report --exclude --count` → `exclude = ["--count"]`, `count = false` — the count mode is lost and the exclusion pattern is a string no blob name contains, so nothing is excluded either.
- `peek report -o --quiet` → `output_file = Some("--quiet")`, `quiet = false` — the preview is written to a file literally named `--quiet`, banner and all.
- `find report --format --tag` → `format_error = Some("--tag")` — the user gets `error: invalid --format "--tag": expected tag, group, or union`, naming a flag they used correctly (as the format shortcut) as the bad value.

The same parsers already know the guard for the optional numeric flags: `--first`/`--last` only consume the next token when it does **not** start with `-` (`!rest[i + 1].starts_with('-')`), and peek's `--lines` only consumes a token that parses as a number, leaving a following flag to be processed as a flag. The required-value flags are the ones missing the guard.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `85537203`)

- `pkgs/id/src/repl/runner.rs` sha256 `2161839d92158abc632db4be5007bfb833746e7f31c9352086f5a54ef7af7b16`, identical in the sandbox and laptop clones.
- Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneB-replflagvalue/` (verbatim copies of `parse_find_args`, `parse_peek_args`, `FindArgs` and `PeekOptions` extracted from that file; output read back from `probe-run.log`):

| Input | Result |
|---|---|
| `find report --dir out` (control) | `dir=Some("out")`, `all=false` |
| `find report --dir --all` | `dir=Some("--all")`, `all=false` |
| `find report --exclude --count` | `exclude=["--count"]`, `count=false` |
| `find report --format --tag` | `format_error=Some("--tag")` |
| `find report --first --all` (guard control) | `first=Some(1)`, `all=true` |
| `peek report -o out.txt` (control) | `output_file=Some("out.txt")`, `quiet=false` |
| `peek report -o --quiet` | `output_file=Some("--quiet")`, `quiet=false` |
| `peek report --lines --head` (guard control) | `lines=5`, `head_only=true` |
| `peek report --exclude --all` | `exclude=["--all"]` |

## Why it matters

The REPL is the interactive surface of `id`. In these cases the command that runs is not the command the user typed, and nothing says so: output goes to a file or directory named after a flag, a mode flag (`--all`, `--count`, `--quiet`) silently does not apply, and an exclude pattern that can never match makes the exclusion look applied when it is not. The CLI side (clap) refuses a missing flag value loudly.

Distinct from #2274 (same parsers: unknown/mistyped flags vanish, value-flags with **no** following token are silently dropped, bare `>` — this issue is a following token that **is** a flag being consumed as the value), #2009 (non-numeric values of the numeric `--first`/`--last`/`--lines` flags becoming queries), #3144 (clap space-form `--new` on the CLI side) and #3415 (the aggregator's record-claude-launch script, a different parser in a different language).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A value-flag (`--dir`, `--format`, `--exclude` in `parse_find_args`; `-o`/`--output`, `--exclude` in `parse_peek_args`) whose next token starts with `-` is reported as missing its value (visible error/usage naming the flag), and the flag token is not consumed as the value.
- [ ] `find report --dir --all`, `find report --exclude --count`, `peek report -o --quiet` and `peek report --exclude --all` no longer produce a dir/file/exclusion named after a flag, and the trailing flag's own effect is not silently lost (it is either applied or the whole command is refused with the error above — triage pins which).
- [ ] A legitimate value that starts with `-` remains expressible or is explicitly documented as unsupported for these flags (triage pins; at minimum the error must not claim the flag token was a bad *value* the user supplied, as `--format --tag` does today).
- [ ] Regression tests in `runner.rs` cover flag-as-value for each affected flag in both parsers, plus the control cases (`--dir out`, `-o out.txt`) and the existing `--first`/`--lines` guard behaviour; existing parser tests still pass.
