body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#139 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #95

## Summary

Decide how the suite is split across matrix legs and how the split is kept balanced as tests are added. Today the whole suite is one job, and one package (`internal/e2e`, 100.7 s, strictly serial) is three quarters of it. The notes propose: split unit from integration, shard the longer one into logical groups, repeat on the longest shard, then fall back to alphabetical ranges balanced by time, and stop when setup/teardown dominates. This issue makes that concrete, gives the stop rule as arithmetic, and recommends a **timing-file-driven splitter** over hand-tuned alphabetical ranges -- while keeping the one real advantage of the alphabetical idea (a shard you can reproduce locally with one `-run`).

## Original notes

> - testing
>   - make a comprehensive github action ci.yaml workflow (or test.yaml) that is as fast as possible,
>     - splitting sets of tests into as small groups as practical, eg split out unit/integration tests into 2 jobs, whichever one takes longer: shard it into 4 logical groups (or however many) based on an appropriate category, then find the longest job at that point and repeat (you dont want to iterate on this forever, at some point start splitting logical units by like, e.g. maybe a-f/g-s/t-z, balance number of letters by time.

> - testing
>   - make a comprehensive github action ci.yaml workflow (or test.yaml) that is as fast as possible,
>     - continue until the jobs can't get much faster considering setup/teardown and then set a ci testing budget which is a hardcoded default input. after the test matrix have a time budget job when subtracts github workflow request time from now. (this catches if the jobs are impacted by matrix size, could lessen by taking initial job end or matrix start time.)

> - testing
>   - make a comprehensive github action ci.yaml workflow (or test.yaml) that is as fast as possible,
>     - repeat this process whenever testing exceeds some time budget. make setup faster, rebalance alpha splits, split groups of tests on the longest shard. maybe flag that never tears down because just killing the box after. anything downloaded should be cached, shallow clone a partial path to mcpx dir, if there's unexplainable job start delays, try to keep all job times balanced, 10 ultrafast ones can give you quick signals but may put pressure on runner infra and cause the longest jobs to last a little longer. all that matters is how long the longest jobs take. job runners have 2 or 4 cores, consider if theres lengthy tests which are '1' test but re-exec N times 'in parallel': they will only run 1-3 at a time and so 30 cases _could_ take up to 10 tests worth of time even in parallel and may need to be examined. we're using go so im not too worried about time budget but its best to get this early. main focus is strong tests as each step of the lifecycle.

## Current state

From run 36673523537 (see #135 for the full step table); the post-#182 run 36693030957 at 05c78b2 is in brackets:

| Package | Time | Tests |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `internal/e2e` | **100.7 s** [108.9 s] | 199 [209] |
| `internal/tui` | 8.6 s | 15 |
| `internal/pool` | 1.5 s | |
| `internal/events`, `internal/mcpserver` | ~1 s each | |
| every other package | < 0.5 s | |
| compile (no working cache) | ~31 s [~39 s incl. module download; #182 fixed the cache key, but this run was a miss by construction -- first warm figure is #143's] | |

`internal/e2e` by file (`rg -c '^func Test'`; at 05c78b2 in brackets):

| File | Tests | Share |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `e2e_test.go` | 128 [129] | 64 % [62 %] |
| `consumer_test.go` | 17 | 9 % |
| `exec_test.go`, `proto_test.go`, `v1ops_test.go` | 11 each | 17 % |
| `settings_test.go` | 10 | 5 % |
| `unread_test.go` | [9, new in #171] | [4 %] |
| `logs_test.go` | 5 | |
| `multiconfig_test.go` | 4 | |
| `runtime_test.go` | 2 | (loops deno/bun/node inside) |

Per-test timings do not exist yet: the log has package totals only (no `-v`, no `-json`). 199 tests in 100.7 s is ~0.5 s each on average (209 in 108.9 s at 05c78b2, the same rate); the distribution is unknown. For contrast, the ~520 unit tests take ~15 s together, ~0.03 s each -- a 17x gap (from #166). 62 of the e2e tests start a JavaScript runtime (53 `"exec"` calls in `e2e_test.go`, 9 in `exec_test.go`, 3 in `runtime_test.go`; unchanged at 05c78b2), so one e2e test is commonly 3-4 processes: the CLI, a daemon, a fake MCP server and deno/bun/node.

Parallelism today:
- **No `t.Parallel()` anywhere** in the module. `go help testflag`: `-parallel n` "Allow[s] parallel execution of test functions that call t.Parallel ... By default, -parallel is set to the value of GOMAXPROCS" -- so it currently does nothing.
- `go help build`: `-p n` is "the number of programs, such as build commands or test binaries, that can be run in parallel. The default is GOMAXPROCS". So `go test ./...` runs up to 4 *package* binaries at once on the runner, which is why every unit package finished inside e2e's 100 s -- but e2e itself is one binary running 199 tests one after another.
- Runner: this repo is public, so `ubuntu-latest` = **4 vCPU / 16 GB**; a private repo gets **2 vCPU / 8 GB**; `ubuntu-slim` is a 1 vCPU container; `macos-latest` is 3 vCPU M1 ([runner reference](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/runners/github-hosted-runners)). The notes' "2 or 4 cores" is right; which one depends on repo visibility.
- Account limits on the Free plan: **20 concurrent standard-runner jobs** (5 macOS), shared by every workflow in the account; 256 jobs per matrix ([limits](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/limits)).

Tests that fan out internally ("1 test that re-execs N times in parallel"):

| Test | Fan-out | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `TestConcurrentRunsGetIsolatedInstances` | 4 concurrent `mcpx run`, each a runtime process + daemon traffic | `internal/e2e/e2e_test.go:319` (func, 05c78b2) |
| `TestConcurrentRunsOfOneScriptKeepTheirOwnLauncher` | 6 concurrent `mcpx run --launcher` | `internal/e2e/e2e_test.go:2938` |
| `TestTwoConfigurationsDoNotShareAGeneratedClient` | 2 | `internal/e2e/e2e_test.go:2826` |
| five pool tests (`TestSharedModeHandlesConcurrentCalls`, `TestSessionModeRespectsMaxAndQueues`, ...) | goroutine fan-out over fakemcp | `internal/pool/pool_test.go:92-475` |

Each `mcpx run` starts Deno/Bun/Node, which is CPU-heavy at startup, so on 4 vCPU a 6-way fan-out runs roughly 3-4 at a time and on 2 vCPU roughly 2 -- the notes' "30 cases could take up to 10 tests worth of time" is the right intuition. These are also the tests that will contend worst once other tests run in parallel. There are also 7 fixed `time.Sleep` waits in e2e (100-500 ms each, e.g. `e2e_test.go:149,403`) that cost wall time regardless of cores.

## The procedure, made concrete

1. **Measure.** Every CI run of e2e uses `go test -json` (keep human output via `gotestsum` or a `jq` filter) and uploads per-test `Elapsed` as an artifact. The final job (#140) merges them into one timing file per main run.
2. **Unit vs integration.** One `unit` job (`go test $(go list ./... | grep -v /internal/e2e)`), and e2e separately. The unit job's test time is ~9 s (tui); it will never be the long pole unless something changes drastically.
3. **Shard e2e** (the approaches below).
4. **Repeat on the longest job** -- which after step 3 will likely be the `nix` job, not a test shard (#143 predicts this). That is the runbook in #140.
5. **Stop** by the rule below.

### Stop rule

Per-leg fixed cost today, from the step table: queue 2-3 s (occasionally ~40 s) + set up 3.4 s + checkout ~2 s + toolchains ~18-26 s (setup-go 10.9 s alone) + compile and binary build (part of the ~31 s, less with a cache) + post 2 s + completion ~3 s ≈ **30-45 s**. With T = 100 s of e2e test time and N equal shards, the longest leg is ≈ fixed + T/N:

| N | T/N | longest leg (fixed ≈ 35 s) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 100 s | 135 s |
| 2 | 50 s | 85 s |
| 3 | 33 s | 68 s |
| 4 | 25 s | 60 s |
| 8 | 12.5 s | 48 s |

Each extra shard saves T/N - T/(N+1) and costs one more runner (and more pressure on the 20-job limit). **Stop when T/N is below the fixed cost** (going from 4 to 8 legs saves 12 s for 4 more runners), or when the leg is no longer the longest job. Today that means N ≈ 3-4. Reducing the fixed cost (the working Go cache, shipping a compiled `e2e.test`, #135 decision 7) moves the optimum up; `t.Parallel` (below) moves T down.

"Many tiny jobs" vs "all that matters is the longest job": more legs are free until they queue. With lint (~3 legs), unit, nix, plugin, docs-examples and #97's environment legs, a 4-shard e2e already puts ~12 jobs in one run; two concurrent runs (a PR and a main push) reach 20 and the 21st waits. Queue time is invisible in the per-job durations and only shows in the run's wall clock -- the budget job reports it separately (#140).

## Approaches

### A -- hand-tuned alphabetical ranges (the notes' fallback), least recommended as the end state

`-run '^Test[A-F]'`, `'^Test[G-S]'`, `'^Test[T-Z]'`, with boundaries moved by hand when the budget is exceeded.
- Pro: no tooling; anyone can reproduce a shard locally from its name; stable membership.
- Con: every test starts with `Test` and the next letter follows English, not runtime -- clusters like `TestRun...`, `TestExec...`, `TestConcurrent...` cannot be split by a range boundary without going to two letters (`^TestC[a-n]`), and after a few rebalances the regexes are unreadable. Balance drifts with every added test, and each rebalance is a workflow edit and a PR -- exactly the "iterate on this forever" the notes warn about. Balancing "number of letters by time" requires the per-test timings anyway, and once you have them, bin-packing uses them better than contiguous ranges can.

### B -- logical shards by feature (file), a static list

One shard per feature file: exec, consumer, v1ops, proto, settings, logs, runtime, multiconfig, plus the rest.
- Pro: a red leg names a feature; stable; readable.
- Con: badly unbalanced by construction -- `e2e_test.go` holds 64 % of the tests, so the "rest" shard is roughly two thirds of the time and needs splitting again. Go cannot select tests by file, so each shard's `-run` regex is a generated list of names (`grep '^func Test' file`). To make B balance, `e2e_test.go` would have to be broken into feature files first -- a worthwhile readability refactor on its own (one file of 2,977 lines and 129 tests at 05c78b2), but not something to do *for* CI balance.
- Variant (from #166): split `internal/e2e` into **subpackages** (`internal/e2e/exec`, `.../proto`, `.../v1ops`, ... with `newEnv` and the fixtures lifted into a shared helper package). Each subpackage is its own test binary, so shards need no regex, survive renames, cannot silently select zero tests, and compile in parallel; `go test ./internal/e2e/...` still means "all e2e". Same arithmetic limit as B: on today's file boundaries the largest shard is still `e2e_test.go`.

### C -- timing-file-driven splitter (recommended)

A small Go program in the repo (e.g. `pkgs/mcpx/internal/ci/shard` or `scripts/ci/shard.go`, run with `go run`; the toolchain is already there):
1. lists tests (`grep '^func Test'` over `internal/e2e/*_test.go` is free; `go test -list .` is exact but compiles the test binary first);
2. reads the latest timing file -- the artifact of the last successful main run (via `gh run download` / `actions/download-artifact` with `run-id`), falling back to a committed `timings.json`, falling back to equal weights;
3. gives tests without a timing the median;
4. computes N = clamp(ceil(total / target_leg_seconds), 1, max_shards), and assigns tests to shards by **longest-processing-time greedy** bin-packing (sort descending, put each into the currently lightest shard);
5. emits the matrix JSON: `[{"name":"e2e-1","run":"^(TestA|TestB|...)$"}, ...]`, and each leg prints its exact `go test -run '...'` line into the job summary.
6. makes each leg assert it ran the number of tests it was assigned. A `-run` regex that matches nothing makes `go test` print "testing: warning: no tests to run" and exit **0** -- a shard that ran nothing is green (from #166).
7. records subtests as their own units: `TestGeneratedClientWorksOnEveryRuntime` and `TestSessionIsolationHoldsOnEveryRuntime` (`internal/e2e/runtime_test.go:13,45`) are one `func Test` each but three runtimes' worth of time, so a packer that weighs by `func Test` under-counts them 3x (from #166 / #168).

Why it beats A: balance within a few percent regardless of naming, rebalancing is automatic on every run (no workflow edits), and "split the longest shard" becomes changing one number (`target_leg_seconds`). The alphabetical idea's real benefit -- a shard you can reproduce locally -- is kept by printing the regex, and the #99 policy can say "rerun the failing leg with the line in its summary". Honest costs: ~100-150 lines to own; shard membership changes between runs (fine, since the summary names the tests); timings are noisy (use the median of the last few main runs, not the last one); a very long `-run` regex is ugly but Go handles thousands of alternatives fine.

Existing tools considered: `gotesplit` splits by test **count**, not time; CircleCI's `tests split --split-by=timings` is CircleCI-only; `gotestsum` records `-json` but does not split. Nothing off the shelf does LPT from Go JSON timings on GitHub Actions without adopting a larger framework, so a small in-repo program is the honest choice.

Hybrid worth considering: keep the `-run` names meaningful by packing whole *files* first (B's readability) and only splitting `e2e_test.go` by LPT. Adds complexity for readability only; decide after the first timings.

### Beyond sharding: `t.Parallel` in e2e (the biggest single win; #52 no longer blocks it)

199 (now 209) serial tests that mostly wait on process start, sockets and runtime startup are the textbook case for `t.Parallel`: on one 4 vCPU runner it could plausibly cut e2e 2-3x with **zero** extra setup cost, and it composes with sharding (fewer legs needed). What stood in the way, and what still does:
- ~~#52: leaked daemons multiply under parallel runs, and the cleanup error is discarded.~~ **Fixed in #182**: cleanup runs `mcpx stop --all` through the info files and logs its error (`internal/e2e/e2e_test.go:71-85`), and every test daemon idles out after 60 s (`:68`, `:92`).
- #138: `newEnv` still starts from `os.Environ()` (`e2e_test.go:52`), so an exported `MCPX_DAEMON_ENDPOINT` or `MCPX_SOCKET` sends every test -- every *parallel* test at once -- to one outside daemon. Fix before parallelising.
- Shared state audit: no `t.Setenv`/`os.Setenv` in e2e (good -- `t.Setenv` forbids `t.Parallel`), and each `newEnv` isolates state/cache/config dirs (`internal/e2e/e2e_test.go:35-87`). Unknown: fixed ports, the stub registry, anything in `$HOME`, and whether a long `t.TempDir()` path pushes two tests' sockets into the shared private runtime dir (`internal/daemon/paths.go:103-133`; hashed per state dir, so a collision is unlikely but the directory is shared -- #88).
- Process count, not test count, is the unit of contention: each parallel test is 3-4 processes (above), so `-parallel 8` on 4 vCPU is 24-32 processes and the 90 s per-command timeout (`e2e_test.go:113`) stops being generous. Measure `-parallel` at 2, 4, 6, 8 and record the chosen value with its reason, rather than taking GOMAXPROCS (from #166 / #168).
- The fan-out tests above should stay serial (or get their own leg) so they do not starve the rest.
- #79 (faster CLI/exec, no self-socket) reduces per-test time directly; every e2e test pays process start.

Recommended order: #143 (unit/e2e split, first static shards, timing capture; the cache line already landed in #182) -> C with N = 3-4 -> #138's allowlist, then `t.Parallel` in e2e at a measured `-parallel`, re-measure, reduce N.

### Unexplained job-start delays

Measure, do not guess: the jobs API gives `created_at` (queued), `started_at`, and per-step times for every job (#140 reports max and sum of queue delay per run). Observed so far: 2-3 s in 9 of the last 10 runs, 37 s once (run 36663358199). If queue delay grows with leg count, merge the smallest legs (lint legs are the obvious candidates) before adding shards.

## Open questions

1. Per-test time distribution of e2e: is it flat (~0.5 s each) or dominated by a few slow tests? Decides whether LPT or "fix the ten slowest tests" comes first. (#143 captures it.)
2. Timing source: last main run's artifact (fresh, no commits) vs a committed file (reviewable, deterministic, needs a bot or manual refresh). Recommendation: artifact with committed fallback.
3. `target_leg_seconds` default: tie to the budget (#140) or set independently?
4. Should unit packages join the packer (as package-granularity items) or stay one leg? Probably one leg until units exceed ~30 s.
5. Split `e2e_test.go` into feature files regardless of CI? (Readability win; separate issue if wanted.)
6. ~~Does `t.Parallel` in e2e need a per-test daemon idle-exit (#52 fix 1) first, or only the stop-error fix?~~ Answered by #182, which landed both. The remaining precondition is #138.
7. A per-shard `-timeout`? A hung shard currently burns the default 10 minutes and #140 would report it as a budget breach rather than a hang (from #166).
8. `internal/tui` (8.6 s) stays in the unit leg: it is the second-largest package but does not justify a leg's fixed cost (from #166).

## Ease · Impact · Related

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#187 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #175

## Summary

Three runtime issues each introduce a content-addressed cache, and each designs it alone: #103 a prepared dependency
directory, #104 a resolved import graph, #107 a resolved flake reference. The one cache mcpx has today is sized and
evicted for something far smaller. Built three times, they get three layouts, three eviction rules and three
concurrency bugs -- and #78 (daemon state and cache correctness) gets three more members. This issue owns one cache
mechanism; the three issues own what they put in it.

This is #181 collision 12.

## Original notes

> - non-ai auto-import dynamic if a script imports something that isnt avaialble

>   - if i import a file in another dir that has its own package.json/lock can it auto-import, prepare dependencies to be available whereever needed

> - accept a flake url as an alternative exec env (devshell/shell.nix in default pwd or tempdir or ad-hoc flake that isfully isolated, path executed before script, script executed inside 

## Current state (05c78b2)

- Exec workdirs are content-addressed and evicted **by count**: `pruneWorkDirs` (`internal/runner/runner.go:808`) keeps
  `defaults.ExecWorkDirs` directories (`internal/defaults/defaults.go:413`). Each holds a generated client -- kilobytes.
- It is already one of three count-based pruners, each written separately: `prunePrograms` (`runner.go:768`, generated
  programs per workdir), `pruneWorkDirs` (`:808`) and `pruneEntries` (`:847`, entry points beside a user's script).
  Their bounds (`exec.programs: 64`, `exec.workDirs: 8`, `exec.entries: 8`, `internal/defaults/defaults.json:96-100`)
  are built-in defaults, not settings.
- Nothing is evicted by size or age, nothing pins an entry a running exec is using, and there is no listing or prune
  command for cached state. Each pruner spares only the caller's own entry (`if p == keep`) and orders the rest by
  mtime, so a concurrent run's directory is protected only by being recent.

The three proposals differ by orders of magnitude, which is the point this issue exists to make:

| Cache | Proposed in | Key (as proposed) | Size of an entry |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| prepared dependencies (`node_modules`, deno/bun cache) | #103 | dependency set | tens to hundreds of MB |
| import graph | #104 | entry file hash + transitive mtimes | kilobytes |
| flake resolution | #107 | reference + lock | bytes -- but the store path it names lives in `/nix/store` and is collected by `nix-collect-garbage` unless mcpx holds a GC root |

Two more candidate tenants are proposed in sibling issues, and they should not become a fourth and fifth design:
#100's compiled JS (`script.compile`, "its own cache keyed by script hash + runtime" is an open question there) and
#105's uv environments per dependency set.

So "one cache" should mean one **mechanism** (layout, keys, index, eviction, pinning), not one blob store.

## Approaches

**A -- each issue keeps its own directory and pruning.** What happens by default. Count-based eviction applied to
`node_modules` trees is unbounded in bytes, and three prune loops race each other and any running exec.

**B -- generalise `pruneWorkDirs` to every kind: one root, evicted by count.** One mechanism, little code. Count is the
wrong unit when entries differ by five orders of magnitude, and it still has no pinning, so a prune can delete the
dependencies of an exec that is running.

**C -- recommended: one cache package with per-kind namespaces.** `<state>/cache/<kind>/<key>`; keys are the SHA-256 of
canonical inputs (for #104, content hashes rather than mtimes, which are not stable across checkouts); entries are
created in a temp directory and renamed into place; a lease (lock file or refcount) pins an entry while an exec uses it;
eviction by total bytes and age, never touching a leased entry; #107's entries register and drop nix GC roots; limits
are settings (`cache.maxBytes`, `cache.maxAge`; names open), and `mcpx cache` lists and prunes (or the existing
`status` gains a section -- prefer that over a new command if it fits). Recommended because it is the only option that
gives the large kind a byte bound and every kind a guarantee that a running script's inputs are not deleted under it.

## Open questions

- Should #103 cache at all, or lean on the runtimes' own content-addressed caches (`DENO_DIR`, bun's global cache with
  hardlinks, npm's cache) and have mcpx cache only the resolved manifest? That would shrink the large kind to bytes.
- Who evicts -- the daemon, or any process that writes? Eviction racing between a daemon and a standalone CLI run is
  the #78 bug class.
- Do the existing exec workdirs (and the program and entry pruners) move onto this, or stay as they are? If they move,
  their three built-in bounds become settings of the mechanism rather than three more constants.
- Timing: this has to be settled before the first of #103/#104/#107 ships a cache. After that, it is a migration.
- The daemon's schema cache is a fourth existing cache with its own invalidation, a hand-bumped `cacheVersion` (`internal/daemon/registry.go:102-106`; #78 item 3). Whether it joins the mechanism (keyed by content instead of a version constant) is the same question as the pruners.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** M · **Impact** med-high -- cheap now, expensive after the first of #103/#104/#107 ships its own.
Related: #103, #104, #107 (users), #100 and #105 (candidate users: compiled JS, uv environments), #78 (cache
correctness), #181 (collision 12).

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#144 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #96

## Summary

Decide how the reference part of the mcpx docs is produced so it cannot drift from the binary: settings, environment variables and flags, global CLI arguments, CLI commands, the `/v1` API, the MCP tools mcpx serves, the protocol matrix, the parity matrix and the man page as HTML.

**This issue was added by the architect.** The user's notes have no "generated reference" bullet. They do ask for pages on "env vars", "cli arguments", "cli commands", "mcp compatibility" and "/v1", and for a compendium where "basically everything that is built can be described". Those pages are the ones that go stale fastest, and mcpx already has single sources for most of them (the settings registry, `Commands()`, the ops table, the protocol feature table). Writing the pages by hand would throw that away. So the reference pages are generated, and this issue picks how. The prose around them (#146, #147) stays hand-written.

The reading below found that some reference docs have already drifted, and that several "single sources" have gaps. Those gaps would be published as-is. They are listed as bug candidates under "Found while reading", separate from the docs work.

## Original notes

> - documentation
>   - make a book using whatever is the most common and simple modern choice
>     - 3 main things, not book sections jsut like levels of detail-
>       - the 'ok i just installed this thing what even is it' layer
>         - a page or section in a page for
>           - env vars
>           - cli
>           - cli arguments
>           - cli commands
>           - mcp
>           - mcp compatibility
>           - /v1
>       - the compendium
>         - basically everything that is built can be described here in as much detail as you want. you don't need to hold back it's an encyclopedia

These lines are the parents plus the reference-shaped children of the level-2 list. The other children of line 52 belong to #146 and #147. The compendium lines are quoted because its reference sections, such as per-area setting tables, should include the same generated fragments rather than copy them.

## Current state

Paths are relative to `pkgs/mcpx/`. Written on `main` (d0b7e01); line numbers re-cited at `05c78b2` in the 2026-09-30 issues pass.

### What each reference surface is generated from today

| Page | Single source in code | Machine output today | Docs today | Checked? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Settings / env vars / flags | `settings.Registry()`, `internal/settings/schema.go` (`Setting`, `FlagName()`/`EnvName()` at :211-243) | `mcpx config --schema [--plumbing]` text (`settings/file.go:175` `Describe`) or `--json` (`file.go:219` `JSON`); roff `SETTINGS` / `PLUMBING` sections (`cli/manual.go:386`, `:412`) | `docs/configuration.md:149-474`, "Every setting": 28 section tables, 149 rows | Presence only (below) |
| CLI commands | `cli.Commands()` (`cli/manual.go:33`), 32 entries | `mcpx man` (roff, `manual.go:333`); `mcpx help <cmd>` (`helpFor`, `cli/root.go:473`); `mcpx completion` (`cli/completion.go:17`) | Roff man page only (`package.nix:88-94` writes `share/man/man1/mcpx.1` and completions); `docs/parity.md:71-111` CLI table by hand | No |
| Global CLI arguments | None: a hand-written `switch` in `cmd/mcpx/main.go:62-104` | Hand-written `usage` const, GLOBAL FLAGS block at `cli/root.go:589-595` | Nowhere else | No |
| `/v1` API | `api.Ops()` in `internal/api/ops*.go`, 60 operations | `api.OpenAPI(version)` (`api/openapi.go:18`) served at `GET /v1/openapi.json` (`daemon/ops.go:38`, `:498`) | `docs/parity.md:23-70` | Code-vs-code only (below) |
| MCP tools mcpx serves | `mcpserver.New(...).WithExtras(mcpserver.OpTools(...))` (`mcpserver/ops.go:30-32` builds one tool per op) | `mcpx openapi` lists them as `/v1/tools/<name>` (`cli/openapi.go:65-81`) | `docs/parity.md` "MCP tool" column | Code-vs-code |
| Protocol matrix | `mcpserver.Supported` (`server.go:778`), `Features` / `FeatureMatrix()` (`revisions.go:292-316`), `capabilities(version, conn)` (`server.go:1389`; per connection since #171) | `GET /v1/protocol` | `docs/protocol.md` §1, §2.1, §2.2, hand-written | No |
| Parity matrix | ops table plus the tool list; the CLI and plugin columns have no source | none | `docs/parity.md`, hand-written | Code only; the file itself is never read |
| Upstream tool types | the user's configured servers | `mcpx schema --format json-schema\|openapi\|typescript\|mcp` (`cli/publish.go:60`), needs a daemon (`publish.go:75`) | n/a | n/a |

The last row is not a docs source. `mcpx schema` publishes the types of whatever servers the builder has configured, not mcpx's own surface, so a docs build must not depend on it. It can appear only as an example.

### The settings table: how it is made, and what the test checks

- There is no emitter in the tree. `| setting | kind | default | scope | hot |` appears only in `docs/configuration.md`, and nothing under `internal/` produces it. The table arrived in 32f49b9 (#56, "adds docs/configuration.md with a generated inventory"), but the generator was not committed. The rendering is inconsistent: an empty default is `` ` ` `` at `configuration.md:166` and `*(empty)*` in 20 other rows, which suggests at least two ad-hoc runs. #171's two new rows (`plugin.remember`, `plugin.annotate`) were appended by hand after `plugin.tools` (`configuration.md:354-355`), out of alphabetical order.
- `docs/configuration.md:151-153` says "Generated from the registry; a test fails if this list and the registry disagree. `mcpx config --schema --plumbing` prints the same thing". Neither half is quite true:
  - `internal/settings/docs_test.go:19-48` fails only if a setting's path or its `MCPX_*` name is missing in backticks. `:52-65` checks that each scope has a `**scope**` explanation somewhere in the file. Kind, default, scope, hot, flag, aliases and description can all drift without failing anything.
  - `mcpx config --schema` prints neither scope nor hot. `Describe` (`file.go:175-208`) and `JSON` (`file.go:219-252`) both omit them, yet the table has both columns.
- Today the table and the registry agree on names: 149 settings in `internal/settings/*.go` and 149 rows, with every one-line `Short` present. Nothing keeps it that way.
- The same `Setting` is projected in four places, with different field names. A generated page must pick one:

  | Projection | Where | Field names |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Schema JSON | `settings/file.go:219` | `short`/`long`, `flag` without `--`, no scope or hot |
  | `/v1/settings` record | `daemon/routes_settings.go:85-99` | `description`/`detail`, `--flag`, `scope` and `hot` |
  | OpenAPI extension | `cli/openapi.go:147` `x-mcpx-settings` | `short`, `--flag`, no scope, hot or long |
  | Roff | `manual.go:386-425` | text |

### Commands: `Commands()` is not the single source it says it is

- `manual.go:12-17` (the `Command` type's doc comment; `Commands()` itself is at `:33`) says commands are "described once so that help, the man page and the command table cannot disagree about what exists". But dispatch is a separate map in `cmd/mcpx/main.go:119-162`. Seven dispatched commands are not in `Commands()`: **`serve`, `adapter`, `registry`, `openapi`, `api`, `man`, `completion`** (plus the undeclared alias `logs`). As a result:
  - `mcpx help serve` answers "no command" (`root.go:488`).
  - The man page and shell completion omit them.
  - A page generated from `Commands()` would omit `mcpx serve --transport stdio`, one of the main integration surfaces.
- `mcpx help` with no argument prints a hand-written const (`root.go:549-611`), not `Commands()`. Its groups (DISCOVERY / RUNNING / MANAGEMENT / DIAGNOSTICS) differ from `Commands()`'s groups (running / discovery / daemon / configuration / inspection). It omits `schema`, `elicit`, `doctor`, `prompts`, `resources`, `tui`, `explore` and `help`.
- Per-command flags are mostly hand-declared: 130 declarations across non-test `internal/cli/*.go` at `05c78b2` (118 `x := fs.String/Bool/Int/Duration` plus 12 `fs.Var`; a count of 118 misses the `fs.Var` ones). Examples are `config --schema/--plumbing/--path` and `man --install`. `settings.Bind` skips a registry flag when a hand-written one already has the name (`settings/bind.go:63-74`). For instance, `mcpx daemon` hand-declares `--log-level` and `--format` (`root.go:98-108`). Those names are also the registry aliases of `logging.level` and `logging.format` (`configuration.md:296`, `:299`), so on `mcpx daemon` the hand-written flags win. ~~They resolve through `os.Getenv("MCPX_FORMAT")` and `os.Getenv("MCPX_LOG_LEVEL")` (`root.go:95-101`), and `MCPX_FORMAT` appears in no table. Whether the documented `MCPX_LOGGING_FORMAT` reaches the daemon's own log writer on this path is not verified; either way, a generated table could not show it.~~ *Fixed in #171:* after the hand-written flag, the daemon now falls back to the resolved `logging.format` / `logging.level` (`root.go:131-146`), so `MCPX_LOGGING_FORMAT` and the config key reach its writer and `MCPX_FORMAT` is read nowhere. The shadowing itself remains: a generated per-command page must show the hand-written flag, not the registry alias. Hand-declared flags are invisible to `helpFor` (`root.go:506-516` lists registry settings only), to the man page and to completion. They appear only in Go's `-h` output.
- Global flags (`--json`, `--tui`, `--profile`, `--skip-default`, `--all-profiles`, `--config`, `--version/-v`, `--help/-h`) are a `switch` in `main.go:63-105`. `usage` lists six of them (`root.go:589-595`).
- `ManPage` stamps `time.Now()` into `.TH` (`manual.go:335`). The same commit therefore yields different bytes on different days, which breaks golden comparison and Nix reproducibility.
- The man page embeds hand-kept lists: launcher placeholders (`manual.go:427-449`) and files (`:450-458`).

### `/v1`, MCP tools and parity

- The architect's context says the ops table generates routes. It does not. The table generates OpenAPI and the MCP proxy tools. Routes are hand-registered with `mux.HandleFunc` (e.g. `daemon/ops.go:28-38`), and `api/parity_test.go:21` reads the route patterns out of the daemon source with a regex. The tests at `:54`, `:73` and `:87` check route ↔ op ↔ tool in code.
- **`docs/parity.md` is already stale, and no test reads it.** 27 of the 60 ops have no row in its `/v1` table (this said 26 until the 2026-09-30 pass; `exec` was missed, see #180):
  - artifacts: `artifact_get`, `artifact_put`, `artifact_delete`, `artifacts_list`
  - ask: `ask_begin`, `ask_poll`, `ask_answers`, `ask_abandon`
  - recipes and intent: `recipes_list`, `recipe_get`, `recipe_save`, `recipe_run`, `intent`, `diagnose`
  - settings: `settings_list`, `settings_get`, `settings_set`, `settings_unset`
  - servers: `servers_list`, `servers_add`, `servers_remove`
  - other: `call_path`, `catalog_history`, `exec`, `protocol`, `resolve`, `tool_invoke`

  The file's own claim (`parity.md:12-16`) is about code, not about the file. This is the drift the whole issue exists to prevent. Its `## Known gaps` section describes gaps within the 33 documented ops, so a reader cannot tell a known gap from a missing row. **#145 owns the fix for that (#181 collision 18):** its drift check fails on an absent row, not only on a wrong one. The page's content belongs to whoever regenerates it (#76 for the CLI column, this issue for the shape).
- `GET /v1/openapi.json` merges in one path per *currently loaded upstream tool* on every request (`daemon/ops.go:498-535`). Fetched from a running daemon, it describes the builder's configuration. `api.OpenAPI(version)` alone is static and callable in-process.
- Every response schema is `{"type": "object"}` (`api/openapi.go:110-120`). Any renderer will show no response shapes.
- There are two OpenAPI documents. `mcpx openapi` (`cli/openapi.go:21`, `:166`) describes the `mcpx serve --transport http` surface: `/mcp`, `/health`, `/openapi.json`, `/v1/tools/<tool>` and `x-mcpx-settings`. `GET /v1/openapi.json` describes the daemon. `cli/openapi.go:16` claims it is generated from "the command table", but it does not read `Commands()`.
- The MCP tool list can be built offline: `mcpserver.New(nil, "mcpx", v).WithExtras(mcpserver.OpTools(nil))` (`parity_test.go:90`).

### Protocol

`docs/protocol.md:61-64` already says "the document defers to the endpoint". Two of its tables can be computed from code today:
- §1: the revisions against the features (`FeatureMatrix()`).
- §2.2: the declared capabilities per revision (`capabilities(v, conn)` for each `Supported` version, unexported). Since #171 the answer depends on whether the connection can push, and `logging` is no longer declared, so the committed §2.2 table (`docs/protocol.md:98-106`) is already wrong (#159 item 18).

§2.1 (methods) is a `switch` in `mcpserver/server.go:504-765`, not data. It stays hand-written unless methods become a table. §2.3, §3-§6 are prose.

### Where the checks run

- CI runs `go test ./... -count=1` (`.github/workflows/mcpx.yml:65`).
- The Nix `checkPhase` (`package.nix:73-81`) runs `./internal/settings/` (and `./internal/mcpserver/`), but not `./internal/api/` or `./internal/cli/`. So `nix build .#mcpx` enforces the settings presence test but not the parity tests.

Docs checks run in CI; see the testing trackers under #91 (CI pipeline #95, integration/environments #97).

## Found while reading: bug candidates (not docs work; the lead should file or fold them)

Filed: all six are tracked in #159 (items 1, 8, 6, 5, 11 and 10 respectively), which owns the fixes. They stay listed here because they are prerequisites of this design.

1. **Seven dispatched commands are missing from `Commands()`.** The top-level help is a hand-written const. Fix: dispatch from the command table, or a test that the dispatch keys are a subset of `Commands()` names plus aliases. This blocks a correct CLI reference.
2. **Hand-declared per-command flags are undocumented everywhere except `-h`.** This blocks a correct per-command page. It is the #74 shape in documentation form: a flag nobody can discover.
3. **Derived names split acronyms letter by letter** (`dashed`, `schema.go:227-243`). Four settings are affected:

   | Setting | Flag | Variable | Where |
   | --- | --- | --- | --- |
   | `daemon.leaseTTL` | `--daemon-lease-t-t-l` | `MCPX_DAEMON_LEASE_T_T_L` | `configuration.md:216` |
   | `proto.askTTL` | `--proto-ask-t-t-l` | | `:403` |
   | `proto.serveMCP` | `--proto-serve-m-c-p` | `MCPX_PROTO_SERVE_M_C_P` | `:407`, and this one is not plumbing |
   | `proto.stateTTL` | `--proto-state-t-t-l` | | `:409` |

   A generated page publishes these as-is, and once published, renaming them is a breaking change. Decide before the site goes live: acronym-aware `dashed()`, or explicit `Flag`/`Env` plus the old spellings as `FlagAliases`/`EnvAliases`.
4. **The man page date is not reproducible** (`manual.go:335`). Use `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` when it is set.
5. **`docs/parity.md` is missing 27 ops,** as listed above.
6. **`mcpx config --schema` omits scope and hot,** although `configuration.md:152` says it prints "the same thing".

## Pages to generate

| Page | Source | Shape | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Settings, env vars, flags | registry, plus the declared table of non-setting `MCPX_*` variables that #172 owns | One full table with one section per top-level key, plus the same sections includable one at a time (per-area pages, compendium entries) | Columns as today: setting, kind, default, scope, hot, flag(s), variable(s), governs. Plus `Long` and enum values. Plumbing marked, not hidden. |
| Global CLI arguments | a new `GlobalFlags()` table that `main.go` parses from | One page | Needs bug candidate 1's refactor, or it is hand-written with a presence test |
| CLI commands | `Commands()` + registry `ForCommand` + the hand-declared flags | An index grouped by `Group` (the man page's titles, `manual.go:354-360`), and one page per command: usage, summary, aliases, detail, examples, flags with scope | One page per command suits search and linking from #147. Subcommands (`settings get/set`, `servers add/remove`, `log sql/record`, `elicit answer`, `recipes run`) are not data today. |
| `/v1` API | `api.Ops()` | Markdown, one section per op: method and path, summary, description, parameters, admin/mutating/destructive/streams, the MCP tool that reaches it (`ToolName()` / `CoveredBy`) | Also publish the raw `openapi.json` next to it. An HTML "try it" renderer is optional (below). |
| MCP tools mcpx serves | the tool list from `mcpserver.New(...).WithExtras(OpTools(nil))` | name, description, annotations (`readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`), input parameters | Covers both the hand-written tools and the `mcpx_<op>` proxies |
| Protocol matrix | `Supported`, `Features`, `FeatureMatrix()`, `capabilities(v)` | The §1 and §2.2 tables | §2.1 methods stay hand-written, with a presence test, until methods are data |
| Parity matrix | ops, tools, plus CLI and plugin columns | The `/v1` table generated. The CLI column needs a source: an Op field naming its commands, which #76 would want anyway. The plugin column comes from `plugin/opencode/mcpx/daemon.ts` method names, or stays hand-written. | Its "Known gaps" prose stays hand-written |
| Man page as HTML | the same data as the per-command and settings pages | The per-command and settings pages *are* the HTML manual. Also link the raw `mcpx.1`. | Converting roff to HTML (mandoc/pandoc) would render a lossy copy of data we already have |

Every generated page must work as-is as its own agent twin (#120): plain markdown, no generator-specific syntax inside the fragment.

## Approaches

### Approach A (least recommended): keep hand-maintained pages with presence tests

This is today's model, extended. Keep writing the tables by hand, add presence tests for `parity.md` and a command page, and fix the empty-default rendering.

Why not:
- A presence test proves that a name appears. It says nothing about whether its default, scope, description or flag is right, and those are what a reader comes for.
- It does not scale to one page per command or per `/v1` op.
- `parity.md` shows the failure under this model: a claim of test coverage sat next to 26 missing rows.
- Every new setting or op needs a hand edit in the same PR, and forgetting it fails a test only when the *name* is missing.

### Approach B (middle): the site generator reads machine output at build time

The docs build starts from the binary's JSON and renders it with templates or a preprocessor in the docs toolchain (#117). With mdBook, that is a preprocessor reading `[context, book]` on stdin.

Inputs:
- `mcpx config --schema --plumbing --json`
- `mcpx openapi` (the serve surface)
- `GET /v1/openapi.json` from a started daemon
- `mcpx man` converted with pandoc

The OpenAPI goes through Redoc (the `redocly build-docs` single HTML file), Scalar or Stoplight Elements for the `/v1` page.

What you get: no change to the Go code, and the HTML renderers give a polished "try it" UI.

What it costs:
- **The inputs are incomplete.** The schema JSON has no scope or hot. No command emits the command table as data, and the hand-declared flags are in no output at all. So B still needs Go changes (JSON output for commands, scope and hot in the schema); it just moves the markdown into templates.
- **`GET /v1/openapi.json` depends on the builder's configuration** (`daemon/ops.go:498-535`). The build must start a daemon with an empty config, an isolated state directory and a clean shutdown. #52 showed how easily that lifecycle leaks. #182 fixed the e2e leak (`stop --all` through the info files, plus `MCPX_AUTOSTART_IDLE_EXIT=60s`, `internal/e2e/e2e_test.go:60-83`), but a docs build would have to repeat that discipline. `api.OpenAPI` in-process avoids it, but that is a Go-side emitter, which is C.
- **The renderers produce HTML, not markdown.** Redoc, Scalar and Elements are JS-rendered HTML. The agent twin (#120) needs markdown, so B also needs an OpenAPI-to-markdown converter. That is one more third-party tool to vet and pin, and the ops table's MCP-specific facts (tool name, `CoveredBy`, admin, destructive) survive only as `x-mcpx-*` extensions that a generic converter ignores.
- The templates live in a different language and toolchain from the types they render. Adding a field to `Setting` or `Op` then means editing Go and the templates, and nothing fails when only one is edited.

### Approach C (recommended): the binary emits markdown itself, from one renderer package, via `--format` on existing commands

A new package, e.g. `internal/refdoc`, holds pure functions from the existing data to markdown:
- settings from `settings.Schema`
- commands and global flags from `Commands()` plus the registry
- `/v1` from `api.Ops()`
- tools from `mcpserver`
- protocol tables from `FeatureMatrix()` / `capabilities`
- the parity table

Existing commands expose it:

| Invocation | Output |
| --- | --- |
| `mcpx man --format roff\|markdown [-o DIR]` | Roff stays the default. Markdown writes the whole reference tree into `DIR`: CLI index, global flags, one page per command, settings, `/v1`, MCP tools, protocol and parity tables. "The manual" is the whole reference, and roff is the terminal subset of it. `man` already has `--install DIR` (`CmdMan`, `root.go:255-276`). |
| `mcpx config --schema --format text\|json\|markdown` | The settings fragment alone, the same bytes as the settings page. `--json` stays as a synonym for `--format json`, and JSON gains `scope` and `hot`. |
| `mcpx openapi` | Unchanged. It is published as a file next to the `/v1` page. A daemon-surface variant (`--surface daemon`) is only needed if someone wants the static daemon spec without a daemon. Open question. |

No new command and no new endpoint.

Why the binary rather than a separate `go run` generator:
- An installed `mcpx` can print a reference that matches itself, offline: `mcpx man --format markdown | less`, or an agent reading it. That is the same argument that put the roff page in the binary.
- `package.nix` can write the tree to `$out/share/doc/mcpx/`, so the docs derivation (#118) copies it from `${mcpx}` instead of building mcpx a second time.

Why the data rather than OpenAPI for `/v1`: the ops table carries the facts a reader of mcpx needs (MCP tool name, `CoveredBy`, admin, destructive), and it is available without a daemon.

**Committed goldens or build-only?** Both have a place. The split is whether the file already has to render on GitHub.

| | Committed and regenerated in place (golden) | Generated at build, never committed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pages | Tables inside `docs/configuration.md`, `docs/parity.md` and `docs/protocol.md`, between markers like `<!-- mcpx:generated settings -->` … `<!-- /mcpx:generated -->` | CLI per-command pages, global flags, `/v1`, MCP tools, the site's settings page |
| Why | These files are read on GitHub and linked from `story.md`. GitHub does not process mdBook's `{{#include}}`, so an include directive there would show as literal text. | They exist only on the site. Committing them adds churn and review noise and buys nothing. |
| Check | A Go test renders each marked region and compares it with the committed bytes, with `-update` to rewrite (the standard Go golden idiom). CI fails on drift. | None needed: they cannot differ from the binary that built them. CI checks that the docs build succeeds. |
| Risk | A contributor must run the update step. The failure message says exactly which command to run. | A reader browsing the repo sees no per-command pages, only `mcpx help <cmd>`. |

On the site, the prose pages include fragments from the generated directory rather than from the marker regions, so the site never depends on a committed copy being current. mdBook's `{{#include file.md:anchor}}` with `ANCHOR:` / `ANCHOR_END:` lines, which it strips, lets one generated settings file serve both the full table and per-area includes. That covers the compendium entries and the #146 config pages with no extra flags.

Prerequisites before any page is published:
- Bug candidates 1 and 2 (complete command table, discoverable per-command flags).
- Bug candidate 3 (names are forever once published).
- Bug candidate 4 (deterministic output).

#74 bears on this directly. A generated per-command page states, from `Setting.Commands`, which flags a command accepts, so the page is only as honest as those lists. For example, `pool.max`/`pool.min`/`pool.idleTimeout` list `status` and `restart` (`settings/registry.go:30-80`) and are daemon-scoped, and #77 notes that `pool.callTimeout` is listed for run/exec/call but is not call-scoped. The page must show scope next to every flag, with a line saying what a daemon-scoped flag does on a command that talks to an already-running daemon. #74's proposed flag-walk test is what earns the page the right to say "accepted". #75 (which closed #74) built that walk for exec's flags. #129 owns extending it to every setting (#181 collision 15).

## Open questions

1. **Markers plus goldens for the three in-repo files, or move those tables out entirely** so the repo files link to the site? Moving is simpler, but the tables disappear from GitHub browsing.
2. **The `/v1` HTML renderer:** is a Redoc/Scalar/Elements "try it" page wanted in addition to the markdown page? It has to point at a daemon the reader runs, over loopback CORS. Deferred unless asked.
3. **Hand-declared flags: capture them, or declare them as data?** Capture works because every command calls `newFlagSet` then `parseFlags` (`root.go:34-67`) before doing any work, so `parseFlags` can record `fs.VisitAll` and return a sentinel. Declaring moves each command's flags into `Command`. Capture is cheap but depends on every command parsing before side effects. Data is more work but also serves #74.
4. **Subcommands** (`settings set`, `servers add`, `log sql`, ...): should `Command` gain `Sub []Command`?
5. **The parity CLI column:** should an `Op` name the CLI commands that reach it, checked against `Commands()`? #76 would then generate from the same field.
6. **Groups:** do per-command pages follow `Commands()` groups or the hand-written `usage` groups? Fixing bug candidate 1 forces a choice.
7. **Does the `/v1` page need response schemas** (today all `{"type":"object"}`)? That is an ops-table change, separate from docs.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** M. The decision itself is small, but it forces the choices about command-table completeness and flag capture. · **Impact** high. Every reference page and the agent twin depend on it, and it stops the drift already visible in `parity.md`. · **Depends on / related**: #117 (mdBook `{{#include}}` and anchors, preprocessor), #120 (fragments double as the twin), #146, #147 (the prose that includes the fragments), #145 (implementation; owns #181 collision 18: the parity drift check fails on an absent row), #118 (the docs derivation), #74 (closed, fixed in #75; a generated page must not advertise ignored flags), #129 (the guard that a flag changes an outcome, #181 collision 15), #76 (CLI for /v1-only ops, same source as the parity CLI column), #77 (protocol follow-ups; `pool.callTimeout` scope), #49 (CI), #52 (closed, fixed in #182; why B's started daemon is a liability), #159 (the bug candidates below, filed), #172 (the outbound `MCPX_*` table the env-var page needs).

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

body:
## Origin

Follow-up to #437 (closed by Drew's decision, 2026-10-28): fixed ports + port-file publication is the standing design for the four `bin/` proxies, AND option (e) from that issue — systemd socket activation — is approved.

## What

Today each proxy (clef 18742, agy 18743, codex 18744, antigravity-ls 18745) binds its own port. When the service restarts or crash-loops, anything connecting in that window is refused, and a previous instance still holding the port crash-loops the new one.

With socket activation, systemd owns the listener from boot and hands the socket to the service: connections queue instead of being refused while the service restarts, and the port can never be double-bound. OpenChamber already works this way (`systemd.user.sockets.openchamber`, home/common/default.nix) — this extends the proven pattern.

## Scope

- One `systemd.user.sockets` unit per proxy, holding its existing fixed port (ports do not change — #437 KEEP ruling).
- Each proxy's `.mjs` accepts the handed-off socket (`LISTEN_FDS` protocol, `server.listen({ fd: 3 })`) and still binds the port itself when launched outside systemd, so manual runs keep working.
- Services become socket-activated (no longer need to bind on start).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Socket units + service changes land in the flake and evaluate in the `amd` host config.
- [ ] After the NixOS switch on the laptop: restarting a proxy service mid-flight no longer refuses a client connection (it queues and completes once the service is back) — demonstrated for at least one proxy.
- [ ] Launching a proxy by hand (no systemd) still works exactly as today.
- [ ] A still-running previous instance can no longer crash-loop its replacement on the port.

body:
Phase 2 of design #1414 (cold-restart upstream HTTP session resume). Depends on Phase 1 (persist + resume). Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-cold-restart-session-resume.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace.

## Scope

Make a resumed session that turns out to be dead indistinguishable from a fresh start, and keep the persisted records honest as config changes:

- **Expiry fallback:** if the first request sent on a resumed session is answered **404** (upstream forgot the session — the streamable HTTP spec's session-expiry signal; mcpx already treats a 404 DELETE as "already forgotten" in `closeSession`, `internal/mcpclient/http.go`), the client drops the persisted record, performs a fresh `initialize`, and retries the call **once**, transparently to the caller. A second failure surfaces exactly as failures surface today.
- **Credential rotation:** the same drop-and-reinitialise-once path on **401/403** to the first request of a resumed session (headers are re-derived from live config at restore, so a refusal means the session/credential pairing is stale, not that the new credentials are wrong — one fresh initialize with the current credentials is the correct test).
- Only the *first* request of a resumed session gets this treatment; a 404 mid-session keeps today's behaviour.
- **Record hygiene on config change:** when a server leaves the config, its persisted record is deleted at reload. A best-effort upstream DELETE is attempted with a transient transport built from the last live config when one is still available (the `TerminateHTTPSession` shape, headers re-derived — never from the record, which holds none); when no live config remains, the removal is logged as left-to-expire — the #260 degradation, made explicit instead of silent.
- Coordinate with the roadmap's "Legacy client robustness" row (`planning/roadmaps/mcpx.md`; nix#200, nix#201, nix#203): this issue is only the resumed-session slice of session-404 handling, not a second general 404 project. If triage finds the general fix landing elsewhere, narrow this issue to wiring the persisted-record drop into it.

Out of scope (Phase 3 of #1414, undecided): graceful-shutdown DELETE semantics, record TTL, dashboard resumed-vs-fresh visibility.

## Acceptance

- Test: upstream that forgets sessions on demand → a call on a resumed-but-forgotten session succeeds; exactly one extra `initialize` observed upstream; caller sees no error.
- Test: resumed session answered 401 on first request → one fresh initialize with current credentials → call succeeds (or surfaces the second refusal unchanged).
- Test: a 404 on a non-first request of a resumed session is NOT retried (today's behaviour preserved).
- Test: server removed from config → its record is gone after reload; DELETE attempted when a live config was available; left-to-expire logged when not.
- Full suite passes: `cd pkgs/mcpx && go test ./...`.

body:
Phase 1 of design #1414 (cold-restart upstream HTTP session resume). Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-cold-restart-session-resume.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace.

## Scope

Persist the resumable half of each legacy streamable-HTTP upstream session in the mcpx daemon state directory and restore it on cold start, reusing the takeover restore path:

- New versioned state file next to `sessions.json`, written/read with the `internal/daemon/sessions.go` discipline: atomic tmp+rename, `defaults.PrivateMode`, version envelope, ignore-and-log on version mismatch or corruption.
- Record per pool instance: instance key (server name + pool scope key), upstream URL, config fingerprint (hash over the session-defining config fields + header/auth **names** — never values), `SessionID`, `Negotiated`, the full `mcpclient.Session` protocol state (as returned by `Client.SessionState()`), `savedAt`.
- The record type has **no field for headers or resolved secret values** — that absence is the security invariant (handoff headers travel over the takeover socket only; see `HTTPHandoff` comment in `internal/mcpclient/http.go`). On restore, headers are re-derived from live config via the existing `httpOptions()` / `resolveAuth()` path.
- Save triggers: successful legacy `initialize` (session established) and any response that installs a new `Mcp-Session-Id` (`internal/mcpclient/http.go:156`). Save failure: log, non-fatal — the daemon behaves exactly as today.
- Restore: at pool connect, if a record exists and its fingerprint matches the live config, seed the transport with `ht.Resume(...)` and build the client with `mcpclient.Resume(...)` — the identical calls the takeover path makes (`internal/pool/handoff.go:238,326`). **No parallel resume implementation.**
- Fingerprint mismatch → record discarded, fresh initialize, no error surfaced.
- Scope limits: legacy-era streamable HTTP only. Modern era (no sessions) and legacy SSE (session lives in the GET stream) are untouched. Takeover behaviour unchanged. The standalone GET stream is re-established on resume exactly as takeover re-establishes it — parity with takeover is the bar.

Out of scope (Phase 2 / Phase 3 of #1414): 404/401 expiry fallback and retry, record removal on config removal, graceful-shutdown DELETE semantics, TTL, dashboard visibility.

## Acceptance

- Defining test passes: daemon against a test HTTP upstream → legacy session established → daemon killed with SIGKILL → daemon restarted → first call succeeds; the upstream saw **no** second `initialize`; the request carried the original `Mcp-Session-Id`.
- Fingerprint-mismatch record is ignored and a fresh initialize happens (test).
- Corrupt / version-mismatched state file is ignored and logged; daemon starts and operates normally (test).
- No test or code path writes a resolved header/secret value into the state file (record type has no such field; assert in test by scanning the written file for a sentinel secret value).
- Takeover tests and the full suite pass: `cd pkgs/mcpx && go test ./...`.

The direction decision sits with Drew on #1414 (`user/review`) — triage may proceed, implementation start should respect that decision.

title: id(web): GitHub alert blockquotes lose their alert on save — [!NOTE] marker is backslash-escaped into plain text

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id

labels.description: Medium: expected under 1 day of work

body:
## Problem

GitHub alert blockquotes (`> [!NOTE]`, `> [!TIP]`, `> [!WARNING]`, …) lose their alert semantics on save in the id web editor: the marker is backslash-escaped, so every CommonMark/GitHub renderer afterwards shows a plain blockquote containing the literal text `[!NOTE]` instead of a rendered alert.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `0cbb91b1`)

Probe: verbatim copy of `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs` in a standalone crate (comrak 0.56.0), `markdown_to_prosemirror` → `prosemirror_to_markdown`. Logs: fleet bookkeeping `probe-2026-10-27-creator-a/out.log`, `out3.log`, `out4.log` (raw-output capture).

Input:

```markdown
> [!NOTE]
> Remember this.
```

The parse direction has no alert concept — the marker becomes ordinary paragraph text `!NOTE` bracketed as `[!NOTE]` — and the save direction escapes it (raw bytes verified, not debug-escaped):

```markdown
> \[!NOTE\] Remember this.
```

Same result for `[!WARNING]` and `[!TIP]`, single- and multi-line, and with following paragraphs (all in the probe logs). The visible text a reader sees after one save is the same words, but GitHub's alert rendering keys on the unescaped `[!NOTE]` marker at the start of the blockquote's first line — after the escape is written, the alert is gone for every future reader, and the literal backslashes are what a raw-markdown reader sees.

Root cause: `commonmark_options` (`pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs:81-91`) enables strikethrough/tasklist/table/footnotes but not comrak's alerts extension, and the codec has no blockquote-variant representation, so the marker is plain text and the CommonMark renderer escapes the `![` sequence exactly as it would for literal bracket text (compare the wikilink case in the same probe: `[[Other Page]]` is likewise escaped — correct for literal text, wrong for a construct the parser should have claimed).

## Why it matters

Alerts are the standard callout syntax in GitHub READMEs and docs — exactly the files a markdown editor like id is used on. The damage is quiet: the words survive, so nobody notices the callout silently demoted to a plain quote (with stray backslashes in raw form) until the doc is viewed on GitHub. Preservation is the floor; rendering alerts distinctly in the editor is the stretch goal, not a requirement here.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `> [!NOTE]` / `[!TIP]` / `[!IMPORTANT]` / `[!WARNING]` / `[!CAUTION]` blockquotes round-trip with the marker unescaped at the start of the first quoted line, and the saved form is a fixpoint.
- [ ] The alert body (including multi-paragraph alerts) is preserved; a blockquote that merely starts with bracketed text that is not one of the five alert markers (e.g. `> [!NOTE] extra words on the marker line` per GitHub's rules, or `> [see appendix]`) round-trips as a plain blockquote without gaining or losing escapes beyond today's plain-text behaviour.
- [ ] The representation decision (codec-level marker preservation vs a dedicated PM node + editor rendering) is noted in the PR; if a new PM node is introduced, `pkgs/id/web/src/editor.ts` gains the matching schema entry so the doc stays valid in the editor.
- [ ] Regression tests in `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs` cover at least NOTE/WARNING round-trips and the non-alert bracket control.

# id(web): collab reconnect cap is defeated by the onopen reset — accept-then-drop server loops forever, never surfaces "error"

## Evidence (verified this run, main 0cbb91b1)

`pkgs/id/web/src/collab.ts`:

- `scheduleReconnect()` caps attempts: `if (reconnectAttempts >= 10)` → status `error`, stop (line ~150); attempts increment per schedule (line ~162).
- `socket.onopen` unconditionally resets the counter: `reconnectAttempts = 0;` (line ~442).

So the cap only counts *consecutive sockets that never open*. If the server accepts the WebSocket handshake and then drops the connection (abnormal close 1006, no Init ever sent — e.g. a server process that accepts the upgrade then panics/restarts, or a proxy that accepts then resets), every cycle resets the counter to 0 and the client reconnects forever at the capped 5s backoff, never reaching the `error` status and never giving the user a failure state.

Reproduced this run with a targeted vitest probe (fake `WebSocket`, fake timers, real `initCollab`; probe removed after verification):

- 15 cycles of open → close(1006) produced **16 sockets**, every cycle logged `Reconnecting in ~250-300ms (attempt 1/10)`, and the status callback sequence never contained `error` (last status `connecting`).

## Why it matters

The 10-attempt cap exists to give up and surface an error state to the user. In the accept-then-drop failure mode — the most common real one for a local/LAN server that is up at TCP level but broken above it — that protection never fires: the tab retries indefinitely, the UI sits at "connecting" forever, and there is no signal that the session is dead.

## Suggested fix

Only reset `reconnectAttempts` once a session is actually established — i.e. when the Init message is handled (the point where the server has proved it can serve this document) — not on bare socket open. A long-lived stable session that later drops should still restart from attempt 1, which the Init-based reset preserves.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] With a server that accepts the handshake then drops abnormally (no Init), the client stops after 10 reconnect attempts and the status callback receives `error`; no further sockets are created.
- [ ] After a successful Init, a later abnormal drop restarts backoff from attempt 1 (stable-session behavior unchanged).
- [ ] New regression tests for `initCollab` reconnect behavior (there is currently no `collab.test.ts`) covering the cap under accept-then-drop cycles.
- [ ] Existing web unit tests and typecheck pass.

## Finding

PR #1013 (merged, merge commit 554dc370b7083c433b5f71b0b7eaa57badcbbdb2) taught the Rust markdown codec to emit two new ProseMirror node types — `footnote_reference` (inline atom, `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs:545`) and `footnote_definition` (block, `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs:558`) — but never added those node types to the web editor's ProseMirror schema.

The parallel change in the same batch did this correctly: PR #1009 added the `html_inline` node type to BOTH the codec and `pkgs/id/web/src/editor.ts` (current main: `editor.ts:216`). For footnotes, `grep footnote pkgs/id/web/src/editor.ts` on current main returns nothing.

## Why it matters

`pkgs/id/web/src/editor.ts` parses the initial document with `Node.fromJSON(editorSchema, initialDoc)` (editor.ts ~line 375). ProseMirror throws `Unknown node type` for a node type absent from the schema, and the catch block in `initEditor` replaces the ENTIRE document with an empty one:

```ts
} catch (err) {
  console.error("[editor] Failed to parse initial doc JSON, using empty doc:", err);
  doc = editorSchema.topNodeType.createAndFill() ?? editorSchema.node("doc");
}
```

So opening any markdown file that contains a footnote in the web editor shows an empty document instead of the file's contents — and a subsequent save risks persisting that empty doc over the real file. The codec round-trip tests added by #1013 (and the follow-up #1031) all pass because they never go through the editor schema; the bug is only visible at the codec/editor boundary. Verified still present on current main (2026-10-27): codec emits the types, editor schema does not define them.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/1013 — `fix(id-web): preserve footnotes in markdown codec (#945)`
- Codec parse direction: `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs:545` (`footnote_reference`), `:558` (`footnote_definition`); save direction `:1366`, `:1378`
- Editor schema: `pkgs/id/web/src/editor.ts` `richSchema` `.append({...})` defines `task_list`, `table*`, `html_inline` — no `footnote_reference` / `footnote_definition`
- Editor load path: `pkgs/id/web/src/editor.ts` `initEditor` — `Node.fromJSON` try/catch falling back to an empty doc
- Dedup: #945 (closed) was the codec mangling; #1031 (closed) was multi-paragraph definition fusion in the codec. Neither mentions the editor schema.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `richSchema` in `pkgs/id/web/src/editor.ts` defines `footnote_reference` (inline atom carrying `label`) and `footnote_definition` (block carrying `label` and inline content), mirroring the `html_inline` pattern from #1009 / PR #1009, with inert `toDOM` rendering (label as text, never innerHTML).
- [ ] Opening a markdown document containing `Text.[^1]` + `[^1]: Body.` in the web editor displays the full document (no "Failed to parse initial doc JSON" fallback, no empty doc).
- [ ] A round-trip through the editor (open -> save with no edits) preserves the footnote reference and definition byte-identically.
- [ ] A test or e2e check covers a footnote document going through `Node.fromJSON(richSchema, ...)` so a future codec node type cannot silently miss its schema entry again.

# orchestrator: resurface the next-horizons discussion (#1240) to Drew on triggers — never let it sit silent

#1240 ("next horizons — what comes after Phase 13") is deliberately **do-not-work**: it waits for Drew's planning input. Drew's rule (2026-10-26): it must not sit there forever without orchestrator input to him. A scheduled check (cron `id-horizons-resurface`, every ~3 days) evaluates these triggers and, when one fires, posts a status comment on #1240 and pings Drew in chat:

1. **Milestone**: the Path-to-Phase-12 queue (#1235) completes — all steps closed — or Phase 12 (tier 2) work begins in earnest.
2. **Running low**: open `app/id` issues drop below 25 (the lined-up work is thinning out), or the tier-1/tier-2 queues are empty.
3. **Time**: 7 days pass without the discussion being resurfaced — and after that, at most once a week, even if plenty of issues exist.

State (last resurfaced date + which trigger fired) lives in `~/workspace/id-dashboard-push/horizons-state.json` so the cadence survives across runs. When a resurface happens, summarize: what's been completed since the last one, current queue depth, and the 2–3 questions from #1240 that most need Drew's answers. If Drew engages on #1240, the output is design issues + a roadmap update — close this issue when #1240 converts into filed Phase 14 plans.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The scheduled check (cron id-horizons-resurface, ~3 days) evaluates all three triggers from the body: milestone (#1235 queue completes or Phase 12 tier-2 begins), running-low (open app/id issues < 25 or tier queues empty), and time (7 days without resurfacing, then at most weekly).
- [ ] When a trigger fires, a status comment is posted on #1240 and Drew is pinged in chat; when none fires, the check is silent and records its state (last resurfaced time / trigger states) where the next run can read it.
- [ ] #1240 itself is never worked or closed by this automation — it only resurfaces the discussion.

Part of epic #1184 (PM stack coherence — wave 2, 2026-10-26).

The dashboard answers questions when Drew goes to it; nothing summarises the day on its own. A scheduled digest closes that gap: once a day (and a weekly roll-up) the PM system generates a digest from the canonical projection — what moved (started, merged, closed), what is blocked and on whom, what needs Drew (the NEEDS DREW tier, with reasons), what was done recently, and a quota outlook (pools near walls, walls predicted before reset) — delivered to chat and archived as a dashboard page so any day's digest can be re-read later. The digest is a rendering of the same projection the pages use (no separate reporting pipeline to drift), states the feed/orchestration freshness it was built from, and links every claim to the item it came from.

Acceptance:
- A daily digest is generated on schedule from the canonical projection and posted to chat, with a weekly roll-up on the configured day.
- Each digest is archived as a dashboard page (dated URL) rendering identical content to the chat delivery.
- Every section (moved / blocked / needs Drew / done / quota outlook) links its items, and the digest header states the data freshness it was derived from.
- A missed or stale source degrades the digest visibly (section marked stale with its age) instead of silently omitting it.

## Acceptance criteria

- A scheduled digest is generated from the canonical projection: daily plus a weekly roll-up, delivered to chat and archived as a dashboard page.
- Every section (moved / blocked / needs Drew / done / quota outlook) links its items, and the digest header states the data freshness it was derived from.

body:
## Finding

PR #727 ("feat(rust): range sessions are selected and answered by method [P3.3]", commit `80c3ce37a5dba062055612b9f75d6634bb97e2b8`) wires range sync into the `/id-sync/1` session: the initiator's `Request` names the method `choose()` picked, the responder answers it, and `run_agreed` gains a Range branch. But the estimate that drives `choose()` can never be satisfied by real data: the `PeerHistory` it needs is never created, updated, or stored anywhere, so a production initiator would always choose LogSync and the range path would be dead code.

The PR's own commit message discloses this as an open follow-up — "It is in memory for now, and storing it is open" — but no issue was ever filed for it (issue search for "PeerHistory" returns 0).

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/727 (OPEN, stale/CONFLICTING; reviewed at head `80c3ce37a5`)
- `pkgs/id/src/sync_method.rs` (PR branch): `choose()` returns `SyncMethod::Log` whenever `stats.last_completed_sync_ms()` is `None`; `PeerHistory` is documented as "What this node remembers about one peer… The caller keeps it. Nothing stores it yet, so it lasts as long as the caller does."
- `git grep PeerHistory` over the whole PR branch returns only: the definition in `sync_method.rs`, the `history: &PeerHistory` parameter of `SharedEventStore::estimate` in `pkgs/id/src/store_traits.rs`, and test code in `pkgs/id/src/log_sync.rs` that fabricates one (`synced_once(1)` with `last_completed_sync_ms: Some(1)`).
- `sync_with()` (`pkgs/id/src/log_sync.rs`, PR branch) takes `stats: &impl SyncStats` from its caller and never records anything when a session completes: no code sets `last_completed_sync_ms` after a successful sync, and nothing maintains or resets `changed_since_sync`. `SharedEventStore::estimate` is called only from tests on the branch.
- On current main (`5db60876`) the range method is still unwired — `run_agreed` in `pkgs/id/src/log_sync.rs` returns `SyncError::NotWired` for `SyncMethod::Range` — so this follow-up belongs with/after the range wiring (PR #727 or a successor), not before it.
- Not a duplicate of the existing Phase 3 sync issues: #179 tracks the shared `/id-sync/1` handshake (which PR #727 implements), #178 tracks `read_flight`'s unbounded buffering (unchanged by PR #727), #180 tracks data-phase batches bounded by count not bytes (also unchanged). Cross-repo check: `PeerHistory` / this sync code exists only in developing-today/code (`git grep` over the opencode, openchamber and nix clones returns nothing).

## Why it matters

Range sync (P3.1/P3.3) exists to cut control bytes when two peers differ by only a few events (crossover ≈ 3.5% of chain count, per `sync_method.rs`). Without a recorded per-peer history, `choose()` degenerates to "always LogSync for every real peer", so the range implementation — reconciliation, `range_entries`, `LogAndRange` responder support — can never be exercised outside tests that hand-fabricate a history.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Something owns a per-peer `PeerHistory`: when a sync session with a peer completes, `last_completed_sync_ms` is set, and `changed_since_sync` is maintained (increments for locally created/received events, resets at a completed sync) — kept at least for the process lifetime in the sync caller, and persisted across restarts if the design requires bootstrapping state to survive.
- [ ] Production code (not only tests) builds the estimate via `SharedEventStore::estimate(topic, &history)` and passes it to `sync_with`.
- [ ] A test demonstrates that a second sync with the same peer, with a small difference, chooses `SyncMethod::Range` using a history produced by the first completed session (not a hand-constructed `PeerHistory`).

body:
# aggregator(backfill-usage-snapshots): unknown, misspelled, joined, and duplicate arguments are silently ignored — a typo'd `--dirr` seeds the rebuilt history into the default store and exits 0

## Evidence

`pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/backfill-usage-snapshots.ts` documents exactly one option (line 27: `Usage: bun run scripts/backfill-usage-snapshots.ts [--dir <storeDir>]`), but argument handling is a single `indexOf` probe (lines 40–46):

```ts
const dirArg = process.argv.indexOf("--dir");
const dirValue = dirArg >= 0 ? process.argv[dirArg + 1] : undefined;
if (dirArg >= 0 && (!dirValue?.trim() || dirValue.trimStart().startsWith("--"))) { /* exit 2 */ }
const storeDir = dirValue ?? process.env.PM_AGG_SNAPSHOTS_DIR ?? join(PKG, "snapshots");
```

Nothing else in `process.argv` is ever examined. #3330 guarded the `--dir` *value* (trailing / flag-like), but the rest of argv is unvalidated — the residual axis of the strict-argument contract its siblings now enforce (collect-fleet-feed #3352/#3509, append-usage-snapshots #6961, compact-usage-snapshots #6967).

Verified this run on the laptop at main `0290574b3e` with the real script, fixture empty quota-view/registry inputs, and `PM_AGG_SNAPSHOTS_DIR` pointed at a fixture default store (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-backfill-argv`):

| invocation | observed |
|---|---|
| `--dir <custom>` (control) | exit 0, appends to `<custom>` |
| `--dirr <intended>` (typo) | exit 0, appends to the **default** store; `<intended>` is never created |
| `--bogus` | exit 0, silently ignored, default store written |
| `somefile` (positional) | exit 0, silently ignored, default store written |
| `--dir=<joined>` | exit 0, silently ignored, default store written; `<joined>` never created |
| `--dir <a> --dir <b>` | exit 0, first value wins silently (`indexOf`), `<b>` ignored with no diagnostic |

With real inputs (the default `QUOTA_VIEW_PATH` / registry), the typo case is not a no-op: it appends the full rebuilt history into the live/default snapshot store the operator explicitly tried to redirect — the exact wrong-store write #3330 fixed for the flag-like-value form of the same mistake.

## Why it matters

This is a one-shot recovery/seed script: it is run rarely, by hand, precisely when the store is being rebuilt — the moment a wrong-store write is hardest to notice and most expensive to unwind. Every sibling operator script in this package now refuses unknown arguments before any I/O; this one still runs the default mode on any typo.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Any argument other than a single separated `--dir <dir>` — unknown flags, misspellings, positionals, the joined `--dir=<path>` form, and duplicate `--dir` — is a usage error: exit 2 with a message naming the offending argument, raised before any input file is read or any store directory is created/written.
- [ ] The documented forms keep working: no arguments (env/default store) and `--dir <dir>`, including the existing #3330 trailing/flag-like value rejection.
- [ ] Regression coverage extends the existing pinning suite (`pm-stack/aggregator/test/backfill-usage-snapshots-dir-3330.test.ts` or a sibling argv suite): the new cases fail pre-fix and pass post-fix, following the `rejectUnknownArgs` pattern from #6961/#6967.

title: id-mail(worker): runtime MAIL_CONFIG/CALLERS JSON is shape-trusted — malformed config throws raw errors out of fetch(), string transports/from are substring-accepted

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job
