labels.name: app/id-mail
labels.description: pkgs/nixos id-mail service and worker

body:
## Problem

The id-mail Worker's runtime handler trusts the shape of its two operator-supplied JSON env values (`MAIL_CONFIG`, `CALLERS`) and of the per-caller grant objects — while the request body in the same file is carefully shape-checked, and the deploy side got a total `validate()` in #6947. Every other failure path in the handler returns the JSON error envelope; these shapes instead throw raw errors out of `fetch()`, or are silently accepted with wrong semantics.

Evidence (verified on laptop @ origin/main `7b618e88fd`, probe `~/git/fleet/probe-idmail-runtime`, real `src/index.js`/`src/limiter.js`/`src/transports/email.js` verbatim, md5-checked; shipped `runtime.test.mjs` 5/5 green; control request 200):

`nixos/services/id-mail/worker/src/index.js`:
- Malformed `MAIL_CONFIG` JSON → bare `SyntaxError` escapes `fetch()` (`JSON.parse(env.MAIL_CONFIG)`, line ~16).
- `MAIL_CONFIG = "null"` → `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'defaultTransport')`.
- `MAIL_CONFIG` without `limits` → `TypeError` at `config.limits.windowSeconds` — thrown *after* authentication.
- `MAIL_CONFIG = {}` with a request naming `transport` → `TypeError` at `config.transports.includes`. (`{}` without a named transport returns 400 only by accident, because the name check fires first.)
- `MAIL_CONFIG.transports` as the string `"email"` → **accepted** (200, mail sent): `String.prototype.includes` does substring matching where an array was meant.
- Malformed `CALLERS` JSON → bare `SyntaxError` from `authenticate()`'s unguarded `JSON.parse`.
- `CALLERS = {"alice": null}` → `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'sha256')`.
- A caller entry with no `transports` → `TypeError: Cannot convert undefined or null to object` at `Object.hasOwn(caller.transports, name)`.

`nixos/services/id-mail/worker/src/transports/email.js` (grant = the caller's entry in `CALLERS`):
- Grant with no `from` → `TypeError` at `grant.from[0]` in `check()`.
- Grant with `from` as a **string** → accepted with wrong semantics: `body.from ?? grant.from[0]` takes the first *character*, `grant.from.includes(from)` substring-matches, and `deliver()` sends with `From: "a"`.
- Template mode with `config.templates` missing → `TypeError` at `config.templates.some(...)`; a `null` template entry → `TypeError` destructuring it in `matchesTemplate`.

## Why it matters

These env values are rendered by the deploy path and edited by hand; a typo or a partial config today either crashes the Worker with a non-JSON platform 500 that names nothing (every request, including valid ones — the parse happens before routing), or, worse, silently sends mail under a corrupted `From`/transport interpretation. The handler's own vocabulary already has the right answer for absent config — `500 {"error":"worker is not configured"}` — it just never applies to malformed or wrong-shape config. #6947 made deploy-time validation total; the runtime boundary was left trusting.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Malformed JSON, non-object, or wrong-shape `MAIL_CONFIG`/`CALLERS` (including missing/non-array `transports`, missing/non-object `limits` with non-numeric fields, non-array `templates` or non-object template entries, null/non-object caller entries, non-string `sha256`, missing/non-object caller `transports`) fails closed with the existing `500 {"error":"worker is not configured"}` envelope — nothing throws out of `fetch()`.
- [ ] Grant shapes are validated before use: `from` must be an array of strings, `maxRecipients` a number, `mode` a string; a wrong-shape grant refuses the request instead of throwing or substring-matching.
- [ ] `transports` as a string and `from` as a string are rejected, never substring-accepted.
- [ ] New regression tests in `runtime.test.mjs` drive the real handler with the shapes above and fail pre-fix; the existing 5 runtime tests and the deploy suite stay green.
- [ ] Valid config behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged (control request still delivers, limiter call order unchanged).

body:
# aggregator(compact-usage-snapshots): unknown or misspelled flags are silently ignored — a typo'd `--month 24` with `--apply` irreversibly compacts months the operator meant to keep raw

## Summary

`pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/compact-usage-snapshots.ts` never validates its argv. The two options are found by membership/index lookup and every other token is ignored:

- `:29` — `const apply = process.argv.includes("--apply");`
- `:30-31` — `const monthsArg = process.argv.indexOf("--months"); const retentionMonths = monthsArg >= 0 ? Number(process.argv[monthsArg + 1]) : 13;`

So any misspelled or unknown flag is silently dropped:

1. **A typo'd `--month 24` silently falls back to the 13-month default retention — and with `--apply` that destroys raw history.** The operator asked to keep 24 months of raw monthly files; the script instead compacts everything at or before the 13-month cutoff, replacing each raw `usage-YYYY-MM.jsonl` with a lossy min/max/last rollup and deleting the raw file. Compaction is one-way: the per-observation records are gone. The run exits 0 and prints a normal report.
2. **Any unknown flag is silently ignored.** `--bogus` alongside a valid `--apply --months 24` invocation changes nothing and exits 0.

The `--months` *value* was hardened by #3285 (values < 1 are a usage error), but the flag set itself was not — this is the same class #6961 just fixed in the sibling `append-usage-snapshots.ts`, and the class the strict-argument-contract design #3352 tracks; sibling scripts got per-script filings and fixes (#3723, #6926, #6961).

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ 073b320eec, probe `~/git/fleet/probe-compact-argv`)

Real script run against fixture stores (each case a fresh copy; raw files `usage-2024-01.jsonl` and `usage-2025-06.jsonl`, 3 records each; today 2026-11-07, so retention 24 → cutoff 2024-11, retention 13 → cutoff 2025-10):

| Invocation | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `--months 24` (control, dry-run) | exit 0, `cutoffMonth: "2024-11"`, only 2024-01 in scope; both raw files untouched |
| `--apply --month 24` (typo) | exit 0, **both** months compacted: `2024-01: 3 records -> 1 rollups (compacted)`, `2025-06: 3 records -> 1 rollups (compacted)`; store afterwards holds only `usage-2024-01.rollup.jsonl` + `usage-2025-06.rollup.jsonl` — the 2025-06 raw file the 24-month retention was meant to keep is deleted |
| `--apply --bogus --months 24` | exit 0, 2024-01 compacted — unknown flag silently ignored |

## Why it matters

This script is the only compactor for the usage-snapshot store (hub design §6, #1117): raw months older than the retention window are replaced in place by rollups. It is run by hand, deliberately, with a chosen retention — exactly the setting where a one-character typo must stop the run, not silently widen the blast radius. A typo'd `--months` in the "keep more" direction is the destructive direction here: the default (13) is *shorter* than any longer retention an operator would type, so the silent fallback always compacts more than asked, irreversibly.

## Acceptance criteria

- Any argv token that is not `--apply`, `--months`, or the value consumed by `--months` is a usage error: exit 2, a message naming the offending token, and the store untouched (validation before the store is read or written — the same before-any-I/O discipline as #6961 / #3295).
- The existing #3285 behavior is unchanged: a malformed `--months` value (missing / non-integer / < 1) still exits 2 with its specific `invalid --months '…'` message (the token consumed as `--months`'s value is not re-interpreted as an unknown argument), and the pinning test `test/compact-usage-snapshots-months-3285.test.ts` still passes.
- Valid invocations are unchanged: no args (dry-run, 13 months), `--apply`, `--months <n>`, and their combination behave exactly as today.
- New regression tests in the style of the #3285 / #6961 pinning tests cover: a misspelled `--month` with `--apply` (asserting exit 2 and both raw files byte-identical), an unknown flag, and a stray positional, each asserting exit 2 and an untouched store.

## Related

- #6961 (closed) — the same defect in sibling `append-usage-snapshots.ts`, fixed with a `rejectUnknownArgs()` pass before any I/O.
- #3285 (closed) — the `--months` *value* guard in this same script.
- #3352 (open, design) — one strict argument contract for the repo's operator scripts.

title: id(shell-contract): parseShellContract never validates frame specs or the contract header — a string phases field substring-matches the phase gate (chat accepted in opening), opens can corrupt the session phase, and negative/fractional bounds pass

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

`parseShellContract` in `pkgs/id/web/src/shell-contract.ts` is the TypeScript port of the Rust shell-contract checker (`pkgs/id/src/shell_contract.rs`). Two earlier fixes hardened its load-time validation: #2657 (every frame's **field specs** are validated at load) and #4323 (three **top-level fields**: `routing_fields`, `projection.redacted_keys`, `max_frame_bytes`). One level remains unvalidated: the **frame specs themselves** and the remaining contract header fields.

`parseShellContract` (shell-contract.ts:112-159) checks only that each frame is an object with an object `fields`, then returns `value as unknown as ShellContract`. It never validates:

- frame `class` — Rust `RawFrame.class: FrameClass` is required and must be one of `event|ephemeral|query|control|admin|delegation|durable|reply` (shell_contract.rs, `RawFrame` / `FrameClass`).
- frame `phases` — Rust `phases: Vec<Phase>`; every entry must be a named phase.
- frame `opens` — Rust `opens: Option<Phase>`; must be a named phase when present.
- frame `forbidden_keys` — Rust `forbidden_keys: Vec<String>`.
- contract header `contract` (String), `version` (u32), `revision` (u32), `transports` (map) — all required by Rust `RawContract` with no `#[serde(default)]`.
- field bounds `min` / `max` / `max_bytes` as integers — Rust deserializes them as `u64` / `usize`; TS `parseField` accepts any finite number, including `-1` and `1.5`.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-shell-contract-frame/`, bun, importing the real `pkgs/id/web/src/shell-contract.ts` @ main `073b320eec`, md5 `8fa5b11c75f51a35bb2a6cbc5cd2d81b`, and the real `pkgs/id/contract/shell-contract.v1.json`, md5 `bda28d789afa8f47213bce6a76ad8201`). Controls on the unmodified contract behave: `chat` in `joined` is `{ok:true}`; `chat` in `opening` is rejected with "`chat` may not be sent in the opening phase".

Against mutated documents, `parseShellContract` **accepts every variant below** — each is a document the Rust parser refuses at load:

- **`chat.phases = "joinedopening"` (a string, not an array)** → accepted; then `checkClientFrame(contract, {type:"chat", text:"hi"}, "opening")` returns `{ok:true}` — `String.includes` substring-matches the phase, so a frame the contract allows only after join is accepted in the opening phase. This is a phase-gate bypass, not just a parse gap (compare the #4323 `routing_fields: "world"` substring failure, same mechanism one level down).
- **`chat.phases = ["joined","bogus"]`** → accepted (Rust `Vec<Phase>` rejects the unknown phase name).
- **`join.opens = "bogus"`** → accepted; a `Conformance` session that sends a valid `join` then reports `phase === "bogus"` with no violation — the session's phase state is silently corrupted to a phase that does not exist.
- **`chat.class` deleted, or `chat.class = "bogus"`** → accepted (Rust: required enum).
- **`version = "1"` (string), `revision` deleted, `transports` deleted, `contract` deleted** → all accepted (Rust `RawContract`: all four required and typed).
- **`chat.text = {type:"string", max_bytes:-1}`** → accepted at load; then every `chat` frame is rejected at check time ("`chat.text` is 2 bytes, more than -1"). `max_bytes: 1.5` and a `u64` field with `min: -1` are likewise accepted (Rust: `usize`/`u64` deserialization refuses both).

Code facts: the phase check is `(spec.phases ?? []).includes(phase)` (shell-contract.ts:299), the forbidden-key loop is `for (const key of spec.forbidden_keys ?? [])` (:302 — iterating a string yields its characters, so a string `forbidden_keys` checks single-character key names instead of the named key), and `Conformance.client` assigns `this.#phase = opens ?? "closed"` from the unvalidated document (:351-352).

Scope honesty: like #2657/#4323, no production web code imports the TS checker today — only `pkgs/id/web/src/world-contract.test.ts`. This is a correctness/parity defect in the conformance library before it gains consumers, not a live outage — hence priority/low. It is distinct from #4323, whose acceptance list covered only `routing_fields` / `projection` / `max_frame_bytes`; the frame-spec and header fields above were not in its scope and remain open after its fix.

## Why it matters

The contract is the conformance boundary every shell proves itself against instead of reading host code. A checker that accepts a document its canonical Rust counterpart refuses — and then substring-matches phases, invents a bogus session phase, or rejects every frame of a type — makes a contract-authoring error look like a shell bug, and in the `phases` case silently weakens the phase gate the checker exists to enforce. Fail-fast-at-load parity is the contract author's safety net; the TS port should offer the same for the whole document, not only the parts two previous issues enumerated.

## Acceptance criteria

- `parseShellContract` rejects, with a named error at load time (frame/field named where applicable):
  - a frame with a missing or unknown `class`;
  - `phases` that is not an array, or that contains a name that is not one of `opening|query|install|joined|closed`;
  - `opens` that is present and not a valid phase name;
  - `forbidden_keys` that is not an array of strings;
  - a missing or wrongly-typed `contract` (string), `version` / `revision` (non-negative integers), or `transports` (object);
  - field bounds `min` / `max` / `max_bytes` that are negative or non-integer.
- After the fix, no document accepted by `parseShellContract` can make `checkClientFrame` / `checkServerFrame` / `Conformance` substring-match a phase, adopt a non-existent session phase, or apply a negative/fractional bound; malformed documents fail at parse.
- Regression tests in `pkgs/id/web/src/world-contract.test.ts` cover each case above, mirroring the existing #4323 top-level tests — including the behavioral pair: `chat` in `opening` under a string-`phases` document is a parse rejection (not an `{ok:true}`), and a session's phase after `join` is never a value outside the phase set.
- The real `contract/shell-contract.v1.json` still parses and all existing shell-contract tests pass; the Rust checker and the contract JSON are unchanged.

labels.name: task/small-fix

body:
# aggregator(append-usage-snapshots): unknown or misspelled flags are silently ignored — a typo'd `--from-provider-usage` silently runs the wrong derivation mode and exits 0

## Summary

`pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/append-usage-snapshots.ts` never validates its argv. The mode is selected with a substring-style membership test and every other token is ignored:

- `:71` — `const fromProviderUsage = process.argv.includes("--from-provider-usage");`
- `:56-59` — `resolveObservedBy` looks up only the exact `--by` token (its value was hardened in #3295; the flag set itself was not).

So any misspelled or unknown flag is silently dropped:

1. **A typo'd mode flag changes what data is written.** `--from-provider-usag` does not match, so the script silently runs the *default* mode (derive records from quota-view.md + the provider registry) instead of the requested `--from-provider-usage` mode (derive from the keeper's provider-usage snapshot). The intended source file is never even opened, the intended records never reach the outbox, and the run exits 0. In the stewardship flow (the script's documented caller, header `:8-16`) the log line reports a normal run, so the loss is invisible.
2. **Any unknown flag is silently ignored.** `--bogus-flag` alongside a valid invocation changes nothing and exits 0.
3. **A typo'd `--byy alice` silently discards the attribution.** `resolveObservedBy` never sees `--by`, so every appended record carries the default `observedBy` (`check-usage` / `stewardship-cycle`) instead of the requested name — provenance is silently wrong, not missing.

This is the remaining unguarded surface of the script whose `--by` value #3295 hardened, and the same class the strict-argument-contract design #3352 tracks; sibling scripts got per-script filings and fixes (#3723, #6926, #6939, #6941).

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ e238c85d5a, probe `~/git/fleet/probe-append-argv`)

Real script run with all four paths redirected to fixtures (`provider-usage.json` = `{"generated_at":"2026-11-07T00:00:00Z","sessions":[{},{}]}`; empty quota-view/registry fixtures):

| Invocation | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `--from-provider-usage` (control) | exit 0, `appended 1 record(s)` — `{"serviceId":"opencode-server","metricId":"sessions-listed","value":2,"observedBy":"check-usage",...}` |
| `--from-provider-usag` (typo) | exit 0, `no records derived; outbox untouched` — default mode ran; the provider-usage records were silently lost |
| `--from-provider-usage --bogus-flag` | exit 0, record appended — unknown flag silently ignored |
| `--from-provider-usage --byy alice` | exit 0, record appended with `observedBy:"check-usage"` — requested attribution silently dropped |

Mode-switch proof: with `provider-usage.json` *deleted*, the typo invocation still exits 0 (`no records derived`), while the correctly spelled invocation fails with exit 1 (ENOENT) — the typo'd run never opens the file it was asked to read.

## Why it matters

This script is a writer in the usage-snapshot pipeline (hub design §4): stewardship runs it unattended right after a quota-view refresh, and hand runs use `--from-provider-usage`. A one-character typo in either caller silently swaps or loses a whole run's records while reporting success — the exact failure #3295's comment warns about for `--by` ("a silent loss of the whole run"), one flag over. Wrong `observedBy` attribution additionally corrupts the provenance the snapshot store's consumers rely on.

## Acceptance criteria

- Any argv token that is not `--from-provider-usage`, `--by`, or the value consumed by `--by` is a usage error: exit 2, a message naming the offending token, and no file read or written (the same before-any-I/O discipline as `resolveObservedBy` / #3295).
- The existing #3295 behavior is unchanged: malformed `--by` (missing / empty / flag-like value) still exits 2 with its specific message (the token consumed as `--by`'s value is not re-interpreted as a flag by the new check), and the pinning test `test/append-usage-snapshots-by-3295.test.ts` still passes.
- Valid invocations are unchanged: no args, `--from-provider-usage`, `--by <name>`, and their combination derive and append exactly as today.
- New regression tests in the style of the #3295 pinning test cover: a misspelled mode flag, an unknown flag, and a misspelled `--byy`, each asserting exit 2 and an untouched outbox.

## Related

- #3295 (closed) — the `--by` *value* guard in this same script.
- #3352 (open, design) — one strict argument contract for the repo's operator scripts.
- #5140 (open) — a different silent-drop axis in the same pipeline (`recordsFromProviderUsage` date gate).

title: id(just-recipes-check): the drift guard reads just-recipes.json relative to the caller's CWD — invoked by path from elsewhere it fails raw or certifies the wrong file

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/id/scripts/just-recipes-check.sh` — the drift guard for the generated `just-recipes.json` (#2729) — resolves both of its inputs relative to the caller's working directory and never anchors to its own location:

- `:5` — `just --dump --dump-format json` dumps whatever justfile `just` finds searching upward from the CWD.
- `:17` — `project just-recipes.json` reads the committed file relative to the CWD.

There is no `cd` anywhere in the script. Both sibling scripts in the same directory establish the opposite convention: `scripts/roc-test.sh:8` and `scripts/rebuild-roc-examples.sh:3` both `cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."`.

The two current call sites pass only by accident of their CWD: the `just-recipes-check` just recipe (justfile:212-213, `just` runs recipes from the justfile's directory) and the `just-recipes-drift` flake check (flake.nix:396, sandbox CWD is `pkgs/id`). Invoking the script the natural way — by path, from anywhere else — breaks it in two directions:

1. **False failure:** from a directory with no `just-recipes.json`, the script dies with a raw `jq: error: Could not open file just-recipes.json` (exit 2), naming neither the script nor the file it actually wanted.
2. **False pass (the dangerous direction):** from a directory that happens to contain a `just-recipes.json` matching the fresh dump, the script prints `✓ just-recipes.json matches the justfile` and exits 0 — while the real `pkgs/id/just-recipes.json` has drifted. The guard certifies a file it never read.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ 4adffb688e)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-just-recipes-cwd` (real script verbatim, stub `just` emitting a fixed dump so the committed-file half is isolated; fixture `just-recipes.json` in the script's directory):

- Control, invoked from its own dir: `✓ matches`, rc 0. Same dir with the fixture's `doc` drifted: diff shown, rc 1 — drift correctly caught.
- Invoked by absolute path from `/tmp`: `jq: error: Could not open file just-recipes.json: No such file or directory`, rc 2.
- Invoked by absolute path from a directory whose own `just-recipes.json` matches the dump, while the script's real fixture is drifted: `✓ just-recipes.json matches the justfile`, rc 0 — **the drifted real file was certified as matching**.

The shipped test (`scripts/just-recipes-check-test.sh`) cannot see this: it `cd`s into its fixture directory before invoking, so the CWD-relative read always lands on the fixture. No case invokes the script from a foreign CWD.

## Why it matters

This script is the only guard against the #2729 failure mode (a recipe change silently getting no nix app because `just-recipes.json` went stale). A guard that can certify the wrong file — or that a developer cannot run by path from the repo root — gives false confidence exactly where the check is trusted: the flake check's pass is meaningful only as long as its sandbox CWD never changes, and any future call site (CI step, hook, docs instruction) that invokes it from elsewhere silently checks a different tree or a different file.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `just-recipes-check.sh` anchors to its own location (e.g. `cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.."` as in `rebuild-roc-examples.sh:3`) before running `just --dump` and reading `just-recipes.json`, so it checks the `pkgs/id` tree it lives in regardless of the caller's CWD.
- [ ] Invoking it by path from an unrelated directory produces the same verdict as invoking it from `pkgs/id`: a drifted `pkgs/id/just-recipes.json` fails (exit 1 with the drift message) and an in-sync one passes.
- [ ] `scripts/just-recipes-check-test.sh` gains a regression case that invokes the script from a foreign CWD (with a decoy `just-recipes.json` present there) and asserts the verdict follows the script's own tree, not the CWD's file; the existing cases keep passing (the fixture will need the script copied into it, as `build-sh-test.sh` already does for `build.sh`).
- [ ] The existing call sites (`just just-recipes-check`, the `just-recipes-drift` flake check) still pass on an in-sync tree.

title: projector(github): GitHub API response bodies are shape-trusted — non-array list pages spread into per-character rows or crash, a null installation reply defeats the token fallbacks, and a token-less access-token reply is returned as a valid app token

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: app/pm-stack

body:
## Problem

The projector's GitHub API client (`pm-stack/projector/src/github.ts`, verified on `origin/main` @ `56b6a47f9b`) casts every `res.json()` result to the expected shape and uses it unchecked. Three call sites fail in three different ways on a 200 response whose body is valid JSON of the wrong shape — the exact class the sibling validators in the same stack guard against (e.g. `parsePositiveDecimalId` for the app/installation ids in this same file, added for #4106/#4139):

### 1. `listResource` (github.ts:205-206): a non-array page spreads or crashes

```ts
const page = (await res.json()) as T[];
out.push(...page);
```

- `null`, object, or number page → raw `TypeError: Spread syntax requires ...iterable…`, which aborts the whole reconcile stream (reconcile.ts records the bare TypeError text as the stream error; the cursor never advances).
- **String page → silent corruption:** `"hello"` spreads into `["h","e","l","l","o"]`, returned as five "rows". Reconcile then iterates the characters as issue/PR/comment objects (`fromIssueOrPr(repo, "h", …)` → a row with `number: undefined`, ref `owner/repo#undefined`).

### 2. `discoverInstallationId` (github.ts:131-132): a `null` body defeats every fallback

```ts
const body = (await res.json()) as { id?: number };
if (typeof body.id === "number") { … }
```

A `null` 200 body throws `TypeError: null is not an object (evaluating 'body.id')`. The throw escapes `apiTokenFor` (github.ts:149) before the fallbacks that follow it are ever tried — the configured `GITHUB_APP_INSTALL_ID` (github.ts:151) and the plain `GITHUB_TOKEN` fallback (github.ts:162) — so one wrong-shape discovery reply takes reconciliation for that repo down instead of degrading to the next credential, unlike the non-200 case right above it (`if (!res.ok) return undefined`, github.ts:130), which falls back correctly.

### 3. `apiTokenFor` access-token reply (github.ts:159-160): a token-less reply is returned as a valid app token

```ts
const body = (await res.json()) as { token: string };
return { kind: "app", token: body.token };
```

- `{}` (no `token` field) → returns `{ kind: "app", token: undefined }` as success; every downstream call then sends `Authorization: Bearer undefined` and fails as a misleading `github_api_401`.
- `{ token: 123 }` → the number is returned unchecked as the token.
- `null` → raw `TypeError` on `.token`.

## Evidence

Verified this run on the laptop, probe `~/git/fleet/probe-projector-github` (real `src/github.ts` imported under bun 1.4.4, stubbed `fetchFn`, generated RSA key for the JWT paths; shipped suite `bun test test/github.test.ts` = 14 pass on current main):

| Case | Result today |
|---|---|
| `listResource`, page `[{n:1}]` | OK `[{n:1}]` (control) |
| `listResource`, page `null` / `{message}` / `42` | **throws** raw `TypeError: Spread syntax requires ...iterable…` |
| `listResource`, page `"hello"` | **OK `["h","e","l","l","o"]`** — silent per-character rows |
| `apiTokenFor`, installation reply `null`, plain `GITHUB_TOKEN` also configured | **throws** `TypeError: null is not an object (evaluating 'body.id')` — fallback never reached |
| `apiTokenFor`, access_tokens reply `{token:"good-token"}` | OK `{kind:"app", token:"good-token"}` (control) |
| `apiTokenFor`, access_tokens reply `{}` | **OK `{kind:"app"}`** — `token: undefined` returned as success |
| `apiTokenFor`, access_tokens reply `{token:123}` | **OK `{kind:"app", token:123}`** — non-string token returned unchecked |
| `apiTokenFor`, access_tokens reply `null` | **throws** `TypeError: null is not an object (evaluating '(await res.json()).token')` |

## Why it matters

Reconcile is the projector's self-healing path beyond webhook delivery (reconcile.ts header): it polls every configured repo on a timer. A single wrong-shape 200 from any of these three endpoints — a proxy/CDN error page served as JSON, an API change, a partial rollout — currently either kills the stream/repo with a bare runtime TypeError that names neither the endpoint nor the shape, silently manufactures per-character rows that flow toward the store as `repo#undefined` items, or manufactures a credential that guarantees opaque 401s downstream. The non-200 paths in the same functions already fail in the module's own vocabulary (`github_api_<status>`, `installation_token_failed_<status>`, fall back to the next credential); the 200 wrong-shape paths should fail — or fall back — the same way.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `listResource` rejects a non-array 200 page with an error in the module's vocabulary (e.g. `github_api_unexpected_shape` naming the path/URL), never a raw spread `TypeError`; a string page is never spread into per-character rows.
- [ ] `discoverInstallationId` treats a non-object/`null` 200 body like a missing id (returns `undefined`), so `apiTokenFor` proceeds to the configured installation id and then the plain-token fallback exactly as it does for a non-200 reply.
- [ ] `apiTokenFor` accepts an access-token reply only when `token` is a non-empty string; any other 200 shape throws `installation_token_failed_…`-style error naming the problem — it never returns an app auth with an undefined or non-string token, and never throws a raw property-access `TypeError`.
- [ ] Well-formed flows are unchanged: array pages (with Link-header pagination), `{id: <number>}` discovery, and `{token: <string>}` replies behave byte-identically; the shipped `test/github.test.ts` suite (14 tests) still passes.
- [ ] New tests in `pm-stack/projector/test/github.test.ts` cover: `listResource` with null/object/string/number pages, discovery with a `null` body falling back to the plain token, and access-token replies `{}`, `null`, and `{token: 123}`.

## Problem

The github-backup queue Worker's webhook endpoint (`POST /github` in `infra/github-backup/worker/src/index.js`) trusts two things it should guard, and both failures escape the handler as unhandled throws instead of responses. Sibling endpoints in the same file were covered by #6882 (`/queue/ack` body shape, corrupt KV on `GET /queue`); the `/github` handler was not.

File: `infra/github-backup/worker/src/index.js` (verified on `origin/main` @ `86afa3b8b6`; the file is unchanged since `63f83bef5a`).

### 1. A signed JSON `null` body crashes the handler (:45-47)

```js
let payload = {};
try { payload = JSON.parse(body); } catch { /* ping has form encoding sometimes */ }
...
const repo = payload.repository && payload.repository.full_name;
```

The `try/catch` guards only the parse. A body of `null` parses successfully to `null`, and `payload.repository` then throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'repository')`. Every other non-object body behaves sanely today (`[]`, `"hi"`, `123`, and non-JSON all get `202 no repository in payload`), and the ping path returns before the deref — `null` is the one shape that crashes the receiver for a legitimately signed delivery.

### 2. An unset/empty `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET` crashes every delivery, naming nothing (:38-41)

```js
const expect = await hmacHex(env.GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET, body);
```

`hmacHex` encodes the secret and calls `crypto.subtle.importKey` with it. With the secret unset or empty, the key is zero-length and `importKey` throws `DOMException: Zero-length key is not supported` — for *every* POST, signed or not, before the signature comparison. A misconfigured deployment (secret not provisioned, or provisioned empty) therefore takes the webhook receiver down with a bare 500 whose error names neither the endpoint nor the missing configuration, instead of an explicit fail-closed configuration error.

## Evidence

Verified this run on the laptop, probe `~/git/fleet/probe-ghb-github` (real `src/index.js` verbatim, md5 `931e7df400d74fb6d60d38698205f2c4` matching `origin/main`, node v24.21.0, stub KV, HMACs computed with node:crypto):

| Case | Result today |
|---|---|
| secret set, correct signature, repo payload | `202 queued`, 1 KV write (control OK) |
| secret set, wrong signature / no signature | `401 bad signature`, 0 KV writes (control OK) |
| secret set, correct signature, body `null` | **throws** `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'repository')` |
| secret set, correct signature, body `[]` / `"hi"` / `123` / non-JSON | `202 no repository in payload` (controls OK) |
| secret set, event `ping`, body `null` | `200 pong` (returns before the deref) |
| secret unset or `""`, any signature (even a correct empty-key HMAC) or none | **throws** `DOMException: Zero-length key is not supported` |

The existing suite (`infra/github-backup/worker/test/index.test.mjs`, 5 tests) has no `/github` coverage at all.

## Why it matters

- This Worker is the freshness signal for the estate mirror system (#3215): webhook events feed the drainer queue. A signed `null` delivery (a malformed or hand-crafted payload from the GitHub App) currently produces an unhandled 500 instead of the `202` the handler already returns for every other repository-less shape — noise in delivery logs and a redelivery loop for a payload that can never succeed.
- A missing secret is exactly the failure a deploy can ship silently (see the deploy-side history in #3475/#6507): today it surfaces only as an opaque per-request exception, indistinguishable from a runtime bug, instead of one clear "secret not configured" response an operator (or an alarm) can act on. The fix must stay fail-closed: no signature is ever accepted without a configured secret.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `POST /github` with a correctly signed JSON `null` body returns `202 no repository in payload` (same as the other non-object shapes); no exception escapes the handler for any parsed JSON value.
- [ ] `POST /github` with `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET` unset or empty returns an explicit 5xx whose body names the missing configuration, for every request; no exception escapes, no KV write occurs, and no signature (including an empty-key HMAC) is accepted.
- [ ] Well-formed deliveries are unchanged: correct signature + repository payload → `202 queued` with the event stored; wrong/missing signature → `401`; `ping` → `200 pong`.
- [ ] New tests in `infra/github-backup/worker/test/index.test.mjs` cover: signed `null` body, unset secret, empty secret; the existing 5 tests still pass (`node --test infra/github-backup/worker/test/index.test.mjs`).

title: github-ci(turso client): a wrong-shape 200 response is read as success or escapes as a raw TypeError — batch() never validates the pipeline envelope

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

labels.name: app/github-ci
labels.description: Package/app: github-ci (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

The github-ci Worker's minimal libSQL client (`pkgs/github-ci/worker/src/turso.ts`) trusts the shape of the Turso `/v2/pipeline` HTTP response:

```ts
const out = (await res.json()) as { results?: PipelineResult[] };
const failed = (out.results ?? []).find((r) => r.type === "error");
...
return out.results ?? [];
```

and in `execute()`:

```ts
const results = await this.batch([{ sql, args }]);
return results[0];
```

A 200 response whose body is valid JSON but not the pipeline envelope is mishandled three ways:

1. **Body `null` → raw `TypeError` escapes.** `out.results` dereferences `null` (`null is not an object (evaluating 'out.results')`), bypassing the client's own `turso pipeline failed: …` error contract. The webhook handler surfaces it only as an opaque `receiver failed: TypeError…` 500.
2. **Body `{}` / `"str"` (no `results`) → the write is reported as success.** `batch()` returns `[]`, `execute()` resolves `undefined`, and callers that ignore the return value — the `workflow_run` `INSERT OR IGNORE INTO ci_events` in `src/index.ts`, and the sink writes in `src/sink.ts` (`advanceSnapshot`, `stampDirtyWatermark`, `appendAgentEvent`) — proceed as if the statement ran. The worker answers GitHub `{ok: true}`, so the delivery is never retried: a results-less 200 (proxy/misroute/partial platform fault) becomes silent event loss instead of a retryable 500.
3. **Body `{}` → `queryText()` crashes downstream.** `execute()` returns `undefined`, and `queryText` dereferences it (`undefined is not an object (evaluating '(await this.execute(...)).response')`) — a second raw TypeError, one layer away from the actual fault. A non-JSON 200 body likewise escapes as a bare `SyntaxError` with no Turso context.

The shipped tests stub Turso only with a well-formed success envelope (`tursoOk()` in `test/worker.test.ts`); no test pins a wrong-shape 200.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ 63f83bef5a, probe `~/git/fleet/probe-turso-shape`)

Real `pkgs/github-ci/worker/src/turso.ts` copied verbatim (md5 `b7b07055809e84b1165ce074c9dfd9c0`, matching the laptop primary) into the probe; global `fetch` stubbed per case; `Turso` driven directly:

- Control — well-formed envelope → `execute()` resolves the ok result; `queryText()` returns `"main"`.
- Control — `results: [{type:"error", error:{message:"no such table"}}]` → throws `Error: turso pipeline failed: no such table` (the intended contract).
- **Bug — body `null` → `execute()` and `queryText()` THREW `TypeError: null is not an object (evaluating 'out.results')`.**
- **Bug — body `{}` → `execute("INSERT INTO ci_events …")` RESOLVED `undefined`** (read as success by callers); **`queryText()` THREW `TypeError: undefined is not an object (evaluating '(await this.execute(sql, args)).response')`.**
- **Bug — body `"ok"` → `execute()` RESOLVED `undefined`** (same silent-success path).
- **Bug — body `[]` → `queryText()` THREW the same `undefined…response` TypeError.**
- **Bug — non-JSON body (`<html>…`) → THREW raw `SyntaxError: JSON Parse error…`** with no `turso pipeline failed` context.

## Why it matters

This client is the worker's only write path to both Turso databases (platform `ci_events` and the fleet-queue snapshot/watermark/event stores). Its one job on a bad response is to fail loudly so the handler returns 500 and GitHub retries. Today a whole class of bad 200s either escapes as a context-free TypeError or — worse — is indistinguishable from success, converting a transient platform/proxy fault into permanently lost CI events and snapshot updates with a green delivery log.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `batch()` validates the decoded body: a non-object body, a missing/non-array `results`, or a non-JSON body throws an `Error` in the client's own contract form (`turso pipeline failed: …` naming the malformed response), never a raw `TypeError`/`SyntaxError`.
- [ ] `execute()` never resolves `undefined` for a sent statement: a results array that lacks the statement's result is an error, so no caller can read a results-less 200 as a successful write.
- [ ] Well-formed behavior is unchanged: ok results resolve as today, per-statement `type:"error"` results keep throwing `turso pipeline failed: <message>`, and HTTP non-2xx keeps throwing `turso pipeline failed: HTTP <status>`.
- [ ] New tests pin the wrong-shape cases (null body, `{}` body, non-JSON body) for `execute`/`queryText`, and the existing github-ci worker test suite passes; the new tests fail pre-fix.

title: id-mail(deploy): validate() crashes on null config entries instead of reporting them, and a config without retire passes validation then crashes the real deploy

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id-mail
labels.description: pkgs/nixos id-mail service and worker

body:
## Problem

`nixos/services/id-mail/worker/deploy.mjs` opens with the promise that it "Validates config.json" before any bws/wrangler/Cloudflare work, and `validate()` (deploy.mjs:124-179) is written as an aggregator: it collects every problem into a list and the caller throws one `config.json is invalid:` error naming them all (deploy.mjs:34-37). That contract fails for two classes of shape the validator itself is the last line of defense against:

### 1. `validate()` crashes on null entries instead of reporting them

`validate()` dereferences nested entries without a null/object check, so a config carrying a null where an object belongs dies with a raw `TypeError` naming no config field, and any other problems in the same config are never reported:

- top-level `null` config → `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'worker')` at deploy.mjs:135 (the very first check)
- `templates: [null]` → `TypeError ... (reading 'subject')` at deploy.mjs:153
- `callers: { "amd": null }` → `TypeError ... (reading 'tokenKey')` at deploy.mjs:163
- a null grant (`callers.amd.transports.email: null`) → `TypeError ... (reading 'mode')` at deploy.mjs:169

Control: a merely *wrong* value (e.g. `worker: "BAD NAME"`) is reported correctly — `Error: config.json is invalid:\n  worker must be a lowercase name` — so the aggregator works for scalar mistakes and only collapses on null object entries.

### 2. A config that passes validation crashes the real deploy: `retire` is optional to `validate()`, required by the deploy flow

`validate()` checks `c.retire ?? []` (deploy.mjs:141 — an absent `retire` is valid), but the deploy sequence iterates it unconditionally at deploy.mjs:87: `for (const name of config.retire)`. A config with no `retire` key:

- passes `validate()` and `--dry-run` exits 0 printing `dry run: mail config is valid, nothing deployed` — the operator is told the config is valid;
- the real deploy then crashes with `TypeError: config.retire is not iterable` at deploy.mjs:87, *after* the bws secret read and the `wrangler deploy --dry-run` step have already run (observed in the stub call log), midway through the deploy sequence.

## Evidence

Verified this run on the laptop against `main` @ `63f83bef5a`, probe `~/git/fleet/probe-idmail-deploy` (the real `deploy.mjs` verbatim, stub `bws`/`wrangler` binaries and a stubbed `fetch`, the same harness as `deploy.test.mjs`):

- control (the committed `config.json`, `--dry-run`): exit 0, `config is valid, nothing deployed`
- bad-name control: clean aggregated validation error, zero external calls
- the four null shapes above: raw `TypeError` from inside `validate()`, zero external calls, no aggregated report
- `retire` omitted: `--dry-run` exit 0; real run exit 1 with `TypeError: config.retire is not iterable` at deploy.mjs:87 after `bws secret list` + `wrangler deploy --dry-run` had already executed

## Why it matters

This deploy script is the guarded door for a production mail Worker: #3281 already established that it must fail closed and say why before touching anything external, because its sequence retires (force-deletes) Workers and resets secrets. A validator that crashes on the malformed shapes it exists to catch — and that blesses a config the deploy flow then crashes on halfway through the sequence — sends the operator debugging the validator instead of their config, at exactly the moment the config is broken.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `validate()` never throws for any JSON value of `config.json` (null/scalar/array top level; null or non-object template, caller, or grant entries): every problem is returned in the aggregated list, each naming the config path it belongs to (e.g. `templates[0] must be an object` / `callers.<name> must be an object`), and the run ends with the existing `config.json is invalid:` error and zero external calls.
- [ ] `retire` optionality agrees between validation and the deploy flow: either validation requires it, or the flow tolerates its absence (`config.retire ?? []`) — a config that passes `--dry-run` must complete the full (stubbed) deploy sequence without a `TypeError`.
- [ ] Regression coverage in `deploy.test.mjs` (same stub harness): the null-entry shapes produce the aggregated validation error with no bws/wrangler calls logged, and a no-`retire` config completes the deploy sequence against the stubs.
- [ ] The committed `config.json` still validates and `--dry-run` still exits 0; the existing #3281 argument tests still pass.

title: atlas-search(worker): GET /v1/cache/inspect accepts a whitespace-only query — the post-normalization empty check the search route has is missing, so an empty query is keyed and its Durable Object is queried

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

labels.name: app/atlas-search
labels.description: pkgs/atlas-search (Atlas search service + atlas-embed)

body:
## Problem

The atlas-search Worker's two gated routes disagree on what an empty query is (`pkgs/atlas-search/worker/src/index.ts` @ def55caf48):

- `POST /v1/search` normalizes the query and rejects an empty result: `const query = normalizeQuery(body.query); if (!query) return errorJson(400, "bad_request", "query must not be empty")`.
- `GET /v1/cache/inspect` (:98-111) guards only the **raw** parameter — `const q = url.searchParams.get("query"); if (!q) return errorJson(400, …, "query parameter is required")` (:102-103) — then normalizes (:104) and never re-checks. A whitespace-only `query` (`?query=%20%20%20`) normalizes to `""` and is accepted: the Worker computes the canonical key for the empty query, resolves the per-query Durable Object for it, and calls its `/inspect` route, returning `200 {"key": …, "query": "", …}`.

So the inspect route — documented as the metadata readback for a real cached query — instantiates/queries a Durable Object for a query that can never exist (the search route can never create an entry for `""`), and returns a success envelope for a request its sibling route defines as a 400.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ def55caf48)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-atlas-inspect/probe.ts` imports the **real** `src/index.ts` (bun) with a stub `QUERY_CACHE` namespace that counts DO calls:

- control: `POST /v1/search` with `{"query":"   "}` → `400 {"error":{"code":"bad_request","message":"query must not be empty"}}`
- control: `GET /v1/cache/inspect` with no `query` → `400 … "query parameter is required"`
- control: `GET /v1/cache/inspect?query=hello` → `200`, DO called once
- defect: `GET /v1/cache/inspect?query=%20%20%20` → `200 {"key":"4588f191…","query":"","exists":false}`, **DO called once** — the empty-after-normalize query reached keying and the Durable Object instead of the 400 both sibling checks imply.

`test/worker.test.ts` has no empty-query case for either route (grep: no `empty`/`must not be empty` test; only a whitespace-normalization comment) — the search route's guard is itself unpinned, and the inspect route has neither guard nor test. Sibling surface: #6879 covers the POST route's null-body crash — a different defect in the same file; this is the inspect route's missing post-normalization check.

## Why it matters

Route-contract consistency is what clients and audit tooling rely on: the same malformed input is a 400 on one route and a 200 with a fabricated cache key on the other. It also spends a Durable Object instantiation (constructor + SQL table creation in `cache_do.ts`) on a key that can never hold a legitimate entry, retained indefinitely per the v1 no-eviction design (#6788).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `GET /v1/cache/inspect` with a query that is empty after `normalizeQuery` (whitespace-only, including tabs/newlines/NBSP-class whitespace the normalizer collapses) returns `400 bad_request` ("query must not be empty", matching the search route's message) and does **not** call the Durable Object.
- [ ] Missing `query` keeps returning `400 "query parameter is required"`; a real query's inspect response is unchanged.
- [ ] A regression test in `test/worker.test.ts` covers the whitespace-only inspect case (400, no DO interaction); adding the search route's whitespace-only case in the same test pins both routes' contract.

title: bitwarden-load-secrets: value-taking options hang forever on a trailing flag and swallow a following flag as the value

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: area/infra
labels.description: Infrastructure, deployment, and operations

body:
## Summary

`lib/bitwarden-load-secrets.sh` parses every value-taking option with an
unguarded `"$2"` + `shift 2` (lines 44, 48, 81, 86, 90, 94: `--item`,
`--field`, `--secret`, `--project`, `--prefix`, `--format`). The script has
no `set -u` and no value check, so:

1. **A trailing value-option hangs forever.** With `--item` as the last
   argument, `$#` is 1, `ITEM_QUERY="$2"` reads empty, and `shift 2` fails
   without advancing the positional parameters — the `while [[ $# -gt 0 ]]`
   loop repeats the same iteration indefinitely. When the script is
   *sourced* (its primary documented mode), this hangs the caller's shell.
2. **A flag in the value position is swallowed as the value.**
   `--item --bws` sets `ITEM_QUERY="--bws"` and consumes the flag: the
   script silently runs in vault mode against an item literally named
   `--bws` instead of switching to Secrets Manager mode (or erroring).

This is the same missing/flag-like-value defect class fixed for the
aggregator scripts in #6926/#6922/#6930 and for record-claude-launch in
#6895, but here the failure mode is worse: an infinite loop instead of a
wrong record.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop main @4c3d00ccb7)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-bw-load-args` (real script verbatim, stub `bw`/`bws`
first on PATH, `HOME` pointed at an empty dir so the script's
`~/.local/bin` prepend cannot shadow the stubs):

- Control `--item StubItem --format json` → rc 0, prints
  `{"API_KEY": "sekrit"}` from the stub item.
- `bash lib/bitwarden-load-secrets.sh --item` → never returns; killed by
  `timeout 3` (rc 124).
- `bash lib/bitwarden-load-secrets.sh --item StubItem --format` → same
  hang (rc 124).
- `bash lib/bitwarden-load-secrets.sh --item --bws` → rc 0 in **vault**
  mode, exporting the stub item's field (`export API_KEY='sekrit'`); the
  `--bws` flag was consumed as the item name and Secrets Manager mode
  never engaged.

The existing contract suite `scripts/tests/test_bitwarden_load_secrets.py`
(4 tests, from #5650) covers multiline values only — no missing-value or
flag-as-value case.

## Why it matters

This loader is sourced into shells to fetch credentials; a typo'd command
(`source lib/bitwarden-load-secrets.sh --item`) freezes the user's shell
with no message, and `--item --bws`-style slips silently query the wrong
backend/item instead of failing fast like every sibling script now does.

## Acceptance criteria

- Each value-taking option (`--item`, `--field`, `--secret`, `--project`,
  `--prefix`, `--format`) with a missing, empty, or flag-like (`--*`)
  value fails fast with a usage error naming the option — exit non-zero
  when executed, and abort the source with non-zero status when sourced;
  never loop.
- Valid invocations are unchanged (all 4 existing tests in
  `scripts/tests/test_bitwarden_load_secrets.py` still pass).
- New regression tests in that suite cover at least: trailing `--item`,
  trailing `--format`, and `--item --bws` (flag-as-value), each completing
  under a timeout with a non-zero status and an error naming the option.

title: aggregator(check-contract-corpus): a flag taken as the --corpus/--publisher value is not a usage error — it becomes a bogus path and fails with a raw ENOENT stack (or a misdiagnosed publisher parse failure)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

body:
# aggregator(check-contract-corpus): a flag taken as the --corpus/--publisher value is not a usage error — it becomes a bogus path and fails with a raw ENOENT stack (or a misdiagnosed publisher parse failure)

## Summary

`pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/check-contract-corpus.ts` parses its two value-taking flags in `args()` (:39-49):

```ts
if (rest[i] === "--corpus" && rest[i + 1]) corpus = rest[++i];
else if (rest[i] === "--publisher" && rest[i + 1]) publisher = rest[++i];
else usage();
```

The only check on the value is truthiness. A following flag is therefore accepted as the value:

- `--corpus --publisher` sets `corpus = "--publisher"`. The script then tries to open `--publisher/orchestration.json` and dies with an unhandled `ENOENT` stack trace (exit 1), instead of the usage error (exit 2) it correctly produces for a trailing flag.
- `--publisher --corpus` sets `publisher = "--corpus"`. All corpus checks pass, then the run reports `FAIL publisher file parses (--corpus) — ENOENT…` (exit 1) — misdiagnosing an operator argument mistake as a broken publisher file, the exact file this pre-publish gate exists to validate.

This is the flag-as-value defect class the sibling aggregator CLIs have been systematically closed against (e.g. #3723 for post-alert, the #3295/#3352/#3509 strict-argument contracts for the snapshot/feed scripts, and #6926 for generate-digest, merged today): a value that is missing, empty, or flag-like is a usage error raised before any file is read. This script guards the missing/empty cases (trailing flag and `""` both reach `usage()`, exit 2) but not the flag-like case.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop, origin/main 1fabdbc2ca; working-tree file md5 5ec8a4bb870f321e3d17bb407a6ac416, identical to origin/main)

Probe: the real script run in place in `pm-stack/aggregator` (Bun 1.4.4, no stubs — the script only reads the checked-in corpus):

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| control: no args | all corpus checks `ok`, `contract check passed`, exit 0 |
| trailing `--corpus` | `usage: check-contract-corpus.ts [--corpus <dir>] [--publisher <orchestration.json>]`, exit 2 (correct) |
| `--corpus --publisher` | unhandled `ENOENT: no such file or directory, open '--publisher/orchestration.json'` with Bun stack trace at `loadJson` (:58), exit 1 |
| `--publisher --corpus` | corpus checks all `ok`, then `FAIL publisher file parses (--corpus) — Error: ENOENT…`, `contract check FAILED: 1 check(s)`, exit 1 |

No existing test covers the script's argument parsing: `test/contract-corpus.test.ts` exercises the validators over the corpus, never the CLI's `args()`.

## Why it matters

This script is the publisher's pre-publish gate (`bun run contract:check -- --publisher <path>`, per its header and the aggregator README) and runs in CI (`pm-aggregator-tests.yml`). An operator typo of the form `--publisher --corpus <dir>` (flags in the wrong order / a value forgotten) currently produces a verdict that blames the publisher file — sending the operator to debug a valid orchestration.json — or a raw stack trace, instead of the one-line usage error every sibling script now gives for the same mistake.

## Acceptance criteria

- `--corpus` or `--publisher` followed by a flag-like value (a token starting with `--`, matching the sibling scripts' guard) is a usage error: the usage line on stderr, exit 2, raised in `args()` before any corpus or publisher file is read — no stack trace, no `FAIL publisher file parses` line.
- A missing (trailing) or empty value remains a usage error (exit 2), as today.
- Valid forms keep working unchanged: no args, `--corpus <dir>`, `--publisher <path>`, and both together, including the `ORCHESTRATION_PATH` env default for the publisher.
- A pinning test in the aggregator test suite (subprocess style, following `test/collect-fleet-feed-args-3509.test.ts`) covers the flag-as-value cases for both flags plus a valid-args control, and fails on the pre-fix script.

body:
# aggregator(generate-digest): a trailing `--kind` silently archives a daily digest — the one unguarded arg() copy left among the aggregator scripts

## Summary

`pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/generate-digest.ts` reads `--kind` through a
local `arg()` helper (:22-25) that returns `process.argv[i + 1]` verbatim —
or `undefined` when the flag is last. In `main()` (:29) that result is
combined with a default:

```ts
const kind = (arg("kind") ?? "daily") as DigestKind;
```

So a `--kind` that is *present but missing its value* is indistinguishable
from a flag that was never passed: the run archives (and, without
`--no-deliver`, push-delivers) a **daily** digest and exits 0. This is the
exact failure the house already settled in #3723 for post-alert.ts ("a
trailing `--severity` silently fell back to the critical default") — and
every sibling script now guards its value-taking flags the same way:
post-alert.ts `arg()`, collect-github-billing.ts `explicitArg` (#3419),
record-claude-launch.ts (#3415), backfill-usage-snapshots.ts `--dir`,
append-usage-snapshots.ts `--by` (#3295), compact-usage-snapshots.ts
`--months`. generate-digest's `arg()` is the unguarded copy left behind.

The flag-token case is also mishandled: `--kind --no-deliver` treats the
next flag as the value and exits 2 with a message that blames the value
("must be daily|weekly, got --no-deliver") instead of naming the missing
value — and the swallowed `--no-deliver` token never takes effect as a
flag.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop main 61f7fedbbe)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-digest-kind/` — the real script, Bun, fixture
source (`PM_AGG_SOURCE=fixtures`), `PM_AGG_DIGESTS_DIR` pointed at the
probe dir, `--no-deliver` on every run:

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| control: `--kind weekly` | exit 0; archived `weekly-2026-11-07.json` ("PM weekly digest … window 168h") |
| control: `--kind daily` | exit 0; archived `daily-2026-11-07.json` ("window 24h") |
| trailing: `--kind` (last token, no value) | exit 0; archived **`daily-2026-11-07.json`** — a daily digest produced by an invocation that named `--kind` and supplied nothing; no error, no warning |
| flag-as-value: `--kind --no-deliver` | exit 2; `generate-digest: --kind must be daily|weekly, got --no-deliver` — the flag token was consumed as the value |

Production callers are the systemd units
`pm-stack/aggregator/systemd/digest-daily.service` /
`digest-weekly.service`, which pass `--kind daily|weekly`; the script is
also the documented manual path (header Usage). A value lost to a unit
edit, a wrapper, or a hand run converts the weekly digest into a daily
one silently — the archive file and the delivered push both say "daily",
so nothing downstream can tell the weekly run ever misfired.

## Why it matters

The digest archive is rendered verbatim at `/digest/<date>` and the push
payload announces the kind; a silently-downgraded weekly run produces a
24h-window digest where subscribers expect the 168h one, with a success
exit and a normal-looking log line. Silent default-substitution on a
present-but-valueless flag is precisely the failure mode #3723 removed
from the alert throat; the same latent copy should not survive in the
digest path.

## Acceptance criteria

- `--kind` with no following value, or with a following token that starts
  with `--`, prints a usage error naming `--kind` and its missing value
  to stderr and exits 2 — no digest is archived and nothing is delivered.
- `--kind daily` and `--kind weekly` behave exactly as today (same
  archive file, same summary line); omitting `--kind` entirely still
  defaults to daily.
- A regression test covers the trailing-flag and flag-as-value cases
  (script-level harness case, as in the sibling scripts' suites).

Distinct from #3333 (produce-charge-candidates `--start`/`--end`/`--out`,
same unchecked-argv family, different script and different silent-write
target) and from #3723 (post-alert, already fixed — this is its residual
sibling copy).

# aggregator(collect-github-billing): the `--by` value is never validated — empty/whitespace fails the whole collection after the gh call, a flag token is recorded as the observer, and a trailing `--by` silently defaults

## Evidence

`pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/collect-github-billing.ts`:

- `:39-42` — `argValue(flag)` returns the next argv token verbatim (or `undefined`).
- `:56-61` — `explicitArg(flag)` exists precisely to reject missing/flag-like values, and #3419 wired it for `--year`/`--month`/`--user` (`:65`, `:74`, `:83`).
- `:112` — `observedBy` still comes from the unguarded helper: `const observedBy = argValue("--by") ?? "collect-github-billing";`
- `:123-126` — records built with that `observedBy` are validated with `isSnapshotRecord`, and ANY invalid record throws, discarding the whole month's collection.

Verified this run on laptop main `5b4aae140e` with the real script and a stub `gh` returning one valid billing item (probe `~/git/fleet/probe-billing-by`):

- control `--print`: exit 0, records carry `observedBy: "collect-github-billing"`.
- `--by "" --print` and `--by "   " --print`: exit 1 — the gh call is made, records are derived, then the run throws `… derived record(s) failed validation` (empty/whitespace `observedBy` fails `isSnapshotRecord`). A usage mistake is reported as a data-validation failure and the month's collection is lost.
- `--by --print`: exit 0 — the flag token is recorded verbatim as the observer (`"observedBy":"--print"` in the printed records) AND the token is consumed a second time as the `--print` flag itself (dry-run mode).
- trailing `--by` (no value): exit 0 — silently falls back to the default observer and appends 3 records to the outbox, instead of the usage error every sibling flag produces.

The settled pattern already exists twice over: #3419 in this same file (`explicitArg` + exit 2 before any gh call) and #3295 in the sibling writer `append-usage-snapshots.ts` (`resolveObservedBy`: a missing, empty, or flag-like `--by` is a usage error, exit 2, outbox untouched). The shipped test `test/collect-github-billing-args-3419.test.ts` covers `--year`/`--month`/`--user` bad values but has no `--by` case; the suite passes 3/3 on current main.

## Why it matters

`observedBy` is the provenance field on every snapshot record this collector writes. A flag token recorded as the observer corrupts provenance permanently in the snapshot store, and the empty-value path converts a one-character CLI typo into a lost month of billing collection with a misleading error (the same misreporting class #3419 fixed for the other flags).

## Acceptance criteria

- `--by` with a missing value, an empty/whitespace-only value, or a value that is another flag token is a usage error: exit 2, message naming `--by`, ZERO gh calls, outbox untouched — resolved before `fetchUsageItems`, consistent with `explicitArg`/`resolveObservedBy` (#3295).
- A valid `--by <name>` is recorded verbatim as `observedBy` on every derived record (control case).
- Omitting `--by` keeps the existing default (`collect-github-billing`).
- Extend `test/collect-github-billing-args-3419.test.ts` (or a sibling test file) with the `--by` bad-value cases (missing / empty / whitespace / flag token) asserting exit 2 + zero gh calls, plus a valid `--by` control asserting the recorded `observedBy`; the existing 3 tests keep passing.

body:
# opencode-acp-adapter: a JSON `null` line on stdin crashes the adapter — dispatch destructures the parsed message unguarded

## Summary

`bin/opencode-acp-adapter.mjs` (the ACP-to-HTTP adapter, #1243) reads newline-delimited JSON-RPC from stdin. A line that is not valid JSON is handled: it is logged and ignored. But a line that is valid JSON with the value `null` kills the whole adapter process — every in-flight session the client (OpenClaw acpx) is driving through it dies with it, and no error is ever returned on the protocol channel.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ 84890c3667)

The readline handler parses the line and calls `dispatch` without checking the parsed value is an object:

- `bin/opencode-acp-adapter.mjs:554-559` — `message = JSON.parse(trimmed)` (only the parse is inside try/catch), then `void dispatch(message);`
- `bin/opencode-acp-adapter.mjs:520` — `async function dispatch(message) { const { id, method, params } = message; … }`

Destructuring `null` throws, `dispatch` is `void`-called, so the throw becomes an unhandled rejection and Node exits.

Probe (laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-acp-null/`, adapter spawned against an unreachable `--server` stub exactly like the shipped test harness; `initialize` is a static handler needing no server):

- Control — `initialize` request alone: correct response, process alive.
- `null` line, then an `initialize` request (id 2): **process exited code 1, no response**. stderr:
  ```
  file:///home/user/git/code/bin/opencode-acp-adapter.mjs:520
    const { id, method, params } = message;
            ^
  TypeError: Cannot destructure property 'id' of 'message' as it is null.
      at dispatch (…/opencode-acp-adapter.mjs:520:11)
      at Interface.<anonymous> (…/opencode-acp-adapter.mjs:559:10)
  ```
- Controls that survive and answer the following `initialize` normally: `42`, `"hi"`, `[]`, `true` — destructuring a primitive/array yields `undefined` fields and `dispatch` returns quietly. `null` is the only JSON value that throws here, which is why this door stayed hidden.

The shipped suite passes today and has no non-object-message case: `node --test bin/opencode-acp-adapter.test.mjs` → fail 0.

## Why it matters

The adapter is a long-lived shim for a shared `opencode serve`; its stdin is fed by another program's output, not by a human typing carefully. One stray `null` frame (a client bug, a proxy/heartbeat artefact, a partially-written line completed as `null`) terminates the adapter mid-session instead of being ignored like the non-JSON lines right next to it in the same handler. The failure is also silent on the protocol channel: the client sees its transport die, not a JSON-RPC error.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `null` line on stdin (and, for completeness, any other valid-JSON non-object line) is ignored with the same debug-log treatment as a non-JSON line; the adapter stays alive and answers the next request.
- [ ] The guard sits where future parse results cannot bypass it (in `dispatch` itself or immediately after `JSON.parse`), not only at one call site.
- [ ] A regression test in `bin/opencode-acp-adapter.test.mjs` drives a `null` line followed by a valid `initialize` request and asserts the response arrives and the process is still running.
- [ ] Existing suite still passes: `node --test bin/opencode-acp-adapter.test.mjs`.

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-a (creator lane A), verified this run; probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-acp-null/` on the laptop.

body:
# codedb-bridge: a null daemon response body crashes codedb_tree out of the handler (no JSON-RPC response is ever sent) and reads as a successful "null" result on the other tools

`bin/codedb-bridge.mjs` trusts the shape of the daemon's JSON body after
`res.json()`:

- The error check uses optional chaining (`data?.error`), so a `null` body
  passes it.
- For `codedb_tree` the result line dereferences the body directly:
  `String(data.tree ?? '')`. With a `null` body that is a raw `TypeError`.
  The throw escapes `callTool` and then `handle()` (the `tools/call` case
  awaits `callTool` with no guard), and in `main()` the dispatch chain's
  `.catch(() => settle())` swallows it — so **no JSON-RPC response is ever
  written for that request id**. The MCP client hangs until its own timeout
  with no error anywhere; the bridge logs nothing.
- For the JSON-kind tools (`codedb_search`, `codedb_hot`, `codedb_outline`,
  `codedb_symbol`, `codedb_word`, `codedb_deps`) a `null` body instead
  returns a *successful* result whose text is the literal string `"null"` —
  a daemon malfunction presented to the caller as a normal (empty-looking)
  answer.

## Verified this run (laptop probe, verbatim origin/main @ ac0bf3e189, file md5 84097d1a)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-codedb-null` on the laptop: the real module
extracted byte-identical from `origin/main`, driven through the exported
`createHandler` with a stubbed `fetchFn` answering HTTP 200:

| Call | Daemon body | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `codedb_tree` (control) | `{"tree":"x"}` | ok, text `x` |
| `codedb_tree` | `null` | **throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'tree')` out of `handle()`** → swallowed by main's catch → no response for the id |
| `codedb_search` | `null` | success result, text `"null"` |
| `codedb_hot` | `null` | success result, text `"null"` |
| `codedb_search` max_results control | `{"results":[1,2]}`, `max_results: 1` | ok, sliced to `[1]` |
| `codedb_outline` | `"weird"` (string body) | success result, text `"\"weird\""` — the daemon's wrong shape passed through as if it were an outline |

The shipped suite (`bin/codedb-bridge.test.mjs`, 13/13 passing on the same
tree) stubs only well-shaped object bodies and daemon errors; no case covers
a null or non-object 200 body.

## Why it matters

The bridge is the per-session shim every MCP client uses to reach the shared
codedb daemon; its design contract (#3352, in the module header) is that
problems are reported by name, never silently dropped. A daemon that answers
200 with a null/wrong-shape body (a partial write, a version-skewed daemon, a
proxy in between) currently produces the two worst outcomes: an indefinite
client hang with zero diagnostics on `codedb_tree` — the tool the header
tells callers to use *first* — and plausible-looking `"null"` successes
everywhere else, which a caller reads as "no results" rather than "the
daemon is broken".

Distinct from #4191 (daemon fetch has no timeout — the fetch never
returning) and #4216 (unknown argument names silently dropped): this is the
response-body shape after a successful fetch. Dedup: searched open and
closed issues for `codedb-bridge` — no issue covers daemon response-body
shape validation.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A daemon 200 body that is `null` or not a plain object produces an
      `isError` text result naming the route and the unexpected shape, for
      every tool kind (tree and json) — never a thrown exception out of
      `handle()`, never a successful `"null"` result.
- [ ] Well-shaped bodies behave exactly as today (existing tests green,
      slicing and `data.error` handling unchanged).
- [ ] New tests in `bin/codedb-bridge.test.mjs` cover at least: null body
      for `codedb_tree`, null body for one json-kind tool, and a non-object
      (string) body — each asserting an `isError` result, not a throw and
      not a success.
- [ ] `node --test bin/codedb-bridge.test.mjs` passes.

body:
# opencode-usage-export: state.json valid-but-wrong-shape JSON wedges every tick (null) or fabricates a store move (non-string storePath)

`pm-stack/opencode-usage-export/opencode-usage-export.mjs` reads its own
`state.json` (the out-dir file recording `{ storePath, lastTickAt }` from the
previous tick) with a bare parse and no shape validation:

- `readState` (`:303-305`) returns `JSON.parse(await readFile(...))` verbatim;
  its `catch` returns `{}` only for a *parse* failure. Valid JSON of the wrong
  shape passes straight through.
- `run()` then dereferences it unchecked (`:341`): `previousPath: state.storePath ?? null`.
  When `state.json` contains the JSON literal `null`, that is
  `Cannot read properties of null (reading 'storePath')` — a raw `TypeError`
  that the outer catch wraps as `read-failed` (exit 6).
- `resolveStore` (`:188`) trusts the type of `previousPath`:
  `previousPath && previousPath !== winner.path ? { from: previousPath, to: winner.path } : null`.
  A non-string `storePath` (e.g. `123`) is truthy and unequal to the winner
  path, so the success document reports a store move that never happened.

## Verified this run (laptop probe, verbatim origin/main @ ac0bf3e189, file md5 13c24364)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-usage-state` on the laptop: the real module extracted
byte-identical from `origin/main`, a fixture `session_v2`/`session_message`
store (same shape as the shipped test) with one fresh session, `run()` invoked
with injectable `home`/`now` exactly as the shipped tests do:

| state.json content | Result |
|---|---|
| (absent — control) | exit 0, `status: "ok"`, 1 session, `moved: null` |
| `null` | **exit 6, `read-failed`**, detail `opencode usage export failed: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'storePath')`; `latest.json` overwritten with the failure document |
| `"just a string"` | exit 0, ok (`.storePath` is `undefined` on a string — survives by accident) |
| `{"storePath": 123}` | exit 0, ok, but **`moved: {"from": 123, "to": "<real store path>"}`** — a fabricated move |
| `{` (truncated) | exit 0, ok — the parse-error path is guarded; only the wrong-shape path is not |
| `[]` | exit 0, ok |

The shipped suite (`opencode-usage-export.test.mjs`, 4/4 passing on the same
tree) writes only well-shaped or absent `state.json`; no case covers a
wrong-shape state file.

## Why it matters

The module's contract is fail-closed *about the store*: a tick that cannot
read the live store writes a failure document so a bad tick "can never be
mistaken for a reading". A wrong-shape `state.json` breaks that in both
directions:

1. **Self-perpetuating wedge.** With `state.json` = `null`, every tick fails
   with `read-failed` and overwrites the last good `latest.json` with a
   failure document, even though the store is fresh and healthy — and the
   failure path never rewrites `state.json`, so the exporter never heals
   until a human edits the out-dir by hand. The detail also misdiagnoses:
   it presents a corrupt bookkeeping file as a store read failure.
2. **Fabricated move report.** The `moved` field exists so a store move is
   "surfaced on the tick it happens" (module header). A non-string
   `storePath` manufactures a move event in an otherwise-good success
   document, sending downstream consumers (#2072 slices) and operators
   chasing a move that never occurred.

Distinct from #4739 (this exporter's `--window-hours`/`--fresh-hours`
validation — the CLI-argument surface; this is the persisted-state surface)
and from the readState-adjacent guards in sibling exporters. Dedup: searched
open and closed issues for `opencode-usage-export`, `state.json`,
`usage-export state`, and `moved` — no issue covers the state-file shape.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `readState` (or its call site) treats any `state.json` whose top level
      is not a plain object — `null`, array, string, number, boolean — the
      same as a missing/unparseable file: no previous path, tick proceeds.
- [ ] A `storePath` that is not a non-empty string is treated as absent:
      no `moved` entry is ever produced with a non-string `from`.
- [ ] A healthy fresh store with a wrong-shape `state.json` produces the
      normal `status: "ok"` document (exit 0), and the tick rewrites
      `state.json` in the correct shape, so the state self-heals.
- [ ] New tests in `opencode-usage-export.test.mjs` cover at least:
      `state.json` = `null`, a non-object top level, and
      `{"storePath": 123}` — asserting exit 0, `status: "ok"`,
      `moved: null`.
- [ ] Existing tests stay green: `node --test pm-stack/opencode-usage-export/`
      passes.
