body:
## Bug: provider-catalog-sync `makeEntry` crashes with a raw SyntaxError when every variant-carrying sibling has `"variants": null`

`bin/provider-catalog-sync.mjs`, `makeEntry` (lines 487–494):

```js
const withVariants = entries.filter((e) => e && typeof e === 'object' && 'variants' in e);
...
if (withVariants.length > 0) {
  const sibId = longestCommonPrefixSibling(modelId, ids.filter((id) => siblings[id]?.variants));
  const clone = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(siblings[sibId]));
```

The two filters disagree about what counts as a variant-carrying sibling:

- the branch gate (line 487) counts an entry whose `variants` key is present with **any** value, including `null`;
- the clone-source filter (line 493) requires `siblings[id]?.variants` to be **truthy**.

When a provider block's only variant-carrying entries have `"variants": null` (a shape a hand-edited `opencode.jsonc` can legitimately contain — the key present, the value nulled out), the branch is taken with zero clone candidates: `longestCommonPrefixSibling(modelId, [])` returns `null`, `siblings[null]` is `undefined`, and `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(undefined))` throws.

### Verified (laptop, main @ 6d2a24b656, probe `~/git/fleet/probe-catalog-sync`, real module imported)

```
A variants:null -> THROWS SyntaxError "undefined" is not valid JSON
C control (variants: {high:{}}) -> OK {"name":"Model B","variants":{"high":{}},"_clonedFrom":"model-a"}
D variants:{} -> OK {"name":"Model B","variants":{},"_clonedFrom":"model-a"}
```

### Why it matters

`makeEntry` is called from `applyAdditions` during `--apply`. The throw escapes as a bare `SyntaxError: "undefined" is not valid JSON` — it names neither the provider, the model, nor the sibling shape — and aborts the whole apply run: no validated additions from any provider are written (the write happens after `applyAdditions` returns). One nulled `variants` key in one provider block silently blocks every catalog update until someone hand-diagnoses a JSON error that has nothing to do with JSON input. The shipped test suite (`bin/provider-catalog-sync.test.mjs`) covers name-only blocks and real-variant clones, but no null-variant sibling.

### Acceptance criteria

- `makeEntry` with siblings whose only `variants` values are `null` (or otherwise non-object) returns a name-only entry instead of throwing — the same result as a block with no variant-carrying siblings — plus the models.dev `limit` when one is available (the existing name-only branch behavior).
- The branch gate and the clone-source filter use one consistent definition of a cloneable sibling (a sibling whose `variants` is a non-null object).
- A regression test in `bin/provider-catalog-sync.test.mjs` covers the null-variants sibling shape; the existing suite still passes (`node --test bin/provider-catalog-sync.test.mjs` or the repo's bin test runner).
- Behavior for real variant objects (clone from nearest-prefix sibling, models.dev limit preference) is unchanged.

title: aggregator(record-claude-launch): empty flag values are recorded verbatim — '--id ""' appends a session with no id, '--parent ""' a parent that is not null, exit 0

body:
## Problem

`pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/record-claude-launch.ts`: the #3415 guard in `valueAfter` (:35-41) refuses a missing value and a value that is itself a flag, but it does **not** refuse an empty (or whitespace-only) value. Its settled siblings do: `post-alert.ts:131` and `collect-fleet-feed.ts:231` both check `value === ""`, and `append-usage-snapshots.ts` (`resolveObservedBy`) checks `value.trim() === ""`. This script is the one value-taking CLI in the set whose guard omits the empty case, so empty strings flow into the appended launch record verbatim, with exit 0.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ 4cd2927643, real script, `--file` pointed at a probe file)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-launch-empty/` (real `record-claude-launch.ts` run via `bun run`, control first):

- Control `--label "Control"` → record with a generated `claude-…` id, `parentId: null`, `status: "launched"`, rc 0.
- `--label "EmptyId" --id ""` → rc 0, appended record is `{"id":"", …}` — an identity record with no identity.
- `--label "EmptyParentStatus" --parent "" --status ""` → rc 0, appended record carries `"parentId":""` (instead of the `null` the default produces) and `"status":""`.
- `--id " "` → rc 0, `"id":" "`. `--label " "` → rc 0, a session whose display name is a single space (the `!label` check at :54 catches only the empty string).
- `--file ""` → not a usage error at all: raw `ENOENT` stack from `appendFile("")`, rc 1, no message naming the flag.

## Why it matters

The collector's reader accepts these records: `parseLaunchRecords` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/registry.ts:105`) admits any record whose `id` is a string — `""` qualifies — and the registry merge keys records by `(source, id)` (:133-135). Every session ever recorded with `--id ""` therefore collides on the same merge key and folds into a single phantom registry entry, silently losing those sessions' task↔session linkage (the file's stated purpose, script header :5-11); a `parentId` of `""` likewise points at that phantom instead of meaning "no parent". Because the script exits 0 and prints the usual `recorded …` line, a launcher passing an unset shell variable (`--id "$SESSION_ID"`) gets no signal that it just registered a nameless session.

## Acceptance criteria

- Every value-taking flag (`--label`, `--id`, `--parent`, `--task`, `--model`, `--status`, `--file`) refuses an empty or whitespace-only value with the existing usage-error path: message naming the flag, exit 2, and **nothing appended** (the launch-records file is byte-identical afterwards).
- Non-empty values, including values with internal spaces (e.g. `--label "Slice 3 builder"`), keep working exactly as today; the #3415 flag-as-value refusals keep working.
- A pinning test in the style of `pm-stack/aggregator/test/record-claude-launch-flag-value-3415.test.ts` covers at least `--id ""`, `--parent ""`, `--status ""`, and a whitespace-only `--label`, asserting exit 2 and an untouched records file.

title: Fix #6883: id(build.sh): a missing or corrupt variant file lets the wrong-variant b

labels.name: source/dispatch
labels.description: Filed by pm-dispatch

body:
Implement GitHub issue #6883 in developing-today/code: id(build.sh): a missing or corrupt variant file lets the wrong-variant binary pass as up to date — a lib binary is served for a web build (and vice versa)

## Problem

`pkgs/id/scripts/build.sh` decides whether the existing binary matches the requested variant (`lib` vs `web` — the same output path `target/debug/id` / `target/release/id`, differing only by `--features web`) from a single marker file, and only in one narrow case:

- `scripts/build.sh:105`: the variant check fires only when the marker file **exists** and its content is exactly the *other* variant:
  ```bash
  elif [[ -f $VARIANT_FILE ]] && [[ "$(cat "$VARIANT_FILE")" == "$OTHER_VARIANT" ]]; then
  ```
- If the marker file is **missing, empty, or contains anything else**, the script falls through to the timestamp scan and can declare `"<variant> <profile> variant up to date"` — with a binary on disk that was built as the *other* variant.
- The marker is written non-atomically at `scripts/build.sh:153` (`echo "$VARIANT" >"$VARIANT_FILE"`), so an interrupted build is exactly how an empty/truncated marker is produced. The marker can also be lost independently of the binary (partial `target/` cleanup, a copied-in binary, a manual `rm target/.build-variant*`).

## Verified (laptop, main @ 8a5cd8ea75, real script verbatim, stubbed cargo/bun)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-buildsh-variant` (fixture tree in the style of `scripts/build-sh-test.sh`; control + 3 failure cases):

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| Control: build `lib`, marker intact (`lib`), run `web` | Correctly rebuilds: `cargo build --features web`, marker becomes `web` |
| Build `lib`, **delete** marker, run `web` | `web debug variant up to date`, **cargo never invoked**, marker still absent — the lib binary (no `--features web`) is left in place as the "web" build |
| Build `lib`, marker **truncated to empty**, run `web` | Same: `up to date`, cargo never invoked |
| Build `lib`, marker contains **`banana`**, run `web` | Same: `up to date`, cargo never invoked |

Symmetric for `web` → `lib` (a web binary silently served as the lib build).

## Why it matters

The two variants produce functionally different binaries at the *same path*. A stale-variant binary that passes as current is a silent wrong-artifact failure: a developer (or a just recipe — `build-lib` / the web build) runs a binary missing the web features (or carrying them unexpectedly) with no diagnostic, and the timestamp logic can keep it "up to date" indefinitely until a source file changes. This is the same script whose variant handling already produced #6869; the marker is the only variant evidence, so an unknown marker state must mean "rebuild", not "trust the binary".

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A missing marker file, or a marker whose content is not exactly the requested variant, forces a backend rebuild (unknown state rebuilds; only an exact match for the requested variant may take the up-to-date path).
- [ ] The marker write is atomic (write to a temp file in the same directory + rename), so an interrupted build cannot leave an empty/truncated marker.
- [ ] `scripts/build-sh-test.sh` gains cases for the missing-marker, empty-marker, and garbage-marker states (build one variant, disturb the marker, request the other variant, assert cargo is invoked with the correct flags and the marker is rewritten) — for at least the debug profile.
- [ ] Existing `build-sh-test.sh` cases (lib debug/release, assets, web control) still pass.

Related: #6869 (the `lib`-variant unbound-variable crash in the same script, fixed + regression-tested in PR #6870).

Rules from the repo owner: (1) Deliver the finished work as a pull request in this run; put "Fixes #6883" in the PR description so the issue closes on merge. (2) Cover the whole set in the one PR: if the issue names a set (files, subcommands, cases), fix every member, and batch any directly related dependency updates into the same PR — never one PR per item or per dependency. (3) Run the relevant tests and checks before opening the PR. (4) Merging is permitted but never required: merge only when checks pass and you are reasonably certain the PR is correct and low-risk — otherwise leave it open, and state your confidence and what a human should check. (5) If you hit a genuine blocker (missing credentials, a decision only the owner can make), stop and say exactly what is needed in your final summary instead of guessing. (6) Detached-session clause: never use the `question` tool — if you hit a question, record it and the default you chose in your final summary and keep working.

title: id(roc): roc-chat + roc-grid build.sh quote multi-word WASM_TOOLS on validate — fallback builds die at the last step (127) after strip

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
# id(roc): roc-chat + roc-grid build.sh quote the multi-word `WASM_TOOLS` command on the validate step — fallback builds die at the last step after the module was already stripped

## Evidence

Every Roc example build script resolves `WASM_TOOLS` to a **command string that can be multi-word**:

- `pkgs/id/examples/roc-chat/build.sh:10-20` (same block in roc-grid, lounge, roc-counter, roc-screen, territory, tic-tac-toe): if `wasm-tools` is not on PATH and no `/nix/store/*-wasm-tools-*/bin/wasm-tools` exists, the fallback is `WASM_TOOLS="nix run nixpkgs#wasm-tools --"`. `WASM_OPT` has the same shape (`"nix shell nixpkgs#binaryen --command wasm-opt"`). Every invocation in all seven scripts therefore relies on unquoted word-splitting (`$WASM_TOOLS strip …`, `$WASM_OPT -Os …`).

Two lines break that contract:

- `pkgs/id/examples/roc-chat/build.sh:43`: `"${WASM_TOOLS}" validate roc-chat.wasm`
- `pkgs/id/examples/roc-grid/build.sh:43`: `"${WASM_TOOLS}" validate roc-grid.wasm`

Quoted, a multi-word value is treated as one executable name. These are the only quoted uses in the tree (the other five scripts, and the strip/opt steps in these same two files, are unquoted). The lines came in with commit 96e95c1455, which added the validate step to these two examples for #1538.

## Verified this run (laptop, main @ a2ea75cb63)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-wasm-quote` (real build.sh files copied verbatim, md5-checked; stub `roc` printing the pinned version and emitting the `--output` file; stub wasm-opt/wasm-tools; `roc-world/build-host.sh` stubbed):

- **roc-chat, `WASM_TOOLS="<stub> --some-flag"` (the fallback shape): exit 127** — `build.sh: line 43: …/wasm-tools-stub --some-flag: No such file or directory`. The calls log shows wasm-opt and the (unquoted) `strip` step already ran, i.e. the checked-in `.wasm` was already optimized, stripped and moved into place when the build failed on validate.
- **roc-grid, multi-word: exit 127**, same line 43.
- Control, roc-chat single-word `WASM_TOOLS`: exit 0, validate runs.
- Control, lounge (all-unquoted sibling) with multi-word `WASM_TOOLS`: exit 0, validate runs with the flag passed through.

So in exactly the environments the fallback exists for (no wasm-tools on PATH, none in the store — e.g. a non-Nix shell), roc-chat and roc-grid builds fail at the final step, after the artifact was already replaced; and any user-supplied multi-word `WASM_TOOLS` wrapper breaks the same way.

## Why it matters

The fallback branch is the documented escape hatch for building the checked-in Roc modules outside the pinned toolchain shell. Two of the seven examples silently diverge from the other five: their builds report failure after mutating the artifact, leaving the operator unable to tell whether the module on disk is valid — the validate step exists precisely to answer that (#1538) and it is the step that cannot run.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `pkgs/id/examples/roc-chat/build.sh` and `pkgs/id/examples/roc-grid/build.sh` invoke the validate step so a multi-word `WASM_TOOLS` (including the built-in `nix run nixpkgs#wasm-tools --` fallback) works, consistent with the other five example build scripts and with the strip/opt steps in the same files.
- [ ] With a multi-word `WASM_TOOLS`, both builds run to completion (exit 0) and the validate step actually executes; with a single-word `WASM_TOOLS` nothing changes.
- [ ] `shfmt -d -i 2 -s` clean and no new shellcheck findings at warning severity (the flake's `shellcheck-check` gate; the sibling scripts' unquoted uses are the precedent).

title: sync_research_workflow: empty or root workflow_docs maps the whole source tree (including .git) into the target

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

body:
## Problem

`scripts/sync_research_workflow.py` validates that a profile's `workflow_docs` is a string (`load_profile`, :50-52) but never that it names a real subdirectory. An empty string or `"."` passes validation, and `Path("")` / `Path(".")` is the repository root — so `source_files` (:82-95) treats the **entire source checkout as the workflow-docs tree**.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ ab37879484)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-sync-docs` (real module, fixture source/target trees; the source profile has `workflow_docs: ""`, the target a normal `docs/wf`):

- `source_files()` returned **25 mappings** instead of the control's 12, including:
  - `docs/wf/.git/HEAD` — the source checkout's `.git` contents are enumerated as portable workflow files
  - `docs/wf/SECRET.txt` — an unrelated top-level source file
  - `docs/wf/.agents/research-workflow.json`, `docs/wf/scripts/research_workflow.py`, plus every skill file duplicated under the docs prefix
- Control (same fixture, `workflow_docs: "docs"`): exactly the 12 expected mappings (9 skills, `docs/wf/a.md`, the two portable scripts).
- Existing suite `scripts/tests/test_sync_research_workflow.py`: 8/8 pass on current main — the shape tests added for #2800 cover non-string `workflow_docs` (`123`, `None`, missing) in both profiles, but not `""` / `"."`.

In `--write` mode `sync()` copies every mapping into the target and records all of them in `.agents/research-workflow.upstream.json`, so a templating typo that empties `workflow_docs` would sweep a copy of the source repo — `.git` included — into the target checkout and bless it in the provenance manifest. A target profile with `workflow_docs: ""` is the mirror hazard: destinations collapse onto repository-root-relative paths.

`inside()` (:28-36) does not catch this: the root is relative to itself, so the escape check passes.

## Acceptance criteria

- `load_profile` rejects a `workflow_docs` that is empty or resolves to the repository root (`""`, `"."`, `"./"` etc.) in **both** the source and target profiles, with the tool's clean diagnostic naming the file and field (e.g. `research-workflow.json: workflow_docs must name a directory inside the repository`), consistent with the existing shape errors.
- Regression tests in `scripts/tests/test_sync_research_workflow.py` cover `""` and `"."` for both profiles, following the existing `assert_clean_failure` pattern.
- Normal profiles (e.g. `docs/workflow`) keep working; the existing suite stays green.
- Out of scope but worth a look while here: a `lifecycle_skills` entry of `""` or `"."` has the same directory-itself shape (maps `.agents/skills` wholesale); reject or explicitly accept it with a test.

title: id(build.sh): the lib variant crashes before cargo — needs_frontend is unbound under set -u outside the web/assets Step 1 block

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Summary

`pkgs/id/scripts/build.sh` — the build script behind the justfile's
`build-lib` and `release-lib` recipes — crashes immediately for the
`lib` variant: `needs_frontend` is only assigned inside the Step 1
block that runs for the `web`/`assets` variants, but line 88 expands
it unconditionally under `set -u`. Every `lib` build dies before
cargo is ever invoked, so the documented "build without web UI / no
bun required" path does not work at all.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ 65beb42c1a, probe `~/git/fleet/probe-buildsh-lib`, real script verbatim, stubbed `cargo` on PATH)

`pkgs/id/scripts/build.sh` (root `pkgs/id/build.sh` is a symlink to it):

- `:15` — `set -euo pipefail`
- `:48-49` — Step 1 runs only `if [[ $VARIANT == "web" || $VARIANT == "assets" ]]`, and `needs_frontend=false` is assigned only inside that block
- `:88` — `frontend_just_built="$needs_frontend"` runs for every variant

Probe results (fixture tree with an up-to-date `web/dist/manifest.json`):

| invocation | result |
| --- | --- |
| `bash build.sh lib debug` | exit 1, stderr `./build.sh: line 88: needs_frontend: unbound variable`; the stubbed cargo log is absent — cargo was never reached |
| `bash build.sh assets debug` (control) | exit 0, `[web] Frontend assets up to date` |
| `bash build.sh web debug` (control) | exit 0, cargo called as `build --features web`, variant file written `web` |

Callers: `pkgs/id/justfile:430` (`build-lib`: `./scripts/build.sh lib debug`) and `justfile:442` (`release-lib`: `./scripts/build.sh lib release`) — both recipes are dead on arrival, in both profiles (the crash is before any profile-dependent code runs).

## Why it matters

The `lib` variant is the bun-free build path — the one a contributor
or a CI job without the web toolchain is supposed to use. It has
presumably been broken since `frontend_just_built` was introduced,
and nothing caught it because the default `web` path masks it: the
variable is always set on the path everyone runs.

## Fix shape

Initialize `needs_frontend=false` before the Step 1 conditional (or
expand `${needs_frontend:-false}` at line 88). One line; no behavior
change for `web`/`assets`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `bash pkgs/id/scripts/build.sh lib debug` with a stubbed cargo reaches cargo (invoked with no `--features web`) and writes `lib` to the variant file; same for `lib release`
- [ ] Controls unchanged: `assets` exits 0 without invoking cargo; `web` still invokes cargo with `--features web` and rebuilds the backend when the frontend was just rebuilt
- [ ] A regression check exercises all three variants with stubbed cargo/bun (fixture tree, up-to-date manifest) so a variant-specific unbound variable cannot silently return

title: repo-universe(generate): field-level wrong shape passes the #6716 entry guard — malformed full_name/html_url forge phantom repos in the artifact, and a string "false" fork silently un-watches an owned repo

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: status/needs-triage
labels.description: Not yet triaged; needs a first look

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/repo-universe
labels.description: scripts/fleet/repo-universe generator + issue checker

body:
## Problem

`scripts/fleet/repo-universe/generate.py` validates enumeration entries at the entry level (#6716: an entry must be a JSON object with a string `full_name`), but it never validates the **fields inside** an object entry. A capture whose entries are objects with wrong-shaped fields is accepted silently and produces a corrupt maintained artifact (`doc/fleet/repo-universe.yaml`) — or silently misclassifies a real repo so it stops being watched.

This is the field-level residual of #6716 on the generator side, the same shape of gap #6757 fixed on the checker side (`check_issues.py`).

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop, origin/main `fc5aa00e79f33c5fd53bc2ad4ff0ccb6285b492d`)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-repo-universe-fields` — the real `generate.py` taken verbatim from `origin/main`, driven through its public `build()`:

- `validate_entry` (generate.py:79-99) checks only `isinstance(entry, dict)` and `isinstance(entry.get("full_name"), str)`. It does not check that `full_name` is a non-empty `owner/name` shape, and it never looks at `html_url` or `fork`.
- **Empty / malformed `full_name` is accepted and classified `owned` + `watch: issues`:** entries with `full_name` `""`, `"noslash"`, and `"/leading"` each produce a `repos:` entry (`- name: ` / `- name: noslash` / `- name: /leading`) with `class: owned`, `watch: issues`, `sources: [github]`.
- **Newline injection through `full_name` forges phantom repos:** `full_name` `"a/b\n  - name: evil/injected\n    url: https://evil.example\n    class: owned\n    watch: issues\n    sources: [github]"` is emitted verbatim at generate.py:327 (`lines.append(f"  - name: {full}")`), so the artifact gains a complete, well-formed-looking second repo entry for `evil/injected` that no enumeration ever returned.
- **Newline injection through `html_url` forges phantom repos too:** `build()` takes the URL as `(repo or {}).get("html_url") or ...` (generate.py:317-321) with no type or content check and emits it verbatim at :328. An `html_url` of `"https://example.com\n  - name: evil/injected"` injects a phantom entry the same way.
- **Non-string `html_url` is rendered as Python syntax:** `html_url: 12345` emits `url: 12345`; `html_url: ["x", "y"]` emits `url: ['x', 'y']`.
- **`fork` is judged by truthiness, not by type:** `classify` (generate.py:213-217) does `if gh_repo.get("fork"): return "fork"`. An entry with `"fork": "false"` (string) is classified `class: fork` / `watch: inventory-only` — a non-fork owned repo silently drops out of issue watching because a capture field carried the wrong JSON type.

Control: a well-formed entry (`full_name` `developing-today/code`, string `html_url`, `fork: false`) builds exactly as before (`class: owned`, correct URL).

## Why it matters

The artifact this generator writes is the fleet's repo universe: `class` and `watch` decide which repos get their issues pulled in and tracked (#1511). A single wrong-shaped capture — a hand-saved API error page, a truncated/edited capture file, a proxy that stringifies booleans — either corrupts the artifact with phantom repos (which downstream consumers then try to watch) or silently un-watches a real owned repo. #6716 made wrong-shape entries fail with a named error precisely so a bad capture cannot silently rewrite the universe; the field-level hole re-opens that door one level down.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `validate_entry` (or an equivalent single gate used by `decode_pages`, `merge_repos`, and `build`) rejects, with the existing named-error style (source + entry index + offending value), any entry whose `full_name` is not a well-formed `owner/name` string (non-empty owner and name, exactly the GitHub shape, no whitespace/control/newline characters).
- [ ] An entry whose `html_url` is present and not a string, or contains whitespace/control/newline characters, is rejected with the same named error; an absent `html_url` keeps the current fallback behaviour.
- [ ] An entry whose `fork` is present and not a JSON boolean is rejected with the same named error (no truthiness coercion); absent `fork` keeps current behaviour.
- [ ] No input accepted today with well-formed fields changes output: regeneration on well-formed captures is byte-identical, and the in-tree `test_generate.py` suite passes.
- [ ] Regression tests in `test_generate.py` cover at least: empty `full_name`, slash-less `full_name`, newline-bearing `full_name`, non-string `html_url`, newline-bearing `html_url`, and string `"false"` `fork`.

Relates to #6716 (entry-level shape, closed) and #6757 (same field-level gap, checker side).

body:
## Problem

The hourly `cargo-target-janitor` (infra/cargo-target-janitor) — the only mechanism enforcing the 150 GiB fleet Cargo-target cap — **fails every run** and has deleted nothing while the laptop disk filled to 100% (#6797 triage, 2026-11-07):

```
cargo-target-janitor: refusing cleanup: queue helper unavailable: /home/user/hatch/tools/repo-queue.py
```

(journalctl --user -u cargo-target-janitor.service, runs at 03:08Z / 04:00Z / 05:03Z on 2026-11-07, all exit 2.)

The janitor reads its never-delete claimed set through the retired Python repo-queue helper at `~/hatch/tools/repo-queue.py` — a path removed by the fleet-binary migration (code#5362/#5412). Fail-closed is the right behaviour for an unavailable safety source; the defect is that the source path is permanently stale, so the refusal is permanent and silent (its run-record dir `~/.local/state/cargo-target-janitor/runs/` holds no recent runs, and nothing alerts on the repeated service failure).

Measured at triage (2026-11-07 ~05:35Z): in-scope targets `~/git/fleet/*/pkgs/id/target` alone sum **274,701 MB vs the 150 GiB cap**. Separately, two build-output classes sit outside the janitor's configured scope entirely: `~/git/fleet/queue/*/pkgs/id/target` ≈ 82 GiB (one level deeper than its glob) and repo-root `~/git/fleet/*/target` ≈ 114 GiB. `~/git/fleet` totals 604 GiB across 1,704 entries (352 registered worktrees).

## Requested change

1. Restore a live queue-claims source for the janitor on the current fleet path: read claimed task IDs via the fleet queue binary / broker, and — while the queue backend is down (code#6619) — via the GitHub fallback claim markers, which are the claim of record in fallback mode. Preserve fail-closed semantics when *no* source is readable. Note #6790 (closed 2026-11-07) fixed offset pagination inside this same read; keep that fix and its tests.
2. Decide the scope question with the numbers above and implement it: either extend discovery to `~/git/fleet/queue/*/pkgs/id/target` and `~/git/fleet/*/target` (with the same safety rules), or document in the README why those classes are excluded and name what owns them.
3. A run record (summary JSONL under `~/.local/state/cargo-target-janitor/runs/`) is written on *every* run, including refusals, so a dead janitor is visible in its own state, not only in the systemd journal.
4. The existing deletion-safety tests cover the new source path (fixture claim sets, no live queue needed). Wiring those tests into CI is #5952 — coordinate, don't duplicate.

## Acceptance

- A manual dry-run on the laptop completes and prints candidates + protected targets instead of the `queue helper unavailable` refusal.
- The hourly user timer's next run after the fix exits 0 (or reports `over_cap` with named protected targets) and leaves a run record.
- Claimed-task, open-PR, and live-process protections behave exactly as before (existing tests pass, extended for the new source).
- If scope is extended: a dry-run enumerates the queue/ and repo-root target classes with sizes; if not, the README names their owner.

Refs: #6797 (triage), #6790 (closed, same read), #5952 (janitor tests in CI), #3372 (prior disk-full occurrence).

title: id world stats fails against a live host: "expected a query frame" (caps/profile frames refused mid-session)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/queue-worker
labels.description: Filed or worked by the queue/worker pilot

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.description: An agent touched this without the required agent-note comment or labels; needs review of why

body:
## Bug revealed by #5238's execution tests (9-8 verb coverage)

`id world stats <node> --capability <cap>` fails against a live world host:

```
Error: expected a query frame
```

## Cause

The stats verb runs four queries over ONE connection (`id/src/commands/world.rs`, `WorldCommand::Stats`): `info_details` → `caps` → `execution_profile` → `metrics`.

The host's session handling splits frames into two disjoint sets:

- First-frame dispatch (`id/src/world_session/mod.rs`, ~lines 1323/1483) handles `Caps` and `ExecutionProfileInfo` as one-shot sessions.
- `query_session` (~line 1590; doc: "Serve query frames (info, records, records_ticket, download_module)") loops only over `Join` / `Info` / `Metrics` / `Records` / `RecordsTicket` / `DownloadModule`; anything else falls to the default arm (~line 1748) and is refused with `expected a query frame`.

So stats' first query (`info`) succeeds, its second (`caps`) is refused, and the verb errors out. Each query works as a standalone verb (`world caps`, `world profile` both execute fine against the same host) — only the combination on one connection fails.

## Evidence

Execution test added under #5238 (live counter world on a spawned host, one committed input event):

- `world logs` tailed the event frame — pass
- `world caps --ceiling time.now` + read-back — pass
- `world profile --wasm-fuel 424242` + read-back — pass
- `world stats` — FAIL: `Error: expected a query frame` (test panicked at the stats call)

The stats execution test is committed `#[ignore]`d under #5238 naming this issue; un-ignore it here.

## Fix options

1. Server: teach `query_session` the read-only `Caps` and `ExecutionProfileInfo` frames (capability-authorized, like `Info`/`Metrics`). The joined phase already serves both (~lines 2749/2684). This matches the frames' query nature.
2. Client: have the stats verb open a fresh connection per query. Works against older hosts; more handshakes.

Option 1 looks like the protocol-level fix; either must keep the malformed-reply validation from #6624/#6636 intact.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `id world stats` succeeds against a live host and prints the joined JSON (world_id, active_module_hash, current_sequence, caps, profile, metrics).
- [ ] The `#[ignore]`d stats execution test from #5238 runs and passes; the ignore is removed.
- [ ] Existing caps/profile/stats-adjacent tests stay green.

body:
## Problem

`idset::expand` (PR #6787, for #4998) evaluates a group entry's `role_min` against the member's role at the pinned frontier, read from the membership layer. The membership layer records **Admin as Manage** — Admin is a policy role the groups fold tracks apart from access (`record.admins`, with `admin_at_position` replaying it at a causal position in `pkgs/id/src/groups/fold.rs`). The layer therefore cannot distinguish an admin from any other manager at a frontier.

Current behaviour (pinned by `test_expand_role_min_admin_is_answered_at_manage_the_layers_top_role` in `pkgs/id/tests/writer_set_expansion.rs`): a `role_min: Role::Admin` entry is evaluated at `Role::Manage`. Admins are admitted, but so are non-admin managers — an Admin-threshold admission is broader than the set's author wrote, and an Admin-threshold exclusion is broader too.

## What exact resolution needs

Plumb the fold's admin-at-frontier state into expansion so a snapshot can carry `Role::Admin` for members who held Admin at the set version's pinned frontier:

- an `admins_at(group, frontier)` source beside `Membership::members_at_position` (the fold's `admin_at_position` replay is the existing model), or fold the distinction into the membership layer itself;
- `Expander` takes that source and marks those members `Role::Admin` in the `GroupMembers` snapshot it builds, dropping the Manage clamp in `clamp_admin_thresholds`;
- tests: an admin admitted by an Admin entry while a non-admin manager is not; a member promoted to Admin only after the frontier not admitted by the earlier version (the Admin analogue of spec test 6).

## Evidence

- Codex P2 finding on PR #6787 (comment 4500186199) raised the original form of this (Admin entries expanding to empty); the clamp fixed the empty-expansion half, this issue tracks the exactness half.
- `pkgs/id/src/idset/expand.rs` module doc states the limitation and names this follow-up.
- The pure projection (`idset::view::expand_set`) already handles Admin correctly when a snapshot carries it — only the store wiring lacks the data.

Parent context: #4998 (spec §9 item 2), #3789.

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/normal

body:
# cargo-target-janitor(queue_claims): offset pagination over the live claimed set can skip a still-claimed task — it loses never-delete protection

## Summary

`queue_claims` in `infra/cargo-target-janitor/bin/cargo_target_janitor.py` (lines 194–221 at origin/main `e48256bb8f`) reads the pilot queue's claimed task IDs — the janitor's never-delete set — by following `limit=1000&offset=N` pages until a short page arrives. The query carries **no `order=` parameter**, and offset pagination is evaluated by PostgREST against the **current** filtered set on every request. The claimed set is live: claimed tasks complete, fail, and are released constantly while a janitor run is paging.

When a row leaves the claimed set mid-pagination, every later row shifts one position toward the front, and the next offset page skips exactly one still-claimed row. That task's cargo target is then treated as unclaimed by both the plan-time read and the apply-loop fresh re-check (both call this same function), so a target directory belonging to a task a worker is actively building in can be selected and deleted.

This is the residual axis #6618 did not close: #6618 made the read *complete-or-fail-closed for a static set* (page past 1000, fail closed past 100 pages). It does not make the read stable for a *changing* set, and no ordering is requested.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Probe on the laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-janitor-offset/` — the real `cargo_target_janitor.py` copied verbatim from origin/main `e48256bb8f` (diff-verified identical to current origin/main), driven through a stub queue client that simulates PostgREST semantics (each request re-evaluates filter + `limit`/`offset` against the current claimed set):

- **Control (static set):** 1,500 claimed tasks → `queue_claims` returns all 1,500. Pagination itself works.
- **Live churn:** 1,500 claimed tasks; after page 1 is served, task 1 completes and leaves the claimed set (ordinary queue churn — claimed tasks finish throughout every janitor run). Page 2 is then requested at `offset=1000` against the shifted set. Result: `queue_claims` returns 1,499 IDs, and **task 1001 — still claimed — is missing** from the returned set.
- Queries issued (both cases): `tasks?select=id,queue,status,payload&queue=eq.repo-health-code-pilot&status=eq.claimed&limit=1000&offset=0`, then `...&offset=1000` — no `order=` parameter in either.

A missed claimed ID has a concrete consequence in this tool, unlike an ordinary listing: in `discover_targets`, `task_id in claimed` is the `live-claimed-task` protection, and in the `--apply` loop `target.task_id in fresh_claimed` is the stop check. A task skipped by both reads has neither.

## Why it matters

The janitor is a deleter whose every other safety input fails closed (stat failures protect the target, unreadable process tables abort the run, page-overflow aborts the run). This read silently returns a plausible, almost-complete set — no error, no short page, nothing in the log — while dropping the one protection that keeps a live build's target directory from being removed under it. The window needs >1,000 simultaneously claimed tasks, so it is latent today; it opens exactly when the queue is busiest, which is also when a wrongful deletion costs the most in-flight work.

## Acceptance criteria

- `queue_claims` pages in a way that a row leaving (or entering) the claimed set mid-read cannot cause a still-claimed row to be skipped — e.g. keyset pagination (`order=id.asc` plus `id=gt.<last-seen-id>`; task IDs are issued in increasing order, so newly claimed rows sort after the cursor), or another scheme whose stability argument is written down at the read site.
- The request explicitly orders the result (`order=id.asc` or equivalent); offset-only paging over the unordered live set is gone.
- A regression test in `infra/cargo-target-janitor/tests/test_cargo_target_janitor.py` models a live set: a stub client that removes an already-served row between pages, asserting every still-claimed ID is returned (the probe above is a ready-made shape); the existing #6618 tests (pages past 1000, cap boundary, never-ending pages fail closed) still pass.
- The apply-loop fresh re-check inherits the fix automatically because it calls the same function — no second, weaker copy is introduced.

## Dedup

Searched open and closed issues for `cargo-target-janitor`, `queue_claims`, `offset pagination`, and `keyset`: #6618 (closed) fixed the single-page truncation and is the static-set axis only; #6622 is the repo-wide pagination-contract design (cursor type / volume / completeness) and does not name ordering stability or mid-read churn for this read. No issue tracks the mutating-set skip.

title: atlas search worker: Cloudflare Worker + per-query Durable Object embedding/result cache over the shard fan-out (successor surface for #5755)
body:
## What Drew ordered (2026-11-06 22:48 CST, verbatim substance)

Build the cross-database search surface as a **Cloudflare Worker** that pulls **all databases** for search; for each search query it **stores a Durable Object**, **automatically inserts the query as an embedding**, and **caches the result — for now, indefinitely** (no TTL/expiry).

This is the successor surface for the Atlas shard consumer wiring in #5755 (slice 1 merged in #6661; rehomed as `fleet serve search` in #6674). It supersedes the 2026-11-05 "Ask-the-ledger" direction (Cloudflare AI Search / AutoRAG over R2 snapshots + a query/miss ledger DB): Drew replaced the managed-AI-Search design with this explicit Worker + Durable Object + embedding cache design. The AI Search proposal is **not** being built; this issue is the record of what replaced it.

## Architecture (v1)

**Components**

1. **Cloudflare Worker** (`pkgs/atlas-search/worker/`) — the only public edge. Inbound gate: a shared bearer secret checked in the Worker (constant-time compare); not public-open. (Cloudflare Access in front of the Worker hostname is a follow-up hardening note below.)
2. **Durable Object class `QueryCache`** — one DO per distinct query. DO name = `sha256(normalized_query || config_fingerprint)` where the fingerprint pins `{ceiling: "personal", model_rev, vec_table, trunc: 0, k}` so a cache entry can never be served across different effective ceilings or embedding spaces (the same rule the search service applies to job dedupe).
3. **The fleet search service** (`fleet serve search` / `atlas-search serve`, laptop loopback :18760) remains the fan-out engine: it discovers the shard set from the Turso Platform API (only `atlas-core-*` databases), reads each candidate's `atlas_manifest` self-description (tier, topic, part, expected chunks), enforces per-client tier ceilings, embeds the query with the one shared resident embedder, runs the parallel cosine scan + merge/rerank. **The Worker keeps no shard list of its own** — new databases join the fan-out by existing in the Turso org with the `atlas-core-` prefix and a manifest; the Worker inherits the set through the service.
4. **Reachability**: the service is exposed to the Worker through the existing `amd-6-pm-stack` Cloudflare Tunnel as `atlas-search.security.cab` → `localhost:18760`, fronted by a Cloudflare Access application whose only policy is a **service token** the Worker presents (`CF-Access-Client-Id`/`CF-Access-Client-Secret`). The tunnel hostname without the service token is rejected by Access before it reaches the laptop.

**Miss path** (first time a query is seen)

1. Worker normalizes the query, computes the DO key, asks the DO for its entry → miss.
2. Worker calls the service's new **`POST /v1/embed`** (added by this work to both `server.rs` copies, parity-guarded): the service's shared embedder returns the production query vector. The Worker stores `{query, normalized_query, embedding, model, model_rev, dims, created_at}` in the DO **first** — the DO is born holding the query's embedding, per Drew's spec, even if the search below then fails.
3. Worker calls `POST /v1/search` (sync one-shot) with the dedicated **`cf-worker` service client** (see boundary below) → merged, reranked results.
4. Worker stores `{result, searched_at, fanout_ms, embed_ms}` in the DO and returns the result with `cache: "miss"` and the timings.

**Hit path**

- The DO returns the stored result verbatim; the fleet service is never contacted. Response carries `cache: "hit"`, the original `searched_at`, and a `hit_count` the DO increments. This is the proof surface: a hit must be byte-identical to the miss response's result and must not move any counter on the service side.

**Retention**

- **Indefinite.** No TTL, no eviction in v1 — Drew's "for now". DO storage is the ledger of every query ever asked through this surface. A future eviction policy (size/LRU) is a deliberate follow-up (filed separately), not a v1 behavior.

## Embedding source — decision and why

**The fleet embedder** (the service's resident ONNX session): model `Snowflake/snowflake-arctic-embed-m-v2.0` pinned at rev `95c2741480856aa9666782eb4afe11959938017f`, query prompt `"query: "`, production vector table `vec_snowflake_m_v2_768_f32` — **768 dimensions**, full width (trunc = 0).

**Workers AI is rejected**: its 384-dim `@cf/baai/bge-small-en-v1.5` lives in a different embedding space (and a different width). Cosine similarity across embedding spaces is meaningless; a Worker-side embedding that cannot be compared against the corpus vectors would silently corrupt every ranking. Any edge embedding must reproduce the corpus's exact space, and the only artifact that does that today is the pinned Snowflake session in the fleet service.

Correction to older notes: several records describe the corpus as "384-dim Snowflake". Production is **768-dim** (`vec_snowflake_m_v2_768_f32` in the live service config; 384 was a Matryoshka truncation option from the Python era, never the production width).

## Secret-tier boundary

- The Worker authenticates to the search service as a dedicated client, **`cf-worker`, with `ceiling_cap: "personal"`** — the service mechanically caps it to the Public + Internal tiers. The Secret tier is unreachable through this client no matter what the Worker asks for.
- The Worker holds **no Turso credentials** and never receives secret-tier shard data, so nothing secret can enter a Durable Object — neither chunk content nor embeddings of secret chunks.
- The `drew-cli` client (`secret-bearing` cap) stays laptop-local and is not used by anything in this build. Secret-tier search remains a laptop-side-only operation, exactly as today.

## What v1 deliberately leaves out

- **Filters / FTS interplay** — the fan-out runs the service's default hybrid search; classification/date filters and the FTS answer remain #6665.
- **Hydration (`--expand`)** — results are the service's standard envelope; expansion remains #6664.
- **Serve-mode snapshot-id integration** — remains #6666.
- **Eviction policy** for the indefinite cache — follow-up issue (Drew: "for now").
- **Access in front of the Worker hostname itself** — v1 gate is the in-Worker bearer check; recorded as a hardening follow-up.
- The live proof in this issue advances #6662 only for the `personal` ceiling path through the Worker; #6662 stays open for its remaining parity scope.

## Open questions (recorded, proceeded on defaults)

- Worker hostname: default `atlas-search` on the account's `workers.dev` subdomain; a custom domain can be bound later without changing the design.
- Whether the DO should also store the FTS match expression / branch pools for debugging: default no — result + embedding + provenance only.

## Proof required (acceptance)

- Deployed Worker + DO; a real query run twice: first response `cache: "miss"` with fan-out executed (service-side evidence), DO created holding a 768-dim embedding; second response `cache: "hit"`, byte-identical result, served from the DO with no service contact; timings for both; DO state read back through the Worker's gated inspect endpoint.

body:
## Problem

PR #6775 (fix for #4210) makes an `issues` `deleted` event remove the item's `pmp_items` row via the new `deleteItem`. Codex review on that PR (finding 4500146162, P2) identified the remaining hole, out of #4210's filed scope:

There is no item-level deletion marker. If an older, previously unprocessed `issues` or `issue_comment` delivery arrives after the deletion, `upsertItem` unconditionally inserts the absent item again (`pm-stack/projector/src/store.ts`), and `applyComment` upserts the containing issue before processing the comment (`pm-stack/projector/src/projector.ts`). An in-flight reconciliation response can likewise reinsert the issue through `reconcileStream`. The deleted issue reappears in `/items`; the comment tombstones retained by #6775's fix do not protect the containing item.

GitHub issue numbers are never reused within a repo, so a durable marker keyed by item ref cannot block a legitimate future item.

## Acceptance criteria

- Deleting an item persists a deletion marker (ref + deletion source timestamp) that survives the row's removal.
- Webhook upsert paths (`issues`, `issue_comment`, `pull_request_review(_comment)`, `push`-adjacent item writes) and `reconcileStream` refuse to recreate an item whose ref carries a deletion marker with a source timestamp >= the incoming event's — i.e. deletions are absorbing for stale replays, mirroring the comment-tombstone contract in `upsertComment`.
- A test at projector level (fake store) and store level: opened → deleted → stale opened/comment replay leaves the item absent; a genuinely newer event is handled per the marker rule decided in implementation and covered by a test.
- Existing projector suite stays green (`bun test` in pm-stack/projector).

## Origin

Filed by repo-worker-code lane code-y from PR #6775's Codex review (finding 4500146162), dispositioned there as: valid, but a new mechanism beyond #4210's acceptance criteria — tracked here instead of expanding that PR.

title: id(web/assets): is_hashed_filename treats any 8+ lowercase dotted segment as a content hash — ordinary names (app.development.js, styles.darkmode.css) get a one-year immutable Cache-Control at a stable URL

labels.name: effort/s

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/id/src/web/assets.rs`: `static_handler` decides an asset's cache lifetime with `is_hashed_filename` (assets.rs:57, fn at assets.rs:85-101). Any file whose stem's last dot-segment is 8+ lowercase-alphanumeric characters is treated as content-hashed and served with:

```
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
```

(assets.rs:62-64) instead of `no-cache` (assets.rs:66-68).

That segment does not have to be a hash. Ordinary dotted names — where the segment is a word, not a bundler hash — match the rule exactly, so a non-addressed asset gets a one-year immutable cache lifetime at a stable URL. If that asset is ever rebuilt or replaced in place, browsers that fetched it keep serving the stale copy for a year; `immutable` also tells them not to revalidate on reload.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe at origin/main `b16c883b2f1163502981bcdd91a6d238286e0704`, probe crate `~/git/fleet/probe-hashed-filename` running `is_hashed_filename` verbatim from `pkgs/id/src/web/assets.rs:85-101`:

| name | is_hashed | desired |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `main.bjbjbv7v.js` (module test control) | true | true |
| `styles.99e0273f.css` (module test control) | true | true |
| `app.development.js` | **true** | false |
| `styles.darkmode.css` | **true** | false |
| `vendor.production.js` | **true** | false |
| `editor.settings.js` | **true** | false |
| `main.js` (control) | false | false |

4/4 ordinary dotted names are false positives. The in-tree tests (assets.rs:152-203) cover hash-shaped positives and plain negatives (`main.js`, `manifest.json`, short segments, uppercase/hyphen/underscore segments) but no dotted word segment of 8+ lowercase letters, so the false-positive class is untested.

## Why the fix needs a decision, not a one-liner

The obvious tightening — require a digit in the segment — breaks a documented real case: Bun's base36 hash in the module's own test, `main.bjbjbv7v.js`, is letters-only. Hex hashes can also be letters-only (`deadbeef`). So "word vs hash" cannot be separated by charset alone; the fix has to choose a rule the build actually guarantees, e.g.:

- match the bundlers' exact hash lengths/alphabets as configured for `web/dist`, or
- treat only segments the build pipeline actually emits as hashes (a naming contract recorded next to the bundler config), or
- drop the heuristic and default everything to `no-cache` unless the name matches the strictest documented hash shape.

`gh search issues` (all states) for "cache-control immutable assets" and "is_hashed_filename" returned no issues on 2026-11-07. No open or closed issue covers this classifier.

body:
Follow-up filed by the #6670 Phase 4 closing inventory (disposition (d) of #6669's validated-reply contract). Not fixed inside the audit, per #6670's acceptance rule.

## Finding

`WorldClient::record_pages` (`pkgs/id/src/world_net.rs:1806` at main `81bdda48`) reads the pagination cursor as `let next_after = reply["next_after"].as_str();` and treats `None` as "final page" (`match next_after { Some(next) => continue, None => return Ok(pages) }` at :1836-1839). A **present-but-mistyped** `next_after` (number, object, bool) therefore reads exactly like a legitimately absent one, and the listing returns as complete when the host may have had more pages — a fabricated-completeness shape under #6669 rules 2 and 4 (optional means absent-or-null, never mistyped; a listing is complete or it errors).

The sibling code in the same file already implements the strict shape: `parse_admin_history_cursor` (`world_net.rs:1905-1925`) dispositions `next_after` as absent → error (required there), `null` → `None`, string → `Some`, anything else → bail. The records path is the inconsistent one.

Scope note: #6622 owns the pagination *cursor contract* (advance/last-key checks, which `record_pages` already performs at :1807-1833). This issue is only the cursor's *field shape* at extraction, which is #6669's contract. If #6622's owners judge the absent-vs-null semantics differently for this reply, record that here and close with the reason.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `record_pages` dispositions `next_after` in the `parse_admin_history_cursor` shape: missing/null → final page only if that is the wire contract for the `records` reply (name which, with the `ServerFrame` evidence), string → cursor, any other type → malformed-reply error naming `next_after`.
- [ ] A rogue-host test in the existing `rogue_host`/`rogue_records` harness (`world_net.rs:2762`/`2798`): a page whose `next_after` is a number is refused, not silently treated as the last page.

Oracle: `parse_admin_history_cursor` in the same file — one cursor-shape rule for both listing paths.

body:
Follow-up filed by the #6670 Phase 4 closing inventory (disposition (a) of #6669's validated-reply contract). Not fixed inside the audit, per #6670's acceptance rule.

## Finding

`WorldClient::set_execution_profile` (`pkgs/id/src/world_net.rs:1110-1134` at main `81bdda48`) checks only `reply["type"] != "execution_profile"` and then returns the whole frame (`Ok(reply)` at :1133). No field of the frame is extracted or validated. This is the remaining leg of #6635: the getter `execution_profile()` was fixed to extract `update.requested` with a "host returned a malformed execution profile" refusal (:1143-1180), but the setter still accepts any `execution_profile`-tagged frame — including one with no `update` at all — as success.

Consumers trust that success:
- `pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs:358-365` — the returned frame is pretty-printed to the operator as the result of the change.
- `pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs:1272` — manifest apply's `SetProfile` step discards the frame after `?`, so a profile-less success frame counts the step applied.

## Fix shape (precedent in the same file)

Validate-then-return, exactly as `parse_caps_ceiling_reply` does for the ceiling frame (`world_net.rs:941-956`): decode/require the constituting field at extraction, return the frame unchanged on success. Here: require `update.requested` to be present and decode as `crate::world_limits::WorldExecutionProfile` (the same extraction `execution_profile()` performs), bail "host returned a malformed execution profile" otherwise. Successful returns stay byte-identical; no caller changes shape.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A scripted/rogue-host or parser test: an `execution_profile` reply with missing or mistyped `update.requested` is refused with the malformed-profile error; a well-formed reply returns the frame unchanged.
- [ ] Existing profile tests keep passing (the old-report/`#[serde(default)]` controls named in #6669's risks are unaffected — this is the reply seam, not the profile struct).

Oracle: the #6635 getter extraction in the same file — setter and getter must agree on what a valid `execution_profile` frame is.

body:
# repo-universe(check_issues): field-level wrong shape passes the #6652 entry guards — a fieldless fetched issue becomes a phantom "None" state entry, a string `number` crashes the run, and a field-missing persisted entry re-crashes daily

## Problem

`scripts/fleet/repo-universe/check_issues.py` was hardened in #6652 at the *entry* level: a fetched item must be a JSON object, a persisted per-repo entry must be an object whose issue values are objects. Neither guard looks *inside* an object at its fields, so valid-JSON entries with missing or wrong-typed fields still break the checker's header contract ("a failed fetch is an explicit ERROR line in the report … a failure never masquerades as an empty repository") — silently, or as a whole-run crash.

Sites (all on current main `7e903f6a75`, origin/main):

- `check_issues.py:109-124` — `normalize_issue` projects with `{field: raw.get(field) for field in ISSUE_FIELDS}` and validates nothing about the values. A dict entry `{}` (or one missing any field, or with wrong-typed fields) normalizes to `{number: None, state: None, title: None, updated_at: None, html_url: None}` instead of raising the `FetchError` a non-object entry now raises.
- Consequences on the fetch side: the phantom issue is persisted in state under the key `"None"` (`diff_repo`, `check_issues.py:186`, keys state by `str(i["number"])`); several fieldless entries collapse into that one key; a diff report prints the phantom verbatim as `- new: #None None (None)`; a `number` given as a string (`"5"`) or a list (`[1]`) is equally accepted (state key `"[1]"`), and a string number that lands in the same report group as integer numbers crashes `sorted(group, key=lambda i: i["number"])` (`check_issues.py:278`) with `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'` — outside the `FetchError` handler in `run_check`, so the whole run dies with no report and no state write.
- `check_issues.py:211-221` — `_valid_prior_entry` checks only that each persisted issue value `isinstance(v, dict)`. A field-missing dict (e.g. `"2": {}` from a partial hand edit or a torn-but-parseable write) passes, then `diff_repo` subscripts it — `old["state"]` at `check_issues.py:198` raises `KeyError: 'state'`. Because `main` writes state only after `run_check` returns, the poisoned entry re-crashes every daily timer run until a human repairs `state.json` by hand — the exact self-perpetuating failure #6652 set out to end, one level down (fields, not entries).

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ `7e903f6a75` == origin/main)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-check-issues-fields` on the laptop, importing the real `check_issues` module from origin/main and driving `run_check` through the real `fetch_issues_fixture` path (controls — well-formed baseline, then a closed-diff — both pass clean):

- Fixture entry `[{}]` on a baseline run: **no error**; state records one phantom issue `{'None': {'number': None, 'state': None, 'title': None, 'updated_at': None, 'html_url': None}}` and the report claims "1 issues recorded (0 open, 0 closed)".
- The same `[{}]` on a diff run: report line `- new: #None None (None)`.
- Fixture entries with `number: "5"` (string) plus a well-formed `number: 2` issue, both new on a diff run: `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'` at `check_issues.py:278` — whole run crashes.
- `normalize_issue({"number": [1], ...})` is accepted; the issue is persisted under state key `"[1]"`.
- Persisted state `{"a/b": {"issues": {"2": {}}}}`: `_valid_prior_entry` returns `True`, then `run_check` crashes with `KeyError: 'state'` at `check_issues.py:198` (`diff_repo`).

## Why it matters

This checker is the daily, scheduled correctness floor for the repo-universe tracker (#1651): it notices new/closed issues across every watched repo. A field-level malformed item from the API or a fixture — or one field-missing entry in its own persisted state — either fabricates a phantom issue that pollutes every later diff, prints nonsense into the dated report, or silences the whole checker with a traceback in a timer log, indefinitely in the persisted-state case.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `normalize_issue` validates the projected fields (at minimum: `number` is an `int` — not a bool, string, or list; `state`/`title`/`updated_at`/`html_url` are strings or explicitly handled when absent) and raises `FetchError` for a missing/wrong-typed field, so both fetch paths report it as that repo's ERROR line with other repos still checked and that repo's state untouched.
- [ ] `_valid_prior_entry` (or `diff_repo`) applies the same field-level rule to persisted issue entries: a field-missing or wrong-typed persisted issue entry is handled as the malformed-state per-repo error #6652 established — never a `KeyError`/`TypeError` traceback.
- [ ] No phantom state: a run can never persist an issue under a `"None"` / `"[1]"`-style key, and no report line can render `#None None (None)`.
- [ ] Valid behaviour is unchanged: baselining, new/closed/reopened/changed deltas, failed-fetch state preservation, and report/state writing work exactly as before on well-formed inputs (in-tree `test_check_issues.py` still passes).
- [ ] Regression tests in `test_check_issues.py` cover at least: fixture entry `{}`, fixture entry with a string `number` alongside an integer-numbered issue, and a persisted issue entry `{}` — each fails on current code as shown above and passes after the fix.

Dedup: residual of closed #6652, whose acceptance covered only entry-level shape (non-object fetch items, non-object persisted entries) — field-level shape inside object entries was neither tested nor guarded; its fix is the reason the entry-level guards exist to be passed. Distinct from #6716 (generate.py entry shape, closed/fixed), #6612 (generate.py offline flag), and the github-backup shape issues (different system, different files). Title/keyword searches for `check_issues` + shape/field return no covering issue.

body:
You are a code-review agent running as a dispatched session in this
repository. Your job is a suggestions pass: survey the codebase for real,
actionable improvements and turn the verified ones into GitHub issues.

## Dispatch context — read this first

- You are running in this repository's LAPTOP CHECKOUT (the repo's primary
  checkout on the owner's laptop). Work there; do not clone the repo
  elsewhere.
- A tracking issue and a queue task were ALREADY created for this run by
  the dispatcher, and this session is already claimed against them. Do
  NOT create another tracking issue for this run, and do not dispatch
  further tasks.
- There is NO plan-approval step. Proceed directly; do not stop to ask
  for approval of a plan.

## What to review

Survey the codebase across these five areas:

- **Cleanup** — dead code, duplicated logic, obsolete files or config,
  leftover scaffolding.
- **Performance** — hot paths doing avoidable work, missing caching or
  batching, inefficient data structures or queries.
- **Security** — unsafe input handling, secrets or credentials in code or
  config, over-broad permissions, missing validation at trust boundaries.
- **Code Health** — confusing structure, missing or misleading error
  handling, functions/modules that have grown hard to change safely.
- **Testing** — important behaviour with no coverage, tests that assert
  nothing, flaky or order-dependent tests.

## Verify before you file — no speculative filings

Every candidate finding MUST be verified against the actual code before
it becomes an issue:

- Read the code at the location you cite. Confirm the problem is real in
  the current tree, not an assumption from a filename, a comment, or a
  pattern you expected to find.
- Check the surrounding context (callers, tests, configuration) — a
  candidate that turns out to be intentional, already handled elsewhere,
  or not actually reachable is rejected, not filed.
- Search the repo's OPEN issues before filing. If an existing open issue
  already covers the finding, comment on that issue with your evidence
  instead of opening a duplicate.

## Filing

- Per real, verified finding, file ONE issue in this repo with
  `gh issue create` from the laptop checkout. Each issue must include:
  - the canonical component label for its area; use `app/pm-stack` for
    PM-stack / aggregator issues in this repo. `app/aggregator` is a legacy
    alias and must not be used for new filings.
  - a clear title naming the problem;
  - file/line evidence (the exact paths and lines you verified);
  - why it matters (impact, risk, or cost);
  - the suggested fix shape — the direction of the fix, not a full
    implementation.
- CAP: at most **5 filings per pass** (new issues plus evidence comments
  on existing issues). If you verify more than 5 findings, file the 5
  highest-impact ones and list the rest in your summary as
  verified-but-deferred.
- Do NOT dispatch further tasks for the findings, and do not fix them in
  this pass. The issues are the record; the fleet's normal lanes pick
  work up from them.

## Finish

End with a short summary — as your session output, and as a comment on
this run's tracking issue if you can identify it — covering:

- **Filed** — each issue you opened or commented on, with its number and
  one line on the finding.
- **Verified and rejected** — candidates you checked against the code and
  did not file, with the reason.
- **Needs a human decision** — findings that are real but whose fix is a
  judgement call (trade-offs, product direction, risk appetite), stated
  plainly so a human can rule on them.

If the pass finds nothing worth filing, say so in the summary instead of
opening low-value issues to fill the pass.

title: repo-universe(generate): wrong-shape enumeration entries crash the whole generator — a non-object entry or a dict without full_name aborts regeneration with a bare TypeError/KeyError

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/repo-universe
labels.description: scripts/fleet/repo-universe generator + issue checker

body:
## Problem

`scripts/fleet/repo-universe/generate.py` (repo-universe piece 1, #1650) has no wrong-shape guard on the enumeration captures it decodes — the exact defect family that #6652 fixed in its sibling `check_issues.py`, where the contract is: valid JSON with the wrong shape must surface as a named, per-item error, never as a bare `TypeError`/`KeyError` that aborts the whole run.

`decode_pages` (generate.py:79-100) flattens every decoded document into a list of entries without checking their shape, and both consumers index the entries blindly:

- `merge_repos` (generate.py:117): `merged.setdefault(repo["full_name"], repo)`
- `build` (generate.py:236): `gh[repo["full_name"]] = repo`

So one bad entry in any of the three captures (org, forks-org, user) kills the entire regeneration with a traceback and no artifact: a non-object entry in a page array (string, number, `null`), an object page that is not a repo (e.g. an API error object `{"message": "API rate limit exceeded"}` saved into a capture), or a repo object missing `full_name`.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop main e632ea0967)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-repo-universe-gen/probe.py` (on the laptop) imports the real `generate.py` and feeds `decode_pages` → `merge_repos` → `build`:

| Input | Result |
|---|---|
| `[{"full_name": "a/b", "fork": false}, "oops"]` | CRASH `TypeError: string indices must be integers` |
| `[{"full_name": "a/b", ...}] {"message": "API rate limit exceeded"}` | CRASH `KeyError: 'full_name'` |
| `[{"name": "b", "fork": false}]` | CRASH `KeyError: 'full_name'` |
| `[{"full_name": "a/b", ...}, null]` | CRASH `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable` |
| well-formed control | OK, artifact lists `a/b` |

`test_generate.py` has no wrong-shape case for enumeration entries (its only "wrong" test is the live-mode account guard).

## Why it matters

The generator is the piece that produces `doc/fleet/repo-universe.yaml`, the inventory the issue checker (#1651) and tracker (#1511) consume. The offline path exists so a regeneration can be run from captures; a single malformed capture entry — a hand-saved `gh` error page, a truncated-then-repaired capture, a schema drift in one repo object — currently aborts the whole run opaquely, with no indication of which capture or entry is at fault. #6612 already established the house rule for this tool: a missing/emptied source must fail loudly and by name, never silently or opaquely. The checker side of the same tool got the per-item shape guard in #6652; the generator side was left out.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A non-object entry, or an object entry without a string `full_name`, in any enumeration capture makes the run fail with a clear error naming the capture source and the offending entry (index or repr) — no bare `TypeError`/`KeyError` traceback.
- [ ] `build` is equally safe when reached with entries that did not pass through `merge_repos` (it re-indexes `repo["full_name"]` at generate.py:236).
- [ ] Well-formed captures (single page, multi-page concatenated, org+forks+user merge) regenerate byte-identically to today (idempotence preserved).
- [ ] New cases in `test_generate.py` cover: non-dict entry in a page array, dict page without `full_name`, and `null` entry.

title: id(tag_claims): compacted_claims diverges from live_claims on a cyclic parents graph — the kept/removed outcome flips with HashMap iteration order

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

`compacted_claims` (the production fold behind the default tag view) does **not** always agree with the reference fold `live_claims` — on a cyclic `parents` graph it keeps a claim the reference removes, and which answer it gives flips with `HashMap` iteration order, so the same input yields different live-claim sets in different processes.

The module documents the equivalence as unconditional:

- `pkgs/id/src/tag_claims.rs:19-24` — "Two folds give the live claims. [`live_claims`] walks the causal past of each clear. It is the reference. [`compacted_claims`] makes one pass over the parent links … Both give the same result (P5.3, #184)."
- `pkgs/id/src/tag_claims.rs:243-247` (`compacted_claims` docs) — "The result is the same as [`live_claims`] …"

No acyclicity precondition is stated or checked anywhere.

## Verified reproduction (this run, origin/main `8e20f10f93`; `tag_claims.rs` sha256 `a1590882…`)

Probe on the laptop at `~/git/fleet/probe-tagfold-cycle` — the real `tag_claims.rs` copied verbatim (byte-identical sha256 to origin/main), plus a minimal `p2panda_core::Hash` shim covering only the API the file uses:

- Input: claim `Set` event 1; `Clear` event 2 naming claim 1; parents graph `1 -> [2]`, `2 -> [1]` (a 2-cycle).
- `live_claims` (the reference): the clear's causal past is the transitive closure (`causal_past`, `tag_claims.rs:169-181`), which contains claim 1 through the cycle → the claim is removed. Result: **0 claims, every run**.
- `compacted_claims`: acyclic control (`2 -> [1]`, `1 -> []`) agrees (0 claims). On the 2-cycle, across 12 fresh processes it **kept the claim in 5 processes (64/64 calls each) and removed it in 7** — the outcome is decided by the iteration order of `parents.keys()`.

## Mechanism

`compacted_claims` folds depth-first from each root in `parents.keys()` order (`tag_claims.rs:255`). The `open` set (`tag_claims.rs:266-269`) silently drops a back-edge into an ancestor that is still being folded. Whichever of the set/clear pair folds *second* decides the result:

- Clear folds first: its `past` is built only from already-folded parents (`tag_claims.rs:281-285`), the set is not in any folded parent's set yet, so the clear removes nothing (`tag_claims.rs:287-289`); the set then inserts itself (`tag_claims.rs:290-292`) and survives.
- Set folds first: the clear sees it and removes it.

`live_claims` has no such order dependence because it computes each clear's past as a full transitive closure.

## Reachability, stated honestly

From today's store this input does not arise: an event's ID is `Hash::digest` of its whole signed bytes (`pkgs/id/src/chain.rs:423`), and its parents are named inside those bytes, so a parents cycle would require a BLAKE3 hash cycle. The production caller is `EventStore::tag_claims` → `compacted_claims` (`pkgs/id/src/event_store/claims.rs:87`), fed by stored events and fork proof headers.

That makes this a **contract/robustness defect, not a live exploit**: the two folds are public pure functions whose documented equivalence is false as stated, the production fold's answer on out-of-contract input is nondeterministic (process-to-process), and nothing detects the out-of-contract input. #4359 already hardened these exact folds against adversarial duplicate-ID inputs for the same reason — the folds are expected to be robust on adversarial `applied`/`parents` values, not only on honest-store ones. The existing equivalence proptest (`pkgs/id/tests/tag_claims.rs:484-518`, `test_the_compacted_fold_agrees_with_the_causal_walk`) cannot find this: its generator builds histories from real signed events, whose parents graphs are DAGs by construction.

## Why it matters

- The default tag view (`tag_claims()` / `tag_index()`) is only as trustworthy as the fold-equivalence contract; a silent, nondeterministic divergence class undermines the P5.3 design claim the rest of Phase 5 builds on (e.g. the persisted incremental index, #183, will bake in whichever answer the fold gives).
- Per the repo's testing doctrine, `live_claims` is a ready-made oracle: the invariant "both folds agree" should be property-tested over generated graphs — including cycles, self-loops, and duplicate IDs — not only over well-formed causal histories.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A property test compares `compacted_claims` against the `live_claims` oracle over generated `parents` graphs that include cycles and self-loops (plus the duplicate-ID shapes from #4359), and either passes or is the failing test this fix closes.
- [ ] `compacted_claims` gives the same result as `live_claims` on the 2-cycle repro above (set 1, clear 2 naming 1, parents `1 -> [2]`, `2 -> [1]` → claim removed), deterministically across repeated runs/processes.
- [ ] The fix shape is chosen explicitly and documented in `tag_claims.rs`: e.g. detect a cycle during the walk (the `open` back-edge case) and fall back to the reference computation for the affected component, fold to a fixpoint, or refuse/document the precondition *and* enforce it at the `EventStore::tag_claims` boundary — silence is not an option.
- [ ] All existing `tag_claims` tests (unit + the `tests/tag_claims.rs` proptests) still pass.

Related: #4359 (duplicate-ID divergence, fixed), #184 (P5.3), #183 (persisted incremental tag index).

```
thread 'world_net::tests::execution_profile_can_be_queried_and_updated_over_iroh' panicked at src/world_net.rs:2615:9:
assertion failed: res.get("wasm_fuel").is_some() || res.get("total_memory_bytes").is_some()
test result: FAILED. 0 passed; 1 failed; 2314 filtered out
```

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop)

- Control: a pristine worktree at `origin/main` (0b8afc92fc, no local changes) running only this test → same failure, same assertion (world_net.rs:2615 on main; :2623 in a branch that adds lines above it).
- Context: the failure surfaced while regression-checking PR #6682 (issue #6647, `read_worlds_reply` default validation). That PR's diff does not touch execution-profile code, and the other 22 `world_net` lib tests passed in the same run — this failure is pre-existing on main, not a regression from #6682.
- The assertion expects the queried execution-profile result to carry at least one of `wasm_fuel` / `total_memory_bytes` after an update round-trip over iroh; on main it carries neither.

## Why it matters

A red lib test on main trains every worker to ignore `world_net` test results — exactly how real regressions in this file (e.g. #6647's silent-default class) hide. ## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] If the cause is reply-shape parsing, the fix follows the validated-reply direction of #6669 rather than another per-field patch, or names why it is distinct.

title: fleet(proxy ssh): recovery SSH paths use literal ~ (passwd home) instead of Fleet's HOME — known-hosts, identity and ControlPath resolve to the wrong directory

labels.name: kind/bug
