labels.name: app/fleet
labels.description: pkgs/fleet multicall binary + platform crates

body:
## Finding (from PR review)

`fleet proxy ssh` (the recovery verb added by PR #6403) builds its known-hosts, identity, and ControlPath arguments from literal `~` paths, which OpenSSH expands from the account database home (`getpwuid()` / `pw_dir`), not from Fleet's `$HOME`-based home — so when the two differ, recovery authentication / strict host-key checking fails and the shared control socket is missed.

Reviewer **chatgpt-codex-connector[bot]** (Codex, P2) on PR #6403, 2026-11-06T00:49:20Z:
https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/6403#discussion_r4487818003

> "Resolve recovery SSH paths from Fleet's HOME — When `$HOME` differs from the account database home, these literal `~` paths select the wrong known-hosts and identity files: OpenSSH's tilde expansion implementation uses `getpwuid()` and `pw_dir`, not `$HOME`. This causes recovery authentication or strict host-key checking to fail even when the required files exist under Fleet's home directory, and the similarly constructed ControlPath misses its shared socket. Fleet configuration already resolves from `$HOME` (`fleet-config/src/lib.rs:225-226`), and the existing SSH integration explicitly constructs these paths from `$HOME` (`fleet-search/src/client.rs:182-197`). Resolve all three paths consistently before constructing the SSH arguments."

Source PR: #6403 `feat(fleet): add proxy ssh recovery verb` (open; parent design issue #5697 does not cover this defect — dedupe searched by PR number, "known_hosts_laptop", "proxy ssh", and HOME/tilde keywords: no existing issue covers it).

## No-response evidence

- The comment is now over 24 hours old (grace period for open PRs passed; first flagged by pr-comment-review 2026-11-06 15:54 CST, rechecked this run).
- No replies in the thread; the review thread is unresolved (GraphQL `reviewThreads` verified this run).
- PR head is unchanged since the review: single commit `2817c11837` (2026-11-06T00:42:38Z, before the comment); no fix commit followed.

## Still-live evidence (verified on PR head `2817c11837` this run)

`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet/src/main.rs` on the PR head, fresh `gh api` raw read — all three literal tilde paths present verbatim in `build_proxy_ssh_argv`:
- Line 702: `"UserKnownHostsFile=~/.ssh/known_hosts_laptop"`
- Line 706: `"~/.ssh/id_ed25519"` (the `-i` identity argument)
- Line 718: `"ControlPath=~/.ssh/cm-%r@%h:%p"`

The argv-builder tests on the same head (lines ~1066-1081) assert these literal `~` strings, so the current tests pin the defective behavior.

## Acceptance criteria

- All three paths (known-hosts file, identity file, ControlPath) are resolved from Fleet's home (the same `$HOME`-based resolution `fleet-config` uses) before the SSH arguments are constructed — no literal `~` is passed to OpenSSH for these.
- Tests updated/added: argv built with a Fleet home that differs from the passwd home contains the Fleet-home absolute paths for all three.
- Or: resolve this issue by a documented decision explaining why passwd-home expansion is intentional for the recovery path.

title: fleet(proxy ssh): clustered SSH options are not parsed — operand-bearing options inside flag clusters (and -P) break the recovery invocation

body:
## Finding (from PR review)

`fleet proxy ssh` argument splitting does not parse operand-bearing SSH options inside flag clusters, and omits at least one operand-bearing option (`-P`), so valid invocations are broken.

Reviewer **chatgpt-codex-connector[bot]** (Codex, P2) on PR #6403, 2026-11-06T00:49:20Z:
https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/6403#discussion_r4487818000

> "Parse operand-bearing SSH options inside flag clusters — For valid invocations such as `fleet proxy ssh -- -vL 127.0.0.1:2222:localhost:22`, the exact-string lookup does not recognize that `-vL` requires an operand. It consequently inserts `user@100.99.113.103` immediately after `-vL`, where OpenSSH consumes it as the forwarding specification and exits with `Bad local forwarding specification`. The table also omits `-P tag`, documented in the OpenSSH manual, causing another operand-boundary error. Parse clustered option characters and account for all operand-bearing options before separating the remote command."

Source PR: #6403 `feat(fleet): add proxy ssh recovery verb` (open; parent design issue #5697 does not cover this defect — dedupe searched by PR number, `split_ssh_options`, "operand-bearing", "proxy ssh", "flag cluster": no existing issue covers it).

## No-response evidence

- The comment is now over 24 hours old (grace period for open PRs passed; first flagged by pr-comment-review 2026-11-06 15:54 CST, rechecked this run).
- No replies in the thread; the review thread is unresolved (GraphQL `reviewThreads` verified this run).
- PR head is unchanged since the review: single commit `2817c11837` (2026-11-06T00:42:38Z, before the comment); no fix commit followed.

## Still-live evidence (verified on PR head `2817c11837` this run)

`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet/src/main.rs` on the PR head, fresh `gh api` raw read:
- Line 638: `fn split_ssh_options_and_command(...)`; line 639-642: `OPTIONS_WITH_OPERANDS` table contains `-B -b -c -D -E -e -F -I -i -J -L -l -m -O -o -p -Q -R -S -W -w` — no `-P`.
- Line 655: `if OPTIONS_WITH_OPERANDS.contains(&arg.as_str())` — exact-string match only; a clustered argument such as `-vL` never matches, so its operand is treated as the start of the remote command and the fixed destination is inserted in the operand's place.

## Acceptance criteria

- Clustered SSH options are parsed character-by-character: an operand-bearing character inside a cluster consumes the rest of the cluster or the next argument as its operand, and the destination is inserted only after the full option prefix.
- `-P` (and any other documented operand-bearing ssh options missing from the table) are accounted for.
- Tests cover at least: `-vL <spec>` clustered forwarding, `-P <tag>`, a separated-operand option (existing behavior), and a plain remote command with no options.
- Or: resolve this issue by a documented decision explaining why clustered forms are intentionally unsupported, with the rejection made explicit (a clear error instead of a malformed ssh invocation).

title: id(access): load_allowed_nodes reads a present-but-unreadable .iroh-allowed as an empty allowlist — no diagnostic, allowed writers silently dropped

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

`id serve`'s write-access allowlist file `.iroh-allowed` is loaded with every read error collapsed to an empty list. A file that exists but cannot be read as UTF-8 text — saved as UTF-16 by a text editor, containing non-UTF-8 bytes, replaced by a directory, or unreadable — silently contributes **zero** writers, exactly as if the file were missing (the one case that is supposed to be empty). Nothing is logged, so the operator's allowed peers are denied writes (`put`/`delete`/blob push) with no diagnostic pointing at the file, while `id serve` startup only prints a writer *count* that mixes the file's entries with the two always-trusted keys and any `--allow-node` flags.

This is inconsistent with the same module's per-line handling: an invalid node ID inside a readable file is warned about by name (`access.rs:116`), but a wholly unreadable file gets no warning at all.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ 207e61203b)

- `pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/access.rs:124-128` — `load_allowed_nodes` is `read_to_string(...).map(parse).unwrap_or_default()`: every `io::Error` kind (NotFound, InvalidData from non-UTF-8, IsADirectory, PermissionDenied) becomes the same empty `Vec`. The function returns no `Result` and logs nothing on this path.
- `pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/access.rs:109-121` — `parse_allowed_nodes` warns per invalid line (`warn!("ignoring invalid node id {l:?} in allow list: {e}")`), so the module's own convention is to name allowlist problems, not swallow them.
- `pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:707` — the only production caller: `writers.extend(load_allowed_nodes(Path::new(".")))` inside `build_access_policy` (serve runs with the data directory as CWD, per `pkgs/id/src/main.rs:219`). `serve.rs:1704-1711` then prints only `"{n} node(s) may write"`.
- Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-allowed-nodes`, a crate depending on the real `id-core` by path, run against main @ 207e61203b): `load_allowed_nodes` returned 0 writers for **every** case — missing file (by design), `.iroh-allowed` as a directory, UTF-16LE content with BOM (what a Windows editor saves), and non-UTF-8 garbage bytes — with no panic and no error surface distinguishing the broken cases from the missing/empty ones.
- Existing tests (`access.rs:226-236`) cover only the missing-file and happy-path cases; no test pins behavior for a present-but-unreadable file.

## Why it matters

The allowlist is the mechanism that lets an operator's other machines write to a store. Its failure mode is fail-closed but invisible: sync/push from an allowed peer is refused as if it had never been listed, and the one artefact that would explain it — the file the operator wrote — is never named in any log. A UTF-16 save is a realistic way to produce this file by hand.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A present-but-unreadable `.iroh-allowed` produces a diagnostic that names the file and the read failure (e.g. a `warn!` distinguishing the error kind, or a propagated error at policy build time); a **missing** file stays silent and empty, as today.
- [ ] The diagnostic fires on the `id serve` policy-build path (`build_access_policy`), not only inside a helper no caller surfaces.
- [ ] Regression tests cover at least: directory-in-place-of-file and non-UTF-8 contents (both must not read as a plain empty list), plus the existing missing-file and valid-file cases staying green.
- [ ] Per-line invalid-ID warnings (`parse_allowed_nodes`) are unchanged; a readable file with garbage lines still loads its valid IDs.

## Scope notes

- Do not change who is trusted by default (server key + client key) or `--open-writes` behavior.
- Fail-closed must be preserved: an unreadable file must never grant writes — the fix is visibility, not leniency.

## Phase 4 of #6669 — closing reply inventory: disposition every WorldClient reply extraction against the validated-reply contract

Design #6669 (a reply is not its defaults — one validated-reply contract for the WorldClient) states the contract in `files/designs/code-worldnet-reply-validation.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace:

1. A field that constitutes the answer is required and typed — missing/mistyped is a malformed-reply error naming the field; success fields are never defaulted.

title: fleet-queue(fallback): parse_ts accepts impossible dates — Feb 31 / non-leap Feb 29 / Apr 31 silently roll into the next month and shift marker lease math by days

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/fleet
labels.description: pkgs/fleet multicall binary + platform crates

body:
## Problem

`parse_ts` in the queue fallback mode (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/fallback.rs:151-158`) validates the day field only as `1..=31`, regardless of month or leap year. Impossible dates are accepted and silently normalized by `days_from_civil` into a different real date, shifting the parsed epoch by days:

- `2026-02-31T00:00:00Z` → parses as 2026-03-03
- `2026-02-29T00:00:00Z` (2026 is not a leap year) → parses as 2026-03-01
- `2026-04-31T00:00:00Z` → parses as 2026-05-01

Marker timestamps are authoritative for all lease math in fallback mode ("The marker's own embedded `ts` is authoritative — comment metadata is never consulted for lease math", `fetch_markers` doc), and `parse_marker` accepts any marker whose `ts` parses. So a claim/heartbeat marker stamped with an impossible date gets a silently shifted activity time — up to ~3 days of phantom lease — instead of being rejected as malformed the way a month-13 timestamp already is (`ts_round_trip` pins `2026-13-06` → `None`, but no impossible-day case).

## Evidence

Verified on the laptop against origin/main @5492f27e02 (probe `~/git/fleet/probe-fallback-contest`, real `fallback.rs` included verbatim, `parse_ts`/`format_ts` called directly):

```
parse_ts(2026-02-31T00:00:00Z) = Some(1772496000) = 2026-03-03T00:00:00Z
parse_ts(2026-02-29T00:00:00Z) = Some(1772323200) = 2026-03-01T00:00:00Z
parse_ts(2024-02-29T00:00:00Z) = Some(1709164800) = 2024-02-29T00:00:00Z   (leap year: correct)
parse_ts(2026-04-31T00:00:00Z) = Some(1777593600) = 2026-05-01T00:00:00Z
parse_ts(2026-01-31T00:00:00Z) = Some(1769817600) = 2026-01-31T00:00:00Z   (control: correct)
```

## Why it matters

Fallback markers are the claim state: a misparsed `ts` moves `last_activity`, which decides Live vs Stale, supersede, and contest outcomes. Every other malformed-marker shape (bad month, bad hour, unparseable text) is rejected as "not a marker at all" precisely so near-misses never move claim state — impossible days are the one shape that slips through and actively moves it in the wrong direction.

## Acceptance criteria

- `parse_ts` returns `None` for day-of-month values that do not exist in the given month/year (Feb 29 on non-leap years, Feb 30/31, Apr/Jun/Sep/Nov 31), while still accepting 2024-02-29 and all valid dates.
- `ts_round_trip` (or a sibling test) gains the impossible-date cases above.
- Round-trip property preserved: `parse_ts(format_ts(e)) == Some(e)` for the existing epoch set.

body:
# github-backup(manifest): a valid-JSON but wrong-shape plan/state entry crashes the whole manifest regeneration — MANIFEST.json (the DR source) is never rewritten

## Evidence

`infra/github-backup/bin/manifest.py`, `build()` (verified on laptop at origin/main `fff580fb1e`):

- `:36` / `:38` — `plan` and `state` are loaded with bare `json.load` and never shape-checked.
- `:41-42` — `for item in plan: repo = item["repo"]` subscripts every plan entry unguarded.
- `:49` — `"last_fetch": (state.get(repo) or {}).get("last_fetch")` assumes every state value is a dict (or falsy).

Verified this run with a probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-manifest-shape/probe_manifest.py`, real `manifest.build()` against temp roots, only `load_config` stubbed):

- Controls pass: valid plan+state → `OK totals={'mirrored': 0, 'missing': 1, 'disk_kb': 0}`; empty plan/state → OK.
- Malformed shapes all raise, and no `MANIFEST.json`/`FAMILIES.md` is written:
  - plan entry `123` → `TypeError: 'int' object is not subscriptable`
  - plan entry `"o/r"` → `TypeError: string indices must be integers`
  - plan entry `[]` → `TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices`
  - plan entry `{"size_kb": 1}` (no `repo`) → `KeyError: 'repo'`
  - plan top-level `{"repo": "o/r"}` (dict, not list) → `TypeError: string indices must be integers`
  - state entry `{"o/r": 123}` → `AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'get'`
  - state entry `{"o/r": "t"}` → `AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get'`
  - state top-level `[]` → `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'`

## Why it matters

`MANIFEST.json` is the disaster-recovery source of record (module docstring: it records what DOES exist, where, and its state; together with `config.json` it rebuilds the whole backup tree). One poison entry in `plan.json` or `state.json` — written by another tool, a hand edit, or a partial migration — wedges every regeneration: the manifest silently goes stale while mirrors keep changing, and the failure surfaces only at DR time, when the stale manifest is trusted. The poison entry also re-crashes every subsequent run until someone hand-edits the JSON. Sibling consumers were hardened/filed separately (#6637 fetch, #6606 reconcile); manifest is the remaining unguarded consumer of the same two files. Distinct from #3240, which covers torn/invalid JSON and non-atomic writes — this is valid JSON with the wrong shape.

## Acceptance criteria

- `build()` validates plan/state shape: a non-list plan, a non-dict state, a plan entry that is not a dict with a string `repo`, or a non-dict state value produces a clear, named error (or a per-entry skipped/error record) instead of a raw `TypeError`/`KeyError`/`AttributeError` traceback.
- Valid entries in the same file still regenerate `MANIFEST.json` + `FAMILIES.md` (or the run fails atomically with the offending entry named — either contract is acceptable if it is explicit and tested).
- Regression tests in `infra/github-backup/tests/` cover the malformed shapes above against the real `build()`.

body:
# repo-universe(check_issues): valid-JSON wrong-shape fetch/state entries crash the whole checker instead of a per-repo ERROR — poison state re-crashes daily

## Problem

`scripts/fleet/repo-universe/check_issues.py` promises in its header that a failed fetch is "an explicit ERROR line in the report (and a non-zero exit); the repo's persisted state is left untouched, so a failure never masquerades as an empty repository." That contract only holds for failures raised as `FetchError`. Every valid-JSON-but-wrong-shape input escapes as an unhandled `TypeError` / `AttributeError`, kills the whole run before any report or state file is written, and — for persisted state — re-crashes every daily timer run until a human repairs `state.json` by hand.

Sites (all on current main `fff580fb1e`, origin/main):

- `check_issues.py:109-113` — `normalize_issue`: `"pull_request" in raw` then `raw.get(field)`. A non-object item (`123`, `"x"`) raises `TypeError` / `AttributeError`, not `FetchError`.
- `check_issues.py:150-161` — `fetch_issues_fixture`: only a dict entry containing `"error"` becomes a `FetchError`. A dict entry without `"error"` (e.g. one issue object instead of a list) is iterated by key; an int entry is not iterable; a list of non-objects reaches `normalize_issue` and crashes the same way. `load_fixture` (:146-147) likewise returns any JSON shape, so a top-level list fixture crashes at `fixture.get` (:151).
- `check_issues.py:116-147` — `fetch_issues_gh` has the same hole on the live path: a parsed JSON page that is not a list of objects (a string, a list containing a scalar) is iterated into `normalize_issue` and raises outside the `FetchError` wrapping that covers the subprocess and the JSON parse.
- `check_issues.py:261-262` + `:202-203` + `:216-217` — persisted state: `main` loads `state.json` with bare `json.loads`; `run_check` does `state.get("repos", {})`, `dict(prior_repos)` and `prior_repos.get(repo)`; a top-level list, a list-valued `repos`, or an int per-repo entry raises before any repo is checked. `diff_repo` (:179-188) then subscripts persisted issue entries (`old["state"]` etc.), so an int entry for one issue number crashes that repo's diff.
- `check_issues.py:207-215` — `run_check` catches only `FetchError` around `fetch(repo)`; the shape crashes above are raised inside the fetch callables and inside `diff_repo`, outside that handler, so one bad repo / one bad state entry takes down every other watched repo's delta for the run.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ `fff580fb1e` == origin/main)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-check-issues/probe.py` on the laptop, importing the real `check_issues` module from origin/main:

- Control — `run_check` with a valid in-memory fetch: Ok (`had_error=False`); control baseline-then-diff with a well-formed persisted entry: Ok.
- Fixture entry `{"number": 1}` (object, no `error`) → `AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get'`; entry `123` → `TypeError: 'int' object is not iterable`; entry `[123]` → `TypeError: argument of type 'int' is not a container or iterable`; entry `["x"]` → `AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get'`; top-level fixture `[1, 2]` → `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'`.
- Persisted state as a top-level list → `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'`; `{"repos": []}` → same; `{"repos": {"a/b": 123}}` → `TypeError: 'int' object is not subscriptable`; `{"repos": {"a/b": {"issues": {"1": 123}}}}` with a current issue #1 → `TypeError: 'int' object is not subscriptable`.

No report file and no state file are written on any of these paths (`main` writes both only after `run_check` returns, :271-280).

## Why it matters

This checker is the daily, scheduled correctness floor for the repo-universe tracker (#1651): it is the thing that notices new/closed issues across every watched repo. Its one job on bad data is to say so per-repo and keep going. Instead, one malformed fixture/API item — or one wrong-shape entry in its own persisted `state.json` (a partial hand edit, a future schema change, a torn-but-parseable write) — silences the whole checker with a traceback in a timer log, and the state poison is self-perpetuating because the crashing run never rewrites the file.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Non-object fetch items (from the fixture path and the `gh api` path alike) and non-list per-repo fixture entries are reported as that repo's `FetchError` — an ERROR line in the report, a non-zero exit, other repos still checked, and that repo's persisted state untouched.
- [ ] A wrong-shape persisted `state.json` (non-object top level, non-object `repos`, non-object per-repo entry, non-object persisted issue entry) is handled under the same rule: named as an error and either skipped per-repo or failed as a single named load error — never an unhandled `TypeError` / `AttributeError` traceback that aborts the run for every repo.
- [ ] Valid behaviour is unchanged: baselining, new/closed/reopened/changed deltas, failed-fetch state preservation, and report/state writing all work exactly as before on well-formed inputs (in-tree `test_check_issues.py` still passes).
- [ ] Regression tests in `test_check_issues.py` cover at least: fixture entry as an object without `error`, fixture entry `[123]`, state as a top-level list, per-repo state entry as an int, and a persisted issue entry as an int — each fails on current code with the exceptions above and passes after the fix.

Dedup: distinct from #6612 (generate.py offline `--forks-org-json` omission — the generator, not the checker), #5945/#1651 (the checker existing / being wired at all), and the github-backup shape issues #6637/#6606/#6575 (different system, different files). Title/keyword searches for `check_issues` + shape/state return no covering issue.

title: id(world_net): read_worlds_reply reads a missing or mistyped 'default' as Ok("") — a malformed worlds reply silently lists no default world

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Bug

`WorldClient::read_worlds_reply` (`pkgs/id/src/world_net.rs:1213`) — the shared reply parser behind the admin `list_worlds` and the public `directory` — reads the reply's top-level `default` field with a silent fallback:

```rust
let default = reply["default"].as_str().unwrap_or_default().to_owned();
```

A `worlds` reply whose `default` is missing, `null`, or mistyped (number, boolean, array, object) reads as `Ok("")` — an empty default name — with no error. The host's wire type makes this a malformed reply by construction: `ServerFrame::Worlds { default: &'a str, worlds: Vec<WorldInfo> }` (`pkgs/id/src/world_session/types.rs:377-380`) always sends a string, and both host arms build it from `hub.default_world()` (`pkgs/id/src/world_session/mod.rs:943-968`).

This is the one top-level field of this reply the parser does not validate: the same function refuses a non-list `worlds` with `context("worlds reply had no list")` (`world_net.rs:1214-1216`). (Per-entry drops in the same function are #6621 — different fields, already filed; this issue covers only the top-level `default`.)

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ fff580fb1e)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-worlds-default-wt` (real `id` crate, integration test `pkgs/id/tests/probe_worlds_default.rs` in the probe worktree only; scripted iroh host answering `list_worlds` with canned frames, harness reused from the #6621 probe), `cargo test --test probe_worlds_default` — **1 passed**:

- Control — `{"type":"worlds","default":"lobby","worlds":[lobby, arena]}` → `Ok(("lobby", [("lobby", true, 3), ("arena", false, 0)]))`.
- `default` missing → `Ok(("", [both worlds]))`.
- `default`: `123` / `true` / `[]` / `{}` / `null` → each `Ok(("", [both worlds]))`. Every malformed shape collapses to the same empty string.
- Oracle — `"worlds": {...}` (not a list) → `Err("worlds reply had no list")`, confirming the function does refuse top-level shape errors for the sibling field.

## Why it matters

- `id world list` is the operator's view of which world is the host's default. With `default` silently `""`, the plain listing marks **no** world with the `(default)` marker (`commands/world.rs:77-83` selects the marker by raw-name equality with the default string), and `--json` output prints `"default": ""` with every entry's `default` flag `false` (`world_hub::directory_json`, `pkgs/id/src/world_hub.rs:161-176`).
- The public `directory()` path shares the parser, so the same malformed reply quietly publishes a directory with no default world — a version-skewed or buggy host degrades the listing invisibly instead of failing loudly, exactly the failure mode the function's own `worlds`-list check guards against.
- A consumer comparing the returned default against a real world name cannot distinguish "host has an empty-named default" from "host sent garbage": the malformed-reply signal is destroyed at the parser.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `worlds` reply whose `default` is missing or not a string makes `list_worlds` / `directory` fail with an error naming the field (e.g. "worlds reply had no default world"), mirroring the existing "worlds reply had no list" check.
- [ ] A well-formed reply returns the host's default name unchanged; an explicitly empty-string default from a conforming host, if triage decides it is legitimate, is a deliberate documented case, not a fallback for malformed shapes.
- [ ] A regression test drives `list_worlds` (or `directory`) against a scripted host covering: string default (control), missing default, and at least number + null mistyped defaults.
- [ ] No change to the per-entry handling (#6621), the refusal path, or the `ServerFrame::Worlds` wire shape.

Related (same function/file, different fields — not this issue): #6621 (per-entry drops + presence), #6620 (compile reply defaults), #6632 (create_world `created` default).

labels.name: source/creator

labels.description: Workflow/app: .github/workflows/bws-freshness.yml + lib/bws-to-sops.sh freshness check

body:
## Summary

The `bws freshness` workflow (`.github/workflows/bws-freshness.yml`) finds "the" open drift issue for an episode by title search alone and takes the first hit — with no exact-title, author, label, or body-marker check. Both consumers of that lookup can therefore act on an unrelated issue: the drift path comments the drift report on it, and the fresh path **closes** it.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ 4e92da9311)

- `.github/workflows/bws-freshness.yml:84` (drift path):
  `existing="$(gh issue list --search "$title in:title state:open" --json number --jq '.[0].number // empty')"` where `title="bws.yaml mirror drift detected"` (:74).
- `.github/workflows/bws-freshness.yml:96` (fresh path): the identical lookup, followed at :98 by `gh issue close "$existing" --comment "A later scheduled freshness check (#5451) found the mirror up to date; closing this drift episode."`
- The drift path at :85-86 runs `gh issue comment "$existing" --body-file issue-body.md` on the same unfiltered first hit.
- The lookup requests only `--json number` — it never fetches author, labels, or body, so nothing downstream can distinguish the workflow's own drift issue (created :88 with only `--label "priority/normal"`, a label any human issue can also carry) from a human-filed issue whose title merely contains the same words (GitHub `in:title` search is a word/substring match, not an exact-title match, and result order is relevance, not creation).
- Nothing else in the workflow pins identity: the created issue carries no hidden marker comment/body token that a later run checks.
- Probe (laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-bws-freshness/probe_bws.py`, run against the real workflow file @ 4e92da9311): extracted lines 84/86/88/96/98 verbatim as above; simulating the `.[0]` selection over a search result where an unrelated same-words issue ("bws.yaml mirror drift detected in staging export", #9001-style) sorts ahead of the workflow's own issue picks the unrelated one — `fresh-path would close #9001; drift-path would comment on #9001`.

## Why it matters

The fresh path is destructive: the first night the mirror is fresh again, the workflow closes whatever issue the search happened to rank first — which can be a human's open issue about drift in a different mirror/context — with a comment claiming the mirror is up to date. The drift path leaks the drift report (key names from `drift.txt`) as a comment on an unrelated issue and, worse, never opens/updates the real drift issue, so the actual episode goes untracked. This is a live risk as soon as `BWS_FRESHNESS_ENABLED` is turned on (#5451 prerequisite gate, workflow :14-23); fixing it after enablement means the first misfire may already have closed someone's issue.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both lookups (drift and fresh paths) identify the workflow's own drift issue deterministically: e.g. exact title equality after fetching candidate titles, plus at least one workflow-owned signal (a dedicated label such as `bws-drift` applied at creation, the `github-actions` author, or a hidden marker in the issue body that the lookup verifies).
- [ ] The fresh/close path never closes an issue that fails that identity check; with no verified drift issue open it is a no-op.
- [ ] The drift/comment path likewise comments only on the verified drift issue, and creates a new one (with the identity signal applied) when none verifies.
- [ ] A fixture/shell test or documented stubbed-`gh` exercise covers: an unrelated same-words title sorting first is ignored; the workflow's own issue is found even when it is not `.[0]`.
- [ ] Related: #5451 (parent freshness check), #6631 (the `--check`/`--dry-run` skip in the script this workflow runs — distinct defect, same surface).

# id(world_net): the lib-test target does not compile on main — `info_details_rejects_malformed_active_module_hash` calls a nonexistent `inject_json` helper (14 errors)

## Summary

On current `origin/main`, `cargo test -p id --lib` fails to compile. The test added with the #6633 fix, `info_details_rejects_malformed_active_module_hash` (`pkgs/id/src/world_net.rs:3426-3519` at `4e92da9311`), drives the client through a helper that does not exist:

- 7 × `error[E0599]: no method named 'inject_json' found for struct 'world_net::WorldClient'` — `client.inject_json(reply).await` at (snapshot lines) :3443/:3455/:3466/:3478/:3490/:3502/:3514. There is no `inject_json` anywhere in `pkgs/id` (`grep -rn "fn inject_json"` = 0 hits on origin/main).
- 7 × `error: cannot find macro 'json' in this scope` — the test uses bare `json!({...})` without importing `serde_json::json` in the test module.

Total: `error: could not compile 'id' (lib test) due to 14 previous errors`. The production half of the same change (the `info_details` match-and-bail on a mistyped `active_module_hash`) is present and correct — only its regression test is broken. The breakage arrived in the repo-keeper snapshot `4ecb3510c9` ("snapshot code 2026-11-06 17:23 CST"), which swept the in-progress fix into main.

## Evidence (verified this run)

- Laptop, worktree at `4ecb3510c9` (== origin/main at the time): `cargo test -p id --lib --no-run` → the 14 errors above, every one inside this single test; no other file errors.
- Re-verified at fresh `origin/main` `4e92da9311` (only intervening commit is the unrelated PR #6639 merge): the test is still present at `world_net.rs:3426`, and `fn inject_json` still has 0 definitions in the crate.

## Why it matters

While the lib-test target does not compile, **no** `id` unit test can run — locally, in a probe worktree, or in CI. Every verification of the pkgs/id work that dominates this repo's current queue (the world_net reply-validation family included) is blocked or forced into workarounds, and the #6633 fix itself has no working regression coverage: the test that was supposed to pin it cannot execute.

Drive it the way the neighboring world_net tests do (a scripted/rogue host via `Router` + `ProtocolHandler` speaking the world ALPN, or a real `#[cfg(test)]` frame-injection helper on `WorldClient` if that is the intended design — implemented, not just called).
- [ ] The malformed-hash cases from the broken test (123, true, ["abc"], {"hash": "abc"}) all appear in the working test.

## Dedup

Distinct from #6633 itself (the reply-validation bug, whose production fix has landed on main via snapshot — this issue is only its broken test). Related: #6641 (filed this run) hit this breakage as a probe blocker and worked around it locally.

body:
# id(world_net): admin_event_history reads a mistyped begin-frame `module_hash` as Ok(None) — a malformed export header records a world with a module as module-less

## Summary

`WorldClient::admin_event_history` (`pkgs/id/src/world_net.rs:1699`) reads the begin frame's module hash leniently:

```rust
let module_hash = begin["module_hash"].as_str().map(str::to_owned);
```

`.as_str()` yields `None` for a JSON `null` (the legitimate no-module case), for a **missing** key (older hosts), and for **any non-string value** (number, boolean, array, object) alike — so a mistyped `module_hash` is silently rewritten to `None`, indistinguishable from a world that genuinely has no active module.

Every sibling field in the same begin frame is strict: `world_id` (`.as_str().context("history reply has no world ID")?`, :1695-1698), `current_sequence` (`.as_u64().context(...)`, :1700-1702), `complete` (`.as_bool().context(...)`, :1703-1705), and `event_count` (type- and range-checked, :1706-1710). The host's typed contract is `ServerFrame::EventHistoryBegin { module_hash: Option<String>, .. }` (`pkgs/id/src/world_session/types.rs:364-370`), which serializes the hash as a string or `null` — never a number/bool/array/object. A non-string, non-null value is a malformed reply by construction (host bug, version skew, or hostile host).

Oracles that refuse exactly this shape:

- `world_fixture`'s own header parser (`pkgs/id/src/world_fixture.rs:592-595`): a persisted fixture header whose `module_hash` is neither string nor null fails with "the header's module_hash must be a string or null". The on-disk format is stricter than the network reader that produces it.
- `info_details` in the same file (`world_net.rs`, module_info reply): `None | Null => None`, a string => `Some`, anything else => bail "host sent malformed active_module_hash". That is the exact pattern this field needs.

## Consumers

- `world_fixture::record` (`pkgs/id/src/world_fixture.rs:310-320`) bakes `history.module_hash` verbatim into the fixture header. A mistyped hash therefore records a fixture claiming the world had **no** active module.
- Replay then refuses that fixture for the wrong reason: `replay` requires `header.module_hash.is_some()` ("the fixture records no active module, so there is nothing to replay", `world_fixture.rs:371-374`), and `check_module` errors "the fixture records no active module" (:328-332). The export "succeeded", the fixture is unusable, and nothing anywhere says the begin frame was malformed — the provenance of which module produced the recorded events is silently lost.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Probe on the laptop @ `4ecb3510c9` (origin/main), worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-admin-hash-wt`, in-crate test `probe_admin_history_module_hash_shape` (rogue iroh host speaking the world ALPN, canned `event_history_begin` + one empty records page per case; real `id` crate):

- CONTROL string `"abc123"` → `Ok`, `module_hash = Some("abc123")`
- CONTROL `null` → `Ok(None)` (legitimate no-module)
- CONTROL missing key → `Ok(None)` (older hosts)
- CASE `module_hash: 123` → `Ok(None)` — **bug: collapsed**
- CASE `module_hash: true` → `Ok(None)` — **bug: collapsed**
- CASE `module_hash: ["abc"]` → `Ok(None)` — **bug: collapsed**
- CASE `module_hash: {"hash": "abc"}` → `Ok(None)` — **bug: collapsed**

## Why it matters

The admin event-history export is the audit/backup path and the fixture-capture path for a world. Its header is the provenance record: which module produced these events. A reader that converts a malformed hash into "no module" manufactures a false provenance statement instead of failing the export — the same class as #6633 (info_details hash, fixed on current main with the match-and-bail pattern), one function over. The begin frame's other four fields already refuse malformed shapes; this one field is the outlier.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] In `admin_event_history`, a begin-frame `module_hash` that is present and neither a string nor JSON `null` (number, boolean, array, object) fails with a malformed-reply error naming the field (mirroring the `info_details` match-and-bail pattern). Missing key and `null` still read as `None`; a string still reads as `Some(hash)`.
- [ ] Regression tests drive `admin_event_history` against scripted/rogue replies covering: string (Ok, `Some`), `null` (Ok, `None`), missing (Ok, `None`), and at least number + boolean + array/object (all Err).
- [ ] Existing world_net / world_fixture tests stay green (conforming hosts always send string-or-null, by construction of `ServerFrame::EventHistoryBegin`).

## Dedup

`gh issue list --search` (all states) on 2026-11-06 for "admin_event_history module_hash", "event_history_begin", and "history reply module": no hits. Distinct from #6600 (the same function's records-loop `next_after` cursor type — different field, different frame) and from #6633 (`info_details`' `active_module_hash` in the `module_info` reply — different function, already fixed on main; this is the remaining unguarded sibling in the begin frame of the admin-history export).

body:
# mcpx(logstore): the read-only log-sql guard still executes bare mutating PRAGMAs (`PRAGMA optimize`, `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint`)

## Finding

PR #3516 closed the value-carrying half of #1664: `CheckReadOnly` now refuses PRAGMAs in `name = value` and `name(value)` form (except an allowlist of function-form reads). But `checkReadOnlyPragma` passes **any bare PRAGMA** — a name with no `=` and no parentheses — and SQLite has bare, no-value PRAGMAs that perform actions instead of answering questions:

- `PRAGMA optimize` — runs ANALYZE over the database and **writes `sqlite_stat1`**.
- `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint` — **checkpoints the live WAL into the main database file** (this store's DSN is WAL mode, see evidence).
- `PRAGMA incremental_vacuum` — performs vacuum work in its bare form (verified mutating in rollback-journal mode; in WAL mode its effect was nil in the probe until a checkpoint, so it needs a disposition either way).

These run on the same writable store connection #1664 was about, through `mcpx log sql`, on a surface whose own contract is: "CheckReadOnly rejects a statement that would change anything."

## Evidence

- Source PR: #3516 (https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/3516), head commit `afcce321e62f258ca290b73b1d1795adde603f38`, merge `8f0c004f738f181615aa0652759f9ffee8366610`. It added `checkReadOnlyPragma` refusing only `=`-carrying and parenthesised non-allowlist forms.
- Current main `4ecb3510c9a46e5392a1c3218743251b1c4ae921` (verified ×2, file byte-identical across both reads):
  - `pkgs/mcpx/internal/logstore/sql.go:24` — "CheckReadOnly rejects a statement that would change anything."
  - `pkgs/mcpx/internal/logstore/sql.go:74` — `checkReadOnlyPragma`: returns nil for any `rest` with no `=` and no `(`; there is no bare-name allowlist.
  - `pkgs/mcpx/internal/logstore/sql.go:151` — `RunSQL` executes the checked statement via `s.db.Query(query)` on the store DB.
  - `pkgs/mcpx/internal/logstore/store.go:134` — the store DSN sets `_pragma=journal_mode(WAL)`, so `wal_checkpoint` has a live WAL to act on.
- Laptop probe (python sqlite3, WAL-mode database matching the store's mode): after `PRAGMA optimize` (bare), `sqlite_stat1` contained 1 row (a persistent write); bare `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint` returned `(0, 414, 414)` — 414 WAL frames checkpointed into the database file. In a rollback-journal database, bare `PRAGMA incremental_vacuum` shrank the freelist 200 → 199 and the file by one page.
- Dedupe: issue searches for `incremental_vacuum`, `PRAGMA optimize`, `wal_checkpoint`, `bare pragma`, and `CheckReadOnly` return only #1664 (CLOSED — the value-carrying issue this PR fixed) and unrelated #1668. No open or closed issue covers the bare forms.

## Why it matters

The guard is the only thing standing between the documented read-only `mcpx log sql` surface and writes to the live log index. #1664's lesson was that this surface executes what it admits, persistently (its assignments survived reopen). The bare forms are the same class with the value removed: `optimize` rewrites planner statistics, `wal_checkpoint` forces WAL frames into the main file on a database the daemon is concurrently writing. Severity is modest — these are maintenance actions, not data destruction — but they break the stated read-only contract and can race/surprise the live writer.

## Acceptance criteria

- `CheckReadOnly` admits bare PRAGMAs only from an explicit allowlist of known reads (e.g. `journal_mode`, `user_version`, `schema_version`, `database_list`, `compile_options`, `integrity_check` as applicable), or equivalently refuses the known action PRAGMAs (`optimize`, `wal_checkpoint`, `incremental_vacuum`, `shrink_memory`, and any other bare form triage finds that changes state).
- Regression tests in `pkgs/mcpx/internal/logstore` (guard-level and `RunSQL`-level, following `TestRunSQLRefusesPragmaAssignments`): `PRAGMA optimize` and `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint` are refused; the established bare reads (`PRAGMA journal_mode`, `PRAGMA user_version;`) still pass.
- `incremental_vacuum` gets an explicit disposition: refused, or a comment/test records why its bare form cannot change this WAL-mode store.
- Existing logstore tests still pass.

body:
# github-backup(fetch): a valid-JSON but wrong-shape plan/state entry crashes the whole daily fetch — one poison entry in plan.json or state.json wedges every repo, every day

## Problem

`infra/github-backup/bin/fetch_mirrors.py` loads `plan.json` and `state.json` with `json.load` and then subscripts / `.get()`s the results with no shape check anywhere. A file that is **valid JSON but the wrong shape** — the class #3240 does not cover (that issue is torn / unparseable JSON) — crashes the daily fetch before it fetches anything, and the same poison entry re-crashes every subsequent daily run until a human repairs the file by hand.

Sites (all on current main `de90338c42`):

- `fetch_mirrors.py:83-85` — `iter_plan_repos`: `return [p["repo"] for p in plan]`. A plan entry of `123`, `"a/b"`, or `{"name": "x"}` (no `repo`), or a top-level plan that is an object instead of a list, raises `TypeError` / `KeyError` and kills `main()` at startup.
- `fetch_mirrors.py:92` + `:100` — `main`: `state = json.load(...)`, then `st = state.get(repo) or {}` and `st.get("last_fetch")`. A top-level list, or a per-repo entry that is a string / int (`{"owner/repo": "oops"}`), raises `AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get'` — before any fetch, state write, or manifest regeneration.
- `fetch_mirrors.py:64-77` — `fetch_repo`: `st = state.setdefault(repo, {})` returns a pre-existing non-dict entry unchanged, so `st.setdefault("fail_days", [])` / `st["last_error"] = ...` raises on the same poison entry even if the main loop is reached another way.
- `fetch_mirrors.py:22` — `record_failure_day(days, today)`: its `try` catches only `TypeError, ValueError, IndexError` around the date walk, but a non-list `fail_days` escapes anyway: a string raises `TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment` at the `days[:] = ...` write after the walk, an int raises `TypeError` on `len()`, and a dict raises `KeyError: 0` (not in the caught set).

Sibling consumers of the same `plan.json` repeat the unguarded pattern and should be checked in the same pass: `manifest.py:41-42` (`item["repo"]`) and `clone_all.py:185-188` (`p["repo"]`). Note the contrast inside the same system: `clone_all.py`'s `clone-status.jsonl` reader (the oracle cited in #6606) wraps each line in `try/except Exception` and skips bad lines, and `reconcile.py`'s `_clone_status_entries` was the subject of #6606 for the same shape class one level down.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ `de90338c42` == origin/main)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-ghb-fetch-shape/probe.py` on the laptop, importing the **real** `fetch_mirrors` module from the repo tree (controls + malformed shapes, `main()` driven with the same patched helpers the in-tree `test_fetch_mirrors.py` uses):

- Control — valid plan: `iter_plan_repos` → `['a/b', 'c/d']` OK.
- Plan entry `123` → `TypeError: 'int' object is not subscriptable`; entry `"a/b"` → `TypeError: string indices must be integers`; entry `{"name": "x"}` → `KeyError: 'repo'`; plan as a top-level object → `TypeError: string indices must be integers`.
- Control — `record_failure_day(["2026-01-01"], "2026-01-02")` → `['2026-01-01', '2026-01-02']` OK.
- `fail_days` as string → `TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment`; as int → `TypeError: object of type 'int' has no len()`; as dict → `KeyError: 0`.
- Control — `main()` with `{"owner/repo": {"last_fetch": 0}}` → exit 0, `{"results": {"missing": 1, ...}, "chronic_failures": []}`.
- `main()` with state entry `"oops"` or `123` → `AttributeError: 'str'/'int' object has no attribute 'get'`; state as a top-level list → `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'`. No fetch attempted, no state/manifest written.

## Why it matters

`state.json` is shared mutable state (the 5-minute drainer writes it too) and `plan.json` is generated by the weekly reconcile sweep — neither is hand-audited before the daily fetch consumes it. One wrong-shape entry (a bad reconcile emit, a partial hand edit, a future schema change landing in one writer before the reader) does not degrade the backup for one repo: it takes the **whole daily mirror fetch** down, silently (a traceback in a timer log), and it is self-perpetuating — the crashing run never rewrites the file, so tomorrow's run hits the identical entry. For a backup system, a poison entry must cost at most that entry, never the estate.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `fetch_mirrors` validates the shape of `plan.json` and `state.json` at load: a non-list plan, a plan entry that is not an object with a string `repo`, a non-object state, or a non-object per-repo state entry is reported by name (repo / entry index) and skipped or failed as a single named error — never an unhandled `TypeError` / `KeyError` / `AttributeError` traceback that aborts the run for every other repo.
- [ ] A non-list `fail_days` (string / number / object) is treated as a malformed entry under the same rule instead of crashing `record_failure_day` / `fetch_repo`.
- [ ] Valid plan/state behaviour is unchanged: coalescing, failure-streak / chronic-failure accounting, and manifest regeneration all work exactly as before on well-formed files (in-tree `test_fetch_mirrors.py` still passes).
- [ ] Regression tests in the github-backup test suite cover at least: plan entry `123`, plan entry missing `repo`, state entry as a string, state as a top-level list, and `fail_days` as a string — each fails on current code with the exceptions above and passes after the fix.
- [ ] The sibling `plan.json` consumers (`manifest.py`, `clone_all.py`) are checked in the same pass and either fixed under the same rule or explicitly recorded as out of scope with a reason.

Dedup: distinct from #3240 (torn/unparseable JSON + non-atomic writes; these files parse fine), #6606 (reconcile's `clone-status.jsonl` non-dict lines), #6575 (drain queue-event shape), and #3270 (missing mirror never records `fail_days`). Title/keyword searches for `fetch_mirrors` + plan/state shape return no covering issue.

body:
# id(world_net): set_caps_ceiling() never validates the reply — a `caps_ceiling` reply with a missing or malformed report reads as Ok, so an admin ceiling change reports success with no report

## Summary

`WorldClient::set_caps_ceiling` (`pkgs/id/src/world_net.rs:851-875`) checks only that the reply's `type` is `"caps_ceiling"` and then returns the whole reply verbatim:

```rust
if reply["type"] != "caps_ceiling" {
    bail!(/* host message */);
}
Ok(reply)
```

It never looks at `report` or `message` at all. The host's typed contract is `ServerFrame::CapsCeiling { report: CapsReport, message: &'static str }` (`pkgs/id/src/world_session/types.rs:405-408`; the host sends it at `world_session/mod.rs:1369-1372`), so a reply that omits `report`, sets it to `null`/`123`, or gives it the wrong shape is indistinguishable from a real ceiling change.

This is the third sibling of #6624 (`caps()`/`update_caps()` return `reply["report"]` unvalidated) — `set_caps_ceiling` is worse: it does not even extract the field.

## Consumers

- `id world caps --ceiling …` (`pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs:299-319`): when no grant/revoke follows, `ceiling_res` becomes the command result and is pretty-printed with exit 0 — a report-less reply prints `{"message": …, "type": "caps_ceiling"}` as if the ceiling change succeeded and was reported.
- Manifest apply `ApplyStep::SetCeiling` (`pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs:1257-1267`): discards the value with `.await?`, so any `caps_ceiling`-typed frame — including one with no report — counts as the step having applied.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Probe on the laptop @ `de90338c42` (origin/main), worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-ceiling-wt`, test `pkgs/id/tests/probe_ceiling_reply.rs` (real `id` crate, scripted host replying with one canned frame per case; 1 passed):

- CONTROL `{"type":"caps_ceiling","report":{valid CapsReport},"message":"the ceiling applies immediately"}` → `Ok(full reply)`
- CASE missing report `{"type":"caps_ceiling","message":"…"}` → `Ok` (no report at all)
- CASE `report: null` → `Ok`
- CASE `report: 123` → `Ok`
- CASE report wrong shape `{"granted":"time.now"}` (string where `CapsReport.granted: Vec<String>`, `pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/world_caps.rs:1426`) → `Ok`
- CASE missing `message` → `Ok`

Sibling oracles in the same file refuse malformed success replies: `set_schedule`/`cancel_schedule` parse via `serde_json::from_value(reply["schedules"].clone()).context("host sent a malformed schedule map")` (`world_net.rs:891-960`), and `records_ticket` requires the ticket string (`world_net.rs:1769-1796`).

## Why it matters

The ceiling is the world's capability bound — the security-relevant limit on what a program may use. An admin (or manifest apply) that believes the ceiling was replaced, based on a reply carrying no valid post-change report, can leave a world running under the old ceiling while every surface reports success. The typed `CapsReport` exists precisely so the client can confirm the resulting state; returning the frame unchecked throws that confirmation away.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `set_caps_ceiling` refuses a `caps_ceiling` reply whose `report` is missing or does not parse as `CapsReport` (route `reply["report"]` through `serde_json::from_value::<CapsReport>` with a "host sent a malformed capability report" context, mirroring `set_schedule`), and returns the validated report (or a value containing it) instead of the raw frame.
- [ ] A well-formed reply still succeeds, and the CLI caps command prints the validated report.
- [ ] A regression test with a scripted host covers at least: missing report, `report: null`, and a wrong-shaped report — all refused; the well-formed control still Ok.
- [ ] Existing world_net / world_session caps-ceiling tests stay green (`cargo test -p id` for the touched modules, on the laptop or CI).

## Dedup

`gh issue list --search "caps_ceiling"` and `--search "ceiling reply"` (all states) on 2026-11-06: #6624 covers `caps()`/`update_caps()` only; #816 (closed) is the world-doctor ceiling checks; no open or closed issue covers `set_caps_ceiling` reply validation.

body:
## Bug

`id world diff` and `id world apply` always read the world's execution profile as the all-default profile, no matter what profile the host has actually persisted. Manifest reconciliation therefore never converges for any world/manifest pair that uses a non-default `[profile]`.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ de90338c42)

- The host answers `execution_profile_info` / `set_execution_profile` with `ServerFrame::ExecutionProfile { update: ExecutionProfileUpdate { requested, applies_on_next_program_install_or_process_restart }, message }` — the profile is nested at `update.requested` (`pkgs/id/src/world_session/types.rs:399-402`, `pkgs/id/src/world/mod.rs:1848-1853`, reply built in `pkgs/id/src/world_session/mod.rs`, `ExecutionProfileInfo` arm).
- `WorldClient::execution_profile` (`pkgs/id/src/world_net.rs:1029-1059`) returns the **whole reply frame** after only a `type` check — unlike `caps()` (`world_net.rs:791`), which extracts `reply["report"]`.
- `current_world_state` (`pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs:1122-1129`) then runs `serde_json::from_value::<WorldExecutionProfile>(whole_frame)` with the context `"host returned a malformed execution profile"`. But `WorldExecutionProfile` (`pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/world_limits.rs:283-309`) is `#[serde(default)]` with all-`Option` fields and no `deny_unknown_fields`, so parsing **any** object frame succeeds and yields the all-`None` default: the frame's real profile sits under the unknown key `update` and is ignored. The malformed-profile error can never fire for an object reply.
- Consequence in the planner (`pkgs/id/src/world_manifest.rs:340`): a step is planned when `desired.profile != default && desired.profile != current.profile`. Since `current.profile` is always the default, every manifest with a non-default `[profile]` plans a `set_profile` step on **every** diff/apply — including immediately after a successful apply set exactly that profile. `id world diff` reports profile drift forever; apply never reaches "no drift".

## Reproduction (probe, laptop)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-exec-profile-frame` (verbatim copy of the `WorldExecutionProfile` type from `world_limits.rs:283-309`, exact client expression from `commands/world.rs:1122-1129`), run on the laptop this run:

- Host frame for a world with persisted `wasm_fuel=1000000, total_memory_bytes=268435456` → client parse returns `WorldExecutionProfile { all fields None }` (== default). **BUG CONFIRMED.**
- Oracle parse of `frame["update"]["requested"]` → `wasm_fuel: Some(1000000), total_memory_bytes: Some(268435456)`.
- Plan rule (`world_manifest.rs:340`) with desired=oracle, current=parsed → `SetProfile` planned on every diff/apply.

## Why it matters

Manifest diff/apply is the declarative path for world configuration (#838/#807 family). A profile read that is silently always-default makes drift detection meaningless for the profile dimension: perpetual false drift for profile users, re-applies on every run, and no way to notice a host whose persisted profile was changed out-of-band to something the manifest does not want (any actual profile reads as default). The dead `"host returned a malformed execution profile"` error string shows the strictness was intended — the frame shape just never matched the parse.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `WorldClient::execution_profile` (or `current_world_state`) extracts the profile from `update.requested` (mirroring how `caps()` extracts `report`), so a host-persisted non-default profile reads back identically.
- [ ] A reply whose `update.requested` is missing or mistyped fails with the existing "host returned a malformed execution profile" context instead of reading as the default profile.
- [ ] Regression test: a scripted/frame-level test where the host's persisted profile is non-default and `current_world_state` (or its extraction helper) returns that profile; and a manifest whose `[profile]` equals the live profile plans zero steps / diffs clean after apply.
- [ ] `set_execution_profile`'s return path checked for the same shape assumption and covered by the same extraction, if it shares the consumer pattern.

Related (same client, different fields/functions — not this issue): #6624 (caps report), #6625 (policy reply), #6626 (manifest_state seed).

title: id(world_records): read_records collapses duplicate keys inside a replicated value — the #6483 receipt caps measure the collapsed value, so an oversized value hidden behind a duplicate passes, unlike parse_records (#6473)

body:
## Problem

`RecordsStore` receipt path `read_records` (`pkgs/id/src/world_records.rs:242`) re-checks the `MAX_RECORD*` caps on replicated records — that was the #6483 fix — but it parses each record's value with plain `serde_json::from_slice` (`world_records.rs:269-270`) and measures the value's size from the **parsed** value (`world_records.rs:271`: `serde_json::to_vec(&value)` length). `serde_json::Value` keeps only the last value for a repeated object key, so a duplicate key inside a replicated value silently collapses **before** the cap is measured:

- A value whose raw bytes exceed `MAX_RECORD_VALUE_BYTES` (8192, `pkgs/id/src/world/mod.rs:1937`) hidden behind a duplicate key — e.g. `{"k":"<8292 x's>","k":"small"}` (raw 8,3xx bytes) — collapses to `{"k":"small"}` and passes the receipt cap.
- The same bytes are refused on the publish path: `parse_records` (`world/mod.rs:1946`) parses through `id_core::json_unique::parse_json_without_duplicate_keys` (#6473, design #6520: a duplicate key is a parse error at every depth), so the identical duplicate inside a published record is a hard error there.

So the replica receipt gate — the one path that exists because a replicated doc is *not* trusted (#6483) — accepts a value shape and size the publisher can never produce, and the size it enforces is the collapsed size, not the size of the bytes actually received and stored in the blob. This is the #6473 exploit surviving on the one receipt path #6483 hardened for caps but not for duplicate keys.

## Evidence

- `pkgs/id/src/world_records.rs:269-271` — `let value: serde_json::Value = serde_json::from_slice(&bytes)...; let size = serde_json::to_vec(&value)...` — no duplicate-key refusal; the cap is measured post-collapse.
- `pkgs/id/src/world/mod.rs:1946-1950` — `parse_records` routes through `parse_json_without_duplicate_keys` with the comment "the caps below must see the document as written, never a last-wins collapse of it" (#6473). That reasoning applies verbatim to receipt.
- `pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/json_unique.rs` — the shared helper already exists in `id-core` (design #6520); `read_records` does not use it. This site should also be dispositioned as a **gate** in the #6521 closing inventory.
- Existing receipt tests (`world_records.rs`, `read_records_refuses_an_oversized_value` etc.) cover caps on duplicate-free values only — no duplicate-key case.

## Verification (this run, laptop @ de90338c42)

Probe test added in a laptop worktree (`~/git/fleet/probe-readrecords-wt`, test `probe_read_records_collapses_duplicate_keys_in_a_value`, using the module's own `write_raw` harness against a real in-memory iroh-docs doc):

- Raw duplicate value `{"k":"<8292 x's>","k":"small"}` written under key `dup`: `read_records` returns **Ok** with `dup = {"k":"small"}` — the oversized first value vanished and the collapsed size passed the 8192 cap.
- Control: `parse_records` on the same value nested in a records document returns **Err** (duplicate key refusal).
- Control (pre-existing test): a duplicate-free oversized value is refused by `read_records` (`read_records_refuses_an_oversized_value`), so the cap itself works — only the duplicate collapse bypasses it.

## Why it matters

`read_records` is the trust boundary for replicated world state: its whole purpose (#6483) is that a non-conforming or hostile doc cannot smuggle over-cap records into a follower. A duplicate key reopens exactly the hole #6473 closed on the publish side — the checker and the byte stream disagree about the value — and it also means two readers of the same blob can disagree about a record's content (the #6520 contract's core concern).

## Acceptance criteria

- `read_records` refuses a record value containing a duplicate object key at any depth, with an error naming the record key (routing the parse through `id_core::json_unique::parse_json_without_duplicate_keys` over the value bytes, or an equivalent checked parse).
- A duplicate-hidden oversized value (raw bytes > `MAX_RECORD_VALUE_BYTES`, collapsed size under) is refused; the value-size cap is evaluated against the document as written, never a collapsed form.
- Duplicate-free conforming values — including values at exactly `MAX_RECORD_VALUE_BYTES` — still read back unchanged; all existing `world_records` receipt tests stay green.
- A regression test in the `world_records` tests uses the existing `write_raw` harness with a duplicate-key value and asserts the refusal.
- The site is recorded as a gate disposition for the #6521 inventory.

body:
## Problem

`WorldClient::info_details` in `pkgs/id/src/world_net.rs` (reply handling at :1473 on main `075b2de904`) reads the `module_info` reply's active module hash with a bare optional coercion:

```rust
let active_module_hash = reply["active_module_hash"].as_str().map(str::to_owned);
```

`as_str()` returns `None` for **every** non-string value, so a present-but-mistyped `active_module_hash` (number, bool, array, object) is silently read as `None` — the exact value that legitimately means "this world has no installed module". The host's `ServerFrame::ModuleInfo` (`pkgs/id/src/world_session/types.rs:330-336`) always serializes this field as either a string or `null`, so a non-string, non-null value can only be corruption, a version-skewed host, or a hostile/buggy peer — and the client should say so instead of inventing "no module".

The same reply is otherwise strict, which is the in-function oracle:

- `world_id` missing/mistyped → error (`"host omitted world id"`, :1469-1472)
- `current_sequence` missing/mistyped → error (`"host omitted sequence"`, :1474-1476)
- a non-null `active_module_provenance` that fails to decode → error (`"host sent invalid module provenance"`, :1477-1482)

Only the hash field collapses malformed → absent.

## Why it matters

Consumers trust `None` as a factual statement about the world:

- `id world download` (`pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs:214-216`) turns the coerced `None` into the operator-facing claim "world has no installed module to download" — wrong diagnosis for a world that does have a module, sending debugging in the wrong direction.
- `capture_world_state` (`pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs:1148`) bakes `module_hash: info.active_module_hash` into the captured `WorldState` manifest — a mistyped reply is recorded as a manifest with **no module**, the same class of fabricated capture state as the manifest seed issue (#6626, different field/function).
- `id world info` JSON output (`commands/world.rs:665`) prints `"active_module_hash": null`, indistinguishable from a genuinely module-less world.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Probe on the laptop against main `075b2de904`, real `id` crate with a scripted iroh host (`~/git/fleet/probe-compile-wt/pkgs/id/tests/probe_info_reply.rs`, test `probe_info_reply_shapes`):

- control, string hash `"abc123"` → `Ok(Some("abc123"))`
- control, `null` hash → `Ok(None)` (the legitimate no-module case)
- mistyped hash `123` / `true` / `["abc"]` / `{"h":"abc"}` → all `Ok(None)` — silently conflated with no-module
- oracle in the same reply: mistyped non-null `active_module_provenance: 123` → `Err("host sent invalid module provenance")`

Dedup: `gh search issues` for `active_module_hash` / `info_details` / `module_info` in this repo returns no issue covering `info_details` reply validation. Neighbours are distinct functions/fields: #6620 (`compile()` reply defaults), #6621 (`read_worlds_reply` entries), #6624 (`caps()` report), #6625 (`policy_request` reply), #6626 (`manifest_state` seed), #6632 (`create_world` flag).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `info_details` errors when `active_module_hash` is present and neither a string nor `null`, with an error naming the malformed field.
- [ ] A string hash still returns `Some(hash)`; `null` (and a genuinely absent field, for older hosts) still returns `None`.
- [ ] Regression tests with a scripted host (or equivalent) covering: string, null, absent, and at least number/object mistyped shapes.
- [ ] No host-side change; `ServerFrame::ModuleInfo` serialization is unchanged.

body:
# id(world_net): create_world reads a missing or mistyped `created` flag as Ok(false) — a malformed `world_created` reply reports "exists" for a world that may not exist

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ origin/main 075b2de904)

`WorldClient::create_world` (`pkgs/id/src/world_net.rs:1226`) checks only that the reply frame's `type` is `"world_created"`, then reads the outcome flag with a silent default:

- `pkgs/id/src/world_net.rs:1245` — `Ok(reply["created"].as_bool().unwrap_or(false))`

`false` is a real, meaningful answer here: the host (`pkgs/id/src/world_session/mod.rs:977-986`) replies `ServerFrame::WorldCreated { world, created }` where `created: false` means the world already existed. So a `world_created` reply whose `created` field is missing or mistyped (host bug, version skew, hostile host) is indistinguishable from "already exists" — the client reports `Ok(false)` and never errors.

The sole caller trusts the bool directly:

- `pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs:772-777` (`id world create`): `println!("{}", if result? { "created" } else { "exists" })` and exits `Ok(())` — a malformed reply prints `exists` and exits 0, telling the operator the world is there when the reply never actually said so.

Sibling `WorldClient` methods refuse exactly this shape instead of defaulting: `set_isolation` requires the field with `.context("host sent no isolation")` (`world_net.rs:1155-1158`), `info_details` requires `world_id`/`current_sequence` with context errors (`:1473-1478`), `set_schedule`/`cancel_schedule` parse via `from_value` with "host sent a malformed schedule map" (`:909`/`:943`), and `manifest_state` does the same (`:979`).

## Reproduction (probe, laptop)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-world-reply-defaults` (verbatim extraction of the reply tail `world_net.rs:1237-1245`; only the transport is replaced by passing the reply `Value` in):

- control `{"type":"world_created","world":"arena","created":true}` -> `Ok(true)`
- control `{"type":"world_created","world":"arena","created":false}` -> `Ok(false)` (legitimate "exists")
- MISSING `created` (`{"type":"world_created","world":"arena"}`) -> `Ok(false)` — silently reads as "exists"
- MISTYPED `created` (`"created":"true"`) -> `Ok(false)` — silently reads as "exists"

PROBE PASS (cargo run --offline, laptop). Note the same probe run also reproduced the `policy_request` null/verbatim behavior — that half is already tracked as #6625 and is NOT part of this issue.

## Why it matters

`id world create` is how an operator provisions a world. Today a garbled success reply produces a confident, wrong answer — "exists", exit 0 — for a world whose creation was never confirmed. The operator (or a script checking the output) proceeds as if the world is ready; the failure surfaces later, elsewhere, with no trace back to the bad reply. This is the same silent-default family as #6620 (compile) and #6621 (read_worlds), in a distinct method with a distinct user-visible lie.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `WorldClient::create_world` rejects a `world_created` reply whose `created` field is missing or not a bool, with an error in the existing style (e.g. "host sent no created flag" / "host sent a malformed world_created reply")
- [ ] Well-formed replies still return `Ok(true)` (newly created) and `Ok(false)` (already existed) unchanged; the refusal path (non-`world_created` type) still surfaces the host's message
- [ ] A regression test feeds `create_world` (or its reply extraction) the missing/mistyped shapes and asserts Err; the two control shapes assert Ok(true)/Ok(false)
- [ ] `cargo test -p id world_net` (laptop or CI) green, including the existing create-world-over-iroh tests (`world_session/tests.rs:1724-1770` region)

Distinct from: #6620 (compile reply defaults), #6621 (read_worlds reply drops), #6624 (caps/update_caps report), #6625 (policy_request policy) — same family, different method and consequence. The typed server side is `ServerFrame::WorldCreated { world, created }` (`pkgs/id/src/world_session/mod.rs:981-984`); only the client extraction is unchecked.

title: bws: lib/bws-to-sops.sh --check is silently skipped when --dry-run is also passed — freshness check exits 0 without comparing (PR #6401)

body:
## Finding (unaddressed PR review comment)

PR #6401 — "feat(bws): names-only --check freshness mode for the SOPS mirror (#5451)" — is merged, and a CodeRabbit finding on it was never fixed or responded to (merged PRs have no grace period; the concern was verified live on current main).

- Reviewer: coderabbitai[bot], 2026-11-06T00:23:10Z (Minor · Functional Correctness)
- Comment: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/6401#discussion_r4487652599
- File: `lib/bws-to-sops.sh:99`

Essence of the comment ("Give `--check` precedence over `--dry-run`"): "When both options are supplied, the script exits successfully after listing keys, even if the mirror is stale. It never compares the mirror. Give `--check` precedence so its exit status reports freshness."

## No-response evidence

- The inline thread contains only the CodeRabbit comment (id 4487652599) — no replies (fresh `gh api pulls/6401/comments` read, 2026-11-06). (The PR's two Codex findings were replied to and fixed in-PR by dezren39; this CodeRabbit finding was not.)
- GraphQL `reviewThreads` for PR #6401: the thread is `isResolved: false`.
- The PR merged at head `36e37f4c62b41898155c21307a6492e5cd80c2fd` with the flagged ordering intact, and no follow-up commit on main has changed it (verified by the current-main read below).

## Still-live evidence

Read on current main (2026-11-06), `lib/bws-to-sops.sh`: argument parsing sets `DRY_RUN=true` and `CHECK=true` independently, and the dry-run branch runs first and exits:

```bash
if [ "$DRY_RUN" = true ]; then
  echo "Would write $COUNT secret(s) to ..."
  jq -r 'keys[] | "  " + .' <<<"$DOC"
  exit 0
fi

if [ "$CHECK" = true ]; then
  # Names-only freshness check ... Exit 0 when the mirror is fresh, 1 on
  # any drift ... and 2 on operational failure
  ...
fi
```

So `lib/bws-to-sops.sh --check --dry-run` (in either order) lists key names and exits 0 without ever decrypting or comparing the mirror — a caller combining the flags gets a "fresh" success signal for a check that never ran. This is the script the scheduled `bws-freshness` workflow relies on for drift detection (#5451).

Dedupe: searched open/closed issues for "dry-run check bws", "6401", "bws-to-sops" on 2026-11-06 — no issue covers this flag-precedence defect. Issue #5451 is the parent freshness-check task PR #6401 implements; it does not record this defect.

## Acceptance criteria

- Fix the defect: when both `--check` and `--dry-run` are supplied, `--check` takes precedence (the freshness comparison runs and its 0/1/2 exit status is reported), or the combination is rejected with a clear error and a non-zero exit — it must never exit 0 without comparing; cover the combined-flags case in `lib/bws-to-sops-check.test.sh`; OR resolve this issue with a documented decision explaining why the current behavior is intended.
- Do not reply to or resolve the source PR review thread from the fix work (per the pr-comment-review job rules); the correction lands as a follow-up change or is decided here.

## Finding (unaddressed PR review comments)

PR #6360 — "ci: register test-suite coverage contract (#6186)" — is still open, and two Copilot review findings on the same defect were never fixed or responded to. The 24-hour grace period for open PRs has passed (comments 2026-11-05T19:10:08Z; rechecked 2026-11-06).

- Reviewer: Copilot, 2026-11-05T19:10:08Z — https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/6360#discussion_r4484834991 — `.github/test-suite-registry.json:33`
- Reviewer: Copilot, 2026-11-05T19:10:08Z — https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/6360#discussion_r4484835054 — `.github/test-suite-registry.json:46`

Essence of the comments: the registry is a machine-readable contract, but some `scope.boundaries[*].path` values are not patterns. Comment 4484834991: "These `scope.boundaries[*].path` values are presented as machine-readable patterns, but this entry embeds two globs in a single string using natural language (`and`). If tooling will consume this registry, it won't be able to reliably interpret the boundary. Split into two boundary entries or change `path` to an array (e.g. `paths: [...]`) so patterns remain unambiguous." Comment 4484835054: "This boundary's `path` value is descriptive prose rather than a path/glob like the other entries, which makes the registry inconsistent and harder to validate mechanically. If this is meant to be a categorical boundary rather than a filesystem pattern, consider introducing a separate field (e.g. `category`) or replacing this with concrete glob patterns."

## No-response evidence

- Neither inline thread has any reply (fresh `gh api pulls/6360/comments` read, 2026-11-06).
- GraphQL `reviewThreads` for PR #6360: both threads are `isResolved: false`.
- No fix followed the comments: the PR's last commit (`b690fac5c8`, 2026-11-05T19:03:41Z — which did fix the separate Codex omitted-suites finding) predates the Copilot review (19:10:07Z), and the PR head is still `b690fac5c895d22b8263a6d1b7c8ef8adc631e2e`.

## Still-live evidence

Read on the PR head (`b690fac5`, 2026-11-06), `.github/test-suite-registry.json` `scope.boundaries` still contains both flagged values verbatim:

- `"path": "doc/**/spikes/** and doc/**/research-round*/**"` (two globs joined by natural-language `and`)
- `"path": "fixtures, golden data, and test helper/generator files"` (descriptive prose, no glob at all)

The other boundary entries are single concrete globs (`pkgs/id/**`, `pkgs/mcpx/**`, `pavex/**`, `pkgs/id/vendor/**`), so a Phase 4 ratchet / inventory consumer parsing `path` as a pattern will silently mis-scope these two boundaries. Issue #6186 itself specifies the registry form as "a machine-readable manifest under `.github/` (parseable by Phase 4's ratchet)" — these two values do not meet that contract.

Dedupe: searched open/closed issues for "test-suite-registry", "6360", "registry boundaries" on 2026-11-06 — no issue covers this defect. Issue #6186 is the parent task PR #6360 implements; it states the machine-readable requirement but does not record that these two boundary values violate it.

## Acceptance criteria

- Fix the defect: make every `scope.boundaries[*].path` value a single machine-readable glob — split the combined `doc/**` entry into two boundary entries (or move to a `paths` array schema), and give the fixtures/helpers boundary concrete glob patterns or a separate non-pattern field (e.g. `category`) that the schema distinguishes from `path`; keep any registry validator green; OR resolve this issue with a documented decision explaining why these values are safe for the Phase 4 consumer as-is.
- Do not reply to or resolve the source PR review threads from the fix work (per the pr-comment-review job rules); the correction lands in the PR itself or is decided here.
