## Finding (unaddressed PR review comment)

PR #6367 — "id(currency_poc): remember failed transfer IDs in InMemoryLedger (IdAlreadyFailed)" — is still open, and a CodeRabbit finding on it was never fixed or responded to. The 24-hour grace period for open PRs has passed (comment 2026-11-05T20:15:12Z; rechecked 2026-11-06).

- Reviewer: coderabbitai[bot], 2026-11-05T20:15:12Z (Minor · Functional Correctness)
- Comment: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/6367#discussion_r4485525977
- File: `pkgs/id/src/currency_poc/ledger.rs:189`

Essence of the comment ("Return `IdAlreadyFailed` for resubmitted failed transfer IDs"): "`validate_and_stage` returns the stored original error for a failed ID. A transfer that failed with `DebitAccountNotFound` keeps returning that error after the account exists. The `TransferError::IdAlreadyFailed` doc comment and the live binding's status mapping both expect `IdAlreadyFailed`." Suggested fix: check `failed_transfers.contains_key(&transfer.id)` and return `TransferError::IdAlreadyFailed` instead of the stored error.

## No-response evidence

- The inline thread contains only the CodeRabbit comment (id 4485525977) — no replies (fresh `gh api pulls/6367/comments` read, 2026-11-06).
- GraphQL `reviewThreads` for PR #6367: the thread is `isResolved: false`.
- PR head is unchanged since the review: head `7d5d64f9402afec929275a8d494611aa727f84d0` is the PR's single commit; no fix commit followed the comment.

## Still-live evidence

Read on the PR head (`7d5d64f9`, 2026-11-06), `pkgs/id/src/currency_poc/ledger.rs:188-190`:

```rust
// Check if this transfer ID was previously recorded as failed
if let Some(error) = self.failed_transfers.get(&transfer.id) {
    return Err(*error);
}
```

The stored original error is returned, not `IdAlreadyFailed`. The contract mismatch is visible in the same tree: `ledger.rs:101-103` defines `IdAlreadyFailed` with a doc comment naming the resubmission (`id_already_failed`) behavior, and the live TigerBeetle binding (`pkgs/id/src/currency_poc/tb_ledger.rs:223`) maps `Status::IdAlreadyFailed => Err(TransferError::IdAlreadyFailed)` — so the in-memory backend and the live backend return different errors for the same resubmission, and the in-memory error can go stale (it keeps naming a cause, e.g. a missing account, after that cause is fixed).

Dedupe: searched open/closed issues for "IdAlreadyFailed", "6367", "6150" on 2026-11-06 — no issue covers this return-value defect. Issue #6150 is the parent task PR #6367 implements; it asks for failed IDs to be remembered, and does not record that the implementation returns the wrong error for them.

## Acceptance criteria

- Fix the defect: `validate_and_stage` in the InMemoryLedger returns `TransferError::IdAlreadyFailed` for any resubmitted ID present in `failed_transfers`, matching the doc comment and the live binding's mapping; add a test where a transfer fails (e.g. `DebitAccountNotFound`), the cause is then fixed, and resubmission still returns `IdAlreadyFailed`; OR resolve this issue with a documented decision explaining why returning the stored original error is the intended contract (and reconcile the doc comment / binding expectation with that decision).
- Do not reply to or resolve the source PR review thread from the fix work (per the pr-comment-review job rules); the correction lands in the PR itself or is decided here.

## Finding (unaddressed PR review comments)

PR #6367 — "id(currency_poc): remember failed transfer IDs in InMemoryLedger (IdAlreadyFailed)" — is still open, and three review findings on the same defect were never fixed or responded to. The 24-hour grace period for open PRs has passed (comments 2026-11-05T20:09–20:15Z; rechecked 2026-11-06).

- Codex P2: chatgpt-codex-connector[bot], 2026-11-05T20:09:19Z — https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/6367#discussion_r4485465073 — `pkgs/id/src/currency_poc/ledger.rs:398`
- CodeRabbit Major: coderabbitai[bot], 2026-11-05T20:15:12Z — https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/6367#discussion_r4485526014 — `ledger.rs:398`
- CodeRabbit Major: coderabbitai[bot], 2026-11-05T20:15:12Z — https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/6367#discussion_r4485526024 — `ledger.rs:398`

Essence of the comments: when a chain fails, the failure-recording block inserts **every** leg of the chain into `failed_transfers` with the failing leg's error. Codex: "Do not mark an already-posted ID as failed when rejecting a conflicting submission" — if a transfer already posted and a later submission reuses its ID with different fields, `ExistsWithDifferentFields` gets permanently cached against the posted ID, and because `validate_and_stage` checks `failed_transfers` before `transfers`, every subsequent byte-identical retry of the original successful transfer returns the cached error instead of `Exists`, breaking the documented idempotent-retry contract. CodeRabbit (6014): "When a chain fails on leg B, every leg, including valid leg A, is stored with B's error. Resubmitting A in a valid chain then returns B's error instead of posting. Legs after B, which were never validated, are also stored. Store only `chain[failing_offset].id`." CodeRabbit (6024): "Skip any ID that is already in `self.transfers`."

## No-response evidence

- None of the three inline threads has any reply (fresh `gh api pulls/6367/comments` read, 2026-11-06).
- GraphQL `reviewThreads` for PR #6367: all three threads are `isResolved: false`.
- PR head is unchanged since the reviews: head `7d5d64f9402afec929275a8d494611aa727f84d0` is the PR's single commit and exactly the commit Codex reviewed; no fix commit followed the comments.

## Still-live evidence

Read on the PR head (`7d5d64f9`, 2026-11-06), `pkgs/id/src/currency_poc/ledger.rs` (failure-recording block, ~lines 386–400):

```rust
if !matches!(
    error,
    TransferError::LinkedEventFailed | TransferError::LinkedEventChainOpen
) {
    for transfer in chain {
        self.failed_transfers.insert(transfer.id, error);
    }
}
```

The loop inserts every chain leg, with no `self.transfers` (already-posted) check and no restriction to the failing offset — all three findings reproduce verbatim on the current head.

Dedupe: searched open/closed issues for "failed_transfers", "6367", "IdAlreadyFailed", "ledger failed transfer" on 2026-11-06 — no issue covers this recording defect. Issue #6150 is the parent task PR #6367 implements (the ledger previously forgot failed IDs entirely); it does not record this over-recording defect in the implementation.

## Acceptance criteria

- Fix the defect: record a failure only for the transfer that actually failed (the failing offset), and never record an ID that is already posted in `self.transfers`; add/extend tests covering (a) a valid sibling leg of a failed chain remains submittable, and (b) a byte-identical retry of an already-posted transfer still returns `Exists` after a conflicting submission with the same ID was rejected; OR resolve this issue with a documented decision explaining why the current behavior stands.
- Do not reply to or resolve the source PR review threads from the fix work (per the pr-comment-review job rules); the correction lands in the PR itself or is decided here.

body:
## Problem

`WorldClient::manifest_state` (`pkgs/id/src/world_net.rs:961-995`, on
`origin/main` 075b2de904) reads the two fields of the `world_state`
reply with opposite strictness:

```rust
Some("world_state") => Ok((
    reply["seed"].as_u64(),                                   // :978
    serde_json::from_value(reply["schedules"].clone())
        .context("host sent a malformed schedule map")?,      // :979-980
)),
```

`schedules` is decoded strictly and a malformed map errors. `seed` is
read with a bare `as_u64()`: a **present but mistyped** seed — `"42"`,
`-1`, `1.5`, `{}` — silently becomes `None`, indistinguishable from
the one legitimate `None` case, a capability-only read where the host
deliberately hides the seed (#240; `world_session/tests.rs:685`
"schedule_and_world_state_frames_round_trip_and_hide_the_seed").

## Verified this run (laptop probe, real `id` crate, scripted host)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-policy-wt/pkgs/id/tests/probe_policy_reply.rs`,
test `probe_manifest_state_seed_shapes`:

- CONTROL `{"type":"world_state","seed":42,"schedules":{"a":1}}` →
  `Ok((Some(42), {"a":1}))`.
- CONTROL no `seed` field (capability-only shape) → `Ok((None, {}))`
  — the legitimate `None`.
- CASES seed `"42"` / `-1` / `1.5` / `{}` → all `Ok((None, {}))`,
  identical to the legitimate hidden-seed result.
- ORACLE mistyped `schedules` (`{"a":"x"}`) → `Err`, proving the
  sibling field in the same reply is validated.

## Why it matters

The consumer is world-manifest capture
(`commands/world.rs:1145`, `capture_world_state`): it takes the
returned seed into `WorldState { seed: seed.unwrap_or(0), .. }`, the
state that `id world apply`/diff reconciles against. An admin read
whose seed arrived mistyped is silently downgraded to the
capability-only shape and then baked in as **seed 0** — a fabricated
install seed in the captured manifest, with no error anywhere. The
reply's own contract already distinguishes the two cases (field absent
= hidden; field present = the seed); the client just has to check
presence before type, the way the schedules arm checks its type.

## Acceptance criteria

- `manifest_state` errors when the `seed` field is present but not a
  `u64` (string, negative, float, object, array, bool), with an error
  naming the malformed seed; a genuinely absent seed still returns
  `None` for capability-only reads.
- Regression tests with a scripted host covering: numeric seed,
  absent seed, and each mistyped-seed shape; mistyped `schedules`
  continues to error.
- No change to the host side or to the #240 seed-hiding behavior.

title: id(world_net): policy_request never validates the policy reply — a missing or mistyped policy reads as Ok(null)/verbatim, so an isolation-boundary change reports success with no policy

labels.name: task/small-fix

labels.name: app/id

body:
## Problem

`WorldClient::policy_request` (`pkgs/id/src/world_net.rs:1112-1127`, on
`origin/main` 075b2de904) — the shared reply path for
`set_cross_world_write` (:1061), `force_cross_world_write` (:1080) and
`set_file_scope` (:1097) — checks only that the reply's `type` is
`"policy"` and then returns the policy field unchecked:

```rust
Ok(reply["policy"].clone())   // :1126
```

A `policy` reply with the `policy` field **missing** returns `Ok(null)`;
a mistyped field (e.g. `123`, `"deny"`) returns `Ok(123)` / `Ok("deny")`
verbatim. These are admin operations on the world's isolation boundary —
whether other worlds may write into this one, and whether its files are
confined to the world root — so a malformed reply silently reads as a
successful policy change whose resulting policy is unknown.

The host's real reply is always a structured object:
`world_session/mod.rs:1058` sends `ServerFrame::Policy { world, policy }`
with `policy: WorldPolicy` (`world/mod.rs:510` — isolation,
cross_world_write, cross_world_forced, file_scope,
file_write_override). And the sibling client method in the same file is
the oracle: `set_isolation` (:1135) refuses a missing/mistyped field
with `.context("host sent no isolation")`. `policy_request` is the
outlier.

## Verified this run (laptop probe, real `id` crate, scripted host)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-policy-wt/pkgs/id/tests/probe_policy_reply.rs`
(scripted host answering one canned frame per connection, same harness
as the #6620/#6621 probes), test `probe_policy_reply_shapes`:

- CONTROL well-formed `policy` object via `set_cross_world_write` →
  `Ok` with the policy object (`cross_world_write: true`).
- CASE `{"type":"policy","world":"arena"}` (field missing) via
  `set_cross_world_write` → `Ok(null)`.
- CASE `policy: 123` via `set_file_scope` → `Ok(123)`.
- CASE `policy: "deny"` via `force_cross_world_write` →
  `Ok("deny")`.

## Why it matters

The CLI prints the returned value as the outcome of the change
(`commands/world.rs` CrossWorldWrite / ForceCrossWorldWrite / FileScope
arms pretty-print the result and exit 0). A buggy, downgraded, or
hostile host that answers `{"type":"policy"}` with no usable policy
leaves the operator believing cross-world writes were enabled/disabled
or the file scope was set — with `null` (or garbage) as the only
"evidence". For an isolation control, "changed, probably" is the
failure mode the reply exists to prevent. Same unchecked-clone family
as #6624 (`caps`/`update_caps`), different endpoint and a
security-boundary payload; the fix here is independent.

## Acceptance criteria

- `policy_request` rejects a `policy` reply whose `policy` field is
  missing or not a well-formed `WorldPolicy` object (deserialize into
  the typed struct, adding `Deserialize` to `WorldPolicy` if needed,
  or validate the object shape explicitly), with an error naming the
  malformed reply — mirroring `set_isolation`'s "host sent no
  isolation" refusal in the same file.
- All three callers (`set_cross_world_write`,
  `force_cross_world_write`, `set_file_scope`) inherit the check via
  the shared helper.
- Regression tests with a scripted host: missing field, numeric,
  string, and array `policy` values all error; a well-formed policy
  reply still returns the policy unchanged.

body:
# id(world_net): caps() and update_caps() never validate the host's capability report — a missing or malformed `report` reads as Ok(null), so an admin grant/revoke reports success with no report

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ origin/main 075b2de904)

`WorldClient::caps` (`pkgs/id/src/world_net.rs:791`) and `WorldClient::update_caps` (`:817`) check only that the reply frame's `type` is `"caps"`, then return the report field unchecked:

- `pkgs/id/src/world_net.rs:809` — `Ok(reply["report"].clone())` (caps)
- `pkgs/id/src/world_net.rs:842` — `Ok(reply["report"].clone())` (update_caps)

serde_json indexing a missing key yields `Value::Null`, and a present-but-mistyped report is cloned verbatim. Neither function ever parses the report as the typed `CapsReport` (`pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/world_caps.rs:1426`: `granted`/`requested`/`missing`/`usage`/`policy`/`catalog`, with `#[serde(default)]` only on `ceiling`/`effective`/`view_failures`).

The strict oracle already exists in-tree, twice:

- `pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs:1119-1121` and `:1231-1233` take the same `caps()` result and run `serde_json::from_value::<CapsReport>(...)` with `.context("host returned a malformed capability report")` — those callers reject exactly what `caps()` itself accepts.
- Sibling `WorldClient` methods validate their payloads the same way: `set_schedule`/`cancel_schedule` (`world_net.rs:909`/`:943`, "host sent a malformed schedule map"), `manifest_state` (`:979`), `metrics` (`:1444`, "host sent invalid metrics"), and `install_wasm` checks the returned hash against the uploaded module's hash (`:1401-1408`).

But other callers trust the `Value` directly:

- `pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs:301-320` (`id world caps`): the `update_caps` result is pretty-printed and the command exits `Ok(())` — a malformed reply prints `null` and reports a successful grant/revoke.
- `pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs:658` (world profile): the `caps()` result is embedded into the profile JSON as `"caps": <value>` — a malformed reply silently becomes `"caps": null` in an otherwise successful profile.

## Reproduction (probe, laptop)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-caps-report` (verbatim extraction from `world_net.rs:801-809`, identical in `update_caps`; `CapsReport`/`CapUsage` copied verbatim from id-core; oracle = the `from_value::<CapsReport>` check from `commands/world.rs:1120`):

- control-valid: `caps()=Ok(<report>)`, oracle Ok
- control-refusal (`type:"error"`): `caps()=Err(<host message>)`
- 8 malformed shapes — missing `report`, `report:null`, `"yes"`, `123`, `[]`, `granted` as a string, `policy` as a number, and a report missing required fields — **all** return `caps()=Ok(<verbatim value>)` while the oracle rejects every one with "host returned a malformed capability report"

PROBE PASS (release build, laptop).

## Why it matters

`update_caps` is an admin mutation: it grants/revokes what a world program may use. Today a host (buggy, older, or hostile) that answers `{"type":"caps"}` with a missing/garbled report gets a success exit and a printed `null` instead of an error — the operator believes the capability change took effect and has no report to check it against. The query path has the same hole in the profile output. This is the same silent-default family as #6620 (compile) and #6621 (read_worlds), in a distinct method pair with a mutation on one side.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `WorldClient::caps` and `WorldClient::update_caps` reject a `caps` reply whose `report` is missing or does not deserialize as `CapsReport`, with an error in the existing style (e.g. "host returned a malformed capability report" / "host sent a malformed capability report")
- [ ] Well-formed reports — including pre-ceiling reports that rely on the `#[serde(default)]` fields (cf. the existing old-report test at `world_net.rs:2621`) — still return Ok and round-trip unchanged for existing `Value` consumers
- [ ] A regression test feeds both methods (or their shared extraction) the malformed shapes above and asserts Err; the refusal-reply path still surfaces the host's message
- [ ] `cargo test -p id world_net` (laptop or CI) green, including the existing caps-over-iroh tests

Distinct from: #6620 (compile reply), #6621 (read_worlds reply), #6600/#6578 (paging cursors). The typed server side is `ServerFrame::Caps { report }` (`pkgs/id/src/world_session/types.rs:396`); only the client extraction is unchecked.

body:
## Summary

`WorldClient::read_worlds_reply` (`pkgs/id/src/world_net.rs:1194-1222`) — the shared reply parser behind the admin `list_worlds` and the public `directory` — validates the reply's top level but silently discards per-entry shape failures:

```rust
let worlds = reply["worlds"]
    .as_array()
    .context("worlds reply had no list")?          // top level: refused
    .iter()
    .filter_map(|w| {
        Some((
            w["name"].as_str()?.to_owned(),          // entry dropped on any miss
            w["open"].as_bool()?,
            w["presence"].as_u64().unwrap_or(0) as usize,  // mistyped presence -> 0
        ))
    })
    .collect();
```

An entry whose `name` is not a string, whose `open` is not a bool, or that is not an object at all is dropped from the listing with no error; an entry whose `presence` is mistyped is kept but reported with presence `0`. The caller receives `Ok` and a listing that looks complete.

## Why it matters

- `list_worlds` is the admin inventory: `id world list` is how an operator sees which worlds a host holds. A world the host lists with a malformed entry (host bug, version skew between host and client) becomes invisible to the operator while still existing — and being served — on the host.
- The fabricated `presence: 0` is worse than a drop: a world reported as empty invites exactly the operations (close, reap, ignore) that an occupied world should not get.
- The function's own top level already refuses shape errors (`worlds reply had no list`), and sibling parsers in the same file refuse missing/mistyped fields (`info_details`: "host omitted world id" / "host omitted sequence"; `install_wasm`: "host omitted installed module hash"). Per-entry silence is the inconsistent outlier.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe at origin/main `075b2de904` (worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-compile-wt`, real `id` crate, integration test `pkgs/id/tests/probe_worlds_reply.rs` in the probe worktree only): a scripted iroh host (raw `ProtocolHandler`, canned frames via the crate's own `frames::read_frame`/`write_frame`) answers `list_worlds`, result printed per case; test 1 passed.

- Control — two well-formed entries → `Ok(("lobby", [("lobby", true, 3), ("arena", false, 0)]))`.
- Mixed — five entries: valid `lobby`; `{"name": 123, ...}`; `{"name": "ghost", "open": "yes", ...}`; `{"name": "arena", "open": false, "presence": "many"}`; `"not-an-object"` → `Ok(("lobby", [("lobby", true, 3), ("arena", false, 0)]))`: three worlds silently gone, arena's presence silently rewritten to 0, no error.
- Top-level control — `"worlds": {...}` (not a list) → `Err("worlds reply had no list")`, confirming the function refuses shape errors at the top level.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `worlds` entry that is not an object, or whose `name` / `open` / `presence` is missing or mistyped, makes `list_worlds` / `directory` fail with an error naming the entry/field — or, if triage prefers partial listings, the drop is surfaced explicitly (count + reason in the result), never silent. Silent `filter_map` + `unwrap_or(0)` is the defect either way.
- [ ] Well-formed replies return exactly the host's entries, unchanged.
- [ ] A test pins the behavior with a scripted host reply containing one malformed entry among valid ones.
- [ ] No change to the refusal path (non-`worlds` replies) or the top-level list check.

title: id(world_net): compile() silently defaults a malformed 'compiled' reply — missing/mistyped module_hash, sequence and diagnostics all read as Ok(("", 0, ""))

labels.name: task/small-fix

body:
## Summary

`WorldClient::compile` (`pkgs/id/src/world_net.rs:773-775`) reads the host's `compiled` reply with `unwrap_or_default()` on every field:

```rust
Some("compiled") => Ok((
    reply["module_hash"].as_str().unwrap_or_default().to_owned(),   // :773
    reply["sequence"].as_u64().unwrap_or_default(),                  // :774
    reply["diagnostics"].as_str().unwrap_or_default().to_owned(),    // :775
)),
```

A `compiled` reply that is missing `module_hash`, or carries it (or `sequence` / `diagnostics`) under the wrong JSON type, is silently read as `("", 0, "")` and returned as success. Every sibling reply parser in the same file refuses exactly this shape:

- `invite` — `reply["capability"].as_str().map(str::to_owned).context("invite reply had no capability")`
- `install_wasm` — `installed["module_hash"].as_str().context("host omitted installed module hash")?` plus an equality check against the locally computed hash ("host acknowledged a different module hash")
- `info_details` — `.context("host omitted world id")?` / `.context("host omitted sequence")?`, and invalid provenance is a hard error
- `metrics` — `serde_json::from_value(...).context("host sent invalid metrics")`

`compile` is the only reply path that manufactures a plausible-looking success value out of a malformed reply.

## Why it matters

- `id world compile` (`pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs:272-280`) prints the returned hash alone on stdout (`println!("{hash}")`) precisely so scripts can capture it. A malformed reply yields an empty line and exit 0 — the caller captures an empty module hash as a successful compile.
- `id world apply`'s `InstallModule` step (`commands/world.rs:1277-1284`) treats `compile()` returning `Ok` as the step having applied; a field-less `compiled` reply counts the step done even though no module hash was ever reported.
- Sequence `0` is a real sequence value (a fresh world's first state), so the default is indistinguishable from a genuine reply — there is no way for a caller to detect the substitution after the fact.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe at origin/main `075b2de904` (worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-compile-wt`, real `id` crate, integration test `pkgs/id/tests/probe_compile_reply.rs` in the probe worktree only): a scripted iroh host (raw `ProtocolHandler`, canned frames via the crate's own `frames::read_frame`/`write_frame`) answers the compile request, and `WorldClient::compile` is called against it.

- Control — `{"type":"compiled","module_hash":"abc123","sequence":7,"diagnostics":"warn"}` → `Ok(("abc123", 7, "warn"))`.
- Missing `module_hash` — `{"type":"compiled","sequence":7,"diagnostics":""}` → `Ok(("", 7, ""))` (silently defaulted).
- Mistyped fields — `{"type":"compiled","module_hash":123,"sequence":"7","diagnostics":42}` → `Ok(("", 0, ""))` (all three silently defaulted).
- Bare — `{"type":"compiled"}` → `Ok(("", 0, ""))`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `compile()` errors (with a message naming the missing/invalid field, in the style of the sibling parsers) when a `compiled` reply omits `module_hash` or `sequence`, or carries any of `module_hash` / `sequence` / `diagnostics` under a wrong JSON type.
- [ ] A well-formed `compiled` reply returns its fields unchanged (existing behavior).
- [ ] A test pins the refusal: a scripted/broken host reply missing `module_hash` makes `id world compile` fail non-zero instead of printing an empty hash.
- [ ] No change to the refusal path (non-`compiled` replies still surface the host's message) or to any other reply parser.

# infra: repo-queue PostgREST `timeout: global` failures are lane-visible again — recurrence after #6450 closed (2026-11-06 ~21:15–21:31Z)

## Evidence (lane code-w shift, 2026-11-06)

Five consecutive `fleet queue` calls failed with the same signature, exit 4:

- `fleet queue health --queue repo-health-code-pilot` — failed ~21:15Z, ~21:17Z, ~21:20Z, ~21:31Z (4 attempts)
- `fleet queue claim --queue repo-health-code-pilot --worker repo-worker-code --lane code-w --lease-seconds 2700` — failed ~21:24Z (1 attempt)

Every call: stderr `repo-queue: PostgREST request failed: timeout: global`, exit 4, each taking ~90s before failing. No task could be claimed; the lane-W shift ended with zero tasks worked. No claim was recorded by the failed claim call as far as the client can tell (the verb errored; atomic claim semantics + the 57014 rollback rationale in #6450 say a timed-out write rolled back — worth a broker-side confirm).

## Why this is a recurrence, not #6450 itself

#6450 closed COMPLETED 2026-11-06T17:44:35Z after PR #6584 deployed the posture (broker health cache 12s TTL, paced enqueues, shared backoff base 500ms ×2 cap 20s ×6 attempts on 57014/PGRST002). Its closing note recorded that in the post-deployment window (~17:48–17:51Z) timeouts still occurred at the DB but **no queue verb surfaced a failure** — calls were slow (~50s worst) but succeeded. Its close rule: the issue closes when a captured failure window proves the root cause, or the posture eliminates the windows.

This window breaks that: verbs are surfacing failures again, repeatedly, over 15+ minutes — either a longer/deeper window than backoff can absorb, a different failing leg (health aggregation was already the expensive verb: one `repo_queue_health` read cost 6,315 ms in the #6450 capture), or the sandbox client vintage (the #6450 note said installed client binaries update at the next fleet install/switch — the client-side backoff may not be live on this sandbox yet).

## Pointers

- Standing capture from #6450 arm (a): cron `queue-capture-6450` + broker failure-events log (`~/.local/state/queue-broker/failure-events.jsonl`) should have this window — check `hidden_files/queue-capture-6450/captures/` for a failure capture covering 21:15–21:31Z and correlate the pg_stat delta.
- Related but distinct: #6616 (backoff `is_retryable` substring-matching can misclassify permanent errors as statement timeouts).
- Prior occurrences: #6450 (2026-11-06, closed), #5370 (2026-11-04, closed).

## Acceptance

- The 21:15–21:31Z window is attributed from the capture stream (failing verb + DB-side cause), or a broker/client fix ships that makes this window class non-lane-visible, with the verification recorded here.
- Confirm no orphan claim was left by the failed 21:24Z claim call (task claimed by repo-worker-code / lane code-w with no checkpoint would be the tell).

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/id/src/conversion.rs` computes conversion quotes and fees with a hand-rolled 256-bit intermediate (`U256`: `mul_u128`, `mul_factor`, shift-and-subtract `divmod`, lines 158–281) so results that fit `u128` are never lost to intermediate overflow. This is money arithmetic: `convert_amount` (line 299) and `fee_amount` (line 347) decide destination amounts and fees for the conversion engine (#2063).

The in-repo property tests only exercise a **bounded** domain:

- `convert_amount_matches_naive_oracle_on_bounded_domain`: amounts `< 2^64`, rate terms `< 2^32`, scales `<= 9`.
- `convert_amount_satisfies_the_floor_invariant`: amounts/rate terms `< 2^50`, scales `<= 6`.
- `fee_amount_matches_naive_oracle`: principals `< 2^100`.

The wide region the U256 exists for — amounts and rate terms above `2^64` up to `u128::MAX`, scale differences up to the full `MAX_SCALE = 38`, the 256-bit-overflow-to-`Overflow` verdict path in `convert_amount`'s scale fold — is covered only by two hand-picked examples (`wide_intermediate_recovers_results_the_poc_quote_loses`, `true_overflow_is_an_error_not_a_saturation`). A regression in `divmod`, `mul_factor`, or the scale fold in that region would pass every existing test.

## Verification this run (2026-11-06, laptop @ 2bb307550b)

Probe crate `~/git/fleet/probe-conversion` (laptop): `U256` + `convert_amount` + `fee_amount` copied verbatim from `src/conversion.rs`, driven by 5,000 randomized vectors (amounts/rate terms drawn from `<1000`, `<2^64`, full `u128`, powers of two ±1, and `u128::MAX`−small; scales 0–44 including 37/38/39; zero rate numerator/denominator cases; fee_bps 0–19,999) against a Python bignum oracle implementing the documented formula and error precedence.

**Result: 5,000 / 5,000 match.** The implementation is correct today — this issue is about locking that in, not fixing a live bug.

Also checked this run and found correct (no issue): `id-core` `unicode::is_format_char` matches the Unicode 16.0 Cf set exactly (170 code points, oracle: Python `unicodedata` 16.0.0).

## Fix

Add property tests to `conversion.rs` covering the wide domain with a named oracle, per the testing doctrine (PBT with an explicit oracle for arithmetic invariants):

- Full-range generators: amounts and rate terms across the whole `u128` range (including values `> 2^64`, powers of two ±1, `u128::MAX`), scales across `0..=MAX_SCALE` in both directions, zero rate numerator, and the boundary where the scale-folded numerator crosses 256 bits.
- Oracle: either an exact bignum reference or the floor invariant in exact arithmetic (the current invariant property bounds its domain precisely because its `u128` check arithmetic would overflow — the wide version needs a formulation that stays exact, e.g. checking via the U256-free decomposition or a dev-dependency bignum used only in tests).
- `fee_amount`: extend the oracle property to full-range principals.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] New proptests in `pkgs/id/src/conversion.rs` generate amounts/rate terms above `2^64` and scales up to 38, and pass.
- [ ] The wide-domain oracle is named in the test docs and shares no code with the U256 implementation under test.
- [ ] The 256-bit-overflow scale-fold path asserts `ConvertError::Overflow` from generated (not only hand-picked) inputs.
- [ ] Existing conversion tests still pass unchanged.

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/normal

body:
# fleet-queue(backoff): is_retryable substring-matches the whole error text — a permanent RPC error naming task 57014 (or 157014, 570149, …) is retried as a statement timeout

## Summary

The shared #6450 retry policy classifies an error as belonging to the
statement-timeout class by substring search over the **entire error text**,
not by the PostgREST error's `code` field. The queue RPCs' own permanent
error messages embed the task ID verbatim, so any permanent failure on a
task whose ID contains the digits `57014` is misclassified as a retryable
statement timeout — at both retry layers.

## Evidence (verified this run, origin/main `2bb307550b`)

`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/backoff.rs:35-36`:

```rust
pub fn is_retryable(err_text: &str) -> bool {
    err_text.contains("57014") || err_text.contains("PGRST002")
}
```

The text searched is the broker's whole error string
(`queue_broker.rs`: `HTTP {status} from PostgREST: {body trimmed to 500}`),
which includes the PostgREST body's `message` field. The RPC functions
raise permanent errors with the task ID interpolated, e.g.
`pm-stack/opencode-claimant/migration-0023.sql:99`:

```sql
raise exception 'fail_repo_task: task % is not claimed by %', p_task_id, p_worker;
```

(same shape at `:209` for `park_task`, and the `bind_repo_task_lane_session`
raises at `:435` / migration-0024 `:146`.)

Probe (laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-backoff-wt`, the real `backoff.rs` compiled
via `#[path]` from a clean `origin/main` export; controls pass):

```
genuine 57014 code      -> true  (want true)
permanent, task 12345   -> false (want false)
permanent, task 57014   -> true  (want false) BUG
permanent, task 157014  -> true  (want false) BUG
permanent, task 570149  -> true  (want false) BUG
BUG_CASES_TRUE=3/3
```

The permanent cases use code `P0001` (the default for `raise exception`)
with messages in exactly the migrations' format.

## Why it matters

- **Compounding retries of a verb that can never succeed.** The broker
  retries 6 attempts (`queue_broker.rs:308-315`), then the repo-queue
  client's `call` sees the same text in the broker envelope and retries the
  whole round trip 6 more times (`client.rs:284-287`) — up to 36 RPC
  attempts and minutes of jittered backoff for a definitive
  "not claimed by you" answer. Task IDs are already past 11000 and grow
  monotonically; IDs containing `57014` (57014, 570140–570149, 157014,
  257014, …) are certainties, not hypotheticals.
- **The safety argument is keyed to the real code.** The policy's
  no-double-apply guarantee (backoff.rs module docs) rests on the error
  *actually* being 57014/PGRST002 — Postgres cancelling the statement. A
  substring false positive steps outside that argument's premise.
- **Spurious failure capture.** On exhaustion the broker appends the error
  to the #6450 failure-events file (`record_failure_event`), so a permanent
  not-claimed error on such a task pollutes the capture the timeout-mining
  job reads as genuine 57014 evidence.

Distinct from #6450 (the outage + the posture itself, closed): this is the
classifier's matching rule, introduced with the posture. Not the
substring-free negative cases already pinned in backoff.rs tests
(`PGRST102`, validation text, `no matching claimed row` with no ID digits).

## Acceptance criteria

- `is_retryable` (or its replacement) decides from the PostgREST body's
  parsed `code` field — exactly `57014` or `PGRST002` — not from a substring
  anywhere in the message/detail/hint text. Where the body is not JSON, the
  match must require the code in a code position (e.g. `"code":"57014"` /
  `"code": "57014"`), never bare digits in prose.
- New tests: permanent RPC errors (`P0001`) whose messages embed task IDs
  57014, 157014, and 570149 classify as **not** retryable; genuine
  `57014`/`PGRST002` code-field bodies still classify retryable; an error
  whose *detail/hint* mentions 57014 while its code is something else is
  not retryable.
- Both call sites (broker `postgrest`, client `call`) keep working with no
  signature change beyond what the classifier needs, and the existing
  backoff tests still pass.

# id(world_ssh): the /records drain never validates its cursor — a non-string next_after silently ends the listing as if complete, and a non-advancing cursor re-requests the same page ~18,700 times

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ origin/main `2bb307550b`)

`pkgs/id/src/world_ssh.rs`, the `Some("records")` arm of the SSH world-session frame handler:

- `:1014` — `let after = value["next_after"].as_str().map(str::to_owned);` A missing **or non-string** `next_after` (number, bool, object) collapses to `None`, indistinguishable from a legitimate end-of-pages.
- `:1018-1035` — continuation is decided purely by `records_prefix.is_some() && after.is_some() && records_drained < MAX_RECORDS_TOTAL_BYTES` (1 MiB of *rendered* text, `:1276`). The only stop marker is `truncated = after.is_some() && records_drained >= MAX_RECORDS_TOTAL_BYTES` (`:1027`). There is **no cursor-advance check and no page-count bound**, and the parse at `:1014` never distinguishes "host said no more pages" from "host sent a malformed cursor".
- `render_records_value` (`:1434-1457`) prints the "more records; fetching next page" line only when `next_after.is_some()`, so the silent-stop case renders exactly like a complete listing.

Probe (laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-ssh-records/probe.py`, exact transliteration of `:1010-1040` + `render_records_value`):

- **Case A** — one page `{records: {a: 1}, sequence: 7, next_after: 123}` → 0 continuations, no truncation note: the drain ends and the partial listing is presented as complete.
- **Case B** — host repeats the same cursor (`next_after: "k1"`, empty page) → **18,724 continuation requests** before the rendered-byte cap finally stops the drain; every response re-renders the same page to the user's terminal.
- **Case C** — empty-string cursor `""` → same 18,724-request loop (the cursor never advances past the start).

## Contrast with the sibling consumers

The `world_net` consumers of the same host pages validate exactly this:

- `WorldClient::records` (`world_net.rs:1605-1632`) requires `next_after` to equal the page's last key and to strictly advance past the previous cursor, and refuses otherwise.
- `admin_event_history` (`world_net.rs:~1740`) ensures the cursor matches the last key and advances (`"admin history record cursor did not advance"`).

The SSH drain is the one records consumer that took the byte-cap fix (its total-bytes bound is real and tested) without the cursor contract — so a buggy or hostile host can silently truncate a user's `/records` listing, or pin the session re-requesting one page tens of thousands of times. This is the same failure family as #6505/#6578 (host-page trust in `world_net`), on the one surface those fixes did not cover.

## Why it matters

`/records` over SSH is an operator's view of a world's structured state. A listing that silently stops mid-world reads as ground truth; a stuck drain floods the terminal and the host with duplicate requests. Both outcomes come from one unvalidated host value.

## Acceptance criteria

- A `records` frame whose `next_after` is present but not a string is treated as a malformed page (error / visible truncation notice), never as a clean end-of-pages.
- A `next_after` that does not strictly advance past the cursor that produced the page stops the drain with a visible notice instead of re-requesting.
- A page-count bound complements the rendered-byte bound (or the advance check makes the count bound unnecessary — say which, in the code).
- Tests cover: non-string `next_after`, repeated cursor, empty-string cursor, and a normal multi-page drain still completing; oracle = the `world_net` cursor contract (#6505/#6578 behavior).

body:
## Summary

`scripts/fleet/repo-universe/generate.py` — offline mode does not require `--forks-org-json`. Omitting it (while providing `--org-json` and `--user-json`) silently regenerates the repo-universe artifact with the entire developing-today-forks enumeration emptied: every GitHub-only forks-org repo disappears from the artifact, with exit 0 and no warning.

This is the exact failure the offline guard exists to prevent, and the exact repo loss #5615 fixed for `--live`: opencode and openchamber live in developing-today-forks since 2026-11-04.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ 083d1a4324, origin/main)

Code, `scripts/fleet/repo-universe/generate.py`:

- `:347-353` — the offline `missing` check lists only `("--org-json", args.org_json)` (:350) and `("--user-json", args.user_json)` (:351). `--forks-org-json` (arg defined :306-307) is absent.
- `:103-105` — `load_enumeration(None)` returns `[]` silently, so the missing capture becomes an empty source, not an error.
- `:359-362` — the forks capture is merged from `load_enumeration(args.forks_org_json)` (:361), so `None` merges as zero repos.
- The comment at `:344-346` states the invariant the check is supposed to enforce: "Both captures are required offline: a missing one would silently regenerate with that source emptied, deleting its GitHub-only repos from the artifact." There are now three captures; the check covers two.

Probe (real `generate.py` as a subprocess, fixture captures in the shape of `test_generate.py`; probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-repo-universe-forks` on the laptop):

- Control, all three captures: exit 0; `developing-today-forks/some-tool` and `developing-today-forks/opencode` present in the artifact.
- Control, omit only `--user-json`: exit 2, no output written, error `offline mode requires --user-json (or use --live)`.
- Control, omit only `--org-json`: exit 2, no output written.
- Case, omit only `--forks-org-json`: **exit 0, output written** (`wrote …: 4 repos, 0 overrides applied`); `developing-today-forks/some-tool`, `developing-today-forks/opencode`, and `developing-today-forks/openchamber` are **all absent** from the artifact, while the org and user repos are still present.

Why the existing test does not catch it: `scripts/fleet/repo-universe/test_generate.py::test_offline_mode_requires_both_captures` passes `--org-json` only — it omits `--user-json` and `--forks-org-json` together, so the user-json guard fires and masks the forks gap. There is no test that omits each capture singly.

Related: #5615 (closed — added the forks-org enumeration), #1650 (closed — piece 1 generator), #1511 (open — parent tracker).

## Why it matters

The artifact `doc/fleet/repo-universe.yaml` is the maintained inventory the issue checker (#1651) consumes to decide which repos get watched. A single forgotten flag on an offline regeneration silently unwatches/drops the forks org — including opencode and openchamber, two of the four fleet repos — and the run reports success, so the loss is only visible as a large unexplained diff (or, if committed without a careful read, as missing repos downstream).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Offline mode with any one of `--org-json`, `--forks-org-json`, `--user-json` omitted fails via `ap.error` (non-zero exit), names the missing flag(s), and writes no output — for each flag singly.
- [ ] `test_generate.py` covers omitting each capture singly (not just two at once), asserting non-zero exit and no output file.
- [ ] All-three-captures and `--live` behavior unchanged; existing repo-universe tests pass.

You are "Bolt" ⚡ - a performance-obsessed agent who makes the codebase faster, one optimization at a time.

Your mission is to identify and implement ONE small performance improvement that makes the application measurably faster or more efficient.


## Boundaries

✅ **Always do:**
- Run commands like `pnpm lint` and `pnpm test` (or associated equivalents) before creating PR
- Add comments explaining the optimization
- Measure and document expected performance impact

⚠️ **Ask first:**
- Adding any new dependencies
- Making architectural changes

🚫 **Never do:**
- Modify package.json or tsconfig.json without instruction
- Make breaking changes
- Optimize prematurely without actual bottleneck
- Sacrifice code readability for micro-optimizations

BOLT'S PHILOSOPHY:
- Speed is a feature
- Every millisecond counts
- Measure first, optimize second
- Don't sacrifice readability for micro-optimizations

BOLT'S JOURNAL - CRITICAL LEARNINGS ONLY:
Before starting, read .jules/bolt.md (create if missing).

Your journal is NOT a log - only add entries for CRITICAL learnings that will help you avoid mistakes or make better decisions.

⚠️ ONLY add journal entries when you discover:
- A performance bottleneck specific to this codebase's architecture
- An optimization that surprisingly DIDN'T work (and why)
- A rejected change with a valuable lesson
- A codebase-specific performance pattern or anti-pattern
- A surprising edge case in how this app handles performance

❌ DO NOT journal routine work like:
- "Optimized component X today" (unless there's a learning)
- Generic React performance tips
- Successful optimizations without surprises

Format: `## YYYY-MM-DD - [Title]
**Learning:** [Insight]
**Action:** [How to apply next time]`

BOLT'S DAILY PROCESS:

1. 🔍 PROFILE - Hunt for performance opportunities:

  FRONTEND PERFORMANCE:
  - Unnecessary re-renders in React/Vue/Angular components
  - Missing memoization for expensive computations
  - Large bundle sizes (opportunities for code splitting)
  - Unoptimized images (missing lazy loading, wrong formats)
  - Missing virtualization for long lists
  - Synchronous operations blocking the main thread
  - Missing debouncing/throttling on frequent events
  - Unused CSS or JavaScript being loaded
  - Missing resource preloading for critical assets
  - Inefficient DOM manipulations

  BACKEND PERFORMANCE:
  - N+1 query problems in database calls
  - Missing database indexes on frequently queried fields
  - Expensive operations without caching
  - Synchronous operations that could be async
  - Missing pagination on large data sets
  - Inefficient algorithms (O(n²) that could be O(n))
  - Missing connection pooling
  - Repeated API calls that could be batched
  - Large payloads that could be compressed

  GENERAL OPTIMIZATIONS:
  - Missing caching for expensive operations
  - Redundant calculations in loops
  - Inefficient data structures for the use case
  - Missing early returns in conditional logic
  - Unnecessary deep cloning or copying
  - Missing lazy initialization
  - Inefficient string concatenation in loops
  - Missing request/response compression

2. ⚡ SELECT - Choose your daily boost:
  Pick the BEST opportunity that:
  - Has measurable performance impact (faster load, less memory, fewer requests)

  - Doesn't sacrifice code readability significantly
  - Has low risk of introducing bugs
  - Follows existing patterns

3. 🔧 OPTIMIZE - Implement with precision:
  - Write clean, understandable optimized code
  - Add comments explaining the optimization
  - Preserve existing functionality exactly
  - Consider edge cases
  - Ensure the optimization is safe
  - Add performance metrics in comments if possible

4. ✅ VERIFY - Measure the impact:
  - Run format and lint checks
  - Run the full test suite
  - Verify the optimization works as expected
  - Add benchmark comments if possible
  - Ensure no functionality is broken

5. 🎁 PRESENT - Share your speed boost:
  Create a PR with:
  - Title: "⚡ Bolt: [performance improvement]"
  - Description with:
    * 💡 What: The optimization implemented
    * 🎯 Why: The performance problem it solves
    * 📊 Impact: Expected performance improvement (e.g., "Reduces re-renders by ~50%")
    * 🔬 Measurement: How to verify the improvement
  - Reference any related performance issues

BOLT'S FAVORITE OPTIMIZATIONS:
⚡ Add React.memo() to prevent unnecessary re-renders
⚡ Add database index on frequently queried field
⚡ Cache expensive API call results
⚡ Add lazy loading to images below the fold
⚡ Debounce search input to reduce API calls
⚡ Replace O(n²) nested loop with O(n) hash map lookup
⚡ Add pagination to large data fetch
⚡ Memoize expensive calculation with useMemo/computed
⚡ Add early return to skip unnecessary processing
⚡ Batch multiple API calls into single request
⚡ Add virtualization to long list rendering
⚡ Move expensive operation outside of render loop
⚡ Add code splitting for large route components
⚡ Replace large library with smaller alternative

BOLT AVOIDS (not worth the complexity):
❌ Micro-optimizations with no measurable impact
❌ Premature optimization of cold paths
❌ Optimizations that make code unreadable
❌ Large architectural changes
❌ Optimizations that require extensive testing
❌ Changes to critical algorithms without thorough testing

Remember: You're Bolt, making things lightning fast. But speed without correctness is useless. Measure, optimize, verify. If you can't find a clear performance win today, wait for tomorrow's opportunity.

title: opencode-claimant(poll/claimant): snapshot rewrite dropped poll.py's test-pinned cap API (36/36 tests error) and inverted cap_room — idle reads as saturated, busy launches unbounded

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: app/pm-stack
labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

body:
## Bug

`pm-stack/opencode-claimant/poll.py` and `claimant.py` no longer implement the session-cap contract that `test_poll.py`, `prompt.md`, and `README.md` describe — and the claimant's cap arithmetic is inverted, so it launches nothing when idle and over-launches when busy.

Verified on laptop primary @ `083d1a4324d0` (== origin/main), 2026-11-06.

### 1. The pinning test suite errors 36/36 — the functions it tests do not exist

`test_poll.py` (36 tests, header: fixtures mirror the live server's session shape verified 2026-10-31) calls `poll.is_active_root`, `poll.count_active_roots`, `poll.summarize_cap`, `poll.is_candidate`, `poll.parse_lease_ms`, and `poll.is_stuck_bound`, and reads `poll.CAP`. None of these exist in current `poll.py` (its only functions are `get_active_root_sessions`, `get_stuck_bound_tasks`, `get_candidates`, `main`).

Probe (laptop, `requests` stubbed, real modules): `python3 -m unittest pm-stack/opencode-claimant/test_poll.py` → `Ran 36 tests — FAILED (errors=36)`, every error `AttributeError: module 'poll' has no attribute …`.

Root cause: repo-keeper snapshot commit `8b8e7a1295` (2026-11-06 00:27 CST) rewrote `poll.py` (571 lines changed) and `claimant.py` in the same pass that left `test_poll.py` untouched (0 lines). The pre-snapshot `poll.py` (`8b8e7a1295^`) had exactly this API: `CAP = 36` (:54), `is_candidate` (:72), `parse_lease_ms` (:105), `is_stuck_bound` (:123), `is_active_root` (:164), `count_active_roots` (:181), `summarize_cap` (:185), plus repo-queue-binary `fetch_claimed`.

### 2. Cap room is the active-session COUNT, in both entry points — inverted

- `poll.py:244`: `cap_room = get_active_root_sessions()` — that function (:37) returns a **count** of active roots (or `None` on error). `prompt.md:62-63` and README say `cap_room = 36 − active_root_sessions`, and "if cap_room is 0 or null, launch nothing". With 0 active sessions poll now reports `cap_room: 0` (launch nothing, though room is 36); with 40 active it would report 40.
- `claimant.py:347`: same assignment. `CONCURRENCY_CAP = 36` (:23) is referenced nowhere else in the file (grep count = 1, the definition). `main()` then: count `<= 0` → prints "Cap saturated … exiting" (:354-356); otherwise "Launching up to {count} tasks" (:360).

Probe (laptop, stubbed `requests.get`, real `claimant.py`): 0 active → count 0 → cap-saturated branch taken; 40 active (over the 36 cap) → count 40 → not saturated, launches up to 40 **more**.

### 3. `poll.py` doesn't recognise the server's session shape

`poll.py`'s counter requires `session.get("isRoot") == True` and reads `time.idle`/`time.prompted`. The verified live shape (test fixtures, and pre-snapshot code) is root = no `parentID`/`parent_id`, activity = `time.updated` falling back to `time.created`, finished = `time.idle` or top-level `outcome`.

Probe: one fresh fixture-shaped root (`time.created` 5 min ago, `time.updated` 1 min ago, no `isRoot` field) → `poll.get_active_root_sessions()` returns **0**; `claimant.py`'s differently-shaped counter returns 1 for the same session (it checks `parent_id` + `time.last_message`/`created` — a third, mutually inconsistent shape).

## Why it matters

The claimant is the lane that launches opencode sessions for handed-off queue tasks. As written: an idle server reads as saturated (no launches — consistent with the symptom in #6533, handed-off tasks cycling claim → handed_off → park with `session_id` still null), and a busy server reads as having the most room (launches bounded by the active count, never by the 36 cap — the over-concurrency the cap exists to prevent, cf. #5016). The 36-test suite that pinned the correct behaviour (#3026 gate, #4758 recovery, fail-closed on an unreadable active set) is still in the tree and still named in `.github/workflows/pm-stack-tests.yml`, but every test in it errors, so the regression is invisible to anyone who doesn't run it by hand.

Related (distinct): #6533 (symptom: handed-off tasks never launched), #4757 (GET /api/session truncates at 50), #5016 (cap consumed by lane runners), #5951 (closed; CI wiring for this suite), #5400 (a different snapshot/migration-dropped claimant binding mode).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `python3 -m unittest pm-stack/opencode-claimant/test_poll.py` passes 36/36 against the real `poll.py` (restore the test-pinned API — `CAP`, `is_active_root`, `count_active_roots`, `summarize_cap`, `is_candidate`, `parse_lease_ms`, `is_stuck_bound` — or, if the API is deliberately being replaced, rewrite the suite in the same change so a green run still pins the cap/candidate/stuck-bound rules; a suite that errors 36/36 is not a pin).
- [ ] `cap_room` reported by `poll.py` and used by `claimant.py` is `CAP − active_root_sessions` (36 cap), is `null`/unknown — never a fabricated number — when the session list or the server active set cannot be read, and the claimant launches nothing in that case.
- [ ] Probe check: 0 active roots → room 36 and launches proceed; 40 active roots → room 0 and no launches (today: the exact opposite in both cases).
- [ ] Both counters recognise the same, verified live session shape (`parentID` root marker, `time.updated`/`created` activity, `time.idle`/`outcome` terminal markers) — one fresh fixture-shaped root counts as 1 in both `poll.py` and `claimant.py`.
- [ ] The restored `poll.py` candidate/stuck-bound logic reads queue state through the repo-queue binary path the pre-snapshot version used (not the `/api/queue/<queue>/tasks` route on the OpenCode server in current `get_candidates`/`get_stuck_bound_tasks`), or documents and tests whatever route replaces it.

## Evidence

- PR #3678 (https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/3678): OPEN, verified twice via REST this run — `mergeable=false`, `mergeable_state=dirty`; head `3453e65cb1` on branch `queue/5518-3013-search-memoize`; created 2026-11-01T12:34:40Z, last updated 2026-11-01T16:18:41Z. Body: "Fixes #3013 (queue task 5518)".

body:
# fleet(dispatch-test): scan counts only the first GitHub page — in-progress runs, per-run jobs, workflows and forks beyond 100 are silently invisible, so `active` undercounts and a busy home can be chosen

## Summary

`fleet dispatch-test scan` (and the scan inside `submit`) decides which execution home has free Actions capacity. Every GitHub list it reads is fetched exactly once with `per_page=100` and no `page` parameter, and the counting helpers count only the items in that single returned page. Anything past item 100 is silently invisible:

- in-progress **runs** past the first 100 are never visited, so none of their jobs count;
- a single run's **jobs** past the first 100 never count (one GitHub run can fan out to 256 matrix jobs, so a single run can hide up to 156 jobs);
- the **workflow** list past 100 can hide `fleet-dispatch-test.yml`, reporting `workflow=no` for a home that has it;
- **forks** past 100 per repo are never discovered as execution homes.

The crate already knows the exact-count pattern: the queued-runs term uses the response's `total_count` (`total_count(&queued)`), which is correct no matter how many pages there are. The in-progress and jobs terms ignore the `total_count` sitting in the same responses and count the page array instead — so the reported `active=<n>` is a lower bound presented as an exact count, and `eligible` (`active < threshold`) can be `yes` for a home that is actually at or over threshold. With a large configured threshold (e.g. `--threshold 1000`) even the jobs of the first 100 runs undercount enough to flip eligibility; at the default 40, a >100-job matrix run whose first page shows <40 active jobs while later pages hold the rest flips it too.

## Evidence (file:line, origin/main @ fa2bb52a4827)

All in `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-dispatch-test/src/lib.rs`:

- `:469` — in-progress runs: one GET `…/actions/runs?status=in_progress&per_page=100`; `:473` — per-run jobs: one GET `…/runs/{run_id}/jobs?per_page=100`; `:478` — queued runs: one GET (but counted via `total_count`, see below); `:481` — workflows: one GET `…/actions/workflows?per_page=100`; `:537` — forks: one GET `…/repos/{repo}/forks?per_page=100` per level in `discover_scopes`.
- A crate-wide grep for `page=` / `Link` finds nothing: no list call ever requests a second page.
- `:374-388` `run_ids()` collects ids only from the returned `workflow_runs` array; `:396-413` `count_active_jobs()` counts only the returned `jobs` array. Neither consults `total_count`.
- `:391-394` `total_count()` exists and `:482` uses it for the queued term — the internal oracle showing the exact shape was available and used for exactly one of the three counted terms.

## Verification (this run, laptop, real crate)

Probe worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-dispatch-scan-wt` (origin/main export; one probe test module appended, no production code changed), `cargo test -p fleet-dispatch-test probe_page_bound_counts` — **1 passed**:

```
PROBE jobs counted=30 total_count=256
PROBE runs ids=100 total_count=250
```

- A jobs body with `total_count: 256` and a 100-job first page (30 in_progress, 70 completed) counts **30** — if the remaining 156 jobs are in progress (a 256-job matrix run), the true active count is 186 and scan reports 30, i.e. `eligible=yes` at the default threshold 40.
- A runs body with `total_count: 250` and a 100-run first page yields **100** run ids; the other 150 runs' jobs are never fetched.
- `fork_full_names` likewise returns exactly the returned page (100 of a larger fork list are discovered, the rest never become scopes).

## Why it matters

- `scan`/`submit` exist to *not* pile work onto a saturated execution home (#6580). An undercount that reports a busy home as free defeats the one job of the capacity check, and the printed/JSON `active` number is wrong on its face — an operator (or the submit path) trusting it dispatches into congestion that the tool claimed was absent.
- The failure is silent: no error, no truncation marker; the JSON output carries the undercount as fact.
- The forks case silently shrinks the fleet of execution homes: copies past page 1 are never chosen, so capacity that exists is never used.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every GitHub list the scan reads is read completely: follow pagination (`page=` until a short page, or the `Link` header) for in-progress runs, per-run jobs, workflows, and forks — or, where a term only needs a count, use the response `total_count` consistently the way the queued term already does, with the choice justified per call site.
- [ ] `active` for a repo with >100 in-progress runs, or a run with >100 jobs, equals the true number of in_progress/queued jobs (tests pin both shapes, plus a >100-workflow and >100-fork shape).
- [ ] Existing counting tests keep passing; the documented queued-run approximation (crate docs) is unchanged — this is about un-read pages, not the approximation.
- [ ] If complete pagination is deliberately rejected for any call site, that site caps loudly (error or an explicit `truncated` marker in text + JSON output) instead of presenting a page-bound count as exact.

Related: #6580 (the design this implements), #6603 (the threshold-zero gap in the same scan path — distinct: that is input validation, this is incomplete reading).

title: fleet-config(dispatch-test): threshold = 0 is never validated — it loads cleanly and makes every execution home permanently ineligible, unlike the #6412 zero rule

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

body:
## Problem

`fleet-config`'s load-time zero rule (#6412) rejects a configured `0` for the three scalar numeric settings that existed then — `[proxy] egress_proxy_port`, `[dispatch] port`, `[proxy] idle_exit_secs` — because "a configured `0` for a scalar numeric setting is a misspelling-class error, never a value" (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs:395-423`, `Config::validate`).

The `[dispatch-test]` section landed later (#6580 / #6589) with a new scalar numeric setting, and it was never added to that rule:

- `DispatchTestConfig.threshold: Option<u64>` (`fleet-config/src/lib.rs:235-237`)
- `Config::dispatch_test_threshold()` returns the configured value verbatim via `unwrap_or(DEFAULT_DISPATCH_TEST_THRESHOLD)` (`fleet-config/src/lib.rs:596-600`) — so `threshold = 0` in `fleet.toml` loads cleanly and surfaces as `0`.
- The CLI path has the same hole: `parse_threshold` in `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-dispatch-test/src/lib.rs:254-263` accepts `--threshold 0` — its error message calls the value "a non-negative integer", so `0` passes.

## Why it matters

Eligibility is `workflow && active < threshold` (`fleet-dispatch-test/src/lib.rs:439-440`). With threshold `0`, `active < 0` is false for every possible count, so:

- `fleet dispatch-test scan` reports every copy `eligible=no` and `chosen: none`, with no hint that the threshold itself is the cause — it looks exactly like genuine fleet-wide saturation.
- `fleet dispatch-test submit` (unforced) always fails with "no eligible scope: no execution-home copy has active < 0 with the generic workflow present (job … remains queued in the store)" (`fleet-dispatch-test/src/lib.rs:973`) — and leaves a queued job row behind for a configuration error, not a capacity fact.

An operator who writes `threshold = 0` most plausibly means "no limit" (or made a typo); under the crate's own stated doctrine there is no zero spelling for that, and the field must be rejected at load naming the field, exactly like the #6412 three. A threshold of 0 can never be a meaningful capacity bound.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop primary `~/git/code` at `fa2bb52a4827300e26a68e1b9e750a0e3eecf54e` (== origin/main, clean). Probe crate on the laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-dispatch-test-threshold`, depending on the real `fleet-config` crate and calling `Config::load_from`:

- control, omitted threshold → loads, `dispatch_test_threshold() = 40` (the documented default)
- control, `threshold = 7` → loads, `dispatch_test_threshold() = 7`
- oracle (#6412 rule), `[proxy] idle_exit_secs = 0` → **rejected** at load: `[proxy] idle_exit_secs must not be 0; omit the field for the default (3600)`
- case, `[dispatch-test] threshold = 0` → **loads**, `dispatch_test_threshold() = 0`
- consequence check: `eligible(active=0, threshold=0, workflow=true)` evaluates to `false` — even a completely idle copy with the workflow present is ineligible.

Dedup: searches for "dispatch-test threshold", "threshold=0", "threshold zero" return the design #6580 and unrelated threshold issues only; #6412 (closed) covers the original three fields, which did not include this later-added setting. The sibling dispatch-test filing #6598 is a different defect (submit marks dispatched before the dispatch call).

## Acceptance criteria

- `Config::load_from` rejects `[dispatch-test] threshold = 0` with a Parse error naming `[dispatch-test] threshold` and the default (40), following the existing `validate()` message shape.
- `fleet dispatch-test scan|submit --threshold 0` fails as a usage error (exit 2) instead of scanning with a threshold nothing can satisfy.
- Tests pin both refusals; omitted threshold still yields 40 and positive values pass unchanged.
- No change to eligibility semantics for threshold ≥ 1, and no "0 means unlimited" spelling is introduced (per the #6412 doctrine).

title: cold-store-reaper(listings): list_backups and s3_list_objects have no page/result bound — a fresh-token page stream loops forever, accumulating rows

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.description: Package/app: cold-store-reaper (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Problem

Both listing loops in `pkgs/cold-store-reaper/cold_store.py` guard against a *stuck* cursor — a missing or repeated token raises — but neither bounds the *number of pages or accumulated results*, so a backend (or a hostile/buggy endpoint, or a proxy that mangles responses) that hands back a **fresh token on every page** makes the listing loop forever, growing the result list without limit:

1. **Drive — `ColdStore::list_backups`** (`cold_store.py:1211`, loop at `:1223`): termination is only `nextPageToken` falsy (`:1251-1253`) or repeated (`:1254-1257`, the #2426 fix). Every page appends to `out` (`:1245-1250`); there is no page cap and no result cap. `list_backups` feeds the `list-backups` CLI (`:2425`) and retention planning (`:1344`).
2. **S3 — `ColdStore::s3_list_objects`** (`cold_store.py:1805`, loop at `:1817`): the docstring states the progress guard — a truncated page must return a usable, advancing `NextContinuationToken`, else raise (`:1810-1816`, implemented `:1827-1834`, the #1632 fix). But a page stream that is *always* `IsTruncated=true` with a *new* token each time satisfies that guard on every iteration: `out.extend(page)` (`:1824`) grows forever and the function never returns.

The existing guards answer "is the cursor advancing?" — nothing answers "has this listing gone on implausibly long?". A real Drive folder of backups or an R2 bucket holds a bounded, knowable number of objects; an endless fresh-token stream is a malfunction, and the correct response is the same one the sibling guards already chose: raise a `ColdStoreError` naming the listing, not hang.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ origin/main fa2bb52a4827)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-coldstore-pages/probe.py` — the real `cold_store` module imported from the laptop primary, transports stubbed (`http_request` for Drive, `_s3_request` for S3), stub gives up with a sentinel after 5,000 calls:

- Drive control, finite: 2 pages (token then none) → returned, 2 calls, 2 rows. ✅
- Drive control, repeated token: same token every page → `ColdStoreError` ("files.list for backups repeated nextPageToken"), 2 calls. ✅
- **Drive defect:** every page returns 1 file and a brand-new `nextPageToken` → **still looping at 5,001 calls**; the stub's sentinel, not the listing, ended it.
- S3 control, finite: truncated page + token, then untruncated page → returned, 2 calls, 2 objects. ✅
- S3 control, repeated token: `IsTruncated=true` with the same token → `ColdStoreError` ("non-advancing NextContinuationToken"), 2 calls. ✅
- **S3 defect:** every page `IsTruncated=true` with a brand-new token → **still looping at 5,001 calls**; only the stub's sentinel ended it.

Probe verdict line: "PROBE PASS: both listings loop unbounded on fresh-token streams".

## Why it matters

These listings are the reaper's view of what exists: `list_backups` drives retention/prune planning and the operator `list-backups` command; `s3_list_objects` enumerates buckets for the same lifecycle work. A wedged endpoint, a token-minting bug server-side, or a response-rewriting proxy turns either call into a permanent hang with unbounded memory growth (the accumulated list) instead of a diagnosable error — in a tool whose whole job is unattended storage hygiene, a silent hang is the failure mode that pages nobody and prunes nothing.

Distinct from closed #2426 (Drive listing did not follow `nextPageToken` at all — now it does) and closed #1632 (S3 missing/empty/repeated token — now guarded): this is the remaining axis, *volume* — page/result count — which neither fix bounded. Sibling in spirit to open #6572 (github-backup drain pagination, different codebase and endpoint).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both `list_backups` (Drive) and `s3_list_objects` (S3) terminate with a `ColdStoreError` naming the listing when a page stream exceeds a generous page and/or result bound sized well above any real backup folder / bucket (the exact bound is the fixer's choice; it must be unreachable by a legitimate listing).
- [ ] Regression tests: a stubbed fresh-token page stream raises the new error for both listings (not a hang); the existing finite multi-page controls and the repeated/missing-token guards keep passing.
- [ ] Existing cold-store-reaper tests stay green.

title: id(world_net): admin_event_history treats a non-string or missing next_after as end-of-pages — the admin export, and fixtures recorded from it, silently truncate while complete stays true

labels.name: task/small-fix

body:
## Problem

In `pkgs/id/src/world_net.rs`, `WorldClient::admin_event_history` (the admin export behind `world_fixture::record`) validates a *string* `next_after` cursor strictly — it must equal the page's last key (`:1740-1748`) and advance past the previous cursor — but it never checks the cursor's *type*:

```rust
match frame["next_after"].as_str() {
    Some(next) => { /* equality + advance checks */ }
    None => break,
}
```

`.as_str()` yields `None` for a JSON `null` (the conforming terminator), for a **missing** `next_after` key, and for **any non-string value** (number, boolean, array, object) alike — and every one of those breaks the loop and returns `Ok(history)`. A malformed cursor is indistinguishable from a complete export.

The conforming host can only ever send a string or `null`: the sender, `event_history_admin_session` in `src/world_session/mod.rs`, sends `ServerFrame::Records { next_after: Option<String> }`, which serializes the key always, as a string or `null`. A missing or non-string cursor is therefore a malformed reply by construction — a host bug, a version-skewed host, or a hostile host — never a legitimate end of pages.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ origin/main 9123103344)

Probe: in-crate test in a laptop worktree (`~/git/fleet/probe-admin-history-wt`, test `probe_admin_history_malformed_cursor_silently_truncates`, rogue iroh host speaking the world ALPN, `event_count: 0`, `complete: true`):

- Control, conforming: page 1 `{a:1}` → `next_after:"a"`, page 2 `{b:2}` → `next_after:null` → `Ok`, 2 records. ✅
- **Defect N:** page 1 `{a:1}` → `next_after:123` (number) → `Ok` with **1 record** — the export silently stops after the first page; any later pages are never read, no error.
- **Defect B:** page 2 `{b:2}` → `next_after:true` (boolean) → `Ok`, 2 records — the malformed cursor accepted as the terminator.
- **Defect M:** page 2 `{b:2}` with **no `next_after` key at all** → `Ok`, 2 records — a missing cursor accepted the same way.

Sibling strictness in the same function shows the intended posture: `current_sequence` is extracted with `.as_u64().context("history reply has no sequence")?`, `complete` with `.as_bool().context(...)`, and `event_count` is type- and range-checked before it is trusted. The records cursor is the one field read leniently. Note this is the mirror of the `record_pages` half of #6578 (same `.as_str()` conflation, different loop): #6578's fix scope explicitly excluded this path as "already strict" — it is, for string *values*; the *type* check is what is missing here.

## Why it matters

This export is how a world's history is captured for fixtures: `world_fixture::record` (`src/world_fixture.rs:310`) embeds `history.records` directly into the fixture header and `history.complete` alongside it. A silently truncated records page stream produces a fixture that reports `complete: true` while its records map is missing every record after the malformed page — replay and verification then run against a world state that was never the world's, with no error anywhere. Admin exports are also the audit/backup path for a world; "the export succeeded" must mean the export is whole.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] In `admin_event_history`'s records loop, a `next_after` that is present but not a string and not JSON `null` (number, boolean, array, object) is a malformed-reply error, not end-of-pages; a missing `next_after` key is likewise an error (the conforming sender always emits the key). Only `null` terminates paging.
- [ ] Regression tests drive `admin_event_history` against stub/rogue replies covering: numeric cursor on the first page (error, not a 1-record `Ok`), boolean cursor on a later page (error), missing cursor key (error), plus the conforming control — string cursors then `null` — still returning `Ok` with all records.
- [ ] Existing world_net / world_session / world_fixture tests stay green (conforming hosts always send string-or-null, by construction).

Distinct from #6578 (the `record_pages` loop: empty advancing pages plus the same cursor-type conflation in that loop) and from #6505 (caps/ordering/non-advancing cursors in `record_pages`): this is the admin-history export loop in the same file, whose string-cursor checks are strict but whose cursor-type check is absent — and whose caller records the result into fixtures as `complete`.

title: fleet(dispatch-test): submit marks the job dispatched before the dispatch call — a failed dispatch leaves a permanently lying row

body:
## Bug: fleet(dispatch-test) `submit` marks the job `dispatched` before the dispatch call — a failed dispatch leaves a permanently lying row

`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-dispatch-test/src/lib.rs`, `verb_submit` (verified at laptop origin/main `867c695518`):

1. `:947` — INSERT the job row with `status='queued'`.
2. `:982` — UPDATE the row: `status = 'dispatched'`, with the chosen `target_repo`.
3. `:990-1004` — only *afterwards*: GET the repo's `default_branch` (`:992`, errors if absent) and POST `/repos/{repo}/actions/workflows/fleet-dispatch-test.yml/dispatches`.

Every failure in step 3 — a workflow that lacks the `workflow_dispatch` trigger (422), a missing workflow file (404), a repo body with no `default_branch`, a transport error — returns `Err` to the caller, but the row already says `dispatched`, and nothing ever corrects it. There is no later writer for a job whose workflow never started: `status` (`:1056`) faithfully reports `dispatched` forever for a job that will never run.

The ordering was clearly considered for the *other* failure window: the no-eligible-scope error at `:974` explicitly notes "(job {id} remains queued in the store)" — true and recoverable there, because step 2 has not run yet. The step-3 window has the opposite property and no such handling.

### Verification (laptop probe, this run)

Probe crate `~/git/fleet/probe-dispatch-test` on the laptop: the crate's real `lib.rs` with exactly two seams redirected — `GITHUB_API_BASE` pointed at a local stub GitHub, `resolve_named` returning a stub token (the Turso URL is config, pointed at a recording stub store). All submit logic byte-identical.

- **Case A (dispatch POST returns 422 "Workflow does not have workflow_dispatch trigger"):** `submit` prints `fleet dispatch-test: HTTP 422: GitHub API: ...` and exits **4**. The recording Turso stub's write sequence for the job ends with `UPDATE jobs SET target_repo = 'acme/fleet', status = 'dispatched', ... WHERE id = 'dt-mw5b5m76-4ac2'` — and **no corrective write of any kind follows**. The store's final state claims the job was dispatched; no workflow run exists.
- **Case B (control, dispatch POST returns 204):** exit 0, report JSON `status: "dispatched"` — the same write sequence, this time truthful.

### Why it matters

The jobs store is the tracking surface for this explicit-dispatch CI system (#6580): operators and agents read row status to know whether a test job ran. A `dispatched` row that never dispatched is indistinguishable from a real in-flight job — it will be waited on, and its missing results read as a hung run rather than a failed submit. The caller does see the submit error, but anyone (or any automation) consulting the store afterwards is misled, and there is no retry path that starts from the row's stated state.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `submit` whose dispatch POST (or the preceding `default_branch` fetch) fails does not leave the row in `dispatched`: either the `dispatched` UPDATE moves after a successful dispatch response, or the failure path writes a truthful terminal/intermediate status (e.g. back to `queued`, or a `dispatch_failed` status carrying the error).
- [ ] A regression test pins the ordering/state: with the dispatch call failing, the row's final stored status is not `dispatched` (stub GitHub + stub store, as in the probe); the success control still ends `dispatched`.
- [ ] The no-eligible-scope behavior (`:974`, row remains `queued`) is unchanged.

Design reference: #6580.

body:
## Finding (unaddressed PR review comment)

PR #6322 — "fix(atlas-search): cap get-chunk --neighbors at 100" — is still open, and a CodeRabbit review finding on it was never fixed or responded to. The 24-hour grace period for open PRs has passed (review 2026-11-05T17:18:47Z; rechecked 2026-11-06T18:08Z).

- Reviewer: coderabbitai[bot], review 5789043954, 2026-11-05T17:18:47Z
- Review: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/6322#pullrequestreview-5789043954
- File: `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-search/src/main.rs:782-785` (test module) / cap call at `main.rs:668`

Essence of the comment ("Add a command-level test for `get-chunk --neighbors` above the cap"): the cap in `cmd_get_chunk` (`main.rs:668`) is covered only by tests that call `count` directly with `Some(100)`. The command-level tests in `tests/cli_parity.rs` pass `--neighbors` only with `0` and `1`. Removing the cap from the `cmd_get_chunk` call would not fail any test. The suggested test invokes `get-chunk 2 --neighbors 101 --backend local` via `run_bin`, asserting exit code 2 and the bound message on stderr.

## No-response evidence

- PR #6322's only review is 5789043954; there are no inline comments and no replies to the review (verified by fresh `gh api pulls/6322/comments` and `pulls/6322/reviews` reads on 2026-11-06).
- PR head `34687774a198bb023399c83ef3a51b4f2295378e` is unchanged since the review and PR `updatedAt` is 2026-11-05T17:18:50Z — no fix commit followed the comment.

## Still-live evidence

Read on the PR head (`34687774`, 2026-11-06):

- `src/main.rs:668`: `let neighbors = count("--neighbors", args.neighbors, 0, Some(100))?;` — the command-path cap.
- `src/main.rs:781-793`: the only above-cap tests call `count("--neighbors", 101, 0, Some(100))` directly (unit level).
- `tests/cli_parity.rs`: `--neighbors` appears only in the `get_chunk_neighbors` case with value `"1"` (lines 150-161, 195-216) — no command-level invocation above the cap exists, so deleting the `Some(100)` at the `cmd_get_chunk` call site would fail no test.
