body:
# fleet(queue): dedupe-key cross-checks only run when the matching identity field is present — a packet whose identity arrives via a different field validates with a dedupe key naming a different issue/PR/set

## Summary

`validate_packet` in `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/validate.rs` cross-checks the packet's `dedupe_key` against the payload identity — but every family check in `dedupe_errors` (validate.rs:327) is conditional on the *matching* identity field being present:

- `fix`/`triage` (validate.rs:379-388): the key's issue number is compared only `if let Some(ino) = issue_no` — a packet whose identity is a `prs` list (or a pre-filing `source`) is never compared.
- `pr` (validate.rs:389-396): the key's PR number is checked only `if !pr_numbers.is_empty()` — a packet whose identity is an `issue` object is never compared.
- `pr-set` (validate.rs:397-413): the key's PR list is checked only `if !pr_numbers.is_empty()`.
- `set` (validate.rs:414-427): the key's origin issue is checked only when the `set` object happens to carry an `origin_issue` field — a non-empty `set` object without one (e.g. `{"prs": [605, 620]}`, the exact shape #5549's own test treats as a valid set identity) is never compared.

Meanwhile `manual_schema_errors` accepts any one of four identity shapes (`issue.number`, a non-empty `prs` list, a non-empty `set` object, or a `source {pr, finding}`), with no rule tying the shape to the dedupe family. So a packet can validate cleanly while its payload describes one piece of work and its dedupe key — the unique identity the queue dedupes on, forwarded verbatim by `task_from_packet` — names a completely different one.

## Evidence (verified this run, origin/main 9e20032d0c)

Probe on the laptop (crate `~/git/fleet/probe-queue-xcheck/probe`, built against the real `fleet-queue` crate from worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-queue-xcheck-wt` at origin/main, calling the real `validate_packet` + `task_from_packet`):

Controls — the cross-check fires when the matching field is present:
- `fix` key `issue:9999` + `issue {number: 9999}` → `errors=[]` (match passes)
- `fix` key `issue:8888` + `issue {number: 9999}` → `errors=["packet.dedupe_key: issue 8888 in key does not match payload.issue.number 9999"]`
- `pr` key `pr:222` + `prs [{number: 222}]` → `errors=[]`; `prs [{number: 111}]` → `errors=["packet.dedupe_key: PR 222 in key is not in payload.prs [111]"]`
- `set` key `set:9999:owed:…` + `set {origin_issue: 9999}` → `errors=[]`; key `set:8888:owed:…` → `errors=["packet.dedupe_key: origin issue 8888 does not match payload.set.origin_issue 9999"]`

Escape cases — mismatched key/identity pairs validate with `errors=[]` and the mismatched key is forwarded verbatim into the task row (`task_from_packet` output shown):
- `fix` key `issue:222` + identity `prs [{number: 111}]` only → `errors=[]`, `task_dedupe_key="repo-health:v1:fix:developing-today/code:issue:222"`
- `triage` key `issue:222` + identity `prs [{number: 111}]` only → `errors=[]` (only warning is the unrelated design-default `max_attempts` warning), key forwarded verbatim
- `pr` key `pr:222` + identity `issue {number: 111}` only → `errors=[]`, key forwarded verbatim
- `pr-set` key `111-222` + identity `issue {number: 9999}` only → `errors=[]`, key forwarded verbatim
- `set` key `set:9999:owed:…` + identity `set {"prs": [605, 620]}` (no `origin_issue`) → `errors=[]`, key forwarded verbatim
- `fix` key `issue:777` + identity `source {pr: 588, finding: "f"}` only → `errors=[]`, key forwarded verbatim
- `pr` key `pr:777` + identity `source {pr: 588, finding: "f"}` only → `errors=[]` — the key's PR (777) is not even the source PR (588), and nothing compares them

## Why it matters

The dedupe key is the queue's only duplicate-work guard: it is the deterministic identity a task is deduplicated on at enqueue. A packet whose key names issue #222 while its payload works PR #111 (a) blocks a later, correct packet for issue #222 as a "duplicate" of work that was never queued for it, and (b) lets a second packet for PR #111 through under a correct key, double-working the same PR. The #5482/#5510/#5549 line of fixes closed the *spelling* and *shape* holes in this same cross-check family (non-canonical numbers, placeholder identities); this is the remaining hole — the check itself is skipped when the identity arrives in a different field than the family expects. Whether the right rule is "each dedupe family requires its matching identity field" or "any identity field present must agree with the key" (with a stated carve-out shape for pre-filing `source` packets, whose key cannot yet name the unfiled issue) is the triage call; what is not defensible is the current silent pass.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validate_packet` rejects, with a field-named error in the existing style, any packet whose dedupe-key number(s)/origin do not match the payload identity it carries — for all five families (`fix`, `triage`, `pr`, `pr-set`, `set`), including when the identity is supplied via a different field than the family names, or explicitly requires the matching identity field per family.
- The pre-filing `source {pr, finding}` identity has a stated, tested rule (either its `pr` is cross-checked where the family allows it, or source-identity packets are restricted to a dedupe shape that cannot name a mismatched issue/PR).
- Every real packet shape in the fleet corpus still validates (the #5549 corpus check pattern: real packets already carry matching identities).
- Regression tests cover each escape case above plus the existing matching/mismatching controls; the broker `/validate` + `/enqueue` path (which shares `validate_packet`) rejects the same packets.

Distinct from: #5549 (identity *shapes* — placeholder `prs`/`set` elements; closed), #5510/#5482 (dedupe-key *spellings*; closed), #6430 (packet string-field *types*; open, different check), #6423/#6426 (`max_attempts`/`not_before` validation; open, different fields).

title: id(attestation): sign_claim never checks the outcome is in compute_state's domain — 'banana', '', 'DRAW' or an uppercase/truncated winner hex signs Ok and is ignored in every view

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

`sign_claim` (`pkgs/id/src/attestation.rs:208`) signs any `ResultClaim` whose body serializes — it never checks that `claim.outcome` is in the domain `compute_state` can ever count. `compute_state` (`attestation.rs:287-291`) counts a claim only when its outcome is `"draw"` or a seated player's lowercase 64-character hex id (`valid_outcome`). A claim signed with any other outcome string is therefore **dead on arrival**: it is ignored in every view, forever, and signing succeeds silently.

This is shape-only and knowable at sign time — `sign_claim` needs no agreement to know these outcomes can never count:

- `"banana"`, `""`, `"0x1234"` — not `"draw"`, not a hex id
- `"DRAW"` / `"Draw"` — the domain string is exact-case
- A winner's hex id in UPPERCASE, or truncated to 63 chars — `compute_state` builds player outcomes as lowercase `{byte:02x}` hex and compares by string equality

## Evidence (verified this run)

Probe on the laptop at `origin/main` `9e20032d0cf3034a2baea117caa60c115119138e` (worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-attestation-outcome-wt`, integration test `pkgs/id/tests/probe_attestation_outcome.rs` against the real `id` crate, 1 passed): two players sign identical genesis, then both sign claims concurring on one outcome, and `compute_state` is run over the signed objects.

- Controls: outcome `"draw"` → sign Ok, state `Agreed`; outcome = player X's lowercase hex → sign Ok, state `Agreed`.
- Malformed: `"banana"`, `""`, `"DRAW"`, `"Draw"`, uppercase winner hex, 63-char winner hex, `"0x1234"` → **sign_claim Ok for both players**, yet state computes `Proposed` — the concurring claims are silently ignored, so the match can never settle from these objects.

## Why it matters

This is the construction-vs-receipt asymmetry the crate has been fixing one signer at a time (#6422 currency, #6424 attestation signer, #6434 match_audit, #5623 artifacts): a signer produces a signed object no verifier will ever accept, with no error at the only moment the mistake is cheap to catch. Here the signer is a legitimate seated player (unlike #6424's non-player signer) making a formatting slip — e.g. an uppercase or truncated winner hex from a UI — and the match silently never reaches `Agreed`.

## Distinct from neighbours

- #6424: `sign_genesis`/`sign_claim` never check the *signer is a player* — different defect, different fix (needs the agreement at the sign site).
- #2868 (closed): `compute_state` never validated the outcome domain — fixed on the read side; the sign side was never gated.
- The remaining domain rule sign time cannot check (outcome names a *seated* player, not a third party's well-formed hex) stays a `compute_state` rule; this issue is only the shape half that is decidable from the claim alone.

## Acceptance criteria

- `sign_claim` refuses (new `SignError` variant, e.g. `InvalidOutcome`) any claim whose outcome is neither `"draw"` nor a 64-character lowercase hex string, before signing.
- Well-formed outcomes (`"draw"`, any 64-char lowercase hex) still sign Ok — including a third party's hex, whose seated-ness remains `compute_state`'s call.
- Tests pin: each malformed class above refused at sign time; controls sign Ok and still compute `Agreed` end-to-end; existing attestation suite (`tests/attestation_poc.rs`) green.
- No change to `compute_state`'s counting rules.

title: id(match_audit): sign_header/sign_footer never check version, roster, signer or seed commitment — signatures verify_integrity always rejects are produced silently

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Summary

`pkgs/id/src/match_audit.rs`: `sign_header` (line 404) and `sign_footer` (line 440) sign any header/footer presented to them — including shapes that `MatchLogV0::verify_integrity` (line ~467) rejects before or independently of the signature — so a caller can produce a well-formed Ed25519 signature that is dead on arrival, and signing succeeds silently.

`sign_header` performs no check at all before `sign_message`: it does not check `header.version == FORMAT_VERSION_V0` (verify_integrity rejects any other version with `UnsupportedVersion` as its first check), it does not call `validate_roster(&header.players)` (line 886: empty or duplicate-key rosters are rejected with `Roster`), and it does not check that the signer is one of `header.players` (`verify_signature_set` rejects a signature set containing a non-roster signer).

`sign_footer` has the same gaps and one more, even though it already receives the `header` it needs to check them: it does not check the signer is in `header.players`, and it does not check `Hash::digest(&footer.seed_reveal) == header.seed_commitment` — verify_integrity rejects a mismatching reveal with `SeedCommitmentMismatch`, and that check runs *before* the footer signatures are verified, so the signature never even gets considered.

This is the same dead-on-arrival signing shape as #6422 (`sign_authorisation` never calls `validate`) and #6424 (`sign_genesis`/`sign_claim` never check the signer is a player), in a module neither issue covers. The precedent for the fix shape is also in-tree: `sign_genesis` already refuses a duplicate-seat agreement at sign time (#2863, cited on #6424), and `chain::sign` refuses an extension that fails `ChainExt::validate` before signing.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ origin/main a2b4345e80)

Probe: laptop worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-match-audit-sign`, test `pkgs/id/tests/probe_match_audit_sign.rs` against the real `id` crate (`cargo test --test probe_match_audit_sign`). A well-formed control log (two roster players, version 0, matching seed reveal, no entries) passes `verify_integrity`. Against that control:

- `sign_header` with `version = 99`: returns Ok; a log assembled with those signatures fails `verify_integrity` with `unsupported match-audit format version 99`.
- `sign_header` with an empty `players` roster: returns Ok; the assembled log fails `verify_integrity` with `invalid match-audit roster`.
- `sign_header` with a duplicate roster (same player twice, different roles): returns Ok; the assembled log fails `verify_integrity` with `invalid match-audit roster`.
- `sign_header` by a signer who is not in the roster: returns Ok; the assembled log fails `verify_integrity` with `match-audit integrity failure: HeaderSignature`.
- `sign_footer` by a non-roster signer: returns Ok.
- `sign_footer` (by a roster player) over a footer whose `seed_reveal` does not digest to `header.seed_commitment`: returns Ok; the assembled log fails `verify_integrity` with `match-audit integrity failure: SeedCommitmentMismatch`.

Probe result: `1 passed` (control verifies; every bad shape above signs Ok and is rejected at verify).

## Why it matters

The match-audit log is the evidence format for contested match outcomes (#2814 lineage): header and footer signatures are what make a log attributable. A signing helper that happily signs an unsupported version, an empty/duplicated roster, a non-participant's attestation, or a seed reveal that contradicts the signed commitment produces evidence that every verifier discards — and the failure only surfaces later, at verification time, attributed to the log rather than to the moment the bad input was signed. Failing at sign time, with the specific `AuditErrorV0` reason, makes the error local and actionable, exactly as the sibling fixes for #6422/#6424 propose.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `sign_header` refuses (with an `AuditErrorV0` naming the reason) a header whose version is not `FORMAT_VERSION_V0`, whose roster is empty or contains duplicate player keys, or whose signer is not in the roster — before producing a signature.
- [ ] `sign_footer` refuses a signer who is not in `header.players`, and a footer whose `seed_reveal` does not digest to `header.seed_commitment` (the checks sign_footer has the inputs for; tick/chain-context checks that need the assembled log stay in `verify_integrity`).
- [ ] Well-formed headers/footers sign exactly as before (existing exporter `export_tic_tac_toe_reference` and the module tests stay green).
- [ ] New tests pin each refusal above, with the valid control still signing Ok — in the style of the #6422/#6424 sign-time refusal tests.
- [ ] No change to `verify_integrity`, the wire format, or any verifier verdict.

🤖 Filed by the fleet new-issue-creator (lane B) — verified with a probe against the real crate this run; see the probe path in the evidence section.

body:
# fleet(queue): repo-queue `list --limit` accepts 0, negative, and unbounded values — 0 silently reports "(no tasks)", and the broker forwards the value verbatim to PostgREST

## Evidence (verified this run, origin/main `669788ab0344`)

Neither end of the `list` path validates the limit's range:

- **Client** — `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/client.rs`: `parse_i64_flag` (:579-582) accepts any `i64` (the #5939 fix made non-numeric values a loud error, but range was never checked), and `cmd_list` (:875, :883) sends the parsed value verbatim as `"limit"`.
- **Broker** — `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/queue_broker.rs`: the `/list` handler (:492) takes `req.get("limit").and_then(|l| l.as_i64()).unwrap_or(20)` and interpolates it unchecked into the PostgREST query (:502-505): `tasks?select=…&limit={limit}`.

Verified on the laptop with the real `repo-queue` binary (built this run from the laptop primary; `client.rs`/`queue_broker.rs` limit paths are identical HEAD..origin/main) against a recording stub broker (probe `~/git/fleet/probe-queue-limit`, `REPO_QUEUE_BROKER_URL` direct transport):

| invocation | recorded `/list` body | exit |
|---|---|---|
| `list --limit 0` | `"limit":0` | 0 |
| `list --limit -5` | `"limit":-5` | 0 |
| `list --limit 999999999` | `"limit":999999999` | 0 |
| `list --limit 20` (control) | `"limit":20` | 0 |
| `list --limit abc` (control, #5939) | — rejected: `argument --limit: invalid int value "abc"` | 2 |

Consequences, by value:

- **`--limit 0`** → PostgREST `limit=0` returns zero rows → the client prints `(no tasks)` and exits 0, even when the queue is non-empty. A typo'd or scripted `0` reads as an empty queue — the false-empty misreport class (cf. #6314, where an empty queue name also reported "(no tasks)").
- **Negative** → forwarded verbatim; PostgREST rejects a negative limit, so the operator gets a downstream database-API error instead of a usage error naming the flag.
- **Huge** → no cap on either side: the broker issues an unbounded select and streams/prints the whole result set.

## Why it matters

`repo-queue list` is the fleet's own visibility surface — lanes and monitors use it to decide whether work exists. A limit that can silently mean "show nothing, successfully" undermines exactly the checks that rely on it (a Step-0 gate or a human checking a queue with `--limit 0` in a script sees an empty queue that is not empty). The fix layer is a triage call: client-side range validation (consistent with #5939's loud-error pattern), a broker-side clamp/reject (the broker is the trust boundary for non-CLI callers, e.g. the claimant's rich list reads), or both.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `repo-queue list --limit 0` and negative values are rejected with a usage error naming `--limit` (exit 2), consistent with the #5939 non-numeric error — or, if a clamp is chosen instead, the chosen semantics are documented in the `--help`/command docs and pinned by tests. Silent `(no tasks)` for a configured 0 is not an acceptable outcome.
- [ ] The broker's `/list` handler validates or clamps the limit it interpolates into the PostgREST query, so a non-CLI caller cannot drive a negative or unbounded select through it.
- [ ] A sane maximum exists (value is triage's call) and is enforced on the client and/or broker; `--limit 20` and the default (absent flag → 20) behave exactly as before.
- [ ] Tests pin the boundary: 0, -1, the maximum, maximum+1, and the default; the existing #5939 non-numeric rejection test still passes.
- [ ] Same-pass audit note: the sibling `get_i64` flags (`--lease-seconds` at claim, `--extend-seconds` at heartbeat, `--delay-seconds`) share the range-unchecked parse — triage records whether each is already validated downstream (SQL/broker) or needs the same treatment; this issue's fix is not blocked on that audit.

body:
## Problem

Concurrent repo-queue worker lane shifts share `/tmp` on the sandbox, and lanes use identical generic scratch filenames (`/tmp/handoff.sh`, `/tmp/note-<task>.md`, `/tmp/claimed.json`, `/tmp/work_one.py`). During the 2026-11-06T00:49Z lane code-r shift, lane code-u overwrote `/tmp/handoff.sh` with its own version mid-shift. Lane R's last two handoffs (task 10531 / issue #5748, task 10756 / issue #6371) therefore executed lane U's script: the agent notes say "lane code-u", the label step set `queue/claimed`/`status/in-progress` instead of the parked set, and no `park` call happened at all. Lane R caught the divergence only because the exec output format changed, then parked both tasks manually and fixed labels (verified by readback).

## Evidence

- `/tmp/handoff.sh` on the sandbox at 2026-11-06T01:14Z identified itself as lane code-u's script (`usage: handoff.sh TASK ISSUE ATTEMPTS`, note template naming lane code-u, no park step) while lane R was mid-bundle using that path.
- Agent notes 6673922995 (issue #5748) and 6673965622 (issue #6371) carry lane code-u text for tasks claimed by lane code-r.
- TOOLS.md already notes `/tmp` is a shared 512M tmpfs; 24 lanes run staggered 40-minute shifts and overlap by design, so filename collisions are guaranteed to recur.

## Acceptance criteria

- Worker runbook (repo-queue-worker-instruction) requires per-lane scratch directories (e.g. `/tmp/lane-<lane>-<shift>/`) for all helper scripts, note files, and claim dumps — no generic shared filenames in `/tmp`.
- Any lane tooling shipped in the repo uses lane-namespaced temp paths by construction.
- A lane that detects its scratch script changed mid-shift (checksum or magic header) stops and reports instead of executing it.

body:
# fleet-config: zero numeric values are never validated — egress_proxy_port=0 and dispatch port=0 dial port 0, and idle_exit_secs=0 makes the broker exit within seconds

## Summary

`fleet-config`'s numeric accessors only substitute a default when the value is *absent* — a configured `0` passes through verbatim for all three numeric settings, and `0` is a broken value for every one of them:

- `[proxy] egress_proxy_port = 0` — the egress CONNECT dial targets port 0, which no proxy can listen on; every tunnel attempt fails with a connection error that names the connection, not the config.
- `[dispatch] port = 0` — the dispatch client probes, dials directly, and tunnels to port 0 (`fleet-dispatch`'s `pick_transport` uses this one port for all three transports); pm-dispatch is unreachable and the errors again point at the network.
- `[proxy] idle_exit_secs = 0` — the broker's keepalive loop compares elapsed idle time against `0`, so the session broker exits (code 0, "success") on its first idle ticks regardless of activity. `0` is also the spelling an operator would naturally choose to mean "never idle-exit" — it currently means the exact opposite: exit almost immediately.

This breaks the crate's stated config policy (crate docs, lib.rs:14-17): a malformed config is a loud error, never a silent fallback. A zero port / zero timeout in a templated `fleet.toml` is a misspelling-class error, and the crate already validates the neighbouring shapes (#6397 covers the `[[proxy.services]]` rows' port 0; the scalar numeric fields here are the unvalidated remainder). Distinct from #2758 (pm-dispatch's own Bun-side env parsing) and #2835 (env-number parsing design) — these values arrive as typed TOML integers, so nothing ever parses or range-checks them.

## Evidence (file:line, origin/main @ 28719695372b)

- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs:332-336` — `egress_proxy_port()`: `self.proxy.egress_proxy_port.unwrap_or(DEFAULT_EGRESS_PROXY_PORT)` — `Some(0)` wins over the default (3130). Field at :121.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs:405-408` — `dispatch_port()`: same shape against `PORT_DISPATCH` (4879). Field at :179.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs:319-321` — `idle_exit_secs()`: same shape against `DEFAULT_IDLE_EXIT_SECS` (3600). Field at :115.
- Consumer, port 0 dialled: `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-dispatch/src/lib.rs:152-175` — `pick_transport` takes `config.dispatch_port()` and uses it for the loopback probe, the direct authority (`127.0.0.1:{port}` / `{target_host}:{port}`), and the tunnel; :206 hands `config.egress_proxy_port()` to `egress_from_env`. The broker path does the same at `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/serve.rs:589` and `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/stdio.rs:55`.
- Consumer, idle 0 exits: `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/serve.rs:526-543` — `keepalive_loop` reads `idle_exit_secs()` once, then every `IDLE_TICK_S` (5s, :51) exits the process when `now - last_used > idle`; with `idle = 0` that condition is true at the first tick where a second has elapsed since the last request — the broker cannot stay up.

## Verification (this run, laptop, real fleet-config crate @ origin/main 28719695372b)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-fleet-config-zero` (extracted `pkgs/fleet` tree at origin/main; an example bin added to the copy drives the *real* `fleet-config` crate's `Config::load_from` on written temp `fleet.toml` files):

```
egress_zero:   load Ok, egress_proxy_port()=0
dispatch_zero: load Ok, dispatch_port()=0
idle_zero:     load Ok, idle_exit_secs()=0
control_default: egress=3130 dispatch=4879 idle=3600
control_set:     egress=3131 dispatch=4880 idle=60
dial_port0:    Err kind=ConnectionRefused msg=Connection refused (os error 111)
```

Every zero case loads with no error and surfaces `0`; defaults and valid values resolve exactly as documented; a dial to port 0 is refused — the failure the dispatch/egress paths will report, with no mention of the config value that caused it.

## Why it matters

- A generated or templated `fleet.toml` that renders a port or timeout as `0` (an unset template variable's classic output) does not fail at load: dispatch and egress fail later as opaque connection refusals, and the broker flaps — starting, exiting 0 within seconds, being restarted — with every log line pointing away from the one-line config mistake.
- `idle_exit_secs = 0` is worse than a typo: "0 disables the timeout" is the common convention for this exact knob shape, so the value most likely to be written deliberately produces the most destructive reading of it.

## Acceptance criteria

- `egress_proxy_port = 0` and `[dispatch] port = 0` are either rejected at load with a loud `ConfigError` naming the field, or treated as unset (documented default applies) — one consistent shape, triage's call, matching however #6397 resolves the services-row port 0 so the crate has a single zero-port rule.
- `idle_exit_secs = 0` gets an explicit, documented semantics: either rejected at load, treated as unset (3600), or honoured as "never idle-exit" in `keepalive_loop` — it must not silently mean "exit at the first tick".
- Pinning tests cover the zero spelling for each of the three accessors alongside the existing `proxy_settings_*` / `dispatch_settings_*` tests; absent and valid values resolve exactly as before.
- No change to `[[proxy.services]]` handling (#6397) or to env-var handling.

Consequences, both verified on the laptop:

2. A `fn` inside `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` without `#[test]` is never executed by the harness. `tsv_row_keeps_control_characters_inside_the_name_field` is the **only** test of `tsv_row` itself — the row-level pin for the #1613 contract that a peer name containing `\n`/`\t` cannot forge a row or shift columns in TSV output. `plain_field` (its callee) is well tested; the row composition (`{hash}\t{field}`, exactly one real delimiter) is not covered by any running test.

The orphaned test is valid: extracted verbatim (with the production `plain_field` / `tsv_row` / `is_format_char` copied byte-for-byte from origin/main into probe crate `~/git/fleet/probe-tsv-row` on the laptop) and given its `#[test]`, it **passes** (`cargo test --lib`: 1 passed). ## Why it matters

This is the "a suite that never runs is not a test" failure class (#6185) in its smallest form: one displaced attribute silently disables the regression pin for a security-adjacent rendering contract (untrusted peer names from unsigned gossip, #1613), while the doubled attribute on the neighbor makes the test count look right. ## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Move the stray second `#[test]` from `list_tsv_row_shows_origin_and_upload_time` to `tsv_row_keeps_control_characters_inside_the_name_field` in `pkgs/id/src/commands/text.rs` (one-attribute move; no test body changes).

- [ ] No other production or test behavior changes.

# fleet-config: a relative HOME is used verbatim — config, state, and broker socket resolve CWD-relative and a planted fleet.toml loads

## Summary

`fleet-config` filters an *empty* `HOME` (it falls back to `"."`, tracked separately as #5737) and treats empty or relative XDG bases as the hazards they are (#5473 closed; #6396 open for relative XDG), but a *non-empty relative* `HOME` is used verbatim as the anchor for every home-relative resolution in the crate. With `HOME=relhome`, `Config::file_path()` returns the relative path `relhome/.config/fleet/fleet.toml`, and `Config::load()` loads a `fleet.toml` planted under the process's current working directory. The state dir, the shims dir under it, the broker socket, and both token-file paths resolve CWD-relative the same way.

This is a distinct trigger from the filed siblings: #5737 covers HOME *unset/empty* (the `"."` fallback); #6396 covers relative *XDG* bases with HOME present and correct (and explicitly puts the HOME cases out of its scope). Neither covers HOME itself being set to a relative path.

## Evidence (file:line, origin/main @ 28719695372b; fleet-config lib.rs is byte-identical between laptop HEAD 1dae17e457 and origin/main, md5-verified this run)

- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs:225-227` — `home_dir()`: `env_path("HOME").unwrap_or_else(|| PathBuf::from("."))`. `env_path`/`non_empty_path` (:217-223) filter only the empty case; a relative value passes through unchanged.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs:252-263` — `file_path_from` joins `.config/fleet/fleet.toml` onto that home value; a relative home stays relative.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs:442-445` — `state_dir_from` joins `.local/state/fleet` onto the same home; `shims_dir()` is `state_dir()/shims`.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs:302-320` — `broker_socket_from` resolves the default `.cache/laptop-agent/broker.sock` under the same home via `resolve_under`; `default_token_file()` (:385) and `secrets_token_file()` (:430) resolve under it too.

## Verification (this run, laptop, real fleet-config crate)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-fleet-config-empty-rel` (path-depends on the real `fleet-config` crate; `paths` bin prints `file_path`/`state_dir`, loads via `Config::load()`, and reports domain flags):

- From a scratch CWD containing a planted `relhome/.config/fleet/fleet.toml` (`[domains] planted = false`), with `HOME=relhome` and XDG/FLEET_CONFIG unset:
  - `file_path=relhome/.config/fleet/fleet.toml` (relative)
  - `state_dir=relhome/.local/state/fleet`
  - `broker_socket=relhome/.cache/laptop-agent/broker.sock`
  - `planted_enabled=false` — **the planted CWD config was loaded** (an unknown domain defaults to enabled; `false` can only come from the planted file)
  - `queue_enabled=true` (control domain untouched)
- Same relative `HOME=relhome` from a CWD with no `relhome` tree: `planted_enabled=true` — defaults rule; the load follows the CWD-relative path, not any fixed location.
- Control, absolute `HOME=<scratch>/abshome`: all paths anchor at the absolute home; its own config loads as expected.

## Why it matters

- A fleet process launched with a relative HOME (a wrapper script, a templated systemd unit with `HOME=.` or a relative `WorkingDirectory`-style spelling, a container entrypoint) silently reads its configuration — including the `[domains]` disable lever the crate docs call an incident lever — from whoever controls its working directory: the exact planted-config hazard #5473 closed for the empty-XDG spelling and #6396 filed for the relative-XDG spelling.
- State, shims, socket, and token-file paths landing CWD-relative means two processes in different directories keep different state and talk to different sockets, with no error anywhere.

## Acceptance criteria

- A relative `HOME` is not used as a resolution anchor: it is treated as unset for anchoring purposes (so the existing #5737 fallback decision governs what happens next), or resolution otherwise fails closed with a loud error — triage picks the shape, consistent with #5737/#6396.
- A planted `./<relative-home>/.config/fleet/fleet.toml` in the working directory is never loaded.
- Pinning tests cover a relative HOME for `file_path`, `state_dir`, and `broker_socket` alongside the existing empty-value tests (`env_paths_ignore_empty_values_and_resolve_under_home`, lib.rs:577).
- Behavior with an absolute HOME is unchanged; existing fleet-config tests stay green.
- Out of scope: HOME unset/empty (#5737), relative XDG bases (#6396), and `FLEET_CONFIG` itself (an explicit per-file override a user may deliberately spell relative).

# fleet-config: a relative XDG_CONFIG_HOME / XDG_STATE_HOME is used verbatim — config and state resolve CWD-relative and a planted ./fleet.toml loads even with HOME set

## Summary

`fleet-config` treats an *empty* XDG base as invalid (#5473), but a *non-empty relative* XDG base is used verbatim. The XDG Base Directory specification requires relative values in these variables to be considered invalid and ignored. As a result, with `HOME` set correctly, `XDG_CONFIG_HOME=relcfg` makes the config path `relcfg/fleet/fleet.toml` — relative to the process's current working directory — and `Config::load()` loads a `fleet.toml` planted in the working directory. `XDG_STATE_HOME` relative likewise puts the state dir (and the materialized shims dir under it) in the CWD.

This is a distinct trigger from the two filed siblings: #5473 (closed) covered *empty* XDG values; #5737 (open) covers HOME unset/empty falling back to `"."`. Neither covers a non-empty relative XDG base with HOME present and correct.

## Evidence (file:line, origin/main @ 967fb229e4; pkgs/fleet unchanged between laptop HEAD and origin/main)

- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs:211-223` — the crate's own comment: "the XDG base-directory spec treats an empty base as invalid; taking one literally here would turn the config file, the state dir, and the broker socket into CWD-relative paths (issue #5473)". `non_empty_path` filters only the empty case; `env_path` returns any non-empty value, relative included.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs:252-263` — `file_path_from`: `let base = xdg_config_home.unwrap_or_else(|| home.join(".config")); base.join("fleet").join("fleet.toml")` — a relative base stays relative.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs:442-445` — `state_dir_from` has the same shape for `XDG_STATE_HOME`; `shims_dir()` is `state_dir()/shims`.
- The XDG spec (Base Directory Specification): "If an implementation encounters a relative path in any of these variables it should consider the path invalid and ignore it."

## Verification (this run, laptop, real fleet-config crate)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-fleet-config-xdg-rel` (path-depends on the real `fleet-config` crate; run from a scratch dir containing a planted `relcfg/fleet/fleet.toml` with `[domains] planted = false`):

- `HOME=/home/user XDG_CONFIG_HOME=relcfg XDG_STATE_HOME=relstate` (FLEET_CONFIG unset):
  - `file_path=relcfg/fleet/fleet.toml`
  - `state_dir=relstate/fleet`
  - `planted_enabled=false` — **the planted CWD config was loaded** (an unknown domain defaults to enabled; `false` can only come from the planted file)
  - `queue_enabled=true` (control domain untouched)
- Control, absolute XDG bases: paths anchor at the given absolute dirs; planted file ignored (`planted_enabled=true`).
- Control, no XDG vars: `file_path=/home/user/.config/fleet/fleet.toml`, `state_dir=/home/user/.local/state/fleet`; planted file ignored.

## Why it matters

- A fleet process launched with a relative XDG base (a templated systemd unit, a wrapper script exporting `XDG_CONFIG_HOME=.config`, a container entrypoint) silently reads its configuration — including the `[domains]` disable lever the crate docs call an incident lever — from whoever controls its working directory: the exact planted-config hazard #5473 closed for the empty spelling.
- The state/shims dirs landing in the CWD means two processes in different directories keep different state and different PATH shims, with no error anywhere.

## Acceptance criteria

- A relative `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` or `XDG_STATE_HOME` is treated as unset (ignored, per the XDG spec), exactly as an empty one is after #5473; resolution falls back to the HOME-anchored default.
- A planted `./<relative-base>/fleet/fleet.toml` in the working directory is never loaded when HOME is set and the XDG base is relative.
- Pinning tests cover relative XDG bases for `file_path` and `state_dir` alongside the existing empty-value tests (`env_paths_ignore_empty_values_and_resolve_under_home`, lib.rs:577).
- Behavior with absolute XDG bases and with HOME set is otherwise unchanged; existing fleet-config tests stay green.
- Out of scope: `FLEET_CONFIG` itself (an explicit per-file override a user may deliberately spell relative) and the HOME-unset fallback (#5737).

body:
# mcpx(conformance-record): an equal-count skip swap escapes the skip guard — `best`/`largest` records diverge, and a swap-plus-pass silently re-baselines `best`

`pkgs/mcpx/scripts/conformance-record.py` maintains the two per-leg conformance records (`best`, `largest`) kept in GitHub variables and saved on `main` by `.github/workflows/mcpx-conformance.yml` (record step at workflow lines 391–410: the script's new state is written back with `gh variable set` whenever it differs). Its guard against silent coverage loss is count-only:

- The skip-increase error (conformance-record.py:120–125) fires only when `cur["skipped_count"] > best["skipped_count"]`. The skipped **names** are used only to decorate that error (`newly = set(names) − set(best["skipped"])`, :122) — a name that becomes skipped while another stops being skipped never triggers anything.
- When the counts tie and `passed` ties, `best` is kept as `dict(best, latest_timestamp=now)` (:139–141) — its `skipped` list stays the **old** run's names.
- At the same total, `largest` is unconditionally replaced with the current run's counts (:156–158) — including the **new** skipped names.
- When the counts tie and `passed` rises, `best` is replaced wholesale as "improved" (:136–138) — including the new skipped names, with no skip alert.

Verified on the laptop at origin/main `cb8eee8d68` (script extracted verbatim from that tree; probe `~/git/fleet/probe-conformance-swap`, stored record: 10 passed / 0 failed / 12 total / 1 warning / 1 skipped, `skipped=["check-A"]` in both records):

1. **Equal-count swap** — current run 10p/0f/12t/1 skipped, `skipped=["check-B"]` (check-A now runs as a warning; check-B, which used to run, is now skipped): exit **0**, no error or warning; the written state has `best.skipped == ["check-A"]` (stale) while `largest.skipped == ["check-B"]` — the two records for the same leg now disagree about which check is skipped, and the workflow saves that state on main. The `best` record's name list is the one the "newly skipped" diff reads, so it is now permanently out of date until some strictly better/worse run happens to replace it.
2. **Swap-plus-pass** — check-A un-skips and passes, check-B (previously a warning) becomes skipped: 11p/0f/12t/1 skipped. Exit **0**, summary reports `best: **improved**`, and `best` is silently re-baselined to `skipped=["check-B"]`. A check that stopped running is absorbed into the baseline with no alert — the exact re-baselining failure the count guard exists to prevent, reached by keeping the count constant.
3. **Increase control** — skipped 1 → 2: exit **3**, error names `newly skipped: check-B`. The guard works, but only on the count.
4. **Identical control** — same counts, same skipped name: exit 0, only timestamps move. Correct.

There is also no test suite for this script at all (`pkgs/mcpx/scripts/test_gotest_report.py` covers its sibling `gotest-report.py`; nothing references `conformance-record.py` outside the workflow and docs), so none of this behavior is pinned.

## Why it matters

These records are the baseline every future conformance run is judged against, and they are written back to repository variables on main. A fixture or capability that goes missing (the script's own docstring: a skip increase "usually means a fixture or a capability went missing") can hide indefinitely behind an unrelated un-skip: the count never rises, the job never fails, and in the swap-plus-pass case the degraded state becomes the new `best` baseline, so even the stale-name evidence is erased. In the plain swap case the records are left internally inconsistent — `best` and `largest` naming different skipped checks for the same leg — which corrupts the "newly skipped" diagnostic the next real increase relies on.

Distinct from #6391 (the same count-only pattern in the sibling `gotest-report.py` skip record, filed separately with its own probe): different script, different record store (GitHub variables vs a committed record file), different mechanics — here the two records diverge from each other, and re-baselining is triggered by a `passed` increase. Sibling precedent for the guard's intent: the gotest-report quarantine/skip discipline (#1973/#6387).

## Acceptance criteria

- A run whose skipped **set** changes against the `best` record — any newly skipped name, regardless of the count — is surfaced explicitly (error/exit 3 like a count increase, or at minimum a prominent summary warning naming the newly skipped checks); it never passes silently.
- After any run the script saves, `best.skipped` and `largest.skipped` cannot disagree about the current run's skipped set when both describe that run; a `best` record that is retained rather than replaced does not keep a skipped-name list the current run contradicts without that being reported.
- A `best` replacement triggered by a `passed` increase does not silently absorb newly skipped names: the swap-plus-pass case above is reported by name.
- Count-increase behavior is unchanged (exit 3, newly-skipped names listed), identical runs still only move timestamps, and incomplete/legacy records are still replaced rather than compared (existing `complete()` semantics).
- A test suite for `conformance-record.py` exists alongside the script (mirroring `test_gotest_report.py`) covering at least: equal-count swap, swap-plus-pass, count increase, and identical-run controls — and it is wired wherever `test_gotest_report.py` is run, or the wiring gap is filed separately.

# atlas-eval: a duplicate query key in a run's `results` object silently replaces that query's ranking — validation never sees the dropped entry

`pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-core/src/eval.rs` is the deterministic offline evaluation harness (#5741): saved rankings are scored against judged qrels, and its reports decide whether a retrieval signal earns a place in the fused ranking and which parameters `select_best_signal` picks. Its module docs promise strict duplicate discipline — duplicate query ids, duplicate qrels, duplicate docs in a ranking, and duplicate signal names are all rejected at parse/validation time — and `EvalData::validate()` (called from `EvalData::from_json`, eval.rs:150) enforces each of them. One duplicate class escapes, because it vanishes before validation runs:

- `Run.results` (eval.rs:125) is `BTreeMap<String, Vec<String>>` — query id → ranked doc ids. serde's map deserialization inserts key by key, so JSON text that names the same query twice in one run's `results` object keeps only the **last** ranking; the first is silently discarded during parsing. `validate()` iterates the post-parse map and cannot detect that anything was dropped.
- Every other duplicate class is detectable post-parse (vectors keep both copies; struct fields are protected by serde derive, which errors on a repeated field) — `results` keys are the only input that arrives through a map.

Verified on the laptop with a probe crate (`~/git/fleet/probe-eval-dupkey`, serde/serde_json, types mirrored field-for-field from eval.rs) against the exact shapes:

- `{"signal":"dense","results":{"q1":["a","b"],"q1":["c"]}}` → parses OK; `results["q1"] == ["c"]` — the `["a","b"]` ranking is gone, with no error at any layer.
- Control, duplicate struct field (`"format"` twice) → parse error `duplicate field 'format'` — confirming the hole is specific to the map-typed field, not a general parser laxity.

## Why it matters

The eval document is a file format (versioned fixtures such as `pkgs/atlas-search/fixtures/eval-smoke.json`, plus generated/hand-merged eval sets per `pkgs/atlas-search/eval/README.md`). A duplicated query entry — a merge artifact, a generator emitting a query twice, a hand edit — does not produce an error; it produces a *wrong report*: the signal is scored on the replacement ranking as if that were its output, and nDCG/recall/MRR means and `select_best_signal` parameter choices are computed from silently truncated evidence. The harness exists to be the trustworthy oracle for signal selection; a silent input-truncation path is exactly the failure its validation section was written to prevent (the same class the deploy registry fix #6384 addressed with an `object_pairs_hook`: discarded text must fail the load, not vanish).

Note the existing pinning test (`validation_rejects_format_violations`, eval.rs:~683) builds its inputs with `serde_json::json!(...)` values — a `Value` object cannot even represent duplicate keys, so that test style structurally cannot express this case; a regression test must feed `from_json` raw text.

## Acceptance criteria

- `EvalData::from_json` rejects, with an error naming the signal and query, any `atlas-eval/v1` document whose `results` object repeats a query key — at any run.
- All currently-valid documents still parse and score identically (including `fixtures/eval-smoke.json` and the existing test corpus); every existing validation rejection (duplicate doc in a ranking, duplicate qrel, unknown query, grade > 30, duplicate signal) still fires.
- A raw-text regression test covers the duplicate-`results`-key case (not via `json!` values, which cannot express it).
- The fix does not change the report format (`atlas-eval-report/v1`) or any metric definition.

Related: #6384 (same silently-discarded-duplicate-key class in the deploy registry; fixed with a pairs hook), #5741 (the eval harness's parent issue, closed), #6046 (eval-set/gate design that will build on this harness).

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/6169 — "aggregator(forecast): design §1 resampling estimator in deriveEpicEta (#5274)" (MERGED 2026-11-05T09:08:34Z, merge commit f2a72d9478fa2a13bb2fb5a004e6432615e535dc, head 2c2a5e9fdbe8bde32d4fe968b0f60cb5459cabfb)
- Comment: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/6169#discussion_r4478536495 (chatgpt-codex-connector[bot], 2026-11-05T09:10:10Z, P2, anchored at `pm-stack/aggregator/src/forecast.ts:152`)
- Essence: "**Keep unfinished trials out of completion-time quantiles.** When remaining work cannot finish within the 100,000-week cap, this records unfinished trials as actual completions, making the forecast optimistic rather than conservative. For example, buckets `[1, 1, 1, 1]` with 100,001 remaining units yield P50 and P80 at 100,000 weeks even though completion takes exactly 100,001 weeks. Preserve capped trials as censored observations and return an unavailable date with a limitation when the requested percentile exceeds the simulation horizon, rather than publishing a completion date before the work finishes."

## No-response evidence

- The comment's review thread is unresolved (GraphQL `reviewThreads`: isResolved=false) and contains only the single Codex comment — no replies (`in_reply_to_id` empty, no later inline comments in the thread).
- The review was submitted at 2026-11-05T09:10:10Z on the merged head 2c2a5e9fdb, after the PR merged at 2026-11-05T09:08:34Z, so no fix commit followed it in the PR; the code on current main is unchanged in the relevant respect (below).

## Still live on current main (verified 2026-11-05 by independent `gh api` raw reads)

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/forecast.ts:125-130` (current main): `RESAMPLE_MAX_WEEKS = 100_000`, with a comment claiming "A capped trial reads as that many weeks, which is conservative for both percentiles" — for a trial whose true completion exceeds the cap, recording the cap value is the opposite: it pulls the percentile earlier than the true completion.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/forecast.ts:145-153`: `resampledWeeksToComplete` pushes `weeks` unconditionally after the capped loop (`samples.push(weeks)`), so an unfinished trial (completed < remainingUnits) is indistinguishable from a trial that finished exactly at the cap.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/forecast.ts:420-425`: the caller unconditionally converts the P50/P80 percentiles of those samples into ETA dates; there is no censored/unavailable path when a percentile falls beyond the simulation horizon.
- Repro by inspection from the reviewer's example: buckets `[1,1,1,1]`, remaining 100,001 units — every trial caps at 100,000 weeks with 100,000 of 100,001 units done, yet both percentiles return a date at 100,000 weeks, one week before the work can finish (and arbitrarily early for larger remaining counts).
- Dedupe: open and closed issues searched by "forecast percentile capped trial", "6169 forecast", "forecast.ts resampling", and the finding title — no issue covers censored/capped trials; the hits are the closed parent design issue #5274 and the closed epic-ETA issue #3982, neither of which names this defect.

## Acceptance criteria

- Capped (unfinished) trials are preserved as censored observations, not recorded as completions at the cap; when a requested percentile exceeds the simulation horizon, the forecast returns an unavailable date with a stated limitation instead of a completion date before the work finishes.
- A regression test covers the reviewer's example shape (uniform buckets with remaining units beyond the cap) asserting no P50/P80 date earlier than true completion is published.
- Or: the finding is resolved on this issue by a documented decision with reasoning recorded.

# Notes incorporation pilot — corpus registry + manifest + 10-doc pilot into developing-today/zettel

Design of record: 2026-11-04 investigation (idea-register-2026-10-20.md + cloud-ideas-log.md, 2026-11-04 ~08:57 CST entry, §§1–7). Authorized by Drew 2026-11-05 ("auth pilot, mint token", main chat), including minting the token the pilot needs.

## Scope (the design's recommended first step, nothing more)
1. Create the notes submission DB (Turso) with the §7 tables — `submissions`, `notes_out`, `upload_attempts`, `corpus_controls` — plus the corpus registry table and the migration manifest table. Mint a DB-scoped Turso auth token for it and file it in Bitwarden (name only recorded here, never the value).
2. Register the five corpora: `dezren39/zettel` (public), `developing-today/zettel` (public), `dezren39/slip` (private, manual hold), `developing-today/slip` (private, manual hold), `dezren39/cairn` (federated private source).
3. Generate the manifest: code `doc/`'s design-named documents + every named registry/inventory, one row each with source repo/path, pinned commit, hash, title, authored datetime, type, sensitivity, target corpus, action, canonical owner.
4. Run ONE end-to-end pilot: ten already-merged design docs from code `doc/` into `developing-today/zettel` as draft-marked notes with mandatory frontmatter + provenance footer (provenance spans recorded), through the submission DB as system of record — with one forced push failure (recorded, retried, recovered) and one kill-switch flip (per-corpus control re-checked immediately before push; upload halts while on, resumes when off) exercised for real.

## Pilot simplifications (explicit, reversible)
- Notes land as source landing notes (full doc import with provenance) — the model-driven explode-into-children draft pass is not exercised in the pilot; no Workers AI drafting occurs, so the ~50k Neurons/day cap binds nothing yet.
- Atlas zettel indexing is recorded per attempt but not wired in this pilot; it remains follow-on work under the Atlas ingestion program.
- The uploader is the pilot operator following the §7 protocol (single writer, lease/attempt rows, kill-switch re-check immediately before push, idempotent retry via remote check) — the sanctioned machine direct-commit to the notes repo applies to this repo only, from the uploader's own worktree, never a primary checkout.

## Acceptance
- 10 notes present on `developing-today/zettel` main, each with valid mandatory frontmatter and a provenance footer matching its `notes_out` row byte-for-byte (hash check).
- Every pilot submission's DB state = `uploaded`; `upload_attempts` shows: successful batch push, one forced failure + successful retry, one kill-switch hold (no push attempted while on) + successful resume.
- Manifest and corpus registry rows present in the submission DB; token filed in Bitwarden and verified working against the DB.

labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/fleet
labels.description: pkgs/fleet multicall binary + platform crates

body:
## Problem

The standalone broker binaries `queue-broker` and `secrets-broker` (the `fleet-brokers` rollback artifacts, `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/bin/queue-broker.rs` and `src/bin/secrets-broker.rs`) ignore argv entirely: their 5-line `main()`s call `queue_broker::run()` / `secrets_broker::run()` directly, and both `run()` functions take no arguments. Every argument — including `--help` — starts the daemon.

This surface is NOT covered by open issue #5568: that issue's acceptance criteria cover `fleet serve <broker-role>` and the fleet binary's argv0 aliases, which route through `fleet`'s `run_domain` in `crates/fleet/src/main.rs`. The standalone `[[bin]]` targets bypass that code entirely, so a #5568 fix in `run_domain` cannot reach them. The sibling standalone binary `fleet-connect-udp` had exactly this defect and was fixed separately in #6134 (closed) with a `classify_bin_args` gate in its bin `main()`; the two broker bins never got the same treatment.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @04f78696ab)

Code:

- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/bin/queue-broker.rs` — `fn main() { std::process::exit(fleet_queue::queue_broker::run()); }` (no argv read).
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/bin/secrets-broker.rs` — identical shape for `secrets_broker::run()`.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/queue_broker.rs:589` — `pub fn run() -> i32` (no args).
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/secrets_broker.rs:189` — `pub fn run() -> i32` (no args).
- Built by the `fleet-brokers` package (`pkgs/fleet/default.nix:115`), so these are shipped artifacts, not dead code.
- Contrast: `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/bin/fleet-connect-udp.rs` classifies argv first (#6134): `--help` prints usage at exit 0, any other argument is a usage error, both before loading config or binding anything.

Probe (real binaries built on the laptop this run, `cargo build -p fleet-queue --features queue-broker,secrets-broker --bins`; `HOME` pointed at an empty dir so the daemon dies at its first startup step — the token-file read — proving which path was entered; probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-broker-argv`):

| invocation | result |
|---|---|
| `queue-broker --help` | `queue-broker: cannot read token file …/.config/queue-broker/token`, exit 3 (daemon startup) |
| `queue-broker --bogus-junk` | identical token-file error, exit 3 |
| `queue-broker frobnicate` | identical token-file error, exit 3 |
| `queue-broker` (bare, control) | identical token-file error, exit 3 |
| `secrets-broker --help` | `secrets-broker: cannot read token file …/.config/secrets-broker/token`, exit 3 (daemon startup) |
| `secrets-broker --bogus-junk` | identical token-file error, exit 3 |
| `secrets-broker frobnicate` | identical token-file error, exit 3 |
| `secrets-broker` (bare, control) | identical token-file error, exit 3 |

With real token files present, the same invocations proceed past the token read into daemon startup (bind), exactly as #5568 observed for the serve route.

## Why it matters

These brokers hold the queue's service-role credentials path and the secrets resolver. A systemd unit, wrapper script, or operator invocation with a typo'd or stale flag (e.g. a removed option) silently starts a daemon with default bind/token settings instead of failing loudly — the fail-open shape the fleet has been stamping out in #6134 (connect-udp bin), #6139 (udp-forward dup flags), and #5568 (serve route). `--help` starting a daemon is the sharpest form: an operator checking usage on a production host starts the broker.

## Acceptance criteria

- `queue-broker --help` / `-h` and `secrets-broker --help` / `-h` print usage on stdout and exit 0, without reading any token file or binding anything.
- `queue-broker <any other argument>` and `secrets-broker <any other argument>` exit 2 with a usage error naming the unexpected argument, before any daemon startup (no token-file read, no bind attempt).
- Bare `queue-broker` / `secrets-broker` still start the daemon exactly as today.
- The gate follows the #6134 precedent (a pure, unit-testable argv classification in the library, called first in the bin `main()`), with pinning tests for the help, junk-arg, and bare controls.
- `cargo test -p fleet-queue` passes on the laptop or in CI.
- Scope boundary: `fleet serve <role>` and the fleet argv0 aliases stay with #5568 — this issue covers only the two standalone `[[bin]]` artifacts in `fleet-queue`.

body:
# id(meta): meta protocol decoders ignore trailing bytes — a padded or double-request stream executes as the bare first request

## Summary

The meta protocol's postcard decoders use bare `postcard::from_bytes`, which stops at the end of the first value and ignores everything after it. The stream contract is exactly one request per stream (the server reads the stream to end-of-stream, then decodes once), so any trailing bytes — padding, garbage, or a second complete request — are silently discarded and the first request executes as if the stream had been well-formed.

The server side is the consequential one: `MetaRequest` includes mutating variants (`Put`, `Delete`, `Rename`, `Copy`, `SetTag`, `DelTag`, `MigrateTags` — `MetaRequest::is_write()`, `pkgs/id/src/protocol.rs:360`), and a decoded request goes straight to `MetaProtocol::handle` (`protocol.rs:554`), which performs the operation for any caller the access policy admits. A malformed frame is never reported as malformed; it is reinterpreted as a clean request.

## Evidence (file:line, main @ fc2e707b5f)

- `pkgs/id/src/protocol.rs:845` — `MetaProtocol::handle_stream`: `let resp = match postcard::from_bytes::<MetaRequest>(&buf)` where `buf` is `recv.read_to_end(MAX_REQUEST_BYTES)` (one stream = one request). Any suffix after the first postcard value is ignored; the `Err` arm that would produce `MetaResponse::Error { "malformed request: …" }` never fires for padded frames.
- `pkgs/id/src/meta_client.rs:112` — the shared client helper `request_over` decodes the response with the same bare `postcard::from_bytes(&buf)`.
- 16 further hand-rolled client response decodes with the same expression (`postcard::from_bytes(&resp_buf)`): `commands/repl.rs:466,617,764,897,1022,1066,1105,1146`, `commands/find.rs:939`, `commands/get.rs:169,340`, `commands/list.rs:86,172`, `commands/peers.rs:259,299`, `commands/serve.rs:2436`. (The #6204 packet explicitly excluded these response sites from its scope as a "separate assessment"; the server request site was not in any filed issue's scope.)

## Verification (this run, laptop, real id crate)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-meta-trailing` (depends on the real `id` crate @ fc2e707b5f; decode expressions verbatim from the production sites; binary re-run after build, identical output):

```
list_len=1
list_clean_ok=true eq=true
list_trailing_0x00_ok=true eq=true          # List + 0x00 decodes as List
list_trailing_garbage_ok=true eq=true       # List + "GARBAGE" decodes as List
list_take_rest_len=1                        # take_from_bytes exposes the ignored suffix
delete_is_write=true
delete_trailing_ok=true eq=true             # Delete{"victim.txt"} + DEADBEEF decodes as the Delete
delete_plus_second_req_ok=true eq_first=true # Delete + a second complete Delete stream-decodes as the first only
delete_truncated_ok=false (expect false)    # control: a genuinely truncated frame IS refused
response_trailing_ok=true success=true      # MetaResponse::Delete{success:true} + 0x00+"EXTRA" decodes Ok
response_take_rest_len=6
```

## Why it matters

- **Framing strictness is the protocol's own contract.** One stream carries one request; the handler's phases (read under deadline → handle to completion → respond) assume the buffer *is* the request. Accepting padded frames means two different byte streams are the same request — the malleability the sibling decoders in this crate were fixed to refuse (full-consumption checks at `world/replication.rs:532`, `event_store/range.rs`, and — merged today in #6198 for #6197 — `chat_presence.rs` / `peer_announcement.rs`).
- **Mutations execute from malformed frames.** A padded `Delete`/`Put`/`Rename` from an admitted writer is indistinguishable from a clean one in logs and responses; there is no "malformed request" signal for corruption, truncation-by-concatenation bugs in a future client, or a peer probing the framing.
- **The second-request form is silently dropped, not refused.** A client bug that concatenates two requests onto one stream loses the second operation with a success response for the first — a silent data-operation loss that a full-consumption check would surface immediately as an error.
- The response side is lower stakes (the client chose the server), but 17 copies of the same lax decode mean a corrupted or confused response stream is likewise reinterpreted instead of refused.

## Related

- Siblings in the same class, each filed/fixed separately per decoder: #6192 (seitan accept), #6197 (gossip frames; fixed by PR #6198), #6202 (match_audit), #6204 (log_sync). This issue is the meta protocol's instance — server request decode plus the client response decodes.
- Strict in-crate precedent to mirror: `pkgs/id/src/world/replication.rs:532` (`take_from_bytes` + empty-rest check) and the tests added by PR #6198.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `MetaProtocol::handle_stream` (`protocol.rs:845`) refuses a request buffer that does not decode as exactly one `MetaRequest` (e.g. `take_from_bytes` + empty-rest check, mirroring `replication.rs:532`), returning the existing `MetaResponse::Error "malformed request: …"` for padded, garbage-suffixed, and double-request streams.
- [ ] The client response decodes (`meta_client.rs:112` and the 16 `commands/*` copies, or a shared helper they converge on) refuse a response buffer with trailing bytes the same way.
- [ ] Pinning tests cover: padded read (`List` + 0x00), padded write (`Delete` + garbage), concatenated double request, and a padded `MetaResponse` — each refused; clean request/response round-trips unaffected.
- [ ] `cargo test -p id --lib protocol meta_client` (and the affected command modules' tests) pass.

title: pm-stack(aggregator): one lined-up task with a non-GitHub ref silently deletes the board's whole in-flight lane — inFlightBoardItems parseRef throws into an unlogged catch

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/pm-stack
labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Summary

`pm-stack/aggregator` — one orchestration-section lined-up task carrying a non-GitHub `ref` silently deletes the board's **entire** orchestrator in-flight lane. `inFlightBoardItems` (`src/sources/live.ts:605`) calls `parseRef` unguarded on the task's ref while reshaping work items into board items; `parseRef` throws on anything that is not `owner/repo#N`. The only caller wraps the lane assembly in a catch that swallows the error with no log line, so the board renders with the Kaneo cards alone and no trace anywhere — no 500, no provenance note, no console output — while every other lined-up task in the section is healthy.

This is the board-lane sibling of #6174 (the same input class 500ing `/today`): different consumer, different failure mode, broader reach. #6174's acceptance criteria can be fully satisfied by guarding the Today objectives render and this defect would remain.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @f78551465f)

Chain of the defect, all on current main `f78551465f888b21620d9834394819af1c1624b3`:

- `src/feed.ts:223` `isLinedUpElement` — the per-element gate for goal `linedUp` arrays — checks `title`, `horizon`, `status`, `horizonWhy`, but never `ref` (not even its type), so a goal-id string, a bare number string, or a non-string all pass `isOrchestrationSection`. (Same gate gap as #6174.)
- `src/work-items.ts:191` `assembleWorkItems` copies `ref: task.ref` onto the canonical work item with no validity check.
- `src/sources/live.ts:621` `inFlightBoardItems` adds `item.ref` to the item's refs unfiltered (title-derived refs go through `refsInText`/`isValidRef` and are safe; the task's own ref does not), and `:634` computes the board item's repo as `parseRef(remainingRefs[0]).repo` — the unguarded throw site. Any invalid task ref is necessarily `remainingRefs[0]`: it is added first, and it can never be deduped away against existing board links.
- `src/sources/live.ts:1173-1184` — the board source calls `inFlightBoardItems(orchSection, merged)` inside `try { … } catch { /* the Kaneo board still renders without the lane */ }`: the throw is swallowed silently (contrast the kaneo change-diff warning a few lines above, which logs), provenance is never annotated, and the lane merge is skipped wholesale — healthy tasks in the same section vanish with the poisoned one.

Probe (laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-inflight-ref/probe.ts`, bun, importing the real `src/feed.ts` and `src/sources/live.ts` at `f78551465f`; section built on the `test/board-in-flight.test.ts` fixture shape, task status `in-progress`, horizon `tomorrow` — the lane is not horizon-gated, unlike `/today`):

```text
PROBE goal-id ref: validator=true -> THREW Error: not a repo-qualified ref: goal_a243772844c3
PROBE numeric ref: validator=true -> THREW Error: not a repo-qualified ref: 12345
PROBE bare-number string ref: validator=true -> THREW Error: not a repo-qualified ref: 812
PROBE good + poisoned mix: validator=true -> THREW Error: not a repo-qualified ref: goal_a243772844c3
PROBE control github ref: validator=true -> returned 1 item(s): [{repo: "developing-today/code", links: [{ref: "developing-today/code#812"}]}]
PROBE control no ref: validator=true -> returned 1 item(s): [{repo: "developing-today/code", links: [{ref: "developing-today/code#944"}, {ref: "developing-today/code#985"}]}]
```

The mix case is the operational one: a single poisoned task throws for the whole section, so the fail-soft catch drops every in-flight entry, not just the bad one.

## Why it matters

The in-flight lane is the board's only view of work being done now (the Kaneo cards under it are a completion record — `render.ts` says so explicitly). The orchestration section is republished by an external job every run, and #6149/#6174 established that this publisher does put goal ids into ref fields in live data. When that happens on a lined-up task, the board silently reverts to showing only the completion record: the failure is invisible in the UI, in provenance, and in the logs, so it can persist for as long as the poisoned task stays lined up (up to its horizon window) with nobody able to see that anything is wrong. A loud 500 (#6174) at least announces itself; this one falsifies the board quietly.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A validator-passing section whose lined-up task carries a non-GitHub ref (goal id, bare number, or non-string) no longer throws in `inFlightBoardItems`; the poisoned task renders title-only (or with its valid title-derived refs), and every other lined-up task in the section still appears in the lane
- [ ] A valid `owner/repo#N` lined-up ref still produces a linked board item with the correct `repo` (control case), and title-derived refs behave as before
- [ ] The board source's lane catch (or the chosen fix layer) leaves an observable trace when a ref is dropped or the lane assembly fails — a log line or provenance note — so a future lane loss is diagnosable from the running service
- [ ] Pinning tests in `test/board-in-flight.test.ts` cover the goal-id ref, the non-string ref, and the good + poisoned mix (lane survives with the healthy task present)
- [ ] The `bun test` aggregator suite passes

## Related

- #6174 — the `/today` sibling: same gate gap (`linedUp[].ref` unchecked), different consumer (`todayFromSection` → objectives render), different failure mode (a loud 500 on one page vs a silent whole-lane loss on the board). Fixing the gate in #6174 would also close this; a render-site-only fix there would not — the PR that closes either should state which layer it chose and check the other consumer.
- PR #6149 — the tier-card fix for this class on the Needs-you page (`isValidRef` guard + plain-text treatment).
- #4952 — the shared `isValidRef` rule the guarded sites route through.
- #2417 / #3897 — the section-gate element-validation line this gap continues.

## Scope notes

- Filed-only from the creator lane; not self-solved (the fix layer — section gate vs `assembleWorkItems` vs `inFlightBoardItems`, shared with #6174 — and the observability treatment of the silent catch are design calls for one deliberate pass).

title: security(identity): confine provider static-file requests to the static root

labels.name: kind/security
labels.description: Security issue or security hardening

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: security-adjacent
labels.description: Touches security-sensitive surface; extra care and review

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: app/identity
labels.description: Package/app: identity (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

The identity provider serves static files by concatenating the untrusted request path into a filesystem path without resolving or confining it to the static directory. In `pkgs/identity/provider/core.sh:376-393`, `/static/../../.env` becomes `./static/../../.env` and is accepted by `-f`/`cat` when the provider runs from `pkgs/identity/provider`.

`pkgs/identity/provider/start.sh:3` changes into that provider directory. The parent `pkgs/identity/.env` is written by `pkgs/identity/provider.sh:79-93` and contains `TURSO_AUTH_TOKEN`, so an unauthenticated HTTP request can disclose provider credentials.

## Required behavior

Resolve and confine every static request beneath the canonical static root before opening it. Reject traversal and symlink escapes; do not rely on string-prefix checks alone.

## Acceptance criteria

- A regression test with a fixture `.env` secret requests `/static/../../.env` using a path-preserving client and gets 403/404 without the marker in the response.
- A normal static asset still returns 200 with its expected bytes.
- A symlink inside the static root pointing outside the root is rejected.
- The test exercises the same path-resolution helper used by the provider request handler.

body:
## Summary

`pm-stack/aggregator` — the `/today` render crashes (throws, served as the error-boundary 500) when an orchestration-section lined-up task carries a ref that is not a GitHub `owner/repo#N` ref. This is the same failure class PR #6149 fixed today for `tierItemCard` on the Needs-you page, left unguarded on the Today page's objectives path — and the section validator that is supposed to be the only gate never checks the lined-up `ref` field at all, not even its type.

Chain of the defect (all on current main `1a069c3ff2`):

- `src/feed.ts:223` `isLinedUpElement` — the per-element gate for goal `linedUp` arrays — checks `title`, `horizon`, `status`, and `horizonWhy`, but **not `ref`**: a string like `goal_b647ff5c92f5`, or even a non-string (`12345`), passes `isOrchestrationSection`.
- `src/work-items.ts:191` `assembleWorkItems` copies `ref: task.ref` onto the canonical work item with no validity check; a tier merge can also supply it (`if (!match.ref && t.ref) match.ref = t.ref`), and tier refs are known to legitimately carry tracked-goal ids (that is exactly the live data that broke Needs-you in #6149).
- `src/derive.ts:724` `todayFromSection` copies `ref: item.ref` onto today's objectives (items with `horizon === "today"` and a goal).
- `src/render.ts:3368` the objectives render calls `refUrl(o.ref)` **unguarded**: `refUrl` → `parseRef` throws `Error: not a repo-qualified ref: …`. The sibling sites fixed in #6149 guard with `isValidRef` (`src/render.ts:2489`, `:2524`), and `sessionRecordLine` wraps `refUrl` in try/catch — the objectives site does neither.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe against the real aggregator sources)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-today-ref/probe.ts` on the laptop (bun, imports the real `src/feed.ts`, `src/derive.ts`, `src/render.ts` at `1a069c3ff2`; section built in the shape of `test/orchestration.test.ts`'s SECTION fixture, one goal with a `horizon: "today"` lined-up task):

- `ref: "goal_b647ff5c92f5"` → `isOrchestrationSection` **true**; `todayFromSection` objective carries the goal-id ref; `renderTodayBody` **THREW `Error: not a repo-qualified ref: goal_b647ff5c92f5`**
- `ref: 12345` (non-string) → validator **true**; `renderTodayBody` **THREW** the same error
- Control `ref: "developing-today/code#812"` → validator true; renders OK (len 1311) with the GitHub link

So one publisher-supplied lined-up task — a goal id copied into `ref` is a realistic shape, since the same publisher puts goal ids in tier refs in live data (#6149) — takes down the whole `/today` page and its `/frag/today` fragment, instead of taking the designed invalid-section fallback or rendering the ref as plain text.

## Why it matters

`/today` is the dashboard's daily front page. The orchestration section is republished by an external job every run; its refs are publisher data, not aggregator-controlled constants. #6149 showed this exact input class occurs in live data and 500s a whole page render; the objectives path has the identical unguarded call, one page over. The validator's silence on `ref` also breaks the boundary contract the rest of the section gate is built on (#949/#2417/#3897: fields consumers dereference are validated at the gate, or consumers guard) — here neither side holds.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A validator-passing section whose lined-up task carries a non-GitHub ref (goal id, slug, or non-string) no longer throws in `renderTodayBody` / the `/today` and `/frag/today` renders; the objective renders with the ref as plain text/code (the #6149 `tierItemCard` treatment), or the ref is dropped at a named boundary — the chosen layer is stated in the PR
- [ ] A valid `owner/repo#N` lined-up ref still renders as a GitHub link on the objective (control case)
- [ ] Pinning tests cover both cases end-to-end (section → `todayFromSection` → render), mirroring the #6149 regression tests in `test/dashboard-overhaul.test.ts`
- [ ] The `bun test` aggregator suite passes

## Related

- PR #6149 (merged today, commit `d634b9b1a3`) — the tier-card fix for the same class on Needs-you; this issue is its Today-page sibling, not a duplicate: different render site, different input field (`linedUp[].ref`, which the section gate shapes), different page.
- #4952 — the shared `isValidRef` rule the guarded sites route through.
- #2417 / #3897 — the section-gate element-validation line this gap continues.

title: id(currency_poc): InMemoryLedger forgets failed transfer IDs — a failed transfer resubmits and posts after funding, real TigerBeetle refuses it forever (IdAlreadyFailed)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: status/in-progress
