body:
## Summary

`pkgs/id/src/currency_poc/ledger.rs` — `InMemoryLedger` never remembers failed transfer IDs, so it can never return `TransferError::IdAlreadyFailed` — while real TigerBeetle remembers a failed transfer's ID permanently and refuses every resubmission of it. A transfer (or linked chain) that fails in the in-memory backend can be resubmitted later — after the blocker clears, e.g. the debit account is funded — and it **posts**. On a real cluster the same recovery resubmission is refused `id_already_failed` and the conversion can never post with those IDs.

- The variant exists and is documented for exactly this: `TransferError::IdAlreadyFailed` (ledger.rs:97–103) — "TigerBeetle remembers failed transfer IDs and refuses their resubmission (`id_already_failed`). A recovery resubmission meeting this is a rejected resubmission, not a posting."
- The real backend maps it: `tb_ledger.rs:223` — `Status::IdAlreadyFailed => Err(TransferError::IdAlreadyFailed)`.
- The in-memory backend never produces it: an exhaustive grep of `pkgs/id/src/currency_poc/` finds `IdAlreadyFailed` only at its definition (ledger.rs:101–103) and the TB mapper (tb_ledger.rs:223) — the only other mention of the concept is the snake_case status name in the live-test comment (tests.rs:1491). `InMemoryLedger` records only posted transfers (`transfers` / `transfer_order`, ledger.rs:152–156); a chain that fails in `create_transfers` (ledger.rs:270ff) stages nothing and records nothing about the failed IDs, so a later resubmission is validated from scratch as if the first attempt never happened.
- The pinned behaviour exists only as a live-cluster test: `live_failed_conversion_recovery_reports_resubmission_rejected` (tests.rs:1478ff, `#[cfg(feature = "currency-poc-tb")]`, `#[ignore]` — requires the pinned TigerBeetle binary) asserts that after a failed conversion, recovery resubmission is refused (`id_already_failed`, comment at tests.rs:1491) and surfaces as `ResubmissionRejected`. There is no in-memory counterpart — and with the current backend there cannot be one that passes: in-memory, once liquidity is restored, `recovery::reconcile` (recovery.rs:110–125) resubmits the legs, they post, and the record is marked `Posted` instead of `ResubmissionRejected`.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe against the real `id` crate)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-failed-id` on the laptop (path dependency on the real `pkgs/id` crate), at laptop primary HEAD `266875e1e02f8312d63baec10cdf03f917687578` (line citations re-verified at this HEAD):

```
PROBE create_accounts: [Ok(()), Ok(()), Ok(())]
PROBE t42 first submit (unfunded): [Err(DebitsMustNotExceedCredits)]
PROBE t42 identical resubmit (still unfunded): [Err(DebitsMustNotExceedCredits)]
PROBE fund USER id=1: [Ok(())]
PROBE USER balance after funding: Some(AccountBalance { debits_posted: 0, credits_posted: 1000 })
PROBE t42 resubmit after funding: [Ok(())]
PROBE lookup_transfer(42): Some((42, 500))
PROBE LP balance: Some(AccountBalance { debits_posted: 0, credits_posted: 500 })
PROBE t43 amount=0 submit: [Err(AmountMustNotBeZero)]
PROBE t43 fixed-amount resubmit (different fields): [Ok(())]
PROBE chain 50/51 first submit: [Err(DebitsMustNotExceedCredits), Err(LinkedEventFailed)]
PROBE fund USER id=2: [Ok(())]
PROBE chain 50/51 identical resubmit after funding: [Ok(()), Ok(())]
PROBE lookup_transfer(50): Some((50, 600))
PROBE USER balance final: Some(AccountBalance { debits_posted: 1100, credits_posted: 2600 })
```

No resubmission ever returns `IdAlreadyFailed`: the failed transfer `42` posts once funded, the validation-failed ID `43` posts with corrected fields, and the failed linked chain `50/51` posts byte-identical after funding.

Controls in the same run: account creation and the funding transfers post normally; the first submission of each failing shape returns the expected original error (the failure itself is modelled — only the *memory* of the failure is missing).

On the real backend each resubmission above returns `IdAlreadyFailed` (tb_ledger.rs:223) and nothing ever posts with those IDs — the exact behaviour the live test at tests.rs:1478 pins for the recovery path.

## Why it matters

`InMemoryLedger` is the executor's test oracle (see #6135 / #6108 for the sibling divergences): every non-live scenario test, including the whole recovery suite, runs against it. The recovery scanner's central promise is "absent from the ledger ⇒ the submission never landed, so the same IDs may be safely resubmitted" (recovery.rs module docs; intent.rs:9) — but on TigerBeetle "absent" has two different meanings: *never submitted* (resubmittable) and *submitted and failed* (poisoned forever). The in-memory backend collapses them into one, so the in-memory recovery tests certify a resubmission path that, against a real cluster, strands the intent as `ResubmissionRejected` — and, worse, a scenario in which a failed conversion later posts after re-funding passes in-memory while being impossible in production. The one test that pins the real behaviour is `#[ignore]`d and needs a live cluster, so CI never runs it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `InMemoryLedger` records the IDs of transfers that failed for their own reason (validation / balance-invariant failures, including the failing leg of a linked chain), and any later submission of a recorded ID returns `Err(TransferError::IdAlreadyFailed)` — regardless of whether the resubmitted fields match or differ, and regardless of whether the original blocker has cleared
- [ ] The treatment of `LinkedEventFailed` legs (siblings of the failing leg) is decided explicitly and pinned by a test, consistent with what the TB binding observes on resubmission of a failed chain (the live test at tests.rs:1478 is the reference: the record surfaces `ResubmissionRejected`)
- [ ] An in-memory counterpart of `live_failed_conversion_recovery_reports_resubmission_rejected` passes: failed conversion → fund the account → `reconcile` with `RecoveryPolicy::Resubmit` yields `ResubmissionRejected`, the record stays `Submitted`/unresolved, and no leg posts
- [ ] Controls unchanged: resubmitting a *posted* transfer still returns `Exists` / `ExistsWithDifferentFields`; resubmitting a chain rejected as unterminated (`LinkedEventChainOpen` — the trait docs at ledger.rs:136 promise those transfers "may be resubmitted (properly terminated) in a later batch") still works; a failed ID's failure does not block unrelated new transfers
- [ ] `cargo test -p id --lib currency_poc` passes

## Related

- #6135 — sibling oracle divergence in the same backend (zero / int-max IDs accepted and posted in-memory, refused by real TigerBeetle).
- #6108 — the real-backend side: unmodelled TB statuses (including the shapes that produce `id_already_failed` verdicts) panic in the `tb_ledger.rs` mappers.
- #6102 — sibling builder gap in `build_conversion_batch`.
- tests.rs:1478 `live_failed_conversion_recovery_reports_resubmission_rejected` — the live-only pin this issue asks to make reproducible in-memory.

body:
Parent: [#6021](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/6021) (classification revalidation scan). Research source: prior-art doc `~/workspace/scratch/atlas-ingestion-brief-2026-11-04/prior-art-research.md` (2026-11-04). Follow-up 29 (Cluster 5).

## Decision to record (research, in substance)

trufflehog is the broader secret scanner (more sources + **live credential verification**), but for Atlas it carries two structural problems:

1. **License:** trufflehog is **AGPL-3.0**, which collides with Drew's 2026-10-24 adoption hard filter ("NOT AGPL, NOT GPL") for our own dependencies. Adopting it needs the adoption-vs-use question answered deliberately, not by drift.
2. **Exfiltration:** verification is **on by default and calls external vendor APIs with candidate secrets**. Inside a secret-tier scan, that behavior would exfiltrate the very material being hunted. Any use must be `--no-verification` only.

**Ruling proposed by the research:** gitleaks-first (MIT, fully local); trufflehog, if ever, only with `--no-verification` and only after the license question is answered on the record (the adoption/upload regime distinction is being worked in the licensing family, #5977/#5984/#5986).

## Done looks like

The decision recorded here (adopt the ruling or amend it), so the classification scanner design (under #6021) builds on gitleaks-class tooling by default.

title: id: research: AGPL/GPL hosting analysis — inspectable-by-default vs copyleft network clauses, self-hoster obligations

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: A design proposal (design-architect): multi-step, phased, decision-bearing

body:
Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Statement S91 of the 2026-11-04 brief. Research, not legal advice — the output informs policy defaults; final policy text gets a lawyer pass separately.

## The question (Drew, in substance)

> The problem is it's exactly the line where AGPL becomes… Is that going to block someone from running their own server if someone hosts AGPL there? Because then it's sharing code over the internet, and generally, in my design, all of this is fully inspectable by all users, so we would meet any GPL requirements. GPL shouldn't be banned per se, but we don't want tricky situations. We want this to be simple.

## Research points

- **AGPL §13 mechanics** applied to our shape: users interacting with a world over a network — who is the "user interacting" with AGPL code when a world *imports* an AGPL library but the world's own code is MIT? What must be offered, to whom, in what form?
- **Does inspectability satisfy it?** Our design makes everything fully inspectable by all users by default. Map that against GPLv3 §6 / AGPL §13 source-offer requirements precisely: is ambient inspectability a Corresponding Source offer, or does the license want a specific offer mechanism regardless?
- **The self-hosting scenario**: a third party runs their own server; a user uploads AGPL content to it. What obligations land on the *server operator* vs the *uploader* vs *us* (protocol/library authors)? This is the scenario the brief worries about — answer it directly.
- **GPL (non-AGPL) in a networked world**: distribution vs mere interaction; why GPLv2/3 are usually *not* triggered by SaaS-style use, and whether our inspect-and-share-everything design changes that (it might convert interaction into distribution — in which case compliance is ambient, or in which case obligations multiply; say which).
- **Combination pressure**: AGPL library inside an MIT world that other worlds import — does the obligation travel? (Feeds the combination-checker child of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955).)
- Precedents: how plugin/theme ecosystems (WordPress), game-mod ecosystems, and federated software (Mastodon is AGPL) have handled exactly this shape.

## Done looks like

A research doc answering the headline question in its first paragraph, with the scenario table (operator/uploader/author × GPL2/GPL3/AGPL) and the design implications listed for the policy child.

body:
Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Statements S101–S105 of the 2026-11-04 brief.

## Requirement (Drew, in substance)

- There should be at least a basic mechanism to say **"you can't combine this with this, because this is a violation of something."** When we say "can't," we mean: **warn heavily**, and have a **checkbox that says "override"**, or a **"request exception"** button to **raise it to an admin who can say "yes, we accept this file."**
- On the user's side it should **just all work**. They should just kind of understand **anything they post is available for others to share**.
- If they edit it, **they either do or don't have to share their edited version** (per its license).
- If they sell things or whatever, the rules are mostly that users think **anything that I see or that I provide could be copied and used in other places**.
- Over time we might have a more nuanced model like the **Google Terms of Service**, where **anything that's on the site can be forked, inspected, and reviewed (even if it's completely unlicensed or whatever)**.

## Design points to settle

- Combination events: what counts as combining — a world importing a library, a DLL linking a dependency, assets bundled into a world upload, a moderation library reused across worlds? Each fires the check at a different moment (import time, upload time, publish time).
- The incompatibility rules v1: copyleft propagation into combined works (GPL-family × permissive distribution), NC × commercial server, share-alike obligations, unlicensed × redistribution. Rules consume the taxonomy (sibling child of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955)) — this design owns the rule table and the UX, not the license list.
- Override vs exception: an override is a self-serve attestation (recorded, attributed, reversible); an exception request is an admin decision (queued, answered, scoped to the file/world). Which violations get which path — AGPL-class probably exception-only; say so explicitly.
- Records: every override/exception is a registry fact (who, when, what pair) so a later admin can audit why a combination exists.
- The user-side norm ("anything posted can be shared; edits may or may not be share-back") must be *stated in the flow*, not only in a ToS document nobody reads — one line at upload, in plain language.

## Related

- License taxonomy & classifier, and licensing policy + ToS children of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955)
- Library imports design child (import time is where combinations physically happen)

## Done looks like

A design doc: the combination-event list, the v1 incompatibility rule table, override vs exception-request flows, and the audit record shape.

# ci(worktree-reaper): test_worktree_reaper.py is run by no workflow — the destructive reap gates are verified nowhere

## Summary

`infra/worktree-reaper/tests/test_worktree_reaper.py` (8 tests) is enumerated by no workflow and no other automation: it runs only when a human follows the README's manual command. That suite is the only automated guard on the reaper's safety gates — the checks that must all hold before the tool deletes a worktree (dry-run, kill switch, the reap matrix, the quiet gate, and the run-log audit trail).

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ 2b476fd0453c8b6de423154b8b645b33ed8e76f4)

- `grep -rn "worktree-reaper" .github/workflows/` → zero references; no workflow mentions the tool or its tests. No justfile/flake step runs the suite either. The only scheduled runner in the repo is `infra/worktree-reaper/systemd/worktree-reaper.{service,timer}`, whose `ExecStart` runs `bin/worktree_reaper.py` itself (the production reaper) — never its tests.
- `infra/worktree-reaper/README.md`, "Tests" section: the sole documented runner is a manual `python3 tests/test_worktree_reaper.py`, with the note "Run them on the laptop — the occupied gate needs a real `/proc`" (a Linux CI runner has a real `/proc`).
- The suite passes today, run on the laptop: `python3 -m unittest discover -s infra/worktree-reaper/tests -v` → `Ran 8 tests in 0.888s — OK` (GateTests ×4, RunLogCollisionTests ×1, UnitTests ×3; the gate tests build synthetic bare-origin/clone/worktree repos in tempdirs).
- This gap has already bitten once: #5716 — a run-log filename collision that made the gate suite fail 6/6 and silently overwrote a prior run's audit log — was found only because a fleet creator happened to run the suite by hand during an unrelated run. The open #5740 (fail closed when `/proc` cannot be scanned before removal) is in the same gate surface this suite exercises. A regression in the kill switch or reap matrix would currently surface as a wrongly deleted worktree, not a failing check.

## Why it matters

The worktree-reaper is a destructive tool running on a timer against the fleet's live worktree farm. Its gates are the entire safety case for unattended deletion, and the tests exist and pass in under a second — but nothing runs them, so gate regressions are discovered in production, after a tree is gone.

## Acceptance criteria

- Some workflow runs `infra/worktree-reaper/tests/test_worktree_reaper.py` and fails when a test fails (a dispatch-triggered workflow is consistent with the house pattern since 5a94833ea3).
- The full suite (8 tests) passes under the new wiring on the workflow's Python on a Linux runner (real `/proc` for the occupied gate).
- A green run cannot be a silently skipped suite: the wiring names the test file/discovery directory explicitly.
- No behaviour change to `bin/worktree_reaper.py`.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues this run for "worktree-reaper tests / workflow / CI" and "test_worktree_reaper": #5740 (the `/proc` fail-closed bug, open — a behaviour fix, not CI wiring), #5716 (the run-log collision, closed — found by a hand run of this suite), and no CI-wiring filing for this suite. Sibling same-class filings cover different suites: #5945 (repo-universe), #5942 (fleet-paperwork), #5937 (github-backup).

title: Session proxy: fail fast (≤2s, not 16-26s), single-flight recovery, timestamped broker log, pool stays 50

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

body:
## Session-proxy: fail fast, size the pool from the ramp, timestamp the broker log (WS-C)

Part of epic #5412. Evidence: WS-C comment on #5701 (2026-11-04) + the #5701 stage-2 ramp.

### Facts
- Ramp (stage 2, #5701): 50/64/128 concurrent tunnels all succeeded (14.6 s wall at 128, latency ≈ serialized CONNECT setup). **No ceiling ≤128** — so pool size is NOT a correctness limit today; `LAPTOP_AGENT_POOL=50` (`~/tools/init-ensure.sh`) stays until the multiplexed-tunnel work (sibling issue) makes pool size moot. Do NOT raise to 128: more idle tunnels = more keepalive traffic and a bigger CONNECT stampede on proxy recovery, for zero measured benefit.
- Failure mode is the real cost: in trips.jsonl (n=1149, 2026-11-04), status 502 trips have p50 **16,294 ms** (n=119) and no-status trips p50 **25,965 ms** (n=73). The broker retries once on a stale connection and the client timeout is 660 s — during a proxy wobble every caller pays 16–26 s before failing, and dozens of callers × retries amplify the herd (the stage-1 addendum found the same chain).
- Keepalive/idle today (Python broker, mirrored by `fleet proxy serve` behavior to confirm): KEEPALIVE_S=180 health ping, broker exits after 3,600 s idle, pool per port.
- Broker log has **no timestamps** and broker ownership has flapped between the Python broker (pool 12) and `fleet proxy serve` (pool 50) with no record of which was live in an incident window (stage-1 addendum, #5701).

### Proposal
1. **Fail fast on dead target**: cap total per-call failure latency at ≤2 s when the tunnel target is unreachable (bounded CONNECT attempt + one stream-level retry, no second full CONNECT inside one call). Healthy-path latency unchanged; the 660 s cap stays ONLY for the daemon-side exec duration, not for transport setup.
2. **Single-flight tunnel recovery**: when the pool/tunnel is down, exactly one reconnect attempt in flight; concurrent callers wait on it or fail fast — never N parallel CONNECTs.
3. **Timestamped, identity-stamped broker log**: every broker start writes one line {ts, implementation, version, pool_size, pid}; every ownership handoff is therefore reconstructable after an incident.
4. **Deterministic single owner**: one implementation owns broker.sock (fleet proxy serve); the Python broker starts only when the fleet binary is absent (the init-ensure gate already expresses this intent — enforce it in the clients' auto-start paths too, which still spawn the Python broker directly: laptop-agent.py `_broker_roundtrip`, repo-queue `spawn_broker`).
5. **Keepalive policy**: keep 180 s application keepalive per tunnel while pooled HTTP remains; re-evaluate under the multiplexed design (PING on the single tunnel). Idle-exit stays 3,600 s.

### Acceptance
- Kill the runtime proxy mid-test: p50 failed-trip latency in trips.jsonl ≤2 s (from 16.3 s), and recovery shows exactly 1 CONNECT stampede in the watcher log.
- broker.log first line after any start is timestamped with implementation + pool size.
- No client auto-start path can spawn the Python broker while a fleet binary exists.

body:
## Problem

Daemon startup can delete a regular file that happens to occupy the configured Unix socket path. In pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/server.go, the cleanup path around lines 342–345 and 479–489 attempts a Unix dial and removes the path whenever dialing fails. A regular file is not a live socket, so the failed dial is followed by os.Remove and its contents are lost before the daemon binds.

A stale Unix socket should be removable, but an unrelated regular file or symlink must not be treated as stale socket state.

## Required behavior

Inspect the path type before removal. Remove only a stale socket file after confirming it cannot be connected to; for any non-socket filesystem entry, preserve it and return a clear startup error that identifies the collision.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A test creates a regular file at the configured socket path, attempts daemon startup, and asserts startup fails while the file contents remain unchanged.
- [ ] A stale Unix socket at that path is still cleaned up and startup succeeds.
- [ ] An active socket remains protected and is not removed.
- [ ] Cover custom MCPX_SOCKET and the default socket path through the same cleanup helper where possible.

body:
# fleet(dispatch): duplicate and contradictory flags are silently resolved — last value wins, `--no-*` always beats `--*`

## Summary

`fleet dispatch launch` / `fleet dispatch enqueue` parse their flags with a hand-rolled parser (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-dispatch/src/lib.rs`) that silently discards user input in three ways:

1. **Duplicate value flags overwrite silently.** `parse_args` stores each `--flag value` with `values.insert(...)` (lib.rs:555), so `--repo developing-today/code --repo dezren39/darwin-nix` launches against the second repo with no error or warning — the first value is silently dropped.
2. **Contradictory boolean pairs resolve by check order, not argument order.** `verb_launch` tests `no-issue` before `issue` and `no-wait` before `wait` (lib.rs:638-649), so `--issue --no-issue` **and** `--no-issue --issue` both send `issue: false`. One of the two flags the user typed is silently ignored, whichever order they wrote them in.
3. **`--prompt` + `--prompt-file` together silently drop the prompt.** `prompt_of` (lib.rs:580-587) prefers `--prompt-file` whenever it is present; an explicitly typed `--prompt <text>` is discarded without a word.

This is the fleet CLI family's established silent-discard class (see #5568, #5572, #5592, #5603, #5607, #5652 — trailing/extra arguments silently ignored, each fixed to a usage error naming the argument). Duplicate and contradictory flags are the same failure one step earlier in parsing, with sharper consequences: `launch` creates real sessions, tracking issues, and queue tasks, so a silently-wrong `--repo`, a silently-dropped tracking issue (`--issue` overridden by a stray `--no-issue`), or a silently-substituted prompt acts on the wrong work instead of merely misreporting success.

## Evidence (main @ af0847d00a2231c71f6ebb59eba4cc7db197599e, read via `gh api` raw; laptop unavailable this run — broker tunnel down, #5708)

- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-dispatch/src/lib.rs:527-570` — `parse_args`: value flags go into a `Map` via `values.insert(name, ...)` at :555 with no duplicate check; bool flags via `flags.insert(...)` at :544. Unknown flags and missing values are usage errors — duplicates are the one malformed shape that is not.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-dispatch/src/lib.rs:638-649` — `verb_launch`: `if parsed.flag("no-issue") { issue=false } else if parsed.flag("issue") { issue=true }`, and the same shape for `no-wait`/`wait`. Both members of a pair can be present simultaneously; the negative always wins regardless of order.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-dispatch/src/lib.rs:580-587` — `prompt_of`: `if let Some(path) = args.get("prompt-file") { read it }` else require `--prompt`. Both supplied → the `--prompt` text never reaches the request body.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-dispatch/src/lib.rs:660-735` — `verb_enqueue` shares the same parser and the same `prompt_of`, so duplicates of `--repo` / `--title` / `--issue-number` / `--dedupe-key` overwrite silently there too.
- The fleet-queue client parser has the same overwrite shape (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/client.rs:471-504`, `opts.insert` at :487/:490) — noted as the sibling surface; this issue's fix is scoped to fleet-dispatch, and the queue parser can be aligned in the same change if the worker judges it in-scope, or filed separately.

## Why it matters

`fleet dispatch launch` is the fleet's own session launcher: it POSTs to pm-dispatch, which creates a tracking issue and a queue task and starts an OpenCode session on the laptop. Silent flag resolution means a mistyped or scripted command can launch work against the wrong repository, skip the tracking issue the operator asked for, wait (or not wait) contrary to the flag they wrote last, or run a prompt read from a file instead of the text they typed — with exit 0 and no indication anything was overridden. Every sibling surface in this CLI family now errors on silently-discarded input; dispatch's parser is the remaining one that resolves it quietly.

## Acceptance criteria

- `parse_args` in fleet-dispatch rejects a repeated value flag (`--repo a --repo b`, including the `--repo=a` inline form) with a usage error naming the flag, before any network call.
- `verb_launch` rejects `--issue` together with `--no-issue`, and `--wait` together with `--no-wait`, with a usage error naming the contradictory pair, before any network call. (Rejecting a repeated identical bool flag is optional; the contradictory pair must error.)
- Supplying both `--prompt` and `--prompt-file` to launch or enqueue is a usage error naming both, instead of silently preferring the file.
- Single, non-contradictory invocations behave exactly as today (including `--help` in any position, per #5560's verb help handling).
- New pinning tests in the fleet-dispatch test module cover: duplicate value flag rejected, both contradictory pairs rejected in both orders, prompt+prompt-file rejected, and the ordinary single-flag controls still parse.
- `cargo test -p fleet-dispatch` passes on the laptop / in CI.

Related: #5560 (dispatch status args, fixed), #5555 (dispatch status endpoint gap), #5413 (absorb dispatch into repo-queue — if that lands first, the same rule should hold in the absorbing parser).

title: fleet-queue(client): HOME unset/empty makes home() empty — broker socket, token, and worker signal paths all anchor at the filesystem root

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

labels.description: pkgs/fleet multicall binary + platform crates

body:
## Problem

In the fleet-queue client (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/client.rs`, the `repo-queue` binary every fleet agent uses to enqueue / claim / signal), the home helper treats a missing or empty `HOME` as the empty string:

```rust
// client.rs:31-33
fn home() -> String {
    std::env::var("HOME").unwrap_or_default()
}
```

Every path the client derives is a `format!("{}/...", home())`, so with `HOME` unset **or empty** each one anchors at the filesystem root instead of the user's home:

- `client.rs:56` — session-proxy socket: `/.cache/laptop-agent/broker.sock`
- `client.rs:76` — direct-broker marker: `/.config/repo-queue/broker-url`
- `client.rs:95` — direct-broker token: `/.config/queue-broker/token`
- `client.rs:148` — session-proxy payload `token_file`: `/tools/queue-broker-token` (the laptop-side proxy is told to read the broker token from the root of its filesystem)
- `client.rs:218` — auto-start fallback program: `/tools/laptop-agent-broker.py`
- `client.rs:223` — `spawn_broker` does `create_dir_all("/.cache/laptop-agent")` and opens `/.cache/laptop-agent/broker.log` there
- `client.rs:1221` — `cmd_signal`'s default signal path: `/workspace/goals/keep-the-four-repos-healthy/hidden_files/repo-queue-signal.json` — the file that wakes the queue worker lands at the root-anchored path, not the goal workspace, so the signal silently never reaches the worker

Same crate, secondary sites: the brokers handle unset loudly but let the empty half through — `queue_broker.rs:592` and `secrets_broker.rs:192` use `std::env::var("HOME").expect("HOME unset")`, so `HOME=""` yields the root-anchored token paths `/.config/queue-broker/token` / `/.config/secrets-broker/token`; `secrets_broker.rs:45` reads the Bitwarden access token from `{home}/.config/bitwarden/access-token` with the same empty-home shape.

## Evidence

Code read at current main `2db40a34e0` (via `gh api` raw reads; the laptop SSH route was down during this run, so no binary probe — the behaviour follows deterministically from the constructions above: `env::var("HOME")` errs on unset and returns `""` on empty, `unwrap_or_default()` maps both to `""`, and `format!("{home}/.cache/...")` with `home == ""` is the root-anchored path shown).

Contrast inside this repo, i.e. the class is known and the fix shape exists:

- fleet-config was fixed for exactly this class in #5473 and now routes through a `non_empty_path` helper (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs`).
- #5640 tracks the sibling pattern in atlas-search / atlas-core / fleet-search (literal `~` fallback, CWD-relative there). It does not name fleet-queue.
- `pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs` treats a missing `HOME` as a hard error with context.

## Why it matters

`repo-queue` is invoked from cron jobs, systemd units, and agent shells — exactly the contexts where `HOME` is most often unset or empty. In that state the client does not fail: it connects to (or tries to spawn) a broker at root-anchored paths, reads a broker URL / token from files the operator never wrote, and writes the worker-wake signal to a path no watcher reads. The failure presents as a silently idle queue or a "cannot connect to session proxy" error pointing nowhere near the cause. If a root-anchored `/.config/repo-queue/broker-url` or token file ever exists (e.g. created by a root-run invocation), a later user-level client would silently trust it.

## Acceptance criteria

- The client's home resolution treats an empty `HOME` as unset, and with `HOME` unset/empty every verb either fails loudly naming `HOME` or resolves the real home another way — one rule, shared with (or matching) fleet-config's `non_empty_path` approach.
- With `HOME` unset/empty, no fleet-queue verb reads, writes, creates, or spawns at a root-anchored path (`/.cache/...`, `/.config/...`, `/tools/...`, `/workspace/...`).
- The brokers (`queue_broker.rs`, `secrets_broker.rs`) treat empty `HOME` the same as unset at the token-file / access-token sites.
- Regression tests pin both shapes (unset and empty) for at least the broker socket path, the direct-broker token path, and the signal path.
- Behaviour with `HOME` set is unchanged: existing fleet-queue tests stay green and the paths resolve exactly as today.

body:
Follow-up from triage task 9456 on issue #5082, confirmed against current main `8de9292b77ff3fbfd72153bf0e6ac6758be635cc`.

## Evidence

On 2026-11-04 at 22:10:34Z, ordinary `curl` probes against the already-running laptop aggregator at `127.0.0.1:4870` returned `curl: (52) Empty reply from server`, 0 bytes, after ~12.0s for `/board` (12.002793s), `/api/board.json` (12.003588s), `/api/overview.json` (12.011524s), `/frag/overview` (12.007072s), and `/program` (12.004105s). `/api/program.json` returned 200 / 64,684B in 3.088804s; `/api/quota.json` returned 200 / 50,995B in 0.018966s. The server process was Bun PID 11116 with cwd `/home/user/git/code/pm-stack/aggregator`, started 09:39:30 local; this task did not launch it and its loaded SHA is unknown.

Current-main source inspection: `pm-stack/aggregator/src/server.ts` awaits the full context before returning on `/board` (1307-1316), `/frag/overview` (1302-1306), `/api/overview.json` (1745-1746), and `/api/board.json` (1748-1761). `boardContext` serially awaits board refs and items (459-464); `overviewContext` waits for its slowest facet (701-712). `Bun.serve` has no explicit `idleTimeout` (2211-2217), and the source reads have individual timeouts longer than the observed cutoff (for example Kaneo 8s per call, projects 20s, Supabase 60s). Current main has no bounded stale/error response for this assembly. The exact source of the 12s cutoff is not proven; an idle timeout is a plausible contributing cause, not a confirmed root cause.

## Scope

Make the affected dashboard assembly routes settle with bytes: return a last-good/stale result when available, otherwise an explicit bounded timeout/error response (including a visible fragment error for `/frag/overview`) rather than allowing the connection to close silently. Add deterministic tests with slow/stalled stub sources that assert each affected route returns the defined stale/error behavior. Do not treat increasing `Bun.serve` `idleTimeout` alone as sufficient; the application still needs a bounded outcome. Preserve fast-path behavior.

## Separate symptom

The historical `/program` HTML size regression (~1.16MB) is not measured by this probe because `/program` itself currently closes at ~12s; its JSON twin returned normally. Re-measure bytes after the response reliability fix and track HTML slimming separately if still present.

Links: #5082

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Under slow dashboard assembly, `/board`, `/api/board.json`, `/api/overview.json` and `/frag/overview` never return an empty reply: each either serves within a bounded time or returns an explicit error/stale response the client can act on.
- [ ] The ~12s empty-reply probes recorded in the evidence (2026-11-04 22:10Z against the laptop aggregator) no longer reproduce, or the remaining slow path is named with its bound.
- [ ] Fast endpoints (`/api/quota.json`, `/api/program.json`) do not regress.
- [ ] Fix is covered by a test or a reproducible probe script showing behaviour before/after.

body:
# atlas-search: CLI `get-chunk --neighbors` has no upper bound — standalone returns the whole message, bypassing the service's 100-neighbor cap

## Summary

The service caps get-chunk neighbor context at 100, but the standalone CLI path for the same command enforces no maximum at all:

- The service's get-chunk handler rejects `neighbors > 100`: `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-search/src/server.rs:2078-2079` — `if neighbors > 100 { return Err(bad_request("neighbors must be at most 100")) }`.
- The CLI's `count()` validation — documented as validating "against the service's request contract" (`pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-search/src/main.rs:583-591`) — validates `--neighbors` only as non-negative, no maximum: `main.rs:664` calls `count("--neighbors", args.neighbors, 0, None)`.
- The standalone path then calls `run_get_chunk(backend, chunk_id, neighbors)` (`main.rs:669`), which feeds `neighbor_map` in `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-core/src/search.rs:283-284, 401-402` — the same `chunk_idx ± n` range machinery, with no cap.

So the identical request is a `bad_request` error via the service and an unbounded whole-message dump via the standalone CLI. This is the sibling of #5593 (`--expand` on the search surfaces, same missing bound, different flag/command/server check); #5593 does not cover the CLI get-chunk path.

## Verified this run (2026-11-04, laptop probe)

Probe DB `~/git/fleet/probe-atlas-neighbors/probe.db` (same fixture schema as the #5593 probe: one message with 300 chunks, chunk 151 mid-message), the `atlas-search` binary built from laptop main `8a8d509f8`, local backend:

- `get-chunk 151 --neighbors 2` → context: 2 before + 2 after (control, as expected).
- `get-chunk 151 --neighbors 100` → 100 before + 100 after (the service cap, honored only by coincidence of the request).
- `get-chunk 151 --neighbors 250` → **150 before + 149 after = 299 context chunks, exit 0** — the whole message, nearly 3× the total the service allows for this exact command.

## Why it matters

- Neighbor context is the response-size multiplier the 100 cap exists to bound; the standalone CLI — the fallback path used exactly when no service is running — defeats it completely.
- This is the CLI↔service contract family of #5407 (closed) and #5593 (open): a count the service rejects must not silently pass on the CLI surface. #5407 fixed the 0/negative clamps; #5593 covers `--expand`; `--neighbors` on get-chunk is the remaining uncapped count.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The CLI's `count()` validation for `--neighbors` enforces the same maximum the service enforces (100), exit 2 with a message naming the bound, before any backend work — mirroring the `--pool` max handling.
- [ ] A pinning test covers `--neighbors` at the bound (accepted) and above it (rejected), alongside the existing `count_validation_mirrors_the_service_contract` test in `main.rs`.
- [ ] If the fix for #5593 introduces a shared neighbor-bound constant, this cap uses it too (one source of truth for the neighbor bound across `expand`, get-chunk service, and get-chunk CLI).

## Evidence

- `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-search/src/server.rs:2078-2079` (service get-chunk neighbors cap 100)
- `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-search/src/main.rs:583-599` (count() contract comment), `:664` (`--neighbors` min 0, no max), `:669` (standalone run_get_chunk call)
- `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-core/src/search.rs:262, 283-284, 401-402` (run_get_chunk → neighbor_map, `n as i64`)
- Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-atlas-neighbors/` (probe.db, out-n2.json / out-n100.json / out-n250.json) on the laptop, 2026-11-04, binary built from `8a8d509f8`
- Related: #5593 (`--expand` unbounded — sibling, open), #5407 (CLI count clamps, closed)

body:
# atlas-search: `expand` has no upper bound anywhere — one search hit can return its whole message, bypassing the 100-neighbor cap the service enforces on get-chunk

## Summary

Atlas search's neighbor expansion is bounded on exactly one surface and unbounded on the search surfaces that use the same backend call:

- The service's get-chunk endpoint caps `neighbors` at 100: `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-search/src/server.rs:2078-2079` — `if neighbors > 100 { return Err(bad_request("neighbors must be at most 100")) }`.
- The service's search validation caps `pool` (1..=400) and rejects `k == 0` and `page_limit == 0`, but places **no bound on `expand`**: `validate_request`, `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-search/src/server.rs:509-525`.
- The CLI, whose `count()` is documented as validating "against the service's request contract" (`pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-search/src/main.rs:578-591`), likewise validates `--expand` only as non-negative, no maximum (`main.rs:606`).
- `expand` feeds the same neighbor machinery as get-chunk's `neighbors`: `atlas-core` `search.rs:391-392` calls `neighbor_map(backend, d, opts.expand)` for **every kept hit**, and `neighbor_map` (`search.rs:401-402`) issues `backend.neighbors(message_id, chunk_idx, n)` — a `chunk_idx ± n` range query in both backends (`atlas-core/src/local.rs:631-639`, `atlas-core/src/turso.rs:624-631`). So one request's response can carry up to `k × 2 × expand` chunk texts, and `k` itself has no upper bound in `validate_request` either (only `k >= 1`).

## Verified this run (2026-11-04, laptop probe)

Probe DB `~/git/fleet/probe-atlas-expand/probe.db` (fixture schema; one message with 300 chunks, chunk 150 carrying the unique term `zebraquux`), run with the installed `atlas-search` binary, local backend, FTS mode, `--k 1`:

- `--expand 2` → context: 2 before + 2 after (control, as expected).
- `--expand 250` → context: **150 before + 149 after = 299 neighbor chunks for a single hit** — nearly 3× the per-request neighbor total the get-chunk endpoint allows, from one hit alone.
- `--expand 1000000` → accepted identically (whole message returned).

The code at HEAD (`aa06c420d`) has the same unbounded paths cited above; the probe corroborates them at the CLI surface, and `validate_request` is the service-side gate a wire request passes through (`server.rs:1299`).

Secondary: `expand` is a `usize` on the wire (`atlas-proto/src/lib.rs:181`); `neighbor_map` casts it `n as i64`, so a JSON `expand` above `i64::MAX` wraps negative and silently yields an empty/inverted neighbor range instead of a validation error.

## Why it matters

- The 100-neighbor cap exists because neighbor context is the response-size multiplier; the search path defeats it — one job with a large `k` and `expand` can force the service to materialize and return effectively whole messages per hit, with no validation error.
- This is the same CLI↔service contract family as #5407 (closed): counts the service rejects must not silently pass on other surfaces, and vice versa. #5407 fixed the 0/negative clamps for `--k`/`--pool`; the missing upper bound for `expand` was left behind on both sides.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `validate_request` (server.rs) rejects a search request whose `expand` exceeds a stated maximum, with a `bad_request` message naming the bound — the bound should be justified against the get-chunk neighbors cap (100) or a documented reason for a different value recorded in the code.
- [ ] The CLI's `count()` validation for `--expand` enforces the same maximum (exit 2, same message shape as `--pool`), keeping the CLI↔service contract in lockstep per #5407.
- [ ] A test pins both surfaces: `expand` at the bound accepted, above it rejected (service validation test and/or CLI parity test).
- [ ] Consider the same treatment for `k`'s missing upper bound in `validate_request`; if left unbounded, the code comment says why (e.g. bounded by corpus/ranking size) — not silent.
- [ ] The `usize as i64` wrap in `neighbor_map` can no longer be reached with an out-of-range value (validation makes it moot, or the cast becomes a checked conversion).

## Evidence

- `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-search/src/server.rs:509-525` (validate_request: pool/k/page_limit only), `:1299` (submit gate), `:2073-2081` (get-chunk neighbors cap 100), `:1410` (page limit clamped ≤ the results length)
- `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-search/src/main.rs:578-607` (count() contract comment; `--expand` min 0, no max; `--pool` max 400 by contrast)
- `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-core/src/search.rs:391-392, 401-402` (per-hit neighbor_map, `n as i64`)
- `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-core/src/local.rs:631-639` and `turso.rs:624-631` (`chunk_idx ± n` range, no LIMIT)
- Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-atlas-expand/` (make_probe_db.py, probe.db, out-e2.json / out-e250.json / out-e1000000.json) on the laptop, 2026-11-04
- Related: #5407 (CLI count clamps, closed), #5375 (atlas LIKE filters — different mechanism)

body:
## Problem

The new `id-native-shell` crate (F13.6 step 1, PR #5573, for issue #5542) is a workspace member of `pkgs/id` but is excluded from `default-members`, and **no check anywhere runs its build, tests, or lints** — not CI, not the flake checks, not `check-all`, not the just recipes. Its contract-parity transcript test is the step-1 conformance gate for the F13.1 shell contract; today that gate exists on paper only, so a change to `pkgs/id/contract/shell-contract.v1.json` or to the frame builders can silently break the native shell's contract conformance and nothing will notice until step 2.

## Evidence (verified on main `857e3413d`, laptop primary, 2026-11-04)

- `pkgs/id/Cargo.toml`: `members = ["crates/id-core", "crates/id-native-shell"]` but `default-members = [".", "crates/id-core"]`. `cargo metadata` on the laptop confirms `workspace_default_members` = `id` + `id-core` only.
- Every cargo entry point runs at the workspace root with no `--workspace` and no `-p id-native-shell`, so all of them scope to the default members:
  - `pkgs/id/justfile`: `cargo-check` = `cargo check --all-targets --all-features`; `clippy-lint` = `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features`; `test-unit` = `cargo test --all-features --lib`; `test-sandbox` = `cargo test --all-features`; the `ci` recipe chains exactly these.
  - `pkgs/id/check-all`: `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features`, `cargo test --lib`, `cargo test --doc` — same scoping.
  - `pkgs/id/flake.nix` checks (`cargo-check`, `clippy-lint`, `test`, `test-unit`, shards, `doc`, `default = ci`) all delegate to those just recipes.
  - `.github/workflows/id-check.yml`: the only direct cargo test invocation is `cargo test -p id` (arm64 snapshot job).
- No occurrence of `native-shell` / `native_shell` exists in `pkgs/id/flake.nix`, `pkgs/id/nix/`, `pkgs/id/default.nix`, `pkgs/id/check-all`, `pkgs/id/justfile`, or `pkgs/id/build.sh` (grep, 2026-11-04).
- PR #5573's status checks were only CodeRabbit — no cargo check exercised the crate on its own PR.
- The tests themselves are real and pass when invoked explicitly on the laptop: `cargo test -p id-native-shell` at `857e3413d`, verified twice in this run — 7 library tests (frame builders + bounds + view fallback) plus the 2 transcript tests in `crates/id-native-shell/tests/transcript.rs` that validate the recorded frames against `contract/shell-contract.v1.json`, all green. They simply never run unless someone types that exact command.
- The design's step-1 "Done when" (`pkgs/id/docs/2026-11-01_design_id788.md` §7) requires "`cargo build -p id-native-shell` succeeds, and the fixture passes" — there is currently no automated gate keeping either true.

## Why it matters

Step 2 of #5542 builds the live contract-parity session harness on top of these frame builders and bounds. If the transcript test or a bound (e.g. paste 4096 bytes, resize 500×200) rots against a contract revision in the meantime, step 2 starts from a silently non-conforming base. This is exactly the class of drift the shell-contract checks exist to catch for the web/terminal shells.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] At least one PR-gating check (flake check in the `id-check` matrix, or an equivalent CI step) runs `cargo test -p id-native-shell` and a compile/clippy pass over the crate (e.g. `cargo check -p id-native-shell --all-targets`), so a contract or builder change that breaks it turns a required check red.
- [ ] The local path agrees: `pkgs/id/check-all` and/or the just `ci` recipe chain includes the native-shell test pass (explicit `-p` is fine; do NOT add the crate to `default-members` — the Bevy-free `cargo build -p id` isolation is a design requirement of #788 step 1).
- [ ] The new check is proven live: a deliberate temporary break (e.g. a paste-bound mismatch against the contract) makes it fail, and it passes again on clean main. Oracle: `pkgs/id/contract/shell-contract.v1.json` is the reference the transcript test validates against.
- [ ] `cargo build -p id` still pulls in no Bevy/desktop dependencies after the change.

Related: #5542 (implementation), #788 (design). Not a duplicate: neither tracks CI/check coverage of the crate.

title: fleet: serve <broker-role> silently ignores all trailing arguments — a typo'd flag starts the daemon instead of erroring

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

body:
## Problem

`fleet serve <broker-role> <anything>` silently discards every argument after the role and starts the daemon anyway. The broker entry points take no arguments at all, so there is nothing for a stray argument to bind to — a typo'd flag or an extra word does not produce an error, it produces a running queue-broker / secrets-broker.

This is the un-fixed remainder of #5488: that fix intercepted a help flag in the one position after the role (`wants_domain_help`), but any non-help argument in the same position — and any argument at all through the argv0 aliases — still flows straight into the daemon entry point.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary at e844ed152)

Code:

- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet/src/main.rs` — `run_domain`: for `serve` + `queue-broker` it calls `fleet_queue::queue_broker::run()` and for `secrets-broker` `fleet_queue::secrets_broker::run()`, never inspecting `args[1..]`. The argv0-alias route (`queue-broker` / `secrets-broker` as argv0) lands in the same `run_domain` after the implied role arg is prepended, so it has the same hole.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/queue_broker.rs:589` — `pub fn run() -> i32` (no args).
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/secrets_broker.rs:189` — `pub fn run() -> i32` (no args).

Probe (fleet binary rebuilt on the laptop from e844ed152, `Source rev: e844ed152dd1`; `HOME` pointed at an empty dir so the daemon dies at its first startup step — the token-file read — proving which path was entered):

| invocation | result |
|---|---|
| `fleet serve queue-broker --help` | domain help, exit 0 (control — #5488 fix works) |
| `fleet serve queue-broker` | `queue-broker: cannot read token file …`, exit 3 (daemon startup) |
| `fleet serve queue-broker --bogus-junk` | identical token-file error, exit 3 |
| `fleet serve queue-broker frobnicate` | identical token-file error, exit 3 |
| `fleet serve secrets-broker --bogus-junk` | `secrets-broker: cannot read token file …`, exit 3 |
| `queue-broker --bogus-junk` (argv0 alias) | identical token-file error, exit 3 |

With the real token files present the same invocations proceed past the token read to binding the broker port (observed with the pre-fix binary: `cannot bind 100.99.113.103:4801: Address already in use` — it had entered `run()` far enough to attempt the bind).

## Why it matters

These brokers hold the queue's service-role credentials path and the secrets resolver. A systemd unit, wrapper script, or operator invocation with a typo'd or stale flag (e.g. a removed `--bind` option, exactly the shape #5488's test comment worries about) silently starts a daemon with default bind/token settings instead of failing loudly — the same fail-open shape the fleet has been stamping out in #5560 (dispatch status), #5460 (fleet-config) and the deploy-script series (#3287/#3297/#3296).

## Acceptance criteria

- `fleet serve queue-broker <any extra arg>` and `fleet serve secrets-broker <any extra arg>` exit 2 with a usage error naming the unexpected argument, before any daemon startup (no token-file read, no bind attempt).
- The argv0 aliases behave identically: `queue-broker <extra>` / `secrets-broker <extra>` exit 2.
- `fleet serve <role> --help` / `-h` / `help` still prints domain help with exit 0 (#5488 behavior preserved), and a bare `fleet serve <role>` still starts the daemon.
- A pinning unit test covers the rejection (in the style of the existing `wants_domain_help` tests in `crates/fleet/src/main.rs`).
- `cargo test -p fleet` passes on the laptop or in CI.

**Found:** 2026-11-04 during the opencode#1414 native repoint verification (deploy-gated #1146 sequence).

## Symptom

The standing server (user unit opencode.service, fork nix module) runs **without the runtime overlay** ~/.local/state/opencode/opencode-runtime.jsonc:

- Process environment of the running server contains OPENCODE_DB only — no OPENCODE_CONFIG.
- systemctl --user show-environment has no OPENCODE_CONFIG either.
- The rendered unit (~/.config/systemd/user/opencode.service) sets only OPENCODE_DB and TMPDIR.
- Consequence: every overlay-only model is unavailable. GET /api/provider reports antigravity-direct with **0 models**; a session on antigravity-direct/gemini-3.8-flash fails provider.no-route / Model unavailable. The overlay also carries settings/models for google, openai, cloudflare-gateway (see the overlay header) — all silently unloaded.

## Timeline / mechanism

- code#4544 split the config: tracked deliberate config in .opencode/opencode.jsonc, runtime catalogs in the overlay, layered via OPENCODE_CONFIG. In home/common/default.nix, OPENCODE_CONFIG exists only as a **home.sessionVariables** entry (~line 1657); shells get it, the systemd user manager does not (~/.config/environment.d/10-home-manager.conf does not carry it).
- Pre-reboot, the long-running server process evidently inherited the variable (last overlay-model success in the route ledger: route_attempt 223202, 2026-11-04 09:00:11 UTC, antigravity-direct/claude-sonnet-5-5 — before the 05:47 CST reboot).
- Since the reboot + generation-528 switch, the server is started purely from the module unit and the overlay has been unloaded. Route traffic kept working (routes and catalog models live in the tracked config / models.dev), which masked the loss.

## Fix

Declare the layer on the unit itself in home/common/default.nix (alongside the module-provided unit), e.g.:

    systemd.user.services.opencode.Service.Environment = [
      "OPENCODE_CONFIG=%h/.local/state/opencode/opencode-runtime.jsonc"
    ];

(Or expose/consume an option in the fork module — deployment-side override is the smaller change and matches how this file already overrides sibling units.)

## Interim repair already applied live (2026-11-04)

Drop-in ~/.config/systemd/user/opencode.service.d/overlay-config.conf with the same Environment line + daemon-reload + restart. **Remove the drop-in once a switch lands the fix above.**

Related: opencode#1414 (the repoint that surfaced this), opencode#1550 (its first post-deploy lane row needs this server whole again).

title: pm-aggregator deploy path: install.sh unit cp fails on the home-manager symlink; hand-unblocked pulls skip pm-git-sync redeploys

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

body:
Found while deploying #5389/#5391 (2026-11-04). Two composed gaps in the aggregator's deploy path on amd-6:

1. **install.sh can no longer complete on this machine.** Its `cp "$UNIT_SRC" "$UNIT_DST"` writes through `~/.config/systemd/user/pm-aggregator.service`, which is now a home-manager store symlink (units went NixOS-managed), and cp dies with `Read-only file system`. The manual install path has therefore been broken since the unit became store-managed; only pm-git-sync's restart-only redeploy (dep step + `systemctl restart`, lines ~166-172 of pm-stack/scripts/pm-git-sync.sh) still works. install.sh should detect the symlink case (skip the unit render when the destination is store-managed, or replace the symlink deliberately) instead of failing mid-install after the env file has already been re-rendered.

2. **pm-git-sync treats an externally moved HEAD as its new baseline.** When the #5389 wedge was unblocked by a manual `git pull --ff-only` (the only way to land the .gitignore fix that the sync itself was blocked on), pm-git-sync's next run diffed only the range it pulled itself (4d13062b3 -> 5acabc82c) and never redeployed the aggregator for the pm-stack changes in the hand-pulled range — the aggregator kept running pre-#5376 code until restarted by hand, with nothing recorded as owed. Diffing from the last *deployed* head (persisted across runs) rather than the last *pulled-by-me* head would close this: any HEAD movement, however it happened, queues the subtree redeploys it implies.

Context: #5389 close-out has the full timeline. Neither gap blocks anything today (the aggregator is current and the sync is cycling normally); both will bite the next hand-unblock or manual install.

body:
# atlas-embed: `embed_ids` silently embeds an empty token list as an all-padding row — and only fails for a lone empty list via a raw ONNX error

## Summary

`Embedder::embed_ids` (`pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-embed/src/lib.rs`, the crate's documented "core path") validates the batch as a whole — empty batch refused (`Error::EmptyBatch`), any list over `MODEL_CONTEXT` refused (`Error::TooLong`) — but never validates an individual entry. An empty token list inside a non-empty batch is padded to the batch's `maxlen` with `PAD_ID` and an all-zero attention mask, run through the model, CLS-pooled and L2-normalized, and returned as a normal unit-norm embedding of *nothing*. A lone empty list fails only by accident, leaking a raw ONNX runtime error instead of a crate error.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe (temporary test against the crate at origin/main `1433b926f`, pinned model snapshot `95c2741480856aa9666782eb4afe11959938017f`, ONNX Runtime 1.31.1 from the atlas v3 venv — the Gate A environment):

```text
tokenize("") -> 2 ids: [0, 2]
embed_ids([[]])        -> Err: onnxruntime: Non-zero status code returned while running Gather node.
                          Name:'/1/Gather' Status Message: indices element out of data bounds,
                          idx=0 must be within the inclusive range [0,-1]
embed_ids([[], real])  -> Ok rows=2  row0_norm=1  row0_nan=false  row1_norm=0.99999976
embed_ids([real])      -> Ok norm=0.99999976        (control)
```

- `embed_ids(&[vec![], real_ids])` returns **Ok**, and row 0 — the empty entry — is a finite, unit-norm 768-dim vector produced entirely from padding positions (attention mask all 0). Nothing distinguishes it from a real embedding downstream.
- `embed_ids(&[vec![]])` errors, but only because `maxlen = 0` produces a `[1, 0]` tensor the graph rejects; the error is `Error::Ort("…Gather node…")`, not a deliberate crate-level validation error.
- The text front door cannot hit this (`tokenize("")` still yields the 2 special-token ids `[0, 2]`), but `embed_ids` is public and is precisely the entry point recorded-id pipelines use: `crates/atlas-embed/tests/gate_a.rs` feeds fixture `token_ids` straight into `embed_ids`, and the corpus pipeline this crate mirrors works from recorded token ids. A chunk whose recorded ids are empty (tokenizer failure upstream, an empty chunk from a splitter) would be indexed with a fabricated vector instead of failing loudly — in a crate whose whole contract is "loud error, never silent" (cf. the `TooLong` design: "a >8192-token input is a loud error here, never a silent cut").

Relevant code: `embed_ids` in `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-embed/src/lib.rs` (batch checks at the top; the padding loop builds `input_ids`/`attn` from each list with no per-entry length check).

## Why it matters

Atlas search quality depends on every stored vector meaning "this text". A padding-fabricated vector is a plausible-looking nearest neighbour for unrelated queries and cannot be detected after the fact (it is finite and unit-norm, like every real row). The failure mode is silent data corruption in the corpus, in the one crate that exists to be parity-exact.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `embed_ids` refuses any batch containing an empty token list, with a crate-level error (a dedicated `Error` variant or a documented reuse of an existing one) — before the session runs, for both the lone-empty and mixed-batch cases.
- [ ] Unit tests cover: lone empty list, empty list mixed with a valid list, and the existing controls (empty batch still `EmptyBatch`, over-context still `TooLong`, a normal batch still embeds).
- [ ] No behaviour change for non-empty inputs: the Gate A fixture path (`gate_a.rs`, `#[ignore]`d, model-gated) is unaffected, and `cargo test -p atlas-embed` (non-ignored tests) passes.

## Problem

The #4742 / #4867 defect class — loading the pm-dispatch action family via the remote form `uses: developing-today/code/.github/actions/<name>@main`, which makes the runner download the whole repo as an action archive and fail with `Could not find file '.../_staging/code-<sha>/archive'` — still exists in these consumers (verified on main b6f36bf35, 2026-11-04, by grep of `.github/`):

- `.github/workflows/jules.yml` — pm-dispatch-start@main (3 steps)
- `.github/workflows/jules-daily-codebase-ideation.yml` — pm-dispatch-start@main
- `.github/workflows/jules-daily-flake-sync.yml` — pm-dispatch-start@main
- `.github/workflows/flake-inputs-update.yml` — pm-dispatch-start@main + pm-dispatch-queue@main

- `.github/actions/pm-dispatch-ci-fix/action.yml` — pm-dispatch-task@main (consumed by `.github/workflows/nix-ci.yml` via pm-dispatch-ci-fix@main)

## Fix pattern (already proven twice)

Check developing-today/code out to `.pm-central` in the job and load the actions from local paths, as in main-broken.yml (#4867) and pm-scheduled.yml (PR #5331 for #4742). pm-dispatch-task's loading contract (header note in its action.yml after PR #5331) requires the `.pm-central` checkout for its nested steps.

## Acceptance

- No `uses: developing-today/code/.github/actions/...@main` references remain under `.github/`.
- Each converted workflow's next run gets past action loading (no `_staging .../archive` error in the log).

Found by queue task 9304 (lane code-c) while fixing #4742.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] No remote-form pm-dispatch action references remain: grep of `.github/` finds no `uses: developing-today/code/.github/actions/<name>@main` for the consumers named in this issue (jules.yml, jules-daily-codebase-ideation.yml, jules-daily-flake-sync.yml, flake-inputs-update.yml, pm-dispatch-smoke.yml, pm-dispatch-ci-fix).
- [ ] Each converted consumer checks developing-today/code out to `.pm-central` and loads the actions from local paths, following the main-broken.yml (#4867) / pm-scheduled.yml (PR #5331) pattern, with pm-dispatch-task's loading contract preserved.
- [ ] Affected workflows validate and the pm-dispatch smoke workflow runs without the `_staging` archive download failure.

- [ ] Each named verb has at least one test that executes it against a fixture/temp world and asserts on output/effect (beyond argument parsing).
- [ ] A test that runs in CI compiles the `world new` scaffold output.
- [ ] Targeted tests pass in CI; the verb-by-verb mapping is posted on #796 and this issue closes with that evidence.
- [ ] Test-only: a revealed bug gets its own issue/PR referenced here and on #796 — not a silent fix under this issue.

body:
## Summary

The versioned `group.event` wire codec landed today in PR #5212 (`pkgs/id/src/groups/event.rs`, for #163) accepts three shapes that no sibling codec in pkgs/id accepts: duplicate causal predecessors in `after`, an event that names **itself** as a causal predecessor, and a `create` body that lists the same member twice with conflicting roles. Its `check_bounds` enforces only counts (≤256 predecessors / create members) and the decline-names-a-group rule — it never deduplicates, and neither the encode nor the decode path compares `after` against the event's own `id`.

## Evidence (verified on `origin/main` @ 3adad8fc, this run)

- `pkgs/id/src/groups/event.rs:218-241` — `check_bounds()` checks `after.len() > MAX_AFTER`, create-member count, and the friendship-decline group rule only. `encode_group_event` (event.rs:134) and `decode` (event.rs:160, which calls `check_bounds` again at the end) both gate on it, so one missing check leaves both paths open.
- Sibling precedent in the same crate: `pkgs/id/src/chain.rs:222` — `ChainExt::validate()` refuses a repeated `after` hash with the named error `ChainError::DuplicateAfter`, and its tests pin that refusal (chain.rs:601-606). The same bug class in `artifact.rs` was filed and fixed as #3196 ("check() accepts duplicate after hashes — the same hash can fill all 32 frontier slots, unlike chain.rs").
- The group fold itself treats a repeated create member as malformed: `pkgs/id/src/groups/fold.rs` — `FoldError::BadMembers`, "The members list repeats an account, or names the author." So a wire `create` with a duplicated member is an event the codec blesses that the fold can only refuse.

Verified with a laptop probe at `origin/main` 3adad8fc9 (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-03-laneA-groupevent/pkgs/id/tests/probe_groupevent.rs`, `cargo test --test probe_groupevent` — 1 passed):

- Control: an ordinary `join` event round-trips encode → decode unchanged.
- `after = [H, H]` (same predecessor twice): `encode_group_event` = Ok, `decode` = Ok with 2 predecessors.
- `after = [own id]` (self-predecessor): `encode_group_event` = Ok, `decode` = Ok with 1 predecessor.
- `create` with members `[([6;32], Read), ([6;32], Admin)]` (same key, conflicting roles): `encode_group_event` = Ok, `decode` = Ok with 2 members.

## Why it matters

This codec is the wire format group events will sync by, and it has no production consumer yet — now is the cheapest moment to tighten it, before lax acceptance is baked into peers' stored logs. A duplicated predecessor inflates the causal frontier with noise every later consumer must tolerate; a self-predecessor is an unplaceable causal cycle (the group log's fold "refuses an `after` it cannot place", and a self-reference can never be placed); a duplicated create member carries two contradictory roles for one account in a single signed object, and which one wins depends on the reader. Every other causal codec in pkgs/id refuses these shapes at the boundary (`DuplicateAfter` in chain.rs, the #3196 artifact fix, duplicate refusals in chat links #4857 and tag claims #4765) — this one should match the house rule while it is still version 1 with no deployed peers.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `check_bounds` (or an equivalent single gate used by both `encode_group_event` and `decode`) refuses a repeated hash in `after` with an `EventError::Shape` naming the duplication, mirroring `ChainError::DuplicateAfter`.
- [ ] The same gate refuses an `after` entry equal to the event's own `id` (a self-predecessor / one-node causal cycle).
- [ ] The same gate refuses a `create` body whose `members` list names the same key twice (regardless of role), matching the fold's `BadMembers` rule.
- [ ] Tests in `groups/event.rs` cover all three refusals on the decode path (hand-built CBOR, not just encode) plus the existing round-trip/golden tests staying green.
- [ ] Existing groups tests still pass (`cargo test -p id groups` on the laptop/CI).

body:
# pm-stack(aggregator): validateStreamEvent accepts impossible and non-ISO `at` timestamps — Date.parse-only gate behind an "ISO timestamp" error

## Evidence

`pm-stack/aggregator/src/events.ts:54` — the only check on a stream event's timestamp is:

```ts
if (typeof v.at !== "string" || !Number.isFinite(Date.parse(v.at))) {
  return { ok: false, error: "event.at must be an ISO timestamp string" };
}
```

`Date.parse` is not an ISO or real-calendar check: it rolls impossible calendar dates forward and accepts free-form date strings. The accepted value is stored **verbatim** (`events.ts`, `validateStreamEvent` returns `at: v.at`), while every consumer parses it again — retention pruning (`pruneEvents`, events.ts:99), newest-first ordering (`filterEvents`, events.ts:121), and rendering — so the stored string and the instant it behaves as disagree.

Verified this run with a laptop bun probe against `origin/main` at `bd4466c63` (worktree `~/git/fleet/scan26`, `/tmp/probe-events.log` on the laptop), calling the real `validateStreamEvent`:

| `at` input | accepted? | stored | `Date.parse` instant |
|---|---|---|---|
| `2026-02-30T10:00:00Z` | yes | `2026-02-30T10:00:00Z` | 2026-03-02T10:00:00Z |
| `2026-04-31T10:00:00Z` | yes | `2026-04-31T10:00:00Z` | 2026-05-01T10:00:00Z |
| `March 2, 2026` | yes | `March 2, 2026` | 2026-03-02T06:00:00Z |
| `03/02/2026` | yes | `03/02/2026` | 2026-03-02T06:00:00Z |
| `2026-03-02T10:00:00Z` (control) | yes | unchanged | 2026-03-02T10:00:00Z |
| `not-a-date` (control) | no | — | — |

Retention consequence, also probed: `pruneEvents([event at "2026-02-30T10:00:00Z"], now = 2026-03-05)` keeps the event — it is pruned and sorted as a March 2 event while the stream displays a February 30 timestamp that does not exist.

## Why it matters

The event log (#1739) is the single chronological stream the dashboard and `/today` read. An impossible or non-ISO `at` that passes validation is persisted verbatim, then silently re-interpreted as a different instant by pruning, sorting, and age rendering — the displayed time and the effective time diverge, and a malformed writer can place an event days away from where it appears to sit. Sibling aggregator gates already refuse exactly this: `isIsoDate`/`parseIsoDate` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/validate.ts:116` / `:66`) are used by tier-items.ts, snapshots.ts, and saas-extract.ts for the same reason (see #4987, #5018, #4968). `events.ts` is the remaining Date.parse-only validator in the store layer.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validateStreamEvent` refuses an `at` that is not a real-calendar ISO timestamp: `2026-02-30…`, `2026-04-31…`, `March 2, 2026`, and `03/02/2026` all return `{ ok: false }` with the existing ISO error message.
- Valid ISO timestamps with offsets/fractional seconds that the stream already accepts in the wild keep validating (no regression for existing writers).
- The fix uses the aggregator's existing ISO helper (`isIsoDate`/`parseIsoDate` in validate.ts) rather than a new ad-hoc parser, or documents why events need a different rule.
- Tests cover the impossible-date and non-ISO cases through `validateStreamEvent` (and, if the load path relies on it, through the events store load/quarantine path), alongside the existing valid/invalid controls.

## Problem

`nixos/home/pm-dashboard-backup.sh` lists the retired Meta exporter's outputs as REQUIRED files in the laptop dashboard backup manifest:

- `required file meta-quota-export/latest.json`
- `required file meta-quota-export/history.jsonl`

The producer was retired 2026-11-03: PR #5040 replaced the dev.meta.ai console scrape with a direct ask of the OpenCode quota module (Drew's ruling — gather quota by asking OpenCode), and PR #5044 removes the exporter code and its home-manager unit. The files under `~/atlas/meta-quota-export/` are now frozen at their last scrape.

Today the backup still passes because the frozen files exist. But the manifest now enshrines a dead producer: if the stale directory is ever cleaned up, the laptop dashboard backup starts failing on a "required" file nothing will ever produce again — and the failure would point at the backup, not at the retirement.

## Fix

- Relax the two meta-quota-export files from required to optional (or drop them from the manifest), and stop sweeping the `meta-quota-export` journal in the same script (the service loop at the journal step names it alongside pm-aggregator and quota-gatherer).
- Update `nixos/home/pm-dashboard-backup-record.test.sh` fixtures accordingly (it fabricates `atlas/meta-quota-export/latest.json` + `history.jsonl` in two places).
- Keep backing up the frozen directory while it exists if history retention is wanted — that call belongs with the change; either way the REQUIRED contract has to go.


## Acceptance criteria

- nixos/home/pm-dashboard-backup.sh no longer lists meta-quota-export/latest.json or meta-quota-export/history.jsonl as required files (optional or removed).
- The same script no longer sweeps the meta-quota-export journal in its service loop.

body:
Writer-set spec **§9 item 2** (`doc/2026-10-30T13-15-00Z_design_id_writer_set_view_projection/`). Slice 1 shipped as #3854 (`pkgs/id/src/idset.rs`: `WriterSet`, `Entry` in all three shapes, `Excludes`, `Rescind`, canonical body encode/decode, sign/decode round-trip). This slice adds the **expansion** both later slices stand on.

## Goal

```text
expand(set_version)       -> BTreeSet<AuthorKey>
expand_retro(set_version) -> BTreeSet<AuthorKey>   // same expansion, narrowed to entries carrying include_history
```

Spec §3.1 and §4.1: `retro` is **per entry**, so one flagged friend must never import another's backlog — `expand_retro(v) ⊆ expand(v)` is an invariant, not an approximation.

## What already exists (verified at main `0467ae0f9`, 2026-11-03)

- `pkgs/id/src/idset.rs` — the types and their canonical encoding; `Entry` carries `include_history` on every shape (§D3). Its module doc still ends: *"This module is types and encoding only. Expansion, projection, and counting are later slices of the spec's routing (§9 items 2–4) and are deliberately absent here."*
- `pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/membership/layer.rs:442` — `Membership::access_at_position(after, group, who)`, the frontier-aware membership check; `:424` — `is_member_at(author, group, &after)`.
- `pkgs/id/src/groups/delegation.rs:312` — a caller of `access_at_position`; `pkgs/id/src/event_store/resolve.rs:397` — a caller of `is_member_at`.
- `pkgs/id/src/groups/fold.rs` — the fold the two above read.

## What to build

- Expansion must go through **`is_member_at` / `access_at_position`**, *not* `members(group)` (§4.5): the answer is pinned to the set version's frontier, and a live roster is not that.
- **One-level flattening** of group entries (§D3/D4) — a group entry expands to its members at the frontier; a nested group reference is not followed.
- **`role_min` filtering** (§D3): include a member whose role is at least the entry's `role_min` *at that frontier*.
- **Exclusions win** (§D6): an exclusion entry removes its target from the expansion regardless of which entry admitted them.
- Cache, if any, keyed `(group, frontier, R)` (§4.5) — and the fork-invalidation test below is what proves the key is right.

## Tests (spec §9 item 2, verbatim requirements)

1. Expansion is **order-independent** — the same set with entries permuted yields the same set of authors.
2. Expansion is **frontier-pinned** — a membership change *after* the set version does not change `expand(v)`.
3. Expansion is **unchanged by a later group-membership event** — the reproducibility guarantee, as a test with the event written after the pin.
4. `expand_retro(v) ⊆ expand(v)`, and a set with no `include_history` entries has `expand_retro` empty while `expand` is not.
5. **Fork proof that invalidates a group grant changes the expansion, and the cache does not serve the stale one** (§4.5) — the test finding 23 added.
6. `role_min` filters at the frontier: a member who holds the role *later* is not admitted by an earlier version.
7. An exclusion removes an admitted writer, and an exclusion of someone never admitted is a no-op rather than an error.

## Out of scope

`AuthorEvents`/retrieval (slice 3), `Projection`/`counted`/`uncounted`/`validity_now` (slice 4), public/sentinel views (Q1 on #2031), abuse budgets (#2032), app/UI rendering.

## Acceptance

`cargo test -p id` green with tests 1–7 above present and named; no counting path enabled (`expand*` returns authors only); `pkgs/id/src/idset.rs`'s module doc updated to say expansion now lives beside the types.

Parent: #3789 · spec §9 item 2 · slice 1: #3854

## Acceptance criteria
- `expand(set_version)` and `expand_retro(set_version)` exist in the id writer-set module, expanding through `is_member_at` / `access_at_position` pinned to the set version's frontier — never a live `members(group)` roster.
- Group entries flatten exactly one level (§D3/D4); `expand_retro(v) ⊆ expand(v)` holds and is test-pinned, including the case where one entry's `include_history` must not import another entry's backlog.
- The idset module doc no longer states that expansion is absent; slice 3/4 consumers can call both functions without further expansion work.

title: pm-stack(aggregator): normalizeResetAt accepts impossible and non-ISO reset dates — its string branch is Date.parse-only, rolling 2026-02-30 to Mar 2 instead of returning null
