body:
## Problem

`normalizeResetAt` in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-gather-map.ts` (lines 44–57, at main `67f97516c`) normalizes a provider reset stamp to ISO. Its numeric branch is guarded (finite, > 0, valid Date), but its string branch is `Date.parse`-only:

```ts
if (typeof v === "string" && v !== "") {
  const t = Date.parse(v);
  return Number.isNaN(t) ? null : new Date(t).toISOString();
}
```

`Date.parse` rolls impossible calendar dates over to a different real date and accepts non-ISO formats, so a drifted/malformed provider stamp is silently converted into a wrong-but-plausible `resetsAt` instead of `null`. Garbage strings do return `null` — the gate is inconsistent within itself: `"not-a-date"` → `null`, but `"2026-02-30"` → a fabricated March 2 reset time.

This contradicts the aggregator's own date contract: `isIsoDate`/`parseIsoDate` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/validate.ts:116`) rejects impossible dates by round-trip, and the feed gates built on it (`isQuotaFreshness` feed.ts:502, `isQuotaWindow` feed.ts:474) already refuse such values.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop bun probe at origin/main `67f97516c`)

Probe: `/tmp/probe-resetat.ts` importing `normalizeResetAt` from the worktree copy of `quota-gather-map.ts`; output in `/tmp/probe-resetat.log` on the laptop:

| input | result |
|---|---|
| `"2026-02-30"` | `"2026-03-02T00:00:00.000Z"` — impossible date rolled over |
| `"2026-04-31"` | `"2026-05-01T00:00:00.000Z"` — impossible date rolled over |
| `"2026-02-29"` (2026 is not a leap year) | `"2026-03-01T00:00:00.000Z"` — rolled over |
| `"March 2, 2026"` | `"2026-03-02T06:00:00.000Z"` — non-ISO format accepted (and TZ-shifted) |
| `"2026-03-02"` | `"2026-03-02T00:00:00.000Z"` — control OK |
| `"2026-03-02T00:00:00.000Z"` | unchanged — control OK |
| `"2024-02-29"` (leap year) | `"2024-02-29T00:00:00.000Z"` — control OK |
| `"not-a-date"` | `null` — garbage already refused |

Call sites that inherit the flaw (all feed the quota-current contract's `resetsAt`, which drives reset-time display and reset-soon guidance):

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/clinepass-adapter.ts:106` — ClinePass window `resetsAt`
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-gather-map.ts:279` — Meta file-export windows
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-gather-map.ts:345` — `entryFromResult` provider windows
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-gather-map.ts:618` — Turso billing period end

Related sites in the same file worth checking in the same pass (not the primary scope): the `credentialExpiresAt` string branch in `entryFromResult` (`Date.parse` + `toISOString`, ~line 340) and the Turso period start/end `Date.parse` pair (~lines 621–622), from which `windowSeconds` is derived.

## Why it matters

`resetsAt` is operator-facing: it tells Drew when a quota pool resets and feeds reset-soon choices. A provider payload that drifts (or a hand-edited file export) carrying an impossible date currently produces a confident, wrong reset time a day or two off, instead of the `null` the same function already returns for unparseable strings. Every sibling date gate in the aggregator was hardened to the `isIsoDate` contract for exactly this failure mode; this shared normalizer — the one four call sites funnel through — was missed.

## Acceptance criteria

- `normalizeResetAt` returns `null` for impossible calendar dates (`2026-02-30`, `2026-04-31`, `2026-02-29`) and for non-ISO date strings (`"March 2, 2026"`).
- Valid inputs are unchanged: ISO date/datetime strings normalize as today, `2024-02-29` passes, epoch-second and epoch-millisecond numbers behave as today, garbage strings still return `null`.
- Regression tests added to `pm-stack/aggregator/test/quota-gather-map.test.ts` covering the refused and accepted cases above.
- Existing aggregator test suites (at minimum quota-gather-map, clinepass-adapter, feed) still pass.
- The related `credentialExpiresAt` / Turso period `Date.parse` sites in the same file are either fixed to the same contract or explicitly called out in the PR as follow-ups.

## Problem

`isCredentialLifecycleRow` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/credential-lifecycle.ts:85-105, new in the credential-lifecycle module) is the gate `sanitizeQuotaView` uses to drop-and-count malformed credential-lifecycle rows before rendering (pm-stack/aggregator/src/feed.ts:617). Its two date fields are validated far more weakly than every other date gate in the same sanitize pass:

- `measuredAt` (credential-lifecycle.ts:95) is checked only as `typeof row.measuredAt === "string"` — any string passes, including `"not-a-date"`.
- `expiresAt` (credential-lifecycle.ts:97) is checked only as `Number.isFinite(Date.parse(row.expiresAt))` — `Date.parse` rolls impossible dates over and accepts non-ISO strings, so `"2026-02-30"` (→ Mar 2) and `"March 3, 2026"` both pass.

The sibling gates in the same file/pass use the strict contract: `isQuotaFreshness` requires `isIsoDate(v.measuredAt)` (feed.ts:502), `isQuotaWindow` requires `isIsoDate(v.resetsAt)` (feed.ts:474), and `isIsoDate`/`parseIsoDate` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/validate.ts:116) rejects impossible calendar dates by round-trip. This is the same defect family as #2199/#4835/#4858 and the validateStreamEvent finding (OB-2026-11-03-096), in a gate that was added after those fixes.

## Verified (laptop bun probe at main b9633324312197a1da81be0d69d778917b56c3f9, /tmp/probe-credlc.log)

```
control valid: true
measuredAt garbage: true            ("not-a-date")
measuredAt impossible 2026-02-30: true
expiresAt impossible 2026-02-30: true
expiresAt non-ISO March 3 2026: true
expiresAt garbage: false            (only the fully-unparseable case is refused)
```

So a lifecycle row with a garbage `measuredAt` or an impossible/non-ISO `expiresAt` survives sanitization and renders (with a bogus measurement/expiry stamp) instead of being dropped and counted in `droppedCredentialLifecycle`, defeating the drop-and-count contract the pass documents (#2429/#3921/#4546 pattern).

## Why it matters

The credential-lifecycle section exists to tell the user when a credential expires or has expired. A row whose dates were never validated can show a wrong expiry state/stamp with no signal that the row was malformed, while every neighbouring section drops such rows and surfaces the drop count.

## Acceptance criteria

- `isCredentialLifecycleRow` refuses a row whose `measuredAt` is not a valid ISO date per `parseIsoDate`/`isIsoDate` (validate.ts), including impossible dates such as `2026-02-30`.
- `isCredentialLifecycleRow` refuses a row whose present `expiresAt` is not a valid ISO date per the same contract (impossible and non-ISO strings refused).
- Well-formed rows produced by `lifecycleForEntry` still pass unchanged.
- Tests in pm-stack/aggregator/test/credential-lifecycle.test.ts (or the feed sanitize tests) cover: garbage `measuredAt`, impossible `measuredAt`, impossible `expiresAt`, non-ISO `expiresAt`, and the valid control.
- `sanitizeQuotaView` counts such rows in `droppedCredentialLifecycle` (existing drop-and-count behaviour once the gate refuses them).

body:
## Problem

In `pm-stack/aggregator/src/dns.ts`, the authoritative register.json builder `dnsSectionFromRegisterJson` accepts a **negative** `renewal_price_usd` — the one money rule its sibling paths already enforce:

- The builder's price guard (dns.ts:136) checks only type/finiteness: `typeof price !== "number" || !Number.isFinite(price)` → return null. A price of `-25` passes.
- The shared gate `isDnsSection` refuses negative money since issue #4226: a present entry `priceUsd` must be `>= 0` (dns.ts:188-191, with the comment "A present price must also be non-negative (#4226)") and `totalAnnualListUsd` must be `>= 0` (dns.ts:170-175).
- The Markdown path can never produce a negative price: `parsePriceUsd` (dns.ts:28-31) matches only `^\$([\d,]+(?:\.\d+)?)$` — no minus sign; anything else becomes `null`.

So the JSON builder certifies sections that the fleet's own shared gate rejects. That breaks the builder/gate invariant the existing tests assert for well-formed JSON (`test/slice3.test.ts:211`: a section built by `dnsSectionFromRegisterJson` satisfies `isDnsSection(section) === true`).

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary at origin/main d1628b4be)

Laptop bun probe (`/tmp/probe-dns-neg.ts` on the laptop, importing `dnsSectionFromRegisterJson` and `isDnsSection` from current main):

- `renewal_price_usd: -25` → section non-null, `priceUsd = -25`, `totalAnnualListUsd = -25`, `isDnsSection(section) = false`
- `renewal_price_usd: -0.01` → section non-null, total `-0.01`, `isDnsSection = false`
- Mixed register (`10` and `-40`) → section non-null, `totalAnnualListUsd = -30`, `isDnsSection = false`
- Controls: `0` and `12.5` → section non-null, `isDnsSection = true`

Downstream consequence: the collector (`scripts/collect-fleet-feed.ts:718`) uses this builder and only falls back to the Markdown parse when it returns null (line 737) — a negative-price register therefore does **not** trigger the documented fallback. Instead the feed carries a section the live source then discards whole at its `isDnsSection` checks (`src/sources/live.ts:1052`, `:1310`), and any direct consumer of the builder output gets the poisoned arithmetic — e.g. `recordsFromDns` (`src/snapshot-records.ts:243`) records `totalAnnualListUsd` verbatim as the `total-annual-usd` snapshot value, exactly the negative snapshot value issue #4226 set out to prevent.

## Why it matters

register.json is the authoritative source for renewal prices (#902 slice 2). One drifted negative price silently understates the annual total, can drive the total itself negative, and — because the builder returns a section instead of null — suppresses the Markdown fallback the builder's contract promises on ANY malformation (dns.ts:100-103). Issue #4226 fixed this rule at the gate only; the producer that feeds the gate was left able to mint the invalid value, the same producer/gate split as issue #4858 (impossible renewal dates in this same function).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `dnsSectionFromRegisterJson` returns null when any row's `renewal_price_usd` is a finite negative number, so the collector falls back to the Markdown parse (zero stays valid, per #4226).
- [ ] Regression tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/slice3.test.ts`: negative price rows (`-25`, `-0.01`, and a mixed register whose total goes negative) are refused by the builder; a built section with valid prices still satisfies `isDnsSection`.
- [ ] Existing slice3 DNS tests stay green (`bun test test/slice3.test.ts`).

Found by new-issue-creator lane A (new-issue-creator-code-a) this run; dedup: issue #4226 (closed) covered only `isDnsSection`, issue #4858 covered only renewal dates in this builder — neither covers negative prices in `dnsSectionFromRegisterJson`.

body:
# id(world_fixture): a partial fixture ending mid-epoch is record-compared anyway — final_epoch_covered checks only that an install exists, not that the window reaches the header sequence

## Summary

`world_fixture::replay` documents that a partial fixture's records "are
compared only when the retained window still covers the final program
epoch". The gate for that comparison, `final_epoch_covered`
(`pkgs/id/src/world_fixture.rs`), is only
`events.iter().any(is_install)` — it never checks that the window
actually reaches the header's `current_sequence`. `decode` /
`check_window` explicitly permit a partial window that ends early
("partial history may end earlier"), so a partial fixture whose last
install is in the window but whose events stop mid-epoch is compared
against the header's head records anyway: the replay can only produce
the records as of the last replayed event, so the verdict is a spurious
`Mismatch`, and `id world replay --allow-partial` fails (the command
bails on `Verdict::Mismatch`) on a fixture shape the format allows and
the docs say must not be compared.

## Evidence (origin/main ea10fd051)

- `pkgs/id/src/world_fixture.rs` `check_window`: for a non-complete
  header, sequenced events need only be contiguous and
  `<= header.current_sequence`; ending before `current_sequence` is
  accepted.
- `pkgs/id/src/world_fixture.rs` `verdict`: when
  `!header.complete && !final_epoch_covered` it returns
  `NotCompared("partial history")`; otherwise it compares the replayed
  records with `header.records`.
- `pkgs/id/src/world_fixture.rs` `final_epoch_covered`:
  `events.iter().any(is_install)` — no check that the last sequenced
  event reaches `header.current_sequence`.
- `pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs` `replay_fixture`: bails
  "the replayed records differ from the fixture's" on
  `Verdict::Mismatch`, so the spurious verdict is a command failure,
  not just a label.
- Probe (laptop worktree at origin/main ea10fd051,
  `pkgs/id/tests/probe_fixture_partial.rs` against the real crate +
  the checked-in tic-tac-toe wasm): the complete fixture
  `tests/fixtures/tic-tac-toe-determinism.jsonl` replays to
  `Verdict::Match` (control). The same fixture truncated to a partial
  window — header `complete:false`, `current_sequence` 7 and head
  records unchanged, events cut after sequence 4 (the
  `program_installed` event at sequence 1 retained) — decodes Ok and
  replays under `--allow-partial` semantics to `Verdict::Mismatch`
  with the mid-game records, instead of `NotCompared`.

## Why it matters

`--allow-partial` exists so retained-window fixtures remain usable for
determinism checks. A window that happens to contain an install but
was cut before the head (retention, a truncated copy, a hand-trimmed
fixture — all shapes `decode` accepts) now reports a false
"records differ" failure, indistinguishable from a real determinism
regression, and `verify`'s header verdict inherits the same false
mismatch.

## Acceptance criteria

- A partial fixture whose sequenced events end before
  `header.current_sequence` is never record-compared: `replay` and
  `verify` report `Verdict::NotCompared` for it, whether or not an
  install event is in the window.
- A partial fixture whose window contains the last install AND reaches
  `header.current_sequence` is still compared exactly as today
  (regression test with the tic-tac-toe fixture truncated at the front,
  not the back).
- Complete fixtures are unchanged (the checked-in determinism fixture
  still verifies `Match`).
- New tests in `world_fixture` cover both partial shapes; existing
  `world_fixture` and CLI fixture tests stay green.

title: mcpx plugin: stamp the generated ops with the API table hash and refuse to run on a stale copy

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

body:
Drew (2026-11-03): 'a stale type hint is worse than not having one.' The generated plugin ops (pkgs/mcpx/plugin/opencode/mcpx/ops.gen.ts) are type hints the plugin codes against. When they drift from the daemon's real /v1 table (as in #4806), everything still type-checks and reviews fine — the types lie with confidence, and the failure only surfaces at runtime against the real API, or worse, a renamed/dropped operation is called wrongly. An untyped surface would at least be honestly dynamic.

#4807 makes nix builds regenerate the file in preCheck, so nix artifacts always carry true types. What remains: from-checkout consumers (code's .opencode/plugin, editor type-checking) can still load a stale copy silently.

Proposal: PluginTS() emits a stamp in the generated file — a hash of the /v1 operation table plus the mcpx version. The plugin's daemon client compares the stamp against the daemon's self-reported table hash at connect time and REFUSES (clear error: regenerate or update the plugin) on mismatch, instead of calling through stale types. Needs the daemon to report its table hash (a /v1 metadata field or a field on the existing version/doctor surface). Acceptance: with a deliberately stale ops.gen.ts, the plugin fails loudly at startup with the mismatch named; with a fresh one, it connects as today.

title: id(local_events): publish records duplicate live claims for a repeated (name, value) tag — the batch is never checked against itself

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/id/src/local_events.rs` — `LocalEvents::publish` (line 272) records a document plus one `tag.set` per entry of its `tags` argument. Every tag is checked individually before anything is recorded (`check_tag`, line 285 → `tag_claims::check_op` on a single `Set`), but the batch is never checked against itself: the same `(name, value)` pair twice in one `publish` call creates two distinct live claims — different event IDs, same author, same subject, same name, same value.

Every other multi-entry validation in this layer refuses duplicates within one operation: `tag.clear` claim lists (tag_claims.rs `check_op`, #4765), `ChainExt.after` (chain.rs `DuplicateAfter`), `note.revise` parents (notes.rs), session-checkpoint participants (session_checkpoint.rs), and `LocalEvents::clear_tag`'s own claim partitioning treats claims as a set. `publish` is the remaining batch entry point that does not.

Consequences: the duplicate claims both appear in `tags_on` / search hits for the document (a contested-looking pair that no second author created), both count toward `MAX_CLEAR_CLAIMS` chunking when the name is later cleared, and `Published.claims` returns two IDs for what the caller described as one tag.

## Evidence (verified this run, origin/main 98d3d07bb)

Laptop probe (worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-scan7`, unit probe in `pkgs/id/src/local_events.rs` against the real crate, `cargo test --lib probe_publish_duplicate_tags`, probe removed after the run):

- `publish("text/plain", b"hello", [("city", Some("Seattle")), ("city", Some("Seattle")), ("city", None), ("city", None)])` → claims returned: 4; live claims on the document: 4 — two identical `city=Seattle` claims and two identical bare `city` claims, all by the same author.

## Fix direction

In `publish`, refuse a `(name, value)` pair that appears twice in `tags` (exact pair equality; same name with different values, and bare vs valued, stay legal — they are distinct claims), before recording anything, so the existing "a bad tag records nothing" guarantee covers it. Alternatively deduplicate silently — but the sibling validators all refuse, and refusal surfaces caller bugs.

## Acceptance criteria

- `publish` with a repeated `(name, value)` pair returns an error and records no events (document or tags).
- `publish` with the same name at different values, or bare plus valued, still succeeds with one claim per entry.
- Regression tests in `pkgs/id/src/local_events.rs` tests cover the duplicate-pair refusal (valued and bare) and the distinct-pair success cases.
- Existing `local_events` and `tag_claims` tests stay green.

body:
## Summary

`pm-stack/opencode-claimant/poll.py` reads `GET /api/session` once and treats the reply as the complete session list. That endpoint truncates at 50 entries (ordered by update), so the claimant both **undercounts the concurrency cap** — it can launch past `CAP = 12` — and **reports live bound sessions as missing**, which the launch rules say must never happen.

Observed 2026-11-03T04:42Z on the laptop server (`http://127.0.0.1:13420`):

- `GET /api/session` → exactly 50 sessions, 50 roots.
- Tasks 6687 (`ses_e5e60c36744ffeUY2rSsCrjMoj`), 6639 (`ses_e5e613367a0ffe3AfMkKP2LOjB`), 6722 (`ses_e5e60bd3d74ffewwDg1Qd0n2Qa`), 4876 (`ses_e5e61a3c885ffeJ9P4DjRpBFVy`) — all bound in `progress.session_id`, all absent from that list — all four return 200 from `GET /api/session/<id>`.

## Impact

1. **Cap overcount of room.** `summarize_cap()` ([poll.py:112-128](https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/main/pm-stack/opencode-claimant/poll.py#L112-L128)) intersects the 50-row page with `/api/session/active`. Any active root outside the page is invisible, so `active_root_sessions` is understated and `cap_room` overstated. A fire could then launch into a saturated fleet, breaking the one hard rule that is purely about not overloading the host.
2. **False "session is gone".** Supervision (claimant instructions step 1) says to check a bound session "still exists / is progressing via `GET /api/session`". On the truncated page an *alive* session reads as gone. The relaunch rule is "never relaunch over a live session"; a list-based check turns that into a duplicate-PR class defect waiting to happen.

## Proposed fix

- Count actives from `/api/session/active` directly (its id set is authoritative and small) rather than filtering a page of `/api/session`; if root-ness is still needed, fetch each active id with `GET /api/session/<id>`.
- Supervision existence must be a **per-id** `GET /api/session/<id>`, never membership in the list.
- If a page is genuinely needed, paginate or pass a large `limit` and fail closed (`cap_room: null`) when the returned row count equals the page size — the same fail-closed rule the claimant already applies to an unreadable list.

## Evidence trail

Fire log lines for 2026-11-03 in `~/.local/state/opencode-claimant/fires.jsonl` carry the full supervision table for that fire.

## Acceptance criteria

- Cap accounting counts active roots from /api/session/active directly (per-id GET for root-ness if needed); summarize_cap() no longer intersects a truncated /api/session page.
- Supervision existence checks for a bound session use GET /api/session/<id>, never membership in the list endpoint.
- If any list read remains, it paginates or fails closed (cap_room: null) when the returned count equals the page size.
- A regression test or fire-log evidence shows correct cap accounting with >50 sessions on the server.

title: id(waiting): WaitingPool::arrived does not drop a ready-queue copy — an event applied through another path is handed out again by take_ready

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

`WaitingPool::arrived` (`pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/waiting.rs:385`) drops a **held** copy of the arriving key — its doc says so: "If `key` was itself held, that copy is dropped without being returned, because the caller now holds the event" (`waiting.rs:383-384`). It does **not** drop a **ready-queue** copy of the same key. An event whose dependencies had all arrived at `insert` time sits in the ready queue (`ready` / `ready_keys`, `waiting.rs:170-176`); if the caller applies that event through another path and calls `arrived(its key)` before `take_ready()` — the documented step-2 call in the module's caller loop (`waiting.rs:21-27`) — the ready copy survives, and the next `take_ready()` (`waiting.rs:421-424`) hands the same event out a second time.

Every other entry point treats the ready queue as a real state a key can be in: the duplicate guards in `insert` (`waiting.rs:243-246`) and `park` (`waiting.rs:281-284`) check `ready_keys`, and that index exists precisely because a key in the ready queue is otherwise invisible (#2001, closed). `arrived` is the one transition that never looks at it. The sibling gap in `restore` is already tracked as #3911; this is the remaining cell in the same matrix — #3911's criteria cover `restore`'s guard only, and fixing #3911 does not make `arrived` drop a ready copy.

## Verified this run (laptop probe, origin/main f961fb8a)

Probe crate on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-arrivedready/`) `#[path]`-includes the real `waiting.rs` extracted from `origin/main` (md5 `9654300d490a030f3f5513c79692e717`, matching the `origin/main` blob) and exercises `WaitingPool<u32, &str>`:

- **Case A:** `arrived(10)` (dependency present), then `insert(author, 1, [10], "ready-copy")` → key 1 sits in the ready queue. `arrived(1)` (caller applied event 1 itself) releases nothing — but `take_ready()` afterwards still returns `["ready-copy"]`: the already-applied event is handed out a second time.
- **Case B (no-deps form):** `insert(author, 7, [], "only-copy")` → ready immediately. `arrived(7)`, then `take_ready()` returns `["only-copy"]` again.
- **Control (held analogue):** `insert(author, 1, [10], "held-copy")` with `10` not yet arrived, then `arrived(1)` → held copy dropped, `len=0`, nothing handed out. The held and ready states behave differently for the same call.
- **Sanity:** the normal flow (`insert` with no deps, no intervening `arrived`) returns the event from `take_ready()` exactly once.

The property suite (`pkgs/id/tests/waiting_properties.rs`) cannot see this: its driver calls `take_ready()` immediately after every single `insert`, so a ready copy is never pending when an `Arrive` op runs, even though the file's stated invariant is "each event is output at most once, by release, by `take_ready`, or by expiry".

## Why it matters

The pool's contract is that a key is in exactly one state — held, ready, or arrived — and is handed out at most once. A caller that applies an event it obtained elsewhere (a duplicate delivery decided as already-applied, a batch that resolves an event before draining the ready queue) and dutifully calls `arrived` will still receive that event from `take_ready` and apply it twice, or route it through a second decision as if it were new. The asymmetry with the held case — which the code and its tests explicitly pin — makes this easy to rely on wrongly: `test_arrival_of_a_held_event_drops_the_held_copy_without_releasing_it` promises a behaviour the ready state does not share.

Note on fix shape (why this is filed-only, not a trivial self-solve): `ready` is a `Vec<E>` with keys kept separately in `ready_keys`, so there is currently no key→position mapping with which `arrived` could remove one specific ready event; the fix needs a small data-structure decision (e.g. storing `(K, E)` pairs in the ready queue) plus care that `take_ready`'s insert-order guarantee and the #2001 guard keep holding.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `WaitingPool::arrived(key)` drops a pending ready-queue copy of `key`: after `arrived`, `take_ready()` never returns an event whose key has arrived, for both the all-deps-arrived and no-deps insert forms.
- [ ] Regression tests at the pool level, alongside `test_arrival_of_a_held_event_drops_the_held_copy_without_releasing_it`: arrived-after-ready hands the event out zero further times, and the ready events of *other* keys are unaffected and still in insert order.
- [ ] The property model in `pkgs/id/tests/waiting_properties.rs` either gains an operation order that can express arrive-before-take-ready, or the unit tests above are noted as covering the gap the driver's sequencing excludes.
- [ ] Existing behaviour is unchanged otherwise: #2001 duplicate guards, the held-copy drop, expiry, caps, and the event store's waiting/waiting_rows tests all stay green. Coordinate with #3911 (restore's guard) so the two fixes land as one consistent key-state matrix.

## Dedup

Open/closed searches for "WaitingPool arrived", "take_ready", and "waiting pool ready arrived duplicate" (2026-11-02) return: #2001 (closed — `insert`'s ready-queue duplicate guard), #3911 (open — `restore` ignores the arrived/ready guards; its acceptance criteria cover `restore` only), #1730 (open — arrived-set growth, a different defect), and #4000 (open design umbrella on restore guards). No issue covers `arrived` failing to drop a ready-queue copy.

title: id(directory): level_in and reaches recurse without memoization — diamond-shaped group nesting makes views, member updates and ensure_admins exponential

labels.name: kind/performance
labels.description: Performance problem or optimization

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`Directory::level_in` and `Directory::reaches` in `pkgs/id/src/directory.rs` recurse over nested groups with no memoization or visited set, so a group-nesting graph shaped as a diamond DAG (each layer's groups both contain both groups of the next layer) is re-traversed once per distinct path — exponential in the nesting depth, even though cycles are refused.

## Evidence (origin/main 9dfc29e56)

- `directory.rs:975-994` — `level_in(account, group)` folds over the group's nested groups and calls itself recursively for each one; a subgroup reachable by N paths is evaluated N times. Its semantics (max over paths of `min(inner, held_at)`) are memoizable per group for a fixed account, but nothing is cached.
- `directory.rs:1749-1759` — `reaches(from, target)` has the same shape: `.any()` recursion with no visited set; for an absent target (the normal case for the cycle check) it explores every path.
- `directory.rs:1647` — `reaches` runs on every `MemberSet` entry that nests a group (the cycle guard in `apply`), so simply adding a nesting member pays the exponential cost.
- `directory.rs:1761-1770` — `ensure_admins()` calls `level_in` for every (account × group) pair, and it runs inside `apply` (call sites :1407, :1496), multiplying the blow-up across the whole directory.
- `directory_view.rs:1548` — the directory view calls `level_in` once per group for the viewer, so rendering the view of a diamond-nested directory hangs the same way.
- No cap on the number of groups exists in `directory.rs` (only name/description length caps), so the depth is bounded only by how many groups an admin/manager creates.

## Verified this run (laptop probe)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-diamond/` extracts `level_in` and `reaches` verbatim from origin/main (snapshots saved alongside the probe; function bodies unchanged, only the standalone `members: BTreeMap<(u64, Member), Level>` field reproduced) and builds a diamond: layer *i* = groups {2i, 2i+1}, each containing both groups of layer *i+1*; the last layer holds the account directly.

| layers | groups | `level_in` | `reaches` (absent target) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 20 | 77µs | 46µs |
| 15 | 30 | 2.7ms | 3.6ms |
| 18 | 36 | 28ms | 18ms |
| 20 | 40 | 104ms | 61ms |
| 22 | 44 | 400ms | 243ms |

Time doubles per added layer (×4 per 2 layers): ~30 layers (60 groups) extrapolates to ~100s for a single `level_in` call, and `ensure_admins`/`view` repeat that call per group/account. A plain 45-group chain control completes in ~17µs, so the cost is the repeated shared-subgraph traversal, not the group count itself.

## Why it matters

Group nesting is the directory's delegation mechanism; layered org/team structures naturally produce diamonds (two parent groups both containing the same shared subgroup). A modest, legitimate structure — or one crafted by any account allowed to manage groups — makes directory views, member updates, and every `apply` that runs `ensure_admins` effectively hang, with no error and no cap to trip.

## Acceptance criteria

- `level_in` evaluates each (account, group) pair at most once per top-level call (memoization or an equivalent DAG traversal), preserving the exact current semantics: max over paths of `min(inner level, level the subgroup is held at)`, direct membership included.
- `reaches` visits each group at most once per call (visited set), preserving its result for present and absent targets.
- A regression test builds a diamond-nested directory (≥25 layers) and asserts `level_in`, the `MemberSet` cycle check, and a directory view complete promptly (or counts evaluations) — the test must fail/hang on the pre-fix code and pass quickly after.
- Existing directory tests pass unchanged, including `nesting_passes_the_lower_level_and_refuses_cycles` (directory.rs:~2371).
- Bonus, if in scope: note the `ensure_admins` account×group multiplication in the fix description; it needs no separate change once `level_in` is memoized per call, but a cross-call cache is out of scope unless trivial.

## Dedup

Searched open and closed issues for `level_in`, `reaches`, directory nesting, and exponential traversal on 2026-11-02 — no covering issue. The cycle itself is already refused (:1647); this is the traversal cost of the DAG that remains, not the cycle case.

title: id(currency_poc): executor submit() and recovery resubmission treat a short create_transfers result vector as success — a backend returning no results marks the conversion Posted with nothing in the ledger

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: status/triaged
labels.description: Triaged and routed (see agent note)

body:
## Problem

In `pkgs/id/src/currency_poc`, neither the executor's submission path nor the recovery scanner checks that `LedgerBackend::create_transfers` returned one result per leg. A backend that returns a short — or empty — result vector is treated as complete success, and the conversion is persisted as `Posted` with nothing (or only part) in the ledger.

- `executor.rs:264-282` — `submit()` iterates `record.legs.iter().zip(results.iter())` (line 270). `zip` stops at the shorter side, so legs with no corresponding result are never examined; the record then advances to `IntentState::Posted` at line 282 unconditionally.
- `recovery.rs:111-124` — the `Resubmit` path computes `failed` by scanning `results` for a non-`Ok`/`Exists` entry. An empty vector has no failing entry, so the record is persisted `Posted` and reported `ReconcileOutcome::Resubmitted`.
- `ledger.rs:134` — the `LedgerBackend::create_transfers` trait contract documents the linked-chain rule a production binding must implement, but never states that the returned vector must carry exactly one result per submitted transfer. The in-repo `InMemoryLedger` happens to return `batch.len()` results; nothing enforces that for the future TigerBeetle client binding this seam exists for (#2289).

This is the same vacuous-success shape the module already hardened against once: #4133 fixed `reconcile` marking an empty/duplicate leg vector `Posted` because `matched == legs.len()` held vacuously (0 == 0). The result-vector side was left unchecked — a short result vector makes "no leg failed" true vacuously in both callers.

## Verified this run (laptop probe, verbatim sources @ 04286381)

Probe crate `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-shortresults/` on the laptop compiles the verbatim `currency_poc` sources (sha256-matched: `executor.rs` d6ad6d84…, `recovery.rs` 3d96f415…) against a `SilentBackend` whose `create_transfers` drops the batch, posts nothing, and returns `Vec::new()`, with accounts/balances delegated to a funded `InMemoryLedger`:

- Control: real `InMemoryLedger` → `execute()` returns `Posted`, 3 legs findable by `user_data_128 = 777`.
- Executor probe: `execute()` returned `Ok` with record state `Posted` while **0 legs** were in the ledger.
- Recovery probe: a genuine `Recorded` record (legs built by `build_legs`) reconciled under `RecoveryPolicy::Resubmit` against the silent backend → outcome `Resubmitted`, record state `Posted`, **0 legs** in the ledger.

`cargo test --offline` on the probe: 2 passed (both probes assert the buggy outcome).

## Why it matters

The intent record is the recovery source of truth. A conversion marked `Posted` that never posted is invisible to the recovery scanner afterwards (the record is resolved), so the user's source funds never move and no operator signal fires — the worst failure mode for a write-ahead design whose whole point (#2289, #2063) is that state on disk never claims more than the ledger proves. A real client binding that batches, pages, or errors per-request rather than per-transfer can plausibly return a short vector exactly when something else already went wrong.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ConversionExecutor::submit` fails (record stays `Submitted`, error names the conversion and the expected/actual result counts) when `results.len() != record.legs.len()`.
- [ ] `reconcile`'s resubmission path treats a short result vector as a rejected resubmission (`ResubmissionRejected`, record left unresolved, scan continues) rather than `Resubmitted`/`Posted`.
- [ ] The `LedgerBackend::create_transfers` trait doc states the one-result-per-transfer contract explicitly.
- [ ] Regression tests in `currency_poc/tests.rs` cover a short-result backend (empty and partial, e.g. 1 of 3) for both `submit` and the recovery resubmission path; existing scenario tests still pass.

Related: #4133 (same vacuous-success class, leg-vector side), #2289 (the PoC), #2063 (design). Distinct from #4578 (FileIntentStore listing).

body:
## Finding (from PR review)

When two sessions have prompts in flight, completing either one clears the streamed-text offsets for both, duplicating already-delivered text for the still-running session. Codex (P2, PR #3997):

> The next cumulative text update for the still-running session is then emitted from character zero, duplicating content already delivered to its ACP client. Exercising the current handlers with session B emitting `Hello`, session A becoming idle, and B updating its part to `Hello world` produces the concatenated output `HelloHello world`. Keep offsets scoped to each session and remove only the completed session's entries.

## Evidence

- Source PR: #3997 — https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/3997 (merged 2026-11-02 as-is)
- Review comment: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/3997#discussion_r4437436112 — chatgpt-codex-connector[bot], 2026-11-01T21:31:18Z, `bin/opencode-acp-adapter.mjs:290`
- No-response evidence: the review thread is unresolved (GraphQL `reviewThreads`, checked 2026-11-02), the comment has no replies, and PR #3997 contains a single commit (8e67215808, 2026-11-01T21:26:51Z) that predates the comment — no fix followed it before merge.
- Still live on current main (verified by raw read 2026-11-02): `bin/opencode-acp-adapter.mjs:290` — `finishPrompt()` calls `partTextSent.clear()`, wiping every session's offsets whenever any one prompt finishes.

## Acceptance criteria

- Streamed-text offsets are scoped per session: finishing one session's prompt removes only that session's entries.
- A regression test covers two concurrent sessions where one completes and the other's cumulative text update is not re-emitted from character zero.
- Or the finding is resolved by a documented decision on this issue.

title: id(journals): a crash-torn final line that splits a multibyte UTF-8 character bricks the journal open — petnames, groups, outbox, artifacts and directory all read_to_string before their torn-tail handling runs

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

Every JSONL journal loader in pkgs/id that promises crash-torn-tail tolerance reads the whole file with `std::fs::read_to_string` **before** its torn-tail logic runs. `read_to_string` fails on any invalid UTF-8 anywhere in the file, so a crash that tears an append **in the middle of a multibyte character** (a name containing `é`, an emoji, CJK text — all legal in these journals) bricks the open entirely: the loader returns the UTF-8 error instead of dropping and truncating the torn final line as its own doc promises. The complete, valid records before the tail are unreachable.

Affected loaders (all verified at the lines below on current main):

- `crates/id-core/src/petname.rs:64` — `Petnames::open`: doc (lines 54–58) promises a torn final line "is dropped and truncated away"; the `read_to_string` at :64 errors first.
- `src/groups/log.rs:56` — `GroupLog::open`: same promise (doc lines 44–50), same `read_to_string` first.
- `src/envelope_outbox.rs:135` — `Outbox::open`: torn-tail handling at :143–175 is unreachable for a UTF-8-split tail.
- `src/artifact.rs:579` — `ArtifactLog::open`: doc (lines 573–576) promises a crash-cut final line "is dropped and the file is truncated"; `read_to_string` at :579 errors first.
- `src/directory.rs:494` — `Directory::replay`: the #1521 torn-tail repair computes `kept_len` from the string it already failed to read.

The world journal in the same codebase does this correctly: `FileJournal::open` (`src/world_store.rs:59`) reads bytes with `read_until(b'\n')` and parses with `serde_json::from_slice`, and `read_journal_entries` (`src/world_store.rs:466`) splits the raw bytes on `b'\n'` — a UTF-8-split torn tail is dropped there exactly as documented.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe (worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-utf8torn`, at GitHub main 9f096d925; all five loader sources md5-matched between the sandbox and laptop clones): an integration test against the real `id_core::petname::Petnames`:

- Control: a valid journal plus an ASCII torn tail (no newline) reopens fine — the existing torn-tail path works for ASCII.
- Probe: a valid journal whose first record sets the petname `José`, followed by a torn second record cut after the first byte (`0xC3`) of an `é` in the name, with no trailing newline — `Petnames::open` FAILS instead of dropping the tail and keeping `José`.

Probe output (`cargo test -p id-core --test probe_utf8_torn -- --nocapture`):

```
CONTROL ascii torn tail: OK (dropped, Ali kept)
test control_ascii_torn_tail_is_dropped ... ok
PROBE utf8-split torn tail: open FAILED: stream did not contain valid UTF-8
test probe_utf8_split_torn_tail ... FAILED (BUG REPRODUCED: utf8-split torn tail bricks Petnames::open)
```

The other four loaders share the identical construction (`read_to_string` returning the same std UTF-8 error before any line logic), so the same torn file bricks each of them; the probe exercises the petname loader against the real crate code as the representative case.

Earlier torn-tail fixes — #1499/#2948 (petnames), #1521 (directory), #1522 (groups), #1620/#2150 (outbox), #2128 (artifacts) — each tested torn tails made of ASCII or complete characters, so this sub-case survived all of them.

## Why it matters

These journals are the durable state of a world (directory, groups, outbox, artifacts, petnames). One crash at the wrong byte turns a recoverable, documented torn tail into a world that will not open at all, with an error ("stream did not contain valid UTF-8") that does not name the torn tail — the exact failure class the torn-tail fixes were written to eliminate, gated on whether the torn record happened to contain non-ASCII text.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each affected loader reads bytes (or otherwise tolerates invalid UTF-8 confined to the unterminated final line), drops and truncates a torn final line even when it splits a multibyte character, and reopens with all complete records intact.
- [ ] A newline-terminated line containing invalid UTF-8 / unparseable content in any earlier position still fails the open as corruption (the torn-tail tolerance must not widen).
- [ ] Regression tests for each fixed loader: valid record with a non-ASCII name + a final line torn mid-character reopens with the valid records and the file truncated to the last complete line; the next append after reopen replays cleanly.
- [ ] Existing torn-tail and journal tests for petnames, groups, outbox, artifacts and directory still pass.

title: mcpx(model+scripting): OpenAI-compatible providers buffer response bodies whole — io.ReadAll uncapped, and the error path embeds the entire body in the error string

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Summary

mcpx's two OpenAI-compatible model providers buffer a provider's entire HTTP response body with no size cap, and on a non-2xx response they embed that whole body in the returned error string:

- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/model/openai.go:123` — `respBody, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)` in `OpenAIProvider.Generate`; the error path at :128-131 formats the full body into the error (`strings.TrimSpace(string(respBody))`, no truncation).
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/scripting/provider.go:121` — the twin code in `OpenAICompatibleProvider.Complete`; the error path at :125-128 likewise embeds the full body.

The `baseURL` of both providers is configuration, not a constant: the model layer's own doc comment (openai.go:17-20) says the same code serves "OpenAI itself, a company gateway, LiteLLM, Ollama and LM Studio", and the scripting provider lists Ollama / local Qwen / vLLM / LM Studio. A misbehaving, compromised, or simply wrong endpoint (e.g. a proxy returning a large HTML error page, or a local server gone wrong) can therefore make the daemon allocate an arbitrarily large body in memory — and on the error path, produce an arbitrarily large error string that callers log and surface.

Contrast inside the same codebase: `internal/mcpclient/http.go:167` and `sse.go` read non-2xx bodies through `io.LimitReader(resp.Body, defaults.HTTPErrorBodyLimit)` (`internal/defaults/defaults.go:400-402`, "bounds how much of a non-2xx body is read"), and the daemon's own request paths use `http.MaxBytesReader` / `io.LimitReader` throughout. These two provider implementations are the un-capped outliers. (Distinct from #4282, which is the mcpclient `Send` success-path fallback in a different package; this issue is the two model-provider implementations and their error embedding.)

## Evidence (verified this run, main bc1bdce04)

- Source files md5-identical between sandbox main bc1bdce04 and the laptop probe tree: model/openai.go b588dd091baea938ff8492476150e2e0, scripting/provider.go 898d9cd168c60971538331c917fa2731.
- Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-modelbody/` (detached worktree of the repo; probe tests only, in-package, against `httptest` servers):
  - `internal/model`: server returns HTTP 500 with a 33,554,432-byte body of `x` → `Generate` returns an error of length **33,554,473 bytes** — the entire body, buffered and embedded. A 200 response with a 32 MiB non-JSON body is likewise read in full before the JSON parse error is produced.
  - `internal/scripting`: same 500/32 MiB setup → `Complete` returns an error of length **33,554,466 bytes**.
  - Both probes pass in the sense that they demonstrate the un-capped behaviour (`go test -run TestProbeHuge -count=1 -v`, both packages).

## Why it matters

- Memory: one provider response can force an unbounded allocation in the long-lived mcpx daemon; nothing else in the response path (timeout aside) bounds it — the client timeout bounds duration, not bytes, and a fast local endpoint can deliver gigabytes within it.
- Log/surface bloat: the non-2xx path copies the whole body into an error string that callers fall back on, log, and may return to users — a 33 MB "error message" in this probe, unbounded in principle.
- The house pattern already exists (LimitReader + `defaults.HTTPErrorBodyLimit` for error bodies); these two sites were simply never brought under it.

## Acceptance criteria

- Both providers read response bodies through a bounded reader with a stated cap (per-path if success and error bodies warrant different bounds; the error body must never exceed a small bound such as `defaults.HTTPErrorBodyLimit` in the produced error string).
- Exceeding the success-path cap produces a clear error naming the provider and the cap, not a silent truncation that then fails JSON parsing with a misleading message — or, if truncation is chosen, the error says the response was truncated at the cap.
- Regression tests in `internal/model` and `internal/scripting`: an `httptest` provider returning an oversized error body yields an error whose length is bounded by the cap (plus fixed overhead); an oversized success body is refused/truncated per the chosen contract; normal small responses (success and error) behave exactly as before.
- `go test ./internal/model/ ./internal/scripting/ -count=1` passes (package-scoped per pkgs/mcpx/internal/AGENTS.md).

body:
## Finding

The #2417 fix (merged today in PR #4176, main c611bf45) deepened the orchestration section gate for the section's top-level arrays: `dependencies` elements must now pass `isDependencyElement` (string `task`, `status` in the DependencyRef union, string-typed optional fields), and tier/action elements gained field checks. Inside goals, however, `isGoalMeasurement` checks `linedUp`/`stalled` elements only with `isRecord` — and a lined-up task's `blockedBy` field, declared as the very same `DependencyRef[]` shape, is not checked at all. `todayFromSection`'s `blockedText` helper calls `.map` on it, so a gate-passing goal whose lined-up task carries a malformed `blockedBy` crashes the today view instead of the section being diagnosed invalid and falling back to the derived view.

Scope boundary with #3897 (open): that issue's acceptance criteria enumerate the `linedUp` element checks as title/horizon/status/horizonWhy and the goal-level fields — `blockedBy` is not named in it, and a fix implementing those criteria verbatim leaves both crashes below alive. This issue covers only the `blockedBy` field; everything else in the goal gate stays #3897's.

## Evidence (main c611bf45, verified this run)

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/model.ts:615-623` — `LinedUpTask.blockedBy?: DependencyRef[]`; `DependencyRef` is the shape `isDependencyElement` validates for top-level `dependencies`.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/feed.ts` — `isGoalMeasurement` (~:197-212, after #2417): `g.linedUp.every(isRecord)` and `g.stalled.every(isRecord)` are the only element checks; no clause touches `blockedBy`. `isDependencyElement` (~:241) shows the house rule for the identical shape one array over.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/derive.ts:688-690` — `blockedText` does `deps?.length ? deps.map(...) : undefined`; `:698` and `:714` call it on `task.blockedBy` unguarded. A string has a truthy `.length` but no `.map`; a `[null]` element reaches `d.task` on null.
- Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-goalblockedby/`, verbatim `src/` from main c611bf45 — feed.ts md5 fcfbd045, derive.ts md5 dcdefb5e, both matched to the sandbox clone), importing the real `isOrchestrationSection`/`orchestrationSectionProblem` and `todayFromSection`:
  - Control (`blockedBy: [{task, status}]`): gate `true`, today renders `blocked by dep-1 (in-progress)`.
  - `blockedBy: "waiting on dep-1"` (string): gate `true`, problem `null` → `todayFromSection` **throws** `TypeError: deps.map is not a function`.
  - `blockedBy: [null]`: gate `true`, problem `null` → **throws** `TypeError: null is not an object (evaluating 'd.task')`.
  - `blockedBy: [{}]`: gate `true` → renders the falsified text `blocked by undefined (undefined)`.

## Why it matters

The orchestration section is machine-published JSON read fail-soft by design: a malformed section is supposed to be diagnosed (`goals (per-goal shape)`) and demoted to the derived view. #2417 closed that hole for the section's top-level `dependencies` array; the identical field nested one level deeper in goals still turns one drifted publisher line into an uncaught TypeError on the today path — or, for `[{}]`, silently falsified blocker text presented as measured state.

## Acceptance criteria

- `isGoalMeasurement` (or a helper it uses) validates each lined-up task's `blockedBy` when present: an array whose every element passes the same DependencyRef rule the gate applies to top-level `dependencies` (reuse `isDependencyElement` rather than duplicating the rule).
- A section failing only on `blockedBy` is diagnosed through the existing machinery: `orchestrationSectionProblem` reports `goals (per-goal shape)`, the section falls back to the derived view, and `todayFromSection` can no longer be reached with a `blockedBy` it throws on.
- Regression tests beside the #2417 orchestration gate tests cover at least: `blockedBy` as a string, `blockedBy: [null]`, `blockedBy: [{}]` — all rejected — plus the well-formed `blockedBy` control still passing and rendering.
- Existing aggregator tests stay green.

Dedup: #3897 (open) covers the goal gate's element/field checks but its enumerated criteria omit `blockedBy` (see scope boundary above); #2417 (closed, fix merged c611bf45) covered top-level `dependencies`, tiers, actions, and record-ness of goal elements. No open or closed issue names `blockedBy` in a goal (title search: no hits).

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-a (Lane A) from a verified laptop probe; filed only, not self-solved — the gate-criteria coordination with #3897 is a triage call.

body:
## Summary

`collectFileExportAdapter` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/token-adapter.ts) is documented as the strict layer over the bare file-export mapping: a success document whose windows are malformed must fail closed as `unparseable` and retain the previous entry, "instead of a partial one being published" (token-adapter.ts:220-228, and the comment at :271: "drift => unparseable, never partial").

Its window validation (token-adapter.ts:272-296) checks only that each window is an object with a non-empty string `name` and a **finite** `usedPct`. It never checks the 0–100 range — but the mapping it wraps does treat out-of-range as malformed: `entryFromFileExport` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-gather-map.ts:139-140) silently `continue`s past any window with `pct < 0 || pct > 100`.

So an out-of-range window passes the adapter's drift check, is silently dropped by the mapping, and the adapter publishes the result as a **fresh `ok`** outcome:

- one bad window among good ones → a partial entry (window missing) presented as fresh, not stale, with no error;
- a document whose only window is out of range → a fresh `ok` entry with **zero windows** — an empty reading that is neither the retained previous value nor an error.

## Evidence (verified this run, main @ 0858c741)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-fileexport/` — verbatim copies of token-adapter.ts (md5 9a6c0009), quota-gather-map.ts (ecf44799), validate.ts (2078ddfd), model.ts (6189406b) from main, run with `bun run probe.ts`, a previous value present in every case:

```
control 42pct+10pct: status=ok stale=false windows=["5h=42","weekly=10"]
negative -5 + 10:    status=ok stale=false windows=["weekly=10"]        <- 5h window silently gone
over100 250 + 10:    status=ok stale=false windows=["weekly=10"]        <- same
only window -5:      status=ok stale=false windows=[]                   <- fresh ok, zero windows
drift control NaN:   status=unparseable stale=true windows=["5h=11"]    <- retained, as designed
```

The NaN control proves the fail-closed path works for the shapes the adapter checks; the range is the one malformed shape it does not check, even though the mapping's own rule (quota-gather-map.ts:140, and the same rule for provider results at :199-200) defines it as malformed.

## Why it matters

The file-export adapter is the framework's reference adapter (#1153) that the per-provider browser-token adapters copy. A producer whose payload drifts into an out-of-range percentage (a dashboard change, a fraction-vs-percent slip like 0.42 → 4200, a signed bug) currently degrades the dashboard quietly: windows disappear one by one, or the entry goes empty, while everything reports fresh/ok and the retained-value safety net never engages — the exact failure mode this module exists to prevent.

## Distinct from

- #2571 (closed): the *mapping* published −20%/1e9% as live ok data. Fixed by the skip at quota-gather-map.ts:140. This issue is the residual at the *adapter* layer: the skip converts bad data into a silently partial/empty fresh entry, and the adapter — whose stated job is to catch exactly that — doesn't.
- #2551 (closed): the adapter's window check threw on a null element / accepted a non-string name. Fixed (isRecord + name check now present at token-adapter.ts:276-285). The range was not part of that fix.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `collectFileExportAdapter` returns the retained `unparseable` outcome (previous value kept, `stale: true`) for a success document containing a window with `usedPct < 0` or `usedPct > 100`, naming the window in the detail — consistent with its existing NaN/non-finite handling.
- [ ] A success document whose only window(s) are out of range no longer yields a fresh `ok` entry with zero windows.
- [ ] In-range documents (including exactly 0 and exactly 100) still produce the fresh `ok` entry with all windows.
- [ ] Tests cover: negative, over-100, boundary 0/100, and the mixed good+bad document case.

body:
## Problem

The projector has no delete path for items. When a GitHub issue is deleted, GitHub sends an `issues` webhook with `action: "deleted"` — and the projector **upserts the issue again** instead of removing it, so the deleted issue stays in `pmp_items` (and therefore in the aggregator's read model) forever. Nothing else can heal it: reconcile only ever upserts.

- `pm-stack/projector/src/projector.ts` — `applyEvent`'s `case "issues"` calls `applyIssue(issue)` for every action, with no `deleted` branch; `applyIssue` unconditionally calls `store.upsertItem(fromIssueOrPr(...))`. Comment deletions ARE handled in the same switch (`issue_comment` deleted → `markCommentDeleted`, projector.ts:158; `pull_request_review_comment` deleted → projector.ts:212) — item deletion is the one missing case.
- `pm-stack/projector/src/projector.ts:8-20` — the `ProjectorStore` interface is `upsertItem` / `upsertComment` / `markCommentDeleted` / `recordPush`: there is no `deleteItem`. `pm-stack/projector/src/store.ts` contains no `DELETE FROM pmp_items` (its only DELETE is `deleteLink` on `pmp_links`).
- `pm-stack/projector/src/reconcile.ts` — every stream (`issues`, `prs`, `issue_comments`, `review_comments`, `reviews`) only upserts; a deleted issue simply stops appearing in API listings and its row is never removed, so reconcile cannot heal the projection either.
- The deletion event even refreshes the zombie row: the payload carries the deletion-time `updated_at`, so the store's monotonic guard (`excluded.source_updated_at >= pmp_items.source_updated_at`) accepts the re-upsert.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneA-projdeleted/` — the real `pm-stack/projector/src/projector.ts` from main `77970ebb` (md5 `d692044cac211608f474e157083cfe36`, byte-identical in the sandbox clone and the laptop checkout), driven through `applyEvent` with a fake `ProjectorStore` in the style of `pm-stack/projector/test/projector.test.ts`:

```
opened:            wrote=true calls=[upsertItem developing-today/code#100 state=open]
issues/deleted:    wrote=true calls=[upsertItem developing-today/code#100 state=open]
item still stored: true state=open
comment/deleted:   wrote=true calls=[upsertItem ...; markCommentDeleted 555]   (control: comment deletion does reach a delete path)
```

## Why it matters

`pmp_items` is the projection the dashboard reads. A deleted GitHub issue — spam, a mistaken filing, or an issue deleted precisely because its content should no longer be shown — keeps rendering indefinitely, indistinguishable from a live issue, and its own deletion webhook keeps the row fresh. Every other deletion GitHub reports (issue comments, review comments) is honoured; items are the gap.

## Acceptance criteria

- An `issues` event with `action: "deleted"` removes the item's `pmp_items` row (new `deleteItem` on the `ProjectorStore` interface + a `DELETE FROM pmp_items` in `store.ts`); the result reports the touched ref. All other `issues` actions behave exactly as before.
- Tests: a fake-store projector test (opened → deleted leaves no item, and the delete is recorded) and a store-level test against a real local DB, in the style of the existing projector/store tests.
- Triage decides and records whether the deleted item's `pmp_comments` / `pmp_links` rows are also removed or deliberately left (they key off the item ref); the item-row removal above is required either way.
- Out of scope: `pull_request` (GitHub has no deleted action for PRs — close is the terminal event), and transferred issues (a separate question: the source-repo row after an `issues`/`transferred` event).

body:
## Problem

`RoadmapAnnotationsStore.doLoad` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/roadmap-annotations.ts) rethrows any non-ENOENT read failure — and because `load()` memoizes the load promise, that one transient failure is latched for the whole process lifetime. Every annotations read/write then rejects until the aggregator is restarted, even after the underlying file is healthy again. The sibling stores in the same directory were specifically fixed not to do this (#2980); the roadmap-annotations store (added later, for #1284) kept the old pattern.

## Evidence (main `199a7d27`)

- `load()` (roadmap-annotations.ts:94-96) memoizes: `if (!this.loadPromise) this.loadPromise = this.doLoad();` — a rejected `doLoad()` is returned to every later caller forever; it is never cleared.
- `doLoad` read path (roadmap-annotations.ts:102-105): only `ENOENT` returns (empty start); any other error is `throw err` — no quarantine attempt, no loud-start-empty fallback.
- Contrast — the #2980 fix in the sibling stores: `CommentsStore.doLoad` (comments.ts:129+) and `ActionsStore.doLoad` (actions.ts:491+) treat a non-ENOENT read failure like the corrupt case: quarantine the original bytes to `<file>.corrupt-<timestamp>`, log loudly, start empty — so their loads never reject and the service keeps working. `ViewsStore` (views.ts:202-208) does the same.
- Consumers have no recovery path: server.ts calls `roadmapAnnotationsStore.forObject(...)` with no `.catch` in the /roadmap page handler (server.ts:969-971, :994), in GET /api/roadmap.json (server.ts:1245, :1261), and in the item-page Promise.all (server.ts:1519) — one latched rejection fails those requests for the process lifetime. `add()`/`addAlias()` (roadmap-annotations.ts:163, :180) also await the latched load, so annotation writes stay broken too.

Verified this run on the laptop with verbatim src copies @199a7d27 (roadmap-annotations.ts md5 `28ef7ae7`, comments.ts md5 `14b8f229`, model.ts md5 `6189406b`), bun 1.4.2:

- Control: valid store file → `all()` returns the seeded annotation; OK.
- Store path is a directory (EISDIR): roadmap store `all()` **REJECTED (EISDIR)**; after replacing the directory with a valid store file at the same path, the same instance's `all()` **REJECTED AGAIN (EISDIR)** and `add()` **REJECTED (EISDIR)**; a fresh instance on the restored file resolves 1 annotation — the failure is the latched promise, not the file.
- chmod 000 (EACCES): same shape — `all()` REJECTED (EACCES), and after restoring permissions the same instance still REJECTED AGAIN (EACCES).
- Sibling control under the identical directory-in-place setup: `CommentsStore.all()` resolved 0 and quarantined the path to `dir-as-file-comments.corrupt-<timestamp>` with a loud warning — the #2980 behaviour.

Probe: laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneB-roadmapload/` (probe.ts + verbatim src copies).

## Why it matters

Roadmap annotations are the dashboard's append-only decision/outcome history on roadmap rows (#1284), and the store sits on the read path of the /roadmap page itself. A single transient read failure at startup — a permissions slip, a momentary I/O error, a directory briefly in place of the file during a deploy/restore — permanently takes down annotation reads and writes *and* the roadmap views that embed them, until someone restarts the aggregator. #2980 already established the house contract for exactly this failure in the sibling stores; this store is the one outlier, and its variant is worse than the original #2980 bug in one respect: there is no silent data loss, but there is also no recovery at all — the memoized rejection never retries the read.

Distinct from: #2980 (closed — covered actions/comments stores only; this store did not exist in its fix scope and reintroduced the pattern), #3732/#3729 (success-path memoization of a transient *null* from bws/Supabase in alerts/push — different stores, different mechanism), #3879 (design epic on success-only memoization for lazy initializers; this is a concrete store instance with a verified latch).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `RoadmapAnnotationsStore.doLoad` handles a non-ENOENT read failure the way the #2980 sibling stores do: only ENOENT takes the silent empty start; any other read error is loud (console.error naming the file and error), attempts the `<file>.corrupt-<timestamp>` quarantine rename before starting empty, and surfaces a failed quarantine explicitly — the load does not reject for a read failure.
- [ ] A transient read failure cannot latch the store for the process lifetime: after the file is restored to a valid store at the same path, the same store instance serves reads/writes again (either because the load no longer fails, or because a failed load is retried rather than memoized).
- [ ] Behaviour for the genuinely-missing-file case is unchanged (silent empty start, first write creates the file), and the corrupt/wrong-shape parse path keeps quarantining as today.
- [ ] Regression tests in pm-stack/aggregator/test/roadmap-annotations.test.ts (or a sibling store test) pin the non-ENOENT case (directory-in-place and/or unreadable file, per platform) plus the recovery-after-restore case, alongside the existing valid/missing cases, which keep passing.

title: codedb-bridge: regex/scope/compact are rejected only on codedb_search and codedb_outline — silently ignored on codedb_word, codedb_symbol, codedb_hot, codedb_tree and codedb_deps (and limit/max_results are silent no-ops on the wrong tool)

body:
## Problem

`bin/codedb-bridge.mjs` promises, in its own header (`:24-31`, per issue #3352):

> arguments the daemon cannot honour are rejected by name, never silently ignored — `project` (the daemon serves exactly one root), `regex: true`, `scope: true`, `compact: true`.

`project` is indeed rejected on every tool (`rejectProject`, `:119-121`, called in every case). But `regex` / `scope` / `compact` are only checked where the author happened to add them:

- `codedb_search` (`:145-149`): rejects `regex`, `scope`, `compact` ✓
- `codedb_outline` (`:138-140`): rejects `compact` only
- `codedb_symbol` (`:142-144`), `codedb_word` (`:151-153`), `codedb_hot` (`:154-156`), `codedb_tree` (`:135-137`), `codedb_deps` (`:157-160`): reject **none** of them

So `regex: true` passed to `codedb_word` is silently dropped and the caller gets exact-word results while believing it asked for a regex search — precisely the silent third path #3352 forbids. The same hole covers misnamed limit arguments: `codedb_search` honours `max_results` and silently ignores `limit`; `codedb_hot` honours `limit` and silently ignores `max_results` (each becomes a `slice` of `[key, undefined]`, a no-op). Unknown arguments generally (e.g. `bogus_arg` on `codedb_tree`) are also silently ignored, though the header's promise is at minimum about the named unhonourable set.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneA-codedb/` (verbatim copy of `bin/codedb-bridge.mjs` from main `199a7d27`, md5 `ca05ede20d2ae1a4760297bbe9320c58`, node v24.21.0), calling `routeForTool` directly:

- `codedb_word {word:"x", regex:true}` → OK, route `/explore/word?q=x` (regex silently dropped)
- `codedb_word {word:"x", scope:true}` → OK (scope silently dropped)
- `codedb_symbol {name:"x", compact:true}` → OK (compact silently dropped)
- `codedb_hot {limit:2, regex:true}` → OK (regex silently dropped)
- `codedb_tree {bogus_arg:1}` → OK
- `codedb_search {query:"x", limit:5}` → OK, `slice:["results",null]` (limit silently ignored; the honoured name is `max_results`)
- `codedb_hot {max_results:5}` → OK, `slice:["files",null]` (max_results silently ignored; the honoured name is `limit`)
- Control: `codedb_deps {path:"a.rs", project:"/elsewhere"}` → THROWS naming `project` — the per-tool rejection machinery works; it just isn't applied uniformly.

Existing tests (`bin/codedb-bridge.test.mjs:36-44`) only assert rejection on `codedb_search` (regex/scope) and `codedb_outline` (compact) — the two tools that already check — so the gap is invisible to the suite.

## Why it matters

Callers (MCP clients, mcpx sessions) passing a familiar argument to the wrong tool get plausible-looking results computed under different semantics than they asked for, with no signal. That is the exact failure mode the bridge's argument contract was written to prevent, and it is asymmetric enough that a client author testing against `codedb_search` would reasonably conclude all tools behave that way.

## Acceptance criteria

- Every tool rejects `regex: true`, `scope: true`, and `compact: true` by name when the daemon route for that tool cannot honour them (or the rejection set is otherwise made uniform and the header updated to match — no silent divergence between tools).
- Misnamed limit arguments are not silent no-ops: either `limit` on `codedb_search` / `max_results` on `codedb_hot` is honoured, or it is rejected by name like the other unhonourable arguments.
- Tests extended beyond the current search/outline-only cases: for each advertised tool, at least one unhonourable-argument case throws naming the argument; the existing route/rejection tests still pass.

body:
## Bug

`pm-stack/aggregator/src/coverage.ts`: `CoverageSnapshotStore.read()` is documented as "corrupt reads as absent" (coverage.ts:214, class comment: "Thin JSON store for the coverage snapshot; corrupt reads as absent"), but its only validation (coverage.ts:222-232) is:

```ts
const parsed = JSON.parse(await readFile(this.file, "utf8")) as CoverageSnapshotFile;
if (!parsed || typeof parsed !== "object" || !parsed.current || !Array.isArray(parsed.current.repos)) {
  return null;
}
return parsed;
```

`baseline` and `weekly` are never checked, and neither are the row fields of any report. A snapshot file whose `current.repos` is an array but whose `baseline` is malformed is accepted as a good snapshot, carried through `nextCoverageSnapshot` (coverage.ts:199-212, which copies `stored.baseline` / `stored.weekly` verbatim into the next file — and promotes `weekly` to `baseline` at the weekly rotation), and then crashes the consumer:

- `diffCoverage` (coverage.ts:168-183) does `baseline.repos.map(...)` unconditionally — a baseline that is a string, or an object without a `repos` array, throws `TypeError` there;
- that call sits on the /projects render path: `coverageSectionHtml` in `render.ts` (diffCoverage at render.ts:5610) and `coverageSnapshot()` in `server.ts:109-128`, which feeds the stored snapshot into `nextCoverageSnapshot` on every panel read;
- a baseline whose rows carry garbage field types (e.g. `openIssues: "ten"`) survives too and produces `NaN` deltas (`deltaOrNull` subtracts unchecked values) that render as `(NaN)` in the panel.

The snapshot file is exactly the kind of artifact that drifts: the format already grew optional `weekly` / `anchorAt` fields with explicit "files written before the field existed" fallbacks (coverage.ts:62-73), so older/hand-edited/partially-migrated files are an anticipated input — the sibling roadmap-annotations store validates every row on load (`isAnnotation`, roadmap-annotations.ts:76-89) and quarantines a bad file instead of trusting it.

## Evidence (verified this run, main @ bc0afe2f)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneB-projcov/` (verbatim `coverage.ts`, md5 e17585a5fee1a752a9be91911a9e79ea; store files written to a temp dir, then `read()` → `nextCoverageSnapshot(...)` → `diffCoverage(...)`):

```
control (well-formed baseline/current/weekly) -> read() NON-NULL, diffCoverage OK, 1 delta entry
baseline: "junk" (string)                      -> read() NON-NULL (accepted); diffCoverage THREW TypeError: undefined is not an object (evaluating 'baseline.repos.map')
baseline: {generatedAt} (no repos)             -> read() NON-NULL (accepted); diffCoverage THREW TypeError (same)
baseline: {repos: "nope"}                      -> read() NON-NULL (accepted); diffCoverage THREW TypeError: baseline.repos.map is not a function
baseline row fields garbage ("ten", null, {})  -> read() NON-NULL (accepted); diffCoverage OK but deltas are NaN
file containing "{not json"                    -> read() null (absent) — the documented behaviour, only for unparseable JSON
```

## Why it matters

One malformed stored snapshot permanently breaks the /projects coverage panel: the bad baseline is re-persisted by `coverageSnapshot()` on every read (it only writes when the snapshot "changes", and the poisoned baseline is part of the compared shape), and the weekly rotation can promote a malformed `weekly` into the baseline slot. The store's own contract says this input should read as absent and self-heal with a fresh snapshot; instead it is a recurring render crash with no recovery short of deleting the file by hand.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `CoverageSnapshotStore.read()` validates the whole file shape — `current`, `baseline` (when non-null), and `weekly` (when present) are each either null/absent or a report object with a string `generatedAt` and a `repos` array whose rows carry a string `repo` and number-or-null count fields — and returns `null` (absent) for anything else, per its documented contract.
- [ ] Files written by the current writer (including pre-`weekly`/pre-`anchorAt` files, which rely on the documented fallbacks) still read back exactly as today.
- [ ] A malformed `weekly` can no longer be promoted into `baseline` by `nextCoverageSnapshot` rotation, because the store never hands one out.
- [ ] Tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/coverage.test.ts`: store reads for a string baseline, a baseline without `repos`, a non-array `repos`, and garbage row field types all return `null`; the existing concurrent-write test still passes.
- [ ] Existing aggregator tests still pass.

Dedup: #3364 (closed) covered the *feed-side census gate* (`isRepoCensus`) letting impossible census rows into a snapshot; this is the separate *file-side* read path — the stored snapshot's own baseline/weekly/current shapes are never validated on load. Searches for `CoverageSnapshotStore` / `diffCoverage` / "coverage snapshot" return no issue covering it.
