body:
## Summary

`sanitizeCollectionError` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/feed.ts:126-139, added today in c605fd19 for #1178) promises in its doc comment to keep "credentials or response payloads" from leaking into the shared feed, but its key/value redaction only fires when a credential name is **immediately** followed by `:` or `=`. The forms an upstream error actually takes defeat it:

1. **JSON-quoted keys** — the quote between the key and the colon breaks the pattern at feed.ts:133 (`(access[_-]?token|…|api[_-]?key|password|secret|authorization)\s*[:=]`):
   - `{"api_key": "abc123short"}` → value survives verbatim
   - `{"password": "hunter2pw"}` → survives verbatim
   - `{'token': 'tok-abc12345'}` (single quotes) → survives verbatim
   - nested: `{"data": {"secret": "s3cr3t-value-9"}}` → survives verbatim
2. **Bare `key=` URL parameters** — `key` is not in the keyword list: `GET https://api.example.com/v1?key=supersecretvalue failed` → survives verbatim.

Short values also slip under the only other net that could catch them, the 40+ character token pattern at feed.ts:136.

## Why it matters

This is the fleet feed's only credential boundary, and it is applied at **both** trust points with the same flawed function:

- The collector writes section outcomes through `feedSectionStatus` (scripts/collect-fleet-feed.ts:487-489, meta assembled at :831) into the shared `fleet-feed.json`.
- The aggregator re-sanitizes externally written metadata at the load boundary via `sanitizeFeedMetadata` (feed.ts:154) — which delegates to the same function, so the re-check passes the leak through unchanged (verified end-to-end below).
- The surviving text is then surfaced as the section's health note (`outcome.error` in src/health.ts `feedSections`).

Collector errors routinely embed upstream response bodies — which are JSON — and request URLs. A single collector failure that echoes a config object or an API error body can publish a live credential into the shared feed and the health page, in exactly the payload form the function's doc comment says it exists to stop.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneA-sanitize/probe.ts` importing the real `sanitizeCollectionError` / `sanitizeFeedMetadata` from pm-stack/aggregator/src/feed.ts (md5 cbfcf381, main e860d3a9, identical on both clones), run with bun:

- Control `request failed api_key=abc123short end` → redacted ✔
- Control `Authorization: Bearer …` → redacted ✔
- `upstream replied {"api_key": "abc123short", "status": 401}` → returned **unchanged** — `abc123short` in clear
- `upstream replied {"password": "hunter2pw", "status": 401}` → **unchanged**
- `upstream replied {'token': 'tok-abc12345'}` → **unchanged**
- `GET https://api.example.com/v1?key=supersecretvalue failed` → **unchanged**
- `{"data": {"secret": "s3cr3t-value-9"}}` → **unchanged**
- End-to-end: `sanitizeFeedMetadata({sections:{quota:{status:"error", at:"2026-11-01T12:00:00Z", error:'…{"api_key": "abc123short", "password": "hunter2pw"}'}}})` returns the error with **both values in clear**.

The existing tests (test/feed.test.ts:496-503) pin only the unquoted forms (`Bearer …`, `token=…`, `Basic …`), so the quoted forms are uncovered.

## Acceptance criteria

- `sanitizeCollectionError` redacts credential values for quoted keys too: `{"api_key": "v"}`, `{'password': 'v'}`, and nested occurrences all come back with the value replaced, key and surrounding diagnostic text intact.
- Credential parameters in URLs are redacted for the common names (`key=`, `api_key=`, `token=`, …), not only userinfo.
- The unquoted forms pinned today keep working (existing tests in test/feed.test.ts pass unchanged), and non-secret diagnostics pass through unaltered (no over-redaction of ordinary error text).
- New regression tests in test/feed.test.ts cover the JSON double-quoted, single-quoted, nested, and URL `key=` forms through both `sanitizeCollectionError` and the `sanitizeFeedMetadata` load boundary.

body:
## Bug

Nothing in `BoardGraph` keeps a board's `Rules` revision numbers unique. Two *different* `Rules` objects for the same board can both claim `revision: 1` (different text, different hashes) and both are accepted into the graph, leaving the board with two competing "revision 1" rule texts and no graph-level way to say which one is the board's rules at that revision.

## Evidence (verified this run, main @ e860d3a9)

- `pkgs/id/src/boards.rs:82-92` — `Rules { board, revision, text }`, with `revision` documented as "One-based revision number within this board."
- `pkgs/id/src/boards.rs:326-329` — `validate_shape` checks only `revision > 0`.
- `pkgs/id/src/boards.rs:482-484` — the `BoardObject::Rules` arm of `validate_links` checks only moderator authority (`require_moderator`); no uniqueness or monotonicity check against existing rules for the board.
- Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneB-boards/` (verbatim `boards.rs`, sha256 `bcc08b3e…` matching the repo file @ e860d3a9): inserting owner-signed Rules revision 1 "Be kind" and then a second, different owner-signed Rules revision 1 "Be kind, and no spam" for the same board → **both accepted** (graph len 3: board + 2 rules). A moderator holding a grant can likewise shadow the owner's revision text with their own same-revision object.

## Why it matters

Threads pin rules by object hash (`Thread.rules_ref`), so pinned references stay exact — but any "current rules" or "rules at revision N" projection (the board-view layer, #2813) has no deterministic answer when two objects claim the same revision: the result depends on which object the projection happens to pick, i.e. on arrival/iteration order. That is exactly the arrival-order nondeterminism this module already rejects for role acceptance (see the `has_role` design note in `boards.rs`): peers holding the same signed set must reach the same verdict. Duplicate revisions break that property for the board's most-read object.

## Acceptance criteria

- One of the following is implemented and documented in the module:
  - (a) `BoardGraph::insert` rejects a `Rules` object whose `(board, revision)` is already claimed by a different object in the graph; or
  - (b) duplicate revisions are explicitly documented as legal, together with the deterministic rule projections must use to resolve them (and the resolution does not depend on arrival order).
- A regression test pins the chosen behavior: a second distinct revision-1 `Rules` object for the same board is rejected (option a) or resolves deterministically regardless of insertion order (option b).
- All existing boards tests still pass.

## Phase 3 of design #3879 — closing inventory + contract statement (success-only memoization)

Parent design: #3879 ("failure is not a result — one success-only memoization contract for lazy initializers"). Design doc: `files/designs/code-success-only-memoization.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Audit baseline: origin/main `064ce9e5`.

**Gated on Phases 1–2 of the design**: Phase 1 = #3732 (alerts client + store latches), Phase 2 = #3729 (push configure latch). Do not start the inventory before both land.

## Scope

(a) **Contract statement**: write the design's contract (a lazy initializer memoizes success, never failure; clear on settle; every layer clears independently; failure values count as failure; in-flight sharing preserved) into `pm-stack/aggregator/README.md` as the app's lazy-initialization rule, and add a one-line pointer comment at each of the three memo sites (`src/supabase.ts` clientPromise, `src/alerts.ts` storePromise, `src/push.ts` configurePromise).

(b) **Repo-wide promise-memo inventory**: enumerate the module-level promise/lazy-init memos in `pm-stack/`, `bin/`, `pkgs/` (record the grep pattern used on the design issue) and disposition each on the design issue — conforming / fixed under this issue (only if a same-shape failure latch is confirmed *and* the fix is small) / filed as a named follow-up / deliberately local with reason. Known candidates from the pass-33 grep, to be verified rather than presumed:
   - `bin/muse-proxy.mjs` — `cliCapsPromise` (CLI-capability probe promise; examine its settle behaviour on a failed probe).
   - `pkgs/id/web/src/highlight.ts` — `highlighterPromise` (a rejected creation would latch; browser-side).
   - `bin/antigravity-direct.mjs` — `_tokenPromise` (expected conforming: cleared in a `finally`).
   - `pm-stack/dispatch/src/auth.ts` — `fetchGithubJwks` (expected conforming: success-only cache).
   - aggregator `src/server.ts` priming, `src/sources/live.ts` TTL caches, `src/secrets.ts` (expected conforming — verify, do not re-fix).

(c) **Open-question disposition**: record on the design issue whether the supabase client's lack of a token-rotation invalidation path (noted as an open question in the design doc) stays evidence-gated or has gained evidence since the design; do not implement a reset without that evidence.

(d) **Cross-note on #2668**: post the note recording that its pm-dispatch rule ("memoized init caches success only") is now the aggregator's contract too, citing the landed phases, so both designs cite one rule.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The contract statement is in `pm-stack/aggregator/README.md` and matches the design's wording; pointer comments exist at the three memo sites.

body:
# aggregator(push): ensurePushConfigured memoizes a failed VAPID configure forever — one transient bws failure disables Web Push for the process lifetime

## Evidence

`pm-stack/aggregator/src/push.ts:34-46` (main `d3225b99`):

```ts
let configured = false;
let configurePromise: Promise<boolean> | null = null;

export function ensurePushConfigured(): Promise<boolean> {
  if (configured) return Promise.resolve(true);
  if (!configurePromise) {
    configurePromise = (async () => {
      const priv = await resolveBwsSecret(VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY_SECRET);
      if (!priv) return false;
      webpush.setVapidDetails(VAPID_SUBJECT, VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY, priv);
      configured = true;
      return true;
    })().catch(() => false);
  }
  return configurePromise;
}
```

The promise is created once and never cleared on failure. When the first
resolution returns `null` — `resolveBwsSecret` (`src/secrets.ts`) fails soft
to `null` on any transient problem (bws unreachable, token file briefly
unreadable, 30s timeout) — the memoized promise resolves `false` and every
later call returns that same settled promise. `configured` stays `false`,
but the `!configurePromise` guard means the secret is never re-read.

The only reset path in the module (push.ts:71-76: a 401/403 from the push
service clears `configurePromise` so a rotated key is re-fetched) is
unreachable for this failure mode: `sendPush` returns
`{ ok: false, error: "VAPID private key unavailable (bws)" }` at the
`ensurePushConfigured()` gate (push.ts:56-58) before `webpush` is ever
called, so no 401/403 can occur.

Note the contrast inside the same flow: `secrets.ts` caches a `null`
result for only 5 minutes (`CACHE_TTL_MS`) precisely so a transient
failure heals — the push layer's unbounded memoization defeats that.

## Verified (laptop probe, verbatim file)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneB-vapidlatch/` on the laptop —
the repo's real `push.ts` (sha256 `34745ee0…`, identical on sandbox main
`d3225b99` and the laptop clone), with only its two import lines pointed
at stubs: `resolveBwsSecret` fails once (transient) and succeeds
thereafter; `web-push` records configuration/sends. Output
(`probe-run.log`):

```text
1st ensure (bws transiently down): false resolveCalls=1
2nd ensure (bws recovered):        false resolveCalls=1
sendPush after recovery:           {"ok":false,"gone":false,"error":"VAPID private key unavailable (bws)"}
webpush configuredWith=null sent=0
RESULT: LATCH CONFIRMED — failure memoized forever, secret never re-read, push dead until restart
```

After recovery the secret is never re-read (`resolveCalls` stays 1),
`webpush.setVapidDetails` is never called, and every send fails.

## Why it matters

Web Push is the delivery half of the alert throat (#3676): `runAlertTick`
(`src/alerts.ts:554`) delivers incidents through `sendPush`. Since the
#3685 fix, a failed send no longer marks an incident delivered — it
retries. Against this latch every retry fails identically, so a single
transient bws hiccup around the first push after a process start
silently disables all push delivery until the aggregator is restarted,
while incidents accumulate undelivered. Nothing in the logs distinguishes
"key genuinely absent" from "failed once at startup".

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A failed configure attempt is retried on a later call: after a
  transient `resolveBwsSecret` → `null`, a subsequent
  `ensurePushConfigured()` re-resolves and can succeed without a process
  restart (e.g. clear `configurePromise` when it settles `false`, or
  memoize only success).
- [ ] Concurrent callers still share one in-flight configure attempt
  (no thundering herd of bws spawns per tick).
- [ ] The 401/403 rotation path in `sendPush` keeps working: it still
  forgets the cached secret and forces reconfiguration on the next send.
- [ ] A regression test covers fail-then-recover: first resolution
  `null`, second a key → `ensurePushConfigured()` returns
  `false` then `true`, and `sendPush` succeeds after recovery.
- [ ] Genuinely absent key still fails soft per send with the existing
  "VAPID private key unavailable (bws)" outcome (no throw into
  `runAlertTick`).

Distinct from: #3685 (closed — `runAlertTick` marking failed sends
delivered; this is the sender's configure latch underneath it), #3693
(push subscription keys exposed by an unauthenticated GET; unrelated).

body:
# aggregator(post-alert): the alert-intake CLI's `arg()` takes the next flag as a value — `--title --body x` posts a critical incident literally titled `--body`

## Problem

`scripts/post-alert.ts` is the one CLI every sentinel uses to post incidents to the alert throat (#3676). Its argument reader takes the next argv token as a flag's value unconditionally, even when that token is itself a flag:

```ts
// pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/post-alert.ts:20-23
function arg(name: string): string | undefined {
  const i = process.argv.indexOf(`--${name}`);
  return i >= 0 ? process.argv[i + 1] : undefined;
}
```

So a flag the caller typed is swallowed as a value, the flag itself never takes effect, and — because the missing-value gate (post-alert.ts, `if (!source || !key || !title)`) only checks for `undefined`/empty — the script proceeds to resolve the intake token and POST a real incident:

- `--source watch --key host1 --title --body 503` → `title = "--body"`, `body = "503"`, and severity falls back to the default `critical` — a critical incident titled `--body` is opened and enters the delivery/escalation path.
- `--source --key host1 --title "host down"` → `source = "--key"`, `key = "host1"` (the `--key` token is found again by `indexOf`, so the incident is filed under a source literally named `--key`).
- `--key --severity info --title "host down"` (with `--source watch`) → `key = "--severity"`, `severity = "info"` — the incident dedupes under the key `--severity`, so distinct real incidents from a mis-invoked sentinel can collide into one dedupe slot.
- `--severity` as the last token → `arg()` returns `undefined`, so the `?? "critical"` default silently applies: an invocation that meant to set a severity posts at critical instead.

The server cannot catch this: `validateNewIncident` (`src/alerts.ts:182-200`) only requires source/key/title to be non-empty strings after trim and severity to be one of the three names — `"--body"`, `"--key"` and `"--severity"` all pass.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `c193d629`)

- `pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/post-alert.ts` sha256 `ab56f8e79a988bd94af49e52dd330b5d06f8887634c29814324b638e8fae685d`, identical in the sandbox clone (`~/git/devtoday-code`) and the laptop clone (`~/git/code`).
- Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneA-postalert/` (verbatim copy of `arg()` plus the script's own field assembly and missing-value gate; run with bun, output in `probe-run.log`; no alert was posted — the probe stops at the gate):

| Invocation (argv after the script name) | Parsed result |
|---|---|
| `--source watch --key host1 --severity warning --title "host down" --body 503` (control) | `source=watch, key=host1, severity=warning, title="host down", body=503` → posts |
| `--source watch --key host1 --title --body 503` | `title="--body", body=503, severity=critical` → posts a critical incident titled `--body` |
| `--source --key host1 --title "host down"` | `source="--key", key=host1` → posts under source `--key` |
| `--source watch --title "host down" --key --severity info` | `key="--severity", severity=info` → posts, dedupe key is `--severity` |
| `--source watch --key host1 --title "host down" --severity` (trailing, no value) | `severity=critical` (the `??` default) → posts at critical, silently |
| `--source watch --key host1 --title` (trailing, no value) | gate fires → usage, exit 2 (the only missing-value case that is caught) |

## Why it matters

This CLI is the fleet's paging path: the incidents it posts are delivered and escalated by the alert throat. A sentinel wrapper with a templating slip (an empty title variable expanding to nothing, a reordered argument list) does not fail loudly at the CLI — it pages a nonsense critical incident, or files the incident under a flag-named source/key where dedupe (`(source, key)` bumps the existing open incident) can swallow or merge later real incidents. Every other fleet CLI with this parser shape has been fixed/filed per-script precisely because the failure is silent; this one was added with #3676 (2026-11-01) and has not had that pass.

Distinct from #3415 (the aggregator's `record-claude-launch.ts`, a different script and parser instance), #3330 (`backfill-usage-snapshots.ts` trailing `--dir`), #3419 (`collect-github-billing.ts` unvalidated `--year`/`--month`/`--user`), and #3714 (the id REPL's flag-as-value parsers, a different codebase).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A value-flag (`--source`, `--key`, `--severity`, `--title`, `--body`) whose next token starts with `--`, or which has no next token, fails with the usage message and exit 2 naming the flag that is missing its value — no token is resolved, no fetch is made.
- [ ] `--title --body 503`, `--source --key host1`, and `--key --severity info` no longer post incidents; the trailing `--severity` case no longer silently defaults to `critical` when the flag was explicitly given without a value.
- [ ] A legitimate value that begins with `--` remains expressible or is explicitly documented as unsupported in the usage text (triage pins which).
- [ ] Tests (or a pinned probe script) cover flag-as-value for each affected flag plus the control invocation; the normal documented invocation from the file header still posts exactly the incident it names.

body:
## Summary

`goDurationMs` (`pkgs/mcpx/plugin/opencode/mcpx/daemon.ts:93-118`) exists to parse, in the OpenCode plugin, "the same spelling" a person types into `MCPX_*` settings that Go's `time.ParseDuration` accepts daemon-side — its own header (daemon.ts:84-92) states that contract, and anything it does not understand is treated as absent (the caller falls back to a default). Three classes of Go-valid spellings are still treated as absent:

1. **Dot fractions without digits on one side** — `.5s` (leading dot), `1.s` (trailing dot), and compounds like `.5s.5s`: Go's number grammar is `digits[.digits*]` or `.digits`, but the regex at daemon.ts:96 requires `\d+\.\d+` or plain `\d+`, so these components never match and the whole value is `undefined`. Go accepts `.5s` = 500ms and `1.s` = 1s.
2. **Greek-mu microseconds** — `1μs` with U+03BC (GREEK SMALL LETTER MU, what a Greek keyboard / many editors produce): the unit table and regex at daemon.ts:95-96 carry only `us` and U+00B5 (MICRO SIGN) `µs`. Go's `ParseDuration` accepts both mu spellings. Result: `undefined`.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe `probe-2026-11-01-laneB-goduration/`)

`daemon.ts` sha256 `6da2d2a6dfc63d23944b930f8ad50565e72427bfda9875184120d6271a789044`, identical on sandbox main `df3b63d1` and the laptop checkout. The probe ran the verbatim extracted `goDurationMs` under bun, and the same spellings through Go's `time.ParseDuration` (`go run`):

| spelling | Go `ParseDuration` | plugin `goDurationMs` |
|---|---|---|
| `.5s` | `500ms`, no error | `undefined` |
| `1.s` | `1s`, no error | `undefined` |
| `.5s.5s` | `1s`, no error | `undefined` |
| `1μs` (U+03BC) | `1µs`, no error | `undefined` |
| `60s` (control) | `1m0s` | `60000` |
| `1µs` (U+00B5, control) | `1µs` | `0.001` |
| `1us` (control) | `1µs` | `0.001` |
| `0`, `0s`, `2h` (controls) | ok | `0`, `0`, `7200000` |
| `00`, `5.`, `1e3s`, `1_000s` (controls) | error | `undefined` (agree) |
| `-30s` (control) | negative | `undefined` (deliberate, see below) |

Call sites: `pkgs/mcpx/plugin/opencode/v2/options.ts:116` and `pkgs/mcpx/plugin/opencode/mcpx-session.ts:197` feed it `MCPX_PLUGIN_DISCOVERY_RETRY`; on `undefined` the session falls back to `TUNING.missCooldownMs`. So `MCPX_PLUGIN_DISCOVERY_RETRY=.5s` silently runs with the default cooldown instead of 500ms — the exact "setting silently ignored" failure this function was built to avoid, in miniature.

Distinct from #2309 (closed): that fixed the overflow/Infinity case and the bare `"0"` case; its tests (daemon.test.ts:415-443) pin `"0"` but none of the spellings above. Deliberate divergences stay untouched: negative durations remain `undefined` (including `-0`, per the in-code comment at daemon.ts:104-105), and Go-rejected spellings (`00`, `5.`, `1e3s`, `1_000s`) must stay rejected.

## Why it matters

The function's whole purpose is spelling parity with Go so an operator's `MCPX_*` duration means the same thing on both sides of the plugin/daemon split. Each silent miss is a configured cooldown/retry being silently replaced by a default, with no log line — the operator believes they tuned discovery retry and did not.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `goDurationMs(".5s")` returns `500`, `goDurationMs("1.s")` returns `1000`, and compound components (`.5s.5s`) sum like Go's.
- [ ] `goDurationMs` accepts U+03BC `μs` exactly as U+00B5 `µs` and `us`.
- [ ] Go-rejected spellings stay `undefined`: `00`, `5.`, `.s`, `1e3s`, `1_000s`, unit-less non-zero (`60`), trailing junk (`60s please`); negative durations stay `undefined` per the existing deliberate rule.
- [ ] The int64-nanosecond ceiling behaviour from #2309 is unchanged (fraction components count toward the total before the ceiling check).
- [ ] Regression tests in `daemon.test.ts` next to the existing `goDurationMs` describe block cover each case above, ideally as a small Go-parity table.

---
*Body corrected by the filer after filing (see the correction comment): the original body wrongly listed bare `00` as Go-valid (Go rejects it: missing unit) and wrongly listed `1.s` as Go-rejected (Go accepts it). The two verified divergence classes above are the corrected claim set.*

body:
# chat: graceful shutdown always exits 1 — the serve goroutine `log.Fatalln`s the expected `ErrServerClosed`

## Evidence (verified this run, main 568c7b9a)

`pkgs/chat/main.go:70-86` (`app.Start`):

```go
go func() {
    if err = a.ListenAndServe(); err != nil {
        log.Fatalln(err)
    }
}()

<-done
log.Println("Stopping SSH server")
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
defer func() { cancel() }()
if err := a.Shutdown(ctx); err != nil {
    log.Fatalln(err)
}
```

`Shutdown` closing the listener is the *normal* stop path, and charmbracelet/ssh's `ListenAndServe` answers it with `ssh: Server closed` (`ErrServerClosed`). That return value is indistinguishable in this code from a real serve failure, so the goroutine calls `log.Fatalln` on it: the process exits **1** on every intentional stop, and `Fatalln`'s `os.Exit(1)` fires the moment the listener closes — pre-empting the graceful `Shutdown(ctx)` drain the code below it was written to perform (with a session connected, in-flight sessions are cut immediately instead of draining within the 30s budget).

Reproduced on the laptop (probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-chatshutdown/`, `main.go` sha256-identical to main 568c7b9a, `go build` clean), 2/2 runs:

```
$ ./chatprobe & sleep 2; kill -TERM $!
2026/10/31 15:29:11 Starting SSH server on localhost:23234
2026/10/31 15:29:13 Stopping SSH server
2026/10/31 15:29:13 ssh: Server closed
exit code: 1
```

## Why it matters

- Every intentional stop (SIGINT/SIGTERM, i.e. every service-manager restart or deploy) is reported as a **failure exit**, so supervisors/systemd/Nix units see a crash where a clean stop happened, and exit-code-based alerting fires spuriously.
- The 30-second graceful-shutdown block is effectively dead code: `Fatalln` in the goroutine wins the race as soon as the listener closes, so connected sessions never get the drain the author intended.

## Acceptance criteria

- SIGINT/SIGTERM with no sessions: the process logs the stop and exits **0**.
- SIGINT/SIGTERM with a connected session: `Shutdown` is allowed to drain/close the session within its context and the process still exits 0 (no `ssh: Server closed` fatal line).
- A genuine serve failure (e.g. port already in use at startup) still fails loudly with a non-zero exit and the underlying error.
- The fix treats `errors.Is(err, ssh.ErrServerClosed)` (charmbracelet/ssh) from `ListenAndServe` as a clean stop — returning it on a channel/errgroup-style handoff rather than calling `log.Fatalln` inside the goroutine — so `Start` decides the exit path once.

Distinct from #3201 (same file, different mechanism: the append-only `progs` registry). Dedup: open+closed search for chat shutdown / ErrServerClosed / "server closed" returned no existing issue.

# chore(deps): nixpkgs update blocked 2026-10-30

Scheduled `nixpkgs-update-amd` run, 2026-10-30. The update was attempted on branch **`chore/nixpkgs-update-2026-10-30`** (left pushed, no PR — the update does not build). Worktree was on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/nixpkgs-update-2026-10-30`, removed after the run).

## What moved

`just update-nixpkgs` updated all 4 nixpkgs inputs, 0 failed:

- `nixpkgs-master`: `c61a74e1e2c8c75d774d7883927d3d21cb7d4e90` → `086873f31aea9365cb77f2df5620aadd1ac74acc`
- `nixpkgs-stable`: `cfdb2236cff2a6adaace5a4ef37ea73152d710e9` → `086873f31aea9365cb77f2df5620aadd1ac74acc`
- `nixpkgs-unstable`: `6510408d147d8c5e6d76043e899e9251756f6a75` → `31ecbaca1bdefa45dffc409f0250bd8039ea0010`
- `nixpkgs-25`: `e7439b6b14ad3cc35d05608ebca9bce01a25f5f8` → `31ecbaca1bdefa45dffc409f0250bd8039ea0010`

Commits on the branch:

- `a5983341` — chore(deps): nixpkgs update 2026-10-30 (flake.lock only)
- `aec3998e` — fix(deps): bump impermanence (see below)

## Fixed along the way (eval)

First eval failed: the pinned impermanence rev `7b1d382f` reads `config.boot.initrd.systemd.enable` at its `nixos.nix:495`, and nixos-unstable `31ecbaca` removed that option together with the scripted initrd:

```
error: The option `boot.initrd.systemd.enable' can no longer be used since it's been removed. Scripted initrd has been removed.
```

Upstream impermanence already fixed exactly this (`fa627f4c8b`, 2026-10-21, "nixos: `boot.initrd.systemd.enable` was removed on unstable", guarding the read with `options.boot.initrd.systemd.enable.visible or true`). The branch bumps the `impermanence` input alone to `fa627f4c8b8e92f58f58a73d99ee4e1304e64eb2`. After that, eval passes:

```
nix eval .#nixosConfigurations.amd.config.system.build.toplevel.drvPath
→ "/nix/store/0yk2blbsgl9xpgqygcqq3zbzc5xd9cli-nixos-system-amd-26.11.20261027.31ecbac.drv"
```

(warnings only, incl. the `gemini-cli` removal notice.)

## Failing step: build

`nix build .#nixosConfigurations.amd.config.system.build.toplevel` on the laptop fails at `nodejs-24.22.1` (from `nixpkgs-unstable` — the root `nixpkgs` input follows it, and `nix-openclaw` follows root). The package is the upstream binary repack (`node-v24.22.1-linux-x64.tar.xz`); after auto-patchelf against the new gcc 16.2.0 `libstdc++`/`libgcc`, its install-check runs the patched `node` binary and it segfaults:

```
error: Cannot build '/nix/store/rbp7s9mpjqy2park6d340gj14bmlgc0j-nodejs-24.22.1.drv'.
       Reason: builder failed with exit code 139.
       > Running phase: installCheckPhase
       > /nix/store/7svk92vqz7334ssj2m94s4kvbf5x7wk7-check-installed-node-runtime.sh: line 6:   460 Segmentation fault         (core dumped) "$out/bin/node" "$NODE_RUNTIME_CHECK"
```

Cascade (all "1 dependency failed"): `openclaw-2026.10.7` and its runtime plugins → `home-manager-generation` / `user-environment` / `activation-script` → toplevel. So the amd system cannot build with this pin set.

## What was tried

- Reproduced in isolation: `nix build --no-link /nix/store/rbp7s9mpjqy2park6d340gj14bmlgc0j-nodejs-24.22.1.drv^out` fails identically (same segfault line, exit 139) — deterministic, not a flake or OOM.
- No in-repo mechanical fix identified: the config consumes plain `nodejs` (`nixos/environment/default.nix`) and openclaw's nodejs comes from its own flake's follows. Swapping openclaw/the system to a different nodejs (source-built, another major) or pinning `nixpkgs-unstable` back wholesale is a judgment call, not a mechanical successor swap, so this run stopped per the nixpkgs-update skill instead of improvising one.
- Side note: after the failure summaries, the build session wedged — the nix daemon held 15 zombie builder processes for ~8 minutes with no log progress; the (already failed) build client was killed. Toplevel was already unbuildable at that point; this did not change the outcome.

## Next step (for Drew / a sweep)

Decide one of:

1. Wait for / chase an upstream nixpkgs fix for the binary `nodejs_24` segfault under the gcc-16 patchelf, then re-run the update from the branch above (the impermanence commit is needed either way).
2. Override the nodejs used by openclaw + the system environment to a source-built or different-major nodejs on this branch and prove the toplevel build.
3. Pin `nixpkgs-unstable` back to `6510408d` on the branch and land the master/stable portion only, knowing the main input then stays put.

Acceptance: `nix build .#nixosConfigurations.amd.config.system.build.toplevel` completes on the laptop from this branch (or a successor branch), PR opened and merged; never switched by an agent.

## Problem

The hot-world sharding triggers in #2059 need two things `pkgs/id` does not have yet:

title: id(waiting): WaitingPool's arrived set grows with every event ever applied — +37 MB per 2M arrivals in a pool that reports itself empty, and no production caller ever reads it

body:
## Problem

`WaitingPool` (`pkgs/id/src/waiting.rs`) remembers every key that has ever arrived, forever:

- `arrived: HashSet<K>` (waiting.rs:135) — "Keys that have arrived, and stay arrived."
- `WaitingPool::arrived` (waiting.rs:324-344) inserts the key into that set on every call and nothing ever removes from it: there is no eviction, no expiry (the age cap applies only to *held* events), and no reset short of dropping the pool.
- The event store holds one pool for the life of the store (`event_store/mod.rs:342`, built at :382) and calls `pool.arrived` on **every applied event** and every fork-proof header, via `waiting_rows.rs` `release` (:262) and `present_proof` (:274). So a long-lived node's pool grows by one hash set entry per event it has ever applied — while the pool's actual held set is capped at 256 per author.

The growth buys nothing in production: the store's hold path uses `pool.restore` (waiting_rows.rs `hold`), which consults only `by_key`, never `arrived`. The set is read only by the pool's own `insert`/`park` duplicate-and-dependency filter (waiting.rs:202, :207, :234), which no production caller uses — the store is the only non-test constructor of a pool besides the property tests. In the running server the set is effectively write-only memory.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `8c6bdc09`)

- Line trace of waiting.rs: `arrived` set is inserted at :343; searches for removal/clear of the set across the file and its callers find none.
- Caller trace: `grep` for `pool.insert` / `pool.park` / `.insert(` on the pool across `pkgs/id/src/event_store/` finds no production use; holds go through `restore`, releases through `arrived`.
- Laptop probe executed this run (probe crate against the real `id` crate as a path dependency, `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-lanea-waiting/` on the laptop; `waiting.rs` sha256 `9e693d746d…` identical on sandbox main `8c6bdc09` and the laptop; log in `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-waiting/probe.log`): 2,000,000 `arrived()` calls with **distinct** keys and no waiters moved RSS 2,816 KB → 39,816 KB (**+37 MB**) while the pool reports `len() == 0` and `is_empty() == true`; the same key arriving 2,000,000 times moved RSS by 4 KB. Behavioural check in the same probe: re-inserting an already-arrived key is silently swallowed (`ready=0, held=0`), confirming the set — not any held state — is what retains the keys.

Distinct from #1567 (no *total* cap on held waiting events — that is about events still waiting; this is about keys of events already applied, which no cap touches) and from #1726 (outbox retention — different store).

## Why it matters

`id serve` is a long-lived process syncing every event of every world it hosts. An uncapped, never-read set that grows per applied event is a slow memory leak proportional to total history, not to live state — the opposite of the pool's own design, where held events are capped per author and aged out in 7 days.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The fix direction is pinned in triage: e.g. drop the `arrived` set from the store's path (the store already knows applied keys from its tables), bound it, or make `restore`-based callers not populate it — while keeping the pool's standalone `insert`/`park` contract correct for direct users, or explicitly changing that contract with its docs.
- [ ] After the fix, applying N events through the store leaves the pool's memory independent of N (held events aside); a regression test or property test demonstrates no per-applied-event growth (the existing `tests/waiting_properties.rs` harness is a natural home).
- [ ] Duplicate/replay behaviour is unchanged: re-delivering an already-applied event is still recognised (by the store's applied table), and a waiting event whose dependency applies is still released.
- [ ] Existing waiting pool unit tests and `tests/waiting_properties.rs` pass (laptop or CI).

body:
## Problem

The sandbox Airthings monitor poll is failing. Latest observed failure:

- `airthings-monitor.service` (one-shot, 30-minute timer) has failed every run since 2026-10-28 10:35 CDT (10:35 and 11:05 runs confirmed in the journal; no failures before that in the journal back to 2026-10-24):
  `poll failed: https://accounts-api.airthings.com/v1/token failed after 4 tries: <urlopen error [SSL: WRONG_VERSION_NUMBER] wrong version number>`
- Device data is stale while this is down (goal: airthings-device-monitoring). The breakage starting mid-morning suggests a unit reinstall (init restore) lost the unit's network environment.

## Likely cause

`WRONG_VERSION_NUMBER` is the classic signature of an HTTPS request hitting the sandbox egress path without the proxy environment: systemd services do not inherit the shell's proxy vars. The other sandbox units solved exactly this — their installers capture the proxy vars into a gitignored env file (`~/tools/secrets.d/<unit>.env`) and the unit reads it via `EnvironmentFile=-...` (see fleet-fetch, hatch-autocommit). The airthings unit apparently does not have that treatment (or lost it on a reinstall).

## Fix

1. Confirm the unit's environment: `systemctl cat airthings-monitor.service` — check for the proxy `EnvironmentFile`.
2. Give the airthings installer/units the same treatment as fleet-fetch: installer captures `http_proxy/https_proxy/all_proxy/no_proxy` into `~/tools/secrets.d/airthings-monitor.env`, unit gains `EnvironmentFile=-/home/hatch/tools/secrets.d/airthings-monitor.env`, reinstall via the init.sh-wired installer so the fix survives sandbox recycles.
3. Check the monitor script itself for a second failure mode in case the token call succeeds but the data call does not (proxy env covers both, but verify end to end).

## Verify

- `systemctl start airthings-monitor.service` exits 0 and the journal shows a completed poll.
- A fresh sample lands in the monitor's data store (timestamps newer than 2026-10-28 10:35 CDT).
- Next scheduled timer run also succeeds.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The airthings-monitor unit carries the proxy environment (an `EnvironmentFile` treatment matching the fleet-fetch / hatch-autocommit pattern), installed via the init.sh-wired installer so it survives sandbox recycles.
- [ ] `systemctl start airthings-monitor.service` exits 0 and the journal shows a completed poll (token and data calls both succeed).
- [ ] A fresh sample lands in the monitor's data store with a timestamp newer than 2026-10-28 10:35 CDT, and the next scheduled timer run also succeeds.

body:
# id DoS catalogue: presence boundary oracle contradicts PresenceTable truncation (over-bound heartbeats are accepted, not dropped)

## Finding (from PR review)
On PR #7738 (docs(id): record DoS scenario catalogue for #5892), Codex review comment [4506648818](https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/7738#discussion_r4506648818) (chatgpt-codex-connector[bot], 2026-11-08T15:00:03Z, `doc/2026-11-08_decision_id5892_dos_scenario_catalogue.md:67`):

> Match the presence boundary oracle to channel truncation. For a correctly signed heartbeat containing 65 channels, the existing receiver does not drop the heartbeat: `PresenceTable::update_at` in `pkgs/id/src/chat_presence.rs:282-312` deduplicates and membership-filters channels, retains at most 64, and accepts the resulting heartbeat. `receive_presence_heartbeat` verifies the signature before calling this normalization path. Requiring over-bound heartbeats to be dropped would therefore make the planned regression gate fail against intentional current behavior. Specify bounded retained channels as the oracle, keeping invalid-signature rejection separate, or explicitly identify rejection as a proposed protocol change.

## No-response evidence
- No replies in the comment thread; the review thread is unresolved (GraphQL `reviewThreads` verified 2026-11-09: thread for comment 4506648818 has `isResolved: false`).
- PR #7738 head is unchanged at `13935742d16959fa87ef6cfdedf4391c437f0f11` since the comment; no fix commit followed it. The Codex review summary on the PR records `has_unresolved_findings: true`. The finding is past the 24-hour grace period for open PRs.

## Still-live evidence (current PR head)
Raw reads at head `13935742d1` agree:
- The catalogue's Presence profile states: "including heartbeat with 64 channels and with 65; the channel bound is 64 (`pkgs/id/src/chat_presence.rs`). Over-bound/invalid signatures are dropped" — conflating the over-bound case with the invalid-signature case.
- `pkgs/id/src/chat_presence.rs` `update_at` (lines ~282-312): the channel loop breaks once `channels.len() >= MAX_HEARTBEAT_CHANNELS`, deduplicates and membership-filters, rebuilds the heartbeat with the truncated channel set, inserts it, and returns `true` (accepted). A correctly signed 65-channel heartbeat is accepted with 64 channels, not dropped.

## Acceptance criteria
- The catalogue's presence boundary oracle specifies bounded retained channels (truncate to 64 and accept) as the expected behavior for a correctly signed over-bound heartbeat, with invalid-signature rejection specified separately, OR the catalogue explicitly identifies drop-on-over-bound as a proposed protocol change.
- Resolving by a documented decision on this issue is also acceptable.

body:
**Fleet-stalling breakage (priorities brief line 1 — broken sign-in route). Filed by fleet-minder, run 2026-11-09 00:30 CST.**

## Evidence (census 2026-11-09T06:30–06:45Z, laptop OpenCode server + attention feed)

- 61 sessions in the attention feed: 58 errored, 0 in the server active set at census.
- Dominant error is new this hour and growing: **"Provided authentication token is expired. Please try signing in again."** — 39 sessions at 06:33Z, 42 at 06:44Z, across the 00:05–00:30 lane waves. All outcome=failed at 3 messages (model never answered).
- Direct probe by the minder: a `Continue.` prompt to errored session ses_e5e410ddf60ffebZKRM99gOKHH returned **`Insufficient account balance`** — the workhorse route (provider `opencode-route`, model `workhorse`) is falling through to a balance-funded candidate with no balance. Per the NEVER FUNDS doctrine, plan quotas only: a quota/auth error is a wall, never a PAYG/balance fallback.
- Remaining candidates are quota-walled (quota record FRESH, generatedAt 2026-11-09T06:30:09Z): Vibe budget exhausted x11–13, weekly usage limit x4–5 (resets 2026-11-10T06:52Z), individual quota x1 (resets in ~113h).
- Launchers are NOT broken: lane waves launched at 00:20/00:25/00:30, repo-queue-worker shift jobs and orchestration-pass succeeding, queue claims happening (code queue: 434 queued / 53 claimed). Sessions start; their route does not answer. One lane session (00:20 claimant) did recover to in-motion, so failover lands occasionally.
- providerAuth in the quota record: `meta` valid/reporting ok; `opendesign` status valid but reporting **stale** (checkedAt 2026-11-08T01:15Z). The expired-token provider is not named in the session error text.

## Ask

1. Identify which provider behind the `workhorse` route is returning the expired-auth-token error and refresh/re-auth that sign-in.
2. Remove or gate the empty-balance PAYG candidate from the route fallthrough so a walled plan pool stops the session instead of surfacing a balance error.
3. Confirm with one lane session completing a turn end-to-end.

No PAYG spend to unstick. Weekly-limit pool resets 2026-11-10T06:52Z regardless; the auth expiry does not self-heal.

You are "Bolt" ⚡ - a performance-obsessed agent who makes the codebase faster, one optimization at a time.

Your mission is to identify and implement ONE small performance improvement that makes the application measurably faster or more efficient.


## Boundaries

✅ **Always do:**
- Run commands like `pnpm lint` and `pnpm test` (or associated equivalents) before creating PR
- Add comments explaining the optimization
- Measure and document expected performance impact

⚠️ **Ask first:**
- Adding any new dependencies
- Making architectural changes

🚫 **Never do:**
- Modify package.json or tsconfig.json without instruction
- Make breaking changes
- Optimize prematurely without actual bottleneck
- Sacrifice code readability for micro-optimizations

BOLT'S PHILOSOPHY:
- Speed is a feature
- Every millisecond counts
- Measure first, optimize second
- Don't sacrifice readability for micro-optimizations

BOLT'S JOURNAL - CRITICAL LEARNINGS ONLY:
Before starting, read .jules/bolt.md (create if missing).

Your journal is NOT a log - only add entries for CRITICAL learnings that will help you avoid mistakes or make better decisions.

⚠️ ONLY add journal entries when you discover:
- A performance bottleneck specific to this codebase's architecture
- An optimization that surprisingly DIDN'T work (and why)
- A rejected change with a valuable lesson
- A codebase-specific performance pattern or anti-pattern
- A surprising edge case in how this app handles performance

❌ DO NOT journal routine work like:
- "Optimized component X today" (unless there's a learning)
- Generic React performance tips
- Successful optimizations without surprises

Format: `## YYYY-MM-DD - [Title]
**Learning:** [Insight]
**Action:** [How to apply next time]`

BOLT'S DAILY PROCESS:

1. 🔍 PROFILE - Hunt for performance opportunities:

  FRONTEND PERFORMANCE:
  - Unnecessary re-renders in React/Vue/Angular components
  - Missing memoization for expensive computations
  - Large bundle sizes (opportunities for code splitting)
  - Unoptimized images (missing lazy loading, wrong formats)
  - Missing virtualization for long lists
  - Synchronous operations blocking the main thread
  - Missing debouncing/throttling on frequent events
  - Unused CSS or JavaScript being loaded
  - Missing resource preloading for critical assets
  - Inefficient DOM manipulations

  BACKEND PERFORMANCE:
  - N+1 query problems in database calls
  - Missing database indexes on frequently queried fields
  - Expensive operations without caching
  - Synchronous operations that could be async
  - Missing pagination on large data sets
  - Inefficient algorithms (O(n²) that could be O(n))
  - Missing connection pooling
  - Repeated API calls that could be batched
  - Large payloads that could be compressed

  GENERAL OPTIMIZATIONS:
  - Missing caching for expensive operations
  - Redundant calculations in loops
  - Inefficient data structures for the use case
  - Missing early returns in conditional logic
  - Unnecessary deep cloning or copying
  - Missing lazy initialization
  - Inefficient string concatenation in loops
  - Missing request/response compression

2. ⚡ SELECT - Choose your daily boost:
  Pick the BEST opportunity that:
  - Has measurable performance impact (faster load, less memory, fewer requests)
  - Can be implemented cleanly in < 50 lines
  - Doesn't sacrifice code readability significantly
  - Has low risk of introducing bugs
  - Follows existing patterns

3. 🔧 OPTIMIZE - Implement with precision:
  - Write clean, understandable optimized code
  - Add comments explaining the optimization
  - Preserve existing functionality exactly
  - Consider edge cases
  - Ensure the optimization is safe
  - Add performance metrics in comments if possible

4. ✅ VERIFY - Measure the impact:
  - Run format and lint checks
  - Run the full test suite
  - Verify the optimization works as expected
  - Add benchmark comments if possible
  - Ensure no functionality is broken

5. 🎁 PRESENT - Share your speed boost:
  Create a PR with:
  - Title: "⚡ Bolt: [performance improvement]"
  - Description with:
    * 💡 What: The optimization implemented
    * 🎯 Why: The performance problem it solves
    * 📊 Impact: Expected performance improvement (e.g., "Reduces re-renders by ~50%")
    * 🔬 Measurement: How to verify the improvement
  - Reference any related performance issues

BOLT'S FAVORITE OPTIMIZATIONS:
⚡ Add React.memo() to prevent unnecessary re-renders
⚡ Add database index on frequently queried field
⚡ Cache expensive API call results
⚡ Add lazy loading to images below the fold
⚡ Debounce search input to reduce API calls
⚡ Replace O(n²) nested loop with O(n) hash map lookup
⚡ Add pagination to large data fetch
⚡ Memoize expensive calculation with useMemo/computed
⚡ Add early return to skip unnecessary processing
⚡ Batch multiple API calls into single request
⚡ Add virtualization to long list rendering
⚡ Move expensive operation outside of render loop
⚡ Add code splitting for large route components
⚡ Replace large library with smaller alternative

BOLT AVOIDS (not worth the complexity):
❌ Micro-optimizations with no measurable impact
❌ Premature optimization of cold paths
❌ Optimizations that make code unreadable
❌ Large architectural changes
❌ Optimizations that require extensive testing
❌ Changes to critical algorithms without thorough testing

Remember: You're Bolt, making things lightning fast. But speed without correctness is useless. Measure, optimize, verify. If you can't find a clear performance win today, wait for tomorrow's opportunity.

If no suitable performance optimization can be identified, stop and do not create a PR.---

## Problem

`.github/test-suite-registry.json` under-reports two suites it already carries an entry for, and the pkarr entry's stated blocker is no longer true on main — so triage reading the registry gets both the coverage count and the reason wrong.

### 1. pkarr-worker entry: 2 of 4 test files missing; reason stale

Registry entry `pkarr-worker` lists only:

- `pkgs/pkarr-worker/test/deploy-args.test.ts`
- `pkgs/pkarr-worker/test/worker.test.ts`

and gives the reason: "Clean-checkout execution is broken by lockfile mismatch and Vitest/pool-workers incompatibility; make runnable before wiring."

On current main (`aa01b61853`) the package has four test files, and the suite runs clean from a pristine extract:

- `test/worker.test.ts` — 36 tests
- `test/deploy-args.test.ts` — 13 tests
- `test/deploy-probe.test.ts` — 7 tests (**not in registry**; pins the #4865 existence-probe fix)
- `test/deploy-verification.test.ts` — 5 tests (**not in registry**; pins the #6476 post-deploy health verification)

Verified this run on the laptop (probe `~/git/fleet/probe-pkarr-20261108`, `git archive origin/main` extract): `package.json` requires `vitest ^3.2.7` and `package-lock.json` pins vitest 3.2.7 (in sync); `npm ci` succeeds and `npm test` reports **Test Files 4 passed, Tests 61 passed**. The lockfile/vitest-4 breakage described in #6093 and repeated in the registry reason has been fixed on main; what remains of #6093 is only the no-workflow wiring gap, not a broken suite.

### 2. cold-store-reaper.worker entry: the #6590 regression suite is missing

Registry entry `cold-store-reaper.worker` lists `test/run-local-proof.mjs` and `test/range-ignored.test.mjs` but omits `pkgs/cold-store-reaper/worker/test/bounded-decompress.test.mjs` — the regression suite for #6590 (zstd decompression bounded by the manifest's expected plaintext size; a hostile bundle member expanding past the Worker memory limit instead of a clean 502). The file is wired into the package's own `npm test` (`package.json` test script runs all three files). Verified this run on the laptop (probe `~/git/fleet/probe-coldstore-20261108`): `node test/bounded-decompress.test.mjs` passes, ending `PASS: bounded decompression (issue #6590)`.

## Why it matters

The registry is the inventory the coverage work (#6185 family, ratchet #6188) and every creator/sweep lane reads to decide what is verified and what is blocked. An entry that omits a third of a suite's files and states a fixed breakage as the current blocker sends fixers to re-diagnose a solved problem and undercounts the tests that would be wired by #6093 / the cold-store venue work.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `pkarr-worker` registry entry lists all four test files under `pkgs/pkarr-worker/test/` (worker, deploy-args, deploy-probe, deploy-verification).
- [ ] The pkarr entry's reason no longer claims a lockfile/runner breakage; it states the current verified state (suite runnable via `npm ci && npm test`, 61 tests passing at the verifying commit) and that the remaining gap is venue wiring (#6093).
- [ ] `cold-store-reaper.worker` registry entry lists `pkgs/cold-store-reaper/worker/test/bounded-decompress.test.mjs`.
- [ ] Registry `uncovered_count` / audit metadata are left consistent with the edited entries (no count change is expected: both suites' venue status is unchanged — this is a paths/reason correction, not a wiring change).

Related: #6093 (pkarr venue wiring — its breakage premise should also be re-checked against this evidence), #6188 (coverage ratchet), #6590, #4865, #6476.

title: mcpx github: fail over across a list of GitHub App identities on soft blocks (rate limits), stop on hard blocks

labels.name: epic/mcpx
labels.description: Epic: mcpx - all issues of this effort carry it

milestone.title: mcpx platform program
milestone.description: mcpx platform program: one canonical mcpx in developing-today/code - dedup, scope-resolved roots, module consolidation, MCP server parity.

body:
## Proposal (Drew, 2026-11-08 22:04 CST)

> "can we make it so we can feed a list of app tokens to mcpx github and it fallback to app? sounds like a minor change to suggest fail over when not hard blocked?"

Give mcpx's `github` namespace a **list of GitHub App credentials** (the fleet's App identities: developing.today, fleet, developing-today-backup) and make it **fail over to the next identity when one hits a soft block** — a rate limit on that identity — because each App identity carries its own rate-limit bucket. On a **hard block** (permission denied, no installation on the target repo, invalid auth), rotation cannot help: stop and surface the error instead of burning the list.

This is the tool-layer twin of Drew's model-leg failover spec (leg errors → short grace → next leg) and of the gh-post ladder the Muse side already uses for its own GitHub writes (user token → App identity when the user bucket is exhausted).

## Why — tonight's evidence (2026-11-08, America/Chicago)

- ~21:05–21:14 CST: the queue broker flapped (restarted 21:05:31 CST). Shift fallback claims then died **in sequence** on: the fleet user token's secondary rate limit ("submitted too quickly"), then its primary rate limit (HTTP 403 at 03:14:36Z), then an App-route failure on that fallback path ("no GitHub App installation for owner developing-today"). Result: **0 tasks worked, 0 GitHub writes landed** in that window. One shared credential bucket took the whole claim path down.
- 21:40 CST: a separate wave of mcpx github-namespace session errors — 3 sessions ACTIVE in the namespace, 1 `tools.github` TypeError (fleet-minder run, report 202). Single-credential, single-server: any credential-level wall is a namespace-level outage.

## Feasibility — checked against the code (2026-11-08)

Drew's "minor change" read is **half right: the concept is small, the surface is not one line.**

- Today the `github` namespace is **one stdio downstream server** (`github-mcp-server`, via the `github-mcp` wrapper) holding **one credential**: the *user* token from `gh auth token` (account dezren39), read **once at server start** (`doc/fleet/mcp.md`). It is not an App credential at all today, and nothing rotates it.
- mcpx's per-server auth (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/mcpauth`) is a single bearer/env credential per server, expanded at connect time. There is **no credential-list, rotation, or failover concept anywhere in mcpx today** (searched `pkgs/mcpx/internal` + docs).
- App credentials are not static tokens: an installation token lives ~1 hour and must be minted from the App private key (JWT → installation token). A minter is required — the fleet already operates this machinery in the gh-post ladder, and the App private key already exists as a vault/org secret (referenced by name only: `FLEET_APP_PRIVATE_KEY` / the developing.today app key in Bitwarden).
- A stdio server keeps its launch env, so per-call failover needs one of: (a) N registered github server instances in mcpx (one per identity) plus error-class-aware retry across instances in the mcpx client layer (`internal/mcpclient`); or (b) a token-broker shim in the wrapper that rotates the credential and restarts the github server on a soft block (the server is effectively stateless per call, so restart is survivable but blunt). Option (a) is the cleaner long-term shape; (b) is the smaller first step. The implementer picks with evidence, but the acceptance criteria below are shape-neutral.
- Error classification is part of the work: today tool errors pass through opaquely (the 21:40 TypeError surfaced raw). mcpx must distinguish soft from hard blocks at the GitHub layer.
- Rotation state (current identity, per-identity cooldown until its rate-limit reset) must survive server restarts — mcpx daemon state or a small state file beside it.

Realistic size: a small-but-real feature in mcpx (config shape + minter + classified retry + state), measured in days, not a config tweak — and not a rewrite.

## Soft vs hard blocks (the classification this issue fixes in one place)

**Soft — rotate to the next identity, after a short grace:**
- HTTP 429 (any GitHub endpoint)
- HTTP 403 with rate-limit markers: `X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0`, a `Retry-After` header, or a body naming a primary/secondary rate limit (including "submitted too quickly")
- HTTP 502/503 from GitHub (transient; grace + retry, same or next identity)

**Hard — stop and surface immediately, never rotate:**
- HTTP 401 / bad credentials / expired or revoked key material
- HTTP 403 with no rate-limit markers (permission forbidden, SSO enforcement, "Resource not accessible by integration")
- HTTP 404 for the installation or the target resource
- HTTP 422 validation errors (the call itself is wrong; no identity fixes it)

## Acceptance criteria

1. mcpx's github namespace accepts a configured **list** of App identities (installation ids + credential references **by vault/secret name only** — no secret values in any config file, log, or this issue's follow-ups).
2. A GitHub tool call that hits a **soft block** on identity #1 completes via identity #2 **without the calling session seeing a fatal error** (demonstrated with a forced rate-limit response or a staged low-limit identity, test named with its oracle per the testing doctrine).
3. A **hard block** surfaces immediately with its real error — no rotation attempts, no retries that burn the remaining identities.
4. Every rotation is **logged with the identity name and the reason** (soft-block class + status), and the current-identity/cooldown state survives a github-server restart.
5. With the list configured, sessions keep the same tool surface (same 43 github tools, same names) — no session or packet changes required.
6. The old single-user-token path remains available as the last list entry or a config fallback, so a bad App config cannot take the namespace down entirely.

## Refs

- Sibling model-layer defect (do not merge): developing-today-forks/opencode#2212 — provider transport timeout kills session.
- Existing prior art: the gh-post ladder (Muse side) — user token → org App identity on rate limit, same doctrine.
- Code: `pkgs/mcpx` (`internal/mcpauth`, `internal/mcpclient`), `doc/fleet/mcp.md` (current github row: stdio `github-mcp` → `github-mcp-server`, `gh` token).

body:
# fleet-paperwork: installations() fetches only page 1 of /app/installations — with 103 installations the developing-today org is page 2, so every App-route write fails 'no installation found'

## Summary

`infra/fleet-paperwork/fleet_paperwork.py` is the fleet's rate-limit fallback
for GitHub writes: when the user token hits GitHub's secondary rate limit,
issue/comment/PR writes are retried as the developing.today GitHub App
(App ID 5454422). That route is currently **down for the developing-today
org**: `AppClient.installations()` fetches exactly one page of
`/app/installations` (`per_page=100`, no `page` parameter, no pagination
loop), and the app now has **103 installations**, so the first page (100,
newest first) no longer contains the `developing-today` org installation.
Every App command for `developing-today/*` dies with
`no installation of the app found for owner 'developing-today'` before it
can mint a token.

## Evidence (verified live 2026-11-09, code @ origin/main 13eb408fe5)

`infra/fleet-paperwork/fleet_paperwork.py`:

- `installations()` (lines 251–263): a single
  `GET /app/installations?per_page=100` — no page loop, and the result is
  cached as if complete. `installation_for()` (lines 265–272) then searches
  only that truncated list.
- The same file paginates correctly in two sibling places:
  `assert_repo_in_scope()` loops `/installation/repositories?per_page=100&page=N`
  (line ~296), and `find_by_exact_title()` pages the Search API
  (line ~385, "the scan pages through the matches … so an exact-title issue
  past the first page is still found"). `installations()` is the one list
  fetch that does not page.

Live reproduction (laptop, 2026-11-09T02:47–02:52Z):

- `fleet_paperwork.py check` lists exactly **100** installations; the
  `developing-today` org is not among them (only `developing-today-vendor`,
  `developing-today-fork`, `developing-today-vendored` are).
- `fleet_paperwork.py create --repo developing-today/code …` fails:
  `no installation of the app found for owner 'developing-today'`.
- Fetching the same endpoint with `page=2` returns the remaining
  installations — **103 across 2 pages** — including the org installation.
  With the paginated list, the identical `create` and `comment` calls
  succeeded and verified by readback (issue #7929 and its agent note,
  comment 6731084039, were filed through this route during the run that
  found this).
- Independent corroboration the same hour: another fleet lane recorded
  "app route down" in its run bookkeeping (sweep.log, 2026-11-09T02:53:00Z)
  and parked its GitHub writes in the action outbox instead.

Context: the user token was under a secondary rate limit at the time
(`gh api` create → HTTP 403 "You have exceeded a secondary rate limit",
request ID 302F:25BDF8:44D395:E39792:6AF134FA, 2026-11-09 02:50:35 UTC) —
exactly the situation this tool exists for — so both write paths were
unavailable at once and only the paginated workaround restored the App
route.

## Why it matters

The App route is the documented fallback (Drew, 2026-11-03) that keeps
fleet GitHub writes flowing when the user token is rate-limited. With it
silently capped at page 1, any owner whose installation falls off the
first page — today the org that owns three of the four fleet repos — loses
the fallback entirely, and every affected write degrades to the action
outbox or is lost to a silent no-op on the limited token. The failure
mode is also deceptive: "no installation found" reads as *the app is not
installed on the org*, which sends diagnosis toward re-installation
instead of a one-line pagination gap. The installation count only grows,
so more owners will fall off page 1 over time.

Related: #6623 (repo-wide pagination inventory — this is a live instance
of that contract failing, in the fleet's own fallback tool); #6864
(closed; response-*shape* validation in the same file — different defect);
#7903 (comment subcommand 422 — different defect).

## Finding

- Status line: "implementation is phased in §8"
- Prerequisites note: "Do not present the existing host journal or the attestation PoC as that prerequisite (§2, §8)"

The document's numbered sections run §1–§7 under "Recommended protocol"; the phased implementation plan the references mean is the unnumbered `## Phased implementation plan` section near the end (the 8-phase table). §2 exists; §8 does not — a reader following the status line to find the phasing, or the prerequisite note to find why the PoC is not the prerequisite, lands nowhere.

## Evidence

- Source PR: #3807 `design(id): #2039 match attestation + audit v1`, commit `65eb6ccc5f2c65d78767cbc81359d5c04d5b6178`; merge `048a01d9b37730038e1d9fa6bd4f487dcde8bba3` (verified an ancestor of main by the compare API).

  - Line 4: "implementation is phased in §8"
  - Line 14: "…as that prerequisite (§2, §8)"
  - Headings: `### 1.`–`### 7.` at lines 43–102, then unnumbered `## Invariants` (:128), `## Acceptance criteria for implementation` (:140), `## Open decisions for Drew` (:154), `## Phased implementation plan` (:164), `## Non-goals` (:179). No §8 heading anywhere.
- The implementation split the design deferred ("Do not create implementation issues in this design change; split them after this design receives its review", :166) has since happened — #3792 is open from #2039 — so this is only the dangling-reference fix, not a request to split anything.

## Why it matters

This doc is the v1 protocol reference for match attestation/audit and is linked from #2039 and epic #2056; its status line is the entry point for anyone picking up a phase. A dangling §8 in the second line a reader sees undermines the doc's own source-precedence discipline (it corrects two investigation docs) and wastes every new reader's first lookup.

## Acceptance criteria

- Both §8 references resolve: either number the existing sections so the Phased implementation plan is §8, or retitle the references to name the "Phased implementation plan" section directly — one consistent choice applied to lines 4 and 14.
- A grep of the doc for `§` references shows every cited section exists in the document.
- No protocol content changes: wording, phases, gates, and open decisions are byte-identical apart from the reference/heading fix.

body:
## Problem

id(web/image-upload): the image upload flow shape-trusts the `/api/upload` response — a wrong-shape 200 response silently inserts an image node with `src: undefined` (or a numeric `src`) into the document, and a `null` body is misreported as an insertion failure for an upload that "succeeded".

`pkgs/id/web/src/image-upload.ts`:

- `:109` — `return (await response.json()) as UploadResponse;` in `uploadImageFile()` is a bare cast; any 200 body is resolved as a well-formed `{ hash: string; name: string; url: string }` with no validation. The `!response.ok` guard at `:104` only covers non-200 statuses.
- `:277-283` — the caller (`handleImageUpload`) treats any resolution as success (`outcome.ok = true`); only a rejection takes the upload-failure path.
- `:312-315` — on "success" the caller creates the image node with `src: outcome.result.url` and `alt: outcome.result.name || fileName`. With a wrong-shape body, `result.url` is `undefined`, so a src-less image node is inserted into the real document and dispatched. With a `null` body, `result.url` throws a raw `TypeError` inside the insertion `try`, which the catch at `:320-328` reports as "Insertion failed" — the wrong diagnosis (the upload response was malformed; nothing about the document insertion was at fault), and the placeholder is removed with no accurate feedback anywhere.
- A wrong-typed body is worse: `{ url: 123 }` inserts an image node with `src: 123`.

The server contract is three required strings (`pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs:1564` `UploadResponse { hash: String, name: String, url: String }`, returned at `:2226`), so a wrong-shape 200 requires deploy skew, a proxy/error envelope with a 200, or a future contract change — exactly the boundary this cast refuses to check. Siblings: #7812 (image-browser `/api/images`, same src-less-insert outcome via a different module), #7811 (home feed).

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ origin/main af4e603e89, image-upload.ts md5 41fa9f0a3ba46a56452fd5c3608fef75)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-upload-shape/probe.ts` (bun, real module imported from a clean `git archive origin/main` snapshot at `~/git/fleet/probe-main-c`, fetch stubbed per case; caller effect mirrors `image-upload.ts:312-315`):

- control (well-formed `{hash:"abc123", name:"cat.png", url:"/blob/abc123?filename=cat.png"}`): resolves the object — image node attrs `src="/blob/abc123?filename=cat.png"`, `alt="cat.png"` — OK
- `null` body: RESOLVES `null` (not rejected) → caller deref throws `TypeError: null is not an object (evaluating 'result.url')`, caught and misreported as "Insertion failed"
- `{}` body: resolves `{}` → image node created with `src=undefined`
- `"abc"` body: resolves `"abc"` → image node created with `src=undefined`
- `[]` body: resolves `[]` → image node created with `src=undefined`
- `{hash:42, name:null, url:123}`: resolves → image node created with `src=123`
- `{hash:"abc123", name:"cat.png"}` (missing `url`): resolves → image node created with `src=undefined`

The existing tests (`pkgs/id/web/src/image-upload.test.ts`, `uploadImageFile` describe at `:231`) mock only the well-formed success body, a non-ok response, and a network error — no malformed-200 cases.

## Why it matters

Paste/drop image upload is a primary editing path. The upload itself succeeded server-side (the blob is stored), so a wrong-shape response today either corrupts the document with a broken src-less image node that then gets saved, or misdiagnoses the failure as an insertion problem — making the real contract break undebuggable from user reports. Failing closed is cheap: validate the shape at the fetch boundary and let the existing upload-failure path (warn + placeholder removal, `:279-282`) handle it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A malformed `/api/upload` 200 payload (null/non-object body, missing `hash`/`name`/`url`, or wrong-typed fields) makes `uploadImageFile` REJECT with a clear upload error — it never resolves a malformed value.
- [ ] On a malformed payload, no image node is inserted, and the failure is reported through the existing upload-failure path ("Upload failed for …"), never as "Insertion failed" and never as a raw TypeError.
- [ ] Well-formed payloads behave exactly as today (existing `uploadImageFile` tests unchanged and green).
- [ ] New regression tests in `pkgs/id/web/src/image-upload.test.ts` cover the malformed cases above and fail pre-fix.
- [ ] Web suite + typecheck green.

body:
## Problem

id(web/image-browser): the image browser shape-trusts the `/api/images` response — a wrong-shape 200 response either dumps a raw engine TypeError into the dialog or, worse, silently renders bogus cards that insert a src-less image node into the document.

`pkgs/id/web/src/image-browser.ts`:

- `:245` — `return (await response.json()) as ImageEntry[];` in `fetchImages()` is a bare cast; the result is consumed unvalidated by the `.then` handler in `openImageBrowser`.
- `:146` — the handler wipes the grid first (`grid.textContent = ""`, clearing the "Loading…" state), then reads `images.length` (`:148`) and iterates (`:156`), dereferencing `img.hash` / `img.url` / `img.name` per element with no shape check.
- `:212` — the `.catch` surfaces the raw exception (`Failed to load images: ${err}`), so a shape failure shows e.g. "Failed to load images: TypeError: {} is not iterable" to the user.
- A string payload is iterable, so it never throws: each character becomes a "card" with `name`/`url`/`hash` all undefined, the Insert button enables on selection, and `insertImage` (`:216-224`) creates an image node with `src: undefined, alt: undefined`.

The server contract is a bare JSON array (`pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs:2238` `images_list_handler` returns `Json(Vec<ImageEntry>)`), so a wrong-shape 200 requires deploy skew, a proxy/error envelope, or a future contract change — exactly the boundary this cast refuses to check. Sibling of #7811 (home feed, same wipe/cast pattern, different module and endpoint).

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ origin/main fd2b0c84f8, image-browser.ts md5 9f5336c522ed40f25ac493a4a7215f24)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-image-browser/probe.ts` (bun, minimal DOM stub, real module imported from a clean `git archive origin/main` snapshot at `~/git/fleet/probe-main-a`; fetch stubbed per case):

- control (well-formed `[{hash:"abc123", name:"cat.png", url:"/api/images/abc123", size:42}]`): renders 1 card, name `cat.png`, hash `abc123` — OK
- `null` body: grid shows `Failed to load images: TypeError: null is not an object (evaluating 'images.length')`, 0 cards
- `{}` body: grid shows `Failed to load images: TypeError: {} is not iterable`, 0 cards
- `[null]`: grid shows `Failed to load images: TypeError: null is not an object (evaluating 'img.hash')`, 0 cards
- `[valid, null]`: throws on the second element; the catch's `grid.textContent =` assignment wipes even the already-appended valid card — 0 cards, raw TypeError
- `"abc"` body: NO error — 3 bogus cards render, every name `undefined`; selecting one enables Insert, and clicking Insert creates an image node with attrs `{}` (`src`/`alt` undefined)

The existing test file (`pkgs/id/web/src/image-browser.test.ts`) mocks only the well-formed array (line 17) — no malformed-shape cases.

## Why it matters

The image browser is how users insert previously uploaded images. Failing closed here is cheap: validate the array shape at the fetch boundary and show the designed failure message. Today a malformed payload either leaks a raw TypeError as the dialog's only content or — in the string case — lets a user insert a broken, src-less image node into a real document with no error anywhere.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A malformed `/api/images` payload (null body, non-array body, null or wrong-typed elements/fields) does NOT render any cards and does NOT enable Insert.
- [ ] A malformed payload surfaces the clean failure message (e.g. "Failed to load images.") — never a raw TypeError/engine message.
- [ ] A partially valid array (`[valid, null]`) does not leave a half-rendered grid (all-or-nothing rendering).
- [ ] Well-formed payloads render exactly as today (existing image-browser.test.ts cases unchanged and green).
- [ ] New regression tests in `pkgs/id/web/src/image-browser.test.ts` cover the malformed cases above and fail pre-fix.
- [ ] Web suite + typecheck green.

body:
# mcpx(plugin): the dogfood `.opencode/plugin` copy has drifted from `pkgs/mcpx` again — `daemon.ts` is pre-#3490 and `biome.json` is missing

## Evidence (verified this run, main `d222177982`)

The sync guard in `.github/workflows/mcpx.yml` (plugin-sync job, lines 99–100; repeated in the test job, lines 130–131) is an exact byte comparison:

```
diff -r pkgs/mcpx/plugin/opencode/mcpx .opencode/plugin/mcpx
diff pkgs/mcpx/plugin/opencode/mcpx-session.ts .opencode/plugin/mcpx-session.ts
```

Run by hand on the laptop primary at `d222177982`, the first diff fails (rc=1) with exactly three drift paths:

```
Only in pkgs/mcpx/plugin/opencode/mcpx: biome.json
Files pkgs/mcpx/plugin/opencode/mcpx/daemon.test.ts and .opencode/plugin/mcpx/daemon.test.ts differ
Files pkgs/mcpx/plugin/opencode/mcpx/daemon.ts and .opencode/plugin/mcpx/daemon.ts differ
```

(`mcpx-session.ts` is in sync; the other five files in the directory are identical.)

What the drift means, concretely:

- `daemon.ts`: the `.opencode` copy is the pre-#3490 `goDurationMs` — its unit table lacks the Greek-mu micro sign (U+03BC) and its grammar rejects Go-valid dot fractions (`.5s`, `1.s`), so those duration spellings silently fall back to the default cooldown; its saturation cap is `9_223_372_036_854.776` where the fixed source has `.775`. `pkgs/mcpx/plugin/opencode/mcpx/daemon.ts` was last fixed by `04f564f211` (#3490); the `.opencode` copy was never updated after it.
- `daemon.test.ts`: the `.opencode` copy lacks the #3490 Go-parity test block (and carries the old `.776` expectation), so even the copied tests would not catch the stale parser.
- `biome.json`: added to the pkgs copy by the #5151 pinned plugin lint/type-check work (`6e50a61760`); absent from the dogfood copy, so the copy the repo's own OpenCode loads is not the linted configuration.

The `.opencode/plugin` copy is the one this repo's own OpenCode sessions actually load (mcpx.yml:121: "The repo dogfoods the plugin"). The fleet's own tooling is therefore running the stale duration parser today.

## Why the guard did not catch it

The guard lives only in `mcpx.yml` (grep over `.github/workflows/*.yml`, `flake.nix`, `justfile`: the two mcpx.yml sites are the only ones), and that workflow currently has no `push`/`pull_request` triggers and is `disabled_manually` — filed separately as the companion CI issue (mcpx.yml trigger/enablement loss). This is the third instance of the same class: #314 (ops.gen.ts 9 ops behind, no guard), #2795 (drifted again; guard push-only). Each sync without a running guard has re-drifted.

## Why it matters

- A declared byte-identity contract is silently false on main; anyone reading `.opencode/plugin` sees code that is not the plugin's current behavior.
- The stale copy is live, not archival: it is the plugin loaded by OpenCode sessions working in this repo.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `diff -r pkgs/mcpx/plugin/opencode/mcpx .opencode/plugin/mcpx` exits 0 on main (biome.json present; daemon.ts and daemon.test.ts at the pkgs versions).
- [ ] `diff pkgs/mcpx/plugin/opencode/mcpx-session.ts .opencode/plugin/mcpx-session.ts` still exits 0.
- [ ] The synced copy's plugin tests pass (the #3490 parity block in daemon.test.ts green against the synced daemon.ts).
- [ ] No change to `pkgs/mcpx/plugin/**` itself — the pkgs tree is the source of truth.

## What

`scripts/tests/test_check_provider_retirement_gate.py` (324 lines, 19 tests) — the contract suite for `scripts/check-provider-retirement-gate.sh`, the #5610 gate that blocks retiring a provider while configuration files still reference it — is run by no workflow, flake check, or just recipe.

- `.github/workflows/scripts-test.yml:34-38` names only three sibling suites from `scripts/tests/` (`test_update_nixpkgs_inputs.py`, `test_worker_preflight.py`, `test_bitwarden_load_secrets.py`); this suite is not among them.

- It has no entry in `.github/test-suite-registry.json` either (`git grep retirement` there: no hits), so the #6185 coverage contract does not even record the gap.
- The other `scripts/tests/` suites in the same directory that do run somewhere are wired by name (program-tending in `program-tending.yml:46-47`; plan_check and the `test_*workflow*.py` glob in `research-workflow.yml:35-37`) — this one's name matches no glob and no explicit step.

## Verified this run (laptop, main 26018ce4e7)

- Hand run exactly as a workflow step would: `python3 -m unittest discover -s scripts/tests -p 'test_check_provider_retirement_gate.py'` → **19 tests, OK** (0.4s).
- The suite pins the gate's fail-closed behaviour added for #5610: unterminated block comments fail closed (c09832df94), empty provider IDs are usage errors, `disabled_providers` tombstones pass only at the top level (52c8b24c81, f86f7e5f18), the deployed runtime overlay is checked despite XDG overrides, substring provider IDs do not false-block. Every one of those fixes landed with its only regression suite exercising them nowhere automatic.
- The gate itself is live infrastructure, not dead code: `home/common/default.nix:748` documents it and `.github/scripts/check-proxy-port-fallbacks.sh:131-133` points maintainers at it as the manual pre-retirement check — so the script is expected to work when someone reaches for it during a provider retirement, which is exactly the high-stakes moment #5610 was filed from (route proxy retired while deployed config still routed through it).

## Why it matters

A gate that is only ever run by hand, whose contract suite runs nowhere, rots silently in the same way the siblings filed as #7664 (test_auto_format_workflow.py) and #7597 (test_hardware_doc_init.py) did: the next change to the gate's comment-stripping or tombstone logic can break a pinned case and nobody will know until a retirement is wrongly blocked — or wrongly allowed through.

- [ ] The suite runs in an automatic venue: a named step in `scripts-test.yml` (the house pattern for this directory) or an equivalent flake/just venue, naming the file explicitly like its siblings.
