body:
## Problem

`.github/scripts/check-workflows.sh` is the only validator for `.github/actions/**` metadata (#5743): actionlint parses every file it is given as a workflow, so composite/action metadata gets this script's dedicated shape validation instead. That validation (the PyYAML branch of `validate_action_metadata`, check-workflows.sh:82-91) checks the per-runtime required field for exactly one runtime and stops:

- `using == "docker"` → `runs.image` must be a non-empty string (:89-91) ✔
- `using` in `node16`/`node20`/`node24` → **nothing further is checked**. GitHub requires `runs.main` (the entry point) for JavaScript actions; a node action without it passes this gate and only fails when GitHub tries to run it.
- `using == "composite"` → `runs.steps` must merely be a non-empty list (:85-88). A step that is a bare string, or a mapping with neither `run` nor `uses`, passes; GitHub rejects both at run time (every composite step must declare `run`+`shell` or `uses`).

The structural fallback branch (no PyYAML) enforces even less — by its own comment it checks top-level keys and the `using` line only — so on a machine without PyYAML all three gaps widen, and the two branches disagree about what "valid action metadata" means.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop, main @ ab37879484)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-check-workflows` — fixtures run through the real `~/git/code/.github/scripts/check-workflows.sh` (unmodified), once on the structural-fallback path (system python3, no PyYAML) and once on the PyYAML path (venv PyYAML 6.0.3 on PATH), with a stub `ACTIONLINT_BIN` (action-only invocations never call actionlint).

PyYAML path results:

| fixture | shape | result | expected |
|---|---|---|---|
| `node-main/action.yml` | node20 + `main: dist/index.js` | rc=0 pass | pass ✔ (control) |
| `node-nomain/action.yml` | node20, no `runs.main` | **rc=0 pass** | fail |
| `comp-badstep/action.yml` | composite, sole step has `name` only (no `run`/`uses`) | **rc=0 pass** | fail |
| `comp-stringstep/action.yml` | composite, `steps: ["just-a-string"]` | **rc=0 pass** | fail |
| `ctrl-noruns/action.yml` | no `runs` | rc=1 fail | fail ✔ (control) |
| `ctrl-banana/action.yml` | `using: banana` | rc=1 fail | fail ✔ (control) |
| `ctrl-docker-noimage/action.yml` | docker, no `runs.image` | rc=1 fail | fail ✔ (control — proves the docker branch is checked) |

The fallback path passes all three gap fixtures too (rc=0). The existing contract suite (`.github/scripts/check-workflows.test.sh`, 6 cases) covers none of these shapes: its action cases are a valid composite, missing `runs`, and `using: banana`.

## Why it matters

This script is the basic-tier gate for every `.github/actions/**` change (workflow-lint.yml), and the repo already carries four real actions there (`pm-dispatch-start`, `pm-dispatch-ci-fix`, `pm-dispatch-task`, `pm-dispatch-queue`). A future node action — or an edit that drops `main`, or a composite step typo'd into a no-op — merges green and fails only when a workflow actually invokes the action, which is exactly the failure class #5743 built this validator to catch before merge. The docker branch shows the intended pattern; node and composite were left half-checked.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A node action (`using: node16`/`node20`/`node24`) whose `runs.main` is missing or not a non-empty string fails validation with a diagnostic naming the file and field (mirroring the docker `runs.image` check).
- [ ] A composite action fails validation when any `runs.steps` entry is not a mapping, or declares neither `run` nor `uses`; a `run` step without `shell` is also flagged (GitHub requires `shell` on composite run steps).
- [ ] All currently-valid metadata still passes: the four `.github/actions/*/action.yml` files in the repo and every fixture in the existing contract suite.
- [ ] `.github/scripts/check-workflows.test.sh` gains contract cases for: node action without `main` (fail), node action with `main` (pass), composite step with neither `run` nor `uses` (fail), composite steps as strings (fail).
- [ ] The PyYAML and structural-fallback branches agree on the new checks, or the fallback's reduced contract is documented in the script header where the "same rules" claim currently stands.

title: grist(update-choice-options): API envelope shape-trusted — get_widget_options/api die as raw Key/Type/Attribute/JSONDecode tracebacks on wrong-shape 200s, bypassing the #6588 exit-1 contract

labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/normal

body:
## Summary

`pm-stack/grist/update-choice-options.py` guards the *inner* stored
`widgetOptions` shape (#6588, `check_widget_options`), but the Grist API
*envelope* around it in `get_widget_options` — and the JSON decode in
`api()` — are still shape-trusted. A wrong-shape 200 response dies as a
raw `KeyError` / `TypeError` / `AttributeError` / `JSONDecodeError`
traceback, even though the module's own contract (docstring, exit
codes) says an unexpected shape is an exit-1 failure reported on
stderr, and `run()` converts exactly the two named error classes
(`TimeoutError`, `WidgetOptionsError`, lines 221–226) to that exit.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ 65beb42c1a, probe `~/git/fleet/probe-grist-envelope`, real file verbatim, stubbed `api` transport)

`get_widget_options` (update-choice-options.py:136–144):

```python
for col in data["columns"]:  # :138
    if col["id"] == column:  # :139
        raw = col["fields"].get("widgetOptions") or ""  # :140
        parsed = json.loads(raw)  # :144 — only JSONDecodeError is wrapped
```

Controls pass (empty widgetOptions → `{}`; valid JSON string →
`{'choices': ['id']}`). Every wrong shape below is a raw error:

| payload | result |
| --- | --- |
| `{}` (no `columns`) | `KeyError: 'columns'` |
| `[]` (top-level list) | `TypeError: list indices must be integers` |
| `{"error": "not found"}` | `KeyError: 'columns'` |
| `{"columns": "abc"}` | `TypeError: string indices must be integers` |
| `{"columns": ["Area"]}` | `TypeError: string indices must be integers` |
| `{"columns": [{"id": "Area"}]}` (no `fields`) | `KeyError: 'fields'` |
| `fields: null` | `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'get'` |
| `fields: []` | `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'` |
| `widgetOptions` already a dict (not a JSON string) | `TypeError: the JSON object must be str, bytes or bytearray, not dict` |
| `widgetOptions: 123` | `TypeError: ... not int` |
| `{"columns": null}` | `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not iterable` |

End-to-end: `run([...])` with a `{}` response **propagates**
`KeyError: 'columns'` instead of returning 1 — the CLI traceback names
no endpoint, column, or field.

Second door, same class: `api()` (:133) returns
`json.loads(raw) if raw and raw != "null" else None` with no decode
guard — a non-JSON 200 body (e.g. an HTML proxy/error page) raises a
raw `JSONDecodeError: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)`
(probe2 in the same probe dir), also uncaught by `run()`.

Why these shapes are realistic: the columns endpoint is a server the
tool does not control — other Grist versions, an error object returned
with 200 by a proxy, or a column whose `fields`/`widgetOptions` were
written by another tool (the exact premise #6588 already accepted for
the inner value). Both the initial read and the post-PATCH read-back
verification go through `get_widget_options`, so a wrong-shape
read-back also crashes *after* a successful PATCH, reporting a
traceback for a change that actually landed.

## Fix shape

Validate the envelope at the same boundary #6588 used for the inner
value: in `get_widget_options`, require `data` to be an object with a
`columns` list of objects each carrying an `id` and an object
`fields`; require a present `widgetOptions` to be a string before
`json.loads`. Raise `WidgetOptionsError` (or a sibling named error
that `run()` already converts) with messages naming the endpoint
payload part that was wrong. In `api()`, wrap the `json.loads` decode
failure the same way, naming method + path. No coercion, no PATCH on a
shape failure (the existing pre-PATCH ordering already guarantees
this for the first read).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each wrong-shape payload in the table above produces a named,
      human-readable error on stderr and exit 1 via `run()` — no
      traceback, no raw `KeyError`/`TypeError`/`AttributeError`.
- [ ] A non-JSON 200 body from `api()` is reported as a named API
      failure (method + path), exit 1, not a raw `JSONDecodeError`.
- [ ] Controls unchanged: empty widgetOptions → `{}`; valid stored
      options merge and read-back verification behave exactly as today.
- [ ] A column genuinely absent from a well-shaped `columns` list
      still exits via the existing "column not found" path.
- [ ] New cases land in `pm-stack/grist/test_update_choice_options.py`
      (stubbed transport, no live Grist), covering at least: missing
      `columns`, non-list `columns`, entry without `fields`,
      non-string `widgetOptions`, non-JSON response body.

body:
## Problem

`pm-stack/opencode-claimant/claimant.py` — the opencode lane claimant/executor — calls two modules it never imports at module level, so in live mode its two active steps can never do their work:

- `requests` is used at lines 197, 226, 252 (`supervision_step`: session GET, messages GET, session DELETE) and 392, 407, 432 (`launch_step`: session POST, cleanup DELETEs) but is never imported (imports at lines 18–24 are only `json, os, sys, time, datetime, pathlib, typing`). `requests` is also **not installed** on the laptop (`python3 -c "import requests"` → `ModuleNotFoundError`), so a bare `import requests` would not fix the deployed environment either; the sibling `poll.py` in the same directory does its HTTP with stdlib `urllib.request`.
- `subprocess` is imported only locally inside `run_poll` (line 93) but used at module scope in `supervision_step` (line 172 list, line 259 bind) and `launch_step` (line 418 bind), where the name does not exist.

Every failure is swallowed by the broad `except Exception` handlers around these steps, so nothing crashes and nothing is logged as an error:

- Supervision: the per-queue `subprocess.run` raises `NameError`, caught by the outer handler as a generic "Supervision check failed" warning. Even with that fixed alone, the session check `requests.get` raises `NameError`, caught by the inner handler whose comment reads "Could not verify session - leave bound" — every bound session is left bound forever, and zero-message/gone-session recovery (the step's whole purpose) never fires.
- Launch: the session-create `requests.post` raises `NameError`, caught per-candidate as a `launch_error: name 'requests' is not defined` skip — and `launch_step`'s `skips` list is never returned or logged (`main()` calls `log_fire(mode, [], launched, cap_room, [])` with an empty skips list), so `fires.jsonl` records only "Launched 0" with no reason. Even past that, the bind `subprocess.run` would raise the same way.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop, main @65beb42c1a)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-claimant-requests` (real `claimant.py` copied verbatim; transport and queue CLI stubbed):

- `hasattr(module, "requests")` → `False`; `hasattr(module, "subprocess")` → `False`.
- `launch_step("live", 3)` with one valid unbound `handed_off` candidate from a stubbed `run_poll` → `[]` (nothing launched, no error surfaced). With stub `requests` and `subprocess` injected into the module namespace, the identical call → one launched session (`ses_1` bound).
- `supervision_step("live")` with a stubbed queue list returning a claimed opencode task whose session 404s with zero messages: with only `subprocess` stubbed (requests still missing) → `[]`; with both stubbed → the task is recovered as a `zero_message` candidate and the delete+bind recovery runs.
- First probe round (no stubs at all) printed `Supervision check failed for queue <each of the 4 queues>: name 'subprocess' is not defined` — the exact warning shape a live run would emit.
- CI never catches this: `.github/workflows/pm-stack-tests.yml` runs only `test_poll.py` for this package (per #6091/#5951); `claimant.py` has no test suite at all.

Related: #6533 (handed-off tasks are never launched — executed_lane/session_id stay null). #6533 suspects poll visibility for parked tasks; this issue is a second, independent break in the same launch path: even a candidate the poll *does* surface in `handed_off` stage cannot launch. Both need fixing for a handoff to result in a session.

## Why it matters

The claimant is the component that turns handed-off opencode-lane queue tasks into running sessions and recovers dead bound sessions. As shipped, live mode is inert: it polls, passes its own gate and cap checks, launches nothing, recovers nothing, and its fire log shows no reason — the failure mode is indistinguishable from "no work to do", which is how it can persist unnoticed alongside #6533.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `claimant.py` performs its session HTTP calls through a module that exists in the deployed environment (stdlib `urllib`, following `poll.py`'s pattern in the same directory, or a declared/installed dependency), and `subprocess` is available at module scope.
- [ ] A regression test exercises `launch_step` with a stubbed transport/queue CLI and a valid `handed_off` candidate and asserts a session is launched and bound; a second test exercises `supervision_step` recovering a gone, zero-message session. The suite is wired into `pm-stack-tests.yml` alongside `test_poll.py`.
- [ ] `launch_step`'s skips are returned and recorded in the `fires.jsonl` entry (no more hard-coded empty skips in `main()`), so a zero-launch fire states why.
- [ ] Negative control: the new tests fail against the pre-fix `claimant.py`.

body:
# fleet-paperwork: API response bodies are shape-trusted — a wrong-shape 200/error body crashes every command with a raw Attribute/KeyError, including inside http()'s own error handler

## Summary

`infra/fleet-paperwork/fleet_paperwork.py` — the tool the fleet's rate-limit fallback (rule 9) depends on for issue/PR writes as the developing.today GitHub App — assumes every GitHub API response body is a JSON **object** whose items are also objects. `http()` is even annotated `-> tuple[int, dict]`, but it returns whatever `json.loads` produced. A parseable-but-wrong-shaped body (a JSON array, string, or number — the shapes an edge/proxy error page or a skewed endpoint can return) crashes every consumer with a raw `AttributeError`/`KeyError` traceback instead of the tool's own `die()` diagnostic — including inside `http()`'s own HTTP-error handler, so the real HTTP status/message is lost exactly when the operator needs it.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ 65beb42c1a)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-paperwork-shape/` on the laptop — the real `fleet_paperwork.py` copied verbatim, transport stubbed (`http_raw`/`http` monkeypatched), controls run alongside. Controls pass: a dict error body dies cleanly (`fleet-paperwork: error: GET … -> HTTP 403: boom-rate`), a well-shaped create/dedupe/installations flow succeeds. The wrong shapes:

| Surface | Code | Wrong shape | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `http()` error handler | `:175-178` — `detail = json.loads(raw)` then `detail.get('message', …)` | 403 body `["a","b"]` / 502 body `"edge string"` / 500 body `42` | raw `AttributeError: 'list'/'str'/'int' object has no attribute 'get'` — the HTTP error itself is never reported |
| `http()` success return | `:179` — `json.loads(raw) if raw else {}` | any non-object 200 body | returned verbatim despite the `-> dict` annotation; every caller below then crashes |
| `cmd_create` | `:367` `created.get("number")` | POST returns `["weird"]` | raw `AttributeError` — the `isinstance(created, dict)` guard written into the die message at `:371` is **unreachable**, because `.get` runs first |
| `cmd_comment` | `:400` `comment.get("id")` | POST returns `"weird"` | raw `AttributeError` |
| `cmd_close` | `:459` `current.get("state")` | GET returns `[1,2]` | raw `AttributeError` |
| `find_by_exact_title` | `:298` `data.get("items", [])`, `:300-302` item filter/`.get` | body `["top-level-list"]`, or an item that is a bare string | raw `AttributeError` (for a string item, `"pull_request" in item` even succeeds as a substring test before `.get` crashes) |
| `AppClient.installations` / `installation_for` | `:198` `inst.get(...)`, `:208` `inst["id"]` | body `{"installations": []}` (dict instead of list) or a string item | raw `AttributeError` (iterating a dict yields its string keys) |
| `AppClient.assert_repo_in_scope` | `:227` `r["full_name"]` | a repository entry without `full_name` | raw `KeyError: 'full_name'` — and this runs at the start of **every** command, including `token`, so one skewed entry wedges the whole tool |

Related latent case in the same pattern: `:198` `inst.get("account", {}).get("login", "")` — the `{}` default only covers an *absent* `account`; an explicit `null`/non-object `account` crashes the same way.

## Why it matters

This tool is the fleet's designated fallback when the user token is rate-limited (it mints the App token and performs verified creates/comments). Its entire value is being the reliable path when GitHub is already misbehaving — which is precisely when non-standard error bodies (edge 502s, abuse/rate-limit responses, proxy pages) are most likely. Today those responses produce an undiagnosed Python traceback with the HTTP status and message swallowed, in the error handler itself. The unreachable `isinstance` guard at `:371` shows the shape case was considered for `cmd_create` but the check was placed after the first unguarded use.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `http()` validates the decoded body shape for its callers: a non-object success body, and a non-object error body, both produce a `die()` diagnostic naming the method, URL, HTTP status, and the received shape (the error path must still surface the raw body excerpt, as it does today for unparseable bodies).
- [ ] No fleet-paperwork command (`create`, `comment`, `close`, `check`, `token`, `api`) can raise a raw `AttributeError`/`KeyError`/`TypeError` from a parseable-but-wrong-shaped response body or response item — each such case ends in `die()` with the response shape named.
- [ ] `cmd_create`'s existing `isinstance` intent is made effective (shape checked before the first `.get`).
- [ ] `assert_repo_in_scope` treats an entry without a string `full_name` as a malformed-response `die()`, not a `KeyError`.
- [ ] Regression tests in `infra/fleet-paperwork/tests/test_fleet_paperwork.py` cover the probe shapes above (list/string/number error bodies, non-object create/comment/close bodies, string search item, dict-shaped installations body, scope entry missing `full_name`), with the well-shaped controls still passing.

## Verification

Probe directory (laptop): `~/git/fleet/probe-paperwork-shape/` (`fleet_paperwork.py` verbatim from main @ 65beb42c1a + `probe.py`); 4 controls pass, 10 wrong-shape cases produce raw tracebacks as tabled above. Sibling dedupe history: #6697 covered `find_by_exact_title`'s PR-matching/pagination only — response *shapes* were not covered; #3068 is the umbrella design for this contract class.

body:
## Problem

`scripts/research_workflow.py`'s `init` command (`scaffold()`) reads the `--outline` JSON file with a bare `json.loads(...)` (research_workflow.py:243-244) and then uses the parsed value's fields raw. Sibling inputs in the same tool were hardened in #6854 (profile/state/trigger shapes) and #6857 (note/resolution shapes), but the outline — the file that seeds a new research package's title, concepts, and state — was not covered. A valid-JSON-but-wrong-shape (or non-JSON) outline therefore surfaces as a bare Python error that names neither the file nor the field, instead of the tool's own `fail()` diagnostic used everywhere else in the file. The CLI (`main()`, research_workflow.py:1079-1088) catches these types, so the run exits 1 with e.g.:

```
$ research_workflow.py init --input transcript.txt --slug x --outline outline.json
error: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'
```

— an operator cannot tell which field of which file is malformed.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ 65beb42c1a70672bed159fe401c2cb1079aa516f, real files verbatim, probe `~/git/fleet/probe-rw-scaffold-outline/`)

The probe copies `scripts/research_workflow.py` (+ its two extension modules) verbatim from `origin/main` (md5 match), builds a fixture repo root with a valid profile, and drives the real CLI (`init --allow-duplicate`, 2-line transcript).

Control: a well-formed outline (object with string `title`, one concept with string `title`/`slug`/`summary` and `source_lines: [[1, 2]]`) scaffolds successfully (rc=0, package created). No malformed case creates a partial package.

Wrong shapes (all raw, none via `fail()`):

- Outline top level `[]` → `error: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'`; `"x"` → same for `str` — `outline.get("title", "")` at research_workflow.py:262 runs before any isinstance guard.
- Outline `title: 42` → `error: expected string or bytes-like object, got 'int'` — `re.search(...)` on the unchecked title at :262.
- Concept entry `"just-a-string"` → `error: 'str' object has no attribute 'get'` — `concept.get("title")` at :271.
- Concept `slug: 42` → `error: expected string or bytes-like object, got 'int'` — `slug()` runs `re.fullmatch` on the unchecked value (:276 → :121-124). An explicit `"slug": null` takes the same path.
- Concept `summary: 42` → `error: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str` — `summary` is concatenated raw at :355 (its `thoughts`/`suggestions` siblings ARE validated as string lists at :294-298; `summary` is not).
- Outline file containing non-JSON (`not json{`) → `error: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)` — the bare `json.loads` at :244; the message names no file.

## Why it matters

The outline is the machine-generated seed for every new research package (produced by the research-prepare step and handed to `init`); a truncated or mis-shaped generation is exactly the corruption this tool's `fail()` idiom exists to diagnose precisely. Today the operator gets a type error with no file, no field, and no expected shape, and must read the source to find which of the outline's fields is wrong. This is one more instance of the #3068 parsed-is-not-validated pattern, in the one `research_workflow.py` input surface #6854/#6856/#6857 did not reach.

## Acceptance criteria

- `scaffold()` validates the outline before use: non-object top level, non-JSON body, non-string `title`/`introduction`, non-object concept entries, non-string concept `slug`, and non-string concept `summary` each fail via `fail()` with a message naming the outline file and the field/expectation.
- Validation happens before any package directory is created (today's no-partial-package property is preserved).
- Regression tests in `scripts/tests/test_research_workflow.py` cover each wrong shape above and assert the clean `fail()` diagnostic.
- A valid outline behaves byte-identically to today (existing test suite green; the probe control above still scaffolds).

body:
# agent-backup: dedup comparison is mode-blind — a permission-only change to a credential file is dropped as "no change"

## Evidence

`pkgs/agent-backup/backup.sh` (verified at origin/main `65beb42c1a`):

- The header states the snapshot contract includes file modes: "files keep their modes, so 0600 secrets stay 0600" (backup.sh:18-19), and copies are made with `cp -p` (backup.sh:75) to preserve them.
- The dedup decision — drop the new snapshot if it is "identical to the previous one" — is a bare content comparison (backup.sh:105):

  ```sh
  if [ -n "$PREV" ] && diff -rq "$ROOT/$PREV" "$DEST" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  ```

  `diff -rq` compares names and file contents only. It does not compare permissions/modes, so a mode-only change compares "identical".

## Reproduction (laptop probe, real backup.sh from origin/main, `~/git/fleet/probe-backup-mode`)

Fake HOME with one candidate, `~/.config/opencode/auth.json`:

1. `auth.json` mode 600 → run 1: `agent-backup: snapshot 2026-11-07T09-24-31 (1 files)`; recorded copy is mode 600.
2. `chmod 644 auth.json` (content untouched) → run 2: `agent-backup: no change since 2026-11-07T09-24-31` — the new snapshot is deleted. The only snapshot on disk still records mode 600 while the live credential file is world-readable 644; `latest` still points at it.
3. Control: appending to the file's content → run 3 creates a new snapshot normally. Content changes are detected; mode changes are not.

`pkgs/agent-backup/test-backup.sh` has no mode/permission case (grep for chmod/mode/perm finds only the test harness's own stub setup).

## Why it matters

This tool exists to snapshot the machine's irreplaceable credential/config files (auth.json files, API keys). A permission loosening on one of those files — 0600 → 0644 — is precisely the kind of change a credential backup history should record: it is a security-relevant state change, and the snapshot set is what a later restore/audit would trust. Today the history silently asserts the file is still 0600. Worse, the mode is part of the tool's own documented contract (`cp -p`, "0600 secrets stay 0600"), so the comparison is inconsistent with the copy: modes are preserved on the way in and ignored when deciding whether anything changed.

## Acceptance criteria

- A mode-only change (e.g. 0600 → 0644) to any candidate file produces a new snapshot whose recorded copy carries the new mode; the run does not report "no change".
- A run where contents, file set, and modes are all unchanged still dedups (snapshot dropped, "no change since <PREV>"), preserving the history-grows-only-on-change property.
- The comparison stays within the tool's dependency discipline (findutils + coreutils + bash builtins; the systemd service PATH has no awk/grep/sed per the comment at backup.sh:95-100).
- Regression coverage in `pkgs/agent-backup/test-backup.sh`: mode-only change snapshots; unchanged run still dedups; existing cases (same-second suffix #3340, future-dated PREV #4602) stay green.

body:
## Problem

`scripts/program_tending.py`'s GitHub API helper never authenticates, even though the scheduled workflow explicitly provides a token for it. Every API call the daily run makes is unauthenticated.

The workflow sets the token (`.github/workflows/program-tending.yml`, "Run program-tending scaffold" step):

```yaml
env:
  GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
run: python3 -I scripts/program_tending.py --run
```

But `_gh_api` (scripts/program_tending.py:48-64) builds each request with only an Accept header, and the module never reads the environment at all (it does not even import `os`):

```python
req = urllib.request.Request(
    url, headers={"Accept": "application/vnd.github+json"}
)
```

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop, main @ 65beb42c1a70672bed159fe401c2cb1079aa516f)

- Probe (~/git/fleet/probe-program-tending on the laptop, real `program_tending.py` verbatim, `GH_TOKEN` set in the environment, `urllib.request.urlopen` stubbed to capture the request): the captured headers are exactly `{'Accept': 'application/vnd.github+json'}` — no `Authorization` header is sent.
- `grep -n "GH_TOKEN|Authorization|environ" scripts/program_tending.py` returns nothing; the only `GH_TOKEN` occurrence in the pair is the workflow env line above.
- Control: the existing suite passes 8/8 on the laptop (`python3 -m unittest scripts.tests.test_program_tending`) — no test captures the request headers, so nothing guards this.

## Why it matters

Unauthenticated GitHub REST calls are limited to 60 requests/hour per source IP, and GitHub-hosted runner IPs are shared — the unauthenticated quota for a runner IP is routinely already exhausted by other tenants. The one live section of the scaffold, `stub_stalled_prs`, follows pagination (`Link: rel="next"`) across four repos, so a rate-limited run degrades to `open_prs: "unverified"` with a 403 error string — indistinguishable in the log from a genuine outage — even though Actions provided a token with the standard 1,000 requests/hour per-repository budget for exactly this purpose. The token is provisioned, named, and silently unused: the failure mode is a daily log that says "unverified" for no repo-side reason.

## Acceptance criteria

- `_gh_api` sends `Authorization: Bearer <token>` when a token is available in the environment (`GH_TOKEN`, falling back to `GITHUB_TOKEN`), and behaves exactly as today when no token is set (local runs without a token still work, subject to unauthenticated limits).
- The token value never appears in the run log, error strings, or test output.
- A new test in `scripts/tests/test_program_tending.py` captures the request `_gh_api` builds (stubbed `urlopen`) and asserts the Authorization header is present when the env token is set and absent when it is not.
- Existing program-tending tests still pass.

body:
# research_workflow_items: the `ids` command reads the package's package.json manifest shape-trusted — wrong shapes surface as bare Attribute/Key/Type errors naming no file or field, not the tool's fail() diagnostics

## Summary

`scripts/research_workflow_items.py` `list_ids` (the `ids` command, :952) reads the research package's own `package.json` manifest with a bare `json.loads(...).get("segments", [])` (:956-957) and projects `[s["id"] for s in segments]` (:976) with no shape validation at all. A valid-JSON-but-wrong-shape manifest therefore surfaces through the CLI's catch-all as a bare Python error that names neither the file nor the field — the exact failure mode #6854 filed for `scripts/research_workflow.py`'s profile/state/trigger inputs, in the sibling module #6854 did not cover (its scope was research_workflow.py only; package.json / list_ids / segments appear nowhere in it).

The rest of this tool family validates with `fail()` diagnostics that name the file and the expectation (e.g. sync_research_workflow.py's `load_json_object`: "expected a JSON object"; research_workflow.py's field-level `fail()` checks). This one read is the unguarded remainder.

## Verified this run (laptop probe, real CLI end-to-end, @65beb42c1a)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-rw-items` (research_workflow.py + research_workflow_items.py + research_workflow_live.py copied verbatim; package created through the real `init` CLI exactly as scripts/tests/test_research_workflow_items.py does; then `ids --package <pkg>` against crafted package.json files). Controls behave as designed:

| package.json | Observed |
|---|---|
| absent (control) | rc=0, ids listed, `segments: []` |
| `{"segments":[{"id":"S1"},{"id":"S2"}]}` (control) | rc=0, segments listed |
| `[{"id":"S1"}]` (list top level) | rc=1, `error: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'` |
| `"hello"` (string top level) | rc=1, `error: 'str' object has no attribute 'get'` |
| `{"segments":"S1S2"}` (segments as string) | rc=1, `error: string indices must be integers, not 'str'` |
| `{"segments":{"id":"S1"}}` (segments as object) | rc=1, `error: string indices must be integers, not 'str'` (iterates the object's keys) |
| `{"segments":[{"name":"x"}]}` (segment missing `id`) | rc=1, `error: 'id'` |
| `{"segments":["S1"]}` (segment as string) | rc=1, `error: string indices must be integers, not 'str'` |
| `not json` | rc=1, `error: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)` — no filename |

No case names package.json, the `segments` field, or the expected shape; the non-JSON case doesn't even name the file that failed to parse. (The CLI catches the exceptions, so there is no traceback — the defect is the undiagnosed message, same as #6854.)

## Why it matters

- `ids` is the inventory command operators and other workflow steps use to enumerate a package's concepts/items/segments; package.json is a hand-editable, generated-and-edited artifact inside every research package — exactly the kind of file that gets truncated, merged badly, or written by another tool in a slightly different shape.
- When that happens, the operator gets `'list' object has no attribute 'get'` with no indication that package.json is the malformed input, out of the several JSON files a package contains (state block, profile, transcripts, receipts). The tool family's whole contract is named diagnostics; this read breaks it.
- Sibling of #6854 (research_workflow.py inputs) and the #3068 parsed-is-not-validated pattern; the fix idiom already exists in the family (`fail()` / `load_json_object`).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `list_ids` validates the manifest before use: top level is a JSON object, `segments` (when present) is a list of objects each with a string `id`; any violation — including a non-JSON manifest — fails via the tool's `fail()` diagnostic naming package.json and the field/expectation, never a bare Attribute/Key/Type/JSONDecode message.
- [ ] Well-formed manifests (including a missing package.json and a manifest without `segments`) behave exactly as today.
- [ ] New tests in scripts/tests/test_research_workflow_items.py cover the probed wrong shapes (list/string top level, segments as string/object, segment missing `id`, segment as string, non-JSON) asserting the single-line `error: …` contract names package.json, plus the controls (oracle: the family's `fail()` diagnostic style, as in #6854).

```
$ research_workflow.py check --repo-root <root with .agents/research-workflow.json = []>
error: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'
```

— an operator cannot tell which file is malformed or what shape was expected.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ 65beb42c1a, real file verbatim, probe `~/git/fleet/probe-rw-shape/`)

Controls all behave as designed: a valid profile loads; a valid state block loads; a valid triggers array passes `check_profile`; a transcript hash mismatch fails cleanly via `fail()`.

Wrong shapes (all raw, none via `fail()`):

- `profile()` (research_workflow.py:79-80): profile JSON `[]`, `"x"`, `null`, `42` → `AttributeError: '<type>' object has no attribute 'get'` (the `.get("version")` check runs before any isinstance guard).
- `read_state()` (research_workflow.py:694-695): state block JSON `[]` / `"x"` / `null` → same raw `AttributeError`.
- `check_package()` transcript (research_workflow.py:753): `transcript` as a string → `TypeError: string indices must be integers`; `transcript` missing → `KeyError: 'transcript'`; `transcript` without `path` → `KeyError: 'path'`. (Unlike `events`/`stage`/`status`/`created_at`, which are validated with `fail()` just above at :741-751.)
- `check_package()` concepts: `concepts` as an object → `TypeError: string indices must be integers`; missing → `KeyError: 'concepts'`; a list of strings → `TypeError`.
- `dependencies()` (research_workflow.py:183-187): missing `dependencies` → `KeyError: 'dependencies'`; a string edge → `AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get'`; `concepts` as an object → `TypeError`.
- `check_profile()` trigger fixtures (research_workflow.py:950): the array itself is isinstance-checked (:948-949), but an entry that is a string → `AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get'` at `entry.get("skill")`.

## Why it matters

This tool is the checker for evidence-preserving research packages; its whole contract is precise, named diagnostics (`fail()` messages name the field and the expectation everywhere else). A hand-edited or partially-written profile/state block — exactly the corruption a checker exists to catch — instead produces a message that points at no file and no field, sending the operator to read the source to find which of the four JSON inputs is malformed. This is one more instance of the #3068 parsed-is-not-validated pattern, in a file that already has the right idiom (`fail()`) and applies it inconsistently.

## Acceptance criteria

- `profile()` rejects a non-object top level with `fail()` naming the profile file and the expected object shape, before the version check.
- `read_state()` rejects a non-object state block the same way, naming the package.
- `check_package()` validates `transcript` (object with string `path`/`sha256`), `concepts` (list of objects), and `dependencies` presence/type with `fail()` messages naming the field, before indexing them.
- `dependencies()` / `frontier()` and the `check_profile()` trigger-fixture loop validate edge/entry shapes with `fail()` instead of raw `.get` on unchecked values.
- Regression tests in `scripts/tests/test_research_workflow.py` cover each wrong shape above and assert the clean `fail()` diagnostic (and the CLI's `error: …` line names the field/file).
- Valid profile/state/triggers fixtures behave byte-identically to today (existing test suite green).

title: mcpx(gotest-report): go-test event lines and the stored skip record are shape-trusted — non-object events, null Package, and wrong-shape records crash the guard with raw tracebacks, and an empty-list record silently resets the ratchet

labels.name: kind/ci

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/mcpx/scripts/gotest-report.py` — the CI guard that holds skipped Go tests to the record stored on main — trusts the shape of both of its inputs:

1. the `go test -json` event file it parses line by line, and
2. the stored skip record (a repository variable) it compares against.

Neither is validated. A valid-JSON-but-non-object event line, a null/non-string field inside an event, or a wrong-shape stored record crashes the step with a raw traceback; one wrong shape (an empty-list stored record) is silently treated as "no record yet" and lets the run re-baseline the skip ceiling from scratch.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ 65beb42c1a, real file verbatim)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-gotest-shape/` (`gotest-report.py` copied verbatim from `origin/main`, driven through its real CLI entry). Controls (well-formed event file + well-formed record; and empty stored string for a first run) exit 0. Malformed inputs, all rc=1 with a raw traceback as the last line unless noted:

Event-file shapes (`read()`, gotest-report.py:31-60):

- an event line that is a bare number `123`, a string `"hello"`, or a list `[1,2]` → `AttributeError: '<type>' object has no attribute 'get'` at :41 — the `try` at :37-40 only catches `ValueError` from `json.loads`, not a successfully-parsed non-object
- an event with `"Package": null` and a `Test` → `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'rsplit'` at :47 (`e.get('Package', '')` returns `None` for an explicit null; the default only covers a missing key)
- an event with a non-string `Output` (e.g. `42`) on a skipped test → `AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'strip'` at :58

Stored-record shapes (`main()` :110, `decide()` :81-103):

- invalid JSON → unguarded `json.loads` at :110, `JSONDecodeError`
- record missing `skipped_count` → `KeyError: 'skipped_count'` at :99
- `skipped_count` a string → `TypeError: '>' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'str'` at :99
- `skipped` an int → `TypeError: 'int' object is not iterable` in `decide()` (:94 `set(stored.get("skipped", []))`)
- stored top-level `[]` → rc=0, **silently** treated as no record (`if not stored` in `decide()` :94 / `main()`), so the run becomes the new record and the skip ceiling resets without any warning

## Why it matters

This record is the ratchet that keeps skipped tests from creeping back (see #3313, #6391 for the guard's history). The event file is machine-generated, but it is assembled from matrix shards and tooling output in the workflow; one non-object line (a stray log line that happens to be valid JSON, a truncated/merged shard) currently kills the report step with a traceback that names neither the line nor the file. A corrupted or hand-edited record variable does the same — or worse, an empty-list value silently zeroes the ratchet. The sibling conformance guard has the same class of gap; the shard packer got this treatment in #6822.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `read()` skips (with a count surfaced in the summary or stderr) event lines that parse to a non-object, instead of crashing; non-string `Package`/`Output`/`Test`/`Action` fields are coerced-or-skipped under one stated rule, never an `AttributeError`.
- [ ] The stored record is validated before `decide()`: non-object top level, missing/non-int `skipped_count`, non-list-of-strings `skipped`, and invalid JSON each produce one named error identifying the record and field — and an empty list is an error, not "no record".
- [ ] No code path in `read`/`decide`/`main` can raise `KeyError`/`TypeError`/`AttributeError` on an input that passed validation.
- [ ] Tests in `pkgs/mcpx/scripts/test_gotest_report.py` cover the shapes above; existing tests and the well-formed controls still pass.
- [ ] Behaviour for well-formed event files and records (including the first-run empty-string case) is unchanged.

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/mcpx/scripts/conformance-record.py` compares each conformance run against the best/largest records stored in a GitHub repository variable, but it never validates the shape of that stored JSON — or of the skipped-names JSON passed as argv[13] — before indexing, comparing, and doing arithmetic on it. Any wrong-shape value crashes the step with a raw Python traceback (no leg, no field, no recovery path), and three wrong shapes are silently *misinterpreted* instead of rejected, so the record the whole skip-guard depends on can be quietly re-baselined onto nonsense.

The stored value is operator-editable (a repo variable), can be truncated or hand-patched (the file's own header notes a record was once "patched in place into a mix of two runs"), and is exactly the kind of input that drifts. Today a single bad edit wedges every conformance leg until someone fixes the variable by hand, with only a traceback to go on.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ 65beb42c1a, real file verbatim)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-conformance-shape/` (`conformance-record.py` copied verbatim from `origin/main`, driven through its real CLI entry exactly as `.github/workflows/mcpx-conformance.yml` calls it). Controls (valid stored record, valid names, matching names) exit 0. Malformed inputs:

Crashes (all rc=1, raw traceback as the last line):

- stored top-level string `"hello"` → `AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get'`
- stored top-level non-empty list / int → `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'` / `TypeError: argument of type 'int' is not a container or iterable` (`complete()`, conformance-record.py:92-98)
- stored invalid JSON (`{oops`) → unguarded `json.loads` at :218, `JSONDecodeError`
- `best` is a string → `AttributeError` in `total()`/`describe()` (:69-84); `best` is an int → `TypeError` in `complete()` (:92)
- `best.passed_count` is a string → `TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str` in `total()` (:71)
- `best.skipped_count` is a string → `TypeError: '>' not supported` at the skip guard (:142)
- `best.skipped` is an int → `TypeError: 'int' object is not iterable` at the #6392 set comparison (:140)
- `largest` is an int → `TypeError` in `complete()`/`total()`
- names argv is an int (`123`) → `TypeError: 'int' object is not iterable` in `record()` `sorted(names)` (:65)
- names argv is a list containing an int → `TypeError: sequence item 0: expected str instance, int found`

Silent misinterpretations (rc=0, wrong semantics):

- names argv is a string `"abc"` → treated as an iterable of characters; the written record's `skipped` list becomes `['a','b','c']`
- names argv is an object `{"a":1}` → treated as its keys; `skipped` becomes `['a']`
- `best.skipped` is a string `"abcde"` → the #6392 newly-skipped set comparison compares *character* sets, so a run skipping `["a"]` reads as no-change

## Why it matters

This script is the gate that stops skipped conformance checks from creeping back (#6392 hardened its set comparison). A gate that dies with a traceback on a malformed record fails every leg opaquely; a gate that silently treats a string as a set of characters can absorb a wrong record and re-baseline `best` onto it, defeating the guard without any signal. The neighbouring guard scripts have been getting exactly this shape treatment (e.g. #6822 for the shard packer); this one was missed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `validate_stored` (or equivalent) step rejects, with one named error identifying the leg and the offending field: non-object top level; `best`/`largest` present but not objects; count fields (`passed_count`, `failed_count`, `total_count`, `skipped_count`, `warning_count`, `info_count`) present but not non-negative ints (bools excluded); `skipped` present but not a list of strings; non-string timestamps/run.
- [ ] Invalid stored JSON produces the same named error, not a `JSONDecodeError` traceback.
- [ ] The skipped-names argv is validated as a JSON list of strings before use; a string/object/int there is a named error, never iterated as characters/keys.
- [ ] No code path in `compare`/`total`/`describe`/`bad`/`complete` can raise `TypeError`/`AttributeError`/`KeyError` on a stored value that passed validation.
- [ ] Tests in `pkgs/mcpx/scripts/test_conformance_record.py` cover the shapes above (crash set + silent set); existing tests and the valid-record controls still pass.
- [ ] Behaviour for well-formed current and legacy (pre-`total_count`/`skipped_count`) records is unchanged.

title: cold-store-reaper: token-endpoint responses are parsed unguarded — a wrong-shape 200 from access_token/auth_exchange raises raw KeyError/TypeError/JSONDecodeError, not ColdStoreError

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.description: Package/app: cold-store-reaper (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/cold-store-reaper/cold_store.py` parses the OAuth token endpoint's
HTTP-200 responses with a bare `json.loads(resp)` and unchecked field
access in both auth flows — the exact assumption the D1 paths in the same
file were hardened against in issue #2618 (which added the guarded
`_d1_parse_payload` helper at :259-285). The token paths never got it:

- `auth_exchange` (:648, payload at :667): `payload.get("refresh_token")`
  on whatever `json.loads` returned. A list body raises a raw
  `AttributeError`; a non-JSON 200 body raises a raw `JSONDecodeError`.
  (A dict body missing `refresh_token` *is* handled with a named
  `ColdStoreError` — the intended pattern, already present one line down.)
- `access_token` (:678, payload at :708): the payload is subscripted for
  the token field and `expires_in` is added to the current timestamp with
  no shape checks at all:
  - dict body missing the token field → raw `KeyError`
  - list body → raw `TypeError: list indices must be integers`;
    string body → raw `TypeError: string indices must be integers`
  - non-JSON 200 body → raw `JSONDecodeError`
  - `expires_in` as a string or `null` → raw `TypeError: unsupported
    operand type(s) for +: 'float' and 'str'/'NoneType'` when computing
    the in-memory expiry
  - a non-string token value (e.g. `123`) is returned unchecked and flows
    into the `Authorization: Bearer …` header built by `_auth_headers`

Every cold-store command goes through `access_token()` before touching
Drive/S3/D1, so a shape-drifted 200 from the token endpoint (or an
intermediary/proxy answering in its place — the transport layer in this
same file documents exactly that class of intermediary misbehavior for
S3) kills the run with a traceback that names neither the endpoint nor
the unexpected shape, instead of the module's own `ColdStoreError`.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop primary `~/git/code` at origin/main
`65beb42c1a70672bed159fe401c2cb1079aa516f`. Probe:
`~/git/fleet/probe-cold-store-state/probe_token.py` (+ `probe_token2.py`)
against the real `cold_store.py` copied verbatim from origin/main
(sha256 `39a1ecb1a8ff10dedcb59538cc6d2691d7a264e3def2afcb41963240dea27f2d`),
with `http_request` stubbed to return HTTP 200 with canned bodies and a
fixture credentials file — no network, no real credentials.

Controls (as expected):
- `access_token` with `{"access_token": "…", "expires_in": 3600}` → token
  returned, expiry set
- `auth_exchange` with a dict carrying `refresh_token` → stored, returned
  summary; dict *without* `refresh_token` → named `ColdStoreError`
  (re-run-the-grant guidance)

Failing shapes:
- `access_token`: missing token field → raw `KeyError`; token `123` →
  returned unchecked; `expires_in` `"3600"` or `null` → raw `TypeError`;
  body `[]` / `"hello"` → raw `TypeError`; body `not json` → raw
  `JSONDecodeError`
- `auth_exchange`: body `[]` → raw `AttributeError: 'list' object has no
  attribute 'get'`; body `not json` → raw `JSONDecodeError`

Dedup: searched open + closed issues for `cold-store token response
shape`, `access_token ColdStoreError` — no hits. Issue #2618 covers only
the D1 response paths (`d1_error_message` / `_d1_select` / sync loop) and
its fix added `_d1_parse_payload` in this same file; the token-endpoint
paths at :667/:708 do not use it. Issue #6845 (filed this run) covers the
*local files* `load_state`/`load_credentials`, a different input surface.

## Why it matters

`access_token()` is on the critical path of every command. When the token
endpoint's 200 body drifts in shape, the operator currently gets a raw
`KeyError`/`TypeError`/`JSONDecodeError` with no indication that the
token response was the problem — and a non-string token silently
propagates into the Authorization header of every subsequent request.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both token-response parses (`auth_exchange` :667, `access_token`
      :708) validate the payload shape — reusing or mirroring the
      `_d1_parse_payload` pattern from #2618 — so a non-JSON or
      non-object 200 body raises a `ColdStoreError` naming the token
      endpoint and the unexpected shape; no raw
      `JSONDecodeError`/`AttributeError`/`TypeError` escapes.
- [ ] `access_token`: a missing or non-string token field raises the
      named `ColdStoreError`; a present `expires_in` must be a number —
      a string/`null`/object value raises the named error instead of a
      raw arithmetic `TypeError` (absent `expires_in` keeps the existing
      3600 default).
- [ ] `auth_exchange`: the existing missing-`refresh_token`
      `ColdStoreError` behaviour is preserved, and a non-string
      `refresh_token` value is refused the same way rather than written
      into `credentials.json`.
- [ ] New tests in `pkgs/cold-store-reaper/tests/test_cold_store.py`
      (transport stubbed, as in the probe) cover: non-JSON body, list
      body, missing token field, non-string token, string/`null`
      `expires_in` for `access_token`; list body and non-JSON body for
      `auth_exchange`; happy-path controls still pass.
- [ ] The full cold-store test suite passes (laptop or CI).

body:
# github-backup(inventory): inventory_owner pagination never terminates on a non-advancing cursor — hasNextPage is trusted with no progress check, page bound, or node-shape guard

## Evidence

`infra/github-backup/bin/ghb_common.py`, `inventory_owner` (verified on laptop at origin/main `f74a3dea13`):

```python
# ghb_common.py:71
while True:
    ...
    # ghb_common.py:126-127
    if conn["pageInfo"]["hasNextPage"]:
        after = conn["pageInfo"]["endCursor"]
    else:
        return repos
```

The loop's only exit is `hasNextPage` becoming false. The cursor is never checked for progress: if a page reports `hasNextPage: true` with `endCursor: null`, the next iteration re-requests the first page (`after=None`); if `endCursor` repeats the cursor just used, the same page is re-fetched forever. There is no page cap. Each iteration is a real `gh api graphql` call and appends the same repos to the result list again, so the loop also grows memory unboundedly.

Node handling in the same loop is unguarded (`ghb_common.py:113`): `n["nameWithOwner"]` is subscripted directly, so a null node or a node missing the field raises mid-loop.

## Verified this run (probe on the laptop, real `ghb_common.py` verbatim, `run` stubbed with canned GraphQL pages; probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-ghb-inventory-pagination`)

- Control (page 1 `hasNextPage=true, endCursor=CURSOR1`, page 2 `hasNextPage=false`): returned 2 repos in 2 calls — terminates correctly.
- `hasNextPage=true, endCursor=null` on every page: **never returned** — exceeded 200 stubbed `gh` calls and was still looping when the probe aborted it.
- `hasNextPage=true, endCursor=CURSOR1` (never advances): **never returned** — same >200 calls.
- A `null` entry in `nodes`: `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable` — the whole owner's inventory raises.
- A node missing `nameWithOwner`: `KeyError: 'nameWithOwner'` — same whole-owner failure.

## Why it matters

- The only caller is the weekly reconcile sweep (`reconcile.py:79` → `inventory(cfg["owners"])`, `github-backup-reconcile.service`, `Type=oneshot`, no timeout set in the unit). A non-advancing cursor wedges that sweep forever: plan.json is never rewritten, no error is recorded, and the run issues one GraphQL request per iteration indefinitely (API quota burn).
- The failure mode bypasses the system's own safety net: reconcile's last-known-good retention (#3229, `reconcile.py:87+`) engages only when `inventory()` records an owner *error* (a raised exception). A hang raises nothing, so the protection never engages and nothing alerts.
- The node-shape crashes are the milder sibling: one malformed node fails the *entire* owner's inventory (caught per-owner by `inventory()`, so the owner falls back to last-known-good and never refreshes while the shape persists), instead of the bad node being named and skipped under the #6637 poison-entry discipline the rest of this system already follows.

## Acceptance criteria

- `inventory_owner` raises a named `RuntimeError` (so `inventory()` records an owner error and reconcile's last-known-good path engages) when a page reports `hasNextPage` with an `endCursor` that is null/empty or equal to the cursor used for that page — i.e. pagination must prove progress on every iteration.
- A hard page bound (generous, e.g. well above the largest owner's real page count) backstops the loop even if cursor semantics change again.
- A null node, or a node without a string `nameWithOwner`, is named and skipped (or fails the owner with a named shape error) — it must not surface as a raw `TypeError`/`KeyError` traceback from the subscript.
- Tests in `infra/github-backup/tests/test_inventory_owner.py` (stubbed-`run` style already used there): null-cursor page, stuck-cursor page, null node, and missing-field node cases, plus the existing terminating two-page control still passing.
- The existing inventory tests and the github-backup test workflow stay green.

body:
## Gap: the Turso queue backend has no revive/requeue verb

Found during the dead-at-cap requeue pass (2026-11-07) executing the staged evaluation in #6463 against `fleet-queue`.

**What exists:** `fleet queue` verbs on the Turso backend (`turso_queue.rs`): enqueue, claim, lane, bind, heartbeat, checkpoint, park, block, cancel, fail, complete, list, health, signal, events-*. `verb_fail` only requeues a *claimed* task on transient failure while attempts remain.

**What's missing:** any supported way to revive a `queued` task whose `attempts >= max_attempts` (the silent-zombie state #6463 is about — 231 such rows fleet-wide at the 2026-11-07 census). Specifically:

1. No `revive`/`requeue` verb that resets `attempts` (and clears `last_error`) on a queued row with an audit event.
2. `verb_enqueue`'s dedupe lookup (`WHERE queue = ? AND dedupe_key = ?`) has **no status predicate** — it returns the existing row even when that row is `cancelled`/`done`/`failed`. The PG backend's revive-on-enqueue semantics (only live rows dedupe-match) were not ported, so cancel + re-enqueue of the same packet silently returns the dead row instead of creating a fresh task.

**Impact:** the 2026-11-07 requeue pass had to reset attempts via direct SQL against fleet-queue (queued rows only, guard predicates `status='queued' AND attempts>=max_attempts`, one `revived` event row per task) because no verb path exists. Cancellations of superseded tasks did go through the `cancel` verb.

**Ask:** add a `revive` verb (task id + worker + reason → attempts=0, not_before=now or supplied, last_error=NULL, `revived` event) and make enqueue's dedupe match only non-terminal rows (reviving/resetting per the PG semantics), with tests naming the oracle (the PG migration-0023 behavior).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A supported broker verb (revive/requeue) resets attempts and clears last_error on a queued dead-at-cap task, with an audit event recorded
- [ ] Enqueue dedupe matches only live rows (queued/claimed/parked/blocked): re-enqueueing a packet whose previous row is cancelled/done/failed creates a fresh task instead of returning the terminal row
- [ ] The fleet monitor's dead-in-queue self-repair (Duty 1 addendum) can be re-pointed from direct SQL to the new verb

# github-backup(drain): drain_queue reads plan.json/state.json with bare json.load — the one consumer bypassing validate_plan/validate_state, and its own drain_* keys crash it

## Evidence

Verified on the laptop at origin/main `e380645a3b7c94e47dabda544564d7fd89c75416`. Every other github-backup consumer of plan.json/state.json now goes through the #6637 shared gates (`ghb_common.load_plan` / `load_state` → `validate_plan` / `validate_state`): fetch_mirrors, clone_all, manifest, and (after #6831 is fixed) reconcile. `infra/github-backup/bin/drain_queue.py` — the 5-minute webhook drainer — imports only `load_config, backup_root` from ghb_common and reads both files raw:

- `drain_queue.py:217` — `state = json.load(open(state_path))` with no shape check.
- `drain_queue.py:227` — `planned = {p["repo"] for p in json.load(open(plan_path))}` subscripts every plan entry unguarded, before any event is processed.

Crash sites on wrong-shape (valid JSON) input:

- Plan entry `"o/r1"` (string) → `TypeError: string indices must be integers`; entry `123` → `TypeError: 'int' object is not subscriptable`; top-level dict → same string-indices error. The planned set never builds, so no queued event is fetched, acked, or even logged — every 5-minute drain tick re-crashes identically until plan.json is hand-fixed.
- State top-level `[]` → `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'` at `drain_queue.py:275` (`state.get(key, 0)`).
- `drain_last::<repo>` as a string or dict → `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for -: 'float' and 'str'` at `drain_queue.py:275` (`now - state.get(key, 0)`). This is the drainer's OWN key: `validate_state` already validates `drain_last::*` as a non-bool number and `drain_fail::*` as an object (ghb_common.py, #6637) — the drainer is the one consumer that never calls it.
- `drain_fail::<repo>` as an int or string, on a fetch failure → `state.setdefault(fkey, {...})` at `drain_queue.py:288` returns the poisoned value, then `fs["count"] += 1` raises `TypeError: 'int' object is not subscriptable` / `string indices must be integers`. The failure is never counted, the DRAIN-CHRONIC escalation never fires, state.json is never rewritten, and the event's ack decision is lost with the run.

Probe (laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-ghb-drain-plan-state/probe.py`, real `drain_queue.main` from origin/main with config/root/queue stubbed to temp files and one queued event for a planned repo; fetch stubbed only where noted):

- Control (valid plan + `{}` state) → rc=0, event fetched+acked.
- Plan entry string / int / top-level dict → the three TypeErrors above.
- State top-level list → AttributeError; `drain_last` string/dict → TypeError at the coalesce subtraction.
- `drain_fail` int/string with fetch returning "fail" → TypeError at the failure counter; `drain_fail` dict control → rc=0, consecutive_failures=2 recorded correctly.

## Why it matters

The drainer is the estate's highest-frequency consumer (every 5 minutes) and the only path that turns webhook events into fetches. A single poison entry in plan.json or state.json — hand edit, older/newer writer, torn write per #3240 — wedges every tick: mirrors stop reflecting pushes, the Worker queue grows unbounded, and because the crash precedes all logging/acking, the failure presents as silence rather than an alarm. The irony is load-bearing: the shared validators were extended in #6637 specifically to cover the drainer's `drain_last::`/`drain_fail::` key shapes, and fetch/clone/manifest all use them — the drainer itself is the remaining bypass, the same pattern as #6831 (reconcile's previous-plan read) but in the live event path.

Distinct from: #6575 (queue EVENT shape inside the drainer — validated separately), #6831 (reconcile.py's previous-plan read), #6637 (built the validators + fixed fetch), #6821 (fetch's `last_fetch` arithmetic on validated state). None touches drain_queue's plan/state loading.

## Acceptance criteria

- `drain_queue.main` loads plan and state through `ghb_common.load_plan` / `load_state` (or equivalent validation with `report_problems`), so a wrong-shape entry is named on stderr and skipped/reset instead of crashing the tick.
- With a poisoned plan entry, the drainer still processes events for the valid planned repos (fetch/ack/coalesce behavior unchanged) and prints its JSON summary.
- With a wrong-shape `drain_last::<repo>` or `drain_fail::<repo>`, the entry is reported and treated as absent (coalesce window not applied / failure count starts fresh), state.json is rewritten clean at the end of the run, and the DRAIN-CHRONIC path still works for genuine repeated failures.
- Regression tests in `infra/github-backup/tests/` cover the probed shapes (string/int plan entry, dict top-level plan, list top-level state, string/dict drain_last, int/string drain_fail) against the real `drain_queue.main`, plus the valid controls; the existing github-backup suite stays green.

body:
# github-backup(clone_all+manifest): a wrong-shape `reference`/`branch` field passes validate_plan and crashes both consumers — the #6637 gate checks only `repo`

## Evidence

Verified on the laptop at origin/main `e380645a3b7c94e47dabda544564d7fd89c75416`. `ghb_common.validate_plan` (`infra/github-backup/bin/ghb_common.py:149-165`, the #6637 gate every plan consumer now shares via `load_plan`) validates exactly one field: an entry is kept iff it is a dict with a string `repo`. The other plan fields consumers actually compute with — `reference` and `branch` — pass through at any JSON shape.

Consumers that break on those fields:

- `infra/github-backup/bin/clone_all.py:202-214` — the main-thread scheduler does `state.get(ref)` (and later `state.get(ref) == "ok"`) on `p.get("reference")`. A list or dict `reference` is unhashable: `TypeError: cannot use 'list' as a dict key`. The crash is in the scheduling loop, not in a worker thread, so the whole clone run dies: remaining pending repos are never submitted, in-flight results are never recorded to `clone-status.jsonl`, and no `DONE` summary prints.
- `infra/github-backup/bin/clone_all.py:147-149` — `mirror_path(root, ref)` would also fail on a non-string reference (`ref + ".git"`), but the scheduler crash fires first.
- `infra/github-backup/bin/manifest.py:58` — `families.setdefault(item["reference"], [])` raises the same unhashable `TypeError` for a list/dict reference; `MANIFEST.json` and `FAMILIES.md` are never rewritten.
- `infra/github-backup/bin/manifest.py:81` — `sorted(families)`: a numeric reference alongside string references raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'`; a lone numeric reference silently writes `## anchor: 123` into FAMILIES.md.
- `infra/github-backup/bin/manifest.py:15-16,50` — `head_sha(path, item.get("branch"))` builds `"refs/heads/" + branch`; a non-string branch (int, list) on a repo whose mirror is present raises `TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str`.

Probe (laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-ghb-reference-shape/probe.py` + `probe2.py`, real `ghb_common` / `clone_all` / `manifest` modules from origin/main, temp roots, controls included):

- `validate_plan([{repo, reference: [..]}, {repo, reference: {..}}, {repo, reference: "o/anchor"}])` → kept=3, problems=[] — the gate is blind to the field shape.
- `clone_all.main` with `reference: ["o/anchor"]` → `TypeError: cannot use 'list' as a dict key (unhashable type: 'list')`; with `reference: {"x": 1}` → same for dict. String and null reference controls complete the run normally.
- `manifest.build` with list/dict reference → same unhashable `TypeError`, no manifest written; string control → `OK totals={'mirrored': 0, 'missing': 1, 'disk_kb': 0}`.
- `manifest.build` with references `123` + `"o/anchor"` in one plan → `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'` at the `sorted(families)` pass.
- `manifest.build` with a present bare mirror and `branch: 123` / `branch: ["main"]` → `TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str`; `branch: "main"` control → OK, mirrored=1.

## Why it matters

plan.json is the shared input to the clone driver and the manifest regenerator, and it is exactly the file class the estate keeps poisoning itself with (hand edits, older/newer writers, torn writes per #3240). #6637 hardened the entry level and #6821 the `last_fetch` field of state entries, but the plan's own field level was never validated: one wrong-shape `reference` wedges the resumable clone driver for every repo (not just the poisoned one) and separately wedges MANIFEST regeneration — the disaster-recovery source of record — on every subsequent run until someone hand-edits the JSON. A numeric reference is worse in one way: it does not crash clone_all at all (it is silently ignored there), so the corruption is invisible until manifest's mixed-type sort or a bogus FAMILIES.md anchor surfaces it.

Distinct from: #6637 (plan entry-level shape + state fail_days/drain_*), #6821 (state `last_fetch` field, fetch consumer), #6653 (manifest entry-level, fixed via load_plan), #6831 (reconcile reading the previous plan bypassing validate_plan), #6822/#6814 (other repos' seed/artifact field shapes). None validates the plan `reference`/`branch` fields.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validate_plan` validates the consumed plan fields: `reference` and `branch` (and `parent`, copied into the manifest) must be strings or null/absent; a wrong-shape field produces a named problem via `report_problems` and is neutralized (field dropped to None, or the entry skipped with the entry named — either contract is acceptable if explicit and tested), never passed through to a consumer.
- With such a plan file, `clone_all.main` completes its scheduling loop (poisoned entries/repos are reported, other repos still clone or fail on their own merits, `DONE` prints) and `manifest.build` still writes `MANIFEST.json` + `FAMILIES.md`.
- A numeric `reference` can no longer produce a bogus `## anchor: 123` family or a mixed-type sort crash.
- Regression tests in `infra/github-backup/tests/` (extending `test_plan_state_shape.py` and the manifest/clone tests) cover list/dict/int `reference`, int/list `branch` with a present mirror, and the string/null controls; the existing github-backup suite stays green.

body:
Credential-scope smell, confirmed during the #5691 repoint (see TURSO-MIGRATION.md 2026-11-06 bullet-4 entry) and re-verified in the 2026-11-07 rename program (#6619).

~/tools/quota-check/JOB-BODY.md says the mirror reads use per-DB tokens by BWS name (turso.fleet-platform-rw-token / turso.fleet-mirror-rw-token, renamed 2026-11-07). In practice the reads go through `~/tools/bin/turso db shell <db>`, which authenticates with the turso CLI's PLATFORM token — one credential that can reach every database in the org. So:
- The per-DB tokens named in the job body are decorative on this route; rotating or revoking them does not change quota-check's access.
- A quota-check run holds org-wide DB authority when it only needs read access to two DBs (agent_quota_records on fleet-platform, agent_mirror_token_usage_daily on fleet-mirror).

Fix direction: make the quota-check reads use the per-DB tokens over the libsql HTTP pipeline (the pattern runtime-db-export's turso_client.py already implements, including its direct-BWS fallback for broker staleness #6767), or explicitly accept and document the platform-token route in the job body so the named tokens stop implying a scope they do not enforce.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] quota-check's mirror reads authenticate with the per-DB BWS tokens named in its job body (turso.fleet-platform-rw-token / turso.fleet-mirror-rw-token) over the libsql HTTP pipeline, OR the job body is explicitly corrected to document the platform-token route as accepted.
- [ ] If the per-DB route is adopted: revoking/rotating a per-DB token demonstrably changes quota-check's access to that DB only, and a quota-check run succeeds end-to-end on the new route.
- [ ] No quota-check run needs org-wide platform-token authority for its routine reads.

title: fleet-proxy: connect/init spawn a detached broker before shims_dir is validated — a shim-path failure leaves the broker running (PR #6444)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.name: source/pr-comment-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-comment-review job

labels.name: app/fleet
labels.description: pkgs/fleet multicall binary + platform crates

body:
## Finding (unaddressed PR review comment)

PR #6444 (open, fleet-config HOME-resolution change) also touches the fleet proxy connect/init flows. CodeRabbit flagged that those flows start the session broker before the shim path is validated, so a shim-path resolution failure leaves a detached broker running.

- Source PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/6444
- Review comment: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/6444#discussion_r4489204567
- Reviewer: coderabbitai[bot], 2026-11-06T05:02:28Z, Minor (Stability & Availability), at `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/client.rs:229`
- Essence: "Resolve and validate the shim path with `Config::shims_dir` before starting the broker in the connect and init flows, propagating resolution failures through the existing ClientError handling. Ensure an invalid or unavailable shim path cannot leave a broker running."

## No-response evidence

- The comment thread has no replies and is unresolved (GraphQL `reviewThreads` verified this run).
- The PR's 2026-11-07 rebase (head `932ca5b212829a4260c1224650d8a3dd1c371d61`) did not change this ordering and did not disposition the comment.
- Comment is >24h old, so the open-PR grace period has expired.

## Still-live evidence (verified on current PR head 932ca5b212 this run)

- `run_connect` (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/client.rs:379`) calls `ensure_broker(...)` - which spawns the detached broker via `spawn_serve` when none answers - and only afterwards calls `sync_shims_from(&services)` (:390), whose first shim step resolves `Config::shims_dir()` (:229) and can fail with `?`, after the broker is already running.
- `run_init` has the same order: `ensure_broker` at :511, `sync_shims_from` at :516. Neither flow resolves/validates `shims_dir` before the spawn.
- Dedupe: searched open and closed issues by file path and keywords (`shims_dir broker`) - no issue covers this ordering defect.

## Acceptance criteria

- In both connect and init flows, resolve and validate the shim path before any broker spawn, propagating failures through the existing `ClientError` handling, so an invalid/unavailable shim path cannot leave a broker running; or resolve by a documented decision on this issue.
- Do not reply to or resolve the source PR review thread from this issue.

body:
Found by lane code-n while verifying #2859 on the laptop (2026-11-07).

TestTargetBearerTokenResolvesTheTargetDaemon (pkgs/mcpx/internal/cli/bearer_test.go) fails deterministically when the operator environment carries a real MCPX_CONFIG (on amd-6: MCPX_CONFIG=/nix/store/...-mcpx-config.json, the fleet's own deployed config):

    bearer_test.go:170: inherited targetBearerToken = "", true; want the parent config's token

The inherited-token case builds a parent/sub .mcpx.json chain in t.TempDir() and expects targetBearerToken to walk up to the parent file; the ambient MCPX_CONFIG short-circuits that resolution and the test reads the operator config instead. With env -u MCPX_CONFIG the test passes on both current main and PR #2714's head (verified this run).

Impact: any worker/operator machine with a real mcpx deployment exports MCPX_CONFIG, so the package suite reports a false failure there — it cost a full stress-verification cycle on #2859 before the env leak was identified. CI is unaffected (no MCPX_CONFIG), which is why this only bites locally.

Acceptance criteria:
- [ ] The test (and any sibling config-resolution tests in internal/cli with the same exposure) isolates MCPX_CONFIG (and equivalent config-path env vars) via t.Setenv, so the suite result does not depend on the host operator config.
- [ ] go test ./internal/cli -run TestTargetBearerTokenResolvesTheTargetDaemon passes WITH a realistic MCPX_CONFIG set in the environment.
