body:
## Port the PG pg_cron queue sweepers to the Turso backend

Follow-up from the Turso queue cutover (#6741, runbook `doc/fleet/queue-turso-cutover.md` deviations 3–5). On Postgres, pg_cron ran three queue jobs inside muse-dev2; the Turso backend covers only the first, and only lazily:

1. `expire_leases` — PORTED, but it runs inside `claim_repo_task` (as in the PG function body). PG also ran it standalone every minute (`agent-expire-leases`). Effect of the gap: expired leases sit until the next claim against any queue (expire is global, so any claim sweeps all queues — the practical gap is small but real when no claims happen).
2. `revalidate_parked_tasks` (daily, `park-revalidation-daily`) — NOT ported: parked tasks whose ready conditions are non-time-based never auto-release in Turso mode. Time parks already release through claim at `not_before`.
3. `prune_events` (daily, `agent-prune-events`, 30-day retention) — NOT ported: the Turso `events` table grows unbounded.

**Work:** add a broker-side periodic task (or a small systemd timer driving a fleet verb) that runs expire_leases on a cadence, revalidates parked tasks per the PG ready-condition semantics (recovered shapes are in the park implementation in `turso_queue.rs`), and prunes `events` older than 30 days. Keep the semantics identical to the PG bodies where they were recovered; note any deviation on this issue.

**Acceptance:** with the sweeper live, (a) a task claimed with a short lease returns to `queued` without any intervening claim, (b) a parked task with a satisfiable non-time ready condition releases, (c) `events` rows older than 30 days are deleted and newer rows untouched — each proven against the live `fleet-queue` DB with readback.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A broker-side periodic mechanism runs lease expiry on a schedule (not only lazily inside claim), demonstrated by an expired lease being swept while no claims occur
- [ ] Parked tasks with non-time ready conditions are revalidated on a schedule in Turso mode, or the gap is explicitly accepted and recorded with reasoning
- [ ] The Turso events table is pruned to the 30-day retention the PG agent-prune-events job enforced, with the prune observable in logs/metrics

title: fleet-paperwork: create dedupe matches PRs — a same-titled PR is reported as 'already filed' and the issue is never created

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/fleet-paperwork
labels.description: Package/app: fleet-paperwork (infra/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

`fleet_paperwork.py create` — the rate-limit fallback path the fleet files issues through as the developing.today GitHub App — can silently refuse to create an issue because a **pull request** shares its exact title.

`find_by_exact_title` (`infra/fleet-paperwork/fleet_paperwork.py:282-291`) queries the Search API with `repo:{repo} "{title}"` and returns the first item whose title is byte-equal. The `/search/issues` index contains pull requests as well as issues (PR items carry a `pull_request` key); the query has no `type:issue` qualifier and the filter never excludes PR items. `cmd_create` (lines 326-338) treats any hit as a dedupe hit: it prints `already filed: <repo>#<number>` — the PR's number — and returns 0 having created nothing.

PR titles in this repo routinely copy the issue title they implement, so the collision is realistic exactly in the fallback path's busiest case: filing a follow-up while a same-titled PR is open.

Secondary gap in the same function: the lookup is a single page of `per_page=20`, and the search matches title **and body** text, so more than 20 phrase matches can push the one byte-exact issue past the page — dedupe misses and a duplicate is created instead.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ f76f83f2e8)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-paperwork-dedupe/probe.py` (laptop) loads the real `fleet_paperwork.py`, stubs `http` to return one search item that is a PR (exact title, `pull_request` key present, as the real Search API returns), and calls `find_by_exact_title`:

```
query path: /search/issues?q=repo%3Adeveloping-today/code%20%22id%3A%20exact%20title%20shared%20with%20a%20PR%22&per_page=20
dedupe hit: (4242, True)
VERDICT: BUG: a PR is returned as an already-filed issue; cmd_create would print already filed and create nothing
```

The existing test does not catch this: `TestExactTitleFilter.test_exact_match_only` (`infra/fleet-paperwork/tests/test_fleet_paperwork.py:103`) never calls `find_by_exact_title` — it reimplements the title comparison inline on hand-built dicts with no `pull_request` items.

## Why it matters

This tool is the fleet's documented fallback when the user token hits GitHub's secondary rate limit (rule: App first, outbox second). A fallback that exits 0 while creating nothing is the worst failure shape for it — the filing agent records success and moves on, and the issue simply never exists. Its own header promises the opposite: "a filing is verified, or it is a failure."

## Acceptance criteria

- `find_by_exact_title` never returns a pull request: add `type:issue` to the search query and/or skip items carrying a `pull_request` key (belt and braces — the filter, not just the query, states the contract).
- The dedupe lookup is not silently limited to the first 20 matches: paginate (or otherwise bound honestly) until the exact-title issue would be found.
- `cmd_create`'s "already filed" output names an issue, verified as one on readback.
- Tests in `infra/fleet-paperwork/tests/test_fleet_paperwork.py` call the real `find_by_exact_title` with a stubbed `http`: a same-titled PR item is not a hit; a same-titled issue past 20 non-exact matches is found; the current exact-match behavior for issues is preserved. Oracle: the stubbed Search-API payloads, shaped as GitHub actually returns them.

body:
## Design: a reply is not its defaults — one validated-reply contract for the WorldClient

`WorldClient` (`pkgs/id/src/world_net.rs`) turns each host JSON reply into the caller's answer, but the file never stated what a reply owes the client. Its readers split in two: a strict population that refuses malformed success replies in the file's own vocabulary (`invite`, `install_wasm`, `set_schedule`, `metrics`, `set_isolation`), and a lax population that manufactures the answer out of defaults, verbatim clones, and dropped entries — where every default is also a real value (sequence 0, `created: false`, `""`, `null`, `None`), so a fabricated answer is indistinguishable from a real one. Ten filings in three days landed on the lax population, one per method, each with a scripted-host probe. Two siblings were fixed while the family filed and are the contract's embodiments: #6633 (`info_details` optional-field match-and-bail, in snapshot 4ecb3510c) and #6635 (`execution_profile` extraction of `update.requested`).

Design doc: `files/designs/code-worldnet-reply-validation.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Audit at origin/main a6951e692.

### The contract

1. **A field that constitutes the answer is required and typed.** Missing/mistyped is a malformed-reply error naming the field, in the file's existing style. Success fields are never defaulted.
2. **Optional means absent-or-null, never mistyped.** The #6633 shape: absent/null => None, correctly typed => Some, anything else => the rule-1 error. Presence is checked before type (the #240 hidden seed stays legitimate).
3. **Typed payloads are decoded at extraction, not cloned.** `CapsReport`, `WorldPolicy`, and peers are validated by decoding at the `WorldClient` seam; on success the method returns what callers already consume (validate-then-return), so no caller changes shape.
4. **A list reply's entries are part of the answer.** A malformed entry fails the listing naming the entry/field — complete, or it errors (the #6622 rule applied to entries).
5. **Extraction lives in `WorldClient`, never in callers.** The caller-side duplicate decodes (`commands/world.rs:1119/1231`) are how the strict/lax split hid.

Wire and host unchanged: `ServerFrame` already states every shape. Alternatives (caller-side validation, typed returns everywhere, partial listings with drop counts, lenient-plus-logging) are considered and rejected in the design doc.

### Phases (adopted origins — no parallel filings)

- **Phase 1 — defaulted scalars:** #6620 (compile), #6632 (create_world), #6647 (worlds `default`).
- **Phase 2 — typed payloads on admin paths:** #6624 (caps/update_caps report), #6636 (set_caps_ceiling report), #6625 (policy_request).

title: fleet-queue(fallback): a contested claim never expires — the fold ignores the lease, the holder cannot heartbeat, and a dead holder bricks the issue for the whole outage

body:
## Problem

In the new GitHub-native queue fallback mode (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/fallback.rs`, merged in PR #6654 for #6619), a **contested claim never expires**. Once a second worker's claim marker lands while a claim is live, the issue is bricked in fallback mode:

- `fold_claim` returns `ClaimState::Contested` whenever a contest was recorded and a holder exists (fallback.rs:448-455) — before and regardless of the lease-age check at :460. Lease expiry, the mode's only recovery mechanism ("If no marker from the holder lands for the lease window, the claim is stale and any other worker may claim the issue", module doc), never applies to a contested issue.
- `cmd_claim` refuses a contested issue (`reason: "contested"`, exit 5, fallback.rs:888), and the tool never posts a claim against one — so the fold's clean-supersede arm (a new claim arriving after the previous claim went stale) can never fire once a contest exists.
- `cmd_heartbeat` refuses a contested issue too (fallback.rs:970), so even a **live, working holder cannot renew** after a single stray claim from a since-dead challenger; the holder's `last_activity` is frozen at its pre-contest value.
- The only exit is a release from the holder — and if the holder is the dead worker (the exact failure fallback mode exists to survive), nobody can ever claim the issue through the tool again. `cmd_release` inconsistently has NO contested check, unlike `cmd_heartbeat`.

## Evidence

Verified on the laptop against origin/main @5492f27e02 (probe `~/git/fleet/probe-fallback-contest`, real `fallback.rs` included verbatim, `fold_claim`/`parse_ts` called directly; lease = 1800s):

- Control: `[claim a @T0]` folded at T0 + 100 leases → `stale`, claimable = true.
- Case 1: `[claim a @T0, claim b @T0+60]` folded at T0 + 100 leases (both workers silent for ~2 days) → `contested`, claimable = false.
- Case 2: same + holder heartbeats at T0+120/T0+240, folded at T0+300 → still `contested` (and per :970 the real heartbeat verb would have refused to post them).
- Case 3: same + challenger release at T0+120, folded at T0 + 100 leases → still `contested`, claimable = false.

Existing test `fold_stale_supersede_and_live_contest` only folds a contest inside the lease window (T0+120); no test covers a contest after lease expiry.

## Why it matters

Fallback mode runs exactly when the queue backend is down (#6619 outage) — the fleet monitor / broker reconciliation that the "a human or the fleet monitor resolves" note relies on may be unavailable at the same time. One bypass-tool claim, one race the readback didn't catch, or one worker claiming with a skewed clock permanently removes an issue from the fallback work pool for the rest of the outage, silently (`scan` ranks contested last, claimable count excludes it).

## Acceptance criteria

- A contest whose holder (and challenger) have both been silent longer than the lease window no longer reports `claimable: false` forever: e.g. `fold_claim` ages a contest out to `Stale` (holder's last activity governs), or an equivalent documented rule lets a new worker supersede.
- A live holder can heartbeat while a contest is younger than the lease (or the resolution rule above makes the heartbeat refusal unreachable in practice), and `cmd_heartbeat` / `cmd_release` treat `Contested` consistently.
- New fold tests: contest folded after lease expiry; contest + holder heartbeats; contest where the challenger goes silent and the holder keeps working.
- Existing behavior inside the lease window is unchanged: a claim against a live claim still contests, `scan`/`status` output shapes unchanged.

title: github-backup(reconcile): a non-dict JSON line in clone-status.jsonl crashes the failed-clone report path — _clone_status_entries tolerates unparseable lines but not valid non-dict ones

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/github-backup
labels.description: infra/github-backup estate mirror system

body:
## Problem

`infra/github-backup/bin/reconcile.py` — a non-dict JSON line in `clone-status.jsonl` crashes the weekly reconcile on exactly the run it is most needed: a failed clone pass.

- `_clone_status_entries` (reconcile.py:52-66) tolerates a line that does not parse as JSON at all (`except Exception: pass`, line 62-63) but appends every line that *does* parse, with no shape check.
- Its only consumer (reconcile.py:147-152, in the `clone_rc != 0` branch) assumes dicts:

  ```python
  clone_failures = sorted(
      {e["repo"] for e in _clone_status_entries(root, status_offset)
       if e.get("status") == "fail" and e.get("repo")}
  )
  ```

  A line containing `123`, `"fail"`, `["owner/bad"]`, `null`, or `true` — all valid JSON, all plausible products of a torn/interleaved append to this shared append-only file, a hand edit, or a future writer change — raises `AttributeError: '<type>' object has no attribute 'get'`.

- The crash site is before everything the failed-clone branch exists to produce: the dated report `reconcile-YYYY-MM-DD.md` is written at reconcile.py:~185 and `manifest_mod.build(root)` runs at :~192, both *after* the clone-failure computation. So one poison line converts "clone pass failed, here is the report naming the failed repos" (the #3300 contract) into an unhandled traceback with no report, no MANIFEST refresh, and no per-repo failure list — on the one run where the clone pass already failed.

Contrast / oracle in the same estate: `clone_all.py:93-100` reads the same file and is safe — its `r.get("status")` call sits *inside* the `try:` whose `except Exception: pass` swallows the shape error along with parse errors. The two readers of one file disagree about what a line may be; reconcile's is the fragile one.

Distinct from: #6575 (drain_queue queue-event shape poison — different file, different consumer), #3331 (drain owner allowlist shape, closed), #3240 (plan.json/state.json/MANIFEST.json bare `json.load` on torn *object* files — clone-status.jsonl is not in its writer/reader list, and its readers already claim per-line tolerance).

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ afdad96108)

Probe on the laptop at `~/git/fleet/probe-ghb-reconcile-status/probe.py`, importing the **real** `reconcile` module from `~/git/code/infra/github-backup/bin` and feeding `_clone_status_entries` a scratch `clone-status.jsonl`, then applying main's exact consumer expression:

- control, dict entries `[{"repo":"owner/bad","status":"fail"}, {"repo":"owner/good","status":"ok"}]` → consumer Ok, failures `['owner/bad']`
- control, malformed JSON line `"{torn line"` before a fail dict → skipped as designed, consumer Ok, failures `['owner/bad']`
- offset control (entries appended after the recorded byte offset only) → Ok
- non-dict `123` → `consumer_CRASH AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'get'`
- non-dict `"fail"` → `consumer_CRASH AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get'`
- non-dict `["owner/bad"]` → `consumer_CRASH AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'`
- non-dict `null` → `consumer_CRASH AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'get'`
- non-dict `true` → `consumer_CRASH AttributeError: 'bool' object has no attribute 'get'`

## Why it matters

Reconcile is the weekly correctness floor of the backup estate. Its clone-failure path (#3300) was specifically built so a failed clone pass is reported, named, and exit-coded. A single non-dict line in the shared status file defeats that path entirely and takes the dated report and the MANIFEST rebuild with it — the failure mode is silent in the place operators look (no report file appears) and the poison line stays in the append-only file, so the next failed-clone reconcile crashes the same way.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `_clone_status_entries` (or its consumer) ignores non-dict JSON lines the way it already ignores unparseable lines — a parsed line is kept only if it is a dict; dicts missing `repo`/`status` keep the current filtered behaviour.
- [ ] A failed clone pass with a poisoned `clone-status.jsonl` still produces the dated report (with the real dict fail entries named, or the existing "no per-repo failures recorded" fallback), still runs `manifest_mod.build`, and still returns exit 1 — no traceback.
- [ ] Regression test: scratch status file mixing a valid fail dict, an unparseable line, and each non-dict JSON shape (`123`, `"x"`, `[]`, `null`, `true`) → consumer returns exactly the valid fail repos; dict-only and malformed-line controls unchanged.
- [ ] The two readers of `clone-status.jsonl` (clone_all and reconcile) end up with the same line-shape contract, stated in one place.

body:
# Design: `fleet dispatch-test` — explicit-dispatch CI over fleet runner capacity

Status: design of record + MVP built same day (2026-11-06). Direction: Drew, 2026-11-06 11:28 CST.
Supersedes the trigger request in #5663 (closed as superseded): **no GitHub Actions
triggers are enabled anywhere** — this mechanism is explicit `workflow_dispatch` only,
consistent with the standing no-auto-CI policy (2026-11-04 ruling, PR #5501). Label:
GitHub Pro / runners program.

## Problem

Fleet CI capacity is spread across several GitHub scopes (personal + two orgs), each
with its own hosted-runner concurrency. Load is wildly uneven: measured 2026-11-06
~11:31 CST (in-progress / queued *runs*): `developing-today/code` 45 / 244,
`developing-today-forks/opencode` 7 / 11, `developing-today-forks/openchamber` 4 / 17,
`dezren39/darwin-nix` 1 / 1, `dezren39/hatch` 0 / 0. There is no single place to ask
"where is a runner free right now?" and no generic way to run a build+test on the
emptiest scope with results written back reliably.

## The subcommand

New domain in the fleet multicall binary (`pkgs/fleet`, epic #5412 family):
`fleet dispatch-test`, verbs `scan`, `submit`, `status`.

### Capacity scan

For each scope repo, in configured order:

1. `GET /repos/{r}/actions/runs?status=in_progress` — for each run,
   `GET /repos/{r}/actions/runs/{run_id}/jobs` and count jobs with status
   `in_progress` or `queued`.
2. `GET /repos/{r}/actions/runs?status=queued` — each queued run counts as 1 active
   unit (a not-yet-started run exposes no jobs; this is the documented
   approximation).
3. Workflow presence: `GET /repos/{r}/actions/workflows` — the scope is eligible
   only if an active workflow file named `fleet-dispatch-test.yml` exists there.

**Eligible = active jobs < threshold AND workflow present.** First eligible scope
wins. Threshold is a tunable: `--threshold` flag / `[dispatch-test] threshold`
config, **default 40** (Drew's tentative figure). Scopes default to
`developing-today/code`, `developing-today-forks/opencode`,
`developing-today-forks/openchamber`, `dezren39/darwin-nix`, `dezren39/hatch`
(config-overridable). At the measurement above, `code` fails the threshold test
outright and `hatch` is the first scope that is both under threshold and
workflow-equipped — the scan demonstrates both rules on real data.

Auth: a GitHub token resolved **by name** through fleet-secrets
(default `github.ghcr-classic-pat` — classic PAT, scopes include `repo` +
`workflow`, verified live 2026-11-06; covers every scope above because the
fleet operates as dezren39 in all of them). Follow-up: move to
developing.today-fleet App installation tokens for least-privilege per scope.

## Job store: Turso (MVP choice)

Chosen: a dedicated Turso database `fleet-dispatch-jobs` (created 2026-11-06),
one table:

```sql
jobs(id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, created_at TEXT NOT NULL, name TEXT,
     target_repo TEXT, target_ref TEXT, script TEXT NOT NULL,
     status TEXT NOT NULL, run_id INTEGER, run_url TEXT,
     exit_code INTEGER, output_tail TEXT, updated_at TEXT NOT NULL)
```

Why Turso over a CF Worker queue endpoint for the MVP: the fleet already runs on
Turso everywhere (brokers, atlas, ledgers), the HTTP pipeline API
(`POST /v2/pipeline`) is callable identically from the laptop binary (ureq) and
from a runner step (curl + jq), there is no new service to deploy or keep alive,
and a dedicated database keeps the blast radius at one table. A CF Worker
front-end remains the right hardening step if runner-side access ever needs
rate-limiting or payload validation — the store schema does not change.
Status flow: `queued → dispatched → running → succeeded | failed | error`.
Token: `turso.fleet-dispatch-jobs-token` (BWS; also the pilot repo's
`DISPATCH_TURSO_TOKEN` Actions secret; DB URL is the repo variable
`DISPATCH_TURSO_URL`).

## Job patterns

**(2) ID-input — built first (MVP).** `fleet dispatch-test submit` generates an
internal id (`dt-<millis base36>-<4 hex>`), stores the payload (script, ref,
name) under that id, scans, records the chosen scope on the row, then dispatches
the pilot workflow with the single input `job_id`. The workflow fetches its job
by id, marks it `running` (with run id + URL), executes the script, and in an
`if: always()` step writes back the terminal status, exit code, and the output
tail (last 6000 bytes) — so status lands **even on failure**, and a crashed or
timed-out run leaves the row in `running` where `status` shows it honestly
instead of pretending success. A job can be re-dispatched by id (fresh run row
fields overwrite); retry is roughly idempotent because the payload is immutable
and keyed by the id.

**(1) No-inputs pull — designed, not built.** A generic workflow dispatched with
no inputs boots, claims the newest `queued` row (single `UPDATE … WHERE id =
(SELECT … ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1) RETURNING` shape), executes it, and
writes back exactly as in pattern (2). This is the better shape for bulk work
(no per-job dispatch call, runners pull when free); it lands as a second
workflow mode once pattern (2) has soaked. The store and write-back contract
are already compatible.

## Pilot workflow

`dezren39/hatch` (chosen: zero active runs at measurement time, PAT-owned, no
real CI to disturb) carries `.github/workflows/fleet-dispatch-test.yml`:
`workflow_dispatch` with required input `job_id`, `permissions: contents: read`,
30-minute timeout, steps fetch → checkout(job ref) → execute → write-back
(always) → upload `job-output.log` artifact (14-day retention). The workflow
must live on the repo's default branch for dispatch to see it (GitHub rule).

## Artifact quotas + return paths

(Research numbers posted as a comment on this issue: per-account artifact
storage GB, cache GB, retention defaults/min/max, private-repo minutes,
concurrency — dezren39 GitHub Pro personal, developing-today org,
developing-today-forks org, with sources.)

Return-path evaluation:

1. **GitHub Actions artifacts (default).** Zero new infra; the output log rides
   the run. Limits: per-account storage pools are small on personal/org plans
   (see research comment) and retention is capped; fine for logs and small
   outputs, wrong for build products.
2. **R2 via a Cloudflare Worker (fallback, when artifacts don't fit).** The
   fleet already operates Workers + R2 patterns (webhook-gateway, hatch
   workers); a presigned-upload Worker endpoint lets a runner stream large
   outputs to R2 with no GitHub storage pressure. Build only when a real job
   outgrows (1).
3. **Tunnel straight to the laptop (last resort).** The lab tunnel
   (`lab.security.cab`) proves the path exists, but runner→laptop transfers
   couple CI results to home-network availability; use only for outputs that
   must never leave fleet hardware.

Recommendation: **(1) by default, (2) when size/retention demands, (3) only on
a stated privacy need.** The store's `output_tail` covers the common case
without any artifact at all.

## MVP scope (this build)

- `fleet dispatch-test` domain: scan / submit / status, threshold tunable,
  config in `[dispatch-test]`, tokens by name. (PR + merge link below.)
- Turso store as above; pilot workflow in `dezren39/hatch`.
- One end-to-end proof: a real submitted smoke job (checkout ref, print
  environment, exit 0) with scan choice, run URL, and final stored status
  recorded on this issue.
- Out of scope for the MVP: pattern (1), App-token auth, R2 return path,
  installing the new binary fleet-wide (rides the normal fleet build/deploy
  path), any change to runner strategy beyond this dispatch mechanism.

## Risks / notes

- `workflow_dispatch` requires the workflow on the default branch of each
  participating repo — adding scopes later is a one-file PR per repo.
- Runner-side store token is full-access to this one small database by
  design; rotation = `turso db tokens invalidate fleet-dispatch-jobs` +
  re-mint + BWS + repo secret update.
- The queued-runs-as-1 approximation can undercount a queued multi-job
  matrix run; acceptable for a capacity heuristic, revisited if it misleads.

## Acceptance criteria
- `fleet dispatch-test scan` reports per-scope in-progress/queued load and workflow eligibility for the five configured scopes, honoring the threshold flag/config (default 40).
- `submit` runs a build+test job on the first eligible scope via explicit `workflow_dispatch` only — no automatic GitHub Actions triggers are enabled anywhere.
- `status` reports the dispatched run's state and result from the Turso job store (`fleet-dispatch-jobs`), including run URL and exit code.
- The design's MVP scope is either landed or split into tracked implementation issues linked from this issue; no part of the design sits silently.

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-secrets/src/lib.rs` — the `bws` CLI fallback source (`BwsSource::resolve`, :383) reads a malformed `bws secret list` listing as "no secret by that name" (`SecretError::NotFound`) instead of "the source could not answer" (`SecretError::Unavailable`). The crate's own type contract separates the two: `NotFound` is documented at :65-67 as "The source answered: no secret by that name", and `Unavailable` as "The source could not answer (transport down, bad status, subprocess failed)". A listing that cannot be understood is the second case, never the first.

Two shapes in `resolve` (:392-410) collapse into `NotFound`:

- `:397-410` — the parsed list JSON is reduced with `.as_array().and_then(...)`: if the top level is not an array at all (an object, a string, a number — e.g. a `bws` CLI output-schema change), `as_array()` is `None`, the `and_then` yields `None`, and `.ok_or_else(NotFound)` at :407 fires. Contrast the same function's get stage (:420-435) and the sibling `BrokerSource::list_names` (:240-267): a 200 response without the expected array/field is `Unavailable` in both. The list stage is the one inconsistent site.
- `:399-405` — the lookup is `items.iter().find_map(...)`: an entry whose `key` matches the requested name but whose `id` is missing or not a string returns `None` from the closure and the search continues/falls through to `NotFound` at :407. The secret demonstrably exists in the listing the source just returned; its record is malformed. That is a source failure, not an absence.

This is a different code path from #6568: that issue is the secrets-*broker server* (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/secrets_broker.rs`, `do_refresh`/`fetch_one`, partial cache installed + false 404 over HTTP). This one is the *client* fallback in the separate `fleet-secrets` crate — the path every fleet consumer takes when the broker is down (crate docs :7-14: broker protocol first, `bws` fallback second; "the one secrets-by-name path for fleet", #5412). Nothing in #6568's body or acceptance criteria covers this crate.

## Verified this run (behavioral probe of the real crate on the laptop)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-secrets-client` (laptop): a binary depending on the real `fleet-secrets` crate at laptop main `b0c472d94d`, driving the public `BwsSource::with_runner` with a stub `CommandRunner` (same fake-runner shape as the in-tree tests at :550-565) whose `secret get` returns `{"value":"fixture-value"}`.

Controls (correct today):
- Well-formed list `[{"id":"id-1","key":"wanted.name"},{"id":"id-2","key":"other.name"}]`, resolve `wanted.name` → `Ok(fixture-value)`
- Same list, resolve `absent.name` → `NotFound` (genuine absence)
- Empty list `[]` → `NotFound` (genuine absence)

Malformed shapes (all incorrectly `NotFound` today):
- Top-level object `{"id":"id-1","key":"wanted.name"}` → `NotFound`
- Top-level string `"hello"` → `NotFound`
- `[{"id":123,"key":"wanted.name"}]` (matching key, numeric id) → `NotFound`
- `[{"key":"wanted.name"}]` (matching key, missing id) → `NotFound`
- `[{"id":null,"key":"wanted.name"}]` (matching key, null id) → `NotFound`

## Why it matters

The distinction is load-bearing in this crate: callers and the `Resolver` chain (:167-185) aggregate per-source errors, and operators triage "not found" (vault contents are wrong — stop, fix the vault) differently from "unavailable" (a source is broken/schema-drifted — fix the source, the secret may well exist). Reporting a drifted or corrupt `bws` listing as a definitive absence sends diagnosis in the wrong direction and, for a caller that treats `NotFound` as authoritative, can act on "this secret does not exist" (provision a replacement, skip a required credential) while the vault record is right there with a malformed id. The crate has repeatedly hardened exactly this confusion class — empty values count as source failures, never successes/absences (#6275, crate docs :21-28) — the list stage is the remaining site that still manufactures a confident wrong answer.

## Acceptance criteria

- A `bws secret list` result whose top level is valid JSON but not an array makes `BwsSource::resolve` return `SecretError::Unavailable` (source `bws`, detail naming the malformed listing), never `NotFound`.
- A list entry whose `key` matches the requested name but whose `id` is missing or not a string returns `Unavailable`, never `NotFound`.
- Genuine absence still returns `NotFound`: an empty list, and a well-formed list with no entry keyed by the requested name (entries for *other* names with malformed ids do not block a lookup they are not part of — or, if the fix instead fails the whole listing on any malformed entry, that choice is stated in the PR and pinned by a test).
- Behavior is pinned by tests in the crate using the existing fake-runner shape (the probe cases above are the regression set).
- Controls unchanged: a well-formed list + get still resolves the value; non-JSON list output still returns `Unavailable` ("output is not JSON").
- `cargo test -p fleet-secrets` green (laptop or CI).

Found by new-issue-creator-code-b (Lane B) during the 2026-11-06 run; verified against the real crate at main `b0c472d94d` (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-secrets/src/lib.rs`). Related: #6568 (the broker-server sibling in fleet-queue — different crate, different path), #5504 (closed, broker get-stage), #6275 (closed, empty-value discipline), #5412 (fleet-secrets epic).

title: fleet(secrets-broker): a malformed bws list entry is silently dropped before the #5504 fail-whole count — the refresh installs a partial cache and evicts the secret

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/fleet

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/secrets_broker.rs` — `do_refresh` silently drops every `bws secret list` entry whose `id` or `key` is missing or not a string, before the fail-whole counting that #5504 added, so a refresh built from a partial listing is installed as the whole cache and reported as a success. The dropped secret is evicted until a later well-formed refresh, and consumers are told `404 {"error":"no such secret"}` for a secret that exists in the vault.

This is a residual hole in the closed #5504 fix, not a reopening of it: #5504 covered per-item `bws secret get` failures (non-zero exit, unparseable output, missing/non-string `value`). Those are now counted (`secrets_broker.rs:181` — a refresh with `failed > 0` errors and keeps the previous cache, per the comment at `:140-145`: a refresh "must fail as a whole … instead of installing the partial map and evicting the secrets it failed to fetch"). The list stage defeats the same invariant one step earlier:

- `:126-137` — the listing is reduced with `.filter_map(|s| Some((s.get("id")?.as_str()?.to_string(), s.get("key")?.as_str()?.to_string())))`: any entry with a missing/non-string `id` or `key` vanishes with no count, no log, and no error.
- `:143` — `let total = items.len();` is taken **after** the filter, so the dropped entries are invisible to the `failed > 0` check at `:181`: the denominator itself shrank.
- `:188-189` — the resulting partial map replaces `state.secrets` wholesale and `last_refresh` advances, exactly the silent-eviction outcome #5504 banned for get failures.

Sibling site, same shape: `fetch_one` (`:198`, read-through on a cache miss, #6275) resolves a name with `find_map` at `:204` — an entry whose `key` matches but whose `id` is missing/non-string is skipped, the lookup falls through to `Ok(None)` at `:213`, and `handle_request` turns that into `404 "no such secret"` (`:364`) instead of the loud 502 a source failure gets. The probe below shows this firing live: after the malformed refresh evicted `beta.name`, the read-through log line was `read-through: "beta.name" is not in Bitwarden` — for a secret that was in the vault listing the whole time.

## Verified this run (behavioral probe of the real binary on the laptop)

Probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-secrets-listdrop` (laptop): the current `secrets-broker` binary built this run from laptop main `d54934a99a` (`cargo build -p fleet-queue --features secrets-broker --bin secrets-broker`), run with `SECRETS_BROKER_BIND=127.0.0.1:14931`, a fake HOME holding only the broker token file, TTL 900s, and a stub `bws` on PATH whose `secret list` output is file-driven and whose `secret get <id>` serves `alpha.name`/`beta.name` by id.

1. Well-formed list `[{"id":"id-alpha","key":"alpha.name"},{"id":"id-beta","key":"beta.name"}]`: `GET /health` → `{"ok":true,"secrets":2,…}`; `GET /secret/beta.name` (authed) → `200 {"key":"beta.name","value":"value-beta"}`.
2. List flipped so beta's entry is malformed — `{"id":123,"key":"beta.name"}` (non-string id), alpha unchanged — then `POST /refresh` → `202`. After it: `GET /health` → `{"ok":true,"secrets":1,"last_refresh_unix":<advanced>}`; `GET /secret/beta.name` → **`404 {"error":"no such secret"}`**; `GET /secret/alpha.name` → still 200. No refresh-failure line in the broker log (the `/refresh` handler discards the result, and `do_refresh` returned `Ok(1)` in any case).
3. Control — list restored to the well-formed shape, `POST /refresh` again: `secrets:2`, `GET /secret/beta.name` → 200. The eviction in step 2 was the malformed entry, not a vault removal.

## Why it matters

The secrets broker is the fleet's one secrets-by-name cache (#5362): the queue broker fetches its Supabase credentials through it and sandbox consumers resolve vault secrets through it. A single malformed or schema-drifted list record (a `bws` CLI output change, one corrupt vault item) silently shrinks the whole cache at the next TTL refresh, and every downstream failure surfaces far away as "no such secret" — the answer for a secret that does not exist — with health presenting the partial load as a successful refresh. That is precisely the failure mode #5504 was filed and fixed for; the list stage is the one entry point the fix did not close.

## Acceptance criteria

- A `bws secret list` entry with a missing or non-string `id` or `key` makes the refresh fail as a whole (previous map and `last_refresh` kept, failure logged), matching the #5504 get-failure behavior — a partial listing is never installed as a successful refresh.
- `fetch_one` treats a key-matching entry with a missing/non-string `id` as a source failure (Err → 502), not as "not in the vault" (Ok(None) → 404).
- The behavior is pinned by a test or a scripted fake-`bws` probe (the probe recipe above reproduces the current behavior end-to-end against the real binary).
- Controls unchanged: a fully well-formed refresh still swaps in new values and advances `last_refresh`; a secret genuinely removed from the vault listing still disappears on the next successful refresh; duplicate-key handling, if the fix touches it, is decided explicitly rather than by parallel-fetch completion order.
- `cargo test -p fleet-queue --all-features` green (laptop or CI).

Found by new-issue-creator-code-b (Lane B) during the 2026-11-06 run; verified against the real binary and the source at main `d54934a99a` (`do_refresh` / `fetch_one` in `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/secrets_broker.rs`). Related: #5504 (closed — the get-stage fix this is a residual of), #6275 (closed — read-through), #5362 (broker design).

title: talos(save-secrets.sh): a failed sops encryption truncates secrets.enc to zero bytes and the script still exits 0

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: area/infra
labels.description: Infrastructure, deployment, and operations

labels.name: app/talos
labels.description: infra/talos cluster secrets workflow

body:
## Problem

`infra/talos/01b.us/save-secrets.sh` — the script that persists the Talos cluster's secrets to their only encrypted copy, `secrets.enc` — writes that copy non-atomically **and** masks the failure:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
tar czf - ./secrets | base64 >secrets.tmp
sops --encrypt secrets.tmp >secrets.enc
rm secrets.tmp
```

- `save-secrets.sh:3`: the shell truncates `secrets.enc` **before** `sops` runs, so any encryption failure (missing/expired sops key, sops error, disk full, interruption) leaves the encrypted copy empty or partial.
- The script has **no `set -e` / `pipefail`** at all (the house style in this repo's sibling scripts, e.g. `infra/dns/*.sh` and `init-talos.sh` itself, is `set -Eexuo pipefail`). After `sops` fails, `rm secrets.tmp` (line 4) still runs and succeeds, so the script **exits 0** — the failure is silent.
- The caller trusts that exit code: `init-talos.sh` (which runs under `set -Eexuo pipefail`) invokes `./save-secrets.sh` at lines 14 and 148 and proceeds with cluster bootstrap on the assumption the secrets were saved.

## Evidence

`infra/talos/01b.us/save-secrets.sh` @ `9c06d0c8a4` (full file, 4 lines, quoted above):

- `secrets.enc` is 43,916 bytes and is the **only** persistent copy: `.gitignore` ignores `secret*` and excepts exactly `!secrets.enc`; the plaintext `./secrets` directory is gitignored, and `load-secrets.sh` can only regenerate it **from** `secrets.enc`.
- Verified this run on the laptop (probe `~/git/fleet/probe-talos-save`, real `save-secrets.sh` copied verbatim — md5 identical to the repo file — stub `sops` on PATH):
  - Stub `sops --encrypt` exits 1: `save-secrets.sh` exits **0** and `secrets.enc` goes from 30 bytes to **0 bytes**.
  - Control (stub `sops --encrypt` succeeds): exit 0, `secrets.enc` holds the new ciphertext, `secrets.tmp` removed.
  - Load path probed for contrast: a failing `sops --decrypt` in `load-secrets.sh` exits 2 via `tar`, so the load side is **not** silently masked in that shape — the defect is specific to the save side.

## Why it matters

`secrets/` holds the cluster's identity material (`secrets.yaml` from `talosctl gen secrets`, plus the generated controlplane/worker configs and talosconfig). `secrets.enc` is the sole durable, committed copy of it. Zeroing it on a transient sops failure destroys the cluster's secrets — a re-run of `init-talos.sh` would generate a **new** cluster identity rather than recover the old one — and because the script reports success, the operator only discovers the loss the next time `load-secrets.sh` is needed, possibly after the plaintext directory has been cleaned up. The intermediate `secrets.tmp` is also an unencrypted base64 tarball of the same secrets: it is removed on the happy path, but nothing guarantees its cleanup if the script is interrupted mid-run.

Related but distinct: #6536 covers the same non-atomic pattern in `infra/dns/save.sh` (different script, different state of record, and that script at least exits non-zero on failure). This issue is the Talos counterpart, with the additional failure-masking defect.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `save-secrets.sh` encrypts to a temporary file in the same directory and atomically renames it over `secrets.enc` only after `sops` exits 0 and the temp file is non-empty; a failed encryption leaves the previous `secrets.enc` byte-identical.
- [ ] The script fails loudly: `set -Eeuo pipefail` (house style) or equivalent explicit checks, so a `tar` or `sops` failure exits non-zero and `init-talos.sh` stops instead of proceeding.
- [ ] Plaintext-bearing intermediates (`secrets.tmp` and any new temp ciphertext) are cleaned up on failure and on interruption (e.g. an EXIT trap), without touching the live `secrets.enc`.
- [ ] A regression probe/test with a failing `sops --encrypt` stub shows `secrets.enc` unchanged **and** a non-zero exit; a succeeding stub shows the new ciphertext in place; `load-secrets.sh` still round-trips a saved `secrets.enc`.

body:
## Problem

`infra/dns/save.sh` writes the encrypted Terraform state of record non-atomically: `sops -e … > terraform.tfstate.enc` (save.sh:50). The shell truncates `terraform.tfstate.enc` **before** `sops` runs, so any encryption failure — missing/expired sops key, sops error, disk full, interruption — leaves the state of record empty or partial, destroying the only encrypted copy the whole DNS workflow treats as canonical.

This is the one unguarded write left in the flow the #1943 campaign hardened: `load.sh` refuses a missing/empty `.enc`, `init.sh` snapshots and byte-verifies the decrypted state around `tofu init`, and `plan.sh` re-verifies lineage and sets `SKIP_SAVE` on its refusal paths so the EXIT trap cannot save a refused state. But `save.sh` itself — including when `plan.sh`'s EXIT-trap cleanup invokes it after a successful plan — can still zero the record on a routine sops failure.

## Evidence

`infra/dns/save.sh` @ `2bcd46e0dc`:

- :44-47 the already-current fast path decrypts and compares first, so the destructive path is only reached when the state actually changed — exactly when the new ciphertext matters most.
- :50 `sops -e "$dir/terraform.tfstate" >"$dir/terraform.tfstate.enc"` — in-place redirection, no temp file, no rename, no post-write verification (contrast `init.sh`'s snapshot + sha256 verify + restore).
- `set -Eexuo pipefail` (save.sh:2) makes the script exit on the sops failure, but the truncation has already happened; nothing restores the previous ciphertext.

Verified this run on the laptop (probe `~/git/fleet/probe-dns-save`, real `save.sh` copied verbatim, stub `sops` on PATH):

- Stub `sops -d` returns differing content (so the already-current fast path is skipped); stub `sops -e` exits 1: `save.sh` exits 1 and `terraform.tfstate.enc` goes from 26 bytes to **0 bytes**.
- Control (stub `sops -e` succeeds): exit 0, `.enc` holds the new ciphertext (15 bytes).

## Why it matters

`terraform.tfstate.enc` is the state of record for the DNS estate: `load.sh` decrypts it, `init.sh` calls it "the decrypted state of record" and refuses to continue without it, and a void/mismatched state is the #1943 failure mode ("151 to add, 0 to destroy" against an empty state). Losing it to a transient sops failure turns a retry-able error into state recovery from the plaintext working copy — if that copy has been cleaned (`cleanup_terraform_tfstate.sh` exists in the same directory) or the failure happens on another machine, the encrypted record is simply gone.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `save.sh` encrypts to a temporary file in the same directory and atomically renames it over `terraform.tfstate.enc` only after `sops` exits 0 (and the temp file is non-empty); a failed encryption leaves the previous `.enc` byte-identical.
- [ ] A post-write sanity check (e.g. the new `.enc` decrypts and its lineage matches the plaintext state, mirroring plan.sh's check) runs before the save is reported successful, or the rename only happens after such a check on the temp file.
- [ ] The temp file is cleaned up on failure without touching the live `.enc`; the `.lock` cleanup behaviour is unchanged.
- [ ] A test/probe with a failing `sops -e` stub shows `.enc` unchanged and a non-zero exit; a succeeding stub shows the new ciphertext in place; the already-current fast path still skips re-encryption.
- [ ] `load.sh`'s analogous in-place decrypt write (`sops -d … > terraform.tfstate`, load.sh:41) is assessed in the same pass: the plaintext target is re-derivable from `.enc`, so it may be documented as safe-by-reconstruction rather than changed — but the reasoning is recorded on this issue.

body:
# github-backup(ghb_common): inventory_owner paginates forever when a page says hasNextPage with a null/empty endCursor — the reconcile sweep hangs re-fetching page 1 instead of raising

`infra/github-backup/bin/ghb_common.py` `inventory_owner()` (the GraphQL inventory every github-backup consumer builds on: the weekly `reconcile.py` sweep, `clone_all.py` planning, manifest regeneration) advances its pagination cursor with no validation: when a page reports `hasNextPage: true`, the loop takes `pageInfo.endCursor` as the next `after` unconditionally (`ghb_common.py:126-127`). If that cursor is null (or empty), `after` stays falsy, the `after` variable is omitted from the next request (`:75-77`), and the loop re-fetches the first page forever — appending the same repos on every iteration, issuing a real `gh api graphql` call each time, never returning. Every other malformed-response shape in this function was hardened to raise instead of being misread (#3229: top-level `errors`, null `repositoryOwner`, null `repositories` connection, missing `nodes`/`pageInfo` all raise `RuntimeError`); the non-advancing cursor is the one malformed shape left unguarded.

## Evidence (file:line, origin/main `2bcd46e0dc`)

- `ghb_common.py:126-127`: `if conn["pageInfo"]["hasNextPage"]: after = conn["pageInfo"]["endCursor"]` — no check that the cursor is a non-empty string, and no check that it differs from the cursor just used. A repeated (stuck) cursor loops the same way.
- `ghb_common.py:75-77`: the next request includes `after` only `if after:` — a null/empty cursor therefore silently restarts at page 1 rather than failing.
- `ghb_common.py:96-124` (contrast): the function's own stated contract — a successful `gh` exit carrying a failed/malformed inventory must raise, never be read as data (#3229 comment, `:96-102`). The cursor path violates that contract by hanging instead of raising.
- Callers hang with it: `reconcile.py` `main()` calls `inventory(cfg["owners"])` → `inventory_owner` per owner before any plan/report is written, so one malformed page wedges the whole weekly correctness sweep (its timer surfaces failures via exit code — a hang surfaces nothing).

## Verification (laptop probe, this run)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-ghb-cursor/` against the real `ghb_common.py` at origin/main `2bcd46e0dc`, with `ghb_common.run` stubbed to return canned GraphQL pages:

- Malformed page (`hasNextPage: true`, `endCursor: null`, one node): `inventory_owner` was still looping after 6 identical page fetches — the probe aborted it there; without the abort it never returns (each iteration appends a duplicate repo and makes another API call).
- Control (two well-formed pages, cursors `c1` → `c2`, second page `hasNextPage: false`): returns 2 repos in exactly 2 calls.

## Why it matters

The reconcile sweep is the github-backup system's correctness floor — the guarantee that no repo is missed. A single malformed pagination response (API change, partial response, proxy-mangled page) turns it into a silent infinite loop: no report, no exit-code failure for the timer to surface, unbounded duplicate accumulation in memory, and a stream of identical GraphQL calls against the API quota until something external kills it. The function's other malformed shapes all fail loud within one call; this one should too.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `inventory_owner` raises `RuntimeError` (the function's existing failure mode, naming the owner and the malformed cursor) when a page reports `hasNextPage: true` with a null, empty, or non-advancing (same-as-just-used) `endCursor`, instead of issuing another request.
- [ ] Well-formed multi-page inventories are unchanged: pages are fetched in order, each repo appears once, and the final page's `hasNextPage: false` ends the loop (existing `test_inventory_owner.py` suite passes unchanged).
- [ ] A regression test in `infra/github-backup/tests/test_inventory_owner.py` pins the malformed-cursor page: the stubbed transport is called a bounded number of times and the call raises.
- [ ] `inventory()`'s per-owner error recording picks the failure up as an owner-level error (the #3229 path), so `reconcile.py` reports it and exits non-zero rather than hanging.

Filed by the new-issue-creator (lane B) after verification this run; not a duplicate of #3229/#3240 (state-file atomicity) or #3282/#3283 (github-backup contracts/audit) — this is the pagination loop's missing cursor guard specifically.

title: cold-store-reaper(repair_dump): a multi-line schema statement is terminated by the first interior line ending in ');' — the fragment is rewritten as the whole statement and the tail passes through raw

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.description: Package/app: cold-store-reaper (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
# cold-store-reaper(repair_dump): a multi-line schema statement is terminated by the first interior line ending in `');` — the fragment is rewritten as the whole statement and the tail passes through raw

`pkgs/cold-store-reaper/scripts/repair_dump.py` — the streaming repair filter between the libsql `/dump` download and the sqlite3 rebuild in `scripts/export-turso.sh` — decides where a multi-line `INSERT INTO sqlite_schema(...)` candidate ends purely by line shape: the first buffered line ending in `');` is taken as the statement's end. A schema object's SQL can itself contain such a line (a `CREATE TRIGGER` whose body has a statement ending in a string literal, e.g. `SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'bad');`, is the natural case — SQLite stores the CREATE text as written, newlines included). When that happens the filter splits the statement at the interior line, "repairs" the fragment as if it were the whole statement, and passes the remaining lines through unfiltered — corrupting the filtered dump so the sqlite3 rebuild fails, where the identical statement on one line repairs and loads correctly.

## Evidence (file:line, origin/main `2bcd46e0dc`)

- `repair_dump.py:142-161` (`main`): once a line starts with `INSERT INTO sqlite_schema(`, every later line is appended to `buffered` (`:147`) until a line ending in `STATEMENT_END` (`b"');"`, `:33`) appears (`:148`), at which point the joined chunk is emitted through `repair_chunk`. Nothing checks that the accumulated text is actually one complete statement — the line shape is the only terminator test.
- `repair_dump.py:90-128` (`repair_statement`): the fragment verifies as a "complete" statement — its final literal, after quote-doubling, parses exactly to the chunk end with `");"` remaining (`:124-127`) — because the fragment genuinely is indistinguishable from a complete statement whose SQL is just the fragment. The rewrite therefore fires on the fragment.
- The docstring (`:22-25`) states the assumption outright: it "buffers only the lines of one candidate statement (which ends at a line ending in `');`)" — the assumption is the bug: a line ending in `');` inside the embedded SQL is not the statement's end.

## Verification (laptop probe, this run)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-repair-dump-earlyflush/probe.py` against the real script at origin/main `2bcd46e0dc`. Input (the final value's SQL spans two lines; line 1 ends in `');` via the trigger body's `RAISE(ABORT, 'bad');`):

```sql
PRAGMA writable_schema=ON;
INSERT INTO sqlite_schema(type,name,tbl_name,rootpage,sql) VALUES('table','ft','ft',0,'CREATE TRIGGER tr AFTER INSERT ON ft BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'bad');
 INSERT INTO log VALUES('x'); END');
PRAGMA writable_schema=OFF;
```

Filtered output — the first line is emitted as a complete, rewritten statement (note `''bad'`), the tail line passes through raw:

```sql
INSERT INTO sqlite_schema(type,name,tbl_name,rootpage,sql) VALUES('table','ft','ft',0,'CREATE TRIGGER tr AFTER INSERT ON ft BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT, ''bad');
 INSERT INTO log VALUES('x'); END');
```

Oracle (stock sqlite3 load of the filtered stream, the same rebuild `export-turso.sh` performs): **FAILS** — the orphaned tail executes as a top-level statement (`OperationalError: no such table: log`) and the schema row that does land carries only the truncated first line of the trigger SQL. Control: the identical statement on a single line is repaired by the same filter and loads cleanly (schema row `ft` present). Filter exit code is 0 in both cases — the corruption is silent.

## Why it matters

This filter is the Turso export path's only defense against the libsql mis-escaping quirk (#1391); its output feeds a `sqlite3 -bail` rebuild of the only portable backup. A dump containing a multi-line trigger (or any schema SQL with an interior `');` line end) is silently mangled: the rebuild either dies (backup export fails) or, worse, a truncated schema statement lands in the restored database. Distinct from #6525 (same file: an *unterminated* candidate is buffered whole — a memory failure with byte-identical output); this is the opposite terminator failure — termination *too early* — and it breaks correctness, not just memory.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A candidate statement is not terminated by an interior line ending in `');` when more of the statement follows: the two-line probe statement above (and equivalents) is repaired as one statement and the filtered stream loads in stock sqlite3 with the full schema SQL intact.
- [ ] Byte-identical output is preserved in every currently-correct case: mis-escaped literals still repaired, valid literals untouched, unterminated-at-EOF still flushed unchanged (existing `TestDumpRepairFilter` in `tests/test_export_turso.py` passes unchanged).
- [ ] A new regression test in `TestDumpRepairFilter` pins the case: a multi-line schema statement whose embedded SQL contains an interior line ending in `');` round-trips through the filter and a sqlite3 rebuild.
- [ ] The docstring's statement-end description matches the implemented termination rule.

Filed by the new-issue-creator (lane A) after verification this run; not a duplicate of #1391 (the mis-escaping quirk) or #6525 (the same filter's unbounded-buffer memory issue — this one terminates too early and corrupts output).

## Root cause (verified by direct read of `agent.tasks`)

Claim filters `attempts < max_attempts`. All 7 queued tasks sat at `attempts == max_attempts`, burned by repeated claim → `handed_off` (execution_lane=opencode) cycles whose bound opencode claimant session never launched:

| task | issue | attempts |
|---|---|---|
| 10555 | openchamber #1652 | 12/12 |
| 10737 | openchamber #1654 | 12/12 |
| 10805 | openchamber #1682 (triage) | 12/12 |
| 10817 | openchamber #1680 (triage) | 12/12 |
| 10883 | openchamber #1660 | 8/8 |
| 10978 | openchamber #1701 | 4/4 → repaired this shift |
| 10854 | openchamber #1685 | 8/8 → repaired this shift |

The affected GitHub issues all still carry `queue/claimed` + `status/in-progress` + `work/assigned` labels while their tasks sit `queued` — the label/task divergence the fleet monitor's Duty 1 addendum was built to auto-repair, except these tasks are neither claimable nor divergent in a way that repair covers.

## Repaired this shift (precedent: 2026-10-26 cap raises for tasks 1063/1111)

- Task 10978: `max_attempts` 4 → 10, claimed by lane openchamber-a, implemented, PR developing-today-forks/openchamber#1712 merged, issue #1701 closed, task done.
- Task 10854: `max_attempts` 8 → 14, claimed, salvaged the earlier session's uncommitted implementation from its laptop worktree, PR #1713 merged, issue #1685 closed, task done.

## Still owed

1. Tasks 10555, 10737, 10805, 10817, 10883 remain at cap and unclaimable. Raising their caps without a claimant only restarts the burn loop — the actual missing step is launching the bound opencode claimant sessions (each task's progress already says `next: claimant launches the bound opencode session`), or re-routing them to a lane that implements directly, as this shift did for 10978/10854.

body:
## Problem

`install_module_session` in `pkgs/id/src/world_session/mod.rs` is the one remaining `ClientFrame` parse path that does not route through the module's strict duplicate-key parser. Every other peer-frame entry point refuses a frame containing duplicate JSON keys at any depth; the module-install path parses chunk and completion frames with plain `serde_json::from_str::<ClientFrame>`, which refuses duplicate *known* fields (serde derive) but silently collapses duplicate keys in fields the frame type ignores — the exact residual class PR #6508 pinned and fixed for `query_session`.

Evidence (`origin/main` 6046e1d7bcda, `pkgs/id/src/world_session/mod.rs`):

- Strict helper: `parse_json_without_duplicate_keys` at mod.rs:880. Used by the first frame (mod.rs:1026), `query_session` (mod.rs:1721–1722, via PR #6508 for issue #6501), and the joined-frame handler (mod.rs:2663).
- Install path: chunk frames parsed at mod.rs:2189 with `serde_json::from_str::<ClientFrame>(&text)`; the `install_end` completion check at mod.rs:2208 matches `serde_json::from_str::<ClientFrame>(text)` the same way. Neither sees the strict helper.
- Issue #6501 described the install path as the strict sibling oracle — true only for duplicate known fields. Duplicate keys in ignored/unknown fields, and duplicates nested inside an ignored object, pass both install parses untouched.

Verified this run on the laptop with a probe driving the real `id` crate's public `run_session_with` against a clean `origin/main` export (probe `~/git/fleet/probe-id-install-dupkeys`; `WorldService` with admin token, `install_begin` with `total_bytes: 1`, one 1-byte chunk `0x00`, then `install_end`; oracle = which error the session ends with — "Wasm module failed validation or initialization" means the frames were accepted and the upload reached module installation, "expected module chunk frame" means the chunk was refused at parse):

- Control: valid chunk + valid `install_end` → "Wasm module failed validation or initialization" (accepted; reached install).
- Chunk `{"type":"install_chunk","offset":0,"data_hex":"00","bogus":1,"bogus":2}` → same Wasm error: duplicate unknown keys silently accepted.
- Chunk with `"extra":{"a":1,"a":2}` → same Wasm error: duplicates nested inside an ignored object silently accepted.
- `install_end` as `{"type":"install_end","bogus":1,"bogus":2}` after a valid chunk → same Wasm error: the completion frame matched despite duplicate keys.
- Chunk with duplicate known field `"offset":0,"offset":0` → "expected module chunk frame" (refused by serde derive) — confirming the gap is precisely the ignored-field class, not all duplicates.

## Why it matters

The install path is the admin module-upload gate: it runs after admin authorization and assembles the exact bytes whose hash is checked and which are then installed as a world module. It is the last session path where two readers of the same frame bytes can disagree about what was sent — the inconsistency the duplicate-key contract (design #6520; sibling fixes #6473, #6474, #6491, #6499, #6504, #6501) exists to remove. #6521 (the gated closing inventory) does not name this site; this issue is its disposition for the install path: it is a gate, not a not-a-gate.

## Acceptance criteria

- Chunk frames and the `install_end` frame in `install_module_session` are parsed through `parse_json_without_duplicate_keys` + `serde_json::from_value::<ClientFrame>` (or an equivalent strict route), so any duplicate key at any depth — known, unknown/ignored, or nested inside an ignored object — refuses the frame before any chunk bytes are appended or the upload is treated as complete.
- Refusal behavior matches the current parse-failure behavior: a refused chunk ends the install with "expected module chunk frame"; a refused completion frame ends it with "expected install_end frame".
- Regression tests (sandbox feature, mirroring the existing `admin_upload_pins_validates_and_activates_a_roc_program` harness and PR #6508's query-session cases) pin: duplicate unknown key in a chunk, duplicate key nested in an ignored chunk object, and duplicate unknown key in `install_end` — each refused; the valid upload flow still installs.
- Existing `world_session` tests keep passing (`cargo test -p id world_session` on the laptop or CI).

Related: #6501 (first/joined/query paths), #6520 (duplicate-key contract), #6521 (closing inventory — install site not named there).

body:
## Summary

The fleet session broker's request-frame parser silently discards a present-but-non-string `token_file` — a number, boolean, object, or array collapses to `None`, and the broker then authenticates the request with the **default** token file instead of the credential the caller named, or instead of refusing the frame. The request is delivered and answered (200) with a credential substitution that neither the caller nor the service can see. A present-but-invalid `token_file` is not an absent one; only an absent one should take the default. Sibling of #6516 (the same collapse for the frame `port`, in the same function).

## Evidence

`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/serve.rs` (at `6046e1d7bc`):

- `parse_request` (:610; the `token_file` chain at :640-643): `frame.get("token_file").and_then(|v| v.as_str()).map(|s| s.to_string())` — every non-string shape (123, true, `{"x":1}`, `["x"]`) fails `as_str()` and collapses to `None`, indistinguishable from the field being absent.
- `Broker::do_request` (:507; the fallback at :512-514): `None` becomes `self.config.default_token_file()` (`$HOME/tools/laptop-agent-token`, fleet-config `default_token_file()`), whose contents are read, trimmed, and sent to the target service as the `X-Agent-Token` header (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/http.rs:195`).
- Contrast in the same call path: a `token_file` that **is** a string but names a missing file is a loud 502 — `broker: cannot read token file /nonexistent/token: No such file or directory`. The invalid shapes are not even consistent: a bad string errors, a non-string is silently replaced with a different credential.
- Contrast in the same function: `method` and `path` are strictly validated and refused when malformed (#5750). The module comment describes the leniency as mirroring the Python's defaults — the Python takes its default only when the key is absent.

## Verified (probe, laptop, real crates)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-broker-tokenfile` (path-deps on the real `fleet-proxy`/`fleet-config`/`fleet-proxy-proto` crates at `6046e1d7bc`): a stub HTTP service on 127.0.0.1:4799 that echoes the `X-Agent-Token` header it received; the real broker (`serve::run`, direct mode, temp socket) in front of it; HOME pointed at the probe dir so the broker's default token file is the probe's own (`default-token`); a custom token file holding `custom-token`:

- `token_file: <custom path>` → 200, service received `custom-token` (control)
- `token_file` absent → 200, service received `default-token` (control — the documented default)
- `token_file: 123` → 200, service received **`default-token`** (bug — the named credential was silently replaced)
- `token_file: true` → 200, service received **`default-token`** (bug)
- `token_file: {"x":1}` → 200, service received **`default-token`** (bug)
- `token_file: ["x"]` → 200, service received **`default-token`** (bug)
- `token_file: "/nonexistent/token"` → 502 `broker: cannot read token file /nonexistent/token: No such file or directory (os error 2)` (the inconsistent contrast)
- `token_file: null` → 200, service received `default-token` (JSON null; arguably absent-equivalent — triage's call, listed for completeness)

## Why it matters

The broker is the fleet's local RPC router, and `token_file` is how a frame names the credential its request should carry. Silently substituting the default credential means a request can succeed against a service under an identity the caller never named — or fail confusingly elsewhere — with nothing in the response or logs saying a substitution happened. Client bugs that serialize the field wrong (a config object, a boolean flag, a numeric id) become silent credential swaps instead of loud errors at the frame boundary, exactly where #5750 established strict validation and #6516 is establishing it for `port`.

## Acceptance criteria

- `parse_request` distinguishes an absent `token_file` (→ the default token file) from a present-but-non-string one, and the broker answers the latter with the standard `{status: 502, body: {error: "broker: …"}}` frame naming the bad shape — no connection is opened and no token is read.
- The rule for `token_file: null` is chosen explicitly (absent-equivalent or refused) and pinned by a test.
- Tests in `fleet-proxy` pin: a string `token_file` sends that file's token, an absent one sends the default token, and each non-string shape (number, boolean, object, array) is refused without touching any service.
- Existing fleet-proxy tests keep passing (`cargo test -p fleet-proxy` on the laptop or CI).

## Scope notes

- Frame-boundary parsing in `serve.rs` only — the `token_file` field. The `port` field's version of this collapse is #6516; the typed `fleet-proxy-proto` `Request` (`token_file: Option<String>`) cannot express these shapes — the gap exists precisely because the broker parses raw frames leniently, which legacy/Python clients still use.
- Not the brokers' empty-token-file authentication behaviour (#6320, closed — a file that exists but is empty, at the queue/secrets brokers) and not fleet-config's empty/blank config strings (#6405).

body:
## Summary

The fleet session broker's request-frame parser silently reroutes a request to the default laptop-agent port (4799) whenever the frame's `port` field is present but not a valid `u16` — out of range, negative, a float, or a string. A request addressed somewhere else (or nowhere valid) is delivered to a service it was never addressed to, with a 200, instead of being refused. A present-but-invalid `port` is not an absent `port`; only an absent one should take the default.

## Evidence

`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/serve.rs` (at `540d3bea3f`):

- `parse_request` (:610; the port chain at :636-639): `let port = frame.get("port").and_then(|v| v.as_u64()).and_then(|p| u16::try_from(p).ok());` — every failure mode of that chain (70000, -1, 4801.5, `"4801"`) collapses to `None`, indistinguishable from the field being absent.
- `Broker::do_request` (:507; the default at :511): `let port = req.port.unwrap_or(fleet_config::PORT_LAPTOP_AGENT);` — the `None` becomes port 4799, and the request (method, path, body, and the caller's token file) is forwarded there.
- Contrast in the same function: `method` and `path` are strictly validated and rejected when malformed (#5750), and `port: 0` — which survives the chain as `Some(0)` — is dialled and fails. The invalid cases are not even consistent: 0 errors, 70000 silently reroutes.

The module's own contract says the lenient parsing "mirrors the Python's dict access" for *defaults* — the Python takes `req.get("port", 4799)` only when the key is absent; a present 70000 is used and the connect fails. The broker's hello also advertises a closed routing table (`services_map`, ports 4799/4800/4801 per fleet-config) with the proto rule that an unadvertised port is "not here" — a frame for port 70000 being served by 4799 breaks that contract from inside.

## Verified (probe, laptop, real crates)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-broker-port` (path-deps on the real `fleet-proxy`/`fleet-config`/`fleet-proxy-proto` crates at `540d3bea3f`): stub HTTP services on 127.0.0.1:4799 and 127.0.0.1:4801 that answer with their own port; the real broker (`serve::run`, direct mode, temp socket/token) in front of them; legacy request frames over the broker socket:

- `port: 4801` → 200, served by 4801 (control)
- `port` absent → 200, served by 4799 (control — the documented default)
- `port: 70000` → 200, **served by 4799** (bug)
- `port: "4801"` (string) → 200, **served by 4799**, not 4801 (bug)
- `port: -1` → 200, **served by 4799** (bug)
- `port: 4801.5` → 200, **served by 4799** (bug)
- `port: 0` → 502 `broker: tunnel to 127.0.0.1:0: Connection refused` (dial failure — the inconsistent contrast)

## Why it matters

The broker is the fleet's local RPC router: a frame's port is its address. Silently delivering a request to the wrong service is worse than failing it — the wrong service acts on a request it was never sent (the laptop-agent daemon executes commands), the caller sees a plausible 200 from a service it did not address, and the misaddressing is invisible in logs. Client bugs that serialize a port as a string or compute an out-of-range port become silent misroutes instead of loud errors at the frame boundary, exactly where #5750 already established strict validation for method/path.

## Acceptance criteria

- `parse_request` distinguishes an absent `port` (→ default 4799) from a present-but-invalid one (non-integer, negative, float, string, or > 65535), and the broker answers the latter with the standard `{status: 502, body: {error: "broker: …"}}` frame naming the bad port value's shape — no connection is opened.
- `port: 0` gets the same frame-boundary refusal instead of a dial attempt (or is explicitly documented and tested as a dial error, consistently with the other invalid values).
- Tests in `fleet-proxy` pin: valid port routes to that port, absent port routes to 4799, and each invalid shape (70000, -1, 4801.5, `"4801"`, 0 per the chosen rule) is refused without touching any service.
- Existing fleet-proxy tests keep passing (`cargo test -p fleet-proxy` on the laptop or CI).

## Scope notes

- Frame-boundary parsing in `serve.rs` only. Not the typed `fleet-proxy-proto` `Request` (its `port: Option<u16>` cannot express these shapes — the gap exists precisely because the broker parses raw frames leniently, which legacy/Python clients still use).
- Not fleet-config's services-table validation (#6397) and not the `proxy connect` CLI flag handling (#5929).

title: fleet-proxy(http): response reader caps every line but nothing caps repetition — endless 1xx heads, header lines, or trailer lines hang an exchange (and its pooled tunnel) forever

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.description: pkgs/fleet multicall binary + platform crates

body:
## Problem

`fleet-proxy`'s HTTP response reader (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/http.rs`) bounds every *unit* a peer can send — one line is capped at `MAX_LINE_BYTES` (:52, enforced in `read_line_bounded` :143), a declared body is capped at `MAX_RESPONSE_BODY_BYTES` before allocation — but nothing bounds *repetition*. Three loops consume peer-controlled units forever:

1. **Interim 1xx heads** — `request()` (:215) loops `read_response_head()` and `continue`s on every 1xx (except 101) with no count limit.
2. **Header lines** — `read_response_head()` (:282, loop at :305) reads header lines until a blank line with no line-count limit.
3. **Chunked trailer lines** — `read_chunked()` (:355, trailer loop :369) reads trailer lines until a blank line with no line-count limit.

A laptop service that is stuck, buggy, or hostile can therefore hang one broker exchange *indefinitely*: every unit arrives promptly, so the tunnel's 660 s per-read timeout (`tunnel.rs` `TUNNEL_READ_TIMEOUT`, applied per read syscall) never fires — each successful read starts a fresh window. The exchange holds its pooled tunnel (per-port pool, `serve.rs`) and broker thread the whole time; repeated requests to the same misbehaving service can pin the whole pool (default 50) one exchange at a time, with no error ever surfaced.

This is the one peer-trust gap left in a module whose stated doctrine (#5579, module doc :16-27) is that peer-declared sizes are never trusted: sizes are capped, counts are not.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-proxy-http` on the laptop (real `fleet-proxy` crate via path dependency, `http.rs` byte-identical at laptop HEAD and `origin/main` 85c435ec6c; loopback fake peer, `HttpConn::request` on a thread with a timed wait):

- Control — peer sends one `100 Continue` head then `200 OK` with `Content-Length: 2`: **RETURNED status=200 body_len=2 in ~202µs**.
- `flood1xx` — peer streams `HTTP/1.1 100 Continue\r\n\r\n` heads at 1 ms intervals: **STILL BLOCKED after 4s** (would run to the peer's 200,000-head budget and beyond).
- `floodhdr` — peer sends `HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n` then streams `X-Fill: y\r\n` header lines: **STILL BLOCKED after 4s**.
- `floodtrailer` — peer sends a chunked head + `0\r\n` then streams trailer lines: **STILL BLOCKED after 4s**.

Dedup: #5579 (closed) capped declared *sizes*; #5921 (closed) made 1xx interim heads consumed rather than returned — it introduced loop 1 without a bound. No open issue covers repetition/count bounds in this reader (searched: "fleet-proxy 1xx", "interim response unbounded", "http.rs trailer").

## Why it matters

The broker is the fleet's single transport chokepoint to laptop services. A hang here is silent and unbounded — not a slow error but a permanently pinned tunnel and thread per exchange — and the trigger is exactly the peer this module already treats as untrusted for sizes. The failure mode also defeats the pool's bounded-wait design: slots are never returned, discarded, or timed out.

## Acceptance criteria

- Each repetition loop in the response reader has an explicit, named bound (interim-head count, header-line count per head, trailer-line count), sized generously above anything a legitimate laptop service sends, and exceeding it returns `HttpError::Malformed` and marks the connection non-reusable — the same failure shape as the existing size caps.
- The probe cases above become tests in `http.rs`' loopback test style: a peer flooding 1xx heads / header lines / trailer lines errors out promptly; the control (one interim head, normal headers, normal trailers) still succeeds.
- Legitimate behaviour is unchanged: #5921's HEAD/204/304/1xx semantics and #5579's size caps keep passing (`cargo test -p fleet-proxy` on the laptop or CI).
- The module doc's peer-trust paragraph names the count bounds alongside the size bounds.

body:
## Finding

PR #3510 (fix for #3475) made the github-backup deploy script advertise the final configured live version as the rollback target instead of the pre-secrets upload — but the new code silently falls back to that same pre-secrets upload whenever the post-provisioning re-read cannot name a live version:

```js
// infra/github-backup/worker/deploy.mjs, normal flow (current main 85c435ec6c59)
const configuredLive = liveVersionIds();
const liveId = configuredLive.join(", ") || version.id;
console.log(`live: ${WORKER_URL} at version ${liveId} (${tag})`);
```

`liveVersionIds()` (same file) swallows every failure into `[]`: a `deployments list` error, unparseable output, a non-array response, or a latest deployment with no version at `percentage === 100` all yield `[]`. In each of those cases the script exits 0 and prints `live: … at version <uploaded id>` — the exact version #3475 established carries no `DRAIN_BEARER` / `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET` bindings and must never be used as a rollback target. The `note: uploaded version … was superseded …` warning is also suppressed in this branch (it only prints when `liveId !== version.id`), so nothing in the run's own summary tells the operator the advertised target is unverified.

## Evidence

- PR #3510: MERGED 2026-11-01T10:56:11Z, merge commit `f5f612871e` (verified ancestor of current main `85c435ec6c59950f59b773776785ee78046ab69c`, compare behind_by 0).
