title: id(world_caps): parse_wants collapses duplicate JSON keys before its checks — a forbidden version, cap, id, or list size hidden behind a duplicate is accepted

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Problem

`parse_wants` (`pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/world_caps.rs:733`) parses a world program's `wants` document into a `serde_json::Value` first (`:738`) and only then runs its checks against the collapsed map:

- the format-version check reads `object.get("v")` (`:742-747`),
- the subscription entry cap reads `object.get("subscribe")` and checks the surviving array's length against `MAX_WANTS_ENTRIES` (`:749-756`),
- the request checks read `object.get("requests")` and, per entry, `entry.get("id")` / `entry.get("cap")` with the `MAX_NAME_BYTES` and control-character rules (`:764-790`).

`serde_json::Value` keeps only the **last** value of a repeated object key, so every one of those checks can be defeated by putting the forbidden value first and a benign duplicate after it. The document the host validates is not the document the program wrote: two readers of the same bytes (this parser vs. any strict reader, a logger, or a human) disagree about what was asked for.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop, real `id-core` crate, origin/main b7a15d73e9; world_caps.rs identical HEAD..origin)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-wants-dup` (path-dep on the real `id-core`), calling `parse_wants` directly:

Controls — each forbidden value standalone is refused, as designed:

- `{"v":99}` → Err (unsupported version)
- a request whose `cap` is 65 bytes (> `MAX_NAME_BYTES` 64) → Err
- a request whose `id` contains a control character → Err
- a `subscribe` array with 65 entries (> `MAX_WANTS_ENTRIES` 64) → Err
- a benign wants document → Ok

Findings — the same forbidden values hidden behind a benign duplicate key all parse **Ok**:

- `{"v":99,"v":1}` → Ok (version 99 never seen by the version check)
- `{"requests":[{"id":"r1","cap":"<65 bytes>","cap":"ok"}]}` → Ok (over-long cap hidden inside the entry object)
- `{"requests":[{"id":"a<CTRL>b","id":"ok","cap":"x"}]}` → Ok (control-character id hidden inside the entry object)
- `{"subscribe":[<65 entries>],"subscribe":["players"]}` → Ok (over-cap subscription list hidden at the top level)
- `{"requests":[{"id":"r1","cap":"<65 bytes>"}],"requests":[]}` → Ok (a whole non-conforming requests array hidden at the top level)

## Why it matters

`wants` is host-parsed, program-supplied input: the checks in `parse_wants` are the host's schema and bounds enforcement for what a world program may ask for (its own doc comment: "The caller treats that as a program failure, like invalid records"). A parser that validates a different document than the one on the wire is the same defect class already filed for the sibling Value-first parsers — #6473 (`parse_records`), #6474 (world fixture decode), #6491 (`parse_surface`) — and the fix pattern is established there: detect duplicate keys before/at parse (a duplicate-recording visitor or a strict typed decode), never validate the collapsed map. `parse_wants` is the remaining Value-first parser in `id-core` with checked fields; `args` values are opaque payloads and are out of scope except that their container keys (`id`/`cap`) are checked fields.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `parse_wants` refuses any document with a duplicate object key in a checked position: the top-level object (`v`, `subscribe`, `requests`) and each request entry object (`id`, `cap`, `args`), naming the repeated key.
- [ ] Each probe form above is refused; the standalone controls stay refused; benign documents (including documents whose `args` payloads legitimately repeat nothing) parse exactly as today.
- [ ] Regression tests pin: duplicate `v` (bad-first and bad-last), duplicate request `cap` over `MAX_NAME_BYTES`, duplicate request `id` with a control character, duplicate top-level `subscribe` over `MAX_WANTS_ENTRIES`, duplicate top-level `requests`.
- [ ] No change to the accepted-document semantics: field order, optional `v`, unknown top-level keys, and `args` contents behave as before for duplicate-free documents.

title: id(world_manifest): validate()/apply() never check the 30-day schedule horizon — a fire time past the horizon parses and plans clean, then fails partway through a live apply (schedules run last)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

`id world apply` accepts a manifest schedule the host can never set. The manifest layer checks only that a schedule's fire time is positive; the host layer refuses any fire time more than 30 days past the host clock — and the live apply runs schedule additions **last**, so the refusal lands only after every earlier step of the same apply has already been executed.

## Evidence (origin/main 32ec450e74)

- `pkgs/id/src/world_manifest.rs:236` — `WorldManifest::validate` schedule check is only `ensure!(*at_ms > 0, "schedule {id:?} must fire in the future")`. Its doc comment (lines 216ff) lists what validate enforces: known capability names, profile floors, schedule count, schedule-id shape, and positive fire times. No horizon bound.
- `pkgs/id/src/world_manifest.rs:423` — the defensive re-check in the pure `apply()` fold repeats only the same `at_ms > 0` rule.
- `pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/world_caps.rs:585-587` — `MAX_SCHEDULE_HORIZON_DAYS = 30`, `MAX_SCHEDULE_HORIZON_MS = 30 days`.
- `pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs:1467-1472` — `check_schedule_inner` (used by both the session `schedule.at` path and `AdminScheduleAt` via `check_schedule_replacing`) refuses `at_ms > now_ms + MAX_SCHEDULE_HORIZON_MS`: "schedule {id:?} is more than 30 days past the host clock".
- `pkgs/id/src/world/tests.rs` (~6488-6492) — the host rule is pinned in-tree: `now + horizon` is Ok, `now + horizon + 1` errors, and a past time (`0`) is Ok (past schedules fire on the next wakeup, by design — this issue is only about the far-future side).
- `pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs:1200-1211,1219` — `ordered_steps` ranks `ScheduleAt` last (rank 5, after cancels, profile, grants, ceiling, module install), and `apply_steps` executes the steps sequentially over the wire. A horizon refusal therefore aborts the apply after the earlier steps have already landed on the host: partial apply, and the failing step is re-planned as drift on every subsequent `diff`/`apply` forever.
- This is the exact failure shape #3015 fixed for profile bounds (see the rationale comment in `validate()`: "an invalid manifest must never parse and plan clean, then fail partway through a live apply") — the schedule horizon is the remaining host-side bound the manifest layer never pre-checks.

## Verified this run (probe, real id crate)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-manifest-horizon` on the laptop (path dependency on the real `id` crate; working tree identical to origin/main for every file involved — none of the 8 behind-commits touch them):

```
now_ms=<run time> horizon_ms=2592000000 horizon_days=30
X1 now+horizon+1day: parse=Ok plan=[ScheduleAt { id: "far", at_ms: <now+horizon+1day> }] apply=Ok(1) folded_schedules={"far": <same>}
X2 at_ms=u64::MAX: parse=Ok plan=[ScheduleAt { id: "far", at_ms: 18446744073709551615 }] apply=Ok(1) folded_schedules={"far": 18446744073709551615}
C1 now+1day: parse=Ok plan=[ScheduleAt …] apply=Ok(1) (control, inside horizon)
C2 at_ms=0: parse=Err "schedule \"far\" must fire in the future" (control, the one rule that is enforced)
```

So a manifest declaring a fire time 31 days out — or `u64::MAX` — parses, plans, and folds clean, while the host's own `check_schedule` refuses the same value at apply time.

## Why it matters

A typo'd or stale manifest (e.g. a fire time in nanoseconds, or a date past 30 days) does not fail fast at parse/dry-run: `id world apply --dry-run` reports the step as applicable, and a real apply mutates the world (grants, ceiling, profile, module, schedule cancels) before failing on the last step. The operator is left with a half-reconciled world and a manifest that can never converge — every later `diff` shows the same schedule drift.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A manifest whose schedule fire time is beyond the host horizon is refused **before any step is applied** — either at manifest validation time relative to an explicit clock, or as a pre-flight check in the `apply` command path (all `ScheduleAt` steps checked against the host clock / a freshly read host time before `apply_steps` executes anything). The refusal names the schedule id, its fire time, and the 30-day horizon.
- [ ] Schedules in the past and schedules within the horizon still parse, plan, and apply exactly as today (past times are legal by design and fire on the next wakeup).
- [ ] A regression test covers the boundary: `now + MAX_SCHEDULE_HORIZON_MS` accepted through the manifest path, `now + MAX_SCHEDULE_HORIZON_MS + 1` refused before any mutation.
- [ ] `id world diff` for such a manifest does not present the un-settable schedule as ordinary applicable drift without the horizon refusal being visible (or the pre-flight refusal covers the apply path and diff output is unchanged but documented — pick one and note it in the PR).

Related: #3015 / #4294 (parse-time validation family), #4769 / #4774 (apply() re-checks), #807 (manifest apply wiring).

body:
# id(world/replication): `SignedReplicationEnvelope::sign` signs envelopes every receiver rejects — version, header version, payload digest, cursor chain, terminal and snapshot-base rules are never checked

## Summary

`SignedReplicationEnvelope::sign` (`pkgs/id/src/world/replication.rs:495`) is the production signing entry point for replication frames (used by `world_replication_net.rs:320` `write_envelope`, the writer feed). It refuses only two things:

- the signing key not matching the envelope's claimed `source`, and
- a payload longer than `MAX_REPLICATION_PAYLOAD_BYTES`.

Every other rule that `ReplicationTracker::accept` (same file, `:744ff`) enforces **before** a frame may advance a replica is unchecked at signing time, and several of those rules are decidable from the envelope alone (no receiver/session state needed). A hand-built `ReplicationEnvelope` (all fields are `pub`, and `tail`/`snapshot`/`terminal` are not the only way to build one) therefore signs `Ok`/`Some` and is then rejected by **every** receiver, unconditionally:

| # | Signed shape | `sign()` | Every `accept()` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `version = 99` | `Some` | `UnsupportedEnvelopeVersion(99)` |
| 2 | `header_version = 0` or `MAX_JOURNAL_VERSION + 1` | `Some` | `UnsupportedJournalVersion(..)` |
| 3 | `payload_digest != payload_digest(payload)` | `Some` | `PayloadDigestMismatch` |
| 4 | `cursor_after != chain_payload(cursor_before, payload)` | `Some` | `EntryChainMismatch` |
| 5 | payload not complete decodable journal entries | `Some` | `MalformedPayload` |
| 6 | `Terminal` with a non-empty payload (or `cursor_before != cursor_after`) | `Some` | `TerminalCursorMismatch` |
| 7 | `Snapshot` with `cursor_before != chain_base_cursor(world_id, source, header_version)` | `Some` | `CursorFork` |
| 8 | Snapshot/tail payload whose journal header does not match the envelope (wrong world/version, duplicate `Created`) | `Some` | `InvalidJournalHeader` (#4486 rule) |

This is the same dead-on-arrival signing pattern as the earlier `sign_*` filings in this crate (e.g. #6422 currency, #6434 match_audit, #6447 `sign_move`): the signer is the writer itself, so a frame signed this way is not an attacker's forgery the receiver heroically stops — it is this node's own output that no peer can ever accept, discovered only when a sync session fails frame-by-frame.

## Evidence

Verified this run on the laptop primary at `6271e067012c360e108fa658ae23b5d9dedf6867` with a probe integration test against the real `id` crate (`~/git/fleet/probe-replication-sign/pkgs/id/tests/probe_replication_sign.rs`, worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-replication-sign`):

- Control: a `ReplicationEnvelope::tail(..)` envelope signs and a fresh `ReplicationTracker` accepts it.
- Cases 1–8 above: each mutated/hand-built envelope's `sign()` returned `Some`, `verify_signature()` passes (the signature is genuinely valid), and a fresh tracker's `accept()` returned exactly the named error in the table. 1 test passed.

Code read confirming the gap:

- `replication.rs:495-508` — `sign()` checks only `source` and payload length, then signs `signing_bytes()`.
- `replication.rs:744-830` — `accept()` checks envelope version, journal header version range (`JOURNAL_VERSION..=MAX_JOURNAL_VERSION`), payload digest equality, `chain_payload(cursor_before, payload) == cursor_after`, the snapshot base cursor, the terminal shape, and `validate_payload_journal_header` — none of which `sign()` mirrors.
- The safe constructors (`tail` :257, `snapshot` :287, `terminal` :313) compute digest/cursors correctly, which is why production frames are fine today — the hole is that `sign()` will sign anything else, and its doc comment ("refusing to sign for a key that is not the envelope's claimed source, and refusing an over-bound payload") presents those two as the refusal contract.
- Precedent that a refusing signer is workable: `replication_receiver.rs:626` tests already contain `sign_unbounded`, a helper that replicates the signing-bytes contract precisely because "the production signer refuses to sign" an over-bound payload. Receiver tests that need a lying signer can use the same bypass technique for the newly refused shapes (the `SignedReplicationEnvelope` fields are `pub`).

Not in scope (receiver-state-dependent, cannot be decided at signing time): world/pinned-source matching, session nonce, `prev_frame_digest` chaining, tail cursor gap/fork vs the receiver's current cursor. Those stay receiver-only.

## Why it matters

Replication is the read-replica path for worlds (#806). A writer that signs an always-rejected frame wastes a sync session and surfaces as an opaque peer-side refusal, far from the construction site that caused it. Every other signing path in this crate that gained a "refuse here what receipt would refuse" check (e.g. `directory::declare_home` #3187, `sign_after` symmetry #5623) did so to move exactly this class of failure to the moment of signing, with the rule named.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `SignedReplicationEnvelope::sign` returns `None` for an envelope that fails any envelope-local rule `accept()` enforces: envelope version, journal header version range, payload-digest equality, payload chaining to `cursor_after` (including malformed payload), snapshot base cursor, terminal shape (empty payload, `cursor_before == cursor_after`), and payload journal-header agreement (#4486).
- [ ] A valid `tail`/`snapshot`/`terminal` constructor envelope still signs `Some` and is accepted by a fresh tracker (existing replication tests keep passing).
- [ ] Tests pin each refused shape at the signer, and receiver tests that intentionally sign lying envelopes construct them via a direct/bypass helper (as `sign_unbounded` already does), not via the production `sign()`.
- [ ] The `sign()` doc comment states the full refusal contract.

## Dedup

Searched open and closed issues for `SignedReplicationEnvelope`, "replication envelope", "replication sign" (2026-11-06): only #806 (the F12.13 feature epic) and closed #4966 (checkpoint splitting) — neither covers signer-side validation. Distinct from #6447 (`sign_move` world-core domain) — different module, different signed type, different receiver rules.

body:
# atlas-eval: select_best_signal's documented tie-break (lexicographically smallest signal) only holds for evaluate()'s own output — a report in any other signal order picks the first-listed tied signal

## Summary

`atlas_core::eval::select_best_signal` documents a deterministic tie rule: "Deterministic: ties go to the lexicographically smallest signal name" (`pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-core/src/eval.rs:622-623`). The implementation does not implement that rule: it iterates `report.signals` in the order they appear in the report and keeps the first strictly-greatest value (`:630-645`, `value > best_value`), so on a tie the winner is whichever tied signal happens to be listed first.

That happens to be the lexicographically smallest only when the report came straight from `evaluate()`, which sorts its signals (`:578-579`). `EvalReport` is a public, `Serialize`/`Deserialize` type with all-public fields (`:496-507`), and the workflow the harness exists for is report-shaped: the `atlas-eval` binary prints the report JSON to stdout (`src/bin/atlas-eval.rs`), and parameter selection is a separate step that operates on a report. A report that was saved, round-tripped through JSON, merged, or simply constructed by a caller with its signals in a different order silently gets a different "best" signal on ties — the exact nondeterminism across input orderings that the rest of this module is careful to eliminate (the module docs promise reports are deterministic and input-order independent, and the fixture test pins that `evaluate()`'s output does not change when the input runs are shuffled — but no test pins the tie rule for `select_best_signal` itself, and none of its callers' reports are required to be sorted).

## Evidence (file:line, origin/main 97648e200c)

- `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-core/src/eval.rs:622-623` — the documented contract: "Deterministic: ties go to the lexicographically smallest signal name."
- `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-core/src/eval.rs:630-645` — `select_best_signal` scans `report.signals` in slice order and replaces the incumbent only on a strict `>`: the first-listed tied signal wins, whatever its name.
- `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-core/src/eval.rs:578-579` — `evaluate()` sorts runs by signal name before building the report; this incidental sort is the only thing that makes the documented rule true today.
- `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-core/src/eval.rs:496-507` — `EvalReport { format, split, signals }` is `pub`, with `pub` fields, and derives `Serialize`/`Deserialize`: nothing about the type requires or restores sorted order, and `SignalReport`/`MetricMeans` are likewise fully public, so any caller can build or load a report whose signal order differs.
- No test covers a tie: `grep select_best_signal` shows assertions only for a single-signal dev report, the test-split refusal, and the smoke fixture (dense wins outright on nDCG, 0.898354 vs 0.846713 — no tie).

## Verification (this run, laptop, real atlas-core crate)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-atlas-tie` (path-depends on the real `atlas-core` crate at origin/main 97648e200c; each case is a real `select_best_signal` call):

```
case1 tie unsorted [zeta, alpha] -> Ok("zeta")     // documented winner: "alpha"
case2 tie sorted [alpha, zeta] -> Ok("alpha")     // control: documented winner
case3 tie deserialized [zeta, alpha] -> Ok("zeta") // report JSON round-trip, same wrong winner
case4 strict winner unsorted -> Ok("zeta")         // control: a strict winner wins in any order
case5 evaluate() tie -> Ok("alpha") (signals order: ["alpha", "zeta"]) // evaluate()'s sort masks it
```

Cases 1 and 3 return `zeta`, contradicting the function's own documented tie rule; the controls (cases 2, 4, 5) behave as documented, which isolates the defect to `select_best_signal` trusting the report's signal order instead of applying its rule.

## Why it matters

- Parameter selection is the harness's decision point (#5741): the signal it names is the one that earns a place in the fused ranking. On a metric tie — common at `round6` precision, where distinct signals routinely round to the same mean — the selection currently depends on the provenance and serialization order of the report, not on the stated rule. Two runs of the same selection step over the same scores can name different signals.
- The failure is silent: the returned name is a real signal with a real (tied) score, so nothing downstream looks wrong; the determinism the module promises ("the same input serializes to byte-identical JSON on every run") is broken at the one step that converts scores into a choice.

## Acceptance criteria

- `select_best_signal` returns the lexicographically smallest signal name among those tied at the best metric value, for a report in ANY signal order (hand-built, deserialized, or `evaluate()` output) — e.g. by comparing names on ties or by selecting over a name-sorted view of the signals.
- A strict (non-tied) winner still wins regardless of order, the test-split refusal is unchanged, and a report with no signals still errors.
- Pinning tests cover: a tie with signals in reverse lexicographic order (directly and via a JSON round-trip of the report), a tie in sorted order, and a strict winner in reverse order, alongside the existing `held_out_test_split_is_refused_for_parameter_selection` and fixture tests.
- `evaluate()`'s own output and ordering are unchanged.

Related: #5741 (the eval harness and its parameter-selection rule), #6390/#6433 (the same module's duplicate-results-key fix — validation-side determinism in this harness).

title: id(directory_mail): CommandSink never calls validate_header_fields — header values both sibling sinks refuse are forwarded verbatim to the external mail program

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/id/src/directory_mail.rs` defines three `MailSink`s for the same `Mail { to, subject, body }`, and a shared header-field validation, `Mail::validate_header_fields` (:35) — recipient must be ASCII and a plain address (`plain_address`), subject must contain no control character. Two sinks enforce it before doing anything with the message:

- `OutboxSink::send` (:79-80) calls `mail.validate_header_fields()?` before creating the `.eml` file (this was the fix for #2404, which had found the outbox writing unvalidated `To:`/`Subject:` headers).
- `SmtpSink::send_with_timeout` (:257) calls `mail.validate_header_fields()?` before connecting to the relay.

`CommandSink` — the sink used for `--world-mail-command` (`commands/serve.rs:773`), i.e. the configured external mail program — never calls it. Its `send_with_timeout` (:134-140) passes the fields verbatim into the child process environment:

```rust
.env("ID_MAIL_TO", &mail.to)
.env("ID_MAIL_SUBJECT", &mail.subject)
.env("ID_MAIL_BODY", &mail.body)
```

So a `Mail` that both sibling sinks refuse — a subject with an embedded newline (`Your code\nBcc: attacker@evil.example`), a recipient with CRLF / SMTP smuggling syntax, a non-ASCII (internationalised) recipient, or a recipient that is not a plain address at all — is handed unchecked to the external program. The shipped program, `nixos/services/id-mail/cloudflare-mail.sh`, forwards `ID_MAIL_TO` / `ID_MAIL_SUBJECT` as the `to` / `subject` of a Cloudflare Email Sending API (or mail Worker) call — i.e. these values do become mail headers downstream, just one process later — and any operator-configured program receives them under the same contract, trusting that the sink enforced the module's one documented invariant ("Validate fields that sinks serialize into mail headers", :34). #2404's acceptance criteria said the validation should be shared so that "no sink writes unvalidated header fields"; the command sink is the one sink that still forwards them unvalidated.

`Mail`'s fields are `pub`, and the sinks are the crate's public mail API, so the guarantee has to live in the sink (as it now does for the other two), not in today's callers.

## Evidence (verified this run, origin/main 917e1a3bdb)

Verified by direct code read of `pkgs/id/src/directory_mail.rs` at origin/main 917e1a3bdb (two independent reads this run — a full read of the sink implementations and a grep line map of every `validate_header_fields` occurrence):

- The only occurrences of `validate_header_fields` in the file are its definition (:35), the `OutboxSink` call (:80), and the `SmtpSink` call (:257). There is no call anywhere in `CommandSink`'s impl (:122-204).
- `CommandSink::send_with_timeout` (:134-199) was read in full: it builds the `Command` with `.env("ID_MAIL_TO", &mail.to)` / `.env("ID_MAIL_SUBJECT", &mail.subject)` / `.env("ID_MAIL_BODY", &mail.body)`, spawns it, and returns Ok on a successful exit — no validation step exists on the path, so for any program that exits 0 (e.g. the recording `/bin/sh` program the module's own tests use, :509) the malformed fields are delivered verbatim.
- The sibling refusals are pinned by in-tree tests: `the_outbox_refuses_subject_header_injection_before_creating_file` and `the_outbox_refuses_crlf_recipient_before_creating_file` assert the exact errors ("the subject has a line break or control character", "the recipient is not a plain address") for a subject of `Your code\nBcc: attacker@evil.example` and a recipient of `a@b.co>\r\nRCPT TO:<x@y.z` — the same values `CommandSink` forwards unchecked. Non-ASCII and non-plain recipients hit the other two arms of the same `validate_header_fields` (:38-47).

A runtime probe (recording command sink in a laptop worktree, `~/git/fleet/probe-mail-cmd-wt`) was prepared this run but the laptop became unreachable before the corrected probe run completed; this filing therefore rests on the code read above, which is deterministic — there is no validation call to find — and the triage packet asks the worker to add the regression tests in the acceptance criteria as the executable proof.

Dedup: #2404 (closed) covered `OutboxSink` only and named `CommandSink` out of scope except for its timeout (#1788, closed). Searches for `CommandSink`, `validate_header_fields`, and `directory_mail` return no open issue covering command-sink header validation.

## Why it matters

The three sinks are interchangeable configuration choices for the same confirmation-mail path (`commands/serve.rs:769-773` picks one from flags). A validation invariant that holds for two of the three is a trap: switching a deployment from the outbox/SMTP sink to a mail command silently drops the header-injection, address-shape, and SMTPUTF8 refusals the module deliberately enforces, and the external program — the component least able to know the invariant — receives exactly the smuggled values the other sinks were fixed to refuse (#2404, #2637).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `CommandSink` refuses a `Mail` whose `to` is non-ASCII or not a plain address, or whose `subject` contains a control character, with the same errors as the other sinks — e.g. by calling `mail.validate_header_fields()?` at the top of `CommandSink::send_with_timeout` (or `send`), before any process is spawned.
- [ ] Regression tests mirror the existing outbox refusal tests for the command sink: a newline subject and a CRLF recipient are both refused and the recording program is never invoked (no output file created).
- [ ] The legitimate path is unchanged: the existing command-sink tests (message passed in the environment, failing command is an error, timeout kill/reap) pass unmodified.
- [ ] No change to `OutboxSink` / `SmtpSink` behaviour, the `Mail` shape, or the `ID_MAIL_*` environment contract for valid mail.

title: id(app_manifest): discovery never checks route↔socket collisions — one app's route can equal another app's socket (or its own) and both register

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

`discover_apps` (`pkgs/id/src/app_manifest.rs`) enforces cross-app uniqueness for web paths in two separate namespaces: a new app's `interfaces.web.route` is compared only against already-registered apps' **routes**, and its `socket` only against their **sockets**. Route↔socket collisions are never checked — neither across two apps nor within a single manifest (`route == socket`).

Routes and sockets are the same namespace at the layer that binds them: `pkgs/id/src/web/app_interface.rs` treats them as one axum path space — it rejects a socket that collides with a host-registered route, and rejects a single section whose route and socket name the same path ("route and socket both bind {path}; they must differ", app_interface.rs:103-105, ~:410). Discovery is the only gate that sees the whole discovered set (the Phase 4 disposition table in app_manifest.rs assigns cross-app uniqueness to discovery: "unique across the discovered set; first folder in sort order wins, the loser is a named error"), and `commands::serve` only logs discovered apps today — no binding pass over the discovered set exists to catch what discovery misses. So two apps that would collide in one router both register cleanly, with no named error, and the collision surfaces only later as a bind failure (or an axum panic) in whatever step eventually binds the set.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ origin/main 50debbc36a)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-manifest-xcollision` (real `id` crate, `discover_apps` over synthetic app folders):

- **X1 route-vs-socket**: app-a route `/shared`, app-b route `/b` + socket `/shared` → `registered=["app-a", "app-b"] errors=[]`
- **X2 socket-vs-route**: app-a route `/a` + socket `/shared`, app-b route `/shared` → `registered=["app-a", "app-b"] errors=[]`
- **X3 self route==socket**: one app, route `/same`, socket `/same` → `registered=["app-a"] errors=[]` (the binding layer rejects exactly this shape for a single section; discovery/parse do not)
- **C1 control** route↔route duplicate → second app rejected with the named duplicate-route error
- **C2 control** socket↔socket duplicate → second app rejected with the named duplicate-socket error
- **C3 control** all-distinct route/socket pairs → both apps register, no errors

Code: app_manifest.rs `discover_apps` — the route check searches `discovery.apps` for an equal `route` only; the socket check searches for an equal `socket` only; `parse_app_manifest` validates each path's shape (`is_safe_web_path`) but never compares the two fields.

## Why it matters

Discovery's contract (Phase 4 disposition, #4203) is that cross-app path collisions are deterministic named errors at scan time, first-folder-wins. The cross-kind hole means the discovered set can be internally inconsistent in exactly the dimension the binding layer treats as one namespace — and because serve currently only logs discovery results, nothing downstream re-checks the set as a set. When a bind step for discovered apps lands, this becomes a startup failure (or panic) caused by two individually "valid" apps, with no error naming either.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `discover_apps` rejects (named per-app error, first folder in sort order wins, other apps unaffected) any app whose route equals an already-registered app's socket, and any app whose socket equals an already-registered app's route — in both folder orders.
- [ ] A manifest whose own `route == socket` is rejected at parse or discovery time with a named error (mirroring the binding layer's existing rule), instead of registering.
- [ ] Same-kind duplicate behavior unchanged: route↔route and socket↔socket duplicates keep their current named errors; all-distinct sets register fully.
- [ ] Tests in app_manifest.rs cover: route-vs-socket, socket-vs-route, self route==socket, plus the existing same-kind and distinct controls.
- [ ] The Phase 4 disposition table rows for `interfaces.web.route` / `interfaces.web.socket` are updated to state the cross-kind rule.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for app_manifest route/socket/discovery: #4060 (closed) covered same-kind duplicate routes and shape validation; #5427 (closed) covered dot-segment spellings evading uniqueness; #4779 (closed) added the route==socket and host-collision checks in the single-section binding layer (`web_interface_from_app_toml`), which discovered apps never pass through. None covers cross-app route↔socket uniqueness at discovery, or route==socket at parse/discovery.

title: id(directory_auth): sign_request never checks the nonce against verify_signed's domain — empty, over-long and bad-character nonces sign Ok yet are always rejected as 'signature does not verify'

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Summary

`pkgs/id/src/directory_auth.rs`: `sign_request` (line 304) signs any nonce presented to it and returns the `Signed` infallibly (`#[must_use]`, no `Result`), while `verify_signed` (line 327) refuses — before it even checks the signature — any nonce that is empty, longer than 64 characters, or contains a character outside ASCII alphanumeric plus `-` (lines 348–353). A caller can therefore produce a correctly-signed request that every verifier rejects, and the signing call gives no signal anything is wrong.

The rejected shapes are all decidable at sign time from `sign_request`'s own inputs: the nonce rule depends only on the `nonce: &str` argument itself. (The other `verify_signed` checks are correctly verify-only: the time window is relative to the server's clock, and replay is server state — neither is asked to move.)

The rejection is also misattributed when it happens: the nonce failure returns the generic `refused()` error, "signature does not verify", so a client debugging a rejected request is pointed at its key/signature, not at the malformed nonce it chose.

This is the same construction-vs-receipt asymmetry as #6422 (`sign_authorisation` never calls `validate`), #6424 (`sign_genesis`/`sign_claim` never check the signer is a player), and #6434 (`sign_header`/`sign_footer` never check version/roster/signer/commitment), in a module none of them covers. The in-tree precedent for the fix shape is #5623: a known kind is signed only when receipt would accept it, so signing fails with the receipt refusal instead of producing a dead-on-arrival object.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ origin/main 9e20032d0c)

Probe: laptop worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-dir-auth-wt`, test `pkgs/id/tests/probe_dir_auth_sign.rs` against the real `id` crate (test binary run directly after the build: `1 passed`). Controls verify Ok through `verify_signed` with a fresh `ReplayGuard`: nonce `"n1"`, `"abc-DEF-123"`, and a 64-character nonce. Against those controls, `sign_request` returns a `Signed` (it has no error channel) and `verify_signed` rejects every one of:

- `""` — empty nonce
- a 65-character nonce — one over the cap
- `"has space"` — space
- `"under_score"` — underscore
- `"plus+sign"` — plus
- `"dot.name"` — dot
- `"unié"` — non-ASCII

Grep at origin/main: the nonce domain rule exists only at `directory_auth.rs:348-353`, inside `verify_signed`; `sign_request` at `:304` and its call sites contain no nonce check. Dedup: `gh search issues` for "sign_request", "directory_auth" and "signed request nonce" returned no filing covering sign-time nonce validation (#6177 is the pending-codes slot in the same file, a different subject).

## Why it matters

`sign_request` is the client helper for the signed-request authentication that `world_hub` / `world_ws` / `world_session` verify (`verify_signed` call sites in `world_hub.rs:473`, `web/world_ws.rs:465`, `world_session/mod.rs:1207`). A client that derives its nonce from anything other than a strict alphanumeric generator — a UUID with dots is fine, but a base64 nonce (`+`, `/`, `=`), a timestamp with separators, or an over-long random string — produces requests that can never authenticate, with the server reporting "signature does not verify". Failing at sign time, naming the nonce rule, makes the error local and actionable, exactly as the sibling fixes for #6422/#6424/#6434 propose.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `sign_request` (or a nonce-validating constructor/helper it uses) refuses a nonce that is empty, longer than 64 characters, or contains a character outside ASCII alphanumeric plus `-`, with an error naming the nonce rule — before producing a signature. The exact API shape (fallible `sign_request` vs a validated nonce type) is triage's call, since the current signature returns `Signed` infallibly.
- [ ] Well-formed nonces sign and verify exactly as before: existing `directory_auth`, `world_ws`, and `world_session` tests stay green.
- [ ] New tests pin each refusal class above (empty / over-long / representative bad characters incl. non-ASCII), with the valid controls (short, alphanumeric+dash, exactly 64 chars) still verifying.
- [ ] No change to `verify_signed`'s verdicts, the wire format (`Signed` fields / headers), the replay guard, or the time-window rule.

🤖 Filed by the fleet new-issue-creator (lane B) — verified with a probe against the real crate this run; see the probe path in the evidence section.

body:
## Parent and context
Parent program: #5678. Product/implementation foundation: #2048. This ticket owns the evidence-backed competitor feature inventory and matrix that the cluster designs can use; it does not implement features or silently settle the program-level open questions.

## Scope
- Define a repeatable enumeration method and a normalized feature vocabulary for Obsidian, Evernote, Notion, OneNote, NotebookLM, Logseq, Joplin, Anytype, and Open Knowledge (whose identity is not yet confirmed).
- Record each product’s data model, sync, sharing/permissions, pricing or lock-in where it affects import/export, and distinguishing capabilities.
- Compare features in a product-by-feature matrix with qualitative notes about depth/quality and meaningful implementation differences; avoid checkbox-only conclusions.
- Use primary documentation and, where authorized and feasible, hands-on evaluation. Record product edition/version, source and observation dates, evidence type, uncertainty, unavailable evidence, and gaps.
- Trace candidate clusters to the existing follow-ons #5837–#5844 and identify any matrix-driven additions or changes. For each candidate, record evidence and adopt/adapt/reject options without treating competitor presence as a default requirement.

## Required outputs
1. A short method and source/provenance note, including how product editions and feature names are normalized.
2. A linked matrix document with product inventories, comparative notes, and evidence links.
3. A findings section connecting observations to the existing cluster designs and recording unresolved decisions rather than deciding them by assumption.

## Read-authority constraint (already ruled; do not re-litigate)
The knowledge layer defaults to public read; owners may grant reads to any number of groups and/or users. Resolution order is **object → user default → server config → public**. Any inventory or recommendation involving sharing, search, graph visibility, or AI-over-notes must describe compatibility with this rule and must not suggest a read path that exposes content the resolved policy denies.

## Open Drew-owned program questions — still open, not assumptions
Carry these questions into the investigation and record whether each affects the matrix or requires an explicit decision; do not answer them by guessing: product versions/editions (free vs. paid); hands-on evaluation vs. documentation-only budget per product; the identity of “Open Knowledge”; graph scope (all ID objects vs. knowledge-only in v1); and AI-over-notes model choice (local, hosted, or user choice) and its read-authority implications.

## Acceptance criteria
- The method, normalized product/feature inventories, and matrix document are complete, sourced, and linked from #5678.
- Every in-scope product is covered or has an explicit evidence/identity blocker; matrix entries distinguish confirmed facts from unknowns.
- Cluster findings link to the existing tickets and state evidence-backed options without silently adopting features or resolving Drew-owned questions.
- Read-authority compliance is explicit, including visibility-sensitive AI/search/graph findings.

# id: five more tests never run — attribute-less and never called (cli.rs, repl/runner.rs, web/markdown.rs, web/templates.rs); corrects #6410's neighbor claim

## Evidence (verified this run, origin/main `28719695372b`)

Each function below is a zero-argument, assertion-bearing test body inside a `#[cfg(test)]` module, carries **no `#[test]` attribute**, and occurs **exactly once** in the repo (`git grep` count 1 — its own definition), so it is never called by another test either. It never runs:

| Site | Test | Pins |
|---|---|---|
| `pkgs/id/src/cli.rs:3638` | `test_cli_rejects_first_and_last_together` | #3059 CLI boundary: `--first` + `--last` together are rejected |
| `pkgs/id/src/repl/runner.rs:1967` | `test_parse_find_args_basic` | REPL `parse_find_args` basic shape |
| `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs:9019` | `test_footnote_multi_paragraph_definition_fixpoint` | #1031: a two-paragraph footnote definition keeps its paragraph boundary on save |
| `pkgs/id/src/web/templates.rs:1329` | `test_render_program_page_escapes_the_world_name` | program page escapes a hostile world name (`a"<b>`) in `data-world-program` |
| `pkgs/id/src/web/templates.rs:1335` | `test_render_world_page_exposes_presentation_controls` | world page exposes the presentation controls / socket wiring |

Verification method: a scan of every `mod tests` in `pkgs/id/src` + `pkgs/id/crates` for attribute-less zero-argument test-shaped functions, then per-site confirmation (raw preceding lines show the previous test's closing brace, a blank line, and the bare `fn`; caller count via `git grep` = 1). Helpers with the same scan shape (e.g. `test_find_match(name)` in runner.rs, `test_store()` in world_ssh.rs, `encode_alpha_key_4_fields()` in tags.rs) were checked and excluded — they take arguments or return fixtures and are called by living tests.

## Relation to #6409 / #6410 — and a correction

#6410 described the five doubled-`#[test]` sites as "pure duplications" with "all neighbors correctly attributed". **That was wrong for two of them**: this run's first neighbor check only looked *before* each doubled site. The dead tests *after* them tell the fuller story — cli.rs's doubled site (:3608) is one test before dead `test_cli_rejects_first_and_last_together` (:3638), and templates.rs's doubled site (:1306) precedes both dead templates tests (:1329, :1335). The runner.rs and markdown.rs:9019 dead tests have no doubled neighbor; their attributes are simply absent. The shared, verified fact across #6409, #6410, and this issue is the dead tests themselves; the doubled attributes are one visible symptom, not the whole mechanism.

## Why it matters

Seven dead regression pins in one crate (2 in #6409/#6410 + these 5), covering CLI argument rejection (#3059), REPL parsing, footnote save behavior (#1031, sibling of #945), and HTML escaping of an untrusted world name on a guest-facing page — the templates escaping test is security-adjacent: a regression in `render_program_page`'s escaping would ship with a green suite. Same class as #6185: a suite that never runs is not a test.

As with #6410, these tests were **not** re-run standalone this run (full-crate test build). If any fails when re-enabled, that failure is a live regression the dead test was hiding — triage it as such; do not weaken or delete the test to make it pass.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Add the missing `#[test]` to each of the five functions listed above (attribute only; no test-body changes).
- [ ] `cargo test -- --list` shows each of the five exactly once; run them — each passes, or a follow-up issue is filed/linked for the regression its failure exposes.
- [ ] No production code changes.

## Notes

- Third in a series from Lane B (new-issue-creator-code-b), same run: #6409 (commands/text.rs), #6410 (web/markdown.rs #945 + doubled sites). A correction comment has been posted on #6410 pointing here.

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/id/worker-poc/smoke/participant-clamp.mjs` — the regression pin for the Codex P2 on PR #3726 — is not run by the worker-poc's aggregate entry point and is not documented, so the pin executes only when someone remembers its private script name.

The pin: the native host clamps participant IDs to `i32::MAX` (`sandbox.rs: i32::try_from(participant).unwrap_or(i32::MAX)`); `PlazaGuest` used to wrap them with `| 0`, so participant `4294967296` became participant `0`. roc-chat routes participant 0 through its host-event handler (input not appended) while any real participant appends, so the wrap is observable in the guest view. The smoke asserts `4294967296` behaves exactly as `i32::MAX` and differently from `0` (`smoke/participant-clamp.mjs:1-28`).

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ origin/main `2fac2b7b0f`)

- `pkgs/id/worker-poc/package.json` — the `smoke` script is `node smoke/counter-smoke.mjs && node smoke/post-update-failure.mjs && node smoke/participant-validation.mjs`. `participant-clamp` has a script of its own (`package.json:15`) but is **not in the `smoke` chain**.
- `pkgs/id/worker-poc/README.md` smoke section (lines 42-52) documents `counter-smoke`, `post-update-failure`, and `participant-validation` — `participant-clamp` is **absent from the README**.
- Repo-wide grep for `participant-clamp` returns only the file itself and its own `package.json` script: no workflow, flake check, justfile, or NixOS module runs it (the poc smokes have no CI venue at all — established for the sibling in #6372).
- This is the leftover of the #6372 fix: PR #6374 (commit `8f2cf5dd62`) added `participant-validation` to the `smoke` chain and the README, and `participant-clamp` — already present with its own script at that commit — was passed over by the same pass.
- The smoke itself is green: on the laptop (Node v24.21.0, files extracted verbatim from `origin/main`), `node smoke/participant-clamp.mjs` exits 0 with `participant-clamp: ok (i32::MAX view "chat seen=0 last= input=x"; participant 0 view "chat seen=0 last= input=")`.

Distinct from CLOSED #6372 (that was `participant-validation.mjs`, which had no script of its own and no chain entry; it is now wired). This file is the remaining orphan smoke in the same directory.

## Why it matters

The clamp-vs-wrap difference is exactly the class of host/isolate divergence the worker-poc exists to catch (#2271), and it was a review-caught regression once already (Codex P2 on PR #3726). A pin that the documented aggregate command (`npm run smoke`) silently skips can regress again unnoticed — the same failure mode #6372 fixed for its sibling.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `npm run smoke` in `pkgs/id/worker-poc` executes `smoke/participant-clamp.mjs` along with the other smokes, and the full chain is green.
- [ ] The README smoke section documents `participant-clamp` (what it pins, how to run it alone via `npm run participant-clamp`), matching the treatment `participant-validation` got in #6374.
- [ ] No behavior change to `participant-clamp.mjs` itself or to the guest/host code it pins.

title: id(flake): alias apps bypass the private/default filter — an alias to a private recipe publishes it, and a dangling alias target breaks every app's evaluation

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: kind/infrastructure
labels.description: Infrastructure / host-portability work

body:
## Problem

In `pkgs/id/flake.nix`, the apps generated from `just-recipes.json` apply the house filter on the recipe side only:

- `publicRecipes` (flake.nix:293-295) excludes private recipes and `default`: `!(recipe.private or false) && name != "default"`.
- The alias side (flake.nix:791-793) is unfiltered: `apps = mapAttrs mkRecipeApp publicRecipes // mapAttrs mkAliasApp (justRecipes.aliases or { }) // { …manual… }`, and `mkAliasApp` (flake.nix:285-290) resolves its target with a bare `justRecipes.recipes.${alias.target}` and feeds it straight to `mkRecipeApp`.

Two consequences, both by construction:

1. **The private filter is bypassable by alias.** An alias whose target is a private recipe publishes that recipe as a public `nix run .#<alias>` app, even though the same recipe is deliberately excluded when named directly. The private recipes in the current JSON are exactly the kind that must not leak: `_nixpkgs-inputs`, `mark-variant-lib`, `mark-variant-release-lib`, `mark-variant-release-web`, `mark-variant-web`. An alias name colliding with a public recipe name also silently overrides that recipe's app (`//` order: aliases win over recipes).
2. **One dangling alias breaks every app.** If an alias target is renamed or removed and the JSON is regenerated inconsistently (or edited by hand), `recipes.${alias.target}` throws attribute-missing during evaluation of the whole `apps` attrset — every generated app fails to evaluate, not just the stale alias. The drift guard (`scripts/just-recipes-check.sh`) projects only top-level recipes/aliases from a fresh `just --dump`, so it cannot catch an alias-to-private or alias-collision shape either: it compares targets, never the filter semantics.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop, origin/main a664c227e8)

Exact-expression `nix eval` probe over the committed `pkgs/id/just-recipes.json` (the flake's own `filterAttrs` predicate and alias resolution, no flake inputs):

```json
{"aliasCount":22,"dangling":[],"exposedPrivate":[],"privateRecipes":["_nixpkgs-inputs","mark-variant-lib","mark-variant-release-lib","mark-variant-release-web","mark-variant-web"],"publicCount":127,"syntheticAliasToPrivateResolves":true}
```

- 133 top-level recipes → 127 public (5 private + `default` excluded) on the recipe side.
- All 22 current aliases happen to target public recipes (`exposedPrivate: []`, `dangling: []`) — the gap is latent today, which is precisely when a filter belongs in code rather than in the data. Nothing in the pipeline prevents the next alias from targeting a private recipe.

## Why it matters

`[private]` in a justfile is an explicit "not a public entry point" decision. The flake honors it for direct names and silently un-honors it for aliases, so the published app surface depends on contributors remembering a rule no tool enforces. The dangling-target failure mode is the inverse robustness problem: one stale alias takes down evaluation of the entire generated app set.

## Acceptance criteria

- Alias apps go through the same admission as recipe apps: an alias whose target is private (or `default`) produces no app, and an alias whose name collides with a public recipe name or a manual app (`default`, `just`) does not silently override it — the collision is refused or the recipe/manual app wins, with the choice pinned by a test or check.
- A dangling alias target does not break evaluation of the remaining apps: it is skipped with a visible warning (e.g. `builtins.trace` / a check failure in `just-recipes-check`), or the drift check fails naming the alias and its missing target.
- `scripts/just-recipes-check.sh` (or a new flake check) covers the alias shapes: alias→private, alias→default, alias→missing target, alias↔recipe name collision. Current clean data (22 aliases, all public targets) keeps passing.
- Existing behavior is preserved for honest data: the same 127 recipe apps + 22 alias apps evaluate as before.

Found by new-issue-creator-code-a; verified at laptop origin/main a664c227e8ffde71fb8af0958301dd4cf3b8af8b.

title: deploy(deploy.py): validate() accepts shapes its own rules reject — newline service names, duplicate targets/secrets, host-less healthCheck URLs

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/deploy
labels.description: Package/app: deploy (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
# deploy(deploy.py): validate() accepts shapes its own rules reject — newline service names, duplicate targets/secrets, host-less healthCheck URLs

`pkgs/deploy/deploy.py`'s module docstring states the contract: validation "is the oracle for 'well-formed definition'... Any violation is reported by field and makes `list` exit non-zero — a registry that cannot be validated must never be enumerated as if it were trustworthy." Three classes of invalid definition currently pass `validate()` and are enumerated by `deploy list` with exit 0.

Verified on the laptop primary @1dae17e457 with a probe driving the real `deploy.py` against hand-written registries (probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-deploy-validate/probe.py` on the laptop):

## 1. Service name with a trailing newline passes NAME_RE

- `NAME_RE = re.compile(r"^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*$")` (deploy.py:52), checked at deploy.py:64. In Python, `$` also matches immediately before a trailing newline, so the name `"svc\n"` is accepted.
- Observed: registry with service name `"svc\n"` → `deploy list` exits 0 and prints the name verbatim, injecting a line break into the table:

  ```
  NAME  CLASS       TARGETS
  svc
    systemd     laptop
  ```

- Control: name `"bad name"` is correctly rejected (exit 1, "name must match ^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*$").
- Why it matters beyond cosmetics: service names are not display-only. The design (doc/2026-11-04_deployment-architecture-services-layer.md §4) puts per-service profiles at `/nix/var/nix/profiles/per-service/<name>`, and later #5766 slices render systemd units / activation paths from these names. A name the validator's own pattern intends to forbid should not reach those consumers. Fix shape: `\Z` instead of `$` (or `fullmatch`), so the pattern means what it says.

## 2. Duplicate `targets` and duplicate `secrets` accepted — while duplicate `ports` are rejected

- deploy.py:124 explicitly rejects repeated ports: "ports must not repeat a port". The same function places no uniqueness check on `targets` (deploy.py:137-142) or `secrets` (deploy.py:102-109).
- Observed: `targets: ["laptop", "laptop"]` → exit 0, list prints `laptop,laptop`. `secrets: ["a.b", "a.b"]` → exit 0. Control: `ports: [4801, 4801]` → exit 1 with the repeat error.
- The asymmetry inside one validator reads as an oversight, not a design choice: a repeated target or secret name is the same class of registry authoring error as a repeated port, and later slices will iterate targets (deploy destinations) and secrets (broker lookups by name) where duplicates cause double work or double resolution.

## 3. `healthCheck` accepts a bare scheme with no host

- deploy.py:128-135 checks only `hc.startswith("http://") or hc.startswith("https://")`. Observed: `healthCheck: "http://"` → exit 0.
- `"http://"` is not a URL any health checker can poll; §3's own example is a full URL with host and path (`http://100.99.113.103:4801/healthz`). A host-less value passes the oracle today and would only fail later, at activation/health-check time, in a slice that trusts validation to have caught it.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validate()` rejects, with field-named errors in the existing style: (a) any service name not fully matching the intended name pattern, including a trailing newline (and generally any control character); (b) repeated entries in `targets` and in `secrets`, mirroring the existing ports rule; (c) a `healthCheck` string that is not a parseable http(s) URL with a non-empty host.
- The existing valid registry (`pkgs/deploy/services.nix` rendered via the flake) still validates and `deploy list` output is unchanged for it.
- Regression coverage: extend the malformed-registry flake check (`deploy-list-malformed`, lib/default.nix:1230) or add equivalent cases so each rejected shape above is exercised — the current check covers only an `entryPoint` type error and an out-of-range port.
- Sane controls keep passing: the probe's valid registry, the space-in-name rejection, and the duplicate-port rejection all behave as before.

Related: #6376 (same file's argument parser silently ignoring trailing args / duplicate `--registry` — a separate parser-layer finding), #5766 (the deploy tool epic this validation gates).

title: deploy(deploy.py): arguments after list are silently ignored and a duplicate --registry silently overrides the first — the typo-flag class, in the parser the activation slices will build on

labels.name: task/triage

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/deploy/deploy.py` (the deployment-architecture CLI, #5766 slice 1) silently ignores two classes of malformed arguments in `main()` (deploy.py:168-186):

1. **Anything after `list` is ignored.** After the `--registry` extraction loop (deploy.py:172-178), `main()` checks only `args[0] != "list"` (deploy.py:186) and never inspects the rest. `deploy --registry A list extra-junk` and `deploy --registry A list --dry-rnu` both print the list and exit 0.
2. **A duplicate `--registry` silently overrides the first.** The `while "--registry" in args` loop (deploy.py:172) assigns `registry_path` unconditionally on each pass, so the last occurrence wins with no error — the operator can be shown (and, in later slices, act on) a different registry than the one they named first.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ origin/main 03d1a21eae, probe `~/git/fleet/probe-deploy-argv`)

Two one-service registries: A = `svc-a` (target `laptop`), B = `svc-b` (target `sandbox`).

- Control `python3 deploy.py --registry regA.json list` → lists `svc-a`, exit 0.
- `... list extra-junk` → lists `svc-a`, exit 0 (stray argument ignored).
- `... list --dry-rnu` → lists `svc-a`, exit 0 (typo'd flag ignored).
- `--registry regA.json --registry regB.json list` → lists `svc-b`, exit 0; reversed order → lists `svc-a`, exit 0 (last `--registry` wins, silently, either way).
- Controls that do fail: unknown subcommand → exit 2; `--registry=regA.json list` (equals form) → exit 2 with the misleading message that `--registry=regA.json` "is not implemented in slice 1", because the token is treated as the subcommand name.

## Why it matters

Slice 1 is read-only, so today the harm is a wrong-registry listing believed to be the requested one. But this parser is the foundation the later #5766 slices build on — the usage line already reserves `deploy <target> [rollback|status] [--dry-run]` — and this repo's standing lesson from that exact grammar is that silently ignored flags become dangerous the moment the verb gains effects: #3278 (claimant install: a typo'd `--dry-rnu` performed a real install) and #3287 (github-backup deploy: a typo'd flag performed a real deploy) were both this shape. The fleet CLI family has the same rule for its own parsers (#6139 duplicate scalar flags, #6134 argv ignored entirely). Fixing the parser now, while `list` is its only verb, is the cheap moment.

## Acceptance criteria

- `deploy ... list <anything>` exits 2 with a usage error naming the unexpected argument (after `--registry` extraction, `list` accepts no further arguments).
- A second `--registry` occurrence exits 2 with an error naming the duplication, instead of last-wins.
- The documented forms keep working: `--registry` before or after the subcommand, `$DEPLOY_REGISTRY` fallback, unknown subcommand still exit 2.
- Tests pin all of the above (there is currently no test file for deploy.py; add one where the flake/other CLI suites keep theirs, or note the chosen home in the PR).
- Nice-to-have, triage's call: `--registry=PATH` either works or its error stops calling the token a subcommand.

title: pm-stack(aggregator): Meta keeper re-arm is all-or-nothing — a partial .backup rename is never restored and the alert falsely says no backups exist

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

body:
## Summary

`pm-stack(aggregator)` Meta session keeper: the exporter re-arm check requires **both** systemd units (or **both** `.backup` copies) to be present, so a partial rename state — exactly the failure family the keeper was built to recover from (the 2026-11-01 → 11-05 incident, units renamed to `.backup`) — can never be recovered, and the alert then falsely states that no `.backup` copies exist.

## Evidence

`pm-stack/aggregator/src/meta-renewal.ts`, `defaultEnsureExporterArmed` (lines 102–125):

- Line 111: returns `"armed"` only if the timer **and** the service both exist.
- Line 114: restores only if the timer backup **and** the service backup both exist.
- Any mixed state (one unit present + the other unit's `.backup` present, or one unit missing with no backup while the other has one) falls through to `"missing"` (line ~123).
- The `exporter-missing` alert (lines 232–233) then says: "…are missing from ~/.config/systemd/user and **no .backup copies exist**" — which is false in the mixed state, and sends the human responder looking for units to recreate instead of a one-rename restore.

Verified this run on the laptop at `1dae17e457` with the real module (probe `~/git/fleet/probe-meta-partial/probe.ts`, fake `$HOME`, `readLatest` → null, `runExporter` injected; `ensureExporterArmed` **not** injected, so the default implementation ran):

| Fake `~/.config/systemd/user` contents | Result |
|---|---|
| `meta-quota-export.timer` + `meta-quota-export.service.backup` | `attention`, recovery `exporter-missing`, alert claims "no .backup copies exist"; the service backup was **not** restored |
| `meta-quota-export.service` + `meta-quota-export.timer.backup` | Same: `exporter-missing`, false alert, timer backup not restored |
| both `.backup` files, neither unit present (control) | Both units restored, exporter run attempted (`still-expired` against the null probe) — the all-or-nothing path works |
| empty dir (control) | `exporter-missing` — correct here |

The existing suite (`src/meta-renewal.test.ts`, 6 tests) injects `ensureExporterArmed` in every case, so the default implementation's filesystem logic has no test coverage at all.

## Why it matters

The keeper exists so the Nov-1 sequence (units renamed away → exporter silent → ~40h of unalerted stale quota data) cannot repeat silently. A partial rename — an interrupted restore, one unit renamed back by hand, one unit deleted while its backup remains — is a plausible variant of that same incident, and in that state the keeper (a) never recovers on its own even though everything needed is on disk, and (b) actively misdiagnoses the state in the one alert a human will read.

## Acceptance criteria

- `defaultEnsureExporterArmed` restores each missing unit independently from its own `.backup` copy when that copy exists (per-unit, not all-or-nothing), and reports `restored` when it restored at least one unit.
- The `exporter-missing` alert is only used when no unit and no `.backup` copy can be found; when a `.backup` copy exists but could not be restored (or only some units are present), the alert/state names the actual per-unit state.
- New tests exercise the **default** implementation against a fake unit directory (temp `$HOME` or an injectable unit dir): partial-backup states for each unit, both-backups, neither, and already-armed.
- Existing `meta-renewal.test.ts` tests still pass (`bun test src/meta-renewal.test.ts`).

Related: the keeper landed for #6079 (PR #6315); standing-rule follow-through is #6120 (this is a code defect in the keeper, not a missing keeper).

body:
## Problem

`nixos/services/id-mail/worker/runtime.test.mjs` — the runtime-contract suite for the id-mail Worker handler and its Limiter Durable Object — is run by no workflow, flake check, justfile recipe, or Nix build. The package's own `npm test` now covers it, but nothing in the repo invokes that script.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ 50237a7deb, HEAD == origin/main)

- `runtime.test.mjs:1-9` documents what it pins: it drives the real `fetch` handler and the real `Limiter` class (from `src/index.js`) against in-memory fakes of the Durable Object storage/namespace APIs. The 5 tests pin the #5739 contract: caller-denied requests short-circuit before recipient-limiter work, caller-allowed requests deliver and consult recipient limiters, the recipient limit and per-request recipient cap still apply, and limiter state is alarm-bounded with alarm cleanup of dormant keys.
- The suite was added in PR #6336 (`fix(id-mail): short-circuit caller denials and expire limiter state (#5739)`) — it postdates #6082, which covered only the sibling `deploy.test.mjs` suite. Since then `package.json`'s `test` script reads `node --test deploy.test.mjs runtime.test.mjs`, but no automation runs it.
- Grep of `.github/workflows/`, `flake.nix`, `justfile`, and the id-mail Nix modules for `runtime.test` / any test invocation: zero references (the Nix files only define the service and the deploy wrapper).
- Laptop run this run: `cd nixos/services/id-mail/worker && node --test runtime.test.mjs` → 5 tests, 5 pass, 0 fail, ~0.65 s, fully offline (node:test, in-memory fakes; no network, wrangler, or secrets).

## Why it matters

These tests are the only regression net for the #5739 throttling fix — a security/availability contract (a throttled caller must not consume recipient-limiter work; limiter state must not grow unbounded). A future change to `src/index.js` can silently reintroduce the pre-#5739 behaviour and nothing will flag it, exactly the failure mode #6082 documented for the deploy suite in the same package.

## Acceptance criteria

- An automated check (workflow, flake check, or equivalent) runs the id-mail worker test script (`node --test deploy.test.mjs runtime.test.mjs`, or `runtime.test.mjs` at minimum) with a fail-if-missing guard, so deleting/renaming the suite fails the check instead of silently unwiring it.
- The check passes on current main (5 runtime tests + 4 deploy tests at filing).
- Breaking a pinned behaviour (e.g. recipient-limiter work performed after a caller denial, or limiter state without alarm cleanup) makes the check fail.

Related: #6082 (deploy.test.mjs wiring, same package), #5739 / PR #6336 (the contract this suite pins).

body:
## Finding (from PR review)

Codex (chatgpt-codex-connector[bot]) raised this finding in its review of merged PR #5764 and it was never fixed or responded to:

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/5764 — "doc: deployment architecture — a services layer outside the system switch" (MERGED 2026-11-05T01:48:25Z on the reviewed head 37f62be9c4)
- Comment: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/5764#discussion_r4475579692 (chatgpt-codex-connector[bot], 2026-11-05T01:40:09Z, P2, anchored at `doc/2026-11-04_deployment-architecture-services-layer.md:142`)
- Essence: "Use the queue broker's unauthenticated health endpoint. For the `fleet serve queue-broker` target shown here, `/health` is not an ordinary HTTP health probe: `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/queue_broker.rs:640-645` permits unauthenticated GET requests only to `/healthz`, while other paths require authentication and POST. A GET to the configured URL therefore returns 401 without credentials or 405 with credentials, causing a healthy deployment to fail its activation check and roll back. Use `http://100.99.113.103:4801/healthz`, which is also the endpoint exercised by the broker smoke test."

## No-response evidence

- The PR's three inline Codex findings have no replies (`in_reply_to_id` empty, no later inline comments); the conversation contains only the Codex review summary and a CodeRabbit rate-limit notice.
- The PR merged on the exact reviewed head (37f62be9c4), so no fix commit followed the comment.

## Still live on current main (verified 2026-11-05 by independent `gh api` raw reads)

- `doc/2026-11-04_deployment-architecture-services-layer.md:142` still reads `healthCheck = "http://100.99.113.103:4801/health";` in the §3 services-layer example for the queue-broker target.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/queue_broker.rs` (current main): the HTTP handler special-cases only `GET /healthz` as unauthenticated (line ~640); any other path without a token gets 401, and with a token a non-POST gets 405. The authenticated POST `/health` command (line ~517) is a different, credentialed operation. A deploy health check following the design example would fail a healthy broker and trigger rollback.
- Dedupe: open+closed issues searched by "healthz queue broker" and PR #5764 — the deployment epic issue #5765 and deploy-tool issue #5766 do not name this endpoint correction.

## Acceptance criteria

- The design doc's queue-broker healthCheck example uses the unauthenticated `GET /healthz` endpoint (and any registry seed copied from the example is corrected with it).
- Or: the finding is resolved on this issue by a documented decision with reasoning recorded (e.g. the broker gains an unauthenticated GET `/health` route, making the example correct).

# Closing ref inventory — disposition every ref consumer and producer against the ref contract

Phase 4 of the aggregator ref-contract design (design issue #6242; design doc `files/designs/code-aggregator-ref-contract.md` in the `keep-the-four-repos-healthy` goal workspace). Gated on Phases 1–3 of #6242 (#6174 + #6195, #6210 + #6211, #6224).

The contract this phase closes out (from #6242): a ref is an annotation, not identity; validity is `isValidRef` only; an invalid ref is dropped at the consumption step beside its gate (the item survives, the drop is traced), producers mint only valid refs, and rendering/deriving reaches `refUrl` for stored/feed-derived refs only through the safe-link helper — never a throw.

## Scope

- An inventory of every `refUrl(` / `parseRef(` consumer in `pm-stack/aggregator/src` (25 `refUrl` sites at the design audit HEAD, origin/main 955ed2344) and every ref-carrying gate, scrape, derivation and store path in `pm-stack/aggregator` + `pm-stack/projector`, each dispositioned against the contract with file:line evidence: gate-dropped (rule 2) / producer-filtered (rule 3) / safe-helper (rule 4) / internal-constructed-safe (code-built refs, `parseRef` throw retained) / fixed-in-this-phase.
- The contract statement landed in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/model.ts` beside the #4952 `isValidRef` comment, so the disposition rules live where the validity rule lives.
- Required dispositions (name each explicitly on this issue, with the evidence or the follow-up issue if one is owed):
  1. `queue-view.ts:113,139` — stored refs reaching `refUrl` unguarded.
  2. `sources/live.ts:368` — the session-row `row.url ?? refUrl(row.ref, …)` fallback.
  3. `comments.ts:494` — `githubCommentUrl` against the post-#4952 store-load gates: is every stored comment's `githubRef` now guaranteed valid, or is a guard owed?
  4. `render.ts:3574` — `ensure()`'s `refUrl` fallback in the overview path (post-#6205 state), and `render.ts:6756`.
  5. `sessionRecordLine` (`render.ts:1912`) — align its omit-the-link treatment with rule 4's plain-text treatment, or record why this surface differs.
  6. A recount of stored `pmp_links` rows (projector registry) whose ref fails `isValidRef`: how many exist, and confirmation that Phase 2's consumption filtering disarms them (no hand-deletion required for safety).
  7. Any raw `matchAll` ref scrape outside `titleRefs` / `refsInText` (rule 3) — the #6205 fix's second vector (a title re-scrape beside `refsInText`) is the shape to grep for.
- Probe evidence: for each surface this phase changes, a bad-ref case (unsafe-integer and non-GitHub forms) rendering/deriving without a throw, with a valid-ref control unchanged.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The inventory is posted on this issue (or in the model.ts contract statement it lands) with a disposition per site and no site left unclassified.
- [ ] The contract statement is on main in `model.ts` beside the #4952 comment.
- [ ] All seven required dispositions are recorded with evidence or a linked follow-up issue.
- [ ] Any site fixed in this phase carries pinning tests in the aggregator suite; the `bun test` aggregator suite passes (via CI per fleet policy).
- [ ] The design issue #6242 is commented with the closing state so its acceptance can be checked off.
