body:
Design doc: `files/designs/code-aggregator-ref-contract.md` in the `keep-the-four-repos-healthy` goal workspace. Filed by the design architect (pass 55, 2026-11-05). Audit HEAD: origin/main 955ed2344. No `user/review` — the validity rule is already landed (#4952) and the layer rulings below are the architect's recorded decisions.

## The defect

The aggregator's pages are stitched together with GitHub refs (`owner/repo#N`). A ref is typed `RefKey` — a promise that `parseRef` accepts it — but producers and gates make that promise without checking it, and renderers trust it: `parseRef` throws, and one bad ref takes down a whole page (/today #6174, /search + project pages #6211, pool project pages + briefs #6224), a whole board (#6210), or silently deletes the board's entire in-flight lane (#6195 — the throw is swallowed by an unlogged catch). Six filings in two days, one per producer/consumer pair, each leaving the same question open — which layer owns it? — and answering it differently: drop at a named boundary (#6174), "a design call for one deliberate pass" (#6195), both layers (#6211), gate-drops-the-item preferred (#6224). This issue is that deliberate pass: it records the disposition contract once and adopts the five open origins as its phases. Per-site fixes that choose different layers will diverge; this design is the layer ruling they share.

## Evidence

- **The validity rule exists.** `pm-stack/aggregator/src/model.ts:454-467` — `parseRef` throws on non-`owner/repo#N` shapes and unsafe-integer numbers; the comment states the #4952 rule (boundary validators route through `isValidRef`, never a local regex). `refsInText` complies (:484; #4890 closed today was its producer instance). Render embodiments exist: PR #6149's `isValidRef` guard → plain text (`render.ts:2489-2524`), `sessionRecordLine`'s try/catch (`render.ts:1912`). The overview instance #6205 closed in-window today.
- **Gates shape-check or ignore ref fields.** `isLinedUpElement` (`feed.ts:223`) never checks `ref`; `assembleWorkItems` copies it verbatim (`work-items.ts:191`). `isProjectPoolItem` (`projects.ts:280-283`) checks `parentRef`/`epicRef` as any string, `blockedBy`/`blocks` as any string array.
- **Producers mint/carry unvalidated refs.** `titleRefs` (`sources/live.ts:538`) adds its explicit-ref and alias-shorthand candidates unguarded (#6210). `projectorLinks` (`sources/live.ts:484`) maps registry rows verbatim (#6211), and the projector's `POST /links` gate is a local regex whose `\d+` admits unsafe numbers (`pm-stack/projector/src/server.ts:246`) — the anti-pattern the #4952 comment names, in the sibling app; legacy `pmp_links` rows bypass even that.
- **Consumers throw.** 25 `refUrl(` sites in `pm-stack/aggregator/src`; the filed unguarded ones on stored/feed-derived refs are at `render.ts:3368` (#6174), `render.ts:1506` + assembly `parseRef` at `sources/live.ts:634` (#6195/#6210), `render.ts:510` + `:6741` (#6211), `brief.ts:96` + `render.ts:6479/:6590/:6645/:6648` (#6224). The board lane's catch (`sources/live.ts:1177-1184`) swallows the throw with no log line.

## The contract (recorded decisions)

**A ref is an annotation, not identity; validity is `isValidRef`; an invalid ref is dropped where it is consumed and rendered as plain text where it is displayed — it never throws, and it never takes its item with it.**

1. **One validity rule** — `isValidRef` only, in both apps; no local regex re-derives it. `parseRef` keeps throwing for internally constructed refs.
2. **Drop the ref, keep the item** (stored/feed data) — at the consumption step beside each gate (`normalizeOrchestrationSection`, `poolFromFeed`, `projectorLinks`), not inside the pure predicates: an invalid ref field/edge is removed, the element survives, the drop is counted/logged. This pins against #6224's drop-the-whole-item gate option (an edge is an element of the item; #2576's drop-element-and-count applies at that granularity — item loss over an annotation is the #6195 harm). Direct user POSTs whose ref *is* the subject keep #4952's landed reject behaviour.
3. **Producers mint only valid refs** — every scrape/derivation routes candidates through `isValidRef`; an unfiltered ref scrape is a defect per se.
4. **Rendering and deriving never throw on a ref** — stored/feed-derived refs reach `refUrl` only through one safe-link helper (valid → anchor, invalid → plain text, the #6149 treatment); derive paths treat an invalid edge as absent. Defence in depth behind rule 2, not a substitute.
5. **Drops are observable** — every rule-2/3 drop leaves a log line or provenance/count note; assembly catches that can hide a lane log what they swallowed.

## Phases (each independently landable; origins adopted, no parallels)

- **Phase 1 — the lined-up seam:** #6174 + #6195 (consumption-step drop + objectives/board consumption via the safe treatment + lane catch logging). #6174's "chosen layer" question is answered by the contract: consumption step + render helper, not the predicate, not render alone.
- **Phase 2 — minting and the registry:** #6210 + #6211 (`titleRefs` filtering; `projectorLinks` consumption filtering incl. legacy rows; projector `POST /links` gate aligned; /search + roadmap rendering via the helper).
- **Phase 3 — pool edges:** #6224 (edges drop / single-ref fields clear at `poolFromFeed`, item retained per rule 2; brief + graph consumers per rule 4). Its dispatch implementation copy #6226 is this phase's vehicle if its holder takes the pin; otherwise triage reconciles the two so the fix lands once.
- **Phase 4 — closing inventory (filed with this design, gated on Phases 1–3):** every `refUrl`/`parseRef` consumer and ref-carrying gate/scrape/store path in aggregator + projector dispositioned; contract statement in `model.ts` beside the #4952 comment; named dispositions for `queue-view.ts`, `sources/live.ts:368`, `comments.ts:494`, `render.ts:3574` + `:6756`, the `sessionRecordLine` alignment, and a stored-`pmp_links` recount.

Open questions stay in the design doc (a typed non-GitHub ref kind for goal ids; drop-count surfacing — shared with #2576's dashboard question; projector bulk-import paths).

## Acceptance

- [ ] All four phases closed or dispositioned with evidence.
- [ ] No stored/feed-derived ref can throw a render or a derivation anywhere in the aggregator (Phase 4 inventory is the proof).
- [ ] Every invalid-ref drop in the filed surfaces leaves the trace rule 5 requires.

## Acceptance criteria
- One ref contract is documented for the aggregator: when a ref can link, when it must render as plain text, and why.
- Every surface that renders refs (board, in-flight, detail views) follows the same contract, with tests for a linkable ref and an unlinkable ref.
- No ref renders as a dead/broken link anywhere the contract applies.

body:
Implementation follow-up from the design decision on #5699 (adopted 2026-11-05, task 10135 triage).

## Scope
Client migrations to probe-based transport selection (explicit URL/env override wins, then the `[<role>] transport` config preference, then probe: socket file exists + connect succeeds -> UDS, else TCP — the dispatch client's probe-then-choose pattern, `crates/fleet-dispatch/src/lib.rs:152-183`):
- queue client direct path (`crates/fleet-queue/src/client.rs:69-84,100-113`)
- queue-broker's `DirectSecrets` hop to secrets-broker (`crates/fleet-queue/src/queue_broker.rs:48-51,604-605`) — gains a `unix://` form or sibling `secrets_socket` setting
- laptop-local `fleet secrets` path
- On the way past: fix the queue client's hardcoded broker-sock path (`client.rs:55-57`) to ask `fleet-config` instead.

Sandbox consumers are untouched — they speak UDS to their local proxy, a different socket.

## Acceptance
- Each migrated client works over UDS when the role socket answers and falls back to TCP when it does not.
- No behavior change when only TCP is configured.

## Acceptance criteria
- Fleet clients select UDS vs TCP per role by probing, with no manual configuration.
- A failed or absent socket probe falls back to TCP within the same connection attempt.
- Probe behavior is covered by tests for socket-present, socket-absent, and socket-stale cases.

body:
# pm-stack(aggregator): board page render throws when a lined-up task's title carries an unsafe-integer ref in a non-first link — titleRefs mints refs parseRef rejects, inFlightBoardItems validates only the first

## Summary

A lined-up (in-flight) task whose **own ref is a valid GitHub ref** but whose **title** mentions a ref with a number above `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (e.g. `code #99999999999999999999`) breaks the whole board page: `renderBoard` throws `ref number is not a safe integer`. Assembly survives because only the first link is ever validated; rendering validates every link and throws on the bad one.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ 04f78696ab)

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/model.ts` — `parseRef` throws `ref number is not a safe integer: <key>` for non-safe-integer numbers, and the shared rule (#4952, comment above `isValidRef`) is that producers must route through `isValidRef`; `refsInText` does (`model.ts:480` guards every candidate with `isValidRef`).
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/sources/live.ts:538` `titleRefs()` scrapes refs from lined-up titles, but its two own regex paths add candidates **unguarded**: the explicit-ref `matchAll` at `:545` and the alias-shorthand `#(\d+)` `matchAll` at `:555`. Neither checks `isValidRef`.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/sources/live.ts:634` — `inFlightBoardItems` calls `parseRef(remainingRefs[0])` only to extract the repo of the *first* remaining ref; every remaining ref is then emitted as a link (`links: remainingRefs.map(...)`) with no further validation.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/render.ts:1506` — the orchestrator in-flight card renders every link with unguarded `refUrl(l.ref)`, which throws via `parseRef`.

Probe (real sources via bun, `~/git/fleet/probe-board-render-ref/probe.ts`, run in `pm-stack/aggregator`):

```
isValidRef huge explicit: false
titleRefs explicit huge: [ "developing-today/code#99999999999999999999" ]
titleRefs alias huge:    [ "developing-today/code#99999999999999999999" ]
inFlightBoardItems OK, links: [[{"ref":"developing-today/code#123","relation":"tracks"},{"ref":"developing-today/code#99999999999999999999","relation":"tracks"}]]
renderBoard THREW: Error: ref number is not a safe integer: developing-today/code#99999999999999999999
control renderBoard OK, len 20262
```

The probe section task has `ref: "developing-today/code#123"` (valid) and title `Fix the thing, follow-up code #99999999999999999999`.

## Why this is distinct from the sibling filings

- #6195: a non-GitHub ref as the task's **first/own** ref throws at `inFlightBoardItems`'s `parseRef` (live.ts:634) during assembly and the lane is silently dropped. Here the first ref is valid, assembly succeeds, and the failure lands later in **page rendering**, taking down the whole board response rather than one lane.
- #6174: /today objectives calling `refUrl` unguarded. Different page, different producer.
- #6205 (fixed): overview's `reconciledInProgress` reaching `refUrl` unguarded. Different derive path.
- Session records already show the house precedent for render-time defence: `sessionRecordLine` wraps `refUrl` in try/catch so one malformed ref omits only its own link.

## Why it matters

Lined-up titles are free text republished by the orchestration pass every run; long digit strings (timestamps, snowflake-ish ids, exaggerated issue numbers in prose) are realistic title content. One such title on one lined-up task currently 500s/breaks the cross-repo WIP board for every viewer until the title scrolls off, and the throw gives no hint which task caused it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `titleRefs` never returns a ref `parseRef` rejects: both its explicit-ref and alias-shorthand paths filter through `isValidRef` (the #4952 shared rule), with tests pinning the unsafe-integer forms.
- [ ] A lined-up task with a valid first ref and an unsafe-integer ref later in its title renders on the board; the invalid ref is omitted (or rendered unlinked), the valid refs stay linked.
- [ ] Board rendering cannot be taken down by any single link ref: either assembly guarantees every emitted link `isValidRef`, or the render site follows the `sessionRecordLine` try/catch precedent.
- [ ] Regression tests in the aggregator suite (e.g. `test/board-in-flight.test.ts`) cover: unsafe refs via the explicit `owner/repo#N` title form, via the alias `#N` shorthand form, and in a non-first link position.

body:
## Summary

`id(log_sync)`: both postcard decode sites in the `/id-sync/1` session transport ignore trailing bytes inside a frame. A frame whose payload is a valid message plus arbitrary appended bytes decodes as the bare message — for the session handshake (`Request`/`Answer`) and for `LogSyncMessage`, including `Operation`, whose header bytes are handed straight to the ingest worker. The frames are length-prefixed, so the appended bytes are inside the frame, not a following frame: they are silently discarded, unauthenticated and unlogged.

## Evidence

- `pkgs/id/src/log_sync.rs:425` — `next_message` (the handshake reader) is a bare `postcard::from_bytes(&frame)`. Its own doc comment states the intended strictness: a first frame that does not decode as the expected message is a `SyncError::Frame` — "the session is refused, never reinterpreted as another protocol" — and the #179 test at `log_sync.rs:1556` pins refusal of a foreign first frame. A `Request` + suffix, however, decodes as the `Request` and the session proceeds.
- `pkgs/id/src/log_sync.rs:470` — the inbound stream for p2panda `LogSync` decodes each frame with a bare `postcard::from_bytes(&frame)`; at `:474-487` a decoded `LogSyncMessage::Operation((header, body))` sends `Arrival::Header(header)` to the ingest worker (or `Arrival::Refused` when a body is present). Padding an operation frame changes nothing about what is ingested.
- Contrast inside the same crate and protocol family: range sync's `decode_frame` (`pkgs/id/src/event_store/range.rs:560`) rejects trailing bytes (pinned by the test at `range.rs:1006`), and the signed replication frame decoder (`pkgs/id/src/world/replication.rs:532`) uses `postcard::take_from_bytes` with an empty-rest check — with a pinning test using an "unsigned suffix" (`replication.rs:1626`). The log-sync transport is the remaining bare-`from_bytes` outlier.

Verified this run on the laptop primary @36b346f399 (probe `~/git/fleet/probe-logsync-trailing`, real `id` crate; the decode expressions are verbatim the two call sites above, on the real types `id::sync_method::{Request, Answer}` and `p2panda_sync::protocols::LogSyncMessage<id::store_traits::ChainLog>`):

- `Request` clean: Ok, equal. `Request` + `0x00`: Ok, equal. `Request` + `GARBAGE`: Ok, equal. (`take_from_bytes` on the padded frame reports the suffix as a non-empty rest.)
- `Answer::Agree(Range)` + 2 trailing bytes: Ok, equal.
- `LogSyncMessage::Done` + `0x00`: Ok, `Done`. `PreSync` + trailing text: Ok.
- `LogSyncMessage::Operation((header, None))` clean: Ok. Same frame + `DE AD BE EF`: Ok, identical header/body delivered — i.e. exactly what the `log_sync.rs:470` closure would pass to ingest.

## Why it matters

Same defect class as #6197 (gossip frames), #6192 (seitan accept) and #6202 (match-audit logs) — non-canonical acceptance of signed/structured wire data — in the one sync transport that had not been converted:

- The session's strictness contract is already stated in the module ("never reinterpreted", first-frame refusal test); trailing-byte acceptance is a hole in that stated contract, not a new policy.
- Operation frames carry signed p2panda headers, but the frame as transmitted is not the unit that is authenticated: a peer or relay can pad frames with arbitrary unauthenticated data that every receiver silently drops — a covert channel on the sync transport and a malleability footgun for any future frame-level hashing, dedup, or logging.
- Inconsistent strictness between the two sync methods on the same store (range frames rejected when padded, log-sync frames accepted) invites protocol-confusion bugs as the transport evolves (#179 split the session shapes deliberately).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both decode sites in `pkgs/id/src/log_sync.rs` (`next_message` and the inbound `LogSyncMessage` decode) reject a frame whose postcard payload does not consume the entire frame (e.g. `postcard::take_from_bytes` + empty-rest check, mirroring `world/replication.rs:532`), surfacing `SyncError::Frame` as the existing malformed-frame path does.
- [ ] Pinning tests: a padded `Request` first frame is refused with `SyncError::Frame` (extending the #179 first-frame test family); a padded `LogSyncMessage` frame errors the session stream instead of delivering an `Arrival`.
- [ ] Clean sessions are unaffected: the existing `log_sync` test suite passes (`cargo test -p id --lib log_sync`), including the bulk-session and range-method sessions that share `next_message`.

🤖 Filed by new-issue-creator-code-a (fleet role map: developing-today/code#2131; implementation #2152). Sibling filings: #6197, #6192, #6202.

labels.name: app/id

body:
## Summary

`pkgs/id/src/chat_presence.rs:474-477` (`decode_frame`) and `pkgs/id/src/peer_announcement.rs:61` (`SignedPeerAnnouncement::decode_frame`) decode signed gossip frames with `postcard::from_bytes`, which returns after the first complete value and never checks that the input is exhausted. Any trailing bytes after the encoded struct are silently ignored, so one signed heartbeat / announcement has many accepted byte spellings: the bare frame, the frame plus a stray byte, the frame plus arbitrary garbage, or the frame plus a second complete value.

Both decoders sit on the live gossip ingestion path:

- `chat_presence::decode_frame` — called for presence heartbeats; the decoded heartbeat's signature is verified over a canonical re-encoding of the parsed fields (`signing_bytes`, chat_presence.rs:137-141), so appended bytes are not covered by the signature and do not affect verification.
- `SignedPeerAnnouncement::decode_frame` — called at pkgs/id/src/commands/peers.rs:473 and pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:2362 on received gossip messages; `verify()` likewise re-encodes the parsed fields (`signing_bytes`, peer_announcement.rs) instead of covering the received bytes, so a valid signed announcement plus arbitrary trailing bytes authenticates identically.

The codebase already treats this exact shape as a defect in the sibling replication decoder — and documents why:

- `pkgs/id/src/world/replication.rs:528-536`: "`take_from_bytes`, not `from_bytes`: trailing bytes after the envelope must refuse the frame, not be silently ignored — the frame digest covers the whole received buffer, so an unsigned suffix would otherwise desynchronize the frame chain." That decoder checks `rest.is_empty()`. The commit that fixed it (395a2b41b5, "fix(id): refuse trailing frame bytes and undecodable entries in replication contract") states the premise verbatim: "decode_frame used postcard::from_bytes, which ignores trailing bytes — an unsigned suffix would desynchronize the frame chain". Only replication.rs was fixed in that commit; the two gossip decoders were missed.
- #6192 filed the same class for the Seitan accept decoder (`rmp_serde::from_slice`); this is the postcard instance of the class, in two more decoders. The event_store range decoder likewise refuses trailing bytes (`decode_frame(&extra).is_err()`, range.rs tests).

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe against the real `id` crate @ 6d9d1c899b)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-postcard-trailing` on the laptop (path dependency on `pkgs/id`, `default-features = false, features = ["world"]`):

```text
raw bare: Ok(Pair { a: 7, b: "hi" })
raw trailing 0x00: Ok(Pair { a: 7, b: "hi" })
raw trailing dup: Ok(Pair { a: 7, b: "hi" })
presence bare ok: true
presence trailing 0x00 ok: true
presence trailing garbage ok: true
```

The first three lines pin the semantics of the exact call both decoders make (`postcard::from_bytes`, postcard 1.x with the `alloc` feature, as pinned by pkgs/id/Cargo.toml:109): a trailing `0x00` byte and a whole duplicated value are both silently dropped. The last three lines run the real `chat_presence::encode_frame` / `decode_frame` pair from the `id` crate: a genuine frame decodes, and the same frame with one appended `0x00` byte — and with the 9 appended garbage bytes `garbage!!` — also decodes to the same heartbeat instead of returning `None`. `SignedPeerAnnouncement::decode_frame` is `pub(crate)`, so it could not be called from the probe; its exposure is the identical `from_bytes` call at peer_announcement.rs:61 on the same pinned postcard version, with the same re-encode-to-verify structure — and the 395a2b41b5 commit message (above) already establishes the `from_bytes` trailing-byte premise for this codebase.

## Why it matters

- Frame malleability on an authenticated gossip plane: two different byte strings are the same authenticated heartbeat/announcement. Anything downstream that hashes, logs, dedupes, rate-limits, or chains off the received frame bytes (the failure mode replication.rs's comment names) can be desynchronized by an unsigned suffix that both of these decoders accept.
- The two decoders' own docs promise refusal of anything that is not exactly their frame ("Anything else on the shared gossip topic — peer announcements included — is refused, never guessed at", chat_presence.rs; "malformed frames … return `None`", peer_announcement.rs) — a frame followed by a second value is not one frame.
- Consistency: replication, event_store ranges, and (per #6192) the intended Seitan fix all enforce full consumption; these two gossip decoders are the remaining `from_bytes` sites on signed peer-facing frames.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `chat_presence::decode_frame` returns `None` when any byte remains after the first complete postcard value (use `postcard::take_from_bytes` + empty-rest check, mirroring world/replication.rs:532-536); pinning tests cover a trailing single byte, trailing garbage, and a trailing second encoded heartbeat.
- [ ] `SignedPeerAnnouncement::decode_frame` returns `None` for the same trailing forms; pinning tests in peer_announcement.rs cover them.
- [ ] Genuine frames produced by `encode_frame` (both modules) still decode and verify; the existing chat_presence and peer_announcement test suites stay green: `cargo test -p id --lib chat_presence peer_announcement` (and the serve/peers callers are unchanged in behaviour for honest frames).
- [ ] The fix checks the decoder's consumed length / remainder; it does not re-encode-and-compare (postcard encodings the current decoder accepts must stay accepted).

## Scope notes

Filed-only from the creator lane. Out of scope: `MatchLogV0::decode` (match_audit.rs:460) and the local meta-client `from_bytes` call sites — those are not signed gossip frames; if the fixer wants the same treatment there it is a separate call. Related: #6192 (Seitan accept, same one-object-many-spellings class, msgpack instance).

# Suite registry — inventory every test suite and name its venue

Phase 1 of the test-suite coverage design (design issue #6185; design doc `files/designs/code-test-suite-coverage-contract.md` in the `keep-the-four-repos-healthy` goal workspace).

The contract (from #6185): a suite counts as covered only when it is **registered** (one registry naming exactly one venue + invocation per suite), its venue is **real** (enabled in Actions / a flake check that actually runs, and dispatchable), the run is **proven** (files named explicitly, existence asserted, SKIP is a visible failure, build/vet does not count), and the suite is **runnable and hermetic** (clean checkout, networking disabled). This phase builds the registry the other phases wire and ratchet against.

## Scope

- Inventory every test suite on current main: the filed family (#5935, #5942, #5946, #5952, #5992, #5993, #6065, #6082, #6084, #6085, #6091, #6092, #6099, #6093, #5582, plus the in-window closed wirings #5937, #5945, #5951, #6034, #6081, #6090, #6094, #6095, #6178, #6179) plus a full tree inventory of test files outside the already-covered in-tree suites.
- Registry form: the design's recorded lean is a machine-readable manifest under `.github/` (parseable by Phase 4's ratchet), summarised in `.github/ci-policy.md`; if implementation chooses another form, record why on this issue. One entry per suite: path(s), venue (workflow + job/step, flake check, or nightly), invocation, enablement state at audit time (from the Actions API, not the tree).
- Suites with no venue get an explicit `uncovered` entry pointing at their Phase 2 issue on #6185 — no silent omissions. Waivers (a suite deliberately not run) only with a recorded reason on the entry.
- Record the registry boundary explicitly: in-tree product suites (pkgs/id, pkgs/mcpx) at per-crate granularity with named exceptions if the inventory supports it; `doc/` spike trees and vendored trees (pavex) out, with the boundary stated so Phase 4's inventory rule has a defined scope.
- The contract statement (the five rules from #6185) lands in `.github/ci-policy.md` beside the tier policy.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The registry exists on main and lists every suite found by the tree inventory, each with a venue or an explicit `uncovered`/waiver entry with a reason.
- [ ] Every filed family member above appears in the registry; #5951's entry is marked uncovered-in-fact (its venue `pm-stack-tests.yml` is `disabled_manually`) pending Phase 3.
- [ ] Enablement states in the registry match a fresh Actions-API read at landing time (evidence quoted on this issue).
- [ ] The five-rule contract statement is in `.github/ci-policy.md`.
- [ ] The design issue #6185 is commented with the registry's uncovered count so its acceptance can be tracked.

Found during the 2026-11-05 OpenClaw fix pass (evidence from the live laptop):

`~/.openclaw/acpx/claude-agent-acp-wrapper.mjs` and `codex-acp-wrapper.mjs` hardcode `installedBinPath` into `~/.openclaw/tmp/plugin-captures/136d25b8-80e8-4290-85db-07ea6667370a/captures/openclaw-plugin-build-*/...` — that capture directory **no longer exists**. The captures present on disk (1a07e52e, f7d349b8) are codedb/native captures, not the ACP plugin-build trees. The gateway's managed cleanup evidently garbage-collected the plugin-build capture the wrappers were staged against (same failure family as the Oct 28 note: captures are load-bearing for the wrappers).

Impact: spawning a **claude** or **codex** ACP session would fail at adapter start. **opencode** (via the #1243 ACP-to-HTTP adapter) and **agy** (system binary) are unaffected — the #6137 ACP proof passed tonight using opencode. Claude/Codex also remain available via their native runtime plugins.

Fix directions (pick one): re-stage the plugin captures and repoint the wrappers; move the wrapper targets into the Nix store (the store-repoint tracked as #1711); or make the capture lifecycle aware that wrapper-referenced captures are pinned. Until fixed, treat claude/codex ACP spawn as known-broken.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The claude/codex ACP wrappers no longer reference the garbage-collected capture `136d25b8-…`: one fix direction from the body is chosen and implemented (re-staged captures + repointed wrappers, Nix-store targets per #1711, or capture-lifecycle pinning for wrapper-referenced captures).
- [ ] Spawning a claude ACP session and a codex ACP session on the laptop succeeds end-to-end (adapter starts; no missing-path failure).

body:
# Rate-limit-proof GitHub posting: outbox / GitHub App fallback path

Drew's order (2026-11-05): "use the feedback outbox / github app when rate limited." Standing rule in AGENTS.md: *WHEN GITHUB RATE-LIMITS A POST, USE THE OUTBOX / THE GITHUB APP*.

Origin failure: the code#1258 Q3/Q6 ruling — decided by Drew 2026-11-03 — failed to post twice on the `gh` secondary rate limit and sat in a prepared file for two days while standing lists reported the questions unanswered. That failure mode must be impossible: a rate-limited post is never parked in a loose file and never silently dropped.

## The path (single documented route for fleet GitHub writes that matter)

1. **Try `gh` as the user** (dezren39) — the normal route.
2. **On a secondary-rate-limit failure, post as the org GitHub App** — the `developing.today` app (App ID 5454422) via `infra/fleet-paperwork/fleet_paperwork.py`. An installation token is a different actor with its own rate-limit bucket. The tool mints the token from the app key in the laptop's sops store (`~/secrets/pm-stack.sops.yaml`, keys by name only), posts, and **verifies by readback** before reporting success. App-posted comments carry the app identity (`developing.today[bot]`) — acceptable for ruling/filing traffic; the identity difference is recorded in the delivery record (fleet-paperwork's local ledger + this issue's proof comments).
3. **If both routes fail, enqueue in the action outbox** — a fully prepared entry in `~/workspace/goals/keep-the-four-repos-healthy/hidden_files/action-outbox.md` per the 2026-10-28 protocol (`files/action-outbox-protocol-2026-10-28.md`). The `action-outbox-processor` cron (every 30 min) is the pusher: it executes entries exactly as prepared, verifies by fresh readback, marks `status: done` with the resulting URL, and hard-stops on a renewed rate limit (attempts/last_error recorded, next run retries). The caller gets a `QUEUED <OB-id>` result — never a silent file.

One outbox, one pusher: this wires into the existing 2026-10-28 action outbox + processor (the same store the external-comms ledger lane is building on), NOT the unbuilt DB creation outbox scoped in #3706 (bounded pilot only, per Drew's 2026-11-04 ruling).

## Entry point for lanes

`~/tools/gh-post` (sandbox) implements the ladder for comments and issue creation:

```
gh-post comment --repo owner/name --issue N --body-file F [--pr]
gh-post create  --repo owner/name --title T --body-file F [--label L ...]
```

It prints the posted URL (identity noted when the App leg delivered), or `QUEUED OB-<date>-<nnn>` with exit code 3 when both live routes fail and the outbox has it. Non-rate-limit errors fail loudly without falling through.

## Follow-ups (noted, not done here)

- The outbox processor currently delivers as the user only; teaching it to prefer the App identity for entries whose live routes were rate-limited would shorten drain time during long limit episodes. (Cron job bodies are not rewritten by this change — this is the recorded follow-up.)
- #3706's DB-backed creation outbox remains a bounded pilot per Drew's 2026-11-04 ruling; if it is ever built fleet-wide, this path folds into it.

## Proofs

Posted as comments on this issue: (1) the App-route proof (comment authored by the App identity), (2) an enqueue → processor-delivered test with its comment URL, (3) the stranded-artifact census from the 2026-10-28 rate-limit episode and the #1258 origin case.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The single documented route exists: `gh` as the user first; on a secondary-rate-limit failure, post as the org GitHub App (`developing.today`, via fleet-paperwork) with readback verification; if both fail, a fully prepared action-outbox entry the processor cron delivers and verifies.
- [ ] A rate-limited post is never parked in a loose prepared file and never silently dropped — every path ends in a delivered post or a tracked outbox entry.
- [ ] App-posted deliveries record the identity difference in the delivery record (fleet-paperwork ledger + proof comment).
- [ ] Proof on this issue: one real ruling/filing post delivered through the fallback path and verified by readback.

body:
## Problem

The three pm-stack quota-exporter test suites — `pm-stack/opencode-usage-export/opencode-usage-export.test.mjs`, `pm-stack/cloudflare-export/cloudflare-quota-export.test.mjs`, and `pm-stack/supabase-export/supabase-quota-export.test.mjs` — are run by no workflow, flake check, or Nix build. Each README documents only a manual local run. The exporters themselves run on production systemd timers and feed the quota plane; their regression pins execute only when a human remembers.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ aee78ac310, HEAD == origin/main)

- `git grep` for each suite name across the whole tree returns only the suites' own READMEs (and, for cloudflare, the test file's own header comment). No reference in `.github/workflows/`, the flake, the justfile, or any Nix file. `pm-stack-tests.yml` runs the aggregator/projector bun suites, the seed/deploy-install smokes, and (since #5953) the claimant/grist Python suites — none of the three exporter suites.
- Hand runs on the laptop this run, all green:
  - `node --test pm-stack/opencode-usage-export/opencode-usage-export.test.mjs` → **4 tests, 4 pass, 0 fail** (~0.5 s; pins store move detection, stale/missing store failure documents and exit codes 3/4).
  - `node --test pm-stack/cloudflare-export/cloudflare-quota-export.test.mjs` → **35 tests, 35 pass, 0 fail** (~0.6 s; pins the #2574 R2 bucket-enumeration "unknown, never partial" contract and the #4325 entry-point checks).
  - `bun test` in `pm-stack/supabase-export/` → **12 tests, 12 pass, 0 fail** (pins the #2492 fail-closed billing rules). Note the runner split: this suite imports `bun:` modules, so `node --test` fails on it with `ERR_UNSUPPORTED_ESM_URL_SCHEME` — wiring must run it under bun, unlike the other two.
- What they guard is live: each exporter ships a `.service`/`.timer` pair in its directory and publishes the `latest.json` documents the aggregator's quota gatherer consumes (#1151/#2072). The pins exist for real incidents — #2574 (partial bucket lists published as complete), #2492 (unpriced addons billed), #4325 (symlinked invocation silently no-opping) — and today none of them can catch a regression before it merges.

## Why it matters

Three production data producers have test suites that are decorative. A regression in enumeration completeness, billing fail-closed behaviour, or store move detection merges silently and surfaces as wrong quota/billing data on the dashboard — the exact failure classes these suites were written to pin.

Related but distinct: #5954 (pm-stack-tests.yml itself is `disabled_manually` in Actions) and #5993 (the pm-git-sync/tailnet script suites, a different set of suites in the same workflow). This issue is about the three exporter suites being absent from every check; wherever they are wired, #5954's enablement is what lets that check actually execute.

## Acceptance criteria

- An automated check runs all three exporter suites on changes under `pm-stack/opencode-usage-export/`, `pm-stack/cloudflare-export/`, and `pm-stack/supabase-export/` (a step in `pm-stack-tests.yml` following its existing explicit-file, fail-if-missing pattern, or an equivalent check).
- The two node suites run under `node --test`; the supabase suite runs under `bun test` (it cannot run under node — see evidence).
- The check passes on current main (4 + 35 + 12 tests at filing).
- Breaking a pinned behaviour (e.g. publishing a partial bucket list as complete, #2574) makes the check fail.

## Problem

`nixos/services/id-mail/worker/deploy.test.mjs` — the only test suite for the id-mail worker deploy script — is run by no workflow, flake check, or Nix build. Its package's own `npm test` exists, but nothing invokes it.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ aee78ac310, HEAD == origin/main)

- `nixos/services/id-mail/worker/package.json:6` declares `"test": "node --test deploy.test.mjs"`, and `deploy.test.mjs:1-9` documents what it pins: it drives the real `deploy.mjs` in a temp dir with stubbed `bws`/`wrangler` binaries and pins the three #3281 cases — `--dry-run` validates only and exits 0, a typo'd `--dry-rnu` is a usage error with **zero** external calls, and a bare run performs the real deploy sequence against the stubs.
- Grep across `.github/workflows/`, `nixos/` (including `nixos/services/id-mail/default.nix` and the worker's `deploy.nix`), `home/`, `infra/`, `scripts/`, and the flake finds no reference to `deploy.test` outside the test file and its package.json. The `deploy tests` comment in `github-backup-tests.yml:21` concerns `infra/github-backup`, a different deploy script.
- Hand run on the laptop this run: `node --test nixos/services/id-mail/worker/deploy.test.mjs` → **4 tests, 4 pass, 0 fail** (~0.25 s). Green, fast, never run.
- What it guards is destructive: #3281 (closed) was `deploy.mjs` silently ignoring unrecognized arguments, so a typo'd `--dry-rnu` entered the real deploy sequence and force-deleted the retired `id-mail` Worker. The sibling github-backup deploy script got the same defect (#3287) and its suite is wired (`github-backup-tests.yml`); this one is not.

## Why it matters

The pin for a deploy script that can delete a live Worker exists but is decorative: a regression in `deploy.mjs` argument handling (or in the stubbed deploy sequence) merges with no signal, and the next typo'd flag re-runs the #3281 failure against production.

## Acceptance criteria

- An automated check (a workflow step following the repo's test-workflow conventions, or an equivalent flake/Nix check) runs `node --test deploy.test.mjs` in `nixos/services/id-mail/worker/` on changes to that directory.
- The check passes on the current main tree (4 tests at time of filing).
- Reintroducing the #3281 behaviour (unknown args reaching the deploy sequence) makes the check fail.

body:
Research (2026-11-04, part of the Modal credits design #6069; full doc `~/workspace/scratch/modal-gpu-design-2026-11-04/design.md` §4): where GPU compute comes from after Modal credits — answering Drew's four questions with evidence. Prices verified from vendor pages, Oct–Nov 2026.

## Q1 — Blacksmith GPU? **No.**
Blacksmith sells CPU Actions runners only (x64/arm to 32 vCPU, Windows beta, macOS on Apple M4; 2 vCPU $0.004/min, 3,000 free min/mo). No GPU runner product exists as of Nov 2026. Third parties do sell GPU Actions runners (machine.dev: T4 spot from $0.00308/min ≈ $0.18/hr, L4 $0.00682/min ≈ $0.41/hr; StarSling: RTX 4090 $0.02522/min) — relevant only for CI-shaped GPU work.

## Q2 — Copilot / Actions / Actions Mac?
- **Copilot: no GPU compute at any tier.** It is a coding-assistant subscription; it confers no compute of any kind.
- **GitHub-hosted GPU larger runner: yes, one shape, expensive.** `gpu-t4-4-core` = 4 vCPU / 28 GB / 1× Tesla T4 16 GB at **$0.052/min ($3.12/hr)**; requires Team/Enterprise Cloud; included minutes never cover larger runners (every minute is cash). ~4× Modal's L4 hourly rate for an older card; ~8–17× third-party T4 runners. Break-glass only.
- **Actions Mac runners: no usable GPU compute.** Arm64 macOS runners are virtualized; GitHub's documented limitations for arm64 macOS runners exclude MPS, and community reports show the MPS backend hard-capped (~1 GB) to uselessness. Metal graphics ≠ ML compute. (Our own Mac is Vertex's work machine — never fleet infrastructure — and is excluded regardless.)

## Q3 — OCI GPU? Real, priced, **stood down**.
VM.GPU.A10.1 (1× A10) $2.00/GPU-hr (≈2.5× Modal L4 for a comparable card); BM.GPU.H100.8 $10/GPU-hr sold as an 8-GPU bare-metal node ($80/hr minimum); VM.GPU3.1 V100 $2.95/hr (preemptible $1.48). No Always-Free GPU; new tenancies have GPU limits of zero until raised. **OCI is stood down (Drew 2026-10-31: no tenancy, PAYG/provisioning on HOLD)** — evaluation only. Unlock condition: Drew lifts the hold + a tenancy exists. Its niche would be a persistent GPU service, not batch work.

## Q4 — Local GPUs? **Effectively none.**
Verified 2026-11-04: the laptop (Ryzen 7 7840U) has only a Radeon 780M iGPU, no discrete GPU; ROCm on gfx1103 is unofficial/fragile → treat as CPU-class (measured local embedding rate 1,529 tok/s). Sandbox VM: no GPU. **There is no owned RTX 3060 Ti** — every 3060 Ti in our records is a Marketplace listing the deal hunt passed on ($250, Kimberly WI, 2026-10-02). A used RTX 3060 12GB (~$200) / 3060 Ti (~$250) in a lab-cluster host would give ~L4-class embedding throughput 24/7 for ~$0.03/hr electricity — best constant-use economics here, and a purchase decision for Drew, not an action.

## The ladder (when Modal credits run out)
1. Modal PAYG overage (same rates, cash) — at our volumes even 10× growth is ~$10–30/mo. Default next step.
2. Third-party GPU Actions runners, if the job is CI-shaped.
3. GitHub native GPU runner — break-glass (price).
4. Local used GPU — only if a recurring always-on need appears (none today).
5. OCI — only after the stand-down lifts, for persistent-service shapes.

Constant-use verdict: nothing we run needs a standing GPU; all workloads are batch-shaped. A live embedding endpoint for ID worlds should run on laptop CPU until volume proves otherwise, with a warm Modal web endpoint as fallback — not a rented always-on card.

Adjacent: #2605 (hosted runner queue saturation — CPU capacity side of the same question).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each of the four questions (Blacksmith GPU, Copilot/Actions/Mac GPU, OCI GPU, local GPU) is answered with cited vendor evidence and prices, as drafted in the body.
- [ ] A single recommendation for the post-Modal-credits GPU source is recorded, with the break-glass option named.
- [ ] The OCI hold (Drew 2026-10-31) is respected: evaluation only, no tenancy or provisioning actions.

So the cost risk is not the corpus — it's **churn**: re-embedding the unchanged 95% on every version of every log, forever, plus 5–20× corpus growth from comments/docs expansion. Against the standing plan cap (Turso scaler $24.92/mo), embedding spend is a rounding error *if* deltas work; storage and DB-count quotas bind first. (https://embeddingcost.com/compare)

## Scope — the ledger

Per batch, log: `(chunks_new, chunks_reused, tokens_embedded, model, $)`. The headline metric is the **delta reuse ratio**: if reuse is **<90% on an append-mostly source, the delta protocol is broken — not the budget** — and the ledger says so as an alert, not a line item. The ledger complements #6019's plan-headroom accounting (Turso storage/writes) with the embedding side, per source class.

## Done looks like

A ledger schema + per-source reuse-ratio baselines + the alert rule.

Parent: [#6021](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/6021) (classification revalidation scan). Research source: prior-art doc `~/workspace/scratch/atlas-ingestion-brief-2026-11-04/prior-art-research.md` (2026-11-04). Follow-up 30 (Cluster 5).

## Finding (research, in substance)

One-time scanning certifies a moment, not a corpus — that is a named dead end. Rules improve, corpora get re-tiered, and sources turn out dirtier than believed, so **revalidation is a recurring gate**: new rules find old leaks. The cadence design has three moving parts:

- **Rule-update-triggered rescans:** when the scanner rules / inventory pack / recognizer set changes, the affected scan re-runs over the corpus (deterministic layer in full; NER layer per its scoping design, sibling under #6021).
- **Sampled human audit per round:** a small random sample of each tier hand-checked, to *estimate the scanners' miss rate* instead of assuming it. "No detector catches everything" is every tool's own disclaimer; the audit sample turns that caveat into a number.
- **Allowlist expiry:** allowlist entries carry reasons and expiry; a stale allowlist is how leaks get grandfathered.

## Scope

This design takes #6021's recurrence recommendation (one-off vs standing gate) as its input and specifies the standing form: triggers, per-layer scope per trigger, audit sample sizes, and where the cadence plugs into the ingestion-operations design (#6019) as a standing gate.

## Done looks like

A cadence spec: trigger table, scope per trigger, audit method with miss-rate estimate, allowlist lifecycle.

## Finding (research, in substance)

Computing "indices 0–16 matched old span A, 17–241 is new, 242+ matched old span B" without aligned chunk boundaries is the **rsync matcher** (Tridgell & Mackerras, TR-CS-96-05, 1996): slide a window one byte at a time over the new file computing a cheap rolling (Adler-32-derived) checksum; only on a weak hit pay for the strong checksum; emit literal/copy tokens. http://oceanpark.com/webmuseum/rsync.html — That sliding-window match at arbitrary offsets is exactly the mechanism the offset-embed design needs.

## Scope

- Rolling-hash choice + window size at embed scale (~1–2 KB spans, not rsync's file blocks); strong-verify hash; minimum match run worth anchoring on.
- Matcher output contract: token stream → span references + literal regions for the span-table schema (sibling follow-up under #6028).
- Cost model: matcher CPU + reads vs embeddings saved, per source type (text vs prepend-heavy logs, where resync behaves worse).

## Done looks like

An algorithm design with parameters, failure cases (reflow/re-wrap phantom diffs), and a worked run over Drew's 17–241 example.

Parent: [#6018](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/6018) (Atlas ingestion program). Statements S16–S20, S29, S30 of the 2026-11-04 brief.

## Requirement (Drew, in substance)

Atlas must understand **content versioning** well enough that:

1. **New versions of files are first-class**: a changed file lands as a new version of the same object, never an overwrite and never an unrelated new object.
2. **Renames are understood**: a renamed file's versions continue the same lineage. For git sources this is simple **if commits are done in the right way** (renames recorded as renames instead of delete+insert) — the design may set commit-hygiene expectations for source repos, and must handle non-git sources (session stores, doc trees) where lineage has to be inferred (segment association, sibling design under [#3125](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/3125)).
3. **Old and new are both kept**, but resolution defaults to **"the max" — the newest version of every file**. Search/retrieval asks for a file and gets its latest version unless it explicitly addresses history.
4. **Old versions roll out to cold storage** over time (2026-11-04 storage ruling: cold tiers → rustfs) — a lifecycle with hot → cold movement, not permanent hot residence.
5. **Old versions are eventually removed** under an explicit policy with three named triggers, any of which can retire a version:
   - **by date** — older than a threshold;
   - **by increments** — N newer versions exist beyond it;
   - **by access** — it has never (or no longer) been retrieved (this trigger consumes the retrieval statistics from the sibling stats/feedback design under [#6018](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/6018)).

## Tensions the design must face honestly

- [#3125](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/3125) carries Drew's 2026-10-31 rule: **keep ALL data; nothing stripped to save space; only byte-identical dupes cleaned**. The deletion policy above is a deliberate evolution of that rule (2026-11-04 brief) — the design must state which rule governs which tier/class, and default to keep unless a trigger AND a class rule both say retire. Deletion of a version must never orphan chunks whose occurrences point at it (occurrence registry semantics per #3125).
- Newest-resolution interacts with fan-out search ([#5755](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5755)) and the parameter surface ([#5774](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5774)): `as-of` / version pinning becomes a query parameter, and full-version logging per run must record WHICH version of each file a result came from (feeds the query-trace design).
- Cold rollout must preserve resolvability: a cold version still resolves (slower) until a deletion trigger fires; deletion is the only hard end.

## Design must answer

- The version object model: identity (file id vs version id), lineage edges (rename, edit, split/merge of files), and how chunks map to versions (shared chunks across versions recorded as occurrences, not copies).
- Per-class retention defaults (code, docs, session logs, chat logs, generated reports likely differ) and who can override them.
- The retrieval-side contract: default-latest semantics, explicit history addressing, and how merge/rescore treats multi-version hits for the same file (one file, best version, unless the query is historical).

## Done looks like

A design doc in code (`doc/`): version model, lineage rules per source type, retention policy table with the three triggers parameterized per class, cold-tier mechanics, and the query-side version contract — with implementation split into follow-ons.

## Requirement (Drew, in substance)

Atlas updates become **semi-automated on a long-term plan** — not ad-hoc manual ingestion runs. The automation:

1. **Ingests the operational source set automatically**: reboots / boot records, session logs, chat logs, statistics, and reports are added to Atlas as they are produced.
2. **Applies a usefulness filter**: data that is useless to have in Atlas is NOT uploaded. Semi-automated ≠ indiscriminate — every source class carries an inclusion test (what question would this ever answer?).
3. **Monitors disk and I/O**: ingestion watches storage consumption and I/O load on the source and target machines and throttles / pauses / reports rather than filling a disk or swamping a host.
4. **Never spends more than the plan**: the current paid plan is a hard ceiling (today: Turso scaler, $24.92/mo yearly). Design treats plan limits (storage, reads/writes, DB count) as the budget envelope; growth that would cross the plan is surfaced to Drew, not silently incurred. Cf. [#5468](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5468) (pm-stack mirror storage surge) for what unmonitored growth looks like.

## Current state

- Ingestion today is script-driven and manual (scripts migrating into code + fleet under [#5670](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5670)); staging tier with merge-on-close promotion exists ([#5669](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5669)).
- Sources produce data continuously (boot records in `~/logs/init.jsonl` + init-status; OpenCode session store; Muse chats; quota/statistical reports) but nothing sweeps them into Atlas on a cadence.
- Storage rulings (2026-11-04): Turso + D1 both used, Turso embedded replicas first-class, huge atlases shard across both, cold tiers → rustfs; TursoDB for all NEW databases; production atlas stays libSQL for now.

## Design must answer

- Trigger model per source class: scheduled sweep vs event-driven (file close, session end, boot completion) vs hybrid; what "semi" means — which steps stay human-approved (new source classes? classification changes? bulk backfills?).
- The usefulness test: per-class inclusion rules, who/what applies them (static allowlist, size/shape heuristics, classifier pass), and how a rejected class is logged (rejection is data — cf. S32's unassociated-log principle).
- Disk/IO guardrails: watermarks, backpressure behavior, where the monitors live (source host vs ingest host), interaction with the delta-only design (companion issue under [#6018](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/6018)) so sweeps stay cheap.
- Cost accounting: per-run and per-source ingest cost (storage delta, write volume) reported against plan headroom; alert before the ceiling, not after.
- Failure posture: a failed/partial sweep never corrupts or double-ingests (idempotent, content-addressed landing per [#3125](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/3125)).

## Done looks like

A design doc (in code, `doc/`) + follow-on implementation issues: per-source trigger table, usefulness rules, guardrail thresholds, cost report format, and the runbook for the recurring sweeps. Implementation itself is follow-on work, not this issue.

**Second Life land** remains the fullest implementation of virtual real estate with in-world permission granularity: parcel permissions, group-deeded land, per-parcel ban lists, per-parcel script permissions — land as a *capability domain*. - A parcel/region inside a world as a capability domain: its own script-permission policy, access/ban list, and asset rules, nested under the world's ceilings (a parcel can only narrow, never widen — attenuation, per the program's delegation semantics).
- Ownership/delegation: parcel control as a delegable, revocable grant (writer-set/delegation substrate), not a token.
- What a self-hoster's server enforces vs what is world-author policy.

A design note: parcel domain model, nesting rule, grant shape — or a recorded decision that worlds don't subdivide this way, with reasons.

Wave-2 follow-up from the prior-art research (Lane B item 41); parent topic issue: [#5970](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5970). Research source: `workspace/scratch/worlds-capabilities-brief-2026-11-04/prior-art-research.md`.

## Scope

GLSL fragment shaders in the **Shadertoy format** (`mainImage(fragColor, fragCoord)` + iChannel inputs) are the de facto portable shader unit; **WGSL** is the emerging WebGPU counterpart. No cross-engine standard exists — so worlds should treat shaders as **data in a named format with declared inputs**, gated by the cost-ranking system (sibling follow-up under #5955), not as code in the world language. This also answers #5970's open question — do user shaders go through the user-function compile/trust pipeline? — with: no; they are data assets with a declared input surface, and their *effect* is bounded by the presentation layer.

- Format v1: Shadertoy-compatible GLSL unit + declared inputs (which asset parts it may read/transform).
- WGSL track: when it lands, a second format name, not a conversion promise.
- Licensing hooks: a shader upload carries the standard license tag (licensing children of #5955). Note the cautionary precedent from the licensing research: Shadertoy's own default for user shaders is CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 — defaults become the de facto license of the whole corpus.

## Done looks like

A format spec (unit shape, input declarations, format registry) the presentation layer can implement.

Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Wave-2 follow-up from the prior-art research (Lane B item 40); parent topic issue: [#5970](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5970). Research source: `workspace/scratch/worlds-capabilities-brief-2026-11-04/prior-art-research.md`.

## Precedent: VRChat, the strong one

VRChat computes an **Avatar Performance Rank** (Excellent → Very Poor) from *measured* metrics — triangles, materials, texture memory, PhysBones, particles, lights, shader complexity. Each user sets a minimum displayed rank; below-threshold avatars are replaced by fallbacks/impostors; **Very Poor is hidden by default**; Quest/mobile has a separate, stricter rank table and only SDK mobile shaders are permitted on Android avatars at all. World/instance settings add another gate layer, and per-user "Show Avatar" overrides exist for trusted individuals — the same override shape as our permission and license systems (https://wiki.vrchat.com/index.php?title=Avatar_Performance_Ranking ; https://vrcreators.net/docs/vrchat/quest-compatibility-checklist).

## Scope

#5970 owns per-world enablement of assets/filters; this follow-up designs the **ranking mechanism** that makes gating automatic and legible:

- Measured cost metrics for sprites/filters/shaders (the shader asset format is a sibling follow-up under #5955) and the rank table.
- Three gate layers: per-world (author policy — e.g. filters off because invisibility cheats), per-viewer (minimum rank), per-person override.
- **Fallback substitution:** below-threshold content is replaced by its authored fallback (per #5970's fallback chain), never just vanished — except where the world says hidden.

Users accept automatic visual downgrade when the rule is legible (a rank) and overridable per-person. That is the usability bar.

## Done looks like

A ranking design: metrics, rank table, gate layers, substitution rules.

Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Wave-2 follow-up from the prior-art research (Lane B item 38); parent topic issue: [#5970](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5970). Research source: `workspace/scratch/worlds-capabilities-brief-2026-11-04/prior-art-research.md`.

## The ladder is the design

Modern tooling (chafa, `vt`, dapple) all implements the same degradation order: **Kitty graphics protocol** (APC `_G`, base64 PNG/raw pixels — kitty/WezTerm/ghostty-family) → **Sixel** (indexed-palette true pixels — xterm/mlterm/foot) → **iTerm2 inline images** (OSC 1337) → **Unicode block/braille/sextant symbols with ANSI color** → **plain ASCII luminance ramp**. Auto-detection probes the terminal and picks the best available; chafa's `-f [iterm|kitty|sixels|symbols]` with symbols fallback is the reference UX (https://manpages.debian.org/unstable/chafa/chafa.1.en.html ; https://github.com/akirco/vt/blob/HEAD/README.md).

## Scope

Distinct from the conversion research under #5955 (media → protocol encoding): this is the **client-side selection ladder** — probing, choice, and runtime behavior.

- Probing method per rung and its failure modes; **tmux passthrough is a recurring breakage** and needs explicit handling.
- The symbols/ASCII tiers must be genuinely good, not an afterthought — kitty/sixel support is fragmented across terminals and multiplexers.
- **Dead end, recorded:** a single "universal" graphics format. The ladder *is* the design.

## Done looks like

A ladder spec (probe sequence, rung obligations, multiplexer rules) the client shells can implement.

Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Wave-2 follow-up from the prior-art research (Lane B item 31); parent topic issue: [#5977](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5977). Research source: `workspace/scratch/worlds-capabilities-brief-2026-11-04/prior-art-research.md`.

## The problem

"Public domain" is not a portable legal act: in Germany's monistic author's-rights system copyright can neither be transferred nor waived — moral rights are inalienable — so a bare dedication simply fails as drafted; several other jurisdictions lack a dedication concept or treat it as revocable. **CC0** is engineered around this: waiver, then a fallback permissive license if the waiver fails, then a covenant not to assert. Caveats to carry honestly: CC0 expressly does *not* license patent/trademark rights (why Fedora reclassified CC0 as not-allowed for *code* in 2022; data/content still fine), and FSF does not recommend CC0 for software. Sources: https://Wiki.CreativeCommons.org/images/6/69/CC0_Jurisdiction_Survey.pdf ; https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=30556049

## Scope

#5977 keeps public domain and CC0 as separate taxonomy entries; this follow-up decides the **storage normalization**:

- A user selecting "public domain" is stored as `CC0-1.0` for content and `0BSD` (or Unlicense) for code — never as a bare "public domain" string.
- One sentence of UI copy explaining why, in plain language.
- What the registry and the combination checker see (the normalized SPDX identifier only).

## Done looks like

A normalization rule + UI copy, adopted by the taxonomy spec.

Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Wave-2 follow-up from the prior-art research (Lane B item 24); parent topic issue: [#5973](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5973). Research source: `workspace/scratch/worlds-capabilities-brief-2026-11-04/prior-art-research.md`.

## Finding that shapes this

Every successful cross-community moderation sharing system is **data, not code**: Discord AutoMod rules are structured per-guild API objects with **no first-party import/export or cross-guild subscription** (https://docs.discord.com/developers/resources/auto-moderation); the reusable unit that actually emerged in third-party bots is a **curated feed** (cross-server network blacklists — scam domains, known raiders) plus a **policy preset** that compiles down to platform rules (Paladin: https://www.shapedimage.com/paladin-docs.html ; Azra: https://www.azrabot.com/docs/moderation.html). Reddit AutoModerator snippets are reuse-by-copy-paste — forks silently, never updates downstream; **subscription/feed beats copy-paste** for anything that must stay current. Rules-as-code packs have no successful mainstream precedent — and Garry's Mod addons (full-trust Lua, recurring malicious Workshop backdoors) are the negative evidence for executable shared moderation.

## Scope

#5973 designs moderation as parameterized libraries; this follow-up pins the pack as a **data format**:

- Static rules (the world's own policy text).
- Feed subscriptions (sibling feed-protocol follow-up under #5955).
- Parameters: report threshold for auto-quarantine, moderator/reviewer set, local exemption lists — kept separate from the shared core so adopting a pack doesn't surrender local judgment (this is Drew's "same thing, different moderators, different threshold" as a format property).
- Format in our manifest language (KDL profile, #5753) unless there's a reason otherwise.

## Done looks like

A pack-format spec (fields, versioning, parameter surface) #5973's interface design can adopt.

body:
Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Statements S47, S107, S109 of the 2026-11-04 brief. Filed as dedicated research per Drew's instruction: an overall design plus research into other common examples — the kinds of features and capabilities, pros and cons, and drawbacks different games and worlds have had.

## Scope

Two intertwined lineages:

**A. Scripted-bot battle games** — games going back to the '80s that take a script from each user and then play it out and see who wins in different scenarios:

- **Core War** (1984) and its descendants/standards (ICWS, Redcode variants, pMARS) — the original: per-warrior instruction budgets are our gas model, 40 years early.
- **Robot War** (Apple II, 1981) and the robot-programming line through RoboWar, Crobots, Robocode.
- Named by Drew: **Crowbots, Gladiabots, Botlands / Botland** — cover each: what the user submits (code? visual logic? DLL-equivalent?), how matches are bounded, how strategies are shared/reused.
- Modern heirs worth one pass: Screeps (MMO of user JS — the closest living relative of this whole program; study its CPU-bucket economics and memory model), Battlecode, Halite/Kaggle sims.

**B. User-programmable worlds** — the late-'90s / early-2000s wave:

- **Second Life** (LSL: per-script memory limits, ll* capability surface, permissions system for objects/scripts — a worked example of capability + licensing UX inside a world, including its failures).
- MOO/lambdaMOO (programmable objects, wizard authority), Furcadia (DragonSpeak), Active Worlds, There, Roblox's long arc from Lua sandboxes to an economy.
- What each did about: user code resource limits, code sharing/reuse as libraries, moderation of user creations, and asset licensing.

## Deliverable

A research doc: per-system entries with the same fields (user submits X; bounded by Y; capabilities granted via Z; sharing model; moderation model; what broke), then a synthesis table feeding the per-user mapping, server-invariants, and governance design children of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955).

## Done looks like

Doc landed; every design child that borrows a mechanism from a predecessor cites it here, and at least the named systems (Core War, Robot War, Crowbots, Gladiabots, Botland, Screeps, Second Life) each have a full entry.

body:
Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Statement S106 of the 2026-11-04 brief.

## The tension (Drew, in substance)

We need to figure out the balance between **Roc being fast to compile and basically nearly the full speed of C**, against the fact that what this program proposes is **highly dynamic and could be very computationally intensive**:

- Per tick, a world may map over **one user function per user**, each hot-swappable, each individually gas/timeout bounded.
- User functions arrive as **server-compiled DLLs**, get cached, get switched at tick/second/minute cadence.
- Presentation adds per-user view projections (FOV/line-of-sight) on top.

## Work for this design

- Build the cost model: per-tick budget = world step + N × (view projection + user function call + metering overhead). Put numbers on each term from the current implementation (`pkgs/id/src/world_session/`, example worlds) — measured, not vibes.
- Identify where the dynamic model spends the C-speed advantage: DLL call boundaries, metering (gas research child of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955)), projection computation, cache misses on strategy switches. Rank them.
- State the design levers: batching user-function calls, view caching across ticks, compiled-world reuse, tick-rate adaptation — and which levers this program takes as defaults vs leaves to world authors.
- Connect to the existing bench infrastructure (`pkgs/id/benches/`) — extend it with a bot-battle-shaped workload (N scripted users, mixed strategies) so the tension is tracked continuously, not re-litigated.

## Related

- Per-function gas/timeout research, per-user mapping design, compile-economics children of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955)
- Deterministic testing / soak runs: [#5779](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5779)

## Done looks like

A cost model with measured terms, a ranked overhead list, chosen default levers, and a benchmark scenario added (or specified) for the many-user-functions workload.

body:
Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Statements S78–S81 of the 2026-11-04 brief.

## Requirement (Drew, in substance)

We're trying to build **a real place in the virtual world** to allow people to share, create, and deal with one another **without absolutely requiring our own interaction**:

- **We might not even host them.** They could do it all on their own.
- They could use **our Rust libraries** to take the appropriate parts to build **their own client or subsystem** — which technically rides along the same protocol networks but is entirely separate and **doesn't automatically work for our intercompatibility requirements**. Or ideally, it does.
- Maybe it works perfectly, and they just **don't want to have our chat and world system** and want to **host their own servers**: it's the **exact same system**, but they're just using it in a different way, and **that should all work**.

## Design points to settle

- What is the **interop contract** exactly: which parts are load-bearing for intercompatibility (wire format, identity, capability negotiation, registry format) and which are our product choices on top (chat UI, our registry, our permission defaults)? A third-party server that implements the contract interoperates; one that doesn't is merely separate — the design must make that line explicit and testable.
- Conformance: the adapter conformance harness / interop matrix in [#5814](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5814) is the natural home for "does it actually interoperate" — this design states the stance, that issue builds the proof.
- Self-hosting a subset: run worlds without chat, run chat without worlds, run only the registry — which subsets are supported shapes vs accidents?
- Defaults travel or don't: our permission defaults, license policy defaults (licensing children of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955)), and moderation defaults are **server-admin choices** on a self-hosted server, not protocol requirements. Say so in the design, because the AGPL/licensing analysis depends on self-hosting being genuinely possible.
- Boundary enforcement across bridges/federation/relays is [#5882](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5882); residency implementation is [#5529](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5529). This issue is the *stance* those implement.

## Related

- Wire format & transport adapters: [#5674](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5674)
- Adapter conformance harness & interop matrix: [#5814](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5814)
- Writer sets v2 / federation: [#5789](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5789)

## Done looks like

A short stance doc: the interop contract's load-bearing list, supported subset shapes, and what is explicitly *not* required of a self-hoster.

body:
Part of the docs migration (hatch-personal/hatch → code). Stay-until-replaced register item **R3**.

## What exists today

hatch-personal `tools/proxy-supervisor/` (proxy-supervise.mjs, proxy-relay.mjs, proxy-port.mjs, config.json) plus `proxy-supervisor.service`, `proxy-supervisor.timer`, and `install-proxy-supervisor-service.sh` supervise local proxy endpoints that non-fleet tools dial. The supervisor is currently **dormant** (its config proxy list is empty) but is still installed and service-checked on every boot.

## What the built-in must do

`fleet serve` provides **built-in supervised local proxy endpoints**: declared endpoints with health checks, drain semantics (config carries drainSeconds / healthTimeoutSeconds today), and state under the fleet state dir — so ad-hoc tools get a stable local proxy without a separate supervisor service living in the sandbox home repo.

## Exit condition

When this ships (or when a deliberate decision records that the dormant supervisor is retired rather than replaced), the 7 hatch files above become historical copies only.

body:
Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Statements S59–S65 of the 2026-11-04 brief.

## Requirement (Drew, in substance)

Libraries need a type system of their own:

- **We need a type for libraries.**
- Libraries and scripts built for a **specific world or game type** may need some sort of **arbitrary definition or subtype**.
- A library may **attach to any given entity ID** — so it could attach to the **genre**, to a **specific game**, or to **nothing** if they want, whatever.
- A library may be **flagged for being built to be used as a DLL** versus **built to be compiled into another program**.
- **Most uploads would probably be worlds or DLL code**, because other libraries can just be **a URL**, essentially.
- Any number of kinds of libraries could be uploaded; the ones **marked as DLLs could be precompiled and cached** (economics: the compile-economics child of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955)).

## Design points to settle

- The library manifest: what fields (kind, subtype/attachment, build mode, platform requirements — from the capability-model child, license — from the licensing children, version). KDL is our config/manifest language ([#5753](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5753)) — the manifest should be a KDL profile unless there's a reason otherwise.
- Attachment semantics: does attaching to a genre make a library *discoverable* by that genre's worlds, *eligible* for them, or *restricted* to them? (Discovery vs eligibility vs restriction are three different designs.)
- Subtype definition: who defines a game-type subtype — the world author publishes an interface, and libraries declare conformance? Checked how?
- URL libraries: identity and integrity (a URL is mutable — pin by hash? by version?), and how a URL library participates in capability subset checking.
- How the taxonomy shows up in the registry next to worlds themselves.

## Related

- Library imports design, capability model, compile economics, licensing children of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955)
- Invites (attachment to entities has a family resemblance): [#5751](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5751)

## Done looks like

A design doc: the library type/manifest schema, attachment semantics, build-mode flags, and the upload taxonomy (world / DLL / source library / URL library) as registry kinds.

## Triage — task 10338 (2026-11-05)

**Verdict: live design issue; stays OPEN.** This is a design/documentation deliverable, not a code fix. At verified current main, the requested library taxonomy, registry and entity-attachment model are not implemented; there is no evidence the issue is handled or superseded.

**Verification:** Issue #5969 is OPEN, has no linked PR, and has no hard-stop labels. The checkout is `main` at `7aae3accaf`, equal to `origin/main`.

**Current-main evidence:** `pkgs/id/src/world_session/types.rs:275-290` install frames carry bytes/hash/signature/seed, not a library type; `pkgs/id/src/world/mod.rs:408-440` records a world module hash with only Artifact/SourceBuild/Fork provenance. `pkgs/id/src/world_compile.rs:38-47,197-210` compiles bounded .roc files and does not fetch packages. The app/world manifests identify a source path or module hash, not a library registry. `src/boards.rs:142-169,335-367` is a content-addressed attachment precedent, but board-specific. `doc/2026-11-05_design_id5965.md` says DLL support is not implemented and defines proposed cache treatment; `doc/2026-11-05_design_id5997.md` proposes content-addressed library identity and capability manifests, also without implementation.

**Scope and ordering:** Produce the design note requested here: distinguish world executable, compile-in source library, DLL/linkable library and URL-addressed library; separate type metadata from entity/world attachment; settle discovery vs eligibility vs restriction; specify immutable identity and URL integrity (URLs are locators, not identities). Parent #5955 stages V1 imports (#5956 → #5957) before the V2 registry/permissions work, then V3 dynamic user functions. Coordinate the import-facing minimum with #5956 before #5957 consumes it; the full taxonomy is V2. A first draft can proceed now. Align capability fields with #5958, license fields with #5977/#6008, and runtime attachment semantics with #6003. Defer DLL ABI/linking claims until #5964/#5995 settle them; reuse #5965's cache decisions and #5997's content-identity proposal rather than reopening them.

**Next action:** design-authoring pass on #5969, explicitly referencing and deferring sibling-owned decisions. No code patch is warranted at triage; these are sequencing constraints, not grounds to close or abandon the issue.

Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Statements S46, S48–S51 of the 2026-11-04 brief. Genre prior art is the separate bot-games research child.

## Requirement (Drew, in substance)

Design the world-side pattern where **a world maps over a set of users' functions** — say, one function per user, all matching the appropriate interface:

- Any user function that takes longer or uses more gas than the world wants is **timed out / cut off individually** (mechanism: the gas/timeout research child of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955)).
- **A human can be in control with a partner or subsystem** — the mixed human+AI case is first-class, not an afterthought (intent blending itself is specified in the tick/intent data-model child).
- Users can **dynamically switch** their function **very often: every tick, every second, every minute, or whatever**.
- The game/world author may provide **a trigger function to switch immediately or on the next load**.
- **Conditional strategy selection** is a supported pattern: "if they ever see a green bot, they load their green-bot strategy; if there are green and blue bots, they switch it out with a generic strategy." The world offers the view; the switching logic can live in a user function, a world-provided trigger, or both — the design says which layer owns what.

## Design points to settle

- The function interface: single entry point per tick? Init/step split? What state persists between ticks and who owns it?
- The mapping's failure table: timeout → intent defaults to what (no-op, last intent, world-defined default)? Gas exhaustion mid-tick? Crash?
- Fairness: N functions × per-function budget vs the world's per-tick budget (server-invariants child) — scheduling order, and whether a slow user's function can starve others' wall-clock.
- Switching mechanics against the DLL/hot-swap design child: a switch is a rebind; who validates the new function's interface conformance and when?

## Related

- Dynamic user functions (DLL) and tick/intent data-model children of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955)
- Bot-game prior art: research child of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955)

## Done looks like

A design doc: the per-user function interface, the per-tick mapping algorithm with its failure table, the switching/trigger model, and the human+partner composition rule.

body:
Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Statements S40–S42 of the 2026-11-04 brief. Filed as dedicated research per Drew's rule for sub-parts that need their own documentation.

## Questions (Drew, in substance)

1. **Per-function gas:** "I don't know if there's a way to rate limit specific functions' gas usage, but that would be ideal." — Is there, in our Roc/wasm/host setup? Options to evaluate: fuel metering at the wasm layer, instruction counting, host-side accounting per capability call, cooperative yield points.
2. **Per-function timeout:** the world code gives a function a certain amount of time; if it doesn't respond in that time, it closes. — What mechanism enforces this against a function that never yields (interruptible execution, epoch interruption, process isolation)?
3. **Multi-threading:** "I know that there were discussions about how to do multi-threading, but I don't know if that ever was fully figured out." — Find those discussions (Roc community + our own repo history) and report the actual state: what was decided, what was left open, what it means for running many user functions per tick.

## Scope notes

- The consumer is the per-user function mapping design (child of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955)): a world maps over N user functions per tick and must bound each one independently.
- Measure against the performance-tension design child too: metering overhead is the tax on the near-C-speed story — quantify it, don't hand-wave it.
- Check what the current host already enforces (world session/compile path in `pkgs/id/src/world_session/`, `pkgs/id/src/world_compile.rs`) before proposing new machinery.

## Done looks like

A research doc answering all three questions with evidence: mechanism options with measured or cited overheads, a recommendation for per-function gas + timeout, and the multithreading state-of-the-art summary.
