body:
Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Statements S24–S27 of the 2026-11-04 brief.

## Requirement (Drew, in substance)

Our side of the bargain is narrow, and it is the whole safety story:

- **Ticks, sessions, or gas stay below a certain amount.** Budgets are platform-enforced, not author-promised.
- **The platform side is solid — it can't be exploited to do more than it's meant to.** The capability ceiling is a security boundary, not a convention.
- **Users are aware of what could be done.** Awareness (registry listing, permission prompts) is a load-bearing part of the model, not decoration.
- Within those bounds — disk size and the rest — **users can pull whatever libraries they want**. No additional gatekeeping is implied by this design.

## Design points to settle

- The budget vocabulary: per-tick gas, per-session totals, per-world aggregate, disk quota per world / per user / per library cache. Which are hard kills, which are throttles, which are bills (see the compile-economics child of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955))?
- Observability: what does a world author / server admin see when a budget trips — and what does the *user whose function tripped it* see? (The brief's program framing names observability as a first-class axis.)
- Exploit-resistance review surface: enumerate the platform functions as an attack surface; for each, what bounds it (path sandboxing, network egress rules, allocation limits). This is the checklist the "can't be exploited" claim will be audited against.
- Failure containment: a world that blows its budget must not degrade co-resident worlds on the same server.

## Related

- Per-function gas/timeout research child of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955)
- Writer-set authority (adjacent boundary): [#5545](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5545)
- Sandbox implementation today: `pkgs/id/src/sandbox.rs`; capability catalog `pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/world_caps.rs`

## Done looks like

A design doc: the budget set with enforcement semantics, the observability surface for each budget, and the platform attack-surface checklist.

body:
Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Statements S19–S23 of the 2026-11-04 brief.

## Requirement (Drew, in substance)

Design the permission system for worlds — at least in the user-friendly examples and main interfaces, a **simple version of what the Play Store does**: before you connect, it tells you what the thing can do.

- The disclosure must distinguish **whose capability is exercised**: "this app connects to the internet **using your client**" is a different sentence from "this app reads things from the internet **through the server side**." Client-side and server-side capabilities are presented as separate lines, because they implicate different parties.
- Granting **server-side** capabilities is a **server admin decision**.
- Admin grant modes to support: approve **generally**; **ignore for all time for specific websites**; ignore for **specific permissions**; **YOLO mode** — don't worry about anything.
- The client-side analog (per-user memory of grants) should mirror the same shape: ask once, remember per world / per permission / globally, with YOLO as an explicit user choice, not a default.

## Design points to settle

- Prompt content: the requested set and the discovered-used set (capability-model child of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955)) — show both when they differ ("asks for X, only uses Y").
- When prompts fire: first connect, capability change (see the change-notices child), never on an unchanged reconnect for a remembered grant.
- What a denial does: world still loads with the denied capability inert, or connection refused? Per-capability granularity implies the former is possible — say which capabilities are load-bearing.
- YOLO mode scoping: per-server, per-user, time-boxed? It must be loud in the UI that it's on.

## Related

- Knowledge-layer sharing & permissions (different layer, same vocabulary problem): [#5840](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5840)
- Capability-change notices and permission precedents research: children of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955)

## Done looks like

A UX design: prompt mock/content spec for client-side and server-side grants, the admin grant-mode matrix, memory/remembering rules, and denial semantics.

body:
## Finding

`scripts/tests/test_program_tending.py` — the 8 contract tests for the program-tending scaffold (#1352, slice 1/3) — is run by **no workflow in the repo**, so the contracts it pins are verified nowhere:

- `.github/workflows/scripts-test.yml` enumerates exactly two files: `test_update_nixpkgs_inputs.py` and `test_worker_preflight.py` (lines 31–33).
- `.github/workflows/research-workflow.yml` runs `test_*workflow*.py` and `test_plan_check.py` (lines 35–37) — neither pattern matches `test_program_tending.py`.
- `.github/workflows/program-tending.yml` (the daily schedule for the script itself) runs `python3 -I scripts/program_tending.py --run` (line 47) and never its tests.
- A repo-wide search for `test_program_tending` / `program_tending` across `.github/workflows/`, `flake.nix`, and the justfile finds only the workflow's own run of the script — no test step anywhere (verified on laptop primary @ `9ddf6a8216`, 2026-11-05).

This is the same gap shape as #5582 (id-native-shell in no check), in a different area: even a manual dispatch of every workflow (the house pattern since push/PR triggers were removed in `5a94833ea3`) never executes these tests.

## What the tests pin (and would silently lose)

Verified by running the suite on the laptop @ `9ddf6a8216`: **8 tests, all pass, ~55 s**.

- the run log always covers all five sections in order (`epics`, `roadmaps`, `projects`, `stalled-prs`, `loose-ends`);
- the scaffold is read-only: `actions_taken == 0`, every section `no-action`;
- the hard-stop labels (`held`, `user/owned`, `do-not-merge`, `do-not-auto-edit`) are named in every log;
- a per-repo fetch failure is reported in-section and never fails the run;
- CLI contract: `--run` prints a valid log and exits 0; no `--run` exits 2;
- the isolated-subprocess run (`python3 -I`) works from a clean interpreter.

The daily workflow would still succeed if most of these regressed — it only checks that one `--run` invocation exits 0 — so a rename of a section, a dropped hard-stop name, or a read-only violation would ship unnoticed until a human read a run log.

## Secondary observation (same fix pass)

Four of the eight tests call `pt.run(...)` / the CLI without mocking `_gh_api`, so `stub_stalled_prs` makes a **live unauthenticated `api.github.com` request** per invocation (plus one more in the isolated subprocess). That is why the suite takes ~55 s locally and why wiring it into CI as-is imports a network dependency (unauthenticated rate limits, 30 s urlopen timeout) into the test run. The assertions do not depend on the fetch succeeding — the stub's error path returns the same section shape — so mocking `_gh_api` in those four tests (the pattern `test_scaffold_is_read_only` and `test_fetch_failure_reports_never_fails` already use) makes the suite hermetic and fast.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Some workflow step runs `python3 -m unittest discover -s scripts/tests -p 'test_program_tending.py'` (e.g. a step in `scripts-test.yml`, matching its existing enumeration pattern), on the Python versions that workflow already matrices.
- [ ] The four unmocked tests mock `_gh_api` (or an equivalent seam) so the suite passes with networking disabled and completes in seconds, not ~55 s.
- [ ] The full suite still passes locally after the change: 8 tests OK.
- [ ] No change to `scripts/program_tending.py` behavior or to the `program-tending.yml` schedule.

## Evidence

- File/line evidence above, read on laptop primary `~/git/code` @ `9ddf6a821658c8700fb78c06b024e2a1b024f754` (HEAD == origin/main, clean tree).
- Suite run on laptop: `python3 -m unittest discover -s scripts/tests -p 'test_program_tending.py' -v` → `Ran 8 tests in 54.951s — OK`.
- Related: #1352 (parent scaffold issue, open), #5582 (same gap shape for id-native-shell).

body:
# Capability-provider field survey — the current option space, per class and cross-cutting

**Kind:** research / option-space inventory. **This document makes no design decision and contains no recommendation.** Each section ends with the open questions a decider would need answered. The one exception to "no verdicts": options that are verifiably dead, archived, or license-changed are flagged as such, with evidence, so nobody designs on them unknowingly.

**Origin:** #5686 bundled five provider targets (ESP32/MQTT, terminal, Bevy, smartphone, web) into one provider-model design. The WS-F gap pass split the filings (#5780 Android, #5781 Bevy, #5783 ESP32 platform, #5898 declaration, #5899 discovery & negotiation, #5900 grants, #5901 constrained-device, #5902 host providers: terminal & website, #5903 embedded providers: engine & smartphone, #5904 offline/degraded, #5905 security model). Drew's ruling (2026-11-04): splitting the filings is not enough — the research widening is its own task, so the design issues inherit a real option space instead of first-idea designs. This is that survey.

**Method / sources:** vendor and project documentation and current-state reporting, surveyed 2026-11-04. Claims carry a status inline where it matters: current versions and dates are as reported by the projects themselves. Anything I could not verify is marked **[unverified]**. Drew's own earlier statements in the ID design issues are treated as context for what a provider must be, per the standing raw-sources rule.

---

## 0. The shape the options are being mapped onto

From #5686, #789 (ceiling model), and the writer-set design behind #5545:

- A **provider** declares typed, described, versioned capabilities (name, input/output shape, units/semantics, rate/size limits, side effects) into the ceiling model: a provider can never offer more than its own ceiling, a consumer can never receive more than the grant.
- Provider **identity** may be the user's, the device's own, or a delegated/pseudo identity; device-owned vs user-owned vs shared/public providers all exist.
- **Declaration** is a signed, versioned artefact (in-repo prior art: #1061 F12.4 provider registry — capabilities as manifest + provider components; #2338 device.info capability manifest). Static (firmware) vs dynamic (runtime-discovered) declaration both occur.
- From the writer-set design (#5545): capability-bearing objects are **signed, versioned, owner-controlled**; **ingest is a validity gate, never an authority gate** — receiving and validating an object never by itself grants authority.
- Discovery (#5899) happens within a world, within a server, and across bridges/federation, under visibility rules.

Every option below is described on its own terms first, then (in §6) mapped against this shape: where it **fits**, where it **fights**.

---

## 1. Terminal providers

*Inherits into: #5902 (host providers: terminal & website). The terminal matters twice in ID: as a surface a user sits at, and as a provider — a shell session offers capabilities (run commands, expose command blocks with exit status, cwd, output) to authorised consumers.*

### 1.1 Multiplexers as the programmatic substrate

| Option | What it is | Maturity | License | How it differs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **tmux** (3.8, Sep 2026) | The incumbent multiplexer. **Control mode** (`tmux -C`) is a documented, line-based protocol used by terminal emulators (iTerm2) to drive tmux programmatically; the full command language (`capture-pane`, `send-keys`, `pipe-pane`, formats) is scriptable from anything. | Ubiquitous, stable for a decade+ | ISC | Deepest scripting surface of the class; no official plugin API — extensions are shell scripts via the third-party TPM ecosystem. |
| **Zellij** (0.45.1, Aug 2026) | Rust "terminal workspace": KDL layouts, session resurrection, built-in web client, native Windows since 0.44. | Active, fast-moving | MIT | **Plugins are WebAssembly/WASI components** — a plugin is a first-class pane that renders UI, reacts to state, and controls Zellij; Zellij's own tab bar/status bar are plugins. Also has a `pipe` CLI for external tools to exchange data with plugins. |
| **WezTerm** | Rust GPU terminal + its own multiplexer domains (local/SSH/TLS), driven by `wezterm cli` (list/activate-pane/send-text/…) and configured/extended in **Lua** with an event system. | Mature; note: stable release line is old (2024) while main stays active **[release-cadence caveat]** | MIT | The multiplexer is *inside* the terminal — one binary is both surface and provider substrate; reconnectable domains are a native concept. |
| **GNU screen / byobu** | The older substrate. | Maintenance-paced | GPL | Included for completeness; strictly less programmable surface than tmux. |

### 1.2 Terminal emulators with remote-control APIs

- **kitty** — a full **remote-control protocol** (`kitten @ …` over a socket, must be explicitly enabled: `allow_remote_control`), plus *kittens* (in-terminal extensions) and two protocols of its own that other terminals adopt: the **graphics protocol** and the **keyboard protocol**. GPL-3.0.
- **Ghostty** — Zig core with an embeddable library (**libghostty**) so a host app can embed a terminal as a component rather than shell out to one; modern protocol coverage (OSC 133 etc.). MIT. The "terminal as a library" shape is unique in this class.
- **iTerm2** — macOS-only; a comprehensive **Python API** and AppleScript surface; the deepest emulator-side API, at the cost of a platform lock. Proprietary freeware.
- **VS Code terminal** — xterm.js + PTY host; shell integration is built in, and extensions interact via the terminal API — but the API is editor-scoped, not a general provider surface.

### 1.3 The protocol layer underneath all of them: shell integration

- **OSC 133** (semantic prompt / command marks, from FinalTerm) is now the de-facto standard for making shell output *structured*: prompt boundaries, command start/finish, **exit codes**. Supported by kitty, WezTerm, Ghostty, iTerm2, VS Code, foot, Zellij 0.45. **OSC 7** (cwd reporting) and **OSC 52** (clipboard) round out the set. This layer is what turns "a terminal" into "a provider of typed command-block events" without scraping heuristics — agent-era tools (e.g. shell-context capture in coding agents) already build exactly this three-layer stack: shell hooks → OSC 133 marks → multiplexer scrollback APIs.
- **DEAD FLAG — Coder AgentAPI**: a terminal-emulator-in-memory with an HTTP API for driving agents; **archived 2026-09-13**. Do not design on it.

### 1.4 Agent-protocol adjacency

Terminals are also where *agents* live: **ACP** (Zed's Agent Client Protocol) standardises editor↔agent driving; **A2A** (see §6.2) is agent↔agent. A terminal provider design will sit next to both — they answer "who drives the agent in the terminal", not "what capabilities the terminal offers", but the boundary must be drawn somewhere.

**Open questions for the decider:** Does the terminal provider expose *raw PTY* (bytes, maximal power, no structure) or *command blocks* (OSC 133-structured, typed, auditable) — or both as different capabilities with different risk classes? Is the provider the multiplexer (session outlives any surface) or the emulator (owns rendering/input)? Does Zellij's WASI-plugin shape — terminal capabilities as sandboxed components — generalise into ID's provider-component shape (#1061), or is it a local coincidence?

---

## 2. Smartphone / Android providers

*Inherits into: #5780 (native Android client), #5903 (embedded providers). The platform moved under this design in the last twelve months: Android now has a first-party "apps as tool providers" mechanism.*

### 2.1 The new platform layer: AppFunctions / "Android MCP"

- **AppFunctions** (Android 16+, Jetpack library): an app annotates functions; the library generates an XML schema of them; the **Android OS itself keeps the registry**; authorised callers discover and execute via `AppFunctionManager`. Callers need the `EXECUTE_APP_FUNCTIONS` permission. Google describes apps as behaving "like on-device MCP servers" and the layer as **Android MCP**; transport is Binder IPC, not HTTP. Status as of this survey: **announced "officially in beta" 2026-10-31** (Android Dev Summit), Jetpack library in **alpha**, Gemini integration in **private preview** with trusted testers — the only public examples are Samsung Gallery (Galaxy S26) and Gemini's Calendar/Notes/Tasks integrations. Docs still say "experimental feature"; access to the full pipeline is limited to a limited set of apps and system agents during evaluation.
- What it is for ID: this is the first time the *operating system* offers the declaration+discovery half of a capability-provider model on a phone — but the registry is the OS's, the caller set is Google's, and authority is Android permissions, not owner-controlled signed objects. It is an **instantiation surface**, not the model.
- **Third-party precedent: Phone MCP** (Premex, open source): an Android app that turns the phone into a real MCP server (photos, sensors, camera, contacts) reachable via an outbound-connection relay or directly on local Wi-Fi — evidence that the phone-as-provider demand exists independent of Google's programme, and that a relay pattern solves carrier/NAT reachability.

### 2.2 The classic platform surfaces (mature, no programme gate)

- **Intents / App Links / bound services (AIDL)**: the original Android capability system — implicit/explicit intents as coarse capability calls, App Links as verified web↔app delegation, bound services as the typed IPC variant. Mature, Apache-2.0 (AOSP), but granularity is app-level and consent is install/permission-time, not per-grant.
- **Runtime permissions + per-use consent**: Android's permission model (dangerous permissions, one-time grants, photo-picker-style mediated access) is the closest mainstream analogue to ID's per-use consent caps (#2341's accuracy-ceiling + per-use consent shape).
- **Accessibility services**: the de-facto "drive any app" capability — powerful enough that Play policy restricts it; a provider built on it inherits the policy fight.
- **WorkManager / foreground services**: the honest background-execution envelope (battery rules) any provider must declare against — #5780 already flags this.

### 2.3 On-device runtimes and agents

- **Termux**: a full Linux userland on the phone — the "phone as a small server" variant. Caveat: the **Play Store build is years stale**; distribution is F-Droid/GitHub **[widely reported; verify current state before relying]**.
- **On-device agent runtimes**: Gemini Nano with native function calling and ML Kit's **Agentic API** (alpha, Oct 2026) run an agent loop *on the device* — the phone as consumer-host, not just provider.
- **Wasm on Android**: Wasmtime and other runtimes have Android targets **[uneven maturity across runtimes — unverified per-runtime]**; relevant if provider components (#1061) are to run on the phone in the same component shape as elsewhere.

**Open questions for the decider:** Does ID's Android client register its capabilities with the OS registry (AppFunctions) as one *projection* of its writer-set declarations — accepting Google's caller gating — or stay self-contained and treat AppFunctions as an interop bridge for *other* apps' functions? How do Android runtime permissions compose with ID grants (permission held by the app ≠ grant held by a consumer)? What wakes a provider on a phone (push, WorkManager windows) given #5904's offline/degraded model?

## 3. Web / browser providers

*Inherits into: #5902 (host providers), #5782 (GUI surface). This class changed the most in 2026: the web platform is growing a native "page as tool provider" API.*

### 3.1 WebMCP — pages declaring tools to agents

- **WebMCP** (W3C Web Machine Learning Community Group; editors from Microsoft and Google): a page calls `document.modelContext.registerTool()` with a name, description, JSON Schema, and an `execute` callback; a declarative form annotates HTML forms into tools. Tools run **in the page, in the user's session, visibly**. It borrows MCP's vocabulary but is *not* MCP: no server process, no JSON-RPC transport, tools exist only while the tab is open. Cross-origin exposure needs explicit grants both ways (`exposedTo` / `fromOrigins`); everything is gated by the `tools` Permissions Policy (default `'self'`); annotations include `readOnlyHint`, `untrustedContentHint`, `consequentialHint` — hints, not enforcement.
- Status: **Draft Community Group Report (current draft 2026-10-20) — not a W3C standard**; Chrome origin trial from Chrome 149; Mozilla's standards position **neutral**, WebKit's **oppose**. Chrome's own guidance: WebMCP is the contextual layer, backend MCP is the service layer; neither replaces the other.
- For ID: a website-as-provider gets a *platform-native declaration surface* for the first time — but declaration honesty and authority stay the page's problem, which is precisely the half ID's writer-set model exists to own.

### 3.2 The extension route (works today, every browser)

- **WebExtensions (Manifest V3)**: an extension can expose page + browser capabilities (tabs, storage, scripting, native messaging to a local host process). MV3's service-worker lifecycle and the removal of blocking webRequest are real constraints on provider shape. Cross-browser baseline is good for core APIs, uneven at the edges. An extension is today the only way to ship a browser provider to all users without an origin trial.
- **Native messaging**: the extension↔local-process bridge — the seam where a browser provider meets a local ID node.

### 3.3 Browser device & platform APIs (Chromium-led)

- **WebUSB, WebSerial, Web Bluetooth, WebHID**: a web page as a *hardware* capability provider (talk to an ESP32 over serial from a tab, etc.) — Chromium-only in practice; Firefox/Safari do not ship most of these. **File System Access**, **WebGPU**, **WebNN** similarly expand what a page can offer. These make "website" and "ESP32" provider classes touch: the browser is a provisioning/bridge surface for constrained devices.

### 3.4 Browser-automation MCP servers (the inverse direction)

- **chrome-devtools-mcp**, **Playwright MCP** and kin expose the *browser itself* as tools to an external agent — the browser as provider to agents rather than pages as providers to the browser's agent. Both directions now exist in the field; a web-provider design has to say which one it means, or both.

### 3.5 Adjacent: MCP Apps

- **MCP Apps** (first official MCP extension, SEP-1865, stable 2026-01-26): MCP servers return interactive UI surfaces rendered in sandboxed iframes inside clients — providers that bring their own UI. Directly relevant to #5782's surface design: the field's answer to "a provider with a GUI" is server-declared UI in a sandbox, not provider-supplied native UI.

**Open questions for the decider:** For a website provider, which declaration is authoritative — the writer-set object, with WebMCP registration as its in-tab projection? Does ID consume *other* sites' WebMCP tools as foreign providers (ingest = validity gate) — and what does WebKit's "oppose" do to a cross-browser story? Are Chromium-only device APIs acceptable as a provider substrate given ID's own browser fleet is Chromium-based?

## 4. Game-engine providers (Bevy)

*Inherits into: #5781 (Bevy incorporation), #5903 (embedded providers). Bevy is both a provider target (engine offers render/input/audio surfaces) and a client shape (a world hosted in an engine).*

### 4.1 The engine itself

- **Bevy** (0.20 current per ecosystem compat tables, late 2026): Rust, data-oriented ECS at the core, **MIT OR Apache-2.0**. Fast release cadence with breaking changes per release — every ecosystem crate pins to a Bevy version (this is the version-policy question #5781 already poses). An official editor is under active development **[status unverified in detail]**.
- **`bevy_ecs` standalone**: the ECS is usable without the engine — including, per Espressif's own developer portal, **Bevy ECS running on an ESP32 in `no_std` Rust**. The class boundary between "engine provider" and "constrained device" is thinner than the issue split assumes; the mapping ID entities↔Bevy entities could in principle run on the device class too.

### 4.2 Scripting / provider components inside the engine

- **bevy_mod_scripting** (0.21–0.23 line, actively released through Oct 2026): the community scripting bridge — **Lua and Rhai** supported (via mlua / rhai), bindings generated from Bevy's reflection, dynamic systems/components registerable from scripts. Self-described work-in-progress with anticipated API churn; version-locked to Bevy patch releases. **FLAG: Rune support is "temporarily on hold"** in the rewrite — do not assume it.
- The engine-native alternative is **plugins in Rust** (Bevy's own plugin architecture): full power, compile-time only — providers as native code vs providers as scripts is a live axis here, not a settled one.

### 4.3 Networking / replication (world state across engines)

- **lightyear** (0.31 for Bevy 0.20): the full-featured option — client-server *and* P2P *and* host-client modes, prediction/interpolation, multiple transports (UDP, WebSocket, WebTransport via aeronet, Steam), deterministic (input-only) replication supported. Built on **bevy_replicon**.
- **bevy_replicon** alone: the replication core (world replication, interest management, pre-spawning) without lightyear's netcode opinions — the "bring your own transport" variant.
- **aeronet**: the transport-abstraction layer both sit on.
- ID-relevant tension: these systems replicate *engine state* under a server-authoritative or lockstep model; ID replicates a *journal* under a writer-set model. They are answers to different authority questions and a design must not conflate them.

### 4.4 Variants outside Bevy

- **Fyrox** (MIT, Rust): a full engine *with* an editor — the "batteries included" Rust alternative; smaller ecosystem.
- **Godot + godot-rust (gdext)** (MIT): the non-Rust-core engine with a live Rust binding story; huge community, different (node/scene) state model.
- **macroquad / miniquad** (MIT/Apache): minimal Rust game loops — if the "engine" need is really "a render/input surface", these are the floor of the class.
- Unity/Unreal exist as proprietary poles; noted for completeness, they do not fit a Rust workspace's seams.

**Open questions for the decider:** Is the Bevy provider face (render/input/audio surfaces) declared through the same manifest as every other provider, with the engine-specific part confined to *how* surfaces are produced? Engine-state replication (replicon/lightyear) vs journal replication (ID): which carries a shared world when both are present — and can replicon-style interest management inform #5899's discovery visibility? Bevy's cadence: pin, track, or abstract (already open in #5781 — the ecosystem's universal version-pinning is evidence, not an answer).

## 5. ESP32 / MQTT / IoT providers

*Inherits into: #5783 (ESP32 platform line), #5901 (constrained-device providers), and the existing bridge design #2343 (`id.device.v1` MQTT bridge). Two independent axes: what runs **on** the device, and what the device **speaks**.*

### 5.1 On-device stacks

| Option | Shape | Maturity | License | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **ESP-IDF** (v5.5 stable, support to Jan 2028; v6.0 in development) | Espressif's C SDK: drivers, esp-mqtt client, OTA with rollback, secure boot/flash encryption | Production standard; 100M+ chips | Apache-2.0 | The default. Everything else in this table is measured against it. |
| **esp-hal + Embassy** (esp-hal **1.0, Oct 2025**) | Bare-metal **Rust, no_std**: esp-hal for peripherals, esp-radio for Wi-Fi/BLE, Embassy async executor/net | 1.0 is new but the esp-rs line is years old; Espressif now blesses a Rust SDK | MIT OR Apache-2.0 | The stack that lets device firmware share the workspace's language — and potentially its capability-subset code. Async drivers have constraints (e.g. not Send across cores in 1.x). |
| **Arduino-ESP32** | The hobbyist-standard C++ core over ESP-IDF | Very widely deployed | LGPL-2.1 | Enormous example/library gravity; weakest fit for a signed/attested firmware lifecycle. |
| **ESPHome** | YAML-configured firmware generator (C++ output) with a native API to Home Assistant; huge component library | Mature for home automation | MIT | **FLAG: its Matter support is explicitly experimental (2025–)**; its native API is a provider model of its own (entities declared, HA consumes) — an interop target and a design reference, per #5783's open question. |
| **Zephyr RTOS** | Vendor-neutral RTOS with an ESP32 port; strong where a project spans many chip vendors | Production, LF-governed | Apache-2.0 | The "not just Espressif" variant; costs ESP32-specific polish. |
| **Tasmota** | Ready-made firmware for commercial ESP devices (MQTT-first) | Mature, deployed at scale | GPL-3.0 | A *product*, not a toolkit — relevant as an interop peer: ID worlds will meet Tasmota devices whether or not ID builds on it. |

### 5.2 What the device speaks

- **MQTT 5.0 / 3.1.1** — the incumbent (#2343's bridge is specified against it). Client side: ESP-IDF's built-in esp-mqtt; Rust side: **rumqttc** (client) / **rumqttd** (broker), **paho** bindings; `no_std` clients exist at smaller scale (mqttrs-based). MQTT 5's user properties and response-topic patterns are the hooks a capability-envelope design would use.
- **MQTT-SN** — the UDP/sleepy-device variant; niche but designed exactly for the power posture #5783 worries about.
- **Matter over Thread/Wi-Fi** — the industry-consortium model: **production-ready on ESP32-C6/C5** (802.15.4 radios) via Espressif's **esp-matter** SDK; Thread 1.3/1.4; Home Assistant / Apple / Google fabrics interoperate today. Two honest caveats from the field: **esp-matter's OTA is not fully wired up** (reflash by hand), and Matter's device-type model is **rigid** — custom capabilities need custom clusters or don't map. Matter also brings its own identity/attestation regime (DAC certificates, CSA certification for distributed products) — a *second* authority system any design must reconcile with ID's device-owned identity (#5686's question), not a transport you bolt on.
- **CoAP / LwM2M** — the carrier/industrial lineage: CoAP (REST on UDP, DTLS) and LwM2M (device management + object-model telemetry). Less consumer gravity, more fleet-management shape (bootstrap, firmware objects) — LwM2M's object model is a worked example of "declared device capabilities" from the telecom world.

### 5.3 Broker side (where the bridge terminates)

| Broker | Maturity | License | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Eclipse Mosquitto** | The default small broker; also now **ported to run on ESP-IDF itself** (Espressif, 2025) — a broker *on* the device class | EPL-2.0 / EDL-1.0 | Single-node by design; dynamic security plugin for auth. |
| **rumqttd** | Rust broker, MQTT 5/3.1.1, clustering in progress historically | Apache-2.0 **[cluster maturity unverified]** | The in-language option for a bridge that lives inside fleet/Rust infrastructure. |
| **NanoMQ** | C, edge-focused, MQTT over QUIC/WebSocket bridges | MIT | Built for edge deployments. |
| **HiveMQ CE** | Java, full MQTT 5 | Apache-2.0 | The enterprise-lineage open core. |
| **VerneMQ** | Erlang, clustered | Apache-2.0 | **Project has had maintenance turbulence historically — verify current maintainership before designing on it [unverified at survey time].** |
| **EMQX** | Largest-scale clustered broker; also gateways MQTT-SN/CoAP/LwM2M and MQTT over QUIC | **⚠ LICENSE CHANGE: BSL 1.1 from v5.9.0 — single-node free; clustering requires a commercial licence (converts to Apache-2.0 per-release after 4 years).** | Flagged so nobody designs a clustered-EMQX bridge on the old Apache assumption. |

**Open questions for the decider:** Which wire does the *capability* semantics ride: MQTT topics/payloads per #2343, with Matter as a foreign-provider interop — or is Matter a second native instantiation of the provider model (its cluster model ≈ capabilities, its attestation ≈ declaration honesty)? For firmware: does the crate split's embedded variant (#5788) target esp-hal/Embassy Rust or ESP-IDF, given the OTA/rollback and 64 KiB frame budget questions in #5783? Broker: is the bridge's broker a component ID operates (in-Rust rumqttd? Mosquitto?) or an external the bridge merely speaks to?

## 6. Cross-cutting: the layer above the classes

*Inherits into: #5898 (declaration), #5899 (discovery), #5900 (grants), #5905 (security model), #5545 (writer-set shape). Four families: agent-tool protocols, component/sandbox systems, object-capability RPC, and capability-token formats. They are not interchangeable — each owns a different layer, and the survey's main cross-cutting finding is that the field has separated into exactly those layers.*

### 6.1 Agent-tool protocols: MCP (and A2A next to it)

- **MCP** — current spec revision **2026-07-28**: JSON-RPC 2.0; transports **stdio** and **Streamable HTTP**; primitives tools/resources/prompts; the 2026-07-28 revision made the core **stateless** (no initialize handshake, no session header), deprecated Sampling/Roots/Logging, and formalised an extensions framework (**MCP Apps** UI extension stable 2026-01-26; Tasks extension for long-running work). Governance moved to the **Agentic AI Foundation** (Linux Foundation) in Dec 2025. Authorization, where present, is an **OAuth 2.1 profile** (protected-resource metadata, audience-bound tokens). The spec is **explicitly silent on policy, quota, and audit** — hosts decide.
- **Fit with ID's shape:** MCP is a *declaration + invocation* surface: `tools/list` ≈ a declaration read, tool calls ≈ invocations. Its stateless 2026 core fits a journal-based world better than its sessionful predecessors did. As a *provider mouth* — an ID provider projected as an MCP server, and foreign MCP servers ingested as providers — it composes cleanly with "ingest is a validity gate": schema-valid ≠ authorised, and the spec never claims otherwise.
- **Fight:** MCP's authorization story is identity-and-token centric (OAuth bearer authority, ambient once granted). ID's authority lives in **owner-controlled signed objects under a ceiling model**. Any design that lets an OAuth token *be* the authority has replaced ID's model, not interfaced with it; the grant check has to stay in the writer-set layer (#5900) with MCP as transport. Also: MCP's consumer is assumed to be an *agent host*; ID's consumers are arbitrary authorised parties — human clients included.
- **A2A** (v1.0 stable 2026, also AAIF): agent↔agent task delegation with Agent Cards. Adjacent, not a provider protocol — it answers "agent hires agent", and would sit *above* a provider layer, not replace it. (Name-collision warning: Zed's editor protocol is also "ACP"; IBM's Agent Communication Protocol was folded into A2A in 2025. Cite carefully.)

### 6.2 The component model: WASI / WIT and the sandbox hosts

- **WASI + Component Model** — WASI 0.2 (Component Model + WIT) is stable and widely implemented; **WASI 0.3 (2026) adds native async** (futures/streams in the canonical ABI). **Wasmtime** is the reference runtime (Bytecode Alliance, Apache-2.0, 2-year LTS lines). WIT gives typed interfaces — records, variants, resource handles — i.e. a *declaration language for components*. Components receive exactly the host interfaces they are linked against: **capability-style by construction at the sandbox boundary**. Threading remains the notable gap.
- **Runtime variants:** **wasmi** (interpreter, tiny footprint — the constrained-host variant), **Wazero** (Go, zero-dependency), **Wasmer** (commercial-backed, broader language SDKs). Same components, different host economics.
- **Extism** (BSD-3): a host-embedding framework over multiple engines with a simple bytes-in/bytes-out plug-in ABI and *custom host functions as the capability surface* — the pragmatic "providers as plug-ins with only granted host functions" shape, production-used.
- **wasmCloud** (CNCF incubating, Apache-2.0): the distributed-systems variant — components + host "providers" for capabilities (messaging/KV/HTTP) linked by signed **link definitions** over NATS; shipped 2.8 in Aug 2026. **FLAG (health, not death): LFX health score "Concerning" (49/100), contributor counts down ~25% year-over-year — active, but a thinner maintainer bench than its CNCF status suggests; weigh accordingly.**
- **Fit with ID:** the component model is the strongest candidate shape for *provider components* (#1061's "provider components" made literal): a provider implementation as a component whose WIT interface *is* its declared capability shape, holding only granted host capabilities. Zellij (§1.1) already proves this shape inside one product.
- **Fight:** WASI capabilities govern what *code* may do inside a sandbox. They are not *delegable grant objects between principals*: no attenuation chains, no owner-controlled signed artefacts, no revocation story across a network. The component layer can enforce a grant; it cannot *be* the grant system (#5900 stays ID's).

### 6.3 Object-capability RPC: Cap'n Proto / CapTP

- **Cap'n Proto** (1.5.0, Jul 2026; MIT): zero-copy serialization + an RPC system whose security model is **CapTP** (from the E language): authority *is* possession of an unforgeable object reference; delegation = handing over a reference; attenuation = handing over a **proxy/facet** that forwards only some methods; promise pipelining and disconnect handling are protocol-level. Reference implementation supports CapTP level 2 (3-party handoff is the unfinished level) **[per project docs; unchanged for years]**. Production home: Cloudflare Workers internals / Sandstorm lineage.
- **Fit:** philosophically the closest system in the field to ID's least-privilege grant model — "no ambient authority" is its founding axiom, and facets are attenuation as a programming pattern, not a policy bolt-on.
- **Fight:** CapTP references are **live, connection-scoped objects**; ID's grants are **persistent, signed, versioned artefacts** in a journal that must survive offline, sync, and audit (#5904). CapTP offers runtime discipline for a live provider session; it cannot serve as the grant ledger. Also honest adoption note: outside its niche, Cap'n Proto RPC remains rare — the ecosystem gravity is Protobuf/gRPC's, and the ocap discipline would be carried by ID alone.

### 6.4 Capability tokens: the grant-object formats

The layer that *does* deal in persistent, delegable, attenuating authority artefacts:

| Format | Model | Status | Notes for ID |
|---|---|---|---|
| **UCAN** (spec 1.0) | Signed delegation chains (JWT-shaped / CID-linked); every delegation must restate-or-attenuate; capability = `{with: resource, can: action}` + caveats | Active WG; production use in the Storacha/web3.storage line | Closest published relative of ID's grant objects: offline-verifiable, owner-rooted, attenuation-only. Identity is key/DID-based rather than OAuth-based. Flat capability URIs (no policy language) is its known limit. |
| **Biscuit** (3.x, Eclipse Foundation) | Append-only signed blocks (Ed25519); policies in a **Datalog** variant evaluated at verification; offline attenuation | Active, Rust-native | The expressive pole: grants that carry *logic* (context-checked rules), not just scope strings. Its block-chain ≈ a delegation chain as data. |
| **Macaroons** (Google, 2014) | HMAC-chained caveats appended by holders | Stable design, many implementations | The original attenuating-token design; shared-secret verification is its structural weakness for multi-party settings. Still cited as the basis for DeepMind's **Delegation Capability Tokens** proposal (Feb 2026 paper) — the agent-delegation literature is converging on this family. |
| **IETF AAT draft** (Oct 2026, -02) | OAuth-profiled *Attenuating Authorization Tokens*: tool-level capability claims (RFC 9396 RAR profile) + per-hop subsumption checks + holder binding | Internet-Draft, expires Apr 2027 | Evidence the IETF agent-auth track is rebuilding capability semantics *inside* OAuth — worth tracking for #5905; not a thing to build on yet. |

- **Fit/fight summary for §6.4:** these formats *are* grant-shaped, so the question is inverted — not "can they express ID's grants" but "what does ID's writer-set object add that they lack": journal integration, world-scoped visibility/discovery, versioning under owner control, and the ceiling model. A design could adopt a token format *as the encoding* of grant objects, or keep ID's objects and borrow the attenuation/subsumption rules. Either way the survey fact stands: **attenuate-only delegation with offline verification is a solved, multiply-implemented pattern in 2026 — ID does not need to invent it, only to choose its encoding and its deltas.**

### 6.5 Embedded scripting as provider logic

- **Lua** (MIT; via mlua in Rust) and **Rhai** (MIT OR Apache-2.0; Rust-native, designed for embedding with host-controlled exposure) are the live pair — proven inside Bevy (§4.2) and across the tooling field. **QuickJS** (MIT) is the JS-shaped variant. The pattern that matters: scripts receive a *host-curated API surface* — capability discipline by API design rather than by sandbox. Weaker isolation than Wasm components, far lower integration cost; the two are complements at different trust levels, not rivals.

### 6.6 Identity plumbing (adjacent, not authority)

- **SPIFFE/SPIRE** (CNCF graduated): workload identity via attested SVIDs — answers "which workload is this provider process" for the *host* side. Like OAuth, it identifies principals; it does not express owner-controlled grants. Relevant to #5905 as the identity layer a provider *host* might present, never as the grant itself.

### 6.7 The cross-cutting picture

The field in 2026 has converged on a **layered** shape, whether or not any single stack admits it:

1. **Declaration/discovery surface** — MCP `tools/list`, AppFunctions' OS registry, WebMCP registration, WIT interfaces, Matter clusters, #2338-style manifests.
2. **Invocation transport** — MCP (stdio/HTTP), Binder, MQTT, CapTP, in-process component calls.
3. **Sandbox/enforcement** — WASI components, Extism hosts, browser origins, Android permissions.
4. **Authority artefacts** — writer-set objects (ID), UCAN/Biscuit/macaroon tokens, OAuth tokens (identity-centric pole).

ID's model, as filed, puts its originality in layer 4 and its *projection* discipline (the same declaration projected onto many surfaces). Every option above can be located in exactly one or two layers — the design risk the split issues should watch is importing a layer-1/2/3 system and accidentally inheriting its layer-4 assumptions (MCP+OAuth being the standing example).

**Open questions for the decider:** Which single layer does each split issue own, and which does it borrow? Is there exactly one grant-object format (ID's writer-set objects) with *projections* (UCAN/Biscuit encodings, MCP surfaces), or are foreign grant formats ingestible as first-class? Does the provider-component runtime (if any) standardise on the component model now, or stay interface-only until a second implementation forces the question?

## 8. What this survey deliberately did not do

- No option was benchmarked, prototyped, or load-tested; maturity claims are the projects' own plus adoption signals, marked as such.
- iOS was out of scope (the filed class is Android, #5780); the AppFunctions/WebMCP pattern has no public iOS counterpart at survey time **[unverified — no survey pass made]**.
- No recommendation is made or implied. Where one option is "the default" or "the incumbent", that is a statement about the field's centre of gravity, offered so the decider knows what choosing otherwise costs.

body:
# fleet(proxy): `proxy connect` silently overwrites duplicate flags and silently drops modes — repeated `--host`/`--port`/`--request`/`--body` last-wins, `--stdio` eats `--request`, `--print-path` eats `--request`, `--host`/`--port` without `--stdio` are no-ops

## Summary

`fleet proxy connect`'s hand-rolled parser (`ConnectArgs::parse`,
`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/client.rs`) silently discards user
input in two ways. This is the #5713 bug class (fleet-dispatch) on the
proxy-connect leaf; #5713's scope is the dispatch crate only, and the
earlier proxy-leaf filings (#5575 proxy serve, #5619 connect/init
--help) do not cover the connect parser's duplicate/mode handling.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Code at `developing-today/code@2c2219b2a1` (laptop primary):

- `src/client.rs:276-291` — `--host` / `--port` assign with
  `out.host = Some(...)` / `out.port = Some(...)`: a repeat overwrites
  with no error.
- `src/client.rs:293-311` — `--request` assigns a fresh
  `RequestArgs { service_port: None, token_file: None, body: None }`:
  a second `--request` silently discards the first request *and* every
  modifier (`--service-port`, `--token-file`, `--body`) already
  attached to it.
- `src/client.rs:335-348` — `--body` likewise overwrites silently.
- `src/client.rs:366-373` (`run_connect`) — the `stdio` branch returns
  first: `--stdio --request GET /x` relays stdio and the request is
  never sent, with no error.
- `src/client.rs:387-391` — without `--stdio`, the `print_path` branch
  returns before the request branch: `--print-path --request GET /x`
  prints the shims path, exits 0, and the request is never sent.
- `--host` / `--port` are only read on the stdio branch
  (`src/client.rs:367-371`); off it they are parsed, stored, and never
  used — `fleet proxy connect --host other.example --port 2222`
  connects to the broker exactly as if they were absent.

Probe (real crate, laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-proxy-connect-args`,
`fleet-proxy` with `default-features = false`, against
`2c2219b2a1`):

```
dup-host-port: host=Some("second.example") port=Some(2202) stdio=true
dup-request: method=POST path=/second service_port=None token_file=None body=None
dup-body: body=Some(Object {"b": Number(2)})
mode-mix: stdio=true print_path=true request=Some(("GET", "/x"))
host-port-no-stdio: host=Some("other.example") port=Some(2222) stdio=false
control: method=GET path=/ok service_port=Some(4800)
```

The control parses exactly; every duplicate/mixed case succeeds
silently with input lost.

## Why it matters

`proxy connect --request` is the scripted one-shot request path over
the session broker, and `--stdio --host/--port` is the SSH
ProxyCommand path. A duplicated or mistyped flag in a script or an
SSH config currently sends a *different* request than written (the
second one, stripped of its service port / token file / body), or no
request at all at exit 0 — the exact silent-success failure shape the
fleet CLI has been eliminating leaf by leaf (#5572, #5592, #5603,
#5652, #5713). The `--request` case is the worst: losing
`--token-file`/`--service-port` changes which service is called and
with what credential, invisibly.

## Acceptance criteria

- Repeating a value flag (`--host`, `--port`, `--request`,
  `--service-port`, `--token-file`, `--body`) is a usage error
  (exit 2) naming the repeated flag, matching the fleet CLI's
  established direction; or, if a repeat is deliberately meaningful,
  it is documented in `CONNECT_USAGE` and pinned by a test.
- Mutually exclusive modes are rejected or given a documented,
  tested precedence: `--stdio` with `--request`, and `--print-path`
  with `--request`, must not silently drop the request.
- `--host` / `--port` without `--stdio` are a usage error naming the
  requirement (or are honored some other documented way).
- Pinning tests in `fleet-proxy` cover each rejected shape plus the
  well-formed control shapes (single `--request` with modifiers,
  `--stdio --host --port`, bare `--print-path`).
- `CONNECT_USAGE` states the rules the parser enforces.

body:
# WS-G stranded-fix audit 2026-11-04: merge drive + regression mechanisms

Drew's directive (19:46 CST): fixes keep resurrecting after restarts/switches — make sure everything built is committed and merged into main. This issue is the audit record. Cross-refs: #5760 (fleet rev lag), #5704 (gatherer), #5768 / PR #5764 (deployment layer), #5701 (incident).

## Merge drive (done under standing merge authority)

**59 PRs merged** across the four repos on 2026-11-04 evening (all merge commits): code ×40 (incl. #5667 design doc + stacked #5689, #5764 WS-E design, #5707 ID answers, and the full mergeable queue/fix backlog #5305–#5754), opencode ×9, openchamber ×6, darwin-nix ×5. Deliberate holds untouched: code#5613/#5614, opencode#1659, openchamber#1604 (forks-rename, Drew's word), code#4760 (patchelf, deliberately open).

## Regression mechanisms (evidence, not speculation)

1. **Quota gatherer (merged ≠ running, cross-repo stale checkout).** `quota-gatherer.service` fails every 15 min: `auth.openCodeLocalCredentialSource is not a function`. The gatherer (code main, current) imports its quota module in-process from a sibling OpenChamber checkout's *built* lib dir (`resolveLibDir()` in pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/gather-quota.ts: `$OPENCHAMBER_LIB_DIR` → `~/git/devtoday-openchamber` (absent) → `~/git/openchamber-fork`). That checkout is frozen at e216864bf0 (2026-10-22 integration branch), **6,733 commits behind** openchamber origin/main; its `lib/quota/providers/claude/auth.js` exports no `openCode*` symbol (on current main the symbol lives in `lib/opencode/auth.js`). Fixes merged in either repo never reach the gatherer. Fix direction: point the gatherer at a checkout that tracks main (or pin/vendor the module), and add the lib-dir resolution + checkout rev to the gatherer's startup log. Gatherer repair itself is owned by the laptop coordinator / #5704.
2. **Fleet binaries (manual flip, no drift check).** Running rev 18f0aa1a68 vs main — see #5760.
3. **Route-proxy (hand state outside any generation).** Fix existed in config; the deployed unit was hand-placed and broken — see #5768 / PR #5764.
4. **pm-stack from checkout.** pm-git-sync (~30 s timer) keeps ~/git/code within ~a minute of origin/main (verified: primary == origin/main c7ad1825ec at audit end, after being a few merges behind mid-drive). Deployment tracks main but is *unpinned* — a bad main lands in production within a minute, and a merge mid-pull can present a mixed tree. Design answer lives in PR #5764 (services layer).

labels.name: task/triage

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Summary

Design **writer sets v2**: composition and federation — views built from other views, writer sets shared and subscribed across servers, and set algebra over the v1 primitives — the step after the single-owner, single-view projection #5545 specifies.

## Motivation

The writer-set design (#2238 spec, closed; #5545 implementation) is deliberately singular: one view owner, one signed writer set (`idset.writer`), one projection tuple, and a discovery query that returns the counted and uncounted sides grouped by author. Its founding rule — "ingest is a validity gate, never an authority gate; a view counts only its writer set" — is exactly what makes composition interesting and undesigned: the moment a user wants to *build on someone else's view* (subscribe to a curator's set, union two communities' sets, publish their own view as an object others can count through), v1 has no objects for it. Tree state today is types and encoding only (`idset.rs`); v1 projection is still being implemented. That is the right order — but the v2 design should exist before v1's shapes ossify, because composition constrains representation: whether a view can *reference* another view, and what a set entry pointing at a set means, are decisions that are cheap now and expensive after #5545's encoding freezes.

## Sketch

- **View-as-object**: a view (or its counted projection) published as a signed object others can reference — what exactly is referenced (the set? the tuple? a snapshot at a frontier?) and what the referencing view counts when the referenced view changes.
- **Set algebra**: union/intersection/difference over writer sets as derived sets with provenance — exclusions still win; derivation chains are auditable back to signed originals; cycles refused by construction.
- **Federation**: writer sets whose entries name authors known only on other servers — resolution through #5675's remote query and #5672's selective sharing; what a set may claim about authors the local server has never seen.
- **Discovery v2**: discovering *views and sets* (not just subjects) — who curates well is itself a discovery problem; the uncounted-side honesty rule extends: a derived view must be able to show what its sources excluded.
- **Abuse shape**: composition as an amplification vector (a popular view silently re-counting a flood) — rate/volume posture, composing with #2033's abuse primitives.

## Open questions

- Is a derived view's projection still a pure function of a tuple (v1's purity rule), and what extends the tuple — source view frontiers per source?
- Retro-import (`include_history`) through a derivation chain: whose history flag governs?
- Do derived sets need their own signing owner, or is derivation unsigned-but-reproducible?

## Relations

Parent: epic #2056. Extends: #5545 (v1 projection + discovery), #2238 (v1 spec). Relations: #5672 (selective sharing), #5675 (remote query), #2033 (abuse primitives), #5732 (typed similarity/recommendation — views are a signal source), and the GUI design (counted/uncounted rendering is where composition becomes visible). Filed in the 2026-11-04 gap pass (WS-F) as a version-ladder design.

## Summary

Design the **feature-leveled build variants** the crate split exists to enable: client-only, server, headless/embedded, and provider-class builds of ID with defined feature sets — which capabilities each variant carries, how the levels are expressed, and how conformance is checked per variant.

## Motivation

The crate split (#3447, Drew-prioritised) is repeatedly justified by what it unlocks. The answers review (PR #5707, §12) states it plainly: "The split is also the mechanism for feature-leveled variants — client-only builds stripping most of the server — once the seams exist." But the variants themselves have no design: the split issues (#4403–#4411) carve the seams, and nothing decides what the *products* on those seams are. The consumers are already queuing up with incompatible needs — the Android client (needs a client-only core with no server), the ESP32 line (needs a provider-class minimal build), Bevy incorporation (needs an embeddable world/client library), the terminal (client + occasional server). Without a variants design, each consumer invents its own feature set and the "levels" become per-consumer accidents. (Note: #3846 specified the F13.8 client-only *boundary*; this issue is the build/product design across all variants, a different artefact. #1797's "build-variants as a cargo artifact" was build hygiene, not this.)

## Sketch

- **The level set**: name the variants (at minimum: client-only, full node/server, headless service, embedded/provider) and the capability matrix each carries — journal, sync, serve, presenters, providers — against the crate seams (#3447's 11 crates).
- **Expression**: cargo features vs per-crate composition vs both — and the rule that a variant is a *composition of crates*, never a thicket of `cfg` inside the monolith's remains.
- **Size/perf budgets**: Drew's stated order for the split — shipped-binary runtime performance first, build time second — applied per variant: what each variant's binary must weigh and do (the client-only variant is where the ≤2 MiB-class discipline from the fleet work is the reference point).
- **Conformance**: the shell contract and receipt contract per variant — which contracts a client-only build must still honour, and how variant conformance is tested (the determinism infrastructure's replay fixtures as cross-variant oracles: same journal, every variant, same state).
- **Upgrade/migration interplay**: F12.9 program upgrade (#1066) semantics per variant — what a client-only build does when a world requires a newer program than it carries.

## Open questions

- Are variants release artefacts (published binaries) or build-time choices for embedders only?
- Does the server variant ever *lose* features to a level (a "lite server"), or is server always the full set?
- Who owns variant drift — what stops a fifth consumer from quietly becoming a fifth variant?

## Relations

Parent: epic #2056. Depends on: #3447 and steps #4403–#4411 (the seams). Consumers: the Android client design, the ESP32 platform design, the Bevy incorporation design, #788 (reference shell). Relations: #3846 (client-only boundary spec), #1066 (upgrade/migration), #5685 (per-interface benchmark matrix — variants belong in it). Filed in the 2026-11-04 gap pass (WS-F).

title: id: design: spill v2 — native spill pools, lease failover and multi-holder fencing (extends #2819)

labels.name: task/triage

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Summary

Design **spill v2**: what happens after the single-spill-node write lease — a *pool* of native spill nodes for a hot world, lease arbitration among them, and lease behaviour under partition between the Durable Object and multiple native holders.

## Motivation

#2819 designed the write lease for exactly one spill target: when a world gets too hot for its hosted DO, execution spills to *a* native `id` node, and the journaled single-writer lease (DO as sole grantor, epoch fencing on append, journaled handoff) decides who may write. That design is landed as a protocol (design doc `doc/2026-11-01_design_id2819.md`; phases #3803–#3805). Its scope is honestly singular — one holder at a time, one spill node. The obvious next step it doesn't take: a world hot enough to spill may be hot enough to need more than one native node — read replicas are easy (the journal is the record), but *write* scaling, failover when the spill holder dies mid-term, and a second spill while the first is still draining are all undesigned. If that day comes with no design, the lease gets stretched by improvisation in exactly the place #2819 said catastrophe lives: "split-brain (DO and native node both accepting writes) is the catastrophic failure."

## Sketch

- **Holder failover**: lease term expiry and revocation when a holder dies or partitions — who detects it, what the DO may assume, and the in-flight command posture (extending v1's retryable not-holder rule) when the holder vanishes mid-term rather than handing off politely.
- **Spill pool**: multiple native nodes eligible for one world — grantor selection policy, whether epochs stay per-world global (recommended by v1's shape) or partition, and how a second node joins as reader-then-holder.
- **Read-your-spill**: native read replicas under a held lease — staleness bounds, and whether a replica may serve presence/session traffic.
- **Multi-world spill**: one native node spilling *many* worlds — per-world leases composing on one host, resource fairness between spilled worlds (composes with #5685's fairness-attack cases).
- **Region interplay**: spill across regions vs #2818's region-seam handoff — when is a hot world spilled, when is it *moved*?

## Open questions

- Is write scaling ever actually needed, or does the honest v2 stop at failover + read replicas? The design should say, with the load argument.
- Lease term/renewal defaults (v1: 30 s / 10 s) under failover — shorter terms trade journal traffic for recovery time; what's the evidence?
- Does the epoch stay a single monotonic counter when holders change across nodes with skewed clocks — v1 says the journal position is the truth; does that survive?

## Relations

Parent: epic #2056. Extends: #2819 (v1 lease — design landed, implementation phasing in #3804/#3805). Relations: #2818 (region-seam handoff), #2059 (hot worlds), #5685 (fairness cases), and the deterministic-testing design (lease fencing is one of its named oracle properties — failover interleavings are its test case). Filed in the 2026-11-04 gap pass (WS-F) as a version-ladder design: design now, implementation when load demands it.

title: id: design: output safety beyond plain text — HTML/JS output modes, safe-plain as a user choice, ingest without execution (follow-on to #3455)

body:
## Summary

Design the output-safety contract **beyond plain terminal text**: HTML/JS-bearing output modes, safe-plain rendering as a user choice, and servers ingesting arbitrary data without executing it. This is the follow-on #3455's own record flags as not covered.

## Motivation

#3455 (closed, sub-issues 4/4) settled the plain-output contract: a value cannot act on the terminal — one Cf/Cc set, escape-at-render, printer-not-ingest. But the answers review (PR #5707, §10) records three extensions Drew raised that the filed contract explicitly does **not** cover, plus one open question the design doc itself left filed-nowhere:

> "Explicitly NOT covered by #3455: ANSI/OSC terminal sequences — 'no filed instance,' listed in the design doc's open questions." And Drew's extensions: "HTML/JS-bearing output modes that some applications require; safe-plain rendering offered as a user choice; servers ingesting arbitrary data without executing it" — "flagged as a candidate follow-on design, not as part of #3455."

This issue is that follow-on. The risk shape is the same one #3455 named — *a value acts on its consumer* — with the consumer changed: a browser DOM, a rendering mode the user picked, or a server process that stores and forwards data it must never execute.

## Sketch

- **HTML/JS-bearing output modes**: which ID surfaces may emit markup at all (programs-as-websites, #2146/#5679, is the obvious one), and under what contract a data value may enter markup — escaping contexts (text, attribute, URL, script), the equivalent of #3455's "one shared set" for markup contexts, and who owns the set.
- **Safe-plain as a user choice**: rendering offered as a user-selected mode (plain-safe vs rich) per surface — what the choice means, its default, and whether it is per-client, per-world, or per-field; the plain mode's contract is #3455's, this design covers the *choice* and the rich side.
- **Ingest without execution**: servers (and bridges/relays) that ingest arbitrary data — the guarantees that stored data is never evaluated anywhere downstream: no template evaluation, no markup rendering without the contract above, no terminal emission without #3455 — stated as one ingest-side rule composing the two render-side contracts.
- **ANSI/OSC**: disposition the open question — are terminal escape sequences a #3455-class problem (values acting on the terminal through a second channel), and if so which surfaces refuse, escape, or pass them?

## Open questions

- Does the markup contract live beside the Cf set as a sibling shared definition, or is one "output safety" module the home for both?
- Is safe-plain a rendering *mode* or a data *classification* (sensitivity-style, per #5675's model)?
- Which existing surfaces already emit markup with data values in them today — the audit list is a deliverable.

## Relations

Parent: epic #2056. Relations: #3455 (the plain contract this extends; its open questions and Drew's extensions are the source), #2146 + #5679 (markup-emitting surfaces), #5675 (classification model), #3231 (receipt-side sibling: values validated as strictly as built — this is the emission-side counterpart). Filed in the 2026-11-04 gap pass (WS-F).

## Summary

Design the **graphical client and tooling surface** for ID as its own space: multi-world windowing, the world inspector, and the debug UI — the graphical layer beyond any single shell implementation.

## Motivation

#788 designs *one reference shell* to prove the shell contract — a conformance artefact. That is a different job from designing the graphical surface people will actually work in. Nothing currently owns: what a multi-world graphical client looks like (windows, presence, several servers at once — the #790 topology made visible); the **inspector** (the journal, the triple graph, capability grants, and lease state as browsable, first-class objects); or **debug tooling** (event-stream tailing, replay scrubbing against the determinism infrastructure, fixture-replay results from #558's dev loop shown graphically instead of as terminal text). Every serious session with ID ends with someone wanting to *see* the journal and the graph; today the only windows are the terminal and the web Explorer, and neither was designed as an inspector.

## Sketch

- **Windowing & presence**: one client, many worlds and servers; what presence means graphically; how worlds are organised, pinned, and found (the #5545 discovery query rendered, not just returned).
- **The inspector**: journal browser (positions, kinds, authors, epochs — including #2819 lease state and handoff history); entity/triple explorer following the graph; grant/capability viewer (who can do what, issued by whom, under which delegation — #5684's objects made legible); the writer-set counted/uncounted sides shown side by side, since "uncounted but findable" is a *visual* idea.
- **Debug UI**: live event tail per world; deterministic replay with a scrubber (step the journal, watch state rebuild — the determinism infrastructure's fixtures as the source); fuzz/soak failure playback.
- **Surface split**: which of this is web (Explorer growth), which is native-only, and which must be identical in both — decided here as requirements; framework choice stays with #788's record.

## Open questions

- Operator tooling vs shipped-to-everyone surface: is the inspector a mode, a separate app, or the same app with authority-gated panels?
- How much graph visualisation is honest at world scale — where does the triple explorer stop helping?
- Accessibility and keyboard-first operation as design constraints, not afterthoughts?
- Does the inspector need write affordances (moderation actions per #835) or is it read-only by design?

## Relations

Parent: epic #2056. Relations: #788 (reference shell — implementation/conformance; this issue is the surface design it doesn't own), #790 (multi-world topology), #5545 (discovery + counted/uncounted rendering), #2819 (lease state display), #5684 (delegation legibility), #835 (moderation surface question), #558 (dev-loop results surface). body:
# Standing-load inventory findings (WS-C, 2026-11-04, follow-up to #5701)

Measured 2026-11-05 01:26–01:36 UTC: 11 snapshots, 60 s apart; sustained %CPU from `ps` TIME deltas over 619 s, cross-checked against `/proc/<pid>/stat` tick deltas. Box: 4 CPUs. Load1 during window 7.4–19.1 (parallel fleet work), overall CPU busy 77.5% (3.10/4 cores).

## Key result: resident daemons are NOT the baseline problem
Every persistent non-platform resident measured ≤0.16% of one core sustained: fleet proxy serve (PID 22878, 2.3 MB RSS), systemd-journald, resource-sampler (cgroup total 2.27 CPU-s since 23:00 UTC), sysstat-collector + sadc (cgroup total 0.23 CPU-s since 23:32 UTC). The dominant standing consumers are the platform itself: **hatch daemon PID 67: +325 CPU-s/619 s = 52.5% of one core, ~680 MB RSS; hatch-execd PID 711: +65 CPU-s = 10.5%, ~57 MB RSS** (independent /proc recheck over 30 s: 50.5% / 14.4%). The rest of the load is concurrent agent exec work, not residents.

## Actions taken
- **Stopped `/tmp/conn-watch.py` (was PID 25624)** — incident watcher from 2026-11-04 23:16 UTC. Evidence it was functionally dead: its log fd pointed to a deleted file (`hatch-personal/workspace/.../connection-watch-2026-11-04.log (deleted)`); last visible log line 00:50:31 UTC, yet it kept spawning ss/ps/pgrep every 10 s (+1.43 MB rchar, +27.8 KB written to the deleted inode per 20 s). No systemd unit/launcher (PPID 1), exact-PID kill, no respawn after 15 s. Script preserved at `/tmp/conn-watch.py` — relaunch if still wanted.

## Proposals needing a ruling (nothing else was killed)
1. **RustDesk client (`.rustdesk-wrapped`)**: NOT resident and NOT supervised — verified absent from `ps` and a full `/proc` cmdline scan, no systemd unit, no cron (no cron daemon exists on this box at all). It is the nixpkgs wrapper `/nix/store/dybnmkvv6y57vy9yh6n00phnday58k67-rustdesk-1.4.5/bin/rustdesk` → `.rustdesk-wrapped` → `../app/rustdesk/rustdesk`, launched on demand only by `~/tools/rustdesk-gl/launch.sh` (nohup, PPID 1, plus Xvfb :99 + a dedicated ssh forward from `forward.sh`). Its ~45% CPU is software-GL (llvmpipe) rendering while a session runs — the risk is a client left running after the session ends. Video leg was fixed 2026-11-04 (#5509), so it does serve a function when used. Proposal: add an idle auto-exit / stop-after-session step to launch.sh rather than banning it; long-term transport replacement is #5694.
2. **quota-recorder.timer every 1 min**: each run ~5 s wall (python + Supabase curl child). Cadence is a rate change, so per standing rules this needs Drew's call — consider 5 min.
3. **Stuck exec sessions**: trees rooted at PIDs 98000 and 105080 (laptop-ssh.sh heredocs started 00:20 / 00:27 UTC) were present in all 11 snapshots at 0 CPU — hung sessions under hatch-execd holding `cat`/`head` children. Worth an execd session-reaping look.
4. Periodic bursts (keep, for the record): fleet-fetch 5.66 CPU-s per 10-min run (~0.94% of a core averaged), hatch-autocommit 2.19 CPU-s per 5-min run (~0.73%), charge-inputs-fetcher ~15–30 s wall per 15-min run.

## sysstat verdict: KEEP at current settings
Custom `sysstat-collector.service` runs `sadc -S ALL 120 5` in a loop to `~/logs/sysstat/sa-YYYY-MM-DD` (persistent, survives recycles — by design; the distro route is inert: `/etc/cron.d/sysstat` exists but there is no cron daemon, `sysstat.service`/timer are disabled, `/var/log/sysstat` is 0 bytes). Measured cost: cgroup CPUUsageNSec 0.23 CPU-s total since start (~0.003% of a core); a timed standalone sadc run used 0.006 CPU-s; sadc RSS 2.5 MB, sleeping between samples. Disk: ~5.9–7.0 KB per sample → ~5 MB/day, pruned at 14 days (~70 MB cap). That is orders of magnitude below anything that could cost a session, and its absence during the #5701 incident is exactly why forensics were missing. Reducing frequency would save ~nothing and lose incident granularity.

Full workstream report: WS-C/B in the 2026-11-04 sandbox performance program (parent session has the complete inventory table).

body:
## Problem

The public router constructors build route trees without the security middleware that the normal serve path attaches later. pkgs/id/src/web/mod.rs publicly re-exports create_router and create_router_for_app (around line 83). Their builders in pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs:487-503 omit middleware, while the private finish_router in web/mod.rs:525-545 attaches the security guard. The production cmd_serve path uses guarded routers, but an embedder calling the public constructors can expose handlers without token or origin enforcement.

## Required behavior

Make the public API safe by default: either attach the required security middleware in the public constructors, or make raw route builders private or explicitly named as unguarded and expose only guarded constructors. Avoid applying middleware twice on the cmd_serve path. Document any intentionally raw embedding seam and its required wrapper.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Integration tests call every public router constructor and prove that unauthenticated, invalid-token, and invalid-origin requests are rejected.
- [ ] The normal serve path keeps exactly one security layer and its current response behavior.
- [ ] Any retained raw route builder is not presented as the safe public API and is documented as requiring an explicit guard.
- [ ] Existing embedding callers compile against the revised API, or receive a migration note.

title: mcpx: prevent custom credential headers from following cross-origin HTTP redirects

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: priority/high

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

The HTTP client in pkgs/mcpx/internal/mcpclient/http.go applies configured custom headers to upstream requests, but its http.Client uses Go's default redirect policy (around lines 75–83 and request header construction around lines 152–155). Go strips selected standard sensitive headers on some cross-origin redirects, but it does not know that arbitrary configured headers such as X-API-Key contain credentials. A malicious or compromised upstream can return a redirect to another origin and receive the configured secret header.

This affects any MCP server/provider configured with a custom credential header and does not require the destination origin to be trusted.

## Required behavior

Do not forward configured secret/custom credential headers across an origin boundary. Prefer refusing cross-origin redirects; if same-origin redirects remain supported, compare normalized scheme/host/port and retain credentials only when the origin is identical. The redirect policy must cover every request through this HTTP transport.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An httptest upstream returns a redirect to a second server; configure a custom X-API-Key header and assert the second server never receives it.
- [ ] The selected behavior for the redirect is explicit and deterministic (reject it or return the 3xx without following).
- [ ] Same-origin redirect behavior is covered if it remains supported.
- [ ] Existing bearer/auth header behavior and normal HTTP MCP calls remain covered by targeted tests.

body:
## Problem

The reusable scheduled-agent workflow accepts an arbitrary comma-separated tasks input but silently ignores unknown names. In .github/workflows/pm-scheduled.yml, the Resolve step uses INPUT_TASKS verbatim, then sets has_bolt/has_palette/has_suggestions only for recognized names around lines 147–164. If a caller passes a typo such as "suggestion" or "boltt", every dispatch step is skipped and the workflow can still succeed while its summary reports blank task/session IDs.

This creates silent missed work for a reusable workflow whose caller is often a cron-only workflow. It differs from the intentionally documented behavior for an empty or unknown schedule: those schedules map to all tasks. The bug is an invalid explicit task list, not schedule fallback.

## Required behavior

Validate each non-empty comma-separated task token against the task steps declared in the workflow (currently bolt, palette, suggestions). Normalize surrounding whitespace. Reject unsupported or empty tokens with a non-zero exit and an error naming the token before any pm-dispatch step runs.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Valid single and multiple tasks continue to dispatch; surrounding whitespace is accepted.
- [ ] A mixed list containing one valid and one unknown task fails before dispatching any task.
- [ ] Unknown, empty, or trailing-comma tokens fail with a clear message; no silently successful no-op.
- [ ] Empty/unknown schedule inputs retain their currently documented fallback to all tasks.
- [ ] Add deterministic tests for valid lists, whitespace, unknown tokens, and schedule fallback.
