body:
# fleet-config: HOME unset/empty falls back to "." — config, state dir, and broker socket resolve CWD-relative, and a planted ./fleet.toml loads

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ a719a69907)

`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs:198-200`:

```rust
fn home_dir() -> PathBuf {
    env_path("HOME").unwrap_or_else(|| PathBuf::from("."))
}
```

`home_dir()` feeds `Config::file_path()` (lib.rs:216-224), `Config::state_dir()` (lib.rs:396-398), and `Config::broker_socket()` (lib.rs:273-291, via `resolve_under_home` / `resolve_under`). #5473 made empty XDG/FLEET_* values count as unset, but when HOME itself is unset or empty — and no absolute XDG base is set — every one of these paths becomes relative to the process's current working directory.

Probe (laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-fleetconfig-home`, real `fleet-config` crate as a path dependency; run from a scratch dir containing a planted `./.config/fleet/fleet.toml` with `[domains] planted = false`; environment explicitly scrubbed):

- `env -u HOME -u XDG_CONFIG_HOME -u XDG_STATE_HOME -u FLEET_CONFIG -u FLEET_BROKER_SOCKET`:
  - `file_path=./.config/fleet/fleet.toml`
  - `state_dir=./.local/state/fleet`
  - `broker_socket=./.cache/laptop-agent/broker.sock`
  - `Config::load()` succeeds and `domain_enabled("planted") == false` — **the planted CWD config was loaded** (an unknown domain defaults to enabled; `false` can only come from the planted file).
- `HOME=` (empty) with empty XDG bases: identical CWD-relative results, planted config loads.
- Control (`HOME=/home/user`): all paths anchor under `/home/user`, planted CWD config ignored.

Note: a process environment that happens to set absolute `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`/`XDG_STATE_HOME` masks the config/state paths (the broker socket has no XDG source and stays CWD-relative), which is presumably why this survived #5473's fix — that issue covered empty XDG values given a present HOME.

## Why it matters

- A fleet process started without HOME (cron, a minimal systemd unit, `env -i`, a container) silently reads its configuration from whoever controls its working directory — the exact planted-config hazard #5473 closed for the XDG spelling of this bug.
- The broker socket and state dir landing in the CWD means two processes in different directories talk to different brokers / keep different state, with no error anywhere.
- Siblings, same class, different crates and different wrong anchors: #5640 (atlas-search / fleet-search, literal `~` CWD dir) and #5673 (fleet-queue client, filesystem root). This one is fleet-config's own copy; neither sibling covers it.

## Acceptance criteria

- With HOME unset or empty (and no absolute XDG/FLEET override), fleet-config never resolves the config file, state dir, or broker socket relative to the CWD: it either resolves a real home (e.g. passwd entry) or fails loudly with an actionable error naming HOME.
- A planted `./.config/fleet/fleet.toml` in the working directory is never loaded in that environment.
- Pinning tests cover HOME unset and HOME empty for `file_path`, `state_dir`, and `broker_socket` (the existing #5473 tests cover empty XDG with HOME present).
- Behavior with HOME set is unchanged; existing fleet-config tests stay green.

title: Design: recommendations for ID — similar objects and similar users, across all object types

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

body:
# Design: recommendations for ID — similar objects and similar users, across all object types

Extends #5675 (querying / discovery). Related: #5677 (notes / boards / multiplayer editing), #5678 (knowledge layer), #5683 (residency & boundaries — sensitivity rules below lean on it), #5669 (staging tier — computation placement).

## The gap

#5675 covers *finding* things in ID when you know what you're looking for (search, local and remote). It does not cover *being shown* things you didn't ask for: "worlds like this one", "documents people in your position read next", "users working on similar things". Search answers intent; recommendations create discovery. Drew (2026-11-04): file this for ID across **all object types**, not just worlds, and take similar-user view metrics into account.

## Scope — all object types

The recommender treats every first-class ID object type uniformly:

- worlds, documents, notes, boards, chats / message threads, programs, and **users themselves** ("people working on similar things").
- Every recommendation is a typed edge: `(subject object, recommended object, signal, score, computed_at)` — so any surface (a world's sidebar, a document's "read next", a home/discovery feed, a board's header) renders the same underlying data.

## Signals (v1 is arithmetic, not a trained model)

1. **Item–item co-occurrence (Jaccard over interaction sets).** Two objects are similar when the sets of users who viewed / joined / edited them overlap. Jaccard similarity over those sets is the score. This is the classic collaborative signal and needs no ML infrastructure — set arithmetic over interaction logs.
2. **User–user similarity ("similar users viewed").** Users are similar when their view / interaction histories overlap (Jaccard or cosine over each user's object-interaction set). A user's recommendations then include objects that *similar users* engaged with and the user has not seen. Drew's requirement (2026-11-04): this signal is in scope from v1, not a later phase — weighted alongside item–item, not replacing it.
3. **Content-based cold start.** A new object has no interactions to overlap. Fall back to the embedding scan (the atlas machinery: dense cosine over descriptions / content) until interaction data accrues; a new *user* starts from content similarity of the objects they first touch. Cold-start edges are labeled with their signal so surfaces can present them differently if wanted.

## Sensitivity rules (hard constraints, from #5683 / #5675)

- A recommendation never crosses a sensitivity boundary: an object is only ever recommended to users who could already access it. The recommender filters by the requester's visibility *before* ranking, not after.
- Similar-user metrics are computed only over interactions with objects visible to the requester. ("People like you read X" must never leak the existence of a private X, nor that a specific user read anything.)
- No per-user reading history is ever surfaced to another user — only aggregate similarity outcomes ("similar users viewed"), never identities or histories. An opt-out from contributing interaction data to similarity computation should exist and be cheap to honor.

## Computation placement (staging tier pattern, #5669)

- Recommendations are **computed periodically into tables**, not per request: interaction aggregates accumulate in a staging DB; a batch pass computes similarity edges and promotes them into the core tier keyed by object, so reads are simple lookups.
- Recency decay: interactions age — a view from a year ago should weigh less than one from this week (decay function is an open question below).
- Recompute cost is bounded by the interaction graph's active slice, not the whole history.

## Open questions for the design pass

- Decay + diversity: pure similarity collapses into an echo of what's already popular — what diversity / serendipity term keeps suggestions non-obvious? (At minimum: cap how many recommendations one very popular object can occupy.)
- Freshness vs stability: how often to recompute so suggestions feel alive without churning between visits?
- Feedback loop accounting: when a user follows a recommendation, that interaction itself becomes similarity data — how do we keep the system from amplifying its own suggestions into fake consensus?
- Evaluation: what do we measure — follow-through rate (clicked / joined / read), and against what baseline (recency-ordered, popularity-ordered)?

## Non-goals for v1

- No trained ranking model / matrix factorization — revisit only if the arithmetic signals measurably plateau.
- No cross-server recommendation federation until #5675's remote querying settles its sensitivity story; v1 is per-server (or per-owner-data) only.

title: Init job duration: ~60s of every ~75s run is a telemetry du of nix-persist that times out and returns 'unknown'

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: status/triaged
labels.description: Triaged and routed (see agent note)

body:
## Init job duration breakdown — why every init run costs ~65–97s (measured 2026-11-04)

Follow-on from #5700 (the re-run loop, fixed). The loop is fixed, but each individual run of `~/tools/init.sh` still costs 68–97s (boot 6989413c runs: 71/68/73/97/79/75s). Drew asked where the time goes. Per-step timings from `~/logs/init.log` + `~/logs/init.jsonl`, cross-checked against `~/tools/init.sh`:

### Ranked breakdown (final SUCCESS run, 23:10:30→23:11:45 UTC, init_secs=75)

| # | Step | Seconds | Why it's slow | What would cut it |
|---|------|---------|---------------|-------------------|
| 1 | `du -sh /home/hatch/nix-persist` (deferred-telemetry block, init.sh:207) | **~60 (the full `timeout 60`)** | Recursive du over the whole persisted nix store tree (15,247 store paths) on a loaded 4-CPU box. It **times out and returns `unknown` in every recent run** — the value is never even obtained. ~80% of the entire init cost buys a telemetry field nobody reads. | Delete it, or cache it (compute at most once per boot into a state file), or move it to the detached-retry pattern the sysstat restore already uses. Any of these cuts init to ~15s. |
| 2 | Quota snapshot (`/opt/hatch/bin/subscription-status status`, init.sh:220, `timeout 30`) | ~2–10 (varies; budget 30) | Network/API call on every init run. | Cache per boot; it is telemetry, not a restore step. |
| 3 | Net check (init.sh:210–216) | ~3–4 | 1 HEAD + 3 full GET samples to cache.nixos.org through the CONNECT proxy (net_lat alone averaged 2.2s). | One sample suffices for a liveness check. |
| 4 | Snapshot counts (`ls /nix/store \| wc -l`, profile bins, init.sh:218–219) | ~1–3 | Directory listing over 15k entries. | Negligible alone; cache with #1 if kept. |
| 5 | All named restore steps combined (nix-ensure 1–2s, nix-profile-sync 1s, nix-wrapper/bash-wrapper/go-check/rust-check/services-verify 0s each) | **~4 total** | — | The actual restore work is already fast. Nothing to fix. |
| 6 | sysstat restore (init.sh:280–306) | 0s when apt lock held (deferred instantly, post-#5700 fix); **minutes when the lock is free** | Its apt-get runs inline under a 600s budget; the platform os-intent replay's own `apt-get update` fetched 41.7 MB in 10m33s at ~66 kB/s through the proxy on this boot. On a boot where init wins the lock race, init eats that cost inline. | Always detach (never run apt inline in init); the deferred-retry path already converges it. |

### The amplifier (context, fixed by #5700 but worth restating)

While FAILURES≥1 kept the boot marker unwritten, `init-ensure` re-spawned this full ~65–75s init on **every agent prelude, all day, every boot** — the ~65s cost was paid hundreds of times per day, and the log shows overlapping invocations serializing (`another init already running, exiting`). Any future FAILURES≥1 cause re-arms that herd at ~75s per prelude. Shrinking the run (items 1–3) shrinks the blast radius of any recurrence; a rate-limit on init-ensure respawns would cap it independently.

### Bottom line

Init's real work is ~4s. ~60s is a single telemetry `du` that times out and returns `unknown`. Removing/caching it (plus detaching the sysstat apt path unconditionally) takes a run from ~75s to ~10–15s.

Evidence: `~/logs/init.log` lines 15997–16016 (two full runs, step-stamped), `~/logs/init.jsonl` (424 runs), `~/tools/init.sh` lines 199–306. Filed from the 2026-11-04 laptop-session coordinator run (Phase 1 addition at Drew's request).

body:
## Root cause (verified 2026-11-04, laptop powered off — source-level, gh api reads only)

### Meta — ok-but-null masks the last good read
- The v1 file-export producer (`~/atlas/meta-quota-export/latest.json`, dev.meta.ai scrape) was retired 2026-11-03 (PR #5040); `FILE_EXPORTS` in `pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/gather-quota.ts` is empty. Its 401/session-expired state is a symptom, not the current source.
- Current source is the explicit module ask (`runMetaModule` in gather-quota.ts): OpenChamber quota module `fetchQuotaForProviderInstances("meta")` — the in-process form of `openchamber quota meta --json` — credentials asked from the OpenCode server (`GET /api/credential`), then Meta's own plan endpoint `POST https://api.meta.ai/muse-code/key` (OpenChamber `packages/web/server/lib/quota/providers/meta.js`).
- That provider returns `ok:true` with both windows present and percentages **null** on a 200 / `is_subs_active:true` response with no `subs_usage` (its documented "post-roll empty state"). That shape has been the gatherer row since after the last good read (weekly 100% @ 2026-11-03T21:00:12Z, reset 2026-11-09T00:00Z).
- Gatherer bug: `entryFromResult` (`src/quota-gather-map.ts`) maps that to a fresh `state:"ok"` entry with null windows, discarding the provider's `failureClass`/`lastSuccessAt`. #1268 retention only fires on **error** runs, so it never engages; `recordsFromEntries` emits nothing for null pct; quota-current.json publishes fresh nulls over the last good percentages, and downstream (quota-check/plan) has to carry the last good read by hand.
- OpenCode's internal `route_attempt` history is not a substitute source: it meters tokens/cost per attempt; Meta's plan percentage exists only on Meta's endpoint. OpenCode core `QuotaSnapshot.derive` is a routing gate derived from the model-plan store + route history, not a provider usage read.

### Command Code — routing-disabled, no explicit ask; plan vs balance
- `commandcode` is disabled in routing (`disabled_providers`, definitions kept). Unlike Meta, the gatherer had **no explicit ask** for `command-code`: if the provider listing drops it, there is no run at all — no error, no retention, a silently missing row. An explicit ask always works (listing filter governs listing, never a named fetch; same rule the CLI documents).
- The module's provider (`command-code.js`) returns PLAN windows (monthly derived from the $10 included-credits bucket, 5h/weekly from `windowLimits`) **and** balance windows (`purchased_credits`, `free_credits`, label-only). Per Drew's 2026-11-01 rule — Command Code reads use PLAN, not BALANCE — the gatherer must strip the balance windows so no consumer mistakes a balance for a plan reading (and, in OpenCode snapshot terms, a non-windowed credits snapshot is `balance:true, percent:null` — reading the plan kind from that snapshot is reading the wrong snapshot kind).

## Fix (patch prepared, NOT yet applied — laptop is powered off)
Patch against `gather-quota.ts` + `src/quota-gather-map.ts` + `src/model.ts` (prepared in the fleet sandbox at `/tmp/gather-quota-fix.patch` on 2026-11-04; applies cleanly with `patch -p1`):
1. `entryFromResult` preserves `failureClass`/`lastSuccessAt` and names the ok-but-null case (`no-data: provider reported ok but no window carried a percentage…`) on the entry.
2. New `finalizeRun` in the gatherer downgrades any ok-but-no-measured-window run to an **error** run carrying that reason, so #1268 retention replaces it with last-known rows stamped `retainedFromFailedTick` — stale-with-reason in quota-current.json + heartbeat, never fresh nulls. (CNY-label measurements, e.g. DeepSeek #1052, count as measured and do not degrade.)
3. New `runCommandCodeModule` explicit ask with Meta's exactly-one-run discipline, plus `keepCommandCodePlanWindows` stripping `purchased_credits`/`free_credits` balance windows from listed and explicit runs alike (raw payload stays on `entry.usage`).

## Verification still owed (laptop off at time of writing)
- Apply the patch in a laptop worktree of `~/git/code`, run the gatherer once, and verify with two independent reads of `~/.local/state/pm-aggregator/quota-current.json` (deployed path per aggregator layout) that Meta shows a measured window or a retained stale row with the no-data reason, and Command Code shows a fresh plan read (monthly/weekly/5h, no balance windows).
- Related: #4889 (usage snapshot append broken on laptop, bad path in the snapshot writer) is a separate defect in the same tick's output path.

Cross-link: summary also posted on #1163 (the Claude-adapter issue this investigation was routed through; the 2026-11-04 Claude ruling there is unaffected).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A Meta quota read that returns ok-but-null no longer masks the last good read; the gatherer surfaces an explicit unknown/stale state instead.
- [ ] Command Code plan state is handled explicitly (plan-on vs plan-off), not inferred from a null payload.
- [ ] The null-payload case is covered by a test or a reproducible fixture in the gatherer.

labels.name: priority/normal

body:
## Quota recorder: move the Supabase write to the laptop (design + recommendation)

### Current state (verified 2026-11-04)

- The sandbox quota recorder runs from systemd units installed by `~/tools/quota-recorder/` (its timer + service). Like every `/etc/systemd/system` unit, **they vanish on every sandbox recycle** and must be reinstalled — today that reinstall is a manual/cron-assisted step (the 2026-11-04 15:08 boot check found them missing again post-recycle and reinstalled them from `~/tools/quota-recorder/`, after which ticks resumed with Supabase acks).
- The recorder writes usage snapshots to Supabase (muse-dev2) from the sandbox, which means the sandbox side holds/uses the Supabase write path directly.
- Recycles are frequent (six boots on 2026-11-04 alone), so "reinstall after recycle" is a recurring failure surface, and a missed reinstall = a silent gap in the quota record the burn plan depends on.

### Proposal (Drew's question, 2026-11-04)

Split the recorder the same way the queue and secrets already work:

- **Sandbox side: record-only.** A small local writer appends quota observations to a local spool (JSONL under `~/tools/quota-recorder/` state or `~/.local/state/quota-recorder/`). No Supabase credentials, no network write on the sandbox. Survives recycles by construction (the spool lives in `/home/hatch`, which persists).
- **Ship via the fleet proxy.** Batches move sandbox → laptop through the existing fleet session proxy, the same transport every other broker call uses.
- **Laptop side: broker-owned ingest.** A laptop endpoint (a `fleet serve` role alongside queue-broker :4801 / secrets-broker :4800, or an ingest route on an existing broker) owns the Supabase connection and performs the insert — credentials live only on the laptop, exactly like the queue-broker holding the Supabase credentials for queue operations today.
- **Ack + trim:** the laptop acks batch ids; the sandbox trims its spool only on ack. A laptop-off window (e.g. 2026-11-04 evening, laptop powered down) becomes a growing local spool, not lost data — recording continues and ships when the laptop returns.

### Evaluation vs. status quo

| | Status quo (sandbox units → Supabase direct) | Proposed (spool → proxy → laptop broker) |
|---|---|---|
| Survives recycle | No — units vanish; reinstall is a step that can be missed | Yes — no unit needed for recording; shipper can be an init-ensure-style prelude check or a tiny timer reinstalled by the same mechanism as other fleet units |
| Credentials on sandbox | Yes (Supabase write path) | No — laptop-only, matching the queue/secrets pattern |
| Laptop off | Recorder still writes (Supabase is remote) | Recording continues to spool; ingest pauses; no loss |
| Failure visibility | Missing ticks noticed by the boot check | Spool depth + last-ack age are directly measurable; alert on spool age |
| New machinery | — | One laptop ingest endpoint + batch/ack protocol (small; mirrors trip-log ingest follow-on on #5343) |

### Recommendation

**Adopt the proposal.** The deciding factors: the recycle-vanish reinstall already failed once today and will keep failing on the same cadence; the credential placement matches the fleet's established broker pattern; and the spool design converts the laptop-off case from data loss risk into mere delay. The one real cost — ingest pauses while the laptop is off — is acceptable because the quota data is consumed on planning timescales (the burn plan reads snapshots, and the gatherer already tolerates staleness by design: a stale read never idles a pool).

### Acceptance / next steps

1. Local spool writer on the sandbox replacing the direct-write recorder; format = the existing snapshot payload, one JSON object per line, batch id per ship.
2. Laptop ingest endpoint with ack; idempotent on batch id (replays after a crash are expected).
3. Shipper on the sandbox (fleet-proxy transport) with spool trim-on-ack and a last-ack watermark.
4. Boot check updated: instead of "reinstall the units," it verifies spool freshness + last ack; a stale ack surfaces like today's missing-timer finding.
5. Old sandbox units retired once the new path has produced a week of clean acks.

Related: #2072 (unified quota attribution/observability) covers the read/attribution side; this issue is only about the recorder write path and where the Supabase connection lives.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The quota recorder runs on the sandbox and ships records via the fleet proxy to ingestion at a laptop broker, per the design in this issue.
- [ ] The retired Supabase path is removed or explicitly disabled, with no silent dual-writing.
- [ ] Recorded quota data matches the previous recorder's output for the same inputs (parity spot-check recorded on the issue).

title: id: design: ID selective sharing and foreign data-store adapters v1

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Summary

Two related capabilities for ID's data layer:

1. **Selective sharing** — an ID server should be able to share *subsets* of its data with peers, instead of the all-or-nothing choice of full replication or no sharing.
2. **Foreign data-store adapters** — ID should be able to expose and query data that does not live in its native REDB store: public Turso databases exposed through ID, and remote database connections to browser IndexedDB, Postgres (via its HTTP interfaces), and Turso/libsql (HTTP protocol) — plus one-shot conversions such as Redis→SQLite export and "query a Redis instance, get a SQLite result."

Relates: #2036 (ID messaging/relay protocol — sharing grants ride on ID identity/relay), #2048 (ID data/zettelkasten layer — selective sharing governs what of that data moves between servers).

## Part A — Selective sharing

### Grants model

- Grant unit: per-object and per-collection grants as the two first-class granularities; per-table/per-database grants as coarse shorthand that expands to collections.
- Grant dimensions: who (identity/key, group, or public), what (objects/collections), which operations (read, read+subscribe to updates, write/append where the data model allows), and duration (standing vs. expiring vs. one-shot snapshot).
- Revocation: how revoking a grant interacts with data already replicated to the peer (state the honest boundary: revocation stops future sync/access via ID; it cannot un-copy bytes the peer already holds in plaintext — encrypted shares may do better, see below).
- Delegation: can a grantee re-share? Default no; any delegation must be explicit, attenuated (never broader than the original grant), and visible to the owner.

### Partial replication

- A peer holding a grant replicates only the granted subset: initial snapshot of the subset + ongoing updates scoped to it, without receiving (or being able to enumerate) ungranted objects.
- Existence privacy: partial replication must not leak the shape of what was withheld — counts, IDs, or metadata of ungranted objects are not exposed to the peer.
- Consistency: how partial replicas handle objects that reference ungranted objects (dangling references, redacted placeholders, or grant closure over references — pick per data type, state the rule).
- Storage/quotas on the receiving side: a peer can cap accepted share size, pause, or drop a share.

### Encrypted shares

- Option for shares that remain encrypted at the peer (peer stores/forwards but cannot read), vs. readable shares — with the key-distribution story for each.
- Interaction with sensitivity classification and remote-query filtering (see the ID query design): grants and classification must compose, not contradict.

### Public data through ID

- Exposing a **public Turso database through ID**: an owner publishes a database (or a view of one) as a public ID share — discoverable, queryable/replicable by anyone, with the owner able to unpublish.
- Public shares need rate limits, size limits, and a clear "this is world-readable" confirmation in the UX; nothing becomes public as a side effect of a private grant.

## Part B — Foreign data-store adapters

General adapter contract (applies to every adapter below): how a foreign store is named/addressed in ID, what schema/type mapping is promised, whether the adapter is live (queries pass through) or materialized (data copied into ID/REDB or SQLite), read-only vs. writable, credential handling (never in ID data itself; referenced, not stored), and error/latency behavior when the foreign store is slow or gone.

### B1. Browser IndexedDB adapter

- Connect ID to a browser's IndexedDB: expose selected object stores as ID-queryable data, and/or materialize them into ID.
- Browser constraints stated plainly: the tab/extension must be alive for live access; origin scoping; structured-clone types vs. ID types mapping.

### B2. Postgres via HTTP interfaces

- Adapter for Postgres reached through its HTTP-facing interfaces (e.g. PostgREST-style or HTTP query endpoints) rather than the native wire protocol — chosen so it works from constrained environments (browsers, sandboxes, HTTP-only egress).
- Query translation scope: which ID query shapes translate, which are refused rather than silently degraded.

### B3. Turso / libsql HTTP protocol adapter

- Adapter speaking the libsql/Turso HTTP protocol: remote Turso databases as first-class ID data sources; also the mechanism behind "public Turso database exposed through ID" (Part A).
- Auth tokens handling, batch/transaction semantics over HTTP, and local materialization/caching options.

### B4. Redis → SQLite export

- One-shot and repeatable export: snapshot a Redis instance (keyspace scan, per-type mapping: strings/hashes/lists/sets/zsets → tables/rows) into a SQLite database file the user can keep, query, and import into ID.
- Type-mapping rules and lossy corners (expiry/TTL, ordering, huge keys) documented in the export report.

### B5. Query a Redis instance, get a SQLite result

- Ad-hoc form of B4: run a query/selection against a live Redis instance and receive the result *as* a SQLite database (file or ID-hosted), shaped by the query — for inspection, joins against ID data, and handing structured results to tools that speak SQL but not Redis.
- Read-only against Redis by definition; no mutation path smuggled in.

## Non-goals (v1)

- Full bidirectional sync with arbitrary foreign stores (adapters are read/materialize-first unless a follow-on design says otherwise).
- Replacing REDB as ID's native store.
- Sharing UX polish — this design covers the model, protocol, and safety boundaries; UI comes later.

## Acceptance for this design

A follow-on reader can split Part A and each adapter (B1–B5) into their own design tickets (see sketch) without re-deciding the grants model, existence-privacy rule, or the adapter contract.

## Decomposition sketch

1. Design: selective-sharing grants model (units, operations, expiry, revocation, delegation).
2. Design: partial replication protocol (subset snapshot + scoped updates, existence privacy, dangling references).
3. Design: encrypted shares & key distribution; composition with sensitivity classification.
4. Design: public shares through ID, incl. public Turso databases (discovery, limits, unpublish).
5. Design: foreign adapter contract (addressing, type mapping, live vs. materialized, credentials).
6. Design: IndexedDB adapter (browser constraints, origin scoping).
7. Design: Postgres-over-HTTP adapter (query translation scope).
8. Design: Turso/libsql HTTP adapter.
9. Design: Redis→SQLite export + query-Redis-get-SQLite (type mapping, lossy corners).

## Open questions

- Grant granularity floor: is per-object enough, or do we need per-field/redacted-field grants in v1?
- Does revocation of an encrypted share give real cryptographic take-back, and is that a v1 promise or a later one?
- Existence privacy vs. useful errors: how does a peer distinguish "no such object" from "not granted" — or must it not be able to?
- Which HTTP interface is canonical for Postgres, and what do we do where none exists?
- Are adapters live-only, materialize-only, or both per adapter — and who decides (owner config vs. query hint)?
- Public Turso exposure: is the published artifact the live DB, a snapshot, or a replicated copy — and who pays its query costs?
- Redis export: how are non-UTF8/binary values and key expiry represented in SQLite output?

title: atlas-search(fleet-search): HOME unset/empty resolves state/config/token paths relative to the CWD (literal ~ dir)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

labels.description: pkgs/atlas-search (Atlas search service + atlas-embed)

body:
## Problem

In atlas-search (and its fleet-search port), every home-directory helper treats a missing `HOME` as the literal relative path `~`, and an empty `HOME` as the empty path — so state/config/token paths resolve **relative to the current working directory** instead of failing or resolving to the user's home.

The helper shape, copied in at least six places:

```rust
std::env::var_os("HOME").map(PathBuf::from).unwrap_or_else(|| PathBuf::from("~"))
```

- `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-search/src/server.rs:202` — `default_service_config_path()` (the `init`/`serve` service config, which contains the client bearer tokens)
- `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-search/src/fetch_model.rs:41` — `state_root()` / `model_dir()` (fetch-model provisioning + lock)
- `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-search/src/service.rs:50` — `home_dir()` (client token config `~/.config/atlas-search/client.json`)
- `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-search/src/main.rs:248` — `home_dir()` (`default_db_path()`, `resolve_model_dir()`, `resolve_ort_lib()`)
- `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-core/src/turso.rs:210` — `home()` (Turso token cache `~/.cache/atlas-search/turso-token.json`)
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-search/src/client.rs:53` — `home_dir()` (serving-host marker + the same client-token path, ported in fleet step 5)

## Verified (this run, laptop, real debug binary, probe `~/git/fleet/probe-atlas-home`)

In a scratch working directory:

- `env -u HOME atlas-search init` → exit 0, prints `wrote service config ~/.local/state/atlas-search/service.json`, and actually creates `./~/.local/state/atlas-search/service.json` under the CWD.
- `HOME= atlas-search init` → exit 0, prints `wrote service config .local/state/atlas-search/service.json`, and creates `./.local/state/atlas-search/service.json` under the CWD.

Current main `beaad887b0` contains the identical helpers at the lines above.

## Why it matters

- `init` reports success while writing the service config — which holds freshly generated client bearer tokens (0600) — into whatever directory the caller happened to be in (potentially a git checkout or shared dir), where a later `serve`/client run with a normal `HOME` will never find it. The service silently appears unconfigured.
- The same CWD-relative drift hits the model snapshot dir, the Turso token cache, and the fleet-search serving-host seat marker, so seat detection and token resolution can silently disagree with the service.
- Contrast inside this repo: `pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs:999` treats a missing `HOME` as a hard error with context (`no HOME for ~/.ssh/known_hosts; pass --ssh-host-key`), and fleet-config was fixed for the empty-env half of this class in #5473. Atlas/fleet-search never got either half.

## Acceptance criteria

- An empty `HOME` is treated as unset at every site above (atlas-search, atlas-core, fleet-search).
- With `HOME` unset/empty, no atlas-search or fleet-search verb creates or reads a path under `./~` or `./.local` / `./.config` / `./.cache`: it either fails loudly naming `HOME`, or resolves the real home directory another way (e.g. passwd entry) — one consistent rule, shared where practical instead of six copies.
- Regression tests pin both shapes (unset and empty) for at least the service-config path and the fleet-search serving-host marker.
- Normal behavior is unchanged when `HOME` is set: `init` writes `~/.local/state/atlas-search/service.json`, and existing path-resolution tests stay green.

body:
## What happened

When the popesdrew OpenCode Go instance was provisioned on 2026-11-03 (17:13:45Z), its console-login OAuth credential was stored in the laptop credential store under integration_id `opencode` instead of `opencode-go.popesdrew`. The route proxy matches credentials by exact leaf provider id (`WHERE integration_id = <leaf provider id> AND active = 1`), so every attempt on `opencode-go.popesdrew` failed with "no credential for provider opencode-go.popesdrew":

- 23 route attempts between 2026-11-03T18:04Z and 2026-11-04T09:00Z, all failing over to other leaves.
- The account sat at 0% usage for ~16 hours while the weighted pool config (PR #5112, drewrypope 2 : popesdrew 1) was correct as deployed — the failure was invisible to quota reporting because the account simply never served.
- Compounding: the known-exhausted gate (#5295) kept the already-walled drewrypope account as the last-resort candidate when no credentialed candidate survived.

Fixed operationally on 2026-11-04: a copy of the credential was inserted under the correct key (`opencode-go.popesdrew`, active=1; original `opencode` row untouched), and the account immediately served 118 consecutive successful workhorse attempts, independently confirmed in the session message store.

## The process gap

Provisioning a new Go instance currently ends at "rows created." Nothing asserts the instance can actually serve before it joins a weighted pool.

## What's owed

Instance registration for a new `opencode-go.*` leaf must assert, before the instance is seated in any pool:

1. A credential row exists under the **exact** instance integration_id (not the bare `opencode` console-login key), active=1.
2. A **successful route_attempt** for that leaf is recorded in the proxy ledger after seating (a real completion, not just a config reference).
3. If either assertion fails, provisioning reports the instance as not-seated and the pool config change does not merge/deploy until it passes.

Watch item from the fix: if the fork's auth later rotates the token under the original `opencode` row, the copied row could diverge (the same pattern drewrypope runs on) — the assertion in (2) is what would catch that too, if run periodically for existing instances.

Related: PR #5112 (weighted Go pool), code#5295 (known-exhausted gate), the 2026-11-04 popesdrew 0% root-cause investigation.

## Acceptance criteria

- Instance registration for a new `opencode-go.*` leaf asserts, before the instance is seated in any pool, that a credential row exists under the exact instance integration_id (not the bare `opencode` key) with active=1; registration fails loudly when the row is missing.
- A successful route_attempt for the leaf is recorded in the proxy ledger after seating; its absence within a bounded window blocks seating or raises an alert.
- A regression test or registration-check entry covers the popesdrew failure shape (credential stored under the bare console-login key while the pool config was correct).

body:
## What happened

Commit e8b4cdc75 ("rewire OpenClaw to the server facade and retire the route proxy (opencode#1153)", landed 2026-11-04 10:57 CST) deleted `bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs` + `bin/opencode-route-proxy-start.sh` and removed the `opencode-route-proxy.service` definition from `home/common/default.nix`. The unit was stopped at 10:54 CST and the files were removed from the live deploy dir (`~/code/bin`).

But the deployed OpenCode config still routes through that proxy: `~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.jsonc` (and the repo's `.opencode/opencode.jsonc`) still carry 52 `opencode-route` references, and every dispatched session runs model `opencode-route/workhorse` against `127.0.0.1:18750`. The opencode#1146 server-façade cutover that was supposed to make the standalone proxy unnecessary has NOT landed in the deployed config.

## Impact

- Every `opencode-route/*` session failed from 10:54 CST onward (surfaced as provider.auth 401s).
- The #3232 receipt-validation audit session burned all 3 of its monitor resume attempts against the dead route and was marked failed-final, even though all four of its gates had closed and the audit itself is still owed (issue closed via PR #5576; the audit deliverable is outstanding).
- Any other workhorse-tier work dispatched in that window hit the same wall.

## Stopgap applied (2026-11-04 ~12:03 CST, laptop only, no repo change)

- Restored `bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs`, `bin/opencode-route-proxy-start.sh`, and the test file into `~/code/bin` from `e8b4cdc75^` (md5-verified byte-identical; untracked files in that checkout).
- Installed a hand-placed user unit `~/.config/systemd/user/opencode-route-proxy.service` replicating the retired nix unit (port 18750, Restart=always), enabled and started it.
- Verified: unit active, listening on 18750, `/health` ok, `/v1/models` serves the tier list, and a live `scout` completion returned HTTP 200 end-to-end. (Workhorse/specialist currently return honest quota 429/502s — the Go Flash carriers are in a trough until popesdrew's 5h reset at 18:47Z; drewrypope weekly is walled until Nov 9. That part is quota, not plumbing.)
- The #3232 session has been resumed with full context.

## What's owed

1. **A retirement gate**: never retire a provider door (files, unit, or port) while the deployed config still references it. The retirement check must grep the deployed `opencode.jsonc` (and the session dispatch state) for the provider id before removing anything.
2. **A durable home for the proxy until the cutover actually lands**: either restore the files + unit in the repo/home config until opencode#1154's cutover changes the deployed config, or formally adopt the hand-placed user unit as the interim mechanism and record it. The stopgap above is deliberately out-of-band and should not silently become permanent.
3. **Remove the stopgap when the façade cutover lands** in the deployed config (opencode-route references gone from the deployed jsonc), and close this issue with that evidence.

Related: opencode#1146 (façade program), opencode#1153 (the retirement), opencode#1154 (cutover), code#5295 (known-exhausted gate), code#3232 (the audit that was blocked).

## Acceptance criteria

- A retirement gate exists: removing a route/proxy component fails or blocks while deployed config or live session routing still references it (checked against the `opencode-route` reference counts in `~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.jsonc` and the repo `.opencode/opencode.jsonc`).
- For the opencode-route retirement specifically, the end state is one of: deployed config migrated to the server façade (the opencode#1146 cutover), or the proxy remains deployed as a repo-managed unit — the hand-placed stopgap unit is not the final state.
- The outstanding #3232 receipt-validation audit deliverable (its monitor attempts were burned against the dead route) is re-run or explicitly re-filed.

Residual scope from #5433, split out when step 5 landed the search **client** surface (PR #5601, merged `18f0aa1a6`): `fleet search` / `get-chunk` now run over the live Atlas service contract, but the service itself still runs as the standalone atlas-search artifact.

## What remains

- Rehome the atlas-search bin crate's **serve half** as the fleet-search serve role, so `fleet serve search` runs the Atlas service (one shared embedder per process, read-only Turso token — the service stays mechanically incapable of production writes, the async job queue, per-client recovery listing, dedupe keyed by the effective request). atlas-core / atlas-embed / atlas-proto stay untouched and consumed as-is.
- Re-point the atlas user unit at `fleet serve search`. The flip must stay reversible to the standalone atlas-search artifact in a single re-point (the standalone name keeps working via the argv0 map from the same workspace).
- Gates before the flip: `fleet serve search` passes the #5354 protocol gates under the fleet binary; the atlas release rule applies — any fleet release touching the search domain re-runs the atlas gates (embedder bit-parity, golden parity) before the tag.

## Why this is separate

Step 5's gate was the #5350 step-6 cutover; destabilizing a just-landed service by rehousing its server in the same step that added its client surface is exactly what the epic's sequencing (§7: search joins *last, at a natural seam*) argues against. The client surface shipped and is proven live (parity + ceiling canary on #5433); the serve rehome is a packaging move with its own risk profile and should be scheduled on its own evidence.

title: atlas-search: build-provenance hardening — Gate A parity must catch a divergent embedder build under the same FOD hash
body:
## Provenance of this issue — read first

This issue exists to examine a claim, not to report a confirmed defect.

During Atlas step 6 (#5356, Gate B + cutover), a mid-run relayed report claimed the embed builds are **bimodal under one FOD hash**: one machine's build embedding ~+0.88% uniformly "hot", another's ~−30% "cold", with both builds passing the startup assertion. That claim **does not appear in step 6's final report** and is **UNVERIFIED**. It may be a misread relay, a scratch-instance artifact, or real; nobody has reproduced it.

What IS verified, from step 6's completed work:

- Gate B's fresh paired run produced **byte-identical top-10 lists on 309/309 questions** (Rust packaged build vs the Python reference, production corpus).
- The cutover battery passed **cross-machine**: via-service ≡ standalone results, and the sensitivity-ceiling canary behaved correctly.
- Conclusion from evidence: the **currently deployed builds are consistent**. There is no known live defect.

## Why file it anyway

If the claim were true, it would be exactly the failure Gate A (embedder parity, #5351) exists to catch — and it would have slipped past it: two divergent embedder builds sharing one fixed-output-derivation hash, both green at startup, silently returning different rankings depending on which machine built or served the closure. Atlas step 7 should not dispatch on an unexamined provenance claim of that shape.

## Asks

1. **Verify or refute the bimodality claim** with a two-builder experiment: build the atlas-search closure on two machines, embed a fixed probe set with each build, and compare against the pinned reference embeddings within a tight cosine tolerance. Record the numbers either way.
2. **If real:** strengthen Gate A (the startup/reference parity check) so a divergent build fails loud instead of passing, and separate per-machine build outputs so divergent artifacts cannot share one FOD hash.
3. **Either way:** record the verdict on this issue and on epic #5350, so step 7's dispatch rests on an examined claim.

## Severity

Hardening / pre-step-7 gate. Not a live defect; no user-facing impact is known or claimed.

title: atlas-search: via-service client should honor proxy env (ureq Proxy::try_from_env)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

body:
Found during the step-6 cutover (#5356): the via-service client in `crates/atlas-search/src/service.rs` builds its ureq agent with timeouts only — no proxy support. On hosts that reach the tailnet only through an HTTP CONNECT proxy (the sandbox: its tailnet tunnel proxy is the same egress host on port 3130), `ATLAS_SEARCH_URL=http://amd-6.raptor-pumpkinseed.ts.net:18760` is therefore unreachable directly: the connect times out and the CLI falls back to standalone. The fallback is loud and correct (verified live — warning on stderr, standalone results identical), so this is a capability gap, not a correctness bug.

Interim state (working, shipped in the cutover): the sandbox's `atlas-search` wrapper asks the shared laptop-ssh control connection to forward loopback:18760 to the laptop and points `ATLAS_SEARCH_URL` at `http://127.0.0.1:18760`. That works (1.7s dedupe-class responses vs ~9.5 min for a standalone hybrid search over the proxy path), but it couples the CLI to the SSH tunnel.

Ask: build the client agent with proxy-from-environment support (ureq 3: `Proxy::try_from_env` or equivalent, honoring HTTPS_PROXY/http_proxy + NO_PROXY), with a test that runs the client against a stub CONNECT proxy. Then the sandbox wrapper reduces to setting `ATLAS_SEARCH_VIA=service` + `ATLAS_SEARCH_URL`, and any other proxied host (codespaces, CI) gets the same path for free.

Note the related asymmetry: the sandbox's egress proxy (port 3128) cannot complete TLS to `tailscale serve --https` endpoints, while the tailnet tunnel proxy (3130) reaches the fleet-standard `tailscale serve --tcp` forwards — the atlas serve mapping is therefore the tcp form. Proxy support in the client makes both forms usable from the sandbox.

Refs #5356, epic #5350.

```
pm-git-sync: FAIL /home/user/git/code working tree is dirty — not pulling. Dirty paths:
?? .cache/
```

## Suggested fixes (any one)

- Add `.cache/` to the repo `.gitignore`, or
- point mcpx's cache at the XDG cache dir when run from the checkout, or
- teach pm-git-sync to ignore this specific path.

## Acceptance criteria
- The primary laptop clone no longer sits dirty solely because of mcpx in-tree `.cache/` writes (one route chosen and recorded: .gitignore, XDG cache relocation, or a pm-git-sync carve-out)

- pm-git-sync's protective dirty-tree refusal is not weakened for real changes

body:
## Symptom

RustDesk login to the laptop (amd-6) now **succeeds**, but the session never delivers video: the client sits at "Connecting…" and then fails with **"Connection error: Timeout"**. Zero PipeWire frames ever flow.

## What is proven working (not the problem)

- **Credentials**: the password reset is complete — Bitwarden `rustdesk.amd-6-password` is now **accepted** by the host (config field 118 chars, prefix `01`; RustDesk service active on :21118). This is **not** a credential issue.
- **Route / transport**: the connection reaches the host and authenticates; this is **not** a routing issue.
- **Client rendering**: the sandbox client's GL/render path was already fixed separately (llvmpipe, direct rendering); this is **not** a client-render issue.

## Evidence (2026-11-04 reset run)

- Post-auth, the session reaches the host's screen-share picker.
- The picker was automated once end-to-end (ydotool + hyprctl geometry on `hyprland-share-picker`; **"Remember this choice" ticked**) and the share was **granted**.
- Despite the granted share, **zero PipeWire frames** flow: client shows "Connecting…" → "Connection error: Timeout".
- Host log shows the connection closed on **Timeout after encoder selection (AV1)** with no frames delivered.

Evidence files:

- `~/workspace/rd-work/rd-portal3.jpg` — live screenshot of the host screen-share picker
- `client-timeout-error.png` (sandbox) — client-side timeout error

## Diagnosis

The stall is in **ScreenCast Start / PipeWire negotiation** on the laptop's Hyprland/portal stack: authentication and share consent complete, encoder selection (AV1) completes, but the PipeWire stream never starts producing frames. RustDesk's own UI flags Wayland capture as experimental.

## Family / cross-link

Same family as #5415 (KRdp dead under Hyprland — its KWallet user store never loads): the laptop's remote-desktop capture paths are rotting under the Hyprland session in different places. #5415 explicitly scoped RustDesk out ("RustDesk is the other fallback … out of scope here"); this issue is that separate failure.

## Acceptance

- A RustDesk session from the sandbox client **displays the laptop desktop** (frames actually flowing, not just auth + consent), **or**
- a documented switch of the laptop's remote-desktop path to a working capture stack, with the RustDesk/Hyprland-PipeWire stall recorded as the reason.

title: opencode-route/workhorse sometimes dispatches to schema-rejecting antigravity-direct

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

body:
## Observed

During the Nov 4, 2026 OpenCode claimant fire for #3026, two Workhorse sessions resolved to `antigravity-direct/claude-sonnet-5-5` and failed immediately after prompt delivery with `provider.invalid-request`:

> `tools.5.custom.input_schema: JSON schema is invalid. It must match JSON Schema draft 2020-12.`

The affected queue tasks were 1484 and 8706. Both sessions remain bound to their tasks and have a terminal failed outcome; no task work began. Other sessions from the same Workhorse route resolved to OpenAI and OpenCode Go models and continued normally.

## Expected

A Workhorse launch should either avoid incompatible tool schemas for this provider/model or fail over to a compatible route before leaving an already-bound queue task stranded.

## Impact

Repeated failures can leave claimed tasks bound to failed sessions. The claimant correctly does not relaunch over a bound session, so these need explicit recovery/watchdog handling.

## Investigation

Check which tool contributes the rejected custom input schema, whether it conforms to JSON Schema 2020-12, and whether the Antigravity provider path supports it. Then determine whether route eligibility or failover should exclude this provider/model for the affected tool set.

## Problem

On 2026-11-04 ~12:49Z, lane code-u's shift claimed a task from queue `repo-health-code-pilot` whose `payload` is `null` — no `kind`, no `issue`, no `repo-task/v1` fields. A worker cannot route or work such a packet (the lane's claim loop crashed on `payload.get("kind")` with `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'get'`), and the claim's task id is not recoverable afterwards from the helper's own views:

- `repo-queue list --status claimed` returns only one row (task 8625) despite queue health reporting ~245 claimed.

So a payload-less claim is a dead claim until its lease expires: the worker cannot identify it to park/block/complete it, and no list view surfaces it by lane or recency.

## Acceptance

- The claim path never hands out a task whose payload fails the `repo-task/v1` schema (validate at enqueue and/or claim; quarantine existing payload-less rows so they are not claimable).
- `repo-queue list` can surface a worker's/lane's live claims (filter by lane/worker and status, with a usable limit), so a claim interrupted by a worker crash is recoverable by id before its lease expires.

## Evidence

- Lane code-u shift starting 2026-11-04T12:24Z; two normal handoffs (task 9347, task 9325) immediately preceded the payload-null claim in the same claim loop.
- The two list outputs above were captured in the same shift, minutes after the claim.

Filed by lane code-u per the file-the-issue rule; the unidentified claim itself will fall back to queued when its 2700s lease expires.

title: nixos: declare linger for the laptop user so user services start at boot

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

body:
## State found (2026-11-04, verified on amd-6)

`loginctl show-user user -p Linger` returns **Linger=yes** (and `/var/lib/systemd/linger/user` exists), so systemd user services on the laptop already start at boot without a login. But that state is **imperative** — set by hand (believed around 2026-10-23, for RustDesk) — and is not declared anywhere in this repo. A reinstall or a config rebuild from a tree that does not know about it would silently lose it, and the failure mode (user services simply not running until someone logs in) is exactly the kind that goes unnoticed.

## Ask

Declare it in the laptop's NixOS configuration in this repo:

```nix
users.users.<name>.linger = true;
```

This should ride the **next natural config change** — no dedicated switch just for this. While the imperative state holds, nothing is broken.

## Boundary worth recording

Linger starts the user manager at boot; it does **not** unlock the GNOME keyring. Keyring-held credentials still require a graphical login — observed 2026-11-04: after the 05:47 reboot, the laptop `gh` CLI credential was dead until a desktop login, even with linger on. Fleet services must keep using file-based secrets (sops / Bitwarden), never the keyring, so they are boot-independent.

title: id(web): .txt save drops footnote_reference atoms — PR #3274 documented the gap, no follow-up filed

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Finding

`.txt` save in the id web editor silently drops every `footnote_reference` atom. PR #3274 (https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/3274, commit f210bff6ba, merged 2026-11-01 as 2c3710942a) fixed the sibling image-atom loss for #1491 and documented this remainder in the code itself, but no follow-up issue was ever filed:

- The PR added this doc comment on `extract_plain_text` in `pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs`: "Known remaining gap: `footnote_reference` atoms are not yet rendered — they contribute nothing; that is explicitly out of scope for the #1491 fix."
- Verified on current main (fd961f654672): the same comment is still at `routes.rs:2406`, and `extract_inline_text` (`routes.rs:2468`) handles only `text`, `hard_break`, and `image`; every other inline node is recursed into via its `content` array.
- A `footnote_reference` is a leaf atom with no `content` — its payload is `attrs.label` (node shape `{"type": "footnote_reference", "attrs": {"label": "1"}}`, see `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs` footnote tests) — so the recursion contributes an empty string and the reference vanishes.

## Why it matters

This is the same loss class #1306/#1491 established as a bug for `.txt` save ("loss-free extraction"): a document whose footnotes were authored or opened in the editor saves to plain text with the `[^1]` markers gone, while the footnote *definition* text survives (definition blocks are containers and are recursed into) — leaving orphaned note text with nothing in the body pointing at it. The gap is acknowledged in the source but untracked, so nothing will ever schedule the fix.

## Acceptance criteria

- `extract_inline_text` (or its caller) renders a `footnote_reference` atom as `[^<label>]` — the same marker the markdown codec emits — at its inline position, using the atom's `attrs.label` verbatim when non-empty.
- New tests in `pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs` pin: a footnote reference between text runs in a paragraph, a reference inside a recursive container (list item or blockquote), and the missing/empty-label case (contributes nothing, does not panic).
- Existing `extract_plain_text` / routes tests still pass; footnote_definition handling is unchanged.

Found by pr-diff-review lane B reviewing PR #3274 (batch 3253–3276, 2026-11-04). Dedupe: searches for `footnote_reference`, `extract_plain_text`, and open footnote issues return only #1347 (richSchema node coverage), #1491 (images, closed by #3274), #945/#1565/#1031 (markdown save path, different defect), and open #1004/#1376 (link-reference definitions / alert blockquotes) — none covers `.txt` extraction dropping footnote references.

title: opencode-route-proxy: per-leg first-response timeout — shed transport-timeout legs inside the client window (#4370b)

labels.name: kind/bug

body:
# opencode-route-proxy: per-leg first-response timeout — shed transport-timeout legs inside the client window (#4370 acceptance (b))

Implementation slice scoped by triage task 8950 (lane W, 2026-11-04) extending #3325 leg-shedding to the #4370 death classes. Findings and full evidence are on #3325 (task 8950 comment) and #4370.

## Problem (verified at main, blob 70f01618, bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs, 1095 lines)

- `callLeaf`'s fetch passes only the shared walk signal — there is no per-leg timeout. A hung/slow leg holds the walk; the only cap is the whole-walk `TIMEOUT_MS` (line 62, default 1,200,000 ms).
- `runCompletion` does fall through on per-leaf transport errors, but only while the signal is not aborted; the OpenCode client's ~10 s no-output window (`provider.transport` "No response output within 10000ms", #4370) kills the session first, and a client abort is terminal in the walk.
- Net effect: a transport-timeout leg is never shed in time — ~30 fleet sessions died this way on 2026-11-01 (#4370).

## Scope

- Per-leaf first-response (headers) timeout in `bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs`, configurable via env in the existing `OPENCODE_ROUTE_PROXY_*` pattern, sized well under the client no-output window; on timeout, record the attempt (outcome `timeout`, tag `Transport`, `failedOverTo` set) and continue the walk.
- Proxy tests: hung first leg sheds to a live second leg inside the timeout; ledger row written.
- Verify whether the client's ~10 s provider.transport window is configurable for proxied routes; if the proxy-side fix cannot beat it, record that on #4370 with the exact client setting named.

Out of scope: in-stream pre-content error shedding (task 8932, #3325), mid-stream fallthrough, route redesign.

## Acceptance criteria

- A transport-timeout leg is shed like a quota-exhausted leg: walk continues, session completes on a live leg.
- Per-leg timeout configurable + documented next to `TIMEOUT_MS`; responding legs unchanged.
- #4370 acceptance (b) satisfied by the merged fix, or closed out on #4370 with provider/client-side evidence.

Refs: #4370 (acceptance (b)), #3325, task 8950, task 7380.

title: id(world-manifest): world.toml [profile] total_memory_bytes is rejected as an unknown field — the #2876 probe struct was never updated for the #557 profile field

body:
## Problem

In `pkgs/id`, a `world.toml` manifest that sets the legitimate execution-profile field `total_memory_bytes` under `[profile]` fails to parse — `world_manifest::parse` rejects it as an unknown field, even though the field is a real, validated member of `WorldExecutionProfile`:

- `WorldExecutionProfile` gained `total_memory_bytes: Option<u64>` in the #557 per-world memory-budget work (`pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/world_limits.rs:307`). It is validated in `WorldExecutionProfile::validate` (`world_limits.rs:351`, nonzero) and resolved/clamped in `resolve` (`world_limits.rs:380-381`).
- `WorldManifest::validate` runs `self.profile.validate()` at parse time, and `parse`'s own docs promise the profile bounds in a manifest are honored (see the #3015 comment in `pkgs/id/src/world_manifest.rs`).
- But the unknown-key probe `reject_unknown_profile_keys` (`pkgs/id/src/world_manifest.rs:179-215`) still lists only the six pre-#557 fields in its `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)] ProfileKeysProbe` (`wasm_fuel`, `wasm_memory_bytes`, `wasm_message_bytes`, `native_memory_bytes`, `native_cpu_seconds`, `native_call_deadline_ms`). `total_memory_bytes` is missing, so the probe — which `parse` runs first (`world_manifest.rs:156`) — refuses the valid key before the real parse ever sees it.

The inconsistency is self-contained: `WorldManifest::to_toml` serializes a manifest whose `profile.total_memory_bytes` is set, emitting `total_memory_bytes = …` under `[profile]`, and `round_trip` (parse of `to_toml`) then fails on the manifest's own output.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe at origin/main ece818d38)

Laptop cargo probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-03-laneA3-manifest` on the laptop, one test added to `world_manifest::tests`, kept for inspection):

- `parse("[profile]\ntotal_memory_bytes = 67108864\n")` → Err: `TOML parse error at line 2, column 1: unknown field 'total_memory_bytes', expected one of 'wasm_fuel', 'wasm_memory_bytes', 'wasm_message_bytes', 'native_memory_bytes', 'native_cpu_seconds', 'native_call_deadline_ms'` — the expected list is exactly the probe's six stale fields
- The same probe test's later assertions (never reached) cover the `round_trip` of a `WorldManifest` with `profile.total_memory_bytes = Some(67108864)`, which fails for the same reason on the manifest's own `to_toml` output
- Controls: all 29 pre-existing `world_manifest::tests` pass on the same binary (the typo-refusal tests for #2876 among them); only the probe test fails

Probe result: `world_manifest::tests::probe_total_memory_bytes_profile_key_parses` FAILED at the first assertion on unmodified main; full module run: 29 passed, 1 failed (the probe).

## Why it matters

The per-world total memory budget (#557) is settable through the server/profile paths and is persisted/restored, but the declarative path — `world.toml` + `id world apply`/`diff` — cannot express it at all: any manifest naming the budget is refused wholesale, so an admin cannot set or pin a world's total memory budget declaratively, and any tooling that round-trips a manifest carrying the field breaks. The probe struct is a hand-maintained mirror of `WorldExecutionProfile`'s field list, so the same failure recurs the next time a profile field is added unless the fix also guards the mirror (see acceptance criteria).

## Acceptance criteria

- `parse` accepts `[profile] total_memory_bytes = <u64>` and the value reaches `WorldManifest.profile.total_memory_bytes`; `validate` still refuses `total_memory_bytes = 0` via the existing `WorldExecutionProfile::validate` rule.
- A manifest carrying `total_memory_bytes` survives `to_toml` → `parse` round-trip unchanged.
- Typo'd/unknown `[profile]` keys are still refused, naming the key (the #2876 behavior is preserved — e.g. `wasm_fuell` still fails).
- A regression test pins the probe's field list against `WorldExecutionProfile`'s actual fields (or the probe is restructured so drift is impossible), so adding a future profile field cannot silently reintroduce this.
- Existing `world_manifest` and `world_limits` tests stay green.

body:
# pm-stack(aggregator): IngestionStore load gates accept impossible/non-ISO gap + checkpoint dates and negative counts

## Evidence

`pm-stack/aggregator/src/activity.ts` (landed today in PR #5141, commit f5c8993c0; verified at origin/main d0a5b039c):

- `isGapRecord` (activity.ts:284-295) checks `from`, `to`, and `detectedAt` with `typeof === "string"` only.
- `isCheckpoint` (activity.ts:297-308) checks `lastEventAt` and `updatedAt` with `typeof === "string"` only, and `deliveries`/`duplicates` with `Number.isInteger` only — negative counts pass.
- Neither gate uses the aggregator's standing rule `isIsoDate` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/validate.ts:116`), which every sibling store gate was moved to for exactly this failure class (e.g. #5078, #5154, #5214).

Verified with a laptop bun probe against `IngestionStore` at d0a5b039c (probe `/tmp/probe-activity.ts` on the laptop, scan worktree `~/git/fleet/scan-2026-11-03-laneA2`):

- A persisted file whose gap has `from: "2026-02-30T00:00:00.000Z"`, `to: "2026-04-31T00:00:00.000Z"`, `detectedAt: "March 2, 2026"`, plus a second gap with `from: "not-a-date"`, `to: "also-bad"`, loads with **no quarantine** — `gaps()` returns both rows verbatim.
- A checkpoint with `lastEventAt: "2026-02-30T00:00:00.000Z"`, `updatedAt: "not-a-date"`, `deliveries: -5`, `duplicates: -2` loads verbatim; after ingesting one real delivery the count is `-4`.
- Consequences in the store's own arithmetic:
  - `recordGap` merge (activity.ts:515-516): extending the open watchdog gap with a real window ending `2026-03-10` did **not** widen `to`, because the stored Apr-31 rolls to May 1 under `Date.parse` — the recorded gap window silently overstates coverage by ~7 weeks.
  - `ingestSerialized` (activity.ts:499): a real delivery at `2026-02-20` does not advance `lastEventAt`, which stays pinned to the impossible Feb-30 stamp (parsed as Mar 2).
  - `gaps()` sort (activity.ts:414) and `resolveGap` extension (activity.ts:549) compare with `Date.parse`; a `not-a-date` value yields NaN, so ordering is undefined and the window never extends.

## Why it matters

The ingestion store is the aggregator's dedupe/coverage memory: gap records are rendered as holes in history ("never as coverage", per the module header), and checkpoints decide what a restart re-emits. An impossible or non-ISO stamp in the persisted file — a hand edit, a partially corrupted write that stays valid JSON, a future producer formatting loosely — currently passes the load gate that is supposed to quarantine malformed rows, and then silently corrupts gap windows and checkpoint progress instead of failing loudly. The negative-count hole additionally lets delivery accounting go below zero.

## Acceptance criteria

- `isGapRecord` requires `from`, `to`, and `detectedAt` (and `resolvedAt` when present) to satisfy `isIsoDate`; `isCheckpoint` requires `lastEventAt` (when non-null) and `updatedAt` to satisfy `isIsoDate`, and `deliveries`/`duplicates` to be integers `>= 0`.
- A persisted file violating these gates follows the store's existing malformed-row path (loud quarantine + empty start), consistent with the events store's discipline.
- Tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/activity-3321.test.ts` (or a sibling) cover: impossible date (2026-02-30), non-ISO date ("March 2, 2026"), garbage date, and negative counts are each refused/quarantined; a valid file loads unchanged (control).
- Aggregator test suite and `tsc` stay green.

body:
## Problem

`recordsFromProviderUsage` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/snapshot-records.ts:274) gates the provider-usage snapshot's `generated_at` with a NaN-only `Date.parse` check at :282:

```ts
if (!ts || Number.isNaN(Date.parse(ts))) return [];
```

`Date.parse` rolls impossible calendar dates (2026-02-30 → Mar 2, 2026-04-31 → May 1) and accepts non-ISO strings ("March 2, 2026"), so such a stamp passes this gate and is copied verbatim onto every derived record — the sessions count and both Codex windows.

## Why it matters

The store's own validator refuses exactly these stamps: `isSnapshotRecord` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/snapshots.ts:330) requires `isIsoDate(r.ts)` — "Real calendar dates only (#2264/#2483)". The only live caller, `scripts/append-usage-snapshots.ts:88` (`--from-provider-usage` mode), silently filters derived records through `isSnapshotRecord`. Net effect: one impossible or non-ISO `generated_at` silently discards the **entire** provider-usage snapshot (sessions observation + Codex pct history) with no legible reason — the run just reports fewer/no records appended. The derivation boundary is the right place to refuse, legibly, exactly as this file's sibling derivations already produce only real-calendar stamps (snapshot-records.ts already imports `parseIsoDate` from validate.ts).

## Evidence (verified this run, origin/main d94b89547, laptop bun probe)

Snapshot: `sessions: [1,2]`, Codex primary window `used_percent: 12, limit_window_seconds: 604800`.

- `generated_at: "2026-02-30T10:59:33Z"` → 2 records returned, ts verbatim; `isSnapshotRecord` = [false, false]
- `generated_at: "2026-04-31T10:59:33Z"` → 2 records returned, ts verbatim; `isSnapshotRecord` = [false, false]
- `generated_at: "March 2, 2026"` → 2 records returned, ts verbatim; `isSnapshotRecord` = [false, false]
- `generated_at: "not-a-date"` → 0 records (control — the current gate catches only this)
- `generated_at: "2026-10-26T10:59:33Z"` → 2 records; `isSnapshotRecord` = [true, true] (control)

Dedup: no open or closed issue covers this function/field — #3460/#2568 (closed) are the `used_percent` range in the same function; #3379 (closed) is the sibling `recordsFromDeepseekBalance` date-shadow bug, a different function.

## Acceptance criteria

- `recordsFromProviderUsage` returns [] for `generated_at` values "2026-02-30T10:59:33Z", "2026-04-31T10:59:33Z", and "March 2, 2026" (gate with `isIsoDate`/`parseIsoDate` from validate.ts, the same strict primitive `isSnapshotRecord` uses).
- Valid control unchanged: "2026-10-26T10:59:33Z" still yields the sessions record plus the Codex window records, all passing `isSnapshotRecord`.
- Garbage ("not-a-date") and missing `generated_at` still yield [].
- New tests in pm-stack/aggregator/test/snapshot-writers.test.ts cover the impossible/non-ISO refusals and the valid control; `bun test` in pm-stack/aggregator passes.

title: pm-stack(aggregator): entryFromFileExport launders impossible and non-ISO measuredAt — Date.parse rolls 2026-02-30 to Mar 2 and accepts 'March 2, 2026'

body:
## Problem

`entryFromFileExport` in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/quota-gather-map.ts:271` gates a file-export document's `measuredAt` with raw `Date.parse` and a NaN check only:

```ts
const measuredMs = doc.measuredAt ? Date.parse(doc.measuredAt) : Number.NaN;
if (doc.status !== "ok" || Number.isNaN(measuredMs)) { /* error entry */ }
const measuredAt = new Date(measuredMs).toISOString();
```

`Date.parse` rolls impossible calendar dates forward and accepts non-ISO strings, so a corrupt or hand-written export stamp is silently rewritten to a different day and published as a successful (`state: "ok"`) quota-current entry — stamped onto the entry and onto every window it carries. The same file already gates both Turso billing-period stamps with `isIsoDate` before `Date.parse` (quota-gather-map.ts:636-637, #5091), and `parseQuotaCurrent` gates its `measuredAt` with `isIsoDate` (#4987); this mapper is the remaining raw-`Date.parse` gate for a `measuredAt` in the quota path.

## Evidence (verified this run, origin/main dd04e9cd4)

Laptop bun probe calling `entryFromFileExport` with a status-`ok` doc (one weekly window at 42%):

| input `measuredAt` | result |
| --- | --- |
| `2026-02-30T12:00:00Z` | state `ok`, stored as `2026-03-02T12:00:00.000Z` |
| `2026-04-31T12:00:00Z` | state `ok`, stored as `2026-05-01T12:00:00.000Z` |
| `March 2, 2026` | state `ok`, stored as `2026-03-02T06:00:00.000Z` (TZ-dependent) |
| `03/02/2026` | state `ok`, stored as `2026-03-02T06:00:00.000Z` (TZ-dependent) |
| `not-a-date` | error entry (correct) |
| `null` | error entry (correct) |
| `2026-11-03T12:00:00Z` | state `ok`, unchanged (correct) |

Callers are live and neither pre-validates the stamp: `scripts/gather-quota.ts:566` (`runFileExport` — `JSON.parse` of the producer's `latest.json` cast straight to `FileExportDoc`) and `src/token-adapter.ts:294` (its fail-closed check validates the windows, not `measuredAt`).

## Why it matters

The entry's `measuredAt` is what freshness/age derivations read for the file-export convention (#1301) — the pattern other laptop exports follow. An impossible stamp that rolls forward (Feb 30 → Mar 2) makes a stale or corrupt export read as measured *later* than it was, and a non-ISO stamp's stored value depends on the host time zone, so the same document yields different quota-current entries on different hosts. Garbage stamps already produce the right outcome (an error entry, never zeros); impossible/non-ISO stamps should take the same path instead of being laundered into a plausible date.

## Acceptance criteria

- `entryFromFileExport` returns an error entry (not `state: "ok"`) for impossible dates `2026-02-30…` and `2026-04-31…` and for non-ISO stamps `March 2, 2026` and `03/02/2026`, by gating `measuredAt` with `isIsoDate` (validate.ts:116) before `Date.parse`, matching the Turso gate in the same file.
- Valid ISO stamps, `null`/missing `measuredAt`, non-`ok` statuses, stale docs, and `doc: null` behave exactly as before.
- New tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/quota-gather-map.test.ts` cover the impossible/non-ISO refusals and the valid control; `bun test` in `pm-stack/aggregator` passes.

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

body:
## Summary

`pm-stack/opencode-usage-export/opencode-usage-export.mjs:383` still uses the pre-#2083 raw-path entry-point check:

```js
if (process.argv[1] && import.meta.url === pathToFileURL(process.argv[1]).href) {
  const { exitCode, doc } = await run({ argv: process.argv.slice(2) });
  ...
}
```

This is the same bug class as #2083 / #2235 / #2350. `process.argv[1]` is the path as invoked; `import.meta.url` is the resolved module URL. Through a file symlink or a path through a symlinked directory (the fleet's own `~/code -> ~/git/code` alias), they never match, so the CLI body never runs and the process **exits 0 with no output and no files written**.

It survived #4325 because that issue scoped itself to four named files (codedb bridge, Supabase and Cloudflare exporters, claimant installer). #4325 has since been fixed and closed by PR #4583 (merge `b7d274c08`), whose own acceptance grep therefore does not hold repo-wide: this instance is the only raw compare left in the repo after that merge.

## Evidence (origin/main `b7d274c08`, laptop, 2026-11-03)

`git grep -nE "pathToFileURL\(process\.argv\[1\]\)|resolve\(process\.argv\[1\]\)" origin/main` returns exactly one hit:

```
origin/main:pm-stack/opencode-usage-export/opencode-usage-export.mjs:383
```

Live probe with a scratch `HOME` and `--out-dir` (no credentials needed):

- Direct: `node pm-stack/opencode-usage-export/opencode-usage-export.mjs --out-dir <scratch>` → exit 3, stdout `{"status":"store-missing","exitCode":3}`, failure document written (`latest.json`, `history.jsonl`).
- Via a file symlink: exit 0, no stdout, no stderr, **out-dir empty**.
- Via a symlinked directory: exit 0, no stdout, no stderr, **out-dir empty**.

So the exporter's failure-visibility design (always write a `store-missing` / `no-token` document so consumers can tell "source down" from a reading) is defeated by symlinked invocation: a timer tick through a symlink leaves `latest.json` silently stale and the unit green.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The entry-point check compares real paths (`fs.realpathSync` on both sides, as in `bin/proxy-supervise.mjs` and now the four files fixed by #4583), or an equivalent. Do not use the raw-path compare.
- [ ] Direct, file-symlink and directory-symlink invocations all run `main()` and write the same `store-missing` document with exit 3 in the no-store case.
- [ ] Importing the module as a library still does not run `main()` (its test suite at `pm-stack/opencode-usage-export/opencode-usage-export.test.mjs` does this).
- [ ] A regression test covers file-symlink and directory-symlink invocation plus inert import, so the check cannot regress again.
- [ ] `git grep -nE "pathToFileURL\(process\.argv\[1\]\)|resolve\(process\.argv\[1\]\)"` on the fix branch is empty (meta-exporter instance, if it reappears, is #2350, not this issue).

Related: #4325 + PR #4583 (the four sibling files, merged), #2083, #2235, #2350.

## Merge Danger

**Door:** one-way. **Blast Radius:** narrow — entry-point detection only; imported-module behavior unchanged. No credential or token path is touched.

Found by repo-health queue triage task 8376 (openchamber scheduled lane).

body:
Follow-up from the issue #2021 babysitter design (task 8584, design doc: `files/opencode-babysitter-design-2026-11-03.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace, §5).

## Problem

Conductor Phase 1's finished-unverified audit (in `hidden_files/openchamber-conductor-instruction.md`) ends in "archive the session" once GitHub verification passes — but the same instruction records that if the archive call is not in the current API inventory, the session is left in place and noted. Verified-finished sessions therefore accumulate as leftovers in the unfinished set, polluting the capacity picture the scripted tally has to explain every cycle. Sessions are never deleted; archiving is the only terminal cleanup, and it is currently not wired.

## Scope

- Verify whether the current OpenChamber API exposes a session archive call (check against `files/openchamber-api-inventory-2026-10-26.md`, gap 4 area, and the live API from the laptop).
- If it exists: add it to the API inventory with the verified request/response shape, and update the conductor instruction's finished-unverified step to call it.
- If it does not exist: file the gap against the OpenChamber side with the exact endpoint shape needed, and record that in the inventory instead.

## Acceptance

- The API inventory states, with fresh evidence, whether an archive call exists and its exact shape.
- A verified-finished session can be archived by the babysitter round (or the blocker is filed and linked here with the endpoint shape specified).
- No session is ever deleted as part of this work.

Refs #2021, #2153


## Acceptance criteria

- The current OpenChamber API's session-archive capability is verified against the live API (not only the 2026-10-26 inventory): the call exists with a recorded request/response shape, or its absence is confirmed with a follow-up filed.
- The API inventory names the archive call (or the confirmed gap) in the gap-4 area.
- The conductor instruction's finished-unverified step archives verified-finished sessions instead of leaving them in place with a note.
- Verified-finished sessions no longer accumulate unexplained in the unfinished set / capacity tally.
