body:
## Finding

The C2 holepunch NAT-emulation lab exists and works, but it cannot be reproduced from the repo: it is bound to one machine's absolute paths.

- `doc/2026-10-11T03-44-33Z_design_groups_events_delegation/spikes/c2-holepunch/Cargo.toml:14` — path dependency on `/home/user/work/spikes/c1-connect`.
- `.../spikes/c2-holepunch/lab/run.sh:24-26` — hardcodes nix-store paths for the `nft`, `iroh-relay` and `c2-holepunch` binaries.
- `.../spikes/c2-holepunch/lab/probe-nat.sh:14` — hardcodes `nft` again.
- No flake app, just recipe, script or CI job runs the matrix: the lab is only reachable by hand from the author's checkout.

## Why it matters

This is the second deliverable of #1826 (Drew's 2026-10-28 ruling: emulated laptop NAT is acceptable for the C2 cells a phone cannot cover, provided results are recorded **as emulated**). The emulation already covers the full matrix, including mixed pairs (`.../c2-holepunch/RESULTS.md:96-123`), and `RESULTS.md:170` records that real NAT devices and real networks remain untested. What is missing is reproducibility: on a clean checkout today the matrix cannot be re-run or re-verified by anyone else.

## What's needed

1. Make `c1-connect` resolvable relatively (workspace member or relative path), not an absolute `/home/user/work/...` path.
2. Resolve `nft`, `iroh-relay` and `c2-holepunch` at runtime — a `nix develop`/flake app that provides them, or env vars with a clear error when unset.
3. One documented entry point (flake app or just recipe) that runs `probe-nat.sh` + the full C2 matrix and writes a timestamped results file under the spike directory.
4. Stay netns-only (`unshare -Urn`): no host network changes, no root requirement beyond user namespaces.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] On a clean checkout, one documented command builds and runs the probe + matrix without editing any absolute path.
- [ ] The run writes a timestamped results artifact that states the NAT types are Linux netfilter emulation, not real NAT devices.
- [ ] The reproducer is exercised at least once end-to-end on the laptop, with the command and output recorded on this issue.
- [ ] Results are posted to #795 labelled emulated (not real-network), and #1826's second acceptance criterion is checked.

Filed by the #1826 triage (queue task 7751) as the split of its actionable half.

body:
Found while triaging #2915 (queue task 8000, coverage pass 2026-11-03).

## Problem

`pm-stack/dispatch/src/server.ts` `handleSessions` creates the GitHub tracking issue in **step 1**, before the queue enqueue (step 2) and the launch (step 3):

- On an **enqueue** failure the handler returns `502 {error, issue_number}` (`server.ts:219-227`) and never comments on or closes the issue it just created. The issue is left as a bare prompt with the footer promising "Queue task and OpenCode session ids follow in a comment below" — a promise that never comes true. Only the *launch* failure path (`launch_failure.ts:46`, which cancels the task and comments) and the success annotation path (`launch_annotations.ts`) write to the issue.
- `parseSessionRequest` puts no floor on spec quality, so a caller sending a generic prompt gets a real repo issue whose entire body is that prompt. Title is `titleFromPrompt(prompt)`, hence a family of issues literally titled `do the thing`.

Consequence in this repo: **59 open issues titled `do the thing`** (`gh issue list --state open --search '"do the thing" in:title'`), created 2026-10-31 through 2026-11-03, several per day. Each one is picked up by the coverage join as "open issue with no live queue task", so it costs a triage lane per issue and produces no work — the exact waste #2915's intake review described ("enqueueing an unspecified task would waste a lane"), except the issue itself now gets enqueued by coverage.

## Work

1. **No orphan issues.** Either create the tracking issue *after* the successful enqueue (preferred: the issue then always has a task id to name), or on the enqueue-failure 502 path comment the failure on the created issue and close it as not planned. Never return an `issue_number` for an issue left dangling with no task.
2. **Minimum spec gate.** Reject (400) a session request whose prompt is trivially short or whose `title` would be derived from such a prompt — e.g. require an explicit `title` when `prompt` is under a small length. Never derive a repo issue title from a placeholder prompt.
3. **Cleanup.** Close the open `do the thing` placeholders (bulk, `state_reason: not_planned`, one comment each pointing here) and clear their queue coverage noise; verify no live queue task references them before cancelling any.
4. **Tests.** Enqueue failure leaves no open issue (or leaves a closed, commented one); a short/generic prompt is rejected at validation; a normal dispatch still posts task/session ids on the issue.

## Evidence

- `pm-stack/dispatch/src/server.ts:194-227` — issue created before `requireQueue().enqueue`; the 502 path returns without a comment or close.
- `pm-stack/dispatch/src/server.ts:197` — `const title = body.title ?? titleFromPrompt(body.prompt)`.
- `pm-stack/dispatch/src/launch_failure.ts:46-93` — the only failure path that annotates the issue.
- `gh issue list --repo developing-today/code --state open --search '"do the thing" in:title'` → 59 open.
- #2915 — triaged and closed as the specimen; its 2026-10-31 intake review already flagged it as unactionable.

Not in scope: the dispatch auth/directory gates (#2903) and the launch failure handler (#2901), both working.

## Acceptance criteria

- On an enqueue failure, the dispatch handler does not leave an orphan: the just-created tracking issue is closed (or commented with the failure and labelled so coverage skips it) in the same request path that returns the 502.
- `parseSessionRequest` enforces a minimum spec floor: a prompt that cannot name work (e.g. the literal `do the thing` family) is rejected with a 4xx naming the missing spec, before any issue is created.
- The 59 existing open `do the thing` placeholder issues are dispositioned in bulk (closed as orphans with a pointer here, or adopted with a real spec) — the open-issue search for that title returns zero unexplained placeholders.
- A test covers the enqueue-failure path asserting no open orphan issue remains.

body:
Residual gap found while triaging #2244 at main `1e3763f` (both phases shipped: #3891 core, #3960 integration).

## Problem

#2244's "Done when" requires that "the counters are visible" so an operator can tune the limits they can see. Today the per-`(local node, remote endpoint)` frame/byte counters exist and are correct, but their only reader is Rust code:

- `WorldProtocol::abuse_counters()` (`pkgs/id/src/world_net.rs:156`) returns `Vec<((NodeId, EndpointId), Counters)>`.
- It has no other caller in the tree (`git grep abuse_counters -- pkgs/id/src`), no CLI verb prints it, and no metrics/status endpoint exposes it.

So an operator running `id` cannot see any counter value, which means the tuning half of the issue is not reachable without writing code.

## Work

- Pick the surface the design allows (metrics **or** `id peers`): add a counter section/flag to `id peers` (`pkgs/id/src/commands/peers.rs`) backed by an `abuse_counters()` snapshot from the live protocol, or expose the same snapshot through the existing metrics/status route used for world state.
- Include both directions (inbound/outbound frames and bytes), the endpoint id in the same rendering `id peers` already uses, and the policy values (rate/burst) alongside so a value can be judged relative to its bucket.
- Keep it read-only and bounded: snapshot per invocation, no unbounded state retention; reuse `CounterRegistry::prune` retention semantics rather than adding a second lifetime.
- Test: a snapshot with two endpoints renders both rows deterministically, and the output stays stable when counters are empty.

Related: #2244 (closed by this triage), #3881, #3882, #2033 (design, `doc/2026-11-01_design_id2033.md`), #2247 (budgets consume the same counters).

body:
# id(text/1): `TextSurface` wrap emits lines wider than the requested width when a single grapheme is wider than the width — contradicting the wrap contract

## Evidence

`pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/world_presentation.rs` — the new `text/1`
surface from #2339 (commit `0ec941645`):

- `wrap_text_line` (line ~157) documents: "a word longer than `width` is
  hard-wrapped on grapheme boundaries **so no output line ever exceeds
  `width` columns** (zero-width graphemes attach to the preceding column)".
- The wrap loop only breaks *before* a grapheme when the current line is
  non-empty (`current_width + grapheme_width > width && !current.is_empty()`).
  A grapheme whose own display width exceeds `width` is therefore placed
  whole on its own line, and that line exceeds `width`.
- `TextSurface::with_width` documents its result as "already wrapped to
  `width` columns" and `parse_surface` accepts a guest `width` as small
  as 1, so a guest document `{"kind":"text","version":1,"width":1,
  "lines":["界"]}` (界 = U+754C, unicode-width 2) validates and produces
  a stored line of width 2 at width 1.

Verified this run with a laptop probe at origin/main `c19c1d8b0`
(worktree `probe-2026-11-03-laneB-scan19`, logs `/tmp/probe-scan19.log`
and `/tmp/probe-scan19b.log` on the laptop, read back from disk):

- `TextSurface::with_width(1, vec!["界"])` → `Ok`, `lines == ["界"]`
  (display width 2 > requested width 1)
- `parse_surface("{\"kind\":\"text\",\"version\":1,\"width\":1,
  \"lines\":[\"界\"]}")` → `Ok(Some(Text(_)))` with the same over-wide line
- Control: `with_width(2, vec!["a界b"])` wraps to lines within width 2,
  and the existing tests at width 3 (`ab界cd`) stay within width — the
  violation needs a grapheme strictly wider than the wrap width itself.

## Why it matters

`text/1` is the main presentation mode for agents and scripts (#2339):
presenters size their output to the negotiated width and trust the
validated surface to fit it. A validated line that exceeds the width
breaks that contract exactly where it is hardest to see — narrow
terminals / width-1..2 viewports and wide CJK/emoji graphemes — and the
module's own doc states the opposite guarantee, so downstream code has
no reason to re-check. The screen side never faces this because a
`ScreenSurface` cell names its column span explicitly; the text side
needs its own rule.

## Acceptance criteria

- Code and docs agree, one of:
  (a) `TextSurface::with_width` / `parse_surface` refuse a line whose
      single grapheme is wider than the requested width (naming the
      width in the error), or
  (b) the wrap contract is amended in the module docs to state that a
      line may exceed `width` by the width of one unsplittable grapheme,
      and presenters are pointed at that exception.
- Regression tests cover: width 1 with a width-2 grapheme, width 2 with
  a width-2 grapheme (accepted, fits exactly), and the existing
  width-3 `ab界cd` case still passing.
- `cargo test -p id-core --lib world_presentation` passes (laptop or CI).

Relates to #2339 (the text/1 contract issue) — this is a specific
wrap-contract violation in the landed implementation, not covered by
that issue's remaining work.

title: pkarr-worker: PUT and DoH POST bodies are fully buffered with arrayBuffer() before the size caps are checked (DoH rate limit also runs after the read)

labels.name: kind/security

labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: app/pkarr-worker
labels.description: pkgs/pkarr-worker

body:
## Finding

In `pkgs/pkarr-worker/src/index.ts`, both request-body size caps are checked **after** the whole body has already been buffered with `request.arrayBuffer()`:

```ts
// current main (eefeab5af), PUT /pkarr/<key> — cap is MAX_RELAY_PAYLOAD = 1072 bytes
120:  const body = new Uint8Array(await request.arrayBuffer());
121:  if (body.length > MAX_RELAY_PAYLOAD) return new Response("payload too large", { status: 413 });

// current main, POST /dns-query — cap is MAX_DOH_BODY = 4096 bytes (index.ts:44)
260:  return handleDoh(request, env, new Uint8Array(await request.arrayBuffer()));
179:  if (queryBytes.length > MAX_DOH_BODY) return new Response("message too large", { status: 413 });
```

For the DoH POST path the ordering is worse: the per-IP rate limiter (`index.ts:198`, inside `handleDoh`) also runs only after the full body has been read, so an oversized DoH body costs the Worker a full buffer before any limit — size or rate — is consulted. (The PUT path does rate-limit before reading; the DoH path does not.)

## Evidence

- Introduced by PR #3234 (merged, merge commit 54ca296c0, verified an ancestor of current main) — "feat(pkarr): pkarr Worker pilot + cf versions deploy standard (#1829)".
- Verified unchanged on current main `eefeab5af648ac612899c65a4c575c20808ef0e1` via two independent contents-API reads (line numbers above).
- Dedupe: searches for pkarr + arrayBuffer / unbounded / body-cap return no issue; the filed pkarr-worker issues (#3252, #3264, #3261) cover deploy-argument handling and RETENTION_SECONDS parsing, not body reads.

## Why it matters

The caps exist to bound what an unauthenticated remote caller can make the Worker handle — 1,072 bytes for a publish, 4,096 bytes for a DoH query. As written, the bound applies to what is *processed*, not what is *buffered*: a caller can send a body up to the platform request-size limit (100 MB on Cloudflare's free plan) and the Worker will allocate for all of it before returning the 413 the cap was supposed to produce cheaply. Against a 128 MB-memory Worker, oversized-body floods are a memory-exhaustion / error-1102 surface instead of a cheap early rejection — exactly the read-then-check pattern the repo's bounded-body work elsewhere exists to remove.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] PUT /pkarr and POST /dns-query reject an over-cap body without buffering it whole: a `Content-Length` pre-check where the header is present, and/or a streaming read that aborts once the cap is exceeded.
- [ ] The DoH path consults its rate limiter (or at least the size pre-check) before reading the body.
- [ ] Over-cap requests still return 413; at-cap and under-cap requests behave exactly as before (existing vitest suite green).
- [ ] A test demonstrates an over-cap body is rejected on the pre-read check (e.g. declared Content-Length above the cap), not only after a full read.

Base: `c0e9d059a` (worktree from `origin/main`, no local changes). Both a default-linker run and a mold run hit the identical errors — the failure is linker-independent and pre-existing:

```
error[E0063]: missing field `checkpoint` in initializer of `ChainExt`
  --> tests/search.rs:84:19
error[E0063]: missing field `checkpoint` in initializer of `ChainExt`
  --> tests/voiding_scenarios.rs:88:19
error: could not compile `id` (test "search") due to 2 previous errors
error: could not compile `id` (test "crash") due to 1 previous error
error: could not compile `id` (test "event_store_properties") due to 4 previous errors
```

`pkgs/id/src/chain.rs` — `ChainExt` now ends with:

```rust
pub checkpoint: Option<SessionCheckpoint>, // #3794 session checkpoint body
```

but literals such as `pkgs/id/tests/search.rs` (`document()`, `tag_ext()`) list `kind/group/after/tag/document/removes/note/link` and stop there — no `checkpoint: None`, and no `..Default::default()` (the struct has no Default impl in use at those sites).

## Impact

- Any `--all-targets` check/test build of `pkgs/id` fails on main until the literals are updated.
- It blocks the #3195 phase-3 mold measurement (queue task 5375): cold check-build timings cannot be taken against a tree that does not compile.

## Done when

Found by: queue worker lane I, task 5375 (#3195 phase 3), 2026-11-03.

## Acceptance criteria

- Every `ChainExt` literal constructed in `pkgs/id` tests supplies the fields required by the #3794 chain contract (no missing-field compile/test failures).

body:
Part of epic #1184; implementation follow-up of design issue #1259 (spend rollups). Design note: `doc/spend-rollups-design-1259.md` (PR linked from #1259).

## Scope
Build the spend-attribution projection in the pm-stack aggregator: a versioned, pure projection that turns existing per-session usage records into per-issue / per-epic / per-project spend facts. Consume existing sources only — do NOT build new collectors:
- `pm-stack/opencode-usage-export` documents (per-session tokens + cost, `parentId`, `directory`, model/provider) — slice 1 of #2072.
- The aggregator usage snapshot store (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/snapshots.ts`, append-only `usage-YYYY-MM.jsonl`).

## Attribution rules (per the design note)
- Queue-bound sessions resolve exactly: lane-ledger session binding → queue task → issue number.
- Fleet-worktree sessions resolve from the worktree directory name (`~/git/fleet/<task>-<issue>-<slug>`).
- Sub-sessions roll up to their root session (`parentId`); never double-counted.
- Epic/project resolution reuses the existing hierarchy seams (`epicRef` / parent chains in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/model.ts`, rollups in `src/epics.ts`); Project Area is a display grouping, not an attribution key.
- Anything unresolved lands in an explicit **unattributed** bucket with a reason code (`no-binding`, `no-worktree`, `parent-left-pool`, `source-gap`). Unattributed spend is shown, never dropped or guessed onto an epic.
- Every projected fact carries `attributionVersion`; raw source records are never rewritten.

## Acceptance criteria
- Projection is a pure, tested module: same inputs + same version → identical output.
- Unit tests cover: bound session, worktree session, sub-session rollup, each unattributed reason code, and a session whose parent chain leaves the fetched pool.
- Totals reconcile: sum(attributed) + unattributed = source totals, per unit, asserted in tests.
- No new collector, exporter, or instrumentation in OpenCode/OpenChamber.

## Checks
- `bun test` and `bunx tsc --noEmit` in `pm-stack/aggregator` pass (CI on the PR).

title: id(tag_claims): check_op accepts a tag.clear naming zero claims — sibling batch rules refuse empty batches and the local producer refuses to create one

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Summary

`check_op` in `pkgs/id/src/tag_claims.rs` accepts a `tag.clear` operation that names zero claims. Every sibling batch rule in the same header-extension family refuses an empty batch, and the local producer refuses to create one — so an empty clear is a shape the library's own client can never make but a remote peer's signed event passes validation, decodes, and applies as a no-op that still occupies a chain sequence number and sync bandwidth.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe at origin/main f0fd3ddd3)

- `pkgs/id/src/tag_claims.rs` `check_op` (CLEAR_KIND arm): checks only `claims.len() > MAX_CLEAR_CLAIMS` (256) and duplicate claims (added for #4765). There is no lower bound: `check_op("tag.clear", &TagOp::Clear { claims: vec![] })` returns `Ok(())` — verified by a probe test against the real `id` crate (`EMPTY_CLEAR_RESULT: Ok(())`).
- The same probe signs a full chain event: `chain::sign` with a `ChainExt { kind: "tag.clear", tag: Some(TagOp::Clear { claims: vec![] }), .. }` succeeds, so the empty clear is a valid signed event on the wire, not just a library-level curiosity. `ChainExt::validate` applies `check_op` on both build and decode (`pkgs/id/src/chain.rs`), so the decoder accepts it on receipt too.
- The local producer refuses the same shape: `LocalEvents::clear_tag` in `pkgs/id/src/local_events.rs` bails with "no live claim … is named {name}" when there is nothing to clear, and only ever records a clear naming ≥1 claim.
- Sibling rules refuse empty batches in the same validation layer: `check_note_op` (`pkgs/id/src/notes.rs`) refuses a revision naming no parents ("a revision names at least one parent"); `check_session_checkpoint` (`pkgs/id/src/session_checkpoint.rs`) refuses a session naming no participants ("a session names at least one participant").

## Why it matters

Validation at the header layer is the contract every consumer relies on: a signed event that passes `check_op` is treated as well-formed by ingest, the folds, and sync. A clear that clears nothing is meaningless work in an append-only log — it advances the author's chain, is stored and replicated to every peer, and can be spammed at zero cost to pad a chain — and its acceptance is an inconsistency in the stated rules: the same module family that refuses an empty parent list and an empty participant list silently accepts an empty claim list. Either the shape is valid (then the local producer's refusal and the sibling rules are the anomaly, and that should be stated) or it is not (then `check_op` should refuse it at build and decode, before it ever reaches a fold).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `check_op` refuses `TagOp::Clear { claims: [] }` with a named `TagError::Field` message in the style of the sibling refusals (e.g. "a clear names at least one claim"), so `ChainExt::validate` refuses the shape on both build and decode.
- [ ] Tests in `pkgs/id/src/tag_claims.rs` cover the empty clear refusal; the existing cap (256) and duplicate-claim refusals and all valid clears (1..=256 claims) behave exactly as before.
- [ ] If an empty clear is in fact intended to be valid, document that explicitly on `TagOp::Clear` / `check_op` instead, with a test pinning the acceptance — one stated rule either way.

Distinct from: #4765 (duplicate claims in one clear — the cap/duplicate arm of the same check), #4772 (duplicate tags in `local_events::publish`), #1720 (clear_tag chunking over the cap, closed).

body:
## Bug

`FileOps::copy` duplicates **all** of the source's metadata tags onto the copy — including the source's `archive.rename` / `archive.replace` references. Those references are ownership records: `FileOps::delete` follows them and hard-deletes every archive they name (blob tag + the archive's metadata). So a copy silently becomes a second owner of the source's archives, and deleting the copy destroys the source's archived versions while the source file still exists.

## Evidence (origin/main c0e61d033)

- `pkgs/id/src/fileops.rs:443` `FileOps::copy` calls `TagStore::copy_all_tags` at `:465` with no exclusions; `refresh_identity_tags` afterwards resets only `name`/`file`, and `stamp` only `created`/`modified`.
- `pkgs/id/src/tags.rs:1079` `copy_all_tags` copies every tag verbatim (key, value, payload).
- Contrast `pkgs/id/src/fileops.rs:32-44`: `ARCHIVE_IDENTITY_TAG_KEYS` deliberately keeps `archive.rename`/`archive.replace` off an archive subject during `archive_existing`, with the comment that letting one travel "orphans every earlier archive from the live file's delete (#4574)" — the same ownership reasoning applies to a second live file, but the copy path has no equivalent exclusion.
- `pkgs/id/src/fileops.rs:496` `FileOps::delete` reads the name's `archive.rename`/`archive.replace` values (`:507`) and deletes each named archive tag and its metadata. Rename moving these references is correct (the source name ceases to exist, and delete's comment at `:501` documents that case); copy leaves the source alive, so the references end up owned twice.

## Reproduced this run (laptop probe, pkgs/id lib test)

Probe test `probe_copy_inherits_source_archive_refs` (worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-scan5` on the laptop, `cargo test --lib probe_copy_inherits_source_archive_refs`):

1. Seed: `put source.txt`, `put other.txt`, `rename other.txt -> source.txt` — replaced `source.txt` is archived as `source.txt.archive.1793681949` and the live `source.txt` carries `archive.replace = source.txt.archive.1793681949`.
2. `copy source.txt -> copy.txt` (copy.txt did not exist): probe printed the copy's `archive.replace` values as `["source.txt.archive.1793681949"]` — inherited verbatim.
3. `delete copy.txt` reported `archives_removed=1`, and afterwards the source's archive tag `source.txt.archive.1793681949` no longer exists (`survives: false`), while `source.txt` itself is untouched.

## Why it matters

Archives are the only record of replaced/original file versions. A routine copy + delete of the copy — with the source never touched — permanently removes the source's archived versions (the blob tag is deleted; the blob bytes are then garbage-collectable). It also misreports the copy's own archive list.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] After `copy`, the destination carries no `archive.rename`/`archive.replace` values that name the **source's** archives (the destination's own `archive.replace` for a file it replaced during the copy, set today after `copy_all_tags`, still works).
- [ ] `delete` of a copy never removes an archive owned by the still-existing source; the source's archives survive and remain deletable via the source.
- [ ] Regression test in `pkgs/id/src/fileops.rs` tests: source with an archive -> copy -> delete copy -> source's archive tag and metadata still present; and the copy's tag set contains no inherited archive references.
- [ ] Existing fileops tests keep passing (`cargo test --lib fileops` on laptop/CI), including `copy_onto_existing_moves_replaced_metadata_and_keeps_single_fresh_stamps`.

## Dedup

Checked open + closed issues 2026-11-03: #4720 (archive namespace not reserved — a user file *named* like an archive) is a different mechanism; #2856/#2862 (closed) cover rename/delete archive tracking and replaced-file metadata merging, not copy inheriting the source's archive references. No existing issue covers this.

body:
# opencode-usage-export: --window-hours / --fresh-hours are never validated — a junk window publishes a zero-filled `status: "ok"` document, a junk freshness reports a fresh store as moved

`pm-stack/opencode-usage-export/opencode-usage-export.mjs` (slice 1 of #2072, merged in PR #4680) parses its two numeric flags with a bare `Number(...)` and never checks the result:

- `parseArgs` (`:311-322`): `--window-hours` → `Number(argv[++i])` (`:317`), `--fresh-hours` → `Number(argv[++i])` (`:318`). No finite/positive check; a missing value is `Number(undefined)` = `NaN`; an unknown flag throws, but a known flag with a bad value does not.
- The window flows unchecked into `sinceMs = now - args.windowHours * 3600000` (`:348`) and the session query `WHERE time_updated >= ?` (`:221` via `:349`).
- The freshness flows unchecked into `freshMs: args.freshHours * 3600000` (`:343`) and the liveness comparison `now - p.newestUpdated <= freshMs` (`:165`).

## Verified this run (laptop probe, verbatim origin/main @ cf74b1ea, file md5 13c24364)

Fixture store with one fresh session (updated 1 min before `now`) and one 48 h-old session, exporter extracted byte-identical from `origin/main` (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-usagewindow/` on the laptop):

| Invocation | Result |
|---|---|
| control (defaults) | exit 0, `status: "ok"`, 1 session |
| `--window-hours banana` | exit 0, `status: "ok"`, **0 sessions**, `windowHours: NaN` |
| `--window-hours` (value missing) | exit 0, `status: "ok"`, **0 sessions**, `windowHours: NaN` |
| `--window-hours -5` | exit 0, `status: "ok"`, **0 sessions** |
| `--window-hours Infinity` | exit 0, `status: "ok"`, **2 sessions** — the 48 h-old session outside any real window is included |
| `--fresh-hours banana` | exit 4, `store-stale`: "no candidate store has session_v2 activity within **NaNh**; newest activity [1 minute ago] — the live store may have moved" |
| `--fresh-hours -1` | exit 4, `store-stale`, same misleading moved-store diagnosis for a store updated 1 minute ago |

## Why it matters

The module's own contract is fail-closed: the header (`:29-31`) promises a tick that cannot read the live store "writes a failure document and exits non-zero — **never a zero-filled success**", and the README repeats that a failed tick can never look like a reading. An invalid `--window-hours` breaks exactly that promise: `latest.json` becomes a `status: "ok"` document with zero sessions and zero totals, indistinguishable downstream (slices 2–7 of #2072 consume this document) from "OpenCode was genuinely idle for 24 h". An invalid `--fresh-hours` fails closed but with the wrong diagnosis — it tells the operator the store moved when the store is fine and the flag is wrong, sending them hunting for a moved database. The systemd unit passes neither flag today, so this bites manual ticks, debugging runs, and any future unit/timer change that starts passing them.

Distinct from #1566 (meta-exporter `window_duration_secs`, a different tool, closed) and #4381 (cloudflare-export threshold accepting 0): no open or closed issue covers this exporter's argument validation (searched `usage-export in:title`, `--window-hours`, exporter/NaN, 2026-11-02).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `--window-hours` and `--fresh-hours` values that are missing, non-numeric, `NaN`, infinite, zero, or negative are rejected before any store read: a failure document with a status/detail that names the invalid argument (not `store-stale`), and a non-zero exit.
- [ ] A valid positive finite value behaves exactly as today (existing tests green).
- [ ] New tests in `opencode-usage-export.test.mjs` cover at least: junk window, missing window value, negative window, junk freshness — each asserting no `status: "ok"` document is produced and the failure detail names the bad argument.
- [ ] No `ok` document can ever carry a non-finite or non-positive `windowHours`.

title: id(world-replication): replication stream serves the full world journal to any peer — no read authorization before the feed opens (PR #4589)

labels.name: kind/security

body:
## Finding (from PR review, never addressed)

World journal replication serves a world's complete journal to any Iroh peer that supplies a nonzero session nonce — no capability, membership, or admin credential is checked before the journal is opened and streamed. Omitting `world` even selects the default world. This bypasses the capability validation used for the existing records replication path and exposes journaled chat, inputs, and host events to nonmembers.

Raised independently by two reviewers on PR #4589:
- Codex (P1), 2026-11-02T21:31:55Z: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/4589#discussion_r4447988604 — "Authorize replication before exposing the journal" (`pkgs/id/src/world_replication_net.rs:114`)
- CodeRabbit (Major, Security & Privacy), 2026-11-02T21:37:25Z: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/4589#discussion_r4448051641 — after `ensure_nonce`, `serve_stream` calls `hub.lease(request.world.as_deref(), None)` and `replication_feed()`; neither checks the peer's identity or credentials; the nonce only rejects an all-zero value; `REPLICATION_ALPN` is also registered without an access policy (`pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:1145-1157`). The participant projection hides chat and zeroes seeds for `/id-world/1`, but this stream sends raw journal bytes without that projection.

## No-response evidence

- PR #4589 (feat(id): serve signed world journal replication, #806 phase 2) had a single commit; both comments predate the merge (merged 2026-11-02T22:21:20Z as-is).
- All 12 review threads on PR #4589 are unresolved (GraphQL `reviewThreads`, checked 2026-11-03); there are no replies to either comment.

## Still live on current main (verified 2026-11-03 via `gh api` raw reads)

`pkgs/id/src/world_replication_net.rs` on main: `serve_stream` calls `ensure_nonce(&request.session_nonce)?` (:109), then `hub.lease(request.world.as_deref(), None)` (:110-113), then `replication_feed()` (:114) — still no authorization check between the nonce check and opening the feed.

## Acceptance criteria

- Replication requires an authorized read credential/capability before the lease/feed is opened; unauthorized peers are rejected before any journal bytes are sent.
- A regression test covers an unauthorized peer being refused (including the default-world case when `world` is omitted).
- Or: a documented decision on this issue explaining why unauthenticated replication is acceptable, with the exposure stated explicitly.

Found by the pr-comment-review job from an unaddressed PR review comment.

**Gated on Phases 1–2 of #4592 landing** (Phase 1 = #4471, the restore range at the envelope; Phase 2 = #4487, snapshot monotonicity). Do not start the audit before both land.

## Scope

Land the contract statement in the `ReplicationTracker` module doc (`pkgs/id/src/world/replication.rs`) and produce the closing admission inventory: every precondition `WorldCore::restore` demands of a journal, dispositioned against a check in `ReplicationTracker::accept` — *holds at accept* / *holds at restore only, with the reason that is safe* / *gap, filed as a named follow-up issue*. The inventory is the deliverable; fixing a confirmed gap inside this issue is out of scope beyond a single-site slip (file it instead).

Disposition with evidence either way.
- **(b) Session-bootstrap version source** — where `ReplicationTracker::new`'s `header_version` argument comes from in the serve wiring, whether #4592's decision 2 (an out-of-range session version makes the tracker inert under the accept-side range check) holds at that call site, and whether a *new* session may legitimately start below the version a previous session reached (monotonicity is per-tracker; answer from the bootstrap code, not assumption).
- **(c) Pre-fix terminal hygiene** — Terminal frames carrying an out-of-range version against a tracker whose version was set by a pre-Phase-1 snapshot: expected to be covered by Phase 1's all-kinds range check — confirm with a test or a code citation, don't assume.

title: id(world_net): route_frame lets a frame's own 'world' key override the session-bound world — a WorldSessions session keyed to one world silently leases another

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

`route_frame` (`pkgs/id/src/world_net.rs:387-396`) only *inserts* the session-bound world when the frame does not already carry a `world` key — it never overrides one. That breaks the contract the rest of the stack is built on:

- `WorldClient.world` is documented (world_net.rs:404) as the "World named in every frame this client sends".
- The host binds a session to a world by the **first frame only**: `run_session_with` (pkgs/id/src/world_session/mod.rs:847-890) removes `world` from the first frame and leases that world for the session's whole lifetime; later frames cannot re-route.
- The new coordinator `WorldSessions` (#3845, merged today in PR #3896) retains sessions keyed by `(endpoint, world)` (world_net.rs:1473-1510) and trusts that key to mean the world the session is actually bound to.

So a session opened/keyed for world **arena** whose first frame already carries `"world": "bazaar"` — the shape hand-built join frames routinely use (cf. world_session/tests.rs:1386, :1403) — silently leases **bazaar** on the host, while the coordinator keeps handing out that client as the arena session. Every later frame routed through it (which `route_frame` stamps `arena`, to no effect — the lease is already bazaar) acts on bazaar. Wrong-world reads/writes with no error anywhere.

## Evidence (verified this run, main @ 6fc3145d5)

Verbatim `route_frame` (world_net.rs:387-396, snippet md5 3644119170747a4a3197b05032d01efc) in a laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-routeframe/` on the laptop):

```
bound=arena frame_world="bazaar" routed={"capability":"1.abc","type":"join","world":"bazaar"}
bare frame routed world="arena"
```

- Frame with its own `world` key + bound world `arena` → routed frame still names `bazaar` (frame wins).
- Control: frame without a `world` key + bound world `arena` → routed frame names `arena` (insert path works).

All current in-tree `route_frame` callers (commands/world.rs:738, world_ssh.rs:2680, :2860, `WorldClient::send_json` world_net.rs:470) build frames without a `world` key, so the override branch is latent today — it activates the moment a caller reuses a world-carrying frame template through a bound session, which the `WorldSessions` API now invites. There are no tests for `route_frame`.

## Why it matters

World selection is a capability boundary (per-world capability checks are the F13.8 design's stated invariant, doc/2026-11-01T17-54-35Z_design_id_concurrent_world_sessions). A client-side coordinator that can silently hold a session to a different world than its key claims undermines that invariant and produces wrong-world actions that look successful.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `route_frame` with a bound world produces a frame naming that world even when the input frame already carries a different `world` key (bound world wins), or the mismatch is rejected with an explicit error — one behavior, documented on `WorldClient.world` / `route_frame`.
- [ ] Unit tests for `route_frame`: insert-when-absent, override/reject-when-present-and-different, no-op when the frame's world already equals the bound world, `None` bound world leaves the frame untouched.
- [ ] A `WorldSessions`-level test (extending the coordinator tests in world_net.rs) shows a session opened for world A cannot end up leased to world B via a pre-keyed first frame.
- [ ] Existing world_net / world_session tests stay green.

title: id(replication): ReplicationTracker accepts a snapshot with a lower header version — replica silently rolls back and re-admits old-version tails

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Problem

In `pkgs/id/src/world/replication.rs`, `ReplicationTracker::accept` treats a `Snapshot` frame as an unconditional rebase: the Snapshot arm (lines 619-714, snapshot branch) checks only that the frame's `cursor_before` is the chain base **for the snapshot's own `header_version`**, then sets `self.cursor = envelope.cursor_after` and `self.header_version = envelope.header_version`. Unlike the Tail and Terminal arms — which refuse any header-version change with `HeaderVersionChanged` — the Snapshot arm never compares the snapshot's header version against the chain's current one. A snapshot carrying a **lower** `header_version` than the receiver has already advanced to is accepted, silently rolling the replica's header version back.

Journal header versions only ever move forward in this codebase: `pkgs/id/src/world/mod.rs` (lines 915-946) documents that a journal's header bumps from `JOURNAL_VERSION` (1) to 2 and then 3 *before* an entry kind an older binary cannot read is appended, and a binary refuses a journal newer than `MAX_JOURNAL_VERSION`. There is no downgrade path for a real journal. A lower-version snapshot therefore cannot be a legitimate writer state — it is either a writer bug or a stale/forged stream — yet the tracker accepts it and, after accepting it, also accepts Tail frames on the old header version that it refused with `HeaderVersionChanged` moments earlier. The version guard the Tail arm enforces is thus defeated by inserting one snapshot frame.

This matters for the phases that build on this contract (#806 phases 2-5: writer feed, durable receiver, spectator serving). The durable receiver will persist `header_version()` alongside the replicated entries; a rolled-back header version over entries that may include kinds only a newer version can read is an internally inconsistent replica — and a silent rollback of verified state is exactly what the tracker's other checks (gap, fork, replay, frame chain) exist to prevent, including for frames the pinned source signed (the module already refuses a signed-but-undecodable payload; see the regression test added for PR #4447).

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe: worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-repldowngrade/` at origin/main `abe917ab6`, `replication.rs` md5 `f807510cedc0884c513f5a49ea81bfe6` — byte-identical to sandbox main `a377f61ed`. Integration test `pkgs/id/tests/probe_repl_downgrade.rs` (probe-only, in the worktree) drives the public `ReplicationTracker` API with the module's own test payload (three real journal entries). One disclosed probe-local shim: the lib does not compile on current main (#4454 — `references.rs` E0277 + E0597), so the worktree carries two minimal compile shims in `references.rs` only (owning the stripped hex string; a `Default` impl for `StoreId`); `replication.rs` is untouched. Probe output (1 passed):

- PROBE1: tail on header v1 accepted; cursor ordinal 3.
- PROBE2: snapshot on header v2 (the documented header-bump rebase) accepted; `header_version()` = 2.
- PROBE3 (control): a tail on v1 is now refused — `Err(HeaderVersionChanged)`, as designed.
- PROBE4: a snapshot on header v1 again (correct session nonce, correct `prev_frame_digest` naming the v2 snapshot, signed by the pinned source) is **accepted**; `header_version()` returns to 1 and the cursor is rebased onto the v1 chain base (ordinal 3, v1-base chain verified equal).
- PROBE5: after that downgrade snapshot, a tail on v1 is **accepted** — the guard PROBE3 demonstrated is gone.
- PROBE6 (control): in a fresh session, a same-version (v1) snapshot rebase — the legitimate compaction case — is accepted (`Ok(Snapshot)`) and must stay accepted.

Dedup: title/keyword searches for `replication snapshot`, `replication header version`, `ReplicationTracker` across open and recently closed issues find only the #806 feature epic (the phased replication plan itself) — no issue covers snapshot header-version regression. Lane A and lane B filings today covered references, serve bindings, chat-presence, currency validation, world_caps, peers, and journal torn-tails — not the replication tracker.

## Why it matters

The tracker is the receiver-side trust boundary for journal replication: every later phase applies whatever it accepts. All of its other state transitions are monotone or refuse regression — cursors refuse gaps, replays, and forks; tails refuse any header change. The snapshot path is the one place state can move *backwards* in version while the frame chain stays perfectly valid, so neither the frame-chain check nor the signature check catches it. If a writer-side bug (or a writer reading a stale journal header after a restart) ever emits an old-version snapshot, every replica silently rolls its header version back and resumes accepting old-version tails — the failure surfaces much later, if at all, as a replica that disagrees with its own persisted header.

## Acceptance criteria

- `ReplicationTracker::accept` refuses a Snapshot whose `header_version` is lower than the tracker's current `header_version` (e.g. `HeaderVersionChanged`, or a dedicated error variant), leaving tracker state unchanged.
- Snapshots with an equal header version (compaction rebase) and with a higher supported header version (header-bump rebase, existing test `snapshot_rebases_the_chain_on_a_header_bump`) are still accepted.
- New unit tests cover: downgrade snapshot refused after a bump; the refused frame leaves cursor and header version untouched; a v1 tail remains refused after the downgrade attempt.
- Existing replication tests pass (`cargo test` for the `world::replication` module, on the laptop or CI).

title: id(repl): PR #3096 source pipe scan mistakes a |> inside $(...)/backticks for an outer pipe — valid lines rejected as trailing-placeholder errors

body:
## Finding

PR #3096 (merged, head `1b0327c346`) added a source-level pipe validation that runs before any substitution stage, to reject a trailing `-` content placeholder before shell code executes. Its pipe locator does not skip command-substitution bodies, so a `|>` that appears inside a `$(...)` or backtick body is mistaken for an outer REPL pipe — and an otherwise valid line is rejected with the trailing-placeholder error. Codex raised this as a P2 on the PR (comment 4432995812); it was never replied to, and the PR's final Codex review state on the merged head is `has_unresolved_findings: true`.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/3096 — merged 2026-11-01, merge commit `d00c6d10aafb479cc92d6ae85b8b78f04c3cba54`, final head `1b0327c3467ddb1b366d6c7b6f7e1aa8a82755eb`.
- Current main (`d1de7ee86`): `pkgs/id/src/repl/input.rs:385` `source_pipe_position` locates pipes with `find_unquoted_from(line, "|>", &[], from)` — the finder tracks quote state only; it has no notion of `$(...)`/backtick nesting, and the source-level call passes no protected spans. The check at `input.rs:442-449` then applies `has_trailing_placeholder` to whatever follows that first `|>`.
- Codex example: `get $(echo filename # |>) -` previously produced `Ready("get filename -")` (correctly requesting stdout); on current main the scan finds the `|>` inside the substitution (where it sits in a shell comment), takes the rest as the pipe's right side, and returns the trailing-placeholder error. The backtick equivalent regresses the same way.
- Verified still present on current main by reading `source_pipe_position` / `find_unquoted_from` at `pkgs/id/src/repl/input.rs:217-251,385-406` — no substitution-body skipping exists.
- Dedupe: searched open + closed issues for `3096 placeholder`, `source_pipe_position`, `substitution bodies pipe` (2026-11-02) — only the parent fix #2280 (closed) and the unrelated rescan issue #2281 (closed) match; neither covers this.

## Why it matters

The REPL preprocessor must not reject a line for an operator that is data/shell-code inside a substitution. This is a behavior regression introduced by a merged PR: a previously working input form now fails with a misleading diagnostic (it blames a trailing placeholder that is not a pipe placeholder at all).

## Acceptance criteria

- `source_pipe_position` (or its replacement) skips `$(...)` and backtick bodies when locating the outer pipe, while retaining the early, pre-substitution validation of genuine outer pipes that #3096 added.
- Regression test: `get $(echo filename # |>) -` (and a backtick equivalent) preprocesses to the same `Ready` result as before #3096.
- Existing #3096 tests still pass: trailing-placeholder rejection happens before substitution execution, here-string payloads stay literal, and the side-effect marker test still proves ordering.
- `cargo test --lib repl::` passes in CI.

title: chat: broadcast fan-out runs each Send in its own goroutine — messages arrive out of order and a stalled session piles up unbounded blocked goroutines

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/chat
labels.description: Package/app: chat (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`app.send` in `pkgs/chat/main.go` fans a chat message out with one new goroutine per recipient (`go p.Send(msg)`, main.go:52-54). Nothing serializes those goroutines, so:

1. **Broadcast order is not preserved.** Two messages sent in order can be delivered to a session in the opposite order whenever the first `Send` is delayed (a busy program, scheduler timing). Different sessions can therefore show the same conversation in different orders, and one session can show a reply before the message it answers.
2. **A stalled session accumulates unbounded goroutines.** `tea.Program.Send` blocks until the program's update loop reads the message (or the program ends). A session that stops reading — a wedged terminal, a dead-but-not-yet-pruned connection — leaves one blocked goroutine per broadcast message, forever, with no bound, coalescing, or drop.

## Evidence (main @ 30ce6be56, verified this run)

- `pkgs/chat/main.go:46-55` — `send` copies the registry under `RLock`, then `for _, p := range progs { go p.Send(msg) }`. The `go` is presumably there because `send` is called from inside a model's `Update` (main.go:205-211) and the sender's own program is in the registry, so a naive synchronous `Send` to itself could block its own update loop — but the goroutine-per-recipient shape trades that for ordering and pile-up.
- Laptop probe (verbatim `main.go`/`main_test.go` from current main, md5 main.go ed60f0ca59fe0cec95101087ca792655; probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-chatorder/` on the laptop):
  - PROBE1: a recipient whose `Send` for the text `first` sleeps 150 ms before recording received two broadcasts issued in order `[first second]` as `[second first]` — order inverted at one recipient.
  - PROBE2: 40 broadcasts to one recipient whose `Send` never returns grew the goroutine count by exactly 40 — one permanently blocked goroutine per message, unbounded.
  - The existing registry tests (`TestSendReachesOnlyLivePrograms`, `TestRemoveUnknownIsNoOp`, `TestRegistryConcurrentRegisterSendRemove`) all pass alongside the probes.

## Why it matters

A chat room's one shared truth is the order of its messages. Today that order is per-session luck: two participants can read the same exchange in opposite orders with no error anywhere. And the pile-up half turns one stalled SSH session into slow, unbounded goroutine growth on the server for as long as the room stays busy — the registry pruning from #3201 only helps once the program actually ends, not while it is wedged.

## Acceptance criteria

- Broadcasts are delivered to each live program in the order `send` was called: a probe in the style of PROBE1 (a recipient whose first `Send` is delayed) records `[first second]`, and a multi-recipient probe shows every recipient recording the same order.
- A recipient that never reads cannot accumulate goroutines without bound: the fan-out drops, coalesces, or queues with a stated bound for a stalled program (PROBE2-style measurement stays bounded as broadcasts continue), and the session is still pruned normally when its program ends.
- Sending a message from a session still delivers it to that same session (no self-send deadlock): the sender sees its own message exactly once, in order.
- Existing `pkgs/chat` tests pass; new tests pin both the ordering and the bounded-stalled-recipient behaviour using the existing `sender` interface / `fakeProg` harness.

Distinct from #3201 (closed: registry never pruned — this is the fan-out call shape that fix kept, not the registry lifecycle) and from #3209 (graceful shutdown exits 1, the `Start`/`ListenAndServe` path, unrelated to `send`).

body:
## Problem

`bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs` is the one proxy the #3186 fix missed. Its chat-completions handler still assembles the request body by string-concatenating each network chunk:

```js
// bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs:988-990 (main 3d5023d0)
if (req.method === "POST" && url.pathname === "/v1/chat/completions") {
  let raw = "";
  for await (const part of req) raw += part;
```

`raw += part` coerces each `Buffer` chunk to a UTF-8 string **separately**. A multibyte character whose bytes straddle a chunk boundary is decoded as U+FFFD replacement characters on both sides of the split — exactly the bug #3186 fixed in the other eight proxies (`bin/request-body.mjs`'s `createRequestBodyCollector`, PR #4322 / commit 7733c688), whose fix commit touched agy, antigravity-ls, claude-code, clef, codex, commandcode, design-code and muse proxies but not this one. #3186's own title scopes it to those 8 proxies, and this file is not among them.

The corrupted body is still valid JSON, so the request succeeds (HTTP 200) and the leaf provider receives silently mangled user content — no error anywhere.

## Verified (this run, laptop probe)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneA-routeutf8/probe.mjs` — runs the real proxy (laptop clone at main 3d5023d0, `bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs` md5 c7ad0712, matching the sandbox clone) against a stub leaf that decodes its received body correctly (Buffer concat), with a raw-socket chunked-encoding client:

- Control (whole body in one chunk): leaf receives `"café ☃ fin"` — intact.
- Test (chunk split inside the `é` bytes 0xC3|0xA9 and inside the `☃` bytes 0xE2|0x98 0x83): leaf receives `"caf�� ��� fin"` — every split character replaced by U+FFFD, response still `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`.

## Secondary facet: no body size bound

The same loop accumulates `raw` with no cap (no 413 / length check anywhere in the file — grep for `413|content-length|maxBytes` is empty). The sibling proxies bound bodies at 20–50 MB via the collector and answer 413. A client (or a stuck sender) can grow this proxy's memory unboundedly with one request.

## Why it matters

This proxy is the fleet's routing door for OpenAI-compatible clients (#2518); chat traffic routinely carries non-ASCII content (accented text, CJK, emoji, math symbols), and TCP chunk boundaries are not under the sender's control — any sufficiently large or unluckily segmented request can be silently corrupted in transit while every health signal stays green.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The `/v1/chat/completions` body is collected as bytes and decoded once after the full body arrives — e.g. via the shared `createRequestBodyCollector` from `bin/request-body.mjs`, as in the other eight proxies.
- [ ] Regression test in `bin/opencode-route-proxy.test.mjs`: a chunked request whose chunk boundary falls inside a multibyte UTF-8 character reaches the leaf byte-for-byte intact (the probe above is a ready-made repro).
- [ ] The body is size-bounded with a 413 response past the cap, consistent with the sibling proxies (20–50 MB range; pick and document one).
- [ ] No other per-chunk string coercion of request bodies remains in this file.

Related: #3186 (closed — the same bug in the other eight proxies), #4259 (this proxy's window-time validation).

title: aggregator(views): ViewsStore load accepts duplicate ids, duplicate names and multiple defaults — one remove(id) then silently deletes two distinct views

labels.name: app/pm-stack
labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

body:
## Problem

`ViewsStore` enforces its cross-row invariants only in the mutating methods, never at load:

- `save()` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/views.ts:276-280) and `rename()` (:296-302) refuse a second view with the same name (case-insensitive) for one owner.
- `setDefault()` (:322-337) maintains at most one default per owner.
- View ids are treated as identity everywhere: `get()` (:268) finds by id, actions address one view by id.

But `doLoad()` (:205-225) validates rows only per-row via `isSavedView` (:88-104) — the #4150 hardening checks each row's shape and quarantines the file if a row is malformed. It performs **no cross-row check**: duplicate ids, duplicate per-owner names, and multiple per-owner defaults all load verbatim (`this.views = rows.filter(isSavedView)`).

## Verified this run

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-viewsload/probe.ts` against the real `views.ts` @ `23c2c514` (md5 `c682e11f5536262812db98431838d6b2`, matched on sandbox and laptop). A store file holding 5 shape-valid rows for one owner — ids `vw-a` (name `Alpha`, default), `vw-b` (name `Beta`, default), `vw-dup` (name `Gamma`), `vw-dup` (name `Delta`), `vw-e` (name `alpha`) — loaded with:

- `loaded_count 5` — no quarantine, no complaint;
- two defaults for the owner; `defaultFor` silently returns `vw-a` (first after the createdAt sort — the two rows even share a timestamp);
- `get("vw-dup")` returns only `Gamma`;
- **`remove("vw-dup", owner)` returned true and deleted BOTH `Gamma` and `Delta`** (count 5 → 3), because `remove()` (:309-316) filters by id — and the deletion was persisted (a reloaded store also shows 3 rows).

So one delete-view action addressed to a single view can silently delete a second, distinct saved view, permanently, the moment a store file ever contains a duplicated id (hand edit, file merge, an older/buggier writer, a restored backup). The duplicate-name pair likewise breaks the invariant `save()` promises later callers, and duplicate defaults make the landing-page default an accident of row order.

## Why it matters

Saved views are per-person dashboard state reached through the audited action path; the store's own discipline elsewhere is fail-loud (quarantine, never silently overwrite — module header, views.ts:10-14). Silently accepting cross-row duplicates converts a data anomaly into silent data loss on the next routine delete, instead of a loud quarantine at load when the file can still be preserved.

## Acceptance criteria

- Loading a store file whose rows violate a cross-row invariant (duplicate view id; duplicate name per owner, case-insensitive; more than one `isDefault` per owner) is refused the same way malformed rows are: the file is quarantined with a loud log naming the violation, and the store starts empty — OR the loader deterministically repairs with an explicit log line per dropped/demoted row. Silent verbatim acceptance is the bug.
- A regression test in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/views.test.ts`: a file with a duplicated id loads per the chosen policy, and a subsequent `remove` of one view can never delete a second distinct view.
- Existing views tests pass (`bun test` in pm-stack/aggregator), including the #4150 malformed-row quarantine cases and the singular-default round-trip.

## Dedup / related

- #4150 (closed) covered per-row malformation at load (missing/non-string name, non-object filters) — this is the cross-row layer it did not check: every row above is individually shape-valid.
- The in-memory duplicate-name and singular-default tests in views.test.ts cover the mutating API only, not a file that already contains duplicates.

title: mcpx(mcpclient): a non-JSON 200 reply is buffered whole with no size cap — Send's fallback io.ReadAll is unbounded while the error path in the same function caps at 4 KB

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/mcpx/internal/mcpclient/http.go` `HTTPTransport.Send` handles a 2xx reply whose body is not SSE by decoding the first JSON value (http.go:204-209). When that decode fails — the body is not JSON at all — the fallback hands the body on whole "for push to judge":

```go
rest, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)   // http.go:218 — no cap
...
b := append(head.buf.Bytes(), rest...)
if len(bytes.TrimSpace(b)) > 0 {
    t.push(b)
}
```

`io.ReadAll` here has **no size bound at all**, and the bytes are also duplicated through the `firstValue` tee buffer on the way in. The same function's non-2xx path, a few lines earlier (http.go:167), is careful to cap its body read at `defaults.HTTPErrorBodyLimit` (4 KB, "enough for a JSON-RPC error, not enough for an HTML error page to matter") — the garbage path for a *successful* status has no equivalent bound. A remote MCP server (or a proxy/error page in front of one) that answers 200 with a large or endless non-JSON body makes mcpx buffer the entire body in memory and deliver it as a single incoming "message". The HTTP client's overall timeout bounds the time, not the bytes: a fast server can push gigabytes inside it.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe (full verbatim copy of `pkgs/mcpx` @ `fa28f499`; `http.go` md5 `691386b8…` identical in both clones; probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-mcpclientbody/`, test `internal/mcpclient/probe_http_test.go`, `go test` on the laptop):

- Test server replies 200, `Content-Type: application/json`, body = `"this is not json "` + 32 MiB of `x`. `Send` + `Recv` deliver a pushed message of **33,554,449 bytes** — the whole garbage body, uncapped.
- Control: a valid single-JSON reply is pushed as-is (`{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"result":{}}`) — the streaming decode path is unaffected.

## Why it matters

mcpx talks to third-party MCP servers by design; their failure modes are not under our control. The one reply shape that is definitionally not a protocol message — a body whose first value isn't even JSON — is the one shape read without any limit, turning a misbehaving/proxied upstream into unbounded memory growth in the client. The house already picked the bound for exactly this situation (4 KB error-body cap in the same function); the fallback just never got it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The non-JSON fallback read in `Send` is bounded (e.g. `io.LimitReader` at a named limit — `defaults.HTTPErrorBodyLimit` or a new explicit one); a body past the limit is truncated or surfaced as an error, never buffered whole.
- [ ] Regression test: an oversized non-JSON 200 body does not produce an oversized pushed message (probe above reproduces at 32 MiB today); a small non-JSON body keeps today's hand-on-whole behaviour; the valid-JSON and SSE paths are unchanged.
- [ ] `go test ./internal/mcpclient/` passes.

Distinct from: #2114 (open — daemon chat-completions proxy buffering an upstream response; different package, direction, and code path), #2082 (closed — daemon *request* bodies bypassing `http.*BodyLimit`).

title: proxy-relay: endpoint.json is never republished after a failover — relayTo keeps naming the first target while /health reports the new preferredTarget

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.name: app/proxy-relay
labels.description: bin/proxy-relay.mjs sandbox-to-laptop relay

body:
## Summary

`bin/proxy-relay.mjs` publishes its discovery file `<name>/endpoint.json` exactly once, at listen time, with `relayTo` naming the then-current preferred target. When a later connection fails over to another target, `preferred` changes in memory — and the relay's own `/health` reports the new `preferredTarget` correctly — but `endpoint.json` is never republished, so the file keeps naming the dead/old target for the rest of the process's life.

## Evidence (verified this run, 2026-11-02)

- `bin/proxy-relay.mjs:60-81` — `publishEndpoint()` writes `relayTo: \`${TARGET_HOST}:${preferred}\``.
- `bin/proxy-relay.mjs:186` — the only `publishEndpoint()` call is in the `server.listen` callback.
- `bin/proxy-relay.mjs` (`tryTargets`, ~line 128-140) — on a successful CONNECT it sets `preferred = p` and returns the socket; no republish.
- The local `/health` handler reads the live variable (`preferredTarget: preferred`), so `/health` and `endpoint.json` disagree after any failover.

Laptop probe (Node v24.21.0, real `proxy-relay.mjs` from this repo, md5 `063d33753752c1ae6541773a2468781f`; fake tunnel proxy that 503s the first target port and 200s the second; `RELAY_TARGET_PORTS=19001,19002`):

```text
endpoint.json BEFORE failover: {"host":"127.0.0.1","port":18999,...,"relayTo":"100.99.113.103:19001"}
health AFTER failover: {"status":"ok",...,"preferredTarget":19002}
endpoint.json AFTER failover: {"host":"127.0.0.1","port":18999,...,"relayTo":"100.99.113.103:19001"}
```

One forwarded request forced the failover (first CONNECT refused, second accepted, `preferred` became 19002); the discovery file still claims the relay forwards to 19001.

## Why it matters

`endpoint.json` is the fleet's discovery surface for these proxies — the file other tooling reads to learn where a service actually points (the relay's header comment: "Like the fleet proxies, it publishes `<name>/endpoint.json`"). Port flips are the relay's normal operating mode (canonical vs +1000 alternate ports, per the same header comment), so after the first flip the published `relayTo` is wrong indefinitely and silently: anyone or anything diagnosing "which laptop port is the sandbox actually reaching?" from the file gets the port that just failed.

Related but distinct: #2847 (bytes dropped during CONNECT), #2234 (no client timeout), #1844 (target-list parsing). None covers the stale discovery file.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] After a failover changes `preferred`, `endpoint.json` is republished with the new `relayTo` (same atomic tmp+rename write as at listen).
- [ ] `/health`'s `preferredTarget` and `endpoint.json`'s `relayTo` agree after a failover in a test/probe like the one above.
- [ ] No republish storm: republishing happens on a preferred-target change, not per connection.
- [ ] A regression test (there is currently no `proxy-relay.test.mjs`) covers: start → failover → endpoint file names the new target.

title: The app folder is the unit of trust — one gate for what an app manifest may name (pkgs/id app_manifest)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: epic

labels.name: effort/l

labels.name: meta/enriched

labels.name: kind/design

labels.name: source/design-architect
