body:
## Summary

The app-packaging design (`doc/2026-10-29T12-50-36Z_design_id_app_packaging` §2) states the model in one line: "Everything is relative to the app folder. No absolute paths, no references outside the folder" — the folder is copyable as a unit, its name must equal the app `id`, and discovery (§3) validates and registers the app, degrading per-app with a named error. Discovery was built under #2324 (closed) and the gate in `pkgs/id/src/app_manifest.rs` has been tightened field by field since (#4063 / PR #4082). Six filings in two days show it is still partial in a patterned way — every one is a place where the gate checks one field, one list, or one level and trusts the rest:

- **#4059** — `[resources].files` is never inspected: `files = ["../../etc/passwd", "/etc/passwd", "assets/**"]` is accepted, while `program.source` is component-checked. The pack step will package and content-hash exactly these entries as a set.
- **#4067** — `discover_apps` follows symlinks (`is_dir`, `join("app.toml")`), and the id-match uses the symlink's name, so an app folder symlinked to a directory **outside** the apps root registers as a local app, errors=0.
- **#4085** — the #4082 duplicate gate covers only `capabilities.request`: duplicate `cli.commands` pass, and the capability duplicate check compares raw strings while the blank check trims, so `" store.read "` is stored verbatim as a distinct request — a capability name no exact-match check will ever match.
- **#4168** — `[resources].files` has no blank/duplicate gate at all (blank, whitespace-only, duplicate, padded-duplicate all parse). Its acceptance explicitly defers its duplicate rule to "the same normalisation rule the #4085 fix chooses".
- **#4060** — `[interfaces.web]` checks only `mode` and `route.starts_with('/')`: `route = "/../escape path"` and `socket = "https://evil.example/ws"` are accepted, and `discover_apps` registers two apps on the same route with zero errors. #2325 (open) will parameterise the host's `/world` route and `/ws/world` channel from these fields.
- **#4061** — `discover_apps` special-cases a missing root (`ErrorKind::NotFound` → default discovery): zero apps, **zero errors**, and serve never logs the root it scanned — a mispointed `ID_APPS_DIR` is indistinguishable from zero apps installed.

Three origins leave a ruling open (#4067's symlink stance, #4085's trim-vs-reject, #4061's layer) and #4168 defers its ruling to #4085's. This design states the contract once and records those rulings. It was the standing candidate named at design-architect pass 35; the currency_poc cluster filed the same evening was assessed and not originated (heterogeneous mechanisms, complete per-issue acceptance, no unrecorded shared rule — recorded in the design doc).

Full design doc: `files/designs/code-id-app-manifest-folder-contract.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Audit baseline: origin/main `cc5effd8` (the whole of `app_manifest.rs` read verbatim at HEAD this pass; all six defects present at the cited sites).

## The contract

> **A discovered app is exactly its folder.** Every path a manifest names resolves inside the folder, under the same component rule `program.source` already carries. The folder itself is a directory under the apps root — a symlink is followed only when its resolved target stays inside the root, otherwise it is a named per-app error. Every list field obeys one entry rule (non-blank, unpadded, no duplicates — the gate names authoring mistakes, it does not absorb or rewrite them). Routing keys are path-shaped and unique across the discovered set, first folder in sort order wins, the loser is a named error. And discovery reports what it could not do: a root it cannot read — missing included — is a named error entry, so "no apps" always means the scan actually looked.

## Recorded decisions

1. **Path fields share `program.source`'s rule (Phase 1, #4059).** `[resources].files` entries get the same component test (non-empty, every component `Component::Normal`); glob metacharacters live inside otherwise-normal components, so the design example (`assets/**`, `web/templates/**`) passes; absolute/`..`/nested-escape entries are refused naming the entry. Glob semantics belong to the future pack step, not the gate.
2. **Symlinked app folders: resolve and contain (Phase 1, #4067).** Canonicalize each candidate folder; resolution failure or a resolved path outside the canonicalized root → not registered + a named `AppDiscovery.errors` entry; a target inside the root registers normally. This generalises the fleet's landed #3999 precedent (pm-dispatch symlink confinement: resolve, require the resolved form inside the boundary) over skip-all-links — an inside-root link breaks nothing in the folder model, and double-registration is self-defeating because the id-match compares the manifest `id` to the *entry* name. Rule stated in the module doc. Symlinks *inside* a folder are not a phase; Phase 4 dispositions them.
3. **One entry rule for every list field; padding is refused, not trimmed (Phase 2, #4085 + #4168).** For `cli.commands`, `capabilities.request` and `[resources].files`: non-blank, entry equals its own trim, no duplicates — refused naming field and entry. Trim-and-store loses: the manifest is "the strict record of what an app asks for" (#4082 gate's own words), and silently rewriting a capability name hides the authoring mistake the gate exists to name — the same rationale the code pins for duplicates (rejected, not deduplicated). This supplies the normalisation rule #4168's acceptance defers to. An empty `files = []` stays legal (optional section; packages nothing) and is dispositioned explicitly by Phase 4.
4. **Routing keys are path-shaped and unique across the set (Phase 3, #4060).** `route`, and `socket` when present: starts with `/`, no `..` segment, no whitespace, no `?`, no `#`. Uniqueness is discovery-level: first in folder sort order keeps the key; a second app on the same route is not registered and gets a named error. **Socket uniqueness is pinned the same way** — a duplicate socket is the same shadowing defect on the live channel #2325 parameterises; this extends #4060's letter by its own logic and is recorded here so its triage does not re-derive it. Uniqueness against the host's own routes belongs to #2325's binding (it owns the host route table); Phase 4 records the disposition.
5. **A missing root is a named error, recorded by discovery (Phase 3, #4061).** The `NotFound` special case goes away; a missing root produces the same named error entry other `read_dir` failures produce, naming the root. Serve's existing warn-per-error loop surfaces it unchanged, every caller gets the signal, and root-missing / present-empty / present-with-N are distinguishable. This pins #4061's "triage picks the layer": the layer is discovery, where the error channel already exists.

Alternatives that lose (in the doc): six independent fixes (the rulings interact and #4168 already defers to #4085); skip-all-symlinks (against the #3999 precedent); trim-and-store (decision 3); serve-side missing-root warning (leaves `discover_apps` lying to other callers); deferring confinement to pack/serve consumers (re-derives the rule per consumer); folding into #3068 (JS/TS parsed-shape contract — different gate, the pass-28 disposition).

## Phased breakdown

- **Phase 1 — the folder is the unit (adopted: #4059 + #4067).** `[resources].files` under `program.source`'s component rule; symlinked folders resolved and contained, outside-root refused with a named error, rule in the module doc. Lands first: the trust boundary every consumer relies on.
- **Phase 2 — one entry rule for every list (adopted: #4085 + #4168).** Duplicate `cli.commands` refused; padded entries refused on all three list fields; the missing blank/duplicate gate for `[resources].files` under the same rule (decision 3). Independent of Phase 1 in code. (#4168 is already claimed/blocked in the fleet — consistent with waiting on exactly this rule.)
- **Phase 3 — routing keys and scan visibility (adopted: #4060 + #4061).** Route/socket segment sanity; route + socket uniqueness in `discover_apps` (first wins, loser named); missing root as a named error entry. Independent of Phases 1–2 in code. #2325 is the named downstream consumer.
- **Phase 4 — closing audit (new issue, gated on Phases 1–3).** Field-by-field disposition of every `AppManifest` field and every `discover_apps` behaviour against this contract, recorded in the `app_manifest.rs` module doc. Required dispositions: in-folder symlinks (`program.source` existence check + pack-time resource resolution); empty `files = []`; route edge spellings (trailing slash, `//`, `route = "/"`); app-`id` uniqueness (structural via folder-name equality — stated); `[program].kind`'s free-string vocabulary; uniqueness against host routes (#2325's disposition).

Open questions stay in the design doc (in-folder symlinks at pack time; glob semantics for the pack step; `ID_APPS_DIR`'s CWD-relative default beyond the new visibility; a `[program].kind` vocabulary once a second kind exists).

Related: packaging design `doc/2026-10-29T12-50-36Z_design_id_app_packaging` (#2026 / epic #2056) — this contract operationalises its §2/§3 at the gate without re-opening its schema; #2324 (closed, built discovery); #2325 (open, Phase 3's consumer); #4063 / PR #4082 (the partial gate); #3999 (symlink precedent); #2898 / #3231 / #3455 (same crate, validate-at-the-gate family, no field overlap).

🤖 Design architect pass 36 (2026-11-01), audit at origin/main `cc5effd8`.

## Acceptance criteria
- Every `AppManifest` field and `discover_apps` behaviour named in the design has an explicit disposition — gated by a named rule, or deliberately ungated with the reason recorded — in the pkgs/id module documentation.
- Phases 1–3 (issues #4059, #4067, #4085, #4168, #4060, #4061) have landed or been dispositioned, and the Phase 4 audit (issue #4203) records the closing field-by-field disposition.
- A manifest naming an absolute path, or a path escaping its app folder, is rejected with a named error at discovery — for every field that can name a path.
- Duplicate, blank, or whitespace-padded entries in any list field are rejected under the one shared entry rule.
- Each dispositioned rule is covered by tests in pkgs/id.

title: codedb-bridge: daemon fetch has no timeout — a hung daemon hangs the call forever and blocks bridge exit on stdin close

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: app/codedb-bridge
labels.description: bin/codedb-bridge.mjs — stdio MCP bridge to the shared codedb daemon

body:
## Problem

`bin/codedb-bridge.mjs` (new in PR #4171, for issue #4120) calls the codedb daemon with no timeout anywhere:

- `createHandler`'s `callTool` awaits the fetch with no signal: `bin/codedb-bridge.mjs:192` — `res = await fetchFn(\`${daemonUrl}${mapped.route}\`)`.
- `main` wires the real fetch the same way: `bin/codedb-bridge.mjs:251` — `fetchFn: (url) => fetch(url)` — no `AbortSignal.timeout(...)`, no `AbortController`, no deadline constant anywhere in the file.

A daemon that accepts the connection but never responds (wedged index rebuild, half-open socket, a daemon stuck behind a lock) therefore hangs that `tools/call` forever.

## Why it matters

1. The caller never gets an error it can act on — not even the bridge's own "daemon unreachable" message (`:194-199`), which only covers a rejected fetch. The line-293 comment says "the caller times out on that one id", but nothing in the bridge ever resolves that id.
2. It defeats the bridge's own exit path: `main`'s `maybeExit` (`:261-262`) refuses to exit while `pending !== 0`, and a hung call never settles (`:269-271`). So after the MCP client closes stdin, the bridge process leaks indefinitely instead of exiting — exactly the per-session process accumulation the bridge was built to eliminate (#4120 / #2225).
3. The shared-bridge design (mcpx can share one bridge across sessions, `:255-258`) makes one wedged daemon call a standing leak for every session that touches it.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneA-codedb/` (verbatim copy of `bin/codedb-bridge.mjs` from main `199a7d27`, md5 `ca05ede20d2ae1a4760297bbe9320c58` on both hosts, node v24.21.0):

- `createHandler` with a never-resolving `fetchFn`: the `tools/call` promise was **STILL-PENDING after 600 ms** (and by construction pending forever — no timer exists in the code path).
- `grep` over the file: no `AbortSignal`, `AbortController`, `timeout`, or `setTimeout` outside the tests.

Distinct from issue #2114 (mcpx's Go chat-completions proxy upstream timeout — a different component and language).

## Acceptance criteria

- A daemon fetch is bounded by a deadline (a named constant; configurable via env if that fits the existing `CODEDB_DAEMON_URL` config style).
- On expiry the `tools/call` returns an MCP error result (`isError: true`) naming the daemon URL, the route, and the timeout — the caller can retry or restart the daemon.
- After stdin closes, the bridge exits even if a call was hung (the hung call is aborted/settled, so `pending` reaches 0).
- New test in `bin/codedb-bridge.test.mjs`: a stub daemon/fetch that never responds produces the timeout error within a bounded, test-scale time; the existing slow-but-finite test (1.2 s daemon delay, PR #4171) and the stdin-close flush test still pass — pick the default deadline comfortably above legitimate slow daemon responses.

title: id(aliases): a whitespace-only alias claim displays as a blank alias — aliases_of excludes empty text but not whitespace-only text

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

In `pkgs/id`, a tag claim whose alias value is only whitespace is treated as a real alias and displayed as the object's name, even though the alias module's own rule is that an empty alias is not an alias.

- `pkgs/id/src/tag_claims.rs` — `check_op` accepts a `tag.set` value of 1..=512 bytes that is NFC. A value of `"   "` (spaces) passes every check, so such a claim is a valid, signed, syncable event.
- `pkgs/id/src/aliases.rs:105-118` — `aliases_of` filters out only a bare tag or a value where `text.is_empty()`. A whitespace-only value is not empty, so it becomes an `Alias { text: "   " }`.
- `pkgs/id/src/aliases.rs` module docs state the intended rule: "A bare tag, or an alias with empty text, is not an alias." A whitespace-only alias renders as blank — indistinguishable from empty — but is not excluded.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneB-aliasws/` with `aliases_of`/`shown_for` copied verbatim from `pkgs/id/src/aliases.rs` @ `11cb8966` (md5 `46b7428bd37db1c5d9c96687db6e0b72`, identical in the sandbox clone and the laptop checkout):

- value `Some("   ")` → `aliases_of` returns 1 alias with text `"   "`, and `shown_for` returns `Shown::Only(..)` — the view shows a blank alias as the object's only name.
- value `Some("")` (control) → 0 aliases, as documented.
- value `Some("  Ann  ")` → stored/displayed verbatim with padding (related display wart; the whitespace-only case is the bug).

## Why it matters

Alias display is what views show instead of a raw ID (`aliases::rows` / `Shown::Only`). Any peer can publish a whitespace-only alias claim on a group or user subject; a lone such claim makes the object display with a blank alias, and alongside a real claim it forces the row to `Contested` with one visibly-empty contender. The fix belongs in one place (`aliases_of` is documented as "the one place that decides what a view shows for an object's aliases").

## Acceptance criteria

- `aliases_of` treats a value whose trimmed form is empty the same as an empty value: it is not an alias (does not appear in `Row::aliases`, does not make a row `Contested`, does not become `Shown::Only`).
- A unit test covers whitespace-only alias values (spaces/tabs) next to the existing empty-value test in `pkgs/id/src/aliases.rs`.
- Existing alias behaviour for non-blank values is unchanged (no silent trimming of real alias text unless that is decided and tested separately).

body:
Follow-up to #1965 / PR #4051 (Codex P2 finding 4438238077, dispositioned in cea81a390).

A paste >1 MiB can be a single ProseMirror replace step. The client now withholds such a step (kept locally, error logged) instead of sending it to be refused by the server's 1 MiB frame cap and discarded by the reconnect re-init — but it never syncs, and later steps queue behind it.

Splitting the step on the wire is not safe: prosemirror-collab confirms unconfirmed steps by count from the server echo. The fix belongs at dispatch time in the editor layer: chunk a large text insertion into several transactions (each producing bounded steps) before the steps enter the collab unconfirmed queue.

Acceptance:
- A >1 MiB text paste syncs to the server in bounded Steps messages and is visible to other joiners.
- No step is lost or double-confirmed; version/history stay consistent under the chunked dispatch.
- Tests cover a single oversized insertion end to end at the client layer.

## Acceptance criteria

- A single-step text insertion larger than the server's 1 MiB frame cap is chunked at dispatch time in the editor layer into several transactions, each producing bounded steps, before the steps enter the collab unconfirmed queue.
- Chunked insertions sync to the server and to other clients in order; no step is withheld locally or discarded on reconnect re-init.
- Insertions at or below the cap keep the existing single-step path unchanged.
- A regression test covers a >1 MiB single-step paste syncing successfully (via CI on the fix PR).

title: id(boards): BoardFork records are in no board's replication set — fork provenance never replicates and replicas still report Complete

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Summary

A signed `BoardFork` record (`BoardObject::BoardFork`, pkgs/id/src/boards.rs:232-238) belongs to **no board's replication set**, so fork provenance can never replicate: `export_board` / `replicate_board_from` never transfer it, and `replica_status_against` still reports the replica `Complete` — the exact silent-lag failure the federation design (#3806) says must never happen.

## Evidence (verified this run, main @ 74a872a4)

- `BoardObject::board_ref()` returns `None` for `BoardFork` (boards.rs:389, grouped with `Board` and `Theme`).
- `board_object_set()` (boards.rs:899-935) seeds the set with objects whose hash is the board root or whose `board_ref() == Some(board)`, then expands only `Board::{forked_from, theme_ref}` and `Theme::forked_from` dependencies. A `BoardFork` matches neither seed rule for its source board nor for its fork board, and no closure step adds it.
- Laptop probe (verbatim `boards.rs` @ 74a872a4, md5 `e142727a25d638136a27ac9ecfb7c3f9`, in `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneB-boardsfork/` on the laptop): source board + one frontier thread + forked board + a valid signed `BoardFork` record citing the thread as its frontier (graph len = 4). Results:
  - `board_object_set(source)` contains fork record: **false**
  - `board_object_set(fork)` contains fork record: **false**
  - `export_board(source)` len = 2, `export_board(fork)` len = 2 (of 4 graph objects)
  - `replicate_board_from(fork)` into a fresh graph: state `Complete`, transferred = 2, replica has **no** fork record; `replica_status_against` reports expected=2 / present=2 / missing=0.
- No test in boards.rs constructs a `BoardFork` object at all (the replication tests cover themes, ancestor roots, and listings only), so the gap is untested as well as unfixed.

Secondary, same fix area: the fork's cited `source_frontier` objects are scoped to the *source* board, so even the fork board's set omits the frontier content the fork record says it starts from.

## Why it matters

The `BoardFork` record is the only signed statement of a fork's provenance and cited starting frontier. A replica that reports `Complete` without it presents an incomplete fork history as fully converged — silently, which the module docs explicitly promise not to do ("a lagging replica is never silently presented as current", boards.rs:1012-1023 area / module header).

## Acceptance criteria

- A `BoardFork` record is included in a well-defined board replication set (its fork board's, its source board's, or both — the choice is stated in the module docs), and `board_object_set`'s dependency closure pulls in everything `validate_links` needs to accept it on a fresh graph (both roots, and the cited frontier objects if the record travels with the fork board).
- `replicate_board_from` transfers the fork record; a replica of a forked board holds it afterwards.
- `replica_status_against` can no longer report `Complete` for a graph missing an in-set fork record.
- New tests construct a real `BoardFork` (none exist today), assert it is in the chosen set(s), and assert end-to-end replication of a forked board including its fork record and cited frontier.
- Existing boards tests still pass.

```
retrying the bulk session after a transport error: the sync session did not finish within 60s
assertion left == right failed: left 0, right 210 (accepted tally)
test result: 1521 passed; 1 failed
```

Re-run in isolation immediately after: **ok in 39.36s** — the test itself takes ~39s of wall time unloaded, so its internal 60s retry deadline has little headroom when the machine is saturated. Not a logic failure: zero events were accepted because the retried session never got scheduled time, not because sync misbehaved.

Context: the same suite at the same code was fully green (1514 passed) earlier the same day at lower load. This is a robustness/headroom issue in the test (deadline vs. work size), worth a look by the log_sync owner — e.g. scale the deadline, or reduce the per-test event volume. priority/low: it only bites on loaded shared machines, but it did block a verification cycle for the #3720 fold.

## Acceptance criteria
- `log_sync::tests::test_a_bulk_session_moves_every_event_across_pages` passes reliably under parallel load comparable to the flake (deadline scaled to work size, or per-test event volume reduced, with the rationale recorded on this issue).
- The full `cargo test -p id --lib` suite is green on a loaded shared machine, not only in isolation.

title: chore(deps): remove the activitywatch overrides (peewee 3 pin + aw-qt wrapper args) once nixpkgs' activitywatch builds stock

labels.name: kind/infrastructure

body:
## Context

Found via #2715 (the 2026-10-30 nixpkgs update). The update moves the `nixpkgs-25` input from e7439b6b to 31ecbaca. `nixos/environment/default.nix` takes `activitywatch` from that input's raw `legacyPackages` segment. On the new pin, `python3.14-aw-core-0.5.17` fails its `pythonRuntimeDepsCheck`:

```
Checking runtime dependencies for aw_core-0.5.17-py3-none-any.whl
  - peewee==3.* not satisfied by version 4.4.0
```

aw-core 0.5.17's wheel metadata pins `peewee==3.*`, but the tree now ships peewee 4.4.0. The identical aw-core derivation (and peewee 4.4.0) appears on the new master and unstable pins too, so no current pin offers a consistent set to source activitywatch from; the failure cascades aw-core -> aw-qt/aw-client -> activitywatch -> man-paths -> system-path and blocks the amd toplevel.

## The temporary fix

`nixos/environment/default.nix` extends the nixpkgs-25 legacyPackages set (`nixpkgs-25-fixed`, next to `nixpkgs-master-fixed`) with a python3 packageOverride that adds `pythonRelaxDeps = [ "peewee" ]` to aw-core, and the activitywatch segment uses the extended set. This rewrites the stale metadata pin so the runtime-deps check accepts peewee 4.4.0. Caveat: it does not prove aw-core's peewee API usage is 4.x-compatible at runtime — it is the standard nixpkgs remedy for this skew class, and activitywatch is a local user application, not a system service.

## Removal condition

Remove once stock activitywatch builds on the pin the segment consumes — i.e. upstream nixpkgs bumps aw-core for peewee 4 (or pins peewee 3 for the aw-* packages), so `python3Packages.aw-core` passes `pythonRuntimeDepsCheck` unmodified.

## Removal test

Point the activitywatch segment back at `inputs.nixpkgs-25.legacyPackages.${system}` (deleting the `nixpkgs-25-fixed` binding) and build `activitywatch` plus `config.system.build.toplevel` for amd; both must succeed, and `aw-core` should still launch (`aw-server --help` or the activitywatch binaries present in the system profile).

## Acceptance criteria

- A current nixpkgs pin (25 / master / unstable, whichever first) ships an aw-core whose `peewee` requirement is consistent with the tree's peewee version — verified by evaluating the activitywatch derivation from that pin with no overrides.
- The peewee 3 pin and aw-qt wrapper-args overrides in `nixos/environment/default.nix` are removed, and activitywatch still builds and launches from the unmodified pin.
- If no pin qualifies yet, the blocking pin state is re-recorded on the issue with the date checked (the issue stays open as the waiting record).

body:
## Problem

The fleet-feed collector's new per-section outcome metadata (#1178, landed in PR #3943) reports the **projects** section as `ok` in exactly the case where the section failed to materialize: a successful GraphQL read that returns **zero items**. The collector omits the section (its own log line calls the outcome out), but `markSection("projects", "ok")` runs unconditionally after the fetch, so the health view shows the projects section as `present: false, status: "ok"` and the dashboard is **not** degraded — the silent-failure shape the per-section status system was built to eliminate.

Every sibling section treats "read produced nothing usable" as an error:

- DNS: a register that parses to zero entries → `markSection("dns", "error", "register did not produce a valid DNS section")` (`collect-fleet-feed.ts:657`)
- Coverage: any failed repo census → `error`; all failed → `error` (`collect-fleet-feed.ts:760-764`)
- Orchestration: a section that fails its structural check → `error` (`collect-fleet-feed.ts:681`)

Projects is the only one that reports success for an omitted section.

## Evidence (verified this run, main e860d3a9)

`pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/collect-fleet-feed.ts:695-705`:

```ts
projects = await fetchProjectPool(token);
if (!projects.length) {
  console.error("collector: GitHub Project read returned zero items; projects section omitted");
  projects = undefined;
}
markSection("projects", "ok");
```

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneB-projstatus/`, Bun, importing the **real** `feed.ts` / `health.ts` / `config.ts` from the laptop clone; all three files sha256-identical to sandbox main e860d3a9 — feed.ts `36078a97…`, health.ts `0730cfd3…`, collector `6cb9a738…`; 4/4 tests pass):

- The collector's zero-items mark, `feedSectionStatus("ok", at)`, survives `sanitizeFeedMetadata` verbatim → `meta.sections.projects.status === "ok"`.
- `buildHealth` over a feed with that meta and **no** projects section yields the projects entry `{"key":"projects","status":"ok","present":false}` and `degraded: false`.
- Control — the same absence with the DNS-style `error` status: health entry shows `status: "error"` and `degraded: true`.
- Control — projects present with `ok`: `present: true`, `degraded: false`.

Consumer side: `pm-stack/aggregator/src/health.ts` `feedSections` reads `feed.meta?.sections[key]` for `status`, and `buildHealth` sets `degraded` when any section's status is `"error"` — so the collector's `ok` is the only thing standing between a zero-item Project read and a visible degradation.

## Why it matters

Project #4 is never legitimately empty (the collector reads the org project the whole dashboard is built on), so a zero-item read means a broken read — a token that lost project scope, a renamed project, a GraphQL shape change that maps to an empty list instead of throwing. Those failure modes throw today only sometimes; when they return an empty list instead, the feed quietly loses its projects section, `items()` falls back to a previous chain, and /health reports the section `ok`. That is precisely the "sections fail silently" complaint #1178 was filed to fix, reintroduced for one section by its own implementation PR (#3943).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A zero-item `fetchProjectPool` result marks the projects section `error` (with a sanitized diagnostic naming the zero-item read), matching the DNS zero-entries treatment; the section remains omitted from the feed.
- [ ] A non-empty result still marks `ok`; no-token still marks `skipped`; a thrown read still marks `error`.
- [ ] Regression coverage: a collector/health-level test shows a feed whose projects section is absent with a zero-item outcome surfaces `status: "error"` on /health and marks the view degraded, where it previously showed `ok` / not degraded.
- [ ] No other section's outcome semantics change.

Dedup: open + closed searches for collector section outcomes / FeedMetadata / projects-omitted returned only the implementation issue #1178 (closed) and Lane A's #3966 (sanitizeCollectionError redaction gaps, a different function) — no issue covers the zero-items projects outcome.

title: aggregator(feed): isQuotaPool never checks credential-row label/freshness or activeSessions — a windows-only credential row or a null session crashes renderQuota

labels.name: app/pm-stack
labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

body:
## Finding

`isQuotaPool` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/feed.ts:321-334) — the gate whose doc comment promises "One quota pool whose own shape is safe to hand to the renderers (#2429)" — validates a pool's credential rows only as *records holding a windows array*, and never checks `activeSessions` at all. `sanitizeQuotaView` (feed.ts:392-408) filters credential-row *windows* and pool windows, but passes credential `label`/`freshness` and every `activeSessions` entry through untouched. `renderQuota` then dereferences both unguarded, so one malformed row or session entry that no producer emits crashes the whole /quota render instead of dropping at the boundary like its sibling fields do (#2429's drop-and-count pattern).

The `QuotaCredentialRow` contract (model.ts:269-282) requires `label: string`, `providerId: string`, and a **required** `freshness: PoolFreshness` (`measuredAt`/`source`/`state`). The only producer, `credentialRows` (quota-current.ts:195-214), always emits all three. `activeSessions` (model.ts:256) is `{ session: string; model: string; tokens: number }[]`; the collector (scripts/collect-fleet-feed.ts:580-587) always emits that shape.

## Evidence (main 33aefa7f, verified this run)

- feed.ts:326-331 — credentials check is only `isRecord(row) && Array.isArray(row.windows)`; no `label`, `providerId`, or `freshness` check. `activeSessions` is never mentioned in the gate.
- feed.ts:399-406 — `sanitizeQuotaView` maps credential rows replacing only `windows`; a row's missing/null `freshness` survives sanitization.
- render.ts:2045-2048 — `c.freshness.state === "ok"`, `esc(c.freshness.state)`, `c.freshness.error` dereferenced unguarded on every credential row.
- render.ts:2035-2040 — `(p.activeSessions ?? []).map((s) => … s.tokens.toLocaleString())`: a non-array value, a `null` element, or an element without `tokens` all throw.
- Laptop Bun probe (~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneB-credrows/, real feed.ts/render.ts/model.ts copied from the laptop primary at 33aefa7f; sha256 feed.ts d62b3096…, render.ts 061fc8ad…, model.ts f987be93… — identical to sandbox main; control pool with a well-formed credential row + active session renders OK, 25,787 bytes):
  - `credentials: [{ windows: [] }]` (no label/providerId/freshness) → gate `true`, droppedPools=0, `renderQuota` throws `TypeError: undefined is not an object (evaluating 'c.freshness.state')`
  - `credentials: [{ …, freshness: null }]` → gate `true`, throws `TypeError: null is not an object (evaluating 'c.freshness.state')`
  - `credentials: [{ …, freshness: "ok" }]` (string) → gate `true`, renders — the row's state silently renders blank (falsified, no crash)
  - `activeSessions: [null]` → gate `true`, throws `TypeError: null is not an object (evaluating 's.session')`
  - `activeSessions: "s1"` → gate `true`, throws `TypeError: (p.activeSessions ?? []).map is not a function`
  - `activeSessions: [{ session: "s1", model: "gpt" }]` (no `tokens`) → gate `true`, throws `TypeError: undefined is not an object (evaluating 's.tokens.toLocaleString')`
  - `activeSessions: [{ …, tokens: "5000" }]` → gate `true`, renders the string verbatim (no crash; type falsified)

## Why it matters

/quota is the fleet's quota page; its feed is a hand-/script-produced JSON document, exactly the input the #2429 gate-and-sanitize boundary exists to fail soft against. Every sibling surface in the same pool — windows, burn segments, charges, subscriptions — drops malformed elements individually and counts the drops. Credential rows and active sessions are the two remaining unguarded dereferences in the same renderer: one bad row takes the whole page down (and the unsanitized shape is also served verbatim by /api/quota.json) instead of losing one row.

## Acceptance criteria

- A pool whose credential rows lack a string `label`/`providerId` or a record `freshness` with a valid `state`, or whose `activeSessions` is not an array of `{ session: string, model: string, tokens: finite number }`, no longer crashes `renderQuota`; the owning layer is pinned (extend `isQuotaPool` vs drop-and-count in `sanitizeQuotaView`, following the #2429 pattern) and applied consistently to both surfaces, with drops counted/surfaced where the sanitizer owns them.
- A well-formed pool with credential rows and active sessions (existing fixtures/tests) renders unchanged.
- Regression tests cover at least: credential row without `freshness`, `freshness: null`, `activeSessions: [null]`, a non-array `activeSessions`, and a session entry without `tokens`.

Dedup: #2429 (closed) built the pool/window gate and sanitizer — its credential check stopped at record+windows and it never touched `activeSessions`. #3427/#3428 cover quota window/burn fields, #3513/#3458 subscriptions/charges, #3897/#2417 the orchestration section — different fields in different gates. Searches for "isQuotaPool" and "activeSessions" across open and closed issues return no covering issue.

body:
## Context

The 2026-10-30 nixpkgs update (tracking: #2715) bumped nixpkgs-unstable 6510408d -> 31ecbaca. Between those revisions, nixpkgs' Haskell builder stopped adding the `pkg-config` wrapper to Haskell package build environments. `haskellPackages.regex-pcre` (pulled into the amd system closure via `haskellPackages.misfortune` -> man-paths -> system-path) runs a Cabal configure check that hard-requires the `pkg-config` program, so its build now fails deterministically:

```
Error: [Cabal-7620]
The program 'pkg-config' version >=0.9.0 is required but it could not be found.
```

Evidence: on the old pin the derivation's `nativeBuildInputs` contain `pkg-config-wrapper-0.29.2`; on the new pin they do not. A solo rebuild on the new pin fails identically (not a flake).

## The temporary override

`nixos/nixpkgs/default.nix` carries a small overlay that overrides `haskellPackages.regex-pcre` to append `pkg-config` to its `nativeBuildInputs`, restoring the old build environment for this one package.

## Removal condition

Remove the overlay when nixpkgs' Haskell builder once again provides `pkg-config` in regex-pcre's build environment (check: the stock derivation's `nativeBuildInputs` contain a pkg-config path), or when regex-pcre/misfortune leaves the amd closure.

## Removal test

Delete the overlay, then build `nix build .#nixosConfigurations.amd.pkgs.haskellPackages.regex-pcre` and the full `amd` toplevel; both must succeed.

## Acceptance criteria

- The removal condition is verified, not assumed: the stock (un-overlaid) `haskellPackages.regex-pcre` derivation's `nativeBuildInputs` contain a pkg-config path, OR regex-pcre/misfortune has left the `amd` closure.
- If the condition holds: the overlay in `nixos/nixpkgs/default.nix` is removed and both `nix build .#nixosConfigurations.amd.pkgs.haskellPackages.regex-pcre` and the full `amd` toplevel build succeed.
- If the condition does not hold yet: the check result (date + nixpkgs revision + what was observed) is recorded on this issue and the overlay stays.

title: Design: failure is not a result — one success-only memoization contract for lazy initializers (aggregator first)

labels.name: task/triage

labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: epic

labels.description: Large: multi-day or open-ended; expect staged check-ins

labels.name: app/aggregator
labels.description: Package/app: aggregator (pm-stack in this repo)

labels.name: app/pm-stack
labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: A design proposal (design-architect): multi-step, phased, decision-bearing

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Summary

Three lazy initializers in the aggregator memoize their first **failure** forever, defeating the one layer that was designed to heal:

- **#3732** — `getSupabaseClient` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/supabase.ts:43`) caches its promise once and never clears it; stacked on top, `getAlertsStore` (`src/alerts.ts:481`) caches the resulting `null` in a second, independent latch. One transient bws hiccup at first use makes the whole alert throat (ledger, dedupe, delivery state, ack) report itself unavailable until restart.
- **#3729** — `ensurePushConfigured` (`src/push.ts:26`) resolves `false` when the VAPID key is unreachable and never clears `configurePromise` on that path; its only reset (a push-service 401/403) is unreachable from the configure failure, because `sendPush` returns at the configure gate. Web Push is dead for the process lifetime after one transient failure.

Both origins are priority/high with verified laptop probes. The shared dependency already states the intended bound: `src/secrets.ts` caches a `null` for only **5 minutes** precisely so failures heal — the consumers widen that to forever.

The rule that fixes this already exists in this repo, stated for one app: #2668 recorded for pm-dispatch that "memoized init caches success only (clear-on-reject, in-flight promise still shared)", generalising `fetchGithubJwks`' success-only cache; its instance #2663 has since closed. The aggregator never adopted the rule. This design generalises it.

Full design doc: `files/designs/code-success-only-memoization.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Audit baseline: origin/main `064ce9e5` (all three latch sites read verbatim at HEAD this pass).

## The contract

> **A lazy initializer memoizes success, never failure.** Concurrent callers share the one in-flight attempt; once that attempt settles, a failure — a rejection, or a fail-soft failure *value* (`null`, `false`) — leaves no memo behind, so the next caller retries. A success is memoized for the process lifetime unless the module already has an explicit invalidation path, which stays. Per-call fail-soft behaviour is unchanged: the contract removes the *permanence*, not the posture.

Conforming embodiments already in-tree: `secrets.ts` (5-minute null cache + `forgetBwsSecret`), `dispatch/src/auth.ts` `fetchGithubJwks` (success-only), aggregator `server.ts` priming (self-clearing + 60s gate), `sources/live.ts` TTL caches (assigned only on success), `bin/antigravity-direct.mjs` token promise (cleared in `finally`).

## Recorded decisions

1. **Clear on settle, not a consumer-side failure TTL.** The shared dependency already bounds retry cost (secrets' 5-minute null cache means a retry re-reads a map, not bws); a second per-site TTL delays healing past the designed bound by an arbitrary per-site number.
2. **Every layer clears independently (stacked-latch rule).** #3732's evidence: fixing the client alone does not heal the store. "The layer below retries" is never a reason for a layer to keep a failure.
3. **Failure values count as failure.** All three sites fail soft (`.catch(() => null/false)`), so the success test is on the resolved value: non-null client/store, `true` configure.
4. **In-flight sharing preserved.** Clear at settle (a `finally`/settle handler), never before — concurrent first callers still trigger exactly one resolution.
5. **Existing invalidation stays.** Push's 401/403 reset + `forgetBwsSecret` remain the rotation path; no timers, reset endpoints, or in-call retry loops are added. Retry drivers already exist: the tick, the next request, the next send.

Alternatives that lose (in the doc): per-site failure TTLs; retry-with-backoff inside the initializer; an operator reset surface; repo-wide scope from day one (unexamined sites get dispositions in Phase 3, not presumed fixes).

## Phased breakdown

- **Phase 1 — the alerts ledger heals (adopted: #3732).** Contract applied at both layers (`getSupabaseClient`, `getAlertsStore`), fail-once-then-succeed tests per layer plus the stacked case. Lands first — every alerts surface, and #3702's throat contract, sits on this store.
- **Phase 2 — push configuration heals (adopted: #3729).** `ensurePushConfigured` clears on `false`; the 401/403 reset preserved verbatim; probe-shaped test. Independent of Phase 1 in code.
- **Phase 3 — closing inventory + contract statement (new issue, gated on Phases 1–2).** Contract into `pm-stack/aggregator/README.md` + pointer comments at the three sites; a repo-wide promise-memo inventory with a disposition per site (known candidates: `bin/muse-proxy.mjs` `cliCapsPromise`, `pkgs/id/web` `highlighterPromise`; expected-conforming sites verified, not re-fixed); a cross-note on #2668 that its rule is now the aggregator's contract too.

Open questions stay in the design doc (supabase client token rotation — no invalidation path, no failure evidence yet; genuinely-absent config cost, bounded by the secrets cache and recorded acceptable; Go/Rust `sync.Once` latches — no filed instance).

Related: #2668 (the rule's first statement), #3702 (neighbouring throat contract — different mechanism, no phase overlap). Not this design: #3701 (batch scheduling), the settings-kind numeric cluster (pass 32's trigger has not fired).

🤖 Design architect pass 33 (2026-11-01), audit at origin/main `064ce9e5`.

body:
## Finding (R2 review, 2026-11-01)

The `webhook-gateway-payloads` bucket (raw GitHub webhook payloads written by the webhook-gateway Worker, `github/<delivery-id>.json`) has **no retention anywhere**: no delete/expiry logic in the Worker code (`~/workspace/webhook-gateway/`), and no bucket lifecycle rule. Every payload since the bucket was created (2026-10-23) is still present.

Measured 2026-11-01 (S3 listing + Cloudflare r2StorageAdaptiveGroups):

- 49,815 objects / 862 MB and growing ~+8,000–9,000 objects/day — the rate tracks this repo's GitHub issues-event volume, including the fleet's own automation bursts.
- Daily max object count: Oct 26: 2,297 → Oct 28: 15,922 → Oct 30: 30,289 → Nov 1: 49,566. Nothing has ever been deleted.
- Storage bytes are still small, but the object count is unbounded: at the current rate this is ~250k objects/month, ~3M objects/year, with matching Class A/B operation and listing costs, and an ever-growing replay/audit surface nobody reads.

The D1 `webhook-gateway` deliveries ledger is the queryable record; the R2 payload bodies are needed for replay of recent/pending deliveries, not forever.

## Ask

Declare and implement a retention for delivered payloads, e.g.:

- Worker-side: delete the R2 payload N days after its ledger row reaches `delivered` (keep payloads for pending/failed deliveries indefinitely), or
- Bucket lifecycle rule expiring `github/` objects after N days.

Pick N (30 days suggested) and note the choice on the Worker README. If payloads are intentionally kept forever as an audit archive, say so in the README instead and close this — the problem is that the growth is currently *undeclared*, not that it exists.

## Acceptance criteria
- A retention period for delivered webhook payloads is declared (30 days suggested) and written into the webhook-gateway Worker README — or, if payloads are intentionally kept forever as an audit archive, that decision is declared in the README instead and this issue closes on that declaration.
- The retention is implemented (Worker-side deletion N days after the D1 ledger row reaches `delivered`, or an R2 lifecycle rule expiring `github/` objects after N days) and verified: the bucket's object count stops growing unboundedly and delivered payloads older than N are gone.
- Payloads for pending/failed deliveries are retained (not expired) so replay stays possible for the deliveries that still need it.

title: run-switch.sh: overlapping switches snapshot stale trees and land surprise generations (gen 524, 2026-11-01, explained)

body:
## What happened

During the flake-fold activation attempts on 2026-11-01, the laptop's system profile advanced 523 -> 524 at 09:30:41 CST through an activation neither fold attempt produced (both died at build). Investigation (laptop-hygiene-2026-11-01.md, Addendum 9) traced it completely:

- The activation was `~/run-switch.sh` started **08:35:22 CST** (its own log: `~/switch-20261101-083522.log`, `SWITCH_EXIT=0`, "Done. The new configuration is /nix/store/vnsmm27..."). It evaluated the laptop primary at **51dee6874** — pre-fold main. The fold's pull to 5828cb8d7 only landed at 08:58:12, while this build was already running. Nix snapshots a path flake's tree at eval time, so the ~55-minute build on the loaded box faithfully built and switched the *stale* tree. Gen 524 therefore contains no fold units (verified), and everything on it is healthy.
- The launcher was an agent session over the sandbox's multiplexed SSH connection (logind session 3462, opened 08:00:06 CST), feeding the sudo password from 1Password item `user@amd` via stdin — the fleet's established deploy pattern (see the archived deploy-chain-2220 executor: run the switch after merges, vault-fed sudo). It was **not** a systemd timer (the laptop has no nixos-upgrade/autoUpgrade unit and `system.autoUpgrade` appears nowhere in the flake), not cron (none exists), and not a local GUI session (no local login; the password arrived via stdin, cf. the 75-byte `sudo: no password was provided` logs at 03:56:01 and 08:59:29 when a feed was missed).
- This is a standing rhythm, not a one-off: successful run-switch activations landed at 03:42, 05:05, 08:10 and 09:31 CST that night (starts 02:07 / 03:56 / 07:11 / 08:35), plus direct `nixos-rebuild switch` runs from the `wt-pm-collector-nix` fleet worktree at 01:11 / 01:48 / 02:21. Agent sessions switch the laptop to current main after merges, roughly every 1-2.5 hours, and builds take 35-95 minutes under load — which is why a switch can land long after, and far away from, the work that launched it.

## Why this is filed

The mechanism works as designed, but it has two sharp edges worth a guard:

1. **No lock.** Two switches ran concurrently on 2026-11-01 (08:35 and the fold's 08:59 attempt) and contended; nothing prevents overlapping builds/activations.
2. **Silent staleness.** A switch whose build spans a merge/pull lands the *old* configuration with a success exit, indistinguishable from a fresh deploy unless you diff the resulting generation. It cost the fold run about an hour of confusion ("an activation neither attempt produced").

Suggested minimal guard for `run-switch.sh`: take an `flock` for the duration, and log the primary's HEAD at eval time into the switch log (plus a warning at the end if HEAD moved during the build). No behavior change otherwise.

## Interaction with the pending fold (code#3720 / PR #3722)

There is no autonomous switcher: nothing fires on a timer. But at the observed cadence, once main is green again (the `id` checkPhase failures, code#3787, are the current blocker), the next routine fleet switch will incidentally complete the fold: the primary is kept at origin main by pm-git-sync (fold modules already merged), and `home-manager.backupFileExtension = "backup"` means the 16 hand-installed unit files still in place will be renamed to `*.backup` rather than blocking activation. Whoever notices the fold land should still run the runbook's verification (store links, timers, one drain run) and retire the reaper's bootstrap worktree, per `~/.local/state/flake-fold-backup-2026-11-01/`.

Filed from the gen-524 investigation, 2026-11-01. Priority: low — documentation/guard, no live breakage.

## Acceptance criteria
- Overlapping `run-switch.sh` invocations cannot silently build stale trees: a second switch started while one is running (or while the tree moved since eval) is refused, queued, or loudly warned with the evaluated commit named — the mechanism is the fixer's choice, the surprise-generation outcome is what must be impossible.
- A switch's log records the evaluated commit and tree state so a landed generation can always be traced to its source tree after the fact.
- The 2026-11-01 gen-524 sequence is reproducible as a test scenario or documented drill: stale-tree switch is caught before activation.

body:
## Problem

`~/run-switch.sh` records its log location in a single shared pointer file, `~/switch-current.logpath`. When two switches run concurrently, the second invocation overwrites the pointer, and the first operator's monitoring reads the WRONG run's log — exit-code attribution for a system switch then depends on each operator happening to track their own log filename privately.

## Evidence (2026-11-01)

During the flake-dedupe activation switch (generation system-524, SWITCH_EXIT=0, verified from the operator's own log file), another actor launched `~/run-switch.sh` twice from a separate worktree effort (08:59:29 — failed instantly, no sudo password; 08:59:51 — ran to completion on a newer main). The second launch clobbered `~/switch-current.logpath` mid-flight; the first operator's final tail read the other run's log. Both switches built from the same main lineage so the system stayed consistent — this time. A wrong-log read on a FAILED switch could equally mask a failure as a success.

## Ask

- Per-invocation logpath: write the pointer to a unique file per run (e.g. `~/switch-<timestamp>-<pid>.logpath`, or print the log path on stdout only and drop the shared pointer), and/or
- A switch lock (`flock` on a lockfile) so a second concurrent switch refuses with a clear message instead of racing — two NixOS switches racing is wasteful even when harmless.

Either change is small; the lock is the stronger guarantee.

## Acceptance criteria

- Two concurrent `run-switch.sh` invocations cannot clobber each other's log attribution: each run's log path is unique to the invocation, or a flock-style lock makes a second concurrent invocation refuse with a clear message.
- A failed switch is never read as a success (or vice versa) because of another run's log: the recorded log path points at the operator's own run from start to finish.
- Single-invocation behaviour is unchanged apart from the pointer/lock mechanics.

body:
## Bug

The REPL heredoc scan takes the delimiter as the raw rest of the line after `<<`, trimmed — it is never parsed as a heredoc delimiter word:

- `pkgs/id/src/repl/input.rs:342-356` (`preprocess_repl_line`): `let delimiter = after.trim().to_owned();` where `after = &line[heredoc_start + 2..]`.
- `pkgs/id/src/repl/input.rs:599` (`continue_heredoc`): a line ends the heredoc only when `line.trim() == delimiter` — an exact match against that raw string.

So two ordinary shell forms produce a heredoc that can never terminate on the word the user expects:

1. **Trailing token:** `put - name <<EOF extra` → delimiter is `EOF extra`. Typing `EOF` on its own line (the prompt says: type 'EOF extra' on its own line to end) never matches unless the user literally types the whole two-word string. The trailing token is also silently discarded — it is part of neither `original_line` nor any argument.
2. **Quoted delimiter:** `put - name <<'EOF'` or `put - name <<"EOF"` → delimiter is `'EOF'` / `"EOF"` including the quote characters. Shell strips the quotes (and a quoted delimiter is the standard way to ask for a literal, unexpanded body); here typing `EOF` never ends the heredoc. The only exits are Ctrl+C / EOF, which cancel and lose the content already typed (`continue_heredoc` returns `Ok(None)` and the runner drops the command).

## Verification (this run, real code)

Laptop probe worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneB-heredocdelim/` at origin/main `e0f683ef` (probe tests appended to `pkgs/id/src/repl/input.rs` in the worktree only, never committed; file sha256 `52215ae162c817cd4753bb9d7b5cd34a0cb63f01c6223abcf9039f229734f9bc`, identical in the sandbox clone at the same HEAD). `cargo test --lib probe_heredoc_delim`:

- control `put - name <<EOF` → delimiter `EOF` — **passed**
- `put - name <<EOF extra` → delimiter was `"EOF extra"`, expected `EOF` — **failed as predicted**
- `put - name <<'EOF'` → delimiter was `"'EOF'"`, expected `EOF` — **failed as predicted**
- `put - name <<"EOF"` → delimiter was `"\"EOF\""`, expected `EOF` — **failed as predicted**

(4 tests: 1 passed, 3 failed; the whole existing `repl::input` module suite passed in the same run.)

## Why it matters

The heredoc is one of the documented `put` input methods (`pkgs/id/src/repl/mod.rs:55`). A user who habitually quotes the delimiter (the shell idiom for literal bodies) or adds a trailing token wedges the REPL in continuation mode with no error naming the actual delimiter expectation beyond the raw string in the hint, and cancelling discards everything they typed. The failure is silent at the point of the mistake: the line is accepted, and the mismatch only shows up as a heredoc that "never ends".

## Acceptance criteria

- The delimiter is parsed as one word: the first whitespace-delimited token after `<<`, with one layer of surrounding single or double quotes stripped (`<<'EOF'` and `<<"EOF"` both terminate on a line containing exactly `EOF`).
- Anything after the delimiter word is not silently swallowed: it is either kept as part of the command (shell behaviour: extra words are arguments to the command in `original_line`) or refused with an error naming the extra text — pick one and pin it in a test.
- New unit tests in `repl/input.rs` cover: plain delimiter (existing behaviour), quoted delimiter (both quote kinds), and the trailing-token case under the chosen rule.
- Existing `repl::input` tests still pass.

## Dedup

Distinct from #1585 (closed: quoted `<<` operator starting a heredoc with a garbage delimiter — the scan's quote-blindness, not delimiter-word parsing) and #2280 (open: the trailing `-` placeholder replace is a literal pattern, in the substitution stage, not the delimiter). Searched open + closed for heredoc/delimiter/here-string on 2026-11-01.

body:
Per Drew's 2026-10-27/30 orders, the PM stack's units are declared in nixos/services/pm-stack/default.nix and land by nixos-rebuild switch (aggregator, projector, pm-git-sync, quota-gatherer, dispatch, tunnel, Kaneo). The fleet-feed collector missed that wiring: when it moved from the sandbox to the laptop on 2026-10-31 it was installed as hand-written files ~/.config/systemd/user/fleet-feed-collector.service and .timer (plain files, not home-manager store symlinks), and the module has no collector declaration (grep: no match for collector/fleet in default.nix).

Fold the collector service + timer into the module with the same environment the hand unit carries today (SUPABASE_PROJECT_REF via bws token file, FLEET_FEED_OUT=~/.local/state/pm-aggregator/fleet-feed.json, QUOTA_VIEW_PATH/QUOTA_REGISTRY_PATH/JULES_STATE_PATH/ORCHESTRATION_PATH into the laptop hatch-personal clone, --out argument as the service invokes it), so the next successful switch owns its lifecycle and home-manager retires the hand files (.backup rename per the module header). Note switches are currently blocked by the nix error 102 problem tracked elsewhere; the module change can land ahead of the switch. Related symptom of hand-managed collector state: #3362.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The fleet-feed collector service + timer are declared in `nixos/services/pm-stack/default.nix` with the same environment the hand-written unit carries today (SUPABASE_PROJECT_REF via the bws token file, FLEET_FEED_OUT, QUOTA_VIEW_PATH/QUOTA_REGISTRY_PATH/JULES_STATE_PATH/ORCHESTRATION_PATH, and the `--out` argument as currently invoked).
- [ ] After a successful `nixos-rebuild switch` on the laptop, the module-owned units are the ones running; the hand-written files under ~/.config/systemd/user are retired (.backup rename per the module header), not left as a second owner.
- [ ] The collector keeps producing a healthy fleet-feed.json on its timer cadence after the switch (AA section present, session counts in the normal range).

## Symptom
Since the collector moved to the laptop (2026-10-31), the laptop's fleet-feed.json (~/.local/state/pm-aggregator/fleet-feed.json) is periodically overwritten by a feed whose AA section is absent (reason: Supabase query failed HTTP 403) and whose session counts are ~24 instead of the laptop collector's 88. The explorer page blanks until the next laptop collector tick restores a good feed.

## Verified timeline (2026-11-01 CDT)
- Good service writes: 00:30:09 (full build, aa-last-good store written), 00:35:09, 00:39:58, 00:54:38 — AA ok, 84-88 sessions.
- Phantom writes (top-level generatedAt): 00:31:50, 00:37:08, 00:47:12 — AA absent/403, attention 24.
- The phantom write is NOT the laptop systemd service (no journal entries at those times; the timer's LAST/NEXT do not match) and NOT the current code: PR #3349's keep-last-good collector degrades to the stored section on failure (forced-failure test 2026-11-01 passed: bogus project ref -> section ok + stale:true). The phantom produces absent, i.e. it runs pre-#3349 code or an equivalent old copy.
- A 7-minute process watch on the laptop (00:49:50-00:56:51) caught only the legitimate service tick; no phantom write landed in the window. SSH logins from the sandbox tailnet peer (100.115.16.3) at 00:32:03 and 00:37:22 correlate with push-sized gaps after the 00:31:50 / 00:37:08 collects. No sandbox cron, systemd timer, or loop process has been found yet. No phantom write observed since 00:47:12.
- Its file-based sections (projects 351, charges 75, DNS) are complete, so it reads the synced hatch-personal tree; its session source sees only ~24 sessions.

## Ask
Identify the launcher (candidates: a leftover sandbox-era push loop, a lane/test session running a stale checkout's collector against the live feed path, an unretired unit somewhere) and stop it. A 30-min watcher is logging feed changes + collector processes on the laptop from ~00:57 CDT (~/tmp/phantom-watch2.log). Related: the collector's own units are hand-written and not yet in the pm-stack NixOS module (separate issue).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The phantom writer is identified by name (process/unit/copy of the collector code) with evidence — not just ruled out as the laptop systemd service or current main.
- [ ] The phantom writer is stopped/removed or updated to current code, and over a >=1h observation window every fleet-feed.json write carries the AA section (or the keep-last-good stale marker) and full session counts — no absent-AA overwrite recurs.
- [ ] The finding and the fix are recorded on this issue with timestamps from the feed file, so the next stale-copy incident has a named suspect list.

body:
# aggregator(charges-producer): a trailing or flag-like `--start`/`--end`/`--out` value is silently replaced by the defaults — the producer overwrites the live candidates file for the wrong period and exits 0

## Summary

`pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/produce-charge-candidates.ts` reads its three
value-taking flags through `argValue()` (`:52-55`), which returns
`process.argv[i + 1]` — or `undefined` when the flag is last. In `main()`
(`:252-257`) every result is combined with `??` defaults:

```ts
const start = argValue("--start") ?? isoDay(<first of current month>);
const end   = argValue("--end")   ?? isoDay(now);
const outPath = argValue("--out") ?? process.env.CHARGE_CANDIDATES_PATH ??
  join(homedir(), "workspace/goals/keep-the-four-repos-healthy/hidden_files/charges-candidates.json");
```

So a flag that is *present but missing its value* is indistinguishable from a
flag that was never passed: no error, no warning, exit 0. There is also no
validation that `--start`/`--end` are real `YYYY-MM-DD` dates, or that
`start <= end`. The candidates file is the live input the fleet-feed collector
consumes (`collect-fleet-feed.ts`: charges-candidates.json → matcher →
charges/chargesAttention), and this producer is run by hand (#2205: it "only
refreshes when an agent runs it by hand"), so a typo lands silently in the
one file that matters.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `d64e83c1`)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneA-chargeargs/` — the real
script (sha256 `999f2dd904924bc718aa278f209441656e85da05db75aa33c6a95e6d8b0eefe3`,
identical on the sandbox main checkout and the laptop checkout), Bun 1.4.2,
with `PLAID_CLI` pointed at a stub that logs its arguments and returns one
valid transaction, and `CHARGE_CANDIDATES_PATH` pointed at a probe-local
default file:

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| control: `--skip-gmail --start 2026-09-01 --end 2026-09-30 --out <probe>/control.json` | exit 0; `control.json` written with period `2026-09-01..2026-09-30`; stub logged `--start-date 2026-09-01 --end-date 2026-09-30`; default file untouched |
| trailing `--out`: `... --start 2026-09-01 --end 2026-09-30 --out` | exit 0; silently wrote the **default** candidates path (`wrote .../default-out.json`) — in a real run that is the live `hidden_files/charges-candidates.json`, overwritten when the operator asked for a custom file and forgot its value |
| trailing `--start`: `--skip-gmail --end 2026-09-30 --out <probe>/trailstart.json --start` | exit 0; period became **`2026-11-01..2026-09-30`** (start after end); the stub was queried with `--start-date 2026-11-01 --end-date 2026-09-30`, and the inverted period was persisted into the written file |
| flag-like `--out` value: `--start 2026-09-01 --end 2026-09-30 --out --skip-gmail` | exit 0; wrote a file literally named **`--skip-gmail`** in the working directory (`producer: wrote --skip-gmail`), and the same token also switched Gmail off |
| unvalidated date: `--skip-gmail --start banana --end 2026-09-30 --out <probe>/banana.json` | exit 0; stub queried with `--start-date banana`; the written file's `period.start` is the string `"banana"` |

## Why it matters

The failure is silent in exactly the dangerous direction: the operator
believes they produced a custom period into a scratch file, while the
script actually (a) regenerates the *current* month into the *live*
candidates file, or (b) persists a candidates file whose declared period is
inverted or not a date at all, which the collector then matches and surfaces
as if it were the requested period. Nothing in the output line looks wrong —
it prints the substituted values as if they were requested.

Distinct from: #3295 (append-usage-snapshots `--by` voiding `observedBy`),
#3330 (backfill `--dir` crash / flag-named directory), #3285 (compact
`--months 0`) — same unchecked-argv family, different script, different
failure: here the `??` fallback *masks* the missing value instead of
crashing or misdirecting, and the target of the silent write is the live
charges pipeline input. Also distinct from #3224/#3120/#3121 (amount/subject
parsing inside this same producer) and #2448 (a garbled Gmail date throwing
inside `gmailCandidates`).

## Acceptance criteria

- `--start`, `--end`, or `--out` with no following value, or with a
  following token that starts with `--`, prints a usage/error message
  naming the flag and its missing value to stderr and exits 2 — no Plaid or
  Gmail call is made and no file is written (in particular the default
  candidates file is untouched).
- `--start` / `--end` values that are not real calendar dates in
  `YYYY-MM-DD` form, or a `start` after `end`, exit 2 with an error naming
  the offending value — nothing is queried or written.
- Valid explicit flags behave exactly as today (same period, same output
  file, same summary line); the no-flag defaults (current month, env /
  default candidates path) are unchanged.
- A regression test (or script-level harness case, e.g. with a stub
  `PLAID_CLI`) covers the trailing-flag, flag-like-value, and
  invalid/inverted-date cases.

body:
## Bug

`docs-history` (the mcpx compendium history / release-stamping tool, landed today in #3266 for #1865) **panics with a Go runtime stack trace** when a value-taking flag is the last argument of `stamp` or `check`.

Both subcommands parse flags with a hand-rolled loop that does `i++; value = rest[i]` with no bounds check:

- `pkgs/mcpx/tools/docs-history/main.go:1119-1127` — `stamp`: `--version`, `--date`, `--changes-dir`
- `pkgs/mcpx/tools/docs-history/main.go:1146-1153` — `check`: `--diff`, `--changes-dir`

## Evidence (verified this run)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneA-docshistory/`): `main.go` copied verbatim from main `2cc551cd`, sha256 `12e1888103e770ed83476d6a65695f978e0c9cfa95e39915c54ba1948dec37b6` on both sides, built with Go 1.26.8.

Bug cases — every one panics:

```
$ docs-history stamp --version
panic: runtime error: index out of range [1] with length 1
goroutine 1 [running]: main.main() …

$ docs-history stamp --version 1.2.3 --date        → panic: index out of range [3] with length 3
$ docs-history stamp --changes-dir                 → panic: index out of range [1] with length 1
$ docs-history check --diff                        → panic: index out of range [1] with length 1
$ docs-history check --changes-dir                 → panic: index out of range [1] with length 1
$ docs-history check doc.md --diff                 → panic: index out of range [2] with length 2
```

Controls — the tool's own intended behaviour for bad usage is a clean usage message:

```
$ docs-history stamp --version file.md   → usage text, exit 2 (no panic)
$ docs-history check                     → usage text, exit 2
$ docs-history bogus-subcommand          → usage text, exit 2
$ docs-history stamp --version 1.2.3 --date 2026-10-31 doc.md
    → exit 0; `since: unreleased` correctly rewritten to `since: 1.2.3`
```

## Why it matters

`stamp` is the release step (docs/release-runbook.md) and `check` is a CI gate. A mistyped release command — a flag whose value was forgotten, or a shell variable that expanded to nothing — currently produces a runtime panic and stack trace instead of the usage text the tool already prints for every other usage error. In CI the panic output buries the actual mistake; at release time it looks like the tool itself is broken. The exit code happens to also be 2 (Go runtime), so scripts cannot distinguish a usage error from a crash by code alone.

## Acceptance criteria

- `stamp`/`check` with any value-taking flag (`--version`, `--date`, `--changes-dir`, `--diff`) as the final argument print the usage text (or a message naming the flag and its missing value) to stderr and exit 2 — no panic, no stack trace.
- All currently-valid invocations behave exactly as before (valid stamp still stamps and exits 0; missing required values still usage + exit 2).
- A regression test covers each value-taking flag in trailing position for both subcommands (the existing `main_test.go` suite tests the library functions; the arg-parsing path in `main()` needs coverage, e.g. by factoring the parse into a testable function or an exec-based test).

Related: #1865 (the tool's implementation issue). Distinct from the unrecognized-argument class filed for other scripts (#3264/#3278/#3281/#3287/#3296/#3297): those silently ignore unknown flags; this one crashes on a *known* flag missing its value.

body:
Phase 3 (closing audit) of design #3282 — "a mirror is what it can prove" (design doc: `files/designs/code-github-backup-mirror-contract.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace). Filed by the design architect, pass 29 (2026-10-31). **Gated on Phases 1–2 of the design** (Phase 1 = #3238 + #3233; Phase 2 = #3250 + #3219 + #3270 + #3257) and on its own phase siblings #3240 + #3229 landing the `ghb_common` state helpers and plan retention it audits against.

## Scope

1. **Closing inventory.** Grep `infra/github-backup/bin/` for every remaining bare `json.load` on a generated-state file and every `open(..., "w")` / `json.dump` write to one (`plan.json`, `state.json`, `MANIFEST.json`, `clone-status.jsonl` appends excluded — append-only logs are not in the torn-write class). Disposition each hit: migrated to the `ghb_common` helpers from #3240, or deliberately local with the reason recorded in this issue. The inventory is complete only when a fresh grep returns no undispositioned hits.
2. **Named dispositions required:** (a) FAMILIES.md and the `reconcile-YYYY-MM-DD.md` report — markdown written non-atomically; expected disposition is migrate via the same atomic-write helper (a torn FAMILIES.md feeds cold-export decisions), or a recorded reason if not; (b) `drain_queue.py`'s per-repo `plan.json` re-read inside its fetch loop (a bare load and an O(events) re-read — disposition: route through the tolerant loader; restructuring the loop is in scope only if triage judges it trivial); (c) the Worker (`worker/src/index.js`) — expected disposition: out of scope with reason (KV is the store; the laptop half's ack discipline is Phase 2's #3219), recorded so the boundary is explicit.
3. **Contract statement.** Write the design's seven rules, in operator language, into `infra/github-backup/README.md` (system contract section) and cross-reference from `docs/RUNBOOK.md` where the DR procedures consume MANIFEST.json — the docs are the system's system-of-record per #3215.
4. **Evidence on the umbrella.** Post the completion evidence (inventory result, contract location, phase closure list) as a comment on #3215.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The grep inventory exists in this issue's closing comment with a disposition for every hit; a re-run grep finds no undispositioned bare load/write on generated state in `infra/github-backup/bin/`.
- [ ] FAMILIES.md / reconcile-report, the drainer plan re-read, and the Worker boundary each carry an explicit disposition (migrated, or out-of-scope/local with reason).
- [ ] README.md states the seven-rule contract and RUNBOOK.md cross-references it from the DR section.
- [ ] Evidence comment posted on #3215 naming this design and its phase closures.
- [ ] This audit does not re-open the decisions recorded on the design issue (validity = resolvability; four destination states; recorded outcomes; ack-on-ok; 3-consecutive-day streak; atomic state via `ghb_common`; plan retention) — a genuine blocker is flagged on the design issue instead.
