title: projector(comments): pmp_comments is keyed by the bare GitHub numeric ID — an issue comment, a review comment and a review with the same ID silently overwrite each other

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

labels.name: app/pm-stack
labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Problem

`pmp_comments` is keyed by the bare GitHub numeric ID alone, but the projector writes **three different kinds of GitHub objects** into that one table — issue comments, PR review comments, and PR reviews — and GitHub assigns those IDs from **independent sequences per object type**. The same number can therefore denote an issue comment and a review on the same (or different) items, and when it does, the second object silently **replaces** the first (main b3f6d2b2):

- `pm-stack/projector/schema.sql:47` — `id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, -- GitHub comment/review id`, no kind or repo qualifier.
- `pm-stack/projector/src/store.ts:207` — `upsertComment` is `ON CONFLICT(id) DO UPDATE SET` over every column including `ref`, `kind`, `body` and `deleted` (guarded only by `source_updated_at >=`, which a later-created colliding object passes).
- Every writer passes the raw per-type ID: webhook `commentCommon` (`src/projector.ts:80`, `String(c.id)`), the delete paths (`src/projector.ts:159` and `:213`, `markCommentDeleted(String(comment.id))` — a delete for one kind can tombstone another kind's row), and reconciliation (`src/reconcile.ts:76` issue/review comments, `:116` reviews, both `String(...id)`).

The unified activity stream (schema view `pmp_v_subject_activity`, `getCommentsForSubject`) then shows the surviving object and has lost the other one — no error anywhere, and reconciliation re-derives the same collision on every poll.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneB-projector/probe.ts`, real `store.upsertComment`/`getComments` against an in-memory libSQL DB migrated from the real schema.sql, main b3f6d2b2): upsert an `issue_comment` with id `424242` (created 2026-01-01), then upsert a `review` with the same id `424242` (created 2026-01-02):

```text
collision: rows=1 kinds=review bodies=review body
pmp_comments total rows = 1
```

The issue-comment row is gone — overwritten in place by the review, including its `ref` and `kind`. (The fixtures hint the namespaces were kept apart by hand: `fixtures/03-issue-comment.json` uses id 9001, `05-pr-review.json` 10001, `06-pr-review-comment.json` 11001.)

## Why it matters

The projector's whole purpose is a trustworthy unified comment/activity projection across the four repos (aggregator requirement #2). A cross-kind ID collision silently drops a real comment or review from every subject view and can cross-wire a deletion onto the wrong object. Because the monotonic guard compares `source_updated_at`, the corruption sticks: re-delivering the overwritten object's webhook is a no-op duplicate or loses the guard comparison, so the lost row does not heal itself.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Comment identity distinguishes the object kind (e.g. a composite key or a kind-qualified ID) at the schema level and in `upsertComment` / `markCommentDeleted`, so an issue comment, a review comment, and a review with the same numeric ID coexist as three rows.
- [ ] A delete event for one kind never tombstones a row of another kind.
- [ ] Store/projector tests pin the same-ID-different-kind case for all three kinds, plus the cross-kind delete case.
- [ ] Existing rows and the read model (`getComments`, `getCommentsForSubject`, `pmp_v_subject_activity`) keep working; the migration path for an existing database is stated in the PR (the DB is documented as disposable/rebuildable in schema.sql, if that is the chosen route).

Distinct from #2455 (deleted comments resurrected by stale upserts — the monotonic guard's key, not the primary key's namespace) and #2456 (failed webhook deliveries unretryable — the deliveries table, not comments).

(Deferred from #1978 deliberately: until the ledger exists, every group is trivially unproven, so gap issues filed earlier would only restate the inventory.)

Refs #1978 (parent item), #1905 (tracker), #1971 (guard policy), #309.

body:
Found 2026-10-30 by Codex review (P1) on the opencode route-audit PR, and verified against the source:

`bin/agy-proxy.mjs` is text-only. It builds its prompt solely from `body.messages` (formatPrompt / extractLatestUserPrompt, ~line 864) and never reads `body.tools`; its chat responses contain only text content with `finish_reason: 'stop'` (~line 1057) and never structured `tool_calls`. `bin/antigravity-ls-proxy.mjs` bridges tool calls; agy does not.

Consequence: seating antigravity-agy as a leaf in a tool-using route pool (gemini-flash-plan, sonnet-plan, opus-plan) silently terminates agent turns — the model answers in plain text, the turn ends as a 'success', and no failover to a tool-capable door happens. Until this is fixed, agy leaves belong only in text/burn roles (its existing argon seats), never as failover for tool-using pools.

Acceptance: the proxy forwards tool definitions to the agy backend and returns structured tool_calls (streaming and non-streaming) in the OpenAI shape, with tests alongside the existing bin/agy-proxy.test.mjs suite. After it lands, the route pools named above can gain agy leaves for a genuine second Antigravity door (the ls proxy outage of 2026-10-24/25 is the motivating incident: 38 ConnectionRefused failures in gemini-flash-plan with nothing to fail over to).

body:
## Summary

The single-instance guard added to the generated `openchamber-serve` wrapper (bc6044f, for dezren39/nix#1117) never matches a running server, so it is a no-op in production: after a restart, a leftover OpenChamber server keeps sharing the socket-activated listener on 127.0.0.1:3000 with the new instance.

## Root cause

In the wrapper as generated into the Nix store, the guard's cmdline capture is:

```
cmd="$(cat "$proc/cmdline" 2>/dev/null | tr '\\0' ' ')"
```

The generated script literally contains `tr '\\0' ' '` (verified byte-for-byte with `grep | cat -A` on the store file). In shell single quotes that passes backslash + backslash + `0` to `tr`, and GNU tr reads `\\` as an escaped backslash, so the translate set is {backslash, `0`} — NUL bytes are never converted to spaces. Bash command substitution then strips the NULs, concatenating the argv words (`...cli.jsserve--foreground--port3000--host...`), so neither the `cli.js serve` pattern nor the `--port 3000 ` boundary pattern can ever match any real process.

Intended text in the generated script: `tr '\0' ' '`.

## Observed impact (2026-10-29 23:50 CDT, laptop)

`systemctl --user restart openchamber.service` with the guarded wrapper: the tracked main (pid 3892827) stopped cleanly, the new instance (pid 483540) started, the guard logged no reap, and the untracked leftover (pid 1668515, started 12:38 CDT) was still holding fd 3 on 127.0.0.1:3000 alongside the new instance (`ss -tlnp` showed both pids). Replaying the guard's three checks (exe match, cmdline match, port match) by hand against the leftover matched all three once `\0` was translated correctly. The leftover had to be TERM'd manually to return to exactly one instance.

## Suggested fix

- Emit `tr '\0' ' '` in the generated wrapper (adjust the Nix string escaping in `home/common/default.nix` where `openchamberStart` is defined).
- Add a regression test that runs the guard scan against a synthetic `/proc`-style cmdline with real NUL separators (or a fake leftover process) and asserts the leftover is selected for reaping.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The generated `openchamber-serve` wrapper contains `tr '\0' ' '` (single backslash) — verified byte-for-byte in the generated store file, not just in the Nix source
- [ ] A regression test runs the guard scan against a synthetic cmdline with real NUL separators (or a fake leftover process) and asserts the leftover is selected for reaping
- [ ] After a restart with a leftover instance present, exactly one openchamber instance holds 127.0.0.1:3000 (the #1117 scenario from dezren39/nix, re-verified)
- [ ] No other generated-wrapper strings with the same double-escaping defect remain (audit the same Nix string for sibling `tr`/escape uses)

body:
## Problem

The `opencode-acp` agent entry added to `home/openclaw/default.nix` (PR #2237, #2229 mechanism 1) makes the whole NixOS configuration fail to evaluate, which blocks every `nixos-rebuild switch` on the laptop:

```
error: The option `home-manager.users.user.programs.openclaw.config.agents.entries.opencode-acp.runtime.acp' does not exist.
       Did you mean `home-manager.users.user.programs.openclaw.config.agents.entries.opencode-acp.runtime.type'?
```

## Root cause (verified with a minimal reproduction)

The generated schema in nix-openclaw (`nix/generated/openclaw-config-options.nix`, locked rev 4e5f444, identical on upstream main) types an agent entry's `runtime` as:

```nix
t.nullOr (t.oneOf [
  (t.submodule { options = { type = enum [ "embedded" ]; }; })
  (t.submodule { options = { acp = ...; type = enum [ "acp" ]; }; })
])
```

Under the pinned nixpkgs, `types.oneOf` is `foldl' either ...`, and a submodule type's `check` accepts any attribute set — so every plain-attrset definition is claimed by the FIRST (embedded) branch, which then rejects the `acp` attribute as an unknown option. The acp branch is unreachable:

- `{ type = "acp"; acp = { ... }; }` → "The option `x.acp' does not exist"
- `{ type = "acp"; }` alone → "A definition for option `x.type' is not of type `value "embedded" (singular enum)'"

Both reproduced against the pinned nixpkgs (6510408) with a 15-line evalModules test, independent of this repo's config.

## Impact

- The laptop has been unable to switch since the entry merged; it is still on the 2026-10-28 generation.
- This blocked the #2220/#2250 deployment chain (2026-10-29) at the switch step.

## Fix plan

1. Remove the `opencode-acp` entry from `home/openclaw/default.nix` (leaving a comment pointing here) so the configuration evaluates and the deployment chain can proceed. The ACP capability itself (acp.enabled, allowedAgents, acpx plugin, per-agent wrappers from #1728) is unaffected — OpenClaw can still spawn OpenCode over ACP from sessions.
2. File the generator bug upstream in openclaw/nix-openclaw with the minimal reproduction (a discriminable encoding would be a single submodule with `type = enum [ "embedded" "acp" ]` plus an optional `acp` attrset).
3. Restore the entry (tracked by #2256) once the schema can express it — either an upstream generator fix + input bump, or a local workaround proven by evaluation.

Acceptance: the entry is restored AND `nixos-rebuild switch` succeeds with it present.


## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A laptop `nixos-rebuild switch` evaluates with the `opencode-acp` agent entry present (or the entry is removed/reworked with the reason recorded here)
- [ ] The workaround or fix is verified against the pinned nixpkgs with the same minimal evalModules reproduction from the body, which must now reach the acp branch or fail with a comprehensible error
- [ ] OpenClaw ACP dispatch (#2229 mechanism 1) either works through the fixed entry or is explicitly deferred with a follow-up issue

body:
Follow-up to PR #2214 / issue #179 (queue task 2970).

`event_store::sync::Outcome` now carries `voided`, mapped from the range session's `Tally` (`event_store/sync.rs`, `Tally::add` → `Ingest::Voided`). `Ingest::Voided` is produced when an arrival is **stored but not applied** (`event_store/ingest.rs`, `Staged::finish`: `is_applied == false`).

Nothing tests that path end to end:

- The range-session test that was meant to (`test_a_range_session_counts_voided_events`, commit `2316d85f` on #2214) actually built the fork into the receiving store before the session, so its arrivals were **refused as frozen** (`db.voided = 0`, `db.refused = 2`). That test now pins the frozen shape under its real name, `test_a_range_session_counts_frozen_arrivals_as_refused`.
- No test anywhere asserts an `Ingest::Voided` outcome today (`grep 'Ingest::Voided'` finds only the label arms in `event_store/sync.rs` and `log_sync.rs`).

What is needed: a shape where an event is stored without being applied and reported as `Voided` — plausibly an event released from the waiting pool by a fork decided in the same batch (`Staged::Stored` → `finish`) — driven through `event_store::sync` and asserted on `Outcome::voided`, plus the same for `log_sync`'s tally. If no such shape is reachable, the `voided` field is dead and should say so in its doc comment instead.

## Acceptance criteria
- A range-session test drives an arrival that is stored but not applied through a real range session and asserts the session tally / `Outcome::voided` reflects it (a voided count greater than zero), distinct from the frozen-refusal shape the current mis-built test pins.
- The same voided accounting is covered for the `log_sync` tally, or the gap is explicitly documented in the test/PR.
- If no stored-but-not-applied shape is reachable through a range session, the `voided` field is documented as dead in its doc comment instead of gaining a forced test.

body:
Follow-up from the capability taxonomy v0 investigation (#2027, record: `doc/2026-10-29T14-05-00Z_investigation_capability_taxonomy/`, PR #2337).

## Goal
Add a `device.info` capability to `pkgs/id/src/world_caps.rs` returning the device's capability manifest (display kind/size/colours, input keys/encoder/pointer/text_entry, sensors with accuracy, audio in/out, transport class), so a world program can adapt one model to web, ESP32 and text/agent devices instead of rendering blind.

## Why first
Every other interface capability in the taxonomy is conditional on it. It is deliberately a capability, not a surface field, so a program asks when it cares.

## Scope
- New catalog name `device.info` (append-only CATALOG rule; existing 17 names unchanged; no `WANTS_VERSION` bump — v1 already admits new names).
- Manifest value shape per taxonomy §3.1: `{manifest:{v:1}, display, input, sensors, audio, network}`.
- One-shot request only; the manifest is node-local, journaled, unsigned — same trust rule as other grants.
- Per-device caching by the adapter; a program must never be able to make the device re-enumerate for free.
- Refusal: `unknown_cap` if the node cannot describe itself.

## Acceptance
- `device.info` in CATALOG, provider in the world actor, and a test asserting the manifest round-trips and that an unknown manifest version is refused.
- Program-side helper (Roc or plain JSON) documented in the module header alongside the existing wants example.
- No change to existing capability semantics.

## Out of scope
`form.*`, `loc.*`, `media.*` (separate follow-ups), MQTT transport (separate follow-up).


## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `device.info` is in the world_caps CATALOG (append-only; existing 17 names unchanged, no WANTS_VERSION bump) with a provider in the world actor
- [ ] A test asserts the manifest round-trips and that an unknown manifest version is refused (`unknown_cap` when the node cannot describe itself)
- [ ] Program-side helper (Roc or plain JSON) documented in the module header alongside the existing wants example
- [ ] No change to existing capability semantics; per-device adapter caching means a program cannot force free re-enumeration

## From the #2053 investigation (embedded playable posts)

Investigation #2053 (queue task 3358, result posted on that issue 2026-10-29) designed the game-post model: a board post carrying a world/app package reference + mode (live-session | async-turns | succession), turns as signed events, save-point objects with handoff/fork semantics, and #2037 attestation as an opt-in plug-in. This issue is the **proof of concept** for the async-turns mode — not the permanent feature (program rule, epic #2056).

## PoC scope

Using the existing tic-tac-toe example (`pkgs/id/examples/tic-tac-toe`) as the game package:

1. A **game-post object** referencing the package (hash + version), mode `async-turns`, two player IDs, attestation mode `concession`.
2. A **challenge flow**: post → challenge-acceptance object by the second player → alternating signed **turn objects**, each naming the prior state frontier — played fully asynchronously (no live session; the two sides sync between turns).
3. Game end emits the #2037 pair of signed **result claims**; agreeing claims compute `agreed` (per the #2037 model / #2248 PoC shapes if it lands first — coordinate, do not duplicate).
4. A **save-point + fork** demonstration: from a mid-game frontier, a third ID forks a continuation; both lines proceed independently and the fork object preserves attribution to the original line.

## Out of scope

Live-session (real-time) games, succession handoff chains (the fork primitive here is their foundation; the chain policy is #2054's), board UI, sandbox policy changes.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] PoC demonstrates scope points 1–4 with the object shapes documented in the PR/issue
- [ ] Findings note posted on this issue: what the PoC proved about the game-post model, what it did not
- [ ] No production game-post feature claimed or merged under this issue

Split from #1971 (its task list + leak 1), filed by queue worker triage (task 2873, 2026-10-29).

## Problem

`TestEveryExecFlagChangesSomething` (`pkgs/mcpx/internal/e2e/e2e_test.go`) does not enumerate the flags it guards. It has four hand-written rows (`--export`, `--launcher`, `--prefix`, `--typecheck`) and a comment "Add a row when you add a flag", while the exec/run flag set (`internal/cli/commands.go`) has ~23 flags — including three fixed by the historical #75 (`--no-launcher`, `--allow-repeat`, `--no-capture-console`) with no row. A new flag with no row passes; the "flag accepted and ignored" class (shipped three times before the guard existed) is not closed — it relies on memory, the thing the guard exists to replace. Its probe half is the model to copy: each row asserts the outcome with the flag and its absence without.

## Scope (per #1971 Approach C)

1. A **unit-speed completeness test** enumerating the real exec/run FlagSet (`flag.FlagSet.VisitAll` over the flag definitions in `internal/cli`) that fails when any flag has neither a probe row nor an exemption with a reason. The completeness half lives outside the e2e test so it fails locally in milliseconds.
2. **Probe rows** for `--no-launcher`, `--allow-repeat`, `--no-capture-console` and every other unprobed flag with an observable effect, in the existing with/without shape.
3. Exemptions explicit, reasoned, and **ratcheted** (pinned set may only shrink without a deliberate reasoned update).

## Acceptance criteria

- Completeness test enumerates the FlagSet and fails on a flag with no row/exemption; runs at unit speed.
- All unprobed flags with observable effects gain with/without probe rows; the rest carry reasoned exemptions.
- `pkgs/mcpx go test ./...` green in CI.
- No flag behaviour changes — this guards existing behaviour only.

body:
## What this is

Drew, 2026-10-29: hunt for "jewels" — AI capabilities already available but not configured — as scheduled tasks, inside GitHub Actions, API/event-triggered, or as failure-triggered triage; plus verdicts on ChatGPT and Claude scheduled tasks. Study: ~/workspace/research_notes/unconfigured-jewels-20261029/findings.md.

Baseline (not an AI desert): Jules runs scheduled (daily ideation/flake-sync/upstream-sync) and as remediation (issue-label + PR-branch CI-failure-fix); a designed main-broken chain (#1779 §5) runs in all four repos (workflow_run → Breakage-ID dedupe → one issue → Jules first, ≤3 concurrent, 24h release → fleet queue); code's flake-inputs-update has a failure→Jules→Claude escalation ladder; OpenChamber has a bot suite (pr-review, help, summarize); opencode has a /review bot; opencode + openchamber now have consolidated LLM repo-sweepers (15-min triage/intake/duplicates). Trigger census across all workflow files: workflow_dispatch 54, schedule 23, workflow_run 5, **repository_dispatch 0**.

## The jewels, ranked by value ÷ effort

1. **Dependabot-alert triage agent.** Live counts: **code ≥100 open alerts (API page cap hit), opencode 33, openchamber 3, nix 0** — and nothing reads them. This is the fleet's largest untriaged queue, and it is the security queue. Design: scout-tier scheduled pass on the repo-sweeper chassis — group by ecosystem/severity/reachability, dismiss dev-only/unreachable WITH recorded reasons, one grouped fix issue per cluster, criticals escalated same-day.
2. **Classifier leg on the main-broken chain + coverage for the other "right kinds."** The chain files and routes well, but nobody reads a failure before Jules/queue spend — and most failures are knowable classes (runner stalls, missing-secret, flakes). Uncovered by construction today: release workflows (goreleaser/Release/publish file nothing), the automation's own workflows (openchamber's repo sweeper failed repeatedly today, unwatched; nix's buffer-backup lock sync likewise), PR-tier failures. Design in the failure-triage section below.
3. **Jules API as a first-class queue executor.** The fleet uses only the jules-action wrapper; the REST API (v1alpha: sessions, activity polling, sendMessage, approvePlan) makes Jules the **only vendor agent Muse can both dispatch AND poll** — it fits the Supabase queue with the same outcome/time review fields as OpenCode/OpenClaw. **BUG: opencode has no JULES_API_KEY secret, so its Jules-first leg cannot fire** (noted in its own main-broken.yml header). Close that gap first.
4. **repository_dispatch bridge (zero today).** The outbound twin of #2072's inbound webhook hot list: fleet/Worker/Supabase events starting GitHub-side agent runs without a laptop runner, replacing several pollers with events.
5. **Port the repo-sweeper to code and nix.** Those two repos still get first-look triage from Claude-side cron sweeps — exactly the "Muse task launching OpenCode" spend Drew wants cut (see #2174). Includes label-only stale handling (Drew's rule; only openchamber has it).
6. **Small ones:** PR-branch failure classifier, comment-only (≥3 same Breakage-ID in 24h → one classification comment; no fix attempts, no Jules budget); code is the only repo with no /oc mention bot; Copilot cloud agent workflows exist in all four repos but seat/usage is unverified — a 10-minute check before counting it as an executor.

## Failure-triage design (the "right kind", scoped narrowly)

In scope: main-tier failures (already chained), release/publish failures, automation-own workflows, repeated PR-tier failures. Never: single PR failures, cancels, experiment branches. Pipeline: the existing deterministic shell step computes the Breakage-ID and dedupes → a NEW scout step (`opencode run` on the repo key, same in-Actions pattern as the sweepers) reads the failing jobs' log tails and classifies: infra-runner / infra-network / quota-or-secret / flake-suspect / real-regression / unknown — attaching 3–5 evidence log lines to the issue as an agent-note:v1 comment BEFORE any fix spend. Routing: quota/secret → immediate escalation to Drew with the exact fix named, zero fix attempts; infra → one automatic re-run of failed jobs, repeat escalates as infrastructure (when Actions itself is stalled, in-Actions triage cannot run — the external fleet-watchdog stays the backstop, and the classifier says "infrastructure" rather than filing code fixes); flake → one re-run, green closes as flake with a strike counter, third strike files a flake-fix issue; real regression → existing Jules-budget/queue routing with the diagnosis attached. Authority limits: the agent may re-run failed jobs once per breakage, comment/label/file within chain labels, dispatch Jules within budget; it may NOT edit code, merge, touch secrets, or disable workflows — anything else is an "escalating:" comment + status/needs-triage. Every step lands as an agent-note so outcome/time/tokens audit into the same review table as the OpenCode/OpenClaw comparison (#2072). Preserve the chain's guardrails: no workflow_run on "*" (#304), per-breakage concurrency, dry-run mode.

## ChatGPT scheduled tasks — verdict: usable niche, fire-and-forget

Relaunched June 2026 (dedicated Scheduled page): one-off/recurring/monitoring tasks, at most hourly, web search + connected apps; event triggers via Gmail/Slack/GitHub on paid plans. Limits by tier: 3 active (Go) / 5 (Plus) / 10 (Business, Edu) / 15 (Pro, Enterprise). Caveats: **Tasks cannot run GPTs** — a Task is generic ChatGPT, not Aster (no persona/memory): a separate, dumber-but-unattended executor. **"ProLite" appears in no published tier table** — Drew's task allowance is unverified until checked on his Scheduled page. Fits only off-fleet monitoring (vendor status/changelog watches, Gmail-event nudges, public-web digests). Monitoring gap: **no API exists to create, list, or audit tasks or runs** — Muse cannot confirm one is alive, and unattended tasks can silently auto-pause. Convention: every task's instructions end with "email the full result to drewrypope@gmail.com, subject [CHATGPT-TASK <name>]" (Muse reads Gmail) or post via the Slack app to a channel Muse reads; the weekly ChatGPT export (#2072) is the retrospective audit; a Claude-side registry treats a missed cadence as presumed-dead and surfaces it. Residual risk: silence is the only failure signal.

## Claude scheduled tasks — verdict: blocked, and a poor fit anyway

All three surfaces (Claude Code Routines — cloud, schedule/API/GitHub-webhook triggers, caps Pro 5 / Max 15 / Team+Ent 25 runs/day, 1-hour minimum interval; Desktop scheduled tasks — app must be open; Cowork scheduled tasks) require a paid claude.ai plan; **Drew's claude.ai is on the free tier**, so the surfaces do not even appear. Even unblocked, the fit is poor: Routines' API trigger is fire-only (returns a session URL; no endpoint reads a result, sends follow-up, or cancels; no idempotency key). The one additive surface (laptop-closed pure-repo work) is already covered by Jules free tier + Actions. **Do not buy a seat for this.** (Distinct pots: Drew's free claude.ai ≠ the assistant's own Muse subscription ≠ the Meta Muse API pool.) If ever used, monitoring is the same self-reporting-output convention as ChatGPT Tasks.

## Worth-it measurement (Drew, 2026-10-29 — applies to every executor surface)

Each surface gets measured per task class against doing the work via OpenCode or Muse directly: outcome quality, Muse supervision minutes, allowance burn (exact tokens where metered; plan-level % delta where not). A class that is not worth it is a finding, not a failure. Companion agents (Aster today; a Claude equivalent later) are additionally valued as chat partners and escalation points independent of task volume, and their task mechanics (what triggers a billable work job vs plain chat, rough work-job cost, effort levels) get learned empirically and recorded. Cross-cutting fact from the study: of every vendor surface examined, only the Jules API gives Muse both dispatch and result polling; ChatGPT Tasks and Claude Routines are fire-and-forget from Muse's seat.

## Acceptance

- Dependabot triage pass running with its first grouped report (all four repos).
- opencode JULES_API_KEY gap closed (or escalated with the reason recorded).
- Classifier leg implemented on the main-broken chain in one repo, dry-run first, with the routing rules above.
- ChatGPT Scheduled-page allowance for Drew's plan verified and recorded here.

Implement #2021 as a MERGE of openchamber-dispatcher + openchamber-babysitter into one session conductor with two phases (Drew approved 2026-10-29):

- DISPATCH: take from the queue head, launch the session on the chosen pool (Workhorse default; Specialist/Summit for complex work), bind session↔task, log, move on to the next. Fire-and-forget; never babysit inside the dispatch phase.
- SWEEP: one pass over ALL live sessions — answer their questions, nudge or kick stalls, and escalate when a session cannot crack its issue: change its routing pool (e.g. Workhorse → Specialist) or move it off an exhausted pool. Update the fleet-watchdog roster to the merged job id. Keep the measurement gate binding: no dispatch without a quota picture ≤60 min old covering all pools.

title: mcpx testing: one seed per run -- format (UUIDv7), derivation, and how it reaches every test

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#121 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #93

## Summary

Decide the **run seed**: what one looks like, how every random input in every test is derived from it, how it reaches every `go test` process (locally and in CI), and how a failure is reproduced from it with one command. Per #91 this is step 1 of the testing strategy: it must land before the first randomized test does, or the first fuzz failure is unreproducible.

Where the seeds are *stored* and *collected* is #122. Which library consumes the seed is #123. Generator registry and versioning detail is #124.

## Original notes

> - testing
>   - agents should make at least 1 simple, new test for every bug observed from any source, when cheap to do so-- aggresively test many permutations. 
>     - you can absolutely rely on fuzzing anywhere you can fit it and you should whenever you can-- but you _must_ use a single seed per-run to generate all inputs. (this could eventually be discussed with careful consideration.) it should be appended into a test tracking structured file in the repo and it can be committed. ideally main branch commit's seed or pr merge seed should make it back into file eventually. to prevent churn, maybe ci appends the seed into a gha var (race/overwrite risk?), or attached as artifact to each workflow in init job before tests begin-- a collector job can scoop them up sometime later. once a day/week/on-release/every-100-commits. im thinking touch tests/seeds/<seed> or uv has a seed generate job. anyways ci it should end up in that dir, then as an artifact if gha and main branch, then passed into the test matrix. if uv test without arg- warn, generate and write it yourself pass it to all tests, if some other testing method there should not be a static seed, throw for empty or setup should make the seed. avoid changing how seed generates data. im not sure if a convenient uuid with time, v7?, is valid, but as long as its enough entropy whatever works. either put nothing in their or compact json, consider seeds/v1/id/<first 2 char>/<seed><--symlink: seeds/yyyy/mm/dd/<seed> avoiding conflicts is important.

"uv test" in the notes: mcpx is Go and has no uv. This issue reads it as **"the test entrypoint/wrapper"** -- a `just` recipe or `pkgs/mcpx/scripts/test.sh` that everyone (agents, humans, CI) calls instead of bare `go test`.

## Current state (re-checked at 05c78b2)

| Fact | Where |
| --- | --- |
| No randomness in any test: 735 `func Test*` across 64 files, no `math/rand`, `testing/quick`, rapid, `Fuzz*`. Clean slate: no existing inputs to preserve. | `rg` over `pkgs/mcpx` |
| No test wrapper. CI calls `go test ./... -count=1` directly; the repo `justfile` has no mcpx test recipe. | `.github/workflows/mcpx.yml`; `rg mcpx justfile` (no hits) |
| `go test ./...` builds **one test binary per package and runs each as a separate process**. Anything minted inside a test process is per package, not per run. | `go help test` |
| e2e passes `os.Environ()` into every `mcpx` subprocess, so an env var reaches the daemon and runtimes for free. | `internal/e2e/e2e_test.go:52` |
| Only flags in a fixed "cacheable" set keep `go test` results cacheable; `-shuffle` and any `-args` flag disable caching. A test that reads an env var is cached keyed on that var's value. | `go help test` lines 76-89 |
| `-shuffle off,on,N`: N is an integer seed and is printed for reproducibility. | `go help testflag` |
| `math/rand/v2`: `NewChaCha8(seed [32]byte)`, `NewPCG(seed1, seed2 uint64)`. `go doc math/rand/v2` makes **no** promise that `Rand` methods (`IntN`, `Shuffle`, `Perm`, ...) return the same values across Go releases; the ChaCha8 stream itself is specified (chacha8rand, C2SP). | `go doc math/rand/v2` |
| `google/uuid` v1.6.0 (already an indirect dep) implements `NewV7` with the 12-bit `rand_a` filled from the sub-millisecond clock, not randomness. | `github.com/google/uuid@v1.6.0/version7.go:80-103` |
| `package.nix` `checkPhase` re-runs 18 unit packages inside the nix sandbox, where no seed env var exists. | `pkgs/mcpx/package.nix` |
| `internal/logging/trace.go:168` records every `MCPX_*` env var into traces, so `MCPX_TEST_SEED` would show up in daemon traces from e2e runs (useful). Settings env names are `"MCPX_" + path` (`internal/settings/schema.go:220-224`), so a future setting under `test.` would collide with `MCPX_TEST_*`. | |
| `MCPX_TEST_SEED` would be an `MCPX_*` variable that the code reads and no setting declares, which is exactly the class #172 (in flight) inventories. #172's recommended guard bans `os.Getenv("MCPX_*")` outside the settings package unless the name is on an allowlist with a reason. The seed helper's read needs that allowlist entry, or `_test.go` files and `internal/testsupport` need to be out of the guard's scope. #171's `TestNoHandRolledSettingEnv` (`internal/settings/consumed_test.go:145`) only covers names the registry owns, so it does not flag the seed variable today. | #172 |

## Design

### 1. Seed format

| Format | Distinct across runs | Human-copyable | Time-ordered | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| u64 integer | 64 bits | yes | no | what `-shuffle` and rapid take; too easy to hand-pick ("seed 1") |
| UUIDv4 | 122 bits | yes | no | standard, but no ordering |
| random 128/256-bit hex | 128/256 bits | long | no | entropy beyond ~64 bits buys nothing here (see below) |
| **UUIDv7** | 74 bits (62 with google/uuid) + ms timestamp | yes | **yes** | recommended |
| derived from `run_id`/`run_attempt` | ~34 bits of run id | yes | yes | CI-only, predictable; evaluated in #122 |

Facts for v7 (RFC 9562 section 5.7): 48-bit `unix_ts_ms`, 4-bit version, 12-bit `rand_a`, 2-bit variant, 62-bit `rand_b`. RFC 9562 section 6.2 lets implementations spend `rand_a` on sub-ms precision or a counter, which is what google/uuid does -- so budget **62** random bits, not 74. Either is ample: a collision needs two runs in the *same millisecond* and then a ~2^31 birthday bound on the random part.

Entropy is not the constraint anyway. A PRNG needs a fixed-size key (ChaCha8: 32 bytes), so the id is **never** used as a key directly: it is hashed into one (section 2). What the id needs is to be *distinct* per run and *easy to copy*; v7 adds free time ordering (ids sort by mint time, and the date is recoverable from the id without a lookup, which #122 uses).

**Recommendation:** mint UUIDv7 (canonical lowercase, 36 chars). On *input*, accept any string matching `[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,128}` (so a human can reproduce with an old id, and the format is not locked in forever); only the wrapper and CI mint, and they mint v7.

Minting without a Go dependency (works in a CI init job before `setup-go`, and on macOS where BSD `date` has no `%3N`):

```sh
python3 -c "import os,time;b=bytearray(int(time.time()*1000).to_bytes(6,'big')+os.urandom(10));b[6]=b[6]&15|0x70;b[8]=b[8]&63|0x80;h=b.hex();print(f'{h[:8]}-{h[8:12]}-{h[12:16]}-{h[16:20]}-{h[20:]}')"
# e.g. 01a0f101-2378-7c1c-9dc1-5a1ae1571eca  (74 random bits)
```

### 2. Derivation: one root, many independent streams

```
root            = SHA-256("mcpx-test-seed/v1\x00" || seedID)
stream(t, g@v)  = SHA-256(root || 0x00 || "g@v" || 0x00 || t.Name())   -> ChaCha8 key
shuffle         = int64(big-endian(SHA-256(root || "shuffle")[:8]) & MaxInt63)   -> go test -shuffle=N
rapid (if used) = non-zero uint64 from SHA-256(root || "rapid")                  -> RAPID_SEED
```

- Adding, removing or reordering tests never shifts another test's inputs (each stream is keyed by test name, not by draw order in the process).
- Changing generator `g` (a new version) never shifts generator `h`'s inputs.
- Renaming a test changes its inputs. Acceptable; documented.
- `v1` in the domain tag is the **derivation** version. Changing the derivation is `v2`; old seeds replay under `v1`.

### 3. "avoid changing how seed generates data"

- **Same commit + same seed reproduces exactly**, always -- the commit pins the generator code. Generator stability matters only for **cross-commit replay** (an old stored seed against today's code), which is what the stored seeds in #122 are for.
- Every generator is `name@version`. Any change that alters its output for the same stream is a new version; the old version is kept while any stored seed references it, or frozen. Registry detail in #124.
- **Guard test:** per `generator@version`, a checked-in hash of its first N outputs from a fixed test-vector key. It fails when a generator's output changes without a version bump -- including when a Go upgrade changes `IntN`/`Shuffle` (not promised stable). The test vector pins the *generator*; it is not a static seed for testing mcpx, which the notes forbid.
- To shrink Go-release coupling: generators draw only `Uint64()` from the ChaCha8 source and do their own range reduction (a few lines), so the only external dependency is ChaCha8's specified stream.

### 4. How the seed reaches tests

- **`MCPX_TEST_SEED`** env var is the one channel. Reserve the `MCPX_TEST_*` prefix (a settings guard can assert no setting path starts with `test.`).
- **`internal/testsupport/seed`** helper, read lazily: `seed.Rand(t, gen)` derives the stream for `(t.Name(), gen@version)` and registers a `t.Cleanup` that, if `t.Failed()`, logs the seed, test, generator and the exact reproduce command. Packages that never call it never read the env var and **stay cacheable**; packages that do are re-run whenever the seed changes (correct).
- No `TestMain` needed anywhere.
- **Wrapper** (`just mcpx-test` or `pkgs/mcpx/scripts/test.sh`; exact home decided with #99): mints **once** if unset, exports it, derives and passes `-shuffle=N`, runs `go test` with any extra args. One seed for every package process.

### 5. No seed given

| Situation | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| Wrapper, `MCPX_TEST_SEED` unset or empty | warn on stderr, mint v7, print `MCPX_TEST_SEED=<id>`, write it to a gitignored `pkgs/mcpx/.cache/test-seed/last` (+ local history), export, run. |
| Bare `go test`, unset or empty | helper mints once **per process** (`sync.Once`), logs a warning on first use: "no MCPX_TEST_SEED; generated <id> for this package only -- use the wrapper for one seed per run". Still reproducible (the id is printed on failure). |
| CI (`CI=true` / `GITHUB_ACTIONS=true`), unset or empty | **fail** (helper `t.Fatal`, wrapper exit 1). CI must never mint inside a test process. |
| Anywhere | never a static default in code. |

"write it yourself": locally the seed is written to a **gitignored** file, not the committed store -- local runs committing into the repo would be the churn the notes want to avoid. Committed seeds come from CI via #122 (open question below).

### 6. Reproduce from a seed (one command)

```sh
MCPX_TEST_SEED=01a0f101-2378-7c1c-9dc1-5a1ae1571eca just mcpx-test -run '^TestX$' ./internal/codegen
```

The wrapper derives the same `-shuffle` value from the seed. The helper prints exactly this line on failure, with the commit. In CI, a `workflow_dispatch` input `seed` re-runs the whole matrix on CI runners with a given seed.

Caveat: this reproduces **inputs and test order**, not timing. Execution is not deterministic (#126); a timing bug may need several tries under the same seed.

### 7. Minting in CI (mechanism only; the matrix is #95's)

```yaml
jobs:
  seed:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      seed: ${{ steps.mint.outputs.seed }}
    steps:
      - id: mint
        env: { SEED_IN: "${{ inputs.seed }}" }   # workflow_dispatch override
        run: |
          seed="${SEED_IN:-$(python3 -c '...v7 one-liner above...')}"
          echo "seed=$seed" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "MCPX_TEST_SEED=\`$seed\`" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
          jq -n --arg seed "$seed" --arg sha "$GITHUB_SHA" --arg ref "$GITHUB_REF" \
                --arg event "$GITHUB_EVENT_NAME" --arg run "$GITHUB_RUN_ID" --arg attempt "$GITHUB_RUN_ATTEMPT" \
                '$ARGS.named' > seed.json
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: test-seed, path: seed.json }
  test:
    needs: seed
    env: { MCPX_TEST_SEED: "${{ needs.seed.outputs.seed }}" }
    # matrix owned by #95
```

- "Re-run failed jobs" reuses the outputs of the already-successful `seed` job, so failed shards re-run **with the same seed** (desired: a same-seed pass is a flake, not a seed-dependent bug -- input for #99's flake policy). "Re-run all jobs" mints a new seed. (Verify on the first real run.)
- The artifact is what #122's collector scoops up.
- **Nix `checkPhase`:** the sandbox has no seed and a nix build should stay deterministic. Recommend `checkPhase` sets `MCPX_TEST_FUZZ=off` (generators run only their checked-in regression inputs), or #95 drops the double run of unit tests entirely. Flagged to #95.

## Approaches

### A -- `TestMain` in every package mints or reads the seed (least recommended)
About 30 `TestMain`s. Bare `go test ./...` then produces ~30 different seeds for one "run", and a new package without a `TestMain` is silently unseeded. Printing happens at process start, far from the failure. Nothing here is better than C.

### B -- a `-seed` test flag (registered in `TestMain`) plus a wrapper
Familiar (`-rapid.seed`, `-shuffle` look like this). But `go test ./... -args -seed=X` **errors** in every package whose test binary does not define `-seed` ("flag provided but not defined"), so every package needs the `TestMain` from A anyway; and any `-args` flag disables `go test` caching for all packages, including the ones that never use randomness. Could be offered *in addition* to the env var for single-package runs, but it adds a second channel to keep in sync.

A variant that fixes bare `go test ./...` without a wrapper: all package test binaries are children of the same `go` process, so the first to start could create `$TMPDIR/mcpx-test-seed.<ppid>` (write temp + `os.Link`, atomic) and the rest read it. Clever, ~30 lines, but breaks under `-exec`, `go test -c`, IDE runners and `go test` inside `nix build`. Not the default; possible later.

### C -- env var + lazy helper + one wrapper that mints once (recommended)
As in sections 4-7. One channel that works for subprocesses (e2e, daemon, runtimes), keeps unrelated packages cacheable, needs no per-package boilerplate, fails closed in CI, and gives a one-command reproduction. The wrapper is also where #99's "what to run locally" policy naturally lives. It does not need to reap daemons: #182 fixed #52's leak in the harness itself (`newEnv` cleans up with `stop --all` and sets `MCPX_AUTOSTART_IDLE_EXIT=60s`, `internal/e2e/e2e_test.go:68,79`).

## Open questions

- Wrapper home: `just mcpx-test` in the repo `justfile`, `pkgs/mcpx/scripts/test.sh`, or both (just calling the script)? Windows (in the #97 env wish-list) favours a script that also runs under Git Bash, or a Go `cmd` under `internal/testsupport/cmd`.
- Should local seeds ever reach the committed store (e.g. only failing ones, via an explicit `just mcpx-seed-keep`)? Default proposed: no.
- `-shuffle` disables test caching; is shuffling on by default locally, or CI-only (#99 decides)?
- Env var name: `MCPX_TEST_SEED` (proposed) vs `MCPX_SEED`. Whichever it is, reserve the prefix in #172's allowlist when that lands, so the "read but never declared" guard treats it as test-only rather than as a missing setting.
- Accept arbitrary strings as seed ids on input, or v7 only? Proposed: accept, but the store (#122) only files v7 ids minted by CI.
- Budget knob (`MCPX_TEST_FUZZ=off|quick|ci|soak`) belongs here or in #124? Proposed: named here, sized in #124 with #95.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** S (helper + wrapper ~150 lines; CI init job ~20 lines) · **Impact** high (every randomized test depends on it)
**Depends on / related:** #91 (strategy step 1), #93, #122, #123, #124, #125 (lands it), #126; #95 (consumes the `seed` job output, owns the matrix and the nix double run), #99 (wrapper as the local entrypoint, `-shuffle` and flake policy), #172 (in flight: its allowlist must admit the seed variable), #52 (closed, fixed in #182; the harness cleans up after itself now, so the wrapper has nothing to reap).

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#95 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #91

## Purpose

CI for mcpx, built to the notes' stated top priority: **"the main priority is being short as possible"**, with its stated focus, **"main focus is strong tests as each step of the lifecycle"**. Those two pull against each other, and this tracker is where the trade is made explicitly rather than by accident.

Where it starts, measured rather than estimated. One workflow, `.github/workflows/mcpx.yml`, one `ubuntu-latest` job. Run 36673523537 (push to main), from the step timestamps in `gh run view 36673523537 --log`:

| Step | Seconds |
| --- | --- |
| Set up job, checkout, nix-installer, setup-go/deno/bun/node | 32.6 |
| `go test ./... -count=1` | **134.8** |
| `nix build .#packages.x86_64-linux.mcpx` | 58.8 |
| Post steps + complete | 1.5 |
| **Total wall clock** | **229 s** |

Inside the test step, `internal/e2e` alone is **100.727 s** of 134.8; `internal/tui` 8.6 s; `internal/pool` 1.5 s; `internal/events` 1.05 s; `internal/mcpserver` 1.03 s; everything else under 0.5 s. The last eight runs sit between 3 m 57 s and 4 m 18 s. So the whole sharding question is, in the first instance, one question: **what do you do about e2e**, which is 44% of wall clock and 199 of 719 tests.

After #182, at 05c78b2 (run 36693030957, push to main): 4 m 09 s wall; setup 22 s; `go test` 148 s with `internal/e2e` at **108.9 s for 209 of 735 tests**; `nix build` 70 s (`checkPhase` 18.5 s). That run's Go cache was a miss by construction (the first main run with the new key), so the warm-cache number is still owed -- #143 records it.

Three facts about today's setup that this tracker exists to fix, all verified:

- ~~**The Go cache has never restored.**~~ **Fixed in #182.** `actions/setup-go@v7` defaults `cache: true` but looked for `go.mod` at the repository root; mcpx's is at `pkgs/mcpx/go.mod`. The log carried `##[warning]Restore cache failed: Dependencies file is not found` and every run re-downloaded every module and compiled cold. #182 added `cache-dependency-path: pkgs/mcpx/go.sum` (`.github/workflows/mcpx.yml:50`); the key now saves. What remains of caching (restore-only on PRs, the Nix store, toolchains) is #135.
- **`treefmt.nix` exists and nothing runs it.** `programs.nixfmt` and `programs.rustfmt` are enabled, `flake.nix` exposes `checks.formatting`, and no workflow invokes either. `treefmt.nix:6` also carries `# programs.shellcheck.enable = true; # failures` -- a linter switched off rather than satisfied, already in the tree, and the precedent any new linter must avoid repeating.
- **Unit tests run twice per CI run.** `package.nix` `checkPhase` re-runs a list of unit packages inside `nix build`, costing 16.55 s (18.5 s at 05c78b2) on top of the `go test` step. That is either free time to reclaim or a deliberate sandbox check worth keeping; #135 decision 6 now argues to keep it (the sandbox has no network, which would have caught #65) but take it off the critical path, and to fix its drifted package list (12 packages with tests never run there).

What this tracker does **not** own: the seed itself (#93 -- the `init` job mints and exports it, but #121/#122 decide what it is), the environment legs that join this matrix (#97 -- nix, container, remote, other OSes), and what an agent runs on its own machine instead of CI (#99).

## Children

- [ ] #135 mcpx testing: CI workflow skeleton -- init, matrix, final job; triggers, concurrency, caching, checkout (its cache one-liner landed in #182)
- [ ] #139 mcpx testing: shard the suite by measured time, and a rule for when to stop splitting
- [ ] #140 mcpx testing: a CI time budget in the final job, and the over-budget runbook
- [ ] #141 mcpx testing: every formatter and linter in the CI matrix, pinned by the flake (and run the plugin's bun test)
- [ ] #142 mcpx testing: format.yaml -- auto-format after a green run; PR head vs main
- [ ] #143 mcpx testing: first CI iteration -- unit + e2e shards + lint + nix build, and a recorded baseline

## Proposed order

1. **#135** -- the skeleton. Workflow name, `init -> matrix -> ci-ok` job graph, triggers (including the notes' "commit/open/undraft to a non-draft pr", which today's workflow does not implement -- it sets no `pull_request: types:`, so it uses the default `[opened, synchronize, reopened]` and `ready_for_review` never fires), concurrency, caching, checkout, and what stays behind in `mcpx.yml`. Everything else plugs into this.
2. **#143** -- build the first real iteration and **record a baseline**. Split unit from e2e, put static shards in, add the lint leg, keep `nix build`. (The Go cache fix it also carried landed separately in #182, as #181's phase 0 asked; #52, which the old order waited on, is closed by the same PR.) This is the issue that produces the timing data every later decision needs; without it #139 and #140 are guesswork. #138 (in #97) is recommended just before or alongside it: it is the remaining isolation gap, and every shard inherits it.
3. **#139** -- replace the static shards with a split driven by measured per-test time, and write down the rule for when to stop splitting. Needs #143's numbers. `t.Parallel` in e2e is no longer blocked by #52; it waits on #138 and a measured `-parallel`.
4. **#140** -- turn the recorded baseline into a gate: the budget job, and the runbook for what to do when it is breached. Needs a number, which #143 supplies.
5. **#141** -- the full formatter and linter set, beyond the first lint leg #143 stands up.
6. **#142** -- `format.yaml`, last, because it only makes sense once the formatters are pinned (#141) and there is a green test workflow for it to key on (#135's `name:`).

The notes describe an iterative loop -- split the longest job, re-measure, repeat, and do it again whenever the budget is breached. That loop is #143 -> #139 -> #140 -> #143, and it is expected to run more than once. #140's runbook is what makes it a procedure rather than a habit.

## Children -- ease and impact

| # | Title | Kind | Ease | Impact |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| #135 | workflow skeleton -- init, matrix, final job, triggers, caching (cache line done in #182) | design | M | **high** |
| #139 | shard by measured time, and when to stop splitting | design | M | **high** |
| #140 | time budget in the final job, and the over-budget runbook | design + implement | S (job) + S (runbook) | med |
| #141 | every formatter and linter in the matrix, pinned by the flake | design | M (mostly clean-up, one style decision) | med |
| #142 | format.yaml -- auto-format after a green run | design | M (needs a token decision) | low-med (convenience; quality comes from the blocking check) |
| #143 | first iteration + recorded baseline | implement | M | **high** -- roughly halves wall clock and produces the data for everything else |

## Warnings carried by this tracker

- **The biggest single win is no longer blocked by #52, but it is not free.** 209 serial e2e tests that mostly wait on process start, sockets and runtime startup are the textbook case for `t.Parallel()` -- plausibly 2-3x on one runner at zero extra setup cost. #182 fixed the leak that made that dangerous (`stop --all` through the info files, 60 s idle exit). What still has to come first is #138: `newEnv` still inherits the caller's environment, so an exported `MCPX_DAEMON_ENDPOINT`/`MCPX_SOCKET` sends every parallel test to one outside daemon. And one e2e test is 3-4 processes (CLI, daemon, fake server, often a JS runtime), so `-parallel 8` on 4 vCPU is 24-32 processes: measure `-parallel`, do not take GOMAXPROCS. #139 has both.
- **Renaming a job invalidates every required check**, and a sharded matrix produces N check names that change on every rebalance. The fix -- one `needs: [...] if: always()` aggregator as the sole required check -- is in #135, along with the trap that without `always()` a skipped aggregator reads as neutral and a red matrix merges.
- **A `paths:`-filtered required check never reports and blocks merges permanently.** Harmless today only because nothing is required yet.
- **Sparse checkout breaks `nix build`**, which evaluates the whole flake. Sparse applies to test legs only.
- **`workflow_run` only fires from the default branch**, checks out the default-branch tip rather than `head_sha`, and `types: [completed]` includes failures. All three bite #142.
- **The `GITHUB_TOKEN` loop guard is the only thing that closes the auto-format loop.** Swapping in a PAT to get past branch protection re-opens it.
- **More shards are not monotonically better.** 22-33 s of setup is the floor per leg (32.8 s on 36673523537, 22 s on 36693030957); ten legs spend 220-330 runner-seconds of setup to save ~90 s of wall clock, and the concurrency cap turns them into two waves -- which is exactly the runner-pressure effect the notes predict. Driving the fixed cost down beats adding a fifth shard.

## Related

#91 (parent), #93 (#121/#122 -- the seed `init` mints), #97 (#134/#136 -- environment legs join this matrix), #99 (#127 -- CI is where "every test" runs so that agents do not), #49 (CI for every flake package -- overlaps this tree directly), #138 (in #97; the isolation gap before parallel shards), #178 (also edits `package.nix`), #52 (closed, fixed in #182), #79, #35, #65, #47, #48.

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

## Acceptance criteria
- mcpx CI runs sharded with a stated time budget; lint and auto-format checks run as their own jobs and fail the build on violations.
- The budget and shard layout are documented, and a deliberately slow test is shown to trip the budget alarm in CI.

body:
# codex-proxy: the app-server WebSocket frame parser has no size cap — one header claiming a huge payload wedges the connection forever and swallows every later frame

## Evidence (verified this run, main `3675a470`)

`bin/codex-proxy.mjs`, `AppServerClient.drainFrames()` (lines 486–525):

- The 64-bit length form is trusted verbatim: `len = Number(this.buffer.readBigUInt64BE(off))` (:500). There is no maximum frame size anywhere in the parser.
- The only guard is `if (this.buffer.length < off + len) return;` (:506) — for an absurd claimed length the parser simply waits for payload bytes that will never arrive. It never errors, never closes, and never resynchronizes.
- Everything the peer sends afterwards is accumulated into `this.buffer` (and, for fragmented messages, into `this.fragments`, also uncapped, :515) as if it were that frame's payload — including perfectly valid frames.
- Contrast in the same repo: the Rust frame reader refuses anything over `MAX_FRAME_BYTES` = 1 MiB (`pkgs/id/src/frames.rs`), and `bin/proxy-relay.mjs:105` caps the tunnel CONNECT response head at 16 KiB. This parser is the outlier.

### Probe (laptop, verbatim parser)

Probe dir: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-codexws/` — `codex-proxy.mjs` copied byte-identical to main (sha256 `494e89732baa3fac58b535f07313bfe31560ebbe41bb4a01a23068918d44ca3a`), `drainFrames`/`wsEncodeFrame` extracted verbatim from that copy and driven with crafted unmasked server-style frames (`node probe.mjs`):

- CONTROL: a small text frame `{"id":1,"result":{}}` → delivered to `onMessage`, buffer empty.
- OVERSIZED: a header claiming `2^40` payload bytes followed by a valid `{"id":2,"result":{}}` frame → **no message, no close, no error**; 32 bytes buffered and the valid frame swallowed as payload. The connection is permanently desynchronized.
- INCOMPLETE: a 65,535-byte claim with 100 bytes present → silently waits, same wedge in miniature.

## Why it matters

The app-server is a separate process; a buggy or desynchronized frame stream (a partial write, a version-skewed peer, one corrupt length byte) turns into a silent, permanent proxy outage rather than a reconnect. `handleClose` never fires, the client still reports ready, pending RPCs reject only on their individual 30 s timeouts, and every subsequent RPC on the wedged connection times out the same way until the proxy process is restarted by hand. A bounded parser would fail the connection at the bad header and let the existing close/reconnect path run.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `drainFrames` refuses a frame whose claimed payload length exceeds a named maximum (choose one in line with the repo's other caps, e.g. the 1 MiB of `pkgs/id/src/frames.rs`, or a documented codex-specific value): the connection is closed via the existing `handleClose`/destroy path with an error naming the claimed length and the cap, instead of waiting for the payload.
- [ ] The accumulated fragmented message size is bounded by the same (or a named) cap, so a peer cannot grow `this.fragments` without bound using non-final frames.
- [ ] A claimed length that does not fit exactly in a safe integer is refused, not rounded by `Number(BigUInt)`.
- [ ] Regression tests in `bin/codex-proxy.test.mjs`: a valid small frame still parses (control); an oversized claimed length closes/errors immediately and does not consume a following valid frame as payload; an over-cap fragmented sequence is refused.
- [ ] Normal-size app-server traffic is unchanged: the existing codex-proxy tests pass.

body:
## Origin

Owner direction (Drew, 2026-10-28), given with the #793 implement decision: 'we need to start deploying Cloudflare and other resources in a controlled way.' This issue designs the standard; the P7.2 pkarr Worker is its pilot. The standard is meant to be **the pattern for all future deployments** — later deployables follow it and add on, and a composed entrypoint eventually deploys everything by running the deployers in the appropriate order. Nobody downstream should have to re-think any of this.

## Requirements (owner's, verbatim in substance)

1. **All code lives in this repo** (developing-today/code) to start.
2. **Deployment is a Nix flake action, never a NixOS switch.** Drew does not deploy by switching his Nix config, and NixOS builds are network-less. Shape to decide in this design: `nix run` on a flake app, OR a deploy binary the flake puts on PATH as its own command, OR a `just` recipe wrapping either — with secrets fetched at deploy time.
3. **Secrets: SOPS-encrypted in the repo, keys in the vaults.** All deploy secrets are stored SOPS-encrypted inside the repo, encrypted to a system age key or a dedicated key generated for this effort. Every key is documented — what it is and where it lives — and the key material is ALSO stored in Bitwarden and/or 1Password, so deployment never depends on the Nix store containing secrets (it must never contain plaintext secrets). Reuse the existing Bitwarden loading mechanism (the bws tooling the fleet already uses) where it fits — 'maybe it's just more of that.'
4. **Rollback = revert + redeploy.** Deployment is a function of the checked-out code: revert the code, deploy again, and the previous version is what's live. The design must state honestly how resources REMOVED from the config are handled — that state problem is the one real argument for Terraform, and the design has to answer it, not wave at it.
5. **Avoid Terraform.** Not strictly forbidden, but the burden of proof is on needing it. Explore first: generating deployable config/JSON from Nix and driving provider APIs directly (for Cloudflare: the API or wrangler under the deploy command). If Terraform (or terranix) is genuinely required, say exactly why, scoped to the piece that needs it.
6. **Composability.** Each deployable follows the same shape; a top-level deploy runs them in a declared order.

## This design must settle

- The deploy entrypoint shape (flake app vs PATH binary vs just recipe) and the per-deployable interface.
- The secrets flow end to end: SOPS layout in-repo, which age key(s) encrypt what, how the deploy command obtains decryption capability at run time (Bitwarden/1Password fetch), how a new secret gets added, how rotation works.
- The Cloudflare driver (direct API vs wrangler vs generated config) and the removed-resource/state answer from requirement 4.
- What 'deploy' verifies before declaring success (health endpoint, version marker), and what a failed deploy leaves behind.
- The documentation standard: every key and secret named, purposed, and located (repo SOPS file + vault entry), in one index a future operator can follow cold.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A design document in `doc/` answering every point above, with the entrypoint shape and Cloudflare driver chosen and justified.
- [ ] The pilot implementation issue (pkarr Worker, linked from #793) is scoped against this design.

body:
# commandcode-proxy: COMMANDCODE_PROXY_TIMEOUT_MS is parsed with a bare Number() — a typo'd, negative, or >2³¹ value makes every request "time out" in ~1 ms instead of failing at startup

## Evidence

`bin/commandcode-proxy.mjs:60` (main `e91098f1`):

```js
const TIMEOUT_MS = Number(process.env.COMMANDCODE_PROXY_TIMEOUT_MS || 240000);
```

No validation follows. `TIMEOUT_MS` drives every timeout in the proxy:

- `:567` — the ACP `request()` timer (`ACP … timed out after ${timeoutMs}ms`),
- `:675` / `:682` — the ACP prompt timer, and the request timer derived as `timeoutMs + 30000`,
- `:945` — the spawn-fallback kill timer,
- `:1067` — the user-visible error text: `` `commandcode timed out after ${TIMEOUT_MS}ms` ``.

The sibling env values in the same `bin/` family were hardened against exactly this failure class: ports go through the strict shared parser in `bin/proxy-port.mjs` (#483, #494 — "a bare parseInt is not a validator"), which fails at startup naming the variable and its value. The timeout never got the same treatment.

### Probe (laptop, verbatim `:60` expression + the same `setTimeout` use as `:567`/`:675`/`:945`)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-cctimeout/probe.mjs`:

| `COMMANDCODE_PROXY_TIMEOUT_MS` | parsed `TIMEOUT_MS` | timer fired after |
|---|---|---|
| `abc` | `NaN` | ~6 ms (`TimeoutNaNWarning … set to 1`) |
| `240000junk` | `NaN` | ~1 ms |
| `-5000` | `-5000` | ~2 ms (`TimeoutNegativeWarning … set to 1`) |
| `9999999999999` | `9999999999999` | ~2 ms (`TimeoutOverflowWarning … does not fit into a 32-bit signed integer … set to 1`) |
| `300` (control) | `300` | ~306 ms |

## Why it matters

One typo in the service environment (a unit, a home-manager option, a hand edit) silently converts the proxy into a machine that fails **every** chat/agency request instantly, while reporting `commandcode timed out after NaNms` (or `after -5000ms`) — an error that points at the upstream engine, not at the configuration. The proxy starts cleanly and answers `/health`, so supervisors see a healthy process. A large-but-sane-looking value (e.g. `9999999999999`, or anything above 2³¹−1 ≈ 24.8 days in ms) overflows Node's timer the same way. Startup is the right place for this to fail, as the port parser already established for this family.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An invalid `COMMANDCODE_PROXY_TIMEOUT_MS` (non-numeric, trailing junk, zero, negative, or above a pinned maximum ≤ 2³¹−1) makes the proxy exit at startup with an error naming the variable and its value, in the style of `proxy-port.mjs`'s `parseProxyPort`.
- [ ] The parsing lives in a shared/strict helper (extending `proxy-port.mjs` or a sibling) rather than an inline copy unique to this proxy, or the triage comment pins why inline is right here.
- [ ] Tests in `bin/commandcode-proxy.test.mjs` (or the helper's test file) cover: unset → 240000 default; a plain value → itself; each invalid class above → startup error.
- [ ] No behaviour change for valid values: ACP request/prompt timers and the spawn kill timer receive the same millisecond values as today.

Related: #483 / #494 (strict port parsing for this same proxy family).

labels.name: kind/ci

labels.name: priority/high

labels.name: effort/m

body:
## Phase 1 — cancel-in-progress across all four repos

Design: #1779 (doc §2.2, §4). **Drew-approved outright 2026-10-28.**
Cross-repo: one issue, one PR per repo.

### Problem

Stale CI runs from superseded pushes queue to completion instead of
cancelling, holding GitHub runner-assignment slots ahead of live
work. 2026-10-28 sample (code#1599): queue branches carried 4–5
queued runs each; 127+ runs queued fleet-wide with ~4 in progress,
while per-job execution is only 0.4–14m — the wait is the disease.

### Scope (audit gaps from the design inventory)

Apply the standard pattern — group keyed by ref for branch/PR runs,
`cancel-in-progress: true`, push-to-main runs keyed by `run_id` so
they are never cancelled:

```yaml
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' && github.run_id || github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true
```

- **developing-today/openchamber:** add concurrency where missing —
  `nix-eval.yml`, `release.yml`, `vscode-extension.yml`,
  `release-desktop-smoke.yml`; set cancel on `pr-review.yml`
  (currently cip=false).
- **developing-today/opencode:** `publish*.yml` — concurrency group
  exists but cancel-in-progress is unset (defaults false); set it
  for PR/branch runs.
- **developing-today/code:** `goreleaser.yml` (no block),
  `auto-assign.yml` (cip=false; metadata-only, align for
  uniformity).
- **dezren39/nix:** audit confirms both PR workflows already carry
  the pattern — verify and close this repo's slice with evidence.

### Explicit non-goals

- code `jules.yml` is NOT touched: its job-level cip=false groups
  are load-bearing (#304 — a shared group let noise completions
  cancel real Jules dispatch runs).
- Scheduled singleton jobs (branch-cleanup, deploys) keep
  cip=false; they are not checks.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] One PR per repo (merge commit) applying the pattern to the
      files above; no other workflow behaviour changes.
- [ ] A superseded push on a test PR shows the earlier run
      `cancelled` (evidence screenshot/comment on the PR).
- [ ] A push-to-main run is never cancelled by a later push
      (run_id keying) — verified on the first main run after merge.

title: id(peers): --max-peers is not a hard cap — the crawl inserts a whole ListPeers response unchecked, and the RPC/gossip paths never consult it at all

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: status/blocked
labels.description: Queue or user escalation state

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: queue/blocked
labels.description: Queue or user escalation state

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`id peers --max-peers` is documented as a hard cap on total discovered peers, but it is not enforced as one. Three of the four collection paths never consult it, and the fourth (the crawl) checks it only *before* issuing a query — never while inserting that query's response — so a single `ListPeers` response can push the result arbitrarily far past the cap.

## Evidence (developing-today/code @ 9874fe59, `pkgs/id/src/commands/peers.rs` unless noted)

- The contract: module doc `:32` — "`--max-peers` caps total discovered peers (default: 1000)"; `PeersOptions.max_peers` doc `:78` — "Hard cap on total peers discovered."; CLI doc `src/cli.rs:1194-1198` — "Maximum total peers to discover. Hard cap to prevent unbounded crawling."
- `cmd_peers` initial RPC results are inserted unchecked at `:144` (`all_peers.insert(peer.node_id, peer.clone())`), crawled results unchecked at `:159`, and gossip results unchecked at `:170`. `max_peers` is passed only to `crawl_peers` (`:148-156`).
- `discover_via_gossip` collects announcements into its own map unchecked at `:432` — no cap at all during the collect window.
- `crawl_peers` checks `all_peers.len() >= max_peers` at `:296` (loop head) and `:313` (before each query), but the response-insertion loop at `:322-331` inserts every vacant entry with no cap check. The checks only stop *further queries*; they never bound what one response adds.

## Verification (this run)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-peers-maxcap/` (cargo, laptop): `crawl_peers` copied structurally verbatim with the peer query stubbed (seed peer answers one response of 100 fresh peers; ID types reduced to `u64`):

- Case 1 — crawl with `max_peers=10`, depth 1, one 100-peer response → **collected 101 peers** (10× the "hard cap").
- Case 2 — the `cmd_peers` initial-insert loop shape with a 2,000-peer RPC result and the default cap 1000 → **all 2,000 retained**.

Note the response itself is separately bounded today only by the 1 MiB read in the hand-rolled clients (see #1761, ~20k peers max per response) — so one response can overshoot the default cap ~20×, and `--max-peers 50` (a value the CLI tests exercise, `cli.rs:2747-2759`) provides almost no protection at all. The overshoot lands in memory, in the sorted output, and — for crawl results — in the next frontier.

## Why it matters

`--max-peers` is the user's only stated safeguard against unbounded crawling (per its own CLI help). A malicious or merely large peer can hand back a huge peer list and the client will absorb, store, sort, print, and crawl from all of it regardless of the flag. Users who set a small cap for a quick, bounded probe get unbounded work instead.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Total peers returned/printed by `id peers` never exceeds `--max-peers` in any mode (RPC, gossip, default, any `--depth`), or the docs/help are corrected to state the real, weaker guarantee and a true bound is enforced elsewhere — triage pins which.
- [ ] The crawl insertion loop enforces the cap while inserting a response (stops at the cap, and the existing "cap reached" warning fires in that case too).
- [ ] The initial RPC insert, the crawl-result merge, the gossip merge in `cmd_peers`, and the `discover_via_gossip` collect loop all respect the same cap.
- [ ] Regression test: a single response larger than the cap yields exactly the cap (extraction of the collection logic for testability is acceptable if the network-facing shape is preserved).
- [ ] Existing `peers` / CLI tests pass (laptop or CI).

title: id(tag): meta-tag TSV output renders subject/key/value raw — a newline in a synced tag value forges extra rows in id tag list, and a tab forges columns

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The plain-text output of `id tag list` / `id tag search` (and the `tag set:` echo) renders the tag's subject, key and value **raw** into a tab-separated one-line-per-tag format. Meta-tag subjects, keys and values are arbitrary bytes with no control-character validation anywhere on the write path, so a value (or key, or subject) containing a newline forges an entire extra row in another node's listing, and a tab forges extra columns. This is the same forgery class as #1611 (claim/doc/group `key=value` renderer, fixed in #1703 via `group::text()`) and #1613 (peer names in `id peers`), but a different renderer, a different store and a different protocol — neither issue covers it: the meta-tag renderer does not go through `tokens()` at all.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `0e245370`)

- Rendering: `print_tag_line` (`pkgs/id/src/commands/tag.rs:373-380`) prints `format!("{subject}\t{key}={}", opts.format_value(v))` where subject/key are `String::from_utf8_lossy` of the raw bytes. `TagDisplayOptions::format_value` (`tag.rs:104-131`) returns valid-UTF-8 values **verbatim** (only length-truncation at 256 bytes on a char boundary); the `<binary N bytes>` / hex summaries apply only to non-UTF-8 values. The `run_set` echo (`tag.rs:249`, `tag set: {subject} [{key}={}]`) prints subject/key raw the same way.
- Write path admits the payload: `TagStore::set_tag` (`pkgs/id/src/tags.rs:800-845`) documents subject/key/value as "arbitrary bytes" and stores them with no validation; the meta protocol handler (`pkgs/id/src/protocol.rs:589-598`) passes them straight through. Tags sync between nodes (α/Ω iroh-docs stores), so the crafted bytes do not have to be typed by the person reading the listing.
- Same class in the sibling TSV listings of the same name space: `id list` prints `{hash}\t{name}` raw (`pkgs/id/src/commands/list.rs:91,110,157`) and the find renderers print `{hash}\t{name}` raw (`pkgs/id/src/helpers.rs:155-176,192-233,246-265`) — a stored blob name containing LF/TAB forges rows there too.
- Probe (verbatim `hex_encode` + `truncate_on_char_boundary` + `format_value` + the `print_tag_line` rendering, run on the laptop; `commands/tag.rs` sha256 `d2d52342…` on main `0e245370`; probe + log in the goal's `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-tagforge/`):
  - Control `README.md / priority=high` → 1 physical line, 2 tab fields.
  - value `x\nEVIL.bin\towner=attacker` → **2 physical lines**; the second is a fully-formed forged tag row naming a different subject.
  - value `a\tb` → 3 tab fields in one row (column forgery).
  - key `k\nEVIL.bin\towner=attacker` → 2 physical lines, forged row.
  - subject `a\nEVIL.bin` → 2 physical lines, forged row.
  - value `a\rb` → raw CR passes through.
  - Non-UTF-8 value `[0xff, 0x0a]` → summarised as `<binary 2 bytes>` — the safe path exists, but only off the UTF-8 branch.

## Why it matters

`id tag list` output is the machine-adjacent listing operators and fleet scripts split on tabs/newlines. A tag synced from a peer (or set once via `--value-file`/the meta protocol with arbitrary bytes) can plant a phantom row attributing tags to a different file in every subsequent listing — the exact output-forgery pattern #1611/#1613 guard against in the neighbouring renderers. The UTF-8 fast path in `format_value` is the odd one out: binary values are already summarised safely.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Plain output of `id tag list` / `search` and the `tag set:` echo is always one physical line per tag, whatever bytes the subject, key or value contain (escape/quote values containing whitespace or control characters, or summarise them like the non-UTF-8 path — the rule is pinned by tests and stated in the module doc at `commands/tag.rs:14-22`).
- [ ] A tab-splitting consumer recovers exactly the real fields: no forged rows and no extra columns from crafted subject/key/value bytes (probe cases above).
- [ ] The same rule is applied (or explicitly scoped out with a reason) for the sibling raw TSV name listings: `id list` (`commands/list.rs`) and the find renderers (`helpers.rs` `print_match_cli`/`print_matches_cli`/`print_match_repl`).
- [ ] Ordinary space-free printable values and names render byte-identically to today; `--hex`/`--binary` behaviours are unchanged.
- [ ] Tests pin the rule at `format_value`/`print_tag_line` level, mirroring the renderer tests added for #1611 in `commands/group.rs`.

Triage note: renderer-side escaping/summarising is likely the load-bearing fix (refusing control bytes at `set_tag` would change what synced stores may hold and would not clean rows already stored); whether to also refuse at write time is the triage pin.

title: Consider: an acpx 'muse' agent — ACP adapter for the Muse CLI (plan-quota coding harness for OpenClaw)

labels.name: source/human
labels.description: Filed directly by a human

labels.name: effort/m
