body:
## What happened (2026-11-07, OpenCode lane sessions)

Three lane sessions died on provider credential/routing errors at or near startup. None failed over to another candidate — against the standing doctrine that sessions must fail over, never error, while candidates remain:

- **(a) 18:35 CST** — session `ses_e5e476b7e03ffe4YdwXaba0m0v` (mcpx script-repair one-off): died in 0.69s before producing any output. `provider.auth`, HTTP 401 — "OAuth access token has been revoked."
- **(b) 20:05 CST** — session `ses_e5e4719223effeYQyhrJHBwDRD` (lane claimant/executor for #3026): did real work for 24.5s, then the next assistant turn failed with `provider.invalid-request`, HTTP 404 "Provider request failed", empty body. Which provider endpoint/model returned the 404 is NOT in the session record — this cause remains unexplained on the evidence.
- **(c) 01:40 CST** — session `ses_e5e4b0cb…v2yvifAqnGqu` (same repair prompt as (a); not flagged by the minder): died in 0.10s. `provider.auth` — the Claude Code OAuth credential in `~/.claude/.credentials.json` had expired and this provider does not refresh the CLI's login; in the provider's own words, requests "fail closed rather than falling back."

## Problem

The session cascade failover covers mid-session errors; startup-phase provider errors (auth expiry/revocation, routing 404s) kill the session outright. Two of the three deaths are the wire-only doctrine's remaining tail: the claude-code provider's OAuth refresh/write-back path.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Startup-phase provider errors (auth, invalid-request, routing 404) enter the same failover cascade as mid-session errors: while candidates remain, the session re-routes instead of erroring.
- [ ] Session outcomes record the provider error text — and for routing errors, the endpoint/model that failed — in the session outcome itself. (Today the session minder's state carried outcome only; finding these causes required a live-API dig.)
- [ ] Case (b)'s 404 is identified (which endpoint 404'd), or explicitly recorded as unidentifiable with the evidence preserved.
- [ ] The claude-code OAuth expiry path (case c) either refreshes or fails over — fail-closed with no fallback is not an acceptable end state.

Source: lane review 2026-11-07 §1.2 (scratch/lane-review-2026-11-07.md). Related: session cascade failover (opencode fork #1853), question-stall cluster (opencode fork #1883/#1884/#1890).

body:
## Incident (2026-11-07, lane code-e, task 11075 / #6819)

The first done-note posting for #6819 was built with an UNQUOTED heredoc. A backticked env segment in the note text executed on the laptop, and the resulting environment dump — values included — was posted as public issue comment 6715474588 on this public repo. The comment was deleted within ~3 minutes and verified 404; a clean repost followed (comment 6715488065). Exposed variable names: BWS_ACCESS_TOKEN (the secrets-broker master key), CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN, MUSE_API_KEY, META_API_KEY, plus CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID.

Credential rotation for that exposure is a separate decision tracked elsewhere. This issue is the PREVENTION work: the incident is recorded on #6819 and in the four-repos backlog, and until now prevention existed only as a backlog sentence ("never use unquoted heredocs for gh body files").

## Rule

Sanctioned note/comment posting must be structurally incapable of shell-evaluating body text:

- Post bodies are passed ONLY via quoted heredocs (`<<'EOF'`) or via body files (`gh --body-file`, base64-decoded body files, or file-body API fields). Unquoted heredocs for post bodies are banned in lane work.
- A pre-post secret-content scan runs on the sanctioned posting path: if body text matches credential-shaped patterns (env-dump shapes, known token prefixes, credential KEY=value lines), the post is blocked and the body must be re-prepared from a file.

## Acceptance

- [ ] The rule is written into the lane instruction bodies lanes actually read — not only a backlog note.
- [ ] One safe shared posting pattern/helper exists and the lane instructions point at it.
- [ ] Grep verification across lane bodies and posting scripts shows no unquoted-heredoc post-body pattern remains.
- [ ] The pre-post scan is in the shared path and demonstrably blocks a synthetic env-dump-shaped body in a dry run.

Refs: #6819 (incident record) · clean repost comment 6715488065 · lane review 2026-11-07 §3 (scratch/lane-review-2026-11-07.md).

- Lane code-m's §1b `fleet queue lane 11895` call returned a ledger row (assigned_lane direct, assigned_at 02:33:01Z) and its first checkpoint appeared to apply, so the shift worked the triage.
- At ~02:38Z a checkpoint failed with the verdict `checkpoint_task: task 11895 is not claimed by repo-worker-code` (broker exit 5 — the backend was healthy; health reads fine).
- Issue #1087 then showed a second, independent pickup (02:40Z) and done (02:41Z) agent-note pair from the queue worker — lane code-f had held the real claim all along, worked the same triage in parallel, and completed task 11895.

**Why it matters**

The atomic claim is the fleet's only protection against double work (worker instruction §0/§1: lanes overlap by design; the shared worker id `repo-worker-code` does not distinguish lanes). A claim call that returns a task another lane already holds — with that lane's stamp already on the row — makes two shifts do the same work and post duplicate agent notes (here: issue #1087 comments 6716245056/6716245301 from lane code-m alongside lane code-f's pair). This instance was benign (read-only triage, same verdict, no labels or code touched by either side beyond notes), but the same race on a small_fix task means competing branches/PRs.

**Evidence to check**

- Task 11895's claim/lease history around 2026-11-08T02:32:59Z: two claim calls (lane code-m, lane code-f) in the same second; the row's lane_id was code-f in the response lane code-m received.
- Whether the claim verb, on losing a race, returns the winner's claimed row as if it were a successful claim instead of moving to the next queued task or returning a refusal.

**Acceptance**

- A claim that loses the race for a task never returns that task as a successful claim: it claims the next eligible task or returns no-task.
- A regression test/fixture exercises two concurrent claims (distinct lane ids, same queue) and shows exactly one winner per task.

title: aggregator(assembly-deadline): no single-flight — concurrent or post-timeout requests for the same bounded URL each start a full assembly, so overload multiplies the heaviest renders

labels.name: task/small-fix

labels.description: Package/app: aggregator (pm-stack in this repo)

labels.name: app/pm-stack
labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

body:
## Problem

`pm-stack/aggregator/src/assembly-deadline.ts` (the #5664 dashboard deadline wrapper, used for every request in `src/server.ts:2292`) bounds how long a caller waits, but it never coalesces concurrent work for the same URL:

- Every request starts its own `assemble()` unconditionally (`assembly-deadline.ts:71`, `const pending = Promise.resolve().then(assemble)`). There is no in-flight entry keyed by the cache key that already exists at `:70`.
- When a request times out, its assembly keeps running by design (to seed the last-good cache, `:92-94`) — but the next request for the same URL starts a **second** full assembly while the first is still running, and a third request starts a third.

The bounded routes (`/board`, `/api/board.json`, `/api/overview.json`, `/frag/overview`, `/program`) are exactly the routes whose assembly is expensive and which die under load (#5082). Under the precise condition this module exists for — assembly slower than the deadline, with the dashboard auto-refreshing and multiple viewers polling — identical assemblies multiply concurrency instead of sharing one run, amplifying the overload that caused the timeouts.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop, real module)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-assembly-deadline` (module copied verbatim from main @801ceb9cb1, md5 `60a86fddb871c30d52c0adc348a5ea3a` both sides), `createDashboardResponseDeadline({ timeoutMs: 50 })`, assemble that resolves after 300 ms and counts concurrent runs:

- 3 concurrent requests for `http://localhost/api/board.json` → statuses `503,503,503`; **assemblies started: 3, max concurrent: 3**.
- Control (fast assemble, 0 ms) → status 200, assemblies started: 1. The deadline/stale-cache behaviour itself works; only coalescing is missing.
- The existing suite `pm-stack/aggregator/test/assembly-deadline.test.ts` covers the deadline, stale, and timeout responses but has no concurrency/coalescing case.

## Why it matters

The deadline wrapper turns a slow dashboard into bounded 503/stale responses for callers, but on the server side it can make overload self-reinforcing: N waiting callers ⇒ N copies of the heaviest renders in the aggregator running at once, competing for the same CPU/IO that made assembly slow. Single-flight per key caps that at 1.

## Acceptance criteria

- Concurrent (or overlapping, post-timeout) requests for the same bounded key share one in-flight `assemble()` run; the probe above reports assemblies started: 1, max concurrent: 1, with each waiter still bounded by its own deadline (503/stale at its own timeout, never waiting for the shared run past it).
- A late-finishing shared run still seeds the last-good cache exactly once; a rejected shared run does not poison the key — the next request starts a fresh run, and waiters observe the same error path as today (server.ts error boundary).
- Non-bounded paths and non-GET requests are untouched (still direct `assemble()`).
- New regression test in `assembly-deadline.test.ts`: concurrent same-key requests coalesce (counting assemble), plus the post-timeout overlap case; existing suite stays green.

Related: #5664 (built the deadline wrapper), #5082 (the overload symptom on these routes).

title: lab-ops-hub(container): POST /crawl trusts Content-Length — a negative or oversized length wedges the single-threaded crawler in an unbounded body read

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/lab-ops-hub
labels.description: Package/app: lab-ops-hub (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Summary

The lab-ops-hub container crawler (`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py`) reads its
`POST /crawl` request body with no validation of `Content-Length` and no read
bound, on a single-threaded server. A negative or oversized declared length
wedges the whole crawler service in `rfile.read()` until the client socket
closes — every other crawl (and the health `GET /`) starves behind it.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @08dd577848)

`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py`, `Handler.do_POST` (:1473-1478):

```python
length = int(self.headers.get("content-length", "0"))
url = json.loads(self.rfile.read(length))["url"]
```

served by the single-threaded server at :1507-1508:

```python
HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0", 8080), Handler).serve_forever()
```

- `Content-Length: -1` → `rfile.read(-1)` reads until EOF: as long as the
  client holds the socket open, the handler never returns.
- `Content-Length: 10000000` with a small body actually sent → `read()` blocks
  awaiting bytes that never arrive.
- There is no cap and no socket deadline on this read. The response side of
  the same file is carefully bounded by contrast: `_fetch_crawl` caps the
  fetched body at `_CRAWL_MAX_BODY_BYTES = 2_000_000` (:1358) under one
  absolute 20 s deadline (`_CRAWL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`, :1357, :1362-1367),
  explicitly so "a peer that keeps dribbling bytes cannot renew the budget".
  The request side has neither protection.
- Secondary: a non-numeric `Content-Length` raises `ValueError` out of
  `int(...)` and is answered by the catch-all as **502** (a container
  failure), not 400 — and per the #7018 contract a 502 is what makes the
  Worker treat the crawl as a container failure and fall back, so a client
  error is indistinguishable from a dead crawler.

## Reproduction (probe, real module, validation/fetch stubbed — the read loop is what is under test)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-labops-bodyread/probe.py` on the laptop (real
`app.py` Handler over a real socket; `validate_crawl_url`/`_fetch_crawl`
stubbed, `idna` stubbed as the sandbox python lacks it):

- Control `POST /crawl` with a well-formed length → `200`; control `GET /` → `200`.
- `POST /crawl` with `Content-Length: -1`, partial body, socket held open →
  no response within 3 s; a concurrent `GET /` on a new connection also gets
  no response within 3 s (the single-threaded server is wedged); after the
  client socket closes (EOF), `GET /` answers `200` again.
- `POST /crawl` with `Content-Length: 10000000` and a partial body, socket
  held open → same wedge and same starvation of the concurrent `GET /`.

## Why it matters

The container is a separate service with its own release cadence (the premise
of #7018); the hub Worker is its only caller today and sends well-formed
lengths, but any client bug, proxy quirk, or future caller that stalls a body
mid-request takes the crawler out for every subsequent crawl until the
connection dies — there is no server-side deadline that releases it, and the
container's `sleepAfter` idle shutdown never engages while a handler is stuck
in a read. It is the one unbounded input left in a file that otherwise bounds
every byte and second it spends.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `do_POST` validates `Content-Length` before reading: a missing,
      non-integer, negative, or over-cap value is rejected with a 400 JSON
      error without reading the body (the cap should be sized for the actual
      payload — a `{"url": ...}` JSON object — and named as a constant, in
      the style of `_CRAWL_MAX_BODY_BYTES`).
- [ ] The body read itself is bounded: the handler cannot block indefinitely
      on a client that declares an in-cap length but never finishes sending
      (e.g. a socket/read deadline consistent with the crawl deadline
      machinery), and the server answers other requests afterwards.
- [ ] Malformed-length requests are answered 400, not the catch-all 502, so
      client errors stay distinguishable from container failures.
- [ ] Regression coverage in the container test suite
      (`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/test/test_container_validate.py` or a sibling):
      negative length, oversized declared length with a partial body, and
      non-numeric length each get a prompt 400 and the server still answers
      a following `GET /`; the well-formed control still returns 200.
- [ ] Existing container + worker suites still pass.

Related: #7018 (the Worker-side shape validation of this container's
responses), #6975 (the hub's POST bind validation). This issue covers the
container's request side, which neither touched.

title: ci(id-check): matrix emit step does not normalise id-pr-checks.txt entries — guard accepts whitespace/CRLF (from #6881), matrix would request malformed installables

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

body:
## Problem

PR #7027 (for issue #6881) made the flake-list guard `check-id-pr-checks.sh` normalise `id-pr-checks.txt` entries before comparison (CR stripped, surrounding whitespace trimmed, duplicates reported as duplicates). The workflow that consumes the same list does not normalise: in `.github/workflows/id-check.yml`, the "Emit PR check list for the matrix" step in the `guard` job emits raw lines —

```bash
checks=$(grep -v -e '^[[:space:]]*#' -e '^[[:space:]]*$' .github/scripts/id-pr-checks.txt | jq -R . | jq -cs .)
```

— and the `check_each` job interpolates each value unchanged into the Nix installable (`nix build -L --no-link "./pkgs/id#checks.x86_64-linux.${{ matrix.check }}"`). A list entry with trailing whitespace or a CRLF ending now passes the guard but would reach the matrix as a whitespace/CR-suffixed attribute name and fail the build with a wrong-cause error.

Found by the Codex review of PR #7027 (finding on `.github/scripts/check-id-pr-checks.sh`, comment 4504478410). It was not fixed in PR #7027 because that task's packet explicitly excluded the id-check.yml workflow wiring; this issue tracks the follow-up so it is not lost.

## Acceptance criteria

- The matrix emit step in `.github/workflows/id-check.yml` applies the same normalisation as the guard: CR stripped and surrounding whitespace trimmed per entry (and, for consistency, duplicates collapsed or rejected — pick one and say which in the PR).
- A whitespace/CRLF variant of the current list emits exactly the same matrix JSON as the current list.
- The guard's behaviour and the current (clean) list are unchanged.

## Evidence

- `.github/workflows/id-check.yml` guard job, "Emit PR check list for the matrix" step (raw `grep | jq -R .` pipeline, no trim/CR handling) and `check_each` job's `nix build` step interpolating `matrix.check` verbatim — both at main commit 08dd577848 / PR #7027 head 863f3def13.
- PR #7027 Codex finding 4504478410 (P2): "Normalize matrix entries alongside the guard".

title: projector(reconcile): list-page elements are shape-trusted — a null/string element crashes the stream and wedges its cursor, a number-less element writes a phantom owner/repo#undefined row

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/projector
labels.description: pm-stack projector

body:
## Problem

`pm-stack/projector` reconcile trusts the *elements* of GitHub list pages, not just the page shape. #6954/#6955 validated the page envelope in `listResource` (`pm-stack/projector/src/github.ts:204-233`: non-array 200 → `github_api_unexpected_shape`), but the returned elements flow unvalidated into the projection:

- `pm-stack/projector/src/reconcile.ts` — the `prs` and `issues` streams call `fromIssueOrPr(repo, obj, ...)` per element with no element guard; the comment streams deref `c.html_url` / `c.created_at` per element likewise.
- `pm-stack/projector/src/projector.ts` — `fromIssueOrPr` reads `obj.number` and evaluates `"merged" in obj` with no plain-object / number check.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @8169bbd899, probe `~/git/fleet/probe-projector-elements`, real `projector.ts` under bun)

Control (well-formed issue object) projects correctly to `o/r#7`. Wrong-shape elements:

- `null` → raw `TypeError: null is not an object (evaluating 'obj.number')`
- `"str"` / `42` → raw `TypeError: obj is not an Object (evaluating '"merged" in obj')`
- `[]` or an object with no `number` → **no throw: a phantom row is produced with `ref = "o/r#undefined"`, `number = undefined`**, which `store.upsertItem` would persist.

## Why it matters

In the `prs`/`issues` reconcile streams the per-element loop is not guarded per item, so one wrong-shape element aborts the whole stream; `reconcileRepos` records the error but never advances that stream's sync cursor (`setSyncCursor` runs only after a successful stream), so every later poll re-reads and re-fails on the same page — the stream wedges permanently and the projection silently goes stale for that repo. The phantom `#undefined` variant is worse: it succeeds, writing a corrupt row keyed `owner/repo#undefined`. This is the element-level residual of the #6954 trust-boundary defect: the API (or any intermediary) returning one malformed entry in an otherwise valid page is enough.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A list page containing a non-object element (`null`, string, number, array) cannot produce a raw `TypeError` out of reconcile or `fromIssueOrPr`, and cannot abort the whole stream's remaining valid elements.
- [ ] An element without a safe-integer `number` never produces an upsert with `ref` ending in `#undefined` / `number: undefined`.
- [ ] The chosen disposition (skip-with-count in the stream result, or a named module-vocabulary error) is applied consistently across the `prs`, `issues`, `issue_comments`/`review_comments`, and `reviews` streams, and a stream that contained bad elements still advances its sync cursor over the good ones.
- [ ] Regression tests feed pages with null/string/array/missing-number elements through reconcile (stub fetch + fake store, as in the shipped reconcile suite) and pin the behavior above; existing projector suite stays green.

title: Restore procedure: reference tables + post-restore row-count diff gate

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: status/triaged
labels.description: Triaged and routed (see agent note)

body:
## Restore procedure: reference tables + post-restore row-count diff gate

**Origin:** the 2026-11-07 fleet-queue restore-completeness audit (#6853, comment 6715020584), prompted by Drew's correction that the lane registry was supposed to be filled from the 2026-11-06 snapshot.

**What happened:** the fleet-queue cutover loaded its backup through a hand-built per-table export whose manifest listed five tables (tasks, leases, workers, checkpoints, repo_task_lane_ledger). `agent.lanes` — a reference table in the same queue core — was never exported, so the recreated store ran a full day with an empty lane registry and every lane claim rejected (`unknown lane_id`, #6853). The audit also found `agent.token_expirations` (10 rows) has no Turso home anywhere. Whole-database moves (fleet-platform, fleet-mirror) could not fail this way — they import every table by construction and had flip-count verification. Only selective per-table restores are exposed, and nothing in the procedure caught the omission: the load "matched the export exactly" because the export itself was incomplete.

### Required changes to the recreate/restore procedure (any selective export → fresh store)

1. **Source-inventory-first checklist.** Before any export is built, enumerate EVERY table in the source scope (for a schema: `information_schema` / dump COPY headers) and record it in the export manifest with its row count. Every source table must appear in the manifest with an explicit disposition: `load`, `archive` (name the destination), or `retire` (name the reason). A source table missing from the manifest fails the export step — silence is not a disposition.
2. **Reference/config tables are named explicitly.** Registries and trackers (lanes-class: lane registries, worker registries, token/credential trackers, watermarks, feature/config tables) are the highest-risk omission class because data tables load fine without them and the failure surfaces later, elsewhere (here: a day of rejected claims). The checklist names this class and requires a second-person/second-lane read of the manifest against the source inventory.
3. **Post-restore row-count diff gate.** After load, an automated per-table diff (snapshot count vs live count, with an allowlist for explained deltas: post-cutover writes, by-design archives like `agent_events_pg_history`, pre-rename duplicate keys) must pass before the cutover is declared complete. Any table that is non-empty in the source and empty or unexplained-short in the target blocks the declaration. The 2026-11-07 audit's diff table on #6853 is the worked example.
4. **Backfill path is additive-only.** Gaps found by the gate are backfilled with INSERT OR IGNORE from the snapshot, before/after counts recorded (lanes precedent: 32 → 47, no deletes, no overwrites).

### Named disposition owed: `agent.token_expirations`

10 rows (credential names, services, expiry/renew-by dates, renewal-watch cron names; never secret values) survive only in the 2026-11-06 snapshot (`~/workspace/scratch/muse-dev2-queue-core-export-2026-11-06/latest-backup.pgdump.sql.zst` on the laptop, and the throwaway PG restore from Lane C). Pick its Turso home and load it:
- Recommendation: **fleet-platform as `agent_token_expirations`**, beside the other human-facing `agent_*` operational tables that landed there (`agent_external_comms`, `agent_quota_records`) — it is a human-maintained tracker read by renewal-watch jobs, not broker state.
- Alternative: fleet-queue with the rest of the audit's queue-core class.
- Either way: load the 10 snapshot rows, then repoint/note the renewal-watch consumers (the GHCR PAT renewal fires 2027-01-15 and the project-token renewal 2027-10-01 per the tracker's own rows) so the tracker is live again, not just preserved.

### Acceptance

- [ ] Restore/recreate runbook (doc/fleet + hatch-personal backup/restore docs) updated with (1)–(4).
- [ ] The diff gate exists as a runnable script/query set, not just prose.
- [ ] `agent.token_expirations` loaded into its chosen store; counts verified; consumers noted.

title: cold-store-reaper(worker): Google token response is shape-trusted and cached — a wrong-shape 200 poisons the DO token cache (Bearer undefined) for up to an hour

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/cold-store-reaper
labels.description: Package/app: cold-store-reaper (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/cold-store-reaper/worker/src/index.js` — `BundleFlight.accessToken()` (the
rehydrator Worker's Google token exchange) trusts the token endpoint's 200
response body completely:

```js
const payload = await resp.json();
const entry = {
  token: payload.access_token,
  expires_at_ms: Date.now() + (payload.expires_in ?? 3600) * 1000,
};
await this.state.storage.put("google_token", entry);
return entry.token;
```

There is no validation that `payload` is an object, that `access_token` is a
non-empty string, or that `expires_in` is a usable number — and the
unvalidated result is **written to Durable Object storage as the cached
token**. The cached entry is then trusted by the early return at the top of
`accessToken()` (`cached.expires_at_ms > Date.now() + 60_000`), so one
wrong-shape 200 poisons every later rehydration on that bundle DO until the
bogus expiry passes.

## Verified (laptop, main @7c8fb3e1ee, probe `~/git/fleet/probe-reaper-token`)

Real `src/index.js` + `src/decoder.js` copied verbatim (md5-checked against
the laptop primary), stub DO storage + stub token endpoint, `BundleFlight`
driven directly (the shipped tests' own harness shape):

- Control `{access_token:"good", expires_in:3600}` → returns `"good"`,
  second call served from cache, token endpoint called once. Correct.
- `{}` (200, no `access_token`) → `accessToken()` returns `undefined` and
  **caches it** (`google_token` entry with a ~1h future `expires_at_ms`);
  the second call returns `undefined` again with the token endpoint still
  called only once. Every `rehydrate()` in that window sends
  `Authorization: Bearer undefined` to Drive and fails 502 — even after the
  token endpoint recovers.
- `{access_token:123, expires_in:3600}` → returns the number `123` and
  caches it the same way.
- JSON `null` body → raw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null
  (reading 'access_token')`.
- Non-JSON 200 body → raw `SyntaxError` out of `resp.json()`.

In `BundleFlight.fetch` the raw errors surface as a 502 with the raw
runtime message (`rehydration failed: Cannot read properties of null…`),
not the module's `HttpError` vocabulary (`google token exchange failed
(HTTP …)` is the only shaped failure, and it covers only non-200 status).

## Why it matters

The rehydrator is the read door for cold-store restores. A single
malformed-but-200 token response (proxy/error-page JSON, a Google-side
shape change, a partial deploy) currently converts a transient exchange
hiccup into up to an hour of hard 502s per bundle DO, with no re-exchange
attempt and an error message that does not say the token response was the
problem. The Python sibling got exactly this boundary shaped in #6846
(`cold_store.py` token endpoint); the Worker door was not covered by it.

## Acceptance criteria

- `accessToken()` validates the parsed body before caching: it must be a
  plain object with a non-empty string `access_token`; anything else
  (null, scalar, array, missing/wrong-typed `access_token`) throws
  `HttpError(502, …)` naming the token exchange as the failure, and
  **nothing is written to the `google_token` storage entry**.
- A non-JSON 200 body produces the same shaped 502, not a raw
  `SyntaxError`.
- `expires_in` is used only when it is a finite positive number;
  otherwise the existing 3600s default applies (no `NaN`/negative expiry
  is ever cached).
- A cached entry whose `token` is not a non-empty string is treated as
  absent (re-exchange), so an already-poisoned entry self-heals.
- Regression tests in the package's node test style (stub token endpoint,
  as in `test/range-ignored.test.mjs`) cover: control cached once;

body:
## Finding

The four Go-module build-verification workflows that `.github/ci-policy.md` groups in one table row — `go-modules-build.yml`, `identity-build.yml`, `map-build.yml`, `mcpx-nixbuild.yml` — cannot run at all on current main (d0703e82ce):

1. **Dispatch-only triggers.** Every one declares only `on: workflow_dispatch:` (identity-build.yml:16-17, map-build.yml:16-17, go-modules-build.yml and mcpx-nixbuild.yml same shape). The Nov 4 sweep commit 5a94833ea3 ("ci: remove push/pull_request triggers (dispatch/schedule only)") deleted their `push: branches: [main]` triggers; the earlier main-only phase (814c5146ad / 285e425b77) had already removed their path-gated `pull_request` triggers.
2. **Disabled in Actions settings.** `gh api repos/developing-today/code/actions/workflows/<file>` reports `state: disabled_manually` for all four — so even a manual `workflow_dispatch` cannot run them until they are re-enabled.
3. **No completed run since 2026-11-03.** `gh run list --workflow <file>` newest entries for each are 2026-11-03T02:19Z push runs, all `completed/cancelled`.

## Why it matters

- ci-policy.md:164 assigns this exact set a PR tier ("class-3 paths only") and a main tier ("always (push to main, no path filter)"). Neither tier exists in reality.
- Each workflow's own header promises the opposite of the current state: identity-build "builds and vets both variants whenever the module changes" (#340, the tagged sqlite/libsql variants nothing else compiles); map-build exists because pkgs/map "rotted silently" once already (#338); go-modules-build covers pkgs/{chat,database,graph,import,launcher,tea} plus per-module tidy checks (#342/#347); mcpx-nixbuild is the only CI build that can catch a stale vendorHash in pkgs/mcpx/package.nix (#297).
- The rot the workflows were created to prevent is already possible again: since 2026-11-03, changes have landed in these modules with zero build verification — e.g. pkgs/identity (bc4fccf9dc "fix(identity): confine provider static-file requests", d442f5def4 property tests) and pkgs/chat (24d38b1eff merging main_test.go lifecycle/registry tests).
- Their concurrency blocks still describe push runs keyed by run_id "so every merged tree gets its own completed run" — dead configuration that makes the files look live.
- Sibling instances of the same sweep damage are tracked per-workflow in #6929 (mcpx fix-test guard), #6953 (opencode-config guard) and #6959 (production-line guard); #6187's venue audit inventories disabled venues but names go-modules-build only, and its dispositions are gated on a #6185 ruling — this set's policy promise (ci-policy.md:164) is specific enough to disposition on its own: restore or retire, per workflow.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] For each of the four workflows, exactly one disposition is recorded on this issue: **restore** (re-enable in Actions settings + restore the ci-policy.md:164 triggers — class-3 path-gated pull_request and push to main) or **retire** (delete the workflow and remove/annotate its ci-policy row and header promises).
- [ ] For every restored workflow, a completed (not cancelled) run on current main is linked as proof, triggered by a real module change or a dispatch after re-enabling.
- [ ] `.github/ci-policy.md` table row for this set matches the workflows' actual triggers and enablement state after the change.
- [ ] pkgs/identity's tagged variants (sqlite, libsql) are compiled by something that runs — if identity-build is retired, name the replacement venue on this issue.

Verified this run on the laptop primary at d0703e82ce: workflow files read on main, sweep commit 5a94833ea3 diff inspected, Actions API state and `gh run list` checked per workflow, post-2026-11-03 module changes confirmed via git log.

body:
## Finding

PR #3725 closed #168 ("production ingest enforces only p2panda-auth membership"), but a whole class of signed store operations still never reaches the groups fold on the production ingest path — they keep the membership verdict alone, so the fold rules the PR lists (only an Admin changes a role or removes an Admin, a create may not repeat a member, a manager acts only through a chain from an owner) do not gate them:

- a group create that does not list its author;
- a group create that lists its author below Manage access;
- any operation naming a group as its member (add/remove/promote/demote of a group);
- friendship/policy bodies the body codec does not carry (per the PR body).

The limits are documented in the code, but no follow-up issue was filed for them — #168 is CLOSED, so as far as the tracker is concerned the production-ingest gap is finished, while these signed operations remain ungated on every path that derives from `resolve()` (ingest, refresh/replay, late-body attach, sync batches).

## Evidence

- Source PR: #3725 (merged, merge commit `60c325f397a548ee7601ef4caa7b977f6d05d559`); its body: "Creates not listing their author keep the membership verdict alone" and "Operations naming a group as a member, and friendship/policy bodies the body codec does not carry, are not bridged; the fold judges those when they travel as group events."
- #168 is CLOSED (verified this run); dedupe searches for a follow-up covering the bridge limits returned no open or recently closed issue.
- On current main (`fc035359245855fd5b3db1d6b85ee60223abcf20`, verified via `git show origin/main`), `pkgs/id/src/event_store/resolve.rs`:
  - Lines 225–231 (doc on `fold_projection`): operations that do not bridge "are left out and keep the membership verdict".
  - Lines 314–324 in `bridge()`: a create listing its author with `!access.is_manage()` returns `None` (does not bridge), and `if !author_listed { return None; }` at lines 322–324.
  - Line 364 (`member_key`): `GroupMember::Individual(AuthId::Group(_)) | GroupMember::Group(_) => None` — a group-as-member operation cannot bridge, so `bridge()` returns `None` for it.

## Why it matters

These are not exotic shapes: a create that omits its author from the member list, or a group nested as a member of another group, are ordinary signed operations a peer can put in the store. For all of them the Admin-only role/removal rules and the no-duplicate-member rule simply do not run on production ingest — the store can apply what group projections refuse, which is the divergence #168 existed to close. If full bridging is impossible for some shapes, that residual needs a tracked disposition (bridge them, refuse them at ingest, or a documented ruling that membership-only is sufficient for those shapes) instead of an untracked code comment.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each unbridged shape (author-unlisted create, author-below-Manage create, group-as-member operation, codec-uncarried friendship/policy body) has a tracked disposition: bridged into the fold, refused at ingest with a named reason, or a documented ruling recorded on this issue explaining why membership-only judgement is sufficient for that shape.
- [ ] For every shape that gets bridged, a production-path test (`ingest_with_body` style) shows a fold-voided operation of that shape does not apply.
- [ ] The disposition is reflected in the `fold_projection`/`bridge` doc comments, so the code no longer presents untracked limits as settled behaviour.

title: mcpx(completion): rate limiter admits before pool validation — unknown server names mint fresh limiter buckets, so the per-server window never binds bogus names and bucket growth is request-rate × window

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

In `handleComplete`, the completion rate limiter is consulted *before* the pool lookup validates the requested server — by design, so a refused request never wakes an upstream. But the limiter keys include the requested server name, and `CanonicalName` passes unknown names through unchanged. So every distinct bogus `server` value mints fresh limiter buckets: the per-server window (`completion.serverPerMinute`) can never bind a name that does not exist (each name has its own budget), the per-caller window is also keyed per server spelling, and bucket growth between sweeps is bounded only by request rate × the sweep interval. The handler's own tests demonstrate the ordering: with an unknown server, an admitted request reaches the pool lookup and gets a 400 — after it has already been counted by the limiter.

## Evidence

- Source PR: #3730 (merged, merge commit `e49c0beeb801f21cec7234accf17139d7ed11b79`) — limiter placed "after shape validation and before `s.reg.Pool(...)`".
- On current main (`fc035359245855fd5b3db1d6b85ee60223abcf20`, verified via `git show origin/main`):
  - `pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/ops.go` line 378: `if refused := s.completeLimiter.admit([]limitCheck{...})` with keys `"caller\x00" + completionCaller(cc) + "\x00" + serverName` and `"server\x00" + serverName`; the pool validation `p, ok := s.reg.Pool(req.Server)` is only at line 397, after admission.
  - `pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/registry.go` lines 1467–1479: `CanonicalName` returns `nameOrNS` unchanged when it matches no pool and no namespace.
  - `pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/ratelimit.go` line 85: admission creates `l.buckets[c.Key] = &rateBucket{start: now, n: 1}` per new key; expired buckets are swept at most once per minute (lines 77–84) and only on the new-bucket path.
  - `pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/completion_ratelimit_test.go`: `TestHandleCompleteRateLimitRefusesBeforePool` uses an unknown server and expects admission to precede the pool's 400 — pinning the ordering without pinning any bound on distinct-name buckets.

## Why it matters

The per-server window is described in the PR as "the backstop that does not depend on caller identity" — for nonexistent servers it is no backstop at all, and a client spraying distinct bogus server names grows the limiter's in-memory map at request rate for at least a full window per name. Impact is bounded (bogus requests still 400 and never wake an upstream), but the limiter's own state should not be client-shaped: validating the server exists before admission, or not minting buckets for names the registry does not know, closes it without changing the refusal-before-pool guarantee for real servers.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Requests naming a server/namespace the registry does not know do not create limiter buckets (e.g. existence is checked before admission, while refusal for known servers still happens before any pool lease is acquired).
- [ ] A handler test pins it: repeated `/v1/complete` calls with distinct unknown server names leave the limiter's bucket count bounded (or are refused without admission).
- [ ] Existing completion rate-limit tests still pass, including refusal-before-pool for a known server and the canonical-spelling sharing test.

body:
## Finding

The guard test added by PR #3715 (`test_command_lists_cover_all_clap_subcommands`) only checks one direction: every live clap subcommand name must be *present* in the two hand-maintained lists. Nothing checks the reverse — that every entry in the lists still corresponds to a real subcommand. If a subcommand is later renamed or removed from clap, its stale entry stays in both lists and the guard still passes. That is exactly the drift class #3126 was filed for (lists diverging from the real command set), in the opposite direction.

## Evidence

- Source PR: #3715 (merged, merge commit `73a21ba36cce18bb30b8b28685ef40889bf34530`) — "Both hand-maintained `id` CLI command lists now name every top-level clap subcommand, and a guard test keeps them in sync".
- `pkgs/id/src/cli.rs` on current main (`fc035359245855fd5b3db1d6b85ee60223abcf20`, verified via `git show origin/main`):
  - The test at line 2800 collects `names` from `Cli::command().get_subcommands()`.
  - Line 2819: `for name in &names {` — asserts each clap name appears in the module-doc list.
  - Line 2840: `for name in &names {` — asserts each clap name appears as a `| \`{name}\`` row in the README CLI Commands table.
  - Neither loop iterates the doc-list lines or the README rows to assert each documented entry is still a real subcommand; there is no subset/reverse check anywhere in the test.

## Why it matters

The two lists are the discoverability surface for the `id` CLI (module docs + README table). A rename/removal is the most likely future edit to the command set, and it is precisely the edit this guard cannot see: it would leave documentation advertising a command that no longer exists, with CI green.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The guard also fails when the module-doc list or the README table contains an entry that is not a current clap subcommand (bidirectional check), accounting for any intentional non-subcommand rows if they exist.
- [ ] A test mutation demonstrates the new direction: temporarily adding a bogus entry to either list makes the guard fail.
- [ ] The existing forward-direction coverage (all current subcommands documented) still passes.

labels.name: kind/ci

labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.description: F11.10 production-line guard (.github/scripts/check-production-line-limit.sh)

body:
## Problem

`check-production-line-limit.sh` enumerates production sources with `find` and never excludes build output, so in any tree that has been built it counts Cargo's generated `.rs` files under `target/` as production code and fails on them. CI never sees this (a fresh checkout has no `target/` — `**/target` is gitignored, `.gitignore:33`), but every local/worktree verification run does — which is precisely how the grandfather splits (#4704/#4715/#4716/#4717) and any fix to this guard would be verified.

## Evidence (verified 2026-11-07 on laptop primary @ e238c85d5a)

- `.github/scripts/check-production-line-limit.sh` (enumeration at the bottom of the script): `find "$ROOT/$base" -name "*.rs" -type f` over `pkgs` and `apps`, with only two exclusions — paths under a `tests/` directory and files named `tests.rs`. No `target/` (or any build-directory) exclusion.
- Fixture probe (laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-line-guard-target`): a tree with one 10-line `pkgs/demo/src/lib.rs` plus one 2,600-line `pkgs/demo/target/debug/build/gen-abc/out/generated.rs` → guard reports `::error::OVER LIMIT pkgs/demo/target/.../generated.rs: 2600 production lines`, "checked 2 production .rs files", exit 1. Control with `target/` removed → "checked 1 production .rs file", OK, exit 0.
- Real tree: running the guard in the laptop primary (which has build output) produced dozens of `OVER LIMIT` errors, all under `pkgs/id/target/debug/build/cranelift-codegen-*/out/*.rs` (generated ISLE code, up to 45,726 "production lines") plus `libsqlite3-sys-*/out/bindgen.rs` — exit 1 for reasons unrelated to the source tree. The same guard on a clean `git archive` export gives the true verdict (524 files; one real over-limit file, `pkgs/id/src/directory.rs`).
- The contract suite `check-production-line-limit.test.sh` passes and has no fixture with a `target/` directory, so this case is untested.

## Why it matters

A guard that cries wolf on every built tree trains everyone to ignore or bypass it locally: a worker splitting a grandfathered module cannot get a trustworthy local verdict, and the failure output buries the real over-limit files among pages of generated-code noise. The fix must not weaken CI: excluding gitignored build output keeps the CI verdict identical (CI has no `target/`), it only makes local runs mean the same thing.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The enumeration skips `target/` directories (at any depth under the scanned roots, matching the repo's `**/target` ignore) — and the skipped set is named in the script header alongside the existing `tests/` exclusions.
- [ ] A contract-test fixture with an over-limit `.rs` file under a `target/` directory passes the guard, while an over-limit file in normal source still fails it (both directions pinned in `check-production-line-limit.test.sh`).
- [ ] Guard verdict on the laptop primary's built tree matches the clean-export verdict for real sources (generated files no longer reported).

Related: #1411 (guard origin). Filed alongside the production-line guard's missing-triggers issue from the same run.

body:
## Problem

The F11.10 production-line guard (#1411) — no production `.rs` file under `pkgs/`/`apps/` may exceed 2,500 production lines — never runs. Its workflow has been `workflow_dispatch`-only since the 2026-11-04 trigger sweep, and current `main` already fails the guard: a non-grandfathered file crossed the limit while nothing was watching.

## Evidence (verified 2026-11-07 on laptop primary @ e238c85d5a)

- `.github/workflows/production-line-guard.yml:7-9` — `on:` is `workflow_dispatch:` only. No `push`, no `pull_request`, not even `merge_group` (the sibling opencode-config guard, #6953, at least kept `merge_group`).
- Sweep commit `5a94833ea3` ("ci: remove push/pull_request triggers (dispatch/schedule only)", 2026-11-04) removed this workflow's path-gated `push` (branches `[main]`, paths `pkgs/**`, `apps/**`, the guard script/test, the workflow) and `pull_request` (same paths) triggers — 15 lines. The workflow's concurrency group (lines 13-16) still keys on `github.event_name == 'push'`, dead code left by the removal.
- `gh run list --workflow production-line-guard.yml`: the newest of the last 30 runs is 2026-11-04T14:26:03Z (`pull_request`) — minutes before the sweep commit landed (08:27 CST). Zero runs since, in over three days of merges to main.
- The guard script `.github/scripts/check-production-line-limit.sh` is invoked by no other workflow (grep over `.github/workflows/`), so nothing else covers it.
- Running the guard on a clean export of current `main` (`git archive HEAD`, probe `~/git/fleet/probe-line-guard-target/clean` on the laptop): **FAILED** — `pkgs/id/src/directory.rs: 2610 production lines (limit 2500)`, and `directory.rs` is **not** in the guard's grandfather list and has no split issue (title searches for `directory.rs` splits return none; 4,961 raw lines). Checked 524 production `.rs` files; the contract tests (`check-production-line-limit.test.sh`) all pass — the guard logic works, it is simply never invoked.
- The four grandfathered files have all grown since the guard landed, unobserved: `web/markdown.rs` 5,325 → 5,742 (#4704), `cli.rs` 2,504 → 2,797 (#4715), `web/routes.rs` 2,573 → 3,021 (#4716), `world_session/mod.rs` 2,821 → 3,079 (#4717). Those split issues' acceptance ("delete the grandfather entry in the same PR") has no automated check behind it.

## Why it matters

The guard exists so module growth is caught at the PR that causes it, while a split is still cheap. With it dark, `directory.rs` crossed the limit unnoticed and the grandfathered files drifted further from their splits — exactly the silent accumulation F11.10 was built to prevent (#1438). Unlike #6929/#6953, ci-policy's tier table does not even list this workflow, so its absence is invisible from the policy side too.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A decision is recorded: restore automatic triggers for `production-line-guard` (the pre-sweep path-gated `push` to main + `pull_request` over `pkgs/**`/`apps/**` + guard files is the obvious candidate) **or** retire the guard explicitly (delete workflow + script + grandfather bookkeeping, and close/update #1438 and the four split issues' enforcement premise accordingly). A dispatch-only guard that nobody dispatches is not a third option.
- [ ] If restored: `.github/ci-policy.md` gains a tier-table row for the workflow, and the dead `push` expression in the concurrency group is either live again or removed.
- [ ] `pkgs/id/src/directory.rs` (2,610 production lines) is dispositioned: split, or grandfathered in the script with a linked split issue, per the guard's own convention — so the restored guard is green on main.
- [ ] A run of the workflow on main after the change is linked from this issue (dispatch counts once triggers are restored; the point is a recorded green run).

Related: #1411 (guard origin), #1438 (enforcement request), #4704/#4715/#4716/#4717 (grandfather splits), #6929 and #6953 (sibling guards darkened by the same sweep).

title: github-ci(worker): a JSON null body crashes fetch — payload.repository dereferences null outside the try/catch, escaping the receiver-failed envelope

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

labels.name: app/github-ci
labels.description: Package/app: github-ci (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

The github-ci Worker (`pkgs/github-ci/worker/src/index.ts`, #5693) parses the webhook body and then dereferences it **outside** its error envelope:

```ts
let payload: Record<string, unknown>;
try {
  payload = JSON.parse(raw);
} catch {
  return new Response("bad json", { status: 400 });
}
...
const repo = (payload.repository ?? {}) as Record<string, unknown>;
```

`JSON.parse("null")` succeeds and yields `null`, so a signed body of literally `null` passes the parse guard and then throws `TypeError: null is not an object (evaluating 'payload.repository')` at the `payload.repository` read — which sits **before** the `try { ... } catch` block that produces the worker's `receiver failed: …` 500 envelope. The exception escapes `fetch` entirely: Cloudflare returns its generic unhandled-exception 500, nothing is logged with the worker's event/repo context, and GitHub records a failed delivery it will retry — a poison delivery that can never succeed, for every event type (the deref happens before routing).

Other non-object JSON bodies survive only by accident of JS semantics: `[]`, `"str"`, and `123` box to objects with an undefined `repository`, land on `repoName = "unknown"`, and exit through the normal skip/ignore paths. `null` is the one valid-JSON body that crashes — and it is exactly the case the shipped test suite does not cover (`worker.test.ts` posts objects only).

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ 63f83bef5a, probe `~/git/fleet/probe-ghci-snapshot`)

Real `pkgs/github-ci/worker/src/*.ts` copied verbatim (md5-checked: index.ts 9b29537d…, sink.ts 487d63ee…) into the probe; `worker.fetch` driven directly with correctly HMAC-signed bodies (the probe signs with the same WebCrypto HMAC the worker verifies):

- Control — body `{}` (event `workflow_run`, valid signature) → HTTP 200, `{"ok":true,"skipped":"not_completed","repo":"unknown",…}`.
- **Bug — body `null` (event `workflow_run`, valid signature) → `worker.fetch` THREW `TypeError: null is not an object (evaluating 'payload.repository')`** — no Response at all.
- **Bug — body `null` (event `push`, valid signature) → same throw** (crash precedes routing).
- Control — body `[]` (event `workflow_run`) → HTTP 200 skip path.

## Why it matters

A webhook receiver's one job is to turn any delivered bytes into a deliberate HTTP answer. A body shape that escapes the handler as an unhandled exception defeats the worker's own failure envelope and logging, produces a retryable 500 for a delivery that can never succeed, and — because the throw happens before the event routing — takes down every event type at once, not just one route. It is also the shape most likely to be hit by a misconfigured sender or a probe, precisely when a clean 400 matters most.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A signed `null` JSON body (and any other non-object JSON body: array, string, number, boolean) gets a deliberate response — 400 is the natural choice — for every event type, with no exception escaping `fetch`.
- [ ] Object bodies keep today's behavior byte-for-byte (ping → pong, workflow_run skip/store paths, push/PR/issues routing, 202 for unknown events).
- [ ] Malformed JSON keeps returning the existing 400 `bad json`.
- [ ] New worker tests pin the null-body case for at least `workflow_run` and one fleet-routed event (`push`), plus one non-object scalar/array body.

# id(cli): `test_cli_rejects_first_and_last_together` never runs — PR #3738's inserted test took its `#[test]` attribute

## Finding

The CLI regression test for the `--first`/`--last` conflict (`conflicts_with`, the #3029 contract) is dead code on current main: it carries no `#[test]` attribute, is never called from anywhere, and therefore never runs — while the suite stays green.

## Evidence

- PR #3738 (merged, merge commit `5fa06504a63c`, verified ancestor of main `63f83bef5ab2` via compare API, behind_by 0) inserted its new test between the existing `#[test]` attribute and the function it belonged to. Its diff hunk (cli.rs, old lines ~2923-2946) shows the context line `#[test]`, then the added `+ #[test]` / `+ fn test_cli_rejects_zero_result_limits()`, and after the inserted body the context line `fn test_cli_rejects_first_and_last_together()` with no attribute.
- Current main `pkgs/id/src/cli.rs:3608-3609`: `test_cli_rejects_zero_result_limits` carries **two** `#[test]` attributes (a duplicated-attribute warning; the test registers twice, per the mechanism documented in issue #6409).
- Current main `pkgs/id/src/cli.rs:3638`: `fn test_cli_rejects_first_and_last_together()` carries **none**. A repo-wide code search for its name returns exactly one hit — its own definition in cli.rs — so nothing else calls it either.
- PR #3754 fixed the *identical* displacement PR #3738 caused for `Command`'s `#[derive(Subcommand)]` (issue #3751), but did not catch this second displacement in the same PR.
- The behaviour the dead test guards is still configured on main: the `--first` fields still carry `conflicts_with = "last"` (e.g. cli.rs ~:883), so the test is expected to pass when re-enabled — its assertions are the oracle.

## Relation to issue #6410

Issue #6410 (OPEN) lists cli.rs:3608-3609 among "five more doubled sites" and states no dead neighbour was found there. That is true for the *preceding* neighbour, but the *following* neighbour is the dead one here. Simply deleting one duplicated attribute at cli.rs (the literal #6410 acceptance step) would leave this test dead. Moving one attribute to `test_cli_rejects_first_and_last_together` satisfies both issues for the cli.rs site.

## Why it matters

PR #3738's body claims "#3029's first/last conflict behaviour is preserved" — the one test that pins that behaviour at the CLI boundary has not run since PR #3738 merged. If a future clap refactor drops the conflict, nothing would say so.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Move one `#[test]` from `test_cli_rejects_zero_result_limits` to `test_cli_rejects_first_and_last_together` in `pkgs/id/src/cli.rs` (no test-body or production-code changes).
- [ ] `cargo test -- --list` for the id crate shows both tests exactly once each.
- [ ] The re-enabled `test_cli_rejects_first_and_last_together` passes; if it fails, that is a live first/last-conflict regression — triage it as such, do not weaken the test.
- [ ] Note the cli.rs site as resolved on issue #6410 when this lands.

# dispatch: the fleet repo list names the nix repo by its pre-rename name — `dezren39/darwin-nix` is not allowlisted, has no queue/dir mapping, and its OIDC callers are rejected; only the redirected `dezren39/nix` spelling passes

## Summary

`pm-stack/dispatch/src/config.ts` names the fleet's nix repo `dezren39/nix` everywhere — but that repo's canonical name is `dezren39/darwin-nix` (the name the rest of the fleet uses, and the origin of the laptop clone at `~/git/nix`). `dezren39/nix` is the pre-rename name; GitHub redirects it, which is why nothing visibly explodes for `gh`/API reads — but every exact-string check inside dispatch fails for the canonical name:

- `FLEET_REPOS` (config.ts:12–19) lists `dezren39/nix`; the default `repoAllowlist` is built from it (config.ts:87), so `assertCallerRepo` (auth.ts:206–212, exact `includes` match) **rejects any request naming `dezren39/darwin-nix`** — and rejects every GitHub Actions OIDC caller from that repo, whose token's `repository` claim is the canonical `dezren39/darwin-nix`.
- `REPO_QUEUES` (config.ts:22–29) has no `dezren39/darwin-nix` key, so `QueueClient.enqueue` (queue.ts:75–76) throws `no queue mapped for repo dezren39/darwin-nix`.
- `REPO_DIRS` (config.ts:32–39) has no canonical key either, so `server.ts:417`'s `REPO_DIRS[body.repo]!` is `undefined` for it. (The directory value under the old key, `/home/user/git/nix`, is correct — that clone's origin is `dezren39/darwin-nix`; only the key is stale.)
- `APP_INSTALLED_REPOS` (config.ts:48) contains only the old name, so for the canonical name dispatch would skip issue creation with a "GitHub App not installed" warning — the opposite of the truth its own comment (config.ts:41–47) records.

The stale name is also baked into the tests (`test/config.test.ts:36,70-71`, `test/auth.test.ts:134,144,158,161,179`, `test/packet.test.ts:19-20`), the README (lines 54, 120, 491), and `src/github.ts:7`, so the suite passes while pinning the wrong name. A secondary effect: `canonicalDedupeKey` (packet.ts:21) embeds the repo string, so any task dispatch did manage to enqueue under the old spelling carries dedupe keys no other fleet producer (which all use `dezren39/darwin-nix`) will ever match.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop, origin/main `def55caf484833e062247c46e5b0c4bb719accd3`)

- `gh repo view dezren39/nix` returns `{"nameWithOwner":"dezren39/darwin-nix"}` — the old name only resolves via GitHub's rename redirect; the canonical name is `dezren39/darwin-nix`.
- Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-dispatch-nix-name/` — the real dispatch modules (`config.ts`, `auth.ts`) under bun, `loadConfig({SUPABASE_URL: dummy})`:

| Check | `dezren39/darwin-nix` (canonical) | `dezren39/nix` (stale) |
|---|---|---|
| default allowlist includes | **false** | true |
| `REPO_QUEUES[repo]` | **undefined → QueueError** | `repo-health-nix-pilot` |
| `REPO_DIRS[repo]` | **undefined** | `/home/user/git/nix` |
| `APP_INSTALLED_REPOS.has(repo)` | **false** | true |
| `assertCallerRepo` (OIDC caller from this repo) | **throws `repo dezren39/darwin-nix is not in the dispatch allowlist`** | OK |

- Baseline: shipped `test/config.test.ts` + `test/auth.test.ts` pass 35/35 on current main — the wrong name is what the tests assert.
- Laptop check: `~/git/nix` exists and its origin is `https://github.com/dezren39/darwin-nix.git` — directory right, name key wrong.

Distinct from #6859 (program-tending's fleet list naming `developing-today/nix` in `scripts/program_tending.py`) — same disease, different file, different wrong name; that fix does not touch dispatch.

## Why it matters

Dispatch is the fleet's cross-repo launch door (Actions OIDC → queue task → OpenCode session). For one of the six fleet repos it can only be addressed by a name nothing real presents anymore: a workflow in dezren39/darwin-nix presents its canonical name in its OIDC token and is rejected at the door, and any caller naming the repo the way every other fleet component names it gets "not in the dispatch allowlist" / "no queue mapped". The redirect masks the rot for read paths, so the failure only appears the first time someone actually tries to dispatch nix work by its real name.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `FLEET_REPOS`, `REPO_QUEUES`, `REPO_DIRS`, and `APP_INSTALLED_REPOS` in `pm-stack/dispatch/src/config.ts` key the nix repo as `dezren39/darwin-nix` (the `REPO_DIRS` value `/home/user/git/nix` stays — it is the actual clone path).
- [ ] A dispatch request naming `dezren39/darwin-nix`, and an OIDC caller whose token repository is `dezren39/darwin-nix`, pass `assertCallerRepo` under the default allowlist; enqueue resolves `repo-health-nix-pilot` and the session directory resolves to `/home/user/git/nix`.
- [ ] Tests updated to the canonical name (`test/config.test.ts`, `test/auth.test.ts`, `test/packet.test.ts` — including the canonical dedupe key expectation) and the full dispatch suite passes; README and `src/github.ts` comments use the canonical name.
- [ ] A note in the fix (PR or issue comment) addresses the dedupe-key spelling change for any dispatch-created nix tasks still live under `dezren39/nix` keys — migrated, or explicitly accepted as a one-time break with the reason recorded.

Related: #6859 (same disease in program-tending's list — different file).

# opencode-usage-export: `--db`/`--out-dir` values are never validated — a trailing or empty `--db` silently exports the default store, a trailing `--out-dir` silently writes the default out dir, and a flag-like value crashes `run()` with no failure document

## Summary

`pm-stack/opencode-usage-export/opencode-usage-export.mjs` validates none of the values of its two path flags. In `parseArgs` (lines 320–330 at `def55caf48`):

```js
if (a === "--db") args.db = argv[++i];
else if (a === "--out-dir") args.outDir = argv[++i];
```

- A **trailing** `--db` sets `args.db = undefined`; `run()` then computes `explicit = args.db ?? env.OPENCODE_USAGE_DB ?? null` and falls back to the default candidate stores — the tick exports a *different store than the operator named*, exit 0, `status: "ok"`.
- An **empty** `--db ""` sets `args.db = ""`; `explicit ? [explicit] : defaultCandidatePaths(home)` treats `""` as absent — same silent fallback.
- A **trailing** `--out-dir` sets `args.outDir = undefined`; the document, `state.json`, and history are silently written to the default `~/atlas/opencode-usage-export/` instead of the requested directory, exit 0.
- A **flag-like** value (`--db --out-dir <path>`) consumes `--out-dir` as the db path and leaves `<path>` as a bare token, so `parseArgs` throws `unknown argument: <path>` — and because `parseArgs(argv)` is called *before* `run()`'s try block (line ~340), the throw escapes `run()` entirely: no failure document is written, the previous tick's `latest.json` keeps looking current, and the CLI dies with a stack trace naming the wrong token.

This is the residual door of #4739, which covers only `--window-hours`/`--fresh-hours`. The open PR #6810 fixes the hour flags (and, in its restructure, routes parse errors into a failure document), but its `parseArgs` still reads `--db`/`--out-dir` with the same unguarded `argv[++i]` — the silent fallbacks above survive that PR unchanged. This issue should land after (or be folded into) PR #6810.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop, origin/main `def55caf484833e062247c46e5b0c4bb719accd3`)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-usage-db-args/` — the real module extracted byte-identical from `origin/main` (md5 `144b35852e1c2ea763626fbdf1f51dea` both sides), driven through the exported `run()` with a fixture home containing a fresh default store (session `ses_DEFAULT`) and a fresh explicit store (session `ses_EXPLICIT`), mirroring the shipped test fixtures:

| Invocation | Result |
|---|---|
| control: `--db <explicit> --out-dir <out>` | exit 0, `status: "ok"`, storePath = explicit store, sessions = `ses_EXPLICIT` |
| `--out-dir <out> --db` (trailing) | exit 0, `status: "ok"`, storePath = **default store**, sessions = `ses_DEFAULT` — the explicit request was silently dropped |
| `--db <explicit> --out-dir` (trailing) | exit 0, `status: "ok"`; document + `state.json` + `history.jsonl` written to the **default** out dir under the fixture home; the requested out dir never used |
| `--db "" --out-dir <out>` | exit 0, `status: "ok"`, storePath = **default store**, sessions = `ses_DEFAULT` |
| `--db --out-dir <out>` (flag-like) | `run()` **threw** `Error: unknown argument: <out>` — no failure document, no exit-code contract |

The shipped suite passes on current main (5/5, `node --test`), and it has no case for a missing/empty/flag-like `--db` or `--out-dir` value.

## Why it matters

The module's contract is fail-closed (header, lines 29–31): a tick that cannot read the intended store must write a failure document and exit non-zero, never a plausible success. Exporting the *wrong store* under `status: "ok"` is worse than a junk window (#4739): the document is internally consistent, names a real storePath, and feeds downstream attribution (#2072) with another store's sessions — with no signal anything was mistyped. The systemd timer invokes this exporter on a cadence; a hand run with a typo'd flag produces a confident, wrong reading.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `--db` and `--out-dir` with a missing (trailing), empty, or flag-like (`--…`) value are usage errors in the #4739 style: an `invalid-argument` failure document naming the flag and the offending value, exit 2, and no store is read or exported.
- [ ] No invocation of the form `--db <value>` ever silently falls back to the env var or the default candidate list; an explicit flag that is present governs, or the run fails.
- [ ] A parse failure of any flag (including the flag-like case above) is routed through `run()`'s failure-document path — `run()` never throws for an argument error (coordinate with PR #6810's restructure; do not regress it).
- [ ] Regression tests in `opencode-usage-export.test.mjs` cover: trailing `--db`, empty `--db`, trailing `--out-dir`, and flag-like `--db`; the control cases (explicit `--db`, explicit `--out-dir`) keep working and the full suite passes.

Related: #4739 (hour-flag validation), PR #6810 (its open fix — this issue is the part it does not cover).

body:
# ci(mcpx): the #1969 fix-test guard never runs — its workflow lost every trigger in the Nov 4 sweep, and ci-policy still assigns it a PR tier and a main tier

## Problem

`.github/workflows/mcpx-fix-test-guard.yml` — the basic-tier enforcement of the
mcpx failing-first rule (#1969, `pkgs/mcpx/docs/testing.md` "A test per bug") —
cannot fire automatically. On current main (`1fabdbc2ca`) its trigger block is:

```yaml
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
```

(`.github/workflows/mcpx-fix-test-guard.yml:13-14`)

- No `pull_request` trigger: the enforcement step
  (`if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'`, :35) is unreachable — under the
  only remaining trigger the step is always skipped, so even a manual dispatch
  runs only the guard's own contract tests, never the guard itself.
- No `push` trigger: the main tier the policy assigns (below) never runs either.

## Evidence

- Commit `5a94833ea3` ("ci: remove push/pull_request triggers
  (dispatch/schedule only)", 2026-11-04) removed this workflow's
  `push: branches: [main]` and `pull_request:` blocks (both path-filtered to
  `pkgs/mcpx/**` + the guard files) in a repo-wide sweep of ~25 workflows.
- Live run history agrees: `gh run list --workflow mcpx-fix-test-guard.yml`
  shows the last runs on 2026-11-04 (latest 14:09Z, event `pull_request`) and
  **no runs at all since** — verified this run.
- `.github/ci-policy.md` was not updated and still promises both tiers:
  - §"mcpx fix-test guard (#1969)" (:65-77): the check runs "on pull requests
    touching `pkgs/mcpx/**`" and the contract tests "also run on pushes to
    main".
  - The tier-assignment table (:167) lists a PR tier ("fix PRs touching
    `pkgs/mcpx/**` must carry a test or a `No test: <reason>` attestation
    (basic tier)") and a main tier ("contract tests for the guard script
    only").
  - The same document's Coverage rule: "Nothing removed from PRs may vanish:
    the union of main-tier + nightly jobs must cover the old PR matrix." This
    guard vanished from both tiers.
- The workflow's own header comment (:9-11) still describes the removed
  behavior: "The path filter is the scope rule: PRs that touch no mcpx file
  never fire this workflow."
- Sibling basic-tier guards from the same sweep were re-armed to gate merges:
  `fleet-search-parity-guard.yml` and `opencode-config-guard.yml` now trigger
  on `merge_group`; `workflow-lint.yml` and `proxy-port-fallbacks.yml` kept
  `pull_request` + `merge_group`. This guard (and its script's contract
  tests) got no equivalent restoration.
- Precedent that this exact loss class is treated as a defect here: #4533
  (closed) restored the policy-listed PR test-tier trigger for mcpx-test
  after the same sweep.

## Why it matters

Since 2026-11-04, an mcpx fix PR can merge with no regression test and no
`No test: <reason>` attestation, and nothing notices — the #1969 rule is
unenforced while the policy doc, the workflow header, and
`pkgs/mcpx/docs/testing.md` all say it is enforced. The guard script itself
(`.github/scripts/check-mcpx-fix-test.sh`) and its contract tests are
maintained and passing; only the wiring is dead.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A decision is recorded on this issue: restore automatic firing
      (e.g. the pre-sweep `pull_request` + `push[main]` path-filtered
      triggers, or `merge_group` like the sibling guards) **or** retire the
      guard deliberately.
- [ ] If restored: a test mcpx fix PR without a test file and without a
      `No test:` line is failed by the check, a dispatch/push run of the
      workflow appears in `gh run list --workflow mcpx-fix-test-guard.yml`,
      and the contract-test step runs on main.
- [ ] If retired: `.github/ci-policy.md` (§ and tier table), the workflow
      header comment, and `pkgs/mcpx/docs/testing.md` are updated in the same
      change so no document claims the rule is enforced.
- [ ] Either way, ci-policy.md, the workflow, and the workflow header agree
      afterwards.

body:
## Problem

`bin/provider-catalog-sync.mjs` — `makeEntry()` crashes `--apply` with a raw `TypeError` when any existing sibling entry in the provider block carries a non-string `name` (a number, boolean, object, or array — all parseable JSONC, all plausible in a hand-edited `opencode.jsonc`).

This is the residual door of #6907 in the same function: that fix taught `makeEntry` that a sibling's `variants` may be present-but-null and not cloneable. The sibling `name` field, read two lines earlier in the same function, has no equivalent guard.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ 9917cfaef0)

- `bin/provider-catalog-sync.mjs:485` — `const suffix = commonSuffix(entries.map((e) => e?.name).filter(Boolean));` — `.filter(Boolean)` drops missing/empty names but keeps every truthy non-string (`42`, `true`, `{}`, `["x"]`).
- `bin/provider-catalog-sync.mjs:454-460` — `commonSuffix(names)` calls `n.match(/(\([^)]*\))\s*$/)` (:457) on each name unconditionally; a non-string name has no `.match`.
- Probe (laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-catalog-name`, real module verbatim, md5 `0a0b30b58067e3ba8584d7a7427338c9` matching the repo file; existing suite 38/38 green):

  | siblings | result |
  | --- | --- |
  | `{a: {name: "GPT-1 Sol (codex)"}}` (control) | OK — `{name: "GPT 1 Terra (codex)"}` |
  | `{a: {}}` (control, no name) | OK — `{name: "GPT 1 Terra"}` |
  | `{a: {name: 42}}` | THROW `TypeError: n.match is not a function` |
  | `{a: {name: true}}` | THROW `TypeError: n.match is not a function` |
  | `{a: {name: {text: "x"}}}` | THROW `TypeError: n.match is not a function` |
  | `{a: {name: ["x"]}}` | THROW `TypeError: n.match is not a function` |
  | one good string name + one numeric name | THROW — a single bad sibling poisons the whole block |

## Why it matters

`makeEntry` runs only on the `--apply` path (`applyAdditions`, called before the config write). One malformed sibling entry in any provider block therefore aborts the entire catalog sync — no validated additions from any provider are applied — and the run dies as a fatal exit-2 stack trace that never names the offending entry, provider, or field. A missing name is already handled gracefully (it simply contributes no suffix); a wrong-typed name should be no worse.

## Acceptance criteria

- `makeEntry` treats a non-string sibling `name` the same as a missing one for suffix purposes (contributes nothing to `commonSuffix`), OR rejects it with a named error identifying the provider/sibling/field — silently crashing with `n.match is not a function` is the failure being fixed, not an acceptable outcome.
- New tests in `bin/provider-catalog-sync.test.mjs` cover numeric, boolean, object, and array sibling names (mirroring the #6907 `variants: null` test), including the mixed good+bad sibling case.
- Existing suite stays green (`node --test bin/provider-catalog-sync.test.mjs`, 38 tests at filing).
- The fix stays inside the sibling-shape guards of `makeEntry`/`commonSuffix`; no change to suffix semantics for well-formed string names.
