body:
# mcpx(ci): e2e-shard-packer assigns `realsoftware`-tagged tests to untagged shards — those legs fail the count check and the tagged tests never run in the PR path

## Summary

`pkgs/mcpx/scripts/ci/e2e-shard-packer.py` discovers tests by regex over the raw text of every `*_test.go` file (`discover()`, e2e-shard-packer.py:54-60), ignoring Go build constraints. The shard legs in `.github/workflows/mcpx-test.yml` then run `go test ./internal/e2e -run '^($RUN_PATTERN)$'` **without** `-tags realsoftware` (mcpx-test.yml:160-163), and the leg's own verifier fails the step when the number of reported tests differs from the packer's assigned count (mcpx-test.yml:~197-199, `EXPECTED_COUNT` = `matrix.count`).

Four e2e tests live behind `//go:build realsoftware` and can never appear in an untagged `go test` run:

- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/e2e/real_filesystem_test.go:1` — `TestRealFilesystemServerRoundTrip`
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/e2e/real_memory_test.go:1` — `TestRealMemoryServerRoundTrip`
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/e2e/real_time_test.go:1` — `TestRealTimeServerTools`, `TestRealLsLatencyRecorded`

(`TestRealSoftwareGuard` in `realsoftware_guard_test.go` is untagged and runs fine — it is not part of this defect.)

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ 6d2a24b65628593adcb9ed02c3f3cdad6d11c690)

1. Packer run against the real tree: `e2e tests: 360 in 6 shards`, and the four tagged tests are dealt into the matrix — shard 0: `TestRealTimeServerTools`, shard 2: `TestRealFilesystemServerRoundTrip`, shard 3: `TestRealLsLatencyRecorded`, shard 4: `TestRealMemoryServerRoundTrip` (each such shard's `count` = 60 including the tagged test).
2. Ground truth from the compiler on the same tree: `go test ./internal/e2e -list '.*'` reports **356** tests; `go test -tags realsoftware ./internal/e2e -list '.*'` reports **360**. The packer's text discovery and the untagged build disagree by exactly the four tagged tests.
3. The workflow verifier counts only top-level pass/fail events whose `Test` is in `RUN_PATTERN`; a tagged test assigned to a shard produces no event, so that leg reports 59 of 60 and raises `SystemExit("shard test count differs from the init assignment")` under `set -e` — the leg fails even though every test that ran passed.
4. Corroborating, not load-bearing: in run 41530429335 (the run the packer's docstring cites for its measurements), e2e shards 2 and 4 failed while the others passed. (That run's job logs were no longer retrievable when checked, so the per-shard cause there is not claimed — the mechanism above is proven locally end to end.)

The packer's own stated contract is "every discovered test must be assigned exactly once, or the job fails rather than running a shard that silently executes nothing" — build-tagged tests break the dual of that contract: they are assigned, counted, and can never execute in the leg that owns them, and the failure surfaces as a misleading count mismatch in the leg rather than a discovery defect in init.

## Why it matters

- Every mcpx-test run that deals a tagged test into a shard (with equal weights today that is 4 of 6 shards) gets a spurious red leg, training everyone to ignore e2e failures in this workflow.
- The timing seed can never contain these tests (shard artifacts only record tests that ran), so the packer's median fallback permanently mis-weights them.
- The realsoftware subset already has its own coverage path (the nightly from #1990); the per-PR shard matrix should reflect the untagged build exactly.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `discover()` (or its replacement) returns exactly the tests an untagged `go test ./internal/e2e` build contains — today 356 names, excluding the four `realsoftware`-tagged tests — verified against `go test -list` output on the real tree.
- [ ] Build-constraint handling is general, not a hard-coded filename/test denylist: a new `*_test.go` file carrying an unsatisfied `//go:build` constraint (e.g. a new tag, or `//go:build ignore`) is likewise excluded, and a file whose constraint is satisfied by the default build (e.g. OS/GOARCH constraints matching linux/amd64) is still included.
- [ ] A regression test for the packer (fixture directory with tagged, untagged, and default-satisfied-constraint files) covers the discovery rule; the packer currently has no test suite.
- [ ] After the fix, every shard leg's `matrix.count` equals the number of tests its untagged `go test -run` invocation can report, so the workflow count check passes when all tests pass.
- [ ] The tagged tests remain covered by their existing nightly path — this change must not add `-tags realsoftware` to the per-PR shard legs.

## Dedup

Checked open + closed issues 2026-11-07: #6822 covers the packer's *timings-seed* shape handling (`load_weights`), not discovery; #1990 (closed) built the tagged subset + nightly; #4961 (closed) was a nightly failure. No issue covers packer discovery ignoring build constraints.

title: mcpx(testsupport): MCPX_TEST_REQUIRE has two divergent parsers, and CI's python3 entry is enforced by nothing

labels.name: kind/test
labels.description: Test coverage, test infrastructure, or test-only fixes

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Finding

`MCPX_TEST_REQUIRE` is parsed by two divergent parsers in the same `testsupport` package, and CI's list contains an entry nothing enforces. The two semantics disagree on case and on the wildcard/labels, and the `python3` entry in CI's list has no consumer — both recreate the silently-green hole the mechanism exists to close.

## Evidence

- Source PRs: #3696 (merged, merge `d55d6c90a5c7a584140ebbe0a299bdde25c882a1`) added `pkgs/mcpx/internal/testsupport/require.go`; #3704 (merged, merge `855372038be7b060a39a6fbecb4f405a454ff112`) added `realRequired()` in `pkgs/mcpx/internal/testsupport/realserver.go`. One finding for the set: same variable, same package, two PRs in the same batch.
- On current main (`4cd2927643453bee47a0f764de534e229220cf88`, verified twice via the contents API):
  - `require.go` `RequiredBinaries()` (line 21) normalises entries with `strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(name))` and knows only exact binary names.
  - `realserver.go` `realRequired()` (line 64) does `strings.TrimSpace(entry)` with **no lower-casing**, and additionally honours `"realsoftware"`, `"real"`, and `"*"`.
  - So `MCPX_TEST_REQUIRE=RealSoftware` (or `REALSOFTWARE`) fails a missing *runtime binary* test via the first parser but only *skips* a missing real server via the second; `MCPX_TEST_REQUIRE=*` demands every real server but no runtime binary.
  - `.github/workflows/mcpx.yml` line 178 sets `MCPX_TEST_REQUIRE: deno,bun,node,python3`, but no call site passes `python3` to `RequireBinary`/`MissingRequired` (the e2e and probe call sites cover only deno/bun/node), and there is no suite-level check that every entry in `RequiredBinaries()` is present on PATH. Enforcement is purely per-test: an entry with no (or a `-run`-filtered-out) consumer silently does nothing.

## Why it matters

The require-list is a contract between CI configuration and the test suite. Two parsers drifting in the same package guarantee the contract means different things for runtimes and for real servers, and an unenforced entry makes CI claim a guarantee it does not check — the exact failure #1983 was filed to eliminate.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] One shared parser for `MCPX_TEST_REQUIRE` lives in `require.go` (with the label/wildcard rules stated once), and `realRequired` uses it.
- [ ] Case handling is identical for runtime binaries and real servers (a test pins `RealSoftware`/`REALSOFTWARE` behaviour).
- [ ] Either a suite-level enforcement fails CI when any listed entry is missing from PATH (covering `python3`), or `python3` is removed from the workflow list with the reason recorded.
- [ ] Existing testsupport tests still pass.

## Finding

The flake builds and the nightly installs six pinned real MCP servers, but only three of them are ever exercised by a test. `mcp-server-git`, `mcp-server-fetch`, and `mcp-server-sequential-thinking` have no test at all, so if one of them breaks, vanishes from the build, or stops speaking MCP, the nightly stays green indefinitely.

## Evidence

- Source PR: #3704 (merged, merge `855372038be7b060a39a6fbecb4f405a454ff112`, head `5e379290ab5efb8ad7720bc52513f3da19a02636`).
- `pkgs/mcpx/real-servers.nix` on current main (`4cd2927643453bee47a0f764de534e229220cf88`, verified twice): six servers in the buildEnv (lines 8–13 inputs, 32–37 paths): time, memory, filesystem, git, fetch, sequential-thinking.
- On main, `pkgs/mcpx/internal/e2e/` contains only `real_filesystem_test.go`, `real_memory_test.go`, `real_time_test.go` (plus the guard) — the only `testsupport.RealServer(t, …)` calls name `mcp-server-filesystem` (:19), `mcp-server-memory` (:24), and `mcp-server-time` (:64, :92). No test names the other three.
- The nightly's only presence check is an unasserted `ls "$servers/bin"`; the guard test enforces tag/helper hygiene per test *file*, not per-server coverage. `MCPX_TEST_REQUIRE=realsoftware` flips a missing server to a failure only for a server some test actually requests.
- No open tracker covers this: #3704's body left the remaining legs on #1990, and #1990 is now CLOSED. Git and sequential-thinking are local stdio servers (no network needed, unlike fetch's HTTP shape), so their absence is not explained by the fetch leg's constraints.

## Why it matters

This is the silently-green failure mode #1990/#1983 exist to prevent, one level up: the subset's value is proving the pinned real servers still work with mcpx. Half the pinned set is currently decoration — built nightly, never run.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] At least a minimal RealServer test (tools/list + one real call) exists for `mcp-server-git` and `mcp-server-sequential-thinking`; fetch is covered too, or its exclusion is recorded in `real-servers.nix`/TESTING.md with the reason and a tracking reference.
- [ ] Removing/renaming one of the covered server binaries makes the nightly fail (require-flip actually engages).
- [ ] Existing real-software subset tests still pass.

body:
## Finding

`fleet-paperwork create`'s readback verification checks only the created issue's title and number — not the body, state, or labels — although the tool's README promises the readback compares "(title, body, state)". A create whose body was dropped or mangled, or whose labels were not applied, passes as "created+verified".

## Evidence

- Source PR: #3692 (merged, merge `ad1b664351d543575828b2d49ed0800fb30432a9`, head `240bab31582b8851ef2717abcd157089ce42a752`).
- `infra/fleet-paperwork/README.md` on current main (`4cd2927643453bee47a0f764de534e229220cf88`): "A filing is verified, or it is a failure. Every create / comment / close is followed by a readback GET, and the result is compared (title, body, state…)".
- `infra/fleet-paperwork/fleet_paperwork.py` on current main (same commit, verified twice): `cmd_create` at line 337; its readback is `if got.get("title") != title or got.get("number") != number: die(...)` — body, state, and the labels sent in the payload are never compared. (`cmd_comment` does compare the comment body; create is the odd one out.)

## Why it matters

The tool's whole contract — relied on by the rate-limit outbox workflow — is that a reported success means the filing is actually there, complete. An issue created with an empty/mangled body carries none of the evidence or acceptance criteria the filer sent, yet every downstream consumer (queue packets, backlog entries, dedupe) treats the create as verified.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Create readback compares at least body and state (and labels when labels were requested) against what was sent, dying on mismatch like the title check does.
- [ ] A unit test with a readback payload whose body differs proves the failure; a matching payload passes.
- [ ] Existing fleet-paperwork tests still pass.

title: worktree-reaper: no single-instance lock, and the pre-removal re-check omits the QUIET and PUSHED gates

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: app/worktree-reaper
labels.description: infra/worktree-reaper

body:
## Finding

The worktree-reaper has no single-instance lock, and its pre-removal re-check re-verifies only two of its five gates (occupancy and dirt) — not QUIET and not PUSHED. A tree can therefore be removed on stale evaluations, and overlapping runs can race each other.

## Evidence

- Source PR: #3698 (merged, merge `6313875c7b505305ccd12ec168c408a37df178c3`, head `434c2eeef33a01d7defde10f9c935d80bbdcaddc`).
- `infra/worktree-reaper/bin/worktree_reaper.py` on current main (`4cd2927643453bee47a0f764de534e229220cf88`, verified twice via the contents API):
  - `main()` at line 589 checks only the `DISABLED` kill switch before running; a whole-file search finds no lockfile/flock anywhere (0 hits). The systemd timer cannot overlap itself, but the README's own rollout procedure uses manual live runs, which can overlap a timer fire; both processes then evaluate the same trees and race the `last-run.json` state write and removals.
  - `reap_tree()` at line 534 re-checks occupancy (fresh `/proc` scan) and dirt (fresh `status_entries`) immediately before removal, per its comment — but never re-runs `pushed_proof` or the quiet check from `evaluate_tree` (line 458). A clean new *commit* made during the run (working tree stays clean, so the dirt re-check passes; branch tip now unpushed) does not stop the removal. `git branch -d` will usually refuse and keep the branch ref, which bounds the loss, but the worktree, its index, and its reflog are deleted under the resumed agent.

## Why it matters

TOCTOU and overlapping execution are the classic failure modes for destructive janitors. The re-check exists precisely to close the evaluation-to-removal window; leaving two of five gates — including PUSHED, the gate that protects unlanded work — outside it leaves the window open for the highest-value case.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A single-instance lock (lockfile/flock in the state dir) makes a second concurrent run exit without evaluating or removing anything, with a log line saying so.
- [ ] `reap_tree` re-verifies QUIET and PUSHED immediately before removal, retaining the tree if either no longer holds.
- [ ] Synthetic tests: a commit landing between evaluation and removal keeps the tree; a held lock makes a second run a no-op.
- [ ] Existing reaper tests still pass.

body:
# meta-exporter: the #6333 re-home regressed three closed fail-closed fixes — decimal-only parsing (#2789), timestamp range checks (#2460), and integer minor units (#2510) are all gone

## Evidence (verified this run, main `4cd2927643`)

`pm-stack/meta-exporter/meta-quota-export.mjs` was recreated by the re-home commit `b4cf60a2db` (PR #6333, 2026-11-05, 626 lines) from a pre-fix version. The three fixes that had landed and closed their issues are absent from current main, and their regression tests are absent from `meta-quota-export.test.mjs` (current suite: 13/13 pass on the laptop, none covering these cases):

- `parseSubscriptionQuota` (line ~83): `const num = (v) => (typeof v === "string" || typeof v === "number" ? Number(v) : NaN);` — the exact line #2789's fix (commit `934b902621`, PR #2864) replaced with a plain-decimal-only guard.
- No timestamp range/plausibility check on `resets_at` / `as_of` — the #2460 fix.
- `parseBillingBanner`: `minor / 100` with only `typeof minor === "number" && isFinite && >= 0` — fractional minor units pass, the #2510 fix.

Probe (laptop @`4cd2927643`, probe `~/git/fleet/probe-meta-rehome/probe.mjs`, importing the real module; valid captured-shape control payload, one field mutated per case):

| input | result on current main | expected (closed-issue contract) |
|---|---|---|
| control (decimal strings) | OK — 5h 10%, weekly 20% | OK (unchanged) |
| `window_weighted_used = ""` | **OK — 5h usedPct exported as 0** | `unparseable` (#2789) |
| `window_weighted_used = "0x10"` | **OK — usedPct 16** (hex reinterpreted) | `unparseable` (#2789) |
| `window_weighted_used = "1e2"` | **OK — usedPct 100** (scientific reinterpreted) | `unparseable` (#2789) |
| `as_of = ""` | **OK — consoleAsOf `1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z`** | null or `unparseable`, never epoch (#2789) |
| `window_resets_at` = ms-scale (`1793080000000`) | **OK — resetAt `+058790-06-11T17:46:40.000Z`** | `unparseable` (#2460) |
| `window_resets_at` = `999999999999999999` | **bare `RangeError: Invalid time value`** (not an `ExportError`; in `main()` this is misclassified as `fetch-failed`, exit 7) | `unparseable`, exit 6 (#2460) |
| `parseBillingBanner({remaining_minor_units: 1050.5, currency: "USD"})` | **OK — exports $10.505** | `unparseable` (#2510) |
| billing control `1050` | OK — $10.50 | OK (unchanged) |

## Why it matters

The exporter's design contract is "a failed tick can never be mistaken for a reading" and its parsers are documented "Throws on any shape drift — fail-closed, never partial zeros." All three regressions silently break that: a drifted empty used-value becomes a measured 0% window the quota gatherer ingests as fact, an ms-scale reset becomes a year-58790 reading in a `status: "ok"` document, and fractional cents become fractional dollars. The fixes already exist in git history (`934b902621` for #2789; the #2460/#2510 fixes likewise) — this is a restore-and-reconcile job, not new design: the re-home's newer features (readiness probe, bounded restart, #6343 entry-point guard) must be kept.

## Acceptance criteria

- `parseSubscriptionQuota` again accepts only plain decimal spellings for its numeric fields (used/limit/duration, inside `resetField`, and `as_of`): `""`, whitespace-only, hex, and scientific strings throw `ExportError("unparseable", 6, …)`; `as_of = ""` yields `consoleAsOf: null` or `unparseable`, never 1970.
- Reset/`as_of` timestamps are range-checked: an ms-scale or otherwise out-of-plausible-range value throws `unparseable` (exit 6), and no input to `parseSubscriptionQuota` can surface a bare `RangeError`.
- `parseBillingBanner` rejects non-integer `remaining_minor_units` as `unparseable`.
- The regression tests from the three original fixes are restored/adapted in `meta-quota-export.test.mjs`; the full suite passes (`node --test pm-stack/meta-exporter/meta-quota-export.test.mjs`), including the re-home's readiness/restart/entry-point tests.
- A note is left on closed #2789, #2460, and #2510 pointing at this regression issue (do not reopen them — this issue tracks the restore).

## Dedup

- #2789, #2460, #2510 are CLOSED (fixed, then regressed by `b4cf60a2db`); no open issue covers the regression — searches for "meta-exporter regression re-home 6333" and "6333 parseSubscriptionQuota" returned nothing.
- #6344 (open) is only about the test file not being run by any workflow — related context, different defect.
- #3469 (open) is the shared `opt()` flag-as-value bug in the exporters' CLI parsing — different function/mechanism.

# aggregator(provider-display): underscore strip breaks one-shot iterables and collapses renamed+plain providers to one display name

## Summary

The leading-underscore display strip added to `providerDisplayNames` in PR #6889 (commit `8dc7e75af7`, the #1823 provider rename) introduced two defects in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/provider-display.ts`:

1. **The function now spreads its `Iterable<string>` parameter twice, so a one-shot iterable produces a garbage map.** `providerDisplayNames` is declared over `Iterable<string>` (line 37), and the pre-rename implementation spread it exactly once. The new code spreads it at line 38 to build the stripped list and again at line 44 (`const originals = [...names]`) to recover the keys. For a one-shot iterable — a generator, a `Map.keys()` / `Set.values()` iterator — the second spread is empty, `originals[i]` is `undefined`, and the result is a single-entry map keyed by `undefined`. Every lookup misses, and `providerDisplayName` silently falls back to the unstripped canonical id.
2. **The underscore strip is not collision-aware, unlike the `-direct` rule in the same function.** The `-direct` strip keeps the suffix when a plain base provider exists in the same set, expressly "so the two stay distinguishable" (module header). The underscore strip has no such guard: a set containing both the renamed id and its plain base — e.g. `_claude` and `claude`, or the new pool series `_commandcode` and the pre-rename series `commandcode` that the rename deliberately kept in the store — renders both providers under the identical display string.

## Evidence

`pm-stack/aggregator/src/provider-display.ts:37-58` at `4cd2927643` (origin/main):

```ts
export function providerDisplayNames(names: Iterable<string>): Map<string, string> {
  const list = [...names].map((name) => { ... });   // first spread (line 38)
  ...
  const originals = [...names];                      // second spread (line 44)
```

Verified this run on the laptop with the real file verbatim (md5 `f16c0bdb00963613ca7b19399f667520`, probe `~/git/fleet/probe-provider-display`, bun 1.4.4):

| Input | Result |
|---|---|
| `["_claude", "_antigravity.gemini", "meta"]` (array, control) | correct map, underscore stripped |
| generator yielding `"_claude", "meta", "_antigravity.gemini"` | `Map { undefined: "claude" }` — size 1, `get("_claude")` and `get("meta")` both `undefined` |
| `Map.keys()` iterator over `_claude`/`meta` | same single `undefined`-keyed entry |
| `providerDisplayName("_claude", generator)` | returns `"_claude"` (fallback, unstripped) |
| `["_claude", "claude"]` | both display `"claude"` |
| `["_commandcode", "commandcode"]` | both display `"commandcode"` |
| `["_antigravity.gemini", "antigravity.gemini"]` | both display `"antigravity.gemini"` |
| `["openai", "openai-direct"]` (contrast) | `-direct` correctly kept: the existing rule is collision-aware |

Control: the shipped suite `pm-stack/aggregator/test/provider-display.test.ts` passes 11/11 on the same tree (run via `git archive origin/main`) — it only ever passes arrays, and has no renamed+plain pair case.

All current call sites (`render.ts:2167`, `render.ts:3364`, `render.ts:3714`) pass arrays, so defect 1 is latent today — but the exported signature promises `Iterable<string>`, and the singular helper `providerDisplayName(name, names)` invites exactly the iterator inputs that break.

## Why it matters

This module is the dashboard's one display-name rule, and its header states the contract: display strings change, ids/keys never do, and names that would collide stay distinguishable. Defect 1 breaks the type contract silently (no throw — wrong markup), and defect 2 makes two different providers/series indistinguishable on the quota board precisely in the migration window the rename created, where old and new ids coexist in the store by design.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `providerDisplayNames` reads its input exactly once: a generator or `Map.keys()` iterator yields the same map as the equivalent array, keyed by the exact input strings.
- [ ] When stripping the leading underscore would make a name's display equal to another distinct input's display in the same set (renamed + plain base both present, plain or dotted), the renamed name keeps a distinguishable display (mirroring the `-direct` rule's keep-on-collision behaviour); when there is no collision, the underscore is stripped as today.
- [ ] New regression tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/provider-display.test.ts` cover: a one-shot iterable input, and a renamed+plain pair (`_claude` + `claude` and/or `_commandcode` + `commandcode`).
- [ ] `bun test test/provider-display.test.ts` passes (existing 11 tests unchanged in behaviour).

Related: #1823 / PR #6889 (the rename that introduced the strip); #6125 (the original `-direct` display rule).

body:
# feature-plan(plan_check): every digit in `Requires:` prose is read as a step number — version and RFC numbers become phantom requirements

## Summary

`plan_check.py` extracts a step's requirements by taking every run of digits in the `Requires:` sentence as a step number. Any number that is not a step reference — a runtime version, an RFC number, a port, a year — becomes a phantom requirement, and the checker fails the plan with a wrong-cause error naming a step that does not exist.

## Evidence

`.agents/skills/feature-plan/scripts/plan_check.py:49-52` (at `0a5c705a23`):

```python
bare = re.sub(r"\([^)]*\)", "", text)
requires = re.search(r"Requires: ([^.\n]*)", bare)
fields["requires"] = (
    [int(n) for n in re.findall(r"\d+", requires[1])] if requires else []
)
```

Parenthesised prose is stripped first, so the canonical `Requires: 1 (the lock layout)` works — but prose outside parentheses is scanned digit-by-digit, and the capture also stops at the first `.`, so a decimal version contributes its major number.

Verified this run on the laptop with the real file verbatim (md5 `53bca2a3f105a4c3a4f2198e6631a46a`, probe `~/git/fleet/probe-plan-check`), using plans in the documented step format (`.agents/skills/feature-plan/references/plan-outline.md` §4):

| `Requires:` text on step 2 | Result |
|---|---|
| `1` (control) | `ok: 2 steps in 2 waves`, exit 0 |
| `1 (the lock layout)` (canonical control) | `ok`, exit 0 |
| `1 and the Node 20 runtime` | exit 1 — `step 2: requires 20, not a lower step` |
| `1, per RFC 8446` | exit 1 — `step 2: requires 8446, not a lower step` |
| `1 and Python 3.12` | exit 1 — `step 2: requires 3, not a lower step` |

The existing suite (`scripts/tests/test_plan_check.py`, 3 tests) passes on the same tree and has no prose-number case.

## Why it matters

`validation.md` §1 makes this checker the gate before the fresh-context validator runs: "Fix everything it prints before launching the validator." A phantom requirement sends the plan author hunting for a step 20 / 8446 / 3 that was never a requirement, or — worse — teaches authors to strip legitimate version references out of `Requires:` prose to make the gate pass. The inverse also holds: a prose digit that happens to equal a real lower step number (e.g. "the HTTP 2 transport" in a plan that has a step 2) silently invents a hard edge the author never declared, which the wave checks then enforce.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Requires:` parsing recognises step references in the documented forms (bare numbers / number lists, parenthetical notes) without treating other digits in the sentence as step numbers; the three repro cases above pass (`ok`, exit 0) while the controls keep passing.
- [ ] A genuinely bad target is still reported: a requirement on a non-existent, self, or later-wave step still fails with the existing messages.
- [ ] New regression tests in `scripts/tests/test_plan_check.py` cover: a version number (`Node 20`), an RFC number, and a decimal version (`Python 3.12`) in `Requires:` prose, plus the canonical parenthetical form.
- [ ] `python3 -m unittest scripts.tests.test_plan_check` passes.

Related: #585 (earlier plan_check duplicate-step defect, closed) — different mechanism, same checker.

title: id(build.sh): a missing or corrupt variant file lets the wrong-variant binary pass as up to date — a lib binary is served for a web build (and vice versa)

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/id/scripts/build.sh` decides whether the existing binary matches the requested variant (`lib` vs `web` — the same output path `target/debug/id` / `target/release/id`, differing only by `--features web`) from a single marker file, and only in one narrow case:

- `scripts/build.sh:105`: the variant check fires only when the marker file **exists** and its content is exactly the *other* variant:
  ```bash
  elif [[ -f $VARIANT_FILE ]] && [[ "$(cat "$VARIANT_FILE")" == "$OTHER_VARIANT" ]]; then
  ```
- If the marker file is **missing, empty, or contains anything else**, the script falls through to the timestamp scan and can declare `"<variant> <profile> variant up to date"` — with a binary on disk that was built as the *other* variant.
- The marker is written non-atomically at `scripts/build.sh:153` (`echo "$VARIANT" >"$VARIANT_FILE"`), so an interrupted build is exactly how an empty/truncated marker is produced. The marker can also be lost independently of the binary (partial `target/` cleanup, a copied-in binary, a manual `rm target/.build-variant*`).

## Verified (laptop, main @ 8a5cd8ea75, real script verbatim, stubbed cargo/bun)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-buildsh-variant` (fixture tree in the style of `scripts/build-sh-test.sh`; control + 3 failure cases):

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| Control: build `lib`, marker intact (`lib`), run `web` | Correctly rebuilds: `cargo build --features web`, marker becomes `web` |
| Build `lib`, **delete** marker, run `web` | `web debug variant up to date`, **cargo never invoked**, marker still absent — the lib binary (no `--features web`) is left in place as the "web" build |
| Build `lib`, marker **truncated to empty**, run `web` | Same: `up to date`, cargo never invoked |
| Build `lib`, marker contains **`banana`**, run `web` | Same: `up to date`, cargo never invoked |

Symmetric for `web` → `lib` (a web binary silently served as the lib build).

## Why it matters

The two variants produce functionally different binaries at the *same path*. A stale-variant binary that passes as current is a silent wrong-artifact failure: a developer (or a just recipe — `build-lib` / the web build) runs a binary missing the web features (or carrying them unexpectedly) with no diagnostic, and the timestamp logic can keep it "up to date" indefinitely until a source file changes. This is the same script whose variant handling already produced #6869; the marker is the only variant evidence, so an unknown marker state must mean "rebuild", not "trust the binary".

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A missing marker file, or a marker whose content is not exactly the requested variant, forces a backend rebuild (unknown state rebuilds; only an exact match for the requested variant may take the up-to-date path).
- [ ] The marker write is atomic (write to a temp file in the same directory + rename), so an interrupted build cannot leave an empty/truncated marker.
- [ ] `scripts/build-sh-test.sh` gains cases for the missing-marker, empty-marker, and garbage-marker states (build one variant, disturb the marker, request the other variant, assert cargo is invoked with the correct flags and the marker is rewritten) — for at least the debug profile.
- [ ] Existing `build-sh-test.sh` cases (lib debug/release, assets, web control) still pass.

Related: #6869 (the `lib`-variant unbound-variable crash in the same script, fixed + regression-tested in PR #6870).

# cloudflare-export: GraphQL group-limit saturation is flagged for only 2 of 7 datasets — workers/kv/d1/queues/r2-ops/ai-total totals at their query limit are published as exact, never as lower bounds

## Summary

`pm-stack/cloudflare-export/cloudflare-quota-export.mjs` states its own discipline in the header (lines 70–73): a grouped result at its query limit "is flagged as a lower bound, never silently truncated — the r2-storage discipline." That discipline is implemented for exactly two datasets and silently absent for the other five:

Implemented:
- `r2StorageAdaptiveGroups` (limit 10000): `parseGraphqlUsage` computes `saturated = storageGroups.length >= R2_STORAGE_GROUP_LIMIT` and marks the `r2-storage` metric `lowerBound: true` with detail prose (lines 313–325).
- `aiInferenceAdaptiveGroupsByDay` (limit 10000): `aiNeuronsDayAlerts` returns `saturated`, alerts carry `lowerBound: true`, and the document carries `aiNeuronsByDaySaturated` (lines 248–266, 385).

Missing — `GRAPHQL_QUERY` (lines 442–449) sets explicit limits and `parseGraphqlUsage`/`classifyR2` sum whatever came back with no at-limit check:
- `workersInvocationsAdaptive` limit 100 → `workers-requests`, `workers-cpu-ms`
- `kvOperationsAdaptiveGroups` limit 100 → `kv-reads`, `kv-writes` (`foldKv`)
- `d1AnalyticsAdaptiveGroups` limit 100 → `d1-rows-read`, `d1-rows-written`
- `queueMessageOperationsAdaptiveGroups` limit 100 → `queues-ops`
- `r2OperationsAdaptiveGroups` limit 1000 → `r2-class-a`, `r2-class-b` (`classifyR2` returns only `{classA, classB, unclassified, nonbillable}` — no saturation field)
- `aiInferenceAdaptiveGroups` limit 100 → `workers-ai-neurons` cycle total / per-day average (the by-day sibling got limit 10000 + a flag in #2287; the cycle-total dataset it is compared against kept limit 100 and no flag)

If any of these datasets returns exactly its limit of rows, the published document reports the partial sum as an exact reading in a `status: "ok"` document — the precise failure mode the r2-storage and #2287 fixes were written to prevent.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ 8a5cd8ea75)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-cf-gql-limits` (real `cloudflare-quota-export.mjs` copied verbatim, md5 780d4ee5dd2905d92c3672859c35c3dd, run under Bun against `parseGraphqlUsage`):

- control payload: all metrics present, no `lowerBound` anywhere (correct).
- kv groups at exactly 100 (the query limit): `kv-reads` = `{"id":"kv-reads","used":100,"unit":"count","source":"cloudflare-graphql-analytics"}` — no `lowerBound`.
- workers rows at exactly 100: `workers-requests` used=100, no flag.
- ai cycle-total groups at exactly 100: `workers-ai-neurons` published with a definitive detail string ("cycle total 1000 neurons"), no flag.
- d1 and queues groups at exactly 100: `d1-rows-read` / `queues-ops` used=100, no flag.
- r2 operations groups at exactly 1000 (the query limit): `r2-class-b` used=1000, no flag; `classifyR2` result keys are only `classA,classB,unclassified,nonbillable`.
- Existing suite as control: `bun test` on the real test file — 35 pass / 0 fail; the only saturation tests cover r2-storage (test line 155) and ai-by-day (line 419).

Dedup: no open or closed issue covers GraphQL-limit saturation for these datasets (#2574 covered REST bucket enumeration; #2287 covered only the by-day neurons dataset).

## Why it matters

The aggregator's Cloudflare card and the quota registry consume these figures as exact readings. A truncated workers/kv/d1/queues/r2/ai total understates usage silently — for the AI neurons cycle total it also corrupts the per-day average that the #2287 alert is compared against. The file already solved this problem twice; the remaining datasets are the residual door of the same fix.

## Acceptance criteria

- Every dataset in `GRAPHQL_QUERY` with an explicit `limit` has a defined saturation behaviour: at-limit results mark the affected metric(s) `lowerBound: true` (the r2-storage pattern) or otherwise surface an explicit document-level flag — no dataset publishes an at-limit sum as an exact reading.
- `classifyR2` reports saturation for `r2OperationsAdaptiveGroups` (limit 1000) and the flag reaches the success document.
- New tests in `cloudflare-quota-export.test.mjs` pin at-limit behaviour for each previously unflagged dataset (at-limit flagged; one-below-limit unflagged), mirroring the existing r2-storage test at line 155.
- Existing 35 tests still pass.

body:
# id(bench-compare): malformed current bench lines read as results — a non-numeric median coerces to 0 (-100% 'ok'), a missing median prints 'not run', duplicate lines silently overwrite

## Problem

`.github/scripts/id-bench-compare.sh` diffs pkgs/id benchmark medians
against the committed baselines and prints the Markdown regression
report that goes to the GitHub job summary. Its parser
(`parse()`, awk) trusts the shape of every `bench` line:

- :65 — `if (kv[1] == "median") median[name] = kv[2] + 0`. awk coerces a
  non-numeric value to 0, so a corrupt current median (`median=abc`, a
  truncated line, a harness format drift) becomes a real 0.000 median:
  the row prints `-100.0%` with status **ok**, and the summary can read
  "No benchmark regressed" over garbage input.
- A `bench` line with no `median=` field at all registers the name in
  the order list (:68) but never in `median[]`, so the row falls into
  the :110 branch and prints **not run** — the benchmark *did* run; its
  line is malformed, which is a different, actionable fact.
- A repeated `bench <name>` line silently overwrites the earlier median
  (last one wins, no note). A +100% regression line followed by a
  duplicate normal line reports `+0.0% ok`.

#1619 (closed) fixed the comparison-side shapes — unit changes and a
zero baseline are now reported as *incomparable* with no verdict, and a
non-numeric threshold exits 2, on the stated principle that broken input
"must be loud, never silently read as flag nothing". The line-level
shapes above are the residual door in the same parser: they are neither
flagged nor marked incomparable, they just become wrong numbers or a
wrong "not run".

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ a2ea75cb63)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-bench-compare` (real script unmodified;
baseline `alpha median=100`, `beta median=200`, `gamma median=50`, all
`unit=ns`):

- Current file with `alpha median=abc`, `beta median=260`,
  `gamma` with **no** median field →
  `alpha | 100.000 | 0.000 | -100.0% | ok`; `gamma | — | — | not run`;
  exit 0. The beta regression (+30%) is flagged correctly in the same
  run, so the machinery works — only the malformed rows lie.
- Current file with two `alpha` lines (`median=200` then `median=100`)
  → alpha reports `100.000 | +0.0% | ok` and the summary prints
  "✅ No benchmark regressed" — the +100% line vanished silently.
- Control (well-formed current file, alpha +10%): all rows ok with
  correct percentages, exit 0.

The existing suite `.github/scripts/id-bench-compare.test.sh` covers
unit change, zero baseline, bad threshold env, ok/regression rows and a
genuinely missing current row ("not run") — none of the three shapes
above.

## Why it matters

This report is the only regression signal for the F11.8 baselines on PRs
(non-blocking by design, #1513), so its readers trust the rows at face
value. A harness hiccup or format drift that corrupts a median today
does not produce a suspicious report — it produces a *perfect* one
(-100%, ok), and a duplicated line can erase a real regression from the
summary entirely. That is the exact failure #1619 was filed to stop,
one door over.

## Acceptance criteria

- A `bench` line whose `median=` value is missing or not a valid number
  (on either the baseline or the current side) produces an
  *incomparable/malformed* row naming the benchmark and the reason —
  never a numeric change, never an `ok`/regression verdict, and never
  `not run` when a line for that benchmark is present.
- A repeated `bench <name>` line in one file is surfaced (flagged in
  the report as a duplicate/malformed input, or rejected with the
  non-zero usage-style exit) — it never silently overwrites an earlier
  median.
- Well-formed inputs are byte-identical to today: the control,
  regression, unit-changed, zero-baseline and genuine not-run/no-baseline
  cases in `.github/scripts/id-bench-compare.test.sh` still pass, and
  the suite gains cases for the three shapes above (non-numeric median,
  missing median field, duplicate line).
- A baseline-side malformed median is reported with its real reason
  (malformed), not as "zero baseline median".

body:
# pm-stack(external-comms): a record spilled while the pusher drains is silently lost — spill() takes no lock and do_push() rewrites the outbox from its stale read set

## Problem

`pm-stack/external-comms/record-external-send` is the external-comms ledger
writer + pusher. Its contract (Drew's 2026-11-05 rule, in the module
docstring) is **EXTERNAL COMMS ARE NEVER SILENT**: every send is recorded
in `agent.external_comms`, DB-first with spill to a local outbox that the
pusher drains. That contract has a lost-update race:

- `do_push()` (:212) takes the pusher flock (:216), reads the whole outbox
  once (:235-236 `lines = [ln for ln in f if ln.strip()]`), inserts those
  records, then rewrites the outbox from that read set alone:
  pending records are written to `OUTBOX + ".tmp"` and
  `os.replace(tmp, OUTBOX)` (:285) swaps it in.
- `spill()` (:137) — the path a concurrent `record` takes when its own DB
  insert fails — appends to `OUTBOX` directly. It never takes the pusher
  lock, and nothing re-reads the outbox before the replace.

A `record` that spills **between the pusher's read and its replace**
appends its line to the inode the pusher is about to replace. The line is
never inserted (it was not in the pusher's read set), is not in the
rewritten outbox, and is not quarantined — it simply vanishes, while the
pusher reports a clean drain (`pending: 0`, `last_drain_ok_at` set). The
failure window is exactly the bad moment: spills happen when the DB is
failing, which is also when a drain takes longest (per-record timeouts),
and a spilled record is by definition one whose direct insert already
failed once.

This is the second silent-loss door in the same file: #6154 (closed)
fixed unparseable lines being dropped by the rewrite; this one loses
*well-formed* lines the rewrite never saw.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ a2ea75cb63)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-extcomms-race` (real `record-external-send`
copied verbatim, md5 `fc7f526a1ee95f58990b7a8e15783a27` = the file on
main; transport stubbed via module attributes):

- Seed outbox with record A only; stub `insert_record` so that, while
  inserting A, a concurrent record B spills via the real `spill()`
  (exactly what `do_record` does after a failed DB insert); run the real
  `do_push()`.
- Result: pusher prints `{"pusher": "ran", "landed": 1, "pending": 0,
  "quarantined": 0, "last_error": null}`; landed = `[A]`; outbox after
  push = `[]`; no quarantine file; health shows `pending_count: 0` with
  `last_drain_ok_at` set. **Record B is nowhere** — not landed, not
  pending, not quarantined.
- Control (same probe, B spilled before the push starts): both records
  land, `landed: 2`. Only the mid-drain timing loses the record.

## Why it matters

The ledger is the audit trail for every external send made under Drew's
or a fleet identity, including the approval basis for each send. A record
lost this way leaves no trace anywhere — no error, no quarantine, a
health file claiming a clean drain — so a later audit reads "no such
send" for a send that happened. The pusher runs every minute
(`external-comms-pusher.timer`), so the race window opens constantly;
it only needs one send recorded during one slow drain.

## Acceptance criteria

- A record spilled at any point during a `do_push()` run is never lost:
  after the run it is either inserted, still present in the outbox, or
  quarantined with a reason — and a run that leaves a spilled record
  behind does not report it as landed.
- The fix preserves the existing contracts: `record` still exits 0 when
  the spill succeeds even with the DB down (recording must not block or
  fail the send it logs); the quarantine behavior from #6154 is
  unchanged; two concurrent pushers still serialize on the flock.
- `pm-stack/external-comms/test_push_quarantine.py` (the #6154/#6217
  pinning suite) still passes, and gains a regression case that
  reproduces this race (e.g. a spill injected mid-drain via a stubbed
  insert) and asserts the spilled record survives the drain.
- Whatever mechanism is chosen (shared lock on the record path, drain
  re-read/merge before replace, append-only pending write, or another
  shape), the module docstring's write-pattern section describes it, so
  the next reader can see why the outbox rewrite is safe.

body:
## Problem

`.github/scripts/check-workflows.sh` supports an explicit-file mode — `check-workflows.sh FILE [FILE..]`, "used by the contract tests" (script header) — but file arguments are resolved **after** the script changes directory, and a missing/unreadable action file is misdiagnosed on both validation branches:

1. **Relative paths break.** The script computes `REPO_ROOT` from its own location and runs `cd "$REPO_ROOT"` (check-workflows.sh:26-28) before it ever looks at `"$@"`. A relative FILE argument that is valid in the caller's working directory is then resolved against the repo root instead. From any other directory the file "does not exist" — and the error says nothing about paths.
2. **PyYAML branch mislabels an OS error as a YAML error.** A missing action file produces `<file>: invalid YAML: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '<file>'` — the file is not invalid YAML; it was never opened.
3. **Structural-fallback branch invents a key.** On a missing file, `grep` fails inside the key extraction, the key list comes out empty, and the validator reports `<file>: unexpected top-level key ''` — an empty-string key that exists nowhere — instead of reporting that the file cannot be read.

The contract suite (`.github/scripts/check-workflows.test.sh`) always passes absolute paths from a controlled temp dir, so none of this is exercised; the failure shows up exactly when a developer runs the gate by hand from a subdirectory or with a typo'd path — the moment a clear diagnostic matters most.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop, main @ ab37879484)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-check-workflows`, invoking the real unmodified script with a stub `ACTIONLINT_BIN`:

- Missing file, fallback path (system python3, no PyYAML):
  ```
  $ bash .github/scripts/check-workflows.sh /tmp/does-not-exist/action.yml
  grep: /tmp/does-not-exist/action.yml: No such file or directory
  /tmp/does-not-exist/action.yml: unexpected top-level key ''
  rc=1
  ```
- Missing file, PyYAML path (venv PyYAML 6.0.3):
  ```
  /tmp/does-not-exist/action.yml: invalid YAML: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '/tmp/does-not-exist/action.yml'
  rc=1
  ```
- Relative path to an existing, valid action file, run from the directory containing it (`~/git/fleet/probe-check-workflows`):
  ```
  $ bash ~/git/code/.github/scripts/check-workflows.sh node-main/action.yml
  node-main/action.yml: invalid YAML: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'node-main/action.yml'
  rc=1
  ```
  The same file passes (rc=0) when given as an absolute path — the path resolution, not the file, is at fault.

## Why it matters

The verdict (rc=1) happens to be right for a missing file, but for the wrong reason in both branches, and a *valid* file given by relative path from a non-root cwd also fails. A gate whose hand-run diagnostics blame YAML syntax or invent an empty top-level key teaches developers to distrust and bypass it — and the fallback branch's `''` verdict would be actively confusing in a CI log if a rename ever left the full-set `find` racing a deleted file.

Sibling finding in the same validator, filed separately: #6871 (missing per-runtime field checks — node `runs.main`, composite step shapes).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Explicit FILE arguments are resolved against the caller's working directory (canonicalized before the `cd`, or the `cd` is scoped so argument resolution is unaffected): `check-workflows.sh node-main/action.yml` from the file's own directory behaves identically to the absolute-path invocation.
- [ ] A missing or unreadable action file fails with a diagnostic that names the file and the OS error (e.g. `cannot read <file>: No such file or directory`) on **both** the PyYAML and structural-fallback branches — never `invalid YAML:` for an open failure, and never `unexpected top-level key ''`.
- [ ] A genuine YAML syntax error still reports as invalid YAML with the parser's message (existing behavior preserved).
- [ ] `.github/scripts/check-workflows.test.sh` gains contract cases: relative path from a foreign cwd (pass for a valid fixture), missing action file (fail, with a cannot-read diagnostic) on whichever branch the test environment exercises.

body:
# opencode-claimant(poll): a session entry with a wrong-shaped `time` crashes all of poll.py — one malformed session kills candidate discovery for every queue

## Summary

`pm-stack/opencode-claimant/poll.py` reads the OpenCode server's session list and classifies every entry through `is_active_root` (:186), `is_stuck_bound` (:145), and `_stuck_entry` (:366). All three do `t = session.get("time") or {}` and then call `t.get(...)` and do arithmetic on `t.get("updated") or t.get("created") or 0` (:175-179, :196-200, :368-380) with no type check on `time` itself or on the timestamp values. A single session entry whose `time` is a non-empty string, an int, or a bool raises `AttributeError`; an entry whose `time.updated`/`time.created` is a string, list, or object raises `TypeError`. Because `main()` (:419) runs `summarize_cap` and `get_stuck_bound` over the whole list with no per-entry guard, one such entry crashes the whole poll: no JSON is printed at all, so the claimant discovers no candidates and no stuck-bound rows for any of the four queues.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ 65beb42c1a)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-poll-time-shape/` on the laptop — `poll.py` copied verbatim from `origin/main` (md5 matches `git show`), existing suite as control, classifiers called directly:

Controls (all pass):
- Existing `test_poll.py` suite on the verbatim copy: **41 tests OK**.
- `is_active_root(fresh root)` → `True`; `summarize_cap([fresh, finished], set(), now)` → `(2, 1, 35)`; timeless dict `{"id": "ses_x"}` → `False` (the pinned `test_non_dict_and_timeless_entries_never_active` case).

Wrong shapes (all raise):
- `time="soon"`, `time=123`, `time=True` → `AttributeError: 'str'/'int'/'bool' object has no attribute 'get'` in `is_active_root`, in `summarize_cap`, in `is_stuck_bound`, and in `_stuck_entry`.
- `time={"updated": "soon"}` / `{"created": "soon"}` (also list/dict values) → `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for -: 'int' and 'str'` in `is_active_root` and `is_stuck_bound`.
- Main-path simulation: `summarize_cap([good_root, root(time="soon")], ...)` raises — one bad entry poisons the entire list; `get_stuck_bound` with the bad session raises the same way.

Falsy non-dict `time` values (`[]`) slip through via `or {}` and are silently treated as timeless — inconsistent with the truthy cases crashing, and for `is_stuck_bound` an empty-list `time` yields `updated=0`, i.e. "silent forever", which can mark a bound task stuck on no evidence.

## Why it matters

poll.py is the claimant's only discovery surface: its own header states the claimant treats its output as the launch decision input for all four pilot queues. The module's documented contract is fail-closed on unknowns — `summarize_cap` returns `None` counts rather than guess, `parse_lease_ms` refuses to call an unparseable lease expired, `is_stuck_bound` says "Fail closed on every unknown". A wrong-shaped `time` is exactly such an unknown, but instead of failing closed it raises out of `main()`: the claimant gets no output whatsoever (worse than the `cap_room: null` no-launch signal the design intends), and the crash repeats every poll cycle for as long as the malformed session remains in the server's list — finished sessions are returned forever until archived, per the module header. The server is an external trust boundary (its payload shape has already changed under this code: #4757 truncation, #6609 cap API), so one unexpected entry shape must not be able to take down discovery fleet-wide.

Related: #6865 (claimant.py missing imports) is a different defect in the sibling file; this issue is only poll.py's session-`time` handling. #4757/#6609 covered fetch truncation and the cap API, not per-entry field shapes.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] No session entry shape raises out of `is_active_root`, `is_stuck_bound`, `_stuck_entry`, `count_active_roots`, or `summarize_cap`: non-object `time` (string/int/bool/list) and non-numeric `updated`/`created` are handled, not raised.
- [ ] Fail-closed semantics preserved: an entry whose timing cannot be read must never be counted as a known-inactive root to manufacture cap room, and never classified stuck-bound on missing timing evidence; the cap summary treats an unreadable-timing entry consistently with the module's unknown-propagation rule (unknown/`None` rather than a guessed count), or documents and tests the chosen equivalent.
- [ ] `main()` still prints its full JSON (candidates + stuck_bound + cap fields) when the session list contains one malformed entry among good ones.
- [ ] Regression tests in `pm-stack/opencode-claimant/test_poll.py` cover: `time` as string/int/bool/list, `updated`/`created` as string/list/object, across the active-root, stuck-bound, and stuck-entry paths, plus the existing 41 tests still pass.

## Verification

Probe directory (laptop): `~/git/fleet/probe-poll-time-shape/` (`poll.py` verbatim from main @ 65beb42c1a, md5-verified; `probe.py`; `test_poll.py` control suite 41/41 OK). Dedup: gh searches (all states) for `poll.py` time/session shape and claimant-poll malformed-session terms — no issue covers per-entry `time` shapes; #6394-style config validation and #2800 sync shapes are different files/mechanisms.

body:
# mcpx(affected-tests): an `all:`-prefixed //go:embed pattern never matches — edits to the embedded opencode skills select no tests at all

## Summary

`pkgs/mcpx/scripts/affected-tests.py` maps a changed non-Go file to the package that embeds it (`embedded_owners`, :312), so an edit to an embedded input selects that package's T0/T1 commands. The matcher builds its candidate prefix from the raw embed pattern text (`base = pat` / `pkg_dir + "/" + pat`, :337-338) and never strips Go's `all:` pattern prefix. The one `all:` embed in the tree — `plugin/opencode/skills/skills.go:18`, `//go:embed all:mcpx-*`, which carries every `mcpx-*/SKILL.md` skill document into the binary — therefore matches nothing: a change confined to the embedded skills selects **no tier commands at all**, and the selector reports it as a no-code change.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ 65beb42c1a)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-affected-embed/probe.py` on the laptop — imports the real `affected-tests.py` from main and calls `embedded_owners` against the real `pkgs/mcpx` tree:

| Changed file | Embed directive | `embedded_owners` result |
|---|---|---|
| `plugin/opencode/skills/mcpx-basics/SKILL.md` | `plugin/opencode/skills/skills.go:18` — `//go:embed all:mcpx-*` | `[]` — **no owner** |
| `internal/dashboard/dashboard.html` (control) | `//go:embed dashboard.html` | `['internal/dashboard']` |
| `internal/mcpspec/schema/mcp.schema.json` (control) | `//go:embed schema` | `['internal/mcpspec']` |
| `internal/defaults/defaults.json` (control) | `//go:embed defaults.json` | `['internal/defaults']` |

Code path: the pattern token is `all:mcpx-*`, so `base` becomes `plugin/opencode/skills/all:mcpx-*`; a real candidate (`plugin/opencode/skills/mcpx-basics/SKILL.md`) is neither equal to it, under `base + "/"`, nor an `fnmatch` match for it (:340-344). With no owner and no `.go` file changed, `main()`'s `pkgs` stays empty (:391-395), so no T0 vet / T1 test command is emitted for the change and the run ends with "# no tier commands selected (no code or registry changes)".

## Why it matters

The skill files are shipped product content, not docs: `skills.FS` is served to every connected MCP host via the skills extension (`internal/mcpserver/skills.go:77`) and read by the CLI (`internal/cli/commands.go:1929,2038`), and content tests exercise exactly these bytes (`internal/mcpserver/skills_test.go` — `TestSkillEntriesListEveryFile`, `TestSkillsListGetRead`; `internal/e2e/skill_examples_test.go` — `TestSkillExamplesRun` runs the skills' examples). TESTING.md's tier contract says an embedded-input change is a code change for its owning package; for the only `all:` embed in the tree the selector silently breaks that contract, so an agent following `just mcpx-test-affected` for a SKILL.md edit is told there is nothing to run. The `all:` prefix is also semantically load-bearing in the other direction (it is what makes dot/underscore files part of the embed, per the comment at skills.go:14-17), so a fix must strip it for matching without losing the pattern itself.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `embedded_owners` attributes a change under `plugin/opencode/skills/mcpx-*/` (e.g. `mcpx-basics/SKILL.md`) to `plugin/opencode/skills`; a dry-run selection for a skills-only change emits that package's T0/T1 commands instead of "no tier commands selected".
- [ ] Pattern handling covers the `all:` prefix generally (any `all:<pattern>` embed), not a special case for this one path.
- [ ] Controls unchanged: the plain-file (`dashboard.html`), directory (`schema`), and plain-glob embeds that resolve today still resolve to the same owners.
- [ ] Regression tests in `pkgs/mcpx/scripts/tests/` (alongside `test_affected_untracked.py`) cover an `all:`-prefixed pattern — file and directory candidates under it — plus the existing plain-pattern controls.

## Verification

Probe directory (laptop): `~/git/fleet/probe-affected-embed/` (`probe.py`, imports the real script verbatim from main @ 65beb42c1a, runs against the real tree): the `all:` case returns `[]` while all three controls return their owning package. Dedup: searches (all states) for `embedded_owners`, `embed owner`, `go:embed affected`, `mcpx skills embed` — no issue covers embed-owner matching; #5649 covers `--run` shell syntax from changed paths, a different mechanism in the same file.

body:
# id(test-shard-sandbox): invalid SHARD/COUNT silently runs the whole unsharded suite — an empty target selection is passed to cargo test unfiltered and exits 0

## Evidence

`pkgs/id/scripts/test-shard-sandbox.sh` (verified at origin/main `65beb42c1a`) is the PR gate's integration-test partition: the four flake checks `test-shard-0..3` (`pkgs/id/flake.nix:347-350`, `test-shard-sandbox 0 4` … `3 4`, via `pkgs/id/justfile:311-312`) together are supposed to run every target under `pkgs/id/tests/` exactly once (script header, lines 5-11; `.github/workflows/id-check.yml:29-30`).

The script never validates its two arguments and never checks that it selected anything:

- `shard=$1` / `count=$2` are taken raw (lines 14-15). There is no integer, range, or positivity check anywhere in the script.
- Selection is one arithmetic test inside a `[ … ]` condition (line 30): `if [ $((i % count)) -eq "$shard" ]`. Arithmetic and test errors inside a condition do not abort the script (they are not covered by `set -e` in that context, and no explicit check follows), so every malformed input simply selects nothing.
- The selected `--test` args are then passed straight to cargo (line 36): `cargo test --all-features "${args[@]}" -- --skip serve_tests`. With an empty `args` array that command has **no `--test` filter at all** — cargo runs the entire test suite (all integration targets plus the lib) — and the script exits 0.

## Reproduction (laptop probe, real script verbatim, `~/git/fleet/probe-shard-sandbox`)

Probe setup: the real `test-shard-sandbox.sh` copied verbatim, a `tests/` dir with 8 stub targets `t0.rs`…`t7.rs`, and a `cargo` stub on PATH that echoes its argv.

Controls (the partition contract working):

- `0 2` → `--test t0 --test t2 --test t4 --test t6`, plus the shard-0 bins/doc runs.
- `1 2` → `--test t1 --test t3 --test t5 --test t7`. Disjoint from shard 0; together they cover all 8 targets.

Malformed inputs (every one exits 0 and runs the suite unfiltered):

- `4 4` (shard out of range) → `test-shard-sandbox 4/4 targets:` (empty), then `CARGO: test --all-features -- --skip serve_tests` — no `--test` filter.
- `9 4` → same empty selection, same unfiltered run, exit 0.
- `-1 4` (negative shard) → same empty selection, same unfiltered run, exit 0.
- `x 4` (non-numeric shard) → `[: x: integer expected` printed once per target on stderr, still empty selection, same unfiltered run, exit 0.
- `0 0` (zero count) → `i % count: division by 0` printed once per target on stderr, still empty selection, same unfiltered run **plus** the shard-0 bins and doc runs, exit 0.
- No arguments at all → the only case that fails, and it fails with a bare `line 14: $1: unbound variable` naming neither the usage nor the expected range.

## Why it matters

The shard arguments are the entire coverage contract of the id PR gate: `flake.nix` hard-codes `0 4`…`3 4`, and the script's header promises "the shards together cover every target". A single typo when that wiring is next touched (a shard renumbered to `4 4`, a count edited in the script's callers but not the flake, a just recipe invoked by hand with swapped arguments) does not fail the gate — it turns one shard check into a full ~25-minute unsharded suite run that passes, while the targets that shard was supposed to own may be run by nobody. The failure mode is the worst kind for CI: slower *and* silently less partitioned, with a green check at the end. Every other malformed-input surface in this script's neighbourhood fails closed with a named diagnostic; this one fails open into the most expensive possible run.

## Acceptance criteria

- `test-shard-sandbox.sh` validates its arguments before selecting anything: exactly two arguments; `count` a positive integer; `shard` an integer with `0 <= shard < count`. Any violation prints a usage diagnostic naming the problem (e.g. `test-shard-sandbox: shard must be in 0..count-1`) to stderr and exits non-zero **without invoking cargo at all**.
- An empty target selection for a valid-looking invocation (e.g. more shards than targets, so a shard legitimately owns nothing) is an explicit, reported outcome — it must never fall through to an unfiltered `cargo test`. (Refusing with a diagnostic is acceptable; so is a clearly-logged intentional no-op for the per-target run, as long as cargo is not invoked unfiltered. The shard-0 bins/doc behaviour on an otherwise valid empty shard should be decided and documented in the script header.)
- Existing valid behaviour is unchanged: `0 4`…`3 4` against the real `pkgs/id/tests/` select the same round-robin partition as today, shard 0 still additionally runs `--bins` and `--doc`, and the four shards' selections remain disjoint and jointly cover every target.
- Regression coverage follows the neighbouring pattern (`pkgs/id/scripts/just-recipes-check-test.sh`: stub binary on PATH, temp cwd): valid partitions cover/disjoint, and out-of-range / negative / non-numeric / zero-count / missing arguments all fail non-zero with cargo never invoked.

body:
## Problem

`scripts/program_tending.py`'s default fleet list names a repository that does not exist, so the daily program-tending run never tends the fourth fleet repo and reports a fetch error for a phantom repo every run.

`FLEET_REPOS` (scripts/program_tending.py:29-34) is:

```python
FLEET_REPOS = (
    "developing-today/code",
    "developing-today-forks/opencode",
    "developing-today-forks/openchamber",
    "developing-today/nix",          # line 33 — this repo does not exist
)
```

The fourth fleet repo is `dezren39/darwin-nix` (the four repos are developing-today/code, developing-today-forks/opencode, developing-today-forks/openchamber, and dezren39/darwin-nix). There is no `developing-today/nix` repository.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop, main @ 65beb42c1a70672bed159fe401c2cb1079aa516f)

- `gh repo view developing-today/nix` → `Could not resolve to a Repository with the name 'developing-today/nix'`; `gh repo view dezren39/darwin-nix` resolves.
- Probe (~/git/fleet/probe-program-tending on the laptop, real `program_tending.py` verbatim, live unauthenticated GitHub API): `GET /repos/developing-today/nix/pulls` → HTTP 404 Not Found; `GET /repos/dezren39/darwin-nix/pulls` → HTTP 200 with a list body.
- `main()` uses the default list whenever `--repo` is not passed (scripts/program_tending.py:173: `repos = args.repo or list(FLEET_REPOS)`), and the scheduled workflow (`.github/workflows/program-tending.yml`) runs `python3 -I scripts/program_tending.py --run` with no `--repo`, so every daily run takes this path.
- In `stub_stalled_prs` the 404 is caught and recorded as `{"repo": "developing-today/nix", "open_prs": "unverified", "error": "HTTP Error 404: Not Found"}` — a permanent, expected-looking error line that trains readers to ignore the section's errors, while dezren39/darwin-nix's open PRs are never counted. The other four sections echo the wrong name in their `checked` lists, so the run log claims a repo that does not exist was "checked".
- The existing tests never catch it: every test in `scripts/tests/test_program_tending.py` passes `--repo developing-today/code` explicitly or mocks `_gh_api`; the control run this run passes 8/8 on the laptop.

## Why it matters

Program-tending is the scheduled care layer for exactly these four repos (#1352). One quarter of its coverage has been silently absent since the scaffold landed, and the standing 404 in the daily log masks real fetch failures for the other repos (the section's contract is "reports, never fails" — an always-present error makes the error channel worthless).

## Acceptance criteria

- `FLEET_REPOS` names the canonical four fleet repos, with `dezren39/darwin-nix` as the fourth entry; `developing-today/nix` appears nowhere in the script or workflow.
- A new test in `scripts/tests/test_program_tending.py` asserts the default repo list equals the canonical four (so a future rename/typo fails the suite instead of the daily log), and a test drives `stub_stalled_prs` over the default list with a mocked `_gh_api` asserting every default repo is queried.
- A default `--run` (mocked API) produces a log whose sections list dezren39/darwin-nix and no nonexistent repo.
- Existing program-tending tests still pass.

title: cold-store(drill_compare): a definitive D1 failure silently downgrades the restore drill to the local manifest — d1()'s own success=false error is swallowed by fetch_source's bare except and mislabeled 'D1 unreachable'

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/cold-store-reaper
labels.description: Package/app: cold-store-reaper (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/cold-store-reaper/scripts/drill_compare.py` is the restore drill's backup-vs-live check: its verdict means "this backup is good". Its docstring promises the local manifest SQLite file is the fallback oracle only "if D1 is unreachable". But `fetch_source()` (drill_compare.py:67-79) wraps the whole D1 path in a bare `except Exception`, so **any** D1 failure — including a definitive, reachable answer — silently downgrades the drill to the local manifest and labels it `local manifest (D1 unreachable)`.

The sharpest case is built into the file itself: `d1()` (drill_compare.py:62-63) deliberately raises `RuntimeError("D1 query failed")` when the API returns a 200 payload with `success: false` (bad SQL, wrong database id, token lacking D1 permission, …). That deliberate error is then swallowed by `d1()`'s own caller, and the drill proceeds against the local file — a file that may be stale or be the very thing being verified — and can exit 0.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ 65beb42c1a, real file verbatim — sha256 matched origin/main — probe `~/git/fleet/probe-drill-fallback/`, stubbed `urllib.request.urlopen`, real local manifest)

- D1 returns `{"success": false, "errors": [{"code": 7404, "message": "…"}]}` → `fetch_source()` returns the local manifest rows with source label `"local manifest (D1 unreachable)"`. No error, no mention of the D1 error code/message anywhere in the output.
- D1 genuinely unreachable (`URLError: connection refused`) → identical result and identical label (the intended fallback).
- The two cases are indistinguishable in the drill's output, and the first is mislabeled: D1 was reachable and answered.

Wrong-shape D1 payloads take the same silent path (`payload["result"][0]["results"]` at :64 raises Key/Index/Type errors inside the same `try`), so a changed API shape also downgrades the oracle instead of failing the drill.

## Why it matters

A restore drill exists to catch the day the backup pipeline and D1 disagree. If D1 rejects the drill's queries — expired/rotated token scope, a renamed database, an API change — the current code reports a verdict computed against a local file and calls D1 "unreachable", so the drill passes (or fails) for reasons nobody can see and the real D1 problem stays invisible until an actual restore depends on it. The fallback should be for transport failure only; a definitive D1 error is drill-relevant information and must fail loudly, naming the API's error.

## Acceptance criteria

- A D1 response with `success: false` aborts the drill with a non-zero exit and a message carrying the API's error code/message — it never falls back to the local manifest.
- A wrong-shape D1 success payload (missing `result`/`results`, wrong types) likewise fails loudly instead of downgrading the oracle.
- Genuine transport failure (connection error / timeout reaching D1) keeps the documented local-manifest fallback, and the output label remains accurate for that case only.
- Regression tests stub the transport for all three cases (definitive error, wrong shape, unreachable) and assert the behavior above; the healthy live-D1 and fallback comparison paths are unchanged.

body:
## Problem

The research-workflow note/resolution JSON blocks — the markers that record how one concept answered another — are shape-trusted at every parse site, while the receipt JSON in the same extension is guarded. A note marker or resolution block whose JSON is valid but not an object (`[]`, `"x"`, `42`, `null`) surfaces as a bare `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'` naming no file or field, instead of the tool's own `fail()` diagnostic. The CLI catches these types (`research_workflow.py` `main()`), so the operator sees only `error: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'` and cannot tell which note or concept file is malformed.

Sibling filings did not cover this surface: #6854 covered `research_workflow.py`'s profile/state/transcript/concepts/dependencies/triggers; #6856 covered `research_workflow_items.py`'s package manifest. The note/resolution blocks in `check_package()` and the whole of `research_workflow_live.py`'s note path were not in either.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ 65beb42c1a, real files verbatim — sha256 matched origin/main — probe `~/git/fleet/probe-rw-note-shape/`)

Controls all behave as designed:

- `research_workflow_live.read_note()` on a valid note returns the note; a dict note with missing fields fails cleanly via `fail()` ("note body hash mismatch", naming the path).
- `research_workflow_live.receipts()` on a receipt whose JSON is `[]` fails cleanly via `fail()` — because `check_receipt()` (research_workflow_live.py:384) checks `isinstance(entry, dict)` first. That is the guarded sibling in the same file.
- `resolve_command()` with a well-formed object resolution block succeeds and writes the receipt.

Wrong shapes (all raw `AttributeError`, none via `fail()`):

- `read_note()` (research_workflow_live.py:348-356): note marker JSON `[]`, `"x"`, `42`, `null`, `[1,2]` → `AttributeError: '<type>' object has no attribute 'get'` at the first `note.get(...)`.
- `resolve_command()`'s already-resolved scan (research_workflow_live.py:469): a concept file containing a resolution block whose JSON is `[]`, `"x"` or `42` → same raw `AttributeError` at `json.loads(block).get("note")`. `resolve-note` therefore dies mid-command on a malformed block in any concept file, before it can write or refuse cleanly.
- Same unguarded pattern by code read in `research_workflow.py` `check_package()`: the resolution scan (:813-816, `entry = json.loads(block)` then `entry.get("note")`) and the notes loop (:838-846, `note = json.loads(found[1])` then `note.get(...)`) — a non-object block there fails `check` the same bare way.

## Why it matters

Notes and resolutions are the audit trail of a research package: who told whom what, and how it was dispositioned. They are hand- and agent-edited Markdown embeds — exactly the content most likely to be pasted wrong — and this tool is the checker whose contract everywhere else is a named `fail()` diagnostic. The one JSON family in the live extension that lacks the guard is the one `resolve-note` parses before doing anything else, so a single malformed block wedges the disposition workflow with a message that points at nothing. One more instance of the #3068 parsed-is-not-validated pattern, in a file that already contains the correct guard (`check_receipt`) applied to only one of its three JSON inputs.

## Acceptance criteria

- `read_note()` rejects a non-object note marker with `fail()` naming the note path and the expected object shape, before any `.get`.
- `resolve_command()`'s resolution scan and `check_package()`'s resolution scan reject a non-object resolution block with `fail()` naming the concept file, instead of raw `.get` on the unchecked value.
- `check_package()`'s notes loop rejects a non-object note marker the same way, naming the note path.
- Regression tests (scripts/tests/test_research_workflow_live.py and/or test_research_workflow.py) cover each wrong shape above and assert the clean `fail()` diagnostic; the guarded receipt path is unchanged.
- Valid notes, resolutions and receipts behave byte-identically; the existing research-workflow suites stay green.
