body:
# cold-store-reaper: Drive API response bodies are parsed unguarded — a wrong-shape 200 from files.list / files.create / files.get raises raw Attribute/Key/Type/Value/JSONDecode errors, not ColdStoreError

## Summary

`pkgs/cold-store-reaper/cold_store.py` treats every Google Drive API response body as if it were the exact JSON object the happy path returns. Only HTTP status is checked; the parsed body's shape never is. A 200 response whose body is valid JSON of the wrong shape (or not JSON at all) crashes the caller with a raw builtin exception instead of the module's own `ColdStoreError`, so the CLI surfaces a traceback and — worse — `upload()` dies *after* the bundle has been uploaded and marked `uploading`, with no verification verdict recorded.

The module already knows the right pattern: `put_backup`'s identical files.get verification readback wraps its parse in `try/except (KeyError, TypeError, ValueError)` and re-raises its `verification_failed` `ColdStoreError` (cold_store.py:1196-1204). The Drive call sites below never got the same guard. This is the Drive-API sibling of #6846 (token endpoints, cold_store.py:667/708) and #6845 (local state/credentials files); the D1 surface was guarded earlier (#2618). Umbrella: #3068.

## Unguarded sites (all at main 65beb42c1a)

- `_find_folder` (cold_store.py:735): `files = json.loads(resp).get("files", [])`, then `files[0]["id"]`.
- `_create_folder` (cold_store.py:750): `return json.loads(resp)["id"]`.
- `_resumable_upload` (cold_store.py:988): `file_id = json.loads(resp)["id"]` on the 200/201 chunk-completion response.
- `upload` verification readback (cold_store.py:1066-1068): `info = json.loads(resp)`; `drive_size = int(info.get("size", -1))` — compare the guarded twin in `put_backup` at :1196-1204.
- `list_backups` (cold_store.py:1257-1267): `page = json.loads(resp)`; `page.get("files", [])`; per entry `f["id"]`, `f["name"]`, `int(f.get("size") or 0)`.
- `get_backup` (cold_store.py:1431-1435): same `.get("files", [])` + `files[0]["id"]` pattern as `_find_folder`.

## Verified this run (laptop probe, real cold_store.py verbatim, stubbed transport, @65beb42c1a)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-cold-store-drive` (`cold_store.py` + `schema.sql` copied verbatim, `http_request` stubbed, controls pass). Results:

| Call | Wrong-shape 200 body | Observed |
|---|---|---|
| `_find_folder` control `{"files":[{"id":"abc"}]}` / `{}` | — | returns `"abc"` / `None` |
| `_find_folder` | `["x"]` or `"hello"` | raw `AttributeError: 'list'/'str' object has no attribute 'get'` |
| `_find_folder` | `{"files":"abc"}` | raw `TypeError: string indices must be integers` |
| `_find_folder` | `{"files":[123]}` | raw `TypeError: 'int' object is not subscriptable` |
| `_find_folder` | `{"files":[{"name":"n"}]}` | raw `KeyError: 'id'` |
| `_find_folder` | `not json` | raw `JSONDecodeError` |
| `_create_folder` control `{"id":"new1"}` | — | returns `"new1"` |
| `_create_folder` | `{}` | raw `KeyError: 'id'` |
| `_create_folder` | `["x"]` | raw `TypeError: list indices must be integers` |
| `list_backups` control (one well-formed file entry) | — | returns the entry |
| `list_backups` | `["x"]` (page) | raw `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'` |
| `list_backups` | `{"files":["abc"]}` | raw `TypeError: string indices must be integers` |
| `list_backups` | `{"files":[{"name":"n","size":"1"}]}` | raw `KeyError: 'id'` |
| `list_backups` | `{"files":[{"id":"f1","name":"n","size":"abc"}]}` | raw `ValueError: invalid literal for int()` |
| `get_backup` | `{"files":"abc"}` | raw `TypeError: string indices must be integers` |
| `upload` readback (real `pack()`-seeded bundle, `_resumable_upload` stubbed) | `["x"]` | raw `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'get'` |
| `upload` readback | `{"size":"abc","md5Checksum":"x"}` | raw `ValueError: invalid literal for int()` |
| `upload` readback | `not json` | raw `JSONDecodeError` |
| `upload` readback control (correct size + md5) | — | returns `verified: True` |

## Why it matters

- Every one of these paths is on the nightly backup/restore route: `ensure_folders` (via `_find_folder`/`_create_folder`) runs before uploads, `list_backups` feeds retention planning in `prune_backups`, and `get_backup` is the restore path. A proxy error page, a partial/truncated body, or an API change returning an error object with a 200 turns a diagnosable `ColdStoreError` into an unhandled traceback that names no endpoint and no expectation.
- `upload()` is the worst case: the bundle row is already `uploading` and the bytes are already in Drive when the readback parse crashes, so the run dies mid-verification — neither verified nor failed — exactly the state ambiguity `put_backup`'s guarded readback (and its trash-on-failure cleanup) was built to avoid.
- The inconsistency itself is the trap: a reader who checks `put_backup` reasonably concludes Drive readbacks are guarded everywhere.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every Drive response parse listed above validates the parsed shape (object at top level; `files` a list of objects; `id`/`name` present strings; `size` numeric) and raises `ColdStoreError` naming the operation and what was wrong — no raw `AttributeError`/`KeyError`/`TypeError`/`ValueError`/`JSONDecodeError` escapes a Drive call site.
- [ ] `upload()`'s verification readback gets the same treatment as `put_backup`'s: an unparseable/wrong-shape readback is a verification failure (`ColdStoreError`), not a crash after upload.
- [ ] Well-formed responses behave exactly as today (existing FakeDrive test suite passes unchanged in behavior).
- [ ] New tests in `pkgs/cold-store-reaper/tests/test_cold_store.py` cover the wrong-shape bodies above for folder find/create, list_backups, get_backup, and the upload readback, asserting `ColdStoreError` (oracle: the guarded `put_backup` readback at cold_store.py:1196-1204).

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/mcpx/scripts/spec-parity.py` — the script behind the `spec-parity` job in `.github/workflows/mcpx-conformance.yml` — `json.loads` every one of its inputs in `main()` (lines 189–202) and never validates a shape before use:

- the two revision lists (`mcpx` from `mcpx protocol --json | jq -c '.asServer.supported | sort'`, suite from the conformance tool's error text via `jq -sc`),
- the two allow lists (workflow env `SPEC_PARITY_ALLOW_ONLY_MCPX` / `SPEC_PARITY_ALLOW_ONLY_SUITE`, workflow lines 40–41),
- the persisted success/failure records (repo variables `MCPX_SPEC_PARITY_SUCCESS` / `MCPX_SPEC_PARITY_FAILURE`, written back by this same job on main).

`decide()` then assumes its inputs: `sorted(set(mcpx))` (line 79), `success or {}` / `failure or {}` followed by `.get(...)` (lines 98–99), `failure["count"] + 1` (line 123), `parse(success timestamp)` and `", ".join(... for v in success["specs"])` (line 183). The only guarded case is an empty/falsy list, which takes the graceful "could not read the lists" path (lines 192–200) that writes `status=error` / `sleep=0` and a summary section. Every other wrong shape either crashes raw or — worse — is silently interpreted.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Probe on the laptop @ `65beb42c1a` (`~/git/fleet/probe-spec-parity-shape/`, real `spec-parity.py` copied verbatim, md5-matched; `decide()` and `main()` driven directly). Controls pass: matching lists → `ok` + a well-formed success record; a one-sided mismatch → `warn`.

Silent misinterpretation (no crash, wrong gate state is persisted on main):

- **Revision list as a bare string** (`"2025-03-26"`, e.g. an extraction change from array to scalar): `set()` iterates the string, so the report claims `Only in mcpx: `-`, `0`, `2`, `3`, `5`, `6`` — single characters as revisions — returns `warn`, and creates a failure record `{count: 1, first_timestamp: now, ...}`. On main that record is saved as the repo variable, starting a false 840-hour deadline clock that will eventually fail the job for a mismatch that does not exist.
- **Revision list as an object** (`{"2024-11-05": true, "2025-03-26": true}`, e.g. `supported` becoming a map): `set()` takes the keys, the comparison passes as `ok`, and a success record is written — a real format change on the tool side is invisible.
- **Allow list as a bare string** (`"2024-11-05"` instead of `["2024-11-05"]`): `stale_allowances` iterates its characters and reports each as a dead entry (`| `2` | `only-mcpx` | mcpx does not have it |`, …), returning an immediate `error` that orders the correct workflow entry removed.
- **Stored success record with `specs` as a string**: the mismatch report renders `At the last success both sides were: `2`, `0`, `2`, `5`, `-`, `0`, `3`, `-`, `2`, `6`.` — characters, again.

Raw crashes (traceback, and via `main()` no `status`/`sleep` files and no summary section at all — the workflow then fails on `cat "$out/status"` with no parity report):

- revision list as a number (`123`): `TypeError: 'int' object is not iterable` (verified end-to-end through `main()`: exception raised, output dir never created)
- list with a nested-list element: `TypeError: cannot use 'list' as a set element`; list with mixed int/str elements: `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'`
- stored success record as a non-empty list or a string: `AttributeError: ... has no attribute 'get'`
- stored failure record as a non-empty list: same `AttributeError`; failure `count` as a string (`"3"`): `TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str` at line 123
- stored success `timestamp` as a number: `TypeError: strptime() argument 1 must be str, not int`

## Why it matters

This gate is the early-warning system for mcpx drifting from the official MCP conformance suite, and its success/failure records are self-persisted state: a corrupted or shape-changed input does not just fail one run, it is written back as the baseline the next runs reason from (deadline clock, failure count, last-success specs). The silent cases are the dangerous ones — a format change in `mcpx protocol --json` output or in either repo variable can manufacture a fake mismatch deadline, or mask a real one behind an `ok`, with a report written in characters that no reader will connect back to the cause. The crash cases lose the one thing the graceful path exists to provide: a readable "could not read the lists" summary naming the bad input.

## Acceptance criteria

- `main()` (or a validator it calls) checks every parsed input before `decide()` runs: revision lists and allow lists are JSON arrays of strings; success/failure are `null` or JSON objects whose used fields are correctly typed (`count` an int, `timestamp`/`first_timestamp`/`latest_timestamp` parseable timestamp strings, `specs` an array of strings, `run` fields strings).
- Any violation takes the existing graceful path — summary section naming which input was wrong-shaped and what it contained, `status=error`, `sleep=0`, no success/failure files written — never a traceback and never a comparison over characters/keys.
- `decide()`'s contract is unchanged for well-shaped inputs: the existing match/mismatch/dead-allowance behavior, deadlines (840 h one-sided, 360 h two-sided) and sleep calculation are byte-identical on the control cases.
- New tests cover at least: string/object/number revision lists, a nested or mixed-type list element, string allow list, list/string success and failure records, string failure `count`, numeric success `timestamp`, and string success `specs` — each asserting the graceful error outcome, plus the well-shaped controls.

body:
# github-backup(app_setup): the App lifecycle helper parses config, bws output and the conversion response unguarded — a wrong-shape config crashes every subcommand at import, wrong-shape bws output raises raw Attribute/Key/JSONDecode errors, and `convert` stores a partial credential set before crashing on a missing field

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ 65beb42c1a)

`infra/github-backup/bin/app_setup.py` is the lifecycle helper for the
developing-today-backup GitHub App (manifest / convert / install-report /
webhook-secret). Every value it reads crosses a trust boundary with no
shape check:

1. **Config is indexed at import time.** `ghb_common.load_config()`
   (`infra/github-backup/bin/ghb_common.py:17-19`) is a bare `json.load`
   with no validation — plan/state got `validate_plan`/`validate_state`
   (#6637), config never got an equivalent. `app_setup.py:34-35` then runs
   `CFG = load_config()` and `NAMES = CFG["app"]["bitwarden_secret_names"]`
   at module top level, so a wrong-shape `config.json` kills **every**
   subcommand — including `manifest`, which needs only two fields — before
   `main` runs. `app_manifest` direct-indexes further fields at :40, :43,
   :48 (`app.name`, `worker.webhook_path`, `app.events`).
2. **bws output is parsed unguarded, and two of the three readers never
   check the return code.** `_bws_list` (:52-58) checks `returncode` but
   returns `json.loads(...)` unchecked; its callers scan it with
   `s.get("key")` (:75, :95). `_project_id` (:61-70) never checks the
   return code and ends at `projects[0]["id"]`. `bws_get` (:94-104) never
   checks the return code and ends at `json.loads(r.stdout)["value"]`.
3. **`convert` stores credentials one at a time from an unvalidated
   response.** `cmd_convert` (:127-144) direct-indexes the
   `/app-manifests/<code>/conversions` response and calls `bws_set` four
   times in sequence (:138-141). A response missing a late field crashes
   **after** the earlier secrets are already stored, leaving a partial,
   inconsistent credential set in Bitwarden (new app id / client id /
   client secret, stale or absent private key).
4. Same pattern in `install-report`: the installations response is
   iterated with `i["account"]["login"]` / `i["id"]` unguarded (:180+).

### Probe (laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-app-setup-shape/`, real files verbatim, stubbed transport/bws)

Control (real `config.json`): import OK, `NAMES` populated.

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| config missing `app` | `KeyError: 'app'` at import |
| config `app` is a list / top level is a list | `TypeError: list indices must be integers...` at import |
| `bitwarden_secret_names` is a string | import passes with `NAMES: str`; first `NAMES["app_id"]` raises `TypeError: string indices...` |
| `bws secret list` returns an error-object dict | `AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get'` |
| `bws secret list` returns `[1, 2]` | `AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'get'` |
| `bws project list` returns a dict | `KeyError: 0` |
| `bws project list` exits 1, empty stdout | misleading `RuntimeError: no Bitwarden projects visible to this token` — the actual bws failure is invisible (no return-code check) |
| `bws secret get` exits 1, empty stdout | raw `JSONDecodeError` (no return-code check) |
| conversion response missing `pem` | `KeyError: 'pem'` **after 3 of 4 secrets already stored** (`app_id`, `client_id`, `client_secret`) |

## Why it matters

This helper runs at the most sensitive moment of the backup system: App
creation and credential rotation for the App the whole mirror estate
depends on. A malformed local config edit (the config file's own header
says adding an owner is "an edit to this file") currently produces a raw
traceback with no field named; a bws hiccup is misreported as "no
projects visible"; and a short conversion response silently leaves
Bitwarden holding half of a new credential set, so the next run mixes
credentials from two different Apps.

## Acceptance criteria

- `load_config` (or an app_setup-local equivalent) validates the config
  shape the github-backup tools actually use — at minimum the `app`
  section (`name`, `events`, `bitwarden_secret_names` as a string->string
  object) and `worker.webhook_path` — and a violation is a clean,
  field-naming diagnostic, never a raw `KeyError`/`TypeError` traceback,
  for every subcommand.
- `_bws_list`, `_project_id`, and `bws_get` check the subprocess return
  code and the parsed shape (list of objects with the fields they read);
  a bws failure reports the bws failure (stderr excerpt), not a shape
  accident or a false "no projects" claim.
- `cmd_convert` validates the full conversion response (all of `id`,
  `client_id`, `client_secret`, `pem`, `slug` present and correctly
  typed) **before** the first `bws_set`, so a bad response stores
  nothing.
- `install-report` validates the installations payload shape before
  indexing `account.login`/`id`.
- Tests in `infra/github-backup/tests/` cover the probe cases above
  (wrong-shape config, wrong-shape bws output, failed bws calls,
  partial conversion response storing nothing); the real-config control
  still passes.

body:
## Finding

The Fly.io service detail page's Sources block names its quota-view section with a literal backslash — `### Fly\.io` — instead of the actual section heading `### Fly.io`. Every other service renders its section name cleanly.

## Evidence

- Source PR: #3677 (merged, merge `0bb007945d`, head `d4107deb86`) — it added `SaasService.sources` and derives the displayed section name from the spec's heading regex.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/saas-extract.ts` on current main (`65beb42c1a70672bed159fe401c2cb1079aa516f`, verified twice via the contents API): line 705 derives `quotaViewSection: spec.heading.source.replace(/^\^/, "").replace(/\$$/, "")` — it strips the regex anchors but not regex escapes.
- Line 664: the Fly.io spec is the only one whose heading contains an escape: `heading: /^### Fly\.io$/`. All other specs (lines 563–676: Cloudflare, Turso, Supabase, GitHub, Vercel, Modal, OCI, Bitwarden, Backblaze B2, Baseten) are escape-free, which is why only Fly.io is affected.
- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/render.ts:2414` (main) renders `svc.sources.quotaViewSection` verbatim inside `<code>` in the detail page's Sources block.
- Laptop probe (Node v24, verbatim derivation over the spec headings): cloudflare → `### Cloudflare — Workers platform`, turso → `### Turso`, baseten → `### Baseten`, fly-io → `### Fly\.io`.
- #3677's own tests (`pm-stack/aggregator/test/usage.test.ts`) assert the section string only for Turso (`### Turso`, escape-free), so the escaped case is unpinned.

## Why it matters

The Sources block is the provenance contract added for #1058: it tells a reader exactly which quota-view.md section a card was built from. For Fly.io the named section does not exist under that spelling — a reader (or a text search) looking for `### Fly\.io` in quota-view.md finds nothing, so the one candidate card whose provenance most needs to be checkable is the one whose citation is wrong.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Fly.io's detail-page Sources block names the section `### Fly.io` (no backslash).
- [ ] The derivation handles regex escapes generally (any future spec heading with an escaped character renders its literal heading text), or the spec carries an explicit display string — either way the rendered text is the literal heading.
- [ ] A regression test pins `sources.quotaViewSection` for the Fly.io service (and ideally asserts no service's section string contains a backslash).

labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Summary

`update-nixpkgs-inputs.py` (two byte-identical copies: `scripts/update-nixpkgs-inputs.py` and `pkgs/id/scripts/update-nixpkgs-inputs.py`; the test suite enforces byte-identity) reads `flake.lock` through five helpers that disagree about shape safety. The Hydra gate added in #4553 validates its remote payloads strictly and fails closed with `HydraGateError`, and some lock readers use `.get` chains — but the local lock readers were never given the same treatment:

- `get_input_info` (line 180) direct-indexes `lock_data["nodes"]["root"]["inputs"]` (:185) and `lock_data["nodes"][node_name]` (:191) — `KeyError` where `get_input_node`/`discover_inputs` guard the same lookups.
- `get_input_info` (:192-193), `get_input_ref` (:228), `get_locked_rev` (:236) and `discover_inputs` (:263) all use `.get("original", {})` / `.get("locked", {})` — the `{}` default does not help when the key is present with an explicit JSON `null`, so a null `original`/`locked` raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'get'`.
- `discover_inputs` (:266) and `get_input_info` (:195) call `.lower()` on `original.type` without a string check — a non-string `type` raises `AttributeError`.
- `get_input_info` (:196-197) does `len(full_rev)` / slicing on `locked.rev` unchecked — and this is the dangerous one: `discover_inputs` never reads `locked.rev`, so a non-string rev **passes the planning pass** and only crashes inside the per-input execution loop (`main`, :487), i.e. potentially *after earlier inputs in the same run have already been updated or pinned and flake.lock rewritten for them*. The run dies with a raw traceback, no summary, and no per-input failure record.
- A node that is a string instead of an object crashes `discover_inputs` and `get_input_ref` with `AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get'`; a root-named node missing from `nodes` is skipped by `discover_inputs` but raises `KeyError` in `get_input_info`.

`flake.lock` is normally nix-generated, but it is also hand-edited (this repo's history includes hand-pinned locks and gated pins written by this very script, `pin_input`), merged, and occasionally truncated/conflicted — exactly the states where the updater is re-run to repair things. A repair tool that tracebacks on the malformed states it may be asked to fix, and that can die mid-run after partially rewriting the lock, is worse than one that refuses cleanly up front.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ 65beb42c1a)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-nixpkgs-inputs-shape/probe.py` imports the real `scripts/update-nixpkgs-inputs.py` and feeds it a well-formed lock plus one mutation at a time. Controls all pass: discover → `['nixpkgs']`, info → `('aaaaaaaaaaaa', 'github:NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-unstable', 'nixos-unstable')`, ref and locked_rev correct.

Malformed shapes (11 cases):

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| node is a string | discover + get_input_ref: `AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get'` |
| `original: null` | discover + get_input_ref + get_input_info: `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'get'` |
| `original.type: 7` | discover + get_input_info: `AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'lower'` |
| `locked.rev: 123` | discover: OK (planning passes); get_input_info: `TypeError: object of type 'int' has no len()`; get_locked_rev returns `123` unchecked |
| `locked: null` | get_input_info + get_locked_rev: `AttributeError` |
| node missing from `nodes` | discover: `[]` (guarded); get_input_info: `KeyError: 'nixpkgs-node'` |
| no `root` node | discover: `[]` (guarded); get_input_info: `KeyError: 'root'` |

## Why it matters

- Mid-run death after partial updates leaves flake.lock half-updated with no summary of what changed — the operator cannot tell which inputs moved.
- The script's own contracts are inconsistent: remote Hydra payloads get strict shape validation and a clean fail-closed error (#4553), while the local file it exists to rewrite gets raw tracebacks.
- Both copies carry the defect; the pkgs/id copy is what the pkgs/id just recipes run (#2783).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All flake.lock readers (`get_input_info`, `get_input_node`, `get_input_ref`, `get_locked_rev`, `discover_inputs`) treat a non-object node, a null/non-object `original` or `locked`, a non-string `type`/`ref`/`rev`, and a missing node/root consistently: either the input is skipped (mirroring the existing missing-node handling in `discover_inputs`) or the run aborts with a clear, named error *before any input is updated* — never a raw `AttributeError`/`TypeError`/`KeyError` traceback.
- [ ] Validation happens in the planning pass (against the pristine lock), so a malformed lock can never crash the execution loop after earlier inputs have been written.
- [ ] Regression tests in `scripts/tests/test_update_nixpkgs_inputs.py` cover the shapes above against both byte-identical copies (root + pkgs/id), following the suite's existing both-copies pattern.
- [ ] Well-formed locks behave exactly as today (existing tests green, including the Hydra gate and byte-identity tests).

🤖 Filed by new-issue-creator-code-b (Lane B), run 2026-11-07 01:20 CST. Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-nixpkgs-inputs-shape/` on the laptop.

title: cold-store-reaper: load_state/load_credentials accept valid-but-wrong-shape JSON — non-object files raise raw AttributeError, non-string folder id is silently used as a Drive id

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: work/assigned
labels.description: Queue worker lifecycle state

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: app/cold-store-reaper
labels.description: Package/app: cold-store-reaper (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/cold-store-reaper/cold_store.py` carefully converts *invalid* JSON in
`credentials.json` / `state.json` into a `ColdStoreError` with repair guidance
(`load_credentials` at :440-446, `load_state` at :455-462; tests exist for the
corrupt-syntax case), but *valid JSON of the wrong shape* slips straight past
both loaders:

- `load_credentials` (:433, :447) calls `creds.get(key)` on whatever
  `json.loads` returned. A top-level list, string, number, bool or `null`
  raises a raw `AttributeError`, with none of the file-naming repair guidance
  the corrupt-syntax path gives.
- The same loader's missing-field check is truthiness-only, so a non-string
  value passes it: `{"client_id": 123, ...}` and `{"client_id": ["x"], ...}`
  are both returned as if they were usable credentials and flow on into the
  token-request encoding downstream.
- `load_state` (:452-455) returns whatever `json.loads` returned unchecked.
  Every caller assumes a dict (`ensure_folders` :754, `_folder_id` :775,
  `_d1_endpoint` :1466-1475 all call `state.get(...)`), so a non-object
  `state.json` crashes the next operation with a raw `AttributeError` far
  from the cause.
- Even a top-level object is not enough: a non-object `folders` field crashes
  downstream (`folders = "abc"` → raw `ValueError` from `dict(...)` in
  `ensure_folders`; `folders = 123` → raw `TypeError` in `_folder_id`;
  `folders = ["root"]` → raw `TypeError: list indices must be integers`),
  and a non-string folder id is silently accepted — `{"folders":
  {"bundles": 123}}` makes `_folder_id("bundles")` return the integer `123`,
  which is then used as a Drive folder id.

These files are operator-managed local state under the cold-store home:
edited by hand when filling credentials from Bitwarden, and rebuilt by the
tool itself. A wrong-shape write (an editor slip, a different tool writing
`[]`/`null`, a partial restore) should produce the same diagnosed refusal
the corrupt-syntax case already produces — not a traceback, and never a
silently mistyped folder id used against Drive (this tool deletes/evicts;
acting on a wrong identifier is the dangerous direction).

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop primary `~/git/code` at origin/main `65beb42c1a70672bed159fe401c2cb1079aa516f`.
Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-cold-store-state/` (`probe.py`, `probe2.py`,
`probe3.py`) against the real `cold_store.py` copied verbatim from
origin/main (sha256 `39a1ecb1a8ff10dedcb59538cc6d2691d7a264e3def2afcb41963240dea27f2d`),
using a temporary home — no network, no real credentials.

Controls (all as expected):
- missing `state.json` → `{}`; dict state → returned unchanged
- dict credentials with string fields → returned unchanged
- syntactically corrupt credentials (`{"client_id": `) → `ColdStoreError`
  naming the file and the repair path

Failing shapes (every one):
- `load_credentials` with top-level `[]`, `[{"client_id":"x"}]`, `"hello"`,
  `123`, `null`, `true` → raw `AttributeError: '<type>' object has no
  attribute 'get'` (never `ColdStoreError`)
- `load_credentials` with `client_id` = `123` or `["x"]` → returned
  unchecked (truthiness check at :447 passes)
- `load_state` with top-level `[]`, `"hello"`, `123`, `null` → returned
  unchecked; `_folder_id` / `state.get(...)` then raise raw `AttributeError`
- `state.json` = `{"folders": "abc"}` → raw `ValueError: dictionary update
  sequence element #0 has length 1`; `{"folders": 123}` → raw `TypeError`;
  `{"folders": ["root"]}` → raw `TypeError: list indices must be integers`
- `state.json` = `{"folders": {"bundles": 123}}` → `_folder_id("bundles")`
  silently returns `123` (int, not a Drive id string)

Dedup: searched open + closed issues for `cold-store`, `load_state`,
`credentials.json corrupt shape`. Related but distinct: issue #3279
(torn-write *invalid* JSON — the fix for that is the corrupt-syntax handling
above), issue #2618 (D1 *response* shapes, closed), issue #6525/#6531
(repair_dump, open). No issue covers the `load_state`/`load_credentials`
shape contract or the `folders` field shape.

## Why it matters

Every cold-store command starts by loading one or both of these files.
A wrong-shape file currently either kills the run with an undiagnosed
traceback (operator cannot tell which file or what shape is wrong) or —
worse for `folders` — silently substitutes a wrong-typed identifier into
Drive operations in a tool whose job includes pruning and eviction.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `load_credentials` raises `ColdStoreError` naming `credentials.json`
      and the unexpected shape (with the existing repair guidance) when the
      top level is not a JSON object; no raw `AttributeError`/`TypeError`
      escapes for any valid-JSON input.
- [ ] Credential values that are present for the known keys
      (`client_id`, `client_secret`, `refresh_token`) must be strings;
      a non-string value raises the same named `ColdStoreError` instead of
      passing the truthiness check.
- [ ] `load_state` raises `ColdStoreError` naming `state.json` and the
      unexpected shape when the top level is not a JSON object.
- [ ] A present `folders` field must be an object mapping string keys to
      string folder ids; any other shape (string/number/list value, or a
      non-string id) raises a named `ColdStoreError` instead of a raw
      downstream `ValueError`/`TypeError` or a silently mistyped id.
- [ ] New tests in `pkgs/cold-store-reaper/tests/test_cold_store.py` cover:
      non-object top level for both files, non-string credential value,
      non-object `folders`, non-string folder id — plus the existing
      corrupt-syntax and happy-path controls still passing.
- [ ] The full cold-store test suite passes (laptop or CI).

title: id(match_audit): sign_footer still signs unsupported-version and duplicate-roster headers — the #6434 refusal left the header checks only in sign_header

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Summary

`pkgs/id/src/match_audit.rs`: `sign_footer` (line 481) is the residual half of the #6434 sign-time refusal fix. PR #6497 gave `sign_header` (line 431) the full header-local checks — version equals `FORMAT_VERSION_V0`, `validate_roster`, signer-in-roster — and gave `sign_footer` signer-in-roster and the seed-commitment check. But `sign_footer` also receives the same `header`, and it still signs two header shapes that `MatchLogV0::verify_integrity` (line 511) rejects before the footer signature is ever considered:

- an unsupported `header.version` — `verify_integrity` returns `UnsupportedVersion` as its first check;
- a duplicate-key roster — `verify_integrity` calls `validate_roster` (line 933) and returns `Roster`.

#6434's acceptance bullet for `sign_footer` named only the signer and seed checks, so this is not a regression of that fix — it is the part of the same dead-on-arrival surface its scoping left behind. Both rules are decidable from `sign_footer`'s own inputs, exactly like the checks `sign_header` now performs. (An empty roster is already refused indirectly: `validate_signer` fails with `SignerNotInRoster` because no signer is in an empty roster.)

Relation to #6487/#6488: this is a concrete gap the Phase 4 closing inventory (#6488) should disposition as "gap — filed as this issue", not a new contract.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ origin/main 07ecb675ef)

Probe: laptop worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-sign-footer` (branch `probe/sign-footer-residual`), three tests added to the module's own test fixture in `pkgs/id/src/match_audit.rs`, run on the laptop with `cargo test -p id --lib match_audit::tests::probe_sign_footer`:

- control (valid header/footer, roster signer): `sign_footer` returns Ok — test passed;
- `header.version = FORMAT_VERSION_V0 + 1` (99-style unsupported version, all else valid): `sign_footer` returned `Ok(PlayerSignatureV0 { ... })` — probe refusal test FAILED as expected, i.e. the bad shape signs;
- duplicate roster (player 1's `PlayerV0` pushed a second time, signer is that player): `sign_footer` returned `Ok(PlayerSignatureV0 { ... })` — probe refusal test FAILED as expected.

Result: 1 passed / 2 failed, where the 2 failures are the defect (a signature produced for a log `verify_integrity` always rejects).

Code reading, same head: `sign_footer` at match_audit.rs:481-497 calls only `validate_signer` and the seed-digest check before `sign_message`; `sign_header` at :431-445 checks version, then `validate_roster`, then `validate_signer`.

## Why it matters

The match-audit log is the evidence format for contested match outcomes. A footer signature over an unsupported-version or duplicate-roster header is dead on arrival: every verifier discards the log, and the failure surfaces later at verification time instead of at the moment the bad header was signed. Mirroring the two remaining header-local checks in `sign_footer` makes the error local and actionable with the existing `AuditErrorV0::UnsupportedVersion` / `AuditErrorV0::Roster` reasons — the same reasons `sign_header` already returns.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `sign_footer` refuses a header whose version is not `FORMAT_VERSION_V0` with `AuditErrorV0::UnsupportedVersion`, before producing a signature.
- [ ] `sign_footer` refuses a header whose roster fails `validate_roster` (duplicate player keys; empty roster may keep surfacing as `SignerNotInRoster` or be reported as `Roster` — either named refusal is acceptable, signing is not) with a named `AuditErrorV0`, before producing a signature.
- [ ] Well-formed headers/footers sign exactly as before (existing `sign_header_and_footer_accept_roster_signers`, exporter, and module tests stay green).
- [ ] New tests pin both refusals with the valid control still signing Ok, in the style of the existing `sign_header_refuses_*` / `sign_footer_refuses_*` tests.
- [ ] No change to `verify_integrity`, the wire format, or any verifier verdict.

🤖 Filed by the fleet new-issue-creator (lane B) — verified with a probe against the real crate this run; see the probe path in the evidence section.

body:
Found during the 2026-11-07 DB rename program (#6619), while repointing runtime-db-export and quota-recorder across machines.

1. The LIVE copies are the sandbox ones. The paused runtime-db-export cron is a sandbox agent job whose body drives ~/tools/runtime-db-export (sandbox). The quota recorder's working home is also the sandbox (its FLEET path ~/tools/bin/fleet resolves there via symlink). Both were repointed to fleet-mirror / fleet-platform on 2026-11-07 and the sandbox hatch commits pushed; the laptop ~/hatch clone fast-forwarded cleanly to the same code.

2. Latent break: laptop ~/hatch/tools/quota-recorder.py resolves its secrets via FLEET = ~/tools/bin/fleet, which does NOT exist on the laptop (the laptop binary is ~/.local/bin/fleet). A manual laptop run on 2026-11-07 failed with turso-error FileNotFoundError: '/home/user/tools/bin/fleet' and left its record pending. Harmless today (the laptop copy is not the live home; the JSONL is backup-of-record and the record stays pending), but anything that ever runs the recorder on the laptop silently stops landing quota records. Its shipped systemd unit is also stale (HOME=/home/hatch, 'Supabase landing' description, timer not installed).

3. ~/git/hatch-dispatch-clone/tools/runtime-db-export on the laptop is a stale PARTIAL copy: no turso_client.py at all (pre-Turso layout), docstrings still naming muse-mirror. It cannot run standalone, but its presence invites exactly the 'which copy is live?' confusion the rename program had to burn time settling.

Fix direction: decide per tool which clone is canonical, delete or clearly mark the stale copies (dispatch-clone is a test fixture — if it must stay, pin it and label it), and make quota-recorder resolve the fleet binary by PATH lookup with a ~/tools/bin/fleet fallback instead of one hardcoded absolute path.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each named tool (quota-recorder, runtime-db-export) has one explicitly named canonical clone, recorded in the issue resolution, and stale copies are deleted or clearly marked as non-live fixtures.
- [ ] quota-recorder resolves the fleet binary by PATH lookup with a ~/tools/bin/fleet fallback (no single hardcoded absolute path), and a manual laptop run lands a quota record without FileNotFoundError.
- [ ] The stale partial copy in ~/git/hatch-dispatch-clone is removed, or pinned and labelled as a test fixture that cannot be mistaken for the live copy.
- [ ] The shipped quota-recorder systemd unit is corrected (HOME, description) or removed if the timer is not installed.

title: github-backup(reconcile): a wrong-shape entry in the previous plan.json crashes the weekly sweep — reconcile is the last plan reader bypassing validate_plan

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/github-backup
labels.description: infra/github-backup estate mirror system

body:
## Problem

`infra/github-backup/bin/reconcile.py` is the one remaining consumer of `plan.json` that reads it with a bare `json.load` and no shape validation — every sibling consumer was moved onto the validated loader in ghb_common (#6637 for fetch_mirrors, #6653 for manifest.py, and clone_all via the same pass), but reconcile's *previous-plan* read was not part of those fixes.

Sites (current origin/main `ed2534c1dd`):

- `reconcile.py:85` — `old_items = json.load(open(old_plan_path))`, bypassing `ghb_common.load_plan` / `validate_plan` (ghb_common.py:149/:224), which every other plan reader uses and which reports a wrong-shape entry by index and skips it.
- `reconcile.py:86` — `old = [p["repo"] for p in old_items]` subscripts every entry unguarded.
- `reconcile.py:96-102` — the last-known-good retention loop (the #3229 path, exercised exactly when an owner's inventory has failed) subscripts `item["repo"]` and calls `item["repo"].split("/")` unguarded a second time.

A `plan.json` that is valid JSON but the wrong shape — a poison entry written by a bad emit, a hand edit, or a schema change landing in one writer before this reader — crashes the weekly reconcile at startup, before it writes the new plan, runs the clone pass, writes its dated report, or regenerates MANIFEST.json. The crash is self-perpetuating: the crashing run never rewrites `plan.json`, so next week's run hits the identical entry.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ origin/main `ed2534c1dd`)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-reconcile-old-plan/` on the laptop: the real `reconcile.py` (sha256 `6f22eb29…`, byte-identical to origin/main), `ghb_common.py`, and siblings copied verbatim, driving the real `reconcile.main()` with `load_config` / `backup_root` / `inventory` stubbed exactly as the in-tree `test_reconcile_clone_pass.py` does, against a temp backup root holding each test `plan.json`:

- Control — valid old plan `[{"repo": "good-owner/newrepo", …}]`: `main()` completes its diff/report flow and rewrites `plan.json` (exit in the probe reflects only the stubbed clone pass reaching the probe dir's missing config, after the plan rewrite).
- Old plan entry `123` → `TypeError: 'int' object is not subscriptable`; `plan.json` unchanged.
- Old plan entry `"good-owner/newrepo"` → `TypeError: string indices must be integers, not 'str'`; unchanged.
- Old plan entry `{"name": "x"}` (no `repo`) → `KeyError: 'repo'`; unchanged.
- Old plan entry `null` → `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable`; unchanged.
- Old plan top level `{"repo": "good-owner/newrepo"}` (object, not a list) → `TypeError: string indices must be integers, not 'str'`; unchanged.
- Old plan top level `"good-owner/newrepo"` (string) → same `TypeError`; unchanged.
- Mixed old plan `[{"repo": "good-owner/old"}, 123]` → `TypeError: 'int' object is not subscriptable` — the one valid entry is lost with the poison one.
- Old plan entry `{"repo": 123}` with an inventory error present → `AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'split'` in the retention path (`item["repo"].split`).

In every malformed case no new plan is written, no report is written, and MANIFEST regeneration (`manifest_mod.build(root)` at the end of `main()`) is never reached.

## Why it matters

Reconcile is the weekly correctness floor for the backup estate (module docstring): it is the sweep that guarantees nothing is missed — it re-plans from fresh inventory, clones newly planned mirrors, retains last-known-good entries for owners whose inventory failed, and refreshes MANIFEST.json, the disaster-recovery source. A poison entry in the previous plan does not degrade one repo: it takes down the whole sweep, silently (a traceback in a timer log), and it recurs every week until a human hand-repairs the file. The validated loader already exists in the same directory and already states the contract this read should follow: a bad entry is reported by name/index and skipped; a wrong-shape top level is a single named problem treated as empty. The previous-plan read is the last place that contract is not applied.

Distinct from: #6637 (fetch_mirrors plan/state shape — fixed, and its sibling pass covered manifest/clone_all but not reconcile's previous-plan read), #6653 (manifest build), #6606 (reconcile's clone-status.jsonl lines), #3240 (torn / unparseable JSON and non-atomic writes — these files parse fine), #6575 (drain queue-event shape).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `reconcile.main()` loads the previous plan through the validated path (`ghb_common.load_plan` / `validate_plan`, or an equivalent guard): a plan entry that is not an object with a string `repo`, and a non-list top level, are reported by name/index via `report_problems` (or an equivalent named warning) and skipped — never a raw `TypeError` / `KeyError` / `AttributeError` traceback that aborts the sweep.
- [ ] Valid entries in the same previous plan still participate exactly as before: the added/removed diff and the #3229 last-known-good retention for failed owners both work off the surviving entries.
- [ ] A fully poisoned / wrong-shape previous plan behaves as an empty previous plan (all currently planned repos read as newly planned), and the run still writes the new `plan.json`, its dated report, and reaches MANIFEST regeneration.
- [ ] Well-formed behaviour is unchanged: the in-tree reconcile tests (`test_reconcile_clone_pass.py`, `test_reconcile_retention.py`) still pass.
- [ ] Regression tests in `infra/github-backup/tests/` cover at least: old-plan entry `123`, entry as a string, entry missing `repo`, entry `{"repo": 123}` on the inventory-error retention path, and a top-level object — each fails on current code with the exceptions above and passes after the fix.

body:
## Finding (unaddressed PR review comment)

PR #6444 (open, fleet-config HOME-resolution change) makes `Config::broker_socket()` and `Config::secrets_token_file()` fallible (they can now return `ConfigError::MissingHome`). CodeRabbit flagged that fleet-secrets' default chain construction propagates those errors with `?`, so a broker path-resolution failure prevents the `bws` fallback from ever being attempted.

- Source PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/6444
- Review comment: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/6444#discussion_r4489204570

body:
# github-backup(fetch): a wrong-shape `last_fetch` field passes #6637 validation and crashes the whole daily fetch

## Summary

#6637 hardened `infra/github-backup` against wrong-shape plan/state **entries**: `validate_state` (bin/ghb_common.py) drops a non-object per-repo entry and resets a non-list `fail_days`, and it validates the drainer's bookkeeping keys by shape (`drain_last::<repo>` must be a number, bool excluded). But the per-repo entry's own fields are not validated — in particular `last_fetch`, the one field the daily fetch does arithmetic on.

A state.json entry such as `{"owner/a": {"last_fetch": "2026-11-01T00:00:00Z"}}` (an ISO string — e.g. from a hand edit, an older/newer writer, or the torn-write shapes #3240 is about) passes `validate_state` with **zero problems reported**, and then crashes `fetch_mirrors.main` before any repo is fetched.

This is the field-level residual of #6637, the same shape as #6757 (field-level residual of #6652) and #6814 (field-level residual of #6716).

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop, origin/main c110f92897605d377b6cbae9b8dfc95f98f429b9)

- `infra/github-backup/bin/ghb_common.py` — `validate_state`: for a per-repo dict entry it checks only `fail_days` list-ness; `last_fetch` (and `last_error`) pass through unchecked, whatever their JSON type.
- `infra/github-backup/bin/fetch_mirrors.py:141` (in `main`):

  ```python
  if not only and st.get("last_fetch") and now - st["last_fetch"] < COALESCE_S:
  ```

  `now` is `time.time()` (float). A string/list/dict `last_fetch` makes this subtraction raise `TypeError` inside the repo loop. Everything after the loop — the state.json rewrite and `manifest_mod.build(root)` — never runs, so the run wedges the same way #6637 described: every repo, every day, until the field is hand-fixed.

- Probe (real `ghb_common.py` + `fetch_mirrors.py` extracted verbatim from origin/main, run on the laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-ghb-lastfetch`): `load_state` returned the poisoned entries with `problems=[]`; `fetch_mirrors.main` then raised, at fetch_mirrors.py:141:
  - `{"last_fetch": "2026-11-01T00:00:00Z"}` → `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for -: 'float' and 'str'`
  - `{"last_fetch": [1762000000]}` → same TypeError ('list')
  - `{"last_fetch": {"ts": 1762000000}}` → same TypeError ('dict')
  - Control `{"last_fetch": 9999999999}` (numeric, fresh) → main returned 0, repo correctly coalesce-skipped.
  - `{"last_fetch": true}` does not crash (bool is an int subclass; `now - True` works) but is silently read as epoch 1 — a wrong-shape value accepted as a timestamp, the same class the `drain_last` check already excludes bool for.

## Why it matters

The daily github-backup fetch is a disaster-recovery input (MANIFEST.json is the DR source, per #6653). One malformed field in one repo's state entry aborts the entire run with a raw traceback — no per-repo report, no state write, no manifest regeneration — and it recurs daily because the poisoned state is never rewritten. #6637's design rule was exactly that one poison entry must not wedge every repo; the fields inside a surviving entry are the remaining hole.

## Suggested fix

Validate `last_fetch` in `validate_state` the way `drain_last::<repo>` is already validated: a per-repo `last_fetch` that is present must be an int/float and not a bool; otherwise report it as a named problem and drop/reset the field (treat the repo as never-fetched) so the fetch proceeds. Mirror the same treatment for any other field a consumer does arithmetic or ordering on, if one exists.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A state entry with a string, list, dict, or bool `last_fetch` produces a named problem from `validate_state`/`load_state` (visible via `report_problems`) and does not reach `fetch_mirrors.main` as a non-number.
- [ ] `fetch_mirrors.main` completes the full repo loop with such a state file: other repos are fetched/skipped normally, state.json is rewritten, and MANIFEST regeneration runs.
- [ ] A numeric `last_fetch` keeps today's behavior exactly: fresh entries coalesce-skip (<12h), stale entries fetch.
- [ ] Regression tests in `infra/github-backup/tests/` (extending `test_plan_state_shape.py` / `test_fetch_mirrors.py`) cover string/list/dict/bool `last_fetch` and the numeric control; the existing github-backup test suite stays green.

## Dedup

#6637 (closed) covered entry-level shapes and the `fail_days`/`drain_*` fields; #6653 (closed) covered manifest regeneration; #3240 (open) covers non-atomic writes that can *produce* torn state. None of them validates the `last_fetch` field inside a surviving entry. Filed by new-issue-creator-code-b, 2026-11-06 run.

body:
# id(world apply/diff): a manifest pinning the default ceiling never converges — current_world_state folds the default ceiling to `None`, but plan() reads `None` as the whole catalog

## Summary

`id world diff` / `id world apply` can never reach "no drift" for a manifest whose `ceiling` is exactly the default ceiling — the natural manifest an admin writes by copying the ceiling out of `id world caps`. Every diff reports a `~ ceiling [...]` step and every apply re-sends a `set_caps_ceiling` for the names the host already has, forever.

The cause is one value with two meanings. Three sites disagree about what `ceiling = None` means:

1. **The host always reports a concrete list.** `WorldCore.caps_ceiling` is a `BTreeSet<String>` initialized to `default_ceiling_names()` (`pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs:153,331`), and `caps_report()` reports it verbatim (`pkgs/id/src/world/actor.rs:1142`). There is no "unset" state on the wire: an untouched world reports the default list.
2. **The client folds that list to `None`.** `current_world_state` (`pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs`, in the block fetching caps for the manifest comparison): if the reported ceiling equals `default_ceiling_names()` it stores `ceiling: None`, with the comment that this folds back to "no ceiling" (#838 — an apply then restores the default ceiling).
3. **The manifest layer reads `None` as the whole catalog.** `WorldManifest`'s docs (`pkgs/id/src/world_manifest.rs`, the `ceiling` field): "(In a `WorldState` and in `ApplyStep::SetCeiling`, `None` instead means the whole catalog.)" And `plan()` implements exactly that: "A live ceiling of `None` is the whole catalog, which no present list equals as a set", so any present manifest ceiling — including the default list itself — plans a `SetCeiling` step against a folded state.

A fourth site sides with (2) against (3): `apply_steps`' `SetCeiling` arm (`commands/world.rs`) treats a `None` step as "restore the **default** ceiling" (the #838 names), while `world_manifest::render_steps` renders the same `None` step as `~ ceiling [*] (whole catalog)` and the model `apply()` folds it as `state.ceiling = None` (whole catalog, per the docs). So even the step value's meaning splits between the model/renderer and the wire executor.

## Evidence

Verified on the laptop at origin/main `fc5aa00e79f33c5fd53bc2ad4ff0ccb6285b492d` with a probe crate (`~/git/fleet/probe-ceiling-fold`) using the **real** `pkgs/id/src/world_manifest.rs` verbatim against the **real** `id-core` `world_caps`/`world_limits`, plus the `current_world_state` fold copied verbatim:

- Default ceiling is a proper subset of the catalog: probe prints "default ceiling: 17 names; catalog: 19 names; default==catalog: false" (the default excludes the `DefaultCeiling::Excluded` providers, #838), so "default" and "whole catalog" are genuinely different sets.
- Case A: manifest `ceiling = [<the default list>]`, host state built exactly as `current_world_state` builds it for a fresh world (report = default list → probe prints "folded state.ceiling = None"): `plan()` returns `[set_ceiling]` instead of no steps.
- Case A round 2: after applying that step through the model (`state.ceiling = Some(17 names)`) and re-reading the host state the same way (the host now holds the default set explicitly — indistinguishable from untouched, so it folds to `None` again), `plan()` again returns `[set_ceiling]`. The plan/apply cycle does not converge; this contradicts `world_manifest`'s own contract ("When `current` already matches, the plan is empty, so applying twice is a no-op", and the `apply_is_idempotent` test's philosophy).
- Controls all behave (probe): a non-default ceiling the host already has plans 0 steps; an omitted ceiling plans 0 steps; the full catalog against a default-ceiling host correctly plans one widening `[set_ceiling]` step (any fix must preserve that step).

## Why it matters

- `id world diff` is the drift oracle for declarative world management (#807/#818 lineage). A whole class of manifests — arguably the most likely one, pinning the reported default — shows permanent phantom drift, training admins to ignore diff output, which is how real drift gets missed.
- Every `apply` performs a journaled admin `set_caps_ceiling` operation that changes nothing, and the run summary counts it as an applied step.
- The split meaning of `None` is a trap for the next change in this area: a future producer of `SetCeiling { ceiling: None }` steps (e.g. a "reset ceiling" manifest spelling) would restore the default on the wire while the model, the diff renderer, and the docs all claim it widened the world to the whole catalog — a security-relevant misdescription of a capability ceiling (cf. #838, where exactly this widening-by-default was the bug).

## Dedup

Checked open + closed: #1519 (closed) fixed ceiling *reorder* set-comparison and the seed-only plan; #817 (closed) fixed *omitted* ceiling widening; #838 (closed) introduced the default ceiling and the fold this issue is about; #6635 (closed) fixed the same function's *profile* non-convergence. None covers the default-list fold vs the whole-catalog reading of `None`, and none names the model/renderer vs wire-executor split for `SetCeiling { None }`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A manifest whose `ceiling` equals `default_ceiling_names()` plans **zero** steps (and `diff` prints "no drift") against a world whose host-reported ceiling is the default list, however that state was reached (never set, or explicitly set to the default names).
- [ ] A manifest pinning the full catalog against a default-ceiling world still plans exactly one widening `SetCeiling` step; a manifest pinning any other list still plans a step iff the sets differ; an omitted ceiling still plans none.
- [ ] One meaning of `ceiling: None` is chosen and stated once, and `world_manifest` (docs, `plan`, model `apply`, `render_steps`) and `commands/world.rs` (`current_world_state` fold, `apply_steps` `SetCeiling` arm) all agree with it — including what a `SetCeiling { ceiling: None }` step does on the wire vs in the model.
- [ ] A regression test exercises the plan → apply → re-read → plan round trip for the default-ceiling manifest and asserts the second plan is empty (the fold in `current_world_state` likely needs extracting into a testable pure function to do this).
- [ ] Existing world_manifest and world command tests still pass.

body:
## Finding

The worktree-reaper's CLEAN gate never looks at **ignored** files, so a fleet worktree whose only non-tracked content is ignored files is classified clean and reaped — and `git worktree remove` deletes the ignored content with the tree, unrecorded in the reaper's audit log.

Found by pr-diff-review reviewing PR #3698 (merged 2026-11-01, merge commit `6313875c7b505305ccd12ec168c408a37df178c3`, verified ancestor of main `bcc090152f3fd7d97d5fbc81c4815224a39d4d30` via compare API, behind_by 0). The code is unchanged on current main.

## Evidence

- `infra/worktree-reaper/bin/worktree_reaper.py`, `status_entries()` (PR #3698 diff; same code on current main at ~line 289): runs `git status --porcelain=v1 -z --no-renames --untracked-files=all` — **no `--ignored`** — so ignored paths appear in neither the tracked nor the untracked list.
- `evaluate_tree()` sets CLEAN ok = no tracked changes and no untracked files beyond the generated-dirt allowlist; `reap_tree()` re-verifies with the same `status_entries()` and chooses `--force` solely from allowlisted *untracked* dirt. Ignored files are invisible at both decision points and are never written to the run JSONL record.
- Laptop probe (2026-11-06, synthetic repo, this review): a worktree containing only an ignored file (`local-state`, matched by `.gitignore`) shows an **empty** reaper-view status; plain `git worktree remove` exits 0 and the ignored file is deleted with the tree. A second worktree with an allowlisted untracked file plus the same ignored file: `git worktree remove --force` exits 0 and the ignored file is deleted too — the reaper's record for that reap would list only the allowlisted dirt.

## Why it matters

The reaper's stated invariant (README in PR #3698) is that it "only removes worktrees whose content is proven on origin". The PUSHED gate proves the *branch tip*; ignored files are never pushed by definition, so they are exactly the content the proof cannot cover — local state files, ignored databases (cf. `pkgs/id/.gitignore`: `.identity.db`, `.identity.redb`), credentials-adjacent scratch, or build/state directories a worker left in a tree that then went quiet for 6 hours. Today such a tree reaps as "clean" and the loss leaves no trace in the audit record.

Related open reaper issues, none of which covers this: issue #5946 (tests run by no workflow), issue #5740 (/proc scan fail-closed), issue #6547 (stale registrations), issue #6394 (config validation). Deduped this run against the open-issue list and searches for "worktree reaper ignored" / "reaper ignored files" — no match.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The CLEAN gate and the pre-removal re-verification enumerate ignored files (e.g. `git status --ignored` / `--ignored=matching`): any ignored file beyond an explicit, config-named ignored-dirt allowlist blocks the reap (fail closed, like the other gates).
- [ ] If an ignored-dirt allowlist is introduced, every ignored path present in a reaped tree is recorded by path in the run JSONL before removal — a reap never silently deletes unlisted content.
- [ ] Synthetic-repo tests in `infra/worktree-reaper/tests/test_worktree_reaper.py` cover: ignored-only tree is kept; allowlisted-untracked + ignored tree is kept (or, if allowlisted-ignored is implemented, reaped with the ignored paths in the record); the existing reap matrix still passes.
- [ ] The README/docstring CLEAN gate description states the ignored-files rule explicitly.

title: fleet-queue(fallback): a contested claim never expires — fold the contest with the lease so a dead holder/challenger cannot brick an issue

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/fleet
labels.description: pkgs/fleet multicall binary + platform crates

body:
## Problem (follow-up fix for triaged issue #6660)

In the GitHub-native queue fallback mode (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/fallback.rs`), a **contested claim never expires**: once a second worker's claim marker lands while a claim is live, the issue is permanently bricked in fallback mode unless the original holder releases it. Verified against main @207e61203b790c525edebd84c906b34df617e741 during triage of issue #6660 (see that issue for the full probe evidence):

- `fold_claim` returns `ClaimState::Contested` whenever a contest was recorded and a holder exists (fallback.rs:448-455) — before and regardless of the lease-age check that follows it. Lease expiry never applies to a contested issue.
- `cmd_claim` refuses a contested issue (`reason: "contested"`, exit 5, fallback.rs:888), so the fold's clean-supersede arm can never fire once a contest exists.
- `cmd_heartbeat` refuses a contested issue too (fallback.rs:970), so even a live holder cannot renew after a stray claim from a since-dead challenger.
- `cmd_release` has no contested check (it matches on `state.holder()`), so a holder release is the only exit — and if the holder is the dead worker, nobody can ever claim the issue through the tool again. A challenger's release does not clear the contest either (the fold's Release arm only acts when the releaser is the holder).

## Fix direction

- In `fold_claim`, a contest should expire with the lease: when the holder's last activity (and the contest) are older than the lease window, the contested state folds to stale/claimable like any other silent claim — a new claim then cleanly supersedes.
- A heartbeat from the holder while contested should be accepted (it proves the holder is alive); consider clearing or aging the contest once the challenger has been silent for a full lease window.
- Keep the within-lease behavior unchanged: a live contest inside the lease window stays hands-off.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] New fold tests: contest folded after lease expiry (both workers silent ~100 leases) is claimable/stale, not contested (issue #6660 Case 1).
- [ ] New fold test: holder heartbeats after a contest keep the claim live/renewable (issue #6660 Case 2), and the heartbeat verb no longer refuses a contested issue for the holder.
- [ ] New fold test: challenger release + lease expiry leaves the issue claimable (issue #6660 Case 3).
- [ ] Existing test `fold_stale_supersede_and_live_contest` still passes (within-lease contest stays contested).
- [ ] `doc/fleet/queue-fallback-mode.md` updated if the contested semantics text changes.

Origin: triage of issue #6660 by repo-worker-code lane code-y (fallback mode, 2026-11-06).
