title: New-router edge design: WAN-on-a-VLAN over bonded SFP+ pairs, dual routers + VRRP (investigation)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: A design proposal (design-architect): multi-step, phased, decision-bearing

body:
## What this is

Investigation (Drew, 2026-11-06): design and later configure Drew's **3 new routers** (each: 10GbE + **2× SFP+** + 3× 1GbE — exact models TBD from inventory) as the home/lab edge, replacing the current TP-Link Deco BE11000 edge (see #1280). Drew: "later we'll need to investigate hooking up my new routers — I need your help [with] the best way to configure" them. Design first; no hardware moves yet.

## Current state (context)

- Edge today: Brightspeed fiber → ONT/bridge → Deco BE11000 in router mode (holds the public WAN directly; #1280 — it advertises an IPv6 default route with no WAN6 path, the current blackhole).
- History correction from Drew (2026-11-06): the pre-Deco router was his **APU2**, which he ripped out "because deco was even more broken before" — i.e. the current Deco-as-router setup was itself the fallback. (Records previously said pfSense → OpenWrt → TP-Link; the APU2 detail is Drew's, 2026-11-06.)

## The concept (Drew's design, in his words as dictated 2026-11-06)

WAN-on-a-VLAN over a bonded SFP+ pair, per router:

- The ISP's single Ethernet handoff lands on a **switch VLAN** instead of a router port.
- **Both** of a router's SFP+ ports **bond (2× 10G)** into the switch; WAN and LAN ride as VLANs over that bond, so neither SFP+ is consumed by a dedicated Internet port.
- Wire **both routers identically**; run **VRRP** so the gateway fails over between them — the SPOF shifts from the router to the switch (accepted trade, to be examined).
- **The primary reason is NOT VRRP** — it is not wasting one of the two SFP+ ports on the Internet link. Failover is the bonus.
- Bandwidth math: the 2× SFP+ bond gives 10G per connection, 20G aggregate; reserving ~2G for ISP traffic and ~2G for WAN traffic on the inside leaves ~16G effective for other routes and networks. If the ISP ever delivers 10G, at 100% ISP utilization the bond is effectively dedicated to ISP work.
- Later WANs to fold in: a **hotspot** and maybe **Starlink** (multi-WAN failover/policy order TBD).

## Pointer owed

Drew documented this concept somewhere on a website he rendered as "mono.si" (dictation, 2026-11-06). Fleet hunt on 2026-11-06 found no copy in memory, the zettel clone, hardware-doc, or hatch-personal. Exact site/URL TBD — when located, link it here and reconcile this issue's description against it.

## Investigation questions

1. Router models/firmware: VRRP + LACP + VLAN trunking support; routing/NAT hardware offload at 10G; can both SFP+ ports bond while carrying WAN+LAN VLANs at line rate?
2. Switch side: LACP + VLAN requirements; is the current/planned switch (see #6073–#6075, #6077) up to it; does removing the new switch SPOF need MLAG/stacking or a second switch later?
3. WAN sharing: can two VRRP routers share the single Brightspeed handoff (DHCP? PPPoE?) and one public IP cleanly?
4. IPv6: does this edge fix the #1280 WAN6/prefix-delegation hole natively?
5. Deco's afterlife: AP-only mesh behind the new edge, or retired?
6. Third router's role: cold spare, lab segment, or third VRRP node?
7. Multi-WAN policy for hotspot/Starlink when they arrive.

Related: #1280 (current LAN/IPv6), #6077 (lab interconnect), #6066 (home-lab parent).

## Acceptance criteria
- The router models are identified from inventory and recorded on this issue (the design depends on exact port/NIC reality).
- A written edge design exists covering: WAN-on-a-VLAN over the bonded SFP+ pair, identical wiring for both routers, VRRP failover, and how the current Deco edge (issue #1280) is retired or demoted.
- The design names the open decisions for Drew explicitly, each with options and a recommendation, rather than burying them in prose.

title: cargo-target-janitor: both deletion-safety liveness reads are single-page — queue_claims caps at 1000 rows and open_pr_branches at 500 PRs, so a claimed task or open-PR worktree past the page silently loses its never-delete protection

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

labels.name: app/cargo-target-janitor
labels.description: Package/app: cargo-target-janitor (infra/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

The cargo target janitor (`infra/cargo-target-janitor/bin/cargo_target_janitor.py`) deletes Cargo target directories under `~/git/fleet`. Its safety policy (README) is absolute — "Never remove a target for a currently claimed `repo-health-code-pilot` task" or for "a worktree whose branch has an open PR" — and it fails closed when a liveness source is *unavailable* (README: "If either source is unavailable, cleanup stops"; an invalid `gh` response raises `SafetyError`, janitor `:246`).

Both liveness reads that implement those two protections are single-page reads with a silent cap, so a source that is *truncated* is indistinguishable from a source that is *complete* — the one failure shape that does not stop cleanup:

1. **Claimed tasks** — `queue_claims` (`:186`), query at `:188-192`:
   `tasks?select=id,queue,status,payload&queue=eq.repo-health-code-pilot&status=eq.claimed&limit=1000`
   One GET, no offset/range follow-up, no check that the page came back full. Claimed task IDs past row 1000 are absent from the returned set, so `discover_targets` never applies the `live-claimed-task` protection (`:309`) to their targets — and the apply loop's per-removal re-check calls the same function (`:512`), so the re-check is blind in exactly the same way.
2. **Open PR branches** — `open_pr_branches` (`:219`), `gh pr list --limit 500` (`:229-230`):
   One call, no page follow. Open PRs past the first 500 contribute no branch names, so their worktrees never get the `open-pr-worktree` protection (`:311`/`:313`), at plan time (`:423`) and at the apply re-check (`:513`) alike.

Same-pattern site to disposition while fixing: `queue_task_states` (`:211`) also ends in `limit=1000`; its ID set is built from local fleet directories, so it is bounded differently, but the fix should state why it is or is not safe.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop primary @ `2bb307550b` (== origin/main). Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-janitor-pages/probe_janitor_pages.py` loads the *real* janitor module and stubs only the two servers, honouring their documented limit semantics (PostgREST `limit=N` returns at most N rows; `gh --limit N` returns at most N PRs):

- Server holds 1005 claimed tasks → `queue_claims` returns **1000**, task IDs 1001–1005 missing, exactly **1** query issued. Control (3 claimed) returns all 3.
- Server holds 600 open PRs → `open_pr_branches` returns **500** branch names, 100 missing, exactly **1** `gh` call (`--limit 500`).
- PROBE PASS, exit 0.

Live headroom today (2026-11-06, `gh pr list`): **259 open PRs** — under the 500 cap, but already past half of it in a repo whose fleet lanes open PRs continuously. The claimed-task count could not be read today (queue backend outage, #6450); nothing here claims either cap has already been exceeded live. The defect is that when a cap *is* crossed, the janitor's two never-delete protections silently stop applying to the overflow — in a tool whose hourly timer runs with `--apply` (README "Run and schedule").

Related: #6605 (same first-page-only flaw in fleet dispatch-test's scan, filed today); #5952 (the janitor's tests run in no workflow — a pagination test added here needs a venue, or it joins that gap).

## Why it matters

Every other safety input in this tool fails closed: unreadable process table, invalid `gh` JSON, helper unavailable, path escaping the fleet root — all raise and stop. A full page is the only degraded input that is silently treated as ground truth, and it degrades precisely the two protections that stand between a live task / open PR and `shutil.rmtree` of its build directory. Deleting a claimed task's target mid-build costs a full recompile of pkgs/id and can fail the task's verification; deleting an open PR's worktree target does the same to its holder.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `queue_claims` returns claimed IDs beyond the first 1000 (offset/range pagination, or an equivalent complete read), OR raises `SafetyError` when a page comes back exactly full so cleanup stops instead of proceeding on a known-incomplete set.
- [ ] `open_pr_branches` likewise pages past 500 open PRs, OR fails closed on a full page.
- [ ] The apply-loop re-checks (`:512`/`:513`) use the same complete/fail-closed reads — no second, weaker copy.
- [ ] `queue_task_states`' `limit=1000` (`:211`) is dispositioned in the change (fixed the same way, or a comment/test records why its locally-bounded ID set cannot exceed it).
- [ ] Tests in `infra/cargo-target-janitor/tests/test_cargo_target_janitor.py` cover the over-page cases for both reads (stub server/gh returning full pages), plus the at-cap boundary; existing 13 tests still pass.
- [ ] README safety policy updated if the chosen behaviour is fail-closed-on-full-page, so the documented contract matches the code.

title: id(world_net): record_pages still loops forever on empty pages with an advancing cursor — the #6505 RecordsBudget checks records, not pages, and a non-string next_after silently ends the read

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

body:
## Problem

Residual of #6505 in `pkgs/id/src/world_net.rs`: the `RecordsBudget` validation that landed on main (snapshot WIP, repaired in PR #6570) checks **records**, not **pages** — so `WorldClient::record_pages` (`:1564`) still loops forever on a page shape that carries no records at all, and still treats a malformed cursor as a clean end-of-read.

1. **Empty pages with an advancing cursor loop forever.** Each received record is run through `RecordsBudget::validate_record` (`:613`, `:619`), which caps key/value/count/order — but an empty page contributes zero records, so the budget never moves. The cursor checks in the loop are:
   - `next_after` must equal the page's last key (`:1606-1612`) — for an empty page there is no last key, and the `else` branch (`:1613-1620`) explicitly carves empty pages out, requiring only that this is not the first request (`after.is_some()`);
   - `next_after` must strictly advance past the cursor sent (`:1623-1629`) — any larger string satisfies this (`z000001`, `z000002`, …).
   
   Each iteration pushes another `(sequence, page)` onto the unbounded `pages` Vec (`:1631`) and issues another request. There is no page-count bound and no aggregate frame-byte budget on this path (`recv_json` discards the frame size), so a buggy or malicious host keeps `records()` / `records_sequenced()` running forever, growing memory page by page.

2. **A non-string `next_after` silently ends the read.** `let next_after = reply["next_after"].as_str()` (`:1606`) yields `None` for a number, boolean, array, or object cursor exactly as it does for a legitimate JSON `null`, and the `match` at `:1632` returns `Ok(pages)` — the caller receives a partial record set presented as complete, with no error. The sibling field in the same reply is handled strictly: `sequence` is extracted with `.as_u64().context("records reply has no sequence")?` (`:1592-1594`).

Neither shape can come from a conforming host: the server side, `records_session` in `src/world_session/mod.rs:1785`, sets `next_after = more.then_some(last_included).flatten()` (`:1826`), and `more` is only set after at least one record was included — an honest server never sends an empty page with a cursor, and always sends the cursor as a string or null. The admin-history client path **in the same file** is the strict oracle: its cursor block (`:1740-1755`) requires `next_after` to equal the last received key *and* to advance past the previous cursor — for an empty page those two requirements contradict each other, so the shape is refused there — and every frame there is charged to a byte budget (`budget.add_frame`).

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ origin/main b0c472d94d)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-records-empty-pages` (real `id` crate + rogue iroh host speaking `/id-world/1`, same harness as the #6505 probe):

- Control, conforming two pages (`{a:1}` → `next_after:"a"`, then `{b:2}` → `next_after:null`) → `Ok`, 2 records. ✅
- Control, empty final page (`{a:1}` → `"a"`, then `{}` → `null`) → `Ok`, 1 record — the legitimate empty-page shape still terminates. ✅
- **Defect E:** first page `{a:1}` → `next_after:"a"`, every later page `{}` with `next_after:"z<n>"` (strictly advancing) → `records()` was **still looping after 3 s; the host saw 55,615 records requests** in that window. No error, no return.
- **Defect T:** second page `{b:2}` with `next_after:123` (a number) → `records()` returned `Ok` with both records, the malformed cursor silently accepted as the terminator.

For contrast, #6505's original shapes are now refused at this HEAD (over-cap page, stuck/non-advancing cursor, out-of-order pages — the budget and the `:1606-1629` checks do catch those). This issue is only the two shapes that remain.

## Why it matters

The plain records query is the read the CLI uses against worlds the client does not operate (the normal join flow). A host that answers with empty advancing pages — a paging bug is enough; malice is not required — hangs every such read indefinitely with unbounded page accumulation, exactly the hang #6505 set out to close, through the one page shape its fix does not inspect. The non-string cursor case is the quieter twin: a malformed host response is indistinguishable from a complete read, so callers act on a silently truncated record set.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `record_pages` refuses an empty page that carries a `next_after` cursor (mirroring the admin-history path in the same file), or equivalently bounds the total number of pages / consecutive empty pages with a loud error naming the bound.
- [ ] A present-but-non-string `next_after` (number, boolean, array, object) is a malformed-reply error, not end-of-pages; only JSON `null` / absent terminates the loop — the same strictness `sequence` already gets.
- [ ] Regression tests drive `WorldClient` against stub/rogue replies covering: empty advancing pages (refused promptly, bounded request count), non-string `next_after` (error), plus the conforming controls — two-page read and empty final page with `next_after: null` both still return `Ok`.
- [ ] Conforming hosts are unaffected: existing world_net / world_session records tests stay green (server pages are non-empty whenever a cursor is present, by construction).

Distinct from #6505 (caps, ordering, and non-advancing cursors in `record_pages` — those landed and are verified refused at this HEAD): this is the residual page-shape hole in the same loop — empty pages are exempt from the last-key check, and the cursor's *type* is never checked.

title: github-backup(drain): a non-dict or id-less queue event crashes the whole drain — the #3331 poison pill one level up (event shape itself is never checked)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/github-backup
labels.description: infra/github-backup estate mirror system

body:
## Summary

`infra/github-backup/bin/drain_queue.py` carefully drops malformed events whose *nested* shapes are wrong (the #3326/#3331 owner-allowlist work: non-dict `owner`/`account`, string owners, missing repository — all DRAIN-DROP + ack, drain continues). But the *event itself* is never shape-checked, and its `id` is never checked:

- `queue_events` (:89-108) validates only that `page["events"]` is a list — its elements are extended into the run unchecked.
- The main loop (:221) calls `event_owner(ev)` / `event_repo(ev)`, which call `ev.get(...)` (:153/:156/:172/:181) — a non-dict element (string, null, number) raises `AttributeError`.
- Dict events without an `id` hit `ack.append(ev["id"])` in the foreign-drop branch (:229) and the no-repo branch (:233), and `ids = [e["id"] for e in evs]` for planned repos (:240) — all raise `KeyError: 'id'`.

Either crash aborts `main()` *before* any fetch, any ack, and before `state.json` is written. The malformed entry stays in the Worker KV (entries carry a 7-day TTL, `worker/src/index.js:5`), so every 5-minute drain tick re-crashes on the same entry: the whole github-backup freshness layer wedges behind one poison event, and valid events queued behind it are never fetched or acked. This is exactly the poison-pill failure #3331 closed for nested shapes — one level up, still open.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ 004fd71699, probe `~/git/fleet/probe-ghb-drain-poison/probe.py`, real `drain_queue.main()` with the test harness's stub Worker/fetch pattern)

- control, valid planned event: `rc=0`, fetched + acked.
- control, #3331 malformed-owner dict event + valid event: `rc=0`, dropped + both acked.
- `"garbage"` / `None` / `42` as an event element, valid planned event behind it: `AttributeError: ... has no attribute 'get'` — `fetched=[] acked=[]`.
- dict event with no `id` (foreign repo / no repo / planned repo): `KeyError: 'id'` — `fetched=[] acked=[]`.

## Why it matters

The drainer is the freshness layer of the estate mirror system (#3215): webhooks queue in the Worker, the drainer fetches mirrors. Its stated contract for malformed input is fail-closed *per event* — drop loudly, keep draining (#3326 docstring: "malformed events whose owner cannot be determined are dropped"). An event-level malformed shape breaks that contract catastrophically instead of per-event: one bad KV entry silently stops *all* mirror fetches for up to the entry's 7-day TTL, with the only signal a crashing timer unit.

Distinct from: #3331 (nested owner/account shapes inside a dict event — fixed), #6572 (queue_events pagination has no page/event bound — the read loop, not per-event shape), #3240 (non-atomic state files).

## Acceptance criteria

- A non-dict event element, or a dict event with a missing/non-string `id`, is DRAIN-DROP logged and skipped (it cannot be acked without an id — log it and move on); it never aborts the run.
- Valid events in the same poll are still fetched/acked exactly as today, and the run summary counts dropped-malformed events.
- Regression tests in `infra/github-backup/tests/test_drain_queue.py` cover: non-dict element first + valid event behind it; id-less dict in each of the foreign / no-repo / planned branches.
- Existing drain suite still passes.

title: worktree-reaper: a stale registration is never pruned — prune runs only when another tree is reaped in the same primary

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/worktree-reaper
labels.description: infra/worktree-reaper

body:
## Summary

`infra/worktree-reaper/bin/worktree_reaper.py` detects a worktree whose directory has already been deleted — `evaluate_tree` returns action `stale-registration` (worktree_reaper.py:417) — but nothing ever removes that registration. The only `git worktree prune` call in the script (worktree_reaper.py:599-600) is gated on `removed_any`, which is set only when a *candidate* tree is successfully reaped in the same primary in the same run (worktree_reaper.py:570, :584). A primary whose only dead trees are already-deleted directories therefore accumulates stale registrations forever: every run logs them as kept (`stale-registration`) and exits 0. The parser even records git's `prunable` flag (worktree_reaper.py:182, :194-195) and no code ever reads it.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary at origin/main 2bcd46e0dc)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-reaper-stale/probe.py` drives the real `worktree_reaper.main()` (in-process, `--no-fetch`, temp config/state under the probe dir) against a scratch primary:

1. Create a linked worktree `wt1`, then delete its directory out from under git (the fleet reality this tool exists for: trees removed by hand, by a crashed cleaner, or by a disk cleanup).
2. `git worktree list --porcelain` before: the `wt1` path is present and marked `prunable`.
3. Run the reaper (not dry-run): exit 0; summary `evaluated: 1, candidates: 0, reaped: 0, kept: {"stale-registration": 1}`.
4. `git worktree list --porcelain` after the reaper: **the stale registration is still present**.
5. Control: a manual `git worktree prune` in the same primary removes it immediately — the remedy exists and works; the reaper just never invokes it on this path.

## Why it matters

The reaper is the fleet's only automatic worktree hygiene (README: born when the standing population grew 187 → 1,511 in five days). Stale registrations are the cheapest dead trees to clear — no gates, no content at risk, the directory is already gone — yet they are the one class it can never clear on its own. They pile up in `git worktree list`, in the reaper's own evaluated/kept counts every run, and in any other tooling that iterates registered worktrees, and they only disappear if some *other*, unrelated tree happens to be reaped in the same primary in the same run (the `removed_any` side effect) or a human prunes by hand.

## Acceptance criteria

- A run that finds a stale registration in a primary (and is not `--dry-run`) leaves that primary with the registration pruned, even when no candidate tree was reaped in that primary.
- `--dry-run` still changes nothing on disk, and stale registrations found in dry-run are reported as would-prune (or an equivalent explicit action), not silently folded into kept counts.
- Prune remains fail-safe: it runs only for primaries that were successfully inventoried this run (the existing fail-closed fetch/list behaviour is unchanged), and a prune failure is surfaced in the run summary/errors rather than swallowed.
- Existing gate semantics are untouched: primaries are never reaped, locked/denied/dirty/unpushed trees keep exactly as today; the post-reap prune behaviour for candidate reaps is preserved.
- Regression coverage in `infra/worktree-reaper/tests/test_worktree_reaper.py`: a primary whose only worktree is a deleted-directory (prunable) registration is pruned by a non-dry-run pass, and is untouched by a dry-run pass.

## Distinct from

- Issue #6394 (worktree-reaper config validation), issue #5946 / issue #6357 (the reaper's test suites have no CI venue), issue #5740 (fail closed when /proc cannot be scanned). None covers the stale-registration/prune path.

title: cold-store-reaper(repair_dump): an unterminated sqlite_schema candidate is buffered whole — the 'constant-memory' filter grows to the size of the remaining dump

labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/cold-store-reaper
labels.description: Package/app: cold-store-reaper (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Summary

`pkgs/cold-store-reaper/scripts/repair_dump.py` — the streaming repair filter between the libsql `/dump` download and the sqlite3 rebuild in `scripts/export-turso.sh` — is documented as constant-memory, but a candidate `INSERT INTO sqlite_schema(` statement whose terminating line never arrives is buffered **in full, without any bound**, so the filter's memory grows to the size of the remaining dump and nothing is emitted until EOF.

## Evidence (file:line, origin/main `6b9e1ec081ac`)

- The promise: `repair_dump.py:22-25` — "The filter is line-oriented and constant-memory: it buffers only the lines of one candidate statement (which ends at a line ending in `');`)"; `export-turso.sh:187-191` repeats it: "streams the dump (constant memory, one statement buffered)".
- The code: `repair_dump.py:142-161` (`main`). Once a line starts with `INSERT INTO sqlite_schema(` and does not end in `');`, every later line is appended to `buffered` (`:146-151`) until a line ending in `');` appears; there is no size cap, no spill, and no flush-through. The accumulated list is only joined and emitted at the terminator (`:149`) or at EOF (`:159-160`).

## Verification (laptop probe, this run)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-repair-dump/` (driver2.py) against the real script exported from origin/main `6b9e1ec081ac`, stdin held open while measuring stdout and RSS:

- Control — 32 MiB of ordinary lines: streamed through; 33,488,896 B already on stdout before EOF; RSS 13,148 KiB.
- Unterminated candidate — the same 32 MiB after one `INSERT INTO sqlite_schema(... 'CREATE TABLE t (` line with no `');` line: **0 B on stdout before EOF; RSS 47,604 KiB** (≈ the full 32 MiB input held in memory, +34 MB over the control). Output after EOF is byte-identical (33,554,534 B, rc 0) — the failure is memory, not correctness.
- Functional controls on the real script: a verifiably mis-escaped FTS5 schema literal is repaired (quotes doubled), and an unterminated statement at EOF flushes unchanged — both pass, matching the existing `TestDumpRepairFilter` expectations.

## Why it matters

The filter sits in the Turso export path (`export-turso.sh:191`) precisely so large dumps can be processed without holding them in memory — the same package's recent #6233 work bounded memory when Drive ignores Range requests. A dump whose schema statement is cut or re-shaped so its terminator line never matches (truncated/corrupt download, a libsql format change such as trailing whitespace after `');`, or a genuinely huge multi-line schema statement) turns the "constant-memory" filter into a whole-dump buffer: on the backup host that is an avoidable OOM risk in the one job whose job is keeping backups restorable, and it fails silently — output stays byte-correct, just unbounded. This is the same shape as the fleet-proxy single-line head bound filed as #6511 (check exists, but only after the unbounded accumulation).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A candidate statement that exceeds a stated, generous bound (well above any real schema statement) is no longer accumulated without limit: e.g. flush the buffered lines through unchanged and resume line-oriented passthrough, or another design that keeps peak memory independent of the remaining dump size.
- [ ] Byte-identical output is preserved in every currently-correct case: mis-escaped literals still repaired, valid literals untouched, unterminated-at-EOF still flushed unchanged (existing `TestDumpRepairFilter` in `tests/test_export_turso.py` passes unchanged).
- [ ] A new regression test in `TestDumpRepairFilter` pins the bound: an unterminated candidate larger than the bound produces output before EOF / bounded memory, with the full stream still byte-identical end-to-end.
- [ ] The docstring and the `export-turso.sh` comment match the implemented bound (name the cap).

Filed by the new-issue-creator (lane A) after verification this run; not a duplicate of #1391 (the original mis-escaping quirk this filter works around) — this is the filter's own memory contract.

title: fleet-search(atlas client): via-service paging never truncates to the requested k — a page longer than k is printed whole instead of the standalone-parity count

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: app/fleet

body:
## Problem

The via-service search clients never truncate the paged results to the requested `k`. Each page is spliced in whole: the paging loop extends the result list with the full page, breaks once the count reaches `k`, and then inserts **all** collected results into the printed envelope. A service whose page contains more results than `k` — one page of 3 against `--k 2`, or the client's own 50-result page limit against the default `--k 10` — makes the via-service route print more results than the caller asked for, where the standalone route for the same request prints exactly `k`.

The clients' own contract says otherwise: paging runs "until the requested result count is satisfied", and the returned value is "the service's envelope with the paged results spliced in, field-for-field what standalone renders for the same request" (fleet-search `client.rs` module/function docs). The cursor guards in the same loop (#5424, #5654) already treat a service that deviates from the protocol as malformed and fall back loudly; an over-`k` ranking is the one deviation that is silently passed through to the user.

## Evidence (origin/main 6046e1d7bc)

- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-search/src/client.rs:31` — `PAGE_LIMIT = 50`: every results page is requested with `limit=50` (:307), larger than the default `k` of 10, so a single conforming-size page can overshoot `k` on its own.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-search/src/client.rs:331-332` — `results.extend(page.results.iter().cloned())`, then break only when `results.len() >= request.k`; nothing truncates.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-search/src/client.rs:364` — the envelope's `results` is replaced with the full collected `Vec`, overshoot included. No downstream truncation exists: `lib.rs` `print_output` / `render::render_text` print the envelope as-is.
- `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-search/src/service.rs:28,202,226-227,259` — the identical loop in atlas-search's own via-service client (fleet-search's header says it is a port of this client, "so the fleet verb and `atlas-search --via-service` speak to the service identically"): same `PAGE_LIMIT`, same extend/break/splice, same overshoot.
- A conforming server's stored ranking is built from the job's `k` (`server.rs` passes `request.k` into the computation), so the overshoot needs a service whose stored ranking is longer than the job's `k` — an older, coalesced, or non-conforming service — which is exactly the class of peer the existing cursor guards defend against.

## Verified this run (probe, real fleet-search crate)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-search-overshoot` on the laptop: a binary calling the real `fleet_search::run` (path dependency on the workspace crate @6046e1d7bc) against a stub HTTP service (submit → 202, status → done, one results page of 3 results, `next_cursor: null`, `total_results: 3`):

```
--k 2  -> printed envelope results: 3  (ids 1, 2, 3), exit 0
--k 1  -> printed envelope results: 3  (ids 1, 2, 3), exit 0
```

Standalone for the same request renders exactly `k` results. No error, no fallback, no truncation.

## Why it matters

`--k` is the caller's result-count contract (scripts and the fleet verb's consumers size output by it). The via-service route is the sandbox seat's default, so the route most likely to be scripted is the one that can silently return 5x the requested count (50 vs the default 10) whenever the service's ranking for a job is longer than the `k` it was submitted with. It also breaks the byte-parity the two clients exist to preserve: the same query prints different result counts via-service vs standalone.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] After paging, the spliced envelope contains at most `request.k` results (truncate the final page's contribution), in both `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-search/src/client.rs` and `pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-search/src/service.rs` — or, if an over-`k` page is judged malformed like the cursor deviations, it returns the malformed-response error and falls back loudly; pick one behavior, apply it identically in both clients, and note the choice in the PR.
- [ ] A stub-service test pins the boundary in each client: a single page longer than `k` yields exactly `k` results (or the malformed error), and multi-page paging that lands exactly on `k` is unchanged.
- [ ] Existing client tests keep passing (`cargo test -p fleet-search`, atlas-search service client tests), including the #5424/#5654 cursor-guard cases and the multi-page happy path.

Related: #5424 / #5654 (paging-loop guards this extends), #5433 (fleet-search port), #5407 (count validation parity).

body:
# Phase 4 of #6520 — closing JSON-parse inventory: disposition every serde_json parse site in pkgs/id against the duplicate-key refusal contract

Phase 4 (closing audit) of design #6520 — *a duplicate key is a parse
error: one duplicate-key refusal contract for `pkgs/id`'s checked JSON
gates*. Design doc: `files/designs/code-duplicate-json-keys.md` in the
keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace.

**Gated on Phases 1–3 of #6520** (#6473 + #6474, #6491 + #6499,
#6504). Do not start the inventory until they have landed; the
dispositions must be written against the as-built shared helper in
its `id-core` home.

## Scope

Inventory every `serde_json::from_str` / `from_value` / `from_slice`
site in `pkgs/id/src` and `pkgs/id/crates` (production code; test
sites may be grouped) and disposition each one against the contract
with file:line evidence:

- **gate** — the parse feeds a check, a store, a forward or a
  comparison: it routes through the shared
  `parse_json_without_duplicate_keys` helper (or is converted by its
  phase), or a follow-up issue is filed for it;
- **not-a-gate** — with the reason named (self-produced round-trip,
  scalar/string decode, test-only, other).

Land the contract statement in the shared helper's module
documentation: the rule (a duplicate key is a parse error, every
depth, naming the key), the one mechanism, and the boundary below.

## Required dispositions

- **(a) Signed-object JSON** — `artifact.rs` `from_slice` struct
  decodes, `boards.rs` `from_value` over artifact bodies: a
  signature covers exact bytes, but a duplicated key inside a signed
  body still makes two readers disagree about what was signed.
  Decide, with reasons: receipt gates for signed objects take the
  refusal too, or stand as deliberately-out (cf. #3231's receipt
  contract).
- **(b) Self-produced files** — serve info and any file the crate
  writes and reads back: the writer cannot produce a duplicate, so
  refusal is defence against hand edits only. Disposition per site,
  not by assumption.
- **(c) Non-JSON decoders** — postcard / MessagePack map types can
  also carry duplicate map keys. No filed instance: record the
  boundary (in this contract's scope as a stated exception, or
  filed as its own follow-up), do not silently extend the helper.
- **(d) The fixture double-collapse** — confirm #6473 + #6474
  landing closed it (header `records` refused at the first parse);
  cite the regression test.

## Acceptance criteria

- The inventory exists (in the helper's module docs or a linked
  crate doc) covering every production `serde_json` parse site in
  `pkgs/id` + `crates/`, each with a gate / not-a-gate disposition
  and file:line evidence.
- Required dispositions (a)–(d) are recorded with their reasons.
- Any site dispositioned as a gate that does not yet route through
  the helper has a filed follow-up issue; no silent exceptions.
- The contract statement is in the helper's module documentation.

🤖 Filed by the repo design architect (fleet), pass 61 — Phase 4 of
design #6520.

title: fleet(dispatch): dechunked_len does unchecked arithmetic on the peer-declared chunk size — overflow panics in debug, wraps in release

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.name: work/assigned
labels.description: Queue worker lifecycle state

labels.name: source/design-architect

labels.name: app/fleet
labels.description: pkgs/fleet multicall binary + platform crates

body:
## Summary

`fleet-dispatch`'s hand-rolled HTTP response reader does unchecked arithmetic on the peer-declared chunk size in `dechunked_len` — the function `read_response` uses to decide whether a chunked body is complete. A chunk-size line naming one of the two largest `usize` values panics in debug/test builds (`attempt to add with overflow`) and, in release builds where overflow checks are off, wraps so the completeness guard and the slice index are computed from wrapped values. The sibling decoder `dechunk` in the same file guards the same declared size before slicing and handles the identical input safely — the two halves of the chunked reader disagree about whether peer-declared sizes can be trusted.

This is the #5579 rule ("peer-declared sizes are never trusted") applied everywhere else in the fleet HTTP readers — fleet-proxy's `http.rs` caps chunk sizes against `MAX_RESPONSE_BODY_BYTES` with `checked_add` before allocating — but missed in the dispatch client.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop, origin/main `540d3bea3f`)

`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-dispatch/src/lib.rs`:

- `:303` — `let size = usize::from_str_radix(size_str.trim().split(';').next()?.trim(), 16).ok()?;` — the chunk size is parsed straight from the response bytes, unbounded.
- `:308` — `if rest.len() < size + 2 { return None; }` — `size + 2` is unchecked: for `size = usize::MAX` or `usize::MAX - 1` this overflows.
- `:311` — `total += size;` — also unchecked.
- `:312` — `rest = &rest[size + 2..];` — slices at the same unchecked expression.
- `read_response` (`:273`, the `complete` closure at `:265-272`) calls `dechunked_len(body)` after every read while filling a chunked body, so the panic/wrap triggers mid-exchange on response bytes alone — no local input needed beyond running `fleet dispatch status|launch|enqueue` against an endpoint that returns such a chunk-size line.
- Contrast `:326` — `dechunk` checks `size == 0 || rest.len() < size` before slicing and never adds to the declared size; and `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/http.rs` `read_chunked`, which does `out.len().checked_add(size)` and refuses anything past `MAX_RESPONSE_BODY_BYTES` before allocating.

### Probe (real crate, laptop worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-dispatch-dechunk-wt` at `540d3bea3f`)

A temporary `#[test]` appended to the crate's own test module, run with `cargo test -p fleet-dispatch probe_dechunked_len_huge_chunk_size -- --nocapture`:

- Control: `dechunked_len(b"4\r\nWiki\r\n5\r\npedia\r\n0\r\n\r\n") == Some(9)` ✔
- Control: `dechunked_len(b"4\r\nWi") == None` ✔
- Control: `dechunk(b"ffffffffffffffff\r\nXX") == []` — the decoder is safe on the same bytes ✔
- `dechunked_len(b"ffffffffffffffff\r\nXX")` → **PANIC** at `crates/fleet-dispatch/src/lib.rs:308:25: attempt to add with overflow`
- `dechunked_len(b"fffffffffffffffe\r\nXX")` → **PANIC** at the same line
- Probe result: `PROBE DONE panics=true true`, test passed (panics caught via `catch_unwind`).

In a release build the same expressions wrap instead of panicking: `size + 2` becomes `1` (for `MAX`) or `0` (for `MAX - 1`), the `:308` guard passes against a 2-byte remainder, `total` wraps, and `rest[size + 2..]` advances by the wrapped index — the completeness verdict for the exchange is then computed from wrapped arithmetic while `dechunk` decodes something else, so the client can finish an exchange early on a body the decoder reads differently.

## Why it matters

`fleet dispatch` is the thin client every seat uses to launch and enqueue sessions through pm-dispatch, over both the direct and the CONNECT-tunnel transports. Its response reader is the one hand-rolled HTTP reader in the fleet workspace that still does raw arithmetic on a peer-declared length. pm-dispatch (Bun.serve) will not emit such a chunk size itself, but the reader's contract — per #5579 and the module's own framing — is that response framing is validated before it is trusted: a buggy, compromised, or mis-proxied endpoint (the tunnel path traverses the egress proxy) turns a status/launch/enqueue call into a client panic in debug builds and a silently wrong completeness verdict in release builds, instead of the crate's normal `DispatchError::Transport` exit-3 path. Panics also bypass the crate's exit-code contract (0/2/3/4) entirely.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `dechunked_len` uses checked arithmetic (e.g. `size.checked_add(2)`, a checked running total, and/or a bound of the declared size against the remaining bytes / the existing 64 MiB body cap) so no peer-declared chunk size can overflow, wrap, or panic in any build profile.
- [ ] A chunk-size line that cannot describe a body within the buffered remainder (including the `usize::MAX` / `usize::MAX - 1` cases) is treated as "not complete" or as a transport error — never as a completed body computed from wrapped values.
- [ ] Unit tests in `fleet-dispatch` pin: the two overflow sizes above, a large-but-plausible size with insufficient bytes (`None`/error, no panic), and the existing happy-path pins (`chunked_bodies_dechunk`) keep passing.
- [ ] `cargo test -p fleet-dispatch` passes on the laptop or in CI.

Scope note: `read_response`'s Content-Length handling and `dechunk` itself are out of scope except where the fix naturally shares a guard; the pooled-connection desync concerns of #5579 do not apply here (one exchange per connection, `Connection: close`).

# deploy(deploy.py): `targets` entries have no shape rule — newline/ANSI/space targets pass validate() and are printed verbatim by `list`, injecting fake table rows

`pkgs/deploy/deploy.py`'s module docstring states the contract: validation "is the oracle for 'well-formed definition'… a registry that cannot be validated must never be enumerated as if it were trustworthy." Service *names* get a shape pattern (`NAME_RE`, deploy.py:52), but `targets` entries — described by the validator's own error text as "host/class names" — get no shape check at all, and `list` prints them verbatim.

## Evidence (verified this run)

At origin/main `85c435ec6c`:

- deploy.py:138-144 — the entire `targets` rule is: a non-empty list of non-empty strings. No character, shape, or control-character restriction.
- deploy.py:182 — `cmd_list` prints `','.join(defn['targets'])` raw into the table.

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-deploy-target-newline/probe.py`, driving the real `deploy.py` from origin/main against hand-written registries; all other fields valid):

- **X1 — newline target:** `targets: ["laptop\nFAKE  systemd     evil"]` → exit 0, and the output contains an injected fake row:
  ```
  NAME  CLASS       TARGETS
  svc  systemd     laptop
  FAKE  systemd     evil
  ```
- **X2 — ANSI target:** `targets: ["lap\x1b[31mtop"]` → exit 0, the raw escape sequence is emitted into the terminal output unchanged.
- **C2 — space target:** `targets: ["bad name"]` → exit 0 (a "host/class name" with a space is not a host or class name in any downstream consumer).
- **C1 — valid control:** the ordinary registry (`targets: ["laptop"]`) → exit 0, normal table. Correct.

## Why it matters

- `list` output is operator-facing and script-consumable; a registry value that can forge table rows (or smuggle terminal escapes) breaks the "enumerated as trustworthy" contract exactly as the service-name newline did in #6383 — through a different field that issue does not cover (#6383 scopes its fix to service names, duplicate targets/secrets, and healthCheck hosts).
- Targets are not display-only: later #5766 slices iterate targets as deploy destinations. A target that is not a plausible host/class name should fail at the oracle, not at activation time on a real host.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validate()` rejects, with a field-named error in the existing style, any `targets` entry that is not a plausible host/class name: at minimum no whitespace, no control or format characters, no ANSI escapes — e.g. reuse the name-pattern discipline used for service names, or an explicitly documented target pattern.
- The existing valid registry (`pkgs/deploy/services.nix` rendered via the flake) still validates and `deploy list` output is unchanged for it.
- Regression coverage: extend the malformed-registry flake check (`deploy-list-malformed`) or add equivalent cases exercising a newline target and a space target.
- Controls keep behaving: valid registry exits 0; the #6383/#6384/#6388 shapes keep their current verdicts.

Related: #6383 (same validator, service-name newline class — names only), #5766 (the deploy tool epic this validation gates).

body:
## Summary

`readDigestArchive` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/digest.ts:418`, origin/main 85c435ec6c) validates only two things about a stored digest archive: `parsed.date === date` and `Array.isArray(parsed.sections)`. Every other field the consumers dereference unconditionally — `freshness` (array of `{facet, state, ageMs}`), each section's `items` array, and each item's `title`/`url`/`ref`/`note` — is unchecked. A malformed archive (partial write, hand edit, schema drift from an older generator) is therefore returned as a valid `Digest`, and both consumers throw on it:

- `renderDigest` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/render.ts:7136`) — the `/digest?date=…` handler in `server.ts` renders the archived digest verbatim when `readDigestArchive` returns non-null, so the throw becomes a failed page instead of the handler's designed fallback (render today's digest with a 404).
- `digestText` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/digest.ts:379`) throws the same way.

Meanwhile `/api/digest.json?date=…` serves the same malformed object verbatim as if it were a valid digest.

## Verified this run (laptop probe, real modules)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-digest-archive/probe2.ts` (bun, real `digest.ts` + `render.ts` from the laptop primary; the relevant functions are byte-identical at HEAD and origin/main 85c435ec6c). Each case is the valid control archive with exactly one field broken:

| case | readDigestArchive | renderDigest | digestText |
|---|---|---|---|
| control (valid archive) | ACCEPTED | rendered | rendered |
| `sections: [null]` | ACCEPTED | THREW `null is not an object (evaluating 's.items')` | THREW |
| section with `items` missing | ACCEPTED | THREW `undefined is not an object (evaluating 's.items.length')` | THREW |
| `freshness` missing | ACCEPTED | THREW `undefined is not an object (evaluating 'digest.freshness.length')` | THREW |
| `items: 42` | ACCEPTED | rendered | THREW `number is not iterable` |
| `items: [null]` | ACCEPTED | THREW `null is not an object (evaluating 'i.url')` | THREW |
| `freshness: [null]` | ACCEPTED | THREW `null is not an object (evaluating 'f.facet')` | THREW |

## Why it matters

The archive is the dashboard's historical record ("the archive IS the dashboard page's data — /digest?date=<date> renders the stored digest verbatim", digest.ts header comment). Its reader already has the right contract for a bad file — return `null`, read as absent, and the `/digest` handler falls back gracefully — but the validation is too shallow to honor it, so one bad archive file permanently breaks that date's page (and its machine twin serves the malformed object as truth). This is the same failure shape as #4140 (CoverageSnapshotStore.read accepts a malformed snapshot and diffCoverage throws instead of the snapshot reading as absent), in the digest store next door.

## Acceptance criteria

- `readDigestArchive` returns `null` for an archive whose `freshness` is not an array of well-formed entries, whose `sections` contain a non-object or a section without an `items` array, or whose items are not objects with the string fields the renderers use — i.e. any shape `renderDigest`/`digestText` would throw on reads as absent.
- A valid archive (as written by `writeDigestArchive` from a real `buildDigest` result) still round-trips and renders.
- Tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/digest.test.ts` (or sibling) pin the malformed shapes above against the reader, naming the oracle: the renderers must never throw on anything the reader accepts.
- `/api/digest.json?date=…` for a malformed archive returns the existing 404 "no digest archived" response rather than the malformed object.

body:
## Problem

`Registry::load` in `pkgs/id/src/publications.rs` parses the persisted publications file directly into the `Registry` struct with serde (publications.rs:372, `serde_json::from_str(&text)`), and only then runs `validate_persisted` (publications.rs:391). Serde's derived decoding collapses duplicate JSON keys — the last value wins — so `validate_persisted` only ever sees the collapsed record. A hand-edited or corrupt file that spells a field twice hides its first, invalid spelling from every load-side invariant the module promises to enforce loudly: empty world name, non-canonical mount path, and duplicate placement (the exact three rules `validate_persisted` exists to re-check, per its doc comment at publications.rs:379–390 and the module's persistence contract: "a malformed file is an error naming the file — a serve that cannot read its persisted publications must say so loudly rather than silently restore nothing").

Evidence (`origin/main` fc073b5f11; `pkgs/id/src/publications.rs` is identical between the laptop primary HEAD and `origin/main`):

- `Registry::load`, publications.rs:356; the struct parse is at publications.rs:372–374, followed by `validate_persisted()` at publications.rs:375–377.
- `validate_persisted`, publications.rs:391: checks world non-empty, mount path stored in canonical form, and no duplicate placement — all on the post-collapse value.
- In-tree load tests pin the single-spelling cases only: publications.rs:619 (duplicate placement), :640 (empty world), :654 (non-canonical mount path). No test spells a key twice.

Verified this run on the laptop with a probe against the real `id` crate (`~/git/fleet/probe-pub-dup`, integration test driving the public `Registry::load` on temp files; `cargo test` 1 passed):

Controls — each invalid record alone is refused by `validate_persisted`, and a valid record alone loads:
- `{"publications":[{world:"", placement path_mount "/empty"}]}` → Err.
- `{"publications":[{world:"bad", placement path_mount "//bad"}]}` → Err.
- `{"publications":[valid, valid]}` (duplicate placement) → Err.
- `{"publications":[valid "/arena"]}` → Ok.

Hidden behind a duplicate key — all load Ok:
- `{"publications":[empty-world record, non-canonical record],"publications":[valid record]}` → Ok, 1 publication: the whole invalid first array is never validated.
- `{"publications":[{"world":"","world":"arena", placement path_mount "/arena"}]}` → Ok, world is "arena": the empty first `world` is hidden.
- `{"publications":[{"world":"bad", placement {"kind":"path_mount","path":"//bad","path":"/good"}}]}` → Ok: the non-canonical first `path` is hidden.

## Why it matters

`publications.json` is restored at boot by `id serve`: the loaded set is what gets published, and `boot_warnings` / shadow handling trust that load validated it. The module's own contract is fail-loud on corrupt persisted records precisely because a silently restored bad set resurrects placements `publish()` refuses. Duplicate keys defeat that contract invisibly — the file on disk and the registry in memory disagree, and no error names the file. This is the same duplicate-key class as #6473 (parse_records), #6474 (world_fixture), #6491 (parse_surface), #6499 (parse_wants) and #6501 (world_session frames), in a persisted-registry loader those fixes did not cover; the sibling persisted loader in deploy.py had the same flaw (#6384, closed).

## Acceptance criteria

- `Registry::load` refuses a publications file containing duplicate JSON keys — at the top level, inside a publication object, and inside a placement object — with an error naming the file, before `validate_persisted` runs on a collapsed value (e.g. parse through a duplicate-rejecting first pass like the #6473-family fixes, or an equivalent strict decode).
- Raw-string regression tests pin: duplicate `publications` (invalid array first, valid second), duplicate `world` (empty first), and duplicate `path` (non-canonical first) — each refused; the existing single-spelling controls at publications.rs:619/:640/:654 keep passing.
- Controls unchanged: a valid registry file loads identically, a missing file still yields an empty registry, and an unreadable file still fails loud naming the file.

# mcpx: callWithLedger ignores operator-declared readOnlyTools — a declared read-only tool that times out after dispatch records an unknown outcome and blocks later writes

## Finding (from PR review)

On PR #6265 ("mcpx: operator-declared readOnlyTools + typed gate refusals (#6116)"), Codex review raised a P2 finding that was never replied to, never fixed, and whose review thread is still unresolved; the PR merged with the finding live.

Reviewer: `chatgpt-codex-connector[bot]`, 2026-11-05T15:38:25Z
Comment: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/6265#discussion_r4482526342
Location: `pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/consumer.go:694` (the flagged call path; the ledger classification itself lives in `registry.go`)

> **Honor read-only declarations when recording unknown outcomes**
>
> When an operator-declared read-only tool without `readOnlyHint` times out or loses its connection after dispatch, `callWithLedger` in `registry.go` still classifies it using only the annotation-based `toolReadOnly` helper. Consequently, a declared search such as `fff.grep` returns `ErrUnknownOutcome` and persists a server-wide block on subsequent non-read-only calls until manually cleared, despite the new declaration classifying it as read-only here. Apply the requested server's declaration to the post-dispatch ledger classification as well, not just the gate and existing-block exemption.

## No-response evidence

- PR #6265 merged 2026-11-05T16:03:17Z (merge commit 4e6cdb92fd2db60fd05624f587532aed5bcd7b01), after the comment.
- The comment has no replies (verified by a fresh `gh api` read of the PR's inline comments, reviews, and conversation comments, cross-checked twice), and its GraphQL review thread reports `isResolved: false`.

## Still-live evidence (current main, verified 2026-11-06)

- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/registry.go`, `callWithLedger` (~line 2330): on a post-dispatch error it records an unknown outcome whenever `!toolReadOnly(p, tool)` — and `toolReadOnly` (~line 2309) classifies solely from cached tool annotations (`policy.Classify(candidate.Annotations).ReadOnly`), treating missing annotations as a write.
- `registry.go` contains no use of the operator declaration at all (zero occurrences of `declaredReadOnly` in the file).
- The declaration helper does exist and is used elsewhere: `pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/consumer.go` defines `declaredReadOnly(server, tool)` (~line 446) and applies it in `confirmDestructive` and in the gate classification — exactly the "gate and existing-block exemption" surfaces the reviewer named — but the post-dispatch ledger path in `registry.go` never consults it.
- Net effect, as the reviewer described: an operator-declared read-only search (e.g. `fff.grep`, declared in `home/common/mcpx-settings.nix`) that times out or disconnects after dispatch returns `ErrUnknownOutcome` and persists a server-wide unknown-outcome block on subsequent non-read-only calls until manually cleared.

## Acceptance criteria

- `callWithLedger`'s unknown-outcome classification also honors the requested server's operator-declared `readOnlyTools` (e.g. via the existing `declaredReadOnly` helper), so a declared read-only tool's post-dispatch timeout/disconnect does not record an unknown outcome or persist a block.
- A regression test covers the declared-read-only + post-dispatch failure case (and the annotation-only behavior for undeclared tools is unchanged).
- Or: the finding is resolved by a documented decision on this issue explaining why the ledger path must remain annotation-only.

body:
# id(world_presentation): parse_surface collapses duplicate JSON keys before its checks — a forbidden version, width, lines, or rows hidden behind a duplicate is accepted

## Summary

`parse_surface` (`pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/world_presentation.rs:419`) is the gate that decides whether a world program's view output is a valid `text/1` or `screen/1` presentation — the module's contract is that guests never supply terminal escapes, control characters, or unsupported versions, and every presenter (`web/world_ws.rs:182`, `world/actor.rs:1473`, `world_session/mod.rs:2404`, the native shell) trusts its verdict.

It parses the guest document into a `serde_json::Value` first (`world_presentation.rs:420`), dispatches on `value.get("kind")`, and only then converts the already-collapsed value into `TextPayload` / `ScreenPayload` (`:428`, `:445`). Duplicate JSON keys therefore collapse last-wins **before** any check runs: the version gate (`:431`, `:448`), the width validation in `TextSurface::with_width`, the control-character rejection, and the screen row/shape checks only ever see the surviving value. A document whose raw form carries a forbidden value is accepted as long as a benign duplicate follows it.

This is the same defect class as #6473 (`world::parse_records`) and #6474 (`world_fixture::decode`) in sibling guest-facing parsers; `parse_surface` is the remaining presentation-path instance. The in-tree tests cannot express it: they build documents via `serde_json::json!` values (world_presentation.rs tests, `fn screen(value: Value)`), which cannot represent duplicate keys.

## Verified (laptop, origin/main 49797dfd49, probe `~/git/fleet/probe-surface-dup`, real id crate, 1 test passed)

Controls — each single-key invalid form is rejected:

- `{"kind":"text","version":99,"lines":["hi"]}` → Err (unsupported version)
- `{"kind":"text","version":1,"width":0,"lines":["hi"]}` → Err (zero width)
- `{"kind":"text","version":1,"lines":["<ESC>[31mred"]}` → Err (control character)
- `{"kind":"screen","version":99,"width":2,"height":1,"rows":["hi"]}` → Err
- `{"kind":"screen","version":1,"width":2,"height":1,"rows":["toolong"]}` → Err

Duplicate-key forms — every one is **accepted** (`Ok(Some(..))`):

- `{"kind":"text","version":99,"version":1,"lines":["hi"]}` → Text
- `{"kind":"text","version":1,"width":0,"width":80,"lines":["hi"]}` → Text
- `{"kind":"text","version":1,"lines":["<ESC>[31mred"],"lines":["clean"]}` → Text
- `{"kind":"screen","version":99,"version":1,"width":2,"height":1,"rows":["hi"]}` → Screen
- `{"kind":"screen","version":1,"width":2,"height":1,"rows":["toolong"],"rows":["hi"]}` → Screen
- `{"kind":"screen","kind":"text","version":1,"lines":["hi"]}` → Text (the kind dispatch itself is last-wins)

## Why it matters

- The version field is the format's compatibility gate: a document that declares an unsupported version anywhere in its raw form is not a v1 document, yet it is admitted as one. Any other reader of the same bytes — a stricter parser, a journal replay, a second implementation — sees a different document than the presenter rendered.
- The hidden values are exactly the ones this module exists to exclude (control characters/escape bytes, zero width, malformed rows). Acceptance depends on key order in a way no other pkgs/id guest parser permits after #6473/#6474.
- `parse_surface` is the single choke point for guest views on the web, SSH/session, and native-shell presenters, so one fix here closes the presentation path.

## Acceptance criteria

- `parse_surface` rejects any `kind: text` / `kind: screen` document containing a duplicate key at any level it inspects (top level at minimum), instead of collapsing last-wins.
- Regression tests use raw string literals (not `serde_json::json!`) covering at least: duplicate `version` (text and screen), duplicate `width`, duplicate `lines` carrying a control character, duplicate `rows`, and duplicate `kind`.
- All previously valid documents still parse identically (existing world_presentation, world_session, sandbox, and native-shell tests green).
- Related: #6473, #6474 (same class, sibling parsers), #2339 (text/1 presentation contract).

body:
# id(world_fixture): `decode` accepts duplicate JSON fields in header and event lines — `check_keys` and the window check only ever see the collapsed last value

## Summary

`world_fixture::decode` (`pkgs/id/src/world_fixture.rs:558`) is documented as "Parse a fixture, refusing anything it cannot replay faithfully", and its field discipline is strict on purpose: `check_keys` (`:1284`) requires **exactly** the expected fields per line — no unknown ones, none missing — and `check_window` (`:1350`) requires sequenced events to be contiguous and within the header's sequence. But both the header (`decode_header`, `:1106`) and every event line (`decode_event`, `:1195`) are first parsed with `serde_json::from_str::<Value>` (`:1108`, `:1199`), and serde_json's `Value` object is last-wins for duplicate keys. By the time `check_keys` runs, a duplicated field has already collapsed to one — so a line that names the same field twice with **different** values is accepted, and the value that survives is whichever came last:

| # | Line shape | Result today | What should happen |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | header with `"world":"first","world":"second"` | `Ok`, `world_id = "second"` | an ambiguous header is refused — the fixture names two worlds |
| 2 | header with `"fixture":99,"fixture":1` | `Ok` (version check sees 1) | the version gate (`:1124`) must see the duplication, not just the surviving value: as written, an unsupported version is hidden in plain sight |
| 3 | chat event with `"sequence":99,"sequence":1` under a header at sequence 1 (complete) | `Ok` | the window check (`check_window`) validates the collapsed sequence; the raw line claimed an out-of-window sequence first and is not a faithful record of any session |
| 4 | header `records` object with a repeated record key | collapsed once by the `Value` parse, then re-serialized (`:1170`) and collapsed **again** inside `parse_records` | refused at the first parse (see companion issue for the `parse_records` side) |

This is the same silent-discard class as #6390 (atlas-eval duplicate results key) and #6384 (deploy.py duplicate registry keys): in a format whose whole purpose is faithful replay (`verify` replays a fixture twice and compares records after every event), an ambiguous line must be a parse error, not a coin the parser flips silently.

## Evidence

Verified this run on the laptop at origin/main `252d430853` with a probe integration test against the real `id` crate (`~/git/fleet/probe-records-dup/pkgs/id/tests/probe_fixture_dup.rs`, worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-records-dup` @252d430853):

- Control: minimal valid fixture (header, `current_sequence` 0, complete, no events) decodes, `world_id = "w"`.
- Case 1: duplicate `world` → `Ok`, `world_id = "second"`.
- Case 2: duplicate `fixture` version (99 then 1) → `Ok`.
- Case 3: duplicate event `sequence` (99 then 1) → `Ok`; the window check passes on the surviving value.

Probe result: 1 passed (all three bug cases reproduce; control behaves).

Code read @252d430853: `decode_header` at `world_fixture.rs:1106` parses `serde_json::from_str(line)` into a `Value`, then `check_keys` over the collapsed map (`:1132`); `decode_event` at `:1195` does the same per event line (`:1199`, `check_keys` at `:1209`/`:1225`/`:1243`/`:1263`); scalar fields are then read with `u64_field`/`string_field`/`bool_field` from the collapsed map. No duplicate detection in either function. The in-tree tests exercise `check_keys` for unknown/missing fields, which duplicates structurally evade.

## Why it matters

Fixtures are the determinism oracle for world programs: `verify`'s verdict is only meaningful if the fixture text denotes exactly one session. A fixture format that silently resolves contradictory fields lets a hand-edited or corrupted fixture (the exact inputs `decode`'s strictness exists to catch — unknown fields, gaps, blank lines are all refused) replay as a different session than the one its text first describes, and lets the version gate be satisfied by a line that also declares an unsupported version. Every other strictness rule in this decoder is defeated the same way if the field it checks can be duplicated.

## Acceptance criteria

- `decode` refuses any header or event line whose JSON object contains a duplicate field, with an error naming the line and the repeated field (line context follows the existing "fixture line {n}" convention).
- All three shapes above are refused; the version, world, and sequence checks operate on a document known to name each field at most once.
- Valid fixtures are unchanged: the existing `world_fixture` tests (encode/decode round-trips of every kind, window checks, key checks) still pass, and `encode` output always decodes.
- New tests pin duplicate-field refusal for the header and for at least one event kind.
- The header `records` field: a repeated record key inside it is refused here as a duplicate field of the records object (not merely by whatever `parse_records` does after re-serialization) — coordinate with the companion `parse_records` issue so the two fixes agree on where nested duplicates are caught.

## Problem

Every Muse queue-worker lane (code, opencode, openchamber, nix) begins its shift by reading the shared instruction file `lane-shift-instruction.md` (tracked in hatch-personal: `workspace/goals/keep-the-four-repos-healthy/hidden_files/lane-shift-instruction.md`; read by workers at `~/workspace/goals/keep-the-four-repos-healthy/hidden_files/lane-shift-instruction.md`).

From ~2026-11-05 11:43 CST (last success) through 2026-11-06 00:15 CST, lane workers' reads of that file were returned with a runtime prompt-injection safety failure, and the workers (correctly, per policy) refused to execute it. Result: nix lane A reached consecutive-failure 20, openchamber A/B and opencode A failed every run in the window; the queues were stalled on the instruction file alone. (One run in the window, openchamber A 23:35, got past the read — the check is non-deterministic — then failed on the separate queue-backend outage, #6450.)

## Root cause

Two passages in the file match the injection-check categories: (1) the GitHub-access section phrased Drew's standing authorization as an approval-disabling imperative (pre-authorized: never pause/park/escalate to ask approval); (2) the rate-limit fallback section framed the ratified App-token/outbox fallback as bold imperatives (mint a token, do NOT just save the text). The content was legitimate standing orders; the phrasing tripped the checker. The file content had not changed since the 2026-11-04 20:50 UTC autocommit snapshot.

## Fix (2026-11-06, Drew-approved: edit the repo copy, deploy to the backend path)

Both passages rewritten in the repo copy with provenance framing (the claimed queue task is the work order; Drew's ratified fallback, same write via the fleet's other authorized actor), mechanics unchanged. New sha256 7bed0ff7b07ee6d9851bcfd2c1efb1f84cb44c2bc553c7dca4da993ea4479a9d (12,166 bytes; was 7b5b3c80..., 12,098). The backend path resolves to the same tracked file; hash verified identical via both paths.

## Verification

- Manual verification run of repo-queue-worker-shift-nix (run 53e0bf8b, 2026-11-06 00:32 CST): the worker read the file IN FULL and executed its gate — the safety halt is gone. The run then failed only on the queue-backend outage (#6450): PostgREST timeouts, one claim attempt returned HTTP 522 with unverified outcome (check for a claimed row by repo-worker-nix/nix-a before re-claiming once the backend recovers).

body:
## Problem

Tasks in `agent.tasks` can die **silently at their attempt cap**: they sit in `queued` forever, unclaimable, invisible to terminal-state counts, with no `failed` event. Measured 2026-11-06 (dead-at-cap evaluation): in queue `repo-health-code-pilot`, **142 of 172 `queued` tasks have `attempts >= max_attempts`** and can never be claimed again. Only 2 tasks in the whole queue are in terminal `failed`.

## Root cause (in the queue's own SQL, `pm-stack/opencode-claimant/migration-0023.sql`)

- `claim_repo_task` increments `attempts` at claim time and only selects `queued` rows with `attempts < max_attempts`.
- `fail_repo_task` is the only path that marks a task `failed` at cap — but it only runs when a worker actively calls fail.
- `expire_leases()` returns a claimed task to `queued` when its lease lapses **without checking attempts**. So every claim that evaporates (bound session never launches, lane dies, backend flaps, quota wall kills the session) burns exactly one attempt and, at the cap, parks the task in `queued` permanently: never claimable, never failed, no terminal event.

Worked example: task 9553 (triage for #5459) burned 24/24 attempts on documented claim→handoff→evaporation cycles (agent notes on #5459, 2026-11-05 17:43Z → 2026-11-06 02:31Z) without the work ever being attempted.

## Fix shapes (either or both)

1. `expire_leases`: when the expiring claim's task is already at `attempts >= max_attempts`, transition it to `failed` (with a `lease_expired_at_cap` event) instead of `queued` — mirror `fail_repo_task`'s terminal branch.
2. A reaper in the fleet monitor's dead-in-queue pass that terminally dispositions `queued` rows at cap (it already detects them — it currently only raises caps, which feeds the same burn loop when the underlying launch failure persists).

Also worth deciding while here: whether claim-time `attempts` increment is the right accounting for claims that never bind a session (a `bind` that never happens arguably shouldn't consume the budget the cap is meant to enforce).

## Evidence

- Census (Management API SQL, 2026-11-06): queued at-cap 142/172 · parked at-cap 29/163 (parked is not attempt-gated) · blocked at-cap 17/231 · failed total 2.
- Full evaluation: dead-at-cap report, 2026-11-06 (scratch/dead-at-cap-evaluation-2026-11-06/report.md in the ops workspace).
- Related: #5459 (task 9553), #6462 (the clippy campaign that sat untouched behind this).

## Acceptance criteria
- expire_leases (or an equivalent reaper) transitions a queued task whose expiring claim is already at attempts >= max_attempts to a terminal failed state with a lease_expired_at_cap event, instead of returning it to queued.
- The claim-accounting question is decided and recorded on this issue: whether a claim that never binds a session should consume attempt budget.
- A regression test or migration-level verification covers the at-cap expiry path, and the 142 silent zombies in repo-health-code-pilot are dispositioned (failed, requeued with a fresh packet, or explicitly kept) with the count recorded.

body:
## Problem

`Registry::publish` (`pkgs/id/src/publications.rs:226`) is the one placement comparison in the module that does **not** compare by the mount a record actually names.

`publish` canonicalises the incoming path mount, then checks whether the placement is taken with raw equality (line 242):

```rust
.any(|existing| existing.placement == publication.placement)
```

Its two sibling operations were both fixed to compare by normalised spelling, because records can exist in the registry that bypassed `publish()` — the field is `pub` (`publications: Vec<Publication>`, line ~129), and the module's own tests simulate such records with direct pushes:

- `unpublish` (line 269) normalises both the wanted placement and every stored placement (`normalise_mount_spelling`, lines 281/293), with the comment: a record stored under a non-canonical spelling "must still be removable by its canonical name".
- `boot_warnings` (line 307) shadow-matches on `normalise_mount_spelling(path)` (line 318), because a stored `//world` "is the `/world` mount".
- `normalise_mount_spelling` itself (line 168) exists, per its doc comment, "so records that bypassed `publish()` (hand-edited files, direct `publications` pushes) still compare and shadow-match by the placement they actually name, not by their raw spelling: `//world` is the `/world` mount, and `/api/` is `/api`."

`publish`'s taken-placement check never got the same treatment, and no test covers it.

## Verified behaviour (code read @ main `917e1a3bdb`, logic trace against the in-tree tests)

1. Direct-push a record the way the module's own tests do (lines 601/675/688): `registry.publications.push(mount("/arena/", false))` — a non-shadow mount, so nothing else interferes.
2. `registry.publish(mount("/arena", false), KNOWN_EXPLORER_ROUTES)`:
   - the incoming path canonicalises to `/arena`;
   - the taken check compares `PathMount { path: "/arena/" } == PathMount { path: "/arena" }` → `false`, so the "placement already published" refusal does not fire;
   - the shadow check finds no shadow for `/arena`;
   - the record is pushed (line 260). The registry now holds **two publications for the same mount**, contradicting `publish`'s own contract: "one program per placement — a second publish must unpublish first, never silently replace".
3. The resulting state is also one the persistence layer refuses to restore: `save()` writes both records, and `load()` → `validate_persisted` (line 391) rejects the non-canonical `/arena/` spelling (and would reject the duplicate) — so a registry `publish` happily built fails loudly on the next boot, instead of the duplicate being refused at publish time.

The same trace holds for `//world` vs `/world` (with the shadow acknowledgement set) and `/games//arena` vs `/games/arena`.

Note the laptop was unreachable during the filing run (agent proxy `proxy closed during CONNECT`, real SSH closed), so no compiled probe was run; the verification is the code read above plus the module's own tests, which pin every premise: direct pushes are a supported state (tests at lines 601/675/688), `normalise_mount_spelling("/api/") == "/api"` semantics (test at line 688), and canonicalisation of `/arena/` being refused as a *stored* spelling while `publish` canonicalises its input (tests at lines 456-466, 660-673).

## Why it matters

`publish` is the write-side guard for the one-program-per-placement invariant (#2147). The two read/remove-side operations already assume non-canonical records can be present; the write side assuming they cannot is exactly how a duplicate mount enters the set — and it then either double-binds at runtime apply or makes the persisted registry unloadable at boot. This is the publish-side counterpart of closed #5179 (load-side: `Registry::load` restores records `publish()` would refuse).

## Acceptance criteria

- `publish`'s taken-placement check compares path mounts by normalised spelling (the same `normalise_mount_spelling` comparison `unpublish` uses), so publishing `/arena` refuses when a stored `/arena/`, `//arena`, or equivalent spelling already names that mount — and vice versa.
- Listener placements keep exact `SocketAddr` equality.
- Regression tests: publish-after-direct-push duplicates are refused for at least a trailing-slash spelling and a doubled-separator spelling, on both a plain mount (e.g. `/arena`) and an acknowledged shadow mount (e.g. `/world`); a publish of a genuinely different mount after a direct push still succeeds.
- Existing publications tests keep passing (`cargo test -p id publications` or the crate's equivalent CI check).
