body:
# id(world/signed): `sign_move` never checks `world_id` or `input` against the acceptance domain — a move for a blank world, or with an empty input, signs Ok yet no world can ever accept it

## Summary

`crate::world::signed::sign_move` (`pkgs/id/src/world/signed.rs:67`) is the player-side signing entry point for world moves (#2814): the player signs each move with their own key before submitting it, and the world verifies at the input seam. It forwards `world_id` and `input` to `chain::sign` after no domain check of its own — `chain::sign` validates only the extension shape and the seq/backlink pairing. Two values that the acceptance side refuses unconditionally therefore sign Ok:

1. **A blank `world_id`** (`""`, `" "`, `"   "`, `"\t"`). `WorldCore::new_with_clock` refuses any world whose ID is empty once trimmed — `ensure!(!world_id.trim().is_empty(), "world ID must not be empty")` (`pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs:291`) — so no world can ever bear a blank ID. `sign_move` hashes whatever string it is given into the signed extension's group (`world_group`, signed.rs:53), producing a well-formed, signature-valid move for a world that cannot exist.
2. **An empty `input`**. `sign_move` signs it Ok, but the resulting header carries **no payload hash at all** (`payload_hash: None` — an empty body is no body to the header builder), so `MoveChain::verify`'s commitment check (`payload_hash == Some(Hash::digest(input))`, signed.rs:154) refuses the move with the misleading reason "signed move does not commit to the submitted input bytes" — the signature is genuine; the move is simply uncommittable. And the production path never gets that far: `WorldCore::prepare_input_signed` (core.rs:1925) refuses empty input *before* verify — `ensure!(!input.is_empty(), "world input must not be empty")` (core.rs:1938; the unsigned `prepare_input` has the same rule at core.rs:2042).

In both cases signing succeeds silently and the failure only surfaces later, detached from the mistake — the same dead-on-arrival pattern as #6422 / #6424 / #6434 / #6441 / #6443 in sibling `sign_*` entry points. For the blank world the gap is widest: `MoveChain::verify` (signed.rs:154) happily verifies the move against the same blank ID, so the refusal lives only in `WorldCore`'s constructor, which the signing side never consults.

## Evidence (main @ 9e20032d0c, laptop probe with the real `id` crate)

Probe: laptop worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-sign-move-wt` at origin/main 9e20032d0c, integration test `pkgs/id/tests/probe_sign_move.rs` (real crate, `cargo test --test probe_sign_move`):

- Acceptance-side oracles: `WorldCore::new("", WorldLimits::default())` errs; `WorldCore::new("   ", …)` errs; `WorldCore::new("ttt", …)` is Ok.
- Control: `sign_move(key, "ttt", 0, None, b"cell-0")` signs Ok and `MoveChain::verify` accepts it.
- Blank worlds: `sign_move` returns Ok for `""`, `" "`, `"   "`, `"\t"`, and `MoveChain::verify` against the same ID also returns Ok for each — a move that verifies in isolation yet can never be accepted by any `WorldCore`.
- Empty input: `sign_move(key, "ttt", 0, None, b"")` returns Ok with `header.payload_hash = None`; `MoveChain::verify(…, b"", …)` returns Err("signed move does not commit to the submitted input bytes") — and `prepare_input_signed` would refuse the empty input at core.rs:1938 before verify in any case. Probe test result: 1 passed.

Code reads (origin/main 9e20032d0c):

- `pkgs/id/src/world/signed.rs:67-91` — `sign_move` builds `ChainExt { kind: MOVE_KIND, group: Some(world_group(world_id)), … }` and calls `chain::sign` with `Some(input)`; no check on `world_id` or `input`.
- `pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs:291` — the world-ID domain rule at construction.
- `pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs:1934-1949` — `prepare_input_signed` checks `input.len() <= limits.input_bytes` and `!input.is_empty()` before `chain.verify(signed_move, &self.world_id, input, &author)`.

Out of scope, deliberately: input *length* is per-world (`limits.input_bytes`, default 16 KiB) and `sign_move` cannot know the target world's limit, so no length claim is made here; seq/backlink consistency is already refused by `chain::sign`.

## Why it matters

Signed moves are the evidence base for match attestation (#2814, #3792): a witness replays both players' signed move logs. A signing API that mints signature-valid moves outside the acceptance domain pushes a preventable, deterministic failure to the worst place — submission/replay time, where it reads as a broken move rather than a caller bug at the signing call. Every sibling `sign_*` surface in pkgs/id that has been audited for this pattern now refuses at sign time (artifact #5623 symmetry, currency #6422, attestation #6424/#6441, match_audit #6434, directory_auth #6443); `sign_move` is the remaining one whose acceptance domain is stated in the same crate and ignored.

## Acceptance criteria

- `sign_move` refuses a `world_id` that is empty or whitespace-only, matching the `WorldCore` construction rule (core.rs:291), with an error that names the rule; it refuses an empty `input`, matching `prepare_input_signed` / `prepare_input` (core.rs:1938 / :2042).
- Pinning tests cover at least: `""`, `" "` and `"\t"` world IDs refused; empty input refused; the control move (`"ttt"`, `b"cell-0"`) still signs and passes `MoveChain::verify`; existing seq/backlink refusals from `chain::sign` unchanged.
- Triage decides whether `MoveChain::verify` should also refuse the same values (defense in depth for the witness-replay path, #4346) — the sign-side refusal is the minimum fix.
- `cargo test -p id --lib world` (or the world test module's filter) passes on the laptop / in CI.

Related: #2814 (signed move capture), #3792 / #4346 (attestation + signed-move ingest), #5711 (the same "names no world can bear" pattern on the serve side). Sibling sign-domain issues: #6422, #6424, #6434, #6441, #6443.

## Parent and context
Parent program: #5678. Object model: #2048. This ticket designs an honest, recoverable OneNote import path into the ID knowledge layer; it does not implement the importer or promise source fidelity that the available export/API cannot provide.

## Scope
- Investigate supported OneNote export/API paths, account/edition prerequisites, format coverage, size/rate limits, and whether notebooks, sections, and pages can be enumerated and retrieved reliably.
- Specify mapping for notebook/section/page hierarchy, text and formatting, embedded files/images, links, tags, tables, and available ink/handwriting/OCR data into the #2048 object model. Explicitly distinguish preserved, transformed, omitted, and inaccessible information.
- Define link and attachment handling, provenance, stable identity, duplicate detection, repeat/incremental import, partial-failure recovery, and safe conflict behavior.
- Provide an honest, per-item fidelity report that users can inspect before/after import; where the source/API cannot expose data, state the limit and a viable user-facing fallback instead of implying full fidelity.
- Define a representative source/test corpus and measurable checks for hierarchy, page content, media, links, fidelity reporting, repeat imports, and failure recovery.

## Read-authority constraint (already ruled; do not re-litigate)
ID knowledge defaults to public read, owners may grant read to any number of groups and/or users, and resolution order is **object → user default → server config → public**. State how source permissions are mapped or disclosed when they cannot be represented. Every imported ID object must follow this order, and import/search/preview paths must not expose content outside the resolved readable set.

## Open Drew-owned program questions — still open, not assumptions
Do not guess the product versions/editions to inventory (free vs. paid), hands-on vs. documentation-only evaluation budget, identity of “Open Knowledge,” graph scope (all ID objects vs. knowledge-only in v1), or AI-over-notes model choice (local, hosted, or user choice) and its authority implications. Record which affect OneNote source access, fidelity, testing, and scope; surface the others as parent-level open questions rather than deciding them.

## Acceptance criteria
- The design compares viable acquisition paths and records their current limits/prerequisites.
- Every supported content type has an explicit mapping or documented fidelity limitation, with a user-visible fidelity report and safe recovery/re-import behavior.
- It defines a test corpus and objective checks, explicitly complies with the ruled read-authority order, and leaves unresolved parent-level choices visible.

title: fleet(queue): packet string fields and string-list elements are never type-checked — body, problem, evidence & friends accept numbers/objects and are forwarded verbatim

body:
## Problem

`validate_packet` in the fleet-queue crate type-checks some packet fields but not the packet's string fields or string-list elements. A packet whose top-level `body` is a number/object/array/bool, whose payload `problem` or `priority_reason` is a number/object/array, whose `evidence` / `acceptance` / `tests` / `context_refs` lists contain numbers, `null`s, objects, bools, or nested arrays, whose `scope.include` / `scope.exclude` / `risk.flags` lists contain non-strings, or whose `dedupe.checked_at` / `dedupe.basis` are numbers validates with **zero errors and zero warnings** — and `task_from_packet` forwards every one of those values verbatim into the `agent.tasks` row the broker inserts on `/enqueue`. The queue worker and every packet consumer downstream then read strings that are not strings.

This is the same shape-vs-type gap #5549 fixed for packet *identity* (placeholder `prs` elements like `[null]`, `[{"number": "5424"}]`, `[{}]` used to pass on the array being non-empty alone). The identity fields got element-type checks; the prose fields never did.

## Evidence (all at origin/main `a2b4345e80`; `validate.rs` md5-identical in the laptop primary, origin, and the probe copy)

- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/validate.rs:38-46` — `is_empty()` returns `false` for any number/bool value, so a non-string can never be "empty".
- `validate.rs:72-76` — payload `problem` / `priority_reason` are checked only with `is_empty(...)`: `problem: 123` and `problem: {"x": 1}` pass.
- `validate.rs:77-88` — payload `evidence` / `acceptance` / `tests` / `context_refs` are checked only for being a list (and, for the first three, non-empty). Element types are never inspected: `evidence: [123]`, `[null]`, `[{"x": 1}]`, `tests: [["t"]]` all pass.
- `validate.rs:91-94` and `:101-103` — `scope.include` and `risk.flags` get the same list-only check; `scope.exclude` gets only the `is_empty` check: `[123]` passes everywhere.
- `validate.rs:115-116` — `dedupe.checked_at` / `dedupe.basis` are checked only with `!is_empty(...)`: the number `123` passes for both.
- `validate.rs:467-474` — top-level `body` is read only `if let Some(Value::String(body))`, for the >250-word warning. A non-string `body` skips even that; an empty-string `body` passes silently too (contrast `title` at `validate.rs:~455`, which is required to be a non-empty string — the probe's `title: 123` control correctly errors).
- `validate.rs:521` — `task_from_packet` copies `packet.body` verbatim into the task row; the whole payload (with the malformed fields above) is copied verbatim at the same time.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/queue_broker.rs:327-347` — the broker's `/validate` and `/enqueue` both run this same `validate_packet`, and `/enqueue` inserts `task_from_packet`'s output. There is no second, stricter layer for non-CLI callers; the tasks table's `payload` is jsonb, so the database accepts the malformed values as-is.

## Verified this run (laptop probe, real crate)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-queue-body` on the laptop, built against the real `fleet-queue` crate (path dependency, `queue-broker` feature), calling `validate_packet` + `task_from_packet` on an otherwise-valid packet (the same base packet shape the #6426 probe used):

- Control (valid packet): `errors=[] warnings=[]`, fields forwarded as strings.
- Controls that must fail, and do: `title: 123` → `["packet.title: required non-empty string"]`; `evidence: []` → `["payload.evidence: must not be empty"]`.
- All 19 malformed cases returned `errors=[] warnings=[]` and were forwarded verbatim in the task row: `body` = `12345` / `{"x":1}` / `["a"]` / `true` / `""`; `problem` = `123` / `{"x":1}`; `priority_reason` = `["r"]`; `evidence` = `[123]` / `[null]` / `[{"x":1}]`; `acceptance` = `[false]`; `tests` = `[["t"]]`; `context_refs` = `[42]`; `scope.include` = `[123]`; `scope.exclude` = `[123]`; `risk.flags` = `[123]`; `dedupe.checked_at` = `123`; `dedupe.basis` = `123`.

## Why it matters

The packet is the queue's contract: producers are scripts and agents, and a producer bug that emits `evidence: [null]` or `problem: 123` (a JSON-serialization slip, a templating bug) currently enqueues a task that *looks* valid in every listing — the worker only discovers the corruption when it tries to read the evidence/acceptance strings mid-task, if it notices at all. The validator already type-checks `title`, `priority`, `dedupe_key`, `issue.number`, and (since #5549) every `prs` element, precisely so malformed packets die at the producer with an error naming the field. The prose fields are the unguarded remainder of the same contract.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validate_packet` rejects a top-level `body` that is present and not a string, with an error naming `packet.body`; string bodies keep the existing word-count warning behavior.
- `validate_packet` rejects non-string `payload.problem` / `payload.priority_reason` and non-string `payload.dedupe.checked_at` / `payload.dedupe.basis`, with errors naming the field.
- `validate_packet` rejects any non-string element in `payload.evidence`, `payload.acceptance`, `payload.tests`, `payload.context_refs`, `payload.scope.include`, `payload.scope.exclude`, and `payload.risk.flags`, with errors naming the field (index included where the codebase's message style allows).
- Every real packet in the fleet corpus still validates (the #5549 fix verified the same property for identity shapes: 87/87 real `prs` elements already conformed — the fix should re-run that corpus check for the newly typed fields).
- Tests pin each malformed case above plus the valid control, in the style of the existing `validate.rs` tests (`placeholder_identities_do_not_validate`).

## Dedup / relations

- Distinct from #6426 (top-level `not_before` value validation), #6423 (top-level `max_attempts` override), and #6420 (client duration flags): none of them touches field/element *types* in `manual_schema_errors` or the `body` read.
- Precedent, not a duplicate: #5549 (closed) applied exactly this fix class to identity fields only; its rationale — a placeholder that passes shape checks becomes a second, broken identity for the work — applies here to the prose contract.
- Scope is the Rust validator + broker path only (they share `validate_packet`); no SQL or RPC changes are needed.

# fleet(queue): packet `not_before` is never validated — garbage and far-future values are forwarded verbatim, and a far-future task is born unclaimable

## Evidence (verified this run, origin/main `a2b4345e80927cb1d8ac652756cb219b971bf635`)

The top-level packet field `not_before` is the one scheduling field `validate_packet` never looks at:

- **Validator** — `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/validate.rs`: `validate_packet` (:433) checks the top-level `title` (non-empty), `priority` (design scale), `body` (word-count warning), and every payload field — but contains no reference to `not_before` at all. `task_from_packet` (:510) forwards it verbatim at :525: `"not_before": packet.get("not_before").cloned().unwrap_or(Value::Null)`.
- **Broker** — `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/queue_broker.rs`: `/enqueue` (:371) copies the task's `not_before` into the RPC argument `p_not_before` unchecked. The `/park` path (:439-440) does the same for the park verb's `not_before`.
- **Client park flag** — `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/client.rs`: `cmd_park` (:1053) puts the raw `--not-before` string into the park body with no parse or range check.
- **SQL** — `pm-stack/opencode-claimant/migration-0023.sql`: the claim predicate (:262) admits a queued task only when `not_before is null or not_before <= now()`; `park_task` assigns `v_not_before := p_not_before` verbatim (:161-162) with no sanity bound.

Verified on the laptop with a probe crate against the real `fleet-queue` crate from origin/main (probe `~/git/fleet/probe-queue-notbefore`, calling the real `validate_packet` + `task_from_packet`):

| packet `not_before` | validate errors | forwarded task `not_before` |
|---|---|---|
| absent (control) | `[]` | `null` |
| `"2026-11-06T12:00:00Z"` (control) | `[]` | `"2026-11-06T12:00:00Z"` |
| `"9999-01-01T00:00:00Z"` | `[]` | `"9999-01-01T00:00:00Z"` |
| `"banana"` | `[]` | `"banana"` |
| `""` | `[]` | `""` |
| `12345` (number) | `[]` | `12345` |
| `{"x": 1}` (object) | `[]` | `{"x": 1}` |
| `true` (bool) | `[]` | `true` |
| `"2000-01-01T00:00:00Z"` (past) | `[]` | `"2000-01-01T00:00:00Z"` |

Consequences, by value:

- **Far-future valid timestamp** (e.g. `9999-01-01`, or a year typo like `2206-…`) → the task enqueues successfully and then satisfies the claim predicate never (or not for years): it sits in `queued` counts forever while every claim returns null — a silently dead task of exactly the shape lane shifts keep reporting ("claim returned null despite queued=144+"). Sibling of #6423's born-unclaimable `max_attempts <= 0`, through a different field.
- **Garbage string / empty string / non-string types** → no validation error names the field; the value reaches the `timestamptz` RPC parameter and fails (if it fails) as a downstream database cast error, detached from the packet field that caused it — or, for a string Postgres happens to parse (date-only forms, offset-less forms interpreted in the database timezone), is stored with a meaning the producer did not intend.
- **Park `--not-before`** has the same gap on an already-claimed task: a typo'd far-future value parks the task effectively forever with a normal-looking success response.

## Relation to existing issues

- #6423 covers top-level `max_attempts` (never validated, overrides the validated payload value). This is the same validator's other unexamined top-level field, with a different failure mode (scheduling instead of attempt counting).
- #6420 covers the duration flags (`--lease-seconds` / `--extend-seconds` / `--delay-seconds`); the park `--not-before` timestamp flag was not in its scope.

## Why it matters

Every producer (creators, pr-diff-review, curators, sweeps) enqueues through this validator, and `not_before` is the field producers use to defer work. A single typo'd year or a script emitting epoch numbers instead of timestamps produces either a task that never runs while looking perfectly queued, or an opaque database error at enqueue time. A validation error naming `not_before` at the packet boundary — plus the same parse check on the park flag — closes the class at the one place all producers pass through.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `validate_packet` rejects a top-level `not_before` that is not a string, is empty, or does not parse as an RFC 3339 timestamp, with an error naming `packet.not_before`.
- [ ] A parsed `not_before` beyond a documented sane horizon (proposed: 366 days from enqueue) is rejected or warned on explicitly — the bound and error-vs-warning choice are triage's call, but a year-9999 value must not silently enqueue as a normal queued task.
- [ ] `repo-queue park --not-before <garbage>` is rejected with a usage error naming `--not-before` (exit 2), consistent with the #5939 non-numeric rejection; valid timestamps park exactly as before.
- [ ] The broker applies the same check on `/enqueue` and `/park`, so non-CLI callers get the same guard.
- [ ] Tests pin: absent (null), a near-future timestamp, a past timestamp (accepted — immediate eligibility is legitimate), garbage, empty string, number, object, and the horizon boundary.

body:
## Problem

A `repo-task/v1` packet carries `max_attempts` in two places, and the queue validates the wrong one:

- `payload.max_attempts` is schema-validated: `manual_schema_errors` (pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/validate.rs:108) requires it to be a positive integer.
- The **top-level** `packet.max_attempts` is never read by `validate_packet` (validate.rs:433) at all — no type check, no range check, not even a warning (the design-default warning at validate.rs:492 also reads only the payload copy).
- But `task_from_packet` (validate.rs:510-518) prefers the top-level field over the payload one:

```rust
let max_attempts = packet
    .get("max_attempts")
    .filter(|v| !v.is_null())
    .or_else(|| payload.get("max_attempts"))
    .cloned()
    .unwrap_or(json!(4));
```

- The queue broker then forwards that value verbatim as `p_max_attempts` to the enqueue RPC (pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/queue_broker.rs:347, :372).

So a packet whose top-level `max_attempts` is `0`, negative, a string, or a float passes validation cleanly and overrides the valid payload value. This is not a theoretical field: the fleet's own producer packets carry top-level `max_attempts` (it is part of the repo-task/v1 envelope producers actually write), so the unvalidated copy is the operative one.

Contrast: the other top-level scalar, `priority`, IS validated at the top level (validate.rs:451-466, design-scale check). `max_attempts` is the odd one out.

## Verified this run (laptop, origin/main a2b4345e80)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-queue-maxattempts` — a crate calling the real `fleet-queue` crate's `validate_packet` + `task_from_packet` (extracted from origin/main, compiled and run on the laptop). A fully valid packet (payload `max_attempts: 4`) with variants:

| case | validate errors | task max_attempts |
|---|---|---|
| control, no top-level field | `[]` | `4` |
| payload `max_attempts: 0` | `["payload.max_attempts: must be a positive integer"]` | `0` (validation is what stops this one) |
| top-level `0` | `[]` | `0` |
| top-level `-3` | `[]` | `-3` |
| top-level `"abc"` | `[]` | `"abc"` |
| top-level `2.5` | `[]` | `2.5` |
| top-level `1000000` | `[]` | `1000000` |

## Why it matters

- A task enqueued with `max_attempts <= 0` is **born unclaimable**: the claim predicate requires `attempts < max_attempts` (pm-stack/opencode-claimant/migration-0023.sql:103 and :261), which is false at `attempts = 0`. The task sits at `status = queued` forever, invisible to every claim, while health counts it as available work — the same silent-stall symptom as #2937, except those tasks exhausted their attempts legitimately; these never had a first attempt available. (Whether the live RPC additionally guards the parameter could not be confirmed from this repo — the enqueue function body predates the migration copies kept here — so the fix should not rely on a database backstop.)
- A non-integer top-level value (`"abc"`, `2.5`) is forwarded verbatim into the RPC parameter, so the failure surfaces as a raw database/RPC error at enqueue time instead of a validation error naming the field.
- An unbounded value (e.g. `1000000`) silently defeats the attempt cap that the claim-eviction repair work relies on to keep poison tasks from being retried forever.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `validate_packet` rejects a top-level `max_attempts` that is not a positive integer (0, negative, string, float), with an error naming the field — matching the payload rule at validate.rs:108.
- [ ] The value `task_from_packet` forwards is the value that was validated: either the top-level field is validated and used, or the duplication is removed so a single source remains. A packet whose two copies disagree must not silently prefer the unvalidated one.
- [ ] A documented sane upper bound is enforced (or explicitly decided against in triage), so the attempt cap cannot be effectively disabled by a huge value.
- [ ] Tests pin: top-level 0 / -1 / "abc" / 2.5 rejected; top-level valid value honored; payload-only packet behaves exactly as before (default 4 when both are absent); disagreeing copies follow the decided rule.
- [ ] Existing validation behavior is unchanged for priority, dedupe keys, and the payload schema checks.

Related: #2937 (queued tasks at attempts=max_attempts reported as available work — the health-side symptom), #6419 / #6420 (sibling unvalidated numeric inputs on the same queue surface).

body:
# id(currency): `sign_authorisation` never calls `validate` — a signed authorisation naming another issuer or with `rate_den = 0` is dead on arrival, and signing succeeds silently

## Summary

`pkgs/id/src/currency.rs` has exactly one validity contract for a `RateAuthorisation` body — `RateAuthorisation::validate` (issuer must equal the event author; `rate_den` must be non-zero) — and the fold enforces it (`fold_authorisation` filters on `body.validate(author).is_ok()`, currency.rs:299 at origin/main `a2b4345e80`). But the signing entry point, `sign_authorisation` (currency.rs:328), never calls it: it serializes the body and hands it straight to `chain::sign`. A signer can therefore produce a properly signed, chain-valid event whose body is invalid by the module's own two hard rules, and nothing anywhere will ever fold it as `Live`:

- **Issuer mismatch:** body names issuer B, signed by A. `fold_authorisation(.., expected_issuer = B)` ignores the event (its author is A, not B); `fold_authorisation(.., expected_issuer = A)` drops the body at the `validate` filter (body names B). The signed object is unreachable in every fold.
- **`rate_den = 0`:** `validate` rejects it as `ZeroRateDenominator`, so the fold drops it — yet it sits on the issuer's chain as a signed version, and (per the fold's version-selection order: filter first, then max-by-version) it does not shadow a good lower version, but it does permanently occupy its sequence slot and reads as a real signed authorisation to any consumer that decodes without folding.

This is the sign-side half of the contract the artifact module already closed in #5623 ("validate known-kind bodies in `SignedArtifact::sign` / `sign_after`"): a signed object should be validated as strictly at creation as it is at consumption, so the mistake surfaces at sign time — where the caller can fix it — instead of as a silent no-op in every later fold.

## Evidence (verified this run, origin/main `a2b4345e80`)

- `git grep -n "validate" pkgs/id/src/currency.rs` returns exactly three sites: the definition (currency.rs:153), the fold filter (currency.rs:299), and one test (currency.rs:513). `sign_authorisation` and `sign_revoke` contain no validation call.
- Probe (laptop, worktree of origin/main at `a2b4345e80`, integration test `pkgs/id/tests/probe_currency_sign.rs` in worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-currency-sign-wt`, run with `cargo test --test probe_currency_sign -- --nocapture`): `sign(issuer-mismatch body) -> Ok`, `sign(rate_den=0 body) -> Ok`, `sign(valid body) -> Ok` (control), and the mismatched body folds to `None` for both the signing issuer and the named issuer — dead on arrival, exactly as the code reading predicts. (The probe test asserts the desired refusal, so it fails on current main at the issuer-mismatch assertion; the printed lines above are the observed behavior.)
- Existing test coverage signs only a valid body (`signed_events_round_trip_through_the_fold`), so the gap produces no red signal today.

## Why it matters

`sign_authorisation` is the only sanctioned way to create these objects (Phase 1 of #2290; the conversion engine #5536 builds on it). An LP tool that mis-sets `issuer_id` (e.g. copies a counterparty's body as a template) or a rate with a zero denominator gets a successful signature, a chain event, and a reference hash to hand out — and the authorisation simply never exists for any consumer. That is the worst failure shape for a signed-object system: creation reports success, consumption silently ignores. Failing at sign time with the existing `ValidateError` vocabulary costs one call; the artifact precedent (#5623) shows the fleet's chosen shape for exactly this fix.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `sign_authorisation` refuses a body that `validate` would reject for the signing key's issuer (issuer mismatch, `rate_den = 0`), surfacing the refusal through `SignError` (a new variant wrapping `ValidateError` is fine); no event is produced for an invalid body.
- [ ] Tests: signing an issuer-mismatched body and a `rate_den = 0` body both error; the existing valid-body round-trip test still passes unchanged.
- [ ] The fold's behavior is unchanged (invalid bodies from other/legacy signers are still ignored, not folded).
- [ ] Out of scope: extending `validate`'s rule set — that is #4071, open separately. This issue only enforces the two rules that already exist, at sign time.

## Notes

- Related: #4071 (validate accepts internally inconsistent bodies — the rule-set extension; complementary, not duplicate: it never mentions the sign path, and its fix would not make `sign_authorisation` call `validate`), #5623 (the artifact-module precedent for sign-side validation), #2290 / #5521 (the RateAuthorisation design/implementation this module serves).
- Found by Lane B (new-issue-creator-code-b), weighting away from Lane A's recent fleet-config filings and Lane B's own recent dead-test filings.

# fleet(queue): repo-queue duration flags (`--lease-seconds`, `--extend-seconds`, `--delay-seconds`) accept 0, negative, and unbounded values — a 0/negative lease is born expired, a negative park delay defeats the park

## Evidence (verified this run, origin/main `a2b4345e80927cb1d8ac652756cb219b971bf635`)

None of the three duration flags is range-validated at any layer — client, broker, or SQL:

- **Client** — `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/client.rs`: `parse_i64_flag` (:579) accepts any `i64` (the #5939 fix made non-numeric values a loud error, but range was never checked), and the three call sites send the parsed value verbatim:
  - `cmd_claim` (:906, :912): `"lease_seconds": args.get_i64("lease-seconds").unwrap_or(2700)`
  - `cmd_heartbeat` (:982, :994): `"extend_seconds": args.get_i64("extend-seconds").unwrap_or(900)`
  - `cmd_park` (:1021, :1054): `"delay_seconds": args.get_i64("delay-seconds")`
- **Broker** — `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/queue_broker.rs`: `/claim` (:382-390) copies `lease_seconds` into `p_lease_seconds`, `/heartbeat` (:412-420) copies `extend_seconds` into `p_extend_seconds`, and `/park` (:432-445) copies `delay_seconds` into `p_delay_seconds` — all verbatim, no range check.
- **SQL** — `pm-stack/opencode-claimant/migration-0023.sql`: `claim_repo_task` (:235) takes `p_lease_seconds integer` and sets `lease_until = now() + make_interval(secs => p_lease_seconds)` (:271) with no guard; `park_task` (:150) computes `v_not_before := now() + make_interval(secs => coalesce(p_delay_seconds, 1200))` (:165) the same way. Both parameters are `integer` (int4), so an i64-scale value from the client also overflows at the RPC boundary.

Verified on the laptop with the real `repo-queue` binary (laptop primary build; the lease/extend/delay code paths are byte-identical HEAD..origin/main — the HEAD..origin client.rs diff touches none of them) against a recording stub broker (probe `~/git/fleet/probe-queue-lease`, `REPO_QUEUE_BROKER_URL` direct transport):

| invocation | recorded broker body | exit |
|---|---|---|
| `claim --lease-seconds 0` | `"lease_seconds":0` | 0 |
| `claim --lease-seconds -5` | `"lease_seconds":-5` | 0 |
| `claim --lease-seconds 999999999999` | `"lease_seconds":999999999999` | 0 |
| `claim --lease-seconds 2700` (control) | `"lease_seconds":2700` | 0 |
| `claim --lease-seconds abc` (control, #5939) | — rejected: `argument --lease-seconds: invalid int value "abc"` | 2 |
| `heartbeat 42 --extend-seconds 0` | `"extend_seconds":0` | 0 |
| `heartbeat 42 --extend-seconds -60` | `"extend_seconds":-60` | 0 |
| `heartbeat 42 --extend-seconds 900` (control) | `"extend_seconds":900` | 0 |
| `park 42 --delay-seconds 0` | `"delay_seconds":0` | 0 |
| `park 42 --delay-seconds -3600` | `"delay_seconds":-3600` | 0 |
| `park 42 --delay-seconds 1200` (control) | `"delay_seconds":1200` | 0 |

Consequences, by value:

- **Claim lease 0 / negative** → `lease_until` is `now()` or in the past: the claim succeeds but is born expired, so the task is immediately reclaimable by another worker while the first holder works it — the double-work failure the atomic claim exists to prevent.
- **Claim lease huge** (e.g. `999999999999`, ~31,700 years as i64 seconds) → either overflows the SQL `integer` parameter (a downstream RPC error instead of a usage error naming the flag) or, where it fits, pins the task for effectively ever if the holder dies.
- **Heartbeat extend 0 / negative** → the holder instantly lapses its own claim mid-work: its follow-up verbs fail and the task becomes reclaimable under it — the claim-evaporation pattern, self-inflicted by a typo'd flag.
- **Park delay negative** → `not_before` lands in the past: the "parked" task is immediately claimable, silently defeating gate waits (e.g. a park waiting on a prerequisite issue). Delay 0 is at best a requeue-now that should be a deliberate verb, not a park.

## Relation to #6419

#6419 covers the sibling `list --limit` range gap; its triage packet explicitly scoped this class out with an audit item — "sibling get_i64 flags (--lease-seconds, --extend-seconds, --delay-seconds): validated downstream or needs the same treatment". This issue is that audit's answer: they are **not** validated downstream (client, broker, and SQL evidence above), and the failure modes here are worse than a misreported list — they corrupt claim/lease/park state rather than just a read.

## Why it matters

Every fleet lane drives the queue through these three verbs. The values are one typo or one bad script variable away (`--lease-seconds $EMPTY_OR_ZERO`), the failure is silent (exit 0, normal-looking output), and the resulting states — born-expired claims, self-lapsed heartbeats, un-parked parks — are exactly the divergence classes the fleet monitor then has to reconcile. A usage error naming the flag at the client, plus a broker-side guard (the broker is the trust boundary for non-CLI callers), closes the whole class.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `repo-queue claim --lease-seconds 0` and negative values are rejected with a usage error naming `--lease-seconds` (exit 2), consistent with the #5939 non-numeric rejection; a documented sane maximum is enforced the same way.
- [ ] `repo-queue heartbeat --extend-seconds 0` and negative values are rejected likewise (naming `--extend-seconds`); the absent-flag defaults (claim 2700, heartbeat 900) behave exactly as before.
- [ ] `repo-queue park --delay-seconds` negative values are rejected (naming `--delay-seconds`); the semantics of 0 are decided explicitly (reject, or documented immediate-requeue) and pinned by a test.
- [ ] The broker rejects out-of-range `lease_seconds` / `extend_seconds` / `delay_seconds` before the RPC call, so non-CLI callers get the same guard.
- [ ] Tests pin 0, -1, the maximum, maximum+1, and the defaults for all three flags; the #5939 non-numeric rejection still passes.

# id(web/markdown): the #945 footnote round-trip test never runs — its `#[test]` sits doubled on the next test; five more doubled `#[test]` sites in pkgs/id

## Evidence (verified this run, origin/main `28719695372b`)

`pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs`:

- Line **7055**: `fn test_footnote_roundtrip_fixpoint()` — the regression pin for #945 (a footnote reference + definition round-trip open→save intact, emitted as `[^label]`, never backslash-escaped, second save byte-identical) — carries **no `#[test]` attribute** (line 7053 closes the previous test, 7054 is blank, 7055 is the fn). A repo-wide `git grep` shows its only occurrence is its own definition: it is never called by another test either. It never runs.
- Lines **7088–7089**: the next test, `test_unreferenced_footnote_definition_survives_save` (:7090), carries **two** `#[test]` attributes — the displaced attribute.

Mechanism (proven on the laptop this run for the identical text.rs instance, filed as #6409): a duplicated `#[test]` is only a rustc `duplicated attribute` warning and registers that test **twice**, so the suite stays green, the count looks right, and the attribute-less neighbor is silently dead.

### Five more doubled sites (no dead neighbor found — the test runs twice)

A repo scan for consecutive `#[test]` lines found 7 sites in `pkgs/id`, all on origin/main. Excluding text.rs (#6409) and markdown.rs (above), the remaining five have all their neighboring tests correctly attributed, so the harm there is double execution (wasted CI time; doubled side effects — e.g. cli.rs's test spawns a thread) plus warning noise:

- `pkgs/id/src/cli.rs:3608-3609` — `test_cli_rejects_zero_result_limits`
- `pkgs/id/src/commands/find.rs:1053-1054` — `test_download_output_path_dash_name_is_not_the_stdout_sentinel`
- `pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:3291-3292` — `test_web_content_target_program_rejects_empty_world`
- `pkgs/id/src/repl/runner.rs:1890-1891` — `test_parse_rejects_zero_result_limits`
- `pkgs/id/src/web/templates.rs:1306-1307` — `test_render_program_page_pins_the_world_and_omits_host_controls`

## Why it matters

Same failure class as #6409 / #6185 ("a suite that never runs is not a test"), in the web markdown codec — a surface with a steady stream of round-trip regressions (#945, #998, #1019, #1565, #6364). The #945 pin has been dead for an unknown span: if footnote round-tripping regressed again, no running test would say so. body:
# fleet-config: empty/blank config-file strings are used verbatim — broker_socket="" resolves to the home directory itself, and a blank dispatch url overrides as Some("")

## Summary

`fleet-config` is careful about empty *environment* values: `env_path` filters them out (#5473), and `dispatch_url()`'s own doc says of `FLEET_DISPATCH_URL` that "empty counts as unset, as with every env path here". Empty or blank *config-file* strings get no such treatment: the accessors use them verbatim. A `fleet.toml` with `broker_socket = ""` makes the broker socket path the home directory itself; `token_file = ""` does the same to the secrets token-file path; `[dispatch] url = ""` (or all-whitespace) is returned as a configured URL, `Some("")`; `token_name = ""`, `target_host = ""`, and `connect_udp_listen = ""` likewise surface as empty values instead of their documented defaults.

This breaks the crate's stated config policy (crate docs, lib.rs:14-16): "a malformed file is a loud error, never a silent fallback". An empty string in a path/URL/name field is a misspelling-class error — a templated config rendering a variable that came out empty — and every env-side equivalent in this same crate is already treated as unset for exactly that reason.

Distinct from the filed siblings: #6397 covers `[[proxy.services]]` row values (duplicate/zero ports, empty service names); #6396/#5737 cover env-base resolution. No filed issue covers the scalar string fields of `[proxy]`/`[secrets]`/`[dispatch]`.

## Evidence (file:line, origin/main @ 28719695372b; fleet-config lib.rs is byte-identical between laptop HEAD 1dae17e457 and origin/main, md5-verified this run)

- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs:302-320` — `broker_socket_from`: the env source goes through `env_path` (empty filtered), but `Some(p) => resolve_under(home, &PathBuf::from(p))` for the config value has no empty check; `resolve_under(home, "")` is `home` itself.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs:430-436` — `secrets_token_file`: `Some(p) => resolve_under_home(p)` — same empty-to-home resolution.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs:390-396` — `dispatch_url`: the env branch trims and rejects empty (`Ok(v) if !v.trim().is_empty()`), the config branch is `self.dispatch.url.clone()` verbatim.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs:324-330` — `target_host`: `as_deref().unwrap_or(DEFAULT_TARGET_HOST)` — `Some("")` wins over the default.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs:350-356` — `connect_udp_listen`: same shape against `DEFAULT_CONNECT_UDP_LISTEN`.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs:398-403` — `dispatch_token_name`: same shape against `DEFAULT_DISPATCH_TOKEN_NAME`.
- Contrast inside the same file: `search_url()` (:415-421) and `search_via()` (:406-412) *do* trim/filter their config values — the scalar fields above are the inconsistent remainder.

## Verification (this run, laptop, real fleet-config crate)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-fleet-config-empty-rel` (`cfg` bin; path-depends on the real `fleet-config` crate; `HOME=/home/tester`; each case is a real `Config::load_from` on a written temp `fleet.toml`):

```
empty broker_socket        -> "/home/tester/"     (the home directory itself)
empty secrets token_file   -> "/home/tester/"     (the home directory itself)
empty dispatch url         -> Some("")
blank dispatch url "   "   -> Some("   ")
empty dispatch token_name  -> ""
empty target_host          -> ""
empty connect_udp_listen   -> ""
control broker_socket "sock/b.sock"   -> "/home/tester/sock/b.sock"
control dispatch url "http://127.0.0.1:9" -> Some("http://127.0.0.1:9")
control dispatch token_name "tok.name"  -> "tok.name"
```

Every empty/blank case loads with no error and surfaces the empty value; every control resolves as documented.

## Why it matters

- A templated or generated `fleet.toml` that renders a variable empty (the routine failure the env-side filtering exists for) does not fail loudly: the session broker tries to use the operator's home directory as a Unix socket path, the secrets flow names a directory as its token file, and the dispatch client is handed an empty base URL that outranks the working default — each surfacing later as an opaque connect/read error far from the config mistake, or, for `target_host = ""`, as a dial to an empty host.
- The crate already decided this question for env values and for `[search]`; the remaining fields are an inconsistency, not a design choice.

## Acceptance criteria

- Empty or all-whitespace values for `broker_socket`, `secrets.token_file`, `dispatch.url`, `dispatch.token_name`, `proxy.target_host`, and `proxy.connect_udp_listen` in the config file are either treated as unset (falling back to the documented default, matching the env-side rule) or rejected at load with a loud `ConfigError` — one consistent shape, triage's call.
- No accessor can return the home directory itself as a socket/token-file path, an empty string as a configured dispatch URL, or an empty token name / target host / listen address.
- Pinning tests cover empty and blank spellings for each affected accessor alongside the existing `dispatch_settings_*` / `proxy_settings_*` tests; valid values resolve exactly as before.
- No change to env-var handling (already correct) or to valid configs.

# fleet-config: [[proxy.services]] is never validated — duplicate ports silently collapse last-wins in the broker's routing map, and port 0 / empty names load

## Summary

The `[proxy] services` table is, by the crate's own docs, the proxy's routing table ("the services map IS the routing table"). `fleet-config` loads it with no validation at all: two rows with the same port both load, a row with port 0 loads, and a row with an empty name loads. Downstream, both consumers build the advertised services map by collecting the rows into a `BTreeMap` keyed by port string, so a duplicate port silently collapses — the *last* row wins and the earlier service vanishes from the hello/routing map with no error anywhere.

That breaks the crate's stated config policy (crate docs, lib.rs:14-16): "a malformed file is a loud error, never a silent fallback" — unknown sections and keys are already loud errors for exactly this reason (#5460). A duplicated port is a misspelling-class error with a worse failure mode: instead of a wrong key being ignored, one live service is silently substituted for another in the routing table.

## Evidence (file:line, origin/main @ 967fb229e4)

- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs:146-155` — `ServiceConfig { port: u16, name: String, version: Option<String> }` with `deny_unknown_fields` only; no value validation anywhere.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs:362-…` — `Config::services()` returns `self.proxy.services.clone()` verbatim when non-empty; no duplicate/zero/empty checks.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/serve.rs:370` — `Broker::services_map()` collects `config.services()` into `BTreeMap<String, ServiceInfo>` keyed by `port.to_string()`: duplicate ports collapse, last row wins.
- `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/client.rs:114` — `built_in_services()` builds the legacy/shim services map the same way, so the collapse happens on both the broker and client paths.

## Verification (this run, laptop, real fleet-config crate)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-fleet-config-xdg-rel` (`services` bin; path-depends on the real `fleet-config` crate; the map step mirrors serve.rs:370's collect verbatim):

```
dup-port:            load_ok rows=2 [4801:queue-broker,4801:impostor] map_len=1 map4801=Some("impostor")
port-zero-empty-name: load_ok rows=1 [0:]                             map_len=1
dup-name:            load_ok rows=2 [4801:queue-broker,4999:queue-broker] map_len=2
valid-control:       load_ok rows=1 [4801:queue-broker]               map_len=1 map4801=Some("queue-broker")
```

So a config that names port 4801 twice advertises exactly one service on 4801 — whichever row came last — and a `port = 0, name = ""` row is advertised as `"0": ""`.

## Why it matters

- The services map is the routing table and the shim source: clients negotiate it in the hello and materialize PATH shims from it. A copy-paste duplicate in a host's `fleet.toml` silently re-points a broker port at the wrong service (or drops a service from the map) on that host, with no parse error, no log, and a config file that reads as if both rows are in effect.
- Every other misconfiguration class in this crate was deliberately made loud (#5460 unknown keys, malformed TOML); this one slipped through because serde accepts the shape.

## Acceptance criteria

- `Config::load_from` (or `services()`) rejects a `[[proxy.services]]` table with a duplicate port, a duplicate name, port 0, or an empty/blank name, with a loud `ConfigError` naming the offending row — consistent with the crate's malformed-is-loud policy.
- The duplicate-port case can never reach the `BTreeMap` collect in fleet-proxy: the collapse is impossible by construction, not just unlikely.
- Pinning tests cover duplicate port, duplicate name, port 0, and empty name alongside the existing `services_*` tests in fleet-config; the valid single-row and built-in-default cases stay green.
- No change to the built-in default table or to valid configs.

body:
# worktree-reaper: config is never validated — typo'd `deny_*` keys and string-typed values silently disarm the denylist, and wrong-shaped config crashes with a raw traceback

`infra/worktree-reaper/bin/worktree_reaper.py` is the tool that deletes fleet worktrees (`git worktree remove` + `git branch -d`) on a timer, gated by the safety rules in its header. Its config — the main `config.json` and the `<state_dir>/config.local.json` overlay that `install-units.sh` uses to denylist the install tree — is merged in `load_config` (worktree_reaper.py:99–139) with no validation of any kind: no shape check, no known-key check, no type check. `main` calls it unguarded (:533).

Verified on the laptop at origin/main `cb8eee8d68` (script extracted verbatim; probe `~/git/fleet/probe-reaper-config`, driving the real `load_config` and the real binary):

1. **Typo'd keys are silently accepted, and the denylist silently vanishes.** Config `{"deny_path": ["/home/user/git/important"], "quiet_hour": 24}` loads OK; the effective config keeps `deny_paths == []` and the default `quiet_hours == 6`, plus two stray keys nothing reads. The same holds in the overlay (`{"deny_path": [...]}` → `deny_paths == []`). For a deletion tool, a one-character typo in a deny key converts an explicit "never reap this" into no protection at all, with no message anywhere.
2. **`deny_paths` as a string silently disarms the check.** `{"deny_paths": "/home/user/git/important"}` loads OK and is kept verbatim; `is_denied` (:221) then iterates the string character by character, deriving 24 nonsense one-character "paths" — the intended path is never denied and nothing complains. (`deny_names` as a string similarly turns :229's membership test into a substring test.)
3. **Wrong-shaped config crashes cryptically.** A top-level JSON list or string fails with `ValueError: dictionary update sequence element #0 has length 10; 2 is required` — a message that never mentions the config file or that an object was expected. A top-level list in the overlay fails with `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'items'` (:122–139).
4. **Malformed JSON crashes with a raw traceback.** Running the real binary with `--config bad.json` (contents `{oops`) exits 1 with an uncaught `json.decoder.JSONDecodeError` traceback from `main` → `load_config` (:533) — no `worktree-reaper: cannot load config …` style error, and no run record is written to the state dir's `runs/` log, so the failure is invisible to the tool's own audit trail.
5. **Type errors pass load and explode mid-run.** `{"quiet_hours": "6"}` is accepted verbatim; the run only fails later at the quiet gate (:455, `now - cfg["quiet_hours"] * 3600`) with `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for -: 'int' and 'str'` — after discovery/fetch work has begun, reported (if at all) as a per-tree anomaly rather than a config error.

## Why it matters

Every other gate in this tool is written fail-closed (a failed fetch skips the primary, an unscannable `/proc` is #5740, the kill switch exits 0) — but the config that *parameterizes* those gates, including the operator's explicit denylist, is trusted blindly. The failure modes above split into the two worst kinds for a destructive tool: silent weakening (cases 1–2: the run proceeds and deletes, minus the protection the operator wrote down) and opaque crashing (cases 3–5: the timer unit fails with a traceback that names neither the file nor the key, and the run-log audit trail has no entry). The overlay case is not hypothetical configuration drift: the overlay is a generated file whose entire purpose is to denylist the install tree.

Distinct from #5946 (the reaper's test suite is run by no workflow — CI wiring) and #5740 (fail-closed when `/proc` cannot be scanned). Sibling pattern in a different tool: #6388 (deploy `validate()` crashing on unhashable values instead of reporting them).

## Acceptance criteria

- `load_config` validates both the main config and the overlay before anything is reaped: top level must be a JSON object; unknown keys are rejected (or at minimum reported loudly by name — rejection preferred, matching the fail-closed posture); the known keys are type-checked (`deny_paths`/`deny_prefixes`/`deny_names`/`primaries`/`generated_dirt_*` lists of strings, `quiet_hours`/`max_removals` numbers, `fetch` a boolean, path settings strings).
- Any config problem — malformed JSON, wrong shape, unknown key, wrong type — aborts the run before discovery/removal with a single clear error naming the file, the key where applicable, and what was expected; exit non-zero; no Python traceback.
- The valid-config behavior is byte-identical: the committed `config.json`, the `install-units.sh` overlay merge (deny lists union, scalars override), CLI overrides (`--quiet-hours`, `--max-removals`, `--no-fetch`), and the existing test suite (`infra/worktree-reaper/tests/test_worktree_reaper.py`, 8 tests) all behave exactly as before.
- Regression tests in that suite cover each verified case above: typo'd deny key in config and in overlay, `deny_paths` as a string, top-level list/string in config and overlay, malformed JSON, and string `quiet_hours` — each asserting the clean, naming-the-file error.

body:
# mcpx(gotest-report): an equal-count skip swap silently re-baselines the skip record — a newly skipped test never fails the run if another test is un-skipped in the same run

`pkgs/mcpx/scripts/gotest-report.py` guards the mcpx Go suite against skip creep. Its own docstring (lines 9–13) states the invariant:

> The record lives in a repository variable … A run that skips more tests than the record fails; the newly skipped tests are named. The record only moves down: a run with fewer skips becomes the new ceiling, **so a skip cannot creep back in.**

The count half of that invariant is enforced; the name half is not. `decide()` (gotest-report.py:81–103) only fails the run when `len(skipped) > stored["skipped_count"]` (:99). When the count is **equal but the names differ**, :101–102 returns the current run as the new record:

```python
if len(skipped) < stored["skipped_count"] or skipped != stored.get("skipped"):
    return cur, False, new_names, gone_names
```

and `main()` exits 0 (:189). The workflow then completes the re-baseline: `.github/workflows/mcpx.yml:225–227` saves the new record to the `MCPX_GO_TESTS` variable on main whenever the record file exists and the step's return code is 0. The summary does note "Same number skipped, different tests" (:152–157), but nothing fails, so on main the swap is ratified silently.

## Verified this run (laptop, real reporter)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-gotest-swap/probe.py` on the laptop, driving the real `gotest-report.py` (file unchanged at origin/main `cb8eee8d68`) with synthetic `go test -json` events. Stored record: `skipped_count: 2`, `skipped: [widgets.TestA, widgets.TestB]`.

| case | events | exit | new record written |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **swap** | pass TestGood; skip TestA; skip **TestC** (new) | **0** | **yes — `[widgets.TestA, widgets.TestC]`** |
| increase (control) | skip TestA, TestB, TestC | 1 | no |
| identical (control) | skip TestA, TestB | 0 | no |
| decrease (control) | skip TestA only | 0 | yes — `[widgets.TestA]` (intended lowering) |

So a single change that un-skips one test and newly skips another passes the guard and rewrites the record to include the new skip. The next run then treats that skip as the established ceiling — exactly the creep the docstring says the record exists to prevent. The existing regression suite (`pkgs/mcpx/scripts/test_gotest_report.py`, wired at mcpx.yml:185) covers increase, decrease, identical-by-implication, and the #1973 quarantine exemption, but has no equal-count swap case.

## Why it matters

The skip record is the only automated check standing between "temporary skip" and "permanently untested mcpx behaviour". A count-only ceiling makes the guard blind to the substitution that matters most in practice: fixing (or deleting, or renaming around) one skipped test while quietly skipping another. Renames are the legitimate look-alike — a renamed test also appears as one name leaving and another arriving — so the fix shape (fail on any new name, fail unless the swap is acknowledged, or report-and-hold the record unchanged) is a triage call; what is not defensible is the current silent re-baseline, which contradicts the module's stated invariant.

## Acceptance criteria

- A run whose skipped set contains a name not in the stored record does not silently become the new record on main: either the run fails naming the newly skipped tests (mirroring the increase path), or the record is held unchanged pending an explicit acknowledgement — triage picks the shape, including how genuine test renames are handled.
- Controls keep behaving as today: identical set → exit 0, no record; fewer skips with no new names → exit 0, record lowers; more skips → exit 1, no record; failing runs never write a record; the #1973 quarantine exemption (#6387's validation concerns aside) is unaffected.
- Regression coverage: add the equal-count swap case (and a pure-rename disposition, whichever way triage rules) to `pkgs/mcpx/scripts/test_gotest_report.py`, naming its oracle — the docstring invariant quoted above.
- The summary output for a swap states the consequence (run failed / record held), not only "Same number skipped, different tests".

Related: #6387 (the same reporter's quarantine exemption is a substring test — a different hole in the same guard, filed separately), #3313 (closed: a package-level fail once poisoned this same record downward — the record's integrity has bitten before), #1973 (the flake/quarantine policy this record supports).

title: mcpx(gotest-report): the #1973 quarantine exemption is a substring test — any skip whose last line says 'quarantined until ' evades the skip record, with no date, link, or expiry check

body:
## Summary

`pkgs/mcpx/scripts/gotest-report.py` — the reporter that holds the mcpx Go suite to its skip record on main — exempts a skipped test from the record whenever the test's last output line merely **contains the substring** `quarantined until ` (gotest-report.py:63). It never parses the date, never checks the issue link, and never checks expiry, although its own header (gotest-report.py:15-19) defines the exemption as a `testsupport.Quarantine` notice of the form `quarantined until <date> (<issue link>)` under #1973.

The Go side enforces that shape strictly — `ValidateQuarantine` (pkgs/mcpx/internal/testsupport/quarantine.go:35-48) requires a GitHub issue link and a `YYYY-MM-DD` expiry that has not passed, and `TestQuarantineGuard` audits every `Quarantine(` call site — but the guard only audits calls to `testsupport.Quarantine`. A plain `t.Skip(...)` / `t.Skipf(...)` whose message (or last output line) contains the phrase is audited by nobody and exempted by the reporter: it never counts against the skip record, never raises the ceiling failure, and is reported in the summary as "quarantined under #1973 (issue + expiry, exempt from the record)" (gotest-report.py:158-161) whether or not any issue or expiry exists.

## Evidence (file:line, main @ 5c56f76053)

- pkgs/mcpx/scripts/gotest-report.py:62 — a skip's reason is only its last non-header output line, truncated to 200 chars: `reasons[k] = (lines[-1] if lines else "(no reason given)")[:200]`
- pkgs/mcpx/scripts/gotest-report.py:63 — the whole exemption test: `"quarantined until " in reasons[k]`
- pkgs/mcpx/scripts/gotest-report.py:64 — exempted tests are removed from `counted`, the list the record/ceiling decision (`decide`, :84-103) and the exit code are computed from
- pkgs/mcpx/internal/testsupport/quarantine.go:24-29,35-48 — the real contract the reporter claims to mirror: `Quarantine` validates (issue link containing `github.com/` + `/issues/`, expiry `YYYY-MM-DD`, not past) and only then emits `quarantined until %s (%s)`
- pkgs/mcpx/internal/testsupport/quarantine_test.go:88-120 — `TestQuarantineGuard` scans for `Quarantine(` call sites only; a direct `t.Skip("quarantined until …")` is outside its pattern and its count check

## Verified this run (laptop, real reporter @ origin/main 5c56f76053)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-gotest-quarantine` ran the real `gotest-report.py` on synthetic `go test -json` streams (1 passing test + 1 skipped test, stored record `skipped_count: 0`):

- Plain skip, reason `just skipping this one` (control): **exit 1**, counted as 1 skipped against the record of 0 — the ceiling works.
- Skip with reason `quarantined until banana (not a link)`: **exit 0**, counted as **0 skipped** — exempt despite a nonsense date and a non-link.
- Skip with reason `quarantined until 2000-01-01 (https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/1973)`: **exit 0**, counted as **0 skipped** — exempt despite an expiry ~26 years in the past (a real `testsupport.Quarantine` call with that expiry would `Fatalf`, per quarantine.go:26-28).
- Skip with reason `this test is not quarantined until further notice, honest`: **exit 0**, counted as **0 skipped** — the bare substring in an unrelated sentence is enough.
- Control, real shape `quarantined until 2027-01-01 (https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/1973)`: exit 0, 0 skipped — the legitimate exemption that must keep working.

## Why it matters

The skip record is the ratchet that stops skipped mcpx tests from creeping back in silently ("a run that skips more tests than the record fails; the record only moves down", header :9-12). The quarantine exemption is the one hole in that ratchet, and today the hole is wider than its documented, guarded shape: any test — including one whose author never heard of #1973 — can opt out of the ceiling forever by putting seven words in its skip message, with no issue, no expiry, and no audit. Because the summary then labels it a #1973 quarantine, the evasion is not just silent, it is misattributed to the tracked, expiring mechanism.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The exemption in gotest-report.py parses the full documented shape — `quarantined until <YYYY-MM-DD> (<github issue URL>)` — instead of a substring test, and validates the date (real calendar date) and the link (a GitHub `/issues/` URL), mirroring `ValidateQuarantine` in quarantine.go
- [ ] A quarantine whose expiry has passed at report time is **not** exempt (it counts against the record like any other skip), or the reporter fails loudly naming it — matching the Go side's "expired quarantine fails" rule
- [ ] A skip whose last line merely contains the phrase, has a malformed/nonsense date, or has no issue link counts against the record and can raise the ceiling failure (exit 1), as the plain-skip control does today
- [ ] The legitimate control keeps working byte-for-byte: `quarantined until 2027-01-01 (https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/1973)` stays exempt and is still reported as quarantined in the summary

## Bug: worker-poc smoke/post-update-failure.mjs fails on clean main — MemoryJournal stub doesn't handle worker.ts's `SELECT step FROM journal` query

Reproduced on clean `origin/main` @ `03d1a21eae` (no local changes), laptop Node v24.21.0:

```sh
cd pkgs/id/worker-poc
node smoke/post-update-failure.mjs
# Error: unexpected SQL: SELECT step FROM journal ORDER BY step DESC LIMIT 1
#     at MemoryJournal.exec (smoke/post-update-failure.mjs:37)
#     at WorldObject.handle (src/worker.ts:128)
```

### Cause

`pkgs/id/worker-poc/src/worker.ts:128` issues ``SELECT step FROM journal ORDER BY step DESC LIMIT 1`` (added by 999414c1ab "fix(worker-poc): report journal step on cold start"). The smoke's `MemoryJournal.exec` stub handles the `SELECT step, snapshot FROM journal ...` shape (worker.ts:98) and the journal INSERT, but not the `SELECT step FROM journal ...` shape, so it throws `unexpected SQL`.

Verified pre-existing: the failure reproduces identically with all local changes stashed (found during task 10764 / issue #6372, which only wires participant-validation into the smoke chain — no source or smoke-file changes). `counter-smoke` and `participant-validation` are green on the same tree.

### Acceptance

- `MemoryJournal` in `smoke/post-update-failure.mjs` handles the `SELECT step FROM journal ORDER BY step DESC LIMIT 1` query (returns the latest step), or worker.ts's query is aligned with the shapes the stub supports.
- `node smoke/post-update-failure.mjs` passes on clean main.

## Acceptance criteria

- `node smoke/post-update-failure.mjs` in `pkgs/id/worker-poc` passes on clean main.

title: pm-stack(aggregator): epic-graph rankedBlocked traversal is exponential on diamond blockedBy graphs — and contributingItems lists duplicates

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/pm-stack
labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

body:
# pm-stack(aggregator): epic-graph rankedBlocked traversal is exponential on diamond blockedBy graphs — and contributingItems lists duplicates

## Evidence

`pm-stack/aggregator/src/epic-graph.ts:25-86` defines two recursive helpers,
`transitiveOpenEpicDescendants` and `contributingDownstreamItems`. They are
functionally identical (both return the set of open Epic items in the transitive
`blockedBy` ancestry of a ref), and both pass `new Set(visited)` — a fresh copy
of the visited set — to **each** recursive call (epic-graph.ts:45 and :76).
A visited set copied per branch only prunes cycles along the current path; it
never prunes a subgraph reached by a second path. On a diamond-shaped
`blockedBy` graph (two items in one layer both blocked by the same two items
in the next layer — the natural shape when parallel work shares blockers),
the number of root-to-leaf paths doubles per layer, and every path is walked
in full. `epicGraph()` (epic-graph.ts:350-353) then runs **both** helpers for
**every** blocker of **every** open member, over the whole pool (`byRef` is
the uncapped pool; the 120-node display cap at epic-graph.ts:237 does not
bound this traversal).

`render.ts:6567` calls `epicGraph()` once per epic section on every project
page render (`epicGraphSections` → `epicGraphOneHtml`), so one diamond
anywhere in the pool's blockedBy graph, reachable from any member's blocker,
stalls the whole page render.

Verified this run on the laptop against origin/main @359996097f, probe
`~/git/fleet/probe-epic-diamond` (bun, real `epicGraph` from the tree; pool
items are otherwise minimal — one member blocked by both layer-0 nodes, each
layer's nodes blocked by both nodes of the next layer, last layer blocked by
one open Epic):

| diamond layers | pool nodes | epicGraph time |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | 11 | 1.3 ms |
| 8 | 19 | 0.9 ms |
| 12 | 27 | 5.8 ms |
| 16 | 35 | 84.7 ms |
| 20 | 43 | 1757.1 ms |

Growth is ~2× per added layer (12→16 layers: ~15×; 16→20: ~21×), so ~24
layers ≈ tens of seconds and ~28 layers ≈ many minutes — from a 43-node
pool, far below any pool-size limit. Control: a plain 40-node chain through
the same code takes 0.3 ms, so the cost is the diamond path multiplicity,
not pool size or depth alone.

Second, simpler defect in the same computation: `rankedBlocked`'s
`contributingItems` is built by flat-mapping the per-blocker contributing
sets with no deduplication (epic-graph.ts:396, `r.sortedBlockers.flatMap(b => b.contributingItems)`),
while `downstreamCount` counts the blockers' sets distinctly per blocker.
In the probe above (member with two blockers that share the same downstream
epic), the output was:

```json
{"ref":"developing-today/code#2","downstreamCount":1,
 "contributingItems":["developing-today/code#9000","developing-today/code#9000"]}
```

`render.ts:6592-6594` renders that list verbatim, so the project page lists
the same "Contributing downstream epics" link twice.

## Why it matters

- The aggregator is a live dashboard service; its project page render path
  can be stalled for seconds-to-minutes by ordinary issue-graph data (two
  shared blockers per layer is a normal shape for epic work), with no cap,
  timeout, or memoization anywhere in the traversal. Nothing about the input
  is exotic or attacker-crafted — it is the fleet's own native blockedBy
  relations (#2399 contract).
- The duplicate `contributingItems` entries are a visible correctness bug on
  the same page, and the duplicated helper (two identical traversals per
  blocker) doubles the exponential cost for no benefit.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The transitive blockedBy traversal visits each reachable pool item at
      most once per query (shared visited set / memoization, not a per-branch
      copy), so a 20-layer diamond pool of ~43 nodes scores in milliseconds,
      comparable to the chain control — with a regression test (named oracle:
      the same diamond fixture, asserting both the result set and a
      node-visit bound or a generous wall-clock bound).
- [ ] Only one traversal implementation remains (the duplicate helper is
      removed or one calls the other), with identical results to today's
      sets on the existing epic-graph tests.
- [ ] `rankedBlocked[].contributingItems` contains each ref at most once
      (distinct, in a deterministic order), pinned by a test with two
      blockers sharing a downstream epic.
- [ ] Existing epic-graph test suite passes unchanged in behaviour for
      chains, cycles (a blockedBy cycle still terminates and returns the
      correct set), and out-of-pool blockers.

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-b (Lane B), verified this run; probe and
timings above are reproducible from `~/git/fleet/probe-epic-diamond`.

body: ## Summary The #5745 fix (PR #6339, merged today) neutralizes executable URL schemes in Markdown **links** at every entry point of `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs` — but **image `src` was left out of the same treatment in every direction**. An image whose source is `javascript:`, `data:text/html`, `vbscript:`, `file:`, or any other non-image scheme survives import, raw-HTML `` import, the raw-ProseMirror-JSON (collab) path, and save — sized images even emit it verbatim into a raw `` HTML tag. Links in the same document, through the same converter, are neutralized to `#`. This is the exact gap #5745's own oracle says not to leave: `link_url_is_safe` (markdown.rs:3943) documents that safety must come from an explicit allowed-scheme set and "do not rely on browser sanitization". Image sources currently rely on browser behaviour alone. ## Evidence (file:line, main @ 6f4e4e37a9) Sanitized (links, for contrast): - markdown.rs:2992 — parse direction: `"href": sanitize_link_url(&link.url)` - markdown.rs:3943 / :3984 — `link_url_is_safe` / `sanitize_link_url` (allowed: `http`, `https`, `mailto`, or scheme-less) - markdown.rs:4016, :5047, :5271, :5616 — raw-HTML anchor href and all save-direction link hrefs also sanitized Not sanitized (images): - markdown.rs:3013-3015 — parse direction, `NodeValue::Image` arm: `"src": image.url` verbatim - markdown.rs:3903 — `parse_img_tag`: raw-HTML `` imported verbatim (`let src = attr("src")?`) - markdown.rs:5060 — save direction, unsized image: `url: src.to_owned()` verbatim - markdown.rs:5023 — save direction, sized image: `format!("` → image src preserved verbatim - `` → src + width preserved verbatim - Control, same converter: `[x](javascript:alert(1))` → link mark `href = "#"` (the #5745 behaviour) Save direction (`prosemirror_to_markdown` on raw ProseMirror JSON — the collab Rich path that never passed the parse-direction converter): - image `src = "javascript:alert(1)"` → saved as `![x](javascript:alert(1))` - image `src = "data:text/html;base64,PHNjcmlwdD4="` → saved verbatim - sized image (width 10) `src = "javascript:alert(1)"` → saved as `` Controls that must keep working: `https://example.com/a.png`, `/local/a.png`, and `data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgo=` all parse with src preserved (see the policy note — the last one is why the image oracle cannot simply reuse the link oracle). ## Why it matters - Stored/collaborative documents are shared content: a doc imported from Markdown, pasted as raw HTML, or pushed as raw ProseMirror JSON over collab can plant an image node whose src is an executable or local-file scheme, and it round-trips indefinitely — every save re-emits it, including as a raw HTML `` tag for sized images. Any present or future consumer that renders that HTML, opens the image in a top-level context, or follows the src outside an `` element inherits the payload. #5745 was filed and fixed at priority/high precisely because this converter must not rely on downstream/browser sanitization. - The asymmetry is invisible: a reader of the #5745 fix reasonably believes "URL schemes in this codec are neutralized", while the image half of the same codec is untouched. ## Policy note (the design call for triage) The image oracle is **not** the link oracle verbatim: `data:image/*` (at least the raster types, e.g. `data:image/png`) is a legitimate, currently-working image source and must not be neutralized. The fix needs an image-specific allowed set — e.g. scheme-less / `http` / `https` / `data:image/` — with everything else (`javascript:`, `vbscript:`, `data:text/html`, `data:image/svg+xml` if script-bearing SVG is in scope, `file:`, unknown schemes, and TAB/LF/CR-obfuscated spellings of them, mirroring `link_url_is_safe`'s stripping probe) neutralized the same way links are. Whether to neutralize to `"#"` (link precedent) or drop/replace the src is part of the same call. ## Acceptance criteria - [ ] An image-specific scheme check exists beside `link_url_is_safe` in markdown.rs, with the allowed set documented as the oracle (including the `data:image/*` decision and its rationale) - [ ] Parse direction: Markdown images and raw-HTML `` imports with a disallowed scheme no longer produce a PM image node carrying that src (neutralized per the chosen shape); TAB/LF/CR-obfuscated and mixed-case spellings are caught - [ ] Save direction: raw ProseMirror JSON image nodes with a disallowed src are neutralized in both the unsized (`![alt](…)`) and sized (``) emission paths, and a sanitized document is a stable round-trip fixpoint (re-parsing/re-saving changes nothing further) - [ ] Controls preserved byte-for-byte in both directions: `http:`/`https:` images, relative/absolute local paths, and the allowed `data:image/*` forms - [ ] Pinning tests in the markdown module cover each path above, in the style of the #5745 tests (`test_link_executable_schemes_neutralized` and siblings), naming the image oracle - [ ] The linked-image case still works: the wrapping link's `linkHref` keeps its #5745 neutralization and the image src check does not break `[![alt](src)](href)` round-trips ## Dedup `gh search issues` for "5745 image", "markdown image src scheme", "sanitize image", "img src" (2026-11-05): #5745 (closed) is links-only in title, body, and fix; #873 (closed) is attribute escaping of src/alt/title, not schemes; no open or closed issue covers image-src schemes. Related: #5745 / PR #6339 (the link fix this extends).

title: id(web/collab): CollabMessage::decode ignores trailing bytes — a frame with a second complete message concatenated decodes as the first and silently drops the second

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

`CollabMessage::decode` (`pkgs/id/src/web/collab.rs:554-555`) decodes every WebSocket collab frame with `rmp_serde::decode::from_slice`, which stops after the first complete MessagePack value and silently ignores the rest of the buffer. A frame is therefore not exactly one message:

- a valid message + one trailing garbage byte decodes as the bare message;
- a valid message + a **second complete message** concatenated decodes as the first message — the second is silently dropped, not errored;
- the same holds for every variant, including the first-frame `Auth` message (decode at `collab.rs:836`, token verified over the parsed fields only) and `Steps` in the main loop (`collab.rs:1104`).

Verified this run on the laptop (probe `~/git/fleet/probe-collab-trailing`, rmp-serde 1.x, the exact tuple shapes `decode` uses):

```
trailing byte:        Ok((8, "secret-token"))
trailing 2nd value:   Ok((8, "secret-token"))
extra array elem:     Err(LengthMismatch(2))   // in-array extras ARE refused
exact:                Ok((8, "secret-token"))
ack trailing garbage: Ok((3, 42))
```

So the gap is specifically trailing bytes after the value. (In-array extra elements are already refused by the tuple decoder.)

## Why it matters

This is the one remaining first-party decoder in pkgs/id that does not enforce the full-consumption invariant the repo has been systematically adopting: seitan `accept::parse` (#6192, fixed), gossip presence/peer-announcement frames (#6197, fixed), `MatchLogV0::decode` (#6202), log_sync frames (#6204), meta protocol (#6209). Collab is network-facing — remote WebSocket clients, not a local socket — so it should not be the weakest decoder in the set:

- One message gains many byte spellings: anything that later logs, hashes, rate-limits, or signs raw collab frames sees a different byte string than the semantics that were executed.
- Concatenated frames lose data silently: a client or middle layer that batches two messages into one frame has the second executed nowhere and reported nowhere — the session just diverges (missed steps/cursor/auth-refresh), instead of a decode failure the client could recover from.
- The try-each-shape structure of `decode` compounds it: the first shape that parses a prefix wins, so a suffixed frame can decode as a *different* variant than the sender framed.

## Acceptance criteria

- `CollabMessage::decode` refuses any input with bytes remaining after the first MessagePack value (e.g. decode through a `Cursor`-backed `Deserializer` and require consumed == input length, the pattern used in `seitan/accept.rs:122-130`), for every variant, while honest encodings produced by `CollabMessage::encode` still round-trip.
- Tests pin: trailing byte, trailing garbage, and a trailing second complete message are refused for at least Auth, Steps, and Ack shapes; genuine frames for every variant still decode (existing codec tests keep passing).
- A property test in the style of #6197 is a plus: for generated messages and arbitrary non-empty suffixes, `decode(encode(m) ++ suffix)` is always `None`.

Found by new-issue-creator-code-a; verified at laptop main 50237a7debf6e9114122c593a15a467858d2bf9a.

(Only hits anywhere are `nixos/home/pm-dashboard-backup.sh`, which consumes the exporter's *output files* under `~/atlas/meta-quota-export/` — it never runs the tests.) `pm-stack-tests.yml` wires aggregator/projector/dispatch bun suites + seed/deploy smoke + two Python suites by name; meta-exporter is absent.
