body:
# aggregator: PR #3411's out-of-domain guard nulls projectedExhaustionAt but still computes and renders projectedPercentAtReset for negative pct values

## Finding

PR #3411 (fix for #2346) guarded `projectPace` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/derive.ts`) so an out-of-domain last pct value (`< 0`) yields no projection: `projectedExhaustionAt` stays `null`. The guard covers only that one field. The very next block computes the sibling projection unconditionally:

```ts
let projectedPercentAtReset: number | null = null;
if (last.resetsAt) {
  const toReset = (Date.parse(last.resetsAt) - Date.parse(last.ts)) / 86_400_000;
  if (toReset > 0) projectedPercentAtReset = Math.round((lastVal + slope * toReset) * 10) / 10;
}
```

There is no `lastVal >= 0` condition, so for a stored poisoned series whose last record carries `resetsAt`, `projectPace` still returns a projection — a large negative percent. Worked example using the PR's own poison fixture (`-1e9 -> -999999999` over 2 days, slope 0.5/day) with `resetsAt` 7 days after the last read: `projectedPercentAtReset = -999999999 + 0.5 * 7 = -999999995.5`.

That value is rendered. The service-detail pace list (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/render.ts`, the `paces` block in the service page) prints `projectedPercentAtReset` whenever it is non-null, independent of `projectedExhaustionAt`:

```ts
${p.pace!.projectedPercentAtReset != null ? ` · projected ${p.pace!.projectedPercentAtReset}% at reset` : ""}
```

So the service page can show "projected -999999995.5% at reset" for exactly the stored-poison records #2346/#3411 set out to neutralise. (The quota-card pace line is safe only incidentally: it returns early unless `projectedExhaustionAt` is set.)

## Evidence

- Source PR reviewed: #3411 "aggregator(derive): projectPace RangeError guard — no projection for out-of-domain pct (#2346)" — https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/3411 (merged, commit 15e9a541f8). Its stated contract: an out-of-domain last value "yields no projection (`projectedExhaustionAt: null`; slope/points still reported)".
- Current main `b830347c2a5398ef5a1846e6ee4a424e9793bd93` (verified via gh api x2): `derive.ts` `projectPace` — the `lastVal >= 0` condition gates only the `projectedExhaustionAt` candidate; the `projectedPercentAtReset` block below it has no domain check. `render.ts:2370` prints `projectedPercentAtReset` whenever non-null; `render.ts:2039` (card pace line) is exhaustion-gated.
- Test gap: #3411's regression tests (`test/usage.test.ts`, "pace: out-of-domain pct yields no projection and never throws (#2346)") construct the poison records with the `rec()` helper without a `resetsAt` argument, so the `projectedPercentAtReset` path is never exercised for out-of-domain values; no test on current main asserts it is null for a negative last value.
- Reachability: the poisoned records at issue are previously stored snapshot rows read back through `SnapshotStore.readAll()` (the #3411 PR itself tests that path); pct snapshot records routinely carry `resetsAt` (it is part of `SnapshotRecord` and set by the quota extractors), so a stored negative-pct row with a reset stamp is the realistic shape.
- Dedupe: #2346 is CLOSED by #3411 and covers the RangeError / exhaustion projection only; a search for `projectedPercentAtReset` returns only #3983 (OPEN, a separate per-pool forecast-interval feature that complements the pace derivation — it does not cover this guard gap). No open or recently closed issue mentions the at-reset projection for out-of-domain values.

## Why it matters

#2346's failure class was one poisoned snapshot record breaking or corrupting the quota surfaces. #3411 closed the crash and the exhaustion date, but left the same poisoned input producing an absurd rendered number on the service page — the projection the PR said would not be yielded is still yielded, just in the sibling field. It is a small, well-bounded remainder of an already-agreed fix, not a new design question.

## Acceptance criteria

- For a pct series whose last value is out of domain (`< 0`), `projectPace` returns `projectedPercentAtReset: null` as well as `projectedExhaustionAt: null` (slope/points still reported, per #3411's contract).
- Regression test in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/usage.test.ts`: the #2346 poison fixtures (e.g. `-1e9 -> -999999999`) with `resetsAt` set on the last record assert both projection fields are null.
- In-domain behaviour unchanged: the existing control case (30 -> 40, `projectedPercentAtReset` 80) and the rest of the usage suite keep passing.
- No change to the `isSnapshotRecord` negative-pct boundary guard or to the render layer required — the fix belongs in `projectPace`, the owning derivation.

body:
# Program ecosystem (share, fork, gallery) — v2 — outline: gallery & updates

Part of the Phase 14 core topic #6278 (Program ecosystem (share, fork, gallery)), filed from the next-horizons discussion #1240 per Drew's 2026-11-05 decision. The Phase 14 epic links the whole map.

**Outline refined in place 2026-11-11 (task 14664).** Design of record: `doc/2026-11-11T05-24-00Z_design_id_program_ecosystem_v2/` — the full v2 design refining core decisions D6 (gallery registry) and D4 (update authority). This body is the tightened outline that record expands; the original rough outline is superseded by the sections below.

## Entry condition — MET

The previous step (v1 — first-iteration design, #6291) has its design written, with open questions answered or explicitly deferred to this step: #6291 is CLOSED (2026-11-11) with the v1 design record landed by PR #8541, and that record explicitly scopes the gallery/registry (D6) and channel/update-policy UX to this v2 step, seeded by #8281. Core topic #6278 is CLOSED; its first-pass findings are the core design record (PR #8288, decisions D1–D6).

## Scope (refined)

1. **The gallery as a registry, in depth (D6).** A registry of bundle records (D1 identity, version, content hash, signature, lineage, manifest) in the same protocol family as world discovery (T2), transported over iroh. Validity is protocol — hash/signature verified at ingest and at read, provenance violations surfaced, never silently resolved; admission and curation are operator policy. Template packages publish through the same registry as a second record type (one protocol, two object types).
2. **Three publishing paths, one record.** Publish to a big hosted registry, publish on pkarr, or self-host a registry; a client reads any of them identically. Publishing and withdrawal are author speech (signed publish, signed tombstone); delisting and annotations are registry speech, presented distinct from author data.
3. **Update channels (D4).** A channel is one author's version line — the (author key, name) pair. The install record's policy field becomes live: `pinned` by default (updates are new install decisions), `tracking` as an explicit per-install owner choice. Lineage is not a channel: a fork is a different line, and no install tracks a parent or a fork.
4. **Update flow into worlds.** A newer bundle arriving by any path (registry, pkarr, self-hosted, local file) runs the v1 import verification pipeline first; policy is consulted second. Inside the D4 envelope (same ABI descriptor, no widened capabilities, F12.9 migration succeeds) a tracking install may update without fresh approval; anything outside the envelope — and every update to a pinned install — needs explicit world-owner approval on a fixed summary: from→to identities, the author's changelog, the ABI/capability delta, the migration outcome. Changelogs are signed author metadata; their absence is shown as "no changelog provided", never filled in. Rollback via F12.9 (#1066) is part of the same act, and a failed update leaves the prior install untouched.

Out of scope for v2: our hosted public gallery as an operated instance (v3, #6294 — curation/abuse/scale are operator policy, not protocol), federation and lineage-aware discovery (v4, #6295), ranking, payments, moderation UX.

## Open questions (explicitly deferred)

- Template storage layout in the reference registry (same index as bundles or not) — implementation choice deferred to #8281's build; the record format and client behaviour are decided.
- Push notification of new versions — deferred; v2 discovery is pull-only at world-owner action. Push, if it ever exists, is a v3 operated-instance concern (#6294), never a protocol requirement.
- Multi-registry annotation disagreement — no resolution rule needed: annotations are per-registry speech and are never merged. Record disagreement is a provenance violation and already has its rule.

## Dependencies

#8280 (bundle format + sideload import — the verification pipeline and install record), #8540 (fork operation — the line boundary), #8282 (template-world packages — the template record's manifest), and the landed specs F12.7 (#1064), F12.9 (#1066), F12.10 (#1067), F12.17 (#1069).

## Next-step breakdown (filed and linked)

- #8281 — gallery registry protocol + reference registry service (D6). Already filed from the core record.
- #8546 — program update channels + update flow into worlds (D4). Filed with the v2 design record (task 14664) — the one v2 item no earlier issue owned.

Drew's Phase 14 principles (#1240) govern this step: local-first always; hostable by anyone at any scale; p2p behavior identical to hosted behavior; our hosted instance is the public backstop, never a requirement.

## Acceptance criteria

- The v1 design (issue #6291) is written, with its open questions answered or explicitly deferred to this step (entry condition met). ✓ #6291 closed, v1 record landed via PR #8541, v2 items explicitly scoped there.
- This issue's outline is updated in place: tightened gallery/update scope, open questions, and dependencies named. ✓ This body, 2026-11-11 (task 14664); full design in `doc/2026-11-11T05-24-00Z_design_id_program_ecosystem_v2/`.
- The next-step issue breakdown for gallery & updates is filed and linked from this issue and from core topic issue #6278 — or this issue is closed with a note that the step dissolved into v1 (drop rule). ✓ #8281 + #8546, linked from both.
- The design honours the Phase 14 principles from discussion #1240: local-first, hostable by anyone, p2p identical to hosted. ✓ Design record §§2, 7 and invariant 7.

body:
# Program ecosystem (share, fork, gallery) — Phase 14 core topic (research + design)

Filed from the next-horizons discussion #1240, decided by Drew on 2026-11-05: **all themes are planned**. This issue is the core topic for **Program ecosystem (share, fork, gallery)**. Its job is research and design — broaden the idea beyond what is already understood, set up multiple next steps, and produce implementation plans. No implementation starts here; the output is design documents and implementation issues.

## Drew's principles for everything in Phase 14 (from #1240, 2026-11-05)
- Local-first is always the goal, AND a hosted version is intended: central coordination supporting a large graph of broadly accessible objects.
- Anything built must be completely usable by others hosting a small or large server themselves. P2P-hosted worlds and data behave the same as a large hosted public server; differences live in backend scale elements and access controls.
- Users connect to each other and transfer/interact directly wherever possible, so hosted resources are an offloadable backstop, not a requirement. The app must not technically need us to function. Collaborative / shared / federated / local-first / p2p.
- Our hosted instance is essentially public; other operators open theirs only as much as they want. Publishing paths: share to a big server, publish on pkarr, or self-host. All comms through iroh on the backend; first-class clients.

## The idea, broadened
Programs are the platform's content. Today they are files you have. An ecosystem asks how a program travels: authorship, versioning, signing, forking with attribution, template worlds, install-into-a-world in one click, and updates flowing to installed copies. Broaden with the trust model first (F12.17 provenance is the foundation) and the local-first rule: a gallery is a registry like any other — ours can be public, anyone can run one, and sideloading a .roc file must always work.

## Research questions (first pass)
- Program identity: name + author key + version + content hash; what a fork records
- Install semantics: pinning vs tracking a channel; what an update may change without world-owner approval (ABI, F12.7)
- Template worlds: a world snapshot as a starting point — state, programs, roles included or stripped
- Gallery as registry: same protocol family as world discovery (T2), different object type

## Dependencies and existing pieces
Builds on F12.7 ABI (#1064), F12.8 guest SDKs (#1065), F12.9 upgrades (#1066), F12.17 provenance (#1069). Registry protocol shared with the discovery topic.

## Next steps — the version ladder
- **v1 — first-iteration design** — its own issue, filed in the same pass and linked in the first comment below
- **v2 — outline: gallery & updates** — its own issue, filed in the same pass and linked in the first comment below
- **v3 — outline: public gallery** — its own issue, filed in the same pass and linked in the first comment below
- **v4 — outline: ecosystem at scale** — its own issue, filed in the same pass and linked in the first comment below

Plus a standing rule for this topic: anything the research surfaces that doesn't fit v1–v4 gets its own issue (Drew's rule: every feature, concept, or idea gets an issue), and future investigations are listed as comments here rather than lost.

## Sequencing
Design queue order: F12.4 provider registry (#1061) and F12.10 scheduling/quotas (#1067) designs land first; Phase 14 v1 designs then run hosted worlds → discovery → agents spike → the rest. Implementation follows Phase 13. The drop rule applies throughout: anything that proves blocked, wrong, or superseded gets parked or closed with a note — never a silent stall.

## Acceptance criteria
- A research + design output exists for Program ecosystem (share, fork, gallery): design documents broadening the topic beyond the current understanding, per the Phase 14 principles in the body (local-first plus hosted coordination).
- Multiple concrete next steps are produced as implementation plans / implementation issues filed from this topic.
- No implementation starts under this issue itself (per its own charter).

body:
## Finding (from PR review)

Codex (chatgpt-codex-connector[bot]) raised this finding in its review of merged PR #5754 and it was never fixed or responded to:

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/5754 — "mcpx: touch-on-read terminal task retention (#2546)" (MERGED 2026-11-05T01:48:30Z on the reviewed head 61f7e52ff4)
- Comment: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/5754#discussion_r4475516678 (chatgpt-codex-connector[bot], 2026-11-05T01:31:40Z, P2, anchored at `pkgs/mcpx/internal/tasks/tasks.go:770`)
- Essence: "Preserve the backing-task retention floor under maxAge. With `tasks.maxAge=100ms` and the default one-second task poll interval, answering a question can turn a successful daemon-backed MCP task into a failure. `StartWithDeadline` deliberately floors backing-result retention at two poll intervals, but this clamp overrides that floor. `driveAsked` sleeps for a full poll interval while a question is open, and `updateAsked` does not wake it after sending an answer; if the upstream finishes during that sleep, the backing result is deleted before the next poll. That poll reaches the 404 branch in `daemon/routes_proto.go`'s `handleAskPoll`, and `driveAsked` converts the retrieval error into a failed outer task. Preserve the collection window for internal backing tasks or prevent incompatible maximum-age/poll settings."

## No-response evidence

- The PR's three inline Codex findings have no replies (`in_reply_to_id` empty, no later inline comments); the conversation contains only the Codex review summary and a CodeRabbit rate-limit notice.
- The PR merged on the exact reviewed head (61f7e52ff4), so no fix commit followed the comment.

## Still live on current main (verified 2026-11-05 by independent `gh api` raw reads)

- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/tasks/tasks.go:80-88`: `deadline()` applies the maxAge ceiling with no floor — `if ceiling := terminalAt.Add(maxAge); ceiling.Before(expires) { expires = ceiling }`.
- `pkgs/mcpx/internal/tasks/tasks.go:767-775`: `armRetentionLocked` recomputes retention through `deadline(...)`, so the two-poll-interval floor that `StartWithDeadline` deliberately applies to the task's TTL (documented at lines 797-810, the Codex-on-#2869 fix) is overridden whenever `tasks.maxAge` is smaller than that floor.
- Dedupe: open+closed issues searched by "backing-task retention", `tasks.maxAge` and PR #5754 — neighbour issue #2498 (closed, task-store limits) does not cover the maxAge-vs-floor interaction.

## Acceptance criteria

- Terminal retention for internal backing tasks is never shorter than the two-poll-interval collection window (floor applied inside `deadline`/arming, or incompatible maxAge/poll settings rejected or clamped at configuration time), with a test using a sub-poll-interval maxAge on the ask path.
- Or: the finding is resolved on this issue by a documented decision with reasoning recorded.

body:
Implementation P1 of the compile-economics design for #5965: `doc/2026-11-05_design_id5965.md` (merged in PR #6230). The design is the spec; this issue is its first implementation phase so the design does not sit unlinked.

## Scope (design §2, §4 tiers 0–1, §7 P1)

- Shared server-side compile cache for `pkgs/id` world compiles, keyed exactly as design §2.1: BLAKE3 over (platform tree hash, source closure hash, DLL closure hash, compiler binary digest — reuse the `compiler_blake3` the compile path already computes, target). Seed and compile limits are not key components.
- Sharing scopes `author` and `server` (design §2.3); `public` scope may be stubbed at `server` behaviour until P3. Unpublished source defaults to `author` scope; wider scopes are opt-in only.
- Eviction tiers 0 (per-job scratch — today's behaviour, unchanged as the compile isolation boundary) and 1 (server LRU over `cache.lru_bytes`, default 2 GiB). No pinning (tier 2 is P3).
- Determinism proof harness (design §2.2): the same spec compiled twice in clean job directories must yield byte-identical artifacts for a compiler/platform pair before `server` scope is enabled for that pair; otherwise that pair stays at `author` scope.
- Metering logged only: measured compiler cost per job is recorded (the P2 penalty model consumes this later); no charging, delay, or gating in this phase.
- Cache hits re-verify the artifact's content hash before install; a cache label is never trusted on its own.

## Out of scope

- Penalty/credits/delay (P2) and pinning/gating matrix (P3) — separate phases of the same design, filed when P1 lands.
- DLL mechanism itself (sibling design under #5955); this phase only reserves the `dll_closure_hash` key component (empty closure = constant).

## Acceptance

- [ ] A second compile of identical inputs (same author) is served from cache with no compiler invocation, and installs an artifact whose content hash matches the first compile's.
- [ ] With determinism proof on record for the pair, a `server`-scope entry hits across authors; without proof, it does not.
- [ ] LRU eviction respects `cache.lru_bytes`; invalidation of a compiler digest or platform tree evicts its entries from all tiers present.
- [ ] Existing compile limits and admin-only gating are unchanged; all current `world_compile` tests pass.

Parent: #5955. Design: #5965 (`doc/2026-11-05_design_id5965.md`).

## Acceptance criteria
- Shared compiled-world cache is implemented per the #5965 P1 design, with cache keys that cannot serve a world compiled for different inputs.
- Repeat compiles of an unchanged world measurably reuse the cache (timing evidence recorded on the issue).
- Cache invalidation on any input change is covered by tests; no stale-world execution is possible.

Implementation follow-up from the design decision on #5699 (adopted 2026-11-05, task 10135 triage).

## Scope
Proxy colocated UDS dialing: when `fleet proxy serve` runs on the laptop itself (`proxy_direct()` mode, `crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs:311-314`), add a port -> socket-path resolution beside `Config::services()` so `open_conn` (`crates/fleet-proxy/src/serve.rs:258-271`) dials the role's Unix socket when the target is local and the socket answers, instead of TCP.

The hello/services map stays port-keyed — it is the negotiated wire contract. The socket is a local dialing detail of the colocated proxy, never advertised. The remote (sandbox proxy) path is unchanged: it still tunnels TCP to target_host:port.

## Acceptance
- Colocated proxy reaches a dual-bound broker over UDS; falls back to TCP when no socket answers.
- Hello/services contract byte-identical to before.

## Acceptance criteria
- In direct mode, a colocated fleet-proxy port dials the role's Unix socket instead of TCP loopback.
- Non-colocated and non-socket cases keep the current TCP behavior, selected without configuration changes.
- Tests cover colocated UDS dialing and the TCP fallback.

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/id/src/match_audit.rs:459-461` — `MatchLogV0::decode` is a bare `postcard::from_bytes(bytes)?`. postcard's `from_bytes` stops after the first complete value and never checks that the input is exhausted, so a match-audit v0 log decodes successfully with arbitrary trailing bytes appended: a stray `0x00`, free-form garbage, or a second complete log concatenated after the first.

Nothing downstream covers the suffix:

- `verify_integrity` (`match_audit.rs:466+`) checks signatures and hashes over **re-encoded** fields (`postcard::to_allocvec(&self.header)`, `entry_hash` over re-encoded entry bodies) — the appended bytes are not part of any signed or hashed value.
- `verify_tic_tac_toe_v0` (`match_audit.rs:700`) is exactly `decode` → `verify_integrity` → replay, so a suffixed log earns the same verdict as the clean log.
- The verifier CLI (`pkgs/id/src/commands/match_audit.rs`, `MatchAuditCommand::Verify`) reads a log file (up to 128 MiB) and passes the whole buffer to `verify_tic_tac_toe_v0` — a log file with garbage appended still prints **RESULT CONFIRMED** and exits 0 via `require_confirmation`.

A match-audit log is the artifact two players submit to prove a match result (`id: match audit v0`, closed #3793; v1 design #2039). Its whole purpose is to be a canonical, self-authenticating record. As decoded today it is malleable: one match has many byte spellings, all equally "confirmed", and anything that stores, dedupes, or compares logs by their bytes (or a hash of the bytes) can be made to treat the same match as different records — or different-looking records as the same match. The rest of this codebase refuses exactly this one-object-many-spellings class (tuple decode #1610/#2421, directory-auth #2517, seitan accept #6192, gossip frames #6197), and the sibling replication decoder in the same crate already does it right: `world/replication.rs:532` uses `postcard::take_from_bytes` and checks the rest.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe against the real `id` crate @ 6d9d1c899b)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-match-audit` on the laptop (path dependency on `pkgs/id`, default features). It exports the reference tic-tac-toe log with `export_tic_tac_toe_reference`, then decodes/verifies mutations of the encoded bytes:

```text
clean len=2907 decode_ok=true verdict=ResultConfirmed { runtime: PinnedRuntime }
trailing 0x00: decode_ok=true verdict=ResultConfirmed { runtime: PinnedRuntime }
trailing garbage: decode_ok=true verdict=ResultConfirmed { runtime: PinnedRuntime }
trailing whole-second-log: decode_ok=true verdict=ResultConfirmed { runtime: PinnedRuntime }
control flipped byte 10: decode_ok=false verdict=InvalidRecord { reason: MalformedEncoding }
```

The control matters: flipping a byte *inside* the value fails decode and yields `InvalidRecord` — the decoder checks the value, just never the suffix. A complete second log concatenated after the first is accepted exactly like the bare log.

Dedup: title/keyword search over open and closed issues for `match-audit` / `match_audit` / trailing found #2039 (v1 design epic), closed #3793 (the v0 implementation), #6192 and #6197 (the same defect class in seitan accept and the gossip frame decoders) — none covers `MatchLogV0::decode`.

## Acceptance criteria

- `MatchLogV0::decode` fails (`AuditErrorV0`) when any byte remains after the first complete postcard value — e.g. via `postcard::take_from_bytes` with an empty-rest check, matching the replication decoder's pattern at `world/replication.rs:532`.
- `verify_tic_tac_toe_v0` on a suffixed log returns `TechnicalVerdictV0::InvalidRecord`, and the `match-audit verify` CLI exits non-zero for such a file; tests pin a trailing single byte, trailing garbage, and a concatenated second log.
- A genuine log produced by `MatchLogV0::encode` / `export_tic_tac_toe_reference` still decodes, verifies, and replays exactly as before: `cargo test -p id match_audit` green, including the reference-export replay test.
- No re-encode-and-compare canonicalisation is introduced for the log as a whole (the check is consumed-length only, so honest non-canonical-width postcard encodings of the same value stay decodable if they were before).

## Why not fixed in this run

Filed-only: the fix itself is small, but `MatchLogV0::decode` is the entry point for stored/submitted logs — whether any already-accepted log files in the wild carry suffixes, and whether the error should be the postcard error or a dedicated `AuditErrorV0` variant, deserves a deliberate pass through the queue rather than a rushed creator self-solve.

body:
## Summary

`ConversionExecutor::preflight` (`pkgs/id/src/currency_poc/executor.rs:141`) — the executor's stated gate: "Failing here means no intent is written and nothing is submitted" — validates the transfer-ID list only for count (`:164-172`) and duplicates (`:173-177`). It never checks the ID *values*. A request carrying a transfer ID of `0` or `u128::MAX` passes preflight, `prepare` persists the write-ahead intent, and `submit` submits the batch: against the in-memory backend the conversion is marked `Posted` and the funds move; against real TigerBeetle the same IDs are refused outright (`IdMustNotBeZero` / int-max class, established in #6135), so the persisted intent strands as a poison `Submitted` record the recovery scanner can only ever report `ResubmissionRejected`.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ origin/main f78551465f; pkgs/id identical at primary HEAD 4b41b86cc3)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-executor-ids`, real `id` crate, funded-ledger setup copied from `currency_poc/tests.rs`: user holds 10_000 source units, LP holds 50_000 destination units; request amount_in 1000, fee 25, quote 2/1):

- CONTROL ids 601,602,603: EXECUTE Ok state=Posted, user_dest_credits=2000, lookups 601/602/603 all present
- transfer_id 0 (T1): EXECUTE Ok state=Posted, user_dest_credits=2000, lookup 0 present
- transfer_id 0 (fee leg): EXECUTE Ok state=Posted, user_dest_credits=2000, lookup 0 present
- transfer_id 0 (T3): EXECUTE Ok state=Posted, user_dest_credits=2000, lookup 0 present
- transfer_id u128::MAX (T1): EXECUTE Ok state=Posted, user_dest_credits=2000, lookup MAX present
- transfer_id u128::MAX (T3): EXECUTE Ok state=Posted, user_dest_credits=2000, lookup MAX present

So every reserved-ID shape executes end-to-end and is recorded `Posted` — the executor's own preflight is the layer that should refuse it before any intent is written, exactly as it already refuses duplicate IDs (#4132), wrong ID counts (#4664), and same-account legs (#4124).

## Why it matters

Transfer IDs are caller-generated and pre-persisted by design (write-ahead intent, recovery by ID lookup). A generator or persistence bug yielding `0`/`MAX` is precisely the class preflight exists to catch: today the first signal is a refused submission *after* the intent is durable — against the real backend the record can never post and never reconcile to a terminal state, and against the reference backend it silently posts, teaching exactly the wrong semantics (the broken-oracle problem of #6135, one layer up).

Related but distinct: #6189 covers the same ID values in the pure batch builder (`conversion.rs::build_conversion_batch`, no ledger/store); #6135 covers `InMemoryLedger` accepting the IDs; #6108 covers the `tb_ledger` status mappers. Fixing any of those adds no check to `preflight`.

## Acceptance criteria

- `preflight` (or `prepare`, before the intent is persisted) rejects any `transfer_ids` entry equal to `0` or `u128::MAX` with an error naming the offending ID, in the same style as the existing duplicate-ID bail.
- No intent record is written and nothing is submitted for such a request (assertable via the intent store staying empty).
- Pinning tests in `pkgs/id/src/currency_poc/tests.rs` cover zero and int-max in each leg position (T1, fee, T3), plus the sane-ID control executing identically.
- `cargo test -p id --lib currency_poc` passes.

## Scope notes

- Filed-only from the creator lane; not self-solved (where the check lives — preflight vs prepare — and whether the executor should also refuse reserved *account* IDs for accounts it did not create are the PoC author's calls).
- Out of scope: builder ID validation (#6189), `InMemoryLedger` ID acceptance (#6135), `tb_ledger` mapper panics (#6108), short result vectors (#4669).

## Finding (from PR review)

Codex (chatgpt-codex-connector[bot]) raised this finding in its review of merged PR #5657 and it was never fixed or responded to:

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/5657 — "id: make tag.clear role-aware in the default view" (MERGED 2026-11-04T21:23:11Z, merge commit e4777f1203753e970d074fd7094d154207bc0bab)
- Comment: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/5657#discussion_r4473530083 (chatgpt-codex-connector[bot], 2026-11-04T21:25:31Z, P1, anchored at `pkgs/id/tests/tag_clear_authority.rs:162`; reviewed head b4b151c36f — the review was submitted just after the merge, so no in-PR fix was possible)
- Essence: "Add generated coverage for settled-role authorization. The new grouped-subject authorization path is covered only by fixed examples. The updated property test in `tag_claims.rs` still generates only missing, ungrouped subjects, so its oracle never exercises owning-group selection or settled Admin membership. Add generated grouped histories checked against an independent authorization model, including different owning groups and membership changes; otherwise the central role-aware invariant remains outside the property/model coverage explicitly required by the repository's testing doctrine." (Codex cites the repo AGENTS.md testing-doctrine lines 41–45.)

## No-response evidence

- The PR's inline review comments are exactly the two Codex findings (r4473530065, r4473530083); neither has any reply (`in_reply_to_id` is empty for both, and no later inline comment exists). The conversation contains only the Codex review summary and a CodeRabbit rate-limit notice.
- No commit after the review touched the flagged tests: the PR merged on the reviewed head, and the current-main reads below were taken on 2026-11-05, after the merge.
- Dedupe (searched 2026-11-05, open + closed, by `tag_claims` + proptest, grouped/property/tag keywords, settled/Admin/tag keywords, and PR number 5657): no existing issue covers generated grouped-subject coverage. Neighbours that do NOT cover it: issue #2090 (closed — the role-aware implementation itself), issue #5656 (open — device-admin identity resolution in tag views, a different defect), issue #5736 / PR #5923 (closed/merged — repaired one stale lib unit-test expectation for the role-aware view; no property coverage added).

## Still live on current main (verified 2026-11-05 by two independent `gh api` raw reads, main 4b41b86cc3db)

`pkgs/id/tests/tag_claims.rs`:

- The history generator used by both `proptest!` blocks (lines 453 and 483) builds every subject event with `group: None` (generator sites at lines 73, 260, 271), and the module documents the property oracle as the ungrouped rule (line 312: "only the claim author may clear these ungrouped test subjects").
- So the generated histories never exercise owning-group selection or settled Admin membership — the exact path PR #5657 added in `pkgs/id/src/event_store/claims.rs` (`default_view_events`, which resolves the subject's owning group and checks the settled projection for `GroupRole::Admin`).

`pkgs/id/tests/tag_clear_authority.rs` (227 lines) covers the grouped path only with fixed examples: a settled group Admin clearing another author's tag (line ~159), a non-member clearer (line ~167), and an Admin with no authority for ungrouped/missing subjects (line ~184). No generated histories, no membership changes, no multiple owning groups.

## Acceptance criteria

- Generated (property-based) grouped histories for tag-clear authorization: subjects owned by different groups, clearers with author / settled-Admin / non-member / removed-member roles, and membership changes mid-history, checked against an independent authorization model (the oracle), per the repo's PBT/MBT testing doctrine.
- The new coverage fails if the grouped authorization path in `default_view_events` is broken (e.g. Admin check dropped or group selection bypassed) — demonstrate by mutation or by a recorded counterexample check.
- Or: the finding is resolved on this issue by a documented decision with reasoning recorded (e.g. an argued case that the fixed examples plus other suites already bound the risk acceptably).

body:
## Summary

`pkgs/id/src/conversion.rs` — the production pure conversion layer (Phase E of #2063, landed under #5536) — builds a linked conversion batch for transfer IDs and account IDs of `0` or `u128::MAX` without any rejection. Both values are reserved in TigerBeetle: an ID of `0` is never a valid account/transfer ID (`id` must not be zero) and `u128::MAX` is the reserved int-max sentinel, so every leg built with one is refused outright at submission. The builder mirrors the ledger's other hard rules as typed pre-ledger `ConvertError`s — `ZeroAmount`, `SameAccount`, duplicate transfer IDs — but has no ID-validity variant at all, so the failure surfaces only at ledger submission time instead of as a typed pre-ledger rejection.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @2f470e0e65; `conversion.rs` unchanged at current main @97cd55c865)

- `build_conversion_batch` (`pkgs/id/src/conversion.rs:430`) validates, in order: zero amount (`:433`), min/max bounds, rate/scale/fee terms (via `convert_amount`/`fee_amount`), same-account for the source/destination/fee legs, fee-account presence, and transfer-ID count + duplicates. A module-wide grep for `u128::MAX` / ID zero checks finds none for IDs: the only `== 0` checks are `amount_in`, `rate_den`, and the computed `amount_out`. Transfer IDs are only counted and deduped; account IDs are only compared for equality between roles.
- Probe (laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-conversion-ids`, real `id` crate): with an otherwise-sane request (ledgers 100/200, amount 1000, rate 3/2, min 10 / max 10_000), each of these returned `Ok` and built a full batch:
  - `transfer_ids = [0, 22]` — source leg built with `id=0`
  - `transfer_ids = [11, 0]` — destination leg built with `id=0`
  - `transfer_ids = [u128::MAX, 22]` — source leg built with `id=u128::MAX`
  - `caller_source = 0`, `lp_source = u128::MAX`, `caller_dest = 0`, `lp_dest = u128::MAX` — legs built debiting/crediting the reserved IDs
  - fee leg shapes: `fee_account = Some(0)` with `fee_bps = 100` (fee 10 > 0) and `transfer_ids = [11, 0, 33]` — fee leg built with `id=0` / crediting account `0`
  - Control (all IDs ordinary) builds the expected 2-leg batch (`amount_out 1500`).
- Real TigerBeetle refuses these IDs at submission: #6135 established (with a probe of the in-memory backend) that TB rejects zero / int-max account and transfer IDs (`IdMustNotBeZero` / int-max class) while accepting ordinary IDs. The Phase F executor persists the intent first and submits exactly the batch built here, so a reserved ID becomes a persisted, submitted, refused conversion instead of a build-time rejection.

## Why it matters

The module's own contract is that rejections happen *before* any ledger write, with typed reasons: "`ConvertError` — Why a conversion quote or batch cannot be built. Every variant is a rejection *before* any ledger write, per the failure table in #2063 §2.4." The builder already mirrors the ledger's hard rules — `SameAccount` mirrors `AccountsMustBeDifferent`, `ZeroAmount` mirrors `AmountMustNotBeZero` — and #6102 covers the one ledger-value mirror it also misses (ledger `0`). ID validity is the remaining unmirrored hard rule: transfer IDs are caller-generated and persisted before submission (write-ahead discipline), so a generator or persistence bug that yields `0`/`MAX` is exactly the class of error this layer exists to catch early; today nothing catches it until the ledger refuses the whole linked chain.

Related but distinct: #6102 covers `source_ledger`/`dest_ledger == 0` in this same function (a ledger *value*, not an ID); #6135 covers `InMemoryLedger` *accepting* zero/int-max IDs (the backend oracle, not the builder); #6108 covers the `tb_ledger` status mappers panicking on the resulting TB statuses. Fixing any of those does not add an ID check here.

## Acceptance criteria

- `build_conversion_batch` rejects any transfer ID equal to `0` or `u128::MAX`, and any account ID (`caller_source`, `lp_source`, `lp_dest`, `caller_dest`, and a supplied `fee_account`) equal to `0` or `u128::MAX`, with a new typed `ConvertError` variant (e.g. `InvalidTransferId { id }` / `InvalidAccountId { id }` or equivalent), before any leg is built.
- The rejection order stays deterministic and is documented alongside the existing validation-order note in `build_conversion_batch`'s docs.
- Pinning tests in `pkgs/id/src/conversion.rs` cover: zero and int-max in each transfer-ID position (source, fee, destination), zero and int-max in each account role, and the existing sane-ID requests still building identical batches.
- `cargo test -p id --lib conversion` passes.

## Scope notes

- Filed-only from the creator lane; not self-solved (the variant shape and its position in the validation order are the Phase F author's call, as with #6102).
- Out of scope: `InMemoryLedger` ID acceptance (#6135), `tb_ledger` unmodelled-status panics (#6108), ledger-zero (#6102), `RateAuthorisation::validate` (#4071).

body:
# Venue-reality audit — enablement state and a disposition for every disabled test venue

Phase 3 of the test-suite coverage design (design issue #6185; design doc `files/designs/code-test-suite-coverage-contract.md` in the `keep-the-four-repos-healthy` goal workspace). **Gated on Drew's ruling on #6185** (re-enable test venues / fold suites into active workflows / accept the dispatch-only coverage definition) — do not start the dispositions until that ruling is recorded; the enablement inventory below can be refreshed at any time.

The contract rule this phase enforces (from #6185): a suite's venue counts only if it is **real** — enabled (Actions state `active`, or a flake check that actually runs) and dispatchable. A suite whose only venue is disabled is uncovered, regardless of what the workflow file says. Enablement is Actions settings state, invisible in the repo tree; at the design audit (origin/main e3626d1e3) **20 of 53 workflows were `disabled_manually`**, including the test venues `scripts-test.yml`, `pm-stack-tests.yml`, `go-modules-build.yml`, `research-workflow.yml`, `mcpx.yml`, `mcpx-test.yml`, `lab-ops-hub.yml`, `cf-container-hello.yml`, `cold-store-reaper.yml`, `opencode-config-guard.yml` and `mod-tidy.yml`.

Phase 3's pm-stack instance is the adopted origin #5954 (its own issue: re-enable `pm-stack-tests.yml` or fold its suites into an active workflow). This audit covers every *other* registry venue from Phase 1 of #6185.

## Scope

- Read the Actions-API enablement state for every venue named in Phase 1's registry and post the table on this issue (workflow, state, suites it carries).
- For each disabled **test** venue, record exactly one disposition, executed or explicitly scheduled: **re-enable** (then dispatch a run on main and confirm the carried suites actually execute — a green run that skipped them does not count), **fold** (name the active destination venue and the Phase 2 wiring issue that moves the suites), or **retire** (the venue and its suites are deliberately not run; the registry waiver records the reason).
- Establish the recurring enablement re-audit this contract needs: a named owner and cadence, living somewhere that cannot be silently disabled itself (not solely inside a workflow file). Record the choice on this issue and in `.github/ci-policy.md`.
- Non-test disabled workflows (goreleaser, mcpx-release, id-bench, etc.) are inventoried for the record only; their dispositions are not this design's to make.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Drew's ruling on #6185 is quoted on this issue before dispositions begin.
- [ ] Every registry venue has a current enablement state recorded; every disabled test venue has exactly one executed/scheduled disposition (re-enable + proven run, fold target named, or retire with reason).
- [ ] #5954's disposition is consistent with the table (its outcome is linked, not duplicated).
- [ ] The recurring enablement re-audit has a named owner, a cadence, and a first completed run evidenced on this issue.
- [ ] The registry (Phase 1 of #6185) is updated so no entry claims a disabled venue as coverage.

title: ci(pm-stack/ready-for-agent): test-install.sh (6 cases) + test-apply-config.sh (5 cases) run by no workflow — the gap that let test-install stay red on main until #5368

body:
## Problem

`pm-stack/ready-for-agent/`'s two shell regression suites — `test-install.sh` (208 lines, 6 installer scenarios) and `test-apply-config.sh` (161 lines, 5 config-apply cases) — are run by no workflow, flake check, or justfile recipe. This is exactly how `test-install.sh` stayed red on main unnoticed until #5368 was filed by hand: nothing executes these suites, so installer/config regressions surface only when someone happens to run them locally.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ f2a72d9478, HEAD == origin/main)

- Whole-tree grep for `test-install` / `test-apply-config` across `.github/workflows/`, `flake.nix`, `justfile`, and Nix files returns zero references. The one pm-stack test workflow, `.github/workflows/pm-stack-tests.yml`, wires the aggregator, projector, and dispatch bun suites, two script smokes, and the claimant/grist Python suites — ready-for-agent is not in it (or anywhere else).
- Hand runs on the laptop this run, both fully offline with stubbed `systemctl`/`npm`/`git`/`curl` and isolated `HOME`:
  - `bash pm-stack/ready-for-agent/test-install.sh` → all 6 cases PASS (`package-change-active`, `unit-change-active`, `unchanged-active`, `inactive`, `first-install`, `clone-fail-retry`), exit 0.
  - `bash pm-stack/ready-for-agent/test-apply-config.sh` → all 5 cases ok (`apply-config.test: PASS`), exit 0.
- What the suites pin:
  - `test-install.sh`: restart-vs-start-vs-no-op decisions on package/unit changes, and the #4839 pending-restart marker — an npm upgrade followed by a failing clone must leave the marker, must not restart early, and the retry must restart, apply config, and clear the marker (the #2513 silent-stale-process class).
  - `test-apply-config.sh`: dry-run plans registration and mutates nothing, `DRY_RUN` parsing is case-insensitive, first apply registers/configures/unpauses, second apply is a no-op, and `DRY_RUN=0` really applies (the closed #5421 regression).
- The code under test is live: `nixos/services/pm-apps/default.nix:117-137` runs ready-for-agent as a systemd user service whose binary is installed by this `install.sh`.
- Distinct from open #5368: that issue tracks `test-install.sh` failing on main; on current main the harness passes (verified above), so this filing is only about the missing automated execution that let it stay red unnoticed — wiring the suites also gives #5368 a permanent guard. Distinct from #6091 (opencode-claimant's `install.test.mjs`, a different package).

## Why it matters

`install.sh` decides whether a pinned-version upgrade or unit change actually restarts the dispatch service or silently leaves the old process serving (#2513 happened). `apply-config.sh` decides whether the declared config is applied at all (#5421: a truthy-looking `DRY_RUN=0` silently never applied). Both failure modes are silent and both already happened once. The suites exist, pass, are fast and offline — they are simply never run.

## Acceptance criteria

- An automated check (a step in `pm-stack-tests.yml` or an equivalent workflow/check) runs both `bash pm-stack/ready-for-agent/test-install.sh` and `bash pm-stack/ready-for-agent/test-apply-config.sh` on changes under `pm-stack/ready-for-agent/`.
- The check asserts both suite files exist first, so a green run cannot be a silently skipped suite.
- The check passes on current main (6 install cases + 5 apply-config cases at filing).
- Breaking a pinned behaviour (e.g. dropping the pending-restart marker on a failed clone, or treating `DRY_RUN=0` as dry-run) makes the check fail.

body:
## Problem

In `pkgs/id`, `DirectoryAuth` keeps **one pending email code per address, shared across both code purposes** — and a correct presentation in the wrong flow burns the code. Three consequences, all verified this run:

1. **Cross-purpose replacement.** `codes: HashMap<String, PendingCode>` is keyed by address alone (`src/directory_auth.rs:109-113`); `PendingCode.purpose` is a field of the single stored record (`src/directory_auth.rs:92-99`). `issue_code` unconditionally inserts over any existing record for the address (`src/directory_auth.rs:167-189`). So a `Purpose::SignIn` issuance replaces a pending `Purpose::Confirm` code for the same address, and vice versa — the earlier code, mailed up to a minute earlier, is useless long before its 15-minute TTL (`CODE_TTL_MS`, `src/directory_auth.rs:24`).

2. **The replacement is remotely triggerable without authentication.** The sign-in flow needs no session: `DirectoryAction::SignInEmail` issues a code for any address that belongs to an account (`src/directory_view.rs`, `SignInEmail` arm). Anyone who knows an address can, once per resend window (`CODE_RESEND_MS` = 60 s, `src/directory_auth.rs:25`), replace that address's pending confirmation code — repeatedly invalidating an address-confirmation the owner is mid-flow on, with a fresh mail sent each time.

3. **A correct code presented in the wrong flow is consumed.** `check_code` removes the pending record on a digest match and only then returns the purpose (`src/directory_auth.rs:198-215`). Both callers match on the purpose *after* the call (`ConfirmEmail` and `ConfirmSignIn` arms in `src/directory_view.rs`): presenting a sign-in code to the confirm form (or the reverse — the user just has a code in their mail, the flows look alike) succeeds at the digest layer, burns the code, and then refuses with "no matching code". The user must wait out the resend window and start over.

## Evidence (verified this run)

- Laptop probe at `~/git/fleet/wt-codeprobe/pkgs/id/tests/probe_directory_auth.rs` against laptop main (worktree of `f2a72d9478`), run with `cargo test --test probe_directory_auth` on the laptop: 3 tests pass, each asserting the current behaviour —
  - a `SignIn` issuance at `sent_at + CODE_RESEND_MS` makes the pending `Confirm` code fail `check_code`;
  - a `Confirm` issuance likewise replaces a pending `SignIn` code;
  - `check_code` on a `Confirm` code returns the purpose and removes the record, so a second presentation (the correct flow) fails.
- Code reading (same tree): the map key, the unconditional insert, and the remove-on-match are at the file:lines above; both `directory_view` callers check purpose only after consumption.
- Dedup: no open or closed issue covers the cross-purpose slot (searched `directory_auth code purpose`, `pending code address sign-in confirm`, `RateAuthorisation`-style title scans). The closed #1732 covered only eviction of expired codes. The per-purpose attempt limit and resend throttle themselves work as documented — this is the shared slot, not the limits.

## Why it matters

Email codes are the directory's account-recovery and address-confirmation mechanism. A single unauthenticated endpoint that can invalidate another flow's in-flight code once a minute is a denial-of-service on address confirmation (and a mail-spam lever against the address owner), and the burn-on-wrong-flow behaviour turns a routine user mix-up into a lost code with a misleading error.

## Acceptance criteria

- Pending codes are keyed per (address, purpose) — or an equivalent shape — so a `SignIn` issuance never replaces, throttles, or consumes a `Confirm` code for the same address, and vice versa; each purpose keeps its own resend window and attempt count.
- A code presented to the wrong flow is **not** consumed: the wrong-flow refusal leaves the pending code usable by its own flow (purpose is checked before, or as part of, the consuming match — e.g. `check_code` takes the expected purpose, or the digest comparison is scoped to the purpose's slot).
- Regression tests (oracle: the two purposes are independent slots) cover: cross-purpose issuance leaves the other purpose's code valid; wrong-flow presentation does not burn the code; same-purpose replacement, the 1-minute resend throttle, the 5-attempt limit, and the 15-minute TTL behave exactly as before.
- Existing `directory_auth` and `directory_view` tests pass unchanged except where they asserted the shared-slot behaviour.

title: fleet-proxy(udp-forward): no cap on per-source CONNECT-UDP sessions — 150 one-datagram sources open 150 sessions (threads on the shim, threads+sockets on the endpoint), retained 120s and unreaped under load

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/fleet
labels.description: pkgs/fleet multicall binary + platform crates

body:
## Summary

`fleet-udp-forward` (pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/udp_forward.rs) opens one CONNECT-UDP session per distinct UDP source address with **no cap on concurrent peers**, and the CONNECT-UDP endpoint it drives has no session cap either — so a stream of one-datagram sources turns into unbounded threads, TCP connections, and target UDP sockets on both processes.

- `serve_socket` (udp_forward.rs:192-193) keeps `peers: HashMap<SocketAddr, Peer>` with no size limit; every new source address inserts an entry.
- `open_peer` (udp_forward.rs:134, thread spawn :149) gives each peer a reply thread plus a `UdpProxyClient` session — one TCP connection to the endpoint and one target UDP socket there per peer.
- Retention is `PEER_IDLE_TIMEOUT` = 120s (udp_forward.rs:37), and `reap` (udp_forward.rs:180) is only called from the recv-timeout arm of the serve loop — while new datagrams keep arriving, the loop never takes that arm, so even dead/idle peers are not reaped during a sustained stream.
- The endpoint side mirrors it: `serve` (connect_udp.rs:538-542) spawns a thread per accepted connection with no limit, and each `serve_session` (connect_udp.rs:355, :432) adds another thread plus the target UDP socket.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop, real binaries @ 266875e1e02f)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-udp-peers/probe.py` on the laptop — real `fleet-connect-udp` (opted-in `FLEET_CONFIG`, loopback 127.0.0.1:39141) + real `fleet-udp-forward` (`--map 48001=127.0.0.1:48002`, UDP echo target), thread counts from `/proc/<pid>/status`, connections from `ss -tn`:

- Baseline: forwarder 2 threads, endpoint 1 thread, 0 connections.
- Control — 50 datagrams from ONE source socket: forwarder 3 threads, endpoint 3 threads (exactly 1 session).
- 150 datagrams, each from a DISTINCT source socket: forwarder **153 threads**, endpoint **303 threads**, ~151 established sessions (302 `ss` lines counting both ends on loopback). The echo target received the datagrams — these are real, fully-opened sessions, not half-open state.

150 small UDP packets from one ordinary host (each `sendto` from a fresh ephemeral port does this with no spoofing) created 150 sessions retained for at least the 120s idle horizon. Nothing bounds the count at 1,500 or 15,000 short of OS thread/socket limits, and the shim's documented use (Moonlight) is to bind it on a LAN (`--bind` is a flag precisely so it need not be loopback), where source addresses are not the operator's own processes.

## Why it matters

This is the client shim and endpoint from the #6109 CONNECT-UDP capability that #5694's remote-desktop design builds on. A per-source session model with no ceiling is a self-inflicted amplification surface: one datagram (~a thread + a connection + a socket on two processes, held 120s) is the cheapest possible unit of work for a sender and one of the most expensive for the shim. Every sibling surface in this crate family that allocates per-peer state has needed the same conversation; this one was never capped because the spike (#6109) proved capability, and the forwarder (#6134/#6139's bin) inherited the model unexamined.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `fleet-udp-forward` enforces a documented maximum concurrent peer count per listen socket (and/or globally); a new source beyond the cap is refused loudly (log line naming the cap) and opens no session — existing peers are unaffected
- [ ] `reap` (or equivalent expiry) also runs on the datagram path at a bounded cadence, so idle/dead peers are reaped during sustained traffic, not only when a listen socket goes quiet
- [ ] The CONNECT-UDP endpoint (`connect_udp::serve`) enforces a documented maximum concurrent session count; connections beyond it are refused/closed without spawning unbounded threads
- [ ] Pinning tests/probe: N distinct sources beyond the cap produce exactly cap sessions on both processes; the one-source-many-datagrams control still produces exactly 1; ordinary forwarding (echo round-trip) is unchanged
- [ ] `cargo test -p fleet-proxy` passes

## Related

- #6109 — the CONNECT-UDP capability spike this ships in (capability only, no cutover)
- #6139 / #6134 — the same bin's argument surface, fixed today; this is its session-state surface
- #5694 — remote-desktop design that would put this shim in front of real LAN traffic

title: id(currency_poc/tb_ledger): status mappers panic on unmodelled-but-ordinary TigerBeetle statuses (zero/int-max IDs, closed accounts) the in-memory backend accepts

body:
## Summary

`pkgs/id/src/currency_poc/tb_ledger.rs` — the `LedgerBackend` over the real TigerBeetle client — maps TigerBeetle result statuses to the PoC's typed errors through two functions with a panic catch-all:

- `map_account_status` (tb_ledger.rs:186–199): `other => panic!("tigerbeetle create_accounts returned unmodelled status {other:?}")`
- `map_transfer_status` (tb_ledger.rs:202–242): `other => panic!("tigerbeetle create_transfers returned unmodelled status {other:?}")`

The module docs (tb_ledger.rs:25–29) call this deliberate — "The scenarios exercise only the mapped subset" — but several unmodelled statuses are not exotic: they are the ordinary per-event validation results for input shapes the PoC types themselves accept, and for state a real cluster can be in. When one arrives, the panic unwinds out of `create_accounts`/`create_transfers` (tb_ledger.rs:277/322) and crashes the calling executor/gateway process instead of returning the per-leg `Result` the `LedgerBackend` trait promises.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ c7a0982d172e, HEAD == origin/main)

- The pinned client is `tigerbeetle = "=0.17.9"` (pkgs/id/Cargo.toml:116). In that crate, `CreateTransferStatus` has ~70 variants and `CreateAccountStatus` ~27; the mappers model roughly a third of the transfer set and 9 account statuses.
- Unmodelled **transfer** statuses reachable from ordinary inputs/state: `IdMustNotBeZero` (5), `IdMustNotBeIntMax` (6), `DebitAccountIdMustNotBeZero` (8), `CreditAccountIdMustNotBeZero` (10), `DebitAccountIdMustNotBeIntMax` (9), `CreditAccountIdMustNotBeIntMax` (11), `FlagsAreMutuallyExclusive` (7), `DebitAccountAlreadyClosed` (65), `CreditAccountAlreadyClosed` (66). (Also unmodelled, if less reachable today: `CodeMustNotBeZero` (20) — codes pass through `wire_code`'s +1 shift — `OverflowsTimeout` (53), and the pending-transfer and imported-event families.)
- Unmodelled **account** statuses reachable the same way: `IdMustNotBeZero` (6), `IdMustNotBeIntMax` (7), `CodeMustNotBeZero` (14), `FlagsAreMutuallyExclusive` (8), `DebitsPendingMustBeZero` / `DebitsPostedMustBeZero` / `CreditsPendingMustBeZero` / `CreditsPostedMustBeZero` (9–12), and `LinkedEventFailed` (1) / `LinkedEventChainOpen` (2) for linked account batches — both of which ARE modelled on the transfer side.
- Backend divergence (probe, below): the in-memory reference backend accepts these shapes — an account with `id = 0` is created `Ok`, a transfer with `id = 0` posts `Ok`, and a transfer debiting account 0 posts `Ok` once account 0 exists. So a scenario exercised only against `InMemoryLedger` (the default in `super::tests`) passes, while the same batch against a real cluster returns e.g. `IdMustNotBeZero` and panics the process.
- Probe (laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-tb-unmodelled`, real `id` crate + pinned `tigerbeetle` 0.17.9 crate; the two mappers copied verbatim from tb_ledger.rs:186–243 since they are private):
  - `P1 create_accounts incl id=0: [Ok(()), Ok(()), Ok(())]` — in-memory backend creates account 0.
  - `P1 create_transfers transfer id=0: [Ok(())]` and `P1 create_transfers debit_account_id=0 (account 0 exists): [Ok(())]` — the same shapes post fine in memory.
  - `P2 transfer IdMustNotBeZero / DebitAccountIdMustNotBeZero / CreditAccountIdMustNotBeZero / IdMustNotBeIntMax / CodeMustNotBeZero / DebitAccountAlreadyClosed / OverflowsTimeout: PANIC (unmodelled)` — all seven.
  - `P2 account IdMustNotBeZero / CodeMustNotBeZero / LinkedEventFailed / IdMustNotBeIntMax: PANIC (unmodelled)` — all four.
  - Control: `P2 control LedgerMustNotBeZero transfer: Err(LedgerMismatch)` — modelled statuses map as designed.
- No existing filing: `gh` searches for `map_transfer_status`, `tb_ledger`, `IdMustNotBeZero`, and "tigerbeetle panic unmodelled status" (all states) return no covering issue. Adjacent but distinct: #6102 is about `build_conversion_batch` accepting ledger 0 at the pure layer; this filing is the TB binding's status mapping, which panics for *any* caller of the trait, conversion or not.

## Why it matters

The `LedgerBackend` contract is per-leg `Result`s: the executor and the recovery machinery treat a rejected leg as data to classify and persist, not as a process-fatal event. A single malformed or unlucky leg — a zero/int-max ID from a bad ID generator, a transfer against an account that has since been closed, a timeout overflow on a pending transfer — currently takes down the whole process on the real backend while the in-memory backend (what CI exercises) sails through. That is exactly the class of divergence a two-backend design exists to prevent, and it hides until the TB harness or a real deployment hits it.

## Acceptance criteria

- Every `CreateAccountStatus` / `CreateTransferStatus` variant of the pinned tigerbeetle crate that is reachable from inputs the PoC types accept (zero/int-max account and transfer IDs, closed accounts, mutually exclusive flags, non-zero initial balances, linked-batch failures) maps to a typed `AccountError` / `TransferError` — new variants added where no existing one fits — instead of reaching the panic arm.
- A unit test exercises both mappers over **every** variant of the pinned crate's two status enums and asserts none of them panics (an exhaustiveness net that fails loudly on the next crate bump instead of in production).
- Any status intentionally left panic-worthy (e.g. imported-event statuses the binding can never emit) is enumerated explicitly in the match with a comment saying why it is unreachable, rather than falling into a bare catch-all.
- The in-memory backend's behaviour for the zero-ID shapes is reconciled or explicitly documented as divergent, so scenario tests mean the same thing on both backends.
- `cargo test -p id --lib currency_poc` passes (with the `currency-poc-tb` feature where the harness requires it).

## Scope notes

- Filed-only from the creator lane; not self-solved — the new error-variant shapes are the currency executor author's call, and the fix touches the recovery classification surface.

title: id(conversion): build_conversion_batch accepts ledger 0 — builds a batch that can never post, with no typed pre-ledger rejection

body:
## Summary

`pkgs/id/src/conversion.rs` — the production pure conversion layer (Phase E of #2063, landed 2026-11-04 under #5536) — builds a linked conversion batch for `source_ledger = 0` or `dest_ledger = 0` without any rejection. A zero ledger can never post: every layer below the builder refuses it, so the batch the Phase F executor will persist and submit is unpostable by construction, and the failure surfaces only at ledger submission time instead of as a typed pre-ledger rejection.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @5f161d2e3c)

- `build_conversion_batch` (`pkgs/id/src/conversion.rs`, the validation sequence in `build_conversion_batch`) checks, in order: zero amount, min/max bounds, rate/scale/fee terms (via `convert_amount`/`fee_amount`), same-account for the source/fee/destination legs, fee-account presence, and transfer-ID count/duplicates. There is **no check on `source_ledger` or `dest_ledger` anywhere in the module** — `grep ledger pkgs/id/src/conversion.rs` shows the fields only copied into the built `Transfer`s.
- The ledger layer the batch feeds refuses ledger 0 twice over:
  - `pkgs/id/src/currency_poc/ledger.rs` — `AccountError::LedgerMustNotBeZero` ("`ledger` must be non-zero"): no account can even be created on ledger 0.
  - `validate_and_stage` in the same file: `if transfer.ledger == 0 || …` → `TransferError::LedgerMismatch` for every leg of a zero-ledger batch.
  - Real TigerBeetle likewise requires a non-zero ledger (see `pkgs/id/src/currency_poc/tb_ledger.rs` module docs on non-zero wire fields).
- Probe (laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-conversion-ledger`, real `id` crate @5f161d2e3c): `build_conversion_batch` with `source_ledger=0` and with `dest_ledger=0` both return `Ok` with a full 2-leg chain; submitting the ledger-0 legs to `InMemoryLedger` fails every leg, and `create_accounts` on ledger 0 returns `LedgerMustNotBeZero`. The sane-ledger control (100/200) builds and posts. Probe output is quoted in the filing agent note.

## Why it matters

The module's own contract is that rejections happen *before* any ledger write, with typed reasons: "`ConvertError` — Why a conversion quote or batch cannot be built. Every variant is a rejection *before* any ledger write, per the failure table in #2063 §2.4." The builder already mirrors the ledger's other hard rules as typed pre-ledger errors — `SameAccount` mirrors `AccountsMustBeDifferent`, `ZeroAmount` mirrors `AmountMustNotBeZero`, duplicate-ID mirrors the staged-transfer ID check. Ledger-zero is the one ledger hard rule with no mirror: a caller (or a bad gateway resolution in Phase B/F) that supplies ledger 0 gets a persisted intent and a submitted batch that can only fail at the ledger, where the executor's recovery machinery (#4669 territory) then has to classify a failure that was knowable at build time.

Related but distinct: #4071 covers `RateAuthorisation::validate` accepting zero/same ledgers in the *authorisation body*. This filing is the new pure batch layer, which takes raw ledger fields (`ConversionBatchRequest.source_ledger`/`dest_ledger`) and does not consume a validated authorisation — fixing #4071 does not add a check here.

## Acceptance criteria

- `build_conversion_batch` rejects `source_ledger == 0` and `dest_ledger == 0` with a new typed `ConvertError` variant (e.g. `ZeroLedger { leg: "source" | "destination" }` or equivalent), before any leg is built.
- The rejection order stays deterministic and is documented alongside the existing validation-order note in `build_conversion_batch`'s docs.
- Pinning tests in `pkgs/id/src/conversion.rs` cover: source ledger 0 rejected, destination ledger 0 rejected, and the existing sane-ledger requests (100/200) still build identical batches.
- `cargo test -p id --lib conversion` passes.

## Scope notes

- Filed-only from the creator lane; not self-solved (the variant shape and its position in the validation order are the Phase F executor author's call to confirm, and #4071's authorisation-side fix is in flight under another holder).

body:
## Proposal — git as a second backup leg for the core knowledge files (from 2026-11-05 file-state investigation)

### Current coverage (verified 2026-11-05; full evidence in the investigation report)
| Class | Disk | hatch-personal git (→ GitHub) | Restic → R2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| research_notes (172 files / 24 MB) | ✅ | ✅ 172/172 tracked | ✅ |
| memory topics (71 files) | ✅ | ✅ 71/71 tracked | ✅ |
| goal files/ (348 files) | ✅ | ✅ 348/348 tracked | ✅ |
| goal hidden_files records | ✅ | ✅ tracked except deliberately-ignored regenerables (probe-*/clone-*/monitor-*/wt-*, node_modules) | ✅ |
| **workspace/scratch (803 files / 104 MB; 221 .md ≈ 0.9 MB)** | ✅ | ❌ **tracked nowhere in git** | ✅ (only backup leg) |

Drew's concern ("core files… supposed to be kept forever") is well-aimed at exactly one class: **scratch** — tonight's briefs/designs (worlds, atlas, docs-migration, modal, mistral) live there and have no git leg. Research notes, topics, and goal records already have three legs (disk + private git + restic/R2).

### Proposal
1. **Bring scratch under hatch-personal git using the existing pattern**: relocate the real tree to `hatch-personal/workspace/scratch` with `/home/hatch/workspace/scratch` as a symlink — identical to how goals/ and research_notes/ were relocated on 2026-10-25. The per-minute autocommit then tracks it with zero new machinery.
2. **Track records, ignore bulk**: add scratch entries to git for documents and small data (md/txt/json under ~1 MB each); gitignore large regenerable payloads inside scratch subdirs (model/data dumps). Starting point: 221 md files ≈ 0.9 MB — the entire current markdown corpus is trivially small. Nothing in scratch today exceeds sane git size except raw data payloads, which restic already covers.
3. **Close the hygiene-scratch hole in the same change** (see the companion security issue): add `workspace/goals/*/hidden_files/hygiene-scratch/` to .gitignore + untrack — regenerable inventory dumps do not belong in git and demonstrably capture credential material.
4. **Promotion convention (Drew's stated end state)**: scratch is a staging area, not a home. At task close, durable deliverables get promoted — research/design docs toward `developing-today/code` doc/ (per the docs-migration batches, tracker #5983) or into research_notes — and the scratch dir is discarded. Truly sensitive material stays in hatch-personal only.
5. **Do not** bulk-add the 9.3 GB goals tree to git: the current split (records tracked, regenerable probe/clone/monitor trees ignored per .gitignore lines 59–75) is correct and should be kept as documented policy.

No files were moved or re-tracked by the investigation itself — this issue is the work order for steps 1–3 when Drew approves.

## Acceptance criteria
- A decision on this proposal is recorded on this issue (adopt / adopt-modified / decline) with the reasoning.
- If adopted: workspace/scratch's knowledge files (the ~221 markdown files at minimum) are tracked by the git second leg, with ignore rules excluding bulk/binary scratch, and hygiene-scratch is untracked as proposed.
- A restore drill from the git leg alone succeeds for a sample of the newly covered files.
- The coverage table in the body is updated to the post-change state (git column no longer empty for the covered classes).

## Problem

`pkgs/chat/main_test.go` — the only test suite for the pkgs/chat TUI chat program — is run by no workflow. The one workflow that touches the module, `go-modules-build.yml`, verifies tidy/build/vet only; it never runs `go test`. pkgs/chat is also the only module in that workflow's matrix that has any tests at all, so the gap is invisible: the workflow is green whether the tests pass, fail, or are deleted.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ e90672dc9e, HEAD == origin/main)

- `.github/workflows/go-modules-build.yml` (matrix line ~57: `module: [chat, database, graph, import, launcher, tea]`) runs exactly three verifications per module: `go mod tidy` cleanliness, `go build ./...`, and `go vet ./...`. There is no `go test` step in the file, and no other workflow mentions `pkgs/chat`.
- Hand run on the laptop this run: `cd pkgs/chat && go test ./...` → **ok, 5 tests pass** (1.128 s, fully offline).
- What the 5 tests pin (`main_test.go` lines 68–207, against the 238-line `main.go`): Enter on empty input broadcasts nothing; Enter on real text broadcasts it verbatim exactly once; `send` reaches only live programs (removed sessions get nothing); removing an unknown session is a no-op; and the registry holds up under concurrent register/send/remove.
- Why these pins matter here: the open chat issues are exactly in this area — #4389 (broadcast fan-out ordering / unbounded blocked goroutines), #4515 (completion waiter can block forever; session never deregistered), #3268 (unbounded per-session history). The registry/broadcast contract tests are the regression net for those fixes, and today a fix for any of them can merge with the net never run.

## Why it matters

Build+vet proves the chat program compiles; it says nothing about the broadcast semantics that are its whole behaviour. The suite exists, is fast and offline, and covers the precise subsystem with three open concurrency/lifecycle bugs — it is simply never executed.

## Acceptance criteria

- An automated check (a `go test ./...` step in `go-modules-build.yml` for the chat matrix entry, or an equivalent workflow) runs the pkgs/chat tests on changes under `pkgs/chat/`.
- The check passes on current main (5 tests at filing).
- Breaking a pinned behaviour (e.g. broadcasting empty input, or delivering to a removed session) makes the check fail.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ e90672dc9e)

- Verified on the laptop: `cd pm-stack/opencode-claimant && bun test test/install.test.mjs` → **13 pass, 0 fail, 98 expect() calls** (~0.1s, offline, stores are temp-dir fixtures).

install.mjs is a write-path tool against live scheduler stores: an argv-validation regression does not fail loudly, it installs into the wrong store (closed #3278). The pinning tests exist and are green; nothing executes them.

- `github-backup-tests.yml` runs exactly one glob: `infra/github-backup/tests/test_*.py`. It never touches `worker/`. `git grep` for `index.test.mjs` and for `worker/test` across the tree returns no workflow, flake, justfile, or Nix reference (the one `worker/test` hit is cold-store-reaper's unrelated `run-local-proof.mjs` comment).

- What it guards is live: per `infra/github-backup/README.md`, the Worker receives the estate's GitHub webhook events and queues them in KV, and the laptop drains that queue every 5 minutes. An auth or pagination regression in the Worker merges with no signal — events silently dropped or the drain loop wedged — and the Python suite that IS wired cannot see it, because it tests the laptop side, not the Worker.

## Why it matters

#5937 closed the "github-backup tests run by no workflow" gap for the Python half and created the impression the estate's tests are covered. The Worker half — the internet-facing half, with the auth checks — is still decorative.

Per the 2026-11-04 storage ruling, old versions roll out to cold storage on rustfs. The cold format must be **self-describing** — a shard file that can be re-imported years later without the hot DB that wrote it:

A format spec + restore/re-import procedure design, with the round-trip (hot → cold → hot, byte-identical spans) as the acceptance shape.

body:
Parent: [#6018](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/6018) (Atlas ingestion program). Statements S7–S10 of the 2026-11-04 brief.

## Questions (Drew, in substance)

1. **Where do agent notes go?** Agents produce notes constantly (working notes, research_notes, goal files, memory entries, scratch findings). There is no single placement rule today, and the answer decides what Atlas ingests and what future agents can find.
2. **What is the difference between the Zettelkasten and the repo** as note homes? (Drew's dictation says "that tile cast" — read as the Zettelkasten, dezren39/zettel, the Emanote slip-box; interpretation recorded in the program inventory.) When does a note belong in the zettel graph vs committed to a code repo vs kept in agent memory/workspace?
3. **Publishing directly into the ID graph**: some notes/objects should be published as ID-graph objects rather than files at all — which classes, and what changes (identity, writer-set, relations) when they are?

## Tie-ins (do not reinvent)

- ID relation methods are already covered elsewhere: writer-set authority [#5545](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5545), the capability/relation family under [#5686](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5686), and tonight's worlds/licensing program ([#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955)). This design **consumes** those relation methods for notes rather than inventing a parallel model.
- Tonight's zettel brain-dump design already fixes part of the shape: every surface emits ONE `note_submission` envelope; zettel notes are first-class Atlas corpus; the Turso submission DB is the system of record; mandatory metadata = content hash + provenance spans; nothing auto-commits (staging → human promotion). The placement design must compose with that pipeline, not bypass it.
- The docs migration ([#5981](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5981) + [#5983](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5983)) is moving the canonical home of fleet/architecture docs into code — placement rules for agent notes must agree with the migration's classification standard (sandbox-environment material stays in hatch-personal; everything else canonicalizes to code / zettel / ID).
- Atlas ingestion (parent program) is the downstream consumer: whatever homes are chosen, each needs an ingestion path with provenance marks (source system @ machine @ date).

## Design must answer

- A placement decision table: note class (ephemeral working note, durable finding, design, research, daily log, user-facing doc) → home (workspace scratch / memory / repo doc / zettel / ID graph) → lifetime → Atlas-ingested? at which tier?
- The zettel-vs-repo distinction stated crisply enough that an agent mid-task can apply it in one step.
- The ID-graph publishing path: which note classes qualify, what an ID-native note's identity/provenance is, and how repo/zettel copies relate to it (canonical vs projection).
- Migration expectations for the existing sprawl (research_notes, goal workspaces, memory topics): swept, grandfathered, or left with pointers.

## Done looks like

A placement design doc + the decision table, cross-linked from the zettel program and the ID epic ([#2056](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/2056)), with any implementation split into follow-on issues.

body:
Parent: [#6018](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/6018) (Atlas ingestion program). Statements S39–S40 of the 2026-11-04 brief.

## Mandate (Drew, in substance)

Alongside the smaller per-topic designs, produce **one larger design that expands the depth and scope of Atlas wherever the research takes it, thinking ahead to v2, v3, and v4** — not a restatement of the brief, but the brief pushed further: what does a personal corpus become when ingestion is automatic, provenance is complete, versions are kept, and every search can be judged by its user?

## Starting threads (research is expected to find more)

- **Feedback-trained retrieval**: thumbs/essay feedback + per-stage score traces (sibling design under [#6018](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/6018)) as training signal — per-user ranking adaptation, query-pattern evolution, and honest evaluation harnesses that distinguish "the corpus lacks it" from "the ranker buried it".
- **Provenance-complete resolution**: with [#3125](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/3125)'s occurrence registry + version lineage, any chunk resolves to every place it ever lived, at every version — citation-grade answers ("this claim came from file X at commit Y, lines 17–241, also present in Z").
- **Cross-source lineage graph**: files, embeds, sessions, issues, notes as one graph (ties to the ID graph and the zettel graph designs; writer-set authority per [#5545](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5545)).
- **Self-curating corpus**: retention driven by measured usefulness (retrieval survival + feedback), not just age — the corpus proposes its own cold-storage and deletion candidates for human approval.
- **Classification-aware retrieval**: tier boundaries enforced inside ranking/expansion (a secret-tier chunk never hydrates an internal-tier context), building on the classification manifest line ([#5410](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5410)).
- **Cost-aware tiering**: hot/warm/cold placement continuously rebalanced against the plan ceiling (Turso/D1/rustfs per the 2026-11-04 storage ruling).
- **Agent-facing corpus**: Atlas as the memory substrate for agents — session/chat/report ingestion (operations design, sibling under [#6018](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/6018)) makes every agent's past work searchable by every future agent, with provenance spans as the trust mechanism.

## Method

Survey before designing: personal-knowledge/search systems (Mem, Rewind-style capture, Khoj, Quivr, personal RAG stacks), provenance systems (W3C PROV, git-like content addressing, datalake lineage), and feedback-loop retrieval research. Label dead ends as dead ends. Each v2/v3/v4 claim must name its dependency on the v1 pieces (delta ingestion, versioning, traces) so the horizon stays buildable, not aspirational.

## Done looks like

A design document in code (`doc/`) laying out the v2/v3/v4 arc with per-stage entry criteria, plus a follow-on issue list for anything the research shows is independently buildable sooner. Breadth is the deliverable; premature implementation commitments are explicitly out of scope.
