body:
Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Wave-2 follow-up from the prior-art research (Lane B item 30); parent topic issue: [#5977](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5977). Research source: `workspace/scratch/worlds-capabilities-brief-2026-11-04/prior-art-research.md`.

## Scope

#5979 surveys the tooling; #5977 designs the taxonomy's declared/detected/inherited distinction. This follow-up specifies the **pipeline** that runs at upload:

- **Tooling facts:** ScanCode Toolkit (nexB) is the leading open-source scanner — 2,000+ curated license texts in ScanCode LicenseDB, detects declared vs detected licenses, computes a License Clarity Score (https://scancode-licensedb.aboutcode.org/help.html ; https://aboutcode.org/blog/scancode-license-clarity-scoring/). GitHub's `licensee` powers GitHub's detection (high-precision text matching). FOSSology is the enterprise option.
- **Shared limit, design around it:** detection identifies license *texts and headers*, not intent — a file can carry an MIT header inside a GPL project, and scanners report both. Detection can never verify *ownership* (that's the attestation flow in the policy child of #5955).
- Pipeline stages: declared license recorded → scan at upload → mismatch handling (declared ∀ detected: which wins, who is told, what is recorded — a registry fact) → inherited licenses from a library's dependency closure flagged for the combination checker (combination child of #5955).
- Cost/latency budget: scanning is an upload-time cost; state where it may be deferred (large uploads) and what state the object sits in meanwhile.

## Done looks like

A pipeline spec (stages, mismatch rules, registry records) the classifier can be built against.

Research source: `workspace/scratch/worlds-capabilities-brief-2026-11-04/prior-art-research.md`.

## Scope

Drew's timeout ask: "the world code could give a function a certain amount of time, and then if it doesn't respond in that amount of time, it closes." Screeps proves the cooperative half of this works when usage is self-observable (`Game.cpu.getUsed()`); the hard half needs an enforcement mechanism from #5966's research (epoch interruption, fuel, process isolation). This follow-up specifies the *contract* between world and user function:

- **Deadline passing:** the world passes a budget/deadline with each invocation; the function's view of its own consumption (sibling metering design under #5955).
- **Checkpoint convention:** where a long-running function is expected to check in, and what state a checkpoint carries so a killed function degrades to a defined intent (composes with the mapping design's failure table: timeout → default intent).
- **Hard-kill semantics:** what the world observes when the backstop fires (error kind, partial results discarded or kept), and how repeat offenders are surfaced to the world author.

## Done looks like

A contract spec (invocation parameters, checkpoint shape, kill outcomes) both the host and function authors code against.

body:
Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Wave-2 follow-up from the prior-art research (Lane B item 17); parent topic issue: [#5966](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5966). Research source: `workspace/scratch/worlds-capabilities-brief-2026-11-04/prior-art-research.md`.

## Scope

The per-function gas/timeout research (#5966) evaluates mechanisms; this follow-up designs the *accounting shape*, from the metering gold standard in production:

- **Screeps model:** per-tick CPU limit; unused limit accumulates into a **bucket** capped at 10,000; a tick may burst up to 500 CPU total drawing on the bucket; exceeding available CPU terminates script execution for that tick. A hard per-tick ceiling exists independently of the average limit. `Game.cpu.getUsed()` lets code self-throttle cooperatively; CPU is treated as a currency, not just a cap (https://docs.screeps.com/cpu-limit.html ; https://wiki.screepspl.us/CPU/).
- **Adaptation needed:** Screeps accounts per *account*; Drew's case (per-user function mapping child of #5955) needs per-*function* sub-accounting. Screeps players built exactly that in userland (process schedulers with per-process CPU accumulators) — evidence the demand is real and the primitive needed is fine-grained `getUsed()` deltas.

## Work

- Two-level design: burst ceiling (hard kill) + average budget with rollover (bucket), per user function, composed with the world's per-tick budget (server-invariants child of #5955).
- Self-observation API: a `getUsed()`-style read so well-behaved functions can check their own consumption; hard termination stays the backstop.
- Bucket parameters as world-author configuration, not constants.

## Done looks like

A metering design doc the mapping design can implement against, with the Screeps parameters mapped to ours term-by-term.

Research source: `workspace/scratch/worlds-capabilities-brief-2026-11-04/prior-art-research.md`.

## Question

Drew recalls "at least in one version of the compiler there is a way to make a DLL." Close this question with evidence before the dynamic-user-functions design (#5964) builds on it.

## What the prior-art pass found (to verify, not assume)

No evidence in Roc docs, FAQ, or examples of a supported DLL/dynamic-loading story for Roc modules. Roc compiles via LLVM to a static executable linked with the host; the FAQ's stated plan is to compile "only to very low-level targets like machine code and WebAssembly" (https://www.roc-lang.org/faq). The recollection most plausibly refers to: (a) the platform *host* being buildable as a shared-library artifact that other programs load — the host is the DLL, not the Roc app; or (b) `roc build --lib`-style outputs discussed for the old compiler for embedding. In neither case can a running world hot-swap a Roc library without recompiling/restarting the host process.

## Work

- Pin the current compiler's actual library outputs (build one, inspect the artifacts) and what a host must do to load one.
- Check both compiler lines the repo cares about (pin vs track, per #5964's design points).
- Deliverable: a short evidence doc — outputs that exist, load mechanics, and the explicit conclusion for #5964: **do not design around native Roc DLL hot-swap**; the mechanism must live at the host/Wasm/process layer (see the hot-swap alternatives follow-up under #5955).

## Done looks like

Doc landed and linked from #5964; the DLL question is answered with artifacts, not recollection.

body:
# ci(pm-stack): pm-git-sync.test.sh (23 checks) and tailnet-bindings.test.sh run by no workflow — pm-stack-tests.yml runs the other two script suites in the same directory

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ ec2ac0e8eb)

- `.github/workflows/pm-stack-tests.yml` runs exactly two of the four shell suites in `pm-stack/scripts/`: `seed-smoke.test.sh` and `deploy-install-smoke.test.sh` (step "Test seed and deploy/install scripts"). The other two are named nowhere:
  - `grep -rn "pm-git-sync.test|tailnet-bindings" .github/workflows/` → zero references; no other workflow, justfile, or flake check runs them either.
- `pm-stack/scripts/pm-git-sync.test.sh` (168 lines, 23 checks): regression tests for `pm-git-sync.sh` — the script the `pm-git-sync` systemd service runs **every 30 seconds** (`nixos/services/pm-stack/default.nix:386-392` timer; ExecStart at :215) to keep the laptop primary clone on clean main and redeploy PM services on subtree changes. Verified on the laptop @ ec2ac0e8eb: `bash pm-stack/scripts/pm-git-sync.test.sh` → **23/23 ok, "all checks passed", exit 0** (checks include restart-failure retry, dispatch-owed record clearing, unusable-state-dir redeploy failure).
- `pm-stack/scripts/tailnet-bindings.test.sh` (89 lines): the #781 regression suite — Pad/Grist compose files must take the tailnet bind address from `PM_STACK_TAILNET_IP` (never hard-code a host IP, never render a public 0.0.0.0 binding) and `GRIST_DEFAULT_EMAIL` from the environment. Verified on the laptop @ ec2ac0e8eb (docker compose available, no SKIP): **"all checks passed", exit 0**. Note the suite self-skips with exit 0 when docker compose is unavailable — see the acceptance criteria.
- Dedup: issue searches for "pm-git-sync test workflow", "tailnet-bindings", and "pm-stack scripts test.sh workflow" found no CI-wiring filing for either suite (#781 is the closed defect the tailnet suite pins, not its CI coverage).

## Why it matters

pm-git-sync is the enforcement mechanism for the primaries-stay-on-clean-main model: it fetches, fast-forwards, and redeploys services on a 30-second timer. Its retry/owed-record/state-dir behaviour is pinned only by a test file nothing runs — a regression lands on the laptop fleet silently, exactly the class #5951/#5952 wired up for the neighbouring suites. The tailnet suite guards a security boundary (no public container bindings) the same way.

## Acceptance criteria

- `pm-stack-tests.yml` (or a successor workflow, per `.github/ci-policy.md`) runs both `pm-stack/scripts/pm-git-sync.test.sh` and `pm-stack/scripts/tailnet-bindings.test.sh`, failing the job when either fails (no continue-on-error).
- The wiring names both files explicitly and asserts they exist first, so a green run cannot be a silently skipped suite; for tailnet-bindings, the step must also fail (or visibly error) when the suite reports its docker-compose SKIP instead of silently passing.
- Both suites pass under the new wiring on a Linux runner.
- No behaviour change to `pm-git-sync.sh`, the compose files, or the deploy scripts.

title: id: design: license taxonomy & classifier — allowed set, copyleft warning ladder, public domain vs CC0, MIT/BSD variants

labels.name: task/triage

body:
Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Statements S82–S89 of the 2026-11-04 brief. Licensing splits into four children: this taxonomy/classifier design, an SPDX/tooling research, a policy + ToS design, and a combination-checker design, plus an AGPL research — all under [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955).

## Requirement (Drew, in substance)

- We need a way to say **this object is licensed with this license or that license** — code, images, documents, worlds, libraries: everything uploadable carries a license tag.
- A system that **automatically flags and warns whenever there's a license other than: MIT, BSD, MPL, Blue Oak, Apache 2** — and it should at least be able to **distinguish between each of those**.
- It must distinguish, individually:
  - **public domain** — because that matters for some countries where they don't actually support the concept of public domain,
  - the **MIT variants**,
  - the **weak copyleft of MPL**,
  - **GPL 2**, **GPL 3**, **AGPL** — each increasingly warning and problematic.
- **By default, we just don't support anything further copyleft than MPL.** That is the default support ceiling; policy (admin-configurable, per the policy child) decides what happens beyond a warning.

## Design points to settle

- The license value type: an enumerated taxonomy with a warning ladder (allowed → informational → warning → strong warning → unsupported-by-default), not a free-text string. Where does "unlicensed / all rights reserved" sit on the ladder (the brief supports it existing — see the policy child — so it needs a taxonomy slot, distinct from public domain).
- Public domain vs CC0: they are not the same object (CC0 is a waiver + fallback license precisely because public domain dedication fails in some jurisdictions) — the taxonomy keeps them separate.
- MIT variants: MIT, MIT-0, and the advertising-clause ancestors are different entries; "BSD" is a family (2-clause, 3-clause, 0-clause) — enumerate which BSDs the allowed set means.
- Creative Commons entries for non-code: CC0, CC-BY, CC-BY-SA allowed-shape; CC-NC variants identified and flagged differently (policy child owns what servers do with them).
- Detection: declared (uploader asserts) vs detected (file headers / package metadata) vs inherited (a library's dependencies carry their own licenses — the combination child consumes this).

## Done looks like

A taxonomy spec: the enumerated license set with per-entry ladder level, the public-domain/CC0 treatment, family expansions (MIT/BSD/CC), and the tag format used in manifests and the registry.

body:
Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Statements S39, S43, S44 of the 2026-11-04 brief.

## Requirement (Drew, in substance)

Compilation is a server resource and the economics must point the cost at whoever causes it:

- **Penalty model:** heavy compiles, and not using a pre-cached server-side object, are a **penalty to that user**. They just keep running the code they'd already published in the meantime — so a slow or expensive compile never stalls the world, and the cost lands on the user who triggered it, reducing impact to the world's performance.
- **Caching:** combinations of libraries and source code might represent a world; if they're compiled, that could be **cached** — and if somebody makes another world with the **same platform and source code**, it would be **reused**. Same for DLL-marked libraries (precompiled and cached).
- **Premium gating candidates:** being able to **upload raw code that gets compiled**, or having a game/world app **cached semi-permanently**, might be things servers **charge for**, mark as **premium**, or **limit to admins, contributors, or patrons**.

## Design points to settle

- Cache key: (platform identity, source hash, dependency closure hash, compiler version) — what exactly, and who else may reuse an entry (same user only, same server, anyone)? A cache hit across users is a feature per the brief; say what it leaks (existence of identical source) and whether that's acceptable.
- Eviction: semi-permanent vs LRU; what "semi-permanent" means concretely for the premium tier.
- The penalty currency: wall-clock delay, quota of compiles per period, literal money, or some mix — and how it composes with the tick/gas budgets (server-invariants child of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955)).
- Custom-compiled platforms (capability-model child) are compiles too: same cache, same penalty rules?
- Free tier shape: what does a non-paying user get — pre-cached popular objects only, compiles with delay, compiles with a small quota?

## Related

- Capability model (custom platforms) and DLL design children of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955)
- Server-side invariants child (budgets this design spends)

## Done looks like

A design doc: cache-key and sharing rules, eviction tiers, penalty model, and the premium/admin/contributor/patron gating matrix — with defaults a server admin can change.

body:
Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Statements S30–S35 of the 2026-11-04 brief.

## The model (Drew, in substance)

- **Libraries themselves are pure.** The core app passes the platform in — or specific functions from the platform.
- An app can thereby **ask what actions some entity should perform**, automatically or in response — effects are requested through the passed-in surface, never reached around it.
- The security property: **an app only has access to the world-level capabilities that are passed to it.** Nothing ambient.
- Convention: access is written as **`context.platform.<function name>`**, and **their code won't compile if it doesn't exist** — absence is a compile error, not a runtime surprise.
- A **context object** was the recommendation that landed in technical discussions Drew saw — but this design must check whether there is a **better best practice** rather than adopting it by default.
- Because this is a peer language, some worlds may **accept specific functions from users**; they can **trust exactly what a function would do** — function-passing is part of the same model, not an exception to it (this is the seed of the dynamic-user-functions design).

## Open questions

- Context object vs explicit function parameters vs a capabilities record: ergonomics in Roc specifically (the existing example protocol in `pkgs/id/examples/roc-world/RocCap.roc` is data point #1 — pure helpers, app owns its model).
- Granularity of what's passed: whole platform, per-domain sub-records (fs, net, time), or individual functions? Passing narrower than the platform is the "asks vs uses" story at the source-code level.
- How does the passed surface appear in a library's type signature so the import checker (library-imports design child) can verify subset-ness mechanically?
- Versioning: when the platform grows a function, do contexts gain it silently (capability expansion — see the change-notices child) or is the context surface pinned per world?

## Related

- Core/app platform design: [#2028](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/2028)
- Capability-model and library-imports design children of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955)
- OCAP prior-art research child of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955) (this model *is* object-capability discipline — the research should say where we follow it and where we deliberately don't)

## Done looks like

A design doc naming the chosen passing mechanism (with the alternatives' rejection reasons), the Roc-level conventions, and how library signatures expose their platform needs.

`infra/cargo-target-janitor/tests/test_cargo_target_janitor.py` (13 tests) is run by no workflow, justfile recipe, or flake check — the same gap class as #5942/#5945/#5946/#5951, for a destructive tool.

The suite pins the janitor's deletion-safety rules: claimed-task targets are protected (:37), open-PR targets are protected (:52), recent/unmapped targets are never candidates (:66), adhoc targets are protected during any fleet build (:100), hardlinked artifacts are counted once (:159), and the default mode logs a plan without deleting (:183). The janitor itself runs hourly in production via `infra/cargo-target-janitor/systemd/cargo-target-janitor.timer` → `cargo-target-janitor.service` (`ExecStart=... cargo-target-janitor --apply`) — the timer runs the deleter, never its tests.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ d82a48a3dd)

- `grep -rn "cargo-target-janitor|cargo_target_janitor" .github/workflows/ .github/scripts/ justfile scripts/ infra/` (excluding the package's own directory) → zero references.
- README:69 documents only a manual run: `python3 ~/git/code/infra/cargo-target-janitor/tests/test_cargo_target_janitor.py`.
- The suite passes today, run by hand on the laptop: `python3 -m unittest discover -s infra/cargo-target-janitor/tests` → Ran 13 tests, OK (0.015s, offline).
- Distinct from closed #5710: that issue fixed two `owner_changed` tests defined after `unittest.main()` so they never ran at all (now :191/:205, inside `JanitorTests`); this issue is that the now-complete suite is wired into no CI, so a future regression in the protection rules surfaces as wrongly deleted build targets.

## Why it matters

The janitor deletes cargo target directories with `--apply` on an hourly timer. Its protection rules are the only thing standing between a fleet build in progress and the deletion of its target dir (or a claimed task's / open PR's build cache). Those rules currently have zero automated regression signal.

## Acceptance criteria

- A CI step (a new small workflow or an existing infra-tests workflow, following `.github/ci-policy.md`) runs `infra/cargo-target-janitor/tests/test_cargo_target_janitor.py` and fails when a test fails (no continue-on-error).
- The wiring names the test file/discovery directory explicitly so a green run cannot be a silently skipped suite.
- The full suite (13 tests) passes under the new wiring on a Linux runner.
- No behaviour change to `bin/cargo_target_janitor.py`.

title: Fix #5612: scope unwrap/expect/panic Clippy exceptions to test modules

labels.name: kind/ci

body:
Implementation follow-up from the clippy triage on #5612 (diagnosis and policy decision: https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5612#issuecomment-6649814769). This is a scoped implementation issue, not a second main-broken holder; #5612 remains the sole tracker for the breakage.

## Problem
`pkgs/id/Cargo.toml` denies `clippy::unwrap_used`, `clippy::expect_used`, and `clippy::panic`. CI runs `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features`, so these lints also apply to the `id` lib-test target. Run #41868296408 at `f28bdee` failed that target with 521 errors (280 unwrap_used, 205 expect_used, 25 expect_err/unwrap_err, 13 panic). The same 521 lib-test errors remained in completed main run #41915614433 at `e4777f`, after PR #5622. The Cargo.toml comment already says test modules should add explicit allows.

## Policy
Keep production denies. Add explicit lint allowances only on affected `#[cfg(test)]` modules whose test code intentionally uses these patterns. Fix any diagnostic originating in production code rather than allowing it. Do not add a crate-wide or package-wide test-build allow, and do not weaken or skip the check.

## Acceptance
- Scope `unwrap_used`, `expect_used`, and `panic` exceptions only to affected test modules in the failing target.
- `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features` passes.
- The id workflow basic `clippy-lint` job passes on the PR.
- The PR description includes `Fixes #5612` and closes this implementation issue too.

body:
**Defect: opencode.service first-start deadlock — `EnvironmentFile` is loaded before the `ExecStartPre` materializer that creates it can run.**

Found during the 2026-11-04 evening switch re-run (the first switch to land the unit in this shape). The deployed unit carries:

```
EnvironmentFile=%h/.local/state/opencode/mistral-api-key.env
ExecStartPre=/nix/store/…-opencode-mistral-key-materialize
```

The materializer creates `mistral-api-key.env` (umask 077, writes `MISTRAL_API_KEY=…`). But when the file is absent, systemd fails the start before the materializer can ever run:

```
opencode.service: Failed to load environment files: No such file or directory
opencode.service: Failed to spawn 'start-pre' task: No such file or directory
opencode.service: Failed with result 'resources'.
… restart counter climbs … Failed with result 'start-limit-hit'.
```

The old server was stopped at activation (21:15:40 CST) and the service stayed down until the materializer was run once by hand, after which `reset-failed` + `start` brought it up clean and the façade verified (401 unauth / 200 authenticated route completion). So the end state is recoverable, but any start from a state where the env file is missing — state-dir cleanup, first deploy, a future activation that prunes it — deadlocks the same way.

**Fix directions (any one):**
- Prefix the EnvironmentFile path with `-` (optional load) so the first start can run the materializer, which creates the file for the ExecStart spawn; or
- Move materialization out of the unit (activation script / tmpfiles-style generation at switch time); or
- Have ExecStartPre itself export the key without the env-file indirection.

**Also observed in the same start's journal** (possibly related config work, separate concern): `provider route "mistral-plan": member "vibe-direct" names no known provider; it contributes no leaves` — the route references a provider id the server doesn't know.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] On a host/state-dir where `mistral-api-key.env` is absent, `opencode.service` starts successfully — no `Failed to load environment files` and no start-limit-hit.
- [ ] The materializer (or an equivalent ordering/`EnvironmentFile=-` mechanism) guarantees the env file exists before the main process reads it.
- [ ] Behaviour with the env file already present is unchanged, and the file's permissions remain 0600/umask 077.
- [ ] Verified by an actual switch + service start from the absent-file state, with the journal showing a clean start.

body:
## Observation (found while fixing #5736, 2026-11-04)

Building the id package from its **standalone flake** (`nix build ./pkgs/id#id-web`) fails its checkPhase on a test that does not fail in the root-flake composition:

```
---- world_compile::tests::version_probe_records_the_reported_version stdout ----
thread 'world_compile::tests::version_probe_records_the_reported_version' panicked at src/world_compile.rs:794:9:
assertion `left == right` failed
  left: ""
  right: "roc version 9.9-test"
test result: FAILED. 2809 passed; 1 failed; 6 ignored
```

The test writes a fake compiler script with a `#!/bin/sh` shebang (`fake_compiler` in `src/world_compile.rs`) and expects `probe_compiler_version` to record its output. In the standalone composition's build sandbox the probe returns "" — consistent with the sandbox lacking `/bin/sh` for the shebang (hypothesis, not proven).

Why this is filed as an observation, not a regression:

- The switch builds the package through the **root flake** composition (`nix build .#id-web` at the repo root), whose checkPhase runs a different test total (2765 in the 2026-11-04 switch log) and does **not** fail this test — the switch log's only failure was the local_events test fixed for #5736.
- `cargo test -p id` in a dev shell also passes it (a shell has /bin/sh).
- The failing mechanism (fake-compiler probe) is disjoint from the #5736 change (docs + one test in `src/local_events.rs`).

Ask: confirm whether the standalone flake is a supported build path for pkgs/id. If yes, make the probe test robust to a `/bin/sh`-less sandbox (skip when the fake compiler cannot execute, or invoke it via an explicit interpreter). If the root composition is the only supported path, record that in pkgs/id's docs so the standalone failure stops surprising people.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `nix build ./pkgs/id#id-web` (standalone flake) passes its checkPhase, including `world_compile::tests::version_probe_records_the_reported_version`.
- [ ] The root-flake composition build of the same package still passes — the fix does not just move the failure.
- [ ] The fix addresses the sandbox environment difference (what `probe_compiler_version` sees under the standalone build) rather than weakening or deleting the assertion.

body:
## Summary

Design the **native Android client for ID as a product**: a first-class client with its own identity custody, local/offline worlds, and the phone's capability-provider role — not a peripheral for driving other machines.

## Motivation

#1831 (2026-10-28) is a proof of concept: an Android app that relays the phone's touch input into a live app running elsewhere, over a deliberately limited interface. It answers "can a phone drive a remote app?" — a real question, and its input-event model work stands. But it is scoped as a PoC and defines the phone as an *input peripheral*. Drew's 2026-11-04 direction names the Android app as its own design line: what ID *is* on a phone — the device most users will actually carry — is a different and larger question that no issue currently owns. #1831 becomes this design's remote-drive feature and its PoC precursor, not its definition.

## Sketch

- **Identity custody on-device**: Ed25519 keys in Android Keystore / StrongBox where available; enrolment and recovery applying the #5684 custody model (including its plainly-stated unrecoverable cases) to mobile realities — device loss, biometrics as unlock (not as identity), multi-device households.
- **Offline worlds**: a local journal on-device with sync on reconnect (the id-sync seams from the crate split, #3447); the journal model itself is the conflict posture — no separate merge design until one is proven needed.
- **Client shape**: the shell contract on mobile — portable-screen presenter plus native surfaces where Android is genuinely better (notifications, share intents, widgets); presence and background-sync limits stated honestly against Android's battery rules.
- **Capability-provider role**: the phone as a #5686 provider — sensors, location, camera, notifications — with Android's runtime-permission model mapped onto ID's grant model, actuation vs observation risk classes respected.
- **Build shape**: Rust core via the crate split's client-only variant; the shell in Kotlin/Compose vs shared Rust UI is an open decision for this design, informed by #788's framework record rather than forking it.

## Open questions

- Thin client, thick client, or per-world choice — and what decides?
- Distribution for a personal fleet: Play, sideload, or both — and what each does to the update story?
- How much of #1831's input-event model survives as remote-drive mode vs is subsumed by the shell contract?
- Push/presence without a central server: what wakes the app when a world changes?

## Relations

Parent: epic #2056. Precursor: #1831 (PoC — input relay; this design supersedes its framing, not its event-model work). Relations: #5684 (identity custody/delegation), #5686 (capability providers — the phone as provider), #788 (shell contract + framework record), #3447 (client-only build variant), #5671 (transport fallback — mobile networks are the UDP-denied case in the wild). Filed in the 2026-11-04 gap pass (WS-F) per Drew's order.

body:
## Summary

Design ID's **deterministic testing infrastructure**: the machinery that makes the system's behaviour reproducible — a simulated clock, deterministic replay of recorded world event streams, a managed seeded fuzz corpus, and long-horizon soak runs with invariant checkers. This is testing *infrastructure* as its own design line, distinct from any one feature's tests.

## Motivation

ID is a journal/event-sourced system: correctness lives in replay, reconstruction, and projection. The pieces that exist are scoped elsewhere — #558's deterministic fuzz harness belongs to the authoring dev loop; #544 is a per-world replay self-check (`id world verify`); #5685 designs the DoS suite and the performance benchmark programme (regression gates on speed and abuse resistance — it says nothing about determinism). The mcpx deterministic-testing work (#1963, #2641) is mcpx-scoped. Nothing designs, for ID itself: how determinism is *achieved* (where nondeterminism can enter), how recorded reality becomes a permanent regression asset, or how the system is exercised over *time* — days of simulated operation, not single runs.

The design's own rules are the natural oracles: "reconstruction is admission" (#2898), lease-epoch monotonicity and single-writer fencing (#2819), writer-set projection purity (#5545 — projection is a pure function of its tuple, so any replay divergence is by definition a bug).

## Sketch

- **Simulated clock**: logical time injected at the core seams; wall-clock reads, RNG, hash-map iteration order, and thread scheduling audited as nondeterminism sources, with the audit itself a deliverable. Where the clock seam lives across the crate split (#3447) is part of the design.
- **Deterministic replay**: capture world event streams (journals plus input frames) into replayable fixtures; replay must reproduce the journal hash bit-exact; divergence is a bug report with a minimal repro, not a flaky test.
- **Seeded fuzz corpus**: corpora as versioned artefacts — seeds that found bugs are pinned forever, minimisation is automated, corpus growth is reviewed like code.
- **Soak runs**: long-horizon runs compressing days of simulated time, with invariant checkers running continuously over live state (not just at checkpoints): admission invariants, lease fencing, projection purity, discovery bounds.
- **CI shape**: a determinism gate (same input → same journal hash) on the fast tier; replay + soak on a slower cadence, sized with #5685's tiering so the two programmes share load machinery instead of duplicating it.

## Open questions

- Corpus storage and size discipline: in-repo, in object storage, or generated-from-seeds only?
- Soak cadence and budget: nightly vs weekly; what simulated-time-per-real-hour is achievable?
- How much of the mcpx determinism pattern (#1963/#2641) is shared doctrine vs per-system machinery?
- Does the simulated clock extend to network/transport simulation (partitions, latency) or stay at the world layer for v1?

## Relations

Parent: epic #2056. Relations: #558 (dev-loop fuzz harness — a consumer), #544 (replay self-check — a consumer), #5685 (DoS + benchmark programme — sibling infra, shared machinery), #2898, #2819, #5545 (oracle rules), #3447 (crate seams). Filed in the 2026-11-04 gap pass (WS-F) per Drew's order that deterministic testing gets its own design issue.

body:
# Home-resolution inventory audit — disposition every remaining site against the contract

Phase 4 of the home-resolution design (design issue #5762; design doc `files/designs/code-home-resolution-contract.md`
in the `keep-the-four-repos-healthy` goal workspace).

The contract: a tool that needs the home directory resolves it
exactly one way — a non-empty `HOME`; empty is unset; unset is a
named error at the first surface that needs a path, never a
substitute directory (no root anchoring, no CWD fallback, no
literal `~`, no hardcoded user). Phases 1–3 cover the filed
crates (#5737 fleet-config, #5673 fleet-queue, #5640
atlas-search/fleet-search). This audit dispositions everything
else the inventory finds, so the contract is a repo property,
not a per-crate accident.

## Known unfiled sites (from the design pass's grep inventory, origin/main c2bf5fca2)

- `pkgs/id/src/world_compile.rs:704` — `std::env::var("HOME").unwrap_or_default()`:
  the fleet-queue shape (root anchoring) in id's own tree, one
  file away from world.rs's hard-error embodiment.
- JS `bin/*` proxies — `process.env.HOME || '/home/user'`
  hardcoded-user fallback (agy-proxy.mjs, sync-models.mjs,
  provider-catalog-sync.mjs) plus template-literal
  `${process.env.HOME}/...` path construction at further sites
  (claude-code-proxy, codex-proxy, commandcode-proxy,
  antigravity-ls-proxy): unset HOME yields `undefined/...`
  relative paths. Disposition may route these to this contract
  or to #3352's env rule — decide with evidence and record it.
- mcpx (Go) — `home, _ := os.UserHomeDir()` discards the error
  at ~8 sites (internal/cli, internal/config, internal/daemon,
  internal/mcpclient): on Unix an unset HOME yields `""` and
  root-anchored joins. Sites that already handle the error
  (`err == nil` guards) are conforming; disposition the rest.

## Acceptance criteria

- A grep inventory of home resolution (Rust `env::var("HOME")` /
  `var_os`, Go `UserHomeDir` / `Getenv("HOME")`, JS/TS
  `process.env.HOME`, Python `os.environ["HOME"]` / `expanduser`)
  is posted on this issue with a disposition per production
  site: conforms / fixed in this phase / filed separately
  (issue link + why its context genuinely differs).
- Same-shape sites (unset/empty HOME silently producing a
  substitute directory) are fixed in this phase with the
  contract's probe matrix as tests (unset and empty both named
  errors; set = unchanged paths).
- No production site remains whose disposition is "unexamined".
- The design issue is commented with the closing inventory so
  its acceptance can be checked off.

title: id(directory): prevent one signing key from exhausting the shared replay budget

labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: app/id

body:
## Problem

The signed-request replay guard has a fixed global capacity but no per-key admission bound. In pkgs/id/src/directory_auth.rs:253-275 and 327-368, verify_signed accepts valid signatures from arbitrary well-formed keys and inserts key:nonce entries into a shared map capped at 4096. WorldHub shares one ReplayGuard across requests (pkgs/id/src/world_hub.rs:438-443 and 473-492). One key can submit 4096 unique valid nonces and consume the global capacity, starving fresh signed requests from other users.

## Required behavior

Keep a hard global memory bound while preventing a single key or principal from consuming the entire replay budget. Preserve duplicate-nonce rejection per key and the existing signature verification contract. The eviction and admission policy must be explicit; a replay must never be accepted merely because the cache is full.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A test fills the replay budget with distinct valid nonces from one key, then proves a fresh valid request from a second key is still admitted.
- [ ] A replay from the first key is still rejected under the chosen policy.
- [ ] Total retained replay state stays within a documented hard bound.
- [ ] Concurrent verification tests prove duplicate requests cannot race past admission.

## Summary

The #2146 phase-2 program-only router (`create_program_router`, merged in PR #5537 commit `bde2ec004f`) pins only its root page to the bound world. The world session bridge it merges is the shared, unpinned bridge: every bridge handler leases whatever world the caller names, so a listener bound to `program:<world-A>` also serves the full world session API for every other world the hub hosts.

## Evidence (verified this run against laptop primary main `57119df82e`)

- `pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs:515-531` — `create_program_router` sets `state.program_world` (read only by `program_page_handler`, routes.rs:614) and merges `world_ws::world_routes_at(&world_socket)` with a `WorldWebState { hub: state.world.clone(), cookie_secure }` — the whole hub, no world restriction.
- `pkgs/id/src/web/world_ws.rs:40-47` — `WorldWebState` has only `hub` and `cookie_secure`; there is no pinned-world field for the bridge to enforce.
- Bridge handlers route by caller-supplied world name:
  - host-view: world_ws.rs:137 `hub.lease(query.world.as_deref(), None)`
  - directory read/write: world_ws.rs:427 `hub.lease(world.as_deref(), token)` (world from `DirectoryQuery`/`DirectoryRequest`)
  - invite: world_ws.rs:545 `hub.lease(request.world.as_deref(), supplied)` — with the hub admin token, an invite can be minted for a different world through this listener, and `lease` with an admin token may create the named world.
  - websocket: `handler` upgrades and `run_session(&hub, ...)` (world_session/mod.rs:857) joins the world the session names.
  - explore routes merged by `world_http_routes` ride along the same way.
- The stated contract this breaks: `create_program_router`'s doc (routes.rs:506-514) says the program surface is the bound world's frontend + bridge "and nothing else", and `program_page_handler` (routes.rs:610-613) 404s for a world the hub does not host because the surface must never become "a lobby for a different world". The existing test `program_router_serves_only_the_program_surface` checks explorer paths 404 and that invite minting without the admin secret is 401 — but never tries a *different hosted world* through the bridge.

## Why it matters

A program binding is the surface an operator deliberately exposes for one world (potentially publicly, per #2146 programs-as-websites). Today that exposure silently includes every other hosted world's session bridge: directory reads/writes, host-view, invite minting, explore pages, and guest session joins for worlds the operator never bound to that listener. Per-world authority inside the bridge (guest caps, admin token) still applies, but the listener-level isolation the phase-2 design promises — one listener, one world — does not exist, and it fails silently: nothing in the router or tests names the gap.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The program router's bridge is pinned to the bound world: requests naming any other world (host-view `?world=`, directory `world`, invite `world`, explore, websocket join) are refused (404, matching `program_page_handler`'s convention) without leasing or creating that world.
- [ ] Requests naming the bound world, or omitting the world where the bridge defaults, work exactly as on the explorer surface.
- [ ] Tests extend `program_router_serves_only_the_program_surface`'s pattern: with a hub hosting two worlds, a program router for world A refuses world B on each bridge entry point (invite, host-view, directory read/write, websocket join) and serves world A.
- [ ] The mechanism is structural (the pin lives in the bridge state or an equivalent single choke point), not per-handler ad-hoc checks that a future bridge route can forget.

Related: #5537 (parent implementation), #5711 (the phase-1 parse-time companion gap: program target names not validated against the world-name rule). Distinct from #5711 — that is about which names parse; this is about which worlds a live program listener serves.

# id(serve): `WebContentTarget` program target accepts world names no world can bear — validate at parse time

## Summary

The #2146 phase-1 web content target (`pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs`, merged in PR #5590 for issue #5537) validates a `program:<world-name>` target only as "non-empty once trimmed". By the design's own selector semantics the target **is** an existing world name — the `--world-name` selector — and world names elsewhere in the same binary are held to `world_hub::validate_world_name`. A binding line naming a world that can never exist therefore passes startup parsing and is carried as a valid binding, instead of failing fast at startup like every other malformed `[web_bindings]` line.

## Evidence (main @ af0847d00a2231c71f6ebb59eba4cc7db197599e, read via `gh api` raw; laptop unavailable this run)

- `pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:418-430` — `WebContentTarget::program()` does `world.trim()` and only ensures non-empty. Its doc comment says it validates "the same way the #2147 publication registry validates its world names: non-empty once trimmed" — but the publication registry is a *mount* registry; the target's name is a **world** name (design `doc/2026-11-01_design_id2146.md:36`: "use the existing world name (the `--world-name` selector, default `lobby`) as the program target").
- `pkgs/id/src/world_hub.rs:48-60` — `validate_world_name`: 1..=64 bytes (`MAX_WORLD_NAME_BYTES`, world_hub.rs:37), characters only `[a-z0-9-_]`, and not `.` or `..`.
- `pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:656-662` — `validate_world_options` applies exactly that validator to `--world-name`.
- `pkgs/id/src/world_hub.rs:515` — world resolution maps `validate_world_name` failure to `ResolveError::InvalidName`: a world named `Arena`, `..`, `a/b`, `a.b`, or 65+ bytes can never be created or opened, so a program target carrying one can never resolve.
- `pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:3293-3300` — the only pinning tests for `program()` rejection are the empty / all-whitespace spellings (`program:`, `program:  `); `program:arena` round-trips. No test pins rejection of an impossible world name.
- `pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:541-553` — `resolve_web_bindings` documents the point of parsing config lines at startup: "a malformed `[web_bindings]` line fails startup naming the line". A never-resolvable target is exactly the class that should fail there, before phase-2 routing (#5537 phases 2-4) turns it into a per-request failure instead.

Accepted today but impossible as worlds (by the reads above): `127.0.0.1:3001 program:Arena`, `program:..`, `program:a/b`, `program:a.b`, `program:` + a 65-byte name.

## Why it matters

Phase 1's stated job was "this type and its validation first" (serve.rs:391-395). The validation it shipped checks the wrong registry's rule: startup now blesses bindings whose target is unresolvable in principle, deferring a config typo (`Arena` for `arena`) to a runtime mystery in phase 2+. It also lets `WebBinding::program` / `WebContentTarget::program` mint identities (`program:..@127.0.0.1:3001`) for content metadata that no world lookup will ever match.

## Acceptance criteria

- `WebContentTarget::program` (and therefore `WebContentTarget::parse`, `WebBinding::program`, and `parse_web_binding_line`) rejects any world name that `crate::world_hub::validate_world_name` rejects — uppercase, `.`/`..`, path separators, dots, over 64 bytes — with an error naming the offending spec, while `program:arena` and other legal names keep working.
- The validation rule lives in one place (reuse `validate_world_name` where feature gates allow, or mirror it with a comment naming the source of truth) so the target grammar cannot drift from the world-name grammar again; the doc comment on `program()` is corrected to cite the world-name rule, not only the #2147 registry rule.
- New pinning tests next to `test_web_content_target_program_rejects_empty_world` cover at least: uppercase, `..`, a name with `/`, a name with `.`, and a 65-byte name — plus a legal max-length / hyphen / underscore name accepted.
- `cargo test -p id --lib commands::serve` (or the serve test module's filter) passes on the laptop / in CI.

Related: implementation epic #5537, design #2146, bindings model #2145, publication registry #2147.

title: id: design: Querying local and remote ID servers v1

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Summary

ID servers hold data in tables; there should be a first-class, designed way to **query** those tables — on a local server and on remote servers — from scripts, from agents, and from the human CLI, with the same semantics in all three. Remote queries are filtered by the data's sensitivity classification; the owner of a server keeps a deliberate override for their *own* server's unencrypted data. This design defines the query surfaces, the filtering model and its hard boundary, and result shaping.

Relates: #2048 (ID data/zettelkasten layer — the tables being queried), and composes with the selective-sharing grants model (grants decide *whether* a peer may reach data; sensitivity filtering decides *what a query returns* — the design must state how the two compose).

## Feature set (expanded)

### 1. Query surfaces

- **Local queries:** querying tables on a local ID server — in-process/embedded where possible, no network round trip, full local performance.
- **Remote queries:** querying tables on a remote ID server over ID transport (including over fallback transports), with the remote server executing the query — not "replicate everything and query locally" as the only option.
- Query language/shape: define what a query is in v1 (table selection, filters, projections, ordering, joins or explicitly no joins) — powerful enough for real use, constrained enough to be safe to execute on someone else's server.
- The same query, unchanged, should be runnable against local and remote targets; only the target and the filtering outcome differ.

### 2. Sensitivity classification & filtered remote queries

- Every table/collection (and where needed, object/row or field) carries a sensitivity classification; the design defines the classification levels, who assigns them, and the default for unclassified data (default must be safe, not permissive).
- A remote query executes **under the requester's clearance**: results are filtered to what the requester's identity is cleared for, server-side, before anything leaves the server. Filtering is not client-side cosmetics.
- Filtered-result honesty: does the requester learn that results were withheld (count of withheld rows, existence of withheld fields) or not? Pick per classification level and state it — silent filtering and existence leaks are both failure modes.
- Field-level behavior: redaction vs. whole-row exclusion vs. query rejection, per classification and query shape.
- Audit: remote queries (who, what query, what classification levels were touched/withheld) are logged on the serving server, visible to its owner.

### 3. The owner override — and its hard boundary

- The local owner may **override sensitivity filtering for data on their OWN server**: when querying their own server, the owner can see past classification filtering.
- **Boundary (state it exactly):** the override applies only when the data is **not encrypted**. Encryption defeats the override — if data is encrypted under keys the querying identity does not hold, no override, admin flag, or local access returns plaintext. Classification is a policy filter; encryption is a cryptographic boundary, and policy never outranks cryptography.
- Override mechanics: explicit, deliberate, and audited (an override flag/mode, never a silent default; override use appears in the server's audit log). Override is per-query or per-session, not a permanent server setting that quietly stays on.
- Override scope: own server only. Being owner of server A grants no override on server B, even for data A originally shared to B.
- Multi-principal servers: if a server hosts data for more than one owner, whose override applies to whose data must be defined — an operator must not gain override over other people's unencrypted data merely by hosting it, if the model can prevent it; where it cannot, say so honestly.

### 4. Parity: scripts, agents, humans

- One query model, three front doors: a scripting/API surface, an agent-facing surface (structured in/out, machine-readable errors, stable result schema), and the human CLI — all executing the same queries with the same filtering.
- No privileged back door: agents and scripts get no broader access than their identity's clearance; the CLI gets no magic local bypass except the explicit owner override above.
- Non-interactive safety: scripts/agents can run read-only queries without prompts; mutating operations (below) require explicit intent that is visible in audit.

### 5. Read-only vs. mutating surfaces

- The query surface is **read-only by default and by design**; v1 query language must not be able to mutate data as a side effect.
- Mutating operations, if exposed at all, are a *separate* surface (distinct commands/endpoints, distinct permissions, distinct audit), designed explicitly — not "query language plus write verbs when you're local."
- Remote mutation: whether a remote principal may ever mutate via this surface, and under what grants (compose with selective sharing), is decided here even if the v1 answer is "no."

### 6. Result shaping & pagination

- Projection (choose fields), ordering, limits — pushed to the executing server, not done client-side over a full dump.
- Pagination: stable cursor-based pagination for large results (no offset drift under concurrent writes), with page-size limits enforced server-side.
- Result formats: structured (JSON/rows) for scripts/agents; human-readable tables for the CLI; a SQLite-shaped result is a candidate format for composability (see the foreign-adapter design's query-Redis-get-SQLite pattern).
- Truncation honesty: when a result is cut (page size, server cap, sensitivity filtering), the result says so and how to continue — never a silent partial answer presented as complete.
- Cost limits: server-side guardrails for expensive queries (timeout, scan cap) so a remote query cannot DoS the serving server.

## Non-goals (v1)

- A general SQL engine over arbitrary foreign stores (adapters are a separate design; this covers ID tables).
- Analytics/aggregation beyond what the v1 query shape explicitly includes.
- Weakening encryption for operability — the override boundary above is absolute.

## Acceptance for this design

A follow-on reader can break this into the decomposition tickets below without re-deciding: the filtering model, the override boundary, surface parity, or pagination/result rules.

## Decomposition sketch

1. Design: ID query language/shape v1 (local + remote execution model, local/remote parity).
2. Design: sensitivity classification model (levels, assignment, defaults, field vs. row behavior).
3. Design: server-side filtered remote query execution + withheld-result honesty + audit.
4. Design: owner override mechanics (scope, audit, multi-principal servers) and the encryption boundary.
5. Design: client surfaces parity — scripting/API, agent, and CLI front doors over one model.
6. Design: result shaping & cursor pagination (formats, truncation honesty, server cost limits).
7. Design: mutating surface separation (permissions, audit) — or an explicit v1 "read-only only" decision record.

## Open questions

- Classification levels: how many, named how, and can owners define their own?
- Withheld-result signaling: counts, yes/no, or nothing — per level?
- Is the query language a new ID-specific shape, a SQL subset, or both (SQL compiled to the ID shape)?
- How do grants (selective sharing) and classification compose when they disagree — deny-wins?
- On multi-principal servers, can the model technically separate operator from data owner for override purposes?
- Cursor stability: snapshot semantics per query, or best-effort with documented drift?
- Should a SQLite-formatted result be a v1 format or a follow-on?

body:
## Context

Follow-up to #2090. Its role-aware `EventStore::tag_claims` default view uses the settled group projection and compares a clear's signing key to the Admin account key. The event-store bridge in `pkgs/id/src/event_store/resolve.rs` currently maps `p2panda_auth::GroupAction` membership operations, but does not carry the newer `id::groups::fold::DeviceGrant` records into that projection.

As a result, a `tag.clear` signed by a device authorized to act for a group Admin is not recognized as that Admin: the marker remains visible/audit-queryable, but it does not hide the claim in the default view.

## Needed

Integrate settled device authorization into the event-store tag-role lookup, or explicitly define that the event-store protocol treats a device key as a distinct non-admin poster. If device authorization is supported, cover an Admin-scoped device, a device with a lower scope, and a revoked/inactive device. Keep device support separate from deletion policy (#2091).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The event-store tag-role lookup in `pkgs/id/src/event_store/resolve.rs` either recognises settled `DeviceGrant` authorization (an Admin-scoped device clear hides the claim in the default view) or this issue records the explicit decision that a device key is a distinct non-admin poster.
- [ ] If device authorization is supported: tests cover an Admin-scoped device, a lower-scoped device, and a revoked/inactive device.
- [ ] Device support stays separate from deletion policy (issue #2091) — no deletion semantics change here.

title: mcpx(affected-tests): --run executes shell syntax from changed paths

labels.name: kind/security
labels.description: Security issue or security hardening

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

`affected-tests.py --run` executes shell commands containing Git-reported paths without quoting them. The script collects changed and untracked paths at `pkgs/mcpx/scripts/affected-tests.py:366-371`, interpolates `.go` paths and package directories into command strings at `:399-404` and `:412-414`, then runs each string with `subprocess.run(..., shell=True)` at `:605-608`. The repo-level `mcpx-test-affected` recipe exposes the `--run` argument (`root.just:187-191`).

A controlled scratch-repository probe confirmed arbitrary shell syntax in a space-free untracked `.go` filename executed during `--run` and created a marker file. The probe ran outside the laptop checkout. Current selector tests explicitly use the dry-run seam and never `--run` (`pkgs/mcpx/scripts/tests/test_affected_untracked.py:12-19,85-99`).

## Why it matters

A developer running the documented affected-test command with `--run` against an untrusted branch can execute commands from a crafted filename. This turns a local test-selection convenience into a shell-execution boundary.

## Suggested fix

Keep Git paths as structured values (prefer NUL-delimited Git output), build argument vectors for `gofmt`, `go vet`, and `go test`, and use `cwd=` rather than shell `cd` strings. Add a scratch-repo regression test with shell metacharacters in a filename and assert that no marker command runs.

title: pm-dispatch: no read/status endpoint for launched or enqueued work (thin clients must cross domains for status)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/m
labels.description: Medium: expected under 1 day of work

body:
Filed from fleet epic #5412 step 4 (#5432, the dispatch thin client), per that step's rule: interface gaps found while building the verbs are filed against pm-stack, not absorbed into the client.

## Gap 1 — no read/status endpoint on pm-dispatch

`pm-stack/dispatch/src/server.ts` exposes exactly three routes: `GET /health` (unauthenticated), `POST /v1/sessions`, `POST /v1/tasks`. A caller that launched or enqueued work has **no way to ask pm-dispatch about it afterwards** — no `GET /v1/tasks/<id>`, no `GET /v1/sessions/<id>`. The thin client shipped in #5432 therefore answers "what happened to task N?" by crossing domains into the queue (`fleet queue list` / the queue store), which works but couples every dispatch caller to queue internals and to a second credential path.

A minimal fix on the pm-stack side would be one authenticated read route reusing the existing auth (`authenticate()` already gates the POSTs), e.g. `GET /v1/tasks/:id` returning the task row's status/worker/progress (the row dispatch itself created and claimed), and ideally `GET /v1/sessions/:id` proxying the session's existence/state from the OpenCode server. Read-only, no new write surface.

## Gap 2 — DISPATCH_API_TOKEN had no by-name vault home (already fixed in the vault; recorded for the docs)

The dispatch README states pm-stack's secrets are filed in Bitwarden/1Password under dotted names. The bearer token was the exception: it existed only in the laptop's `~/secrets/dispatch.env`, so the fleet-secrets resolver chain (the fleet's one secrets-by-name path) could not resolve it for a client. It has been filed in Bitwarden as **`pm-dispatch.api-token`** (value verified byte-identical to the service's, by hash) as part of #5432. The durable part of this gap is documentation: `pm-stack/dispatch/install.sh` / the dispatch README should name the token's vault home alongside the other pm-stack secrets so a future rotation updates both places.

## Not gaps (checked and fine)

- Auth shapes: the static bearer is sufficient for local clients; GitHub Actions OIDC remains the CI form.
- Dedupe: `POST /v1/tasks` with a consumed `dedupe_key` returns the pre-existing task with `pre_existing: true` — exactly what a thin client needs.
- The design note for the fleet epic claimed a rendered state dir at `~/.local/state/pm-dispatch/`; none exists. Not a pm-stack defect — the note was wrong; corrected on #5432.

## Acceptance criteria
- pm-dispatch exposes an authenticated read route for a launched/enqueued task (and ideally a session) returning status/worker/progress
- The dispatch README / install docs name the `pm-dispatch.api-token` vault home alongside the other pm-stack secrets
- A thin client can answer "what happened to task N?" from pm-dispatch alone, without crossing into queue internals

title: id(world): many_worlds p99 is blocking fdatasync on Tokio workers, capped at ~1.5k commits/s (not algorithmic)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## What

The F11.8 \`many_worlds\` reference measurement (\`benches/BASELINES.md\`, #557) misses its p99 target: 5,650.8 ms vs 50 ms, with completed throughput 1,523.1/s against 2,000/s scheduled. The cause is **not** an algorithmic O(n) problem in the journal. Each durable commit runs a synchronous \`fdatasync\` on a Tokio worker thread, so concurrent commits are capped at the worker count and the rest queue.

## Evidence

**Per-append path** (no O(journal) work — checked):

- \`src/world/actor.rs:444-469\` — \`WorldActor::persist\` is synchronous and calls \`journal.append\` inline from the actor task.
- \`src/world_store.rs:184-204\` — \`FileJournal::append\`: one \`write_all\`, then \`self.file.sync_data()\` at **:202**. No directory fsync, no re-read, no re-encode of the journal.
- Per input: 1 fsync, 1 write, 3 full JSON encodes (\`actor.rs:482-485\` for replication, \`core.rs:29-31\` / \`:1983-1985\` for admin-history sizing, plus the journal line), and ~4 event clones (\`actor.rs:1370\`, \`core.rs:1964,1968\`).

**Concurrency cap** (\`benches/world_bench.rs:704-708\`): the runtime is \`new_multi_thread().worker_threads(available_parallelism())\` = 16 on the reference laptop. The bench drives 100 active worlds at 20 commits/s = **2,000 fsyncs/s**. Each fsync blocks one worker, so at most 16 are ever in flight.

**Micro-benchmark** (same filesystem, 64-byte appends to 100 files, \`fdatasync\` timed):

| concurrency | fsync/s | p50 |
|---|---|---|
| 1 thread | 168 | 5.5 ms |
| 16 | 1,190–1,456 | — |
| 32 | 2,083 | — |
| 64 | 2,648 | — |

The bench's 1,523 completed/s sits at the 16-way ceiling. Backlog ≈ (2000−1523)/1523 ≈ 3 s, which matches the p99.

**Secondary (smaller, same area):**

- \`src/world/core.rs:503-506\` — open re-serializes every journal entry with \`serde_json::to_vec\` just to charge the memory budget, on the async worker.
- \`src/world_store.rs:416-421\` — \`WorldCore::restore_with_runtime\` runs on the runtime worker in \`open_world\`, while \`FileJournal::open\` is offloaded.
- \`src/world_hub.rs:601-622\` — eviction shuts victims down before the requested world opens (\`:539-541\`), serialising leases behind the victim's in-flight command.

## Proposed fix (ranked)

1. **Take the fsync off the runtime worker.** Give \`FileJournal\` a dedicated writer thread (request channel → write + \`fdatasync\` → reply) so \`WorldJournal::append\` keeps its contract and ordering. Do not use \`block_in_place\`: \`FileJournal\` is also called from \`spawn_blocking\` during open. Estimated 40–50 lines. Expected to lift the cap from ~1.5k to ~2.5k fsyncs/s.
2. **Group commit.** One flusher writes all pending per-world appends and issues one \`syncfs(2)\` per batch. This is the only design that reliably sustains 2,000 durable events/s under 50 ms p99 on this device. Risky (per-world error attribution, compaction ordering, replication snapshots), so it deserves its own design doc per \`pkgs/id/AGENTS.md\`.
3. Move \`restore_with_runtime\` into the existing \`spawn_blocking\` in \`open_world\` and drop the redundant encode/clones listed above.

## Acceptance

- \`cargo bench --bench world_bench\` on the reference machine: \`many_worlds\` p99 < 50 ms, or a recorded result with the target still missed and a reason.
- \`journal_append_fsync\` baseline unchanged (5.18 ms/append) or explained.
- Checkpoint/eviction/reopen assertions in \`many_worlds\` still pass.

Related: #557 (the target this measurement belongs to). Found while profiling for PR #5500 (Bolt, #5489); not addressed there.

body:
## What is broken

`basic: proxy port fallbacks` (`.github/workflows/proxy-port-fallbacks.yml` → `.github/scripts/check-proxy-port-fallbacks.sh`) fails on every PR and on main:

```
::error::.opencode/opencode.jsonc has no {env:ANTIGRAVITY_DIRECT_PORT:-18751} baseURL — the fallback must match the antigravityDirectProxyPort definition (18751); a bare {env:ANTIGRAVITY_DIRECT_PORT} resolves to an empty port outside a home-manager shell (#434).
```

Because `basic: proxy port fallbacks` is the required check for the `main` merge queue (`.github/ci-policy.md`), **no PR can currently merge**.

## Why

The guard table (`check-proxy-port-fallbacks.sh`, line ~57) still marks the antigravity-direct door `has_config=yes`:

```
"ANTIGRAVITY_DIRECT_PORT|antigravityDirectProxyPort|bin/antigravity-direct.mjs|yes"
```

But the provider was deliberately repointed in `.opencode/opencode.jsonc` on 2026-11-04 (opencode#1414 / #5483): `antigravity-direct` now rides the native in-fork provider (opencode#1457) and has no `baseURL`/`apiKey`, so the `{env:ANTIGRAVITY_DIRECT_PORT:-18751}` fallback no longer exists by design.

This is the same shape as the codex precedent already recorded in the script header: the door program still exists, only its `opencode.jsonc` provider was re-seated elsewhere, so the row keeps its *script* check and drops the *config* expectation.

## Fix

One character-class change: set the antigravity-direct row's last field to `no` (keep the `bin/antigravity-direct.mjs` fallback check, which still passes), and update the retirement note in the script header to name the #1414/#5483 repoint. The `:18751` door unit and `bin/antigravity-direct.mjs` retire later after the zero-traffic window; when the script retires too, the row goes away entirely.

## Evidence

- main `ffc19be78`: `bash .github/scripts/check-proxy-port-fallbacks.sh` → exit 1 with the error above.
- Confirmed on the merged tree of PR #5036 (`queue/5906-805-screenpatch-phase-2`) — the failure is not caused by that branch.
- Reproduced in CI on run 41846464347 job 126632250062 (re-run after a runner-less cancellation).

## Impact

Fleet-wide: it blocks the merge queue, not just one PR.

body:
## What

The fleet's placement capability — deciding WHERE a build job runs
across the fleet's GitHub Actions copies and runner providers, and
dispatching it there — currently exists as a reference
implementation in the org fork of the fleet umbrella:

- Spec + frozen client interface: `docs/placement.md` in
  **developing-today/fleet** (branch `fleet-place`, commit `1258ed8`;
  lands on the fork's main once the fork is added to this app's
  installation — see below).
- Reference implementation: `tools/fleet-place` + the data registry
  `tools/fleet-surfaces.json` in the same repo.

Drew's direction (2026-11-04): this capability belongs in the binary
clients already use — **repo-queue** — so lane workers and Muse
clients trigger jobs in the appropriate location through one
interface, with sessions that outlive the client (reconnect by
handle). The crates are being refactored in another line of work
today; this issue is the absorption spec so that work inherits the
architecture instead of redesigning it. **Do not treat the Python
dispatcher as the destination.**

## The contract to implement (from placement.md, frozen v1)

```bash
repo-queue dispatch --repo developing-today/code \
  --command 'nix build .#mcpx' [--ref SHA] \
  [--runner auto|github|blacksmith] [--surface ID] \
  [--push-nix-cache] [--actions-cache KEY:PATH] \
  [--allow-paid-blacksmith MINUTES]
# -> session handle (fp_...), chosen surface, reasoning

repo-queue session status HANDLE    # mapped state + run URL
repo-queue session result HANDLE    # terminal result
repo-queue session list [--mine]
```

Non-negotiables:

1. **Registry as data.** Surfaces live in `tools/fleet-surfaces.json`
   (id, kind, owner, repo, workflow, app installation, capacity /
   budget posture, eligibility). Adding a location = adding an
   entry (+ app installation + a fleet copy). The binary reads the
   same registry format; no surface is ever hardcoded.
2. **Adapters per placement kind.** github-actions dispatch,
   blacksmith (runner variant, org-only, budgeted), codespace
   (session handoff, last resort), laptop (recorded handoff) —
   each behind eligible/capacity/dispatch/status. A new placement
   type = a new adapter + a `kind` value; dispatch/session logic
   untouched.
3. **App-only dispatch.** Every dispatch mints an installation
   token for the host repo's owner through the fleet-paperwork
   flow (App private key from the sops secrets file). Both
   installations (org 174792676, personal 175747567). No user-token
   path; a surface the app cannot reach is ineligible, loudly.
4. **Sessions server-side.** Handle = `fp_` + 128-bit random.
   Record: payload, surface + why, run id/URL, submitter, state,
   timestamps. DDL for `agent.placement_sessions` is in
   placement.md (the Python stopgap is a local JSON store with
   identical semantics — migrate records, don't redesign them).
5. **Spill cascade.** GitHub-hosted capacity per owner (live
   running+queued vs plan cap) → Blacksmith inside its free
   3,000 min/mo budget (paid only via explicit per-job allowance or
   the registry's paid cap) → Codespaces when Actions is tapped and
   the laptop is saturated → otherwise the job stays queued in
   repo-queue. Nothing is dropped for lack of a surface.
6. **Caching passthrough.** fleet-run jobs may carry per-entry
   cache options (nix closure → fleet R2 cache via the existing
   signing machinery; actions/cache for non-nix artifacts). The
   dispatch command exposes them as flags, unchanged.

## Proof state of the reference implementation (2026-11-04)

- Dry-run cascade verified, incl. simulated spill to Blacksmith and
  the all-tapped → queued outcome.
- Real dispatch as the app: session `fp_5ccf1d4ca63f4ca0939fd909345bd9ad`,
  run https://github.com/dezren39/fleet/actions/runs/41819899125
  (triggering actor `developing-today[bot]`), pin-check job read
  back to `succeeded` via the session handle.

## Blockers that also gate this

- developing-today/fleet is not yet in this app's installation
  scope (org-owner grant pending) — the reference branch waits on
  it to push.
- org-run (this repo) is pre-registered as a surface; when it lands,
  flip its registry status and give it the `runner` input for
  Blacksmith parity (small follow-up PR, noted in placement.md).

Unassigned on purpose; pick up with the queue refactor.

## Acceptance criteria
- fleet placement (dispatch + session commands per docs/placement.md in developing-today/fleet) is absorbed into repo-queue.
- No regression: existing tests/checks for the touched area remain green, and the change lands via PR referencing this issue.
- Evidence (PR link, test/CI output, or verification note) is posted on this issue before it is closed.

body:
Found by Codex review of PR #5399 (comment 4466514775), verified against live state during task 9348 (2026-11-04):

## Defect
`agent.bind_repo_task_lane_session` live today has **no guarded recovery branch**: the recovery `launched_by` values (`opencode-claimant-recovery:zero-message-deleted`, `opencode-claimant-recovery:gone-session`) from migration-0022.sql are unhandled, and the function rejects expired leases. The claimant prompt (`pm-stack/opencode-claimant/prompt.md` steps 1c-1d) explicitly invokes those recovery operations after lease expiration, so they raise instead of atomically clearing the bindings — deleted/vanished sessions stay bound and the documented relaunch flow (#4758 recovery rule) cannot run.

## Evidence
- migration-0022.sql (on main) defines the recovery branch (compare-checks both stores, clears atomically, increments attempts, records `launch_failed`).
- migration-0023.sql (PR #5349 record copy) redefines the function with the bind-time claim guard and contains **zero** `recovery` references; the live definition extracted with `pg_get_functiondef` on 2026-11-04 (before migration-0024 was applied) matched the 0023 body exactly and likewise had no recovery branch (`has_recovery=false` on the live def probe). So the recovery mode was dropped when migration-0023 was applied live, not by migration-0024 (#5393), which preserved the live body and only added the task-row `FOR UPDATE` lock.
- Live overload check 2026-11-04: exactly one `bind_repo_task_lane_session(bigint, text, text, text)` in the agent schema.

## Fix shape
A new claimant migration (next free number after 0024) that merges both behaviors against the current live body: migration-0022 recovery branch + migration-0023 claim guard + migration-0024 lock order (task row FOR UPDATE before ledger access, including in the recovery branch). Exercise in a rolled-back transaction: recovery bind with each reserved `launched_by` value against an expired-lease task with matching bindings clears both stores and increments attempts; mismatched prior session id is refused.

## Acceptance
- [ ] Recovery calls from prompt.md steps 1c-1d succeed against live for verified-gone / verified-empty-deleted sessions
- [ ] Normal bind still requires a claimed task with a live lease
- [ ] Lock order stays task-row-first in every branch
- [ ] Record copy lands via PR referencing this issue

body:
## Problem

`pm-stack/ready-for-agent/test-install.sh` — the regression harness for `install.sh` — fails on current `main` at its very first case, so none of its six install scenarios can run.

## Evidence (verified 2026-11-04, origin/main `fd961f654`)

Run on the laptop, twice, same result:

```text
$ bash pm-stack/ready-for-agent/test-install.sh
installing ready-for-agent@1.1.0 (found: 1.0.0)
waiting for the harness UI...
ready-for-agent@1.1.0 is running after restart: http://127.0.0.1:6056
/tmp/tmp.XXX/package-change-active/deploy/install.sh: line 192: ./apply-config.sh: No such file or directory
FAIL: package-change-active: installer exited unsuccessfully
exit=1
```

Root cause, from the sources:

- `pm-stack/ready-for-agent/install.sh:192` runs `./apply-config.sh` unconditionally at the end of every verified-serving success path (added by the #1203 declarative-config change, commit `dcea7fa21`).
- `pm-stack/ready-for-agent/test-install.sh` builds each case's deploy dir by copying only two files into it: `install.sh` and `systemd/ready-for-agent.service`. It never copies `apply-config.sh` (or `config.json`), and provides no stub for it — so the success path the harness exists to exercise always dies at line 192.
- `install.sh:31` does `cd "$(dirname "$0")"`, so the `./` call resolves inside the copied deploy dir, not the repo checkout.
- The companion harness `test-apply-config.sh` passes on the same tree, so `apply-config.sh` itself is not the failure.
- No PR CI covers `pm-stack/**` (already tracked as #2936), which is how this stayed red unnoticed.

## Why it matters

`test-install.sh` is the only automated coverage for the installer's trickiest behavior — the #4839 pending-restart marker, restart-vs-start-vs-unchanged verification, and the clone-fail retry. With the harness red at case 1, all of that coverage is inert, and future installer changes have no working safety net.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `bash pm-stack/ready-for-agent/test-install.sh` passes all six cases (`package-change-active`, `unit-change-active`, `unchanged-active`, `inactive`, `first-install`, `clone-fail-retry`) on current `main`.
- [ ] The fix keeps the #1203 behavior covered: the harness asserts `apply-config.sh` is actually invoked on a successful install (e.g. the fixture copies the real script plus `config.json` with its dependencies stubbed, or provides a recording stub) — simply deleting or skipping the call in `install.sh` does not count.
- [ ] `bash pm-stack/ready-for-agent/test-apply-config.sh` still passes.

body:
## Finding

`infra/github-backup/systemd/drain-wrapper.sh` — the systemd drainer's only Bitwarden credential path for the github-backup estate mirror — had its credential-loading logic changed twice in one evening, and none of it is tested:

- PR #3222 (https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/3222, commit a0d2da4587) replaced the hard `source ~/tools/bws-env.sh` with a three-way branch (sandbox `~/tools`, laptop `~/hatch/tools`, raw access-token file).
- PR #3226 (https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/3226, commit 6361b89737) replaced that again: export `~/.config/bws/access-token` when present, then probe `bws secret list` and only on failure source a `bws-env.sh` from either candidate path, with sourcing failures masked (`source "$f" || true`).

Both PRs touched only `drain-wrapper.sh` (verified from both merge commits' file lists). On current main (3adad8fc9e2e) the fallback logic is at `drain-wrapper.sh:11-18`, and there is no test for the wrapper anywhere in the repo: `infra/github-backup/systemd/` contains no test file (directory listing verified), and a code search for `drain-wrapper` returns only `nixos/home/github-backup.nix` and the drain service unit.

## Why it matters

The fallback branch is precisely the code that runs only on a machine where the primary credential path has already failed — the situation both PRs were written for (the laptop drain). Its failure modes are silent or late:

- If bare `bws` fails and `bws-env.sh` is missing or itself fails, the `|| true` mask lets the script continue to the Python `eval`, which then dies with a raw traceback/KeyError at timer fire time, not at deploy time.
- Path drift (the wrapper already moved conventions once: `~/tools` vs `~/hatch/tools` vs `~/.config/bws`) breaks the fallback without any signal until a drain run fails and the estate mirror silently stops draining.

The sibling scripts in this fleet's backup tooling carry stubbed tests (e.g. `pkgs/cold-store-reaper/tests/`); the drain wrapper — which handles live credentials — has none.

## Acceptance criteria

- A stubbed shell test for `drain-wrapper.sh` (fake HOME, stub `bws`, stub drain target — no real Bitwarden, no network) covering all four branches:
  1. `BWS_ACCESS_TOKEN` already set in the environment → no token-file export, no `bws-env.sh` sourcing, drain proceeds.
  2. Token file present at `~/.config/bws/access-token` → exported, bare `bws` succeeds, no fallback sourcing, drain proceeds.
  3. Bare `bws secret list` fails and a `bws-env.sh` exists (each candidate path) → it is sourced, credentials load, drain proceeds. This is the PR #3226 branch that currently has zero coverage.
  4. No working credential path → the wrapper exits non-zero before invoking the drain, with a comprehensible error.
- The test runs in the same place/convention as the repo's other shell-script tests and passes.
- Production behavior of `drain-wrapper.sh` is unchanged unless a branch is shown broken by the new test, in which case the fix is part of this issue.

Found by pr-diff-review lane B reviewing PRs #3222 and #3226 (batch 3217–3251, 2026-11-03). Cross-checks that this is not already covered: open tracker issue #3215 (estate mirror system) does not mention wrapper tests; issue #3240 covers non-atomic state JSON writes in the fetch/drain scripts, a different defect.

title: pm-stack(aggregator): an unparseable coverage-snapshot anchorAt silently disables weekly rotation forever — the bad anchor is re-persisted verbatim on every panel read
