title: id(abuse): check_bytes/check_frame promise a retry for requests larger than bucket capacity — oversize can never be admitted, but refusal is temporary with retry_after_ms

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`AbuseEvaluator::check_bytes` (pkgs/id/src/abuse.rs:505-528) refuses a byte request larger than the bucket's burst capacity as a **temporary** `BudgetExhausted` refusal with a bounded `retry_after_ms` — but such a request can **never** be admitted. `TokenBucket` caps `tokens_milli` at `capacity_milli` on refill (abuse.rs:145-155), so a cost above capacity is unreachable at any future time. The refusal contract promises "wait this long and retry" for a wait that cannot help, forever.

The same trap exists on the frame path whenever a policy's `frame_burst` is 0 (cost 1 > capacity 0, abuse.rs:474-492).

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe crate `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneB-abuseoversize/` — verbatim `abuse.rs` from main @3dbc7006 (sha256 `625bcd348fe4dbe528dd67f813ce2b290d35ff8d1365774194d0b8441ed1358e`, identical on sandbox and laptop clones), default `AbusePolicy` (byte_burst 4 MiB, bytes_per_sec 512 KiB):

- Control: `check_bytes(ep, true, 4*1024*1024, 0)` → **Ok** (exact burst admitted).
- `check_bytes(ep, true, 4*1024*1024 + 1, 0)` → `Err(Refusal { reason: BudgetExhausted, retry_after_ms: Some(1000) })`.
- Retried at `now = 1000` (the promised wait) → still `Err`, `retry_after_ms: Some(1000)` again.
- Retried at `now = 1_000_000_000` ms (~11.6 days) → still `Err`, `retry_after_ms: Some(1000)` again.
- At that same instant the exact-burst request succeeds, proving the bucket is full — the oversize cost is simply above capacity, not below a refill horizon.
- Zero-burst frame policy (`frame_burst = 0`): `check_frame` refuses with `retry_after_ms: Some(1000)` and still refuses at `now = 1_000_000_000`.

Why the retry number is also wrong on its own terms: `TokenBucket::retry_after_ms` (abuse.rs:176-186) computes `deficit.div_ceil(rate_per_sec)` against *current* tokens without checking cost against capacity — for the oversize case it yields 1 ms, clamped to the 1 s floor by `Refusal::new` (abuse.rs:103-113). Every retry is told "1 s" indefinitely.

## Why it matters

The structured `Refusal` is the one contract every comms surface will consume (#2244 / #2033 design; the core landed in #3881, wiring is #3882). #3882 maps these refusals to HTTP `429` + `Retry-After` and frame-path refusals: an oversize request (e.g. a byte charge above 4 MiB) will be answered "retry in 1 s" forever, inviting well-behaved peers into an infinite retry loop and giving operators no signal that the request is permanently inadmissible rather than momentarily over budget. Fixing the contract is cheapest now, before Packet B (#3882) builds the mapping on top of it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A request whose cost exceeds the bucket's capacity is refused **permanently**: `retry_after_ms` is `None` (a dedicated reason such as `RequestTooLarge`, or documented reuse of the permanent-refusal shape) — on both `check_bytes` and `check_frame`.
- [ ] `retry_after_ms` is only ever `Some(..)` for requests that can actually be admitted after the stated wait.
- [ ] Regression tests: oversize byte request refused with no retry at t=0 and at a far-future time; zero-burst frame policy likewise; a within-capacity request over a drained bucket still gets a bounded temporary refusal; the exact-burst control is still admitted.
- [ ] The module doc / `Refusal` doc states the permanent-oversize semantics so the #3882 wiring maps it distinctly from `429` (e.g. a non-retryable refusal), or explicitly records why it still maps to 429.

Related: #3881 (core, closed — introduced the contract), #3882 (integration that will consume it), #2244 (parent), #2033 (design).

body:
Parent design: #2051 (ID chat v1), with investigation inputs #2049/#2050 and hosted-bridge constraints from #2058.

Implement the durable, IRC-shaped channel core selected by #2051. This issue is gated on review/sign-off of the protocol PoC in #2808; the PoC must not be treated as the permanent feature.

## Scope
- Use the signed group ID as the canonical channel identity and the existing group log/policy for channel membership, roles, and history. Names and nicknames are local client aliases, not a global registry.
- Add a versioned `chat.message.v1` signed event in the channel group. The event body carries bounded text plus optional `{kind, hash, author, hint?}` object references; only `blob` and `event` are v1 link kinds. Use the existing signed event/event-store/sync path; do not add a chat ALPN or bridge-assigned ordering.
- Use the channel's group history policy for new-member history. Keep world chat behavior intact. Presence and typing are explicitly out of this issue (see #2809); attachment multi-provider retrieval remains in #2260/#2261.
- Authenticate message authors with the existing signing identity in the event, not the transport peer or a server-assigned world participant number. The Iroh EndpointId is a routing/connection identity, not a substitute for the event signature.

## Acceptance criteria
- Two independent members can create/join a channel and exchange signed message events; signatures, channel/group binding, replay, duplicate delivery, and out-of-order delivery are tested.
- Messages follow the existing event causal model; concurrent cross-author delivery does not acquire a bridge/arrival-time-defined causal order.
- Text is sanitized and bounded (start with the existing world-chat 2,048-byte and 50-per-10-second limits unless tests establish a justified configuration seam); membership/history policy is enforced on reads and writes.
- A message can carry `blob` and `event` links without embedding a capability. Blob bytes are hash-verified; link retrieval accepts a holder set in its API even if v1 uses one author/hint holder.
- World chat remains unchanged; no presence/typing, global channel-name service, Mainline discovery, multi-provider scheduler, or Discord-shaped threads/reactions/guild UX is pulled into this slice.
- No permanent feature is built on the #2808 PoC until its review/sign-off is recorded.

title: design(queue): durable task data model — blocker links, park revalidation, status reasons + notes, full event history, actor provenance

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: queue/queued
labels.description: Has a queued queue task

body:
## Direction (Drew, 2026-11-01 ~02:40 CST)

Make the repo-queue data model durable — "make this system to last." Six pieces, one design:

### 1. External waits take a real datetime
Today `park` accepts only `--delay-seconds`; the `not_before` column is a timestamp and enqueue already accepts an absolute datetime (helper example: `2026-10-25T12:00:00Z`), but a mid-work park cannot name one. External events have known instants (a quota reset, a review window): park should accept an absolute `not_before` datetime as well as a relative delay.

### 2. Blockers are links, not text
A task's blockers are recorded as typed links — to other queue tasks (preferred: they are queryable, so claim can exclude a task whose blocker task is incomplete, and completing a blocker can surface its dependents), and to PRs and issues. Today `block` stores a free-text reason in progress/last_error; nothing can query it, so blocked-on relationships are invisible to the claim query.

### 3. Long parks get re-verified on a schedule
A maintenance check re-verifies every long park per item on a cadence (default daily): are the linked blockers still real, has anything changed around them that the time, the queue state, or the GitHub number doesn't capture? The check writes `last_checked_at` and its outcome onto the item; a park confirmed still-valid stays parked untouched; a stale park is flagged with a note (piece 4) for pickup or release.

### 4. Status reason column + a notes table, mirrored out
Every status transition records a `status_reason`, which automatically lands as a row in a notes/comments table (task, actor, kind — status_reason / finding / handoff — body, timestamp). Findings and notes from previous pickups, and insights from related items, accumulate there instead of evaporating between shifts. The system comments notes back automatically (to the linked GitHub issue) so the record lives where the work is discussed.

### 5. Full event history — resurrect any moment
An append-only events table records every change to a task (status, priority, park, claim, links, notes) with before/after values and the actor. Any past state of any task is reconstructable from the event stream.

### 6. Actor provenance on every write
Every create/update records who made it: lane, runtime (opencode / Muse / whichever system), session id, hostname, pid, ip address, task id and the task's start, and — at creation — which system found/filed the originating issue. Provenance rides on tasks, notes, and events alike.

## Migrations question (part of the design's scope)
Schema changes for this system should land as proper versioned migrations, in order, in a repo — the design must first inventory how the muse-dev Supabase schema (agent schema: tasks, claim/park RPCs) is currently changed, and establish the migration discipline before adding pieces 1–6.

## Acceptance
- Design record covering pieces 1–6: schemas for blocker links, notes, events; the park-datetime change; the revalidation check's cadence/config and where it runs; provenance field set.
- Migration discipline decided and the current schema state inventoried as the baseline migration.
- Implementation packets split per piece and enqueued, each independently landable.

Related: #3418 (budget-aware claiming — the claim-side companion; blocker links and budget requirements both belong in the claim query), opencode#1014 task 5256 (the capacity-wait park that started this line of design).

Named starting candidates (disposition, do not pre-judge): `pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/compact-usage-snapshots.ts` (validates its `--months` value, membership-parses unknowns), `bin/provider-catalog-sync.mjs`, `pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/collect-fleet-feed.ts`, `bin/record.mjs`, `pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/confirm-charges-surfaced.ts`.

6. Write the contract where operator tools are documented (script header-comment conventions / contributing docs — name the exact places in the evidence), and post the closing evidence on design issue #3352.

body:
Design (design-architect pass 30, 2026-11-01). Full design doc: `files/designs/code-operator-argument-contract.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Audited at origin/main `5de8ee19`. No `user/review`: every origin carries explicit acceptance with a verified laptop probe, and the judgment calls below are the architect's recorded decisions.

## Summary

The repo's operator scripts parse their command lines by membership test — `args.includes("--dry-run")`, `argv.indexOf("--store")` — and are silent about everything else. Ten filings in three days are that silence, in two costumes plus a sibling:

- **Unknown argument silently ignored → the mutating operation runs.** #3264 (pkarr-worker deploy: `--dry-rnu` deploys for real; `--deploy-version=<id>` falls through to deploying HEAD), #3287 (github-backup worker deploy, written *after* #3264 was filed), #3281 (id-mail worker deploy: a typo'd preview force-deletes the retired Worker, then deploys), #3278 (opencode-claimant install: typo'd `--dry-rnu` installs for real; typo'd `--stor` silently re-aims at the real OpenChamber store), #3296 (proxy-supervise: `--dry-rnu` starts real proxies; `--statuz` reconciles instead of reporting status), #3297 (sync-models: a typo'd preview rewrites the live OpenCode config and reloads opencode).
- **A value option present but valueless is silently replaced / consumed / crashed on.** #3333 (charges producer: trailing `--out` overwrites the live candidates file via the `??` default), #3330 (snapshot backfill: trailing `--dir` raw TypeError; `--dir --print` writes into a directory named `--print`), #3295 (snapshot append: trailing `--by` silently discards the run's records, exit 0), #3312 (mcpx docs-history, Go: trailing value flag panics instead of printing usage).
- **Sibling:** #3252 — the *recognized* `--dry-run` is dropped on pkarr deploy's `--deploy-version` branch, so a rollback preview creates a real 100% deployment.

The strict behaviour already exists in-tree (`lib/bws-to-sops.sh:53` dies on `unknown argument`; `scripts/stage-docs.sh:45`; `compact-usage-snapshots.ts:28-31` exits 2 naming a bad value). No operator script uses a strict platform parser (zero `parseArgs` hits). Sibling contracts: #2835 governs env numbers, #3005 measurement strings, dezren39/nix#1145 another repo's scripts — this repo's argv has no stated contract.

## The contract (recorded decisions)

> **Every argument is accounted for before anything happens.** A script declares its whole command line and parses strictly; anything unaccounted for is a usage error naming the offending argument, exit non-zero (2 where no usage code is established), before any subprocess / network / file write / lock / deploy step.

1. Unknown means stop — unknown flag, stray positional, and typo'd flag are the same event.
2. `--opt=value` either works identically to `--opt value` or is refused under (1) — never a silent fall-through to a different operation (per-tool pin in triage, stated in usage text).
3. Present-but-valueless is not absent — trailing, flag-valued, or (where non-empty is required) empty values are usage errors naming the option; defaults apply only when the option was not given.
4. A parsed safety flag (`--dry-run`, `--status`) is honoured on every path; tests cover the flag × path matrix.
5. Per-tool strict parsing (tools deploy independently, three languages, no shared imports); the contract and one probe matrix are shared: unknown flag → zero stubbed side-effect calls; typo'd safety flag → same; value-option edge forms → pinned behaviour; previously valid invocations unchanged.

## Phases (adopted origins — no parallel issues)

- **Phase 1** = #3264 + #3252, #3287, #3281, #3278, #3296, #3297 (unknown means stop on the side-effecting tools; lands first).
- **Phase 2** = #3333, #3330, #3295, #3312 (present-but-valueless; independent of Phase 1).
- **Phase 3** = closing inventory audit + contract statement (filed as a sub-issue, gated on Phases 1–2): every remaining hand-rolled argv parser in `bin/`, `pm-stack/*/scripts/`, deploy/install scripts and the Go tools, dispositioned covered / strict / deliberately lenient with reason (interactive REPL #2274 named deliberately-local; env-value #3261 dispositioned against #2835/#2837, not adopted).

Open questions stay in the design doc (repeated value options; short-flag style; a mechanical net; leading-dash values).

Displacement note: this pass's standing candidate was the pkgs/id plain-output rendering family (#2839/#3111/#3089, pass 29). It is displaced by this cluster per pass 29's own watch condition (unknown-args "revisit at a third tool" — now six, plus four) and remains the standing candidate for pass 31.

<!-- agent-note:v1 design-architect pass 30 -->

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every operator script in the audit scope either rejects unknown arguments with a non-zero exit and a named error, or is explicitly dispositioned as deliberately lenient with its reason recorded (per the design doc's contract statement).
- [ ] Phases 1-3 (the origin issues named in the design) are filed as linked implementation issues and land or are dispositioned; the closing argv-parser inventory (Phase 3, #3353) finds no un-dispositioned hand-rolled parser in scope.
- [ ] A typo'd flag on a mutating script (e.g. `--dry-rnu` on a deploy script) provably performs no mutation — verified by probe on at least one script per family.

## Problem

The 2026-10-31 22:40 CDT code lane wave lost 5 of its 6 root sessions terminally when the workhorse route reached a quota-exhausted leg, instead of the route rotating those sessions to a live leg.

Content-verified from the laptop OpenChamber API (`/api/session/<id>/message`) by the conductor cycle 2026-10-31 22:52 CDT:

- Failed roots (all `opencode-route/workhorse`, Queue lane code 22:40): ses_e5e6ace9855ffeRyqRUjjNVoeg, ses_e5e6ace9f3affe0Xg8PG6Ytl5H, ses_e5e6acea082ffe20Y7BWyRJVaq, ses_e5e6acea3f2ffeDkwnSH52qMIm, ses_e5e6acea9b5ffeCBemgz5smt7h
- Every one contains `provider.rate-limit` 429: "Subscription quota exhausted. Your usage window resets at 2026-11-02T00:00:00Z." on the muse-spark leg; one also shows `provider.internal` 502 "Direct Meta route request failed: fetch failed" (muse-direct).
- Zero `provider.auth` hits and zero thought_signature hits — this is NOT a recurrence of #3216.
- In the same sessions, earlier attempts on another leg (gpt terra via openai) produced normal assistant turns, so a live alternative existed while the sessions died on the exhausted leg.
- The sixth code root and all other lanes' 22:40 roots succeeded.

## Why it matters

A quota-exhausted leg is routine (pools are expected to run out before reset when alternatives exist). A route that lets the session die on the exhausted leg instead of falling through turns a routine pool state into lost lane work and burned attempts.

## Acceptance criteria

- A 429 quota-exhausted response from a route leg is treated as a leg failure and the session's next attempt falls through to the next live leg in the route, without terminating the session.
- A 502/fetch-failed on a direct leg likewise falls through rather than ending the session where another leg is available.
- Verified by a route attempt ledger / session transcript showing a session surviving a quota-exhausted leg and completing on an alternative leg.

body:
Drew's order (2026-10-31): the /aa explorer should let him switch between AA dataset versions (import batches) to compare — e.g. the current v5 data vs earlier vintages — instead of only ever showing the newest.

Current state (verified 2026-10-31):
- The collector's AA payload (pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/collect-fleet-feed.ts) is hardwired to `ainventory.v_latest_workbook_batch` — every query filters `import_batch = (select import_batch from ainventory.v_latest_workbook_batch)`. The payload carries the batch id (`aa.ts` raw.batch) but only ONE batch is ever emitted.
- `ainventory.ingest_batches` holds the batch register (id, source_kind, source_ref, ran_at, inserted_counts). Caveat: many rows are #1248 Phase-1 backfill carriers re-importing the same 2026-10-21 workbook (identical 62 measurement events under different ran_at dates) — a raw batch list would show near-duplicates.

Build:
1. **Batch index**: the collector emits the list of available batches with human labels (ran_at date + short source_ref + inserted counts), collapsing carrier duplicates that carry identical content (same source_ref + identical inserted_counts + identical payload where cheaply checkable) into one selectable entry.
2. **Per-batch payloads**: /api/aa.json serves the selected batch (`?batch=<id>`); default remains the latest batch (today's behavior). Keep collector cost sane — a batch's payload only needs rebuilding when that batch is newest or newly imported; historical payloads can be built once and cached as files beside the feed.
3. **UI selector on /aa**: a dataset-version control (visible on both tabs) listing the labeled batches, newest first, with the ACTIVE batch labeled on the page and reflected in downloads (a download taken while viewing batch X contains batch X's data). Switching swaps the entire explorer dataset — charts, tables, recommendations, both perspectives.
4. Out of scope: side-by-side diff rendering (switching + labels is the ask); the #1400 parity items; #3298 chart chrome.

Acceptance:
- Selector present on /aa; choosing an older batch visibly changes the data (verify with a batch whose counts differ) and the page labels which batch is active.
- Default load = latest batch, byte-identical behavior to today.
- Downloads follow the selected batch.
- Verified live on the laptop aggregator after deploy from the primary clone.

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/pkarr-worker/deploy.mjs` ignores `--dry-run` on the `--deploy-version` (rollback / redeploy) path: the flag combination that should be the safest way to preview a rollback instead creates a **real** Cloudflare deployment at 100%.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `5e08e198`)

- Arg parsing is global: `deploy.mjs:40-45` — `dryRun = args.includes("--dry-run")`, `deployVersion` from `--deploy-version <id>`.
- The deploy-version branch runs **before** any dry-run handling and never checks `dryRun` (`deploy.mjs:84-88`):

  ```js
  if (deployVersion !== null) {
    createDeployment(deployVersion);
    reportLive();
    process.exit(0);
  }
  ```

  `createDeployment` (`deploy.mjs:161-170`) unconditionally runs `cf workers deployments create --strategy percentage --versions [{version_id, percentage: 100}]`.
- Both other paths honour the flag: the bootstrap path pushes `--dry-run` into `cf deploy` and exits (`deploy.mjs:99-105`), and the versions path pushes `--dry-run` into `cf workers versions create` and exits (`deploy.mjs:118-124`). The deploy-version branch is the only one that drops it.
- Laptop probe (sha-matched copy of `deploy.mjs`, sha256 `805d407348729bf00a6010a5502b66455d66c559d79d4659a786faf067d80ff9`, stub `cf`/`bws` on PATH, `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` stubbed; probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneA-pkarr-dryrun/` on the laptop):
  - `node deploy.mjs --dry-run --deploy-version v-rollback-123` → stub `cf` log records a real call: `cf -q workers deployments create --worker pkarr --strategy percentage --versions [{"version_id":"v-rollback-123","percentage":100}]`, exit 0.
  - Control `node deploy.mjs --dry-run` → `cf` receives only `workers get` and `workers versions create ... --dry-run`; no deployment is created. The flag works everywhere except this branch.

## Why it matters

`--dry-run` is the safety affordance for the deploy tool, and `--deploy-version` is the rollback path — the moment an operator is most likely to reach for a preview before committing. The combination silently doing the live thing (100% traffic shift to the named version) is worse than having no dry-run at all: it teaches the operator the preview was clean when in fact the rollback already happened.

## Acceptance criteria

- `deploy.mjs --dry-run --deploy-version <id>` creates no deployment: it prints what it would do (worker, version id, 100%) and exits 0 without calling `deployments create`.
- The non-dry-run `--deploy-version` path is unchanged (creates the deployment, then reports live deployments).
- Unknown/conflicting argument handling is not weakened: `--deploy-version` with no id still errors.
- A regression test (stub `cf`/`bws`, as in the probe) covers all three paths: plain `--dry-run` (no create), `--deploy-version` (create), and `--dry-run --deploy-version` (no create) — the third fails on current code.

Related: #1828 / #1829 (the deployment standard this script implements; the deployable-shape and strategy fixes landed today in #3241/#3242/#3244 — this branch was not touched by them).

body:
Filed by the #2792 Phase 3 closing audit (queue task 4373, 2026-10-31). The audit swept the repo's TS/JS/mjs for plain-object tables indexed by a dynamic key (vendored assets excluded). The sites below are indexed by keys spelled from outside the process — live request input, ingested API/config data, documents, or issue text — with only an `undefined` / `??` / truthiness miss guard, so a prototype spelling (`constructor`, `__proto__`, `toString`, …) resolves to an inherited member instead of taking the site's miss path. Same class as #2787 / #2734 / #2781 / #2790 / #2757; the fix at each site is the #2792 rule: `Object.hasOwn(table, key)` at the read site (or a Map / null-prototype table), with the shared probe matrix asserted equal to unknown-key behaviour. Each site is small; they are grouped here because the audit is one pass — split per site if triage prefers.

## pm-stack/aggregator — ingested-data keys

1. `src/aa.ts:350` — `AA_EFFORT_ORDER[effort.toLowerCase()] ?? 50`: effort names from ingested AA data; `constructor` yields the Object constructor instead of the 50 default (numeric context → NaN risk).
2. `src/aa.ts:859` — `AA_PLAN_FACTS[providerId]` (used as `fact?.note`): provider ids from provider config/data; a prototype-spelled id yields a function as the "fact".
3. `src/aa.ts:886` — `AA_GO_CAPS[norm] ?? null`: normalized provider id, same shape.
4. `src/aa.ts:998` — `CAI_CREATORS[slug.toLowerCase()] ?? slug`: creator slug from data; prototype spelling yields a function as the creator string.
5. `src/derive.ts:760-761` — `PRIORITY_ORDER[(priority ?? "normal").toLowerCase()] ?? 2`: priority strings derive from issue/label data; prototype spelling defeats the `?? 2` fallback and poisons the sort comparator with a function (NaN ordering).
6. `src/quota-current.ts:283` — `TURSO_WINDOW_META[w.name]` guarded by `if (!meta …) continue`: window names from Turso data; `constructor` passes the truthiness guard and emits a metric with undefined label/limit/unit. (Sibling of #2781, different file.)
7. `src/sources/live.ts:127` — `KANEO_PROJECT_REPOS[p.slug] ?? fallback`: project slugs from the Kaneo API.
8. `src/sources/live.ts:446` — `TITLE_REPO_ALIASES[m[1].toLowerCase()]`: keys regex-captured from issue titles.
9. `src/quota-extract.ts:367,386` — `POOL_DOOR_PROVIDER_ID[poolId] ?? …`, `POOL_DOOR_PROVIDER_IDS[poolId] ?? …`: pool ids from ingested quota data; prototype spelling returns a function where a provider-id string/array is expected.

## bin/ proxies — live request / document keys

10. `bin/antigravity-ls-proxy.mjs:125-136` — `MODEL_MAP[cand]` (`?.enum` and a direct read): candidate model names from live request traffic.

Sites the audit dispositioned internal-only (allowlist-guarded dispatch repo tables, mcpx OPS literals, regex-bounded MONTHS, aggregator render enums, fixture tables) are named in the closing-audit comment on #2792 and are NOT in scope here.

body:
# ci(id): every main run builds the pkgs/id checks twice — the PR-tier matrix and the full flake check both run on push/schedule since the main-only trigger change

## Evidence (main `0f84fe08`, verified this run)

`.github/workflows/id-check.yml` has had no `pull_request` trigger since `814c5146` ("ci: main-only workflow triggers, cancel-in-progress everywhere", 2026-10-30, Drew's main-only order). Its `on:` block (id-check.yml:44-58) is now: `push` to main (paths `pkgs/id/**` + the workflow/guard files), a nightly `schedule` (41 8 * * *), and `workflow_dispatch`. But the job graph still contains BOTH tiers, and nothing gates either one off for push/schedule events:

- **PR tier:** `guard` ("basic: guard PR check list") → `check_each`, a matrix over the **26 checks** in `.github/scripts/id-pr-checks.txt` → the `check` aggregator ("nix flake check"). No `if:` on `guard` or `check_each`.
- **Main tier:** `full-flake-check` ("full (main tier): nix flake check"), whose only gate is `if: github.event_name != 'pull_request'` — a dead condition, since the workflow can no longer receive that event. It has no `needs:` on the matrix, so it starts in parallel and cannot reuse the matrix jobs' cache uploads from the same run.

The matrix set is a subset of the full check by construction: the guard script `check-id-pr-checks.sh` exists to keep `id-pr-checks.txt` in sync with `pkgs/id/flake.nix`'s checks (every flake check is either listed or explicitly excluded as heavy), and the workflow's own comment on `full-flake-check` says the full check is the PR set "including the heavy checks the PR list excludes". So every push-to-main run — and every nightly schedule run — builds each of the 26 fast derivations twice: once as its own matrix job, once inside the full flake check.

Live confirmation: run `41183833194` (push, 2026-10-31T08:15Z) — the jobs API shows, in one run, `basic: guard PR check list`, all 26 `basic: nix flake check (<name>)` matrix jobs, and `full (main tier): nix flake check` (28 jobs at query time; the aggregator is created once the matrix completes, for 29). The 2026-10-31 nightly main-broken report (#3038) likewise names both a `basic:` matrix failure and the full `nix flake check` failure from the same tree.

The docs still describe the pre-814c5146 world: the workflow header says it "Runs on push to main and PRs that touch pkgs/id/ files", the concurrency comment explains how "Pull-request runs keep sharing a per-ref group", and `.github/ci-policy.md`'s table still lists the id PR tier as "guard + affected-crate matrix (`id-pr-checks.txt`)" — a tier that can never run on a PR again.

## Why it matters

The matrix split (#869) and the PR-tier slimming (#1781) existed to stop paying for the same derivations repeatedly; the main-only trigger change silently reintroduced the duplication on the one event that now fires most — every merge to main that touches pkgs/id. That is ~26 extra Nix builds per merge (plus the guard and aggregator jobs), competing for the same runner pool the fleet already queues on (#1599), and doubling the surface for flaky-check noise on main (a matrix flake and the same check inside the full run can disagree, producing two differently-named failures for one tree, as #3038 shows). This is not a request to restore PR triggers — the main-only order stands — it is about making the job graph match it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A push-to-main (and schedule) run of the `id` workflow builds each pkgs/id check derivation at most once: e.g. the PR-tier jobs (`guard`/`check_each`/`check`) are removed or gated off for push/schedule, OR `full-flake-check` is restructured so it no longer re-runs the matrix set — with the chosen shape recorded in the workflow header.
- [ ] The drift guards (`check-id-pr-checks.sh`, `check-crash-gate-coverage.sh`) still run exactly once per main run, in whichever job survives.
- [ ] The dead `github.event_name != 'pull_request'` condition on `full-flake-check` is resolved, and the workflow header comment + `.github/ci-policy.md`'s id row describe the main-only reality (no PR tier that cannot fire).
- [ ] Evidence on the closing PR: the job list of a post-change push run, showing no check name appearing in both a matrix job and the full-tier job.

Distinct from: #3039 (host-eval job not a required check in nix-ci), #2936 / #1579 (pm-stack paths with no PR CI at all), #1780/#1781 (the original tier design, closed), #1599 (runner queueing — this issue reduces load, it is not the queueing bug).

title: id(serve): serve-lock staleness check tests pid existence, not serve identity — a reused pid wedges serve discovery on a dead endpoint

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: effort/xs

body:
## Summary

`get_serve_info()` decides whether the serve lock (`.iroh-serve.lock`) is stale by checking only that the recorded pid **exists** — `is_process_alive(pid)` is `kill(pid, 0) == 0` (`pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:200-210`). It never checks that the process holding that pid is the serve that wrote the lock. When a serve dies without removing its lock (crash, `kill -9`, power loss) and the OS later hands that pid to an unrelated long-lived process, the lock passes the staleness check forever: `get_serve_info` returns the dead serve's `ServeInfo` (serve.rs:171-185), and every command that consults the lock first — `get` (commands/get.rs:101), `list` (commands/list.rs:72), `put`, `peers`, the REPL, the meta client (meta_client.rs:103) — tries to connect to the recorded addresses of a serve that no longer exists instead of falling back to opening the local store directly. The failure presents as a connection error against a phantom endpoint; nothing points at the lock file.

This is the reuse sibling of #2142, which covers sentinel pids read from disk (`0`, `u32::MAX`) answering "alive" for no process at all. #2142's fix (refuse non-positive / out-of-range pids) does nothing here: a reused pid is an ordinary in-range pid held by a real process — just the wrong one.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `a9df3018`)

The gate in `get_serve_info` is straight-line: read the lock JSON → parse `ServeInfo` (serve.rs:130-141) → `is_process_alive(info.pid)` → `Some(info)`, else delete the lock and return `None`. The only staleness test is pid existence.

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-pidreuse/`; `is_process_alive` copied verbatim from serve.rs:200-210 with `libc::kill` spelled as the FFI call it wraps; serve.rs md5 `9a3eba3e2c09114e28d6932f8a102fea` identical in the sandbox and laptop clones):

```text
pid 2086858: comm=sleep state=S
gate accepts lock while pid is held by sleep: true
gate accepts same lock after sleep exits:    false
RESULT: the lock staleness check tests pid existence, not serve identity
```

The probe spawns an unrelated `sleep 120` (verified live and running via `/proc/<pid>/comm` = `sleep`, state `S` — not a zombie, not an `id serve`), writes a lock naming that pid with a dead endpoint's addresses, and the gate accepts it; the moment the sleeper exits, the same lock is refused. So the check cannot distinguish "serve alive" from "any process alive with that pid".

## Why it matters

Serve discovery is the front door for most CLI commands in a served directory. A crashed serve plus ordinary pid reuse (routine on long-uptime machines and in containers with small pid namespaces, where wraparound is fast) turns a recoverable state into persistent, misleading connection failures in that directory until a human deletes `.iroh-serve.lock` by hand — the same wedge class as #2142, reached by a mundane path rather than a corrupt file.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The staleness check verifies the pid holder is the serve that wrote the lock (e.g. the lock records the serve's start time / exe identity and `get_serve_info` compares it, or an equivalent identity check), so a lock whose pid was reused by an unrelated process is treated as stale: removed, and `None` returned.
- [ ] A lock written by a live serve behaves exactly as before (discovery still succeeds against the running serve).
- [ ] A lock with an ordinary dead pid behaves exactly as before (removed, `None`).
- [ ] Regression tests cover: live serve pid accepted; dead pid refused; live **unrelated** pid refused.
- [ ] The fix states how it behaves on non-Unix platforms, where `is_process_alive` currently always answers `true`.

Dedup: #2142 (open) covers sentinel pids `0`/`u32::MAX` only; its acceptance criteria do not include pid-reuse identity. Searches for `serve lock pid reuse`, `is_process_alive`, and `stale lock` returned no other covering issue.

title: id(world): journal restore never enforces the participant limit — a journal with more Issued entries than WorldLimits.participants restores fully, and the excess participants act

labels.name: task/triage

body:
## Problem

`WorldCore::restore` (`pkgs/id/src/world/core.rs`, the `JournalEntry::Issued` arm) rebuilds every journaled capability and inserts it into `core.capabilities` — but it never counts them against `WorldLimits::participants`, the world's maximum number of active capabilities (`src/world/mod.rs`: "Maximum number of active capabilities in this world"; default 256).

Every live path that creates a capability enforces the limit:

- `WorldCore::mint` (core.rs, the single funnel under `issue_capability` / `issue_for_account` / `attenuate`) counts the non-revoked records first: `active < self.limits.participants`, else "world participant limit reached".
- Restore's neighbouring arms enforce their caps in the same style: the `ScheduleSet` arm refuses a journal that holds more than `MAX_PENDING_SCHEDULES` pending schedules.

The `Issued` arm validates the neighbouring fields — digest shape, duplicate participant id, parent must already exist, `uses >= 1`, a delegate's expiry may not outlive its parent's — but not the count. A journal no live code path can produce (hand-edited, corrupted, or fork-copied — restore's own contract is "a bad journal is refused, never partially applied") therefore restores with more active capabilities than the world allows, and every excess participant is fully live: its token authorizes `snapshot()` / `chat()` like any minted participant. The limit is a resource bound (capability records, presence, snapshot participant lists), so the bypass is not cosmetic: after such a restore the world operates permanently above its configured capacity, and `mint` then refuses all new issuance (the restored excess already saturates the count) while the excess tokens keep working.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `51033658`)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneA-restorecap/`, a detached worktree of `origin/main` at `51033658f73a`; integration test `pkgs/id/tests/probe_restorecap.rs` against the real `id` crate, token digests built exactly as `mint` builds them — SHA-256 of `"<id>.<hex secret>"`):

- CONTROL: live `issue_capability` under `participants: 2` admits two participants and refuses the third ("world participant limit reached").
- CONTROL: restore of `Created + Issued(1) + Issued(2)` under `participants: 2` returns `Ok`.
- CASE A: restore of `Created + Issued(1) + Issued(2) + Issued(3)` under `participants: 2` returns `Ok`; the excess participant 3's token then passes `snapshot()` (snapshot lists 3 participants) and `chat()` — the over-limit participant acts normally.
- CASE D (boundary): `Issued(1) + Issued(2) + Revoked(2) + Issued(3)` under `participants: 2` also restores `Ok` — active-in-order counting (revokes applied as they appear) is the semantics that keeps this legitimate shape valid.

Code points (main `51033658`): restore's `Issued` arm is at `src/world/core.rs:168-222` (validations at :178-202, unchecked insert at :212-221); the limit check in `mint` is at `core.rs:854-861`; the participants bound is defined at `src/world/mod.rs:60-61` (default 256 at `mod.rs:89`); the schedule-cap precedent in the same function is at `core.rs:263-275`.

A counting check cannot break legitimate compacted journals: `checkpoint_entries` (core.rs:445+) re-emits participants in id order with each `Revoked` immediately after its own `Issued`, so the in-order active count of a compacted journal never exceeds the count the live world had when each participant was minted, which `mint` already bounded.

## Why it matters

Restore is the trust boundary for persisted world state, and it already refuses journals that break the schedule cap, the delegate-expiry rule, and the duplicate-id rule. The participant cap is the same kind of invariant — a configured resource bound on the world's authority surface — enforced by the one producer (restore) that rebuilds state wholesale. A journal that exceeds it yields a world that is simultaneously over capacity and unable to issue to anyone new, with the excess capabilities indistinguishable from legitimate ones.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Restore refuses an `Issued` entry that would make the active (non-revoked, counting entries in journal order) capability count exceed `limits.participants`, with an error naming the participant/limit in the style of the neighbouring restore errors.
- [ ] Regression tests beside the existing restore tests (cf. `restore_refuses_a_delegate_outliving_its_parent`): over-limit restore refused; at-limit restore passes; issue → revoke → issue at the limit passes (revokes count in order); a checkpoint/compacted journal at the limit still restores.
- [ ] Triage confirms the counting semantics for delegates (mint counts every non-revoked record, whatever its parent — mirror that) and for `Issued` entries whose participant is revoked later in the same journal.
- [ ] Cross-check the adjacent `Issued` fields triage has not yet ruled on (display-name sanitization is filed separately this run; scopes are #2890).

Dedup checked this run: open+closed search for world journal restore / participant limit — #2890 (restore never validates `Issued` *scopes*; same arm, different invariant), #2894 (restore never validates Committed/Checkpoint *event authors*), #2882 (schedule-replacement flag vs the cap restore *does* enforce for schedules). No filing covers the participant-count cap in restore.

body:
## Bug

`pkgs/id/src/tuple.rs` — the FLOAT64 decoder admits the stored form of **-0.0**, an encoding the encoder can never produce. This is the one canonical-form gap left by #1610 (which closed the negative-int range, non-minimal int, and NaN cases in the same decoder).

## Evidence (verified this run, main `5a34fa70`)

- Encoder canonicalizes -0.0 away: `push_f64` at `src/tuple.rs:355-357` — "Canonicalize -0.0 to +0.0" (`let v = if v == 0.0 { 0.0f64 } else { v };`). Encoding `-0.0` and `+0.0` both emit `[0x21, 0x80, 0x00 ×7]`.
- The stored form that *would* represent -0.0 under the sort transform is `[0x21, 0x7F, 0xFF ×7]` (bits of -0.0 are `[0x80, 0x00 ×7]`; the negative branch flips all bits).
- Decoder FLOAT64 branch at `src/tuple.rs:500-522` reverses the transform and rejects NaN (`ensure!(!v.is_nan(), …)`, line 520, added by #1610) but has **no -0.0 rejection**: the payload above reverses to exactly -0.0 and is returned as `Ok(Float(-0.0))`.

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-laneA-negzero/`, real `tuple.rs` from `origin/main` — md5-identical to the sandbox clone — compiled as a crate with only an `anyhow` dep):

```
decode(-0.0 stored form) = Ok([Float(-0.0)])
value: -0 is_sign_negative=true eq_zero=true
encoder(-0.0) = [21, 80, 00, 00, 00, 00, 00, 00, 00]
encoder(+0.0) = [21, 80, 00, 00, 00, 00, 00, 00, 00]
encoder emits neg-zero stored form: false
neg-zero key sorts after -5e-324 key: true
neg-zero key sorts before +0.0 key: true
nan rejected: true
roundtrip -1.5: [Float(-1.5)]
```

## Why it matters

Tuple keys are sort-preserving binary keys: byte order is supposed to *be* value order. The phantom -0.0 key sorts in the negative-float region (after the key of -5e-324, before the key of +0.0) while its decoded value compares equal to 0.0. So:

- A range scan for floats `< 0.0` returns a key whose value is `== 0.0`; a scan bounded at the encoder's 0.0 key never sees it.
- Two distinct stored keys decode to values that compare equal — the exact harm #1610's NaN refusal cites ("two different keys decode to floats that compare unequal to everything, including themselves"), here in the equal-but-different-key direction.
- Keys are persisted and exchanged between peers (event store / sync), so a non-canonical key admitted once propagates; the decoder is the choke point that #1610 established as the enforcement layer for every other type.

## Acceptance criteria

- `decode` rejects the -0.0 stored form `[0x21, 0x7F, 0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF]` with an error, mirroring the NaN refusal in the same branch (encoder unchanged).
- Regression tests alongside `test_decode_nan_float_rejected` cover: the -0.0 stored form is rejected; encoder output for `-0.0`/`+0.0` still decodes to `Float(0.0)`; `-5e-324`, `-1.5`, and ±infinity still round-trip/decode.
- No other decoder branch changes behavior; existing tuple tests stay green.

## Dedup

body:
Follow-up from the capability taxonomy v0 investigation (#2027, record: `doc/2026-10-29T14-05-00Z_investigation_capability_taxonomy/`, PR #2337).

## Goal
Semantic style tokens on `WorldSurface`: a program names intent (`emphasis`, `muted`, `heading`, `code`, `warning`, `success`, `link`) and each adapter resolves it to its own CSS variables, ANSI attributes or 1-bit dithering.

## Why
The issue asks for a styling tool across GUI and web that is neither all-web-elements nor Electron. Emitting DOM breaks the trusted-adapter rule on terminals and ESP32; bundling Electron drags a browser onto a 128×64 display. Tokens keep program intent portable and looks adapter-owned, extending today's `ScreenCell` (xterm-256 + bold) rather than replacing it.

## Scope
- Token runs alongside existing style spans in `ScreenSurface`; tokens are a superset with a defined mapping to the current xterm-256/ANSI projection so terminals degrade predictably.
- Adapter contract: each adapter must resolve every token (a table in the module header), with a documented fallback for unknown tokens.
- Degradation: 1-bit pixel screens map tokens to on/off/dither; text mode strips them.
- Bounded like style spans (`MAX_SCREEN_STYLE_SPANS`).

## Acceptance
- Parse/validate token runs; a test asserting an unknown token is refused (`bad_args`) rather than dropped silently.
- A test asserting the ANSI projection of a token run matches the documented mapping.
- No CSS, HTML or escape sequences reachable from a token document.

## Out of scope
A theme document, design system, per-world palettes, font selection, layout.


## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Token runs (emphasis, muted, heading, code, warning, success, link) parse and validate alongside existing ScreenSurface style spans, bounded like style spans (MAX_SCREEN_STYLE_SPANS)
- [ ] A test asserts an unknown token is refused (bad_args) rather than dropped silently, and the adapter contract table (every adapter resolves every token, documented fallback) is in the module header
- [ ] A test asserts the ANSI projection of a token run matches the documented mapping to the current xterm-256/ANSI projection; 1-bit screens map to on/off/dither and text mode strips tokens
- [ ] No CSS, HTML or escape sequences reachable from a token document

body:
The one product/policy pin in the #2065 design (`doc/2026-10-29T12-10-00Z_design_refundable_grants_pending_transfers/` §3, PR #2293). Filed so it is decided deliberately rather than defaulted in code.

## Decision 1 — window length

How long a Steam-key grant stays pending (unspendable) before it vests.

| Option | Refund exposure closed | User waits | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. 14 days (Steam's refund window)** — design recommendation | essentially all Steam refunds | up to 14 days | the rule the user experiences is the rule that protects the ledger |
| B. 48 hours | refunds inside 48h only | 2 days | leaves a 12-day hole that looks safe and is not |
| C. 14 days with early vest on evidence | most, sooner | hours–14 days | needs a trustworthy 'refund window closed' signal; Steam does not reliably expose one |
| D. none (post immediately) | none | 0 | the status quo #2065 exists to replace |

## Decision 2 — spendability of pending tokens

Recommendation: **not spendable, at all.** Allowing purchases against pending balance reintroduces the clawback problem through the front door.

## What I reviewed

The intake review on #2065 asked for this to be surfaced rather than buried; the design doc does that and carries a recommendation for each. Nothing here blocks the design doc landing — the value is a config, and the build issues read it from config.

## Answer needed

Pick a window (A unless told otherwise) and confirm pending tokens are unspendable. A one-line answer closes this.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Decision 1 recorded on this issue: refund/vesting window length chosen (A/B/C/D or an alternative), with the chooser named
- [ ] Decision 2 recorded on this issue: pending tokens spendable or not, explicitly confirmed
- [ ] The chosen values are reflected as the config defaults the #2065 build issues read (issue or PR link recorded here), and this issue is closed with the decisions in the closing comment

body:
From the #2032 investigation ([record](https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/2243/files)). Blocked by #2244 (counters must exist before a budget can be evaluated).

## Problem

The issue's requirement is "configurable budgets — max MB per window across the whole app, per IP, or per ID, and message/MB caps for a **SPECIFIC counterparty**, not just any counterparty". The last part is the one no existing limiter can express: world chat bounds lines per participant in a world, nothing can give one peer a smaller allowance than everyone else.

## Work

- Rolling-window byte budgets: app-wide inbound 32 MiB/s / 20 GiB/h, outbound 64 MiB/s / 40 GiB/h; per peer 100 MiB/h burst 8 MiB/min; per IP 250 MiB/h (direct connections only).
- **Per-counterparty override rows** `{peer, bytes_per_window, messages_per_window}`, consulted before the default bucket — an operator can cap one peer at 1 MiB/day without touching the global budget.
- Configuration in `id-server-config.toml` (`server_config/parse.rs`), defaults in code so an unchanged config behaves as today.
- Budget exhaustion is a `budget_exhausted` refusal with `retry_after_ms` (from #2244), not a disconnect.

## Done when

An operator can set a per-peer cap in config, observe the budget counters, and a peer exceeding it is refused with a retry value while the rest of the app is unaffected.

body:
From the #2032 investigation ([record](https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/2243/files)). This is the control an operator actually reaches for during an incident.

## Problem

There is no block list of any kind in `pkgs/id` — `grep -i 'block|ban|deny'` over `peers`, `connectivity` and `petname` returns nothing — and `ServerConfig` (`server_config/mod.rs:58-70`) has no key that could hold one.

## Work

- Persisted `blocks` table in the per-node store: `{kind: peer_key | ip | topic_tag, value, added_at, reason, expires_at}`; `expires_at = null` is the permanent block the issue asks for.
- **Public key** (endpoint ID): refuse new sessions, refuse to serve blobs, drop gossip subscriptions, filter their objects out of views. Blocks change serving/subscribing/rendering — they must **not** reject already-signed objects, or the graph diverges between nodes (see #2030).
- Web UI: **Block** / **Mute** on each peer row, a Blocks page with unblock, and a one-click action that writes the row.
- IP and topic/tag kinds: IP enforced at the listener only (best-effort; a relayed peer has no visible IP), topic/tag composed with the existing `PullPolicy`.

## Done when

An operator can block a peer from the peer list in one click, see it in the blocks page, and the peer's live frames and served objects stop without any signed object being discarded.

body:
Throwaway prototype: run the existing collaborative-editing live path through a session header, MAC-authenticated frames and segment checkpoints, and prove a late joiner can reconstruct from a checkpoint.

## Why

[#2034](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/2034) investigation (doc: `doc/2026-10-29T10-45-00Z_investigation_ephemeral_live_data_retention/`) found the current live path is already unsigned and bounded — `web/collab.rs` carries steps and cursors as unsigned MessagePack frames, cursors are dropped 5 min after disconnect, document state 1 h after the last client leaves (`world/mod.rs` limits) — but nothing produces a *signed checkpoint* that makes that low-retention stream auditable afterwards. This PoC answers whether the checkpoint shape actually works before anyone commits to it.

## Scope (prototype only)

- Take `pkgs/id/src/web/collab.rs` steps/cursors and put them behind a session header + per-session MAC key (no per-keystroke signature).
- Emit segment checkpoints every ~2 s or ~256 events, plus on commit/blur, chained to the previous checkpoint's signature.
- Demonstrate: a late joiner loads the latest checkpoint and reconstructs state; a reconnecting peer reconciles at the next checkpoint boundary; a truncated tail is detectable by a verifier.
- Measure the signature count and bytes saved versus signing every event.

## Hard rule (program, #2056)

**Proof of concept — must NOT be merged into the permanent feature, and no permanent feature may be built on it before a review round.** Land it as a throwaway (branch or `examples/`) that the reviewer can run, not as a change to the production path.

## Blocked by

- #2240 (session header + segment checkpoint design) — the wire shape comes from there.

Refs #2034, #2056.

body:
Design (fleet design architect, pass 13): finish the spec-revision choice work originated in #1974 (ex-nix#307) — every revision conflict gets a disposition, the `internal/spec` predicates get their callers, and the policy is demonstrated end to end.

Full design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-spec-revision-choice.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace (register: `files/potential-projects.md`).

## Audit summary (origin/main 319e6c21)

The foundation of #1974 is LANDED: settings `spec.precedence` / `spec.first` (`--mcp-spec`, `MCPX_MCP_SPEC`) / `spec.lenient` (`internal/settings/spec.go`), the `internal/spec` Policy (`Governs`, `Winner`, `Strict`, predicates `AtOrAfter`/`Before`/`Only`/`Between`), `adoptSpec` (`internal/cli/root.go:236`), and reporting on `GET /v1/protocol` (`internal/daemon/routes_proto.go:761`).

What is not finished:

- Exactly TWO behaviours consult the policy: progress `message` stripping (`internal/mcpserver/relay.go:106`) and answering 2026-07-28 server-initiated requests when lenient (`internal/mcpclient/client.go:550`). `docs/protocol.md` §1.1 says so itself.
- The predicates have ZERO callers outside `internal/spec`. Scattered comparisons remain: a duplicate package-local `AtLeast` (`internal/mcpserver/revisions.go:40`), raw `>=` in `Modern()` (`internal/mcpserver/server.go:1285`), `internal/mcpclient/modern.go` (`CallerLegacy`), `internal/mcpclient/client.go:455`.
- `docs/spec/revision-conflicts.md` still claims headline items 1, 3–13 are all "not yet converted", lumping together peer-settled decisions (disconnect-as-cancel by session presence, `server.go:1988`; cursor era key, `client.go:1214`; batches, `transport.go:110`), recorded readings of intra-revision contradictions (subscription teardown, `listen.go:347`), and stale text (C5's `-32022` claim — replaced by the counter-offer at `server.go:1341`; C23's `protocolVersions` claim — code emits `supportedVersions`, `server.go:851`).

## Decision recorded by this design

Precedence is for conflicts the peer cannot settle — `docs/protocol.md` §1.1 already scopes it that way. #1974's "every conflict resolves through the precedence list" is reinterpreted deliberately: every conflict gets a DISPOSITION of exactly three kinds — (1) peer-settled (code site + era key named; no policy consultation), (2) precedence-governed (`spec.Current()` decides, both behaviours implemented), (3) recorded reading (intra-revision contradiction; the reading is recorded, as headline 1 already does). A conflict with no disposition is the defect. This reinterpretation is also posted on #1974 (Phase 1 acceptance).

## Phases (each independently landable)

1. **Classification and truth-up (docs only).** Every headline (1–13) and per-area (A–E) item in `revision-conflicts.md` gets a disposition naming its code site; the header's blanket claim is replaced by the disposition index; stale C5/C23 fixed; `protocol.md` §1.1 updated to match; unclassifiable items listed as *undisposed* with their specific question. Reinterpretation posted on #1974.
2. **One predicate vocabulary (no behaviour change).** `mcpserver.AtLeast` delegates to `spec.AtOrAfter` or is deleted for direct predicate use; `Modern()`, `CallerLegacy`, and the `>= "2025-03-26"` check use `spec` predicates. Acceptance: no test changes its verdict. Genuine identity equalities (e.g. `request.go:54`) stay, named out of scope.
3. **Demonstrate the policy in the full stack + #1974 closure.** Daemon-level e2e (the `internal/e2e/proto_test.go` harness) showing `--mcp-spec 2024-11-05` stripping a relayed progress `message` end to end, and `MCPX_SPEC_LENIENT=2026-07-28` answering a 2026 server-initiated request that the default drops; then evidence posted on #1974 and it is closed or its remaining acceptance lines named precisely.

## Open questions (in the design doc, NOT filed)

Headline 5's validation-error form vs #1481's recorded -32602 decision at the client choke point (should the MCP serve seam era-split?); headline 7's non-object `structuredContent` translation for object-only hosts; headline 9's logging relay gating; whether `Governs` should gain any more call sites at all.

Origin: #1974 — its triage must not re-file these phases; this design's Phase 1 posts the disposition plan there and Phase 3 closes it with evidence.

title: Full-quota utilization: burn-rate projections, cascade plan, and 4–6h audibles for every plan

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: status/triaged
labels.description: Triaged and routed (see agent note)

body:
## What this is

Drew, 2026-10-29: OpenCode work burns mostly DeepSeek, so other plans that do not offer DeepSeek (Gemini, ChatGPT, eventually Claude again, others) risk ending their periods under-used. Standing rule from this issue: **if a plan is not on track to be used in full by its reset, queue more useful work. Leftover quota is waste; useful work done sooner is not a bad thing.**

## The requirement

At all times there is a **theoretical full-utilization plan for every quota** — for each provider's largest window (weekly or monthly): current %, reset instant, the burn rate that lands it at ~100% exactly at reset, and where it fits in the cascade.

- **Burn rates come from history**: per-model/per-pool run rates over time from the data we already keep (Supabase agent.quota_records, aggregator quota series, agent.mirror_token_usage_daily/hourly joined to agent models). Rates are measured per pool, not assumed.
- **Cascade modeling**: when pool A exhausts at its projected date, route pools fall through to the next provider — project that provider's exhaustion in turn, across ALL pools and across consecutive resets, not just the next one. A plan that hits 100% for this reset but strands the following period is not a plan.
- **Audibles are planned, with dates**: when projections say a pool will finish under-used or over-paced, the plan names the change in advance — route-pool priority/weight changes on a specific date, work-class shifts, or more work queued — rather than discovering the miss at the reset.
- **Check cadence: every 4–6 hours.** Each check recomputes projections from fresh quota reads + recent burn, compares against the standing plan, and either confirms on-track or escalates the approach dynamically (more work queued, weights adjusted per the plan).
- **Over-pace flag**: when a pool projects to exhaust materially early, raise the flag to Drew: slow down, or keep progressing? Default bias per Drew: keep doing useful work — but the flag is asked, not assumed.

## Build

1. Projection model over the recorded series (per pool: % trajectory, per-model burn attribution, reset calendar incl. the reset after next).
2. The standing plan document (per pool: target trajectory, cascade position, dated audibles) — regenerated each check, diffed against the previous plan.
3. The 4–6h check itself: evolve the existing go-plan-expiry-watch (already 6h, already projects in its daily report) or a sibling job; integrate with pool-quota-steward rather than duplicating it. Any job cadence change is Drew's call per the standing rate rule — this issue carries his explicit 4–6h direction for THIS check.
4. Under-pace output must name the work to queue (which backlog/queue, which job class fits the stranded provider's models); over-pace output is the flag to Drew.

## Acceptance

- A current written plan exists covering every pool's largest window, with cascade projections across at least two resets.
- Two consecutive 4–6h checks ran, recomputed from fresh reads, and either confirmed the plan or executed/escalated an audible.
- One real under-pace pool was caught by the check (not by Drew) with work queued against it, or a written proof that every pool was on track.

title: agy-proxy: four numeric env vars parsed with bare Number() — 'abc' disables the worker cap and idle eviction and freezes the model catalog, a typo'd turn timeout fires in ~1ms, and MAX_LIVE_WORKERS=0 crashes the eviction loop

labels.name: app/agy-proxy

body:
## Problem

`bin/agy-proxy.mjs` parses all four of its numeric environment knobs with a bare `Number(...)` and no validation (main `bd880194`, file sha256 `7de2c21d…`):

- `bin/agy-proxy.mjs:168` — `MODELS_TTL_MS = Number(process.env.AGY_PROXY_MODELS_TTL_MS || 300000)`
- `bin/agy-proxy.mjs:453` — `TURN_TIMEOUT_MS = Number(process.env.AGY_PROXY_TURN_TIMEOUT_MS || 300000)`
- `bin/agy-proxy.mjs:456` — `MAX_LIVE_WORKERS = Number(process.env.AGY_PROXY_MAX_LIVE_WORKERS || 32)`
- `bin/agy-proxy.mjs:457` — `SESSION_IDLE_TTL_MS = Number(process.env.AGY_PROXY_SESSION_TTL_MS || 30 * 60 * 1000)`

The proxy starts healthy with any of these typo'd, and each bad value silently breaks a different safety/behaviour knob instead of failing at startup.

## Verified behaviour (laptop probe, verbatim parsing + consumer expressions)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneA-agyenv/probe.mjs` on the laptop, against the shipped parsing shape and the exact consumer comparisons. Control (unset / `300`) behaves correctly in every case.

- **`AGY_PROXY_*='abc'` → `NaN` everywhere:**
  - Model catalog never refreshes: `:290` `Date.now() - modelsFetchedAt > MODELS_TTL_MS` is `3600000 > NaN` = **false** even an hour later — the proxy serves the stale/fallback catalog forever.
  - Idle sessions never evict: `:695` `now - w.lastUsedAt > SESSION_IDLE_TTL_MS` is false at any age.
  - The live-worker cap never fires: `:701` `live.length >= MAX_LIVE_WORKERS` is `100 >= NaN` = **false** — warm `agy` workers accumulate unbounded.
  - Every turn "times out" immediately: `:641` `setTimeout(..., TURN_TIMEOUT_MS)` with `NaN` is clamped to 1 ms (Node `TimeoutNaNWarning`), so each turn is killed and reported as `agy turn timed out after NaNms`.
- **`AGY_PROXY_TURN_TIMEOUT_MS='-5'` or `'9999999999999'` (>2³¹):** Node clamps both to 1 ms (`TimeoutNegativeWarning` / `TimeoutOverflowWarning`) — measured firing at ~3–7 ms vs the 300 ms control firing at 301 ms. Same total breakage as the typo case, with a plausible-looking value in the unit file.
- **`AGY_PROXY_MAX_LIVE_WORKERS='0'`:** the eviction loop at `:701` runs `while (live.length >= 0)`, which is true even for an **empty** list; `live.shift()` yields `undefined` and destructuring it throws `TypeError: undefined is not iterable` inside `evictLiveWorkersIfNeeded` (called from the 60 s interval at `:708` and from `acquireWorker`). Reproduced verbatim in the probe.
- **Negative TTLs** invert the gates the other way: `MODELS_TTL_MS=-5` re-pulls the catalog on every check, `SESSION_IDLE_TTL_MS=-5` evicts every live worker on every sweep.

## Why it matters

These are operator knobs in systemd unit environment lines — exactly the place a typo lands. Today a typo does not fail the unit; it disables the resource caps that keep resident warm workers bounded, freezes the model catalog, or makes every request fail as a "timeout" whose message (`after NaNms`) points at the upstream, not the config. The sibling case in commandcode-proxy is tracked as #1809; this is the same class in a different proxy with four knobs and three distinct failure shapes (never / always / crash), so it needs its own pin — including whether `MAX_LIVE_WORKERS=0` is a legitimate "no live workers" setting or an invalid value.

## Dedup

Searched open + closed issues for `agy-proxy`, `AGY_PROXY_`, and `bare Number`: #1809 covers only `COMMANDCODE_PROXY_TIMEOUT_MS` in `bin/commandcode-proxy.mjs`; #483/#661 covered proxy **ports** via the strict `parseProxyPort` helper in `bin/proxy-port.mjs`. No issue covers agy-proxy's duration/count env vars.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All four `AGY_PROXY_*` numeric env vars are validated at startup through one strict parser (positive finite integer in a stated range; durations also within the 2³¹−1 `setTimeout` bound): an invalid value fails startup loudly, naming the variable and the offending value — no silent `NaN`/negative/overflow behaviour.
- [ ] The pinned contract for `AGY_PROXY_MAX_LIVE_WORKERS=0` is implemented and tested (either refused as invalid, or honoured without the eviction loop throwing on an empty worker list).
- [ ] Tests in `bin/agy-proxy.test.mjs` (or a shared helper's tests) cover each var with: unset (default), a valid value, `'abc'`, a negative, `0` where it matters, and a >2³¹ duration.
- [ ] Valid configurations are unchanged: defaults 300000 / 300000 / 32 / 1800000 and the model-refresh, turn-timeout, idle-eviction, and cap behaviours they drive.

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#138 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #97

## Summary

The e2e harness starts every test's environment from the developer's own `os.Environ()`, then overrides four variables. Anything else set in the caller's shell reaches the test binary. That includes `MCPX_DAEMON_ENDPOINT`, which the opencode mcpx plugin injects into every shell it opens. So an agent running `go test ./internal/e2e` inside opencode can point the suite at the user's real daemon. Separately, several code paths read `$HOME`/`XDG_*` directly, and the harness does not isolate those.

The fix: build the child environment from an **allowlist**, not by inheriting and overriding, and add a guard that catches new `MCPX_*` leaks. (The short autostart idle-exit this issue also asked for landed in #182, which fixed #52; the inheritance itself is untouched and is what remains.)

This is the precondition for "very few shouldn't work if user has own real daemon running" (#134): isolation has to be strong enough that "very few" is true.

## Original notes

> - testing
>   - a general goal is to ensure all features have one or more integration tests
>     - for both binary && app entrypoint (consider binary a superset)
>       - all tests should pass for nix flake & container
>         - all local also but may need impractical setup
>           - very few shouldn't work if user has own real daemon running

## Current state (written on d0b7e01; re-checked at 05c78b2)

`newEnv` (`internal/e2e/e2e_test.go:35-87` at 05c78b2) sets `envVars: append(os.Environ(), MCPX_REGISTRY_URL=..., MCPX_STATE_DIR=..., MCPX_CACHE_DIR=..., MCPX_CONFIG=..., MCPX_AUTOSTART_IDLE_EXIT=60s)` (`:52-69`). `os/exec` keeps the last value for a duplicated key, so these five win. **Everything else is still inherited** -- #182 added the fifth variable and changed the cleanup to `stop --all` with a logged error (`:71-85`), but did not touch the `os.Environ()` base. A developer's or agent's `MCPX_DAEMON_ENDPOINT`, `MCPX_SOCKET` or any other `MCPX_*` still reaches every test.

The table below comes from reading the code; the suite was not run for this issue. The first implementation step confirms these reads with a test.

| Inherited from the caller | Effect in a test | Where read |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MCPX_DAEMON_ENDPOINT` | every client command targets that daemon and refuses to start a local one | `daemon.endpoint`, `internal/settings/registry.go:350`. The plugin injects it into every opencode shell: `plugin/opencode/mcpx-session.ts:696-701` |
| `MCPX_SOCKET` | replaces the socket path outright, for both bind and connect (its precedence over the info file is #88's to decide, #181 collision 8) | `internal/daemon/paths.go:103-105` |
| any `MCPX_<SETTING>` (derived from each setting's path, `internal/settings/schema.go:220-224`), e.g. `MCPX_SCRIPT_RUNTIME`, `MCPX_DAEMON_INLINE` | the test runs under the developer's settings, not the documented defaults | `settings.ApplyEnv`, `bind.go:163` |
| `MCPX_SESSION_ID`, `MCPX_PARENT_SESSION_ID`, `MCPX_HARNESS_*` | session scoping and lease keys come from the outer agent session | several `internal/*` |
| `HOME`, `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` | recipe dirs include the user's (`internal/cli/scripts.go:71-72`, `internal/daemon/consumer.go:141-142`, `internal/recipes/dirs.go:28`), so the user's real recipes can change `TestRecipesAreMatchedDeterministically`-style results. A `--persist user` or `servers add --scope user` test would write the user's real config (`internal/config/write.go:33-40`) | as listed |
| `XDG_DATA_HOME`, `OPENCODE_DB` | the opencode v1 DB lookup finds the user's real `opencode.db` | `internal/opencode/opencode.go:35-50` |
| `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` | the fallback socket dir is shared with the user's daemons. The name is hashed per state dir (`paths.go:115-116`), so there is no collision; leaked test daemons used to accumulate there for hours (#52), and since #182 they idle out after 60 s | `paths.go:141-148` |
| `XDG_STATE_HOME`/`XDG_CACHE_HOME` | masked, because `MCPX_STATE_DIR`/`MCPX_CACHE_DIR` win (`paths.go:36-45`) | -- |

Related, from #52 (closed, fixed in #182): `newEnv` now sets `autostart.idleExit` (`internal/settings/wire.go:135`) to 60 s through `MCPX_AUTOSTART_IDLE_EXIT` (`e2e_test.go:68`, `testIdleExit` at `:92`), and cleanup runs `mcpx stop --all` through the `daemon-<key>.json` info files, logging rather than discarding its error (`:71-85`). That bounds a leak; it does not stop a test from reaching the caller's daemon, which is this issue.

The **in-process** runner (#133) inherits all of this through `os.Getenv` in the same process. The fix below has to apply to both runners.

## Approaches

### A -- denylist: unset known-dangerous variables (least recommended)
Strip `MCPX_DAEMON_ENDPOINT` and `MCPX_SOCKET` after `os.Environ()`. It is the smallest diff, and it fixes today's concrete hole. It fails open: every future `MCPX_*` setting, and every new `XDG_*`/`HOME` read, leaks again until someone notices. That is the pattern the history shows (#65 registry, #52 leaks). Not recommended as the end state.

### B -- strip every `MCPX_*` and override `HOME`/`XDG_*`
Drop every inherited variable that starts with `MCPX_`, and set `HOME`, `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, `XDG_DATA_HOME`, `XDG_STATE_HOME`, `XDG_CACHE_HOME` and `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` under `e.dir` (short names, for the 100-byte socket cap, `paths.go:75`). This is robust against new settings. It still inherits unrelated variables: `DENO_DIR`, `BUN_INSTALL`, `NODE_OPTIONS`, `OPENCODE_*`, proxies. Some of those are wanted (runtime caches), some are not (`NODE_OPTIONS=--require ...`).

### C -- allowlist plus a guard (recommended)
- **Child environment** = an explicit allowlist from the parent: `PATH`, `TMPDIR`, `LANG`/`LC_*`, `TERM`, `SYSTEMROOT` (for Windows later, #136), and runtime cache dirs (`DENO_DIR`, `BUN_INSTALL_CACHE_DIR`, npm cache) so runs stay fast. Add B's `HOME`/`XDG_*` under `e.dir`, then the five variables `newEnv` already sets (including #182's `MCPX_AUTOSTART_IDLE_EXIT=60s`).
- **Opt-in pass-through** for the rare test that needs the outer world: `e.inherit("NAME")`. The tests labelled "needs the user's default paths" (#134, `RequireNoUserDaemon`) are the ones that use it.
- **Guard test**, `TestTheHarnessInheritsNoMCPXVariable`. It sets `MCPX_DAEMON_ENDPOINT=http://127.0.0.1:1`, `MCPX_SOCKET=/nonexistent`, `MCPX_SCRIPT_RUNTIME=bogus` and `HOME=/nonexistent` in its own process (`t.Setenv`), builds an env, runs `mcpx doctor -v`, `mcpx settings list` and `mcpx recipes`, and asserts the output is local, default and home-free. This is the regression test that makes the fix stay fixed (#99: a test per bug, a guard per bug class). Make its variable list *derived*, not typed (from #162): enumerate the settings registry and require every `EnvName()` and `EnvAliases` entry (`internal/settings/schema.go:220-224,284`) to be either set by the harness or on an explicit safe-to-inherit list, so a new setting is covered the day it is added. Undeclared `MCPX_*` reads are not in the registry; take them from #172's allowlist once it lands rather than keeping a second list here.
- **Backstop**: `TestMain` in `internal/e2e` fails fast, with a clear message, if the *parent* has `MCPX_DAEMON_ENDPOINT` or `MCPX_SOCKET` set and the allowlist is somehow bypassed. That turns a silent "tests passed against the user's daemon" into a loud failure.
- **Machine-level check** (from #162): `TestMain` records `mcpx daemons` for the caller's real environment at start and end and fails on any difference. It is the one assertion of "the suite does not disturb your machine" that cannot rot, and it also catches a regression of #182's leak fix.

Recommended because it fails closed. A new setting, or a new read of `$HOME`, is isolated by default, and the guard catches the regression if someone widens the allowlist.

## Implementation steps

1. Write the guard test first, expecting it to fail on main. That confirms the table above.
2. Replace `append(os.Environ(), ...)` with the allowlist builder in `internal/testsupport` (shared with the plugin harness in #132 and the in-process runner in #133).
3. ~~Add `MCPX_AUTOSTART_IDLE_EXIT=30s`, and record the `stop` error rather than discarding it (#52 fixes 1 and 2).~~ Done in #182 (60 s; `stop --all`, error logged).
4. Add the `TestMain` backstop.

## Open questions

- Should a caller's `DENO_DIR`/bun cache be shared with tests (fast) or isolated (hermetic)? Proposal: shared on laptops, isolated in the container entry.
- Does anything need `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`/git credentials? The `repo`/`worktree` scopes use git (`package.nix` comment), but only locally. (The GIT architect is replacing the `git` subprocess with native resolution in `internal/config/scope.go`; if that lands, `git` may drop out of the allowlist question entirely.)
- Should the plugin's `shell.env` injection skip `go test` commands? No: the harness must be robust against any caller, and special-casing a command name in the plugin is the wrong layer.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** S-M · **Impact** high (a correctness hole in every e2e run started from opencode with the plugin, and the foundation for the "user's daemon" subset)
**Depends on / related**: #52 (closed, fixed in #182 -- step 3 is done), #139 (this is the remaining precondition for `t.Parallel` in e2e), #88 (owns `MCPX_SOCKET` precedence, #181 collision 8), #172 (the undeclared `MCPX_*` allowlist the guard should reuse), #134 (the labelled subset; the `inline`/`spawn`/`remote` run modes), #133 (the in-process runner needs the same env), #132 (the plugin harness), #99 (guard-per-bug-class), #65 (the registry precedent for "never the real thing").

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

## Acceptance criteria

- The e2e harness builds the child environment from an allowlist (no inherited MCPX_* or caller daemon endpoints), a guard test catches new MCPX_* leaks, and CI is green.
- The work described in the Summary/Scope above is delivered via a branch + PR (no direct push to main); verification runs in GitHub Actions CI, not on the sandbox.
- Evidence (CI links, timings, or probe output as applicable) is recorded on this issue before it is closed.
