title: fix(home): run sync-models from checkout, not a store bin copy (#883)
body:
## Summary

Fixes the remaining store-path bin refs for #883 (task 6513).

**The pin, named:** the home layer is sourced via `lib.from-root`, which resolves to `inputs.self.outPath` (`lib/default.nix`) — the flake source snapshot of the git tree. Every `${...}` path coercion in `home/common/default.nix` inherits whatever that snapshot contains; the Oct-25 `-bin` store copy with 16 of 25 files was such a snapshot baked into the units.

**Probe (2026-11-12, amd):** `(builtins.getFlake "git+file:///home/user/git/code?ref=main").outPath` = `/nix/store/ymada22lj4q2qzhj76qp3fy42b3lpyan-source`; its `bin/` holds all 35 tracked bin files, an exact match with `git ls-files bin` at HEAD — the committed tree snapshots completely today, so the fix is to stop baking bin/ into store copies at the remaining sites.

**Change:** the only remaining `${../../bin}` refs on main were the three `sync-models.mjs` sites (the clef/agy/codex/antigravity shims from the original report were removed in the 2026-11-06 proxy decommission). All three — the `sync-models` user service and the `sync-models` / `update-models` shims — now run `"$HOME/code/bin/sync-models.mjs"`, the checkout pattern the #2107 proxy migration adopted and this file already uses for its stamp-gated sync (lines 157-158). A `#883` comment at the service site records why.

## Verification

- `nixfmt --check home/common/default.nix` — pass
- `nix-instantiate --parse home/common/default.nix` — pass
- Eval probe above (flake source bin list == tracked bin list, 35 files)
- No other `${../../bin}` refs remain in `home/common/default.nix`

Deploy (nixos-rebuild switch on amd) stays with the operator per the task packet — this PR does not switch the machine.

Refs #883 (does not close it: the switch-time acceptance — declarative unit serving after a switch, managed opencode rev — can only be verified at deploy).

body:
## Problem

The Rust workspace at pkgs/fleet/Cargo.toml contains ten members, including fleet-queue and fleet-dispatch. Its unit/integration tests are not built or run by the workflows inspected on main. The fleet-specific workflow found, fleet-search-parity-guard.yml, checks generated search parity rather than compiling/testing the workspace; nix-ci.yml evaluates selected flake outputs rather than building the Fleet test targets. As a result, regressions in queue, dispatch, proxy, config, and registry crates can merge without their Rust tests running.

This is separate from #6400: that issue wires pkgs/fleet/smoke.sh against four existing variant binaries, while this issue covers Cargo library, binary, and integration tests.

## Scope

Add a CI check for the existing Fleet Rust workspace using its own lockfile/toolchain. Run it on changes to pkgs/fleet/** in the repository's policy-approved tier, and on demand if the normal runner/build cost requires a manual or scheduled entry. Reuse existing CI/Nix build conventions; do not create duplicate package definitions or turn the unrelated #6400 smoke suite into this work.

## Acceptance criteria

- The check runs a locked workspace test command that compiles and executes all supported Rust unit and integration tests under pkgs/fleet (including fleet-queue and fleet-dispatch tests).
- Workflow triggers and branch policy agree with .github/ci-policy.md; the result is a required signal in the intended tier and cannot silently skip when a Fleet path changes.
- The test job uses the workspace's declared rust-toolchain.toml and lockfile and does not require the developer laptop's broker or credentials.
- Add a workflow/registry contract test if that is the repository's standard for CI wiring; retain #6400's separate per-variant smoke acceptance.
- Document runtime and build-resource cost so CI placement is deliberate rather than accidentally making an expensive test a PR gate.

## Evidence

- pkgs/fleet/Cargo.toml:17-29 lists the ten workspace members.
- .github/workflows/nix-ci.yml:85-99 evaluates the devShell, mcpx package, and format-check program; it does not test Fleet.
- .github/workflows/fleet-search-parity-guard.yml:23-32 checks parity, not Cargo tests.

## Problem

Two NixOS Cloudflare Tunnel units currently pass their tunnel token as a `cloudflared` command-line argument:

On Linux, command-line arguments can be observable through process inspection. The PM tunnel also has an established readiness/watchdog path because `cloudflared` may remain alive while its edge connections are down; the lab tunnel has `Restart=on-failure` but no equivalent recovery check. A live-but-disconnected connector can therefore persist without systemd restarting it.

## Scope

Harden the two NixOS tunnel service definitions without changing their public hostname/ingress behavior or secret-source ownership. Confirm the pinned `cloudflared` version's supported credential-file mechanism before selecting the implementation. Reuse existing service/module conventions rather than adding a new secret store.

- Neither unit renders the tunnel token into `ExecStart` or another process argument; credentials are supplied through a supported file/credential mechanism with restrictive permissions.
- Add a focused rendered-unit or module test proving the token is absent from command arguments and the credential file is wired to the service.
- Add a lab-tunnel readiness probe and bounded watchdog/recovery path modeled on the PM tunnel's existing `/ready` behavior. A healthy tunnel is not restarted; a persistently degraded one is recovered with a bounded retry/backoff policy.
- Add tests for healthy, degraded, and probe-error paths, and preserve existing PM tunnel behavior.
- Document any cloudflared-version limitation and the chosen fallback if token-file support is unavailable.

## Evidence

- `nixos/services/pm-stack/default.nix`: PM tunnel unit and existing readiness/watchdog implementation.
- `nixos/services/lab-tunnel/default.nix`: lab tunnel unit currently lacks readiness recovery.

## Verification

Run the focused NixOS/module test or rendered-unit test, then the repository's relevant formatting/check target. Validate both systemd unit outputs and confirm no credential value appears in rendered `ExecStart`.

title: id(grants): reject duplicate grant IDs when restoring snapshots

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

body:
## Evidence

On fresh `origin/main` (`5f31d7a921a9ed4714e52acb088958367b021b45`), `pkgs/id/src/grant_service.rs:301-305` exposes `StoreSnapshot` as a deserializable record with a public `grants` vector. `GrantStore::restore` at `:334-346` builds `order` from every vector entry, then collects the entries into a map keyed by `grant_id`; duplicate IDs silently overwrite in the map while remaining duplicated in `order`. `stranded_presented` at `:287-294` walks `order` and resolves through that map, and `GrantService::reconcile` at `:730-732` processes every returned occurrence. Thus a malformed/imported snapshot with duplicate IDs silently loses one record and can cause the surviving `Presented` record to be reconciled more than once. Normal snapshots generated by `snapshot()` need not contain duplicates, but the public serde input allows malformed snapshots to reach restore.

The relevant code was added by merged PR #8614 under the broader lifecycle issue #2723; all-state issue/PR searches for grant snapshot restore and duplicate grant IDs found no specific tracked follow-up.

## Why it matters

Restore is the restart boundary for the grant intent protocol. Silently accepting a malformed snapshot breaks the one-record-per-ID invariant and can repeat recovery work instead of surfacing corrupted state.

## Acceptance

- Validate snapshot grant IDs before rebuilding indexes; reject duplicate IDs without returning a partially restored store (for example, with a fallible restore API).
- Add a regression test constructing/deserializing a snapshot with two records sharing one `grant_id`; assert restore rejects it.
- Keep normal snapshot/restore round trips and insertion-order reconciliation behavior passing.

## Finding (unaddressed PR review comment)

Codex P2 on open PR #8624 — comment https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/8624#discussion_r4536166816 by chatgpt-codex-connector[bot], 2026-11-11T09:30:07Z, at `pm-stack/aggregator/src/server.ts:1487`:

A token with an unknown `kid` also forces a fresh JWKS request for every entry, even with a warm cache. Verify the request-level token once before the loop and retain only the asserted-author contradiction check per entry.

## No-response evidence

`pm-stack/aggregator/src/server.ts` at head 2809e82e5a: the `/api/actions/batch` handler (route at line ~1455) loops over up to 100 entries and calls `await enforceAccessAuthor(req, parsed.value.author)` per entry at line ~1487. `pm-stack/aggregator/src/access-identity.ts` at the same head: `fetchJwks` (lines ~77–95) caches only successful responses and fetches with `AbortSignal.timeout(5_000)`; `verifyAccessJwt` (lines ~116–123) forces a fresh JWKS fetch on an unknown `kid` on every verification. body:
## Finding (unaddressed PR review comment)

Codex P1 on merged PR #8705 — comment https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/8705#discussion_r4539123543 by chatgpt-codex-connector[bot], 2026-11-11T14:30:10Z, at `pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py:1493`:

> **Use single-read chunks to enforce the absolute body deadline** — If a client declares an in-cap body and keeps sending bytes less than 10 seconds apart, this call can block far beyond the intended deadline: `self.rfile` is a buffered reader whose `read(n)` repeatedly receives until all `n` bytes arrive, with the socket timeout applying separately to each underlying receive. Because the entire allowed body fits in one chunk, the loop cannot recheck the deadline while those bytes trickle in, leaving every subsequent request blocked on the single-threaded server for potentially days. Use `read1()` and recheck the absolute deadline between reads, as `_fetch_crawl` already does.

## No-response evidence

- PR #8705 merged 2026-11-11T14:28:30Z; the flagged code merged in the reviewed shape (reviewed commit ec9d1b6e31).
- Fresh re-read (2026-11-12, this run): the PR's only inline comment is this Codex original, with no replies; no conversation comment addresses it.
- GraphQL `reviewThreads` check (2026-11-12): the thread is unresolved, 1 comment.
- Searched open and closed issues for "8705", "4539123543", "read1 deadline", and "lab-ops-hub body deadline" — no existing issue covers this finding. Parent issue #7036 (closed) is the Content-Length validation this PR implemented; it does not cover the trickle/deadline defect in the read loop itself. Issue #532 (closed) covered the same per-read-timeout flaw on the response-fetch side (`_fetch_crawl`), which was fixed with `read1()` — the request-body side was left with the buffered `read()`.

## Still live on current main (verified 2026-11-12, two `gh api` reads)

`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py` on main: `_read_request_body` (lines ~1480–1500) still calls `chunk = self.rfile.read(min(remaining, _CRAWL_READ_CHUNK_BYTES))` at line ~1493. `_CRAWL_REQUEST_MAX_BODY_BYTES` is 65,536 and `_CRAWL_READ_CHUNK_BYTES` is 65,536, so the entire allowed body fits in a single `read(n)` call; the deadline is only rechecked after that call returns, and each underlying receive gets its own socket timeout — a client dribbling bytes less than 10s apart wedges the single-threaded server indefinitely. By contrast `_fetch_crawl` (lines ~1421–1428) uses `res.read1(...)` and rechecks the absolute deadline after every chunk.

## Acceptance criteria

- `_read_request_body` reads with `read1()` (single underlying receive per call) and rechecks the absolute deadline between reads, so a trickling in-cap body is rejected at the deadline — or the finding is resolved by a documented decision on this issue.
- Regression coverage exists for a slow-drip request body (bytes arriving less than the socket timeout apart) being cut off at the absolute deadline rather than blocking until the full declared length arrives.

## Evidence

On current `main` (`51121b4c00528698c434e1f9f72c637688c0f0a8`), `pkgs/id/src/web/security.rs:139-143` extracts only the authority from an Origin and discards its scheme. The middleware at `:213-221` then decides whether Origin matches Host using only `authority_normalized` at `:218-219`.

For `Host: localhost:3000` and `Origin: https://localhost:3000`, `origin_authority` returns `localhost:3000`; both values normalize identically, so the guard treats the request as same-origin even though `https://localhost:3000` and `http://localhost:3000` are different origins. This follows directly from the current helper and comparison; no in-browser exploit was reproduced in this pass.

The module contract at `security.rs:12-18` says the Origin must match by host and port, but the security purpose at `:12-15` is to reject cross-origin browser fetches and WebSocket handshakes. #814 fixed the different-port case and records the general origin definition as scheme + host + port, but its acceptance criteria cover port and host only. This is a residual scheme-comparison gap, not a duplicate of #814. It is also distinct from #8880/#8883, which handle malformed bracketed-authority syntax rather than scheme mismatches. Fresh all-state issue searches for Origin scheme/scheme mismatch and all-state PR search found no specific follow-up.

## Why it matters

The guard can accept a cross-origin request when the Origin and Host authorities match but their schemes differ, undermining the same-origin policy the middleware documents for CSRF and cross-site WebSocket protection. Browser reachability depends on the served protocol and browser mixed-content behavior; this issue does not assert a demonstrated exploit.

## Acceptance criteria

- Define how the request scheme is determined for the supported serving/deployment modes (including any TLS-terminating proxy behavior the app supports) and compare it with the Origin scheme, not just host and port.
- Reject a scheme-mismatched Origin with the existing forbidden response, including same-host/same-port HTTP versus HTTPS cases.
- Preserve valid same-scheme cases, the #814 different-port refusal, the portless-authority policy, and opaque `Origin: null` refusal.
- Add guard-level regression tests for matching and mismatching schemes; run them when the current web build is available (the current-main web test build has unrelated tracked failures under #8795).}

title: fleet gh: one passthrough that rotates personal + App tokens for every fleet gh call

labels.name: task/triage

labels.description: Has a queued queue task

labels.name: meta/follow-up

body:
## Directive (Drew, 2026-11-12)

All fleet GitHub work should be done using the fleet app, which seamlessly switches between the personal token and each of the 3 GitHub App installation tokens. Build this in two steps:

1. **Now: a `fleet gh` subcommand** on the fleet multicall binary. It selects a token (personal PAT + the 3 App installations), exports it as `GH_TOKEN`, and passes every argument through to the real `gh` binary unchanged. On a rate-limit or permission failure it retries with the next token in the rotation instead of failing the caller.
2. **Later: dedicated higher-level tools** (project sync, queue sync, etc.) built on top of the same rotation, so callers stop shelling out to raw gh at all.

## Why

- Project reconciliation (single writer to Project #4) currently runs on the single fine-grained PAT `github.project-token` (Projects read/write only, no repository access). On 2026-11-12 it partially failed: milestone writes were refused with **"Resource not accessible by personal access token"** — 6 updates landed, 49 left pending (tracker: #1408).
- The user token has hit GitHub secondary rate limits mid-shift repeatedly (content creation blocked); App installation tokens carry separate rate-limit buckets and broader repo permissions.
- Today every caller picks its own token ad hoc (reconcile script fetches the PAT by name; paperwork mints App tokens separately — see also the closed #7930 pagination break in that path). One rotation point ends the ad-hocery.

## Acceptance

- `fleet gh <args...>` behaves exactly like `gh <args...>` (stdout/stderr/exit code passthrough) with a working token selected.
- Rotation covers the personal token and all 3 App installations; a rate-limited or permission-denied attempt fails over to the next token and the caller sees only the final result.
- Tokens are resolved by name from the fleet secrets broker at runtime; no token value is ever printed, logged, or written to a file.
- `project-reconcile.sh` is rewired to call `fleet gh` instead of fetching `github.project-token` directly, and a full reconcile pass completes with zero "Resource not accessible" failures.
- The follow-on (higher-level sync tools) is filed as its own issue when step 1 lands; this issue covers step 1 + the reconcile rewire.

body:
# pm-stack notifications: section-risk class — phone push only when a whole route section fails or is at severe risk, with the pending-wall pools shown compactly

Drew's order, 2026-11-12 ~01:58 CST (verbatim): "update push on phone add a option that shows pools that are pending wall, only alert me when each major section of workhorse speed specialist summit or small fail or severe risk and in that scenario show compact what is failed or at risk which are walled and soonest related resets"

## What exists today

- Six notification classes in `pm-stack/aggregator/src/notifications.ts` (`NOTIFICATION_CLASS_DEFAULTS` / `NOTIFICATION_CLASSES`), toggled per subscription on `/alerts/preferences`. Quota alerting is per-pool: `quota-wall` (pool walled well before reset, or sole-door pool walled) and `quota-near-wall` (sole-door pool ≥85%).
- `buildNotificationCandidates` derives quota candidates from the quota snapshot with the wall test already in code: pool walled = `state === "walled"` or any measured window ≥100%; pools in `error`/`stale`/`lapsed` state are skipped (never derive from retained windows).
- `src/aa.ts` already reads the deployed OpenCode config's `experimental.model_routes` and computes route leaf sets (`routeLeafSets`) — the section→door mapping source.
- Design context: `pm-stack-notifications-design-2026-11-11.md` (keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal files); Phase 1 producers landed under #8568 (closed).

## The new option

A seventh notification class, id **`section-risk`**, label **"Section failure / severe risk"**, blurb: "A whole route section (workhorse, speed, specialist, summit, small) fails or is at severe risk. Shows the pools pending wall, which are walled, and the soonest resets." Default ON for new subscriptions, and added to the preferences page like the other classes (same `NOTIFICATION_CLASSES` mechanism, test-send support included).

### Definitions (v1, measured windows only — no pace projection)

- **Major sections**: exactly the route names Drew listed — `workhorse`, `speed`, `specialist`, `summit`, `small`. (Scout is deliberately NOT in the list; Drew's 2026-11-12 list omits it. Variants like `small-100k` roll up under `small` only if the config's leaf analysis says they share its doors — otherwise they are out of scope for v1; record the choice in the PR.)
- **Section membership**: the pools serving a section = quota pools whose provider door appears in the section's route leaf set (reuse `aa.ts` routeLeafSets over the deployed config; join to pools on the same provider/credential keys the quota view already uses — pin the exact join in the PR and unit-test it).
- **Pool walled**: the existing test (state `walled` or any measured window ≥100%). Pools in `error`/`stale`/`lapsed` state do not count as serving.
- **Pool pending wall**: not walled, and any measured window ≥85% (the existing near-wall threshold).
- **Section FAILED**: at least one serving pool exists and every serving pool is walled.
- **Section SEVERE RISK**: not failed, and every non-walled serving pool is pending wall — i.e. no serving pool has all windows <85%; the section's remaining headroom sits entirely in pools about to wall.

### Candidate + delivery rules

- One candidate per section per state, objectRef `section:<name>`, derived in `buildNotificationCandidates` alongside the quota loop; existing dedupe/cooldown/fingerprint machinery applies unchanged (state fingerprint must change when the walled/pending membership or the soonest reset changes materially).
- FAILED is a breakthrough (bypasses quiet hours and digest), like a sole-door wall. SEVERE RISK is not a breakthrough.
- When a section leaves FAILED, emit the recovery through the same disappearance/recovery semantics the engine already has for quota states (a state that disappears cancels its pending digest entry); do not invent a second recovery mechanism.
- Landing URL: `/quota`.

### Compact push format (this is the point of the feature — keep it short)

Title: `Section failed: workhorse` / `Section at risk: summit`
Body, one line per affected section, soonest reset first within the section:

`walled: openai-plan (resets Fri 14:28Z), cline-pass (resets Sun 06:52Z) · pending: go-drewrypope 97% (resets Mon 11:04Z)`

- FAILED sections list their walled pools, each with its soonest reset (the exhausted window's reset / `wallLiftsAt`, same computation as the existing quota-wall candidate).
- SEVERE RISK sections list their pending-wall pools with the window percent and that window's reset.
- No prose paragraphs, no pool that is neither walled nor pending in the affected section.

## Subscription flip (part of the same change, after the class is live)

Drew's rule is "only alert me when" a section fails or is at severe risk: once `section-risk` is deployed and enabled on Drew's existing phone subscription, set his subscription's per-pool `quota-wall` and `quota-near-wall` classes OFF, so pool-level quota pushes stop reaching his phone. Other subscriptions and the classes themselves are untouched. Record the flip (timestamp, before/after class map) on this issue.

## Acceptance (Drew's terms)

1. Preferences page shows the new "Section failure / severe risk" toggle; a per-class test send lands on `/quota`.
2. Fixture/unit tests: a snapshot where every workhorse pool is walled produces exactly one FAILED candidate with the compact body (walled pools + soonest resets); a snapshot where workhorse's only non-walled pool is ≥85% produces one SEVERE RISK candidate; a snapshot with one healthy workhorse pool under 85% produces NO section candidate even if individual pools are walled/near (per-pool classes may still fire for other subscriptions).
3. Live proof on the laptop board: with the current real quota state, the candidate derivation runs without error against the live snapshot (whatever sections it flags or doesn't flag is evidence, recorded on this issue).
4. Drew's phone subscription: `section-risk` on, `quota-wall`/`quota-near-wall` off, flip recorded on this issue.
5. CI green on the PR; deployed to the laptop aggregator (primary-clone deploy discipline) and the running server serves the new class (verify via the preferences endpoint it exposes).

## Out of scope

- Pace/projection-based pending-wall (percent deltas over gatherer ticks) — v1 is measured windows only.
- Scout and any section Drew did not name.
- Changes to the per-pool classes' derivation rules for other subscriptions.
- The Phase 2 edge relay (#8569) and Phase 3 consolidation (#8570).

body:
## Ask (Drew, 2026-11-12)

Drew asked how to access the decision question sets in the PM stack — all the ones asked, new today, new this week, or all. Today there is no way: each raised set lives only at its own token link (`/decisions/<setId>?t=<token>`), delivered solely inside its push notification. There is no list route, no index, no grouping by date.

## Build (complete, not a pilot)

In `pm-stack/aggregator`:

1. A decision-sets index page listing EVERY set in the decisions store (`~/.local/state/pm-aggregator/decisions.json`): set title, setId, raised date/time (America/Chicago), item count, question count, OPEN question count (questions with no resolution), and answered/deferred state.
2. Views/filters: **New today**, **This week**, **All** — plus an open-only toggle. Default view: All, newest first.
3. Each row links through to that set's existing decisions page (the token-carrying URL, exactly as the push carries it). Do NOT weaken the per-set token model: the index itself must sit behind the same access as the rest of the aggregator (tailnet origin / pm.security.cab behind Cloudflare Access) — no new public unauthenticated route.
4. Counts computed live from the store at request time (no cached snapshot that can go stale), consistent with how the set page itself counts open questions.
5. Tests in the aggregator's existing test setup covering: listing multiple sets, open-count correctness (resolved + deferred questions excluded), today/week grouping boundaries in America/Chicago, and the empty-store case.
6. Deploy through the normal pm-stack path and verify the page live (HTTP 200 on the tailnet origin, correct counts against the live store).

## Current live store (2026-11-12 00:54 CST) — acceptance fixture

- `decisions-2026-11-11` — 15 items / 24 questions / 0 open
- `decisions-reraise-2026-11-11` — 2 items / 2 questions / 2 open
- `decisions-2026-11-11-design-blocked` — 11 items / 11 questions / 11 open

The index must show exactly these three with these counts before any new set is raised.

## Out of scope

- No changes to the per-set page, submit/defer/request-info flows, or the push system.
- The hourly pending-questions ledger items are raised as sets separately (orchestrator-side); this issue is the index page only.

title: id(chat-presence): separate future clock skew from the presence TTL

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

Presence accepts a heartbeat timestamp up to a full `PRESENCE_TTL_SECS` into the future, then computes liveness and pruning from that sender-provided timestamp. A node whose clock is ahead can therefore remain reported live for nearly two TTLs after its heartbeat is received, despite the documented TTL describing how long a heartbeat keeps a node live.

## Evidence (current `main` `12b3fb6b29914f9f675558ea3d9e27f13ca31487`)

- `pkgs/id/src/chat_presence.rs:61-63` sets the presence TTL to 75 seconds.
- `PresenceTable::update_at` (`:277-280`) accepts a heartbeat as far as 75 seconds in the future.
- `liveness_at` and `prune_at` (`:330-335, 440-446`) use `now.saturating_sub(heartbeat.ts) <= PRESENCE_TTL_SECS`. Thus, with receipt `now=1000` and accepted `ts=1075`, the node is live immediately and through `now=1150`: up to 150 seconds after receipt. `roster_at` (`:384-398`) uses the same age calculation for liveness and typing; it also exposes the sender's future timestamp as `last_seen` (`:390-393`).
- The tests reject `u64::MAX` (`:688-690`) but do not cover the accepted future-skew boundary or expiry relative to receipt time.
- The #2809 protocol contract specifies a 60–90 second TTL but does not define a future-clock-skew allowance. Reviewed #4004 and #4502 as adjacent presence work; neither tracks this timestamp/expiry behavior.

## Why it matters

Clock skew—or a self-signed heartbeat with a future timestamp—can make an absent member appear online substantially longer than the advertised TTL. Future `last_seen` values and typing indicators can also mislead roster consumers.

## Suggested fix

Define a future-skew allowance independently of the liveness TTL, and make the expiry contract explicit. Consider tracking local receipt time for presence expiry while retaining the signed sender timestamp only as metadata, or another policy that prevents permitted future skew from extending liveness beyond the documented bound. Apply the same rule consistently to liveness, typing, roster output, and pruning.

## Acceptance criteria

- Document the maximum future-skew allowance separately from `PRESENCE_TTL_SECS` and define whether expiry is measured from sender timestamp or local receipt.
- Add boundary tests at the allowed skew and just beyond it.
- Test that an accepted future-dated heartbeat cannot keep liveness/typing past the documented bound from receipt; ensure `last_seen` has defined behavior and cannot misleadingly be future-dated unless explicitly intended.
- Preserve out-of-order and replay protections.

Codex P1 on merged PR #8667 — comment https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/8667#discussion_r4537729037 by chatgpt-codex-connector[bot], 2026-11-11T12:14:34Z, at `pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:3279`:

> **Add property coverage with an independent start-time oracle** — The regression obtains `actual` through the same parser used by `is_process_alive`, so accidentally extracting another numeric `/proc/<pid>/stat` field would still pass both assertions. The new parser has a meaningful invariant—extracting field 22 regardless of spaces or parentheses in `comm`—but only receives this self-referential example coverage. Extract the string parsing into a helper and add property tests using generated process names and an independently selected field-22 value, as required by the repository's testing doctrine.

## No-response evidence

- PR #8667 merged 2026-11-11T12:18:32Z, ~4 minutes after the comment; the flagged tests merged unchanged.
- Fresh re-read (2026-11-11, this run): the PR's only inline comment is this Codex original, with no replies; no conversation comment addresses it.
- GraphQL `reviewThreads` check: the thread is unresolved.
- Searched open and closed issues for "8667", "is_process_alive proc stat", and "start-time oracle" — no existing issue covers this finding (parent issue #3040 is closed and does not cover the test-oracle gap).

## Still live on current main (verified 2026-11-11, two `gh api` reads)

`pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs` on main: `get_process_start_time` (line ~225) still parses the stat string inline (no extracted string-parsing helper), and the regression tests still use the parser as its own oracle — `test_is_process_alive_current_process` asserts `is_process_alive(pid, get_process_start_time(pid))` and `test_is_process_alive_reused_pid` derives `actual` from `get_process_start_time(pid)` (lines ~3274–3290). If the parser extracted the wrong field, both assertions would still pass. The proptest cases in this file cover web-bindings parsing, not the stat parser.

## Acceptance criteria

- The `/proc/<pid>/stat` start-time parsing is covered by tests whose expected value is selected independently of the parser under test (e.g. an extracted string-parsing helper plus property tests over generated `comm` values with spaces/parens and an independently chosen field-22 value), or the finding is resolved by a documented decision on this issue.

body:
## Evidence

On current `origin/main` (`f1ea4f0857970a8579b7273ef3750e79aeccf3b2`), `pkgs/id/src/server_config/parse.rs:391-414` validates `window_seconds` only against zero, then converts it with `row.window_seconds.saturating_mul(1_000)` at line 410. A valid `u64` such as `18446744073709552` seconds exceeds the millisecond representation, is accepted, and silently becomes `u64::MAX` milliseconds. That is about 1,000 times shorter than the configured duration. Existing counterparty parsing coverage at lines 1098-1122 checks normal windows but not the overflow boundary.

## Why it matters

An operator can believe a per-counterparty budget lasts for the configured interval while the running policy uses a silently truncated interval. This makes configuration semantics misleading and can cause the budget to reset much earlier than intended.

## Acceptance criteria

- Reject `window_seconds > u64::MAX / 1000` as a configuration error, or otherwise preserve the requested duration without lossy saturation.
- Add regression tests for the largest representable seconds value and the first overflowing value; assert the accepted boundary converts exactly and overflow is rejected (or preserved exactly).
- Keep existing zero-window and ordinary-window behavior covered.

## Finding (unaddressed PR review comment)

Codex P2 on merged PR #8647 — comment https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/8647#discussion_r4537028885 by chatgpt-codex-connector[bot], 2026-11-11T10:57:07Z, at `pkgs/id/src/world_dev.rs:999` (at review time):

> **Reject unhealthy candidate actors before committing promotion** — For a session with no input history and empty active records, such as the `roc-grid` example, a candidate whose records export traps or returns invalid JSON can pass this equality check. `WorldHandle::spawn_durable_inner` catches the records error, marks the program unhealthy, and substitutes empty records (`world/handle.rs:201–209`), while capability issuance still lets `DevScratchWorld::launch` succeed. With no inputs to replay, those substituted records equal the old records, so promotion replaces the working world with an actor that rejects subsequent inputs as unavailable. Propagate initialization failures or explicitly check candidate health before committing.

## No-response evidence

- PR #8647 merged 2026-11-11T10:55:02Z; the comment was posted after merge, on the merged head.
- Fresh re-read (2026-11-11, this run): all 5 inline comments on the PR are Codex originals with no replies; no conversation reply addresses this.
- GraphQL `reviewThreads` check: this thread is unresolved.

## Still live on current main (verified 2026-11-11, two `gh api` reads)

The file has since moved to `pkgs/id/crates/id-worlds/src/world_dev.rs`. `DevSession::promote` on main launches the candidate, replays the recorded inputs, and commits when `candidate.records() == migrated_records` (~lines 997–1045) — there is no `program_healthy` check anywhere in `promote` (the only `program_healthy` uses on main are the `DevScratchWorld` accessor ~line 329 and the fuzz path ~line 1747). With no inputs to replay and empty active records, an unhealthy candidate whose records were substituted with empty records passes the equality check and is committed (`self.world = candidate`), replacing a working world with one that rejects subsequent inputs. Parent feature issue: #5541; no existing issue covers this (searched before filing).

## Acceptance criteria

- Promotion rejects a candidate whose program is unhealthy (explicit health check before commit, or initialization failures propagated), with a regression test: a no-input, empty-records session does not promote a candidate whose records export traps / returns invalid JSON, **or**
- the issue is resolved by a documented decision explaining why this case cannot occur or is acceptable.

Filed by the pr-comment-review job (source: unaddressed PR comment; see the agent note on this issue).

title: id-store: legacy metadata migration marks complete after load failure
body:
## Evidence

On current `main` (`eeee505783`), `pkgs/id/crates/id-store/src/tags.rs:1217-1222` treats every `load_meta(store)` error as an empty `MetaDoc` via `unwrap_or_default()`. The migration then reaches lines 1248-1249, sets `registry.legacy_meta_imported = true`, and saves that completion flag. Subsequent calls return immediately at lines 1219-1220.

`load_meta` can fail while fetching the `.meta` blob or deserializing it (`tags.rs:1907-1914`). A malformed metadata JSON blob therefore gets interpreted as “nothing to import”; `migrate_legacy_meta` returns `Ok(0)` and permanently records migration complete. Correcting or restoring the blob afterward cannot recover the legacy tags because later calls skip the import.

Repro from the code path: place invalid JSON in the store's `.meta` blob, call `migrate_legacy_meta`, then replace it with valid legacy metadata and call again. The first call returns success with zero imported tags and marks `legacy_meta_imported`; the second returns `Ok(0)` without reading/importing the corrected data. This is a static trace; a targeted regression test should pin the behavior.

## Why it matters

A transient blob read failure or corrupt-but-repairable metadata can silently lose legacy tags during one-time migration. The success flag prevents retries, so users may permanently lose metadata without an error explaining the skipped import.

## Acceptance criteria

- A `.meta` read or decode error is not treated as an empty document.
- On such an error, migration returns an error and leaves `legacy_meta_imported` unset so a later retry can succeed.
- Add a regression test that makes the first load fail, verifies the completion flag remains false, then supplies valid metadata and verifies a subsequent call imports it.
- Preserve the successful empty/missing `.meta` behavior if that is the intended compatibility contract.

You are a code-review agent running as a dispatched session in this
repository. Your job is a suggestions pass: survey the codebase for real,
actionable improvements and turn the verified ones into GitHub issues.

## Dispatch context — read this first

- You are running in this repository's LAPTOP CHECKOUT (the repo's primary
  checkout on the owner's laptop). Work there; do not clone the repo
  elsewhere.
- A tracking issue and a queue task were ALREADY created for this run by
  the dispatcher, and this session is already claimed against them. Do
  NOT create another tracking issue for this run, and do not dispatch
  further tasks.
- There is NO plan-approval step. Proceed directly; do not stop to ask
  for approval of a plan.

## What to review

Survey the codebase across these five areas:

- **Cleanup** — dead code, duplicated logic, obsolete files or config,
  leftover scaffolding.
- **Performance** — hot paths doing avoidable work, missing caching or
  batching, inefficient data structures or queries.
- **Security** — unsafe input handling, secrets or credentials in code or
  config, over-broad permissions, missing validation at trust boundaries.
- **Code Health** — confusing structure, missing or misleading error
  handling, functions/modules that have grown hard to change safely.
- **Testing** — important behaviour with no coverage, tests that assert
  nothing, flaky or order-dependent tests.

## Verify before you file — no speculative filings

Every candidate finding MUST be verified against the actual code before
it becomes an issue:

- Read the code at the location you cite. Confirm the problem is real in
  the current tree, not an assumption from a filename, a comment, or a
  pattern you expected to find.
- Check the surrounding context (callers, tests, configuration) — a
  candidate that turns out to be intentional, already handled elsewhere,
  or not actually reachable is rejected, not filed.
- Search the repo's OPEN issues before filing. If an existing open issue
  already covers the finding, comment on that issue with your evidence
  instead of opening a duplicate.

## Filing

- Per real, verified finding, file ONE issue in this repo with
  `gh issue create` from the laptop checkout. Each issue must include:
  - the canonical component label for its area; use `app/pm-stack` for
    PM-stack / aggregator issues in this repo. `app/aggregator` is a legacy
    alias and must not be used for new filings.
  - a clear title naming the problem;
  - file/line evidence (the exact paths and lines you verified);
  - why it matters (impact, risk, or cost);
  - the suggested fix shape — the direction of the fix, not a full
    implementation.
- CAP: at most **5 filings per pass** (new issues plus evidence comments
  on existing issues). If you verify more than 5 findings, file the 5
  highest-impact ones and list the rest in your summary as
  verified-but-deferred.
- Do NOT dispatch further tasks for the findings, and do not fix them in
  this pass. The issues are the record; the fleet's normal lanes pick
  work up from them.

## Finish

End with a short summary — as your session output, and as a comment on
this run's tracking issue if you can identify it — covering:

- **Filed** — each issue you opened or commented on, with its number and
  one line on the finding.
- **Verified and rejected** — candidates you checked against the code and
  did not file, with the reason.
- **Needs a human decision** — findings that are real but whose fix is a
  judgement call (trade-offs, product direction, risk appetite), stated
  plainly so a human can rule on them.

If the pass finds nothing worth filing, say so in the summary instead of
opening low-value issues to fill the pass.

BOLT'S PHILOSOPHY:
- Speed is a feature
- Every millisecond counts
- Measure first, optimize second
- Don't sacrifice readability for micro-optimizations

BOLT'S JOURNAL - CRITICAL LEARNINGS ONLY:
Before starting, read .jules/bolt.md (create if missing).

Your journal is NOT a log - only add entries for CRITICAL learnings that will help you avoid mistakes or make better decisions.

⚠️ ONLY add journal entries when you discover:
- A performance bottleneck specific to this codebase's architecture
- An optimization that surprisingly DIDN'T work (and why)
- A rejected change with a valuable lesson
- A codebase-specific performance pattern or anti-pattern
- A surprising edge case in how this app handles performance

❌ DO NOT journal routine work like:
- "Optimized component X today" (unless there's a learning)
- Generic React performance tips
- Successful optimizations without surprises

Format: `## YYYY-MM-DD - [Title]
**Learning:** [Insight]
**Action:** [How to apply next time]`

BOLT'S DAILY PROCESS:

1. 🔍 PROFILE - Hunt for performance opportunities:

  FRONTEND PERFORMANCE:
  - Unnecessary re-renders in React/Vue/Angular components
  - Missing memoization for expensive computations
  - Large bundle sizes (opportunities for code splitting)
  - Unoptimized images (missing lazy loading, wrong formats)
  - Missing virtualization for long lists
  - Synchronous operations blocking the main thread
  - Missing debouncing/throttling on frequent events
  - Unused CSS or JavaScript being loaded
  - Missing resource preloading for critical assets
  - Inefficient DOM manipulations

  BACKEND PERFORMANCE:
  - N+1 query problems in database calls
  - Missing database indexes on frequently queried fields
  - Expensive operations without caching
  - Synchronous operations that could be async
  - Missing pagination on large data sets
  - Inefficient algorithms (O(n²) that could be O(n))
  - Missing connection pooling
  - Repeated API calls that could be batched
  - Large payloads that could be compressed

  GENERAL OPTIMIZATIONS:
  - Missing caching for expensive operations
  - Redundant calculations in loops
  - Inefficient data structures for the use case
  - Missing early returns in conditional logic
  - Unnecessary deep cloning or copying
  - Missing lazy initialization
  - Inefficient string concatenation in loops
  - Missing request/response compression

2. ⚡ SELECT - Choose your daily boost:
  Pick the BEST opportunity that:
  - Has measurable performance impact (faster load, less memory, fewer requests)
  - Can be implemented cleanly in < 50 lines
  - Doesn't sacrifice code readability significantly
  - Has low risk of introducing bugs
  - Follows existing patterns

3. 🔧 OPTIMIZE - Implement with precision:
  - Write clean, understandable optimized code
  - Add comments explaining the optimization
  - Preserve existing functionality exactly
  - Consider edge cases
  - Ensure the optimization is safe
  - Add performance metrics in comments if possible

4. ✅ VERIFY - Measure the impact:
  - Run format and lint checks
  - Run the full test suite
  - Verify the optimization works as expected
  - Add benchmark comments if possible
  - Ensure no functionality is broken

5. 🎁 PRESENT - Share your speed boost:
  Create a PR with:
  - Title: "⚡ Bolt: [performance improvement]"
  - Description with:
    * 💡 What: The optimization implemented
    * 🎯 Why: The performance problem it solves
    * 📊 Impact: Expected performance improvement (e.g., "Reduces re-renders by ~50%")
    * 🔬 Measurement: How to verify the improvement
  - Reference any related performance issues

BOLT'S FAVORITE OPTIMIZATIONS:
⚡ Add React.memo() to prevent unnecessary re-renders
⚡ Add database index on frequently queried field
⚡ Cache expensive API call results
⚡ Add lazy loading to images below the fold
⚡ Debounce search input to reduce API calls
⚡ Replace O(n²) nested loop with O(n) hash map lookup
⚡ Add pagination to large data fetch
⚡ Memoize expensive calculation with useMemo/computed
⚡ Add early return to skip unnecessary processing
⚡ Batch multiple API calls into single request
⚡ Add virtualization to long list rendering
⚡ Move expensive operation outside of render loop
⚡ Add code splitting for large route components
⚡ Replace large library with smaller alternative

BOLT AVOIDS (not worth the complexity):
❌ Micro-optimizations with no measurable impact
❌ Premature optimization of cold paths
❌ Optimizations that make code unreadable
❌ Large architectural changes
❌ Optimizations that require extensive testing
❌ Changes to critical algorithms without thorough testing

Remember: You're Bolt, making things lightning fast. But speed without correctness is useless. Measure, optimize, verify. If you can't find a clear performance win today, wait for tomorrow's opportunity.

title: fix(fleet-queue): outbox reconcile of issue_comment/pr_comment entries can never match — search hit's issue number is read back as a comment id

body:
## Problem

For `issue_comment` / `pr_comment` outbox entries, marker reconciliation can never verify a landed comment, even once the search call works. `find_by_marker` (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/client.rs:2589-2608`) takes `item.number` from a `search/issues` hit, which is the **issue/PR number**, and passes it to `read_back`. For comment kinds, `read_back` (client.rs:2578-2581) treats that number as a **comment id** and fetches `repos/{repo}/issues/comments/{number}`. Comment ids are a separate namespace, so this never matches and the drainer concludes the comment is absent and re-creates it (a duplicate comment).

## Evidence (verified on origin/main fb97fae771, scratch repo dezren39/fleet-outbox-trial-3706)

- Search indexes comment text and returns the parent issue: a phrase that exists only in the comment on issue #7 returns `num=7`.
- The comment lookup by that issue number fails; by the real comment id it works:

```
$ gh api repos/dezren39/fleet-outbox-trial-3706/issues/comments/7
{"message":"Not Found",...}  (HTTP 404)
$ gh api repos/dezren39/fleet-outbox-trial-3706/issues/comments/6781256653 --jq .id
6781256653
```

- The create path is right (`create` parses `#issuecomment-<id>`, client.rs:2535-2541), so only the reconcile path mixes the two id spaces. The reconciled `github_url` would also be the parent issue's `html_url`, not the comment's.
- Minor, same loop: `let number = item.get("number")...?;` (client.rs:2601) aborts the whole scan on one item without a number instead of skipping it.
- No test touches comment kinds against `GhCreator` (the trials all use `kind: issue` with `FakeCreator`).

## Acceptance criteria

- Reconciling an `issue_comment` / `pr_comment` entry resolves the marker to a comment id (for example list `repos/{repo}/issues/{n}/comments` for each candidate issue and match the marker) and records the comment's `html_url` and id.
- A malformed search item is skipped, not fatal.
- A test with a stubbed `gh` covers a landed comment being reconciled (no second comment), for both kinds.
- Depends on the `gh` seam from the companion issue (#8361: find_by_marker POST/404); related: #8331, #3706.

title: fleet-search parity guard red on clean main: atlas-search and fleet-search server.rs have drifted (blocks clean CI signal for search PRs)
body:
## Problem

The fleet-search parity guard is red on clean main (verified 2026-11-10, lane code-b, while shepherding PR #7954 for #6665):

- `bash .github/scripts/check-fleet-search-parity.test.sh` exits 1 on clean main AND on PR #7954's branch.
- `bash .github/scripts/check-fleet-search-parity.sh` exits 1 on clean main AND on PR #7954's branch.

The atlas-search and fleet-search copies of server.rs have drifted; one visible hunk is a request guard (`if req.k == 0 { return Err(ServerError::bad_request("k must be at least 1")) }`) present in one copy and absent in the other. This is the drift class the guard exists to catch (#5920 contract tests, #5433 writer parity) — but because the guard runs on PRs, every atlas-search/fleet-search PR now shows a red check that is not its own, and shepherds cannot tell PR-caused red from main red without a local both-trees run.

## Work

Diff the two server.rs copies end to end, decide per hunk which side is correct (the k>=1 guard's side should be argued from the API contract, cf. #6524's paging-truncation findings), bring the copies back into parity, and confirm both guard scripts exit 0 on main. If a hunk is an intentional divergence, encode it as an explicit guard exception instead of silent drift.

title: queue: stamp the claiming session's own model on the task at claim time
body:
## Order

Drew, 2026-11-10 10:53 CST: "sessions should provide their own model to the queue when picking up an item. opencode should expose current model to the active session."

## Part 1 (fork — DONE, pre-existing)

developing-today-forks/opencode#1891 (serving leaf invisible to the session) was implemented by fork PR #1929 (merged 2026-11-07, squash `03c8dc44`): the in-session `route_usage` tool, given a `session` input, returns `serving` (per-step leaves) and `lastServing` (provider/model/variant of the leaf that served the last step, plus `attemptedLeaf`/`failedOver`), derived from `route_attempt`. Verified present on current fork `main` and in the deployed pin (`ff9858ae`, fork PR #2237's merge — ancestry confirmed via the compare API: the deployed pin descends from the #1929 merge). No new fork work needed; this issue covers the queue half.

## Part 2 (this issue — queue claim stamp)

When a session picks up (claims) an item, the claim records the session's own current model on the task:

- Additive columns on `tasks` (Turso backend, `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue`), existing rows NULL: `claim_provider`, `claim_model`, `claim_variant` — the claiming session's serving leaf at claim time, read from the Part 1 `route_usage` surface.
- The broker claim verb (`claim_repo_task`, both the pick path and the by-id path) accepts optional `model_provider` / `model_id` / `model_variant` request fields and stamps them on the claimed row; the `claimed` event detail carries them too.
- The `repo-queue claim` CLI gains `--model-provider` / `--model-id` / `--model-variant` flags (validated: provider and model required together; variant optional).
- Claimant/lane surfaces pass the stamp on a normal claim without extra manual steps. Claims by non-session actors (Muse lanes) carry a distinct marker in the provider field (`muse-lane`) instead of a fabricated model.
- Semantics: the stamp is the model at claim time. A later failover changes the serving leaf (visible via `route_usage`) but not the stamp.

## Acceptance

- One real claim through the production path on a scratch task reads back with `claim_provider`/`claim_model`/`claim_variant` matching the claiming session's `route_attempt` leaf.
- Existing behavior unchanged for claims that carry no model fields (stamp stays NULL).

You are "Bolt" ⚡ - a performance-obsessed agent who makes the codebase faster, one optimization at a time.

Your mission is to identify and implement ONE small performance improvement that makes the application measurably faster or more efficient.


## Boundaries

✅ **Always do:**
- Run commands like `pnpm lint` and `pnpm test` (or associated equivalents) before creating PR
- Add comments explaining the optimization
- Measure and document expected performance impact

⚠️ **Ask first:**
- Adding any new dependencies
- Making architectural changes

🚫 **Never do:**
- Modify package.json or tsconfig.json without instruction
- Make breaking changes
- Optimize prematurely without actual bottleneck
- Sacrifice code readability for micro-optimizations

BOLT'S PHILOSOPHY:
- Speed is a feature
- Every millisecond counts
- Measure first, optimize second
- Don't sacrifice readability for micro-optimizations

BOLT'S JOURNAL - CRITICAL LEARNINGS ONLY:
Before starting, read .jules/bolt.md (create if missing).

Your journal is NOT a log - only add entries for CRITICAL learnings that will help you avoid mistakes or make better decisions.

⚠️ ONLY add journal entries when you discover:
- A performance bottleneck specific to this codebase's architecture
- An optimization that surprisingly DIDN'T work (and why)
- A rejected change with a valuable lesson
- A codebase-specific performance pattern or anti-pattern
- A surprising edge case in how this app handles performance

❌ DO NOT journal routine work like:
- "Optimized component X today" (unless there's a learning)
- Generic React performance tips
- Successful optimizations without surprises

Format: `## YYYY-MM-DD - [Title]
**Learning:** [Insight]
**Action:** [How to apply next time]`

BOLT'S DAILY PROCESS:

1. 🔍 PROFILE - Hunt for performance opportunities:

  FRONTEND PERFORMANCE:
  - Unnecessary re-renders in React/Vue/Angular components
  - Missing memoization for expensive computations
  - Large bundle sizes (opportunities for code splitting)
  - Unoptimized images (missing lazy loading, wrong formats)
  - Missing virtualization for long lists
  - Synchronous operations blocking the main thread
  - Missing debouncing/throttling on frequent events
  - Unused CSS or JavaScript being loaded
  - Missing resource preloading for critical assets
  - Inefficient DOM manipulations

  BACKEND PERFORMANCE:
  - N+1 query problems in database calls
  - Missing database indexes on frequently queried fields
  - Expensive operations without caching
  - Synchronous operations that could be async
  - Missing pagination on large data sets
  - Inefficient algorithms (O(n²) that could be O(n))
  - Missing connection pooling
  - Repeated API calls that could be batched
  - Large payloads that could be compressed

  GENERAL OPTIMIZATIONS:
  - Missing caching for expensive operations
  - Redundant calculations in loops
  - Inefficient data structures for the use case
  - Missing early returns in conditional logic
  - Unnecessary deep cloning or copying
  - Missing lazy initialization
  - Inefficient string concatenation in loops
  - Missing request/response compression

2. ⚡ SELECT - Choose your daily boost:
  Pick the BEST opportunity that:
  - Has measurable performance impact (faster load, less memory, fewer requests)
  - Can be implemented cleanly in < 50 lines
  - Doesn't sacrifice code readability significantly
  - Has low risk of introducing bugs
  - Follows existing patterns

3. 🔧 OPTIMIZE - Implement with precision:
  - Write clean, understandable optimized code
  - Add comments explaining the optimization
  - Preserve existing functionality exactly
  - Consider edge cases
  - Ensure the optimization is safe
  - Add performance metrics in comments if possible

4. ✅ VERIFY - Measure the impact:
  - Run format and lint checks
  - Run the full test suite
  - Verify the optimization works as expected
  - Add benchmark comments if possible
  - Ensure no functionality is broken

5. 🎁 PRESENT - Share your speed boost:
  Create a PR with:
  - Title: "⚡ Bolt: [performance improvement]"
  - Description with:
    * 💡 What: The optimization implemented
    * 🎯 Why: The performance problem it solves
    * 📊 Impact: Expected performance improvement (e.g., "Reduces re-renders by ~50%")
    * 🔬 Measurement: How to verify the improvement
  - Reference any related performance issues

BOLT'S FAVORITE OPTIMIZATIONS:
⚡ Add React.memo() to prevent unnecessary re-renders
⚡ Add database index on frequently queried field
⚡ Cache expensive API call results
⚡ Add lazy loading to images below the fold
⚡ Debounce search input to reduce API calls
⚡ Replace O(n²) nested loop with O(n) hash map lookup
⚡ Add pagination to large data fetch
⚡ Memoize expensive calculation with useMemo/computed
⚡ Add early return to skip unnecessary processing
⚡ Batch multiple API calls into single request
⚡ Add virtualization to long list rendering
⚡ Move expensive operation outside of render loop
⚡ Add code splitting for large route components
⚡ Replace large library with smaller alternative

BOLT AVOIDS (not worth the complexity):
❌ Micro-optimizations with no measurable impact
❌ Premature optimization of cold paths
❌ Optimizations that make code unreadable
❌ Large architectural changes
❌ Optimizations that require extensive testing
❌ Changes to critical algorithms without thorough testing

Remember: You're Bolt, making things lightning fast. But speed without correctness is useless. Measure, optimize, verify. If you can't find a clear performance win today, wait for tomorrow's opportunity.

If no suitable performance optimization can be identified, stop and do not create a PR.---

body:
# Atlas source-mark grammar: repository mark omits captured_at, breaking the registry round-trip

## Finding (from PR review)
On PR #7629 (docs(atlas): source-mark grammar spec for composite provenance marks, #6044), Codex review comment [4505856175](https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/7629#discussion_r4505856175) (chatgpt-codex-connector[bot], 2026-11-08T10:18:21Z, `doc/2026-11-08T10-17-00Z_design_source_mark_grammar/2026-11-08T10-17-00Z_design_source_mark_grammar.md:54`):

> Preserve capture time in the repository mark mapping. For two registry occurrences captured at different times from the same revision, path, and content hash, this production emits identical marks because it has no `captured_at` field. That conflicts with §6's registry tuple and the requirement that the total formatter round-trip every registry-shaped `OccurrenceRef`: parsing cannot recover which capture time was formatted. Include capture time in repository marks, or explicitly define a repository-specific record contract that excludes it and narrow the round-trip requirement accordingly.

## No-response evidence
- No replies in the comment thread; the review thread is unresolved (GraphQL `reviewThreads` verified 2026-11-09).
- PR #7629 head is unchanged at `aac41eefd44cec7480e1e7dca4263802ba1b7678` since the comment; no fix commit followed it. Past the 24-hour grace period for open PRs.

## Still-live evidence (current PR head)
Raw read of the spec at head `aac41eefd4`: §3 defines `repo-mark = "repo@" revision ":" path hash?` — no captured-at component — while `host-mark` carries `captured-at`. Two occurrences differing only in capture time still format to identical repository marks, so the §6 round-trip cannot recover capture time.

## Acceptance criteria
- Repository marks carry capture time, OR the spec defines a repository-specific record contract excluding it and narrows the total-formatter round-trip requirement to match.
- Resolving by a documented decision on this issue is also acceptable.

# ci(ci-policy checker): agreement checker counts any `push` trigger as the main tier — a push that never runs on main is certified as agreeing, and its waiver is ordered deleted

## Summary

The CI-policy agreement checker merged in PR #7945 (Phase 1 of #7089, parent #7090) claims to enforce the tier→trigger mapping "exactly" as pinned in `.github/ci-policy.md`, but for the **main tier** it checks only that a trigger *named* `push` exists — never what that push trigger targets.

The contract it enforces:

- `.github/ci-policy.md:199` — main tier is satisfied by "a `push` trigger on `branches: [main]` (path gates as before), or a named equivalent main-tier venue".
- `.github/scripts/check-ci-policy-agreement.sh:20` — the script header repeats the pin: `main (main tier) -> push trigger (branches: [main])`.
- `.github/ci-policy.md` §"CI-policy agreement contract" — "**Tier → trigger mapping** (the checker below enforces exactly this)".

The implementation:

- `check-ci-policy-agreement.sh:93` `triggers_of()` prints only the trigger *names* from the workflow's `on:` block; branch/tag filters under a trigger are never read.
- `check-ci-policy-agreement.sh:170` — the leg agrees iff the required name matches exactly: `printf '%s\n' "$triggers" | grep -qx "$req"`, with `required_trigger main` = `push` (`:80`).

So a `push` trigger that cannot run on main — `branches: [release]`, `branches-ignore: [main]`, or tags-only — satisfies the main leg. Worse, for a currently waived workflow it flips the verdict to **STALE WAIVER … "main leg now agrees — delete the waiver in this PR"**, and once the waiver is deleted as instructed, the checker passes: it certifies a main tier that never runs on main.

## Verified behavior (this run)

Probe on the laptop: `~/git/fleet/probe-ci-policy-branches-20261108/` (`probe.sh` + `probe.log`), using a byte-identical copy of the checker from origin/main `e744a9bb0016` (md5 `3f4cdd4a5bc5740c24e72f047c59eb69`, verified against `git show origin/main:`), driven with fixture trees in the same shape as the checker's own contract tests.

- **Control** — a tree in the current-main shape (every main leg waived): checker exits 0, `ci-policy-agreement: OK`. The checker's own contract suite (`check-ci-policy-agreement.test.sh`, run unmodified) also passes all 5 cases — its `wf()` helper (`test.sh:14`) only ever emits bare trigger names with no sub-keys, so no existing test exercises a branch filter.
- **Case 1** — `mcpx-nixbuild.yml` gains `push: branches: [release]` (never main): checker reports `STALE WAIVER mcpx-nixbuild.yml: main leg now agrees (trigger 'push' declared) — delete the waiver for issue #6981 in this PR`.
- **Case 2** — `push: branches-ignore: [main]` (explicitly *not* main): identical STALE WAIVER verdict.
- **Case 3** — `push: tags: ["v*"]` only: identical STALE WAIVER verdict.
- **Case 4** — following the checker's own instruction for Case 2 (waiver removed from a copy of the checker, logic untouched; workflow still `branches-ignore: [main]`): checker exits 0, `ci-policy-agreement: OK` — a false agreement end-state.
- **Case 5 (sanity)** — `push: branches: [main]`: same STALE WAIVER verdict, correctly — the checker cannot distinguish Case 5 from Cases 1–3 at all.

No in-scope workflow on current main declares a filtered `push` trigger, so no live workflow is mis-certified today. The hazard is prospective and concrete: every main leg in the registry is currently waived against Phase 2–3 of #7089 (#6953, #6929, #6981), and the re-arm PRs those phases produce are exactly the PRs this checker will judge. A re-arm that restores `push` with the wrong branch filter — or a deliberate `branches-ignore` — would be certified as agreement, with the waiver deleted in the same PR, removing the record that the leg was ever disputed.

## Why it matters

The agreement contract exists so "dispatch-only and nobody dispatches" cannot persist by default (#7089). A checker that certifies by trigger name alone re-creates that failure in a subtler form: the tree, the policy, and the waiver set all *appear* to agree while the main-tier check never runs on main — and the stale-waiver machinery actively deletes the evidence trail.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] For the main tier, the checker verifies the `push` trigger actually targets main: an explicit `branches:` filter must include `main` (a bare/unfiltered `push:` still counts, as today); `branches-ignore:` containing `main`, a `branches:` list without `main`, and a tags-only `push:` do **not** satisfy the main leg (they keep the leg waived/disagreeing, never stale).
- [ ] Contract tests in `check-ci-policy-agreement.test.sh` cover at least: `branches: [release]`, `branches-ignore: [main]`, tags-only push, and `branches: [main]` (agreeing), using fixture workflows with real trigger sub-keys.
- [ ] The existing 5 contract tests and the current-main tree still pass (checker stays green on main with the recorded waiver set unchanged).
- [ ] Out of scope: changing any workflow's triggers, tiers, or waivers; the named-equivalent-venue clause of the main tier (a prose disposition, not tree-checkable) is unchanged.

Related: #7089 (agreement contract epic), #7090 (Phase 1 checker), #6981 / #6953 / #6929 (the waived main legs this checker will judge).

Fix the root cause triaged on #6829: the laptop's `~/hatch/tools/op-env.sh` (line 41) fetches the 1Password service-account token via a hardcoded `"${HOME}/tools/bin/bws"` path. That path does not exist on the laptop (`/home/user/tools/bin/` does not exist at all; the working `bws` is `/run/current-system/sw/bin/bws` 2.1.0 on PATH), so the fetch exits 127 with empty stdout, the line's `2>/dev/null` swallows the error, and the downstream Python JSON parse dies with `JSONDecodeError: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)` — reproduced verbatim 2026-11-08, full evidence on #6829 (agent note, comment 6731508081).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `op-env.sh` resolves `bws` from PATH (with `~/tools/bin/bws` as a fallback if present), never a single hardcoded path — on both the laptop (`~/hatch/tools/`) and sandbox (`~/tools/`) copies.
- [ ] `op-env.sh` fails loudly naming the failing step (binary resolution / `bws secret get` / JSON parse) when a fetch returns empty or non-zero, instead of surfacing a downstream `JSONDecodeError`.
- [ ] `source ~/hatch/tools/bws-env.sh; source ~/hatch/tools/op-env.sh` on the laptop completes with `OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN` non-empty (verified by length only — never print the value).
- [ ] The 1Password copies owed for the tokens minted during the 2026-11-07 rename program (`turso.fleet-mirror-rw-token`, `turso.fleet-platform-rw-token`, the rotated atlas-ask-ledger token) are filed, restoring the both-vaults rule from #6829.
- [ ] The stale "bws lives in ~/tools/bin" comment in `bws-env.sh` is corrected to match the resolution order.

Parent: #6829 (triage findings, root cause, and evidence live there).

body:
## Session error wave 2026-11-07 21:00–22:00 CST — _claude credential blanked; 49 sessions dead, still ongoing

**Diagnosis (session-minder triage, 2026-11-07 ~22:15 CST, from laptop opencode.db route_attempt + minder snaps):**

- 49 sessions newly errored across the 21:00 / 21:10–21:35 / 21:40 / 22:00 lane batches (failed in top-200: 2 → 51). Error class: **656 of 664 post-switch Claude-model attempts are `_claude` Authentication failures** — "Claude Code is not signed in on this machine: no OAuth credential in ~/.claude/.credentials.json and no CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN in the environment." Since the current server started, `_claude` is **656 attempts / 0 successes**.
- **Root cause:** `~/.claude/.credentials.json` was rewritten at **19:02 CST** with EMPTY `accessToken` (len 0), EMPTY `refreshToken` (len 0), `expiresAt` 0 (subscription metadata retained: max, sign_in). Preceded by the 18:35 CST revoked-OAuth 401. Whatever wrote the file at 19:02 persisted empty tokens over a live credential.
- The old fastlane server held a working in-memory credential, so Claude legs kept working until the **nixos-rebuild switch restarted the server at 21:04:34 CST** (base unit opencode.service, 2.0.30+4b2fc8a). The new process read the blanked file → total _claude outage from that moment. The switch exposed the blanking; it did not cause it. The speed/_muse config edit (22:04) is exonerated: later, different provider, no restart.
- **Amplification:** sonnet-plan made 263 decisions since the switch, ALL choosing `_claude/claude-sonnet-5-5` — the `_antigravity` Claude leg is quota-closed (AG Claude+GPT weekly 100%) and never attempted, so sonnet-plan has exactly one live candidate and no failover target when it auth-fails. Sessions on Luna/Vibe/DeepSeek legs survived (146 succeeded). This is the #7073 failure shape at fleet scale.
- **Still ongoing** at 22:11 CST: 72 _claude auth failures in the trailing 10 minutes. Every new batch will keep dying on Claude legs until the credential is restored.

## Fix
1. **Re-provision the Claude Code OAuth credential fleet-side on the laptop** (2026-11-06 restore route; the refresh token is also empty, so a refresh alone cannot recover it — a sign-in/OAuth flow is required). Cf. #6120 (Claude auth auto-renewal gap).
2. **Restart opencode.service** so the provider re-reads the credential; then restart the OpenClaw gateway (known coupling) and verify both; spot-check `_claude` attempts succeeding in route_attempt.
3. **Fork defect (developing-today-forks/opencode):** a credential write must never persist empty tokens over an existing credential — on refresh failure, preserve the existing file. Whatever wrote empties at 19:02 CST is the bug.
4. Failover amplification is tracked on #7073 — this issue is its largest exhibit; no duplicate work there.

Acceptance: `_claude` success attempts > 0 in route_attempt after restore; a lane batch completes with failed-count back to baseline; the minder's next check shows no new provider.auth session deaths.


## Acceptance criteria
- The problem described above is confirmed against current main (reproduced or traced to the named code path), or the issue is closed with that evidence.
- A fix/implementation addressing the described behaviour is merged via PR referencing this issue, with tests naming their oracle where the change has meaningful invariants.
- Related/sibling issues from the same filing batch are cross-linked and any dependency is recorded as a native blocked-by relation.

# muse-dev2 decommission: confirmatory platform-schema sweep at first recovery window

Context: Postgres wrap-up bullet 5 audit (2026-11-06, recorded on #6619) proved by code/config search that **no live fleet system reads or writes** muse-dev2's Supabase platform schemas (`auth`, `storage`, `realtime`, `vault`), and the 2026-11-06 inventory (`hatch-personal/workspace/supabase/turso-migration/inventory-supabase-2026-11-06.md`) showed every data table in those schemas at **0 rows** (only the platform's own `schema_migrations`/`migrations` tables hold rows: auth 82, realtime 91, storage 74). Per Drew's 2026-11-06 ruling the project will be **decommissioned, not deleted** — these schemas are safe to leave behind.

The one thing that cannot be verified while the data plane is down (#6619): that the counts are still 0 today. No fleet code path can write to these schemas, so this is a formality — but it must be run and recorded before the decommission is signed off.

## At the first verified-green window, run (Management API SQL / supabase-exec):

```sql
select 'auth.users', count(*) from auth.users
union all select 'auth.identities', count(*) from auth.identities
union all select 'auth.sessions', count(*) from auth.sessions
union all select 'auth.refresh_tokens', count(*) from auth.refresh_tokens
union all select 'auth.audit_log_entries', count(*) from auth.audit_log_entries
union all select 'storage.buckets', count(*) from storage.buckets
union all select 'storage.objects', count(*) from storage.objects
union all select 'realtime.subscription', count(*) from realtime.subscription
union all select 'vault.secrets', count(*) from vault.secrets;
```

Expected: all zero. Record the result on #6619 and close this issue. Any non-zero count: stop, identify the writer before decommission proceeds — nothing in the fleet is expected to have written there.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] At the first verified-green recovery window, the confirmatory counts for muse-dev2's platform schemas (auth/storage/realtime/vault data tables) are run and recorded on this issue
- [ ] The recorded result is attached to the #6619 decommission sign-off trail, and this issue closes with the counts as evidence

## Finding (unaddressed PR review comment)

PR #6444 (open, "fix(fleet-config): reject CWD-relative paths without an absolute HOME (#5737)") makes home-dependent config resolution fail with `ConfigError::MissingHome` when HOME is unset/empty. CodeRabbit flagged that the fleet smoke suite's clean-environment checks were not updated for that behavior, so the documented smoke suite now fails.

- Source PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/6444
- Review comment: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/6444#discussion_r4489204560
- Reviewer: coderabbitai[bot], 2026-11-06T05:02:28Z, Major (Functional Correctness), at `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs:248`
- Essence: "Both `env -i` version checks now exit 2 because `HOME` and the config overrides are absent. The documented smoke suite therefore fails. Assert the missing-HOME error and separately test successful version output with an absolute override."

## No-response evidence

- The comment thread has no replies and is unresolved (GraphQL `reviewThreads` verified this run).
- A later rebase of the PR (2026-11-07T04:41:04Z, head `932ca5b212829a4260c1224650d8a3dd1c371d61`, agent note by the queue worker claiming issue #5737) combined the config semantics but did not touch `pkgs/fleet/smoke.sh` and did not disposition this comment.
- Comment is >24h old, so the open-PR grace period has expired.

## Still-live evidence (verified on current PR head 932ca5b212 this run)

- `pkgs/fleet/smoke.sh:816-817` still runs both checks expecting exit 0: `env -i "$CONNECT_OUT/bin/fleet" version` and the static variant.
- `fleet`'s `main()` calls `fleet_config::Config::load()` before any version dispatch (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet/src/main.rs`), and `Config::load()` -> `file_path()` returns `ConfigError::MissingHome` when HOME, `FLEET_CONFIG`, and `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` are all absent (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs`, `file_path_from`), so under `env -i` the binary exits 2 before `version` runs.
- Dedupe: searched open and closed issues by PR number, file path, and keywords - no issue covers the stale smoke expectations. Issue #5737 is the parent config defect, not the smoke update; issue #6400 (smoke.sh not run by CI) is a different gap.

## Acceptance criteria

- Update the clean-environment smoke checks to match the MissingHome behavior: assert the expected error when HOME is absent, and separately verify successful version output with an absolute config override, keeping the two outcomes independently verified; or resolve by a documented decision on this issue.
- Do not reply to or resolve the source PR review thread from this issue.

Implements the design in #5687 (fleet init location awareness). That design is complete in the #5687 body (§1–§6 + recommendation summary) and was triage-verified 2026-11-07 by lane code-l:

- Verified at current main `d98f52fe34209ac70fc6d494ba7f6916bafc22bf` (2026-11-07T04:24Z): no `HostConfig`, `FLEET_LOCATION`, or `FLEET_HOST_CONFIG` exists anywhere under `pkgs/fleet/crates/` — the design is NOT implemented.
- Paths in the #5687 body have moved since filing: read `crates/fleet/...` as `pkgs/fleet/crates/...` (e.g. `cmd_init` is at `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet/src/main.rs:686`; `fleet-config` still uses `deny_unknown_fields`).
- Parent epic #5412 is CLOSED; this issue is the implementation step the design's Next steps called for "under #5412".

## Gate before starting

The #5687 Next steps reserve one decision to Drew: confirm the design, or amend the §1/§2 names — `[host]` section in `fleet.toml`, `FLEET_LOCATION`, `FLEET_HOST_CONFIG`. #5687 carries `user/escalated` for that confirmation. Do not start implementation until that confirmation lands on #5687; if Drew amends the names, this issue's spec follows the amended names.

## Scope (per #5687 §5–§6)

- `HostConfig` + location/role resolution in `fleet-config`, with unit tests for precedence (env-contents > env-location > file, no cross-source merging), mismatch, unknown-role (loud error), and malformed-env (loud, exit 2).
- Location-aware `cmd_init` / `run_init`: unknown location ⇒ report state, start nothing, exit 69.
- `spawn_serve` switches to `["serve", "proxy"]`; `fleet proxy init` goes through the identical resolution.
- `[domains]` kill switch still wins over the manifest; gated-off roles are reported as skipped with reason.
- Migration sequencing per §6: provision the sandbox `[host]` manifest + `FLEET_LOCATION=sandbox` pin in `init-ensure.sh` BEFORE deploying the location-aware binary; the `deny_unknown_fields` rollback gotcha (a `[host]` section parse-errors the old binary) goes in the runbook.
- Smoke cases per §6: manifest-fixture no-op, unknown-location report (exit 69, nothing spawned), laptop-manifest-on-sandbox roles.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Drew's name confirmation recorded on #5687
- [ ] Resolution + tests landed; `fleet init` on the provisioned sandbox prints its location and is a strict no-op against a live broker, exit 0
- [ ] Unknown-location machine: report + exit 69 + nothing spawned, verified
- [ ] Provisioning change sequenced before the binary flip, rollback note written

Filed by lane code-l triage of #5687 (fallback mode, queue backend down) so the design does not sit without a linked implementation issue.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `fleet init` is location-aware per the #5687 design: it reads a HostConfig [host] manifest and honors the FLEET_LOCATION / FLEET_HOST_CONFIG overrides.
- [ ] When location or host config cannot be determined, init reports what is missing and stops (report-don't-guess) instead of silently assuming a location.
- [ ] Behavior on the sandbox and on the laptop matches the #5687 design's recommendation summary, with tests covering the override and missing-config paths in CI.
