# Phase 4 of #6622 — closing pagination inventory: disposition every paginated loop in the repo against the complete/bounded/honest contract

Phase 4 (closing inventory) of design #6622 — *complete, bounded, or say so: one pagination contract for the repo's paged reads* (design doc: `files/designs/code-pagination-contract.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace; audit at origin/main `075b2de90`).

## Scope

GATED on Phases 1–3 of #6622 (#6578 + #6600 + #6615 cursor validity; #6572 + #6532 + #6602 volume bounds; #6605 + #6618 completeness honesty) — do not start the inventory until they have landed; keep this issue `status/blocked` until then.

Inventory every paginated loop in the repo — every place code follows a cursor/token/page parameter across requests, or reads a list it presents as complete — and disposition each one against the contract's three rules (cursor validated where read: type + progress; volume bounded with a named-listing error; truncation never silent: complete, fail-closed, or explicitly marked): **conforms** (name the guard), **filed** (a follow-up issue, if a gap is found), or **deliberately local/unbounded** (the reason named). The inventory covers at least: the pkgs/id page consumers beyond Phase 1's three (any other `next_after`/records/history readers, and the sender side in `world_session`); github-backup's remaining page followers beyond Phase 2's two (clone/fetch/reconcile loops); cold-store-reaper's remaining listings beyond `list_backups`/`s3_list_objects`; the aggregator/projector page and cursor reads; fleet crates' list reads beyond dispatch-test's scan (including the queue brokers' list paths); and the operator scripts under `infra/` and `bin/` that page GitHub or PostgREST.

Land the contract's final statement form: confirm each Phase 1–3 system carries the three-rule statement in its module docs (or the nearest equivalent), in the terms recorded on #6622.

## Required dispositions (name each one explicitly in the closing evidence)

- (a) **The github-backup shape filings:** #6575 (drain queue-event shape) and #6606 (reconcile clone-status line shape) are parsed-shape defects in the same system as Phase 2's legs. Confirm they are dispositioned under #3068's shape contract / #3282's estate (filed follow-ups or explicit assignment), and that nothing in this contract claims them.
- (b) **The #3283 cross-reference:** design #3282's closing audit (#3283) inventories github-backup state access. State how the two inventories divide the github-backup page loops (pagination axes here; state access there) so neither audit re-covers or drops a loop.
- (c) **Sender-side cursor emission:** for each Phase 1 protocol, confirm the sender always emits the cursor in the pinned type (string-or-null for the id worlds protocol) — or file the sender gap. A receiver-side refusal whose sender can emit the refused shape is a compatibility break, not a contract.
- (d) **Pin verification:** confirm Phase 1 landed cursor-type refusal as recorded on #6622, and Phase 3 landed #6618 as fail-closed-or-complete (never page-as-set) — cite the tests that pin each.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An inventory (posted on this issue or landed in docs) lists every paginated loop above with a disposition and file:line evidence.
- [ ] The four required dispositions (a)–(d) are each answered explicitly.
- [ ] Any gap found is filed as its own issue and linked; no gap is fixed silently inside the inventory.
- [ ] The contract statement's final form is present in the Phase 1–3 systems' docs, and design #6622 is commented with the closing evidence.

*Filed by the design architect as Phase 4 of #6622. Triage: record the gating on Phases 1–3, keep `status/blocked` until they land, and do not re-scope the contract — the decisions are recorded on #6622.*

# Phase 4 of #6487 — closing sign-surface inventory: disposition every public signing entry point in pkgs/id against the sign-time refusal contract

Design: #6487 (sign only what receipt would accept — one sign-time
refusal contract for `pkgs/id`). Design doc:
`files/designs/code-id-sign-time-refusal.md` in the
keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace.

**Gated on Phases 1–3 of #6487** (Phase 1: #6422 + #6443;
Phase 2: #6424 + #6434; Phase 3: #6447 + #6451 + #6469). Do not
start the inventory until they have landed; keep this issue
`status/blocked` until then.

## Scope

Produce a closing inventory of **every public signing entry point
in `pkgs/id`** (every `pub fn sign_*`, `Signed*::sign`, and any
public method whose purpose is producing a signed object),
dispositioned against the #6487 contract with file:line evidence:

- **enforced** — the signer mirrors every unconditional receipt
  rule decidable from its own inputs; name the phase that did it;
- **deliberately receipt-only** — every unchecked receipt rule is
  class (d) receiver-state; name the rule and the reason it is
  not decidable at the seam;
- **gap** — a decidable unconditional receipt rule is still
  signable-around: file it as a follow-up issue from the audit
  (do not fix it inside this phase).

Required dispositions (named in the design doc):

# Closing queue-validation inventory — disposition every forwarded field, client flag and broker verb value against the validation contract (Phase 4 of #6448)

## Summary

Design #6448 ("Validate what you forward", design doc `files/designs/code-fleet-queue-validation-contract.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace) states the fleet queue's validation contract once: every value the queue forwards is validated — type, range, agreement — at the boundary, and refused with a field-named error rather than forwarded verbatim. Phases 1–3 adopt the six filed instances (#6423, #6426, #6430, #6446, #6419, #6420). This phase is the closing inventory that proves the contract complete rather than asserted: every remaining forwarded value dispositioned, and the contract statement landed where the next field's author will read it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] **Forwarded-field inventory:** every field `task_from_packet` (validate.rs) forwards, and every payload field `manual_schema_errors` touches or skips, is dispositioned against the contract with file:line evidence — validated (cite the check), deliberately unvalidated (state why the value cannot harm: e.g. free-text by design), or filed as a follow-up issue. The inventory, not the design doc, is the completeness proof.
- [ ] **Client-flag inventory:** every `get_i64` flag in `client.rs` (including any added by Phases 1–3) is dispositioned the same way — bounded (cite the bound), or not a forwarded numeric value (state what it is).
- [ ] **Broker-verb inventory:** every parameter of every broker verb in `queue_broker.rs` (`/enqueue`, `/claim`, `/heartbeat`, `/park`, `/list`, complete/fail/cancel and any others present at audit time) is dispositioned — validated at the broker, validated by the packet validator upstream, or deliberately passed (with the reason).
- [ ] **Contract statement landed:** the contract rule and the bounds table from design #6448 are recorded in the `validate.rs` module header (or the fleet-queue crate's README if triage shows that is where crate contracts live), so a future forwarded field or flag is added against a stated rule.
- [ ] **Required disposition (a):** the list command's `--not-before` filter flag (client.rs:876) — a read filter, not a forwarded value: state whether a garbage filter value can produce a false-empty listing in the #6419 shape, and file/fix accordingly.
- [ ] **Required disposition (b):** the SQL-guard question — design #6448 decision 2 leaves the SQL layer unchanged because every evidenced path passes through the validator or the broker. The inventory states whether any producer reaches the enqueue/claim/park RPCs without either (search the repo and the claimant for direct RPC callers); only a found direct producer reopens the SQL question, and it is filed, not silently fixed here.
- [ ] **Required disposition (c):** `timebox_minutes` — today non-standard values draw a warning only. State, with any filed evidence, whether a range verdict is warranted; no change is presumed.
- [ ] **Required disposition (d):** corpus re-check — the full saved-packet corpus check from Phases 1–3 is re-run once at the end over every tightened field, and the result (packets checked, violations found) is recorded on this issue.
- [ ] **Gating:** this phase starts only after Phases 1–3 of #6448 have landed; until then it stays `status/blocked`. If a disposition files a follow-up, that follow-up references this issue and #6448 — it is not folded into this phase's own diff.

## Out of scope

Implementing any follow-up the inventory files; broker response-side (read-back) validation; SQL migrations (unless disposition (b) finds a direct producer, which is filed separately).

Design #6448 and its doc; Phases 1–3: #6423, #6426, #6430, #6446, #6419, #6420. Precedent closing audits: #6243 (ref contract), #3069 (parsed-shape contract).

body:
# id(attestation): `sign_genesis` / `sign_claim` never check the signer is a player — a non-player's signed genesis or claim is dead on arrival, and signing succeeds silently

## Summary

`pkgs/id/src/attestation.rs` enforces its authority rules in the viewer: `compute_state` (attestation.rs:258) counts a genesis only when *each of the agreement's two players* has signed the identical agreement, and counts a claim only when its author is one of those players ("Claims answering a different agreement, **from non-players**, or with an outcome other than … are ignored", attestation.rs:254-255). The signing entry points enforce only one viewer invariant — `sign_genesis` (attestation.rs:171) refuses a duplicate-seat agreement, mirroring the viewer's malformed-agreement rule from #2863. Neither signer checks the other authority rule:

- `sign_genesis` never checks that the signing key is one of `agreement.players`. A third party can sign the agreement and produce a well-formed `attestation.genesis` event that no viewer will ever count toward the genesis pair.
- `sign_claim` (attestation.rs:208) never checks that the signing key is one of the players of the agreement the claim answers (it cannot check from the claim alone — see acceptance criteria for the shape this implies).

So a caller holding the wrong key — the realistic failure: a harness or wallet layer selects the wrong identity, or an operator signs with a witness/service key — gets a successful signature, a chain event, and an event id to hand out, and the object simply never exists for any viewer. That is the same failure shape closed for currency in #6422 ("creation reports success, consumption silently ignores") and for artifacts in #5623: a signed object should be refused at creation when the module's own consumption rules make it unreachable, so the mistake surfaces where the caller can fix it.

## Evidence (verified this run, origin/main `a2b4345e80`)

- Code: `sign_genesis` (attestation.rs:171-205) checks only `first == second` (duplicate seat) before serializing and calling `chain::sign`; `sign_claim` (attestation.rs:208-232) performs no check at all. `compute_state`'s genesis rule (`agreement.players.iter().all(|player| genesis.iter().any(|(author, signed)| author == player && …))`) and per-player claim collection (`author == player`) make non-player objects unreachable by construction.
- Probe (laptop, worktree of origin/main at `a2b4345e80`, `~/git/fleet/probe-attestation-wt`, integration test `pkgs/id/tests/probe_attestation_sign.rs`, `cargo test -p id --test probe_attestation_sign -- --nocapture`, 1 passed): `sign_genesis` by a third key naming neither seat → **Ok** (event produced); `sign_claim` by the same third key → **Ok**; `compute_state` over both players' genuine genesis events plus only the stranger's claim → **Proposed** (the stranger's claim is ignored, exactly as documented). Controls in the same probe: both players' sign calls succeed, and the existing duplicate-seat refusal errors as documented.

## Why it matters

The attestation PoC's own module doc states the principle: "Reconstruction is admission, not deserialization: derive conclusions from signature-verified authors and compare claims with the selected agreement. Reject, ignore, or dispute inconsistent input according to the API's rules; **never silently repair it or let an input's own claims establish authority**." The viewer side honors that; the signer side is the remaining half. This module is explicitly the shape later production attestation APIs would be built on (#2039 design, epic #2056 review gate), so the sign-side contract should be settled while it is still a PoC surface. The duplicate-seat refusal in `sign_genesis` already establishes the house shape: viewer invariants that make an object meaningless are refused at sign time with a typed `SignError`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `sign_genesis` refuses to sign when the signing key's `player_id` is not one of `agreement.players`, surfacing a typed `SignError` variant (e.g. `NotAPlayer`); no event is produced.
- [ ] `sign_claim` gains a way to refuse a non-player signer — e.g. it takes the `GenesisAgreement` (or its player set) alongside the claim, or a sibling checked entry point is added and the unchecked one is crate-private/test-only, mirroring the `sign_unchecked` pattern in artifact.rs. The chosen shape is the fixer's call; the requirement is that the public signing path cannot silently produce a claim no viewer will count.
- [ ] Tests: a non-player genesis signing and a non-player claim signing both error; both players' genuine genesis + claim flow still computes `Agreed` (the existing `attestation_poc.rs` demonstration passes unchanged).
- [ ] `compute_state` behavior is unchanged: non-player objects from other/legacy signers are still ignored, never counted.
- [ ] Out of scope: the witness slot (present and unused by design in this PoC) and objection handling (#2038/#2039).

## Notes

- Related: #2863 (duplicate-seat: the sign-time refusal precedent in this same function), #2868 (claim outcome domain, viewer side), #6422 (the currency sign-side validation gap — same failure shape, different module and rule; complementary, not a duplicate), #5623 (artifact sign-side precedent), #2898 (the reconstruction-is-admission design epic this module's doc cites).
- Found by Lane B (new-issue-creator-code-b), weighting away from Lane A's recent fleet-config/queue filings and Lane B's own recent dead-test and currency filings.

title: Implement RustDesk raw-stream splice through fleet proxy

labels.name: epic/fleet-orchestration
labels.description: Reprioritization program epic (2026-11-12)

body:
Parent design: #5694. Related remote-GUI evaluation: #5924; dedicated SSH forward: #5509.

## Goal
Implement the first-build recommendation from #5694: let the fleet proxy expose the laptop's RustDesk direct-access TCP endpoint through a loopback-only raw stream splice, using the existing CONNECT tunnel path. Keep `forward.sh` as the fallback until the splice is verified.

## Current-main evidence
At current main (`04f78696abfbdf6567f58e623d80520436f002fa`), `fleet-config` registers laptop-agent port 4799 but not RustDesk 21118 (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs:27,368`); the proxy advertises `ProxyServe` only (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/serve.rs:488`); and `tunnel.rs` applies a 660-second read timeout (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src/tunnel.rs:22,196`). PR #6088 is merged and explicitly says RustDesk remains on its SSH forward until this splice is built. PR #6140 is merged credential durability work, not transport.

## Scope
- Register the RustDesk TCP service at laptop port 21118.
- Add an explicit raw-splice capability in the fleet proxy handshake; older brokers must not advertise it.
- Add the client-side loopback listener at `127.0.0.1:21118`; per accepted client, check out one CONNECT tunnel to laptop:21118 and relay bytes bidirectionally. Do not wrap as HTTP or return a spent stream to the pool.
- Make the long-lived splice opt out of the HTTP tunnel read/write timeout.
- Keep broker configuration and logs free of RustDesk credentials; the broker is only a byte pipe.

## Non-goals
Do not change `forward.sh` until verified; do not pre-warm RustDesk sockets; do not run `hbbs`/`hbbr`; do not implement per-connection virtual desktops (separate design/follow-up).

## Acceptance
- New and old broker capability negotiation is tested; old brokers keep existing behavior.
- A local loopback RustDesk client can establish a session through the splice; a bidirectional byte-stream test proves framing is transparent and concurrent splices work.
- An idle session remains connected beyond the current 660-second timeout (the acceptance target in #5694 is >30 minutes).
- No RustDesk password/proof is added to broker config or logs; the existing SSH forward remains an available fallback.
- Targeted tests and applicable Nix/build checks pass; findings and any activation caveat are recorded on #5694.

body:
Drew's standing rule (2026-11-05 01:10 CST): no provider integration may depend on a browser cookie/session that silently expires. Every browser-dependent auth must have (a) an auto-renewing long-lived token, or (b) built-in cookie auto-renewal (automatic re-capture/refresh, e.g. via CDP against the standing signed-in laptop Helium profile, on cadence and on auth failure), with an alert BEFORE hard expiry when renewal fails. Manual re-import steps and one-shot fix-it crons are not an end state.

LANDED with this issue's opening pass:
- OpenDesign session keeper in the quota gatherer (pm-stack aggregator src/opendesign-renewal.ts): per-tick session read (the Better Auth session slides — verified live 2026-11-05: expiresAt = read-time + 7 days), horizon recorded in ~/.local/state/pm-aggregator/opendesign-renewal.json, CDP re-capture from the laptop Helium with validate-before-store when the stored session fails or runs low, and an alert state while days remain when renewal cannot complete. The one-shot opendesign-cookie-reimport-nov5 cron is retired once the keeper verified live.

REMAINING GAPS (each is follow-through under the rule, not a new decision):
1. Meta portal fetcher (#6079): the auto-renewal requirement is recorded on that issue (comment 6652154440) — the restore must ship with CDP cookie re-capture + pre-expiry alert built in, not a manual capture step.
2. Mistral console credits leg (openchamber#1630): /api/billing/credits is cookie-only (both API keys 401). If the usage producer lands on that leg, it needs the same CDP re-capture pattern as the OpenDesign keeper. The plan leg (whoami / account-context) is key-authed and needs no browser.
3. OpenDesign browser re-arm: the laptop Helium profile currently holds NO Open Design session (verified 2026-11-05 — the profile cookie DB has no open-design rows; the Oct 29 import's session lived in a profile state that did not survive). The keeper's capture leg therefore cannot renew from the browser until someone signs into Open Design in that profile once (Google SSO click-through — proven agent-doable 2026-10-29, no Drew-only step hit then). Until re-armed, renewal-by-use (sliding session, ~7d horizon, checked every 15-min tick) is the live mechanism and the keeper alerts with days of lead if it degrades.
4. Claude Code leaf credential: ~/.claude/.credentials.json holds an OAuth pair whose refreshTokenExpiresAt is 2026-11-09T06:27Z. Renewal is the CLI's built-in refresh — automatic when the CLI runs — but the claude-code provider is disabled in config, so nothing runs it; if the refresh token lapses, re-login is Drew-only (interactive OAuth). Surface before 2026-11-09 if the provider is to be re-enabled. Side observation: the gatherer's recorded credentialExpiresAt for claude (2026-11-05T14:31:57Z) reads +8h against the file's expiresAt (06:31:57Z, same minutes/seconds/ms) — check the lib's normalizeTimestamp for an offset bug before relying on it for alert lead times.
5. ClinePass native adapter (dormant — CLINEPASS_CREDENTIAL_REF unset on the laptop gatherer unit): its dashboard token is session-class by design (401/403 = session-expired + needsRelogin in src/clinepass-adapter.ts). Do not enable it without a renewal story. The live module read uses the ClinePass API key and is unaffected.
6. Alert surfacing: the OpenDesign keeper's alert today is its state file + the gatherer journal. Surface renewal alerts (opendesign-renewal.json status=attention, and equivalents as other providers gain keepers) on the aggregator board / morning readout so a failing renewal is seen without reading state files.

Full inventory: provider-quota-registry.md (auth inventory section, 2026-11-05) and ~/memory/topics/provider-auth-renewal-2026-11-05.md.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Meta portal fetcher (#6079) ships with CDP cookie re-capture + pre-expiry alert built in — no manual capture step.
- [ ] The Mistral console credits leg (openchamber#1630), if used, has the same CDP re-capture pattern; the key-authed plan leg needs no browser path.
- [ ] The OpenDesign browser re-arm gap is closed: the laptop Helium profile holds a live Open Design session the keeper can slide/renew, or the keeper's alert fires before hard expiry.
- [ ] Every browser-dependent provider auth in the fleet has (a) an auto-renewing long-lived token or (b) built-in cookie auto-renewal with a pre-expiry alert — an inventory on this issue proves none is left on manual re-import.

Parent: [#6018](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/6018) (Atlas ingestion program tracker). Research source: prior-art doc `~/workspace/scratch/atlas-ingestion-brief-2026-11-04/prior-art-research.md` (2026-11-04). Follow-up 16 (Cluster 3). Implementation home: the provenance registry #3125; audit consumer: #6029.

## Finding (research, in substance)

The brief's marks — `repo@hash:path` and "OpenCode DB @ AMD laptop on this day" — are **composite marks**, and proven grammars exist to steal: git blob/commit SHAs (content identity + tree state), Go module pseudo-versions (`v0.0.0-20261104120000-abcdef123456` — compact time+commit at ecosystem scale), OCI digests (`name@sha256:…` — the `locator@digest` shape). For non-git sources the mark needs the tuple `(system, host, locator, captured-at, content-hash)` — Drew's prose mark is that tuple; the work is making it **one parseable grammar with one formatter**, so the existing-embed audit (#6029) is a parse-and-validate job, not a regex safari.

## Scope

- Grammar covering: `repo@commit:path`, `system@host@date` (session stores, DBs), `chat@session@timestamp`, plus the general fallback form.
- The content hash rides *in* the mark (a `repo@commit:path` mark must stay resolvable even if the repo is later lost).
- Validation rules the audit can execute mechanically: parseable? fields in range? hash verifies against stored content?

## Done looks like

A grammar spec (EBNF or equivalent) + formatter/parser contract + the validation rule list #6029 consumes.

Parent: [#6028](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/6028) (delta-only ingestion + offset embeds). Research source: prior-art doc `~/workspace/scratch/atlas-ingestion-brief-2026-11-04/prior-art-research.md` (2026-11-04). Follow-up 1 (Cluster 1).

## Finding (research, in substance)

The offset-embed model makes a file version an **ordered list of span references** `(embed_id, start, end)` — the restic/borg content-addressed span-list shape applied to embeddings. A new version then costs only its genuinely new spans plus a manifest row. The span's stored text *is* what was embedded, and spans are reused only when the text is byte-identical (embeddings are not hashes: the same paragraph embedded with different neighbors is a different vector).

## Scope

- The span table: `(file_version_id, start, end)` + the span's own embedded-text snapshot + vector + provenance link.
- How spans and today's chunk store (~107,639 chunks) coexist during migration: dual-read, backfill, or cutover — and what happens to chunk IDs that existing traces/feedback reference.
- Span context metadata (heading path / section) versions with the *reference*, not the span (a reused span under a new "Deprecated:" heading must not inherit stale context).

## Done looks like

A schema design: tables, keys, migration path from the chunk store, and the invariants (byte-identical reuse only; context versioned per reference).

body:
Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Wave-2 follow-up from the prior-art research (Lane B item 45); parent topic issue: [#5989](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5989). Research source: `workspace/scratch/worlds-capabilities-brief-2026-11-04/prior-art-research.md`.

## State of the art (2025)

Goblins (Guile + Racket; Hoot compiles to WebAssembly) models objects in **vats** processing transactional **turns**, with promise pipelining and distributed GC; *The Heart of Spritely* (May 2025) is the canonical design doc (https://spritely.institute/static/papers/spritely-core.pdf). **OCapN** is the cross-implementation protocol suite: **CapTP** for capability-preserving remote invocation over pluggable netlayers, references as unforgeable sturdyrefs (`ocapn://…`). **Caveat in Spritely's own docs: CapTP support "is still in its early days — do not rely on the protocol being stable"** (https://files.spritely.institute/docs/guile-goblins/0.13.0/OCapN.html).

## Position for id (from the research)

**Dead end for now:** adopting OCapN as id's wire protocol in v1. Adopt the *discipline* (no ambient authority; authority travels by reference passing) — which Roc already enforces one level down by platform exclusivity and explicit context passing — design handle semantics to be OCapN-*compatible*, and revisit when CapTP stabilizes.

## Work

- Watch: re-check CapTP/OCapN stability status on a cadence; record dated state changes here.
- Spike (when the watch says it's worth it): a minimal CapTP interop test between a Goblins vat and an id-side stub — feasibility evidence before any v2 commitment.

## Done looks like

A dated watch log plus, when triggered, a spike report with a go/no-go for bridge work.

Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Statements S75–S76 of the 2026-11-04 brief.

## Requirement (Drew, in substance)

- Worlds could **build their own rules**, **pre-approve specific designs**, and build **content moderation, approval, or report capabilities**.
- The best ones could end up as **libraries, which could be reused by different worlds** — and then it would be standard because it's **literally the same thing** from a different world, but maybe with a **different set of moderators or reviewers or approvers**, or a **different threshold for reports to have automatic quarantine**.

So moderation is not a platform feature bolted on top: it is **world code**, subject to the same library model as everything else in this program — typed, attachable, importable, parameterized per world.

## Design points to settle

- The moderation-library interface: what hooks exist (submission approval, report intake, quarantine action, appeal), and which are world-provided vs platform-provided. A moderation library receives capabilities like any other code — which means its powers are exactly the platform surface passed to it (programming-model child of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955)); say which capability set a moderation library legitimately needs (read content? hide content? ban principals?) and how that interacts with writer-set authority ([#5545](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5545)).
- Parameterization: moderator/reviewer sets and report thresholds are **per-world configuration** of the same library — config, not forks. KDL profile ([#5753](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5753)).
- Pre-approval of designs: what is a "design" here (a world object submission? a library? a user function?) and what does approval bind (content hash, capability set)?
- Relation to the boards moderation line: [#5680](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5680) and its hooks split [#5861](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5861) are board-surface designs; this issue is the world-level generalization. Cross-pollinate, don't duplicate.

## Related

- Boards next steps / moderation hooks: [#5680](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5680), [#5861](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5861)
- Sharing & permissions cluster (knowledge layer): [#5840](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5840)
- Library typing child of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955) (a moderation system is a library with an attachment and a capability footprint)

## Done looks like

A design doc: moderation-as-library interface, per-world parameterization model, pre-approval semantics, and the capability/authority set a moderation library runs with.

body:
## Problem

The worktree-reaper can treat a process-scan failure as proof that a worktree is unoccupied, then pass its final removal gate. In infra/worktree-reaper/bin/worktree_reaper.py, the /proc scan helper around lines 377–394 returns an empty process list when os.listdir("/proc") fails; tree_occupied around lines 397–403 interprets that empty list as unoccupied. The fresh pre-removal check around lines 479–487 therefore fails open on an inspection error.

This is distinct from the recent run-log collision fix in #5716/#5718. The reaper is destructive, so “could not determine” must not mean “safe to delete.”

## Required behavior

Represent process-scan failure distinctly from a successful scan with zero matching processes. If occupancy cannot be established, retain the candidate and emit a clear warning/error; do not call git worktree remove, remove the branch, or delete the path.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Inject an os.listdir("/proc") failure and assert the candidate is treated as occupied/unknown and retained.
- [ ] The failure-path test asserts git worktree remove and branch deletion are not called.
- [ ] Preserve the existing behavior for a successful empty scan and for a confirmed matching process.
- [ ] The test is discovered by the documented CI/test command for infra/worktree-reaper/tests/test_worktree_reaper.py.

body:
Follow-up from Phase 4 audit issue #5048 (epic #5047); intentionally not changed in the audit PR.\n\nIn `HostedBindingService::cancel_rebind`, the request is marked `Cancelled` before the binding lookup and re-attestation. If either later operation returns `NoBinding` or `RecordEncoding`, the method returns an error after changing the request, while the binding can remain `RebindPending`; this contradicts the no-mutation-on-failure contract in the `RebindError` docs.\n\nPrepare and validate the restored binding (including its attestation) before committing either state mutation, then add a regression test using inconsistent internal fixture state or an injectable failure.

## Acceptance criteria
- `cancel_rebind` prepares and validates the restored binding (including its attestation) before committing any state mutation.
- On `NoBinding` / `RecordEncoding` failure paths, neither the request state nor the binding state is mutated (the documented no-mutation-on-failure contract holds).
- A regression test using inconsistent internal fixture state or an injectable failure proves the atomicity, and existing hosted-binding tests still pass.

title: flake: root opencode input re-resolves on fresh eval — committed flake.lock is not evaluable as-is

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: epic/opencode-platform
labels.description: Reprioritization program epic (2026-11-12)

body:
## Symptom

Evaluating the flake from a clean checkout of main (329b23bb2) requires a lock file change. A faithful build is impossible:

```
nix build --no-update-lock-file .#nixosConfigurations.amd.config.system.build.toplevel
error: flake 'git+file:///.../tree' requires lock file changes but they're not allowed due to '--no-update-lock-file'
```

## Evidence (2026-11-04, #5477/#5449 switch round)

A plain eval rewrites exactly ONE lock node — the root `opencode` input:

- committed: owner `developing-today-forks`, rev `4175c630bf8314c6934a8b581648b86999bb8a8a`, narHash `sha256-FTesfhNqsK8cRQO+GZP7pmAMBXp2GZ3PT6UmWyDGM58=`
- re-resolved: owner `developing-today`, rev `c1dea598daa5429c8025b90db2d5c8e6751de73a`, narHash `sha256-wyGc+CihesnbHIv8qiK9pMo7Yolz5dKSm/FmE/vRWK4=`

No other node changes. The pinned server input `opencode_2` stays at `ae5d592093e8d9e190a2101ad82d2e1ffc64bc44` and is unaffected. A grep of the tree's flake.nix files shows no literal `developing-today/opencode` URL, so the stale declaration is indirect (an override/follows or a nested flake's input) — residue of the developing-today → developing-today-forks org transfer repoints.

## Impact

- The committed lock cannot be evaluated as-is; any cold-cache evaluation (including `nixos-rebuild switch`) silently substitutes the root `opencode` input with the old org's current HEAD.
- In a live/dirty worktree the mid-eval lock rewrite races the flake source copy and kills the build: `store path ('/nix/store/...-source') was hashed to avoid a full copy at first, but upon reading it again, the contents have changed` (observed 2026-11-04 in the switch-round pre-build).

## Suggested fix

Align the root `opencode` input declaration and the lock on one owner + explicit rev (presumably `developing-today-forks`), so a fresh eval leaves `flake.lock` byte-identical and `--no-update-lock-file` builds succeed.

body:
## Observed

The Nov 4, 2026 claimant fire (14:33Z) re-discovered three tasks as launch candidates, created a session for each, and had `bind` reject all three because the lane ledger still held an older binding:

- task 4924 — already bound to `ses_e5e59622aafffeKleYpA1NrmWc`
- task 6719 — already bound to `ses_e5e5961e557ffe77gDqN8yhAC8`
- task 6774 — already bound to `ses_e5e595f0ef9ffe3LOpHRLqutug`

All three sessions are absent from `GET /api/session`. Each task's `progress.session_id` is null and carries a `progress.session_cleared` record written by `fail_repo_task` / `park_task` on 2026-11-04 around 13:00Z. The previous fire hit the same three conflicts.

## Defect

`poll.py`'s candidate filter checks only `progress.session_id`. The bind guard checks the lane ledger (`bind_repo_task_lane_session`). When a terminal verb clears progress but leaves the ledger binding, the task is permanently re-offered: every fire creates a session, then deletes it on the bind conflict.

## Impact

- One wasted session create/delete per affected task per fire.
- Candidate counts and cap accounting stay noisy.
- The true state (ledger-bound, session gone, progress unbound) matches neither the claimant's launch path nor its recovery rule, because recovery is keyed on `progress.session_id`.

## Fix direction

Reconcile the two stores when a terminal verb clears a session, and make `poll.py` treat an existing lane-ledger binding as bound (or surface it as a distinct stale-binding row). Ensure the fix also clears ledger bindings for the affected legacy rows.

Related: #5001 (requeue/lease expiry binding clear), #5400 (guarded recovery branch missing live).

## Verified 2026-11-04 ~12:16Z (during nix queue task 9426, PR dezren39/nix#1461)

From a laptop fleet worktree (`~/git/fleet/9426-1460-integrity-sigpipe`), `git push` to the HTTPS remote fails:

- `git push`: `(ssh-askpass) cannot open display` / `fatal: could not read Username for 'https://github.com'`
- `gh auth status` on the laptop: `Failed to log in to github.com account dezren39 (default) - The token in default is invalid.`
- `ssh -T git@github.com` (BatchMode): `Permission denied (publickey)` — the laptop's `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` is not a registered GitHub key.

The sandbox's `gh` login is healthy (verified same hour), so this is laptop-local credential rot, not an account problem.

## Impact

Fleet policy puts all worktrees/builds on the laptop, but a laptop worktree currently cannot push its branch or open PRs from the laptop. Workaround used for task 9426 (kept the work moving, but it is a detour every shift will now hit): commit on the laptop, `git bundle` the branch, fetch the bundle into the sandbox clone, verify the SHA, push from the sandbox.

## Fix / acceptance

- [ ] A push credential works on the laptop again: either `gh auth login` refreshed on the laptop (device flow, needs Drew at the laptop or its browser) followed by `gh auth setup-git`, or the laptop SSH key registered on the GitHub account and remotes switched to SSH.
- [ ] Proof: `git push` of a scratch branch from a laptop fleet worktree succeeds, and `gh auth status` on the laptop is green.

Found by lane nix-a (repo-queue-worker-shift-nix) while landing dezren39/nix#1461 for dezren39/nix#1460.

body:
## Bug: atlas-core topics/projects filters are unescaped SQL `LIKE` patterns — `%`/`_` in a filter value act as wildcards and a `"` crosses JSON element boundaries

`pkgs/atlas-search/crates/atlas-core/src/filters.rs` builds the topics/projects
filter (the values stored in `l.topics` / `l.projects` are JSON list text such as
`["nixos","backup"]`) as a raw `LIKE` pattern with the user-supplied value
interpolated verbatim:

- `Filters::where_clause` (filters.rs:177-182):
  `clauses.push(format!("{col} LIKE ?"))` with param `format!("%\"{v}\"%")`
  for `l.topics` and `l.projects`.
- `Filters::session_clauses` (filters.rs:213-218): the identical construction
  for the Turso vector branch's session subquery.

There is no escaping and no `ESCAPE` clause anywhere in atlas-core. SQL `LIKE`
treats `%` as "any run of characters" and `_` as "any single character", so a
filter value is a pattern, not a literal topic/project name:

### Verified (laptop, origin/main a65000aeabf)

1. Rust probe through `atlas-core` itself (temporary test in a scan worktree at
   a65000aeabf, `cargo test -p atlas-core --test probe_like`): `Filters::new`
   with topics `["my_topic", "100%", "a\",\"b"]` and projects `["%"]` emits
   `l.topics LIKE ?` / `l.projects LIKE ?` clauses whose params are the raw
   interpolations `%"my_topic"%`, `%"100%"%`, `%"a","b"%`, `%"%"%` in both
   `where_clause` and `session_clauses`.
2. SQLite probe of exactly that pattern against JSON-list rows:
   - filter `my_topic` matches `["my-topic","other"]` and `["myXtopic"]`
     (the `_` wildcard) — neither row has a topic named `my_topic`;
   - filter `%` matches every non-empty topics list
     (`["my-topic","other"]`, `["myXtopic"]`, `["a","b"]`, `["100 days"]`) —
     the filter silently becomes a no-op;
   - filter `a","b` matches `["a","b"]` — the embedded `"` crosses the JSON
     element boundary, so two distinct topics satisfy a filter for one
     (nonexistent) topic;
   - filter `100%` matches `["100 days"]`;
   - control filter `my-topic` matches only `["my-topic","other"]`, as intended.

### Why it matters

Filter-before-rank with exact classification filters is a headline contract of
atlas-core (filters.rs module doc; step-2 PR #5352). A topic or project whose
name legitimately contains `_` (common: `my_topic`, `pm_stack`) over-matches
unrelated sessions, and a `%` value disables the filter entirely — wrong
results are returned as if the filter had been applied, with no error or note.
Because both branch constructions share the flaw, FTS and vector results are
affected identically, so fusion cannot mask it. The step-3 CLI (#5353) will
surface these filters directly to users.

Note on parity: the construction is inherited from the production Python's
`Filters` (the port mirrors its SQL byte-for-byte and the parity fixtures pin
it). This is a deliberate-deviation candidate: the fix changes the recorded
SQL/params for values containing `%`, `_`, `\`, or `"`, so the parity fixtures
should gain these cases as documented deviations rather than silently
diverging — the Python side carries the same bug and should get the same fix
or an explicit waiver.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A topics/projects filter value matches only a JSON element exactly equal
      to it: `%`, `_`, and `\` in the value are treated as literal characters
      (e.g. escaped with an explicit `ESCAPE` clause), and a value containing
      `"` cannot match across element boundaries.
- [ ] Both construction sites are fixed consistently: `where_clause`
      (filters.rs, FTS/local) and `session_clauses` (filters.rs, Turso vector
      branch subquery).
- [ ] New tests pin at least: filter `my_topic` does not match `my-topic` or
      `myXtopic` rows but does match a `my_topic` row; filter `%` matches only
      a literal `%` element (not every list); filter `a","b` does not match
      `["a","b"]`; ordinary values (`nixos`) behave exactly as before.
- [ ] The parity fixtures / step-6 Gate B (#5356) record the changed params
      for wildcard-bearing values as an intentional deviation from the Python,
      or the Python construction is fixed in step with a note on this issue.
- [ ] Existing atlas-core unit + parity tests pass (`cargo test -p atlas-core`),
      excepting fixture expectations updated per the previous criterion.

body:
Parent: #1929 (Approach C — prompt hooks with declared effects).

## Scope

Add the first safe prompt-action slice to the existing `on: script` exec hook list. A hook may be either the already-supported deterministic script action or a prompt action with declared `effect: advise` (default `advise`). Resolve through the configured `internal/model.Provider` layer (provider-keyed configuration/profiles are already on main); keep the current no-provider behavior deterministic: emit a warning/advice-unavailable hook frame and continue the script unchanged.

Prompt context/template values follow `docs/decisions/0001-hook-vocabulary.md`: user placeholders and built-ins such as `@result`, `@error`, `@diagnostic`, `@calls`, `@artifacts`, and `@source` are JSON-encoded/delimited as data, never raw text substitution. Keep the hook frame before the final result/error frame, report action/effect/model/duration, and attach advice without changing the run outcome. Preserve existing deterministic hooks and config-before-per-call declaration order.

## Acceptance

- Prompt and script actions share the current script-hook list; invalid/unsupported action/effect combinations fail validation rather than silently doing nothing.
- `advise` prompt output is surfaced in the hook frame and does not transform the result or error.
- Configured model and per-hook model selection use the provider layer; unavailable/provider-error paths warn and continue the deterministic run.
- Regression tests cover success/error phases, built-in and user placeholder data delimiting, advice frame placement, provider unavailable/error fallback, and unchanged script hooks.
- Targeted Go tests pass; CI review confirms the change against current main.

## Explicitly deferred

Effects `ask`, `propose`, `apply`, and `run` (including elicitation, replacing outcomes, or executing generated code); prompt actions on non-script hook points; any opencode plugin-provider backend work. Those remain with #1929 / their owning work.

## Design references

`pkgs/mcpx/docs/decisions/0001-hook-vocabulary.md` (accepted action/phase/template/frame contract) and `0002-autonomy-dial.md` (accepted effect/autonomy vocabulary and ceilings). The provider layer and provider profiles are merged in #2592/#4836; `sampling.answerLocally` is merged in #4947. The deterministic hook foundation is PR #2616.

body:
## Problem

`Petnames::open` (pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/petname.rs:59) replays `petnames.jsonl` through `apply` (petname.rs:196-209), which inserts each `Record::Set` name verbatim. The write path, `Petnames::set` (petname.rs:128-163), refuses:

- names that fail `normalize_name` — empty, longer than 64 chars, or containing control/format (Cf) characters (petname.rs:262-278);
- a name whose `fold` equals another contact's petname for the same owner (Conflict);
- a name whose UTS #39 `skeleton` matches another contact's petname or a directory-alleged account name (the anti-mimicry guard the module doc states as its purpose: "the store refuses a petname that could be taken for someone else's name").

None of those invariants are re-checked at load. A journal written by an older build, a hand edit, a partial restore, or another writer therefore loads state the store itself would never create: two contacts of one owner holding fold-equal petnames (`PayPal` / `paypal`), a petname carrying U+200B, or an 80-char name — and the display/labels path consumes them as if they had passed the guards.

## Evidence (verified this run, origin/main a51be0e22)

Probe test on the laptop (worktree of origin/main, `cargo test -p id-core --test probe_petname_load`): a hand-written journal with four `set` records — fold-duplicate names for two accounts, a name containing U+200B, and an 80-char name — loads with all four records present verbatim; `Petnames::open` returns Ok.

This is the same shape as #5179 / PR #5190, where `Registry::load` for publications was fixed to validate persisted records against `publish()` invariants at load. The petname store was not covered by that fix. Related audits: #2898 Phase 3 and #4001 both name "directory/petname persistence restores" in their closing-inventory scope — this issue is the concrete, reproduced instance for the petname store and can serve as that inventory's named follow-up for this seam.

Note the deliberate legacy tolerance in the comparison paths (`fold`/`skeleton` strip Cf "so a name stored with one (before they were refused) cannot spoof by the comparison path", petname.rs:236-243): the fix must disposition legacy stored names explicitly — fail-loud like the publications registry, quarantine-with-warning, or normalise — rather than silently breaking existing journals.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Petnames::open` dispositions every replayed `Set` record against the `set()` invariants (normalisability, per-owner fold uniqueness, per-owner skeleton uniqueness), with the chosen behaviour for violations (error naming the line / skip-with-warning / normalise) stated in the module doc.
- [ ] The alleged-name skeleton check that needs directory state is either applied where the directory is available at open time or explicitly documented as a load-time exemption with the reason.
- [ ] Tests: journal with fold-duplicate names, a Cf-carrying name, and an overlong name each produce the documented disposition; a journal written by current `set()` calls reopens unchanged.
- [ ] Existing petname tests stay green (laptop or CI).

🤖 Filed by new-issue-creator-code-a (lane A), 2026-11-03.

body:
# pm-stack(aggregator): isAuditEvent accepts impossible/non-ISO ingestedAt — the v2 audit load gate Date.parse-checks the one stamp validateStreamEvent's isIsoDate rule skips

## Evidence

`pm-stack/aggregator/src/events.ts` at origin/main `3adad8fc9`:

- `validateStreamEvent` (events.ts:142) gates the event time `at` with the shared `isIsoDate` primitive (validate.ts:116) — the #5154 fix, with the comment at :145 explaining that `Date.parse` rolls day-overflow dates over (2026-02-30 parses as March 2).
- The v2 load gate `isAuditEvent` (events.ts:303-311) re-checks the record's second timestamp far more loosely: `typeof v.ingestedAt === "string" && Number.isFinite(Date.parse(v.ingestedAt))`. `Date.parse` accepts impossible calendar days and non-ISO spellings, so `2026-11-31…` and `November 2, 2026` both pass.
- `isAuditEvent` is the shape gate `EventsStore.doLoad` applies to every v2 row (events.ts:438-455): a row that fails it in a v2 file is treated as a damaged audit record and the whole file is quarantined. A row with a bad `at` triggers exactly that; a row with a bad `ingestedAt` sails through.
- `ingestedAt` is not decorative: it is part of the hash-covered canonical form (`canonicalFields`, events.ts:228), so a rolled/non-ISO ingest stamp becomes a permanent, chain-verified part of the audit record and is rendered as the record's ingest time. The store's own writers always set it from `new Date().toISOString()` (events.ts:696), and v1 migration sets it from the already-gated `at` (events.ts:293) — only the load gate lets a foreign spelling in.

## Verified (laptop probe, this run)

Probe at origin/main `3adad8fc9` (laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-03-laneB-ingested/probe.ts`, importing the real `events.ts`): each trial writes a one-row v2 events file whose `hash` is the genuine `eventHash(EVENT_CHAIN_GENESIS, row)`, then loads it with `EventsStore`:

```
control loaded: 1 ingestedAt: 2026-11-02T00:00:01.000Z      ← valid ISO control loads
feb30   loaded: 1 ingestedAt: 2026-11-31T00:00:00.000Z      ← impossible day (rolls to Dec 1) loads, kept verbatim, chain verifies
noniso  loaded: 1 ingestedAt: November 2, 2026              ← non-ISO spelling loads, kept verbatim
bad-at  loaded: 0                                           ← same impossible day in `at`: file quarantined as damaged (the #5154 gate working)
```

## Why it matters

The events store is the audit trail: its load path was hardened (#3322/#5137, #5154) so that a damaged or hand-edited record is caught at the shape gate instead of being silently absorbed — an empty-hash v2 row throws, a v1-shaped row in a v2 file throws, and an impossible `at` quarantines the file. `ingestedAt` is the one timestamp that escaped that hardening. A record whose ingest stamp names a day that never existed (or a locale spelling that parses differently per timezone) loads as a healthy audit record, is covered by the hash chain as-is, and misstates when the record entered the audit trail — the exact silent-absorption failure the neighboring gates exist to prevent.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `isAuditEvent` gates `ingestedAt` with `isIsoDate` (validate.ts:116), matching the `at` gate in `validateStreamEvent`: `2026-11-31…`, `2026-02-30…`, and `November 2, 2026` no longer count as valid v2 audit records (in a v2 file the row is treated as damaged, like a bad `at` today).
- [ ] Genuine ISO ingest stamps — including fractional seconds and offset spellings `isIsoDate` accepts — still load, and v1 migration (which derives `ingestedAt` from the gated `at`) is unaffected.
- [ ] Aggregator tests cover the refused impossible/non-ISO `ingestedAt` cases and a valid control through the store load path; existing events tests still pass.

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-b (Lane B), verified this run at origin/main `3adad8fc9`. Dedup: issue searches for `ingestedAt` and `isAuditEvent` (open and closed) return nothing; #5073/#5154 cover `at` in `validateStreamEvent` only, not the v2 load gate's `ingestedAt` check.

body:
# pm-stack(aggregator): isProjectPoolItem accepts impossible/non-ISO updatedAt — pool items carry rolled dates into momentum and board-recency math

## Evidence

`pm-stack/aggregator/src/projects.ts` at origin/main `9380bf6d7`:

- `isProjectPoolItem` (line 272) gates the pool item's only timestamp with a bare type check: `(p.updatedAt === undefined || typeof p.updatedAt === "string")`. Any string passes — impossible calendar dates, non-ISO spellings, and outright garbage. This predicate is the whole feed-side gate: `projectPoolSectionProblem` in `feed.ts` delegates per-item validation to it, and the collector parses against it too.
- `poolItemToGhItem` (projects.ts:282) copies the stamp through verbatim: `updatedAt: p.updatedAt ?? ""`.
- Consumers do arithmetic on it with `Date.parse`, which rolls impossible days forward and parses non-ISO spellings timezone-dependently:
  - `derive.ts:815` — the weekly "accomplished" list for project momentum is `(state === "merged" || "closed") && Date.parse(i.updatedAt) >= weekAgo`;
  - `derive.ts:820` — `recent = Date.parse(i.updatedAt) >= twoDaysAgo` feeds the momentum state itself (`moving` vs `stalled`, derive.ts:824);
  - `derive.ts:786` — board ordering sorts on the raw string (`localeCompare`), so non-ISO spellings also misorder.
- Sibling gates in the same codebase refuse exactly these stamps: the tier-item delegation parser ISO-gates its `updatedAt` (`tier-items.ts:179`, via the local `isIso`), `isSessionRecord` ISO-gates `lastSeenAt`/`startedAt` (registry.ts, #5078), and `isSubscriptionRow` ISO-gates `renewsAt` with `isIsoDate` (feed.ts, validate.ts:116). The pool item is the remaining typeof-only stamp.

## Verified (laptop probe, this run)

Probe at origin/main `9380bf6d7` (laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-03-laneB2-poolupd/probe.ts`, importing the real `projects.ts`; `now` fixed at 2026-03-01T00:00:00Z for the momentum predicate):

```
{"updatedAt":"2026-02-30T00:00:00Z","gate":true,"parsed":1772409600000,"countsAsThisWeek":true}   ← rolls to Mar 2 — a future day that never existed counts as this week's activity
{"updatedAt":"2026-04-31T00:00:00Z","gate":true,"parsed":1777593600000,"countsAsThisWeek":true}   ← rolls to May 1
{"updatedAt":"March 2, 2026","gate":true,"parsed":1772431200000,"countsAsThisWeek":true}          ← non-ISO, parsed timezone-dependently
{"updatedAt":"not-a-date","gate":true,"parsed":null,"countsAsThisWeek":false}                     ← garbage passes the gate (only the downstream NaN comparison happens to exclude it)
{"updatedAt":"2026-02-25T00:00:00Z","gate":true,"parsed":1771977600000,"countsAsThisWeek":true}   ← valid control
```

## Why it matters

Project momentum is a headline dashboard signal: it decides whether a project reads as "moving" or "stalled" and which merged/closed items are listed as this week's accomplishments. One pool item carrying an impossible stamp (a collector glitch, a hand-edited feed, a future producer that formats dates loosely) silently fabricates recent activity — Feb 30 becomes Mar 2, Apr 31 becomes May 1 — and a project with no real activity in weeks can read as moving. Every other timestamp the feed gate owns has already been moved to the `isIsoDate` rule for this exact failure class; this one was missed.

One nuance the fix must preserve: the collector itself emits `updatedAt: c.updatedAt ?? ""` (projects.ts:163), so a missing GraphQL stamp arrives as `""`. Items must not start dropping solely for a missing stamp — treat `""` as absent (or have the collector omit the field) rather than requiring a date on every item.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `isProjectPoolItem` refuses a present, non-empty `updatedAt` that is not a real ISO calendar date (`isIsoDate`, validate.ts:116): `2026-02-30…`, `2026-04-31…`, `March 2, 2026`, and `not-a-date` all fail the gate and the item drops individually, as with the other feed gates.
- [ ] A pool item with `updatedAt` absent — including the collector's current `""` spelling for a missing GraphQL stamp — still passes, so no legitimate item is dropped for lacking a stamp.
- [ ] Tests in the aggregator suite cover the refused cases, the `""`/absent case, and a valid ISO control; existing projects/feed/derive tests still pass.
- [ ] Existing aggregator tests still pass.

Filed by new-issue-creator-code-b (Lane B), verified this run at origin/main `9380bf6d7`. Dedup: searches for `isProjectPoolItem`, "pool item updatedAt", and "ProjectPoolItem date" surface only the closed number/labels/truncation filings (#3514, #2418, #2453, #2459) — none covers the `updatedAt` stamp.

body:
Filed by queue triage task 6875 (2026-11-03) from the design record on main, `doc/2026-11-01_design_id2031.md` §2, which names this as "a prerequisite missing from #3788–#3790's current dependency graph" — it has no issue of its own, so the gap is invisible to the fleet.

## The gap (per the design record, verified against main 2026-11-03)

- `ChainExt` carries a free-string `kind` and optional group (`pkgs/id/src/chain.rs`, root `id` package), and the signed header commits to a body's hash and size while the body itself is separate.
- Ingest accepts and verifies a supplied body (`pkgs/id/src/event_store/ingest.rs`), but `store_event` writes `event.bytes` (the signed header) only (`pkgs/id/src/event_store/mod.rs`); range sync sends stored events and fork-proof headers (`pkgs/id/src/event_store/sync.rs`).
- Consequence: a `didit.*` CBOR body can be validated at ingest but is not yet available for later retrieval or cross-device replication.

## Scope

Design + implement generic application event-body persistence, retrieval, and range-sync in `pkgs/id` (not didit-specific), so any `kind` with a CBOR body — starting with the four `didit.*` kinds from issue #3788 — round-trips: stored at ingest, retrievable by event id/hash, and carried by range sync with the same integrity checks as headers.

## Acceptance

- A stored event with a generic body can be retrieved byte-identically after restart.
- Range sync between two nodes transfers bodies for events the peer lacks, with hash/size verification against the signed header.
- Existing header-only kinds are unaffected; tests cover body-present and body-absent events.

## Relations

- Blocks the app phase: issue #3790 (Phase 3 of #2031) cannot read tracker state back without this.
- Does NOT block issue #3788 (Phase 1: library-only schema types + pure evaluator, golden tests only).
- Parent: issue #2031.

## Acceptance criteria

- Generic event-body persistence exists for `pkgs/id`: bodies can be stored, retrieved by event id, and range-synced without per-type bespoke code.
- Retrieval of a missing body returns a typed not-found (not a panic or silent empty).
- Range-sync is idempotent: re-syncing a range does not duplicate bodies.
- Covered by tests exercising persistence, retrieval, and a repeated range-sync.

body:
## Finding (from PR review)

Codex (chatgpt-codex-connector[bot]) raised a P2 on PR #4384 — "Synchronize the completion waiter with program startup":

> If this goroutine runs before Wish starts the program, `p.Wait()` blocks forever: in the pinned Bubble Tea v0.25.0 implementation, `finished` is initialized by `Run`, not `NewProgram`, and `Wait` receives directly from that channel. The Wish middleware calls this handler before `p.Run()`, so there is no initialization ordering guarantee. An early waiter receives from a nil channel permanently, leaking the new goroutine and preventing that session from ever being deregistered; concurrent initialization also introduces a data race. Tie removal to a lifecycle hook with guaranteed startup ordering or to the return of `Run`.

## Evidence

- Source PR: #4384 (https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/4384), merged 2026-11-02T14:12:01Z
- Review comment: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/4384#discussion_r4443380736 — chatgpt-codex-connector[bot], 2026-11-02T14:11:05Z, on `pkgs/chat/main.go:126`

1. **Contract statement landed**: the contract from #4502 (a gossip claim is stored only in the form its table's guards produce — canonical, scoped, and bounded — and every ingest path enters through those guards) is written into the `chat_presence.rs` module doc as an admission section, with a cross-reference at `PeerDiscovery::update`'s doc in `crates/id-core/src/discovery.rs`, where the next ingest path will look.
2. **Ingest inventory**: every frame-decode / claim-ingest site in `pkgs/id` (production code; test code excluded) is dispositioned against the contract — through its table / fixed in this audit if a single-site slip / filed as a named follow-up. The inventory is recorded on #4502 or in the module doc beside the contract statement. The grep surface includes at least: `decode_frame` (presence), `SignedPeerAnnouncement::decode_frame`, `PresenceTable::update` / `update_scoped` / `update_at` callers, and `PeerDiscovery::update` callers.
3. **Required dispositions** (each recorded on #4502 with its reason):
   - **`PresenceTable::update`** (the explicitly unscoped admission entry): per #4502 decision 5, it remains public only if a production caller that legitimately needs the transport view is named; otherwise it is removed or made crate-private in this audit.
   - **The RPC paths merged in `cmd_peers`** (`crawl_peers`, `query_remote_peers`, `query_local_peers`): RPC answers are a different trust surface from gossip — disposition each as deliberately-unguarded or guarded, naming the reason, including whether the merge order in `cmd_peers` is safe once Phase 4 (#4377) has landed.
   - **Any `decode_frame` caller outside `serve` / `peers`** the inventory grep finds: through-the-table or a named exception with its reason.
   - **The gossip frame-size bound above the table**: #3991 demonstrated a ~3.3 MB signed presence frame; after Phase 1 bounds the *stored* form, state which layer owns the *frame* bound (iroh-gossip's message limits vs a `decode_frame`-level refusal) and file a follow-up if neither layer bounds it.
4. **Closing evidence on #4502**: all five origins (#4404, #3991, #4004, #4363, #4377) closed or verified already-fixed, the contract statement landed, and the inventory complete.

## Acceptance criteria

- The contract statement is present in the `chat_presence.rs` module doc and cross-referenced from `PeerDiscovery::update`'s doc, and matches #4502's five decisions.
- The ingest inventory covers every production frame-decode / claim-ingest site in `pkgs/id`, each with a disposition and a reason or a follow-up link.
- All four required dispositions are recorded on #4502.
- No behaviour change beyond the `PresenceTable::update` disposition (removal / crate-private) and a single-site slip fix; anything larger is filed as a named follow-up, not fixed inside the audit.

title: id(chat-presence): PresenceTable has no node-count bound — every distinct self-signed key is stored for a full TTL, so minted keys grow serve's memory without limit

body:
## Summary

`pkgs/id` chat presence bounds a heartbeat's *contents* (channels cap, TTL) but never the *number of nodes* the table will hold. `PresenceTable` is a `HashMap<AuthorKey, Entry>` with no capacity limit, and the production receiver in `serve` inserts an entry for every signature-valid heartbeat it hears on the public gossip topic. A signature proves only that the sender holds the key the heartbeat names — keys are free to mint — so any peer can grow a receiver's table by one entry per minted key, and every fresh entry is guaranteed retention for a full `PRESENCE_TTL_SECS` (75 s), or ~150 s for a heartbeat stamped at the future edge of the freshness window. The periodic prune removes only entries older than the TTL, so re-announcing fresh keys each window sustains the growth indefinitely.

## Evidence (verified this run, main b5fc3f06)

- `PresenceTable` storage is an unbounded map: `entries: Arc<RwLock<HashMap<AuthorKey, Entry>>>` (pkgs/id/src/chat_presence.rs, `PresenceTable` struct). No constant caps the node count — contrast `MAX_HEARTBEAT_CHANNELS = 64` (chat_presence.rs:77), which bounds one heartbeat's channels, and `PRESENCE_TTL_SECS = 75` (chat_presence.rs:63), which bounds one entry's life, not their count.
- `PresenceTable::update_at` (chat_presence.rs:261-301) checks freshness and ordering, filters channels, then unconditionally `entries.insert(node, Entry { heartbeat })` (line 299). No size check precedes the insert on any path (`update`, `update_scoped`, `update_at`).
- `prune_at` (chat_presence.rs:428-435) retains every entry with `now - ts <= PRESENCE_TTL_SECS`; serve's cleanup task runs it every 60 s (`STALE_CHECK_INTERVAL`, crates/id-core/src/discovery.rs:318; serve.rs cleanup loop). Pruning therefore cannot shrink a flood of fresh entries at all.
- The production receiver (pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:1575-1588): `decode_frame` → `heartbeat.verify()` → `recv_presence.update(heartbeat)`. Verification is self-signing: the heartbeat's own key signs it, so a minted key verifies trivially. There is no membership scoping on this path (`update`, not `update_scoped`) and no count limit.
- Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneA-presencenodes/` (verbatim `chat_presence.rs` from current main, md5 68590664a175bd4a17937c28a2f0fb6b, matching both clones at b5fc3f06-era main; minimal `groups`/`waiting` stubs, same scaffolding as the #3991 probe):
  - CASE1: 100,000 distinct self-signed keys, each heartbeat naming one channel at `ts = now` → `accepted=100000 count=100000`; the heartbeats' frames total 15,000,000 bytes on the wire (150 B each, before in-memory overhead). `prune_at(now)` removed 0; `prune_at(now + 75)` removed 0 — every entry survives the full TTL.
  - CASE2: a heartbeat stamped `now + PRESENCE_TTL_SECS` (the future edge `update_at` accepts) is accepted and is still present at `prune_at(now + 2*TTL)` — ~150 s of guaranteed retention per minted key.
  - CONTROL: re-announcing one existing key replaces its entry instead of adding one — growth is exactly per distinct key, which is the attacker's free resource.

## Why it matters

Presence is an always-on, public-topic gossip surface in every long-running `id serve`. Per-heartbeat bounds (channels, typing — see #3991) limit how big one entry can be; nothing limits how many entries a stranger can plant. Memory growth is linear in minted keys (≈150 wire bytes each, more resident with the map, the signature vector, and channel vectors), each batch is retained at least 75 s regardless of the 60 s prune cadence, and sustained re-announcement makes the growth permanent for as long as the flood runs. This is the same unbounded-table shape as #2944 (discovery's `PeerDiscovery`), repeated in the presence table that #2809 added afterwards — #2944's fix scope is the discovery table only, and presence heartbeats being signed does not close it, because the scarce resource was never identity, it is distinct keys.

## Acceptance criteria

- `PresenceTable` refuses (or evicts to make room for) entries beyond a stated maximum node count, on every insert path (`update`, `update_scoped`, `update_at`); the cap is named next to `MAX_HEARTBEAT_CHANNELS`/`PRESENCE_TTL_SECS` with its rationale.
- The eviction/refusal rule is deterministic and does not let a flood of fresh minted keys evict long-standing legitimate entries wholesale (e.g. refuse new nodes at capacity, or evict the soonest-expiring entries first) — the chosen rule is stated in the code and covered by a test.
- Regression tests: inserting more distinct signed nodes than the cap leaves `count() <= cap`; entries within the cap behave exactly as before (freshness, ordering, roster/liveness reads unchanged); existing chat_presence tests keep passing.
- The serve receive path needs no workaround: the bound holds for the verbatim `verify()` → `update()` sequence serve runs today.

Distinct from: #3991 (per-heartbeat `typing` size — one entry's bytes, not the entry count), #2944 (the separate discovery peer table; unauthenticated announcements — presence is signed but count-unbounded), #2809 (the presence protocol itself, closed — this is a bound its implementation never had), #1730/#1726 (other unbounded-growth items, different structures).

- Tests cover a dropped event repaired by reconciliation, producer outage/recovery, event journal loss/reset, quiet-but-healthy sources, and stale data remaining visibly stale.

The five-minute reconciliation target may be narrowed per source after API-read cost is measured; record any slower source-specific window and its missed-event detection bound.

Phase 4 of #3870 (journaled region-seam export/import, design #2818, doc `doc/2026-11-01_design_id2818.md` in PR #3875, §8 packet 4). GATED on Phase 3 (destination import) landing.

**Scope:** Coordinator state machine + recovery.
- Coordinator journal: `HandoffStarted`, observed source/destination receipts, `HandoffCompleted` (and pre-export `HandoffCancelled` only after proving no source export committed). Coordinator journal stores NO entity payloads.
- Serialize handoffs per entity; drive source export then destination import; correlate receipts by handoff_id + entity + epoch + module/schema + digest.
- Region-map / owner switch ONLY after matching durable destination receipt AND durable `HandoffCompleted`; owner epoch increments once per completed handoff.
- Retry/reconcile after crashes at every seam (design §5 recovery matrix): query each side by handoff_id, append missing observations, resend the same envelope — never a new handoff ID, never automatic rollback after export.

**Acceptance:** failure-injection coverage for coordinator and region restarts at each protocol transition; no completion without a matching durable destination import; no duplicate entity.

title: pm-stack(quota-exporters): opt() in all three exporters takes a flag token as a value — '--out-dir --cdp-port 19222' writes the export into a directory named '--cdp-port', the flag token is consumed twice, and a non-numeric --cdp-port becomes a NaN CDP outage

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage

body:
## What

All three pm-stack quota exporters share an identical `opt()` argv helper that takes the next token as a flag's value **blindly** — including when that token is itself another flag — and each affected flag's value is then consumed a second time by its own lookup. A flag-like value also passes silently for the value-taking flags that are never range-checked.

The helper (identical in all three files):

```js
const opt = (name, fallback) => {
  const i = args.indexOf(name);
  return i >= 0 && args[i + 1] ? args[i + 1] : fallback;
};
```

- `pm-stack/meta-exporter/meta-quota-export.mjs:372-375` — call sites `:376-378` (`--out-dir`, `--cdp-port`, `--team-id`)
- `pm-stack/cloudflare-export/cloudflare-quota-export.mjs:437-440` — call sites `:441` (`--out-dir`), `:447` (`--account-id`)
- `pm-stack/supabase-export/supabase-quota-export.mjs:372-375` — call sites `:376-377` (`--out-dir`, `--project-ref`)

## Verified this run (laptop, real scripts, main 98371127, sha256-matched copies)

Probe dir: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneB-exporteropt/` on the laptop.

| Run | Observed |
|---|---|
| `meta-quota-export.mjs --out-dir --cdp-port 19222` | Created a directory literally named `--cdp-port` in the cwd and wrote the failure document's `latest.json`/`history.jsonl` there (status `no-console-page`, exit 5). `--cdp-port`'s token was consumed twice: once as the out-dir value, once as the port flag. |
| `cloudflare-quota-export.mjs --out-dir --account-id probeacct` | Created a directory literally named `--account-id` and wrote the `no-token` failure document there (exit 2). |
| `supabase-quota-export.mjs --out-dir --project-ref proberef` | Created a directory literally named `--project-ref` and wrote the failure document there; the API call still went to `/projects/proberef` (HTTP 400, exit 5) — the flag token served as both the out-dir value and the ref flag. |
| Control: `meta-quota-export.mjs --out-dir out` | Wrote `out/latest.json` + `out/history.jsonl` as intended. |
| `meta-quota-export.mjs --out-dir out --cdp-port banana` | No validation of the port: `Number("banana")` is `NaN`, and the run failed with `cdp-unavailable: CDP http://127.0.0.1:NaN/json/list unreachable` (exit 4) — a typo'd port is reported as a CDP outage. `--cdp-port --team-id x` produces the same NaN path. |

The systemd units invoke these exporters on a timer, and the failure-document path is exactly the path that fires on a mis-typed manual run: the failure doc — the artifact an operator reads to diagnose the tick — lands in a directory named after a flag, while the real atlas out-dir keeps its previous `latest.json` and looks merely stale.

## Why it matters

- A single mis-ordered or doubled flag silently redirects the exporter's only output to a junk directory in the cwd; the aggregator keeps reading the old export and the quota picture goes stale with no error anywhere expected.
- Flag tokens are also accepted as an account id (cloudflare) / project ref (supabase) value in the mirror-image invocation (`--account-id --out-dir …`): the flag string is sent to the API as the account/ref, and the resulting 4xx is blamed on token scope — the same misdiagnosis shape as #3419 (collect-github-billing).
- The unvalidated `--cdp-port` turns a typo into a reported infrastructure outage (`cdp-unavailable … NaN`).

## Distinct from

- #3449 (provider-catalog-sync): same failure class, different file and a different `opt()` implementation (`bin/provider-catalog-sync.mjs:689-698`); that issue's fix does not touch these three exporters.
- #3352/#3353: the umbrella strict-argv design + inventory audit; this filing is the concrete verified instance for the three exporter scripts, as with #3415/#3333.
- #3419/#3333/#3415: same class in `collect-github-billing`, `produce-charge-candidates`, `record-claude-launch` — different scripts, different argv code.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] In all three exporters, a value-taking flag followed by another `--flag` token (or by nothing) fails fast with a usage error naming the flag, before any directory is created, any token is resolved, or any API/CDP call is made.
- [ ] No token is consumed twice: `--out-dir --project-ref X` can never both name the out-dir `--project-ref` and use `X` as the ref.
- [ ] Meta `--cdp-port` must be a plain decimal integer in 1-65535; anything else is the same usage error, never a `NaN` CDP URL.
- [ ] Unknown/unrecognized arguments are rejected (or at minimum never silently ignored in a way that changes where output goes), matching the contract chosen under #3352.
- [ ] Regression tests in each exporter's existing `*.test.mjs` cover: flag-as-value for each value-taking flag, trailing flag, and (meta) a non-numeric port; the normal `--out-dir out` control still writes `latest.json` + `history.jsonl` to the named dir.

body:
## Order

Drew, 2026-11-01 (~03:23 CST, main chat): "prioritize the crate splitting work."

This elevates the crate-shape work out of #3195's sequencing. #3195 scoped splitting as "only if the above is insufficient" (after profile separation, release audit, build hygiene). Drew's order makes the split a first-class work item now, in parallel — the profile work in #3195 continues on its own track and is not a precondition.

## Why

pkgs/id is one giant compilation unit and the cost is now gating production work:

- #3195's table: 150 src .rs files, 125,722 lines (2026-10-31), up from 71,723 lines on 2026-10-11 — compile time tracks the crate's own size, superlinearly under LTO with `codegen-units = 1`.
- #3195 measured a cold nix build of the package at ~16 min under shared load (2026-10-31).
- 2026-11-01: the NixOS switch that deploys the fleet-feed collector (#3363) sat behind this compile for over an hour of wall time — the `id` release build (cargo, ~200-crate dependency graph, LTO) ran 53+ minutes under fleet load, and two stale/duplicate builds of the same package were found competing with it and had to be killed by hand.
- Every check/test build recompiles the one crate end-to-end for any change anywhere in it. Splitting along the existing module seams makes most changes recompile only the touched sub-crate and lets the graph build in parallel.

## Scope

- Identify the split seams from the crate's existing module structure and dependency directions (the program's areas — artifact, world, sandbox, web, dht/ssh, core types — are the starting hypothesis; the triage verifies against real import graphs).
- Sequence the extraction into phased, independently mergeable packets (one sub-crate per packet), each keeping the full test suite green.
- Keep the public surface of the resulting top crate/binary unchanged for consumers (the NixOS module, mcpx, and the flake checks build the same binary).

## Acceptance (inherited from #3195, non-negotiable)

- Shipped-binary runtime performance unchanged-or-better, with evidence: the deterministic fuel baselines in `src/sandbox.rs` identical after each phase; runtime spot benchmark before/after.
- Cold check-build time materially reduced, before/after timings recorded on this issue from the laptop.
- No test coverage removed and no check weakened to buy speed.

Program context: #3195 (build-time review), Drew's 2026-10-28 id program directive. Sibling storage/duplication problem: the fleet target-dir duplication issue filed alongside this one.

title: aggregator(actions): validateNewAction accepts impossible calendar dates — a snooze until 2026-02-30 is stored verbatim and Date.parse reads it as Mar 2, so the card stays snoozed ~2 extra days
