labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem
`BackupStore` can mark an identity authoritative after confirming a restore receipt that did not notify every device bound at confirmation time.

On current `origin/main` (`be6bf9a3af0e04cde337b40c33974601cbcde106`):
- `pkgs/id/src/backup.rs:662-690` snapshots `bound_devices` when `download_for_restore` creates the receipt and stores one pending token.
- `pkgs/id/src/backup.rs:740-746` allows `bind_device` to add another device without changing the pending restore.
- `pkgs/id/src/backup.rs:758-778` accepts the original token, clears the pending state, and then reports the identity authoritative.

Repro at the store API: create/upload a backup; bind device A; call `download_for_restore` and retain its receipt; bind device B; call `confirm_restore_notifications` with that receipt token. It succeeds and `is_authoritative` becomes true, although B was not included in the receipt's notifications. Existing restore tests cover devices bound before download and stale tokens, but not binding during pending delivery.

This is a store-model contract gap; I found no production callsites for these methods in this checkout, so this report does not claim a live endpoint exploit. It violates the documented invariant in the method/module comments that bound devices are notified before the restored key becomes authoritative.

## Why it matters
A restore can complete while a newly bound device has not received the restore notice required by the backup lifecycle. Callers relying on `is_authoritative` may then permit new group epochs before all currently bound devices have acknowledged the restore.

## Acceptance criteria
- Add a regression test for binding device B after a restore receipt has been created for device A.
- Define and enforce the lifecycle: either reject/defer binding while restore notification delivery is pending, or add B to the pending notification/acknowledgement set.
- Confirming the old receipt alone must not make the identity authoritative while B still requires notification; authority becomes true only after the defined pending-device acknowledgements complete.
- Preserve stale-token protection and normal ordered delivery for devices bound before restore.

body:
## Evidence

On `origin/main` (`6741fc50a4`), `pkgs/id/src/app_manifest.rs:381-445` validates each web app's route and optional socket by repeatedly scanning every previously registered app with `discovery.apps.iter().find(...)`. With N valid web apps whose paths are all distinct, all four scans miss for each new app, so discovery performs Θ(N²) route/socket comparisons. `commands::serve` calls `discover_apps` during startup (`pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:1451`), making this cost part of serving startup when an installation has many local apps.

The current contract intentionally rejects duplicate routes and cross-kind route/socket collisions (#6454); this is a performance gap in implementing that contract, not a request to change its semantics.

## Why it matters

Adding apps increases discovery work quadratically. A large but valid local app set can make `id serve` startup disproportionately slow, and the current repeated scans make future growth harder to reason about.

## Acceptance criteria

- Keep route uniqueness, socket uniqueness, and route↔socket collision behavior (including the existing first-conflict diagnostics) unchanged.
- Track already-registered route and socket values in lookup structures so each app's collision checks are expected O(1), rather than rescanning all registered apps; preserve the conflicting app identity/path needed by errors.
- Add/adjust tests covering duplicate routes, duplicate sockets, and both cross-kind collision directions, with an oracle that checks the same winning app and rejection/error behavior as today.
- Add a non-timing-based structural or benchmark check demonstrating discovery no longer performs a full prior-app scan per new app; avoid flaky wall-clock thresholds.
- Run the focused `pkgs/id` app-manifest tests and relevant formatting/checks.

body:
## Evidence

`pkgs/id/src/serve_proxy.rs` documents `Frame::stream_id` as `0` only for leg-level frame types (for example PING and RESUME), and `Frame::seq` as a DATA-only sequence number that is `0` for other types (lines 32–36). However, `Frame::validate` currently checks only payload and total frame sizes (lines 98–112). As a result, `Frame::new(FrameType::Data, 0, 0, vec![])` succeeds, and `Frame::decode_prefix` accepts the same invalid values from the wire because it calls that same validator (lines 141–149). The generic serve-proxy implementation issue #7569 is closed; the open design issue #5792 does not specifically track this validation gap.

## Why it matters

Malformed peers or local callers can create frames whose stream/leg scope and sequencing contradict the documented wire contract. Downstream multiplexing and stream state handling then have to interpret invalid control/data frames inconsistently instead of rejecting them at the codec boundary.

## Acceptance criteria

- Define/enforce the allowed stream-ID and sequence-number combinations for each frame type according to the serve-proxy protocol decision; do not assume every frame is stream-scoped.
- Reject invalid combinations through both `Frame::new`/`encode` and `Frame::decode_prefix`.
- Add regression tests for DATA on stream 0, a non-DATA frame with nonzero sequence, and valid leg-level and stream-level frames.
- Keep existing size-cap and incremental-decoder behavior unchanged.

body:
## Evidence

`pkgs/id/src/commands/key.rs:70,89-99` defines and enforces an 8-byte minimum for `id key export`. In contrast, the public `backup` module exposes `create_backup` at `pkgs/id/src/backup.rs:839-844`; it sends every byte slice to `key_envelope::encrypt` and only returns an optional advisory `passphrase_warning`. An empty passphrase therefore produces a valid offline-guessable backup envelope through the public API, bypassing the CLI guard.

The adjacent open PR #8911 only warns about repeated-character passphrases and explicitly keeps weak passphrases accepted; it does not add a minimum-length guard. The closed envelope feature issue #2279 does not specify this public-API floor.

## Why it matters

Backup envelopes can be attacked offline. A caller using the public API can accidentally create a backup with no passphrase entropy at all, even though the CLI rejects inputs below 8 bytes. Returning a warning is not equivalent to enforcing the existing minimum at the API boundary.

## Acceptance criteria

- Define one documented minimum passphrase length and apply it consistently to the CLI and `backup::create_backup` (preserve at least the existing 8-byte CLI floor unless the security policy chooses a stronger one).
- Reject below-floor inputs, including empty input, before deriving the KDF key or returning an envelope.
- Add boundary tests for below-floor rejection and exact-floor acceptance, plus a restore round trip for an accepted passphrase.
- Keep the weak-passphrase warning for accepted inputs that meet the floor but remain low entropy.

body:
## Evidence

On current `main` (`3e05759bc97e4d573a6921d1ffb60ef4d5019cc7`), `pm-stack/opencode-usage-export/opencode-usage-export.mjs:363-373` assigns each parsed value directly into `args`; a repeated scalar flag overwrites the earlier value without a usage error. The two `--out-dir` values can therefore silently retarget the failure document and the normal export.

Reproduced using the real exported `run()` function with isolated temporary paths:

```text
argv: --out-dir <first> --out-dir <second> --db <missing.db>
result: exitCode=3, status=store-missing
first/latest.json: absent
second/latest.json: written
```

The parser fails closed on unknown/missing/bad values, but accepts conflicting repeated values. The operator-argument design #3352 explicitly left repeated value-option semantics as an open question. #3353 is its closed inventory; #3469 and open PR #4480 cover `opt()` defects in meta/cloudflare/supabase exporters, not this separate exporter or duplicate flags. Fresh all-state issue/PR searches for this exporter and duplicate value options found no specific item.

## Why it matters

A duplicated `--out-dir` can route the tick or its failure artifact somewhere other than the operator's intended first destination, leaving the expected export looking stale. Last-value-wins is undocumented here and can conceal a duplicated argument in a timer or manual invocation.

## Acceptance criteria

- Reject repeated scalar value options (`--db`, `--out-dir`, `--window-hours`, `--fresh-hours`) as an `invalid-argument` usage failure before store probing or export writes.
- For repeated `--out-dir`, do not write an artifact to either conflicting destination; report the duplicate flag and exit non-zero (2).
- Add regression tests for duplicate options, especially two distinct `--out-dir` paths, and retain controls showing each option works once with existing behavior.

body:
## Evidence

On current `main` (`a5b2326379d540614ef62681b7b78ecd5fca84fc`), `pkgs/id/src/web/security.rs:118-127` normalizes every bracket-prefixed authority by taking text through the first `]`; if the tail is not `:<non-empty port>`, it discards the tail and returns the bracketed host. `origin_authority` at `:138-143` passes that authority through, and the guard compares normalized Origin and Host at `:213-221`.

This leaves an Origin-side counterpart to the Host fix in #8776. With `Host: [::1]` and `Origin: http://[::1]attacker.example`, the actual helper functions extracted from current `security.rs` produce:

```text
origin_authority="[::1]attacker.example"
origin_normalized="[::1]"
host_normalized="[::1]"
same_origin=true
```

The complete bracketed authority is malformed, but its suffix is ignored and it matches the valid Host. #8776 fixed `host_only` and explicitly scoped the fix to that helper; `authority_normalized` remains permissive. Browser-originated requests generally cannot produce this malformed serialized Origin, so the realistic caller is a non-browser client that can set an arbitrary Origin header; this is a validation/guard-consistency gap, not evidence of a browser CSRF exploit.

## Why it matters

The Origin guard accepts malformed bracketed authority text as same-origin. Callers relying on this check should not have to assume every client serializes Origin exactly as a browser would.

## Acceptance criteria

- Reject malformed bracketed Origin authorities, including `[::1]attacker.example`, rather than normalizing them to `[::1]`.
- Preserve valid bracketed IPv6 origins with no port or a numeric port, and preserve the existing host-and-port equality behavior from #814.
- Add a guarded-router regression test showing the malformed Origin is refused while valid same-origin IPv6 controls pass.
- Prefer making bracketed authority normalization report invalid syntax (for example, `Option`) and have the Origin guard reject it; do not weaken or undo the `host_only` fix from #8776.

labels.name: kind/bug

body:
## Evidence

On current `main` (`12b3fb6b29914f9f675558ea3d9e27f13ca31487`), the normal event paths reject sequence exhaustion with `checked_add(1)` (for example `pkgs/id/crates/id-worlds/src/world/core.rs:1670-1674,2318-2321`). The program-install path does not:

- `pkgs/id/crates/id-worlds/src/world/actor.rs:2583-2612` creates `ProgramInstalled` with `self.core.sequence.saturating_add(1)`, persists `JournalEntry::Committed`, then calls `commit_prepared`.
- `pkgs/id/crates/id-worlds/src/world/core.rs:2483-2488` also compares against `self.sequence.saturating_add(1)`, so at `u64::MAX` it accepts another event whose sequence is still `u64::MAX`.
- Restore now requires the committed event to be a checked successor (`core.rs:1098-1104`), and rejects a committed `MAX` event after a checkpoint already at `MAX`; the existing regression test pins this at `pkgs/id/crates/id-worlds/src/world/tests.rs:1191-1239`.
- A checkpoint at `u64::MAX` is an accepted restored state (`tests.rs:1172-1188`). Thus installing a program into that state can succeed and append a journal entry that prevents the world from restoring after restart.

This is distinct from closed #8370, which fixed only the restore-side committed-event predicate, and from #4000's restore-admission scope. That design says live writers cannot produce refused state, but this program-install writer currently can.

## Why it matters

A world at the sequence limit can report program installation as successful and become unrecoverable on the next restart. The install-specific saturating sequence path bypasses the checked exhaustion handling used by other event writers.

## Acceptance criteria

- Program installation refuses sequence exhaustion before persisting any `Committed` entry or changing the active program; surface the existing checked-successor error.
- `commit_prepared` independently rejects `u64::MAX` as an exhausted sequence rather than accepting a saturated same-sequence event.
- Add a regression test starting from a valid checkpoint at `u64::MAX`: installation is refused, the journal remains restorable, and no `ProgramInstalled` event is appended. Preserve the ordinary install path.

title: id(web): avoid reporting success when restoring an absent file

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

body:
## Evidence

`pkgs/id/src/web/routes/file_handlers.rs:936-963` implements `restore_handler` by calling `tag_store.del_by_key(..., b"deleted")` and then returning `DeleteResponse` with HTTP 200. It does not check whether the file exists or whether a deleted marker was present. By contrast, `delete_handler` at `:896-904` explicitly returns 404 for an unknown file. `pkgs/id/WEB.md` describes `/api/restore` as “Restore deleted file,” and the only matching E2E coverage (`pkgs/id/e2e/tests/file-operations.spec.ts:283-307`) covers restoring a file that was first deleted; it does not pin absent/non-deleted behavior.

A request such as `POST /api/restore` with `{"name":"typo.txt"}` can therefore receive a success response even though no file was restored. The caller cannot distinguish a real restore from a stale name or a request for a file that was never soft-deleted.

## Why it matters

A successful response is misleading for API clients and can hide stale references or user typos. The neighboring delete endpoint already establishes that unknown files are not silently treated as successful operations.

## Acceptance criteria

- Define the endpoint behavior for both a missing file and an existing file with no soft-delete marker; do not return an indistinguishable success response when no restoration occurred (unless idempotency is intentional and explicitly represented/documented).
- Preserve the existing successful soft-delete-then-restore behavior.
- Add regression coverage for missing and non-deleted names, plus the existing restore case; keep lookup/storage errors distinct from a no-op result.

A 404 for a missing file and an explicit no-op result for an existing non-deleted file would be one reasonable shape, but the API contract should be chosen deliberately.

body:
## Problem

A write-authorized id-sync peer can attach an `archive.rename` or `archive.replace` tag to one file while naming an archive owned by a different file. Deleting the first file then hard-deletes that unrelated archive and its metadata.

## Evidence (fresh `origin/main` `671088b42ce21882f6e40f77288e758847fcaaf6`)

- `pkgs/id/crates/id-sync/src/protocol.rs:691-699` gates `SetTag` and `Delete` on write authorization; `:792-800` forwards arbitrary `SetTag` subject, key, and value to `TagStore::set_tag` without reserving archive-reference keys or checking ownership.
- `pkgs/id/crates/id-store/src/tags.rs:811-847` stores the supplied subject/key/value without archive-reference validation.
- `pkgs/id/crates/id-sync/src/fileops.rs:602-615` accepts any reference whose value has the general `<name>.archive.<digits>` shape; it does not require the archive name to belong to the file being deleted.
- `fileops.rs:661-676` then deletes each referenced archive tag and all metadata for that archive name.

## Reproduction shape

1. Create a normal archive for `other-file` (for example `other-file.archive.123`) so its tag and metadata exist.
2. Through `MetaRequest::SetTag`, set `archive.replace = "other-file.archive.123"` on `my-file` from a peer granted write access.
3. Through `MetaRequest::Delete`, delete `my-file`.
4. The unrelated archive tag and its metadata are removed, although `other-file` was not renamed or deleted. The archive blob tag is lost and its blob may later be garbage-collected.

This differs from #4761 (now closed), which fixed normal `FileOps::copy` duplicating internally generated source references. This path allows an authorized protocol client to forge a cross-file ownership reference through the general metadata write endpoint. It is a concrete follow-up to the Rule 3 ownership audit in #4766/#4767.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Protocol metadata writes cannot create or change an archive ownership reference to an archive not owned by that subject; choose and document an explicit policy for reserved `archive.rename`/`archive.replace` keys.
- [ ] Regression test covers a write-authorized peer attempting the cross-file reference, then deleting `my-file`; `other-file`'s archive tag and metadata remain intact.
- [ ] Existing FileOps-generated archive references and legitimate rename/delete behavior continue to work.
- [ ] Focused id-sync protocol/FileOps tests pass.

Consequently, a 20-character repeated passphrase such as `aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa` has one class but returns `None`.

This is a concrete false negative in the warning surfaced during backup creation: the repeated-character passphrase has negligible guessing cost, while the code's no-warning result implies it passed the weak-passphrase assessment. Backup envelopes are subject to offline guessing, as the warning text and nearby comment note.

## Suggested fix / acceptance criteria

- Add a regression test proving a long repeated-character passphrase is warned about.

title: id(libsql): limit half-open circuit breaker to one recovery probe
body:
## Evidence

In `pkgs/id/src/foreign_libsql.rs`, `CircuitBreaker::allow` returns `true` for every call in `BreakerState::HalfOpen` (around lines 923–936). The first caller after `BREAKER_HALF_OPEN_AFTER` changes `Open` to `HalfOpen` and is admitted; while that remote call is still in flight, any number of other callers are also admitted. The state remains half-open until a call records success or transient failure. This is the recovery path in the adapter shipped by #8115 (merged; #7577 is closed).

The breaker is intended to probe a recovered endpoint before resuming regular traffic. Admitting an unbounded concurrent burst defeats that purpose and can overload an endpoint that is only beginning to recover.

## Acceptance criteria

- Half-open admits at most one in-flight recovery probe per breaker; concurrent callers are rejected or wait according to the chosen API policy.
- A successful probe closes the breaker and resets the failure count.
- A failed probe reopens the breaker and starts a fresh recovery delay.
- Tests cover repeated calls while one probe is outstanding, plus success and failure transitions; include a concurrent test if the implementation can be exercised concurrently.
- Closed-state admission and the existing open-state delay behavior remain unchanged.

Follow-up to merged implementation PR #8115 and issue #7577; this is a newly identified edge case, not a duplicate of the adapter implementation request.

## Work

Extend the existing webhook-to-Cloudflare-Worker-to-Turso sink (live for CI events under #5693) to mirror GitHub issue and PR state into the fleet-queue database: issues (title, body hash, state, labels, assignees), pull requests (state, merged, head/base, draft), comments count and latest agent note pointer, label changes. title: id(libsql): accept chunk extensions and reject incomplete HTTP chunk framing
body:
## Evidence

`pkgs/id/src/foreign_libsql.rs:864-875` parses the entire chunk-size line as hexadecimal. A valid HTTP/1.1 chunked body `4;foo=bar
Wiki
0

` therefore returns `bad chunk size` rather than `Wiki`. Production `HttpTransport::round_trip` passes responses through `parse_http_response` at lines 759-765, which invokes `dechunk` at 851-856. A compliant server or proxy using chunk extensions can thus break foreign libSQL requests.

The same parser treats the CRLF after chunk data as optional (`:885`) and returns immediately for a zero chunk (`:876-877`), accepting incomplete framing such as `4
Wiki0
` or `0
`. Existing unit cases at `:1256-1282` do not cover these inputs. This is based on source inspection; no runtime test was run.

Related: #8504 fixed UTF-8 decoding across chunk boundaries and called for malformed-frame errors, but its byte-based replacement still leaves these framing cases.

## Acceptance criteria

- Accept valid chunk extensions and decode chunk data correctly, including a valid terminal chunk and trailers.
- Reject missing chunk-data delimiters and incomplete terminal/trailer framing with a transport error rather than accepting a truncated response or panicking.
- Add focused parser regression tests for valid extensions, malformed and truncated frames, and ordinary responses; use expected decoded bytes or explicit errors as the oracle. Consider a transport-level test exercising a response from a local server.

title: lab-ops-hub(container): symbol-host parity conflict — #588 category check refuses what #659 test and the Worker accept (😀.com)

labels.name: app/lab-ops-hub
labels.description: Package/app: lab-ops-hub (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Summary

The container copy of the lab-ops-hub crawl validator (`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py`) and its own test suite disagree about symbol hosts, and the suite fails on clean main:

- `test/test_container_validate.py::test_returns_idn_hosts_in_alabel_form` (added by #659, commit 120dd96bdf) expects `http://😀.com/` → `http://xn--e28h.com/`.
- `container/app.py::_judge_idna_label` (category check added by #588, commit d7d0692dc0) refuses every label containing a punctuation/symbol/separator-category character (categories P/S/Z, plus Co/Cs), so `😀` (So) raises `ValueError: ... IDNA-disallowed punctuation, symbol or separator character`.

The Worker copy (`src/lib.ts::validateCrawlUrl`) judges the WHATWG-parsed host (`new URL` punycodes it) and carries no category check — it accepts the host. Verified with Node's WHATWG `domainToASCII` this run: `😀.com → xn--e28h.com`, `¤.com → xn--bba.com`, `×.com → xn--rca.com`, `€.com → xn--lzg.com`, while `¨.com`, `´.com`, `‾.com` → rejected (empty). So WHATWG accepts So/Sc/Sm symbols broadly and refuses only some — the container check is both stricter than the Worker (So/Sc/Sm) and matched to it elsewhere; #588's comment ("a currency/math symbol passed while the Worker refuses it") does not hold for the URL-parser path the Worker actually uses.

## Evidence (2026-11-11, lane code-v, task 14507)

- On pristine current main, in a venv with the pinned `container/requirements.txt` (idna 3.18): `npm test` — TypeScript suite passes; Python suite 73/74, sole failure the case above.
- This is one of the divergences that merged unverified while the lab-ops-hub workflow was dispatch-only + disabled_manually (#7715).

## Decision needed / acceptance

- Decide the intended policy for symbol labels in the container validator: match WHATWG/Worker (accept what `domainToASCII` accepts, refuse what it refuses) or keep the stricter IDNA2008 stance and change the #659 test expectation — with the security rationale recorded either way (this is the SSRF guard for a publicly reachable crawler, so the choice is a policy call, not a mechanical fix).
- Whichever way it lands: container suite + TS suite both green, and the two copies' behavior on a shared symbol-host corpus (😀, ¤, ×, €, ¨, ´, ‾) is identical or the divergence is documented in both codebases.

Found by: queue lane code-v while restoring the #7715 workflow (task 14507, PR #8426).

body:
## What happened

pm-git-sync.service (user unit, 30s timer) failed every run from 2026-11-08 until fixed 2026-11-10 ~09:00 CST. The service itself was healthy and behaving exactly as designed — it refuses to pull unless ~/git/code is on a clean main. The clone was neither:

1. **A queue lane worked directly in the primary clone.** ~/git/code sat on branch queue/13790-5954-deploy-smoke-fixture (checked out 2026-11-08 16:43 CST, one commit 9d7f54fda6, also pushed to origin under the same branch name) with uncommitted WIP edits across 9 tracked files (claimant, fleet-paperwork, mcpx; all stamped 2026-11-09 21:31:21) plus untracked files (incl. a whole nested checkout base-agg/). Because the sync was stalled, merged config had to be written into the live OpenCode config by hand during the 2026-11-10 deploy (PRs #8162/#8164).
2. **A stale lane worktree squatted main.** ~/git/fleet/12652-main held the main branch checked out (same commit as ~/git/fleet/12652 and 12652-3939-quota-uninstrumented), so even after cleaning, git checkout main in the primary clone was refused. Its apparent dirt was stale-base drift (Nov 8 base), not unique work.

## Fix applied (2026-11-10)

- All dirt preserved first: ~/git/code-dirt-rescue-2026-11-10/ on the laptop (tracked patch, two copies of every untracked file, 12652-main full diff + status, README). The opencode.jsonc edit was already byte-identical to origin/main; the remaining edits are stale-base versions of files that moved substantially on main since — recoverable from the rescue dir if any lane still needs them.
- Clone restored to clean main; stale worktree removed; sync restarted. Proof: one full cycle pulled 436 commits (1e46b89399 → 68dda495eb), restarted pm-projector + pm-dispatch, exit 0; follow-up timer run: ok clean main, up to date. HEAD == origin/main == 68dda495ebd5b439f22642164a6c49324fbc2adf; live config byte-identical to main.

## Prevention gap (the ask)

Lane/worker setup must never check out a branch or edit files in the primary clone (~/git/code), and must not create worktrees that hold main. Options: lane launcher refuses to start when its working dir resolves to the primary clone; a periodic check that no registered worktree holds main; pm-git-sync could also page louder than a journal FAIL when stalled >1h. Acceptance: a lane attempting to work in ~/git/code is stopped or redirected to a worktree, and a main-holding worktree raises a visible alert within one sync cycle.

# Currency gateway: Balance/History reads are rejected for frozen/sunset currencies

## Finding (from PR review)
On PR #7650 (feat(id): add currency gateway request envelope, #2319), Codex review comment [4506000715](https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/7650#discussion_r4506000715) (chatgpt-codex-connector[bot], 2026-11-08T11:13:36Z, `pkgs/id/src/currency/gateway.rs:692`):

> Allow authorized reads for inactive currencies. When a currency is frozen or sunset (`active == false`), this call rejects both `Balance` and `History` with `InactiveCurrency`, even for the holder and issuer. The control-plane design defines those statuses as restricting new writes (design_currency_control_plane §2.2), while §4.2 gates reads by ownership or role. Consequently, freezing a currency also prevents users from inspecting their existing balances and history. Look up the registered currency without requiring it to be active for read operations.

## No-response evidence
- No replies in the comment thread; the review thread is unresolved (GraphQL `reviewThreads` verified 2026-11-09).
- PR #7650 head is unchanged at `abef5c07e7bcd45b92210dd659f6480f717ec7e5` since the comment; no fix commit followed it. Past the 24-hour grace period for open PRs.

## Still-live evidence (current PR head)
Two independent raw reads of `pkgs/id/src/currency/gateway.rs` at head `abef5c07e7` agree: the read path resolves the currency through `active_currency(...)`, whose helper returns `Err(GatewayError::InactiveCurrency)` whenever `!record.active` — so reads inherit the write-side active requirement.

## Acceptance criteria
- Authorized `Balance`/`History` reads succeed for frozen/sunset currencies (gated by ownership/role per the control-plane design §4.2), while writes remain rejected.
- Tests cover read-after-freeze and read-after-sunset for holder and issuer.
- Resolving by a documented decision on this issue is also acceptable.

body:
# id(web/main): /api/tags response shape-trusted in loadFileTags — a wrong-shape 200 shows the file as untagged, leaves the previous file's tags on screen, or renders '[object Object]' pills

## Summary

`loadFileTags` in `pkgs/id/web/src/main.ts` (lines 759–776 on origin/main `5ad9688450`; the web tree is unchanged from `1aea9b5f75`) trusts the shape of the `GET /api/tags?subject=…` response:

```ts
const raw = await response.json();
// API may return { tags: [...] } or a flat array
const tags = Array.isArray(raw) ? raw : raw.tags || [];
const userTags = tags.filter(
  (t: { key: string }) =>
    t.key !== "created" && t.key !== "modified" && t.key !== "deleted" && !t.key.startsWith("archive."),
);
this.renderEditorTags(userTags);
```

There is no validation that the body is an object/array, that `tags` is an array, or that entries have string `key`/`value`. Every failure mode is silent: either the panel is re-rendered wrong, or a `TypeError` is swallowed by the surrounding `catch` as a `console.warn` and the panel keeps showing whatever it showed before.

## Verified behavior (this run)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-filetags` (laptop) — `loadFileTags` + `renderEditorTags` extracted **byte-verbatim** from `main.ts:759-817` (diff-checked against the source slice, md5 `8fce00a3ebdb4199a0f2b9cfbd089fcc`), driven in Node 24 with a minimal DOM stub and stub `fetch` returning HTTP 200 with each body. The panel starts each case showing a sentinel pill (`STALE-PILL`, standing in for the previously opened file's tags):

| Response body | Observed |
|---|---|
| `{tags: [{key:"project",value:"alpha"},{key:"created",…},{key:"plain",value:null}]}` (control) | renders `project: alpha`, `plain` — system tag filtered ✅ |
| `[{key:"project",value:"alpha"}]` (control, flat array) | renders `project: alpha` ✅ |
| `{}` | panel re-rendered as **"none"** — the file falsely appears untagged |
| `"abc"` (bare string) | panel re-rendered as **"none"** |
| `{tags: null}` | panel re-rendered as **"none"** |
| `null` | `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'tags')` → caught, `console.warn` only — **panel left stale** (previous file's tags still shown for this file) |
| `{tags: "abc"}` | `TypeError: tags.filter is not a function` → caught — **panel left stale** |
| `[null]` | `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'key')` → caught — **panel left stale** |
| `[{key: 123, value: null}]` | `TypeError: t.key.startsWith is not a function` → caught — **panel left stale** |
| `[{key: "note", value: {a: 1}}]` | renders a pill literally labelled **`note: [object Object]`**, whose remove button would send that bogus key/value back to the API |

## Why it matters

- The stale-panel cases are cross-file: open file A (tagged), then file B whose tags response is wrong-shaped, and the editor shows **A's tags as B's** — and the pill remove buttons act on B's filename with A's key/value, so a click issues a real `DELETE /api/tags` for a tag B may not have (and misses the one it does).
- The `{}` / bare-string / `{tags: null}` cases silently present a tagged file as untagged, indistinguishable from the genuine empty state.
- This is the same shape-trust pattern as #7837 / #7839 (save/identity endpoints in the same file), but a distinct endpoint and function — the tags path was noted as an unprobed lead in the 2026-11-08 creator-b run and is verified here.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The `/api/tags` GET response is parsed through a validating parser: body must be a flat array or an object whose `tags` is an array; every rendered entry must have a string `key` and a `value` that is a string or `null`. Anything else fails closed.
- [ ] On a wrong-shape 200, the tag panel is **not** re-rendered as "none" and does **not** keep the previous file's pills: it shows an explicit load-failure/unknown state (or retains a clearly-marked stale state) and logs a diagnosable error — never a silent `console.warn`-only swallow.
- [ ] No pill is ever rendered with a non-string key or a coerced `[object Object]` value.
- [ ] Regression tests cover `{}`, `null`, bare string, `{tags: "abc"}`, `{tags: null}`, `[null]`, numeric `key`, and object `value`, plus both control shapes (object form with system-tag filtering, flat array).
- [ ] pkgs/id web vitest suite + typecheck green.

## Scope notes

- Fix belongs at the fetch boundary in `main.ts` `loadFileTags` (a small parser next to the function or in `tags`-adjacent code is fine); server contract unchanged.
- Out of scope: the POST/DELETE `/api/tags` callers (`addTagInline`, `removeTag`, `bulkAddTag`) — they only check `response.ok`; the Tags WebSocket handler is a separate path.

body:
## Problem

id(web/home): the home feed refresh shape-trusts the `/api/home/feed` response — a wrong-shape 200 response wipes the already-rendered home lists and leaves raw engine errors / bogus rows in place of the feed.

`pkgs/id/web/src/home.ts`:

- `:105` — `const feed = (await response.json()) as HomeFeed;` is a bare cast; the result is dereferenced unvalidated at `:107-110` (`feed.recent`, `feed.popular`, `feed.recent_tags`, `feed.popular_tags`, `feed.scope`).
- `:28` / `:55` — both renderers (`renderList`, `renderTagList`) call `list.replaceChildren()` FIRST and only then read `documents.length` / iterate, so a malformed payload destroys the previously rendered (good) list before it throws.
- `:114` — the catch surfaces the raw exception text (`error.message`) as the status line, so a shape failure shows e.g. "null is not an object (evaluating 'tags.length')" to the user instead of a clean unavailable message.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ main 3bf18dc57d, home.ts md5 b3b0b3734c290dec5be5053834a871f4)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-home-feed/probe.ts` (bun, minimal DOM stub, real module imported from the laptop tree):

- control (well-formed tag list): renders OK — `topic:rust — 4 documents`
- `renderTagList(list, null)`: THROW `TypeError: null is not an object (evaluating 'tags.length')` — list children after throw = 0 (previous good row wiped)
- `renderTagList(list, {})`: THROW `TypeError: {} is not iterable` — list wiped
- `renderTagList(list, [null])`: THROW `TypeError ... (evaluating 'tag.subject')` — list wiped
- `renderTagList(list, [valid, null])`: THROW on the second element — list left half-rendered (1 new row, previous content gone)
- `renderTagList(list, "abc")`: no throw — silently renders 3 bogus rows: `undefined — undefined documents` ×3

`renderList` (documents) shares the same wipe-first shape (`:28` then `documents.length`), and a `null` feed body throws at `feed.recent` itself. The refresh polls every 15s (`home.ts` poll loop), so one bad response (deploy skew, an error envelope returned with 200, a future server field change) blanks the home page's lists until a well-formed response arrives, with a raw TypeError as the only explanation.

The existing test file (`pkgs/id/web/src/home.test.ts`) covers only well-formed `renderTagList` inputs (XSS text rendering, occurrence counts) — no malformed-shape cases.

## Why it matters

The home page is id's front door. Every other feed consumer in this repo that was audited in this class (projector, aggregator, atlas worker) validates the shape at the boundary before touching state; the home refresh instead mutates the DOM first and validates never. Failing closed here is cheap: keep the last good render and show the designed unavailable message.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A malformed feed payload (null body, non-object body, missing/non-array `recent`/`popular`/`recent_tags`/`popular_tags`, null or wrong-typed elements/fields) does NOT clear or partially replace the currently rendered lists.
- [ ] A malformed payload surfaces a clean user-facing message (e.g. "Feed is temporarily unavailable.") — never a raw TypeError/engine message.
- [ ] Well-formed feeds render exactly as today (existing home.test.ts cases unchanged and green).
- [ ] New regression tests in `pkgs/id/web/src/home.test.ts` cover the malformed cases above and fail pre-fix.
- [ ] Web suite + typecheck green.

body:
Implementation step 5 of the design in #5683 (design record: `doc/2026-11-08_design_id5683.md` §6, PR #7781).

## Scope

Intranet-mode servers:

- Boundary mechanisms, strongest first: mTLS client identity / org IdP assertion (strong), VPN/overlay membership (medium), source IP ranges (weak).
- Gate generic user activity from outside the boundary via `evaluate()` with `Plane::Transport`; no new gate.
- 2FA step-up at: new network, privilege escalation, admin actions. Bounded window (declared per scope, default short, e.g. 15 min), logged.
- Org-escrowed credentials: proxy **assertions** ("member of group G", "residency attested"), not raw values, wherever an assertion suffices. Every proxy use audited; user can see what was shared.
- **Fail closed** for generic activity when boundary / IdP / VPN is unreachable. Break-glass held by a named role, use logged loudly and surfaced to admins — never an automatic fallback.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Property test: with the boundary unreachable and no break-glass, generic activity is never allowed.
- [ ] Step-up window expiry forces re-step-up on the next privileged action.
- [ ] Every proxy use and every break-glass use produces an audit record.

Design: `doc/2026-11-08_design_id5683.md` §6. Parent: #5683.

- The problem described above is confirmed against current main (reproduced or traced to the named code path), or the issue is closed with that evidence.

# ci(lab-ops-hub): test workflow is dispatch-only AND disabled_manually — the SSRF validator suites have not run since 2026-11-01 (last run: failure) while three validator fixes merged

## Problem

`pkgs/lab-ops-hub`'s only CI venue, `.github/workflows/lab-ops-hub.yml`, can never run:

- Its only trigger is `workflow_dispatch:` (`.github/workflows/lab-ops-hub.yml:22-23`) — no push, pull_request, or schedule trigger.
- The Actions API reports the workflow's state as `disabled_manually`, so it cannot even be dispatched. A disabled dispatch-only workflow is a dead venue, not a manual one.
- Its newest run is 2026-11-01T22:15:37Z — and that run's conclusion was **failure**. The suites have had no CI signal for a week.

Meanwhile the package keeps changing in exactly the area the suites pin: three fixes merged 2026-11-07 — #7018 (validate the container crawler response shape), #7037 (validate the Workers AI summary result), #7087 (validate the POST /api/files multipart body). None of them could be verified by the suite that exists for this purpose.

The suites pin the SSRF guard for a publicly reachable crawler, implemented twice (TypeScript Worker copy + Python container copy) under a documented "same policy" contract (workflow header, citing #470). The Python half is currently **red on main** and CI cannot show it: the pinned WHATWG-alignment test tracked by #5947 fails, and there is no venue in which a #5947 fix could be verified either.

This is the same shape as #7663 (cold-store-reaper), filed for the identical dispatch-only + `disabled_manually` combination; the general enablement audit is #6187, which this issue gives a per-package disposition target for lab-ops-hub.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop primary @ 83b7a024b8)

```
$ gh api repos/developing-today/code/actions/workflows/lab-ops-hub.yml
disabled_manually  lab-ops-hub

$ gh run list --workflow lab-ops-hub.yml --limit 3
2026-11-01T22:15:37Z push failure      <- newest run
2026-11-01T22:02:24Z push success
2026-11-01T16:48:26Z push success

$ git log --oneline --since=2026-11-01 -- pkgs/lab-ops-hub
b3c6a90794 fix(lab-ops-hub): validate the POST /api/files multipart body and file field (#7087)
ae4dfc702a fix(lab-ops-hub): validate the Workers AI summary result before storing it (#7037)
7307ab56dc fix(lab-ops-hub): validate the container crawler response shape before archiving or binding (#7018)

# Hand run on the laptop (the workflow's own commands):
$ cd pkgs/lab-ops-hub && npm run test:ts
113 tests, 113 pass

$ pip install -r container/requirements.txt  (scratch venv)
$ python3 -m unittest discover -s test -p 'test_*.py'
Ran 74 tests — FAILED (errors=1)
ERROR: test_returns_idn_hosts_in_alabel_form (test_container_validate.TestValidateCrawlUrl)
  ValueError: refusing to crawl host 😀.com: label '😀' contains an IDNA-disallowed
  punctuation, symbol or separator character      <- the #5947 pin
```

Dedup: no open or closed issue names the lab-ops-hub workflow's enablement state (searches: "lab-ops-hub workflow disabled", "lab-ops-hub disabled_manually"). Closed #5663 asked for PR triggers and was settled by the dispatch/schedule-only policy (5a94833ea3) — this issue does not re-ask for PR triggers; it asks for a disposition for a venue that cannot run at all. Open #6187 is the cross-repo venue audit; open #5947 tracks the failing pin itself, not the missing venue.

## Why it matters

- The crawl validators are the SSRF boundary for a publicly reachable crawler, duplicated in two languages with a parity contract — precisely the code that must not drift silently.
- The suite is red today (#5947) and the redness is invisible: no run since 2026-11-01, and that run failed for reasons nobody can now attribute.
- Every future validator fix (including the #5947 fix) lands unverified until a venue exists again.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A disposition is chosen and recorded on this issue: re-enable the workflow (dispatch stays acceptable per the 5a94833ea3 policy — but a dispatchable workflow must not be `disabled_manually`), move the suites to a live venue (e.g. the fleet dispatch-test pattern of #6580 or a schedule), or retire the suites with the parity contract's new home named.
- [ ] After the disposition, one real run of both suites exists on current main and its result is linked here (expected state at filing: TS 113/113 pass; Python 74 tests with the single #5947 error — a run that reproduces exactly that is a working venue).
- [ ] The run is reproducible from the workflow's documented commands (`npm test` in `pkgs/lab-ops-hub`, with `container/requirements.txt` installed for the Python half).
- [ ] #5947 and #6187 are cross-linked from the disposition comment so the audit and the failing pin point at the live venue.

# ci(aggregator): check-provenance-matrix.ts (#1200 consistency check) is run by no workflow, flake check, just recipe, or npm script

## Evidence (verified this run, main `8a0a1c0cea`)

`pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/check-provenance-matrix.ts` (116 lines) is the #1200 consistency check: it derives the load-bearing capability-provenance facts from the code of record and fails (exit 1, naming each divergence) when the pm-stack README, the aggregator README, `src/program.ts` (/program), `src/sources/live.ts`, `install.sh`, or the NixOS pm-stack module contradict them. Its own header says: "Run after changing any facet's source, the projector's deployment, or the matrix itself: `bun run scripts/check-provenance-matrix.ts`."

Nothing runs it:

- No match for `check-provenance-matrix` or `provenance-matrix` in `.github/workflows/`, `flake.nix`, `justfile`, or any `package.json` in the repo (grep verified this run).
- The aggregator's `package.json` wires its sibling check as a named script — `"contract:check": "bun run scripts/check-contract-corpus.ts"` — but has no equivalent entry for the provenance check.
- Hand run on the laptop primary this run: all 15 checks pass, exit 0 (`check-provenance-matrix: matrix, READMEs, /program, code and NixOS module agree.`) — the check is healthy; it is simply verified nowhere, so the next divergence it exists to catch will land silently, recreating the #1200 failure mode (prose surfaces diverging unnoticed).

## Why it matters

#1200 exists because the provenance claims lived as prose in three places and silently diverged. The fix produced a mechanical check — but an unrun check is prose again: facet, projector, and deployment changes merge without it, and nobody learns the matrix went stale until a human trips over the contradiction.

## Acceptance criteria

- The check runs automatically on changes to the surfaces it guards (at minimum: the aggregator subtree, `pm-stack/README.md`, `install.sh`, and the NixOS pm-stack module) — e.g. a step in the pm-stack tests workflow or an aggregator `package.json` script invoked by one, following the `contract:check` pattern.
- The wiring names the script explicitly and fails loudly if the script is missing or exits non-zero; a green run can never be a silently skipped check.
- A deliberately introduced divergence (e.g. a stale claim edited into `src/program.ts` in a test branch) makes the wired job fail, demonstrating the gate bites.
- The check itself still passes unmodified on current main.

body:
## Problem

The `developing-today[bot]` automation closes an issue seconds after a PR that merely **references** it merges, and labels it `status:done` — even when the PR deliberately carries **no closing keyword** because the issue must stay open for a recorded remainder.

## Evidence (2026-11-08, lane code-k shift, task 12836 and task 12785)

- Issue #5866: PR #7588 body said "Refs #5866 — deliberately no closing keyword"; squash merge commit `8f16bcc10c63861cf704307762f7c870eabe4bd9` message contains no closing keyword. Timeline: `developing-today[bot]` labeled `status:done` at 2026-11-08T09:14:05Z and **closed** issue #5866 at 09:14:07Z (stateReason COMPLETED), 8s after the merge. The task 12836 packet explicitly required #5866 to stay open for the decision record's §6 remainder (blocked on issue #5867 / issue #5681). Worker reopened it (note 6719705368).
- Issue #5767: PR #7592 (phase 1 only; later phases remain on #5767) merged `b413e06d0ecbb07b599c0550fc2715f64306251d`; `developing-today[bot]` labeled `status:done` at 09:31:51Z and **closed** issue #5767 at 09:31:52Z. Worker reopened it (note 6719854174).
- Same bot also manages the `status:` family around the event (adds `status:in-review` on PR open, `status:to-do` after a reopen), so the close appears to be part of that status automation, not GitHub's native closing-keyword behavior (native close would be attributed to the merging user and requires a closing keyword).

## Why it matters

Phase/remainder work is a standing fleet pattern: a PR lands one phase with `Refs #<n>` and the issue stays open for the rest. Auto-closing hides the remainder, marks it `status:done`, and makes closure state unreliable for the queue's revalidation (workers must spend a cycle reopening + correcting, as happened twice in one shift).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A merged PR that references an issue **without** a closing keyword does not close the issue and does not add `status:done`.
- [ ] A merged PR **with** a closing keyword (Closes/Fixes/Resolves #<n>) still closes the issue as today.
- [ ] The automation's rule is documented where the status automation lives, naming which signal it keys on.
- [ ] Regression evidence: one Refs-only merge and one Closes merge after the fix, with timeline excerpts on this issue.

## Acceptance criteria

- A merged PR that references an issue without a closing keyword does not close the issue and does not add `status:done` (the issue's own checklist, consolidated here).
- A merged PR with a closing keyword (Closes/Fixes/Resolves) still closes the issue as today.
- The automation's rule is documented where the status automation lives, naming the signal it keys on.
- Regression evidence covers both cases above (the #5866 / PR #7588 and #5767 / PR #7592 events replayed or reproduced).

body:
## Finding

PR #3746 added inline code-span tracking to `protect_newline_destinations` so a destination-shaped string inside a *closed* code span is not protected. The tracking has no reset: a backtick run opens a span that only an equal-length run closes, and the state is carried across blank lines, headings, and every other block boundary to the end of the document. In CommonMark an unmatched backtick run is literal text, not a code span — so after any stray/unmatched backtick in prose (a common typo in notes), the scanner believes the rest of the document is code, and every genuine newline destination after it silently loses protection. That is the exact load/save corruption the protection exists to prevent, reintroduced for a whole class of real documents.

## Evidence

- Source PR: #3746 (merged, merge commit `40f561e8a69d6c272bc2a099e1690de756802714`) — "fix(id/web): newline-destination protection skips literal code contexts (#1707)". #1707 is CLOSED; dedupe searches (`protect_newline_destinations`, "newline destination backtick span", "unmatched backtick") return no covering issue.
- Current main `2aca793a345a88b2f11a815fc190da4df07e0ee0`, `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs`:
  - `:2444` `fn protect_newline_destinations`
  - `:2469` `let mut span: Option<usize> = None;` — the only span state; nothing in the function ever resets it at a blank line or block boundary.
  - `:2514` protection is gated on `span.is_none()`.
  - `:2573-2575` a backtick run sets `span = Some(n)` when none is open and clears it only on a run of exactly the same length.
- Probe (this run): a faithful line-for-line Python port of the function as on current main, run twice with identical results:
  - Control `"[x](<a\nb>)\n"` → protected, token issued.
  - Closed span ``"`[x](<a\nb>)`\n"`` → not protected (the intended #1707 behaviour).
  - `"the \`foo flag does x\n\n[x](<a\nb>)\n"` (one stray backtick, destination in a later paragraph) → **not protected**.
  - Same-paragraph stray backtick and a stray double-backtick run → also **not protected**.
- PR #3746's own test (`test_newline_destination_protection_skips_literal_contexts`) pins only a properly closed span, fences, and indented blocks; no unmatched-run case is covered.

## Why it matters

The id web editor's notes are exactly the kind of prose that accumulates a stray backtick. From that character on, every link or reference definition whose destination contains a newline is parsed without the token protection, so its URL is handled by comrak's default path instead of the round-trip-safe one — silent link corruption on load/save for the remainder of the document, with no error anywhere.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A document containing an unmatched backtick run still gets newline-destination protection for genuine destinations after it (span state ends at the paragraph/block boundary at the latest, matching CommonMark's treatment of an unclosed span as literal text).
- [ ] The #1707 cases still pass: destinations inside properly closed inline spans, fences, and indented blocks remain unprotected.
- [ ] A regression test pins the unmatched-backtick case (same-paragraph and later-paragraph destinations).

body:
## Finding

PR #3719 fixed the non-total call-stat tie-break by applying the same field-wise comparator (TotalMs descending, then Server ascending, then Tool ascending) as two verbatim copies — one in the eventstore, one in the logstore. The bug it fixes (the two stores disagreeing on row order) had to be fixed twice for exactly this reason, and any future ordering change (e.g. a third tie-break field) must again be hand-applied to both copies; fixing only one silently reintroduces store disagreement, and the agreement test only catches divergence for fixtures it happens to include (the `("a","bc")` / `("ab","c")` collision pair was absent until this PR).

## Evidence

- Source PR: #3719 (merged, merge commit `1778b54941678b1241d70786dcc0d1e4435610c5`) — "Both stores now tie-break field-wise: Server ascending, then Tool ascending".
- On current main (`fc035359245855fd5b3db1d6b85ee60223abcf20`, verified via `git show origin/main`):
  - `pkgs/mcpx/internal/eventstore/stats.go` lines 93–99: the comparator (`TotalMs` desc, `Server <`, `Tool <`).
  - `pkgs/mcpx/internal/logstore/stats.go` lines 108–114: the identical comparator, character-for-character in the sort closure.
  - The only guard against the copies diverging is `TestCallStatsAgreeWithLogstore`, which compares outputs on its fixture set.

## Why it matters

Duplicated ordering logic across two stores that must agree is a recurring-bug shape: #3136 itself was the second manifestation (concatenation collision). A single shared comparator (or a shared `CallStat` sort helper used by both stores) eliminates the class instead of relying on fixture coverage to catch the next divergence.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] One shared implementation of the call-stat ordering is used by both `eventstore` and `logstore` (or an equivalent structural guarantee replaces the two copies).
- [ ] `TestCallStatsAgreeWithLogstore` still passes, including the `("a","bc")` / `("ab","c")` collision fixture.
- [ ] No change to the current ordering semantics (TotalMs descending, Server ascending, Tool ascending).

body:
## Problem

`.github/workflows/opencode-config-guard.yml` — the workflow that runs the metered/PAYG provider guard (`bin/check-opencode-metered-providers.mjs` + its fixtures) over the canonical `.opencode/opencode.jsonc` — no longer runs on the events its own policy assigns it:

- Current `on:` (workflow lines 4–6) is only `merge_group:` + `workflow_dispatch:`.
- `.github/ci-policy.md` ("OpenCode metered-provider config guard", lines 117–118) still states the workflow "runs the static guard and its fixtures on pull requests, merge groups, and pushes to `main`", and the job is named `basic: OpenCode metered-provider guard` — `basic:` is the PR tier in this repo's policy.
- Commit 5a94833ea3 (2026-11-04, "ci: remove push/pull_request triggers (dispatch/schedule only)") deleted the `pull_request:` trigger — which was deliberately path-gated to the four files the guard cares about (`.opencode/opencode.jsonc`, `bin/check-opencode-metered-providers.mjs`, `bin/check-opencode-metered-providers.test.mjs`, the workflow itself; #1401, to avoid runner-backlog queueing) — and the unfiltered `push: branches: [main]` trigger. The pre-sweep header comment recorded the design: "merge_group and push to main stay unfiltered, so the queued head and main are always validated."
- Live run history confirms the effect: the 30 most recent runs of this workflow are all push/pull_request runs on or before 2026-11-03T02:21Z — **zero runs since the sweep**, in a repo that merges PRs daily. The retained `merge_group:` trigger has produced no recorded run in that window either.

This is the same sweep and the same failure shape as issue #6929 (mcpx fix-test guard), in a different workflow: a guard that exists, is policy-assigned to the PR and main tiers, and silently never executes — so a metered provider selection (a direct PAYG `deepseek` route or a `cloudflare-*` target without a `payg-exception` comment) can now land in the canonical OpenCode config with no CI signal at all. The policy's Coverage rule ("Nothing removed from PRs may vanish") is violated in the same way.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ 56b6a47f9b)

- `sed -n 1,20p .github/workflows/opencode-config-guard.yml`: `on:` = `merge_group:` + `workflow_dispatch:` only; job name `basic: OpenCode metered-provider guard`.
- `grep -n "opencode-config-guard" .github/ci-policy.md` → lines 117–118 promise pull requests, merge groups, and pushes to `main`.
- `git show 5a94833ea3 -- .github/workflows/opencode-config-guard.yml`: removes the path-gated `pull_request:` block and `push: branches: [main]`, keeps `merge_group:` + `workflow_dispatch:`.
- `gh run list --workflow opencode-config-guard.yml --limit 30`: newest run 2026-11-03T02:21:31Z (push, cancelled); all 30 are push/pull_request on or before 2026-11-03; no merge_group, push, or pull_request run since.
- Dedup: `gh` searches for "opencode-config-guard" / "metered-provider guard" (open + closed) find issue #2288 (closed — the guard's creation), issue #4694 (closed — a symlink bug in the checker script itself), and issue #6065 (open — opencode-config-normalize test suite unwired, a different package). No issue covers this workflow's lost triggers. Sibling issue #6929 covers the mcpx fix-test guard only. Checked and not filed: `fleet-search-parity-guard.yml` is also merge_group+dispatch only, but it was born that way in bfbd19e9e9 (#5920) and ci-policy.md makes no PR/push promise for it.

## Why it matters

This guard is the only CI check standing between the canonical OpenCode config and a metered/PAYG provider selection — the exact exposure the house rules treat as a money leak (disabled providers are checked too, so a later re-enable cannot silently restore metered routes). It has been dark for four days while its policy text, its `basic:` job name, and its fixtures all claim it runs on PRs and main. Either the triggers come back (path-gated, as #1401 designed them) or the policy and the guard's claimed tier must be retired honestly — the current state is a guard that reads as coverage and provides none.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A decision is recorded on this issue: restore the triggers, or retire the policy promise (restore-vs-retire is triage's call, as with issue #6929).
- [ ] If restored: `pull_request:` returns with the #1401 path gate (`.opencode/opencode.jsonc`, `bin/check-opencode-metered-providers.mjs`, `bin/check-opencode-metered-providers.test.mjs`, `.github/workflows/opencode-config-guard.yml`) and `push: branches: [main]` returns unfiltered; `merge_group:` and `workflow_dispatch:` stay. No duplicate push+pull_request execution of the same suite for the same commit (ci-policy Dedup rule).
- [ ] After the fix, a recorded workflow run on a relevant PR (or a dispatch run plus the next relevant merge) proves the guard executes again; the run link is posted on this issue.
- [ ] If retired instead: `.github/ci-policy.md`'s OpenCode metered-provider guard section and the job's `basic:` naming are corrected in the same change, so no document claims coverage that does not run.
- [ ] Either way, ci-policy.md and the workflow agree afterward, and the #6929 sibling is cross-linked (same sweep commit 5a94833ea3).

title: github-ci(worker): HMAC gate fails open when GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET is unset — unsigned POSTs are processed and written to Turso

body:
## Problem

The github-ci Worker (`pkgs/github-ci/worker/src/index.ts`, #5693) is the GitHub webhook receiver: its header comment states the gate plainly — "Gate: HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body, X-Hub-Signature-256 header, verified with Web Crypto against GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET … the HMAC is the gate" (:3-9), and the README calls it the "HMAC-SHA256 gate". The secret is a required deployment secret per `wrangler.toml` ("HMAC gate; NEW value minted for this Worker, vaulted in BWS").

The implementation only verifies when a secret happens to be present:

```ts
// src/index.ts:73-80 @ def55caf48
const secret = env.GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET ?? "";
if (secret) {
  const given = (req.headers.get("x-hub-signature-256") ?? "").replace("sha256=", "");
  const expected = await hmacHex(secret, raw);
  if (!timingSafeEqual(given, expected)) {
    return new Response("bad signature", { status: 401 });
  }
}
```

When `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET` is empty or the binding is missing — a deploy before `wrangler secret put` lands, a renamed/mistyped binding, a preview/dev deployment (`workers_dev = true` in `wrangler.toml`) — the gate is skipped entirely and **every POST is processed as if it were an authentic GitHub delivery**, including the writes behind the gate:

- `workflow_run` → `INSERT OR IGNORE INTO ci_events` in fleet-platform Turso (failure conclusions keep the raw forged payload for forensics),
- fleet-repo `push` → advances `agent_repo_snapshots.head_sha` to an attacker-chosen SHA + appends a sink event,
- fleet-repo `pull_request` / `issues` → sink event + `dirty:<repo>` watermark.

The sibling atlas-search Worker fails closed on the same condition (`gateOk`: `if (!presented || !env.GATE_TOKEN) return false`). This Worker fails open.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop @ def55caf48)

Probe `~/git/fleet/probe-ghci-gate/probe.ts` imports the **real** `src/index.ts` (bun) with a stub Turso pipeline server that records statements:

Controls — secret configured:
- unsigned `ping` → `401 bad signature`
- validly signed `ping` → `200 pong`
- bad-signature `ping` → `401 bad signature`

Defect — no signature presented at all:
- `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET: ""`, unsigned `ping` → `200 pong`
- secret binding missing entirely, unsigned `ping` → `200 pong`
- `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET: ""`, unsigned completed `workflow_run` for `developing-today/code` → `200 {"ok":true,"repo":"developing-today/code","run_id":999,"conclusion":"success"}`, and the stub recorded **1 pipeline call containing `INSERT OR IGNORE INTO ci_events`** — an unauthenticated request reached the Turso write.

Existing tests (`test/worker.test.ts`) always run with the secret bound (vitest.config.ts bindings) and cover only the bad-signature case; there is no missing/empty-secret case.

Related: #5693 (the Worker's tracking issue), #6925 (same Worker's sink reachability).

## Why it matters

A webhook receiver whose only authentication silently disables itself on a configuration miss is a forge-anything endpoint: CI history, repo snapshot heads, and agent events/watermarks are all downstream of these writes, and a forged `push` head_sha or failure `workflow_run` payload is indistinguishable from a real delivery once stored. The failure mode is silent — nothing logs that the gate was skipped — so a misconfigured deploy would not be noticed until forged data is found downstream. Fail-closed is the house pattern for exactly this condition (atlas-search `gateOk`, cold-store, pkgs/id fail-closed fixes).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] With `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET` unset or empty, every POST (including `ping`) is rejected with a 5xx configuration error (e.g. 500/503 "webhook secret not configured") and **no** Turso/sink write is attempted; the rejection is logged server-side without logging any credential value.
- [ ] With the secret configured, behavior is unchanged: valid signature processes normally, missing/bad signature → 401 (existing tests keep passing).
- [ ] The GET liveness response stays unauthenticated (it exposes no data and takes no writes) — or, if it is also gated, the README/wrangler notes say so explicitly.
- [ ] New worker tests cover the unset-secret and empty-secret cases for at least `ping` and one writing event (`workflow_run` or `push`), asserting rejection and zero Turso pipeline calls.
- [ ] Header comment / README wording and the code agree: the HMAC is the gate, unconditionally.

body:
# mcpx(ci): e2e-shard-packer crashes with raw tracebacks on a wrong-shape timings seed — non-object `tests` field and non-finite weights are unguarded

## Summary

`pkgs/mcpx/scripts/ci/e2e-shard-packer.py` (the #1994 measured-time shard packer that produces the mcpx-test e2e matrix) carefully guards its *discovery* side — the coverage assertion fails with a named `coverage defect: ...` message rather than emitting a bad matrix — but its *timings seed* side (`load_weights`) trusts the shape of `e2e-timings.json`:

1. If the seed's `tests` field is present but not an object (a list, a string — a hand edit, or a future seed generator emitting pairs), `load_weights` raises a raw `AttributeError` from `raw.items()`.
2. A weight of `Infinity` (which Python's `json.load` accepts by default in a seed file) passes the `seconds > 0` check, poisons the total, and `pack` raises a raw `OverflowError: cannot convert float infinity to integer`. (`NaN` is filtered only by accident, because `NaN > 0` is false.)
3. A `true` weight is accepted as 1.0s, because `bool` is an `int` subclass and the `isinstance(seconds, (int, float))` check does not exclude it — the same bool-as-number class the fleet's other validators (#6637's `drain_last` check) explicitly exclude.

In every case the mcpx-test init job dies with an interpreter traceback instead of either the script's equal-weights fallback or a named error saying the seed is malformed and which entry is wrong — so a malformed seed regeneration blocks the whole e2e workflow with a message that points at the packer's internals, not at the seed.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop, origin/main c110f92897605d377b6cbae9b8dfc95f98f429b9)

Probe: real `e2e-shard-packer.py` extracted verbatim from origin/main, driven through its own `load_weights`/`pack` (`~/git/fleet/probe-shard-packer`):

- Control `{"tests": {"TestA": 10, "TestB": 20, "TestC": 30}}` → weights as measured, `pack` → 1 shard, OK.
- `{"tests": [["TestA", 10]]}` → `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'items'` at `load_weights` (`raw = doc.get("tests", doc)` then `raw.items()`).
- `{"tests": "TestA=10"}` → same `AttributeError` ('str').
- `{"tests": {"TestA": Infinity, "TestB": 20, "TestC": 30}}` → accepted as a measured weight (`inf`), then `pack` raises `OverflowError` at `math.ceil(total / target_seconds)`.
- `{"tests": {"TestA": true, ...}}` → weight silently becomes 1.0s.
- (For reference: a wholly non-object seed, e.g. a top-level list, already falls back to equal weights, because `raw` becomes `{}` — only the `tests`-field shape and the weight values are unguarded.)

## Why it matters

The seed is a committed file that timing tooling regenerates; the failure mode for a bad regeneration should be the packer's own contract style — fall back to equal weights with the note printed, or fail with a named error identifying the seed problem — never a raw traceback that fails the init job and every e2e leg behind it. This is the same wrong-shape-inside-a-valid-container class fixed for repo-universe (#6716/#6814) and github-backup (#6637/#6821).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `load_weights` treats a non-object `tests` field as a malformed seed: named error (or equal-weights fallback with the reason in the weight note), never an `AttributeError` traceback.
- [ ] Weights must be finite positive numbers and not bools: `Infinity`, `-Infinity`, `NaN`, and `true`/`false` values are rejected per-entry (skipped with the entry named, or the seed refused by name), and cannot poison the median or the shard-count arithmetic.
- [ ] Well-formed seeds behave byte-identically to today (same matrix output for the committed `e2e-timings.json` and for the no-seed fallback).
- [ ] Tests for the packer cover: list `tests`, string `tests`, infinite weight, bool weight, and the well-formed control; the mcpx-test workflow's init step still emits its matrix for the committed seed.

## Dedup

Searches (all states) for "shard-packer" and "e2e-timings": #1994 (closed, built the packer), #1992/#1985/#1901 (open, other mcpx testing topics). None covers the seed-shape guards. Filed by new-issue-creator-code-b, 2026-11-06 run.

body:
## Problem

When the laptop's `/home` filesystem filled to 100% on 2026-11-06/07 (#6797), the first signal was builds dying with `No space left on device (os error 28)` mid-compile. Nothing in the fleet watches disk headroom: the cargo-target-janitor was failing silently every hour (filed separately), and no monitor reported the filesystem state at 90%, 95%, or 99%.

Measured trajectory (2026-11-07): 0–9 GiB avail (~05:05Z) → 217 MB avail (start of lane code-d's shift) → 39 GiB avail after incidental lane cleanups (05:31Z). `~/git/fleet` alone holds 604 GiB of worktrees/targets, so the swing between "fine" and "dead" is a handful of parallel Rust builds.

## Requested change (triage scopes the exact home)

Add a disk-headroom check to the fleet's existing monitoring (repo-fleet-monitor is the natural owner; triage confirms) that, hourly:

- reads `df` for the laptop `/home` filesystem,
- at ≥95% used, surfaces an alert in the monitor's normal report naming the filesystem, the avail figure, and the largest build-output consumers (the `~/git/fleet` target classes by size, e.g. top 5 directories),
- repeats/escalates at ≥98% or when avail drops under ~10 GiB regardless of percentage,
- stays silent below threshold (no new noise class in the hourly report).

## Acceptance

- The check exists in the monitor's run and its state records the last-observed used% / avail.
- A threshold crossing (or a fixture simulating one) produces exactly one alert entry naming the top consumers; a non-crossing produces none.
- The alert text distinguishes "janitor healthy but targets growing" from "janitor failing" when that state is readable from the janitor's run records.

Refs: #6797 (triage), #3372 (prior occurrence, also discovered by failure).

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] A fleet monitor/watchdog check reports laptop /home disk headroom and warns at 95% full (before ENOSPC), naming the largest target/worktree directories contributing.
- [x] The alert reaches a surface the fleet actually reads (monitor summary / watchdog log) with the measured usage, threshold, and top contributors.
- [x] The check is quiet below the threshold and does not duplicate-alert every cycle while the condition persists unchanged.

body:
## Decision needed: one ONNX Runtime version for atlas, deliberately chosen

Filed from the #6663 investigation (lane code-m, 2026-11-07). Gate A itself is now guarded against cross-version runs (PR #6764), but the underlying version split is real and still open:

- **Production corpus** was embedded by the Python pipeline (`~/atlas/v3/embed_onnx.py`) under **ONNX Runtime 1.31.1** (atlas venv). The Gate A fixtures record the same version in their provenance.
- **The live service** (`pkgs/atlas-search/default.nix`, step 5 #5355; now `fleet serve search`, #5604) bakes the nix closure's **ONNX Runtime 1.27.1** as `ATLAS_SEARCH_ORT_LIB_DEFAULT`.

Measured effect of the split (controlled re-run, amd-6, #6663): same embedder code + fixtures pass bit-identically under 1.31.1 and differ by ~1e-7 max|d| (~740–757 of 768 components) under 1.27.1. Retrieval impact of 1e-7 is negligible; the costs of the split are (a) Gate A cannot certify the production runtime as shipped, and #5604's release rule requires a Gate A run before any search-domain tag; (b) query embeddings (1.27.1) and corpus embeddings (1.31.1) come from different runtimes indefinitely, so any future drift investigation starts from a known-mismatched baseline.

## Options

1. **Bump the nix runtime to 1.31.1** (nixpkgs update or an override in `pkgs/atlas-search/default.nix`). Corpus, fixtures, gate, and service all align on the recorded version. Cheapest in artifact terms — no re-embed, no fixture ceremony. Cost: packaging work; nixpkgs' onnxruntime may lag or need an override pin.
2. **Re-embed the corpus under 1.27.1 and re-record the Gate A fixtures** through the `gen_fixtures.py` ceremony (provenance becomes 1.27.1; the PR #6764 guard follows automatically). Aligns everything on the hermetic nix version — arguably the better long-term anchor since the service is nix-deployed. Cost: a full corpus embedding pass on the laptop + fixture regeneration + re-verification of Gate A against the new fixtures.
3. **Accept the split** and downgrade Gate A to a version-matched-only gate permanently (the guard already makes this explicit). Not recommended: leaves query/corpus runtimes permanently split and the #5604 release rule effectively ceremonial.

## Recommendation

Option 1 if nixpkgs (or a tractable override) can supply 1.31.1; otherwise Option 2 as a scheduled laptop-side ceremony. Either way the end state is one version everywhere, with the gate certifying the exact runtime production ships.

Acceptance: whichever option lands, `fleet serve search`'s baked ORT version equals the Gate A fixture provenance version, and a Gate A run against the service's own `ATLAS_SEARCH_ORT_LIB_DEFAULT` library passes bit-identically.

body:
## Problem

`power-guard` never notices when its `systemd-inhibit` child dies. The daemon's only protection against UPower's single-sample CriticalPowerAction is the block inhibitor it holds while it confirms a critical reading (#1687); if that child exits, the guard keeps believing it holds the block for the rest of the process lifetime, logs nothing, and never tries to re-engage — so the machine is exactly as unguarded as if power-guard were not running, while the daemon reports a healthy state.

## Evidence

`nixos/services/power-guard/power-guard.py` @ `2bcd46e0dc`:

- `Inhibitor.engage()` (:153-173): returns immediately when `self.proc is not None` (:154-155); otherwise `Popen`s `systemd-inhibit … sleep infinity` (:160-172), discards its stdout/stderr to DEVNULL (:170-171), and logs "engaged" (:173). Nothing ever calls `poll()` / `wait()` on the child.
- `Inhibitor.held` (:183-185): `return self.proc is not None` — handle non-None is treated as lock held, regardless of whether the process is alive.
- `Inhibitor.release()` (:175-181) is the only place `self.proc` returns to `None` (plus `terminate()` without `wait()`).
- Main loop (:208-215): the low-battery path calls `inh.engage()` every poll; with a dead child every one of those calls is a no-op.

Verified this run on the laptop (probe `~/git/fleet/probe-pg-inhibit`, real `power-guard.py`, stub `systemd-inhibit` on PATH):

- Stub exits 1 immediately: after `engage()`, `inh.proc.poll() == 1` (child dead) yet `inh.held == True`; a second `engage()` did not invoke `systemd-inhibit` again (stub invocation log: exactly 1 call). The daemon would sit in this state forever.
- Control (stub `exec sleep 30`): `poll() is None`, `held == True`, `release()` clears `held` — the live path works as intended.

A child can die for ordinary reasons: `systemd-inhibit` failing to acquire the lock, the inhibitor being killed, a logind restart/reload, or the `sleep infinity` being signalled. Because stderr goes to DEVNULL, even the child's own complaint is invisible.

## Why it matters

The guard exists because of the 2026-10-28 incident (#1687): UPower hybrid-slept the laptop for 2h40m on a glitched reading. A silently dead inhibitor recreates that exact exposure with a false sense of coverage — the unit is active, the log says "INHIBIT(block sleep) engaged", and the first glitched critical sample sleeps the machine. Silent loss of a safety control is worse than the control failing loudly.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The daemon detects a dead inhibitor child (e.g. `held` reflects `poll() is None` for a real process, checked on engage and/or each poll cycle).
- [ ] On detection it acts, per a stated policy: re-engage the inhibitor (logging the death and the child's exit status loudly) and/or exit non-zero so the unit surfaces as failed — it must not continue indefinitely believing it holds a lock it does not hold.
- [ ] The child's stderr is no longer unconditionally discarded, or its exit status is logged on death, so the failure is diagnosable from the journal.
- [ ] `release()` reaps the child (`wait()` or equivalent) instead of leaving a zombie.
- [ ] Tests in `test_power_guard.py` (the suite added for #6477) cover: a child that exits immediately is detected and handled; a live child is not disturbed; the NO_INHIBIT stub path is unchanged.
- [ ] Existing power-guard tests still pass.
