body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#82 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #173

**Capability boundary (#181 collision 10):** this issue owns where "declared" ends and "enforced" begins for plugin capabilities (declarable now, enforceable later; security stays deferred). The decision is being recorded by SURFACES under `pkgs/mcpx/docs/decisions/` (in flight; linked here when it merges); point 3 of Approach C below is input to it. **Hook registration** here adopts #81's vocabulary (collision 2, recorded in the same place) rather than defining its own.

## Summary

The notes ask for a plugin tier that is not "expose some tools" but "be part of the application": register its own hooks, read and write variables, invoke internal commands that are also reachable from the CLI and from a script, call the app's public *and private* functions, and optionally detach — fork, configure its own socket, shut itself down, and keep interacting over RPC.

Most of that already exists as `/v1`, and the parts that do not are the parts that should not exist. This issue takes the bullet apart clause by clause, says which clause is already served, which needs a small named addition, and which is a request for in-process code loading that should be refused for the reasons the Go standard library gives.

## Original notes

> - plugins
>   - go/ts(/py) can directly interact with app set own hooks, get/set vars, trigger any external command internally which can be triggered outside the app or in a script, call public and private functions of app, fork configure socket shutdown and independently interact (maybe this mode also supports still get/set vars transport types rpc anything they could do inside.

## Current state (what mcpx does today, with file refs)

The clause-by-clause reading against the code:

| clause | served today | by what |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "directly interact with app" | yes | `/v1`, 60 declared operations in `internal/api/ops*.go`, over a unix socket; also as MCP tools, because every non-streaming op is proxied (`internal/cli/serve.go:344`, `v1OpTools`) |
| "set own hooks" | **no** | nothing registers a subscriber at runtime; `pool.Hooks` is Go-internal (`internal/daemon/hooks.go:24`), the bus has no registration API |
| "get/set vars" | mostly | `GET/PUT /v1/settings`, `DELETE /v1/settings/{path}` for a runtime override (`internal/api/ops_settings.go:63`); one registry gives every setting a config key, env var, flag, `/v1` path and MCP tool (`internal/settings/`). There is no *arbitrary* key-value store. |
| "trigger any external command internally, which can be triggered outside the app or in a script" | partly | adapters are exactly this for command-line programs (`internal/adapter/adapter.go`), recipes are exactly this for saved scripts (`internal/recipes/`, `mcpx prompt`, `POST /v1/intent`), and `POST /v1/exec` runs arbitrary TypeScript |
| "call public and private functions of app" | no, and see below | `/v1` *is* the public function set. There is no export of unexported Go functions and there should not be. |
| "fork configure socket shutdown and independently interact" | partly | the daemon writes `daemon-<key>.json` with `pid`/`socket`/`endpoint`; the discovery ladder (`docs/plugin-discovery.md`) is exactly "find a daemon's socket and interact independently". A *plugin* doing this to itself is new. |
| "transport types rpc" | yes | stdio, HTTP, SSE, unix socket, MCP over `/mcp`, `/v1` over the socket |

Two observations that decide most of the design:

- **`/v1` is already the plugin API.** `internal/api/ops.go` opens with the rule: "anything the CLI can do can be done from a plugin, from /v1, and from MCP", enforced by a parity test. A plugin given `MCPX_SOCKET` has the whole surface, in any language, with an OpenAPI document (`internal/api/openapi.go`) to generate a client from. That is a better answer to "interact with the app" than any in-process API, because it is already written, already tested for parity, and already reachable from a script, the CLI, a harness plugin and curl.
- **"private functions" is the one genuinely incoherent clause.** In Go there is no mechanism to expose unexported functions to a dynamically loaded object; `plugin.Open` resolves *exported* symbols only, and even for those the toolchain/dependency-identity requirements make it unusable (see the plugin-model sibling issue, which quotes `go doc plugin` in full). The useful reading is not "unexported Go functions" but "operations that exist inside mcpx and are not on `/v1` yet" — and the fix for those is to put them on `/v1`, where the CLI and MCP get them too. #76 is already that work for five operations.

## Approaches

### Approach A — least recommended: an in-process extension API, via `plugin.Open` or an exported Go interface with reflection

Load the plugin into the daemon and hand it a `*daemon.Registry`, the `*events.Bus`, the settings store and an escape hatch for everything else. This is the literal reading of the bullet and it is the one to refuse.

Mechanically it cannot work portably: `go doc plugin` states plugins are "supported only on Linux, FreeBSD, and macOS", that a plugin "cannot be closed", and that "runtime crashes are likely to occur unless all parts of the program ... are compiled using exactly the same version of the toolchain, the same build tags, and the same values of certain flags", plus "unless all common dependencies of the application and its plugins are built from exactly the same source code". It requires cgo and external linking, so the daemon could never again be built as a static `CGO_ENABLED=0` binary — which it can be today (#182 verified one), even though the shipped nix package and Containerfile use cgo by choice (#136).

Design-wise it is worse than it is mechanically. Handing a plugin the registry makes every internal type part of the public API forever: `pool.Pool`, `events.Bus`, `elicit.Broker` and `settings.Store` could not be refactored without breaking plugins built against the last release. A plugin that panics kills the daemon and every pooled instance under it. And it creates a second, parallel capability surface that the `/v1` parity test does not cover, which is precisely the drift `internal/api/ops.go` was written to prevent.

The only thing it buys is the "private functions" clause, which is the clause with no real requirement behind it.

### Approach B — middle: extend `/v1` with the missing verbs, and stop there

Take the clauses that are not served and add them as ordinary operations, with no new plugin concept at all:

- **`set own hooks`** → hook registration on the daemon: register a subscriber with a filter and a target, list them, remove them. The target for a plugin is one of its own MCP tools, which means the daemon calls back into the plugin through the same connection it already has. This is the runtime twin of the config-declared hook table in the hooks sibling issue, and must share its vocabulary and its `events.Filter`.
- **`get/set vars`** → either settings (typed, validated, already there) or a genuinely new scratch store. Almost every real use is "a plugin wants to remember something across calls", which is a namespaced key-value store keyed by plugin and optionally by session, with a declared lifetime. Keep it *out* of the settings registry: the registry's value is that every key is declared, documented, flagged and env-var'd, and an arbitrary plugin key has none of those properties. Two stores with different guarantees, clearly named, beats one store that is sometimes typed.
- **`trigger any external command internally`** → this is a *named command* registry: a thing with a name, declared inputs, and an implementation that may be a command, a script, a recipe or a plugin tool — invocable from the CLI, from `/v1`, from MCP and from a script, which is exactly what "can be triggered outside the app or in a script" asks for. mcpx has three partial versions of this already (adapters, recipes, `/v1` op tools); the honest move is to notice they are the same thing viewed three ways.
- **`fork configure socket shutdown`** → nothing new is needed for a plugin to fork: it is a process, it may fork. What it needs is a way to *tell* the daemon "I have moved; reach me at this socket" — a re-address, which is a small addition to the plugin handshake, plus an orderly "I am going away" so the daemon drops the namespace rather than logging a crash.

B is the right *content*. Its weakness is that it treats the plugin as an API consumer with no identity: there is no answer to "which plugin registered this hook", "whose variables are these", "who may call this", and no way to tear a plugin's registrations down when it exits. That gap gets filled ad hoc by whoever hits it first.

### Approach C — recommended: B, with a plugin session as the unit of identity and lifetime

Same verbs as B, but every one of them is scoped to a **plugin session**: an identity the daemon issues when a plugin connects (or that a detached plugin presents), carried on every `/v1` call the plugin makes, and the key under which everything it created is tracked.

```
plugin connects (spawned, or dials in)
  → daemon issues a plugin session id + the socket endpoint
  → plugin registers hooks, publishes events, stores vars, declares commands
  → all of it keyed by that session
plugin exits or detaches-and-dies
  → every registration it owns is dropped, atomically
```

What falls out of that one decision:

1. **Teardown is automatic.** A crashed plugin does not leave a hook pointing at a dead socket, which is the failure mode B walks into.
2. **`mcpx ls` / `/v1/status` can answer "what is extending this daemon".** Which hooks, which commands, which namespaces, and who owns each. A plugin system you cannot introspect is one you cannot debug.
3. **Capabilities become declarable.** The plugin manifest says what it intends to use — hooks, settings-write, server-add, exec, events-publish — and the daemon can report and later enforce that. Declaring is useful even before enforcing, because it is documentation the daemon can print.
4. **Detachment is a first-class transition, not a trick.** "fork configure socket shutdown and independently interact" becomes: the plugin forks, the child presents the same plugin session id on a new connection, the daemon re-points the namespace and the hooks at it, and the parent exits cleanly. The re-address is one operation and the session is what makes it safe. The discovery ladder already solves the inverse — a plugin finding the daemon — so both directions exist (`docs/plugin-discovery.md`).
5. **The "call private functions" clause gets a real answer.** A plugin may call every declared operation, and anything it wants that is not declared is a missing declaration to be added to `internal/api/ops*.go` — where the CLI and MCP get it too, and the parity test keeps it honest. State this as policy in the issue: **there is no private surface; there is a surface and a backlog.** #76 is the existing instance of that backlog.
6. **A plugin may publish to the bus.** Its events carry its identity, so a hook can subscribe to `plugin.<name>.*` and the whole thing composes. This is what makes plugin-to-plugin extension work without a plugin-to-plugin protocol.

Recommended because it costs one concept — a session — and turns a list of loosely related verbs into a system with lifetimes, ownership and introspection, without loading a single line of foreign code into the daemon's address space. It also keeps every existing guarantee: one capability surface, one parity test, one crash domain per process.

The cost is honesty about what is deferred: capability *enforcement* is security work and is out of scope here; the plugin session must be designed so enforcement can be added later without changing the shape.

## Open questions

- Is a plugin session the same object as the existing session concept used for leasing, attribution and elicitation routing (`--session`, `MCPX_SESSION_ID`, `_meta["ai.opencode/sessionID"]` per #47)? They have different lifetimes and probably should not be unified, but they must be distinguishable in logs and events.
- Variables: namespaced-per-plugin only, or is a shared namespace wanted so two plugins can coordinate? Shared is requested eventually and is a coupling nobody can undo.
- Do variables persist across daemon restarts? A plugin that caches an auth handle wants yes; a daemon that must be stateless wants no. Probably: declared per key, with in-memory as the default.
- What exactly may a runtime-registered hook be attached to — only `observe` phase, or the blocking phases too? A blocking hook whose target is a plugin that may vanish is a hang waiting to happen; scoping to a plugin session is what makes that recoverable.
- "trigger any external command internally which can be triggered outside the app or in a script" — should the named-command registry subsume adapters and recipes, or sit beside them? Subsuming is right and is a larger, separate piece of work.
- Detachment: does a detached plugin still count against pooling and idle reaping? It has no pooled process any more, so probably it becomes a `url`-shaped server pointing at a unix socket — which is the `unix://` transport question from the plugin-model issue.
- Does the daemon ever *restart* a plugin, or is that the user's problem? The pool restarts servers; a detached plugin cannot be restarted by definition.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease:** L — the verbs are individually small, the session, ownership and teardown are the real work. **Impact:** med-high; high if plugins land, near zero without them.

**Depends on / related:** #80 (the plugin loader; this is meaningless without it), #81 (runtime registration adopts its vocabulary, collision 2), #84 (a detached plugin becomes a `unix://` server — its transport), #76 (operations that exist on `/v1` but not on the CLI — the same parity argument runs the other way here), #6 (event store: a plugin publishing to the bus should land there; gap contract, collision 13), #87 (a plugin session's lifetime should follow the same touch-on-read rule), #112 (another hook list adopting #81's vocabulary), #48, #5, #77.

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

milestone.description: mcpx platform program: one canonical mcpx in developing-today/code - dedup, scope-resolved roots, module consolidation, MCP server parity.

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#154 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #98

## Summary

The compendium's research chapter holds what was learned while building mcpx, and while doing anything else in this repository, filed so it is not lost in session transcripts. It has four parts:

1. A section outline for every topic note 91 names.
2. A large standalone **Nix** section that does not need to mention mcpx.
3. A seed list of findings that already exist in the repository, with file references.
4. A harvesting process and a quality bar, so findings from sessions, PRs and issues keep arriving and stay trustworthy.

Scope, recorded as the note gives it: fiction is **allowed, not requested**. The deliverable is "an overview intro and reference website and manual".

## Original notes

> - documentation
>   - make a book using whatever is the most common and simple modern choice
>     - 3 main things, not book sections jsut like levels of detail-
>       - the compendium
>         - you dont have to just put strict mcpx things here
>           - any research or incidental findings into ai, llm, harnesses, plugins, token providers, cloudflare, the typescript ecosystem, SSE, sockets/rpc/websockets/tcp/mcp/openapi/rest/oauth/command-line, really whatever you come across or we talk about. compendium can have an entire section on nix that is a hundred pages and doesnt mention mpcx at all. you could write a short science fiction in there and i wouldnt mind. i'm not asking you to write a short science fiction story i'm asking for an overview intro and reference website and manual.

Note 91's last sentence ("i'm asking for an overview intro and reference website and manual") describes the whole book, not just this chapter. It is recorded here because it is part of the line, and it is also relevant to #89.

## Current state

Findings exist, but they are spread across feature entries, design docs, commit messages and PR descriptions. Nothing collects them by topic, and nothing marks which ones are measured, which are read from a source, and which are hearsay. `docs/ideas.md` already has the discipline this chapter needs ("an answer that only exists in a conversation is lost"), but only for design questions.

## Section outline, with seed findings

Every seed below already exists in the repository. File references are to `pkgs/mcpx` on `main` unless another path is given.

| Section (note 91 term) | Seed findings |
| --- | --- |
| **AI and LLMs** | **Cost model**: `ls` ~171 tokens, `search` ~61, `types` 675-4,402 per namespace (`docs/story.md` "Zero-context discovery"). **Cloudflare's argument** that models write code better than they call tools, because tool-call tokens are synthetic training data (blog.cloudflare.com/code-mode). **MCP client best-practices**: switch to progressive discovery at 1-5% of the context window; mutating the `tools` array mid-conversation invalidates the provider's prompt cache (modelcontextprotocol.io client best-practices). |
| **Harnesses** | **Harnesses and plugins**: `docs/opencode-plugin.md` (opencode v1 vs v2, and which parts are opencode's rather than general); `story.md` "The harness knows what the agent does not" and "Statistics from opencode"; `AGENTS.md` as the cross-harness instruction file; #48 harness-free core (codex, claude code, pi, manus). **opencode code mode**: v1 ships it behind `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE` (`OPENCODE-V2.md` correction block). |
| **Plugins** | **Plugin without the binary**: `docs/plugin-discovery.md` (the connection ladder, `GET /v1/resolve`) and #44 (fixed in #53). **Plugin logging**: the plugin logs over the socket (#36). **Plugin install**: `plugin/opencode/README.md`. |
| **Token providers** | Ambiguous (see open questions). **Model providers**: this repository patches opencode for them (`opencode-copilot-business-support.patch`, `opencode-copilot-compaction-fix.patch`, `opencode-openai-response-id-caching.patch` at the repo root) and has skills to maintain those patches. **Credential providers**: `story.md` "Credentials". |
| **Cloudflare** | **Code Mode mechanics**: Worker Loader API isolates; `fetch()`/`connect()` throw; bindings hide API keys from generated code. Shared with #153. |
| **The TypeScript ecosystem** | **Node type stripping**: Node v24.20.0 runs TypeScript by stripping types, erasable syntax only. A file with `enum` fails. Constructor parameter properties failed too, which is why the generated client uses plain fields (`ASSESSMENT.md` bug 3; `story.md` "Runtime portability"). **Runtime detection** is deno, then bun, then node (`script.runtime`, `--runtime`, `MCPX_SCRIPT_RUNTIME`). **`--typecheck`** runs `deno check`, Deno only, ~80 ms repeat, ~400 ms for a new program (#79). **`ts-morph`**: constructing a TypeScript compiler per request was lootbox's memory problem (`ASSESSMENT.md`). The runtime comparison belongs in #101 (`docs/runtimes.md`). Versions here: Deno 2.9.6, Bun 1.3.11. |
| **SSE** | **SSE over WebSockets**: `story.md` "Server-sent events, not WebSockets": SSE is plain HTTP, `EventSource` reconnects on its own, and WebSocket upgrades are mishandled by middleboxes. **Reconnection**: "Lossless reconnection". |
| **Sockets, TCP** | **Transport costs**: `story.md` "What each transport costs": spawning `mcpx status` 23.12 ms, unix socket keep-alive 0.17 ms (135x), TCP loopback keep-alive 0.65 ms. **Socket path limit**: macOS `sun_path` is 104 bytes, and deep state dirs failed with `bind: invalid argument` (`ASSESSMENT.md` bug 4). **Loopback address**: `localhost` resolved to IPv6 only while the compiled build bound `127.0.0.1` (`ASSESSMENT.md`). |
| **RPC, WebSockets** | **JSON-RPC framing** is standard library (`docs/dependencies.md`). **Lootbox's WebSocket**: lootbox used a WebSocket RPC channel (`lootbox.config.json` `serverUrl: ws://127.0.0.1:9420/ws`). |
| **MCP** | **Protocol eras**: `story.md` "Two protocol eras" and "What 2026-07-28 actually asks of a client". **Revision matrix**: `docs/protocol.md`, every revision in both directions, plus "What is still missing". **Sampling bug**: `story.md` "Sampling" -> "It did not work, and nothing said so". Capabilities are declared in the handshake, but the handler was installed after it, and every test called the passthrough directly. **Elicitation bug**: "The bug that came first". **Doctor**: "mcpx doctor" -> "It found a bug immediately". **Remote transport**: "Remote servers without a shim" (Streamable HTTP, no `mcp-remote`). **Registry**: the official one publishes an OpenAPI spec; HAPI is not open source and returns 404 (`story.md` "Which registry"). |
| **OpenAPI, REST** | **Specs as tools**: `story.md` "Specifications as tools" -> "Two things easy to get wrong": a relative server URL must resolve against the document's location, and only read methods are exposed by default. **Wrong spec**: "The specification described the wrong thing": the spec described mcpx's ten tools, not the hundreds it fronts. **Ops table**: one table generates the routes, MCP tools and OpenAPI (`internal/api/ops*.go`). |
| **OAuth** | **Status**: `story.md` "Credentials"; "OAuth for remote servers" is `status: proposed`. |
| **Command line** | **CLIs as servers**: `story.md` "Command-line programs as servers". **Derived flag names**: `daemon.leaseTTL` becomes `--daemon-lease-t-t-l` (`docs/configuration.md:216`). **Ignored flags**: accepted and ignored (#74, fixed by #75). **Help coverage**: `internal/cli/manual.go` `Commands()` lists 32 commands, but `cmd/mcpx/main.go`'s dispatch table also routes `man`, `completion`, `serve`, `openapi`, `adapter`, `registry` and `api`, so help/man do not list them. |

### The Nix section (need not mention mcpx)

A hundred pages is allowed. The seeds below are real, and several are not about mcpx at all.

**Go on Nix.**

- **`vendorHash` repair.** Renovate can bump `go.mod` but cannot compute the vendored-tree hash, so every Go dependency bump broke the Nix build and "merged silently". `.github/workflows/mcpx.yml` blanks the hash, reads `got: sha256-...` from the failed build, commits it back to bot branches only, and fails any PR that still does not build.
- **Sandbox tests.** `package.nix` sets `subPackages = [ "cmd/mcpx" ]`, which confines `go test` to a package with no tests. So `checkPhase` lists the internal packages explicitly: a new package is untested in the sandbox until someone adds it there (`package.nix:69`).
- **Pure-Go SQLite.** Using `modernc.org/sqlite` instead of cgo keeps the derivation free of a C toolchain and keeps cross-compilation working (`docs/dependencies.md` "Why this driver").

**Wrapping and generated artefacts.**

- `wrapProgram --suffix PATH` with git, deno, `bun-bin` and nodejs, so behaviour does not depend on the calling shell. git is there because `repo`/`worktree` scopes are silently weaker without it.
- The man page and shell completions are generated by the just-built binary in `postInstall` ("A man page maintained separately is wrong within two releases").

**Beyond mcpx: this repository.**

- The nix-darwin flake layout, homebrew brews/casks/masApps.
- Custom packages (`pkgs/`: `bun-bin`, `codedb`, `flake-tidy`, `opencode-share`, `opencode2`, ...).
- Patching opencode from the flake, and keeping those patches alive across updates (the `update-opencode` and `fix-opencode-patches` skills).
- The justfile workflow.
- Renovate on a flake.

**Containers and CI (seeds from #182; not Nix-specific).**

- **Static Go builds.** `os/user` and `net` pull in libc only under cgo. `CGO_ENABLED=0` produced a fully static linux binary of the same size (within ~100 bytes) that still runs `exec` (`docs/container.md` section 4). The cost is Linux-only: pure-Go `os/user` reads `/etc/passwd` instead of NSS, and the pure-Go resolver ignores `nsswitch.conf`. On macOS, since Go 1.20, `net` and `os/user` use the system libraries without cgo, so the flag changes nothing there.
- **Where image size goes.** In `debian:bookworm-slim`, `git` with `--no-install-recommends` costs 105 MB, more than bun (79 MB), because Debian's git depends on perl (`docs/container.md` section 5).
- **`actions/setup-go` in a monorepo.** Without `cache-dependency-path` it looks for `go.sum` at the repository root, logs "Restore cache failed: Dependencies file is not found" on every run, and never restores (`.github/workflows/mcpx.yml:46-50`, fixed in #182).
- **Test daemons must be stopped the way they record themselves.** Plain `stop` recomputes the socket path from the environment, which a long state path moves elsewhere, so e2e daemons survived for hours (#52, closed). The fix stops them through the info files they write (`stop --all`) and sets a short idle exit as a backstop (`internal/e2e/e2e_test.go:61-83`, #182).

**macOS findings.**

- **The temp-dir sweep.** The per-user temp directory `/var/folders/.../T/` is swept by the OS. That silently destroyed ~3,000 tracked files across git worktrees, while `git status` reported clean from a stale fsmonitor index (`instructions/worktrees.md`).
- **macOS-only tests.** Two tests only passed on macOS (#35).

### Scope note on fiction

"you could write a short science fiction in there and i wouldnt mind. i'm not asking you to write a short science fiction story". Recorded as scope: **allowed, not requested**. If anything like it is ever written, it is labelled as fiction, kept out of search results mixed with facts, and left out of the agent twin (#120). Nothing in this issue produces it.

## Approaches: how findings get here

- **A -- write them up when someone remembers (least recommended).** This is today's process. Findings stay in session transcripts, PR bodies and commit messages. The ones in feature entries are organised by feature, not topic. Nothing marks a measurement as stale. A reader cannot tell a verified number from a guess. It costs nothing, and that is roughly what it recovers.
- **B -- issues labelled `research`, compiled by hand into pages.** GitHub is the intake: any session, PR or person files an issue (or comments with a link) under the existing `research` label, and someone periodically writes pages from them. Intake is better and discussion can thread, but compilation is manual. Issues close and get forgotten, and the page format is undefined, so the quality varies.
- **C -- a findings entry format, a label for intake, and a harvest step (recommended).**
  - **Entry format.** Reuse the runbook key block, so #150/#151 tooling (IDs, `since`, `changed`, history) works unchanged:

    ```
    created:      2026-09-29T15:00:00-05:00
    last-updated: 2026-09-29T15:00:00-05:00
    status:       verified
    tags:         topic:mcp, topic:sampling, area:protocol
    sources:      docs/story.md#sampling, 28f2cdc (#39)
    checked:      mcpx 0.1.0 @ d0b7e01
    description:  a capability handler installed after the handshake is never offered.
    ```

    `status` gets finding-specific values: `verified` (reproduced here), `measured` (with environment), `read-in-source`, `reported` (someone else's claim, cited), `hearsay`, `superseded` (struck through, not deleted, per the runbook's "Never delete an entry"). `topic:` is a new tag key alongside the runbook's `area`, `platform` and `cost`.
  - **Intake.** A `finding` label, or the existing `research` label, on issues and PRs. A PR template line: "Anything learned that is not about this change? Link or label it." And a sentence in the agent instruction files telling agents to file a `finding` issue for a verified surprise, not bury it in a transcript.
  - **Harvest.** A per-release runbook step moves labelled items into topic pages as entries and closes the issues with a link. A finding stays an issue until it is written up, so nothing is lost in between.

  C reuses every mechanism the compendium already needs and makes provenance explicit.

## Quality bar for an encyclopedia entry

- **Sources.** Every claim has at least one: a file with line, a commit, an issue, or an external URL with the date it was read.
- **Measurements.** A measurement carries its environment (machine, OS, runtime and tool versions) and the command that produced it, following the story's rule "re-run the command, paste the result".
- **Provenance.** Say how it is known: reproduced, read in source, read in docs, or someone said so. Never let hearsay read like a measurement.
- **Dates.** Every entry is dated, and a re-check updates `checked`. When an entry is wrong, strike or supersede it with a link. Never edit it silently; the history (#150) shows the change.
- **Standalone.** Where possible an entry is readable without mcpx context. That is the point of the Nix section.

## Open questions

1. "token providers": model providers (Copilot, Anthropic, OpenAI and the opencode patches for them), credential/OAuth token providers, or both? The outline assumes both.
2. Does the Nix section live in this book, or in a separate book for the whole `dezren39/nix` repo that this one links to? The mcpx book is a project site inside a monorepo (#117, #118), and a hundred-page Nix section is about the monorepo, not mcpx.
3. A new `finding` label, or reuse `research`?
4. One page per topic with many entries, or one page per finding?
5. Should findings stated inside feature entries (the sampling bug, transport costs) move here, or be excerpted here with the feature entry as the source of truth? The latter avoids two copies.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** L (ongoing; the first cut of the outline plus seeds is M) · **Impact** med · **Depends on / related**: #150 and #151 (entry format, history), #152 (chapter placement), #153 (Cloudflare and opencode overlap), #117 and #118 (where a Nix section is published), #120 (fiction and hearsay excluded from the agent twin), #101 (runtimes comparison), #48 (harness-free core), #79 (typecheck timing), #74 (closed, fixed in #75: flags accepted and ignored), #134 and #136 (container and platform findings).

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

body:
## Bug

`bin/sync-models.mjs` — the "existing model" update branches judge drift by `limit.context` only, so two kinds of drift are **never reconciled** and the sync reports the config up-to-date while it stays wrong:

- `bin/sync-models.mjs:543` (antigravity-agy / antigravity-ls): `if (prov.models[baseId].limit?.context !== limits.context)` — the whole `limit` object is replaced only when `context` differs. If `context` already matches, a wrong or stale `limit.output` (the sync's own desired values come from `defaultLimits`, `bin/sync-models.mjs:488-492`: claude 64000, gpt-oss 16384, otherwise 65536) is kept forever.
- `bin/sync-models.mjs:538`: variants are written only when the existing entry has none (`&& !prov.models[baseId].variants`). If a model's effort set changes upstream (an effort dropped or added), an existing `variants` map is never updated: stale efforts stay offered and new efforts never appear.
- `bin/sync-models.mjs:583` (openai-codex): the same shape — `if (codexProv.models[m.slug].limit?.context !== 1000000)` — so a codex entry with the right context but any other `output` than the sync's 128000 is never corrected.

Because no edit is recorded for these cases, the run's summary counts no update, and a later run sees the same state and again does nothing: the sync does not converge.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-laneB-syncmodels/probe.mjs` (node v24; source `bin/sync-models.mjs` sha256 `5e21fe06…` on the laptop, identical to sandbox main `e91098f1`; all three condition strings asserted present verbatim, then the two branches copied verbatim and run over fixtures):

```text
A control context-drift: changed=true limit={"context":1048576,"output":65536}
B agy output-drift: changed=false limit={"context":1048576,"output":9999} (desired output 65536)
C agy variants-drift: changed=false variants=["low"] (desired high,medium)
D codex output-drift: changed=false limit={"context":1000000,"output":1} (desired output 128000)
E control codex context-drift: changed=true limit={"context":1000000,"output":128000}
BUG CONFIRMED: output-limit and variants drift are never reconciled when context matches
```

Controls A/E show the branches do fire when `context` differs (and fix `output` only as a side effect of replacing the whole object); B/C/D show that with `context` already correct, nothing ever fires.

## Why it matters

`sync-models` is the tool that keeps the opencode config's model entries honest against the live catalogs. An entry whose output limit was set wrong — by a hand edit, an older sync with different defaults, or a changed `defaultLimits` — is silently permanent, and the operator is told "All providers are already up-to-date". The same holds for the reasoning-effort variants a model is offered with: once written, they are frozen at whatever the first sync saw.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The agy/ls update branch reconciles the full desired state: if the existing `limit` differs from `defaultLimits(id)` in `context` **or** `output`, the limit is replaced (one edit, counted as an update); if the existing `variants` differ from the variants built from the current effort set, they are replaced the same way.
- [ ] The codex update branch likewise fires when `output` differs from 128000, not only when `context` differs from 1000000.
- [ ] Regression tests in `bin/sync-models.test.mjs` (verbatim-extraction style, as for `parseJsonc`): output-only drift is corrected, variants drift is corrected, and an already-correct entry records no edit.
- [ ] A genuinely up-to-date entry still produces no edits and no count changes (no write churn on every run).

Found by new-issue-creator-code-b. Dedup: `gh issue list --search 'sync-models'` (open + closed) on 2026-10-28 shows only #704 (parseJsonc), #591 (Nix store path), #1754 (provider-catalog-sync, a different script) and unrelated mentions — nothing on limit/variants reconciliation.

body:
## The gap (found in fleet review, 2026-10-27)

The PR diff reviewers (`pr-diff-review` + `pr-diff-review-b`) are static: they read commits and diffs, verify findings against current main *by reading*, and file issues. They never execute the changed behavior. A regression that only appears at runtime — a config interaction, a timing/ordering effect, a behavior that typechecks and reads correctly but acts wrong — is invisible to them and is caught later, by CI if the suite happens to cover it, or by the fleet fixing it after it lands.

The fleet already pays for this gap in the other direction: several of the queue's small_fix tasks in October were follow-up fixes for behavior that a diff read as fine.

## Scope (assess per repo, then build the bounded version or record why not)

- Design a bounded runtime-verification step for high-risk findings only: when a reviewer files a finding it labels high-risk (a named risk class in the packet — e.g. behavior-change-no-test, config/routing touch, data-path change), a verification pass runs the touched package's targeted tests on the laptop against the PR head (or against main + the diff's scenario where a PR head isn't runnable) and attaches the result to the finding's issue — turning "reads wrong" into "reproduces" or "does not reproduce" before a solver lane picks it up.
- Bound it hard: targeted tests only, laptop or CI only (never the sandbox), per-run cap in line with the reviewer batch caps, and no verification step for findings that are already test-covered or purely structural.
- Per-repo verdict required: for each of the four repos, either the lane operates there or the issue records why CI coverage makes it unnecessary there (suite strength, runtime surface, cost).
- Guardrail interaction: reviewers still never fix and never merge; verification output is evidence on the issue, and the queue keeps owning the fix.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A per-repo assessment exists (comment on this issue): CI coverage strength vs the runtime-regression classes the static review has missed, with 2–3 concrete past examples.
- [ ] The high-risk finding class is defined and the reviewer instructions name it (labels/packet field).
- [ ] A verification pass is demonstrated on at least one real finding end-to-end (laptop, targeted tests, result attached to the issue), or the per-repo record shows why it is unnecessary in every repo.

Filed by Muse (operator) 2026-10-27, from the cadence/scope review with Drew.

body:
## What happened (2026-10-27, fixed ~02:29 CDT)

The AA explorer page (`/aa` + `/api/aa.json`, shipped in #1250) showed `{"status":"absent","reason":"no AA explorer section in the fleet feed yet"}` even though the aggregator deploy was current and a manual collector run at 00:29 CDT produced a perfect AA section (138 rankings / 1,144 thresholds / 35 configs / 183 test runs).

**Root cause: the feed's actual producer is not the laptop deploy — it's the sandbox clone `~/git/pm-feed`.** `fleet-feed-collector.timer` (sandbox, ~5 min) runs `~/git/pm-feed/pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/push-fleet-feed.sh`, which collects in that clone and scp's the result to the laptop. The clone sat at merge-of-#994 (`14dd66b6`); its collector (18,570 bytes) predates the AA section entirely — zero `ainventory` references — so every push overwrote the laptop feed with a section-less one. The 00:29 good run came from `~/pm-stack-update/aggregator` (the deploy working copy), which the timer never executes.

## Fix applied tonight (operational, not in this repo)

- `git merge --ff-only origin/main` in `~/git/pm-feed` (`14dd66b6` → `3a32780c`, includes #1250). Collector is now the merged 25,633-byte version.
- The clone is a **sparse checkout** (only `pm-stack/aggregator`); the new collector reads `.opencode/opencode.jsonc` at the repo root for the AA coverage lists and failed soft ("opencode.jsonc unreadable; AA coverage omitted"). Added `.opencode` to the sparse checkout.
- Verified end-to-end: collector summary `aa 138 rankings / 35 configs / 183 test runs`, feed pushed, `/api/aa.json` → `status: ok` with coverage (4 lists), `/aa` + board HTTP 200.

## Why this will recur

Nothing keeps `~/git/pm-feed` current: laptop deploys (`pm-stack-update` + `install.sh`) refresh the server, but the producer clone only moves when a human fast-forwards it. It drifted ~250 PRs behind silently — the only symptom was a dashboard section going "absent", and the stale collector can't even log the new design's loud `collector: AA section absent (...)` error because it doesn't contain that code.

## Proposed durable fix (pick one)

1. **Updater step:** a tiny `pm-feed-sync` oneshot (or a pre-step in `install-collector-units.sh`'s units) that `git fetch` + `merge --ff-only`s the feed clone before collector runs — never auto-resolving, failing loud on divergence. Must not edit the running push script in place mid-run (pull in a separate unit, then start the collector).
2. **Staleness guard in `push-fleet-feed.sh`:** before collecting, compare clone HEAD to `origin/main`; if behind by more than N commits, log a loud journal error (and optionally stamp the feed with the producer commit so `/api` can surface "producer is stale").
3. **Feed provenance:** embed the collector's git HEAD in the feed envelope (`generatedAt` already exists); the aggregator's absent/stale states could then name the producer commit.

Option 1 is probably the real fix; 2 is the cheapest loud tripwire. Also worth documenting in the aggregator README that the producer is the sandbox feed clone, not the laptop working copy — that fact cost most of the diagnosis time.

## Acceptance criteria

- A durable mechanism (updater step, staleness guard, or equivalent) keeps the sandbox `~/git/pm-feed` producer clone current with `origin/main`, or fails loud in the journal when it cannot — never silently pushing a section-less feed again.
- The feed envelope or `/api` surface can name the producer commit, so a stale producer is diagnosable from the feed itself.
- The aggregator README documents that the producer is the sandbox feed clone, not the laptop working copy.
- Verified end-to-end: after a simulated stale-clone state, the next collector cycle either self-heals or reports the staleness loudly, and `/api/aa.json` returns `status: ok`.

The babysitter (#1185) will run on the sandbox and watch sessions on the
laptop's OpenChamber over Tailscale. OpenChamber's remote access model

  session reads, session-activity, quota reads, message injection

  name in the babysitter's config and docs — never a value in a file,

  per route) in the API inventory doc; mark any route that still
  refuses and why.

      projects and sessions and reads one session's activity

body:
Part of epic #1184 (PM stack coherence — ideal-system design series, 2026-10-26).

## Why
The stack's own reliability is currently vibes: pages degrade silently, the watchdog concept (#1148) alerts after the fact, and common failures (collector stopped, feed not pushed, a facet down) wait for a human or an hourly job. The ideal stack declares per-facet freshness SLOs with error budgets on the health page, and the watchdog remediates the known failure classes itself — restart the collector, re-push the feed, re-render config — escalating to Drew only when remediation fails or budget burns.

## Design questions to answer
- SLO definitions per facet (feed age, quota read age, orchestration freshness, per-service up): targets, windows, and how budget remaining is computed and displayed.
- Remediation catalogue: which failures are auto-fixable (collector restart, feed re-push, aggregator restart, tunnel restart), with what guardrails, attempt caps, and cooldowns?
- Verification after remediation: how does the watchdog prove the fix worked before standing down, and where is the attempt logged?
- Escalation: what pages Drew (via the PWA/push design) vs lands in NEEDS ORCHESTRATOR, and how does a burning error budget change that threshold?
- Safety: what the watchdog must never do (data writes, deploys, credential changes) and how its own failure is detected.

## Acceptance
- Design note landed in repo `doc/` + implementation issues filed and linked as sub-issues of #1184; open questions needing Drew named explicitly in the design note.

## Acceptance criteria

- A design note answering every question listed under "Design questions to answer" is landed in the repo `doc/` tree and linked from this issue.
- Implementation issues are filed and linked as sub-issues of epic #1184 (developing-today/code), each with its own acceptance criteria — this design issue does not itself carry implementation work.
- Every open question that needs Drew is named explicitly in the design note (not buried in prose).
- The remediation catalogue carries per-action guardrails, attempt caps, and cooldowns, and the design names what the watchdog must never do (data writes, deploys, credential changes).

body:
## Pilot — OpenClaw integration, information gathering

The long-term design (OpenChamber dispatch + babysitter design,
2026-10-26) ends at babysitting-by-comment for OpenClaw: the monitor
posts a routine status-request comment on the issue; OpenClaw sees it,
answers with its session report in the thread, and acts on
instructions left there — GitHub as the bus, no API polling of the
gateway. This pilot proves or kills that loop on ONE issue before
anything is built on it.

## Run

- One real but low-risk task owned by an OpenClaw session (the gateway
  install landed via PR #1025, 2026-10-26).
- The monitor (a human-driven pass by Muse is fine for the pilot)
  posts a status-request comment in the agreed format.
- Measure: does OpenClaw notice, how fast, and does its reply contain
  the fields the babysitter needs (progress verdict, pool/route used,
  quota left, blockers)?
- Then post an instruction comment (checkpoint, then continue; or hand
  back) and record whether it is obeyed precisely.
- Cost the loop: tokens/messages per check-in round vs an API-driven
  babysitter round over the same session.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A written pilot report: loop latency, reply completeness against
      the babysitter's field list, instruction obedience, cost per
      round, failure modes seen.
- [ ] A go / no-go recommendation for mirror mode (babysitter posts
      verdicts as comments for OpenClaw locations), with the comment
      format pinned if go.
- [ ] Any OpenClaw-side setup the loop needs is listed as concrete
      follow-up work, not left as folklore.

Filed by Muse (operator) 2026-10-26 at Drew's direction.

Read replicas that follow a world's journal over a signed stream. A world keeps a single writer, so there are no write conflicts. Replicas serve spectators and survive the writer being offline. The rollback and format rules from F11.12 apply to the stream.

body:
## Finding

PR #530 added U+200C (ZWNJ) and U+200D (ZWJ) to the container validator's `_IDNA_DISALLOWED` set, so `validate_crawl_url` now refuses **every** host containing a zero-width joiner — including hosts where the joiner is in a valid joining context and IDNA/UTS-46 (with `CheckJoiners`, as the WHATWG URL parser applies it) accepts it.

ZWNJ/ZWJ are not DISALLOWED in IDNA2008; they are CONTEXTJ (RFC 5892 Appendix A.1/A.2):

- **ZWJ (U+200D)** is allowed when the preceding character has Canonical_Combining_Class 230 (a virama) — the standard Indic conjunct spelling, e.g. Devanagari क + ् + ZWJ + य.
- **ZWNJ (U+200C)** is allowed after a virama, or in a valid Arabic-script joining context — routine in ordinary Persian words, e.g. می‌خواهم.

PR #530's own regression test only pins the no-context case (`exam<ZWJ>ple.com`, comment: "no joining context here"), which both validators do refuse — but the implementation is a blanket `ord(c) in _IDNA_DISALLOWED` check with no context evaluation.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/530 (merged, commit `43a89a81`, merge `a8a3bf7e`)
- `pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py` on current main: `_IDNA_DISALLOWED` (line ~55) contains `0x200C, 0x200D`, and the forbidden-character check refuses any host containing them, with no CONTEXTJ context rule.
- Verified on current main (`a8a3bf7e`) with the actual `validate_crawl_url` from `container/app.py`:
  - `http://क्‍य.com/` (U+0915 U+094D U+200D U+092F) → **refused**: "refusing to crawl host with a forbidden character"
  - `http://می‌خواهم.com/` (with U+200C in joining context) → **refused**, same error
  - `http://exam<ZWJ>ple.com/` → refused (correct — matches the Worker)
- Verified the Worker side with the WHATWG URL parser (Node `new URL`, the same UTS-46 + CheckJoiners processing the Worker's `validateCrawlUrl` in `pkgs/lab-ops-hub/src/lib.ts` relies on — it has no joiner check of its own):
  - `http://क्‍य.com/` → accepted, hostname `xn--11b6c9d222i.com`
  - `http://می‌خواهم.com/` → accepted, hostname `xn--mgbn2ecje63gr19l.com`
  - `http://exam<ZWJ>ple.com/` and `http://exam<ZWNJ>ple.com/` → rejected, matching the container

## Why it matters

This is the same Worker/container parity class as #516/#526/#529, in the fail-closed direction: the Worker validator accepts these public IDN hosts and dispatches the crawl, and the container — the component that actually fetches — then refuses them, so legitimate crawls of Persian/Arabic-script and Indic domains whose names contain a contextual joiner fail at crawl time. ZWNJ in particular is not exotic: it appears in everyday Persian orthography, so a large class of real .ir / Persian-script hostnames is affected.

Single-repo: the validator pair (`container/app.py` + `src/lib.ts`) lives only in this repo (checked the opencode/openchamber/nix clones — no copies).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `validate_crawl_url` evaluates U+200C/U+200D under the RFC 5892 CONTEXTJ rules (A.1 for ZWNJ, A.2 for ZWJ) instead of blanket-refusing them: a joiner in a valid context (after a virama; valid Arabic-script joining context for ZWNJ) no longer triggers the forbidden-character refusal.
- [ ] Joiners with no valid context (e.g. `exam<ZWJ>ple.com`, `exam<ZWNJ>ple.com`, a label-leading joiner) are still refused, keeping PR #530's #516 regression tests green.
- [ ] New tests in `pkgs/lab-ops-hub/test/test_container_validate.py` pin both directions: at least one virama+ZWJ Indic host and one Arabic-script ZWNJ host accepted, plus the existing no-context refusals.
- [ ] A differential probe against the Worker's WHATWG parsing over a host battery including the CONTEXTJ cases shows no container/Worker mismatch for joiner hosts.

body:
## Finding

`pm-stack/invariant-sweeper.py:186-199` runs `gh api` through `gh_graphql` and `gh_run` with no subprocess timeout; line 364 does the same for `docker exec ... psql` in `kaneo_links()`. These helpers are called from the live `main()` path and the `pm-invariant-sweeper.timer` runs the script daily with `--act --post-epic` (`pm-stack/systemd/pm-invariant-sweeper.service` and `.timer`). Because this is a Type=oneshot unit with no `TimeoutStartSec`, systemd disables its default start timeout; a stuck GitHub CLI or Docker/psql process can wedge the run indefinitely.

## Suggested fix

Give the subprocess helpers explicit timeouts, convert `TimeoutExpired` to a clear report/failure, and consider a systemd `TimeoutStartSec` as a final outer bound. Test each helper with a timed-out fake process.

Not enqueued in this pass: the dispatch explicitly prohibits creating/dispatching further tasks for findings.

labels.name: kind/bug

body:
## Finding

`infra/cargo-target-broker/bin/cargo_target_broker.py:265-282` chooses an idle LRU directory, calls `shutil.rmtree(victim.path, ignore_errors=True)`, and then unconditionally deletes its `dirs` row and increments `evictions`. If removal fails (for example permissions or a filesystem error), the directory remains on disk but is no longer accounted for. The size cap can then be exceeded indefinitely; the orphan may later be re-adopted by `adopt_strays` (lines 236-255), repeating the accounting failure. The path is reachable through `checkout()` when the cache is over cap (line 320).

There are no tests for this broker module in the repository.

## Suggested fix

Make eviction conditional on successful removal (surface/report failures and preserve the DB row), and add a test that injects a failed removal and verifies both the row and byte accounting remain intact.

Not enqueued in this pass: the dispatch explicitly prohibits creating/dispatching further tasks for findings.

body: ## Finding `pm-stack/aggregator/src/render.ts:399-409` embeds `FRAG_WATCHDOG_SCRIPT` in every fragment shell, but line 406 emits `p.innerHTML = "the live view did not arrive — load the full page";`. The doubled quotes terminate the JS string; extracting the script body and running `node --check` reports `SyntaxError: Unexpected string` at that line. Consequently the browser cannot parse/execute the watchdog at all, so failed fragment loads remain stuck on their skeleton instead of showing recovery UI. This code is included by `renderBoardShell`, `renderAttentionShell`, `renderTodayShell`, `renderQueueShell`, and `renderOverviewShell` (see `render.ts:1743, 3646, 3884, 3961, 4161`). Existing `pm-stack/aggregator/test/frag-watchdog-1503.test.ts:20-39` only asserts rendered HTML contains the strings; it does not parse or execute the embedded JS. ## Suggested fix Use a valid JS string/template literal and construct/escape the link safely (e.g. DOM APIs or a correctly escaped constant). Add a regression test that extracts and syntax-checks the emitted watchdog script or executes it in a DOM test environment.

title: fix(hosted-worker): KV usage and ceiling count UTF-8 characters, not bytes

labels.name: kind/bug

body:
## Evidence

`pkgs/id/hosted-worker/src/user-do.ts:152` computes `kv_bytes` with SQLite `SUM(LENGTH(value))`; for SQLite TEXT, `LENGTH` counts Unicode code points, not UTF-8 bytes. The overwrite lookup at `:334` uses the same character count as `priorBytes`, while the PUT path at `:347` measures the incoming value with `TextEncoder` (bytes). This mixes units in storage usage and ceiling calculations.

Verified against the real `UserDO` with its in-memory SQLite test harness pattern and a 100-byte ceiling: PUTting 17 distinct values of `"😀😀😀😀😀"` (20 UTF-8 bytes each) returned 200 for all 17. The test state then held 340 UTF-8 bytes, while `/v1/usage` reported `kv_bytes=85`, `storage_bytes=85`, and `at_cap=false`. This is reproducible because SQLite reports `LENGTH("😀😀😀😀😀") = 5` while `LENGTH(CAST(value AS BLOB)) = 20`.

## Why it matters

A user can store substantially more data than the configured per-user ceiling by using multibyte text. Usage reports and the at-cap signal are also wrong, undermining the ceiling and its read-only-at-cap behavior. The unit mismatch also means subsequent write decisions combine character-based stored usage with byte-based incoming deltas.

## Acceptance criteria

- Stored KV byte usage and prior-value accounting use UTF-8 byte lengths consistently with the ceiling contract and `TextEncoder`.
- Add regression coverage with multibyte/astral Unicode values proving the ceiling cannot be exceeded and usage/`at_cap` report actual bytes.
- Existing ASCII accounting, overwrites, and delete/recovery behavior remain correct.

title: fix(hosted-worker): front door buffers every non-GET body with arrayBuffer() before routing, so the PR #11336 early refusal never runs

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: status/triaged
labels.description: Triaged and routed (see agent note)

body:
## Summary

The hosted data-plane front door reads every non-GET/HEAD request body into memory before routing, so the body cap added to the user DO in PR #11336 (closing #11332) can never refuse an oversized request early. The early refusal (`Content-Length` check and `readTextUpTo` cap in `pkgs/id/hosted-worker/src/user-do.ts:341-344`) only runs after the Worker has already buffered the whole body.

## Evidence (origin/main `c4a5fb592e`)

- `pkgs/id/hosted-worker/src/worker.ts:42-47`:
  ```ts
  const forwarded = new Request(req.url, {
    method: req.method,
    headers,
    body: req.method === "GET" || req.method === "HEAD" ? undefined : await req.arrayBuffer(),
  });
  return await stub.fetch(forwarded);
  ```
  `req.arrayBuffer()` reads the full body for every method other than GET/HEAD, on every route, before any size check, and before the DO's storage ceiling is consulted.
- `pkgs/id/hosted-worker/wrangler.toml:6` deploys `src/worker.ts` as `main`, so this is the production entry point, not a test shim.
- `pkgs/id/hosted-worker/src/user-do.ts:341-344`: the KV PUT path checks `content-length` against headroom and caps `readTextUpTo` before reading. By the time the DO receives `forwarded`, the body is already a fully materialised `ArrayBuffer` supplied to `new Request`, so that cap bounds nothing at the front door.
- #11332 (closed, fixed by PR #11336, merged 2026-11-17 20:11Z) described the defect as "KV and blob PUT buffer the whole request body before the storage ceiling check". The merged fix changed only `user-do.ts` and `test/usage.test.ts`; `worker.ts` is unchanged, so the buffering that #11332 reported still happens at the front door.
- Fresh search of issues (all states) for hosted-worker, arrayBuffer, and body-buffering terms found no tracker for `worker.ts:45`. #11332 and #11336 are the nearest; they cover the DO-side check only.

## Why it matters

- Memory: a single unauthenticated-size PUT/POST of arbitrary length is held in the Worker isolate before the storage ceiling or any per-route limit applies. The DO-side fix is therefore ineffective for the exact case it targets.
- Cost and reliability: the buffer is paid even for requests the DO will refuse with 413 after the fact.
- Scope: every mutating route in the hosted data plane (KV, blob, and any future POST) shares this path, so the gap is not specific to one route.

## Suggested fix shape

- In `worker.ts`, enforce a front-door body limit for non-GET/HEAD requests before `arrayBuffer()`: refuse a declared `Content-Length` above the largest per-route limit with 413, and pass the request body through as a `ReadableStream` (or a capped reader) so no route reads more than its limit into memory.
- Keep the DO's per-route check as the authority for storage ceilings. The front-door check only bounds memory.
- Route-specific limits should be defined once and used by both the front door and the DO, so the two cannot drift.

## Acceptance criteria

1. An oversized PUT with a declared `Content-Length` above the limit is refused with 413 at the Worker front door, and the forwarded body is never read into memory (test: a body stream that records bytes read, asserting the read stops at the limit).
2. An oversized chunked PUT (no `Content-Length`) is refused after reading at most the limit plus one chunk (same instrumentation).
3. A normal-size KV PUT and blob PUT still succeed end to end through `worker.ts`, not only through the DO in isolation. The existing `test/usage.test.ts` tests call `UserDO` directly and do not exercise `worker.ts`, so add a test that goes through the default export.
4. Mutation check: removing the new front-door cap fails test 1.

## Related

- #11332 (closed) and PR #11336 (merged): DO-side early refusal. This issue is the front-door half that #11336 does not reach.
- #11335 (open): the same buffering-before-verification shape in `pkgs/github-ci` and `infra/github-backup`. Separate deployment, separate fix.

labels.description: Package/app: github-ci (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Evidence (origin/main cb96495039)

- `pkgs/github-ci/worker/src/index.ts:76` (`const raw = await req.text();`) buffers the whole webhook body. The HMAC is computed only afterwards, at `:78`, and compared at `:79`. Auth fails closed on the secret (`:70-74`), but the body read runs before the signature check.
- `infra/github-backup/worker/src/index.js:44` (`const body = await req.text();`) has the same order. The secret check is at `:41-43`, the HMAC at `:46`, and the signature comparison at `:50`.
- Neither handler checks `Content-Length` or caps the read. A grep of both `src/` trees for `content-length`, `413` and size limits finds nothing.

Result: any unauthenticated POST to either receiver makes the Worker buffer an arbitrary body in memory before a 401 is returned. The platform request limit is the only bound. This is the same order-of-operations problem that #11331 and #11332 describe for other Worker routes.

Not reproduced at runtime. The claim is about the code path.

## Why it matters

GitHub's webhook payloads are bounded (about 25 MB per GitHub's documented limit; confirm the exact figure before setting the cap). A legitimate delivery never needs more, so a cap can refuse oversized input cheaply without changing behaviour for real deliveries. Today an oversized or drip-fed unauthenticated body costs the Worker its full memory before the signature fails.

## Fix shape

- Reject with 413 when `Content-Length` is present and exceeds the cap, before reading the body.
- For bodies without a length, read through a size-capped reader that stops at cap + 1 byte and returns 413.
- Keep the existing HMAC check as the authoritative gate, unchanged in order after the bounded read.
- Apply the same helper to both receivers rather than two copies.

## Acceptance criteria

- A POST whose declared `Content-Length` exceeds the cap returns 413 without reading the body, on both `github-ci` and `github-backup`.
- A chunked POST larger than the cap stops reading at the cap and returns 413.
- A correctly signed delivery under the cap is processed exactly as before (existing tests stay green).
- A test covers the early reject and the chunked cap on each worker.

## Dedupe

Searched open and closed issues for `github-ci worker body`, `github-backup worker`, `webhook signature body`, `X-Hub-Signature`, `HMAC verify before read` and `buffers body before signature`. Related but different: #6936 (fail-open secret, closed), #6946 and #6951 (JSON null bodies, closed), #9445 and #9454 (projector webhook intake design; the projector already caps at 10 MB and is a different component). No open issue or PR covers a body cap on these two workers.

Queue: `repo-queue` is not available in this environment, so no queue item was enqueued. Coverage needs a follow-up pass.

## Evidence (origin/main ccb195b946)

- \`pkgs/id/hosted-worker/src/user-do.ts:291-300\` (KV PUT): \`const value = await req.text();\` runs before any size check. The byte delta is computed only afterwards, in \`this.assertWritable(new TextEncoder().encode(value).byteLength - priorBytes)\` at \`:295\`.
- \`pkgs/id/hosted-worker/src/user-do.ts:237\` (blob PUT): \`const bytes = new Uint8Array(await req.arrayBuffer());\` has the same order. \`assertWritable\` runs at \`:246\`.
- \`assertWritable\` (\`:135-146\`) checks the storage ceiling only. Nothing in \`hosted-worker/src\` caps the request body size (grep for content-length, 413, too_large and bodyLimit finds only the storage 413 in \`assertWritable\`).

Result: a write that is already over the ceiling is still fully buffered into the Durable Object's memory before it is refused with a 413. A body larger than the DO's memory limit would fail inside the isolate rather than return the documented \`ceiling_exceeded\` response.

Not yet reproduced at runtime. The claim is about the code path, not a measured OOM.

## Why it matters

The ceiling is documented as a fail-closed guard for writes. The guard runs after the most expensive step, so an oversized write can crash the DO instead of being refused cleanly. The user then gets an opaque error and the DO may reset.

## Fix shape

- Reject early from \`Content-Length\` when it is present and already exceeds the remaining headroom (\`ceiling - usage\`), before reading the body.
- For bodies without a length, read through a size-capped reader that stops at the remaining headroom plus one byte, then returns \`ceiling_exceeded\`.
- Keep the existing \`assertWritable\` check as the authoritative delta check.

## Acceptance criteria

- A PUT to \`/v1/kv/:key\` or \`/v1/blobs\` whose declared length exceeds the remaining headroom returns 413 \`ceiling_exceeded\` without reading the body.
- A chunked PUT larger than the headroom stops reading at the cap and returns the same 413.
- Existing under-cap writes and overwrite deltas behave as before.
- A test covers the early reject and the chunked cap.

## Dedupe

Searched open and closed issues for \"user-do KV body\", \"request body size limit hosted-worker\" and \"user-do\": no matching issue or open PR. Related but different: #6880 and #2791 (cloudflare-export numeric handling) and #3000 (aggregator regex), none of which touch this path.

title: atlas-search(worker) + id-mail(worker): POST handlers read request bodies with no size cap
body:
## Problem

`pkgs/atlas-search/worker/src/index.ts` reads the `POST /v1/search` body with a bare `req.json()` (line ~75). There is no `Content-Length` check and no byte cap, so the whole body is buffered and parsed regardless of size. The route only needs `{ query, k }`.

The gate check (`gateOk`) runs before the read, so only callers holding the gate token reach it. That limits exposure to authenticated callers, but a single oversized request still costs the Worker full memory and CPU before the handler can reject it.

The same bare read pattern appears in `nixos/services/id-mail/worker/src/index.js` (`authenticate` runs first, then `request.json()`). The pm-stack dispatch server already has the equivalent guard (`content-length` checked up front, then a streamed byte cap in `readJsonBody`), so the fleet has a tested pattern to copy.

## Scope

- `pkgs/atlas-search/worker/src/index.ts`: `POST /v1/search`.
- `nixos/services/id-mail/worker/src/index.js`: the POST handler.

## Proposed fix

Reject declared `Content-Length` above a small cap (for example 64 KiB) before reading, and read the stream with a byte cap that returns the route's existing 413/400 envelope. Add a test for oversized and drip-fed bodies on each route, and keep the existing 400 envelopes for non-JSON and non-object bodies.

## Oracle

A request whose body exceeds the cap gets a 4xx envelope and the handler never parses it. A normal `{ query, k }` body is unchanged.

title: fix(id-core): canonical CBOR encoders accept values their decoders reject
body:
## Problem

The canonical CBOR encoders do not enforce the nesting-depth limit enforced by their decoders. Rust's `encode_into` recurses through arrays and map values without a depth parameter or guard (`pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/canonical_cbor.rs:132-179`), while `Reader::value_inner` rejects depth greater than `MAX_NESTING_DEPTH` (64, `:194-199, :270-273`). The TypeScript mirror has the same mismatch: `encodeInto` recurses without a limit (`pkgs/id/hosted-worker/src/canonical-cbor.ts:79-127`), but `Reader.valueInner` rejects over-depth values (`:184-185`).

Consequently, a caller-built value with 65 nested arrays can be encoded successfully, but decoding those bytes returns `TooDeeplyNested`. Still deeper caller-built values recurse without a bound during encoding and can exhaust the stack. This breaks the encoder/decoder round-trip contract and leaves the producer path without the decoder's stack-safety bound.

## Requested change

Apply the same depth policy to both encoders and return the existing typed `TooDeeplyNested` error when a value exceeds it. Add Rust and TypeScript tests for the boundary and over-limit nesting, including parity between the implementations.

## Related work

Closed #2121 addresses unbounded nesting in a different ID tuple decoder. It does not cover these canonical CBOR encoders. No open issue or PR specifically tracking this encoder/decoder mismatch was found in the dedupe search.

title: mcpx: http.streamBufferInit > http.streamBufferMax silently defeats the documented line ceiling

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/mcpx
labels.description: Package/app: mcpx (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
Found while probing http.streamBufferInit for the #8469 coverage burn-down (queue task 20151, PR #11307).

Documented behaviour: http.streamBufferMax is the event-stream line ceiling — "a line over this ends the stream". But the stream reader is a bufio.Scanner, which only consults the max when its buffer must GROW past the initial capacity. So when http.streamBufferInit > http.streamBufferMax, lines over the documented ceiling are silently delivered instead of ending the stream: the two settings contradict each other, and streamBufferMax does not mean what its documentation says whenever init is larger.

Evidence: standalone bufio trials plus the (removed) draft probe during task 20151 — with init pinned small, the streamBufferMax probe behaves as documented (PR #11307 pins init at 64 bytes in both phases for exactly this reason); with init > max, over-ceiling lines pass through.

Decide and fix: either clamp the effective scanner maximum to at least the initial capacity explicitly (and document that max < init raises max), or reject/warn on streamBufferInit > streamBufferMax at settings validation, or correct the streamBufferMax documentation. Then the http.streamBufferInit exemption in the #8469 burn-down can be probed against whichever semantics is chosen.

title: mcpx(daemon): handleAskAbandon reads r.Body unbounded — TestNoUnboundedBodyReaders red on main, blocks amd toplevel
body:
Found during the 2026-11-17 amd toplevel build for the Dot SSH activation: `mcpx-0.1.0.drv` fails its check phase on current main —

```
--- FAIL: TestNoUnboundedBodyReaders (0.01s)
    body_limits_test.go:114: routes_proto.go:909: r.Body read without a size ceiling: if r.Body != nil {
    body_limits_test.go:114: routes_proto.go:910: r.Body read without a size ceiling: _ = json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&body)
FAIL github.com/developing-today/code/pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon
```

Reproduced deterministically outside nix: `go test ./internal/daemon/ -run TestNoUnboundedBodyReaders -count=1` fails at main 8fef1ad620.

Cause: `handleAskAbandon` in `pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon/routes_proto.go` decodes its optional `{taskCancelled}` body with a bare `json.NewDecoder(r.Body)` — the one daemon handler that missed the #2082 rule (every body read goes through `http.MaxBytesReader` at the route class's configured limit). The guard test is doing exactly its job; the handler is a real unbounded read (small struct today, but the ceiling is the contract).

Fix: wrap the decode in `http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, s.bodyBytes("http.controlBodyLimit", defaults.HTTPControlBodyLimit))`, matching the control-class idiom (cf. upgrade.go). The existing error tolerance stays: an absent/empty body still decodes to the zero value.

Also seen in the same nix check run, not reproduced locally yet and possibly load-related: `TestDefaultConfigStdioRunsSupervised` (internal/pool) — "supervised child still alive after the reap" at its 10s bound under heavy parallel build load. Noted here for now; if it reproduces on a quiet run it deserves its own issue.

Impact: mcpx is in the amd system closure, so this blocks the amd switch (and any main-based toplevel build) until fixed.

body:
## Evidence

On current `main`, `EventStore::open_with` runs `recover_device_ops` inside a write transaction during every store open (`pkgs/id/crates/id-events/src/event_store/mod.rs:449-455`). The one-time recovery helper in `event_store/ingest.rs:140-156` collects every `EVENTS` row into `Vec<Event>` and every waiting row into another `Vec<Event>` before scanning. It then accumulates all missing device-op rows in a third `Vec` (`:156, :178-185`) before writing any of them. `EVENTS` is persistent historical state; there is no global row-count cap, and pruning is explicit (`EventStore::prune_behind_cut`). Thus an upgrade of a large but valid store has temporary memory proportional to its entire history while holding the startup write transaction, and can stall or OOM before the store opens.

The recovery is being added by open PR #11283 as part of #8160. That PR provides the right recovery semantics but retains this whole-store materialization; this issue tracks the independent memory-bound requirement and should be cross-linked, not treated as a duplicate.

## Why it matters

A large long-lived store, especially one that has not pruned old events, can require multiple copies of its history in memory during the one-time upgrade. The failure occurs on open, so affected users may be unable to start the store to recover or prune it.

## Acceptance criteria

- Recovery scans stored and waiting rows without retaining all decoded events simultaneously; any staging is bounded by a documented fixed batch/size limit (or equivalent constant-space approach).
- Preserve the existing verified-body check, idempotence, recovered count, and incomplete-recovery warning/report.
- Add a test with a large synthetic legacy store that exercises recovery across multiple batches and proves every eligible operation is recovered, missing bodies are reported, and restart does not duplicate rows.
- Keep recovery transactional or document and test a safe resumable strategy if bounded batching requires multiple transactions.

Related implementation: #11283 / #8160.

body:
## Problem

`basic: workflow lint`'s ci-policy agreement checker fails on current main against the **real tree** (not a fixture):

```
$ bash .github/scripts/check-ci-policy-agreement.sh
::error::PR-derived trigger forbidden: .github/workflows/note-submission-pr.yml
ci-policy-agreement: checked 10 workflows, 0 waived disagreement(s)
ci-policy-agreement: FAILED - disagreement(s) without a recorded waiver listed above
```

Reproduced on fresh `origin/main` 14333e4bd8 (2026-11-17, triage task 20245). The contract test (`.github/scripts/check-ci-policy-agreement.test.sh`) fails at its first step for the same reason — it copies the real workflows and runs the checker over them.

## Cause

`.github/workflows/note-submission-pr.yml` declares a `pull_request` trigger (path-filtered to `pkgs/note-submission/**`). The trigger contract in `.github/ci-policy.md` (Nov-13 policy, Nov-16 nightly ruling) forbids it categorically: "No `pull_request`, `pull_request_target`, PR review/comment, or `merge_group` triggers. PR-only venues become manual-only, not new deployments on main." The WAIVERS array in the checker is empty (2026-11-11 re-arm, #7089), so the disagreement is unwaived.

This is the successor failure to #8945: that issue's stale waiver-era fixtures were resolved by the wholesale fixture rewrite under the new policy (issue closed COMPLETED 2026-11-17), but the checker now disagrees with a real workflow instead of a fixture.

## Fix shape

Bring the workflow into agreement: remove the `pull_request` trigger from `note-submission-pr.yml`, keeping `push` to main (path filters unchanged); per the policy, the PR-era venue becomes manual — add `workflow_dispatch` if a manual run path is wanted. If evidence shows the PR trigger is load-bearing for a gated path, record a WAIVERS entry in the checker with the ruling reference instead (the waiver comment in the checker requires the disposition to name its ruling, not just the disagreement).

Verify: `bash .github/scripts/check-ci-policy-agreement.sh` exits 0 on the real tree and `bash .github/scripts/check-ci-policy-agreement.test.sh` passes end to end.

Filed from triage task 20245 (lane any-g) during verification of #8945.

    --> crates/id-worlds/src/world_session/mod.rs:1449:24

## Problem
On current main (verified at e5eab191db, 2026-11-17), `cargo check -p id-worlds --lib` fails: the revision-10 pointer landing (#1831 slice S2) added `Pointer`/`Hover` variants to `ClientFrame` without dispatch arms, leaving two matches non-exhaustive (E0004 in `world_session/session_core.rs` run_world_session and `world_session/mod.rs` handle_client_frame). Behind the lib errors, the test build has further pre-existing breakage from the same era:
- `shell_contract/tests.rs`: the pointer test binds `let contract = contract();` and later calls `contract()` (E0618).
- `world/actor.rs` test modules `device_info_tests` / `form_tests` use `Request` (and `form_tests` also `CapError`) from `crate::world_caps` without importing them (E0422/E0425).

Evidence: clean worktree at e5eab191db, `cargo check -p id-worlds --lib` -> RC 101, exactly the two E0004 errors (run by lane any-e, task 20044, 2026-11-17).

## Interim fix (in the #7913 PR)
- First-frame match: Pointer/Hover join the joined-only refusal group.
- Joined dispatch: Hover accepted as ephemeral no-op (no host consumer yet); Pointer refused explicitly with `input_refused` / `unknown_or_unsupported_event`, per the contract rule that an input event is never silently dropped.
- The two test-build import/shadowing fixes above.

## Remaining (owned by #1831 follow-up)
Real pointer routing: manifest `interfaces.input` declaration checks, journaling pointer events like input (the journaled-vs-ephemeral contract test's `pointer` expectation — sample commits exactly one event — is written ahead of that routing and will fail until it lands), and hover delivery if a consumer appears.
