title: fix(fleet-paperwork): http_raw urlopen has no timeout — a stalled GitHub connection hangs every App write, and a read timeout escapes as a traceback

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: app/fleet
labels.description: pkgs/fleet multicall binary + platform crates

body:
## Problem

`infra/fleet-paperwork/fleet_paperwork.py` makes every GitHub App call through one transport, `http_raw`, and that transport has no timeout.

- `fleet_paperwork.py:163` — `with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as resp:` passes no `timeout=`. Python's socket default is "block indefinitely", so a connection that is accepted and then stalls hangs the command for as long as the kernel keeps the socket open.
- `http_raw` is the only network call in the file. It is the transport for `http()` (`:210`), which backs `create`, `comment`, `close`, `check`, and the installations lookup, and for `cmd_api` (`:610`).
- The same function has a second gap. Its `except` clauses are `urllib.error.HTTPError` and `urllib.error.URLError`. A read-phase timeout during `resp.read()` raises a plain `TimeoutError` (not a `URLError`), so once a timeout is added it would escape as a raw traceback instead of a `die(...)` diagnostic.

## Evidence

Checked on `origin/main` `8e04b8ad59` with python3 3.14.8, against a local socket server:

- Server sends `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` with `Content-Length: 10` and then stalls. `urlopen(req, timeout=1)` followed by `resp.read()` raises `TimeoutError: timed out` (not `URLError`). `http_raw` does not catch it, so the traceback surfaces.
- Server accepts and never responds. Without a timeout the call blocks; the fleet command does not return and writes nothing, with no diagnostic.

## Why it matters

Fleet paperwork runs in bulk (for example one decision issue per preserved branch during worktree cleanup). A single stalled connection currently hangs the whole batch silently, and the caller cannot tell a hang from slow GitHub. The ledger write happens after the call, so the operator also loses the record of what was sent.

Dedupe: searched `urlopen timeout` and `fleet_paperwork timeout` on developing-today/code, open and closed. The only hit is closed #4434 (grist), a different tool. Other fleet-paperwork issues (#9150, #6864, #7930, #5109) cover pagination, shape validation and pacing, not transport timeouts.

## Suggested fix

- Add a module-level request timeout constant (e.g. 30 s) and pass it to `urlopen`.
- Catch `TimeoutError` / `socket.timeout` in `http_raw` and route it through `die(...)` with the method and URL, the same way `URLError` is reported.
- Do not add retries in this change; that is a separate policy decision.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `urlopen` in `http_raw` is called with a finite timeout.
- [ ] A read-phase timeout returns a `die` diagnostic naming method and URL (exit non-zero), not a traceback.
- [ ] A test in `infra/fleet-paperwork/tests/` starts a local socket server that stalls (accepts and sends nothing, or sends headers and then stalls the body) and asserts `http_raw` fails within a bound of about 2x the timeout. The oracle is the timeout bound itself, which fails on the current code.
- [ ] Existing `fleet-paperwork` tests stay green.

Scope: only `developing-today/code` has this file (`infra/fleet-paperwork`). No other fleet repo carries the transport.

body:
# mcpx: prompt hooks — effect: propose (Approach C slice 1 of the #1929 remainder)

Parent: #1929 (Approach C prompt hooks with declared effects). Design of record: the sequencing design note posted on #1929 by queue task 19661 (2026-11-17), against `pkgs/mcpx/docs/decisions/0001-hook-vocabulary.md` (hook vocabulary) and `pkgs/mcpx/docs/decisions/0002-autonomy-dial.md` (effect levels). Previous slice: `effect: advise` prompt hooks, #5276, landed in PR #9021 — `pkgs/mcpx/internal/execsvc/prompt_hooks.go` implements advise only, and `validateHooks` in `pkgs/mcpx/internal/execsvc/hooks.go` refuses any other prompt effect, naming #1929.

## Scope

Implement the `propose` effect for **prompt hooks only**, at the `script` point:

- A prompt hook may declare `"effect": "propose"`. Validation accepts it at phases `onSuccess` and `onError` only; `before` (nothing exists to propose against yet) and `suffix` (clamped to at most `advise` by 0001) refuse it at validation, in the existing refusal style.
- The provider's reply is parsed as a hook output object (the 0001 output shape): a `propose` key carries the proposed replacement (any JSON value); a reply that is not a JSON object is treated as a plain-text proposal (a plan is a legitimate proposal per 0002) and carried as a string value. Keys above the declared effect (`apply`, `run`) are dropped and named in the frame's `dropped` list, per 0001 — never honoured, never silent.
- The proposal rides in the hook frame beside the original: `HookFrame` gains a `propose` field (the proposed value, JSON). The run's result and error are **never** modified by a propose hook, in any phase — that is the whole definition of the level (0002: "return a replacement beside the original, unapplied").
- The prompt system text for a propose hook differs from advise's (which states the reply cannot change anything): it instructs the model to answer with the proposal, and keeps the same data-not-instructions guard for placeholder values.
- No provider configured: the frame reports the proposal as unavailable and the run continues, exactly like advise — propose is not a gate, so it keeps prompt hooks' fail-soft contract.

Out of scope: `ask` and `apply` prompt effects (later #1929 slices, sequenced on #1929), the `run` effect (the #1929 design concludes it is not built for prompt hooks), script/module hooks' output keys (their fixed per-phase effects are unchanged), and any `hooks.autonomy` / `autonomy.max` registry ceiling work (0002's separate track).

## Acceptance

- A prompt hook declaring `effect: propose` at `onSuccess` produces a hook frame carrying the proposal and the run's original result, with the result delivered to the caller byte-identical to a run without the hook.
- At `onError`, the frame carries the proposal beside the untouched error; the error still propagates.
- `effect: propose` at `before` or `suffix` is refused at validation with a named reason.
- A reply carrying `apply` or `run` keys has them dropped and reported in the frame's `dropped` list.
- With no provider configured, the frame states the proposal is unavailable and the run is otherwise unchanged.

## Tests (oracle: a propose hook can never change the outcome — only add a frame-carried proposal beside it)

- Frame carries the parsed proposal (object reply and plain-text reply cases); `res.Result` / `res.Error` unchanged in both phases.
- Validation refusals for `before` / `suffix` propose declarations.
- Dropped-key reporting for `apply` / `run` keys in a propose reply.
- No-provider frame (proposal unavailable, run unchanged), mirroring the advise slice's no-provider tests in `prompt_hooks_test.go`.

title: OpenDesign session keeper misclassifies transient get-session failures as session rejection (false 'sign-in needed' alerts)
body:
Evidence 2026-11-16/17 (second flap; first was 2026-11-15, flagged 10:53 CST, valid by 11:48 with no sign-in):

- Tick 2026-11-17T05:15:22Z: keeper reported status=attention, horizonHours=unknown, capture=no-browser-session, with the 'session no longer accepted / sign-in in laptop Helium profile needed' alert (steward 448).
- Every tick since — 23:21 / 23:30 / 23:45 / 00:00 / 00:15 / 00:30 CST plus a manual keeper run at 00:43 CST — shows providerAuth.opendesign VALID (real authenticated GET /auth/get-session), sessionExpiresAt 2026-11-24T03:30:34Z, horizon ~165h. The session never died.

Mechanism (pm-stack/aggregator/src/opendesign-renewal.ts): fetchSession catches ANY fetch error and returns null (~lines 100-107), so a slow/failed read is indistinguishable from a server-side rejection: session=null triggers a CDP re-capture attempt, which finds no browser session, and the keeper fires the full rejection alert. Gatherer legs were running 36-43s that evening; one bad read is enough.

Fix shape: distinguish transport failure from true rejection — only fire attention on a definitive unauthenticated response (a completed get-session returning no session), and/or require two consecutive failed validations before alerting. A transport error should record a read failure and retry next tick, keeping the last-known horizon.

Related: code#6120 (standing-rule tracker, closed) — the re-arm gap noted there is real and separate: the Helium profile holds no Open Design session cookie, so re-capture has nothing to capture if the stored session ever truly dies.

body:
## Problem

`POST /ingest-status` on the voice-line worker (`pm-stack/voice-line-worker/src/index.ts:106-124`) has no input guard between the bearer check and the store:

1. `const body = (await request.json()) as Record<string, unknown>;` has no try/catch. A malformed body throws out of the handler and the Worker answers a generic 500 instead of a 400 with a JSON error. A body of JSON `null` throws too (`Cannot read properties of null`). Every other write route in the stack answers these as 400 (compare `decision-events-worker/src/index.ts:96,173`).
2. Each count is `Number(body.x ?? 0)` with no range check. Anything that is not a number becomes `NaN`, which `JSON.stringify` stores as `null`. Negative and fractional values are stored as-is.
3. The stored snapshot is what `queue_state` reads back: `buildAnswer` (`src/intent.ts:35-47`) interpolates the fields directly, so a bad count is spoken aloud.

## Repro (node 22, same expressions as the handler)

```
malformed JSON  -> throws: SyntaxError (-> Worker 500, no 400)
JSON null       -> throws: TypeError Cannot read properties of null (reading 'queued')
{"queued":"abc","claimed":"3","parked":-4,"blocked":1.5}
                -> stored {"queued":null,"claimed":3,"parked":-4,"blocked":1.5}
```

`buildAnswer` on that stored row produces "The fleet queue has null tasks waiting, 3 being worked, and -4 parked." A missing field (`{}`) is stored as zeros, which can look like an empty queue.

## Why it matters

The endpoint is bearer-authenticated, so the risk is a pusher bug rather than an outside attacker. But the failure is silent: a bad push is accepted, stored, and then read back as a false queue state. The route has no test in `pm-stack/voice-line-worker/test/` (grep for `ingest` finds none).

## Acceptance criteria

- A body that is not valid JSON, or is not a plain object, returns 400 with `{"error":"invalid_json"}` or `{"error":"expected_object"}`, and does not write a row.
- Each of `queued`, `claimed`, `parked`, `blocked` must be present or defaulted to 0 and must be a non-negative safe integer. Anything else returns 400 naming the field, and no row is written.
- Add tests in `voice-line-worker/test/` for: malformed JSON (400), `null` (400), string count (400), negative (400), fractional (400), `{}` (200 and zeros), a valid body (200 and the stored row). The oracle is the response status plus the stored payload.

Suggested fix shape: parse with `try`/`catch` into `unknown`, check `typeof body === "object" && body !== null && !Array.isArray(body)`, then validate each count with `Number.isSafeInteger(v) && v >= 0` after the `?? 0` default.

## Evidence

- Handler: `pm-stack/voice-line-worker/src/index.ts:106-124` (origin/main `72b930750b`).
- Read-back: `pm-stack/voice-line-worker/src/ledger.ts:126-132` (`putSnapshot` stores `JSON.stringify(payload)`), `src/intent.ts:35-47`.
- Dedupe: no open or closed issue mentions `ingest-status`, `STATUS_INGEST`, or `queue_state` snapshot validation. Related but distinct: #10921 (CLOSED, the WebSocket control frame in `session.ts`, a different route).

title: mcpx docs workflow: Deploy to GitHub Pages fails - artifact not found
body:
## Failure Details

**Run:** https://github.com/developing-today/code/actions/runs/44014450921
**Workflow:** mcpx docs
**Job:** deploy: GitHub Pages
**Failed Step:** Deploy to GitHub Pages (step 9)
**Head SHA:** c7708460664317c10b90f7348cb81e16196f7a0b
**Run Time:** 2026-11-17T04:04:07Z - 2026-11-17T04:05:02Z

## Error

The  step fails with:
```
Fetching artifact metadata for "github-pages" in this workflow run
Found 0 artifact(s)
Error: No artifacts named "github-pages" were found for this workflow run. Ensure artifacts are uploaded with actions/upload-artifact@v4 or later.
```

However, the  step (step 8) **successfully uploads** the artifact:
```
Artifact github-pages successfully finalized. Artifact ID 14297553256
Artifact github-pages has been successfully uploaded! Final size is 4980868 bytes.
Artifact download URL: https://github.com/developing-today/code/actions/runs/44014450921/artifacts/14297553256
```

## Root Cause Hypothesis

This appears to be a race condition in GitHub Actions where the  action cannot immediately find the artifact that was just uploaded by . The artifact upload completes successfully (as evidenced by the artifact ID and download URL), but the subsequent deploy step reports "Found 0 artifact(s)".

This is a known intermittent issue with GitHub Pages deployments where there's a propagation delay between artifact upload completion and artifact availability for the deploy action.

## Suggested Fix

Add a retry/wait mechanism before the deploy step, or use the  action's built-in retry configuration. The workflow already has  and  configured, but the error suggests the artifact metadata fetch itself is failing rather than a deployment retry.

Possible solutions:
1. Add a  step or explicit sleep before deploy-pages
2. Use a newer version of deploy-pages with better artifact handling
3. Check if the artifact name mismatch (upload uses "github-pages", deploy looks for "github-pages") - they match, so this isn't the issue
4. The issue may be that  creates a different artifact type than what  expects

## Workflow File

The workflow is likely at  or similar.

body:
## Summary

`pm-stack/voice-line-worker/src/session.ts` parses WebSocket control frames with `JSON.parse` and then reads `control.type` outside any guard. A text frame whose JSON value is `null` parses successfully, so `control.type` throws `TypeError` and the handler exits without sending the `error` reply that every other malformed control frame gets.

## Evidence

- `pm-stack/voice-line-worker/src/session.ts` (`webSocketMessage`): `control = JSON.parse(message)` is inside a `try` that only catches parse failures. Line after it: `if (control.type === "start")`, with no check that `control` is a non-null object.
- Node probe of the same expression, on the text frames a client can send:
  - `"null"` → throws `Cannot read properties of null (reading 'type')`
  - `"1"`, `"\"stop\""`, `"[]"`, `"{}"` → `type` is `undefined` → falls through to the `unknown control type` error reply (correct)
- So the only failing shape is `null`. Other non-object JSON gets the proper error frame; `null` gets an uncaught exception, no reply, and an error in the worker log.
- `pm-stack/voice-line-worker/test/` has `intent`, `ledger`, `vad`, `wav` tests and no session/control-frame test, so nothing exercises this path.
- Searched open and closed issues for `voice-line-worker`, `webSocketMessage`, `control frame`: no tracker. Open PRs mentioning "voice": none touching this file.

## Why it matters

Low severity (one client, one malformed frame), but it is a missing guard on external input in the same handler whose siblings already validate: the client gets no answer and the failure shows up as an unexplained worker exception rather than the documented `error` frame. It is also the only control-frame branch with no test.

## Acceptance criteria

- A control frame that parses to a non-object (including `null`) gets the same `{ type: "error", error: "control frame must be JSON" }` (or a dedicated "control frame must be an object" error) reply as malformed JSON, and the handler does not throw.
- Narrow guard suggestion: after the `try` block, treat `control` as invalid unless `typeof control === "object" && control !== null`, reply with an error, and return.
- A test in `pm-stack/voice-line-worker/test/` covering `"null"`, `"1"`, `"[]"`, and `"{}"` frames against the control-frame handler (or an extracted pure parse helper if the Durable Object is hard to instantiate in bun test), with the existing `bun test` suite staying green.

title: fix(id-core): reconcile full holder announcements with prior holdings
body:
## Evidence

`pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/holders.rs:177-181` implements `ProviderTable::apply_announcement` by recording every hash in the incoming announcement, but it never removes that endpoint's previously announced hashes that are absent from a later complete announcement. The `HolderAnnouncement::truncated` flag is ignored by this method. The only cleanup is `remove_stale` at `:206-220`, which retains records until their age exceeds the stale threshold.

A minimal sequence demonstrates the issue: apply a non-truncated announcement from endpoint E containing hashes A and B, then apply a non-truncated announcement from E containing only A. `holders(world, B)` still returns E until stale cleanup expires it, despite the refreshed complete announcement saying E no longer holds B. This can direct retrieval toward a peer that no longer has the content. The existing `apply_announcement` test only covers insertion (`:312-320`), not replacement/removal.

## Why it matters

Fresh announcements refresh records but cannot correct changed holdings. Provider results therefore remain false-positive for a full staleness window, degrading lookup and retrieval reliability.

## Suggested fix / acceptance criteria

- Treat non-truncated announcements as a complete snapshot for that `(world, endpoint)`: remove that endpoint's records for hashes omitted from the snapshot, then record the included hashes.
- For truncated announcements, do not interpret the prefix as a complete set; retain omitted prior records (or define another explicit reconciliation mechanism).
- Add regression tests showing complete announcements remove omitted hashes, truncated announcements do not remove omitted hashes, and empty complete announcements clear the endpoint's holdings for that world.
- Preserve other endpoints and other world buckets during reconciliation.

Related context: closed #2260 established the provider-table foundation and stale expiry; open PR #10576 implements that foundation but does not add snapshot reconciliation.

## Goal

Complete the remaining F13.4 presentation work tracked by #786. The shared bounded detector/profile from merged PR #5023 is in place; this issue owns the unimplemented tier renderers and acceptance proof, not another detector rewrite.

## Source and design

- Parent: #786 — Phase 13 F13.4 presentation capability tiers
- Design: [F13.4 decision-ready design](https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/main/doc/2026-11-01_design_id786.md), especially phased steps 3–5
- Detector baseline: merged PR #5023 (5ad9688450c5e5dca36aee36002b11f71c59a770)
- Prerequisites #561 and #562 are now closed/merged; verify their landed behavior against current main before integrating.

## Scope

1. Implement Tier 2 cell-grid rendering and Tier 3 line-mode rendering for both SSH and interactive iroh TTY paths, retaining non-TTY iroh JSON-lines behavior.
2. Implement Tier 1 graphics/synchronized-output rendering behind the existing positive feature evidence; do not activate Kitty keyboard parsing or add guest-authored image payloads.
3. Use shared batching across all tiers, cell diffs for screen tiers, and text deltas for line mode. Preserve full repaint on attach/resize/invalidation and restore terminal modes on every exit.
4. Prove equivalent behavior using the same transcript-driven harness over SSH and iroh, including the three requested tiers, no-reply/malformed/interleaved input, byte-for-byte input replay, and no probe replies entering world input or the journal.
5. Record frame/byte comparisons against a full-render control and the F11.9 baseline.

## Acceptance criteria

- One harness selects and renders all three tiers correctly over both SSH and iroh from equivalent terminal transcripts.
- Every tier consumes shared server-side batching; Tier 1/2 diff parity and Tier 3 text-delta parity are asserted against the full-render oracle.
- No-TTY, timeout, malformed/conflicting replies conservatively fall back; unmatched user input is replayed byte-for-byte and in order.
- Non-TTY iroh JSON-lines behavior and unrelated SSH input/command behavior remain unchanged.
- Rich terminal sequences are emitted only after positive feature-specific evidence, and modes are restored on success, error, and disconnect.
- Reported output preserves the shell/journal contract; no capability frame or guest image payload is added.

## Out of scope

- Reworking the detector already delivered by #5023 except for a demonstrated integration defect.
- Kitty keyboard protocol work owned by #787/F13.5.
- New guest content, asset protocol, or unrelated terminal UX.

## Parent tracking

Keep #786 open until these criteria are met; this issue is the scoped implementation follow-on for its remaining F13.4 acceptance.

title: fix(mcpx): affected-tests changed_test_names still diff-only — untracked e2e tests lose changed-test prioritization at the T2 budget (PR #4398 residual of #3320)

body:
## Finding

PR #4398 (merge `545be40ba6f4`, closes #3320) taught `pkgs/mcpx/scripts/affected-tests.py` to render untracked files as added diff lines for the T1b exported-identifier scan, the T2 registry-name scan, and the e2e `newEnv` harness check. One diff consumer was left unpatched: `changed_test_names` still derives its changed-line ranges solely from `git diff`, which is silent about untracked files — so tests in an untracked e2e file never receive the changed-test prioritization the function exists to provide.

## Evidence (verified on current main `b337e1ac8b41f4c3b48e9ef47acf9e5c4d06bf0f`)

- `pkgs/mcpx/scripts/affected-tests.py:266` — `changed_test_names(mcpx, e2e_rel_paths, root, base)`; at `:280` it runs `git diff --unified=0 <base> -- pkgs/mcpx/<path>` per e2e file and builds test line ranges from the hunks. For an untracked file `git diff` prints nothing, the range list is empty, and the function `continue`s past the file.
- `pkgs/mcpx/scripts/affected-tests.py:550` — the call site passes `edited_e2e_all`, which includes untracked e2e files (they are in the change set via `git ls-files --others`), so untracked files reach the function and are silently dropped by it.
- `pkgs/mcpx/scripts/affected-tests.py:584` — `prioritized = [t for t in changed_e2e_tests ...]` is placed ahead of ranked name matches and the alphabetical fill precisely so changed tests are not truncated away at the 15-test T2 budget (see the comment block above it). Untracked-file tests miss that protection.
- The untracked render added by #4398 is applied at `:467` (T1b/T2 diff text) and `:547` (e2e `newEnv` diff) — never to `changed_test_names`.
- Partial mitigation already present: the `edited_e2e` all-names path adds every test of an edited e2e file (untracked included) to `e2e_selected`, but only in the final alphabetical segment of the ordering. Selection parity therefore holds in small runs — the PR's own parity tests in `pkgs/mcpx/scripts/tests/test_affected_untracked.py` pass — and breaks exactly when the T2 budget truncates: a staged new e2e file's tests are prioritized, the identical untracked file's tests can be cut. (CI runs the full suite either way; this is local-selector fidelity, the same contract #3320 fixed for the other three consumers.)
- The parity tests added by #4398 assert the T1b importer command, the T2 registry run-set, and the harness sample for staged vs untracked — none asserts changed-test prioritization for an untracked e2e file under a full T2 budget.

## Why it matters

#3320's contract is staged/untracked parity for the selector's content-derived decisions. The one remaining consumer silently treats an untracked e2e file's tests as unedited, so the exact regression test a developer just wrote in a new file is the one the local selector may drop when the budget is tight — the failure mode the prioritization code was added to prevent.

## Acceptance criteria

- `changed_test_names` (or its call site) accounts for untracked e2e files — e.g. an untracked file's tests are treated as changed (whole-file added ranges), matching the staged-new-file result.
- A parity regression in `pkgs/mcpx/scripts/tests/test_affected_untracked.py`: identical e2e content staged vs untracked yields the same prioritized ordering, including a scenario where the T2 selection exceeds the 15-test budget.
- Existing selector tests keep passing (`python3 -m unittest discover -s pkgs/mcpx/scripts/tests`).

---
Filed by pr-diff-review-b from the review of PR #4398. Dedupe: `gh search issues` for `changed_test_names` returned nothing; `affected-tests untracked` returned only the closed parent #3320, whose fix this residual survives.

title: secrets-broker: a hung bws child wedges the refresh guard forever (no subprocess deadline)
body:
## Problem

The secrets-broker background refresh can wedge permanently when a single `bws` child process never returns. Nothing in the refresh path has a deadline, so the `refreshing` guard is never cleared and every later refresh is rejected.

## Evidence

`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/secrets_broker.rs`:

- `BwsRunner::run` (~L118-136) spawns `bws` with `Command::new(program).args(args).env(...).output()`. There is no timeout and no kill.
- `do_refresh` (~L226-268) runs `bws secret list`, then spawns 8 worker threads that each call `bws secret get` through `bws_run` (~L143). It then does `for h in handles { let _ = h.join(); }` (~L266-268). A hung child blocks its worker forever, so `join` never returns.
- `refresh` (~L151-171) sets `*refreshing = true` before calling `do_refresh`, and clears it only after `do_refresh` returns (~L170). A stuck `do_refresh` therefore leaves `refreshing == true` for the life of the process.
- The background loop (~L718-728) calls `refresh` and then sleeps `ttl_s`. Once wedged, every iteration returns `"refresh already in progress"`, so the cache is never refreshed again.
- `GET /health` reports `refreshing` (~L543). It shows `true` indefinitely with no alarm, and `last_refresh_error` is not updated because the guard returns before the bookkeeping.

## Why it matters

The broker is the single source of vault secrets for consumers. Stale-while-revalidate only helps if a refresh eventually finishes. A hang in Bitwarden's CLI, a network stall, or a credential prompt turns "secrets are slightly old" into "secrets are frozen until someone restarts the broker". Restart is the only recovery, and `/health` does not say why.

## Fix shape

- Give each `bws` invocation a deadline: spawn, poll `try_wait` against a bound, kill and reap on expiry, and return an error. Reuse the existing timing constants where possible.
- Optionally bound the whole `do_refresh` join, so one slow item cannot hold the guard indefinitely.
- Make `/health` or the error log report the timeout, so the wedge is visible.

## Acceptance criteria

- A unit test with a `CommandRunner` or fake `bws` that never exits: `refresh` returns an error within the deadline, `refreshing` is `false` afterwards, and the next refresh is attempted.
- Existing refresh tests still pass.
- `/health` `refreshing` cannot stay `true` past the deadline.

## Related

- #10578 (closed): broker client exchange had no timeout. This issue is the separate `bws` child-process path inside the broker.
- #10868 (open): live-but-broken broker is never replaced. Different failure mode.
- #10743 (closed): `bws` NotFound and gh shim hang. Different cause.

title: secrets-broker: live-but-broken instance (stripped PATH, cannot spawn bws) is never replaced by init-ensure liveness check
body:
## Symptom

On sandbox boot 64c3d6a0 (2026-11-16), the sandbox-local secrets-broker (pid 3771, started 19:17Z) ran with a PATH missing `/home/hatch/tools/bin`, so it could not spawn `bws`; its cache never populated ("refresh failed: bws secret list -o json failed: spawn failed: entity not found" in `~/.config/secrets-broker/secrets-broker.log`). Every `fleet secrets get` degraded to ~120s (broker timeout, then Bitwarden fallback). The quota-recorder's 60s token timeout expired on every flush, so Turso acks stalled from 19:10Z and the pending backlog grew to 20 records (file-first, no data lost).

## Evidence

- Measured `fleet secrets get turso.fleet-platform-rw-token` at 120.1s / 120.2s before the fix.
- `/proc/3771/environ` PATH lacked `/home/hatch/tools/bin`.
- After killing the broker and re-running `~/tools/init-ensure.sh`, the respawned broker (pid 57865) had the correct PATH, logged "refreshed 202 secrets", token fetches went to ~0s, and the 20:55:03Z recorder tick acked all 20 records.

## Scope

Fleet/init tooling — the broker spawn environment and init-ensure's liveness check (socket exists + process alive passes a live-but-broken broker).

## Acceptance

1. Broker spawn is PATH-proofed (bws resolved by absolute path, or PATH guaranteed at spawn regardless of the spawning phase), and/or
2. init-ensure's health check verifies the broker can actually serve (e.g. a refresh succeeded / a test get returns promptly) and replaces an instance that cannot.

A repeat of the stripped-PATH start is detected and self-healed without manual intervention.

## Refs

- Quota-recorder stall 2026-11-16 (pending 1→20, resolved by manual broker restart).
- Sandbox broker dual-hosting since 2026-11-15, #10578.

title: main-breakage: mcpx examples suite leaks supervise processes — nix checkPhase fails, amd toplevel blocked

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

body:
# main-breakage: mcpx examples suite leaks `supervise` processes — nix checkPhase fails, amd toplevel build blocked

Found by lane any-b, task 17502 (2026-11-16), while trying to build-verify PR #10817 (nixpkgs-update 2026-11-16) for darwin-nix#1913.

## Symptom

`pkgs/mcpx`'s nix build fails its checkPhase: every test passes, but the `examples` package fails the testsupport process sweep (#1971):

```
testsupport: 8 process(es) still executing from the suite's build temp dirs after the suite ran (#1971)
FAIL github.com/developing-today/code/pkgs/mcpx/examples 66-86s
```

8 survivors = 4 example daemons' worth. Inspection of a survivor shows it is not the daemon itself but its server supervisor:

```
/tmp/mcpx-bin-<tmp>/mcpx supervise --socket /tmp/TestExamplesdiscover<...>/001/state/sup-2a97516c354b6884.sock -- /tmp/mcpx-fake-<tmp>/fakemcp
```
still alive 38s+ after the test suite ended (the sweep polls a 10s shutdown budget before declaring a leak). The example's own cleanup (`mcpx stop --all`, t.Cleanup in examples_test.go) exits without error, yet the supervise process and its fakemcp child survive. Supervise processes from e2e subset runs were likewise still alive an hour later on the laptop.

## Reproduction (no nix involved)

On current main (95ef2ba25e):

```
cd pkgs/mcpx && go test ./examples/ -count=1
# PASS for every test, then:
# testsupport: 8 process(es) still executing ... FAIL
```

A single subtest reproduces it: `go test ./examples/ -run 'TestExamples/discover' -count=1 -v` — test PASSes, 2 survivors (1 supervise + 1 fakemcp).

## Impact

- `nix build .#nixosConfigurations.amd.config.system.build.toplevel` fails on the mcpx derivation (builder exit 1) — verified in 3 full attempts on PR #10817's branch (which has current main merged) on 2026-11-16; the mcpx derivation was the ONLY failing dependency (full-log + --keep-going runs; logs at ~/git/fleet/17502-build-full.log and 17502-build-retry.log on the laptop).
- This blocks PR #10817 (nixpkgs-update 2026-11-16) and therefore darwin-nix#1913 / queue task 17502, which is dep-blocked on this issue.
- A second, load-sensitive failure was seen once under load ~30 (`internal/pool` TestDefaultConfigStdioRunsSupervised: "supervised child still alive after the reap") — same supervise-reap family; it passed at low load. The examples leak reproduces at load ~1.5, so it is not a load flake.

## Suspected area

The supervise lifecycle: a `mcpx supervise` parent for a supervised stdio server (fakemcp here) is not reaped when the owning command/daemon stops. Either `stop --all` does not signal supervisors, or the supervisor ignores the daemon's shutdown. The #1971 sweep (commits 6599706647, ff4b38a0d3, 7beef75422) is doing its job — the leak is real.

## Acceptance

- `go test ./examples/ -count=1` exits 0 with no surviving supervise/fakemcp processes after the suite.
- The mcpx nix derivation builds green and the amd toplevel build completes on PR #10817's branch.

title: id(grants): reconcile panics on restored grant whose storefront is missing from config
body:
## Defect

`RegistrationService::reconcile` unconditionally unwraps the grant's storefront config on the retry path (`pkgs/id/src/grant_service.rs:792-796`):

```rust
let cfg = self
    .config
    .get(&grant.storefront_id)
    .expect("grant's storefront is configured")
    .clone();
```

The comment above it (`769-770`) claims a store invariant: "a grant in the store always has its storefront in the config built from the same store." That invariant does not hold: the store and the config arrive through independent channels.

- `GrantStore::snapshot` / `GrantStore::restore` (`347-369`) persist and reload every grant record, including `storefront_id`, with only a duplicate-grant-id check. Nothing validates that the restored storefronts exist in the operator config.
- `RegistrationService::new` (`562-576`) takes `store: GrantStore` and `config: HashMap<String, StorefrontConfig>` as independent constructor arguments. No constructor or startup path checks coverage of stored storefronts.
- `register` correctly returns `RegistrationError::UnknownStorefront` for an unconfigured storefront (`601-607`), but `reconcile` replays stored grants without that guard.

## Trigger

1. Register a grant for storefront `sf-a` (grant reaches `Presented`).
2. Persist via `snapshot()`, restart the process with a config that no longer contains `sf-a` (storefront decommissioned, config typo, snapshot copied from another deployment).
3. Restore via `GrantStore::restore(snapshot)`, build the service with the reduced config, let the grant go stale (`stranded_presented`, `300-308`).
4. Next `reconcile()` scan: if the ledger lookup for the grant's deterministic transfer id returns `Ok(None)` (transfer absent — the normal retry case), the `.expect()` fires and the reconciler thread panics instead of counting the grant as still-pending/blocked.

Note the transfer-present branch (`Ok(Some(_))` -> `confirm`) needs no config, so the panic is conditional on the ledger-miss path — a crash-looping reconciler on exactly the retry path that should be most robust.

## Expected

Match `register`'s behavior: treat a stored grant with no configured storefront as a terminal/skip outcome (count it, e.g. `still_pending` or a new `unknown_storefront` counter, keep the record untouched) instead of panicking. At minimum replace the `expect` with a graceful skip; ideally also add a startup coverage check (stored storefronts ⊆ config keys) and a regression test: restore a snapshot containing storefront `sf-a` with an empty config, stub ledger `try_lookup_transfer -> Ok(None)`, call `reconcile` past the freshness bound, assert no panic.

## Duplicates checked

Searched open + all issues for reconcile/storefront/UnknownStorefront — nearest are #2295/#2294 (reconciler feature), #2723/#2254 (lifecycle spec), #8913/#8915 (snapshot duplicate ids). No existing issue covers the store/config divergence panic.

title: fix(dispatch): optNonBlankString returns padded values verbatim — padded dedupe_key defeats dedupe

labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

body:
## Summary
`optNonBlankString` (`pm-stack/dispatch/src/validate.ts:138-141`) trims only for the blank check but returns the original untrimmed string:

```ts
function optNonBlankString(body: Record<string, unknown>, field: string): string | undefined {
  const v = optString(body, field);
  return v !== undefined && v.trim() !== "" ? v : undefined;  // returns v, not v.trim()
}
```

So `"  abc  "` passes the non-blank check and is stored verbatim. It applies to session `title`/`directory` (`:174/:176`) and task `dedupe_key` (`:336`).

## Verified on origin/main `bbe8d38be`
Node repro of the exact function shape:

```
> optNonBlankString({title:"  hello  "},"title")  === "  hello  "  (padding kept)
> optNonBlankString({dedupe_key:"  abc  "},"dedupe_key") === "  abc  "
```

Consequences (code-read, `server.ts:502-505,534-544`):
- Task `dedupe_key`: the padded key is used verbatim for `findExisting`/`enqueue`, so `"abc"` and `"  abc  "` are distinct dedupe keys — a caller typo/mirror-padding double-enqueues work that dedupe exists to collapse.
- Session `directory`: `" /clone "` fails the absolute-path check (or misses the in-clone prefix) and 400s on input the caller meant as valid; trailing-space `"/clone "` resolves lexically and is rejected rather than normalized.
- Session `title`: cosmetic — padded titles reach `maybeCreateIssue` (`:474`) verbatim.
- Contrast: `reqString`, `parseModel`, and `promptRaw.trim()` all normalize; only the `optNonBlankString` path keeps padding.

## Dedupe
- Open/closed `gh search issues` for `optNonBlankString`: no tracker (one closed hit #6428 is an unrelated shepherd note for #2664).
- Nearest fixed sibling #10739 (blank `dedupe_key` falls through to the canonical key, now CLOSED) covers empty/whitespace-only keys only; padded-but-nonblank keys are a distinct gap. Existing tests pin only already-trimmed verbatim values (`validate.test.ts:356-365` `"My session"`, `:384-387` canonical key) — no padded case.
- #10825 (OPEN) is outbound-fetch timeouts, unrelated.

## Fix shape
Trim inside `optNonBlankString` (`return v.trim()`), and extend the two verbatim tests with padded inputs (`"  My session  "` → `"My session"`, padded canonical key → trimmed key). Effort is trivial; directory behavior then matches the documented missing/empty/whitespace-only → repo-default rule with accidental padding forgiven.

body:
Every outbound fetch in pm-stack/dispatch except the JWKS one has no timeout or abort signal, so a stalled upstream parks the dispatch handler (and its worker slot) indefinitely — Bun/Node fetch has no default timeout.

Evidence (origin/main 92e96ddaab, read-only):
- pm-stack/dispatch/src/queue.ts:72 (rpc), :115 (patchTask), :145, :195, :224, :259 — bare `await fetch(...)`, no signal.
- pm-stack/dispatch/src/opencode.ts:55 (`api()`) — bare fetch. The catch there maps only connection-refused to a 502 OpenCodeError; a stall never resolves at all.
- pm-stack/dispatch/src/github.ts:147 (`appApi()`) — bare fetch to api.github.com (installation lookup :166, token mint :177).
- Exhaustive: `grep -rn 'AbortSignal|AbortController|timeout' pm-stack/dispatch/src/` returns zero hits.
- Adjacent but distinct: #10738 covers only the JWKS fetch in auth.ts:105 (`fetchGithubJwks`); this issue is the other six call sites. Open-issue search for timeout/fetch-timeout returns #10738 plus unrelated items (#500, #4191, #4191-class in other packages) — no tracker for the Supabase/opencode/GitHub paths; no open PR touches these files for timeouts.

Why it matters: dispatch awaits these inline on the request path. One slow Supabase query, one wedged opencode server, or one api.github.com stall hangs that handler forever; under load this exhausts server concurrency and blocks queue operations fleet-wide. The OIDC path at least fails closed after #10738; these paths hang open with no error at all.

Suggested fix shape: a shared `fetchWithTimeout` helper (sane default, e.g. 10–15s, longer budget for known-slow ops), wired through queue.ts rpc/patchTask/claim paths, opencode.ts api(), and github.ts appApi(); a timeout surfaces as 502/503 (upstream failure, matching opencode.ts's existing unreachable mapping), never a raw 500. Test: stub upstream that never responds, assert rejection within budget.

Acceptance:
- All outbound fetches in dispatch/src carry a timeout.
- Timeout errors map to 5xx upstream-failure responses, not hangs and not raw 500s.
- A regression test pins the bound (never-responding stub rejects within the budget).

title: fix(cold-store): non-UTF-8 state.json/credentials.json still leak a raw UnicodeDecodeError — PR #4361's corrupt-file wrap catches only JSONDecodeError

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/cold-store-reaper
labels.description: Package/app: cold-store-reaper (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Finding

Merged PR #4361 made cold-store's private-JSON loads fail usefully on corrupt files: `load_state` and `load_credentials` wrap `json.loads(...)` and raise `ColdStoreError` naming the file, instead of leaking a raw `JSONDecodeError`. The wrap catches only half of what a corrupt file can do:

Both loaders call `Path.read_text()` (default UTF-8, strict) **inside** the same expression, but the `except` clause names only `json.JSONDecodeError`. A state.json or credentials.json whose bytes are not valid UTF-8 — binary garbage, a file torn by a non-atomic writer outside this module, latin-1 bytes from a manual edit — raises `UnicodeDecodeError` from `read_text()` before `json.loads` ever runs, and it propagates raw: no file name, no repair guidance, and not the `ColdStoreError` type callers are told to expect for corrupt files. (`UnicodeDecodeError` and `JSONDecodeError` are sibling `ValueError` subclasses; catching one does not catch the other.)

The PR's corrupt-file tests write truncated *text* JSON, so this path is untested as well as unhandled.

## Evidence

- PR #4361 (MERGED, commit `d64a9e9d9b`, merge commit `d1de7ee869c7dede6e7538b9f2acde85df30f71c`, ancestor-verified against main `856d00f1d322a5724aa4ba85c728eaec5e341c7a`, compare behind=0), fixes #3279 (CLOSED, verified): https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/4361
- On current main, `pkgs/cold-store-reaper/cold_store.py:528` — `creds = json.loads(self.credentials_path.read_text())` guarded by `except json.JSONDecodeError` at `:529`; same shape at `:558-559` for `load_state`. No `UnicodeDecodeError` handling at either site — a grep of the full file on main finds zero occurrences of `UnicodeDecodeError`.
- The module's own later hardening shows the intended contract: wrong-shape JSON was separately fixed to raise `ColdStoreError` (#6845, CLOSED; the `isinstance` checks now at `cold_store.py:537+` and `:566+`) — decode failure is the remaining raw-exception hole in the same two functions.
- Dedupe: searched open + closed issues for `UnicodeDecodeError` and `cold-store corrupt` on 2026-11-16 — no issue covers non-UTF-8 corruption of these files; #3279 covered torn writes / `JSONDecodeError`, #6845 covered valid-JSON wrong shape.

## Why it matters

The point of #4361 (and #6845 after it) is that a wedged cold-store run tells the operator which file is corrupt and how to repair it, in one typed error. A non-UTF-8 file — a realistic corruption shape for a credentials file handled by external tools — still wedges every run with a bare traceback that names neither the file nor the remedy.

## Acceptance criteria

- `load_state` and `load_credentials` raise `ColdStoreError` (naming the file, with the existing repair guidance) when the file contains invalid UTF-8, not a raw `UnicodeDecodeError`.
- Regression tests cover a non-UTF-8 state.json and a non-UTF-8 credentials.json (bytes, not truncated text), alongside the existing corrupt-text cases.
- Existing cold-store tests keep passing (`python3 -m unittest tests.test_cold_store` in `pkgs/cold-store-reaper`).

## Shadow verdict (PoC)

Stage A window already closed (summary on developing-today/code#2313) — no shadow verdict recorded.

body:
## Finding

Merged PR #4355 fixed `graphemeWidth` in the id web presenter so U+FE0F widens a cluster only when the preceding code point can start an emoji presentation sequence. The gate is `EMOJI_PRESENTATION_SEQ_RANGES` — a table of 183 ranges / 371 code points in `pkgs/id/web/src/world-surface.ts`, transcribed by hand from unicode-width 0.2.2's `starts_emoji_presentation_seq` bit table.

The transcription has no committed test that can catch a transcription error:

- The PR's own verification was a one-off differential probe (14,607 base+FE0F clusters against a Rust probe pinned to unicode-width =0.2.2, zero mismatches) — run manually, **not committed**, so nothing re-checks the table when it is next edited.
- The committed test added by the PR asserts ~33 spot glyphs (11 narrow, 22 wide). A wrong boundary in any of the other ~150 ranges — e.g. one code point shifted at a range edge — passes the whole suite.
- The shared screen-cell parity corpus (`pkgs/id/web/src/test-fixtures/screen-cell-parity.json`, from #5237/#6110) contains exactly one U+FE0F case (⚠️ U+26A0+FE0F), which is also in the spot list.

## Evidence

- PR #4355 (MERGED, commit `382eb52c17`, merge commit `30ce6be56b7ecacf3e23071f62488f914c8a8a62`, ancestor-verified against main `856d00f1d322a5724aa4ba85c728eaec5e341c7a`, compare behind=0), fixes #3265 (CLOSED, verified): https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/4355
- Table on current main: `pkgs/id/web/src/world-surface.ts:354` (`EMOJI_PRESENTATION_SEQ_RANGES`, spanning to just before `isEmojiPresentationSeqBase` at `:540-541`); the FE0F branch at `:615-616`. PR body states the table was "decoded verbatim" from the crate's bit table and the differential probe was a verification step, not a test.
- Committed coverage on current main: `pkgs/id/web/src/world-surface.test.ts:453` — the #3265 test with the 11 narrow + 22 wide spot glyphs; parity fixture `test-fixtures/screen-cell-parity.json` has 6 cases total, one with U+FE0F.
- Later parity work did not close this: PR #4491 (for #2962, CLOSED) synced `WIDE_RANGES` for single code points and likewise relied on a manual differential re-run; it did not touch the FE0F presentation table.
- Dedupe: searched open + closed issues for `FE0F parity`, `emoji-presentation`, and `world-surface test` on 2026-11-16 — matches are #3265/#4355 themselves, #2962/#4491 (single-code-point scope), #6110/#5237 (the 6-case corpus); none covers the presentation table's transcription.

## Why it matters

This table is the TS half of a TS↔Rust wire contract: the Rust validator decides which cells are legal, and the presenter refuses the whole screen when its width measurement disagrees. A silent one-point transcription error reintroduces exactly the #3265 failure mode (a Rust-valid screen refused, or an invalid one accepted) for the affected glyph, with no test positioned to notice.

## Acceptance criteria

- A committed test checks every range in `EMOJI_PRESENTATION_SEQ_RANGES` at its boundaries (low−1, low, high, high+1) against the expected emoji-presentation membership derived from unicode-width 0.2.2 (e.g. a generated fixture from the crate's table, or an equivalent exhaustive base+FE0F sweep committed as a fixture), so any future edit to a range edge fails a test.
- The test runs in the existing `pkgs/id/web` vitest suite (no manual probe step).
- Existing world-surface tests keep passing.

title: test(pkarr-worker): RETENTION_SECONDS guard is never exercised through the real Durable Object alarm path — invalid values only reach a mock that re-implements it (PR #4352)

labels.name: kind/test
labels.description: Test coverage, test infrastructure, or test-only fixes

labels.name: task/triage

labels.name: app/pkarr-worker

body:
## Finding

Merged PR #4352 guarded the pkarr-worker's retention alarm: malformed, non-positive, or out-of-range `RETENTION_SECONDS` values now fall back to seven days instead of scheduling a deletion alarm at/before now (or `NaN`). The guard itself (`retentionMilliseconds`) is well unit-tested — but the invalid-value cases never exercise the real Durable Object path they protect:

- The parameterized `RETENTION_SECONDS` tests drive `worker.fetch` with a **mock** `PKARR_STORE` whose `putPacket` re-implements the production alarm computation inline (`now + retentionMilliseconds(retentionSeconds, now)`). The real `PkarrStore.putPacket` — the code that reads `this.env.RETENTION_SECONDS` and calls `this.ctx.storage.setAlarm` — is never invoked for any invalid or valid non-default value.
- The only assertion against a real Durable Object alarm is in the pre-existing publish test, which uses the default environment (no `RETENTION_SECONDS` set) and expects the seven-day default.

So the seam the fix exists for — env value → `retentionMilliseconds` → `setAlarm` inside the real DO — is unpinned: if the wiring in `src/index.ts` regressed (wrong env field, alarm computed from a stale `now`, guard bypassed), every retention test would still pass, because the mock copies the intended wiring instead of using it.

## Evidence

- PR #4352 (MERGED, commit `388d8c1dcf`, merge commit `f1330f3f09ee3dad97f51aa9f7e54510643ffb34`, ancestor-verified against main `856d00f1d322a5724aa4ba85c728eaec5e341c7a`, compare behind=0), closes #3261 (CLOSED, verified): https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/4352
- Production wiring on current main: `pkgs/pkarr-worker/src/index.ts:88-89` — `const retentionMs = retentionMilliseconds(this.env.RETENTION_SECONDS, now); await this.ctx.storage.setAlarm(now + retentionMs);`. Guard: `pkgs/pkarr-worker/src/retention.ts:5-22`.
- Test gap on current main: `pkgs/pkarr-worker/test/worker.test.ts:33` defines `mockStore`, whose `putPacket` (lines 33-45) computes the alarm itself from `retentionMilliseconds`; the `RETENTION_SECONDS` describe block at `:136` routes every case (missing, `0`, `-1`, `7d`, whitespace, `1e9`, `3600.5`, `+3600`, out-of-range, `604800`, `3600`) through that mock. The sole real-DO alarm readback is at `:196-199` (`runInDurableObject` + `state.storage.getAlarm()`), in the default-env publish test only.
- Dedupe: searched open + closed issues for `RETENTION_SECONDS alarm`, `retentionMilliseconds`, and `cold-store corrupt` analogues on 2026-11-16 — only #3261 (the parent issue #4352 closed) and #4352 itself match; no issue covers this test seam.

## Why it matters

#3261 was a data-loss bug: a bad env value made stored packets vanish right after a 204, or never expire. The regression suite for it should fail if the protection stops being wired into the real object — today it cannot, because the tests substitute a hand-copied version of the wiring for the thing itself.

## Acceptance criteria

- At least the invalid-value cases (e.g. `0`, `7d`, out-of-range) and one valid non-default value (e.g. `3600`) are exercised through the real `PkarrStore` Durable Object (e.g. `runInDurableObject` / SELF with per-test env bindings), asserting the alarm the DO actually scheduled via `state.storage.getAlarm()`.
- The mock-based cases are removed or reduced so the alarm expectation is not computed by re-implementing the production expression in the test.
- Existing pkarr-worker tests keep passing (`npm test` in `pkgs/pkarr-worker`).

## Shadow verdict (PoC)

Stage A window already closed (summary on developing-today/code#2313) — no shadow verdict recorded.

title: fleet-queue: unify max_attempts defaults at 1000 (live table defaults to 4, outbox stamps 8)
body:
## Problem

Drew's standing order (2026-11-12) is that every fleet-queue task carries `max_attempts = 1000`. That order was implemented as after-the-fact patching (the queue-hygiene sweep raising rows batch by batch) instead of unifying the defaults at creation. The mismatch never stops regenerating: **72 tasks created since 2026-11-15 landed below 1000**, three of them live on 2026-11-16 (tasks 17481 @ 3, 17492 @ 4, 17507 @ 4). On 2026-11-16 Drew ordered a bulk normalization: **13,025 rows** were raised to 1000 in the Turso `fleet-queue` tasks table (one `hygiene_fix` event per row recording its old value); the table now verifies 0 rows ≠ 1000. Without this source fix, the drift restarts with the next task created on a stale-default path.

## Root cause: four different defaults in `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue`

1. **The live Turso `tasks` table itself defaults to 4.** Read directly from the live DB: `max_attempts INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 4`. The current code's SCHEMA constant (`turso_queue.rs`, CREATE TABLE for tasks) says `DEFAULT 1000`, but `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` never alters an existing table, so the live table keeps 4 forever. Any insert that relies on the column default lands at 4.
2. **The creation outbox stamps 8.** `creation_outbox.rs:45`: `pub const DEFAULT_MAX_ATTEMPTS: i64 = 8;` used at line 371; the `creation_outbox` table also defaults its own `max_attempts` to 8. Worse, `turso_queue.rs` (~line 8129) carries a comment/test asserting the outbox "intentionally stays at its own DEFAULT_MAX_ATTEMPTS" — the divergence is deliberate and test-locked.
3. **Legacy Postgres-era tasks carry 3.** `migrations/0008_repo_queue_pilot.sql:62`: `coalesce(p_max_attempts, 3)` — tasks from that era were carried into Turso with 3 (thousands of historical rows).
4. **Assorted producers pass explicit small caps** (observed live values: 2, 5, 6, 9, 10, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48).

The one correct path: `validate.rs:913` `TASK_DEFAULT_MAX_ATTEMPTS: u64 = 1000`, used as the enqueue fallback in `turso_queue.rs` (~line 2116).

## Fix

- Make the live `tasks` table default 1000 in fact, not just in the schema constant: rebuild/migrate the table default, or stamp `max_attempts` explicitly on every insert path so the column default is never relied on.
- Set `creation_outbox::DEFAULT_MAX_ATTEMPTS` to 1000 and remove/replace the intentional-divergence comment and test in `turso_queue.rs`.
- Audit enqueue call sites that pass explicit sub-1000 caps; any that remain need a named reason on this issue.

## Acceptance

- A task created via each path — direct insert relying on the column default, creation outbox, enqueue API with no explicit cap — lands at `max_attempts = 1000`.
- A hygiene-sweep run afterwards finds zero rows to raise.

body:
## Summary

`replay_grants` (`pkgs/id/crates/id-worlds/src/world/audit.rs:125`) claims to fold the retained log back into the final grants state, but it skips every record whose outcome is not `"accepted"` and only folds `UpdateCaps` / `SetCapsCeiling`. First-use provider grants are audited as `provider_use` / `first_use_grant` and also persist `JournalEntry::CapsGranted` — so after any grant-on-use, replayed `granted` is missing a capability the live ledger holds.

## Evidence (origin/main @ aa3472c037)

- `pkgs/id/crates/id-worlds/src/world/audit.rs:128`: `if record.outcome != "accepted" { continue; }`, then match only on `UpdateCaps` / `SetCapsCeiling`; `_ => {}` swallows `provider_use`.
- `pkgs/id/crates/id-worlds/src/world/actor.rs:647-665` `audit_provider_decision`: `Decision::AllowAndGrant => "first_use_grant"`, `action: "provider_use"`, `parameters: {"capability": capability}`.
- `pkgs/id/crates/id-caps/src/world_caps.rs` `CapLedger::decide_for`: under `grant_on_use`, inserts cap into `granted` and returns `AllowAndGrant`.
- Actor persists on all three `AllowAndGrant` sites (`:1533`, `:1757`, `:1823`): `persist(JournalEntry::CapsGranted { granted })`.
- Existing exit test `retained_audit_log_replays_to_the_final_grants` (`pkgs/id/crates/id-worlds/src/world/tests.rs`, F12.6 #1063) covers only admin UpdateCaps/SetCapsCeiling actions — no first-use path, so the divergence is untested.

## Why it matters

Any consumer using `replay_grants` (audit export, restore verification, grants reconciliation) silently under-reports grants on worlds with `grant_on_use` enabled — the exact worlds where grants change without admin action. The journal says granted; the replay says not granted.

## Acceptance criteria / fix shape

- Fold `provider_use` / `first_use_grant` capability from `parameters.capability` into `replayed.granted` (insert single cap; respect ceiling semantics if needed).
- Extend the F12.6 replay test with a first-use grant: enable grant-on-use, exercise one provider use, assert `replay_grants(&records).granted == caps_report().granted`.
- Keep refused/denied replaying as nothing.

## Finding (from PR review)

CodeRabbit (COMMENTED review, 2026-11-16) on merged PR #10624 — "feat(antigravity): track newest agy via antigravity-cli-nix overlay":

That package set does not receive `nixpkgs.overlays`. The system profile therefore installs the unoverlaid package (1.4.8 at the linked nixpkgs revision) instead of the 1.5.9 overlay package. The home profile, `mcpx`, and `t3code` already use `pkgs.antigravity-cli`. Selecting `pkgs.antigravity-cli` here makes every install use the same package.

`nixos/environment/default.nix` on main (blob sha acda5bb4c658):

- Line 872: the system package list block opens with `++ (with inputs.nixpkgs-unstable.legacyPackages.${system}; [`
- Line 885: `antigravity-cli # google, mainProgram "antigravity"` — still the bare entry resolved from the unoverlaid legacyPackages set.

title: fleet-queue(validate): a non-ASCII byte in a maintenance dedupe key panics the broker thread — /validate answers 500 with no field named

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: app/fleet
labels.description: pkgs/fleet multicall binary + platform crates

body:
## Symptom

A packet whose `dedupe_key` carries a non-ASCII character inside the maintenance week field makes the **running queue-broker panic** instead of rejecting the packet:

```
$ repo-queue validate /tmp/bad-key-packet.json
repo-queue: queue-broker error
exit=3
```

Expected: exit 2 with `packet.dedupe_key: '…' matches no design pattern` (the module's documented contract is reject-with-a-named-field). Observed: an opaque broker error, and in the broker journal:

```
Nov 16 07:23:53 amd fleet[2163]: thread '<unnamed>' (3123350) panicked at crates/fleet-queue/src/validate.rs:493:48:
Nov 16 07:23:53 amd fleet[2163]: end byte index 4 is not a char boundary; it is inside 'é' (bytes 3..5 of string)
```

`POST /validate` for that packet answers **HTTP 500 with an empty body**; the same request with an ASCII week (`2026-W46`) answers HTTP 200 with the normal `errors` array.

## Root cause

`match_dedupe` parses the maintenance family by **byte-slicing the client-supplied key**:

`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/validate.rs:491-498`

```rust
let week_ok = week.len() == 8
    && all_digits(&week[..4])      // :493  <-- panics when byte 4 is mid-character
    && week.as_bytes()[4] == b'-'
    && wb[5] == b'W'
    && all_digits(&week[6..])      // :496  <-- same hazard at byte 6
    && week[6..].parse::<u32>()...
```

`week.len() == 8` counts **bytes**, not chars. A key like

```
repo-health:v1:maintenance:developing-today/code:fmt:202éW01
```

has an 8-byte week tail (`202` + 2-byte `é` + `W01`) whose byte 4 falls inside `é`, so `&week[..4]` panics. The panic kills the per-request thread (main.rs spawns one per connection), so the client gets no envelope at all — not even a validation error.

## Why it matters

- The broker is the fleet's **trust boundary** for non-CLI producers (`validate.rs` module doc): a value it cannot honour must be refused with an error naming the field, never crash the request path.
- Any authenticated producer can trigger it with a hand-written or templated key (encoding artifact, pasted en-dash/é, a copied key with a smart quote). The enqueuer then sees `queue-broker error` / exit 3, which reads like an infrastructure fault and invites blind retries; the only real signal is a journal panic.
- `validate_packet` is also used in-process by `repo-queue`, so the same input has no safe path anywhere.

## Affected copies

- `developing-today/code` — `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/validate.rs:493,496,497` (live; serves `queue-broker.service`, PID 2163 at time of filing).
- `dezren39/darwin-nix` — `pkgs/fleet-brokers/src/crates/queue-broker/src/validate.rs:233` (vendored port; identical expression, verified by a local `cargo test` probe: `panicked at …:233:48: end byte index 4 is not a char boundary`). Same guard needed whenever that port is refreshed.

## Fix shape

Make the week test byte-safe instead of string-slicing untrusted input, e.g. reject `!week.is_ascii()` up front, then compare `week.as_bytes()` against `b"YYYY-Www"` and parse only ASCII digits. Keep the ISO-week range check (`01..=53`) from #5482 — the current test `maintenance_keys_name_real_iso_weeks` (`validate.rs:1374`) already pins W00/W54/W99 rejection and must keep passing.

## Acceptance criteria

- `match_dedupe` / `validate_packet` never panic for arbitrary UTF-8 input. Add a property test (proptest is already a dev-dependency in `pkgs/id`; any generator is fine) that throws random unicode strings at `match_dedupe` and random packets at `validate_packet` and asserts they return `None` / `Vec<String>`.
- Regression test: `repo-health:v1:maintenance:developing-today/code:fmt:202éW01` (and the equivalent at the byte-6 position, e.g. `2026-Wé`) are rejected as "matches no design pattern"; `2026-W44` still matches and W00/W54/W99 still do not.
- `POST /validate` for the repro packet returns HTTP 200 with a `packet.dedupe_key` error; no panic line in the broker journal.
- `repo-queue validate` on that packet exits 2 and names `packet.dedupe_key` (not exit 3 `queue-broker error`).
- Mirror the same guard in the `dezren39/darwin-nix` vendored copy if that port is being kept.

## Dedupe

Searched all states for `validate.rs`, `validate_packet`, `dedupe_key`, `char boundary`, `panicked`, `maintenance week`: nearest are CLOSED #5482 (added the ISO-week range check and this slicing code), #5510 (leading-zero spellings), #6430 (element type checks), and OPEN #10739 (`blank dedupe_key` is accepted — different defect), #9028/#9029 (producer bypass / bounds table). No open PR touches `validate.rs`. Nothing tracks this panic.

title: main-broken: id-0.1.0 fails to compile — mismatched closing delimiter in pkgs/id/crates/id-worlds/src/world_ssh.rs (blocks amd toplevel)
body:
# main-broken: `id-0.1.0` fails to compile — mismatched closing delimiter in `pkgs/id/crates/id-worlds/src/world_ssh.rs`

Found by the 2026-11-16 nixpkgs-update run (branch `chore/nixpkgs-update-2026-11-16`) while acceptance-building the amd toplevel. **This failure is pre-existing on main and is not caused by the nixpkgs update** — proof below.

## Failing step

`nix build .#nixosConfigurations.amd.config.system.build.toplevel` fails at exactly one root derivation:

```
error: Cannot build '/nix/store/0a18cs3qqfn3v83iqc306gsslcxyhcz0-id-0.1.0.drv'.
       Reason: builder failed with exit code 101.
       >    Compiling id-worlds v0.1.0 (/build/id/crates/id-worlds)
       > error: mismatched closing delimiter: `}`
       >     --> crates/id-worlds/src/world_ssh.rs:3813:24
       >      |
       > 3760 |     fn terminal_shell_frames_conform_to_the_shell_contract() {
       >      |                                                              - closing delimiter possibly meant for this
       > 3813 |         sent.push(check(
       >      |                        ^ unclosed delimiter
       > 3858 |     }
       >      |     ^ mismatched closing delimiter
       > error: could not compile `id-worlds` (lib) due to 1 previous error
```

In the source, the `sent.push(check(&serde_json::json!({…}).to_string(),` call in `terminal_shell_frames_conform_to_the_shell_contract` is never closed (the closing `));` is missing before the following `let more_documents = …` statement).

Dependents that consequently cannot build: `unit-id-primary.service` → `system-units` → `etc` → the amd toplevel.

## Proof it predates / is independent of the nixpkgs update

- The update branch changes only `flake.lock` (`nixpkgs-25` 1d060086d60c → d5cc68339997). `git diff origin/main -- pkgs/id/crates/id-worlds/src/world_ssh.rs` is empty, and `git show origin/main:pkgs/id/crates/id-worlds/src/world_ssh.rs` shows the identical unclosed call at line 3813.
- `nix-store -q --requisites` of the failing `id-0.1.0` derivation contains **zero** references to the updated nixpkgs-25 source and none of its packages (misfortune / activitywatch / regex-pcre) — the `id` package builds from the main pkgs set, which the update does not move.
- Last commits touching the file on main: 2f78741e8a / 2f76243fe0 (#3762, id session documents frames).

## What was tried

- Full amd toplevel build on the laptop from the update branch: this was the only root builder failure (all other `Cannot build` entries are its dependents).
- The nixpkgs-25 segment itself (regex-pcre / misfortune / activitywatch at d5cc68339997) is being realised solo and store-validity-checked separately; results are reported on the update PR.

## Impact

Any amd toplevel build from current main fails until this delimiter is fixed, including the nixpkgs-update acceptance build. The 2026-11-16 nixpkgs update PR is therefore opened **unmerged** under the #2696 exception (update's own breakage: none; remaining red: this issue only), to be merged once `id` builds on main again.

Fix is presumably the missing `));` — left to the id lanes, who are actively committing in this file, rather than folded into the deps-update PR.

title: fleet gh: document the credential lifecycle and current limitations
body:
## Problem (five words: fleet gh behavior is undocumented)

The credential behavior of `fleet gh` is documented nowhere an operator would look. It took a full source read (gh.rs, 1,218 lines) plus live probes on 2026-11-14 to establish facts that should be written down:

- Credentials resolve by name through the fleet secrets broker (session proxy first, Bitwarden CLI fallback). Exact secret names per leg (personal hosts file, three app keys/IDs).
- Minting is in-process (RS256 JWT via openssl fd, installation lookup, token exchange, GH_TOKEN exported to the child gh only).
- NO cross-invocation caching: every call re-resolves, re-signs, re-lists, re-mints (issue #10742 (the caching-daemon issue) addresses fixing this; this issue is about documenting reality until then, and the design after).
- Leg lists are compiled-in constants per app, overridable via FLEET_GH_*_OWNERS env vars; FLEET_GH_ORDER grammar; owner-hint behavior (hint reorders within existing legs, never adds).
- Unknown-org behavior: never mints dynamically; scoped calls fail 403 under a wrong-org leg; the personal-first default masks the gap for an admin user.
- Exit code 3 semantics; FLEET_GH_BIN and FLEET_GH_RAW behavior.

## Acceptance

- A doc page in the fleet docs (alongside the fleet gh material from code#8887) covering every bullet above, written from the source with file references, reviewed against live behavior.
- The doc states plainly which parts are interim (per-invocation cost, compiled-in lists) and links code#10311 and issue #10742 (the caching-daemon issue) as the tracked fixes, so the limitation is visibly owned rather than tribal knowledge.

body:
The default `gh` route on the Muse sandbox is dead: every call through the fleet gh shim hangs indefinitely while the pristine gh binary works instantly.
The secrets broker cannot refresh its vault (`bws secret list` spawn fails), so it serves 503 "not loaded yet" for the github-cli hosts secret the shim's token fetch depends on — no fleet GitHub work can run through the normal route until this is fixed.

## Evidence (2026-11-16, verified twice this run)
- Broker log `~/.config/secrets-broker/secrets-broker.log` (last write 2026-11-16T12:27:50Z), repeated line: `secrets-broker: refresh failed: bws secret list -o json failed: spawn failed: entity not found` (5 occurrences in the current log; the prior broker incarnation in the same log refreshed 198 secrets successfully).

## Why this is fleet-stalling (Drew's Priorities Brief, line 1)
Brief line 1: "a broken sign-in or secrets route" outranks all feature work. The `gh` shim is the standing route for Muse-side GitHub work (shim installed 2026-11-14, Drew); with the broker unable to load secrets, that route hangs instead of failing visibly.

title: fleet gh: credential/token caching daemon for sandbox and laptop
body:
## Problem (five words: every call re-mints everything)

`fleet gh` caches nothing across invocations (source-verified 2026-11-14, gh.rs): every call re-resolves secrets through the broker, re-signs RS256 JWTs, re-lists app installations, and re-mints installation tokens for each leg it attempts. All caching is in-memory per process. For interactive use this is seconds of overhead per call; for automation it compounds badly — the closure watchdog (code#10138) pages issue events across four repos and makes a `fleet gh` call per check, and on 2026-11-16 it could not clear a ~41h event backlog within a 10-minute run, leaving the closure guard impaired. The cost is structural, not a bug in any caller.

## Proposal (Drew, 2026-11-16)

A small credential daemon, running on the sandbox and on the laptop, that caches what `fleet gh` currently re-derives per call:

- Secret resolution results (short TTL), app JWTs (within their expiry), installation tokens (until shortly before expiry), and installation lists per app.
- Memory-only: tokens and keys are never written to disk; the daemon is the only process holding them.
- Single-flight minting: concurrent callers share one mint per leg instead of stampeding the broker/API.

### Addressing (per Drew's sketch)

- The daemon address is **a setting in the app** (fleet config), not a hardcoded constant.
- A flag or CLI arg overrides the setting for a single invocation.
- Client resolution order: **try the localhost daemon first, then the laptop daemon**. The same logic works on the laptop itself (there, localhost IS the laptop), so one code path serves both machines.
- If an address has **no port, a default port applies**.

### Fallback

If no daemon answers, `fleet gh` falls back to today's in-process resolution — with a visible note that it did so, never silently (silent degradation is the failure mode this program keeps hitting elsewhere).

## Acceptance

- Repeat `fleet gh` calls on both machines reuse cached tokens: no broker round-trip, no re-mint, while a valid cached token exists (prove with TRACE timings before/after).
- Daemon restart clears all cached material; nothing secret persists on disk at any point.
- Address setting + flag/arg override + localhost-then-laptop order + default-port behavior all covered by tests, including the no-daemon fallback.
- Closure watchdog catch-up over a multi-day backlog completes in a small fraction of today's time (measure against the 2026-11-16 baseline).

Refs: code#10311 (configurable rotation — companion piece), code#10138 (watchdog cost symptom).

title: id(world): FileJournal byte cap is bypassed by append_transaction (journal can grow past MAX_JOURNAL_BYTES)
body:
## Evidence

`pkgs/id/crates/id-worlds/src/world_store.rs` (verified on origin/main `bb57b6f5`):

- `FileJournal::append` enforces the cap before writing (:344-356): `new_bytes = self.bytes + line.len()`, `ensure!(new_bytes <= self.max_bytes, ... "byte cap" ...)`, and the in-crate + `world_dos` tests pin exactly this ("appends refuse at the byte cap, the file never exceeds it").
- `FileJournal::append_transaction` (:397-423) reads the journal, extends the entry list, and calls `self.compact(&entries)` with **no size check**.
- `FileJournal::compact` (:425+, sibling-file build + rename, re-baselines `self.bytes = compacted_bytes`) likewise has **no cap check**.

So a two-entry atomic write succeeds where the equivalent appends would refuse: fill a journal to just under the cap with `append`, then `append_transaction(&[e1, e2])` pushes the file over the cap and re-baselines the tracker to the over-cap size. The very next `append` refuses (bytes > max), but the invariant the tests assert — "the file never exceeds the cap" — is already broken.

Production callers go through this path: `WorldActor::persist_transaction` (`pkgs/id/crates/id-worlds/src/world/actor.rs:890`) wraps the signed-move pair (:~2959, `Committed` + `SignedMoveAccepted`) and the builder-install pair (:~3330, install event + `BuilderInstalled` audit) as transactions precisely so a crash cannot split them. Near a full journal, the crash-safety write is the one that overflows.

## Why it matters

#560 (option B, landed via #10702) closed the F12.18 journal-size bullet on the promise that the byte cap is a backstop: "when an append would cross the cap the append is refused before anything is written". With the transaction path uncapped, the DoS bound is advisory, not enforced — a hostile or buggy program driving signed moves / installs near a full journal grows the file past `MAX_JOURNAL_BYTES` (64 MiB default), and the over-cap journal then refuses *all* further appends until an operator trims it. Availability-wise this is the worst outcome: unbounded growth followed by total refusal.

## Acceptance criteria / suggested fix

- `append_transaction` refuses **before writing anything** when the encoded transaction would cross `max_bytes`, with the same "byte cap" refusal shape as `append` (atomicity preserved: refuse the whole transaction, never a prefix).
- `compact` itself stays available as the shrink path: checkpoint trim (`compact_journal`, actor.rs:454) and any rewrite that *reduces* size must succeed even on an over-cap journal; only growth past the cap refuses. Cleanest split: size-check in `append_transaction` (and the append path, as today), not a blanket check inside `compact`.
- The bump-on-first-write rewrite inside `append` (:335-340) should also stay cap-exempt or be accounted: it rewrites the same entries under a new header version and must not turn a version bump into a spurious refusal.
- Tests: extend the in-crate cap test (`journal_appends_are_refused_at_the_byte_cap`) and/or `world_dos::journal_size_is_bounded_by_the_file_journal_byte_cap` with a transaction that would cross a small explicit cap — assert refusal, file length still <= cap, and replay equals the accepted prefix.

Deduped: `gh search issues` for `append_transaction` + byte cap and `MAX_JOURNAL_BYTES` returns only #560 (the tracking issue, whose remaining journal-size bullet #10702 claimed to close) and unrelated items; #10702 touched only `append` + tests, no transaction path. No open PR touches `world_store.rs` transaction/cap logic.

title: queue: a blocked task is re-claimed within ~30s, so lane escalations cannot hold (task 15848, attempt 13)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Symptom

A queue task that has been **blocked** by a lane can be back in `claimed` within ~30 seconds, so a lane's escalation never holds and the same task is re-claimed by a different lane minutes later. The visible cost is a park→claim→park cycle that repeats for days, with each lane re-doing the same verification and re-posting the same escalation.

## Evidence (2026-11-16, queue `repo-health-code-pilot`)

Task **15848** (issue #1822, socket activation, small_fix) is at attempt 13:

- `11:04:02Z` — lane code-i ran `repo-queue block 15848 --worker repo-worker-code --reason-class escalated-to-user --blocker …`. The command **returned a success row** for 15848.
- `11:04:1xZ` — `repo-queue list --task 15848` reported **`queued`**.
- `11:04:34Z` — 15848 was **claimed again** (`muse-lane`), 32 s after the block.
- `11:05:53Z` — the task shows `muse-lane/muse-lane` as owner again in `repo-queue timeline`.

Control: the same verb on an unrelated task (`5797`) wrote `blocked` as expected, and that row was also **claimed again within ~30 s** by a different owner. So the block write is not the failing part; something re-queues or claims blocked rows.

Prior escalations that were silently undone the same way: lane code-f at `05:13Z` and lane code-h at `04:06Z` (both reported `state=blocked` on 15848 in agent notes; the row kept being re-claimed).

## Why it matters

- Fleet lanes are instructed to write a terminal queue verb at the first moment an outcome exists. When `block` does not survive, lanes cannot leave a terminal state, and the queue converts a human decision into unbounded worker churn.
- Attempt counts inflate (`max_attempts` churn), and every re-claim burns a scheduled window on a task that cannot progress.

## Scope of investigation (suggested)

1. Which process can move a `blocked` row to `queued`/`claimed`? Candidates: `wake` on a parked row, `release` from a stale lease holder, an external orchestrator (muse-lane) using direct SQL rather than the verb, or a broker sweep.
2. Whether `repo-queue block` on a row whose claim is held by another identity can report success without writing (15848 had multiple overlapping owners in the minutes around the block).
3. Whether `claimed_by` accepts a stale `leases` row, letting a second process take a task that another process's block just cleared.

Related: #5444 (packet validation quarantine visible in 15848's `last_error`), #6838 (`revive`), #8276 (typed dependency blocks).
