body:
# Home is not optional — one home-resolution contract for the repo's tools

Design doc: `files/designs/code-home-resolution-contract.md` in the
`keep-the-four-repos-healthy` goal workspace. Filed by the design
architect (pass 53, 2026-11-04). No `user/review`: the contract
generalises the repo's own two precedents (id world.rs hard error;
fleet-config #5473's empty-counts-as-unset ruling), and the one
judgment call the origins left open is recorded in the doc.

## The defect

Three filings in two days are one defect with three addresses: a
tool that cannot find the user's home directory invents one, and
the invention differs per copy of the helper —

- **Filesystem root** — fleet-queue's client `home()`
  (`unwrap_or_default()`) anchors the broker socket, broker token
  and worker-wake signal at `/...` when HOME is unset *or empty*
  (#5673); its brokers are loud on unset, silent on empty.
- **Current working directory** — fleet-config's `home_dir()`
  falls back to `"."`, so config/state/socket resolve CWD-relative
  and a planted `./.config/fleet/fleet.toml` is loaded, probe-
  verified (#5737) — the HOME spelling of the hazard #5473 closed
  for XDG in the same crate.
- **A literal `~` directory** — atlas-search / atlas-core /
  fleet-search copy a helper mapping missing HOME to `"~"`, so
  `atlas-search init` exits 0 creating `./~/.local/state/...`
  (#5640, probe-verified).

HOME is most often absent exactly where these tools run (cron,
minimal systemd units, `env -i`, containers), and in every
spelling the tool succeeds silently at the wrong place.

## The contract (recorded decision)

**A tool that needs the home directory resolves it exactly one
way: a non-empty `HOME`. Empty is unset. Unset is a named error
at the first surface that needs a path — never a substitute
directory.**

1. Empty = unset, for HOME itself as #5473 ruled for XDG/FLEET_*.
2. Unset = fail loudly naming HOME (the world.rs precedent),
   before any home-derived read/write/spawn/connect. No root
   anchoring, no CWD fallback, no literal `~`, no hardcoded user.
3. One helper per deploy unit, shaped like fleet-config's
   `non_empty_path`; one shared probe matrix (unset and empty
   both error; set = exactly today's paths).
4. Absolute XDG/FLEET_* overrides keep working as #5473 left
   them; relative/empty ones are not a home substitute.

**Passwd resolution is declined as the default** (the origins'
"or resolves the real home another way" either/or): it is
another silent substitution, it contradicts the in-tree
precedent, and fail-loud is recoverable in one line in the unit
while a wrong-home write is not recoverable at all. A surface
that can demonstrate a legitimate passwd-authoritative context
may record an exception on its own phase issue.

## Phases (each independently landable)

- **Phase 1 — fleet-config: #5737** (adopted; holds the
  `non_empty_path` precedent the others mirror)
- **Phase 2 — fleet-queue: #5673** (adopted)
- **Phase 3 — atlas-search + fleet-search: #5640** (adopted)
- **Phase 4 — closing inventory audit** (filed with this design):
  disposition every remaining home-resolution site on main —
  `pkgs/id/src/world_compile.rs:704` (`unwrap_or_default`), the
  JS `bin/*` hardcoded `/home/user` fallbacks, mcpx's discarded
  `os.UserHomeDir()` errors, and any further copies the inventory
  turns up. Same-shape sites fixed in-phase; genuinely different
  contexts filed separately with the reason.

## Acceptance

- [ ] All four phases closed or dispositioned with evidence.
- [ ] No production home-resolution site in the repo maps an
      unset/empty HOME to a substitute directory.
- [ ] Register (`files/potential-projects.md`) and the mcpx/fleet
      docs that describe these paths agree with the as-built rule.

title: Quota gatherer ticks fail at import: lib dir resolves to stale openchamber checkout parked on a queue branch

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

body:
## Quota gatherer: every tick fails at import — lib dir resolves to a stale openchamber checkout parked on a queue branch

**Symptom (live 2026-11-04 evening):** `quota-gatherer.service` fails every tick in ~13ms with:

```
quota-gatherer: tick failed before providers ran: quota module import failed: auth.openCodeLocalCredentialSource is not a function. (In 'auth.openCodeLocalCredentialSource({ dbPath })', 'auth.openCodeLocalCredentialSource' is undefined)
```

(heartbeat `~/.local/state/pm-aggregator/quota-gatherer-heartbeat.json`, tickAt 2026-11-05T00:30:13Z, ok:false. Same failure at 18:18 and 18:23 CST ticks; the gatherer stall first observed 2026-11-04 ~18:30:15Z is consistent with this breakage starting earlier that day.)

**Root cause:** `resolveLibDir()` in `pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/gather-quota.ts` picks the first candidate containing `quota/index.js`: `$OPENCHAMBER_LIB_DIR`, else `~/git/devtoday-openchamber/...` (doesn't exist), else `~/git/openchamber-fork/packages/web/server/lib`. The fork checkout `~/git/openchamber-fork` is currently parked on branch `queue/8357-224` (an old integration merge, e216864bf) with a dirty tree; its `packages/web/server/lib/opencode/auth.js` predates `openCodeLocalCredentialSource`. `origin/main` of the fork **has** the function (auth.js:214). The gatherer is therefore coupled to the mutable state of an unrelated work checkout — any queue lane that parks that checkout on an old branch breaks quota gathering fleet-wide, silently (heartbeat only).

**Verified workaround (used for the #5704 verification run):** a clean worktree of the fork at origin/main + `OPENCHAMBER_LIB_DIR=<worktree>/packages/web/server/lib` makes the gatherer run green.

**Fix options:**
1. Pin the deployed lib: set `OPENCHAMBER_LIB_DIR` in the quota-gatherer unit (Nix module) to a dedicated, main-tracking checkout/worktree of the fork that lanes never work in.
2. Vendor or bundle the quota module with the aggregator so no external checkout is on the runtime path.
3. At minimum: fail loud — a tick that dies at import should surface somewhere other than a heartbeat file (the stall went unnoticed for hours).

Do NOT fix by switching/cleaning `~/git/openchamber-fork` in place: it holds another lane's dirty queue work (queue/8357-224).

Found during the 2026-11-04 laptop-session coordinator run (Phase 2 of the #5704 verification — that fix itself is landed via PR #5719; the timer stays red until this issue is resolved).

body:
## Context

Part of epic #5412 (one `fleet` multicall binary), following the laptop-agent design #5343. Companion to the one-daemon serve-all design issue #5698.

Every fleet role is reached on its own TCP port today: laptop-agent :4799, secrets-broker :4800, queue-broker :4801, dispatch :4879, search service :18760 (`crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs:27-29,72`). For consumers **on the same machine** as a role, this issue evaluates Unix domain sockets (UDS) — and briefly other process-stream options — against loopback/tailnet TCP, verifies from source which transports each role actually binds today, and designs the dual-stack: UDS locally, TCP via the fleet proxy remotely. **Design only — no implementation here.**

## Findings: transports as they actually are today

### 1. The two brokers bind TCP on the tailnet IP only — not loopback, not UDS

- `crates/fleet-queue/src/queue_broker.rs:589-591` — `run()` binds `tiny_http::Server::http(&bind)` where bind = `$QUEUE_BROKER_BIND` or default `100.99.113.103:4801` (the laptop's tailnet address, hardcoded as a string — `fleet-config`'s `PORT_QUEUE_BROKER` const is not used here).
- `crates/fleet-queue/src/secrets_broker.rs:189-191` — same shape, default `100.99.113.103:4800`; the crate doc says it plainly (`:6-7`): *"Binds the laptop tailnet IP only; consumers reach it through the sandbox session proxy."*
- Neither broker has any Unix-socket code. Same-machine callers therefore pay for — and are exposed on — a network interface even when caller and broker are the same host and the same user.

### 2. The one UDS in the system is real, live, and already the Rust proxy's — but it belongs to the proxy protocol, not to any role

- `crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs:25` — `DEFAULT_BROKER_SOCKET = ".cache/laptop-agent/broker.sock"`, resolved by `Config::broker_socket()` (`:265-290`, env `FLEET_BROKER_SOCKET` > config > default, relative paths under `$HOME`).
- Yes, the Rust proxy uses it: `crates/fleet-proxy/src/serve.rs:543-562` — `fleet proxy serve` binds `UnixListener` at exactly that path (stale-file probe: connect first; if connect fails, unlink and bind, `:554-561`), chmods the socket dir `0700` (`:545-552`), and serves the framed fleet-proxy-proto protocol, thread per session (`:618-626`). This is the session broker succeeding the Python `laptop-agent-broker.py` at its historical path.
- Who connects over it: **sandbox-side clients talking to the proxy**, never clients talking to a role directly. E.g. the queue client (`crates/fleet-queue/src/client.rs:181-197` `unix_roundtrip`) and the secrets resolver (`crates/fleet-secrets/src/lib.rs:263-264`, broker-first chain, `:8-13`) both `UnixStream::connect` the socket and send a framed request naming a **port**; the proxy then dials TCP `target_host:port` through a CONNECT tunnel (or directly) and forwards HTTP (`crates/fleet-proxy/src/serve.rs:258-271` `open_conn`, `:312-368` `do_request`; port defaults to 4799, `:316`).
- One wart worth recording: the queue client hardcodes the socket path itself (`client.rs:55-57` `broker_sock()` = `$HOME/.cache/laptop-agent/broker.sock`) instead of asking `fleet-config`. Any new socket-path conventions should fix this class of duplication, not add to it.

So the system's current shape is asymmetric: **client → proxy is UDS; proxy → role is TCP; same-machine client → role is TCP on the tailnet IP.** The UDS question is only about that last leg (and the proxy → role leg when the proxy is colocated).

### 3. Same-machine consumers today: three different TCP workarounds, no UDS

- **Queue client on the laptop:** direct TCP when `REPO_QUEUE_BROKER_URL` or `~/.config/repo-queue/broker-url` is configured (`crates/fleet-queue/src/client.rs:69-84`), a raw `TcpStream` HTTP exchange (`:100-113`); otherwise it falls back to the session-proxy/UDS path (`:139-142`) — which on the laptop means a proxy that may not even be running there.
- **Queue-broker → secrets-broker (colocated!):** plain HTTP to the tailnet IP, `secrets_url` default `http://100.99.113.103:4800` (`queue_broker.rs:604-605`), via the `DirectSecrets` source whose doc notes *"the two brokers are colocated; no session proxy sits between them"* (`:48-51`). Two processes on one host, talking over the tailnet interface.
- **Dispatch client:** probes loopback first — `pick_transport` tries `TcpStream::connect_timeout(127.0.0.1:4879, 750ms)` and goes direct if it answers, else direct-to-target or CONNECT tunnel (`crates/fleet-dispatch/src/lib.rs:152-183`). This probe-then-choose pattern is an in-codebase precedent for transport selection.
- **Search client:** HTTP to `http://127.0.0.1:18760` (`crates/fleet-search/src/client.rs:27` `DEFAULT_SERVICE_URL` — the standalone atlas-search service binds loopback), with routing preference resolved flag → env → `[search] via` in fleet.toml → host default (`crates/fleet-search/src/lib.rs:308-328` `resolve_route`; `fleet-config` `search_via()`/`search_url()` at `lib.rs:369-386`). The `search_via` precedent: a config value that shapes *a preference between two working routes*, deliberately not a loud-error disable lever.

### 4. The proxy's routing model is port-keyed end to end

- The routing table *is* a port map: `Config::services()` returns `(4799, laptop-agent)`, `(4800, secrets-broker)`, `(4801, queue-broker)` (`fleet-config/src/lib.rs:321-338`), advertised in the hello; request frames carry a numeric `port`; tunnel pools are keyed by port (`serve.rs` `TunnelPool`). A socket-backed role therefore cannot be reached by the existing proxy without either (a) the role also binding TCP (dual-bind), or (b) the proxy learning a port → socket-path mapping for the colocated case. This is the main integration cost, and it is in the proxy, not in the roles.

## Evaluation: UDS vs TCP for same-machine consumers

- **Latency / connection cost:** both are local IPC; UDS skips the TCP handshake, checksums, and Nagle interaction and is measurably a bit faster per round trip, but at fleet's request rates (queue ops, cached secret lookups, search jobs) the difference is not user-visible — the expensive parts are `bws` refreshes, Supabase RPCs, and tunnel setup to reach the laptop at all. Honest verdict: **latency is not the reason to do this.** The real wins are the three rows below. Per-connection cost slightly favors UDS (no TIME_WAIT accumulation on a fixed port pair under the thread-per-connection + `Connection: close` pattern the direct queue client uses, `client.rs:104-107`), but this is a minor operational nicety, not a driver.
- **Discovery:** ports are compiled-in consts plus a config table — global, collision-prone (anything can squat :4801), and invisible to `ls`. Socket paths are filesystem objects: discoverable (`ls`, `ss`), self-describing per role, namespaced per user, and existence *is* a liveness hint (with the stale-file caveat the proxy already handles by connect-probing, `serve.rs:554-561`). Cost: a path convention to define and keep under the 108-char `sockaddr_un` limit.
- **Permissions / auth:** today both brokers check an `X-Agent-Token` header per request (`queue_broker.rs:581-587` `token_ok`, `secrets_broker.rs:181-187`; `/health(z)` exempt) — necessary, because binding the **tailnet IP** exposes them to every device on the tailnet, token or not. Binding loopback TCP instead would expose them to *every local process of every local user* — on the laptop that is a strictly worse audience for secrets-broker, which holds the entire vault cache in memory. A UDS under a `0700` directory (the proxy socket already does exactly this, `serve.rs:545-552`) restricts callers to the owner's processes by filesystem permissions, and the server can additionally verify the peer with `SO_PEERCRED` (uid/pid) — a credential a local process cannot forge, unlike a bearer token in a file any same-user process can read. **But:** the token must stay on the proxy-forwarded path — when the proxy forwards, the peer *is* the proxy, so peer credentials say nothing about the original caller — and the token should stay on UDS too in v1 (defense in depth; removing it is a separate auth decision, not a transport side effect).
- **Operational cost:** TCP wins on familiarity (curl, `ss`, health checks, the existing `services()` hello map). UDS costs: stale-file handling (solved pattern already in-tree), socket-file cleanup on crash, no `curl` without `--unix-socket`, and Windows is out of scope (fleet is unix-only already — `std::os::unix` throughout the proxy). systemd offers a middle path worth naming: **socket activation** (`.socket` units hand the role a pre-bound fd) gives per-role socket lifecycle and restart granularity for free; repo precedent: the socket-activation audit in #1822.
- **Other process-stream options, briefly:** *abstract-namespace UDS* (`@fleet-queue-broker`) — no stale files, auto-cleanup, but undiscoverable by `ls` and Linux-only spelling; *systemd socket activation* — see above, pairs naturally with per-role units; *vsock* — for VM↔host, not same-host processes; *shared memory / io_uring rings* — wildly disproportionate for JSON RPC at this rate. Plain filesystem UDS is the only alternative that beats TCP on the rows that matter.

## Design: the dual-stack

1. **Roles dual-bind.** Each broker binds its TCP address *and* a Unix socket when both are configured; either alone when only one is. Default behavior on the laptop flips the local leg to UDS while the tailnet TCP bind stays for the proxy's remote path — no flag day, existing clients keep working byte-for-byte (the brokers' wire is HTTP either way: `tiny_http` is TCP-only, so the UDS listener needs a minimal HTTP-over-`UnixStream` accept loop or a small shim — this is the one real implementation cost in the roles; the proxy's framed protocol is *not* reused for roles).
2. **Path convention in `fleet-config`.** One helper deriving every role's socket from the existing dirs, mirroring `broker_socket()`'s precedence (env > config > default): `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/fleet/<role>.sock` when `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` is set (tmpfs, per-login, auto-cleaned — the right home for a runtime socket), else `Config::state_dir()/run/<role>.sock` (`fleet-config/src/lib.rs:396-410`). Directory `0700`, socket `0600`, both enforced at bind like the proxy does today. The historical `.cache/laptop-agent/broker.sock` stays as-is for the proxy (its path is a compatibility contract); only *role* sockets are new.
3. **Client choice — probe, with a config preference, following the two in-tree precedents.** Resolution order, per role: explicit URL/env override (today's `REPO_QUEUE_BROKER_URL` shape wins, unchanged) → `[<role>] transport = "socket" | "tcp"` config preference in the `search_via` style (a preference between working routes, not a disable lever) → **probe**: if the role's socket file exists and a connect succeeds, use UDS; else TCP (the dispatch client's probe-then-choose pattern, `fleet-dispatch/src/lib.rs:163-173`, and the proxy's own stale-socket connect-probe). Same-machine consumers that change: the queue client's direct path, queue-broker's `DirectSecrets` (`secrets_url` gains a `unix://` form or a sibling `secrets_socket` setting), and the `fleet secrets` path when it runs on the laptop. Sandbox consumers are untouched — they still speak UDS to their *local proxy*, which is a different socket.
4. **What the proxy does with a socket-backed role.** Nothing new for the remote case: the sandbox proxy still tunnels TCP to `target_host:port`, and the role's surviving TCP bind answers it. For a proxy running **on the laptop itself** (`proxy_direct()` mode, `fleet-config/src/lib.rs:311-314`), add a port → socket-path resolution beside `Config::services()`: when the target is local and the role's socket answers, `open_conn` dials the UDS instead of TCP. The hello/services map stays port-keyed (it is the negotiated wire contract); the socket is a local dialing detail of the colocated proxy, never advertised.
5. **Auth unchanged in v1.** `X-Agent-Token` required on both transports, `/health(z)` exempt as today. Peer-credential checking (`SO_PEERCRED` uid == owner) is logged-and-allowed in v1 and becomes a candidate v2 requirement for the secrets-broker socket specifically. Token files, read per request on the proxy path, are untouched.

## Recommendation

**Adopt the dual-stack: filesystem UDS as the preferred same-machine transport for the two brokers, TCP retained everywhere it is used today, probe-based client selection with a `search_via`-style config preference, and the proxy learning UDS dialing only in its colocated (`direct`) mode.**

Do it for the discovery and permissions wins — a per-user, `0700`-namespaced, `ls`-visible endpoint for the process that holds the whole vault cache — not for latency, which is a wash at fleet's rates. Do **not** do: UDS-only roles (breaks the proxy's port-keyed remote path and every TCP client), abstract sockets (loses discoverability, the main win), or dropping the token as part of the transport change.

Sequencing note: this is independent of the serve-all design (roles in one process could later swap the queue→secrets hop for an in-process call — but that is an optimization to earn with measurements, not a premise of either design).

## Next steps

- [ ] Decide this issue (dual-stack, path convention, probe order, auth unchanged, proxy UDS dialing only when colocated).
- [ ] Split out `fleet-config` work: role-socket path helpers + `[<role>] transport` preference parsing (deny-unknown-fields discipline preserved).
- [ ] Split out per-broker UDS listeners (HTTP over `UnixStream` alongside `tiny_http` TCP), with the proxy's stale-socket probe reused as the bind pattern.
- [ ] Split out client migrations: queue client direct path, queue-broker `DirectSecrets`, laptop-local `fleet secrets`; fix the queue client's hardcoded broker-sock path to use `fleet-config` on the way past.
- [ ] Split out the proxy's colocated port → socket dialing; verify the hello/services contract is untouched.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A decision is recorded: which fleet roles use ports vs Unix-socket local transports, and the dual-stack requirements for each.
- [ ] The decision is linked from the affected fleet role configs/docs.
- [ ] Implementation follow-ups are filed as linked issues if the decision changes current behavior.

title: design: one-daemon serve-all — multi-role `fleet serve` in a single process

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: A design proposal (design-architect): multi-step, phased, decision-bearing

labels.name: epic/fleet-orchestration
labels.description: Reprioritization program epic (2026-11-12)

body:
## Context

Part of epic #5412 (one `fleet` multicall binary), following the laptop-agent design #5343.

Drew's question, from dictation: can we say `fleet serve queue broker secret broker search` — or `fleet serve` / `fleet serve all` — and have **one process** run queue-broker + secrets-broker + search + proxy together?

Today the laptop runs the roles as separate systemd user services invoking the same binary once per role (`fleet serve queue-broker` on :4801, `fleet serve secrets-broker` on :4800), the session proxy is a separate invocation again (`fleet proxy serve`, auto-spawned on demand), and the search service role does not exist in fleet at all yet. This issue answers the one-daemon question from the code, evaluates the invocation shapes, and recommends one. **Design only — no implementation here.**

## Findings (from source, fleet 0.1.0)

### 1. `serve` today takes exactly one role, by construction

- `crates/fleet/src/main.rs:394-406` — `required_capability()` reads only `args.first()` for the `serve` domain and maps it to exactly one capability (`QueueBroker` | `SecretsBroker` | `SearchServe`); anything else is a usage error: *"'fleet serve' needs a role: queue-broker, secrets-broker, or search"*.
- `crates/fleet/src/main.rs:485-492` — `run_domain()` then dispatches that single role to a blocking `run()`. Extra role words are never validated: `fleet serve queue-broker secrets-broker` today silently runs only queue-broker (unlike `fleet proxy serve`, whose leaf explicitly rejects stray args). Any multi-role grammar has to fix this arg handling, not just loop over it.
- The role vocabulary is hyphenated registry tokens — `queue-broker`, `secrets-broker`, `search` (`crates/fleet-registry/src/lib.rs`, `serve` domain: subcommands `["queue-broker", "secrets-broker", "search"]`). Drew's dictated `queue broker secret broker` is two tokens per role in speech; the grammar should keep the existing hyphenated tokens rather than invent a second spelling.

### 2. Every role is a blocking, synchronous, thread-per-connection server — there is no async runtime anywhere

- No `tokio`, no `async fn`, no `.await` anywhere in the workspace. The brokers are `tiny_http` servers: `crates/fleet-queue/src/queue_broker.rs:630` (`Server::http(&bind)`) with an accept loop at `:635` that `std::thread::spawn`s one thread per request; `crates/fleet-queue/src/secrets_broker.rs:231,236-239` is the same shape, plus a background cache-refresh thread (`:220-228`).
- The proxy is the same shape over a Unix socket: `crates/fleet-proxy/src/serve.rs:618-626` — `listener.incoming()` with a thread per session, plus preconnect and keepalive threads (`:597-609`).
- Each standalone bin is a 9-line shim over the same blocking entry point, e.g. `crates/fleet-queue/src/bin/queue-broker.rs`: `std::process::exit(fleet_queue::queue_broker::run())`.

Consequence: **co-hosting the roles in one process needs no runtime merger.** Each role's `run()` can move to its own OS thread under a small supervisor that joins them. This is the single fact that makes serve-all cheap here — it would be a different answer in a codebase where each role owned a tokio runtime with its own reactor and shutdown protocol.

### 3. The roles share less than it looks — and what they do share is files, not memory

- `crates/fleet/src/main.rs:736-746` — `main()` loads `fleet_config::Config` once, but only the proxy and the client domains receive it (`run_proxy` passes `&surface.config` to `fleet_proxy::serve::run(config)`, `main.rs:565-587`). The brokers' `run()` takes **no arguments at all** (`queue_broker.rs:589`, `secrets_broker.rs:189`): each re-reads its own env vars (`QUEUE_BROKER_BIND`, `SECRETS_BROKER_BIND`, token-file vars) and its own token files, and calls `std::process::exit(3)` itself if a token file is unreadable (`queue_broker.rs:595-603`, `secrets_broker.rs:195-203`).
- The one real inter-role dependency is already network-shaped: queue-broker resolves secrets by calling secrets-broker over HTTP (`queue_broker.rs:48-58` `DirectSecrets`, `:604-605` `secrets_url` default `http://100.99.113.103:4800`). Co-hosting does not remove that hop unless someone deliberately replaces it with an in-process channel (see the companion transports design issue).
- So the honest "sharing wins" list is modest: one binary load, one config parse, one log facility (already unified via `fleet_queue::log`), and in a future step the option — not the obligation — of sharing a `ureq::Agent`/connection pool. There is no shared in-memory state today that separate processes are wastefully duplicating, except secrets-broker's vault cache, which only it holds either way.

### 4. The blockers are failure semantics, not plumbing

- **Process-exit landmines:** both brokers `std::process::exit(3)` deep inside `run()` on bind or token failure (`queue_broker.rs:602,615,632`; `secrets_broker.rs:202,233`). In a combined process, one role's missing token file kills every role. Serve-all requires converting these to returned errors the supervisor can act on per-role.
- **Blast radius:** in one process, a panic in a role's accept loop, a deadlock, a memory blow-up, or an abort takes down queue + secrets + proxy together. Handler-thread panics are already contained today (thread-per-request), but the accept loops and secrets-broker's refresh thread are not supervised by anything inside the process. Note the coupling that already exists across processes: if secrets-broker dies today, queue-broker degrades (its `DirectSecrets` calls fail) but the proxy and the laptop-agent path keep working, and clients keep their `bws` fallback (`crates/fleet-secrets/src/lib.rs:8-13`). One-daemon must not silently widen that coupling.
- **Restart granularity:** today systemd restarts exactly the failed role. A naive one-daemon loses that: restarting a wedged secrets-broker would drop the proxy's warm tunnel pools (`serve.rs` `TunnelPool`, per-port pools of 50) and every in-flight queue request with it. Keeping the granularity means building an internal supervisor (spawn role threads, watch them, restart the failed one in-process) — i.e. re-implementing the slice of systemd we actually use, inside the binary, where it is harder to observe (`systemctl status`, per-unit logs and resource limits all go away).
- **Idle-exit asymmetry:** the proxy is a warmth cache that exits after an idle hour by design (`crates/fleet-proxy/src/lib.rs`, `serve.rs` keepalive/idle logic; `fleet-config` `DEFAULT_IDLE_EXIT_SECS`). The brokers are resident services with no idle exit. A merged process cannot idle-exit without killing the resident roles, so `proxy` does not belong inside the same lifetime as the brokers (see Recommendation).

### 5. `search` cannot join yet — there is no search server role to co-host

- `crates/fleet-search/src/lib.rs:48-52`: *"The service role is not this domain: `fleet serve search` remains the step's registry stub (the atlas user unit still points at the standalone atlas-search service…)"*. `fleet-search` is a client crate (its `run()` is the client surface, and `serve` as a search-domain verb is a usage error, `lib.rs:535-543`).
- `main.rs:485-522` confirms it mechanically: `run_domain` has serve arms for queue-broker and secrets-broker only; `serve search` resolves `SearchServe` in `required_capability` and then falls through to the capability stub even in a build that carries `search-serve`. The serve help text says the same (`main.rs:367-370`).
- Any serve-all grammar must therefore treat `search` as "joinable when the role lands", and until then either stub it per-role (69) or reject it — never silently omit it from a supposedly complete set.

### 6. The proxy is not a `serve` role today — it is a separate domain

- The registry puts the session broker under `proxy` (`fleet proxy serve`, capability `ProxyServe`, argv0 alias `laptop-agent-broker`), while `serve`'s capabilities are exactly `QueueBroker + SecretsBroker + SearchServe` (`crates/fleet-registry/src/lib.rs`, `serve` domain; `alias_route()` maps `queue-broker`/`secrets-broker` → `serve` with an implied arg, `laptop-agent-broker` → `proxy serve`).
- The proxy also has a different lifecycle owner: clients auto-spawn it on demand when the socket is missing (`crates/fleet-proxy/src/client.rs:139-160` `ensure_broker`, `:182-216` `spawn_serve`; the queue client does the same at `crates/fleet-queue/src/client.rs:204-220`). Folding it into a systemd-owned serve-all would give it two owners.

### 7. Capability-selected builds already draw the line serve-all must respect

- `crates/fleet/Cargo.toml` feature sets: `full` = everything; `serve` = `proxy-serve, queue-broker, secrets-broker, search-serve, secrets`; the connect variant is base-only (`proxy-connect` is compiled into every variant and is not a feature). The registry mirrors this: `serve_capabilities()` vs `connect_capabilities() = {ProxyConnect}` (`crates/fleet-registry/src/lib.rs`).
- So serve-all must be a **dispatch-time composition of per-role capability checks** (the `required_capability` idea, applied per requested role, stubbing 69 for any role not in the build/profile/config), never a new monolithic feature. A client-only build must render `fleet serve …` exactly as it does today — registry help plus the exit-69 stub — and grow no server code.

## Options

**(i) Multi-role list — `fleet serve queue-broker secrets-broker search`**
Explicit set, composes with everything: argv0 aliases keep meaning `serve <one role>`; systemd can run one unit per role, or one unit with several roles, pointing at the same binary; capability stubs stay per-role. Cost: slightly more typing for the common "everything" case.

**(ii) `fleet serve all`**
`all` = every serve role compiled into this build. Ergonomic, but `all` is build-dependent — the same command starts different sets on full vs serve builds, and silently shrinks when a role is config-disabled. That ambiguity is exactly what the capability-stub machinery (exit 69, explicit wording) exists to avoid. Would need `all` to print its resolved role list loudly and fail if a role it names is unavailable rather than skip it.

**(iii) Bare `fleet serve` = all**
Worst of (ii) plus a breaking change: bare `fleet serve` today is a usage error that teaches the role list (`main.rs:402-404`); making a bare word start several daemons is a footgun in scripts and in the #5488 bug class (a help/stray-arg path accidentally starting a daemon is a bug this codebase has already fixed twice).

**(iv) Status quo — separate processes only**
Keeps systemd's supervision, restart granularity, and per-role logs for free, at the cost of Drew's ask: N units to babysit, and no single "bring the laptop's fleet up" command.

## Recommendation

**Adopt (i): an explicit multi-role list, with the supervisor kept outside the process.**

1. Grammar: `fleet serve <role> [<role> …]` where each role is an existing registry token (`queue-broker`, `secrets-broker`, `search`). `fleet serve all` may be added later as sugar that *expands to the explicit list and prints it*; bare `fleet serve` stays a usage error. No space-separated `queue broker` spelling.
2. Runtime shape: parse and capability-check **all** roles up front (any role not compiled in / narrowed by invocation name / disabled in `[domains]` → the whole invocation fails with that role's 69 stub before anything binds; no partial starts). Then run each available role's existing blocking loop on its own thread and join; a role thread that returns or panics is fatal to the process (exit non-zero naming the role) so the *external* supervisor restarts the unit. Do **not** build an in-process restarter in v1 — systemd already is the supervisor, with better observability.
3. Precondition refactor (small, do first): the brokers' `run()` must stop calling `std::process::exit(3)` internally and return a `Result`/exit code to their caller, and accept the already-loaded `Config` the way `fleet_proxy::serve::run(config)` does. The standalone bins keep their exact behavior by exiting with the returned code — the rollback inventory (design §7) is untouched.
4. Deployment shape: **keep one systemd unit per role as the default** (`ExecStart=fleet serve queue-broker`, etc. — same binary, different role args, per-role restart/logs/limits preserved). The multi-role list is then an operator convenience for hosts without systemd or for a deliberate single-unit host, not a replacement for per-role units. This directly answers Drew's question — yes, `fleet serve queue-broker secrets-broker search` can bring everything up in one process — without giving up the granularity that makes the current setup debuggable.
5. Keep `proxy` out of the list for now: it stays `fleet proxy serve`, client-auto-spawned and idle-exiting, a different lifetime from the resident brokers. If a role-like spelling is wanted later, add `--with-proxy` as an explicit opt-in that also disables the proxy's idle-exit for that process, and decide it in its own step.
6. `search` joins the grammar the day its server role actually lands; until then `fleet serve … search …` gets the honest per-role stub (69, "not implemented yet" form), consistent with `main.rs:367-370`.

## Next steps

- [ ] Decide this issue (grammar (i), external supervision, proxy excluded, search stubbed until its role lands).
- [ ] Split out the precondition refactor: brokers return errors instead of `process::exit(3)`; thread `&Config` into broker `run()`s; bins unchanged externally.
- [ ] Split out the dispatch change: `required_capability` → per-role checks over the whole arg list, rejecting unknown/duplicate roles and stray args before any bind.
- [ ] Write the systemd guidance (per-role units by default; one multi-role unit as the documented alternative) alongside the implementation step.
- [ ] Revisit `--with-proxy` and the `all` sugar only after the list form has run live.

body:
**Design scope only — no data moves in this issue's first pass.**

## What moves
- From: Supabase (`muse-dev2`) — 20 `agent.mirror_*` tables (171,236 live rows, 136.9 MB): `mirror_sessions`, `mirror_agent_agents`, `mirror_scheduler_jobs`, `mirror_scheduler_job_runs`, `mirror_goals_goals`, `mirror_goals_updates`, the token/session/run/concurrency `*_daily`/`*_hourly` aggregates, `mirror_top_daily`, `mirror_export_state`, and peers
- To: Turso, core tier (internal sensitivity level per §4), topic = agent analytics

## Why
This is the single largest block in the project and it is mirrored, derived analytics copied from Muse's local stores — rebuildable from source, aggregate-upsert shaped (e.g. `mirror_token_usage_daily`: 200,769 updates re-aggregating 27,191 rows in the window), with no FK or multi-writer transaction requirement. Under the §9 placement rule it never needed Postgres; it pays Postgres costs (size, vacuum, backup weight) for scan-shaped reads Turso serves natively.

Design doc: §9 of `doc/2026-11-04T21-27-34Z_design_atlas_scaler_revision/` (PR #5667, addendum PR #5689).

## Risks
- Open question (§9.4 Q1): is the mirror analytics/reporting (safe to move) or a backup of record? If backup, the Turso placement must keep the §7 nightly Drive cold-store export.
- The mirror writer (export pipeline keyed on `mirror_export_state` watermarks) is a single producer whose Turso write path must respect the single-writer-per-DB rule — batch by export run, per §4's aggregator pattern.
- Aggregate tables are upsert-heavy, not append-only: the Turso design must use merge-on-export-run semantics, not naive row streaming.

## Sketch of steps
1. Confirm the mirror's purpose with Drew (§9.4 Q1) and inventory its readers (dashboards/reports).
2. Design the Turso schema (one DB, internal tier; current-state tables + aggregate tables; export-run partitioning).
3. Point the exporter at Turso in parallel (dual-publish), diff aggregate outputs against the Postgres mirror for several export cycles.
4. Flip readers; stop the Postgres mirror writes; retain the Postgres copy read-only for one reporting cycle before any drop decision (separate approval). The 5 duplicate `mirror_history_*` tables and 3 empty mirror shells are RETIRE class (§9.2) and are handled as cleanup, not migration.

Links: design doc PR #5667 · addendum PR #5689 · tracking dezren39/hatch-personal#21

title: id: design: KDL as human presentation format + triples + ANSI graph SQL (SQL/PGQ) for ID data

labels.name: epic/id-program
labels.description: Reprioritization program epic (2026-11-12)

body:
## Summary

Expand KDL into the **human presentation format for ID data**, backed by an
**atomic-triples data model** and queried with the **ANSI-standard graph
query work in SQL (SQL/PGQ, SQL:2023)**.

Three layers, kept strictly separate:

1. **Presentation / interchange — KDL.** Compact, human-readable,
   authorable by non-developers. KDL is *not* the wire format and *not*
   the query substrate.
2. **Canonical data — atomic triples.** Every compound statement
   decomposes into `(subject, action/predicate, target)` facts, one fact
   per triple, referencing IDs. Real data is resolved / carried through
   those IDs.
3. **Query — ANSI graph SQL.** Target SQL/PGQ property-graph views over
   the triple table as the query model, rather than inventing a private
   query language.

This is an expansion-style design issue: it defines the full feature set
in enough detail that a later pass can break it into further design
tickets, and then into implementation tickets. It does not itself build
the feature.

Umbrella: epic #2056

Relatives:

- #2048 — zettelkasten layer (the tagging home; see "Tagging" below)
- #5675 — querying ID servers (the query design here composes with that
  work; this issue supplies the triple/graph model it queries)
- #5678 — knowledge layer program (this is one presentation + storage
  shape under that program)
- #2036 — wire format (KDL is **not** the wire format; see below)

---

## 1. KDL as the human presentation format for ID data

### 1.1 Why KDL

- Compact and readable: node / child / property syntax reads as
  structured prose rather than markup. A non-developer can read an ID
  export and, with modest guidance, author one.
- It expresses nesting (compound statements, qualified facts) naturally,
  without the punctuation noise of JSON or the indentation fragility of
  YAML.
- It has typed values, comments, and a formal spec, and — importantly for
  us — prior in-house familiarity (see Prior art).

### 1.2 The conversion contract

KDL is a presentation / interchange layer, with lossless-enough
conversion both ways:

- KDL ⇄ JSON — the primary canonical conversion (see §2).
- KDL ⇄ XML
- KDL ⇄ YAML

"Lossless-enough" must be defined precisely by the follow-on design
ticket, not left as a slogan. The definition needs to cover at least:

- node names, ordered children, properties / arguments, and typed
  scalars survive a round trip;
- ordering guarantees (where order is semantically load-bearing vs.
  incidental);
- comments and formatting: explicitly out of the losslessness promise
  (they are presentation, not data), unless a follow-on ticket decides
  otherwise;
- type fidelity across formats with different type systems (dates,
  numbers, nulls, binary);
- an explicit list of known-lossy edges, each with a test.

### 1.3 What KDL is NOT

- **Not the query substrate.** Nobody queries raw KDL. KDL is converted,
  decomposed into triples (§2), and the triples are queried (§3).
- **Not the wire format.** #2036's wire-format decision stands:
  **postcard stays** for machine-to-machine ID traffic. Wire traffic is
  optimized for size, determinism, and machine decode, not human
  readability; KDL optimizes for the opposite. Conflating the two would
  compromise both. KDL may be *carried* as a payload/document where a
  human is in the loop, but it does not replace postcard on the wire.

### 1.4 Presentation uses

1. **Human-readable exports.** Any ID dataset can be exported as KDL a
   person can read, diff, annotate, and check into a repo.
2. **Hand-authored data upload.** A person writes (or edits) a KDL
   document and uploads it; the ingest pipeline (§2) validates it and
   decomposes it into triples.
3. **Agent-authored statements.** Agents emit KDL as their statement
   format — readable in logs and reviewable by a human before commit —
   and the system validates + decomposes it exactly as it does a
   hand-authored upload. Same pipeline, no agent-only back door.

---

## 2. Ingest pipeline: compound statements → JSON → atomic triples

### 2.1 The shape of the problem

Uploaded KDL expresses **compound statements**. Drew's canonical example
shape:

> this person did activity with other person; other activity with other
> person; third activity with three people

One authored statement bundles multiple facts, multiple participants,
and shared context. Storing it as one blob would make it unqueryable;
decomposing it naively would lose the grouping that makes it meaningful.

### 2.2 Pipeline stages

1. **Parse + validate KDL.** Syntax validation, then schema validation
   against the statement shapes ID accepts. Reject early, with errors a
   non-developer author can act on.
2. **Convert to the most conventional JSON form preserving the compound
   shape.** This intermediate JSON is the canonical record of *what was
   authored*: the compound statement as a whole, in the most boring,
   conventional JSON representation that does not flatten or split it.
   It is the audit / provenance anchor for the decomposition that
   follows, and the form other JSON-native tooling consumes.
3. **Decompose into atomic triples.** Each compound statement breaks
   down into `(subject, action, target)` triples — one fact each. From
   the example shape: one triple per person–activity–person fact, not
   one triple per sentence.
4. **Resolve through IDs.** Triples reference **IDs**, not embedded
   copies of data. The subject, action, and target are IDs; the real
   data behind them is resolved / carried through those IDs at read /
   query time. A triple is a claim about identified things, not a
   denormalized copy of them.

### 2.3 Namespaces and qualifiers: more triples, never special cases

- **Namespaces** are expressed as additional triples about a term / ID,
  not as a syntactic special case in the store.
- **Qualifiers** (time, place, certainty, source, role-in-activity, …)
  are likewise additional triples. An n-ary fact decomposes into a
  statement node (itself ID'd) plus binary triples hanging off it.
- Rule for implementers: if a design proposes a special column, a
  special table, or a special parser branch for a qualifier/namespace,
  that is a smell — decompose it into triples instead. Any exception
  needs explicit justification in its follow-on ticket.

### 2.4 The payload boundary

Some payloads legitimately remain **data objects attached to triples**
rather than being decomposed further — e.g. a long text body, an image,
a geometry, a document. The design must define this boundary explicitly:

- Decompose what is *queried, joined, tagged, or reasoned over*.
- Attach as payload what is *carried, displayed, or stored verbatim*.
- A payload is attached to an ID / statement, is referenced by triples,
  and is not itself silently flattened into triples.
- The follow-on ticket owns the decision procedure + worked examples of
  payloads on both sides of the line, including the grey cases.

### 2.5 Tagging

Tagging in ID is **already triples-shaped** — `(thing, tagged-with, tag)`
is a triple. Build on that explicitly rather than treating tags as a
separate subsystem: tags are triples, tag vocabularies are data, and the
zettelkasten layer in #2048 is the home where those tag triples are
authored and browsed. Any tagging feature that cannot be expressed as
ordinary triples over IDs needs to say why.

---

## 3. Query: ANSI graph SQL (SQL/PGQ) over triples

### 3.1 Target

Target the **ANSI-standard graph query work in SQL — SQL/PGQ as
standardized in SQL:2023** — as the query model for triple-shaped data.
Rationale: a standard property-graph query surface over relational
storage, instead of betting the knowledge layer on a private query
language or a separate graph database.

### 3.2 The model

- A **triple table** is the storage fact: subject ID, predicate ID,
  object/target ID (plus the statement/provenance linkage from §2.2).
- **Property-graph views** are defined over that triple table:
  predicates (or predicate classes) become edges, ID'd entities become
  vertices, and attached payloads / qualifier triples supply properties.
- Queries are written against the graph view (SQL/PGQ `GRAPH_TABLE` /
  `MATCH` style), not hand-rolled recursive joins, wherever the engine
  supports it.

### 3.3 Honest engine assessment (to be completed by follow-on ticket)

This design does **not** assume our current stores speak SQL/PGQ. The
follow-on investigation must assess, with evidence:

- What **libsql / SQLite** and the stores ID actually uses today can do:
  native SQL/PGQ support (expected: none/limited), recursive CTEs,
  JSON functions, and where each falls short of the PGQ model.
- What needs a **translation layer**: PGQ-shaped queries compiled down
  to the SQL our engines do run, vs. a restricted supported subset, vs.
  waiting on upstream support.
- Performance characteristics of graph patterns over a single triple
  table (indexing strategy: predicate/subject/object permutations) and
  the point at which that stops being good enough.
- How this composes with #5675 (querying ID servers): the remote query
  surface should expose the same graph model, not a second one.

The deliverable of that ticket is a capability matrix (engine × PGQ
feature × native / translated / unsupported), not an opinion.

---

## 4. Honest adapter assessment: the KDL layer is ours to build

**No KDL-in-database adapter is known to exist.** There is no off-the-
shelf component that stores/query KDL in libsql/SQLite or speaks KDL to
a triple store. **The KDL ⇄ JSON conversion layer is ours to build.**
Saying so plainly here so no later ticket plans around a phantom
dependency.

Sketch of what we build:

- **Parser / serializer options (Rust-first):**
  - the `kdl` crate — the reference Rust implementation;
  - `knuffel` — derive-style parsing onto typed structures, attractive
    for schema-validated statement shapes;
  - evaluate both against: spec compliance (KDL v1 / v2 posture), error
    quality for non-developer authors, round-trip fidelity, maintenance
    health.
- **Prior art in-house:** `developing-today/hygge` (2022) is a
  rudimentary KDL builder / "cerealizer" on the `kdl` crate v3 — proof
  the approach works in our hands, and a reference (not a dependency to
  resurrect uncritically; the crate ecosystem has moved since v3).
- **Conversion layer shape:** KDL AST ⇄ canonical JSON (§2.2 stage 2) as
  a standalone, separately testable component with the round-trip test
  corpus from §1.2, usable by ingest, export, and agent tooling alike.
- Explicit non-goals: no KDL query language, no KDL-native storage
  format, no fork of a parser unless the evaluation ticket proves one
  is necessary.

---

## Prior art in our own trees

Verified by a doc hunt 2026-11-04 — stated exactly as found:

NO standalone old KDL brainstorming doc exists in the code repo `doc/`,
hatch-personal notes, or the zettel corpora. What exists:

1. `pkgs/id/README.original.md` line ~38: "hash-based ids different
   formats including custom treed hash of structured data
   kdl/json/xml/automerge (each part breaks out into it's own entity)"
2. `pkgs/roc/out-in.kdl` — an actual KDL file brainstorming Roc language
   syntax
3. `pkgs/screen/README.md` listing kdl among data formats of interest
   alongside sparql/turtle/json-ld
4. The 2022 repo `developing-today/hygge` — "a rudimentary KDL
   builder/cerealizer", Rust, kdl crate v3
5. Memory summaries of Drew's ChatGPT export place the deep
   KDL/graph-DB/RDF brainstorming in late-2023 ChatGPT conversations —
   likely never a repo file.

Consequence: recovering that late-2023 ChatGPT cluster is a source-hunt
follow-on (see Decomposition sketch) — the design record should cite
what it recovers rather than reconstructing the brainstorming from
memory.

Note the sparql/turtle/json-ld adjacency in (3): the triples direction
has been in the air in-tree for a long time; this issue is where it
becomes a design.

---

## Decomposition sketch

Follow-on **design** tickets (each then breaks into implementation
tickets; ~7):

1. **KDL ⇄ JSON canonical conversion + round-trip contract** — define
   "lossless-enough" (§1.2), the canonical JSON shape for compound
   statements, XML/YAML edges, and the round-trip test corpus.
2. **Parser evaluation: `kdl` crate vs `knuffel`** — spec posture, error
   quality for non-developer authors, hygge lessons; pick the stack for
   the conversion layer (§4).
3. **Triple decomposition rules** — compound → atomic decomposition
   (§2.2–2.3): statement nodes, n-ary decomposition, namespaces and
   qualifiers as triples, worked examples starting from Drew's
   person/activity example.
4. **Payload boundary** — the decompose-vs-attach decision procedure
   (§2.4) with grey-case examples, and how payloads are referenced by
   triples and resolved through IDs.
5. **SQL/PGQ capability investigation** — libsql/SQLite and our stores
   vs SQL:2023 PGQ (§3.3): capability matrix, translation-layer design
   or supported-subset definition, triple-table indexing strategy.
   Composes with #5675.
6. **Presentation surfaces** — human-readable export, hand-authored
   upload UX, and agent-authored KDL statements (§1.4): one validation
   + decomposition pipeline, three front doors.
7. **Source hunt: recover the late-2023 ChatGPT KDL/graph-DB/RDF
   cluster** — locate, extract, and summarize the brainstorming from
   Drew's ChatGPT export; file what it changes about this design as
   amendments to the tickets above.
8. **Tagging-as-triples alignment with #2048** — confirm the
   zettelkasten layer's tagging model is the triple model of §2.5, and
   reconcile any divergence in vocabulary/namespace handling.

## Open questions

- KDL spec version: pin to v1, adopt v2, or accept both on ingest and
  emit one? What does each parser option actually support today?
- How is the canonical JSON form versioned when the KDL statement
  schemas evolve — schema IDs as triples too?
- Where does decomposition happen for agent-authored statements from
  untrusted agents: same trust path as hand uploads, or sandboxed
  staging until approved?
- What is the identity of a statement node — content-hashed (per
  `pkgs/id/README.original.md`'s treed-hash idea), minted, or derived
  from its decomposition?
- SQL/PGQ: full translation layer, supported subset, or dual surface
  (PGQ where available, documented fallback elsewhere)? Who owns that
  call after the capability matrix lands?
- Payload size/format limits for objects attached to triples, and do
  payloads ever get content-addressed independently of their statement?
- Does export-to-KDL need to re-compose atomic triples back into
  compound statements for readability, and if so, what grouping rules
  make the round trip author → triples → KDL recognizable to the author?
- Provenance: every decomposed triple should trace to its source
  compound statement and upload — is that trace itself triples, a
  column, or the canonical-JSON anchor from §2.2?

title: design: fleet init location awareness — role manifest, env overrides, report-don't-guess failure rule

labels.description: pkgs/fleet multicall binary + platform crates

labels.name: epic/fleet-orchestration
labels.description: Reprioritization program epic (2026-11-12)

body:
## Context

Part of epic #5412; related design #5343. Naming + behaviour approved by Drew 2026-11-04 (approval recorded in a comment on #5412): all daemons move under `fleet serve` (the sandbox session broker becomes `fleet serve proxy`); `fleet proxy` becomes the client-only domain; `fleet init` becomes location-aware.

Today `fleet init` is location-blind. It is hard-wired to exactly one role, the sandbox session proxy, wherever it runs:

- `crates/fleet/src/main.rs` — `cmd_init()`: gates on `Capability::ProxyServe` for domain `"proxy"`, then calls `run_init_call()`; root dispatch is `Some("init") => cmd_init(...)` in `run_root()`. Help text (same file): `init — Autostart the session proxy if it is not running (no-op when it is)`.
- `crates/fleet-proxy/src/client.rs` — `run_init()`: probes `config.broker_socket()`, syncs PATH shims, and otherwise spawns a broker; `spawn_serve()` spawns the current exe with args `["proxy", "serve"]`, detached via `setsid`. `ensure_broker()` has the same spawn path, so `fleet proxy connect` shares it.
- There is no host/role concept anywhere: `gh search code FLEET_HOST` in this repo returns nothing, and `crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs` has no host, location, or roles field.

Failure mode this creates: run today's `fleet init` on the laptop (or any future node) and it will try to start a session proxy there — a daemon that machine should not run — because init never asks *where am I, and what is this machine for?*

This is a design issue only. It proposes the design built **on the existing `fleet-config` crate**, not a parallel config system. No implementation in this issue.

## What already exists to build on (`crates/fleet-config/src/lib.rs`)

- `Config::file_path()` — `$FLEET_CONFIG`, else `${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-~/.config}/fleet/fleet.toml`; `Config::load()` / `load_from()` — a missing file yields defaults, a malformed file is a **loud** `ConfigError::Parse`/`Read`, never a silent fallback.
- `Config` is `#[serde(default, deny_unknown_fields)]` with sections `[domains]`, `[proxy]`, `[secrets]`, `[dispatch]`, `[search]`. Unknown sections/keys are a parse error on purpose (#5460: a misspelled disable must not silently no-op).
- `Config::domain_enabled()` — the `[domains]` per-host disable / incident lever (§7).
- `Config::services() -> Vec<ServiceConfig>` — the proxy routing table (port → name → version); built-in defaults are ports 4799 `laptop-agent`, 4800 `secrets-broker`, 4801 `queue-broker` (consts `PORT_LAPTOP_AGENT` / `PORT_SECRETS_BROKER` / `PORT_QUEUE_BROKER`, plus `PORT_DISPATCH` 4879).
- `Config::state_dir()` (`~/.local/state/fleet`), `Config::shims_dir()`, `DEFAULT_BROKER_SOCKET = ".cache/laptop-agent/broker.sock"`.
- Env-first precedents already in the crate: `FLEET_CONFIG`, `FLEET_BROKER_SOCKET`, `FLEET_DISPATCH_URL`; and the #5473 rule that an **empty env value counts as unset**, never as a literal path.

Registry facts (`crates/fleet-registry/src/lib.rs`, `crates/fleet/src/main.rs`): the `serve` domain today accepts exactly `queue-broker`, `secrets-broker`, `search` (`required_capability()` maps them to `QueueBroker` / `SecretsBroker` / `SearchServe`); the `proxy` domain has subcommands `serve`, `connect`, `init`, with `serve → ProxyServe` and `connect`/`init → ProxyConnect`. The search serve role is still a stub ("the search role lands in a later step"); `fleet laptop-agent` is a **client** domain whose capability `LaptopAgent` currently stubs at exit 69.

## 1. Role manifest — recommendation: a `[host]` section in the existing `fleet.toml`

**Evaluated options**

| Option | Verdict |
|---|---|
| (a) Extend the existing fleet-config file with a `[host]` section | **Recommended.** One file, one parser, one precedence story. Reuses `file_path()`/`load()`/`ConfigError`, the loud-malformed rule, and the `[domains]` lever. `fleet capabilities`/help already point operators at this path. |
| (b) Dedicated host/role file (e.g. `~/.config/fleet/host.toml`) | Rejected. Two files that can disagree (which wins when `fleet.toml` says laptop and `host.toml` says sandbox?), two parse paths, and a second place every tool must look. The only gain — separate ownership — is not a real need on our machines. |
| (c) `/etc/fleet/…` system-level file | Deferred, not adopted now. Our installs are per-user (sandbox VM, NixOS laptop user units); a root-owned file adds a root/user precedence layer and a write path nobody owns yet. If a future lab node runs fleet as a system service, revisit as a *fallback read* below the user file — do not design it speculatively now. |

**Exact contents** — a new `HostConfig` in `fleet-config`, all fields optional at parse time (absence = "no manifest", handled by §4):

```toml
# ${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-~/.config}/fleet/fleet.toml
[host]
location = "sandbox"        # this machine's location/role-set name
init_mode = "spawn"          # "spawn" (sandbox) | "systemd" (laptop/lab) — see §5

[host.roles]
proxy = {}                   # key = serve role name; value = per-role options
# queue-broker = {}
# secrets-broker = { enabled = false }   # per-role override: skip without editing the set
```

- Role names are the **`fleet serve` role names**: `proxy`, `queue-broker`, `secrets-broker`, `search`, `laptop-agent`. The role set is the key set of `[host.roles]`; there is no second list to keep in sync.
- Per-role overrides are deliberately thin in v1: `enabled` (bool, default true). Everything else a role needs already has a home — `[proxy] broker_socket`/`idle_exit_secs`, `[dispatch]`, `[search]`, and the `[domains]` kill switch — and must **not** be duplicated under `[host.roles.*]`.
- Parse semantics follow the crate's existing rules: `deny_unknown_fields` (a misspelled role option is a loud parse error), an **unknown role name is a loud error** (not silently ignored — a typo'd role that never starts is exactly the failure this design exists to prevent), and role → capability is a fixed table in code: `proxy → ProxyServe`, `queue-broker → QueueBroker`, `secrets-broker → SecretsBroker`, `search → SearchServe`, `laptop-agent →` a **new** serve-side capability (see §5 note; the existing `LaptopAgent` capability is the client domain and must not be reused for the daemon role).

**Who writes it:** provisioning, not the binary. The Nix/install step that puts `fleet` on a machine writes its `[host]` section (the laptop's NixOS config; the sandbox install step); hand-editing is fine and expected. `fleet init` **never writes** `[host]` — a first-run auto-write would cement a guess into the file that is supposed to be the authority. First run on an unprovisioned machine hits the §4 unknown-location path and tells the operator exactly what to write.

## 2. Env overrides — recommendation: `FLEET_LOCATION` + `FLEET_HOST_CONFIG`

Two vars, mirroring the crate's existing `FLEET_*` env-first pattern:

| Var | Carries | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `FLEET_LOCATION` | Just the location name | `FLEET_LOCATION=sandbox` |
| `FLEET_HOST_CONFIG` | The `[host]` table's contents, inline, as TOML | `FLEET_HOST_CONFIG='location="sandbox" init_mode="spawn" [roles] proxy={}'` |

- `FLEET_HOST_CONFIG` exists for containers / ephemeral sandboxes where writing the config file is awkward. It is parsed with the **same** `HostConfig` parser as the file section — one grammar, no JSON dialect.
- Failure semantics (all following existing crate precedents): empty string = unset (#5473 rule); malformed TOML = loud error, exit 2, same `ConfigError` shape as a malformed file — never a silent fall-through to the file (a silently ignored env manifest is the §7 disable-lever failure in a new costume); unknown role name = loud error; a *syntactically valid* manifest naming an unknown location is **not** a parse error — it flows to the §4 failure rule.
- `FLEET_LOCATION` alone does not carry roles: it selects the location, and roles then come from the file's `[host.roles]` **only if** the file's location matches (see §4), else from the built-in role map for that location (§5), else unknown.

## 3. Detection fallbacks — recommendation: detection informs the report, it never selects roles

Signals evaluated for **our** machines (sandbox VM, NixOS laptop, future lab nodes):

| Signal | Trustworthy for *what* | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Hostname | A hint. The laptop's is set by its NixOS config (stable there); sandbox/lab hostnames are generic and renamable without any fleet-visible event. | Report only. Never a role source. |
| Tailnet self-identity (own tailnet IP / DNS name; cf. `DEFAULT_TARGET_HOST = "100.99.113.103"`, the laptop's tailnet address in `fleet-config`) | Moderately strong *identity* evidence on the laptop vs the sandbox (the sandbox dials that address; it is not its own). But learning it means shelling out to `tailscale` or reading daemon state at init time — a new runtime dependency for every `init`, including the tiny connect build, and it is absent exactly in the ephemeral cases §2 covers. | Report only, and only if obtainable without a new hard dependency. Never the sole basis for starting a daemon. |
| systemd presence (`/run/systemd/system`) | Says nothing about *which* machine this is; says a lot about *how* daemons should be managed (unit vs detached spawn). | Not a location signal at all. It cross-checks `init_mode`: manifest says `systemd` but no systemd is present (or vice versa) ⇒ warn loudly in the report. |
| OS (`/etc/os-release`: NixOS vs the sandbox's distro) | Weak discriminator, trivially true of unrelated machines. | Report only. |

**Conclusion:** no detection signal we have is trustworthy enough to start daemons on. Detection's job is to make the unknown-location report (§4) useful — "here is what this machine looks like, here is the manifest to write" — and to cross-check `init_mode`. Any future proposal to promote a signal to authoritative must argue it against the failure mode in the Context section.

## 4. Precedence and the failure rule

Location + role-set resolution, highest first. Resolution is **not** field-merged across sources (merging is how a stale laptop file's roles end up running on the sandbox):

1. **`FLEET_HOST_CONFIG`** — a complete inline manifest; wins outright.
2. **`FLEET_LOCATION`** — sets the location. Roles: the file's `[host.roles]` if the file's `location` equals it; otherwise the built-in role map for that location (§5); otherwise unknown.
3. **File `[host]` section** — location and roles as written.
4. **Detection** — fills the *report* only; selects nothing.

After a manifest resolves, the existing gates still apply, in the existing order: role compiled into this build → not narrowed out by the invocation name → not disabled by `[domains]` (`domain_enabled()` remains the incident lever and **wins over the manifest**). A gated-off role is reported as skipped with its reason (the §3 stub wording classes), not silently dropped.

**Failure rule (the core of this design): unknown location ⇒ `fleet init` REPORTS state and starts nothing. It never guess-starts roles.** Unknown means: no manifest from any of 1–3, a location with no roles from any source, or a file/env location mismatch with no built-in map. The report (stdout) names every source consulted and what detection found; the exit code is **69** (`EX_UNAVAILABLE` — "not here", the binary's existing D3 semantics), so autostart callers fail visibly instead of silently succeeding with nothing running.

```text
$ fleet init            # on an unprovisioned machine
fleet: location: unknown — starting nothing
fleet:   manifest: none (checked $FLEET_HOST_CONFIG, $FLEET_LOCATION,
         ~/.config/fleet/fleet.toml [host])
fleet:   detected: hostname=<host>, os=<os>, systemd=<present|absent>,
         tailnet=<self identity if known>
fleet: to provision this machine, add a [host] section to
       ~/.config/fleet/fleet.toml or set FLEET_LOCATION / FLEET_HOST_CONFIG
(exit 69)
```

## 5. Per-machine role maps (approved naming: all daemons under `fleet serve`)

Role command lines after the approved rename: `fleet serve proxy` (was `fleet proxy serve` — `spawn_serve()` in `fleet-proxy/src/client.rs` must spawn `["serve", "proxy"]`), `fleet serve queue-broker`, `fleet serve secrets-broker`, `fleet serve search`, `fleet serve laptop-agent`. `fleet proxy` keeps only its client verbs (`connect`, `init`).

| Location | `init_mode` | Roles (`[host.roles]` keys) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sandbox` | `spawn` | `proxy` | Exactly today's behaviour, now *because the manifest says so*. |
| `laptop` | `systemd` | `queue-broker`, `secrets-broker`, `search`, `laptop-agent` | Brokers already run as user units re-pointed at `fleet serve <role>` (README, step 2); `search` joins when the serve role lands (today's atlas user unit is the separate cutover); `laptop-agent` joins when the daemon exists (#5343). |
| `lab-01` (future example) | `systemd` | `queue-broker`, `search` | A headless worker: takes queue work and serves search; no proxy, no secrets-broker — it *consumes* secrets through the laptop's broker like any client. Shows the map is per-machine, not per-OS. |

`init_mode` decides what "ensure" means per role:

- `spawn` (sandbox): today's semantics per role — probe; if already running, report + sync shims and stop (strict no-op); if not, spawn detached and report what was started. For `proxy` this includes the legacy-broker rule already in `run_init()`: a proto-0 (Python) broker answering the socket counts as *running*; init never fights an incumbent.
- `systemd` (laptop/lab): init does **not** detached-spawn daemons that systemd owns. It reports each role's unit state (`fleet-<role>.service`), and starting a stopped role means asking systemd (`systemctl --user start …`), never a `setsid` spawn — a spawned copy would fight the unit for the socket/port on next boot.

What `fleet init` prints/does:

```text
# sandbox — first run, then every subsequent run
$ fleet init
fleet: location sandbox (source: ~/.config/fleet/fleet.toml [host])
fleet: role proxy: started `fleet serve proxy`; shims at ~/.local/state/fleet/shims […]
$ fleet init
fleet: location sandbox (source: ~/.config/fleet/fleet.toml [host])
fleet: role proxy: already running (proto N); shims current

# laptop
$ fleet init
fleet: location laptop (source: ~/.config/fleet/fleet.toml [host])
fleet: role queue-broker: unit fleet-queue-broker.service active — nothing spawned
fleet: role secrets-broker: unit fleet-secrets-broker.service active — nothing spawned
fleet: role search: unit fleet-search.service active — nothing spawned
fleet: role laptop-agent: not yet available in this build (capability stub, exit 69 class) — reported, skipped
fleet: role proxy: not assigned to this host — not started

# lab-01
$ fleet init
fleet: location lab-01 (source: $FLEET_HOST_CONFIG)
fleet: role queue-broker: unit fleet-queue-broker.service active — nothing spawned
fleet: role search: unit fleet-search.service inactive — started via systemctl --user
```

Note on `laptop-agent`: today that name is a **client** domain (`fleet laptop-agent run|status|poll|kill`, capability `LaptopAgent`, stub 69). The daemon role `fleet serve laptop-agent` needs its own serve-side capability (parallel to `search` client vs `search-serve`). Naming that capability is an implementation-step decision; this design only reserves the role name and flags the collision so the client capability is not silently reused.

## 6. Migration from today's proxy-only init

Existing caller that must keep working: the sandbox's `init-ensure.sh`, which calls `fleet init` on shell/tool start and depends on (a) exit 0 when the proxy is up or startable, (b) strict no-op semantics against a live broker of either dialect, (c) no arguments. It is not in this repo (`gh search code init-ensure` returns nothing) — it is sandbox-local — so the migration is a deployment sequence, not just a code change:

1. **Land the `[host]` parsing + location resolution in `fleet-config`/`fleet init`, with the legacy behaviour preserved behind "manifest resolves to sandbox".** (No guessing fallback is added — see step 3.)
2. **Provision before flipping the binary on the sandbox:** write `[host] location="sandbox"`, `init_mode="spawn"`, `[host.roles] proxy={}` into the sandbox's `fleet.toml`, **and** update `init-ensure.sh` to call `FLEET_LOCATION=sandbox fleet init` as belt-and-braces (the env var is idempotent, wins over a lost/truncated file location, and makes the caller's assumption explicit at the call site). Verify: `fleet init` prints `location sandbox`, second run is the no-op, exit 0 both times.
3. **Only then deploy the location-aware binary.** Deliberately **no** "no manifest ⇒ assume proxy" compatibility guess in the binary: that guess is the bug being designed out, and a time-boxed version of it would still start a proxy on any laptop that got the new binary before its manifest. The provisioning-first sequence is what keeps `init-ensure.sh` working — same command, same semantics, same exit codes on the sandbox.
4. **`fleet proxy init`** (the proxy-domain alias path into the same `run_init()` in `main.rs`) goes through the identical resolution — there is one init implementation, not two.
5. **Smoke suite** (`pkgs/fleet/smoke.sh`): the existing `fleet init is a no-op when the broker runs` case gains a manifest fixture (`FLEET_HOST_CONFIG` is the natural hermetic vehicle); add cases for the unknown-location report (exit 69, nothing spawned) and the laptop-manifest-on-sandbox-roles case. The `connect variant stubs fleet init at 69` case is unchanged — that 69 comes from the capability gate, which still runs first.
6. **Rollback gotcha, flagged explicitly:** `Config` uses `deny_unknown_fields`, so a `fleet.toml` containing `[host]` is a **parse error to the current (pre-change) binary**. Rolling the binary back therefore requires removing the `[host]` section (or rolling config and binary back together). This must be in the implementation step's runbook, not discovered during an incident.

## Recommendation summary

Adopt: `[host]` in the existing `fleet.toml` (provisioning-written, init never writes it); `FLEET_LOCATION` + `FLEET_HOST_CONFIG` env overrides with loud-parse / empty-is-unset semantics; detection as report-only; precedence env-contents > env-location > file, no cross-source merging, `[domains]` still wins as the kill switch; **unknown ⇒ report + start nothing + exit 69**; role maps `sandbox={proxy, spawn}`, `laptop={queue-broker, secrets-broker, search, laptop-agent, systemd}`, lab nodes per-machine under systemd; migration by provisioning the sandbox manifest (plus `FLEET_LOCATION=sandbox` in `init-ensure.sh`) **before** the binary flip, with the `deny_unknown_fields` rollback gotcha in the runbook.

## Next steps

- [ ] Drew confirms this design (or amends §1/§2 names) — the naming in §5 is already approved; the manifest/env names are this issue's proposal.
- [ ] Implementation step under #5412: `HostConfig` + resolution in `fleet-config` (with unit tests for precedence, mismatch, unknown-role, malformed-env), location-aware `cmd_init`/`run_init`, `spawn_serve` → `["serve", "proxy"]`, smoke cases per §6.
- [ ] Provisioning change: sandbox `[host]` manifest + `init-ensure.sh` env pin, sequenced per §6, with the rollback note.
- [ ] Separate follow-ups, not this issue: the `fleet serve laptop-agent` capability name; the search serve-role cutover that makes the laptop `search` role real; the `/etc`-level file if a system-service install ever materialises.
