body:
## Summary

Design **client-side capability providers**: the mechanism by which a client — any client — offers capabilities (sensors, actuators, storage, compute, UI surfaces, local services) into the same data / capability model the rest of `id` uses, so other authorised parties can discover and use them under least-privilege grants.

This extends #789 (Phase 13 F13.7 client-side capability providers under the ceiling model). Drew's framing: this is **a huge part of the project — arguably the core feature.** The test of the model is that the *same* data / capability model works, unchanged in its essentials, when the provider is:

- an **ESP32** emitting data over an **MQTT bridge**,
- a **terminal** acting as client *or* as server,
- a **game engine** integration (**Bevy** named),
- a **smartphone**, and
- a **website**.

If the model needs a special case per target, the model is wrong; this issue exists to find the model that does not.

Relates to: #789.

## Core model to design

### Providers and capabilities

- A **provider** is any client-side entity that declares capabilities it offers: typed, described, and versioned (capability name, input/output shape, units / semantics, rate / size limits, side effects).
- Capabilities are offered **into the ceiling model** (#789's framing): a provider can never offer more than its own ceiling allows, and a consumer can never receive more than the grant — the provider model must compose with, not bypass, existing capability / grant machinery.
- Provider identity: a provider is bound to an identity in the system (which one — the user's, the device's own, a pseudo / delegated identity?) and the design must cover device-owned vs user-owned providers and shared / public providers.

### Declaration

- How a provider declares what it offers: a manifest / declaration artefact — contents, signing, versioning, update and withdrawal of declarations.
- Static vs dynamic declaration: fixed firmware capabilities (ESP32) vs runtime-discovered capabilities (phone sensors present, terminal tools installed, engine features enabled).
- Declaration honesty: a declaration is a claim — what, if anything, verifies that a provider can actually do what it declares (test invocations, attestation, nothing — reputation only)? State the choice per target class.

### Discovery

- How consumers find providers and their capabilities: within a world, within a server, across a bridge / federation — and the visibility rules (a provider is discoverable by whom, by default?).
- Discovery metadata minimisation: discovery must not leak a device inventory to parties with no grant (what does an unauthorised browser learn — existence? type? owner?).
- Stale discovery: providers that vanish (device off, tab closed, game quit) — TTLs, heartbeats, tombstones, and what a consumer's cached view may assume.

### Negotiation

- Before use, provider and consumer negotiate: capability version, data format / encoding, rate, quality / resolution, session lifetime.
- Negotiation failure is a normal outcome: partial agreement (lower rate, coarser data), counter-offers, and clear failure reasons — design the shape, per target class where bandwidth / latency differ wildly (MQTT bridge vs in-process engine plugin).
- Who initiates, who can refuse, and whether negotiation itself requires a grant or is pre-grant metadata exchange (see discovery minimisation).

### Least-privilege grants

- Use of a capability requires a **grant**: scoped to capability, provider, consumer, purpose where expressible, rate / volume, and expiry. Default is no access; grants are explicit, revocable, and auditable.
- Grant issuance flows per target class: who approves a grant to read a phone's location vs an ESP32's temperature vs a terminal's command execution — the sensitivity range here is enormous and the UX must scale with it (standing grants for low-sensitivity telemetry; per-use approval for actuation / execution).
- Delegation and attenuation: can a consumer pass on a narrower grant? Must compose with the system's existing delegation model.
- **Actuation vs observation are different risk classes** and the grant model must treat them differently (reading a sensor vs firing a relay vs running a terminal command).

### Offline / degraded behaviour

Per target class, define what happens when connectivity, the server, or the consumer disappears:

- Provider keeps sensing / buffering? Buffer size, drop policy, backfill on reconnect, ordering and gap signalling in emitted data.
- Grants while offline: cached grants with expiry, no-new-grants-while-offline rule, actuation while offline (allowed under a standing grant? never? per class?).
- Degraded modes: reduced rate / resolution, local-only operation, store-and-forward via bridge (MQTT QoS levels and their mapping onto the model's delivery guarantees).

## Target classes (the model must fit all five)

For each: declaration form, transport, constraints (power, bandwidth, CPU, sandbox), identity binding, and the offline story — as instantiations of the one model, with differences listed explicitly and justified.

1. **ESP32 over an MQTT bridge** — constrained device, intermittent connectivity, firmware-fixed capabilities, the bridge as translator between MQTT topics and the capability model: topic ↔ capability mapping, bridge trust (the bridge sees / can forge what?), provisioning a device identity and its ceiling.
2. **Terminal as client or server** — a CLI host offering capabilities (files, commands, local services) as a client, and the dual case: the terminal host *is* the server others connect to. Command execution as the highest-sensitivity capability class; sandboxing expectations stated, not assumed.
3. **Game engines (Bevy named)** — an engine plugin / component model: in-game entities offering and consuming capabilities, tick-rate and latency constraints, capabilities that exist only while a world / session runs, and the boundary between game state and the wider system (what may an external consumer do to a running game, and vice versa).
4. **Smartphone** — OS permission systems (location, sensors, notifications) composed with `id` grants: two gates, both must pass; background execution limits; provider lifecycle tied to app state; battery-aware rates.
5. **Website** — a browser tab as provider: sandbox limits, per-origin identity, capabilities that die with the tab, user-gesture requirements for sensitive grants, and what a website may offer other clients vs only the user viewing it.

## Cross-cutting requirements

- **Data model uniformity:** data emitted by any provider lands in the same model (same typing, provenance, and access rules) regardless of origin target. Provenance records at minimum: provider identity, capability, grant under which it was obtained, and time.
- **Security model:** provider impersonation, rogue providers, malicious consumers probing declarations, bridge compromise (MQTT case), and capability confusion (a grant for one capability replayed against another) — each named with its mitigation or its accepted risk.
- **Versioning & evolution:** capability schemas evolve; consumers pinned to old versions; providers withdrawing a capability version — the compatibility story.
- **Ceiling composition:** every design element must state how it interacts with the ceiling model from #789; any place the provider model would punch through a ceiling is a design bug to be caught here.

## Non-goals

- Implementing providers for all five targets (design the model; prototypes / spikes only where the Decomposition sketch calls for them).
- Designing the MQTT bridge as a standalone product (only its provider-model surface is in scope).
- A general IoT device-management platform (provisioning fleets, OTA updates) beyond the identity / declaration hooks the provider model needs.
- Replacing the existing grant / ceiling machinery — this issue extends it client-side, per #789.

## Acceptance criteria for the design deliverable

- [ ] A design document covering declaration, discovery, negotiation, least-privilege grants, and offline / degraded behaviour as one model, linked from this issue.
- [ ] All five target classes instantiated from that model, with per-target differences listed and justified — no silent special cases.
- [ ] Grant model distinguishing observation vs actuation, with issuance / approval flows scaled by sensitivity.
- [ ] Offline behaviour specified per target class, including cached-grant and actuation-while-offline rules.
- [ ] Security analysis: impersonation, rogue providers, bridge compromise, capability confusion.
- [ ] Ceiling-model composition stated for each mechanism.
- [ ] Follow-on design tickets filed from the Decomposition sketch (or the sketch revised with reasons).

## Decomposition sketch

Follow-on design tickets to be filed from this issue (indicative; revise during the work):

1. Design: provider declaration model — manifest contents, signing, versioning, dynamic vs static capabilities.
2. Design: discovery & negotiation protocols — visibility / minimisation rules, negotiation shape, stale-provider handling.
3. Design: capability grants for providers — least-privilege scoping, observation vs actuation classes, approval flows by sensitivity, attenuation.
4. Design: constrained-device providers — ESP32 + MQTT bridge instantiation, topic mapping, bridge trust, device identity / ceiling provisioning.
5. Design: host providers — terminal (client and server modes) and website instantiations, sandbox and lifecycle rules.
6. Design: embedded providers — Bevy engine integration and smartphone instantiation, OS-permission composition, session-bound lifecycles.
7. Design: offline & degraded operation for providers — buffering, backfill, cached grants, per-class actuation rules.
8. Design: provider security model — impersonation, rogue providers, capability confusion, and ceiling-composition audit.

## Open questions

- Is a provider's identity its own first-class identity, the owner's identity, or a delegated / pseudo identity — and does the answer differ for a $5 sensor vs a phone?
- How much declaration verification is worth it: is an unverified-but-signed claim enough for v1, with attestation left as a later capability?
- Can negotiation be one protocol across an in-process Bevy plugin and a multi-hop MQTT bridge, or does the model need transport profiles — and where exactly is that line?
- What is the default discoverability of a new provider: invisible until granted, visible-but-metadata-minimised within its world, or visible to the server only?
- Actuation while offline under a standing grant: is there any target class where this is acceptable, and who is accountable for an action taken on a stale grant?
- When a provider is a website tab or a game session, do grants outlive it — and what does a consumer holding a grant to a dead provider experience?
- Does the MQTT bridge become a trusted central point that the rest of the model must route around, or is bridge trust acceptable if it is explicit and scoped per device?

---

*Extension of #789. Framing per Drew: a huge part of the project — the core feature; one model across ESP32/MQTT, terminal, game engines (Bevy), smartphone, and web.*

body:
## Summary

ID servers should be reachable from networks where UDP is denied. Today ID's native transport assumes UDP (QUIC/iroh-style reachability). Many real networks — corporate egress, locked-down sandboxes, some cloud and CI environments, captive Wi-Fi — allow only TCP, and often only outbound HTTP/HTTPS through a proxy. This design expands #785 (the UDP-denied SSH fallback design) from "SSH still works" into a general transport-fallback feature set for ID itself: any ID traffic, not just SSH, should degrade gracefully to TCP/HTTP transports without giving up end-to-end encryption.

Relates: #785 (extends it — #785 is the SSH-specific case; this is the general ID transport), the serverless/rendezvous direction in #2046 (Cloudflare Workers edition — a Workers rendezvous/relay is one candidate component here).

## Motivating case

Our own fleet sandbox: no direct UDP egress; outbound traffic goes through an HTTP CONNECT proxy only. We need, from inside that sandbox:

- Access to ID servers (data, queries, sync) with no UDP path available.
- SSH-class reachability through the same constrained egress — ideally locally terminated, so tools on the sandbox side see a local endpoint rather than a fragile chain of tunnels.
- The same pattern the fleet already uses for sandbox→laptop proxying, generalized so it is a property of ID, not a one-off fleet workaround.

If ID works from our sandbox, it works from most restricted networks.

## Feature set (expanded)

### 1. Fallback ordering and transport negotiation

- Defined attempt order: **direct UDP → relay-assisted UDP (hole-punch / relay) → TCP → HTTP/HTTPS proxy (CONNECT, and where necessary plain HTTP/WebSocket-style framing)**.
- Negotiation is automatic by default, with per-peer and per-network memory: remember which transport last worked for a peer/network and try it first next time, re-probing periodically.
- Explicit override surface: config and CLI flags to pin a transport, forbid a transport, or force proxy use (for testing and for networks where probing is noisy/slow).
- Failure classification: distinguish "UDP blocked" from "peer offline" from "proxy auth required" so error messages and retries are correct, and so fallback does not mask real outages.
- Connection migration: when a better transport becomes available (e.g. the client moves to an unrestricted network), upgrade in place where the protocol allows, without dropping sessions.

### 2. Broker / relay role

- A broker that proxies ID traffic over HTTP/TCP for clients that cannot use UDP: clients connect out to the broker over TCP/443 (directly or via their HTTP proxy); the broker forwards to the target ID server (or to a rendezvous point the server also connects out to, for servers themselves behind UDP-denied or NAT-only egress).
- **Ideally native to ID itself:** a serve/proxy role inside the `id` binary (`id serve`-adjacent mode) so any ID node can act as a broker for peers it is authorized to help — no separate daemon to deploy.
- Fleet-side surface (future): a `fleet id` subcommand that stands up/configures this broker role for fleet machines, mirroring the existing fleet sandbox→laptop proxy pattern.
- Broker is a dumb pipe by design: it routes opaque, end-to-end-encrypted traffic (see trust model). It must not need, hold, or be able to derive session/content keys.

### 3. Discovery and rendezvous

- How a UDP-denied client finds its server and a usable broker: rendezvous records (signed, verifiable) advertising a server's available transports, broker endpoints, and priority.
- Candidate rendezvous substrates to evaluate, with a recommendation: DNS-based records, a well-known HTTPS endpoint, and a **Cloudflare Workers rendezvous/relay component** (cheap, globally reachable over 443, no server to run) — including when Workers is the right shape vs. when a self-hosted `id` broker is required (sovereignty, cost, data-residency).
- Rendezvous must itself be reachable over plain HTTPS, or the fallback is circular.
- Stale/spoofed rendezvous handling: signature verification, TTLs, and fallback to last-known-good endpoints.

### 4. Relay trust model

- What the broker/relay **can** see: connection metadata (endpoints, timing, volume) — state this honestly and minimize it (no logging defaults, padding/batching options if cheap).
- What it **cannot** see: payload contents. ID payloads stay end-to-end encrypted between the true endpoints; the broker forwards ciphertext. SSH through the broker likewise stays end-to-end (broker never terminates SSH).
- Broker authorization: who may use a given broker (open, allowlist by identity/key, capability token), and who a broker will forward for — an open relay is an abuse magnet; default to authenticated.
- Compromised-broker analysis: worst case is metadata exposure + denial of service, never content exposure; design must keep it that way (no key escrow, no TLS termination of ID payloads at the broker).
- Local termination option: where the client side runs a local `id` proxy endpoint, applications (including SSH) connect to localhost and the encryption boundary is the local process — document exactly where plaintext exists in each topology.

### 5. Latency and performance budget

- Stated budgets per fallback tier (e.g. interactive SSH and ID queries must stay usable on the HTTP-proxy path; bulk sync may be slower but must complete).
- Overhead sources to measure: proxy CONNECT setup, TLS-in-TLS, framing, broker hop latency, head-of-line blocking on a single TCP stream (and whether multiple streams / multiplexing are needed).
- Keepalive and idle-timeout behavior for long-lived connections through proxies that kill idle TCP.
- Reconnection/resumption: dropped proxy connections resume sessions rather than restarting sync from zero.

### 6. What stays end-to-end encrypted (explicit list)

- ID data/sync payloads: E2E, broker-blind.
- ID queries and results (see the ID query design): E2E.
- SSH sessions tunneled through the fallback: E2E, broker is a pipe.
- Control/rendezvous traffic: authenticated and integrity-protected; confidentiality requirements stated per message type.
- Anything that is **not** E2E (if any) must be named in the design with justification — silence is not acceptable here.

## Non-goals (v1)

- Defeating deliberate, policy-enforced egress restrictions the user is not authorized to bypass — this is for reaching *your own* ID servers from restrictive networks, with the broker as an authorized endpoint.
- A public, open relay network.
- Replacing the native UDP transport; fallback is additive.

## Acceptance for this design

A follow-on reader can break this into the decomposition tickets below without re-deciding: fallback order, broker role shape (in-`id` vs Workers vs both), trust model, or the E2E boundary.

## Decomposition sketch

1. Design: transport negotiation & fallback ordering (probing, per-peer memory, overrides, failure classification).
2. Design: `id` broker/serve-proxy role — protocol, framing over TCP/HTTP(S), multiplexing, keepalive/resumption.
3. Design: rendezvous & discovery for UDP-denied clients (signed transport advertisements; substrate selection).
4. Design: Cloudflare Workers rendezvous/relay component — when it is the right shape, limits, self-host parity.
5. Design: relay trust model & broker authorization (capabilities/allowlist, metadata minimization, compromised-broker analysis).
6. Design: HTTP CONNECT proxy traversal (proxy auth, corporate proxies, locally terminated endpoint for SSH-class traffic).
7. Design: latency budget & measurement plan per fallback tier (interactive vs bulk).
8. Design: fleet surface — future `fleet id` subcommand wiring the broker role into fleet sandbox→laptop patterns.

## Open questions

- Broker in `id` itself, a Workers component, or both — and which ships first?
- What rendezvous substrate is authoritative when several disagree?
- How are brokers discovered by strangers vs. only by pre-configured peers (sovereignty vs. convenience)?
- Proxy-auth credentials: where stored, and how are they kept out of logs/config dumps?
- Is multiplexing over one TCP connection sufficient, or is head-of-line blocking disqualifying for mixed interactive+bulk traffic?
- Cost/ownership model for a hosted relay (who runs it, who pays, what are the abuse controls)?
- How does fallback interact with #785's SSH-specific design — supersede, wrap, or coexist?

body:
Implementation of §4 of the Scaler-era data architecture revision (design doc PR #5667, `doc/2026-11-04T21-27-34Z_design_atlas_scaler_revision/`).

**Scope:**
- `atlas_stage` v1 schema DDL (`items`, `chunks_raw`, `notes`, `kv`, `_schema_version`) + one provisioning tool that creates a staging DB per work unit (queue task / session / epic / notes batch) and applies the schema.
- Registry (internal core tier): unit id → staging DB, owner, sensitivity level, state (open/closing/merged), schema version. (Design §6 proposes the registry be born as a TursoDB `--tursodb` pilot DB once the account toggle is enabled — sequencing note, not a blocker for the libSQL version.)
- Aggregator (`fleet serve` role, laptop): on unit close, embed new chunks with the resident Snowflake model, promote survivors into core in bounded batches (≤500 rows/txn), write the merge manifest (unit id, rows in/promoted, content hash), bump the core snapshot id per batch (consumed by the §3 result cache), branch the staging DB as archive, deregister. Partial periodic promotion for long-lived units (epics).
- Core stores per design: exactly three physical sensitivity levels (public / internal-default / secret — separate DBs + credentials); within a level, scan stores per corpus + one content store per level; reclassification = verified mechanical row move (counts + hash) with a manifest log entry.
- Session-close extraction hook as the canonical staging producer (sessions write staging only; core never sees session-rate writes).

**Acceptance:** an end-to-end demo unit (one session) flows staging → close → promotion → searchable in core with correct ceiling behavior per level; a reclassification move round-trips counts/hashes; promotion never holds a core writer > seconds (batch bound enforced); core DDL only via maintenance path. PBT/MBT per the testing doctrine (schema-version invariants, manifest hash oracle).

Design: #5667 §4 (+ §5 sizing, §6 pilot). Parent context: hatch-personal#21.

## Acceptance criteria

body:
Implementation of §3 of the Scaler-era data architecture revision (design doc PR #5667, `doc/2026-11-04T21-27-34Z_design_atlas_scaler_revision/`). Builds on the search service from epic #5350 (esp. #5354 serve mode).

**Scope:**
- Query-embedding cache: key `sha256(model_id || model_rev || normalized_text)`, no TTL; service-memory LRU (~10k entries) + shared Turso cache DB in the internal tier; cache writes async/best-effort, never in the request path.
- Result cache: key `sha256(query || snapshot_id || ceiling || flags)`; reused while the snapshot id (publish manifest hash) is current; 24 h TTL as GC bound only; in-service memory per the #5354 privacy rule (no cross-client result sharing by default).
- Flags end-to-end (CLI + service protocol): `--no-cache` (bypass reads, refresh writes), `--wait` (block for full fused result vs job handle + first page), `--expand N` (hydrate top N to full chunk/file text from the content store), `--raw` / `--raw=branches` (ungrouped rows, pre-fusion option). All flags are part of the cache key.
- Snapshot id plumbing: aggregator promotion batches bump the snapshot id; the service must observe bumps without restart.

**Acceptance:** golden-311 parity unchanged with caches cold and warm (eval runs use `--no-cache`); a repeated identical query against an unchanged snapshot is served from cache with no Turso round-trip for the ranking; a snapshot bump invalidates all result entries at once; PBT over cache-key construction (flag sensitivity, ceiling sensitivity) + MBT for the snapshot-rotation invalidation, per the testing doctrine (every test names its oracle).

Design: #5667 §3. Parent context: hatch-personal#21.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Query-embedding cache: key `sha256(model_id || model_rev || normalized_text)`, no TTL, service-memory LRU (~10k) plus shared Turso cache DB; writes async/best-effort, never in the request path.
- [ ] Result cache: key `sha256(query || snapshot_id || ceiling || flags)`; hits only while the snapshot id is current; 24h TTL as GC bound only; per-service memory per the #5354 privacy rule (no cross-client result sharing by default).
- [ ] Flags work end-to-end (CLI + service protocol) and are part of the cache key: `--no-cache`, `--wait`, `--expand N`, `--raw` / `--raw=branches`.
- [ ] Snapshot id from aggregator promotion batches (issue #5669) invalidates stale result-cache entries.

body:
## Receipt-audit follow-up from #3232 / design #3231

Envelope.verify currently verifies the signature but does not validate Envelope.id's producer shape (16 random bytes rendered as 32 lowercase hex characters). Directory.receive persists any correctly signed ID into request/seen state. A noncanonical signed request ID such as r1 can flow through Directory.friendship_requests into a friend_remove artifact, whose receipt validation rejects it under #3146; the friendship then cannot be removed through the normal artifact path.

## Scope

- Validate the canonical ID shape at fresh friend-request admission (and relevant persisted-entry boundaries).
- Preserve a safe removal path for already-persisted noncanonical IDs; do not make old friendships permanently unremovable.
- Add regressions for admission and legacy-state removal.
- Keep this separate from the #3232 audit; do not weaken the friend_remove.requests receipt contract.

Evidence: #3232 comment https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/3232#issuecomment-6578677909; current source pkgs/id/src/directory.rs (Envelope::verify, Directory::receive, Directory::friendship_requests) and pkgs/id/src/artifact.rs (friend_remove parsing).

## Acceptance criteria
- Fresh friend-request admission validates the canonical envelope ID shape (16 random bytes as 32 lowercase hex characters) before persistence.
- Already-persisted noncanonical IDs retain a safe removal path — old friendships are not permanently unremovable.
- Regression tests cover both fresh admission rejection and legacy-state removal.
- The `friend_remove.requests` receipt contract (#3146) is not weakened.

Use `ainventory.measurement_events` as the canonical append-only store for AA v5 and v4.3.2 measurements, consistent with the event-log design recorded on #1248. Treat `v_current_measurements` as the intended current read surface. Do not retire `benchmark_results` or change its live aggregator consumers in this slice; those are a later step after consumer migration.

## Current-state caveat
#1248 is still open and blocked. Its 2026-10-27 phase-1 comment describes the intended schema and an earlier backfill, but at current `developing-today/code` main `48cb3fe219e01edbaada53bde7c9e5d6f36235db`, no tracked `measurement_events`, `0013_aa_event_log`, or `backfill_event_log.sql` artifact exists. The last verified live counts are from the 2026-11-03 #4401 readback (comment #6617281563 and earlier #6612157519); revalidate everything read-only against muse-dev2 before any write.

## Scope and safety gates
1. Inspect the live table/view definitions, append-only guards, source columns, and existing rows read-only. Count the Rankings source rows separately for AA v5 and v4.3.2; identify each stable source row id, original import-batch UUID, snapshot date, and estimated flag. Stop and report a blocker if the live schema or source mapping differs from the cited design.
2. Add a repeatable, insert-only backfill artifact for only those two Rankings versions. Preserve source identity, batch, snapshot date, raw fields and estimated flags; use a stable source reference so reruns cannot duplicate events. Do not update/delete existing events or use an upsert that updates rows.
3. Dry-run the exact selection and projected counts first. Execute only after source counts, target schema and provenance mapping reconcile. Read back per-version counts and provenance samples; verify source `sheet_rows` and `benchmark_results` counts are unchanged.
4. Add `pm-stack/aggregator/ARCHITECTURE.md` naming the canonical table/read view and explicitly noting that the existing `benchmark_results` consumer cutover is out of scope and remains a later step.

## Acceptance
- Fresh per-version source counts for AA v5 and v4.3.2 exactly match the new canonical event counts.
- Every inserted event has traceable source id, original batch, snapshot date, and preserved estimated/raw metadata; reruns insert no duplicates.
- `sheet_rows` and `benchmark_results` counts are unchanged; no table/view retirement or consumer migration occurs.
- The backfill SQL and architecture note are reviewed in a PR; include the exact readback evidence and production write summary in the task result.

Risk: high (`production-data`, `multi-step-migration`). Keep the work scoped to this backfill only.

popesdrew is a fully fresh Go account (0% on every window) sitting idle while its sibling pool is walled for ~4.5 more days and opendesign is walled on its 7d window. Daily-pass verdict on PR #5112: OpenAI prong WORKED (openai.main weekly 20%, drawing); Go prong NO EFFECT. Until this is explained, the fleet's Go balance cannot be corrected by weights alone.

1. Is the popesdrew credential able to generate at all (a one-shot smoke through the live server)? If it errors (auth/scope/402), the zero draw is a credential problem, not a routing one.

body:
<!-- agent-note:v1 design-architect pass 45 -->

# A name is claimed once — the hosted binding lifecycle contract (pkgs/id `hosted_binding`)

Design doc: `files/designs/code-id-hosted-binding-lifecycle.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Audit HEAD: origin/main `8e151e89`. Module: `pkgs/id/src/hosted_binding.rs`.

## Summary

`hosted_binding.rs` binds a Google identity (`sub`) to an Iroh root key — the §3 challenge/pairing ceremony (slice 1, #3808) and the §4 delayed rebind protocol (slice 2, #3809 via #4885), both landed 2026-11-03. The module's header states its §3.4 failure table and §4 no-mutation contract in prose, but the transitions of its ephemeral state were never stated as one lifecycle, and three filings in one day are one counterexample per transition:

- **Consumption (#4868):** `submit_proof`'s expiry branch inserts the expired challenge into `consumed_challenges` (hosted_binding.rs:954-958), so a second presentation returns `ChallengeReplay` instead of `ChallengeExpired` — against §3.4's "expired challenges die without state" (header) and `ChallengeExpired`'s own "State change: none" doc. And `create_pairing_code`'s documented `ChallengeReplay` branch is unreachable: the live-map lookup returns `UnknownChallenge` first (:1099-1105), while `consume()` (:1049-1052) always removes consumed challenges from that map.
- **Supersession (#4871):** `create_pairing_code` never invalidates earlier codes for the same challenge (:1093-1147) and `exchange_pairing_code` honours every live code (:1150-1168) — up to 10 simultaneously valid bearer codes per ceremony, none revocable, so "give me a new code" does not retire a leaked one.
- **Reservation (#4887):** a pending delayed rebind reserves the account but never its target key — `request_delayed_rebind` checks the target only against `binding_by_iroh` at request time (:1269), `submit_proof`'s conflict check likewise (:996-1000), `effect_due_rebind` re-checks nothing (:1462-1503), and `apply_rebind` unconditionally overwrites the other binding's `binding_by_iroh` entry (:1538-1540). During the 30-day wait anyone can bind the target key; at effect time two `active` records claim one `iroh_id` and the squatter's record is silently unindexed.

This audit adds a fourth surface of the same missing lifecycle: the rebind paths' shared `verify_challenge_proof` (:1171-1205) also consumes on expiry, and `RebindError::ChallengeExpired`'s doc states the opposite of the ceremony side's — "it is consumed and dead." One module, two contradictory expiry semantics for the same challenge object.

**The contract:** every name the ceremony mints — a challenge, a pairing code, a rebind target key — is claimed exactly once, by exactly one holder, for exactly its stated lifetime, and every transition out of a live state (consumption, supersession, expiry, reservation, release) is named in the §3.4/§4 tables. Dead means the same thing on both error surfaces.

Checked and NOT stating this contract: #3809 (closed implementation slice) and #3818 (open, blocked — hosted bridge transport, gated on the #3808 contract, states no ceremony transitions). The Worker API slice (#3811) that will expose pairing over HTTP is not yet built; this contract lands before it does.

## Decisions recorded

1. **Expiry creates no state, on both surfaces.** Expired challenges are removed from the live map and NOT inserted into `consumed_challenges`, in `submit_proof` and in `verify_challenge_proof`; `RebindError::ChallengeExpired`'s doc is amended to match §3.4 in the same change. (The docs-amended-the-other-way alternative loses: replay is a security signal, expiry is not.)
2. **A consumed challenge reports as consumed, everywhere.** Every entry point checks the consumed set before the live map (the order `submit_proof` already uses), making `create_pairing_code`'s `ChallengeReplay` reachable; `UnknownChallenge` means never-issued or expired away.
3. **Minting supersedes.** `create_pairing_code` removes every existing code for the challenge first — at most one live code per challenge. Rate limits unchanged.
4. **A pending rebind reserves its target key.** Reservation is a predicate over `Pending` requests (not a second index — a second index is a second place for state to disagree, the #4887 failure family). `submit_proof` refuses a reserved key with `IrohIdBoundElsewhere`; `request_delayed_rebind` refuses a reserved target with `NewKeyBoundElsewhere`; the fast path gains the same check. Cancel/effect releases implicitly (the predicate reads only `Pending`).
5. **Effect re-checks; the index write refuses a foreign entry.** `effect_due_rebind` re-checks before any mutation (`NewKeyBoundElsewhere`, no state change, request stays `Pending`), and `apply_rebind` itself refuses to overwrite a `binding_by_iroh` entry naming a different binding.

## Phases (sub-issues of this design)

- **Phase 1 — #4868 (ADOPTED):** expiry creates no state (both challenge gates) + consumed-check order everywhere; docs amended in the same change.
- **Phase 2 — #4871 (ADOPTED, independent):** minting a pairing code supersedes all earlier codes for the challenge.
- **Phase 3 — #4887 (ADOPTED, independent):** target-key reservation + effect-time recheck + `apply_rebind` foreign-entry refusal.
- **Phase 4 — NEW (closing audit):** transition-table audit of every public method, the table written into the module header beside §3.4, four required dispositions (expired pairing-code sweep; `consumed_challenges` growth bound; reservation scan cost vs a target-key index; old-key-side symmetry confirmation), gated on Phases 1–3.

## Open questions (recorded in the design doc, not phased)

- Must "expired" be sticky (a tombstone) once the Worker API (#3811) maps these errors to HTTP? A client-contract question for that slice.
- Reservation notices to third parties whose ceremony is refused — a disclosure question, Drew's call if ever wanted, not a phase.

## Acceptance for this design issue

All four phases closed with evidence; the module header carries the lifecycle transition table; #4868/#4871/#4887 closed by their phases (not re-filed).


## Acceptance criteria

- The lifecycle contract is recorded (design doc + this issue) stating claim-once semantics for each ephemeral state in hosted_binding: pairing challenge, pairing code, rebind target key — holder, lifetime, and every named transition out of a live state (consumption, supersession, expiry, reservation, release).
- Each of the three counterexample transitions (consumption #4868, supersession, rebind) has a named disposition in the contract.
- The phase/implementation issues (#4868, #4871, #4887, #5048) are linked to this epic as native GitHub relations (sub-issues / blocked-by), not only as prose references (protocol §11).

body:
Split from #2381 (encrypted identity backup) as the design-first half. The local envelope half is #2279; the seed-phrase half stays on #2381.

## Problem
#2381 proposes a passphrase-wrapped identity backup stored server-side, with a memory-hard KDF and a rate-limited *blinded* unwrap (OPRF-style) so the server can throttle guessing without learning the passphrase or the key. Nothing of that exists at main `048da81f1`:

- No backup blob format anywhere in `pkgs/id/src` (`grep -rln "backup"` hits only `world_doctor.rs`, `repl/input.rs`, `currency_poc/tests.rs`, `web/routes.rs`, `cli.rs`).
- No OPRF or blinded-unwrap primitive anywhere in `pkgs/id/` or `doc/` (`grep -rli "oprf\|blinded"` → no matches).
- The identity key is still the raw file `KEY_FILE = ".iroh-key"` (`pkgs/id/src/lib.rs:314`).

Implementing this without a recorded decision would invent a wire format, a server-side key-custody posture and an unwrap-throttling protocol in one PR.

## What this design must settle
1. **Blob format** — AEAD + KDF versioned envelope (reuse #2279's header shape rather than defining a second one), keyed by identity-public-key hash; server stores ciphertext bytes only.
2. **Server-side custody posture** — restate that the server never holds plaintext or passphrases, and what it does hold (ciphertext, size, access timestamps). #2060's trust constraint still forbids custodial keys.
3. **Unwrap throttling** — whether an OPRF-style blinded unwrap is adopted, which curve/construction, and how throttle state is keyed so it reveals nothing. If OPRF is rejected, record the cheaper alternative (e.g. per-identity attempt budget over the existing fixed-window limiter shape from #2333) with its guessing-cost analysis.
4. **Storage surface** — which hosted storage the blob lives in, retention, and deletion on key revocation.
5. **Restore-forces-rotation** — the flag's representation, which is #2380's keyset substrate.

## Acceptance
- [ ] A decision is recorded on this issue for items 1–5, or each is explicitly deferred with rationale.
- [ ] The server-never-sees-plaintext claim has a concrete protocol sketch (who computes what) that a reviewer can falsify.
- [ ] Follow-up implementation issues are filed from the decision, or the decision is to decline the server-side backup entirely.

## Out of scope
- Local envelope export/import (#2279), seed-phrase export/restore (#2381), guardian/social recovery (#2382), issuer key rotation (#2804).

## Sources
`doc/2026-10-29T11-28-18Z_investigation_key_recovery_hosted/` §4, §7, §11 slice 2; #2060 (closed); #2279; #2380; `pkgs/id/src/lib.rs:314`.


## Acceptance criteria

- A design is recorded settling: the backup blob format (AEAD + KDF versioned envelope, reusing #2279's header shape), the blinded-unwrap (OPRF-style) protocol, server-side rate limiting / throttling, and the server key-custody posture.
- The design names what the server learns and cannot learn (passphrase, key, blob contents) for each protocol step.
- An implementation issue is filed and linked as a native relation in the same pass the design lands (protocol §11 — a design with no implementation link is not finished work).

body:
## Summary

The opencode-claimant's 12-session cap is consumed almost entirely by sessions that
are **not** the work it is trying to launch, so the claimant starves: 44 eligible
unbound opencode-lane candidates existed at the 2026-11-03 10:10 CT fire and the
gate closed with `cap_room: 0` for the third fire running (also 15:45Z and 16:03Z).

Measured at 2026-11-03T16:12-16:13Z, via `GET /api/session/active` + a per-id
`GET /api/session/<id>` (per-id reads because the list truncates, #4757):

| component | count | note |
|---|---|---|
| active root sessions | 14 | 0 children |
| scheduled lane runners from the 10:00 CT fire | 11 | titles `Queue lane (scheduled) - code/opencode 2026-11-03 10:00` |
| bound task worker sessions | 1 | task 8067, genuinely running (50 msgs, last message 0.4 min before the check) |
| **the claimant session itself** | 1 | `ses_e5e5dd34a9fffehVF6gEz57StG`, this fire |
| unbound orphan session, idle ~18h | 1 | see below |

Cap is 12, so the fire was over by 2 and launched nothing.

## Two concrete problems

1. **The claimant counts itself against its own cap.** Each fire is a root session,
   so a fire with plenty of capacity still spends one slot on the gatekeeper. At
   the margin that is the difference between launching and not.

2. **A live-looking zombie holds a slot indefinitely.** Session
   `ses_e5e61b938bfffeywl78cVRVoec`, title `Queue lane (scheduled) - opencode
   2026-11-02 16:00`, is in `/api/session/active` (`{"type": "running"}`) with
   **no** `outcome` and no `time.idle`, but its last message is
   `2026-11-02T22:18:51Z` (~17.9 h idle). No task row carries its id in
   `progress.session_id` (ledger query returns `[]`), i.e. it is not a bound
   task session, so supervision correctly will not touch it and no worker owns
   it. It simply occupies one of the 12 slots.

## Secondary

`poll.py` reported `live_root_sessions: 50` — exactly the `GET /api/session`
page size — so the fleet total is still truncated (#4757). `cap_room` itself is
computed from `/api/session/active`, which is unaffected, so the gate is not
wrong here; only the reported total is.

## Asks

- Decide whether the claimant's own session (and scheduled lane-runner
  sessions) should count against the 12-session cap, or whether the cap should
  count *launchable work* instead. Same question applies to the opencode lane's
  admission control (#1187).
- Give the fleet watchdog a disposition rule for sessions the server reports
  `running` with no terminal marker and no activity for hours, that are bound to
  no task row: cancel/close them so the slot returns.
- Note for the parallel-run gate (#3026 slice 2): while 11 lane runners can be
  in flight at once, the claimant's cap room is structurally near zero, so
  slice 2 cannot be evaluated on launch counts alone.

## Evidence

Fire log lines: `~/.local/state/opencode-claimant/fires.jsonl` at
`2026-11-03T16:12:52Z` (fire) and its `16:13Z` supplement (cap composition +
stall report). Read-only fire; nothing was claimed, bound, launched or mutated.

## Acceptance criteria
- The claimant's session-cap accounting no longer counts the claimant's own fire session against the cap it enforces (or the cap is explicitly defined to include it and the starvation math is re-derived and documented).
- Sessions present in `/api/session/active` with no queue binding, no outcome, and no activity beyond a stated staleness threshold are reaped or explicitly owned, so a zombie cannot hold a cap slot indefinitely.
- A claimant fire with eligible unbound candidates and real capacity launches work; the `cap_room: 0` starvation measurement from 2026-11-03T16:12Z no longer reproduces under the same session mix.

body:
Two defects found by an OpenChamber scheduled lane while working queue task 7636 (repo-health-code-pilot).

## 1. `repo-queue.py complete` is a silent no-op when the claim has lapsed

Sequence: claim 7636 at 14:01Z (1200 s lease), one heartbeat at 14:05Z (extended to 14:20:43Z), merge finished 14:20:13Z, `complete` invoked ~14:26Z.

- `repo-queue.py complete 7636 --worker repo-worker-code --result '…'` printed a full row of `null` fields and **exited 0**.
- The DB showed the task back in `queued` with `result = null`; the lease had lapsed at 14:20:43Z and the claim was released.
- `heartbeat` on the same task correctly errors (`heartbeat_task: task 7636 is not claimed by repo-worker-code`), so the RPC knows how to refuse. `complete_task` returns SQL NULL instead, and `_require_row` passes that NULL through as an all-null row.

Effect: a worker that runs long (or loses its lease) can believe it closed a task and walk away from a still-queued one — the exact anti-evaporation failure the runbook warns about, but produced by the tool rather than the worker. Suggested fix: make `complete_task` raise when the row is not claimed by the caller, and have `_require_row` treat an all-null row as "no matching row" (exit 5) rather than success.

## 2. The merge-gate check never runs on pull requests

`.github/ci-policy.md` says the merge requirement is the basic PR tier and names `basic: proxy port fallbacks` as the required context, but `.github/workflows/nix-ci.yml` only triggers on `push` to `main`, `schedule` and `workflow_dispatch` — there is no `pull_request` (or `merge_group`) trigger. The job comment still claims it "runs on every PR".

Confirmed on PR #3944: `gh pr checks` showed only a neutral CodeRabbit entry; no `basic:` check ever reported, and the PR merged with zero CI checks (as did #4935 the same day). So the policy's stated gate is not actually enforced, and a PR-tier regression can only surface in the main-tier run or `main-broken.yml`.

body:
Found 2026-11-03 during laptop verification of #4815 (pre-existing; unrelated to that PR): `nix develop` (the default devShell) fails on x86_64-linux — cargo-llvm-cov-0.9.0.drv fails to build because its own test suite fails under cargo 1.99.0 (14 failing tests), which cascades into nix-shell-env.drv and aborts the shell entry before any tool runs.

Impact: the default shell is the front door for new contributors and for verification workflows; every default-shell consumer is blocked until this is fixed or the dependency leaves the shell.

Workarounds that work today: the lean shells substitute fine — `nix develop .#fleet` (go 1.27.3, treefmt) and .#mcpx-lint were both used successfully for the #4815 verification.

Fix directions (not prescribed): bump or pin cargo-llvm-cov to a release whose tests pass under cargo 1.99.0, drop it from the default shell into a dedicated coverage shell, or mark its check phase off if the package is only needed as a binary.

body:
Design doc: `files/designs/code-acp-adapter-prompt-lifecycle.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Audit at origin/main `cf13a269456d3c4fb733af312d89dc741140836c` — every defect below re-verified present at the cited sites this pass (2026-11-02, adapter and dispatch client read at that commit).

## Summary

`bin/opencode-acp-adapter.mjs` (558 lines) lets OpenClaw's acpx runtime drive the fleet's one standing `opencode serve` over ACP (#1243, landed by PR #3997). PR #3997 merged as-is with four Codex review findings unresolved; they were filed on 2026-11-02 as #4614, #4616, #4617 and #4618 (`source/pr-comment-review`). They are one unstated contract in two halves:

- **The adapter does not speak its server's contract.** The file header (:11–20) documents a v1 mapping and the code follows it — `session/new` posts `/session?directory=…` and expects a bare `id` (:449); prompts go to `/session/:id/prompt_async` (:470); the permission reply (:340) and abort (:487) are likewise v1-shaped. The target is the pinned OpenCode 2.x standing server, and the fleet's own client for that same server, `pm-stack/dispatch/src/opencode.ts`, uses the v2 contract throughout: `POST /api/session` with `location.directory` in the body and a `{data: …}` envelope (:58), `POST /api/session/:id/prompt` (:66), `DELETE /api/session/:id` (:70), `GET /api/session` (:74). Per #4614 the v1 flow does not create working sessions against the intended server at all.
- **Prompt state has no lifecycle.** Three module-level containers (:187–191) — `pendingPrompts`, `cancelledSessions` (a bare session-id set), `partTextSent` (keyed by part id alone, no session) — are written at prompt start and cleared, if at all, on exactly one exit path each. `finishPrompt` (:349–352) clears **all** sessions' text offsets (#4616: a still-running session's text is re-emitted from character zero); `session/cancel` (:484) records a marker unconditionally and only the pending-gated `session.idle` branch (:371–372) ever deletes it, while the `session.error` path finishes without clearing it (#4618: the next prompt is mislabelled `cancelled`); and the event-stream loop (:247–256) reconnects after a drop with no reconciliation of `pendingPrompts` (#4617: a prompt whose idle event was lost hangs forever and blocks its session permanently). Even the submission-failure path (:475) deletes only the pending entry.

Both halves are the same omission: the adapter was written against an assumed server and an assumed happy path, and neither assumption was ever stated as a contract the code is checked against.

## The contract

> **The pinned server's v2 API is the only contract, and a prompt's state lives and dies with the prompt: scoped to its session, recorded only while the prompt is in flight, cleared on every terminal path through the one terminal function — and lost event continuity is itself a terminal path, settled by reconciling against the server's state or failing explicitly, never by waiting.**

Recorded decisions (full reasoning, alternatives and risks in the design doc):

1. **Every route is v2-shaped or explicitly dispositioned.** Session create and prompt submission per #4614's acceptance, tested against a v2-shaped stub (not the v1 stub). Phase 1 also dispositions the routes #4614 does not name — abort, permission reply, event stream — against the pinned server, and pins the v2 prompt submission semantics (blocking vs fire-and-event) that Phase 3 depends on.
2. **Offsets are scoped to (session, part)** and a prompt's cleanup removes exactly its own session's entries (#4616's acceptance, stated as the general rule).
3. **Cancellation is recorded only for an in-flight prompt** and cleared on **every** terminal path — idle, error, submission failure, reconciliation failure — because all of them exit through the one terminal function, which clears pending entry, cancellation marker and offsets for that session together (#4618's acceptance, stated as the general rule).
4. **Reconnect reconciles, then fails only the unprovable.** On event-stream reconnect, each pending prompt is reconciled against the server's v2 session read: proven finished/idle → finished normally; state not provable → the ACP request is failed explicitly. This pins #4617's either/or (reconcile *or* fail) as reconcile-first: stream drops are routine and the server's state is readable, so failing every pending prompt would discard completed work; waiting — the current behaviour — is the defect being fixed.

## Phased breakdown

Phases adopt the four origins as sub-issues (no parallels). Phase 4 is a new closing-audit issue, gated on Phases 1–3.

- **Phase 1 — speak the server's contract** (adopted: #4614). v2 session create + prompt submission per the origin's acceptance; required dispositions: abort / permission-reply / event-stream routes against the pinned server, and the v2 prompt submission semantics. (#4614 is currently `status/parked` with a holder — its agent note under this design records the phase structure; the design does not reassign it.)
- **Phase 2 — scoped state, one terminal cleanup** (adopted: #4616 + #4618). Decisions 2–3. Independent of Phase 1 in code — the containers are adapter-local. (#4618 is currently claimed/in-progress; its note records the shared terminal-function rule so its fix and #4616's land as one cleanup, not two.)
- **Phase 3 — reconnect reconciliation** (adopted: #4617). Decision 4, using the v2 session read Phase 1 establishes and the terminal function Phase 2 completes. Gated on Phases 1–2 in substance; the gating is recorded on the origin (its parked/assigned state is its holder's, not changed by this design).
- **Phase 4 — closing state-and-route inventory + contract statement** (new issue, gated on Phases 1–3): every module-level state container and every serve route in the adapter dispositioned against this contract; the header mapping comment rewritten to the v2 contract + lifecycle rules. Required dispositions: (a) the `sessions` map's lifetime (no close path exists); (b) `pendingClientRequests` cleanup when a client never answers; (c) the permission flow's v2 shape if Phase 1 did not land it; (d) `partTextSent` keying after Phase 2.

## Open questions (in the design doc, not filed)

Whether a prompt needs a wall-clock timeout independent of stream continuity (no filed instance; decision 4 covers the observed hang); whether `sessions` should be deleted server-side when an ACP client disconnects (needs a filed instance or Phase 4 evidence); whether a second server-contract version is ever supported (the header comment is the contract's home; revisit when the pin moves).

## Related

- Origins adopted as phases: #4614 (Phase 1), #4616 + #4618 (Phase 2), #4617 (Phase 3).
- Landed sibling from the same PR: #4615 (standing-server credential loading, closed — its code is in the file at audit HEAD). The four origins are the complete filed defect inventory for this adapter (verified by title/body search this pass).
- Feature origin: #1243 (share one opencode serve via an ACP adapter, closed).
- The fleet's v2 reference client: `pm-stack/dispatch/src/opencode.ts` (see also design #2668 for dispatch's own contract).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Phase 1: the adapter speaks the v2 contract (session create + prompt submission per issue #4614's acceptance), with abort / permission-reply / event-stream routes dispositioned against the pinned server and the v2 prompt-submission semantics pinned.
- [ ] Phase 2/3 contract points hold in code: prompt offsets scoped to (session, part); cancellation recorded only for in-flight prompts and cleared on every terminal path through the one terminal function.
- [ ] Each child finding (issue #4614, issue #4616, issue #4617, issue #4618) is closed by its phase or explicitly dispositioned on this issue.

| Rung | II (v5.0) | TTFT (s) | TTFT as read 2026-10-27 |

Phase 4 (closing audit) of design #4302 — a projection writes only what the event proves: one application contract for the PM projector. Design doc: `files/designs/code-projector-application-contract.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace.

**Gated on Phases 1–3 of #4302 landing** (Phase 1 = #2456 + #2982, Phase 2 = #2694 + #2455 + #3087, Phase 3 = #4158 + #4210). Do not start the audit before they land.

## Scope

1. **Contract statement landed**: the contract from #4302 (real delivery identity + success-only dedupe; kind-namespaced object identity; guard key = the source object's last-update time, never creation or delivery time; absence writes nothing; deletion reachable for every projected kind and absorbing for comments) is written into the `schema.sql` header / projector README, where the "applied at most once" comment already lives, replacing that comment's now-stale wording.
2. **Writer inventory**: every writer of `pmp_items`, `pmp_comments`, `pmp_deliveries` and `pmp_push_events` — every `applyEvent` branch in `projector.ts`, every reconcile stream in `reconcile.ts`, `recordPush`, and the links writers — is dispositioned against the contract's six decisions (conforms / fixed in this audit if a single-writer slip / filed as a named follow-up). The inventory is recorded on #4302 or in the projector README beside the contract statement.
3. **Required dispositions** (each recorded on #4302 with its reason):
   - **Transferred issues**: the source-repo row after an `issues`/`transferred` event — delete, keep, or re-key — decided with the transfer payload's actual shape in hand (#4210's explicit out-of-scope, dispositioned here).
   - **The item row's own `new Date()` created-at fallback** (`projector.ts:43`): unreachable for real issue/PR payloads, which always carry `created_at` — remove for symmetry with Phase 2's comment rule, or record as deliberately-local with the reason.
   - **`recordPush` dedupe under Phase 1**: verify pushes inherit the real-identity + success-only contract (they key on the same delivery id) — verify, don't assume.
   - **Secondary comment fields under the absence rule**: `review_state`, `path`/`line`, `diff_hunk` — presence semantics checked per field, not assumed from Phase 3's item rule.
4. **Closing evidence on #4302**: all seven origins (#2456, #2982, #2694, #2455, #3087, #4158, #4210) closed or verified already-fixed, the contract statement landed, and the inventory complete.

## Acceptance criteria

- The contract statement is present in the schema/README location named above and matches #4302's six decisions.
- The writer inventory covers every writer of the four tables, each with a disposition and a reason or a follow-up link.
- All four required dispositions are recorded on #4302.
- No behaviour change beyond a single-writer slip fix; anything larger is filed as a named follow-up, not fixed inside the audit.

Design note: `doc/2026-11-01T21-05-00Z_design_aggregator_dependency_graph_1257.md` (proposed by the linked design PR).

## Goal
Rank unresolved blockers per selected epic by the number of distinct open epic items in their transitive `blockedBy` ancestry. This is downstream reach, not a promise that every counted item becomes immediately unblocked. Preserve the existing longest chain as secondary structural context.

## Acceptance criteria
- The primary list is sorted by descending distinct open downstream item count, descending known effort weight as the tie-break, then canonical ref for deterministic order; unsized items are separately reported.

- Shared dependency paths count each downstream item once; out-of-pool blockers stay unresolved and do not disappear from the explanation.
- The longest dependency chain remains visible as a separate diagnostic and is not conflated with the new primary ranking.
- Add focused tests for a shared blocker, a multi-blocked descendant, ties, closed nodes, unknown refs, and deterministic ordering.

body:
## pm-stack backups silently produced empty day-dirs for 3 days

`~/backups/pm-stack/` has day directories for 2026-10-30, 2026-10-31, and 2026-11-01 that were created on schedule but contain **no archive** — the last good tarball before today was 2026-10-29. Nothing alarmed; the gap was found by hand during the 2026-11-01 Kaneo/PostgreSQL incident (#3849), where the Oct 29 `kaneo.dump` turned out to be the only logical fallback.

Cause: `~/tools/pm-stack-backup.sh` creates the day dir up front, then `set -e` kills it mid-run, leaving the empty dir as camouflage. The mid-run deaths were stale container names from the compose→oci migrations: `docker exec pm-stack-postgres-1` failed while the compose stack was down for the pm-apps activation (Oct 30), and after Grist/Pad became oci containers the script still targeted `grist-grist-1` / `pad-pad-1` (live names: `pm-grist` / `pm-pad`).

Already fixed on the laptop (2026-11-01): names updated in `~/tools/pm-stack-backup.sh` (original kept as `pm-stack-backup.sh.orig-2026-11-01`), and a rerun produced a verified archive for 2026-11-01 (manifest-checked by the script itself, sha256 d7a8881df26333269d4cb9b732b3daafbb5a6fdf8a7ee18a084d1baae7551833).

What remains worth doing:
- The script (or its scheduling service, code#1516) should treat "day dir exists but no verified archive" as a failure worth surfacing — an empty dir currently reads as a completed backup day in any casual listing.
- Container names are migration-fragile; resolving targets by label/project (or failing with the container list in the log) would have made this a one-day, self-explaining failure instead of a silent 3-day gap.


## Acceptance criteria
- A backup run that ends without a verified archive is surfaced as a failure (alarm, non-zero service result, or filed issue) — an empty day-dir no longer reads as a completed backup day.
- Backup targets are resolved robustly against container renames (by label/project, or the run fails loudly with the actual container list in the log), so a compose-to-oci migration cannot silently break targeting again.
- A drill or log excerpt demonstrates the failure path firing on a simulated missing-container run.

body:
## What

Implement the D1-040 design: a `documents`/`document` ClientFrame/ServerFrame pair in the world-session protocol, modelled on `records`, so web and CLI clients can read the public documents — today reachable only from the SSH shell, which reads the shared server blob store directly. Scope is server-wide parity (the design's Decision 1): the frames expose exactly the set SSH exposes today; per-world scoping waits on the deferred per-world document store and is out of scope here.

## Design

`doc/2026-11-01T16-05-00Z_design_documents_session_frames/2026-11-01T16-05-00Z_design_documents_session_frames.md` (lands with PR #3760; tracker #535 item D1-040). The design is decided — frame shapes, authorization, bounds, the serving-logic move, and test expectations are all pinned there. Read it first; this issue is the delivery vehicle, not a second design pass.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ClientFrame::Documents { capability, prefix, after }` and `ClientFrame::Document { capability, name }` in `pkgs/id/src/world_session/types.rs`; `ServerFrame::Documents { names, next_after }` and `ServerFrame::Document { name, size, text }` per the design (no `sequence` on the list frame — the design records why)
- [ ] Serving logic (`list_public_documents` / `read_public_document` and their name/bounds rules) lives in the session layer next to `records_session`; authorization is the records rule (join capability → `participant_id`, else `join denied`); the design's one structural unknown — how the session layer reaches the blob store the SSH shell holds today — is resolved and noted on this issue
- [ ] SSH shell is frame-backed: `command_frame` gains `documents` / `documents_continue` / `document` arms mirroring `records`; rendered SSH output (`public named files:` listing, `[listing truncated]`, `--- {name} ({size} bytes; read-only) ---` header, `/help`) is byte-identical to before
- [ ] Contract updated on both sides: frames named in `pkgs/id/src/shell_contract` and the shared frame contract; web contract tests extended; web client gains the minimal list + read documents panel the design specifies
- [ ] Tests per the design's test expectations: session tests mirroring `records_session` (paging, prefix, `after` exclusivity, oversized/non-viewable/missing refusals, `join denied`), contract accept/refuse cases, existing SSH document shell tests passing against the frame-backed path
- [ ] Existing mcpx/id CI green in GitHub Actions on the PR (note: pkgs/mcpx conformance has a pre-existing compile break on main — features_test.go:308 — do not chase it here)

## Out of scope

- Document writes/publishing (unchanged), a `documents_ticket` replication frame (design non-goal), any change to which documents are public (#548 owns the store).

## Links

- Tracker: #535 (D1-040). Design PR: #3760. Prerequisite: #548 (closed).
- Model: `records` frames in `pkgs/id/src/world_session/types.rs`, `records_session` in `pkgs/id/src/world_session/mod.rs`.
