milestone.description: mcpx platform program: one canonical mcpx in developing-today/code - dedup, scope-resolved roots, module consolidation, MCP server parity.

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#133 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #97

## Summary

Today every e2e test runs `mcpx` as a subprocess. This issue proposes an in-process entrypoint alongside it: move the dispatch in `cmd/mcpx/main.go` into `cli.Run(ctx, args, env, stdio) int`. Then run most integration tests in-process, which is faster, gives coverage, and lets you set breakpoints. Keep a binary suite as a superset that also covers what only a real process has: signals, exit codes, argv parsing, the detached daemon, and the nix wrapper. Let the binary suite point at a **prebuilt** binary (the nix `result`, a container image), not only at a fresh `go build`. Separately, replace the fixed-behaviour `fakemcp` with a scriptable mock so each test states the server behaviour it needs.

## Original notes

> - testing
>   - a general goal is to ensure all features have one or more integration tests
>     - the mcp servers can be specialized mocks but the app entrypoint or binary is used and config is passed in or config path set to appropriate test
>     - for both binary && app entrypoint (consider binary a superset)
>       - all tests should pass for nix flake & container

## Current state (main d0b7e01)

**Binary.**
- `testsupport.MCPXBinary` always runs `go build -o <tmp>/mcpx ./cmd/mcpx` once per test binary (`internal/testsupport/build.go:54-73`).
- **No override exists** to test a prebuilt binary. So in CI "the binary" means a fresh plain `go build`, never the artifact users install. The installed artifact is `result/bin/mcpx`: a `makeBinaryWrapper` C wrapper that puts nix-pinned git/deno/bun/node on PATH (`package.nix` `postInstall`) in front of `.mcpx-wrapped`. There is now a second shipped artifact, the binary inside #182's `pkgs/mcpx/Containerfile` image.
- So there are three drivers, not two (from #160): in-process ⊂ built binary ⊂ installed output. Only the installed output exercises the wrapper's PATH pinning, the ldflags version (`internal/testsupport/build.go:63` builds without `-ldflags`, so `mcpx --version` differs between the test binary and the package -- #178), the generated man page and the completions. That rung should be a small suite -- a dozen assertions, not the whole e2e run -- and it is where #134's nix-build leg and #178's assertions run.
- The temp dirs from `os.MkdirTemp` (`build.go:28,56`) are never removed.

**Entrypoint.** `main()` (`cmd/mcpx/main.go:52-204`) does all of the following, and none of it is reachable from a test:
- reads `os.Args`;
- handles global flags inline (`--json`, `--profile`, `--config`, `--tui`, ...);
- builds `&cli.App{Version, Paths: daemon.ResolvePaths()}`;
- sets the package global `cli.SetPlumbingSource(app)` (`internal/cli/scripts.go:95`);
- dispatches through a local `handlers` map (`main.go:119-162`);
- exits through `os.Exit` at five sites (`main.go:74,103,179,188,202`).

Process-global state that an in-process runner would share between tests:
- `daemon.ResolvePaths` reads `os.Getenv` (`internal/daemon/paths.go:34-52`);
- `settings.Environ()` is `os.Environ()` (`internal/settings/bind.go:218`);
- `internal/cli` non-test files reference `os.Stdout/Stderr/Stdin/Exit/Getenv` 86 times.

**Autostart re-executes itself.** `EnsureDaemon` spawns `autostart.bin` or, if that is unset, `os.Executable()` (`internal/cli/client.go:281-287`). In-process, `os.Executable()` is the **test binary**, which would be started as a "daemon". An in-process runner must set `autostart.bin` to the built mcpx, or use `daemon.inline=true` (`internal/settings/registry.go:379`).

**Mocks.**
- `fakemcp` (`internal/testsupport/fakemcp/main.go`, 321 lines) answers from compiled-in behaviour, with two knobs: `FAKEMCP_FAIL_START` and `FAKEMCP_START_DELAY` (`main.go:35,39`).
- `askmcp` (272 lines) exists separately for elicitation (`build_proto.go:19-39`).
- A new behaviour means editing a shared binary that every test uses.

**Config.** Each test writes `.mcpx.json` into its temp dir, with `FAKE` replaced by the fakemcp path, and sets `MCPX_CONFIG` (`internal/e2e/e2e_test.go:41-60`). That already matches "config path set to appropriate test". "Config passed in" (`--config`, `main.go:88-94`) is a separate path that nothing tests specifically.

**Coverage.** e2e contributes nothing to coverage, because the binary is built without `-cover`. Since Go 1.20, `go build -cover` produces a binary that writes coverage data to `$GOCOVERDIR` on exit. `go tool covdata percent|textfmt -i=<dir>` reads it, and `go test -cover ./... -args -test.gocoverdir=<dir>` writes unit coverage into the same directory so the two merge. Source: https://go.dev/doc/build-cover. A process killed by a signal writes nothing, so a detached daemon killed by `stop` must exit through its normal path for its coverage to count.

## Approaches -- entrypoint

### A -- in-process only (least recommended)
Replace the subprocess with `cli.Run` everywhere. This is the fastest option, and it loses exactly what an integration test is for:
- real exit codes and signal handling (`signal.NotifyContext`, `main.go:53`);
- argv parsing as the shell delivers it;
- the detached daemon (`Setsid`, `client.go:312`);
- the process-group kill of runtimes (`runner.go:413-432`);
- the nix wrapper's PATH;
- environment inheritance: #138 is a bug that exists *only* in the subprocess path.

Shared process globals would also make in-process tests interfere with each other. Not recommended.

### B -- binary only, instrumented
Keep today's suite and add two things: a `-cover` build of the binary under `$GOCOVERDIR`, and an override (`MCPX_TEST_BINARY=/path/to/mcpx`, name to be decided) so the same suite runs against `result/bin/mcpx` or inside a container. It needs almost no code change, gives coverage, and makes "tests pass for nix flake & container" mean the shipped artifact (#134). It does not help speed (each call still pays a fork+exec plus daemon start) or debugging (a breakpoint in a subprocess needs `dlv attach`).

### C -- both, with the binary suite as a superset (recommended)
1. **Refactor**: `func Run(ctx context.Context, args []string, env Env, stdio Stdio) int` in `internal/cli`, where `Env` is an environ slice or lookup function and `Stdio` is `{In io.Reader; Out, Err io.Writer}`. `main()` shrinks to signal setup plus `os.Exit(cli.Run(ctx, os.Args[1:], os.Environ(), cli.Stdio{...}))`. Global-flag parsing, `looksRunnable` and the `handlers` table move with it. The table becomes an exported `cli.Commands()`, which #132's guard needs.
2. **Thread the environment in stages.** Stage 1: `Run` takes `env` but internals still read `os.Getenv`, so in-process tests use `t.Setenv` and cannot use `t.Parallel`. Stage 2: `ResolvePaths`, `settings.Environ` and `plumbingApp` take their inputs from `Run`, so in-process tests can run in parallel. That is the real speed gain, and it pairs with the CI time budget in #95.
3. **Harness**: `newEnv` gets a `runner` interface with `binary` and `inproc` implementations. A test says what it needs, for example `e := newEnv(t, cfg, needsProcess)`. The **binary suite runs every test** (the superset). The in-process suite runs the ones that do not need a process. The daemon stays a real process in both, via `autostart.bin` set to the built binary. An in-process daemon in a goroutine would leak goroutines and listeners between tests, which is the in-process version of #52 (fixed for the subprocess path in #182).
4. **Binary override and `-cover`** from B, so the binary suite can target the nix result or a container image and produce coverage.

Recommended because it matches the notes (binary a superset) and makes the fast path the default for day-to-day agent runs (#99). It also avoids building a second harness. Its risk is the size of the refactor. Stage 1 is small; stage 2 touches every `os.Getenv` in `internal/cli` and `internal/daemon`.

The user's framing is right. One refinement: "app entrypoint" should mean `cli.Run`, **not** `cli.App` methods called directly. Calling `app.CmdExec` directly skips global-flag parsing and `SettingsErr` (`main.go:183-189`), so it would test a code path users never take.

## Approaches -- mock MCP servers

### A -- ad-hoc mocks per test (least recommended)
Each test that needs an unusual server writes its own Go program or `httptest` server. It is flexible, but it multiplies binaries to build (each is a `go build`, about 1 s) and duplicates the protocol plumbing each time.

### B -- more knobs on fakemcp
Keep adding `FAKEMCP_*` environment variables. This is the path today. It stays cheap until the knobs interact, and then the fake becomes a second product with its own bugs.

### C -- one scriptable mock (recommended)
`fakemcp` reads an optional behaviour file (`--script <path>` or `FAKEMCP_SCRIPT`), which declares:
- tools and their schemas and results;
- delays and failures, per call number;
- server-initiated requests (elicitation, sampling, `list_changed` notifications);
- the protocol revision to claim.

With no file it behaves exactly as it does today, so the existing e2e tests (199 at d0b7e01, 209 at 05c78b2) are unchanged. `askmcp` folds into it later, or stays if its opposite-behaviour rationale (`build_proto.go:19-22`) still holds. The script sits next to the test that uses it. The same file format can drive a **remote** mock (#134): the fake is baked into a container and gets its script over a mounted path. A behaviour that randomises (for example "fail 1 call in N") takes the run seed (#93).

Config: keep `MCPX_CONFIG` as the default and add one test each for `--config <path>` and for `.mcpx.json` found by the directory walk (`internal/config/config.go:549-565`), so all three ways config reaches the binary are covered once. When `MCPX_CONFIG` is unset, the walk also reads user-level files, so the walk test needs `HOME`/`XDG_CONFIG_HOME` isolated (#138).

## Open questions

- Which runner is the default for a new test: in-process, with the binary run in CI only? Policy for agents belongs to #99.
- What should the override be named (`MCPX_TEST_BINARY`, or a `-mcpx.binary` test flag)? A test flag does not leak into child processes, which is an argument for it.
- `--tui` and bare `mcpx` need a TTY. They are binary-only, or run under a pty via `github.com/creack/pty` (a new test-only dependency).
- Should the in-process suite count toward coverage at all, given that `-cover` on the binary already covers the same code?
- Does a `-cover` binary run slowly enough to trip the daemon-start timeouts that `internal/testsupport/build.go` warns about? Measure before making it the CI default (from #160).
- Where do the `GOCOVERDIR` artifacts go in CI, and is there a coverage floor? That belongs to #95 and #99.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** L (stage 1 plus override plus `-cover`: M; stage 2 env threading: L; scriptable fake: M) · **Impact** high
**Depends on / related**: #132 (exported command table), #134 (prebuilt-binary runs per environment), #138 (env isolation is a subprocess-path property), #79 (faster CLI/exec; the same `main.go` code), #178 (the ldflags version the installed-output rung checks), #52 (closed, fixed in #182), #93 (seeded mock behaviour), #95 (coverage artifacts, parallel shards), #99 (which runner agents use).

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

## Acceptance criteria

- An in-process entrypoint exists beside the binary suite: the dispatch in `cmd/mcpx/main.go` is reachable as `cli.Run(ctx, args, env, stdio) int` (or the equivalent shape the implementer pins on this issue), and most integration tests can run in-process against it.
- The binary suite is retained as the superset (signals, exit codes, argv parsing, detached daemon, nix wrapper) and can target a **prebuilt** binary (nix `result`, container image), not only a fresh `go build`.
- The fixed-behaviour `fakemcp` is replaced or supplemented by a scriptable mock MCP server whose behaviour each test states.
- The work described in the Summary/Scope above is delivered via a branch + PR (no direct push to main); verification runs in GitHub Actions CI, not on the sandbox.
- Evidence (CI links, timings, or probe output as applicable) is recorded on this issue before it is closed.

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#295 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #83

## Summary

Writing an adapter declaration by hand is the tax on every binary somebody wants
to reach. #83 puts "generated declarations for bare binaries" last in its ship
order (step 5) and #114 sketches the deterministic parse inside a much larger
view/generator design. Both are right and both are large. This issue is the
narrow, shippable front half that neither owns: **`mcpx adapter import`**, a
command that writes a declaration *file the user keeps*, from sources that are
already machine-regular, with no model anywhere in the loop.

It also settles the thing people actually ask for first — "can I just declare
`git` and pass subcommands through?" — as `--bare`: supported, opt-in, and loud
about what it costs.

## Original notes

> is there an issue for automating binary to mcpx (outside the ai version,
> using idk, --help or something) can i just say `git` is an mcp with a command
> that accepts the subcommand and flags and args? not ideal but fast? ideally
> with some easy command `adapter import --bare` or something. go can exec a
> program so that it cant shell escape right?

## Current state

**Declarations are hand-written, and that is the whole input path.**
`loadAdapters` (`internal/cli/adapter.go:22`) reads `paths.adapters`
(`internal/settings/registry.go:298`), unmarshals `AdapterFile` or a bare array,
validates and de-duplicates by name. There is no writer — nothing in the binary
ever produces a `Spec`.

**`mcpx adapter` has four subcommands and none of them generate.** `CmdAdapter`
(`internal/cli/adapter.go:66`) dispatches `list`, `check`, `call` and `tools`.
The doc comment explains the subcommand-over-flag choice: "the three things
somebody wants -- what is declared, does it work, run one -- are different
questions". Generation is a fourth different question.

**The execution model is already argv-only.** `Spec.Call`
(`internal/adapter/adapter.go:206`) builds an argv and runs
`exec.CommandContext(cctx, s.Command, full...)` at
`internal/adapter/adapter.go:237`. No shell is interposed at any point, so there
is no word-splitting, no globbing, no `;`, no `$()`, no `|`. This matters for
`--bare` below and is the reason it is defensible at all.

**Both parent designs already want this and both defer it.** #114 contains the
most concrete plan on record: run `--help`, `help`, `-h`, `--help=full`, parse
usage lines, indented flag blocks and subcommand tables, noting that
"Cobra/clap/argparse produce highly regular help text" and that a model's job
reduces to descriptions and ambiguous types. #83 asks the sceptical question
back: "is `--help` parsing worth it at all, given how irregular help output
is?", and separately asks whether a generated declaration should record the
binary's version. This issue exists to answer both with a shipped command.

**The degenerate case is on record as acceptable-but-unloved.** #83 Approach A
rejects a generic shell escape, and its Approach B calls the argv passthrough
"Approach A wearing a hat", to be "opt-in and loud". That is a specification,
not a rejection, and nothing implements it.

## Approaches

### Approach A — least recommended: infer the declaration at runtime

Parse `--help` on daemon start and synthesise tools on the fly, no file.

Zero friction and badly wrong, for the reason #83 already recorded: a tool
surface that changes when somebody upgrades a CLI. An agent's context silently
shifting because Homebrew bumped `jq` is a bug that costs a day to find and
cannot be reproduced from the repository. It also makes `mcpx catalog` budgets
unpredictable and makes every generated client non-reproducible. Rejected.

### Approach B — middle: `--help` parsing only

Implement exactly #114's plan and stop. Useful, and it is most of the value, but
it leads with the *least* regular source available and leaves the "I just want
`git` now" request unanswered, which is the request that actually recurs.

### Approach C — recommended: a source ladder, best-evidence-first, emitting a file with provenance

```
mcpx adapter import <binary> [--out FILE] [--source auto|completion|man|help|bare]
mcpx adapter import --completion <file> [--shell bash|zsh|fish] [--name NAME]
```

Sources are tried in descending order of regularity and the winner is recorded.

1. **Shell completion scripts** — `--source completion`. Cobra, clap and
   argparse all emit bash/zsh/fish completions, and these are *generated data
   structures*, not prose: fish's `complete -c tool -l flag -d 'desc'` lines are
   almost a declaration already, and zsh `_arguments` specs carry flag, argument
   type and description in a fixed grammar. This is the highest-fidelity source
   that exists for the widest range of programs and #114 does not mention it.
   Lead with it.

   **Two ways in, and both are required.**

   - **Extract from the binary.** `import <binary>` probes for the program's own
     completion output — `tool completion {bash,zsh,fish}`, Cobra's hidden
     `__complete`, clap's `--generate-completion`. Convenient, and it only works
     when the program ships a generator and names it conventionally.
   - **Accept one as input.** `import --completion <file>` takes a completion
     script directly. This matters more than it looks:
     - Distributions **already ship them**, for programs that have no generator
       at all — `/usr/share/bash-completion/completions/*`,
       `/usr/share/zsh/site-functions/_*`, `$(brew --prefix)/share/...`, and
       Nix's `$out/share/bash-completion`. These are often hand-written by
       packagers for old tools whose `--help` is worst, which is exactly the
       case extraction cannot reach.
     - It makes the parser **testable without the binary present**. A corpus of
       completion files is a fixture; probing a binary is an integration test
       that needs the program installed. This alone justifies the input path.
     - It lets a user **fix the source** rather than the output — hand-edit a
       completion script and re-import, instead of hand-editing generated JSON
       and losing it on the next import.
     - It covers the program mcpx cannot run: a different architecture, a
       container image, a binary you have the completion for but not the tool.

   So the extraction path is sugar over the input path — probe the binary, then
   feed whatever came back to the same parser. Build the file parser first; it
   is the part with the logic, and the testable one.
2. **A published machine interface** — `--source spec`. If the program ships an
   OpenAPI or JSON Schema document, this is not an adapter problem at all: hand
   it to `paths.apis`, which already exists. `import` should *detect this and
   say so* rather than producing a worse declaration.
3. **man pages** — `--source man`. `SYNOPSIS` and `OPTIONS` are a fixed troff
   structure, and `mandoc -T markdown` gives a stable intermediate. Less
   complete than completions, more regular than help text.
4. **`--help` text** — `--source help`. #114's plan, as the fallback it should
   be rather than the lead.
5. **`--bare`** — the escape hatch, below.

**Emit a file, never a live inference**, which is #83's non-negotiable. The
emitted file carries provenance as a comment header *and* machine fields: the
source used, the binary's resolved path, its `--version` output, and the date.
That answers #83's open question directly — on a version mismatch `mcpx adapter
check` says "this declaration was written against jq 1.7, found 1.8" rather than
drifting silently. Making `check` do that comparison is part of this issue.

**`--bare`, specifically.** One tool per binary taking `args: string[]`, plus
optional `stdin`:

```jsonc
{ "name": "git", "command": "git", "bare": true,
  "description": "git, unrestricted — argv passed through" }
```

To answer the question in the notes directly: **yes, Go's `exec` makes this
meaningfully safer than a shell escape.** `exec.CommandContext` takes an argv
slice straight to `execve`; there is no `/bin/sh -c` anywhere in
`internal/adapter`, so a model cannot inject `;`, `$()`, backticks, globs or
redirections. It is an *argv* hole, not a *shell* hole, and that is a genuinely
smaller one.

It is still a real hole, and the declaration should say so:

- It gives the model `git` with every subcommand, including `push --force`,
  `config` and anything with `--exec`/`-c` that reaches a shell *itself*. The
  sandbox is only as good as the binary's own argv surface, and `git -c
  core.pager='sh -c ...'` is a shell escape that mcpx cannot see. **`--bare` on
  a program with an argv-level exec escape is equivalent to Approach A**, and
  the docs must say which common binaries those are.
- No schema beyond "array of strings", so there is nothing for an agent to
  reason about and nothing for `mcpx doctor` to check past existence.

So: opt-in per declaration, never a default, never what bare `import` produces
without the flag; rendered in `mcpx adapter list` with a visible `bare` marker
next to `ok`/`missing`; and `description` **required** when `bare` is set, so
the author has to state the intent. A settings gate (`adapters.allowBare`,
default off) is worth considering so an organisation can forbid it centrally.

Ship order, each step useful alone: (1) `--bare` plus the `list` marker and the
required description — this is a day and answers the recurring request; (2)
`--source help`, since #114 already designed it; (3) provenance fields and the
`check` version comparison; (4) completions, parser first and extraction after;
(5) man.

## Open questions

- Does `import` write to `paths.adapters`' first entry, or to stdout by default?
  Writing a file by default is friendly and surprising; stdout with `--out` is
  unixy and makes the common case two commands. Leaning stdout-by-default with a
  printed hint.
- Extraction needs the *program's* completion output, which means guessing a
  subcommand (`completion`, `__complete`, `--generate-completion`). Acceptable
  to probe, or does it need a declared hint?
- Should `import` also *search* the system completion directories for a matching
  file before probing the binary — `/usr/share/bash-completion/completions/<n>`,
  zsh `site-functions`, the Homebrew and Nix prefixes? That turns the common
  case into `mcpx adapter import jq` finding a packager-written completion with
  no probe at all, and it is the strongest version of this feature.
- Which shell's completion is the best parse target when several are available?
  fish is the most declarative and the easiest; zsh carries the most type
  information; bash is the most widely shipped and the least structured.
  Probably parse fish or zsh where present, bash as a last resort.
- Should `import` run the binary at all? It must, for `--help`/`--version`. On an
  untrusted binary that is already an execution. Probably fine — you are about
  to expose it as a tool — but it deserves a sentence in the docs.
- Re-import of an edited declaration: merge, or refuse and emit beside it? Merge
  needs a notion of which fields are hand-edited. Refusing is honest and
  annoying.
- Does `--bare` belong in `Spec` as a field, or is it a distinct `kind` once #83's
  tool-source interface exists? Field now, revisit under #83.
- Does a bare tool get a `cwd` parameter? `git` without a working directory is
  nearly useless, and `Spec.Dir` is fixed at declaration time.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease:** S for `--bare` and the list marker; M for `--source help` and
provenance; M for the completion-file parser and S for extraction on top of it;
M–L for man. **Impact:** high — this is the
difference between "mcpx can wrap any CLI" as a property of the design and as a
property somebody actually gets without an afternoon of JSON.

**Depends on / related:** #83 (owns the tool-source design; this is its step 5
pulled forward, and it answers two of its open questions), #114 (owns generators
that emit declarations; its `--help` plan is this issue's step 2), #102 (an
adapted binary is not script-callable — an imported one inherits that defect
until #102 lands), #106 and #105 (a declaration `runtime` for scripts is the
adjacent resolution problem), #107 (a flake ref as a program — another source a
declaration could point at), #113 (`mcpx doctor`/operation surface, where the
version-drift check surfaces).

## Acceptance criteria

- `mcpx adapter import <binary>` writes a declaration file the user keeps, generated deterministically from completions, man pages, and/or `--help` output — no model in the loop.
- `mcpx adapter import --bare <binary>` produces a pass-through declaration and prints a loud warning about what pass-through costs (no per-subcommand validation).
- Generated declarations load through the existing `loadAdapters` validation/dedup path unchanged, and a generated declaration for a well-known binary (e.g. `git`) passes `mcpx adapter check`.
- Sources that are not machine-regular fail with a clear error naming what could not be parsed, rather than emitting a partial declaration silently.

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#120 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #90

## Summary

Every page of the docs site gets a machine-readable twin written for agents. On top of that, the site publishes `llms.txt` and `llms-full.txt`. The agent twin of the home page carries a **one-shot install prompt**: a procedure an agent can execute to install mcpx, verify it, and wire it into the harness it is running in. The same agent docs should also ship inside the binary, so an offline agent gets docs that match its version.

## Original notes

> - documentation
>   - make a book using whatever is the most common and simple modern choice
>     - specialized agent markdown all pages
>       - home page has install prompt built into the bot version

## Current state

- **`AGENTS.md`** (109 lines) is already agent markdown: the loop (`ls` / `search` / `types` / `run`|`exec`), scripts, profiles, the script contract, results, stateful servers, and a do-not list. It is only a file in the source tree:
  - `package.nix` installs the binary, the man page and completions, not `AGENTS.md`;
  - the only `go:embed` is `internal/defaults/defaults.json`.

  An agent that has `mcpx` but not the repository never sees it.
- **`mcpx man`** renders roff only. Its one flag is `--install DIR` (`internal/cli/root.go:257`). `mcpx help [command]` renders the same `Commands()` table (`internal/cli/manual.go`) as text. Neither emits markdown.
- **Plugin install today** is copying files (`plugin/opencode/README.md` "Install": `cp -R mcpx-session.ts mcpx ~/.config/opencode/plugin/`, skills separately). There is no package. Since #53 (closing #44) the plugin works without the binary: it reaches the daemon over the unix socket and spawns `mcpx --json status` only as the last-resort rung 4 of its discovery ladder (`plugin/opencode/README.md:99-138`). An install prompt has to fetch these files from somewhere (#158).
- `mcpx doctor [-v]` already "diagnoses the installation" and says what to do about each failed check (`manual.go:261`). It is the natural verification step, alongside `mcpx ls`.
- No site exists yet (#117, #118).

## The conventions (llms.txt v2)

Fetched from [llmstxt.org](https://llmstxt.org/) (v2, modified 2026-08-10):

- **`/llms.txt`** is markdown in a fixed order:
  1. an H1 with the project name (the only required part);
  2. a blockquote summary;
  3. optional non-heading prose;
  4. H2 sections that are "file lists" of `[name](url): notes`.

  An `## Optional` section by convention holds links an agent can skip. The file may sit at any path and covers the pages under it, e.g. `/docs/llms.txt`.
- **A clean markdown version of each page at the same URL**, with `.md` appended (`page.html.md`) or replacing the extension (`page.md`). URLs without a file name use `index.html.md` / `index.md`.
- **Discovery**: `<link rel="alternate" type="text/markdown" href="...md">` in each page, and `rel="describedby"` pointing at the `llms.txt` that covers the page. These can also be sent as an HTTP `Link:` header, but GitHub Pages cannot set headers, so we use HTML `<link>` elements only.
- **`llms-full.txt`** is not in the spec. It is a widely used convention: every page concatenated, used by Starlight, Docusaurus and Mintlify plugins.
- **No content negotiation.** GitHub Pages is static: it cannot answer `Accept: text/markdown` with the markdown twin at the same URL, and it cannot set `Link:` headers. Agents have to be pointed at `.md` URLs explicitly (in `llms.txt`, the `<link>` element and the home page). Say so on the site, so nobody expects negotiation to work.

Caveat: Zensical's own analysis ([ZAP 009](https://zensical.org/spark/proposals/zap-009-structured-docs-for-the-agentic-era/)) notes limited evidence that vendors' agents consume `llms.txt`. The per-page `.md` twin and the embedded docs are the parts that pay off regardless. `llms.txt` is cheap once the twin exists.

## What "specialized" means

A raw copy of the markdown source is not enough. An agent page should:

- **Drop decoration**: the video, copy buttons, the rotating prompt, `<details>` wrappers (expanded instead), badges, theme HTML.
- **Inline what the HTML page links or includes**: the generated reference (#144), i.e. settings, flags and env vars, command usage, as plain markdown tables or text, with `{{#include}}` and shortcodes already resolved. Zensical makes the same point: markdown must be an **output** of the pipeline, not a copy of the source.
- **Carry agent instructions**:
  - a short header (what this page is for, what to run next, the one command that answers the page's question: `mcpx help <cmd>`, `mcpx config --schema`, `mcpx types <ns>`);
  - version-matched: "these docs describe mcpx vX.Y. If `mcpx --version` differs, prefer `mcpx help`."
- **Be sourced from `AGENTS.md`** where it applies. It already is the agent-facing instruction file, so the site's agent pages for the loop, scripts and results should be derived from it or include it, not rewritten. There should be one agent-facing text, not two that drift.
- **Keep the version history** (#150) flattened but present. Agents need "since vX" more than humans do.

## The bot home page: the install prompt

`/index.md` and the top of `/llms.txt` carry a procedure an agent can execute end to end, written as numbered imperative steps with the exact commands and the checks between them:

1. **Detect** OS and architecture, the available package managers (nix, brew, go, ...) and the harness it is running in (opencode, claude code, codex, ...).
2. **Pick the channel** from the list in #158: nix profile / flake, Homebrew, `go install`, release binary, `curl <short> | sh`. Prefer one that installs **per-user** and needs no root. Say which channel was chosen and why.
3. **Install**, then **verify**: `mcpx --version`, `mcpx doctor`, and `mcpx ls`, which must list namespaces or say clearly that none are configured.
4. **Wire the harness plugin** for the detected harness: opencode via the plugin files (today a copy; a package once #158 exists), or others via #48's adapters or mcpx as an MCP server. Then verify from inside the harness.
5. **Optionally** move the user's existing MCP servers behind mcpx. After the agent **shows the diff and gets confirmation**, it comments out (never deletes) the user's existing MCP server entries in the harness config, so that the servers are reached through mcpx instead of loaded directly. This echoes the home page prompts in #155. Whether mcpx should import them first (`mcpx init` or registry add) is an open question.
6. **Report** what was installed, where, and how to undo it.

The human home page (#155) shows the same prompt behind a copy button. The bot page *is* the prompt, with nothing around it. Keep a single source for the text so the two cannot drift.

## Shipping the agent docs in the binary

An agent with `mcpx` on `PATH` but no network, or with a different version than the site, should get docs that match the binary it has.

Prefer a **format flag on an existing command** over a new command:

- `mcpx help --format markdown` (or `mcpx man --format markdown|roff`) prints the agent version of the command reference, generated from `Commands()` like the man page.
- `mcpx help agents` (or a topic argument) prints the embedded `AGENTS.md`.

Coordinate with #144: the markdown emitter that feeds the site's reference pages should be the same one behind this flag, so the site's agent pages and the binary's output are byte-identical for the same version. Embedding `AGENTS.md` costs a few KB, and `go:embed` is already in use.

## Approaches: how the twin is produced

### Approach A (least recommended): generator plugin only

Examples: `starlight-llms-txt`, `docusaurus-plugin-llms`, `mdbook-llms-txt-tools`, or Hugo's built-in `markdown` output format with `.RawContent`.

- It is fast to turn on.
- But these plugins emit the **source** (or lightly cleaned HTML-to-markdown): shortcodes and includes are raw or dropped, decoration leaks in, there is no agent header, and the output shape changes with the plugin version.
- It ties the twin to the generator chosen in #117, and cannot produce the in-binary docs.

### Approach B (middle): a build step emits `.md` + `llms.txt` from the same source

- A small program in this repo reads the book **after** preprocessing and writes, per page:
  - `<page>.md`, with decoration stripped, includes resolved and an agent header prepended;
  - `llms.txt` (ordered like the site navigation, one `##` per top-level section, with a one-line note per page taken from its lede);
  - `llms-full.txt`.
- The source can be an mdBook preprocessor over the JSON book, as in [fluree/db#1340](https://github.com/fluree/db/pull/1340), or a Hugo template.
- It adds `<link rel="alternate" type="text/markdown">` to every HTML page via the theme.
- The result is deterministic, generator-light and checkable in CI. It still only derives the twin mechanically. Pages that need a different shape for agents (the home page, the install prompt) have no place to live.

### Approach C (recommended): B, plus hand-written agent sources where they add value, plus the same emitters in the binary

- The twin is **derived by default**, as in B, for every page.
- A page can carry an **agent-only override or supplement**: a sibling `page.agent.md`, or a fenced `agent` block the HTML renderer hides. The bot home page / install prompt and the loop from `AGENTS.md` live there.
- `AGENTS.md` becomes a source of the site rather than a separate document.
- The reference parts use the **same Go emitters** as `mcpx help --format markdown` (#144 / #145), so the site's twin and the binary agree for a given version.
- CI checks that every HTML page has a twin, every twin is linked from `llms.txt`, and the twin is current. Docs checks run in CI; see the testing trackers under #91 (CI pipeline #95, integration/environments #97).

Why C: it is the only option that gives agents something better than the human page with the chrome removed, and still keeps one source of truth per fact.

## Open questions

1. Where are hand-written agent pages allowed? Only the home page and the loop, or any page? Too many overrides and the twin drifts from the human page.
2. Size budgets. `llms.txt` should stay small (a few KB; it is meant to be read whole). `llms-full.txt` for the whole compendium (#152) could run to megabytes (Fluree's is ~1.9 MB). Should we split it into `llms-full.txt` (levels 1 and 2) and a separate compendium file, or cap it and list the rest under `## Optional`?
3. Twin URL shape: `page.md` or `page.html.md`? Both are allowed by the spec. `page.md` is shorter; `page.html.md` never collides with a source file.
4. Should the install prompt be versioned (pinned to the release it was published with), or always install latest?
5. Which harnesses does the prompt cover at first: only opencode, or all of #48's list?

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** M (B is S once #117 is chosen; the install prompt and the in-binary docs make it M) · **Impact** high (agents are a primary audience of mcpx) · **Depends on / related**: #117, #118, #155, #158, #144, #145, #150, #152, #44 (closed, fixed in #53), #48, #49

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#115 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #176

## Summary

Two things: add four specific servers (Dropbox, Google Drive, Outlook, Tailscale), and give mcpx a channel for "you should add this" / "this one is slow, host it locally" so that the first thing is not a manual pipeline forever.

The second is the more interesting one, and the finding is that mcpx should **not** grow a curated vendor list. It already has registry search, live server add, and CLI→MCP adapters; what it is missing is the *memory and the ranking* — a record of what a user wanted and could not find, and enough metadata to answer "is there a better instance of this than the one I am using". A curated list of four servers is a snapshot that rots; a good search-add-record loop keeps working.

## Original notes

> - mcp-owned opencode api support
>   - add the dropboxMcp, googleDriveMcp, outlookMcp, tailscaleMcp
>   - please make an alias for the tailscaleMcp except it should not require auth it should accept the creds i already used to connect to it and the only skill it should provide is listTailnet and listHostnames
>   - accept user feedback, requests, routinely implement features/interfaces that are good idea. "you should add this mcp it's free." "this mcp is very good you should consider hosting it locally because the public one is slow and limited" 

## Current state (what mcpx does today, with file refs)

| capability | where |
| --- | --- |
| search the public MCP registry | `GET /v1/registry/search`, `internal/registry/registry.go:153` (pins `version=latest` at `:158`; matches server names only, as a substring), `mcpx registry search\|show\|add` (`internal/cli/registry.go:15`) — there is no `mcpx connect` |
| add a registry server to config | `mcpx registry add <name>` prints the entry and the variables it needs; `--write` adds it (`internal/cli/registry.go:92-124`). No verify-it-starts step, no rollback. |
| add a server live, project or user scope | `POST /v1/servers` (`internal/api/ops_settings.go:82`) — `command`/`args`/`env` or `url`/`headers`/`transport`, plus `mcpx` extras |
| remove a server live | `DELETE /v1/servers/{name}` |
| expose one server as several filtered namespaces | `aliasOf` + `mcpx.tools` (`docs/story.md` §"Profiles and aliases") |
| wrap a CLI program as a server | `internal/adapter`, `paths.adapters` |
| wrap an OpenAPI service as a server | `internal/openapi`, `paths.apis`, `mcpx api --spec` |
| credentials | `mcpauth.Auth` on a server entry; `${VAR}` expansion in `APISpec.Headers`; OAuth for remote servers is **declared and not performed** (`docs/protocol.md` §6) |
| per-server latency and error statistics | `GET /v1/stats` — `calls`, `servers`, `instances`, `errors`, `sessions`, `volume`, `slowest` |
| a feedback channel | **none** |
| a record of a search that found nothing | **none** |

The statistics row matters: mcpx already measures exactly the thing the note's second quote is about ("the public one is slow and limited"). It measures it and does nothing with it.

## What exists for the four requested servers

Queried the official registry, `https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io/v0/servers?search=<name>`, on 2026-09-30. Results are noisy — the same package is returned several times under different versions — and deduplicated here. (That is the raw API queried *without* `version=latest`. mcpx always sends the pin, `internal/registry/registry.go:158`, and gets distinct names — see #179.)

| requested | found | notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Dropbox** | `io.github.pipeworx-io/dropbox` ("Dropbox MCP Pack — wraps the Dropbox API v2"), `ai.smithery/cindyloo-dropbox-mcp-server` (search/browse/read), `io.usefulapi/dropbox-sign` (a *different* product — Dropbox Sign) | no first-party Dropbox entry; all third-party |
| **Google Drive** | `search=google drive` → **0 results**; `search=gdrive` → **0 results**. Only `com.mcparmory/google-drive` surfaced, under `search=drive` | no first-party Google entry in the registry. The best-known Drive server is the `gdrive` **reference server** from `modelcontextprotocol/servers`, which was moved to the archived set. Effectively: nothing well-maintained and official. |
| **Outlook** | `io.github.chrischall/office-outlook-mcp` (mail, calendar, contacts, tasks), `io.github.0xka13b/microsoft-outlook-mcp` (read/search/send), `com.mintmcp/outlook-email`, `com.mintmcp/outlook-calendar` | no first-party Microsoft entry under this search. Microsoft ships MCP for other products; Outlook coverage here is third-party. |
| **Tailscale** | `io.github.YawLabs/tailscale-mcp` ("manage your tailnet from AI assistants"), `ai.dinglebear/rtailscale` (devices, routes, DNS, keys, users, ACLs — MCP **and** CLI), `ai.dinglebear/tailscale-rmcp` (Rust MCP server and CLI) | no first-party Tailscale entry. |

Two conclusions:

1. **None of the four has a first-party server.** Every option is community-maintained, of unknown quality, and requires handing it a credential to a fairly consequential account. That is a reason to prefer the thinnest possible wrapper, not the richest one.
2. **Three of the four have an excellent official CLI or HTTP API, which mcpx can already consume without any MCP server.** `tailscale` the CLI covers `status --json` (hostnames, tailnet, devices) and the Tailscale API is documented and simple; Microsoft Graph and the Dropbox API v2 both publish OpenAPI-ish documents. So `internal/adapter` and `internal/openapi` are a **better** route than adopting a third-party server: the declaration is reviewable, the credential handling is `${VAR}` expansion, and there is no extra process from an unknown author in the trust path.

**For the specific tailscale request** — an alias exposing only `listTailnet` and `listHostnames` — the cheapest correct answer is an **adapter spec over the `tailscale` CLI**, about fifteen lines:

```jsonc
{ "name": "tailscale", "command": "tailscale",
  "tools": [
    { "name": "listTailnet",   "args": ["status", "--json"], "json": true },
    { "name": "listHostnames", "args": ["status", "--json"], "json": true }
  ] }
```

It requires no auth because the local `tailscale` CLI is already authenticated — which is the literal reading of "it should accept the creds i already used to connect to it". The renaming and narrowing that an *alias over a real MCP server* would need is the `toolViews` work in #114; the adapter route needs none of it, because an adapter declares its own tool names. Worth doing as the first proof that adapters are the right default for this class of request.

## Approaches

### Approach A — least recommended: ship a curated list of vendor servers in mcpx's defaults

Bundle known-good entries for Dropbox, Drive, Outlook, Tailscale and others in `internal/defaults`, so `mcpx registry add dropbox` just works.

Why not:

- **It is a snapshot of a directory that already exists and is maintained by someone else.** The registry is the curation layer; duplicating a slice of it into a Go binary means every entry rots at its own rate and a stale one is worse than no entry, because it carries mcpx's implicit endorsement.
- **It makes mcpx an opinion about third-party code quality** across products it does not use, for a trust decision (handing over a Dropbox or Microsoft 365 credential) that is genuinely consequential and genuinely the user's.
- **It answers the wrong question.** A user asking for "the Dropbox MCP" wants Dropbox capability, not a specific package. The registry answers "which packages exist"; nothing today answers "which of these should I use", and a hard-coded list does not answer it either — it just hides the question.
- It also scales badly: there are thousands of servers and four is not a stopping point anyone will respect.

### Approach B — middle: make discovery and adoption good, and document the four as recipes

Improve what exists rather than adding a list:

1. **Registry metadata in search output.** The registry carries more than name and description; surface what it has — package type, transport, remote-or-local, version recency, whether it is official. "Is this maintained" is the first question and today the answer requires leaving mcpx. Part of it is already fetched and thrown away: each result's `_meta` is decoded into `listResponse` (`internal/registry/registry.go:137-146`) and dropped at `:168-169`. It carries `io.modelcontextprotocol.registry/official` with `status`, `publishedAt`, `updatedAt` and `isLatest` (checked live 2026-09-30).
2. ~~**Deduplicate registry results.** The raw responses above return the same server up to nine times across versions. `internal/registry` should collapse by name and show the newest version, which is a small, clearly-correct fix (visible directly in the query output quoted above).~~ **Struck (issues pass, 2026-09-30, at 05c78b2):** mcpx never sees those duplicates. `Search` pins `version=latest` on every query (`internal/registry/registry.go:158`), every caller goes through it, and five live searches returned all-distinct names (#179). The duplicates belong to the un-pinned raw query above, which mcpx does not issue. What #179 found instead, and owns: `registry.pageSize` is only consulted when `limit <= 0` (`:155`), and `nextCursor` is parsed (`:143`) and dropped, so a search silently stops at one page.
3. **`mcpx registry add <name>` end to end** (this issue first called it `mcpx connect`, which does not exist; the command is `mcpx registry`): search, pick, show what it will run and what credentials it wants — `registry show`/`add` already do this much — add it at project or user scope, verify it starts and lists tools, and roll back if it does not. `POST /v1/servers` plus `/v1/health` already provide the rest.
4. **Prefer an adapter or an OpenAPI declaration when one is available.** When a requested capability has a well-known CLI or published API document, say so: *"`tailscale` is installed; an adapter declaration needs no credential and no third-party process. Generate one?"* That is a better default than adopting an unknown server, and it connects directly to the spec-generation work in #114.
5. **Ship the four as documented example declarations**, in `docs/`, not in defaults — copy-pasteable, reviewable, and obviously not endorsed-and-maintained by mcpx.

This is all deterministic and most of it is small.

### Approach C — recommended: B, plus a recorded feedback loop that mcpx can actually act on

Do B. Then close the loop the second bullet is asking for — and note that the useful version of it is mostly **evidence mcpx already has**, not free text.

**1. Record the misses.** Every `mcpx search` and `registry search` that returned nothing or was followed by no call is a data point. Store them (the event store, #6, is the natural home) and expose `mcpx feedback` / `GET /v1/feedback` as the local list: *"you searched for calendar 6 times in 3 sessions and never called a tool."* That is a concrete, unarguable statement of a missing capability, derived at zero cost from telemetry that already flows through `/v1/log`.

**2. Turn statistics into a recommendation.** "This mcp is very good you should consider hosting it locally because the public one is slow and limited" is a *measurement*, and `/v1/stats` already has `slowest`, `errors` and `volume` per server. A `mcpx doctor` check — and `doctor` already exists (`internal/cli/doctor.go`) as the place mcpx tells you what is wrong — can say: *"`notion` (remote): p95 4.2s over 340 calls, 6% errors. A local package exists in the registry. Switch?"* Remote-versus-local is visible in the config (`url` versus `command`), and the registry says whether a local package is published. This is the single best item in this issue: it is deterministic, it uses only data mcpx already collects, and it produces exactly the advice the note quotes.

**3. Accept explicit feedback as a first-class record.** `mcpx feedback "add a calendar mcp"` / `POST /v1/feedback`, appended to a local file with the context mcpx can attach automatically (which servers are configured, which searches failed, what the daemon version is). Local by default and never transmitted anywhere. Its purposes, in order: it gives the user a place to put the thought, it gives `mcpx prompt` something to act on, and it gives a maintainer a file to paste into an issue if the user chooses to.

**4. Let the prompt layer read it.** With #113's `intent --scope ops`, *"add the thing I keep failing to find"* becomes: read the miss log, search the registry, propose a server or an adapter declaration, show the plan, add on confirmation. Every step is an existing declared operation; the model only chooses among them. That is "routinely implement features/interfaces that are good idea" in the only form that is safe — mcpx proposing, the user approving.

**5. Explicitly out of scope: mcpx modifying itself in response to feedback.** The note's "routinely implement features" could be read as self-modification. It should not be. The loop ends at a proposal a human accepts; anything past that is the arbitrary-provisioning question deferred in #113.

Recommended because it converts a vague "accept feedback" into three concrete, mostly-deterministic features built on data mcpx already has; because the slow-remote-server recommendation is genuinely valuable and genuinely cheap; and because it avoids taking on the maintenance and the implied endorsement of a vendor list.

## Open questions

- Where do feedback and miss records live — the event store (#6), a plain JSONL file in the state dir, or the log store? The log store has query, filtering and retention already; a separate file is simpler to hand to a maintainer.
- Should a miss record capture the *query text*? It is the useful part and it is also the most sensitive thing in the file. Local-only mitigates it; an explicit opt-out setting is probably still required.
- Does `mcpx registry add` verifying a server by starting it constitute running untrusted code before the user consented? Almost certainly — the consent has to come before the first launch, not after.
- Is there a registry field for "official/verified"? The `io.github.*` versus `com.*`/`ai.*` namespacing implies provenance but does not assert maintenance. Partly answered: per entry, `/v0/servers` returns `_meta["io.modelcontextprotocol.registry/official"]` with a lifecycle `status` (e.g. `active`) and dates — registry lifecycle, not a quality or verification signal.
- Should mcpx ever propose *self-hosting* a remote server automatically (pull the package, run it locally, rewrite the config, keep the credential)? Attractive and a large step; the rollback story if the local one is worse must exist first.
- For Google Drive specifically: with no maintained server, is a Google Drive **OpenAPI declaration** (Drive API v3 publishes a discovery document) the better answer? Probably, and it generalises to every Google API at once.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** M (S for richer metadata + the four example declarations — registry dedup struck, see #179; M for `mcpx registry add` end-to-end and the doctor recommendation; M for the feedback/miss store) · **Impact** medium-high — the doctor recommendation and the miss log are the parts that keep paying; the four servers are a day's config each once adapters are the route.

**Depends on / related**: #179 (registry search gaps: unreachable `registry.pageSize`, dropped `nextCursor`; disproved the dedup premise), #6 (event store, for miss records), #76 (ops/CLI parity for any new operation), #5 (config chain, for add scope). Siblings: #114 (`toolViews.from` is what an alias over a *real* tailscale MCP server would need; adapter/OpenAPI generation is the recommended route for all four), #109 (a miss is a search that found nothing — the two share the record), #113 (`intent --scope ops` is what acts on the feedback), #110.

Security/auth deferred; see tracker.

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#106 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #175

## Summary

Two limits on what `mcpx exec` and `mcpx run` will accept. First, they run
TypeScript and nothing else: there is no way to run a shell script, a Python
one-liner, or anything with a shebang, on any surface. Second, `/v1/exec`
accepts a `file` field but resolves it as a raw path on the daemon's
filesystem, while the CLI resolves a script *name* against a search path — so a
named script is a local-only concept and the two sides disagree about what a
"file" is.

## Original notes

> - can exec call bash across the modes?
>   - nearly just allow any shebang
>     - drop the user in <user_config>||<config>||pwd
>     - if not shebang or --shell||--bash||--shell python3||--#!/usr/bin/python
>     - then configured typescript
>   -  ./mcpx -exec 
> - any exec local or remote should allow file scripts, server looks where it finds scripts and tries to find, same as local.

## Current state

### Nothing runs but TypeScript

`runner.Detect` returns one of three JavaScript runtimes and `runner.Run`
spawns it. There is no shell, no interpreter selection, no shebang handling
anywhere — `rg -n "shebang|#!|--shell"` across `internal/cli` and
`internal/adapter` finds only `mcpx completion bash`.

The nearest existing thing is `script.launcher = none` (`runner.LauncherNone`,
`internal/runner/runner.go:493-497`), documented as "the escape hatch for a
script that wants the runtime and none of the harness". Since #75 it, and
`--launcher`/`--no-launcher`/`--export`/`--allow-repeat`/`--no-capture-console`,
apply to `exec` snippets as well as `run` files (#74 closed). It removes mcpx's
shim; it does not change the interpreter.

Related but different: `paths.adapters` wraps an existing CLI *as an MCP
server*, so a shell tool can be reached from a script. That is "call out to a
command", not "this script is a shell script".

### `file` means two different things

- **CLI, local**: `resolveScript(arg)` (`internal/cli/scripts.go`) — an argument
  that looks like a path is used verbatim; otherwise the name is looked up on
  the script search path (every `.config/mcpx/scripts` and `.mcpx/scripts` from
  the working directory up, then the user directory, with `paths.scripts` and
  the `null` splice), trying `.ts`, `.mts`, `.js`, `.mjs`. A miss produces a
  good error listing every directory searched and the `mkdir` to fix it.
- **CLI, remote**: `execOnDaemon` (`internal/cli/exec.go:448`) calls
  `resolveScript` **locally**, reads the file, and sends its *text*. So a named
  script works remotely — by being resolved here and shipped as source.
  `--export` is refused with an explicit message because it needs a module on
  the runtime's disk (`exec.go:453-458`; only for files — on an inline snippet
  `--export` is not refused and not sent). The other exec flags are not refused,
  they are dropped: `runScript` hands off to `execOnDaemon` (`internal/cli/commands.go:556-559`)
  before `--launcher`, `--no-launcher`, the phase flags, `--typecheck`, `--env`,
  `--no-capture-console` and `--allow-repeat` are read (`:573-843`), and
  `execsvc.Options` has no field for most of them (`internal/execsvc/execsvc.go:101-124`).
  #75 closed that class for the local path only. Part 4 below moves resolution
  to the daemon; it should carry these flags on the wire or refuse them, as it
  already refuses `--export`.
- **`/v1/exec` and MCP**: `execReq.File` (`internal/daemon/routes_exec.go`) is
  passed through `execsvc.Request{File: …}` into `runner.Options.File`
  (`internal/execsvc/execsvc.go:327`), and the runner does `filepath.Abs` and
  runs it (`internal/runner/runner.go:293`).
  **No search path, no name resolution, no error naming where it looked.** A
  caller that is not the mcpx CLI — the opencode plugin, a remote agent, an MCP
  client — can therefore only name absolute or cwd-relative paths on the
  daemon's machine.

`docs/exec.md` says "A remote run sends the script's *text*, not its path",
which is true of the CLI and not true of the endpoint. That is the gap the
user's second bullet names.

## Approaches

### Approach A — least recommended: a `--shell`/`--bash` flag pair on exec

Add `--shell`, `--bash`, `--python` flags that swap the interpreter.

Why not: it is a fixed list that will never be the right fixed list — the user's
own note already escalates from `--shell` to `--bash` to `--shell python3` to
`--#!/usr/bin/python` within one line, which is the flag set discovering it
wants to be a string. Every addition is a new flag on two commands, a new
`ExecOptions` field and a new MCP tool parameter. The project has a settings
registry precisely so that one declaration reaches every surface; a flag family
bypasses it. It also leaves the file-resolution half of this issue untouched.

### Approach B — middle: an `script.interpreter` setting plus shebang detection

One setting, `script.interpreter`, whose value is a command line: empty means
"use the configured language/runtime", anything else is argv the script path is
appended to (`bash`, `python3 -u`, `/usr/bin/env -S deno run -A`). Plus: if the
source or file begins with `#!`, honour it — on a file by making it executable
and running it directly, on a snippet by writing it to a temporary file with
the shebang intact.

`--shell` and `--bash` become aliases for `script.interpreter=sh` and `=bash` if
they are wanted at all, which keeps the user's spelling available without the
combinatorics. `KindString` already exists; `FlagAliases` already exists; the
value reaches CLI, env, config, `/v1/settings` and MCP for free.

This answers "can exec call bash across the modes?" — yes, everywhere, because
it is a setting and settings are already everywhere. It stops short of two
things: it does not say what the *working directory* should be (the user's
"drop the user in `<user_config>||<config>||pwd`"), and it has no story for what
the harness means when there is no TypeScript client — a bash script gets no
`tools`, no `emit`, no `artifact`, and mcpx becomes a slower `bash -c`.

### Approach C — recommended: shebang-first dispatch, with the harness offered rather than assumed, and one script-resolution rule for every surface

Three parts.

**1. Dispatch order.** Exactly the order the user wrote, made explicit:

| rank | condition | result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | source or file starts with `#!` | run under that interpreter, verbatim |
| 2 | `script.interpreter` is set (or `--shell`, `--interpreter`) | that command line |
| 3 | `script.language` (see the Python sibling issue) or the file extension | that language's runtime |
| 4 | otherwise | the configured TypeScript runtime — today's behaviour, unchanged |

Unset defaults mean nothing changes for anyone. A shebang is self-describing,
travels with the script text, and therefore works identically for a local run, a
remote exec and a named script — which is the property that makes it the right
primary rule rather than a flag.

**2. The harness is opt-in per interpreter, and its absence is stated.** A
non-JS interpreter gets, at minimum: `MCPX_ENDPOINT`, `MCPX_SESSION`,
`MCPX_SOCKET`, `MCPX_RUNTIME` and the script's args in the environment, so a
bash script can `curl` the daemon; and `stdout`/`stderr`/exit code handled by
the same `execsvc` machinery, so frames, logs, artifacts-by-reference and
timeouts work unchanged. What it does not get is the generated client, and mcpx
should say so once rather than let the author discover it. This is the same
posture `runner.Permissions` takes about bun and node having no sandbox, and
`preflight.TypeCheck` takes about type checking — state the limitation, do not
pretend.

A shell script that can reach `$MCPX_ENDPOINT` with `curl` is genuinely useful
and costs almost nothing to enable, because the daemon already binds a
loopback HTTP endpoint for exactly this reason (a unix socket is not portable
across runtimes — `docs/dependencies.md`).

**3. Working directory becomes a named policy, not an accident.** The user's
`<user_config>||<config>||pwd` is asking for a rule. Propose `script.cwd` with
values `caller | script | config | workdir`:

- `caller` (default) — today's behaviour and `runner.Run`'s stated intent: "a
  relative path in a script should mean what it means on the command line".
- `script` — the directory the script file lives in, which is what a named
  script in `.config/mcpx/scripts` usually wants.
- `config` — the nearest mcpx config directory, the user's `<config>`.
- `workdir` — the content-addressed exec workdir, i.e. isolated.

This matters more once shebangs exist, because a shell script's relative paths
are far more load-bearing than a TypeScript one's, and `ExecOptions.cwd` already
crosses the wire so the remote case has somewhere to put the answer.

**4. One resolution rule, both sides.** Move `resolveScript` out of
`internal/cli` into a package `internal/execsvc` can call, and have the daemon
resolve `file` the same way — search path, `null` splice, extension list, and
the same error that names every directory it looked in. Then:

- `POST /v1/exec {"file": "report"}` finds `report.ts` on the *daemon's* search
  path, which is what the user's bullet asks for and what the opencode plugin
  needs (#48; since #53 closed #44 the plugin reaches the daemon over its socket
  without the binary, so it cannot resolve a name locally the way the CLI does).
- The CLI's existing behaviour — resolve locally, send text — stays the default
  for `--remote`, because `mcpx run ./report.ts --remote` means the file in
  front of you. A new `--remote-file`/`file:` form asks the daemon to resolve
  instead. The two are genuinely different requests and both are wanted.
- `--export` becomes possible on a remote run when the daemon resolved the file
  itself, since there *is* then a module on the runtime's disk. That removes one
  of the two refusals `docs/exec.md` lists under "Not done".

**On `./mcpx -exec`**: the most useful reading is mcpx as a shebang interpreter —
`#!/usr/bin/env -S mcpx run` at the top of a `.ts` file, making a script
directly executable while still getting the client, the launcher and the tool
namespaces. It should be listed as done-when.

Corrected 2026-09-30 (this paragraph said `mcpx exec` and called it a two-line
change):

- The interpreter must be `mcpx run`, not `mcpx exec`. The kernel appends the
  file's path, and `exec` takes source text, so `mcpx exec ./x.ts` would run the
  string `./x.ts` as TypeScript.
- With `run` it probably works already. A file script is imported unchanged by
  the launcher (`runner.go:292-310`), and all three runtimes skip a line-1
  hashbang in an imported module. Verified here with deno 2.9.6, bun 1.3.11 and
  node 24.20.0: a module starting `#!/usr/bin/env -S mcpx run`, imported by
  another, loads and runs. Not yet verified end to end through mcpx. The work is
  a test, not a feature.
- A snippet starting with `#!` does fail under `exec`. The prelude is prepended
  (`runner.go:282`), and a hashbang is only legal on line 1 (a `#!` on line 2 is
  a syntax error on all three). That is part 1's snippet case, not this one.

## Open questions

- Does a shebang override `script.runtime` silently, or warn when both are
  specified and disagree? Silently winning is the usual Unix rule; a warning is
  more in keeping with this project's habits.
- Shebang on a *snippet*: `mcpx exec '#!/bin/bash\necho hi'` must be written to
  a file to run. Where — the content-addressed exec workdir, subject to the same
  pruning? And does it get the `+x` bit, or is the interpreter parsed out and
  invoked directly (safer, and works where the workdir is `noexec`)?
- `script.permissions` is meaningless for a shell script. Warn, ignore, or
  refuse when a non-default permission profile is set?
- Should the daemon's script search path be the same setting as the CLI's
  (`paths.scripts`) with its own scope, or a distinct `paths.daemonScripts`? A
  daemon resolving names from the invoking user's home directory is a different
  thing from resolving them from its own.
- Does `internal/diagnose`'s static tool-call scan simply not run for non-JS
  interpreters, or does it report "not analysable for this interpreter"?
- Does a shebang'd script still get `--typecheck`? Under Approach C's
  `script.check`, `onUnsupported` already has the vocabulary for this.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease** M (dispatch and cwd policy) / L (shared script resolution across CLI and
daemon) · **Impact** high — it turns `exec` from "run TypeScript" into "run a
script", and it closes a real CLI-vs-`/v1` divergence of the kind #76 tracks.

**Depends on / related**: #76 (CLI ↔ `/v1` parity), #48 (harness-free plugin
core; a plugin with no binary is the caller that needs daemon-side
resolution), #44 (closed, fixed in #53 — the plugin no longer needs the
binary), #75 (merged: exec honours its flags locally; the remote path is still
open, above), #5 (`paths.config`, the config-directory chain `script.cwd=config`
would follow), #40 (closed, fixed in #57 — ExecOptions), #7 (launcher, which a
non-JS interpreter bypasses), and siblings #100 (runtime selection;
`script.checkOnUnsupported`), #105 (Python parity; dispatch rank 3) and #107
(flake execution environments; `exec.env` composes on the interpreter seam).
