body:
## Evidence

`pkgs/id/crates/id-render/src/compose.rs:384-413` implements `pick_winner` by iterating candidates and immediately returning an error when it sees two different tokens at equal specificity. It does not first determine the maximum specificity.

This makes the result depend on input order when a lower-specificity pair conflicts but a higher-specificity declaration exists. I reproduced this with the same three assertions on the same button:

1. `[KindDefault(accent), KindDefault(brand), Instance(accent)]` → compose returns a tie error.
2. `[Instance(accent), KindDefault(accent), KindDefault(brand)]` → compose succeeds and silently ignores the lower-specificity conflict.

A temporary probe test run with `~/tools/fleet-build-lock cargo test -p id-render --test zz_probe_order_dependence` printed `order A ... true`, `order B ... false` and failed its equality assertion. The probe was removed and is not part of the checkout.

The behavior contradicts `doc/2026-11-08_decision_id5854_per_target_composition.md` §2.2 / invariant 2: source order is not a cascade input; and invariant 9: every tie is reported. `pick_winner` is shared by semantic assertions, style overrides and presentation overrides, so the same defect affects all three callers.

## Why it matters

An author can reorder equivalent declarations and change a build from error to success, with conflicting lower-specificity data becoming silently accepted. This breaks deterministic validation and can hide configuration mistakes.

## Acceptance criteria

- Tie validation has the same result for every permutation of a given candidate set.
- Conflicting declarations at the winning specificity still produce an error; lower-specificity declarations do not alter the winner.
- Add permutation-focused tests for assertions, style overrides, and presentation overrides (or otherwise demonstrate shared coverage for all callers).
- Existing `id-render` composition tests pass.

Suggested fix: determine the maximum specificity before tie-checking tokens at that specificity, or otherwise make tie detection independent of iteration order.

  - **NixOS System Infrastructure & Web Services**: Modules, cloud functions, background daemons, and system services.

### 2. UNRESTRICTED INNOVATION & NEW FEATURE GENERATION - You are NOT restricted by what currently exists. Brainstorm things that *should* exist, would be exceptionally useful, or incorporate frontier concepts:
  - Edge architectures using Cloudflare Workers, Durable Objects, KV, and Queues.
  - Distributed SQLite / libSQL / Turso primitives for offline-first, syncable state.
  - Advanced autonomous coding loops, speculative tool execution, and local verification loops.
  - Cross-platform bridges, native desktop integrations, and performance optimizations.
- **Bias Toward Capture**: It is far better to create an issue to triage later than to let a valuable opportunity or insight pass.
### 3. ACTIVE ISSUE & PR MAINTENANCE - **Scope Variety**: Create single large architectural vision issues for strategic direction, or narrow, highly focused issues for targeted improvements. - **Issue Decomposition**: If an existing issue is too broad, ambiguous, or monolithic (including issues created by others), break it apart into a series of clear, modular, linked sub-issues with explicit dependencies. - **Deduplication & Consolidation**: Identify overlapping or duplicate proposals/issues and consolidate them into unified, high-quality reference issues. - **Comments & Spec Refinement**: Leave comments or edit existing issues/PRs to provide missing technical specifications, edge-case analysis, data schemas, or suggested test cases. - **Zero-Context Hand-off Standard**: Every issue you author must be self-contained, citing exact file paths, interfaces, architectural rationale, and verifiable acceptance criteria so a new agent with zero prior context can execute it.

### 4. OPPORTUNISTIC IMPLEMENTATION (QUICK-WIN PRS) - If you identify straightforward bugs, unhandled edge cases, missing test coverage, or clean opportunities to refactor code to prevent future merge conflicts:
  - You are actively encouraged to open small, focused Pull Requests implementing the fix or feature directly.
  - Ensure all added code follows repository standards, includes tests, and passes formatting/linting hooks (`treefmt`, `conform`).
  - Never introduce breaking regressions to existing stable flows.
  - **One PR per coherent set**: batch every instance of the same problem — and all related dependency updates — into a single PR, or a few PRs split by coherent group. Never one PR per item or per dependency.
  - **Prefer tracked, higher-impact work**: before inventing a new micro-fix, check the open issues and implement the highest-impact one you can complete and verify, even when it spans several files.
  - **Merging is permitted, never required**: merge your PR only when checks pass and you are reasonably certain it is correct and low-risk. Otherwise leave it open and state your confidence and what a human should check in the description.

labels.name: source/dispatch

body:
Perform the daily configuration review for developing-today/code. Do NOT update the `opencode` or `openchamber` flake inputs — the flake-inputs-update workflow owns them.
Follow these instructions and rules:
### 1. FLAKE INPUTS — OWNED ELSEWHERE, DO NOT BUMP - The `opencode` and `openchamber` flake inputs are owned by the deterministic
  `flake-inputs-update` workflow, which bumps, validates, and merges them daily.
  Do NOT run `nix flake update` for them, do NOT change their pins in `flake.lock`,
  and do NOT open PRs that bump them. If their pins look stale, leave them — the
  owning workflow handles them the same day.
- Do NOT casually bump root `nixpkgs` (root nixpkgs is pinned deliberately per system stability policies). - Clean up any stale input overrides or unused flake dependencies in `flake.nix` (e.g. warnings about non-existent input overrides like gitignore or devshell).
### 2. CONFIGURATION & INFRASTRUCTURE IMPROVEMENTS - Investigate potential configuration improvements in `nixos/`, `home/`, `lib/`, and package definitions under `pkgs/`. - Check for:
  - Deprecated NixOS or Home Manager options
  - Suboptimal build phases or missing binary wrappers
  - Systemd service resilience (e.g. restart policies, socket activation)
  - Modularity and decoupling to prevent merge conflicts
- Clean up any dead code, unused flags, or documentation drift in Nix configurations.
### 3. EVALUATION & VALIDATION - Verify that all system and host configurations evaluate cleanly without errors:
  `nix eval --raw .#nixosConfigurations.nixos.config.system.build.toplevel.drvPath`
- Ensure git hooks, commit messages, and treefmt formatting pass cleanly.

### 4. PULL REQUEST & MERGE - If updates or improvements are present:
  - Open a clear Pull Request documenting any configuration enhancements made. Keep every related change in this one PR — never split changes into one PR per item.
  - Merge into `main` only when you are reasonably certain it is correct: all Nix evaluations and checks succeed, the PR is conflict-free, and the changes are limited to the intended bumps and fixes. Merging is permitted, never required — when any of that is uncertain, leave the PR open and explain what a human should check.

labels.description: pm-stack (Pad/Grist) in developing-today/code

body:
## Problem

`deserializeState()` trusts the shape of persisted `dailyGlobal` and returns its `count` without checking that it is a finite, non-negative integer (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/remediation.ts:629-645`). `decideRemediation()` compares that value with `GLOBAL_DAILY_CAP` (`:453-472`), so malformed same-day values such as a string make the comparison false. `recordAttempt()` then increments the string by concatenation (`:589-592`), leaving the counter nonnumeric and the global cap bypassable across facets.

## Reproduction

A direct probe passed `{ dailyGlobal: { date: "2026-11-19", count: "corrupt" } }` through `deserializeState()` and repeatedly called `decideRemediation()` / `recordAttempt()` across the catalogue's six facets, with cooldowns elapsed and each attempt verified. All 16 attempts were allowed even though `GLOBAL_DAILY_CAP` is 15; the per-facet caps remained active. The persisted counter became `"corrupt1111111111111111"`.

The existing corrupt-input test only covers invalid JSON text (`"not json"`), not structurally valid JSON with malformed counter fields. Closed #9989 implemented the executor and explicitly accepted a global daily cap of 15; focused all-state searches for remediation/global daily cap, `deserializeState` malformed state, and related PRs found no tracker for this persisted-state validation gap.

## Acceptance criteria

- Validate or safely normalize persisted daily counter dates and counts before they reach the decision logic; malformed values must fail closed or reset safely without weakening the cap.
- Ensure counter updates preserve a numeric, non-negative integer invariant.
- Add regression coverage for malformed same-day `dailyGlobal.count` and malformed per-facet counter data, asserting that malformed state cannot permit more than the configured daily limits.
- Keep the existing valid-state serialization round-trip and daily-cap tests passing.

title: fix(id/serve): prevent concurrent servers from replacing the shared serve lock

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

labels.name: status/triaged
labels.description: Triaged and routed (see agent note)

body:
## Problem

The serve lock is a single shared discovery path, but startup does not claim it exclusively. `cmd_serve()` calls `create_serve_lock()` at `pkgs/id/crates/id-cli/src/commands/serve.rs:1973-1976` after binding listeners, and no existing-lock/singleton check guards startup. `create_serve_lock()` writes a temporary file and calls `temporary.persist(lock_path)` at `serve.rs:317-322`; this replaces an existing destination instead of failing if another live serve already owns it.

Two overlapping `id serve` starts can therefore both remain running while the later one overwrites the earlier server's discovery record. The earlier process's graceful shutdown then calls `remove_serve_lock()` at `serve.rs:329-331`, which unconditionally removes the shared path and can erase the later server's lock too. This leaves a live server undiscoverable by local CLI/REPL clients. This is distinct from #12094, which fixed stale-snapshot cleanup deleting a replacement lock; the remaining issue is exclusive ownership and shutdown cleanup across two live serve instances.

## Evidence

- `cmd_serve()` binds listeners and then writes the shared lock without first rejecting an already-running server (`serve.rs:1973-1976`).
- `create_serve_lock()` publishes through `NamedTempFile::persist(lock_path)` (`serve.rs:297-323`), allowing replacement of a pre-existing lock.
- `remove_serve_lock()` unconditionally removes `SERVE_LOCK` (`serve.rs:325-331`), without confirming the lock still belongs to the shutting-down process.
- Focused all-state GitHub searches for concurrent/multiple serve found no matching issue; the open PR search found no matching fix. #12094 addresses stale-read cleanup, not concurrent live owners.

## Acceptance criteria

- A second serve startup must not replace the discovery lock of an already-running serve; use an exclusive claim/ownership protocol and return a clear startup error or otherwise preserve the incumbent.
- Shutdown may remove the lock only when it still owns the lock record, so one process cannot erase another process's discovery state.
- Add deterministic regression coverage for two startup attempts and for the first process shutting down after an ownership change; the incumbent/remnant live server remains discoverable throughout.
- Preserve atomic publication so readers do not observe a partially-written lock.

  - Reference any related performance issues

⚡ Add React.memo() to prevent unnecessary re-renders

⚡ Cache expensive API call results
⚡ Add lazy loading to images below the fold
⚡ Debounce search input to reduce API calls

⚡ Add pagination to large data fetch

BOLT AVOIDS (not worth the complexity):

❌ Large architectural changes

❌ Changes to critical algorithms without thorough testing

title: fix(id/serve): stale-lock cleanup can unlink a replacement serve lock

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

`pkgs/id/crates/id-cli/src/commands/serve.rs:209-217` reads and parses `.iroh-serve.lock`, checks whether that snapshot's process is alive, and then removes the shared path if the snapshot looks stale. The check and unlink are not tied to the same file contents or inode. Meanwhile, `create_serve_lock()` at `serve.rs:245-261` writes a new lock to that path during server startup.

Interleaving: a discovery caller reads an old stale lock; a new serve instance writes its valid lock; the first caller finishes its stale check and `remove_file(SERVE_LOCK)` unlinks the new instance's lock. Later CLI commands then fail to discover/connect to the live server until it restarts. This is distinct from the fixed PID-incarnation, sentinel-PID, and EPERM cases (#3040, #2142, #2384): those validate liveness of the lock snapshot but do not prevent deleting a replacement written after the read.

## Evidence

- `get_serve_info()` reads at lines 209-211, checks the parsed PID/start time at 213-214, then unconditionally removes the shared path at 215-216.
- `create_serve_lock()` writes to the same `SERVE_LOCK` path at lines 245-261.
- Fresh all-state title search for `serve-lock` found only #3040, #2142, #2384, and #3028; body search for `get_serve_info` found the existing liveness issues, but no replacement/unlink race. Open PR title search found no race fix.

## Acceptance criteria

- Stale cleanup can remove a lock only if the path still refers to the exact stale lock that was read (or use an equivalent atomic ownership/locking protocol); it must not unlink a replacement created by a concurrent serve startup.
- Add a deterministic regression test that pauses between stale-snapshot validation and cleanup, writes a fresh lock, resumes cleanup, and verifies the fresh lock remains discoverable.
- Preserve the current stale-lock cleanup behavior when the path still contains the stale snapshot.

title: id(find): an empty --dir value resolves downloads under filesystem root
body:
## Verified behavior

`download_output_path` combines a supplied directory and the safe final component with `format!("{}/{}", dir, file_name)`. With `Some("")`, this returns `/<filename>` rather than a path in the current directory or a validation error. The current CLI accepts `--dir` as `Option<String>` and uses this helper in `id find`/`id search` downloads. An empty variable passed as `--dir "$OUT_DIR"` can therefore direct downloaded content to the filesystem root; a privileged process may write there.

Evidence: `pkgs/id/crates/id-cli/src/helpers.rs:311-335` (current main), called from `commands/find.rs` and `repl/runner.rs`.

## Why it matters

An empty path value unexpectedly changes the destination from the intended working context to `/`, risking failed downloads or writes outside the user's intended output directory.

## Acceptance criteria

- Reject an empty `--dir` value at the CLI/REPL boundary, or normalize it to `.` before constructing output paths.
- Add a regression test proving an empty directory value cannot produce an absolute root path.
- Preserve explicit absolute directory paths supplied by the user.

title: id(find): local tag-list failures are silently reported as empty or partial search results
body:
## Verified behavior

The local-search branch of `cmd_find_matches` suppresses both failure modes while traversing local tags:

- `if let Ok(mut list) = store_handle.tags().list().await` treats a failure to start listing as an empty tag set.
- `if let Ok(item) = item` skips individual stream errors and continues with partial results.

The function returns `Result<Vec<FindMatch>>`, and the remote branch propagates connection, protocol, and response errors. A local database/list failure can therefore be reported to callers as a successful empty or incomplete search result.

Evidence: `pkgs/id/crates/id-cli/src/commands/find.rs`, local branch of `cmd_find_matches` (around lines 955–957 on current main).

## Why it matters

A damaged, inaccessible, or otherwise failing local tag store looks indistinguishable from “no matches,” which can mislead users and downstream commands. Stream failures can also silently produce incomplete results.

## Acceptance criteria

- Propagate tag-list initialization and item-stream errors as errors (or provide an explicit partial-result contract; do not silently return empty/partial success).
- Add tests for failure to initialize the tag listing and for an item-stream error, asserting the caller receives visible failure rather than an empty/partial successful result.
- Preserve normal local and remote search behavior.

body:
## Evidence

In `pm-stack/aggregator/src/genealogy.ts:47-60`, each explicitly historical parent is used as the start of a chain that follows its *current* `parentRef` links. At lines 55-57, those current ancestors are added to `ancestors` as relation `parent`, the same relation used for the item's live parent chain. At line 100, all historical chains are flattened into one list and joined with ` → ` under “Formerly part of”.

I reproduced both cases with temporary focused Bun tests (removed after the run):

1. Item #100 has historical parent #99. After the split, #99 is re-parented under #500. The sentence renders “Formerly part of Former epic (#99) → Post-split reorg epic (#500)”, implying #100 was formerly under #500 even though that edge was created after the split. The API also labels #500 as relation `parent`, not historical.
2. With two historical parents (#99 → #500 and #80 → #90), the sentence emits one continuous arrow chain `#99 → #500 → #80 → #90`, fabricating cross-chain links.

The existing `bun test test/genealogy.test.ts` suite passes (4 tests), but has no re-parent-after-split or multiple-history-chain case. This conflicts with the design contract in `doc/2026-11-12T22-50-00Z_design_pm-board-hierarchy-genealogy/note.md` §6: chain breaks must be honest and links must never be fabricated. #9066 covers recording/validating historical link metadata, while #9070 (the read-model implementation) is closed; neither tracks the read-side temporal boundary bug.

## Why it matters

The genealogy sentence and `/api/item/<id>.json` can present a post-split parent as part of an item's former lineage, or combine unrelated historical parent chains into a false lineage. Consumers cannot distinguish these fabricated ancestors from current parent edges.

## Acceptance criteria

- Historical links render only the ancestry known to have applied during that historical relationship; post-split current parents are not implied as the item's former ancestors.
- Distinct historical-parent chains remain distinct in the sentence/API and are never concatenated into one arrow path.
- API ancestry distinguishes historical relations from current `parent` relations (or otherwise represents historical edges without claiming they are current parents).
- Add regression tests for a former parent re-parented after the split and for multiple independent historical parent chains.

body:
## Evidence

`pkgs/id/src/serve_proxy.rs:382-390` implements `FrameDecoder::feed` by extending `self.buf` with the entire caller-provided slice, then calling `Vec::drain(..consumed)` once for every decoded frame. For a large batch of small frames, each drain shifts the remaining suffix, so total byte movement grows with the number of frames rather than one pass. The full input batch is also copied into `self.buf` before any frame is decoded; `MAX_FRAME_BODY` caps each frame, not the aggregate `bytes` argument or buffered batch.

The module's existing chunking/round-trip property test at `pkgs/id/src/serve_proxy.rs:541-559` checks decoded behavior across splits, but does not exercise bounded buffering or decode work for large batches. `FrameDecoder` has no other source call sites in `pkgs/id/src` today, so this is a codec robustness/performance gap rather than a reported production incident.

## Why it matters

A large read or caller-supplied batch of many small frames causes avoidable copying and temporary memory growth in a public incremental decoder. If fed network data in large batches, this can amplify CPU and memory cost before frames are handed to the caller.

## Suggested fix

Parse using a cursor/read offset and compact the buffer at most once after the loop (or otherwise consume frames without shifting the remaining suffix on every iteration). Consider imposing/documenting a maximum aggregate feed size or processing input incrementally so a single oversized slice is not copied wholesale before parsing.

## Acceptance criteria

- Decoding remains identical for arbitrary chunk boundaries, including incomplete trailing frames and multiple complete frames in one feed.
- A regression test or benchmark covers a large concatenation of small frames and demonstrates linear-ish processing/one compaction rather than repeated front-drains.
- Aggregate buffering behavior is explicitly bounded or the API documents and tests its caller-side input-size contract.

## Problem
Concurrent `GraphIndex::append` calls can leave the persisted metadata count inconsistent with the actual rows. `append` reads metadata before opening its write transaction, so multiple callers can base updates on the same stale count/digest state.

## Evidence
On `origin/main` at `fc0547ee67e7313937f608478e3c7c94e1d80f24`, `pkgs/id/crates/id-store/src/graph_index.rs` reads metadata before its write transaction. A temporary focused concurrency probe synchronized 24 threads appending distinct rows, then called `verify()`; reproduced failure: `Corrupt { table: "spo", problem: "row count differs from meta" }`. The probe has been removed; no product files were changed.

## Acceptance criteria
- Concurrent append operations update rows and metadata atomically from transaction-current state, without lost count/digest updates.
- Add a regression test that synchronizes concurrent appends and verifies the index count and integrity afterward.
- Preserve existing rebuild, append, and verification behavior for serial callers.

body:
## Problem
`DedupLedger::complete` validates the registered request ID and binding digest, but does not validate that the supplied identity is internally valid (its ID derives from its origin, nonce, and binding). A caller can register a valid identity, mutate only `origin`, and still complete the registered entry with an arbitrary outcome. This violates the identity contract and lets completion proceed with a forged/inconsistent identity.

## Reproduction
In `pkgs/id/crates/id-sync/src/federation/slices/b20_request_identity.rs`, create and observe a `RequestIdentity`, clone it, change `origin`, then call `complete` with the clone. The clone has `binding_is_valid() == false`, but `complete` currently returns `Ok(())`. Reproduced by `cargo test --test b20_completion_identity_probe` from `pkgs/id` (1 passed; the test asserts the incorrect acceptance).

## Expected behavior
Completion must reject an identity whose claimed ID does not derive from its origin, nonce, and binding, without changing the ledger entry. Preserve success for the original registered identity and existing outcome/idempotency semantics. Add regression coverage for altered origin and nonce (and verify the valid identity can still complete afterward).

Related completed slice: #10184 (B20 request identity/dedup ledger). This is a focused post-completion gap, not a request to rework B20 or B21 result dedup.

title: id: record join, revoke (and maybe run) times in the world journal for the owner report
body:
## Problem

The world owner report (`id world owner`, #11774 / #11826, #11775, #11777) ships without join times: no journal entry records when a capability was issued, so `joins.in_window`, `joins.available_since` and per-join times are reported as unavailable (`JoinTimeNotRecorded`). Revokes and program runs have the same gap: the journal records that they happened, not when, and records no program runs at all. Drew decided on 2026-11-18 to ship the report without them and plan the journal change here.

## Plan

1. **Record the time on new entries.** Add `issued_at` (Unix ms, `Option<u64>`, serde default, skipped when `None`) to `JournalEntry::Issued`, set from the same world clock that sets `expires_at`, for host-issued and delegated capabilities. Add `revoked_at` to `JournalEntry::Revoked` the same way.
2. **Journal version.** The fields are optional, so older journals still read. But an older binary would parse the entries, ignore the times and drop them when it compacts. Following the existing contract (`JOURNAL_VERSION_*` in `world/journal.rs`), add a new header version required by any entry that carries a time, so older binaries refuse such a journal instead of silently losing the times.
3. **Keep times through compaction and forks.** Checkpoints rewrite every issued capability: carry `issued_at` and `revoked_at` through the rewrite and checkpoint parts. A fork keeps the source's times for inherited joins and says so in the report's existing `inherited_from_fork` coverage.
4. **Owner report.** Fill `JoinSample` with its time, compute `in_window` from the requested window, and set `available_since` to the earliest point from which every later join carries a time (joins from before the upgrade stay "time not recorded", never zero). A window that starts before `available_since` is reported as incomplete. Add revoke times the same way. The report schema stays major version 1 (added optional fields only).
5. **CLI.** `id world owner` shows join and revoke times and the `available_since` boundary in text and JSON.
6. **Program runs (follow-up, separate PR).** Decide whether durable program-run history (start, end, outcome) belongs in the journal at all or stays a live-only snapshot (#11775). If durable, it needs its own entry kind, bounds and version, so it is a design note first, not part of steps 1 to 5.

## Acceptance

- Fixture journals mixing pre- and post-upgrade entries give exact counts, times, window edges and `available_since`; unavailable stays distinct from zero.
- Compaction, checkpoint parts and restore keep every time (round-trip test); an older-version binary refuses the new header.
- Existing journals with no times still read and report exactly as today.
- Property tests for window aggregation and report serialization, as in design §8 (`doc/2026-11-18_design_id6308_creator_owner_basics_v1.md`).

Refs #6308, #11774, #11777

title: id-sync: bounded revocation sweeps quarantine records admitted after expiry
body:
## Problem

`RevocationRecord::covers` defines a bounded interval as `[effective_from, effective_until)`, but `RevocationRegistry::apply_revocation` sweeps previously accepted records using only `effective_from`. If a bounded administrative suspension is learned/applied late, records admitted at or after its exclusive `effective_until` are incorrectly changed from `Accepted` to `Quarantined` (or `Flagged`), even though they were admitted outside the asserted interval.

Relevant code:
- `pkgs/id/crates/id-sync/src/federation/slices/b02_key_revocation.rs`: `covers` checks the exclusive end; `apply_revocation` captures `from` and transitions matching records based only on `admitted_at >= from`.
- `pkgs/id/crates/id-sync/tests/federation_b02.rs`: `bounded_interval_blocks_only_inside_and_quarantine_is_sticky` checks admission blocking at the end boundary and sticky state, but does not cover applying a bounded revocation after a record beyond the end has already been admitted.

Impact: late synchronization of a bounded suspension can withhold valid, post-suspension data from normal release and mark its historical validity indeterminate.

## Acceptance criteria

- Add a regression to `cargo test -p id-sync --test federation_b02` that admits records before, within, and at/after a bounded interval, then applies that revocation after all admissions.
- The sweep flags/quarantines only records whose admission falls within `[effective_from, effective_until)` according to the existing B02 policy; records admitted at or after the exclusive end remain `Accepted`.
- Preserve the existing behavior that quarantine already applied is sticky; expiry alone does not revalidate records previously swept while the interval covered their admission.
- Keep the reference-state-machine oracle aligned with the interval-boundary policy and ensure the dedicated test passes.

title: FileOps: archive-tag classifier disagrees between writer and reader
body:
Found by the #4767 FileOps audit (PR #11788).

`classify_tag` (`pkgs/id/crates/id-web/src/routes.rs:359-385`: rfind, digits, `parse::<u64>`) and `is_archive_tag_name` (`pkgs/id/crates/id-sync/src/fileops.rs:165`: rsplit_once, nonempty stem, digits) disagree on two inputs:

- `.archive.5` (empty stem): the writer accepts it, the reader classifies it as Archive.
- Digit strings that overflow u64: the writer refuses, the reader classifies them as Primary.

Acceptance: one shared classifier used by writer and reader, with a test covering both inputs. Oracle: the writer's accept set is the reference.

title: fleet creator tasks: clock-derived scratch worktree paths collide across runs — a crashed run's tree is adopted by the next run and then force-removed

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: effort/s

body:
## Problem

The improvement-issue-creator scheduled tasks build their scratch worktree path from a per-day counter, not from a run identity:

```
~/git/fleet/improvement-issue-creator-<repo>-<YYYYMMDD>-lane-b-<N>
```

Any later run that computes the same counter finds the path already on disk, silently adopts it, skips its own `git fetch` / base verification, and at the end removes it with `git worktree remove --force`. A run killed mid-work leaves a worktree behind, and the next run in the same slot inherits and then deletes a tree it did not create — with `--force` discarding whatever uncommitted work the dead run left in it. The same shape applies to the lane-A and single-lane creator tasks, which use plain date suffixes.

## Evidence

**1. The 12:30 lane-B run left a worktree behind.** Session `ses_e5e153a18deffeXNjy7x6pWWL0` (Improvement issue creator — lane B, 2026-11-17 12:30) ran

```
git -C ~/git/openchamber-fork fetch origin main -q && git rev-parse origin/main &&
git worktree add --detach ~/git/fleet/improvement-issue-creator-openchamber-20261117-lane-b-3 origin/main -q 2>&1 | tail -3
```

created the tree at `8726d55da`, worked in it through an issue filing, then died at 12:32:08 CST with `provider.invalid-output: "Gemini stopped with MALFORMED_RESPONSE"`. The worktree stayed registered and on disk.

**2. The 15:00 lane-B run adopted that tree instead of creating its own.** Session `ses_e5e14b0c236ffeTqatGhbwCswN` computed the same path and guarded it with

```
cd ~/git/fleet && (test -d improvement-issue-creator-openchamber-20261117-lane-b-3 && echo exists ||
  git -C ~/git/openchamber-fork fetch -q origin main &&
  git -C ~/git/openchamber-fork worktree add --detach ~/git/fleet/improvement-issue-creator-openchamber-20261117-lane-b-3 origin/main 2>&1 | tail -n 2)
```

The `test -d` succeeded, so the `||` branch — the only place a `fetch` and a base check happen — never ran. The run then read code out of the leftover tree, evaluated freshness against it, and filed from it. Its own closing message:

> "the scratch path I used already existed before this run, so my cleanup removed a worktree I did not create. Its status was clean and detached at `8726d55da`, so no uncommitted work was lost."

**3. The cleanup is unconditional and forced.** Same session, final tool call:

```
cd /home/user/git/openchamber-fork && git worktree remove --force ~/git/fleet/improvement-issue-creator-openchamber-20261117-lane-b-3
```

`--force` removes a tree even when it is dirty. In this instance the tree happened to be clean, so nothing was lost; the guard against loss is the dead run's good luck, not the design.

**4. The path is not per-run.** Other runs of the same task in the same day used `improvement-issue-creator-openchamber-20261117-lane-b` (`ses_e5e15dedab2ffeTmoac5fMzqYw`, 09:30), `…-lane-b-2` (`ses_e5e155592aaffeLO8ELG17jTIc`, 12:00) and `…-c` (`ses_e5e14f57015ffe7uavuSE9O4AR`, 13:45). The counter is the only distinguishing element, so any run that recomputes an occupied counter collides, and a crashed run's path stays occupied until the counter advances.

**5. `worktree add` failure is invisible.** The add is piped (`… 2>&1 | tail -3`, `… | tail -n 2`), so the recorded exit status is `tail`'s. Both runs recorded `exit 0`; neither status proves the add succeeded.

## Why it matters

- A crashed creator run does not fail cleanly: it holds a path that the next run adopts, so the fleet's "fresh worktree from `origin/<base>`" rule (doc/agents/parallel-writers-and-subsessions.md) is silently skipped and issues can be filed against a stale tree.
- The adopting run's `--force` removal can destroy uncommitted work belonging to another run, and nothing records that it happened.
- Concurrent invocation is not excluded: the path is a function of the clock, not of the run.

## Suggested fix shape

- Put a per-run unique id in the path (`…-lane-b-<YYYYMMDDTHHMMSSZ>` or the session id), so no two runs can ever name the same directory.
- Refuse, loudly, to adopt a pre-existing scratch path: `test -d` should abort the run with a message naming the path, not fall through to reuse.
- Drop `--force` on cleanup, or gate it on the tree being clean and belonging to this run; record what was removed.
- Stop masking `worktree add` failure: don't pipe it through `tail`, or check the real status.

## Acceptance test (one line)

Two runs of the same creator task — including a run that follows a crashed one — never share a scratch worktree: each path carries a per-run unique id, adoption of an existing path aborts with a loud error, and no run removes a worktree it did not create.

## Filing note

Filed by the builder's-advocate run of 2026-11-17 15:00 CST from the fleet census. The scheduled-task brief that produces these paths lives in the laptop OpenChamber project store (`~/.config/openchamber/projects/path_L2hvbWUvdXNlci9naXQvY29kZQ.json`, task `8560b7ff…` "Improvement issue creator — lane B"), which doc/fleet-schedule-registry.md §2a points at; the brief text and the registry pointer both change under this issue. A triage packet is enqueued in `repo-health-code-pilot` in the same pass.

title: Guard: fleet Cargo.lock drifts from atlas path-deps — second occurrence (first: #8260)

labels.name: epic/fleet-orchestration
labels.description: Reprioritization program epic (2026-11-12)

body:
Twice now, an atlas-search crate gained a dependency and `pkgs/fleet/Cargo.lock` silently fell behind, because fleet-search path-depends on atlas crates whose manifests live outside the fleet workspace:

1. #8260 — missing atlas-proto edge, fixed by hand.
2. 2026-11-14 — atlas-core's `unicode-normalization` (+`tinyvec`) missing; the #10322 switch build died at `fleet-0.1.0.drv` with "no matching package named `unicode-normalization` found". Fixed in PR #10362 by regenerating the lock.

Crane's lockfile-consistency check does NOT catch this: it compares the lock against the vendor dir's copy of the same lock, so a stale lock validates against itself.

Wanted: a cheap guard that fails before a switch build does — e.g. a flake check or smoke step that re-resolves the fleet workspace lock offline against the real manifests (`cargo metadata` / `cargo tree --locked` over the combined source, or a generate-lockfile diff) and fails when the committed lock is not the resolved lock. Should run in the fleet smoke suite (#6400) and/or as a PR check on changes under `pkgs/atlas-search/**` and `pkgs/fleet/**`.

title: Signed/validated routing updates and protection against poisoning, suppression and manufactured loops
body:
## Problem and goal
Signed/validated routing updates and protection against poisoning, suppression and manufactured loops as an independently reviewable contract and implementation increment.

## Version and design basis
Version: V3. Settled design: https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/main/doc/2026-11-13T03-40-00Z_design_id-atlas-summit/part-b/versioned-design.md#routing-validation-and-reputation-policy (section: **Routing validation and reputation policy**).
Tier: **recommended**.
Statement IDs: S1.77, S1.78
Enables: Periodically checks observed topology with nonce-bound probes.

## Scope and ownership
Parent: #9146 (native component/meta parent).
- `pkgs/id/crates/id-sync/src/federation/slices/b24_topology_probe.rs` (new; owner: B24)
- `pkgs/id/crates/id-sync/tests/federation_b24.rs` (new; owner: B24)
Hard dependencies (native blockers): 9110-02 — Minimum output from #9110-02: root federation/slices registry scaffolding and Cargo convention, with this exact module path recorded but not exported before it exists. Slice PRs do not edit shared roots/Cargo/lib.rs; #9110-09 wires versioned public exports after module outputs land.; B23 — Minimum output: Routing-state freshness, periodic validation, and detection of peer/topology changes; stable interface needed by B24.
Soft sequencing (not blockers): none

## Test / evidence first
Create or validate `pkgs/id/crates/id-sync/tests/federation_b24.rs` first. Proposed command: `cargo test -p id-sync --test federation_b24`
Oracle: **invariant** — expected `Probe response binds nonce and peer; stale/vanished/appeared edges update only local scoped routing state.`; verifier: `Independent reference state machine or golden fixture in the dedicated integration test; cryptographic tests use independent vectors, not the implementation under test.`.

## Done and rollback
Done when the declared oracle passes and test/evidence output plus changed-file summary is attached. Research evidence: not applicable.
Rollback: Disable probes and expire probe-derived edges; keep configured peers and signed policy.

body:
Follow-on of #5873 (decision record: `doc/2026-11-08_design_id5873.md`, PR #7614), from parent #5682, under epic #2056.

## What to implement

The terminal surface for object discussions, exactly as decided in #5873. Three parts:

1. **Terminal flow verbs** — extend the shared `world_line` parser (`pkgs/id/src/world_line.rs`) and the three surfaces that already share it (SSH `cmd:` command mode, the `id world join` stdin pump, the `id world` CLI) with `/anchor [confirm|list]`, `/talk`, `/anchors`, `/resolve`, `/queue`, `/flush`. Unknown `/` verbs must keep returning `WorldLine::Message` rather than falling through to chat text.
2. **Textual anchor rendering** — render anchors as `[surface](id://<target-id>)` using the #2259 reference form; render a header line for anchored conversations; always render `disputed` and tombstoned states; degrade unresolvable targets to a bare `id://<target-id>` with no distinguishable error.
3. **Offline compose** — compose and sign locally while disconnected, queue on the existing durable `Outbox` (`pkgs/id/src/envelope_outbox.rs`), replay on reconnect in composed causal order without re-parenting, and surface per-event admission rejections with their reason while keeping the event retryable.

## Gate

Same gate as #6222, and closed today (verified 2026-11-08):

- **#5870** (chat anchor data model) — owns the link-type vocabulary and the part-selector grammar. #5873 §5.2's part-anchor rendering is conditional on it. OPEN, no decision record.
- **#5871** (talk-page semantics) — owns binding authority, lifecycle and the visibility-intersection rules. #5873 §4.3 requires its answer to be binary. OPEN, no decision record.

Do not start this until both land their decisions; #5873 must then be amended if #5870's part-selector grammar cannot be expressed as a URL fragment.

## Acceptance

The eleven invariants in #5873 §7 are the acceptance criteria, in particular:

- One grammar, three surfaces (same `WorldLine` for each verb on all three).
- No terminal-only protocol state; a terminal-produced log projects identically in a GUI client.
- Capability parity: every conversation operation a GUI client has is reachable from the grammar.
- Reference round-trip: printed `id://` references parse back; the `[surface](...)` form is byte-identical to #2259's resolution output.
- No capability leak in rendering (hidden and nonexistent targets render identically).
- Offline durability across process exit, exactly-once delivery, no re-parenting, and visible rejections.

## Out of scope

The anchor data model (#5870), talk-page lifecycle and permissions (#5871), thread resolution mechanics (#5874), notification/watch/presence fan-out (#5875). A full-screen TUI is a later optional rendering over this grammar, not part of this issue.

body:
Follow-up from the capability taxonomy v0 investigation (#2027, record: `doc/2026-10-29T14-05-00Z_investigation_capability_taxonomy/`, PR #2337).

## Goal
`speech.*` for human-conversation mode: `speech.transcribe` (client-side STT, the default), `speech.capture` (audio to server, per-app opt-in), `speech.synthesize`.

## Why client-side first
The world model only needs text, and `chat.say`/events already carry text: client-side transcription costs ~no bandwidth and keeps audio on the device. `speech.capture` exists for devices that cannot run STT (most ESP32s) and for apps that need a better model. Per-app, not global — consent and provider choice differ per app.

## Scope
- Caps and their refusal vocabulary: `cap_denied` + `consent_required` (no consent), `unknown_cap` + `device_lacks_affordance` (no mic), `failed` + `asr_unavailable`.
- `speech.capture` reuses the `media.stream` frame ceiling and consent rules; audio is never retained unless the program asks for an artifact (link the `media.*` follow-up).
- Interaction with the form/chat path: a transcribed utterance becomes a `chat.say`-shaped or form-value input, not a new message type.
- Provider boundary: the taxonomy stays provider-neutral; which STT (browser engine, local WASM model, server ASR) is a runtime choice.

## Acceptance
- Cap names in CATALOG with providers; a test for consent refusal and for a device without a microphone.
- Documented default (client-side) and the per-app opt-in path for server capture.
- No audio bytes in the journal by default.

## Out of scope
Speaker diarisation, wake-word detection, continuous conversation loop, TTS voice selection.


## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] speech.transcribe / speech.capture / speech.synthesize are in CATALOG with providers; transcription is client-side by default and server capture is per-app opt-in, documented
- [ ] Tests cover consent refusal (cap_denied + consent_required) and a device without a microphone (unknown_cap + device_lacks_affordance); asr_unavailable surfaces as failed
- [ ] speech.capture reuses the #2342 media.stream frame ceiling and consent rules; no audio bytes in the journal by default (retention only via an explicit artifact request)
- [ ] A transcribed utterance enters as a chat.say-shaped or form-value input, not a new message type; the taxonomy stays provider-neutral

title: fleet: codify the laptop route forms — tier 0 + 3 methods × 2 shapes + the laptop-ssh wrapper (route-form family)
body:
## Proposal

Codify how this estate reaches the laptop as a **matrix of eight literal forms** — tier 0 (the generic tiered fleet command), 3 methods × 2 shapes, and the `laptop-ssh` wrapper — build the missing fleet-shape forms as endpoint-grade clients, and demote `laptop-ssh` from the primary surface to its codified place: the fallback / simplified tier. Design direction: Drew, 2026-11-23 14:56 + 14:59 + 15:07 CST. Companion to #13654 (the commander subcommand, which becomes tier T1 of this matrix).

## Why a matrix, not a ladder

The platform execution-risk behaviour observed all day 2026-11-23 keys on the **literal command shape** an agent runs: the same laptop operation returned via one route comes back clean, via another trips the check. A single opaque command that papers over every route would hide which form actually works for a given operation, and would remove the raw forms an agent sometimes needs when the wrapper itself is the obstacle. So the raw commands are first-class tiers, not implementation details — and tier 0, the one generic command, still reports exactly which tier served the call.

## The codified matrix — tier 0, 3 methods × 2 shapes, the wrapper

| Tier | Method | Shape | Literal command |
|---|---|---|---|
| T0 | tiered | fleet subcommand | `fleet laptop exec [--timeout S] -- cmd...` — the generic tiered command: walks T1 → T2 → T3 internally and reports the tier that served |
| T1 | commander | fleet subcommand | `fleet commander exec [--cwd D] --timeout S -- cmd...` |
| T2 | http-direct | fleet subcommand | `fleet http exec [--cwd D] --timeout S -- cmd...` (the laptop-agent daemon HTTP API, HTTP legs only) |
| T3 | ssh | fleet subcommand | `fleet ssh exec --timeout S -- cmd...` (binary-owned ssh client contract, below) |
| T4 | commander | raw command | the documented curl recipe against `https://commander.security.cab/mcp` (bearer fetched by name at call time, browser UA, MCP initialize → `tools/call`, SSE `data:` lines) |
| T5 | http-direct | raw command | literal curl to the daemon API (`/health`, `/exec`) through the session proxy, token read from its file at call time |
| T6 | ssh | raw command | the literal `ssh` invocation (pinned host key, proxy CONNECT, multiplexing) written out in full in the mechanics doc |
| T7 | wrapper | simplified tier | `laptop-ssh 'cmd...'` — final fallback, and the one-command form for an agent that doesn't carry the full matrix |

**Composition.** Tier 0 is the first option. It attempts T1 → T2 → T3 **in order, each attempt a literal invocation of that tier's own implementation**, advancing only when a tier fails to *serve* (transport / auth / connect failure or a tier-level timeout) — never on a served result, whatever its exit code — and it names the serving tier. Tier 0 does **not** fall through to the wrapper: when tier 0 fails, the individual forms come into play as their own literal commands — the fleet subcommands (T1–T3) again, because an attempt under tier 0's process shape is a different literal invocation than the standalone subcommand — then the raw commands (T4–T6), then the wrapper (T7). `fleet laptop tiers` prints this table.

## Endpoint-grade builds (the commander pattern, applied to all three methods)

Each fleet-shape form is a real client with a clean contract — auth, timeout discipline, session hygiene — not a script wrapper with flags:

- **Commander (T1)**: bearer resolved in-process from the secrets broker by name (`desktop-commander.machine-bearer`); one MCP session per invocation; `timeout_ms` always sent; spawned processes polled to completion and terminated — no orphaned sessions; remote exit code extracted and propagated.
- **HTTP (T2)**: the laptop-agent daemon already is the endpoint; the work is contract, not transport. `fleet http` builds its ladder from the daemon client's HTTP legs only (broker socket → Cloudflare tunnel → Tailscale CONNECT) — the SSH leg is excluded by construction, so T2 can never silently become T3. Daemon contract as codified: `X-Agent-Token` auth, `/exec` runs the command in its own process group and reaps the whole group on timeout/cancel/disconnect, exit codes propagate, local backstop exits 124.
- **SSH (T3)**: the endpoint-grade shape for SSH is a **binary-owned client contract**: the binary constructs the ssh invocation itself (pinned host key in `~/.ssh/known_hosts_laptop`, `StrictHostKeyChecking=yes`, proxy CONNECT helper, `IdentitiesOnly`) instead of delegating to a shell script; a mandatory overall deadline enforced by the binary (child kill → exit 124; the record stays honest that sshd owns the remote process and cannot be cancelled protocol-side); session hygiene as verbs — fleet-owned ControlMaster path with bounded persist, and `fleet ssh close` to tear the master down. A native in-process SSH protocol implementation is the recorded horizon, not this build.

## Selection doctrine

- Circumstance decides which form is the right way through. There is no single blessed invocation.
- An agent tries each form as **its own literal command** — never a blended invocation.
- **Form visibility**: every result and log line names the exact form used, as method × shape (e.g. `form T2 http/fleet`, `form T4 commander/raw`). Tier 0 reports the serving tier; a tier that failed to serve is reported with its reason before the next is tried.
- Raw forms must exist, stay documented, and stay exercised — they are the route around a wrapper that has itself become the obstacle.

## Constraints carried from #13654 and the standing rules

- **Timeouts required by construction** on every fleet-shape form: no invocation path exists without one (tier 0 sets a per-attempt timeout; commander sends `timeout_ms`; http sets the daemon timeout plus local backstop; ssh carries ConnectTimeout plus the binary deadline).
- Secrets by name only; no token in argv, files, or logs beyond the estate's existing token-file pattern.
- **Deprecation is documentation-and-defaults, not removal**: `laptop-ssh` keeps working for every existing caller (heal/init scripts, crons, lane habits). What changes: the mechanics doc (`TOOLS.d/laptop.md`), the fleet help text, and the shim's own header teach the matrix and the tier-0-first order, and name `laptop-ssh` as tier T7 — fallback / simplified tier.

## Acceptance

- Each fleet-shape form smoke-verified from the sandbox: `hostname` → `amd`; a trivial file read returns its content; a failing remote command propagates its exit code; the serving form is named in the output.
- Each raw form's documented literal command runs as written from the sandbox and returns the same proof.
- Tier 0 serves via T1 on a healthy estate and reports `form T1 commander/fleet`; pinned to a single tier (`--form T2`) it attempts only that tier.
- No secret value appears in any output, log, or file written by the new code.
- The tier table, endpoint contracts, and selection doctrine are recorded in-repo (design record + fleet registry help) and in `TOOLS.d/laptop.md`; `laptop-ssh.sh`'s header names its T7 status.

## Recorded horizon (Drew, 2026-11-23)

Longer-term design threads named alongside this codification, not part of this build: host selection and access without Tailscale; a direct iroh transport for non-Muse agents; a generic pooling system.

## Intake correction to #13654

#13654's premise that the fleet binary's `laptop-agent` domain is a registry stub (exit 69) is **stale**: the domain landed under #10796 (epic #5412) and `fleet laptop-agent health` answers live from the sandbox today (`{"ok":true,...}`). In the Rust client the ladder's SSH leg is an absent stub, so the daemon route is effectively HTTP-only already — T2 builds its HTTP-only ladder explicitly rather than relying on that. #13654 proceeds as T1 of this matrix.

title: mcpx: TestScriptViewCommandTimeoutKillsSpawnedWorkers fails in Fleet executor containers

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

body:
## Summary

`pkgs/mcpx/internal/daemon` test `TestScriptViewCommandTimeoutKillsSpawnedWorkers` fails deterministically inside the Fleet executor container, while it passes on local runs and on GitHub-hosted runners.

## Evidence

- Fleet run (fleet-forks, package suite, `go test ./internal/api ./internal/daemon -count=1`): https://github.com/developing-today-forks/fleet/actions/runs/45251450436
  - `scriptview_test.go:1142: worker 1637 survived the call's timeout: the process group was not terminated`
- Fleet run (fleet-personal, single test, `-run TestScriptViewCommandTimeoutKillsSpawnedWorkers`): https://github.com/dezren39/fleet/actions/runs/45258438959
  - `worker 609 survived the call's timeout: the process group was not terminated`
- Local: the same test passes alone (0.5s).
- The test and `scriptview.go` are unchanged between `origin/main` and PR #13660, so the failure is not caused by that PR.

## Likely cause (unverified)

The test checks `syscall.Kill(pid, 0)` for the spawned `sleep`. In a container whose PID 1 does not reap orphans, a killed orphan can remain a zombie, and `kill(pid, 0)` still succeeds on a zombie. Confirm by checking for zombie state (`/proc/<pid>/stat`) inside the executor, then either make the test treat zombies as gone, or run the container with an init.

## Acceptance

- `TestScriptViewCommandTimeoutKillsSpawnedWorkers` passes in the Fleet executor container.
- Process-group termination behaviour in `scriptview.go` is unchanged.

Found while completing #13577 (PR #13660).

Refs #13660

title: route wall scoping: walled models keep getting hit — scope inference, alias providers for mixed plan+free, per-model free caps
body:
## Spec (Drew, 2026-11-23)

Walled models aren't being skipped and keep getting hit indefinitely. Root-cause it, and work **wall scoping** into the route design: walls must apply at the scope the cap actually binds, a paid side walling must not take the free side down with it, and one capped free model must not kick its free siblings. Automatic scope inference first; config declaration only as the fallback override. Lane WALL-SKIP coordinates; slices land as PRs under this issue.

Related, not duplicated: the point fixes already landed — opencode#2256 (fork combined-signal wall, closed via fork PR #2598), #5295 (proxy known-exhausted gate), #12228 (proxy leaf wall on reset-carrying 429 + auth bench; fork failover slices; merged 2026-11-23, one-week soak to 2026-11-29), fork #2479 (provider-scope gate for single-entry gathered readings). This issue is the scoping layer those fixes don't have. Also linked: #2732 (pace guards advisory at seating time), #10128 (Command Code wall marking), #13675 (DECISION-API — designations + proxy endpoints), #13677 (WIRE-FREE — provider wiring). Census cap shapes: `~/workspace/free-census-2026-11-23.md` (Google free = per-model-per-project; Groq = per-model-per-org).

## Root cause (evidence read first-hand, 2026-11-23)

**RC-1 — Reset-less walls never gate at the proxy.** `bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs`: the only seating-time *exclusion* for quota walls (`knownExhaustedPairs`, #5295) requires the pair's latest quota-bearing failure to carry a parseable reset. `classifyHttp` records a reset only from a seconds-form `Retry-After` header or a body ISO reset (`bodyResetMs`, #13208). Whole classes of real walls record none: HTTP-date `Retry-After` (recorded as `retryAfterMs: null`), duration prose ("try again in 20s"), Google-style `retryDelay: "30s"`, small-number `retry_after: 30` (parsed as NaN), and every 402 (`paymentRequired: true` by construction). The code says it itself at `quotaResetMs`: a quota record with no reset "cannot gate… demotion remains its only handling" — and demotion is reorder-only. Those pairs are walked on every request, indefinitely.

**RC-2 — A later reset-less failure dissolves a recorded wall.** `knownExhaustedPairs` judges only the pair's *latest* quota-bearing failure. Providers vary whether a given 429 carries `Retry-After`; when a reset-less 429 lands after a reset-carrying one, the gate silently disengages mid-wall and the pair is re-hit until another reset-carrying failure happens to land.

**RC-3 — In the fork, wall scope follows the gatherer's shape, not the cap's shape.** `packages/core/src/model-route.ts`: per-model gathered windows → correct model-scope plants (`plantGatheredQuotaWall`, `plantGatheredNearEmptyWall`). A single-entry provider-wide reading → a provider-scope gate (`observeGatheredProviderWall` → `providerQuotaBlocked`) that blocks **every** model of the provider — including free models sharing the provider id with a walled paid plan (the mixed plan+free case). Several entries (per-account readings) → `bindingGatheredReading` returns undefined: no gathered wall at any scope, even when every account reads full; only reactive per-target benches cover it, one failure per session wave (the #2479 symptom — opendesign took 42 attempts in 6h — still open for the multi-entry shape). Nothing infers scope from error shape or sibling evidence, and no config declaration exists to correct a wrong scope.

**RC-4 — All-walled pools walk forever.** The proxy's fail-safe (gate would empty the route → walk anyway) is right when gate knowledge is soft, but when every candidate is gated on a *known* future reset, every request still pays failed attempts on walled legs until the reset. There is no pacing on the last-resort path. (Today's live example: all four OpenCode Go workspaces monthly-walled at once.)

## Design

**Wall units.** Every wall record carries: scope — `(provider, model)` pair, provider, account/key, or pool leg; reason class (quota-window / rate-limit / auth / balance); `until` (stated reset, or a bounded inferred fallback); origin (gathered / attempt / config); evidence. Walls lift on reset or a successful probe — never silently forever, never instantly re-hit in a loop.

**Scope inference (automatic first).**
1. Error/gatherer evidence that names a model (per-model window full, model-scoped quota error) → pair wall.
2. Provider-wide window full → provider wall **only over the models that draw on that window**. A model of the same provider with a recorded success *after* the gate's evidence is exempt — its own pair state governs (sibling-evidence narrowing); its own quota-class failure revokes the exemption.
3. Per-account readings: if **every** account entry of a provider reads known-full, the provider is walled at every account → provider gate from the aggregate. A proper subset states no provider wall (accounts are addressed by alias providers — see below — not by target identity).
4. A sibling model's success under a capped provider narrows a provider-scope wall automatically (rule 2); a capped free model therefore never benches its free siblings once any of them is demonstrably serving.

**Alias providers for mixed plan+free.** Where one provider id carries plan models and free models under one key (unlike OpenCode Go vs Zen, which are already separate), split it into two alias providers sharing the same credential source: `<id>` (plan models) and `<id>-free` (free models only), `instanceOf` the same base. Pools seat free models via the free alias. A wall on either alias never touches the other, because walls key on provider id. The gatherer publishes the plan window against the plan alias and per-model caps against the free alias's models.

**Per-model free caps.** Free providers whose caps bind per model (Google per-model-per-project, Groq per-model-per-org) are judged per model everywhere: gathered plants at pair scope, proxy gates at pair scope (already pair-keyed), and rule 2's narrowing keeps a provider-scope record from swallowing them.

**Config fallback.** An optional `wallScope` field on a provider block — `per-model` | `provider` | `account` — validated by `bin/check-opencode-route-rules.mjs`, consumed by fork and proxy. Absent = inferred. This is the worst-case override when inference gets a provider wrong, not the primary mechanism.

**Reset-less walls (proxy).** (a) Parse the reset shapes real providers send: HTTP-date `Retry-After`, duration prose, `retryDelay`-style duration strings, small-number `retry_after` seconds, `x-ratelimit-reset` headers. (b) Judge the pair's current failure *run* (since its last success), taking the latest reset any failure in the run carried — a reset-less failure no longer dissolves a standing wall. (c) A bounded **inferred wall**: a pair with ≥3 quota-class failures (429 quota or 402) in the demotion window and no success since the first is excluded for a bounded window (15 min, doubling per re-inference, capped 2h); expiry makes the next seating the probe; a success clears the inference and its escalation. This is the combination doctrine translated to the attempt path — repeated plan-limit failures, never one failure, never forever. (d) Fail-safe pacing: when every candidate is gated on known future resets and a walk happened within the last 60s, answer 503 with `Retry-After` = earliest reset instead of walking again; soft gates (inferred/auth) keep today's walk-anyway behaviour.

**Doctrine guardrails (unchanged).** Gathered walls still require the combination (binding window <1% remaining AND plan-limit failures — Drew, 2026-11-10; opencode#2256). One failed call alone never benches anything forever. A failed or stale quota read never idles a pool. Never `disabled_providers` for quota.

## Slices

- **F (fork)** — sibling-evidence narrowing in `providerQuotaBlocked`'s gathered/fed provider gates + all-accounts-full aggregation in `observeGatheredProviderWall`; tests in `model-route.test.ts`.
- **P (proxy)** — reset-shape parsing, failure-run judging, bounded inferred wall, fail-safe pacing in `bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs`; tests in `bin/opencode-route-proxy.test.mjs`. Sequenced with #13675 Part 2 (same file): first proxy PR to merge is the base; the other rebases.
- **C (config/checker)** — `wallScope` validation in the route-rules checker + the first alias split for a mixed provider. Sequenced **after** #13677 and #13675 Part 2 land their config work — no parallel config edits.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Test: a model walled with a stated reset is skipped until the reset or a successful probe (proxy + fork).
- [ ] Test: one capped free model leaves its free siblings serving (per-model caps honoured at pair scope).
- [ ] Test: a wall on a paid alias leaves the free alias (same key) untouched, and vice versa.
- [ ] Test: a mis-scoped (provider-wide) wall self-corrects from sibling evidence — a serving model is re-admitted without a config change.
- [ ] Reset-less quota pairs (429 without reset, 402) stop being walked indefinitely: bounded inferred wall with probe recovery, proven by test.
- [ ] Both checkers + the proxy and fork suites green; root cause and design recorded here (this issue) with the fork link (opencode#2256) bidirectional.

title: SSO (#13658): SAML IdP — design slice (no prior art)
body:
Refs #13658 (Slice 3's SAML half). The story's prior-work search is unambiguous: **there is no SAML prior art in this estate** — no design, no issue, no library. SAML is genuinely new design work, and per the story's slice plan it gets its own design slice before any build.

## Why this issue exists

The #13658 reconciliation ADR settles the OIDC core (separate minimal provider, #13409's stand-up). It deliberately does **not** settle SAML: hand-building SAML (XML signatures, assertion profiles) is the highest-risk protocol work in the program, and the SAML component gets a fresh adopt-vs-build decision of its own, informed by the OIDC build's evidence.

## Design questions to settle (in a dated design record under `doc/`)

1. **Component choice:** adopt a maintained SAML IdP library/component vs build minimal SAML responses into the provider — evaluated against the same hard requirements as the OIDC ADR (signing keys from our PKI — the Slice 2 `saml-signing` key; one account row; #1253 roles as attributes).
2. **Profiles:** Web Browser SSO only, or also ECP/artifact; signed responses vs signed assertions; encryption requirements for assertions.
3. **Metadata:** provider metadata publication + signing (Slice 2 key), SP metadata onboarding model (per-SP config, no dynamic trust by default).
4. **Identity shape:** NameID policy (persistent vs email), attribute mapping onto the provider's account row and the #1253 role set.
5. **Conformance plan:** how the implementation is tested (known SAML test harnesses / interop checks) before any real SP depends on it.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Dated design record under `doc/` answering the five questions, decision recorded on #13658.
- [ ] Build slices filed from the record (not before).
- [ ] No SAML code lands under this issue — design only.

title: SSO (#13658): Slice 2 — issue OIDC (JWKS) and SAML signing keys from the IdP PKI
body:
Refs #13658 (Slice 2 of the story's slice plan). Consumer: #13409 (provider stand-up scopes "JWKS + key rotation" — this slice sources those keys from our PKI instead of provider-local generation). Custody constraints from #13409 / #2060 apply: no pkgs/id keypair custody in the login path; these are the provider's own signing keys, issued by the IdP CA.

## Scope

Using `pkgs/idp-pki`'s `idp-ca` on the laptop `amd`, against the live hierarchy from Slice 1 (root fingerprint `45:49:3A:F7:…:D1:3D`, issuing `B6:9F:25:C5:…:6A:42`):

1. `issue-leaf --profile oidc-signing` — the OIDC token-signing key (RSA 2048, 1095 d per the package defaults).
2. `issue-leaf --profile saml-signing` — the SAML signing key (RSA 2048, 1095 d).
3. Verify both chains (`verify-chain --leaf …` and `--with-crl`).
4. Escrow both private keys in Bitwarden Secrets by name — `idp.oidc-signing.key`, `idp.saml-signing.key` — alongside the CA keys from Slice 1. Key material never in git, never printed, never in logs.
5. Publish the public certificates (the package's `trust/` pattern from Slice 1) and record fingerprints + the JWKS kid convention on this issue: Slice 3's provider publishes the OIDC public key as a JWK whose `kid` is the certificate's SHA-256 thumbprint (x5t#S256), so relying parties can pin either form.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Both leaves issued and chain-verified, including the CRL check.
- [ ] Both private keys escrowed in the vault under the names above; no key material in any commit or log.
- [ ] Public certs published; fingerprints recorded here and on #13658.
- [ ] Automated rollover (story Slice 5) consumes these profiles unchanged — issuance is repeatable, not a one-off.

title: id: research/design: embedded display tier — ESP32 screens (tiny, round, touch) as world presenters
body:
## Direction (Drewry, 2026-11-23)

Support embedded screens as a world-presenter tier, separate from terminal/text rendering: ESP32-family devices (ESP-IDF) driving displays of varied sizes — including very small panels, round panels, and touch-enabled panels. Drewry confirmed this is its own track, distinct from the terminal presenter work (#13623 is terminal-only and is not blocked by this).

Origin: the "IDF tools" reference in #5971's brief resolved to ESP-IDF (see #5971, comment of 2026-11-23). The #5971 conversion research scoped ESP-IDF out as a different surface; this issue takes that surface up deliberately.

## Scope of the research

Produce a research/design record (the #5971 form: one doc PR) answering, with evidence:

1. **Hardware envelope.** ESP32 / ESP32-S3 (and any variant worth naming) with the display controllers this tier should support first: small rectangular (e.g. ST7789-class), round (e.g. GC9A01 240×240), very small panels; touch controllers (e.g. CST816 / FT6236 class). Framebuffer over SPI, PSRAM limits, refresh realities.
2. **Rendering path.** How world state becomes pixels on a microcontroller: ESP-IDF components (esp_lcd, LVGL, esp_new_jpeg and friends), what renders on-device vs. what a gateway renders and pushes (raster/tiles/diffs). Asset conversion belongs at upload time for this tier (fixed geometry known in advance — the opposite of the terminal tier), reusing the #5971 conversion findings where they apply.
3. **Connectivity.** How an ESP32 device joins or is fed: WiFi/BLE/USB-serial, and the bridge pattern if the device cannot speak the world's native transport directly. Session, identity, and input back-channel (touch events as world input).
4. **UI model.** What of a world fits a 240×240 round screen or a very small panel: glanceable state, a small interaction vocabulary, touch gestures. Round and tiny viewports are design constraints, not scaled-down rectangles.
5. **Licensing/dependency posture.** ESP-IDF is Apache-2.0; inventory any component whose license would block bundling, in the #5971 manner.

## Non-goals

- No implementation in this issue; build slices get filed from the research, as #13623 was filed from #5971.
- Does not change the terminal presenter track or the kitty graphics work.

## Acceptance

Research/design record merged naming: the first hardware target(s), the rendering path (on-device vs gateway split), the connectivity/bridge pattern, the touch input model, and the first build slice filed as its own issue.

body:
## Problem
`GatewayService::open` (pkgs/id/src/currency/gateway_service.rs:862-881) replays posted freeze/sunset intents at restart with `moved.map_err(ServiceError::Registry)?`. Any single lifecycle intent naming an unknown currency, or a transition the registry now refuses (e.g. stale/ordering edge, sunset-terminal composition from the #13401 residue work), aborts the whole `open` with `Err`. One dangling intent bricks restart for every currency in the store.

This is inconsistent with the service's own recovery philosophy in the same module: the intent log joins against the ledger in both directions and records mismatches as durable `IntentFinding`s instead of refusing to boot (invariant 7, `reconcile_intents`).

## Evidence
- pkgs/id/src/currency/gateway_service.rs:867-881: `for target_op in ["freeze", "sunset"] { for intent in &all { ... moved.map_err(ServiceError::Registry)?; } }` — `?` propagates `UnknownCurrency`/`InvalidTransition` out of `open`.
- Same file intent/ledger join (reconcile/audit path) appends findings instead of failing open.
- Existing restart test `freeze_survives_restart_via_intent_replay` covers only the happy path (one currency, freeze posted, reopen succeeds); no test covers a dangling/terminal-violating lifecycle intent alongside healthy currencies.

## Acceptance
- `open` boots with healthy currencies even when the intent log contains a posted freeze/sunset that the rebuilt registry refuses (unknown currency or illegal transition).
- The skipped/refused lifecycle intent is surfaced durably (findings log or equivalent operator-visible record), never silently dropped.
- Per-currency final status still matches the posted order for the healthy intents (freeze-then-sunset semantics preserved).
- Regression test: register A+B, freeze A, inject a dangling freeze/sunset intent (unknown currency), reopen succeeds and A is still frozen.
