title: Atlas Python↔Rust parity: six named divergences from the atlas_search.py port (book survey, #13251)
body:
Found by the Atlas book surveys (#13251, surveys A + C). The Rust CLI is presented as a parity port of atlas_search.py; these named divergences are where the parity claim does not hold. The book states the Rust (shipped) behaviour and names each divergence.

1. **search --context default differs.** Python: --context defaults to `local-owner` for both verbs, hardcoded and unvalidated (unknown values fail closed inside the disclosure logic). Rust: search defaults to `fleet-internal`, get-chunk to `local-owner`, unknown value is a hard exit-2 error.
2. **Python get-chunk has --max-sensitivity; Rust get-chunk does not.** Python default `secret-bearing`. Rust: the ceiling arrives via --context local-owner instead; passing --max-sensitivity to Rust get-chunk is a clap error.
3. **Topics/projects LIKE matching diverges deliberately (#5375).** Python records `l.topics LIKE ?` with param `%"<value>"%`; atlas-core escapes `%`, `_`, `\` and the JSON `\"` so a value matches only an exactly-equal JSON element. fixtures/README.md records the deviation and notes "The Python Filters is unchanged and has the same wildcard bug; fixing it is a separate follow-up." filters.rs's "faithful port" header and the byte-parity claim carry this exception.
4. **FTS match expression: three constructions exist.** Rust production (fusion::fts_match_expr) keeps words >3 chars PLUS short digit-bearing tokens. Python hybrid (eval3.py fts_query_hybrid) keeps only >3 chars. Python baseline additionally removes the 23-word STOP list. Only the Rust one ships.
5. **index_depths at pool 0.** Python loops forever (0 doubles to 0); Rust returns vec![0] for IndexFill — a named, intentional non-parity in a crate whose header claims a semantics-exact port.
6. **Python die() inside threaded branches** raises SystemExit in worker threads, ferried to the caller (DieError); observable behaviour matches the Rust port, but backend failures in Python can surface as tracebacks with exit 1 where Rust prints the message — the Rust header calls this out as intentional.

title: Atlas CLI help vs source: ten disagreements in the atlas-search/atlas-stage/atlas-classify help surfaces (book survey, #13251)
body:
Found by the Atlas book survey (#13251, survey A: full CLI dump of the installed binaries, help vs source vs live probes). The book documents source behaviour and calls each of these out; the fixes belong on the help/source side.

1. **atlas-stage has no version flag; atlas-search does.** `atlas-search --version` prints `atlas-search 0.1.0`, exit 0. `atlas-stage --version` / `-V` is a clap error, exit 2 — its `#[command]` sets no `version`. The other four hand-rolled binaries have no version surface either.
2. **atlas-stage's own source header is stale.** It opens with "Two verbs:" and later says "All three are offline" — the binary has six verbs, and `promote` is not offline in the same sense (it needs the embedding model + ONNX runtime). The verb list itself is complete; the counts/framing are wrong.
3. **atlas-stage ingest --language default is misleading.** Help shows `[default: ""]`; source silently replaces an empty value with the staged file's extension. The help never mentions the extension fallback.
4. **atlas-search search --shards is a real flag that help hides.** `#[arg(long, env = "ATLAS_SHARDS", hide = true)]` — absent from --help, fully functional (probed). Its EXPERIMENTAL doc comment (#5755) exists only in source.
5. **--config / --service-url env claims are not clap env.** Help says `(env ATLAS_SEARCH_SERVICE_CONFIG)` / `(env ATLAS_SEARCH_URL)`, but neither arg carries a clap `env =` attribute; the env is honoured by hand. Behaviour matches help; mechanism does not. By contrast --model, --vec-table and --shards really do use clap env.
6. **atlas-classify help gives no defaults; source has several.** Window-days 90, actor `atlas-classify/remainder-sweep`, schema-version 1, reviewer-model `atlas-classify`, --now = current time, max-decisions unbounded — all source-only. The usage text is also printed for --help with exit 2 (no successful help path).
7. **Three binaries have no help path, with two different failure codes.** atlas-classify --help → usage, exit 2. atlas-eval --help → usage, exit 2. atlas-sweep --help → `unknown action`, exit 2. atlas-github-comments --help → `unknown argument`, exit 1.
8. **atlas-search traces report writes files its help never mentions.** Help: "weekly statistics report into the statistics-and-reports source set". Source also writes a Markdown rendering `atlas-statistics-report-<day>.md` into the traces dir and reports both paths (`report_file`, `markdown_file`) in the JSON output.
9. **Via-service eligibility restrictions are in no help text.** --via-service reads as a simple preference; source: a `--backend local` request, a non-default --vec-table, or any --shards spec each disqualify the service route (the third silently, with no attempt at all).
10. **atlas-search feedback help omits the vote-shape rule.** Exactly one of --up/--down, or --get, is enforced only at runtime with an exit-2 message; clap enforces the conflict but not the "at least one" half.

Book chapters carrying the source behaviour: pkgs/atlas-search/book/reference/atlas-search.md, atlas-search-admin.md, atlas-stage.md, atlas-classify.md.

body:
**Commission (Drew, 2026-11-23): build the Atlas book, the same way the fleet book was built.**

The fleet book (55 chapters, live at https://developing-today.github.io/code/fleet/, tracking #13165) is the form to mirror, via the bookwright skill: survey the subject from ground truth first, fix the chapter skeleton before prose, prove coverage mechanically, zero-warning build as a release gate, and join the repo's ONE existing Pages deploy under the subpath **`/code/atlas/`** (a standalone deploy would wipe the mcpx and fleet books).

**Subject:** the Atlas system in this repo — the atlas crates and Worker, the ingest scripts and pipelines, the Turso store and its shards, the embedding pipeline (Snowflake Arctic Embed M v2.0), hybrid retrieval, the `fleet search` consumer surface, the Atlas MCP server, and the REST/CLI access paths.

**The book covers the system as it stands AND the forward design** (the investigation program on #13241 is the source for the planned half):
- Automatic ingest of all data sources (the #9097 Workstream E target list) — sources, chunking, content addressing, model-versioned vectors, shadow-index cutover.
- Query planning — classification, transforms, routed retrieval, fusion.
- Layered search characteristics on top of Snowflake Arctic — hybrid FTS+vector, RRF, metadata pre-filtering as a security boundary, MRL two-resolution indexing, sparse/ColBERT options.
- Reranking — cross-encoder stage over the fused candidate set, model choice, latency budget.
- The single-user recommender — profile, session, and graph signals; no cross-user collaborative filtering.
- Search integration for fleet AND for ID (the #6062 / #9109 Part C line) — one retrieval core behind CLI, REST, and MCP.
- MCP and programmatic access — tool surface, client ceilings, sensitivity tiers as a hard boundary.
- The evaluation programme — golden sets, ablation harness, CI gating.
- Operations: the D1 cache layer, backup/restore, the census, failure shapes.

**Acceptance:**
- Book sources committed beside the subject (mirroring `pkgs/fleet/book/` + `book.toml` placement), built by a Nix package mirroring `pkgs/fleet/docs.nix`, staged into the existing Pages deploy under `/code/atlas/`.
- Live URL verified after deploy; sibling books (mcpx root, /code/fleet/) verified still serving.
- Coverage proved mechanically and stated in the completion report: every CLI command/flag, config key, MCP tool, REST route, crate entry point, and named design in the survey maps to a chapter or section.
- Docs-sync wired the way fleet's is: the DOC-01-style contract where Atlas contributors and agents look (package README / agent docs) names the book, so surface changes update it in the same change.
- Disagreements found between code, help text, and existing docs are filed as issues in the same pass, per the standing file-the-issue rule.
- This issue closes with the full record; #13241 (the program tracking issue) stays open.

Privacy absolutes from the program stand: the book documents the tier system and its enforcement, and publishes no secret-tier content, no credentials, and no private corpus text.

title: id(invites): reject over-cap delegation depth when decoding signed events
body:
## Evidence

`pkgs/id/crates/id-directory/src/invites/event.rs:388-405` (`InviteEvent::from_v2_bytes`) enforces the wire version, body-size limit, and exact postcard consumption, then returns the decoded `InviteBody` without validating its delegation depth. The only current cap check is in `sign_terms` (`:334-354`), so it protects locally minted events but not externally supplied signed event bytes.

Reproduction on current `origin/main`: construct an `InviteBody` with `depth_remaining = 200` and a `parent_digest`, sign it with a valid Ed25519 key, serialize with `to_bytes`, then call `InviteEvent::from_bytes`. It returns `Ok`; `verify_signature()` also succeeds; the decoded depth is 200 while `MAX_SOURCE_DEPTH` is 3. A temporary unit test ran successfully demonstrating this and was removed. Focused test: `cargo test --manifest-path pkgs/id/Cargo.toml -p id-directory repro_from_bytes_accepts_over_cap_depth -- --nocapture` (1 passed).

This is distinct from the closed signing-side fix #13217: that prevents `sign_terms` from producing over-cap events, but decode accepts externally signed events that do not go through that constructor.

## Why it matters

Consumers that trust a decoded, signature-valid invite can observe delegation authority beyond the protocol cap. The parser is the common boundary for serialized invite events, so constructor-only validation leaves the invariant dependent on every producer being this implementation.

## Acceptance criteria

- `InviteEvent::from_bytes` rejects v2 events whose `depth_remaining` exceeds `MAX_SOURCE_DEPTH`, regardless of whether `parent_digest` is present.
- Add a regression test using a correctly signed, directly constructed over-cap body; assert decode fails, and retain valid source/child round-trip coverage.
- Keep valid legacy v1 decoding behavior unchanged.
- Focused id-directory invite tests pass.

title: id(invites): sign_terms accepts child depth above the delegation cap

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

body:
## Evidence

At `pkgs/id/crates/id-directory/src/invites/event.rs:332-343`, `InviteEvent::sign_terms` applies `MAX_SOURCE_DEPTH` only when `terms.parent_digest.is_none()`. A child invite can therefore bypass the cap: `InviteTerms` is public and can be constructed directly with `parent_digest: Some(...)` and `depth_remaining: 255`, without going through `InviteBody::child_terms` (`:526-550`), then `sign_terms` accepts it (the encoded body remains well below the 512-byte limit). `child_terms` itself enforces strict decrease, but it is not the only public way to construct terms.

This makes the signing API accept a child delegation depth outside the documented cap (`MAX_SOURCE_DEPTH = 3`, `:50-52`) and defeats the invariant that delegated authority strictly decreases when callers supply terms directly. I inspected the related invite implementation/issue inventory; closed #12983 delivered the terms extension but does not describe this validation gap. Targeted open/closed searches for `MAX_SOURCE_DEPTH` and child invite depth found no matching tracker; no matching open PR was found.

## Acceptance criteria

- `sign_terms` rejects child terms whose `depth_remaining` exceeds `MAX_SOURCE_DEPTH` (and preserves valid decreasing child terms).
- Add a regression test that constructs `InviteTerms` directly with a parent digest and over-cap depth, asserts signing fails, and retains coverage for a valid child.
- Keep source-invite and existing invite wire/signature behavior unchanged.

title: fleet-queue: sweep_wiring_runs_the_detective_beside_the_recheckers fails on main (whitespace-sensitive source assertion)
body:
## Problem

On current main (`c22ec1948eb`), the fleet-queue test suite has one failing test:

```
turso_queue::closed_bound::tests::sweep_wiring_runs_the_detective_beside_the_recheckers
```

```
thread '...' panicked at crates/fleet-queue/src/turso_queue/closed_bound.rs:822:9:
assertion failed: flat.contains("run_closed_bound_checks( t, req_i64(req, \"closed_bound_limit\")")
```

## Root cause

The test flattens `turso_queue/core.rs` by splitting on whitespace and joining with single spaces, then asserts the call appears as `run_closed_bound_checks( t, ...` — with a space after the open paren, which only holds when the call is formatted across multiple lines.

The call in `core.rs` (line 1654) is currently formatted on one line:

```rust
match run_closed_bound_checks(t, req_i64(req, "closed_bound_limit").unwrap_or(200)) {
```

so the flattened text contains `run_closed_bound_checks(t,` and the assertion fails. The wiring itself is correct — the detective does run beside the recheckers; only the whitespace-sensitive source assertion broke, most likely when the call was reformatted onto one line.

## Evidence

Found while running the full fleet-queue suite for the #13191 repair-verb work: 556 passed, 1 failed (this test). Both `core.rs` and `closed_bound.rs` are untouched by that change — the failure is pre-existing on main.

## Fix options

- Make the assertion whitespace-insensitive (e.g. strip all whitespace from both sides before comparing), or
- Reformat the call in `core.rs` back to multi-line form.

The first is more durable: source-shape assertions should not depend on formatter line-breaking.

title: id-store: admission.rs expect() on Mutex locks breaks the clippy gates on main (PR #13156)
body:
## Defect

`cargo clippy -p id-native-shell --all-targets` (the `clippy-native-shell` gate, #5582) fails on current main — not in the shell crate, but in its dependency `id-store`: the admission module that landed with PR #13156 (#10192) uses `.expect(...)` on `Mutex::lock()` results in production code, and `clippy::expect_used` is denied in this workspace.

Nine error sites, all in `pkgs/id/crates/id-store/src/admission.rs`:

- lines 263, 273 — "follow-up sink poisoned"
- lines 439, 447 — "operation ledger poisoned"
- lines 501, 508, 517 — "outbox journal poisoned"
- lines 696, 784 — (same pattern)

Reproduced 2026-11-23 (Lane QD, while running the clippy gate for #12657 step 2a): `error: used expect() on a Result value` × 9, `could not compile id-store (lib) due to 9 previous errors`. The crate's tests pass (nextest 81/81 for id-native-shell) — this is a lint-gate break only, but it means the clippy-native-shell gate has been red since PR #13156 merged.

## Fix shape

Follow the neighbouring modules' convention for poisoned locks: either propagate the poison as the module's own error type, or scope an `#[allow(clippy::expect_used)]` with a comment arguing the poison case is unreachable-by-construction — the workspace's standing rule (#5950) scopes unwrap/expect exceptions to test modules, so propagation is the preferred shape for production code. The three lock owners (follow-up sink, operation ledger, outbox journal) each need one decision.

## Acceptance

- [x] `cargo clippy -p id-native-shell --all-targets` compiles `id-store` with no `expect_used` errors. (PR #13252, fleet-command run 45171765844: clippy clean.)
- [x] `cargo test -p id-store` (or the admission suites) stays green. (PR #13252, same run: 383 passed, 0 failed.)

title: fix(fleet-dispatch): nix develop commands fail in the fleet-command container (nix config shaped for a daemon that is not there)
body:
## Problem

Remotely dispatched verification commands that use `nix develop` (the documented way to run pkgs/id suites) fail in the `fleet-command` runner container before any user code executes. Three consecutive dispatches of the same command against `developing-today/code` @ `lane-pv-7916` (for #7916) each failed on a different environmental layer:

1. Run [45154835360](https://github.com/dezren39/fleet/actions/runs/45154835360) — `cd pkgs/id && nix develop --command cargo test -p id-caps`:
   `error: experimental Nix feature 'nix-command' is disabled; add '--extra-experimental-features nix-command' to enable it`
2. Run [45155700465](https://github.com/developing-today-forks/fleet/actions/runs/45155700465) — same command with `--extra-experimental-features "nix-command flakes"`:
   `error: the group 'nixbld' specified in 'build-users-group' does not exist`
3. Run [45156461202](https://github.com/dezren39/fleet/actions/runs/45156461202) — same, plus `--option build-users-group ""`:
   `error: home directory "/homeless-shelter" exists; please remove it to assure purity of builds without sandboxing`

So the container's nix is configured for a multi-user daemon shape (build-users-group = nixbld) that the container does not provide, the experimental features are off, and the no-sandbox fallback trips the purity check. Net effect: the dispatch-first verification route cannot run any flake dev-shell command today; lanes fall back to local runs and the gap is invisible unless they read run logs.

## Ask

Make `nix develop` work out of the box in the fleet-build container image (or in the fleet-command action's setup): e.g. ship a nix config in the image with `experimental-features = nix-command flakes` and a build-users-group that exists in the image (or empty with the sandbox/purity shape resolved), so a dispatched command of the documented shape runs the tests instead of the environment. Alternatively, if a different command shape is the supported one for dev-shell suites, record it in `pkgs/fleet/doc/agents/remote-build-and-test.md` and in the dispatch verb's help.

## Evidence notes

- The #7916 change itself was verified locally in the same dev shell on the laptop (full `cargo test -p id-caps` green) and merged as PR #13182; this issue is only about the dispatched route.
- fleet-run caveat from prior art: a green inside the fleet container does not prove sandbox-environment correctness — but here the container cannot start the command at all, which is the defect.

title: fleet dispatch: nix develop commands fail in the fleet-build container (nix config / build-users-group / homeless-shelter purity)
body:
## Problem

`fleet queue dispatch` cannot run a `nix develop`-based command (the standard pkgs/id oracle shape) inside the `fleet-build:full` container today. Verified 2026-11-23 by Lane OR (archer) while verifying the #10191 conformance oracle — four dispatches against `developing-today/code` @ `lane-or-10191`, each failing at a successive environment layer before any test code ran:

1. Run [45146910204](https://github.com/dezren39/fleet/actions/runs/45146910204): `error: experimental Nix feature 'nix-command' is disabled` — the container's nix config does not enable `nix-command`/`flakes`, so plain `nix develop` fails immediately. (The runbook from PR #13128 shows `nix build .#<pkg>` as an example command; that hits the same wall.)
2. Run [45147692449](https://github.com/developing-today-forks/fleet/actions/runs/45147692449) (with `--extra-experimental-features "nix-command flakes"`): `error: the group 'nixbld' specified in 'build-users-group' does not exist`.
3. Runs [45148497025](https://github.com/developing-today-forks/fleet/actions/runs/45148497025) / [45151466620](https://github.com/dezren39/fleet/actions/runs/45151466620) / [45152850260](https://github.com/dezren39/fleet/actions/runs/45152850260) (with `--option build-users-group ""` and HOME/passwd workarounds attempted): `error: home directory "/homeless-shelter" exists; please remove it to assure purity of builds without sandboxing`. Moving the directory aside and rewriting the passwd entry from inside the dispatched command did not clear it — the check appears to run against state the dispatched command cannot change (the build's home is resolved outside the command's environment).

## Impact

The dispatch-first guidance (runbook `pkgs/fleet/doc/agents/remote-build-and-test.md`) works for plain shell/cargo/go commands — proven the same night — but any repo whose checks need its nix dev shell (pkgs/id is the standing example: "pkgs/id work runs in `nix develop`") cannot be verified through dispatch today and falls back to laptop builds, which is what the guidance exists to avoid.

## Ask

Make the fleet-build container able to run `nix develop` / `nix build` commands as dispatched, without per-command workarounds. Any of: bake the nix config into the image (experimental features on, a build-users-group that exists or is empty, a home setup that passes the unsandboxed-purity check), or document a supported container entry/wrapper for nix commands in the runbook and have `fleet-command.yml` use it. Acceptance: a dispatched `cd pkgs/id && nix develop --command cargo test --manifest-path Cargo.toml --test conformance` (or the documented equivalent) reaches cargo and reports the suite result.

Related: #13122 (dispatch unreachable from sandbox seats — separate, seat-side gap).

title: fleet: repo-queue dispatch fails with TLS UnknownIssuer behind the egress proxy (Rust TLS ignores SSL_CERT_FILE)
body:
## Symptom

`fleet queue dispatch` fails on its GitHub POST with:

```
repo-queue: github api POST /repos/developing-today/fleet/actions/workflows/fleet-command.yml/dispatches: io: invalid peer certificate: UnknownIssuer
```

## Evidence

- The seat's egress proxy MITMs TLS; `SSL_CERT_FILE=/run/hatch/egress-tls/ca-bundle.pem` (bundle present, 181489 bytes).
- Go `gh` honors the bundle: pooled `fleet gh api --method POST markdown` succeeds.
- Fleet's own Rust HTTP client does not: the dispatch POST above fails with UnknownIssuer. Same failure for the fleet-run.yml dispatch path.
- Pooled `fleet gh` writes otherwise work (header-defect fix #12500 is installed and verified: 40-char GH_TOKEN, markdown POST exit 0).

## Likely cause

The Rust TLS stack used by fleet's GitHub API calls (repo-queue dispatch path, and probably the queue broker's GitHub client too) does not load the native roots / does not honor `SSL_CERT_FILE`.

## Impact

All `fleet queue dispatch` verification from this seat is blocked. Workaround in use: dispatch the workflow directly via `gh workflow run fleet-command.yml --repo developing-today/fleet -f repo= -f ref= -f command=` through pooled `fleet gh` (Go client, works).

## Suggested fix

Load native roots / honor `SSL_CERT_FILE` in fleet's Rust HTTP client (and audit the broker's client for the same gap), with a regression test that a POST succeeds with the egress bundle present.

title: fix(id-bench): recover stress_gen after interrupted generation
body:
## Evidence

`pkgs/id/benches/world_bench.rs:2126-2132` deletes an existing stress output root before generation, but writes `manifest.json` only at the end (`2249-2253`). If generation exits after creating the root but before writing the manifest, a retry refuses to proceed because the directory exists without a manifest.

Reproduced on the current `origin/main` bench binary: with `ID_BENCH_STRESS_OUT=<fresh path>` and `ID_BENCH_STRESS_HOT_MEMBERS=0`, `--quick --only stress_gen` exits 1 after creating the output directory (`stress world hot-000 needs at least one member`). Re-running with the same output path exits 1 with `stress output root ... exists and holds no stress manifest; refusing to overwrite it`. The failed run leaves generated files behind and no documented recovery other than manual deletion.

## Why it matters

The 100x tier is explicitly expected to hit resource walls, and the run protocol treats such walls as results. Recoverable generator failures (including a resource/interruption during materialization) instead strand the deterministic output path and make reruns fail before useful work can proceed.

## Acceptance criteria

- Generation is recoverable after a failure before manifest publication; retrying the same `(seed, tier, output)` succeeds or reports a clear resumable/cleanup action.
- Never recursively delete an existing directory based only on the presence of an arbitrary `manifest.json`; verify generator ownership/identity, and preserve unrelated files.
- Add a regression test that induces a mid-generation failure, retries with the same output root, and verifies a valid manifest and restorable worlds (or verifies the documented safe recovery behavior).
- Keep manifest publication atomic so consumers cannot mistake a partial generation for a complete fixture.

title: pkgs/fleet docs drift: README variant count + missing design-note citation, fleet-rust-tests comment, services registry laptop-agent naming
body:
Found while surveying for the fleet book (#13165). Documentation drift around pkgs/fleet:

1. `pkgs/fleet/README.md` says `default.nix` exposes "four variant packages"; `mkFleet` returns six attrs (fleet, fleet-serve, fleet-connect, fleet-brokers, fleet-static, fleet-connect-static).
2. The README cites a design note under `pkgs/fleet/doc/2026-11-04T…_design_fleet_multicall_binary/` that is not in the tree (doc/ holds only `agents/remote-build-and-test.md`). The README itself also records the note's "4-byte frame" as a census error against the real 8-byte wire format — the citation should point at wherever the note actually lives now.
3. `.github/workflows/fleet-rust-tests.yml`'s concurrency comment describes push-to-main runs, but the workflow has no push trigger (nightly + dispatch only).
4. `pkgs/deploy`'s services registry names a Nix `laptopAgent` package for the laptop-agent profile while the operational artefact in tree is `laptop-agent.py` — one of the two is stale.

Fix shape: correct each text (or the registry entry), and note the book (#13165) documents the verified behaviour in the meantime.

title: fleet queue: repo-task-v1 schema enums drift from the validator (kind 4 vs 6, repo 8 vs 9)
body:
Found while surveying for the fleet book (#13165). `pkgs/fleet/repo-task-v1.schema.json` and the queue validator disagree on two enums:

- `kind`: the schema lists 4 kinds; the validator accepts 6 (adds `second_pass`, `feature_slice`).
- `repo`: the schema lists 8 repos; the validator accepts 9 (adds legacy `dezren39/nix`).

Tasks valid under the validator can fail schema validation and vice versa. Fix shape: decide which side is canonical per enum (the validator's `second_pass`/`feature_slice` kinds look intentional; the legacy repo looks like a deliberate grandfather) and regenerate/align the other, with a test that keeps schema and validator enums in lockstep.

title: fleet help: stale "later step of epic #5412" wording on shipped domains + stub text
body:
Found while surveying for the fleet book (#13165). Shipped, fully-implemented surfaces still describe themselves as future work from epic #5412's step 1:

- `fleet gh` domain help claims its implementation "lands in a later step of epic #5412" — the gh passthrough is fully implemented (rotation, cache, shadow verbs).
- `fleet laptop-agent` domain help carries the same claim — the client is fully implemented.
- The Available-form stub text still reads "the step-1 skeleton of epic #5412".

Fix shape: rewrite the three texts to describe the shipped behaviour; the stub wording in particular is what an operator sees first when a domain is unusable, so it should name the actual state (not-in-build / narrowed-by-name / disabled-by-config / not-implemented) without the step-1 framing.

title: fleet help gaps: missing/erroring --help surfaces (laptop-agent, gh closures/tiers, queue session, shell, serve, built-ins) + TOP_USAGE omissions
body:
Found while dumping the full help surface for the fleet book (#13165). Several surfaces have missing, erroring, or misleading `--help`:

- `fleet laptop-agent` has no `--help` anywhere: per-verb help invocations fall through to live behaviour (a "poll" of a job literally named `--help` was observed).
- `fleet gh closures` produces no help output at all; `fleet gh tiers --help` errors.
- `fleet queue session status|result --help` treats `--help` as a job handle and errors; the flags are only discoverable from source.
- `fleet shell`'s top-level help lists only `targets` and hides every flag (`--build`, `--detach`, targets semantics).
- `fleet serve` role lists reject `--help` outright; the broker roles have no role-specific help.
- Built-ins (`version`, `capabilities`, `help`) reject `--help` as a usage error (exit 2).
- TOP_USAGE omissions: the fallback group's line omits `complete`; the `release` line omits `[--lane <id>]` that the per-verb usage, help, and implementation all have (same class: `--lane` on heartbeat/checkpoint/fail/complete). The parity test does not cross-check TOP_USAGE.
- Fallback group usage shows `scan <repo> <issue-number>` but `fallback scan` takes no positionals (usage error if given).
- Bridge/agent per-verb help is one byte-identical shared USAGE despite status lines advertising per-verb options.

Fix shape: give every verb a real help path (or an explicit shared usage that names the verb), correct TOP_USAGE, and extend the parity test to cover TOP_USAGE and the no-help surfaces.

title: fleet help: required flags documented as optional (release/checkpoint/cancel/fail) + dead complete --queue flag
body:
Found while surveying for the fleet book (#13165). In the fleet-queue client, four flags are shown as optional in help/usage but are required by the parser (missing them exits 2):

- `queue release --reason` — required by source (#8217 gate), optional in help.
- `queue checkpoint --stage` — required by source, optional in help.
- `queue cancel --reason` — required by source, optional in help. Cancel's default worker is also `fleet-monitor`, not the `repo-worker-code` the surrounding text implies.
- `queue fail --error` — required by source, optional in help. `--reason-class` is a hidden closed enum defaulting to `transient` and appears in no usage string.

Also: `queue complete --queue` is parsed and shown in help but never read anywhere in the source — a dead flag.

Fix shape: correct the usage strings (per-verb usage() in the client support module), decide the dead flag (wire it or remove it), and extend the usage↔parser parity test so required-vs-optional is part of the checked contract.

title: fix(fleet): fleet-command Run step lacks the toolchain on PATH — dispatched cargo commands fail 127
body:
## What happened

A dispatched cargo command fails on the fleet-command runner with
exit 127 before doing any work:

```
Run command step (cwd $GITHUB_WORKSPACE/target):
  bash -euo pipefail -c "$FLEET_RUN_COMMAND"
  FLEET_RUN_COMMAND: cargo test --manifest-path pkgs/fleet/Cargo.toml -p fleet-queue --features client,queue-broker
  -> bash: line 1: cargo: command not found
```

Evidence: run 45150362527 on dezren39/fleet (job 137609977212),
dispatched 2026-11-23 for the #13146 verification; the identical
command with `export PATH=$CARGO_HOME/bin:$PATH;` prefixed runs
(run 45151395564).

## Why

The workflow's Run command step executes on the runner host (not
in the fleet-build container) with `CARGO_HOME` / `RUSTUP_HOME`
pointed at the restored dependency cache — the rustup shims live
in `$CARGO_HOME/bin` — but the step never adds that directory to
`PATH`. Shell built-ins and git work, so trivial probe commands
(the only kind exercised in the first dispatch verifications)
pass; any cargo/go toolchain command fails 127. The runbook
(`pkgs/fleet/doc/agents/remote-build-and-test.md`) shows bare
`--command 'cargo test --workspace'`, which hits this on its
first real use.

title: fleet-command container: dispatched nix develop/build commands fail out of the box (3 stacked env defects)
body:
## Problem

The runbook (`pkgs/fleet/doc/agents/remote-build-and-test.md`) advertises dispatching `nix build` / `nix develop` commands through `fleet queue dispatch` (fleet-command.yml, `fleet-build:full` container). As of 2026-11-23, a plain `nix develop` command fails out of the box in that container on three stacked environment defects, each hit in sequence while verifying PR #13147 (`cargo test -p id-native-shell` in the pkgs/id dev shell):

1. **Experimental features off** — run [45145807796](https://github.com/dezren39/fleet/actions/runs/45145807796): `error: experimental Nix feature 'nix-command' is disabled; add '--extra-experimental-features nix-command' to enable it`. The command context carries no NIX_CONFIG enabling `nix-command flakes`.
2. **Missing build-users group** — run [45146728602](https://github.com/developing-today-forks/fleet/actions/runs/45146728602): after passing the flags explicitly, evaluation succeeded but the build died with `error: the group 'nixbld' specified in 'build-users-group' does not exist`. The container's nix.conf names a group the image does not create.
3. **/homeless-shelter shipped in the image** — run [45147861730](https://github.com/dezren39/fleet/actions/runs/45147861730): with `build-users-group` overridden empty, sandboxing auto-disables in the container and the build then dies with `error: home directory "/homeless-shelter" exists; please remove it to assure purity of builds without sandboxing`.

## Workaround (verified shape, run 45150189636)

```
rm -rf /homeless-shelter; nix --extra-experimental-features "nix-command flakes" --option build-users-group "" develop --command <cmd>
```

## Ask

Make dispatched nix commands work verbatim in the fleet-build:full environment: bake the equivalent of the workaround into the image/workflow env (NIX_CONFIG with `experimental-features = nix-command flakes` and an empty or existing build-users-group; no `/homeless-shelter` in the image, or `sandbox = false` with the purity check addressed). Acceptance: the runbook's example commands (`nix build .#<pkg>`, a `nix develop --command cargo test ...` in pkgs/id) succeed via `fleet queue dispatch` with no caller-side flags or cleanup.

body:
## What

A complete, self-contained documentation book for the `fleet` binary, in a dedicated folder under `pkgs/fleet`, mirroring the form of the existing mcpx book (mdBook: `book.toml` + markdown sources) so the form can be copied for future binaries.

A reader with only the book must be able to understand the binary completely: purpose and architecture, every domain/subcommand/flag with defaults and examples, concept guides (queue lifecycle, placement and remote dispatch, secrets broker semantics, bridge, agent intake, proxy/recovery, Atlas search, gh passthrough), using fleet as a library (the crates and their public APIs), a development guide (including how to add a subcommand and how to add a flag), step-by-step tutorials, and operations/troubleshooting/FAQ/glossary.

## Deployment

Static site via GitHub Pages from this repo (GitHub Actions workflow building the book with the same tooling as the mcpx book). Default github.io address only for now; the custom-domain/CNAME step comes later and is documented in the book's deployment chapter, not wired.

## Docs-sync rule

The change also wires the "update the book in the same change" rule into the places contributors and agents look (pkgs/fleet agent docs and the book's own development guide), following any equivalent pattern the mcpx book already has.

## Acceptance

- Book builds clean with the exemplar's tooling; internal links checked.
- Coverage proven against a full recursive dump of the binary's help surface: every command and flag documented.
- Pages workflow green on main after merge; Pages enabled with source = GitHub Actions (or the single manual step named if permissions block it).

title: id: import ingest — apply a verified export under normal admission rules with a per-entry report (§6.2 step 4; slice 4b of #2852, from #3810)

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: New feature or capability request

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
Slice 4b (ingest half) of #2852, remainder of #3810. The §6 core — export format + import verification (§6.2 steps 1–3) — landed in PR #9396 as slice 4a (`pkgs/id/src/hosted_export.rs`: `build_export` / `verify_import`, 9 tests green at main `3a941eff430e`, verified 2026-11-23). What 4a deliberately left, in its own module doc: "Ingest itself (§6.2 step 4) follows the platform's normal rules and is likewise downstream of a verified import."

## Scope

Apply a verified export at the importing (self-hosted) node:

1. Downstream of `verify_import` only — an export that fails any §6.2 step 1–3 rule ingests nothing (already guaranteed by 4a; this slice must not weaken it).
2. Ingest each verified object under the platform's normal rules (#2030: validity at ingest, counting at view). Import is not a privileged write path: hosted-origin objects are indistinguishable from self-hosted ones at the object layer (§6.2 step 4).
3. Place each verified blob into the node's blob store by its hash, so `document.put` citations resolve locally.
4. Return a per-entry outcome report to the operator: every object and blob named as applied, already-present, or refused with the rule that refused it. Refused entries are reported, never silently dropped (#3810's scope requirement).

## Acceptance

- Round-trip test: store → export → `verify_import` → ingest into a fresh node; the target's canonical object/hash set is identical to the export's set.
- Re-ingesting the same export is idempotent: every entry reports already-present, nothing double-applies.
- An entry that passes verification but fails a normal ingest rule (e.g. validity at ingest) is refused, named in the report with its rule, and does not block the remaining entries.
- Blobs land by hash and are retrievable from the target node's blob store after ingest.

title: fix(pm-dispatch): session-list completeness probe asks for limit=1000, server caps at 200 — cleanup sweep can never list sessions
body:
## Defect

`pm-stack/dispatch/src/opencode.ts` line 9:

```ts
const SESSION_LIST_LIMITS = [1_000, 10_000, 100_000] as const;
```

`listSessions()` probes the OpenCode server with `GET /api/session?limit=<n>` and treats a response shorter than the requested limit as the completeness proof. But the server caps `limit` at **200**: the very first probe (1000) is rejected with HTTP 400 (`Expected a value less than or equal to 200 at ["limit"]`). So `listSessions()` **always throws**, on every call, in the currently deployed build.

## Live evidence (2026-11-23, laptop journal, repeating)

```
[pm-dispatch] task worktree /home/user/git/fleet/dispatch-code-21301 retained: session list unavailable; cannot rule out a live session in the worktree: opencode GET /api/session?limit=1000 failed (HTTP 400): {"_tag":"InvalidRequestError","message":"Expected a value less than or equal to 200\n  at [\"limit\"]","kind":"Query"} — retained
```

## Impact

The dispatch worktree cleanup sweep can never obtain the session list, so it can never rule out a live session in any dispatch worktree — **every dispatch worktree is retained forever**. `~/git/fleet/dispatch-*` worktrees accumulate without bound (disk + clutter), and the sweep's retention log chatter drowns the pm-dispatch journal.

## Fix shape

Probe at the server's actual ceiling: `SESSION_LIST_LIMITS = [200]`. Semantics preserved exactly: a response with fewer than 200 entries is complete; a response at the cap is unprovable and still throws (the sweep stays conservative and retains, with the error naming the cap). Update/extend the `listSessions` coverage in `pm-stack/dispatch/test/opencode.test.ts` to pin the 200 probe and the at-cap throw.

Found during the #6992 pm-dispatch 502 investigation (Lane PG, 2026-11-23).

title: impl(fleet): placement sessions to the queue backend (placement_sessions) — centralize decision state, keep placement decentralized
body:
## Context

Drew's directive, 2026-11-23: improve fleet placement dispatch along the
hybrid lines agreed in chat — dispatch stays **decentralized** (each
seat's fleet binary decides placement locally; that resilience is
deliberate and was proven the same night, when dispatch kept working
while the queue broker's session-proxy leg was down), and only the
**decision state** gets centralized.

Today the placement session records (the `fp_…` handles) live only in a
per-seat JSON file, `~/.local/state/fleet-place/sessions.json`
(`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/placement.rs`). The intake design
(`doc/placement-intake/placement.md`, absorbed under #5413) labeled
that store a stopgap and carried DDL for a dedicated session table.
The queue backend has since consolidated on Turso behind the
queue-broker, so the table lands there as `placement_sessions` (the
Supabase `agent.` schema in the intake DDL is historical). Dispatch
itself was verified end to end on 2026-11-23; the sandbox-seat gap is
#13122. #4986 (placement records on dispatches) is related but
distinct — this issue is the session store only.

## Design (slice 1)

**Schema** — one new table in the Turso queue backend, added to the
`SCHEMA` set in `turso_queue/core.rs` so `ensure_schema` creates it
with `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` on every broker start:

```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS placement_sessions (
  handle       TEXT PRIMARY KEY,   -- 'fp_' || 32 hex chars
  record       TEXT NOT NULL,      -- the full session record JSON;
                                   -- the client record shape is the contract
  state        TEXT,               -- extracted: queued|running|succeeded|failed|cancelled|dispatched
  surface      TEXT,               -- extracted: registry surface id
  submitted_by TEXT,               -- extracted: for list --mine
  run_id       INTEGER,            -- extracted: correlated Actions run
  created_at   TEXT NOT NULL,
  updated_at   TEXT NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS placement_sessions_created
  ON placement_sessions(created_at);
```

**Broker verbs** — new `turso_queue` verbs, dispatched and
authenticated exactly like the existing queue verbs (the broker shell
does not change):

- `/placement-put` `{record}` — upsert by handle (a seat refreshing a
  session's state is the authority for that update).
- `/placement-get` `{handle}` — the stored record, or null.
- `/placement-list` `{submitted_by?, limit?}` — newest first, bounded.
- `/placement-sync` `{records}` — `INSERT OR IGNORE` batch; the
  migration path. Never overwrites a row the backend already holds.

**Client** (`placement.rs` + one transport helper):

- The local JSON store stays the always-available store and the
  **only** input to placement decisions: `build_ctx` and the
  Blacksmith budget reconcile read local state exactly as today.
  Decisions never depend on the backend.
- Session records additionally mirror to the backend, best-effort,
  through a **bounded** broker roundtrip (new helper in the client
  transport: same routes as the queue client — direct broker URL /
  broker socket, else the session proxy — with short timeouts, no
  broker auto-spawn, and errors returned, never a process exit).
- Write path: local commit first (unchanged semantics, unchanged
  lock), then a best-effort `/placement-put`. Any failure is silent —
  a dispatch can never fail or stall because the backend is down.
- Read paths (`session status` / `session result`, the `--followup`
  lookup, `session list`): consult the backend, prefer the record
  with the newer `updated_at` across the two stores, refresh state
  from GitHub exactly as today, and persist the refreshed record to
  both stores.
- Migration of existing local sessions: after a successful dispatch
  commit, and on `session list`, a best-effort `/placement-sync`
  pushes local records the backend lacks (bounded, most recent
  first). Pre-existing per-seat stores converge into the backend
  without an operator step.
- Escape hatch: `FLEET_PLACE_REMOTE=off` disables the remote mirror
  (operator + test use).

## Acceptance criteria

1. Dispatch on seat A; `fleet queue session status <fp_ handle>` on
   seat B (empty local store) returns the session.
2. With the broker unreachable, dispatch + status/result/list behave
   exactly as today (local store only).
3. A pre-existing local `sessions.json` migrates: after one dispatch
   or list against a reachable backend, its records are readable
   from another seat, and sync never overwrites a backend row.
4. Placement decisions (dry-run output, Blacksmith budget accounting)
   are unchanged with the backend up, down, or disabled.
5. Tests name their oracles: backend verb tests against the stub
   pipeline (SQL + reply mapping), client fallback/merge tests
   against a fake remote, and a boundedness test for the transport
   helper.

## Breakdown

- **Slice 1 (this issue):** schema + broker verbs + client mirror
  with local fallback + opportunistic migration + runbook update
  (the broadcast string gains the binary-acquisition block).
- **Later slice (recorded, not in scope):** a fleet-wide Blacksmith
  minute ledger — only if Blacksmith spend grows; the per-seat local
  ledger stays until then.
- **Later slice (recorded, not in scope):** hard cap enforcement at
  decision time (admission control against the caps placement
  currently only steers by).

title: pm-git-sync frozen since 2026-11-23 02:34 CST: uncommitted registry edit in the laptop primary blocks every deploy
body:
## Symptom

`pm-git-sync` (the timer that keeps the laptop primary `~/git/code` on clean main; PM services deploy by merge -> pull, #8171) has failed every run since 2026-11-23 02:34:20 CST:

```
pm-git-sync: FAIL /home/user/git/code working tree is dirty — not pulling. Dirty paths:
 M doc/fleet-schedule-registry.md
```

The primary is frozen at `d3bec26356c4` while GitHub main has advanced well past it (e.g. PR #13134 merged 08:57:48Z is not deployable to the laptop until this clears). Everything that deploys from the primary — pm-console, the opencode-claimant, the rest of the pm-stack — is stale until the sync resumes.

## The dirt (named, deliberately left untouched by the reporter)

- File: `doc/fleet-schedule-registry.md` in `~/git/code`, mtime 2026-11-23 02:35 CST, +22 lines / -0.
- Content shape: a "Surface 2a amended 2026-11-23" note (queue-lane prompts now use `fleet agent next` as intake front door) and a new "Surface 8 — Codex desktop scheduled tasks" section. It reads as another seat/session's registry documentation work written directly in the primary checkout instead of a worktree.
- Per the standing rule for the primaries (stay on main + clean; work happens in worktrees; dirt you did not create is named and left, never stashed/committed/discarded by someone else), the reporting lane did not touch it.

## Ask

The edit's owner: land the change properly (move it into a worktree on a branch, PR, merge) or discard it if it was scratch, so the primary returns to clean main and pm-git-sync resumes. If registry updates are being generated by a tool that writes into the primary, that writer needs a worktree/PR route instead — a generated file that dirties the primary will keep freezing every laptop deploy.

## Evidence

- `journalctl --user -u pm-git-sync.service` from 2026-11-23 02:34:20 CST: repeated FAIL with the dirty path above.
- `git -C ~/git/code status --porcelain` → ` M doc/fleet-schedule-registry.md`; `git diff --stat` → 22 insertions.
- Found during #13112's live verification: PR #13134 (claimant poll gate timeout) is merged on GitHub but cannot reach the claimant until the primary syncs.

title: mcpx: check phase e2e timing tests fail under parallel build load (two runs, two different tests)
body:
**Measured (amd-6, 2026-11-23, during the #2490 openchamber pin verification):** realising the amd config's openchamber package — which builds `pkgs/mcpx` in its chain — failed twice in a row in the mcpx check phase, on a **different** load-sensitive e2e timing test each run, with the laptop saturated by parallel lane builds. Every other mcpx package passed both runs.

Run 1:
```
--- FAIL: TestProxyUpstreamTimeoutIsReachableFromTheEnvironment (3.98s)
    proxy_test.go:44: Post "http://mcpx/v1/chat/completions": net/http: request canceled (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers)
FAIL    github.com/developing-today/code/pkgs/mcpx/internal/e2e 1566.479s
```

Run 2 (one retry):
```
--- FAIL: TestAutostartPingTimeoutBoundsEachReadinessPing (4.87s)
    effect_test.go:3397: at the default autostart.pingTimeout the daemon should start:
        mcpx: no daemon reachable: ... daemon did not become ready
FAIL    github.com/developing-today/code/pkgs/mcpx/internal/e2e 1800.098s
```

Both failures are wall-clock/readiness deadlines expiring under CPU contention, not assertion failures about behaviour. The pattern matches the earlier observation recorded by Lane GS on #12909 (the canonical `nix build .#deploy` stuck in the mcpx check phase ~35 min under multi-lane load).

**Effect:** any full-graph build on a loaded laptop (local package verification, the primary-seat `nixos switch`) can wall on this suite even when the change being verified is unrelated to mcpx. CI on main remains the authoritative gate, but local verification loses its signal.

**Possible directions:** make the two tests' deadlines load-tolerant (deadline scaled by measured startup latency, or retry-once on timeout-class failures only), or split the timing-sensitive e2e cases out of the default check phase into a separately-run suite. Not prescribing; recording the measured failures.

Found by Lane IV, 2026-11-23.

title: Scheduled Bolt — developing-today/code

labels.name: source/dispatch
labels.description: Filed by pm-dispatch

body:

title: fix(fleet): remote dispatch is unreachable from sandbox seats (stale binary + TLS UnknownIssuer on direct GitHub API calls)
body:
## What

Remote build/test dispatch (`fleet queue dispatch`, `fleet queue session`, `fleet shell --target actions`) is landed on main and verified working end-to-end from the laptop on 2026-11-23 (proof runs below). It is **not reachable from Muse sandbox seats** today, for two independent reasons:

1. **The sandbox fleet binary predates the verbs.** The sandbox seat's binary (source rev `d26fa16`, 2026-11-22 build) has no `queue dispatch` / `queue session` / `queue surfaces` verbs and its `fleet shell targets` knows only laptop/codespace/local — no `actions` target. A newer binary rollout to all seats was ordered 2026-11-23 and is tracked outside this issue; this issue is the sandbox-seat record of the gap.

2. **Direct GitHub API calls from the sandbox fail TLS validation.** With the current sandbox binary, `fleet dispatch-test scan` fails immediately:

   ```
   fleet dispatch-test: GitHub API unreachable: io: invalid peer certificate: UnknownIssuer
   ```

   The sandbox's egress path presents a certificate the binary's TLS stack does not trust. Placement's capacity probes and the dispatch-test scan/submit path call the GitHub API directly (not through the queue broker), so updating the binary alone may not restore dispatch from sandbox seats — this needs a verified fix (system CA store use, or routing those calls through a trusted path) or a documented working route for sandbox seats.

## Proof the server side works (from the laptop, 2026-11-23)

- `fleet queue dispatch --repo developing-today/code --ref main --command "echo fleet-dispatch-proof && git rev-parse HEAD" --dispatch --json` → placement picked surface `fleet-personal` (dezren39/fleet) because the developing-today owner showed 62 active jobs vs cap 20 (0 free), dezren39 0 vs cap 40. Handle `fp_30152cf76e232b2e0a3dc89cbc337323`, run https://github.com/dezren39/fleet/actions/runs/45139454074 — completed/success; log shows the command output and the target HEAD.
- `fleet queue session result <handle> --json` returned the full session record (actor: the developing-today GitHub App).
- The same `fleet-command.yml` workflow dispatched raw via `gh workflow run` from the sandbox also completed/success (run 45139195957 in developing-today/fleet), so the workflow layer is reachable from the sandbox — only the fleet binary's own API path is not.

## Acceptance

- From a Muse sandbox seat, `fleet queue dispatch --repo developing-today/code --command 'true' --dispatch --json` returns a handle and the run completes; `fleet queue session result` reads it back.
- `fleet dispatch-test scan` from a sandbox seat prints scope lines instead of the TLS error.
- The agent runbook (`pkgs/fleet/doc/agents/remote-build-and-test.md`) names the working route for sandbox seats once fixed.

## Notes

- The local session store (`~/.local/state/fleet-place/sessions.json`) is a labeled stopgap; under multi-lane load a session read can answer "session store is locked by another fleet-place process; retry shortly" (observed once; retry succeeded). The designed `agent.placement_sessions` table removes this class.
- Placement decision latency observed at ~4-5 minutes from invocation to run creation under heavy fleet load (capacity probes across owners). Not part of this issue's acceptance, recorded for visibility.

- Speed is a feature
- Every millisecond counts
- Measure first, optimize second
- Don't sacrifice readability for micro-optimizations

BOLT'S JOURNAL - CRITICAL LEARNINGS ONLY:
Before starting, read .jules/bolt.md (create if missing).

Your journal is NOT a log - only add entries for CRITICAL learnings that will help you avoid mistakes or make better decisions.

⚠️ ONLY add journal entries when you discover:
- A performance bottleneck specific to this codebase's architecture
- An optimization that surprisingly DIDN'T work (and why)
- A rejected change with a valuable lesson
- A codebase-specific performance pattern or anti-pattern
- A surprising edge case in how this app handles performance

❌ DO NOT journal routine work like:
- "Optimized component X today" (unless there's a learning)
- Generic React performance tips
- Successful optimizations without surprises

Format: `## YYYY-MM-DD - [Title]
**Learning:** [Insight]
**Action:** [How to apply next time]`

BOLT'S DAILY PROCESS:

1. 🔍 PROFILE - Hunt for performance opportunities:

  FRONTEND PERFORMANCE:
  - Unnecessary re-renders in React/Vue/Angular components
  - Missing memoization for expensive computations
  - Large bundle sizes (opportunities for code splitting)
  - Unoptimized images (missing lazy loading, wrong formats)
  - Missing virtualization for long lists
  - Synchronous operations blocking the main thread
  - Missing debouncing/throttling on frequent events
  - Unused CSS or JavaScript being loaded
  - Missing resource preloading for critical assets
  - Inefficient DOM manipulations

  BACKEND PERFORMANCE:
  - N+1 query problems in database calls
  - Missing database indexes on frequently queried fields
  - Expensive operations without caching
  - Synchronous operations that could be async
  - Missing pagination on large data sets
  - Inefficient algorithms (O(n²) that could be O(n))
  - Missing connection pooling
  - Repeated API calls that could be batched
  - Large payloads that could be compressed

  GENERAL OPTIMIZATIONS:
  - Missing caching for expensive operations
  - Redundant calculations in loops
  - Inefficient data structures for the use case
  - Missing early returns in conditional logic
  - Unnecessary deep cloning or copying
  - Missing lazy initialization
  - Inefficient string concatenation in loops
  - Missing request/response compression

2. ⚡ SELECT - Choose your daily boost:
  Pick the BEST opportunity that:
  - Has measurable performance impact (faster load, less memory, fewer requests)
  - Can be implemented cleanly in < 50 lines
  - Doesn't sacrifice code readability significantly
  - Has low risk of introducing bugs
  - Follows existing patterns

3. 🔧 OPTIMIZE - Implement with precision:
  - Write clean, understandable optimized code
  - Add comments explaining the optimization
  - Preserve existing functionality exactly
  - Consider edge cases
  - Ensure the optimization is safe
  - Add performance metrics in comments if possible

4. ✅ VERIFY - Measure the impact:
  - Run format and lint checks
  - Run the full test suite
  - Verify the optimization works as expected
  - Add benchmark comments if possible
  - Ensure no functionality is broken

5. 🎁 PRESENT - Share your speed boost:
  Create a PR with:
  - Title: "⚡ Bolt: [performance improvement]"
  - Description with:
    * 💡 What: The optimization implemented
    * 🎯 Why: The performance problem it solves
    * 📊 Impact: Expected performance improvement (e.g., "Reduces re-renders by ~50%")
    * 🔬 Measurement: How to verify the improvement
  - Reference any related performance issues

BOLT'S FAVORITE OPTIMIZATIONS:
⚡ Add React.memo() to prevent unnecessary re-renders
⚡ Add database index on frequently queried field
⚡ Cache expensive API call results
⚡ Add lazy loading to images below the fold
⚡ Debounce search input to reduce API calls
⚡ Replace O(n²) nested loop with O(n) hash map lookup
⚡ Add pagination to large data fetch
⚡ Memoize expensive calculation with useMemo/computed
⚡ Add early return to skip unnecessary processing
⚡ Batch multiple API calls into single request
⚡ Add virtualization to long list rendering
⚡ Move expensive operation outside of render loop
⚡ Add code splitting for large route components
⚡ Replace large library with smaller alternative

BOLT AVOIDS (not worth the complexity):
❌ Micro-optimizations with no measurable impact
❌ Premature optimization of cold paths
❌ Optimizations that make code unreadable
❌ Large architectural changes
❌ Optimizations that require extensive testing
❌ Changes to critical algorithms without thorough testing

Remember: You're Bolt, making things lightning fast. But speed without correctness is useless. Measure, optimize, verify. If you can't find a clear performance win today, wait for tomorrow's opportunity.

If no suitable performance optimization can be identified, stop and do not create a PR.---

title: opencode-claimant starved: poll.py latency (~60-100s) exceeds claimant's 30s gate timeout, every fire ends gate_unknown with zero launches
body:
## Symptom

The standing opencode-claimant (live mode) has stopped launching entirely. Last 40 fire-log lines in `~/.local/state/opencode-claimant/fires.jsonl` (as of 2026-11-23T08:06Z):

- 21x `gate_unknown` (poll.py exceeded claimant.py's internal 30s gate timeout)
- 10x `sink_claim_failed`
- 7x `already_running`
- 0 sessions launched across all 40 fires

## Evidence

- `python3 pm-stack/opencode-claimant/poll.py` run by hand succeeds (exit 0) but takes **55s–100s wall** with only ~2s CPU — the time is waits (turso ledger reads / broker queries), not compute.
- claimant.py's gate runs poll.py with `timeout=30`, so every fire fails closed at the gate: `candidate discovery unknown. Exiting.`
- A manual poll that completed showed a **real waiting candidate**: task 20708 (`repo-health-code-pilot`, `handed_off`, issue #3321, lane `opencode`, unbound), `cap_room=36`, `stuck_bound=[]`. Work is queued and cap is free; only the gate timeout blocks it.
- Queue backend is healthy (`repo-queue health --worker opencode-claimant` exit 0) and the OpenCode server answers `GET /api/session` in ~0.1s — this is not the backend-outage fallback case, it is poll latency vs gate timeout.

## Filing note (one-queue rule: file + enqueue in same pass)

The triage packet for this issue is enqueued in the same pass via `repo-queue enqueue --queue repo-health-code-pilot` (dedupe `repo-health:v1:triage:developing-today/code:issue:<N>`).

## Acceptance

- A live claimant fire passes the gate and launches the waiting unbound opencode-lane candidate(s), or
- The gate timeout is raised / poll.py is sped up so p99 poll latency fits inside it with margin, with a regression note on which side moved.

## Tests

- Five consecutive live fires each log a gate pass (or a non-gate skip with a reason) instead of `gate_unknown`.
- `poll.py` timed over 10 runs: p99 wall time < gate timeout.

title: bootstrap.sh check: missing 1Password CLI fails the check even when restore was skipped
body:
## What happened

`scripts/muse/bootstrap.sh` check always requires a working `op` CLI + service-account token:

```bash
if command -v op >/dev/null 2>&1 && [ -n "${OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN:-}" ] &&
  OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN="$OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN" op whoami >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  say "check: 1Password CLI and service account answer"
else
  say "check: 1Password CLI/token did not verify (op is restored from ~/tools or login data is missing)"
  rc=1
fi
```

On a non-Muse grok seat run with `--skip restore,persist,init`, the service-account token file is present, but `op` is not on PATH because the restore that would bring `~/tools` / login data back was intentionally skipped. Check logs the line above and sets `rc=1`.

After the three broker tokens were provisioned from BWS and the session broker was started, `fleet secrets list`, `fleet queue health`, `fleet bridge hello`, `fleet agent enroll`, and `fleet agent doctor` all succeeded (all four legs and all four `next` rungs). The check phase would still have failed solely because `op` was missing.

The message itself says `op` is restored from `~/tools`, so treating this as a hard check failure after `--skip restore` is inconsistent with the skip.

## Suggested fix

When the restore phase was skipped (or `op` is not expected on this seat), log a warning and do not fail the check. Keep the hard failure for a full Muse bootstrap that did restore and still cannot verify 1Password.

Seen on developing-today/code `main` at 65f492138, seat name/kind/groups `grok`, 2026-11-23 around 1:24 AM CST. Related: the check then went on to hang on bridge hello, filed separately.

title: bootstrap.sh check: bridge hello hangs with no timeout when the session broker is down
body:
## What happened

`scripts/muse/bootstrap.sh` check runs `fleet bridge hello` with no timeout. On a grok seat that ran:

```bash
bash scripts/muse/bootstrap.sh --skip restore,persist,init
```

the token, tailnet, and fleet phases succeeded, and check itself got as far as:

- `check: laptop agent port answers on the tailnet`
- `check: fleet secrets resolve`
- `check: no session broker answering yet (init.sh starts it; bws fallback still works)`
- `check: 1Password CLI/token did not verify (op is restored from ~/tools or login data is missing)`

Then it blocked on `fleet bridge hello --agent grok --groups grok` (the #12897 fix is in effect; this was not `--groups muse`). There is no timeout around that probe. An outer `timeout 600` killed the script (exit 124) with no `check: bridge hello failed` or `check: all good` line.

`init` was skipped, and the leftover `fleet proxy serve` process on this seat was already dead, so `~/.cache/laptop-agent/broker.sock` had no live broker. Check treats a missing session broker as a warning and then calls hello anyway, which hung instead of failing fast.

After starting `fleet proxy serve` so it picked up the newly provisioned `~/tools/laptop-agent-token`, the same hello returned in seconds (exit 0) and enroll reported `registered: true`.

## Why it matters

`--skip init` (or a stale/dead session broker) turns check into an unbounded hang instead of a named failure. The script's documented "exit 1, the message names the phase" path never runs.

## Suggested fix

- Wrap the check-phase `fleet bridge hello` (and the follow-up inbox read) in a timeout, then treat a timeout as `check: bridge hello failed`.
- Optionally start or restart the session broker before the hello probe when init was skipped or the broker socket is stale, since hello appears to depend on it in practice.

title: Backup Drive leg: restore download throughput measured at ~8 KB/s during the #10300 drill
body:
Found by the 2026-11-23 cold-restore drill for #10300 (report: doc/pm-stack/restore-drills/2026-11.md).

During the drill, a full byte-download of the 30,720,065-byte dashboard archive from the Google Drive leg (`drive:Cloud/cold-store/db-backups/pm-aggregator/2026-11-22/dashboard-2026-11-22.tar.zst`, via the laptop's rclone `drive` remote) ran at roughly 8 KB/s — about 2 MB in 4.5 minutes — and was abandoned; the leg's byte-identity was proven instead via Drive's stored MD5, which matched the R2 copy exactly.

Why it matters: the Drive leg is the fallback if R2 is the lost leg. At the observed rate a Drive-only restore of today's archive takes ~1 h (inside the 4 h core RTO, but it consumes the margin), and the archive only grows. The R2 leg fetched the same archive in ~40 s in the same drill.

Ask: measure the Drive leg's real throughput outside a drill (repeat download, different hours), determine whether the rate is Drive-side throttling of the rclone remote, the remote's configuration (chunk size / pacing), or the path, and record the measured number where the #1514 routine's record lives. If the leg cannot sustain a materially better rate, say so in the backup record so restore planning treats R2 as the only practical full-restore source and Drive as a verify-by-hash copy.

Related: #10300 (drill), #1514 (backup routine), #6816 (execution home).

title: fleet queue fallback: no complete verb -- decide broker-parity disposition recording or record acceptance of release-done
body:
## fleet queue fallback: no `complete` verb — fallback completion is only `release --outcome done`

Observed 2026-11-22 during the session-proxy outage (Lane FN's closeout, recorded on #12777 by Lane GR): the GitHub-fallback verb group had neither `unblock` nor `complete`. The unblock half landed with #12777 (PR #13021: `fallback unblock`). This issue is the remaining half's own home so it is not silently dropped by #12777's close.

Current state: in fallback mode, completion is `release --outcome done` — holder-scoped, `--summary` required. That covers the basic "work landed" record. What it does not carry is the broker `complete`'s disposition/evidence shape (the fix-class completion checks that `verify-disposition` reads back), so a task completed from a fallback seat leaves a thinner record than one completed through the broker.

Ask (design first, small): decide whether fallback completion needs broker parity — a `complete` verb (or a release extension) that records a disposition in the marker stream in a shape `verify-disposition` can consume when the broker returns — or whether `release --outcome done` + the summary is the accepted fallback contract, in which case record that acceptance here and close. Either outcome closes this issue; what it must not do is sit undecided.

Related: #12777 (parent gap, closed), PR #13021 (fallback unblock).

title: id-store: bound untrusted paging cursor size before hex decoding
body:
## Evidence

`pkgs/id/crates/id-store/src/array_query.rs:481-483` passes the caller-provided `Cursor` string directly to `hex_decode`. That helper (`:366-377`) first allocates `Vec::with_capacity(s.len() / 2)` and decodes every byte before the cursor authentication/shape checks. `Cursor::from_string` explicitly accepts an unvalidated string, and `next_page` accepts it as input.

A very large malformed cursor therefore makes each page request allocate roughly half its input size before returning `MalformedCursor`/`UnauthenticatedCursor`. If the paging API is reachable from a remote caller, an oversized cursor can cause avoidable memory pressure or OOM; repeated requests multiply the cost. The existing body/cursor shape is fixed-size except for caller-bound tenant/namespace strings, so an explicit practical cap (or a cap derived from the issued-format maximum) is feasible before decoding.

## Acceptance criteria

- Reject cursor strings longer than a documented maximum before allocating decoded storage.
- Ensure the maximum still admits every cursor that `seal_cursor` can legitimately issue for supported scope/address limits (or define and enforce those limits consistently).
- Add a test proving an over-limit cursor returns promptly as malformed without invoking unbounded decoding/allocation; retain round-trip, tamper, and context-binding tests.

title: id: implement #5751 invite terms extension — InviteBody target/uses/depth/redeemer/parent, postcard versioning, 512-byte budget
body:
Refs #5751, #12922.

## Scope

Implement step 1 of the #5751 design record's implementation shape (§5): extend the signed invite event's body with the delegation terms the record specifies. Today `InviteBody` (`pkgs/id/crates/id-directory/src/invites/event.rs`) is a fixed-layout format carrying only inviter / ticket_digest / group / role / expires_ms — none of the §2–§4 terms exist in code yet, and every later #5751 step (redemption journaling, per-link listing) plus the #5959 §7 `capability_pin` term (#12922) attaches to this terms object.

- Extend `InviteBody` (postcard, versioned, per #5674): `target` (group, or world + its fronting group), `uses_cap: Option<u32>` + redemption counting, `depth_remaining: u8`, `parent_digest: Option<[u8; 32]>`, `redeemer: Option<[u8; 32]>`.
- Enforce the §1 budgets: event body ≤ 512 bytes as a hard parser limit (an over-budget body is refused at decode), and the paste form ≤ 512 chars at mint.
- Defaults per §3/§4: source invites under open delegation mint `depth_remaining = 1` (policy may raise to at most 3), moderator-grant invites default 0; link invites default to 7-day expiry and a 25-use cap unless the inviter sets otherwise.
- The existing fixed-layout events are the v1 wire form: the versioned body must keep reading them (or name the migration explicitly) — do not silently break invites already minted.

## Dependency / ordering

This is the prerequisite slice for #12922 (invite `capability_pin` term): the pin is one optional field in the terms object this issue creates. #12922's redemption side additionally rides #12921 (baseline store + release-record resolution).

## Test oracles

- Round-trip: a body carrying every term encodes/decodes byte-identically; a v1 fixed-layout event still parses.
- Budget: a body encoded over 512 bytes is refused at decode; mint refuses a paste form over 512 chars.
- Terms: redeemer-pinned invite refuses a different redeemer and accepts the pinned one; depth never increases along a re-mint (child depth < parent depth); default expiry/use-cap land when the inviter sets neither.

Design of record: #5751 §1–§5. Filed by Lane HH (archer) from the #12922 premise check, 2026-11-23: #12922 named this terms object as its home and no tracking issue existed for it.

title: id: add `class` field to ProviderManifest + shipped/reserved class table (#5999 §2.4/§10 follow-up)
body:
Refs #5999 (§2.2–§2.4, §10 follow-up 1), #12921 (gated on this), #5959 §10.

## Scope

Implement the first follow-up named in the #5999 diff-semantics record (§10): the record is a design deliverable and deliberately landed no code, and no implementation issue was ever filed for this follow-up — this issue is that filing, and its first slice.

- **`class` field on `ProviderManifest`** (`pkgs/id/crates/id-caps/src/world_caps.rs`): a class id, as registry data — explicitly not prefix parsing (§2.4 rejects coupling to `is_sensor_cap`). Every registered provider entry carries its class from the §2.2 table.
- **The shipped class table**: the nine classes of §2.2 (`cap.none`, `world.presence`, `chat.read`, `chat.write`, `world.records`, `world.schedule`, `device.screen`, `device.keyboard`, `device.location`) with their §2.2 member assignments for all 19 current registry names, **plus the reserved classes of §2.3** (`fs.sandbox`, `fs.read.arbitrary`, `net.out`) so the first `fs.*`/`net.*` provider lands with a warning slot instead of none, **plus the `unknown` class** (§2.4: disclosing, subsumed by nothing).
- **Name → class lookup** through the manifest field: an unregistered capability name maps to `unknown` (§2.4, mirroring the ledger's `<unknown>` usage bucket); a class id not in the shipped table also resolves to `unknown` at lookup time (fail-closed).
- **Table version**: the class table is versioned with the client build (§2.4); expose the current version as a constant the baseline/diff work (#12921) records alongside a comparison.

## Out of scope

- The comparison itself, the baseline store, the connect stage, and the notice surface — that is #12921, which this issue gates (§10 of #5999; §10 of #5959: "the `class` field on `ProviderManifest` remains #5999's own follow-up and gates it").
- The registration-time "class id must exist in the shipped table" check (§9.3) — it belongs with whichever change first registers an `fs.*`/`net.*` provider.
- Final notice wording — #5960's wording review owns the copy; §2.2's sentences are the semantics.

## Test oracles

- Every name in the production registry maps to exactly the class §2.2 assigns it (table-driven test over all entries).
- The reserved classes of §2.3 exist in the shipped table with their ids, and no current registry name claims one.
- An unregistered name resolves to `unknown`; a manifest class id outside the shipped table resolves to `unknown`.
- Existing id-caps suites stay green (the field addition must not break the generated `CATALOG` view or any manifest consumer).

Design of record: #5999 §2.2–§2.4, §10. Consumer: #12921. Parent program: #5955.

