body:
# Build performance: fleet cargo builds pile up — lock orphaned, per-worktree target dirs, GNU ld storm (measured 2026-11-10)

Drew's order 2026-11-10 18:26 CST: "make the build and test take less and share resources. run targeted tests instead of every one, change to a different linker, crate split, and so on."

Trigger: laptop load ~31 on 16 cores with 131 rustc/cargo/ld processes; THREE fleet queue lanes simultaneously running `cargo test -p id --features web` in separate queue worktrees — ~40 GNU ld linkers at ~2.0–2.5 GB RSS each (~30 GB aggregate), ~34 rustc (~17 GB). RAM was fine (49/123 GB); the cost was CPU/linker pileup slowing everything on the host.

## Measurement — representative verification: `cargo test --lib --features web web::markdown` in pkgs/id

Source for all runs: `git archive origin/main` @ `45638b8643281de354b3e41145f873cdd4ac81bb`, byte-identical scratch copies, run through `~/tools/fleet-build-lock`. Peaks are machine-wide process counts sampled every 2s (they include other lanes' processes — that is the point: they show the fleet-wide pileup each run lived in).

| Run | Config | Wall | Load at start | Peak rustc | Peak GNU ld | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| BEFORE | sccache wrapper; no `jobs` cap in cargo config; GNU ld | **1024s (17m04s)** | 30.61 | 37 | **38** | 266 passed, RC=0 |
| AFTER | + `jobs = 8` in `~/.cargo/config.toml`; lld via `rustflags = ["-C", "link-arg=-fuse-ld=lld"]` | **1144s (19m04s)** | 21.02, spiking to ~128 mid-run (two NixOS system builds + a clippy lane competing) | 62 (incl. nix builds) | **3** | 266 passed, RC=0 |
| SHARED | AFTER config; a second, separate source tree pointed at the AFTER run's target dir | **1s** | falling 46→17 | 4 | 0 | fully fresh, RC=0 |

Honest read of the wall numbers: the cold-build wall did NOT improve in this pairing. The AFTER run paid (a) a one-time fingerprint change — new rustflags invalidate sccache entries, so it compiled cold (fleet Rust sccache hit rate fell 67% → 46% across the measurement day), and (b) far heavier competing load than the BEFORE run. The structural wins are the ones that compound:

- **The GNU ld storm is gone**: machine-wide GNU ld peak 38 → 3, and the remaining 3 were other builds. Our links now run lld — verified on the wire in the rustc command line (`-C link-arg=-fuse-ld=lld`). No ld.lld RSS sample was captured (links were too brief for the 2s sampler); the BEFORE-era GNU ld RSS of ~2.0–2.5 GB each was observed live.
- **The jobs cap now binds every cargo invocation**, not just lock users (see lock findings below).
- **Shared target dir works**: a duplicate verification of an identical tree drops from ~17 min to 1s; differing trees still reuse all ~580 dependency-crate builds and only rebuild changed workspace crates. One targeted run produces a 7.4 GB target dir — multiplied by per-worktree dirs this is also the disk problem in #6797 (103 queue worktrees on disk; two measured at 92 GB and 64 GB; /home 87% full).

## Findings

### 1. The build lock exists but was never wired in
`~/tools/fleet-build-lock` (2026-11-04, flock, FLEET_BUILD_SLOTS default 2, defaults CARGO_BUILD_JOBS to half the cores) is referenced by NOTHING in ~/tools, the fleet surfaces, or ~/.config. Lanes run bare `cargo test`. Slot files in ~/.fleet-build-locks/ sat untouched during today's 3-way pileup.
**Lock proof (live)**: with a measurement build holding slot 1, a second invocation took slot 2 immediately and held it for a 25s sleep; a third invocation acquired a slot only at T+30s, after the sleep released. The cap of 2 holds — when the wrapper is used.
**Fix applied**: the damage from bypassing the lock is now bounded at the config layer (below), and the AGENTS.md build-discipline bullet (companion PR) routes lanes through the lock. The lock itself remains cooperative — it cannot force a caller that ignores it.

### 2. Config change applied to the laptop (reversible)
`~/.cargo/config.toml` (backup kept at `~/.cargo/config.toml.bak-20261110-buildperf`):
- `[build] jobs = 8` — half the 16 cores, applies to EVERY cargo invocation by the laptop user, including lanes that skip the lock. `CARGO_BUILD_JOBS` env still overrides.
- `[target.x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu] rustflags = ["-C", "link-arg=-fuse-ld=lld"]` — see linker decision.
- Unchanged: sccache rustc-wrapper, CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0, SCCACHE_DIR, 50G cap.
Note: the rustflags change alters build fingerprints, so each worktree pays ONE full rebuild on its next build; after that the new fingerprints are the shared norm.

### 3. Linker decision: lld now; mold blocked on a nix change + generation switch
- mold is NOT installed on the laptop. `ld.lld` IS (lld 21.1.8, system profile) — wired in via user cargo config above: reversible, no generation switch needed.
- The old mold park ("gated on step 0 / PR #3674", task 5379) is STALE: PR #3674 merged 2026-11-02. Mold remains available as a future step if lld proves insufficient, but it needs a nix config change + generation switch, which this lane was ordered not to run tonight.

### 4. sccache: live and shared for compilations; links/artifacts were the unshared part
Stats 2026-11-10 ~19:20 CST: 14,160 compile requests, 53.39% overall hit rate, Rust 46.40% — down from 69.35% earlier the same day because of fresh-target churn across ~103 worktrees plus the deliberate fingerprint change. One of today's lane runs set `RUSTC_WRAPPER=` (empty), bypassing the cache entirely; the AGENTS.md bullet now forbids that. sccache already shares compilations across worktrees; the per-worktree CARGO_TARGET_DIR was defeating sharing of links and final artifacts — fixed by the shared-target-dir practice proven in the SHARED run above (1s).

### 5. Crate split (#3195 / #3447): foundation landed, all 7 steps open and parked/blocked
pkgs/id workspace already includes `crates/id-core` and `crates/id-native-shell`. Step issues, all OPEN, all priority/high + expedite (checked 2026-11-10 ~18:47 CST): #4403 step 1 (parked), #4405 step 2 (parked), #4406 step 3 (parked), #4407 step 4 (blocked), #4408 step 5 (claimed+parked), #4409 step 6 (parked), #4411 step 7 (parked). #3195's own data agrees with today's: cold check ~16 min while the tests themselves take 12s — the cost is compilation fan-out, which is exactly what the split attacks. Evidence comment posted on #3195.

### 6. Side discovery: origin/main did not compile pkgs/id --features web
`pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs:1263` calls `serve_pull_policy(_started_server_config.as_ref())` but the binding at line 1243 (`#[cfg(feature = "world")]`) is `started_server_config` — E0425 on origin/main @ 45638b86. The measurement copies carried a scratch-only fix for this line. A fix already exists in flight in a queue worktree (task 14074 / #5119 lane) — flagged here for cross-reference, not filed as a duplicate.

## Follow-ups
- [ ] Wire a shared per-package CARGO_TARGET_DIR into the queue claimant/lane launch path (practice proven here; AGENTS.md bullet in the companion PR).
- [ ] Consider raising FLEET_BUILD_SLOTS or making the lock mandatory in the claimant once the shared-target practice lands (duplicate builds become cheap; contention changes shape).
- [ ] Re-measure the cold id test build after the lld fingerprints are the warm norm, under comparable load, to get a clean before/after wall number.
- [ ] Unpark the crate-split steps (#4403, #4405, #4406, #4409, #4411) — they are the long-term fix for test-build fan-out.

Cross-refs: #6797 (per-worktree target dirs / disk), #3195, #3447, #4403, #4405–#4411, #5119.

body:
Implementation follow-up for #6805 (Atlas search Worker cache policy). The decision record is on #6805 (task 14163, lane code-d, 2026-11-10). Of the adopted policy, exactly one piece is worth building now; the rest is deliberately deferred behind named scale triggers recorded on #6805.

## Build now: gated manual purge route for the search cache
- A gated Worker route that purges the cached entry for one query key (the per-query Durable Object in pkgs/atlas-search/worker/src/cache_do.ts), for "this result is wrong, drop it" operations. Per-prefix purge too if the key structure makes it trivial; if not, record why not on this issue.
- Gate: same auth posture as the Worker's other non-public routes; purge is an operator action, never reachable from the search path.
- A purge must be verifiable: after purge, the same query re-runs the fan-out and re-caches (test: seed entry -> purge -> next search is a miss that re-caches).

## Explicitly NOT in scope (deferred behind triggers recorded on #6805)
- Corpus-generation (registry epoch) key component: trigger = first same-space re-ingest changing >5% of chunks, or a user-visible stale-result complaint.
- LRU eviction sweeper + index DO: trigger = 10,000 cached queries or 1 GB aggregate cache storage.
- Any TTL: none, per Drew's standing order on #6805.

## Acceptance
- Purge route merged with tests (purge-then-miss-re-cache; unauthenticated purge refused).
- The two deferred triggers are restated in the Worker README or cache_do.ts header comment so they are discoverable where the code lives.

## Ask

Drew, 2026-11-10: after the #8187 redesign, the queue events table is the append-only audit trail — every claim, lane assignment, session bind, park, wake, completion and failure writes an event carrying task id, queue/pool, platform, lane, model (provider/id/variant) and session id. But there is no fleet verb to READ one task's timeline: `fleet queue show` is an unknown command, and today the history is only readable by querying the store directly (the #8187 acceptance read task 11300's events 161565-161659 that way).

## Wanted

`fleet queue history <task-id>` (name negotiable) that prints one task's full event timeline in order: timestamp, event kind, actor/worker, lane, platform, pool, model, session id, and the reason/note fields where present (lane_assigned reason, park ready-condition, queue_reset scope event 161670 is the shape to match).

- Marks are shown as recorded; a missing mark prints as absent, never invented.
- Human table by default; a --json form for lanes/scripts.

- Run it on task 11300 and show the full ordered trail (claimed, parked, woken, lane_assigned with reason, completed) matching the event ids recorded under #8187.

title: _openai provider: self-contained main OpenAI door that does it all without Codex (Drew top priority)

labels.name: expedite
labels.description: Important - do this very soon, before anything not expedited

body:
## Drew's direct order (2026-11-10, pool-intelligence chat) — TOP PRIORITY

"make _openai that does it all without codex" — supersedes the prove-the-Codex-sync mandate for the openai.main door.

## Problem

The openai.main door's credential is fed by the Muse: `codex-sync.ts` copies `~/.codex/auth.json` into the store and stamps the credential `externalRefresh`, so the provider itself never refreshes it. When the sync path broke, the door auth-died for ~a day (0/9,897 Authentication on 2026-11-10's pool-intelligence window) while quota reads called it healthy. openai.alternate already proves the self-renewing pattern: its own in-store OAuth credential (chatgpt-headless), refreshed in-process, no Codex involvement (#8102 self-renewal audit).

## Build

A self-contained `_openai` provider door for the drewrypope ChatGPT account:

- Own credential in the OpenCode credential store under its own integration id, obtained via the fork's existing OpenAI OAuth flows (seeded from the currently-valid drewrypope tokens if that avoids a fresh consent; the seeded row must NOT carry the externalRefresh stamp).
- Own refresh token, refreshed in-process by the provider (Integration connection resolve), exactly like openai.alternate. No reading `~/.codex/auth.json`, no codex-sync in its path, no Muse involvement at any point.
- Direct HTTPS plan auth to the ChatGPT backend in-process (native openai provider wire), no proxy hop.
- The Codex sync must never write this door's credential (explicit guard + test in the fork).
- Config: seat `_openai` as the main door in `openai-plan` (replacing openai.main's seat; openai.alternate untouched). Keep the openai.main definition until `_openai` is proven, then retire the Codex-sync dependency for the main door.

## Proof standard (traffic, never a quota read alone)

- route_attempt rows under the `_openai` provider id: successes, or — while the weekly quota wall lasts (reset Fri Nov 13 08:28 CST) — attempts that pass auth and fail only QuotaExceeded.
- A successful in-process token refresh cycle in the provider's own store with `~/.codex/auth.json` untouched/unread.
- Negative proof: the door still works with the Codex sync path disabled for it.

Refs: #7991 (closed, the auth-death incident), #5705 (Luna re-lead off openai.main), #8102 (self-renewal audit). Fork: developing-today-forks/opencode.

title: opencode-claimant: slice-1 fire implementation diverges from packet spec (supervision selection, hard-rule labels, audit fields)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: effort/m

labels.name: epic/opencode-platform
labels.description: Reprioritization program epic (2026-11-12)

body:
## Summary

`pm-stack/opencode-claimant/claimant.py` is the deterministic fire implementation for the opencode execution lane (slice 1 of #3026). It runs, and its atomic bind/recovery mechanics are correct — but reading it against the packet spec shows several steps are not implemented, and one supervision branch is inverted. All references are to `main` at the time of filing.

Found during the live fire at 2026-11-09T12:22Z while chasing a repeated `bind_failed` skip.

## 1. `candidates_seen` is always `[]` (step 6)

`claimant.py:681` calls `log_fire(mode, [], launched, cap_room, skips)`; the same hardcoded `[]` appears at `:654`, `:663`, `:668`. The fire log's `candidates_seen` field therefore never carries the candidates, so the record cannot answer "what was eligible at this fire" — it only shows launches and skips. Every `fires.jsonl` line to date has `"candidates_seen": []`.

`gate_step()` (`:333`) and `cap_step()` (`:355`) both discard the poll data they fetch.

## 2. No single-instance lock, no bounded pool

The packet describes the fire as launching "distinct candidates in parallel under a bounded pool and a single-instance lock". `launch_step()` (`:427-634`) is a plain sequential `for` loop, and `claimant.py` contains no `fcntl`/`flock`, no thread pool, no `concurrent` import.

Consequence: two overlapping fires both poll, both see the same unbound candidate, both create a session, and only the second bind wins — the loser's session is an orphan the fire deletes (`:579-589`). That is survivable, but it is not what the packet promises, and the orphan-delete path is exercised in practice (see the `bind_failed` skips in `fires.jsonl` for 2026-11-09T10:01Z, `13932`).

Note `~/.local/state/opencode-claimant/claimant.lock` exists on the host, which suggests a lock wrapper existed at some point outside the script.

## 3. Supervision diverges from the #4758 recovery rule, with an inverted marker test

`supervision_step()` (`:204-330`) reimplements stuck-bound detection instead of consuming `poll.py`'s `stuck_bound` (which the module docstring and the packet both designate as the source), and the reimplementation disagrees with the spec on four points:

- **Inverted terminal-marker test** (`:249-257`): when a session *has* `time.idle`/`outcome` (`has_terminal` true) the code falls through to delete + reclaim; when it has *no* marker (`has_terminal` false) it `continue`s. The spec's case is the opposite — the stuck session is the marker-less, silent one, and a terminated session is not the recovery target.
- **No lease-expiry gate.** The packet says to note a live-lease binding and let Tend's fleet-watchdog see it. `claimant.py` never reads `lease_until`, so a bound-but-unprompted task can be reclaimed while its lease is still live.
- **No 30-minute silence gate** (`ACTIVE_WINDOW_MS`) and **no active-set check**. `poll.py.is_stuck_bound()` (`poll.py:164-198`) requires both; supervision does not. So a session created shortly before the fire, awaiting a prompt, is deletable.
- **No step 1e.** When `attempts >= max_attempts` (`:265` guards with `<`) the task is skipped entirely — it is never terminally failed with `--error "bound session <id> unavailable without terminal outcome; attempts exhausted"` and the `launch_failed_attempts_exhausted` execution record. Those tasks sit bound and dead with no watchdog-visible terminal state.

The zero-message verification (`:266-287`) and the delete-before-unbind ordering (`:298-324`) *are* correct, and I verified at 2026-11-09T12:22Z that seven sessions deleted by this path are gone from `GET /api/session` — so the ordering fix (#4758's core) holds. The selection criteria around it do not.

## 4. Hard-rule label check is missing

The packet hard rule: never launch for a task whose issue carries `held`, `user/owned`, `do-not-merge`, or `do-not-auto-edit`. `launch_step()` never inspects issue labels — grepping the file for `do-not-merge`, `user/owned`, `do-not-auto-edit` or `held` returns nothing. A handed-off packet on a held issue would launch today.

## 5. Step 4e (launch agent-note) is not implemented

Nothing in `claimant.py` posts `agent-note:v1 state=handed off` naming task id + session id after a bind. The prompt at `:602-611` is also abbreviated: it does not inline the queue runbook (step 4d), only the packet, and it omits the lease-heartbeat cadence guidance beyond a one-line mention.

## 6. Minor: gate does not call the CLI `health`

Step 2 specifies running `repo-queue health` for the four queues. `gate_step()` (`:339-352`) relies on `run_poll()` alone. The outcome is equivalent for the launch decision, but the per-queue health line no longer appears anywhere in the fire record.

## 7. Recovered tasks are eligible in the same fire, not the next

The packet says "a task recovered during supervision is eligible on the next fire, not this one." `main()` runs supervision (`:644-646`) and then `launch_step()` re-polls (`:470`), so a task recovered seconds earlier is launch-eligible in the same fire. Harmless today (the fired run's candidates were unchanged by recovery), but it means the retained start-of-fire candidate list the packet describes is not what the launch loop uses — `launch_step` re-polls three times (`:441`, `:470`, `:497`).

## Suggested split

The mechanics worth fixing first are **3** (wrong sessions are selectable, and exhausted tasks never terminate) and **4** (a hard rule that can be violated). **1** and **5** are record-keeping gaps that make every fire's log harder to audit than the packet claims.

## Gap

#5703's design step 4 — "instead of 'reinstall the units,' the boot check verifies spool freshness + last ack; a stale ack surfaces like today's missing-timer finding" — is only half implemented.

- #6148 (closed 2026-11-05) added the init restore block (`~/hatch/tools/init.sh`, ~L401-433): if `quota-recorder.timer` is not `is-active`, reinstall the units from `~/tools/quota-recorder/`, daemon-reload, `enable --now`. That catches a missing or stopped timer.
- Nothing checks whether ticks are actually **landing**. The file-first spool (`~/workspace/goals/stewardship-commission-recurring-review-and-dispatch/hidden_files/visibility/quota-records-YYYY-MM.jsonl`) can stop growing, or accumulate `turso-error` receipts / a non-zero `pending`, while the timer stays active. The DB then goes quiet with no signal — the same silent-gap class #6148 fixed for the units, one layer up.

## What to add

1. A freshness check (init prelude, or a tiny timer next to the recorder): age of the last record `ts` and of the last ack's `through` in the current month file; trailing `turso-error` count and `pending` in the last receipt.
2. Surface the result where the other boot findings already surface (`~/logs/init-status`, and a genuine staleness counts in init's failure total), so it is comparable to today's "missing timer" finding. Optionally feed the /quota view too — #1175 owns read-side freshness there.
3. Thresholds must respect the recorder's fail-soft contract: a recording gap is the alarm; a transient flush error that a later tick self-heals is not.

## Context

Residual of #5703, closed as superseded by the already-landed file-first spool → Turso path (#5690 / PR #6655). Deployment mechanism for the units is #5770. Read-side freshness: #1175. Laptop/sandbox copy drift and the broken laptop FLEET path: #6830.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A stale spool (no new record, or unacked beyond threshold, timer still active) produces a visible finding, not silence.
- [ ] A healthy recorder (ticks landing, acks through) produces no finding.
- [ ] Verified once with a simulated gap: timer active, spool file untouched for the threshold window.

Parent: #6022 (placement policy). Related: #6062 (ID-graph publication format), #6267 (note_submission pilot), #3125 (provenance registry), #5669 (Atlas staging and sensitivity tiers).

Implement the placement policy from #6022 in the existing note_submission pipeline. This issue does not redefine the submission envelope or ID relation vocabulary, and it does not replace the #6267 pilot or #6062 publication-format design.

## Scope
- Classify submissions into the canonical home chosen by the placement policy: workspace/memory (not published), repo document, registry-selected Zettelkasten corpus, or ID-native publication when the #6022/#6062 eligibility and format are satisfied.
- Keep each submission in the Turso submission DB with content hash and provenance spans; preserve source system, machine, date, author/owner and sensitivity decision.
- Enforce staged review and human promotion. Uncertain classification or sensitivity remains staged; nothing auto-commits or auto-promotes.
- Record canonical identity and source revision/hash on any approved projection; maintain an auditable mapping of source to destination.
- Use Atlas physical tiers `public`, `internal`, and `secret` only after applying the separate source/caller sensitivity ceiling. Default to `internal`; public/secret changes are explicit.

## Acceptance
- Table-driven tests cover every note class in #6022's decision table and their selected destination, Atlas treatment, and ID-native eligibility.
- Uncertain/unsupported destinations stay staged and are not published.
- Approval is rechecked immediately before publication; rejected/held attempts leave an audit record and do not push.
- Repo and Zettelkasten projections preserve provenance and cannot silently become a second canonical owner.
- ID-native publication calls the format from #6062 and existing writer/capability authority; no parallel relation or permission schema is introduced.
- A small end-to-end test proves stage → human approval → selected destination and verifies content hash/provenance against the submission record.

## Dependencies
Blocked by #6022 design review/merge and #6062 publication-format decision. Reuse the #6267 submission DB pilot.

## Acceptance criteria

- Submissions are classified into exactly the #6022 canonical homes (workspace/memory unpublished, repo document, registry-selected Zettelkasten corpus, ID-native publication when #6022/#6062 eligibility + format are met).
- Every submission stays in the Turso submission DB with content hash, provenance spans, source system/machine/date, author/owner, and its sensitivity decision.
- Uncertain classification or sensitivity remains staged: nothing auto-commits or auto-promotes, and promotion is a recorded human action.
- Any approved projection records its canonical identity and source revision/hash, and the audit trail can reconstruct who promoted what, when, and why.

body:
Follow-on 1 of the staging-shard ingest gate design (#6057). Design record: `doc/2026-11-08T13-45-00Z_design_atlas_staging_shard_ingest_gate/`.

Depends on the staging-tier registry from #5669. Parent: #6018.

## What this implements

The gate's **record and state machine** — the audit trail the gate exists to produce, and the fail-closed rule that makes every later stage checkable.

1. **Gate record** — one durable row per batch in the internal registry DB: batch (staging unit) id, stage reached, per-stage verdict (`pass` / `fail` / `skip` + reason), reason codes, row counts, content hashes, and the publish manifest id when published. Written at the sensitivity of its batch: counts, classes, row ids and locations only — never content (design §8).
2. **State machine** — `open → closing → gated → published | quarantined`, with the transition set owned by the aggregator (#5669). A batch in `quarantined` retains its staging DB (archived, not deleted).
3. **Fail-closed rule** — a batch with no verdict for a stage has not passed it. Absence of a record is never success; only the write stage (empty batch) and publish (zero survivors) may record `skip`, and each requires a recorded reason. `skip` never advances a snapshot id.
4. **Three-strikes quarantine bound** — a batch quarantined on the same reason code three times escalates to `needs-review` and stops auto-retrying (design §5.5).
5. **Resume-at-failing-stage retry** — a retried batch re-enters at the stage that failed, except `write_invalid` / `write_bypass`, which require the producer to fix and re-write (design §5.3).

## Done when

- A deliberately failing batch, fed through the aggregator, lands a gate record naming the failing stage and reason codes, is quarantined, publishes nothing, and is not retried past three strikes.
- A batch with a missing stage verdict is rejected as not-passed (a test asserts the fail-closed rule directly).
- The gate record for a secret-tier batch contains no content (a test asserts the redaction).

## Out of scope

The five stage checks themselves (follow-ons 2–5 of #6057), and the staging schema/provisioning (#5669).

## Acceptance criteria

- One durable gate-record row exists per batch: batch id, stage reached, per-stage verdict (pass/fail/skip + reason), reason codes, row counts, content hashes, and the publish manifest id when published — counts/classes/ids/locations only, never content.
- The state machine implements exactly `open → closing → gated → published | quarantined`; a quarantined batch retains its staging DB (archived, not deleted).
- Fail-closed is enforced: a stage with no recorded verdict has not passed, and absence of a record is never treated as success (covered by a test).
- Transition ownership follows the #5669 staging-tier registry, as the design specifies.

Implementation follow-on for the design recorded for #6053 (design doc: `doc/2026-11-08T09-15-51Z_design_atlas_license_capture_ingest/` — PR linked from #6053; parent gate #6024; substrate #3125; detection survey #5979).

## Scope

1. **Schema**: add the `ingest_repo_provenance` table to the #3125 provenance registry exactly as designed (fields, PK (repo_id, ingest_generation), append-only). Migration + invariant tests for I1–I4 (PBT over the registry: generation monotonicity, D.6 flag derivation, SPDX parseability).
2. **Detection cascade at ingest**: GitHub license API → licensee → ScanCode (notice files only) → manifest fields → manual, recording `detection_source`, `detection_evidence` (notice file path + content hash), and `detector_version` per row. Every external ingest writes its provenance row in the same transaction window as its first chunks (I1).
3. **D.6 derivation**: `d6_applicable` computed from `has_license_notice` only (`no`/`contested`); `yes` remains unemitted until the #6024 lawyer answer lands.
4. **Re-evaluation surface**: implement the §5 latest-generation difference query against a versioned `policy_eval` stub (zone/license/flag inputs), plus the tombstone-generation purge-candidate listing.

## Acceptance

- Ingesting an external repo with a detectable license produces a provenance row whose SPDX expression, evidence hash, and zone match a hand-checked fixture set (incl. an escaped edge: unlicensed repo → `license_spdx` NULL row, `d6_applicable = no`).
- A detector-version bump re-evaluates from recorded evidence without network fetches (test with network disabled).
- The policy difference query returns exactly the repos whose treatment changes between two rule versions on a fixture registry.

Design authority: the #6053 design record — deviations need a design note amendment, not a silent change.

## Acceptance criteria

- Ingesting an external repo with a detectable license writes an `ingest_repo_provenance` row (PK (repo_id, ingest_generation), append-only) in the same transaction window as its first chunks, with SPDX expression, evidence hash, and zone matching a hand-checked fixture set — including the escaped edge: unlicensed repo → `license_spdx` NULL row, `d6_applicable = no`.
- Invariant tests cover I1–I4 with named oracles (generation monotonicity, D.6 flag derivation from `has_license_notice` only, SPDX parseability) — PBT over the registry where the invariants allow.
- A detector-version bump re-evaluates from recorded evidence with the network disabled (test proves it).
- The §5 latest-generation difference query against the versioned `policy_eval` stub returns exactly the repos whose treatment changes between two rule versions on a fixture registry, and the tombstone-generation purge-candidate listing works.

body:
## What happened

Two independent observations in one OpenChamber scheduled lane run (lane `262eb403-3347-4a7c-ba6b-e7bc263ca853`, worker `repo-worker-code`, 2026-11-08 ~08:40–09:10Z, queue `repo-health-code-pilot`).

**1. A claim I made came back stamped with another lane's id.**

```bash
repo-queue claim --queue repo-health-code-pilot --worker repo-worker-code \
  --lease-seconds 2700 --lane 262eb403-3347-4a7c-ba6b-e7bc263ca853
```

returned task **12016** with `"lane_id": "code-w"` in the response, and the row in `tasks` carried `lane_id = code-w`. The `claimed` event detail for that claim also recorded `lane_id: code-w`.

Context for that same task from `events`, all within ~6 seconds:

| event id | at | lane_id |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 26782 | 08:41:02 | `code-m` |
| 26783 | 08:41:02 | `code-w` |
| 26784 | 08:41:02 | `code-l` |
| 26785 | 08:41:03 | `262eb403-3347-4a7c-ba6b-e7bc263ca853` |

Four different lane ids claimed the same task in two seconds, and the row kept the third one. My own checkpoint then failed with `task 12016 is not claimed by repo-worker-code`, and `heartbeat` failed the same way — so the claim was live in the response but not addressable by the worker that made it.

**2. Other lanes' live claims carry *my* lane id.**

At 09:07Z, `SELECT id, lane_id, lease_until … WHERE status='claimed' AND lease_until > now` showed tasks **12832** and **12851** holding live leases with `lane_id = 262eb403-3347-4a7c-ba6b-e7bc263ca853` — a lane id this session never used for any claim. (This run's actual claims were 12722, 11049, 11938, 12840.)

## Why it matters

- **Attribution is wrong in both directions.** The `lane_id` column is the only per-lane attribution the queue keeps, and it currently cannot be trusted to say who claimed a task. Any per-lane throughput, cost, or "which lane abandoned this" report built on it is measuring noise.
- **The claim is not addressable by its claimant.** Observation 1 is worse than misattribution: `checkpoint` and `heartbeat` both rejected the claim with `not claimed by repo-worker-code`, so a worker that wins a claim can be locked out of the row it just won. That is a direct route to the evaporation pattern #6528 describes.
- **It looks like the same family as #7068 and #6985** (a losing claim call returning another lane's live claim; two lanes claiming one task), but the symptom here is different: the claim *succeeded* and still carries a foreign `lane_id`.

## What is not established

I have not reproduced this from the broker side, and I have not determined whether `lane_id` is being overwritten by a concurrent `UPDATE … SET lane_id = ?` from another lane's claim statement, or whether the value is being echoed from a stale read. The `claim_repo_task` SQL in the binary is a single `UPDATE … WHERE id = (SELECT … LIMIT 1) AND status IN ('queued','parked')`, which should be atomic for the row selection — so the suspect is either the `lane_id` parameter binding/validation path, or a second writer touching the same row.

## Suggested investigation

1. Reproduce with N concurrent `claim` calls against one queue, each with a distinct `--lane`, and assert every response's `lane_id` equals the caller's. Repeat several hundred times; this looks timing-dependent.
2. Check whether `claim_repo_task` validates `lane_id` against the `lanes` table (there is a `SELECT lane_id, worker_id, queue, enabled FROM lanes WHERE lane_id = ?` in the binary) and what it does with an unknown id — #4780 and #6853 suggest this path has history.
3. Check for any other writer to `tasks.lane_id` besides `claim_repo_task`.
4. Decide whether `checkpoint`/`heartbeat` should accept a claim whose `lane_id` matches the caller's `--lane` even when `worker_id` comparison fails, so a mis-stamped claim is still recoverable by its owner.

## Related

- #7068 — losing claim returned another lane's live claim
- #6985 — task claimed by two lanes concurrently
- #6528 — handoff tasks burning attempts and becoming unclaimable
- #7358 — bare `claim` silently defaults to the shadow queue (hit in this same run; the work was parked back)

## Acceptance criteria

body:
## Problem

Queue task 11164 (repo-health-code-pilot, triage of issue #6310) was claimed and worked by two worker lanes at the same time, despite the runbook's premise that \"claiming is atomic across lanes\".

## Evidence (2026-11-08, all times UTC)

- Lane code-x (cron repo-queue-worker-shift-x, run started 2026-11-07 17:59 CST): claimed task 11164, triaged issue #6310, and posted its completion agent note on #6310 at 2026-11-08T00:05:58Z (note footer: `agent-note:v1 agent=repo-worker-code state=done task=11164 at=2026-11-08T00:08:00Z`).
- Lane code-a (cron repo-queue-worker-shift, run started 2026-11-07 18:00 CST): `fleet queue claim --queue repo-health-code-pilot --worker repo-worker-code --lane code-a --lease-seconds 2700` returned task 11164 as a fresh claim in the same window; `fleet queue lane 11164` created lane ledger row 3413 at 2026-11-08T00:05:36Z with assigned_lane `direct`, and a `claimed` checkpoint was accepted.
- Minutes later, lane code-a's heartbeat returned the verdict `heartbeat_task: task 11164 is not claimed by repo-worker-code` — the task had already reached its terminal state under the other lane's work. Lane code-a stopped per the runbook heartbeat-verdict rule and posted no duplicate note.

## Why it matters

The atomic claim is the fleet's only protection against double work when lanes overlap by design (the lane locks are per-lane, not global). A double claim wastes two shifts on one task and risks divergent writes (notes, labels, terminal verbs) on the same issue; here the collision was visible only because both lanes post agent notes on the issue.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Reproduce or explain from queue event history how task 11164 came to be claimed by two lanes (concurrent claim race, completion-then-reclaim, or another path), with the task's claim/complete event rows cited.
- [x] `claim_repo_task` (or its successor) cannot return a task that is already claimed-and-live or already terminal to a second claimer; a regression test or a documented invariant check covers the concurrent-claim case.
- [x] If the root cause is that a completed task was re-presented, the claim path filters terminal tasks and the event history for task 11164 shows where the filter failed.

## Verification (2026-11-23)

- `fleet queue timeline 11164 --json` returns event **1792** (`claimed`, 2026-11-08T00:05:23Z) and event **1842** (`completed`, 2026-11-08T00:06:12Z). Together with the incident's lane code-a claim/ledger evidence at 00:05:36Z, this places code-a's second claim after the initial claim and before completion: a concurrent live-claim race, not completion-then-reclaim. The old history has no separate event for code-a's second claim, which is the observability defect; merged PR #10939 records refused live by-id claims and exposes displacement events in timelines.
- The single-winner invariant is covered by merged PR #8107 (`claim_race_two_lanes_exactly_one_winner_per_task`, task 11895 fixture); PR #10939 adds the same-worker/two-lane refusal event; PR #11803 makes lifecycle verbs reject another lane's claim. On current main, `fleet shell --target local --cwd "$PWD/pkgs/fleet" -- cargo test -p fleet-queue --all-features claim_race_two_lanes_exactly_one_winner_per_task` passed (1 test).
- The terminal-representation condition does not apply to this incident: the second-claim evidence predates event 1842. Current `default_pick_predicate` only selects queued, eligible parked, or eligible handoff work (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/turso_queue/claim.rs:2143-2153`); claimed and terminal statuses are excluded.

The repo-health OpenChamber queue worker cannot claim any task: the queue lane registry rejects its registered lane id.

Verified 2026-11-07 ~08:07Z by the event-hook worker (`repo-worker-openchamber`, generation 1912):

- `fleet queue health` (laptop binary) succeeds and reports the Turso store (`fleet-queue-dezren39.aws-us-east-1.turso.io`): `repo-health-openchamber-pilot` = 32 queued, 0 claimed, 5 parked, 11 blocked.

- `fleet queue claim --queue repo-health-openchamber-pilot --worker repo-worker-openchamber --lane openchamber-a --lease-seconds 2700` returns: `claim_repo_task: unknown lane_id openchamber-a` (broker exit 4).

## Impact

Per the runbook §1/§0b, a lane-id rejection from a healthy backend is a verdict, not a backend failure: the worker stops and reports rather than retrying or switching to GitHub fallback. All 32 queued OpenChamber tasks are unclaimable by this worker until the registry is fixed.

## Fix needed

Register/restore lane `openchamber-a` (worker `repo-worker-openchamber`, queue `repo-health-openchamber-pilot`) in the lane registry backing the Turso queue store, or publish the replacement lane id and update `repo-queue-worker-instruction-openchamber.md` to match. Verify with a live claim by the hook worker.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `fleet queue claim --queue repo-health-openchamber-pilot --worker repo-worker-openchamber --lane openchamber-a` (and the code/opencode/nix lane equivalents) succeeds against the Turso store, or the lane registry is corrected so the pinned lane ids in the runbooks are the registered ones
- [ ] A claim rejected for lane reasons is distinguishable in logs from a backend outage (verdict vs failure) without reading broker internals
- [ ] Regression coverage: a test or probe claims with each fleet lane id (code-a/b, opencode-a/b, openchamber-a/b, nix-a/b) and asserts no `unknown lane_id`

# Phase 4 of #6582 — closing read-site inventory: disposition every frame/peer value read in fleet-proxy + fleet-dispatch against the validated-and-bounded contract

Phase 4 (closing inventory) of design #6582 — *validate it where you read it: one validated-and-bounded contract for the fleet proxy's frame and peer values* (design doc: `files/designs/code-fleet-proxy-validated-bounded.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace; audit at origin/main `b0c472d94`).

## Scope

GATED on Phases 1–3 of #6582 (#6516 + #6518 frame fields, #6509 repetition counts, #6512 dispatch arithmetic) — do not start the inventory until they have landed; keep this issue `status/blocked` until then.

Inventory every read site in `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy/src` and `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-dispatch/src` where a caller-frame or peer value is consumed, and disposition each one against the contract (validated where read — type, range, arithmetic, count — present-but-invalid refused in the surface's own error shape): **conforms** (name the guard), **filed** (a follow-up issue, if a gap is found), or **deliberately local** (the reason named). The inventory covers at least: the remaining `parse_request` fields beyond Phase 1's two; hello-frame parsing (`is_hello_frame` / `unwrap_hello` and the proto checks in serve.rs); `read_frame`'s declared-size handling; the `client.rs`, `stdio.rs`, `shims.rs` and `udp_forward.rs` readers; the tunnel's read expectations (`tunnel.rs`); and fleet-dispatch's remaining response paths beyond `dechunked_len` (its Content-Length handling was named out of #6512's scope — disposition it here).

Land the contract's final statement form: confirm the `http.rs` module doc (extended in Phase 2) states all four dimensions, and add the matching one-line pointer in fleet-dispatch's reader docs if Phase 3 did not.

## Required dispositions (name each one explicitly in the closing evidence)

- (a) **Unadvertised ports:** a frame naming a valid u16 port outside the hello's advertised services table — refused at the boundary, or stays routable? Answer from `do_request`'s actual consumers (who legitimately addresses a non-table port today), not by assumption.
- (b) **The `body` field's shape rule:** today any non-null JSON value is forwarded verbatim (serve.rs:635). State whether verbatim forwarding is the contract (the body is the *service's* input, validated by the service) or a gap, with the reasoning.
- (c) **The #6515 brokers cross-reference:** the queue/secrets brokers' transports carry the same stance under tracker #6515 (their Content-Length leg #6527 landed copying `http.rs`'s rule). Decide whether the contract statement is cited from the brokers' docs, or stays proxy-local with a pointer recorded here.
- (d) **Pin verification:** confirm Phase 1 landed the two rulings recorded on #6582 as recorded — port 0 refused at the frame boundary, `token_file: null` treated as absent — and cite the tests that pin them.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An inventory (posted on this issue or landed in the module docs) lists every read site above with a disposition and file:line evidence.
- [ ] The four required dispositions (a)–(d) are each answered explicitly.
- [ ] Any gap found is filed as its own issue and linked; no gap is fixed silently inside the inventory.
- [ ] The contract statement's final form is present in `http.rs`'s module doc (all four dimensions) and design #6582 is commented with the closing evidence.

*Filed by the design architect as Phase 4 of #6582. Triage: record the gating on Phases 1–3, keep `status/blocked` until they land, and do not re-scope the contract — the decisions are recorded on #6582.*

body:
## Problem

The fleet queue backend (Supabase project muse-dev2, `agent.tasks` via PostgREST + queue-broker) degraded and then went fully inaccessible during 2026-11-06 ~06:20Z–08:10Z+ (still down at filing time), blocking ALL queue verbs fleet-wide mid-evaluation.

## Observed progression (all times UTC, 2026-11-06)

- ~06:20Z onward: Supabase Management API SQL intermittently returns **HTTP 544** "Failed to run sql query: Connection terminated due to connection timeout" (~50% of calls, including trivial queries); `select 1` succeeds at 06:35Z.
- ~06:40Z: one full status census succeeds. After that, aggregate queries consistently time out; single-status indexed counts succeed sporadically.
- ~07:05Z: queue-broker `/list` returns **HTTP 522** (PostgREST via Cloudflare, 90s timeout).
- ~07:35Z: broker `/list` returns **HTTP 503** "upstream connect error or disconnect/reset before headers … delayed connect error: 111" — PostgREST cannot connect to Postgres at all.
- ~07:39Z: brief recovery flicker (`select 1` OK, one count query OK), then:
- ~07:55Z onward: Management API returns **HTTP 400** "Database is possibly not accessible at the moment" for every query, including `select id from agent.tasks where id=9553`.

## Impact

- No claims, heartbeats, completions, or enqueues are possible while it lasts — every lane cycle that touches the queue fails, and per the expire-leases semantics (#6463) evaporated claims keep burning attempts against caps.
- This is the second queue-backend outage in three days (cf. the 2026-11-04 PostgREST outage with a DB rollback during the outage, recorded in orchestration state). A rollback/restore during that event silently regressed queue totals (done 4241→4158), so post-recovery reconciliation of queue state is owed this time too.

## Ask

- Restore service and confirm: PostgREST → Postgres connectivity, connection limits/pooler health on muse-dev2, and whether a restart/rollback occurred (if a rollback occurred, publish the point-in-time and reconcile queue rows written after it).
- Post-recovery: re-run the queue census (the dead-at-cap evaluation's staged requeues are waiting on a stable backend) and verify counts against the 06:40Z baseline: code-pilot done 4885 / blocked 231 / cancelled 197 / queued 172 / parked 163 / claimed 21 / failed 2.

Filed from the 2026-11-06 dead-at-cap evaluation, which this outage partially blocked.

## Acceptance criteria
- Post-recovery queue census published on this issue and reconciled against the 06:40Z baseline recorded in the body (code-pilot done 4885 / blocked 231 / cancelled 197 / queued 172 / parked 163 / claimed 21 / failed 2), with every delta explained.
- The rollback question is answered with evidence: whether a restart/rollback occurred on muse-dev2 during the outage, and if so the point-in-time and the disposition of rows written after it.
- PostgREST-to-Postgres connectivity and pooler/connection-limit health on muse-dev2 are confirmed healthy by a named check, not just by verbs succeeding once.

body:
## Parent and context
Parent program: #5678. Object model: #2048. This ticket designs both a broadly interoperable interchange export and a separate full-fidelity ID-native export; it does not implement either exporter or assume a format before evidence is gathered.

## Scope
- Compare candidate interchange formats against the goal of round-tripping into Obsidian, Logseq, and Joplin. Evaluate Markdown with frontmatter and attachments as a candidate, alongside relevant alternatives (for example OPML, HTML, or a documented JSON representation), and justify the recommendation against actual target-tool behavior.
- Specify representation for pages/blocks, hierarchy, stable IDs, links/backlinks, tags, properties, relations, and attachments; define collision handling, filenames, escaping, and a clear manifest for data that cannot be represented.
- Define loss/omission warnings and safe behavior for partial exports, naming collisions, and repeated exports. Round-trip expectations must state which properties survive and where a target tool necessarily degrades them.
- Separately specify a full-fidelity ID-native export containing complete object data and required metadata, with integrity/validation and restore/import considerations; explain how users distinguish/select the two export modes.
- Define a small representative export corpus and validation/round-trip checks using Obsidian, Logseq, and Joplin, covering links, tags, and attachments at minimum.

## Read-authority constraint (already ruled; do not re-litigate)
ID knowledge defaults to public read, owners may grant reads to groups and/or users, and resolution order is **object → user default → server config → public**. Export only content readable under the resolved policy for the requesting actor; do not leak denied objects through link targets, manifests, indexes, or the ID-native archive. Specify how any exported access metadata is represented without weakening this rule.

## Open Drew-owned program questions — still open, not assumptions
Do not guess product versions/editions (free vs. paid), hands-on vs. documentation-only evaluation budget, the identity of “Open Knowledge,” graph scope (all ID objects vs. knowledge-only in v1), or AI-over-notes model choice (local, hosted, or user choice) and its read-authority implications. Record whether these affect destination-tool testing or export scope and keep unresolved choices explicit; do not silently choose a format based on them.

## Acceptance criteria
- The design compares plausible standards/formats and recommends one based on evidence from real or reproducible target-tool round trips.
- It specifies both interchange and full-fidelity ID-native exports, including mapping/loss reporting, security/read-authority handling, and how the user chooses between them.
- It defines objective tests demonstrating round-trip preservation of links, tags, and attachments in Obsidian, Logseq, and Joplin, with documented known losses.

Parent: [#6021](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/6021) (classification revalidation scan). Related: [#6048](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/6048) (Presidio design, closed); [#10413](https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/10413) (Layer 1 report, merged). Research source: prior-art doc `~/workspace/scratch/atlas-ingestion-brief-2026-11-04/prior-art-research.md` (2026-11-04). Follow-up 28 (Cluster 5).

## Fix packet — secret-backed owner-inventory matching (Layer 3)

Implement the owner-inventory matcher as a usable scanner component without collecting, reconstructing, or checking real personal identifiers into the repository. The inventory is runtime secret-tier input referenced by name; engineering and automated tests use synthetic fixtures only.

### Scope

- Define and document one versioned inventory format with pattern classes (address, phone, family-name, account/ID fragment) and a single secret-store reference; updates happen at that one source, with no copied plaintext inventory.
- Load the inventory at runtime through the existing secret access path. Missing or malformed input must fail closed for this layer and be clearly reported without exposing values.
- Match against internal-tier scan inputs; emit a high-severity/quarantine candidate with only the pattern class and opaque record identifier. Never emit matched content, pattern values, or plaintext inventory to logs, reports, or persisted artifacts.
- Add synthetic-fixture tests for matching, class attribution, missing/malformed inventory behavior, and redaction. If no reusable scan entry point exists yet, deliver the matcher behind a narrow interface and document the exact integration seam rather than inventing a second scan pipeline.
- Document the single-source maintenance/update procedure.

### Acceptance

- A synthetic inventory is loaded by secret reference and matching produces class-only, opaque-ID findings.
- Tests prove raw matching values do not appear in result serialization or logs, and that absent/malformed inventory cannot silently report a clean scan.
- No real identifiers or actual owner inventory are read, written, or required for the PR.
- A real-data internal-tier sweep and its counts-by-class-only report are separate operational validation after the scanner is provisioned; they are not a precondition for implementing this component.

Original research and rationale remain in the issue history. This packet does not authorize assembling an inventory from files, memory, or unrelated data.

body:
Parent: [#6018](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/6018) (Atlas ingestion program). Statement S6 of the 2026-11-04 brief. **This is a task to execute, not only a design.**

## Task (Drew, in substance)

**Revalidate that there is nothing sensitive in the wrong classification level.** Atlas is tiered — internal (28 shards / 107,001 chunks) vs secret (exactly 1 shard / 638 chunks), with the standing rule that secret material exists ONLY in the 2 secret DBs. Corpus growth since the tiers were established (shard restoration 2026-11-04: 31 new TursoDB shards, all counts verified) makes a fresh, deliberate revalidation pass necessary: ingestion has many sources, and a single mis-tiered secret in an internal shard is the failure this task exists to catch.

## Scope

- Sweep the internal tier for secret-class content: credential-shaped strings, private keys/tokens, personal/financial/medical details, anything matching the secret tier's inclusion profile. Combine pattern scanning with a classifier pass over samples + over chunks nearest the secret tier's content profile (vector-neighborhood check: internal chunks embedding-close to secret chunks get human/agent review).
- Verify the converse boundary: secret-tier contents are actually secret-class (no large volumes of mundane content inflating the most-protected tier), and confirm secret material exists in exactly the 2 secret DBs and nowhere else (including the production libSQL monolith and local replicas/caches).
- Check the staging path ([#5669](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5669)) and recent ingestion runs for tier-assignment mistakes: which source classes fed each tier, and does any source class straddle tiers without a rule?
- Relate findings to the classification manifest work ([#5410](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5410)) — the manifest is the natural home for the per-source tier rules this scan validates against.

## Handling rules

- Findings are handled at the SECRET tier's sensitivity: the report names counts, classes, and locations (DB + chunk IDs), never reproduces secret content in this issue, chat, or logs.
- Any confirmed mis-tiered chunk gets a remediation path (move + re-embed at the correct tier, purge from the wrong tier incl. replicas) filed as a follow-on before this task closes.

## Done looks like

A dated revalidation report (counts scanned per tier, methods, findings by class, remediations filed/done) linked from this issue, and a recommendation on recurrence (one-off vs folded into the ingestion-operations design under [#6018](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/6018) as a standing gate).

Part of the docs migration (hatch-personal/hatch → code). Stay-until-replaced register item **R1**.

## What exists today

The sandbox's fallback path to the laptop lives in hatch-personal `tools/` and cannot move or retire until fleet has an equivalent built in:

- `tools/laptop-ssh.sh` — connection-multiplexing SSH wrapper (stock SSH drops burst pre-auth setups; see hatch TOOLS.d/laptop.md)
- `tools/laptop-ssh-real.sh` — the real-SSH route used for stdin pushes and sudo-fed switches
- `tools/laptop-proxy-connect.py` — proxy-connect helper
- `tools/laptop-agent.py`, `tools/laptop-agent-daemon.py`, `tools/laptop-agent-broker.py` — laptop-side agent trio
- `tools/board-agent.service`, `tools/install-board-agent-service.sh`

## What the built-in must do

`fleet` gains a **fallback connection mode**: when the normal fleet proxy path to a host is unavailable, fleet connects directly (SSH with connection multiplexing, burst-safe) with the same verbs and semantics, so callers never need a separate wrapper script. Must cover: multiplexed connection reuse, stdin-pipe transfers (the current real-SSH use), and non-interactive sudo feeding for switch runs.

## Exit condition

When this ships and is verified in a proxy-down drill, the 8 hatch files above become historical copies only, and their canonical home (if any is still needed) is decided in the docs migration.

body:
Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Statements S52–S58 of the 2026-11-04 brief.

## Requirement (Drew, in substance)

Specify the per-tick data flow between world, clients, and user functions:

- **What can be seen** is a mixture of **data passed in for that given tick** and **state stored in the world**.
- The world **gets the inputs** — this user went left, this other user went right — **updates their positions on the map and any calculations**.
- The world then provides that data **for client-side presentation**, and **also to the user's own function**.
- The user's function reads its view: **you are now at X, Y; you have a field of view of Z radius; there are three enemies within your line of sight, at these XY positions** — and whatever other information the world wants to provide.
- The user function uses the provided interface to decide and **pass on the intent for the next tick**.
- Intents might come from **users' inputs on the client**, from **users' functions passing them directly**, or **both**.
- The mixed case is canonical: a human is moving around as Sonic, and they have an **AI playing Tails** following them around — one entity's intent is human, its partner's is computed, in the same tick loop.

## Design points to settle

- The view is a **projection**, not the world state: per-user visibility (FOV, line of sight, team knowledge) is computed by the world and is an anti-cheat boundary — a user function must not be able to read what its view doesn't contain. Say how this composes with the capability model (is the view a capability?).
- Intent schema: per-entity, per-tick, with what validity window? Late intents (function timed out — see the mapping design child) fall back how?
- Precedence/blending when both a human input and a function intent target the same entity in the same tick.
- Replay/determinism: the tick inputs + intents are the log from which a match replays (connects to the deterministic-testing split [#5779](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5779)).
- Presentation data vs function view: same projection at different fidelity, or two separate projections owned by different layers?

## Related

- Per-user function mapping child of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955)
- Deterministic testing over time: [#5779](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5779)
- Existing capability protocol in the examples (`RocCap.roc`: worlds answer with subscribe/requests) — the tick model must extend it, not replace it silently

## Done looks like

A design doc with the tick sequence specified step-by-step, the view-projection rules, the intent schema and blending rules, and the replay story.

body:
Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Statements S8–S16 of the 2026-11-04 brief.

## Where we are (verified 2026-11-04)

An app's capabilities are already bounded upward by the platform used to compile it, and that bound can be securely listed per platform: the capability catalog and compile-time ceilings live in `pkgs/id/crates/id-core/src/world_caps.rs`.

## Requirement (Drew, in substance)

- **First, answer: do we currently have more than one platform?** (S9 — an inventory fact this design starts from.)
- Direction: **allow greater capabilities** — this is a step towards reading and writing files from disk and using system resources. (S10)
- A world should be able to **say** what capabilities it requires — or, ideally, we can **automatically derive and discover** them. (S11)
- Capability vocabulary must at least express: **standard**, **file read+write in the sandbox**, **arbitrary file read**, **arbitrary network out**. (S12)
- The required capabilities are **listed in the world's registry entry**. (S13)
- If no existing platform fits, **custom-compile the appropriate platform** for that world. (S14)
- Handle the expansive-platform case: a user may give a world a platform with **more capability than it uses**. (S15)
- Therefore track two sets: **requested** (what the platform grants) and **discovered-used** (the exact functions really used). The registry says both: "it asks for all these, but it only uses this subset" — that helps users judge what they're connecting to. (S16)

## Open questions

- Discovery mechanism: static analysis of the compiled world, platform-call instrumentation during a profiling run, or both? How are the two reconciled when they disagree?
- Is the used-set a property of the code (same for every run) or can it vary by path taken at runtime — and how does the registry present a path-dependent set honestly?
- Custom-platform compilation: who pays, how long does it take, is the result cached and shared across worlds with identical requirement sets (interacts with the compile-economics child of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955))?
- How does the requested/used pair interact with writer-set authority ([#5545](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5545)) — is a capability grant an authority grant, or a separate axis?

## Related

- Capability-provider parent: [#5686](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5686); field survey [#5931](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5931)
- Provider registry (capabilities as manifest): [#1061](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/1061)
- Core/app platform design: [#2028](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/2028)

## Done looks like

Design covering: platform inventory answer, capability vocabulary v1, declaration vs discovery, registry schema for requested/used sets, and the custom-platform compile path — each with the open questions above resolved or explicitly deferred with a reason.

body:
## Summary

Design the **incorporation of ID worlds into Bevy**: how a world's entity/triple state maps onto Bevy's ECS, how journal events drive a Bevy application, and what it means for a Bevy app to host or join a world — as Bevy's own design line.

## Motivation

Bevy currently appears only as a name inside other designs: #788 lists "Bevy or Qt" as candidate frameworks for the reference native shell (a conformance question), and #5686 lists "a game engine integration (Bevy named)" as one of five capability-provider targets (a provider-model question). Neither designs the incorporation itself — the state mapping, the event flow, the authority model. Drew's 2026-11-04 instruction is explicit: each platform thing gets its own design issue rather than riding inside a bundle. A game engine is also the stress case for the whole client story: tick-driven, frame-budgeted, and stateful in ways a terminal never is — if the shell contract and the triple model survive Bevy, they survive anything.

## Sketch

- **State mapping**: ID entities ↔ Bevy `Entity`; triples/components ↔ Bevy `Component`s; the mapping's ownership rules (which side is authoritative for what) stated per data class — world state, presentation state, purely local state.
- **Event flow**: journal appends and state deltas in; shell-contract input events out. How journal positions map to Bevy schedules/ticks, and what a frame is allowed to *not* apply yet (interpolation, prediction) without violating the presenter contract.
- **Authority postures**: Bevy app as presenter-client; as world host (an embedded server); as both (#790's simultaneity) — and which posture the design blesses first.
- **Determinism**: the game loop against the deterministic replay infrastructure (its own design issue) — a recorded world stream replayed through Bevy must land on identical state; the soak/replay oracles are how engine integration bugs get caught.
- **Provider face**: what the engine offers as a #5686 capability provider — render surfaces, audio, input devices — under the same grant model as every other provider.

## Open questions

- Where the bridge lives: inside `id-worlds`, as a separate bridge crate on the #3447 seams, or as a Bevy plugin crate owned outside the workspace?
- Bevy version policy: Bevy's release cadence vs the workspace's — pin, track, or abstract behind the mapping?
- Does the WIT/component-model decision in #788 change the bridge's shape, or is the bridge contract-level only?
- 2D-first, 3D-first, or headless-logic-first as the proving target?

## Relations

Parent: epic #2056. Relations: #788 (shell contract + framework decision record — this design consumes it), #5686 (capability providers — Bevy as one provider class, designed there in the abstract, here concretely), #790 (client/server simultaneity), #3447 (crate seams). Filed in the 2026-11-04 gap pass (WS-F) per Drew's order that Bevy gets its own design issue.

title: Containers: Nix-build audit — mcpx Containerfile, duplicate lab-ops Dockerfile, amd-crd definition-or-waiver

labels.name: epic/fleet-orchestration
labels.description: Reprioritization program epic (2026-11-12)

body:
Containers track of the deployment-architecture epic (design: PR #5764 §5).

Rule from the design: software we own → Nix-built images, from scratch by default (`dockerTools.streamLayeredImage`/`buildLayeredImage` or `nix2container`; exactly the binary's closure + cacert/tzdata when needed). Third-party software → digest-pinned images, still tracked as deploy targets. A Dockerfile for our own software is a migration bug.

Current state (2026-11-04 inventory):
- lab-ops-hub crawler: already Nix-built (`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container-image.nix`, crane push) — the precedent. But a parallel `container/Dockerfile` builds "the same app" for Docker machines. → Delete the Dockerfile path once the Nix image is the deploy target's artifact.
- mcpx: 3-stage `pkgs/mcpx/Containerfile` (golang build + bun copied in + debian-slim runtime), built in CI for verification. → Replace with a Nix image package; the bun sidecar becomes a closure question in the package.
- identity packages: `pkgs/identity/Dockerfile` is already `FROM scratch` (good shape, prebuilt binary — make the binary a flake package so the image is one derivation); `pkgs/identity/provider/Dockerfile` is `FROM ubuntu` + apt-get (the anti-pattern — Nix-compose it).
- pm-apps (Grist, Pad): third-party, digest-pinned via oci-containers — correct; bring the pins under deploy-target tracking. Kaneo/PostgreSQL are compose-managed outside pm-apps (per the pm-stack module) — bring under the same pin discipline or record why not.
- **amd-crd (Chrome Remote Desktop): no definition exists in any repo** — the only trace is a secret name (`chrome-remote-desktop.amd-pin`, sops). → Definition-or-waiver: either Nix-build it (likely the "fuller userspace, still Nix-composed" exception: explicit contents list, never apt-get) or record it as a named exception with an owner and a reason.
- Cloudflare's 4 container classes (CrawlerContainerV2, HelloContainer, HelloLite, CrawlerProbe) become image targets; the orphaned legacy `CrawlerContainer` app gets an explicit retire-or-keep decision instead of "left in place, unused".

Acceptance: an inventory table in this issue's closing comment listing every container in the estate with {builder, base, target?}; zero Dockerfiles remain for fleet-owned software except any carrying a written exception; amd-crd resolved one way or the other.

body:
# Atlas search: Jaccard as a third signal (rescore + ingest dedup); SPLADE as a triggered follow-on

Context: the atlas hybrid design settled 2026-11-04 (see the shard-restore work under #5669 and the spike verdict on hatch-personal#20): retrieval = **dense cosine scan + FTS/BM25**, one fan-out per shard carrying both scorers, merged with reciprocal rank fusion. Dot product adds no independent signal on normalized embeddings. Drew (2026-11-04) asked where Jaccard fits in atlas specifically — this issue records the answer as a design task.

## Proposal: Jaccard as a THIRD signal, at rescore — not at retrieval

- Each chunk gains a stored **token-shingle set** (hashed word shingles) alongside its embedding and text.
- Retrieval stays two-scorer (cosine + BM25). Jaccard is computed **only over the candidate union** (the top ~100 merged candidates), as a rescore-stage feature:
  - **Near-exact boost**: a candidate whose shingle overlap with the query is very high is probably *the* text the user pasted or quoted (an error message, a passage, a title) — cosine alone ranks it "topically similar among many"; Jaccard identifies it as *the match*. Boost it decisively.
  - **Tie-breaker / confirmation**: among semantically-equal candidates, prefer higher literal overlap when the query contains rare exact tokens.
- Why not a full-corpus third scorer: set intersection per row across every shard is real scan cost for a signal that only matters near the top. Rescore-stage keeps it ~free.

## Second use: ingest / promotion dedup

- At ingest (and at staging→core promotion, #5669), compute shingle overlap of a new chunk against recent / same-source chunks: **≥ ~0.9 Jaccard = near-duplicate** — flag or suppress instead of silently double-indexing. The corpora most at risk: brain-dump explosions, repeatedly-versioned design docs, re-ingested repos.
- Dedup findings are data, not deletions: record the edge (chunk, near-dup-of, score) and let promotion policy decide; never auto-delete on a similarity score alone.

## SPLADE — investigated only on a trigger (Drew, 2026-11-04: "no reason to investigate SPLADE?")

There IS a reason — quality, not speed: learned sparse retrieval can beat BM25 where vocabulary mismatch hurts (the model expands terms with learned weights), and it would collapse hybrid retrieval into a single vector scan (TursoDB even has an experimental sparse-IVF index). The costs are also real: a SPLADE encoder must run at **ingest and at query time**, a model must be hosted, and our corpora are technical text where exact terms dominate — BM25's home turf.

So: **triggered follow-on, not a standing task.** Investigate SPLADE only if the shipped hybrid's held-out evaluation shows the lexical half is the weak side (e.g. recall@10 on the eval set improves materially when an oracle lexical ranker is substituted). Bar for adoption: a measured recall@10 gain over the BM25 half on the held-out query set, large enough to justify a permanent inference dependency at ingest + query time. Until the trigger fires, this stays a named paragraph, not a project.

## Acceptance shape

- Design note covering: shingle construction (size, hashing, storage cost per chunk), the rescore formula (how the Jaccard feature enters the fused ranking), dedup thresholds + the promotion-policy hook, and the eval-set methodology that would (a) prove the rescore signal helps and (b) arm the SPLADE trigger.
