body:
Design from the design-architect pass 16 (2026-10-29). Full design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-error-honesty.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Origins: conformance gap `errors-local-errors-not-mistaken-for-peer` (ex-nix#206) and the `accept-unadvertised` + `32021-broker-fallback` gap keys of #1957 (ex-nix#257 — split out under its own acceptance rule, same pattern as #2192). Audited against origin/main `5a34fa70`.

## Problem

mcpx sits between two peers and speaks for both, but its errors do not say whose they are:

1. **A peer's failure arrives dressed as mcpx's own.** Pass-through relays an upstream JSON-RPC error whole (`UpstreamError`, `internal/mcpserver/capability.go`). The gateway path flattens the same failure to text at the daemon `/v1` surface, then `internal/cli/serve_ask.go` (~L225-255) *reconstructs* it by guessing at the text — with exactly one structured special case (-32021 at serve_ask.go:241). Structured `data` is destroyed and heuristically rebuilt. Spec (2026-07-28, lowercase should): local errors surfaced in JSON-RPC-shaped structures "should ensure they cannot be mistaken for errors received from the peer."
2. **mcpx answers methods it did not advertise.** `capabilities()` (server.go:2410) declares `completions` only where the revision defines it — with the comment that `completion/complete` "is answered for every revision" — so a 2024-11-05 peer is served a method that cannot be advertised to it; `resources/subscribe` is dispatched unconditionally (server.go:938) even when `resources.subscribe` was advertised `false`. The 2026 schema's MethodNotFoundError guidance asks for -32601 for a method "gated behind a server capability the server did not advertise". The `Removed()` check (server.go:785) is the precedent seam; modern HTTP already pairs -32601 with 404 (`modernStatus`).
3. **`-32021` exists only in islands.** Emitted correctly by tasks `missingTasks` (tasks.go:199) and `subscriptions/listen` (listen.go:138), relayed in pass-through — but when a gateway call cannot finish without a capability the host never declared, the question waits in the broker even when no broker audience can answer it. ERR-08 (`pkgs/mcpx/docs/compare/register/errors.md`) + conflict #8 (`docs/spec/revision-conflicts.md`) already record the resolution: mcpx never *requires* the capability while a broker audience can answer — the complement (no audience ⇒ required ⇒ -32021) is unimplemented.

## Decisions recorded

1. **One structured error carriage through the gateway.** The `/v1` call reply gains a structured upstream-error field (code/message/data); the gateway relays it verbatim via `UpstreamError`; text-reconstruction heuristics are deleted wherever the structured field is present. mcpx's OWN errors are minted through one helper that stamps `error.data` with an origin marker (`"mcpx": {"origin": "local"}`) — peer errors never gain it, local errors always carry it. That asymmetry is the "cannot be mistaken" mechanism. No new codes, no message prefixes.
2. **Dispatch consults the same map advertisement used.** One gate after the `Removed()` check: refuse -32601 any method whose gating capability is absent/false in the `capabilities()` map for that peer. Initial gated set is only the two proven disagreements: `completion/complete` ← `completions` (pre-completions revisions), `resources/subscribe`/`unsubscribe` ← `resources.subscribe`. Accept-liberally stands for everything else; the gate's table grows by evidence. Tasks keep their own gating.
3. **`-32021` exactly when waiting is not an answer.** At the ask seam: question needs a capability the peer did not declare AND the broker has no audience that can answer it ⇒ modern peer gets -32021 with `data.requiredCapabilities` (existing shape; HTTP 400 via `modernStatus`); legacy keeps existing behaviour. When any audience can answer, the broker fallback is unchanged.

## Phases

- Phase 1: structured carriage + origin marker (independent).
- Phase 2: advertised-capability gate (independent).
- Phase 3: -32021 at the ask seam + register/conflict truth-up + gap rows retired + #1957/#206 evidence (gated on Phase 1).

Open questions stay in the design doc (client-side origin marker vs #1481's choke point; prompts-validate-io deliberately excluded — it neighbours #1481, not this seam; gated-set growth needs evidence; ERR-09/ERR-13 belong to #2209's classification, not absorbed here).

🤖 Design-architect pass 16 — agent note: this issue is the design of record; phases are its sub-issues. Do not re-derive the decisions above in triage; flag genuine blockers here instead.

## Acceptance criteria

- The three implementation phases (#2435, #2436, #2438) stay linked from this design issue until each merges or is explicitly declined with rationale recorded here.
- Each phase meets its own acceptance criteria; no phase widens scope beyond the design doc (`files/designs/code-mcpx-error-honesty.md`).
- When all phases have landed or been declined, this issue closes with a summary linking the merged PRs.

body:
Follow-up from the key-recovery investigation on #2060 (doc: `doc/2026-10-29T11-28-18Z_investigation_key_recovery_hosted/`, §4/§7 and §11). Parent epic: #2056.

## Ordering (triaged 2026-11-03)

Slices per the investigation's §11; this issue is the **umbrella** for the export/server-backup/rotation remainder, not one implementation task:

- **Slice 1 — `id key export` / `id key import` passphrase-wrapped envelope: #2279** (open, queued, not started). Prerequisite for everything below; do not build a second envelope format here.
- **Seed-phrase (BIP39-style) export/restore** — unique to this issue; shares #2279's KDF/envelope module; dispatch after #2279.
- **Server-side backup blob + rate-limited blinded unwrap (OPRF)** — design decision first (no OPRF or backup-blob code exists at main); ciphertext-only server storage; depends on slice 1.
- **Restore-forces-rotation flag** — needs the keyset log substrate in #2380 (device keys, revocation, bindings).
- Guardian/social recovery is #2382; issuer key rotation is #2804 (different scope).

## Problem
If the only ID key is lost and no device survives, there is no recovery path that keeps the server from holding keys. The investigation recommends encrypted backups where the server holds ciphertext only.

## Proposal
1. Seed-phrase (BIP39-style) export/restore of the identity secret in the `id` CLI — zero server involvement; doubles as the hosted-edition exit ramp.
2. Passphrase-wrapped backup stored server-side (hosted edition): memory-hard KDF, and a rate-limited blinded unwrap (OPRF-style) so the server can throttle guessing without learning the passphrase or the key.
3. A backup-restored key is flagged until a keyset rotation retires it (restore may follow theft).

## Acceptance
- [ ] `id` CLI can export a seed phrase and restore an identity from it, with tests.
- [ ] Server backup format + unwrap throttling designed and documented; server never sees plaintext key material at any step.
- [ ] Restore flow forces/prompts rotation of the restored key.

body:
Follow-up from the capability taxonomy v0 investigation (#2027, record: `doc/2026-10-29T14-05-00Z_investigation_capability_taxonomy/`, PR #2337).

## Goal
Formalise text-only mode as the **main** presentation mode for agents and scripts: a `text/1` contract plus a required text projection for every `WorldSurface` variant.

## Why
`parse_surface` already accepts non-screen documents as legacy UTF-8 text, so text works today by accident. Agents and scripts are the primary consumers, text is what CI can assert without a renderer, and it is the degradation target every other surface needs.

## Scope
- `Text(TextSurface)` variant (`kind: text`) — UTF-8 lines, no escapes, no cursor addressing, no redraw, append semantics.
- Width-aware wrapping, default 80, capped like `MAX_SCREEN_WIDTH`.
- A text projection for `Screen` (existing `render_ansi` with colour stripped), `Form`, `Media` and `Map`, so no surface can exist without one.
- Contract documentation in `world_presentation.rs` header and `pkgs/id/ARCHITECTURE.md` if it describes surfaces.

## Acceptance
- `kind: text` parses and round-trips; a surface without a text projection is rejected at the type level or by a test.
- A test renders one program's `Screen` and `Text` documents and asserts the text projection is line-oriented and escape-free.
- Legacy plain-string documents stay valid.

## Out of scope
A styling/theme system, cursor animation, terminal detection heuristics.


## Acceptance criteria

- [x] `kind: text` (Text/TextSurface) parses and round-trips: UTF-8 lines, no escapes, no cursor addressing, append semantics, width-aware wrapping (default 80, capped like MAX_SCREEN_WIDTH)
- [x] Every `WorldSurface` variant on main (`Screen`, `Text`, `Form`, `Scene`, `Audio`, `Widget`) has a text projection, enforced by the exhaustive, wildcard-free match in `WorldSurface::text_projection`. `Media`/`Map` are not variants — the Media remainder is design-first in #13679.
- [x] A test renders one program's Screen and Text documents and asserts the text projection is line-oriented and escape-free
- [x] Legacy plain-string documents stay valid; contract documented in the world_presentation.rs header (and pkgs/id/ARCHITECTURE.md if it describes surfaces)

body:
Follow-up from the currency control plane design (#2062), §4 of
`doc/2026-10-29T12-42-21Z_design_currency_control_plane/`.

## Scope

The gateway's signed request envelope and the pre-ledger write path.

- Reuse the existing `pkgs/id` scheme: `directory_auth.rs` `Signed { key, at, nonce, signature }` over `id-request-v1\n{method}\n{target}\n{at}\n{nonce}\nsha256(body)`, 5-minute window, `ReplayGuard`, **`verify_strict`** (never `verify`) (design §4.1, §4.6).
- Per-op canonical CBOR bodies, domain-tagged (`id.currency.request.v1`), with strict decoding like `chain.rs`.
- Device → **account** resolution before authorization; issuance binds to the account key (design §4.1b).
- Deterministic idempotency-ID derivation and the typed-error surface (design §4.3).
- Resolve the idempotency-ID vs TigerBeetle monotonic-ID guidance tension (design §9.3).

## Acceptance

- A signed request round-trips: sign in a client, verify in the gateway, reject a tampered body, a stale `at`, and a replayed nonce.
- A forgery fixture proves the gateway rejects a signature that only plain `verify` would accept.
- Signature verification alone never authorizes: a valid signature from a non-minter is rejected.

## Depends on

Nothing hard; F1/F2 for the end-to-end path.

Follow-up C from the Durable Object jurisdiction investigation on #2061
(doc: `doc/2026-10-29T11-43-02Z_investigation_do_jurisdiction_pinning/`, §5 and §1.5).

Parent epic: #2056. Context: #2044.

Needs a Cloudflare account to deploy a scratch Worker — not doable from a repo-only worker session. Two halves: code mechanics (small PoC) and a written vendor ask (not code).

## Half 1 — PoC (one deployed scratch Worker, no user data)

1. `idFromName(name)` vs `jurisdiction("eu").idFromName(name)` produce different IDs in this account (docs assert it; confirm).
2. `ctx.id.jurisdiction` reads back `eu` inside the object, including from an alarm; confirm both `undefined` cases (unrestricted namespace; alarm scheduled before 2026-03-15).
3. A mismatched namespace/ID pair throws; an unrestricted namespace silently accepts a foreign ID (the failure mode the design guards against).
4. Export from an `eu` object, import into a `us` object: signatures still verify (migration path).
5. R2: create an `eu`-jurisdiction bucket, confirm the Worker binding needs the `jurisdiction` field and that the S3 jurisdiction endpoint cannot reach outside the jurisdiction.

## Half 2 — the written ask to Cloudflare (blocks any DPA that claims EU residency)

The docs guarantee the *object* "only run[s] and store[s] data within a region" and that it is never migrated out of the jurisdiction's data-centre list. They do **not** say that DO SQLite's storage replication path stays inside the jurisdiction:

- SQLite commits are forwarded to **five follower machines, each in a different physical data center**, and WAL batches/snapshots go to **object storage** ([blog](https://blog.cloudflare.com/sqlite-in-durable-objects/)). No jurisdiction statement appears in that post.
- Point-in-time recovery / bookmark retention: jurisdiction-confined? Not documented either way.
- Does `fedramp` jurisdiction for Durable Objects require a separate entitlement (R2's FedRAMP jurisdiction explicitly does; DO's docs say nothing)?

Ask Cloudflare support/account team in writing and record the answer on this issue. A negative or evasive answer changes the hosted edition's residency claim, so this is not optional polish.

## Acceptance

- PoC results recorded as a comment (or short doc) with what was observed, including failures.
- The vendor answer, or the exact question as sent plus the date, recorded here.
- Any gap the answer exposes filed as an issue.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] PoC results recorded here (or in a short doc): all five Half-1 mechanics confirmed or the failure recorded, including both ctx.id.jurisdiction undefined cases
- [ ] The Cloudflare written ask (Half 2) sent verbatim and dated on this issue; the vendor answer recorded when it arrives
- [ ] Any residency gap the answer exposes is filed as its own issue

## Implement: fleet OpenCode scheduled-task pattern (systemd timers + `opencode run`, per-job route)

Follow-on from the #2019 investigation (LIST 4a, fleet program #2055). The investigation's verdict: OpenCode has no native scheduler (upstream anomalyco/opencode#41906 still open); the proven pattern is an OS timer firing `opencode run --model opencode-route/<tier>` — verified live 2026-10-29 with a one-shot systemd user timer on the laptop (fired on schedule, route resolved to opencode-go DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, exit 0, zero Muse tokens in trigger or execution).

### Scope
1. A small, committable job registry for fleet scheduled OpenCode tasks: one unit (or unit pair) per job under a managed directory, each naming cadence, workdir, prompt/command, and route (`opencode-route/workhorse|specialist|summit|speed`).
2. Per-job run logs in a fixed location, readable by the babysitter/monitor (directory-scoped server-API reads are the reliable session surface; `opencode session list` is not).
3. Migrate ONE real low-risk fleet job as the proof (a quota probe or census refresh — fire-and-forget, failure visible next round), and record the before/after Muse-token cost of its trigger.
4. Considered and deferred (do not silently switch): adopting the v1 `different-ai/opencode-scheduler` plugin (needs a v2 port — the fleet fork cannot run v1 plugins) and waiting for upstream #41906.

### Out of scope
- Stall supervision: scheduling is not supervision. The preliminary-babysitter design is #2021; this issue only provides the trigger mechanism it can run on.
- The placement-framework decisions (#2024 synthesis stays gated on its inputs; #2019's report is one).

### Acceptance
- One real fleet job running on the pattern for at least one full cadence cycle, observed firing on schedule with logs.
- Registry + units committed via PR; route per job visible in the unit itself.
- A short note on #2019 with the migrated job's name and its first observed run.

body:
Implementation follow-on from the #2138 triage (queue task 3168, 2026-10-29). Parent decision: #2138 (CONVERT to feeder — decision + evidence recorded there); fleet epic: #2055; roles: #2131.

Convert `issue-sweep-rotating` from a direct executor into the Make role's triage feeder for developing-today/opencode, developing-today/openchamber, and dezren39/nix:

1. **New body, feeder-only.** Per run (hourly rotation, one repo per run, up to 5 items — cadence and volume unchanged): pick the repo's highest-value unqueued open issues, triage each (reproduction/evidence notes on the issue), and **enqueue a triage packet into that repo's pilot queue** (`repo-health-opencode-pilot` / `repo-health-openchamber-pilot` / `repo-health-nix-pilot`) with `queue/queued` set on the issue in the same pass. The feeder never fixes, never opens PRs, never self-assigns — execution belongs to the queue lanes and the conductor alone. The one exception is clerical: closing an issue as already-fixed/duplicate with evidence, which is triage, not execution.
2. **Dedupe before enqueue:** check the repo queue's live tasks and the issue's labels (the fleet-monitor safety net pattern); an issue with a live task or a `work/*` label is skipped and logged, never double-fed. (Today's collision — sweep fixing opencode#831 while queue task 3137 held it — is the failure this step exists to prevent.)
3. **Backlog files stay:** the feeder keeps the per-repo backlog files (`backlog-devtoday-opencode.md` etc.) as its triage record; sweep.log lines name the enqueued task ids.
4. **Retire-revisit trigger (from the #2138 decision):** if two consecutive weekly token-usage reviews show the feeder's enqueued packets substantially duplicating producer coverage (pinned creators + pr-diff-review for those repos), or the conductor + producers demonstrably keep all three backlogs triaged without it, file the retirement as a fresh decision on #2138 — do not retire by drift.

Acceptance:
- [ ] issue-sweep-rotating body rewritten to feeder-only; no direct-fix language remains
- [ ] One evidenced feeder run per repo (3 runs) with packets enqueued and task ids logged; zero PRs opened by the feeder
- [ ] fleet-watchdog roster / role map (#2131) updated: sweep listed as Make feeder
- [ ] First weekly review after conversion reports feeder cost per enqueued item; result posted on #2138; #2055 linked

body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#300 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #253

## Summary

#253 implements the authorization *interface*: the OAuth endpoints exist, `/mcp`
acts as a resource server, credentials are accepted, and the shape matches the
spec. Deliberately, it authorizes **everyone** — present anything and the answer
is yes.

That is the right first move, because it separates two jobs that are usually
tangled and have completely different risk profiles. Making the interface exist
is mechanical, unblocks every conformance row that only checks the interface is
*there* and well-formed, and cannot break anybody — a daemon that authorizes
everyone is exactly as secure as today's daemon, which authorizes everyone by
having no interface at all.

This issue is the second job: the conformance rows that require an **invalid**
credential to be *rejected*. Those rows cannot pass against a permissive
interface by construction, and they are the ones that change runtime behaviour
and can lock a user out of their own daemon.

**Nothing is blocked on this issue.** It is not a precondition for any surface,
transport or feature. A permissive interface is a complete answer for a local
daemon, and remains one until somebody actually wants rejection.

## Original notes

> if an interface is not to spec because you must accept a user and password,
> accept a user and password and tell them good job, you're authorized. if the
> spec requires the interface and that invalid fails then go ahead and have a
> separate issue to make the correct interface have the correct behavior.

## Current state

**No interface and no validation.** mcpx has no OAuth client, `/mcp` performs no
authorization, and the conformance matrix (`docs/spec/conformance-matrix.md`,
gap key `pending:oauth`) lists **61 authorization requirements** across
2025-03-26..2026-07-28 that are unimplemented (#253).

**Configured auth is parsed and dropped.** `mcpauth.Resolve` has no caller
(#240) and the per-server `auth:` block is parsed and never applied (#205). So
there is already credential *configuration* with no credential *use* — which
means the permissive interface is closer than it looks, and real validation has
existing structure to hook into.

**The local model is unauthenticated on purpose.** The daemon is explicitly
unauthenticated with socket file permissions as the access control
(`internal/daemon/server.go:214`, `internal/daemon/origin.go:13`,
`internal/api/openapi.go:40`). That remains correct and this issue does not
change it.

## The split, concretely

Of #253's 61 rows, they divide by what a test actually asserts:

| row asserts | satisfied by | owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the endpoint exists and is well-formed | a permissive interface | #253 |
| metadata discovery returns the right document shape | a permissive interface | #253 |
| a valid credential is accepted | a permissive interface (accepts all) | #253 |
| **an invalid credential is refused** | **real validation** | **this issue** |
| **an expired token is refused** | **real validation** | **this issue** |
| **a token for the wrong resource is refused** | **real validation** | **this issue** |
| **scope is enforced** | **real validation** | **this issue** |

Splitting the matrix along that line is the first task here, because it also
tells #253 exactly how far it can get — and the answer is probably "most of
them", which is the point.

## Approaches

### Approach A — least recommended: skip the permissive stage, build validation first

Do it "properly" in one go.

This is the default instinct and it is why auth work stalls. It couples a large
behavioural change to a mechanical interface change, so no conformance row moves
until all of it lands, and the first thing that ships is also the first thing
that can lock somebody out. Rejected — it is the shape #253's split exists to
avoid.

### Approach B — middle: validation behind a setting, default off

One `auth.enforce` flag. Off, everything is authorized; on, credentials are
checked.

Simple and most of the value. Its weakness is that it is a single switch over a
set of independent checks — signature, expiry, audience, scope — which in
practice land at different times and have different confidence levels. One flag
means either shipping them as a block (Approach A again, with a flag) or having
the flag mean different things in different releases.

### Approach C — recommended: per-check enforcement, defaulting to permissive, with the permissive answer always logged

Each validation step is independently enforceable and independently defaulted
off. Signature verification can be real while scope enforcement is still
permissive, and the conformance matrix shows precisely which rows that buys.

The piece that makes this safe to adopt: **a permissive decision is still a
decision, and it gets logged**. Before anyone enables enforcement they can read,
from their own daemon, exactly what would have been refused — the dry-run that
auth rollouts normally lack. `mcpx` can report "17 requests in the last day
would have been refused by scope enforcement, all from your own plugin", which
turns enabling a check from a leap into a verification.

Ship order: (1) split the matrix rows along accepts/refuses and record the split
in the matrix itself, so #253's target is exact; (2) the decision log, while
everything is still permissive, since it has no behavioural risk; (3) checks one
at a time, each defaulting off; (4) flip defaults individually once the log says
it is boring.

## Open questions

- Does the permissive interface need to be *visibly* permissive? A daemon that
  says "authorized" to everything should probably say so loudly at startup and
  in `mcpx doctor`, so nobody deploys it believing otherwise. Leaning strongly
  yes — this is the one real hazard of the permissive-first approach.
- Does the conformance matrix gain a third state? Today a row passes or is
  `pending:oauth`. "Interface present, validation permissive" is honestly a
  different state from both, and recording it is what keeps the split legible.
- Which checks are even meaningful for a local socket daemon? Audience and
  resource binding matter for a remote resource server and are close to
  meaningless on a unix socket. The per-check defaults probably differ per
  surface.
- Do #240 and #205 (configured auth never applied) belong to the permissive
  stage or this one? Applying a configured upstream credential is mcpx acting as
  a *client*, which is a different direction from mcpx validating an inbound
  one — probably they stay independent of both and are simply bugs.
- Is there a conformance row that requires rejection *and* is cheap? If so it
  should be pulled into #253 rather than waiting here.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease:** S for the matrix split and the decision log; M per check; L for all of
them. **Impact:** low until somebody wants a non-local surface, which is the
honest statement — this is conformance completeness rather than a capability.
**Blocks nothing.**

**Depends on / related:** **#253 (the auth implementation — this is ordered
strictly behind it and should not start until the permissive interface is in)**,
#240 and #205 (configured auth never applied — mcpx as client, independent of
this), #298 (principals and per-operation permissions — the authorisation model
this would eventually enforce against; also ordered behind #253 and also
blocking nothing), #204 (Origin validation — a separate browser-threat defence,
already shipped-shaped and unrelated to credentials).

## Acceptance criteria

- The conformance rows that require refusal (invalid/expired/wrong-audience credentials against the #253 interface) are enumerated from the matrix and pass.
- Valid credentials still authorize; the permissive rows from #253 do not regress.
- Rejection responses match the spec for status, error shape, and `WWW-Authenticate` behaviour per revision.
- A local daemon with no credentials configured keeps today's complete local answer — nobody is locked out of their own daemon by default.

Parent: #175

## Summary

Roc is worth an issue for a reason that has nothing to do with "another
interpreter". Roc's defining idea is the **platform/application split**: an
application is pure, and a *platform* supplies every effect it is allowed to
have. That is the exact shape of an mcpx script — pure logic whose only effects
are tool calls — and no other language in the runtime list models it natively.

So this issue has two halves, and they should not be confused. The cheap half is
Roc as a script language alongside TypeScript and Python (#105): a codegen
backend and a runner. The interesting half is **mcpx as a Roc platform**, where
`call`, `readResource`, `log` and `emit` are not a generated client but the
platform's effect API, and a script is incapable by construction of doing
anything mcpx did not hand it.

The second half is a research bet on a pre-1.0 language. This issue recommends
shipping the first and scoping the second honestly rather than pretending they
are one piece of work.

## Original notes

> add another for roc support
>
> you can imagine what i might want build out your dreams

## Current state

**Three JavaScript runtimes, nothing else.** `runner.Detect` picks from
`candidates := []string{"deno", "bun", "node"}` (`internal/runner/runner.go:73`)
and `runner.Run` spawns one. There is no interpreter selection, no shebang
handling and no second codegen backend. #106 is the issue for shebangs and a
`--shell` family; #105 is Python 1:1 with TypeScript; #175 is the tracker over
both.

**The generated client is the whole ergonomic story.** `internal/codegen` emits
TypeScript from the catalog, and that typed surface — `tools.<namespace>.<fn>()`
— is what makes a script worth writing instead of a pile of `mcpx call`
invocations. Any new language is a codegen backend first and a runner second,
which is the framing #105 already uses ("a second codegen backend and a second
runner, not a second product").

**Nothing in the codebase knows about Roc**, and the issue tracker has no Roc
mention at all. This is a greenfield proposal, not a gap.

**What Roc actually is, for the record.** A pure functional, ML-family,
statically typed language compiling through LLVM. No runtime exceptions, no
`null`, tags and records with structural typing and full inference. Its
distinguishing feature is that an application declares a platform —
`app [main] { pf: platform "..." }` — and the platform defines both the type of
`main` and every effect available. The host is ordinarily written in Rust, Zig
or C and is linked with the compiled application.

**The honest status caveat:** Roc is pre-1.0, has no stable release channel, and
makes no compatibility promise between versions. Anything built here is
signing up for breakage on a cadence the project does not control. That is a
real cost and it should be stated in the issue rather than discovered in six
months.

## Approaches

### Approach A — least recommended: let #106 cover it and call it done

Once `mcpx exec` runs any shebang, `#!/usr/bin/env roc` works, and Roc is
"supported" in the sense that the process starts.

This is genuinely zero work and genuinely worthless for Roc specifically. The
script gets no typed client, so every tool call is hand-rolled JSON over the
daemon API — in a language whose entire selling point is that the compiler
proves your data handling correct. Using Roc without generated types is strictly
worse than using TypeScript with them. If this is all that ever happens, do not
open the issue; #106 already covers it and no Roc-shaped work is justified.

### Approach B — middle, and what to actually ship: a Roc codegen backend and runner, on an existing platform

Treat Roc exactly as #105 treats Python. A `roc` runtime in the resolver, and an
`internal/codegen` backend emitting Roc type definitions and call functions from
the same catalog that drives TypeScript. Scripts run with `roc run` against a
community platform (`basic-cli`), and tool calls go over the daemon's HTTP API
like any other non-native client.

Roc is an unusually *good* target for this, which is the argument for doing it
at all:

- Tool input schemas map onto Roc records with inferred structural types, and
  enum/`oneOf` schemas map onto tag unions, which is a closer fit than
  TypeScript's structural-but-unsound interfaces and much closer than Python's
  type hints.
- Roc has no exceptions, so a tool error has to be a value — `Result` — and the
  compiler will not let a script ignore a failed call. Today a TypeScript script
  can drop a rejected promise and mcpx finds out from the exit code.
- Schema-to-type generation is a solved shape in this codebase already; the
  backend is mostly a new emitter, not new design.

B stands alone, ships against today's Roc, and does not depend on resolving any
of the hard questions in C.

### Approach C — the destination, staged behind research: mcpx as a Roc platform

Write a platform whose effects *are* mcpx. A script becomes:

```roc
app [main] { pf: platform "https://.../mcpx-platform/main.roc" }

main =
    issues = Mcpx.call! "github.listIssues" { repo: "dezren39/nix", state: "open" }
    Mcpx.emit! { count = List.len issues }
```

What that buys over B is not syntax, it is a property: **the capability boundary
becomes the type system**. A Roc application cannot open a socket, read a file or
spawn a process unless the platform exposes it. Today mcpx's sandboxing story is
Deno's permission flags (`internal/runner/runner.go:43` notes only Deno has a
permission model worth the name, and bun and node run unrestricted). With a Roc
platform the guarantee is static and total, and it is the same guarantee for
every runtime Roc targets.

It also makes the generated client disappear. There is no emitted `tools.ts` to
drift from the catalog — the platform *is* the surface, and a catalog change is a
platform version bump. That retires a whole class of the drift problems #159 and
#145 exist to police.

**The blockers, stated plainly:**

- **The host would have to be Go, and Roc hosts are not.** A platform host
  exposes a specific symbol set and is linked against the compiled application.
  Rust, Zig and C are the trodden paths; a Go host means cgo, a C shim and a
  build story materially harder than anything in this repository today. The
  realistic shape is a small Rust or Zig host that speaks to the mcpx daemon over
  its existing HTTP/unix-socket API — at which point the platform is a separate
  artefact with a separate toolchain in the release pipeline (#158).
- **Pre-1.0 churn.** Platform authoring is among the parts of Roc that have moved
  most.
- **Distribution.** Platforms are fetched by URL. That interacts with #187's
  content-addressed cache and with whatever #158 decides about release
  artefacts.

So: do B. Open C's research as a tracked question — "can a useful mcpx platform
be hosted without owning a Rust toolchain in this repo?" — and revisit when Roc
cuts a stable release. Do not block B on it.

## Open questions

- Is anyone actually going to write Roc here, or is the platform model the only
  real draw? If the latter, the honest framing is a *capability-sandbox*
  research issue where Roc is one candidate and WASM is another, and this issue
  is a sub-case of that.
- Does the Roc backend share the schema→type layer with Python (#105) and
  TypeScript, or is a third hand-rolled emitter acceptable? #111 (shared schema
  validation) is the adjacent consolidation.
- `roc run` compiles before running. What is the cold-start cost against the
  script cache (#187), and does a compiled Roc script become a cacheable
  artefact keyed by source hash + catalog hash?
- Roc's effects are explicit (`!`). Does the generated client expose every tool
  as an effect, or are read-only tools modelled differently? There is a real
  design here about annotating tools as pure/impure that would also benefit the
  TypeScript side.
- Version pinning: which Roc does a declaration target, and does `mcpx doctor`
  check it? Same drift problem as a generated adapter declaration's binary
  version.

## Ease · Impact · Related

**Ease:** M for the codegen backend and runner (Approach B), mostly mirroring
whatever #105 establishes for Python; **XL and speculative** for the platform
(Approach C), with a hard dependency on a non-Go toolchain. **Impact:** low in
users reached, high in what it would prove — C is the only proposal on the
tracker that makes the sandbox a *type-system* property rather than a flag set.

**Depends on / related:** #105 (Python 1:1 — establishes the second-backend
pattern this follows; do that first), #106 (shebangs — Approach A, and the floor
below this issue), #175 (parent tracker: runtimes, languages, dependencies),
#100 and #108 (runtime selection and its sharp edges), #103/#104/#187
(dependencies, import graphs and the cache a compiled platform would use),
#111 (shared schema validation), #158 (release artefacts, if a platform host
ever ships), #84 (embedding — a C ABI would make a Roc host dramatically more
tractable and is the single highest-leverage dependency for Approach C).

## Acceptance criteria

- A written decision splits the two halves: Roc as a script language (codegen backend + runner) vs mcpx as a Roc platform, with a recommendation for each.
- If the script-language half proceeds: a Roc script can call at least one catalog tool through a generated client surface comparable to the TypeScript one, selected via the existing runner detection.
- The platform half is scoped honestly (pre-1.0 risk, maintenance cost) with a named trigger for revisiting, rather than silently dropped.
- Existing TypeScript/Python script behaviour is unchanged.

body:
## Phase 3 — main-gate + remediation chain (Jules → issue → priority-90 Muse packet)

Design: #1779 (doc §5). Reference implementation in
developing-today/code (its Jules integration exists), then port to
opencode, openchamber, nix.

### Problem

Once PRs merge on basic validation (Phase 2), main will sometimes
go red. Today nothing owns that: code's `jules.yml` `ci-failure-fix`
job explicitly excludes main (`branches-ignore: [main]`), and a red
main is discovered by whichever lane trips over it. Drew's
directive: a main failure triggers Jules to remediate; if Jules
cannot resolve it, an issue is filed following the pattern and the
work is released so a Muse queue task picks it up at high
priority — with orchestrator-safe ownership so nothing
double-assigns and dropped items are picked back up.

### Design

1. **Main-gate:** one thin workflow per repo on push to main that
   runs/aggregates the full suite and produces a single conclusion.
   The chain watches only this workflow (no workflow_run fan-out —
   the #304 lesson).
2. **Identify + file:** on main-gate failure, compute
   Breakage-ID = sha256(`repo|workflow|sorted failing jobs`)[:12].
   If an open `main-broken` issue already carries the ID, append
   the run link and stop. Else file: title
   `main-broken: <repo> <workflow> @<short sha> — <first failing
   job>`; body = run URL, failing jobs, first error excerpt, head
   commit + originating PR/issue, `Breakage-ID:` line. Labels:
   `kind/ci`, `priority/critical`, `main-broken`, `queue/queued`,
   `status/needs-triage`.
3. **Jules first:** if the Jules budget allows (free tier:
   15 tasks/day, 3 concurrent — counted from open `main-broken`
   issues carrying the label), apply the **`jules` label**; code's
   existing `issue-labeled` job starts remediation. Record
   `holder: jules, since <ts>` as an agent-note:v1. Repos without
   an issue-labeled Jules job (opencode, openchamber) gain the
   same job shape in this phase; nix starts at step 4 until a
   Jules door exists (triage decides).
4. **Release to Muse:** on no Jules PR within 24h, or Jules PR
   resolved but main-gate still red for the same Breakage-ID, or
   budget exhausted at filing: remove the `jules` label, note
   `holder: released by chain at <ts>, reason: <which>`, enqueue
   the fix packet — **priority 90**, dedupe
   `repo-health:v1:fix:<repo>:main-breakage:<breakage-id>`,
   45m timebox, body carrying run URL + failing jobs + routing
   instruction (claiming lane fixes it, or routes to Aster /
   a dispatched OpenCode session and records the route).
5. **Singular ownership:** exactly one of {`jules` label, live
   queue task with the breakage dedupe key} holds a breakage at
   any moment. Claims add `queue/claimed` + `work/assigned`;
   every transition is an agent-note:v1 with holder + timestamp,
   so the orchestrator/monitor reconstructs ownership from the
   issue alone. Dropped packets are recovered by the fleet
   monitor's existing claim-evaporation / dead-in-queue repairs.
6. **Close:** fixing lane closes the issue with evidence when
   main-gate passes on a SHA containing the fix; `main-broken`
   comes off only at close.
7. **Release gate:** publish/goreleaser workflows refuse to cut a
   release from a SHA whose main-gate conclusion is not success.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Main-gate workflow live in code; a deliberately broken main
      (test commit) produces exactly one breakage issue with the
      pattern above, and a second identical failure appends
      instead of duplicating.
- [ ] The `jules` label path fires remediation on the test
      breakage (or the budget guard demonstrably routes around
      Jules when exhausted).
- [ ] Release path demonstrated: with Jules stood down, a
      priority-90 packet with the breakage dedupe key lands in
      repo-health-code-pilot and the issue shows the full
      holder-transition trail.
- [ ] Ported to opencode and openchamber (gate + filing + Jules
      job); nix files the Muse packet directly.
- [x] Release workflows check main-gate status before publishing.

body:
Part of the OpenCode-half redesign (design: `files/opencode-half-redesign-2026-10-28.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace; tracking: #1425). Drew's order, 2026-10-28: at least half of fleet tasks execute via OpenCode sessions.

## Scope

Make keeper (`jules-review`) and babysitter (`openchamber-babysitter`) supervision explicitly binding-aware for queue-spawned OpenCode sessions:

- Sessions launched by queue shifts carry a binding (session id ↔ task id ↔ issue) recorded in the task's progress at launch. The babysitter's rounds already enumerate every session at the laptop location; add the queue binding to its per-session record so queue sessions are distinguishable from dispatcher-launched and interactive ones.
- Keeper retry/failover rules apply to queue sessions (error-stopped: one retry, then model failover per the registry ladder) — but question-answering does NOT: a queue session waiting on a question is reported to its owning shift's lane, never answered by the keeper (the shift owns the packet context and the claim).
- Intervention caps: queue-session interventions are counted separately in the keeper state file so a burst of queue-session failures cannot silently consume the whole run's intervention budget; overflow is reported, not dropped.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Babysitter round output identifies queue-spawned sessions with their task/issue binding for 100% of sessions launched under the executor mode.
- [ ] An error-stopped queue session receives the standard retry/failover treatment and the intervention is logged with its binding.
- [ ] A queue session waiting on a question is never answered by the keeper; it appears in the keeper report as owned-by-shift.
- [ ] Keeper state separates queue-session interventions from Jules/OpenChamber ones.

body:
## Work (Drew, 2026-10-27)

Stand up the babysitter as a live scheduled job (`openchamber-
babysitter`, every 20m), implementing #1185's design with #1192's
detector:

- Every round: enumerate ALL sessions at the laptop OpenChamber
  location (and any future locations), bound or unbound, and give
  each a verdict: progressing / stalled / done-unreported / blocked
  / walled (402-class) / idle.
- Stall rule (from #1192's census): suspect when ≥20 min since the
  session's last activity AND no live CI on its bound PR; confirm on
  a second suspect round or on expiry-equivalent silence. Nudge at
  most twice (message injection where the API shape is verified —
  verify by the session's next assistant message), then escalate to
  the fleet as a stuck-holder case.
- Report per round only what changed: new stalls, nudges sent,
  harvests ready (done-unreported sessions whose PR merged or work
  completed → the owning queue task gets completed by its lane, the
  babysitter flags it), quota snapshot per pool in use, and which
  pool each active session is drawing on + whether that choice looks
  effective (progress per the session's own checkpoints).
- Data out: append round observations to the babysitter log in the
  goal workspace (the pool-intelligence and meta-reviewer jobs read
  it); unbound sessions are observed, never driven.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The job exists and has completed three rounds with per-session
      verdicts recorded.
- [ ] One real (or synthetic) stall is detected inside two rounds
      of the rule's threshold.
- [ ] Every report names each active session's pool; a session on a
      walled pool is flagged the round it happens.

Extends #1185; depends on openchamber#524 for the clean last-activity
field (rounds poll what's available until then). Child of the pool &
routing intelligence epic. Filed by Muse (operator) 2026-10-27.

## Work (Drew, 2026-10-27)

The code queue has two 40-minute lane shifts (A/B) with per-lane
locks and atomic claims; the opencode, openchamber, and nix queues
are still worked by the single 2-hourly agent-queue-worker — the
evaporation factory behind #530/#495's near-deaths. Give every queue
the lane treatment:

- `repo-queue-worker-shift-opencode` + `-b` (queue
  repo-health-opencode-pilot, repo developing-today/opencode)
- `repo-queue-worker-shift-openchamber` + `-b` (repo-health-
  openchamber-pilot, developing-today/openchamber)
- `repo-queue-worker-shift-nix` + `-b` (repo-health-nix-pilot,
  dezren39/nix)

Same discipline as the code lanes: bundle ≤10, ~90-minute budget,
per-lane lock files, claim-before-work, checkpoint on claim, park
instead of waiting, verified terminal states, label sync, delivery
only when a task was worked. One shared multi-queue instruction file
parameterized by queue/repo/lane (the code instruction stays as-is).

The 2-hourly agent-queue-worker stays as the fallback sweep until
the lanes prove out; the Phase 2 evaluation notes the overlap.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Six new shift jobs exist (cron list) and each has completed a
      first shift or gated out cleanly at an empty queue.
- [ ] Tasks 1149 (#530) and 1157 (#495) reach terminal states under
      lane discipline without another operator cap raise.
- [ ] Evaporation repairs for these queues trend to zero in the
      fleet monitor's daily count within a week.

intelligence epic. Filed by Muse (operator) 2026-10-27.

body:
# id: next horizons — investigation + discussion with Drew (planning, not a work order)

Drew (2026-10-26): "We need to start preparing for further phases and next steps. Ensure there are designs either built or on the roadmap to be made... Investigate and find things we could do, and then another issue to discuss with me, and we'll come up with a plan." **This is that discussion issue. Nothing here starts until we agree a plan in the comments.**

## Where the design coverage stands today (checked 2026-10-26)
- Phases 0–11: designed and built; validation audits queued (#1075–#1078) to prove it.
- Phase 12: epic #534 runs each F-item through the research/design workflow before implementation; item issues exist for all of F12.1–F12.18. The two that most need design depth first: **F12.4 provider registry** (#1061 — the registry shape constrains everything) and **F12.10 scheduling/quotas** (#1067 — policy, not just code).
- Phase 13: client shells + capability providers; F13.1/F13.2 done, F13.3–F13.8 filed (#785–#790). No design docs yet for F13.6 native shells (#788) beyond the shell contract.
- Beyond Phase 13: **nothing is designed or roadmapped.** That's the gap this issue is for.

## Candidate directions worth a Phase 14+ (from the current architecture and open threads)
1. **Hosted worlds / always-on hosting** — worlds that live on a host (e.g. the basement cluster) instead of a participant's machine: persistence, backups/snapshot export, world DR, uptime. Builds on F12.11 multi-node and F12.13 replication.
2. **Discovery & federation** — the world directory (#812 feed is the seed), signed catalogs, cross-node invites, popularity/quality signals. Global chat exists; worlds are still islands.
3. **Program ecosystem** — share/fork Roc programs and template worlds, a gallery, one-click install into a world; provenance from F12.17 makes this safe to open up.
4. **More shells** — mobile/PWA shell with offline mode, native apps (#1072), the ratatui TUI (#1071), and hardware shells — the ESP32 wing line of work already running in the fleet could become a physical id terminal/input device.
5. **Agents in worlds** — agent participants as first-class programs: MCP bridge so an agent can join a world, read screens, act — id as a place agents and people share, not just people.
6. **Scale & performance hardening** — large-world stress program (entity counts, journal growth, bandwidth budgets), snapshot/compaction policy, chaos tests across nodes.
7. **Creator tooling & insight** — world analytics for authors, in-world search across worlds, moderation tooling for public worlds (needed before any public directory).

## Also on the table
- The dashboard build-out (#1239) — how much of the platform's operational picture belongs there vs in `id world doctor`-style CLI surfaces.

## Questions for Drew
- Which 1–2 themes feel like the real Phase 14? (My instinct: hosted worlds + discovery, because they turn id from a tool into a place — but agents-in-worlds is the most differentiating.)
- Local-first forever, or is a hosted tier an explicit goal?
- How public should discovery be at first — tailnet friends, invite-only catalogs, or open?
- Anything on your mind that isn't in the candidate list?

When we've talked it through here, the output is: chosen themes → design issues filed → roadmap "Later" section updated. Until then this stays `priority/low` discussion.

## Acceptance criteria

- A discussion with Drew in this issue's comments produces an agreed plan: which post-Phase-13 directions (from the candidate list or new ones) become Phase 14+ design work, and in what order.
- Each agreed direction gets a design/roadmap issue (or an explicit 'not now' record) in the same pass — no agreed direction is left as comment-only text.
- Until that agreement exists, no implementation work starts from this issue (it is a planning/discussion issue, not a work order).

body:
Priority P2 — order 11. Horizon: Month. Design: quota-plane-design-2026-10-26.md (usage-billing-hub goal files), Stage 2. Parent context: epic #1047. (§6)

Design Stage 3 — predictive, self-tuning quota operations — so the next stage is planned before it is needed:
- Pace forecasting per window (projected exhaustion) driving placement BEFORE caution zones, not at them.
- Automatic pool re-weighting PROPOSALS as repo PRs (never silent config edits) with the forecast evidence attached.
- Anomaly detection: burn spikes, adapter schema drift, vendor plan changes wired to the evidence-baseline diff protocol.
- A weekly design review folding forecast accuracy back into the rules.
Method: one design doc (stage-3-design) in the usage-billing-hub goal files, using >=2 weeks of gatherer history as its evidence base; Drew reviews; then granular issues per component under a Stage-3 epic, same filing pattern as Stages 1-2.
Acceptance: design doc delivered + linked from the hub GOAL.md; Stage-3 epic filed with prioritized children (or an explicit Drew decision to defer).

body:
## F12.5 — First new providers

From the Phase 12 plan (`.opencode/plans/phase-12-platform-flexibility.md`, workstream B):

- `kv` — a bounded, durable, per-world key-value store
- `blob` — content-addressed blobs, over iroh-blobs
- `http.fetch` — admin allowlist, size and rate bounds, no redirects off the list, **off by default**
- `notify` — user-visible outbound notifications, rate limited (this also covers the roadmap's 'outbound notifications' idea)

Each ships behind a ceiling, with an audit entry per use, and **no new Wasm import**. Depends on F12.4 (provider registry).

**Exit:** each provider has bound, refusal, and replay tests; `http.fetch` has a test that proves an unlisted host is refused.

**Coordination (2026-10-26 reprioritization, per Drew):** every id roadmap item now has its own GitHub issue, and priority encodes the order: (1) the path to Phase 12 — `now` + `priority/high`; (2) Phase 12 itself — `next`; (3) Phase 13 and long-term ideas — `priority/low`. The dashboard mirrors this list (org Project "Developing Today" #4, Area `id-train`; Grist Program roadmap, Area `id`). If this item turns out to be blocked, wrong, or superseded, park or close it with a note rather than letting it stall the queue — dropping an issue is always allowed; silently stalling is not.

body:
## Problem

On 2026-10-25 the laptop's OpenCode sessions failed on the `meta` provider with 401 `invalid_api_key`, even though `~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json` held the correct funded key. Root cause: agent-shell-env (BASH_ENV env.sh, `__ase_load META_API_KEY`) loads the key from `/run/secrets/agent-auth/muse-sdk-token` (fallback `~/.config/muse/api-key`), and the OpenChamber server process carried that env value, overriding auth.json. Both files held a **stale** key (sha256 prefix `7d4f5006`).

## Hot-fix applied 2026-10-25 (live, verified)

Both secret files were replaced with the funded key (Bitwarden + 1Password item `meta.api-key-funded`, sha256 prefix `6b1ea8ee`) and openchamber.service was restarted; laptop sessions then answered on meta/muse-wonder-1.0, content-verified.

## The gap

The sops source in this repo — `nixos/agent-auth/` — still encrypts the OLD key. Any secrets regeneration or laptop reboot restores the stale `/run/secrets/agent-auth/muse-sdk-token` and the 401s return.

## Fix

- Re-encrypt the agent-auth secret with the current funded key from the vault (`meta.api-key-funded`).
- After the next regeneration/reboot, verify the deployed file's sha256 prefix is `6b1ea8ee` and that a laptop OpenCode session answers on meta/muse-wonder-1.0.
- Fold into the laptop declarative-module cleanup so the imperative hot-fix doesn't drift again.

Key values are referenced by name/hash prefix only — never paste the key into this issue, a commit, or chat.

## Acceptance criteria

- The agent-auth secret in `nixos/agent-auth/` (sops) is re-encrypted with the current funded key (vault item `meta.api-key-funded`, referenced by name only — the key value never appears in a commit, issue, or chat).
- After a secrets regeneration or laptop reboot, the deployed `/run/secrets/agent-auth/muse-sdk-token` has sha256 prefix `6b1ea8ee` (not the stale `7d4f5006`).
- A laptop OpenCode session on the `meta` provider (meta/muse-wonder-1.0) answers successfully after that regeneration/reboot, content-verified.
- The imperative hot-fix is folded into the laptop declarative-module cleanup so the secret source cannot drift stale again.

body:
## Finding

Phases 9 and 10 added many capabilities quickly and their own follow-up record says they "were delivered faster than they were verified." There are no dedicated Phase 9/10 issues carrying that verification debt, so the acceptance criteria for individual P9/P10 slices have no issue to close against.

## Evidence

- `doc/2026-10-17T15-00-00Z_architecture_next_stage_platform/2026-10-17T15-00-00Z_architecture_next_stage_platform.md`: Phases 9/10 "were delivered faster than they were verified."
- `.opencode/plans/phase-9-portable-platform.md` records P9.1–P9.11 and P10.1–P10.3 as complete, each with a feature record, but the acceptance criteria (e.g. the P9.1 acceptance list at the bottom) are not individually tracked in issues.
- Phase 9 PRs #214/#219 were closed unmerged on 2026-10-18 while equivalent work landed via the platform stack (#209–#256), leaving a fragmented PR trail.
- Phase 11 (`.opencode/plans/phase-11-foundations.md`, issues #539–#555) covers a subset of the debt (fuel budgets F11.6, benchmarks F11.8, bytes-per-frame F11.9, replay self-check F11.16, module size F11.15, compiler pin F11.18). It does NOT cover per-slice acceptance verification for every P9/P10 feature.

## Why it matters

The Phase 11 issues will make the platform measurable, but they do not individually verify each P9/P10 acceptance criterion (screen DTO bounds/parity, keyboard/viewport/paste parity, execution profile ceilings, RocJson/RocGrid/RocCap/RocText correctness, roles/directory, fixtures, scheduled events). Without a tracking issue, that debt is carried only in prose and can silently drop out of view.

## Suggested scope (for the implementer to plan)

Enumerate the P9/P10 acceptance criteria that lack a test or an issue, and either file a per-item issue or add the missing verification. Defer to Phase 11/12 issues where they already cover the criterion (reference, don't duplicate).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every remaining verification-debt item in the child inventory comment (9-2 parity harness, 9-3 DTO determinism/caps, 9-5 chat.history/records.read bounds, 9-6 SSH window-change + paste/ResizeObserver wiring, 9-7 source-only compiler check, 9-8 CLI verb coverage, 10-2 schedule fire visibility/ceiling) has a proving test added, or is split into its own issue linked from here.
- [ ] No production code changes unless a new proving test reveals a bug — a revealed bug gets its own issue/PR reference rather than being fixed silently under this tracker.
- [ ] Items already split out (#811, #812, #813) and items covered by Phase 11 issues (#539–#555) are referenced, not duplicated.
- [ ] This issue closes only when every inventory item is test-covered or separately tracked.
